profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-17T09:27:59.015+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Dìjì Dìyī Xuāndì
Xuānhuángdì, personal name Yǐ,
courtesy name Zhòngdá,
was a native of Xiàojìnglǐ, Wēn Xiàn, Hénèi.
His family name was Sīmǎ.
His ancestors were descended from Zhònglí, son of Dì Gāoyáng,
who served as Zhùróng, the Summer Official.
Throughout the eras of Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng,
his family held this office in succession.
By the Zhōu dynasty,
the Summer Official became the Sīmǎ (Master of Horse).
Later, Chéng Bóxiūfù,
during the reign of Zhōu Xuān Wáng,
using his hereditary office, pacified Xúfāng,
and was granted his official title as his clan name,
thus adopting it as his surname.
Between the Chǔ and Hàn dynasties,
Sīmǎ Áng was a general of Zhào,
and joined the feudal lords in attacking Qín.
When Qín fell,
he was established as King of Yīn,
with his capital in Hénèi.
Hàn made his territory a commandery,
and his descendants settled there.
Eight generations after Áng,
was born Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Jūn,
courtesy name Shúpíng.
Jūn begot Yùzhāng Tàishǒu Liàng,
courtesy name Gōngdù.
Liàng begot Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Jùn,
courtesy name Yuányì.
Jùn begot Jīngzhàoyǐn Fáng,
courtesy name Jiàngōng.
The Emperor was Fáng's second son.
In his youth, he possessed extraordinary qualities,
was intelligent and perceptive with grand strategies,
extensively learned and widely informed,
and devoted himself to Confucian teachings.
During the great chaos at the end of Hàn,
he often sighed with concern for the world.
Yáng Jùn, the Prefect of Nányáng and a man of the same commandery, known for his ability to judge people,
saw the Emperor
before he reached manhood,
and considered him an extraordinary talent.
Cui Yǎn of Qīnghé, a Shàngshū, was close to the Emperor's elder brother Lǎng,
and also said to Lǎng:
"Your younger brother is intelligent, discerning, and just,
resolute and exceptionally brilliant,
not someone you can match."
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān of Hàn,
the commandery recommended him as a Shàngjì Yuàn.
Wèi Wǔ Dì, then Sīkōng,
heard of him and summoned him.
The Emperor knew that the Hàn dynasty's fortune was waning,
and did not wish to compromise his principles by serving the Cáo family,
so he declined, feigning wind-arthralgia,
unable to get up and move.
Wèi Wǔ sent someone to secretly spy on him at night;
the Emperor remained firmly lying down, not moving.
When Wèi Wǔ became Chéngxiàng,
he again summoned him as a Wénxué Yuàn,
and instructed his messenger, saying:
"If he hesitates again,
arrest him."
The Emperor, fearing, took up the post.
Thus, he was made to accompany the Crown Prince,
then promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
transferred to Yìláng, and Chéngxiàng Dōngcáo Shǔ,
and soon after, transferred to Zhǔbù.
He followed in the campaign against Zhāng Lǔ,
and said to Wèi Wǔ:
"Liú Bèi, through treachery and force, captured Liú Zhāng;
the people of Shǔ have not yet submitted, and he is far away contending for Jiānglíng.
This opportunity must not be missed.
If we now display our might in Hànzhōng,
Yìzhōu will be shaken.
If we advance our troops upon it,
it will certainly collapse.
Taking advantage of this situation,
it will be easy to achieve success.
A sagely person cannot go against the times,
nor does he miss the opportune moment."
Wèi Wǔ said:
"People are never satisfied;
having gained Lǒngyòu,
they still want to gain Shǔ!"
He did not follow the advice.
Afterwards, he followed in the campaign against Sūn Quán,
and defeated him.
When the army returned,
Quán sent an envoy to beg for surrender,
submitted a memorial proclaiming himself a subject,
and explained the Mandate of Heaven.
Wèi Wǔ Dì said:
"Does this child wish to put me on hot coals!"
He replied:
"The Hàn dynasty's fortune is nearing its end.
Your Highness possesses nine-tenths of the world,
and yet serves it.
Quán's declaring himself a subject is the will of Heaven and man.
Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu did not yield out of modesty
because they feared Heaven and knew their destiny."
After the state of Wèi was established,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Whenever he participated in major deliberations,
he always offered brilliant strategies,
and was trusted and valued by the Crown Prince.
He, along with Chén Qún, Wú Zhì, and Zhū Shuò, were known as the "Four Friends."
He was promoted to Jūnsīmǎ,
and said to Wèi Wǔ:
"In ancient times, Jīzǐ, when presenting his counsel,
placed food first.
Today, those who do not farm number over two hundred thousand;
this is not a long-term strategy for governing the state.
Although military conflicts have not yet ceased,
it is still appropriate to both farm and defend."
Wèi Wǔ adopted his advice,
and consequently, agriculture flourished and grain accumulated,
making the national treasury abundant.
The Emperor further stated that Hú Xiū, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, was crude and violent,
and Fù Fāng, the Prefect of Nánxiāng, was arrogant and extravagant,
and that neither should be stationed on the border.
Wèi Wǔ did not heed this.
When the Shǔ general Guān Yǔ besieged Cáo Rén at Fán,
and Yú Jìn's seven armies were all destroyed,
Xiū and Fāng indeed surrendered to Yǔ,
and Rén's encirclement became very urgent.
At this time, the Hàn emperor resided in Xǔchāng,
and Wèi Wǔ considered it too close to the enemy,
wanting to move the capital north of the Yellow River.
The Emperor remonstrated, saying:
"Yú Jìn and others were submerged by water,
it was not a loss due to battle or defense.
It has not yet caused any damage to the state's grand strategy.
If we move the capital now,
it will show weakness to the enemy,
and the people of Huáinmǐan will be greatly unsettled.
Sūn Quán and Liú Bèi are outwardly close but inwardly estranged;
Quán does not wish for Yǔ to succeed.
We can instruct Quán
to attack his rear,
then the siege of Fán will naturally be lifted."
Wèi Wǔ followed his advice.
Quán indeed sent his general Lǚ Méng west to attack Gōng'ān,
captured it,
and Yǔ was consequently captured by Méng.
Wèi Wǔ, considering the remaining people of Jīngzhōu and those in the garrison farms in Yǐngchuān to be too close to the southern invaders,
wished to relocate them all.
The Emperor said:
"The people of Jīngchǔ are fickle and impulsive,
easily moved and difficult to settle.
Guān Yǔ has just been defeated,
and all those who committed wrongdoings are hiding and watching.
If we now relocate the good people,
it will not only hurt their feelings,
but also cause those who leave not to dare to return."
He followed this advice.
Afterwards, all those who had fled returned to their homes.
When Wèi Wǔ died in Luòyáng,
the court and country were in perilous fear.
The Emperor managed the funeral arrangements,
and everything inside and outside was solemn.
Then he escorted the coffin back to Yè.
When Wèi Wén Dì ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Hèjīn Tínghóu
and promoted to Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ.
At that time, Sūn Quán led his troops west,
and the court debated that Fán and Xiāngyáng had no grain
and could not withstand the invaders.
Cáo Rén was then stationed in Xiāngyáng,
and they requested to recall Rén to Wǎn.
The Emperor said:
"Sūn Quán has just defeated Guān Yǔ;
this is his moment to ally himself,
he will surely not cause trouble.
Xiāngyáng is a crucial point for both water and land routes,
a vital stronghold for defending against invaders,
and cannot be abandoned."
His advice was not followed.
Rén then burned and abandoned the two cities,
and Quán indeed did not become an invader.
Wèi Wén regretted this.
When Wèi received the abdication from Hàn,
the Emperor was made Shàngshū.
Soon after,
he was transferred to Dūjūn, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and enfeoffed as Ānguó Xiānghóu.
In the second year of Huángchū,
the office of Dūjūn was abolished,
and he was promoted to Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
In the fifth year,
the Son of Heaven traveled south,
reviewing the troops on the border of Wú.
The Emperor was ordered to remain in charge of Xǔchāng,
was re-enfeoffed as Xiàngxiāng Hóu,
and promoted to Fǔjūn and granted the privilege of the Jiǎjié.
He was given command of five thousand troops,
and additionally appointed Jìshìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
The Emperor firmly declined.
The Son of Heaven said:
"As for the myriad affairs,
I work day and night,
without a moment's rest.
This is not to gain glory,
but to share my worries."
In the sixth year,
the Son of Heaven again extensively mobilized a naval force to conquer Wú,
and again ordered the Emperor to stay behind to guard,
pacify the populace internally,
and supply military provisions externally.
Before departing,
the imperial edict stated:
"I am deeply concerned about the aftermath of affairs,
hence I entrust them to you, my lord.
Although Cáocān had military achievements,
Xiāohé was more important.
If you can ensure I have no worries about the west,
would that not be good!"
The Son of Heaven returned to Luòyáng from Guǎnglíng,
and issued an edict to the Emperor saying:
"When I go east,
Fǔjūn shall oversee affairs in the west;
when I go west,
Fǔjūn shall oversee affairs in the east."
Thereupon, the Emperor remained in charge of Xǔchāng.
When the Son of Heaven was critically ill,
the Emperor, along with Cáozhēn, Chénqún, and others, met him in the south hall of Chónghuá Diàn,
and jointly received the deathbed instructions to assist in governance.
The edict to the Crown Prince stated:
"If anyone sows discord among these three high ministers,
be sure not to doubt them."
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
the Emperor was re-enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Hóu.
When Sūnquán besieged Jiāngxià,
and sent his generals Zhūgějǐn and Zhāngbà to concurrently attack Xiāngyáng,
the Emperor commanded all the armies to campaign against Quán,
and drove him away.
He then pressed the attack,
defeated Jǐn,
beheaded Bà,
and captured over a thousand heads.
He was promoted to Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
In the sixth month of Tàihé First Year,
the Son of Heaven ordered the Emperor to garrison in Wǎn,
and additionally made him Grand Supervisor of all military affairs in Jīng and Yù provinces.
Initially,
when the Shǔ general Mèngdá surrendered,
the Wèi court treated him very generously.
The Emperor, believing Dá's words and actions to be cunning and untrustworthy,
repeatedly advised against it but was not listened to.
Instead, Dá was appointed Prefect of Xīnchéng,
enfeoffed as a marquis,
and granted the privilege of the Jiǎjié.
Dá then allied with Wú and strengthened ties with Shǔ,
secretly plotting against Zhōngguó.
The Shǔ Chancellor Zhūgěliàng disliked his duplicity,
and also feared he would become a problem.
Dá had a feud with Shēn Yí, the Prefect of Wèixīng.
Liàng wanted to accelerate Dá's move,
so he sent Guōmó to feign surrender,
who passed by Yí,
and thus leaked Dá's plan.
When Dá heard his plan was leaked,
he was about to raise troops.
Fearing Dá would act too quickly, the Emperor
sent a letter to dissuade him, saying:
"General, in the past you abandoned Liúbèi,
and entrusted yourself to the state.
The state entrusted you, General, with responsibilities on the frontier,
and relied on you, General, for plans against Shǔ;
it can be said your heart shone bright as the sun.
Among the people of Shǔ, foolish and wise alike,
none do not gnash their teeth at you, General.
Zhūgěliàng wants to destroy you,
but is only troubled by having no way to do so.
What Mó said
is no small matter,
how could Liàng take it lightly and let it be revealed?
This is probably easy to understand."
Dá was greatly pleased to receive the letter,
but still wavered and could not decide.
The Emperor then secretly advanced his army to suppress him.
All the generals said that Dá was colluding with the two enemies,
and it was advisable to observe and then act.
The Emperor said:
"Dá is without trustworthiness or righteousness.
This is the time when they doubt each other;
we must strike before they are settled and make a swift decision."
So he marched day and night,
arriving at the city walls in eight days.
Wú and Shǔ each sent their generals to Xi chéng Ānqiáo and Mùlán Sāi to rescue Dá.
The Emperor divided his generals to resist them.
Initially,
Dá had written to Liàng, saying:
"Wǎn is eight hundred *lǐ* from Luò,
and one thousand two hundred *lǐ* from me.
When they hear I raise an army,
they will report it to the Son of Heaven.
By the time they react,
a month will have passed,
and my city will be fortified,
and all the armies will be ready.
My location is deep and treacherous,
Sīmǎ Gōng will certainly not come himself;
if only other generals come,
I have nothing to fear."
When the army arrived,
Dá again told Liàng:
"I raised the army eight days ago,
and the troops are already at the city walls.
How incredibly swift!"
The city of Shàngyōng was blocked by water on three sides,
and Dá built a wooden palisade outside the city to fortify himself.
The Emperor crossed the water,
broke through the palisade,
and directly reached the city walls.
He attacked it from eight directions.
After sixteen days,
Dá's nephew Dèngxián and general Lǐfǔ and others opened the gates and surrendered.
Dá was executed,
and his head was sent to the capital.
Over ten thousand people were captured,
and the army returned triumphantly to Wǎn.
He then encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
and prohibited extravagant expenditures,
and the southern regions were pleased and submitted.
Initially,
Shēn Yí had been in Wèixīng for a long time,
wielding exclusive authority on the frontier,
often unilaterally carving seals,
and making many unauthorized appointments.
After Dá was executed,
Yí felt self-doubt.
At that time, all the commandery governors, knowing the Emperor had achieved a new victory,
came with respectful felicitations,
and all were allowed.
The Emperor sent someone to subtly hint at Yí.
When Yí arrived,
he was questioned about his unauthorized actions,
arrested,
and sent to the capital.
The Emperor also relocated over seven thousand households of Mèngdá's remaining followers to Yōuzhōu.
The Shǔ generals Yáojìng, Zhèngtā, and others, along with over seven thousand of their subordinates, came to surrender.
At that time, the newly submitted border commanderies
often lacked household registers,
and the Wèi court wanted to increase their actual population.
When the Emperor was summoned to the capital for an audience,
the Son of Heaven consulted him.
The Emperor replied:
"The bandits used a tight net to bind the lower classes,
hence the lower classes abandoned them.
It is best to broaden the general principles,
then they will naturally be peaceful and content."
He was also asked which of the two enemies should be attacked first.
Which should be first?
He replied:
"Wú, because Zhōngguó is not accustomed to naval warfare,
dares to scatter its forces in Dōngguān.
Whenever attacking an enemy,
one must seize its throat and pierce its heart.
Xiàkǒu and Dōngguān are the heart and throat of the bandits.
If we send a land army towards Wǎncity,
drawing Quán eastward,
and send a naval army towards Xiàkǒu,
striking them while they are undefended,
this would be a divine army falling from the sky,
and they will certainly be defeated."
The Son of Heaven agreed with both points,
and again ordered the Emperor to garrison in Wǎn.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn,
additionally made Dà Dūdū and granted the privilege of the Jiǎhuángyuè,
and along with Cáozhēn, campaigned against Shǔ.
The Emperor himself cut mountains and opened roads from Xīchéng,
advancing by both land and water,
sailing upstream on the Miǎn river,
reaching Qúqú,
and capturing its Xīnfēng county.
When the army reached Dānkǒu,
they encountered rain,
and returned to base.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi,
and his enfeoffment was repeatedly increased.
When the Shǔ general Mǎ Dài invaded,
the Emperor dispatched General Niú Jīn to defeat him,
beheading over a thousand.
Fú Shuāng and Qiáng Duān, the Dī kings of Wǔdū, led their six thousand and more followers to surrender.
There was a famine in Guāndōng,
so the Emperor transported five million hú of grain from Cháng'ān to the capital.
In the fourth year,
a white deer was captured
and presented.
The Son of Heaven said:
"In ancient times, Zhōu Gōngdàn assisted King Chéng
and received a tribute of a white pheasant.
Now, you have taken on the responsibility for Shǎnxī
and presented a white deer.
Is this not a sign of loyal devotion aligning with the symbols
and a contract shared across a thousand years,
benefiting the state
to eternally secure its prosperity?"
When Gōngsūn Wén Yì, the Administrator of Liáodōng, rebelled,
the Emperor was summoned to the capital.
The Son of Heaven said:
"This is not enough to trouble you,
but for the matter to be surely victorious,
I must bother you.
What strategy do you think he will adopt?"
He replied:
"Abandoning the city and fleeing in advance
is the best plan.
Holding the Liáoshuǐ to resist the great army
is the second best plan.
Sitting and defending Xiāngpíng
is to be easily captured."
The Son of Heaven said:
"Which plan will he likely choose?"
He replied:
"Only the wise can deeply assess both sides
and prepare to abandon something;
this is beyond his capability.
Now, with our army far from home,
he will assume we cannot endure for long.
He will surely first resist at Liáoshuǐ and then defend,
which is a middle-to-low-tier plan."
The Son of Heaven said:
"How long will the round trip take?"
He replied:
"One hundred days to go,
one hundred days to return,
one hundred days to attack,
with sixty days for rest.
One year will be sufficient."
At this time, grand palace constructions were underway,
and coupled with military expeditions,
the common people were suffering from hunger and hardship.
When the Emperor was about to embark on the military campaign,
he remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Zhōu Gōng established Luòyì,
and Xiāo Hé built Wèiyāng.
Now, the palace buildings are not yet complete,
which is my responsibility.
However, north of the Yellow River,
the common people are impoverished,
with tasks both inside and outside the court.
It is not possible to prosper both simultaneously.
It is advisable to temporarily suspend internal affairs
to alleviate the urgent crisis."
In the second year of Jǐngchū,
leading Niú Jīn, Hú Zūn, and others, with forty thousand infantry and cavalry,
he set off from the capital.
The imperial carriage saw him off past Xīmíngmén.
An edict ordered his younger brother Fú and son Shī to see him past Wēn,
and bestowed upon him grain, silk, oxen, and wine.
It was decreed that all regional administrators and agricultural officials below them should gather to meet him.
He met with elders and old acquaintances,
feasting for several days.
The Emperor sighed,
feeling a deep sense of emotion,
and sang:
"Heaven and Earth began,
sun and moon rekindled their light.
Meeting this auspicious time,
I exert my strength in distant lands.
About to sweep away all impurities,
then return and pass through my old hometown.
Clearing the ten thousand li,
unifying the eight directions.
Completing my task and retiring to old age,
awaiting my sentence in Wǔyáng."
Then he advanced his army,
passing through Gūzhú,
crossing Jiéshí,
and encamping at Liáoshuǐ.
Wén Yì indeed dispatched tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
blocking Liáosuì,
building strong fortifications and defending,
stretching sixty to seventy lǐ north and south,
to resist the Emperor.
The Emperor spread out many troops and displayed numerous banners to the south;
the rebels committed all their elite forces there.
Then he secretly crossed by boat to emerge to their north,
approaching the rebel camp.
He sank the boats and burned the bridges,
building a long circumvallation along the Liáoshuǐ,
bypassing the rebels and heading towards Xiāngpíng.
His generals said:
"Not attacking the rebels but building a circumvallation
is not how to show our strength to the populace."
The Emperor said:
"The rebels have strong camps and high ramparts,
intending to wear out our soldiers.
Attacking them
would play right into their plan;
this is why Wáng Yì was shamed at Kūnyáng.
The ancients said:
'Even if the enemy has high ramparts,
they will inevitably have to fight us
if we attack what they must save.'
The bulk of the rebels are here,
so their lair is empty.
If I head straight for Xiāngpíng,
they will feel internal fear.
When they fear and seek battle,
we are sure to defeat them."
So he straightened his formation and passed.
When the rebels saw the army emerge behind them,
they indeed intercepted it.
The Emperor said to his generals:
"The reason I did not attack their camp
was precisely to achieve this;
we must not lose this opportunity."
Then he unleashed his troops to counterattack,
greatly defeating them,
winning all three battles.
The rebels held Xiāngpíng,
and the army advanced to besiege it.
Initially,
when Wén Yì heard of the Wèi army's departure,
he sought aid from Sūn Quán.
Quán also sent troops to create a distant diversion for him,
and sent Wén Yì a letter saying:
"Sīmǎ Gōng is skilled in warfare,
changing like a god,
irresistible in all directions.
I am deeply worried for my brother."
It happened that there was a continuous downpour,
and the great waters rose several feet on level ground.
The three armies were afraid
and wanted to move camp.
The Emperor ordered that anyone in the army who dared to speak of moving would be beheaded.
The Commander-in-Chief's clerk, Zhāng Jìng, violated the order
and was beheaded.
Only then did the army settle down.
The bandits relied on the water,
and went about their woodcutting and pasturing as usual.
The various generals wanted to attack them,
but he would not listen to any of them.
Sīmǎ Chén Guī said:
"Previously, when we attacked Shàngyōng,
the eight divisions advanced simultaneously,
day and night without rest.
Thus, in half a旬 [ten-day period],
we were able to capture the fortified city
and behead Méng Dá.
Now, having come from afar, we are instead acting with ease and slowness.
I am privately bewildered by this."
The Emperor said:
"Méng Dá's forces were few, but they had provisions for a year.
My officers and soldiers are four times as many as Dá's, yet our provisions will not last a month.
To plan for a year with one month's provisions,
how can one not be swift?
To attack one with four [times the force],
even if we suffer half losses,
we should still do it.
Therefore, we did not consider casualties,
but raced against the provisions.
Now, the bandits are numerous and we are few;
the bandits are hungry and we are sated.
The water and rain are like this,
so no effort can be exerted.
Even if we were to rush them,
what would it achieve?
Since departing the capital,
I have not worried about the bandits attacking,
only feared their escape.
Now the bandits' provisions are nearly exhausted,
but the encirclement is not yet complete.
To plunder their cattle and horses,
and intercept their woodcutting and foraging,
is precisely to drive them to flee.
Now, warfare is a deceptive art,
and one must be skilled at adapting to circumstances.
The bandits rely on their numbers and the rain,
so although they are hungry and distressed,
they are not willing to surrender.
We should feign incompetence to make them feel secure.
To seek small gains to alarm them
is not a wise plan."
When the imperial court heard that the army encountered rain,
they all requested its recall.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Sīmǎ Gōng, facing danger, adapts to changes;
he will capture them in a matter of days."
Soon after, the rain stopped,
and they completed the encirclement.
They built earth mounds and dug tunnels,
and with shields, towers, and grappling hooks,
they launched arrows and stones like rain,
attacking day and night.
At this time, there was a long star,
white in color,
with a radiant mane,
which flowed from the southwest of Xiāngpíng city to the northeast,
and fell into the Liángshuǐ.
The city was shaken with fear.
Wén Yì was greatly alarmed,
and so he sent Wáng Jiàn, whom he had appointed as his Prime Minister (Xiàngguó), and Yǔshǐ Dàfū Liǔ Fǔ to beg for surrender,
requesting that the siege be lifted and they bind themselves.
He did not permit it,
seized Jiàn and the others,
and beheaded them all.
He issued a proclamation to Wén Yì, saying:
"In ancient times, Chǔ and Zhèng were feudal states,
yet the Earl of Zhèng still bared his torso and led a sheep to greet them.
I am an envoy of the King,
and my position is that of a high duke.
Yet Jiàn and the others want me to lift the siege and retreat,
how can this be compared to Chǔ and Zhèng!
These two men are old and foolish,
they must have misreported your intent;
I have already had them beheaded.
If your intention is not yet fully expressed,
you may send a younger person of clear judgment to come again."
Wén Yì again sent his Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Wèi Yǎn to beg for a date to send hostages.
The Emperor said to Yǎn:
"In military affairs, there are five major principles:
if one can fight, one should fight;
if one cannot fight, one should defend;
if one cannot defend, one should flee.
The remaining two options are only surrender or death.
You are unwilling to bind yourselves,
this means you have decided to face death.
There is no need to send hostages."
Wén Yì attacked the southern encirclement to break out.
The Emperor let his troops attack and defeat them,
beheading him at the spot where the star fell over the Liángshuǐ.
Upon entering the city,
two markers were erected to distinguish between the old and new.
Over seven thousand men aged fifteen and above were all killed,
forming a Jingguan [mound of corpses].
All the pseudo-dukes and ministers down to the lowest ranks were executed,
and over two thousand of their generals, such as Bì Shèng, were put to death.
Four tens of thousands of households and
over thirty tens of thousands of mouths [people] were collected.
Initially,
Wén Yì usurped the position of his uncle Gōng and imprisoned him.
When he was about to rebel,
generals Lún Zhí and Jiǎ Fàn, among others, earnestly remonstrated,
but Wén Yì killed them all.
The Emperor then released Gōng from his imprisonment,
sealed the tombs of Zhí and the others,
and elevated their surviving descendants.
He issued an order saying:
"In ancient times, when states were punished,
only the 'whales' and 'sharks' [major offenders] were executed.
All those whom Wén Yì misled
are to be pardoned.
Chinese people who wish to return to their former homes
are freely permitted to do so."
At that time, there were soldiers who were cold and frozen,
begging for short padded jackets,
but the Emperor did not give them.
Someone said:
"Fortunately, there are many old padded jackets,
they can be given to them."
The Emperor said:
"Padded jackets are government property;
a subject has no right to bestow them privately."
He then reported to the throne that over a thousand soldiers aged sixty and above were to be discharged and sent home,
and the remains of officers and officials who died in the campaign were to be returned to their families for burial.
Then he returned with the army.
The Son of Heaven sent envoys to commend the army at Jì,
and increased his enfeoffment with Kūnyáng,
adding it to the two previous counties.
Initially,
when the Emperor arrived at Xiāngpíng,
he dreamed that the Son of Heaven was resting his head on his lap,
and said:
"Look at my face."
He looked down and saw it was different from usual,
and he was inwardly disturbed by it.
Before this,
an imperial edict had ordered the Emperor to proceed to garrison Guānzhōng;
when he reached Báiwū,
an edict summoned the Emperor.
Within three days,
five imperial edicts arrived.
A handwritten edict said:
"I have been anxiously awaiting your arrival.
Upon arrival, enter directly through the inner chambers,
and look at my face."
The Emperor was greatly alarmed,
and so he rode in a 'chasing vanguard' carriage day and night,
traveling over four hundred *lǐ* from Báiwū,
arriving in one night.
He was led into the sleeping quarters of the Jiāfú Diàn,
and ascended the imperial couch.
The Emperor wept as he inquired about the illness,
and the Son of Heaven held the Emperor's hand,
looking at the King of Qí, saying:
"I entrust the future affairs to you.
Death can now be endured.
I endured death awaiting you,
having met you,
I have no more regrets."
He and the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Cáo Shuǎng together received the deathbed edict to assist the young lord.
When the King of Qí ascended the throne,

he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Bearer of Imperial Credentials (Chíjié), Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn), and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
He and Shuǎng each commanded three thousand troops,
jointly managed court affairs,
and took turns on duty in the palace.
The imperial carriage entered the palace.
Shuǎng wanted the Imperial Secretariat to report matters to him first,
so he spoke to the Son of Heaven,
and transferred the Emperor to the position of Grand Commander (Dà Sīmǎ).
The court deliberated and believed that previous Grand Commanders had repeatedly died in office,
so the Emperor was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
entering the palace without hurrying,
being announced for obeisance without his name being called,
and allowed to wear his sword and shoes in the palace,
following the precedent of Xiāo Hé of Hàn.
His marriage, mourning, and burial expenses were provided by the state.
His heir, Shī, was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì),
and three of his sons were made 列侯 (Lièhóu),
four were made Cavalier Commandant (Qí Dūwèi).
The Emperor firmly declined the official positions for his sons and did not accept them.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Zhèngshǐ (240 CE),
the eastern Wō [Japan], after repeated translations, presented tribute.
The kingdoms of Yānqí, Wēixū, and other states,
south of the Ruòshuǐ,
and the renowned kings of the Xiānbēi,
all sent envoys to offer tribute.
The Son of Heaven attributed the achievements to the chief ministers,
and further increased the Emperor's enfeoffment.
Initially,
Emperor Míng of Wèi was fond of constructing palaces and residences.
Their designs were extravagant and beautiful,
which caused distress to the common people.
When the Emperor returned from Liáodōng,
there were still more than ten thousand laborers,
and countless carved ornaments and playthings.
By this time, all these projects were halted,
expenses were cut, and agriculture was prioritized.
The common people rejoiced and relied on this.
In the second year, in the fifth month of summer,
Wú general Quán Cóng attacked Sháopī.
Zhū Rán and Sūn Lún besieged Fánchéng,
while Zhūgě Jǐn and Bù Zhì plundered Zāzhōng.
The Emperor requested to personally lead an expedition against them.
The advisors all said,
"The bandits have come from afar to besiege Fánchéng,
and it cannot be taken quickly.
If they are frustrated beneath a strong city,
they will naturally defeat themselves.
It is advisable to use a long-term strategy to counter them."
The Emperor said,
"When border cities are under attack, and one sits idly in the ancestral temple,
the frontier will be disturbed,
and the people's hearts will be filled with doubt.
This is a great worry for the state."
In the sixth month,
he then commanded all armies to march south,
and the imperial carriage was sent off through Jīnyángmén.
The Emperor considered the southern climate to be hot and humid,
unsuitable for a prolonged campaign.
He sent light cavalry to provoke them,
but they dared not move.
Thereupon, he rested the warriors,
selected elite troops,
recruited vanguards,
and issued commands,
demonstrating a certain intention to attack.
The Wú army fled during the night.
They were pursued to Sānzhōukǒu,
where more than ten thousand people were beheaded and captured.
Their boats and military supplies were seized before returning.
The Son of Heaven sent the Grandee Secretary Chángshì to comfort the troops at Wǎn.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the Emperor's fiefdoms of Yǎn and Línyǐng were increased.
Together with the previous four counties,
his household totaled ten thousand.
His eleven sons and younger brothers were all made marquises.
The Emperor's achievements and virtues grew daily,
yet he became even more humble and respectful.
Because Tàicháng Cháng Lín was an old senior from his hometown,
the Emperor would always bow when he saw him.
He constantly admonished his sons and younger brothers, saying,
"Excessive fullness is what the Daoists forbid.
Even the four seasons undergo changes,
what virtue do I have to bear such prosperity?
Diminish it again and again,
perhaps then I can be spared!"
In the third year, in spring,
the Son of Heaven posthumously enfeoffed and conferred the title of Wǔyáng Chéng Hóu upon his late imperial father, the Jīngzhàoyǐn.
In the third month,
a memorial was submitted to excavate a wide漕渠 (cáoqú, transport canal),
drawing water from the Yellow River into the Biàn River,
to irrigate the various reservoirs in the southeast.
Large-scale agricultural garrisons were first established north of the Huái River.
Prior to this,
Wú sent general Zhūgě Kè to garrison Wǎn.
The border regions suffered greatly from this,
and the Emperor wished to personally attack Kè.
Many advisors thought that since the bandits occupied a strong city,
and had accumulated grain,
they intended to lure the imperial army.
Now, if we commit a detached force to a distant attack,
their relief forces will surely arrive,
making advance and retreat difficult.
They did not see any advantage in this.
The Emperor said,
"The bandits' strength lies in water.
Now, we will attack their city
to observe their reaction.
If they utilize their strength,
abandon the city and flee,
this will be a victory achieved in the temple (i.e., through strategic planning).
If they dare to hold firm,
the lake water is shallow in winter,
and boats cannot navigate.
They will inevitably abandon their naval advantage to provide relief,
thus revealing their weakness,
which will also be to our advantage."
In the fourth year, in the ninth month of autumn,
the Emperor commanded all armies to attack Zhūgě Kè.
The imperial carriage was sent off through Jīnyángmén.
When the army reached Shū,
Kè burned his accumulated supplies,
abandoned the city, and fled.
The Emperor considered the key to defeating the bandits
to be the accumulation of grain.
He then greatly promoted garrison farming,
opened the two canals of Huáiyáng and Bǎichǐ,
and also repaired various reservoirs north and south of the Yǐng River,
totaling over ten thousand qǐng.
From then on, granaries north of the Huái River were seen everywhere,
from Shòuyáng to the capital,
with agricultural officials and garrisoned soldiers continuously linked.
In the fifth year, in the first month of spring,
the Emperor returned from Huáinán.
The Son of Heaven sent a special envoy to comfort the troops.
Shàngshū Dèng Yáng, Lǐ Shèng, and others wished to allow Cáo Shuǎng to establish merits and fame,
and urged him to attack Shǔ.
The Emperor tried to stop them,
but to no avail.
Shuǎng indeed returned without achieving any merits.
In the sixth year, in the eighth month of autumn,
Cáo Shuǎng dismantled the Zhōnglěi and Zhōngjiān camps,
and transferred the troops to his younger brother, Zhōnglǐngjūn Xī.
The Emperor tried to forbid this based on the old regulations of the former emperor,
but could not.
In the twelfth month of winter,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict allowing the Emperor to ride in an imperial carriage and ascend the hall during court assemblies.
In the seventh year, in the first month of spring,
Wú bandits raided Zāzhōng.
Over ten thousand Hàn and non-Hàn families fled the bandits and crossed the Miǎn River northward.
The Emperor believed that Mǐannán was close to the bandits,
and if the common people were to return,
they would certainly invite further attacks.
It was advisable to temporarily keep them there.
Cáo Shuǎng said,
"We cannot maintain defenses in Mǐannán while keeping the common people there;
this is not a long-term strategy."
The Emperor said,
"Not so.
Generally, things are safe when placed in a safe place,
and dangerous when placed in a dangerous place.
Therefore, the military treatise says, 'Success or failure
is about form;
safety or danger
is about momentum.'
Form and momentum
are crucial for commanding armies,
and must not be neglected.
Suppose the bandits use twenty thousand men to block the Miǎn River,
thirty thousand men to hold the imperial forces in Mǐannán,
and ten thousand men to rampage in Zāzhōng,
how then would you rescue them?"
Shuǎng did not comply,
and ultimately ordered them to return south.
The bandits indeed raided and destroyed Zāzhōng,
with losses in the tens of thousands.
In the eighth year, in the fourth month of summer,
Lady Zhāng passed away.
Cáo Shuǎng, following the advice of Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, and Dīng Mì,
moved the Empress Dowager to Yǒngníng Palace,
monopolized court affairs,
and his brothers jointly commanded the imperial guard.
He established many kinsmen and partisans,
and repeatedly altered regulations.
The Emperor could not stop him,
and thus there was a rift between him and Shuǎng.
In the fifth month,
the Emperor claimed illness and did not participate in state affairs.
People at the time composed a ballad about it, saying:
"Hé, Dèng, Dīng,
cause chaos in the capital."
In the ninth year [of Zhèngshǐ], in the third month of spring,
Huángmén Zhāng Dāng secretly brought out eleven palace women, including Càirén Shí Yīng, from the Yètíng,
to serve as entertainers for Cáo Shuǎng.
Shuǎng and Hú Hú Yàn believed the Emperor was gravely ill,
and thus harbored intentions of disrespecting the ruler.
They conspired secretly with Dāng,
planning to endanger the state and its altars,
and the date was set.
The Emperor also secretly made preparations for this.
Shuǎng's followers also harbored considerable suspicion of the Emperor.
At this time, Lǐ Shèng, the Hénán Yǐn, was about to take up his post in Jīngzhōu,
and came to visit the Emperor.
The Emperor feigned a critical illness,
having two maids attend him.
He let his clothes fall,
pointed to his mouth, and said he was thirsty.
When the maids offered him porridge,
the Emperor could not hold the cup to drink,
and all the porridge spilled out, drenching his chest.
Shèng said,
"Everyone says that your previous ailment has flared up again.
How can your honorable body be in such a state!"
The Emperor, making his voice and breath barely audible,
said,
"I am old and confined to bed by illness,
death is imminent.
You should be posted to Bīngzhōu.
Bīngzhōu is near the Hú people,
so be well-prepared.
I fear we will not meet again,
I entrust Zǐshī and Zhāo, your brothers, to you."
Shèng replied,
"I am returning to my original province,
not Bīngzhōu."
The Emperor then confused his words, saying,
"You are going to Bīngzhōu."
Shèng again said,
"I am going to Jīngzhōu."
The Emperor said,
"Old age makes my mind wander,
I don't understand what you are saying.
Now you are returning to your original province,
with your magnificent virtue and valor,
do well to establish great achievements!"
Shèng withdrew and reported to Shuǎng, saying,
"Sīmǎ Gōng is merely a corpse with a remnant of breath;
his spirit has already departed from his body,
there is nothing to worry about."
Another day,
he further said,
"The Grand Tutor cannot recover,
it is truly saddening."
Therefore, Shuǎng and others no longer made preparations.
In the first year of Jiāpíng, in the first month of spring, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Son of Heaven went to worship at Gāopíng Líng,
and Shuǎng and his brothers all accompanied him.
On that day,
Tàibái (Venus) encroached upon the moon.
The Emperor then memorialized Empress Dowager Yǒngníng to depose Shuǎng and his brothers.
At that time, Jǐng Dì was the Zhōnghùjūn,
leading troops and stationed at Sīmǎmén.
The Emperor arrayed his troops outside the palace gate,
passing by Shuǎng's residence.
Shuǎng's Zhàngxià Dū Yán Shì ascended the tower,
drew his crossbow, and was about to shoot the Emperor,
but Sūn Qiān stopped him, saying,
"The outcome of this matter is still uncertain."
He drew it three times and was stopped three times,
each time his elbow was held, preventing him from firing.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture, Huán Fàn, went to join Shuǎng.
Jiǎng Jì said to the Emperor,
"The 'bag of wisdom' has gone."
The Emperor said,
"Shuǎng and Fàn are inwardly distant, and Shuǎng's intellect is inferior.
A weak horse is attached to its short tether;
he will surely not be able to make use of him."
Thereupon, he temporarily appointed Sītú Gāo Róu with a staff of authority (jié),
to act as Grand General,
and take charge of Shuǎng's camp.
He said to Róu,
"You will be Zhōu Bó."
He ordered Grand Coachman Wáng Guān to act as Zhōnglǐngjūn,
and take command of Xī's camp.
The Emperor personally led Grand Commandant Jiǎng Jì and others with their troops to welcome the Son of Heaven,
stationing them at the floating bridge on the Luòshǔi.
He submitted a memorial saying,
"The late Emperor commanded Your Majesty, Qín Wáng, and your servant to ascend the imperial bed,
and grasped my arm, saying, 'Be deeply concerned about affairs after my death.'
Now, Grand General Shuǎng has forsaken the dying Emperor's charge,
and has corrupted the state's statutes.
Internally, he usurps power,
externally, he monopolizes authority.
He has placed his cronies in all the important official positions;
the old imperial guards
have all been dismissed.
His power is entrenched and intertwined,
and his wantonness grows daily.
Moreover, he appointed Huángmén Zhāng Dāng as Dūjiān,
who is specifically involved in collusion,
watching for an opportunity to seize the sacred instruments (imperial power).
The empire is in turmoil,
everyone harbors fear and anxiety.
Your Majesty has become a temporary occupant,
how can you long remain secure?
This is not the original intention of the late Emperor when he commanded Your Majesty and your servant to ascend the imperial bed.
Although your servant is old and infirm,
how dare I forget those former words?
In ancient times, Zhào Gāo indulged his desires to the extreme,
and Qín consequently perished;
Lǚ and Huò were promptly eliminated,
and the Hàn dynasty's rule was prolonged.
These are solemn lessons for Your Majesty,
and this is the moment for your servant to fulfill his mandate.
The dukes, ministers, and all officials believe that Shuǎng harbors intentions of disrespecting the ruler,
and that he and his brothers should not command the troops of the imperial guard;
we have memorialized the Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager has ordered that it be carried out as memorialized.
Your servant has already ordered the responsible officials and the Huángmén Lìng to dismiss Shuǎng, Xī, and Xùn's officers and soldiers,
and to return them to their residences with their original titles as Marquises.
Should they delay the imperial carriage,
they shall be dealt with according to military law.
Your servant, despite his illness, is leading troops to the floating bridge on the Luòshǔi,
to observe any extraordinary events."
Shuǎng did not accept the memorial,
and kept the imperial carriage overnight south of the Yīshuǐ,
cutting down trees to make deer-horns (defenses),
and deploying several thousand garrison troops to guard.
Huán Fàn indeed urged Shuǎng to escort the Son of Heaven to Xǔchāng,
and issue a proclamation to summon troops from throughout the empire.
Shuǎng could not bring himself to do so.
Instead, he sent Attendant-in-ordinary Xǔ Yǔn and Minister Chén Tài to the Emperor that night,
to observe his intentions.
The Emperor enumerated Shuǎng's transgressions,
saying the matter would end with his dismissal from office.
Tài returned and reported this to Shuǎng,
urging him to accept the memorial.
The Emperor also sent the Palace Commandant Yǐn Dàmù, whom Shuǎng trusted, to convey a message to Shuǎng,
making an oath by the Luòshǔi,
and Shuǎng believed him.
Huán Fàn and others cited examples from ancient and modern times,
offering numerous pieces of advice and persuasion.
Ultimately, he could not be convinced,
and said,
"Sīmǎ Gōng merely wants to seize my power.
I can return to my residence as a marquis,
and still be a wealthy old man."
Fàn clasped his chest and said,
"Because of you,
my clan will be wiped out!"
Thereupon, Shuǎng accepted the Emperor's memorial.
Afterwards, the relevant officials impeached Huángmén Zhāng Dāng,
and also exposed Shuǎng's rebellion with Hé Yàn and others.
Then Shuǎng and his brothers, along with their partisans, including Hé Yàn, Dīng Mì, Dèng Yáng, Bì Guǐ, Lǐ Shèng, and Huán Fàn, were arrested and executed.
Jiǎng Jì said,
"The merits of Cáo Zhēn
cannot go without sacrifices."
The Emperor did not listen.
Originally,
Shuǎng's Sīmǎ Lǔ Zhī and Zhǔbù Yáng Zōng cut through the gates and fled to Shuǎng.
When Shuǎng was about to surrender,
Zhī and Zōng tearfully admonished him, saying,
"You hold the responsibilities of Yī and Zhōu.
You hold the Son of Heaven,
and wield heavenly might,
who would dare not obey?
To abandon this and seek death in the Eastern Market,
is this not painful!"
The relevant officials memorialized to arrest Zhī and Zōng and punish them.
The Emperor pardoned them,
saying,
"To encourage those who serve their lord."
In the second month,
the Son of Heaven appointed the Emperor as Prime Minister,
and increased his enfeoffment with Fánchāng, Yānlíng, Xīnjí, and Fùchéng in Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Together with the previous eight counties,
his fief amounted to 20,000 households,
and he was not addressed by name when presenting memorials.
He firmly declined the position of Prime Minister.
In the twelfth month of winter,
the rites of the Nine Bestowals were added,
and he was exempted from bowing at court assemblies.
He firmly declined the Nine Bestowals.
In the first month of spring of the second year,
the Son of Heaven ordered the Emperor to establish an ancestral temple in Luòyáng,
to appoint Zǔoyòu Chángshǐ,
and to increase his clerks and attendants to a full ten people.
Annually, one clerk was to be recommended for a censor's post, and one for a Xiùcái degree.
One hundred additional official cavalry were added,
and fourteen musicians.
His son, Róng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglè Tíng,
and Lún as Marquis of Ānlè Tíng.
The Emperor, due to prolonged illness, was unable to attend court.
Whenever there was a major affair,
the Son of Heaven would personally visit his residence to consult him.
The Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Línghú Yú,
and Grand Commandant Wáng Líng were disloyal to the Emperor,
and conspired to enthrone Chǔ Wáng Biāo.
In the first month of spring in the third year,
Wáng Líng falsely claimed that the Wú people had blocked the Túshuǐ River
and requested troops to attack them.
The Emperor secretly knew of his plot
and did not assent.
In the fourth month of summer,
the Emperor personally led the central army,
traveling by boat downriver,
and arrived at Gānchéng in nine days.
Líng had no recourse,
so he went to meet him at Wǔqiū,
〔一一〕bound himself at the waterside,
and said,
“If Líng is guilty,
Your Grace should simply summon Líng with a written note;
why bother coming yourself?”
The Emperor said,
“It is because you are not the type of person to be summoned by a mere note.”
He then took Líng back to the capital.
On the way, passing by Jiǎ Kuí’s temple,
Líng cried out,
“Jiǎ Liángdào!
Wáng Líng is a loyal minister of Dà Wèi;
only you with your spirit will know this.”
Upon reaching Xiàng,
he looked up and swallowed poison, dying.
His remaining partisans were rounded up,
and all their three clans were exterminated,
and Biāo was also killed.
All the princes and dukes of Wèi were gathered and placed in Yè,
and officials were ordered to monitor them,
forbidding them from interacting.
The Son of Heaven sent the侍中 (shìzhōng) Wéi Dàn with a jié (節) to comfort the army at Wǔchí.
When the Emperor returned from Gānchéng,
the Son of Heaven again sent the concurrently appointed Dà Hónglú (大鴻臚) and Tàipú (太僕) Yú Ní with a jié,
and issued an edict appointing the Emperor as Xiàngguó (相國),
and enfeoffing him as the Duke of Ānpíng Commandery.
His grandson and one nephew were each made列侯 (lièhóu).
His total fief income amounted to fifty thousand households,
and there were nineteen enfeoffed marquises.
He firmly declined the positions of Xiàngguó and Duke of the Commandery and did not accept them.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor fell ill.
He dreamed that Jiǎ Kuí and Wáng Líng were causing mischief,
which greatly troubled him.
On the Wùyín day of the eighth month of autumn,
he passed away in the capital,
aged seventy-three.
The Son of Heaven wore plain clothes and came to mourn.
The funeral rites and solemn procedures followed the precedents of Huò Guāng of Hàn.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Xiàngguó and Duke of the Commandery.
His younger brother Fú submitted a memorial, stating his late brother’s wishes,
declining the title of Duke of the Commandery and the wēnliángchē (轀輬車) carriage.
On the Gēngshēn day of the ninth month,
he was buried at Héyīn,
and given the posthumous title Wén.
Later, this was changed to Xuānwén.
〔一二〕Before this,
he had made his final will in advance,
constructing an earthen tomb at Shǒuyángshān,
without a mound or trees.
He composed three chapters of deathbed instructions,
to be interred in ordinary clothes,
without funerary objects,
and that later deceased family members should not be buried together with him.
Everything was carried out according to his will.
When the state of Jìn was first established,
he was posthumously honored as Xuānwáng.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he was honored with the exalted title Xuānhuángdì,
his陵 (líng) was named Gāoyuán,
and his ancestral temple was called Gāozǔ.
The Emperor was inwardly jealous but outwardly generous,
suspicious and full of stratagems.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi observed that the Emperor had ambitions of a hero-tyrant,
and heard that he had the physiognomy of a “wolf-gaze,”
and wished to verify it.
So he summoned him to walk forward,
and then bade him look back.
His face turned directly backward while his body remained still.
He also once dreamed of three horses eating from the same trough,
which greatly disturbed him.
He then told Crown Prince Pī,
“Sīmǎ Yì is no mere subject;
he will surely meddle in your family affairs.”
The Crown Prince had always been on good terms with the Emperor,
and always protected and supported him,
thus he was spared.
The Emperor then diligently performed his official duties,
working late into the night, forgetting sleep.
Even concerning matters of fodder and pasturage,
he personally oversaw everything.
Because of this, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi’s suspicions were finally allayed.
When he pacified Gōngsūn Wényì,
he carried out a great slaughter.
At the time of executing Cáo Shuǎng,
his partisans were all exterminated along with their three clans.
Men and women, regardless of age,
and even his paternal aunts and sisters who were married, were all killed.
Afterward, he indeed deposed Wèi Qí (魏𣇓), it is said.
During Emperor Míng’s time,
Wáng Dǎo was in attendance.
The Emperor asked how his predecessors had gained the empire.
Dǎo then recounted the beginning of the Emperor’s founding of the dynasty,
and the incident involving Gāoguì Xiānggōng at the end of Emperor Wén’s reign.
Emperor Míng covered his face with his mat and said,
“If what you say is true,
how can the Jìn dynasty last long!”
Tracing his suspicious cruelty,
it indeed matched the “wolf-gaze.”
An edict stated: Of the vastness of Heaven and Earth,
the common people are the foundation;
of the nobility of states,
the sovereign is supreme.
Order and chaos are impermanent,
rise and fall have their destiny.
Therefore, from the time of the Five Dì and earlier,
those who held the myriad chariots considered it a sorrow;
since the Three Wáng,
they have found joy in their sorrow.
They competed in wisdom and strength,
contended over gains and losses;
the small swallowed the large,
the strong preyed upon the weak.
By the time of the Wèi dynasty,
the three powers stood in fierce contention,
weapons never ceased,
and mist and fog flew in all directions.
Xuān Huáng, with his heaven-endowed talent,
arose at the opportune moment to assist in establishing the dynasty.
He governed with refinement,
and awed with martial prowess.
He used men as if they were part of himself,
sought out worthy individuals as if he could not reach them.
His emotions were deep and inscrutable,
his nature broad and accommodating.
He harmonized his light with the dust,
expanded and contracted with the times.
He sheathed his scales and folded his wings,
thinking to align himself with the winds and clouds.
He feigned loyalty with a treacherous heart,
and prolonged security for a life on the brink of peril.
Observing his grand strategy and decisive internal judgment,
his brilliant plans executed externally,
he annihilated Gōngsūn Yuān in a hundred days,
and captured Méng Dá within a single ten-day period.
He himself believed his military movements were like those of a god,
and his strategies flawless.
Later, leading his army westward,
he engaged Zhūgě Liàng in a standoff.
He suppressed his armed forces,
having no initial fighting spirit.
When Zhūgě Liàng sent him women's headwear and ornaments,
only then did he become indignant.
Holding his imperial staff at the gate,
his grand ambitions were suddenly curbed.
He requested battle from a thousand *lǐ* away,
falsely intending to show his might.
Moreover, the people of Qín and Shǔ,
brave and timid, were not equals;
the roads, rugged and easy,
presented different levels of hardship and ease.
To contend for success with these conditions,
the advantage was clear.
Yet, he retreated, closed his army within strongholds,
and dared not engage.
He was truly timid and did not advance,
then later, suspicious of an empty fort, still fled.
The way of a good general,
was it lost here?
During the reign of Wén Dì,
his influence as an auxiliary was immense.
In Xǔchāng, his trust was like that placed in Xiāo Hé;
in Chónghuá, his commission exceeded that of Huò Guāng.
It should be said that he exhausted his sincerity and devotion,
and could be compared to Yī Yǐn and Fù Yuè.
But when Míng Dì was about to die,
the pillars of the state were entrusted to him.
He received the dying charge from two emperors,
and assisted three imperial courts.
Having accepted the trust of an emperor enduring death,
he never repaid it with his own life.
When the Son of Heaven was outside,
he stirred up armed forces within.
The burial mound had not yet dried,
when he hastily began mutual slaughter.
The conduct of a loyal minister,
how could it be like this?
The path of ultimate good,
by this, is confused.
For strategies of conquest,
how could one be wise in the east and foolish in the west?
For the heart of an assistant,
how could it be loyal before and chaotic after?
Therefore, Jìn Míng Dì covered his face,
ashamed that success was achieved through deceit.
Shí Lè spoke freely,
laughing at the treacherous and cunning means by which the dynasty was established.
The ancients said,
"After three years of accumulating good deeds,
few know of them;
after a single day of evil,
it is heard throughout the world."
Is this not true?
Although he concealed his faults during his lifetime,
he was ultimately ridiculed by later generations.
It is like stealing a bell and covering one's ears,
thinking that others will not hear;
or eagerly stealing gold,
thinking that no one in the market will see.
Thus, one knows that those greedy for immediate gain neglect the distant,
and those drowned in profit harm their reputation.
If one does not harm oneself to benefit others,
then one will harm others to benefit oneself.
Acting in accordance with reason is easy;
acting against the times is difficult to succeed.
Moreover, with the still incomplete foundation of the Jìn,
to press upon the abundant mandate of the Wèi?
Even if his Dao encompassed the universe,
and his virtue covered the common people,
yet if Heaven had not yet opened the time,
the imperial throne would still be obstructed.
It could not be competed for by wisdom,
nor contended for by force.
Although blessings flowed to later descendants,
he himself died facing north (as a subject).
Collation Notes
Annals of the Emperors, Chapter Two: Jǐng Dì
Emperor Jǐng, personal name Shī,
courtesy name Zǐyuán,
was the eldest son of Xuān Dì.
He possessed elegant demeanor,
and was resolute and rich in grand strategies.
In his youth, he enjoyed a fine reputation,
and was as renowned as Xiàhóu Xuán and Hé Yàn.
Hé Yàn often said:
"Only one who possesses profound insight can accomplish the affairs of the world,
and Sīmǎ Zǐyuán is such a one."
During the Jǐngchū era of Wèi,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and successively promoted to Zhōnghùjūn.
He established methods for selecting and employing officials,
where promotions were based solely on merit,
and officials had no private interests.
When Empress Xuān Mù passed away,
he was known for his extreme filial piety during mourning.
When Xuān Dì was about to execute Cáosrǔang,
he secretly planned the deep stratagem
exclusively with Emperor Jǐng,
Wén Dì did not know of it.
He was only informed the evening before the action was to be taken.
Later, Xuān Dì sent someone to observe them;
Emperor Jǐng slept as usual,
while Wén Dì could not rest easy.
In the morning, the troops gathered at Sīmǎ Mén,
calming both inside and outside,
and the formations were very orderly.
Xuān Dì said:
"This son is indeed capable."
Initially,
Emperor Jǐng had secretly maintained three thousand sworn followers,
scattered among the populace.
On that day, they assembled in one morning,
and no one knew where they had come from.
When the matter was settled,
for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Chángpíng Xiānghóu,
with a thousand households as his stipend,
and soon after was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn.
When Xuān Dì passed away,
the deliberators all said,
"Once Yī Yǐn died,
Yī Zhì succeeded him in his duties."
The Son of Heaven commanded Emperor Jǐng to assist in governance as Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn.
In the first month of spring in the fourth year of Jiāpíng of Wèi,
he was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and held the imperial staff, overseeing all military forces both inside and outside, and supervising the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
He ordered all officials to recommend worthy talents,
distinguish between the young and the old,
show compassion for the poor and solitary,
and rectify neglected affairs.
Zhūgě Dàn, Guànqiū Jiǎn, Wáng Chǎng, Chén Tài, and Hú Zūn were appointed area commanders of the four directions;
Wáng Jī, Zhōu Tài, Dèng Ài, and Shí Bāo governed prefectures and commanderies;
Lú Yù and Lǐ Fēng managed elections;
Fù Gǔ and Yú Sōng participated in strategic planning;
Zhōng Huì, Xiàhóu Xuán, Wáng Sù, Chén Běn, Méng Kāng, Zhào Fēng, and Zhāng Jī participated in court discussions.
The entire realm looked to him,
and the court and populace were solemn.
Some requested changes to existing institutions,
but Emperor Jǐng said:
"'To be unconscious and unaware,
following the rules of the Dì,'
this is the praise of the poets.
The systems established by the Three Ancestors
should be upheld.
Except for military matters,
no arbitrary reforms are permitted."
In the fifth year, in the fifth month of summer,
Zhūgě Kè, Grand Tutor of Wú, besieged Xīnchéng.
The court deliberated, fearing that he might divide his forces to raid Huái and Sì,
and wished to garrison various river mouths.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) said:
“Zhūgě Kè has just gained power in Wú,
and wishes to gain a temporary advantage.
He will combine his troops at Héféi,
hoping for a slim chance of success.
He will not have time to cause trouble for Qīng and Xú.
Moreover, there is more than one river mouth;
garrisoning many would require a large army,
while garrisoning few would be insufficient to repel invaders.”
Kè indeed concentrated his forces at Héféi,
exactly as predicted.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) then sent Zhèn​dōng Jiāngjūn Guànqiū Jiǎn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Wén Qīn, among others, to resist him.
Jiǎn and Qīn requested to fight,
but the Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) said:
“Kè has plunged deep into our territory with his armor rolled up,
committing his troops to a death trap.
His vanguard is not easily matched.
Furthermore, Xīnchéng is small but strong,
and cannot be taken by assault.”
He then ordered his generals to build high ramparts to wear him down.
They remained in a standoff for several months.
Kè's assault on the city exhausted his strength,
and more than half his troops were killed or wounded.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) then ordered Qīn to lead crack troops to Hélí
to intercept Kè's retreat,
with Jiǎn leading the other generals as a follow-up force.
Kè, in fear, fled.
Qīn met him in battle
and thoroughly defeated him,
beheading over ten thousand.
In the first month of spring in the first year of Zhèngyuán,

the Son of Heaven conspired with Lǐ Fēng, Censor-in-chief, Zhāng Jī, Father of the Empress and Guānglù Dàfū, Sū Shuò, Supervisor of the Yellow Gates, Lè Dūn, Prefect of the Yǒngníng Directorate, and Liú Bǎoxián, Aide-de-camp for Retainers, among others, to replace the Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) in assisting the government with Xiàhóu Xuán, Grand Minister of the Court.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) secretly learned of this
and sent Wáng Xiàn, a chamberlain, to bring Fēng by carriage.
Fēng, feeling pressured,
followed Xiàn to the palace.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) reproached him.
Fēng, knowing disaster was upon him,
then unleashed evil words.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī), enraged,
sent warriors to bludgeon him to death with sword hilts.
He arrested Xuán, Jī, and others,
and exterminated their three clans.
In the third month,
he subtly urged the Son of Heaven to depose Empress Zhāng,
and then issued an edict saying:
“The treacherous minister Lǐ Fēng and others, with their perverse slanders and devious schemes,
secretly plotted evil.
The Grand General (Sīmǎ Shī) has diligently carried out the heavenly punishment,
bringing them to justice.
How could Zhōu Bó's defeat of the Lǚ clan
or Huò Guāng's capture of Shàngguān
surpass this?
His fiefdom should be increased by nine thousand households,
making a total of forty thousand with the previous grants.”
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) declined to accept.
The Son of Heaven, deeply unsettled by the executions of Xuán and Jī,
felt very insecure.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) also feared that trouble would arise
and secretly plotted to depose and enthrone an emperor.
He then secretly hinted to Empress Dowager Wèi Yǒngníng.
In the ninth month of autumn, on the Jiǎxū day,
the Empress Dowager issued an order saying:
“The Emperor's age is already advanced,
yet he does not attend to the myriad affairs of state,
indulging in inner chamber favorites,
and sinking into immoral female conduct.
Daily he draws close to entertainers,
allowing their丑虐 (disgraceful and cruel acts).
He welcomed family members of the Six Palaces to reside in his inner chambers,
destroying human relationships
and disrupting the decorum between men and women.
Furthermore, being coerced by petty individuals,
he is about to endanger the state and its altars,
and cannot be allowed to continue serving the ancestral temple.”
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) summoned his officials for a meeting,
and weeping, said:
“The Empress Dowager's order is thus.
What will you gentlemen do about the imperial house?”
All replied:
“Yī Yǐn banished Tài Jiǎ to pacify Yīn,
and Huò Guāng deposed Chāngyì to secure Hàn.
They established authority over the state,
bringing peace to all under heaven.
These two precedents were carried out in antiquity;
Your Excellency must now undertake this task.
Today's matter,
we will only obey your command.”
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) said:
“The expectations of you gentlemen are great;
how can I dare to shirk this?”
Then, with all the dukes, ministers, and gentry, he jointly memorialized the Empress Dowager, saying:
“We humbly hear that the Son of Heaven
is for nurturing the populace
and bringing eternal peace to all nations.
The Emperor's age is already advanced,
yet he does not attend to the myriad affairs of state.
He daily allows petty entertainers Guō Huái and Yuán Xìn, among others, to perform naked and licentious plays.
He also built a 'Liaodong demon woman' beneath Guǎngwàng Guān,
where passersby on the road all covered their eyes.
Lìnghú Jǐng, Prefect of Qīngshāng, remonstrated with the Emperor,
and the Emperor burned him with hot iron.
When the Empress Dowager suffered the funeral of Hèyáng Jūn,
the Emperor remained playfully joyful as usual.
Páng Xī, Assistant Prefect of Qīngshāng, remonstrated with the Emperor,
but the Emperor did not listen.
When the Empress Dowager returned to the Northern Palace,
the Emperor killed Lady Zhāng,
and the Emperor was greatly resentful.
When Xī remonstrated,
the Emperor became angry
and again shot Xī with a pellet.
Whenever documents arrived,
the Emperor would not examine them.
The Empress Dowager ordered the Emperor to lecture in the Shìgān Diàn,
but the Emperor again refused to comply.
He cannot succeed to the heavenly mandate.
We request to follow the precedent of Huò Guāng of Hàn,
to seize the Emperor's imperial seals and ribbons,
and return the King of Qí to his fiefdom.”
The memorial was approved.
Thereupon, the officials in charge reported to the ancestral temple with a grand sacrifice,
and the King took the imperial carriage and secondary carriage.
The officials followed to the West Yè Gate.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) wept and said:
“My late father received extraordinary favor from successive generations.
When the late Emperor was on his deathbed,
he entrusted me with his dying wishes.
I, your humble servant, am again burdened with heavy responsibilities,

All you dukes, ministers, and gentry,
consider the old precedents from afar,
