preferring to fail the sacred person
so that the ancestral temple may have blood sacrifices.”
Then he sent envoys with imperial credentials to escort him,
and settled him at Chóngmén in Hénèi.
He executed Guō Huái, Yuán Xìn, and others.
On that day,
he discussed with his officials who should be enthroned.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) said:
“At this moment, the universe is not yet at peace.
The two barbarian enemies contend for supremacy.
The ruler of all under heaven
must be a wise and sagacious one.
Péngchéng Wáng Jù,
a son of Tàizǔ,
is, in terms of wisdom,
benevolent, sagacious, brilliant, and trustworthy.
In terms of age,
he is the eldest of the imperial house.
The heavenly throne is of utmost importance;
if the right talent is not obtained,
it will be insufficient to pacify the six directions.”
He then, with all the dukes, memorialized the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager considered Péngchéng Wáng Jù to be an uncle of the late Emperor,
and thus, in the order of ancestral lineage, not in sequence.
Then the lineage of Lièzǔ would never have an heir.
The King of Dōnghǎi,
a younger brother of Míng Dì,
wished to enthrone his son, Gāoguì Xiānggōng Máo.
The Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) firmly contended but did not prevail,
so he complied with the Empress Dowager's order
and sent envoys to welcome Gāoguì Xiānggōng from Yuánchéng and enthrone him.
The reign title was changed to Zhèngyuán.
When the Son of Heaven received the seals and ribbons,
his steps were high,
and the Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) heard of it and was worried.
When the grand assembly was about to take place,
the Emperor (Sīmǎ Shī) instructed the Son of Heaven, saying:
“A sagely king values beginnings,
rectifies the root, and respects the origin.
This is what the ancients were cautious about.
Tomorrow there will be a grand assembly;
the multitude will look upon your serene countenance,
and the dukes and ministers will listen to your harmonious voice.
The *Shī* says: 'He shows people not to be frivolous,
and they take him as their model.'
The *Yì* says: 'If his words are good,
they will be responded to from a thousand *lǐ* away.'
Even with complete rituals and ceremonies,
it is still appropriate to add reverence and solemnity,
to meet the eager expectations and admiration of all under heaven.”
On the guǐsì day,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict saying:
"We have heard that a ruler who establishes a dynasty
must rely on loyal and capable ministers;
a sovereign who preserves the existing order
also depends on supportive and assisting figures.
Thus, Wénwǔ relied on Lǚ and Zhào to achieve their mandate,
and Xuānwáng leaned on Shānfǔ to enjoy the revival of his enterprise.
The Grand General has carried on illustrious virtue for generations,
and has appeared at the opportune moment to assist.
Faced with heaven-sent perils,
when the imperial house suffered many difficulties,
and Qíwáng governed,
he did not follow the established norms.
You, Duke, uphold righteousness and maintain loyalty,
thereby bringing peace to the Central Plain,
setting an example for all the lords,
and managing all affairs.
Internally, you crushed the tyrannical rebels;
externally, you brought peace to the treacherous and wicked.
From dawn to dusk, you have toiled diligently,
laboring day and night.
Your virtuous reputation shines above and below,
and your glorious achievements extend to the four quarters.
Reflecting deeply on grand strategies,
you first proposed brilliant plans,
stabilized the state,
and supported Our person,
allowing the ancestral temples to find peace,
and the myriad people to rejoice and rely on you.
The way Yī Zhì preserved the Yīn state,
and Duke Dàn pacified and secured the Zhōu house,
cannot surpass this.
We greatly commend you for this.
Indeed, those whose virtue is abundant receive high positions,
and those whose merit is great receive ample emoluments;
this is a universal principle of ancient and modern times.
Therefore, you are to ascend to the position of Grand Chancellor (xiàngguó),
with an additional fief of nine thousand households,
making a total of forty thousand households including previous grants;
you are promoted to Grand Commander (dà dūdū) and granted the yellow battle-axe (jiǎ huángyuè),
allowed to enter court without hurrying,
address Us without being named,
and wear swords and shoes into the palace;
you are bestowed with five million coins
and five thousand bolts of silk,
to celebrate your supreme achievement."
The Emperor firmly declined the position of Grand Chancellor.
He also submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven, admonishing him, saying:
"Though the uncarved jade from Jīngshān is beautiful,
without polishing, it will not become a treasure;
though the talents of Yán and Rǎn are abundant,
without study, their capacity will not expand.
Zhòngní said: 'I am not one who was born with knowledge;
I am one who loves antiquity and is diligent in seeking knowledge.'
Looking up at the five generations of rulers from Huáng and Xuān,
none did not have something to emulate and follow.
Zhuānxū received instruction from Lǜtú,
and Gāoxīn sought wisdom from Bózhāo.
By the time of Zhōu Chéng,
Duke Dàn and Duke Wàng acted as his輔,
thus enabling him to distinguish principles and discern aspirations,
and to find peace in the Dao and joy in his work.
Because of this,
the ruler's way was clear above,
and the myriad commoners were compliant below.
The flourishing of a state where punishments were unnecessary
truly originated from this.
It is fitting to follow the principle of the former kings, who sought advice from those below,
so that lectures and recitations are frequently heard by you,
and the words of the canons and counsel are daily presented by your side."
At that time, the Son of Heaven was rather fond of extravagant embellishments,
and the Emperor again admonished him, saying:
"At the beginning of your reign,
it is appropriate to uphold simplicity and plainness."
The Son of Heaven respectfully accepted both.
In the eleventh month,
a white vapor passed across the sky.
In the first month of spring in the second year,
a comet was seen in the region of Wú and Chǔ,
extending across the sky to the northwest.
Zhèn Dōng Dà Jiāngjūn Wúqiū Jiǎn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Wén Qīn raised troops and rebelled,
falsely issuing an order from the Empress Dowager to send manifestos to the commanderies and states,
building an altar to swear an oath outside the west gate,
and each sending four sons as hostages to Wú to request aid.
In the second month,
Jiǎn and Qīn led a force of sixty thousand,
crossed the Huái River and advanced westward.
The Emperor met with his high officials to devise a plan for the punitive expedition.
Many in the court suggested sending various generals to attack them,
but Wáng Sù, Shàngshū Fù Gǔ, and Zhōngshū Shìláng Zhōng Huì advised the Emperor to personally lead the campaign.
On the wùwǔ day,
the Emperor commanded a central army of over one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry to campaign against them.
Doubling marches and advancing swiftly,
he summoned troops from three directions,
gathering a large force on the plains of Chén and Xǔ.
On the jiǎshēn day,
he reached Qiáo,
where Jiǎn's generals Shǐ Zhāo and Lǐ Xù surrendered one after another.
Jiǎn and Qīn moved into Xiàngchéng,
and the Emperor dispatched Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jī to advance and occupy Nándùn to press Jiǎn.
The Emperor deeply fortified his encampment with high ramparts,
awaiting the assembly of the eastern army.
The generals requested to advance and attack their city,
but the Emperor said:
"Gentlemen, you have grasped one aspect,
but not the other.
The officers and soldiers of Huáinán originally had no intention to rebel.
Furthermore, Jiǎn and Qīn wish to follow the tactics of the 'vertical and horizontal alliances,'
imitating the persuasions of Yí and Qín,
believing that distant and near forces would surely respond.
However, on the day the rebellion broke out,
Huáiběi did not follow,
and Shǐ Zhāo and Lǐ Xù scattered one after another.
Disunited internally and betrayed externally,
they know they are doomed to fail.
A cornered beast thinks of fighting,
so a quick battle would only suit their intentions.
Although victory is certain,
many people would also be injured.
Moreover, Jiǎn and others are deceiving their officers and soldiers,
employing countless deceptions.
If we prolong the engagement slightly,
their fraudulent intentions will be exposed by themselves;
this is to conquer without fighting."
He then sent Zhūgě Dàn to lead the various armies of Yùzhōu from Ānfēng towards Shòuchūn,
and Zhēng Dōng Jiāngjūn Hú Zūn to lead the various armies of Qīng and Xú to march between Qiáo and Sòng,
cutting off their retreat.
The Emperor camped at Rǔyáng,
and sent Yǎanzhōu Cìshǐ Dèng Ài to lead the various armies of Tàishān to advance and camp at Lèjiā,
feigning weakness to lure them.
Qīn advanced his army, intending to attack Ài.
The Emperor secretly moved his army, silencing his troops,
and directly proceeded to Lèjiā,
where he encountered Qīn.
Qīn's son, Yāng,
eighteen years old,
was the bravest in the three armies.
He said to Qīn:
"Before they are settled,
please let me ascend the city and beat the drums to create a clamor; we can defeat them."
After plotting and acting,
he made three war cries, but Qīn could not respond.
Yāng retreated,
and together they withdrew eastward.
The Emperor said to his generals:
"Qīn has fled."
He ordered his elite troops to pursue them.
All the generals said:
"Qīn is an old general,
and Yāng is young and fierce.
They led their army inward,
and have not yet suffered defeat,
so they surely will not flee."
The Emperor said:
"The first drumbeat invigorates the spirit,
the second diminishes it,
and the third exhausts it.
Yāng made three war cries,
but Qīn did not respond.
Their momentum is already broken;
what are they waiting for if not to flee?"
When Qīn was about to flee,
Yāng said:
"Unless we first break their momentum,
we cannot leave."
Then, with over ten valiant riders, he charged and broke through the enemy lines,
sweeping away all in his path,
and then withdrew.
The Emperor sent Zuǒ Chángshǐ Sīmǎ Lián to lead eight thousand valiant cavalry to pursue them,
and ordered General Lè Lín and others to lead infantry to follow them.
By the time they reached Shāyáng,
they had repeatedly broken Qīn's formations.
Arrows rained down,
and Qīn rode shielded.
His army was utterly routed,
and all his troops threw down their weapons and surrendered.
Qīn, his son, and their immediate subordinates fled to Xiàng for safety.
Jiǎn, hearing of Qīn's defeat,
abandoned his troops and fled eastward to Huáinán under the cover of night.
The Commander of Ānfēngjīn pursued Jiǎn,
beheaded him,
and sent his head to the capital.
Qīn then fled to Wú,
and Huáinán was pacified.
Initially,
the Emperor had a tumorous illness in his eye,
and ordered a physician to excise it.
When Yāng came to attack,
he was startled and his eye popped out.
Fearing the alarm of the six armies,
he covered it with a quilt.
The pain was intense,
and he gnawed through the quilt, but those around him did not know.
In the intercalary month, his illness became critical.
He commanded Wén Dì to take overall command of all the armies.
On the Xīnhài day,
he passed away in Xǔchāng,
at the age of forty-eight.
In the second month,
the Emperor’s coffin arrived from Xǔchāng.
The Son of Heaven, in plain clothes, attended the mourning,
and issued an edict saying:
"The Duke had the meritorious service of saving the age and pacifying the state,
and the achievement of quelling disaster and disorder.
Compounded by dying in service to the king,
it is fitting to bestow special honors.
Let the dukes and ministers discuss and establish the regulations."
The relevant officials deliberated, believing that he was loyal in securing the altars of soil and grain,
and his achievements benefited all under Heaven.
It was appropriate to follow the precedent of Huò Guāng,
to posthumously add the title of Dà Sīmǎ to precede Dà Jiāngjūn,
increase his fief by fifty thousand households,
and grant him the posthumous title of Wǔ Gōng.
Wén Dì submitted a memorial declining, saying:
"My late father dared not accept the nine rites of the Chéngxiàng and Xiāngguó,
and my late elder brother dared not accept the position of Xiāngguó,
truly because these were the ranks my Grand Progenitor had constantly ascended.
Now, the posthumous title is the same as the two progenitors,
which is certainly a source of awe and trepidation.
In the past, Xiāo Hé, Zhāng Liáng, and Huò Guāng all had the meritorious service of assisting and supporting.
Hé was posthumously titled Wénzhōng,
Liáng was posthumously titled Wénchéng,
and Guāng was posthumously titled Xuānchéng.
If a posthumous title with 'Wén' or 'Wǔ' must be given,
I request that it be added according to the precedent of Hé and others."
The edict granted permission,
and he was posthumously titled Zhōngwǔ.
When the state of Jìn was established,
he was posthumously honored as Jǐng Wáng.
When Wǔ Dì received the abdication,
he was given the esteemed title of Jǐng Huángdì,
his mausoleum was called Jùnpíng,
and his ancestral temple was named Shìzōng.
Wén Dì,
Wén Huángdì, personal name Zhāo,
courtesy name Zǐshàng,
was the younger full brother of Jǐng Dì.
In the second year of Jǐngchū of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnchéng Xiāng.
At the beginning of Zhèngshǐ,
he served as the Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiāng of Luòyáng.
Coming after the extravagance of Wèi Míng,
the Emperor abolished harsh and petty regulations,
and did not interfere with farming seasons,
which greatly pleased the common people.
He was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì.
When Dà Jiāngjūn Cáo Shuǎng attacked Shǔ,
the Emperor was made Zhēngshǔ Jiāngjūn,
and, as deputy to Xiàhóu Xuán, went out through Luògǔ,
and stationed at Xīngshì.
Shǔ general Wáng Lín attacked the Emperor's camp by night,
but the Emperor lay firm and did not move.
When Lín retreated,
the Emperor said to Xuán:
"Fèi Yī relies on the dangerous terrain to hold his ground,
we cannot advance to fight, nor can we attack.
It is advisable to quickly withdraw the army,
and make plans for later."
Shuǎng and others then withdrew.
Yī indeed sent troops quickly to Sānlǐng,
and it was only by contending for the perilous pass that they were able to get through.
Thereupon, he returned,
and was appointed Yìláng.
When Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
he led the multitude to guard the two palaces,
and for his merit, his fief was increased by a thousand households.
When Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi invaded Lǒngyòu,
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Guō Huái defended against him from Cháng'ān.
The Emperor was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn, with a Jié,
stationed in Guānzhōng,
to command all armies.
Huái attacked Jiāng Wéi's subordinate Jù Ān at Qū,
but it remained undecided for a long time.
The Emperor then advanced to Chángchéng,
and headed south towards Luògǔ to create a diversion.
Wéi was afraid,
and retreated to protect Nánzhèng.
Jù Ān's army had its support cut off,
and he led his troops to surrender.
He was transferred to Āndōng Jiāngjūn, with a Jié,
and stationed at Xǔchāng.
When the main army attacked Wáng Líng,
the Emperor supervised all military affairs north of the Huái River,
and led his army to rendezvous at Xiàng.
His fief was increased by three hundred households,
and he was granted a gold seal and purple ribbon.
Soon after, he was promoted to the title of Dūdū,
and commanded Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Hú Zūn and Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Dàn to attack Wú,
fighting at Dōngguān.
Both armies were defeated,
and he was stripped of his marquisate for this failure.
Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi again invaded Lǒngyòu,
and announced his intention to attack Dídao.
The Emperor was appointed acting Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and stationed at Cháng'ān.
The Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Chén Tài wanted to occupy Dídao before the enemy,
but the Emperor said:
"Jiāng Wéi attacked the Qiāng,
collected their hostages,
accumulated grain and built granaries,
and then moved to this location.
He merely wants to deal with the Qiāng beyond the pass,
to provision himself for the coming year.
If he were truly heading for Dídao,
how could he possibly announce it
and let outsiders know?
Now he loudly declares his departure,
this means he intends to retreat."
Wéi indeed burned his camp and left.
At this time, the Qiāng and Hú of Xīnpíng rebelled.
The Emperor defeated them,
then displayed his military might at Língzhōu.
The northern barbarians were terrified and trembled,
and all the rebels surrendered.
For his merit, he was again enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnchéng Xiāng.
When Gāoguìxiāng Gōng was enthroned,
for his participation in determining the plan,
he was promoted to Marquis of Gāodū,
with an increase of two thousand households in his fief.
During the rebellion of Guànqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn,
the main army campaigned in the east,
and the Emperor concurrently held the position of Zhōnglǐngjūn,
remaining to guard Luòyáng.
When Jǐng Dì became gravely ill,
the Emperor personally visited the capital to inquire about his illness,
and was appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn.
When Jǐng Dì passed away,
the Son of Heaven ordered the Emperor to be stationed at Xǔchāng,
and Shàngshū Fù Gǔ led the six armies back to the capital.
The Emperor, using Gǔ's and Zhōng Huì's stratagems,
personally led the army back.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
he was promoted to Dà Jiāngjūn,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn, Lù Shàngshūshì,
to assist in governance,
with the privilege of wearing swords and shoes onto the audience hall.
The Emperor firmly declined to accept.
In the first month of spring in the first year of Gānlù,
he was given the additional title of Dà Dūdū,
and was not referred to by name when submitting memorials.
In the sixth month of summer,
he was promoted to Duke of Gāodū,
with a territory of seven hundred *lǐ*,
and was granted the nine bestowals,
given the ceremonial axe,
and promoted to the title of Dà Dūdū,
with the privilege of wearing swords and shoes onto the audience hall.
Again, he firmly declined to accept.
On the Gēngshēn day of the eighth month of autumn,
he was given the additional grant of a yellow ceremonial axe,
and an increase of three counties in his fief.
On the Xīnwèi day of the fifth month of summer in the second year,
Zhèndōng Dà Jiāngjūn Zhūgě Dàn killed the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Lè Lín,
and started a rebellion in Huáinán,
sending his son Jìng as a hostage to Wú to request aid.
Discussants urged a swift punitive expedition,
but the Emperor said:
"Dàn saw Guànqiū Jiǎn's swift downfall,
and now he must be colluding with the Wú enemy externally.
This is a great but slow-unfolding change.
I should join forces with all quarters
to achieve complete victory over him."
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, when Qíng Bù rebelled,
Hàn Zǔ personally led the expedition;
when Kuí Xiāo defied,
Guāng Wǔ campaigned westward;
Lìzǔ Míng Huángdì repeatedly went forth in his imperial carriage: all these were to demonstrate awe-inspiring might
and manifest majestic power.
Your Majesty should temporarily oversee the military affairs,
so that the generals and soldiers can rely on heavenly might.
Now, the various armies number perhaps five hundred thousand.
With a large force attacking a small one,
there is nothing we cannot overcome."
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Emperor and Empress Dowager were escorted to the east for a campaign.
Troops were levied from Qīng, Xú, Jīng, and Yù provinces,
and scattered armies from Guānzhōng were gathered.
All converged north of the Huái River.
The army reached Xiàng.
Jiǎ Tíngwèi Hé Zhēng was given a staff of authority
and sent to Huáinán
to reassure the officers and soldiers,
clarify the difference between loyalty and rebellion,
and demonstrate rewards and punishments.
On the jiǎxū day,
the Emperor advanced his army to Qiūtóu.
Wú sent Wén Qīn, Táng Zī, Quán Duān, Quán Yì, and over thirty thousand others to relieve Wú Dàn.
Our generals met them in battle,
but could not withstand them.
General Lǐ Guǎng did not advance when facing the enemy,
and Tàishān Administrator Cháng Shí feigned illness and did not come out.
Both were beheaded and their heads displayed to the public.
In the eighth month,
Wú General Zhū Yì led over ten thousand troops,
leaving their baggage train at Dūlù,
and with light troops reached Líjiāng.
Supervisor of the Army Shí Bāo and Yǎnzhōu Provincial Inspector Zhōu Tài resisted them,
and Zhū Yì retreated.
Tàishān Administrator Hú Liè used surprise tactics to attack Dūlù,
burning their grain and supplies.
Shí Bāo and Zhōu Tài again advanced and attacked Zhū Yì,
severely defeating him.
Zhū Yì's remaining soldiers were extremely hungry;
they ate kudzu leaves and fled.
The Wú people killed Zhū Yì.
The Emperor said:
"Zhū Yì failed to reach Shòuchūn,
which was not his fault,
yet the Wú people killed him.
This merely served to apologize to Shòuchūn and strengthen Wú Dàn's resolve,
making him still hope for rescue.
If not for this,
he would have broken through the encirclement
and risked his life in a decisive battle.
Some say our grand army cannot last long,
and suggest reducing food and personnel,
hoping for another change.
Judging the enemy's intentions,
they will not deviate from these three possibilities.
We must now use various methods to confuse them
and prepare for their escape.
This is a winning strategy."
He then ordered the encirclement to be completed,
dispatched the weak and sick to gather grain north of the Huái River,
and provisioned the soldiers with soybeans,
three sheng per person.
Wén Qīn heard of this
and indeed rejoiced.
The Emperor further displayed a weakened appearance to them,
sent many double agents,
and spread rumors that Wú reinforcements were about to arrive.
Wú Dàn and his confederates then indulged in eating more freely,
but soon the city ran out of provisions.
Shí Bāo and Wáng Jī both requested to attack,
but the Emperor said:
"Wú Dàn's rebellious scheme
was not conceived in a day;
he amassed provisions and fortified his defenses,
colluding with Wú outsiders,
believing he could hold Huáinán.
Wén Qīn, being complicit in evil,
will certainly not flee easily.
If we attack them fiercely now,
it will deplete the strength of our mobile forces.
Should external invaders suddenly arrive,
we would be attacked from both front and rear;
this is a dangerous path.
Now, the three rebels are gathered in an isolated city;
perhaps Heaven intends for them to be exterminated together.
I should use a long-term strategy to contain them,
only maintaining strong defenses on three sides.
If the enemy comes by land,
their army provisions must be scarce.
I will use mobile troops and light cavalry to cut off their supply lines,
and we can defeat the external enemy without battle.
Once the external enemy is defeated,
Wén Qīn and the others will surely be captured."
Quán Yì's mother,
a daughter of Sūn Quán,
had fallen out of favor with Wú.
Quán Duān's nephews Yī and Yí escorted their mother and defected.
Yí's brother Jìng was then in Shòuchūn.
Using Zhōng Huì's plan,
letters from Yī and Yí were forged to deceive Jìng.
Jìng and his five brothers led their followers to surrender,
causing great panic in the city.
In the third year, spring, the first month, on the rén yín day,
Wú Dàn, Wén Qīn, and others sallied out to attack the long siege lines.
Our armies counterattacked
and drove them back.
Initially,
Wú Dàn and Wén Qīn were not in harmony internally.
As they faced utter destitution,
they grew suspicious and distrustful of each other.
When Wén Qīn's strategy clashed with Wú Dàn's,
Wú Dàn personally slew Wén Qīn.
Wén Qīn's son Wén Yāng attacked Wú Dàn,
but failed.
He scaled the city wall and surrendered.
He was appointed general
and enfeoffed as a marquis,
and Wén Yāng was sent to patrol the city and shout [to the defenders].
The Emperor saw that the archers on the city walls did not shoot,
and said to his generals:
"We can attack now!"
In the second month, on the yǐ yǒu day,
they attacked and captured the city,
beheading Wú Dàn
and exterminating his three kindreds.
Wú generals Táng Zī, Sūn Màn, Sūn Mí, Xú Sháo, and others, with their subordinates, all surrendered.
[一０]Their ranks and titles were increased,
and provisions were given to their hungry and sick.
Some suggested that the Wú soldiers would certainly not be useful [to us]
and requested to bury them alive.
The Emperor said:
"Even if they return [to Wú],
it will only show the magnanimity of Zhōngguó."
Thereupon, they were relocated to Sānhé.
In summer, the fourth month,
the Emperor returned to the capital, Jīngshī.
The Wèi Emperor commanded that Qiūtóu be renamed Wǔqiū,
to commemorate the military achievement.
In the fifth month,
the Emperor enfeoffed the Emperor [Sīmǎ Zhāo] as Duke of Jìn,
granting him eight commanderies: Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, Lèpíng, Xīnxīng, Yànmén from Bìngzhōu, and Hédōng, Píngyáng from Sīzhōu,
an area of seven hundred li.
He was granted the Nine Bestowals (Jiǔxī),
and advanced to the position of Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
The State of Jìn was allowed to establish its own officialdom.
He declined nine times,
and then it was stopped.
Thereupon, his fief was increased by ten thousand households,
and he was granted revenue from three counties.
All his sons without titles were enfeoffed as列侯 (lièhóu, marquises of various ranks).
In autumn, the seventh month,
a memorial was submitted to record the descendants of the illustrious officials, great meritorious servants, and heroes of previous generations,
and employ them according to their talents.
In the fourth year, summer, the sixth month,
Jīngzhōu was divided, and two Military Governors (Dūdū) were appointed:
Wáng Jī garrisoned Xīnyě,
and Zhōu Tài garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Shí Bāo was made Military Governor of Yángzhōu,
Chén Qiān Military Governor of Yùzhōu,
Zhōng Yù Military Governor of Xúzhōu,
and Sòng Jūn Supervisor of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu.
In the first year of Jǐngyuán, summer, the fourth month,
the Emperor again commanded that the Emperor's [Sīmǎ Zhāo's]爵秩 (juézhì, rank and emolument) be as before,
but he again declined to accept.
Since the Emperor [Cáo Máo] knew that the Emperor [Sīmǎ Zhāo] had been the chief minister for three generations,
and policies did not originate from himself,
he could not feel at ease.
Moreover, fearing dismissal and disgrace,
he planned to summon all officials before the throne and carry out a deposition.
In the fifth month, on the wùzǐ night,
he ordered Eunuch Attendant Director Lǐ Zhāo and others to deploy armored guards at Língyúntái,
summoning Palace Attendant Wáng Shěn, Palace Aide to the Imperial Censors Wáng Yè, and Minister of Works Wáng Jīng.
He took out a yellow silk edict from his bosom and showed it to them,
ordering them to prepare for an emergency and await dawn.
Wáng Shěn and Wáng Yè galloped to inform the Emperor [Sīmǎ Zhāo],
who summoned Palace Guard Commander Jiǎ Chōng and others to make preparations.
[一一]The Emperor [Cáo Máo] knew the plan had been exposed,
and led his attendants to attack the Chancellor's residence,
proclaiming that he was "going to punish someone," and that "any who dared to move would have their families exterminated."
The Chancellor's soldiers hesitated and dared not fight.
Jiǎ Chōng rebuked the generals, saying:
"The Duke raised you
precisely for this day!"
Crown Prince's Household Administrator Chéng Jì drew his halberd, violated the imperial carriage,
and stabbed him.
The blade emerged from his back,
and the Emperor [Cáo Máo] collapsed in his carriage and died.
The Emperor summoned his many officials to discuss the reason for this,
but the Chancellor, Chén TàI, did not arrive.
The Emperor sent his maternal uncle, Xún Yǐ, to bring him in a carriage,
and invited him into a private chamber,
saying,
“Xuánbó,
what can the world do about me?”
TàI replied,
“Only by having Jiǎ Chōng cut in half at the waist
can we slightly apologize to the world.”
The Emperor said,
“Please think of a lesser alternative.”
TàI replied,
“I only see the best option,
not a lesser alternative.”
Thereupon, the blame was placed on Chéng Jì, who was then executed.
The Empress Dowager issued an order saying,
“In the past, Liú Hé, the Prince of Chāngyì of the Hàn dynasty, was deposed as a commoner due to his crimes.
This child should also be buried with the rites of a commoner,
so that all within and without may know his conduct.”
The Minister Wáng Jīng was killed
for being disloyal to me.
On the day Wùshēn,
[一二] the Emperor submitted a memorial stating:
“The late Gāoguì Xiānggōng led his retainers and soldiers,
drew their blades and beat their drums towards my location.
I feared that weapons would clash,
so I immediately ordered the generals and officers not to cause any harm;
those who disobeyed would be dealt with according to military law.
The cavalry commander Chéng Cuì’s younger brother, Chéng Jì, a Palace Attendant, entered the ranks
and fatally wounded the Duke.
I have heard that the principle for a minister
is to die rather than be disloyal,
and the duty of serving a superior
is not to shrink from danger.
Earlier, a sudden change occurred,
and disaster struck like a trigger.
I truly wished to commit myself to death,
letting fate decide.
However, considering the original plot,
it aimed to endanger the Empress Dowager
and overthrow the ancestral temple.
I, who unworthily hold the position of Chief Grand Tutor,
had a duty to pacify the nation,
and immediately issued repeated orders
not to approach the imperial carriage.
But Jì recklessly intruded,
leading to this great calamity.
My sorrow and bitter regret
tear my inner organs apart.
Jì disturbed the nation and violated discipline;
his crime is beyond pardon.
I have forthwith arrested Jì’s family
and handed them over to the Court of Judicial Review.”
The Empress Dowager assented,
and Jì’s three familial exterminations were carried out.
After consulting with the dukes and ministers,
Huáng, the Duke of Chángdào Xiāng, son of Yánwáng Yǔ, was established as Emperor.
In the sixth month,
the reign title was changed.
On the day Bǐngchén,
the Son of Heaven promoted the Emperor to Chancellor,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Jìn,
increased his territory by ten commanderies,
and bestowed the Nine Bestowments as before.
His kinsmen and younger brothers who had not yet been enfeoffed as marquises were granted the title of Tínghóu,
and he was granted ten million coins
and ten thousand bolts of silk.
He firmly declined,
and the matter was dropped.
In the winter, eleventh month,
Xiāo Shèn, the Supervisor of Jíyáng in Wú, sent a letter to the General Who Guards the East, Shí Bāo, pretending to surrender
and requesting welcome.
The Emperor knew it was a trick,
so he instructed Bāo to outwardly show he would welcome him,
but inwardly to prepare for it.
In the second year, autumn, eighth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
[一三] the Son of Heaven sent the Grand Commandant Gāo Róu to present the seal and ribbon of Chancellor to the Emperor,
and the Minister of Works Zhèng Chōng to present the Duke of Jìn’s enfeoffment land and Nine Bestowments.
[一四] He firmly declined.
In the third year, summer, fourth month,
Sùshèn came to present kǔshǐ arrows, stone arrowheads, bows and armor, sable furs, etc.
The Son of Heaven ordered them to be returned to the Grand General’s office.
In the fourth year, spring, second month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
the Son of Heaven again commanded the Emperor as before,
but he again firmly declined.
In the third month,
an edict ordered the Grand General’s office to add one Sīmǎ,
two Supervisors of Records,
and ten Palace Attendants.
In the summer,
the Emperor was about to campaign against Shǔ,
and thus consulted with the assembled officials, saying:
“Since the pacification of Shòuchūn,
six years have passed without military campaigns.
We have trained our troops and repaired our armor
to prepare for the two enemies.
To roughly estimate taking Wú,
building warships,
and opening waterways,
would require over ten million man-days of labor.
This is a matter of one hundred thousand men for several tens of days.
Moreover, the southern lands are low and wet,
which will inevitably lead to illness and epidemics.
Now, it is appropriate to first take Shǔ.
After three years,
we can utilize the downstream advantage from Bāshǔ,
advancing by both water and land.
This is the strategy to destroy Yú and pacify Guó,
and swallow Hán and annex Wèi.
Calculating Shǔ’s warriors at ninety thousand,
those garrisoned in Chéngdū and guarding other commanderies are no less than forty thousand.
Thus, the remaining forces do not exceed fifty thousand.
Now, we will tie up Jiāng Wéi in Tàzhōng,
preventing him from looking eastward,
and march directly towards Luògǔ,
striking their undefended territory
to attack Hànzhōng.
If they fortify cities and defend strategic points,
their military strength will inevitably be dispersed,
and their head and tail will be cut off.
We will use the main army to besiege cities,
and deploy elite troops to raid the countryside.
Jiàngé will not have time to defend its strategic pass,
and the passes will not be able to hold themselves.
With Liú Shàn’s dimwittedness,
and their border cities broken from without,
and their men and women trembling within,
their downfall is predictable.”
The General Who Conquers the West, Dèng ÀI, believed there was no opportune moment yet,
and repeatedly expressed dissenting opinions.
The Emperor was troubled by this,
and sent his Chief Clerk, Shī Zuǎn, to serve as ÀI’s Sīmǎ to explain the plan to him,
whereupon ÀI accepted the command.
Thereupon, troops were conscripted from the four directions, eighteen myriad,
and Dèng ÀI was ordered to attack Jiāng Wéi in Tàzhōng from Dídào.
Zhūgě Xù, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, was to march from Qíshān to Wǔjiē,
cutting off Wéi’s retreat.
Zhōng Huì, the General Who Guards the West, was to lead the Former General Lǐ Fǔ, the Protector of the Army for Conquering Shǔ Hú Liè, and others to attack Hànzhōng from Luògǔ.
In autumn, eighth month,
the army departed Luòyáng.
Great rewards were bestowed upon the generals and soldiers,
and the army was arrayed and sworn in.
General Dèng Dūn said that Shǔ was not yet ready for conquest,
and the Emperor had him beheaded as a warning.
In the ninth month,
he further ordered Wáng Qí, the Administrator of Tiānshuǐ, to attack Wéi’s camp,
Qiān Hóng, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, to intercept him from the front,
and Yáng Xīn, the Administrator of Jīnchéng, to advance on Gānsōng.
Zhōng Huì divided his forces into two columns,
entering from Xiégǔ.
He ordered Lǐ Fǔ to besiege Wáng Hán at Lèchéng,
and also ordered his subordinate general Yì Kǎi to attack Jiǎng Bīn at Hànchéng.
Huì advanced directly towards Yáng’ān,
and the Protector of the Army Hú Liè captured the pass city.
Jiāng Wéi, hearing of this,
led his forces back.
Wáng Qí pursued and defeated Wéi at Qiángchuān.
Wéi, along with Zhāng Yì and Liáo Huà, combined their forces to defend Jiàngé,
which Zhōng Huì attacked.
In winter, tenth month,
the Son of Heaven, seeing that various feudal lords’ reports of victories were constantly arriving,
reiterated his previous command, saying: “I, with meager virtue,
have been fortunate to succeed the heavenly mandate,
inheriting the grand accomplishments of my ancestors.
I have encountered many difficulties in the family
and am unclear in instruction.
In the past, villainous rebellions frequently arose,
and
bandits insulted us domestically.
I greatly feared that the four seas would be lost,
thereby destroying the great enterprise of the three ancestors.
You, Duke, have practiced virtue and walked the path of wisdom,
with bright integrity and profound breadth.
You have propagated the martial and civil arts,
and for generations served as guardian and tutor
to assist the royal house.
Enduring wind and rain,
you have journeyed through campaigns
and conquests,
toiling for the royal house
for over twenty years.
You assisted your predecessors
and then took charge of major state affairs,
successfully suppressing disorder
and stabilizing the altars of soil and grain.
When the disturbances of Jiǎn and Qīn
occurred,
you, Duke, mobilized your forces and rallied the multitude.
You dispatched armies,
and with proper organization and strategy,
you brought peace to Huái pǔ.
Thereafter, Bāshǔ repeatedly invaded,
and the western lands were not peaceful.
You, Duke, with extraordinary plans
giving instructions,
you achieved victory a thousand *lǐ* away.
Thus, in the Battle of Duàn Gǔ,
you seized the opportune moment and achieved a great victory,
beheading generals and seizing banners,
with tens of thousands of heads counted.
When Sūn Jùn caused trouble in Huáxià,
leading invaders to Xú
fāng,
your war chariots were first on the road,
your awesome spirit advancing ahead.
Before the yellow battle-axe was even unsheathed,
the whales and leviathans had fled.
When Sūn Yī caused a rift,
leading to mutual suspicion and obstruction,
your profound insight shone far,
and your marvelous strategies
penetrated the subtle.
Distant people pledged allegiance,
serving as a bulwark in the southern Huáxià.
Thereupon, you were granted crack troops,
and exerted all your strength in military campaigns.
When Zhūgě Dàn's rebellion reached monstrous proportions,
raising an army in Yángchǔ,
Qīn and
Zī harbored guilt,
colluding with the wicked.
They led their insect-like bandits
into Shòuchūn,
relying on the barriers of Huáishān,
daring to resist the royal command.
You personally donned armor,
executing Heaven's
punishment.
With profound foresight and plans from the ancestral temple,
you patiently bided your time.
Your elite troops struck with thunderous force,
and Zhū Yì was utterly defeated;
your divine adaptability responded to circumstances,
and Quán Cóng submitted;
taking advantage of the chaos and darkness,
Gāo Yōng could not be defended.
You combined the grand strategies of the Nine Punishments,
and perfected the true measure of the Five Weapons.
Thus, you were able to fight without exhausting military might,
yet annihilated great enemies;
without waving the banner twice,
the chief rebels surrendered their heads.
You gathered the eminent officials of the powerful Wú,
and captured the fleeing fugitives.
They clasped their arms and bent their knees,
entrusting their lives to your subordinate officials,
capturing and beheading a hundred thousand,
their corpses piled up like a
capital city.
You washed away the accumulated shame of the ancestral temple,
and saved the common people from hardship.
You pacified the region,
and established awe throughout Wúhuì.
Then you sheathed the weapons of war,
bringing peace to our territory.
Heaven and Earth,
and the spirits of the dead,
all benefited.
At that time, when the royal house faced difficulties,
and troubles arose within the court,
it relied on your spiritual power,
greatly overcoming the perils.
The ancestral temple, in peril, found peace,
and the altars of Soil
and Grain, fallen, were restored to tranquility.
Your loyalty reached the August Heaven,
and your achievements aided the six directions.
Therefore, consulting ancient teachings,
and examining the classics and records,
it is commanded that you be elevated to the position of Grand Chancellor,
surpassing all
other marquises,
to open territory at Cānxū,
and be enfeoffed with the domain of Jìn.

Beyond the nine regions,

From the corners of the seas and remote

You assist my person,

the eight extremities.
Because Yōngshǔ was not yet submissive,

You selected and trained generals and commanders,

As soon as they set foot in enemy

The wild and cunning fled north,

You captured their barbarian commanders,

Bāhàn was shaken,

You have the merit of pacifying the six directions,

You upheld the Five Constants to promote benevolence,

Even Shàngfù, who assisted Wén and Wǔ,

you.
In ancient times, the former kings selected and established enlightened virtues,

This was to protect and assist the royal domain,
and bequeath their legacy for a hundred generations.
Therefore, the enfeoffments of Qí and Lǔ

In the difficulties of Huì and Xiāng,
Huán and Wén, through their

But your merits surpass previous achievements,
yet the rewards fall short of the old
system.
All officials and the populace are saddened,

In summer,

Wèi house.

You, Gōng, harmonize

Therefore, you are granted the Gǔnmiǎn robes,

You, Gōng, widely spread manifest virtue,
benevolence

You, Gōng, pacify the universe,

Distant lands hasten to embrace righteousness,

Therefore, you are granted a vermilion door for your residence.
You, Gōng, select the worthy and assess talent,
seeking out the eminent
and exceptional,

Therefore, you are granted a sloping approach for ascending.
You, Gōng, are solemn, respectful, and awe-inspiring,

Therefore, you are granted three hundred Wǔbēn warriors.
You, Gōng, are discerning and cautious in applying punishments,

Therefore,

You, Gōng, array the six armies,

Those who defy commands and transgress righteousness

Therefore, you are granted one vermilion bow and one hundred vermilion
arrows,

You, Gōng, offer sacrifices with increasing fervor,

wine,

The state of Jìn shall establish its offices and below,

Go forth, be reverent!
Respectfully obey my command,
widely spread the teachings and canons,
bring glory and favor to all quarters,

and greatly manifest the excellent decree of me, the lone one.
All dukes, ministers, generals, and commanders went to the mansion to convey the imperial edict,
but the emperor courteously declined.
Sīkōng Zhèng Chōng led the assembled officials in urging acceptance, saying:
"We humbly observe that the auspicious decree has clearly arrived,
and we hear that you, Míng Gōng, are firmly declining.
Chōng and others are deeply concerned,
and indeed have foolish thoughts.
We believe that the institutions established by sagely kings
have been followed for a hundred generations,
and the commendation of virtue and reward for merit
has a long history.
In the past, Yī Yǐn
was merely a minister of Yǒu Shēnhù,
but by assisting Chéng Tāng once,
he received the title of Ā Héng.
Zhōu Gōng, relying on an established power,
and resting on a secured foundation,
gloriously resided in Qūfù,
and possessed Guī Méng.
Lǚ Shàng
was a fisherman of Pánxī,
but in one morning, upon his command,
he was enfeoffed in Yíngqiū.
Since then,
those whose merits were modest but rewards great
are countless,
yet wise and sagely individuals
still consider them fine tales.
How much more so since your esteemed father, the former Xiàngguó,
your family has possessed illustrious virtue for generations,
assisting the Wèi house,
to pacify the world.
There are no corrupt policies at court,
and no slanderous words among the people.
Previously, Míng Gōng marched west to Língzhōu,
and north to the desert,
causing areas west of Yúzhōng
to tremble and submit at the mere rumor.
The Qiāng and Róng came galloping,
turning their heads inwards.
You suppressed rebels in the east,
and entirely achieved victory alone.
You captured the generals of Hélǘ
and took tens of thousands of light-armed soldiers prisoner,
extending your prestige to the South Sea,
and striking fear into the Sān Yuè.
The universe is peaceful and stable,
and wickedness does not arise.
Therefore, the people of the time revere and cherish you,
and the Eastern Yi present their dances.
Thus, the sagely emperor has reviewed the rites and old statutes from ancient times,
to establish a state and glorious residence,
and manifest this in Tàiyuán.
Míng Gōng should accept the imperial decree,
receive this great blessing,
which truly accords with Heaven and man.
Your original merits and grand achievements
are so glorious;
the blessedness of the land
is so magnificent.
Internal and external are in harmony,
without fault or transgression.
By this expedition,
you can cross the Jiāng in court attire,
sweep away Wú and Huì,
block the source of the Jiāng in the west,
and offer sacrifices to Mínshān.
Turn your halberd and stop your chariot,
to command all under Heaven,
so that none are unsubmissive in the distance,
and none are disrespectful nearby.
Let the virtue of Great Wèi
shine more brightly than Táng and Yú;
let Míng Gōng's grand achievements
surpass those of Huán and Wén.
Then, standing by the vast sea, you can decline like Wén Bó,
and ascending Jīshān, you can bow to Xǔ Yóu.
Would this not be grand!
Utterly just and impartial,
who could be your equal?
Why must you be so diligently modest?"
The emperor then accepted the command.
In the eleventh month,
Dèng Ài led over ten thousand men from Yīnpíng, crossing treacherous terrain to Jiāngyóu,
defeated the Shǔ general Zhūgě Zhān at Miánzhú,
beheaded Zhān,
and sent his head.
He advanced his army to Luòxiàn,
and Liú Shàn surrendered.
The Son of Heaven commanded Jìn Gōng, as Xiàngguó, to oversee all government affairs.
Thereupon, he presented the credentials,
and removed the titles of Shìzhōng, Dà Dūdū, and Lù Shàngshū.
He memorialized Dèng Ài as Tàiwèi,
and Zhōng Huì as Sītú.
Huì secretly plotted rebellion,
and thus secretly sent slander against Ài.
In the spring, the first month of the first year of Xiánxī,
a caged cart was sent to summon Ài.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor, with the Son of Heaven, marched west,
reaching Cháng'ān.
At this time, all the Wèi princes and marquises were in Yèchéng.
He ordered Shān Tāo, the Aide to the Military Counselor, to act as Army Commander,
to guard Yè,
and dispatched Hùjūn Jiǎ Chōng, bearing the staff of authority, to supervise all the armies,
to hold Hànzhōng.
Zhōng Huì then rebelled in Shǔ.
Jiān Jūn Wèi Guàn and Yòu Jiāngjūn Hú Liè attacked Huì,
and beheaded him.
Previously,
when Huì was campaigning against Shǔ,
Shào Tì, a clerk of the Xīcáo, said to the Emperor:
“Zhōng Huì is untrustworthy,
he should not be allowed to proceed.”
The Emperor smiled and said:
“Taking Shǔ is like pointing to the palm of one's hand,
yet everyone else says it cannot be done;
only Huì and I share the same view.
After Shǔ is destroyed,
the generals and soldiers of Zhōngguó
will all wish to return home.
The remaining people of Shǔ
are still filled with terror.
Even if they have different intentions,
they will be powerless to act.”
It turned out exactly as he had predicted.
On the day Bǐngchén,
[一五]the Emperor arrived back from Cháng'ān.
In the third month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor's rank was advanced to King,
and his enfeoffment was increased to twenty commanderies, including previous grants.
In the summer, the fifth month, on the day Guǐwèi,
the Son of Heaven posthumously honored Wǔyáng Xuānwén Hóu as Jìn Xuān Wáng,
and Wǔyáng Zhōngwǔ Hóu as Jìn Jǐng Wáng.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Emperor memorialized that Sīkōng Xún Yǐ should establish the rites and ceremonies,
Zhōnghùjūn Jiǎ Chōng should rectify the laws,
Shàngshū Púyè Péi Xiù should deliberate on the official system,
and Tàibǎo Zhèng Chōng should take overall charge and make decisions.
The system of five ranks of nobility was first established.
In the winter, the tenth month, on the day Dīnghài,
he memorialized sending Xú Shào, the Aide to the Prime Minister from Wú, and Sànqí Chángshì Shuǐcáo Shǔ Sūn Yù, as envoys to Wú,
[一六]to inform Sūn Hào about the pacification of Shǔ,
and to present horses, brocades, and other items,
to display both might and benevolence.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Son of Heaven ordered Zhōng Fǔjūn Xīnchāng Xiānghóu Yán to be Jìn Shìzǐ.
In the spring, the second month of the second year, on the day Jiǎchén,
Qú Xiàn presented a spirit turtle,
which was delivered to the Prime Minister's residence.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Sūn Hào sent Jì Zhì to pay tribute,
and also to present local products.
In the fifth month,
the Son of Heaven ordered that the Emperor wear a crown with twelve streamers,
display the Son of Heaven's banners and standards,
have a vanguard when going out and clear the way when entering,
ride in a golden-rooted carriage,
drawn by six horses,
be equipped with five seasonal auxiliary carriages,
and have the máotóu and yúnhǎn standards.
His music and dance included eight rows of performers,
and he had bells and bell stands in a palace-style arrangement.
His position was above that of the King of Yān.
The King's consort was promoted to King's Queen,
the heir apparent to Prince,
and the titles and ranks of the King's daughters and grandsons were all to follow the etiquette of the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor memorialized the removal of all prohibitions, cumbersome regulations, and inconvenient laws and statutes of the time.
The state of Jìn established the offices of Yùshǐ Dàfū, Shìzhōng, Chángshì, Shàngshū, Zhōng Lǐngjūn, and Wèi Jiāngjūn.
In the autumn, the eighth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor passed away in the open-air sleeping chamber,
aged fifty-five.
In the ninth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
he was buried in Chóngyáng Líng,
and was posthumously given the title Wén Wáng.
When Wǔ Dì received the abdication,
he posthumously honored him with the title Wén Huángdì,
and his temple was called Tàizǔ.
The court historians comment: Shìzōng established the foundation with his sagacious strategies,
and Tàizǔ accomplished great deeds with his heroic talent.
The legacy of serving Yīn remained empty,
and the ambition to cut down Shāng became distant.
Dividing the world into three,
their achievements lie therein.
When crossing the Sword Gate to dispel the troubles,
and floating down the Huái to quell the unrest,
the resentments in Tónggōng
were perhaps unbearable for some.
As for embodying the spirit of a renowned minister,
and ranking him among the chief ministers,
Zhōu Gōng lingered in these years,
and Wèi Wǔ achieved his ambition on this day.
The music of Xuánxuán
was greatly expanded in Nányáng,
and the plans of Shī Zhì
[一七]were carried out by facing north.
How grand it was!
He embraced both Heaven and man!
To be the master of an emperor,
is it not difficult?
A eulogy says: Shìzōng succeeded Wén,
the nation's power was not yet divided.
Three thousand warriors,
followed him like clouds.
Tàizǔ was supreme,
[一八]the Spirit Pass was pacified.
Though the rebellion was to suppress a bandit,
it ultimately amounted to regicide.

Annals of Emperor Wǔ, Volume 3
Emperor Wǔ, personal name Yán,
courtesy name Ānshì,
was the eldest son of Emperor Wén.
He was tolerant, kind, benevolent,
and profound with great magnanimity.
During the Jiāpíng era of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as Běipíng Tínghóu,
and successively held the posts of Jǐshìzhōng, Fèngchē Dūwèi, Zhōnglěi Jiāngjūn,
and was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
He was successively transferred to Zhōnghùjūn and given the provisional authority of Jiǎjié.
He welcomed Chángdào Xiānggōng in Dōngwǔyáng,
was transferred to Zhōng Fǔjūn,
and advanced to Xīnchāng Xiānghóu.
When the state of Jìn was established,
he was made Shìzǐ,
appointed Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
given an open administration, and made the second in command to the Prime Minister.
Initially,
Emperor Wén, considering that Emperor Jǐng was the legitimate son of Emperor Xuān
and had died young without an heir,
intended to make Emperor's younger brother Yōu his successor.
He showed him special affection and distinction,
believing that he was only temporarily occupying the Prime Minister's position,
and that after a hundred years,
the great enterprise should rightfully belong to Yōu.
He often said:
“This is the realm of King Jǐng,
what do I have to do with it?”
When discussing the establishment of an heir apparent,
his intention was on Yōu.
Hé Zēng and others firmly argued:
“Zhōng Fǔjūn is intelligent and divinely martial,
possessing talent that surpasses his generation.
His hair reaches the ground,
and his hands pass his knees;
this is not the appearance of a mere subject.”
Thus, the decision was made.
In the fifth month of the second year of Xiánxī,
he was made Jìn Wáng Tàizǐ.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Emperor Wén passed away.
The Prince succeeded to the position of Prime Minister and King of Jìn.
He issued an order to loosen punishments and pardon crimes,
to comfort the populace and cease conscription,
and the entire nation observed mourning for three days.
In this month,
a tall man appeared in Xiāngwǔ,

In the ninth month, on the day Wùwǔ,

In the eleventh month,
the four Hùjūn positions were first established,

second, filial piety and full observance of rites;
third, fraternal affection towards brothers;
fourth, integrity and humble diligence;
fifth, trustworthiness and reliability;
sixth, learning for self-cultivation.

We wish to share with all nations
this auspicious prosperity."
Thereupon, a great amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed.
Titles of nobility were bestowed upon all under Heaven,
five ranks per person;
grain was given to the widowed, solitary, orphaned, and helpless,
five hú [hú] per person.
All land taxes, levies, and market duties were remitted for one year,
and all outstanding debts and old arrears were waived.
Old grudges were cleared,
and prohibitions were lifted.
Those who had lost their offices or titles were all reinstated.
On the day Dīngmǎo [Dīngmǎo],
Grand Equerry Liú Yuán [Liú Yuán] was sent to announce to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Emperor Wèi [Wèi Dì] was enfeoffed as Chénliú Wáng [Chénliú Wáng],
with an estate of ten thousand households,
residing in Yè Gōng [Yè Gōng] (Yè Palace);
all kings of the Wèi [Wèi] clan became county marquises.
King Xuān [Xuān Wáng] was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuān [Xuān Huángdì],
King Jǐng [Jǐng Wáng] as Emperor Jǐng [Jǐng Huángdì],
King Wén [Wén Wáng] as Emperor Wén [Wén Huángdì],
and King Xuān's [Xuān Wáng] consort, Lady Zhāng [Zhāng Shì], as Empress Xuānmù [Xuānmù Huánghòu].
Grand Consort Wáng [Wáng Shì] was honored as Empress Dowager,
and her palace was named Chónghuà [Chónghuà].
His imperial grand-uncle Fú [Fú] was enfeoffed as Ānpíng Wáng [Ānpíng Wáng],
his imperial uncle Gàn [Gàn] as Píngyuán Wáng [Píngyuán Wáng],
Liàng [Liàng] as Fúfēng Wáng [Fúfēng Wáng],
Zhòu [Zhòu] as Dōngguǎn Wáng [Dōngguǎn Wáng],
Jùn [Jùn] as Rǔyīn Wáng [Rǔyīn Wáng],
Róng [Róng] as Liáng Wáng [Liáng Wáng],
Lún [Lún] as Lángyá Wáng [Lángyá Wáng],
his imperial younger brother Yōu [Yōu] as Qí Wáng [Qí Wáng],
Jiàn [Jiàn] as Lè'ān Wáng [Lè'ān Wáng],
Jī [Jī] as Yàn Wáng [Yàn Wáng],
his imperial cousin-once-removed Wàng [Wàng] as Yìyáng Wáng [Yìyáng Wáng],
his imperial cousin Fǔ [Fǔ] as Bóhǎi Wáng [Bóhǎi Wáng],
Huàng [Huàng] as Xiàpí Wáng [Xiàpí Wáng],
Guī [Guī] as Tàiyuán Wáng [Tàiyuán Wáng],
Guī [Guī] as Gāoyáng Wáng [Gāoyáng Wáng],
Héng [Héng] as Chángshān Wáng [Chángshān Wáng],
his son Wén [Wén] as Pèi Wáng [Pèi Wáng],
Tài [Tài] as Lǒngxī Wáng [Lǒngxī Wáng],
Quán [Quán] as Péngchéng Wáng [Péngchéng Wáng],
Suí [Suí] as Fányáng Wáng [Fányáng Wáng],
Suì [Suì] as Jìnán Wáng [Jìnán Wáng],
Xùn [Xùn] as Qiáo Wáng [Qiáo Wáng],
Mù [Mù] as Zhōngshān Wáng [Zhōngshān Wáng],
Líng [Líng] as Běihǎi Wáng [Běihǎi Wáng],
Bīn [Bīn] as Chén Wáng [Chén Wáng],
his imperial cousin Hóng [Hóng] as Héjiān Wáng [Héjiān Wáng],
and his imperial cousin Máo [Máo] as Dōngpíng Wáng [Dōngpíng Wáng].
General of Agile Cavalry Shí Bāo [Shí Bāo] was made Grand Marshal,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Lèlíng [Lèlíng Gōng].
General of Chariots and Cavalry Chén Qiān [Chén Qiān] was made Duke of Gāopíng [Gāopíng Gōng].
Palace General Jiǎ Chōng [Jiǎ Chōng] was made General of Chariots and Cavalry and Duke of Lǔ [Lǔ Gōng].
Director of the Imperial Secretariat Péi Xiù [Péi Xiù] was made Duke of Jùlù [Jùlù Gōng].
Court Attendant Xún Xù [Xún Xù] was made Duke of Jìběi [Jìběi Gōng].
Grand Tutor Zhèng Chōng [Zhèng Chōng] was made Grand Preceptor and Duke of Shòuguāng [Shòuguāng Gōng].
Grand Commandant Wáng Xiáng [Wáng Xiáng] was made Grand Tutor and Duke of Suīlíng [Suīlíng Gōng].
Chancellor Hé Zēng [Hé Zēng] was made Grand Commandant and Duke of Lánglíng [Lánglíng Gōng].
Censor-in-Chief Wáng Shěn [Wáng Shěn] was made General of Agile Cavalry and Duke of Bólíng [Bólíng Gōng].
Minister of Works Xún Yǐ [Xún Yǐ] was made Duke of Línhuái [Línhuái Gōng].
General-in-Chief Who Guards the North Wèi Guàn [Wèi Guàn] was made Duke of Zīyáng [Zīyáng Gōng].
The rest received varying increases in their fiefs and advancements in their noble ranks.
All civil and military officials universally had their ranks increased by two grades.
The Jǐngchū [Jǐngchū] calendar was changed to the Tàishǐ [Tàishǐ] calendar.
The Làyǐ [Làyǐ] sacrifice was held in the month of Yǒu [Yǒu],
and the Shèyǐ [Shèyǐ] sacrifice in the month of Chǒu [Chǒu].
On the *wùchén* day,
an edict was issued extensively promoting frugality,
and jewels, jades, and cherished objects from the imperial storehouse were brought out
and bestowed upon princes, dukes, and officials below them, each according to their rank.
A General of the Central Army was appointed
to command the Seven Imperial Guard Armies.
On the *jǐsì* day,
an imperial decree ordered that the King of Chénliú, Cáo Huàn, use the Son of Heaven's banners and flags,
be provided with five seasonal secondary carriages,
observe the Zhèngshuò calendar of Wèi,
perform sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
and that all rites, music, and institutions should follow the old Wèi customs.
When submitting memorials, he was not to refer to himself as a subject.
The son or younger brother of Liú Kāng, Duke of Shānyáng, and Liú Shàn, Duke of Ānlè, was granted the position of Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
On the *yǐhài* day,

Sīmǎ Fú, King of Ānpíng, was appointed Grand Tutor (*tàizǎi*), given the honorary title of Axe of Authority (*jiǎ huángyuè*), and made Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (*dà dūdū zhōngwài zhūjūn shì*).
The edict stated:
"In the past, Wáng Líng plotted to depose Qí Wáng,
but Wáng Lín was ultimately unable to maintain his position.
Although Dèng Ài boasted of his achievements and lost his integrity,
he submitted to punishment with his hands bound.
Now, a general amnesty is granted to his family,
allowing them to establish an heir.
We shall revive extinguished states and continue severed lines,
pruning laws and lightening punishments.
The prohibitions on the imperial clan of Wèi are lifted.
All generals and officials who are undergoing a three-year mourning period
are to be sent home to complete their mourning.
The corvée labor for the common people is to be reinstated.
The system of hostages for lower-ranking officers of *bùqǔ* generals and magistrates is abolished.
The imperial levies from commanderies and kingdoms are to be reduced.
The luxurious performances and various entertainments of the Music Bureau, as well as elaborately carved decorations and hunting equipment, are prohibited.
The path for straightforward speech is opened,
and remonstrance officials (*jiànguān*) are established to oversee it."
That month,
six Fenghuang, three Qīnglóng, two Báilóng, and one Qílín each were seen in various commanderies and kingdoms.
In the first month of spring of the second year, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Hóu Shǐguāng and others, acting as assistant palace attendants (*jiān shìzhōng*), were dispatched with imperial credentials to the four directions
to inspect customs
and abolish prayers and exorcisms not included in the sacrificial canon.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the relevant officials requested the establishment of seven ancestral temples,
but the emperor, mindful of the burden,
did not approve.
On the *gēngyín* day,
the "Crowing Cock" song was abolished.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Lady Yáng, the consort of Emperor Jǐng, was posthumously honored as Empress Jǐnghuáng,
and her palace was named Hóngxùn.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Empress Yáng was enthroned.
In the second month,
the prohibitions on the imperial clan of Hàn were lifted.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Sīmǎ Héng, King of Chángshān, passed away.
An edict stated:
"The enfeoffments of the Five Ranks
are all recorded based on old merits.
Those who were originally county marquises (*xiánhóu*) shall have their second sons enfeoffed as village marquises (*tínghóu*);
township marquises (*xiānghóu*) as marquises within the passes (*guānnèihóu*);
and village marquises (*tínghóu*) as marquises within the central pass (*guānzhōnghóu*).
All shall receive one-tenth of the tax households of their original fiefs."
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Emperor Xuān was sacrificed to in the suburbs, to match Heaven,
and Emperor Wén was sacrificed to in the Míngtáng, to match the Supreme Deity.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"In ancient times, all officials
were expected to criticize the king's shortcomings.
However, the *bǎoshì* in particular had the duty of remonstrance.
Today's Palace Attendants (*shìzhōng*) and Regular Attendants (*chángshì*) actually hold this position.
Select those who can maintain a serious demeanor, assist in correcting errors, and remedy deficiencies
to concurrently hold this selection."
In the third month, on the *wùxū* day,
people from Wú came to offer condolences and sacrifices.
The relevant officials proposed drafting a reply edict.
The emperor said:
"In the past, Emperor Wén of Hàn and Emperor Guāngwǔ pacified Wèi Tuō and Gōngsūn Shù,
but they had not yet established the proper protocol between ruler and subject,
thus merely holding them loosely without full submission.
When Hǎo first sent envoys,
he did not know of our nation's celebration,
so just reply with a letter."
In the fifth month of summer, on the *wùchén* day,
an edict stated:
"Cáo Huàn, King of Chénliú, is still modest and reserved,
and he memorializes on every matter,
which is not the way to honor and exalt him.
Let the officials concerned understand this intention,
and for matters not of great importance, let the king's own officials memorialize on his behalf."
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Wáng Shěn, the General of Agile Cavalry (*piàojì jiāngjūn*) and Duke of Bólíng, passed away.
In the sixth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Sīmǎ Suì, King of Jìnán, passed away.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *xīnsì* day,
the Grand Ancestral Temple was constructed,
using timber from Jīngshān
and stone collected from Huàshān;
twelve bronze pillars were cast,
coated with gold,
carved with various objects,
and adorned with bright pearls.
On the *wùxū* day,
Sīmǎ Xùn, King of Qiáo, passed away.
On the last day of the month, the *bǐngwǔ* day,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the eighth month, on the *bǐngchén* day,
the office of Right General was abolished.
Initially,
although the emperor followed the Hàn and Wèi systems of removing mourning attire after burial,
he still wore deep robes and plain caps,
lowered his seat, and reduced his meals,
showing grief and reverence as if still in mourning.
On the *wùchén* day,
the relevant officials proposed changing his attire and resuming normal meals,
but he did not permit it,
and thus completed the rituals before returning to auspicious practices.
When the empress dowager passed away,
the same practice was followed.
In the ninth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
Huángfǔ Táo and Fù Xuán, Regular Attendants for Scattered Cavalry (*sànqí chángshì*), took charge of the remonstrance officials.
They submitted memorials offering remonstrance,
and the relevant officials proposed dismissing them.
An edict stated:
"Generally, to speak about the ruler
is extremely difficult for a subject,
and the suffering of not being heard and accepted
has been the indignation of loyal ministers and honest gentlemen throughout history.
Whenever a matter is presented and handed over to the officials concerned,
they often interpret it too harshly,
even saying that leniency and favors must come from the emperor.
What kind of talk is this?
Let it be thoroughly discussed and deliberated."
On the *wùxū* day,
the relevant officials memorialized:
"The Great Jìn succeeds the path of the Three Sovereigns
and treads in the footsteps of Shùn and Yǔ.
Responding to Heaven and aligning with the times,
it received the abdication from Wèi.
Therefore, it is fitting to entirely adopt the Zhengshuo calendar and official colors of previous dynasties,
all following the precedents of Yú and Táng."
The memorial was approved.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *bǐngwǔ* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
an edict stated:
"In the past, when Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
farmers did not alter their fields;
when Yǔ was buried in Chéngjì,
markets did not change their stalls.
Considering the pure and simple intentions of my ancestors,
moving residents within ten *lǐ* of the mausoleum
causes much trouble and disturbance.
Let it be entirely halted."
In the eleventh month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
people from Wō came to present local products.
The Circular Mound (*yuánqiū*) and the Square Mound (*fāngqiū*) were combined at the southern and northern suburbs,
and the sacrifices of the two solstices were combined at the two suburbs.
The military superintendency of the Duke of Shānyáng's state was abolished,
and its prohibitions were lifted.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Lady Xiàhóu, the consort of Emperor Jǐng, was posthumously honored as Empress Jǐnghuái.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the spirit tablets of ancestors were moved to the Grand Ancestral Temple.
In the twelfth month,
the agricultural officials were abolished and replaced by commanderies and counties.
That year,
six Fenghuang, ten Qīnglóng, nine Huánglóng, and one Qílín each were seen in various commanderies and kingdoms.
In the first month of spring of the third year, on the *guǐchǒu* day,
two Báilóng were seen in Hóngnóng and Miǎnchí.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the imperial son Sīmǎ Zhōng was established as the Crown Prince.
An edict stated:
"I, with my unworthiness,
have been entrusted with ruling the four seas.
Trembling with awe and reverence,
I fear being unable to bring peace and prosperity to the realm.
I desire to establish the kingly way with the world,
to rectify the root and purify the source.
Regarding the establishment of an heir and the designation of a crown prince,
this is not my foremost task.
Moreover, in recent times, whenever a crown prince was established,
acts of leniency and bestowal of favors occurred.
Reluctantly, I have followed the discussions of the princes, dukes, ministers, and gentry.
Currently, the fortune of the age is approaching peace.
I intend to display virtue and righteousness,
and reveal my likes and dislikes,
so that the common people may cast aside thoughts of excessive good fortune
and cultivate actions of sincerity from beginning to end.
Petty favors and minor acts of benevolence
are therefore not to be taken.
Let all be informed."
In the third month, on the day Wùyín,
an initial decree permitted officials of two thousand dàns salary to observe a full three-year mourning period.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the sky was dark during the day.
The office of Grand General Wǔwèi was abolished.
Lǐ Xǐ was appointed Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
A rockslide occurred on Mount Tài.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Wùwǔ,
Jiāo Shèng, Administrator of Zhāngyè Commandery, reported,
"At the mouth of the Dàliǔ Valley in Díchí County, there is a dark stone
on which patterns appear in broad daylight.
This is truly an auspicious omen for the great Jìn dynasty."
He submitted a drawing of it.
An imperial edict ordered ritual silks to be made and offered to the Grand Ancestral Temple,
then stored in the imperial treasury.
In autumn, the eighth month,
the office of Grand Protector General was abolished,
and its five subordinate offices were returned to the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
an imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, rank was bestowed according to virtue,
and emolument was granted according to merit.
Even a lower-ranking scholar received enough to sustain an upper-class farmer,
sufficient externally to serve the public and forget private concerns,
and internally to support one's parents and extend favors.
Currently, the emoluments of those in office are not enough to replace their farming income,
which is not the way to promote the foundation of transformation.
Let there be a discussion on increasing official salaries."
Princes and dukes and those below them were granted varying amounts of silk.
Hé Zēng, Grand Commandant, was appointed Grand Mentor;
Wàng, Prince of Yìyáng, was appointed Grand Commandant;
Xún Yǐ, Minister of Works, was appointed Minister of the Masses.
In winter, the tenth month,
soldiers and commoners who suffered the loss of their parents
were permitted to go home to mourn,
unless they were stationed on the border.
In the twelfth month,
Kǒng Zhèn, Marquis of Zōngshèng, was transferred to be Marquis of Fèngshèngtíng.
Liú Kāng, Duke of Shānyáng, came to court.
The study of astrology, prognostications, and apocrypha was prohibited.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on the day Xīnwèi,
Péi Xiù, President of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Minister of Works.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the statutes and ordinances were completed,
and varying ranks and silk grants were awarded.
A comet appeared in the constellation Zhěn.
On the day Dīnghài,
the Emperor ploughed the ceremonial field.
On the day Wùzǐ,
an imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, symbolic punishments were established, and the masses did not transgress;
now, although punishments are severe, transgressions do not cease.
How far apart are virtue and punishment!
The late emperor deeply pitied the common people,
and had compassion for the myriad prisons.
He commanded the various princes
to examine and rectify the laws and punishments.
I, inheriting his legacy,
constantly contemplate preserving the imperial foundation,
and desire to govern all nations through non-action.
Currently, the warmth of spring nourishes all things,
and the spring ploughing has just begun.
I have personally led the princes, dukes, ministers, and gentry to plough a thousand *mǔ* of the ceremonial field.
Furthermore, since the statutes and ordinances have been completed,
and promulgated throughout the empire,
I intend to simplify laws and emphasize fundamentals,
to nurture and benefit all within the four seas.
It is fitting to show leniency to the guilty,
to allow them to reform themselves.
Therefore, there shall be a general amnesty throughout the empire.
Chiefs of counties, adjutants of commanderies, and chief clerks shall each be granted one horse."
In the second month, on the day Gēngzǐ,

additional officials were appointed for the Duchy of Shānyáng: a Chancellor, a Gentleman-of-the-Household, a Mausoleum Administrator, various craftsmen and servants, and varying numbers of drums, trumpets, carriages, and horses.
The office of Grand General of the Central Army was abolished,
and the office of Central Inspector of the Northern Army was established.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Liú Jiǎn of Dōnghǎi, for his utmost integrity,
was appointed Gentleman.
Yáng Hù, Grand General of the Central Army, was appointed Left Grandee Secretary;
Zhòu, Prince of Dōngguǎn, was appointed Right Grandee Secretary.
In the third month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Empress Dowager Wáng died.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Wùxū,
Wáng Xiáng, Grand Mentor and Duke of Suīlíng, passed away.
On the day Jǐhài,
Empress Wénmíng Wáng was interred with him at Chóngyáng Mausoleum.
The offices of Commander of Zhenwēi and Commander of Yángwēi were abolished,
and the Left and Right Grand Generals of Accumulating Crossbows were established.
In the sixth month, on the first day, Bǐngshēn,
an imperial edict stated:
"Commandery Administrators and Chancellors of Principalities
shall conduct a tour of inspection of their subordinate counties once every three years,
always in spring.
This is how the ancients reported on their duties, proclaimed moral influence, and demonstrated righteousness.
They shall visit the chief officials,
observe local customs,
harmonize rites and laws,
examine weights and measures,
inquire after the aged,
and personally see centenarians.
They shall record prisoners,
redress injustices,
thoroughly investigate the successes and failures of governance and punishments,
and learn what the people suffer from.
Regardless of distance,
it should be as if I personally preside over it.
They shall earnestly explain the Five Teachings,
encourage diligence in agricultural work,
and urge scholars
to diligently study the orthodox classics,
not to engage in the trivialities of the Hundred Schools,
which lead inevitably to error.
If there are scholars or commoners who are fond of learning and devoted to the Way,
filial and fraternal, loyal and trustworthy,
pure and upright in extraordinary conduct,
they shall be promoted.
If there are those who are unfilial and disrespectful to their parents,
not reverent towards their elders in the clan,
who violate rites and abandon norms,
or who do not abide by laws and decrees,
they shall be prosecuted and punished.
If fields are cultivated,
livelihoods are improved,
ritual education is established,
and prohibitions are enforced,
then this is the ability of the chief officials.
If people are impoverished,
agricultural work is neglected,
banditry arises,
judicial cases are numerous,
inferiors disrespect superiors,
and rites and righteousness do not flourish,
then this is the incompetence of the chief officials.
Furthermore, if chief officials are upright and honest in office,
their thoughts not extending to private matters,
firm in integrity and unadorned by reputation;
as well as those whose conduct is corrupt and defiled,
who fawn and flatter to seek favor,
whose public integrity is not upheld,
but whose private wealth grows daily—
both types shall be carefully observed.
To commend the pure and condemn the corrupt,
to promote the good and censure transgressions—
this is how I, by sitting with folded hands, manage the overall principles
and hold capable officials of two thousand *dàns* salary accountable.
Alas, be warned!"
In autumn, the seventh month,
a rockslide occurred on Mount Tài,
and all the stars flowed westward.
On the day Wùwǔ,
an envoy, Hóu Shǐguāng, was dispatched to tour the empire.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
a visit was made to Chóngyáng Mausoleum.
In the ninth month,
the four prefectures of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù experienced great floods;
the Yī and Luò Rivers overflowed,
merging with the Yellow River.
Granaries were opened to provide relief.
An imperial edict stated:
"Although an edict may express a desire,
if upon submission it is deemed acceptable but inconvenient for the matter,
the true situation must not be concealed."
In winter, the tenth month,
Shī Jì, a general of Wú, entered Jiāngxià;
Wàn Yù raided Xiāngyáng.
Wàng, Prince of Yìyáng and Grand Commandant, was sent to garrison Lóngpí.
Hú Liè, Inspector of Jīng Province, defeated Yù.
Gù Róng, a general of Wú, raided Yùlín;
Máo Jiǒng, the Administrator, severely defeated him,
beheading Liú Jùn, Inspector of Jiāozhōu, and General Xiū Zé.
In the eleventh month,
Dīng Fèng and other Wú generals advanced to Sháopí;
Jùn, Prince of Rǔyīn and General of Protecting the East, along with Wàng, Prince of Yìyáng, attacked and repulsed them.
On the day Jǐwèi,
an edict was issued to princes, dukes, ministers, administrators, and commandery and principality chancellors
to recommend virtuous, upright, and outspoken gentlemen.
In the twelfth month,
five imperial decrees were promulgated to the commanderies and principalities: one was to rectify oneself,
two was to be diligent for the people,
three was to comfort the orphaned and widowed,
four was to emphasize fundamentals and curb excesses,
and five was to eliminate private favors.
On the day Gēngyín,
the Emperor personally oversaw trials at the Tīngsòng Observation Tower,
recorded prisoners from the Grand Judge's jail in Luòyáng,
and personally resolved their cases.
Fúnán and Línyì each sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the fifth year, spring, the first month, on the day Guǐsì,
decrees were reaffirmed for commandery and principality record keepers, administrators, magistrates, and chiefs,
urging them to fully utilize land resources and
prohibiting itinerant merchants and traders.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor personally oversaw trials at the Tīngsòng Observation Tower and recorded prisoners,
pardoning and releasing many.
Two azure dragons appeared in Xíngyáng.
In the second month,
Qínzhōu was established from the five commanderies of Lǒngyòu in Yōngzhōu, Jīnchéng in Liángzhōu, and Yīnpíng in Liángzhōu.
〔一一〕On the *xīnsì* day,
two white dragons were seen in Zhàoguó.
There were floods in Qīng, Xú, and Yǎn three prefectures,
and envoys were dispatched to provide relief.
On the *rényín* day,
Yáng Hù, Grand Master of Remonstrance and Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu.
Wèi Guàn, General Who Attacks the East, was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu.
Zhōu, Prince of Dōngguǎn, was appointed General Who Guards the East and Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Xúzhōu.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, the competence of all officials was recorded annually,
and after three years, rewards and punishments were administered.
However, the clerks, both past and present,
have only been dismissed if incompetent or inferior,
but there has been no encouragement or promotion,
which is not what is meant by 'evaluating and promoting or demoting.'
Therefore, select those who are diligent, capable, and notably outstanding,
making this an annual practice.
I will then consider their merits.”
On the *jǐwèi* day,
〔一二〕an imperial edict decreed that Zhūgě Jīng, grandson of the Shu chancellor Zhūgě Liàng, should be appointed to office according to his talent.
In summer, fourth month,
there was an earthquake.
On the *xīnmǎo* day, the first day of the fifth month,
a phoenix was seen in Zhàoguó.
A partial amnesty was granted to those sentenced to five years of punishment in Jiāozhǐ, Jiǔzhēn, and Rìnán.
In the sixth month,
Guō Yì, the supervisor of the Xīguān in Yè, submitted a memorial advising on five matters,
his words being very earnest and direct.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Túnliú.
Qū Lùfá from Xīpíng beat the Dengwen Drum,
and his words contained many ominous slanders.
The officials proposed that he be executed in the marketplace.
The Emperor said:
“This is my fault.”
He pardoned him and did not question him.
The office of General Who Guards the Army was abolished,
and the offices of Left and Right Generals were reinstated.
In autumn, seventh month,
the Emperor summoned the grandees
to seek honest advice.
In the ninth month,
a comet appeared in the Purple Palace constellation.
In winter, on the *bǐngzǐ* day of the tenth month,
Wáng Hóng, Administrator of Jí郡, was granted a thousand *hú* of grain for his administrative achievements.
In the eleventh month,
the Emperor's younger brother Zhào was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title of Āi Prince of Chéngyáng.
The Emperor's son Jǐngdù succeeded him.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict ordered prefectures and commanderies to recommend talented individuals who were brave, fierce, and outstanding.
In the spring of the sixth year, on the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the first month,
the Emperor attended court in person,
without music.
Dīng Fèng, a general of Wú, entered Wōkǒu,
but Qiān Hóng, Inspector of Yángzhōu, attacked and drove him away.
In the third month,
an amnesty was granted to those sentenced to five years of punishment and below.
In summer, fourth month,
two white dragons were seen in Dōngguǎn.
In the fifth month,
Chéng, Marquis of Shòu'ān Tíng, was established as Prince of Nángōng.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the sixth month,
Hú Liè, Inspector of Qínzhōu, attacked rebellious barbarians at Wànhúdū,
fought bravely,
and died.
An imperial edict dispatched Shí Jiàn, a State Affairs Department Secretary, to act as General Who Pacifies the West and Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Qínzhōu,
to suppress them together with Tián Zhāng, Protector of the Army Who Displays Might.
In autumn, on the *dīngyǒu* day of the seventh month,
