and Qīn Dàn raided externally.
Although their secret plots were intricate,
they were bound to be detected at the critical moment;
the Huáipǔ region was disturbed twice,
yet
Xǔ and Luò were not shaken: all heterodox schemes were suppressed,
and the former achievements were thus consolidated.
Thereafter, he entrusted Zhōng and Dèng with command,
and marched swiftly into Yōng and Shǔ.
The three passes were swept away like lightning,
and Liú Chán submitted as a vassal.
The
celestial mandate and human affairs
were thus confirmed.
Initially, he was granted extraordinary rituals,
and ultimately received comprehensive gifts.
As for Emperor Shìzǔ,
he eventually enjoyed imperial supremacy.
He was benevolent and generous to his subordinates,
frugal and sufficient in his expenditures;
harmonious but not lax,
lenient yet decisive.
Thus, the people sang of renewal,
and the four seas rejoiced and were encouraged.
He earnestly pursued the aspirations of his ancestors,
and considered the suffering
of the warring states period.
His close advisors disagreed,
and the high officials held differing opinions,
yet he alone adopted Yáng Hù's strategy,
and relied on the decisions of Wáng and Dù.
The campaign took no more than two seasons,
and Jiāng and Xiāng were united.
He covered
the ancient territory of Táng and Yú,
and proclaimed the correct calendar to the eight wildernesses.
Throughout the realm, writing was standardized,
and carriage tracks were uniform.
Cattle and horses covered the fields,
and surplus grain was piled high in the furrows.
Therefore, at that time there was
a saying,
"There are no poor people
under heaven."
Although universal peace was not yet fully achieved,
it was sufficient to demonstrate that officials upheld the law,
and the people enjoyed their lives.
After Emperor Wǔ passed away,
and his mausoleum was not yet dry,
Yáng Jùn was executed,
and the Empress Dowager was deposed.
Soon after, due to the rebellion of the two Dukes and the Prince of Chǔ,
the imperial princes had no protective
assistance,
and the grand tutors and chief ministers had no revered status to command general respect.
It even came to changing the Son of Heaven to the title of Tàishàng,
and there were rumors of dismissals from office.
The people saw no virtue,
hearing
only of chaos.
In the morning they were like Yī and Zhōu,
in the evening they became Jié and Zhí.
Good and evil were trapped by success and failure,
and praise and blame were swayed by worldly gain.
Internal and external affairs were in confusion,
officials lacked talent,
names and realities were
reversed,
and the imperial order was unraveled.
State power shifted repeatedly among unruly individuals,
and the forbidden troops were dispersed to the four quarters.
The regional governors had no steadying influence,
and the passes had no strategic defenses.
Indeed!
Why is it that Lǐ Chén and Shí Bīng devastated Jīng and Yáng,
Yuán Hǎi and Wáng Mí troubled Qīng and Jì,
the Róng and Jié claimed imperial authority,
and the two emperors lost their dignity?
What is the reason?
It is because the establishment
of power was flawed,
trust was given to the untalented,
the four cardinal virtues were not upheld,
and opportunistic governance was rampant.
If laws are made in times of order,
their flaws can still lead to chaos;
if laws are made in times of chaos,
who can save the situation!
That Yuán Hǎi
was merely a commanding officer from Líshí;
and Wáng Mí
was
a mere demoted official from Qīngzhōu.
They were all men of the bow and horse,
mere drifters,
not possessing the abilities of the former lord of Wú or Zhūgé Kǒngmíng;
they were newly risen
bandits,
a disorganized rabble,
no match for the states of Wú or Shǔ;
they dropped their plows to become soldiers,
tore their clothes to make banners,
not wielding the weapons of the Warring States;
they rose from below to rebel against above,
not possessing the power
of neighboring states.
Yet, they disturbed the empire as if driving a flock of sheep,
captured the two capitals as if picking up lost trifles,
and generals, ministers, kings, and nobles were executed en masse,
while empresses, consorts, and princesses were captured
and humiliated by common soldiers.
Is this not lamentable!
The empire [tiānxià]
is a great vessel;
the common people [qúnshēng]
are precious livestock.
Love and hate contend,
benefit and harm struggle,
this is the constant state of affairs.
It is like water accumulating at a dam,
or fire burning in a field;
it never ceases for a moment.
A great vessel [qì]
cannot be governed by petty means;
a heavy force [shì]
cannot be disturbed by contention.
The ancient sage kings knew this to be true,
therefore they guarded against great troubles
and repelled great disasters.
The common people all knew that the highest virtue [shàngdé] gave them life,
and did not attribute it to having been drained [jùn]
to give life.
Therefore, they were moved and responded,
pleased and submitted to it,
like the morning wind gathering in the northern woods,
or dragons and fish seeking out marshes.
Only then did they establish rites and regulations to govern
them,
and punishments to awe them,
carefully displayed what was liked and disliked to them,
clearly explained fortune and misfortune to them,
sought out the perceptive and appointed them to office,
and honored kindness and love to secure them.
Therefore,
the multitude knew their direction,
all delighted in their lives and grieved at their deaths,
pleased with their teachings and at peace with their customs;
gentlemen diligently observed rites,
and commoners exerted their utmost effort.
Integrity and shame were firmly established in every household and village,
and wickedness and perversity vanished from their hearts.
Thus, their people would face danger and give their lives,
rather than seek life at the expense of righteousness;
how much less would they raise their arms and shout,
gathering to violate
discipline and cause rebellion!
When the foundation is broad, it is difficult to overturn;
when the roots are deep, it is difficult to pull up;
when principles are ordered, there is no chaos;
when things are firmly bound, they do not shift.
This is why those who possessed the empire in the past
endured for a long time.
How could there be no perverse rulers?
It was by relying on morality, virtue, and established laws that they were maintained.
When the Zhōu dynasty arose,
Hòujì was born to Jiāngyuán,
and Heaven's mandate was clearly manifest.
The achievements of Wén and Wǔ originated from Hòujì.
By the time of Gōngliú,
he encountered the chaos of the Xià people,
[四九] and left Tái for Bīn,
personally enduring hardships.
By the time of Tàiwáng,
he was pressured by the Róng and Dí,
but could not bear to endanger the lives of his people,
so he took his staff and departed
from them.
Thus, people followed him as if going to market;
in one year, a town was formed;
in two years, a capital was established;
in three years, the population was five times its original.
By the time of Wángjì,
he could spread his virtuous reputation;
by
the time of Wénwáng,
he renewed Heaven's mandate.
From this perspective,
the Zhōu house accumulated loyalty and magnanimity for generations,
its benevolence extended to plants and trees,
internally it prospered its nine ancestral clans,
externally it respected and served the aged and virtuous,
thereby
achieving its blessings and prosperity.
And its empresses personally practiced the four virtues,
respected their teachers,
wore washed and simple clothes,
and undertook troublesome and humble tasks,
transforming the empire to perfect
the way of women.
Therefore, the women by the Hàn River
maintained a pure and white resolve,
and the gentlemen in the woods
possessed a pure and unified virtue,
starting with worry and diligence,
and ending in ease and joy.
With
the wisdom of the three sages,
they attacked the tyrannical Zhòu,
yet they still rectified their moral teachings,
saying: "Taken by rebellion, maintained by righteousness."
When Zhōugōng encountered difficulties,
he displayed how the civilizing influence of Hòujì and the former dukes
led to
the arduousness of establishing the royal enterprise;
these were all matters of clothing and food for farmers and women artisans.
Therefore, from the time Hòujì first established the foundation to bring peace to the people,
it was fifteen kings later that Wénwáng
first pacified it,
sixteen kings later that Wǔwáng first brought it to rest,
and eighteen kings later that Kāngwáng finally secured it.
Thus, their establishment of foundations and roots,
ordering of rites and customs,
regulation of human
emotions,
and compassion for the people's affairs,
was intertwined and meticulous to such an extent.
Now, the rise of Jìn
had merits surpassing a hundred kings,
and achievements swifter than the Three Dynasties.
Xuānwáng and Jǐngwáng encountered a time of great difficulties,
and eliminated junior branches of the family to facilitate matters,
not having time to cultivate
the benevolence of Gōngliú and Tàiwáng.
Receiving a will to assist in governance,
they repeatedly encountered depositions and enthronements.
Thus, Qíwáng was not enlightened,
and could not meditate on virtue at Bó;
Gāoguì Chōngrén,
could not
restore his bright lord.
The two ancestors were pressed by the time of abdication and succession,
not having leisure to await the gathering of eight hundred feudal lords for three parts.
This was how their establishment of foundations and roots
differed from earlier dynasties.
Furthermore,
the court lacked men of pure virtue,
the countryside lacked elders of unwavering loyalty,
customs were licentious and perverse,
and the sense of shame and honor had been lost.
Scholars took Lǎo and Zhuāng as their masters and rejected the Six
Classics;
debaters considered empty and unrestrained talk as eloquent and disdained moral strictures;
those who conducted themselves in society considered indulgence and impurity as open-mindedness and scorned integrity and trustworthiness;
those who entered officialdom considered opportunistic gain as noble and disdained
righteous conduct;
and those in office considered empty talk as superior and laughed at diligence and conscientiousness.
Therefore, when Liú Sòng repeatedly spoke of governance,
and Fù Xián constantly corrected the right and wrong,
they were all called vulgar officials;
while those who relied on emptiness and detachment,
and blindly conformed without conviction, were all famous throughout the land.
As for Wénwáng, who was too busy to eat even at dusk,
or Zhòngshānfǔ, who was diligent day and night without slack,
they were probably
all ridiculed and dismissed as mere dust.
Consequently, praise and blame were confused regarding the reality of good and evil,
and evil desires ran rampant on the path of greed.
Selectors chose officials for others,
and officials
Those who seek benefit for themselves,
while the officials who hold power
simultaneously hold dozens of posts.
The great ones have their highest honors,
the minor ones record their essentials.
And the sons
and younger brothers of aristocratic clans and imperial relatives
surpass and excel,
not constrained by seniority.
Throughout the vast world,
everyone is an official scrambling for power,
thousands of officials,
with no act of yielding to the worthy.
Zǐzhēn's (子真) writings advocated
yielding but no one heeded them;
Zǐyǎ (子雅) established the nine ranks but they were not adopted.
As for the women,
their dressing, combing, weaving, and spinning were all completed by maids and servants.
They never knew the work of female crafts, silk
and hemp industries,
nor the matters of domestic cooking and food.
They married early,
and acted on their impulses.
Therefore, they were not ashamed of the faults of promiscuity,
nor restrained by the evils of jealousy.
Fathers and elder brothers did not punish them,
and the world did not condemn them.
How then can one demand that they learn the four teachings of antiquity,
and cultivate chastity and obedience in the present,
to assist gentlemen
indeed!
Ritual, law, punishment, and government were greatly corrupted at this time,
like water accumulating and breaking its dikes,
like fire being stoked and separated from its fuel.
When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first collapse.
Is this not what it refers to?
Therefore, observing Rǔan Jí's (阮籍) conduct,
one realizes the origin of the collapse and decline of ritual and teaching.
Examining the dispute between Yǔ Chún (庾純) and Jiǎ Chōng (賈充),
one sees the many perversions of the imperial mentors;
investigating
the achievements of conquering Wú (吳),
one knows the lack of humility among generals and commanders;
reflecting on Guō Qīn's (郭欽) strategy,
one realizes the Róng Dí (戎狄) had opportunities;
reading Fù Xuán (傅玄) and Liú Yì's (劉毅) words,
one understands the wickedness of the hundred officials;
analyzing Fù Xián's (傅咸) memorials and the "Discourse on the God of Money,"
one perceives the prominence of favoritism and bribery.
With such popular customs and national power,
even if a ruler of mediocre talent
who upholds tradition
were to govern,
Xīn Yǒu (辛有) would surely foresee it in the sacrifices,
Jì Zhá (季札) would surely detect it in the music,
Fàn Xiè (范燮) would surely ask to die for it,
and Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) would surely weep bitterly for it.
How much more so when our Huì Dì (惠帝) presided over it with a dissolute character!
Huái Dì (懷帝) ascended the throne amid chaos,
constrained by powerful ministers.
Mǐn Dì (愍帝), after fleeing,
was merely given an empty
title.
The governance of the realm had already departed,
and without a heroic talent born for the age,
it could not be recovered!
As the legacy of Chún Yào (淳耀) had not yet faded,
the great mandate once again settled upon Zhōng Zōng Yuán
Huángdì (中宗元皇帝).
Eulogy: Huái Dì (懷帝) held the jade seal,
Mǐn Dì (愍帝) resided in the yellow house.
The great tortoise fell from the three mountains,
the whale swallowed the nine regions.
The Xūn (獯) entered Jīnshāng (金商),
the Xióngnú (穹) resided in Wèiyāng (未央).
Round-headed people all fell,
square-footed ones all stumbled.
Officials turned their backs,
moving us to Píngyáng (平陽).
The lord worried, his subjects wept;
how could it not be bad!
Collation notes
Imperial Annals Chapter 6, Yuán Dì (元帝)
Yuán Huángdì's (元皇帝) given name was Ruì (睿),
courtesy name Jǐngwén (景文).
He was the great-grandson of Xuān Dì (宣帝)
and the son of Lángxié Gōng Wáng Jìn (琅邪恭王覲).
He was born in Luòyáng (洛陽) in the second year of Xiánníng (咸寧).
There was a divine light anomaly;
the whole room was illuminated,
and the mat he lay on was as if freshly cut.
When he grew up,
white hairs grew on the left side of his sun angle,
he had a high nose and a dragon face,
his eyes had a radiant brilliance,
and his gaze was dazzling.
At fifteen,
he succeeded to the title of Prince of Lángxié (琅邪王).
In his youth, he had a good reputation.
During the time of Huì Huáng (惠皇),
the imperial family had many troubles,
but the Emperor always remained respectful, frugal, humble, and yielding,
thus avoiding disaster.
He was deep and discerning with magnanimity,
not revealing any prominent deeds,
so people at the time did not recognize him.
Only Court Attendant Jī Shào (嵇紹) found him extraordinary,
and said to others:
"The Prince of Lángxié (琅邪王) has extraordinary bone structure;
he is probably not the physiognomy of a subject."
In the second year of Yuánkāng (元康),
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
He was successively promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍),
and followed in the punitive expedition against Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎).
During the defeat at Dàngyīn (蕩陰),
his uncle Dōng'ān Wáng Yáo (東安王繇) was killed by Yǐng (穎).
The Emperor feared disaster would strike him too
and intended to flee.
That night, the moon was bright,
but the imperial guard was strict,
and the Emperor had no way to leave,
being in great distress.
A moment later,
clouds and fog made it dark,
and a sudden thunderstorm arrived.
The guards all relaxed,
and he was able to slip out.
Yǐng (穎) had previously ordered all passes not to let noble persons out.
When the Emperor reached Héyáng (河陽),
he was stopped by the ferry officer.
His attendant Sòng Diǎn (宋典) arrived later,
and whipped the Emperor's horse with his riding crop, laughing:
"Innkeeper!
The officials forbid nobles,
are you also being detained?"
The officer then let them pass.
Upon reaching Luòyáng (洛陽),
he welcomed the Grand Consort and returned to his domain.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) gathered troops in Xiàpī (下邳),
he temporarily appointed the Emperor as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
Soon after, he was promoted to Píngdōng Jiāngjūn (平東將軍) and Supervisor of all military affairs in Xúzhōu (徐州),
stationed in Xiàpī (下邳).
Shortly after, he was transferred to Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) and Commander of all military affairs in Yángzhōu (揚州).
Yuè (越) went west to welcome the imperial carriage,
leaving the Emperor to guard the capital.
In the early years of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
following Wáng Dǎo's (王導) plan,
he first garrisoned Jiànyè (建鄴).
He appointed Gù Róng (顧榮) as Jūnsīmǎ (軍司馬),
Hè Xún (賀循) as Cānsǎ (參佐),
Wáng Dūn (王敦), Wáng Dǎo (王導), Zhōu Yí (周顗), and Diāo Xié (刁協) as his closest advisors and crucial aides.
He treated famous worthies with respect,
and inquired about local customs,
thus winning the hearts of the people of Jiāngdōng (江東).
When the Grand Consort died in his domain,
he personally requested leave to attend the funeral.
After the burial,
he returned to his post,
and was granted an additional 20,000 households in Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery,
and promoted to Zhèndōng Dà Jiāngjūn (鎮東大將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
He received Yuè's (越) command
to attack Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Zhōu Fù (征東將軍周馥),
and drove him away.
When Huái Dì (懷帝) was captured in Píngyáng (平陽),
Sīkōng Xún Pán (司空荀藩) and others issued a proclamation to the world,
nominating the Emperor as the alliance leader.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Huá Yì (江州刺史華軼) did not comply,
so Yuè (越) ordered Yùzhāng Nèishǐ Zhōu Guǎng (豫章內史周廣) and former Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wèi Zhǎn (江州刺史衞展) to attack and capture him.
When Mǐn Dì (愍帝) ascended the throne,
the Emperor was promoted to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng (左丞相).
After more than a year,
he was further promoted to Chéngxiàng (丞相) and Dà Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (大都督中外諸軍事).
He dispatched generals to pacify Jiāngdōng (江東),
executed the rebel Sūn Bì (孫弼) in Xuānchéng (宣城),
pacified Dù Tāo (杜弢) in Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
and by imperial authority, pardoned Jīngzhōu (荊州) and Yángzhōu (揚州).
When the Western Capital could not be defended,
the Emperor led his army, camping in the open,
personally donning armor,
issuing proclamations to the four directions,
mobilizing troops from throughout the realm,
and set a date for a punitive expedition.
At that time, a jade tablet was seen in Lín'ān (臨安),
and a white jade qílín (麒麟) divine seal was found in Jiāngníng (江寧),
with the inscription
"Longevity for ten thousand years."
The sun had double halos.
All considered these signs of a restoration.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ, in the second month of spring, on the xīn-sì day
Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Sòng Zhé arrived,
and proclaimed the edict of Xuānmǐn Dì, which said:
"Fortune has been adverse,
and the imperial order has faltered.
I, with my meager virtue,
received this great heritage,
but was unable to pray to Heaven for a long mandate,
or to restore the glorious revival.
This has led to the vicious Hú daring to lead their dog-like hordes,
and besiege the capital.
I am now confined in a remote city,
with ten thousand anxieties,
fearing an imminent collapse.
You are to proceed to the Prime Minister,
and fully convey my intentions,
to have him oversee all affairs of state,
to timely occupy the old capital,
to restore the imperial tombs and temples,
and thereby wipe away this great shame."
In the third month,
the Emperor, dressed in plain clothes, left his residence
and mourned for three days.
Xīyáng Wáng Róng and the various officials, aides, provincial governors, and local administrators petitioned for an imperial title.
The Emperor did not allow it.
Róng and the others insisted with their lives,
even repeatedly.
The Emperor sighed and shed tears, saying:
"I
am a sinner;
I only wish to uphold integrity and die for righteousness,
to wipe away the shame of the empire,
and perhaps atone for the punishment of the axe.
I was originally Lángxié Wáng.
Why do you, worthy gentlemen, keep pressuring me?"
He then called his private slave to prepare his carriage,
intending to return to his fief.
The officials then dared not press him,
and requested that he become Jìn Wáng according to the precedents of Wèi and Jìn.
He assented.
On the xīn-mǎo day,
he assumed the title of Wáng,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
Those who killed their grandparents or parents,
and those who killed Liú Cōng or Shí Lè,
were not exempt from this order.
All Assistant Military Administrators were appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi,
and Secretaries Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Over a hundred secretaries were appointed,
and people at the time called them
"The Hundred and Six Secretaries."
Then all government offices were established,
and ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain were erected in Jiànkāng.
At that time, signs of auspiciousness were reported from all directions,
to which the Emperor said:
"I bear the responsibility of the four seas,
but have not yet been able to reflect.
What auspicious omens can there be?"
On the bǐng-chén day,
he established his heir Shào as Jìn Wáng Tàizǐ.
He appointed Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Xīyáng Wáng Róng, as Tàibǎo;
Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, Hàn'ān Hóu Wáng Dūn, as Dàjiāngjūn;
Yòujiāngjūn Wáng Dǎo as Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnjì, Piàojì Jiāngjūn;

His son, Xuānchéng Gōng Póu, was enfeoffed as Lángxié Wáng.
In the sixth month, on the bǐng-yín day,
Sīkōng, Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ, Guǎngwǔ Hóu Liú Kūn;

Chányú, Guǎngníng Gōng Duàn Chén;

saying: "Your subjects have heard that Heaven gives birth to the myriad people,

Yú,

Since Yuánkāng,

barbarians.

Auspicious signs

Internally,

All ministers will be timely in their duties at the top,

In the past, when Shàokāng (少康) flourished,

How much more so now, when your great merits reach to August Heaven,

Furthermore, among the descendants of Xuānhuáng (宣皇),

The

and all will be
exceedingly fortunate.
Your ministers have heard that an honorable position cannot be left vacant for long,
and the myriad affairs of state cannot be neglected for long.
If it is vacant for one day,
then the honorable position is endangered;
if it is neglected for a full cycle,

chaos.
Currently, we are at the end of the hundred kings,
at a time of great misfortune.
Cunning enemies lurk and spy,

The common people are adrift and scattered,
with nowhere to anchor their hearts.
How can this be neglected
and left unaddressed?
Although Your Majesty wishes to hesitate,
what about the ancestral temple?
What about the common people?
In the past, when Huìgōng (惠公) was captured by Qín (秦),
the state of Jìn (晉) was shaken.
Lǚ (呂) and Xì (郤) conspired
to establish Zǐ Yǔ (子圉),

Therefore, it was said:
"If the lord is lost but there is a new lord,

Not forgetting past events
is a great guide for later generations.
Your Majesty's wisdom rivals the sun and moon,

Deep strategies and far-reaching
plans
originate from your own mind.
Unable to bear the feelings of a dog or horse worrying for the state,

we hereby present our sincerity
and lay it before the officials.
We, your ministers,
have been unworthy of our positions
and have long been in distant lands,
unable to attend the court
and witness the grand ceremony.
Our feelings of joyful anticipation,
looking south, are boundless.
The Emperor graciously ordered a reply,
the text of which is in Kūn (琨)'s biography.
Shí Lè's (石勒) general Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) besieged Qiáochéng (譙城).
General of the Pacified West, Zǔ Tì (祖逖), attacked and repelled him.
On the day Jǐsì (己巳),
the Emperor issued a proclamation throughout the realm, saying:
"The rebel Shí Lè (石勒)
has ravaged Héshuò (河朔) with cruelty,
escaping punishment for years,
wandering freely and unrestrained.
He has again dispatched his vicious faction, Shí Jìlóng (石季龍),
with his dog-and-sheep multitude,
to cross south of the Hé (河) and
spread his venomous poison.
General of the Pacified West, Zǔ Tì (祖逖), led his troops to attack,
and they immediately scattered.
Now We dispatch the General of Chariots and Cavalry, the Prince of Lángyá (琅邪) Póu (裒), and others of the nine armies,
three thousand elite soldiers,
by four routes, water and land,
directly to the rebels' camp,
under Zǔ Tì (祖逖)'s command.

shall be rewarded with three thousand bolts of silk,
fifty catties of gold,
enfeoffed as a county marquis,
with an income of two thousand households.
Furthermore, if a rebel faction member can take and deliver Shí Jìlóng (石季龍)'s head,
the enfeoffment and reward shall be the same."
In the seventh month,
Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary Zhū Sōng (朱嵩) and Department Affairs Administrator Gù Qiú (顧球) died.
The Emperor was grieved
and intended to observe mourning for them.
The relevant officials submitted a memorial,
stating that observing mourning for a former Department Affairs Administrator was not customary.
The Emperor said:
"In times of decline and chaos,
we particularly mourn for each other."
Thereupon, he observed mourning
and wept bitterly.
On the day Dīngwèi (丁未),
Prince of Liáng (梁) Kuī (悝) died.
Grand Commandant Xún Zǔ (荀組) was made Minister of Education.
The prohibitions on mountains and marshes were relaxed.
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),

and thus rebelled together with Dù Zēng (杜曾).
In the ninth month, on the day Wùyín (戊寅),
Wáng Dūn (王敦) sent the Administrator of Wǔchāng (武昌), Zhào Yòu (趙誘), the Administrator of Xiāngyáng (襄陽), Zhū Guǐ (朱軌), and the General of Língjiāng (陵江), Huáng Jùn (黃峻), to attack Dìwǔ Yī (第五猗).

and Zhào Yòu (趙誘) and the others all died.
Shí Lè (石勒) killed the Administrator of Jīngzhào (京兆), Huá Xǔ (華諝).
The Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州), Zhōu Fǎng (周訪), attacked Dù Zēng (杜曾),

In the tenth month, on the day Dīngwèi (丁未),
the Prince of Lángyá (琅邪) Póu (裒) died.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Rǔnán (汝南)'s son Bì (弼) was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīncài (新蔡).
On the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Minister of Works Liú Kūn (劉琨) was made Grand Commandant.
Historical officials were established,
and the Imperial Academy was founded.
That year,
Yángzhōu (揚州) suffered a severe drought.
In the first month of spring of the first year of Tàixīng (太興), on the day Wùshēn (戊申), the first day of the month,
the Emperor attended court,
but remained sorrowful and dispirited.
In the third month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
the news of Mǐndì's passing arrived.
The Emperor wore the deepest mourning and resided in a hut.
On the day Bǐngchén,
all the officials presented a respectful imperial title.
An edict stated:
"Though I am unworthy,
I have reached the extremity of an unlucky fate.
My duty as a subject is not yet established,
and my efforts to rectify and rescue have not yet been undertaken.
This is why, morning and night, I forget sleep and food.
Now, the ancestral temples are abandoned and severed,
and the myriad people have no anchorage.
The multitude of officials and regional administrators
have all urged me to undertake the great administration.
How dare I refuse?
I shall reverently follow their resolve."
On this day,
he ascended the imperial throne.
An imperial edict proclaimed:
"In the past, our Gāozǔ Xuānhuángdì, born in response to the opportune moment,
broadly established the imperial foundation.
Jǐnghuángdì and Wénhuángdì, generation after generation, shone with renewed brilliance,
bringing order and prosperity to all of Huáxià.
Down to Shìzǔ,
responding to Heaven and conforming to the times,
received this clear mandate.
His merits reached Heaven and Earth,
and his benevolence benefited the universe.
But the Vast Heaven did not sustain us,
sending down this extreme misfortune.
Huáidì's life was cut short,
and he was removed from the royal capital.
Heaven's calamities repeatedly struck,
and the late Emperor passed away,
leaving the altars of soil and grain without a lord.
Therefore, the multitude of lords, the Three Ministers, and the Six Officers,
after consulting the various administrators,
from the civilized to the barbarian,
have brought the great mandate to My person.
I, the sole person, fear the majesty of Heaven,
and therefore dare not defy it.
Thus, I ascended the altar on Nányuè,
received the end of the mandate from Wénzǔ,
burned firewood and distributed auspicious tokens,
and reported the sacrifice to Shàngdì.
But I am of meager virtue,
inheriting our grand enterprise,
like crossing a great river,
not knowing how to reach the other shore.
It is you, my trusted aides, my claws and teeth,
my civil and military officials, my 'bears and tigers,'
who can assist in bringing peace to the Jìn house,
and aid me, the sole person.
I wish to share with all nations
this common prosperity and joy."
Thereupon, a great amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
and civil and military officials were promoted by two ranks.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Wáng Tàizǐ Shào was established as the Crown Prince.
On the day Rénshēn,
an imperial edict proclaimed:
"In ancient times, those who governed
moved people by actions, not by words;
they responded to Heaven with substance, not with superficiality.
Therefore, when I am pure and calm, people rectify themselves.
Next, they listen to words and observe actions,
testing merits clearly.
Those whose administrative achievements are notable,
whose judgments in legal cases are fair,
so that people have no grievances or complaints,
and who improve with time;
as well as those who are weak in office,
who 'swallow the soft and spit out the hard,'
whose conduct is corrupt and defiled,
and who cultivate a reputation for the moment –
let each be reported by name.
Let those currently in office
look up to the achievements of their predecessors,
unite their hearts and exert their strength,
and deeply consider how to alleviate the burdens of the populace and ease their labor,
and benefit the hundred clans.
Do not neglect my command.
All distant and near ceremonial gifts
are to be entirely abolished."
In summer, the fourth month, on the first day Dīngchǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
Wáng Dūn was promoted to Grand General and Governor of Jiāngzhōu;
Piaojì Jiāngjūn Wáng Dǎo was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
On the day Wùyín,
the practice of 'summoning the soul' for burial was first prohibited.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
there was an earthquake in Xīpíng.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
Liú Kūn, who held the titles of Shǐchíjié, Shìzhōng, Dūdū, Tàiwèi, Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Guǎngwǔ Hóu, was killed by Duàn Pǐdī.
In the sixth month,
there was a drought.
The Emperor personally conducted the rain sacrifice.
The title Dānyáng Nèishǐ was changed to Dānyáng Yǐn.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Diāo Xié, Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng;
Xún Sōng, Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Qǔlíng Gōng, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
On the day Gēngyín,
Lǐ Jǔ, the Administrator of Xíngyáng, was appointed Dūdū Sīzhōu Zhū Jūnshì and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Wùxū,
the imperial prince Xī was enfeoffed as Wǔlíng Wáng.
The谏鼓 (admonition drum) and谤木 (slander-post) were first established.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Wùshēn,
an imperial edict proclaimed:
"The royal house has suffered many misfortunes,
the wicked and malicious have run rampant,
the imperial order has slackened and fallen,
overturning the great principles.
I, being unworthy,
have succeeded to the grand enterprise,
and day and night I worry and am anxious,
thinking of reforming these evils.
The 'two thousand piculs' (high officials) and the magistrates are to strictly adhere to the old laws,
rectify their conduct and clarify the laws,
suppress and regulate the powerful and overbearing,
and care for the orphaned and solitary.
They are to conceal and verify household registers,
and encourage and supervise agriculture and sericulture.
The provincial governors and inspectors are to mutually examine each other,
and must not let private interests compromise public duty.
If there are senior officials who are dedicated to public service but are not promoted,
or who are greedy and corrupt but secure themselves through wealth and power—
if any of these are not reported,
the reporter shall be guilty of knowingly letting evil go and concealing good.
If they exist but are unknown,
the reporter shall be held accountable for being ignorant and obstructive.
Let each clearly and carefully follow these instructions."
Liú Cōng died,
and his son Càn succeeded to the usurped throne.
In the eighth month,
Jì, Xú, and Qīng provinces suffered from locusts.
Jìn Zhǔn assassinated Liú Càn
and styled himself King of Hàn.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Guǐwèi,
Táo Kǎn, Governor of Guǎngzhōu, was promoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn.
Liú Yào usurped the imperial throne at Chìbì.
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
the sun appeared at night,
three zhàng high,
with red and blue solar ears within it.
Xīncài Wáng Bì died.
Dà Jiāngjūn Wáng Dūn was promoted to Governor of Jīngzhōu.
On the day Gēngshēn,
an imperial edict proclaimed:
"I, being of meager virtue,
have inherited the grand enterprise.
Above, I cannot harmonize yin and yang;
below, I cannot sustain and nourish the multitude of living beings.
Disasters and anomalies have repeatedly arisen,
and portents of misfortune continue to appear.
On Rénzǐ and Yǐmǎo,
there was thunder and torrential rain.
These are surely Heaven's calamities and warnings,
intended to manifest my lack of virtue.
Let all the dukes and ministers
each submit sealed memorials,
fully detailing gains and losses,
without any concealment.
I will personally examine them."
The Tīngsòng Guān (Audience Hall for Hearing Legal Cases) was newly constructed.
Sūn Fán, son of the late Guīmìng Hóu Sūn Hào, conspired to rebel
and was executed.
In the twelfth month,
Wáng Téng, Mǎ Zhōng, and other former generals of Liú Cōng executed Jìn Zhǔn
and sent the Imperial Seal of State to Liú Yào.
There was an earthquake in Wǔchāng.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Huàn, Xiǎnyì Tínghóu, was enfeoffed as Lángyá Wáng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Lángyá Wáng Huàn died.
On the day Guǐsì,
an imperial edict proclaimed:
"Hàn Gāo passed through Dàliáng
and praised the worthiness of Wú Jì;
the Qí army entered Lǔ
and repaired the tomb of Liǔxià Huì.
If there are any eminent and virtuous worthies of Wú who have not yet been honored or recorded,
let them be fully listed and reported."
The three commanderies east of the Jiāng River suffered from famine,
and envoys were dispatched to provide relief.
Zhōu Fǔ, Administrator of Péngchéng, killed Zhōu Mò, Administrator of Pèi, and rebelled.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Chóngyáng Líng was destroyed. The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and wept for three days;
he sent Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Liáng Kān, Shǒutàicháng Mǎ Guī, and others to repair the imperial tomb.
They attempted to welcome the imperial coffin from Píngyáng
but were unsuccessful and returned.
In the second month,
Xú Kān, Administrator of Tàishān, beheaded Zhōu Fǔ
and sent his head to the capital.
In the fourth month of summer,
Chén Chuān (陳川), General of the Soaring Dragon, rebelled at Jùnyí (浚儀),
and surrendered to Shí Lè (石勒).
Xú Kān (徐龕), Administrator of Tàishān (太山), rebelled with his commandery,
proclaimed himself Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
and attacked Jì (濟) and Dài (岱).
Chén Ān (陳安), Inspector of Qínzhōu (秦州), rebelled
and surrendered to Liú Yào (劉曜).
On the day guǐchǒu of the fifth month,
the Tàiyáng (太陽) Mausoleum was destroyed.
The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and wept for three days.
Xú (徐), Yáng (楊), and the various commanderies west of the Yangtze River suffered from locusts.
Wújùn (吳郡) experienced a great famine.
Zǔ Tì (祖逖), General Quelling the North, and Shí Jìlóng (石季龍), a general of Shí Lè, fought at Jùnyí,
and the imperial army was defeated.
On the day rénxū,
an edict stated:
"The empire is in distress,
exacerbated by disasters and famine.
The common people are in dire poverty,
and national resources are depleted.
In Wújùn, hundreds have died of starvation.
Heaven gives birth to the multitudes and establishes rulers over them,
selecting and appointing sagacious and wise individuals to assist them.
We should deeply reflect on how to remedy these ills.
In the past, Wú Qǐ (吳起), for King Dào (悼) of Chǔ (楚), clarified laws and regulations,
eliminated non-essential offices,
removed distant members of the imperial clan who were without merit,
thereby benefiting the generals and soldiers,
and the state became rich and its army strong.
How much more so in today's distress,
with the common people suffering and in poverty!
Therefore, non-urgent matters should be eliminated,
and anything not essential for the military should be cut."
On the day jiǎzǐ,
Zhōu Fǎng (周訪), Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州), fought Dù Zēng (杜曾) at Wǔdāng (武當),
beheaded him,
and captured Dìwǔ Yī (第五猗).
On the day bǐngzǐ of the sixth month,
Zhōu Fǎng was granted the title General Quelling the South.
The imperial bureaus and all commandery assistants were abolished,
and five Erudites were appointed.
On the day jǐhài,
Hè Xún (賀循), Grand Minister of Ceremonies, was granted the privilege of 'opening a mansion and holding office on par with the Three Excellencies.'
On the day yǐchǒu of the seventh month of autumn,
Hè Xún, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, passed away.
In the eighth month,
the Sùshèn (肅慎) offered kūshǐ (楛矢) arrows and stone arrowheads.
Xú Kān attacked Dōngguǎn (東莞).
Yáng Jiàn (羊鑒), Commander of the Crown Prince's Left Guard, was dispatched as acting General Quelling Barbarians,
to lead Cài Bào (蔡豹), Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州), to suppress him.
In the tenth month of winter,
Zǔ Tì (祖逖), General Quelling the North, sent Dūhù (督護) Chén Chāo (陳超) to raid Táo Bào (桃豹), a general of Shí Lè.
Chāo was defeated
and died in battle.
On the day wùyín of the eleventh month,
Shí Lè usurped the throne and declared himself king,
naming his state Zhào (趙).
On the day yǐhài of the twelfth month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
An edict commanded all officials to submit sealed memorials,
and to reduce various public services.
Mùróng Kuì (慕容廆) of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) attacked Liáodōng (遼東).
Cuī Bì (崔毖), Colonel Protector of the Eastern Barbarians and Inspector of Píngzhōu (平州), and Gāogōulí (高句驪) were besieged.
In this year,
Sūn Bǎo (孫保), Prince of Nányáng (南陽), proclaimed himself King of Jìn (晉) at Qíshān (祁山).
The three Wú (吳) commanderies suffered a great famine.
On the day dīngyǒu, the first day of the first month of spring in the third year,
King Bǎo of Jìn (晉) was besieged by Liú Yào (劉曜)
and relocated to Sāngchéng (桑城).
On the day xīnwèi of the second month,
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍), a general of Shí Lè, attacked Yàncì (猒次).
Shào Xù (邵續), General Quelling the North and Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州), attacked him.
Xù was defeated
and died in battle.
In the third month,
Mùróng Kuì sent three imperial seals of jade.
In the intercalary month,
Zhōu Yǐ (周顗), a Shangshū (尚書), was appointed Shangshū Púyè (尚書僕射).
On the day rénchén of the fourth month of summer,
a stray arrow (comet) streamed through the constellations Yì (翼) and Zhěn (軫).
On the day bǐngyín of the fifth month,
Quán (詮), the Crown Prince of Emperor Xiàohuái (孝懷), was murdered in Píngyáng (平陽).
The Emperor wept for three days.
On the day gēngyín,
there was an earthquake.
In this month,
King Bǎo (保) of Jìn was killed by his general Zhāng Chūn (張春).
Liú Yào sent Chén Ān (陳安) to attack Zhāng Chūn,
and destroyed him.
Ān then rebelled against Yào.
Xú Kān (徐龕), a general of Shí Lè, led his troops to surrender.
In the sixth month,
there were great floods.
On the day dīngyǒu,
bandits killed Zhāng Shí (張寔), General of the Western Palace, Colonel Protector of the Qiāng (羌), Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Xīpíng (西平).
Shí’s younger brother Mào (茂) succeeded him,
taking the titles General Quelling the West and Inspector of Liángzhōu.
On the day dīnghài of the seventh month of autumn,
an edict stated:
"My late father King Wǔ (武) and my late grandfather King Gōng (恭) governed Lángyá (琅邪) for over forty years,
bestowing favors upon the common people,
and leaving behind love that bound human hearts.
I, responding to the heavenly mandate,
established the foundation in the Jiangbiǎo (江表) region,
where the myriad people have settled their hearts
and come with their infants in swaddling clothes.
There are nearly a thousand households of Lángyá (琅邪) natives here.
They are now established as Huáidé (懷德) County,
subordinate to Dānyáng (丹楊) Commandery.
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Hàn made Pèi (沛) his 'bath and wash-up' fief,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) likewise restored Nándùn (南頓).
The regulations for their preferential treatment shall entirely follow the precedents of the Hàn (漢) dynasty."
Wèi Cè (衞策), a subordinate of Zǔ Tì (祖逖), heavily defeated a detached army of Shí Lè at the Biànshǔi (汴水).
Tì was granted the title General Quelling the West.
On the day wùwǔ of the eighth month,
Empress Yú (虞氏), the respected queen, was honored as Empress Jìng (敬).
On the day xīnyǒu,
the spirit tablets were moved to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the day xīnwèi,
Zhōu Fǎng (周訪), Inspector of Liángzhōu and General Quelling the South, passed away.
The Crown Prince performed the rite of Shìdiàn (釋奠) at the Imperial Academy.
Gān Zhuó (甘卓), Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘州), was appointed General Quelling the South and Inspector of Liángzhōu.
In the ninth month,
Xú Kān (徐龕) rebelled again
and surrendered to Shí Lè (石勒).
On the day bǐngchén of the tenth month of winter,
Cài Bào (蔡豹), Inspector of Xúzhōu, was executed for cowardice.
Wáng Dūn (王敦) killed Xiàng Shuò (向碩), Administrator of Wǔlíng (武陵).
In the second month of spring in the fourth year,
Xú Kān (徐龕) again led his troops to surrender.
Mòbō (末波) of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) offered the Emperor's imperial seals.
On the day gēngxū,
it was announced at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and then they were accepted.
On the day guǐhài,
there was a sun dog (sun fighting).
In the third month,
Erudites for the Zhōu Yì (周易), Yí Lǐ (儀禮), and Gōngyáng (公羊) were established.
On the day guǐyǒu,
Cáo Yì (曹嶷), General Quelling the East, was appointed General Pacifying the East.
On the day xīnhài of the fourth month of summer,
the Emperor personally inspected various prisons.
Shí Lè (石勒) attacked Yàncì (猒次)
and captured it.
Duàn Pǐdī (段匹磾), General Supporting the Army and Inspector of Yōuzhōu (幽州), was captured by Lè.
In the fifth month,
there was a drought.
On the day gēngshēn,
an edict stated:
"In the past, the two founders of Hàn and Wèi Wǔ (魏武) all exempted commoners [from slavery].
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
after the defeat in Liángzhōu (涼州), those who had become slaves were also restored to their household registers.
These are established precedents across generations.
Therefore, commoners from the central plains who suffered misfortune and became bondservants in the various commanderies of Yángzhōu (揚州) shall be exempted [from this status]
to be ready for conscription."
In the seventh month of autumn,
there were great floods.
On the day jiǎxū,

Dài Ruòsī (戴若思), a Shangshū, was appointed General Conquering the West, Governor-General of military affairs in the six provinces of Sī (司), Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), Bìng (并), Jì (冀), and Yōng (雍), and Inspector of Sīzhōu (司州),
stationed at Héféi (合肥).

Liú Wèi (劉隗), Administrator of Dānyáng (丹楊), was appointed General Quelling the North, Governor-General of military affairs in the four provinces of Qīng (青), Xú (徐), Yōu (幽), and Píng (平), and Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州),
stationed at Huáiīn (淮陰).
On the day rénwǔ,
Wáng Dǎo (王導), General of Agile Cavalry, was appointed Minister of Works.
In the eighth month,
Chángshān (常山) collapsed.
On the day rényín of the ninth month,
Zǔ Tì (祖逖), General Quelling the West and Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州), passed away.
On the day rénwǔ of the tenth month of winter,
Zǔ Yuē (祖約), Tì’s younger brother and a Gentleman-in-Waiting, was appointed General Quelling the West and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
In the twelfth month,
Mùróng Kuì (慕容廆) was appointed as an Imperial Envoy with credentials, Governor-General of military affairs for Yōu (幽) and Píng (平) provinces and the Eastern Barbarians, and Governor of Píngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Liáodōng (遼東) Commandery.
On the day yǐmǎo, the first month of spring in the first year of Yǒngchāng (永昌),
a general amnesty was proclaimed
and the era name was changed.
On the day wùchén,
Wáng Dūn (王敦), Grand General, raised an army at Wǔchāng (武昌),
using the pretext of executing Liú Wèi (劉隗).
Shěn Chōng (沈充), General of the Soaring Dragon, led his troops to respond.
In the third month,
Dài Ruòsī (戴若思), General Conquering the West, and Liú Wèi (劉隗), General Quelling the North, were recalled to defend the capital.
Wáng Dǎo (王導), Minister of Works, was appointed Grand Commander of the Vanguard.
Dài Ruòsī was appointed General of Agile Cavalry.
All commanderies in Dānyáng (丹楊) were granted military titles.
Zhōu Yǐ (周顗), Púyè (僕射), was granted the title Shangshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射).
Wáng Suì (王邃), Leading General, was appointed Shangshū Yòupúyè (尚書右僕射).
Zhōu Yán (周莚), Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard, was appointed acting General Champion of the Army,
to lead three thousand troops to suppress Shěn Chōng.
On the day jiǎwǔ,
Yù (昱), the Imperial Prince, was enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá (琅邪).
Liú Wèi’s army was at Jīnchéng (金城).
Zhōu Zhá (周札), Right General, defended Shítóu (石頭).
The Emperor personally donned armor and reviewed the six armies in the suburbs.
Táo Kǎn (陶侃), General Pacifying the South, was sent to take charge of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Gān Zhuó (甘卓), General Quelling the South, was sent to take charge of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
each to lead their respective forces to pursue Dūn from the rear.
In the fourth month,
Wáng Dūn's (王敦) vanguard attacked Shítóu (石頭).
Zhōu Zhá (周札) opened the city gates to respond to them.
Fènwēi Jiāngjūn (奮威將軍) Hóu Lǐ (侯禮) died.
Wáng Dūn occupied Shítóu.
Dài Ruòsī (戴若思) and Liú Wèi (劉隗) led their troops to attack him.
Wáng Dǎo (王導), Zhōu Yǐ (周顗), Guō Yì (郭逸), Yú Tán (虞潭) and others engaged in battle from three routes.
The six armies suffered a crushing defeat.
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Diāo Xié (刁協) fled to Jiāngchéng (江乘),
where he was killed by the rebels.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (鎮北將軍) Liú Wèi (劉隗) fled to Shí Lè (石勒).
The Emperor sent an envoy to Wáng Dūn, saying:
"If you do not forget the imperial court,
and cease hostilities here,
then the whole world can still enjoy peace together.
If not,
I shall return to Lángxié (琅邪)
to make way for your eminence."
On the *xīnwèi* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Wáng Dūn then appointed himself Chéngxiàng (丞相), Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn (都督中外諸軍), Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事),
and was enfeoffed as Wǔchāng Jùngōng (武昌郡公),
with ten thousand households.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) and Mòlíng Hóu (秣陵侯) Dài Ruòsī (戴若思),
and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射), Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍), and Wǔchéng Hóu (武城侯) Zhōu Yǐ (周顗) were killed by Wáng Dūn.
Wáng Dūn's general Shěn Chōng (沈充) captured Wúguó (吳國).
Wèi (魏) captured Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Wúguó Nèishǐ (吳國內史) Zhāng Mào (張茂)
and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (湘州刺史) Qíáo Wáng Chéng (譙王承) were both killed.
In the fifth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Wáng Dūn made Tàibǎo (太保) Xīyáng Wáng Ráng (西陽王羕) the Tàizǎi (太宰),
and added Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) to Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Dǎo (王導).
On the *yǐhài* day,
Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn (鎮南大將軍) Gān Zhuó (甘卓) was killed by Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu (襄陽太守) Zhōu Lǜ (周慮).
The Shu (蜀) rebel Zhāng Lóng (張龍) plundered Bādōng (巴東).
Jiànpíng Tàishǒu (建平太守) Liǔ Chún (柳純) attacked and drove him away.
Shí Lè (石勒) sent cavalry to plunder Hénán (河南).
Sixth month.
Drought.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Wáng Dūn himself appointed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) as Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍).
Shí Lè's (石勒) general Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) captured Tàishān (太山),
and seized the defending general Xú Kān (徐龕).
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) retreated from Zōushān (鄒山) to defend Héfēi (合肥).
Eighth month.
Wáng Dūn appointed his elder brother Hán (含) as Wèijiāngjūn (衞將軍),
and personally assumed the governorship of Níng (寧) and Yì (益) two *zhōu* as Dūdū (都督).
Lángxié Tàishǒu (琅邪太守) Sūn Mò (孫默) rebelled
and surrendered to Shí Lè (石勒).
In winter, the tenth month,
a great epidemic occurred,
killing two or three out of ten people.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Dūdū Jīng Liáng Èrzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (都督荊梁二州諸軍事), Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍), Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史), and Wǔlíng Hóu (武陵侯) Wáng Yì (王廙) passed away.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Xiàpí Nèishǐ (下邳內史) Wáng Suì (王邃) was appointed Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn (征北將軍) and Dūdū Qīng Xú Yōu Píng Sìzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (都督青徐幽平四州諸軍事),
stationed at Huái'yīn (淮陰).
Xīnchāng Tàishǒu (新昌太守) Liáng Shuò (梁碩) raised an army and rebelled.
A great fog enveloped the capital,
black air obscured the sky,
the sun and moon lost their light.
Shí Lè (石勒) captured Xiāngchéng (襄城) and Chéngfù (城父),
then besieged Qíáo (譙),
and defeated Zǔ Yuē's (祖約) detached force.
Zǔ Yuē (祖約) retreated to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Eleventh month.
Sītú (司徒) Xún Zǔ (荀組) was made Tàiwèi (太尉).
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
〔一一〕Tàiwèi (太尉) Xún Zǔ (荀組) died.
The office of Sītú (司徒) was abolished,
its duties merged with Chéngxiàng (丞相).
In the intercalary month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor passed away in the inner palace,
at the age of forty-seven.
He was buried at Jiànpíng Líng (建平陵),
with the temple name Zhōngzōng (中宗).
The Emperor was by nature simple and frugal, calm and pure.
He was receptive to frank advice,
and treated others with humility.
When he first took charge of Jiāngdōng (江東),
he often neglected affairs due to drink.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) strongly admonished him about it.
The Emperor ordered a drink to be poured,
raised the cup and overturned it,
and from then on, he abstained.
The officials once proposed that the wide hall of Tàijí Diàn (太極殿) be adorned with crimson curtains.
The Emperor said:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn (漢文) used a black sack for a curtain when reading memorials."
So he ordered blue cloth curtains to be used in winter,
and blue *shū* (綀) curtains in summer.
When he was about to enfeoff a noble lady,
the officials requested to buy sparrow hairpins.
The Emperor, deeming it an unnecessary expense, refused.
His favored lady, Fūrén Zhèng (鄭夫人), wore clothes without patterns or colors.
When his maternal cousin Wáng Yì (王廙) built a house for his mother exceeding the prescribed limits,
the Emperor wept and stopped him.
However, the Jìn (晉) dynasty encountered turmoil,
the imperial carriage was forced to wander,
yet Heaven's mandate remained unchanged,
and human efforts combined to assist.
Though the commander-in-chief often moved,
he did not leave the Jiāngjī (江畿) region.
His strategies were confined to a small area,
barely preserving Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚).
Ultimately, he suffered humiliation from those below and above,
dying of sorrow and indignation.
Although his virtues of humility and frugality were abundant,
his capacity for heroism and martial prowess was insufficient.
In the Qín (秦) dynasty, an observer of *wàngqì* (望氣) said
"Five hundred years later, Jīnlíng (金陵) will have the aura of an emperor."
Therefore, Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) traveled east to suppress it,
renaming the place Mòlíng (秣陵),
and cutting a trench in the northern mountains to sever its power.
When Sūn Quán (孫權) assumed his title,
he considered himself the one destined to fulfill it.
Sūn Shèng (孫盛) believed that from Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) to the Sūn (孫) family was four hundred and thirty-seven years,
and examining the calendar,
it was still not enough.
When Emperor Yuán (元) crossed the river,
it was five hundred and twenty-six years,
which truly corresponded to the rise of a true ruler.
In the early Xiánníng (咸寧) reign,
a wind blew and broke a tree in the Grand Altar of the Land (Tàishè),
and there was a green *qì* (氣) within the altar.
Diviners believed this was an auspicious sign of an emperor in Dōngguǎn (東莞).
Because of this, the King of Dōngguǎn (東莞王) was moved and enfeoffed in Lángxié (琅邪),
who was Emperor Wǔ (武).
When Wú (吳) fell,
Wáng Jùn (王濬) was indeed the first to reach Jiànyè (建鄴),
yet Hào (晧)'s surrender letter
sent the imperial seal far back to Lángxié (琅邪).
Heaven's will and human affairs
thus coincided with the omen of restoration.
During the Tàiaān (太安) period,
a children's rhyme went:
"Five horses float across the river,
one horse transforms into a dragon."
And in the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Suì (歲), Zhèn (鎮), Yínghuò (熒惑), and Tàibái (太白) gathered between Dǒu (斗) and Niú (牛) constellations.
Those who understood believed that a king would rise in the land of Wú (吳) and Yuè (越).
In that year,
the royal house collapsed,
and the Emperor, along with the five princes of Xīyáng (西陽), Rúnán (汝南), Nándùn (南頓), and Péngchéng (彭城), managed to cross the river.
And the Emperor indeed ascended to the great position.
Initially,
the Xuánshí Tú (玄石圖) had the phrase
"Niú (牛) succeeds the Mǎ (馬)."
Therefore, Xuāndì (宣帝) deeply feared the Niú (牛) clan,
and made two wine containers
with a shared mouth,
to hold wine.
The Emperor first drank the good one,
and poisoned his general Niú Jīn (牛金) with the toxic wine.
However, Gōng Wáng (恭王)'s consort, Xiàhóu Shì (夏侯氏), eventually had an affair with a petty official named Niú (牛), giving birth to Emperor Yuán (元),
which also matched the prophecy.
The Grand Scribe comments: The Jìn (晉) clan was unprepared.
From the middle reaches and beyond,
the Five Hú (五胡) seized the tripod of state.
The seven ancestral temples were overturned.
As overwhelming forces took the stage,
the people remembered their former virtues.
In ancient times, Guāngwǔ (光武) added his name with only a few commanderies;
Yuánhuáng (元皇) ascended to the supreme position with but a single province.
Could it be that Wǔxuān's (武宣) lingering influence still flourished in Lángyá (琅邪),
and Wénjǐng's (文景) extended benevolence spread its fragrance in Nándùn (南頓)?
This is what is meant by falling behind the opportune moment,
but being ahead in human affairs.
Chapters were rushed forth, titles presented,
and grand canopies formed shade.
Stars and constellations presented auspicious signs,
and Jīnlíng (金陵) announced its felicitations.
Táo Shìxíng (陶士行) commanded the armies of three provinces,
and the area outside Yǐng (郢) was secure.
Wáng Màohóng (王茂弘) made plans for partition,
and Jiāngdōng (江東) could be established.
Some, even before their tall banners were unfurled,
had their distant ambitions quelled.
Turning their heads towards the morning sun,
they looked up, hoping for the pillar of heaven.
Yet the emperor repeatedly declined,
refusing six times, and only accepting after the seventh refusal.
With simple cloth tents and linen curtains,
laws were meticulously examined and simplified,
upholding and promoting previous policies,
thus brightly initiating the restoration.
In ancient times, private households did not hoard weapons,
and great ministers did not wield power and authority.
This was the constant rule of the king,
to instruct his trusted officials.
Zhōngzōng (中宗) lost control of powerful ministers,
and voluntarily forfeited the imperial axe.
In the Two Capitals, the Hú (胡) and Jié (羯) tribes were seen facing each other amidst dust and wind.
Although there was no record of the sixth month's imperial tour,
the song of the wild geese echoed far.
Their reign was short-lived,
alas!
Emperor Míng (明帝)
Emperor Míng (明皇帝), personal name Shào (紹),
courtesy name Dàojī (道畿),
was the eldest son of Emperor Yuán (元皇帝).
He was intelligent and brilliant from a young age,
and thus favored and admired by Emperor Yuán.
When he was several years old,
he was once seated on his father's knee.
An envoy from Cháng'ān (長安) arrived,
and Emperor Yuán asked him:
"Which do you think is further, the sun or Cháng'ān?"
He replied:
"Cháng'ān is closer.
I have not heard of anyone coming from the sun,
so it is obvious."
Emperor Yuán was surprised by this.
The next day,
he hosted a banquet for his officials
and asked him again.
He replied:
"The sun is closer."
Emperor Yuán's expression changed,
and he said:
"Why is your answer different from yesterday's?"
He replied:
"When I look up, I see the sun,
but I do not see Cháng'ān."
From this, Emperor Yuán esteemed him even more.
At the beginning of Jiànxīng (建興) era,
he was appointed Eastern Middle Commander,
garrisoning Guǎnglín (廣陵).
When Emperor Yuán became King of Jìn (晉王),
he was made Crown Prince of Jìn (晉王太子).
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he was established as Crown Prince.
He was extremely filial by nature,
possessed both civil and military talents,
respected the virtuous, loved guests,
and had an elegant fondness for literature.
At that time, renowned ministers,
such as Wáng Dǎo (王導), Yǔ Liàng (庾亮), Wēn Jiào (溫嶠), Huán Yí (桓彝), and Ruǎn Fàng (阮放),
were all treated with intimacy and respect.
He once debated the meaning of a true versus a false sage,
and Wáng Dǎo and others were unable to refute him.
He also practiced martial arts
and was skilled at commanding soldiers.
At that time, the Eastern Court was bustling,
and people far and near placed their hopes in him.
During the rebellion of Wáng Dūn (王敦),
when the six armies were defeated,
the emperor wanted to lead his generals and soldiers to a decisive battle.
As he ascended his chariot, about to depart,
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠), his Middle Administrator, earnestly advised against it,
drew his sword, and cut the chariot's traces.
Only then did the emperor stop.
Wáng Dūn, knowing the emperor's divine martial prowess and brilliant strategy,
and that he was admired and trusted by both court and commoners,
wished to falsely accuse him of unfilial conduct and depose him.
He convened a grand meeting of officials and asked Wēn Jiào:
"By what virtue is the Crown Prince renowned?"
His voice and demeanor were stern,
determined to elicit a specific answer.
Wēn Jiào replied:
"To delve into the profound and reach the distant
is surely not something to be measured by shallow judgment.
Judging by ritual,
he can be called filial."
Everyone believed this to be true,
and Wáng Dūn's plan was thus thwarted.
On the *jǐchǒu* day of the intercalary month of Yǒngchāng (永昌) first year,
Emperor Yuán passed away.
On the *gēngyín* day,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne,
declared a general amnesty,
and honored his birth mother, Lady Xún (荀氏), as Lady of Jiàn'ān (建安郡君).
yellow fog filled all four quarters,
and the capital caught fire.
Lǐ Xióng (李雄) sent his generals Lǐ Xiāng (李驤) and Rèn Huí (任回) to raid Táidēng (臺登).
General Sīmǎ Jiǔ (司馬玖) died there.
Lǐ Zhāo (李釗), Administrator of Yuèsuí (越巂), and Wáng Zài (王載), Administrator of Hànjiā (漢嘉), rebelled with their commanderies
and surrendered to Lǐ Xiāng.
In the second month,
Emperor Yuán was buried in Jiànpíng (建平) Mausoleum.
The emperor walked barefoot to the mausoleum.
Huá Yì (華軼), an Intendant of the Imperial Household, was appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn, 驃騎將軍) and Supervisor of the Land and Water Forces of Shítou (石頭).
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
yellow fog filled all four quarters.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
frost fell.
On the *rénshēn* day,
frost fell again,
killing the crops.
In the third month, on the *wùyín* day, the first day of the month,
the reign title was changed.
The emperor attended court,
suspended banquets,
and eschewed music.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
frost fell,
killing vegetation.
Ráo'ān (饒安), Dōngguāng (東光), and Ānlíng (安陵) three counties suffered disaster,
with over seven thousand homes burned,
and fifteen thousand people killed.
Shí Lè (石勒) attacked and captured Xiàpī (下邳).
Biàn Dūn (卞敦), Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州), retreated to defend Xūyí (盱眙).
Wáng Dūn (王敦) offered one imperial seal.
Wáng Dūn was planning usurpation,
and subtly suggested to the imperial court that he be summoned.
The emperor then personally issued an edict to summon him.
In the fourth month of summer,
Wáng Dūn moved his troops to Hú (湖),
transferred Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Dǎo (王導) to Sītú (司徒),
and personally assumed the post of Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州牧).
Liǔ Chún (柳純), Supervisor of Bādōng (巴東), was harmed by Wáng Dūn.
Shàngshū (尚書) Chén Zhěn (陳眕) was appointed Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Yōu (幽) and Píng (平) Provinces, and Inspector of Yōuzhōu (幽州刺史).
In the fifth month,
the capital suffered a great flood.
Inspector Wáng Xùn (王遜) sent general Yáo Yuè (姚岳) to engage them in battle at Tángláng (堂狼),
where he inflicted a great defeat.
Liáng Shuò (梁碩) attacked and captured Jiāozhōu (交州).
Inspector Wáng Liàng (王諒) died there.
On the *rénzǐ* day of the sixth month,
Empress Yǔ (庾氏) was established.
General Who Pacifies the South, Táo Kǎn (陶侃), sent his aide Gāo Bǎo (高寶) to attack Liáng Shuò,
beheaded him,
and sent his head to the capital.

Táo Kǎn was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, 征南大將軍) and granted the privilege of establishing a general's office with the full honors of the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, 開府儀同三司).
On the *bǐngzǐ* day, the first day of the seventh month of autumn,
the pillars of the Tàijí (太極) Palace were struck by lightning.
In this month,
Liú Yào (劉曜) attacked Chén Ān (陳安) at Lǒngchéng (隴城)
and destroyed him.
In the eighth month,
General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn, 安北將軍) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng, 尚書令).
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍), general of Shí Lè (石勒), attacked and captured Qīngzhōu (青州).
Inspector Cáo Yì (曹嶷) was killed.
In the eleventh month of winter,

Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed his elder brother Wáng Hán (王含), General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, 征南大將軍), as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn, 征東大將軍) and Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Yángzhōu (揚州) west of the river.
Due to military and national famine,
he adjusted the rice rations for officials from Inspector downwards, each by a different amount.
In the first month, *dīngchǒu* day, of spring, second year,
the emperor attended court,
suspended banquets,
and eschewed music.
On the *gēngchén* day,
amnesty was granted to those sentenced to five years of imprisonment or less.
The sorcerer Lǐ Tuō (李脫) created subversive texts to mislead the public,
and was beheaded in the market of Jiànkāng (建康).
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍), general of Shí Lè (石勒), raided Yǎozhōu (兗州).
Liú Xiá (劉遐), Inspector of Yǎozhōu, retreated from Péngchéng (彭城) to defend Sìkǒu (泗口).
In the third month,
Kāng Píng (康平), general of Liú Yào (劉曜), raided Wèixīng (魏興)
and Nányáng (南陽).
In the fifth month of summer,
Wáng Dūn (王敦) forged an imperial edict, appointing his son Yìng (應) as Grand General of the Martial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn),
and his elder brother Hán (含) as Grand General of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn).
Gōngchéng Xióng (公乘雄) and Rǎn Zēng (冉曾), the imperial guards (chángcóng dū) whom the Emperor trusted and favored, were both killed by Dūn.
In the sixth month,
Dūn was about to raise an army and march toward the capital.
The Emperor secretly learned of this,
and so, riding a swift horse from Bādiān (巴滇), he traveled incognito,
reaching Hú (湖).
He secretly observed Dūn’s camp and then left.
A soldier suspected the Emperor was no ordinary person.
Furthermore, Dūn was taking a midday nap
and dreamt that the sun encircled his city.
He awoke with a start and said,
“This must be the yellow-bearded Xiānbēi (鮮卑) slave coming!”
The Emperor’s mother, Lady Xún (荀),
was from Yāndài (燕代).
The Emperor resembled his maternal relatives,
with yellow whiskers,
which is why Dūn called him that.
Thereupon, Dūn sent five horsemen to search for and pursue the Emperor.
The Emperor also galloped away,
and whenever his horse left dung,
he immediately poured water over it.
He saw an old woman selling food at an inn
and gave her a whip adorned with seven treasures,
saying,
“Later, when horsemen arrive,
you can show them this.”
Soon after, the pursuers arrived
and asked the old woman.
The old woman said,
“He has already gone far.”
She then showed them the whip.
The five horsemen passed it around, admiring it,
and delayed for a long time.
They also saw that the horse dung was cold,
concluding that he was indeed far away, and so they stopped the pursuit.
The Emperor barely escaped.
On the day of Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Grand Minister of Works Wáng Dǎo (王導) was granted the additional title of Grand Chief Controller (Dà Dūdū) and acting Commander with Imperial Insignia (Jiǎjié),
and concurrently held the post of Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ).
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠), Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn), was appointed General of the Central Bulwark (Zhōnglěi Jiāngjūn),
and with General of the Right Biàn Dūn (卞敦), he was to defend Shítóu (石頭).

Guānglù Xūn (光祿勳) Yìng Zhān (應詹) was appointed General of the Household Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn), acting Commander with Imperial Insignia, and Controller of Military Affairs South of Zhūquè Bridge (Zhūquèqiáo Nán Zhūjūnshì).
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) was appointed acting General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn) and Controller of all troops accompanying the Emperor (Cóngjià Zhūjūnshì).
Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監) Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) was appointed concurrently General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
Shàngshū (尚書) Biàn Hú (卞壼) was appointed acting General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn).
General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ) Wáng Suì (王邃),
General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ) Zǔ Yuē (祖約),
General of the Northern Central Army (Běizhōngláng Jiāng) and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ) Liú Xiá (劉遐),
General Who Displays Martial Prowess (Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of LínHuái (Línhuái Tàishǒu) Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
General Who Displays Awe (Fènwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu) Táo Zhān (陶瞻), and others were summoned back to guard the capital.
The Emperor stationed himself in the central hall.
On the first day of the seventh month of autumn, Rénshēn (壬申),
Dūn dispatched his elder brother Hán (含), along with Qián Fèng (錢鳳), Zhōu Fǔ (周撫), Dèng Yuè (鄧岳), and others, leading 50,000 troops by land and water,
to the southern bank.
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) moved his troops to the north side of the water
and burned the Zhūquè Pontoon Bridge (Zhūquèhéng)
to blunt their vanguard.
The Emperor personally led the six armies
and stationed them at Nán Huángtáng (南皇堂).
On the night of Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
he recruited brave warriors
and sent General Duàn Xiù (段秀), Central Army Staff Officer Cáo Hún (曹渾), Left Guard Adjutant Chén Sōng (陳嵩), Zhōng Yín (鍾寅), and others, a thousand armed soldiers, to cross the water
and attack them before they had finished deploying.
At dawn,
they fought at Yuèchéng (越城),
utterly defeating them
and beheading their vanguard general Hé Kāng (何康).
Wáng Dūn (王敦) died of indignation and vexation.
Former Grand Master of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng) Yú Tán (虞潭) raised an army of righteousness in Kuàijī (會稽).
Shěn Chōng (沈充) led over 10,000 men to join Hán (含) and others.
On the day of Gēngchén (庚辰),
they built a rampart at Língkǒu (陵口).
On the day of Dīnghài (丁亥),
Liú Xiá (劉遐), Sū Jùn (蘇峻), and others arrived with 10,000 elite soldiers.
The Emperor met them at night,
comforted them,
and bestowed different rewards upon the generals and soldiers.
Zhōu Jiǎn (周蹇) of Yìxīng (義興) killed Liú Fāng (劉芳), whom Dūn had appointed as Administrator.
General Who Pacifies the West Zǔ Yuē (祖約) drove Rèn Tái (任台), whom Dūn had appointed as Administrator of Huáinán (Huáinán Tàishǒu), from Shòuchūn (壽春).
On the day of Yǐwèi (乙未),
the bandit forces crossed the water.
General of the Household Guard Yìng Zhān (應詹) led General Who Establishes Awe (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) Zhào Yìn (趙胤) and others to resist them in battle,
but were unsuccessful.
The bandits reached Xuānyáng Gate (Xuānyángmén).
General of the Northern Central Army Liú Xiá (劉遐), Sū Jùn (蘇峻), and others launched a flanking attack from the Southern Dike (Nántáng),
utterly defeating them.
Liú Xiá (劉遐) also defeated Shěn Chōng (沈充) at Qīngxī (青溪).
On the day of Bǐngshēn (丙申),
the bandits burned their camp and fled during the night.
On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the Emperor returned to the palace
and granted a general amnesty,
pardoning no one except Dūn’s (敦) faction.
Thereupon, he dispatched various generals to pursue Dūn’s (敦) partisans
and completely pacified them.
Grand Minister of Works Wáng Dǎo (王導) was enfeoffed as Duke of Shǐxīng Commandery (Shǐxīng Jùngōng),
with an estate of 3,000 households,
and awarded 9,000 bolts of silk;
Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn) Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) as Duke of Jiànníng County (Jiànníng Xiàngōng);
Shàngshū (尚書) Biàn Hú (卞壼) as Duke of Jiànxīng County (Jiànxīng Xiàngōng);
Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監) Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) as Duke of Yǒngchāng County (Yǒngchāng Xiàngōng);
General of the Northern Central Army Liú Xiá (劉遐) as Duke of Quánlíng County (Quánlíng Xiàngōng);
General Who Displays Martial Prowess Sū Jùn (蘇峻) as Duke of Shàolíng County (Shàolíng Xiàngōng);
each with an estate of 1,800 households
and 5,400 bolts of silk;
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) as Marquis of Gāopíng County (Gāopíng Xiànhóu);
General of the Household Guard Yìng Zhān (應詹) as Marquis of Guānyáng County (Guānyáng Xiànhóu);
each with an estate of 1,600 households
and 4,800 bolts of silk;
General Who Establishes Awe Zhào Yìn (趙胤) as Marquis of Xiāngnán County (Xiāngnán Xiànhóu);
General of the Right Biàn Dūn (卞敦) as Marquis of Yìyáng County (Yìyáng Xiànhóu);
each with an estate of 1,600 households
and 3,200 bolts of silk.
Other enfeoffments and rewards varied according to rank.
In the tenth month of winter,
Grand Minister of Works Wáng Dǎo (王導) was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo) and concurrently Grand Minister of Works;
Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi) and Prince of Xīyáng (Xīyáng Wáng) Yáng (羕) was concurrently appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi);
Yìng Zhān (應詹) was appointed General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn), Controller of all military affairs of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Zhūjūnshì), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ);
Liú Xiá (劉遐) was appointed Overseer of military affairs north of the Huái River (Huáiběi Zhūjūnshì) and Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ);
Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) was appointed General of the Household Guard.
An imperial edict stated that Wáng Dūn’s (王敦) relatives and dependents would not be investigated.
At this time,
Shí Lè’s (石勒) general Shí Shēng (石生) was stationed in Luòyáng (洛陽).
Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ) Zǔ Yuē (祖約) retreated to defend Shòuyáng (壽陽).
On the day of Rénzǐ (壬子) in the twelfth month,
the Emperor paid respects at Jiànpíng Mausoleum (Jiànpínglíng),
observing the ritual for the second anniversary of a parent's death (dàxiáng zhī lǐ).
Administrator of Liángshuǐ (Liángshuǐ Tàishǒu) Cuàn Liàng (爨亮) and Administrator of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Tàishǒu) Lǐ Dì (李逷) rebelled in Xìnggǔ (興古)
and surrendered to Lǐ Xióng (李雄).
Shěn Chōng’s (沈充) former general Gù Yáng (顧颺) rebelled in Wǔkāng (武康),
attacking and burning cities and towns.
The prefectures and counties suppressed and executed him.
On the day of Wùchén (戊辰) in the second month of spring in the third year,
but women were exempted.
In the third month,
Inspector of Yōuzhōu (Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ) Duàn Mòbō (段末波) died.
His younger brother Yá (牙) succeeded him.
On the day of Wùchén (戊辰),
Imperial Prince Yǎn (衍) was established as Crown Prince,
a general amnesty was granted,
civil and military officials were promoted two ranks,
a grand feast was held for three days,
and the widowed, orphaned, and lonely were given silk,
two bolts per person.
On the day of Guǐsì (癸巳),
the reclusive scholars Rèn Xù (任旭) of Línhǎi (臨海) and Yú Xǐ (虞喜) of Kuàijī (會稽) were both summoned to serve as Erudites (Bóshì).
In the fourth month of summer,
an imperial edict stated:
“The great affair has just been settled,
and the mandate is renewed.
Let the Grand Preceptor, Grand Minister of Works, and those below them
gather at the capital to participate in discussions on governance,
and in all matters of reform and change,
endeavor to do what is best.”
Another imperial edict stated:
“Speak frankly,
and introduce upright and honest individuals.
I trust that all worthy officials understand this intention of mine.
If I err, you should assist me – this is how Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) conducted the relationship between ruler and minister.
Though I am humble and unenlightened,
I hope not to reject words that are harsh to the ear.
The responsibilities of Jì (稷) and Xiè (契),
you, my lords, now bear.
I hope we all strive together.”
On the day of Jǐhài (己亥),
there was a hailstorm.
Shí Lè’s (石勒) general Shí Liáng (石良) invaded Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Inspector Tán Yūn (檀贇) fought bravely
and died.
and Shí Lè (石勒) captured all the territories of Sī (司), Yǎn (兗), and Yù (豫) prefectures.
In the fifth month,

General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn) Táo Kǎn (陶侃) was appointed General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn), Controller of all military affairs of Jīng (荊), Xiāng (湘), Yōng (雍), and Liáng (梁) four prefectures, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Wáng Shū (王舒) was appointed General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn) and Controller of all military affairs of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Zhūjūnshì), and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the sixth month,
Shí Lè’s (石勒) general Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) attacked Liú Yào’s (劉曜) general Liú Yuè (劉岳) at Xīn’ān (新安)
and captured him.
Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ) Wáng Shū (王舒) was appointed Controller of all military affairs of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Zhūjūnshì) and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).

Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ) Liú Yǐ (劉顗) was appointed General of the Central Army Who Pacifies the Yuè (Píngyuè Zhōngláng Jiāng) and Controller of all military affairs of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Zhūjūnshì), and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ).
There was a great drought;
it had not rained since the first month
until this month.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Xīnwèi,
Xī Jiàn, President of the Department of State Affairs, was made General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Qīng and Yǎn Provinces, and granted the Imperial Mace.
He was stationed at Guǎnglíng.
Biàn Hú, General of the Palace Guard, was made President of the Department of State Affairs.
An imperial edict stated:
“The Three Reverent Guests and the Two Kings
have been held in high regard by generations;
to restore the fallen and continue the broken
is what the path of government prioritizes.
Furthermore, those sagely kings of the imperial clan who rendered meritorious service at the time of the Great Jìn’s reception of the Mandate,
founding officials who assisted in establishing the dynasty,
and eminent virtuous and renowned worthies
with whom the Three Ancestors jointly maintained the great enterprise,
all of whom established states, were granted land, and swore oaths to be as steadfast as mountains and rivers—
yet have all been abolished and cut off,
their ancestral sacrifices unperformed,
causes me deep sorrow.
The appropriate officials shall deliberate in detail on those who should have heirs established and report back.”
Another imperial edict stated:
“Sacrificing to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs
is a weighty matter for emperors.
Since the restoration,
only the southern suburban sacrifice has been performed;
the northern suburban sacrifice has never taken place,
and the rites of the four seasons and five suburbs are no longer observed at all.
The Five Sacred Mountains, Four Great Rivers, famous mountains, and great rivers recorded in the sacrificial canon that should be honored
have all been abolished and not yet performed.
The appropriate officials shall carefully arrange these matters according to old customs.”
In the eighth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, King Wǔ of Zhōu, upon conquering Yīn,
ennobled the tomb of Bǐ Gān;
Gāo of Hàn, passing through Zhào,
recorded the descendants of Yuè Yì.
This was to give prominence to the past
and encourage the future.
Among the descendants of the generals, ministers, and renowned worthies of the Wú period,
if there are any who can compile and cultivate family instructions,
and are loyal, filial, benevolent, and righteous,
who quietly maintain their integrity,
but are not known to their contemporaries,
the provincial and commandery censors shall promptly report their names,
leaving none out.”
In the intercalary month,
Xún Sōng, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was made Grand Master of Glorious Happiness and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Dèng Yōu, Minister of State Affairs, was made Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor fell ill.
He summoned Yáng, the Grand Tutor and Prince of Xīyáng;
Wáng Dǎo, the Minister of Education;
Biàn Hú, President of the Department of State Affairs;
Xī Jiàn, General of Chariots and Cavalry;
Yú Liàng, General of the Palace Guard;
Lù Yè, General of the Palace Guard;
and Wēn Jiào, Administrator of Dānyáng, all to receive his dying wishes
to assist the Crown Prince.
On the day Dīnghài,
an imperial edict stated:
“From ancient times, there has been death,
common to sages and saints.
Longevity or brevity, poverty or prosperity,
all return to the same fate;
what is there to be particularly grieved about?
I have been ill for a long time,
always fearing a sudden end.
Reflecting upon the grand foundation of my ancestors,
I am unable to complete the imperial structure,
the great shame is not yet avenged,
and the hundred clans suffer terribly—
this is what causes my sigh.
On the unfortunate day of my passing,
wrap me in seasonal clothes,
follow the former precedents completely,
emphasizing simplicity and frugality.
Troubling the populace with lavish decorations
shall all be avoided.
Yǎn is young and weak,
and has unworthily assumed a heavy responsibility;
he must rely on loyal and worthy officials
to instruct and perfect him.
In ancient times, Duke Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
and the Huò family nurtured Emperor Xiàozhāo;
their righteousness is recorded in previous annals,
and their achievements surpassed two generations.
Were these not the ways of ministers of the imperial clan?
All these high officials are
the hopes of the age.
Respectfully heed my dying command,
bear the heavy trust placed in you,
unite your hearts like cutting metal,
to plan for the royal house.
All regional commanders and garrison generals,
inspectors and administrators,
are all my defenders,
who give counsel from afar.
Although matters are internal and external,
their purpose is one.
Therefore, if there are no travelers,
who will guard the herds and pastures?
They are like lips and teeth,
reliant on each other for protection.
You should all strive with one heart,
as if matching tallies,
pondering the beauty of excellence,
making the successful completion of affairs your goal.
All myriad officials and ministers,
you shall collectively obey the Grand Administrator,
protect the young heir,
and broadly aid in these difficulties,
so that the spirits of our ancestors
may forever rest in peace above the nine heavens.
Then, even if I perish beneath the earth,
I will have no regrets in the Yellow Springs.”
On the day Wùzǐ,
the Emperor passed away in the Eastern Hall,
at the age of twenty-seven.
He was buried in Wǔpíng Líng.
His temple name was Sùzǔ.
The Emperor was intelligent and decisive,
and particularly skilled in understanding principles of governance.
At that time, there were fierce wars and famine,
more than half the population died of plague.
The state was extremely depleted,
and affairs were in the utmost difficulty.
It happened that Wáng Dūn wielded the power to intimidate the ruler,
and was about to seize the imperial authority.
The Emperor, with great effort, nourished and preserved the state,
controlling the strong with the weak,
secretly planning and making independent decisions,
