this
clearly shows that the essence of the moon gives birth to water.
Wáng Shēng also says that it appears round because it is far away.
If this were truly the case,
then when the moon first appears and after it wanes,
why
does it not appear round?
And solar eclipses occur sometimes from above or below,
starting from the side,
sometimes like a hook until it is complete.
If it appears round when viewed from afar,
it should not show its partial defects
or where it starts from the left or right.
This then confirms
the principles of Húntiān theory
with evidence.
Yíxiàng
in Yú Shū says:
"It is in xuánjī yùhéng,
to regulate the seven government bodies (celestial bodies)."
Kǎo Língyào says:
"An inch of gnomon shadow,
generated by the heavenly qi,
determines squareness and roundness.
Once squareness and roundness are established,
they are measured with compass and square.
Dusk and dawn govern the times,
thus observing the central stars and the movements of the jade instrument."
Zhèng Xuán believes it refers to a jade armillary sphere.
Chūnqiū Wényào Gōu says:
"When Táng Yáo ascended the throne,
Xīhé erected the Húnyí."
This shows that the establishment of astronomical instruments
goes back a long way.
Passed down through generations,
the historical officials kept it secret,
and scholars could not see it,
hence Xuān and Gài theories were in fervent debate.
Until the Taichū era of the Hàn dynasty,
Luò Xiàhóng, Xiānyú Wàngrén, Gěng Shòuchāng, and others built an armillary sphere to study calendrical degrees.
Later, during Emperor Hé's time,
Jiǎ Kuí revised it,
also adding the ecliptic.
By Emperor Shùn's time,
Zhāng Héng further constructed a Húnxiàng,
complete with inner and outer rings, north and south poles, and the yellow and red (ecliptic and celestial equator) paths,
listing the twenty-four qi, twenty-eight xiu, internal and external stellar officials, and the sun, moon, and five planets.
He used dripping water to turn it in a chamber in the palace hall,
with stars appearing and disappearing in sync with the sky.
Following its mechanisms,
he also rotated the ruìlún mìngjiá below the steps,
which waxed and waned with the moon,
opening and closing according to the calendar.
Afterwards, Lù Jì (陸績) also constructed an armillary sphere.
In the time of Wú (吳),
Zhōng Chángshì (中常侍) Wáng Fān (王蕃) of Lújiāng (廬江) was skilled in mathematics and calendrical calculations.
He transmitted Liú Hóng’s (劉洪) Qiánxiàng Lì (乾象曆),
and based on its methods, he devised an armillary instrument
and established his theories and calculations, saying: Previous scholars’ old theories
held that the forms of Heaven and Earth
resembled a bird’s egg.
Heaven enveloped Earth from without,
like a shell encasing the yolk.
It revolved without end,
its shape being
perfectly round,
hence it was called the Húntiān (渾天) (celestial sphere) theory.
The circumference of Heaven is three hundred sixty-five and one hundred forty-five five-hundred-eighty-ninths degrees.
Half of it covers the ground,
and half is
beneath the ground.
Its two ends are called the South Pole and the North Pole.
The North Pole is thirty-six degrees above the horizon,
and the South Pole is thirty-six degrees below the horizon.
The two poles are separated by one hundred
eighty-two and a half degrees, plus a little.
The circle around the North Pole, with a radius of seventy-two degrees,
is always visible and never hidden;
this is called the upper boundary (shàngguī, 上規).
The circle around the South Pole, with a radius of seventy-two degrees,
is always hidden and never
seen;
this is called the lower boundary (xiàguī, 下規).
The celestial equator is the belt (hóng, 紘) of Heaven,
and it is a little more than ninety-one degrees away from each of the two poles.
The ecliptic
is the path of the sun.
Half of it is outside the equator,
and half is inside the equator.
It intersects the equator to the east at Jiǎo (角) five degrees, a little less,
and to the west at Kuí (奎)
fourteen degrees, a little more.
Its furthest extent outside the equator
is twenty-four degrees from the equator,
which is Dǒu (斗) twenty-one degrees.
Its furthest extent inside the equator
is
also twenty-four degrees,
which is Jǐng (井) twenty-five degrees.
The winter solstice is at Dǒu (斗) twenty-one degrees,
a little more than one hundred fifteen degrees from the pole.
On this day, the sun is at its southernmost point,
hence the shadow is
longest.
At Dǒu (斗) twenty-one degrees on the ecliptic,
the sun rises in Chén (辰) and sets in Shēn (申),
so the sun also rises in Chén (辰) and sets in Shēn (申).
During the day, the sun travels above the ground for a little more than one hundred forty-six degrees,
hence the day is
short;
at night, it travels below the ground for a little less than two hundred nineteen degrees,
hence the night is long.
After the winter solstice,
the sun gradually approaches the pole,
hence the shadow gradually shortens.
The sun travels
more degrees above the ground during the day,
hence the day gradually lengthens;
it travels fewer degrees below the ground at night,
hence the night gradually shortens.
The sun’s position is gradually northward,
so the sun moves gradually northward,
until
the summer solstice,
when the sun is at Jǐng (井) twenty-five degrees,
a little more than sixty-seven degrees from the pole.
On this day, the sun is at its northernmost point,
closest to the pole,
and the shadow is shortest.
At Jǐng (井)
twenty-five degrees on the ecliptic,
the sun rises in Yín (寅) and sets in Xū (戌),
so the sun also rises in Yín (寅) and sets in Xū (戌).
During the day, the sun travels above the ground for a little less than two hundred nineteen degrees,
hence the day is long;
at night, it
travels below the ground for a little more than one hundred forty-six degrees,
hence the night is short.
After the summer solstice,
the sun gradually moves away from the pole,
hence the shadow gradually lengthens.
The sun travels
fewer degrees above the ground during the day,
hence the day gradually shortens;
it travels more degrees below the ground at night,
hence the night gradually lengthens.
The sun’s position is gradually southward,
so the sun’s rising and setting are gradually southward,
until
the winter solstice, when it returns to its initial state.
Dǒu (斗) twenty-one and
Jǐng (井) twenty-five correspond to forty-eight degrees between north and south.
At the spring equinox, the sun is at Kuí (奎) fourteen degrees, a little more;
at the autumn equinox, the sun is at Jiǎo (角) five degrees, a little less.
These are the midpoints of the intersections of the ecliptic and the celestial equator.
They are both a little more than ninety-one
degrees from the pole,
and their north-south positions are between Dǒu (斗) twenty-one and Jǐng (井) twenty-five.
Hence, the shadow is midway between the longest and shortest of the two solstices.
Kuí (奎) fourteen and Jiǎo (角) five
correspond to rising in Mǎo (卯) and setting in
Yǒu (酉),
so the sun also rises in Mǎo (卯) and sets in Yǒu (酉).
During the day, the sun travels above the ground;
at night, it travels below the ground.
Both are a little more than one hundred eighty-two and a half degrees.
Hence, the duration of the sun’s visibility is fifty
kè (刻),
and the duration of its invisibility is fifty kè (刻).
This is called equal day and night.
The day and night of Heaven are divided by the sun’s rising and setting,
while human day and night are limited by dusk and dawn.
It becomes bright two and a half kè (刻) before sunrise,
and it becomes dark two and a half kè (刻) after sunset.
Thus, five kè (刻) are subtracted from night to add to day,
which is why the spring and autumn equinoxes have fifty-five kè (刻) of daylight.
The movements of the three luminaries
are not necessarily constant.
Mathematicians calculate them using various methods,
each having similarities and differences,
so the calendrical systems of various schools are uneven and inconsistent.
The Luòshū Zhēnyào Dù (洛書甄曜度) and Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu (春秋考異郵) both state:
"The circumference of Heaven is one million seventy-one thousand li.
One degree is two thousand nine hundred thirty-two li, seventy-one bù (步), two chǐ (尺),
seven cùn (寸), and three hundred sixty-two four-hundred-eighty-sevenths of a fēn (分)."
Lù Jì (陸績) said:
"The east-west and north-south diameter of Heaven is three hundred fifty-seven thousand li."
This implies that the circumference is three times the diameter.
Examining this, the diameter is not merely one-third of the circumference.
If the circumference is one hundred forty-two and the diameter is forty-five,
then the diameter of Heaven is three hundred twenty-nine
thousand four hundred one li, one hundred twenty-two bù (步), two chǐ (尺), two cùn (寸), and ten seventy-firsts of a fēn (分).
"On the summer solstice, the shadow (jǐng, 景) is one chǐ (尺) and five cùn (寸) long,
which is called the center of the earth (dìzhōng, 地中)."
Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) explains:
"The earth-gnomon (tǔguī, 土圭) is one chǐ (尺) and five cùn (寸) long.
On the summer solstice,
an eight-chǐ (尺) gnomon is erected.
If its shadow is equal to the earth-gnomon,
it is called the center of the earth.
This is the land of Yǐngchuān Yángchéng (潁川陽城) today."
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said:
"Generally, for the sun’s shadow on the ground,
it differs by one cùn (寸) per thousand li.
A shadow of one chǐ (尺) and five cùn (寸) means
it is fifteen thousand li south of the sun’s subsolar point."
Based on this,
the sun should be eighty thousand li away from the ground below it.
If the sun shines obliquely on Yángchéng (陽城),
then this distance is half the diameter of Heaven.
The celestial body is round like a projectile,
Earth is in the middle of Heaven,
and Yángchéng (陽城) is at the center.
Then the sun in spring, autumn, winter,
and summer,
and dusk, dawn, day, and night,
would all be equidistant from Yángchéng (陽chéng),
with no variations.
Therefore, we know that the distance from the sun shining obliquely on Yángchéng (陽chéng)
is half the diameter of Heaven.
Using the Gōugǔ (句股) method,
the horizontal distance of fifteen thousand li
is the gōu (句);
the vertical height of eighty thousand li
is the gǔ (股);
the distance from the sun shining obliquely on Yángchéng (陽chéng)
is the xián (弦).
Applying the Gōugǔ (句股)
method to find the xián (弦),
we get eighty-one thousand three hundred ninety-four li, thirty bù (步), five chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸), and six fēn (分).
This is half the diameter of Heaven and the distance from the Earth to Heaven.
Doubling it,
we get one hundred sixty-two thousand seven hundred eighty-eight li, sixty-one bù (步), four chǐ (尺), seven cùn (寸), and two fēn (分),
which is the diameter of Heaven.
Multiplying it by the circumference
ratio and dividing by the diameter ratio,
we get five hundred thirteen thousand six hundred eighty-seven li, sixty-eight bù (步), one chǐ (尺), eight cùn (寸), and two fēn (分),
which is the circumference of Heaven.
This is fifty-five thousand seven hundred twelve li and some fraction less than the figures of Zhēnyào Dù (甄曜度) and Kǎoyì Yóu (考異郵).
One degree is one thousand four hundred six li, one hundred twenty-four
bù (步), six cùn (寸), and nineteen thousand forty-nine one-hundred-seven thousand five hundred sixty-fifths of a fēn (分),
which is one thousand five hundred twenty-five li, two
one hundred fifty-six bù, three chǐ, three cùn, and one hundred sixty thousand seven hundred thirty out of two hundred fifteen thousand one hundred thirty parts.
The Yellow and Red Paths are divided,
intertwining with each other,
their separation being twenty-four dù.
By extrapolating with the two primary forces (Yǐn and Yáng),
both paths are three hundred sixty-five dù
and a fraction.
From this, we know that the celestial body is spherical like a pellet.
However, Lù Jì made a armillary sphere,
its shape like a bird's egg.
In that case, the Yellow Path should be longer than the Red Path.
Jì said,
"The celestial sphere's east-west and north-south diameters are three hundred fifty-seven thousand lǐ."
If so, then Jì also considered the celestial body to be perfectly spherical.
Yet, his armillary sphere was like a bird's egg,
which means it
contradicts itself.
The old armillary sphere used two fēn for one dù,
its total circumference being seven chǐ three cùn and half a fēn.
Zhāng Héng later remade it,
using four fēn for one dù,
its total circumference being one
zhàng four chǐ six cùn and one fēn.
Fān considered the old system too small,
with stars densely packed,
and Héng's instrument too large,
difficult to move.
He remade the armillary sphere,
using three fēn
for one dù,
its total circumference being one zhàng nine cùn five fēn and three-quarters of a fēn.
The "Hóngfàn Commentary on Astronomical Constellations" says:
"Clear and bright
is the body of Heaven.
When Heaven suddenly changes color,
this is called 'deviating from the norm.'
When Heaven cracks,
Yáng is insufficient;
this is called 'ministers becoming strong.'
When Heaven cracks and people are seen,
war arises and the state perishes.
When Heaven roars with sound,
the sovereign is worried and alarmed.
All these
are born of a chaotic state."
Mǎ Xù said:
"Among the astronomical records and maps that are clearly knowable,
the fixed stars and constant asterisms in the Inner and Outer Officials total one hundred eighteen names,
accumulating to seven hundred eighty-three,
all bearing resemblances to states, countries, officials, palaces, and types of objects."
Zhāng Héng said:
"The brilliant luminaries are arrayed in the heavens.
Those that move are seven:
the sun, moon, and five planets.
The sun
is the patriarch of Yáng essence;
the moon
is the patriarch of Yīn essence;
the five planets
are the essences of the Five Phases.
The multitude of stars are scattered and arranged.
Their bodies are born from the earth,
their essences are formed in the heavens.
They are arrayed, residing and standing intertwined,
each having its own affiliation.
In the wilderness, they symbolize objects;
in the court, they symbolize officials;
among people, they symbolize events.
Those with divine prominence
have five arrays,
totaling thirty-five names.
One resides in the center,
called Běidǒu.
Four are spread in each direction, seven each,
making twenty-eight xiù.
The sun and moon move,
indicating auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
The five planets traverse their stations,
used to announce calamities and blessings.
The Inner and Outer Officials,
those always bright, number one hundred twenty-four.
Those that can be named are three hundred twenty,
making two thousand five hundred stars.
The number of faint stars is probably eleven thousand five hundred twenty.
All creatures, teeming and swarming,
are all able to have their fates connected to them.
Otherwise,
how could they be generally governed?"
Later, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
the Grand Astrologer Chén Zhuó compiled the star charts authored by the three schools of Gān, Shí, and Wūxián,
totaling two hundred eighty-three officials
and one thousand four hundred sixty-four stars,
taking them as the established standard.
Now, we briefly list the clear ones
to complete the Celestial Officials account.
Central Palace:
The five stars of Běijí,
and the six stars of Gōuchén,
are all within the Zǐgōng.
Běijí,
the most revered Běichén,
its pivotal star,
is the pivot of Heaven.
Heaven's rotation is endless,
the three luminaries shine in alternation,
yet the polar star remains unmoved.
Hence, it is said,
"It resides in its place, and all stars gather around it."
The first star governs the moon,
it is the Crown Prince.
The second star governs the sun,
it is the Emperor;
it is also the seat of Tàiyǐ,
said to be the reddest and brightest.
The third star governs the five planets,
it is the various sons.
If the central star is dim,
it means the sovereign does not attend to affairs;
if the right star is dim,
the Crown Prince is troubled.
Gōuchén
is the inner palace,
the principal consort of the Great Emperor,
the constant residence of the Great Emperor.
The four northern stars are called the Palace of Female Consorts,
symbolizing eighty-one imperial concubines.
One star within Gōuchén's mouth is called Tiānhuáng Dàdì.
Its spirit is called Yàopòbǎo,
who governs all spirits
and holds the chart of myriad deities.
The four stars embracing Běijí are called the Four Supports,
which assist Běijí in issuing degrees and bestowing governance.
The nine stars above Tiānhuáng Dàdì are called Huágài,
which cover and shield the Great Emperor's seat.
The nine stars below Huágài are called Gāng,
the handle of the canopy.
The five stars below Huágài are called the Inner Seats of the Five Emperors,
arranged as the residence of the compliant emperors.
If a guest star offends the central seat of Zǐgōng,
it signifies a minister offending the sovereign.
The six stars beside Huágài Gāng are called Liùjiǎ,
which can divide Yīn and Yáng and match seasonal nodes.
[一三]Therefore, they are beside the Emperor,
to spread political decrees and grant agricultural times.
One star to the far east is called Zhùxià Shǐ,
who is in charge of recording transgressions;
the Left and Right Scribes
are symbolized by this.
One star north of Zhùxià Shǐ is called Nǚshǐ,
a minor female official,
who is in charge of transmitting the water clock's drip;
hence, the Hàn Dynasty had court ladies (shìshǐ).
The nine stars of Chuánshè are above Huágài,
near the Milky Way,
the lodging for guests,
presiding over Hú people entering China.
If a guest star guards it,
it indicates guarding against treacherous envoys,
also said to mean the rise of Hú soldiers.
The five stars in the Milky Way south of Chuánshè are called Zàofù,
the official in charge of chariots;
also called Sīmǎ,
or Bólè.
If this star disappears,
horses become very valuable.
To its west, nine stars in the Milky Way, shaped like a hook,
are called Gōuxīng;
if they become straight, there will be an earthquake.
Tiānyī star is to the south of the right star of the Zǐgōng gate,
it is the spirit of the Celestial Emperor,
in charge of battles and knowing the good and bad fortunes of people.
Tàiyī star is south of Tiānyī,
close by,
also a spirit of the Celestial Emperor,
in charge of commanding sixteen spirits,
knowing the countries where wind and rain, floods and droughts,
military conflict and famine, plague and disaster are located.
The fifteen stars of the Zǐwēiyuán enclosure:
seven are in the western screen,
eight in the eastern screen,
north of Běidǒu.
One name for it is Zǐwēi,
the seat of the Great Emperor,
the constant residence of the Son of Heaven,
and it governs destiny and standards.
Another name is Chángyuán,
another is Tiānyíng,
and another is Qíxīng.
They serve as a protective screen,
representing the vassal ministers.
If there is military action in the palace,
and the Qíxīng are straight,
the Son of Heaven will emerge
and personally lead the palace guards.
Below the eastern screen are five stars called Tiānzhù,
which establish governance and teaching,
and promulgate laws and regulations.
Within the gate, at the southeast corner, five stars are called Shàngshū,
who are responsible for receiving counsel,
advising day and night;
the dragon acting as a receiver of counsel is
symbolized by this.
West of Shàngshū are two stars called Yīndé and Yángdé,
which are responsible for aiding the distressed and providing for the destitute.
To the left of the palace gate, within it, two stars are called Dàlǐ,
〔一四〕which are responsible for impartially handling punishments and judgments.
Outside the gate are six stars called Tiānchuáng,
which govern the resting quarters,
for relaxation and repose.
Outside the southwest corner are two stars called Nèichú,
which govern the food and drink within the six palaces,
and the banquets of the empress, consorts, and crown prince.
Outside the northeast corner are six stars called Tiānchú,
which govern elaborate feasts.
The seven stars of Běidǒu are north of Tàiwēi,
the pivot of the seven regulators,
the prime origin of yin and yang.
Therefore, it revolves in the center of the heavens,
overseeing and controlling the four directions,
thereby establishing the four seasons
and balancing the Five Phases.
The four stars of the Kuí form Xuánjī,
and the three stars of the Sháo form Yùhéng.
It is also said
that Běidǒu is the symbol of the sovereign,
the master of commands.
It is also called Dìchē,
taking its meaning from its movement.
Furthermore, the first star of the Kuí is called Tiānshū,
the second is Xuán,
the third is Jī,
the fourth is Quán,
the fifth is Yùhéng,
the sixth is Kāiyáng,
and the seventh is Yáoguāng;
one to four form the Kuí,
and five to seven form the Sháo.
Shū represents heaven,
Xuán represents earth,
Jī represents humanity,
Quán represents time,
Yùhéng represents sound,
Kāiyáng represents law,
and Yáoguāng represents stars.
Shíshì said:
"The first is called Zhèngxīng,
governing yang virtue,
the symbol of the Son of Heaven.
The second is called Fǎxīng,
governing yin punishment,
the position of the empress.
The third is called Lìngxīng,
governing central calamities.
The fourth is called Fáxīng,
governing heavenly principles,
punishing the lawless.
The fifth is called Shāxīng,
governing the center,
assisting the four directions,
and executing the guilty.
The sixth is called Wēixīng,
governing heavenly granaries and the five grains.
The seventh is called Bùxīng,
also called Yìngxīng,
governing military affairs."
It is also said:
"One governs heaven,
two governs earth,
three governs fire,
four governs water,
five governs earth,
six governs wood,
seven governs metal."
It is also said:
"One governs Qín,
two governs Chǔ,
three governs Liáng,
four governs Wú,
five governs Yān,
six governs Zhào,
seven governs Qí."
The four stars within the Kuí form the prison of nobles,
called Tiānlǐ.
The Fǔxīng is attached to Kāiyáng,
thus assisting Běidǒu in accomplishing its tasks,
a symbol of the prime minister.
If the seven regulator stars are bright,
the state will prosper;
if Fǔxīng is bright,
then the ministers will be strong.
The three stars south of the Sháo and the three stars west of the first star of the Kuí are all called Sāngōng,
who are officials responsible for spreading virtuous influence,
regulating the seven regulators,
and harmonizing yin and yang.
The six stars of Wénchāng
are in front of the Běidǒu Kuí,
the six treasuries of heaven,
responsible for compiling and calculating the heavenly way.
The first is called Shàngjiàng,
the Grand General establishing prestige and power.
The second is Cìjiàng,
the Shàngshū rectifying left and right.
The third is Guìxiàng,
the Tàicháng managing cultural affairs.
The fourth is Sīlù, Sīzhōng,
the Sīlì rewarding merit and promoting.
The fifth is Sīmìng, Sīguài,
the Tàishǐ dispelling calamities.
The sixth is Sīkòu,
the Dàlǐ assisting in managing treasures.
The so-called "first"
refers to the one closest to the Nèijiē in front of the Běidǒu Kuí.
If they are bright and moist,
and equal in size,
heavenly auspicious signs will arrive.
North of Wénchāng are six stars called Nèijiē,
the steps of the Heavenly Emperor.
Xiàng is a single star south of Běidǒu.
Xiàng,
the prime minister, oversees all offices and manages national education,
assisting the emperor in securing the state
and gathering all affairs.
If this star is bright,
it is auspicious.
Tàiyángshǒu is a single star
west of Xiàng,
a symbol of grand generals and high ministers,
responsible for guarding against unforeseen events
and preparing military defenses.
To the northwest are four stars called Shì.
Shì refers to
castrated prisoners.
Tiānláo are six stars
below the Běidǒu Kuí,
the prison for nobles.
Tàiwēi,
is the Emperor's court,
the seat of the Wǔ Dì,
and the mansions of the twelve zhūhóu.
Its outer fence
represents the Jiǔ Qīng.
One account says Tàiwēi is Héng.
Héng
presides over fairness.
It is also the Heavenly Court,
governing laws and legal discourse,
overseeing the promotion and bestowal of virtue,
where constellations receive their tallies,
various deities are tested,
and emotions are soothed and doubts examined.
Between the two stars in the southern fence is called Duānmén.
To the east is Zuǒ Zhífǎ,
the symbol of the Tíngwèi.
To the west is Yòu Zhífǎ,
the symbol of the Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Zhífǎ
are those who bring forth accusations against the wicked and treacherous.
To the east of Zuǒ Zhífǎ
is Zuǒyèmén.
To the west of Yòu Zhífǎ
is Yòuyèmén.
The four stars of the eastern fence:
The first star to the south is called Shàng Xiàng,
[one five] to its north
is Dōng Tàiyángmén;
the second star is called Cì Xiàng,
to its north
is Zhōnghuá Dōngmén;
the third star is called Cì Jiàng,
to its north
is Dōng Tàiyīnmén;
the fourth star is called Shàng Jiàng: these are known as the Sì Fǔ.
The four stars of the western fence:
The first star to the south is called Shàng Jiàng,
to its north
is Xī Tàiyángmén;
the second star is called Cì Jiàng,
to its north
is Zhōnghuá Xīmén;
the third star is called Cì Xiàng,
to its north
is Xī Tàiyīnmén;
the fourth star is called Shàng Xiàng: these are also called the Sì Fǔ.
If the eastern and western fences have rays or shake,
it means the zhūhóu are plotting against the Emperor.
[one six] If Zhífǎ moves,
punishments and penalties become particularly severe.
If the moon or the five planets enter Tàiwēi
and follow their orbits,
it is auspicious.
If they violate the central seats,
it portends legal penalties.
The three stars outside its southwest corner are called Míngtáng,
the palace where the Emperor promulgates his policies.
The three stars west of Míngtáng are called Língtái,
the observatory,
which presides over observing cloud phenomena,
examining auspicious signs,
and monitoring calamities and changes.
One star northeast of Zuǒ Zhífǎ is called Yèzhě,
who presides over introducing guests.
The three stars northeast of Yèzhě are called Sāngōng Nèizuò,
the place where court assemblies are held.
The three stars north of Sāngōng are called Jiǔ Qīng Nèizuò,
who preside over governing all affairs.
[one seven] The five stars west of Jiǔ Qīng are called Nèi Wǔ Zhūhóu,
who attend the Emperor internally
and do not go to their states.
If the rites of Bìyōng are correctly observed,
then Tàiwēi and the Zhūhóu will be bright.
Huángdì sits in the middle of Tàiwēi,
the spirit embodying the celestial pivot.
If the Emperor's movements align with the heavens and
his stillness with the earth's will,
following the middle path with ease,
then the Tàiwēi Wǔ Dì seats will be bright and radiant.
If the Huángdì seat is not bright,
the ruler should seek worthy officials to assist with the law,
otherwise, power will be usurped.
The four Dì stars flank the Huángdì seat:
the eastern Cāng Dì,
the spirit of Língwēiyǎng;
the southern Chì Dì,
the spirit of Chìbiāonù;
the western Bái Dì,
the spirit of Báizhāojǔ;
the northern Hēi Dì,
the spirit of Yèguāngjì.
One star north of the Wǔ Dì seats is called Tàizǐ,
the imperial heir.
One star north of Tàizǐ is called Cóngguān,
the attendant officials.
One star northeast of the Emperor's seat is called Xìngchén.
Píng, four stars, are inside Duānmén,
close to Yòu Zhífǎ.
Píng
serve to screen and shelter the imperial court.
Zhífǎ preside over accusations and impeachments;
if subjects respect their sovereign,
then the stars will be bright, moist, and lustrous.
Lángwèi, fifteen stars, are northeast of the Emperor's seat,
one account calls them Yīwū Lángfǔ.
The yuánshì of the Zhōu officials
and the Guānglù, Zhōngsàn, Jiànyì, Yìláng, and Sānshǔ Lángzhōng of the Hàn officials,
this is their function.
Láng
presides over guarding and protecting.
If these stars are incomplete,
the empress or consorts will die,
or favored officials will be executed.
If the stars are very bright or a guest star enters them,
high-ranking officials will create disorder.
Lángjiàng are north of Lángwèi,
presiding over reviewing equipment,
for military preparedness.
Wǔbēn, one star,
is north of the Tàiwēi western fence,
south of Xiàtái,
the cavalry officer of Jìngshì Máotóu.
Chángchén, seven stars,
resembling the constellation Bì,
are north of the Emperor's seat,
representing the Emperor's guard and Wǔbēn soldiers,
established for strong defense.
If the stars shake,
the Emperor will personally go out;
if bright, military forces will be used,
if dim, forces will be weak.
Sāntái, six stars,
residing in pairs,
beginning from Wénchāng,
extending to Tàiwēi.
One account calls them Tiānzhù,
the positions of the Sāngōng.
Among humans, they are Sāngōng,
in heaven, they are Sāntái,
presiding over initiating virtue and proclaiming tallies.
The two stars to the west, near Wénchāng, are called Shàngtái,
serving as Sīmìng,
presiding over longevity.
The next two stars are called Zhōngtái,
serving as Sīzhōng,
presiding over the imperial clan.
The two eastern stars are called Xiàtái,
serving as Sīlù,
presiding over military affairs,
thus manifesting virtue and curbing transgression.
Another account says Sāntái are the Heavenly Steps,
which Tàiyī ascends and descends.
One account calls them Tàijiē.
For the upper steps,
the upper star is the Emperor,
the lower star is the Empress or female ruler;
for the middle steps,
the upper star is the zhūhóu and Sāngōng,
the lower star is the qīng and dàfū;
for the lower steps,
the upper star is the shì,
the lower star is the common people: this is how yin and yang are harmonized and all things governed.
If ruler and subjects are in harmony
and the stars are in their normal state,
any change indicates an omen for the person they represent.
The four southern stars are called Nèipíng,
the officials close to the Zhífǎ who preside over judging crimes.
One star north of Zhōngtái is called Tàizūn,
representing noble relatives.
The six stars of Shè tí,
situated directly south of the Dipper's handle,
govern the establishment of seasons
and observe auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Shè tí acts as a shield,
enclosing and protecting the Heavenly Emperor's seat,
and presides over the Jiǔ Qīng.
If they are bright and large,
the Sān Gōng are unrestrained.
If a guest star enters them,
the sage ruler will be constrained.
The three stars to the west are called Zhōu Dǐng,
and they indicate dynastic decline.
Dà Jué is between the Shè tí stars.
Dà Jué
is the seat of the Heavenly King.
It is also the heavenly ridgepole,
rectifying the warp and weft of affairs.
The three stars to the north are called Dì Xí,
presiding over banquets, offerings, and reciprocal toasts.
The three stars to the north are called Gěng Hé,
the Heavenly Spear.
One interpretation is Heavenly Vanguard,
governing the foreign (Hú) troops.
It also signifies mourning,
thus its changes correspond to warfare and mourning.
If the star disappears,
that state will have military plans.
The star to its north is called Zhāo Yáo,
one interpretation is Spear and Shield.
The star to its north is called Xuán Gē,
both govern foreign (Hú) troops,
and their prognoses are generally similar to Gěng Hé.
The space between Zhāo Yáo and the handle of Běi Dǒu is called Tiān Kù.
If a star deviates from its position,
there will be an auspicious sign for the treasury.
If Zhāo Yáo aligns with Dòng Xīng, Gěng Hé, and Běi Dǒu,
then the foreign (Hú) people will come to accept orders from Zhōngguó.
Xuán Gē also presides over the northern Yi tribes.
If a guest star guards it,
the foreign (Hú) people will suffer a great defeat.
The three stars of Tiān Qiāng
are east of the Běi Dǒu's handle.
One interpretation is Heavenly Axe,
the military armaments of Heaven.
Thus, they are to the left of the Zǐ Gōng,
serving to ward off difficulties.
The three stars of Nǚ Chuáng
are north of Jì Xīng,
representing the imperial harem,
and presiding over women's affairs.
The five stars of Tiān Bàng
are north of Nǚ Chuáng,
the vanguard of the Son of Heaven,
presiding over disputes and punishments,
and concealing weapons to also ward off difficulties.
Qiāng and Bàng
are both for preparedness against emergencies;
if one star is missing,
that state will face military uprising.
The seven stars to the east are called Fú Kuāng,
a vessel for holding mulberries,
presiding over encouraging sericulture.
The seven stars of Qī Gōng
are east of Zhāo Yáo,
the Heavenly Ministers,
an emblem of the Sān Gōng,
presiding over the seven regulators.
Guàn Suǒ, nine stars, are in front of them,
the prison for commoners.
One interpretation is Lián Suǒ,
another is Lián Yíng,
another is Tiān Láo,
presiding over laws,
and restraining the violent and powerful.
One star at the mouth of the prison serves as a gate,
wishing it to open.
If all nine stars are bright,
the empire's prisons will be busy;
if seven stars are visible,
there will be a minor amnesty;
six stars or five stars,
a major amnesty.
If they move, axes and execution blocks will be used;
if the center is empty, the reign title will change.
The Hàn Zhì states fifteen stars.
Tiān Jì, nine stars,
are east of Guàn Suǒ,
representing the Jiǔ Qīng,
presiding over the records of all affairs,
and resolving grievances and lawsuits.
If they are bright, there will be many lawsuits in the empire;
if they disappear, governance will deteriorate,
and state records will be in disorder;
if they scatter and break apart, there will be earthquakes and mountain collapses.
Zhī Nǚ, three stars,
are at the eastern end of Tiān Jì,
the Heavenly Maiden,
presiding over fruits, silks, and precious treasures.
If the king is extremely filial,
and the gods are all pleased,
then the Zhī Nǚ stars will all be bright,
and there will be peace throughout the empire.
If the large star's points are angry,
cloth and silk will be expensive.
The four stars of the eastern foot are called Jiàn Tái,
a platform overlooking water,
presiding over gnomon, clepsydra, and pitch-pipe affairs.
The five stars of the western foot are called Niǎn Dào,
the path where the king enjoys strolling.
The Hàn Niǎn Dào connected the southern and northern palaces,
this is its celestial counterpart.
The two stars between the left and right horns are called Píng Dào Zhī Guān.
One star west of Píng Dào is called Jìn Xián,
presiding over the recommendation of outstanding talents by ministers and chancellors.
Kàng.
Dōng Xián and Xī Xián, each with four stars,
are north of Fáng and Xīn,
the path of the sun, moon, and five planets.
They are the doors of Fáng,
serving to prevent excess and indulgence.
If the stars are bright, it is auspicious;
if the moon or the five planets transgress or guard them,
there is a secret plot.
Jiàn Bì, one star,
is northeast of Fáng,
near Gōu Qín,
presiding over keys and locks.
Tiān Shì Yuán, twenty-two stars,
are northeast of Fáng and Xīn,
presiding over weights and measures,
and assembling crowds.
One interpretation is Tiān Qí Tíng,
presiding over executions.
If the stars within the market are numerous and lustrous,
the year will be bountiful.
If Yíng Huò guards it,
disloyal ministers will be executed.
If a comet sweeps through it,
it means moving the market or changing the capital.
If a guest star enters it,
a great war will arise;
if it exits,
there will be a death of a noble.
Dì Zuò, one star,
is west of Hòu Xīng in the center of Tiān Shì,
the Heavenly Court.
If it is bright and lustrous, the Son of Heaven will be auspicious,
and his authority and decrees will be effective.
Hòu, one star,
is northeast of Dì Zuò,
presiding over observing Yin and Yang.
If it is bright and large,
the輔臣 (Fǔ Chén) are strong,
and the four Yi tribes are open;
if Hòu is faint and subtle,
the state is secure;
if it disappears, the ruler loses his position;
if it moves, there is unrest.
Huàn Zhě, four stars,
are southwest of Dì Zuò,
attendants of the ruler who have undergone punishment.
If the stars are dim,
it is auspicious;
if they are not in their usual state,
the eunuchs will have worries.
Zōng Zhèng, two stars,
are southeast of Dì Zuò,
the Imperial Clan Grand Masters.
If a comet guards them,
or if they lose their color,
the Zōng Zhèng will have trouble;
if a guest star guards them,
the imperial edicts will change.
Zōng Rén, four stars,
are east of Zōng Zhèng,
presiding over recording kinship and offerings.
If the clan members are orderly,
they will be like brocade patterns, clear and upright.
If they move, there will be changes among the Son of Heaven's relatives;
if a guest star guards them,
a noble will die.
Zōng Xīng, two stars,
are east of Hòu Xīng,
an emblem of the imperial clan,
ministers related by blood to assist the Emperor.
If a guest star guards them,
the imperial relatives will be in disharmony.
The four stars of Tiānjiāng,
to the north of Wěi,
govern the Tàiyīn.
If the Jiāng stars are incomplete,
then the ferries, rivers, passes, and roads throughout the world will be impassable.
If they are bright and moving,
great floods will occur,
and great armies will rise;
if they are uneven, horses will be expensive.
If Yínghuò guards them,
a king will be established.
If a guest star enters them,
river ferries will be cut off.
The eight stars of Tiānyuè are to the west of the Nándǒu柄,
governing closures.
The six stars of Jiànxīng are to the north of Nándǒu,
also called Tiānqí,
the celestial capital's passes.
They represent planning matters,
celestial drums,
and celestial horses.
The two southern stars are
the celestial treasury.
The two central stars are
the market,
or axes and choppers.
The two upper stars are
the flag base.
Between Dǒu and Jiàn is
the path of the Three Luminaries.
If the stars move, the common people will suffer.
If the moon halos them,
dragons will appear,
and cattle and horses will suffer from plague.
If the moon and the five planets offend them,
ministers will slander each other and conspire,
and also passes and bridges will be impassable,
and there will be great floods.
The four southeastern stars are called Gǒuguó,
governing Xiānbēi, Wūwán, and Wòqiě.
If Yínghuò guards them,
foreign barbarians will cause trouble.
The two stars north of Gǒuguó are called Tiānjī,
governing the monitoring of time.
The nine stars of Tiānbian,
to the north of Jiànxīng,
are the head of market officials,
through which market treasures are known.
If the stars are bright,
it is auspicious.
If a comet offends or guards them,
grain will be expensive,
and prisoners will raise armies.
The three stars of Hégǔ,
and the nine stars of Qí,
to the north of Qiānniú,
are the celestial drum,
governing military drums
and axes.
One account says they are Sānwǔ,
governing the Son of Heaven's three generals;
the large central star is the Grand General,
the left star is the Left General,
and the right star is the Right General.
The left star
is also the southern star,
used to guard passes and bridges and resist difficulties,
to set up defenses in dangerous places,
and to understand strategic plans.
The Qí is the flag of the Tiāngǔ,
used as a banner and sign.
The nine stars of Zuǒqí
are to the left side of the Gǔ.
If the Gǔ is straight and bright,
with a yellow and lustrous color,
the generals will be auspicious;
if it is not straight,
it indicates military worries.
If the stars are angry,
horses will be expensive.
If they move, soldiers will rise;
if they bend, generals will lose their plans and power will be seized.
If the Qí stars are disordered and crooked,
the chaotic will oppress each other.
The four stars at the end of the Qí arranged north-south
are called Tiānfú,
the drumsticks.
If the stars are not bright,
the clepsydra will lose time.
Close to Hégǔ in front,
if the Fú and Gǔ are directly aligned,
they are all used as Fúgǔ.
The five stars of Lízhū,
to the north of Xūnǚ,
are Xūnǚ's treasury,
the stars of women.
The nine stars of Tiānjīn,
lying across the middle of the river,
are also called Tiānhàn,
and also Tiānjiāng,
governing the ferries and bridges of the four major rivers,
used to cross and connect the four directions.
If one star is missing,
ferries and roads will be impassable.
The twenty-two stars of Téngshé,
to the north of Yíngshì,
are the celestial snake,
governing water creatures.
The five stars of Wángliáng,
to the north of Kuí,
reside in the middle of the river,
the Son of Heaven's charioteer and imperial official.
Its four stars are called Tiānsì,
the one star beside them is called Wángliáng,
also called Tiānmǎ.
If these stars move,
it signifies whipping horses,
and chariots and cavalry filling the fields.
It is also called Liáng,
the celestial bridge,
governing the control of wind, rain, and waterways,
thus sometimes indicating chariots and cavalry,
and sometimes ferries and bridges.
If a guest star guards it,
bridges will not connect roads.
The one star in front is called Cèxīng,
Wángliáng's whip,
governing the Son of Heaven's servants,
beside Wángliáng.
If it moves behind the horse,
then chariots and cavalry will fill the fields.
The six stars of Gédaò,
in front of Wángliáng,
are flying paths.
From Zǐgōng to the river,
that which spirits ride,
one account says,
the Gédaò stars
are the paths for the Son of Heaven to travel to separate palaces.
The one star of Fùlù,
to the south of Gédaò,
is a side path.
The ten stars north of Dōngbì are called Tiān,
the official responsible for horses,
like today's post stations,
responsible for transmitting orders and setting up relays,
racing against the clepsydra,
meaning their movement is urgent and swift,
competing with the gnomon and clepsydra.
The twelve stars of Tiānjiāngjūn,
to the north of Lóu,
govern military forces.
The large central star is
the celestial Grand General.
The one southern star is called Jūnnánmén,
governing who questions those entering and exiting.
The eight stars of Tàilíng to the north of Wèi,
also called Jījīng,
govern great mourning.
If there are many stars in Jījīng,
then feudal lords will mourn,
the people will be sickly,
and troops will rise.
One star in Tàilíng is called Jīshī,
if bright, dead bodies will be like mountains.
The nine northern stars are called Tiānchuán,
also called Zhōuxīng,
used to cross impassable areas.
The one central star is called Jīshuǐ,
monitoring water disasters.
The two stars west of Mǎo are called Tiānnánjiē,
the path of the Three Luminaries,
governing the monitoring of passes and bridges, both internal and external borders.
The six stars of Juǎnshé,
to the north of Mǎo,
govern speech,
used to know flattery and slander.
If curved,
it is auspicious;
if straight and moving,
there will be harm from gossip throughout the world.
The one central star is called Tiānchán,
governing shamans and doctors.
The five stars of Wǔchē,
and the nine stars of Sānzhù,
are north of Bì.
Wǔchē
is the carriage-shelter of the Five Emperors,
the seat of the Five Emperors.
It presides over the five types of weapons of the Son of Heaven,
and some say it presides over the abundance or scarcity of the five grains.
The large star in the northwest is called Tiānkù,
presiding over Tàibái,
and over Qín.
The next star in the northeast is called Yù,
presiding over Chénxīng,
and over Yān and Zhào.
The next star in the east is called Tiāncāng,
presiding over Suìxīng,
and over Lǔ and Wèi.
The next star in the southeast is called Sīkōng,
presiding over Tiánxīng,
and over Chǔ.
The next star in the southwest is called Qīngxīng,
presiding over Yínghuò,
and over Wèi.
If the five planets undergo changes,
all predictions are made based on what they preside over.
Sānzhù is also called Sānquán.
If the Son of Heaven observes the ceremony of the Língtái,
then Wǔchē and Sānzhù will be equally bright and constant.
The five stars within it are called Tiānhuáng.
The three stars south of Tiānhuáng are called Xiánchí,
which is a fish preserve.
If the moon or the five planets enter Tiānhuáng,
war will break out,
roads will be impassable,
and the world will be in chaos.
The six stars south of Wǔchē are called Zhūwáng,
observing the survival or destruction of the feudal lords.
The eight stars to its west are called Bāgǔ,
presiding over the annual harvest.
If one star of Bāgǔ disappears,
one grain will not ripen.
The single star Tiānguān,
south of Wǔchē,
is also called Tiānmén,
the path of the sun and moon.
It presides over border affairs
and closures.
If it has sharp rays,
there will be war.
If the five planets guard it,
many noble persons will die.
The four stars in front of the axe-handle of Dōngjǐng are called Sīguài,
presiding over the observation of extraordinary changes in heaven, earth, sun, moon, and stars, and omens of birds, beasts, plants, and trees.
When an enlightened ruler hears of calamity,
he cultivates virtue to preserve blessings.
The nine stars northwest of Sīguài are called Zuòqí,
which are the markers for the establishment of positions for ruler and ministers.
The four stars west of Zuòqí are called Tiāngāo,
the height of terraces and pavilions,
presiding over observing atmospheric phenomena from afar.
The single star west of Tiāngāo is called Tiānhé,
presiding over observing strange phenomena in mountains and forests.
Nánhé and Běihé each have three stars,
flanking Dōngjǐng.
One account calls them Tiāngāo,
the gates of heaven,
[一九] presiding over bridges.
Nánhé is called Nánshù,
also Nángōng,
also Yángmén,
also Yuèmén,
also Quánxīng,
presiding over fire.
Běihé is called Běishù,
also Běigōng,
also Yīnmén,
also Húmén,
also Héngxīng,
presiding over water.
The area between the two River Guards
is the regular path of the sun, moon, and five planets.
If the River Guards move,
war will break out in the central states.
The three stars south of Nánhé are called Quēqiū,
presiding over the external structures of palace gates.
The five stars of Wǔzhūhóu
are north of Dōngjǐng,
presiding over impeachment and investigation,
warning against the unexpected.
Also, they are said to govern yin and yang,
and observe gains and losses.
They are also said to preside over the emperor's heart.
The first is the imperial preceptor,
the second is the imperial friend,
the third is the three excellencies,
the fourth is the erudite,
and the fifth is the grand astrologer.
These five constantly resolve doubts and deliberations for the emperor.
If the stars are bright, large, and lustrous,
then there will be great order in the world;
if they have sharp rays,
then misfortune will be in the central states.
The three stars south of Wǔzhūhóu are called Tiānzūn,
presiding over providing gruel and porridge to the poor and hungry.
The single star Jīshuǐ,
northwest of Běihé,
is the Water River,
used to supply wine and food properly.
The single star Jīxīn is northeast of Jīshuǐ,
supplying the kitchen properly.
The four stars of Shuǐwèi
are east of Jīxīn,
presiding over water control.
If a guest star, like water or fire, guards or offends it,
all rivers will overflow.
Xuānyuán has seventeen stars,
north of Qīxīng.
Xuānyuán
is the spirit of the Yellow Emperor,
the body of the Yellow Dragon;
the ruler of empresses and consorts,
and the post of scholars.
One account calls it Dōnglíng,
another Quánxīng,
presiding over the spirits of thunder and rain.
The large star in the south
is the empress.
The next star to the north
is the lady,
also the screen,
also the commander-in-chief.
The next star to the north
is the imperial concubine,
also the second-in-command.
The subsequent stars
all belong to the retinue of the second-ranking concubines.
The small star south of the empress
is the female attendant.
The star to the left is Shàomín,
the empress's kin.
The star to the right is Dàmín,
the grand empress's kin.
Their color should be yellow, small, and bright.
The three stars south of the right horn of Xuānyuán are called Jiǔqí,
the banner of the wine official,
presiding over banquets and feasts.
If the five planets guard Jiǔqí,
there will be great feasting throughout the world,
with wine, meat, and wealth,
bestowed upon or granted noble titles to the imperial clan.
The three stars south of Jiǔqí are called Tiānxiàng,
the image of the prime minister.
The four stars west of Xuānyuán are called Guàn,
Guàn refers to
the beacon fires,
the warning signals of border stations.
The four stars north of Guàn are called Nèipíng,
the official who settles crimes,
making punishments clear.
Shàowēi has four stars west of Tàiwēi,
the positions of scholars and grandees.
One name is Chǔshì,
also the deputy ruler of the Son of Heaven,
or the official of the erudite,
one says it presides over the side gate of the imperial palace.
The first star in the south is the Chǔshì,
the second star is the Yìshì,
the third star is the Bóshì,
the fourth star is the Dàfū.
If they are bright, large, and yellow,
then worthy scholars will be promoted.
If the moon or the five planets transgress or guard them,
the Chǔshì and empress will be worried,
and the prime minister will be replaced.
The four stars in the south are called Chángyuán,
presiding over borders and the Hú and Yí peoples.
If Yínghuò enters it,
the Hú will invade the central states;
if Tàibái enters it,
the nine ministers will plot.
Twenty-eight Mansions
In the east,
the two stars of Jiǎo are the Celestial Pass,
and the space between them is the Celestial Gate;
inside it is the Celestial Court.
Therefore, the Yellow Road passes through it,
where the seven luminaries travel.
The left Jiǎo is the Celestial Field,
it governs justice,
and presides over punishment.
To its south is the Way of the Grand Yang.
The right Jiǎo is the General,
presiding over military affairs.
To its north is the Way of the Grand Yin.
Indeed, the three Celestial Gates
are like the four pillars of Fáng.
If these stars are bright and large,
the King's Way is peaceful,
and worthy individuals are in court.
If they move or shift,
the King travels.
The four stars of Kàng
are the inner court of the Son of Heaven,
overall managing all memorials to the throne,
hearing lawsuits, administering justice, and recording merits.
One interpretation calls it Shūmiào,
presiding over epidemics.
If the stars are bright and large,
loyal辅 are accepted,
and the world is at peace.
The four stars of Dǐ
are the King's imperial lodging palace,
the residence of the Empress and imperial concubines,
and a chamber for rest and relaxation.
The front two stars
are the official consorts;
the rear two stars
are the secondary consorts.
If the rear two stars are large,
then ministers abide by the rules.
The four stars of Fáng
are the Míngtáng,
the palace where the Son of Heaven issues policies,
and also the Four Assistants.
The lowest first star
is the Grand General;
the next
is the Secondary General;
the next
is the Secondary Chancellor;
the top star
is the Grand Chancellor.
The two southern stars are the Sovereign's position,
the two northern stars are the Madam's position.
It is also the Four Pillars,
the space in between is the Celestial Thoroughfare,
also known as the Celestial Pass,
where the Yellow Road passes.
The southern space is called the Yang Ring,
to its south is the Grand Yang;
the northern space is called the Yin Space,
to its north is the Grand Yin.
If the seven luminaries travel through the Celestial Thoroughfare,
then the world is peaceful;
if they travel through the Yang Way, there will be drought and death;
if they travel through the Yin Way, there will be floods and war.
It is also called the Celestial Quadriga,
as the Celestial Horses,
presiding over carriages.
The southernmost star is the Left Outer Horse,
the next is the Left Inner Horse,
the next is the Right Inner Horse,
the next is the Right Outer Horse.
It is also called Heaven,
and also presides over opening and closing,
as the channel for animal storage.
If the Fáng stars are bright,
then the King is enlightened;
if the Outer Horse stars are large,
then war arises;
if the stars are scattered,
the people disperse.
Furthermore, the two small northern stars are called Gōujiàn,
the key and bolt of Fáng,
the celestial pipe and flute,
presiding over locking and bolting the celestial heart.
If they are bright and close to Fáng,
the world will be of one mind.
If there are stars in the space between Fáng and Gōujiàn or if it is scattered and cracked,
then there will be earthquakes and rivers will run clear.
The three stars of Xīn
are the proper position of the Celestial King.
The central star is called Míngtáng,
the position of the Son of Heaven,
it is the Grand Constellation,
presiding over rewards and punishments in the world.
When the world changes and moves,
the Xīn stars show omens.
If the stars are bright and large,
the world will be in harmony.
The front star is the Crown Prince,
the rear star is the secondary son.
If the Xīn stars are straight,
then the King loses power.
The nine stars of Wěi
are the site of the imperial harem,
the residence of consorts and empresses.
The uppermost first star
is the Empress;
the next three stars
are the Madams;
the next stars
are the concubines.
Beside the third star is a star named Shéngōng,
the inner chamber for disrobing.
Wěi is also the Nine Sons;
if the star colors are evenly bright,
and their sizes are in succession,
then the imperial harem will have
many children and grandchildren.
The four stars of Jī
are also the residence of the imperial harem's consorts and empresses.
It is also called Tiānjīn,
one interpretation calls it Tiānjī,
presiding over the eight winds.
Whenever the sun and moon dwell in Jī, Dōngbì, Yì, or Zhěn, winds will arise.
It also presides over slander and disputes,
and over foreign guests, barbarians, and northern tribes.
Therefore, when barbarians are about to move,
they are first indicated by Jī.
In the north,
the six stars of the Southern Dǒu
are the Celestial Temple,
the position of the Chancellor and Grand Minister,
presiding over praising the worthy and promoting scholars,
and granting noble titles and emoluments.
It also presides over military affairs;
one interpretation calls it Tiānjī.
The two southern stars are Kuí,
the Celestial Beam.
The two central stars
are the Celestial Assistant.
The two northern stars
are the Celestial Treasury Court,
and also determine the length of life.
If there are matters concerning the Son of Heaven,
they are prognosticated from Dǒu.
If the Dǒu stars are grand and bright,
the King's Way is peaceful,
and noble titles and emoluments are granted.
The six stars of Qiānniú
are the celestial barrier and bridge,
presiding over sacrificial matters.
Its two northern stars,
one is called Jílù,
one is called Jùhuǒ.
It is also said,
the uppermost star presides over roads,
the next two stars preside over barriers and bridges,
the next three stars preside over Nányuè.
If they shake or change color, then prognosticate.
If the stars are bright and large,
the King's Way flourishes,
and barriers and bridges are open.
The four stars of Xūnǚ
are the Celestial Lesser Treasury.
Xū
is a term for a humble concubine,
a lowly female attendant,
presiding over cloth, tailoring, marriage, and weddings.
The two stars of Xū
are the official post of the Grand Minister,
presiding over northern cities, residences, ancestral temples, sacrifices, and prayers,
and also presiding over death, mourning, and weeping.
The three stars of Wēi
preside over the celestial treasury, celestial market, and house building;
the rest is prognosticated the same as Xū.
The four stars of Fénmù
are below Wēi,
presiding over death, mourning, and weeping,
representing tombs.
The two stars of Yíngshì
are the palace of the Son of Heaven.
One interpretation calls it Xuángōng,
one calls it Qīngmiào,
and it also represents the granary for military provisions and earthworks.
If the stars are bright,
the nation flourishes;
if they are small and dim,
sacrifices to ghosts and spirits are not accepted.
The six stars of Lí Gōng
are the detached palace of the Son of Heaven,
presiding over places of concealment and rest.
The two stars of Dōngbì
govern literature
and are the secret repository of all books and records in the world.
If the stars are bright,
a king will rise,
the Way and its arts will flourish,
and the state will have many upright gentlemen.
If the stars lose their color,
differing in size,
the king will be fond of military matters,
scholars of the classics will not be employed,
and books and records will be hidden.
If the stars move,
there will be earthworks.
Western Region.
The sixteen stars of Kuí
are the celestial arsenal.
One name for it is Heavenly Boar (Tiānshǐ),
also called Fēngshǐ.
It presides over using military force to suppress violence
and also over canals and ditches.
The large star in the southwest
is called the Eye of the Heavenly Boar (Tiānshǐ Mù),
also called the Grand General (Dàjiàng),
and it is desired that it be bright.
The three stars of Lóu
are the celestial prison,
presiding over parks, pastures, and sacrificial animals,
supplying the suburban sacrifices.
The three stars of Wèi
are the celestial kitchen and storehouse,
presiding over granaries
and being the repository of the five grains.
If they are bright, there will be peace.
The seven stars of Mǎo
are the ears and eyes of Heaven,
presiding over the Western Region
and over judicial affairs.
They are also called Máotóu,
the Hú stars.
The space between Mǎo and Bì is the Celestial Street (Tiānjiē).
When the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) goes out,
Máotóu rides before Bì as the vanguard.
This is its meaning.
It is the path traversed by the Yellow Road (Huángdào).
If Mǎo is bright,
then the prisons of the world will be peaceful.
If all six stars of Mǎo are bright
and equal to the great star,
there will be great floods.
If all seven stars are yellow,
a great war will arise.
If one star is lost,
it signifies war and mourning.
If they shake and move,
a high minister will be imprisoned,
or there will be a gathering of commoners.
If they are large and numerous, and all move as if leaping,
Hú armies will rise in great numbers.
The eight stars of Bì
preside over border armies
and over hunting with arrows.
Its large star is called Tiāngāo,
and also Biānjiàng,
presiding over the commanders of the Four Barbarians (Sì Yí).
If the stars are bright and large,
then distant barbarians will come to pay tribute,
and the world will be peaceful.
If they lose their color,
then the border armies will be in disarray.
The single star Fù'ěr,
below Bì,
presides over listening for successes and failures,
observing transgressions and evil,
and discerning inauspicious signs.
If the stars are flourishing,
then the central states will be weak,
there will be robbers,
the border guards will be alarmed,
and foreign states will rebel.
If they move,
flattery and slander will prevail.
If the moon enters Bì,
there will be much rain.
The three stars of Zīxuē
are the scouts of the three armies,
the storehouse of armies on the march,
presiding over encampments and travel,
and gathering all things.
If they are bright, army provisions will be abundant,
and generals will gain power.
The ten stars of Shēn
are also called Shēnfá,
also Dàchén,
also Tiānshì,
and also Fǔyuè,
presiding over cutting down.
They are also the celestial prison,
presiding over killing and punishment.
They also preside over weights and measures,
thereby bringing about fairness.
They also preside over border cities
and the Nine Interpreters (Jiǔ Yì),
so it is undesirable for them to move.
Shēn
is the body of the White Beast.
Its three central stars arranged horizontally
are the three generals.
The northeast is called the Left Shoulder (Zuǒjiān),
presiding over the Left General.
The northwest is called the Right Shoulder (Yòujiān),
presiding over the Right General.
The southeast is called the Left Foot (Zuǒzú),
presiding over the General of the Rear.
The southwest is called the Right Foot (Yòuzú),
presiding over the Auxiliary General.
Therefore, the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) interpreted Shēn as corresponding to the seven generals.
The three small central stars are called Fá,
the celestial commanders,
presiding over the states of Hú, Xiānbēi, Róng, and Dí.
Thus, it is undesirable for them to be bright.
If all seven generals are bright and large,
the armies of the world will be elite.
If the royal way is deficient, then the pointed horns will extend.
If the Fá stars are bright and equal to Shēn,
all high ministers will conspire,
and war will arise.
If the Shēn stars lose their color,
the army will disperse and be defeated.
If the pointed horns of Shēn move and shake,
there will be an emergency at the border,
war will arise,
and there will be cutting down and punishment.
If the Shēn stars shift,
guests will attack the host.
If Shēn's Left Foot enters the Jade Well (Yùjǐng),
a great war will arise,
Qín will suffer a great flood,
or there will be mourning,
and mountains and rocks will behave strangely.
If the Shēn stars are out of alignment,
the king's ministers will be disloyal.
Southern Region.
The eight stars of Dōngjǐng
are the southern gate of Heaven,
where the Yellow Road (Huángdào) passes,
Heaven's pavilion and watchtower,
presiding over water-level affairs,
where laws and regulations are made equitable.
If the king applies laws fairly,
then the Jǐng stars will be bright and arranged properly.
The single star Yuè,
attached before Jǐng,
presides over observing and executing the extravagant and licentious.
Thus, it is undesirable for it to be bright.
If it is bright and equal to Jǐng,
then the axe will be used on high ministers.
If the moon is in Jǐng,
there will be wind and rain.
The five stars of Yúguǐ
are the eyes of Heaven,
presiding over observation,
clearly discerning treacherous plots.
The northeast star presides over accumulated horses.
The southeast star presides over accumulated weapons.
The southwest star presides over accumulated cloth and silk.
The northwest star presides over accumulated gold and jade,
interpreted according to changes.
The central star is the accumulated corpses (Jīshī),
presiding over death, mourning, and sacrifices.
One name for it is Fǔzhì,
presiding over execution and beheading.
If the Guǐ stars are bright,
great harvests will be achieved.
If they are not bright,
the common people will scatter.
Zhì is desired to be dim and not bright.
If it is bright, war will arise,
and high ministers will be executed.
The eight stars of Liǔ
are Heaven's chief cook,
presiding over royal food,
and harmonizing flavors,
and also over thunder and rain.
The seven stars of Qīxīng,
also named Tiāndū,
preside over clothing, embroidery,
and also over urgent military matters and bandits.
Therefore, if the stars are bright, the royal way flourishes.
If they are dim, worthy and good people will not remain,
and the world will be empty.
The six stars of Zhāng
preside over precious treasures, items used in ancestral temples, and clothing,
and also over celestial food and drink, rewards and gifts.
If the stars are bright, the king will perform the five rites
and attain the mean of Heaven.
The twenty-two stars of [Yì] 翼,
are the celestial music bureau.
They govern actors, entertainers, and musicians.
[二０]They also govern foreign barbarians, distant guests, and visitors from beyond the seas.
When these stars are bright and large,
ritual and music flourish,
and the four barbarian tribes submit.
If they move, barbarian envoys will come.
If they are scattered, the Son of Heaven will raise an army.
The four stars of [Zhěn] 軫
govern the prime minister,
who is a supporting minister;
they govern chariots and cavalry;
they govern transport and burden.
Whenever armies move in or out,
all omens are observed in [Zhěn] 軫.
They also govern wind,
and govern death and mourning.
If the [Zhěn] 軫 stars are bright,
then the imperial carriage is prepared;
if they move, the imperial carriage will be used.
The [Xiá] 轄 stars flank [Zhěn] 軫 on both sides,
governing kings and marquises.
The left [Xiá] 轄 represents kings of the same surname as the emperor,
the right [Xiá] 轄 represents those of a different surname.
If the stars are bright,
a great army will be raised.
If they are far from [Zhěn] 軫,
it is inauspicious.
If [Xiá] 轄 rises,
the southern barbarians will invade.
The single star [Chángshā] 長沙,
is within [Zhěn] 軫,
and governs longevity.
If it is bright, it means long life for the ruler,
and flourishing descendants.
It is also said:
If the chariot has no [Xiá] 轄,
the state has worries;
if [Zhěn] 軫 gathers,
a great army will be raised.
Constellations outside the Twenty-Eight Mansions:
[Kùlóu] 庫樓 has ten stars,
the six large stars are [Kù] 庫,
the southern four stars are [Lóu] 樓,
located south of [Jiǎo] 角.
One account calls it [Tiānkù] 天庫 (Heavenly Storehouse),
the armory for military chariots.
The fifteen stars clustered in groups of three nearby,
are the [Zhù] 柱 (Pillars).
The four small stars in the center,
are [Héng] 衡 (Balance),
governing the deployment of troops.
The two stars to the northeast are called [Yángmén] 陽門 (Yang Gate),
governing the guarding of passes and strategic points.
The two stars of [Nánmén] 南門 (Southern Gate),
are south of [Kùlóu] 庫樓,
they are the outer gate of Heaven,
governing the guarding of soldiers.
The two stars of [Píng] 平 (Level),
are north of [Kùlóu] 庫樓,
they judge legal cases throughout the empire,
they are the symbol of the Grand Judge.
The two stars of [Tiānmén] 天門 (Heavenly Gate),
are north of [Píng] 平 stars.
Seven stars south of [Kàng] 亢 are called [Zhēnwēi] 折威 (Breaking Majesty),
governing executions.
The two stars of [Dùnwán] 頓頑 (Stubborn),
are southeast of [Zhēnwēi] 折威,
governing the examination of prisoner's situations,
and detecting fraud and deception.
[Qíguān] 騎官 has twenty-seven stars,
south of [Dǐ] 氐,
like the Son of Heaven's elite guards,
governing the palace guard.
The easternmost star is [Qízhèn Jiāngjūn] 騎陣將軍 (General of the Cavalry Formation),
a cavalry general.
The three southern stars are [Chēqí] 車騎 (Chariots and Cavalry),
generals of chariots and cavalry.
The three stars of [Zhènchē] 陣車 (Battle Chariots),
are northeast of [Qíguān] 騎官,
they are leather chariots.
[Jīzú] 積卒 has twelve stars,
south of [Fángxīn] 房心,
governing the guard.
If other stars guard it,
close ministers will be punished.
The two stars of [Cóngguān] 從官 (Attendant Officials),
are northwest of [Jīzú] 積卒.
[Guī] 龜 has five stars,
south of [Wěi] 尾,
governing divination to predict good and ill fortune.
The single star [Fùyuè] 傅說,
is behind [Wěi] 尾.
[Fùyuè] 傅說 governs prayers and blessings,
he is a shamanic official.
The single star [Yú] 魚 (Fish),
is behind [Wěi] 尾 in the river,
governing yin affairs,
and knowing the timing of clouds and rain.
[Chǔ] 杵 has three stars,
south of [Jī] 箕,
the [Chǔ] 杵 (Pestle) provides for the kitchen.
If a guest star enters [Chǔjiù] 杵臼 (Pestle and Mortar),
there will be an emergency in the empire.
The [Kāng] 穅 (Chaff) star is in front of [Jīshé] 箕舌 and northwest of [Chǔ] 杵.
[Biē] 鼈 has fourteen stars,
south of [Nándǒu] 南斗.
[Biē] 鼈 (Turtle) is a water creature,
and belongs to the Greater Yin.
If a star guards it,
the common people will gather,
signifying a water command.
The single star [Nóngzhàngrén] 農丈人 (Elder Farmer),
is southwest of [Nándǒu] 南斗,
the old farmer governs harvest.
The two stars [Gǒu] 狗 (Dog),
are in front of [Nándǒu Kuí] 南斗魁,
governing barking and guarding.
[Tiāntián] 天田 has nine stars,
south of [Niú] 牛.
[Luóyàn] 羅堰 has nine stars,
east of [Qiānniú] 牽牛,
they are dams,
used to hold back and store floodwaters,
and irrigate canals.
[Jiǔkǎn] 九坎 has nine stars,
south of [Qiānniú] 牽niú.
[Kǎn] 坎,
are canals,
used to channel spring sources,
to drain excess and discharge overflow,
and to connect ditches and waterways.
The ten stars between [Jiǔkǎn] 九坎 are called [Tiānchí] 天池 (Heavenly Pool),
one account calls it [Sānchí] 三池 (Three Pools),
another calls it [Tiānhǎi] 天海 (Heavenly Sea),
governing the irrigation of fields.
The two stars south of [Xū] 虛 are called [Kū] 哭 (Weep),
the two stars east of [Kū] 哭 are called [Qì] 泣 (Cry),
[Qì] 泣 and [Kū] 哭 are both near tombs.
The thirteen stars south of [Qì] 泣 are called [Tiānlěichéng] 天壘城 (Heavenly Rampart City),
resembling a chain,
governing the northern barbarians [Dīnglíng] 丁零 and [Xiōngnú] 匈奴.
The two southern stars are called [Gàiwū] 蓋屋 (Covering Houses),
officials who manage palaces and residences.
The four stars to their south are called [Xūliáng] 虛梁 (Empty Beams),
the location of imperial gardens, tombs, and ancestral temples.
[Yǔlín] 羽林 has forty-five stars,
south of [Yíngshì] 營室,
one account calls it [Tiānjūn] 天軍 (Heavenly Army),
governing military cavalry,
and also governing the protection of the king.
[Lěibìzhèn] 壘壁陣 has twelve stars,
north of [Yǔlín] 羽林,
the rampart of [Yǔlín] 羽林,
governing military defense and encampments.
If the Five Planets are within [Tiānjūn] 天軍,
it always means war,
especially [Yínghuò] 熒惑, [Tàibái] 太白, and [Chénxīng] 辰星.
The single star [Běiluòshīmén] 北落師門,
is southwest of [Yǔlín] 羽林.
[Běi] 北 (North) means,
the mansion is in the northern quarter;
[Luò] 落 (Falling) refers to,
the fences of Heaven;
[Shī] 師 (Teacher) means,
multitude;
[Shīmén] 師門 (Multitude's Gate),
is like a military gate.
The north gate of [Cháng'ān] 長安 city is called [Běiluòmén] 北落門,
in imitation of this.
It usually governs observing military movements.
If a star guards it,
the barbarians will enter the border,
and war will break out.
To its northwest are ten stars,
called [Tiānqián] 天錢 (Heavenly Coin).
The single star southwest of [Běiluò] 北落 is called [Tiāngāng] 天綱 (Heavenly Net),
governing military tents.
The nine stars southeast of [Běiluò] 北落 are called [Bākuí] 八魁 (Eight Chiefs),
governing the capture of wild animals.
[Tiāncāng] 天倉 has six stars,
south of [Lóu] 婁,
where grain is stored.
The four southern stars are called [Tiānyǔ] 天庾 (Heavenly Granary),
where stored kitchen provisions are kept.
[Tiānqūn] 天囷 has thirteen stars,
south of [Wèi] 胃.
[Qūn] 囷,
is a type of granary,
governing the supply of imperial provisions.
The four stars of Tiān Lǐn (天廩) are south of Mǎo (昴).
One name for them is Tiān Kuì (天廥).
They govern the storage of millet and panicled millet for offerings and sacrifices.
What is called Yù Lǐn (御廩) in the *Chūnqiū* (春秋)
is an image of this.
The sixteen stars of Tiān Yuàn (天苑)
are south of Mǎo (昴) and Bì (畢).
This is the Son of Heaven’s (天子) imperial park,
a place for raising beasts.
South of Yuàn (苑) are thirteen stars called Tiān Yuán (天園),
a place for planting fruits and vegetables.
The eight stars south of Bì Fù Ěr (畢附耳) are called Tiān Jié (天節).
They govern what envoys carry.
Below Tiān Jié (天節) are nine stars called Jiǔ Zhōu Shū Kǒu (九州殊口).
These are officials who understand local customs
and communicate with those who require multiple translations.
The nine stars of Cān Qí (參旗) are west of Cān (參).
One name for them is Tiān Qí (天旗),
and another is Tiān Gōng (天弓).
They govern the deployment of bows and crossbows,
observing changes and repelling difficulties.
The four stars of Yù Jǐng (玉井)
are below Cān Zuǒ Zú (參左足),
governing water and beverages to supply the kitchen.
To the southwest are nine stars called Jiǔ Yóu (九游),
the flag of the Son of Heaven (天子).
Southeast of Yù Jǐng (玉井) are four stars called Jūn Jǐng (軍井),
the well for an army on the march.
If Jūn Jǐng (軍井) has not been reached,
the general does not speak of thirst.
The name is derived from this.
The thirteen stars of Jūn Shì (軍市) are southeast of Cān (參).
This is the market for the celestial army’s trade,
enabling the exchange of goods.
Yě Jī (野雞) is one star,
governing strange transformations,
located within Jūn Shì (軍市).
Southwest of Jūn Shì (軍市) are two stars called Zhàng Rén (丈人).
East of Zhàng Rén (丈人) are two stars called Zǐ (子).
East of Zǐ (子) are two stars called Sūn (孫).
Southwest of Dōng Jǐng (東井) are four stars called Shuǐ Fǔ (水府),
officials who govern water.
East of the southern wall of Dōng Jǐng (東井) are four stars called Sì Dú (四瀆),
the essences of the Jiāng (江), Hé (河), Huái (淮), and Jì (濟) rivers.
Láng (狼) is one star,
southeast of Dōng Jǐng (東井).
Láng (狼) acts as a field general,
governing invasion and plunder.
Its color is usually fixed;
it is undesirable for it to move.
The northern seven stars are called Tiān Gǒu (天狗),
governing the protection of wealth.
Hú (弧) has nine stars,
southeast of Láng (狼).
It is the celestial bow,
governing the prevention of thieves and robbers,
always pointing towards Láng (狼).
If Hú Shǐ (弧矢) moves or shifts in an unusual way,
there will be many thieves and robbers,
and Xú (胡) troops will rise in great numbers.
If Láng (狼) and Hú (弧) are stretched,
harm reaches the Xú (胡),
and the empire is in disarray.
It is also said,
if the celestial bow is drawn,
the world will be filled with war.
South of Hú (弧) are six stars forming Tiān Shè (天社).
In ancient times, Gòng Gōng Shì (共工氏)’s son Gōu Lóng (句龍)
was able to pacify the waters and land,
so he was sacrificed to, paired with Shè (社),
and his essence became a star.
Lǎo Rén (老人) is one star,
south of Hú (弧).
One name for it is Nán Jí (南極).
It is usually seen in the east at dawn on the autumnal equinox,
and sets in the west at dusk on the vernal equinox.
When it appears, there is peace and order.
It governs longevity and prosperity.
It is always observed at the southern suburban altar on the autumnal equinox.
South of Liǔ (柳) are six stars called Wài Chú (外廚).
South of Chú (廚) is one star called Tiān Jì (天紀),
governing the ages of birds and beasts.
Jì (稷) has five stars,
south of Qī Xīng (七星).
Jì (稷)
is the official in charge of agriculture,
named after the chief of all grains.
South of Zhāng (張) are fourteen stars called Tiān Miào (天廟),
the ancestral temple of the Son of Heaven (天子).
If a guest star guards it,
the sacrificial officials will have worries.
South of Yì (翼) are five stars called Dōng Qū (東區),
the stars of the southern barbarians.
South of Zhěn (軫) are thirty-two stars called Qì Fǔ (器府),
the storehouse for musical instruments.
Qīng Qiū (青丘) has seven stars,
southeast of Zhěn (軫),
the national title of a barbarian state.
West of Qīng Qiū (青丘) are four stars called Tǔ Sī Kōng (土司空),
governing boundaries and territories,
also called Sī Tú (司徒).
North of Tǔ Sī Kōng (土司空) are two stars called Jūn Mén (軍門),
governing camp guards and the Tiger Tail (彪尾) banner.
The Rise and Set of Tiān Hàn (天漢)
Tiān Hàn (天漢) rises in the east,
passing between Wěi (尾) and Jī (箕),
and is called Hàn Jīn (漢津).
It then divides into two paths.
Its southern path passes through Fù Yuè (傅說), Yú (魚), Tiān Yuè (天籥), Tiān Biàn (天弁), and Hé Gǔ (河鼓).
Its northern path passes through Guī (龜),
penetrates below Jī (箕),
then links to Nán Dǒu Kuí (南斗魁) and Zuǒ Qí (左旗),
and merges with the southern path below Tiān Jīn (天津).
It then travels southwest,
again dividing to flank Páo Guā (匏瓜),
linking to Rén Xīng (人星), Chǔ (杵), Zào Fù (造父), Téng Shé (騰蛇), Wáng Liáng (王良), Fù Lù (傅路), the northern end of Gé Dào (閣道), Tài Líng (太陵), Tiān Chuán (天船), and Juǎn Shé (卷舌), then travels south,
linking to Wǔ Chē (五車),
passing south of Běi Hé (北河),
entering the water position of Dōng Jǐng (東井), and traveling southeast,
linking to Nán Hé (南河), Què Qiū (闕丘), Tiān Gǒu (天狗), Tiān Jì (天紀), and Tiān Jì (天稷),
south of Qī Xīng (七星), and then sets.
Degrees of the Twelve Xiù (十二次)
The twelve xiù (次).
Bān Gù (班固) matched the twelve xiù (次) of the Sān Tǒng Lì (三統曆) with the twelve yǎo (野),
and his words are the most detailed.
There are also Fèi Zhí (費直)’s explanation of the *Zhōu Yì* (周易) and Cài Yōng (蔡邕)’s *Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù* (月令章句),
whose statements sometimes differ in order.
Wèi (魏) Grand Astrologer Chén Zhuó (陳卓) further discussed the mansion degrees corresponding to commanderies and states.
[二一] Now they are appended and listed.
From Zhěn (軫) 12 degrees to Dī (氐) 4 degrees is Shòu Xīng (壽星).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Chén (辰).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Zhèng (鄭),
belonging to Yǎn Zhōu (兗州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直)’s *Zhōu Yì* (周易) yǎo (分野) states Shòu Xīng (壽星) begins at Zhěn (軫) 7 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕)’s *Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù* (月令章句) states Shòu Xīng (壽星) begins at Zhěn (軫) 6 degrees.)
From Dī (氐) 5 degrees to Wěi (尾) 9 degrees is Dà Huǒ (大火).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Mǎo (卯).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Sòng (宋),
belonging to Yù Zhōu (豫州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Dī (氐) 11 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Kàng (亢) 8 degrees.)
From Wěi (尾) 10 degrees to Nán Dǒu (南斗) 11 degrees is Xī Mù (析木).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Yín (寅).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Yān (燕),
belonging to Yōu Zhōu (幽州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Wěi (尾) 9 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Wěi (尾) 4 degrees.)
From Nán Dǒu (南斗) 12 degrees to Xū Nǚ (須女) 7 degrees is Xīng Jì (星紀).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Chǒu (丑).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Wú Yuè (吳越),
belonging to Yáng Zhōu (揚州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Dǒu (斗) 10 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Dǒu (斗) 6 degrees.)
From Xū Nǚ (須女) 8 degrees to Wēi (危) 15 degrees is Xuán Xiāo (玄枵).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Zǐ (子).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Qí (齊),

(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Nǚ (女) 6 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Nǚ (女) 2 degrees.)
From Wēi (危) 16 degrees to Kuí (奎) 4 degrees is Zōu Zī (諏訾).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Hài (亥).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Wèi (衞),
belonging to Bìng Zhōu (并州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Wēi (危) 14 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Wēi (危) 10 degrees.)
From Kuí (奎) 5 degrees to Wèi (胃) 6 degrees is Jiàng Lóu (降婁).
In terms of cyclical characters, it is Xū (戌).
It is the yǎo (分野) of Lǔ (魯),
belonging to Xú Zhōu (徐州).
(Fèi Zhí (費直) states it begins at Kuí (奎) 2 degrees.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) states it begins at Kuí (奎) 8 degrees.)
From Wèi 7 degrees to Bì 11 degrees is Dàliáng.
Its earthly branch is Yǒu.
It is the *fēnyě* of Zhào.
It belongs to Jìzhōu.
(Fèi Zhí,
starts from Lóu 10 degrees.
Cài Yōng,

From Bì 12 degrees to Dōngjǐng 15 degrees is Shíshěn.
Its earthly branch is Shēn.
It is the *fēnyě* of Wèi.
It belongs to Yìzhōu.
(Fèi Zhí,
starts from Bì 9 degrees.
Cài Yōng,
starts from Bì 6 degrees.)
From Dōngjǐng 16 degrees to Liǔ 8 degrees is Qúnshǒu.
Its earthly branch is Wèi.
It is the *fēnyě* of Qín.
It belongs to Yōngzhōu.
(Fèi Zhí,
starts from Jǐng 12 degrees.
Cài Yōng,
starts from Jǐng 10 degrees.)
From Liǔ 9 degrees to Zhāng 16 degrees is Qúnhuǒ.
Its earthly branch is Wǔ.
It is the *fēnyě* of Zhōu.
It belongs to Sānhé.
(Fèi Zhí,
starts from Liǔ 5 degrees.
Cài Yōng,
starts from Liǔ 3 degrees.)
From Zhāng 17 degrees to Zhěn 11 degrees is Qúnwěi.
Its earthly branch is Sì.
It is the *fēnyě* of Chǔ.
It belongs to Jīngzhōu.
(Fèi Zhí,
starts from Zhāng 13 degrees.
Cài Yōng,
starts from Zhāng 12 degrees.) Stellar Allotments of Provinces and Commanderies
