In Astronomical Treatise Chapter Two (Seven Luminaries, Miscellaneous Stellar Phenomena, Auspicious Stars, Ominous Stars, Guest Stars, Meteor Showers, Clouds and Vapors, Ten Luminosities, Miscellaneous Vapors, Historical Records and Verifications, Celestial Anomalies, Solar Eclipses and Lunar Changes, Lunar Occultations and Transgressions of the Five Planets, Conjunctions of the Five Planets)
Seven Luminaries
The sun is the essence of the great yang.
It presides over birth, nourishment, and benevolence.
It is the image of the sovereign.
If the sovereign has flaws,
they will inevitably reveal their evils to give a warning.
Therefore, when the sun and moon travel over a country ruled by the Dao, they are bright,
the sovereign is auspicious and prosperous,
and the populace is peaceful.
When the sovereign reigns by virtue of the element Earth,
and their governance is perfectly peaceful,
then the sun will display five colors without a dominant one.
If the sun changes color,
and there is an army,
the army will be defeated;
if there is no army,
a marquess or king will die.
If the sovereign is without virtue,
and their ministers bring chaos to the state,
then the sun will be red and without light.
If the sun loses its color,
the country it shines upon will not prosper.
If the sun is dim at noon,
travelers cast no shadows,
and it does not cease until dusk,
it indicates that punishments are severe at the top,
and the populace struggles to survive at the bottom.
Within a year, there will be great floods.
If the sun is dim at noon,
and crows and birds cry in flocks,
the state has lost its proper governance.
If crows are seen at midday,
the ruler is not clear-sighted,
and governance is chaotic.
The state will have an assembly of people in white clothing,
generals will emerge,
and banners and flags will be raised.
If there are black spots, black qi, or black clouds in the sun,
appearing sometimes three, sometimes five,
ministers will depose their sovereign.
A solar eclipse,
where yin invades yang,
is a sign of ministers overshadowing the ruler,
and there will be a state that perishes.
The moon is the essence of the great yin.
When it is paired with the sun,
it is the image of the empress.
When it is compared to virtue,
it signifies punishment.
When it is placed in the imperial court,
it represents the various marquesses and high ministers.
Therefore, if the ruler is enlightened,
the moon will follow its proper course;
if ministers usurp power,
the moon will deviate from its path;
if high ministers are in charge,
and military and penal affairs are handled improperly,
the moon will travel sometimes south, sometimes north;
if the empress or maternal relatives wield unauthorized power,
the moon will sometimes advance, sometimes retreat.
If the moon changes color,
there will be a disaster.
If the moon is bright during the day,
villainy and evil will arise concurrently,
the ruler and ministers will contend for power,
the empress will behave improperly,
the strength of the northern (yin) states will increase,
the central states will suffer famine,
and everyone under heaven will conspire to usurp.
If the moon is seen twice in a few months,
the state will fall into chaos and perish.
Suìxīng [Jupiter] is said to be the wood of the East and spring.
For people,
of the five constant virtues,
it is benevolence;
of the five affairs,
it is appearance.
If benevolence is lacking and appearance is lost,
going against the spring command [season],
and harming the wood qi,
then punishment will be seen in Suìxīng.
The waxing and waning of Suìxīng [Jupiter] [or its apparent forward and backward motion] determines the fate of the nations in its lodge.
If it stays long in a lodge,
that nation will have abundant virtue,
the five grains will be plentiful and prosperous,
and it cannot be attacked.
If it is opposite to a lodge,
that year there will be disaster.
If Suìxīng [Jupiter] is quiet and follows its proper course,
it is auspicious.
If its waxing and waning [or motion] is out of order,
that nation will have worries,
and should not undertake any ventures or deploy troops.
It also says,
it is the image of the human sovereign;
its color should be bright,
its light and color should be moist and lustrous,
and its virtue should be harmonious.
It also says,
if it advances and retreats according to its measure,
villainy and evil will cease;
if its color changes and its motion is disordered,
the sovereign will be without blessings.
It also presides over blessings,
presides over the grand minister of agriculture (Dàsīnóng),
presides over Qí [Qi] and Wú [Wu],
presides over the faults of all marquesses and sovereigns under heaven,
and presides over the five grains of the year.
If it is red and pointed,
its nation will prosper;
if it is reddish-yellow and dim,
its countryside will have a great harvest.
Yínghuò [Mars] is said to be the fire of the South and summer.
It is ritual,
it is sight.
If ritual is lacking and sight is lost,
going against the summer command [season],
and harming the fire qi,
then punishment will be seen in Yínghuò.
The law of Yínghuò [Mars] dictates that its movement is erratic.
When it emerges, there will be soldiers;
when it retracts, the soldiers disperse.
By its lodge, it determines the fate of nations,
bringing chaos and banditry,
sickness and death,
famine and war.
The nation it resides in will suffer disaster.
If it circles and forms a hook [Jǐ (己) character],
its rays and points shake,
its color changes,
sometimes forward, sometimes backward,
sometimes left, sometimes right,
its disaster will be even more severe.
In the south, men will die; in the north, women will die.
If it revolves and then stops,
it indicates death and mourning;
bandits will cause chaos in its countryside,
and territory will be lost.
If its movement is disordered and swift,
troops will gather beneath it.
Those who follow it will win battles.
It also says,
Yínghuò [Mars] presides over the Grand Usher (Dàhónglú),
presides over death and mourning,
and presides over the Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
It also acts as the Minister of War (Sīmǎ),
presiding over Chǔ [Chu], Wú [Wu], Yuè [Yue], and the regions to the south;
it also oversees the faults of all ministers under heaven,
oversees arrogance, extravagance, downfall, chaos, and calamities,
and presides over the success or failure of the year.
It also says,
if Yínghuò [Mars] is still,
troops will not fight,
and a general will be executed.
If its color is outstandingly red and furious,
and it retrogrades to form a hook [Jǐ (己) character],
battles will be ominous,
and armies will be besieged.
If it forms a hook [Jǐ (己) character],
with rays and points like a sharp blade,
the human sovereign should not leave the palace,
and there will be hidden troops below;
if the rays are large, the populace will be enraged.
It also represents governance.
Externally, it governs military affairs;
internally, it governs political affairs.
It is the governance of the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, it says,
even if there is an enlightened Son of Heaven,
he must observe the location of Yínghuò.
If it enters and guards or infringes upon Tàiwēi [Taiwei], Xuānyuán [Xuanyuan], Yíngshì [Yingshi], Fáng [Fang], or Xīn [Xin],
it portends an ill fate for the ruler.
Tiánxīng (Saturn) pertains to the center, mid-summer, earth,
trustworthiness,
and reflection.
Of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom,
trustworthiness is primary.
Of appearance, speech, sight, and hearing,
the mind is central.
Therefore, if the four stars (other planets) all go astray,
Tiánxīng moves for them.
If it moves and is full,
the marquises and kings will not be at peace.
If it shrinks,
an army will not return.
If it resides in a xù (lunar mansion),
the state is auspicious,
gaining territory and women,
having blessings,
and should not be attacked.
If it departs,
territory is lost,
or there is sorrow for women.
If it resides in a xù for a long time,
the state's blessings are abundant;
if it changes quickly, they are meager.
If it deviates from its proper position and moves two or three xù upward, it is called "full,"
indicating that the ruler's commands will not be accomplished,
or there will be great floods.
If it deviates from its proper position and moves downward, it is called "shrunken,"
indicating sorrow for the empress;
that year will not return to normalcy,
or there will be a crack in the sky or an earthquake.
Another saying:
Tiánxīng embodies the virtue of Huángdì,
and is the symbol of empresses and royal women.
It controls the pivot of thick virtue, peace, danger, existence, and demise,
and oversees the transgressions of empresses and royal women throughout the world.
Furthermore, it is said:
It is the star of the Son of Heaven.
If the Son of Heaven loses trustworthiness,
then Tiánxīng moves greatly.
Tàibái (Venus) pertains to the west, autumn, metal,
righteousness,
and speech.
If righteousness is deficient and speech is amiss,
going against the autumn order
and harming the metallic energy,
punishment is seen in Tàibái.
Tàibái's advance and retreat forecast military campaigns;
its height, lowness, slowness, speed,
stillness, agitation, appearance, and concealment
all symbolize the use of troops,
auspiciously.
If it appears in the west
out of its proper course,
the Yídí (barbarians) will be defeated.
If it appears in the east
out of its proper course,
Zhōngguó (China) will be defeated.
If it does not complete its period,
passing over the Tiān (Orion) constellation,
the opposing state will suffer.
If it traverses the sky,
the world will undergo a revolution,
and the people will change kings.
This is called a disruption of order,
and the populace will flee and disperse.
If it is seen during the day,
competing with the sun for brightness,
strong states will weaken,
small states will strengthen,
and empresses and royal women will prosper.
Furthermore, it is said:
Tàibái controls high ministers;
its title is Shànggōng.
The position of Dàsīmǎ (Grand Minister of War) should carefully observe this.
Chénxīng (Mercury) pertains to the north, winter, water,
wisdom,
and hearing.
If wisdom is deficient and hearing is amiss,
going against the winter order
and harming the watery energy,
punishment is seen in Chénxīng.
When Chénxīng appears,
it governs punishments,
the Tíngwèi (Minister of Justice),
and the states of Yān and Zhào,
also referring to Yān, Zhào, Dài, and the regions to their north;
it is the symbol of prime ministers.
It is also the energy of killing and conquering,
and the symbol of battles.
Furthermore, it is said:
If an army is in the field,
Chénxīng is the symbol of a subordinate general.
If there is no army, it signifies criminal matters.
If it harmonizes Yin and Yang,
its effects are sometimes effective and sometimes not;
at such times, there is disharmony.
If it appears out of its proper time,
and the cold and heat lose their regularity,
the state will suffer a great famine.
If it should appear but does not,
this is called "striking the soldiers,"
and a great war will break out.
If it is between Fáng and Xīn (Scorpio's head and heart),
there will be an earthquake.
It is also said:
Chénxīng's swift and agitated appearance and disappearance
always govern the Yídí.
Furthermore, it is said:
It is the star of the Mányí (southern barbarians) and
also governs the success or failure of penal laws.
If its color is yellow and it is small,
there will be a great earthquake.
If its brightness catches up with the moon,
that state will suffer great floods.
All five planets have colors and
different sizes,
each following its course and aligning with the seasons and their divisions.
If their colors change, there are classifications:
all green compares to the left shoulder of Cān (Orion),
red compares to the large star of Xīn (Antares),
yellow compares to the right shoulder of Cān,
white compares to Lángxīng (Sirius),
and black compares to the large star of Kuí (Andromeda).
If they do not lose their original color and respond to the four seasons,
it is auspicious.
If the color harms its course,
it is inauspicious.
When any of the five planets appears, moves, or is in direct alignment with a certain chén (celestial branch/lunar mansion),
that state is considered to have obtained its position.
Having obtained its position means:
Suìxīng (Jupiter) brings virtue,
Yínghuò (Mars) brings propriety,
Tiánxīng brings blessings,
Tàibái brings strong military,
and Chénxīng brings harmony of Yin and Yang.
When they move or are in direct alignment with a certain chén,
those that follow their color and have "horns" (points of light) win,
while those whose color harms them lose.
Residing in "real" (full) indicates
possessing virtue.
Residing in "empty" (deficient) indicates
lacking virtue.
Color overcomes position,
movement overcomes color,
and complete success is achieved when movement is obtained.
Yíngshì (Pegasus' Square) is the Pure Temple,
the temple of Suìxīng.
Xīn (Scorpio's heart) is the Bright Hall,
the temple of Yínghuò.
Nándǒu (Sagittarius) is the Grand Hall of Literature,
the temple of Tiánxīng.
Kàng (Virgo) is the Sparse Temple,
the temple of Tàibái.
Qīxīng (Ursa Major) is the Round Palace,
the temple of Chénxīng.
When the five planets reach their temples,
observe their commands carefully.
When any of the five planets is "full," "shrunken," or out of position,
their essence descends to earth as humans.
Suìxīng descends as noble officials;
Yínghuò descends as children,
singing songs and playing games;
Tiánxīng descends as old men and women;
Tàibái descends as strong men,
dwelling in forests and mountains;
Chénxīng descends as women.
The responses of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
follow their symbolic announcements.
Regarding the five planets:
When Jùpǐter and Sāturn conjoin,
it signifies internal strife
and famine.
When Jùpǐter and Mèrcury conjoin,
it signifies changing plans and altering affairs.
When Jùpǐter and Màrs conjoin,
it signifies famine
and drought.
When Jùpǐter and Vènus conjoin,
it signifies gatherings of common people (white-clad people),
conjunctions mean fighting,
the state will have internal strife,
there will be a defeated army in the countryside,
and it signifies floods.
When Vènus is in the south
and Jùpǐter is in the north,
this is called "female and male,"
and the year's grain harvest will be bountiful.
When Vènus is in the north
and Jùpǐter is in the south,
the year's harvest may or may not occur.
When Màrs and Vènus conjoin,
it signifies melting,
and mourning,
and it is not auspicious to undertake military campaigns.
If one follows the army,
it will cause military distress;
if one deviates from it,
the army will retreat.
If it emerges from the Yin side of Vènus,
territories will be divided;
if it emerges from its Yang side,
a partial general will fight.
When Màrs and Sāturn conjoin,
it signifies distress
and troubles for the chief ministers.
When Màrs and Mèrcury conjoin,
it signifies a northern army,
and undertaking military affairs will result in a great defeat.
One interpretation says:
When Màrs and Mèrcury conjoin,
it signifies scorching,
and it is not auspicious to undertake military campaigns.
When Sāturn and Mèrcury conjoin,
it signifies blockage and obstruction,
and it is not auspicious to undertake military campaigns;
there will be a defeated army and a demoted commander.
Another interpretation says:
It signifies changing plans and altering affairs,
and there will certainly be a drought.
When Sāturn and Vènus conjoin,
it signifies illness,
gatherings of common people,
internal military conflict,
and the state losing territory.
When Sāturn and Jùpǐter conjoin,
the state will suffer famine.
When Mèrcury and Vènus conjoin,
it signifies changing plans
and military distress.
If it enters the midst of Vènus and then exits upwards,
the army will be defeated, generals killed,
and the guest (invader) will win;
if it exits downwards,
the guest will lose territory.
Observe where the flag points
to determine the defeated army.
If it circles Vènus
as if fighting,
there will be a great battle,
and the guest will win.
Whenever Jùpǐter, Màrs, Sāturn, or Vènus fights with Mèrcury,
it all signifies battle.
If the troops are not external,
it all signifies internal strife.
Conjoining in the same constellation is called "hé" (合, conjunction);
overriding each other is called "dòu" (鬬, fighting).
If two stars are close,
the calamity is great;
if they are far apart,
there is no harm.
Calamity certainly occurs within seven cùn.
Whenever the moon eclipses one of the five planets,
that state will perish.
Jùpǐter signifies famine,
Màrs signifies chaos,
Sāturn signifies killing,
Vènus signifies a strong state waging war,
and Mèrcury signifies women causing chaos.
Whenever the five planets enter the moon,
if Jùpǐter,
there will be a banished minister in its corresponding territory;
if Vènus,
generals will be humiliated.
Wherever the five planets gather,
that state will become king,
and the world will follow.
Jùpǐter leads by righteousness,
Màrs leads by ritual,
Sāturn leads by gravity/importance,
Vènus leads by military might,
and Mèrcury leads by law;
each brings the world into submission according to its affairs.
If three stars conjoin,
this is called "startling establishment, absolute movement";
that state will have internal and external military conflict and mourning,
the common people will suffer hunger and destitution,
and a new marquise or king will be established.
If four stars conjoin,
this is called "great Yang";
in that state, military conflict and mourning will arise simultaneously,
the gentlemen will be worried,
and the common people will be displaced.
If five stars conjoin,
this is called "changing movement";
those with virtue will receive blessings,
a new king will be established,
he will seize control of the four directions,
and his descendants will flourish;
those without virtue will suffer calamity,
lose their state,
have their ancestral temples destroyed,
and the common people will depart,
spreading across the four directions.
If the five planets are all large,
the events will also be large;
if all are small,
the events will also be small.
Regarding the colors of the five planets:
If all are round:
white signifies mourning
and drought;
red signifies internal unrest
and military conflict;
green signifies worry
and floods;
black signifies epidemic disease
and many deaths;
yellow signifies auspiciousness.
If all are pointed (angled):
red
signifies an attack on our city;
yellow
signifies territorial disputes;
white
signifies sounds of weeping;
green
signifies military distress;
black
signifies floods.
If the five planets are of the same color,
the world will cease military activities,
the common people will be peaceful,
they will go about singing and dancing,
no disasters or illnesses will be seen,
and the five grains will flourish.
Regarding the five planets:
Jùpǐter:
If governance is lenient, it will not proceed;
if too strict, it will exceed its bounds;
if it moves in retrograde, it is an omen.
Màrs:
If lenient, it will not emerge;
if too strict, it will not enter;
if it deviates from its path, it is an omen.
Sāturn:
If lenient, it will not return;
if too strict, it will pass its dwelling;
if it moves in retrograde, it is an omen.
Vènus:
If lenient, it will not emerge;
if too strict, it will not enter;
if it moves in retrograde, it is an omen.
Mèrcury:
If lenient, it will not emerge;
if too strict, it will not enter;
if not at its proper time, it is an omen.
If the five planets do not deviate from their courses,
then the year's grain harvest will be abundant and prosperous.
Whenever the five planets gather in the center of the sky,
accumulating in the east,
it is advantageous for the central states;
accumulating in the west,
it is advantageous for foreign states engaged in military action.
If Mèrcury does not emerge,
Vènus acts as the guest (invader);
if it emerges,
Vènus acts as the host (defender).
If Mèrcury emerges and does not follow Vènus,
or if they each emerge from a different direction,
this is called "gé" (格, confrontation);
although there may be armies in the countryside,
there will be no battle.
When the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) appear or disappear, stay, move forward or backward, and vary in speed, in accordance with calendrical calculations,
it is considered their proper movement,
and governance is in harmony with the norm.
When they deviate from the calendar and err in their degrees,
losing their path and expanding or contracting,
it is considered irregular movement.
Irregular movements give rise to celestial arrows (tiānshǐ), comets (huì), and broom stars (bèi),
portending the downfall of states, changes in government,
and calamities of war, famine, mourning, and chaos.
Regarding miscellaneous stars (záxīng) and atmospheric phenomena (záxīngqì) –
the old sayings of the Celestial Sphere Charts (Túwěi)
and also from the end of the Hàn dynasty, when Liú Biǎo (劉表) was the Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he ordered Liú Ruì (劉叡), the Administrator of Wǔlíng (武陵), to compile a collection of celestial observations,
named the Jīngzhōu Zhān (荊州占).
The bodies of these miscellaneous stars
include auspicious stars (ruìxīng),
ominous stars (yāoxīng),
guest stars (kèxīng),
shooting stars (liúxīng),
auspicious qi (ruìqì),
ominous qi (yāoqì),
and qi phenomena alongside the sun and moon (rìyuè bàngqì).
Their names and descriptions are briefly stated,
and their divinatory validations are presented
sequentially here.
Auspicious Stars (Ruìxīng)
1. Jǐngxīng (景星), like a half-moon,
appears at the new and last quarters of the moon,
aiding the moon's brightness.
Some say
it is a large star with a hollow center.
Others say
there are three stars
in the red qi (chìfāngqì),
connected with the green qi (qīngfāngqì),
with a yellow star in the red qi;
it is also called Déxīng (德星).
2. Zhōubóxīng (周伯星), yellow in color,
shines brilliantly.
Its appearance portends great prosperity for the observed country.
3. Hányù (含譽), its light resembles a comet (huì),
when joyful, Hányù shoots.
4. Gézé (格澤), like a blazing fire,
large at the bottom and pointed at the top,
yellowish-white in color,
rising from the ground upwards.
Its appearance indicates harvests without sowing,
large earthworks,
and the arrival of an important guest.
Ominous Stars (Yāoxīng)
1. Huìxīng (彗星), also known as Sǎoxīng (掃星).
Its head resembles a star,
its tail a broom.
The small ones are several inches,
the long ones may span the sky.
Its appearance indicates the rise of wars
and great floods.
It presides over sweeping away,
removing the old and establishing the new.
It has five colors,
each corresponding to the essence of the Five Phases (Wǔxíng) it governs.
The imperial historians note:
A comet's (huì) body has no light;
it is illuminated by the sun.
Therefore, when seen in the evening, it points east;
when seen in the morning, it points west.
Whether it is north or south of the sun,
it always points with the sunlight.
Its radiance may be broken or bent,
long or short.
Wherever its light and radiance reach, there will be disaster.
2. Bèixīng (孛星), a type of comet (huì).
If it points in one direction, it is called Huì (彗);
if its radiating qi spreads in all four directions, it is called Bèi (孛).
Bèi (孛) means
extraordinary and strange;
it is born of evil qi.
If there is no great internal chaos,
then there will be great external warfare.
The world will conspire,
darkened and unclear,
and there will be harm.
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) said:
"If the lord does not change,
the Bèixīng (孛星) will appear;
what is there to fear from the Huìxīng (彗星)!"
From this, it is said
its disaster is worse than that of a comet (huì).
3. Tiānbàng (天棓), also named Juéxīng (覺星).
Its head resembles a star,
its tail is sharp and four zhàng long.
It may appear in the northeast or west,
presiding over fierce struggles.
4. Tiānqiāng (天槍).
Its appearance does not exceed three months,
and there will certainly be a state ruined, a ruler thrown into chaos,
and those guilty will die hidden deaths.
If the calamity is not exhausted,
it will lead to drought, famine, and sudden epidemics.
5. Tiānchán (天欃).
Shí Shì (石氏) said
it resembles a cow-shaped cloud.
Gān Shì (甘氏) said
its head resembles a star,
its tail is sharp.
Wū Xián (巫咸) said
a comet (huìxīng) appearing in the west,
two or three zhàng long,
presides over capture and control.
6. Chīyóuqí (蚩尤旗), resembles a comet (huì) but with a curved tail,
shaped like a flag.
Some say
it is a solitary red cloud.
Some say
its color is yellow at the top and white at the bottom.
Some say
it is like a planted rush, long,
named Chīyóu's flag.
Some say
it is like a winnowing basket,
can be two zhàng long,
with a star at the end.
It presides over punitive expeditions against injustice and rebellion,
and over confusion and chaos.
Wherever it is seen, there will be military conflict,
and great wars will break out;
otherwise,
there will be mourning.
7. Tiānchōng (天衝), appears like a person,
in blue clothes and a red head,
motionless.
Its appearance means ministers conspire against their lord,
soldiers rise up,
and the Son of Heaven perishes.
8. Guóhuáng (國皇), large and red,
resembles the Nánjí Lǎorén Xīng (南極老人星).
Some say
it is one or two zhàng from the ground,
like a torch,
presiding over internal banditry and internal difficulties.
Some say
that troops will rise up beneath it,
and the army will be strong.
Some say
there will be internal and external military conflicts and mourning.
9. Zhāomíng (昭明), its image is like Tàibái (太白),
radiant,
and stationary.
Some say
it is large and white,
without corners,
appearing sometimes high, sometimes low.
One account says,
a red comet (chìhuì) divides to become Zhāomíng (昭明),
Zhāomíng (昭明) extinguishes its light,
as a sign of the rise of hegemons (qíbà) and virtuous rulers (qídé).
The country where it appears will have many military changes.
Another account says,
it signifies great men's misfortune
and the outbreak of great wars.
10. Sīwēi (司危), like Tàibái (太白),
with an eye.
Some say
it appears directly in the west,
a wild star (yěxīng) of the west,
about six zhàng from the ground,
large and white.
Some say
it is large and hairy,
with two horns.
Some say
it resembles Tàibái (太白),
moving frequently.
If observed to be red,
it is a sign of discord and strife,
presiding over the defeat of strong armies.
Its appearance means the ruler loses the law,
heroes rise,
the Son of Heaven loses his country due to injustice,
and influential ministers assume the ruler's virtue.
Eleventh is Tiānchán.
A comet appears in the northwest,
shaped like a sword,
four or five zhàng long.
Some say
it is like a hook,
four zhàng long.
Some say
it is small and white in appearance,
moving frequently.
It portends slaughter and punishment.
When it appears, there is internal chaos in the state,
its subordinates slander each other,
there is famine and warfare,
a thousand lǐ of scorched earth,
and bones scattered everywhere.
Twelfth is Wǔcán,
also named Wǔfēng.
It appears in the due east,
an eastern star.
Its shape resembles Chén,
and it can be six or seven zhàng from the ground.
Some say
a dark comet disperses into Wǔcán,
like the Chén star,
appearing in Jué.
Some say
there is an aura around the star like a halo,
with bristles.
Some say
it is large and red,
moving frequently,
and when observed closely, it is blue.
It portends separation and destruction;
it is a five-fold division,
a sign of ruin and defeat,
and also signifies urgent military preparations.
When it is seen, it portends the execution of the ruler,
political power held by the hegemon (bó),
chaos in the countryside,
urgent military matters,
and mourning.
It is unfavorable for attacking.
Thirteenth is Liùzéi.
It is seen appearing in the due south,
a southern star.
It can be six zhàng from the ground,
large and red,
moving with light.
Some say
it is shaped like a comet.
When Wǔcán and Liùzéi appear,
calamity spreads throughout the world,
and rebellious forces invade crucial passes;
there are troops below it,
and attacking is unfavorable.
Fourteenth is Yùhàn,
also named Xiánhàn.
It appears in the due north,
a wild star of the north,
about six zhàng from the ground,
large and red,
moving frequently,
and when observed closely, it is blue inside.
Some say
it has a red surface,
with three comets below it, following horizontally and vertically.
It portends the banishment of the king,
and the assassination of the king.
When it appears, the yin essence is askew,
and troops rise below it.
It also portends mourning,
and its movement startles the feudal lords.
Fifteenth is Xúnshǐ.
It appears beside the Běidǒu,
like a rooster.
When it is agitated,
it has bluish-black colors,
resembling a crouching turtle.
Some say,
when agitated,
it is female,
and portends disputes and warfare.
It is also said
that a yellow comet divides into Xúnshǐ,
which is a sign for establishing a ruler,
portending chaos,
and inviting horizontal forces (disorder).
When it is seen, rebellious ministers incite warfare,
feudal lords are cruel,
and within ten years,
sages rise to punish,
and various villains run rampant.
Some say
that when it appears, the feudal lords crow like roosters.
Sixteenth is Tiānfēng,
a comet shaped like a spearhead.
When there is horizontal and vertical conflict in the world,
the Tiānfēng star appears.
Seventeenth is Zhúxīng,
like Tàibái.
When it appears, it does not travel,
and once seen, it soon disappears.
Some say
that above the main star, three comets appear pointing upwards.
Where it appears, cities and towns are in chaos,
there are great bandits who fail,
and it is also interpreted by its five colors.
Eighteenth is Péngxīng,
as large as two dòu containers,
white in color,
also named Wángxīng.
Its shape is like the light of a night fire,
often four or five,
sometimes one or two.
One says,
Péngxīng is in the southwest,
several zhàng long,
bright on both sides.
It appears and changes position.
When the star is seen,
within three years,
rebellious ministers are executed.
It is also said
that where it appears, there are great floods and great droughts,
the five grains are not harvested,
and people resort to cannibalism.
Nineteenth is Chánggēng,
like a bolt of cloth stretching across the sky.
When seen, warfare arises.
Twentieth is Sìtián.
A star appears in the four corners,
over six zhàng from the ground.
Some say it can be four zhàng.
Some say
the star is large and red,
two zhàng from the ground,
always appearing at midnight.
When seen,
warfare arises within ten months,
and it always leads to warfare in that area.
Twenty-first is Dìwéicángguāng.
It appears in the four corners.
Some say
it is large and red,
two or three zhàng from the ground,
like the moon when it first appears.
When seen, there is chaos below,
the chaotic perish,
and the virtuous prosper.
The Hétú says: The essence of Suìxīng
flows into Tiānbàng, Tiānqiāng, Tiānhuá, Tiānchōng, Guóhuáng, Fǎndēng,
and Cānghuì.
Yínghuò disperses into Zhāodàn, Chīyóuzhīqí, Zhāomíng, Sīwēi, Tiānchán, and Chìhuì.
Zhènxīng disperses into Wǔcán, Yùhàn, Dàfèn, Zhāoxīng, Chùliú, Xúnshǐ, Chīyóu, Hóngní, Jījìu, and Huánghuì.
Tàibái disperses into Tiānchǔ, Tiānfú, Fúlíng, Dàbài, Sījiān, Tiāngǒu, Tiāncán, Zúqǐ, and Báihuì.
Chénxīng disperses into Wǎngshǐ, Pò Nǚ, Fúshū, Mièbǎo, Ràotíng, Jīnglǐ, Dàfènsì, and Hēihuì.
The multi-colored comets
each have their length and shortness,
curving and bending according to their manifestations.
Jīng Fáng of the Hàn dynasty wrote the Fēngjiǎo Shū, which contains the Jíxīng Zhāng.
The ominous stars recorded therein all appear beside the moon,
interspersed with five-colored square clouds,
appearing on the Wǔyín days,
and each associated with the star from which they are born: Tiānqiāng, Tiāngēn, Tiānjīng, Zhēnrúo, Tiānyuán, Tiānlóu, Tiānyuán
are all born of Suìxīng.
They appear on Jiǎyín day,
and their stars each have two
green squares beside them.
Tiānyīn, Jìnruò, Guānzhāng, Tiānhuò, Tiāncuī, Chìruò, Chīyóu
are all born of Yínghuò.
They appear on Bǐngyín day,
and have two red
squares beside them.
Tiānshàng, Tiānfá, Cóngxīng, Tiānshū, Tiānzhái, Tiānfèi, Jīnghuì
are all born of Zhènxīng.
They appear on Wùyín day,
and have two yellow squares
beside them.
Ruòxīng, Sàoxīng, Ruòhuì, Zhúhuì, Qiángxīng, Yuánxīng, Báiguān
are all born of Tàibái.
They appear on Gēngyín day,
and have two white
squares beside them.
Tiānměi, Tiānchán, Tiāndù, Tiānmá, Tiānlín, Tiānhāo, Duānxià
are all born of Chénxīng.
They appear on Rényín day,
and have two black
squares beside them.
The thirty-five stars mentioned above
are born of the qi of the Wǔxíng (Five Phases),
all appearing within the square qi around the moon,
each according to when the star that birthed it is about to appear or not appear.
The sun is counted according to the celestial periods.
When it is seen before it emerges,
its appearance signifies floods and droughts,
wars and deaths,
famine and chaos.
What it points to means the fall of states,
loss of territory,
death of kings,
defeat of
armies,
and killing of generals.
Guest Stars
Zhāng Héng says:
"The four stars of Lǎozǐ, along with Zhōu Bó, Wáng Péngxù, and Ruì, each appear
interspersed among the five planets.
Their appearance has no fixed time,
and their movement has no fixed path."
A prognosticator from Jīngzhōu said:
"The Lǎozǐ star is a pure white color.
The state where it is seen
will suffer famine and misfortune,
good and evil,
joy and anger.
The Zhōu Bó star is bright yellow;
the state it reaches will greatly prosper.
The Péngxù star is green and shimmering;
the state it reaches will have irregular winds and rains,
scorching droughts,
plants will not grow,
the five grains will not ripen,
and there will be many locusts."
It also says:
"If three stars appear in the southeast,
named Dào Xīng,
their appearance means great bandits will appear in the world.
If three large stars appear in the southwest,
named Zhǒng Líng,
their appearance means the price of grain in the world will increase tenfold.
If three large, white stars appear in the northwest,
named Tiāngǒu,
their appearance means people will cannibalize each other,
a great misfortune.
If three large stars appear in the northeast,
named Nǚbó,
their appearance means there will be a great mourning."
Shooting Stars
Shooting stars
are messengers from Heaven.
Those that descend from above are called 'liú' (flowing);
those that ascend from below are called 'fēi' (flying).
Large ones are called 'bēn' (rushing);
'bēn' is also a type of shooting star.
Larger stars signify major events,
smaller stars signify minor events.
If there is a rumbling sound,
it is a sign of anger.
Those that move quickly indicate an imminent event;
those that move slowly indicate a delayed event.
Large and without light signifies
matters concerning the common people;
small and with light signifies
matters concerning noble people;
large and bright signifies
that the person is noble and has many followers.
Those that alternately brighten and dim signify
the success or failure of rebels.
Those that are large at the front and small at the back signify
fear and worry;
those that are small at the front and large at the back signify
joyful events.
Those that move like a snake signify
treacherous affairs;
those that move swiftly signify
going and not returning.
Long ones signify
that the event will be long-lasting;
short ones signify
that the event will be swift.
Where a 'bēn' star falls,
there will be war beneath it.
If there are no winds or clouds,
and a shooting star is seen,
lingering for a long time before disappearing,
it foretells a great wind
that will blow down houses and break trees.
If hundreds of small shooting stars move in all four directions,
it is a sign of the common people migrating.
Among the types of shooting stars,
if one has a sound like a torch falling to the ground,
and wild pheasants cry out,
it is a sign of Heaven's protection;
the state where it falls will be safe
and there will be joy.
If a small shooting star is greenish-red,
named Dìyàn,
where it falls, an army will rise.
If a shooting star is bright greenish-red,
two or three zhàng long,
named Tiānyàn,
it is the essence of an army;
in that state, an army will rise,
and the general should follow the direction of the star.
If a shooting star is brightly radiant,
its light is white,
and it stretches across the sky,
it is the star of the ruler of men;
the prime minister and general should follow the direction of the star.
If a flying star is as large as a fǒu or wèng,
bright white at the back,
lower at the front and higher at the back,
this is called Dùnwán;
those who follow it will suffer many deaths.
If a flying star is as large as a fǒu or wèng,
bright white at the back,
and after the star disappears,
the white part forms a curved ring like a chariot wheel,
this is called Jiěxián;
in that state, people will kill each other for titles and emoluments.
If a flying star is as large as a fǒu or wèng,
bright white at the back,
several zhàng long,
and after the star disappears,
the white part transforms into clouds and descends,
named Dàhuá;
where it descends, there will be flowing blood and piled bones.
Wǎngshǐ are
like shooting stars,
dark blue-black in color,
moving like a snake;
when looked at, they seem to have fur,
with eyes several pǐ long,
touching the sky.
They signify rebel sprouts,
and signify shooting at fools.
Their appearance means that rebellious armies will unite and be shot at and executed,
and also means using chaos to suppress chaos.
Tiāngǒu
has the appearance of a large 'bēn' star,
yellow in color,
with sound;
when it lands,
it resembles a dog.
Where it falls,
it looks like a fiery light,
flaming up to the sky,
sharp at the top,
round at the bottom,
like a place of several qǐng of fields.
Some say
the star has fur,
with short comets on the side,
and a dog shape underneath.
Some say
when the star appears,
its form is reddish-white and bright,
and its descent is Tiāngǒu.
One account says
a shooting star with light,
showing a human face,
falling silently,
as if with feet,
is named Tiāngǒu.
Its color is white,
yellow in the middle,
the yellow resembling a discarded fire.
It signifies awaiting an army to suppress rebels.
Its appearance means the four directions will attack each other,
and armies will be defeated and generals killed for a thousand lǐ.
Some say
the five generals will fight,
people will cannibalize each other,
and there will be flowing blood in the areas it goes to.
The ruler will lose territory,
a great army will rise,
the state's government will change,
and one should guard against attacks.
Yíngtóu:
A cloud like a falling broken mountain
is what is called the Yíngtóu star.
Where it falls,
armies below it will be overwhelmed,
and blood will flow for a thousand lǐ.
It is also said that a shooting star falling during the day is named Yíngtóu.
Cloud Qi
Auspicious *qì*: The first is called Qìngyún.
Like smoke yet not smoke,
Like cloud yet not cloud,
Lush and numerous,
Sparse yet coiled,
This is called Qìngyún,
Also called Jǐngyún.
This is a joyful *qì*,
An omen of great peace.
The second is called Guīxié.
Like a star yet not a star,
Like a cloud yet not a cloud.
Alternatively, it is said,
A star has two red comets pointing upwards,
With a canopy,
Connected below to the star.
When seen,
There will surely be someone returning to their country.
The third is called Chāngguāng,
Red,
Shaped like a dragon;
When a sage arises,
And an emperor accepts the mandate,
It appears.
Inauspicious *qì*: The first is called Hóngní,
A *qì* beside the sun,
A disordered essence of the Dǒu constellation.
It portends confused minds,
It portends internal debauchery,
It portends ministers plotting against their ruler,
The Son of Heaven will be humbled,
Empresses and consorts will monopolize power,
Wives will be disloyal.
The second is a cloud,
Like a dog,
Red in color,
With a long tail;
It portends a chaotic ruler,
It portends warfare and death.
The Ten Huī
In the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
The Jìn Shì held the methods of the Ten Huī,
To observe ominous and auspicious signs,
And distinguish good fortune from bad.
The first is called Jìn,
Refers to the *qì* of *yīnyáng* and the five colors,
Which infiltrates and encroaches upon each other.
Alternatively, it is said,
It belongs to phenomena like Bào'ěr and Bèiqióng,
Which are like rainbows but short.
The second is Xiàng,
Refers to cloud *qì* forming shapes,
Shaped like a red crow,
Such as flying beside the sun.
The third is Xī,
A *qì* beside the sun,
Piercing the sun,
Shaped like the bone awl worn by children.
The fourth is Jiān,
Refers to cloud *qì* approaching and being above the sun.
The fifth is Àn,
Refers to solar and lunar eclipses,
Or it is said to be the loss of light.
The sixth is Méng,
Refers to a dim and unbright appearance.
The seventh is Mí,
Refers to a white rainbow stretching across the sky and penetrating the sun.
The eighth is Xù,
Refers to *qì* resembling mountains and being above the sun.
Alternatively, it is said,
It is Guān'ěr and Bèiqióng,
Layered and sequential,
Located beside the sun.
The ninth is Jī,
Refers to halo *qì*.
Alternatively, it is said,
It is a rainbow,
As in the *Shī Jīng* which says
"In the morning, a rainbow rises in the west."
The tenth is Xiǎng,
Refers to *qì* of five colors with recognizable shapes,
Green signifies famine,
Red signifies warfare,
White signifies mourning,
Black signifies sorrow,
Yellow signifies harvest.
Alternatively, it is said,
Xiǎng,
Means to ponder,
Red *qì* takes the shape of a person hunting,
From which one can ponder and know its fortune or misfortune.
Whenever wandering vapor obscures the sky,
and the sun and moon lose their luster,
these are omens of wind and rain.
If the sky is heavily overcast,
and the sun and moon are both without light,
with no sun visible by day,
and no stars visible by night,
due to cloud obstruction,
then if two enemies are facing each other,
it indicates their clandestine plotting.
If the sun is dim and without luster,
it means internal strife among soldiers.
It is also said:
If several suns appear together,
as if fighting,
troops will rise throughout the land,
leading to a great war.
If the suns fight,
below there will be city-taking.
A "sun-bearer" (rì dài 日戴)
is a phenomenon that appears straight,
slightly raised above the sun,
which is called dài (戴) when it is above the sun.
Dài (戴)
signifies virtue,
and the state will have joy.
One account says,
"Standing on the sun is dài (戴)."
If a blue and red vapor embraces the sun from above,
a small one is called a "crown" (guān 冠),
and the state will have joyous events.
If a small blue and red vapor intersects below the sun, it is called a "tassel" (yīng 纓).
If blue and red vapors are small and round,
one or two appearing below or to the sides of the sun are called "buttons" (niǔ 紐).
If blue and red vapors resemble a small half-crescent,
appearing above the sun, it is called "bearing" (fù 負),
and "bearing" (fù 負) signifies gaining territory, which is auspicious.
It is also said:
If blue and red vapors are long and lean diagonally beside the sun, they are called a "halberd" (jǐ 戟).
If blue and red vapors are round and small,
appearing to the left or right of the sun, they are called "earrings" (ěr 珥);
if they are yellow and white, there will be joy.
It is also said:
If there is an army,
one "earring" (ěr 珥) on the sun is auspicious.
If it is to the west of the sun,
the western army will win.
If it is to the east of the sun,
the eastern army will win.
The same applies to north and south.
If there is no army and an "earring" (ěr 珥) appears,
it signifies appointment of a general.
Furthermore, if a half-ring appears beside the sun,
facing the sun, it is called "embracing" (bào 抱).
If blue and red vapors resemble a new moon,
appearing opposite the sun, it is called "turning away" (bèi 背).
It is also said:
If the "turning away" (bèi 背) vapor is blue and red and curved,
facing outwards, it is an omen of rebellion,
indicating cities turning rebellious.
Qióng (璚) resembles a sash;
qióng (璚) appears on all four sides of the sun.
If blue and red vapors are long and stand beside the sun, they are called "straight" (zhí 直).
If there is one "straight" (zhí 直) beside the sun,
it means an enemy on one side wishes to establish itself.
The one who attacks in the direction of the "straight" (zhí 直) will win.
If there are two "straights" (zhí 直) and three "embraces" (bào 抱) beside the sun,
those wishing to establish themselves will not succeed.
The one who attacks in accordance with the "embraces" (bào 抱) will win,
and generals will be killed.
If the vapor forms a triangle,
appearing on the four sides of the sun, it is called "lifting" (tí 提).
If blue and red vapors appear horizontally above and below the sun, they are called "blocking" (gé 格).
If the vapor is like a half-halo,
appearing below the sun, it is called "supporting" (chéng 承).
"Supporting" (chéng 承) signifies
a minister supporting the ruler.
It is also said:
If there are three layers of yellow vapor below the sun, like an embrace,
it is named "receiving blessings" (chéng fú 承福),
and the ruler will have auspicious joy,
and will gain territory.
If blue and white vapors resemble shoes,
appearing below the sun, they are called "shoes" (lǚ 履).
If the sun has five layers of "embraces" (bào 抱) around it,
battles fought in accordance with the "embraces" (bào 抱) will be victorious.
If the sun has one "embrace" (bào 抱) and one "turning away" (bèi 背),
it signifies a rout.
"Embracing" (bào 抱)
represents compliant qi (氣);
"turning away" (bèi 背)
represents contrary qi (氣).
When two armies face each other,
the one that attacks the contrary (nì 逆) based on the compliant (shùn 順) "embrace" (bào 抱) will win,
hence it is called a rout.
If the sun has an "embrace" (bào 抱) and two "earrings" (ěr 珥),
and a rainbow penetrates the "embrace" (bào 抱) reaching the sun,
the one who attacks in accordance with the rainbow will win,
and generals will be killed.
If the sun has an "embrace" (bào 抱), two "earrings" (ěr 珥), and a qióng (璚),
and two rainbows penetrate the "embrace" (bào 抱) reaching the sun,
the one who attacks in accordance with the rainbows will win.
If the sun has a double "embrace" (bào 抱),
with qióng (璚) inside,
the one who attacks in accordance with the "embrace" (bào 抱) will win.
It also means
there are those within the army who wish to rebel.
If the sun has a double "embrace" (bào 抱),
with two "earrings" (ěr 珥) on its sides,
and a white rainbow penetrates the "embrace" (bào 抱),
attacking in accordance with the "embrace" (bào 抱) will lead to victory,
and two generals will be captured.
If there are three rainbows,
three generals will be captured.
If the sun's "embrace" (bào 抱) is yellow and white and moist,
red inside and blue outside,
the Son of Heaven will have joy,
and amicable relations will be established with those who surrender;
the army will not fight,
the enemy will surrender,
and the army will be dismissed.
If the color is blue-yellow,
the general will be joyful;
if red,
generals will dispute over military matters;
if white,
the general will experience mourning;
if black,
the general will die.
If the sun has a double "embrace" (bào 抱) and a "turning away" (bèi 背),
the one who attacks in accordance with the "embrace" (bào 抱) will win,
gaining territory,
or there will be a dismissal of troops.
If the sun has a double "embrace" (bào 抱),
with qióng (璚) inside and outside the "embrace" (bào 抱),
and two "earrings" (ěr 珥),
the one who attacks in accordance with the "embrace" (bào 抱) will win,
breaking the army;
the army will be disharmonious,
and there will be no trust.
If there is qi (氣) beside the sun,
round and surrounding it,
red inside and blue outside,
it is called a "halo" (yùn 暈).
A solar "halo" (yùn 暈)
is an omen of military camps.
If it completely surrounds the sun,
without varying thickness,
the enemy and the army are equally matched.
If there is no army outside,
the Son of Heaven will lose control,
and many people will rebel.
If a solar "halo" (yùn 暈) has five colors,
there will be joy;
if it does not have five colors, there will be sorrow.
In all divinations,
when two armies face each other,
one must carefully observe the sun and moon's halos and vapors,
to know where they arise,
their distance of stay or movement,
whether they correspond or not,
their speed,
size,
thickness,
length,
how many "embraces" (bào 抱) or "turnings away" (bèi 背) there are,
presence or absence,
emptiness or fullness,
duration or brevity,
density or sparseness,
and moistness or dryness.
If they are equally matched, the forces are equal.
Nearness overcomes distance,
swiftness overcomes slowness,
largeness overcomes smallness,
thickness overcomes thinness,
length overcomes shortness,
"embrace" (bào 抱) overcomes "turning away" (bèi 背),
multitude overcomes scarcity,
presence overcomes absence,
fullness overcomes emptiness,
duration overcomes brevity,
density overcomes sparseness,
and moistness overcomes dryness.
A double "turning away" (bèi 背) means a great defeat;
a double "embrace" (bào 抱) means peace and alliance;
if there are many "embraces" (bào 抱),
there will be more allies;
"turning away" (bèi 背) signifies disharmony in the world.
Separation and departure:
"turning away" (bèi 背) within signifies separation within,
and "turning away" (bèi 背) without signifies separation without.
Miscellaneous vapors
The aura of the Son of Heaven:
red on the inside, yellow on the outside,
extending in all four directions.
Where it emanates, a king is destined to appear.
If the Son of Heaven wishes to travel to a place,
this aura will also first appear in that land.
Sometimes it resembles a city gate, dimly visible in the misty aura,
carrying a chilling, murderous intent.
Sometimes it resembles a huágài in the misty aura,
or an aura like a qīngyī person without hands,
appearing in the west at sunset.
Sometimes it resembles a dragon-horse,
or a variegated, luxuriant aura that shoots up into the sky.
These are all auras of an emperor or king.
The aura of a fierce general:
like a dragon,
or like a fierce beast;
or like fire and smoke;
or white like boiling powder;
or like a firelight,
illuminating people at night;
or white with a red aura surrounding it;
or like mountains, forests, bamboo, and trees;
or purple-black like a tower above a gate;
or black above and red below,
shaped like a black banner;
or like a drawn crossbow;
or like dust,
with a sharp, low top,
and a large, high base.
These are all auras of fierce generals.
When an aura gradually rises like a cloud,
transforming into a mountain shape,
there will be deep schemes.
Generally, the aura of a victorious army
is like a dike or a slope,
grinding the ground front and back.
Or like a firelight;
the general is brave,
and the soldiers are fierce.
Or like a mountain dike,
with what looks like trees on the mountain;
the generals and soldiers are valorous.
Or like dust boiling up,
its color yellow and white;
or like a person holding an axe facing the enemy;
or like a snake raising its head towards the enemy;
or an aura like an overturned boat,
and clouds like an ox being led;
or there are clouds like fighting cocks,
red and white accompanying each other,
within the aura;
or yellow aura emanates.
These all indicate spirited and brave generals and soldiers.
Generally, an aura that is yellow above and white below
is called a benevolent aura;
for the army it presides over,
the enemy will seek peace and retreat.
Generally, an aura of defeat
is like the color of a horse's liver,
or like a dead gray color;
or resembling an inverted canopy,
or resembling an inverted fish;
or black aura like a collapsing mountain falling onto the army.
This is called the aura of the camp commander.
Or like a flock of sheep or a herd of pigs
within the aura.
These are auras of decline.
Or like hanging clothes,
or people following each other;
or fluttering like rolling tumbleweeds,
or like scattering ashes;
or clouds like rolled mats,
or like tangled pieces of cloth.
These are all signs of defeat.
Aura like a tethered ox,
like a person lying down,
like two snakes,
like flying birds,
like a breached dike,
like a ruined house,
like startled deer chasing each other,
like two chickens facing each other.
These are all auras of a defeated army.
Generally, the aura of people surrendering
is like people in groups of ten or five,
all with clasped hands and bowed heads;
also, it is said,
like people clasping hands facing each other.
Or an aura like a black mountain,
edged with yellow.
These are all signs of impending surrender.
Generally, above a strong city,
if there are black clouds like stars,
it is called the essence of the army.
Or white aura like banners and flags,
or green clouds or yellow clouds over the city.
These all signify great joy and celebration.
Or an aura of green color like an ox's head butting people,
or an aura above the city like smoke and fire,
like two snakes,
like a pestle shape pointing outwards,
or clouds divided into two comet-like shapes.
These all mean the city should not be attacked.
Generally, the aura of a city to be massacred:
either red like flying birds,
or red aura like a broken chariot,
or red and black aura like a patterned civet cat skin;
or the aura within the city gathers like a tower,
visible from the outside;
if there are clouds above the camp like many human heads,
red in color.
Then that city and camp can all be massacred.
Aura like a male pheasant over the city.
Below it, there will certainly be those who surrender.
Generally, hidden troops have a black aura,
dense and long,
with red aura within it;
or white aura boiling up,
rising like a tower;
or like banners and pennants,
within dark clouds;
or like a red pestle in dark clouds,
or like a dark figure in red clouds.
Generally, the aura of an unexpected army:
white,
like interconnected melon vines,
troops chasing each other,
dispersing for a moment and then reappearing;
or white aura like xiānrén,
like xiānrén's robes,
thousands interconnected,
troops chasing each other,
dispersing and then rising again.
This means troops will come from a thousand lǐ away.
Or an aura like a person holding a knife and shield,
clouds like people,
red in color.
To the city or town it covers, sudden troops will arrive.
Or red aura like a person holding a staff of authority;
the troops coming will not cease.
Clouds like a square rainbow.
These are all signs of an unexpected army.
Generally, the aura of battle:
green and white like fat;
like a person without a head;
like a dead person lying down;
like a red snake,
with red aura accompanying it.
There will certainly be a great battle,
and generals will be killed.
If there are no clouds in all four directions,
and a red aura like a dog enters the camp,
there will be flowing blood beneath it.
Generally, if it is continuously overcast for ten days,
the sun is not seen during the day,
the moon is not seen at night,
chaotic winds rise in all four directions,
threatening rain but without rain.
This is called méng,
and ministers are plotting.
Mist-like aura, whether day or night,
its color green and yellow,
covering each other,
sometimes gathering, sometimes dispersing.
The same applies.
If one consistently sees large clouds of five colors in all four directions,
beneath them, a worthy person is in hiding.
Green clouds, moist and thick, obscuring the sun,
in the northwest.
This indicates the promotion of the worthy and good.
Cloud aura like tangled straw.
A great wind is coming.
Observe its direction of origin.
Clouds that are very moist and thick.
A heavy rain will certainly arrive suddenly.
On the day of the Four Beginnings,
if there is a black cloud aura like an army formation,
thick, large, and heavy.
There will be much rain.
Aura like mist but not mist,
clothes and hats not getting wet.
When seen, the city will arm itself and rush forth.
If there are misty clouds horizontally crossing the sun at sunrise and sunset,
white ones signify mourning,
black ones signify alarm.
If it rains within three days, these will each resolve.
If there are clouds like a jiāolóng,
wherever they are seen, the general will lose his composure.
If there are clouds like a swan's tail coming to overshadow the state,
the state will perish in three days.
If there are clouds of reddish-yellow color filling all four directions,
illuminating the ground all day and night.
High officials are acting unrestrainedly.
If there are clouds like an aura,
dim and turbid.
Worthy people will leave,
and petty people will be in office.
All white rainbows
are the root of a hundred calamities,
the foundation of all disorders.
Fog
is the vapor of all邪 (xié) influences,
Yīn (yīn) coming to obscure Yáng (yáng).
Whenever there is a white rainbow or fog,
treacherous ministers conspire against the sovereign,
usurping power and establishing authority.
Fog by day and brightness by night
means ministers' ambitions are realized.
Whenever night fog and a white rainbow appear,
ministers have worries;
whenever day fog and a white rainbow appear,
the sovereign has worries.
If the head and tail of a rainbow reach the ground,
it is an omen of bloodshed.
Whenever fog and vapor do not conform to the four seasons,
and are disordered and intertwined,
with light breezes and small rain,
it is an omen of chaotic Yīn (yīn) and Yáng (yáng) energies.
If it accumulates for days without dissipating,
and day and night are dim and obscure,
the empire is on the verge of separation.
Whenever the heavens, earth, and four directions are dim and hazy as if dust is falling,
for five days or more,
or a month,
or a season,
and the rain does not dampen clothes but contains earth,
it is called mài (mái).
Hence it is said,
"When the heavens and earth are hazy (mái),
sovereign and ministers are estranged (guāi)."
Whenever vapors by the sea resemble terraces,
and vapors in vast plains form palaces,
the vapors of the northern Yí (yí) resemble herds of cattle and sheep and felt tents,
and the vapors of the southern Yí (yí) resemble boats and banners.
South of Huá (huá),
the vapors are black below and red above;
in the vicinity of Sōnggāo (Sōnggāo) and Sānhé (Sānhé),
the vapors are pure red;
north of the mountains,
the vapors are green;
between Bójié (Bójié) and Hǎidài (Hǎidài),
the vapors are all pure black;
between the Jiāng (Jiāng) and Huái (Huái) rivers,
the vapors are all white;
the vapors of the Eastern Sea resemble a round umbrella;
near the Hàn (Hàn) River,
the vapors resemble unrolled cloth;
the vapors of the Jiāng (Jiāng) and Hàn (Hàn) are strong like a loom shuttle;
the vapors of the Jǐ (Jǐ) River are like black…
the vapors of the Wèi (Wèi) River are like a wolf with a white tail;
the vapors of Huáinán (Huáinán) are like white sheep;
the vapors of Shàoshì (Shàoshì) are like white rabbits with green tails;
the vapors of Mount Tài (Tài) are like black oxen with green tails.
The vapors of the Eastern Yí (yí) resemble trees;
the vapors of the Western Yí (yí) resemble houses;
the vapors of the Southern Yí (yí) resemble watchtowers,
or are like boats.
Battle clouds are like standing walls.
Shuttle clouds resemble an axle,
coiled,
with pointed ends.
Dipper clouds are like a rope,
stretching across the sky in front,
half of them covering half the sky;
those that are segmented resemble fragmented banners.
Hook clouds are curved.
Whenever these clouds appear,
omens are divined by their five colors.
If the clouds are dense and cohesive,
and their appearance stirs people,
then war will certainly arise,
〔一０〕and battles will be fought directly.
Vapors resembling three bolts of silk,
wide in front and narrow behind,
are the qi (qì) of a large army on the march.
Hán (Hán) clouds resemble cloth;
Zhào (Zhào) clouds resemble oxen;
Chǔ (Chǔ) clouds resemble the sun;
Sòng (Sòng) clouds resemble chariots;
Lǔ (Lǔ) clouds resemble horses;
Wèi (Wèi) clouds resemble dogs;
Zhōu (Zhōu) clouds resemble chariot wheels;
Qín (Qín) clouds resemble traveling pedestrians;
Wèi (Wèi) clouds resemble mice;
Zhèng (Zhèng) clouds resemble crimson robes;
Yuè (Yuè) clouds resemble dragons;
Shǔ (Shǔ) clouds resemble granaries.
The qi (qì) of chariots is sometimes high, sometimes low,
gathering here and there.
The qi (qì) of cavalry is low and dispersed.
The qi (qì) of infantry is condensed.
When the front is low and the rear is high,
it indicates speed.
When the front is square and high, and the rear is pointed and low,
it indicates retreat.
When the qi (qì) is level, its movement is slow.
When the front is high and the rear is low,
it indicates stopping and returning.
The qi (qì) of elite cavalry
is pure dark green and black,
hundreds of zhàng (zhàng) long.
The qi (qì) of roving troops resembles a broom-like comet,
sometimes hundreds of zhàng (zhàng) long,
without a root.
Joyful qi (qì) is yellow above and red below;
angry qi (qì) is red above and below;
worried qi (qì) is black above and below.
Qi (qì) of earthworks is yellow and white.
Qi (qì) of migration is white.
The method for observing qi (qì)
is that when the qi (qì) first emerges,
it is like a cloud yet not a cloud,
like fog yet not fog,
vaguely visible.
When it first emerges, it is dense and luxuriant,
above mulberry and elm trees,
five or six chì (chǐ) high,
which means it is one thousand five hundred lǐ (lǐ) away.
Looking level, it is a thousand lǐ (lǐ);
looking up, it is five hundred lǐ (lǐ);
looking up at the middle of the sky,
it is within a hundred lǐ (lǐ).
Looking level,
between mulberry and elm trees is two thousand lǐ (lǐ);
ascending to a height and looking,
that which extends to the ground
is three thousand lǐ (lǐ).
If the enemy is to the east,
observe it at sunrise;
if to the south,
observe it at midday;
if to the west,
observe it at sunset;
if to the north,
observe it at midnight.
For an army's qi (qì),
high overcomes low,
thick overcomes thin,
solid overcomes empty,
long overcomes short,
moist overcomes dry.
If the qi (qì) is seen, one knows its magnitude,
and if during the period of observation there is a great wind and rain,
or prolonged overcast weather,
then the disaster will not form.
Historical Records: Verification of Celestial Changes
In the second month of the second year of Yuánkāng (Yuánkāng) of Emperor Huì (Huì),
the sky split greatly in the northwest.
According to Liú Xiàng's (Liú Xiàng) explanation:
"A split in the sky
means insufficient Yáng (yáng);
an earthquake
means excessive Yīn (yīn)."
At that time, the ruler was dim-witted,
and empresses and consorts wielded exclusive power.
In the eighth month, gengwǔ (gēngwǔ) day, of the second year of Tài'ān (Tài'ān),
〔一一〕the sky split in the middle into two,
with three sounds like thunder.
This was an omen of the sovereign's path being deficient and his ministers usurping power.
On that day,
〔一二〕Wáng (Wáng) of Chángshā (Chángshā) escorted the emperor to confront the Two Wáng (Wáng) of Chéngdū (Chéngdū) and Héjiān (Héjiān);
later, the Wáng (Wáng) of Chéngdū (Chéngdū), Héjiān (Héjiān), and Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi) successively monopolized authority and commands,
which was the fulfillment of this omen.
On the night of the jǐmǎo (jǐmǎo) day in the eighth month of the fifth year of Shēngpíng (Shēngpíng) of Emperor Mù (Mù),
the sky split in the middle,
three or four zhàng (zhàng) wide,
with a sound like thunder,
and all wild pheasants cried out.
Thereafter, Emperor Āi (Āi) suffered from illness,
Hǎixī (Hǎixī) lost virtue,
the Empress Dowager held court,
Tàizōng (Tàizōng) managed all affairs,
Huán Wēn (Huán Wēn) monopolized power,
his prestige shaking both inside and outside the court,
Yīn (yīn) energy was strong,
and Yáng (yáng) energy was weak.
On the wùxū (wùxū) day in the eighth month of the second year of Tàixīng (Tàixīng) of Emperor Yuán (Yuán),
the sky thundered in the southeast,
with a sound like wind and water clashing.
Jīng Fáng's (Jīng Fáng) Yìyāo Zhān (Yìyāo Zhān) states:
"When the sky makes a sound,
the ruler has worries."
In the tenth month, rénchén (rénchén) day, of the third year,
the sky thundered again,
stopping on the jiǎwǔ (jiǎwǔ) day.
Thereafter, Wáng Dūn (Wáng Dūn) entered Shítóu (Shítóu),
and the imperial army was defeated.
Emperor Yuán (Yuán) was humiliated,
controlled by powerful ministers,
and soon after died,
his great shame unavenged.
In the intercalary month, *guǐchǒu* day, of the 5th year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān,
the sky roared in the southeast.
In the 9th month, *wùzǐ* day, of the 6th year,
the sky roared again in the southeast.
After this, Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
Emperor Ān was exiled,
and there was no greater sorrow.
The roaring always came from the southeast,
presumably because the restoration was south of the Yangtze,
and Heaven roared in response.
In the 8th month of the 1st year of Yìxī,
the sky roared,
in the southeast.
The *Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
“When the myriad common people are toiling,
the omen is the sky roaring.”
At this time, although Emperor Ān had returned to his rightful place,
wars continued year after year,
and the populace was suffering and toiling.
Solar Eclipses
In the 6th month, *wùchén* day, the last day of the month, of the 2nd year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
there was a solar eclipse.
The officials concerned proposed dismissing the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
but an imperial edict said:
“Calamities and anomalies arise
to admonish the sovereign,
yet faults are attributed to the chief ministers (gǔgōng);
how can this be the meaning of Yǔ and Tāng blaming themselves?
Let all officials diligently perform their duties.
Henceforth, should there be celestial or terrestrial omens,
do not again impeach the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng).”
In the 1st month, *bǐngyín* day, the first day of the month, of the 3rd year,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the 11th month, *gēngshēn* day, the last day of the month,
there was again a solar eclipse.
In the 11th month, *wùshēn* day, the last day of the month, of the 5th year,
there was a solar eclipse.
At the beginning of the Tàihé era of Emperor Míng,
the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng) Xǔ Zhī reported that
a solar eclipse was due,
and proposed praying and averting misfortune at the Lingtai with the Grand Commandant.
The Emperor said:
“I have heard that when the ruler’s governance lacks virtue,
Heaven frightens them with calamities and anomalies,
thereby admonishing and instructing them
to cultivate themselves.
Thus, when the sun and moon are eclipsed,
it clearly indicates that the way of governance is improper.
Since I ascended the throne,
I have been unable to illuminate the sagely virtue of the former emperors,
and my policies have not been in harmony with the august spirits,
therefore, High Heaven has used this to awaken me.
I ought to rectify my governance and cultivate myself,
to respond to the gods and spirits.
Heaven's relationship with man
is like a father's relationship with his son.
There has never been a father who wishes to reprimand his son,
but can be appeased by offerings of rich food to seek exemption.
Now, to want to send a high-ranking duke with the Grand Astrologer to perform averting sacrifices,
I have never heard of such a practice in terms of righteousness.
All dukes, ministers, and grandees,
each of you should strive to fulfill your duties.
If there is anything that can compensate for my shortcomings,
each of you should seal and present it.”
In the 11th month, *wùxū* day, the last day of the month, of the 5th year of Tàihé,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the 1st month, *wùchén* day, the first day of the month, of the 6th year,
there was a solar eclipse.
Seen in the *Wú Lì*.

〔一四〕there was a solar eclipse.
In the 10th month, *wùshēn* day, the first day of the month,
there was again a solar eclipse.
In the 2nd month, *gēngwǔ* day, the first day of the month, of the 8th year,
there was a solar eclipse.
At this time, Cáo Shuǎng wielded exclusive power,
and Dīng Mì, Dèng Yáng, and others frequently altered laws and regulations.
There occurred a solar eclipse anomaly,
and an edict commanded ministers to inquire about gains and losses.
Jiǎng Jì submitted a memorial saying:
“Formerly, when Great Shùn assisted in governance,
he warned against forming cliques.
When Duke of Zhōu assisted in government,
he was cautious about his companions.
When the Marquis of Qí asked about calamity,
Yànzǐ responded by advocating the distribution of beneficence;
When the Lord of Lǔ asked about anomalies,
Zāng Sūn replied by suggesting the easing of corvée labor.
To avert changes and respond to Heaven,
these are truly human affairs.”
Jiǎng Jì's analogy was extremely poignant,
but the ruler and his ministers did not comprehend,
ultimately leading to defeat and destruction.
In the 1st month, *yǐwèi* day, the first day of the month, of the 9th year,

In the 2nd month, *jǐwèi* day, the first day of the month, of the 1st year of Jiāpíng,

the ruler is weak and ministers are strong.
Sīmǎ will lead troops,
to rebel against their king.”
In the 5th month,
there was the incident of Chéng Jì.

from Mǎo to Dǒu.
Dǒu
is the celestial division of Wú.
Thereafter, Sū Jùn caused a rebellion.
In the second year of Xián-Hé of Emperor Chéng, on the *jiǎ-shēn* day of the fifth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in Jǐng (Well) mansion.
Jǐng
rules over wine and food,
and it is also an omen for the empress.
The following year,
the Empress Dowager passed away from sorrow.
In the sixth year, on the *rén-xū* day of the third month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
At this time, the Emperor was already of age,
but whenever he visited Sī-Tú Wáng Dǎo’s residence,
he still paid respects to Wáng Dǎo’s wife, Lady Cáo, as if she were a senior relative to a junior.
For a ruler to show such deference to the wife of his minister
was an omen of a deficiency in imperial virtue.
In the ninth year, on the *yǐ-wèi* day of the tenth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
[一九]At this time, the Emperor had already come of age (performed the capping ceremony),
and ought to have personally attended to all affairs of state,
yet he delegated governance to his great ministers,
indicating a deficiency in the way of a ruler.
In the first year of Xián-Kāng, on the *yǐ-wèi* day of the tenth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.

there was a solar eclipse.
In the third month,
Empress Dù passed away.
In the eighth year, on the *yǐ-wèi* day of the first month, the first day of the lunar month,
[二０]there was a solar eclipse.
Heavy rain fell in the capital,
and the commanderies and states reported it.
This is called “three morning eclipses,”
which rulers dread.
Six months later, the Emperor passed away.
In the second year of Yǒng-Hé of Emperor Mù, on the *jǐ-yóu* day of the fourth month,
[二一]in the seventh year, on the *dīng-yóu* day of the first month,
and in the eighth year, on the *xīn-mǎo* day of the first month,
there were all solar eclipses.
In the twelfth year, on the *guǐ-sì* day of the tenth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse,
in Wěi (Tail) mansion.
Wěi
is the division of Yān,
an omen for the Northern Dí.
At this time, Yáo Xiāng and Fú Shēng on the frontier borders were devouring each other,
causing worry and toil for the court,
and military campaigns were incessant.
In the fourth year of Shēng-Píng, on the *xīn-chǒu* day of the eighth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was almost entirely within Jiǎo (Horn) mansion.
For all eclipses,
shallow ones portend minor misfortunes,
and deep ones portend great misfortunes.
Jiǎo is the Gate of Heaven,
which rulers dread.
The following year, the Emperor passed away.
In the first year of Lóng-Hé of Emperor Āi, on the *jiǎ-yín* day of the third month, the first day of the lunar month,
[二二]and on the *wù-wǔ* day of the twelfth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there were both solar eclipses.
The following year, the Emperor fell ill,
and was unable to attend to affairs of state.

and in the fifth year, on the *guǐ-yóu* day of the seventh month, the first day of the lunar month,
there were both solar eclipses.
These were all portents for the deposition of Hǎi-Xī.
In the third year of Níng-Kāng of Emperor Xiào-Wǔ, on the *guǐ-yóu* day of the tenth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the fourth year of Tài-Yuán, on the *jǐ-yóu* day of the intercalary month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
At this time, Fú Jiān attacked and captured Xiāng-Yáng,
and seized Zhū Xù.
In the sixth year, on the *gēng-zǐ* day of the sixth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the ninth year, on the *xīn-hài* day of the tenth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.

there was a solar eclipse.

there was a solar eclipse.
The following year, the Emperor passed away.
In the fourth year of Lóng-Ān of Emperor Ān, on the *gēng-chén* day of the sixth month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
At this time, Yuán Xiǎn was in charge of government.
In the second year of Yuán-Xīng, on the *guǐ-sì* day of the fourth month, the first day of the lunar month,

In the third year of Yì-Xī, on the *wù-xū* day of the seventh month, the first day of the lunar month,

The following year,
the Emperor passed away.
In the first year of Yuán-Xī of Emperor Gōng, on the *dīng-hài* day of the eleventh month, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
From the first year of Yì-Xī until this time,
solar eclipses all began from the top (of the sun),
all being omens of revolution.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states that the *Shì-Jìn-Shì* (Officer in Charge of Celestial Omens) was responsible for the ten *huī* (lustres) methods,
to observe strange and auspicious phenomena,
and discern good and bad fortune.
There are *jìn*, *xiàng*, *xuán*, *jiān*, *àn*, *méng*, *mí*, *xù*, *qī*, and *xiǎng*, totaling ten.
Later generations changed their names,
and commentators did not agree.
Now, we record those with clear correspondences in order, it is said.
In the second month of the eleventh year of Chì-Wū of Sūn Quán of Wú,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
Sūn Quán issued an edict expressing fear and caution.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Tài-Shǐ of Emperor Wǔ, on the *jiǎ-yín* day,
a double solar halo appeared,
and a white rainbow pierced it.
In the first month of the first year of Tài-Kāng, on the *jǐ-chǒu* day, the first day of the lunar month,
a five-colored aura crowned the sun,
from *mǎo* (5-7 AM) to *yóu* (5-7 PM).
The prognostication stated:
"The way of the ruler has lost its brilliance.
*Chǒu* (ox, second earthly branch) signifies Dǒu (Dipper) and Niú (Ox) mansions,
which rule over Wú and Yuè."
At this time, Sūn Hào was debauched and tyrannical,
and he surrendered in the fourth month.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Yuán-Kāng of Emperor Huì, on the *jiǎ-shēn* day,
there was a solar halo,
double,
blue-red and luminous.
In the first month of the ninth year,
something like a flying swallow appeared in the sun,
which dissipated after several days.
Wáng Yǐn considered it an omen for the deposition and death of Mǐn-Huái.
In the first month of the first year of Yǒng-Kāng, on the *guǐ-hài* day, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar halo,
triple.
In the tenth month, on the *yǐ-wèi* day,
the sun was darkened,
and yellow fog filled all four directions.
The prognostication stated:
"Within three years,
there will be a great battle below with cities taken."
In the twelfth month, on the *gēng-xū* day,
there was black qi in the sun.
The *Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn* states:
"If sacrifices to Heaven are not compliant, this is called rebellion,
its omen is black qi in the sun."
In the ninth month of the first year of Yǒng-Níng, on the *jiǎ-shēn* day,
there was a black spot in the sun.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhàn* states:
"Black is *yīn*;
if ministers do not conceal the ruler's flaws,
allowing them to be seen by those below,
and the common people dislike the ruler,
then this change will occur."
It also states:
"Ministers have obscured the ruler's brilliance."
In the eleventh month of the first year of Tài-Ān,
there was black qi in the sun.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Yǒng-Xīng,
there was black qi in the sun, dividing the sun.
In the fifth month of the first year of Guāng-Xī, on the *rén-chén* and *guǐ-sì* days,
the sunlight scattered in all directions,
red like flowing blood,
illuminating the ground all red.
On the *jiǎ-wǔ* day, it was also like this.
The prognostication stated:
"The way of the ruler has lost its brilliance."
In the eleventh month, *yǐhài* day, of the first year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái's [reign],
a yellow and black *qì* obscured the sun.
Everything it shone upon turned yellow.
According to the divination in the *Hétú*, it says:
"The sun is obscured."
Its explanation says:
"All solar eclipses occur on the first or last day of the lunar month.
If it does not occur on the last or first day of the month, it is an 'obscuration of the sun.'
Although it is not when the sun and moon are in conjunction,
it is when the *yīn* *qì* is strong,
obscuring the sunlight."
Its divination is similar to a solar eclipse.
In the first month, *wùshēn* day, of the second year,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
In the second month, *guǐmǎo* day,
a white rainbow pierced the sun,
with a greenish-yellow halo,
fivefold.
The divination says:
"When a white rainbow pierces the sun,
close ministers will cause chaos,
or else the feudal lords will rebel.
A fivefold halo
means that those who possess states will receive its good omen,
but there will be wars in the world,
and their lands will be destroyed and lost."
The next year,
Sīmǎ Yuè became tyrannical and disrespectful towards the sovereign.
In the fifth year,
Liú Cōng destroyed the capital,
and the emperor was disgraced in the enemy's court.
In the third month, *gēngshēn* day, of the fifth year,
the sun scattered light,
flowing down like blood,
and everything it shone upon was red.
Within the sun, there was something like a flying swallow.
In the first month, *xīnwèi* day, *chénshí* (7-9 AM), of the second year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn's [reign],
[二三]the sun fell to the ground.
Also, three suns appeared in succession,
rising from the west and moving eastward.
In the first month, *gēngzǐ* day, of the fifth year,
three suns shone together,
and a rainbow [*hóngní*] filled the sky.
The sun had a double halo,
with two ears on either side.
The divination says:
"A white rainbow
is the *qì* of war.
When three, four, five, or six suns appear together and contend,
wars will break out in the world,
and *dīngsì* is also among their numbers."
[二四]It also says:
"When three suns appear together,
within three *xún* (30 days),
feudal lords will contend for emperorship.
A double halo on the sun
means there will be established kings in the world.
A halo with ears
means there will be established marquises in the world."
Therefore, Chén Zhuó said:
"There will be great celebrations,
and the world will be divided into three!"
Three months later, Jiāngdōng changed its era name to Jiànwǔ,
and Liú Cōng and Lǐ Xióng also encroached upon the territories of Cáo and Liú.
Thus, wars continued for generations.
In the eleventh month, *yǐmǎo* day, of the first year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán's [reign],
the sun appeared at night,
three *zhàng* high,
with red and green ears within it.
In the second month, *guǐhài* day, of the fourth year,
the sun fought.
In the third month, *guǐwèi* day,
there was a black spot in the sun.
[二五]On *xīnhài* day,
the emperor personally investigated and interrogated prisoners.
[二六]
In the tenth month, *xīnmǎo* day, of the first year of Yǒngchāng,
there was a black spot in the sun.
At that time, the emperor favored Liú Wèi,
who wielded power and authority,
damaging the imperial way.
Wáng Dūn thereupon raised an army,
approaching the capital,
and the disaster affected loyal and virtuous officials.
