Collation Notes
Treatise Six: The Calendar, Part One
The Yì says:
"That which is above forms is called the Dào;
that which is below forms is called a tool."
Indeed, the divine Dào is vast and great,
its wondrous essence rooted in Yīn and Yáng;
the forms and tools are subtle and refined,
their meaning preceding the Lǜ and Lǚ.
The Sages observed the changes of the four seasons,
carving jade to record their waxings and wanings;
they examined the sounds of the five elements,
casting metal to balance their clarity and turbidity.
This was how they brought about the eight winds and promulgated the nine virtues,
harmonizing great music to perfect the way of governance.
However, metal, being moldable,
has no fixed measure for its expansiveness or contraction;
bamboo, being round and hollow,
is easily regulated in length and shortness.
Therefore, Shéngǔ created the Lǜ,
using them to transcribe the sounds of bells.
They were recorded in threes,
balanced in sixes,
and completed in twelves—
this is the Way of Heaven.
Furthermore, they aligned the seasons and days with sundial measurements,
and tested the earthly qi with ash tubes.
Thus, when Yīn and Yáng are in harmony, the solstice arrives;
when the Lǜ-qi resonates, the ash flies.
When the ash flies and the Lǜ-qi communicates,
and one blows into it to name it,
then it is the central sound of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, it can encompass all standards,
and transform all things.
This is what the Yú Shū calls
"aligning the months with the seasons and rectifying the days,
and unifying the pitch-pipes, measures, and weights."
The central sound, structured into patterns,
and virtuous music, manifest and complete in harmony,
can move Heaven and Earth,
inspire ghosts and spirits,
guide dispositions and emotions,
and transform customs.
It can express intentions through songs and chants,
and discern prosperity and decline through order and chaos.
Therefore, the junzǐ discerns sounds to know music,
discerns music to know melodies,
and discerns melodies to know governance.
This all follows this path.
Tàishǐgōng's Lǜshū says:
"Kings who establish affairs and create objects,
whose laws and regulations, standards and norms,
are all derived from the six Lǜ.
The six Lǜ are the foundation of all matters,
and are especially important for military weapons.
Therefore, it is said that by observing the enemy, one knows good and ill fortune;
by hearing their sounds, one can predict victory or defeat.
This is a constant principle for all kings."
When the Qín clan destroyed learning,
this Dào gradually faded.
When the Hàn dynasty first rose,
Chancellor Zhāng Cāng was the first to speak of musical temperament,
but it was not yet fully precise.
Emperor Xiàowǔ established the office of Xiélǜ,
and Sīmǎ Qiān spoke in detail about the sequential generation of the Lǜ and Lǚ.
During the time of Wáng Mǎng,
the principles of musical temperament were examined,
and Liú Xīn presented a memorial,
which largely contained five categories: First, counting numbers—
one, ten, hundred, thousand, myriad;
Second, harmonized sounds—
gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ;
Third, precise measurements—
fēn, cùn, chǐ, zhàng, yǐn;
Fourth, excellent capacities—
yuè, hé, shēng, dòu, hú;
Fifth, weights and balances—
zhū, liǎng, jīn, jūn, shí.
Bān Gù then recorded these in a treatise.
Cài Yōng also recorded those who discussed the Lǜ and Lǚ after Jiànwǔ,
and Sīmǎ Shào compiled and continued it.
At the end of Hàn, the world was in great chaos,
musicians scattered and died,
and instruments and methods were destroyed.
Wèi Wǔ first acquired Dù Kuí,
and ordered him to set the pitch and tone of musical instruments.
Kuí, based on the standards of his time,
temporarily prepared the regulations.
When Wǔdì received the Mandate,
he followed it without change.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ [274 CE],
Guānglù Dàfū Xún Xù memorialized to create new standards
and recast the Lǜ and Lǚ.
In the middle of Yuánkāng [291-300 CE],
Xù's son Fān continued his work,
but before he could succeed,
due to the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
the central court's regulations
were all lost to Shí Lè.
When Yuándì moved south,
the imperial standards were rudimentary,
and all ceremonial vessels and musical instruments
were completely swept away.
Although some efforts were made to collect them,
many were lost,
and by the time of Gōng and Ān,
they could not be fully restored.
Now, we study the ancient sequence of Lǜ generation,
and those who discussed musical temperament and measurements after Wèi Wǔ,
to record them in this chapter.
Tradition says:
“The twelve *lǜ*
were created by Huángdì.
He sent Líng Lún west from Dàxià,
thence to the shady side of Kūnlún,
to take bamboo growing in Xiè Gǔ.
Those with uniformly thick holes
were cut to three *cùn* and nine *fēn* long between two nodes and blown,
to make the *gōng* note of Huángzhōng.
It was called Hánshǎo.
Next, twelve bamboo pipes were made,
imitating the cry of the phoenix;
six for the male cry,
and six for the female cry,
to match the *gōng* note of Huángzhōng.
All could be used to generate the *lǜlǚ* and establish the pitches.
Thus, when the *lǜ* were first created,
bamboo was used for the pipes,
taking advantage of its natural roundness and hollowness.”
It also says:
“Huángdì created the *lǜ*
using jade as pipes,
one *chǐ* long,
with six holes,
to represent the sounds of the twelve months.
By the time of Shùn,
Xīwángmǔ presented the Zhāohuá *guǎn*,
which was made of jade.”
By the time of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Xī Jǐng, a literary scholar from Línglíng, obtained a white jade *guǎn* beneath Shùn’s temple in Língdào.
Also, in the first year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ,
thieves in Jí Jùn broke into the tomb of King Xiāng of Wèi from the time of the Six States,
and also found jade *lǜ*.
Thus, in ancient times, jade was also used for the pipes.
Jade was chosen
because its body contained purity and luster.
However, during the reign of Emperor Píng of Hàn,
Wáng Mǎng made them out of bronze.
Bronze,
named for its ability to ‘harmonize,’
was intended to unify the world
and standardize customs.
As a material of utmost refinement,
it does not change its temperament with dryness, wetness, cold, or heat.
It is firm and constant,
like the conduct of a noble scholar,
hence its use.
In the Zhōu Lǐ,
the Tàishī was in charge of the six *lǜ* and six *lǚ*,
to harmonize the sounds of *yīn* and *yáng*.
The six *lǜ*, which are *yáng* sounds, are
Huángzhōng, Tàicù, Gūxiǎn, Ruíbīn, Yízé, and Wúshè;
the six *lǚ*, which are *yīn* sounds, are
Dàlǚ, Yìngzhōng, Nánlǚ, Línzhōng, Zhònglǚ, and Jiázhōng.
Furthermore, the Tàishī would hold a harmonizing *lǜ* to listen to military sounds
and announce good or ill omens.
The Diǎntóng was in charge of the harmony of the six *lǜ* and six *lǚ*,
to distinguish the *yīn* and *yáng* sounds of heaven, earth, and the four directions,
to make musical instruments.
All were made according to the measurements of the twelve *lǜ*,
and their standardization was based on the twelve sounds.
When King Jǐng of Zhōu was about to cast Wúshè,
he asked Líng Zhōujiū about the *lǜ*.
He replied:
“The sixth,
the color of the center,
is therefore named Huángzhōng,
and serves to proclaim and nourish the six *qì* and nine virtues.
From this, they are ordered.
The second is Tàicù,
which serves as the metal chime to aid the emergence of *yáng* from stagnation.
The third is Gūxiǎn,
which serves to purify all things,
examine the spirits, and receive guests.
The fourth is Ruíbīn,
which serves to calm spirits and people,
and to make offerings and share drinks.
The fifth is Yízé,
which serves to sing praises of the nine virtues,
and ensure people have no doubts.
The sixth is Wúshè,
which serves to disseminate the excellent virtues of sagely people,
and show people proper conduct.
There are six intermediate notes,
to elevate the submerged and hidden, and suppress the scattered and chaotic.
The first intermediate note is Dàlǚ,
which helps to proclaim things.
The second intermediate note is Jiázhōng,
which brings out the subtleties of the four gaps.
The third intermediate note is Zhònglǚ,
which proclaims the central *qì*.
The fourth intermediate note is Línzhōng,
which harmonizes and expands all matters,
ensuring none fail to be serious, pure, and diligent.
The fifth intermediate note is Nánlǚ,
which assists the flourishing of *yáng*.
The sixth intermediate note is Yìngzhōng,
which standardizes the utility of tools,
ensuring they respond and return.”
These all serve to describe the seasonal *qì* and regulate the seasonal changes.
When Qín Shǐhuáng burned books and destroyed records,
the canons and policies were lost and incomplete.
Scattered sayings of the various philosophers still had some remnants.
Lǚ Bùwéi’s Chūnqiū states: The *gōng* note of Huángzhōng
is the root of the *lǜ*.
It generates Línzhōng downwards.
Línzhōng generates Tàicù upwards.
Tàicù generates Nánlǚ downwards.
Nánlǚ generates Gūxiǎn upwards.
Gūxiǎn generates Yìngzhōng downwards.
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn upwards.
Ruíbīn generates Dàlǚ downwards.
Dàlǚ generates Yízé downwards.
Yízé generates Jiázhōng upwards.
Jiázhōng generates Wúshè downwards.
Wúshè generates Zhònglǚ upwards.
When generating notes, from a length divided into three parts:
one part is added for upward generation;
one part is subtracted for downward generation.
Later generations who spoke of musical pitches largely followed this theory.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
inheriting the deficiencies of Qín,
Zhāng Cāng first worked on *lǜlì*,
but could not elaborate fully.
Therefore, Emperor Xiàowǔ rectified music,
and established the office of Xiélǜ.
Although the clear and turbid forms of the *lǜlǚ* were roughly corrected,
and the high and low sounds of metal and stone instruments had standards,
he merely gathered existing remnants
to create a temporary system,
and the number still used five.
At that time, Huáinán Wáng Ān invited scholars,
and also worked on *lǜlǚ*.
He said: The *lǜ* of Huángzhōng is nine *cùn* long, and its *gōng* note is regulated.
Multiplying it by nine,
nine times nine is eighty-one,
thus the number for Huángzhōng is established,
its position is *zǐ*.
Línzhōng’s position is *wèi*,
its number is fifty-four.
Tàicù’s number is seventy-two.
Nánlǚ’s number is forty-eight.
Gūxiǎn’s number is sixty-four.
Yìngzhōng’s number is forty-two.
Ruíbīn’s number is fifty-seven.
Dàlǚ’s number is seventy-six.
Yízé’s number is fifty-one.
Jiázhōng’s number is sixty-eight.
Wúshè’s number is forty-five.
Zhònglǚ’s number is sixty,
which is the extreme and generates no more.
Huángzhōng is taken as *gōng*,
Tàicù as *shāng*,
Gūxiǎn as *jué*,
Línzhōng as *zhǐ*,
Nánlǚ as *yǔ*.
*Gōng* generates *zhǐ*.
*Zhǐ* generates *shāng*.
*Shāng* generates *yǔ*.
*Yǔ* generates *jué*.
*Jué* generates Yìngzhōng.
This does not conform to the main notes,
hence it is called *hé* (harmony).
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn.
This does not conform to the main notes,
hence it is called *móu* (discord).
At the winter solstice,
the sound gradually becomes more turbid like Línzhōng.
At the summer solstice,
the sound gradually becomes clearer like Huángzhōng.
The twelve *lǜ* correspond to the changes of the twenty-four solar terms.
Jiǎzǐ
is the *zhǐ* of Zhònglǚ.
Bǐngzǐ
is the *yǔ* of Jiázhōng.
Wùzǐ
is the *gōng* of Huángzhōng.
Gēngzǐ
is the *shāng* of Wúshè.
Rénzǐ
is the *jué* of Yízé.
In terms of sound,
one *lǜ* generates five notes,
and the twelve *lǜ* make sixty notes.
Multiplying this by six,
six times six is thirty-six,
thus three hundred and sixty notes correspond to the days of a year.
Therefore, the numbers of *lǜlì*
are the Way of Heaven and Earth.
Sīmǎ Qiān’s eight treatises discuss lǜlǚ,
broadly outlining the general principles,
which are recorded in previous histories.
He states that the primordial qi of Tài jí contains three and forms one,
and that movement begins in the zǐ hour.
The generation of the twelve lǜ
must have originated there.
Then, by combining one with the chǒu, three is obtained,
and consequently, this is multiplied by nine-thirds.
Taking the base position and combining it with the ten earthly branches,
one obtains 19,683,
which is called the "completion number,"
and is used as the rule for Huángzhōng.
Further, by combining it with the lǜ of the twelve earthly branches,
one obtains 177,147,
which is called the "total number,"
and is used as the actual value for Huángzhōng.
When the actual value is divided by the rule,
the lǜ length of Huángzhōng is found to be nine cùn,
corresponding to the qi of the winter solstice in the eleventh month.
Indeed, when yin and yang combine their virtues,
qi accumulates in zǐ,
and gives rise to all things.
Thus, all things born cannot but contain three.
Therefore, the hollow diameter of the twelve lǜ is three fēn,
and when generating upwards and downwards,
all are incremented or decremented by three.
The method is based on the nine-cùn length of Huángzhōng.
For those generated downwards, their actual value is doubled,
and their rule is tripled.
For those generated upwards,
their actual value is quadrupled,
and their rule is tripled.
This illustrates how yang generates yin downwards,
and yin generates yang upwards.
Starting with zǐ,
Huángzhōng is nine cùn,
or one.
Chǒu,
two-thirds.
Yín,
eight-ninths.
Mǎo,
sixteen twenty-sevenths.
Chén,
sixty-four eighty-firsts.
Sì,
one hundred twenty-eight two hundred forty-thirds.
Wǔ,
five hundred twelve seven hundred twenty-ninths.
Wèi,
one thousand twenty-four two thousand one hundred eighty-sevenths.
Shēn,
four thousand ninety-six six thousand five hundred sixty-firsts.
Yǒu,
eight thousand one hundred ninety-two nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-seconds.
Xū,
thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-eight fifty-nine thousand forty-ninths.
Hài,
sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six one hundred seventy-seven thousand one hundred forty-sevenths.
Following this cycle of twelve earthly branches,
when a lǜ is one of the six lǜ (yang),
it naturally obtains its position and generates yin downwards.
When a lǜ is one of the six lǚ (yin),
it obtains its balanced position and generates yang upwards.
The method of calculation has no rule for repeated upward generation.
This is what is meant by lǜ taking a wife,
and lǚ giving birth to a son,
the ascending and descending of yin and yang,
which are the grand principles of lǜlǚ.
However, Sīmǎ Qiān also discussed the lengths of the twelve lǜ,
and now, according to the jiǔjiǔ method of Huáinán,
Ruíbīn is considered a "repeated upward generation."
He also spoke of the mutual generation of the five notes,
where gōng generates jiǎo,
jiǎo generates shāng,
shāng generates zhǐ,
zhǐ generates yǔ,
and yǔ generates gōng.
When trying to find the reasoning behind this,
no clear path is seen.
During the Yuánshǐ era,
when Wáng Mǎng was regent,
he widely recruited those knowledgeable in zhōnglǜ
to examine their sounds and meanings.
He appointed Xīhé Liú Xīn to oversee their adjustment and performance.
Bān Gù, in his Hànshū, adopted and recorded this.
Although his preface and discussion are extensive,
when discussing the order of increment and decrement of the twelve lǜ,
starting from Huángzhōng being nine cùn long,
one-third is subtracted,
generating Línzhōng downwards,
which is six cùn long.
One-third is added,
generating Tàicù upwards, and turning left,
with positions of eight-eighths.
One up, one down,
finally ending with Wúshè,
generating Zhōnglǚ downwards.
Comparing the results of their mutual generation,
they are exactly the same as Sīmǎ Qiān’s.
Bān Gù adopted this for his monograph.
During the reign of Yuán Dì,
Lángzhōng Jīng Fáng understood the numbers of the five notes and sixty lǜ.
The emperor sent Crown Prince Grand Tutor Xuán Chéng and remonstrating counselor Zhāng to jointly question Jīng Fáng at the Music Bureau.
Jīng Fáng replied:
"I studied under the late magistrate of Xiǎohuáng, Jiāo Yánshòu.
The method of generating the sixty lǜ is: when generating downwards from above,
all are three generating two;
when generating upwards from below,
all are three generating four.
Yang generates yin downwards,
yin generates yang upwards,
ending with Zhōnglǚ,
and the twelve lǜ are complete.
Zhōnglǚ generates Zhíshǐ upwards,
Zhíshǐ generates Qùmiè downwards.
Generating upwards and downwards,
finally ending with Nánshì,
and the sixty lǜ are complete.
The variations of the twelve lǜ to sixty
are like the variations of the eight trigrams to sixty-four.
Fú Xī created the Yì,
recording the beginning of yang qi as the lǜ method.
The sound established on the winter solstice day,
taking Huángzhōng as gōng,
Tàicù as shāng,
Gūxǐ as jiǎo,
Línzhōng as zhǐ,
Nánlǚ as yǔ,
Yìngzhōng as biàngōng,
Ruíbīn as biànzhǐ.
These are the origin of sounds and qi,
the correct forms of the five notes.
Therefore, each governs one day,
the others follow in sequence,
and on their respective days, they each become gōng,
with shāng, jiǎo, zhǐ, and yǔ following their categories.
The Lǐyùn says, ‘The five sounds, six lǜ, and twelve pipes cycle and become gōng for each other.’
This is what it refers to.
By dividing the days of the year with the sixty lǜ,
Huángzhōng begins from the winter solstice,
and returns at the winter solstice.
Predictions of yin and yang, heat and cold, wind and rain arise from this.
This is used to examine and control all sounds,
and evaluate their pitch.
If it is not the sound of革 (animal hide) or 木 (wood),
then there is nothing that does not match.
The Yúshū says, ‘Lǜ harmonize sounds.’
This is what it refers to."
Jīng Fáng also said:
"Bamboo sounds cannot be used to measure pitch,
so I made a zhǔn to determine the numbers.
The zhǔn looks like a sè,
but is ten chǐ long,
with thirteen strings.
The hidden interval is nine chǐ,
corresponding to the nine-cùn lǜ of Huángzhōng.
The central string
has markings of cùn below it,
to serve as the divisions for the clear and turbid notes of the sixty lǜ."
Jīng Fáng’s discussion of lǜ is more detailed than what Xīn presented.
His method was put into practice by the court historians,
and used by the observation department.
The text is too extensive to include in full.
Cutting bamboo pipes to make lǜ,
blowing them to test sounds,
arranging them to observe qi,
is the fundamental principle.
Practitioners of the art considered its sounds too subtle and its physical form difficult to discern,
and its fractions unclear,
so they made a zhǔn to replace it.
The sound of the zhǔn is clear, fluent, and easy to transmit,
and its measurements are also coarse.
However, strings vary in speed, clarity, and turbidity,
and without pipes, they cannot be corrected.
If the middle string is tuned
to match Huángzhōng,
and other lǜ are found by referring to the markings,
then none will fail to correspond exactly to the numbers.
The Xù Hàn Zhì fully records the zhǔn’s sixty lǜ scale and measurements,
and their order of generation is the same as in the Lǚ Lǎn and Huáinán.
In the first year of Yuánhé of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
the Waiting Attendant Hóu Zhōnglǜ Yīnrǒng presented a memorial, saying:
"The court lacks individuals who understand the sixty *lǜ* (pitches) to standardize and tune music.
Therefore, the Waiting Attendant Yán Chóng has thoroughly taught his son Xuān the standard methods,
and I wish to summon Xuān to be appointed to the Bureau of Music,
to be in charge of tuning musical instruments."
An imperial edict stated:
"If Chóng's son studies and truly understands the *lǜ*,
can distinguish their categories,
and harmonize their sounds,
he shall be thoroughly tested.
He must not rely on his father's learning
and pretend to be clever when he is deaf.
Sound is subtle;
if it is solely incorrect, no one knows;
if it is solely correct, no one understands.
If he can play with *lǜ* pipes and
accurately name the twelve *lǜ* without a single mistake,
only then can he be said to have inherited Chóng's learning."
Xuān was tested on the twelve *lǜ*.
Two were correct,
four were incorrect,
and for six, he did not know what *lǜ* they were.
Xuān was consequently dismissed.
From then on, no one in the *lǜ* family could standardize pitches.
In the sixth year of Xīpíng of Emperor Líng,
the Dōngguān summoned Zhāng Guāng and others, who were *tàizǐ shèrén* (Palace Gentleman for the Crown Prince) and experts in *lǜ*, to ask about the principle of standardization.
Guāng and the others did not know,
and after returning to review old collections,
they found the instrument.
Its form was like a book on rooms (or measurements),
yet they still could not determine the tension of its strings.
Sound
cannot be written down to instruct people;
those who know it wish to teach but have no means,
and those who intuitively grasp it understand it but have no teacher.
Thus, officials who could distinguish clear and turbid notes eventually disappeared.
That which could be transmitted
was only the observation of *qì*.
During the turmoil at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
the *yǎyuè* (ritual music) was lost.
In the time of Wèi Wǔ,
Dù Kuí of Hénán was skilled in recognizing musical rhythms.
He was appointed *yǎyuèlángzhōng* (Gentleman of Ritual Music)
and ordered the bronze caster Chái Yù to cast bells.
Their sounds, both clear and turbid, often did not conform to the standards.
He repeatedly ordered them to be destroyed and remade.
Yù grew very weary of this
and accused Kuí of arbitrarily determining clear and turbid notes,
reporting the mutual grievances to King Wèi Wǔ.
King Wèi Wǔ took the bells cast by Yù and mixed them up for further testing.
Only then did he realize Kuí's expertise,
and consequently punished Yù.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ,
Zhōngshūjiān Xún Xù and Zhōngshūlìng Zhāng Huá brought out twenty-five sets of bronze and bamboo *lǜ* from the imperial treasury.
They appointed *tàilè láng* Liú Xiù and others to examine and test them.
Three sets were consistent with the *lǜ* methods of Dù Kuí and Zuǒ Yánnián;
for the other twenty-two sets,
looking at their inscribed titles and dimensions,
they were *dí* (flute) *lǜ*.
They questioned Xiélǜ Zhōnglángjiàng Liè Hé,
who responded:
"In the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
I was ordered to receive *dí* sounds to create these *lǜ*.
The intention was to have scholars reside in a separate quarter,
to sing, recite, and practice,
tuning according to these *lǜ*.
When it came to harmonizing all music,
one only needed to recognize the names of their dimensions,
and then stringed instruments, wind instruments, and singing
would all be harmonized.
Singers with turbid voices used long *dí* and long *lǜ*,
and singers with clear voices used short *dí* and short *lǜ*.
Generally, the system for tuning stringed instruments and singing for clarity and turbidity,
if not named according to the *dí* dimensions,
cannot be understood."
Xù and others memorialized:
"When the former kings created music,
it was to invigorate customs,
feast the spirits, and assist the worthy.
They invariably harmonized the *lǜlǚ*
to regulate the eight sounds.
Therefore, for suburban sacrifices and court banquets,
its use was regulated,
and in performance and singing,
clarity and turbidity were appropriate.
Hence it is said, 'The five sounds and twelve *lǜ* return to each other as their *gōng* (tonic).'
This is what can be known from the classics, commentaries, and records.
As for Hé's reply,
the length of the *dí* had no principle to emulate;
it was made arbitrarily,
not following any melodic structure.
When examined against the standard *lǜ*,
they all did not correspond;
when their pitch was played,
they were mostly out of harmony.
Moreover, he said, 'My former teachers transmitted the *dí*,
distinguishing their clarity and turbidity
simply by length.
Craftsmen made them;
they were traditionally not based on *lǜ*.'
This means the *dí* were made without standards.
Yet Hé based the creation of *lǜ* on the *dí*,
and furthermore made *qín*, *sè*, and singing
follow them as correct.
This is not how to investigate the ancients and former sages
to establish laws for posterity.
We respectfully list the various *lǜ* and inquire about Hé's intentions as shown on the left.
And according to the traditional system,
making twelve *dí* pipes based on the twelve *lǜ*,
with their pitches harmonized and instruments convenient to use.
Will practice, playing, and striking
necessarily accord with the *lǜlǚ*?
How much more so for banquets of all nations
and performances in the imperial ancestral temple?
Although Lǐng Kuí is distant and
the ultimate sound is difficult to master,
it is still appropriate to model after antiquity
to seek its essence,
conforming to ritual propriety,
which is detailed in its regulations.
If it can be implemented,
we request to again assign *dí* craftsmen to select bamboo and make them,
and have the *Tàilè Yuèfǔ* implement it.
We suggest that all *lǜ* of Dù Kuí and Zuǒ Yánnián be kept,
and one set each of the *dí zhèngshēng* (main pitch) and *xiázhǐ* (lower *zhǐ* note) from the imperial treasury
should be inscribed with the names of their makers.
The rest, having no use,
should be returned to the imperial treasury and destroyed."
The memorial was approved.
Xù then asked Hé again:
"Can *dí* be made by creating twelve *dí* according to the twelve *lǜ*,
so that one hole corresponds to one *lǜ*,
and then consider that to be music?"
Hé replied:
"The long *dí zhèngshēng* in the east wing of the *Tàilè* is already four *chǐ* and two *cùn* long.
Now, if we were to take its *xiázhǐ* sound,
according to the method,
for a turbid sound, the *dí* should be long.
Calculating its dimensions, it would be over five *chǐ*,
and when I made it in the past,
it was unplayable.
Moreover,
although the various holes of the *dí* have not been tested,
I don't think it's possible for one hole to correspond to one *lǜ*."
Upon investigation, the four *chǐ* two *cùn* *dí zhèngshēng* of the *Tàilè* corresponds to *Ruíbīn*.
By applying the principle of the twelve *lǜ* returning to each other as their *gōng*,
the *xiázhǐ* hole should correspond to the *lǜ* *Dàlǚ*.
A *Dàlǚ* *dí* is two *chǐ* six *cùn* and a fraction long,
and cannot be over five *chǐ* long.
They immediately ordered *Tàilè láng* Liú Xiù and Dèng Hào and others to make a *Dàlǚ* *dí* according to the *lǜ* to show Hé.
They also played seven *lǜ*,
testing one hole at a time,
and the sounds all corresponded.
Then, they had Hǎo Shēng play the *zhēng* and
Sòng Tóng play the *dí*,
performing various *zá yīn* and *xiānghé* pieces.
Hé then said:
"Since the Hàn dynasty, my father and grandfather's generation,
the *dí* family has transmitted knowledge without knowing this method.
To achieve tuning that matches the *lǜ*
is truly beyond our capability."
Hǎo Shēng, Lǔ Jī, Zhǒng Zhěng,
and Zhū Xià all agreed with Hé.
Then [he] also asked Hé:
"A flute has six holes,
and its internal cavity makes seven,
can Hé fully name its gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ?
As for whether the holes are in tune or not,
how is this checked and known?"
Hé replied:
"My former teachers passed down [the teaching] that
when playing the flute, one only composes music.
They would tell each other, for a certain piece, which fingers to use,
but at first did not know what sound each of the seven holes should produce.
If one were to make a flute,
the imperial flute makers would first follow old patterns,
and simply blow to get it to sound,
never again checking whether its various holes were in tune or not."
According to the Zhōu Lǐ, when tuning metal and stone musical instruments,
there is a fixed pitch.
Therefore, those who make bells and chimestones first tune them according to the lǜ,
and then hang them in the musical stands.
When making music,
all notes are harmonized according to the standard pitch of the bells and chimestones,
which means they all correspond to the lǜ.
As for banquets in palace halls,
there are no musical stands with bells and chimestones.
Since the flute has a fixed tuning,
all string and vocal music follows the flute as the standard.
This means that the flute is like bells and chimestones,
and ought to conform to the lǜlǚ.
As Hé stated,
if one makes them simply by intuition,
for example, one cùn too short,
and the sounds of the seven holes are all uniform,
without knowing what lǜ each should correspond to,
and whether they are in tune or not,
there is no way to check and correct them.
Simply taking a piece of bamboo that makes a sound
is to be without a proper system.
Therefore, the secretaries Liú Xiù, Dèng Hào, Wáng Yàn, Wèi Shào, and others, together with the flute makers, jointly made flutes.
The artisans created their form,
and the lǜ experts determined their sounds.
Only then would the instruments have a proper system,
and the pitches be harmonious and coordinated.
Then [he] also asked Hé:
"If one makes music without knowing the meaning of lǜlǚ,
how should the tunings of high and low, clear and turbid pitches
be named?"
Hé replied:
"Every time music is performed,
according to the clarity or turbidity of the singer's voice,
flutes of different lengths are used.
For example, if a singer's voice is turbid, a three-chǐ-two flute is used,
and it is then called 'this three-chǐ-two tuning';
if the voice is clear, a two-chǐ-nine flute is used,
and it is then called 'this two-chǐ-nine tuning'.
This practice has been passed down from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
and is universally followed."
According to the Zhōu Lǐ, when performing the six musical pieces,
one plays Huángzhōng and
sings Dàlǚ;
one plays Tàicù and
sings Yìngzhōng.
All these are based on the meaning of lǜlǚ,
to record the clarity and turbidity of singing and playing.
However, what Hé calls naming by two chǐ or three chǐ,
though used in Hàn and Wèi,
is common and not classic.
The secretaries Liú Xiù, Dèng Hào, and others made flutes according to the lǜ.
A three-chǐ-two-cùn one corresponds to the lǜ of Wúshè.
If a long flute is appropriate,
the musician says, "Please play Wúshè."
A two-chǐ-eight-cùn-four-fēn-four-lí one corresponds to the lǜ of Huángzhōng.
If a short flute is appropriate,
the musician says, "Please play Huángzhōng."
Then the meaning of singing and playing
will accord with classical rites,
and when examined against classical texts,
this system is elegant.
The Shū [Jīng] says:
"I wish to hear the six lǜ, the five sounds, and the eight timbres,
in their order."
The Zhōu Lǐ and Guó Yǔ record the six lǜ and six tóng.
The Lǐ Jì also says:
"The five sounds and twelve lǜ revolve around each other to form the gōng."
Liú Xīn and Bān Gù, in compiling the Lǜlì Zhì, also recorded the twelve lǜ.
Only Jīng Fáng first created sixty lǜ.
By the time of Emperor Zhāng,
his method had already died out.
Although Cài Yōng later recorded his words,
he also said that no one today can practice it.
Based on classical texts and what current musicologists use,
the sixty lǜ have no application in music.
Therefore, carefully following classical records,
with the method of the five sounds and twelve lǜ revolving around each other to form the gōng,
twelve flute patterns were created,
and notes were inscribed beside the diagrams.
As shown separately,
reviewing the diagrams
is not as good as observing the holes of the flute itself.
Therefore, the Ruíbīn fúkǒng flute was remade.
Its system states:
The Huángzhōng flute,
its primary sound corresponds to Huángzhōng,
and its lower zhǐ corresponds to Línzhōng.
It is two chǐ, eight cùn, four fēn, four lí and a fraction in length.
(The method for the primary sound tuning:
taking Huángzhōng as the gōng,
then Gūxǐ is the jué.
The sound of the xī flute corresponds to Gūxǐ,
thus the length of the four jué [finger holes] is used for the Huángzhōng flute.
Its gōng sound is primary and not doubled,
hence it is called the primary sound.)
Zhèngshēng Diàofǎ: Huángzhōng is Gōng,
(the first hole.
) Yìngzhōng is Biàngōng,
(the second hole.
) Nánlǚ is Yǔ,
(the third hole.
) Línzhōng is Zhēng,
(the fourth hole.
) Ruíbīn is Biànzhēng,
(the fifth auxiliary hole.
) Gūxǐ is Jué,
(the middle sound within the flute body.
) Tàicù is Shāng.
(the hole at the rear of the flute.
The Shāng sound is lower in pitch than Jué,
and should be below Jué.
However, since the Jué sound is in the middle of the body,
the Shāng hole is placed above it,
making it higher in pitch than Gōng.
It is higher in pitch than Gōng.
Thus, Gōng and Shāng are correct,
while all other sounds are doubled.
Therefore, from Gōng downwards,
the holes gradually become lower in pitch.
This section records the names and order of the flute holes from top to bottom.
The next section explains the mutual generation of the lǜ and lǚ,
and the construction of the flute.
) Zhèngshēng Diàofǎ:
Huángzhōng is Gōng.
(When making a Huángzhōng flute,
to find the Gōng hole,
use the Gūxǐ and Huángzhōng lǜ.
Measure downwards from the flute head.
The hole is made at the end of the length of the two lǜ,
and then the Gōng sound is obtained.
) Gōng generates Zhēng;
Huángzhōng generates Línzhōng.
(Using the Línzhōng lǜ, measure downwards from the Gōng hole.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Zhēng sound is obtained.
) Zhēng generates Shāng;
Línzhōng generates Tàicù.
(Using the Tàicù lǜ, measure upwards from the Zhēng hole.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Shāng sound is obtained.
) Shāng generates Yǔ;
Tàicù generates Nánlǚ.
(Using the Nánlǚ lǜ, measure downwards from the Shāng hole.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Yǔ sound is obtained.
) Yǔ generates Jué;
Nánlǚ generates Gūxǐ.
(Using the Gūxǐ lǜ, measure upwards from the Yǔ hole.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Jué sound is obtained.
However, this would be above the Shāng hole,
beyond the reach of the flutist's left hand.
Measuring downwards from the Yǔ hole,
making a hole at the end of the lǜ,
would also produce the Jué sound,
but it would be below the auxiliary Shāng hole,
beyond the reach of the flutist's right hand.
Therefore, no Jué hole is made.
Pushing it downwards,
it again doubles its pitch.
This is why the Jué sound is in the middle of the flute body,
according to ancient practice.
In the old methods of musicians,
even if it is doubled once or twice,
as long as the pitch is the same,
it is sufficient for singing and harmony,
and does not harm the melody.
The Guóyǔ states,
"Páo and zhú are made to facilitate;
discussions should be appropriate,"
meaning that they should be convenient for practical use and in accordance with what is appropriate.
) Jué generates Biàngōng;
Gūxǐ generates Yìngzhōng.
(The aforementioned spot that should be the Jué hole but is above Shāng,
mark it with an ink dot.
Using the Yìngzhōng lǜ.
Measure downwards from this dot.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Biàngōng sound is obtained.
) Biàngōng generates Biànzhēng;
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn.
(Using the Ruíbīn lǜ, measure downwards from Biàngōng.
Make a hole at the end of the lǜ,
and then the Biànzhēng sound is obtained.
In the construction of the twelve flutes,
each takes its Gōng as the principal,
and the method of mutual generation,
whether doubled or halved,
for practical use,
is all the same.
Xiàzhēng Diàofǎ: Línzhōng is Gōng,
(the fourth hole.
Originally the Zhēng of the Zhèngshēng Huángzhōng.
Zhēng is high-pitched,
and should be above Gōng.
For the convenience of the flute,
it is doubled to make it lower in pitch,
hence it is called Xiàzhēng.
Xiàzhēng becoming Gōng again
refers to the saying
"The five sounds
and twelve lǜ cycle back to become Gōng."
Thus, the Zhèngshēng is clear,
and Xiàzhēng is low-pitched.
) Nánlǚ is Shāng,
(the third hole.
Originally the Yǔ of the Zhèngshēng Huángzhōng,
now the Shāng of Xiàzhēng.
) Yìngzhōng is Jué,
(the second hole.
Originally the Biàngōng of the Zhèngshēng Huángzhōng,
now the Jué of Xiàzhēng.
) Huángzhōng is Biànzhēng,
(in the Xiàzhēng tuning,
Línzhōng is Gōng,
Dàlǚ should be Biànzhēng.
However, the Huángzhōng flute originally has no Dàlǚ sound,
so Huángzhōng is borrowed to serve as Biànzhēng.
The method of borrowing is that,
when the sound of Biànzhēng is desired,
the Huángzhōng, Tàicù, and Yìngzhōng holes are all opened.
Huángzhōng should be low-pitched while Tàicù is high-pitched,
and the Dàlǚ lǜ is between these two lǜ.
By opening all three holes and slightly adjusting the pitch,
the Biànzhēng sound of Dàlǚ is obtained.
The method for finding Biànzhēng in the Xiàzhēng tuning for all flutes
is the same.
) Tàicù is Zhēng,
(the hole at the rear of the flute.
Originally the Shāng of Zhèngshēng,
now the Zhēng of Xiàzhēng.
) Gūxǐ is Yǔ,
(the constricted sound in the middle of the flute body.
Originally the Jué of Zhèngshēng,
now the Yǔ of Xiàzhēng.
) Ruíbīn is Biàngōng.
(This is the auxiliary hole.
Originally the Biànzhēng of Zhèngshēng,
now the Biàngōng of Xiàzhēng.
Thus, in the Zhèngshēng tuning,
the holes become lower in pitch as they go down;
in the Xiàzhēng tuning,
the holes become higher in pitch as they go up.
Qīngjué Diào: Gūxǐ is Gōng,
(this is the constricted sound in the middle of the flute body.
In Zhèngshēng, it is Jué;
in Xiàzhēng, it is Yǔ.
In the Qīngjué Diào, it is taken as Gōng,
and blown with a clear, whistling sound,
hence it is called Qīngjué.
It is only suitable for melodious poems and popular tunes,
and not for elegant music.
) Ruíbīn is Shāng,
(correct.
) Línzhōng is Jué,
(not correct.
) Nánlǚ is Biànzhēng,
(not correct.
) Yìngzhōng is Zhēng,
(correct.
) Huángzhōng is Yǔ,
(not correct.
) Tàicù is Biàngōng.
(not correct.
In the Qīngjué Diào,
only Gōng, Shāng, and Zhēng correspond to the lǜ;
the other four sounds are incorrect and low-pitched.
By blowing one lǜ with a clear, whistling sound,
it is borrowed for use,
and the principle is the same.
In general, flutes are constructed according to the *jiǎo*-lü
scale. The long ones are based on eight units,
(these are the *Ruíbīn* and *Línzhōng* flutes.)
The short ones are based on four units.
(The remaining ten flutes
all have four *jiǎo*.)
The actual volume of the empty space
for the long ones is sixteen units.
(The bamboo for short flutes should accommodate eight *lü* of millet.
If the length, short-ness, or size do not conform to this,
then the instrument's use may not be conducive to the harmony of the sounds and the standardization of the musical system.
However, flute bamboo typically tapers, being larger at the top and smaller at the bottom,
so it cannot be perfectly uniform.
If there is no other option,
prioritize sound harmony.)
There are three *gōng* modes:
(the first is *zhèngshēng*,
the second is *xiàzhǐ*,
and the third is *qīngjiǎo*.)
There are twenty-one variations.
(Each *gōng* has seven notes,
which are used in various combinations,
hence twenty-one variations.
This applies to all flutes.)
There are four hidden holes,
which are for practical use.
(The first is *zhèngjiǎo*,
which emerges above *shāng*;
the second is *bèijiǎo*,
which is near the bottom of the flute;
the third is *biàngōng*,
which is close to the *gōng* hole,
making it twice as low;
the fourth is *biànzhǐ*,
which is far from the *zhǐ* hole,
making it twice as high.
Whether doubled or halved,
or quartered,
the principle is taken from the frets of the *qín*.
None of these four holes are actually made,
but their measurements are taken
to correspond to the rules of ascending, descending, and moving up and down,
thus harmonizing the pitches
and facilitating practical use.
Their original holes are hidden and not visible,
hence they are called "hidden holes.")
For the *Dàlǚ* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Dàlǚ*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Yízé*.
Its length is two *chǐ*, six *cùn*, six *fēn*, three *máo*, with a fraction.
For the *Tàicù* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Tàicù*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Nánlǚ*.
Its length is two *chǐ*, five *cùn*, three *fēn*, one *máo*, with a fraction.
For the *Jiázhōng* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Jiázhōng*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Wúshè*.
Its length is two *chǐ*, four *cùn*.
For the *Gūxǐ* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Gūxǐ*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Yìngzhōng*.
Its length is two *chǐ*, two *cùn*, three *fēn*, three *máo*, with a fraction.
For the *Ruíbīn* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Ruíbīn*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Dàlǚ*.
Its length is three *chǐ*, nine *cùn*, nine *fēn*, five *máo*, with a fraction.
(*Biàngōng* is near the *gōng* hole,
so it is made one and a half times lower,
for ease of use.
The *Línzhōng* flute is similar.)
For the *Línzhōng* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Línzhōng*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Tàicù*.
Its length is three *chǐ*, seven *cùn*, nine *fēn*, seven *máo*, with a fraction.
〔一一〕
For the *Yízé* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Yízé*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Jiázhōng*.
Its length is three *chǐ*, six *cùn*.
(The method for *biàngōng*
is also like that of *Ruíbīn*.
It uses four *jiǎo*,
so one quarter is added.)
For the *Nánlǚ* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Nánlǚ*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Gūxǐ*.
Its length is three *chǐ*, three *cùn*, seven *fēn*, with a fraction.
〔一二〕
For the *Wúshè* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Wúshè*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Zhōnglǚ*.
Its length is three *chǐ*, two *cùn*.
For the *Yìngzhōng* flute,
the *zhèngshēng* corresponds to *Yìngzhōng*,
and the *xiàzhǐ* corresponds to *Ruíbīn*.
Its length is two *chǐ*, nine *cùn*, nine *fēn*, six *máo*, with a fraction.
〔一三〕 The Five Sounds and Twelve *Lǜ*
Earth sound is *gōng*,
its number is eighty-one,
it is the beginning of sounds.
It belongs to Earth,
because it is the most turbid, and is the image of the ruler.
When the *jìxià* (late summer) *qì* is harmonious,
the *gōng* sound is in tune.
If *gōng* is disordered, it leads to desolation,
and the ruler is arrogant.
The *gōng* of *Huángzhōng*
has the longest *lü*.
Fire sound is *zhǐ*,
generated by subtracting one-third from *gōng*,
its number is fifty-four.
It belongs to Fire,
because its *zhǐ* is clear, and is the image of affairs.
When the summer *qì* is harmonious,
the *zhǐ* sound is in tune.
If *zhǐ* is disordered, it leads to sorrow,
and affairs are laborious.
Metal sound is *shāng*,
generated by adding one-third to *zhǐ*,
its number is seventy-two.
It belongs to Metal,
because its turbidity is second to *gōng*, and is the image of ministers.
When the autumn *qì* is harmonious,
the *shāng* sound is in tune.
If *shāng* is disordered, it leads to bias,
and officials are corrupt.
Water sound is *yǔ*,
generated by subtracting one-third from *shāng*,
its number is forty-eight.
It belongs to Water,
because it is the clearest, and is the image of things.
When the winter *qì* is harmonious,
the *yǔ* sound is in tune.
If *yǔ* is disordered, it leads to danger,
and resources are depleted.
Wood sound is *jiǎo*,
generated by adding one-third to *yǔ*,
its number is sixty-four.
It belongs to Wood,
because its clarity and turbidity are intermediate, and is the image of people.
When the spring *qì* is harmonious,
the *jiǎo* sound is in tune.
If *jiǎo* is disordered, it leads to anxiety,
and the people complain.
In general, the highness and lowness of sounds
take their imagery from the Five Phases.
Those with larger numbers are turbid,
those with smaller numbers are clear.
The largest does not exceed *gōng*,
the smallest does not fall below *yǔ*.
In the eleventh month,
the *lü* corresponds to *Huángzhōng*,
which is the beginning of the *lü*.
Its length is nine *cùn*.
When the *qì* of mid-winter arrives,
its *lü* resonates,
thereby proclaiming and nurturing the six *qì* and nine virtues.
〔一四〕Bān Gù subtracted one-third,
producing *Línzhōng* below.
In the twelfth month,
the *lü* corresponds to *Dàlǚ*,
the *lü* not yet generated below by Sīmǎ Qiān.
Its length is four *cùn* and fifty-two parts out of two hundred forty-three *fēn* of a *cùn*.
Doubling this gives eight *cùn* and one hundred four parts out of two hundred forty-three *fēn* of a *cùn*.
When the *qì* of late winter arrives,
its *lü* resonates,
thereby assisting in the manifestation of things.
Adding one-third
generates *Yízé* above;
Jīng Fáng subtracted one-third,
generating *Yízé* below.
In the first month,
the *lü* corresponds to *Tàicù*,
the *lü* not yet generated above.
Its length is eight *cùn*.
When the *qì* of early spring arrives,
its *lü* resonates,
thereby assisting the emergence of *yáng* and the release of stagnation.
Subtracting one-third
generates *Nánlǚ* below.
In the second month,
the lǜ (pitch-pipe) corresponds to Jiázhōng,
the lǜ generated downward from Yǒu,
its length is three cùn and one thousand six hundred thirty-one parts of two thousand one hundred eighty-seven parts of a cùn.
When doubled, it is seven cùn and one thousand seventy-five parts of two thousand one hundred eighty-seven parts of a cùn.
When the qi of mid-spring arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby indicating the subtlety of the four cardinal points.
By adding one-third,
Wúshè is generated upward.
Jīng Fáng's method of subtracting one-third
generates Wúshè downward.
In the third month,
the lǜ corresponds to Gūxǐ,
the lǜ generated upward from Yǒu,
its length is seven cùn and one-ninth of a cùn.
When the qi of late spring arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby purifying all things,
and examining the spirits to welcome guests.
By subtracting one-third,
Yìngzhōng is generated downward.
In the fourth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Zhōnglǚ,
the lǜ generated downward from Hài,
its length is three cùn and six thousand four hundred eighty-seven parts of nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three parts of a cùn.
When doubled, it is six cùn and twelve thousand nine hundred seventy-four parts of nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three parts of a cùn.
When the qi of early summer arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby disseminating the central qi.
In the fifth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Ruíbīn,
the lǜ generated upward from Hài,
its length is six cùn and twenty-six parts of eighty-one parts of a cùn.
When the qi of mid-summer arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby tranquilizing human spirits,
and offering and returning toasts.
By subtracting one-third,
Dàlǚ is generated downward.
Jīng Fáng's method of adding one-third
generates Dàlǚ upward.
In the sixth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Línzhōng,
the lǜ generated downward from Chǒu,
its length is six cùn.
When the qi of late summer arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby harmonizing and displaying all things,
causing none not to be reverently and purely observant.
By adding one-third,
Tàicù is generated upward.
In the seventh month,
the lǜ corresponds to Yīzé,
the lǜ generated upward from Chǒu,
its length is five cùn and four hundred fifty-one parts of seven hundred twenty-nine parts of a cùn.
When the qi of early autumn arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby chanting the nine virtues,
and bringing peace to the common people without leniency.
By subtracting one-third,
Jiázhōng is generated downward.
Jīng Fáng's method of adding one-third
generates Jiázhōng upward.
In the eighth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Nánlǚ,
the lǜ generated downward from Mǎo,
its length is five cùn and one-third of a cùn.
When the qi of mid-autumn arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby aiding the flourishing of yang.
By adding one-third,
Gūxǐ is generated upward.
In the ninth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Wúshè,
the lǜ generated upward from Mǎo,
its length is four cùn and six thousand five hundred twenty-four parts of six thousand five hundred sixty-one parts of a cùn.
When the qi of late autumn arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby announcing the virtuous deeds of the wise,
and showing people the proper conduct and ritual.
By subtracting one-third,
Zhōnglǚ is generated downward.
Jīng Fáng's method of adding one-third
generates Zhōnglǚ upward.
In the tenth month,
the lǜ corresponds to Yìngzhōng,
the lǜ generated downward from Sì,
its length is four cùn and twenty parts of twenty-seven parts of a cùn.
When the qi of early winter arrives,
its lǜ responds,
thereby equalizing useful implements,
to ensure their return.
By adding one-third,
Ruíbīn is generated upward.
The various scholars like Huáinán, Jīng Fáng, and Zhèng Xuán, when speaking of lǜlì (pitch-pipes and calendar),
all generated them both upward and downward.
Up to Ruíbīn, Dàlǚ is again generated upward,
its length being eight cùn and one hundred four parts of two hundred forty-three parts of a cùn.
Yīzé generates Jiázhōng upward,
its length being seven cùn and one thousand seventy-five parts of one thousand one hundred eighty-seven parts of a cùn.
Wúshè generates Zhōnglǚ upward,

its length being six cùn and twelve thousand nine hundred seventy-four parts of nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three parts of a cùn. These three items, compared to the cùn measurements and fractions generated by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù, are all doubled,
while the rest are identical.
This is what Língzhōu Jiū called the "Way of the Six Intervals,"
raising what is hidden and low,
and eliminating what is scattered and transgressing,
making use of these.
Change and adaptation are half and half,
following what is appropriate for each matter,
it is a method of assistance.
The essence of all sounds
lies in harmony and evenness.
When increased, it doubles;
when decreased, it halves,
its relation to the original sound is always faultless.
Thus, when speaking of "one upward and one downward,"
it refers to the method of generation;
when speaking of "repeated upward generation,"
it refers to the use in blowing and observing the seasons.
The repeated upward generation for Ruíbīn
coincidentally meets the numerical requirement for its use,
thus those who speak of lǜ follow this,
it is not the correct method of generation.
Yáng Zǐyún said:
"Sound is generated from the sun.
(This means jiǎ and jǐ are jué,
yǐ and gēng are shāng,
bǐng and xīn are zhǐ,
dīng and rén are yǔ,
and wù and guǐ are gōng.)
Lǜ are generated from the earthly branches.
(This means zǐ is Huángzhōng,
chǒu is Dàlǚ, and so on.)
Sound is based on its essential nature.
(Zhì means
correctness.
Each is correct according to the inherent nature of its element.)
Lǜ harmonize sound.
(One should use lǜ pipes and bells to harmonize the clear and turbid sounds.)
When sound and lǜ accord, the eight tones are produced.
(Xié means
harmony.)
"Gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ
are called the five sounds.
Metal, stone, gourd, hide, silk, bamboo, earth, and wood
are called the eight tones.
When sounds are harmonious and tones accord,
this is called the five joys.
When yin and yang are in harmony, the shadows arrive.
When the lǜ qi responds, the ashes disappear.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven would always, on the days of the winter and summer solstices, preside over the front hall,
gather scholars skilled in eight abilities,
display the eight tones,
listen to the musical harmony,
measure the gnomon shadow,
observe the bell lǜ,
weigh the earth-ashes,
〔一五〕and verify yin and yang.
At the winter solstice, when the yang qi responds, the ashes disappear,
and thus the musical harmony is clear,
the shadow is at its longest,
Huángzhōng resonates,
and the earth-ashes are light and the balance rises.
At the summer solstice, when the yin qi responds, the musical harmony is turbid,
the shadow is at its shortest,
Ruíbīn resonates,
and the earth-ashes are heavy and the balance lowers.
The advances and retreats occur within five days before and after,
and each of the eight skilled individuals reports their observations,
which the Grand Astrologer then seals and submits.
If they match, it is harmonious;
otherwise, it is a prognostication.
The method of observing qi
involves three layers of rooms.
The doors are closed,
and the walls are sealed thoroughly.
Fine curtains are hung.
Inside the room, wooden tables are set up,
one for each *lǜ* (pitch-pipe).
These tables are lower on the inside and higher on the outside,
corresponding to their cardinal directions.
The *lǜ* pipes are placed on them.
Reed pith ash is used to fill the inner end of each pipe.
One observes them according to the calendar: when the *qì* arrives, the ash disperses;
if it is moved by *qì*,
the ash scatters;
if moved by humans or wind,
the ash gathers.
In the imperial palace, twelve jade *lǜ* pipes were used for observation,
but only at the two solstices.
At the Língtái, bamboo *lǜ* pipes were used.
Yáng Quán's record states:
"Bamboo from Jīnménshān in Yíyáng county, Hóngnóng, was taken for the pipes,
and reed pith from Hénèi for the ash."
Some say the *lǜ* pipes were placed inside a room,
buried according to the twelve terrestrial branches,
with their tops level with the ground.
Reed pith ash was filled into the *lǜ* pipes,
and silk gauze was placed over the *lǜ* and *lǚ*.
When the *qì* arrived, it would blow the ash and move the gauze.
A slight movement indicated harmony;
a large movement,
that the ruler was weak and ministers strong;
no movement,
an indication of a severe and tyrannical ruler.
The correct method for
establishing the standards
is described in detail in the *Hàn Zhì*.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
the Zhōngshū Jiān, Xún Xù, calibrated the imperial music (Tàilè).
The eight sounds were out of harmony,
and it was then realized that from the Later Hàn to Wèi dynasties,
the *chǐ* (foot) measure was more than four *fēn* longer than the ancient one.
Xù then ordered the Zuòzuò Láng, Liú Gōng, to create a *chǐ* according to the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
which was the so-called ancient *chǐ*.
Based on the ancient *chǐ*, new bronze *lǜ-lǚ* (pitch-pipes) were cast
to adjust the pitches and rhythms.
When the ancient instruments were measured with this *chǐ*,
there was no discrepancy with the dimensions inscribed on them.
Furthermore,
tomb robbers in Jí Jùn broke into the tomb of Wèi Xiāng Wáng from the Warring States period,
obtaining ancient jade *lǜ* pipes, bells, and *qìng* (stone chimes) from the Zhōu dynasty,
which matched the pitch and rhythm of the new *lǜ* pipes.
At that time, some commanderies and kingdoms also obtained old Hàn dynasty bells,
and when a *lǜ* pipe was blown to test their pitch, they all responded correctly.
Xù inscribed his *chǐ* as follows:
"In the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Jìn,
the Zhōngshū examined ancient artifacts,
and compared them to the current *chǐ*,
finding it to be four and a half *fēn* longer.
The ancient standards compared were of seven types: one, the Gūxǐ jade *lǜ*;
two, the Xiǎolǚ jade *lǜ*;
three, the Xī Jīng bronze *wàngniè*;
four, the gold-inlaid *wàngniè*;
five, the bronze *hú*;
six, ancient coins;
seven, the Jiànwǔ bronze *chǐ*.
The Gūxǐ was slightly stronger,
the Xī Jīng *wàngniè* slightly weaker,
and the rest were identical to this *chǐ*."
The inscription had eighty-two characters.
[一六] This *chǐ* was Xù's new *chǐ*,
and the "current *chǐ*" was Dù Kuí's *chǐ*.
Xún Xù created new bells and *lǜ* pipes which harmonized with ancient instruments,
and people at the time praised their precision.
However, Sànqí Shìláng Ruan Xián of Chénliú criticized their high pitch,
saying that a high pitch
leads to sadness,
and is not the music of a rising state,
but rather the music of a perishing state.
The music of a perishing state is mournful and sorrowful,
and its people suffer.
The current pitch does not conform to the *yǎ* (elegant music),
and I fear it is not the music of virtuous rectitude and supreme harmony,
but must be due to the difference in length between ancient and modern *chǐ*.
Just then, Xián died of illness.
Emperor Wǔ, seeing that Xù's *lǜ* pipes matched Zhōu and Hàn instruments,
therefore put them into use.
Later, in Shǐpíng, someone digging in the ground found an ancient bronze *chǐ*,
which was on the verge of corrosion from age.
It was not known from which dynasty it originated,
but it was indeed four *fēn* longer than Xù's *chǐ*.
People at the time admired Xián's insight,
but no one could act upon it.
The court historian comments: Xù, from a thousand years later,
derived the methods of a hundred generations.
His measurements were appropriate,
and the pitches and rhythms also matched.
This can be called precise and meticulous,
trustworthy and verifiable.
Yet, people at the time lacked understanding;
relying on an unknown *chǐ*,
they disregarded the two instruments of Zhōu and Hàn,
echoing praise or condemnation without thought.
How mistaken they were!
The *Shì Shuō* states:
"A farmer found a Zhōu dynasty jade *chǐ* in a field.
This was the correct *chǐ* for all under heaven.
Xún Xù tested it against the metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments he had created,
and all were shorter by one *mǐ*."
Also,
during the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Xī Jǐng, a Lǐnglíng scholar, obtained a jade *lǜ* pipe from Shùn's temple in Língdào.
He used it to determine the *chǐ*,
which was handed down and called the Hàn official *chǐ*.
When compared to Xún Xù's *chǐ*,
Xù's *chǐ* was four *fēn* shorter;
the Hàn official *chǐ* and the Shǐpíng *chǐ*
had the same length.
Furthermore,
Dù Kuí's *chǐ* used for tuning *lǜ* pipes,
when compared to Xù's new *chǐ*,
was one *chǐ* four *fēn* seven *lí* longer.
In the fourth year of Jǐngyuán of Wèi,
Liú Huī's commentary on the *Jiǔ Zhāng* states: Liú Xīn's *hú* (measure) *chǐ* during Wáng Mǎng's time was four *fēn* five *lí* shorter than the current *chǐ*.
Compared to the Wèi *chǐ*, its *hú* was nine *cùn* five *fēn* five *lí* deep;
this is what Xún Xù meant by the "current *chǐ* being four and a half *fēn* longer."
After Emperor Yuán,
the *chǐ* used in Jiāngdōng was one *chǐ* six *fēn* two *lí* longer than Xún Xù's *chǐ*.
In the fourth year of Guāngchū of Zhào's Liú Yào, a celestial armillary sphere was cast;
in the eighth year, an earth gnomon (tǔguī) was cast.
Their *chǐ* was one *chǐ* five *fēn* longer than Xún Xù's *chǐ*.
Xún Xù's new *chǐ* was only used for tuning musical pitches;
it had not yet widely circulated among the populace.
Thus, the instruments from Jiāngzuǒ and Liú Yào
generally conformed to the Wèi *chǐ*.
The Jiāliáng (standard measure)
*Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"The Lì Shì made measures.
The *fǔ* (bushel) was one *chǐ* deep,
one *chǐ* square on the inside and round on the outside,
holding one *fǔ*.
Its *dòu* (dipper) was one *cùn*,
holding one *dòu*.
Its *ěr* (handle or spout) was three *cùn*,
holding one *shēng*.
It weighed one *jūn*,
and its sound corresponded to the zhōnghuángzhōng (central yellow bell).
[一七] It was leveled without additional tax.
Its inscription reads: 'At this time, Wén sought deeply,
and truly reached the ultimate.
The auspicious measure (Jiāliáng) is now complete,
to be observed by the four states.
It shall eternally enlighten future generations,
this instrument serving as a standard.' "
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn* says:
"Qí's old four measures were
*dòu*, *qū*, *fǔ*, and *zhōng*.
Four *shēng* make one *dòu*,
each of these quadrupling itself
to reach a *fǔ*."
Four *dòu* make one *qū*;
a *qū* is sixteen *shēng*.
Four *qū* make one *fǔ*;
a *fǔ* is sixty-four *shēng*.
Ten *fǔ* make one *zhōng*;
a *zhōng* is sixty-four *dòu*.
Zhèng Xuán believed that a *fǔ* was one *chǐ* square,
with a volume of one thousand cubic *cùn*.
Compared to the *sùmǐfǎ* (grain calculation method) of the *Jiǔ Zhāng*, it was short by two *shēng* and twenty-two eighty-firsts of a *shēng*.
[一八] Calculated by arithmetic,
the volume of an ancient *hú* was one thousand five hundred sixty-two and a half cubic *cùn*.
Square inside and round outside,
with a reduction of one *lí* eight *háo* on the sides,
its diameter was one *chǐ* four *cùn* one *fēn* four *háo* seven *miǎo* two *hū* and a remainder,
and its depth was one *chǐ*.
This was the system for the ancient *hú*.
The Jiǔ Zhāng Shāng Gōng (《九章商功》) method states that one *hú* of millet
occupies 2,700 *cùn*;
one *hú* of hulled rice
occupies 1,627 *cùn*;
[一九]one *hú* of beans, lentils, hemp, or wheat
occupies 2,430 *cùn*.
This is based on their fineness and coarseness as a ratio,
making their prices equal,
but not equating the volumetric measurements of their containers.
Taking the *hú* of hulled rice as the standard
would be consistent with the *Hàn Zhì* (《漢志》).
In the 4th year of Jǐngyuán (景元) of King Chénlíu (陳留王) of Wèi (魏),
Liú Huī (劉徽) annotated the Jiǔ Zhāng Shāng Gōng (《九章商功》) saying:
"The current Grand Minister of Agriculture's *hú*
has a circular diameter of 1 *chǐ*, 3 *cùn*, 5 *fēn*, 5 *máo*,
a depth of 1 *chǐ*,
and a volume of 1,441 and 3/10 *cùn*.
Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) bronze *hú*,
measured with today's *chǐ*, has a depth of 9 *cùn*, 5 *fēn*, 5 *máo*,
and a diameter of 1 *chǐ*, 3 *cùn*, 6 *fēn*, 8 *máo*, 7 *háo*.
Calculated with Liú Huī's (劉徽) method,
it holds 9 *dǒu*, 7 *shēng*, 4 *hé* and a fraction according to today's *hú*."
The Wèi (魏) *hú* was larger and its *chǐ* longer,
while Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) *hú* was smaller and its *chǐ* shorter.
衡權 (Héng Quán)
Héng Quán (衡權) means:
*Héng* (衡) is
level;
*Quán* (權) is
weight.
*Héng* (衡) is used to bear *quán* (權) and balance things,
to equalize light and heavy.
Anciently there were units like *shǔ*, *léi*, *chuí*, *zī*, *huán*, *jūn*, *lüè*, and *yì*,
[二０]which varied across dynasties.
The *Hàn Zhì* (《漢志》) describes the principles of *héng quán* (衡權) in great detail.
Subsequent changes
are not fully known.
During the Yuánkāng (元康) period,
Péi Wěi (裴頠) believed that medical prescriptions were critical for human life,
and that the *liǎng* (兩) measurement was not consistent with ancient times,
causing particularly serious harm.
Therefore, he suggested reforming the weights and measures,
but this was not adopted.
In the 7th month of the 18th year of Zhào Shílè (趙石勒),
while constructing the Jiàndé (建德) Palace,
a round stone was found,
shaped like a water pestle,
with an inscription that read:
"Standard weight stone,
weighing four *jūn*,
conforming to the standard measures of length, volume, and weight.
Made by the Yǒuxīn (有辛) clan."
Xù Xián (續咸) proposed
that it was an object from Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) time.
校勘記 (Jiàokānjì)
志第七律曆中 (Zhì Dì Qī Lǜlì Zhōng)
In ancient times, the sages imitated the celestial pole to operate the armillary sphere,
observed the movements of the heavens, and ordered the brilliant luminaries.
They divided the celestial regions and terrestrial fields,
distinguished the lunar mansions and calendars,
respected agricultural seasons,
and promoted the benefits of things,
all to connect with and follow the two cosmic principles,
and to govern all things.
Thus, observing phenomena and setting up hexagrams,
and dividing yarrow stalks to form divination lines,
the origin of calendrical calculations
lies herein.
When it came to Yán Dì (炎帝),
he divided the eight seasons to begin agricultural work.
Xuānyuán (軒轅) recorded the three principles and elucidated written characters.
Then he ordered Xīhé (羲和) to observe the sun,
Chángyí (常儀) to observe the moon,
Yúqū (臾區) to observe astral氣 (qì),
Línglún (伶倫) to create the *lǜlǚ* (律呂) pitches,
Dànáo (大撓) to create the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) cycle,
and Lìshǒu (隸首) to invent arithmetic.
Róngchéng (容成) synthesized these six arts,
examined and determined celestial phenomena,
established the five phases,
observed expansion and contraction,
initiated waxing and waning,
corrected intercalary errors,
and recorded and published them,
calling it Tiáolì (調曆).
Down to Shàohào (少昊), the phoenix bird oversaw the calendar.
During Zhuānxù (顓頊), the Southern Controller oversaw the heavens.
Táo Táng (陶唐) commanded Xīhé (羲和) to divide their duties.
Yú Shùn (虞舜) followed Yáo's (堯) methods.
When Xià (夏) and Yīn (殷) succeeded in their rule,
and the Zhōu (周) clan responded to their destined time,
the official first month differed,
and the founding methods varied.
The tradition says:
"When the fire star appears,
it is the third month for Xià (夏),
the fourth month for Shāng (商),
and the fifth month for Zhōu (周)."
Therefore, the Son of Heaven appointed sun officials,
and the feudal lords had sun charioteers,
to harmonize the myriad states
and coordinate the three luminaries.
As for the signs of cold and heat, darkness and light,
the numbers of Yin and Yang's birth and destruction,
the records of opening and closing, rising and falling,
and the regulations of waxing and waning, filling and emptying,
all correspond to the celestial positions without deviation.
Thus, they could encompass all living beings
and support heaven and earth.
When Zhōu's (周) virtue declined,
the historians lost their positions,
the calendar specialists dispersed,
and auspicious and inauspicious signs were not managed.
When Qín (秦) unified the world,
it largely promoted the theory of Five Victories,
believing itself to have obtained the auspicious omen of Water virtue,
and used the tenth month as the beginning of the year.
When the Hàn (漢) dynasty first rose,
it had many other preoccupations,
and for over a hundred years,
it adopted Qín's (秦) calendar.
It was not until Emperor Wǔ (武帝) that he first decreed Sì Mǎqiān (司馬遷) and others to discuss the creation of the Hàn (漢) calendar,
and then the Xià (夏) calendar was implemented.
Later, Liú Xīn (劉歆) further created the Sāntǒng (三統) system
to explain the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (《左傳》).
His arguments were specious and not factual,
but Bān Gù (班固) was misled by them
and adopted them in his treatise.
When Guāngwǔ (光武) revived the dynasty,
Grand Master of the Imperial Stud Zhū Fú (朱浮) repeatedly stated that the calendar had errors.
At that time, the empire was newly settled,
and it was not possible to investigate thoroughly.
Towards the end of Yǒngpíng (永平),
the Sìfēn (四分) calendar was adopted,
and after more than seventy years,
its systems were complete.
During Guānghé (光和),
Liú Hóng (劉洪) and Cài Yōng (蔡邕) were commanded to jointly revise the *lǜlì* (律曆).
Later, Sì Mǎbiāo (司馬彪) continued their work
to succeed Bān Gù's (班固) history.
Now, we select from those who discussed calendrical calculations and events after Wèi Wén (魏文) Emperor's Huángchū (黃初) era,
to continue Sì Mǎbiāo's (司馬彪) account.
During Emperor Líng's (靈帝) reign of Hàn (漢),
Liú Hóng (劉洪), the Eastern District Commandant of Kuàijī (會稽),
examined the historical records of calendrical annotations from antiquity to his time.
He investigated the advancement and regression of their movements,
observed the verification of their appearances and disappearances,
watched their comings and goings,
and measured their beginnings and endings.
He finally realized that the Sīfēn (四分) calendar was too coarse in its celestial observations,
due to the *dǒufēn* (斗分) being too large.
He revised the fundamental divisor to 589,
and the *dǒufēn* (斗分) to 145.
He created the Qiánxiàng (乾象) method,
setting the winter solstice sun's position at 22 degrees in the *dǒu* (斗) mansion.
Using this method to trace the movements of the sun, moon, and five planets,
projecting upwards, it matched ancient records;
projecting downwards, it corresponded to the present.
In its creation,
it established numbers based on the *Yì* (《易》),
with hidden movements named,
and concealed positions sought,
named the Qiánxiànglì (乾象曆).
He also innovated calculations for the varying speed of the sun's motion
and concurrently examined the moon's motion,
where Yin and Yang intersect on the ecliptic
and the sun's movement along the ecliptic
causes further advancements and regressions in its celestial longitude relative to the equator.
Compared to previous methods,
it became more precise.
In the 1st year of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Emperor Xiàn (獻帝),
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) received his method,
considering it profound and subtle,
and added annotations to it.
During the Huángchū (黃初) period of Wèi Wén (魏文) Emperor,
the Grand Astrologer Gāotáng Lóng (高堂隆) further meticulously discussed calendrical calculations
and made more reforms.
The Assistant Grand Astrologer Hán Yì (韓翊) believed that the Qiánxiàng (乾象) calendar reduced the *dǒufēn* (斗分) too much,
which would cause it to lead the celestial phenomena later.
He created the Huángchūlì (黃初曆),
using 4,883 as the fundamental divisor
and 1,205 as the *dǒufēn* (斗分).
Thereafter, Shàngshūlìng [尚書令] Chén Qún [陳羣] memorialized,
holding:
"Calculating the calendar is difficult to clarify,
and in previous generations, eminent scholars have often disputed it.
In the first year of Huángchū [黃初], as the Four Quarters calendar was ancient and imprecise,
and the Great Wèi [大魏] received the Mandate,
it was fitting to revise the calendar to clarify the seasons.
Hán Yì [韓翊] first proposed it,
but there was still concern about its accuracy,
so the Qiánxiàng [乾象] method was used for mutual verification.
The verified movements of the sun and moon,
the full and new moons, and the first and last quarters,
after three years,
were still constantly being disputed,
with no resolution.
Examination of the discussions of the Sāngōng [三公] shows they thoroughly covered all principles,
reaching the same conclusion through different paths:
that it should be made to conform to the xuánjī [璿璣] (armillary sphere),
with each method fully applied,
and within one year,
its accuracy or inaccuracy would be determined."
The memorial was approved.
Tàishǐlìng [太史令] Xǔ Zhī [許芝] said:
"Liú Hóng's [劉洪] lunar movement method has been in use for nearly forty years,
and it has been found to be off by more than one chén [辰] (two hours)."
Sūn Qīn [孫欽] argued:
"Sǐqiān [史遷] created the Tàichū [太初] calendar.
Afterwards, Liú Xīn [劉歆] considered it imprecise
and revised it into the Sāntǒng [三統] calendar.
In the Zhānghé [章和] era,
it was changed to the Sìfēn [四分] (Four Quarters) calendar,
using the armillary sphere to measure the heavens.
When examining and comparing its predictions,
there were occasional discrepancies,
and solar eclipses were found to be off by more than half a day.
By the Xīpíng [熹平] era,
Liú Hóng [劉洪] revised it into the Qiánxiàng [乾象] calendar,
which calculated the omens of the seven luminaries in the heavens
and brought them into accord with heaven and earth."
Dǒng Bā [董巴] argued:
"Sages trace the sun by the shadow of the gnomon,
verify the moon by the full and new phases,
clarify the five planets by their visibility and disappearance,
and correct errors by the new and full moons.
The full and new moons, and the visibility and disappearance of planets,
are the guiding principles of calendrical calculations and the clearest means of verification."
Xú Yuè [徐岳] argued:
"Liú Hóng [劉洪], in developing his calendar,
dedicated himself to profound internal reflection for over twenty years,
comparing and verifying the Hàn [漢] dynasty's Tàichū [太初], Sāntǒng [三統], and Sìfēn [四分] calendrical methods,
and calculating the full and new moons against the interval of the Liǎngyí Guōjiān [兩儀郭間].
The moon's movement completes a cycle in nine years,
which is called jiǔdào [九道] (nine paths);
nine chapters,
one hundred seventy-one years,
the nine paths complete a minor cycle;
eighty-one chapters,
five hundred sixty-seven parts complete nine cycles,
advancing or retreating four and five-tenths degrees before Niú [牛] constellation.
Scholars striving to align with the Sìfēn [四分] method
merely reduce one path by sixty-three parts,
but the parts do not extend downwards,
which is why it is imprecise,
all due to too many dòufēn [斗分] (dipper divisions).
When calculating the full and new moons, one should determine the moon's position by the twilight and dawn degrees,
thus understanding the meaning of advancing or delaying the time,
and the Liǎngyí Guōjiān [兩儀郭間] should not be used.
Hóng [洪] added twelve jì [紀] to the first year of Tàichū [太初],
subtracted the lower parts of ten dòu [斗],
starting the first year from Jǐchǒu [己丑],
and also devised methods for the moon's acceleration and deceleration in conjunction, the inclination of the ecliptic, and the five planets.
His principles are truly refined and precise,
and can indeed be long-lasting.
Now, what Hán Yì [韓翊] has created
all uses Hóng's [洪] methods,
with a slight increase in the lower parts of dòu [斗],
so there are few errors.
Yì's [翊] additions and subtractions
also involved careful thought,
but the ten new methods he established
are not yet fully complete;
as for solar eclipses,
they are not fully accurate.
The key to verifying a calendar
lies in solar eclipses.
During the Xīpíng [熹平] period,
when Hóng [洪] was a Láng [郎],
wishing to revise the Sìfēn [四分] calendar,
he first presented a verified solar eclipse:
'The eclipse is in the evening,
the added time is in chén [辰],
the eclipse ascends from below,
two-thirds are obscured.'
After the matter was presented to the emperor, it happened as Hóng [洪] said,
and those in the realm who understood the truth
all heard and saw it;
since Liú Xīn [劉歆],
no one has surpassed Hóng [洪].
For instance, on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month of the second year of Huángchū [黃初] (wùchén [戊辰]), the solar eclipse with added time in wèi [未],
the Qiánxiàng [乾象] method predicted added time at half shēn [申] or slightly later;
the Xiāoxī [消息] method predicted added time in wèi [未];
the Huángchū [黃初] method predicted added time slightly past xīn [辛].
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was later than heaven by one and a half chén [辰], closer;
Huángchū [黃初] was later by two and a half chén [辰], further;
Xiāoxī [消息] was closer to heaven.
On the first day of the first month of the third year (bǐngyín [丙寅]), the solar eclipse with added time in the northern part of shēn [申],
Huángchū [黃初] predicted slightly after yǒu [酉];
Qiánxiàng [乾象] predicted slightly before wǔ [午];
Xiāoxī [消息] predicted in wèi [未].
Huángchū [黃初] was later than heaven by half a chén [辰], closer;
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was earlier than heaven by slightly less than two chén [辰];
Xiāoxī [消息] was earlier than heaven by more than one chén [辰],
making it further from heaven.
On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month of the third year (gēngshēn [庚申]),
the solar eclipse with added time in the southwest,
Qiánxiàng [乾象] predicted the beginning of wèi [未];
Xiāoxī [消息] predicted shēn [申];
Huángchū [黃初] predicted slightly past wèi [未].
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was earlier than heaven by one chén [辰], further;
Huángchū [黃初] was earlier than heaven by half a chén [辰], closer;
Xiāoxī [消息] and Qiánxiàng [乾象] were closer to the zenith.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the second year (guǐwèi [癸未]),
the sun was in rén [壬], the moon in bǐng [丙] for the eclipse.
Qiánxiàng [乾象] predicted the moon in shēn [申];
Xiāoxī [消息] predicted in wèi [未];
Huángchū [黃初] predicted the moon slightly past zǐ [子],
entering jiǎshēn [甲申] day.
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was later than heaven by two chén [辰];
Xiāoxī [消息] was later by one chén [辰], closer;
Huángchū [黃初] was later than heaven by six chén [辰], further.
On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of the third year (yǐsì [乙巳]),
the sun was in chǒu [丑], the moon in wèi [未] for the eclipse.
Qiánxiàng [乾象] predicted the moon at half sì [巳];
Xiāoxī [消息] predicted in wǔ [午];
Huángchū [黃初] predicted the moon slightly past yǒu [酉] on bǐngwǔ [丙午] day.
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was earlier than heaven by two chén [辰], closer;
Huángchū [黃初] was later than heaven by slightly more than two chén [辰], further;
Xiāoxī [消息] was earlier than Qiánxiàng [乾象] by one chén [辰].
In all five instances of calculating solar and lunar eclipses,
Qiánxiàng [乾象] was four times further,
and Huángchū [黃初] was once closer."
Yì [翊] challenged Xú Yuè [徐岳] regarding the calculations:
"The Qiánxiàng [乾象] Xiāoxī [消息] can only be subtracted,
not added.
There is no explanation for adding it,
so it cannot be used."
Yuè [岳] said: "The original method inherently has xiāoxī [消息],
received from the master's teachings,
taking xiāoxī [消息] as the key.
I cannot change the terminology,
so I list it as the correct xiāoxī [消息] method."
Yì's [翊] method is itself imprecise.

(Huángchū [黃初] predicted the seventeenth day of the fifth month (gēngchén [庚辰]),

Venus was seen on the eleventh day of the ninth month of the third year (rényín [壬寅]);

Mercury was seen in the morning on the seventeenth day of the eleventh month of the second year (guǐwèi [癸未]);

Huángchū [黃初] predicted disappearance on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month (gēngxū [庚戌]).
