*Lángzhōng* Lǐ Ēn deliberated:
"By comparing the *Tiāndù* with the historical astronomical records,
the full moon dates in the 7th month of the 2nd year and the 11th month of the 3rd year both differ from the *Tiāndù* dates.
The time of the lunar eclipse was six and a half *shí* later than *Tiān*,
which is not what is meant by 'following three degrees',
but is definitively more than half a day later than *Tiān*."
Dǒng Bā deliberated, saying:
"In ancient times, Fúxī first created the Eight Trigrams,
drawing three lines,
to symbolize the twenty-four solar terms.
Huángdì followed this,
and first created the *Diàolì* calendar.
Through eleven generations,
and five thousand years,
there have been seven calendars in total.
Zhuānxù took the present *mèngchūn* (first month of spring) as the beginning of the year.
At that time, the new moon of the first month coincided with the beginning of spring (*lìchūn*),
the five planets gathered in the celestial temple,
in the *Yíngshì* constellation.
The ice began to thaw,
hibernating insects began to stir,
roosters began to crow three times,
Heaven was said to be creating the seasons,
Earth was said to be creating prosperity,
and humans were said to be creating joy.
Birds, beasts, and all things responded in harmony.
Therefore, the sage Zhuānxù was the patriarch of calendars.
Tāng created the *Yīnlì* calendar,
but no longer took the new moon of the first month coinciding with the beginning of spring as the seasonal marker.
Instead, he took the new moon of the 11th month coinciding with the winter solstice as the year's beginning.
Down to the Zhōu, Lǔ, and Hàn dynasties,
all followed this seasonal marker,
thereby rectifying the four seasons.
The Xià dynasty gained the mandate of Heaven
by succeeding Yáo and Shùn,
because it followed Zhuānxù.
The *Lǐjì Dà Dài* states, 'The calendars of Yú and Xià
established the beginning of the year in the *mèngchūn*.'
This is what is meant. "
Yáng Wěi requested:
"The density and sparsity within sixty days can be known;
there is no need to wait ten years.
If one does not follow the method,
it is like squaring a circle and abandoning the compass and square,
or weighing heavy and light things and disregarding the scales,
or measuring length and breadth and discarding the ruler,
or discussing right and wrong and violating principles.
If we do not first establish the fundamental method for calibrating the calendar,
but rather suspend judgment and listen to terminal disputes that abandon the method,
then it is what Mèng Kē called, 'a foundation of one square inch
can be made higher than a high tower.'
Now, Hán Yì, based on Liú Hóng's method,
knows and values his method,
and treasures his technique.
Yet he discards its theory,
goes against its method,
rejects its words,
and violates its principles.
This will surely prevent Hóng's wonderful formulas from being passed down to future generations.
If he knows and yet violates it,
it is holding onto old ideas and betraying his teacher;
if he does not know and yet relies on it,
it is holding onto ignorance and pretending to know."
The discussions on calibration were not settled,
when the emperor died, and they were suspended.
By the 1st year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng,
*Shàngshū Láng* Yáng Wěi created the *Jǐngchū* calendar.
He presented it in a memorial,
and the emperor then corrected the calendar and beginning of the year,
and implemented Wěi's calendar.
He took the month of *jiànchǒu* as the first month,
changing the third month of that year to *mèngxià* (the first month of summer).
Although its *mèng*, *zhòng*, and *jì* months (first, middle, and last months of each season) differed from the Xià calendar,
for imperial sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, hunting expeditions,
and issuing seasonal decrees,
*jiànyín* (the first month of spring according to the Xià calendar) was always taken as the first month.
In the first month of the 3rd year, the emperor died,
and the Xià calendar was again used.
As for the Liú clan in Shǔ,
they still used the Hàn *Sìfēnlì* calendar.
The *Wú Zhōngshū Lìng* Kān Zé received Liú Hóng's *Qiánxiàngfǎ* from Xú Yuè of Dōnglái,
and added explanations and annotations.
*Zhōngchángshì* Wáng Fān, finding Hóng's method precise and subtle,
used it to deduce the principles of the armillary sphere,
and to construct instruments and write treatises.
Therefore, the Sūn clan used the *Qiánxiànglì* calendar
until the fall of Wú.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
in the 1st year of Tàishǐ,
he adopted Wèi's *Jǐngchūlì* calendar,
renaming it the *Tàishǐlì*.
Yáng Wěi's calculations for the five planets were particularly coarse and imprecise.
Therefore, after Emperor Yuán crossed south of the Yangtze River,
the *Qiánxiàng* method for the five planets was used to replace Wěi's calendar.
Since the *Huángchū* era,
subsequent revisions and creations of calendar methods

all considered the reductions in *dòufēn* (degrees of the Dipper), *shuòyú* (excess at new moon), and the varying speeds (yin and yang, fast and slow) of the moon's movement in the *Qiánxiàng* calendar,
to seek a compromise.
Hóng's method served as a model for later generations of astronomers,
hence it is listed first here.

to the *bǐngxū* of Jiàn'ān 11th year,
the accumulated years are 7,378.

To calculate the entry into the *Jǐ* (epoch):
Place the years from the *shàngyuán* (beginning of the grand epoch) to the desired year.
Divide by the *Qiánfǎ*.
If less than the *Qiánfǎ*,
divide by the *Jǐfǎ*.
The remainder, if less than the *Jǐfǎ*,
means entering the *jiǎzǐ* year of the inner *Jǐ*.
If it reaches the *fǎ* (divisor), remove it,
meaning entering the *jiǎwǔ* year of the outer *Jǐ*.
To calculate the new moon.
Insert the current *jìnián* (紀年)
for which a calculation is desired.
Multiply it by the *zhāngyuè* (章月).
Divide by the *zhāngsuì* (章歲) to obtain
the "fixed accumulated months" (*dìngjīyuè* 定積月).
The remainder is the *rùnyú* (閏餘).
If the *rùnyú* is twelve or more,
that year has a leap month.
Multiply the *dìngjīyuè* by the "general method" (*tōngfǎ* 通法)
to get "hypothetical accumulated days" (*jiǎjīrì* 假積日).
Divide by the "full day method" (*mǎnrìfǎ* 滿日法) to get "fixed accumulated days" (*dìngjīrì* 定積日).
The remainder is the *xiǎoyú* (小餘).
Subtract sixty (*liùxún* 六旬) from the *jīrì* (積日)
to get the *dàyú* (大餘).
Assign it to the entered *jì* (紀),
and outside the calculation,
this is the day of the new moon of the eleventh month (*tiānzhèng shíyīyuè shuòrì* 天正十一月朔日) of the desired year.
To find the next month,
add *dàyú* twenty-nine
and *xiǎoyú* seven hundred seventy-three.
If the *xiǎoyú* reaches the *mǎnrìfǎ*, carry over to the *dàyú*.
If the *xiǎoyú* is six hundred eighty-four or more,
that month is long.
Calculating the Winter Solstice
Insert the current *jìnián*
for which a calculation is desired.
Multiply it by the *yúshù* (餘數).
Divide by the *jìfǎ* (紀法) to get the *dàyú*.
The remainder is the *xiǎoyú*.
Subtract sixty from it,
[一０]assign it to the *jì* (紀),
and outside the calculation,
this is the Winter Solstice day (*tiānzhèng dōngzhìrì* 天正冬至日).
Calculating the Twenty-Four Solar Terms
Insert the *xiǎoyú* of the Winter Solstice.
[一一]Add *dàyú* fifteen
and *xiǎoyú* five hundred fifteen.
If it reaches two thousand three hundred fifty-six, carry over to the *dàyú*.
Assign as per the method.
Calculating the Leap Month
Subtract the *zhāngsuì* from the *rùnyú*.
Multiply the remainder by the "middle of the year" (*suìzhōng* 歲中).
Divide by the *zhāngrùn* (章閏) to get one month.
If there's a remainder,
and it's half of the method or more, it also counts as one.
There are advances and retreats
with no *zhōngyuè* (中月).
[一二]
Calculating First and Last Quarters, and Full Moon
Add *dàyú* seven
and *xiǎoyú* five hundred fifty-seven and a half.
If the *xiǎoyú* reaches the *rìfǎ* (日法), carry over to the *dàyú*.
Assign the remainder as before
to get the first quarter (*shàngxián* 上弦).
Add again to get the full moon (*wàng* 望).
Add again to get the last quarter (*xiàxián* 下弦).
Add again to get the new moon of the next month (*hòuyuèshuò* 後月朔).
If the *xiánwàng* (弦望) *dìngxiǎoyú* (定小餘) is four hundred one or less,
multiply it by one hundred *kè* (刻).
Divide by the *rìfǎ* to get one *kè*.
If there's a remainder, multiply by ten
to find the *fēn* (分).
By checking which nearby solar term's night leak has not yet ended,
the calculation will be in days.
Calculating *Mò* (沒)
Insert the current *jìnián*
for which a calculation is desired.
Multiply it by the *yúshù*.
Divide by the *jìfǎ* to get "accumulated *mò*" (*jīmò* 積沒).
If there's a remainder, add it to the "exhausted accumulated" (*jìnjī* 盡積) to make one.
Multiply it by the *huìtōng* (會通).
Divide by the *mòfǎ* (沒法) to get the *dàyú*.
The remainder is the *xiǎoyú*.
Assign the *dàyú* to the *jì*,
and outside the calculation,
this is the *mò* day after the Winter Solstice.
To find the next *mò*,
add *dàyú* sixty-nine
and *xiǎoyú* sixty-four.
If it reaches the *fǎ* (法), carry over to the *dàyú*.
No *fēn* means *miè* (滅).
Calculating the Sun's Degree
Multiply the *jīrì* by the *jìfǎ*.
Subtract a full circle (*zhōutiān* 周天).
Divide the remainder by the *jìfǎ*.
The result is the degree.
Assign the degree, starting five degrees before *Niú* (牛) constellation.
Divide by the *sùcì* (宿次).
If it doesn't reach a full *sù* (宿),
that is the location of the Sun at midnight of the *tiānzhèngshuò* (天正朔).
To find the next day,
add one degree.
If it passes *Dǒu* (斗), subtract *fēn*.
If the *fēn* is small,
subtract one degree for the *jìfǎ*,
and add it.
Calculating the Moon's Degree
Multiply the *jīrì* by the *yuèzhōu* (月周).
Subtract a full circle.
The remainder, if it reaches the *jìfǎ*, is the degree.
The remainder is the *fēn*.
Assign as above,
then it is the location of the Moon at midnight of the *tiānzhèngshuò*.
To find the next month,
for a short month, add twenty-two degrees
and two hundred fifty-eight *fēn*.
For a long month, add one day,
thirteen degrees,
and two hundred seventeen *fēn*.
If it reaches the *fǎ*, one degree is gained.
In the latter half of winter,
the moon is in *Zhāng* (張) and *Xīnshǔ* (心署).
[一三]
Calculating the Degree of Conjunction and New Moon (*Héshuò dù* 合朔度)
Multiply the *shuòxiǎoyú* (朔小餘) by the *zhāngsuì*.
If it reaches the *huìshù* (會數), it is a *dàfēn* (大分).
If not, it's a *xiǎofēn* (小分).
Add the *dàfēn* to the *shuòyèbànrìfēn* (朔夜半日分).
If it reaches the *jìfǎ*, carry over to degrees.
Assign as before.
This is where the Sun and Moon converge at *tiānzhèng héshuò* (天正合朔).
To find the next month,
add twenty-nine degrees,
three hundred twelve *dàfēn*,
and twenty-five *xiǎofēn*.
[一四]If the *xiǎofēn* reaches the *huìshù*, carry over to the *dàfēn*.
If the *dàfēn* reaches the *jìfǎ*, carry over to the degrees.
[一五]If it passes *Dǒu*, subtract *dàfēn*.
To find the Sun's degree at the first quarter, full moon, and last quarter,
add to the *héshuò dù* seven degrees,
two hundred twenty-five *fēn*,
and seventeen and a half *xiǎofēn*.
Assign the *dàxiǎofēn* (大小分) and degrees as before.
This is the Sun's degree at the first quarter.
Add again to get the full moon, last quarter, and the next month's conjunction.
To find the Moon's degree at the first quarter, full moon, and last quarter,
add to the *héshuò dù* ninety-eight degrees,
four hundred eight *dàfēn*,
and forty-one *xiǎofēn*.
Assign the *dàxiǎofēn* and degrees as for *héshuò*.
This is the Moon's location at the first quarter.
Add again to get the full moon, last quarter, and the next month's conjunction.
To find the Sun's and Moon's degrees for dawn and dusk,
for the Sun, use the *jìfǎ*;
for the Moon, use the *yuèzhōu*.
Multiply by the night leak of the nearest solar term.
Divide by two hundred to get the dawn *fēn*.
For the Sun, subtract from the *jìfǎ*;
for the Moon, subtract from the *yuèzhōu*.
The remainder is the dusk *fēn*.
Add each to midnight,
and according to the method, convert to degrees.
Calculating Lunar Eclipses
Insert the *shàngyuán nián* (上元年)
for which a calculation is desired.
Subtract the *huìsuì* (會歲).
Multiply the remaining years by the *huìshuài* (會率).
Divide by the *huìsuì* to get "accumulated eclipses" (*jīshí* 積蝕).
If there's a remainder, add one to the accumulated.
Multiply by the *huìyuè* (會月).
Divide by the *huìshuài* to get "accumulated months" (*jīyuè* 積月).
The remainder is the *yuèyú* (月餘).
Multiply the remaining years by the *zhāngrùn*.
Divide by the *zhāngsuì* to get "accumulated leap months" (*jīrùn* 積閏).
Subtract this from the *jīyuè*.
Subtract the remainder by the *suìzhōng*.
If there's a remainder,
the count starts from *tiānzhèng*.
To find the next eclipse,
add five months,
one thousand six hundred thirty-five *yuèyú*.
If it reaches the *huìshuài*, one month is gained.
The month is at the full moon.
Calculating the Hexagrams on Duty
Based on the Winter Solstice *dàyú*,
double its *xiǎoyú*.
This is the day *Kǎn* (坎) is on duty.
Add *xiǎoyú* one thousand seventy-five.
If it reaches the *qiánfǎ* (乾法), carry over to the *dàyú*.
This is the day *Zhōngfú* (中孚) is on duty.
To find the next hexagram,
add *dàyú* six
and *xiǎoyú* one hundred three to each.
For the four cardinal hexagrams (*sìzhèng* 四正), each is based on its middle day,
and its *xiǎoyú* is doubled.
Calculating the Five Phases on Duty
Place the major and minor remainders of the Winter Solstice.
[一六] Add twenty-seven to the major remainder,
and nine hundred twenty-seven to the minor remainder.
If it reaches two thousand three hundred fifty-six, it is counted from the major remainder.
This gives the day on which the element Earth takes charge.
Add eighteen to the major remainder,
and six hundred eighteen to the minor remainder.
This gives the day on which the element Wood takes charge at the Beginning of Spring.
Add seventy-three to the major remainder,
and one hundred sixteen to the minor remainder.
This again gives the element Earth.
Add Earth again, and it is like obtaining Fire.
Metal and Water follow this pattern.
To calculate the added *shí* (時, 'hour' or 'moment'):
Multiply the minor remainder by twelve.
When it reaches its *fǎ* (法, 'divisor'), one *chén* (辰, 'double hour') is obtained.
The count starts from *zǐ* (子).
Excluding calculations,
*shuò* (朔, new moon), *xián* (弦, first/last quarter), and *wàng* (望, full moon) are used to determine the minor remainder.
To calculate the *lòukè* (漏刻, 'clepsydra marks'):
Multiply the minor remainder by one hundred.
When it reaches its *fǎ*, one *kè* (刻, 'unit of time') is obtained.
If there is a remainder, divide it by ten.
To find the *fēn* (分, 'sub-unit'):
Examine the nearest *jiéqì* (節氣, 'solar term').
It starts from the end of the night division.
If the upper water of the night has not finished,
it is discussed in relation to what is nearest.
Calculations involve advancement and recession.
Advancement means adding, recession means subtracting what is obtained.
There are discrepancies in advancement and recession.
It starts after the two-part *dù* (度, 'degree').
The rate increases or decreases every four *dù*.
When the decrease is by half each time,
it changes by three.
The discrepancy stops when it reaches three.
After five *dù*, it decreases as before.
Method for the Moon's Three Paths:
The Moon's motion is either slow or fast,
with a complete cycle of advancement.
The total count is derived from the total numbers of Heaven and Earth.
Multiply the remaining rate by itself.
Divide by the total count.
This gives the fractional part beyond the cycle.
Take the total celestial circumference.
Divide by the Moon's cycle.
This is the number of calendar days.
Slowness and quickness have a diminishing rate;
their change is the 'force' (*shì*, 勢).
Add the diminished rate to the Moon's motion rate.
This gives the daily rotational *dù* and *fēn*.
Add the left and right diminishing rates to each other.
This gives the increase/decrease rate.
Increases are successively added,
and decreases are successively subtracted.
This is the accumulated *yíngsuō* (盈縮, 'waxing and waning').
Multiply the half minor cycle by the general *fǎ*.
Divide by the general number.
Subtract it from the calendar cycle.
This gives the *shuò* motion *fēn*.

Calculating the inclusion of the *héshuò* (合朔, 'conjunction of the Sun and Moon') into the calendar:
Multiply the accumulated months from *shàngyuán* (上元, 'prime epoch') by the *shuò* motion major and minor *fēn*.
If the minor *fēn* reaches the general number thirty-one, it is counted as one major *fēn*.
If the major *fēn* reaches the calendar cycle, subtract it.
The remainder, if it reaches the cycle *fǎ*, gives one day.
The incomplete part is the day's remainder.
The day's remainder determines the calculation beyond.
This is the *héshuò* to be included in the calendar.
To find the next month,
add one day.
The day's remainder is five thousand eight hundred thirty-two,
and the minor *fēn* is twenty-five.
To find the *xiánwàng*,
add seven days for each.
The day's remainder is two thousand two hundred eighty-three,
and the minor *fēn* is twenty-nine and a half.
Each *fēn* forms a day according to the *fǎ*.
When the days reach twenty-seven, subtract them.
The remainder is treated as a cycle *fēn*.
If it is insufficient for division,
subtract one day
and add the cycle void.
Determining the major and minor remainders for *xiánwàng*:
Place the *yíngsuō* accumulation included in the calendar.
Multiply it by the total cycle to get the dividend.
Let the general number multiply the day's remainder *fēn*,
then multiply by the increase/decrease rate.
Subtract this from the increase/decrease dividend.
This gives the *yíngsuō* for the added *shí*.
For the *zhāngsuì* (章歲, 'cycle year'), subtract the Moon's motion *fēn*.
Multiply by the half cycle to get the discrepancy *fǎ*.
Divide by it.
The result is that *yíng* (waxing) subtracts and *suō* (waning) adds to the major and minor remainders.
If it is *yíng* or *bùzú* (不足, 'insufficient') according to the day *fǎ*,
the *shuò* added *shí* is before or after the day.
For *xiánwàng*, advance or recede the major remainder
to determine the minor remainder.
Calculating the fixed *dù* for *shuò*, *xiánwàng* at the added *shí*:
Multiply the *yíngsuō* of the added *shí* by the *zhāngsuì*.
Divide by the discrepancy *fǎ*.
If the result reaches the total number, it becomes the *yíngsuō* major and minor *fēn*.
Subtract *yíng* and add *suō* to the Sun and Moon's current positions on this day.
If *yíng* or *bùzú*,
advance or recede the *dù* according to the *jìfǎ* (紀法, 'epoch divisor').
This gives the fixed *dù* and *fēn* for the Sun and Moon's positions.
Calculating the Moon's motion at midnight for inclusion in the calendar:
Multiply the *shuò* minor remainder by the half cycle.
Divide by the general number.
Subtract this from the day's remainder included in the calendar.
If the remainder is insufficient,
add the cycle *fǎ* and then subtract.
Go back one day.
Going back gives the cycle day plus its *fēn*.
This directly gives the inclusion at midnight.
To find the next day,
advance one day.
Due to the day's remainder reaching twenty-seven days,
if the day's remainder reaches the cycle day *fēn*, subtract it.
It does not align with the cycle day.
If it does not align,
add the cycle void to the remainder.
All remainders are then the day's remainder for the next day's inclusion in the calendar.
Calculating the Moon's fixed *dù* at midnight:
Multiply the day's remainder for midnight inclusion in the calendar
by the increase/decrease rate.
If it reaches one according to the cycle *fǎ*,
the incomplete part is the remainder.
With the increase/decrease *yíngsuō* accumulation,
if there is no remainder to decrease,
divide the whole by the *fǎ* for subtraction.
This gives the *yíngsuō* at midnight.
If it reaches the *zhāngsuì*, it becomes a *dù*.
The incomplete part is a *fēn*.
Multiply the *fēn* and the remainder by the general number.
If the remainder reaches the cycle *fǎ*, it is counted as a *fēn*.
If the *fēn* reaches the *jìfǎ*, it is counted as a *dù*.
Add *yíng* and subtract *suō* from the original midnight *dù* and remainder.

To calculate midnight's entry into the calendar:
Multiply the *chāilǜ* (差率) by the new moon's small remainder.

Add the obtained day division to its division.
Reduce the minute division by the *huìshù* (會數) to get the small division.
This is midnight's entry into the calendar on the new moon day.
To calculate the next day,
add one day.
The day remainder is thirty-one,

If the small division follows the remainder like the *huìshù* (會數),

Then add one day again.
When the calendar calculation ends,

This is the beginning of the calendar's entry.

Add a remainder of 2702,

To calculate the fixed day for midnight:
Multiply the common number by the midnight excess and deficit (盈縮) and remainder from the calendar of speed and slowness.
If the remainder reaches half a cycle, it becomes the small division.
Add the excess and subtract the deficit from the Yīn-Yáng day remainder.
If the day remainder is in excess or deficit,
adjust the day by advancing or retreating with the lunar cycle to fix it.
Multiply the fixed day remainder by the gain/loss rate.
If it yields one like the lunar cycle,
use the combined number for gain/loss
as the fixed number for midnight.
To calculate the number for bright and dark:
Multiply the gain/loss rate by the night clepsydra of the nearest solar term.
Two hundredths of this is bright.
Subtract the gain/loss rate to get dark.
Use the midnight number for gain/loss as the fixed number for bright and dark.
To calculate the moon's distance from the pole (ecliptic latitude):
Set the added time or the fixed number for bright and dark.
Divide it by twelve to get degrees.
Divide the remainder by three to get *shǎo* (少).
If it does not divide evenly by one, it is *qiáng* (強).
Two *shǎo* (少) is *ruò* (弱).
The result is the moon's distance from the ecliptic.
For the Yáng Calendar, add the ecliptic distance from the pole at the location of the day.
For the Yīn Calendar, subtract it.
This gives the moon's distance from the pole.
*Qiáng* (強) is positive, *ruò* (弱) is negative.

Terms of different names cancel out.
When subtracting,

Terms of different names combine.

Forecasting the Five Planets
Set the [number of years from] shàngyuán to the year sought,
multiply it by the Zhōulǜ.
When it reaches the Rìlǜ, one [cycle] is obtained,
named jīhé,
the remainder is héyú.
Divide it by the Zhōulǜ.
If one is obtained,
the planet aligns with the previous year.
If two,
it aligns before the previous year.
If nothing is obtained,
it aligns with the current year.
Subtract the Zhōulǜ from the héyú to get the dùfēn.
For Jīn and Shuǐ jīhé,
odd is dawn,
even is dusk.
Forecasting the planetary alignment with the moon
Multiply the Yuèshù and Yuèyú respectively by the jīhé.
When it reaches the Héyuèfǎ, count it as a month;
the remainder is Yuèyú.
Subtract the jīyuè from the jìyuè;
the remainder is the rùjìyuè.
Separately, multiply it by the Zhāngrùn.
When it reaches the Zhāngyuè, one leap month is obtained.
Subtract this from the rùjìyuè.
Then subtract the remainder by the Suìzhōng.
This is called tiānzhèngsuànwài,
which is the héyuè.
If it is at the leap month juncture,
use the shuò to manage it.
Forecasting the day of entering the month
Multiply the Yuèyú by the Tōngfǎ,
and the Shuòxiǎoyú by the Héyuèfǎ.
Then simplify both by the Huìshù.
When the result reaches the Rìdùfǎ, one [day] is obtained,
then the planet aligns on the day of entering the month.
If it does not reach, it is Rìyú,
called shuòsuànwài.
Forecasting the planetary degree
Multiply the Dùfēn by the Zhōutiān.
When it reaches the Rìdùfǎ, one degree is obtained.
The remainder is yú,
the degrees begin from five degrees before Niú.

Wèi Shàngshū Láng Yáng Wěi's memorial stated:
"Your servant has reviewed historical records
and analyzed the calendar calculations.
Time is used to record agricultural seasons,
and months are used to record events.
The origin of this
is ancient and long-standing.
Starting from Shǎohào,
Xuánniǎo supervised the divisions;
during Zhuānxū and Dì Kù,
Chóng Lí supervised the heavens;
during Emperor Táng and Yú Shùn,
Xī Hé managed the sun.
The Three Dynasties followed this,
so there were sun officials (rìguān) for generations.
The sun officials managed the calendar,
which was then distributed to the feudal lords.
The feudal lords received it,
and then distributed it within their territories.
In the time of the Xià Hòu clan,
Xī Hé indulged in revelry,
neglecting the seasons and disrupting the days,
which is recorded in the 'Yìn Zhēng'.
From this perspective,
valuing agricultural seasons and emphasizing human affairs
has been the case throughout the generations.
By the time the Zhōu dynasty declined,
and the Warring States contended fiercely,
the 'sheep of the monthly sacrifice' (gàoshuò zhī yáng)
was abolished and not continued;
the 'rites of ascending the platform' (dēngtái zhī lǐ)
were extinguished and not followed.
The intercalation divisions were out of sequence and unrecognized,
the first month of spring lost its regularity and no one was aware.
The Great Fire star still flowed westward,
yet people wondered why hibernating insects did not hide.
At that time,
the Son of Heaven did not align with the seasons,
the calendar officials did not record the days,
the feudal lords did not receive their duties,
and the sun attendants did not divide the first day of the month.
Human affairs were neglected,
and agricultural seasons were abandoned.
When Zhòngní rectified disorder in the Spring and Autumn period,
he used praise and censure to correct;
if the calendar official missed an intercalation,
he criticized and recorded it;
if one ascended the platform to announce the first day of the month,
he called it 'observing the rites'.
From that time onward,
up to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
they again took the eleventh month (mèngdōng) as the beginning of the year,
and the intercalary month as the 'ninth month afterward'.
The mid-season points were mismatched,
and the timing of months was erroneous.
Time was added after heaven,
eclipses did not occur on the first day of the month.
This accumulated over many years,
and was not reformed for a long time.
Not until the seventh year of Yuánfēng during Emperor Wǔdì's reign
did they finally realize the error.
Thereupon, they corrected the beginning of the year and the first day of the month,
revised the calendar calculations,
and commissioned great talents and well-versed individuals
to create the Tàichū Lì.
They calibrated the discrepancies in the mid-month and first-month calculations
to correct the intercalation divisions;
and measured the degrees of the mid-constellation stars
to examine their density and sparsity.
They took the month of Jiànyín as the first month of the year and the first day of the month,
and the month of Huángzhōng as the beginning of the calendar.
Its 'doufen' (degrees of the Dipper) was too large,
and later became sparse and loose.
By the second year of Yuánhé,
the Sīfēn Lì was again adopted,

Up to the present day,
observations of solar eclipses
frequently occur on the last day of the month (huì).

After detailed refinement,

and aligns with the mid-heaven of ancient and modern times.
Just as in ancient times during Emperor Táng's reign,

truly setting in order the hundred officials,

I wish that the current state ceremonies,

Your servant believes that in ancient imperial times,

When Emperor Xiàowǔ of Hàn reformed the beginning of the year and the first day of the month,

Now the era name has been changed to Jǐngchū,

The Jǐngchū Lì proposed by your servant

To govern with it is to save effort,

Even if one were to employ Yánsāng for mental arithmetic,

The *Ji* difference for conjunctions and oppositions is 103,610.
To find the origin of this number:
Take the accumulated months of one *Ji*,
multiply by the common divisor,
subtract the common conjunction/opposition value.
The remainder after subtraction
is the *Ji* difference.
Add this progressively to the previous *Ji*
to obtain the next *Ji*.
If, after adding, it does not reach the common conjunction/opposition value,
then the new moon at the beginning of the *Ji* year, in the first month of *Tiānzhèng*, is when the moon is at the north pole of the ecliptic.
If it reaches the value and is subtracted,
then the moon is at the south pole of the ecliptic.
When adding to the south pole,
if it reaches the full value, it is at the north pole;
when adding to the north pole,
if it reaches the full value, it is at the south pole.
The *Ji* difference for acceleration/deceleration is 30,180.
To find the origin of this number:

multiply by the common divisor,
subtract the common *Zhōu* (period).
Subtract the remainder from the common *Zhōu*.
The remainder after this subtraction
is the *Ji* difference.
Subtract this progressively from the previous *Ji*
to obtain the next *Ji*.
If it is insufficient for subtraction,
add the common *Zhōu*.
To find the *Yuán* difference rate:
progressively subtract from the *Jiǎyín* *Ji* difference rate of the previous *Yuán*.
The remainder is the *Jiǎzǐ* *Ji* difference rate of this *Yuán*.
To find the next *Ji*,
use the method above.
Method for calculating accumulated months for new moons: From the *Rénchén Yuán* [era]
up to the desired year,
exclude the desired year.
Divide by the *Ji* rule.
The quotient,
excluding the remainder, is the number of the *Ji* entered.
The remainder is the number of years within the *Ji*.
Multiply by the *Zhāng* months.
For each *Zhāng* year,
this gives the accumulated months.
The remainder is the leap remainder.
If the leap remainder is 12 or more,
that year has a leap month.
A leap month is determined by having no *Zhōngqì*.
Method for calculating new moons: Multiply the accumulated months by the common divisor
to get the new moon accumulated points.
Divide by the day rule.
The quotient is the accumulated days.
The remainder is the small remainder.
Divide the accumulated days by 60.
The remainder is the large remainder.
Assign the large remainder according to the *Ji*,
excluding the quotient.
This is the new moon day of the eleventh month (*Tiānzhèng*) of the desired year.
To find the next month,
add 29 to the large remainder,
and 2419 to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the day rule, carry one to the large remainder.
Assign as before.
This is the new moon day of the next month.
If the small remainder is 2140 or more,
that month is a long month.
To calculate first and last quarters and full moons:
Add 7 to the large remainder of the new moon,
1744 to the small remainder,
and 1 to the small fraction.
If the small fraction reaches 2, carry one to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the day rule, carry one to the large remainder.
If the large remainder reaches 60, subtract 60.
Assign the remainder according to the *Ji*,
excluding the quotient.
This is the day of the first quarter.
Add again
to obtain the full moon, last quarter, and the new moon of the following month.
For the full moon of a lunar eclipse,
determine the small remainder as it is for the middle *Jiéqì* (or determine the small remainder as the number of intervals from the nearest middle *Jiéqì*, for numbers below that),
calculate upwards as days.
If the full moon is within four days before or after a middle *Jiéqì*,
observe the limit number.
If the full moon is five days or more before or after a middle *Jiéqì*,
observe the interval limit.
Method for calculating the twenty-four *Qì*: Take the year of the entered *Ji*.
Exclude the desired value.
Multiply by the remainder.
If it reaches the *Ji* rule, it becomes the large remainder.
The remainder is the small remainder.
If the large remainder reaches 60, subtract 60.
Assign the remainder according to the *Ji*,
excluding the quotient.
This is the winter solstice day of the eleventh month (*Tiānzhèng*).
To find the next *Qì*,
add 15 to the large remainder,
402 to the small remainder,
and 11 to the small fraction.
If the small fraction reaches the *Qì* rule, carry one to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the *Ji* rule, carry one to the large remainder.
Assign as before.
This is the day of the next *Qì*.
Method for calculating leap months: Subtract the leap remainder from the *Zhāng* year.
Multiply the remainder by the mid-year value.
If it reaches the *Zhāng* leap rule, one month is gained.
If the remainder is half the rule or more,
one month is also gained.
Count starting from the eleventh month (*Tiānzhèng*).
Excluding the quotient,
this is the leap month.
Leap months may advance or retreat,
governed by the absence of a *Zhōngqì*.

Method for calculating occultations and disappearances: For the accumulated days of the winter solstice that have a small remainder,
add 1 to the accumulated days.
Multiply by the occultation fraction.
Divide by the occultation rule.
The quotient is the large remainder.
The remainder is the small remainder.
If the large remainder reaches 60, subtract 60.
Assign the remainder according to the *Ji*,
excluding the quotient.
This is the day of the occultation after the winter solstice of the previous year.
To find the next occultation,
add 69 to the large remainder,
and 592 to the small remainder.
If the small remainder reaches the occultation rule, carry one
to the large remainder.
Assign as before.
If the small remainder is zero,
it is a disappearance.
Method for calculating the days when the Five Phases take charge: *Lìchūn*, *Lìxià*, *Lìqiū*, *Lìdōng*
are the days when Wood, Fire, Metal, and Water respectively begin to take charge.
Subtract 18 from their respective large remainders,
483 from the small remainders,
and 6 from the small fractions.
Assign the remainder according to the *Ji*,
excluding the quotient.
These are the days when Earth takes charge,
before each of the Four Beginnings (*Lìchūn*, *Lìxià*, *Lìqiū*, *Lìdōng*).
If the large remainder is insufficient for subtraction,
add 60.
If the small remainder is insufficient for subtraction,
subtract 1 from the large remainder
and add the *Ji* rule.
If the small fraction is insufficient for subtraction,
subtract 1 from the small remainder
and add the *Qì* rule.
Method for calculating the day of hexagram application: Based on the great remainder of the Dōngzhì,
six times its small remainder
is the day for applying the Kǎn Guà.
Add 10,091 to the small remainder,
and when it reaches the full fundamental method, starting from the great remainder,
that is the day for applying the Zhōngfú hexagram.
To find the next hexagram,
add six to each great remainder,
and 967 to the small remainder.
For each of the four cardinal points, use its middle day,
and six times its small remainder.
Method for calculating solar degrees: Multiply the accumulated days from the new moon by the calendrical divisor.
Subtract full circuits.
Divide the remainder by the calendrical divisor.
The quotient is the degree,
and the remainder is the fractional part.
The degrees are reckoned starting from the fifth position before Niú,
and divided according to the order of the lunar mansions.
If it does not fill a mansion,
then it is the degree and fractional part of the sun at midnight on the new moon of the eleventh month of the Tiānzhèng calendar.
To find the next day,
add one degree to the day;
do not add to the fractional part.
If it passes Dǒu, subtract the Dǒu divisions.
If the fractional part is insufficient,
retreat one degree.
〔一四〕
Method for calculating lunar degrees: Multiply the accumulated days from the new moon by the lunar circuit.
Subtract full circuits.
Divide the remainder by the calendrical divisor.
The quotient is the degree,
and the remainder is the fractional part.
Calculating as per the method above,
this gives the degree and fractional part of the moon at midnight on the new moon of the eleventh month of the Tiānzhèng calendar.
To find the next month,
for a short month, add 22 degrees
and 806 fractional parts;
for a long month, also add one day,
13 degrees,
and 679 fractional parts.
When the fractional parts reach the full calendrical divisor, it yields one degree.
This gives the degree and fractional part of the moon at midnight on the new moon of the next month.
In the latter ten days of winter,
record the moon in Zhāng and Xīn.
〔一五〕
Method for calculating the conjunction degree at new moon: Multiply the small remainder of the new moon by the *zhāng* year.
When it reaches the full common divisor, it becomes the great fractional part;
the remainder is the small fractional part.
Add the great fractional part to the sun's degree and fractional part at midnight on the new moon.
〔十六〕When the fractional part reaches the full calendrical divisor, add it to the degrees.
Proceed as before,
this gives the shared conjunction degree of the sun and moon at the new moon of the eleventh month of the Tiānzhèng calendar.
To find the next month,
add 29 degrees,
977 great fractional parts,
and 42 small fractional parts.
When the small fractional part reaches the full common divisor, add it to the great fractional part.
When the great fractional part reaches the full calendrical divisor, add it to the degrees.
If it passes Dǒu, subtract its fractional parts.
This gives the shared conjunction degree of the sun and moon at the new moon of the next month.
Method for calculating the solar degree at first quarter and full moon: Add 7 to the conjunction degree,
705 great fractional parts,
10 small fractional parts,
and 1 minute fractional part.
When the minute fractional part reaches two, add it to the small fractional part.
When the small fractional part reaches the full common divisor, add it to the great fractional part.
When the great fractional part reaches the full calendrical divisor, add it to the degrees.
Proceed as before,
this gives the solar degree at the first quarter.
Add again
to obtain the full moon, last quarter, and the subsequent month's conjunction.
Method for calculating the lunar degree at first quarter and full moon: Add 98 to the conjunction degree,
1279 great fractional parts,
and 34 small fractional parts.
When the number is full, proceed as before.
〔一七〕This is the lunar degree at the first quarter.
Add again
to obtain the full moon, last quarter, and the subsequent month's conjunction.
Method for calculating the degrees of sun and moon visibility: For the sun, use the calendrical divisor;
for the moon, use the lunar circuit.
Multiply by the night clepsydra value of the nearest solar term.
Divide by 200.
This is the brightness fractional part.
For the sun, subtract this from the calendrical divisor;
for the moon, subtract from the lunar circuit.
The remainder is the darkness fractional part.
Add each fractional part to midnight,
and apply the method to obtain the degrees.
Method for calculating conjunction and node crossing for lunar eclipses: Place the accumulated new moon integrals for the current epoch.
Add the difference rate of node crossing for the current epoch.
Subtract full cycles of node crossing.
The remainder is the degrees and fractional parts from the node at the new moon of the eleventh month of the Tiānzhèng calendar for the requested year.
Add the common number.
Subtract full cycles of node crossing.
The remainder is the degrees and fractional parts from the node at the new moon of the next month.
Add the sum of new and full moon for each month to its degrees and fractional parts from the node at the new moon.
Subtract full cycles of node crossing.
The remainder is the degrees and fractional parts from the node at the full moon for each month.
If the new and full moon's fractional parts from the node
are below the sum of new and full moon,
or above the limit number for node crossing,
then a new moon indicates a node crossing (solar eclipse),
and a full moon indicates a lunar eclipse.
Method for calculating whether the moon at the conjunction and node crossing for a lunar eclipse is above or below the ecliptic: Place the accumulated new moon integrals for the current epoch.
Add the difference rate of node crossing for the current epoch.
〔一八〕Subtract double cycles of node crossing.
If the remainder does not fill a full cycle of node crossing,
then at the beginning of the epoch, it is above the ecliptic,
and at the Tiānzhèng new moon conjunction, the moon is above the ecliptic;
if at the beginning of the epoch, it is below the ecliptic,
then at the Tiānzhèng new moon conjunction, the moon is below the ecliptic.
If it fills a full cycle of node crossing,
when above the ecliptic, it becomes below the ecliptic;
when below the ecliptic, it becomes above the ecliptic.
To find the next month,
add the common number.
Subtract full cycles of node crossing.
If below the ecliptic becomes full, it goes above the ecliptic;
if above the ecliptic becomes full, it goes below the ecliptic.
For those where node crossing precedes lunar eclipse,
if the new moon is above the ecliptic, the full moon is above the ecliptic;
if the new moon is below the ecliptic, the full moon is below the ecliptic.
For those where lunar eclipse precedes node crossing,
observe the eclipsed moon: if the new moon is below the ecliptic, the full moon is above the ecliptic;
if the new moon is above the ecliptic, the full moon is below the ecliptic.
If the node crossing and lunar eclipse are below the sum of new and full moon,
then the crossing precedes the conjunction.
If they are above the limit number for node crossing,
then the conjunction precedes the crossing.
If the former (crossing before conjunction) is close to the limit number,
then monitor it proactively;
〔一九〕if the latter (conjunction before crossing) is close to the limit number,
then monitor it retrospectively.
Method for calculating degrees from the node: For cases where the crossing precedes the conjunction,
if the current degrees and fractional parts from the node are like one unit of the solar method,
the result is the degrees and fractional parts retreating from the node.
For cases where the conjunction precedes the crossing,
subtract the degrees and fractional parts from the node from the node-crossing cycle.
The remainder, if like one unit of the solar method,
the result is the degrees advancing from the node.
All other remainders are degrees and fractional parts.
If the degrees from the node are 15 or more,
although there is a crossing, there is no eclipse.
If 10 or less, there is an eclipse.
If above 10,
the eclipse is very slight,
and only the light and shadow are involved.
The magnitude of the eclipse
is calculated using 15 as the divisor.
Method for calculating the starting point of a solar eclipse: If the moon is on the outer path,
and the crossing precedes the conjunction,
the eclipse begins from the southwest corner;
〔二一〕if the conjunction precedes the crossing,
the eclipse begins from the southeast corner.
If the moon is on the inner path,
and the crossing precedes the conjunction,
the eclipse begins from the northwest corner;
if the conjunction precedes the crossing,
the eclipse begins from the northeast corner.
The magnitude of the eclipse,
as above, uses 15 as the divisor.
If the crossing coincides with the center,
the eclipse is total.
For a lunar eclipse at the opposition to the sun,
the eclipse corners are the reverse of the above.

Method for incorporating lunar eclipse conjunction and node crossing into the speed and slowness calendar: Place the accumulated new moon integrals for the current epoch.
Add the difference rate of speed and slowness for the current epoch.
Subtract full common cycles.
If the remainder fills the solar method, it yields one day;
the remainder is the day remainder.
Beyond the daily calculation,
this is the calendar entry day for the new moon conjunction of the eleventh month of the Tiānzhèng calendar for the requested year.
To find the next month,
add one day
and a day remainder of 4,450.
〔二五〕To find the full moon,
add 14 days
and a day remainder of 3,489.
When the day remainder fills the solar method, it becomes a full day.
When the days reach 27, subtract them.
Then, divide the remainder as per the cycle day remainder.
If the day remainder is insufficient for division,
subtract one day
and add to the cycle void.

To calculate the large and small remainders for conjunctions, oppositions, and lunar eclipses: 〔二六〕 Multiply the remainder of days entered in the calendar by the rate of increase/decrease of the entered calendar,
and integrate the increase/decrease, expansion/contraction [values]
to obtain the definite integral.
Subtract the lunar motion fraction of the entered calendar from the `zhāngsuì`,
and divide the remainder by it.
Add the resulting quotient from the waxing part and subtract from the waning part to the original small remainder.
〔二七〕 If it fills the day modulus when added,
the added time of conjunction falls on the following day;
if it is insufficient when subtracted,
the added time of conjunction falls on the preceding day.
For lunar eclipses,
the added time of the day is determined according to the large and small remainders.
For entries in the calendar on a `zhōurì`,
multiply the `zhōurì` day remainder by the integral of contraction
to obtain the definite integral.
Multiply the remainder of days entered in the calendar by the rate of loss,
then multiply it again by the `zhōurì` day remainder,
and combine with the small fraction of `zhōurì` degrees.
Subtract the definite integral of loss,
the remainder is the subsequent definite integral.
Subtract the lunar motion fraction of the `zhōurì` from the `zhāngsuì`,
multiply the remainder by the `zhōurì` day remainder,
and combine with the small fraction of `zhōurì` degrees.
Divide the subsequent definite integral by this,
add the result to the original small remainder,
following the method above.
To calculate the added time: Multiply the determined small remainder by twelve.
If it fills the day modulus, it yields one `chén`.
Counting from `zǐ` (11 PM-1 AM),
if beyond the calculation,
then it is the `chén` where the added time of new moon and full moon falls.
If there is a remainder, multiply it by four.
According to the day modulus, one is minor,
two is half,
three is major.
If there is a further remainder, multiply it by three.
According to the day modulus, one is strong.
Above half modulus, arrange it;
below half modulus, discard it.
〔二八〕 Combining strong with minor yields minor strong,
with half yields half strong,
with major yields major strong.
Obtaining two strongs yields minor weak;
combining this with minor yields half weak;
combining this with half yields major weak;
combining this with major yields one `chén` weak.
Name it by its `chén`,
then each obtains its minor, major, half, and strong, weak attributes.
For lunar eclipses where the full moon falls within four days before or after the `zhōngjié`,
〔二九〕 refer to the limit number;
for those falling five days or more before or after the `zhōngjié`,
refer to the interval limit.
If the determined small remainder is within the interval limit,
or below the limit number,
the calculated result is taken as the day.

Method for Calculating the Five Planets
The Five Planets are:
Wood is called `Suìxīng` (Jupiter),
Fire is called `Yínghuòxīng` (Mars),
Earth is called `Tiánxīng` (Saturn),
Metal is called `Tàibáixīng` (Venus),
Water is called `Chénxīng` (Mercury).
The movements of the Five Planets
have slow and fast periods,
and have stationary and retrograde periods.
From the time of creation,
when the clear and turbid first separated,
the sun, moon, and Five Planets converged at `Xīngjì`.
Starting from `Xīngjì`,
they travel together in the heavens,
with slow, fast, stationary, and retrograde motions,
mutually catching up with each other.
When a planet meets the sun,
residing in the same lunar mansion and sharing the same degree,
it is called a conjunction.
The days from one conjunction to the next
are called a cycle.
Each cycle's days are correlated with the days of a year using common fractions.
The ratio of the cycle [to the year] yields:
the number of years in a cycle is called the conjunction cycle year number,
and the number of conjunctions in a year is called the conjunction cycle conjunction number.
〔五二〕 Once these two ratios are determined,
the modulus numbers arise.
Multiply the conjunction number by the `zhāngsuì`
to get the conjunction month modulus.
Multiply the conjunction number by the era modulus
to get the daily degree modulus.
Multiply the year number by the `zhāngyuè`
to get the conjunction month fraction;
dividing by the conjunction month modulus yields the conjunction month number.
The remainder of the conjunction month is the month remainder.
Multiply the conjunction month number by the common number,
dividing by the day modulus (and taking the quotient) as the unit
yields the large remainder.
Subtract sixty from the large remainder,
the remainder is the star conjunction new moon large remainder.
The remainder of the large remainder is the new moon small remainder.
Multiply the month remainder by the common number,
multiply the new moon small remainder by the conjunction month modulus,
combine them,
and divide by the product of the day modulus and the conjunction month modulus.
The result is the number of days the star enters the month in conjunction.
Approximate the remainder by the common modulus,
which is the remainder of days entered in the month.
〔五三〕 Subtract the day modulus from the new moon small remainder,
the remainder is the new moon void fraction.
Multiply the conjunction number by the calendar `Dǒu` fraction
to get the star degree `Dǒu` fraction.
For Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn, subtract the year number from the conjunction number,
multiply the remainder by the full celestial circle,
dividing by the daily degree modulus (and taking the quotient) as the unit.
The result is the planetary degree number,
and the remainder is the degree remainder.
For Venus and Mercury, multiply the year number by the full celestial circle,
dividing by the daily degree modulus (and taking the quotient) as the unit.
The result is the planetary degree number,
and the remainder is the degree remainder.

The method for calculating the Five Planets says: Take the years from the Yuán of Rénchén up to the sought year,
multiply it by the "number of conjunctions in the cycle,"
and for every full "number of years for the conjunction cycle," you get one,
called "accumulated conjunctions."
The remainder is called "conjunction remainder."
Subtract the "number of conjunctions in the cycle" from the "conjunction remainder."
If the result is one, the planet has already conjuncted the previous year.
If the result is two, the conjunction will be in the coming year.
If there is no result,
it is conjuncting in that year.
The remainder is then subtracted from the "number of conjunctions in the cycle"
to obtain the degree fraction.
For Jīn and Shuǐ, if the "accumulated conjunctions"
is even, it is a morning appearance;
if odd, it is an evening appearance.
To calculate the planetary conjunction month: Multiply the "number of lunar months" and "lunar month remainder" respectively by the "accumulated conjunctions."
For every full "lunar period modulus," add one to the month,
which becomes the "accumulated months."
The remainder is the "lunar month remainder."
Divide the "accumulated months" by the "Jì month."
The quotient, outside of the calculation,
is the "Jì" entered,
and the remainder is the "entered Jì month."
Also, multiply it by the "Zhāng intercalary month."
Subtract this from the "entered Jì month."
The remainder is then subtracted from the "years in the cycle."
The remainder is the "entered year month."
Starting from Tiānzhēng,
the result, outside of the calculation,
is the month of planetary conjunction.
If it falls within an intercalary month boundary,
use the new moon to govern it.
To calculate the new moon of the conjunction month: Multiply the "entered Jì month" by the "general number."
For every full "day modulus," you get one,
which is the "accumulated days."
The remainder is the "small remainder."
Divide the "accumulated days" by sixty.
The remainder is the "great remainder."
Designate it with the "Jì" it entered.
The result, outside of the calculation,
is the day of the planetary conjunction's new moon.
To calculate the day of entry into the month: Multiply the "lunar month remainder" by the "general number."
Multiply the "small remainder for the new moon" by the "lunar period modulus."
Add them together.
Divide them by the "general modulus."
For every full "daily degree modulus" obtained, you get one,
which is the day of the planetary conjunction's entry into the month.
The remainder is the "daily remainder."
Designate the day by the new moon.
The result, outside of the calculation,
is the day of entry into the month.
To calculate the planetary conjunction degrees: Multiply the "Zhōutiān" by the "degree fraction."
For every full "daily degree modulus" obtained, you get one degree.
The remainder is the "remainder."
Starting from five degrees before Niú,
the result, outside of the calculation,
is the degree of planetary conjunction.
To find the next conjunction month: Add the "number of lunar months" to the "entered year month,"
and add the "remainder" to the "lunar month remainder."
For every full "lunar period modulus," one month is obtained.
If the months do not complete a year,
it is in the current year.
If a year is completed, subtract it.
If there is an intercalary month, account for it.
The remainder is for the next year.
If it completes another year,
it is in the year after next.
For Jīn and Shuǐ, adding morning appearance gives evening appearance,
and adding evening appearance gives morning appearance.
To find the next conjunction new moon: Add the "new moon great and small remainders" to the "conjunction month great and small remainders."
If the "lunar month remainder" completes a month,
add another twenty-nine to the "great remainder"
and two thousand four hundred and nineteen to the "small remainder."
When the "small remainder" completes the "day modulus," carry it over to the "great remainder."
Designate it as per the previous method.
To find the next day of entry into the month:
For every full "daily degree modulus" obtained, you get one.
If the "small remainder of the previous conjunction new moon" completes its "empty divisor,"
subtract one day.
If the "subsequent small remainder" is two thousand four hundred and nineteen or more,
subtract twenty-nine days.
If it is not full,
subtract thirty days.
The remainder is then the day of entry into the next conjunction month.
Designate it by the new moon.
To find the next conjunction degree,
use the number of degrees and fractions,
Mù: [Jī-xīng] 晨 (chén) and the sun meet,
retreating.
It moves prograde [shùn],
for sixteen days and 9,978,332 parts, the planet moves two degrees and 1,795,238 parts,
and in the morning it appears in the east,
behind the sun.
It moves prograde [shùn],
rapidly [jí],
at eleven fifty-sevenths of a degree per day,
moving eleven degrees in fifty-seven days.
It moves prograde [shùn],
slowly [chí],
at nine parts of a degree per day,
moving nine degrees in fifty-seven days and then stopping.
It remains stationary for twenty-seven days and then retrogrades [xuán].
It moves retrograde [nì],

During the reign of Emperor Wǔ, the Court Attendant (Shìzhōng) Liú Zhì (劉智) from Píngyuán
revised the calendar based on the Dǒulì,
extrapolating from the Sìfēn method.
He posited a reduction of one day every three hundred years,
using 150 as the degree unit,
and 37 as the dou fen.
He traced the jiǎzǐ back to the Yuán.
By the tenth year of Tàishǐ,
the year was jiǎwǔ.
It had been 97,411 years

and the sun, moon, and five planets began in Xīngjì,
thus obtaining the beginning of the Yuán.
Adorned with superficial theories,
it was named Zhènglì (正曆).
Dù Yù (杜預), Marquis of Dāngyáng, wrote the Chūnqiū Chánglì.
It states: "The sun moves one degree a day,
the moon moves thirteen and seven-nineteenths degrees, with a remainder.
The astronomy officials should gather these varying speeds
to calculate the new and full moons,
and thereby establish
intercalary months.
Intercalary months have no central qi,
and the Northern Dipper points diagonally between two chén (zodiacal branches),
which is why they differ from other months.
Accumulating these to connect them,
the four seasons and eight festivals will have no
discrepancies,
and thus the year can be completed.
Its subtlety is profound."
To grasp its essence
and align with the Way of Heaven,
then affairs will not go amiss.
Therefore, the commentary says:
"Intercalary months rectify
the seasons,
and the seasons govern affairs."
However, the movements of yin and yang
deviate with motion.
This deviation, if unchecked,
eventually leads to errors in the calendar.
Therefore, Zhòngní (孔子) and Qiūmíng (左丘明) always commented on the new moon and intercalary months
in their writings,
presumably to correct errors and gains,
and thereby expound on the calendar and its computations.

The principle is not

For the Five Planets' approximate methods,
their first appearance is taken as the standard,
not tied to the original root.
Therefore, while calculations are ultimately derived from the initial origin,
the approximate methods are applied to current use.
Seeking their purpose meticulously,
each has its suitability.
Thus, the author established both methods.
Jí inspected the location of the sun's lodging during lunar eclipses,
which was considered the standard by calendrical astronomers.
He also wrote the Húntiānlùn (Discussion on the Armillary Sphere),
to calculate the sun's position on the ecliptic,
refuting the errors of earlier scholars,
and thereby grasping its essence.
Collation Notes
Treatise 9, Rítuàn (Rites, Part 1)
Humans possess the spiritual essence of Heaven and Earth, Yīn and Yáng,
and have emotions of sorrow, joy, happiness, and anger.
Therefore, the Sages established models
to serve as the people's ultimate standard,
restraining their arrogance and indulgence,
to prevent their violence and disorder;
they revered Heaven and Earth,
and devoutly honored ghosts and spirits,
arranged the order of noble and humble,
and perfected the righteousness of husband and wife.
Only then could states and families
be well-governed.
The tradition says:
"If one can subdue oneself and return to ritual,
all under Heaven will return to benevolence."
However, when Tàiyī first differentiated,
Suìrén drilled for fire,
where aspiration found expression in reverence and frugality,
and emotions were not swayed by jade and silk;
drawing clear water from the right of spring streams,
and burning wild boars outside autumn forests –
even these should not be omitted.
Xuānyuán and Xū embraced the spirits,
Táng and Yú emulated antiquity,
and by the flourishing Zhōu Dynasty,
the rituals were fully complete.
Some set the standard for all officials,
establishing unalterable laws;
some had three hundred articles of ritual classics,
and three thousand rules of decorum.
All these were for the purpose of widely proclaiming the will of Heaven,
and deeply shaping human principles.
In later ages, as customs became corrupt and erroneous,
the royal influence waned and faded.
Affairs diverged from the glorification of the state,
and ritual also erred in the family.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Tàishú about the rites of bowing and yielding, turning and circling,
who replied:
"These are merely what are called manners, not ritual."
The way of Heaven's immutable principles and Earth's righteousness
has been particularly lacking since then.
In the eleventh year of Āigōng,
Kǒngzǐ returned from Wèi to Lǔ,
investigated the classics of the Three Dynasties,
and bequeathed teachings for a hundred kings.
But there was no enlightened ruler at the time,
and his way was obscured and not practiced.
As for emotions diverging,
the benevolence of dikes and defenses was abandoned;
corrupt and erroneous different methods arose,
and the tradition of Zhūsì vanished.
Therefore, Hàn Wén Dì abolished the two-year mourning period,
and the Middle Revival (Zhōngxīng) period performed sacrifices at a single suburban altar.
Is not adapting to the times a natural course?
Yes!
Yet, during the Yuándǐng era of the Western Jīng,
and the Yǒngpíng era of the Middle Revival,
scholars of profound knowledge were invited and officials were promoted,
the gate of Confucianism was opened, and various students were drawn in.
The flourishing of both Jīng Dynasties
was beautiful in this regard.
However, when mountain fish were placed on sacrificial altars,
and marsh pigs deviated from the classics (meaning, when rituals became corrupted),
ritual and music were often neglected,
and superficiality was valued.
Yet, the system of suburban sacrifices
still somewhat survived.
When the Wèi Dynasty gained power,
this beautiful system was emulated.
Wáng Sù, Gāo Tánglóng, and their followers
were broadly learned in past records,
with three thousand articles of ritual,
and seventeen chapters of scholarship.
Each, using old texts, augmented and reduced them for their contemporary era.
How could this be what is called the way to bring the ruler to the level of Yáo and Shùn?
The era was characterized by extravagant decorations,
and the times met with corrupt governance.
The institutions based on the Zhōu Dynasty
often conflicted with contemporary customs,
yet even the surviving fragments and incomplete records still contained admirable things.
In the first year of Jǐngchū,
a round altar was constructed on Mount Wēisù south of Luòyáng.
On the day of the sacrifice, the founding ancestor Dì Shùn was associated with it.
With fish on the sacrificial dishes,
and plain wine in earthen vessels,
if not for the gentry establishing its guidelines,
who could have participated in this?
During the military campaigns of Xuān and Jǐng,
there was no time to establish rituals.
When Tàikāng pacified Wú,
the nine provinces were united,
ritual classics were all brought forth,
and musical instruments were brought together.
Thus, scholars from Qí and Lǔ each brought their yellow silk scrolls.
Emperor Wǔ had also just pacified the rebellions,
and his intention was first to establish proper conduct.
For auspicious rites,
three tufts of hair were not cut,
and the jade disc for observing the sun was put away.
For inauspicious rites,
there were deep robes and cloth caps,
lowered mats, and cleared meals.
The meaning of "one humility, three benefits" was made clear,
and thus education and moral transformation spread.
When Emperor Yuán brought about the restoration,
many matters were handled by expediency,
and old texts and former institutions
remained unbroken like strands of hair.
Therefore, Regular Attendant Dài Miǎo went to the palace gate and presented a memorial, saying:
"At present, heaven and earth have renewed,
all things are in their infancy.
Let us sweep away the abuses of recent generations,
and establish noble precedents for a thousand years.
Hence, the regulation of 'double swords' is esteemed,
and the custom of 'flying white' is formed;
the adornment of 'holding a qín' is observed,
and the harmony of 'responding to music' is created."
His intention was to initiate ritual customs
and urge the emperor to set an example.
After Mù and Āi,
royal authority gradually declined.
Huán Wēn held the reins of government,
and policies originated from him.
Yet the officials in charge sometimes displayed this culture,
adding splendor to their duties,
while the sovereign's authority long faded,
and the minister's way prevailed exclusively.
The *Record* says,
"If one does not have the position,
one cannot create rituals and music."
Is this not what it refers to?
At the beginning of the Jìn dynasty, Xún Yǐ and Zhèng Chōng compiled national statutes;
in Jiāngzuǒ, Xún Sōng and Diāo Xié made additions and subtractions to court ceremonies.
The *Zhōu Guān* lists five rites:
auspicious, inauspicious, military, guest, and festive.
Among the great auspicious rites,
none surpassed sacrifices.
Thus, among the eight governmental matters in the *Hóngfàn*,
the third is sacrifice.
Sacrifice
is for demonstrating filial piety to ancestors
and communicating with the spirits.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
following Qín's destruction of scholarship,
many institutions could not be restored to their ancient form.
Through the more than four hundred years of the Eastern and Western Jīng,
they were often altered.
The Wèi clan succeeded the great chaos at the end of Hàn,
and old regulations were obliterated.
They ordered Palace Attendant Wáng Càn and Minister Wèi Yǐ to draft court ceremonies.
When the Jìn state was established,
Emperor Wén again ordered Xún Yǐ to compile new rites
based on the precedents of the Wèi period,
referring to ancient and modern practices,
and changing their articles and clauses.
Yáng Hù, Rèn Kǎi, Yǔ Jùn, and Yìng Zhēn together edited and finalized them,
resulting in one hundred sixty-five chapters,
which were then presented.
In the early Tàikāng period,
Minister of Personnel Zhū Zhěng submitted a memorial entrusting them to the Minister's Secretary Zhì Yú for discussion.
Yú presented a memorial detailing what should be added or removed, saying: "Your subject has reviewed and collated the Five Rites compiled by the late Grand Commandant Yǐ.
Your subject believes that revolution to establish a lasting lineage
is a glorious undertaking for emperors,
and promoting rites to guide instruction
is a great affair for the
state.
Therefore, your subject previously memorialized that ritual matters were being delayed
and requested their speedy completion and implementation.
Furthermore, as mourning rites contain the most doubts and deficiencies,
they should be rectified and supplemented.
Also,
as the current ritual chapters are cumbersome and heavy,
they should be combined according to type.
As the matter has long been unreleased,
I fear it may be shelved in silence.
Indeed, the auspicious rites for capping, marriage, sacrifices, and gatherings
have undergone few changes in their regulations;
but as for mourning rites,
which are of crucial importance to the world,
they are particularly prone to misinterpretation.
Hence, Zǐzhāng doubted Emperor Gāozōng's
three-year mourning in the 'weeping hut,'
Zǐsī did not allow his son to perform mourning for his birth mother after she was remarried,
Zǐyóu considered paternal half-siblings to require *dàgōng* mourning,
while Zǐxià considered it *qīcuī*,
and after Confucius's death, his
disciples were uncertain about what to wear.
These individuals were all clear-minded and practiced in rites,
looking up to study the *Zhōu Diǎn*,
and down to emulate Zhòngní.
Steeped in sacred teachings,
they lectured and practiced for years,
yet when they encountered mourning
matters,
they were still thus.
This clearly shows that mourning rites are easily misunderstood
and must be thoroughly explained.
Moreover, since then,
chapters have been burned and scattered,
and we have moved ever further from the sages.
That mourning regulations are strange
and erroneous
is only natural.
Therefore, a single scroll on mourning rites,
no more than a handful,
gives rise to endless disputes.
For the three-year mourning,
Zhèng says twenty-seven months,
while Wáng
says twenty-five months.
For mourning after reburial,
Zhèng says *sī* mourning for three months,
while Wáng says it is removed after the burial.
For a stepmother who remarries,
Zhèng says one mourns for all of them,
while Wáng says one mourns only if
she raised one as a stepmother.
For a child who dies young for whom no mourning is prescribed,
Zhèng says if a child lives one month, mourn for one day,
while Wáng says to convert the days of weeping into months of mourning.
Such
cases are numerous.
The main text of the mourning rites is abbreviated,
and the meaning of the matters only becomes clear with annotations;
its commentary and explanations are somewhat detailed,
and the world attributes it to Zǐxià.
Zhèng and Wáng both based
themselves on the classics and their commentaries,
yet they have differences and similarities,
causing uncertainty throughout the land,
with no one knowing what to decide.
However, Yǐ merely transcribed the ancient classic text,
completely omitting Zǐxià's commentary and the annotations of previous scholars,
making the matter impractical.
When it comes to actual practice,
one would still have to issue divergent explanations,
one saying this, another saying that,
which is not the way to establish fixed regulations.
Your subject believes that
it is now appropriate to consult the *Lǐjì*,
select relevant commentaries,
supplement what is incomplete,
and unify divergent meanings.
It can be patterned after the mourning and removal regulations compiled by Wáng Jǐnghóu,
so that the categories are clearly
defined and correct,
to resolve disputes.
Then, there will be no two doors to regulations,
and all will follow the same path.
Moreover, these rites are to be promulgated throughout the empire,
so they should not be overly verbose.
Yǐ compiled one hundred sixty-five chapters,
each chapter forming a scroll,
totaling over one hundred fifty thousand words.
Your subject still
finds the scrolls too numerous and the text too verbose,
with many repetitions.
Consider the *Yáo Diǎn* in the *Shàngshū*: for the rites of sacrificing to mountains and rivers,
only for Mount Dōng did it fully state the number of sacrificial animals and goods,
and describe the ceremonies
to be used;
for the others, it simply said
"as before."
The *Zhōu Lǐ* for sacrificing to Heaven and Earth, the Five Thearchs, and honoring former kings,
for matters that were the same, all said
"also as such,"
with concise text
but clear meaning.
The present rites, however, for matters that are similar but have different names,
are always made into separate chapters,
making the scrolls verbose and unclassical.
All should be made concise and uniform,
combined by category.
If a matter is not
same,
then listed their differences.
In this way,
one-third was reduced.
Yú finished discussing the new rites,
and submitted them in the first year of Yuánkāng.
What he presented concerned only the Míngtáng, the Five Emperors, the Two Shè, the Six Zōng, and the 吉凶王公 (Auspicious and Inauspicious Royal and Ducal) systems,
amounting to fifteen chapters in total.
An imperial edict approved his proposal.
Later, Yú and Fù Xián continued the work,
but never completed it.
When the Central Plains fell,
Yú's Juéyí Zhù (Notes on Resolving Doubts)
was his unfinished work.
By the time of Jiāngzuǒ,
Púyè Diāo Xié and Tàicháng Xún Sōng supplemented and compiled the old texts,
and Guānglù Dàfū Cài Mó again continued to revise the work.
In the first month, dìngwèi day, of the first year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Emperor Wǔ was worshipped in the suburban sacrifice to match Heaven,
and Emperor Wén was worshipped in the ancestral sacrifice at the Míngtáng to match Shàngdì.
At this time,
the complete system of the two suburban sacrifices
was still in place, so the additions and reductions made by Wèi are discernible.
In the eighth month of the fourth year,
the Son of Heaven made an eastern tour,
and passing through Fánchāng,
ordered Zhí Jīnwú Zāng Bà to act as Tàiwèi,
and sacrificed a special ox at the Shòuchán Tán (Altar of Receiving Abdication).
In the tenth month, yǐmǎo day, of the first year of Jǐngchū,
the building of the Yuánqiū (Round Altar) began on Wěisù Shān, south of Luòyáng.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the early Hàn dynasty,
following Qín's destruction of learning,
fragments were collected
to provide for suburban sacrifices.
From Gānquán Hòutǔ
and Yōnggōng Wǔzhì,
the positions of gods and spirits
were often not based on classic texts,
and because their establishment and abolition were inconsistent,
shifting back and forth,
for over four hundred years,
the Dì ceremony was abolished,
and those established in ancient times
were consequently missing.
The Cao clan's lineage
originated from the Yǒu Yú clan.
Now, in the sacrifice at the Yuánqiū, our founding ancestor Dì Shùn shall be matched,
and the Yuánqiū shall be called Huáng Huángdì Tiān (August Imperial Heaven).
What is sacrificed at the Fāngqiū (Square Altar) shall be called Huáng Huánghòu Dì (August Empress Earth),
with Shùn's consort Yī Shì matched.
What is sacrificed at the Heavenly suburban altar shall be called Huáng Tiān zhī Shén (Spirit of August Heaven),
with Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì matched.
What is sacrificed at the Earthly suburban altar shall be called Huáng Dì zhī Qí (Deity of August Earth),
with Wǔxuān Huánghòu matched.
The imperial father, Gāozǔ Wén Huángdì, shall be worshipped ancestrally in the Míngtáng,
to match Shàngdì."
On the twelfth month, rénzǐ day, during the winter solstice,
the sacrifice to Huáng Huángdì Tiān at the Yuánqiū began,
with the founding ancestor Yǒu Yú Dì Shùn matched.
From Zhèngshǐ onwards,
suburban sacrifices were not performed again throughout the Wèi dynasty.
In the twelfth month, jiǎzǐ day, of the second year of Xiánxī of Emperor Yuán of Wèi,
the acting emissary, attendant, Grand Tutor Zhèng Chōng, and concurrently Grand Commandant and Capital Commandant Lǐ Xǐ, presented the imperial seal and ribbon and the instrument of abdication,
ceding the throne to Jìn.
On bǐngyín day,
Emperor Wǔ set up an altar in the southern suburbs,
and performed the cháiliáo (wood-burning sacrifice) to announce to Shàngdì,
at which time there was no ancestral match yet.
In the first month of the second year of Tàishǐ,
an imperial edict stated:
"The officials previously proposed temporarily using Wèi rites for suburban sacrifices,
and I, not considering the difficulty of reform,
ordered them to be made permanent.
Public opinions were conflicting,
and thus it was not settled in time,
preventing the timely offering of sacrifices to gods and spirits,
and matching them with ancestors.
Day and night I long for it,
losing appetite and forgetting comfort.
Let the suburban sacrifices be performed."
At this time, the assembled officials also argued that
the Five Emperors are in fact Heaven,
and royal fortunes differ with the times,
hence their distinct names;
though there are five names,
they are actually one deity.
In the Míngtáng and southern suburbs,
the seats of the Five Emperors should be removed,
the names of the Five Essences in the five suburban altars changed,
all uniformly called Hàotiān Shàngdì,
with only one seat established for each.
The earthly suburban altar should also remove the matching sacrifice to the Former Queen.
The Emperor followed all of them.
On the second month, dīngchǒu day,
Emperor Xuān was sacrificed in the suburban ceremony to match Heaven,
and Emperor Wén was worshipped ancestrally in the Míngtáng to match Shàngdì.
In the eleventh month of this year,
the officials again proposed that
in ancient times the qiū (hills) and jiāo (suburban altars) were not distinct,
so the Yuánqiū and Fāngqiū should be combined with the northern and southern suburban altars,
and altars and ritual grounds be re-established,
and the sacrifices of the two solstices be combined with the two suburban altars.
The Emperor again followed this,
all in accordance with Wáng Sù's proposal, which Emperor Xuān had adopted.
In the same month, gēngyín day, during the winter solstice,
the Emperor personally sacrificed at the Yuánqiū in the southern suburbs.
From then on,
the Yuánqiū and Fāngzé were not established separately.
In the first month of the third year of Tàikāng,
the Emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifice,
with the Crown Prince and Imperial Princes all attending the sacrifice.
In the tenth month of the tenth year,
another edict stated:
“The Xiàojīng says: 'Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburbs to match Heaven,
and worship King Wén in the Míngtáng to match Shàngdì.'
However, the Zhōu Guān says: 'Sacrifice to Heaven, and make a tour to Shàngdì,'
and also says: 'Sacrifice to Earth, and make a tour to the Four Directions.'
If the Four Directions are not Earth,
then Shàngdì in the Míngtáng cannot be Heaven.
Previously, the public discussion abolished the Five Emperors' seats in the Míngtáng,
which is not correct when examined against the ritual texts.
Moreover, the Shī Xù (Great Preface to the Classic of Poetry) says: 'The achievements of King Wén and King Wǔ
originated from Hòujì,'
thus he was accordingly pushed to match Heaven.
Emperor Xuān, having founded the dynasty with divine martial power,
was already matched with Heaven,
so to again match the Former Emperor with Heaven
is also ethically unsettling.
Let the Míngtáng and the Five Emperors' seats in the southern suburbs be restored."
Emperor Mǐn resided in Cháng'ān,
but perished before he could establish suburban temples.
When Emperor Yuán crossed the Jiāng,
discussions on establishing the suburban sacrifice ceremony began in the second year of Tàixīng.
Shàngshū Lìng Diāo Xié and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Dù Yí argued that
they should wait until the capital returned to Luòyì to carry it out.
Sītú Xún Zǔ argued, based on Emperor Xiàn of Hàn establishing suburban altars immediately after moving the capital to Xǔ,
that it was appropriate to carry it out here.
Piàojí Wáng Dǎo, Púyè Xún Sōng, Tàicháng Huá, and Zhōngshū Shìláng Yú Liàng all agreed with Zǔ's proposal,
and the matter was consequently implemented,
establishing the southern suburban altar on sìdì.
Its system was all determined by Tàicháng Hè Xún,
mostly following the rites of Hàn and early Jìn.
On the third month, xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifice,
the rituals of feasting and matching were all according to the precedent of Emperor Wǔ's first suburban sacrifice.
At this time, the northern altar had not yet been established,
and the terrestrial deities and various spirits were all together at the Heavenly suburban altar.
In the seventh month of the third year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
an edict first ordered the establishment of the northern suburban altar,
but the Emperor passed away before it could be built.
Then, in the first month of the eighth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
recalling the former directive,
it was established south of Fùzhōu Shān.
For the Heavenly suburban altar, there were the assistants of the Five Emperors,
the sun and moon, the Five Planets, the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions, Wénchāng, Běidǒu, Sāntái, Sīmìng, Xuānyuán, Hòutǔ, Tàiyī, Tiānyī, Tàiwēi, Gōuchén, Běijí, Yǔshī, Léidiàn, Sīkōng, Fēngbó, Lǎorén,
a total of sixty-two deities.

For the Earthly suburban altar, there were the Five Peaks, the Four Directions, the Four Seas, the Four Rivers, the Five Lakes, the assistants of the Five Emperors, Yí Shān, Yuè Shān, Bái Shān, Huò Shān, Yīwúlǘ Shān, Jiǎng Shān, Sōng Jiāng, Kuàijī Shān, Qiántáng Jiāng, Xiānnóng,
a total of forty-four deities.
The small mountains south of the Jiāng
were probably established by the Jiāngzuǒ regime,
just as in Hàn's Western Capital, all small waters in Guānzhōng had sacrificial rites.
In the same month, xīnwèi day,
the northern suburban sacrifice was performed,
and for the first time, Xuānmù Zhāng Huánghòu was matched,
this being a Wèi precedent,
not a Jìn tradition.
In the first month of the first year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Kāng,
when about to perform the northern suburban sacrifice,
there was a point of doubt.
Tàicháng Gù Hé memorialized:
"In Tàishǐ,
the rites of the two solstices were combined with the two suburban altars.
For the month of the northern suburban sacrifice,
there is no clear ancient text,
some take it as the summer solstice,
others use the same month as yángfù (return of yang).
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, on the first month, xīnwèi day,
first established the northern suburban altar,
which means it was in the same month as the southern suburban altar.
During the restoration and initial establishment,
all systems were simplified,
combining the seven suburban altars into one mound.
The regulations were not fully prepared,
and this rite was adopted temporarily,
which was probably appropriate for the time.
By Xiánhé,
