it was decided to establish the northern suburban altar separately,
and use the first month for both.
Wèi inherited from Later Hàn, sacrificing to Heaven in the first month with Earth matched.
At that time, Gāo Tánglóng and others believed that the rites for sacrificing to Heaven should not have Earth matched,
and cited the Zhōu Lǐ (Rites of Zhōu) stating that the suburban sacrifices of the Three Kings all used the summer calendar's first month."
Thereupon, Hé's proposal was followed.
In the same month, xīnwèi day for the southern suburban sacrifice,
and xīnsì day for the northern suburban sacrifice,
the Emperor personally performed both.
In the third year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān,
Liú Yù campaigned against Huán Xuán
and drove him away.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
he reported his righteous achievement to the Southern Suburb.
In that year,
the Emperor was in distress in Jiānglíng and had not yet returned.
The following year, it was time for the suburban sacrifice,
and the court debated, believing it proper to follow the Rites of Zhōu,
with the Zōngbó acting in his stead
and the Three Dukes performing the rites.
Wáng Nàzhī, the Secretary of the Left in the Ministry of Personnel, alone said:
"Since the sacrifice in the suburb for the departed,
the Son of Heaven is certainly in authority.
With a sovereign present,
acting under his command,
what is there to dispute?
Whether or not to perform the suburban sacrifice
is hardly comparable to the present situation!"
Other debaters further said:
"It is proper to perform the suburban sacrifice now;
it is therefore by imperial decree that the Three Dukes perform the rites."
Also,
"Sacrificing to Heaven in the suburb is of the utmost reverence,
and it is unique.
Thus, only the Son of Heaven may offer this sacrifice.
From commoners upwards,
all perform seasonal offerings,
but if the legitimate son is away,
and a younger son performs the duties,
there has never been a case where one could sacrifice to Heaven without personally receiving the command."
Nàzhī again said:
"When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he performed the suburban sacrifice in the second month.
When Emperor Yuán restored the dynasty,
he performed it in the third month.
The time for the suburban sacrifice has not yet passed.
We look forward to the imperial carriage returning daily.
There is no need to rush,
thereby causing the imperial carriage to turn back
and lose the chance to personally offer the sacrifice."
Thereupon, Nàzhī's proposal was followed.
Regarding the colors of the sacrificial animals, silks, jade discs, and jade tablets for the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
although there were established texts,
during the Qín dynasty, mostly young male horses were used,
while the Hàn merely mentioned calves,
without distinguishing their colors.
To the east of the Jiāng River, both the northern and southern suburban sacrifices uniformly used dark-colored animals,
while the Míngtáng and ancestral temples uniformly used red-colored animals.
The Rites contain texts about reporting affairs to the ancestors in the ancestral temple and the altars of earth and grain,
but there is no precedent for reporting to the suburban altars.
According to Hàn rituals,
upon the death of the Son of Heaven, the Tàiwèi was sent to announce the posthumous title at the Southern Suburb;
nothing else is recorded.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
when the Emperor was about to embark on an eastern tour,
because a large army was to be dispatched,
he ordered the Tàicháng to offer a sacrifice of a single special ox at the Southern Suburb.
When Emperor Wén died,
Tàiwèi Zhōng Yáo announced the posthumous title at the Southern Suburb;
all these were affairs conducted at the suburban altars.
To the east of the Jiāng River, this practice was abolished.
According to the Rites,
on the spring equinox, one worships the rising sun in the east,
and on the autumn equinox, one worships the setting moon in the west.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, when sacrificing at Tàizhì,
emerged from the bamboo palace at dawn,
bowed to the east facing the sun,
and that evening, bowed to the west facing the moon.
This was done on the day of the suburban sacrifice,
and not necessarily in the eastern or western suburbs.
Later, it became a regular practice to bow morning and evening.
Thus, Emperor Wén of Wèi issued an edict stating:
"The Hàn dynasty did not worship the sun in the eastern suburb,
but instead regularly bowed to the sun and moon morning and evening below the palace hall,
which is troublesome and informal, like a family affair,
and not the way to serve Heaven and commune with spirits."
On the day Yǐhài of the first month of the second year of Huángchū,
the sun was worshipped outside the eastern gate,
which also violated the principle of the two equinoxes in the Rites.
On the day Dīnghài of the second month of the first year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the sun was worshipped in the eastern suburb.
On the day Jǐchǒu of the eighth month,
the moon was worshipped in the western suburb,
thus finally conforming to the ancient Rites.
However, in the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
officials submitted a memorial, stating:
"For the spring equinox, according to old custom, the imperial carriage worships the rising sun,
but as the weather is not yet suitable,
His Majesty need not personally attend."
The edict stated:
"Rituals should be constant.
If we follow what has been memorialized,
it will differ from what the late Tàiwèi compiled,
and again there will be no fixed system.
Recently, difficulties have not yet been pacified,
so we have followed memorials each time.
Now that military affairs are settled,
only this (ritual) is of great importance."
According to this edict,
the Emperor again personally worshipped the rising sun.
After this, the practice was abolished.
The Rites state:
"Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburb to match Heaven,
and sacrifice to King Wén in the Míngtáng to match the Supreme Lord."
When Emperor Wén of Wèi ascended the throne,
he used the Hàn Míngtáng but without a match.
In the first year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng,
King Wén of Wèi was first sacrificed in the Míngtáng,
and King Qí also performed the ritual.
In early Jìn, Emperor Wén was matched,
later Emperor Xuān was matched,
and soon after, Emperor Wén was again matched.
There were no other changes.
Thus, the suburban sacrifice and the Míngtáng,
with different matches or the same,
varied inconsistently.
Zhì Yú argued:
"According to Hàn and Wèi precedents,
the Míngtáng sacrificed to the spirits of the Five Emperors.
In the new Rites,
the Five Emperors are the Supreme Lord,
that is, the Heavenly Emperor.
The Míngtáng abolished the positions of the Five Emperors,
and only sacrificed to the Supreme Lord.
According to Zhòngní, he said: 'Sacrifice to Hòujì in the suburb to match Heaven,
and sacrifice to King Wén in the Míngtáng to match the Supreme Lord.'
The Rites of Zhōu state:
Sacrifice to Heaven as host for the Supreme Lords;
sacrifice to Earth as host for the Four Directions.
If the directions are not Earth,
then the Supreme Lords are not Heaven;
this can be clearly understood.
For the suburban mound sacrifice,
the ground is swept and the sacrifice is offered.
The sacrificial animals used are small and young,
and the vessels used are of pottery and gourds,
reverting to their primitive origins,
thus matching with distant ancestors.
For the Míngtáng sacrifice,
all items are fully prepared for offering,
jade and sacrificial animals are presented together,
and bamboo and wooden vessels are arranged in rows.
The ritual is similar to that for human spirits,
thus matching with recent ancestors.
The locations for the suburban altars and Míngtáng
are clearly distinct entities.
The sacrificial animals and offerings
have different qualities and refined purposes.
Moreover, matching with both distant and recent ancestors
is not an expression of supreme reverence,
and sacrificing twice in three days
is not a meaning of non-profanity.
That they are not one single deity
is also sufficiently clear.
In ancient times,
those who were enlightened kings in life,
upon death, were matched with the Five Elements.
Thus, Tàihào was matched with Wood,
Shénnóng with Fire,
Shàohào with Metal,
Zhuānxū with Water,
and Huángdì with Earth.
These Five Emperors
are the spirits matched with Heaven.
They are sacrificed together at the four suburbs,
and honored in the Míngtáng.
When sacrificing to Heaven, one wears a great fur robe and a crown.
When sacrificing to the Five Emperors, it is also the same.
Some believe that the Five Elemental Emperors
are those who assist Heaven in nurturing all things.
Previous generations followed this tradition,
none ever abandoning it,
until the early Jìn, when different opinions began to be followed.
The edict of Gēngwǔ stated that
the Míngtáng and Southern Suburb should abolish the positions of the Five Emperors,
and only sacrifice to the Heavenly Spirit.
The new Rites adopted and used this.
Former Imperial Physician Hán Yáng submitted a memorial, stating
that it was appropriate to sacrifice to the Five Emperors as before.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
an edict had already put this into practice.
It is proper to fix the new Rites,
and for the Míngtáng and suburban sacrifices, to sacrifice to the Five Emperors as in the old system."
The edict followed this.
After the period east of the Jiāng River,
there was no time for reconstruction.
According to the Hàn rituals,
the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ) every year presented the calendar for that year.
Before Lìchūn (Start of Spring), Lìxià (Start of Summer), Dàshǔ (Great Heat), Lìqiū (Start of Autumn), and Lìdōng (Start of Winter), the five seasonal ordinances were regularly read.
The emperor's attire
varied according to the colors of the five seasons.
When the emperor ascended the imperial throne,
the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) and those below him took their seats.
The Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng placed the ordinances on a desk,
presented them, and entered.
After taking their seats and kneeling to read them,
they were granted a cup of wine.
The Wèi dynasty consistently followed this rite.
In the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the Attendant Officer for Reporting (Tōngshì) reported, saying:
“Previously, only the ordinances for the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—were read.
As for the time when yellow robes were worn,
it was uniquely omitted and not read.
Now, I do not understand the reason for this.”
Gāotáng Lóng, Regular Grandee Remonstrant (Sànqí Chángshì) and concurrently Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ Lìng), believed that
“yellow among the Five Phases (wǔxíng)
is central earth.
Earth governs the four seasons, eighteen days each.
Earth is born from fire.
Therefore, at the end of the period when fire is ascendant, yellow is worn.
This is not the case for the other three seasons.
The ordinances, however, follow the four seasons
and are not based on the Five Phases (wǔxíng) as ordinances.
[一０]This is why there is no ordinance for wearing yellow.”
This indicates that the Wèi dynasty did not read the Dàshǔ (Great Heat) ordinance.
When Jìn received the Mandate,
it also had this system.
Fù Xián said:
“On the first day of Lìqiū (Start of Autumn),
the white royal chariot shines in the purple court,
and white banners are arrayed on the jade steps.”
Thus, on that day, the banners and chariot were all white.
In the sixth month, Dīngwèi day, of the fifth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
the relevant authorities memorialized to read the autumn ordinance.

Xún Yì, concurrently Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng) and Regular Grandee Remonstrant (Sànqí Chángshì), and Cáo Yǔ, concurrently Palace Aide to the Imperial Censorate (Huángmén Shìláng) and Cavalier Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng), refuted, saying:
“The Shàngshū Sāngōng Cáo has memorialized to read the autumn ordinance.
The ceremonial notes and old statutes are not complete on this matter.
Your servants have consulted and discussed with Grand Master of Bright Luster (Guānglù Dàfū) Huà Yì,
who holds that Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì), due to the intense heat of autumn and summer,
often omitted reading the ordinance;
it was not abolished in spring and winter.
The reason why the former kings read the ordinances in accordance with the seasons
was to follow heaven and respect the celestial times,
and to rectify the revered and solemn attire.
Now, many ritual vestments are missing,
and the current heat is intense.
Your servants believe it is acceptable to follow the suggestion,
and in accordance with past practice, omit it and not read it.”
An imperial edict approved this.
In the third month of the sixth year,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
“The sixteenth day of this month is Lìxià (Start of Summer).
Now that the official attire is gradually being restored,
reading the ordinances for the four seasons
is to respectfully narrate the way of heaven's harmony, flourishing, and decline.
We believe it is now appropriate to read the summer ordinance.”
The memorial was approved.
According to the rites for the first month of spring,
“a propitious day is chosen.
The Son of Heaven personally loads the plows and hoes,
placing them between the imperial chariots of Cān and Bǎojiè.
He leads the Sāngōng, Jiǔqīng, feudal lords, and grandees to personally plow the imperial field.”
After Qín destroyed scholarship,
this rite had long been abandoned.
After Emperor Wén of Hàn,
this tradition was first revived.
The Three Ancestors of Wèi
also all personally plowed the imperial fields.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
the relevant authorities memorialized to begin plowing and sacrificing to the First Farmer (Xiānnóng),
suggesting that the relevant officials be ordered to carry out the rites.
An imperial edict stated:
“The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifice and agriculture.
Therefore, the sage kings of antiquity
personally plowed the imperial fields
to supply the sacrificial grains for the suburban and ancestral temples,
and also to instruct and transform the world.
In recent times,
the imperial plowing was confined to a few paces,
with only the name of admiring antiquity,
but without the reality of supplying sacrifices or instructing farmers,
yet incurring the expenses of numerous officials, carriages, and attendants.
Now, we are restoring the system of a thousand *mǔ*.
We should, along with the various dukes, ministers, and gentlemen, personally experience the difficulties of farming and harvesting,
to lead the world by example.
The responsible officials should thoroughly detail the system,
send it to Hénán,
and allocate land in the south of the eastern suburb,
north of the Luò River.
If there is no official land, suitable exchanges should be made as convenient,
but private land should not be encroached upon.”
Thereupon, the imperial carriage used a wooden chariot for plowing,
and a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) was offered to the First Farmer (Xiānnóng).
After Emperor Huì,
this practice was abandoned.
In Jiāngzuǒ, Emperor Yuán was about to restore the plowing of imperial fields.
The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) sent a query asking
“whether the supreme one should personally offer sacrifices to the First Farmer (Xiānnóng) for the imperial fields or not.”
Hè Xún replied:
“The Hàn rituals do not explicitly state that the supreme one should personally offer sacrifices,
[一一]however, the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōulǐ) state that when the king sacrifices to the four directions (sìwàng), he wears a feather robe (cuìmǐan),
and when sacrificing to the altars of land and grain (shèjì) and the five sacrifices (wǔsì), he wears a fine linen robe (chīmǐan).
From this, it is not without the meaning of personal sacrifice.
Two sets of ceremonial notes should be established.”
The ceremonial notes submitted by Hè Xún and others were not sufficiently detailed or appropriate,
and the matter was ultimately not carried out.
Later, Emperor Āi again wished to implement this tradition,
but was also unable to succeed.
According to the Hàn rituals,
counties and towns regularly offered sacrifices to the First Farmer (Xiānnóng) on an Yǐwèi day,
then plowed in the Yǐ direction.
On a Bǐngxū day, sacrifices were offered to the Earl of Wind (Fēngbó) in the Xū direction.
On a Jǐchǒu day, sacrifices were offered to the Master of Rain (Yǔshī) in the Chǒu direction.
Sheep and pigs were used for the sacrifices.
On the day of Lìchūn (Start of Spring),
all displayed green banners and turbans to welcome spring in the wild outside the eastern suburb.
When spring arrived from the wild,
they welcomed it with bows and returned,
without sacrificing.
For the other three seasons, there was no welcome.
Although the Wèi dynasty had the Son of Heaven plow the imperial fields,
the feudal governors (fānzhèn) omitted the rites of the feudal lords' hundred *mǔ*.
Towards the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
“In antiquity, feudal lords plowed imperial fields of a hundred *mǔ*,
personally holding the plow to serve the altars of land and grain (shèjì) and the ancestral temples,
to encourage agricultural work.
Now, as various kings govern their states,
they should follow the principle of restoring the plowing of imperial fields.”
However, this was ultimately not implemented.
According to the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōulǐ),
the Queen led the inner and outer noblewomen in sericulture in the northern suburb.
According to the Hàn rituals,
the Empress personally picked mulberry leaves in the eastern suburban park.
In the silkworm chamber, sacrifices were offered to the silkworm gods,
named Yuànwā Fùrén and Yùshì Gōngzhǔ.
A lesser sacrifice (shàoláo) was used for the offerings.
In the first month of the seventh year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
an order was issued for the imperial palace (zhōnggōng) to conduct sericulture in the northern suburb,
following the Zhōu tradition.
In the sixth year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ,
Huá Qiáo, Attendant in Ordinary, memorialized:
"The system of the former kings
was that the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords personally plowed the thousand mú of the Cultivated Field,
while the empress and her consorts personally tended silkworms and mulberry.
Now, Your Majesty, with sagely wisdom and utmost benevolence,
continues the legacy of the former kings;
the Empress embodies the virtue of fostering life
and accords with the principle of complementing Qían.
However, the path of Kūn is not yet radiant,
and the silkworm ceremony is still lacking.
I propose that it would be appropriate to follow ancient customs
and fully establish this grand ceremony."
An imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven personally cultivated the fields
to provide sacrificial grains,
and the empress and her consorts personally tended silkworms
to prepare sacrificial robes.
This was to diligently follow filial piety and reverence,
and to clearly demonstrate instruction.
Now, the system for the Cultivated Field is in place,
but the silkworm ceremony is not performed,
due to the multitude of tasks in between,
leaving no time to fully establish it.
Today, the world is at peace;
it is fitting to establish the ceremony to demonstrate to the four seas.
Let the details be based on ancient classics
and recent precedents,
to consider what is currently appropriate,
and implement it next year."
Thereupon, the silkworm ceremony was held in the western suburb,
which was facing the Cultivated Field.
Then, Chéng Càn, Attendant Official, was ordered to draft the ritual.
The Altar for the First Silkworm was one zhàng high
and two zhàng square,
with four ascending steps,
each five chǐ wide.
It was located outside the outer gate of the curtained palace, southeast of the Empress's Mulberry Picking Altar,
and ten zhàng southeast from the curtained palace,
southwest of the silkworm house,
with the mulberry grove to its east.
Six wives of marquises were chosen as silkworm mothers.
When the silkworms were about to hatch,
on an auspicious day,
the Empress wore twelve hairpins with pendants (bùyáo).
Following the precedents of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
she wore a green gown
and rode in an oiled, painted mica chariot (ānjū),
drawn by six black horses.
Female court officials, wearing diāo chán (marten and cicada decorations) and carrying imperial seals, accompanied her,
carrying baskets and hooks.

Princesses, the three Fūrén, nine Pín, Shìfù, all imperial elder consorts (Tàifēi), ladies (Tàifūrén), as well as Xiàn-Xiāngjūn, Jùn-Gōnghóu special function fūrén, external Shìfù, and Mìngfù all wore bùyáo,
dressed in green,
each carrying a basket and hook, and followed the silkworm ceremony.
Two days before the mulberry picking,
silkworms were placed on thin sheets in the silkworm palace.
On the day of mulberry picking,
before the Empress arrived,
the Grand Invocation Officer at dawn offered a grand sacrifice of one tàiláo,
with one usher supervising the sacrifice.
After the sacrifice, the offerings were removed,
and the remaining meat was distributed to those attending the mulberry ceremony and those performing the sacrifice.
The Empress arrived at the western suburb and ascended the altar;
the princesses and those below them lined up to the east of the altar.
The Empress faced east and personally picked mulberry,
collecting three branches.
Each of the imperial consorts and princesses picked five branches,
and Xiàn-Xiāngjūn and those below each picked nine branches.
All the mulberry was handed to the silkworm mothers,
who returned to the silkworm house.
After the event,
the Empress returned to her temporary seat,
and the princesses and those below then took their places.
A banquet was held,
and silk was bestowed in varying amounts.
The Former Hàn dynasty only established official shè (altars of the god of earth) but no official jì (altars of the god of grain).
Wáng Mǎng established official jì,
but they were later abolished.
Therefore, from Hàn to Wèi, only the Tàishè had jì,
while the official shè had no jì,
thus there were always two shè and one jì.
In the early Jìn dynasty, this practice continued from Wèi,
without any additions or reductions.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng,
when the ancestral temple was rebuilt,
the Shèjì altar was also moved along with the temple.
An edict then stated:
"Shè is truly one deity;
combine the sacrifices of the two shè."
Thereupon, Fù Xián, Cavalier Attendant-in-Chief and Grand Minister, memorialized: "The 'Jìfǎ' (Treatise on Sacrifices) states that the royal shè (Wángshè) and the grand shè (Tàishè)
each have their own meaning.
The Son of Heaven respectfully serves the suburban and ancestral temples,
hence he wears a crown and personally plows.
The personal plowing
is to emphasize the importance of filial offerings
of sacrificial grains.
He plows personally, therefore he makes offerings on his own behalf.
Those who establish a shè for themselves
do so for the Cultivated Field and to offer thanks.
The state is based on its people,
and people depend on grain for life,
therefore, a shè is also
established for the common people to pray and offer thanks.
The matters are different, and the offerings vary;
this is why there are two shè.
Wáng Jǐnghóu's discussion of the Wángshè
also states that it is for praying for the Cultivated Field in spring
and offering thanks in autumn.
Regarding the Tàishè,
he said that the ruler establishes it for the common people
within the territory
under his rule,
calling it Tàishè,
and does not establish it for himself in the capital.
Jǐnghóu's argument here is based on the 'Jìfǎ'.
The 'Jìfǎ' says:
'From grandees downwards, when groups establish a
shè,
it is called zhìshè (established shè).'
Jǐnghóu explained,
'This is what is now called lǐshè (village shè).'
Jǐnghóu's interpretation of the 'Jìfǎ' thus takes zhìshè as the shè of the common people.
And
in a separate discussion, he again takes Tàishè as the shè of the common people;
I do not understand this meaning.
Tàishè
is where the Son of Heaven sacrifices for the common people,
hence it is called the Son of Heaven's Shè.
The 'Jiāotèshēng' states:
'The Son of Heaven's Tàishè
must receive frost, dew, wind, and rain.'
Because of the multitude of common surnames,
the ruler universally establishes a shè for them,
hence it is called Tàishè.
As for zhìshè,
their number is not uniform;
they are probably named after the villages,
as in the 'Zuǒshì Zhuàn' where it says 'pledging at the shè of Qīngqiū.'
The shè of the common people
are not called 'Tài';
if they were also not established in the capital,
where would they be established?
The 'Jìfǎ' also says,
'The king establishes seven sacrifices for the myriad surnames,
and the king establishes seven sacrifices for himself.'
When it says 'for himself,'
it means sacrificing for himself;
when it says 'for the myriad surnames,'
it means sacrificing for the myriad surnames.
The text concerning Tàishè and the seven sacrifices is exactly parallel.
Commentators, having exhausted this point,
then say that the ancient texts only mention five sacrifices,
not seven sacrifices.
Examining
the sacrifices,
the five sacrifices are the great sacrifices of the state,
while the seven are minor sacrifices.
What the 'Zhōulǐ' refers to as 'all minor sacrifices'
belongs to the category of wearing black caps.
Jǐnghóu explained 'Dàlì' (Great Pestilence) by saying,
'Like Dù Bó of Zhōu,
when ghosts have a place to return to,
they do not become pests.'
Now, those who say there are no two shè claim Jǐnghóu,
but the 'Jìfǎ' does not say there are no two;
they then say,
'there is no such text in oral tradition.'
Given Jǐnghóu's sagacity,
he pondered and then provided his interpretation.
To want to eliminate a clear text with an oral argument,
in this way, not only would the two shè be subject to reconsideration,
but Jǐnghóu's later explanation would also not be easily removed.
Formerly, I was instructed
that Shàngshū Zhào Gào established a shè in the new city,
with only one tàiláo,
which is not the clear meaning of two shè.
Examining the 'Jiāotèshēng,' it says 'Shèjì tàiláo.'
If one must cite the text of 'one tàiláo' to argue that there are no two shè,
then Jì would have no sacrificial animal.
Commentators say,
'mentioning Shè implies Jì.'
If one can mention Shè
to clarify Jì,
why not just mention one to clarify two?
The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifices and warfare.
If there are two and one is removed,
it is not better than having too many and keeping them.
Moreover,
Is it righteous to preserve it,
and baseless to abolish it?
The Rites of Zhōu says that the Fēngrén (officer in charge of borders) was responsible for setting up the shèwěi (altars of the earth god),
without the character jì (god of grain).
Currently, the Dìshè (imperial altar of the earth god) has no jì,
which likely originated from this.
However, the state masters shèjì (altars of earth and grain),
hence the classics and commentaries often mention
shèjì.
The Rites of Zhōu states that when the king sacrifices to shèjì, he wears a chǐmiǎn (ceremonial cap and robe made of fine silk),
which is evidence that the Wángshè (king's altar) included jì.
Regarding the absence of the character jì in the shèwěi managed by the Fēngrén,
〔一二〕commentators
believe it is an abbreviated text,
from which it can be inferred.
It is suggested that it is appropriate to retain the old system of establishing two shè,
and additionally establish the jì of the Dìshè.
At the time, Chéng Càn (成粲)'s deliberation cited Jǐnghóu (景侯)'s argument that the Tàishè (Grand Altar) should not be established in the capital,
intending to refute Zhèng Shì (鄭氏)'s scholarship.
Xián (咸) strongly argued in response:
"If we follow Càn (粲)'s argument,
Jǐnghóu (景侯)'s interpretation of the text would be ruined by this.
The Dàyǎ (大雅) says 'Then he established the zhǒngtǔ' (冢土),
and Máogōng (毛公) explained,
'Zhǒngtǔ (冢土)
is the Tàishè (太社).'
Jǐnghóu (景侯)'s interpretation of the Shī (詩) (Classic of Poetry) adopted this very explanation.
The Yǔgòng (禹貢) says 'The earth has five colors,'
and Jǐnghóu (景侯) explained,
'The king takes earth of five colors to make the Tàishè (太社),
and enfeoffs the regional lords of the four directions,
each receiving earth of their respective directional color to cover the four directions.'
If this is the case,
the Tàishè (太社) would again be established in the capital.
I do not know where this argument comes from,
and it contradicts his own interpretation,
above violating the clear text of the classics and records,
and below ruining Jǐnghóu (景侯)'s explanation.
Although I am dull and ignorant,
having grown up in scholarly circles,
I cannot remain silent.
I respectfully present this continuation of the matter."
Liú Shí (劉寔) agreed with Xián (咸)'s argument.
An edict stated:
"The shè is truly one deity,
yet two altars have been successively maintained.
Public opinions differ,
why must we change it?
It is expedient to maintain the old system,
entirely following the Wèi (魏) regulations."
Subsequently, Zhì Yú (摯虞) submitted a memorial,
stating:
"I have examined the Jìfǎ (祭法) (Treatise on Sacrifices): 'The king establishes an altar for the multitude of surnames, called Tàishè (太社);
the king establishes an altar for himself, called Wángshè (王社).'
The Zhōulǐ Dà Sītú (周禮大司徒) (Great Minister of War in the Rites of Zhou) says 'He sets up the altars of shèjì (社稷),'
and also says 'He sacrifices to shèjì (社稷) with blood,'
which refers to the Tàishè (太社).
It also says 'The Fēngrén (封人) is in charge of setting up the king's shèwěi (社壝),'
and there are also rituals for military campaigns that are appropriate for the shè (社),
which refers to the Wángshè (王社).
The Tàishè (太社) is for the multitude of surnames to pray for and give thanks;
there are specific times for prayers and thanks,
and its principal deity cannot be abolished.
Thus, in all rituals of expelling evil from the shè (祓社) and consecrating drums (釁鼓),
the principal deity is respectfully honored and followed.
These are all clear texts regarding the two shè,
honored by previous generations.
Citing the Shàngshū Zhàogào (尚書召誥) (Announcement of Shào from the Book of Documents) regarding three different kinds of sacrificial animals for the shè (社) in the new city,
and the Shī (詩) (Classic of Poetry) stating 'Then he established the zhǒngtǔ' (冢土),
which contain no mention of two shè,
the Dìshè (帝社) was thus abolished,
and only the Tàishè (太社) was established.
What the Shī (詩) and Shū (書) (Book of Documents) mention
each refers to a single matter,
and both predate Gōng Dàn (公旦)'s (Duke of Zhōu) compositions.
They cannot be used to change the clear canonical texts of the Zhōulǐ (周禮) (Rites of Zhou)
or the correct principles of the Jìfǎ (祭法).
The previous alteration in establishing the altars,
setting up a single shè,
led to widespread debate in court,
with many upholding ancient practices to rectify current ones.
Shìzǔ Wǔhuángdì (世祖武皇帝) personally issued an illuminating edict,
settling the principle of two shè,
to be an eternal regulation.
It is fitting to establish the new rites
following the two shè."
The edict was followed.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武), Yuándì (元帝)'s reign,
two shè and one jì were again established, following Luòjīng (洛京) (Luoyang).
The prayer for the Tàishè (太社) read:
"The virtue of Earth universally bestows,
its benevolence preserved boundless.
Hence is the Tàishè (太社) established,
to protect and bless all states.
Vast are the four seas,
all rely on its auspicious blessings."
The prayer for the Dìshè (帝社) read:
"The deep virtue of Kūn (坤) supports all,
the imperial domain is thus protected.
Hence is the Dìshè (帝社) established,
to divinely manifest the Way of Earth.
Bright sacrifices are offered in due season,
great blessings arrive."
According to Hàn (漢) protocol,
on the first day of each month,
the Tàishǐ (太史) (Grand Astrologer) would present the month's calendar.
The Sīláng (侍郎) (Attendant Official) of the Yǒusī (有司) (relevant department) and the Shàngshū (尚書) (Minister) would read its directives,
and ensure their proper execution.
Two days before and after the new moon,
cattle and wine were brought to the shè (社) for the sacrifice of the sun.
〔一三〕If there was a solar anomaly,
a sheep was slaughtered to offer to the shè (社),
to avert the solar anomaly.
Officials performing the ritual wore a chángguān (長冠) (tall cap),
a crimson robe with a red collar and cuffs over an inner garment, and crimson trousers and stockings,
〔一四〕following the old custom.
Since the Jìn (晉) received the Mandate,
when the sun and moon were about to conjoin,
the Tàishǐ (太史) would present the calculated new moon.
Three days before the event, the Shàngshū (尚書) would
declare a state of emergency both inside and outside the palace.
Zhì Yú (摯虞)'s resolution to doubts stated:
"In all cases of averting a solar eclipse,
one wears a red cè (幘) (headband),
to assist the yang energy.
When an eclipse is imminent,
the Son of Heaven wears plain clothes and retreats to the main palace,
and a strict alert is maintained inside and out.
The Tàishǐ (太史) ascends the Língtái (靈臺) (Spirit Tower),
observes the solar anomaly,
and immediately beats drums at the gate.
Upon hearing the drum sound,
all attendant officials don red cè (幘)
and enter to serve with swords.
All officials from the Lìshǐ (令史) (scribes) of the Sāntái (三臺) (Three Departments) upwards each hold a sword
and stand before their doors.
The Wèiwèi Qīng (衞尉卿) (Minister of the Palace Guard) rides around the palace,
observing and guarding,
circulating repeatedly.
Drums are also beaten at the shè (社),
following the Zhōulǐ (周禮).
Furthermore, a rope of red silk is used to tie the shè (社),
and the zhùshǐ (祝史) (prayer official) recites an admonishing speech.
The shè (社)
is the deity Gōulóng (勾龍),
the Son of Heaven's high duke,
hence an admonishing speech is recited to him.
When the sun returns to normal,
they cease."
During the Jiàn'ān (建安) era of Hàn (漢),
when the New Year's assembly was about to take place,
the Tàishǐ (太史) reported
that a solar eclipse was due on New Year's Day.
Court officials doubted whether the assembly should proceed and
collectively consulted Shàngshū Lìng Xún Yù (尚書令荀彧).
At that time, Liú Shào (劉邵), an accountant from Guǎngpíng (廣平), was present
and said:
"Zǐ Shèn (梓慎) and Pí Zào (裨竈),
excellent historians of ancient times,
still miscalculated celestial phenomena when divining water and fire.
According to the Rites,
there are four instances when regional lords, visiting the Son of Heaven,
are not allowed to complete the ritual upon entering the gate;
a solar eclipse is one of them.
However, the sages established regulations
not to preemptively abolish court ceremonies due to anomalies,
either because the calamity might dissipate or the anomaly subside,
or because the calculations might be erroneous."
Xún Yù (荀彧) and the others all praised and followed this,
and thus the court assembly proceeded as usual.
The sun also did not eclipse,
and Liú Shào (劉邵) became famous for this.
In the third and fourth years of Xiánníng (咸寧), Wǔdì (武帝)'s reign,
the New Year's assembly was postponed due to the new moon falling on New Year's Day,
changing the old Wèi (魏) custom.
In the fourth month of the first year of Tàixīng (太興), Yuándì (元帝)'s reign,
during a new moon,
Zhōngshū Shìláng Kǒng Yú (中書侍郎孔愉) memorialized:
"According to the Chūnqiū (春秋) (Spring and Autumn Annals),
if there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven beats drums at the shè (社)
to attack the yin forces;
regional lords beat drums at court
to attack themselves.
However, according to the Shàngshū Fú (尚書符) (Book of Documents tally),
if there is a solar anomaly,
drums are immediately beaten at all gates,
which violates the old canon."
The edict stated:
"What you have presented has correct principles,
so an order shall immediately be issued to the external authorities to change it."
When Emperor Kāng [Kāngdì] ascended the throne in the first year of Jiànyuán [Jiànyuán],
the Grand Astrologer [Tàishǐ] reported a new moon at the start of the year.
Later, doubts arose again as to whether the assembly should be postponed or not.
Yǔ Bīng [Yǔ Bīng] was assisting in governance,
and he showed Liú Shào's [Liú Shào] deliberation to the Eight Ministers [Bāzuò].
At that time, some said that Shào [Shào] did not grasp the meaning of the rites.
Xún Yù [Xún Yù] agreed with this,
which was one of his faults as a superior person.
Therefore, Cài Mó [Cài Mó] wrote a memorial refuting him,
saying:
“Shào’s [Shào] argument that disasters fade and reappear,
and that even Zǐ Shèn [Zǐ Shèn] and Pí Zào [Pí Zào] made mistakes,
and that the Grand Astrologer’s [Tàishǐ] report,
is not necessarily accurate,
is indeed logical.
However, his claim that the Sages [Shèngrén] established regulations
and would not abolish court rituals in advance due to anomalies
is mistaken.
The manifestation of auspicious and inauspicious signs
is to warn the ruler,
a matter which kings [Wángzhě] take seriously.
Therefore, one wears plain clothes, stops music,
retreats to the main chamber,
officials present offerings,
coins are used, drums are beaten,
and the ruler personally intercedes.
In matters of reverence and warning,
rather than abandoning them out of doubt,
it is better to proceed with caution.
Thus, Confucius [Kǒngzǐ] and Lǎo Dān [Lǎo Dān] assisted a funeral in Xiàngdǎng [Xiàngdǎng],
and because a funeral procession should not proceed if stars are not visible,
when there was an eclipse, they stopped the coffin,
saying, 'How do we know the stars are not visible?'
But Shào [Shào] would abolish this,
which is to discard the established rules of the Sages [Shèngrén] and Worthies [Xián].
When Duke Huán of Lǔ [Lǔ Huángōng] had a disaster on the Rénshēn [Rénshēn] day,
he performed the Cháng [Cháng] sacrifice on the Yǐhài [Yǐhài] day,
which the Spring and Autumn Annals [Chūnqiū] criticized.
Even after the disaster had passed,
fear and dread still lingered,
leading to the suspension of ancestral temple sacrifices.
How much more so when one hears that a celestial calamity is imminent,
and yet holds celebratory gatherings?
This is contrary to the rites.
What the Lǐjì [Lǐjì] says about feudal lords entering the gate and not completing the ritual
refers to when the celestial officials [Rìguān] did not predict it in advance,
and the feudal lords, having entered,
only learned of the eclipse when they saw it.
It does not mean that having heard of an impending eclipse, the court assembly would not be suspended.
Citing this
can be said to miss its essential meaning.
The text Liú Shào [Liú Shào] relies on is the Lǐjì [Lǐjì],
and the matter of the Master [Fūzǐ] and Lǎo Dān [Lǎo Dān] in Xiàngdǎng [Xiàngdǎng] is also spoken of in the Lǐjì [Lǐjì].
Yet he contravenes and reverses it,
making his arguments baseless.
However, what Xún Lìng [Xún Lìng] praised,
and what the Hàn [Hàn] court followed,
has caused this statement to be praised even now,
without anyone knowing its error.
Later gentlemen [Jūnzǐ] will model themselves after it,
therefore I rectify it.”
Thereupon, Bīng [Bīng] followed the general opinion,
and the assembly was postponed.
During the Yǒnghé [Yǒnghé] period,
Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào] assisted in governance
and again wished to follow Liú Shào's [Liú Shào] proposal not to postpone the assembly.
Wáng Biāozhī [Wáng Biāozhī] cited the precedents of Xiánníng [Xiánníng] and Jiànyuán [Jiànyuán],
and also said:
“The rites state that there are four instances
when feudal lords visiting the Son of Heaven [Tiānzǐ]
may not complete the ritual and must abandon it.
This refers to sudden and violent occurrences,
not to pre-existing events.
Nor is it an opportunistic hope that the astrological official’s calculations are erroneous,
thereby avoiding the need to postpone court rituals.”
Thereupon, Biāozhī’s [Biāozhī] proposal was followed.
In the Shàngshū [Shàngshū],
“Yīn [Yīn] sacrifice to the Six Zōng [Lùzōng],”
various scholars offered differing interpretations,
often inconsistent.
Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng] equated them with the Six Sons of Yì [Yì Lùzi],
and consequently established shrines for the Six Zōng [Lùzōng].
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi [Wèi Míngdì], he doubted this matter
and inquired of Wáng Sù [Wáng Sù],
who also believed they were the Six Sons of Yì [Yì Lùzi],
hence they were not abolished.
When the Jìn [Jìn] received the Mandate,
Sīmǎ Biāo [Sīmǎ Biāo] and others memorialized that the sacrifices to the Six Zōng [Lùzōng] should not establish new rites.
Consequently, these sacrifices were abolished.
Later, Zhì Yú [Zhì Yú] memorialized,
again arguing:
“Examining Shùn’s [Shùn] acceptance of the Mandate,
‘he performed the Lèi [Lèi] sacrifice to the Supreme Deity [Shàngdì],
the Yīn [Yīn] sacrifice to the Six Zōng [Lùzōng],
and Wàng [Wàng] sacrifices to the mountains and rivers.’
Thus, the Six Zōng [Lùzōng] are not the deities of the Supreme Deity [Shàngdì],
nor are they the spirits of mountains and rivers.
The Zhōulǐ [Zhōulǐ] in the office of Sīshī [Sīshī] states: ‘Sacrifices with animals are made to the Shè [Shè] and Zōng [Zōng].’
The office of Dǎngzhèng [Dǎngzhèng] states: ‘In spring and autumn, the Yíng [Yíng] sacrifice is also performed.’
The Zōng [Zōng] of the Sīshī [Sīshī],
being listed alongside the Shè [Shè],
has the same status as the Shè [Shè].
The Yíng [Yíng] of the Dǎngzhèng [Dǎngzhèng],
not being linked to the Shè [Shè] in the text,
implies a different deity from the Shè [Shè].
Among the sacrifices ordained by Zhōu [Zhōu],
none were more important than the Jiāo [Jiāo] and Shè [Shè].
If Zōng [Zōng] is equivalent to Shè [Shè],
then its noble divinity is clear.
Furthermore,
the Yuèlìng [Yuèlìng] mentions praying to the Tiānzōng [Tiānzōng] in the first month of winter.
Thus, the Jìyíng [Jìyíng] sacrifice in the Zhōulǐ [Zhōulǐ],
and the Tiānzōng [Tiānzōng] in the Yuèlìng [Yuèlìng],
are the deities of the Six Zōng [Lùzōng].
Emperor Guāngwǔ [Guāngwǔ] of Hàn [Hàn], upon his ascension in Gāoyì [Gāoyì],
performed the Yīn [Yīn] sacrifice to the Six Zōng [Lùzōng] according to the Yúshū [Yúshū].
In the Yuánchū [Yuánchū] period of Emperor Ān [Āndì],
a sacrifice was established in the Qián [Qián] position,
with rites similar to the Tàishè [Tàishè].
The Wèi [Wèi] dynasty followed this,
until the second year of Jǐngchū [Jǐngchū],
when a great debate arose regarding these deities,
with court officials in disarray,
each holding their own views.
Only Sànqí Chángshì [Sànqí Chángshì] Liú Shào [Liú Shào] believed that all things carry yin [yīn] and embrace yang [yáng],
and their vital breath [chōngqì] achieves harmony.
The Six Zōng [Lùzōng]
are the harmonious vital breath [chōnghé zhī qì] of the Great Ultimate [Tàijí],
the ancestors of the six energies [liùqì].
The Yúshū [Yúshū] calls them Six Zōng [Lùzōng],
and the Zhōushū [Zhōushū] calls them Heavenly Zōng [Tiānzōng].
At that time, when discussing the similarities and differences,
his proposal was followed.
The Hàn [Hàn] and Wèi [Wèi] dynasties successively
established them as noble sacrifices.
For all esteemed sacrifices to the myriad deities,
if they are neglected and not performed,
once they are established,
no one dares to abolish them.
It is fitting to establish new rites
and sacrifice to the Six Zōng [Lùzōng] as before.”
The edict followed him.
According to the rites,
the king established seven sacrifices for the common people:
to Sīmìng [Sīmìng], Zhōngliú [Zhōngliú], Guómén [Guómén], Guóháng [Guóháng], Dàlì [Dàlì], Hù [Hù], and Zào [Zào].
On the day when the swallows arrived in mid-spring,
a Grand Sacrifice [tàiláo] was offered to Gāoméi [Gāoméi].
In the chapter “Sī Yī” [Sī Yī] of the Máoshī [Máoshī],
Gāo Zǐ [Gāo Zǐ] said it was the image of Língxīng [Língxīng].
When the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty arose,
Emperor Gāo [Gāodì] also established a Língxīng [Língxīng] shrine.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ [Wǔdì],
due to Lǐ Shǎojūn [Lǐ Shǎojūn], sacrifices to Zào [Zào] began;
and after the birth of Crown Prince Lì [Lì Tàizǐ],
Gāoméi [Gāoméi] was established.
The Hàn Yí [Hàn Yí] states that
the state also had five sacrifices,
which officials performed.
Their rites were somewhat lighter than those of the Shèjì [Shèjì],
thus their traditions were also preserved.
It also states that
in the month of mid-spring,
a Gāoméi [Gāoméi] shrine was established south of the city,
and a single animal was sacrificed.
Also,
in that same month,
the Lǎorénxīng [Lǎorénxīng] was sacrificed to at the Lǎorénxīng Miào [Lǎorénxīng Miào] in the southern suburb of the capital.
In early summer, Zào [Zào] was sacrificed to.
In late autumn, the Xīnxīng [Xīnxīng] was sacrificed to at the Xīnxīng Miào [Xīnxīng Miào] on the altar south of the city.
During the Yuánkāng [Yuánkāng] period,
Luòyáng [Luòyáng] still had a Gāoméi [Gāoméi] altar.
The common people sacrificed beside it,
some calling it Luòxīng [Luòxīng].
After this,
nothing more was heard of these sacrifices.
Since the time of Jiāngzuǒ [Jiāngzuǒ],
the seven sacrifices were not established.
Língxīng [Língxīng] was instead included in the Southern Suburban [Nánjiāo] sacrifices,
and no longer separately established.
Zuǒshì Zhuàn
states, “When dragons are seen, a rain sacrifice is offered.”
Such classics are ancient.
According to Hàn rituals,
from Lìchūn (Start of Spring) to Lìxià (Start of Summer),
and until the end of Lìqiū (Start of Autumn),
if there was a severe drought in commanderies and states,
the commanderies and counties would each sweep the altars of the earth and grain.
When drought occurred,
the Gōngqīng (Grandees) and officials would in turn perform the yù (rain sacrifice) ritual to pray for rain,
closing off all yang influences,
wearing black robes,
raising earthen dragons,
erecting earthen figures,
and having two lines of boy dancers.
This changed every seven days,
as was the custom.
In the second year of Wǔdì’s Xiánníng era (276 CE),
there was a prolonged spring drought.
On the Dīngsì day of the fourth month,
an imperial edict stated,
“In all places suffering drought, prayers should be extensively increased.”
On the Gēngwǔ day of the fifth month,
prayers for rain were first offered to the altars of the earth and grain, mountains, and rivers.
On the Wùzǐ day of the sixth month,
a downpour was received.
This was the old tradition of the yù (rain sacrifice).
In the fourth month of the third year of Tàikāng (282 CE),
and the second month of the tenth year (289 CE),
the same was done.
If there was too much rain, a yíng (a sacrifice to avert disaster) was offered,
with red turbans and vermillion robes,
closing off all yin influences,
winding red ropes around the earth altar,
and striking vermillion drums.
According to the Zhōu Lǐ,

the king sacrificed to Hàotiān Shàngdì (August Heaven Supreme Thearch), the sun, moon, and stars, Sīzhōng and Sīmìng, Fēngbó (Earl of Wind) and Yǔshī (Master of Rain), the altars of the earth and grain, the Wǔtǔ (Five Soils), the Wǔyuè (Five Sacred Mountains), mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, and all things in the four directions.
Sacrifices were made to the four classes of spirits and the four quarters,
following the same custom.
In the sixth month, Gēngzǐ day, of the second year of Wèi Wéndì’s Huángchū era (221 CE),
rituals were first performed for the Wǔyuè (Five Sacred Mountains) and Sīdú (Four Great Rivers),
arranging all sacrifices in order,
and burying and submerging guī (jade tablets) and bì (jade discs).
In the seventh month of the sixth year (225 CE),
the Emperor entered the Huái River with a boat army.
On the Rénxū day of the ninth month,
envoys were sent to submerge bì (jade discs) in the Huái River.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Wèi Míngdì’s Tàihé era (230 CE),
the Emperor made an eastern tour,
and sent envoys to sacrifice a special ox at Mount Zhōngyuè.
In the first year of Wèi Yuándì’s Xiánxī era (264 CE),
he traveled to Cháng’ān,
and sent envoys with bì (jade discs) and silk to perform ritual sacrifices at Mount Huàshān.
During Mùdì’s Shēngpíng era,
Hé Qí discussed the repair of the Wǔyuè (Five Sacred Mountains) temples, saying:
“According to the system of Táng and Yú,
the Son of Heaven made an inspection tour every five years,
following the seasonal directions,
burning sacrifices on the Wǔyuè,
looking out over mountains and rivers,
and extending to all spirits.
Therefore it is said,
‘He ascended to Heaven by means of famous mountains,’
thereby making a clear announcement to the gods,
and recompensing their merits.
Hence, calamities did not arise,
and wind, rain, cold, and heat occurred in due season.
When it came to the Sāndài (Three Dynasties),
though the number of years differed,
their rituals remained unchanged.
The Wǔyuè were regarded as the Sāngōng (Three Dukes),
and the Sīdú as the Zhūhóu (feudal lords).
This is recorded in the classics,
as is said,
‘Those who established it, none dared abolish it.’
When Qín and Hàn established their capital in Xījīng,
the Jīng, Wèi, and Cháng Shuǐ rivers,
though not included in the regular sacrificial canon,
because of their proximity to Xiányáng,
all received sacrifices comparable to the great rivers.
How then could the properly established sacrifices be omitted?
Since the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
when Shénzhōu (China) was overturned,
this matter has fallen into disuse.
Only Mount Tiānzhù in Qián,
which was within the royal domain,
formerly had a hundred officials and soldiers selected by the court
to perform its duties.
During the period of restoration (Zhōngxīng),
there were no official posts,
so Lújiāng Commandery often sent a senior official to temporarily handle the seasonal prayers and sacrifices,
praying for relief from cold in spring and for ice in winter.
From Xiánhé until now,
this has again fallen into disuse.
Calculating the number of currently unauthorized shrines,
it can be said to be not just one.
Examining their proper names,
they are illicit and confused spirits;
considering their extravagance,
they are parasites on the common people.
Yet the great spirits of mountains and rivers are increasingly neglected,
rituals and customs are degenerate and disordered,
humans and spirits are mixed and disturbed,
and public and private matters are rushed and constrained,
gradually becoming more numerous.
This is truly because the state has faced many difficulties recently,
having no time to spare,
and hastily establishing and neglecting things,
with some matters not yet attended to.
Now that the prime culprits have been eliminated,
the old traditions should be restored.
In the regions of the sacred mountains and rivers,
where virtuous teachings have spread,
the masses who have come to life again
have all benefited from benevolent grace.
Yet the veneration and sacrifices to the spirits,
have not been distinguished or clarified.
The inspection tours and burning sacrifices
have long been abandoned.
To uphold previous traditions,
we await the imperial carriage’s return north,
to examine ancient statutes and regulations,
and greatly reform the systems.
As for the sacrificial vessels, animals,
and the texts of prayers and blessings,
the old chapters are no longer recorded.
The officials of rites can be ordered to create a new standard,
to be based on sincerity and simplicity,
to convey bright virtue and fragrant devotion,
and that is all.
As for other malevolent cults,
they can be roughly dealt with according to laws and decrees,
first eliminating the worst of them,
so that the proper and the heterodox are not defiled.”
At the time, this was not heeded.
Formerly, when King Wǔ entered Yīn,
before he even alighted from his chariot, he enfeoffed the descendants of previous dynasties,
likely out of remembrance of their virtue.
Kǒngzǐ, though a great sage, died as an inferior minister,
and had no enfeoffment or noble title.
It was not until Hàn Yuándì,
that Kǒng Bà, as the emperor’s teacher, was granted a noble title,
named Bāochéng Jūn,
to serve Kǒngzǐ’s descendants.
In the first month of the second year of Wèi Wéndì’s Huángchū era (221 CE),
an edict made Yìláng Kǒng Xiàn the Zōngshèng Hóu,
with an estate of a hundred households,
to maintain the sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ.
It ordered Lǔ Commandery to repair the old temple,
and assign a hundred officials and soldiers to guard it.
Later, in the eleventh month of the third year of Wǔdì’s Tàishǐ era (267 CE),
Zōngshèng Hóu Kǒng Zhèn was re-enfeoffed as Fèngshèng Tíng Hóu.
An edict also instructed the Imperial University (Tàixué) and Lǔ State
to offer three sacrificial animals seasonally to Kǒngzǐ.
In the third year of Míngdì’s Tàiníng era (325 CE),
an edict ordered that Fèngshèng Tíng Hóu Kǒng Tíng be provided with the expenses for the seasonal sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ,
as was the custom in Tàishǐ.
According to the Rites,
when schools were first established, a dì (offering) ceremony was performed for the Former Sages and Former Teachers,
and when performing official duties, ceremonial silks were always used.
Although schools were established during the Hàn dynasty,
this ritual was not heard of.
In the second month of the second year of Wèi Qíwáng’s Zhèngshǐ era (241 CE),
the Emperor lectured on the Lúnyǔ (Analects) and understood it.
In the fifth month of the fifth year (244 CE),
he lectured on the Shàngshū (Book of Documents) and understood it.
In the twelfth month of the seventh year (246 CE),
he lectured on the Lǐjì (Book of Rites) and understood it.
In all cases, the Tàicháng was ordered to perform the dì ceremony,
sacrificing a tài láo (grand sacrifice) to Kǒngzǐ at the Bìyōng,
with Yán Huí as his co-sacrificed.
In the seventh year of Wǔdì’s Tàishǐ era (271 CE),
the Crown Prince lectured on the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) and understood it.
In the third year of Xiánníng (277 CE),
he lectured on the Shī (Book of Odes) and understood it.
In the third year of Tàikāng (282 CE),
he lectured on the Lǐjì (Book of Rites) and understood it.
In the third year of Huìdì’s Yuánkāng era (293 CE),
the Crown Prince lectured on the Lúnyǔ (Analects) and understood it.
In the second year of Yuándì’s Tàixīng era (319 CE),
the Crown Prince lectured on the Lúnyǔ (Analects) and understood it.
The Crown Princes personally performed the dì ceremony,
sacrificing a tài láo to Kǒngzǐ,
with Yán Huí as his co-sacrificed.
In the first year of Chéngdì’s Xiánkāng era (335 CE),
the Emperor lectured on the Shī (Book of Odes) and understood it.
In the third month of the first year of Mùdì’s Shēngpíng era (357 CE),
the Emperor lectured on the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) and understood it.
In the seventh month of the third year of Xiàowǔdì’s Níngkāng era (375 CE),
the Emperor lectured on the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) and understood it.
In all cases, the dì ceremony was performed as was customary.
Mùdì and Xiàowǔdì provisionally used the central hall as the Imperial University.
According to old custom,
Gāo Táo 皋陶 was sacrificed to in the Tíngwèi Sì 廷尉寺 (Court of the Grand Judge).
The new rites moved the sacrifice to the Lǜshǔ 律署 (Department of Laws),
so that it might be offered concurrently with the sacrifices to the Former Sages at the Tàixué 太學 (Imperial Academy).
According to old custom,
the sacrifice was performed on a shè rì 社日 (earth god day);
the new rites changed this to the first month of autumn (mèngqiū zhī yuè 孟秋之月),
to correspond with the autumn governance (qiū zhèng 秋政).
Zhì Yú 摯虞 opined:
“According to the Yú Shū 虞書,
Gāo Táo 皋陶 served as the shìshī 士師 (Grand Judge),
being both discerning and trustworthy.
The state valued his achievements,
and the people thought of his uprightness.
Therefore, the prison officials honored his spirit,
and those in bondage offered him sacrifices.
His merit lay in the successful resolution of legal cases,
not in the promulgation of laws and regulations.
The establishment of the Tàixué 太學,
[一六] whose significance is considered weighty by the Tàicháng 太常 (Grand Minister of Ceremonies),
is why sacrifices are made there.
This is to revere the sages and follow what is important.
The establishment of the Lǜshǔ 律署 is
inferior to the Tíngwèi 廷尉.
To move the sacrifice to the Department [of Laws]
is to abandon what is important and turn to what is minor.
The Department of Laws is not the main office;
its establishment and abolishment are not constant.
It should remain as it was, sacrificed to in the Tíngwèi 廷尉.
Furthermore,
the sacrifice was performed in mid-spring,
taking the meaning of cherishing life.
Changing it to the first month of autumn,
to correspond with punishments and killings,
is not sufficiently logical to warrant the change.
The new rites should be established
to all follow the old customs.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Granted.”
At the start of the year (suì dàn 歲旦), reed stalks and peach branches were always set up,
and chickens were sacrificed at the gates of the palace and all hundred temples,
to ward off evil influences.
According to Hàn Yí 漢儀 (Han Rites), this was done in midsummer,
with peach talismans,
but no sacrificed chickens.
It was during the reign of Wèi Míngdì 魏明帝 that great reforms to the rites of exorcism were made;
hence, Hé Yàn Ἡ晏, in his discourse on exorcism sacrifices, mentioned the specific offering of a chicken for the rituals of exorcism and averting misfortune.
The sacrificing of chickens likely originated in Wèi 魏,
while the peach talismans were originally a Hàn 漢 system,
intended to complement the *mǎo jīn* (卯金, a type of talisman).
It is also likely that Wèi 魏 abolished them.
However, it is not clear when the change from midsummer to the start of the year occurred.
In the first year of Qīnglóng 青龍 (233 CE) of Wèi Míngdì 魏明帝,
an edict was issued to the commanderies and states that mountains and rivers not listed in the sacrificial canon should not be sacrificed to.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (265 CE) of Wǔdì 武帝,
an edict stated:
“In antiquity, the sagely emperors and enlightened kings maintained the Five Sacred Mountains and the Four Great Rivers, as well as famous mountains, rivers, and marshes,
each with established regulations,
to repay the merits of yin and yang.
However, for those who govern the world with the Dao,
their ghosts do not manifest as spirits,
and their spirits do not harm people.
Therefore, the祝史 *zhùshǐ* (prayer-scribes) made their offerings without reproachful words,
and consequently, the people respected and were cautious of the unseen,
and excessive sacrifices did not occur.
In later generations, faith in the Dao weakened,
rituals were usurped and spirits profaned,
and desires were indulged in prayers and petitions,
without even respecting and keeping them at a distance.
Instead, people merely sought good fortune through stealth,
and strange delusions incited each other,
abandoning the righteous for the perverse.
Therefore, the Wèi Cháo 魏朝 (Wei court) abhorred this.
Let the old rites be followed, and a system be fully established,
so that those whose achievements are manifest among men will certainly receive their due rewards,
and perverse and excessive spirits will not cause disorder in between.”
In the first month of the second year,
the officials proposed sacrificing to malignant spirits at the spring equinox and performing exorcism sacrifices.
An edict stated:
“These are not in the sacrificial canon;
abolish them.”
According to the Wáng Zhì 王制,
the Son of Heaven had seven ancestral temples,
and feudal lords and below had their respective ranks,
the ritual texts being detailed.
In the fifth month of the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (213 CE) of Hàn Xiàndì 漢獻帝,
Wèi Wǔdì 魏武帝 was enfeoffed as Wèi Gōng 魏公 (Duke of Wei) with ten commanderies north of the Yellow River.
In the seventh month of that year,
he first established an ancestral temple at Yè 鄴,
constructing five temples according to the rites for a feudal lord.
Later, although he was elevated to the rank of king,
nothing was changed.
In the first year of Yánkāng 延康 (220 CE),
Wén Dì 文帝 succeeded to the kingship.
In the seventh month,
he posthumously honored his imperial ancestor as Dàwáng 大王 (Great King),
and Lady Dīng 丁 as Dàwáng Hòu 大王后 (Queen of Great King).
In the eleventh month of the first year of Huángchū 黃初 (220 CE), he received the abdication.
He further posthumously honored the Dàwáng 大王 as Dà Huángdì 大皇帝 (Great Emperor),
and his deceased father, Wǔ Wáng 武王 (King Wu), as Wǔ Huángdì 武皇帝 (Emperor Wu).
In the sixth month of the second year,
as the ancestral temple in Luòjīng 洛京 (Luoyang) was not yet completed,
he sacrificed to Wǔ Dì 武帝 in the Jiànshǐ Diàn 建始殿,
personally performing the offerings of food and libations,
as in the rites for a common family.
According to the rites, when building palaces, the ancestral temple takes precedence.
Commoners have no temple,
so they sacrifice in their bedchambers.
For an emperor to do so
is highly contrary to the rites.
It is exceedingly improper.
In the sixth month of the third year of Tàihé 太和 (229 CE) of Míng Dì 明帝,
Gāozǔ Dà Chángqiú 高祖大長秋 (Grand Chief of the Household to the High Ancestor) was posthumously honored as Gāo Huáng 高皇 (High Emperor),
and Lady Wú 吳氏 as Gāo Huánghòu 高皇后 (High Empress),
both being placed in the Yè Miào 鄴廟 (Yè Temple).
The persons sacrificed to in the temple were Wén Dì's 文帝 high ancestor, the *chǔshì* 處士 (hermit), his great-grandfather Gāo Huáng 高皇, and his grandfather Dà Huángdì 大皇帝, all sharing one temple;
his father Tàizǔ Wǔ Huángdì 太祖武皇帝 had a separate temple,
which would not be destroyed for a hundred generations.
Thus, the sacrifices were limited to the four chambers of the immediate ancestral temples.
In the eleventh month of that year,
the Luòjīng Miào 洛京廟 (Luoyang Temple) was completed.
Then, the *chǔshì* 處士 (hermit), whose kinship was too distant, was moved to a garden dwelling.
The acting Tàifù Tàicháng Hán Jì 行太傅太常韓暨 and acting Tàicháng Zōngzhèng Cáo Kè 行太常宗正曹恪, bearing imperial credentials,
were sent to welcome the spirit tablets of Gāo Huáng 高皇 and those below him.
They all shared one temple,
still consisting of only four chambers.
Until the sixth month of the first year of Jǐngchū 景初 (237 CE),
the *qún gōng yǒu sī* 羣公有司 (various dukes and officials) first proposed and finalized the system of seven ancestral temples,
stating:
“The Great Wèi 魏 has had three sagely ancestors succeeding each other,
thereby establishing the imperial enterprise.
Wǔ Huángdì 武皇帝 initiated the grand foundation,
restoring order and leveling dangers,
and is designated Wèi Tàizǔ 魏太祖.
Wén Huángdì 文皇帝 succeeded Heaven in revolutionizing (the mandate),
responding to the opportune moment to receive the abdication,
and is designated Wèi Gāozǔ 魏高祖.
The present emperor gathered the great mandate,
brought peace and order to Huáxià 華夏,
and instituted rites and music,
and should be designated Wèi Lièzǔ 魏烈祖.
To the north of Tàizǔ's 太祖 temple, two *tiāo* 祧 (distant ancestral temples) shall be established;
on the left shall be Wén Dì's 文帝 temple,
named Gāozǔ Zhāo Tiāo 高祖昭祧,
and on the right shall be a temple for Míng Dì 明帝,
named Lièzǔ Mù Tiāo 烈祖穆祧.
The temples of these three ancestors
shall not be destroyed for ten thousand generations.
The remaining four temples
shall be moved in succession as kinship becomes too distant,
in accordance with the rites of the *tiāo* 祧 temples of Hòujì 后稷, Wén Wǔ 文武 of Zhōu 周.”
Wén Dì's 文帝 Empress Zhēn 甄 Hòu 后 was given death,
and therefore was not listed in the temple.
When Míng Dì 明帝 ascended the throne,
the officials proposed posthumously honoring her as Wénzhāo Huánghòu 文昭皇后 (Empress Wenxiao),
and the Sīkōng Wáng Lǎng 司空王朗, bearing imperial credentials, was sent to present the ceremonial tablet and make sacrifices at her tomb.
The Sān Gōng 三公 (Three Ducal Ministers) further memorialized, saying:
“From ancient times, the people of Zhōu 周 attributed their ancestry to Hòujì 后稷,
and also specially established a temple to sacrifice to Jiāng Yuán 姜嫄.
Now, the sagely virtue and transformative power of Wénzhāo Huánghòu 文昭皇后 for her descendants,
how can it be measured!
Indeed, for a revered imperial consort,
whose spiritual essence has departed,
to have no sleeping temple for receiving sacrifices and enjoyment,
is not to repay her manifest virtue
and display filial reverence.
Examining ancient regulations,
it is appropriate to follow the rites of Zhōu 周
and establish a separate sleeping temple.”
The memorial was approved.
The memorial was granted.
In the second month of the first year of Tàihé 太和 (227 CE),
a temple was established at Yè 鄴.
In the fourth month,
when the ancestral temple was first being built in Luòyì 洛邑,
a jade seal was unearthed,
measuring one *cùn* and nine *fēn* square (approx. 2.9 cm square).
Its inscription read:
“The Son of Heaven yearns and misses his kind mother” (tiānzǐ xiànsī cípīn 天子羨思慈親).
Míng Dì 明帝 changed his expression for it
and announced it to the temple with a *tàiláo* 太牢 (grand animal sacrifice).
Until the *jǐwèi* 己未 day in the twelfth month of the first year of Jǐngchū 景初 (237 CE),
the officials again memorialized that Wénzhāo Huánghòu 文昭皇后's temple should be established in the capital,
for eternal enjoyment of sacrifices,
with music and dance the same as the ancestral temple,
and the Yè Miào 鄴廟 (Yè Temple) abolished.
In the first year of Xiánxī 咸熙 (264 CE) of Wèi Yuándì 魏元帝,
Wén Dì's 文帝 rank was advanced to king.
Wǔyáng Xuān Wén Hóu 舞陽宣文侯 was posthumously titled Xuān Wáng 宣王 (King Xuan),
and Zhōngwǔ Hóu 忠武侯 as Jǐng Wáng 景王 (King Jing).
In the eighth month of that year,
Wén Dì 文帝 passed away,
and was posthumously named Wén Wáng 文王 (King Wen).
In the twelfth month, on the day *bǐngyín*, in the first year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
he received the abdication.
On the day *dīngmǎo*,
he posthumously honored his imperial ancestor, King Xuān, as Emperor Xuān;
his senior cousin, King Jǐng, as Emperor Jǐng;
and his father, King Wén, as Emperor Wén.
King Xuān’s consort, Lady Zhāng, was honored as Empress Xuānmù,
and King Jǐng’s lady, Lady Yáng, as Empress Jǐng.
In the first month of the second year,
the relevant officials proposed to establish seven ancestral temples.
The Emperor considered this undertaking burdensome,
and issued an edict that it would be proper to temporarily establish one temple.
Thereupon, the assembled ministers deliberated and presented:
“In high antiquity, there was a single ‘Clear Temple’ (Qīngmiào),
to venerate distant deities.
Upon reaching the Zhōu dynasty,
the system of seven ancestral temples was established,
to distinguish the generations of the clan.
Your sacred intention is profound and far-reaching,
tracing back to ancient times,
and upholding the traditions of Táng and Yú.
Discarding the elaborate seven temples,
you follow the distant principle of a single palace.
In the past, Shùn succeeded Yáo by abdication,
received the mandate in the temple of Wénzǔ,
and then ascended the imperial throne.
After some thirty years,
on the first day of the first month,
he again sacrificed at Wénzǔ,
and then ascended the imperial throne.
This shows that the Yú clan did not alter the Táng temple,
but continued to use the old palace.
It is appropriate to follow the precedent of the Yú clan,
and use the Wèi temple.”
The memorial was approved.

Thereupon, posthumous sacrifices were offered to the General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn), the Prefect of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Fǔjūn), the Prefect of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān Fǔjūn), and the Prefect of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Fǔjūn),
forming, with Emperor Xuān, Emperor Jǐng, and Emperor Wén, three *zhāo* and three *mù* generations.
At this time, Emperor Xuān had not yet been enshrined,
and the position of Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) was vacant.
Therefore, sacrifices were offered to six generations,
making seven temples with Emperor Jǐng.
This rite was based on Wáng Sù’s (Wáng Sù) teachings.
In the seventh month,
an edict was again issued, saying:
“The officials previously proposed
to use the old Wèi temple,
which indeed has a precedent.
However, in reverently serving the divine spirits,
my feelings are still uneasy.
It is proper to undertake new construction.”
Thereupon, the ancestral temple was rebuilt.
In the eleventh month,
Emperor Jǐng’s lady, Lady Xiàhóu, was posthumously honored as Empress Jǐnghuái.
Rèn Mào (Rèn Mào) argued that when Lady Xiàhóu first married into the family,
the imperial enterprise had not yet been established.
The Emperor did not follow this advice.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
Princess Língshòu (Língshòu Gōngzhǔ) was enshrined in the Grand Temple,
a precedent unseen in the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties.
Emperor Míng of Wèi, however, had separately established a temple for Princess Píngyuán (Píngyuán Zhǔ),
and Jìn was different from Wèi.
In the sixth year,
due to the collapse of the temple,
it was to be renovated and rebuilt.
The assembled ministers again deliberated and presented, saying:
“In ancient times, the seven temples had separate locations;
it is appropriate to follow the rites.”
The edict again stated:
“Although anciently there were seven temples,
since recent times, all have been a single temple with seven chambers.
This does not violate the rites,
and it is more convenient.
It is also appropriate for the times.
Therefore, it should remain as it is.”
By the tenth year,
it was finally rebuilt inside Xuānyáng Gate (Xuānyángmén),
achieving the utmost grandeur and beauty.
However, the arrangement of the chambers remained as it was initially.
When the temple was completed,
the Emperor, following Zhì Yú’s (Zhì Yú) proposal,
led the hundred officials in moving the spirit tablets to the new temple.
From the General Who Conquers the West downwards,
their chariots, attire, and retinues all followed the etiquette due to emperors.
When Emperor Wǔ died, the General Who Conquers the West was moved out.
When Emperor Huì died, Yùzhāng was again moved out.

During Emperor Huì’s reign, Crown Prince Mǐnhuái (Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ) and his two sons, the Crown Grandson Āi (Āi Tàisūn) Zhāng and the Crown Grandson Chōng (Chōng Tàisūn) Shàng, were all enshrined in the temple.
During Emperor Yuán’s reign, Crown Prince Shāng (Shāng Tàizǐ) of Emperor Huái was also enshrined in the temple,
known as the “Four Young Deaths of the Inner Chambers” (Yīnshì Sìshāng).
At the beginning of Emperor Huái’s reign,
Empress Yáng of Emperor Wǔ was posthumously given the imperial title Empress Wǔdào (Wǔdào Huánghòu),
reburied beside Jùnyáng Ling (Jùnyáng Líng),
and separately worshipped in the Hóngxùn Palace (Hóngxùn Gōng),
not listed in the ancestral temple.
After Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he succeeded Emperor Wǔ,
treating Emperor Wǔ as his great ancestor,
similar to Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn succeeding Emperor Yuán (Yuándì) in ancient times.
At this time,
the spirit tablets in the Western Capital (Xījīng) were buried and destroyed by the barbarians.
In Jiāngzuǒ, new temples were built,
all newly constructed.
Soon after, when Emperor Huái’s tablet was enshrined,
Yǐngchuān was again moved out.
Although there were seven chambers,
in reality there were five generations,
presumably following Diāo Xié’s (Diāo Xié) view of counting brothers as generations.
At that time, everything was in its initial stages,
and the old rites were not fully prepared.
Destroyed tablets were temporarily placed in separate chambers.
By the first month, on the day *yǐmǎo*, in the third year of Tàixīng,
an edict stated:
“Although I succeed Emperor Shìzǔ,
I faced Emperors Huái and Mǐn and declared myself a subject.
Now when sacrificing at the Grand Temple,
I do not personally hold the wine vessels,
but instead have officials perform the rites,
which is unsettling both in sentiment and rite.
It should be handled according to the rites.”
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) deliberated:
“Now His Majesty succeeds Emperor Wǔ,
and should follow the precedent of Emperor Shìzǔ of Hàn,
not personally holding the wine vessels.”
It also stated:
“Now the Emperor succeeds Emperor Wǔ,
but the *zhāo* and *mù* generations in the temple are only four.
Former Grand Minister of Ceremonies Hè Xún (Hè Xún) and Erudite Fù Chún (Fù Chún)
both believed that Emperors Huì, Huái, and Mǐn
should have separate temples established.
However, your humble subject believes that the temple chambers should be limited by the number of tablets they can accommodate,
without being restricted by a fixed number.
In the Yīn dynasty, there were two ancestors and three founders.
If restricted to seven chambers,
then only the great ancestor would be sacrificed to.
Extrapolating from this argument,
it is appropriate to restore Yùzhāng and Yǐngchuān,
to complete the rites of the seven temples.”
Wēn Jiǎo (Wēn Jiǎo), the Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Chángshǐ), deliberated:
“The saying that brothers do not enter each other’s temples
is not a matter of ritual texts.
Moreover, Emperor Guāngwǔ rose up with a sword,
did not formalize his claim through Emperor Xiàopíng,
and strove to divinize his deeds
to fulfill the prophecy of nine generations.
Also, in antiquity, temples were not shared,
hence they were separately established.
Now, if we speak of His Majesty’s formal claim,
it differs from Emperor Guāngwǔ’s situation.
Personally offering sacrifices
is both correct according to the classics
and comforting to one’s feelings.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies constantly desires to restore the two prefects
to complete the seven generations,
which Jiǎo believes is proper.”
Wáng Dǎo (Wáng Dǎo), the General of Agile Cavalry, agreed with Jiǎo’s deliberation.
Jiǎo also said:
“For those who are not sons,
one can simply say ‘Emperor (name) dares to address Emperor (name)’.
Also, if one considers one emperor as one generation,
then the great ancestor would not be sacrificed to,
which would be inferior to commoners.”
The Emperor followed Jiǎo’s deliberation
and implemented all of it.
Thereupon, a new system was established,
restoring Yùzhāng and Yǐngchuān to their *zhāo* and *mù* positions,
to conform to Emperor Huì’s succession to Emperor Wǔ.
Emperors Huì, Huái, and Mǐn, however, followed the Spring and Autumn Annals’ principle of honoring the exalted,
and remained in the temple without being replaced.
When Emperor Yuán died,
Yùzhāng was again moved out.
However, Emperor Yuán’s divine tablet was still below Emperor Mǐn,
thus there were ten chambers.
When Emperor Míng died,
Yǐngchuān was again moved out,
still ten chambers.
At that time, the Grand Temple was extended,
so the tablets of the three moved individuals were all returned to the western side storage,
named *tiāo*,
to serve as distant temples.
In the fifth month of the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
the spirit tablet of Empress Wǔdào was first made,
enshrined in the temple,
and offered sacrifices alongside Emperor Shìzǔ.
When Emperor Chéng died, Emperor Kāng succeeded to the throne.
As brothers were considered one generation,
Jīngzhào was not moved out,
making eleven chambers in total.
When Emperor Kāng崩 (bēng),
Emperor Mù立 (lì).
In the seventh month of the second year of Yǒnghé,
the relevant officials memorialized:
“For the Yīn祭 (jì) in the tenth month,
the Jīngzhào Fǔjūn當 (dāng) should be moved to the tiāo室 (shì) [storage chamber].
In the past, the three Fǔjūn of Zhēngxī, Yùzhāng, and Yǐngchuān had their spirit tablets destroyed (huǐ zhǔ),
and at the beginning of the Central Revival, they were temporarily placed in the tiānfǔ [imperial treasury],
to the west of the temple gate.
In the Xiánkāng (Xiánkāng) period,
Tàicháng Féng Huái (Féng Huái) submitted a memorial asking to restore them to the west side chamber (xī chú jiā shì),
calling it a tiāo [ancillary shrine].
We suspect this was also not in accordance with ritual.
Now, the Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào) is to be moved in,
making him the fourth-generation distant ancestor (sì shì yuǎn zǔ),
who would long be above the Tàizǔ.
In ancient times, when the Tàizǔ of the Zhōu (Zhōu) house was too distant,
he was moved to a designated place.
Now, in the Jìn (Jìn) ancestral temple, Xuānhuáng (Xuānhuáng) is the principal (zhǔ),
and four ancestors reside there,
which means the ancestors are made to yield to their descendants.
The Yīn xiá [grand triennial sacrifice] being held above [Xuānhuáng]
means replacing the Tàizǔ.”
The Supervising Sītú Cài Mó (Cài Mó) deliberated:
“The four Fǔjūn (Fǔjūn) should have a separate chamber built.
If this cannot be accomplished immediately,
they should be placed within the chambers of the Tàimiào.
No one dares to humble their ancestors;
Wén Wǔ (Wén Wǔ) did not precede Bù Qū (Bù Qū).
On the day of the Yīn (Yīn) sacrifice,
Zhēngxī (Zhēngxī) faces east,
placed above Xuānhuáng (Xuānhuáng).
Thereafter, the spirit tablets moved from the temple
are stored in the tiāo (tiāo) of Zhēngxī (Zhēngxī),
and the sacrificial offerings are not interrupted.”
The Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Féng Huái (Féng Huái) deliberated:
“According to ritual,
for those without a temple, an altar is erected for sacrifice.
A separate chamber can be built to store them,
and for the Yīn dì [quinquennial sacrifice], they are sacrificed at the altar.”
The Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Qiáo Wáng Sīmǎ Wújí (Sīmǎ Wújí), and others deliberated:
“Various scholars say that the spirit tablets of Tàiwáng (Tàiwáng) and Wáng Jì (Wáng Jì) were moved
and stored in the tiāo (tiāo) of Wén Wǔ (Wén Wǔ).
If this is the case,
the Fǔjūn’s (Fǔjūn) moved spirit tablets should be within Emperor Xuān’s (Xuān) temple.
However, there is no ancestral sleeping chamber (qǐnshì) now,
so it is appropriate to adapt and build a new one.
Moreover, for the Yīn xiá (Yīn xiá) in the Tàimiào (Tàimiào),
Zhēngxī (Zhēngxī) faces east.”
Shàngshū Láng Sūn Chuò (Sūn Chuò) agreed with Wújí’s (Wújí) deliberation,
saying:
“Although the Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ) began with the highest position of the Numinous Number Nine,
his way was to be accommodating,
to forgo the honor of human rank,
and to uphold the principle of natural kinship,
thereby establishing the foundation of teaching and glorifying hundreds of generations.”
Shàngshū Láng Xú Chán (Xú Chán) deliberated:
“The ritual says, ‘Removing the tiāo (tiāo) makes an altar;
removing the altar makes a cleared ground (shàn)’;
they are sacrificed to during the annual xiá (xiá).
Now, the four ancestors’ moved spirit tablets
can be stored in a stone chamber,
and when there is a prayer, they are sacrificed to at the altar or cleared ground.”
Chán (Chán) was also sent to Kuàijī (Kuàijī)
to consult the recluse Yú Xǐ (Yú Xǐ).
Xǐ (Xǐ) replied:
“During the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, Wéi Xuánchéng (Wéi Xuánchéng) and others buried the destroyed spirit tablets in the imperial garden.
The Wèi (Wèi) court deliberated that they should be buried between the two steps.
Furthermore, spirit tablets were originally in the Tàimiào (Tàimiào);
if they are now to be sacrificed in a separate chamber,
it would be better to store them permanently.
Moreover, the four lords have no ritual of posthumous titles,
which further indicates they should be destroyed and not sacrificed to.”
At this time, Jiǎnwén (Jiǎnwén) was Fǔjūn (Fǔjūn) and, along with Shàngshū Láng Liú Shào (Liú Shào) and others, memorialized:
“The four ancestors reside together in the western tiāo (tiāo),
with their spirit tablets stored in a stone chamber,
and are sacrificed to only during the dì xiá (dì xiá),
following the old custom of previous dynasties.”
At that time, Fàn Xuān’s (Fàn Xuān) nephew from Chénliú (Chénliú) asked about this ritual,
and Xuān (Xuān) replied:
“Those sacrificed in Shùn’s (Shùn) temple
were all commoners.
When their descendants became distant and their tablets were destroyed,
they were not placed above Shùn (Shùn)
and were not arranged according to zhāomù [generations].
Now, the titles of the four lords still follow their original ones;
they are not honored for their accomplishments or virtues.
If we follow the burial of Yú (Yú) spirit tablets,
they would still be stored where their descendants are.
If we follow the burial of Xià (Xià) spirit tablets,
it would not be the steps of the main temple.
It is appropriate to consider a change:
build a single chamber.
