While kinship is not yet exhausted, they would be placed above Emperor Xuān (Xuān) during the dì xiá (dì xiá);
when kinship is exhausted, there is no reason for them to be placed below among the descendants.”
Thereafter, Tàicháng Liú Xiá (Liú Xiá) and others agreed with Cài Mó’s (Cài Mó) deliberation.
Bóshì Zhāng Píng (Zhāng Píng) deliberated:
“Some suspect that those placed before the Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ)
are all the destroyed spirit tablets of his descendants.
Píng (Píng) examines ancient texts and finds no distinction between earlier and later.
Yǔ (Yǔ) did not precede Gǔn (Gǔn),
so what doubt is there in moving the spirit tablets to a place above the Tàizǔ (Tàizǔ)?”
Thus, Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào) was moved into the western side chamber (xī chú),
together called a tiāo (tiāo),
following the ritual of moving the spirit tablets of the previous three ancestors.
Therefore, the main chambers remained eleven.
When Emperor Mù (Mù) died, Emperor Āi (Āi) and Hǎixī (Hǎixī) were brothers,
and there was no one to ascend or succeed.
At the beginning of Xián'ān (Xián'ān),
Emperor Jiǎnwén (Jiǎnwén) succeeded Yuánhuáng (Yuánhuáng),
and the generations advanced in rank.
Thus, the two spirit tablets of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān) and Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào) returned to their zhāomù (zhāomù) positions.
When Jiǎnwén (Jiǎnwén) died,
Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān) was moved again.
In the twelfth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ, in the fifth month, on the day of Rénxū,
an edict stated:
“When the Grand Ancestral Temple was first built,
everything was done with frugality.
The position for the Grand Ancestor was left vacant,
and the Míngtáng has not yet been constructed.
The suburban sacrifice is a great affair of the state,
yet the ancient system is incomplete.
This should be deliberated upon in detail.”
Xú Mò, the Lángzhōng of the Ministry of Rites, deliberated:
“For the suburban sacrifice at the Yuánqiū,
the classics allow no two ways.
Emperor Xuān once debated this principle
and verified it with the sacred canons.
Down to the restoration,
it was thoroughly researched and examined,
thus establishing the northern and southern suburban altars,
which indeed cannot be lightly altered by other doctrines.
I suggest adhering to the old system for security.”
“Emperor Wǔ established temples for six generations,
three Zhāo and three Mù ancestors.
Emperor Xuān, the founder of the dynasty,
is truly the Grand Ancestor,
and personally, the royal paternal grandfather.
The four ancestral tablets are above,
not yet having been moved out by generational transfer,
so the eastward-facing position was temporarily left vacant.
Brothers succeeding each other
does not constitute two generations.
Therefore, for the current temple sacrifices,
the number of generations is not yet sufficient.
If one wishes for the Grand Ancestor to assume the proper position,
it would violate the principle of 'serving seven'.”
“Moreover, the Rites state that a common son who becomes king also offers the Dì sacrifice to his ancestor and establishes a temple.
This refers to a collateral descendant who is enthroned,
in which case the close relatives must be restored.
The Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào is now six generations removed.
It is appropriate to restore this chamber,
meaning Emperor Xuān is not yet above the six generations.
Only after the earlier generations have been moved out
can the Grand Ancestor's position be settled.
When the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào is moved out and his tablet destroyed,
it should be buried in a stone chamber,
even if the Dì and Xiá sacrifices would not include him.
Why?
The commentary says that a destroyed tablet is 'raised' and 'joined' with the Grand Ancestor.
'Raised' is a term indicating ascending from below,
not descending from a place of honor to a lower one.
The Crown Prince and the Grandson of the Crown Prince,
as well as the four tablets in the inner chamber,
due to the importance of the heir apparent,
are raised to be associated with the imperial ancestor.
The temples they are associated with,
being distant in generations, should be moved out.
Then, the grandsons who enjoy the sacrificial offerings
are destroyed along with them.”
“The principles of the square and round forms of the Míngtáng
have already been established;
it is inappropriate to omit the sacrifice to the associated emperor.
Furthermore, a king considers all under heaven his home,
not necessarily a single state.
Thus, King Píng of Zhōu and Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn did not abolish the two capitals.
The deities to be associated with the Míngtáng
have accumulated doubts and cannot be clarified.
According to the Yì Jīng, 'Yīn offered sacrifices to Shàngdì,
and associated the ancestors.'
If ancestors are associated together,
then Shàngdì is also Heaven,
and the principle of revering the father is manifest.
Those who offered Lǚ sacrifice to Shàngdì in the Rítuals of Zhōu,
when there was an important matter, announced it to Heaven.
This used the same four ceremonial jade tablets as the regular suburban sacrifice,
hence they are mentioned together.
If Shàngdì were the Five Emperors,
why would the classic text not say 'sacrifice to Heaven and Lǚ to the Five Emperors,'
or 'sacrifice to Earth and Lǚ to the Four Sights'?”
Shìzhōng Chē Yìn agreed with this deliberation.
He further stated:
“The system of the Míngtáng
is already difficult to ascertain in detail.
Moreover, music emphasizes harmony,
and ritual emphasizes reverence.
Therefore, the plain and ornate differ,
and musical instruments also vary.
Since thatched huts and grand halls
do not share a single standard,
why must one cling to their specific forms
and not broadly follow the fundamental principles and adapt to customs?
When the nine regions are all peaceful,
and there is no dust in Hèshuò,
then the Míngtáng and Pìyōng can be exalted and repaired.”
At that time, the court deliberations mostly concurred,
so it was carried out,
without any changes.
In the sixteenth year,
the Grand Ancestral Temple hall was first rebuilt.
The main chamber had fourteen bays,
with one storage bay each to the east and west,
totaling sixteen bays.
The ridgepole was eight *zhàng* and four *chǐ* high.
The imperial carriage was fully prepared to move the spirit tablets to the temporary temple.
The four tablets of the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào and the Crown Prince and Grandson of the Crown Prince were brought, each using the ceremonial attire appropriate to their status.
The four tablets did not follow the imperial ritual,
which differed from the Tàikāng era.
After all the tablets entered the temple,
offerings of dried meat and pickles were laid out.
When the new temple was completed,
the spirit tablets returned to their chambers,
and offerings of dried meat and pickles were again laid out.
In the nineteenth year, in the second month,
Emperor Jiǎnwén’s mother, Concubine Zhèng of Kuàijī, was posthumously honored as Empress Xuān, mother of Emperor Jiǎnwén,
and a temple was erected for her west of the Grand Ancestral Temple path.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào was again moved out,
following the precedent of the four Tíao during Emperor Mù’s reign.
In the ninth year of Yìxī, in the fourth month,
when the Yīn sacrifice was about to be performed,
an edict called for broad deliberation on the rites of moving out and destroying tablets.
Dà Sīmǎ Lángyá Wáng Déwén deliberated:
“At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
the position for the Grand Ancestor was left vacant.
And due to sentiment, it extended far back,
up to the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào.
Therefore, when the generations ended, they should have been destroyed,
and Emperor Xuān should have rightly occupied the Grand Ancestor’s position.
Furthermore, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn moved the tablets of eleven emperors to Luòyì,
meaning destroyed tablets were not set up;
the principle can be inferred.
It is appropriate to construct a separate chamber
to house the tablets of the four Grand Administrators,
to be stored permanently without sacrifice.”
Dà Sīnóng Xú Guǎng deliberated:
“The four Grand Administrators once held the foremost position in the temple hall,
receiving sacrifices from all under heaven.
If they were to be buried in the netherworld,
it might not fully satisfy emotional and rational considerations.
I suggest they be moved and stored in the western repository,
to serve as distant Tíao,
and the Dì and Xiǎng sacrifices would be permanently cut off.”
Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn Yuán Bào deliberated:
“Adhering to the old system without change,
the Yīn sacrifice would still reach the four Grand Administrators,
which is emotionally and rationally acceptable.”
At that time, Liú Yù served as regent,
and his opinion was the same as that of the Dà Sīmǎ.
He waited until the next Yīn sacrifice to implement the change.
However, Emperor Ān died,
and before the Dì sacrifice could be performed, his imperial mandate ended.
In the fifth year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ, in the eleventh month, on the day of Jǐyǒu,
Empress Dowager Yáng, who was Hóngxùn, died.
Sacrifices in the ancestral temples ceased for a time.
Music was removed from the Heaven, Earth, and Míngtáng sacrifices,
and the sacrificial meat was not offered.
In the fifth year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù, in the eleventh month, on the day of Jǐmǎo,
the Yīn sacrifice was held,
but no music was played after the Emperor's demise.
In the eleventh year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ, in the ninth month,
an imperial daughter died.
When the Zhēng sacrifice was due,
Zhōngshū Shìláng Fàn Zòu stated:
“According to the Commentary on Mourning Garments, if someone dies in the palace, sacrifices are not offered for three months,
without distinguishing between old and young, or noble and humble.
Although the imperial daughter was an infant,
I humbly find this questionable.”
Therefore, the Shàngshū submitted a memorial asking the Three Ducal Ministers to perform the rites.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ, in the fourth month,
when the Emperor was about to personally perform the sacrifice,
he drove to inspect the sacrificial animals in the evening,
but the ceremonial protocol did not require him to bow upon return.
An edict inquired about the reason,
and the Bóshì reported that it had been inherited thus through successive generations.
The Emperor said:
“This is not a ritual of utmost reverence for the ancestral temple.”
Therefore, he actually bowed and returned,
and this was established as a rule:
one must personally attend and bow when inspecting the sacrificial animals in the evening.
However, since the Jiāngzuǒ era, this practice ceased again.
According to the old system of Wèi,
the Son of Heaven had a secondary hall north-east of the temple hall,
and entered through the north gate.
According to the new ritual,
the secondary hall was set up to the right outside the central south gate,
and the Son of Heaven entered through the south gate.
Zhì Yú believed:
“The secondary hall is a place for rest.
Generally, approaching a place of honor requires reverence through inconspicuousness,
and compliance through hidden entry.
Setting it up in a superior position
and entering through the south gate
does not embody the principle of humility and restraint.
It is appropriate to establish the new ritual
to follow the old说法.”
This was adopted.
According to ritual,
for major affairs, one would report to the ancestral temple (zǔní 祖禰);
for minor affairs, one would report specifically to the father’s temple (ní 禰).
This practice had long been abolished during the Qín 秦 and Hàn 漢 dynasties.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Huángchū 黃初 (223 CE), during the reign of Emperor Wén of Wèi 魏文帝,
when he was about to embark on an eastern tour,
as a large army was to be dispatched,
he ordered the Grand Astrologer (Tàicháng 太常) to report to the Southern Suburb (Nánjiāo 南郊) with a special ox.
When Emperor Wén 文帝 later passed away,
the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉) was again ordered to report the posthumous title (shì cè 諡策) to the Southern Suburb.
From then until the Jìn 晉 dynasty, this practice was inherited;
after reporting to the suburb, they would still report to the temple.
This ritual was abolished in the Jiāngzuǒ 江左 (Eastern Jìn 晉) period.
In the third year of Xiánhé 咸和 (328 CE), during the reign of Emperor Chéng 成帝,
when Sū Jùn 蘇峻 caused chaos and overthrew the capital,
Wēn Jiào 溫嶠 and others established a temporary ancestral temple (xíngmiào 行廟) at Báishí 白石,
and revived this ceremony.
They reported to the former ruler and empress, saying:
“The rebellious minister Sū Jùn 蘇峻
overturned the state (shèjì 社稷),
destroyed and abandoned the three uprights (sān zhèng 三正),
and disgraced all within the four seas.
Your ministers Kǎn 侃, Jiào 嶠, Liàng 亮, and others personally slew the chieftain of the barbarians (róng shǒu 戎首),
and respectfully carried out the celestial punishment.
We pray that the spirits of Emperor Zhōngzōng Yuán 中宗元, Emperor Sùzǔ Míng 肅祖明, and Empress Míngmù 明穆
will look down upon the guilty,
cut short their lives,
and exterminate these numerous evildoers,
thereby bringing peace to the ancestral temples.
Though your ministers may perish and be dismembered,
we shall yet live for many years.”
In the third year of Tàihé 太和 (229 CE), Emperor Míng of Wèi 魏明帝
issued an edict, stating:
“According to ritual,
if a queen has no heir,
a collateral son is chosen and established
to continue the main lineage (dàzōng 大宗).
Then he must inherit the legitimate succession (zhèngtǒng 正統) and uphold public righteousness;
how can he again consider his private relations?
Emperor Xuān of Hàn 漢宣繼 succeeded Emperor Zhāo 昭帝,
and bestowed the imperial title upon his deceased father (dàokǎo 悼考).
Emperor Āi 哀帝 was supported and established from a collateral branch (wàifān 外藩),
yet Dǒng Hóng 董宏 and others cited the defunct Qín 秦 dynasty,
confused and misled the court discussions,
and consequently honored the reverent emperor (Gōng Huáng 恭皇)
and established a temple for him in the capital.
They also favored the concubines of the feudal lords (fān qiè 藩妾),
making them comparable to the Empress Dowager (Chángxìn 長信),
an act of presumptuousness and lack of ritual,
which neither gods nor men would bless.
This was not due to the fault of Master Shī Dān 師丹's loyal and upright remonstrance,
but led to the calamity of Dīng Fù 丁傅's burning.
Thereafter,
this practice was followed in succession.
Let the dukes, ministers, and relevant officials
take deep warning from previous generations.
Should a future heir, by chance, enter the great succession from among the feudal lords,
he must clearly understand the principle of being an adopted heir.
Anyone who dares to be cunning and wicked, flatter the ruler above,
and presumptuously establish an illegitimate title,
calling a father 'Emperor' (huáng 皇)
and a mother 'Empress' (hòu 后),
shall be executed without pardon by the chief ministers.
This shall be inscribed on golden tablets (jīncè 金策)
and stored in the ancestral temple.”
After this, when Gāoguì 高貴 and Chángdào 常道 were enthroned,
none were externally honored.
In the fourth year of Jiànxīng 建興 (316 CE), during the reign of Emperor Mǐn 愍帝,
Sītú Liáng Fēn 司徒梁芬 proposed a ritual for posthumous honors,
but the Emperor did not follow it.
The Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zuǒ Púyè 左僕射) Suǒ Qín 索綝 and others also cited the Wèi 魏 system,
considering it unacceptable.
Therefore, the King of Wú 吳王 was only posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàibǎo 太保).
In the second year of Tàixīng 太興 (319 CE), during the reign of Emperor Yuán 元帝,
the relevant officials suggested that Lángxié Gōng Wáng 琅邪恭王 should be called 'Imperial Deceased Father' (huángkǎo 皇考).
Hè Xún 賀循 argued, saying:
“According to the meaning of ritual canons,
a son must not use his own rank to add to his father’s title.”
The Emperor again followed this.
Collation Notes:
Volume 10, Rites (Lǐ 禮).
Among the five categories of rites,
the second is mourning (xiōng 凶).
From the Son of Heaven to the common people,
their bodies, hair, and skin
are received from their parents.
Since their principle is the same,
their emotions are also equal.
They are nourished in life
and mourned in death.
Therefore, the three-year mourning period
is a universally understood ritual.
According to Hàn 漢 rites,
when the Son of Heaven passed away,
from the time of illness to his demise and burial,
the regulations for mourning
differed from those of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài 三代).
From Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉 onwards,
the general framework was similar to Hàn 漢.
However, since Emperor Wén of Hàn 漢文 reformed the mourning ritual system,
later generations followed it,
and the three-year mourning rite was no longer observed.
When Wèi Wǔ 魏武 was nearing death,
he left a will:
“The world is not yet settled,
so ancient practices cannot be followed.
Among the officials who are to attend the palace hall,
fifteen will mourn aloud,
and after the burial, mourning will cease.
Those commanding troops and stationed in garrisons
are not to leave their posts.”
Wèi Wǔ 魏武 passed away on the day of gēngzǐ 庚子 in the first month,
was immediately interred on xīncǎo 辛丑,
and buried on dīngmǎo 丁卯 of the same month.
This means it did not exceed one month.
When Emperor Xuān (宣帝) and Emperor Jǐng (景帝) passed away,
their funerals both followed provisional regulations.
When Emperor Wén (文帝) passed away,
the country mourned for three days.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) also followed the precedents of the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
removing mourning attire after burial.
However, he still wore deep mourning robes and plain caps,
lowered his seat, and reduced his meals.

Grand Chancellor Sīmǎ Fú (司馬孚), Grand Tutor Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖), Grand Guardian Wáng Xiáng (王祥), Grand Commandant Hé Céng (何曾), Minister of Works and concurrently Central Leader of the Army Sīmǎ Wàng (司馬望), Minister of Works Xún Yǐ (荀顗), General of Chariots and Cavalry Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), Prefect of the Masters of Writing Péi Xiù (裴秀), Assistant Prefect of the Masters of Writing Wǔ Gāi (武陔), Protector-General Guō Jiàn (郭建), Palace Attendant Guō Suí (郭綏), Central Secretariat Director Xún Xù (荀勖), Central Army General Yáng Hù (羊祜), and others memorialized, saying:
"Your servants have heard that the rites and regulations
should be adapted to the times,
and that the Yú (虞), Xià (夏), Shāng (商), and Zhōu (周) dynasties
did not follow each other's practices,
which certainly had its reasons.
The Great Jìn (晉) dynasty inherits from Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏),
with some changes and some continuations,
aiming only to be sufficient to promote transformation,
thus it has not yet been able to fully revert to ancient simplicity
and conform to the practices of high antiquity.
Your Majesty has already humbly followed the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) precedents of reduced mourning,
to manage current affairs,
and yet personally practices great filial piety,
with feelings exceeding normal grief.
Wearing plain caps and deep mourning robes,
lowering your seat and reducing your meals,
though Wǔ Dīng (武丁) did so in the Yīn (殷) era,
and Zēng (曾) and Mǐn (閔) did so as commoners,
it cannot be surpassed.
At present, Jīngmán (荊蠻) is not yet pacified,
and various government affairs are not yet settled.
The myriad affairs of state are pressing,
and every action taxes your mind.
How can Your Majesty have the leisure to fully pursue your sacred will
and follow your utmost feelings?
Your servants believe Your Majesty should restrain your feelings to stabilize the times and assist the populace.
Therefore, we urge you to order the imperial wardrobe to change your clothes,
the inner attendants to restore your seat,
the imperial kitchen to restore your meals,
and all other ongoing practices
to revert to the old regulations."
The edict said:
"Whenever I contemplate the departed in the netherworld,
and am unable to wear the full mourning attire of rough hemp for the rest of my days,
to preserve this pain,
how can I eat fine rice and wear splendid clothes?
This truly pierces and agitates my heart,
and is not a way to console myself.
I am originally from a family of scholars,
where the rites have been passed down for a long time.
How can I bear to suddenly change these feelings for my heaven-sent father?
You have already followed me a great deal;
please try to review Confucius's reply to Zǎi Wǒ (宰我),
and do not cause further commotion.
Speaking of this brings intense sorrow.
Alas!
Alas!"
Fú (孚) and others submitted another memorial:
"We humbly read Your Majesty's sacred edict,
and are filled with sorrow.
We recall how Zhòngní (仲尼) suppressed Zǎi Wǒ's (宰我) question,
and how Your Majesty's sacred thoughts cannot cease,
which is profoundly deep and sincere.
However, at present, weapons have not been sheathed,
military affairs have not ceased,
the myriad affairs of state are of utmost importance,
and the people of the world are exceedingly numerous.
Your Majesty, with the dignity of ten thousand chariots,
observes the rites of a commoner,
sits on a rough mat,
drinks water, and eats coarse food.
Deep sorrow fills you internally,
and emaciation shows externally.
Yet, you personally diligently attend to the myriad affairs of state,
sitting until dawn,
humbling yourself to receive your subordinates,
and are too busy to eat.
The effort expended is thus exceedingly great.
Therefore, your servants are filled with apprehension and unrest,
sincerely fearing that your vital spirit will be damaged,
thereby jeopardizing the great affairs of state.
We have already ordered the relevant officials
to restore your seat and revert to normal,
following the old regulations.
We humbly request Your Majesty to consider and accept our foolish sincerity,
to comfort the heart of the Empress Dowager."
Another edict said:
"Upon reviewing the memorial again,
my grief intensifies,
and I cannot control myself.
Alas!
Alas!
The three-year mourning period
has been the accepted rite since ancient times.
Truly, the sages established the central principle based on human feelings,
acting with enlightened empathy.
With the divine spirit becoming more distant each day,
I have nowhere to express my grief.
Even if my feelings are shallow,
eating delicious food and wearing beautiful clothes
is unbearable.
It is improper to repeatedly argue,
further wounding my heart.
My words are cut short.
Alas!
Alas!"
The Emperor thus observed this rite for the full three years.
Later, when mourning for the Empress Dowager, he did the same.
In the eighth month of the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
an edict said:
"This upper ten-day period
is the day the late emperor left the world,
marking the completion of a full year.
How can I, the desolate one,
ever again experience the feelings of a son?
My thoughts and longing are intensely painful.
I wish to visit the imperial mausoleum to pay my respects,
to fully express my sorrow and indignation.
Let the relevant officials make preparations for the journey."
Grand Chancellor Prince Ānpíng Fú (安平王孚), Prefect of the Masters of Writing Péi Xiù (裴秀), Assistant Prefect of the Masters of Writing Wǔ Gāi (武陔), and others memorialized:
"Your Majesty's utmost filial piety is profoundly evident,
and your grief and sorrow are boundless.
Although the rough hemp mourning attire has been removed,
your sorrowful emaciation and coarse diet
have harmed your vital harmony.
Though it is now autumn,
there is still lingering heat.
Visiting the mountain mausoleum
will cause immense grief and emotional damage.
Your subordinates secretly hold their breath in apprehension,
believing that Your Majesty should restrain your sacred feelings,
to comfort the myriad nations."
The edict said:
"My loneliness has endured,
and a full year has passed.
My pain, longing, and anguish
will never be assuaged.
I wish to pay respects at the mountain mausoleum,
to express my sorrow and indignation.
My physical condition is fine.
Moreover, it has already cooled down.
I will depart soon,
and cannot follow what is proposed in your memorial.
Let the relevant officials make preparations for the journey immediately."
Another edict said:
"Emperor Wén (漢文) did not compel the whole world to mourn fully,
which also demonstrated the utmost humility of an emperor.
When I see the mountain mausoleum,
how can I be without mourning attire?
Let me wear rough hemp mourning attire for the journey."
Fú (孚) and others submitted another memorial, saying:
"Your servants have heard that in high antiquity, there was no fixed mourning period,
and later generations gradually established mourning for specific months and years.
Emperor Wén (漢文帝), in accordance with the spirit of the times,
decreed a shorter mourning period,
which was passed down to later generations.
Your Majesty, considering the importance of the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temples,
and the welfare of the myriad regions and countless people,
has already followed provisional regulations,
removed the rough hemp mourning attire,
and your officials and the populace are in celebratory attire.
Now, to visit the mausoleum
in sorrowful longing,
if you were to add rough hemp mourning attire,
it would be inconsistent with your previous actions.
We dare not comply with the edict."
The edict said:
"I also know it is not merely about this hemp cloth.
However, a son's feelings
wish for objects of sorrow and mourning to be on his person;
this is close to human nature.
Let the officials act according to the old regulations themselves."
Fú (孚) and others again memorialized:
"Your servants have heard that when sages create institutions,
they must follow what is appropriate for the times.
Thus, the Five Emperors had different music,
and the Three Kings had different rites.
This is why ancient and modern times differ,
and why simplicity and refinement are used alternately.
Your Majesty, in accordance with what is appropriate for the times,
has already humbled your heart and restrained yourself,
and acceded to provisional regulations.
Since rough hemp mourning attire has been removed,
and you observe the rites of inner mourning,
to now resume mourning attire
would have no basis in principle.
If the ruler wears mourning attire while the subjects do not,
we would not dare to feel at ease.
The discussion should follow the previous memorial."
The edict said:
"My concern is that my feelings cannot fully reach [the departed],
what do clothes matter?
Gentlemen, your utmost diligence,
how can I casually oppose it?"
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
The officials concerned memorialized:
"According to the precedents of previous dynasties,
a white silk canopy, mat, and plain couch are set up within the mourning hut,
and a cloth-wrapped clod of earth is used.
Chariots, palanquins, and small calf-carts are all adorned with silk streamers."
An imperial edict did not permit this,
ordering only that the carts be covered with plain cloth,
and that the other mourning rituals
should not deviate from the established rites.
The officials concerned again memorialized:
"The late Empress Dowager is to be interred on the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month.
According to precedent,
one wears mourning clothes for the Yú ritual [the third day after burial]
and removes them after the Yú.
All civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, shall attend the morning and evening mourning rituals,
and after His Majesty has removed his mourning clothes,
each shall return to their assigned post and remove their mourning clothes."
The imperial edict said:
"The three-year mourning period
is a universal principle of the realm.
To receive a lifetime of love
and yet offer no years in return,
how can one immediately return to auspiciousness after burial?
My heart cannot bear it."
The officials concerned again memorialized:
"The world has its times of danger and ease,
the Dao has its high and low points.
The circumstances one encounters differ,
and there are indeed reasons for this,
not a disregard for ritual.
Currently, military horses are not yet dispersed,
and state affairs are extremely pressing.
It is necessary to make decisions
to promote various achievements.
In antiquity, when King Kāng of Zhōu first ascended to the throne,
he still wore his crown and presided over court.
From the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onward,
mourning was concluded after burial.
The ritual of liàng'àn [deep mourning]
has been abolished since ancient times.
We beseech Your Majesty to set aside the system of Gāozōng [Emperor Wǔ of Hàn]
and follow what is appropriate for the present time."
The imperial edict said:
"The three-year mourning period
is for expressing deepest feelings and fulfilling rites.
To remove mourning immediately after burial
is something I cannot bear.
In my sorrowful state,
words fail me.
How can it be!
How can it be!"
The officials concerned again earnestly pleaded.
The imperial edict said:
"If one cannot be truly filial,
do not worry about causing damage to oneself [by excessive mourning].
Indeed, I know that clothing is a minor matter,
but now, thinking of the simple earth [of the grave],
to immediately replace it with auspicious items
would only deeply wound my sincere heart,
not show consideration for me.
The ritual codes of each dynasty, whether plain or elaborate, have all differed.
Why restrict us with recent regulations
and leave this profound mourning incomplete?"
The ministers again earnestly pleaded,
and the Emperor wept for a long time before finally assenting.
When Empress Wénmíng died and when Empress Wǔyuán, Lady Yáng, died,
officials and commoners throughout the realm mourned for only three days.
When Emperor Mù died,
Emperor Āi ascended the throne.
Emperor Āi was Emperor Mù's paternal cousin.
Chǔ Xīn, Emperor Mù's maternal uncle, submitted a memorial.
The Secretariat replied that the court had no such protocol,
and an imperial edict was issued for deliberation.
Shàngshū Púyè Jiāng Bīn and three others all said,
"Mǐn and Xī were brothers,
yet [Mǐn] was treated as a son, so Emperor Āi should be Emperor's heir."
Wèijūn Wáng Shù and twenty-five others said:
"Emperor Chéng did not prioritize his own kin
but passed on the heavenly mandate.
Emperor Kāng received the mandate from Xiǎozōng [Emperor Chéng].
The weight of the altars of soil and grain [the state]
has already shifted to the designated successor.
The order of succession
should follow Emperor Kāng."
Shàngshū Xiè Fèng and six others said:
"The correct line of succession
should be based on natural kinship.
Considering human sentiment,
it should follow Xiǎozōng."
The imperial edict followed the deliberation of Shù and others,
to succeed Xiǎozōng.
In the seventh month of the second year of Níngkāng,
Emperor Jiǎnwén died. Two anniversaries [of his death] encountered a leap month.
Doctor Xìe Yōu and Kǒng Càn deliberated:
"In the twelfth month, Yǐwèi day, of the twenty-eighth year of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ,
the Viscount of Chǔ died.
It was actually a leap month, but it was referred to as the twelfth month,
which means attaching the intercalary month to the preceding month.
Since mourning rituals give precedence to distant dates,
the words of Doctor Wú Shāng should be applied,
using the leap month for the xiáng [grand sacrifice]."

Shàngshū Púyè Xiè Ān, Zhōnglǐngjūn Wáng Shào, Sànqí Chángshì Zhèng Xí, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Yīn Kāng, Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Yuán Hóng, Sànqí Shìláng Yīn Mào, Zhōngshū Láng Chē Yìn, Zuǒchéng Liú Zūn, and Lìbù Láng Liú Dān all shared the same view.
Kāng said:
"If it has passed the seventh month but not yet reached the eighth month,
how can it be called 'exceeding a year'?
If there is truly uncertainty,
then one should follow the more serious interpretation."
Hóng said:
"If one were to encounter a leap twelfth month and not count it,
then the year would not be complete,
which is certainly impossible.
The Hànshū considers the leap month as a 'latter ninth month,'
indicating its integral nature."
Xí said:
"Emperor Zhōngzōng and Sùzǔ both died in leap months,
and the changes for the xiáng removal all used the month after the leap month.
The previous court still used the month after it,
and now, with the leap month attached to the seventh month,
what doubt is there in using it?
It also aligns with the saying of 'extending the feeling through distant days.'
Furthermore, a leap month is a 'later seventh' and not an eighth,
so how can there be a suspicion of 'exceeding a month'?"
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Biāozhī, Shìzhōng Wáng Hùn, Zhōngchéng Qiáo Wáng Tián, Yòuchéng Dài Mì, and others held differing views.
Biāozhī said:
"Wú Shāng was a mediocre talent and minor official,
not a renowned worthy, esteemed scholar, or high-ranking minister who served as a standard for the times.
Moreover, there is no evidence for counting the leap month;
he merely grasped the meaning of 'distant days,'
exceeding the xiáng taboo,
and taking it outside the prescribed limit,
which does not conform to the principle of considering distant dates.
Furthermore, Chancellor Huán Gōng once argued that
according to ritual, the grand sacrifice is at twenty-five months.
How can one exceed a year and count a leap month,
making it twenty-six months?"
Thereupon, they memorialized:
"Some believe that since the leap month is attached to the seventh month,
it should be used for the removal of mourning.
Others believe that although the leap month is nominally attached to the seventh month,
it is in reality a separate month of three decades,
and therefore the seventh month should be used for the removal.
We, along with Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Chōng, have carefully considered
this great ritual of the dynasty,
which should be based on the classics.
The three-year mourning period,
with the liàn [minor sacrifice] at thirteen months
and the completion [dàxiáng, grand sacrifice] at twenty-five months,
is clearly stated in the rites.
According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū,
if a leap month is within the year,
it is briefly mentioned but not counted.
It is clear that if the leap month is outside the year,
it should not be counted to exceed the grave taboo of a full year,
because the ritual system dictates that the xiáng removal must be precisely at the full month."
On the last day of Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor removed his white mourning clothes and returned to auspiciousness.
Xú Guǎng commented:
"Generally, in distinguishing meanings and examining principles,
when there is no clear evidence or explicit text to definitively decide and alter,
how can one not have doubts?
When in doubt about ritual, one follows the more serious interpretation;
for mourning, it is better to hasten to sorrow than to ease.
To align with human sentiment and adapt to circumstances
are indeed established principles.
Biāozhī was unable to cite correct interpretations
to refute others,
but merely used his position and status to overpower people.
A gentleman, though open to receiving,
has no personal preferences.
How can this be so?
The executive officials followed and implemented it,
which was probably a mistake."
Wèi Wǔ died in the first month.
Emperor Wén of Wèi, in the seventh month of that same year, arranged for entertainers and various performances,
which shows that Wèi did not abandon music due to mourning.
From Emperor Wǔ onward,
when the state experienced a grand mourning,
music was always suspended for the entire three years.
In the first year of Tàiān of Emperor Huì,
the太子 mourning had not yet concluded,
and at the Yuán Huì [New Year's court assembly], music was also suspended.
During the Yǒnghé period of Emperor Mù,
because the imperial tombs in the Central Plains had not yet been repaired,
music was suspended for the Yuán Huì for several consecutive years.
At that time, the Empress Dowager was regent.
When her father, Chǔ Póu, died,
music was also suspended for the Yuán Huì.
In the sixth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
due to the mourning for Empress Wáng,
music was also suspended.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
Tàifù Lù Shàngshū Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ deliberated:
"After the imperial burial,
marriages are permitted, but music is not to be played,
with one full year as the cutoff."
According to Han
custom, when the Grand Empress Dowager or Empress Dowager passed away,
the Chánglè Tàipú and Shǎofǔ Dàchángqiū presided over the funeral affairs.
The Sāngōng oversaw the regulations,
and all other matters followed the rites.
The Wèi and Jìn dynasties also observed the rites for the Son of Heaven.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ (274 CE),
when Empress Wǔyuán Yáng died,
and was about to be interred at Jùnyánglíng,
according to the old system,
after the burial,
the Emperor and his officials would remove their mourning clothes and resume auspicious activities.
Previously,
the Shàngshū Cíbù had reported a proposal from Dr. Zhāng Jìng,
that the Crown Prince should also follow the system and remove his mourning attire.
Dr. Chén Kuí argued,
believing
that "the current system is based on
an expedient measure by the Han emperors,
arising from particular circumstances,
not the true essence of rites.
The Crown Prince has no state affairs to manage,
and should therefore observe the full mourning period."
An edict was issued for further deliberation.
Shàngshì Dù Yù believed:
"In antiquity, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords observed the three-year mourning period, beginning with the same 'qiīzhǎn' (coarsest sackcloth).
After burial, they would remove their mourning clothes,
live in 'liàng'àn' (deep mourning),
and observe 'xīn sāng' (mourning in the heart) for the full term,
not following the same rites as commoners.
The Han dynasty inherited from the Qín,
requiring the whole realm to observe a three-year mourning period for the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Wén of Hàn, seeing that this could not be sustained indefinitely by his subjects,
and unaware of the ancient system,
instead devised a system of 'xiángdǎn' (sacrifices at the end of mourning),
removing mourning clothes immediately after the burial.
The Wèi dynasty simply took the completion of burial as the endpoint,
and succeeding rulers no longer observed 'liàng'àn' for the full term.
Scholars have long criticized this,
yet they ultimately did not thoroughly investigate the classics and commentaries,
or examine their actual practices,
insisting solely that the three-year mourning for a king
should involve wearing 'suīmá' (sackcloth) for twenty-five months.
If a succeeding ruler were to do this,
then the Emperor and all officials would not be able to remove their mourning clothes.
Although the intention is to show deep mourning,
it would be compelled and impractical.
Even today, rulers follow the lenient custom of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
because those who devised the system did not understand the system.
Now the Crown Prince shares the same body with the esteemed (Emperor),
and should revert to the ancient custom:
removing 'suīmá' after 'zúcū' (the end of wailing ritual),
and concluding the mourning period with 'liàng'àn'.
In principle, it should not be unremoved,
nor should it adopt the custom of Emperor Wén of Hàn;
this is how to deepen the mourning rites."
Thereupon, Shàngshū Púyè Lú Qīn and Shàngshū Wèi Shū asked Dù Yù for the evidence supporting his view.
Yù said:
"The commentaries state that 'the three-year mourning applies to the Son of Heaven,'
which means that the Son of Heaven observes a full year of mourning,
but only has a three-year mourning period in name.
It does not mean wearing mourning clothes for three years,
the same as commoners.
Therefore, regarding the mourning for a queen or crown prince,
Shū Xiàng stated that there were 'two three-year mourning periods.'
The Duke of Zhōu did not say that Gāozōng observed mourning for three years,
but rather 'liàng'àn' for three years;
this is a text explaining the removal of clothing and mourning in the heart.
Shū Xiàng did not criticize King Jǐng for removing his mourning clothes,
but rather for his early banqueting and revelry,
indicating that removal after burial was appropriate,
but violating the rule of 'liàng'àn'.
In the 'Chūnqiū,'
when the Marquis of Jìn entertained the feudal lords,
Zǐchǎn assisted the Earl of Zhèng;
at that time, Duke Jiǎn had not yet been buried,
and Zǐchǎn requested to be exempted from mourning to heed the command;
gentlemen considered this to be in accordance with the rites.
Zǎi Xuān returned the funeral gifts for Duke Huì's son,
and the commentary says: 'condolences for the living do not precede mourning.'
These all serve as evidence for removing mourning clothes and observing 'liàng'àn' after burial.
Former scholars' old sayings
also appear from time to time,
but scholars have not contemplated them.
In mourning rites,
a feudal lord also wears 'zhǎncī' for the Son of Heaven;
how can one say this means wearing them for the full three years?
Looking back at the seven dynasties,
I do not know of any king, minister, or commoner who wore 'suīmá' for three years;
looking forward to the future,
I fear that the principle will be the same for rulers of a hundred generations.
It is not necessarily an inability,
but rather circumstances that prevent it.
Therefore, we know that the sages did not idly establish impractical systems.
Confucius said, 'Though a hundred generations pass, the additions and subtractions in ritual can be known,'
this is what he meant."
Thereupon, Qīn and Shū agreed with him,
and ordered Yù to draft the proposal,

months,

Valuing
and promoting filial piety

It is fitting

Your Servants Qīn, Shū, and Yù respectfully consider the arguments of Jìng, Kuí, and others,

and not understanding the common rites for emperors in mourning, ancient and modern.
From top to bottom,
among the esteemed and the humble, the noble and the lowly,
everything has its appropriate measure.
Thus, in rites, there are those where abundance is valued,
those where scarcity is valued,
those where height is valued,
and those where lowness is valued;
only that which is appropriate (to its measure)
is correct.
Otherwise,
the fundamental and the trivial will be inconsistent,
and their practice will not last.
Between the Son of Heaven and his officials,
although the feelings of sorrow and joy
may be the same,
their appropriate positions are truly different,
and thus the rites cannot be the same.
The 'Yì' states:
"In ancient times, mourning periods were innumerable."
The 'Yúshū' states:
"For three years, the four seas blocked
and silenced the eight sounds."
There is no later text on this.
It was not until the Duke of Zhōu
that it was said:
"Gāozōng of Yīn observed 'liàng'àn' for three years and did not speak."
Its commentary says:
"'Liàng'
means truth;
'Àn'
means silence."
Over five hundred years later,
Zǐ Zhāng doubted this
and asked Confucius.
Confucius replied:
"Why only Gāozōng?
The ancients all did so.
When a ruler
died,
the hundred officials took charge of their own affairs and listened to the Grand Minister for three years."
King Jǐng of Zhōu had the mourning of a queen and crown prince.
After the burial, he removed mourning and engaged in revelry.
Shū Xiàng of Jìn criticized him
saying:
"The three-year mourning,
even the noble should observe it fully,
that is the rite.
Even if the king did not observe it fully,
his banqueting and revelry were too early,
which is also not according to rite."
These are all matters of the Son of Heaven's mourning found in
ancient texts.
It is said that Gāozōng did not observe mourning clothes for three years,
but rather 'liàng'àn' for three years;
this is a text explaining the removal of clothing and mourning in the heart.
The criticism of King Jǐng did not censure him
for removing his mourning clothes,
but for his early banqueting and revelry,
making it clear that removal after burial was appropriate,
but he violated the rule of 'liàng'àn'.
When Yáo died,
Shùn observed 'liàng'àn' for three years,
hence it is said that he 'blocked
and silenced the eight sounds.'
From this, it can be said
that when the Son of Heaven observes mourning,
the system of 'qiīzhǎn',
with simple staff and head-fillet,
should be followed completely.
After burial, it is removed,
and 'liàng'àn' is observed to the end.
For three years, one did not alter the way of one's father.
Therefore, the hundred officials all submitted themselves and listened to the Grand Minister (zhǒngzǎi).
The mourning attire had already been removed,

making it clear that one would no longer sleep on straw mats and use a clod for a pillow,
thereby neglecting important state affairs.
The Lǐjì (Lǐjì) states:
“The three-year mourning period,
extends from the Son of Heaven down.”
It also says:
“For the mourning of parents,
there is no distinction between noble and humble; it is all one.”
It also says:

coarse hemp mourning attire and funeral carriages are all without distinction.”
This generally refers to the Son of Heaven observing mourning,

and the礼 of heart-mourning concludes after three years.

for three years.

Zǐzhāng (Zǐzhāng) raised

The Qín (Qín) burnt books,

Hànzǔ (Hànzǔ) started from scratch,

More recently, during Míngdì’s (Míngdì) reign,

to serve as definitive proof
and elucidate the main points.
If any biographies or records coincided with the current deliberation,
he also listed them in full,
presenting both sides extensively,
clarifying their convergence,
to corroborate the matter.
The text is extensive and not recorded here.
After Emperor Wǔ's Empress Yáng Dào had fostered Emperor Huái,
when the empress encountered difficulties,
Emperor Huái was still young.
Upon his ascension,
an imperial edict praised the empress's grace and affection.
When the empress's ancestral offerings were conducted,
officials debated whether the emperor should wear mourning attire for her.
Some argued that, as a concubine who had shown maternal kindness,
the prescribed ritual was "small mourning" (xiǎogōng) for five months.
Others believed that mourning for a kind mother should be like mourning for one's own mother, meaning "mourning for one year" (qīcuī).
The opinions of the multitude differed.
Lǘqiū Chōng argued:
"Empress Yáng maternally raised the Son of Heaven,
which was due to her special affection.
Now, if we pursue her veneration through grace and ritual,
it would not be appropriate for Emperor Shìzǔ's temple.
Kings do not wear mourning for foster mothers;
it is appropriate that on the day of the ancestral offerings,
he should wear plain clothes for three days and express sorrow, and that is all."
This was then followed.
In the first month of the first year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Kāng, on the last day,
it was the first anniversary (zhōujì) of Empress Chénggōng Dù.
The officials reported that
the emperor should change his mourning attire after one year.
The imperial edict stated:
"The relationship between ruler and parent
is of great importance in the established moral teachings;
the expedient regulations (quánzhì) originated only in recent times."
Thereupon, plain clothes were worn as before.
This was certainly not the practice of the Hàn or Wèi dynasties.
In the first year of Xīngníng,
Emperor Āi's Grand Consort Zhāng (Zhāng huángtàifēi) passed away.
The emperor wished to wear heavy mourning.
Jiāng Pī submitted a memorial:
"The rites established by the former kings
stipulate 'fine hemp mourning' (sīfú)."
The emperor wished to reduce it to "one year" (jī).
Pī again submitted:
"Suppressing personal feelings
is how one reveres ancestors."
Therefore, "fine hemp mourning" (sīmá) for three months was prescribed.
In the Níngkāng era of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Empress Chóngdé Chǔ passed away.
The empress was the emperor's paternal cousin's wife (cóngsǎo),
and there was doubt regarding his mourning attire.
Doctor Bóshì Xú Zǎo argued,
believing:
"Serving one's father and serving one's ruler are equally respectful.
Moreover,
according to ritual,
for those whose husbands hold the position of a father,
their wives all hold the position of a mother.
Thus, if the husband holds the position of a ruler,
the wife also holds the position of an empress.
Mourning for an empress should follow the principle of a foster mother.
Lǔ criticized perverse sacrifices
to demonstrate respect for elders.
Now, the emperor personally performs the sacrifices for Emperors Kāng, Mù, and Āi, as well as Empress Jìng,
showing reverence equivalent to that for one's parents.
How can one honor her with the respect due to a ruler,
yet discard mourning for one's original kin?
It is appropriate to wear 'mourning for one year' (qīcuī jī)."
Thereupon, the emperor prescribed one year of mourning.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān,
Emperor Xiàowǔ's Grand Empress Dowager Lǐ passed away,
and there was doubt about the mourning attire.
The Minister of Personnel Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Hé Chéng, Right Minister of Personnel Yòupúyè Wáng Yǎ, Minister Shàngshū Chē Yìn, Kǒng Ānguó, and Director of Sacrifices Cíbùláng Xú Guǎng argued:
"The Grand Empress Dowager holds a most rightful position and title,
her substance is like the Imperial Ultimate (huángjí),
the principles of the system are fully applied,
and the emotional and ritual obligations are further extended.
According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū,
a mother is honored through her son.
Since she is called 'Lady' (fūrén),
the ritual mourning should follow the principal status.
Therefore, Chéng Fēng (the Spring and Autumn Annals) clearly designates the title of 'Lady',
and Duke Wén observed three years of mourning.
A child, regarding the mother of his father,
holds her in high regard due to her exalted status and profound meaning.
Moreover, ritual states:
'A grandfather does not observe mourning for a grandson.'
It is indeed appropriate to observe mourning without reduction,
and to establish regulations based on sentiment.
If it is feared that there is no clear text,
then this doubt should lead to heavier mourning.
It is appropriate to observe 'mourning for one year' (qīcuī jī), as for a paternal grandmother."
For Empress Yǒng'ān, no mourning was observed,
but only a single expression of sorrow,
and all officials also observed a one-year period.
The edict approved this.
In the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Shūyuàn Chén passed away.
She was the mother of the Crown Prince.
The officials consulted and considered that 'a mother is honored through her son',
and posthumously granted Shūyuàn the title of Fūrén,
establishing a household steward (jiālìng) to manage the funeral affairs.
The Crown Prince's Front Guard Commander Tàizǐ Qiánwèilǜ Xú Miǎo argued:
"The 'Rites of Mourning' states that one forms a single body with the exalted,
and thus does not wear mourning for their private kin.
Furthermore,
what the ruler and father do not wear mourning for,
the son also dares not wear mourning for.
Therefore, a concubine's son of a king or duke wears a hemp cap and plain clothes for his birth mother,
removing them after burial,
which is not among the usual five types of mourning attire,
and is thus called 'no mourning'."
This was followed.
In the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán,
Emperor Xiàowǔ passed away.
Empress Xiàowǔ observed three years of mourning.
In the third month of the first year of Tàipíng of Emperor Huì,
the Imperial Grandson Shàng passed away prematurely.
The officials reported that
the emperor should wear "mourning for one year" (qīcuī jī).
The imperial edict was sent down for general deliberation.
The Palace Attendant Sànqí Chángshì Xiè Héng believed:
"For the crown princes of feudal lords,
whether they have been formally designated or not,
their statuses differ in honor and humility.
The 'Rites of Mourning' refers to 'premature death of a legitimate son' (dízi chángshāng) as meaning not yet formally designated;
if already formally designated, then it is not considered premature death."
The Director of the Central Secretariat Zhōngshūlìng Biàn Cuì said:
"From the moment a crown prince is born,
he is already respected;
he does not await formal designation.
If Héng's argument is that one formally designated is not premature,
then a child for whom no mourning is worn should observe three years of 'unhemmed mourning' (zhǎncuī);
if not formally designated and dying prematurely,
then even at nineteen, one would observe nine months of 'major mourning' (dàgōng).
The difference between being formally designated and not formally designated
is subtle;
the difference between 'unhemmed mourning' (zhǎncuī) and 'major mourning' (dàgōng)
is vast.
And yet the current commentary says
'feudal lords do not reduce mourning for the premature death of a legitimate son.'
If 'no mourning' is considered,
then 'major mourning' is considered mourning for a legitimate son.
Then, even if formally designated,
there is clearly no longer any reason for three years of mourning.
A male who can protect the altars of earth and grain,
and a female who can uphold the conduct of a wife,
in an age when they can achieve things, and having already achieved things,
can thus not be considered prematurely dead;
this is not about young children.
Regarding the mourning for one who died prematurely, if he is honored like a father,
he still observes only the mourning for premature death without any addition.
How much more so for the Son of Heaven,
to observe the rites for an adult for one for whom no mourning is worn and who died prematurely!
All cases of premature death that are considered 'heavy'
do not involve additional mourning for scholars and officials,
and it has never been heard before
that the Son of Heaven alone would bear such heavy mourning."
Doctor Bóshì Cài Kè agreed with Cuì.
The Director of the Imperial Library Mìshūjiān Zhì Yú said:
"From the moment a crown prince is born,
he is treated with the rites of an adult;
thus, the principle of 'premature death' is abolished.
The Imperial Grandson also embodies the ruler's continuation of weighty responsibility;
mourning is observed because of his established position,
not entirely because of his age.
The Son of Heaven has no tradition of mourning for premature death
because the one-year mourning period is abolished."
This was then followed.
According to the precedents of the Wèi clan,
when the state suffered a great mourning,
the assembled officials wore mourning attire,
using silk for their sash-pouches [shòunáng],
and cloth for their sword-covers [jiànyī].
The New Rites [Xīnlǐ]
cited the commentary [zhuàn] stating,
"When mourning is over, there is nothing one may not wear,"
implying that during mourning, one should wear no ornaments.
Therefore, it was enacted that during the mourning of Qīzhǎn, one should not wear a sword or sash.
Zhì Yú [摯虞] thought,
"According to the Rítuals of Zhōu [Zhōulǐ], the Wǔbēnfù [武賁氏]
are officials of the shī-dàfū [士大夫] class.
All of them guard the royal palace with weapons.
If the state suffers a mourning,
they wear mourning clothes [shuāigé], hold spears and shields, and guard the gates.
During the funeral, they follow the hearse and weep.
Furthermore,
when King Chéng [Chéngwáng] passed away,
the Grand Protector [Tàibǎo] ordered all dàfū [大夫] to be on internal and external alert with shields and spears.
This clearly indicates that during times of mourning,
the defense of the palace guard was emphasized.
The phrase 'When mourning is over, there is nothing one may not wear'
refers to matters of dress and adornment,
not to matters of defense.
It is fitting to establish the New Rites [Xīnlǐ] to keep the cloth sword-covers [bùyī jiàn] as before,
and the rest as per the new regulations."
An imperial edict [zhào] agreed to this.
According to the precedents of the Hàn [Hàn] and Wèi [Wèi],
when a funeral was to take place,
auspicious and inauspicious imperial equipage [lǔbù] were set up,
all accompanied by drum and wind music [gǔchuī].
The New Rites [Xīnlǐ] held that since the rites contained no text on auspicious carriages leading the procession,
ministers and sons should not remove their mourning clothes [shuāimá] to wear dark yellow [xuánhuáng].
Thus, the auspicious carriages and equipage [jílúbù] were abolished.
Furthermore,
since there should be no music for inauspicious events,
and the eight tones [bāyīn] should be silenced,
the drum and wind music [gǔchuī] for mourning attire was abolished.
Zhì Yú [摯虞] thought:
"Funerals have 'auspicious carriages [xiángchē] leaving the left side empty,'
which are equivalent to today's funerary carriages [róngchē].
After the burial,
at midday, one returns for the Yú sacrifice [yú],
meeting the spirit and returning.
The Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary [Chūnqiū Zhuàn] states that
when the Zhèng [Zhèng] dàfū [大夫] Gōngsūn Chài [Gōngsūn Chài] died,
the Son of Heaven [Tiānzǐ] posthumously bestowed upon him a grand carriage [dàlù],
ordering it to be used.
In the Rites of the Shī's Funeral [Shìsānglǐ],
funerals include carriages that carry other carriages,
to transport clothes worn during life.
All these are not solely for carrying the coffin;
they also contain clear provisions for auspicious carriages [jíjià].
Since auspicious carriages [jíjià] are set up,
there should be a procession,
to symbolize the appearance during life,
and to clarify the meaning of not leading to death.
Although ministers and sons should not remove their mourning clothes [shuāimá] for themselves,
it is permissible for their sovereign or father.
The 'Chapter on Testamentary Instructions' [Gùmìng zhī piān] is sufficient to clarify this.
It is fitting to establish the New Rites [Xīnlǐ] to keep the auspicious attire [jífú] and procession as before,
while the drum and wind music [gǔchuī] for mourning attire should be abolished."
An imperial edict [zhào] agreed to this.
According to the precedents of the Hàn [Hàn] and Wèi [Wèi],
during a great mourning or the mourning of a high minister,
those who pulled the coffin ropes [zhífú] sang dirges [wǎn'gē].
The New Rites [Xīnlǐ] held that dirges [wǎn'gē] originated from the labor songs of workers under Emperor Wǔ of Hàn [Hàn Wǔdì],
and their mournful and plaintive sound [shēng'āiqiē]
was subsequently adopted as a funeral rite.
Although the music was sorrowful and heart-rending [yīnqǔcuīchuàng],
it was not prescribed by the classics [jīngdiǎn]
and violated the principle of the rites to wear gags [xiánméi].
While in a state of intense grief [hàomù],
it was inappropriate to use singing as a form.
Thus, dirges were abolished.
Zhì Yú [摯虞] thought:
"Dirges [wǎn'gē], when sung in harmony, become a sorrowful sound,
and gags [xiánméi] are for preserving grief;
both are intended to move the multitude.
Although not recorded in the classics [jīngdiǎn],
this has been a practice through successive dynasties.
The Shījīng [Shī] states, 'The noble man [jūnzǐ] makes songs,
using them to express grief.'
To use singing as a form
is therefore not objectionable.
It is fitting to establish the New Rites [Xīnlǐ] as before."
An imperial edict [zhào] agreed to this.
In the second year of Xiánníng [Xiánníng],
Ānpíng Mùwáng [Ānpíng Mùwáng] died without issue.
Therefore,
his younger brother Dūn [Dūn] (by the same mother) was appointed to succeed Xiànwáng [Xiànwáng].
The Grand Courtier [Tàicháng] was asked what mourning attire should be worn.
The Erudite [Bóshì] Zhāng Jìng [Zhāng Jìng] replied that
it should follow the precedent of the three-year mourning by Dǔ Xī [Dǔ Xī] for Mǐn [Mǐn].
The Minister [Shàngshū] Fú Jié [Fú Jié] questioned Jìng [Jìng]:
"Mùwáng [Mùwáng] was not a minister to Dūn [Dūn],
nor did Dūn [Dūn] succeed Mù [Mù].
This differs from the case of Mǐn [Mǐn] and Xī [Xī]."
Sūn Yù [Sūn Yù] and Sòng Chāng [Sòng Chāng] deliberated,
considering that Mùwáng [Mùwáng] did not go to his state,
and Dūn [Dūn] did not serve as an official to the feudal lords [zhūhóu],
so a three-year mourning was not applicable.
From the perspective of principle,
Dūn [Dūn] should wear his original mourning attire,
remove it after one year,
and preside over Mùwáng's [Mùwáng] funeral and sacrifices for three years.
Only then should he perform auspicious sacrifices to Xiànwáng [Xiànwáng].
Yù [Yù] said:
"According to the Rites [Lǐ],
the reason why the sovereign's sons and grandsons serve their elder brothers as ministers [chén zhū xiōng]
is because they preside over the state.
The Rites [Lǐ] also state that for a feudal lord [zhūhóu] who becomes a brother and wears 'cut-off' mourning [zhǎn],
it refers to a minister of a neighboring state to the ruler of a neighboring state,
who holds a position like that of a ruler.
Now, Mùwáng [Mùwáng] did not go to his state,
nor did he have his brothers as ministers.
Dūn [Dūn] did not serve as an official to the feudal lords [zhūhóu],
and thus has no 'neighboring minister' relationship.
This differs from the case of Mǐn [Mǐn] and Xī [Xī],
as the edict of Fú [Fú] stated.
However, since there is no one to preside over the mourning,
and Dūn [Dūn] has received the imperial edict to succeed the state,
he is entrusted with the heavy responsibility of presiding over the mourning [zhǔsāng]
and overseeing the sacrifices.
'For a great mourning [dàgōng] where one is the host of the mourning [zhǔrén zhī sāng],
if there is someone for whom a three-year mourning is observed, then two additional sacrifices must be performed for them.'
Zhèng [Zhèng]'s commentary says,
'This refers to the paternal cousin of the deceased who comes to be the host of the mourning.
Someone for whom a three-year mourning is observed refers to a wife or young child.'
The phrase
'two additional sacrifices' refers to the Lesser and Greater Shàng [xiǎoxiáng] sacrifices.
The consort of Mù [Mù] and the state officials [guóchén] are all, according to the rites, to observe three years of mourning.
This means there are 'those for whom a three-year mourning is observed,'
and Dūn [Dūn] should preside over their two sacrifices, the Lesser and Greater Shàng [xiǎoxiáng].
Moreover,
sorrow and joy should not be mixed,
and auspicious and inauspicious events should not interfere with each other.
With mourning attire in the palace [gōng],
and weeping not yet ceased,
if Dūn [Dūn] were to immediately preside over Mùwáng's [Mùwáng] mourning [zhǔ Mùwáng zhī sāng],
and the state mourning regulations [guózhì] were not yet concluded,
then he would not be able to remove his own filial mourning attire and perform auspicious sacrifices to Xiànwáng [Xiànwáng]."
In the fourth year of Xiánníng [Xiánníng],
the State of Chénliú [Chénliú] reported:
The Duke of Yān [Yāngōng] was the father of the king [wáng].
The king [wáng] had been adopted out to perform sacrifices to Emperor Míng [Míngdì].
Now, to the king [wáng], the Duke was a paternal cousin.
The authorities proposed that he should observe one year of mourning [fú qī],
without any reduction based on closeness or distance of kinship, or rank.
An imperial edict [zhào] stated:
"The king [wáng] serves the Wèi [Wèi] clan,
and the responsibility he bears is great.
He must not observe mourning for his private kin."
During the time of Emperor Mù [Mùdì],
the State of Dōnghǎi [Dōnghǎi] reported:
Āiwáng [Āiwáng] had died more than a year ago,
and the succeeding king [sìwáng] had only then come to succeed him.
He did not pursue mourning again.
Since all the officials had already returned to auspicious attire,
the royal consort [guófēi] should also remove her mourning.
An imperial edict [zhào] stated:
"The reason why the court [cháotíng] follows expedient regulations [quánzhì]
is because the king's [wáng] duties supersede them;
it is not to alter the rites.
For women, the responsibility of transmitting weighty principles is great.
If expedient regulations [quánzhì] were followed,
where would this principle be placed!"
Consequently, the royal consort [guófēi] completed the three-year mourning rites.
Sūn Shèng [Sūn Shèng] thought:
"To abolish the three-year mourning rite opens the door to shallowness.
The Hàn [Hàn] and Wèi [Wèi] made a great mistake in this.
Now, if we say that dàfū [大夫] should forgo mourning due to the king's [wáng] duties,
but women can complete their original mourning,
then auspicious and inauspicious ceremonies would be mixed in the palace chambers,
and the regulations for colored and plain attire would be discordant inside and outside.
Would this not violate both emotion and ritual,
and cause sorrow and joy to lose their proper place!"
In the seventeenth year of Tàiyuán,
Tàicháng Chē Yìn submitted a memorial,
saying: "I respectfully examine the 'Rites of Mourning Garb,'
which states: 'A shùzǐ (son by a concubine) observes three months of sīmá (fine hemp mourning) for his mother.'
The commentary says:
'Why sīmá?
Because one takes the zūnzhě (honored one) as the primary body,
and dares not wear mourning for one's private kin.'
This is the clear text of the classic and its commentary,
a maxim of the sages and worthies.
However, recently, from the ennobled dukes and marquises
down to the qǐngshì (ministers),
whenever a shùzǐ (son by a concubine) becomes the heir,
each indulges their private emotions,
observing mourning for their shùmǔ (concubine mother),
treating it as equal to that for a dí (main wife's) mother.
This is a defect of recent customs,
drowning in emotion and harming instruction.
If it is indulged and not reformed,
then it will stray and be forgotten, never to return.
Moreover, honoring the honored and loving one's kin,
though it is the great root of ritual,
the suppression of kin-love for the sake of honoring the honored
has a long history.
The 'Lǐjì' states:
'One who succeeds his father
does not wear mourning for his birth mother,
because she is not sacrificed to.'
Furthermore,
according to ritual,
when the Son of Heaven is in mourning for his parents,
before burial,
he must set aside the mourning rope to offer sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the altars of grain and soil.
These all illustrate the elevation of solemn reverence,
daring not to abandon the honored for the sake of private matters.
Now, a person bears the heavy responsibility of his ancestors,
yet for the private matter of a shùmǔ (concubine mother),
he neglects the duties of ancestral sacrifices.
The five ancestral temples are deprived of offerings
due to the death of one concubine.
If one seeks for reason in emotion and ritual,
no loss is greater than this.
The whole world acts this way,
with no one to correct or demote it.
Even if their inner feelings differ,
they dare not act differently.
Thus, proper ritual gradually declines,
and accumulated error becomes custom.
This is why the 'Guófēng' longs for ancient times,
and the 'Xiǎoyǎ' laments.
Now, the nine provinces are gradually pacified,
and the king's transforming influence is renewed.
It is truly fitting to uphold and clarify ritual instruction,
to unify customs.
I request that the Tái (Secretariat) and Shěng (Chancellery) examine and revise the classics,
to make clear the king's proper measure."
There was no reply.
In the eighteenth year,
Yìn again submitted a memorial,
saying: "Last year, I submitted that
from the ennobled dukes and marquises
down to the qǐngshì (ministers),
those shùzǐ (sons by concubines) who become heirs
mourn for their shùmǔ (concubine mother),
treating it as equal to that for a dí (main wife's) mother.
This violates ritual and transgresses regulations,
and should be curtailed and suppressed.
The matter has been before Your Majesty for a year,
and no reply has been given.
I do not know what the court discussion finds doubtful.
If it is thought that my statements might be erroneous,
then the classics have the texts;
if it is thought that ancient and modern times differ,
then Jìn has established precedents.
In the fourth year of Shēngpíng,
when the birth mother of the late Tàizǎi, Wǔlíng Wáng, died,
he memorialized requesting qīcuī (coarse hemp mourning) for three years.
An imperial edict ordered him to follow the old precedent of Lè'ān Wáng,
stipulating dàgōng (medium mourning) for nine months.
In the third year of Xīngníng,
when the birth mother of the late Liáng Wáng Xiè again died,
he also requested three years.
An edict issued in the Gēngzǐ year followed the Tàizǎi precedent,
imposing dàgōng (medium mourning).
If one carefully follows the rites of Zhōu,
it is sīmá (fine hemp mourning) for three months;
if one adheres to the Jìn regulations,
it is dàgōng (medium mourning) for nine months.
Neither ancient rites nor current regulations
contain any mention of dwelling in a mourning hut for three years.
However, in recent years,
everyone has indulged their private emotions,
imitating each other,
gradually making it a custom.
If indulged and not forbidden,
then the sacred canons will be extinguished.
Indeed, honoring the honored and loving one's kin,
these are the foundations of human conduct,
and the source of the king's transforming influence,
nothing more than these two principles.
Therefore, the former kings established teachings,
striving to promote them to the utmost,
exalting the reverence of the suburban sacrifices,
establishing the rite of setting aside mourning ropes,
solemnizing ancestral temple sacrifices,
and suppressing the mourning garb for shùzǐ (sons by concubines).
These were for ordering human culture
and transforming the world.
Indeed, subordinating family affairs to the royal way,
and suppressing private affections for the sake of ancestors,
is this not how superiors act toward inferiors,
and fathers toward sons!
If the heart of honoring the honored sometimes falters,
and the emotion of proper suppression is indulged in every situation,
then reverence for ancestors will diminish,
and the ritual of lord and minister will be impaired.
If solemnity and respect are diminished towards ancestors,
and utmost reverence is impaired in serving superiors,
then to wish for stable customs and flourishing transformation,
is that not difficult?
What I value deeply
lies precisely in this.
In my official capacity,
I dare not keep silent.
I request the Tái (Secretariat) to deliberate carefully."
The Shàngshū (Grand Secretary) reported:
"As per the memorial, we shall refer it to the relevant officials for detailed consideration.
According to ritual,
a shùzǐ (son by a concubine) takes the zūnzhě (honored one) as the primary body,
and dares not wear mourning for his private kin.
This is the meaning of honoring ancestors and revering the ancestral lineage.
Recently, this custom has declined,
and this ritual has thus been abandoned.
Princes of ennobled states neglect the importance of the five ancestral temples,
and commoners among gentry and ordinary people fail to observe the rites of ancestral sacrifices.
This has become a decadent custom,
which ought to be corrected.
After internal and external deliberations,
we believe it is proper to accept Yìn's memorial,
and that dàgōng (medium mourning) as per Lè'ān Wáng's precedent should be the correct practice.
We request to issue an official announcement as follows,
to be circulated internally and externally,
to establish a permanent regulation,
and to ensure universal adherence.
This matter can be implemented."
An imperial edict approved it.
According to ritual,
the King wore xīcuī (light mourning) for the Three Dukes and Six Ministers,
and yícuī (uncertain mourning) for dafù (grandees) and shì (scholars),
with a bìan (cap) and dìe (hair band) as headwear.
The Son of Heaven and feudal lords all observed three months of mourning for honored ministers and honored concubines.
There is no record of the Hàn dynasty establishing mourning regulations for high ministers.
During the reign of Hàn Míngdì,
when Dōnghǎi Gōngwáng died,
the Emperor went to Jīnmén Tíng to express his sorrow.
And in the eleventh month of the second year of Wǔdì's Xiánníng era,
an edict stated:
"When princes, dukes, or high ministers die,
those who should express sorrow for three days
shall cease music after one month.
Those who express sorrow for one day
shall cease music for three days."
When the aunt of Yuán Dì, Guǎngchāng Xiāngjūn, died,
before her burial,
Zhōngchéng Xióng Yuǎn submitted a memorial, stating:
"According to the Rites, 'When a lord mourns for a minister or a grandee,
he does not eat meat until the burial,
nor does he perform music until the Zúkū ritual' [Editor's note: which marks the end of the initial mourning period, typically three months].
This is because his compassionate heart cannot bear to engage in auspicious matters.
We have received a decree from the Shàngshū stating that
there will be a small assembly two days after the Winter Solstice.
Your subject believes that on the day of Guǎngchāng Xiāngjūn's funeral,
His Sacred Majesty will be in deep sorrow.
According to the Rites,
when a grandee dies,
sacrifices for a period are suspended.
If sacrifices can be suspended,
how much more so other matters.
On the Winter Solstice, it is only appropriate for subjects to offer congratulations,
a small assembly is not suitable."
An imperial edict ordered Xióng Yuǎn's memorial to be shown to Hè Xún,
and also stated:
"The precedent set by Emperor Wǔ in the second year of Xiánníng states, 'When a king, duke, or high minister dies,
mourning is observed for three mornings, and music is performed after a month;
for those for whom mourning is observed for one morning,
music is performed after three days.'
This is a clear old precedent."
Hè Xún replied:
"According to the 'Zá Jì' (Miscellaneous Records) in the Rites,
'When a lord mourns for a minister or a grandee,
he does not eat meat until the burial,
nor does he perform music until the Zúkū ritual.'
In ancient times, the righteousness between lord and minister was held in high regard.
Even with the utmost veneration due to his position,
the lord would condescend to wear no mourning attire,
but within three months,
he would still wear 'xīcuī' [sackcloth mourning attire] and reside [in mourning],
not engaging in auspicious matters.
Thus, in the Spring and Autumn period, when Jìn's grandee Zhì Dàozǐ had not yet been buried,
Píng Gōng performed music,
and was criticized by Tú Kuǎi.
As Xióng Yuǎn has proposed,
it is in accordance with ancient principles.
Although the Xiánníng imperial edict does not fully align with the classics,
it was established to suit the times
and became a fixed regulation.
It is certainly not something that subjects are at liberty to discuss or comment upon."
In the first year of Shēngpíng,
when Emperor [Mù]'s aunt, Lúlín Gōngzhǔ, had not yet been buried,
a decree inquired of the Tàicháng,
whether music should be performed at the small assembly during the Winter Solstice.
Bóshì Hú Nà deliberated, saying:
"For a lord mourning a minister or grandee,
music is not performed until the Zúkū ritual.
The princess is a close relative by blood,
so music should appropriately be suspended."
Tàicháng Wáng Biāozhī said:
"According to Emperor Wǔ's edict,
for three mornings of mourning,
music is performed after thirty days;
for one morning of mourning,
music is performed after three days.
In the spring of the tenth year of Tàishǐ, when Chánglè Chánggōngzhǔ died,
and in the autumn of the seventh year of Tàikāng, when Fúfēng Wáng Jùn died,
Emperor Wǔ
only observed three days of mourning in both cases.
After the mid-restoration,
this system was re-examined and not changed.
Therefore, music should be performed at the small assembly now."
These two deliberations ultimately
left it unknown which to adopt.
The 'Sāngfú Jì' (Records of Mourning Attire) states that
for a duke who is a guest in another state,
he wears Qīcuī for three months.
The New Rites abolished this chapter,
believing that such a situation no longer exists.
Zhì Yú believed:
"The 'Zhōulǐ' (Rites of Zhōu) was composed during a time when punishments were put aside,
yet it records twelve policies for times of famine.
The Rites are comprehensive in their regulations, awaiting circumstances,
they do not abolish grand ceremonies due to the decline of the times,
nor do they omit teachings for declining morality during prosperous eras.
Previously, Minister Wáng Sītú, having lost his territory and been forced to wander,
referred to himself as a 'jìgōng' (guest duke).
At that time, there were many similar cases in the empire,
all of which are covered by the Rites.
It is appropriate to establish the New Rites to follow the old classics."
An imperial edict approved this.
In the precedents of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
there was no system of five ranks of feudal lords.
When dukes, ministers, and court officials observed mourning,
the degree of closeness and remoteness [of relatives] was determined by their actual kinship.
The New Rites stipulate that for kings, dukes, and the five ranks of feudal lords who establish states and appoint ministers,
as well as for the titles of dukes and lone officials in the court,
collateral relatives observe mourning for a full year,
and these collateral relatives wear Zhǎcuī [the heaviest mourning attire],
while ministers and officials whose positions are equivalent to grandees observe mourning with Sī [lightest mourning attire].
Zhì Yú believed:
"In ancient times, feudal lords ruled over their states
and had their paternal uncles and elder brothers as subjects.
Today's feudal lords are not the same as those of ancient times.
Since they are not the same as ancient times,
their veneration is not complete,
and it is not appropriate to follow the system of a full year's mourning,
nor to make collateral relatives wear the heavy Zhǎcuī.
Since this is the case for feudal lords,
the titles of dukes and lone officials should also remain as before.
In the Jiàn'ān era, Emperor Wèi Wǔ Dì had already submitted a memorial
stating that the Hàn court's regulations, though based on ancient customs,
differed from ancient practices and should not all be implemented;
those that were implemented were recorded in the Wèi statutes.
The Great Jìn adopted these and recorded them in its decrees,
so it is appropriate to establish the New Rites all in accordance with the old."
An imperial edict approved this.
The 'Sāngfú' (Mourning Attire) has no regulation for disciples mourning their teachers,
but the New Rites stipulate that disciples wear Qīcuī for three months for their teachers.
Zhì Yú believed:
"Since ancient times, there has been no system of mourning attire for teachers.
Thus, at the death of Zhòngní (Confucius),
his disciples were uncertain about what to wear.
Zǐgòng said: 'When our Master mourned Yán Huí,
it was like mourning a son without wearing [formal] mourning attire.
I request that we mourn our Master as if mourning a father,
but without wearing [formal] mourning attire.'
Then they observed heart-mourning for three years.
This means they felt three years of sorrow
but without the system of Qīcuī.
When in a group, they wore the 'dié' [mourning headband],
but not when out,
which is called 'diàofú jiāmá' (adding hemp for mourning during condolences).
The ancient sages established rites
that were necessarily easy to follow and transmittable.
The righteousness between teacher and disciple is indeed weighty,
but the mourning system is not explicitly defined.
This has been passed down through generations without being considered a defect.
Furthermore, those who seek teachers consider it advantageous to find ever-loftier ones,
hence they frequently change teachers without objection;
those who pursue learning consider daily renewal as beneficial,
hence they discard the old without hesitation.
Zhòngní said, 'When three people walk together,
there must be a teacher among them.'
Zǐgòng said,
'How can one have a constant teacher?'
For teachers of shallow learning,
or temporary teachers,
one cannot observe mourning for all of them.
If there are differences in the weight of righteousness,
and variations in the practice of mourning,
then praise and blame will arise from it,
and right and wrong will be disputed because of it.
Love and hate will clash,
leading to regrets and misfortunes.
It is appropriate to establish the New Rites to have no mourning attire [for teachers], as before."
An imperial edict approved this.
In ancient times, the funeral rites for the Son of Heaven and feudal lords were roughly prepared,
but during the Hàn dynasty, many changes were made.
From Wèi and Jìn onwards, there were generational changes,
but largely adhering to the Hàn system.
However, Wèi Wǔ, concerning the system of funeral rites for the deceased,
