the number of shrouds,
found them cumbersome and useless,
and moreover, the popular custom went too far.
He personally prepared four chests of clothing for his own funeral,
inscribing them,
for spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
If he were to pass away any day,
they would be used for his burial according to the season.
No gold earrings, pearls, jade, copper, or iron objects
were permitted to be interred.
Wén Dì followed this instruction
without any additions.
Upon receiving the abdication,
he had a golden seal carved,
and bestowed additional honorary titles.
He dared not open the burial chamber,
but instead made a stone chamber
to store the seal at the entrance of the burial chamber,
to show that there were no gold, silver, or other treasures within the mausoleum.
The Hàn rites included many mingqì (burial objects),
but from then on, all were reduced.
In the third year of Huángchū of Wèi Wén Dì,
he again composed his own final testament, saying:
"According to the rites,
when a ruler ascends the throne, a bi (memorial tablet) is made,
so that while alive, one does not forget death.
The shòulíng (longevity tomb) should use the mountain as its body,
without creating a mound or planting trees,
without erecting a sleeping hall,
or constructing a garden city,
or opening a spirit road.
For burial (zàng) means to conceal (cáng),
desiring that people should not see it.
The rites do not include tomb sacrifices,
desiring that the living and the dead should not be defiled.
Empresses and noble consorts and those below who do not follow the king to his state,
upon their demise,
shall all be buried west of the gully,
the location of which has already been indicated."
This edict was stored in the ancestral temple,
with copies in the Shàngshū, Mìshū, and the Three Ministries.
Míng Dì also observed and upheld it.
Although Míng Dì was inclined to extravagance,
he did not hastily undertake the construction of mausoleums.
Xuān Dì had already prepared an earthen tomb for himself on Shǒuyáng Shān,
without a mound or trees,
and composed his final testament (gù mìng zhōng zhì),
to be clothed in seasonal attire,
and without setting up mingqì.
Jǐng Dì and Wén Dì both scrupulously followed these established commands,
without adding anything.
When Jǐng Dì passed away,
the funeral arrangements also followed Xuān Dì's precedents.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Wǔ Dì,
when Empress Wénmíng Wáng passed away,
and was to be interred together,
Chóngyáng Líng was opened.
Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Wàng was sent to offer sacrifices
and present the emperor's secret seal and ribbon at the spirit seat in the side chamber.
In the early days of Jiāng Zuǒ,
Yuán Dì and Míng Dì favored frugality,
and furthermore, all institutions were just being founded.
The mountain mausoleums and funeral rites
were simplified and complete.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Chéng Dì,
Empress Dù passed away.
An edict instructed external officials to attend the wake once every five days,
and internal officials once every morning only,
stopping after the burial and the Yú sacrifice.
The officials concerned memorialized,
proposing to construct a xiōngmén (mourning gate) and bòlì mén (cypress gate) at the site of the late empress's mausoleum,
named Xiǎnyáng Duānmén.
The edict said:
"The gate shall be as located.
But the xiōngmén and bòlì
involve great trouble and expense,
so stop them."
According to Cài Mó's explanation,
two pottery vessels containing the initial sacrifice for the deceased
were tied to wood,
wrapped in reed mats,
and placed in the courtyard,
near the south.
This was called chóng (weight);
today's xiōngmén is its representation.
According to the rites,
the zhǔ (spirit tablet) is made after the Yú sacrifice.
Since the burial had not yet taken place,
there was no zhǔ,
so chóng was used in its place.
The rites called this the zhǔdào (path of the spirit tablet).
This is its meaning.
Fàn Jiān also said:
"The xiōngmén is not part of the rites.
The rites include xuán chóng (hanging weights),
which resemble the xiōngmén in form.
Later generations placed them outside the gate to mark mourning,
and this custom subsequently became widespread.
Bózhang (thin curtains)
are similar to the ancient diàomù (mourning curtains)."
At that time,
an edict also said:
"Beneath the heavy earth,
how can useless adornments be promoted?
The mausoleum should only be kept clean."
The officials concerned again memorialized,
proposing to select sixty sons of officials from the sixth rank and below to be wǎnláng (mourning chanters), as was customary.
The edict again halted this.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔ Dì,
Empress Wáng passed away.
An edict said:
"Funeral affairs should only follow frugality and promptness."
Another edict said:
"Neither near nor far shall send shānlíng shǐ (mausoleum envoys)."
The officials concerned memorialized to select twenty-four wǎnláng.
The edict halted this.
In ancient times, there was no custom of tomb sacrifices.
The Hàn, inheriting from Qín,
all had garden sleeping palaces.
On the first Dīng day of the first month,
after the sacrifice at the southern suburb was completed,
followed by the northern suburb, Míngtáng, Gāomiào, and Shìzǔ Miào,
these were called the Five Offerings.
When Wèi Wǔ was buried at Gāolíng,
the officials concerned, following Hàn precedent, erected a sacrificial hall above the mausoleum.
By the third year of Huángchū of Wén Dì,
an edict then stated:
"The late emperor personally practiced frugality,
and his遗诏 (final testament) instructed reduction.
A son is filial by following his father,
and a subject is loyal by continuing affairs.
Ancient rites did not include tomb sacrifices;
all were set up in the temple.
All halls above Gāolíng shall be dismantled,
carriages and horses returned,
and clothing stored in the treasury,
to follow the late emperor's will for frugal virtue."
Wén Dì's own final testament
also said,
"The shòulíng shall have no sleeping hall
or garden city built."
From then on, garden cities and sleeping halls were abolished.
Qí Wáng reigned for nine years,
only visiting Gāopíng Líng once before Cáo Shuǎng was executed.
After that, the practice was abandoned
and ceased during the Wèi dynasty.
When Xuān Dì passed away,
his final testament instructed
"that sons, brothers, and all officials shall not visit the mausoleums."
Thus, Jǐng Dì and Wén Dì followed this instruction.
By Wǔ Dì,
he still visited Chóngyáng Líng twice
and Jùnpíng Líng once,
but then dared not visit Gāoyuán Líng.
This practice ceased again by Huì Dì.
Upon reaching the south of the Yangtze River,
after Emperor Yuán’s death,
the various dukes first began to have the custom of visiting tombs and making declarations.
This was probably due to a feeling of closeness like friends and colleagues,
acting on emotion,
and was not a former custom of Luòjīng.
During Emperor Chéng’s reign,
the Empress also visited the mausoleum annually.
Those who debated the matter considered it to be against ritual,
so it was then stopped,
and established as a permanent regulation.
During Emperor Mù’s reign,
Empress Dǒwager Chǔ oversaw the court,
and also visited the mausoleum,
because the Emperor was young.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
Piaòqí Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Dàozǐ said:
“Although we are now temporarily released from mourning attire,
as for the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month and other festivals,
it is appropriate to express our feelings at the mausoleum,
with one year as the period.”
So, upon reaching the mausoleum,
they changed into plain clothes and single garments,
the bother and profanation were without standard,
which was not in line with ritual principles.
In the first year of Yuánxīng under Emperor Ān,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Huán Qiān memorialized:
“The hundred officials visiting the mausoleum
began during the Central Revival,
and was not an old custom of Jìn.
Accumulated practice became constant,
and thus became a recent law.
Recalling Emperor Wǔ’s edict,
he did not even allow the sovereign or kings to visit the mausoleum,
how much less the hundred officials!
It is advisable to follow and uphold this.”
Thus it was put into effect.
However, at the beginning of Yìxī,
the old custom of the south of the Yangtze River was revived again.
In the seventh year of Tàikāng,
Dàhónglú Zhèng Mò’s mother passed away.
After the burial,
he was supposed to resume his duties according to old custom,
but he firmly refused to rise.
Thereupon, it was first decreed that high officials could observe a three-year mourning period.
However, during Yuánkāng,
Chén Zhǔn, Fù Xián and others
were still compelled by circumstances
and could not complete the full ritual,
and from then on,
this was considered an established precedent.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
Dōngpíng Wáng Máo memorialized, saying
that Xiāng Wáng Chāng’s father, Bì,
originally resided in Chángshā
and had a wife and children.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he was sent into the Central Plain.
He encountered Wú’s rebellion
and served as Huángmén Láng in Wèi.
Separated from his former wife and children by life and death,
he remarried Chāng’s mother.
Now that the Jiangbiǎo region is unified,
Chāng heard that his former mother had been in mourning for a long time,
and claiming illness, sought an impartial deliberation.
Shǒu Bóshì Xiè Héng 議曰：
「雖有二妻，
蓋有故而然，
不為害於道，
議宜更相為服． 」
Shǒu Bóshì Xǔ Měng 以為
「地絕，
又無前母之制，
正以在前非沒則絕故也．
前母雖在，
猶不應服． 」
Duàn Chàng, Qín Xiù, Zōu Chōng 從 Měng．
Sànqí Chángshì Liú Zhì'ān 議：〔一三〕
「禮為常事制，
不為非常設也．
亡父母不知其死生者，
不著於禮．
平生不相見，
去其加隆，
以朞為斷． 」
Dū Lìngshǐ Yú Pǔ 議曰：
「臣以為禮不二嫡，
所以重正，
非徒如前議者防妬忌而已．
故曰『一與之齊，
終身不改』 ，
未有遭變而二嫡．
苟不二，
則 Chāngfù 更娶之辰，
是前妻義絕之日也．
使 Chāngfù 尚存，
二妻俱在，
必不使二嫡專堂，
兩婦執祭，
同為之齊也． 」
Qín Xiù 議：
「二妾之子，
父命令相慈養，
而便有三年之恩，
便同所生．
Chāngfù 何義不命二嫡依此禮乎！
父之執友有如子之禮，
況事兄之母乎！ 」
Xǔ Měng 又議：
「夫少婦稚，
則不可許以改娶更適矣．
今妻在許以更聘，
夫存而妻得改醮者，
非絕而何． 」
Shìzhōng Lǐng Bóshì Zhāng Yùn 議：
「昔 Shùn 不告而娶，
婚禮蓋闕，
故 Yáo Diǎn 以釐降二女為文，
不殊嫡媵．
傳記以妃夫人稱之，
明不立正后也．
夫以聖人之弘，
帝者嫡子，
猶權事而變，
以定典禮．
Huáng Chāng 之告新妻使避正室，
時論許之．
推 Jī Shì 之讓，
執 Huáng Qīng 之決，
宜使各自服其母． 」
Huángmén Shìláng Cuī Liàng, Xún Kuī, Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù, Lǐng Zhōngshū Lìng Hé Qiáo, Shìláng Xiàhóu Zhàn 皆如 Pǔ 議．
Shìláng Shān Xióng, Jiān Shìláng Zuòshù Chén Shòu 以為：
「Pǔ 駁一與之齊，
非大夫也，
〔一四〕禮無二嫡，
不可以並耳．
若 Chāngfù 及二母於今各存者，
則前母不廢，
已有明徵也．
設令 Chāngfù 將前母之子來入 Zhōngguó 尚在者，
當從出母之服．
苟 Chāngfù 無棄前妻之命，
Chāng xiōng 有服母之理，
則 Chāng 無疑於不服． 」
Zéicáo Shǔ Biàn Cuì 議：
「Chāngfù 當莫審之時而娶後妻，
則前妻同之於死而義不絕．
若生相及而後妻不去，
則妾列於前志矣．
死而會乎，
則同祔於葬，
無並嫡之實．
必欲使子孫於沒世之後，
追計二母隔絕之時，
以為並嫡，
則背違死父，
追出亡母．
議者以為禮無前母之服者，
可謂以文害意．
愚以為母之不親而服三年，
非一無異於前母也． 」
Cāocáo Shǔ Wèi 議：
「或云，
嫡不可二，
前妻宜絕．
此為奪舊與新，
違母從子，
禮律所不許，
人情所未安也．
或云，
絕與死同，
無嫌二嫡，
據其相及，
欲令有服．
此為論嫡則死，
議服則生，
還自相伐，
理又不通．
愚以為地絕死絕，
誠無異也，
宜一如前母，
不復追服． 」
Zhǔbù Liú Biàn 議：Bì 在南為邦族，
於北為羈旅，
以此名分言之，
前妻為元妃，
後婦為繼室．
何至王路既通，
更當逐其今妻，
〔一五〕廢其嫡子！
不書 Jiāng Shì，
絕不為親，
以其犯至惡也．
Zhào Jī 雖貴，
必推 Shú Kuí；
Yuán Tóng 雖寵，
必嫡 Xuān Mèng．
若違禮苟讓，
何則春秋所當善也！
論者謂地絕，
其情終已不得往來．
今地既通，
何為故當追而絕之邪！
Huáng Chāng 見美，
斯又近世之明比． 」
Sīkōng Qí Wáng Yōu 議：
「禮記『生不及祖父母、諸父昆弟，
而父稅喪，
己則否』 ，
諸儒皆以為父以他故子生異域，
不及此親存時歸見 之，
父雖追服，
子不從稅，
不責非時之恩也．
但不相見，
尚不服其先終，
而況前母非親所生，
義不踰祖，
莫往莫來，
恩絕殊隔，
而令追服，
殆非稱情立文之謂也．
以為 Chāng 不宜追服． 」
Sītú Lǐ Yìn 議：
「Bì 為 Huángmén Shìláng，
Jiāngnán 已叛．
Shí Hòu 與焉，
大義滅親，
況於 Bì 之義，
可得以為妻乎！ 」
Dà Sīmǎ Qiān Bù 議，
Tàiwèi Chōng, Fǔjūn Dà Jiàngjūn Rǔnán Wáng Liàng 皆從主者．
Pǔ 又駁 Cuì 曰：
「喪從 Níng Qī，
謂喪事尚哀耳，
不使服非其親也．
夫死者終也，
終事已故無絕道．
分居兩存，
則離否由人．
夫婦以判合為義，
今土隔人殊，
則配合理絕．
彼已更娶代己，
安得自同於死婦哉！
Bó Yí 讓 Gū Zhú，
不可以為後王法也．
且既已為嫡後服，
復云為妾，
生則或貶或離，
死則同祔於葬，
妻專一以事夫，
夫懷貳以接己，
開偽薄之風，
傷貞信之教，
於以純化篤俗，
不亦難乎！
今 Chāng 二母雖土地殊隔，
據同時並存，
何得為前母後母乎！
設使 Chāng mǔ 先亡，
以嫡合葬，
而前母不絕，
遠聞喪問，
當復相為制何服邪！
Indeed, when regulations do not accord with ritual,
actions lead to greater error.
A filial son does not bring his parents into unrighteousness,
nor does a chaste wife enter recklessly and compromise her integrity.
Now, to have a stepmother and a former嫡 wife in the same position after death,
making the later wife occupy the principal position and perhaps neglecting the former,
would there be no shame
in the hearts of the two sons?
To then speak of "slandering the father and abandoning the mother,"
I fear that such artfully crafted words
can hardly determine right from wrong.
According to ritual,
when a feudal lord departs from his suzerain to serve the Son of Heaven,
he does not serve his former ruler.
If so, then Chāngfù (昌父) severed ties with his former ruler.
If he married a second wife
and discarded his former wife,
then why should there be any question of whether she "should be punished" or "should be placated"?
Moreover, for a woman to have a serious illness
is something a compassionate husband would pity,
yet it is among the "seven grounds for divorce."
This is truly because human reason dictates severance.
Now, with husband and wife separated by different regions,
it is like having no wife at all.
Compared to a serious illness,
there is no logical difference.
Based on his own remarriage,
there is evidence of severing the former tie,
so to say she "should be mourned for"
—on what principle does that stand? "
The Eight Ministers of the Shàngshū (尚書) thought,
"Suppose there is someone here
whose father was the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
and the son later held office in Luò (洛).
If the father married a wife,
not only would the son not see her,
but he might even not know her.
However, upon her death,
he would have no choice but to wear mourning.
It is merely that the one who nurtured him inspires deeper sorrow,
while not seeing them is merely a matter of regulation.
the act of wearing mourning for them is the same.
Furthermore,
to treat two wives as equally principal
is said to violate ritual,
not to be an extraordinary event that should be dealt with according to ordinary ritual.
In the past, Zǐsī (子思) wept for his divorced mother in the ancestral temple.
His disciples said, 'The daughter of the Shù (庶) family has died;
why weep for her in the Kǒng (孔) family's temple?'
Zǐsī (子思) was alarmed and
wept in another room.
If Chāng (昌) does not wear mourning,
he would have to inform his father and ancestors,
dig up the corpse of his former mother,
and move it to another location.
If he does not move it,
Chāng (昌) would be a criminal.
Why?
Because a woman of a different clan is not allowed to be buried with the paternal aunt (i.e., the first wife's relatives),
and her tomb is hidden.
Moreover, a wife follows her husband,
and there is still someone to respect.
The action of Zhào Jī (趙姬)
was permissible by the flexibility of ritual.
Therefore, the former historians elaborated on it
and did not criticize the matter.
Now, Chāng's (昌) two mothers
have both died,
so there is no question of them sharing a principal position or their relative importance.
Chāng's (昌) former mother
should be compared to Shúkuí (叔隗).
If she died before Chāng (昌) was born,
then Chāng (昌) should not wear mourning again.
If he was born and his mother was alive,
he should, according to ritual, formally wear mourning for three years.
Let this be formally drafted as a document
and submitted to the Tài Cháng (太常) to inform Máo (楙) to implement."
The Imperial Edict stated:
"All matters that are extraordinary
should be decided according to ancient precedents
and established rulings.
The current deliberation on this matter,
citing Zhào Jī (趙姬) and Shúkuí (叔隗), is broadly correct.
However, the Dí (狄) and Jìn (晉) were in harmony then,
hence Jī (姬) could welcome Shúkuí (叔隗) and bring her down.
The Wú (吳) bandits' obstruction separated [Bì] (毖) and his former wife,
severing their ties forever.
If there truly can be no two principal wives,
then Zhào Shuāi (趙衰) could have solely decided on the Wěi (隗) family.
How could Chāng (昌), as a son, arbitrarily dismiss his mother?
Moreover, Bì's (毖) two wives both died after the separation,
so his son is merely the son of the later mother.
Therefore, Chāng (昌) should not wear mourning."
In the early Tàixīng (太興) era,
the Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎) Gān Bǎo (干寶) commented on this, saying:
"Ritual has constant principles, adaptations, and expedients.
The case of Wáng Bì (王毖)
was a matter of necessity.
One cannot demand adherence to the principle of consistency from beginning to end,
nor seek conformity with ordinary ritual texts.
Why is there such confusion in the opinions of the various deliberators?
Among those born of the same parents, there is no distinction between principal and secondary,
but the one born earlier is the elder brother.
Among feudal lords of the same rank, there is no difference in status,
but the one enfeoffed earlier is the senior.
Now, the entry of two wives
has no distinction of noble or humble in ritual,
so it is appropriate to rank them by order of entry,
following the principle of sequence.
Currently, those who live in the same household are few,
while those who share an ancestral temple after death are many,
and their spirit tablets
certainly have a hierarchy.
Therefore, the 'Spring and Autumn Annals' praises Zhào Jī (趙姬) for encountering a change in ritual and obtaining the essence of ritual.
Moreover, joy and sorrow, happiness and grief,
are moved by emotion.
The system of the Five Rites
is to align with emotions and adapt to circumstances.
Now, these two mothers
were originally strangers.
They became kin by name,
but their affection varied with the times.
Respect did not extend to their lives,
and love did not extend to their deaths.
So, how could there be a way to wear posthumous mourning?
Zhāng Yùn (張惲) and Liú Biàn (劉卞)
understood the principle of precedence.
Qí Wáng (齊王) and Wèi (衞)
understood the system of suspending mourning.
This can be decisive.
The imperial court, in this matter,
should guide them with the example of Zhào Jī (趙姬),
and align them with an imperial edict,
so that the former wife embodies the virtue of broad tolerance,
the later wife upholds the way of humility and deference,
the household members understand the order of seniority,
and the common people see the appropriateness of adapted ritual.
If this is done,
it can be applied to life,
how much more so to death!
Ancient kings
treated their ministers with the rites due to a teacher or friend,
and the ministers dared not exalt themselves.
Now, if the former wife treats the latter as part of one body,
and the later wife dares not resist,
and their descendants wear mourning for each other,
this is an excellent manifestation of ritual.
Therefore, on the day Wáng Chāng (王昌) and his brothers reconcile,
they should perhaps offer a joint sacrifice to their two mothers,
equalizing their ritual offerings,
ordering them by precedence,
positioning them left and right,
with the brothers solemn and harmonious,
exchanging toasts and presenting offerings,
thereby above fulfilling their late father's wishes,
middle exalting the virtues of their two mothers,
and below harmonizing the good relations between the brothers,
making the wind of righteousness spread through royal teaching,
and compassion and deference pervade urgent difficulties.
Would this not be obtaining the essence of ritual? "
At that time,
Liú Zhòngwǔ (劉仲武) of Pèiguó (沛國) had first married a woman of the Wúqiū (毋丘) clan,
and had two sons, Zhèngshū (正舒) and Zhèngzé (正則).
After Wúqiū Jiǎn's (毋丘儉) rebellion failed,
Zhòngwǔ (仲武) divorced his wife
and married a woman of the Wáng (王) clan,
who bore him Táo (陶).
Zhòngwǔ (仲武) had a separate residence for the Wúqiū (毋丘) woman but did not declare a complete severance.
When the Wúqiū (毋丘) woman died,
Zhèngshū (正舒) sought to be buried with her,
but Táo (陶) did not allow it.
Shū (舒) did not remove his mourning attire,
sued at all levels,
wept blood and exposed his bones,
his mourning clothes tattered and worn,
for decades he could not achieve his goal,
until his death.
At that time, Zhū (朱) of Wúguó (吳國) had married a woman of the Chén (陳) clan,
who bore him a son, Dōngbó (東伯).
Upon entering Jìn (晉),
Jìn (晉) bestowed upon him a wife of the [unnamed] clan,
who bore him a son, Suíbó (綏伯).
In the middle of Tàikāng (太康),
the [unnamed] wife had died.
Suíbó (綏伯) took his mother and returned to his clan.
The brothers showed mutual love and respect,
the two mothers showed sincere regard for their order of precedence,
and there was perfect harmony among the people.
When they eventually died,
the two sons wore mourning for each other,
and gentlemen considered this virtuous.
Chéng Liàng (程諒), the Administrator of Ānfēng (安豐), already had a wife,
but later he married again,
thus establishing two principal wives.
When his former wife died,
the son of his later wife, Zǐxūn (子勳), was unsure about the mourning attire to wear.
Zhāng Huà (張華), the Grand Secretary, posed the "Question of A and B," saying:
"A marries B as his wife,
then later marries C,
concealing the fact that he has B,
and in the household, they are treated as two principal wives,
without any distinction of noble or humble.
B dies,
what mourning attire should C's son wear?
Originally they were truly co-equal,
with no distinction between principal and secondary wives.
Although having two principal wives is not proper,
this fault lies with the deceased father.
How can a son unilaterally decide and break up his family relations?
If he wears mourning for a secondary mother,
then she is not considered secondary.
I do not know which way to proceed."
Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖), the Grand Tutor, deliberated, saying:
"A committed a breach of禮 (lǐ) in the household.
With two principal wives coexisting,
it is truly not something a son can rectify.
Therefore, the sons of both B and C should observe three years of mourning,
as in cases of doubt in ritual, one should follow the heavier observance."
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), the General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Rèn Kǎi (任愷), the Attendant-in-ordinary and Junior Tutor, largely agreed with Zhèng.
Xún Yǐ (荀顗), the Grand Commandant, deliberated, saying:
"In the Spring and Autumn period, co-equal queens were treated as principal wives;
this is a clear ancient canon.
Now, one cannot violate 禮 (lǐ) by establishing two wives concurrently,
and not distinguishing their seniority and inferiority, thereby perpetuating the error.
Therefore, it must be decided by 禮 (lǐ):
the one who arrived first is the principal wife,
the one who arrived later is the secondary wife.
C's son should wear mourning for B as his principal mother,
and B's son should serve C as a secondary mother.
In ancient times, Qū Jiàn (屈建) left the mallow [robe];
the ancients considered this to be contrary to 禮 (lǐ) yet in accordance with 禮 (lǐ).
C's son is not suppressing his own mother;
this is simply following the principle of seniority and inferiority based on the order of observance of 禮 (lǐ)."
Xún Xù (荀勖), the Grand Secretary, deliberated, saying:
"In the past, Zhèng Zǐqún (鄭子羣) from our village married the younger sister of Chén (陳), the Minister of Works.
Later, due to the chaos of Lǚ Bù (呂布),
they lost contact and did not know whether each other was alive or dead,
so he married a woman from our village, of the Cài (蔡) clan.
When Xúzhōu (徐州) was pacified,
Lady Chén (陳氏) was able to return,
and so both wives coexisted.
The son of Lady Cài (蔡氏), courtesy name Yuánxìn (元釁),
wore mourning for Lady Chén (陳氏) as his principal mother,
and served Duke Chén (陳公) with the rites due to a maternal uncle's family.
My clan elder Zōngbó (宗伯) once criticized Yuánxìn (元釁),
saying he was suppressing his own mother,
but the village elders considered Yuánxìn (元釁)'s action appropriate.
I wonder if this matter is roughly similar?"
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武) [317 CE],
Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) was appointed as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) declined the appointment, stating that his mother had died during a period of banditry,
so he could not personally attend to her funeral,
and he wished to arrange for a reburial,
thus he firmly refused to accept the post.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) issued an edict saying:
"Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) declines the appointment,
because he has not yet been able to select a new burial site and perform the funeral rites,
and there are also differing opinions in the court discussions.
Is this truly the reason?
When there are obstructions in the world,
those who manage ritual and regulate affairs should ensure that reason can prevail.
The ancients' regulation of three years [of mourning]
was not the full extent of human emotion,
but rather to make a distinction between the living and the dead,
not to injure the living because of the dead.
Those who wear mourning bands and engage in military service,
do they seek official positions?
They act according to the urgency of state affairs.
Now, the rebels are not yet suppressed,
and the road to Píngyáng (平陽) is cut off.
The armies sent to welcome [the emperor] still cannot advance directly.
Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) is but one person;
how can he fulfill his private difficulties,
and doubt himself due to obstacles of principle, refusing to obey the imperial command?
Let the Three Ducal Ministers, the Eight Senior Ministers, the Three Departments of the Palace Secretariat, and all officials, both within and outside the court,
thoroughly discuss such cases as Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠)'s in common deliberation.
I will personally make the final decision."
Thereupon, Yáng (羕), the Grand Tutor and Prince of Xīyáng (西陽);
Zǔ (組), the Minister of Works and Duke of Línyǐng (臨潁);
Dǎo (導), the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Viscount of Jìqiū (即丘);
Jì Zhān (紀瞻), the Attendant-in-ordinary;
Zhōu Yǐ (周顗), the President of the Board of Civil Office;
Xún Suì (荀邃), the Regular Attendant-in-ordinary, and others deliberated,
stating that
"In the past, Wǔ Yuán (伍員) departed Chǔ (楚) with his bow,
serving as a traveler for Wú (吳) to plot against Chǔ (楚).
His true intention was to avenge himself,
not to carelessly destroy his life.
Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) encountered calamity
in the past in Hésuò (河朔),
daily facing conflict.
His ambition was to wipe out the evil enemies.
Traveling thousands of miles, he offered himself
and came to the imperial court,
intending to seize the opportunity to exert his strength,
relying on imperial might,
to fulfill his ambition.
This is Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠)'s aspiration.
There is no reason, with roads not yet open
and armies not yet advanced,
for him to abandon imperial service
and remain focused on his private affairs.
We believe it is truly appropriate as stated in the clear edict."
Thereupon, the relevant officials memorialized, saying:
"According to the general opinion,
following the decree issued on the Xīnwèi (辛未) day of the ninth month of the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武) [317 CE],
according to ritual texts,
in the case of a father's funeral not yet performed,
[one seven] only the chief mourner does not cease [mourning].
If the funeral is not performed for other reasons,
it is human nature
that one cannot live with the coffin and cease mourning.
Therefore, the period is until the funeral is completed,
without distinction of distance.
If the death occurred during banditry or disaster,
and the body has no fixed place,
and efforts to find it are cut off,
then one should indeed cease mourning after three years,
and not follow the precedent of an unburied death.
If flesh and blood were destroyed by banditry,
and deaths are widespread across the Central Plains,
and this is followed by the fact that the remaining rebels are not yet suppressed,
the deceased have no actual place of burial,
and the living lack the rites of rushing to them,
yet it is human nature
that sorrow is ceaseless,
and they follow the principle of an unburied death,
long refusing to cease mourning.
If their feelings are indulged,
then people would observe unlimited mourning,
which is not the meaning of 'there are rituals for all times, and none are unattainable.'
In all such cases,
following the precedents of Dōngguān (東關),
mourning is limited to the completion of the three-year rite before ceasing.
Only in cases where both parents are separated alive,
and their fate (auspicious or inauspicious) is not yet determined,
observing mourning means the inauspicious event is not yet confirmed,
and following auspicious practices raises doubt about their survival.
Inner sorrow and living in plain attire
arise from human nature.
For such cases,
it is not within the scope of official regulations to decide.
Now, Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) has repeatedly offered sick leaves,
because he has not been able to find a new burial site and rush to it.
According to the Xīnwèi (辛未) decree,
there is already a definitive ruling;
none are allowed to indulge their private feelings
and disobey imperial commands,
thereby harming the legal system.
The joint deliberation suggests that Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) should accept the appointment as per the previous edict,
and it should be re-announced by the Imperial Censor and Minister of Works
that all others like Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠)
should follow the precedents of Dōngguān (東關) and the Xīnwèi (辛未) decree."
Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) had no choice
but to accept the appointment.
At this time, the Central Plains were in chaos,
families were separated,
and the court debated whether mourning attire should be observed for parents trapped in banditry.
Hé Xún (賀循), the Grand Master of Ceremonies, said:
"If both parents are separated alive,
and their fate (auspicious or inauspicious) is not yet determined,
observing mourning means the inauspicious event is not yet confirmed,
and following auspicious practices raises doubt about their survival.
Inner sorrow and living in plain attire
perfectly align with human nature."
Emperor Yuán (元帝) ordered that Xún (循)'s deliberation be considered correct.
In the second year of Tàixīng (太興) [319 CE],
Xún Zǔ (荀組), the Minister of Works, said:
"For parents trapped in banditry,
where there is one chance in ten thousand,
they should be allowed to follow royal law
and observe mourning according to precedent."
Yǔ Wèizhī (庾蔚之) said:
"For parents broken by barbarians,
whose survival is unknown,
efforts to seek them out should be exhausted.
If the reason for seeking them out is cut off,
beyond three years,
it is appropriate to marry and hold office,
as the lineage cannot be cut off,
and royal governance cannot be abolished.
It is still appropriate to live in sorrowful plain attire,
not participate in auspicious celebrations,
and wait until middle age to wear mourning.
If the internal banditry and chaos are pacified,
and after a general amnesty,
no trace is found through searching,
then it is appropriate to institute mourning."
In the second year of Xiánkāng,
Lǐ Fán's elder sister from Línglíng had previously married Chén Shēn from Nánpíng Commandery.
She bore four sons and then encountered bandits.
The sister threw herself before the bandits,
begging them to spare her mother-in-law's life.
The bandits took the sister away by force.
Shēn then married a second wife, a woman of the Yán clan,
and she bore three sons.
Later, Fán received news of his sister,
went to retrieve her, and brought her back to Shēn.
Shēn registered both wives in the household records.
When Lǐ's mother died,
Shēn was uncertain about the mourning attire.
[一八]He reported the matter to the office of the Grand General of the Western Expedition, Yǔ Liàng, for deliberation.
At the time, opinions often varied.
Sīmǎ Wáng Qiānqī deliberated, saying:
"According to the rites, there is no second principal wife.
Therefore, Duke Huì's principal consort was Mèngzǐ.
When Mèngzǐ died,
she was succeeded by Shēngzǐ as the principal wife.
If this is so for feudal lords,
how much more so for commoners!
The 'Shì Sàng Lǐ' (Ritual for the Burial of a Scholar) states that
a stepmother is essentially a successor wife,
hence she is called a stepmother.
One serves her like a principal wife,
hence it is said 'like a mother.'
Shēn could not foresee and avoid the calamity,
leading to the loss of his wife.
She was not divorced by Shēn for violating the 'seven outcasts'.
She was not divorced initially,
and was later welcomed back.
She nurtured his mother in the hall,
her son is the eldest principal son,
and her name is listed in the official household register.
Thus, she is Shēn's wife.
As Shēn's wife,
she is then Huī's mother.
Huī's mourning attire should be beyond doubt.
The ritual states that one wears mourning for a stepmother but not for a former mother.
For cases like Lǐ,
such instances are rare throughout the ages.
Only after a former mother has died
does a stepmother come into being.
Later sons do not have a connection to the former mother,
thus there is no text specifying mourning attire for her.
However, for the seasonal sacrifices (yuè, cí, zhēng, cháng),
there is no instance where the former mother is not treated as the mother.
If she is still considered a mother when lost,
how much more so when she is alive!
Shēn has an elderly mother
who cannot be left unprovided for,
and with no return date for his wife,
it was permissible to take a concubine.
Although Lǐ was taken by bandits,
there was still hope for her survival.
Shēn's efforts to find her were not exhausted,
yet he immediately married another wife.
This is truly Shēn's shortcoming.
However, he is a man of the fields,
unfamiliar with rituals and righteousness.
To examine him by the standards of historical records is to be overly demanding.
[一九]Shī Xiàoshū's wife lost her purity to Xí Chōu yet was not cast aside,
because it was not her fault.
Shēn had two wives,
but he did not intentionally violate the law.
Lǐ, though a countrywoman,
was able to beg for her mother-in-law's life in a crisis.
In danger, she did not forget filial duty;
she can be called a Lǐ wife.
Those who argue wish that, while she was in captivity,
she should have maintained absolute purity,
preferring death over a second union.
This is expecting all common people to be Sòng Bó Jī.
Although Shēn should not have married a second wife,
he did indeed take Yán as his wife.
As a wife, she is a successor wife,
not originally the principal one.
Although she is not the principal wife,
righteousness lies in maintaining the situation to the end.
How can one argue that because Shēn should not have had two wives, she herself should then involve herself in two households?
If she can humble herself,
then it is the righteousness of Zhào Jī.
If it is said she cannot,
the government should have a regulation.
The first principal, then the successor,
is a tradition.
The general opinion's criticism is too severe,
so I briefly present a different view."
Liàng followed Qiānqī's deliberation and made his decision.
The Wǔ Jīng Tōng Yì holds that if one has virtue, one is given a good posthumous title;
if one has no virtue, one is given a bad posthumous title.
Therefore, even a lord and his minister can share the same title.
In the early Wèi dynasty, Emperor Xuān was initially given the posthumous title Wén Hóu,
and King Jǐng was given Wǔ Hóu.
King Wén stated that it was inappropriate to share titles with the two imperial ancestors,
so they were changed to Xuān Wén and Zhōng Wǔ.
When King Wén received the title of King of Jìn,
the Wèi emperor again posthumously named Xuān Wén as King Xuān,
and Zhōng Wǔ as King Jǐng.
In the tenth month of the eighth year of Tàikāng,
the Grand Master of Ceremonies posthumously titled the late Grand Master of Ceremonies, Baron of Pínglíng Guō Yì, as Jǐng Hóu.
The relevant officials memorialized, saying:
"Since Jìn received the Mandate,
among the titles and posthumous names of our imperial ancestors, none have been shared by their subjects.
Therefore, Guō Yì being titled Jǐng, which is the same as Emperor Jǐng,
is unacceptable.
He should be titled Mù instead."
Wáng Jì, Yáng Pú, and others all said:
"For an endless dynasty,
posthumous titles are not unique.
If all are to be avoided,
it will be difficult to maintain the system completely.
If none are avoided,
it is again not the禮 (lǐ) of honoring and exalting.
It is appropriate to follow the principle of avoiding taboo names,
but only for the ancestors of the seven ancestral temples,
not for the temples that have been moved or destroyed."
Chéng Càn, Wǔ Mào, and Liú Nà all said:
"Shared posthumous titles are not a concern.
Posthumous titles are a great ritual of the state,
used to encourage the times and establish teachings,
and to extend the profound principles between heaven and humanity.
Thus, even for a lord and father,
there are instances where their righteousness is not exalted,
and for ministers and sons,
they may become prominent through their conduct.
Therefore, it enables those above and below to advance in virtue,
without any slackness or neglect.
Your minister wishes that this holy age will align with Yáo and Shùn,
and follow the Zhōu custom of shared posthumous titles,
abandoning the recent Hán and Wèi practice of avoiding shared titles."
They also cited the Duke of Zhōu and his son both being posthumously titled Wén.
Emperor Wǔ issued an edict saying:
"It is not that a lord and minister cannot share the same title;
it is simply that Yì's title Jǐng is inappropriate.
He should be titled Jiǎn."
In the fourth year of Tàiyuán,
the侍中 (shìzhōng) Wáng Xīnzhī memorialized that a lord and minister sharing posthumous titles was not a concern.
The Shangshū memorialized that Xīnzhī's words were correct.
The emperor approved.
General of Agile Cavalry Wēn Jiào's former wife, Lady Lǐ,
died when Jiào was still of humble status.
He later married Lady Wáng and Lady Hé,
both of whom died before Jiào.
When Jiào passed away,
the court asked Chén Shū:
"Should all three be considered夫人 (fūrén)?"
Shū replied:
"The Lǐ Jì states, 'If a wife dies as a fūrén,
[二０]and her husband later does not become a Grandee,
then she is interred with her wife,
and the sacrificial animals are not changed.
If a wife dies,
and her husband later becomes a Grandee,
then when she is interred with her husband,
the sacrificial animals for a Grandee are used.'
Thus, if the husband is honored at court,
the wife is esteemed in the household.
Although she died before her husband,
honor and disgrace always follow the husband.
The Lǐ Jì says, 'A wife is interred with her ancestral grandmother.
If there are three ancestral grandmothers,
she is interred with the one she is closest to.'
According to the rites,
then all three are fūrén.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the system of one man marrying nine women has been abolished.
In recent times, there is no longer the rite of a successor wife;
if the first wife dies, one marries again.
If they were treated with禮 (lǐ) in life,
then they should not be demoted in death."
Yǔ Wèizhī said:
"A wife from humble times cannot simultaneously be a fūrén,
unless there is an imperial decree of posthumous enfeoffment."
Wēn Jiào's biography states
that Lady Wáng and Lady Hé were posthumously granted the seals and ribbons of a fūrén,
but Lady Lǐ was not.
In the eleventh year of Yǒnghé,
the Kingdom of Péngchéng requested a posthumous title for Consort Lǐ Tàifēi.
Bóshì Cáo Dānzhī deliberated, saying:
"The conduct of a husband and wife need not be the same;
one cannot use the husband's posthumous title for the wife.
In the Chūnqiū, there are many women with posthumous titles,
and the Jīng contains no critical remarks,
indicating that it is permissible by rites to have a posthumous title."
Hú Nà said:
"According to the rites,
a wife lives by her husband's rank,
and dies by her husband's posthumous title.
That the夫人 (Fūrén) in the Chūnqiū had posthumous titles
simply means they did not follow the rites.
Consort Lǐ of Ānpíng Xiànwáng, Consort Zhūgě of Lángyé Wǔwáng, and Consort Péi of Tàifù Dōnghǎi Wáng all have no posthumous titles.
Today, it is proper to follow the old precedents."
Wáng Biāozhī said:
"If women have posthumous titles,
it is because the rites have fallen into disuse.
That Shēngzǐ was given a posthumous title
was considered improper by Fú Qián and other scholars.
Dù Yù also said, 'According to the rites,
women have no posthumous titles.'
The absence of critical remarks in the Chūnqiū
is what is meant by 'self-evident without needing to be condemned.'
In recent times, only empresses have had posthumous titles."
Tàiwèi Xún Yǐ presented a posthumous title law, stating:
"If a posthumous title is bestowed but the distance is too great for the burial to be attended,
all sealing documents should be sent down to the subordinate officials,
who shall dispatch the overseeing chief officers to present the documents and bestow the posthumous title at the family sacrifice."
In the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán,
Kǒng Ānguó was summoned to be Shìzhōng.
Ānguó submitted a memorial stating that Huángmén Láng Wáng Yú's name violated his private taboo,
and thus he could not jointly sign,
requesting to be relieved of his duties.
The responsible officials deliberated, saying:
"To taboo a name eternally
is something everyone agrees with in their hearts;
to be startled in one's heart upon hearing a name
also clarifies previous admonitions.
Yet the rites also say, 'The ruler has no private taboos,
while a Dàfū has public taboos,'
implying no private taboos.
It also says, 'The Shī and Shū do not taboo,
and one does not taboo when reading texts.'
Is this not the public good overriding private sentiment,
and the royal regulations superseding family rites?
Shàngshū Ānzhòng Nán Chén had previously submitted a memorial stating that Bīngcáo Láng Wáng Yòu's name violated his father's taboo,
requesting to be relieved of his post.
A clear imperial edict was issued,
allowing him to switch departments.
This was an act of grace outside the regulations.
However, recently people have been imitating each other,
and once the source and flow are opened,
there is no knowing its limit.
The imperial court's rites are grand,
all officials are at their posts,
and officials are arrayed in their departments,
constantly coming into contact.
If, because of private taboos,
people follow their hearts,
then changing offices and altering positions
will be endless,
which not only violates the laws and regulations
but also undermines the political system.
We request a definitive ruling on this."
This was agreed to.
Textual Criticism Notes
Among the five classes of rites,
the third is called 'guest rites,'
which refers to the ceremonies of homage, audience, and assemblies.
From the Zhōu dynasty onwards,
these rites became increasingly complex.
After Qín destroyed scholarship,
the old traditions were fragmented.
When Hàn arose,
Shūsūn Tōng was first tasked with formulating rites,
drawing upon the ceremonies of previous generations,
though often making changes.
The Hàn ceremonies included the 'grand assembly rite':
on the first day of the year,
seven *kè* before the night clepsydra finished,
bells would ring to receive congratulations.
Dukes and Marquises and those below them would hold ceremonial gifts and line the courtyard,
while those of two thousand *shí* and above would ascend the hall and proclaim 'Wànsuì!'
Then music would be played and a banquet held.
When Wèi Wǔdì made Yè his capital,
the grand assembly was held in Wénchāng Diàn,
using Hàn ceremonies,
and also featured hundreds of elaborate lanterns.
When the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate,
Wǔdì revised the Yuánhuì ceremony,
which is recorded in the Xiánníng notes.
Fù Xuán's Yuánhuì Fù says:
"He examined the remnants of the Xià Hòu's teachings,
synthesized the traditions and arts of Yīn and Zhōu,
adopted the old ceremonies of Qín and Hàn,
and established the grand assembly of the first month."
This shows that he drew upon various dynasties.
The commentary of Xiánníng 咸寧 says:
"On the day of the first lunar month,
officials responsible for each department would set up their accommodations.
When ten *kè* 刻 of the night clepsydra had not yet passed,
all the ministers gathered and arrived,
and the court torches were lit.
The Emperor offered felicitations,
stood up,
presented a report,
and then offered felicitations to the Empress.
Upon returning,
he entered through the Yúnlóng 雲龍 and Dōng Zhōnghuámén 東中華門 gates,
proceeded to the area below the Dōnggé 東閤,
and sat down.
When seven *kè* 刻 of the clepsydra had not yet passed,
all officials, from the *shòuzhì lángguān* 受贄郎官 (officials receiving ceremonial gifts) downwards to the *jìlì* 計吏 (accountants), entered and stood in their designated places.
Those guarding the steps were arrayed as in the ceremony of 'facing the balcony'.
When five *kè* 刻 of the clepsydra had not yet passed,
the *Yèzhě* 謁者, *Púshè* 僕射, and *Dàhónglú* 大鴻臚 each reported that the ministers had taken and settled in their positions.
When the clepsydra finished its count,
the *Shìzhōng* 侍中 reported that preparations outside were complete.
The Emperor emerged,
bells and drums played,
and all officials bowed down.
The *Tàicháng* 太常 led the Emperor to ascend to the imperial seat,
the bells and drums stopped,
and all officials rose.
The *Dàhónglú* 大鴻臚 knelt and reported, 'I request the morning felicitations.'
The *Zhǎnglǐláng* 掌禮郎 announced, 'The Emperor invites the kings to ascend.'
The *Dàhónglú* 大鴻lú knelt and announced, 'Your vassal kings, such-and-such, present one white jade disk each,
and offer felicitations with two bows.'
The *Tàicháng* 太常 reported, 'All kings have ascended.'
The *Yèzhě* 謁者 led them up the hall,
facing the imperial seat.
The Emperor rose,
and the kings bowed twice.
The Emperor sat,
and they bowed twice again.
They knelt and placed the jade disks before the imperial seat,
and bowed twice again.
Once the ceremony was complete,
the *Yèzhě* 謁者 led them down the hall,
and they returned to their former positions.
The *Zhǎnglǐláng* 掌禮郎 announced, 'The Emperor invites the *Tàiwèi* 太尉 and others.'
Thereupon, the *Gōng* 公, *Tèjìn* 特進, *Xiongnú Nán Chányú* 匈奴南單于, and *Jīnzǐ Jiāngjūn* 金紫將軍 positioned themselves west of the *Dàhónglú* 大鴻臚;
the *Zhōng Èrqiānshí* 中二千石, *Èrqiānshí* 二千石, *Qiānshí* 千石, and *Liùbǎishí* 六百石 positioned themselves west of the *Dàxínglìng* 大行令;
all faced north and prostrated.
The *Hónglú* 鴻臚 knelt and announced, 'The *Tàiwèi* 太尉, *Zhōng Èrqiānshí* 中二千石, and others present jade disks, furs, silks, lambs, geese, and pheasants,
and offer felicitations with two bows.'
The *Tàicháng* 太常 announced, 'The Emperor invites the *Gōng* 公 and others to ascend.'
The *Zhǎnglǐ* 掌禮 led the *Gōng* 公 up to the *Jīnzǐ Jiāngjūn* 金紫將軍's position in the hall.
The Emperor rose,
and they all bowed twice.
The Emperor sat,
and they bowed twice again.
They knelt and placed the jade disks, furs, and silks before the imperial seat,
and bowed twice again.
Once the ceremony was complete,
the *Yèzhě* 謁者 led them down the hall,
and they returned to their former positions.
When the *Gōng* 公 placed the jade disks and completed the ceremony,
the *Dàxínglìng* 大行令 simultaneously announced to those below the hall,
and the *Zhōng Èrqiānshí* 中二千石 and lower followed suit.
Once the ceremony was complete,
the ceremonial gifts were handed to the *Zhìláng* 贄郎,
who handed the jade disks and silks to the *Yèzhě* 謁者,
and the lambs, geese, and pheasants to the *Tàiguān* 太官.
The *Tàiyuèlìng* 太樂令 knelt and requested the performance of elegant music,
and the music played in succession.
The *Chénghuánglìng* 乘黃令 then brought out the imperial carriage,
the Emperor withdrew and entered,
and all officials sat down.
When six *kè* 刻 of the day clepsydra had passed,
the various barbarian and Hu 胡 guests entered in succession,
and after all had bowed twice,
they sat down.
Three *kè* 刻 after the Emperor had entered, he emerged again,
and bells and drums played.
The *Yèzhě* 謁者 and *Púshè* 僕射 knelt and reported, 'We request all ministers to ascend.'
The *Yèzhě* 謁者 led the kings, *Gōng* 公, and *Èrqiānshí* 二千石 up the hall,
while the *Qiānshí* 千石 and *Liùbǎishí* 六百石 remained in their original positions.
The *Yèzhě* 謁者 led the kings to the wine vessel to pour longevity wine,
and kneeling, handed it to the *Shìzhōng* 侍中.
The *Shìzhōng* 侍中 knelt and placed it before the imperial seat,
and the kings returned.
The kings poured wine for themselves and placed it before their positions,
and the *Yèzhě* 謁者 knelt and reported, 'Your vassal kings, such-and-such, present wine cups,
and with two bows, offer wishes for ten thousand years of longevity.'
Music from the four sides played,
and all officials bowed twice.
After drinking,
they bowed twice again.
The *Yèzhě* 謁者 led the kings and others back to their original positions.
Those below the steps were passed word to take their seats,
and all ministers knelt and assented.
The *Shìzhōng* 侍中, *Zhōngshūlìng* 中書令, and *Shàngshūlìng* 尚書令 each presented longevity wine in the hall.
The ascending music began,
and the *Tàiguān* 太官 then served imperial wine.
When the imperial wine reached the steps,
the *Tàiguānlìng* 太官令 knelt and handed it to the *Shìláng* 侍郎,
who knelt and presented it before the imperial seat.
Then wine was served to all officials.
The *Tàiyuèlìng* 太樂令 knelt and reported, 'Play the ascending music,'
and it ceased after three repetitions.
The *Tàiguānlìng* 太官令 knelt and requested the imperial meal to be prepared,
and when it reached the steps,
all ministers rose.
The *Tàiguānlìng* 太官令 held the soup and knelt to hand it to the *Sītú* 司徒,
held the rice and knelt to hand it to the *Dàsīnóng* 大司農,
and the *Shàngshí* 尚食 held the tray and simultaneously handed it to the *Chíjié* 持節,
who knelt and presented it before the imperial seat.
The ministers took their seats.
The *Tàiyuèlìng* 太樂令 knelt and reported, 'Play the meal music.'
The *Tàiguān* 太官 served meal trays to all officials.
After the meal,
the *Tàiyuèlìng* 太樂令 knelt and reported, 'We request the music to begin.'
Music played in succession.
The *Gǔchuīlìng* 鼓吹令 then advanced and knelt to report, 'We request the various performances to proceed in order.'
Then the *jìlì* 計吏 from all commanderies were summoned forward,
to receive imperial instructions and admonitions below the steps.
When the banquet and entertainment concluded,
one *Yèzhě* 謁者 knelt and reported, 'We request dismissal.'
Bells and drums played,
all ministers faced north and bowed twice,
and departed."
Thus, the period when seven *kè* 刻 of the night clepsydra had not yet passed was called the "morning felicitations."
When three *kè* 刻 of the day clepsydra had passed, the Emperor emerged again,
and the officials presented longevity wine;
this was called the "daytime assembly."
Thirty female musicians were separately placed outside the yellow tent,
to perform "songs of the inner chambers."
Due to much turmoil south of the Yangtze,
the morning felicitations were no longer observed.
When ten *kè* 刻 of the night clepsydra had not yet passed,
the Xuānyángmén 宣陽門 was opened.
The hall gates were only opened at dawn.
When five *kè* 刻 of the day clepsydra had passed,
the Emperor would emerge to receive felicitations.
When the Crown Prince attended the assembly,
he was positioned below the *sānkè* 三恪 (three eminent guests) but above the kings and *Gōng* 公.
For the Grand Assembly on New Year's Day,
a white beast *zūn* 樽 (wine vessel) was placed in the palace courtyard.
A white beast was placed on top of the *zūn* 樽's lid.
If anyone could offer honest criticism,
this *zūn* 樽 would be opened for them to drink wine.
According to the rites,
the white beast *zūn* 樽 was an ancient custom from Dù Jǔ 杜舉.
The white beast lid,
however, was a later addition,
to symbolize reverence and apprehension.
Under the Wèi 魏 dynasty,
vassal kings were not permitted to have imperial audiences.
During the reign of Emperor Míng 魏明帝 of Wèi,
any who had an audience did so by special grace,
and it was not to be a regular practice.
Then, in the Tàishǐ 泰始 era,
the relevant officials reported:
"As for the feudal states,
the kings, *Gōng* 公, and lower officials who come to court
from the four directions shall be divided into two groups,
rotating every three years,
and then restarting the cycle.
If there is a temporary reason for delay,
it shall be postponed until the following year.
After coming to court in the following year,
they must complete another three years before attending court again,
not deviating from the original number.
For the court ceremony, they shall personally hold the jade disks,
according to the old court regulations.
In years when they do not attend court,
each shall send a *qīng* 卿 to present tribute."
The report was approved.
The kings and marquises south of the Yangtze did not reside in their feudal states.
If they received appointments and resided outside,
they followed the rites of *fāngbó* 方伯, *cìshǐ* 刺史, and *èrqiānshí* 二千石,
and there was no system of court audiences and tributes,
hence this ritual was subsequently abolished.
The Hàn dynasty, in the tenth month of Gāo Dì's reign, pacified Qín
and made that the beginning of the year.
When Wǔ Dì ascended the throne,
although he adopted the Xià calendar,
on the first day of each month,
up until the first day of the tenth month,
there were still regular feasts and gatherings.
The ritual involved,
before seven khắc of the night watch had passed,
receiving congratulations and tributes:
dukes and marquises presented jade bi;
officials ranked Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí and Èr Qiān Shí presented lambs;
officials ranked Qiān Shí and Liù Bǎi Shí presented geese;
and officials ranked Sì Bǎi Shí and below presented pheasants.
The Sān Gōng presented the jade bi on the steps before the imperial throne,
facing north.
The Tàicháng praised, saying, "The Emperor rises as sovereign!"
The Sān Gōng prostrated themselves.
The Emperor sat,
and then they advanced with the jade bi.
All officials offered congratulations,
and those ranked Èr Qiān Shí and above ascended the steps to shout "Wàn Suì!"
and raised their wine cups.
For the imperial meal,
the Sītú presented the soup,
and the Dà Sī nóng presented the cooked rice,
while the music of "Shí Jǔ" was performed.
All officials received gifts,
feasted,
and grand music was played,
just like the rituals of Yuán Zhèng.
During the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, on the winter solstice, envoys from various states and all officials offered congratulations,
followed by a small gathering.
This ceremony was secondary to that of the New Year's Day.
In ancient times, no emperors failed to conduct巡狩 (xún shǒu) tours.
Wèi Wén Dì's reign coincided with the division of the realm into three,
with many affairs in various regions,
and the imperial chariot moved frequently,
with no year of peace for the people involved in service.
This was a response to the needs of the time,
not an adherence to old regulations.
Míng Dì conducted three eastern xún shǒu tours in total.
Wherever he went, he inquired after and comforted the elderly,
alleviated the suffering of the sick,
and sometimes bestowed grain and silk,
displaying the style of ancient imperial tours.
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ of Qí Wáng,
he toured Luòyáng County,
bestowing gifts upon the elderly and diligent farmers, each according to their circumstances.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Wǔ Dì,
an edict was issued to the cìshǐ, èr qiān shí, and zhǎng lì, saying:
"Ancient kings
conducted xún shǒu tours to the regional mountains at seasonal times.
Next were the two Bó who reported on their duties,
or else the xíngrén who inspected on behalf of the emperor.
Therefore, even the most remote and humble
felt no obstruction in their hearts,
and the sentiments of the lower classes reached the top,
while the imperial directives were widely communicated,
so that even the [⿰魚眾]guǎ (isolated and widowed)
all obtained what they needed,
thereby establishing a lasting legacy and
a glorious reputation that still endures.
I have been on the throne for several years,
feeling as if standing on the edge of a deep abyss,
rising early and being vigilant until evening,
unable to sleep when dawn breaks,
sitting and waiting for day,
pondering the droughts, floods, and calamities in the four directions,
and feeling distressed by them.
I diligently humble myself,
wishing that everything be appropriate.
I constantly fear that officials act out of personal feelings,
with insufficient sincerity,
and that the myriad affairs are numerous and complicated,
fearing some oversight,
leading to errors in governance and punishment,
which I might not be able to fully review.
If the common people have faults,
it rests with me alone.
As the years are not easy,
I have not had time to consult or undertake xún shǒu inspections.
How then can I relieve the distress of those below?
Now I send envoys, holding the imperial credentials as shìzhōng, fù gěishì, huángmén shìláng, bearing my mandate to go out in four directions,
traveling throughout the realm,
personally meeting the cìshǐ, èr qiān shí, and zhǎng lì,
reiterating my intentions,
seeking information on gains, losses, benefits, and detriments, and all suitable matters,
observing and inspecting governance and education,
and inquiring about the sufferings of the people.
The Zhōu classics state: 'Make a book of the benefits and harms to the myriad people,
a book of the appropriateness and inappropriateness of rituals, customs, governance, and prohibitions,
a book of violent rebellions, evil deeds, and violations of decrees,
a book of pestilence, famine, hardship, and poverty,
and a book of prosperity, harmony, peace, and stability.
In each state, differentiate them,
and report back to the king.'
These old regulations and former instructions
are to be followed.
Upon their return, they shall present a detailed report,
so that I may clearly observe the distant and hidden,
as if personally traveling.
You Dàfū and Jūnzǐ,
each give your utmost attention,
attend to your duties,
offer good plans and excellent strategies,
sincere advice and serious warnings,
and express them fully to the envoys,
concealing nothing.
I shall humbly await
your efforts and exhortations,
to fulfill my intentions."
According to the Xīn Lǐ,
when conducting xún shǒu tours to the regional mountains,
a chai (burnt offering) and wàng (distant sacrifice) are performed, and an earthen altar and palace are erected according to ritual.
When vassal lords came for an audience,
the reception and presentation of tribute were all according to court rituals,
but no banners were erected.
Zhì Yú believed:
"In the audience ritual,
when vassal lords have an audience with the Son of Heaven,
each erects their banner.
Banner symbols distinguish rank and mandate,
showing hierarchy.
The Shī Jīng says, 'When the jūnzǐ arrive,
one observes their banners.'
It is fitting to establish in the new ritual
that banners be erected as in the old ritual."
The emperor approved this proposal.
However, throughout the Jìn dynasty,
this ritual was not implemented.
There is no mention of Fēng Shàn in the classics.
The Lǐ Jì states that one serves Heaven in accordance with Heaven,
and serves Earth in accordance with Earth,
and ascends to Heaven via famous mountains,
whereupon phoenixes descend
and qílín appear.
The reason the Son of Heaven conducts xún shǒu tours,
reaching the regional mountains,
is to burn faggots and sacrifice to Heaven,
to announce his accomplishments.
This ritual is similar but not identical to Fēng Shàn.
All the apocryphal and prognostication texts say
that a king performs fēng on Tài Shān
and shàn on Liángfǔ,
changing the dynastic name and recording the reign title.
The Qín and Hàn dynasties carried out this ceremony,
and previous historians have each described their systems.
In the Huángchū reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Jìang Jì, the Protector-General, submitted a memorial, saying:
“Of the great rites of an emperor,
the imperial tour is foremost;
to glorify ancestors and enshrine spirits,
the Feng and Shan sacrifices are paramount.
Therefore, from ancient times, those who revolutionized and received the mandate
have never failed to tread Liángfù,
ascend Mount Tài,
engrave eternal names,
and record the interactions between Heaven and man.
Hence Sīmǎ Xiāngrú said that since the advent of writing,
seventy-two rulers
either followed the path of their predecessors
or observed the legacy of those who followed.
The Grand Historian said,
‘If a ruler possesses sagely brilliance but fails to declare it,
it is the fault of the officials.’
Thus, if magnificent achievements and illustrious virtues
are not carved on the stones of Liángshān,
there is no way to manifest the emperor’s accomplishments
and display an immortal spectacle to the multitude.
The saying goes,
‘To praise the beauty of Yáo and Shùn while being a ruler
is like a son praising another’s father in the presence of his own parents.’
Now, the great Wèi succeeded a hundred kings in their decay and disorder,
rescued those wandering in distress and peril,
took up the thread of decline after a thousand years,
and continued the defunct enterprise of a hundred generations.
Starting from Wǔ and Wén,
down to Your Sacred Person,
you have participated in perfecting the Way of Heaven and Earth,
and managed the transformation of men and spirits.
Heaven’s recompense,
auspicious omens, and manifest signs,
when compared to ancient times,
find no suitable analogy.
Yet, through generations until now,
the great rites have not been performed.
Although the intention is to completely eradicate bandits
and cleanse remaining impurities,
there has been no time for this matter.
If that were the case,
had the Sānmiáo been stubbornly rebellious in the Jiānghǎi region,
the great Shùn should have abandoned the eastern tour ceremony;
had the Xú Yí been unruly in the Huái and Sì regions,
Zhōu Chéng should have halted the Dàiyuè rites.
Moreover, last year the Wú barbarians were defeated in the Jiānghàn region,
and this year the Shǔ rebels were slaughtered in Lǒngyòu.
Their tremors and internal collapse
will not last long,
and will not hinder the matter of the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
This ceremony has long been neglected,
and cannot be decided hastily.
It is proper to instruct the high officials
to extensively compile the rites,
divine the year and examine the time,
and announce it to Shangdì,
to fulfill the expectations of all under Heaven.
I, your servant, holding a military post,
cannot bear the weight of this great wish,
and brave death to make it known.”
The edict said:
“Hearing these words from Jìang Jì
makes me sweat profusely.
Since the beginning of the world,
there have been only seventy-odd rulers who performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
Hence the Grand Historian said,
‘Although there were rulers who received the mandate,
their accomplishments were not always sufficient,
which is why there were gaps of over a thousand years,
or in recent times several centuries,
during which the ceremonies were incomplete and could not be recorded.’
What virtues have I cultivated
to dare hope for such a thing!
Does Jì perhaps think that there is no Guǎn Zhòng in this age,
and that I have the ambition of Duke Huán to ascend Mount Tài!
I do not deceive Heaven.
What Jì said,
though ornate,
does not help me.
Let the Grand Councillors, Court Attendants, Presidents of the Boards, and Palace Regular Attendants simply dismiss it,
and do not discuss it further,
nor is there any need to reply to the edict.”
Although the Son of Heaven rejected Jì’s proposal,
he did in fact have Gāotáng Lóng draft the Feng and Shan ceremonies,
but because the empire was not yet unified,
he did not wish to immediately perform the great rites.
When Lóng died,
they were no longer performed.
When Emperor Wǔ pacified Wú
and unified the empire,
in the ninth month, on the Gēngyín day of the first year of Tàikāng,

Wèi Guàn, President of the Board, Shān Tāo, Left Chief Administrator of the Board, Wèi Shū, Right Chief Administrator of the Board, Liú Shí, President of the Board, Zhāng Huá, Minister of Works, and others submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servants have heard that from the beginning of living beings,
there have been rulers,
but the number of years and reigns
cannot be fully recorded.
Those who established virtue and saved the world,
spreading benevolent influence,
and ascended Mount Tài for the Feng sacrifice were seventy-four houses,
of which fourteen had discernible posthumous titles.
Those who sank into oblivion and left no trace
are innumerable.
The virtue of great Jìn
originated with Chónglí,
who indeed aided Zhuānxù,
and down to Xià and Shāng,
their generations ordered Heaven and Earth.
When it came to Zhōu,
they did not lose their lineage.
When the Metal virtue was about to rise,
generations produced enlightened sages,
pacifying Shǔhàn externally,
and uniting hearts within the seas.
The flourishing of military prowess
truly stemmed from civil virtue.
As for Your Majesty,
having received the mandate and ascended the throne,
you have grandly established a great enterprise,
and all living beings look up to you.
Only the regions of Jiānghú, Yuán, and Xiāng,
where fierce and defiant rebels were entrenched,
had for generations not submitted.
With divine wisdom and sole decision,
you commanded generals to campaign,
and with temporary application of military might,
in a few tens of days, they were pacified.
You captured their tyrants,
pardoned their crimes and rebellions,
and with cloud-like cover and rain-like bounty,
the eight directions came to unity,
and your fame and teachings reached
the four extremities.
Even the campaigns of Huáng and Xuān,
the distant strategies of great Yǔ,
and the successive generations of Zhōu,
how can they surpass the present!
As for the mysterious stones and plain texts,
recording ancient titles,
symbolized by numbers and
announced by events,
even the omens of the ancient Hé Tú and Luò Shū
are no more than these.
It is fitting to proclaim the great ceremony,
perform rites to the central sacred mountain,
perform the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
and the Shan sacrifice on Liángfù,
declare your virtuous title,
manifest your supreme status,
receive heavenly blessings,
and strengthen the common people,
engraving a monument for a thousand years,
and spreading fame for future generations,
so that descendants for a hundred ages
will all be inspired.
This is the grand undertaking of emperors,
and the ultimate hope of Heaven and man.”
The edict said:
“Though the remaining rebels are now annihilated,
externally there are frontier alarms,
and internally the common people are not yet settled.
This matter of great virtue
is not yet to be discussed.”
Guàn and others again submitted a memorial, saying:
“Now, extending eastward to the sea,
and westward to the flowing sands,
to the north of the great desert,
and to the southern gates of the sun,
all are connected and subject.
The vast traces of Yǔ
are now indeed surpassed.
The Way of Heaven and man is complete,
and illustrious achievements are manifest.
It is fitting to perform rites to the Earth Spirits,
ascend Mount Tài for the Feng sacrifice,
and offer sincerity to Shangdì,
to respond to the wishes of men and spirits.
We beg to proceed as previously memorialized.”
The edict said:
“Now, yin and yang are not yet harmonious,
and criminal governance is not yet appropriate.
The common people have not yet found their proper place.
How can one engrave merits and proclaim success! ”
The edict did not grant permission.
Guàn and others further memorialized, saying:
“Your subjects have heard that those who occupy the position of emperor or king
must have a preordained period of cosmic fortune
and a response from Heaven’s Mandate;
those who achieve the meritorious work of saving the myriad people
must possess a countenance of flourishing virtue
and the grand ceremony of reporting success.
There is nothing that can be falsified,
and there is nothing that one dares to decline—
this has been the way since antiquity.
However, your sagely edict is humble and self-effacing,
repeatedly declining this ritual.
Although flourishing virtue resides in Your Majesty,
you push it away and do not accept it.
The Three Ducal Ministers’ offices are in charge of Heaven and Earth,
and they indeed manage people and things.
The great affairs of the state
are discussed here.
Therefore, the Fēngshàn ceremony during the Hàn dynasty
was not the responsibility of these officials,
nor was it within their purview.
Your subjects’ previous memorial
expounded on the merits of your ancestors,
the corresponding response of Heaven’s Mandate,
and Your Majesty’s virtue,
which unites the four seas.
Tracing antiquity and examining the present,
it is fitting to perform this ritual.
As for determining the specific year and month,
it requires deliberation by the Five Bureaus
before being reported to Your Majesty.”
The edict said:
“Although the lands south of the river have been cleared and pacified,
this is entirely due to the efforts of those who dealt with the affairs;
how can it be sufficient to report success?
I merely hope that the multitude of officials will contemplate promoting great transformations
to bring peace to the realm,
so that the common people may benefit
and rest with it.
This is my constant hope, day and night;
there is no need to send it down to the various bureaus again.”
Guàn and others further memorialized:
“Your subjects have heard that among the rulers of the Táng, Yú, and Three Dynasties who saved the world and achieved great deeds,
none failed to receive Heaven’s blessing from above
and accord with the will of the people below,
ascending Jièqiū
and treading Liángfù.
None ever declined,
for indeed it is not to be declined.
Now, Your Majesty’s achievements surpass those of a hundred kings,
and your virtue is unparalleled.
Your magnificent accomplishments and grand designs,
your august enterprise,
are indeed beyond what your subjects can fully elaborate.
Yet the sagely will is humble and self-effacing,
repeatedly diminishing itself.
When the time comes, you do not respond;
you push away glory and do not accept it.
This would omit the supreme ceremony of a glorious era
and block the earnest hopes of the spirits.
It would cause the ordinances and plans of the great Jìn
to be out of step with the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Your subjects truly dare not obey the edict,
and request that the previous memorial be put into effect.”
The edict said:
“We should rather collectively think about promoting the Way
to bring peace to the myriad achievements.
Let us wait for other years;
there is no need for further contention.”
The ducal ministers and responsible officials further memorialized:
“Since antiquity, sagely and enlightened rulers,
who gloriously settled the four seas,
performed Fēngshàn on famous mountains,
recorded in historical annals;
seventy-four rulers have done so.
When Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world,
they made inspection tours to the Four Peaks,
personally practicing their Way.
The Yì records ‘observing customs and examining the regions,’
the Lǐ has ‘ascending to the central altar for Heaven,’
and the Shī praises ‘ascending its high mountains’—
all are recorded in books and documents.
Wénwáng, as the Xībó, served Yīn,
and Zhōugōng, as a vassal of Lǔ, was ranked among the feudal lords;
some offered sacrifices on Qíshān,
others performed ceremonies on Tàishān.
Merely because of their sagely virtue,
they were still able to perform these rites.
Since then,
those whose merits were meager but usurped this ritual
are countless,
yet their posthumous titles and appellations have not been extinguished,
persisting to this day.
What more of Gāozǔ Xuānhuángdì, who founded the royal enterprise
and brought peace to all lands beyond the seas;
Shìzōng Jǐnghuángdì, who accomplished great deeds
and pacified the realm;
Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì, who received the Mandate to establish Jìn
and pacified Shǔ-Hàn;
and Your Majesty, who responded to the opportune moment, rising like a dragon,
unifying the six directions,
spreading benevolence to all living beings,
and whose might shakes all beyond comparison?
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty lost its rule,
Wú and Shǔ stood like tripods,
and since the outbreak of war,
nearly a hundred years have passed.
The terrain was perilous, customs varied,
and people’s hopes were cut off by impassable barriers.
Now, the unrestrained rebels
have been pacified in two generations.
Without Your Majesty’s brilliant divine martiality,
which anticipates and does not contravene Heaven’s will,
who could achieve such august success as this?
Your subjects are fortunate to have encountered this epochal gathering in a thousand years,
personally experiencing great transformations
and witnessing grand peace.
This is the ultimate in impartiality and beauty;
who would contend for the right to yield it?
It is fitting to follow the example of previous dynasties,
and make ancient times your model,
engraving achievements on Dàiyuè,
performing Fēng and Shàn ceremonies to report completion,
promoting the institutions of rites and music,
rectifying the ordinances of the Sān Yōng,
and making your name known for ten thousand generations,
to glorify your ancestors.
Therefore, overcome with this great aspiration,
we dare to risk death to report this.
We request to inform the Tàicháng
to fully prepare the rituals and report back.”
The edict said:
“The matter discussed is indeed a grand event for successive generations,
but for now, it cannot be so.”
And then it was definitively rejected.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
he wished to honor Grand Consort Zhāng Huángtài.
Huán Wēn deliberated that she should be called Tàifūrén.
Jiāng Bìn, the Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs, deliberated, saying:
"Emperor Yú Shùn embodied the nature of benevolence and filiality,
fulfilling the rites of serving his parents.
He was noble as the Son of Heaven,
possessing all within the four seas,
yet Gǔsǒu had no place to stand,
no rank or title.
His profound filial heart,
vast as the boundless heavens,
would he tolerate his father's low status
and not manifest him with an honorable title?
Was it not because a son has no right to ennoble his father,
that reason was exhausted and righteousness yielded,
leaving no way to express his feelings?
The Spring and Autumn Annals states, 'Jì Jiāng of Jì returned to the capital,'
and the Commentary says, 'Regarding their children,
even if she becomes the Queen of the Son of Heaven,
they still call her "our Jì Jiāng."'
This means a child's exalted status does not extend to their parents.
Some believe that a child's exalted status does not extend to their parents,
so why did King Wǔ posthumously grant titles to Grand King, King Jì, and King Wén? The Three Kings of Zhōu,
whose virtues matched heaven and earth,
and from whom the rise of kingly rule began,
it was from this point.
Therefore, King Wǔ looked back to his ancestors' legacy,
then received the mandate of heaven,
posthumously honoring his ancestors,
clarifying that a son's exalted status does not add to his parents.
According to the Rites, 'The young do not eulogize the old,
the lowly do not eulogize the noble.'
If the young and lowly are still not allowed to praise the old and noble,
how much less dare one bestow them with an honorable appointment!
Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ was moved by the words of the household master and honored Tài Gōng.
Xún Yuè believed that no filial piety is greater than revering one's father,
but to add a son's nobility to parents,
the household master's words were excessive.
When it came to Emperor Xiàozhāng,
he did not bestow an honorable title upon Lady Jiǎ,
but instead greatly enriched her with gold, jewels, money, and silk.
This was not because his filial piety was lacking,
but because the sacred canons could not be overstepped.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
when an adopted son succeeded to the state,
his mother could become a Fūrén.
I am unsure if the son directly appointed his mother,
or if it was announced at the ancestral temple by the command of the former ruler to appoint her.
I secretly observed the imperial edict, it said that
you are to personally go to the imperial hall to confer upon Lady Guì the title of Huáng Tàifēi.
Now, to say the emperor gives a command and appoints Lady Guì,
this is a son ennobling his mother.
For Lady Guì to bow facing north and accept,
this is a mother acting as a subject to her son.
Heaven is noble and earth is lowly,
positions are established; mother is noble and son is lowly,
human relations are ordered.
Though you wish to exalt Lady Guì,
you are actually debasing her;
though you clarify the national codes,
you are actually abolishing them.
Moreover, the emperor's actions
will certainly be recorded by historians.
If they are to be inscribed in records
to be shown to future generations,
would this not be unfilial?
I secretly believe it should be announced at Xiǎnzōng's temple,
stating that Lady Guì's benevolence and virtue are supreme,
and it is proper to bestow special rites,
to repay the kindness of her nurture and upbringing.
This act would be by the command of the former spirit,
not a matter initiated by the current ruler.
Although 'Fēi' and 'Hòu' are titles for consorts of the ruler,
yet from Hòu downwards there are Fūrén and Jiǔpín,
but no title of Fēi.
Grand Administrator Huán said it is appropriate to advance her title to Tàifūrén,
which is not inappropriate.
If Fūrén is considered too low,
one could say Huáng Tàifūrén.
Huáng
means ruler;
calling her 'Ruler's Tàifūrén' would be appropriate in name and rite."
The Emperor specifically issued an edict to appoint her Huáng Tàifēi.
On the day of Bǐngchén in the third month,
he sent Wáng Tián, acting as Grand Tutor, to confer the imperial seal and ribbons, and ceremonial robes,
all exactly like those of an Empress Dowager.
He also issued an edict saying:
"Should court officials not show respect to the Grand Consort,
is this in accordance with the rites or not?"
Jiāng Yōu, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, deliberated:
"If the rank is not supreme,
one should not offer full respect."
Emperor Xiàowǔ posthumously honored Grand Consort Zhèng of Kuàijī as Empress Dowager Jiǎnwén,
and an edict asked,
"Should her tomb be opened?"
Wáng Xún replied:
"According to the posthumous enfeoffments of the Three Ancestors and Empress Jìng of Zhōngzōng,
none of their tombs were opened,
but rather their burial grounds and structures were reorganized."
When Empress Dowager Chǔ held court,
there was a discussion about the protocol for Chǔ Póu's audience.
Cài Mó and Wáng Biāozhī both stated:
"Even Yú Shùn and Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ still adhered to the filial duties of a son,
let alone an Empress Dowager!
A king is not required to bow to his father."
The eight ministers of the Department of State Affairs deliberated, believing:
"If purely a son, the kingly way is incomplete;
if purely a subject, filial piety is lacking.
It is fitting to act as a subject in public court,
but to maintain strict fatherly respect in private audiences."
According to the precedents of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
the Crown Prince referred to himself as a subject.
The new rites, considering that the Crown Prince is named as a son,
and yet also refers to himself as a subject,
making him both subject and son,
this is illogical.
The system of the Crown Prince calling himself a subject was abolished.
Zhì Yú believed:
"The Classic of Filial Piety says, 'Drawing from serving one's father to serve one's ruler,'
implies the dual role of subject and son,
thus there is no objection to calling oneself a subject.
It is appropriate to reinstate the old system of the Crown Prince calling himself a subject in the new rites."
The emperor followed this.
In the third month, on the day of Wùchén, in the third year of Tàiníng,
Emperor Míng established his imperial son Yǎn as Crown Prince.
On Guǐsì,
an edict stated:
"There is no one noble from birth according to the rites;
thus, the emperor's primary son is treated like a scholar.
However, since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
the heir apparent has been highly honored,
his officials address him as subject,
and all court officials bow to him.
This is completely unreasonable.
When I was formerly in the Eastern Palace,
I did not have time to propose its reform.
Now, at Yǎn's young age,
for him to be treated as a subject by his elders,
will cause him to become accustomed to what he sees daily,
considering it natural.
How can this be taught?
Let the responsible officials refer this to the dukes, ministers, and internal and external officials for full deliberation,
