ensuring it is in strict accordance with the rites."
Biàn Hú, the Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs, deliberated, believing:
"The Rites of Zhōu state that the empress and crown prince do not participate in formal assemblies,
clearly showing that their rites are similar to the ruler's.
All this serves to emphasize the importance of the heir apparent,
distinguishing him as the legitimate heir.
If he is honored as a ruler,
one must bow to him.
If the Crown Prince maintains humility,
he should appropriately return the bow.
I believe that for the establishment of the Crown Prince,
sacrificial announcements are made to Heaven and Earth,
formally positioning him in the heir apparent's palace.
How can this be treated merely as an imperial son's respectful salutation?
I suggest we follow the precedents of Hàn and Wèi,
where the entire court bows."
This was followed.
During the Tàiyuán period,
the Grand Secretary's edict inquired about the etiquette for dukes and princes and below when seeing the Crown Prince, and their clothing.
Chē Yìn, the Palace Attendant and Erudite of the National Academy, deliberated:
"Court officials should wear vermilion robes and black headscarves,
bowing in respect,
and the Crown Prince should return the bow.
The classics and commentaries do not show any such text,
hence Grand Tutor Yáng Hù's memorial congratulating the Crown Prince
says 'I kowtow, worthy of death,'
which is proof of bowing.
Moreover, the edict of the third year of Tàiníng discussed this protocol,
and Grand Secretary Biàn Hú believed it should follow the precedents of Hàn and Wèi,
with the entire court bowing.
As for vermilion robes and ceremonial crowns,
they are only for the imperial court;
a black headscarf is sufficient."
The court's deliberation largely agreed.
In the twelfth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a discussion about the order of precedence between the successors of the Two Kings and the Crown Prince.
Yú Hóngzhī, the Erudite, and the deliberating officials of the Department of State Affairs
all believed:
"The King of Chénliú is the most honored guest of the state.
Although the Crown Prince is the heir apparent of the state,
he is still in the position of a subject,
so the King of Chénliú should sit above the Crown Prince."
Chénliú Wáng Mài submitted a memorial stating that he had been ill for many years
and requested to be dismissed.
The emperor ordered the officials of rites and erudites to deliberate on this.
Erudite Cáo Dān said:
"Mài is the principal sacrificer but has no fixed time for performing sacrifices;
his situation should be similar to Mùzǐ and Mèngzhí."
Wáng Biāozhī said:
"The successors of the Two Kings should not be lightly appointed or deposed.
No record or commentary mentions anyone who, having become a ruler, retired due to illness;
it must be understood that there was no such rite in antiquity.
Mèngzhí and Mùzǐ were at the point of needing to become rulers,
not comparable to Chénliú."
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng,
Emperor Chéng attended court from the imperial carriage,
and dispatched envoys to appoint the Grand Tutor, Grand Commandant, and Minister of Works.
According to ritual protocol,
the imperial music was placed in the courtyard of the hall.
The Palace Gate Bureau submitted a memorial, stating:
"Except for sacrifices and banquets,
there is no regulation for setting up music."
Cài Mó, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, deliberated and said:
"Whenever one respects an affair, one prepares its rites;
when rites are prepared, then the regulations include music.
Music
is for respecting affairs and clarifying righteousness,
not for the entertainment of eyes and ears.
Therefore, it is also used for capping ceremonies,
not just for banquets.
The presence of music at banquets
is also for respecting guests.
Thus, when Xì Zhì was sent to Chǔ,
the Viscount of Chǔ hosted a banquet for him.
Xì Zhì declined, saying: 'We do not forget the good relations of your former ruler,
and you bestow upon us a grand ceremony,
augmented with complete music.'
Examining this statement,
the meaning of banquet music can be understood.
The dukes, marquises, and great ministers
are held in high regard by the ruler;
thus, the emperor rises from his seat for them,
dismounts from his carriage for them,
and addresses them as 'uncle-brother'.
The Zuo Zhuan says, 'A state's ministers
are the ruler's assistants.'
Therefore, on the day of their appointment by envoy,
the emperor personally attends court from the imperial carriage,
and all officials are present in attendance.
This is the meaning of respecting the affair.
In ancient times,
when the Son of Heaven hosted envoys from vassal states,
and when appointing generals and commanders,
or dispatching envoys,
music was always present.
Thus, the 'Preface to the Odes' says: 'Huánghuáng Zhě Huá'
is when the ruler dispatches envoys.'
It also says: 'Cǎi Wēi' is for sending them off,
'Chū Jū' is for comforting them upon their return,
and 'Tuó Dù' is for showing concern for their homecoming.'
All these involve making music and singing.
Now, when dispatching a grand envoy
to appoint chief ministers,
comparing it to the ministers of a vassal state,
the significance is vastly different.
If it is indeed used for minor occasions,
it should certainly be used for major ones.
Therefore, for attending court from the imperial carriage and dispatching envoys,
there should appropriately be music of bells and chimes."
The memorial was presented and accepted.
According to Hán and Wèi customs,
when the concubines of princes and dukes met the official wife,
the official wife did not return the bow.
The new rites stipulated that there should be no unreturned bows,
and a new rule was made for the official wives of consorts and dukes to return the bow to concubines.
Zhì Yú believed:
"According to the rites,
a concubine serves the madam as a daughter-in-law serves her mother-in-law.
A concubine observes mourning for the madam for one year;
if the madam does not return the bow,
then the respect shown is the same as that of a daughter-in-law, yet the concubine is of lower status.
Their names and positions are different,
so there is fundamentally no reciprocity.
'No unreturned bows' does not apply to this situation.
The former sages distinguished between primary and secondary wives
to prevent the gradual erosion of respect.
Even with strict delineation of boundaries,
transgressions still occurred.
It is appropriate to set the new rites
to revert to the old practice."
An imperial edict approved his deliberation.
Among the five categories of rites,
the fourth is military rites,
which serve to harmonize external relations, pacify internal affairs,
preserve the great and establish merit.
However, warfare is an inauspicious affair,
so it is practiced through autumn hunts.
According to Hán protocol,
on Lìqiū (the beginning of autumn),
after the suburban sacrifice was completed,
military might would begin to be displayed,
and an animal would be slaughtered at the east gate,
to be offered at the imperial ancestral temple.
The ritual involved
the emperor riding in the war chariot,
drawn by white horses with red manes,
personally holding a crossbow to shoot the animal,
which was a deer fawn.
The Grand Steward and an usher each carried the fawn in a hunting carriage,
swiftly sending it to the imperial ancestral temple.
Returning to the palace,
envoys were dispatched with bundles of silk
to bestow upon military officials.
Military officials would practice military drills
and battle formations.
The rite of slaughtering the animal
was called chūliú.
All military officers practiced Sūn Wú's sixty-four formations.
Upon returning,
dukes, ministers, and those below them lined up on the front street of Luòyáng.
When the imperial carriage arrived,
the dukes, ministers, and those below them bowed.
The Son of Heaven descended from his carriage,
and the dukes and ministers personally observed his countenance,
before he returned to the palace.
The ancient saying 'descend from the carriage while in the carriage'
was implemented only at this time.
This was a regular practice throughout the Hán dynasty.
In the twenty-first year of Jiàn'ān, during Emperor Xiàn's reign,
officials of the Wèi kingdom memorialized:
"In ancient times, military training was conducted four times a year,
always during agricultural off-seasons.
The Western Hán dynasty, inheriting the Qín system,
did not conduct training for three seasons,
only a grand review in the tenth month.
Now, as military conflicts have not ceased,
and the troops are already well-practiced,
there is no need for four seasonal military trainings.
Instead, on Lìqiū, choose an auspicious day for a grand court assembly of chariots and cavalry,
named 'Yuebīng' (Reviewing the Troops).
[一０] This aligns with ritual names above
and follows the Hán system below."
The memorial was approved.
That winter,
during the military review,
the King of Wèi personally wielded the drum and gong to command advance and retreat.
In the first year of Yánkāng,
Emperor Wén of Wèi became the King of Wèi.
That year, Lìqiū was in the sixth month.
A military review was held in the eastern suburbs,
with dukes and ministers observing the ceremony.
The King rode in a flowered canopy,
personally commanding the rhythm of the drum and gong.
In the tenth month of the first year of Tàihé, during Emperor Míng of Wèi's reign,
another military review was held.
In the ninth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
and in the first year of Xiánníng,
and the fourth year of Tàikāng,
and the winter of the sixth year,
the emperor personally observed the grand review of all armies from Xuānwǔ Guān,
but did not personally command their advance and retreat.
After Emperor Huì,
this rite was abolished.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng during Emperor Yuán's reign,
an imperial edict commanded the Left and Right Guards and various camps to practice,
following the grand practice ceremony to form the 'Goose Feather Formation'.
In the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng,
an imperial edict commanded internal and external armies to perform mock battles in the southern suburban training ground,
hence the place was named 'Dòuchǎng' (Battlefield).
Thereafter, the regional governors such as Huán and Yú frequently conducted reviews,
but the imperial court itself did not conduct such affairs.
According to Hán and Wèi customs,
when dispatching a general on an expedition,
the Fújié Láng (Official of Tallies and Seals) would present the tally and axe in the court hall.
Later, in the new rites established by Xún Yǐ and others,
when dispatching a general,
the emperor would attend court from the imperial carriage,
and the Shàngshū (Minister) would receive the tally and axe,
in accordance with the ancient military texts' meaning of kneeling and pushing the chariot wheels (to encourage).
Among the five categories of rites,
the fifth is auspicious rites,
which encompass the ways of banquets, capping ceremonies, and weddings.
During the chaotic end of the Zhōu dynasty,
the rules for guest archery and banquets were rarely practiced,
and the customs for capping ceremonies, weddings, and dining underwent many changes.
Although the Rites of Zhōu mentions the numbers for robes and caps,
there is no text for the Son of Heaven's capping ceremony.
Moreover, the Yí Lǐ states
that the capping ceremony for dukes and marquises
originated at the end of the Xià dynasty.
Wáng and Zhèng both believed that at the end of Xià, superiors and inferiors were in disorder,
leading to usurpation and regicide.
Therefore, the capping ceremony for dukes and marquises was created,
which clearly indicates the absence of a Son of Heaven's capping ceremony.
Furthermore, great officers had no capping ceremony.
In ancient times, one was only granted a noble title after reaching fifty.
How could there be a capping ceremony for great officers?
If a person of the Zhōu people reached fifty and possessed talent,
they would be tested with the duties of a great officer,
yet still perform the rites of a shi (scholar-official).
Therefore, divining the day and the guest,
performing the capping ceremony at the eastern steps to signify succession,
offering libations at the guest's seat,
and the three additions (of caps) to increasingly honor,
all these were merely rites for shi.
However, since the Hàn dynasty,
the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords have largely adopted this ceremony.
The *jiǎzǐ* or *bǐngzǐ* day of the first month was considered auspicious,
suitable for the capping ceremony (*guānfú*).
This followed the *guānlǐ* (capping ritual).
When Hàn Shùndì was capped,
they also adopted Cáo Bāo's new rites,
where the imperial carriage first added the *zī bù jìnxián* (black cloth cap for officials),
followed by the *juébàn* (sparrow cap) and *wǔbàn* (military cap),
then the *tōngtiān* (heaven-connecting crown).
All of these took place at the High Temple (*gāomiào*),
to respectfully present themselves to the temple of Shìzǔ according to the rites.
For kings and dukes downwards,
only the *jìnxián* was added initially.
According to this text,
the initial capping with the black cloth
followed the ancient system,
and capping at the ancestral temple was correct.
The Wèi Son of Heaven was capped with a single addition.
The explanation for this states:
the capping ritual for a *shì* (scholar-official) involves three additions,
each addition signifying completion.
As for the Son of Heaven and feudal lords, there is no text specifying the number of additions,
because they ascend the throne and rule over all,
their dignity is supreme and their virtue complete.
How could they be the same as a *shì*?
The Wèi dynasty's crown prince received two additions,
while imperial sons, kings, and ducal heirs received three additions.
Sūn Yù considered both one and two additions
to be incorrect.
The libation text for the ritual says:
"In this auspicious month and propitious day,
with the beginning of the year,
and the excellence of the month."
Records show that Lǔ Xiānggōng was capped in winter,
and Hàn Huìdì was capped in the third month,
indicating no fixed month.
However, since the Later Hàn dynasty,
emperors performing the *guānfú* always did so in the first month.
In the second year of Xiánníng (276 CE), during the intercalary ninth month of autumn,
an envoy was dispatched to cap Rǔnán Wáng Jiǎn.
This shows it was not necessarily at the beginning of the year.
The rites prescribe capping at the temple.
However, when Wǔ and Huì capped their crown princes,
the crown princes immediately presented themselves at the temple.
This also emulated the ceremony at the temple.
Before Mùdì and Xiàowǔ were capped,
they both first presented offerings to the temple
and then presented themselves at the temple afterwards.
When Huìdì was crown prince and about to be capped,
Wǔdì presided from the imperial pavilion,
and commanded the acting *sītú* (Minister of Education), Gāoyáng Wáng Guī, to perform the capping,
while the acting *guānglù dàfū* (Grand Master of Ceremonies) and *túnqí xiàowèi* (Colonel of Garrison Cavalry), Huà Yì, assisted in the capping.
When the emperors of Jiāngzuǒ were about to be capped,
musical instruments were set up overnight,
and all officials attended.
Also, a large bed was prepared in advance on the main hall,

and the Imperial Storeroom Director (*yùfǔ lìng*) presented the crown (*miǎn*), turban (*cè*), hairpin (*zāndǎo*), and ceremonial robes (*gǔnfú*) to the *shìzhōng* (Palace Attendant) and *chángshì* (Grandee Remonstrant).
The *tàiwèi* (Grand Commandant) added the turban,
and the *tàibǎo* (Grand Protector) added the crown.
Before adding the crown,
the *tàiwèi* knelt and read the prayer text, saying:
"In this auspicious month and propitious day,
the *guānfú* is first added.
The Emperor, solemn and dignified,
contemplates the expansion of imperial duties.
Reverently following Heaven,
the Six Directions are his model.
Following the ancestors,
enduring endlessly.
May his long life be auspicious,
and this great fortune be bestowed."
After the crown was added,
the *shìzhōng* tied the black ribbon.
The *shìzhōng* removed the emperor's crimson gauze robe
and added the ceremonial robes and crown (*gǔnfú miǎn guān*).
When the ceremony was complete,
the *tàibǎo* led all officials in offering a toast for long life.
Kings and dukes downwards shouted "Long Live!" three times before retiring.
According to the ritual records,
only one addition of the turban and crown was performed.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ (274 CE),
Nángōng Wáng Chéng, being fifteen years old,
should have been capped according to old customs.
Officials discussed and reported:
"The rites state that
at fifteen one becomes an adult male (*chéngtóng*),
and a ruler at fifteen can have a son,
indicating the appropriateness of capping.
Moreover, the Hàn and Wèi dynasties dispatching envoys to cap princes
is not an ancient custom."
Thus, a decree was issued that princes should be capped at fifteen,
and no longer required the dispatch of envoys.
Wáng Biāozhī said:
The rites and commentaries both state that capping should take place in the ancestral temple.
Records show that after Chéngdì received the *guānfú*,
the imperial carriage proceeded to bow at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
to announce the completion.
This was also an emulation of the ceremony at the temple.
In the fourth year of Zhèngshǐ (243 CE), during the reign of Wèi Qí Wáng,
Empress Zhēn Shì was established,
but the details of her ceremony are not preserved.
In the second year of Xiánníng (276 CE), during the reign of Wǔdì,
the emperor presided from the imperial pavilion,
and dispatched the *tàiwèi*, Jiǎ Chōng, to formally appoint Empress Yáng Shì,
and to receive the mourning empress.
A grand amnesty was then proclaimed,
and kings, dukes, and others were granted gifts according to their rank.
All officials offered congratulations.
In the eighth year of Tàikāng (287 CE),
officials reported:
"For the marriage rites' betrothal gifts (*nàzhēng*),
a grand wedding uses black and crimson silk bundles,
with an added *guī* (jade tablet)
and two teams of horses.
For kings and marquises, black and crimson silk bundles,
with an added *bì* (jade disc)
and riding horses.
For *dàfū* (ministers), black and crimson silk bundles,
with an added sheep.
Anciently, skins and horses were used as court offerings (*tíngshí*).
The Son of Heaven added a *gǔguī* (jade tablet with grain pattern),
and feudal lords added a *dàzhāng* (large jade blade).
It is permissible to change the *bì* to a *zhāng* according to the Rites of Zhōu,
while the sheep, geese, wine, rice, black and crimson silk remain as before.
For the marriage rites of feudal lords,
for the *nàcǎi* (proposal), *gàoqī* (announcement of date), and *qīnyíng* (personal reception) each require five bolts of silk,
and for the *nàzhēng*, four horses.
All these should be prepared by the groom's family.
Only the *zhāng*
shall be provided by the government."
Shàngshū (Minister) Zhū Zhěng deliberated:
"According to Wèi dynasty precedents,
for the marriage of kings and princesses,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords used skins and horses as court offerings.
The Son of Heaven added a *gǔguī*,
and feudal lords added a *dàzhāng*.
Hàn Gāohòu's regulations for betrothal gifts stipulated:
for an empress, two hundred *jīn* of gold
and twelve horses;
for a *fūrén* (lady), fifty *jīn* of gold
and four horses.
The Wèi dynasty's rites for a king's marriage to a consort and a princess's marriage
used one hundred ninety bolts of silk.
When Jìn arose,
the precedent was three hundred bolts of silk."
The imperial edict said:
"Princesses' marriages are arranged by the groom's family,
it is inappropriate for us to provide all items.
Give them money to suffice.
Only the *zhāng* shall be provided,
the rest according to precedent."
In the second year of Xiánkāng (336 CE), during the reign of Chéngdì,
the emperor presided from the imperial pavilion,
and dispatched the envoy bearing a *jié* (scepter), acting *tàibǎo* and *lǐngjūn jiāngjūn* (General-in-Chief of the Army) Zhūgě Huī,
and acting *tàiwèi* and *hùjūn jiāngjūn* (General Protecting the Army) Kǒng Yú,
with all six rites' items,
to formally appoint Empress Dù Shì.
She entered the palace on the same day.
The emperor presided at the Tàijí Hall,
and all officials offered congratulations.
This congratulation
was not part of the rites.
For the marriage rites of rulers,
the rites do not specify such a system.
The *Chūnqiū*
states, "Jì Gōng met the Queen at Jǐ."
The explanations in *Gǔliáng* and *Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn* differ from *Gōngyáng*.
And the remaining practices from Hàn and Wèi are all incomplete and brief.
When Wǔ and Huì received their empresses,
Jiāngzuǒ also had no further ritual records.
Therefore, when Chéngdì was about to receive Empress Dù,
the *tàicháng* (Grand Minister of Ceremonies) Huá Shǐ and the academicians discussed and finalized the ceremony.
According to Dù Yù's explanation in *Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn*,
the main purpose of the marriage ceremony was merely to provide the ceremonial silks.
Furthermore,
when Zhōu Líng Wáng sought a marriage alliance with Qí,
Qí Hóu consulted Yàn Huánzǐ.
Huánzǐ replied:
"If the children born to the husband and wife are like ordinary people,
then the paternal aunts and sisters are referred to as 'the surviving daughters of such-and-such a lord, who first held office,' if they are like ordinary people."
This means that the Son of Heaven's commands could be issued directly downwards,
and his subjects' replies could be directly communicated upwards.
Earlier scholars believed that Qiū Míng recorded this matter in detail
as a rite for royal marriages.
Therefore, Chéngdì presided from the imperial pavilion
and dispatched envoys to appoint the empress by imperial decree.
However, the details of that ceremony are again not fully preserved.
In the first year of Jiàn-yuán during the reign of Emperor Kāng,
Empress Chǔ-shì was taken in,
but the ritual protocol for ascending the steps did not include a máo-tóu (yak-tail banner).
The Palace Censor reported:
"Now that the Empress is being welcomed,
following the objects used when Empress Chéng-gōng entered the palace,
and with the ritual protocol for the Supreme One ascending the hall in a ceremonial robe and crown,
the máo-tóu is not set up.
We request consideration for this matter."
"Furthermore, upon investigation,
when Empress Gōng-hòu was welcomed in the past,
only a Qīng-lóng Qí (Green Dragon Banner) was made;
all other items were existing imperial possessions.
Today, when the envoy is dispatched from before the veranda,
the Wǔ-niú Qí (Five Ox Banners) are set up.
The máo-tóu and bì (shield-like banners) are all brought out for immediate use,
thus leading to the current omission."
The imperial edict stated:
"The reason for rectifying the ceremonial robes and ascending the Tàijí (Grand Ultimate Hall)
is to show reverence for the beginning,
and therefore to complete the rites.
How can we now omit something so important and remove ceremonial objects?"
"Furthermore, when the spirit tablet of Empress Gōng-hòu entered the ancestral temple,
the late Emperor decreed that the Empress's rites should be reduced,
and that the Wǔ-niú Qí should not be established.
Why are they still being set up now?
Since the Wǔ-niú Qí are not to be set up,
the máo-tóu and bì are easy to procure."
Another edict stated:
"Since the old regulations are difficult to follow,
and providing for them now
is also not appropriate.
The stores in the imperial treasury
should only be used to fund military and national expenses.
The ceremonial robes and decorations should be roughly prepared;
all other supplementary and miscellaneous items are to be stopped."
In the first year of Shēng-píng during the reign of Emperor Mù,
Empress Hé-shì was to be taken in.
Tài-cháng Wáng Biāo-zhī extensively cited classics, commentaries, and various historical precedents to establish the rites,
strongly disagreeing with the Gōng-yáng (Commentary)'s principle that the host should not be mentioned in wedding ceremonies.
He also said:
"Among the Four Seas, the King
has no one who is not a subject or a servant.
Even beloved fathers and elder brothers,
or wise teachers and friends,
are all pure subjects.
To uphold the beginning of the Three Bonds,
and to establish the ritual of Heaven and Earth (qián-kūn),
how can there be the reverence of a heavenly father,
yet use the command of a subordinate to take a consort?
How can there be the lowliness of a subordinate,
yet use the name of a heavenly father to perform a great rite?
Searching ancient rites far back,
there is no such system for kings;
looking through recent historical records,
there is no such precedent for kings.
Emotionally, it is unsettling;
ethically, it is incomprehensible.
Upon examining the second year of Xián-níng,
when Empress Dào-hòu was taken in,
Empress Dowager Hóng-xùn was overseeing the realm,
yet there was no text stating that an imperial relative was commanded to act as the father or elder brother of Emperor Wǔ for the wedding.
Furthermore, considering the events already performed in the Great Jìn,
since the Xián-níng precedent did not mention father, elder brother, teacher, or friend,
then the rites proposed by Huá-suǒ in Xián-kāng were in line with the old ways.
Your ignorant subject believes that the current ritual for taking in the Empress
should entirely follow the Xián-kāng precedent."
Thereupon, it was followed.
The rites established by Huá-suǒ
which is why Biāo-zhī largely followed Xián-kāng.
This is the reason.
Only regarding the custom that the bride's family should not play music for three days,
and the Xián-kāng officials offering congratulations,
was considered a breach of etiquette.
Therefore, only the Xián-níng rites were followed for the offerings,
and no congratulations were offered.
The rituals such as announcing to the ancestral temple and the texts for the Six Rites were
all established by Biāo-zhī.
The sealed document for the nà-cǎi (presenting betrothal gifts) read:
"The Emperor addresses Qí, the former Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary to the Grand Commandant, Hé Qí.
The primordial origin gives rise to all things,
inaugurating human relations,
extending to husband and wife,
thereby serving Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain.
Having consulted with the Duke-ministers,
they all agree that the old codes should be followed.
Now, I send the envoy, Grand Chamberlain Biāo-zhī, holding the insignia of authority, and Grand Steward Zōng, to perform the nà-cǎi rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
seeking a marriage within this humble clan,
has fully considered and chosen.
This daughter, left by my distant cousin, the late Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Zhǔn-zhī,
is unskilled in instruction,
her attire and conduct are merely human.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system.
Your humble servant Hé Qí, former Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary to the Grand Commandant and Marquis of Dū-xiāng, bows his head to the ground,
prostrating twice to receive the edict."
Next, the document for wèn-míng (asking the name) read:
"The Emperor says: I address a certain official of a certain surname.
The two cosmic principles are united,
inheriting Heaven to govern all things,
establishing the proper position within the inner court,
which must await a noble family,
to reaffirm the old codes.
Now, I send the envoy, a certain Grand Chamberlain, holding the insignia of authority,
and a certain Grand Steward, to perform the wèn-míng rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
your envoy (a certain person) has arrived,
reiterating the imperial edict,
to ask about my family's name.
This daughter of my clan was born of her parents,
a great-great-granddaughter left by my late ancestor, the late Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Marquis of Yú-lóu, Zhēn-zhī;
a granddaughter of my late ancestor, the late Grand Administrator of Ān-fēng, Marquis of Guān-zhōng, Ruì-zhī;
and a daughter left by my late ancestor, the late Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Zhǔn-zhī.
On her mother's side, she is a great-great-granddaughter of my late ancestor, the late Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, Kǒng Zhòu,
and a granddaughter of my late ancestor, the late Palace Attendant, Marquis of Guān-nèi, Yí.
She is seventeen years old.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system."
Next, the document for nà-jí (accepting auspiciousness) read:
"The Emperor says: I address a certain official of a certain surname.
Human counsel and tortoise divination agree,
all say it is auspicious and propitious;
reverently following the rites.
Now, I send the envoy, a certain Grand Chamberlain, holding the insignia of authority,
and a certain Grand Steward, to perform the nà-jí rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
your envoy (a certain person) has reiterated the imperial edict,
the Grand Diviner reports great auspiciousness.
Our humble clan is lowly and base;
we are filled with worry and fear, unable to bear it.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system."
Next, the document for nà-zhēng (presenting wedding gifts) read:
"The Emperor says: I address the daughter of a certain official of a certain surname,
who possesses the virtue of a mother-model
and a graceful and modest demeanor,
like mountains and rivers,
fit to serve the ancestral temples,
and eternally receive Heaven's blessing.
With black and red silks, skins, and fabrics,
horses, sheep, money, and jades,
to manifest the ritual code.
Now, I send the envoy, a certain Minister of Works, holding the insignia of authority,
and a certain Grand Chamberlain, to perform the nà-zhēng rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
descending to marry into our lowly family,
honoring us as grand dukes,
gracing us with ritual codes,
and providing all ceremonial objects.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system."
Next, the document for qǐng-qī (requesting the date) read:
"The Emperor says: I address a certain official of a certain surname.
Having consulted with the Duke-ministers,
and performed the great tortoise divination,
there is nothing inauspicious;
following the ritual codes.
Now, I send the envoy, a certain Grand Chamberlain, holding the insignia of authority,
and a certain Grand Steward, to perform the qǐng-qī rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
your envoy (a certain person) has reiterated the imperial edict,
that a certain auspicious day is suitable for welcoming.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system."
Next, the document for qīn-yíng (personal welcoming) read:
"The Emperor says: I address a certain official of a certain surname.
The year is auspicious, the month favorable,
and a certain auspicious day;
I will follow the rites to welcome.
Now, I send the envoy, a certain Grand Protector, holding the insignia of authority,
and a certain Grand Commandant, to perform the welcoming rite."
The host replied:
"The Emperor's auspicious command,
your envoy (a certain person) has reiterated the imperial edict,
that on an auspicious month and auspicious hour,
the rites will be complete for the welcoming.
Grand Dukes and Imperial Kinsmen have arrived together,
along with over a hundred close ministers and escorts.
Our ant-like clan,
unworthily receiving such a great rite,
is filled with worry, fear, and trembling.
We reverently accept the old regulations,
and solemnly observe the established system."
A certain person bowed his head to receive the edict,
all as initially answered.
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) took Empress Wáng (王皇后).
Her ceremonies were also like this.
For the *nàcǎi* (納采), *wènmíng* (問名), *nàjí* (納吉), *qǐngqī* (請期), and *qīnyíng* (親迎),
they all used one white goose and one white sheep,
and twelve *hú* (斛) each of wine and rice.
However, for the *nàzhēng* (納徵), there was one sheep,
three bolts of black and crimson silk,
two bolts of scarlet silk,
two hundred bolts of plain silk,
two pieces of animal hide,
two million *qián* (錢),
one jade *bì* (璧),
six horses,
and twelve *hú* (斛) each of wine and rice.
This is what Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) called the "five geese and six rites".
The system of *guī* (珪) and horses,
and the number of items prepared,
differed again from what was presented in the Tàikāng (太康) era.
In ancient times, both weddings and capping ceremonies had *jiào* (醮) rituals.
The three *jiào* (醮) texts of Master Zhèng (鄭氏) are still extant.
In the eighth year of Shēngpíng (升平) [364 CE],
[一三] a request from the Secretariat asked,
"Should there be drum and wind music for the Empress's grand procession?"
Dr. Hú Nà (胡訥) deliberated:
"The ceremonial procedures for appearing at the imperial hall are incomplete;
there is no place specified for arranging drum and wind music,
nor are there provisions for raising banners and sounding bells."
Tàicháng (太常) Wáng Biāozhī (王彪之) believed:
"Wedding ceremonies do not involve music.
Drum and wind music is also a general term for music.
The reason it is absent from the ceremonial procedures
is in accordance with wedding rites.
It should now be fully prepared but not performed."
This deliberation was adopted at the time.
In the second year of Yǒnghé (永和) [346 CE], when the Empress was taken,
[一四] there was a debate about whether to offer congratulations.
Wáng Shù (王述) said:
"Marriage is an auspicious ceremony.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* (春秋傳) says: 'Taking a wife is greatly auspicious,
extraordinarily auspicious.'
The *Zhuàn* (傳) also says: 'Zǐhǎn (子罕) of Zhèng (鄭) went to Jìn (晉)
to congratulate the lady.'
Even neighboring states congratulated each other,
how much more so should subjects!
In this case,
congratulations should be offered,
but not within three days.
Now, to congratulate upon the completion of the ceremony at the ancestral temple is
also a valid point."
Wáng Biāozhī (王彪之) deliberated, saying:
"Wedding rites prohibit music and congratulations;
this is clearly stated in the Rites.
The *Zhuàn* (傳) mentioning Zǐhǎn (子罕) going to Jìn (晉) to congratulate the lady
has no corresponding *Jīng* (經) text,
nor does the *Zhuàn* (傳) say it was a rite.
According to the Rites,
for three days after taking a wife, no music is performed,
implying that music is appropriate after three days.
As for not congratulating,
there is no stipulation of a three-day period,
so it is likely that there is no rite of congratulation even after three days."
He further said:
"The reason the *Lǐjì* (禮記) mentions congratulating on taking a wife
is because it refers to auspicious words spoken during a feast with food and drink.
I believe there is no direct form of mutual congratulation,
[一五] but there is the meaning of celebrating together with gifts and gatherings,
which is commonly practiced in today's world."
At that time, in the end, no congratulations were offered.
Emperor Mù (穆帝) wished to take the Empress in the ninth month,
but the ninth month was considered an inauspicious month.
Fàn Wāng (范汪) asked Wáng Biāozhī (王彪之),
who replied:
"The Rites have no mention of inauspicious months.
I dare not say something does not exist
merely because I have not seen it."
Drs. Cáo Dān (曹耽), Xún Nà (荀訥), and others all stated there was no text about inauspicious months,
and thus no impediment should exist.
Wáng Qià (王洽) said:
"If there were inauspicious months,
there would also be inauspicious years."
In the twelfth year of Tàiyuán (太元) [387 CE],
a request from the Secretariat asked,
"After the Crown Prince pays respects at the ancestral temple, should court officials present gifts of congratulation?"
Chē Yìn (車胤), National University Doctor, said:
"All high-ranking officials and nobles
participated in the grand ceremony,
showing respect through bowing and prostrating;
there is no need to present additional gifts.
Only regional governors and administrators,
who did not witness the grand ceremony,
unless they contribute wine and food,
have no means to express their sincerity.
Therefore, they should present gifts.
This is like the grand celebrations on New Year's Day,
when regional governors all present gifts,
while court officials only offer jade *bì* (璧)."
Yú Hóngzhī (庾弘之), Imperial Academy Doctor, deliberated:
"Upon examining the records from the third year of Xiánníng (咸寧) [277 CE], when the Princes of Shǐpíng (始平) and Púyáng (濮陽) were newly appointed,
the officials proposed that, in accordance with precedent,
close officials from the capital, princes, and princesses who were to offer court congratulations should again present gifts.
Now that the Crown Prince, the state's heir apparent,
has been established with such solemnity,
the entire realm rejoices.
Therefore, gifts of congratulation should be presented."
Xú Mò (徐邈) agreed.
He also cited the saying, "Once there is a virtuous heir,
joy lies therein."
Since there were precedents for presenting gifts for the enfeeoffment of princes and the completion of new palaces,
and everyone has already shown respect and reverence,
and furthermore offered wine cups for longevity,
there should also be no doubt.
Since the relocation to the south of the Yangtze,
for the Crown Prince's wedding, the *nàzhēng* (納徵) ceremony used one jade *bì* (璧)
and two pieces of animal hide.
It is unclear what this was based on.
Perhaps the animal hides were chosen for their fierceness and patterned colors,
and jade to symbolize virtue and its warm luster.
Upon reflection, *guī* (珪) and *zhāng* (璋) are also beautiful jades,
and leopard skin's vibrant patterns are used to metaphorically compare to a *jūnzǐ* (君子).
Wáng Sù's (王肅) *nàzhēng cí* (納徵辭) states:
"Bundles of black and crimson silk,
pairs of hides, geese, and sheep."
The Western Hàn (漢) betrothal of an empress
involved two hundred *jīn* (斤) of gold
and twelve horses,
but made no mention of using sheep.
Zhèng Shì (鄭氏)'s "Praise for Wedding Items" says,
"Sheep (*yáng*) is auspicious (*xiáng*)".
If so, the use of sheep in weddings
began in the late Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The "six rites" of kings
had not yet adopted them.
Therefore, during the Tàikāng (太康) era, officials proposed:
"For the Crown Prince's wedding,
the *nàzhēng* (納徵) should use bundles of black and crimson silk,
with the addition of two pairs of sheep and horses."
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) [274 CE] of Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
it was planned to appoint and enfeoff three *fūrén* (夫人) and nine *pín* (嬪).
Officials proposed:
"According to the Rites,
an Empress is betrothed with a *gǔguī* (穀珪),
but there is no system of ceremonial gifts for concubines and female attendants."
The imperial edict stated:
"The appointment and conferral can follow the precedents of the Wèi (魏) dynasty."
Thereupon, before the imperial hall,
envoys holding imperial credentials and concurrently serving as Grand Minister of Ceremonies appointed the three *fūrén* (夫人),
and concurrently serving as Vice Censor-in-chief appointed the nine *pín* (嬪).
The Rites of Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) state that
princesses reside in their own mansions,
and those marrying princesses come to the mansion to complete the wedding.
Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Lǎng (王朗) considered this unacceptable,
and it was later reformed.
During the Tàiyuán (太元) era,
for the *nàzhēng* (納徵) of princesses,
one set each of animal hide and leopard skin was used as ceremonial gifts.
Could it be that since wedding rites did not distinguish the hierarchy of princes and dukes,
animal hides and leopard skins were used to emphasize their noble status?
[一六]
The Rites contain texts about the Three Kings (三王) nourishing the elderly and establishing schools,
and regulations for banquets, archery, and drinking ceremonies,
which fell into disuse by the end of the Zhōu (周) dynasty.
In the third month of the second year of Yǒngpíng (永平) [59 CE] of Emperor Míng (明帝) of Hàn (漢),
the Emperor first led his officials to personally nourish the Three Elders (三老) and Five Seniors (五更) at Bìyōng (辟雍),
and performed the Grand Archery Ceremony.
Commanderies, kingdoms, counties, and districts performed the Village Drinking Ceremony at schools,
all sacrificing to the former sages and former teachers, the Duke of Zhōu (周公) and Kǒngzǐ (孔子),
with a grand sacrificial ox.
[一七] The same was done in the first month of winter.
And in the second year of Gānlù (甘露) [257 CE] of Emperor Gāoguìxiāng (高貴鄉公) of Wèi (魏),
the Son of Heaven personally led all officials to perform the ceremony of nourishing the elderly.
Thereupon, Wáng Xiáng (王祥) served as a Three Elder,
and Zhèng Xiǎotóng (鄭小同) as a Five Senior.
Their ceremonial procedures are not extant,
but the Hàn (漢) rites still existed.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) [270 CE] of Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
the Emperor presided over Bìyōng (辟雍),
and performed the Village Drinking Ceremony.
An imperial edict stated:
"Ritual ceremonies have been abandoned for a long time,
and now the old statutes are finally being reviewed and practiced again."
He bestowed one hundred bolts of plain silk upon the Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and oxen and wine upon the Assistant, Doctors, and students.
In the third year of Xiánníng (咸寧) [277 CE],
and the ninth year of Yuánkāng (元康) [299 CE] of Emperor Huì (惠帝),
the ceremony was performed again.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign of Wèi,
every time Qí Wáng finished lecturing on the Classics,
he would invariably have the Tàicháng perform the Shìdiàn ceremony to the former sages and teachers at the Bìyōng,
without personally attending.
When Huì Dì and Míng Dì were crown princes,
and when Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ completed his classical studies,
they all personally performed the Shìdiàn at the Tàixué.
The Crown Prince offered a libation to the former teachers,
and the Zhōngshùzǐ offered a libation to Yán Huí.
Emperors Chéng, Mù, and Xiàowǔ
also all personally performed the Shìdiàn.
During Xiàowǔ's time,
because the Tàixué was far away to the south of the water,
the officials concerned proposed to temporarily establish a "traveling Tàixué" in the central hall,
following the precedent of the first year of Shēngpíng.
At that time, there were no Guózǐ students remaining,
so the officials submitted a memorial:
"There should be a restoration of 120 students of two types.
Sixty Tàixué students should be selected from existing personnel,
and sixty Guózǐ students should be temporarily selected from the sons and grandsons of high-ranking officials.
They will be dismissed after the matter is concluded."
The memorial was approved.
After the Shìdiàn ceremony concluded,
officials of the sixth rank and above were assembled.
According to Hàn custom,
on the third day of the third month in late spring (Shàngsì),
officials and common people alike performed the Xì ceremony on the flowing waters to the east,
washing away old dirt and impurities.
However, from Wèi onwards,
only the third day was used,
not necessarily the Shàngsì.
From the public ministers and high officials down to the common people in the central court of Jìn,
all performed the Xì ceremony by the Luò River.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
on the third day, he met at the Tiānquán Pond
and executed Zhāng Lín.
Huái Dì also met at the Tiānquán Pond
and composed poems.
Lù Jī said:
"To the south of Tiānquán Pond, a stone channel draws water from the Yù Gōu,
and to the west of the pond, piled stones form a Xì Hall."
Originally, wine was drunk from cups floated on the water,
but it was not called Qūshuǐ.
Yuán Dì further decreed the discontinuation of the third-day amusements.
Hǎixī established a "flowing cups and winding stream" (liúbēi qūshuǐ) at Zhōng Shān,
inviting all officials;
these were all related to this matter.
On the ninth day of the ninth month,
there was horse archery.
Some say that
"autumn,
the season of metal,
for practicing military skills and archery,
symbolizes the ritual of Lìqiū."
Jiàokān Jì
Zhì dì shí'èr Yuè shàng
As for the manifestations of the spirit,
we do not know how they give rise to chants and songs;
as for the origin of emotions,
we do not know how they relate to the hands and feet.
That which originates in the heart is called the Way,
that which takes form is called function.
Comparing it to heaven and earth,
it is like shadow and echo.
Even a hundred beasts dance,
how much more so humans!
Admiring its peace and lamenting its chaos,
they used this to regulate pitch,
and then broadcast its sounds.
Nóng's qín and Xī's qín,
Chuí's bells and Hé's chimes,
reaching the spiritual and forming the character,
embodying objects and manifesting achievements –
from this, it can be said
that their origin is ancient.
When the Yīn clan was without proper governance,
its lingering customs and remaining evils
led to the rise of licentious music,
and the elegant chapters scattered.
The regulations for refined music
had probably already become obscure.
Confucius said:
"It is man who can broaden the Way,
not the Way that broadens man."
The Zhōu began with the Èrnán,
and its influence extended through six generations.
Of old, Huáng Dì composed the Yúnmén,
Yáo composed the Xiánchí,
Shùn composed the Dàsháo,
Yǔ composed the Dàxià,
Yīn composed the Dàhù,
and Zhōu composed the Dàwǔ.
These are what are called following the rituals of former kings,
establishing postures of bowing and looking up,
where harmony and submission accumulated within
and effulgence manifested outwardly.
The Shū mentions commissioning Kuí to oversee music,
teaching the noble youths.
This is what the Zhōu Guān refers to as performing the Dàlǚ
and singing the Huángzhōng.
Heaven's blessings descended,
and both men and spirits were moved.
Regulating and promoting the Zhōu's standards,
to spread refined music.
But when Bàoyàn caused disaster
and Píng Wáng met with turmoil,
rituals for kin and strangers were abandoned,
and music sank into rivers and seas.
This is why Yánlíng Jìzǐ, upon hearing the songs of Xiǎoyǎ, said:
"Is this not the decline of Zhōu's virtue!
Yet there are still remnants of the former kings' customs."
Then, various feudal states, calling themselves solitary rulers,
each created their own chants and poems.
Wèi Wénhóu listened to ancient music and feared falling asleep;
Jìn Pínggōng listened to new music and forgot to eat.
The Way of the former kings
gradually declined.
The eight directions had different customs,
and the nine provinces had different rules.
When the Qín clan unified the realm,
they monopolized laws and institutions.
As for string music, songs, poems, and odes,
and shields, axes, yak tails, and feathers,
they were all cast into fire
and completely wiped out.
Hànzǔ, wielding his sword, pacified the world,
subduing all under heaven.
He focused on moral transformation through culture
and intended to establish institutions through military power.
The Empress Dowager rejected the doctrines of the Confucians,
and the high officials opposed the words of Jiǎ.
Thus, the gentry and scholars sighed deeply,
but Zǐzhèng and Zhòngshū still could not stop.
During the restoration of the glorious Hàn,
when Míng Huángdì ascended the throne,
he marked the gnomon and shadows, and arranged the pure ancestral temple;
he planted scholarly locust trees and cleared the bi-shaped water channels.
He sacrificed to Guāngwǔ in the Míngtáng,
matching him with the Lord on High;
he summoned Huán Róng to the Tàixué,
bared his arm, and cut the sacrificial animal.
How grand and
magnificent it was,
truly worth seeing.
From then on,
rituals and music became increasingly elaborate.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng,
the official in charge of music
was renamed Dàyǔ,
to promote ceremonies and rituals,
and to extensively seek out diagrams and prophecies,
whose ways were akin to the Yǎ and Sòng,
and whose affairs were close to central harmony.
As for the music of the five directions,
it is what is meant by
"the great music has nine transformations,
through which the gods of heaven can be honored."
As for the music of the ancestral temple,
it is what is meant by
"solemn, harmonious, and melodious,
our ancestors will listen."
As for the music of the altars of soil and grain,
it is what is meant by
"qin, se, and drums are played,
to welcome the god of the fields."
As for the music of the Bìyōng,
it is what is meant by
"to transform customs and change practices,
nothing is better than music."
As for the music of the Huángmén,
it is what is meant by
"entertaining the assembled officials,
dancing gracefully."
As for the music of the short flute (duǎnxiāo),
it is what is meant by
"when the king's army achieves a great victory,
order a victory song in the camp."
Wèi Wǔ, holding the emperor, commanded the feudal lords,
hoping to unify the nine regions with one military campaign.
At that time, facing annexation,
institutions and regulations were all swept away.
After pacifying Liú Biǎo,
he first acquired Dù Kuí,
who played the war drums and marshaled the shields and axes,
thus following the former records.
The three ancestors were prolific,
all skilled in poetry.
Although songs and chants had additions and deletions,
the delight lay in their ornate verses.
Therefore, Wáng Càn and others each composed new poems,
drawing upon their elegant thoughts,
chanting praises to the spirits,
and extolling those who came to partake in the offerings.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn adopted the enduring traditions of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties.
He observed the established rules of Jǐngwén,
renewing the imperial court
without altering its former principles.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ (268 CE),
Grand Master of Bright Favor Xún Xù first created the ancient measuring rule
to regulate musical tones and rhythms.
He then used the profound compositions created by Zhāng Huà and others
to arrange the lower pipes.
During the Disorder of Yǒngjiā (311 CE),
the number of musicians greatly diminished.
The Qǔtái and Xuānxiè pavilions
were all transformed into overgrown wilderness.
Even though the elephant dancers and singers
returned from the Hu to Jìn,
as for the pipes of Gūzhú,
the zithers of Yúnhé,
the lutes of Kōngsāng,
and the stone chimes of Sìbīn,
those capable of fully equipping these
were not even one in a hundred.
Humans receive the spiritual essence of heaven and earth,
containing the vital essence of energy.
Rigidity and flexibility are used in turn,
with sorrow and joy expressing different emotions.
Passing through the spring sunshine, one naturally feels joyful;
encountering the autumn decay, one is displeased.
It flows through the ends of metal and stone,
and emerges beyond pipes and strings.
It changes and passes away with things,
riding the current without turning back.
Therefore, King Chǔ ascended a light carriage at Pénglǐ,
and Emperor Shùn of Hàn listened to singing birds at Fánqú.
Sages, when their work is accomplished, create music;
when transformation is complete, they compose melodies.
Thus, they broadcast rhythms
to express moderation and harmony,
to adorn joy,
and to stop at sorrowful thoughts.
In the way of music,
the five notes, eight sounds, six pitches, and twelve pipes
are its fundamental principles.
The five notes: Gōng is the ruler;
the meaning of Gōng is "center."
The way of moderation and harmony
is applicable everywhere without being incorrect.
Shāng is the minister;
the meaning of Shāng is "strong,"
referring to the firm strength of metal.
Jiǎo is the people;
the meaning of Jiǎo is "to touch,"
referring to all yang qi touching things and being born.
Zhǐ is the affairs;
the meaning of Zhǐ is "to stop,"
meaning that when things are abundant, they stop.
Yǔ is the things;
the meaning of Yǔ is "to spread out,"
meaning that when the yang qi is about to return,
all things multiply and grow in a spreading manner.
The ancients had a saying:
"Ritual and music cannot leave one's side for a moment."
To transform the superior and move towards goodness
is as if one cannot attain it quickly enough.
Therefore, hearing the Gōng note
makes people gentle, kind, and magnanimous;
hearing the Shāng note
makes people upright, honest, and fond of righteousness;
hearing the Jiǎo note
makes people compassionate and benevolent;
hearing the Zhǐ note
makes people joyful in nurturing and fond of generosity;
hearing the Yǔ note
makes people respectful, frugal, and fond of ritual.
The eight sounds
are the winds of the eight directions.
The sound of Qián is stone;
its wind is Bùzhōu.
The sound of Kǎn is hide;
its wind is Guǎngmò.
The sound of Gèn is gourd;
its wind is Róng.
The sound of Zhèn is bamboo;
its wind is Míngshù.
The sound of Xùn is wood;
its wind is Qīngmíng.
The sound of Lí is silk;
its wind is Jǐng.
The sound of Kūn is earth;
its wind is Liáng.
The sound of Duì is metal;
its wind is Chānghé.
The six yang pitches are called Lǜ: Huángzhōng, Tàicù, Gūxǐ, Ruíbīn, Yízé, Wúshè;
the six yin pitches are called Lǚ: Dàlǚ, Yìngzhōng, Nánlǚ, Línzhōng, Zhònglǚ, Jiázhōng. In total there are twelve,
which are matched with the twelve earthly branches.
The meaning of Lǜ is "law,"
meaning that the yang qi, in giving rise to life, each has its own law;
the meaning of Lǚ is "to assist,"
which is to assist in achieving the yang's accomplishments.
The earthly branch of the first month is called Yín;
Yín means "passage,"
referring to the passage of living things.
The earthly branch of the second month is called Mǎo;
Mǎo means "flourish,"
meaning that the yang qi is born and multiplies.
The earthly branch of the third month is called Chén;
Chén means "to shake" or "to vibrate,"
meaning that at this time all things shake and grow.
The earthly branch of the fourth month is called Sì;
Sì means "to rise,"
meaning that all things at this time fully rise.
The earthly branch of the fifth month is called Wǔ;
Wǔ means "to grow,"
and "great,"
meaning that all things grow large.
The earthly branch of the sixth month is called Wèi;
Wèi means "taste,"
meaning that at this time all things are nearing completion
and have flavor.
The earthly branch of the seventh month is called Shēn;
Shēn means "body,"
meaning that at this time the bodies of all things are fully formed.
The earthly branch of the eighth month is called Yǒu;
Yǒu means "to shrink,"
meaning that at this time all things shrink.
The earthly branch of the ninth month is called Xū;
Xū means "to extinguish,"
meaning that at this time all things decay and are extinguished.
The earthly branch of the tenth month is called Hài;
Hài means "to indict" or "to investigate,"
meaning that at this time the yin qi investigates and kills all things.
The earthly branch of the eleventh month is called Zǐ;
Zǐ means "to multiply" or "to breed,"
meaning that the yang qi at this point regenerates and multiplies.
The earthly branch of the twelfth month is called Chǒu;
Chǒu means "to knot" or "to tie,"
meaning that at the juncture of beginning and end,
it is named after tying a knot.
The pipe for the eleventh month is called Huángzhōng (黃鍾).
Huáng (黃),
is the central color of Yin and Yang.
Heaven has six qì (氣),
Earth has five cái (才),
and the numbers of Heaven and Earth are complete.
Some say,
that at the winter solstice, the virtue qì (德氣) is earth;
the color of earth is huáng (黃),
hence it is called Huángzhōng (黃鍾).
The pipe for the first month is called Tàicù (太蔟).
Cù (蔟) means gathering,
meaning that all things gather and sprout due to the abundant Yang qì (陽氣).
The pipe for the third month is named Gūxǐ (姑洗).
Gūxǐ (姑洗) means: Gū (姑),
is withered;
Xǐ (洗),
is washing,
meaning that things are born fresh and clean,
washing away their withered parts,
changing branches and leaves.
The pipe for the fifth month is named Ruíbīn (蕤賓).
Wēiruí (葳蕤) means drooping;
Bīn (賓) means respect,
meaning that at this time, the Yang qì (陽氣) descends,
and Yin qì (陰氣) begins to rise,
showing mutual respect.
The pipe for the seventh month is named Yízé (夷則).
Yí (夷) means level;
Zé (則) means law,
meaning that as all things are about to mature,
they are all level and have a regular pattern.
The pipe for the ninth month is named Wúshè (無射).
Shè (射) means to emerge;
it means that at this time, the Yang qì (陽氣) rises,
and all things are stored away and no longer emerge.
The pipe for the twelfth month is named Dàlǚ (大呂).
Lǚ (呂) means to assist,
meaning that the Yang qì (陽氣) is about to develop,
and the Yin qì (陰氣) assists.
The pipe for the tenth month is named Yìngzhōng (應鍾).
Yìng (應) means to harmonize,
meaning that all annual tasks are completed,
harmonizing with the achievements of Yang,
collecting and gathering them.
The pipe for the eighth month is named Nánlǚ (南呂).
Nán (南) means to bear,
meaning that at this time, all things are in bloom,
having the appearance of bearing fruit.
The pipe for the sixth month is named Línzhōng (林鍾).
Lín (林) means lush,
meaning that at this time, things are flourishing in the wilderness.
The pipe for the fourth month is named Zhònglǚ (仲呂).
Lǚ (呂) means to assist,
meaning that the Yang qì (陽氣) is strong and growing,
and Yin assists in its success.
The pipe for the second month is named Jiázhōng (夾鍾).
Jiá (夾) means to assist,
meaning that at this time, things have not yet fully emerged,
and Yin virtue assists Yang in bringing forth things.
After the great chaos in the Eastern Hàn (漢),
there was a complete absence of music from metal and stone instruments.
Musical scores were lost and incomplete,
and could no longer be understood.
When Wèi Wǔdì (魏武帝) pacified Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he captured Dù Kuí (杜夔) of Hénán (河南), an elegant music officer of the Hàn (漢),
who understood the old methods.
He was appointed Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ (軍謀祭酒) [advisor and libationer]
and tasked with establishing and fixing elegant music.
At that time, there were also Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎) Dèng Jìng (鄧靜) and Yǐn Shāng (尹商) who were skilled in explaining elegant music,
and the singer Yǐn Hú (尹胡) could sing the songs for ancestral temples and suburban sacrifices.
The dancers Féng Sù (馮肅) and Fú Yǎng (服養) understood the dances of previous generations.
Kuí (夔) took overall charge of all of them.
He meticulously consulted the classics and books,
collected historical accounts,
and compiled ancient music,
then for the first time set up the xuánxuán (軒懸) bells and chimes.
However, during the Huángchū (黃初) era, Chái Yù (柴玉) and Zuǒ Yánnián (左延年) and others
again gained favor with new melodies,
changing their sounds and rhythms.
At the beginning of Wǔdì's (武帝) reign,
all systems were newly established.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
an imperial edict decreed that for suburban sacrifices and the Míngtáng (明堂), the rituals and music of the Wèi (魏) dynasty should be temporarily used,
following the principle of the Zhōu (周) dynasty adopting the Yīn (殷) rituals.
Only the musical scores were changed,
and Fù Xuán (傅玄) was ordered to compose the lyrics.
Song for Evening Sacrifice to Heaven, Earth, and the Five Suburbs
Heaven's mandate for great Jìn (晉),
Solemn and resplendent.
We, day and night,
Reverently serve the supreme spirits.
Always at this auspicious time,
We complete our task.
We offer black oxen,
Presenting the evening sacrifice.
Exalting virtue, making music,
The gods and spirits listen.
Song for Greeting and Sending Off Spirits at Sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the Five Suburbs
May Xuānwén (宣文) flourish!
May he calm the four directions daily.
May he forever protect them,
Toil day and night without rest.
Glorifying Heaven's mandate,
The Supreme Lord is emperor.
Excellent music, grand offerings,
Spiritual blessings, great auspiciousness.
Gods and spirits descend,
Enjoying boundless fortune.
Song for Feasting Heaven, Earth, and the Five Suburbs
Heaven blesses the great Jìn (晉),
Its mandate is new.
Receiving the end from Wèi (魏),
Possessing all the people.
Reaching up to august Heaven,
Harmonizing all the gods.
Greatly manifest the enduring legacy,
Its virtue pure.
Enjoying its black oxen,
Thus beginning the burning sacrifice.
Gods and spirits come,
Blessings and prosperity arrive.
At the right time, he marches,
The vast Heaven treats him as its son.
Protecting and enjoying the Jìn (晉),
All people begin to uphold him.
Awe-struck by Heaven's might,
Reverently bestowing timely actions upon men.
Greatly manifest, greatly inherit,
Constantly thinking of the path.
The imperial ultimate is thus established,
All achievements flourish.
May we strive day and night,
For the well-being of Jìn (晉).
Xuānwén (宣文) as empress,
Is able to match Heaven.
Soothing and pacifying the four seas,
Possessing years of peace.
Oh, how bright and continuous!
Thus pacifying the people.
She establishes laws and institutions,
She reforms rites and records.
Becoming the standard for the people,
Everything originates from her.
She makes her descendants prosper,
Forever protecting them.
Song for Evening Sacrifice at Heaven's Suburb and the Míngtáng (明堂)
How majestic is the great Jìn (晉)!
Its virtue proceeds with the times.
Receiving the end from Heaven,
Gloriously bringing aid to all nations.
When all nations are glorious,
The spirits affirm their auspiciousness.
Piously performing suburban sacrifices,
Reverently serving the Supreme Lord.
Reverently serving the Supreme Lord,
A hundred blessings arrive.
How grand are the ancestors!
They can match Heaven.
Not coveting fine sacrifices,
Only enjoying the fragrance of virtue.
Receiving Heaven's blessings,
The divine transforms the four directions.
Song for Invoking Spirits at Heaven's Suburb and the Míngtáng (明堂)
Oh, how illustrious is the great Jìn (晉)!
Responding to Heaven with great auspiciousness.
The two emperors advanced virtue,
Proclaiming this double glory.
Our august emperor received the mandate,
Possessing all lands.
Suburban sacrifices and matching offerings,
Rites and music are grand.
Gods and spirits enjoy the offerings,
Ancestors are august.
May their descendants prosper,
Their reign boundless.
Song for Feasting Spirits at Heaven's Suburb
Arranging the Tàitán,
worshiping the imperial deities.
Essence and qi respond,
all spirits attend.
Hidden crimson fire,
igniting fragrant kindling.
Purple smoke drifts,
crowning the green clouds.
The body of the gods,
without form or shape.
Vast and boundless,
profound and clear.
When the gods arrive,
light and shadow are manifest.
Listening hears nothing,
seeing sees no omens.
When the gods reach,
all is pleased.
Spirits and souls harmonize,
stirring my heart.
When the gods are seated,
we share joy and delight.
Benevolent clouds soar,
transforming into gentle breezes.
Auspicious music is played,
eloquent sounds.
The eight tones harmonize,
the gods listen.
All are pure and tidy,
all are fragrant.
Offering whole sacrifices,
presenting jade goblets.
The gods delight in the offerings,
accepting the sacrifice.
Blessing the great Jìn,
sending down abundant blessings.
Building the capital city,
extending to the four seas.
Protecting the celestial years,
to the end of the earthly era.
Song for the suburban earth altar offering to the gods
Arranging the Tàizhì,
awaiting the imperial Dí.
All gods are moved,
all spirits are solemn.
The yin sacrifice is established,
auspicious rites are performed.
Night is at its deepest,
the hour has not yet changed.
The body of the Dí,
without image or form.
Hidden in profound darkness,
penetrating the vast wilderness.
When the Dí appears,
obscurely as if present.
The spirit is not far,
mother of all under heaven.
When the Dí comes,
leaving light and shadow.
Clearly as if existing,
ultimately in the dark unknown.
When the Dí arrives,
all is joyful.
The dance displays virtue,
the song forms patterns.
When the Dí is seated,
we share joy and delight.
Beneficial rain is dispensed,
transforming into spreading clouds.
Music changes eight times,
its sounds and teachings spread.
All things prosper,
the Dí is pleased.
The fast is pure,
attendants are solemn.
Jade goblets are presented,
all are reverent.
Feasting on choice delicacies,
savoring the fragrance of virtue.
Blessing the house of Jìn,
and all living beings.
Overflowing the nine regions,
reaching the heavenly court.
Preserving myriad lifespans,
extending billions of years.
Song for the Míngtáng offering to the gods
Starting the Míngtáng,
offering sacrifices tirelessly.
Oh, august and exalted ancestor,
whose brilliance matches the Shàngdì.
Resplendent Shàngdì,
both high and lofty.
The sage ancestor matches Him,
his bright virtue shines brightly.
All within the four seas respectfully perform their duties,
ten thousand regions come to offer sacrifices.
Always at this time He grants,
preserving the dynasty for eternal generations.
Song for the evening sacrifice in the ancestral temple
My evening sacrifice,
Oh, how reverent it is.
Choice provisions are timely,
supplied for this offering.
The spirits perceive their sincerity,
accepting the ample offerings.
Ancestors descend to partake,
to comfort the heart of the filial grandson.
Song for welcoming and sending off the gods in the ancestral temple
Alas, how distant,
the sun watches over this.
Offering sacrifices in due season,
the deities descend.
The deities descend,
and bless and accept the offerings.
Blessing us without limit,
receiving the blessings of Heaven.
Illustrious Tàishàng,
lofty sage ancestors.
Brilliant and exalted ancestors,
grandly inheriting the succession.
Song for the sacrifice to the Commander of the Western Expedition
Starting the ancestral temple,
the deities arrive.
Repeatedly bestowing boundless gifts,
reverently accepting the sacrifices.
Gracious imperial ancestors,
comforting your grandsons.
Reaching later generations,
bestowing abundant blessings.
Song for the sacrifice to the Lord of Yùzhāng
Auspicious music spreads through the feast,
offerings are presented in the hall.
Majestic ancestral temple,
our ancestors, our emperors.
Numerous lords and dukes,
assisting our autumn and summer sacrifices.
The offerings are without error,
bestowing blessings in abundance.
Song for the sacrifice to the Lord of Yǐngchuān
Oh, the distant former sages,
truly in charge of Heaven.
Illustrious imperial ancestors,
imperial blessings first arrived.
The main lineage can prosper,
initiating the founding era.
Benefiting us boundlessly,
enjoying the dynasty for eternal years.
Song for the sacrifice to the Lord of Jīngzhào
Oh, the great imperial ancestor,
whose virtuous conduct was clearly manifest.
High, bright, and clear,
not contending but gentle and subduing.
Protecting fate and blessing,
his founding mandate was the model.
Giving birth to the sage ancestor,
brilliantly saving the four states.
Song for the sacrifice to Emperor Xuān
Oh, glorious imperial ancestor,
whose sacred virtue was reverent and enlightened.
Diligently spreading his influence in the four directions,
respectful morning and night.
Establishing the civilizing teachings,
raising the military prestige.
Stabilizing the altars of soil and grain,
executing heavenly punishment.
Starting the great enterprise,
founding the imperial base.
Fearing the mandate of Heaven,
thus preserving it.
Song for the sacrifice to Emperor Jǐng
Vigorous Emperor Jǐng,
able to enlighten and be wise.
Extensively acting with reverence,
only reverent and fearful.
Continuing the legacy of Xuān,
establishing his achievements.
Ascending to this eminence,
rectifying those villains.
Diligent in his position,
the Emperor was indeed hardworking.
The mandate of Heaven,
oh, is eternally continuous.
Song for the sacrifice to Emperor Wén
Oh, the Jìn of that time,
truly Emperor Wén was cultured.
Intelligent and wise,
sacred, reverent, and martial.
When myriad affairs were disordered,
the Emperor brought order to them.
When serpents and boars acted recklessly,
the Emperor pacified them.
He was gentle with the distant and able with the near,
selecting and appointing outstanding talents.
Founding the enterprise and establishing the lineage,
his merits reached august Heaven.
Two songs for the ancestral temple offering to the gods
It is the constant way of Jìn,
to offer seasonal sacrifices.
Reverence is paid at the ancestral temples,
and rites and music are fully performed.
When they come to sacrifice,
all under Heaven and all the land [are included].
The sacrificial vessels are already set,
and the clear wine is already poured.
There are also harmonious soups,
and all kinds of delicacies are prepared.
With profound and eternal yearning,
thoughts arise at the opportune moment.
Songs are sung and dances are performed,
and the divine music is harmonious.
Ancestors come and descend,
blessing our state and family.
Under the vast sky,
nothing is without beauty and praise.
Reverent ones are in their places,
and numerous ministers and officials are present.
All within the Four Seas come,
with dignified禮儀 (lǐyí).
Bells and drums vibrate,
pipes and strings are tuned,
dances begin in primordial splendor,
songs sing of eternal beginnings,
and the spirits are all joyful!
Reverent ones are in their places,
and ministers and officials are numerous.
Great and small alike are reverent,
and upper and lower ranks observe proper礼 (lǐ).
Pipes and strings are tuned,
drums and bells vibrate,
dances emulate virtue,
songs praise achievements,
and the spirits are all joyful!
Reverent ones are in their places,
with those who come in harmony.
The august Son of Heaven,
assisted by the various dukes.
Rites have their proper forms,
music has its rules,
dances emulate achievements,
songs praise virtue,
and the spirits are all joyful!
Dù Kuí (Dù Kuí) transmitted four ancient *yǎyuè* (yǎyuè) pieces:
The first is called "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng),
the second "Zōu Yú" (Zōu Yú),
the third "Fá Tán" (Fá Tán),
and the fourth "Wén Wáng" (Wén Wáng),
all ancient melodies and lyrics.
During the Tàihé (Tàihé) reign,
Zuǒ Yánnián (Zuǒ Yánnián) altered Dù Kuí's (Dù Kuí) "Zōu Yú" (Zōu Yú), "Fá Tán" (Fá Tán), and "Wén Wáng" (Wén Wáng) three pieces,
composing new melodies and rhythms himself.
Although their names remained,
their sounds were truly different.
Only Dù Kuí's (Dù Kuí) "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng)
was completely unchanged.
Whenever there was a grand assembly on New Year's Day,
the Grand Commandant offered jade discs,
and the various princes performed their rites;
the *yǎyuè* (yǎyuè) regularly performed in the east wing was this.
Later, the ceremonial poems of these three pieces were also changed.
The first was called "Yú Hè Piān" (Yú Hè Piān),
eulogizing Wǔ Dì (Wǔ Dì),
with a melody and rhythm identical to the ancient "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng).
The second was called "Wēiwēi Piān" (Wēiwēi Piān),
eulogizing Wén Dì (Wén Dì),
using the "Zōu Yú" (Zōu Yú) melody as altered by Yánnián (Yánnián).
The third was called "Yángyáng Piān" (Yángyáng Piān),
eulogizing Míng Dì (Míng Dì),
using the "Wén Wáng" (Wén Wáng) melody as altered by Yánnián (Yánnián).
The fourth reused "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng).
The "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng) melody was used twice,
and the ancient "Fá Tán" (Fá Tán) was removed.
At the beginning of the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty,
the banquet music also used "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng).
By the fifth year of Tàishǐ (Tàishǐ) (269 CE),
the Secretariat reported,

instructing Grand Coachman Fù Xuán (Fù Xuán), Central Secretariat Director Xún Xù (Xún Xù), and Palace Attendant Zhāng Huá (Zhāng Huá) to each compose songs and poems for the New Year's Day ceremony, the royal and ducal longevity wine offering, and the banquet music.
Xún Xù (Xún Xù) said:
"During the Wèi (Wèi) dynasty's ceremonies and banquets,
the 'Lù Míng' (Lù Míng) from the *Shī Jīng* (Shī Jīng) was twice adopted as a musical piece.
Moreover, 'Lù Míng' (Lù Míng) is for feasting honored guests,
and has no place in the court.
Examining old records,
it is unclear why it was applied there."
So Xún Xù (Xún Xù) removed the old "Lù Míng" (Lù Míng) songs
and composed four new ceremonial poems,
first presenting the meaning of the three courts' homage.
He also composed songs and poems for the New Year's Day grand assembly and the royal and ducal longevity wine offering, as well as songs and poems for the banquet music,
totaling thirteen pieces.
He also noted that the Wèi (Wèi) dynasty's songs and poems were sometimes two-character,
sometimes three-character,
sometimes four-character,
or sometimes five-character,
unlike ancient poetry,
and he asked the Commandant of Music, Chén Qí (Chén Qí), about this.
Chén Qí (Chén Qí) said:
"When set to metal and stone instruments,
they may not all be appropriate."
Therefore, the Jìn (Jìn) songs composed by Xún Xù (Xún Xù)
were all four-character,
except for the piece for the royal and ducal longevity wine, which was three-character and five-character.
Zhāng Huá (Zhāng Huá) believed
that "the Wèi (Wèi) dynasty's longevity and banquet poems, and those used by the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty,
had irregular line lengths,
not all conforming to ancient standards.
This is probably because they followed the existing string melodies,
which had inherent traditions.
And those who understood music and rhythm
were capable enough to compose melodies and tunes.
The methods used were generally not something ordinary people could change.
Across two dynasties and three capitals,
they were inherited and remained unchanged.
Although the poetic lyrics differed
and rose and fell with the times,
their rhymes, pauses, and melodic turns
were all tied to the old forms,
and there was a reason for this.
Therefore, I have simply followed them,
not daring to make any alterations."
This shows the differing views of Zhāng Huá (Zhāng Huá) and Xún Xù (Xún Xù).
At that time, an imperial edict also instructed Palace Attendant Chénggōng Suí (Chénggōng Suí) to compose pieces,
and now they are all collected and listed here.
Songs for the Four Wings of Music: Songs for the New Year's Day Grand Assembly Ceremony (by Chénggōng Suí)
The august Son of Heaven,
shines upon myriad nations.
Numerous scholars fill the court,
none without outstanding virtue.
His transforming influence is boundless,
his royal policies truly secure.
At the splendid gathering, wine is set,
honored guests fill the courtyard.
Feathered banners glitter at the imperial zenith,
bells and drums resonate through the clear sky.
Myriad lords pay homage at the three courts,
resplendent in their bright forms.
Numerous and resonant,
like the sound of metal and jade.
Rites and music are complete,
feasting honored guests.
Long life blesses the sagely emperor,
great fortune renews daily.
The various lords arrive,
coming in harmony.
Offering and receiving gifts,
exalting this ceremonial demeanor.
Abundant delicacies on myriad tables,
fine wine in a thousand goblets.
All rejoice in the feast,
fortune and prosperity are shared.
How joyful!
The world is peaceful and stable.
The Dao's transformation spreads,
customs are purified.
The *xiāosháo* (xiāosháo) music is performed,
singing the nine accomplishments.
Years are bountiful,
the world is greatly peaceful.
How perfectly governed,
joy is endless.
The sovereign is wise and enlightened,
his ministers are loyal.
He establishes great bounty,
and spreads pure influence.
Auspicious omens appear,
divine responses manifest.
Qílín (Qílín) are seen,
Fènghuáng (Fènghuáng) soar.
Sweet springs gush forth,
flowing through the central hall.
Auspicious grains grow,
ears filling the bins.
Great blessings descend,
bestowing upon the sagely emperor.
He holds the heavenly position,
ruling myriad nations.
He received the Mandate and met the opportune time,
endowed with sagely virtue.
Four generations shine with renewed glory.
Xuān Dì (Xuān Dì) initiated the grand enterprise,
Jǐng Dì (Jǐng Dì) greatly flourished,
Wén Dì (Wén Dì) was reverent and enlightened,
his virtue ever more manifest.
Founding the Jìn (Jìn) state,
his blessings are boundless.
In the first year of the Tàishǐ era,
the phoenix and dragon arose.
Why did the dragon arise?
To enjoy the throne of a myriad chariots,
possessing all the eight directions,
nurturing and educating the common people.
The charts and writings shone brightly,
and the bronze and stone tablets bore witness.
His virtue shone brilliantly,
his Way flourished grandly.
It spread throughout the four quarters,
reaching the imperial heaven.
Numerous descendants will be illustrious,
brightly and conspicuously eminent,
achieving a glorious end.
Preserving this eternal reign,
equal in loftiness to Heaven.
The sagely emperor rules the four seas,
following human will and responding to Heaven's mandate.
Three generations united in renewed glory,
the Tàishǐ era inaugurated the grand foundation.
His brilliance rivals the sun and moon,
his achievements and transformations are like the four seasons.
The universe is clear and peaceful,
the common people are all harmonious and prosperous.
How excellent, harmonious and prosperous!
It is Heaven that bestows the mandate,
assisting the benevolent and protecting the sagely.
Oh, how majestic are the Three August Ones,
their virtue increasingly abundant.
They unified and harmonized the xúanqí (celestial spheres),
and brightly governed the qīzhèng (seven celestial bodies).
All affairs were in their proper order,
their transformations like those of gods and sages.
The four seas shared a common custom,
giving rise to utmost benevolence.
They saved the people and nurtured creation,
emulating the potter's wheel.
Emulating the potter's wheel,
they bestowed grace and moistening.
Splendid are the assembled worthies,
lofty are the heroes and prodigies.
Their virtuous influence is proclaimed,
their fragrance spreads to future generations.
Spreading to future generations,
it extends to later descendants.
How solemn and majestic is the pure ancestral temple,
the imperial gate (huángjí) opens on four sides.
The imperial gate opens on four sides,
all affairs of state are comprehensively managed.
Diligent and cautious,
never indulging in excess pleasure,
nor delaying meals even in hunger.
When the grand rites are performed,
joy knows no bounds.
Ascending Kūnlún,
reaching the layered city.
Riding flying dragons,
ascending to the Great Purity (Tàiqīng).
Crowned with the sun and moon,
wearing the five planets.
Unfurling rainbows,
erecting comet banners.
Donning auspicious clouds,
sheltered by luxuriant growth.
Surveying the eight extremes,
traveling through the celestial court.
Following Heaven and Earth,
harmonizing yin and yang.
Ordering the four seasons,
illuminating the three luminaries.
Spreading the imperial net,
rectifying the imperial system.
Disseminating benevolent customs,
spreading beneficial peace.
Advancing grand transformations,
wielding divine might.
Embracing all lands,
receiving the Nine Yí.
Holding court at Chānghé,
feasting in Zǐwēi.
Setting up five banners,
arranging bells and stands.
Displaying four sets of instruments,
playing Sháo and Wǔ music.
Clanging bronze and stone instruments,
waving banners and plumes.
Performing the bāyì dance,
and the Bāyú dance.
Reciting Yǎ and Sòng odes,
harmonizing the pitches (lǜlǚ).
Oh, how joyful,
joyful for the sagely ruler.
His transformations are vast,
pure winds emanate.
He gathers heroes,
and commands outstanding talents.
He opens up the universe,
and sweeps away the four barbarians.
His glory shines brightly,
he is lauded as a sage and philosopher.
Surpassing a hundred generations,
extolling his glorious achievements.
His auspicious reign flows,
manifest for myriad generations.
Illustrious is the Manifest Ancestor (Xiǎnzǔ),
who assisted the world and aided the times.
He pacified and brought peace to the six directions,
receiving the mandate at the appointed time.
His divine martial prowess soared like an eagle,
and his great transformations were all glorious.
He vastly opened the imperial road,
thus establishing the imperial foundation.
Bright is Emperor Jǐng (Jǐnghuáng),
whose achievements are unrivaled.
He corrected the times and saved the populace,
his glorious merits covering the world.
The universe was made peaceful,
the nine regions were unified.
Heaven's mandate descended,
inaugurating the reign for the wise and discerning.
Majestic is the Illustrious Deceased Father (Lièkǎo),
who was sagacious and outstanding.
Truly Heaven endowed him with virtue,
