he was born to respond to the auspicious fate.
He initiated and established the imperial enterprise,
founding the state of Jìn.
His virtue spread through generations,
bestowing blessings upon his great descendants.
Bright is the Sagely Emperor,
soaring like a dragon in the sky.
United with the spiritual covenant,
his virtue connected to the profound and mysterious.
Looking up, he transformed the azure clouds,
looking down, he nurtured the many rivers.
Receiving divine blessings,
for ten thousand years.
Song for the Grand Assembly of Kings and Dukes on New Year's Day to Offer Wine for Longevity (by Xún Xù)
Treading on the prime auspicious day,
extending to the eminent and glorious ones.
Offering winged goblets,
praying for a glorious end.
Our Emperor is long-lived and great,
our Emperor is flourishing and lofty.
His lineage thrives for a hundred generations,
auspicious blessings gather upon his sacred person.
Songs for the East and West Aisles of the Banquet Music (by Xún Xù)
Splendid are the Qīyào (seven luminaries),
their double brightness flowing smoothly.
We have esteemed guests,
who are here by invitation and as a gift.
After the state affairs are planned,
they are received with a grand feast.
People who are fond of me,
follow the principles of virtue and deference.
At the guests' initial banquet,
they are dignified and orderly.
After the morning court, then the banquet,
to harmonize all ceremonies.
They are assigned positions,
either in the courtyard or on the steps.
Those who ascend the platform for guests,
also include brothers.
Assisting officials and subordinates,
they exemplify these standards and models.
Observing and nourishing rectitude,
blessings descend abundantly.
In the past, our Three Sovereigns (Sānhòu),
maintained great enterprises.
Now our Sagely Emperor,
shines brilliantly like the former radiance.
His generations repeat the rule,
brightly illuminating the nine regions (Jiǔjī).
He thinks of unifying to glorify,
and at no time does he deviate.
Following the path of Yǔ,
all do not fail to be awed.
Heaven bestows manifest blessings,
and peace and prosperity are secured.
Mighty is the Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ),
who greatly expanded bright virtue.
He vastly opened the universe,
corrected the world and established rules.
His transformations were extraordinary,
the people were without blemish or fault.
He founded the enterprise and established the lineage,
initiating our state of Jìn.
Illustrious and cultivated is the Elder Deceased Father (Báikǎo),
who was Emperor Jǐng (Dì Jǐng).
He pacified dangers and suppressed chaos,
awesome but not fierce.
He governed without error,
the imperial path brightly illuminated.
His seven virtues were all proclaimed,
and his peace was eternal.
Oh, what grandeur!
The sagely writings of the former emperor
are as vast as Heaven, inspiring trust.
Great indeed is he as a ruler.
He diligently observes the Five Constants,
and is assiduous in his imperial duties.
His civilian and military virtues are manifest,
establishing splendid achievements.
He cultivates himself and brings order to governance,
so the people live in peace and prosperity.
He embraces the distant and illuminates the obscure,
his profound teachings pervasive.
He benefits the world without boasting,
and the three parts of the empire serve him.
His virtue is broad, his transforming influence profound,
his Dao flourishes without limit.
His profound transformation is boundless,
the imperial mandate spreads widely.
He ascends to our Jìn (晉) Way,
he is indeed a sagely king.
The dragon flies, changing the times,
his benevolent sway covers the eight directions.
He is wise, discerning, revered, and enlightened,
matching the footsteps of Yú (虞) and Táng (唐).
He establishes his blessings,
and auspicious signs vigorously appear.
Three dynasties have practiced what is good,
and ultimately it is truly excellent.
What is this excellence?
He unites all lands.
Princes and regional lords,
the Four Peaks and vassal kings.
They appear seasonally and offer tribute,
following this constant practice.
They bow in the courtyard,
distinguished guests in the hall.
Sòng (宋) and Wèi (衞) have arrived,
Chénlíu (陳留) and Shānyáng (山陽).
There are guests and envoys,
beholding the glory of the state.
They offer worthy men and submit strategies,
presenting jade disks and scepters.
Heaven protects and bestows upon him,
granting boundless blessings.
Herons fly gracefully,
wild geese spread their wings.
The capital city is serene,
a model for the four directions.
None can contend with such a ruler,
the royal綱 is truly ordered.
Gentlemen come to court,
to observe his ultimate standard.
How majestic is the great ruler,
the one whom the people look up to.
He truly governs according to Heaven's work,
his benevolence and peace are inexhaustible.
He will keep away the unbenevolent,
and instruct with purity and sincerity.
The dark and the bright have their order,
the talented are in their positions.
The nine clans are harmonious,
the various states follow and comply.
He establishes new beginnings and promulgates laws,
the four seas gather like scales.
He harmonizes with the times and rectifies the tradition,
different paths lead to the same goal.
His profound virtue sustains all things,
his spiritual heart is esteemed and noble.
He spreads and presents upright words,
accepting them without reservation.
He establishes models and regulations,
and teaches the categories of righteousness.
The teaching from above is like the wind,
the response from below is like grass.
When one man is blessed,
the myriad people prosper.
Our sovereign enjoys his feasts,
his excellent reputation never fades.
Having feasted and rejoiced,
all the myriad states are united.
Rites and ceremonies are perfectly observed,
things assume their proper forms.
Bright, bright are the courtyard torches,
resounding, resounding are the drums and bells.
Sheng (笙) pipes and qìng (磬) chimes chant his virtues,
the myriad dances symbolize his achievements.
The eight musical sounds harmonize perfectly,
customs are transformed and followed.
Their harmony is like music,
the myriad things are eternally peaceful.
Peaceful and refined,
the whole world is united.
Our ancestor, Xuān (宣),
awed and pacified the different neighbors.
First, he settled Jīngchǔ (荊楚),
then pacified Yān (燕) and Qín (秦).
How diligent was the enlightened emperor,
extending his virtue and benevolence.
He created order from chaos,
responding to Heaven and conforming to the people.
Spiritual omens announced their agreement,
auspicious signs resonated.
Heaven and Earth did not resist,
thus harmonizing gods and men.
He captured Yōng (庸) and Shǔ (蜀),
and Wúhuì (吳會) became his guest.
Sùshèn (肅慎) performed its duties,
presenting kǔ (楛) arrows.
Hán (韓) and Huì (濊) presented music,
with clear gōng (宮) and zhǐ (徵) notes.
The Western tribes offered mastiffs,
Fúnán (扶南) presented treasures.
The barbarian tribes, after multiple translations,
with black teeth and tattooed bodies.
Our emperor soothed them,
the glorious mandate renewed.
Quiet and harmonious is the grand assembly,
heard without sound.
The clear wine is already poured,
the biān (籩) and dòu (豆) dishes are already presented.
Rites are complete, music is prepared,
the xiāosháo (簫韶) music plays nine times.
Joyfully they drink wine,
getting drunk but not excessive.
The whole land rejoices,
the states are thus peaceful.
The royal rule is truly solid,
unshaken for ten thousand years.
Song for the Small Assembly on the Winter Solstice, the Beginning of the Year (by Zhāng Huà (張華))
Sun and moon do not tarry,
the four seasons cycle through.
Festivities succeed each other,
all nations share the joy.
The various officials and high lords
offer congratulations and ascend to court.
I have a congratulatory ritual,
to feast all officials.
Luxurious dishes are intricately arranged,
fine wine flows from springs.
Shēng (笙) pipes and yōng (鏞) bells play in harmony,
qìng (磬) chimes and guǎn (管) pipes emit sounds.
The emperor's love is profound,
the subjects offer their utmost sincerity.
He clears away their obstructions,
and instructs them with virtuous words.
Thus he clears and instructs,
sharing and enjoying universal harmony.
Forever he will carry the benevolent wind,
long ruling without external boundaries.
Song for a Feast (by Zhāng Huà (張華))
How diligent is our emperor,
matching Heaven and shedding light.
He concentrates his essence from dawn till dusk,
his administration is boundless.
Having leisure from court audiences,
he extends an invitation to all his ministers.
Hats and carriages gather like clouds,
goblets and stands are arrayed like stars.
Many kinds of cooked delicacies,
the eight treasures change in variety.
Feathered goblets are countless,
enjoying the ultimate in music and feasting.
Singers pour forth their voices,
dancers toss their sleeves.
Every movement is rhythmic,
strings and bamboo instruments are all present.
They display various postures,
with intricate and urgent movements.
Joy is sufficient to generate harmony,
getting drunk without forgetting propriety.
Loving music without excess,
they are dignified and orderly.
Song for Commissioning a General to Go on Campaign (by Zhāng Huà (張華))
Chónghuá (重華) elevated the imperial Dao,
but the southern barbarians were sometimes disobedient.
The Eastern Yi (夷) rose up against Zhōu (周),
the Guǐfāng (鬼方) also defied Yīn (殷).
Now in this glorious and enlightened age,
bandits and tyrants stir in the four corners.
Wolves dye their fangs and claws with blood,
all living beings cry out to the vast sky.
The Grand Marshal commands the central land,
sending forth chariots to pacify Liáng (涼) and Qín (秦).
The multitude of loyal ones must act according to rules,
good and bad truly depend on people.
His prestige and trust extend to different tribes,
even the remote Di (狄) long to be close.
How could plain wine have any flavor?
But a single quilt touches with utmost benevolence.
Martial merit values ceasing aggression,
the seven virtues beautify the pacification of the people.
Distant lands are thus brought in,
for eternal peace without conflict.
Song for Rewarding Returning Troops (by Zhāng Huà (張華))
The Xiǎnyǔn rebelled against Heaven's virtue,
stirring up chaos and disturbing the capital region.
War chariots thundered in the northern wilderness,
and all the commanders assisted the imperial might.
Generals and soldiers, united in purpose,
felt the call of righteousness and forgot their private concerns.
Their amassed power was like a drawn crossbow,
they advanced to the beat like a released mechanism.
Their shouts shook valleys and mountains,
golden light gleamed in the clear dawn.
Wielding halberds, they overran formidable foes,
their martial steps trod on fallen corpses.
All the whales and monsters were captured,
and the northern lands were forever pacified.
In the past, they ventured forth amidst the scorching heat,
now, white snow falls upon their return.
The conscripted soldiers indeed toiled diligently,
as has been sung since ancient times in "Cǎiwēi."
They will reap glory upon laying down their shields,
and rejoice in their triumphant return.
Song of the Central Palace (Zhāng Huà)
The former kings unified great undertakings,
their profound transforming influence spread to the eight directions.
Their exemplary conduct inspired all nations,
and their inner teachings flourished in the women's quarters.
August sagely rulers bequeathed imperial canons,
and the "Dàyǎ" sang of the three consorts.
Upholding virtue, they proclaimed profound teachings,
rectifying their positions to manage their affairs.
Containing inner brilliance, they embodied gentleness and compliance,
leading with ritual and treading with humility and reverence.
Like locusts, they spread benevolence and kindness,
like entwined trees, they reached the humble and obscure.
Their excellent reputations were like a pure breeze,
their noble righteousness was vast and unattainable.
Their inherited glory partakes of the sun and moon,
for a hundred generations their lingering radiance is looked up to.
Song for Clan Gatherings (Zhāng Huà)
Clan feasts embody decorum and harmony,
eating and drinking arranged by kinship.
Flesh and blood, though dispersed, are not different,
how could brothers be strangers?
The main branch cherishes common joy,
"Tángdì" speaks of the ancients.
Oh, the august sagely and enlightened empress,
her heavenly covering is vast and benevolent.
She bestows ritual to honor relatives,
spreading it widely to unite clans and in-laws.
They feast to their heart's content,
enjoying an array of delicacies.
Harmony and joy are widely spread,
high and low share in the happiness.
Moral teachings reach the four seas,
friendship extends without bound.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
Guānglù Dàfū Xún Xù, using the pitch pipes created by Dù Kuí,
compared the music of Tàilè, Zǒngzhāng, and Gǔchuī with the eight sounds.
Finding discrepancies with the pitch pipes,
he then devised an ancient standard ruler,
and created new pitch pipes,
to harmonize the sounds and rhythms.
The matter is fully detailed in the Lǜlì Zhì.
Once the pitch pipes were completed,
they were then promulgated to the Tàicháng,
for Tàilè, Zǒngzhāng, Gǔchuī, and Qīngshāng to implement.
Xù then took charge of music affairs,
inviting court scholars knowledgeable in music to manage it together.
He had Guō Xià, Sòng Shí, and others create the two dances, Zhèngdé and Dàyù,
whose musical lyrics are also said to have been composed by Zhāng Huà.
Song for the Zhèngdé Dance (Zhāng Huà)
Says the August Supreme Heaven,
its profound illumination is brilliant.
The sacred vessel rotates,

The mandate of rule belongs to Jìn,

Greatly assisting and saving the central lands,

The imperial Way is pure,

Metal and stone instruments are hung,

Symbolic forms display good fortune,

Surpassing Wǔ and Huò,
taking their rhythm from the "Liùyīng."
Advancing, retreating, and yielding together,

Great harmony proclaims its widespread reach,
extending to the dark netherworld.
Song for the Dàyù Dance (Zhāng Huà)
Only the mandate of Heaven,
the cosmic fortune has a place to return.
Illustrious and mighty is Dà Jìn,

Continuing brilliance through generations,
gloriously pacifying the nine regions.
Our emperor inherits the epoch,
thus residing in the celestial sphere.
All beings depend on his mandate,
swiftly possessing all nations.
Diligently observing the Five Canons,
profound teachings extend afar.
All regions share the same tracks,
the whole land is harmonious.
Thus was Dàyù created,
proclaiming virtue and the dance's merit.
Profound transformation is serene,
the kingly way flourishes in harmony.
Benevolence reaches plants and trees,
kindness extends to insects.
Billions of common people,
joyfully look up to the imperial style.
Great achievements are splendidly manifest,
eternally revered for generations.
Xún Xù also created twelve new pitch flutes,
to tune the pitch pipes,
and correct the court music.
He performed them in the court of Zhènghuì Hall,
claiming that the Gōng and Shāng modes were perfectly harmonious.
However, critics still said Xù had a shallow understanding.
At that time, Ruǎn Xián was wonderfully adept at the eight sounds,
and critics called his understanding divine.
Xián often secretly criticized Xù's new pitch pipes for their high sound,
believing they were too high and close to sorrow,
not conforming to moderation and harmony.
Whenever music was played at public gatherings,
Xù felt Xián considered it disharmonious,
deeming him an antagonist,
and so he exiled Xián to become the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng.
Later, a farmer plowing in the wilderness
found a jade ruler from the Zhōu dynasty.
Xù used it to calibrate his own adjusted bells, drums, metal, stone, strings, and bamboo instruments,
and all were found to be short by one mì.
At this, he acknowledged Xián's brilliance,
and recalled Xián to court.
After Xù had created two dances with the new pitch pipes,
he next began to correct the sound of the bells.
without completing his work.
In the third year of Yuánkāng,
an imperial edict commanded his son Fān to revise and set the metal and stone instruments,
for use in suburban and ancestral temples.
Soon after, due to chaos and disorder,
no one recorded this.
When Hàn Gāozǔ led his forces from Shǔ-Hàn to pacify the Three Qín,

After pacifying Qínzhōng,

Their custom was to enjoy dancing,
and Gāozǔ delighted in their fierce spirit,
frequently watching their dances.
Later, he had musicians learn them.
There was the Yú River in Lángzhōng,
and because of their dwelling there,
it was named Bāyú Wǔ.
The dance music included "Máoyú Běnqǔ," "Ānnǔyú Běnqǔ,"

Their lyrics were ancient,
and no one could understand their phrasing or meter.
In the early Wèi dynasty,
Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ Wáng Càn was ordered to revise their lyrics.
Càn asked the Bāyú chiefs, Lǐ Guǎn and Zhǒng Yù, about the meaning of the songs,
and had them sing,
listening to them,
to compare and verify the songs.
He then revised them to "Máoyú Xīnfú Gēqǔ," "Nǔyú Xīnfú Gēqǔ," "Āntái Xīnfú Gēqǔ," and "Xíngcí Xīnfú Gēqǔ,"
with "Xíngcí" describing Wèi's virtue.
In the third year of Huángchū,

By the first year of Jǐngchū,

after examining the surviving ritual music of the Three Dynasties,

all performed holding feathers and flutes.
In the Jìn dynasty, Zhāowǔ Wǔ was again renamed Xuānwǔ Wǔ,

In the first year of Xiánníng,

Collation Notes
Zhì, Chapter 13, Music (Part II)
During the Disorder of Yǒngjiā,
the realm disintegrated,
and court musicians and musical instruments
were all lost to Liú and Shí.
When the ancestral temple was first established on the Left Bank of the Jiāng River,
the Minister of the Secretariat submitted a request to the Grand Master of Ceremonies for the names of the music to be used in the sacrifices.
Hè Xún, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, replied:
"The Wèi dynasty augmented and diminished Hàn music
to create the rites for their own era.
I am not aware of the differences in the names of the music of the great Jìn dynasty.
Having endured times of sorrow and disorder,
the old institutions no longer exist.
However, all these musical pieces are harmonized with bells and pitch-pipes,
embellished with the five tones,
sung in lyrical verses,
and presented in dance formations.
Bell and chime sets are suspended in the courtyard,
qín and sè are in the hall,
the eight sounds are played in alternation,
and yǎyuè music is performed simultaneously.
The 'ascending songs' and 'descending pipes'
each have their regular chants,
which are remnants of the Zhōu people.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
this ritual has been emulated,
with only new poetry created.
The old capital is desolate,
and now everything is scattered and lost.
The intricacies of the melodies and rhythms
are also unknown to anyone now,
so it is difficult to express them by intention today."
At that time, due to the lack of yǎyuè instruments and musicians,
the offices of Grand Music Master and Drum and Pipe Master were abolished.
After this, 'ascending songs' were gradually recovered,
but the music for the 'food presentation' ritual
was still incomplete.
At the end of Tàiníng,
Emperor Míng again consulted Ruǎn Fú and others to augment it.
During Xiánhé,
Emperor Chéng re-established the office of Grand Music Master,
gathering scattered remnants,
but still lacked metal and stone instruments.
When Yǔ Liàng served as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he collaborated with Xiè Shàng to restore yǎyuè music,
but Liàng died before it was completed.
Yǔ Yì and Huán Wēn were solely preoccupied with military campaigns,
and the musical instruments in storage
consequently decayed and were ruined.
When Mùróng Jùn pacified Rǎn Mǐn,
even amidst the warfare,
many musicians from Yè came.
In the eleventh year of Yǒnghé,
Xiè Shàng was stationed at Shòuyáng,
and thereupon collected musicians
to complete the Grand Music,
and also manufactured stone chimes,
whereupon yǎyuè music gradually became somewhat complete.
When Wáng Měng pacified Yè,
the music obtained by the Mùróng clan also entered the Guān Yòu region.
During Tàiyuán,
Fú Jiān was defeated,
and his court musicians such as Yáng Shǔ were captured,
who were skilled in the old music.
Thus, the four-sided metal and stone instruments were finally complete.
Then Cáo Pí, Wáng Xún, and others were commissioned to compose new songs for the ancestral temple,
but music was still not provided for the suburban sacrifices.
Their lyrics are listed below.

During the Hàn dynasty, there was the music of "Short Flute and Náo Songs."
Its tunes included Zhū Lù, Sī Bēi Wēng, Ài Rú Zhāng, Shàng Zhī Huí, Yōng Lí, Zhàn Chéng Nán, Wū Shān Gāo, Shàng Líng, Jiāng Jìn Jiǔ, Jūn Mǎ Huáng, Fāng Shù,
Yǒu Suǒ Sī, Zhì Zǐ Bān, Shèng Rén Chū, Shàng Xié, Lín Gāo Tái, Yuǎn Rú Qī, Shí Liú, Wù Chéng, Xuán Yún, Huáng Jué Xíng, Diào Gān, and others.
They were listed among the military music,
mostly describing matters of battles and formations.
When the Wèi received the mandate,
they changed twelve of these tunes,
and commissioned Miù Xí to compose new lyrics,
describing how their merits and virtues replaced the Hàn.
Zhū Lù was changed to Chǔ Zhī Píng,
referring to Wèi.
Sī Bēi Wēng was changed to Zhàn Xíng Yáng,
referring to Cáo Gōng.
Ài Rú Zhāng was changed to Huò Lǚ Bù,
referring to Cáo Gōng besieging Lín Huái in the east,
and capturing Lǚ Bù.
Shàng Zhī Huí was changed to Kè Guān Dù,
referring to Cáo Gōng fighting Yuán Shào,
and defeating him at Guān Dù.
Yōng Lí was changed to Jiù Bāng,
referring to Cáo Gōng defeating Yuán Shào at Guān Dù,
and returning to Qiáo to collect the dead and wounded soldiers.
Zhàn Chéng Nán was changed to Dìng Wǔ Gōng,
referring to Cáo Gōng first conquering Yè,
and the pacification of Wǔ Gōng beginning from this.
Wū Shān Gāo was changed to Tú Liǔ Chéng,
referring to Cáo Gōng crossing the northern frontier,
passing through Bái Tán,
and defeating the three-commander U-Huán at Liǔ Chéng.
Shàng Líng was changed to Píng Nán Jīng,
referring to Cáo Gōng pacifying Jīng Zhōu.
Jiāng Jìn Jiǔ was changed to Píng Guān Zhōng,
referring to Cáo Gōng campaigning against Mǎ Chāo,
and pacifying Guān Zhōng.
Yǒu Suǒ Sī was changed to Yìng Dì Qī,
referring to Wén Dì receiving the mandate with his sagely virtue,
in response to the destined era.
Fāng Shù was changed to Yōng Xī,
referring to the Wèi clan governing their state,
with harmonious relations between ruler and minister,
and all achievements flourishing.
Shàng Xié was changed to Tài Hé,
referring to Míng Dì succeeding to the throne and continuing the lineage,
with the era name changed to Tài Hé,
and his benevolent favor spreading widely.
The rest retained their old names.
At this time, Wú also had Wéi Zhāo compose twelve new tune names,
to describe their merits and virtues in receiving the mandate.
Zhū Lù was changed to Yán Jīng Quē,
referring to the decline of the Hàn house,
Sūn Jiān's vigorous resolve to rise up,
his mind set on restoring and saving,
and the beginning of his royal achievements from this.
Sī Bēi Wēng was changed to Hàn Zhī Jì,
referring to Sūn Jiān mourning the decline of the Hàn,
grieving over Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
raising an army to vigorously strike,
and his achievements covering the land within the seas.
Ài Rú Zhāng was changed to Shū Wǔ Shī,
referring to Quán inheriting his father's enterprise and embarking on campaigns.
Shàng Zhī Huí was changed to Wū Lín,
referring to Wèi Wǔ Dì having broken Jīng Zhōu,
sailing eastwards downstream,
intending to contend for supremacy,
and Quán ordering general Zhōu Yú to counter-attack him at Wū Lín and defeat him, making him flee.
Yōng Lí was changed to Qiū Fēng,
referring to Quán delighting in employing people,
and people forgetting their fear of death.
Zhàn Chéng Nán was changed to Kè Wǎn Chéng,

Shàng Líng Qǔ was changed to Tōng Jīng Zhōu,

Jiāng Jìn Jiǔ was changed to Zhāng Hóng Dé,

Shàng Xié Qǔ was changed to Xuán Huà,
referring to the ruler of that time cultivating both civil and martial arts,
acting in accordance with Heaven,

and the world rejoicing.

The Píbǔ Dance,
its origin is unclear,
but in the Hàn dynasty, it was already performed at banquets.
The odes composed by Fù Yì and Zhāng Héng
all concern it.
The old tunes had five pieces:
1. "There is a virtuous lady east of the pass,"
2. "In the second year of Zhānghé,"
3. "May happiness be long-lasting,"
4. "The Four Directions' Emperor,"
5. "A cassia tree grows before the palace,"
their lyrics are all lost.
Cáo Zhí's preface to the Píbǔ Dance poems says:
"In the western park of Emperor Líng of Hàn, among the drummers and pipers, there was one Lǐ Jiān,
skilled in the Píbǔ Dance.
When the world fell into chaos,
Jiān fled to Guānxī,
following General Duàn Wēi.
The former emperor heard of his old skill
and issued a decree summoning Jiān.
Jiān was over seventy,
and had ceased performing in the interim.
Moreover, the ancient tunes contained many errors,
and writings from different eras
were not necessarily inherited.
Therefore, based on the old tunes, five new songs were composed."
And in the Tàishǐ reign,
new lyrics were again composed.
The dance traditionally involved two eights (sixteen dancers).
When Huán Xuán was about to usurp the throne,
Yuán Míngzǐ, the palace attendant in the Department of State Affairs, memorialized to increase it to a full eight ranks (sixty-four dancers).
The Tàishǐ era song lyrics are listed hereafter.

and those who exhaust their loyalty are sure to be honored.
Orchids and *zhǐ* plants emerge from the wilderness,
ascending ten thousand *lǐ* to the purple court.
Thorns and weeds defile the hall steps,
they are swept away and cannot live.
The capable and incapable do not deceive each other,
the hundred officials correct their names.
He is respectful and prudent in action,
and whatever he undertakes, nothing fails.
A benighted ruler lacks self-confidence,
his subordinates hold deviant views.
The upright are slandered,
and treacherous ministers seize his power.
Even wishing to be utterly loyal,
they seal their mouths and dare not speak.
But why be afraid to seal one's mouth?
Utter loyalty becomes a personal affliction.
How can a clear stream not be pure?
Flying dust muddies its source.
Forked paths lead one astray,
it is better not to return than to wander far.
A loyal minister stands in the ruler's court,
upright and heedless of himself.
Evil and upright cannot coexist,
like the Hú and Qín.
Though Hú and Qín might one day unite,
evil and upright each follow different paths.
When a loyal minister meets an enlightened ruler,
he strives diligently, renewing himself daily.
All eyes are on the main rope,
all stars revolve around the North Star.
Should he encounter a benighted lord,
he is dismissed and becomes a common man.
Though humble in its use,
white cogongrass is still cherished.
Ice and frost form day and night,
orchids and cassia are broken for firewood.
Treacherous ministers have many tricks,
how devious their intentions.
They flatter and follow the ruler's inclinations,
acting at his every whim.
They seek temporary ease and present pleasure,
without questioning purity or impurity.
They accumulate falsehoods to deceive the current lord,
and maintain connections to secure their emoluments.
Their words and actions contradict,
their greed is harder to satisfy than valleys.
If they hide their crimes, they secretly profit;
if discovered, their clan is exterminated.
Fúwǔ,
originated in Jiāngzuǒ.
It was formerly called Wúwǔ,
but examining its songs,
they are not Wú lyrics.
It was also performed in the palace courtyard.
Yáng Hóng's preface states:
"Since arriving in Jiāngnán and seeing the White Talisman Dance,
or some say White Mallard-Dove Dance,
it is said to have existed for several decades.
Examining its lyrics,
it is actually about the people of Wú suffering from Sūn Hào's tyrannical rule,
and longing to belong to Jìn."
Now, they are listed below.
Fúwǔ Songs and Poems, Five Sections: White Dove Section
Fluttering white doves,
flying and singing again and again.
Cherishing your lord's virtue,
they come to gather in your lord's courtyard.
White sparrows present auspicious signs,
with pure feathers bright and fresh.
Soaring in the courtyard, dancing with wings,
to respond to benevolent Heaven.
Clear-singing doves,
some crimson, some yellow.
Delighting in your lord's grace,
they beat their wings and come to soar.
The lingering light of the eastern wall,
fish in rivers and lakes.
Gracious yet not extravagant,
respecting my humble self.
Harnessing my good steeds,
practicing my driving.
Associating with you,
delighting in the Dao and forgetting hunger.
My heart is empty and serene,
my will is moistened and nourished.
Playing the qín and beating the sè,
thereby amusing myself.
Ascending to the clouds and climbing the terrace,
floating and roaming in the Great Purity.
Clinging to dragons and attaching to phoenixes,
naturally feeling light in body.
Jìjì Section
Unrestrained, flying, dancing, with fragrant energy flowing,
〔二二〕recalling the great beauty of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Losses exist,
times are opportune,
comings and goings are together in this Wèiyāng Palace.
Time slips by,
nearing the evening years,
we should only drink wine for pleasure.
Aging and departing,
what is the appointed time?
〔二三〕Many worries disturb the heart.
The deep pool is vast,
fish are scarce,
would that I could find refuge in the masses of Huángpǔ.
Grace moves people,
unrivaled in the world,
sad songs and dances will never cease.
Dúlù Section
Solitary and hesitant,
〔二四〕the water is deep and the mud is turbid.
Turbid mud is still bearable,
but deep water kills me.
Harmonious pair of geese,
playing by the fields.
I wish to shoot the geese,
but I think of your lonely scattering.
Fluttering duckweed,
lightly swaying with the wind.
How can my heart harmonize,
and be alongside it?
The empty bed with low curtains,
who knows there is no one?
Dressed in brocade at night,
who can distinguish false from true?
The saber clangs in its sheath,
leaning against the bed, useless.
My father's grievance unavenged,
what purpose is there in living?
Striped fierce beasts,
playing in the mountains.
The beasts wish to bite people,
sparing neither the powerful nor the worthy.
Jiéshí Section
Eastward I ascend Jiéshí,
to view the vast sea.
How boundless the water,
mountain islands stand tall.
Trees grow densely,
all grasses lush and abundant.
Autumn winds rustle,
great waves surge.
The journey of the sun and moon,
seems to issue from within.
The brilliant Milky Way,
seems to emerge from within.
How fortunate and splendid,
I sing to express my aspirations.
(Guān Cānghǎi)
In the first month of winter, the tenth month,
the north wind lingers.
The weather is clear and crisp,
dense frost flutters down.
Kūn jī crow in the morning,
wild geese fly south.
Birds of prey hide,
bears and grizzly bears dwell in their dens.
Hoes and rakes are laid aside,
harvested crops are piled in the threshing ground.
Inns are prepared,
to facilitate merchants.
How fortunate and splendid,
I sing to express my aspirations.
(Dōng Shíyuè)
The lands are different,
the north of the Yellow River is bitterly cold.
Floating ice drifts,
boats are difficult to navigate.
An awl cannot pierce the ground,
the rich sound of the wind is deep and profound.
Water runs dry and does not flow,
the ice is firm enough to walk on.
Hermit scholars are poor,
valiant heroes disregard wrongdoing.
Their hearts constantly sigh and complain,
troubled and full of sorrow.
How fortunate and splendid,
I sing to express my aspirations.
(Tǔ Bùtóng)
Though the divine turtle lives long,
it still has an end.
Though the flying serpent rides the mist,
it eventually turns to dust.
A fine steed, old in the stable,
〔二五〕its ambition is still to travel a thousand lǐ.
A hero in his twilight years,
his grand aspirations never cease.
The duration of life and death,
is not solely determined by Heaven.
The blessing of nurturing good health,
can bring a long life.
How fortunate and splendid,
I sing to express my aspirations.
(Guī Suī Shòu) Huáinánwáng Section
The King of Huáinán,
calls himself honorable,
his hundred-foot tall building connects with the sky.
In the rear garden, a well is dug with a silver bed,
a golden jar and white rope draw cold water.
Drawing cold water,
given to young men to drink,
how can these graceful young men be worthy?
Raising their voices, they sing sad songs that pierce the sky.
I wish to cross the river, but the river has no bridge,
I wish to become a pair of yellow swans,
and return to my homeland.
Returning to my homeland,
entering my old village,
lingering in my homeland,
my body toils endlessly.
〔二六〕Numerous dances and wondrous songs, none are not grand,
wandering among the mulberries and catalpas, roaming beyond the heavens.
Drum and Horn Transverse Flute Music.
Drum,
according to the Zhōulǐ
"use large drums to beat for military affairs."
Horn,
commentators say,
when Chīyóu led his demons and monsters to fight Huángdì at Zhuōlù,
the Emperor then first commanded the blowing of horns to make a dragon's roar to resist them.
〔二七〕Later, when Wèi Wǔ campaigned north against the Wūhuán,
crossing the desert, the soldiers longed to return home,
so it was reduced to a mid-range sound,
which was even more mournful.
The barbarian horn (Hújiǎo)
was originally used to accompany the sound of the barbarian reed pipe (hújiā),
later it was gradually used for transverse blowing,
there are double horns,
which is barbarian music.
Zhāng Bówàng entered the Western Regions,
and transmitted its methods to the Western Capital,
only obtaining the tune Móhēdōulè.
Lǐ Yánnián then created twenty-eight new melodies based on barbarian tunes,
which the imperial carriage used as military music.
The Later Hàn provided it to border generals,
〔二八〕during the reign of Hédì,
the general of ten thousand men was allowed to use it.
〔二九〕Since Wèi and Jìn,
the twenty-eight melodies no longer fully exist,
those used include Huánghú, Lǒngtóu,
Upon examination, in the era of Wèi and Jìn,
there was Sūn Shì who was skilled at performing old tunes,
〔三二〕Sòng Shì who was skilled at beating time and singing in harmony,
Chén Zuǒ who was skilled at clear singing,
Liè Hé who was skilled at flute playing,
Hǎo Suǒ who was skilled at zither playing,
〔三三〕Zhū Shēng who was skilled at pipa playing,
and who particularly created new melodies.
Hence, Fù Xuán wrote in his book:
“If people admire what they hear but overlook what they see,
is it not bewildering!
If these six individuals had been born in antiquity,
they would have been unmatched across ages,
and not merely Kúi and Yá have been close companions!”
According to this statement,
from then on,
all were merely descendants of the traditions of Sūn Shì, Zhū Shēng, and others.
Xiānghé was
an old Hàn dynasty song.
Strings and winds harmonized,
and the time-keeper sang.
Originally it was a single piece,
but Emperor Míng of Wèi divided it into two,
to be performed alternately during night vigils.
Originally there were seventeen pieces,
but Zhū Shēng, Sòng Shì, Liè Hé, and others recombined them into thirteen.
Dàn Gē,
four pieces,
originated in the Hàn era.
〔三四〕Without strings or rhythm,
it was performed as the first act of an entertainment,
with one person singing and
three others harmonizing.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi particularly enjoyed it.
At that time, there was Sòng Rónghuá,
who had a clear and beautiful voice,
and was skilled at singing this tune,
considered exceptionally wonderful at the time.
From the Jìn dynasty onwards, it was no longer transmitted,
and thus ceased to exist.
All ancient lyrics of musical compositions
that survive today
are Hàn era street ballads and chants,
such as “Jiāngnán Kě Cǎilián,” “Wū Shēng Shíwǔ Zǐ,” and “Báitóu Yín.”
Wú Gē and miscellaneous tunes all originated in Jiāngnán.
From the Eastern Jìn dynasty onwards,
they gradually expanded.
As for Zǐyè Gē,
a woman named Zǐyè
created this melody.
During the Tàiyuán reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
a ghost sang Zǐyè Gē in the household of Wáng Kē of Lángxié,
indicating that Zǐyè lived before this time.
〔三五〕
Fèng Jiāng Chú Gē
is an old tune.
Yīng Qú’s Bǎiyī Shī says,
“It is said to be Fèng Jiāng Chú,”
which means its origin is very ancient.
Qiánxī Gē
was composed by the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Shěn Chōng.
〔三六〕
As for Ā Zǐ and Huān Wén Gē,
in the early Shēngpíng reign of Emperor Mù,
after a song, he would always call out,
“Ā Zǐ,
do you hear?”
This account is found in the Wǔxíng Zhì.
Later generations elaborated on the melody,
making these two pieces.
As for Tuánshàn Gē,
the Central Secretariat Director Wáng Mín had feelings for his sister-in-law's maid,
loving her very deeply.
His sister-in-law beat the maid too cruelly.
The maid was naturally skilled at singing,
and Mín liked to hold a white round fan,
hence this song was composed.
Ào Gē
was a popular folk song or rumor from the early Lóng'ān period,
the account of which is in the Wǔxíng Zhì.
Zhǎngshǐ Biàn
was composed by the Left Senior Clerk to the Minister of Education, Wáng Xīn, at the time of his defeat.
All these tunes
were initially sung *a cappella*,
and then accompanied by wind and string instruments.
There were also songs created to be accompanied by strings, winds, bronze bells, and stone chimes,
such as the songs of the three modes in the Wèi era.
These are examples.
As for the Bēipán Wǔ (Cup and Tray Dance),
it is recorded that during the Tàikāng reign, the world was preoccupied with the “Jìn Shì Níng Wǔ,”
which involved using hands to receive cups and trays and turn them over.
〔三七〕This indicates that in the Hàn era, there was only the Pán Wǔ (Tray Dance),
and the Jìn dynasty added cups
and the action of turning them over.
Gōngmò Wǔ
is today's Jīn Wǔ (Scarf Dance).
Tradition says that when Xiàng Zhuāng performed a sword dance,
Xiàng Bó used his sleeve to block him,
preventing him from harming Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
and also told Xiàng Zhuāng,
“Gōng mò!”
Ancient people addressed each other as Gōng,
meaning, “Gōng, do not harm the Hàn King.”
The use of a scarf today is likely an imitation of Xiàng Bó's sleeve.
However, the Qín Cāo contains the tune Gōngmò Dù Hé,
which indicates that its origin is already ancient,
and the folk tradition attributing it to Xiàng Bó
is incorrect.
Báizhù Wǔ (White Ramie Dance).
The dance lyrics mention a "scarf robe."
Ramie originally came from the Wú region,
so it should be a Wú dance.
A Jìn era comic song also says:
“Jiaojiao báixù,
jiéjié wèi shuāng.”
The Wú dialect pronounces xù as zhù,
so Báizhù is probably Báixù.
There is one piece of Duó Wǔ Gē (Bell Dance Song),
one piece of Fān Wǔ Gē (Banner Dance Song),
and six pieces of Gǔ Wǔ Jì (Drum Dance Entertainment),
all performed at the Yuánhuì (New Year's court assembly).
On the first day of the New Year in the Later Hàn dynasty,
the emperor would preside over the Déyáng Palace to receive felicitations.
Shèlì came from the West,
performing tricks in front of the palace,
transforming water into flounder,
which jumped and spurted water,
creating mist that obscured the sun.
Afterwards,
they transformed into dragons,
eight or nine *zhàng* long,
playing in the water,
dazzling the sunlight.
Two large silk ropes were tied to two pillar tops,
several *zhàng* apart.
Two female performers danced facing each other,
walking on the ropes,
meeting shoulder to shoulder without falling.
From Wèi and Jìn to the Eastern Jìn,

there were still entertainments like Xià Yù Gáng Dǐng (Xià Yù lifting tripods), Jù Xiàng Xíng Rǔ (Giant elephants suckling), Shén Guī Biàn Wǔ (Divine turtles clapping and dancing), Bèi Fù Líng Yuè (Carrying sacred mountains on their backs), Guìshù Báixuě (Cassia trees and white snow), and Huà Dì Chéng Chuān (Drawing on the ground to form rivers).
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
the Minister of Personnel Cài Mó memorialized:
“For the eighth year's New Year's court assembly protocol,
only drum and wind music and bells and drums should be performed;
all other entertainment music should be suspended.”
Attendant Counselor Zhāng Chéng and Imperial Household Aide-de-camp Chén Kuí rebutted,
believing that
“the king observes the times to establish teachings,
and distinguishing between auspicious and inauspicious is
an unchanging principle.
Now, the four directions observe the rites:
there is a position for condolence ceremonies at the mausoleum,
while court music is performed in the hall.
With two rites used concurrently,
sorrow and joy are not separated.
In structuring the state and regulating institutions,
nothing is more significant than this.”
The imperial edict stated:
“Now, since the empire is of great importance,
the rites shall follow expediency.
For the three regular feasts,
auspicious rites should be fully employed.
As for entertainment for the ears and eyes,
I cannot bear to hear it,
hence it is omitted.
The greatest matters
are no more than presenting longevity wine
and proclaiming ‘Long Live!’
Since its greatness has been acknowledged,
it is not appropriate to further omit bells, drums, and wind music.”
Chéng and Kuí again memorialized:
“Although the great rites are now reduced,
the matters in court are auspicious.
However, as condolence ceremonies are evident at the imperial mausoleum,
sorrow has not yet ceased;
the ceremonial robes are stipulated in the classics,
and it is not righteous to be entirely auspicious.
Therefore, at the Xiánníng assembly,
there was the precedent of suspending music,
which was truly an ancient standard established by previous courts,
setting a model for ten thousand generations.”
The imperial edict stated:
“If on the New Year's Day grand assembly,
when all nations pay homage,
the performance of bells and drums is abolished in the court,
and the rituals of daily life are thus omitted,
the court will lack the sounds of musical stones,
and the guests will lack the decorum of dancing steps.
In terms of its meaning and propriety,
is this not a deficiency!
One can only weigh the importance
to devise a moderate solution.”
Sànqí Shìláng Gù Zhēn (散騎侍郎 顧臻) reported:
“Your servant has heard that enlightened kings formulate music
to praise the Way of governance,
nurture with benevolence and righteousness,
and prevent extravagance and excess.
Upwardly, it is offered in the ancestral temple;
downwardly, it instructs the common people.
It embodies the correct sounds of the Wǔ Xíng (五行)
and harmonizes with the Bā Fēng (八風) to transform all things.
The Gōng (宮) tone is upright and fond of righteousness;
the Jué (角) tone is firm, orderly, and accords with ritual.
The compositions of strings, songs, bells, drums, and metal-and-stone instruments are all complete.
Therefore, through divine communication and ultimate transformation,
there is the feeling of everyone dancing in unison,
transforming customs and changing habits,
leading to the peak of harmony and joy.
The skills of later generations,
however, establish spectacles outside of ritual.
Backwards walking, continuous tumbling,
and the like, such as a head and feet entering a basket,
[three-eight] skin being peeled off,
and the liver and heart being crushed internally.
'Do not tread on those abundant reeds,'
even the 'Xíng Wěi' (行葦) ode advises,
how much more so with living beings,
should one not feel sorrow and pain?
Furthermore, when envoys from the four seas come to pay respects at court,
they come to observe the imperial palace.
Their ears hear the sounds of elegant songs,
and their eyes behold the order of dignified deportment.
With feet to tread on Heaven,
and heads to walk on Earth,
it reverses the ultimate order of Heaven and Earth,
and harms the great principles of human relations.
Now, with barbarians on the opposite bank,
external defense is urgent.
Soldiers receive seven *shēng* (升) of rations,
forgetting themselves as they rush to meet difficulties.
Yet, the performers of these 'excessive' entertainments
receive five *dǒu* (斗) of rations daily.
As we are about to sweep clean Shénzhōu (神州)
and plan the central regions,
such matters
should not be shown to distant peoples.
It is fitting to instruct the Tài Cháng (太常)
to compile and prepare elegant music.
Let the nine movements of Xiāo Sháo (簫韶)
be renewed in this prosperous era,
and the praises of meritorious virtue
be eternally recorded for future generations.
This is what is meant by 'to feast even the August Heaven,
and make their descendants prosper.'
All performances that harm people
should be abolished.
Let the virtue of simplicity and frugality flow,
surpassing the singing of 'Kāng Zāi' (康哉).
When the pure wind circulates,
the people below respond like grass.
This is what is meant.
May my foolish sincerity
be considered and observed!”
Thereupon, the performances known as Gāo (高), Zǐlù (紫鹿), Qì Xíng (跂行), Biē Shí (鼈食), as well as Qí Wáng Juǎn Yī (齊王捲衣) and Záchér (笮兒), were abolished.
Their rations were also reduced.
Afterwards, Gāo (高) and Zǐlù (紫鹿) were reinstated.
Collation Notes
Volume 14, Official Ranks
The *Shū* (書) says:
“Táng Yú (唐虞) studied the ancients,
and established a hundred official positions.”
This was to encourage and guide the populace
and to regulate and complete various governmental affairs.
The *Yì* (易) says:
“Heaven displays its images;
the Sages take them as their model.”
The enforcers of law are to the right of the Nángōng (南宮);
the chief ministers are outside the Duānmén (端門).
And the bird and dragon officials hold their positions;
the cloud and fire officials have their names recorded.
Former historians have detailed this,
it is indeed ancient.
Huáng Dì (黃帝) established the ranks of Sān Gōng (三公)
to bring intimacy to the common people.
Shào Hào (少昊) assigned the names of Jiǔ Hù (九扈)
to be agricultural officials.
Chóng (重) and Lí (黎) were appointed to Heaven and Earth;
Róng (融) and Míng (冥) were commanded over water and fire.
These can be spoken of.
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) said:
“The Sān Gōng (三公) harmonize Yin and Yang;
the Jiǔ Qīng (九卿) communicate cold and heat;
the Dàfū (大夫) understand human affairs;
and the Liè Shì (列士) abandon their selfishness.”
When Chéng Tāng (成湯) resided in Bó (亳),
he first established two prime ministers,
making Yī Yǐn (伊尹) and Zhòng Huǐ (仲虺) them.
All crucial matters
were submitted for the ruler's command.
Generally, from King Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周) dismounting his chariot,
to Kings Chéng (成) and Kāng (康) setting their standards,
the Liù Qīng (六卿) divided their duties,
and the two Gōng (公) spread transformation.
All established their supervising officials,
each with clear standards.
If not according to the Way,
people would not vainly seek honor.
To leave a legacy for descendants,
this was how its foundation was solidified.
When Qín (秦) changed the Zhōu (周) official system,
Hàn (漢) followed the old Yíng (嬴) practices.
Some adapted to the times,
some changed due to needs.
The principles of a hegemon king
lie in this.
Having achieved peace,
this is what is called 'acting in accordance with the times.'
The Four Expeditions (Sì Zhēng, 四征) arose in the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
the Four Pacifiers (Sì Ān, 四安) began in early Wèi (魏);
the Four Garrison Generals (Sì Zhèn, 四鎮) were employed to pacify distant regions;
the Four Stabilizers (Sì Píng, 四平) ceased during times of chaos.
Those crossing the Liáo (遼), traversing the Jiāng (江),
light chariots, strong crossbows,
used to spread influence far and wide,
and to signify attacks and conquests.
They rose and were then destroyed,
their titles became increasingly numerous.
When Dāng Tú (當塗) achieved its ambition
and pacified all of Huá Xià (華夏),
it first had the Jūnshī Jìjiǔ (軍師祭酒)
to jointly manage military regulations.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (208 CE),
the Hàn (漢) court's Sī (司) officials were abolished,
and a Chéngxiàng (丞相) was established instead,
with Cáo Gōng (曹公) holding the position,
thus combining the duties of the prime minister.
Sūn Wú (孫吳) and Liú Shǔ (劉蜀)
largely followed the Hàn (漢) system.
Although they temporarily assigned titles,
they did not disgrace the old regulations.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Wǔ (武), Shìzǔ (世祖),
Ānpíng Wáng Fú (安平王 孚) was made Tài Zǎi (太宰),
Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖) was Tài Fù (太傅),
Wáng Xiáng (王祥) was Tài Bǎo (太保),
Sīmǎ Wàng (司馬望) was Tài Wèi (太尉),
Hé Zēng (何曾) was Sītú (司徒),
Xún Yǐ (荀顗) was Sīkōng (司空),
Shí Bāo (石苞) was Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬),
Chén Qiān (陳騫) was Dà Jiāngjūn (大將軍).
These were what the world called the 'Eight Gōng (公) of the same era,'
those who climbed to the clouds and attached themselves to wings.
If it were to complete a building,
it would not be the strength of a single branch;
if it were to manage affairs,
they would be called a match for ten thousand men.
Some led sheep in a dream,
some dangled a fishing line to express their Way,
some offered their art from an empty mulberry tree,
some held a wooden board to enlighten their hearts.
Wòlóng (臥龍) and Fēihóng (飛鴻),
comparable to gold and precious jade;
Qín Xī (秦奚) and Zhèng Chǎn (鄭產),
Chǔ (楚) talents used by Jìn (晉).
These were also excellent talents of former times,
and even more illustrious ones.
After Xuān Wáng (宣王) executed Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽),
governance came from himself.
He gathered heroes and talents
to fill the imperial offices.
When Lán Qīng (蘭卿) was restrained
and noble Gōng (公) were publicly executed,
although they were listed in the Wèi (魏) clan's records,
their hearts were devoted to the imperial Jìn (晉).
When Wén Wáng (文王) inherited the enterprise,
he first established the Jìn Tái (晉臺).
He first set up the Two Guards (Èr Wèi, 二衞),
with Yǎng Yóu (養由)'s crossbowmen as the vanguard.
Then he established the Three Divisions (Sān Bù, 三部),
with the forces of Xióng Qú (熊渠) and Cì Fēi (佽飛).
Thus, when Emperor Wǔ (武) ascended to power,
he soared with these wings,
just as King Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周) managed the people of Yīn (殷) with his ten able ministers.
Thus, from Tàishǐ (泰始) to Tàikāng (太康),
towering branches and luxuriant leaves
came to occupy these positions.
From Tàixīng (太興) to Jiànyuán (建元),
southern gold and northern fine metal
were used to fill these ranks.
Although they could not be compared to Kuí (夔) playing the drum or Lóng (龍) speaking,
or Heaven's work being done by men,
it was almost like appointing officials based on their virtue
and assigning duties based on their ability.
Chéngxiàng (丞相) and Xiàngguó (相國)
were both Qín (秦) offices.
When Jìn (晉) received the abdication from Wèi (魏),
they were not established.
After Emperor Huì (惠),
they were abolished and re-established without consistency.
Those who held these positions
included Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫), Liáng Wáng Róng (梁王肜), Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎), Nányáng Wáng Bǎo (南陽王保), Wáng Dūn (王敦), Wáng Dǎo (王導), and others.
They were no longer the ordinary duties of human subjects.
The Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), Grand Preceptor (Tàifù), and Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo)
were the offices of the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) in the Zhōu dynasty.
In the early Wèi dynasty, only the Grand Preceptor (Tàifù) was established,
with Zhōng Yáo serving in that role.
In the later years, the Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) was also established,
with Zhèng Chōng serving in that role.
In the early Jìn dynasty, due to Emperor Jǐng's (Jǐng Dì) taboo name,
and also by adopting official titles from the Zhōu dynasty,
the Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi) was established to replace the duties of the Grand Master (Tàishī).
Its rank was increased to be above the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī),
and it, along with the Grand Preceptor (Tàifù) and Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo), became the Supreme Ducal Ministers (Shànggōng),
responsible for discussing the Way to govern the state,
and harmonizing Yin and Yang.
If no suitable person was available, the post remained vacant.
Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú was appointed to this position.
Since the crossing of the Jiāng river,
the title has not been abolished,
but very few held the post.
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Minister of Education (Sītú), and Minister of Works (Sīkōng)
were all ancient offices.
From the Hàn dynasty through the Wèi dynasty,
they were established as the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng).
When the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate,
and up to the Eastern Jìn (Jiāng Zuǒ),
these offices were successively inherited without change.
The Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ)
was an ancient office.
Under the Hàn system, it was placed above the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), and General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn),
and served to replace the duties of the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Thus, it was established alternately with the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
not simultaneously.
When the Wèi dynasty had a Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
the Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ) and Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) each became separate offices,
ranking above the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī).
When the Jìn dynasty received the abdication from Wèi,
it followed this system,
appointing Ānpíng Wáng Fú as Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi),
Zhèng Chōng as Grand Preceptor (Tàifù),
Wáng Xiáng as Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo),
Yìyáng Wáng Wàng as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
Hé Zēng as Minister of Education (Sītú),
Xún Yǐ as Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Shí Bāo as Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ),
and Chén Qiān as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
All eight ducal ministers were simultaneously established,
with the sole exception of the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
After Yìyáng Wáng Wàng served as Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ),
the regulations were set as before,
placing it above the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī).
The Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn)
was an ancient office.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (Hàn Wǔ Dì) established it,
crowning it with the title Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ),
making it a highly esteemed position.
In the Eastern Hàn (Hàn Dōngjīng),
the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) was not a permanent position,
and those who held it often wielded absolute court power.
When Emperor Jǐng (Jǐng Dì) served as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
he also undertook extraordinary responsibilities.
Later, his paternal uncle Fú was made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and he proposed that the Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) be placed below the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
When the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate,
it still followed this system,
placing it below the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī).
Later, it reverted to the old system,
placing it above the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī).
In the first year of Tàikāng (Tàikāng Yuánnián),
Lángxié Wáng Zhòu was promoted to Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
and the system was again set to be below the Three Judicial Ministers (Sānsī).
After Zhòu's death, it returned to the old system.
To Open a Residence and Enjoy Treatment Equal to the Three Judicial Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī)
was a Hàn official title.
In the first year of Yánpíng (Yánpíng Yuánnián) of Emperor Shāng (Shāng Dì),
Dèng Zhì was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn),
with treatment equal to the Three Judicial Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī);
the name "Yítóng"
originated from this.

In the Wèi dynasty, Huáng Quán was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) and permitted to open a residence and enjoy treatment equal to the Three Judicial Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī);
the name "Kāifǔ"
originated from this.

Grand Generals such as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì), General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), General Fúbō (Fúbō), General Fǔjūn (Fǔjūn), Protector-General (Dūhù), General Zhènjūn (Zhènjūn), General Zhōngjūn (Zhōngjūn), Four Expeditionary Generals (Sì Zhēng), Four Garrison Generals (Sì Zhèn), General Lóngxiáng (Lóngxiáng), General Diǎnjūn (Diǎnjūn), General Shàngjūn (Shàngjūn), General Fǔguó (Fǔguó), etc.,
Left and Right Grand Masters of the Palace (Zuǒyòu Guānglù Dàfū) and Grand Master of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū),
those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) all held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng).

Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), Grand Preceptor (Tàifù), Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo), Minister of Education (Sītú), Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Left and Right Grand Masters of the Palace (Zuǒyòu Guānglù Dàfū), and Grand Master of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū),
those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) who held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng) were civil service Ducal Ministers (Wén Guān Gōng),
wearing a three-ridged cap (Jìnxián Sānliáng),
and a black kerchief (Jièzé).

Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ), Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì), General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), and other Grand Generals,
those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) who held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng) were military service Ducal Ministers (Wǔ Guān Gōng),
all wearing military caps (Wǔguān),
and a flat-topped black kerchief (Píngshàng Hēi Zé).
Both civil and military Ducal Ministers (Wénwǔ Guān Gōng)
were granted golden seals and purple ribbons (Jīnzhāng Zǐshòu),
and wore five-colored seasonal robes (Wǔshífú).
The Chancellor (Xiàngguó) and Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng)
all wore ceremonial robes and crowns (Gǔnmiǎn),
with green sash-ribbons (Lǜ Jìshòu),
thus distinguishing them from ordinary Ducal Ministers (Cháng Gōng).
All Ducal Ministers (Zhū Gōng) and those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) who held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng),
were of the first rank (Pǐn Zhì Dìyī),
and received a daily stipend of five hù of grain.
In the second year of Tàikāng (Tàikāng Èrnián),
silk was also provided,
one hundred bolts in spring,
two hundred bolts of silk in autumn,
and two hundred catties of floss silk.
In the first year of Yuánkāng (Yuánkāng Yuánnián),
ten qǐng of vegetable fields were provided,
with ten field servants (Tiánzōu),
and for those who did not cultivate the fields after the beginning of summer,
a year's stipend was given.
One Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) was appointed,
with a salary of one thousand dàn of grain;

one Libationer of the Western and Eastern Gates (Xīdōng Gé Jìjiǔ), one Chief in charge of Western and Eastern Bureaus (Xīdōng Cáo Yuàn), one clerk for Household, Granary, and Robbery bureaus (Hùcāng Zéicáo Lìshǐ Shǔ) each;

one clerk for Imperial Guards' subordinates and attendants (Yùshǔ Géxià Lìshǐ), one clerk for the Western and Eastern Bureaus' Granary, Household, and Robbery sections (Xīdōng Cáo Cānghù Zéicáo Lìshǐ), one Gate Clerk (Mén Lìshǐ), one Record Keeper's clerk for official duties (Jìshì Shěngshì Lìshǐ), one Attendant's Record Keeper's clerk for writing (Géxià Jìshì Shū Lìshǐ), and one clerk for Western and Eastern Bureaus' scholarly affairs (Xīdōng Cáo Xuéshì) each.
Twenty Imperial Guards (Wǔbēn) were provided,
carrying swords of rank (Bān Jiàn).
One court carriage drawn by four horses (Cháo Chē Jià Sì) and one plain carriage with black blinds drawn by three horses (Ānchē Hēi'ěr Jià Sān) were provided;
seven small white-covered carriages (Bái Gài Xiǎo Chē) for Libationers, Chief Clerks, and subordinates;
one lightweight carriage with black blinds and a rear door (Yáochē Shī'ěr Hòuhù), and one calf-drawn carriage with black wheels (Zào Lún Dú Chē) each.
From the Libationer (Jìjiǔ) downwards,
and upwards from the clerks (Lìshǐ),
all wore black-collared ceremonial robes (Zào Líng Pì Cháofú).
Although the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) did not command troops,
all his subordinates wore crimson robes (Jiàngfú).
The Minister of Education (Sītú) was additionally provided with one Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) and one Right Chief Clerk (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) each,
with a salary of one thousand dàn of grain;
one Master of Records (Zhǔbù) and one Chief in charge of the Left Western Bureau (Zuǒ Xīcáo Yuàn) each,
the Western Bureau was referred to as the Right Western Bureau (Yòu Xīcáo);
the number of staff from the Left Western Bureau Clerk (Zuǒ Xīcáo Lìshǐ) downwards was as per old regulations.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) was additionally provided with one Chief in charge of Waterways and Bridges (Dǎoqiáo Yuàn).
All Ducal Ministers (Zhū Gōng) and those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) who held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng) and commanded troops,
were additionally provided with one Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
with a salary of one thousand dàn of grain;
two Central Clerks for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
with a salary comparable to one thousand dàn of grain;
one Master of Records (Zhǔbù) and one Supervisor of Record Keepers (Jìshì Dū) each;
four Chamberlains (Shèrén);
one clerk each for Soldiers and Armor (Bīng Kǎi), Military Personnel (Shì Cáo),
Camp Army (Yíng Jūn), Interception of Spies (Cì Jiān), Under-Tent Commanders (Zhàngxià Dūdū),
and Outer Commanders (Wài Dūdū),
and one clerk for each section.
From the Master of Records (Zhǔbù) downwards,
and upwards from the clerks (Lìshǐ),
all wore crimson robes (Jiàngfú).
The Army Commander (Sīmǎ) was provided with staff and soldiers like a Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ),
the Central Clerks for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng) were each provided with two attendants,
and the Master of Records (Zhǔbù) and Supervisor of Record Keepers (Jìshì Dū) were each provided with one attendant.
For other temporary enhancements,
the commendations and additions were based on the specific circumstances and served as temporary regulations,
not as permanent fixtures.

All Ducal Ministers (Zhū Gōng) and those with the privilege to open a residence (Kāifǔ) who held positions equivalent to Ducal Ministers (Cóng Gōng) and served as Inspectors with Credentials (Chíjié Dūdū),
had their Military Advisers (Cānjūn) increased to six;

the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ), Army Commander (Sīmǎ), Central Clerks for Military Affairs (Cóngshì Zhōngláng), Master of Records (Zhǔbù), Supervisor of Record Keepers (Jìshì Dū), Libationers (Jìjiǔ), Chief Clerks (Yuànshǔ), and Chamberlains (Shèrén) followed the standard system for Ducal Ministers (Gōng) who commanded troops.
Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn)
was a Hàn official title.
In the two Hàn dynasties and the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, it was an additional office, with its carriages and attire following the principal office,
and it had no staff or soldiers.
When the Grand Coachman (Tàipú) Yáng Xiù resigned,
he was appointed Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn),
and additionally Grandee-Consultant for the Cavalier Attendants (Sànqí Chángshì),
with no other offices,
thus he was provided with staff, soldiers, carriages, and attire.
For others appointed Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn),
they only received its stipend and rewards,
and occupied its rank,
without separate provision of staff, soldiers, carriages, or attire for the Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn).
This was later regulated.
The Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn) was of the second rank (Pǐn Zhì Dì'èr),
its position ranked below the Ducal Ministers (Zhū Gōng),
and above those with the privilege to open a residence and the General of Agile Cavalry (Kāifǔ Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
wearing a two-ridged cap (Jìnxián Liángliáng),
a black kerchief (Jièzé),
five-colored seasonal court robes (Wǔshí Cháofú),
wearing an aquamarine jade pendant (Pèi Shuǐcāng Yù),
without seals or ribbons (Wú Zhāng Shòu),
and receiving a daily stipend of four hù of grain.
In the second year of Tàikāng (Tàikāng Èrnián),
for the first time, fifty bolts of silk for spring attire were granted,
one hundred fifty bolts of silk in autumn,
and one hundred fifty catties of floss silk.
In the first year of Yuánkāng (Yuánkāng Yuánnián),
eight qǐng of vegetable fields were provided,
with eight field servants (Tiánzōu),
and for those who did not cultivate the fields after the beginning of summer,
a year's stipend was given.
One Master of Records (Zhǔbù), one Merit Clerk (Gōngcáo Shǐ), one Gate Pavilion Chief (Mén Tíng Zhǎng), and one Subordinate Scribe of the Imperial Secretariat (Ménxià Shūzuǒ) each were appointed,
provided with one plain carriage with black blinds (Ānchē Hēi'ěr) and one driver (Jiàyù),
and one lightweight carriage with black blinds and a rear door (Yáochē Shī'ěr Hòuhù).
The Grand Masters of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū) of the Left and Right,
granted with golden seals and purple ribbons.
Those Grand Masters of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū) who were additionally granted golden seals and purple ribbons
ranked second in official grades.
Their stipends, court seating, caps, headscarves, carriages, clothing, and jade pendants,
as well as the assignment of clerks, soldiers, Yúlín guards, and foot soldiers,
and all other provisions, were equivalent to those of a Special Advance (Tèjìn).
For those appointed as "additional officials" (jiāguān),
only the seals, ribbons, stipends, and court seating were granted;
they were not separately provided with carriages, clothing, clerks, or soldiers.
Furthermore, when someone was posthumously granted this rank,
if they already held the rank of a Minister (Qīng) in life,
clerks and soldiers were not granted again;
all others were granted.
Grand Masters of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū) granted with silver seals and green ribbons
ranked third in official grades,
their position was below that of a General with Golden and Purple (Jīn Zǐ Jiāngjūn)
but above all Ministers (Qīng).
In the Hàn dynasty, no fixed number was established for this position;
it was often used for envoys appointed to bestow condolences and funeral gifts,
and to supervise funeral rites.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
its importance and prestige have increasingly grown,
and it ceased to be a position for envoys.
All Dukes (Zhūgōng) who retired due to old age
were appointed to this rank in their homes;
and those holding prominent positions in the court
were again additionally granted it.
When the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven,
the old system was maintained without change,
again establishing it as a measure of high honor.
However, when the Dukes (Zhūgōng) resigned their positions,
this rank was no longer added;
instead, some were appointed as Senior Dukes (Shànggōng),
or enjoyed ducal stipends based on their original enfeoffment.
The number of Ministers (Zhūqīng), Yin (Yǐn), and high officials of the central court (zhōngcháo) who retired due to old age,
and those holding internal and external positions who were additionally granted this rank,
was very numerous, both before and after.
Consequently, some were able to establish their own government offices (kāifǔ),
or were promoted to receive golden seals and purple ribbons,
and it was also again used as a rank for ceremonial endowments.
During the Tàishǐ period,
only Yáng Yáo, the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì), was additionally granted the title of Attendant Palace Grand Master (Gěishì Zhōng Guānglù Dàfū).
For the system of "additional troops" (jiābīng),
all provisions were based on a third-rank general.
The rest followed the old system,
throughout the reigns of Wǔ, Huì, and Xiàohuái.
The Grand Master of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū) shared the rank of "Minister (Qīng) of Two Thousand Piculs (Zhōng Èr Qiān Dàn)" (Qīng Tóng Zhì Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí),
wore a two-beamed cap of a 'worthy advanced' (jìnxián liǎngliáng guān),
a black jiècè headscarf,
five-season court robes,
wore a dark green jade pendant,
and received a daily stipend of three húl of grain.
In the second year of Tàikāng,
they began to be given a spring gift of fifty bolts of silk,
and in autumn, one hundred bolts of silk
and one hundred catties of floss.
In the first year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
they began to be given six qǐng of vegetable fields,
six field servants,
and one chief clerk (zhǔbù), one merit officer (gōngcáoshǐ), one gate director (méntíngzhǎng), and one gate attendant clerk (ménxià shūzuǒ) each.

Grand Generals (Dàjiāngjūn) below a General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) and all other Grand Generals who did not establish their own government offices (kāifǔ) and were not Inspector-Generals (Dūdū) holding an imperial credential (chíjié),
ranked second in official grades,
and their stipends were the same as those of a Special Advance (Tèjìn).
They appointed one chief clerk (zhǎngshǐ) and one cavalry commander (sīmǎ),
with a rank of one thousand piculs (qiānshí);
one chief clerk (zhǔbù),
one merit officer (gōngcáoshǐ),
one gate director (ménxià dūdū),
one registrar (lùshì),
one officer for soldiers, armorers, and bandits (bīngkǎi shìzéicáo),
one camp commander (yíngjūn), one spy catcher (cìjiān), one tent commander (zhàngxià dūdū),
one merit officer's clerk and gate official (gōngcáo shūzuǒ ménlì),
and one gate attendant clerk (ménxià shūlì) each.
Those who were granted an imperial credential (jiǎjié) and acted as Inspector-Generals (Dūdū),

their establishments were the same as those of the Four Pacifying Generals (Sìzhēng Jiāngjūn), Guarding Generals (Zhèn Jiāngjūn), Pacifying Generals (Ān Jiāngjūn), and Leveling Generals (Píng Jiāngjūn), and additional Grand Generals (Dàjiāngjūn) who did not establish their own government offices (kāifǔ) and served as Inspector-Generals (Dūdū).

The Four Pacifying Generals (Sìzhēng Jiāngjūn), Guarding Generals (Zhèn Jiāngjūn), Pacifying Generals (Ān Jiāngjūn), and Leveling Generals (Píng Jiāngjūn), and additional Grand Generals (Dàjiāngjūn) who did not establish their own government offices (kāifǔ) and were Inspector-Generals (Dūdū) holding an imperial credential (chíjié),
ranked second in official grades,
and appointed aides, clerks, soldiers, and camp cavalry according to the regular Inspector-General (Dūdū) system,
but their court attendance and stipends followed the precedent of second-rank generals.
However, there was no fixed number for those holding an imperial credential (chíjié) or Inspector-Generals (Dūdū).
In the Former Hàn dynasty, envoys first held imperial credentials.
At the beginning of Emperor Guāngwǔ’s Jiànwǔ reign,
during expeditions to the four directions,
Inspector-General Censors (Dūjūn Yùshǐ) were temporarily appointed as needed;
they were dismissed once the task was completed.
In the Jiàn'ān period,
when Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) was Chancellor (Xiàng),
Grand Generals were first dispatched to supervise.
In the twenty-first year, when he returned from campaigning against Sūn Quán,
Xiàhóu Dūn supervising twenty-six armies is an example of this.
In the third year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
Inspector-Generals of Military Affairs for various prefectures (Dūdū Zhūzhōu Jūnsì) were first established,
sometimes concurrently holding the position of Prefect (Cìshǐ).

Furthermore, Cáo Zhēn, the Grand General of the Upper Army (Shàngjūn Dàjiāngjūn), was Inspector-General of All Armies Internal and External (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnsì) and was granted a yellow battle-axe (jiǎ huángyuè),
thus he commanded all armies, both internal and external.
In the autumn of the fourth year of Tàihé of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Emperor Xuān (Sīmǎ Yì) campaigned against Shǔ,
and was given the additional title of Grand Inspector-General (Dà Dūdū).
In the second year of Zhèngyuán of the High and Noble Duke of Xiāng (Gāoguì Xiānggōng),
Emperor Wén (Sīmǎ Zhāo) was Inspector-General of All Armies Internal and External (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn),
and soon after was additionally granted the title of Grand Inspector-General (Dà Dūdū).
When the Jìn dynasty received the abdication,
Inspector-General of All Armies (Dūdū Zhūjūn) was the highest,
Supervisor of All Armies (Jiān Zhūjūn) was next,
and Inspector of All Armies (Dū Zhūjūn) was the lowest.
An envoy holding an imperial credential (shǐchíjié) was the highest,
one holding an imperial credential (chíjié) was next,
and one granted an imperial credential (jiǎjié) was the lowest.
An envoy holding an imperial credential (shǐchíjié) was authorized to execute officials ranked two thousand piculs (èrqiānshí) or lower;
one holding an imperial credential (chíjié) could execute commoners,
or, in military affairs,
could have the same authority as an envoy holding an imperial credential (shǐchíjié);
one granted an imperial credential (jiǎjié) could only execute those who violated military orders in military matters.
Since the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ) era,
the position of Inspector-General of All Armies Internal and External (Dūdū Zhōngwài) became especially important,
and only those with great power, such as Wáng Dǎo, held it.
Generals of the third rank (sānpǐn jiāngjūn) who held the rank of "Minister (Qīng) of Two Thousand Piculs" (Qīng Tóng Zhì Zhōng Èr Qiān Dàn)
wore a military cap (wǔguān),
a flat-topped black headscarf (píngshàng hēicè),
five-season court robes,
wore a dark green jade pendant,

and their stipends, spring and autumn silk and floss allowances, vegetable fields, and field servants were according to the system for Grand Masters of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū) and all Ministers (Qīng).
They appointed one chief clerk (zhǎngshǐ) and one cavalry commander (sīmǎ),
with a rank of one thousand piculs (qiānshí);
one chief clerk (zhǔbù),
one merit officer (gōngcáo),
one gate director (ménxià dūdū),
one registrar (lùshì),
one officer for soldiers, armorers, and bandits (bīngkǎi shìzéicáo),
one camp commander (yíngjūn), one spy catcher (cìjiānlì), one tent commander (zhàngxià dūdū),
one merit officer's clerk and gate official (gōngcáo shūzuǒ ménlì),
and one gate attendant clerk (ménxià shūlì) each.
As for Recording Grand Minister (Lù Shàngshū):
According to the Hàn Wǔ period,
the various officials of the Left and Right Bureaus (Zuǒyòu Cáo) divided and managed the memorials presented to the Grand Minister (Shàngshū),
and those who understood the key affairs first held the responsibility of the Grand Minister (Lǐng Shàngshūshì).
Zhāng Ānshì as General of Agile Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn),
Huò Guāng as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
Wáng Fèng as Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ),
and Shī Dān as General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) all concurrently held the responsibility of the Grand Minister (Lǐng Shàngshūshì).
Later, during Emperor Zhāng’s reign in the Later Hàn,
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Zhào Xǐ and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Móu Róng both recorded the affairs of the Grand Minister (Lù Shàngshūshì).
The name "Recording Grand Minister" (Lù Shàngshū) likely originated with Xǐ and Róng;
it was also the responsibility of holding the Grand Minister (Lǐng Shàngshū) in the Western Capital,
akin to the great Prime Minister (Dàlù) position of Táng and Yǔ.
During Emperor Hé’s time,
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Dèng Biāo became Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
recording the affairs of the Grand Minister (Lù Shàngshūshì),
holding the rank of Senior Duke (Shànggōng),
above the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng).
The Hàn system then made this a permanent practice:
whenever a young emperor ascended the throne, a Grand Tutor (Tàifù) who recorded the affairs of the Grand Minister (Lù Shàngshūshì) was appointed,
which was similar to the ancient concept of the Prime Minister (Zǒngzǎi) taking overall charge;
the position was always abolished upon their death.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
it was also held by powerful Dukes (Gōng) and Ministers (Qīng).
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng)
held a rank of one thousand piculs (qiānshí),
was granted a bronze seal and a black ribbon,
wore a two-beamed cap of a 'worthy advanced' (jìnxián liǎngliáng guān),
a nàyan headscarf,
five-season court robes,
wore a dark green jade pendant,
and received a monthly stipend of fifty húl of grain.
Upon appointment, they were given an imperial edict (cè mìng)
because they were at the front-right of officialdom.
In the second year of Tàikāng,
they first began to be given silk allowances:
thirty bolts in spring,
seventy bolts in autumn,
and seventy catties of floss.
In the first year of Yuánkāng,
they first began to be given six qǐng of vegetable fields
and six field servants.
If they did not receive fields after the beginning of summer,
they would receive a year's stipend.
Jiǎ Chōng, when he was Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
requested to establish four provincial clerks (shěngshì lì) due to an eye ailment;
the "provincial clerks" (shěngshì) likely originated from this.
The Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Púyè)
wore the same robes, rank, seal, and ribbon as the Director (Lìng).
According to the Hàn system, originally only one was appointed.
Until the fourth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
when Róng Hé, the Grand Palace Guardian (Zhíjīnwú), was appointed as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
the Vice Director (Púyè) position was divided into Left and Right;
this likely originated from then.
Through the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
up to the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ),
sometimes none were established,
sometimes two were established,
in which case they were the Vice Directors of the Left and Right (Zuǒyòu Púyè),
or sometimes not both were established,
and it was simply called Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè).
If the Director (Lìng) position was vacant,
the Left Vice Director (Zuǒ Púyè) would be in charge of the department;
if both the Left and Right Vice Directors (Zuǒyòu Púyè) were vacant,
then a Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè) would be appointed to take charge of the Left's affairs.
Various Departments of the Shàngshū.
According to records, the office of Shàngshū was established by the Hàn dynasty, inheriting from the Qín.
When Emperor Wǔ Dì hosted banquets in the inner court,
he first employed eunuchs to manage the Zhōngshū,
appointing Sīmǎ Qiān to this role.
In the interim, this office was abolished,
and its functions were transferred to the Zhōngshū.
In the fourth year of Jiànshǐ during Emperor Chéng Dì's reign,
the eunuchs of the Zhōngshū were dismissed,
and five Shàngshū were again appointed.
One was the Púshè,
and the other four were divided into four Cáo (departments).
They jointly managed matters concerning maps, secret records, memorials, and petitions,
each having their specific duties.
The first was called Chángshì Cáo,
responsible for matters of the Chéngxiàng, Yùshǐ, and Gōngqīng.
The second was called Èrqiānshí Cáo,
responsible for matters of the Cìshǐ and commanderies/kingdoms.
The third was called Mín Cáo,
responsible for petitions from officials and common people.
The fourth was called Zhǔkè Cáo,
responsible for matters concerning foreign tribes and barbarians.
Later, Emperor Chéng Dì also established the Sāngōng Cáo,
responsible for adjudicating legal cases,
making it five Cáo.
In the Later Hàn dynasty, Guāngwǔ used the Sāngōng Cáo to handle the annual evaluation of various prefectures and commanderies at year-end,
renamed Chángshì Cáo to Lìbù Cáo,
which was responsible for selections and sacrifices.
The Mín Cáo was responsible for construction, public works, salt ponds, and imperial gardens.
The Kè Cáo was responsible for escorting Qiāng and Hú tribes during court audiences.
The Èrqiānshí Cáo was responsible for litigation.
The Zhōngdūguān Cáo was responsible for matters of flood, fire, and banditry.
These combined to form six Cáo.
Together with two Púshè and one Lìng,
they were called the Bāzuò (Eight Seats).
Although the Shàngshū had Cáo names,
they were not used as titles.
When Emperor Líng Dì appointed Shìzhōng Liáng Hú as Xuǎnbù Shàngshū,
the use of Cáo names first appeared.
When the Wèi dynasty changed Xuǎnbù to Lìbù,
responsible for selection matters,
there were also Zuǒmín, Kè Cáo, Wǔbīng, and Dùzhī.
In total, there were five Cáo Shàngshū, two Púshè, and one Lìng, forming the Bāzuò.
When the Jìn dynasty established Lìbù, Sāngōng, Kè Cáo, Jiàbù, Túntián, and Dùzhī, making six Cáo,
there was no Wǔbīng.
In the second year of Xiánníng,
the Jiàbù Shàngshū was abolished.
In the fourth year,
one Púshè was abolished,
and the Jiàbù Shàngshū was re-established.
During the Tàikāng period,
there were Lìbù, Diànzhōng, Wǔbīng, Tián Cáo, Dùzhī, and Zuǒmín, making six Cáo Shàngshū,
but no Jiàbù, Sāngōng, or Kè Cáo.
During Emperor Huì Dì's reign, there was also a Yòumín Shàngshū,
limited to six Cáo,
but it is unknown which Cáo was abolished at this time.
Upon crossing the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
there were Lìbù, Cíbù, Wǔbīng, Zuǒmín, and Dùzhī, five Shàngshū.
