The Cíbù Shàngshū often shared duties with the Yòupúshè and was not appointed.
Instead,
the Yòupúshè served concurrently.
If the Yòupúshè position was vacant,
the Cíbù Shàngshū would temporarily manage the affairs of the right.
Zuǒyòuchéng:
Since Emperor Wǔ Dì of Hàn established the Shàngshū in the fourth year of Jiànshǐ,
four Chéng were immediately appointed.
When Guāngwǔ first reduced their number by two,
only a Zuǒchéng and Yòuchéng were appointed.
The Zuǒyòuchéng system thus began from this point.
From then until the Jìn dynasty, it remained unchanged.
The Jìn Zuǒchéng was responsible for internal prohibitions within the court,
ancestral temple sacrifices,
court ceremonies and rituals,
selection and appointment of officials,
and urgent leave.
The Yòuchéng was responsible for the court's treasuries, storehouses, and residences,
all kinds of utensils and equipment,
and grain distribution, human taxes, and cloth.
They also handled criminal cases, military weapons,
and supervised and recorded documents, memorials, and petitions from distant regions.
When the Bāzuò Láng were first appointed,
they all followed the old Hàn system,
gathering at the capital for formal exchanges,
and resigned from these exchanges upon promotion.
Shàngshū Láng:
The Western Hàn dynasty originally appointed four,
to manage the Shàngshū by division.
One was responsible for the Xiōngnú Chányú's camps and departments,
one for Qiāng and Yí officials and common people,
one for households and cultivated land,
and one for wealth and tribute collection.
After Guāngwǔ divided the Shàngshū into six Cáo,
a total of thirty-four were appointed,
with a rank of four hundred shí.
Including the Zuǒ and Yòuchéng, there were thirty-six people.
The Láng were responsible for drafting documents,
rotating duties every five days within the Jiànlǐmén.
Shàngshū Láng initially came from the Sānshǔ to the court for trials.
Those who served as Shǒu Shàngshū Láng (probationary Shàngshū Láng)
were called Shàngshū Láng after a year,
and Shìláng after three years.
Those with administrative ability were selected for the position.
In the Wèi dynasty,

there were Diànzhōng, Lìbù, Jiàbù, Jīnbù, Yúcáo, Bǐbù, Nánzhǔkè, Cíbù, Dùzhī, Kùbù, Nóngbù, Shuǐbù, Yícáo, Sāngōng, Cāngbù, Mín Cáo, Èrqiānshí, Zhōngbīng, Wàibīng, Dūbīng, Biébīng, Kǎogōng, and Dìngkè—
a total of twenty-three Láng.
In the second year of Qīnglóng,
Shàngshū Chén Jiǎo proposed establishing Dūguān and Qíbīng,
making a total of twenty-five Láng.
Whenever a Láng position became vacant,
five filial and honest individuals capable of drafting documents were selected for trial,
and their names were carefully sealed and reported for appointment.
When the Jìn dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven,
Emperor Wǔ Dì abolished Nóngbù and Dìngkè,

and established Zhíshì, Diànzhōng, Cíbù, Yícáo, Lìbù, Sāngōng, Bǐbù, Jīnbù, Cāngbù, Dùzhī, Dūguān, Èrqiānshí, Zuǒmín, Yòumín, Yúcáo, Túntián, Qǐbù, Shuǐbù, Zuǒyòuzhǔkè, Jiàbù, Chēbù, Kùbù, Zuǒyòuzhōngbīng, Zuǒyòuwàibīng, Biébīng, Dūbīng, Qíbīng, Zuǒyòushì, Běizhǔkè, and Nánzhǔkè,
totaling thirty-four Cáo Láng.
Later, Yùncáo was also established,
making a total of thirty-five Cáo,
with twenty-three Láng appointed,
who mutually supervised each other.
Upon crossing the Jiāng (Yangtze River) to the east,
there were no Zhíshì, Yòumín, Túntián, Chēbù, Biébīng, Dūbīng, Qíbīng, Zuǒyòushì, and Yùncáo, ten Cáo Láng.
After Kāngmù,
there were also no Yúcáo and Èrqiānshí Láng,
only Diànzhōng, Cíbù, Lìbù, Yícáo, Sāngōng, Bǐbù, Jīnbù, Cāngbù, Dùzhī, Dūguān, Zuǒmín, Qǐbù, Shuǐbù, Zhǔkè, Jiàbù, Kùbù, Zhōngbīng, and Wàibīng—eighteen Cáo Láng.
Later, Zhǔkè, Qǐbù, and Shuǐbù were again abolished,
leaving fifteen Cáo.
Shìzhōng:
According to records, Fēng Hòu served as Shìzhōng during the time of the Yellow Emperor,
which was the role of Chángbó in the Zhōu dynasty.
The Qín dynasty adopted the ancient name to establish Shìzhōng,
and the Hàn dynasty followed suit.
Both Qín and Hàn had no fixed number of members,
and one person with high merit was appointed as Púshè.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards, four were appointed,
with additional officials not counted in this number.
They were responsible for court reception, ceremonies, and imperial dignity.
When the emperor's grand carriage departed, the attending Shìzhōng would guard it in succession.
The upright Shìzhōng would carry the imperial seal and ride in the imperial carriage.
They did not wear swords,
and all others followed on horseback.
When the emperor ascended the hall,
they would assist him along with the Sànqí Chángshì,
with the Shìzhōng on the left
and the Chángshì on the right.
They were prepared for immediate questions and direct responses,
and to retrieve omissions and correct deficiencies.
In the fourth year of Xīngníng during Emperor Āi Dì's reign of the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
Huán Wēn proposed abolishing two positions,
but it was later restored.
Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng:
This was a Qín official.
The Hàn dynasty and later dynasties inherited it,
managing various affairs of the Ménxià along with the Shìzhōng,
with no fixed number.
In the Jìn dynasty,
four members were appointed.
Sànqí Chángshì:
This was originally a Qín official.
The Qín dynasty established Sànqí,
and also Zhōngchángshì.
The Sànqí rode on horseback behind the imperial carriage,
while the Zhōngchángshì were allowed into the forbidden palace.
Neither had a fixed number of members,
and were also considered honorary appointments.
At the beginning of the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
Sànqí was abolished,
and Zhōngchángshì were eunuchs.
At the beginning of Huángchū during Emperor Wén Dì's reign of Wèi,
Sànqí was re-established
and combined with Zhōngchángshì.
They jointly managed admonitions and remonstrations,
but did not handle specific affairs.
They wore diāo diāng (sable tails and cicada ornaments) on the right,
and followed on horseback.
This remained unchanged until the Jìn dynasty.
During the Yuánkāng period,
Emperor Huì Dì first appointed the eunuch Dǒng Měng as Zhōngchángshì,
but this practice later ceased.
It was always a prominent position.
Jǐshìzhōng:
This was a Qín official.
Those appointed included Dàfū, Bóshì, or Yìláng.
They were responsible for consultations and responses,
ranking below Zhōngchángshì.
The Hàn dynasty inherited this.
It was abolished in the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
re-established in the Wèi dynasty,
and remained unchanged until the Jìn dynasty.
It ranked below Sànqí Chángshì
and above Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
with no fixed number of members.
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì:
According to records, at the end of the Wèi dynasty, there were Sànqí Chángshì outside the fixed number.
In the tenth year of Tàishǐ,
Emperor Wǔ Dì ordered two individuals to be included in the fixed roster of Sànqí Chángshì,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Four were appointed in the Eastern Jìn dynasty.
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì:
Established at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
with no fixed number of members.
There were four Sànqí Shìláng.
In the early Wèi period, they were established together with the Sànqí Chángshì.
From Wèi to Jìn,
the Sànqí Chángshì and Shìláng, together with the Shìzhōng and Huángmén Shìláng, jointly reviewed memorials to the throne from the Shàngshū.
This practice was abolished south of the Yangtze River.
There were four Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng.
Initially,
Emperor Wǔ established Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
In the first year of Tàixīng,
Emperor Yuán made two of them serve jointly with the Sànqí Shìláng,
hence they were called Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng.
Later, their number was increased to four.
Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng
were established by Emperor Wǔ
with no fixed number.
Fèng Cháoqǐng
was not originally an official post
and had no fixed number.
In the Eastern Hàn, many former Sāngōng, imperial relatives (wàiqī), members of the imperial clan (zōngshì), and feudal lords (zhūhóu) served as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Fèng Cháoqǐng
meant simply receiving invitations to imperial audiences and assemblies.
Emperor Wǔ also appointed members of the imperial clan and imperial relatives as Fèngchē, Fùmǎ, and Qí Sāndūwèi, and they also served as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
When Emperor Yuán was King of Jìn,
he appointed Cānjūn as Fèngchē Dūwèi,
Yuánshǔ as Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and Xíng Cānjūn Shèrén as Qí Dūwèi.
All of them served as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Later, the Fèngchē and Qí two Dūwèi were abolished,
and only the Fùmǎ Dūwèi remained as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Liú Tàn and Huán Wēn, who married princesses, all held this post.
Zhōngshū Jiān and Lìng.
According to records, during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's leisure in the imperial harem,
he first assigned eunuchs to manage the affairs of the Shàngshū,
calling them Zhōngshū Yèzhě,
and established Lìng and Púyè.
Emperor Chéng changed the name Zhōngshū Yèzhě Lìng to Zhōng Yèzhě Lìng
and abolished the Púyè.
In the Eastern Hàn, the Zhōng Yèzhě Lìng was abolished,
but there was a Zhōngguān Yèzhě Lìng,
which was not its original function.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was King of Wèi,
he established the Mìshū Lìng
to manage memorials to the throne from the Shàngshū.
In the early Huángchū era, Emperor Wén changed it to Zhōngshū
and established a Jiān and a Lìng.
He appointed Mìshū Zuǒchéng Liú Fàng as Zhōngshū Jiān
and Yòuchéng Sūn Zī as Zhōngshū Lìng.
The posts of Jiān and Lìng perhaps originated from this.
Jìn adopted this system,
establishing one incumbent for each post.
Zhōngshū Shìláng.
In the early Huángchū era of Wèi,
after the Zhōngshū established the Jiān and Lìng,
it also established Tōngshì Láng,
ranking next to Huángmén Láng.
After the Huángmén Láng had signed the documents,
the Tōngshì Láng would then sign their names.
Once signed,
the memorials were presented,
read by the emperor for review,
and then approved in writing.
In Jìn,
they were renamed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
with four incumbents.
The Zhōngshū Shìláng perhaps originated from this.
In the early Jiāngzuǒ period,
Zhōngshū Shìláng were renamed Tōngshì Láng,
but soon reverted to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Zhōngshū Shèrén.
According to records, in the early Jìn, one Shèrén and one Tōngshì were initially established.
South of the Yangtze, the Shèrén and Tōngshì were combined and called Tōngshì Shèrén,
responsible for presenting memorials and documents.
[一０]Later, this was abolished,
and one Zhōngshū Shìláng was assigned to duty in the Xīshěng,
also taking charge of imperial edicts.
Mìshū Jiān.
According to records, in the second year of Yánxī during Emperor Huán of Hàn's reign, the Mìshū Jiān was established,
[一一]but later abolished.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was King of Wèi,
he established Mìshū Lìng and Chéng.
In the early Huángchū era of Emperor Wén,
he established Zhōngshū Lìng
to manage memorials to the throne from the Shàngshū,
and the Mìshū Lìng was changed to Mìshū Jiān.
Later, Hé Zhēn was appointed Mìshū Chéng,
but since there was already a Mìshū Chéng,
Zhēn was appointed Mìshū Yòuchéng.
When Jìn received the Mandate,
Emperor Wǔ combined the Mìshū and Zhōngshū provinces,
but the Mìshū's functions of compilation and writing were not abolished.
During the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Huì,
the Mìshū Jiān was re-established.
Its subordinate officials included a Chéng
and a Láng,
and it also oversaw the Zuòzhù Shěng.
Zuòzhù Láng
held the responsibility of the Zhōu Zuǒshǐ.
In the Eastern Hàn, imperial records were kept in the Dōngguān,
so renowned scholars were appointed to compile works in the Dōngguān,
giving it its name,
though there was not yet an official post.
During the Tàihé era of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
an edict established Zuòzhù Láng,
which was the beginning of this official post,
subordinate to the Zhōngshū Shěng.
When Jìn received the Mandate,
Emperor Wǔ appointed Miào Zhēng as Zhōngshū Zuòzhù Láng.
In the second year of Yuánkāng,
an edict stated:
"The Zuòzhù traditionally belonged to the Zhōngshū.
However, since the Mìshū now manages literary records,
we hereby change the Zhōngshū Zuòzhù to Mìshū Zuòzhù."
Thus, it was made subordinate to the Mìshū Shěng.
Later, a separate office was established for it, but it remained subordinate to the Mìshū.
There was one Zuòzhù Láng,
called Dà Zuòzhù Láng,
specifically responsible for historical records,
and eight Zuǒ Zuòzhù Láng were also established.
When a Zuòzhù Láng first took office,
they were required to compile a biography of one renowned minister.
The Tàicháng, Guānglùxūn, Wèiwèi, Tàipú, Tíngwèi, Dàhónglú, Zōngzhèng, Dàsīnóng, Shǎofǔ, Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng, the three Qīng for the Empress Dowager, and Dàchángqiū
were all Leìqīng,
each with a Chéng, Gōngcáo, Zhǔbù, Wǔguān, and other officers.
The Tàicháng
had positions for Bóshì and Xiélǜ Xiàowèi.
It also oversaw the various Bóshì and Jìjiǔ of the Tàixué, as well as the Lìng of the Tàishǐ, Tàimiào, Tàiyuè, Gǔchuī, and Líng.
The Tàishǐ also had a separate Língtái Chéng.
Tàicháng Bóshì
was a Wèi official post.
Emperor Wén of Wèi first established it,
and Jìn adopted it.
They were responsible for guiding the imperial carriage.
For princes, dukes, and others below them who were due posthumous titles,
the Bóshì would discuss and decide.
Xiélǜ Xiàowèi
was the post of Hàn's Xiélǜ Dūwèi.
Dù Kuí of Wèi held this post.
In Jìn,
it was renamed Xiélǜ Xiàowèi.
In early Jìn, following the Wèi system,
nineteen Bóshì were established.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng,
Emperor Wǔ first established the Guózǐxué,
setting one Guózǐ Jìjiǔ and one Bóshì each,
and fifteen Zhùjiào,
to instruct students.
Bóshì were all chosen from those with pure conduct
and thorough understanding of classical texts and principles,
such as those holding the ranks of Sànqí Chángshì, Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ, or higher,
who would then be summoned for an examination.
In the early Jiāngzuǒ period,
their number was reduced to nine.
In the late reign of Emperor Yuán,
one Bóshì for Yílǐ and one for Chūnqiū Gōngyáng were added,
making a total of eleven.
Later, it was again increased to sixteen,
no longer specializing in the Five Classics,
and they were called Tàixué Bóshì.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
the number of Guózǐ Zhùjiào was reduced to ten.
Guānglùxūn

oversaw the WǔbēnMídlángjiàng, Yǔlín Lángjiàng, Rǒngcóng Púyè, Yǔlín Zuǒjiān, Wǔguān Zuǒyòu Zhōnglángjiàng, and the Lìng of Dōngyuán Jiàng, Tàiguān, Yùfǔ, Shǒugōng, Huángmén, Yètíng, Qīngshāng, Huálín Yuán, and Bàoshì.
In the second year of Xīngníng during Emperor Āi's reign,
the Guānglùxūn was abolished
and merged into the Sītú.
It was re-established in the first year of Níngkāng during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign.
Wèiwèi
oversaw the Lìng of Wǔkù, Gōngchē, Wèishì, and various Zhūyě,
the Zuǒyòu Dūhòu,
and the Nánběi Dōngxī Dūyě Yuàn.
[一二]Upon crossing the Yangtze,
the Wèiwèi was abolished.
Tàipú
oversaw the Diǎnnóng and Diǎnyú Dūwèi,
Diǎnyú Chéng,
Zuǒyòu Zhōng Diǎnmù Dūwèi,
Chēfǔ Diǎnmù,
and the Lìng of Chénghuáng, Huá liú, Lóngmǎ, and others.
Diǎnmù also had a separate Yángmù Chéng.
The Tàipú,
after Emperor Yuán crossed the Yangtze, was sometimes abolished and sometimes re-established.
When the Tàipú was abolished,
the duty of Huá liú became a post of the Ménxià.
Tíngwèi
was in charge of criminal law and legal cases.
Its subordinate officials included Zhèng, Jiān, and Píng,
and also a Lǜ Bóshì.
Dàhónglú
oversaw the Lìng of Dàxíng, Diǎnkè, Yuánchí, Huálín Yuán, and Gōudùn.
It also had Qīnggōng Lièchéng and Yè Xuánwǔ Yuánchéng.
In the Jiāngzuǒ period,
it was temporarily established when there were affairs to manage,
and abolished when there were none.
Zōngzhèng
administered the imperial clan's genealogical records and registers.
It also managed the Tàiyīling and his scribes,
and it had Sīmù yuán (herding officials) and their subordinates.
After crossing the Jiāng,
Emperor Āi abolished and merged it with the Tàicháng.
The Tàiyī were then assigned to the Ménxiàshěng.
The Dàsīnóng
managed the three directors of the Tàicāng, Jítián, and Dǎoguān,
the Xiāngguó Dūshuǐzhǎng,
and the Hùcáo yuán of the eastern, western, northern, and southern sections.
After crossing the Jiāng,
Emperor Āi abolished and merged the Dūshuǐ,
but Emperor Xiàowǔ re-established it.
The Shǎofǔ
managed the directors of the Cáiguān Xiàowèi, the three Shàngfāng (Central, Left, and Right), the Zhōnghuáng Zuǒyòuzàng, the Zuǒxiào, Zhēnguān, Píngzhǔn, and Xīguān, etc.,
and the assistants of the Zuǒxiàofáng, Yèzhōnghuáng Zuǒyòuzàng, Yóuguān, etc.
After crossing the Jiāng,
Emperor Āi abolished and merged it with the Dānyáng Yǐn,
but Emperor Xiàowǔ re-established it.
Since crossing the Jiāng, only one Shàngfāng was established,
and the Yùfǔ was also abolished.
The Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng
was established when there were tasks,
and abolished when there were none.
The three ministers of the Empress Dowager –
the Wèiwèi, Shǎofǔ, and Tàipú –
were established during the Hàn dynasty.
Their titles were named after the Empress Dowager's palace,
ranking above the ministers of the same name.
They were absent when there was no Empress Dowager.
The Wèi dynasty changed the Hàn system,
placing them below the Jiǔqīng.
When Jìn restored the old system,
they ranked above the ministers of the same name.
The Dàchángqiū
was the Empress's minister.
It was established when there was an Empress,
and abolished when there was none.
The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
was originally a Qín official.
During the Qín dynasty,
the Yùshǐ Dàfū had two Cchéng:
one was the Yùshǐchéng,
and the other was the Zhōngchéng.
The Zhōngchéng externally supervised the Bù Cìshǐ,
and internally managed the Shìyùshǐ.
He received memorials from the Gōngqīng,
and impeached and investigated cases.
The Hàn dynasty followed this system.
In the first year of Suíhé of Emperor Chéng,
the Yùshǐ Dàfū was renamed Dàsīkōng,
and a Zhǎngshǐ was established,
but the office of Zhōngchéng remained as before.
In the second year of Jiànpíng of Emperor Āi,
it was restored to Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the second year of Yuánshòu,
it became Dàsīkōng again,
and the Zhōngchéng went out to be the head of the Yùshǐtái.
Throughout the Eastern Hàn and up to the Jìn dynasty, this system was followed,
with the Zhōngchéng as the head of the Tái.
Regarding the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ,
it is said that Emperor Xuān of Hàn once resided in the Xuānshìzhāi and resolved matters,
ordering two Shìyùshǐ to manage documents by his side.
Later, a separate office was established,
called Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ,
which was probably its origin.
During the Wèi dynasty,
a Zhìshū Zhífǎ was also established,
in charge of impeachment,
while the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ was in charge of laws and decrees.
Both offices were established.
During the Jìn dynasty,
only the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ was established,
with four members.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ,
one Huángshāyù Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ was also established.
His rank was the same as the Zhōngchéng,
and he was in charge of imperial prison cases and all inappropriate matters of the Tíngwèi.
Later, when Hénán was merged,
the Huángshā Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ was abolished.
During the Tàikāng period,
two Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ were also abolished.
Regarding the Shìyùshǐ,
during the Two Hàn dynasties, there were five sections under their charge: first, the Lìngcáo,
in charge of laws and decrees;
second, the Yìncáo,
in charge of carving seals;
third, the Gòngcáo,
in charge of fasts and sacrifices;
fourth, the Wèimǎcáo,
in charge of horses;
fifth, the Chéngcáo,
in charge of escorting the imperial carriage.
The Wèi dynasty established eight members.
During the Jìn dynasty,
nine members were established.
Their rank was the same as the Zhìshū,
and there were thirteen sections: Lìcáo, Kèdìcáo, Zhíshìcáo, Yìncáo, Zhōngdūdūcáo, Wàidūdūcáo, Méicáo, Fújiécáo, Shuǐcáo, Zhōnglěicáo, Yíngjūncáo, Fǎcáo, and Suàncáo.
At the beginning of the Jiāngzuǒ period,
the Kèdìcáo was abolished,
and a Kùcáo was established,
in charge of managing cattle, horses, and market taxes.
Later, the sections were divided,
and the Wàizuǒkù and Nèizuǒkù were established.
Regarding the Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
it is said that the Wèi Lántái sent two Yùshǐ to reside in the palace,
to observe and investigate illegal activities,
which was its origin.
During the Jìn dynasty,
four members were established.
Two were established in Jiāngzuǒ.
It is also said that the official rank regulations of Wèi and Jìn also included the Jìnfángyùshǐ of the seventh rank.
During the Tàiyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ, there was a Jiǎnjiàoyùshǐ Wú Kūn,
The Fújié Yùshǐ
was the office of the Qín Fúxǐlìng.
The Hàn dynasty followed this,
ranking after the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
During the Wèi dynasty,
it became a separate Tái,
ranking after the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
in charge of bestowing credentials, bronze military tallies, and bamboo emissary tallies.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
Emperor Wǔ abolished and merged the Lántái,
establishing the Fújié Yùshǐ to manage its affairs.
Regarding the Sīlì Xiàowèi,
it is said that Emperor Wǔ of Hàn initially established thirteen zhōu,
each with one Cìshǐ.
He also established the Sīlì Xiàowèi,
to inspect the seven commanderies of Sānfǔ, Sānhé, and Hóngnóng.
Throughout the Eastern Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn dynasties,
this office was not abolished.
Subordinate officials included Gōngcáo, Dūguān Cóngshì, Zhūcáo Cóngshì, Bùjùn Cóngshì, Zhǔbù, Lùshì, Ménxià Shūzuǒ, Shěngshì, Jìshì Shūzuǒ, Zhūcáo Shūzuǒ Shǒu Cóngshì, Wǔměng Cóngshì, etc.,
totaling one hundred officials
and thirty-two soldiers.
After crossing the Jiāng,
the office of Sīlì Xiàowèi was abolished.
Its duties were then performed by the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Yèzhě Púyè
was a Qín official.
From Hàn to Wèi, this system was followed.
The Wèi dynasty established a Púyè,
in charge of great appointments and the ranking of all officials,
supervising ten Yèzhě.
Emperor Wǔ abolished the Púyè,
merging the Yèzhě with the Lántái.
Jiāngzuǒ re-established the Púyè,
but later abolished it again.
The Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě
was the office of the Hàn Shuǐhéng.
The Hàn dynasty also had Dūshuǐ Zhǎngchéng,
in charge of reservoirs and irrigation,
and maintaining rivers and canals,
subordinate to the Tàicháng.
The Eastern Hàn abolished the Dūshuǐ,
establishing the Hédī Yèzhě.
The Wèi dynasty followed this.
with the Hédī Yèzhě as subordinate officials of the Dūshuǐ.
In Jiāngzuǒ,
the Hédī Yèzhě was abolished,
and six Yèzhě were established.
The Zhōnglǐngjūn Jiàngjūn
was a Wèi official.
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān of Hàn, the Wèi Wǔ Chéngxiàngfǔ established it on its own.
When Hánzhōng was captured,
Cáo Xiū was made Zhōnglǐngjūn.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
the Lǐngjūn Jiàngjūn was first established,
with Cáo Xiū as its holder,
in charge of the five battalions, Zhōnglěi, and Wǔwèi, etc., three camps.
Emperor Wǔ initially abolished it,
making Zhōngjūn Jiàngjūn Yáng Hù manage the two guards, Qian, Hou, Zuo, You, and Xiāowèi, etc., camps,
which were the duties of the Lǐngjūn.
During the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái,
Zhōngjūn was renamed Zhōnglǐngjūn.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
it was renamed Běijūn Zhōnghóu,
and soon restored to Lǐngjūn.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng,
it was restored to Zhōnghóu,
and soon restored to Lǐngjūn.
The Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (Protector Army General)
was originally the Hùjūn Dūwèi (Protector Army Commandant) of Qín.
Hàn adopted it.
Gāozǔ appointed Chén Píng as Hùjūn Zhōngwèi (Protector Army Central Commandant).
Emperor Wǔ later reappointed him as Hùjūn Dūwèi,
subordinate to the Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal).
When Wèi Wǔ was Chancellor,
he appointed Hán Hào as Hùjūn (Protector Army)
and Shǐ Huàn as Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Army).
[一六] These were not Hàn officials.
In the twelfth year of Jiàn'ān (207 CE),
Hùjūn was changed to Zhōnghùjūn (Central Protector Army),
and Lǐngjūn was changed to Zhōnglǐngjūn (Central Commander of the Army),
with a Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) and Sīmǎ (Military Advisor) appointed.
In the early Wèi,
the Hùjūn Jiāngjūn was established,
responsible for the selection of military officials,
and subordinate to the Lǐngjūn.
In the Jìn period, it was no longer subordinate.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng (311 CE) of Emperor Yuán,
the Hùjūn was abolished
and merged with the Lǐngjūn.
In the second year of Tàiníng (324 CE) of Emperor Míng,
Lǐng and Hù were re-established,
each commanding camp soldiers.
Since the move to the east of the Jiāng (river),
the Lǐngjūn no longer separately commanded camps,
but was in overall command of the two Wèi (Guards), Xiāoqí (Valiant Cavalry), Cáiguān (Trained Officials), and other camps.
The Hùjūn still had its own camps.
Those with high seniority became Lǐngjūn and Hùjūn,
while those with lower seniority became Zhōnglǐngjūn and Zhōnghùjūn.
Subordinate officials included Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo (Merit Officer), Zhǔbù (Registrar), and Wǔguān (Five Officers).
If ordered to go on campaign, a Cānjūn (Staff Officer) was appointed.
The Zuǒyòu Wèijiāngjūn (Left and Right Guard Generals).
Emperor Wén initially established the Zhōngwèi (Central Guard) and Wèi (Guards).
[一七] Emperor Wǔ, upon receiving the mandate,
divided them into Zuǒyòu Wèi (Left and Right Guards),
appointing Yáng Xiù as the Left
and Zhào Xù as the Right.
Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo, and Zhǔbù were all appointed.
After the move to the east of the Jiāng, the Chángshǐ was abolished.
The Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (Valiant Cavalry General) and Yóují Jiāngjūn (Skirmishing General)
were both miscellaneous generals of Hàn.
Wèi established them as Zhōngjūn (Central Army).
By Jìn,
Lǐng, Hù, Zuǒyòu Wèi, Xiāoqí, and Yóují constituted the Liùjūn (Six Armies).
The Zuǒyòu Qiánhòu Jūnjiāngjūn (Left, Right, Front, and Rear Army Generals).
In Emperor Míng of Wèi's time, there was a Zuǒjūn (Left Army),
so the Zuǒjūn was a Wèi official,
and it remained unchanged in Jìn.
Emperor Wǔ initially also established a Qiánjūn (Front Army) and Yòujūn (Right Army).
In the eighth year of Tàishǐ (272 CE), a Hòujūn (Rear Army) was also established,
forming the Sìjūn (Four Armies).
The Tuánqí (Cantonment Cavalry), Bùbīng (Infantry), Yuèqí (Vietnamese Cavalry), Chángshuǐ (Long Water), and Shèshēng (Sound-Shooting) Xiàowèi (Commandants)
were the Wǔxiào (Five Commandants),
all Hàn officials.
In Wèi and Jìn, down to the move to the east of the Jiāng,
they still commanded camp soldiers,
and all had Sīmǎ, Gōngcáo, and Zhǔbù.
Later, the Zuǒjūn, Yòujūn, Qiánjūn, and Hòujūn were abolished and replaced by Zhènwèi Jūn (Garrison Guard Army).
Their left and right camp commandants remained as before,
all commanded by the Zhōnglǐngjūn.
The two Wèi initially established Qiánqū (Vanguard), Yóujī (Light Cavalry), and Qiángnǔ (Strong Crossbow) as Sānbù Sīmǎ (Three Department Military Advisors),
each with a Dūshǐ (Supervising Clerk).
The Zuǒwèi had Xióngqú Wǔbēn (Bear-Quiver Martial Braves);
the Yòuwèi had Cìfēi Wǔbēn (Swift-Flying Martial Braves).
Each of the two Wèi had Wǔbù Dū (Five Department Supervisors).
The Zhōngwǔbēn (Central Martial Braves) were commanded by the Xiāoqí and Yóují respectively.
Wǔbēn, Yǔlín (Feathered Forest), Shàngqí (Upper Cavalry), and Yìlì (Exceptional Strength) four departments were also established,
together with Zhōng as Wǔdū (Five Supervisors).
The Wèi Zhèn Sìjūn (Guard Garrison Four Armies) were like the Wǔxiào,
each with one thousand men.
The Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn (Palace Center General),
Zhōngláng (Gentleman of the Household), Xiàowèi, and Sīmǎ were newly established and ranked with the Xiāoqí.
[一八] The Chúichúi Fǔwǔbēn (Mallet and Axe Martial Braves)
were divided and assigned to the two Wèi.
The Wèi Zhōngwǔbēn (Guards' Central Martial Braves), [一九] the Chíchú Róngcóng (Halberd-Bearing Supernumerary Retainers), and Yǔlín Sīmǎ
each had a varying number of regular attendants.
Emperor Wǔ greatly valued military officials,
so military commandants were often selected from upright and respected individuals in the court.
Previously,
Chén Xié was favored by Emperor Wén,
possessing exceptional talent and skill,
and a clear understanding of military regulations.
When the Emperor was King of Jìn,
he entrusted him with military affairs.
After the fall of Shǔ,
he ordered Xié to learn Zhūgě Liàng's methods of encirclement, battle formations, and concealed deployment.
Also, the system of 'A' and 'B' markers and banners;
Xié was thoroughly familiar with them.
Consequently, Xié was made Diànzhōng Diǎnbīng Zhōnglángjiāng (Palace Center Military Superintendent Gentleman of the Household),
and later promoted to Jiāngjūn (General).
After a long time,
whenever Emperor Wǔ went out or came in,
Xié held the white beast banner to the left and right of the imperial carriage,
and the imperial retinue was arranged with precision and solemnity.
Towards the end of Tàikāng (290 CE),
Emperor Wǔ once went pheasant hunting.
Xié, who was then Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě (Director of Waterways),
followed loosely.
The imperial carriage returned late, as darkness approached.
The hour for closing the gates had passed.
The imperial carriage needed to be assembled.
The imperial carriage was stopped,
and for a long time, it could not be assembled.
An edict then ordered Xié to assemble it.
Xié raised the white beast banner and gave commands.
In a moment, the carriage was assembled.
Everyone praised Xié for his familiarity and understanding,
and he was greatly trusted by Emperor Wǔ.
The Tàizǐ Tàifù (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince) and Shàofù (Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince)
were both ancient officials.
In the third year of Tàishǐ (267 CE),
Emperor Wǔ first established these offices,
[二０] appointing one person to each.
The Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Heir Apparent's Household) had not yet been established,
so all official matters, great or small,
[二一] passed through the two Fù.
Both had Gōngcáo, Zhǔbù, and Wǔguān.
The Tàifù was rank "middle two thousand piculs,"
and the Shàofù was "two thousand piculs."
In their instruction and guidance,
the Tàifù was in front,
and the Shàofù was behind.
When the Crown Prince bowed first,
the Fù would then respond.
Emperor Wǔ later, considering the dignity of the heir apparent,
commanded various Dukes to hold these positions.
Because their original ranks were high,
they sometimes concurrently held the positions (Xíng) or temporarily managed them (Lǐng).
At that time, the Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court) Rèn Kǎi,
whom Emperor Wǔ highly respected,
was again made to manage them,
which was a temporary arrangement.
In the first year of Xiánníng (275 CE),
Yáng Yáo, who was Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng (Attendant-in-ordinary at the Yellow Gate), was appointed Zhānshì,
taking charge of palace affairs.
The two Fù no longer managed their official subordinates.
When Yáng Yáo became Wèijiāngjūn (Guard General)
and also held the Shàofù,
the Zhānshì was abolished.
Consequently, the system of Fù instruction was greatly promoted,
and Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Jiǎ Chōng was commanded to hold the Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian),
and Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Qí Wáng Yōu was commanded to hold the Tàifù.
The appointed subordinate officials were restored to the old system.
The two Fù wore Xiánliǎngguān (Double-Beam Cap) for advancement of worthies,
Hēijièzé (Black Helmet-like Headwear),
Wǔshícháofú (Five-Season Court Robe),
and wore a Shuǐcāngyù (Aquamarine Jade pendant).
Their food allowance was three hú per day.
In the second year of Tàikāng (281 CE),
they were first given a spring gift of fifty bolts of silk,
and in autumn, one hundred bolts of silk
and one hundred catties of cotton.
Afterwards, Tàiwèi Rǔnán Wáng Liàng, Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) Yáng Jùn, Sīkōng Wèi Guàn, and Shí Jiàn all held Fù Bǎo positions.
The Zhānshì was still not established,
and this continued until the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign.
In the first year of Yuánkāng (291 CE) of Emperor Huì,
the Zhānshì was re-established.
The two Fù were given six qǐng of vegetable fields
and six Tiánzōu (field servants).
For those who could not cultivate the fields after the beginning of summer,
they received one year's food allowance.
One Chéng (Assistant) was appointed,
with a salary of one thousand piculs.

One Zhǔbù, Wǔguān Yuàn (Five Officers' Clerk), Gōngcáo Shǐ (Merit Officer's Scribe), Zhǔjì Ménxià Shǐ (Chief Scribe of the Gate Department), Lùshì (Record Keeper), Hùcáo Fǎcáo Cāngcáo Zéicáo Gōngcáo Shūzuǒ (Secretary for Households, Law, Granary, Robbery, and Merit), Ménxià Tíngzhǎng (Head of the Gate Department's Pavilion), Ménxià Shūzuǒ (Gate Department's Secretary), and Shěngshì (Investigator) were each appointed.
They were given one Chì'ěr Ānchē (red-eared comfortable carriage).
When Mǐnhuái established his administration,
Six Fù were then established,
three Tàis (Grand) and three Shǎos (Junior).
Because of Emperor Jǐng's taboo on the name Shī (Teacher),
Tàishī (Grand Preceptor) was changed to Tàibǎo.
[二三] They jointly managed the affairs of the Shàngshū (Grand Secretariat),
and all documents of the Zhānshì passed through the Six Fù.
However, from Yuánkāng onwards,
there were sometimes two or three,
or four or six Fù.
In the Yǒngkāng period, the Zhānshì was again not established.
Since Tàian, the Zhānshì had been established
and continued until the end of Emperor Huái's reign.
After crossing the Jiāng,
there were Tàifù and Shàofù,
but no Shī (Preceptor) or Bǎo (Guardian) were established.
There were four Zhōngshùzǐ (Gentlemen of the Inner Household),
whose duties were like those of the Shìzhōng.
Four Zhōngshèrén (Central Palace Attendants) were established in the fourth year of Xiánníng (278 CE).
They were selected from Shèrén (Palace Attendants) with excellent talent and learning,
and together with the Zhōngshùzǐ, they managed literary affairs.
Their duties were like those of Huángmén Shìláng (Attendant-in-ordinary at the Yellow Gate),
ranking below the Zhōngshùzǐ,
but above Xǐmǎ (Groom).
One Shíguān Lìng (Director of Food Officials),
whose duties were like those of the Tàiguān Lìng (Director of the Grand Provisioner).
Four Shùzǐ,
their posts were comparable to Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngshū Jiānlìng.
Sixteen Shèrén,
their posts were comparable to Sànqí and Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Eight Xǐmǎ,
their posts were like Yèzhě and Mìshū,
in charge of maps and documents.
When offerings were made and scriptures lectured, they were in charge of those affairs;
when the prince went out, the one on duty would precede him,
guiding the ceremonial procession.
The Shuàigēng Lìng
was in charge of official palace gates and doors, and matters of reward and punishment;
their post was like Guānglù Xūn and Wèiwèi.
The Jiālìng
was in charge of criminal justice, grain and goods, and food and drink;
their post was comparable to Sīnóng and Shàofǔ.
In the Eastern Hàn, the Zhǔshíguānlìng
and Shíguānlìng, and in Jìn they became independent officials,
no longer subordinate to the Jiālìng.
The Pú
was in charge of chariots, horses, and clan affairs; their post was like Tàipú and Zōngzhèng.
The Zuǒyòu Wèishuaì.
According to Emperor Wǔ's establishment of the Eastern Palace,
〔二四〕Wèishuaì were set up,
initially called Zhōngwèishuaì.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (269 CE),
they were divided into Left and Right,
each commanding one army.
During Emperor Huì's reign,
when Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ was in the Eastern Palace,
Front and Rear commanders were added.
Upon the move to the east of the Yangtze River (Jiāngzuǒ),
the Front and Rear commanders were abolished,
but during Emperor Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era, they were re-established.
The King established one Shī, one Yǒu, and one Wénxué each.
Due to the taboo name of Emperor Jǐng,
Shī was changed to Fù.
The Yǒu title was adopted from King Wén and Zhòngní's "four friends."
Tàishǒu was changed to Nèishǐ,
and Xiàng and Pú were abolished.
There were Lángzhōnglìng, Zhōngwèi, and Dànóng as the three Qīng.
Large states established one Zuǒ Chángshì and one Yòu Chángshì each,
abolished Lángzhōng,
and set up two Shìláng.
One Diǎnshū, Diǎncí, Diǎnwèi, Xuéguānlìng, and Diǎnshūchéng each.
Four Zhìshū.
One Zhōngwèi Sīmǎ, one Shìzǐ Shùzǐ, and one Língmiào Mùzhǎng each.
Four Yèzhě.
Six Zhōng Dàfū.
Ten Shèrén.
One Diǎnfǔ each.
In the third year of Xiánníng (277 CE),
Wèijiāngjūn Yáng Yáo and Zhōngshūjiān Xún Xù, seeing Qí Wáng Yōu's considerable prestige,
feared future difficulties for Emperor Huì.
They thereupon followed the intent of the late Sīkōng Péi Xiù's five-grade enfeoffment system,
and gently presented the current expediency to Emperor Wǔ,
thinking:
"In ancient times, establishing marquises
was for the purpose of protecting the royal house.
Now the Wú bandits are not yet eliminated,
and the regional responsibilities are great.
While the various princes act as commanders,
they administer their enfeoffed states.
Since each does not treat their subordinates as subjects,
it is greatly inappropriate for the current situation.
Moreover, generals of other surnames reside on the borders;
it is appropriate to involve relatives,
but all the princes and dukes are in the capital,
which does not conform to the principle of a protective city,
nor to a secure foundation for ten thousand generations."
The Emperor initially did not pay attention,
but then issued an edict to discuss its regulations.
The responsible officials memorialized to follow the proposal for the princes and dukes,
revising their households and territories,

The states of Píngyuán, Rǔnán, Lángyé, Fúfēng, and Qí were designated as large states.
Liáng, Zhào, Lè'ān, Yān, Ānpíng, and Yìyáng were designated as secondary states.
The rest were small states.
All were regulated to increase their nearby counties to fill up to ten thousand households.
Regulations for commandery dukes were also established, like those for small state kings,
and the Zhōngwèi also commanded their troops.
Commandery marquises, like kings with less than five thousand households,
established one army of one thousand one hundred men,
also commanded by the Zhōngwèi.
At that time,
only Lǔgōng’s state’s households and territory were specially increased.

Furthermore, Nángōng Wáng Chéng and Suí Wáng Wàn were each enfeoffed as county kings during the Tàishǐ era,
〔二五〕with one thousand households.
By this time, the county kings’ households were revised and increased to three thousand households.
Their regulations were like those of a commandery marquis,
and they also established one army.
From this point, only imperial sons could be kings.
The collateral descendants of these princes, who were closely related to the imperial family,
also received enfeoffment based on their land and grace.
The collateral sons of kings originally enfeoffed in large and secondary states became dukes.
The collateral sons of kings succeeding to an enfeoffment became marquises.
The collateral sons of kings succeeding to a second enfeoffment became earls.
For small states of five thousand households or more,
the collateral sons of originally enfeoffed kings became viscounts.
For those with less than five thousand households, the collateral sons of originally enfeoffed kings, as well as the collateral sons of originally enfeoffed dukes and marquises, all became barons.
Without this, none could be enfeoffed.
The regulations for dukes were like states of five thousand households.
The regulations for marquises were like states of less than five thousand households.
They also established one army of one thousand men,
commanded by the Zhōngwèi.
Earls, viscounts, and barons downwards had different grades
and did not establish armies.
The grandsons of originally enfeoffed large states abolished their lower army.
Their great-grandsons also abolished their upper army.
The sons and grandsons of originally enfeoffed secondary states also abolished their lower army.
The rest consistently maintained one army.
Large states had a central army of two thousand men,
and upper and lower armies of one thousand five hundred men each.
Secondary states had an upper army of two thousand men,
and a lower army of one thousand men.
For those who had not yet gone to their states,
large states established one hundred retainers.
Secondary states eighty retainers.
Small states sixty retainers.
Commandery marquises and county dukes also followed the regulations of small states.
After implementation,
those whose households were increased or transferred were sent to their states as originally memorialized,

and departed in tears.
After the pacification of Wú,

The Central Court (Zhōngcháo) system

Dukes and marquises downwards established official retinues;

Famous mountains and large marshes were not enfeoffed.

When households were fewer than three hundred,

for three hundred or more,

those with five thousand or more established three Xiāng;

one Shǐ and

Each Xiàn generally appointed one Lǐlì for every one hundred households.

For one thousand households or more,

Yè and Cháng'ān appointed officials according to the system for Xiàn with three thousand or more households.
The four Zhōnglángjiàng
were established by the Later Hàn dynasty,
and their positions existed through Wèi and Jìn dynasties,

becoming even more important during the Jiāngzuǒ period.
Concerning the Hù Qiāng, Yí, Mán, etc., Xiàowèi:
It is recorded that Emperor Wǔ established the Nánmán Xiàowèi in Xiāngyáng,
the Xīróng Xiàowèi in Cháng'ān,

During the Yuánkāng era,

At the beginning of the Jiāngzuǒ period,

Concerning the Hù Xiōngnú, Qiāng, Róng, Mán, Yí, Yuè Zhōnglángjiàng:
It is recorded that Emperor Wǔ established four Zhōnglángjiàng,
some of whom also held the title of Cìshǐ,
or wielded imperial authority (Chíjǐe) as such.
Emperor Wǔ also established the Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng,
residing in Guǎngzhōu,
primarily responsible for protecting the Nányuè.

"A ruler of a state (guójūn) does not ride a strange chariot (qíchē)."
A strange chariot (qíchē) is also a hunting chariot (lièchē).
In antiquity, the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) would ride a wooden chariot (mùlù) for hunts;
later generations replaced it with a hunting chariot (lièchē).)
The traveling chariot (yóuchē),
nine in number,
drawn by four horses,
was the chariot used as the vanguard.
The 'cloud banner chariot' (yúnhǎnchē),
drawn by four horses.
The 'leather canopy chariot' (píxuānchē),
drawn by four horses,
had its canopy (xuān) made of animal hide.
The 'phoenix banner chariot' (luánqíchē),
drawn by four horses,
was carried in front of the imperial carriage (lù).
The 'phoenix banner' (luánqí)
refers to feathers and yak tails (máozāo) split and woven,
then arranged and tied to the sides of banners.
The 'adorned chariot' (jiànhuáchē),
drawn by four horses,
consisted of two chariots in total,
which, when in motion, positioned themselves to the left and right.
The light chariot (qīngchē),
drawn by two horses,
was the war chariot of antiquity.
There were twenty chariots in total, positioned
to the left and right.
The body and wheels were entirely vermilion,
without covering or canopy.
Spears (máo), halberds (jǐ), pennants (huī), and banners (chuáng) were erected,
and crossbows (nǔ) and quivers (fú) were placed on the armrest (shì).
When the grand imperial carriage (dàjià) and ceremonial carriage (fǎjià) were dispatched,
the Shooting Sounds Commander (Shèshēng Xiàowèi), Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ), officers (lìshì), and warriors (zhànshì) rode them,
as a sequence of attendant chariots (shǔchē).
The 'South-pointing Chariot' (sīnánchē),
also called the 'chariot pointing south' (zhǐnánchē),
was drawn by four horses.
Its lower part was constructed like a pavilion,
with three tiers.
At its four corners, golden dragons (jīnlóng) held feathered decorations (yǔbǎo) in their mouths.
Carved wooden immortals (xiānrén)
wearing feathered cloaks (yǔyī)
stood on the chariot.
Even if the chariot turned, their hands always pointed south.
When the grand imperial carriage (dàjià) traveled,
it served as the leading chariot.
The 'mile-drum chariot' (jìlǐgǔchē),
drawn by four horses,
was similar in form to the South-pointing Chariot (sīnán).
Inside, there was a wooden figure holding a mallet towards a drum.
For every li (lǐ) traveled, it would strike the drum once.
The 'goat chariot' (yángchē),
also called the 'hand-pulled chariot' (niǎnchē),
had its upper part resembling a small chariot (yáo).
It had a 'crouching rabbit' box (fútùxiāng)
and lacquered and painted wheels (lún) and yokes (è).
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì),
the Commander of the Guards (Hùjūn), Yáng Xiù (Yáng Xiù), sometimes rode a goat chariot (yángchē).
The Director of Retainers (Sīlì), Liú Yì (Liú Yì), impeached him for this offense.
The 'painted wheel chariot' (huàlúnchē),
drawn by oxen,
had its wheel hubs (lúngǔ) painted with colored lacquer,
hence its name 'painted wheel chariot' (huàlúnchē).
Above, four standing staffs were erected,
with four open viewing windows on the left and right,
a green oiled canopy (yóuchuáng),
red silk cords (zhūsīluò),
and green crisscrossing patterns (qīngjiāolù).
Its upper structure resembled a hand-pulled chariot (niǎn) in every respect,
but its lower part was just like a calf cart (dúchē).
In antiquity, the noble did not ride ox carts (niúchē).
Towards the end of Emperor Wǔ's (Hàn Wǔdì) benevolent policies (tuīēn),
the feudal lords (zhūhóu) became weak and few.
The poor even rode ox carts (niúchē),
and thereafter, they gradually came to be considered noble.
From the time of Emperors Líng (Líng) and Xiàn (Xiàn) onwards,
it became a common vehicle for everyone from the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) to scholars (shì).
The most revered even rode it when leaving the imperial court (cháotáng) to express grief.
The attendant chariots (shǔchē)
were also called 'secondary chariots' (fùchē),
or 'auxiliary chariots' (èrchē),
or 'left chariots' (zuǒchē).
The Hàn (Hàn) dynasty followed the Qín (Qín) system.
The grand imperial carriage (dàjià) had eighty-one attendant chariots (shǔchē),
which, when in motion, divided into lines in the center, left, and right.
The ceremonial carriage (fǎjià) had thirty-six attendant chariots (shǔchē).
The last chariot had a leopard tail (bàowěi) suspended from it.
Before the leopard tail (bàowěi), the arrangement was comparable to the imperial palace (shěngzhōng).
All attendant chariots (shǔchē) had black canopies and vermilion awnings (zàogài zhūyuán).
The imperial clothing chariot (yùyīchē), imperial book chariot (yùshūchē), imperial small chariot (yùyáochē), and imperial medicine chariot (yùyàochē)
were all drawn by oxen.
The 'four-sided view fine-silk window black-wheeled small chariot' (yángsuí sìwàng suìchuāng zàolún xiǎoxíngchē)
was drawn by oxen.
The elephant chariot (xiàngchē)
was at the very front of the Hàn (Hàn) imperial procession (lǔbù).
After Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) pacified Wú (Wú) during the Tàikāng (Tàikāng) period,
Nányuè (Nányuè) presented trained elephants.
An imperial edict commanded the construction of large chariots to be drawn by them,
to carry dozens of imperial musicians (huángméngǔchuī).
Yuè (Yuè) people were made to ride them.
During the grand assembly on the first day of the year (yuánzhēng dàhuì),
the elephants were driven into the courtyard.

The Mica carriage,
a calf carriage decorated with mica.
Subordinates are not allowed to ride it;
it is granted only to princes and dukes.
The Black-Wheeled carriage,
drawn by four oxen,
its form is like that of a calf carriage,
but with black lacquered wheel hubs,
and a green oiled canopy added above,
with red silk ropes.
Princes and Three Gōng (三公) with meritorious deeds are specially granted this.
Those whose rank reaches Gōng (公) may have a Sìwàng (四望), Sānwàng (三望), or Jiāwàng (夾望) carriage.
The Oiled-Canopy carriage,
drawn by oxen,
its form is like the Black-Wheeled carriage,
but without lacquered hubs.
Princes, dukes, and high ministers with meritorious deeds are specially provided this.
The Tōngxiǎn (通幰) carriage,
drawn by oxen,
its structure is still like today's calf carriages,
but its canopy is raised to fully cover the top of the carriage.
All princes and Three Gōng (三公) ride this.
All Gōng (公) are granted one court carriage drawn by four horses, and one comfort carriage with black ears drawn by three horses,
and one black-wheeled calf carriage each.
From the Jìjiǔ Yuànshǔ (祭酒掾屬) downwards, including the Lìngshǐ (令史),
all wear black scarves
and court robes.
For military officials who are Gōng (公), a large carriage is additionally provided.

Those of special distinction, and those from the Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) and Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) downwards among the great generals who do not establish a staff and do not hold a credential to command,
are granted a comfort carriage with black ears drawn by two horses,
and one Yáo carriage with ears and a rear door.

The Sān Gōng (Three Dukes), Jiǔ Qīng (Nine Ministers), Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí (Central Two Thousand Piculs), Èr Qiān Shí (Two Thousand Piculs), Hénán Yǐn (Governor of Hénán), and Yèzhě Púyè (Attendant-in-ordinary to the Palace Usher)
used grand chariots (dàchē) with standing positions (lìchéng) when attending suburban sacrifices (jiāomiào) or the Mingtáng (Bright Hall),
a regulation.
They were pulled by four horses (jiàsì).
The escort vehicles (dǎocóng dàchē) accompanying them, front and back, were pulled by two horses (jià’èr),
with the right horse as a trace-horse (yòu fēi).
For other outings, they rode in comfortable carriages (ānchē).
When they retired from office due to old age,
they were granted an ānchē (comfortable carriage) with four horses.
Commandery and county dukes and marquises
rode in ānchē pulled by two horses,
with the right horse as a trace-horse.
All had vermilion painted wheels (zhū bān lún),
elbow-rests like deer horns (yǐ lù jiào),
a front board decorated with a crouching bear (fú xióng shì),
black curtains (hēi zī),
and a black silk canopy (zào zēng gài).
The banners (qíqí) of dukes had eight pennants (liú),
marquises seven pennants,
and ministers five pennants.
All were painted with descending dragons.
Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí and Èr Qiān Shí
all had black canopies,
vermilion mudguards on both sides (zhū liǎng fān),
bronze ornaments in five colors (tóng wǔ cǎi),
and were pulled by two horses.
Those of Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí rank and above
had the right horse as a trace-horse.
Qiān Shí (One Thousand Piculs) and Liù Bǎi Shí (Six Hundred Piculs)
had a vermilion left mudguard.
The carriage mudguards were six cùn long,
eight cùn wide at the bottom bend,
and one chi two cùn wide at the top edge,
nine zhàng (long overall),
twelve initial measurements,
with a one cùn recession at the rear,
like a waxing moon,
indicating they dared not be complacent.
The heir apparents (shìzǐ) of kings and dukes who governed on their behalf
rode in ānchē,
pulled by three horses.
Their banners had seven pennants,
while the heir apparents of enfeoffed marquises had five pennants.
In the fourth year of Tàikāng (283 CE),
a regulation was made:
"Following the precedent of the Hàn dynasty,
each of the Jiǔ Qīng shall be provided with one court chariot (cháochē) pulled by four horses and one ānchē."
In the eighth year (287 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"All Shàngshū (Secretaries) and military officers (jūnxiào) who concurrently hold the titles of Shìzhōng (Attendant-in-ordinary) or Chángshì (Regular Attendant)
shall be provided with light carriages (yáochē) for official errands (chuánshì chéng yáochē),
be given swords,
and be permitted to enter the palace hall and inner chambers,
ascending and descending with the attendants."
The Grand Envoy's chariot (dàshǐchē) was a standing carriage,
pulled by four horses,
with red curtains (chì wéishang),
and escorted by cavalry (zōu qí dǎocóng).
(In former times, Sān Gōng, Jiǔ Qīng, and Èr Qiān Shí used the dàshǐchē when attending suburban sacrifices and imperial tombs, or accompanying the emperor.
For other outings, they used ānchē.)
The Minor Envoy's chariot (xiǎoshǐchē) was not a standing carriage,
pulled by four horses,
and was a type of light chariot (qīngchē).
The Orchid carriage (lányú) was all vermilion,
with red hubs (chì gū),
red mudguards (chì píngní),
a white canopy,
and red curtains,
escorted by forty cavalry.
There was also another type of xiǎoshǐchē (Minor Envoy's chariot),
with red hubs and a black canopy,
used by those who pursued, captured, investigated, or seized.
All envoy chariots (shǐchē) had vermilion painted wheels
and red crossbars and yokes (chì héng'è).
The "Chasing the Vanguard" chariot (zhuīfēngchē)
removed the small flat canopy
and added a covering that extended on all sides (tōngxiǎn),
resembling a yáochē (light carriage),
pulled by two horses.
The name "Chasing the Vanguard"
was probably taken from its swiftness,
and when used in military formations,
it was called a chuánchéng (relay carriage).
The yáochē (light carriage)
was a military chariot in ancient times.
A yáochē pulled by one horse was called a yáochē;
by two horses, a yáochuán.
In the Hàn dynasty, the zīpíng (covered carriage) was esteemed and the yáochē was disdained.
In the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, the yáochē was esteemed and the zīpíng was disdained.
Generals of the third rank and above, and the Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat), used yáochē with black "ears" (covered sides) and a rear door (hòuhù).
The Púyè (Grand Assistant) had only a rear door but no "ears,"
and both had black wheels.
Shàngshū (Secretaries) and generals of the fourth rank had no rear door
and had lacquered hubs and wheels.
The Zhōngshū Jiān (Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary) and Lìng (Director), Shìzhōng (Attendants-in-ordinary), Huángmén (Palace Gatekeepers), and Sànqí (Mounted Attendants)
were also permitted to ride in them
when first appointed or when visiting imperial tombs and temples.
The formal carriage (fǎjià) of the Empress Dowager and Empress
was the heavy-pheasant-feather-canopied golden-root chariot (zhòng dí yǔ gài jīn gēn chē),
pulled by a blue chariot (qīng lù),
with blue curtains,
cloud-painted shafts (yún huà yuán),
and gold-plated in five colors.
The canopy claws (gài zhuǎ) were adorned with golden flowers,
pulled by three horses,
with trace-horses on the left and right (zuǒyòu fēi).
For the lesser formal carriage (xiǎojià) used for ancestral temple visits,
they rode in a purple felt covered carriage (zǐ jì píngchē),
with cloud-painted shafts,
gold-plated in five colors,
pulled by three horses.
When not using the formal carriage, the Empress Dowager rode in a palanquin (niǎn),
and the Empress rode in a painted-wheel carriage (huà lún chē).
When the Empress offered the first silk cocoons,
she rode in an oil-painted mica ānchē (comfortable carriage),
pulled by six dappled horses (guīmǎ).
(Guī
means light black.)
An oil-painted two-shaft ānchē,
pulled by five dappled horses,
served as a副 (deputy/secondary carriage).
Also,
a gold-leaf stone-mountain covered carriage (jīn bó shí shān píng) and a purple-crimson felt covered carriage (zǐ jiàng jì píngchē)
were both pulled by three dappled horses
as deputy carriages.
Twelve female attendants holding yak-tail standards (nǚ máotóu),
two holding halberds (chí qǐ jí),
collectively rode in an ānchē,
drawn by a matched pair (lìjià).
Twelve female palanquin bearers (nǚ shàng niǎn)
rode in a covered carriage (zīchē),
drawn by a matched pair.
Eight female high-ranking attendants (nǚ chángyù)
rode in an ānchē,
drawn by a matched pair.
The Sān Fūrén (Three Ladies) used oil covered carriages (yóu píngchē),
pulled by two horses,
with the left horse as a trace-horse.
The Guìrén (Honored Ladies) rode in carriages with decorated shafts.
When the Sān Fūrén assisted in sericulture,
they rode in blue interlaced carriages (qīng jiāolù) or ānchē,
pulled by three horses.
All used purple-crimson felt covered carriages.
The Jiǔ Pín (Nine Concubines) and Shìfù (Court Ladies) rode in covered carriages,
pulled by three horses.
The Elder Princesses (Chánggōngzhǔ) used red felt covered carriages,
pulled by two horses.
Princesses (Gōngzhǔ), Queens Dowager (Wáng Tàifēi), and Princess Consorts (Wáng Fēi)
all used oil covered carriages,
pulled by two horses,
with the right horse as a trace-horse.
Princesses used oil-painted ānchē,
pulled by three horses,
blue interlaced carriages,
with a purple-crimson felt covered carriage pulled by three horses as a deputy,
and Queens Dowager and Sān Fūrén also did likewise.
When Princesses assisted in sericulture,
they rode in oil-painted ānchē,
pulled by three horses.
Princesses who had already been designated to marry (yǒu xiānzhì zhě)
rode in blue interlaced ānchē,
pulled by three horses.

The Princess Consorts (Wáng Fēi), Grand Ladies of Dukes (Gōng Tàifūrén), Ladies (Fūrén), Commandery and County Ladies (Xiàn Xiāng Jūn), and the wives of commandery and county dukes and marquises who held the rank of Tèjìn (Special Advance) and assisted in sericulture,
rode in black interlaced ānchē,
pulled by three horses.
The court ladies (shìfù) of the heir apparents of kings who supervised the state,

and the court ladies (shìfù) and noble wives (mìngfù) of Shìzhōng (Attendants-in-ordinary), Chángshì (Regular Attendants), Shàngshū (Secretaries), Zhōngshū Jiān (Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary), Lìng (Director), Qīng (Ministers), and Xiào (Officers) who assisted in sericulture,
rode in black interlaced ānchē,
drawn by a matched pair.
The wives of commandery and county dukes and marquises, Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí, and Èr Qiān Shí, when attending court or assisting in sericulture,
each rode in their husband's ānchē.
All had the right horse as a trace-horse,
black interlaced carriages,
and black curtains.
Unless it was for a public gathering,
they were not permitted to ride in yáochē,
only in lacquered cloth covered carriages (qī bù zī píng)
with bronze ornaments in five colors.
Princess Consorts (Wáng Fēi), Tèjìn Fūrén (Special Advance Ladies), and enfeoffed Commandery Ladies (Fēng Jùn Jūn)
rode in ānchē,
pulled by three horses,
black interlaced carriages.
Enfeoffed County and Township Ladies (Fēng Xiàn Xiāng Jūn) used oil covered carriages,
pulled by two horses,
with the right horse as a trace-horse.
Since crossing the Yangtze River,
many old regulations have been missing.
When Yuán Dì ascended the throne,
he first had one Dàlù and one Rónglù made,
both following the ancient Jīngēn system,
without the elaborate court displays of old.
As for important events like suburban sacrifices,
other carriages were temporarily adorned to serve the purpose.
When the six armies personally went on campaign, the Rónglù was used;
its canopy was removed, and it was ridden.
There were only five attendant carriages.
It was fitted with a green oil canopy,
a red silk bridle,
decorated with blue cross-straps,
and gilded with five colors,
but its wheels and hubs remained plain,
and the two sides lacked gold brocade decorations.
One of these carriages was also a Yáochē.
According to old customs,
the Son of Heaven’s carriage was drawn by six horses.
At this time, there were no longer carriages drawn by six horses;
all five types of carriages were drawn by four horses,
all using black horses,
which were called Xuánmǔ.
The carriages for the five seasons no longer existed.
When needed, horse-drawn carriages were temporarily used in their place,
with banners erected on them.
Later, only five-colored wooden oxen were used to represent the five-season carriages,
with banners erected on the oxen's backs.
When moving, people would carry them.
The meaning behind using oxen
was probably that they are stable and secure in carrying heavy loads and traveling long distances.
The flags were usually wrapped and not unfurled,
which was called "Déchē jiéjīng".
Only when the Son of Heaven personally went on campaign were the five flags unfurled,
which was called "Wǔchē suíjīng".
The Zhǐnánchē
was lost after crossing the Yangtze.
In the fifth year of Yìxī
when Liú Yù
massacred Guǎnggù,
it was finally recovered.
He then had the artisan Zhāng Gāng repair and restore it for use.
In the thirteenth year,
Liú Yù pacified Guānzhōng,
and also recovered the Sīnán and Jìlǐ carriages,
and the system was finally complete.
As for the niǎn (imperial litter),
its system was also lost after crossing the Yangtze.
During the Tàiyuán era, Xiè Ān
made one according to his own ideas.
When Fú Jiān was defeated at Huáinán,
the old imperial litter from the capital was recovered.
Its form and design were identical,
and its size was the same,
which people at the time praised for his precise memory.
In the fifth year of Yìxī,
when Liú Yù captured Mùróng Chāo,
the Jīnzhēng niǎn and leopard tails were recovered,
and the old style still survived.
In the third year of Tàixīng of Yuán Dì,
the Crown Prince performed the Shìdiàn ceremony.
A decree stated:
"As it is a new beginning,
there is no Gāochē yet; an Ānchē may be used."
During the Tàiyuán era,
when the Eastern Palace was established,
there were blue and red banners on the carriage used for the procession,
causing doubt.
Xú Miǎo deliberated,
and since the Crown Prince did not have all five types of carriages,
the red banner should be removed.
According to the Hàn system,
the Crown Prince’s luánlù were all called Ānchē.
Since the Jìn crossed the Yangtze,
the rites and ceremonies have been disorderly and inconsistent.
From princes and dukes downwards,
their carriages and attire were humble and mixed.
Only the Eastern Palace’s ritual status was elevated and distinct,
ranking above the stars,
and including marquises and kings below.
However, Ān Dì, when he was Crown Prince, rode a Shíshān Ānchē,
whose design was like the Jīnlù.
This was not seen in the classics,
and had no precedent.
When the Empress's palace was first established and during the sacrifice to the first silkworm goddess,
the Fǎjià was used.
The Tàipú’s wife served as charioteer,
the Dàjiāngjūn’s wife rode as attendant,
the Shìzhōng’s wife as a secondary attendant,
while the wives of the Dānyáng Yǐn, Jiànkāng Lìng, and high officials and nobles led the procession.
Each rode in her husband’s carriage and attire,
and often palace women were temporarily assigned to these roles.
According to the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
the Biànshī was in charge of the six kinds of miǎn,
and the Sīfú was in charge of the six kinds of robes.
From the regulations of the empresses and kings down to the common people,
〔一七〕there were different grades.
When the Qín dynasty changed the ancient system,
the robes for suburban sacrifices were all in dark uniform,
and the old laws were completely swept away.
The Hàn dynasty inherited the failings of Qín,
and for over two hundred years in the Western Capital, they were still unable to establish anything.
After the restoration,
Emperor Míng then began to draw upon the *Zhōu Guān*, *Lǐ Jì*, *Shàngshū*, and the records and interpretations of various Confucians,
and thus restored the *gǔnmiǎn* robes.
The Son of Heaven's carriages, rides, hats, and robes followed the interpretations of the Ōuyáng clan.
From the gōng and qīng downwards, they followed the interpretations of the Elder and Younger Xiàhóu clans.
They first established the robes for the Son of Heaven, the Sāngōng, the Jiǔqīng, and the Tèjìn.
Those attending sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the Míngtáng,
〔一八〕all wore *liúmiǎn* crowns,
combining the system of the five *miǎn*,
into a single type of attire.
The Son of Heaven was adorned with twelve symbols,
the Sāngōng and zhūhóu used nine symbols, including mountains and dragons,
and from the Jiǔqīng downwards, they used seven symbols, including flowery insects.
All were made with five colors.
Emperor Míng of Wèi, considering the *gǔnyī* of the gōng and qīng with their *fǔfú* decorations
to be too similar to the Supreme Sovereign,
made many reductions.
He first ordained that the Son of Heaven's robes should have embroidered patterns,
and the gōng and qīng's robes should have woven patterns.
When the Jìn dynasty received the mandate,
they followed this without change.
When the Son of Heaven performed suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and visited the Míngtáng and ancestral temples,
or held grand assemblies from the imperial veranda,
he wore a black *jièzé*,
〔一九〕a *Tōngtiān* crown,
and a flat *miǎn*.
The *miǎn*
was black on the outside
with red and green lining,
seven cùn wide,
and two chǐ two cùn long.
〔二０〕It was placed on top of the *Tōngtiān* crown,
round in front and square at the back,
with white jade beads hanging down,
forming twelve *liú*,
with a red silk cord for the chin strap,
and no streamers.
He wore a white jade pendant,
with hanging yellow and large *liú* pearls,
and a yellow, red, light blue, and dark blue four-colored sash.
The upper garment was black,
the lower garment scarlet,
three panels in front,
and four panels at the back.
The upper garment was painted and the lower garment embroidered,
with images of the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, flowery insects, algae, fire, white rice, *fǔ*, and *fú*,
in total twelve symbols.
The plain belt was four cùn wide,
with a red lining,
and its sides were adorned with red and green embroidery.
The inner garment was edged with scarlet on its collar and sleeves.
A red leather *fú* was worn,
scarlet trousers and socks,
and red *xī* shoes.
Those who had not yet undergone the capping ceremony wore
an open-topped *jièzé*.
For the ceremony of "spreading the mat" for the Former Sages,
he wore a black gauze robe,
an inner garment with scarlet trim,
scarlet trousers and socks,
and black *xī* shoes.
When presiding from the imperial veranda,
it was also the *gǔnmiǎn*.
For court attire,
the *Tōngtiān* crown was nine cùn high,
with a golden *Bóshān* decoration in front,
a black *jièzé*,
a scarlet gauze robe,
and an inner garment with black trim.
When performing ancestral rites at the imperial tombs,
he wore a black *jièzé*
and a plain unlined robe.
His miscellaneous attire
included blue, red, yellow, white, light yellow, and black colors,
a *jièzé*,
five-colored gauze robes,
a five-beamed *Jìnxián* crown,
a *Yuǎnyóu* crown,
and a flat-topped *zéwǔ* crown.
His plain attire
was a white unlined robe.
Since the Later Hàn,
the Son of Heaven's *miǎn*
used real white jade beads for the front and back *liú*.
Emperor Míng of Wèi, fond of women's adornments,
changed them to coral beads.
In the early Jìn, the old practice remained unchanged.
However, after crossing the river,
many parts of the attire and insignia were lacking,
and the *miǎn* was adorned with kingfisher feathers, coral, and various pearls.
Shìzhōng Gù Hé memorialized:
"According to the old rites,
the *miǎn* has twelve *liú*,
using white jade beads.
As beautiful jade is difficult to obtain now,
and cannot be fully provided,
white *xuánzhū* pearls can be used."
This was adopted.
The *Tōngtiān* crown
was originally a Qín system.
It was nine cùn high,
stood straight,
with the top slightly slanted backward,
then went straight down.
It had an iron coiled beam,
a projecting cylindrical front,
and a golden *Bóshānshù* added to the front of the crown.
It was usually worn by the emperor.
The flat *miǎn*
was worn by kings, dukes, and qíng assisting in sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples.
Kings and dukes had eight *liú*,
and qíng had seven *liú*.
The chin strap was made of silk cord,
its color matching their sash.
Kings and dukes wore nine symbols, including mountains and dragons,
and qíng wore seven symbols, including flowery insects.
The *Yuǎnyóu* crown,
Fù Xuán said, was a Qín crown.
It was similar to the *Tōngtiān* but without the front mountain decoration,
and had a projecting cylindrical front horizontally across the crown.
The Crown Prince, descendants of kings, brothers of the emperor, and sons of the emperor enfeoffed as kings of commanderies wore it.
Kings who held additional official posts wore the crown and robes appropriate to their office,
but only the Crown Prince and descendants of kings consistently wore this crown.
The Crown Prince wore kingfisher feathers for the streamers,
adorned with white pearls,
while others merely used green silk.
The black cloth crown,
Cài Yōng said, was the *Wěimào* crown.
In ancient times, caps were made of cloth,
and when purified, they were dyed black.
The black cloth crown
was the crown first worn at the capping ceremony.
Its design had four shapes:
one resembled the *Wǔguān*,
another resembled the *Jìnxián*,
one was square at the top
and shaped like a headband front at the bottom;
the other was pointed at the top and square at the bottom.
When performing the communal archery ritual, the gōng and qīng wore the *Wěimào* crown,
made of black silk.
Its shape was like an inverted cup,
of the same design as the *Píbiàn*,
seven cùn long,
and four cùn high.
The upper garment was black and the lower garment plain,
with the inner garment having black trim on its collar and sleeves.
Those in attendance wore the *Píbiàn*,
made of deerskin.
The *Jìnxián* crown
was an ancient remnant of the black cloth crown,
and was probably the attire of literary scholars.
It was seven cùn high in front,
three cùn high at the back,
and eight cùn long.
It had five beams, three beams, two beams, or one beam.
When the sovereign underwent the capping ceremony,
and first wore the black cloth,
he wore the five-beamed *Jìnxián* crown.
The Sāngōng and those enfeoffed as dukes of commanderies, dukes of counties, marquises of commanderies, marquises of counties, and marquises of xiāng or tíng
wore the three-beamed crown.
Qíng, dàfū, the Bāzuò, the Shàngshū,
inner marquises of Guānzhōng, officials of two thousand *dàn* and above one thousand *dàn*
wore the two-beamed crown.
Zhōngshū Láng, Mìshū Chéngláng, Zhùzuò Láng, Shàngshū Chéngláng, Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ Shèrén, officials of six hundred *dàn* and below, down to lìshǐ and ménláng, xiǎoshǐ,
all wore the one-beamed crown.
In the middle of Jiànchū era of Hàn,
the Tàiguān Lìng wore a two-beamed crown,
due to the importance of personally inspecting the imperial meals.
Bóshì wore two beams,
to honor scholars.
Members of the imperial clan, the Liú family, also received two-beamed crowns,
to show their elevated status.
The Wǔguān (武冠),
also known as Wǔbiàn (武弁),
also known as Dàguān (大冠),
also known as Fánguān (繁冠),
also known as Jiànguān (建冠),
also known as Lóngguān (籠冠),
is the ancient Huìwén Guān (惠文冠).
Some say it was created by King Zhào Huìwén (趙惠文王),
hence its name.
It is also said
that Huì (惠) here means huì (蟪, cicada),
as its pattern was light and delicate like cicada wings,
thus named Huìwén (惠文).
Others say
that people of Qí (齊) saw the spirit of a thousand-year-dry marsh,
named Qìngjì (慶忌),
who wore a Dàguān (大冠),
rode a small carriage,
and enjoyed speeding;
thus, they emulated its cap and wore it.
When Hànyuán Hóngrú (閎孺), a favored minister of Hàn, became a Shìzhōng (侍中),
all wore the Dàguān (大冠).
The Son of Heaven's (Tiānzǐ) regular attire also first included the Dàguān (大冠);
attendant ministers on the left and right, as well as various generals and military officials, all wore it.
Shìzhōng (侍中) and Chángshì (常侍) would add a gold pendant (jīn dāng),
adorned with cicadas (fù chán),
and inserted with sable (diāo) fur,
with a golden rod (huángjīn gān).
Shìzhōng (侍中) inserted it on the left,
and Chángshì (常侍) on the right.
Hú Guǎng (胡廣) said:
"In the past, King Zhào Wǔlíng (趙武靈王) adopted Hú (胡) attire,
decorating his head with gold sable (jīn diāo).
When Qín (秦) destroyed Zhào (趙),
they bestowed its ruler's cap upon attendant ministers."
Yìng Shào's (應劭) Hàn Guān (漢官) states:
"Commentators believe that gold symbolizes strength,
as it does not diminish after a hundred refinements.
The cicada dwells high and drinks pure (dew),
with its mouth under its armpit.
The sable is fierce internally but soft and supple externally."
Also, the cicada is valued for its purity and high dwelling, drinking dew without eating;
the sable for its purple-green softness and moistness, with its fur not being ostentatious;
and gold for its precious gleam.
Each of these had a symbolic meaning.
Some believe that the northern lands are often cold,
and Hú (胡) people commonly used sable fur to warm their foreheads;
later generations imitated this,
and thus attached it to their caps.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the sable used was reddish-black;
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) used yellow sable,
each being attached according to the preferred color of their attire.
The Gāoshān Guān (高山冠),
also known as Cèzhù (側注),
was nine cùn (寸) high,
with an iron coiled beam (juǎliáng),
its form similar to the Tōngtiān (通天) cap.
Its top stood straight up,
not leaning back,
and lacked the mountain-shaped ridge (shānshù) and projecting tube (zhǎntǒng).
Gāoshān (高山, high mountain) refers to the verse from Shī (詩, Book of Odes),
"Gāoshān Yǎngzhǐ (高山仰止, high mountains are looked up to),"
signifying solemnity and respect for distant ones.
It was worn by internal and external officials, Yèzhě (謁者), and Yèzhě Púshè (謁者僕射).
[二一] Hú Guǎng (胡廣) said:
"Gāoshān (高山)
was the cap of the King of Qí (齊).
The legends say, 'Duke Huán (桓公) loved high caps and broad belts.'
When Qín (秦) destroyed Qí (齊),
they bestowed its ruler's cap upon the Yèzhě (謁者) and close ministers."
Yìng Shào (應劭) said:
"The Gāoshān (高山)
is today's Fǎguān (法冠);
Qín (秦) envoys and officials also wore it."
However, the Hàn Guān Yí (漢官儀) states
that "the Emperor (Chéngyú) wore the Gāoshān Guān (高山之冠)
with a Fēihé Zhī Yīng (飛翮之纓, flying feather tassel),"
implying that the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) also occasionally wore it.
Fù Zǐ (傅子) said:
"Emperor Míng (明帝) of Wèi (魏), seeing its design resembled the Tōngtiān (通天) and Yuǎnyóu (遠游) caps,
therefore ordered it to be made lower."
The Fǎguān (法冠),
also known as Zhùhòu (柱後),
or Xièzhì Guān (獬豸冠).
It was five cùn (寸) high,
made with silk ribbon (xǐ) for the projecting tube (zhǎntǒng).
Iron was used for the coiled pillar (zhùjuǎn),
symbolizing its inflexibility.
Shìyùshǐ (侍御史), Tíngwèi Zhèngjiānpíng (廷尉正監平),
and all law enforcement officials wore it.
Some say the Xièzhì (獬豸) is a divine ram,
capable of butting evil and corrupt individuals.
The Yìwù Zhì (異物志) states:
"In the northern wilderness,
there is a beast named Xièzhì (獬豸),
with a single horn,
whose nature is to discern right from wrong.
When it sees people fighting,
it butts the one who is in the wrong.
When it hears people arguing,
it bites the one who is unjust.
The King of Chǔ (楚王) once captured this beast,
and thus emulated its form to create garments and caps."
Hú Guǎng (胡廣) said:
"In the Zuǒshì Zhuàn (左氏傳) of Chūnqiū (春秋), when Lord Jìn (晉侯) observed the military arsenal,
he saw Zhōng Yí (鍾儀) and said,
'Who is that person wearing a southern cap and bound?'
The southern cap was the Chǔ (楚) cap.
When Qín (秦) destroyed Chǔ (楚),
they bestowed its cap and attire upon law enforcement officials."
The Chángguān (長冠),
also known as Qíguān (齊冠).
It was seven cùn (寸) high,
three cùn (寸) wide,
made of lacquered silk ribbon (qīxǐ),
its shape like a plank,
with a bamboo frame (zhúwǔ).
When Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖) was a commoner,
he made this cap from bamboo bark,
and his family thus called it the Liú (劉) family cap.
Later, bamboo was replaced with lacquered silk ribbon (qīxǐ).
Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪) said:
"The Chángguān (長冠) is probably a Chǔ (楚) design.
People sometimes call it the Quèwěi Guān (鵲尾冠, Magpie Tail Cap),
which is incorrect.
During a solar eclipse rescue ritual, the Chángguān (長冠) was worn,
and it was also worn during sacrifices at ancestral temples and other rituals.
This cap, created by Gāozǔ (高祖),
was later used as sacrificial attire,
showing the utmost reverence."
The Jiànhuá Guān (建華冠),
had an iron coiled pillar (zhùjuǎn),
threaded with nine large copper beads.
In ancient times, assorted wooden beads were used;
the Huáguān (華冠) worn by Yuán Xiàn (原憲) was of this type.
Also, the Zuǒshì Zhuàn (左氏傳) of Chūnqiū (春秋) mentions that Zǐzāng (子臧) of Zhèng (鄭) liked to collect jǔguān (鷸冠),
which refers to the Jiànhuá (建華).
During sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the five altars (wǔjiāo), and the Míngtáng (明堂),
dancers wore it.
It was worn by the Yù Mìng (育命) dancers and musicians during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Fāngshān Guān (方山冠),
its design resembled the Jìnxián (進賢) cap.
Dèng Zhǎn (鄧展) said:
"The Fāngshān Guān (方山冠)
was made of five-colored gauze (wǔcǎi gǔ)."
It was worn by the Dàyǔ (大予), Bāyì (八佾), and Wǔxíng (五行) musicians of the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
their caps and robes matched the colors of their respective directions as they danced.
The Qiǎoshì Guān (巧士冠),
was seven cùn (寸) high at the front,
connecting at the waist and back,
standing straight up.
This cap was not commonly used;
the Hàn (漢) dynasty only wore it when sacrificing to Heaven at the suburban altar (jiāotiān),
with four Huángmén Cóngguān (黃門從官) wearing it;
in the imperial procession (lǔbù),
they stood beside the Emperor's (Chéngyú) chariot,
to represent the four stars of the eunuchs (huànzhě sìxīng).
Some say
it was worn by the sweeping attendant officials.
The Quèfēi Guān (却非冠),
was five cùn (寸) high,
its design similar to the Chángguān (長冠).
Palace gate officials and Púshè (僕射) wore it.
They carried red banners,
with blue wings and swallow tails;
all Púshè (僕射) banners were like this.
The Quèdí Guān (却敵冠),
was four cùn (寸) high at the front,
four cùn (寸) long in total,
three cùn (寸) high at the back,
its design similar to the Jìnxián (進賢) cap.
All palace gate guards wore it.
The Fánkuài Guān (樊噲冠),
was nine cùn (寸) wide,
seven cùn (寸) high,
protruding four cùn (寸) at the front and back,
its design similar to the Píngmiǎn (平冕).
In the past, when Chǔ (楚) and Hàn (漢) met at Hóngmén (鴻門),
Xiàng Jí (項籍) plotted to endanger Gāozǔ (高祖).
Fán Kuài (樊噲) always carried an iron shield;
hearing of the urgency,
he tore his robe to wrap the shield,
wore it as a cap,
pushed his way into Yǔ's (羽) camp,
and then enumerated Yǔ's (羽) crimes,
allowing King Hàn (漢王) to escape in the interim.
Later generations admired his spirit,
and thus created a cap in its likeness.
All palace gate Sīmǎ (司馬) and guards wore it.
The Shùshì Guān (術氏冠),
was round in the front,
a Wú (吳) design,
with four staggered layers.
King Zhào Wǔlíng (趙武靈王) liked to wear it.
Some say
it was the cap worn by King Chǔ Zhuāng (楚莊王) for revenge.
The Héguan,
has a double héguan tail added,
inserted vertically on both sides.
Hé
is the name of a bird,
similar in shape to a kestrel but slightly darker,
with a fierce and courageous nature.
Its fights only cease upon death.
Shàngdǎng offered it as tribute,
and Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng used it to signify brave warriors.
Up to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
it was still worn by military men.
The Píbìan
was made from light-haired, yellowish-white deerskin.
The Rítu
states, "The king wears the píbìan,
adorned with five-colored jade,
with a xiàngdǐ yùjī,"
which refers to a cap made of joined leather.
[二二] The seam in the middle is called Huì,
and it is made of colorful jade zhu. Zhū,
means "to knot."
The Son of Heaven wears five colors,
and the feudal lords wear three colors.
(Dǐ
is the base beneath the cap,
made of ivory,
pronounced dì.)
The Son of Heaven's cap has twelve seams,
a gōng's has nine,
a hóubó's seven,
a zǐnán's five,
a gū's four,
and a qīngdàfū's three.
The Wéibiàn
is similar in style to the píbìan,
pointed at the top,
dyed with mào grass,
its color like a light crimson.
The Juébìan
is also known as Guǎngmiǎn.
It is eight cùn high
and one chǐ two cùn long,
[二三] shaped like a jué,
smaller in the front and larger in the back.
Its upper part is augmented to resemble the color of a jué's head.
It has a shōu to hold the jī,
which is what is called Xiàshōu Yīnxū.
Those who perform the Yúnqiáo dance and music at the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the Five Suburbs, and the Míngtáng,
wear it.
[二四]
The Zé
was the headwear of commoners in ancient times who did not wear crowns.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn had thick hair,
and he was the first to adopt the zé.
Wáng Mǎng was bald,
so he added a roof to it.
A Hàn commentary states:
"A Guān Jìnxián should have long ears,
now it is the Jièzé.
A Guān Huìwén should have short ears,
now it is the Píngshàngzé."
At first, each followed what was suitable,
and consequently, the caps became distinct.
The Jièzé was worn by civil officials,
and the Píngshàngzé by military officials.
A child's zé had no roof,
indicating that they were not yet adults.
There was also the Nàyánzé,
which had an additional layer at the back of the zé,
three cùn square.
There was also the Chìzé,
worn by cavalry officers, military officers, and those in the imperial retinue with drums and wind instruments.
During a solar eclipse,
