all civil and military officials would remove their caps and wear zé,
accompanying their court attire,
to display military might.
According to the Hàn rituals,
on Lìqiū, when hunting,
one wore a xiāngzé.
When it came to the Jiāngzuǒ,
Emperor Āi followed the deliberation of Bóshì Cáo Hóngzhī and others,
and when reciting the imperial decree on Lìqiū,
they changed to using plain white.
It is recorded that at the end of the Hàn dynasty, many princes and renowned scholars discarded royal attire,
considering the fújīn elegant.
Thus, people like Yuán Shào and Cuī Jūn,
even as generals,
all wore jiānjīn.
Wèi Wǔ, seeing the world in chaos and scarcity of resources,
modeled it after the ancient píbìan,
cutting silk to make
a tóujīn,
in line with the principle of simplicity and adapting to the times.
It distinguished their status by color,
originally used for military decoration,
not for state formality.
Xú Yuán said:
"Popular belief states that originally there was no qí.
When Xún Wénruò's jīn snagged on a tree branch, creating a qí,
it was deemed auspicious,
and thus it was not changed."
Today, it is commonly worn for celebrations and mourning.
The Jīn
was made of kudzu,
shaped like a tóujīn and worn horizontally.
In ancient times, both high and low status people wore it.
Thus, at the end of the Hàn dynasty, rebel bandits wore yellow jīn,
and the world called them Huángjīn Zéi.
The name Mào is like guān,
its meaning derived from covering the head.
Its original form was the sī.
In ancient times, guān had no zé,
but under the guān was a sī,
made of silk.
Later generations applied the zé to the guān,
and sometimes cut the sī to make a mào.
From the emperor in his private residence
down to commoners without rank, all wore it.
In the ninth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng,
it was decreed that Shàngshū bāzuò chéngláng and Ménxià sānshěng shìguān were allowed to ride in carriages,
[二五] with white low curtains,
entering and exiting the yèmén.
Also,
the Zhíguān of the two palaces wore wūshā tóujīn.
Then, scholars often wore them in their private residences.
And in the Jiāngzuǒ era, commoners already wore mào,
and scholars often did so as well,
but their tops were round,
and later the roof was raised.
According to Hàn regulations,
from the Son of Heaven to all officials,
none did not wear a sword.
Later, only those in court wore swords with their belts.
In the Jìn dynasty, it was initially replaced by wood,
with nobles still using jade pommels,
and commoners also using horn, gold, silver, and tortoiseshell for carving and decoration.
The Imperial Six Seals
were a Qín system.
They were called
"Huángdì Xíngxǐ,"
"Huángdì Zhīxǐ,"
"Huángdì Xìnxǐ,"
"Tiānzǐ Xíngxǐ,"
"Tiānzǐ Zhīxǐ,"
"Tiānzǐ Xìnxǐ."
The Hàn followed Qín without change.
There was also the Qín Shǐhuáng Lántián Yùxǐ,
with a chīshòu handle,
which was outside the Six Seals,
inscribed with the words
"Shòu Tiān Zhī Mìng,
Huángdì Shòuchāng."
Hàn Gāozǔ wore it,
and later generations called it the Chuánguó Xǐ,
which, along with the Zhǎnbáishé Jiàn, was treasured by the emperor.
The Zhǎnbáishé Jiàn was burned in a fire in the imperial armory during Emperor Huì's time,
and was thus lost.
When Emperor Huái was captured by the Hú,
the Chuánguó Xǐ fell into the hands of Liú Cōng,
and later into Shí Lè's hands.
After Shí Jìlóng died,
and the Hú became chaotic,
it was returned to Jiāngnán during Emperor Mù's reign.
The Gédài
was the ancient Pándài,
also called Pángé.
All civil and military officials, governors, prefects, chief clerks, and magistrates, down to palace attendants, wore it.
Those with a Nángshòu,
[二六] would attach it to the gédài.
For military attire, a Píluòdài was used instead.
The Bāzuò Shàngshū wore Hèzǐ,
[二七] which was a lined pouch made of raw purple silk,
attached to the outside of the attire,
placed over the left shoulder.
In ancient times, Zhōu Gōng carried King Chéng on his back,
and this attire was prescribed,
and it is still used as court attire today.
Some say that in the Hàn dynasty, it was used to hold memorials for presentation,
carried on the back while walking,
but this is not certain.
The Chēqián Wǔbǎi
refers to a qīng's entourage,
where five hundred people formed one lǚ.
The Hàn dynasty unified the empire,
so they removed the "people" (人),
but retained the name.
The system of *kùzhě*
has an unknown origin.
In recent times, whenever the emperor personally went on military campaigns or there was a general alert inside and outside the capital, these were worn.
The clothing had no fixed color.
A black cap was worn,
adorned with a purple *biāo*.
The *biāo* was made of silk,
four *cùn* long
and one *cùn* wide.
A *luòdài* was worn at the waist in place of a *pán*.
Officials of the imperial household wore purple *biāo*,
while external officials wore crimson *biāo*.
There were also ceremonial military uniforms (*zǎnyán róngfú*) without *biāo* attached,
worn by all civil and military officials whether traveling or staying put.
For hunting and imperial tours,
only accompanying officials wore military uniforms with leather *pán*,
civil officials did not lower their cap tassels (*yīng*),
and military officials removed their caps.
According to Hàn regulations,
there were five suburban sacrifices (*wǔjiāo*) annually.
The emperor and those performing the duties each wore clothes corresponding to the color of the direction.
Officials not performing duties wore their regular crimson robes to attend.
Qín Jìng, the Secretariat Director (*Mìshūjiān*) of Wèi, said:
"The Hàn dynasty, following Qín,
changed the system of the six ceremonial caps (*liùmiǎn*),
and simply wore a black cap (*xuán’guān*) and crimson robes (*jiàngyī*)."
Since Wèi, these were called five-season court robes (*wǔshí cháofú*).
There were also four-season court robes (*sìshí cháofú*),
and simply court robes (*cháofú*).
From the Crown Prince (*Huángtàizǐ*) downwards, they were issued according to rank.
Although officials wore five-season court robes,
currently only four-season court robes are issued,
lacking the autumn attire.
They were replaced every three years.
Those who were granted seals and sashes (*yìnshòu*) but whose offices did not provide *pánnáng*
were permitted to make their own.
Those who were only granted seals but not sashes
were not permitted to wear sashes.
*Pán*
was an ancient system.
In the Hàn era, those who wore *pánnáng*
had them at their waist,
sometimes called *bàngnáng* (side pouch),
or *shòunáng* (sash pouch).
Thus, it was a purple pouch used to hold the sash.
Sometimes it was enclosed, sometimes loose,
each having its proper time.
As for the *hù* (tablet),
in ancient times, both nobles and commoners held *hù*.
If they had matters to attend to, they tucked it into their waist belt.
The so-called "scholars who tuck and hang" (*jìnshēn zhī shì*)
were those who tucked their *hù* and let their *shēndài* (sash belt) hang.
The hanging *shēn* was three *chǐ* long.
As for the *hù*,
if there were matters, they would write on it,
so a brush was always stuck in it.
Today's white brush (*báibǐ*) is its remnant.
Civil officials of the second rank in the Three Bureaus (*Sāntái*) and Five Ministries (*Wǔshěng*) wore them.
Princes (*Wáng*), Dukes (*Gōng*), Marquises (*Hóu*), Counts (*Bó*), Viscounts (*Zǐ*), Barons (*Nán*), Ministers (*Qīngyǐn*), and military officials did not wear them,
unless they were additionally assigned to an inner service position (*nèishì wèizhě*), then they wore them.
The *shǒubǎn* (hand tablet) is the ancient *hù*.
The Secretariat Director (*Shàngshūlìng*), Grand Astrologer (*Púyè*), and Imperial Secretary (*Shàngshū*) had a white brush at the top of their *shǒubǎn*,
wrapped in purple leather,
and called *hù*.
The Crown Prince (*Huángtàizǐ*) had a golden seal with a tortoise knob (*jīnxǐ guīniǔ*),
a vermilion and yellow sash (*zhūhuáng shòu*),
with four colors: red, yellow, dark blue, and deep purple.
He was issued five-season court robes,
a far-traveling cap (*yuǎnyóuguān*),
an armored headscarf (*jièzé*), and kingfisher feather tassels (*cuìruí*).
He wore *yúyù* jade,
and a hanging cord (*chuízǔ*).
He wore vermilion robes (*zhūyī*) with a crimson gauze collar (*jiàngshā bǒ*),
black-edged white gauze (*zàoyuán báishā*),
and his inner garment was a white curved-collar robe (*bái qǔlǐng*).
He carried a sword,
with a fire-pearl and plain hilt (*huǒzhū sùshǒu*).
He wore a leather belt (*gédài*),
with a jade hook (*yùgōu*) and beast-head *pánnáng*.
For major and minor assemblies, ancestral temple sacrifices, and court appearances on the first and fifteenth of the month, he wore court robes.
When regularly returning to the imperial palace (*shànggōng*), he wore vermilion robes.
When attending major imperial palace assemblies, he removed his sword and clogs (*xiè*) below the hall.
He also had a three-beamed advanced-scholar cap (*sānliáng jìnxiánguān*).
When attending sacrifices, he wore a flat ceremonial cap with nine strings of beads (*píngmiǎn jiǔliú*),
a ceremonial robe with nine patterns (*gǔnyī jiǔzhāng*),
a white gauze inner garment with crimson edges (*báishā jiàngyuán zhōngdān*),
crimson silk,
a painted and woven ceremonial belt (*cǎihuà zhīchéng gǔndài*),
a golden *bìxié* head,
a purple and green two-colored belt,
one painted wide-collar garment (*cǎihuà guǎnglǐng*) and one curved-collar garment (*qǔlǐng*) each,
and red clogs and crimson socks (*chìxiè jiàngwà*).
When lecturing,
he wore an armored headscarf (*jièzé*) and a single robe (*dānyī*);
when performing the *shìdiàn* ceremony (sacrifice to Confucius),
he wore a far-traveling cap (*yuǎnyóuguān*),
a black court robe (*xuán cháofú*),
a crimson-edged inner garment (*jiàngyuán zhōngdān*),
crimson trousers and socks (*jiàngkùwà*),
and black clogs (*xuánxiè*).
If he had not yet undergone the capping ceremony (*jiā yuánfú*),
then the Inner Attendant (*Zhōngshèrén*) would carry his ceremonial cap and follow,
and he would wear an armored headscarf (*jièzé*), a single robe, and a black robe.
[二八]
Princes (*Zhūwáng*) had golden seals with tortoise knobs (*jīnxǐ guīniǔ*),
vermilion sashes (*xūnzhū shòu*),
with four colors: vermilion, yellow, dark blue, and deep purple.
They had five-season court robes,
a far-traveling cap (*yuǎnyóuguān*) and an armored headscarf (*jièzé*).
They also had a three-beamed advanced-scholar cap (*sānliáng jìnxiánguān*).
They wore vermilion robes with crimson gauze collars and black edges (*zhūyī jiàngshā bǒ zàoyuán*),
and their inner garment was plain (*biǎo sù*).
They wore a leather belt (*gédài*),
black clogs (*hēixiè*),
a mountain-black jade pendant (*pèi shānxuányù*),
a hanging cord (*chuízǔ*),
and a great sash (*dàdài*).
If they were appointed to additional offices,
they wore the attire of that additional office.
When the Empress (*Huánghòu*) visited the temple,
her attire was black above and black below.
When personally engaged in sericulture (*qīncán*), it was blue above and dark blue below.
All were of the *shēnyī* style,
with concealed collars and sleeve edges trimmed with braid (*táo*).
Her head ornaments included a false chignon (*jiǎjì*),
and a *bùyáo* (trembling ornament),
which commoners called "pearl pines" (*zhūsōng*).
She wore hairpins (*zān*) and earrings (*ěr*).
The *bùyáo* was made of gold for the mountain-shaped top (*shāntí*),
threaded with white pearls for the intertwined branches.
It featured eight birds and nine flowers,
six beasts: bear (*xióng*), various beasts (*shòu*), [二九] red bear (*chìpí*), celestial deer (*tiānlù*), *bìxié*, and large southern mountain ram (*nánshān fēngdàtè*).
All the birds and beasts were adorned with kingfisher feathers,
with golden tops and white pearl pendants (*dāng*),
and encircled with kingfisher feathers to form flowers.
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng
an edict stated:
"Since Wèi, the empress's sericulture attire has all been embroidered,
which is not in accordance with ancient principles.
Now, plain blue attire should be worn,
and this should be made a permanent regulation."
Noble Consorts (*Guìrén*), Furen (*Fūrén*), and Guìpín (*Guìpín*)
were the three *Fūrén*.
All had golden seals with purple sashes (*jīnzhāng zǐshòu*).
The inscription on the seal read: "Seal of *Guìrén*, *Fūrén*, *Guìpín*."
They wore Khotanese jade (*yútiányù*).
Shúfēi (*Shúfēi*), Shúyuàn (*Shúyuàn*), Shúyí (*Shúyí*), Xiūhuá (*Xiūhuá*), Xiūróng (*Xiūróng*), Xiūyí (*Xiūyí*), Jiéyú (*Jiéyú*), Rónghuá (*Rónghuá*), Chōnghuá (*Chōnghuá*)
were the nine *Pín*.
They had silver seals with green sashes (*yínyìn qīngshòu*),
and wore colorful patterned jade (*cǎizhēnyù*).
*Guìrén*, *Guìpín*, and *Fūrén* who assisted in sericulture
wore plain dark blue for both top and bottom, [一０] all in the *shēnyī* style.
They wore the Taìpíng chignon (*Taìpíngjì*),
a seven-tiered concealed chignon (*qītǎ bìjì*) made of
black tortoiseshell,
and additionally wore hairpins and earrings.
The nine *Pín*, princesses (*Gōngzhǔ*), and *Fūrén* wore five tiers (*wǔtǎ*).
Court Ladies (*Shìfù*) wore three tiers (*sāntǎ*).
The principle of assisting in sericulture
has existed since ancient times.
The Crown Princess (*Huángtàizǐfēi*) had a golden seal with a tortoise knob (*jīnxǐ guīniǔ*),
a vermilion sash (*xūnzhū shòu*),
and wore *yúyù* jade.

The Grand Consorts (*Taìfēi*) and Consorts (*Fēi*) of princes, Elder Princesses (*Zhū Chánggōngzhǔ*), Princesses (*Gōngzhǔ*), and Enfeoffed Ladies (*Fēngjūn*) had golden seals with purple sashes (*jīnyìn zǐshòu*),
and wore mountain-black jade (*shānxuányù*).
When Elder Princesses and Princesses attended meetings,
they wore the Taìpíng chignon (*Taìpíngjì*),
and a seven-tiered concealed chignon (*qītǎ bìjì*).
The Elder Princesses were allowed to have *bùyáo*.
All had hairpins and earrings,
and their clothing was of the same style.
From Princesses and Enfeoffed Ladies upwards, all wore sashes,
with colored cords for the sash-belt (*gǔndài*),
each matching the color of their sash.
A golden *bìxié* head served as the belt buckle (*dàijué*).
Grand Ladies (*Taìfūrén*) and Ladies (*Fūrén*) of commandery dukes (*jùngōng*), marquises (*hóu*), and county dukes (*xiàngōng*) and marquises had silver seals with green sashes (*yínyìn qīngshòu*),
and wore aquamarine jade (*shuǐcāngyù*).
Those specially honored received golden and purple.

Grand Ladies and Ladies of dukes, special promotion officials (*tèjìn*), marquises, ministers (*qīng*), high officials (*xiào*), court ladies (*shìfù*), and those with salaries of two thousand *dàn* (full and middle) wore dark purple silk headbands (*gàngzēng guó*),
with a golden dragon head holding a white pearl in its mouth,
and fish whiskers one *chǐ* long for hairpins and earrings. [一二]
Those assisting in sacrifices at the temple wore black silk top and bottom.
Those assisting in sericulture wore dark blue silk top and bottom.
All were of the *shēnyī* style with borders.
From ladies of two thousand *dàn* salary upwards to the Empress,
all used sericulture attire as court robes.
Collated Notes
Treatise 16, Food and Goods
In antiquity, the former kings measured the land to establish settlements,
surveyed the land to settle the people.
They utilized the Three Powers to regulate their affairs,
reverently followed the Four Seasons to complete their undertakings.
They observed the local customs and rectified the guiding principles.
They encouraged the fundamentals of agriculture and sericulture,
facilitated the benefits of fish and salt.
They ascended auspicious mountains to gather auspicious jades,
and sailed the vast seas to net pearls.
At midday, markets were established,
gathering all the commoners under Heaven.
First, cloth and silk,
then currency,
were traded for what was needed or lacked,
each getting what they desired.
The Rites of Zhōu state:
“In the first month, when harmony begins,
teachings are promulgated at the Huábiǎo.”
As for a common man,
a ten-mǔ homestead,
three days of labor service,
and a nine-fold tax system,
they implemented benevolent rites to foster humility,
and commanded spring communal altars to encourage plowing.
That which Heaven values is humanity;
that which sagacity seeks is learning.
When one studies the classics and enters officialdom,
then the way of the jūnzi is realized.
The Shī says:
“On the third day, to our spades;
on the fourth day, we raise our feet.”
Therefore, agricultural officials, marsh and forest wardens,
each had their proper sequence of duties.
The practices of fathers and elder brothers
were perfected without effort.
At fifteen, they engaged in duties,
and began to manage their clothes.
In the countryside, there were no idlers;
in the towns, no time was wasted.
This is what is meant by "when the people were first born,
each followed their own occupation."
Thus, Tàigōng facilitated the trade of market goods
to achieve the strength of the Qí state;
Chīyí excelled at managing wealth and commerce
to prosper the enterprise of Zhōngtáo.
Formerly, during the reign of Jīntiān,
he diligently attended to the affairs of the people.
He commanded spring for plowing and planting,
summoned summer for weeding and hoeing,
autumn for harvesting and gathering,
and winter for storing away.
The Shū says:
“He charted the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
and respectfully provided the people with the seasons.”
The Zhuàn says:
“Yǔ and Jì personally tilled the land and possessed the world.”
When the Nine Earths were settled,
the Four Peoples followed the norms.
Dōngwú had an abundance of ivory and horns;
Xīshǔ had a wealth of cinnabar.
Yǎnyù had stores of lacquer and silk;
Yānqí had treasuries of strange stones.
Qín Bīn had yak tails and feathers,
and a vast region with exquisite jade.
Jīngyǐng had cassia forests,
and was crisscrossed by bamboo groves.
By the riverbanks were oranges and pomelos;
beyond the river, boats and carriages.
Liáoxī was a land of woolens and felts;
Cōngyòu had swift Púshāo horses.
The variety of plants and goods was astonishing,
what was there that was not available?
Thus, they emulated the celestial phenomena above,
and surveyed everything below.
They utilized the advantages of Heaven and Earth,
and collected the abundance of mountains and seas.
A hundred mǔ of land
was taxed at one-tenth.
After nine years of personal cultivation,
there was a three-year reserve.
This could provide for the young,
and sustain the elderly.
They relied on the people,
and used them for the state.
Palaces and residences had their proper measures;
flags and banners had their order.
Court audiences and diplomatic visits followed their rituals;
banquets and feasts adhered to their regulations.
When families were prosperous and the state affluent,
those from afar came and those nearby were at peace.
They rescued from the calamities of floods and droughts,
and had compassion for the hardships of the world.
Only then did the king's regular meals
occasionally include sheng and yǒng music.
The rise of Shāng and Zhōu
was due to this way.
Xīn Zhòu was tyrannical and cruel,
squandering the state's expenses.
He constructed Qīnggōng Palace with gold inlays,
extending over a hundred lǐ.
He adorned Lùtái Terrace with jade,
rising a thousand rén high.
Within the palace were nine markets,
each managed by female officials.
Heavy taxes were levied to fill Lùtái with money;
great requisitions were made to increase the grain at Jùqiáo.
Many beautiful women were conscripted to fill the splendor of Qīnggōng;
a vast collection of treasures was amassed for pleasure excursions at Shāqiū.
Meat was hung to form a forest;
fermented liquor was piled to create a pond.
He made men and women chase each other naked within,
and over three thousand people would lie prostrate, drinking like cattle from the wine pond.
Inside the palace, brocade and fine silk were used for mats,
and damask and thin silk for cushions.
When King Zhōu punished Zhòu,
he respectfully bowed at Yīnxū.
He then distributed all the wealth from Lùtái,
and issued the grain from Jùqiáo.
Heaven sent down blessings,
and the Yīn people greatly rejoiced.
When King Nǎn was in his later years,
he moved the capital to Xīzhōu.
The Nine Cauldrons were lost,
and the Èr Nán were utterly destroyed.
He borrowed from the common people,
but had nothing with which to repay them.
So he ascended a high terrace to avoid his debts.
The Zhōu people called the king's residence "Táozétái" (Debt-Evading Terrace).
Formerly, Duke Jī of Zhōu established the Six Codes.
The Director of the Domains presented the Nine Tributes.
Wealth was distributed from the inner treasury,
to be perpetually unchangeable.
But as criminal law and administration declined,
and fine white grass became scarce,
Lord Lǔ first imposed the mū tax,
and Lord Qín collected a two-thirds share of income.
The models of the former kings
were utterly lost.
The court historian says: Bān Gù wrote the Zhíhuò Zhì,
covering from the Three Dynasties to the execution of Wáng Mǎng.
He extensively documented previous records,
and his text is detailed and comprehensive.
Guāngwǔ was magnanimous and benevolent,
carrying out a heavenly punitive expedition.
After Wáng Mǎng,
and with the Chìméi's recent defeat,
although the three luminaries (Sun, Moon, and Stars) again turned their gaze,
the nine provinces were desolate.
When Lǒng was gained and Shǔ was in sight,
the common people settled down.
From this time, the five-zhū coin began to be circulated.
Land rent was set at thirty-to-one (one-thirtieth).
For those among the people who gave birth to a child, the tax exemption was extended by three years.
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
the world was at peace and tranquil.
The people suffered no arbitrary levies,
and years saw consecutive bumper harvests.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng, a Ever-Full Granary was built,
and a grain market was established to the east of the city.
A hú of grain was worth twenty qián.
Grass and trees flourished,
cattle and sheep stretched as far as the eye could see.
Taxes were exceptionally light,
and the government granaries were again full.
Treachery and deceit were not tolerated,
and ritual and righteousness were exclusively practiced.
At that time, as the east brightened,
officials attended the imperial court.
The relatives of the empress and the households of marquises
rushed around.
Carriages flowed like water,
horses like flying dragons,
illuminating the corridors and eaves,
their splendor borne forth.
The tradition states:
"The origins of the Three Systems
have nine types of Yin and Yang,"
which are the constant numbers of Heaven and Earth.
In the third year of Yǒngchū of Āndì,
there were floods and droughts throughout the land,
and people cannibalized each other.
The Emperor granted the land of Hóngpí to the poor people.
Due to insufficient funds,
the Three Dukes again submitted a memorial requesting that officials and commoners be allowed to contribute money or grain to be granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng of Huándì,
less than half of the commanderies and kingdoms suffered from locusts.
The Yellow River overflowed for several thousand lǐ,
displacing over ten thousand households.
Relief supplies were provided wherever they were needed.
By the beginning of Jiànníng and Yǒnghé,
the Western Qiāng rebelled.
For over twenty years, warfare was continuous, exhausting the armies.
Military expenses amounted to over 32 billion,
emptying the imperial treasury
and extending to the inner commanderies.
Chōng and Zhì had short reigns;
Huán and Líng were wayward.
In the second year of Zhōngpíng,
the Southern Palace caught fire,
extending to the Northern Gate.
Thereupon, a tax of ten qián per mù of farmland was again collected from the entire realm
to construct the palace buildings.
The Emperor came from a marquis's family,
having been poor when he ascended the throne.
He often said:
"Huándì was unable to manage his household;
he had no private savings."
Therefore, he built the Wànjīntáng in the Western Garden
as his private treasury.
He also entrusted private money to the xiǎohuángmén,
with each household accumulating immense wealth.
Thereupon, he hung up the Hóngdū placards
and opened the path for selling official positions.
From dukes and ministers downwards,
all had their ranks differentiated by price.
Tíngwèi Cuī Liè paid five million qián to buy the position of Sītú.
When刺史 (Cìshǐ) and officials earning two thousand shí were promoted or transferred,
they were all required to contribute money for the construction of palace buildings.
For large commanderies, this amounted to twenty million qián.
Those who could not fulfill it sometimes committed suicide.
Xiàndì minted five-zhū coins,
but they had four lines connecting to the edge.
Knowledgeable people criticized this, saying:
"Perhaps the capital is being destroyed,
and these coins are scattering in four directions."
When Dǒng Zhuó engaged in warfare,
burning the palaces,
he then kidnapped the imperial carriage
and moved west to Cháng'ān.
He destroyed all the five-zhū coins
and cast smaller coins.
He collected all the bronze figures and flying beasts in Cháng'ān and Luòyáng
to be used for casting.
Furthermore, the coins lacked rims
and their inscriptions were inconvenient.
People at the time believed that Qín Shǐhuáng saw giants in Líntáo
and then cast bronze figures.
Zhuó was
a man from Líntáo,
and though their rise and fall differed,
their ominous portents were similar.
After Zhuó was executed,
Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì attacked each other,
using the city of Cháng'ān as their battlefield.
At this time, one hú of grain cost five hundred thousand,
and beans and wheat cost two hundred thousand.
People cannibalized each other,
white bones piled up,
and decaying corpses and remaining flesh
fouled the roads.
The Emperor sent Shìyùshǐ Hóu Wèn to distribute rice and beans from the grand granary
to make gruel for the starving people.
After days of distribution, more people died.
The Emperor then began to suspect that the officials were stealing his grain,
so he personally supervised the distribution in front of him.
All the hungry people wept, saying:
"Now we finally receive it!"
When the Emperor returned east,
Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and others pursued and defeated the imperial retinue at Cáoyáng.
That night, they secretly crossed the river,
and the six palaces (imperial consorts) all walked.
When they first left the camp,
the Empress held several bolts of silk.
Dǒng Chéng ordered the Fújié Lìng Sūn Huī to threaten her with a blade and seize them,
killing the attendants nearby,
and blood splattered on the Empress's clothes.
Upon reaching Ānyì,
the imperial robes were tattered,
and they only had wild dates and garden vegetables as provisions.
From then on, the entire city of Cháng'ān was empty,
everyone having scattered in all directions.
For two or three years,
there were no travelers in Guānzhōng.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
the imperial carriage reached Luòyáng.
The palace inner quarters were completely desolate,
and officials lived amidst thorns and brambles.
Each province and commandery held strong armies,
but supplies failed to arrive.
Shàngshū Láng officials went out to forage for themselves,
some unable to return,
dying in the ruined streets.
In the early days of Wèi Wǔ,
the nine provinces were in turmoil.
As cities were besieged and land plundered,
and the people were protected,
military resources
were temporarily allocated.
At that time, Yuán Shào's soldiers all relied on mulberries and dates for sustenance,
while Yuán Shù's warriors subsisted on snails and cattails.
Wèi Wǔ then recruited good citizens to cultivate fields in Xǔxià,
and also established agricultural officials in various provinces and commanderies.
Annually, tens of millions of hú were harvested,
to be used for military expenses.
When Yuán Shì was initially pacified,
and Yèdū was settled,
he ordered a land tax of four shēng of grain per mù,
two bolts of silk and two jīn of cotton per household.
All other arbitrary levies were forbidden,
preventing the strong from hiding their wealth and the weak from being overly taxed.
In the second year of Huángchū of Wén Dì,
due to high grain prices, the five-zhū coins were abolished.
At that time, the world was not yet unified,
and war chariots moved annually.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Add to this the marching armies,
and follow it with famine."
This refers to the malevolent strategies of war and the corresponding baleful qi.
At that time, the people of the three regions
were intent on devouring each other.
In victory and conquest,
farmers abandoned their plows.
The regions of Jiāng and Huái
particularly lacked stored provisions.
The Grand General Lù Xùn of Wú submitted a memorial requesting that all generals expand their fields.
Quán replied:
"Excellent.
Now I and my son will personally receive fields,
with eight oxen in the carriage,
arranged as four pairs.
Though we cannot compare to the ancients,
I also wish to share the labor with the masses."
The emphasis on agriculture and grain in Wú
began here.
Wèi Míngdì was disrespectful
and indulged in palace pleasures.
All officials were assigned to manual labor,
and the people throughout the land neglected their farming.
After this, Guāndōng suffered from floods,
and the people lost their livelihoods.
Yet, armies were raised in Liáoyáng,
and troops were stationed in Jiāngdiàn.
All this was due to the nation's lack of funds for expenditure.
How can one fully express it?
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ, Shìzǔ,
after Sūn Hào had been pacified,
the wealth of Sānwú was exhausted, having absorbed a million [people],
and the resources of Xīshǔ were brought under control, having taken over a thousand [years of accumulation].
Shields and spears were stored in armories,
and boats were broken up in rivers and ravines.
Riverbanks and coastlines,
Sānqiū and Bābǒu,
places untouched by plows and hoes,
were all granted to people.
The god of agriculture appeared in the morning,
arranging the eastern labor.
Those carrying hoes and provisions
were like spreading clouds.
Indeed, relying on heaven for the five planets,
and relying on earth for the five materials,
the era belonged to peace and prosperity,
goods flowed into storehouses.
Official mansions were increasingly embellished,
clothing and ornaments shone brightly against each other.
Thereupon, Wáng Jūnfū, Wǔzi, Shí Chóng, and others competed in extravagance,
the splendor of carriages, clothes, tripods, and sacrificial vessels,
allied with the imperial household,
spreading gold in their ponds,
and pulverizing coral trees.
When things prosper, they decline,
which is certainly fitting.
In the early Yǒngníng period,
Luòzhōng still had four million bolts of brocade and silk,
and over a hundred hù of pearls, jewels, gold, and silver.
When Empress Huì campaigned in the north,
and the imperial carriage was turned back at Dàngyīn,
with cold peaches served to the emperor,
and only one chicken provided,
her two quilts of common cloth,
and three thousand coins in her purse,
were used as provisions for the imperial carriage.
When Emperor Huái was besieged by Liú Yào,
the imperial army suffered repeated defeats.
The state treasury was depleted,
and officials were extremely hungry.
No smoke from cooking fires was seen in any house,
and hungry people resorted to cannibalism.
At Emperor Mǐn’s western residence,
famine was widespread.
A dòu of rice cost two catties of gold,
and more than half the population died.
When Liú Yào deployed his troops,
inside and outside communications were cut off.
Ten [dòus] of grain mash
was ground and offered to the emperor.
The sovereign and his ministers looked at each other,
all weeping.
When Empress Yuán crossed the Jiāng,
military preparations were rudimentary.
The tribute cloth from the barbarian tribes
had no fixed standard.
What was stored in the central treasury
amounted to four thousand bolts.
At that time, Shí Lè was brave and fierce,
stirring up trouble south of the Huái.
The emperor feared his encroachment,
and was greatly troubled by it.
He then issued an edict to the regional commanders, saying,
“Whoever cuts off Shí Lè’s head
shall be rewarded with a thousand bolts of cloth.”
Since Dǒng Zhuó’s rebellion in the Hàn dynasty,
the common people had been displaced,
grain prices reached over five hundred thousand shí per stone,
and many people cannibalized each other.
After Wèi Wǔ broke the Yellow Turban rebels,
he wanted to administer the four directions,
but suffered from insufficient military provisions.
Yǔlín Superintendent Zǎo Zhī of Yǐngchuān proposed the establishment of garrison farms (túntián).
Wèi Wǔ then issued an order, saying:
“The art of stabilizing the state lies in strong armies and sufficient food.
The Qín people unified the world through urgent agriculture,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ secured the Western Regions through garrison farms.
These are excellent models from previous generations.”
Thereupon, Rèn Jùn was appointed Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng,
and common people were recruited to cultivate garrison fields near Xǔ.
A million hù of grain were obtained.
Garrison farm officials were established in various commanderies and states.
Within a few years,
grain was accumulated everywhere,
and granaries were all full.
After Zhī died,
Wèi Wǔ later recalled his achievements
and enfeoffed his son with a noble title.
In the early Jiàn’ān period,
over ten thousand households of common people from Guānzhōng flowed into Jīngzhōu.
When they heard their homeland was peaceful,
they all yearned to return,
but had no means to sustain themselves.
Thereupon, Wèi Jì proposed,
“Salt is a great treasure of the state.
Since the chaos and turmoil, it has been dispersed.
Now, it should be managed as before, with commissioners overseeing its sale,
using the proceeds to buy more plowing oxen,
and providing them to the returning common people.
By diligently farming and accumulating grain,
Guānzhōng will be enriched.
Those far away, hearing of this,
will surely rush to return.”
Consequently, Wèi Wǔ dispatched an Attendant Officer, Púshè, to supervise the salt officials,
and moved the Sīlì Xiàowèi to reside in Hóngnóng.
The displaced people indeed returned,
and Guānzhōng became prosperous.
Soon after, Liú Fù of Pèiguó was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu,
stationed at Héféi,
where he greatly expanded garrison farms,
and repaired the dams of Sháopí, Rúpí, Qīmén, and Wútáng,
to irrigate rice fields.
Both public and private sectors accumulated reserves,
providing benefits for generations.
When Jiǎ Kuí served in Yùzhōu,
which bordered Wú to the south,
he repaired defensive and offensive equipment,
dammed the Rǔ River,
and constructed new dikes.
He also opened a transportation canal over two hundred lǐ long,
which was called Jiǎhóu Qú.
During the Huángchū period,
commandery governors in all directions further expanded cultivated land,
thus ensuring the state's resources were not depleted.
At that time, Yán Fěi of Jìběi served as Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào.
Since Mǎ Chāo’s rebellion, the people of Jīngzhào
had not focused on agriculture,
and thus had no carts or oxen.
Fěi then instructed the people
to gather materials for carts during idle months,
and to teach each other craftsmanship.
Those without oxen were told to raise pigs,
selling them when prices were high to buy oxen.
At first, everyone found it troublesome,
but within one or two years, every registered household had carts and oxen.
Labor for farming was reduced and supplied sufficiently,
and Jīngzhào became prosperous.
Zhèng Hún served as Grand Administrator of Pèijùn.
The commandery was low and wet,
suffering from floods,
and the people were hungry and destitute.
Hún built dams in Xiāo and Xiāng counties
and opened rice fields.
The people of the commandery did not consider it beneficial.
Hún believed it would ultimately bring long-term benefits,
and personally led the people to start the work,
completing it all in one winter.
In successive years, there were great harvests,
acreage increased annually,
and tax revenue doubled the usual amount.
The commandery relied on its benefits,
and an inscription was carved in its praise,
calling it Zhèngpí.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi, Xú Miǎo served in Liángzhōu.
The land received little rain,
and often suffered from grain shortages.
Miǎo proposed repairing the salt ponds of Wǔwēi and Jiǔquán
to obtain grain from the barbarians.
He also extensively opened irrigated fields,
recruiting poor people to cultivate them.
Every household became prosperous,
and granaries were overflowing.
Furthermore, the surplus military provisions from the Dùzhī in the region
were used to purchase gold, brocade, dogs, and horses,
which were then supplied for the expenses of the central plains.
People from the Western Regions offered tribute,
and goods circulated,
all thanks to Miǎo’s efforts.
Later, Huángfǔ Lóng served as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
The custom in Dūnhuáng was not to use seed drills or plows,
nor did they know how to use water for irrigation.
Both human and ox labor was wasted,
and grain harvests were even smaller.
Upon his arrival, Lóng
taught them how to make seed drills and plows,
and also taught them how to irrigate.
By the end of the year, calculations showed
that saved labor was more than half,
and grain yields increased by five times,
making the western region prosperous.
In the fourth year of Jiāpíng,
there was a famine in Guānzhōng.
Xuāndì memorialized to relocate five thousand farmers from Jìzhōu to cultivate land in Shàngguī.
He also developed salt ponds in Jīngzhào, Tiānshuǐ, and Nán'ān
to augment military supplies.
In the first year of Qīnglóng,
the Chéngguó Canal was opened.
From Chéncāng to Huáilǐ, the Línjìn Dyke was built,
drawing water from the Qiān River and Luò River to irrigate over three thousand qǐng of saline-alkaline land,
which greatly enriched the state.
In the fourth year of Zhèngshǐ,
Xuāndì again commanded his armies to attack the Wú general Zhūgě Kè,
burning his accumulated supplies.
Kè abandoned the city and fled.
The Emperor thus wished to expand cultivated land and accumulate grain,
as a strategy for annexation.
He then sent Dèng Ài to survey the land east of Chén and Xiàng,
reaching the region of Shòuchūn.
Ài believed that while the land was fertile, water was scarce,
and it was insufficient to fully exploit the land's potential.
He suggested that canals should be opened,
which would allow for large accumulations of military provisions,
and also facilitate transport by water.
He then authored the Jìhé Lùn to explain his reasoning.
He also believed that in the past, after defeating the Yellow Turbans,
military agricultural colonies (túntián) were established,
accumulating grain in Xǔdū
to control the four directions.
Now that the three corners (of the realm) were settled,
the matter lay in Huáinán.
Whenever a large army was raised for an expedition,
more than half the (expeditionary force) was engaged in transport,
with enormous costs and efforts,
constituting a major burden.
The land between Chén and Cài
was low-lying and fertile,
and the rice fields around Xǔchāng could be reduced,
with their water channeled eastward.
Twenty thousand people from Huáiběi and thirty thousand from Huáinán could be assigned to alternate periods of rest,
cultivating and guarding simultaneously.
When water was abundant,
the harvest would consistently be three times that of the west.
After deducting all expenses,
five million hù of grain could be annually completed as military provisions.
Within six or seven years,
over thirty million hù could be accumulated in the Huái River region.
This would be enough food for one hundred thousand men for five years.
With this, attacking the enemy
would ensure victory.
Xuāndì approved of this
and implemented everything according to Ài's plan.
Subsequently, along the Huái River to the north,
from Zhōnglí southward and west of Héngshí,
encompassing the Bǐ River region for over four hundred lǐ,
a camp was established every five lǐ.
Each camp consisted of sixty men,
who would cultivate and guard simultaneously.
The Huáiyáng and Bǎichǐ canals were simultaneously repaired and expanded,
drawing water from the Hé River upstream
and connecting to the Huái River and Yǐng River downstream.
Numerous reservoirs were greatly improved south and north of the Yǐng River,
and canals totaling over three hundred lǐ were dug,
irrigating twenty thousand qǐng of land.
Huáinán and Huáiběi were all connected.
From Shòuchūn to the capital,
agricultural officials and soldier-farmers
could be heard with the sound of chickens and dogs,
and fields stretched endlessly.
Whenever there was military activity in the southeast,
and a large army was dispatched,
they would embark on boats and sail downstream,
reaching the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
With ample provisions,
and no water-related hazards,
this was all Dèng Ài's establishment.
When the Jìn Dynasty received the Mandate,
Wǔdì wished to pacify the region south of the Jiāng River.
At that time, grain was cheap and cloth and silk were expensive.
The Emperor wished to establish a "level purchase and sale" (píngdí) system,
using cloth and silk to purchase grain
for storage.
Those who discussed it believed that military provisions were still scarce,
and it was inappropriate to exchange expensive goods for cheap ones.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
the Emperor issued an edict saying:
"If the common people have an abundant year, they become extravagant;
if there is famine, they become destitute.
This is the natural cycle.
Therefore, the ancients assessed state expenditures,
taking surpluses and dispersing stagnation,
employing methods of 'light and heavy' (price control) and 'level purchase and sale'.
To manage finances and distribute (resources) equitably,
benefiting without cost,
is an excellent policy.
However, this practice has long been abandoned,
and the world is rarely accustomed to its appropriateness.
Furthermore, official reserves are not extensive,
speakers hold differing views,
and the system for circulating wealth has not been fully implemented.
This has resulted in national treasures being scattered in abundant years without the state collecting them,
while the poor and weak suffer in famine years without the state being prepared.
Powerful individuals and wealthy merchants,
with their light capital,
hoard large accumulations,
thereby controlling the profits.
Thus, farmers suffer in their occupation,
and secondary occupations cannot be prohibited.
Now, we reduce corvée and emphasize fundamentals,
uniting efforts in cultivation.
We wish to increase agricultural output
and encourage cultivators,
yet prices sometimes still soar,
resulting in harm to farmers.
Now, it is appropriate to facilitate sales and purchases
to alleviate scarcity.
Let the responsible officials deliberate
and formulate specific regulations."
However, the matter was ultimately not implemented.
At this time, Jiāngnán was not yet pacified,
and the court exerted itself greatly in agriculture.
In the first month, Dīnghài day, of the fourth year,
the Emperor personally ploughed the ceremonial field (jìtián).
On Gēngyín day,
an edict stated:
"To make all within the four seas
abandon secondary pursuits and return to fundamental ones, vying in agriculture and diligence,
who can effectively convey Our will
and make the common people enthusiastic in their work and content in their occupations,
but the chief officials of commanderies and counties?
To lead them and exert effort,
lies in tireless dedication.
Whenever We think of their management of duties,
they are indeed diligent.
Let the Zhongzuǒ Diǎnmù who breed and graze horses
be granted one horse each to the county magistrates and chiefs and the commandery and state assistant officials."
In this year,
the Ever-Normal Granaries (chángpíngcāng) were established,
buying in times of abundance
and selling in times of scarcity,
to benefit the common people.
In the first month, Guǐsì day, of the fifth year,
an imperial order warned the auditors of commanderies and states,
and the administrators, chiefs, and magistrates of all commanderies and states,
to diligently exploit the land's potential
and prohibit idle merchants and peddlers.
Those on leave should participate in the labors of their fathers and elder brothers,
and powerful figures should not exploit the weak
or privately enlist them under their names.
In the tenth month,
an edict stated that
"Shī Jiàn, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, has reported that Wáng Hóng, the Administrator of Jí Commandery, diligently cares for the common people,
guides and transforms them with effective methods,
and encouraged the reclamation of over five thousand qǐng of wasteland.
Despite a widespread famine in that year, his commandery alone experienced no shortages.
He can truly be said to have excelled through persuasion and instruction,
achieving different results from others in the same era.
Let him be granted a thousand hù of grain,
and let this be announced throughout the empire."
In the eighth year,
Sītú Shí Bāo memorialized:
"There is no system for evaluating the best and worst in agriculture and sericulture among the provinces and commanderies.
It is advisable to increase the number of clerks and scribes
to conduct inspections."
The Emperor followed this.
The details are in the biography of Shí Bāo.
Since Bāo was effective in encouragement and instruction,
the common people were content.
In the tenth year,
Guānglù Xūn Xiàhóu Hé memorialized to repair the Xīnqú, Fùshòu, and Yóupō canals,
which in total irrigated fifteen hundred qǐng of land.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Xiánníng,
an edict stated:
"Going out to battle and returning to cultivate,
though a constant since ancient times,
yet as military efforts have not ceased,
we have never not thought of the soldiers.
Now, let the eunuchs' slaves and maidservants from Yè be settled in Xīnchéng,
to replace the military farmers in planting rice.
Fifty slaves and maidservants each shall form one túntián unit,
with a Sīmǎ appointed for each unit,
and all shall follow the túntián regulations."
In the third year,
another edict stated:
"This year, the continuous rain has been excessive,
and there has also been insect damage.
In Yǐngchuān and Xiāngchéng,
since spring, planting has been almost impossible,
which is a deep concern.
What measures should the responsible officials take for the common people?
Act promptly to address this."
Dù Yù submitted a memorial saying: "Your subject has pondered,
the current floods are particularly severe in the southeast.
Not only are the five grains not harvested,
but dwellings and livelihoods are also damaged.
Low-lying fields everywhere are inundated,
and high ground is all
largely barren.
This means the people’s destitution is still to come next year.
Although imperial edicts urgently instruct chief officials and the Ěrqiānshí to devise plans,
if a grand policy is not broadly implemented
to determine the appropriate course of action,
I fear it will be mere empty words,
offering only meager benefits.
At present, during the season of summer and autumn vegetables,
the common people already lack sufficiency.
When winter
and spring arrive,
with no green grass in the fields,
they will surely look to official grain
for their survival.
This is a major matter for one region,
which cannot but be considered in advance.
Your foolish subject believes that since they are afflicted by water,
they should rely on fish, vegetables, and snails.
However, with the vast, overflowing waves,
the poor and weak will ultimately be unable to obtain them.
Now, it is advisable to largely breach
the various dikes on the eastern borders of Yǎn and Yù Prefectures,
guiding the water according to its natural course.
Let the hungry fully obtain the bounty of aquatic products.
The common people need not leave their boundaries,
eating wild produce morning and evening.
This is an immediate daily benefit.
After the water recedes,
the silted fields
will yield several zhōng per mù.
Come spring, if large quantities of the five grains are planted,
the five grains
will surely be abundant.
This is another benefit for the coming year.
Your subject previously proposed that
the breeding cattle of the Diǎnmù are not sufficient for plowing and hauling.
Those that are old and have not had their noses pierced are useless,
incurring only the expense of provisions and fodder for officials and soldiers.
The number of cattle
sent out for hauling each year is very small,
and they are also untrained.
It would be advisable to sell a large number of them
to exchange for grain or as rewards.
The imperial edict stated:
“Breeding animals
should not be reduced or dispersed.”
The matter was subsequently shelved.
Upon inquiring with the responsible officials,
currently, the Diǎnyú Yòudiǎnmù’s breeding cattle,
including large and small,
number over forty-five thousand head.
If they do not benefit worldly use,
though the number is large,
the expenses daily increase.
In ancient times, a single horse or ox
was used for plowing when at home
and for battle when going out;
they were not like pigs and sheep.
Now, merely raising cattle that ought to be useful
ultimately results in useless expenses,
which is a great deviation from what is proper.
In the southeast, rice paddies are the primary occupation,
and people have no cattle.
Now that the dikes have been breached,
thirty-five thousand head of breeding cattle can be distributed
to the generals, officials, gentry, and commoners of the two prefectures,
so they can be used for spring plowing.
After the grain harvest,
each head will be charged three hundred hú.
〔一０〕 This transforms useless expenses
into a yield of seven million hú of grain from the irrigated land.
This is another benefit for several years hence.
Moreover, with the common people moving down from the hills to settle the land,
the future abundance for both public and private will be immeasurable.
The ten thousand good breeding cattle that are retained
can be immediately handed over to the officials of the Yòudiǎnmù Dūwèi to raise.
Where there are many people and few livestock,
the pasture lands can be combined and managed,
clarifying their assessment and evaluation.
Furthermore, in the near-suburbs of the three Wèi,
several hundred thousand hú of grain will be re-entered annually,
and the cattle will all be trained
and ready for hauling.
All these are things that can be preserved today.”
Yù also said: "Those who wish to cultivate paddy fields
all find ‘fire-plowing and water-weeding’ convenient.
It is not that it isn't so,
but this method is only applied to new fields and overgrown land
that are isolated
from where people live.
In the past, the southeast was newly developed and sparsely populated,
thus benefiting from 'fire-plowing'.
Since recently, the population has daily increased,
and dikes and dams burst annually,
good fields
turn into reeds and rushes.
People live by marshes and swamps,
with unsuitable land and water conditions.
Grazing is impossible,
and trees stand withered.
These are all harms caused by the dikes.
When there are many dikes, the soil is thin
and the water shallow,
so floods do not penetrate deep.
Therefore, whenever there is heavy rain,
the water overflows again,
extending to dry fields.
Those who speak do not consider the cause,
thus saying this soil is unsuitable for dry
farming.
Your subject estimates the population of the Hàn dynasty,
and examining the current dike locations,
all were dry land occupations.
If there are any old dikes or old dams,
they are sturdy, complete, and well-maintained,
not what is
now called harmful to people.
Your subject previously saw Shàngshū Hú Wēi petitioning to breach the dikes,
his words were sincere and earnest.
Your subject recently saw Sòng Hóuxiàng Yīng Zūn submitting
a memorial on what was expedient,
requesting to breach the Sì Dike and
relocate the transport canal.
At that time, the Dūdū and Dùzhī discussed the matter together,
each presenting their views,
and did not follow Zūn's suggestion.
Your subject has reviewed Zūn's memorial:
the transport canal goes east to Shòuchūn,
where there is an old canal,
so it need not pass through the Sì Dike.
The Sì Dike, within Zūn's jurisdiction, damages some thirteen thousand qǐng of land,
destroying established livelihoods.
Zūn's
county governs two thousand six hundred tenants,
which can be said to be very few,
yet they still complain of narrow land,
insufficient to exert their full strength.
All this is the harm caused by water.
This should be jointly remedied,
yet the Dūdū and Dùzhī still hold differing opinions,
not because their views are difficult to reconcile,
but simply because their disagreement harms what is right.
Since people's views differ,
the interests and harms
also vary.
The military, the commanderies and counties,
the scholar-officials, and the common people—
their intentions are none alike.
This is because each focuses on their own benefits and forgets the harms.
This
is why the principles are not fully understood,
and why affairs often suffer from problems.
Your subject further notes that
the tenants led by the two Dùzhī in Yù Prefecture,
including officials, soldiers, and miscellaneous personnel from the prefecture and commanderies,
altogether use only some seven thousand five hundred qǐng of paddy fields.
Calculating
three years' worth of reserves,
it amounts to no more than twenty thousand qǐng.
According to common sense,
there is no need to accumulate so much useless water,
especially now when water overflows,
causing great
disasters.
Your subject believes that rather than mismanaging it,
it is better to drain it than to store it.
An enlightened edict should be issued,
instructing the Cìshǐ and Ěrqiānshí
that the old dikes and old dams of the Hàn dynasty
and small private dikes in mountains and valleys
should all be repaired to store water.
As for those constructed since the Wèi dynasty,
and those that burst due to rain and overflow, forming reed-filled, 'horse-intestine' dikes
and the like,
they should all be breached and drained.
Chief officials and Ěrqiānshí should personally encourage the work,
and all able-bodied people should assist in the work orders at the same time.
By the time the water freezes,
the ground should be roughly dry
and hardened.
Those who performed the actual work should all be rewarded for it.
For the old dikes, dams, and irrigation channels that need repair or blocking,
all traces should be sought out
and restored exactly as they were in Hàn times.
As was the custom,
preliminary divisions should be made and reported.
Wait until winter when the troops in the southeast are rested and rotated,
each to remain for one month to assist.
Rivers have constant flows,
and terrain has a fixed
form.
The Hàn dynasty, with its large population,
still had no such troubles.
Now, by addressing what causes trouble and draining it,
tracing ancient practices to illuminate the present,
the great principle is clear
and can be argued.
and gained it.
Your humble servant, unable to control his foolish thoughts,
ventures to say that this is the most practical benefit for today.
The imperial court followed it.
After the pacification of Wú,
the relevant authorities again memorialized:
"The imperial edict states, 'Princes and dukes treat their states as their homes,
and it is inappropriate for them to own lands and residences in the capital city.
Although there is no time to build residences for the various states now,
there should be places for them to stay in the city
and fields for fodder in the nearby suburbs.'
Now, this can be restricted:
kings, princes, dukes, and marquises
may have one residence in the capital city.
For suburban fields:
fifteen qǐng for large states,
ten qǐng for medium states,
and seven qǐng for small states.
Those who have no residence within the city but own one outside
are all allowed to keep them."
A system for household tax was also established: households of able-bodied men
paid annually three bolts of silk,
and three jīn of floss;
households of women or second-class able-bodied men paid half.
For some frontier commanderies, it was two-thirds,
and for distant ones, one-third.
The Yí people paid cōngbù,
one bolt per household,
or one zhàng for distant ones.
Each man was allotted seventy mǔ of land,
and each woman thirty mǔ.
In addition, able-bodied men were obligated to cultivate fifty mǔ,
able-bodied women twenty mǔ,
second-class able-bodied men half of that,
and women of this class were not obligated.
Men and women aged sixteen and above to sixty were considered zhèngdīng;
those aged fifteen and below to thirteen, and sixty-one and above to sixty-five were considered cìdīng;
those aged twelve and below, and sixty-six and above were considered elderly or young,
and were not obligated for service.
Distant Yí who were not obligated to cultivate land paid yì mǐ,
three hú per household,
five dòu for distant ones,
and extremely distant ones paid suàn qián,
twenty-eight wén per person.
For officials from the first to the ninth rank,
land was allotted according to their noble or humble status:
first rank occupied fifty qǐng,
second rank forty-five qǐng,
third rank forty qǐng,
fourth rank thirty-five qǐng,
fifth rank thirty qǐng,
sixth rank twenty-five qǐng,
seventh rank twenty qǐng,
eighth rank fifteen qǐng,
ninth rank ten qǐng.
Furthermore, according to their rank, they could shelter their relatives:
those of high rank up to the nine generations of relatives,
those of lower rank up to three generations.
Imperial clansmen, honored guests of the state, descendants of former sages, and sons and grandsons of scholars also followed this.
They could also shelter people as retainers (yīshíkè) and tenant farmers (diànkè).
Those of sixth rank and above could have three yīshíkè;
seventh and eighth ranks two persons;
ninth rank one person, including jǔniǎn, jìqín, qiánqū, yóujī, qiángnǔ, sīmǎ, yǔlínláng, diànzhōngrǒngcóngwǔbēn, diànzhōngwǔbēn, chíchuífǔwǔqíwǔbēn, chísháirǒngcóngwǔbēn, and mìngzhōngwǔbēnwǔqí.
As for those entitled to diànkè:
first and second rank officials could have no more than fifty households of diànkè;
third rank ten households;
fourth rank seven households;
fifth rank five households;
sixth rank three households;
seventh rank two households;
eighth and ninth ranks one household.
At this time, there was peace throughout the land,
taxes were fair,
and everyone enjoyed their livelihoods and took pleasure in their work.
After Emperor Huì,
governance declined,
and by the time of Yǒngjiā,
chaos and disorder intensified.
East of Yōngzhōu,
many people suffered from hunger,
selling each other,
fleeing and migrating,
in countless numbers.
Yōu, Bìng, Sī, Jì, Qín, and Yōng six zhōu suffered a great locust plague,
consuming all vegetation and even the hair of cattle and horses.
There was also a great epidemic,
coupled with famine,
and the common people were further killed by bandits,
filling rivers with floating corpses,
and covering fields with white bones.
When Liú Yào pressed,
the imperial court debated moving the capital to Cāngyuán,
but people were often cannibalizing each other,
and hunger and disease arrived together,
with eighteen or nineteen out of ten officials fleeing.
When Emperor Yuán was King of Jìn,
he spurred agricultural work,
issuing an edict that the performance of officials receiving two thousand dàn of grain (èrqiānshí zhǎnglì) would be judged by the amount of grain they collected.
Those not in urgent palace guard duties
should all go to the fields,
making the army cultivate their own land,
which would then serve as their granary.
In the first year of Tàixīng,
it was stated:
"The lands of Xú and Yáng two zhōu are suitable for three types of wheat.
They should be instructed to dry the land,
plant in autumn,
and harvest in summer,
connecting the old and new harvests,
thereby providing great relief
and immense benefit.
In the past, the Hàn sent the light chariot envoy Fàn Shèngzhī to oversee wheat cultivation in the three Fǔ,
and Guānzhōng subsequently had a bumper harvest.
Do not delay."
Afterwards, although there were droughts and locusts in subsequent years for wheat,
the benefits were still great.
In the second year,
the three Wú suffered a great famine,
with deaths numbering in the hundreds.
Dèng Yōu, the Grand Administrator of Wújùn, promptly opened granaries to provide relief.
During Emperor Yuán's time, the Imperial Household Attendants Yú and Huán Yí were sent to open granaries for relief,
[一一] and many government services were reduced.
All officials submitted sealed memorials.
The General of the Rear Army, Yìng Zhān, memorialized:
"If one person does not plow,
there will surely be someone in the world who suffers hunger.
Since the outbreak of war,
with campaigns and transport,
and the expenses of the imperial court, ancestral temples,
and all officials already vast,
down to merchants, artisans, vagrants, and servants who do not engage in agriculture or sericulture but wander and live off others,
numbering in the tens of thousands.
If one does not think of establishing great benefits,
and yet hopes for the state to be self-sufficient and the people provided for,
how can it not be difficult!
The ancients said,
'When hunger and cold arrive together,
even Yáo and Shùn cannot prevent bandits in the wilderness.'
'When wealth and poverty are combined,
even Gāoyáo cannot prevent the strong from oppressing the weak.'
Therefore, those who possess a state or a family,
how can they not diligently promote agriculture and value grain?
Recently, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi adopted the proposals of Zǎo Zhī and Hán Hào,
extensively establishing military agricultural colonies (túntián),
and even during campaigns,
he allocated armed soldiers
to reclaim land as appropriate,
so the populace was not overly burdened,
and great achievements were accomplished.
Lately, refugees have fled to Eastern Wú,
but Eastern Wú is now suffering from scarcity,
so they have all returned.
The fertile lands west of the Jiāng River,
though long abandoned,
[一二] can be cleared by fire and tilled by water,
which is relatively easy work.
It is advisable to select these refugees,
re-establish agricultural officials,
and ensure that their merits and rewards
are all according to the precedents of the Wèi dynasty:
in the first year, they share with the common people;
in the second year, they share the tax;
in the third year, taxes are calculated and imposed on them,
thereby benefiting both public and private interests.
Then granaries will be full,
and one can count the days until prosperity."
He also said:
"In the past, Gāozǔ sent Xiāo Hé to pacify Guānzhōng;
Guāngwǔ ordered Kòu Xún to guard Hénèi;
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi entrusted Zhōng Yáo with affairs in the west.
Thus, they were able to pacify the entire realm
and bring peace to the interior.
Now, the central plains are desolate
and have not yet received proper governance.
This is what the common people yearn for.
Shòuchūn, a regional hub,
is not far from here.
An inspector-general (dūdū) with both civil and military strategy should be selected,
to secure the strategic positions of Héluò from afar,
and serve as a frontier governor (fānzhèn) for Xú and Yù nearby,
to gather and settle the dispersed populace,
providing people with a place to rely on,
and to exclusively focus on agricultural work,
ensuring affairs are properly managed.
Zhào Chōngguó engaged in agriculture in Jīnchéng,
thereby pacifying the western Líng;
Zhūgě Liàng cultivated by the Wèibīn River,
planning to resist the superior state.
Now, all armies that are not facing the enemy
should all be assigned to collective cultivation."
In the fifth year of Xiánhé,
Emperor Chéng first measured the common people's land,
taking one-tenth,
at a rate of three shēng of rice tax per mù.
In the sixth year,
due to pirate raids,
and the inability to maintain grain transport,
surplus able-bodied men from princes and dukes downwards were conscripted,
each to transport six hú of rice.
After this, there were frequent floods, droughts, and locust plagues for several years,
and land harvests were insufficient.
At the beginning of Xiánkāng,
the calculated land tax on rice
showed a deficit of over fifty thousand hú,
and Shàngshū Chǔ Póu and others were dismissed from office.
there were frequent large military campaigns,
and grain transport was insufficient.
A decree was issued that thirteen households, from princes and dukes downwards, should jointly provide one person
to assist with duózhī transport.
At the beginning of Shēngpíng,
Xún Xiàn became the Dūdū of Běifǔ,
stationed in Xiàpī.
He established fields in Shíbiē of Dōngyáng,
which benefited both the state and private individuals.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
he reduced the land rent,
collecting two shēng per mù.
In the second year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the system of measuring land and collecting rent was abolished.
From princes and dukes downwards, a head tax of three hú was imposed,
exempting only those in active service.
In the eighth year,
the rice tax was further increased
to five shí per head.
By the latter years,
the empire was at peace,
the climate was favorable, and the harvests were abundant.
The common people were content in their work,
and grain and silk were plentiful,
almost to the point where every household had enough and every person was satisfied.
The Hán currency formerly used five zhū coins.
Since Wáng Mǎng's reforms,
the common people all found it inconvenient.
When Gōngsūn Shù usurped the imperial title in Shǔ,
a children's rhyme said:
"Yellow ox with white belly,
the five zhū shall return."
Those who loved omens secretly said
that Wáng Mǎng claimed yellow,
and Shù wanted to succeed him,
hence he called himself the White Emperor.
The five zhū was Hán currency,
meaning Hàn would again unite the empire.
Upon Gǔangwǔ's restoration,
Wáng Mǎng's coinage was abolished.
In the sixteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
Mǎ Yuán again submitted a memorial, saying:
"The foundation for enriching the state
lies in food and currency.
It is proper to cast five zhū coins as before."
The Emperor agreed.
Thereupon, five zhū coins were again cast,
and the people of the empire found it convenient.
During Emperor Zhāng's time,
the prices of grain and silk were high,
and the county treasury's expenses were insufficient,
which worried the court.
Shàngshū Zhāng Lín said:
"Now it is not only grain that is expensive,
but all goods are expensive.
This is because the currency is cheap.
It is appropriate to order the entire empire to use cloth and silk for rent,
and to use them for all market purchases.
Seal the coins and do not circulate them;
in this way, coins will be scarce and goods will be cheap.
Furthermore,
salt is essential for food.
The county officials can sell salt themselves,
a practice implemented during Emperor Wǔ's time,
named jūnyūn."
Thereupon, the matter was submitted to the Shàngshū for general discussion.
Shàngshū Zhū Huī argued, saying:
"According to the royal system,
the Son of Heaven does not speak of abundance or scarcity,
nor do the feudal lords speak of much or little.
Those who receive salaries do not contend with the common people for profit.
The law of jūnyūn
is no different from that of merchants.
If cloth and silk are used for rent,
officials will be prone to corruption.
For officials to sell salt themselves
is to contend with the common people for profit,
which is not something an enlightened ruler should do."
The Emperor originally thought Lín's words were correct,
but upon receiving Huī's argument,
he became angry.
He then adopted Lín's proposal,
but stopped it a short time later.
During Emperor Huán's time, someone submitted a memorial saying:
"People are impoverished because currency is light and coins are thin.
It is appropriate to recast larger coins."
The matter was submitted to the officials of the Four Prefectures and scholars of the Grand Academy who could speak.
Xiàolián Liú Táo submitted his argument, saying:
and the discussion on balancing heavy and light,
inquiring into the subtle and profound,
not neglecting the poor and lowly.
Therefore, even a person who eats humble fare
has been mistakenly included.
The current concern,
I believe,
is not about currency,
but about people's hunger.
Therefore, the former kings observed celestial phenomena to nurture creatures,
and respectfully taught the people the seasons,
so that men would not neglect
their fields
and women would not leave their looms.
Thus, the way of ruler and minister was practiced,
and the teaching of the royal path was understood.
From this, it can be said
that food is the treasure of the state,
and the most
precious thing to the common people.
I secretly observe that in recent years,
good crops have been consumed by locusts and other pests,
and looms and shuttles are empty due to public and private demands.
What is urgent is food for the morning and evening,
and what causes distress are matters of
extravagance and waste.
How can it be about the thickness or thinness of coins,
or the weight of zhū and liǎng?
Even if sand and gravel were to turn into southern gold,
and tiles and stones were to transform into rare jade,
if the common
people have nothing to drink when thirsty
and nothing to eat when hungry,
even the pure virtue of Huáng Xī
and the civilization of Táng and Yú
still could not secure what is within the palace walls.
Indeed, the common people
can go a hundred years without currency,
but cannot endure a single morning of hunger.
Therefore, food is the most urgent matter.
Those who discuss this do not understand the foundation of agriculture
and often speak of the convenience of casting and smelting.
Some wish to exploit this opportunity to commit fraud,
to appropriate state profits.
When state profits are almost depleted,
those who take will compete
fiercely,
and the source of casting will thus arise.
Indeed, if ten thousand people cast them,
and one person takes them,
it is still not enough.
How much more so now, if one person casts them and ten thousand people take
them?
Even if yin and yang were used as charcoal,
and all things as copper,
and people not needing to eat were employed,
and those not hungry were made to work,
it still would not satisfy insatiable desires.
If one wishes for the people's wealth to be abundant,
the key is to stop forced labor and prevent confiscation.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue
pities the worries and sorrows within the seas [of the empire],
and is grieved by the difficulties of the world,
wishing to cast coins and standardize currency
to remedy these ills.
This is like trying to raise fish in a boiling cauldron,
or perch birds on a raging fire.
Wood and water
are
originally
where fish and birds thrive,
but if used at the wrong time,
they will inevitably be scorched and destroyed.
I wish Your Majesty would relax the prohibitions on reducing coinage
and postpone the discussions on casting and smelting.
The Emperor ultimately did not cast coins.
When Emperor Xiàn's
Chūpíng reign began, Dǒng Zhuó then re-minted small coins.
Consequently, currency became light and goods became expensive,
with one hú of grain reaching several million coins.
When Wèi Wǔ was chancellor,
he abolished them
and reverted to using Wǔzhū coins.
At this time, no coins had been minted for a long time,
so the currency stock was not large,
and there was no increase;
thus, grain became indefinitely cheap.
In the second year of Huángchū,
Emperor Wén of Wèi abolished Wǔzhū coins,
instructing the people to use grain and silk for trade.
By Emperor Míng's reign,
after coins had been abolished and grain used for a long time,
human artifice and fraud gradually increased.
People competed to wet grain to gain profit,
and made thin silk for trade.
Even though severe penalties were applied, it could not be prohibited.
Sīmǎ Zhī and others raised a great discussion in court,
believing that using coins not only enriched the state,
but also reduced punishments.
If Wǔzhū coins were now re-minted,
the state would be enriched and punishments reduced,
which would be advantageous for affairs.
Emperor Míng of Wèi then re-established Wǔzhū coins.
They were used until the Jìn Dynasty,
and no reforms or innovations were heard of.
In the fifth year of Jiāhé,
Sūn Quán cast large coins, each worth five hundred.
In the first year of Chìwū,
he again cast coins worth a thousand.
Thus, when Lǚ Méng pacified Jīngzhōu,
Sūn Quán bestowed one hundred million coins.
As the coins were too valuable,
they were merely an empty name,
and people suffered from them.
Quán heard that the people did not find them convenient,
so he reduced and halted them,
casting them into implements.
Officials were not to issue them again.
Those privately held
were all to be handed over to storehouses,
their value equitably lowered,
with no injustice.
Since the Jìn Dynasty's central plain was lost in chaos,
Emperor Yuán crossed the river.
Sūn's old coins were used,
with varying weights circulating.
The larger ones were called Bǐlún,
and the medium ones Sìwén.
Shěn Chōng of Wúxīng also cast small coins,
called Shěnláng coins.
As there were not many coins,
they gradually became more valuable.
In the third year of Tàiyuán during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
an edict stated:
"Coins
are the state's precious treasure.
Petty people, coveting profit,
endlessly melt and destroy them.
The inspecting authorities should pay attention to this.
The barbarians of Guǎngzhōu treasure bronze drums,
and the province has always not produced copper.
It is heard that both official and private merchants, coveting the slightly heavier weight of Bǐlún coins,
take them into Guǎngzhōu,
trade them with the barbarians,
and have them melted down to make drums.
This is to be strictly prohibited and controlled.
Those caught will be punished."
In the Yuánxīng period of Emperor Ān,
Huán Xuán, assisting in government,
proposed to abolish coins and use grain and silk.
Kǒng Línzhī argued: "Of the Eight Policies in the Great Plan,
currency is second only to food.
Is it not because it is the means of exchange
and thus the most essential for use?
If the people were to exert effort in making coins,
that would impede their livelihood,
and prohibiting it would be acceptable.
But now, farmers devote themselves to grain,
and artisans devote themselves to tools,
each adhering to their profession.
How do they ever labor for coins?
Therefore, the sagely
kings instituted currency of no inherent use
to facilitate the exchange of useful goods.
This not only avoids the cost of damage and waste,
but also saves the hardship of difficult transport.
This is why coins have succeeded the achievements of tortoise shells and cowries,
and have never been abandoned throughout
generations.
Grain and silk, as treasures,
are fundamentally for clothing and food.
If divided for currency,
it would cause much loss.
Moreover, they are damaged by the hands of merchants
and wasted
by cutting and measuring.
The disadvantages of this
were evident in the past.
Thus, Zhōng Yáo said,
'Deceptive and fraudulent people
compete to wet grain to gain profit,
and make thin silk to serve as
currency.'
In the Wèi era, even with severe penalties,
it could not be prohibited.
Therefore, Sīmǎ Zhī believed that using coins not only enriched the state,
but also reduced punishments.
The non-use of coins
was due to prolonged military strife,
which naturally led to their abandonment.
There was a reason for this,
as seen at the end of the Hàn Dynasty.
Now, to abolish them after they have been in use,
would suddenly deprive the people of their benefit.
If all the grain in the world were gathered
to provide food for all the world,
some granaries would overflow,
while others would have no stored provisions.
If they were to assist each other,
the poor would rely on
the rich.
The way to achieve wealth
truly depends on coins.
To suddenly cut them off
would make them useless objects.
Thus, those with money but no grain
would all sit and starve.
To decide
based on this
would again create a disadvantage.
Furthermore, where coins are currently used,
people do not consider themselves poor;
where grain is used,
people do not consider themselves rich.
Moreover, people have been accustomed to this for a long time,
and changing it would surely cause confusion.
The saying
goes,
'Unless the profit is a hundredfold,
one does not change profession,'
how much more so when coins are more convenient than grain!
When coins were abolished in Emperor Míng of Wèi's time,
and grain had been used for a long time,
it did not benefit the people.
So the entire court
held a great discussion.
All talented and perceptive officials believed it was appropriate to resume the use of coins;
there was no differing sentiment below,
and no differing opinion in court.
Even they abandoned grain and silk for coins,
which is
sufficient to show that the disadvantages of grain and silk were already evident and served as a warning.
Some in the world say that the Wèi clan, having not used coins for a long time,
accumulated millions,
and therefore wished to implement them,
to benefit the public and enrich the state.
This is most likely not true.
Jìn Wén, after his maternal uncle Jiùfàn's
counsel,
first established the trust of Chéng Jì,
believing that even with temporary merit,
it is not as good as benefits for ten thousand generations.
At that time, renowned worthies were in the ranks,
and gentlemen filled the court,
making great
plans for the advantages and disadvantages of the world,
and about to settle on essential statecraft.
If grain were truly more convenient than coins,
they would not have obscured the immediate benefits of the time,
and abandoned a universal practice for eternal use.
This can be definitively known.
This was truly due to distress and a desire for reform,
to change and make new arrangements.
Towards the end of Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
the world was at peace,
the times were harmonious, and the years were abundant.
The people were happy in their
work,
and grain and silk were plentiful,
almost to the point where every household had enough and every person was satisfied.
Examining the facts,
coins also did not hinder people.
Recently, military conflicts have repeatedly arisen,
and famines have followed one after another.
Hunger and cold have not yet been overcome,
which is precisely due to this.
Since Your Grace has come to rescue and relieve them,
greatly reforming what is seen and heard,
and generously strengthening the foundation
of instruction,
illuminate the policies for promoting agriculture,
reverently grant people their seasons,
each following their own occupation,
those who wander know to return,
those engaged in peripheral tasks spontaneously cease,
all competing with effort in the southern fields,
and there will be no uncultivated
land in the wilds.
From this point onward,
peace and prosperity will surely arrive,
so why worry about food and clothing!
Your humble servant believes that the method for rectifying abuses
does not require the abolition of currency.
The court council mostly agreed with Lín Zhī,
hence Xuán's proposal was not implemented.
Collation Notes
Zhì, Volume 17, Page 5, Line 1, Above
Indeed, the emperor-kings,
match their virtue with Heaven and Earth,
align with Yīn and Yáng,
issue commands and decrees,
their actions affecting the visible and the hidden,
and omens of good and ill fortune
arise in response to their influence.
Therefore, the Shū [Jīng] says:
"Follow the Way, and there is good fortune;
go against it, and there is ill fortune,
like an echo and a shadow."
In ancient times, Fúxī Shì succeeded Heaven as king,
received the Hétú,
and based on it drew [the trigrams],
which are the Bāguà.
Yǔ controlled the floods,
was granted the Luòshū,
and based on it arranged [the principles],
which is the Hóngfàn.
When the sages practice their Way [dào]
and cherish its truth,
Heaven assists them,
and there is nothing but good fortune.
From Sān Wǔ [the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors] downward,
each had their administrators.
It extended to Jīzǐ of Yīn,
