who held the position of Grand Tutor,
and presided over this great norm.
When Zhōu conquered Yīn,
Jīzǐ was brought back,
and King Wǔ humbly questioned him.
Jīzǐ replied with the Luòshū that Yǔ had obtained,
giving him its teachings.
Thus, the Hétú and Luòshū serve as warp and weft for each other,
and the Bāguà and Jiǔzhāng are its outer and inner layers.
When the Way of Yīn [dào] ended,
King Wén expanded the Zhōu Yì;
when the Way of Zhōu [dào] was in decline,
Kǒngzǐ wrote the Chūnqiū.
They upheld the Yīn and Yáng of Qián and Kūn,
and demonstrated the good and ill omens of the Hóngfàn,
the Way of Heaven and humanity becoming brilliantly clear.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
succeeding the Qín's destruction of learning,
during Emperor Wén's reign,
Fú Shēng created the Dàzhuàn,
and its words covered the Wǔxíng and various omens comprehensively.
Later, around the time of [Emperors] Jǐng and Wǔ,
Dǒng Zhòngshū studied the Gōngyáng Chūnqiū,
and first deduced Yīn and Yáng,
becoming a patriarch among scholars.
Between [Emperors] Xuān and Yuán,
Liú Xiàng studied the Gǔliáng Chūnqiū,
counted its misfortunes and blessings,
and transmitted it with the Hóngfàn,
differing greatly from Zhòngshū in many respects.
When Liú Xiàng's son, Liú Xīn, studied the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn,
his discussions of the Chūnqiū and Wǔxíng
were even more divergent.
Bān Gù, based on the Dàzhuàn,
and drawing from Zhòngshū, Liú Xiàng, and Liú Xīn, compiled the Wǔxíng Zhì,
and the transmission recorded the actions presented by Sūi Mèng, Xiàhóu Shèng, Jīng Fáng, Gǔ Yǒng, Lǐ Xún, and others,
concluding with Wáng Mǎng,
broadly interpreting auspicious and anomalous changes,
to append to the Chūnqiū.
To summarize,
there are three methods.
The first is:
if the ruler governs with the Way,
and ministers assist with utmost loyalty,
and all things fulfill their nature,
then harmonious energy responds,
auspicious signs appear,
and the state is at peace.
The second is:
if the ruler deviates from the Way,
petty individuals are in power,
and the populace loses its norms,
then discordant energy responds,
inauspicious signs appear,
and the state perishes.
The third is:
if the ruler and high ministers observe calamities and anomalies,
retire and reflect upon themselves,
take responsibility and cultivate virtue,
and together prevent and correct errors,
then misfortunes are averted and blessings arrive.
These are the general outlines.
Whenever these examples are cited,
interwoven with changes of the times,
subtly forming chapters,
they are indeed worth observing.
When Sīmǎ Biāo compiled the events of the Hàn dynasty after Emperor Guāngwǔ,
his explanations of calamities and misfortunes did not exceed the previous rules.
Now, we collect statements regarding auspicious and anomalous events from Huángchū onward
and record them in this chapter.
The Jīng says:
"The Wǔxíng are: first, water;
second, fire;
third, wood;
fourth, metal;
fifth, earth.
Water moistens downward;
fire flames upward;
wood bends and straightens;
metal yields and transforms;
earth allows planting and harvesting."
The Zhuàn says:
"If one hunts without lodging overnight,
eats without proper offering,
enters and exits without restraint,
seizes farmers' time, or harbors evil schemes,
then wood will not bend and straighten."
The Shuō says: Wood
is the east.
In the Yì,
wood above ground is Guān [Observation].
In royal affairs,
dignity, deportment, and appearance are also things to be observed.
Therefore, walking has the measure of jade pendants,
mounting a chariot has the rhythm of phoenix bells,
there is the system of three hunts,
and eating has the rites of offering and presenting;
coming and going have their proper names,
people are employed at the right time,
efforts are focused on encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
and plans are aimed at bringing peace to the common people.
If this is so,
then wood attains its nature.
If, however, one hunts and races about,
not returning to the palace;
indulges in food and drink,
disregarding laws and regulations;
arbitrarily raises labor service,
thereby taking away farmers' time;
or engages in treachery and deceit,
thereby harming people's wealth,
then wood loses its nature.
In such cases, artisans making wheels and arrows often suffer damage and failure,
and wood transforms into abnormalities,
which is "not bending and straightening."
In the first month of the sixth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
it rained,
and trees froze.
According to Liú Xīn's explanation,
if the upper Yáng influence does not descend,
and the lower Yīn influence does not ascend,
then it rains,
and trees freeze because of it,
and the misty air is cold,
so wood does not bend and straighten.
Liú Xiàng said:
Ice is the abundance of Yīn;
wood is lesser Yáng,
symbolizing noble ministers, high officials, and grand masters.
If such people are about to suffer harm,
then Yīn energy threatens wood,
and wood first becomes cold,
hence it rains and freezes.
In the sixth month of that year,
Cài Fāng and other soldiers of Lìchéng Commandery killed the Administrator Xú Zhì,
seized the commandery, and rebelled.
The Administrator [Tàishǒu]
was like the feudal lords of old,
an omen of harm to noble ministers.
Another theory considers tree freezing as "wood armor" [mù jiè],
and "armor" [jiè] is a symbol of soldiers and weapons.
In that year,
after Cài Fāng was suppressed,
in the eighth month, the Son of Heaven himself led a naval force to conquer Wú,
with over ten myriad garrison soldiers,
extending banners for several hundred Lǐ,
reviewing troops by the river,
and it was also a time of constant rain.
On Xīnwèi day in the second month of the third year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
it rained,
and trees froze.
Two years later,
Zhōu Yí and others were killed;
this was the upper Yáng influence not descending.
In the eighth year of Yǒnghé, in the first month, on the day Yǐsì, during the reign of Mùdì,
there was rain,
and trees were covered in ice.
In this year, Yīn Hào led a northern expedition;
the next year, his army was defeated;
and in the tenth year, he was deposed.
It is also said that
Xún Xiàn's and Yīn Hào's northern expeditions
were portents for Huán Wēn's entry into the pass.
In the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán, in the twelfth month, on the day Yǐsì, during the reign of Xiàowǔdì,
there was rain,
and trees were covered in ice.
The next year, in the second month, Wáng Gōng became the Northern Commander;
in the eighth month, Yú Kǎi became the Western Commander;
in the ninth month, Wáng Guóbǎo became the Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
and soon after, he was appointed General of the Army;
in the seventeenth year, Yīn Zhòngkān became the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Although the righteous and the wicked had different aims,
they ultimately met the same end of destruction,
which was the fulfillment of these portents.
In the second year of Jiànxīng, during the reign of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
Zhūgě Kè campaigned against Huáinán.
Afterwards, the central beam of the hall where he used to sit broke.
Kè wantonly raised troops for campaigns,
disrupted agricultural seasons,
formed wicked plots,
and damaged the nation's financial resources.
Thus, the wood lost its natural properties and caused the damage and breakage.
Upon his return, he was executed and exterminated.
In the *Zhōu Yì*, this is also
“the ill omen of a broken ridgepole.”
In the fifth year of Tàikāng, in the fifth month, during the reign of Wǔdì,
the ground of Xuāndì's ancestral temple caved in,
and beams broke.
In the eighth year, in the first month,
the Grand Ancestral Temple hall again caved in.
The temple was rebuilt,
and the foundation was laid down to the spring.
In the ninth month of that year,
a new temple was eventually constructed,
with fine timber brought from afar,
mixed with bronze pillars.
Chén Xié was the master craftsman,
and six thousand people worked on it.
It was completed in the fourth month of the tenth year.
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngyín, a beam broke again.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say:
the caving in of the ground signifies separation;
the breaking of beams means wood not being straight or curved.
The next year, the Emperor passed away,
and the royal house subsequently fell into chaos.
In the second year of Tàiyì, during the reign of Huìdì,
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng sent Lù Jī to lead troops towards the capital
to attack Chángshā Wáng.
When the army began to march, the general's standard pole broke.
Soon after, the battle was lost,
Lù Jī was executed,
Yǐng subsequently fled and collapsed,
and was eventually granted death.
This was the punishment for treacherous plots,
meaning wood not being straight or curved.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng, during the reign of Yuándì,
Wáng Dūn was in Wǔchāng.
Under his bell, the ceremonial standard grew flowers like lotuses,
which withered and fell after five or six days.
This was the wood losing its natural properties.
Gān Bǎo believed that wild flowers growing on dead wood,
and also within the bell chamber,
indicated that the splendor of authority,
and the flourishing of glory,
were all like the blooming of wild flowers,
unable to last long.
Afterwards, Wáng Dūn ultimately faced execution, his corpse being mutilated for his rebellious actions.
Another explanation is also that it was a calamitous bloom,
which in the *Zhōu Yì* is
“a withered poplar growing flowers.”
When Huán Xuán first usurped power,
the pole of the dragon banner broke.
At that time, Xuán was excessively engaged in hunting,
indulged in extravagant food and drink,
his construction projects interfered with agriculture,
and he also engaged in many treacherous plots.
Therefore, the wood lost its natural properties.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say:
a banner is used to display the three luminaries,
making them clearly visible.
The breaking of the banner pole
means that high brightness has departed.
Xuán indeed failed.
The tradition states:
“If one abandons laws,
expels meritorious ministers,
kills the heir apparent,
and takes a concubine as wife,
then fire will not rise upwards.”
The explanation says: fire,
being of the South,
is that which radiates light and brilliance to bring illumination.
As for a ruler,
he faces south, towards the light, and governs.
The *Shū* says:
“To know men is to be wise,
and to be able to appoint officials.”
Thus, Yáo and Shùn elevated all worthy men and appointed them to court,
and sent away the four wicked ones, banishing them to the wilderness.
Confucius said:
“If insidious slanders
and direct accusations
make no headway,
he may be called enlightened.”
If the worthy and the wicked are distinguished,
officials are appointed in order,
following old regulations,
meritorious achievements are respected,
and legitimate and illegitimate children are clearly separated,
then fire will attain its natural properties.
But if one's faith in the Way is not firm,
or if one displays falsehoods,
if slandering men flourish,
and evil overcomes righteousness,
then fire will lose its natural properties.
From above descending,
and when uncontrolled flames rise wantonly,
burning ancestral temples,
and incinerating palaces and mansions,
even if a large army is mobilized,
it cannot save it,
this is what is meant by fire not rising upwards.
In the fifth year of Tàihé, in the fifth month, during the reign of Wèi Míngdì,
Qīngshāng Hall caught fire.
Initially,
when the Emperor was Prince of Píngyuán,
he took a Lady Yú from Hénán as his consort.
Upon his ascension,
he did not make her Empress,
but instead established the daughter of Máo Jiā, a common carriage maker, as Empress.
The Empress was originally of humble origin,
unsuitable for such elevation,
this was the punishment for taking a concubine as wife.
In the sixth month of the first year of Qīnglóng,
the Jūshì chamber of Luòyáng Palace caught fire.
In the fourth month of the second year,
Chónghuá Hall caught fire,
extending to the southern chamber,
and was repaired.
In the seventh month of the third year,
this hall caught fire again.
The Emperor asked Gāotáng Lóng:
“What is the cause of this calamity?
Is there a ritual meaning to praying or averting it?”
He replied:
“The occurrence of disasters and anomalies
are all for the purpose of clarifying warnings and instructions.
Only by following rituals and cultivating virtue can one overcome them.
The *Yì Zhuàn* says: 'If the superiors are not frugal,
and the inferiors are not restrained,
calamitous fire will burn their dwellings.'
It also says: 'If the ruler elevates his platforms,
heavenly fire will be the calamity.'
This means that if a ruler merely adorns his palaces,
unaware of the people's destitution,
Heaven responds with drought,
and fire starts from the high halls.
According to old divination records,
the outbreak of calamitous fires
are all warnings regarding platforms, pavilions, palaces, and mansions.
Now, it is appropriate to dismiss the laborers,
strive for frugality,
clean the areas affected by the fire,
and not engage in any construction there.
Auspicious *shāpú* and excellent grain will surely grow in this place,
to reward Your Majesty's devout and reverent virtue.”
The Emperor did not follow this advice.
He subsequently rebuilt Chónghuá Hall,
renaming it Jiǔlóng.
Because there were nine reports of dragon sightings from various commanderies and states,
it was given this name.
He largely abandoned laws and regulations,
exhausted the populace to indulge his desires,
which was the fulfillment of taking a concubine as wife.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Jiànxīng of Wú Sūn Liàng,
the Duānmén gate in Wǔchāng was damaged by fire.
It was rebuilt,
but Duānmén was damaged by fire again.
The inner palace gate
was where imperial decrees were issued;
the palace
was where political affairs were conducted.
At this time, Zhūgě Kè held power,
and was arrogant and unrestrained.
Sūn Jùn commanded the imperial guards,
and his sinister intentions eventually came to light.
Wǔchāng
was where the Sūn clan began their imperial title.
Heaven’s warning seemed to say:
“It is appropriate to eliminate the heads of those who are noble and powerful.”
Sure enough, Zhūgě Kè lost his army and annihilated people,
and Sūn Jùn handed over political power to Sūn Chēn,
who then deposed Sūn Liàng.
Some say that
Sūn Quán demolished Wǔchāng to augment the Tàichūgōng Palace,
and Zhūgě Kè had the intention of relocating the capital,
rebuilding gates and palaces.
The timing was inappropriate for these actions,
hence the disaster.
Jīng Fáng’s Yì Zhuàn says:
“If the ruler does not contemplate the Dao,
the omen is fire burning the palace.”
On the first day of the second month of the first year of Tàipíng,
Jiànyè caught fire,
a fire caused by man.
That autumn,
Sūn Chēn began to hold power,
falsely using Sūn Liàng’s edict to kill Lǚ Jù and Téng Yìn.
The next year,
he again arbitrarily killed Zhū Yì.
This was the punishment for abandoning laws and expelling meritorious officials.
In the second month of the fifth year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Xiū,
the north tower of the west gate of the city caught fire.
In the tenth month of the sixth year,
the small city of Shítóu caught fire,
burning one hundred and eighty zhàng in the southwest.
At this time, the favorite Zhāng Bù monopolized state power,
committing many acts of disrespect,
while Wéi Zhāo and Shèng Chōng were ultimately dismissed and not used.
Moreover, he dispatched inspectors and generals to serve as internal officials,
alarming and disturbing the provinces and commanderies,
leading to the rebellion in Jiāozhǐ.
This was his fault.
In the third month of the second year of Jiànhéng of Sūn Hào,
there was a great fire,
burning over ten thousand households,
and seven hundred people died.
According to the Chūnqiū, there was a great disaster in Qí.
Liú Xiàng believed that Dàihán Gōng was fond of inner palace affairs,
listened to women,
and frequently changed wives and concubines, which was the punishment.
At that time, Sūn Hào’s decrees were perverse and cruel,
abandoning laws and regulations.
Many hardworking officials and famous scholars
were executed or banished.
There were over ten thousand women in the harem,
and female courtiers frequently intervened.
Among them, many received great favor and wore the imperial seals and sashes of empresses,
hence the great fire.
On the yǐchǒu day of the third month of the eighth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
a fire disaster struck the west wing, the quarters where the King of Chǔ resided, and the windows of the Línshāngguān pavilion.
On the guǐchǒu day of the fourth month of the tenth year,
the Chóngxiándiàn Palace caught fire.
On the gēngchén day of the eleventh month,
the Hánzhāngjūshì room, the front corridor of Xiūchéngtáng hall, the east house of Jǐngfāng, and the south wing of Huīzhāngdiàn Palace caught fire.
At that time, someone submitted a memorial saying:
“In the Hàn dynasty, the Wáng clan had five marquises,
brothers successively holding office.
Now the Yáng clan has three dukes,
all in high positions.
Thus, heavenly anomalies have appeared repeatedly.
I secretly worry about this for Your Majesty.”
Because of this, Yáng Yáo requested to retire.
At this time, the Emperor accepted Fēng Dǎn’s slander,
abolished Zhāng Huà’s merits,
listened to Yáng Jùn’s calumny,
and estranged Wèi Guàn from his favor.
This was the punishment for expelling meritorious officials.
The next year,
the imperial carriage passed away (the emperor died).
After this, the King of Chǔ (Sīmǎ Wéi) carried out his secret instructions,
killing and harming the two dukes (Yáng Jùn and Wèi Guàn),
but he himself did not escape.
The fire disaster struck his quarters—
was this also Heaven’s will?
On the gēngyín day of the intercalary month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
the imperial armory caught fire.
Zhāng Huà suspected chaos,
first ordered a firm defense,
and then put out the fire.
As a result, treasures accumulated over generations,
Wáng Mǎng’s head,
Kǒngzǐ’s clogs,
Hàn Gāozǔ’s sword that cut the white snake, and weapons for two million men
were all consumed at once.
This was the punishment for the later killing of the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái.
Heaven’s warning seemed to say:
“Setting up defenses and beating watchtowers
is how one secures the state.
Stockpiling military equipment
is how one guards against unforeseen dangers.
Now the heir apparent is about to fall,
the state is about to perish,
the imperial army has nowhere to be deployed again,
and who will protect the imperial forces?”
The Emperor and Empress did not realize this,
and eventually lost the four seas.
This was its fulfillment.
Zhāng Huà and Yán Zuǎn
both said,
“When the imperial armory burned and the Dī and Qiāng rebelled,
and the Crown Prince was deposed,
then the fate of the realm was known.”
In the eleventh month of the eighth year,
the Gāoyuánlíng tomb caught fire.
At this time, Empress Jiǎ was cruel and unrestrained,
and Jiǎ Mì monopolized the court.
Their evil accumulated and their crimes ripened,
they deserved to be executed.
Heaven’s warning seemed to say:
“Those who are unfit as ministers or servants,
even if their closeness and nobility are unmatched,
should still be endured and then executed,
just as I burned the Gāoyuánlíng tomb.”
The Emperor was already feeble-minded,
and Zhāng Huà did not accept the advice of Péi Wěi and Liú Biàn,
so the Empress and Jiǎ Mì eventually killed the Crown Prince.
Gān Bǎo believed that
“the fire at Gāoyuánlíng
was the omen for the Crown Prince’s deposition.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the Gāoyuánbiàndiàn Palace caught fire,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū’s interpretation was the same as this omen.”
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
the Emperor took Empress Yáng as his wife.
When the Empress was about to enter the palace,
fire suddenly appeared in her clothes,
which everyone found strange.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
the King of Chéngdū (Sīmǎ Yǐng) then deposed the Empress,
and she was confined in the Jīnyōngchéng city.
After this, she was reinstated,
and was deposed and reinstated four more times.
An edict also ordered her to commit suicide,
but Xún Fān petitioned for her life.
Although she returned to her position,
the distress, coercion, and humiliation she suffered
were unheard of throughout history.
This was the fulfillment of the ominous fire.
On the jiǎwǔ day of the seventh month of the second year of Yǒngxīng,
fire broke out in the various offices of the Shàngshū province,
extending to the Chónglǐtà gate and the covered walkway.
The hundred offices are the foundation of royal governance;
this was the omen of the king abandoning laws and regulations.
Later, King Qīnghé (Sīmǎ Tán) entered to succeed,
but did not remain in his position until the end,
and this was also the punishment for killing the Crown Prince.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái,
Xiāngyáng caught fire,
burning over three thousand people to death.
At this time, Wáng Rú proclaimed himself Grand General and Inspector of the Yǒng and Sī provinces,
with a force of forty to fifty thousand,
attacking and plundering commanderies and counties.
This was the omen of inferiors encroaching upon superiors,
and the Yang principle losing its proper measure.
During the Tàixīng reign of Emperor Yuán,
Wáng Dūn was stationed in Wǔchāng,
and Wǔchāng suffered a fire.
Fire broke out,
and he raised a crowd to extinguish it.
While putting it out here, it flared up there,
appearing simultaneously in dozens of places to the east, west, south, and north,
and continued for several days.
The old saying states,
“When a rampant blaze arises without cause,
even if an army is raised, it cannot extinguish it.”
This is what it refers to.
Gān Bǎo believed that
“this was a minister acting as a ruler,
the excessive Yang principle losing its proper measure.
This was Wáng Dūn encroaching upon his superiors,
having a heart without a ruler,
hence the disaster.”
On the guǐsì day of the first month of the second year of Yǒngchāng,
the capital suffered a great fire.
In the third month,
the three counties of Ráonán, Dōngguāng, and Ānlíng caught fire,
burning over seven thousand households,
and fifteen thousand people died.
In the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng, in the first month,
the capital caught fire.
At this time, Wáng Dūn insulted and belittled the imperial court,
acting with much irreverence.
Officials, both internal and external, all harbored resentment and malice,
which was an extreme yin generating yang.
In the second year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng, in the fifth month,
the capital caught fire.
In the first year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Kāng, in the seventh month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Wújùn suffered a disaster.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù, in the sixth month,
a lightning strike damaged Shí Jìlóng's Tàiwǔ Hall and the front gates of the two ancestral temples.
The lightning-induced fire raged for over a month before it was extinguished,
destroying all metal and stone.
Afterward, Jìlóng died,
great chaos ensued,
and his state was consequently destroyed.
During the Tàihé reign of the Duke of Hǎixī,
Xī Yīn served as the Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the sixth month, there was a great drought,
and fire burned down several thousand households,
extending to the Shānyīn granary, destroying several million hù of rice.
The flames and smoke obscured the sky,
making it impossible to extinguish.
This too was a response to Huán Wēn's growing power,
as he was about to depose the Duke of Hǎixī,
an extreme yin generating yang.
In the first year of Níngkāng of Emperor Xiàowǔ, in the third month,
a great wind and fire broke out in the capital.
At this time, Huán Wēn entered the court,
with the ambition to usurp the throne.
The young emperor had just ascended,
and people were filled with worry and fear.
This was similar to the fire during the Tàiníng era.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán, in the first month,
students of the Guózǐ (National Academy) set fire with the aid of the wind,
burning down over a hundred rooms.
Thereafter, performance reviews were not strict,
and rewards and punishments lacked clear criteria.
There was the name of nurturing talent,
but no reality of recruiting worthy individuals.
This was a premonition of the punishment for a lack of wisdom.
In the thirteenth year, in the twelfth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
the Yánxián Hall suffered a disaster.
In the same month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Zhōngsī Zébǎi Hall, the guest quarters, and the Pàoqí Commandant's armory all suffered disasters.
At that time, the court had many corrupt policies,
and decline was increasingly evident.
The punishments for a lack of wisdom
all had symbolic significance,
but the emperor and ministers did not realize it,
ultimately leading to chaos and destruction.
Wèi Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ favored Buddhist nuns and foster mothers,
each promoting their relatives,
even allowing them to enter and exit the imperial palace,
and be formally received by the ruler.
Heaven's warning seemed to say,
"Those who enter the Yánxián Hall and guest quarters are mostly not the right people,"
hence the disaster.
Moreover,
Emperor Xiàowǔ did not establish an empress,
but favored the low-born Fūrén Zhāng.
The Fūrén was arrogant and jealous,
and the imperial princes were not numerous,
going against
the principle of "Zhōngsī Zébǎi" (numerous descendants),
hence the disaster to that hall.
Dàozǐ also awarded rewards without restraint,
hence the armories suffered disasters,
this too being his punishment.
In the second year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān, in the third month,
two dragon boats caught fire,
which was water harming fire.
Thereafter, Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
and the emperor was exiled.
Heaven's warning seemed to say,
"The king will be exiled,
and will no longer ride dragon boats,"
hence the disaster.
In the first year of Yuánxīng, in the eighth month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
the Xìashècáo of the Shàngshū caught fire.
At the time, Huán Xuán was remotely overseeing the Shàngshū (Secretariat),
so Heaven sent fire
to indicate that he would no longer reside there.
In the third year,
Lú Xún attacked and plundered Guǎngzhōu.
The governor, Wú Yǐnzhī, closed the city gates and held firm.
On the night of the day Rénxū in the tenth month,
a fire broke out.
At that time, the city was full of people avoiding the bandits.
Yǐnzhī feared there were collaborators with the bandits,
and only focused on strict military enforcement,
not first extinguishing the fire.
Consequently, the government buildings were burned down,
and over ten thousand people died in the fire.
The people then scattered and collapsed,
all captured by the bandits.
In the fourth year of Yìxī, in the seventh month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the Lìbùcáo of the Shàngshū Diànzhōng caught fire.
In the ninth year,
the capital suffered a great fire,
burning several thousand households.
In the eleventh year,
great fires occurred everywhere in the capital,
especially severe in the Wú region.
Fire prevention measures were very strict,
yet the fires continued.
Wáng Hóng, then Administrator of Wújùn,
was in the public office during the day
when he saw a red object descend from the sky,
shaped like a signal banner,
remotely landing on the roof of a house south of the road,
and a great fire immediately erupted.
Hóng knew it was a disaster caused by Heaven,
so he did not punish the fire's owner.
This was a sign of the decline of the imperial house.
The commentary says:
"If one repairs palaces,
decorates terraces,
engages in internal debauchery,
offends relatives,
insults fathers and elder brothers,
then crops will not mature."
The explanation says: Earth,
in the center,
is that which gives birth to all things.
For a ruler,
it pertains to internal affairs,
palaces, husband and wife, relatives,
who also generate each other.
In ancient times, for the Son of Heaven and feudal lords,
there were regulations on the size and height of palaces and ancestral temples.
There were limits on the number of empresses, consorts, and concubines.
The nine clans, near and distant, old and young, had their proper order.
Confucius said:
"In rites,
rather than being extravagant,
it is better to be frugal."
Thus, Yǔ had humble palaces,
and King Wén set an example for his wife.
This is how the sages made their civilizing influence manifest.
If this were so,
then earth would attain its proper nature.
But if there is extravagance, debauchery, arrogance, and rudeness,
then earth loses its proper nature.
Even without floods or droughts, crops and grains do not ripen,
this is what is meant by "crops not maturing."
During the time of Sūn Hào of Wú,
there were no floods or droughts year after year,
and the sprouts and crops were abundant and beautiful, but the grains did not form.
The common people suffered from hunger,
and this was true throughout the entire region,
continuing for consecutive years.
The people of Wú thought it was due to dew damage,
which was incorrect.
According to Liú Xiàng's commentary on the Chūnqiū, it states:
"Floods and droughts should be recorded.
If floods and droughts are not recorded, but it is said that there was 'a great lack of wheat and grain,'
it means the earth's energy did not nourish,
and crops did not mature."
This is its meaning.
Hào initially moved the capital to Wǔchāng,
then soon returned to Jiànyè.
He also built new halls,
decorated with pearls and jade,
exceedingly magnificent.
He destroyed various camps
and expanded the imperial gardens,
transgressing against the heat and hindering farming,
causing fatigue to both officials and private citizens.
The Yuèlíng states that
one should not undertake earthworks in late summer,
but Hào violated all of these.
This was the punishment for repairing palaces and decorating terraces.
In the second year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
Wújùn, Wúxīng, and Dōngyáng had no wheat or grain,
and there was a great famine.
In the fifth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
there was no wheat or grain,
and a great famine afflicted the whole realm.
In the tenth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù,
the three types of wheat failed to ripen.
In the twelfth year,
there was a great lack of wheat.
In the sixth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
there was no wheat or grain,
and a great famine afflicted the whole realm.
In the first year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān,
there was no wheat or grain,
and a great famine afflicted the whole realm.
The commentary says:
"If one is fond of warfare and attacks,
disregards the common people,
adorns city walls,
and invades border regions,
then metal will not be pliable."
It is said: Metal [Jīn],
is the West,
where all things are fully formed,
and the beginning of the killing aura.
Therefore, at the beginning of autumn [Lìqiū], falcons and hawks strike;
at the autumn equinox [Qiūfēn], a light frost descends.
As for the affairs of the king,
it is to dispatch armies and march troops,
to hold banners and wield battle-axes,
to rally the soldiers and masses,
to display might and valor,
thereby conquering rebels [pànnì]
and suppressing violent uprisings.
The Odes [Shī] say:
"Reverently he holds the battle-axe,
like a blazing fire."
And it also says:
"We sheathe our shields and spears,
we store our bows and arrows."
Movement and stillness should be appropriate;
when incited to face difficulties,
people forget their deaths,
and metal [Jīn] obtains its nature.
But if one is greedy and self-indulgent,
focused on establishing power and victory,
and disregards human lives,
then metal [Jīn] loses its nature.
When artisans cast metal and iron,
if it freezes, becomes stagnant, dries up, and hardens,
many will not succeed,
and this results in anomalies and monstrosities.
This is called metal [Jīn] not yielding to change [bù cónggé].
During the Wèi [Wèi] period, a stone omen [shíruì] in Zhāngyè [Zhāngyè]
was indeed a propitious sign for Jìn [Jìn],
but for Wèi [Wèi] it was an omen of disaster [yāo].
Fond of warfare,
disregarding the common people,
adorning cities and walls,
encroaching on borders—
all three ancestors of the Wèi [Wèi] clan engaged in such acts.
The stone inscription [Shítú] revealed an extraordinary text;
this was an anomaly of not yielding to change [bù cónggé].
When Jìn [Jìn] established its great enterprise,
many of the Cáo [Cáo] clan perished;
the stone omen text [Shíruìwén]
was an echo of "greatly attacking Cáo [Cáo]".
According to Liú Xīn [Liú Xīn], the stone speaking in Jìn [Jìn] during the Spring and Autumn [Chūnqiū] period
was because metal [Jīn] and stone [shí] are of the same category.
This is an instance of metal [Jīn] not yielding to change [bù cónggé],
losing its nature.
Liú Xiàng [Liú Xiàng] believed that white stones were primary,
belonging to auspicious white omens [báixiáng].
During the Qīnglóng [Qīnglóng] reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi [Wèi Míngdì],
extravagant construction of palaces took place.
Golden sculptures of barbarians [Jīndí] were taken from Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān] in the west.
The dew-collecting plate [chénglùpán] broke,
its sound heard for dozens of *lǐ*.
The golden barbarians [Jīndí] wept,
and so they were left in Bàchéng [Bàchéng].
This was metal [Jīn] losing its nature and becoming an anomaly.
During the Wú [Wú] period,
in Lìyáng [Lìyáng] county, there was a rock fissure [yánchuān]
resembling a seal.
Everyone said,
"When the stone seal [shíyìn] is opened,
all under heaven will be at peace."
In the first year of Tiānxǐ [Tiānxǐ] of Sūn Hào [Sūn Hào],
the seal was opened.
Also,
in Yángxiàn [Yángxiàn] mountain, there was a stone cave [shíxué]
over ten *zhàng* long.
Hào [Hào] initially renovated the Wǔchāng [Wǔchāng] palace,
with the intention of moving the capital.
At this time, Wǔchāng [Wǔchāng] was a detached palace [lígōng].
Bān Gù [Bān Gù] said,
"A detached palace [lígōng] and a city wall [chéngguō] have the same omen,"
referring to the adornment of cities and walls.
Three years after Bǎodǐng [Bǎodǐng],
Hào [Hào] went out through the Eastern Pass [Dōngguān],
sending Dīng Fèng [Dīng Fèng] to Héfèi [Héfèi].
In the third year of Jiànhéng [Jiànhéng], Hào [Hào] again launched a major expedition from Huálǐ [Huálǐ],
referring to encroaching on borders.
Thus, metal [Jīn] lost its nature,
and Wú [Wú] ultimately perished, with Hào [Hào] bound and facing his demise.
In the third intercalary month of Yuánkāng [Yuánkāng] (third year) of Emperor Huì [Huìdì],
all six bells in front of the palace shed tears,
stopping after five *kè*.
The previous year, Empress Jiǎ [Jiǎhòu] had killed Grand Empress Dowager Yáng [Yáng Tàihòu] in Jīnyōng Chéng [Jīnyōng Chéng],
and Empress Jiǎ's [Jiǎhòu] wickedness did not cease.
Therefore, the bells shed tears,
still grieving her.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng [Yǒngxīng],
Chéngdū [Chéngdū] attacked Chángshā [Chángshā].
Every night, the tips of the spears and halberds had a fiery glow like hanging candles.
This shows disregard for human life and a fondness for warfare,
where metal [Jīn] lost its nature and became a luminous anomaly.
Heaven's warning seemed to say,
"Weapons are like fire;
if not contained, they will burn oneself."
Chéngdū [Chéngdū] did not realize this,
and ultimately perished in defeat.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā [Yǒngjiā] of Emperor Huái [Huáidì],
in Xiàng [Xiàng] county, on the stone tablet of Jiǎ Kuí [Jiǎ Kuí], the Inspector of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu] for Wèi [Wèi],
gold grew and could be harvested.
This was metal [Jīn] not yielding to change [bù cónggé] and becoming an anomaly.
In the fifth month,
Jí Sāng [Jí Sāng] rebelled,
and bandits arose like a storm.
When Qīnghé Wáng Tán [Qīnghé Wáng Tán] was the heir apparent,
the golden bell he wore suddenly grew protuberances like millet grains.
King Kāng's [Kāng Wáng] mother suspected it was inauspicious [bùxiáng]
and destroyed and discarded it.
Later, when he became Emperor Huì's [Huìdì]太子 [tàizǐ],
he did not complete his tenure,
and was ultimately killed by Sīmǎ Yuè [Sīmǎ Yuè].
In the fifth year of Jiànxīng [Jiànxīng] of Emperor Mǐn [Mǐndì],
a stone spoke in Píngyáng [Píngyáng].
At this time, the emperor, in distress, was also in Píngyáng [Píngyáng].
Therefore, an object incapable of speech spoke,
which was the greatest of omens of disaster [yāo].
Soon after, the emperor was murdered by rebel Hú [Hú].
In the first year of Yǒngchāng [Yǒngchāng] of Emperor Yuán [Yuándì],
Gān Zhuó [Gān Zhuó] was about to attack Wáng Dūn [Wáng Dūn],
but later stopped.
When he returned,
his household experienced many strange occurrences;
he looked in the mirror and could not see his head.
This was metal [Jīn] losing its nature and becoming an omen of disaster [yāo].
Soon after, he was attacked by Dūn [Dūn],
and was utterly annihilated.
During Shí Jìlóng's [Shí Jìlóng] time,
two golden phoenixes on the Fèngyáng Mén [Fèngyáng Mén] gate of Yèchéng [Yèchéng] flew into the Zhāng Hé [Zhāng Hé] river.
During the Tàihé [Tàihé] reign of Hǎixī [Hǎixī],
a granary was built in Kuàijī Shānyīn [Kuàijī Shānyīn] county.
While digging, two large boats were found,
full of coins.
All the coins had a large circular pattern.
It was nearing dusk,
so the diggers rushed to report to the officials.
The officials dispatched a strict guard that night.
By dawn,
the money was gone,
only the boats remained.
Upon inspection,
all the places where the money had been were visible.
In the early Yìxī [Yìxī] reign of Emperor Ān [Āndì],
Yīn Zhòngwén [Yīn Zhòngwén], the Administrator of Dōngyáng [Dōngyáng], looked in the mirror and could not see his head.
Soon after, he was also executed,
the omen being the same as Gān Zhuó [Gān Zhuó].
The tradition says:
"If ancestral temples [zōngmiào] are neglected,
sacrifices and prayers are not offered,
rites are abandoned,
and the timing of Heaven is defied,
then water will not flow downwards."
It is said: Water [Shuǐ]
is the North,
that which ultimately stores all things.
In terms of human conduct,
when life ends, the body is stored,
and the spirit disperses.
The sages established ancestral temples [zōngmiào] for them,
to gather the souls and vital energy,
and offered sacrifices in spring and autumn,
to fulfill filial piety.
When a king ascends the throne,
he must offer suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth [jiāosì tiāndì],
pray to gods and spirits,
attend to the ranks of mountains and rivers,
and conciliate all deities;
none are left unserved.
He meticulously observes fasting and abstinence,
and displays solemn reverence.
Therefore, ghosts and spirits accept the offerings,
and bestow abundant blessings and assistance.
This is how sage kings comply with the *yīn* [yīn] energy,
and harmonize gods and humans.
And when issuing decrees and commands,
they also adhere to the timing of Heaven.
If all twelve months obtain their proper *qì* [qì],
then *yīn* [yīn] and *yáng* [yáng] are harmonious, and beginning and end are completed.
If this is so,
then water [Shuǐ] obtains its nature.
But if ghosts and spirits are not revered,
and government decrees defy the seasons,
water [Shuǐ] loses its nature.
Misty waters erupt violently,
a hundred rivers overflow in reverse,
destroying towns and villages,
drowning people,
and excessive rain damages crops.
This is called water [Shuǐ] not flowing downwards.
Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn says:
"He who is wholly devoted to affairs is promoted.
When punishments and penalties violate reason,
the disaster is water.
When it is water,
there is rain,
killing people,
with falling frost,
and a great wind that makes the sky yellow.
When there is famine but no reduction in labor,
this is called tài (excess),
the disaster is great floods,
water kills people.
When the virtuous are obstructed and suppressed,
this is called kuáng (madness),
the disaster is water,
and the flowing water kills people.
After the water, the earth produces insects.
When imprisonment is not released,
this is called zhuī fēi (pursuing wrong),
the water is cold,
killing people.
When executions are pursued endlessly,
this is called bù lǐ (unreasonable),
the disaster is water and the five grains are not harvested.
When great defeats are not resolved,
this is called jiē yīn (all yin),
the disaster is water flowing into cities and towns,
and frost killing the grain."
Dǒng Zhòngshū says:
"When armies clash and enmities form,
corpses lie scattered and blood flows,
the common people are distressed and resentful,
yin energy flourishes,
hence great floods."
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
there was heavy continuous rain.
The Yī and Luò rivers overflowed,
reaching the city gates of Jīnyáng,
sweeping away several thousand homes,
and killing people.
Initially,
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
he moved from Yè to Luò,
constructing palaces and chambers,
but did not establish ancestral temples.
The spirit tablets of Tài Zǔ were still in Yè.
He once held offerings and sacrifices in Jiànshǐ Diàn as if for family rituals,
and throughout Huángchū he never returned to Yè.
Moreover, the deities of the suburban sacrifices
had no fixed position.
This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples and abandoning sacrifices.
In the summer of the eighth year of Chìwū of Sūn Quán of Wú,
Chálíng County experienced a great flood,
sweeping away over two hundred homes.
In the autumn of the thirteenth year,

It is recorded that Quán reigned as emperor for thirty years,
yet never established seven ancestral temples in Jiànyè.
Only one temple for his father, Sūn Jiān, was far away in Chángshā,
and the suburban sacrifice rituals were incomplete.
In the early Jiāhé period,
officials petitioned that suburban sacrifices should be performed,
but he did not permit it.
Although he performed one southern suburban sacrifice in his later years,
the northern suburban sacrifice was never heard of.
The veneration for Wú and Chǔ was also not given due order,
instead, he sacrificed to the demonic deities of Luóyáng,
seeking blessings and assistance.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
Quán neglected ancestral temples,
did not offer prayers and sacrifices,
and abandoned rituals,
therefore this punishment was shown,
hoping he would be enlightened.
In the first year of Tàiyuán,
there was again an anomaly of great winds and surging waters.
That winter,
Quán performed the southern suburban sacrifice.
Perhaps this was a reflection on the ominous omens!
Upon returning, he fell ill,
and died in the fourth month of the following year.
Some say
that Quán at that time readily believed slander and accusations.
Even though Lù Xùn had great merit,
and Sūn Hé was the heir apparent,
they still did not have a good end,
which is similar to Emperor Ān of Hàn believing slander and dismissing Yáng Zhèn, and deposing the Crown Prince.
Furthermore, during the Chìwū period, there was no year without military campaigns,

In the autumn of the eighth year,

In the ninth month of the first year of Jǐngchū of Emperor Míng of Wèi,

Water overflowed in the four provinces of Jì, Yǎn, Xú, and Yù,

From the beginning of his reign,
the Emperor indulged in extravagance and extreme desires,
appropriating many young girls,

He excessively decorated palaces and chambers,
hindering agriculture and warfare,
and indulged his passions and desires,
which became even worse by this time.
His decrees were contrary to the times,

This was the manifestation of water not moistening the lower regions.
In the summer of the first year of Wǔfèng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,

Liàng only established a temple for Quán four years after his ascension.
Moreover, throughout the Wú dynasty, the ancestors were not given imperial titles,

Liàng, Xiū, and Hào also both abolished the two suburban sacrifices,

This was the punishment for neglecting ancestral temples and not offering sacrifices.
Furthermore,
at this time, Sūn Jùn held exclusive power,
