The Classic says:
"The common practice involves five matters: first, demeanor;
second, speech;
third, sight;
fourth, hearing;
fifth, thought.
Demeanor should be respectful (gōng);
speech should be compliant (cóng);
sight should be clear (míng);
hearing should be acute (cōng);
thought should be discerning (ruì).
Respect (gōng) produces solemnity (sù);
compliance (cóng) produces [missing character in source, often 'mù'];
clarity (míng) produces wisdom (zhé);
acuteness (cōng) produces deliberation (móu);
discernment (ruì) produces sageliness (shèng).
Auspicious omens: for solemnity (sù), timely rain;
for [missing character], timely sunshine;
for wisdom (zhé), timely warmth;
for deliberation (móu), timely cold;
for sageliness (shèng), timely wind.
Inauspicious omens: for wildness (kuáng), excessive rain;
for usurpation (jiàn), excessive sunshine;
for indulgence (yù), excessive warmth;
for urgency (jí), excessive cold;
for obscurity (méng),
〔一三〕excessive wind."
The Commentary says:
"When demeanor is not respectful,
it is called lack of solemnity (bùsù).
Its affliction is wildness (kuáng),
its punishment is rain,
its extreme is evil.
At such times, there are ominous dress omens,
at such times, there are turtle abnormalities,
at such times, there are chicken calamities,
at such times, there are illnesses where the lower body grows above,
at such times, there are green misfortunes and green auspicious signs.
This is when metal afflicts wood."
The commentary says: All things of the grass and tree category are called *yāo*.
*Yāo* is like a fetus that dies prematurely (*yāo tāi*),
indicating something still subtle.
All things of the insect and worm category are called *niè*.
*Niè* means sprouts or shoots.
As for the six domestic animals,
they are called *huò*,
meaning something manifest.
As for humans,
they are called *ē*.
is the appearance of illness,
meaning it is deep.
If it is severe, strange things are born,
called *shěng*;
if they come from outside,
they are called *xiáng*.
*Xiáng*
is like *zhēn*.
If *qì* injure each other,
it is called *lì*.
*Lì* is like overlooking or overseeing,
meaning disharmony.
For each matter, the phrase
"at that time, then"
is used to cut it off,
meaning they do not necessarily all arrive,
some may exist, some may not,
some may be earlier, some later.
During Emperor Xiàowǔ’s reign,
Xiàhóu Shǐchāng was thoroughly versed in the Five Classics,
and skilled in deducing the *Wǔxíng Zhuàn*,
which he transmitted to his clansman Xiàhóu Shèng.
Down to Xǔ Shāng,
they all taught it to their esteemed disciples.
Their transmission was the same as Liú Xiàng’s,
only Liú Xīn’s transmission was uniquely different.
"Lack of reverence in outward demeanor
is called disrespect (*bù sù*)."
*Sù*
means reverence.
Within is *gōng*,
without is *jìng*.
If a ruler conducts himself
with an irreverent demeanor,
being lazy, arrogant, and haughty,
then he cannot respect all matters.
If he errs, he becomes reckless and changeable,
hence his fault is recklessness.
If the superior is lax and the inferior violent,
then *yīn qì* prevails,
hence the punishment is constant rain.
If water damages all grains,
and clothing and food are insufficient,
then villainy and treachery arise together,
hence the extreme is wickedness.
Another explanation is that
many people are subjected to punishment,
or their appearance is ugly and evil,
which is also this.
If customs are reckless and lax,
changing norms and altering standards,
then there are light, strange, and peculiar garments,
hence there are clothing *yāo*.
If water creatures move,
hence there are turtle *niè*.
In the *Yì*,
*Xùn* is the chicken.
The chicken has a comb and spurs,
the appearance of both culture and military might.
But if it does not act with authority,
its appearance and *qì* are damaged,
hence there is chicken *huò*.
Another explanation is that
in a water year, many chickens die or become strange,
which is also this.
If the superior loses dignity and decorum,
then there are powerful ministers who harm the ruler and superiors,
hence there is the *ē* of a lower body growing on an upper one.
The color of wood is green,
hence there are green *shěng* and green *xiáng*.
In general, those whose demeanor is harmed suffer from wood *qì* disease.
If wood *qì* is diseased, then metal *lì* it,
as opposing *qì* communicate.
In the *Yì*,
*Zhèn* is in the east,
representing spring and wood;
*Duì* is in the west,
representing autumn and metal;
*Lí* is in the south,
representing summer and fire;
*Kǎn* is in the north,
representing winter and water.
In spring and autumn, day and night are equally divided,
and cold and heat are balanced,
thus the *qì* of metal and wood easily transform each other.
Hence, if demeanor is harmed, it leads to autumn *yīn* and constant rain;
if speech is harmed, it leads to spring *yáng* and constant drought.
As for winter and summer,
day and night are opposite,
cold and heat are utterly distinct,
and the *qì* of water and fire cannot combine.
Hence, if sight is harmed, it is always warm; if hearing is harmed, it is always cold –
this is the nature of their *qì*.
To go against it,
its extreme is called wickedness;
to follow it,
its blessing is called "loving virtue."
Liú Xīn’s *Mào Zhuàn* says there are *niè* of scaled creatures,
[一四] sheep *huò*,
and nose *ē*.
The explanation is that in astronomy, the eastern constellation *Chén* is the Dragon Star,
hence it represents scaled creatures.
In the *Yì*,
*Duì* is the sheep,
and wood is harmed by metal,
hence it leads to sheep *huò*,
which corresponds to constant rain.
This explanation is incorrect.
In spring and autumn, the *qì* of *yīn* and *yáng* are equally matched;
if wood is diseased and metal flourishes,
then they can combine,
but this is only for this one matter.
*Huò* is of the same category as *yāo*, *ē*, *xiáng*, and *shěng*;
it should not be uniquely different.
Dèng Yáng, a minister of the Imperial Secretariat of Wèi, walked with a loose and unrestrained gait,
his muscles not binding his body.
When sitting or standing, he swayed and leaned,
as if he had no hands or feet.
This is the disrespect of demeanor.
Guǎn Luò called it "ghostly agitation."
Ghostly agitation
is a sign of a bad end,
and he was eventually executed.
In the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì,
noble youths engaged in drinking parties with loose hair and naked bodies,
openly toying with maidservants and concubines.
Those who opposed them were harmed;
those who criticized them were ridiculed.
Men who sought to conform to the world considered it shameful not to participate.
This lack of reverence in demeanor
was the harbinger of the Hú and Dí invading Zhōngguó.
Afterwards, there were indeed the rebellions of the two Hú,
which was another fault of recklessness.
In the Yuánkāng era,
Jiǎ Mì was powerful and favored,
frequently entering the two palaces
to play with the crown prince,
without a sense of deference.
He also once argued over a path during a game of *yì*,
whereupon Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng sternly said:
"The Imperial Crown Prince is the heir to the nation;
how dare Jiǎ Mì be so disrespectful!"
Mì still did not repent,
hence he met with disaster.
This was the punishment for irreverent demeanor.
Qí Wáng Jiǒng, after executing Zhào Wáng Lún,
stayed on to assist in governance.
He sat while officials bowed,
and issued orders and decrees to the Imperial Secretariat and other ministries.
He was dissolute, arrogant, and haughty,
not attending court for a single day.
This was the fault of reckless indulgence and disrespect.
Everyone in the realm praised his achievements but worried about his downfall.
Jiǒng ultimately did not change,
and thus brought about his own destruction.
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ set up stalls within his residence garden,
had his concubines sell goods,
and personally engaged in trade.
Gān Bǎo considered this an omen of a nobleman losing his position
and falling to the status of a menial servant.
Soon after, Dàozǐ was deposed
and died as a commoner.
This was the consequence of irreverent demeanor.
In the seventh year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān,
Liú Yì was about to be appointed as a princely heir.
Yì, considering the importance of the royal decree,
intended to host a banquet,
and personally requested his subordinates to oversee it.
On the day of the appointment,
the national officials did not report the matter with due solemnity,
but silently made the appointment in the stables.
When the royal messenger was about to return with the report,
Yì then learned of it,
and was greatly resentful,
dismissing Liú Jìngshū, the Langzhong Ling, from office.
Heaven's warning seemed to say
that this was a *yāo* of lazy neglect of auspicious rites and disrespect.
Afterwards, Yì was indeed killed.
Regarding "many rains" (*shù zhēng yǔ*),
Liú Xīn considered it "heavy rain" (*dà yǔ*) in the *Chūnqiū*,
while Liú Xiàng considered it "great flood" (*dà shuǐ*).
In the first year of Tài-Hé
extravagant practices flourished,
encroaching on farming seasons.
Therefore, water lost its nature and rain became a punishment.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tài-Hé,
there was continuous heavy rain for over thirty days.
The Yī, Luò, Hé, and Hàn rivers all overflowed,
and the year was marked by severe famine.
In the second month, jiǎ-yín day, of the second year of Tài-Píng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
there was heavy rain
with thunder and lightning.
On the following day, yǐ-mǎo,
it snowed,
and the cold was severe.
According to Liú Xīn’s explanation,
at this time, it should have rained but not heavily.
Heavy rain
was a punishment by rain.
For snow and severe cold
to occur the day after the initial thunder and lightning
was also a punishment of unusual cold.
Liú Xiàng believed that since there had already been thunder and lightning,
snow should not have fallen again.
These were all anomalies due to being out of season.
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
"If the ruler is out of sync with the times,
treacherous ministers will arise."
Thunder and lightning first, followed by snow, indicated
that yin saw an opening,
rising to overcome yang,
and the calamity of regicide was about to occur.
Liàng did not understand,
and was soon deposed.
This is similar to Duke Yǐn of Lǔ in the Spring and Autumn period.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of Tài-Shǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
there was continuous heavy rain.
On the jiǎ-chén day,
the Hé, Luò, Yī, and Qìn rivers all overflowed simultaneously,
flooding over four thousand nine hundred households,
killing over two hundred people,
and submerging over one thousand three hundred sixty qǐng of autumn crops.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Tài-Kāng,
Rèn-Chéng and Liáng-Guó experienced torrential rain,
harming beans and wheat.
In the ninth month,
Nán-Ān commandery had continuous rain and heavy snow,
trees were broken,
harming autumn crops.
That autumn,
Wèi commandery, Xī-Píng commandery’s nine counties, Huái-Nán, and Píng-Yuán had continuous rain and torrential floods,
and frost damaged autumn crops.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yǒng-Níng of Emperor Huì,
Yì-Yáng, Nán-Yáng, and Dōng-Hǎi had continuous rain,
inundating and harming autumn wheat.
In the third year of Tài-Xīng of Emperor Yuán,
spring rain continued into summer.
At this time, Wáng Dūn held power,
and this was a punishment for his disrespect.
In the first year of Yǒng-Chāng,
spring rain lasted over forty days,
and thunder and lightning roared day and night for over fifty days.
At this time, Wáng Dūn raised an army,
and this was an omen of the imperial army's defeat.
In the fourth year of Xián-Hé of Emperor Chéng,
spring rain lasted over fifty days,
with thunder and lightning.
Although Sū Jùn was executed at this time,
his remaining partisans still held Shí-Tóu,
and only after their extermination
did the excessive rain clear.
In the eighth month, yǐ-chǒu day, of the first year of Xián-Kāng,
the three counties of Yōu, Lǐ-Líng in Cháng-Shā prefecture of Jīng-Zhōu, and Lóng-Yáng in Wǔ- Líng,
experienced floods,
which floated away houses,
killed people,
and damaged autumn crops.
At this time, the emperor was young,
and power was held by those below.
**Inauspicious Clothing**
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi, seeing the world in chaos and famine,
and resources scarce,
first emulated ancient leather caps,
cutting silk to make white headcloths (bái-qiá)
to replace old attire.
Fù Xuán said:
"White is for military attire,
not national attire."
Gān Bǎo believed
"white plain cloth
is a symbol of mourning."
Naming it "qiá"
was a term of destruction and humiliation,
indicating that after the change of dynasties,
it was an omen of robbery and slaughter.
Emperor Míng of Wèi wore an embroidered hat
and a light blue silk half-sleeve robe.
When he often appeared before the upright minister Yáng Fù,
Yáng Fù remonstrated:
"What kind of ceremonial attire is this!"
The emperor remained silent.
This was a recent instance of inauspicious clothing.
Light blue
is not a color for ritual.
Even informal wear should not use red or purple,
much less for meeting officials?
The ruler personally wearing illegal attire
is what is called "creating one's own misfortune, which cannot be averted."
The emperor did not enjoy a long life,
his body perished, and his emoluments departed from the royal house,
his descendants did not last,
and thus the empire was lost.
In the first year of Jǐng-Chū,
copper was cast to make two giant figures,
called Wēng-Zhòng,
placed outside the Sī-Mǎ Gate.
According to ancient records, the appearance of giant men
portended the downfall of a state.
When the Cháng-Dí appeared in Lín-Táo,
it was a harbinger of Qín’s demise,
but Shǐ-Huáng did not realize it,
instead taking it as an auspicious sign,
and cast bronze figures to imitate them.
Wèi cast implements of a doomed nation,
and truly gained nothing from it in terms of righteousness.
This was indeed an inauspicious garment.
Shàng-Shū Hé Yàn enjoyed wearing women's clothes.
Fù Xuán said:
"This is inauspicious attire.
The regulations for clothing
are to distinguish between high and low, and internal and external.
The Dà-Yǎ says, 'Black robes and red shoes,
hooked breastplates and carved cheekplates,'
singing of its elegance.
The Xiǎo-Yǎ says, 'Majestic and awe-inspiring,
their martial attire,'
praising its martiality.
If internal and external are not distinguished,
the royal system is lost.
Once inauspicious clothing appears,
the person perishes with it.
Mò-Xī wore a man's cap,
and Jié lost the empire;
Hé Yàn wore women's clothes,
and also lost his family;
their faults are the same."
Among the women of Wú who practiced self-adornment,
they tightly bound their hair and filed their temples extremely close to their ears.
This indicates that their custom of self-restraint was too strict,
leading to a loss of moderation in their principles.
Thus, the customs of Wú
drove each other to extremes,
with sharp and critical remarks,
valuing severity and harshness.
Those observing the three-year mourning period
often damaged themselves to the point of death.
Zhū-Gě was troubled by this,
and wrote the Zhèng Jiāo Lùn (Treatise on Correcting Relationships).
Although it could not rectify the chaos through canonical teachings,
it was also an effort to save the times.
After Sūn Xiū,
the style of clothing became long at the top and short at the bottom,
with five or six layers for the collar, but only one or two for the skirt.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The top is excessively luxurious,
the bottom is meager and constrained.
This is an omen of excess above and insufficiency below."
When Sūn Hào arrived,
he indeed indulged in extravagance and tyranny above,
while the common people were impoverished below,
ultimately leading to the downfall of the state.
This was its fulfillment.
In the early years of the Tàishǐ reign of Emperor Wǔ,
the fashion of clothing was plain on top and full below.
Those who wore them all disliked their seams.
This was an omen of the ruler's weakness,
the ministers' indulgence,
and the lower subjugating the upper.
By the end of the Yuánkāng reign,
women wore two-paneled bodices
over their cross-collared garments.
This symbolized the inner being exposed to the outer.
Those who made carriages and carts excessively valued lightness and fineness,
and frequently changed their shapes,
all using white bamboo strips for decoration.
This was probably a remnant image of ancient funeral carts.
A carriage,
after all, is a vessel for a junzǐ (noble person).
However, the junzǐ lacked firmness in their intentions,
and their actions did not uphold substance.
Gān Bǎo considered this an omen of disaster for the Jìn dynasty.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
power and control resided with favored ministers,
which was the fulfillment of the lower subjugating the upper.
By the end of the Yǒngjiā reign,
the talented women of the six palaces were scattered and lost among the Róng Dí barbarians,
which was the fulfillment of the inner being exposed to the outer.
When the world fell into chaos,
many high-ranking ministers (zǎifǔ) and regional governors (fāngbó) failed in their responsibilities,
and were frequently replaced, which was the fulfillment of not upholding substance.
After the Tàishǐ reign,
people in Zhōngguó began to adopt Hú chairs and Mò pans,
and practiced Qiāng stewing and Mò roasting.
Noble and wealthy families
would certainly possess these utensils.
During auspicious feasts and joyous gatherings,
these were always given priority.
In the Tàikāng reign,
they also used felt for head coverings, belts, and trouser cuffs.
The common people joked among themselves, saying,
"Zhōngguó will surely be defeated by the Hú barbarians."
Indeed, felt originates from the Hú,
and the people of the realm used it for head coverings, belts, and trouser cuffs.
Since the Hú had thus controlled these three things,
how could there be no defeat?
By the Yuánkāng reign,
the Dī and Qiāng rebelled against each other.
After Yǒngjiā,
Liú and Shí successively usurped the central capital (zhōngdū).
Thereafter, the Four Barbarians alternately occupied the Huá lands.
This was the fulfillment of the clothing omens.
When clogs were first made,
women's clogs had round toes,
and men's clogs had square toes.
Roundness symbolized compliance,
thus distinguishing men from women.
By the early Tàikāng reign,
women's clogs had square toes,
indistinguishable from men's.
This was an omen of Empress Jiǎ's tyranny and jealousy.
During the Tàikāng reign,
the people of the realm performed the "Jìn Shì Níng" dance,
catching cups and plates with their hands and turning them over.
They sang,
"The Jìn world is peaceful,
dance with cups and plates."
Those who understood said:
"Music arises from the human heart,
and is therefore used to observe affairs.
Now, to catch cups and plates in one's hands and turn them over,
is an extremely perilous act.
Cups and plates
are vessels for food and drink,
yet they are named 'Jìn Shì Níng' (The Jìn world is peaceful),
meaning that the gentlemen of the Jìn era merely sought temporary pleasure in food and drink,
their knowledge not extending far.
The peace of the Jìn era is like cups and plates in one's hand."
During Emperor Huì's Yuánkāng reign,
women's ornaments included the 'five weapons pendant',
and they also used gold and silver settings,
fashioned into axes, battle-axes, spears, and halberds,
to serve as hairpins.
Gān Bǎo believed that
"the distinction between men and women is a great principle of the state.
Therefore, clothing and objects differ in status,
and gifts and offerings are not the same.
Now, for women to use weapons as ornaments,
this is an extreme feminine perversion.
This then led to the affair of Empress Jiǎ."
Ultimately, the empire perished.
At this time, when women's hair was braided and styled,
they used silk to tightly bind the coils,
calling it a 'jiézi jì'.
It originated from the imperial palace,
and the whole realm adopted it.
Later, this was the fulfillment of Empress Jiǎ deposing and harming the Crown Prince.
During the Yuánkāng reign,
people throughout the realm began to emulate each other in using 'wūzhàng' (black staffs) as walking sticks.
Later, they gradually added metal ferrules to them,
so that when stopped, they could stand upright.
Wood,
which is the element of the East,
is subservient to Metal.
A staff is a tool to support the body.
Having its head blackened
made it particularly convenient to use.
The necessity of leaning on it for support
symbolized external rescue.
Adding metal to it,
so that it could stand upright when stopped,
meant that wood, relying on metal,
could stand alone.
By the time of Emperors Huái and Mǐn,
the royal house faced many difficulties,
and the central capital was defeated.
Emperor Yuán, as a regional vassal, established virtue in the East,
maintaining the realm,
which was the fulfillment of support and rescue.
When the altars of soil and grain were without a master,
and the entire country turned to him,
he then received the Mandate of Heaven,
established his capital outside the Jiāng region,
which was the fulfillment of standing alone.
Between Yuánkāng and Tài'ān,
in the Jiānghuái region, there were worn-out straw sandals gathering by themselves on the roads,
sometimes as many as forty or fifty pairs.
People would throw them into pits and valleys,
but the next day they would reappear as before.
Some said
they saw civets carrying and gathering them.
Gān Bǎo believed that
"straw sandals
are humble garments of people,
associated with toil and humiliation,
symbolizing the common people (qiánshù).
Worn-out symbolizes
exhaustion and dilapidation;
the road
is for movement in all directions,
thus facilitating the king's commands.
Now, worn-out sandals gathering on the road
symbolize the common people being tired and sick,
and gathering to cause chaos,
thereby severing the king's commands."
During the Tài'ān reign,
soldiers were conscripted in the rénwǔ year,
and the common people resented and rebelled.
Zhāng Chāng of Jiāngxià initiated the rebellion,
and the Jīng Chǔ region followed him like a flood.
Thereupon, warfare broke out year after year,
which was the fulfillment of the clothing omen.
Originally,
the Wèi dynasty made white headbands,
sewing a horizontal seam in the front to distinguish the back,
and called them 'Yánqià',
which became widespread.
By the Yǒngjiā reign,
the seam was gradually removed,
and they were called 'Wúyánqià' (faceless headbands).
Women's hair, when bound,
became increasingly loose,
the bun unable to stand firm by itself.
Hair covered the forehead,
with only the eyes exposed.
Wúyán means
shame.
Covering the forehead means
a look of embarrassment.
The increasing looseness
meant that the world lacked propriety and righteousness,
indulging in emotions and desires,
and ultimately
leading to great disgrace.
After Yǒngjiā,
the two emperors did not return,
and the world was ashamed.
During Emperor Xiàohuái's Yǒngjiā reign,
scholars and officials competed to wear single garments of raw silk gauze.
Those who understood pointed it out, saying:
"This is the ancient suīcuī (mourning clothes of coarse silk),
which feudal lords wore for the Son of Heaven.
〔一七〕Now, to wear it without cause,
is there perhaps a corresponding omen?"
Afterwards,
there was indeed the rebellion of the Hú bandits,
and the emperor was killed.
During Emperor Yuán's Tàixīng reign,
soldiers bound their hair buns with crimson bags.
Those who understood said:
"The hair bun is on the head,
representing Qián (heaven),
the way of the ruler.
The bag is Kūn (earth),
the way of the minister.
Now, to bind the hair bun with a crimson bag
is an omen of the minister's way encroaching upon the ruler's."
Thereupon, Wáng Dūn encroached upon the emperor.
Formerly, a feather fan handle
was carved from wood in the shape of a bone,
and ten feathers were arranged,
taking the full number.
From the beginning of the *Zhōngxīng* era,
when Wáng Dūn marched south,
it was first changed to a long handle,
extending downwards to be grasped,
and the number of feathers was reduced to eight.
Discerning people criticized this, saying:
"A feather fan,
is named for its wings.
He who first made the long handle,
will grasp its handle to control the wings.
He who changed ten to eight,
will take what is not yet ready from what is already ready.
This is probably Wáng Dūn's usurpation of power to control the handle of the court,
and his desire, with untalented individuals, to steal what is not rightfully his."
At that time,
those who made clothes also made the tops short,
the belt only reaching the armpit,
and those wearing hats also bound their necks with a strap.
The lower part pressed the upper part,
leaving the upper part no room.
Those who made trousers made the legs straight at the opening,
without a tapering cut,
an omen of the lower being large.
Soon after, Wáng Dūn plotted rebellion,
and attacked the capital again.
When Hǎixī succeeded to the throne,
he forgot to set up the leopard-tail banners.
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
that leopard-tail banners
are the chief of ceremonial attire,
by which great men effect a "leopard transformation."
But on the day of Hǎixī's leopard transformation,
he forgot something that should not have been forgotten.
He was not a man fit to rule the state,
hence he forgot his leopard-tail banners,
indicating he would not last.
Soon after, he was deposed.
In the *Tàiyuán* era of Xiàowǔ,
people no longer wore *qiáotóu* (head-wraps).
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
"The head is the sovereign,
and the *qiáo* (head-wrap) is that which assists the sovereign in his ceremonial attire.
Now it is suddenly abolished,
as if the ruler stands alone without assistance,
leading to peril and destruction."
When Án Dì came to the throne,
Huán Xuán then usurped it.
Formerly, for *jī* (clogs),
the teeth (soles) all extended above the plank,
called *lùmǎo* ("exposed tenon/notch").
In the *Tàiyuán* era, they suddenly did not extend through,
called *yīnmǎo* ("hidden tenon/notch").
Discerning people believed that *mǎo*
means "scheme" or "plot,"
and there would surely be a hidden conspiracy.
Towards the end of Lìezōng's reign,
Yuán Yuèzhī, a Staff Officer in the Cavalry, began to collude internally and externally,
and in the *Lóng'ān* era, they conspired to deceive and overthrow each other,
leading to great chaos.
In the *Tàiyuán* era,
princesses and women necessarily loosened their hair and tilted their hairpins,
considering it grand adornment.
Using much false hair,
it was impossible to wear directly,
so they first arranged it on wood or a cage,
called *jiǎjì* ("fake chignon") or
*jiǎtóu* ("fake head").
As for poor families,
unable to afford it themselves,
they called themselves "headless"
and borrowed "heads" from others.
This then spread throughout the realm,
also a sartorial omen.
Not long after,
Xiàowǔ passed away, and the realm was in turmoil,
with countless executions,
many losing their heads.
For the grand interment,
heads were carved from wood and wax or bound from cogongrass,
which was the fulfillment of *jiǎtóu*.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
a crimson curtain was hung in the hall,
with a golden face carved,
and golden dragons at the four corners holding five-colored feathered canopies with tassels.
The subordinates said to each other:
"It somewhat resembles a funerary carriage."
Soon after, Huán Xuán was defeated;
this was the omen of the attire.
At the end of the Jìn dynasty, all wore small caps and wide, flowing robes,
a fashionable imitation,
which became a common custom even among commoners.
Discerning people said:
"The upper part is small and the lower part is large;
this is an omen of abdication."
Soon after, Sòng received the mandate.
Portents of Chickens
In the second year of Jǐngchū of Wèi Míngdì,
a hen in the office of the Grand Judge transformed into a rooster,
but did not crow or lead.
Gān Bǎo said:
"That year, Xuāndì pacified Liaodōng,
and the common people began to have the idea of 'sharing power.'
This was its omen.
However, the three empresses of the Jìn dynasty all ended as subjects;
not crowing or leading
was also heaven's will."
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng of Huì Dì,
in the state of Chén, a hen laid a rooster chick without wings,
which, when it grew large,
fell into a pit and died.
Wáng Yǐn believed:
"The rooster
is an omen of an heir or son.
The pit
is an omen of the mother.
Now a chick born without wings,
falling into a pit and dying,
means this son will have no support,
and will be harmed by his mother?"
Later, Empress Jiǎ falsely accused and killed Mǐnhuái;
this was its fulfillment.
In the *Tài'ān* era,
a hen in Zhōu Qǐ's house escaped into a drainpipe,
and after six or seven days came down,
flapping its wings and crowing and leading,
but its feathers alone did not change.
After this, there was the affair of Chén Mǐn.
Although Mǐn controlled the region south of the Yangtze,
he ultimately lacked discipline and cultural refinement;
this was probably its omen.
Ultimately, he was destroyed by Zhōu Qǐ.
The omen of the chicken appearing in Zhōu Qǐ's house
was also heaven's will.
The *Jīngfáng Yìzhuàn* says:
"When a hen crows like a rooster,
the ruler will not prosper."
In the *Tàixīng* era of Yuán Dì,
Wáng Dūn was stationed in Wǔchāng,
and a hen transformed into a rooster.
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
"A hen transforms into a rooster,
meaning a subject will usurp his superior."
Later, Wáng Dūn attacked the capital again.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year of *Tàiyuán* of Xiàowǔ,
a hen in Yán Sōng's house in Gǔanglíng Gāopíng was born without a right wing,
and a chicken in Liú Xiàng's house in Péngchéng had three feet.
The *Jīngfáng Yìzhuàn* says:
"If the ruler uses the words of women,
then chickens will produce strange phenomena."
At that time,
the ruler and prime minister both listened to the words of Buddhist nuns and old women,
bestowing excessive favor,
hence these ominous signs appeared.
In the eighth month of the first year of *Lóng'ān* of Án Dì,
a blue hen in Wáng Dàozǐ's house in Lángyá transformed into a red rooster,
but did not crow or lead.
This was an omen that Huán Xuán would usurp,
but would be unable to establish his enterprise.
In the fourth year,
in Jīngzhōu, a chicken grew a horn,
which soon fell off.
At this time, Huán Xuán had just begun to dominate the western regions,
acting wildly and disrespectfully,
hence this chicken omen.
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
"The horn
is an omen of military power;
that it soon fell off
is an omen of a temporary rise that will not last."
All these were later fulfilled.
In the second year of *Yuánxīng*,
in Héngyáng, a hen transformed into a rooster,
and after eighty days its comb withered.
The heavenly warning seemed to say,
"Héngyáng
was part of Huán Xuán's territory for the state of Chǔ."
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he was indeed defeated after eighty days;
this was its fulfillment.
Green Auspices
In the first year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ, in the eighth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
a great wind broke the tree of the Great Shè altar.
A green aura emerged from it.
This was a green omen.
The prognostication stated:
"There will be an emperor from Dōngguǎn."
The following year,
Emperor Yuán was born.
At this time,
the emperor's great-grandfather, King Wǔ, was enfeoffed in Dōngguǎn.
Because of this, he was moved and enfeoffed in Lángyá.
Sūn Shèng considered this an omen of the restoration.
During the disturbances of the Jìn dynasty,
none of Emperor Wǔ's descendants remained.
This was the fulfillment of the breaking of the Shè tree,
and also a punishment by an abnormal wind.
During the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì,
horseflies made a sound on the southern mountain of Luòyáng,
saying,
"Hán Shīshī."
Those who understood said:
"The Hán clan will perish.
The repetition 'Shīshī'
means a complete annihilation."
Later, Hán Mì was executed and the Hán clan was exterminated.
This was a green omen.
Metal overpowering Wood.
In the seventh year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi, in the first month,
the emperor went to Xǔchāng.
The south gate of Xǔchāng city collapsed without cause.
The emperor felt it was an ill omen
and therefore did not enter,
returning to Luòyáng.
This was metal overpowering wood,
causing the wood to move.
In the fifth month,
the imperial carriage passed away.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn states:
"When superiors and inferiors are all perverse,
the ominous sign is the collapse of a city gate."
In the second year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán, in the sixth month,
a rice storehouse in Wújùn collapsed without cause.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say that
a rice storehouse
is a place for storing grain.
Its collapsing without cause
signified that grain would become extremely expensive,
so there would be no grain to sell.
That year, there was indeed a great famine,
and thousands died.
In the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
Zhōu Yán submitted to Wáng Dūn.
[一八]After his residence was built,
the five bays and six beams that were erected
suddenly leaped out and fell to the ground,
while the remaining rafters still spanned the pillar tops.
This was metal overpowering wood.
The following year, in the fifth month,
Qián Fèng plotted a rebellion,
and consequently, Yán's clan was exterminated.
And Húshú soon also became a ruin.
In the first year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān, in the first month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yuánxiǎn, the heir apparent of the King of Kuàijī, was about to attack Huán Xuán.
He erected a battle standard at the south gate of Yángzhōu.
The eastern one was difficult to set up,
and only after a long time was it straightened.
This was a near ominous omen.
And Yuánxiǎn was soon captured by Xuán.
In the third year, in the fifth month,
the Lèxián Hall collapsed.
At that time, the emperor was dull and confused,
without a heart for delighting in the worthy.
Therefore, this hall was affected by the malevolent influence.
In the ninth year of Yìxī, in the fifth month,
the Guózǐ Shèntáng collapsed.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say that
the Shèntáng,
the foundation of rites and music,
collapsing without cause,
was an omen that the imperial enterprise and prosperity would fall.
Less than ten years later, the throne was abdicated.
Collation notes
Chapter 18, fifth line
The biography states:
"If words are not followed,
this is called disorder.
Its fault is usurpation,
its punishment is yang,
its ultimate consequence is worry.
Then there will be poetic omens,
then there will be infestations of shelled insects,
then there will be dog calamities,
then there will be diseases of the mouth and tongue,
then there will be white calamities and white omens.
This is wood overpowering metal."
Words not followed,
to follow
means to obey.
This is called disorder, disorder
means governance.
Confucius said:
"When a gentleman stays in his room
and utters ill words,
people a thousand *lǐ* away will disobey him,
how much more those nearby!"
The Shī says:
"Like cicadas, like grasshoppers,
like boiling water, like stew."
It means that if the ruler's commands do not accord with the people's hearts,
and there is empty clamor and confusion,
then he cannot govern the land within the seas.
The error lies in excessive deviation,
therefore its fault is usurpation and deviation.
If punishments are applied arbitrarily,
and the common people do not attach themselves,
then the yang energy will prevail.
Therefore its punishment is constant yang.
If drought harms the hundred grains,
then there will be banditry and calamities,
and both superiors and inferiors will worry.
Therefore its ultimate consequence is worry.
If the ruler is overbearingly yang and tyrannical,
and officials, fearing punishment, hold their tongues,
then the qi of resentment and slander will manifest in songs and ballads.
Thus there are poetic omens.
Infestations of shelled insects
refer to small insects with shells that fly,
produced by yang energy.
In the Chūnqiū, they are called *zhōng*,
today they are called locusts,
all of these are of that type.
In the Yì,
Duì is the mouth.
Dogs bark and guard but are not to be trusted,
meaning qi is corrupted.
Therefore there are dog calamities.
Another explanation says,
in drought years, many dogs die madly or become monstrous,
which is also this.
And among people,
there are many who suffer from diseases of the mouth, throat, and coughing.
Therefore there are diseases of the mouth and tongue.
The color of metal is white,
therefore there are white calamities and white omens.
Generally, when one speaks of being harmed,
it is a disease of metal qi.
When metal qi is diseased,
then wood overpowers it.
Its ultimate consequence of worry,
if followed,
its blessing is health and peace.
Liú Xīn's biography states: "Then there will be infestations of hairy creatures."
It is explained that in astronomy, the Western constellation Shēn (Orion) is the beast star,
hence hairy creatures.
In the early Jiāpíng era of King Qí of Wèi,
there was a rumor in Dōngjùn
that a demonic horse came out of the Báimǎ River.
At night, it passed by the official pastures and neighed,
and all the horses responded.
The next day, its tracks were seen,
as large as a *hú*,
traveling several *lǐ*,
then returning into the river.
King Chǔ, Biāo, was originally enfeoffed in Báimǎ.
Lìnghú Yú, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, considered Biāo intelligent and brave,
and upon hearing this rumor,
he conspired with Wáng Líng to enthrone him.
The plot was exposed,
Líng and Yú were executed,
and Biāo was granted death.
This was the punishment for words not followed.
The Shī says:
"The deceitful words of men,
why are they not punished?"
When Liú Chán of Shǔ succeeded to the throne,
Qiáo Zhōu said:
"The given name of the former ruler was Bèi,
which means 'to be fully prepared'.
The given name of the later ruler was Chán,
which means 'to bestow'.
It is as if to say that the Liú (dynasty) is already fully prepared
and should be bestowed upon others.
This is even more ominous than the names given to their sons by Duke Mù of Jìn and Emperor Líng of Hàn."
Shǔ indeed perished.
This was a case of words not followed.
After Liú Bèi died,
Liú Chán ascended the throne.
Before the burial,
and before a month had passed,
the era name was changed to Jiànxīng.
This was a case of words not followed.
According to the rites,
a ruler who ascends the throne should change the era name only after a year
because the hearts of his subjects cannot bear to have two rulers in one year.
Now, it can be said that he was too hasty and did not understand the rites and righteousness.
Later, he surrendered.
During the Tàihé reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
Jiāng Wéi defected to Shǔ,
and lost his mother.
The Wèi people had his mother write a letter calling for Wéi to return,
and also sent Dāngguī (angelica root, also a pun on "ought to return") to persuade him.
Wéi replied, saying:
"A hundred qǐng of good land,
one mú is not counted.
I only see Yuǎnzhì (Polygala tenuifolia, also a pun on "far-reaching ambition"),
there is no Dāngguī (ought to return)."
Wéi ultimately did not return.
In the first year of Jǐngchū,
officials memorialized that
the Emperor should be designated Lièzǔ,
and have his temple be one of the "indestructible temples" alongside those of Tàizǔ and Gāozǔ;
this was followed.
According to the regulations for ancestral temples,
the titles of Zǔ and Zōng
are only formally bestowed and perfected after one's death.
Therefore, even if one's merits shake heaven and earth,
and one's virtue surpasses previous kings,
there was no precedent for such a pre-determined decree.
This is likely an instance where not following good advice led to severe consequences.
Two years later, the imperial carriage ascended to heaven (the Emperor died),
and thereupon the imperial authority weakened and political affairs became lax.
During the time of Sūn Xiū of Wú,
a man from Wūchéng suffered from a serious illness.
After he recovered,
he was able to speak with a resonant voice,
speaking here and being heard there.
From where he himself listened,
he did not perceive the loudness of his own voice.
From a distance, listening to it,
it was like someone speaking face-to-face,
one did not perceive the voice coming from afar.
The direction of the sound
followed his intention,
traveling over ten li for the furthest listeners.
One of his neighbors had a debt of interest owed from outside
which had not been returned for years.
He then borrowed the man to scold and reproach the debtor,
frightening him with threats of misfortune or blessings.
The debtor, thinking it was a ghost or spirit,
immediately poured out and gave it to him,
the man himself did not know why this happened.
This was the fault of not following advice.
During the Wèi dynasty, the Ānshì Palace was built,
and Empress Wǔ later resided there.
Ānshì
was Emperor Wǔ's courtesy name.
Whenever Emperor Wǔ invited his officials,
he often spoke of ordinary matters from his life,
never touching upon statecraft or long-term plans.
This is an instance of not following advice.
Hé Céng said to his son, Zūn:
"The state has no plan for future generations,
it only cares for the present generation,
how perilous for the heirs!
This is a worry for the descendants."
After Yǒngxī, the imperial house gradually fell into chaos,
and during Yǒngjiā, the world was utterly ruined.
When Hé Suí was unjustly killed,
everything was as Céng had predicted.
Zhào Wáng Lún deposed Emperor Huì at Jīnyōngchéng,
and renamed Jīnyōngchéng as Yǒng'ān Gōng.
The Emperor was soon restored to his position and Lún was executed.
In the first year of Emperor Huì's Yǒngxīng reign,
an edict abolished Crown Prince Tán and reinstated him as Qīnghé Wáng,
and established Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng as Imperial Younger Brother (皇太弟),
further granting him the titles of Shìzhōng and Dà Dūdū,
leading the Chéngxiàng (Chancellor),
bestowing him with the Nine Bestowals (九錫),
and enfeoffing him with twenty commanderies,
following the precedent of the Wèi King.
According to the Rites of Zhōu, succession is based on lineal descent, not merit;
therefore, even the sage Gōng Dàn did not change the heir of King Chéng,
in order to completely cut off covetous ambitions
and forever unify the ancestral lineage.
Later generations followed this,
and changing it led to chaos.
Now, the imitation does not match reality,
and the usurpation and deviation are already extreme.
Furthermore, having already become the heir of the state,
he should not have been additionally enfeoffed with land
or concurrently held various official positions.
This is an instance of not following advice,
where advancement and retreat were contradictory,
thus after the Emperor was exiled,
Yǐng also came to a bad end;
this was the consequence of his transgression.
Later, they still did not realize their error,
and again established Emperor Huái as Imperial Younger Brother.
Huái eventually suffered murder in exile,
and did not enjoy a long reign;
this was another consequence.
The saying goes,
"Changing ancient ways and altering constant norms,
if not chaos, then destruction,"
is this what it refers to?
In the second year of Emperor Yuán's Yǒngchāng reign,
Generalissimo Wáng Dūn descended and occupied Gūshú.
The common people spread rumors of a "worm disease,"
which ate large holes in people,
entering the abdomen in a few days,
and causing death once inside;
there was a cure,
which required the gall of a white dog as medicine.
From Huái-Sì, it spread to the capital,
and within a few days,
the common people were in a panic,
everyone claiming to have contracted the worm disease.
It was also said that,
when it was still outside the body,
one should burn iron to cauterize it.
Thereupon, everyone rushed to it,
and seventeen or eighteen out of ten were cauterized by burning iron.
White dogs suddenly became very expensive,
leading to people fighting over them,
their price multiplying tenfold.
Some people even claimed to be able to perform the burning iron cauterization,
and charged the common people for it,
earning fifty to sixty thousand (cash) a day,
stopping only when exhausted.
After four or five days, things gradually quieted down.
An explanation states:
"Naked creatures are mankind,
and humans are their masters.
Now it is said that worms eat people,
meaning those of the same kind harm each other.
From below to above,
indicates rebellion.
It must enter the abdomen,
meaning the harm comes from within, not from outside.
Dogs have a nature of guardianship,
white is the color of metal,
and the gall is used by a martial ruler.
In the destiny of emperors and kings,
the king and hegemon will meet at Xū (戌, the eleventh earthly branch, associated with dogs and metal).
Xū governs the use of military force,
metal is the element of Jìn,
burning iron to treat the illness
means that one must remove one's own kind and let fire and metal combine their virtues
to jointly eliminate the worm pestilence."
Consider that during the period of restoration,
the Generalissimo was originally entrusted with the crucial responsibility of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
yet in Emperor Yuán's later years,
he attacked the capital.
During Emperor Míng's period of mourning,
he again harbored rebellious intentions.
This is why the lower rebelled against the upper,
and the heart (trusted official) rotted from within.
When the rebellious forces of Qián Fèng, Shěn Chōng, and others converged from all sides,
they were repelled by the imperial army,
and could not cross the river for over a month.
Liú Xiá, Northern Commander of the Guards, and Sū Jùn, Administrator of Huáilíng, led the forces from Huái-Sì to rescue the court.
Hence, the rumor first started in Huái-Sì.
The court ultimately used weakness to control strength,
and the culprits were apprehended.
This is the effectiveness of the white dog's gall in saving the situation.
During the time of Hǎixī Gōng,
Yǔ Xī enjoyed composing dirges for four or five years,
shaking a large bell himself to lead the singing,
and having his attendants join in harmony.
Also, at banquets, he would often order singers and courtesans to perform "Xīn'ān Ren Gēwǔ Líbíe Zhī Cí" (songs and dances of separation from Xīn'ān people),
the sounds of which were mournful and poignant.
People at the time found this strange,
and later he indeed suffered defeat.
During Tàiyuán,
children would strike two pieces of iron together in the dirt,
calling it "Dòu Zú" (fighting tribes/clans).
Later, Wáng Guóbǎo and Wáng Xiàobó, within the same clan, attacked each other.
When Huán Xuán first changed the reign name to Dàhēng,
people far and near excitedly said,
"The second month is over" (a pun on 二月了, referring to the end of a reign or dynasty, as '二' and '月' combine to form '玄', Huán Xuán's name),
thus the righteous uprising occurred in mid-spring.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
he again changed the reign name to Jiànshǐ,
which was the same as Zhào Wáng Lún's,
then changed it to Yǒngshǐ,
and Yǒngshǐ was again the year Wáng Mǎng received his enfeoffment.
He first relocated Sīmǎ Dàozǐ to Ānchéng.
Emperor Ān abdicated his position,
departed Yǒng'ān Gōng,
and was enfeoffed as Pínggù Wáng.
Lángxié Wáng Déwén was enfeoffed as Shíyáng Gōng.
Both were sent to Xúnyángchéng.
Those who understood considered all these to be ominous signs of usurpation, stemming from not following advice.
In the early reign of Emperor Wǔ,
Hé Céng considered the imperial cuisine from the Grand Provisioner (Tài Guān) to be paltry,
and thus brought his own private food.
His son, Shào, surpassed him in this regard,
and Wáng Kǎi in turn surpassed Shào.
Wáng Kǎi and Yáng Xiù's ilk
indulged excessively in pleasures of sound and sight,
exhausting all kinds of rare and beautiful things.
By the Yuánkāng era,
extravagance had become a custom,
with people vying to outdo each other.
Shí Chóng's extravagance
eventually surpassed that of Wáng and Hé,
and rivaled that of the sovereign himself.
After Chóng was executed,
the empire soon fell into ruin.
This was the consequence of overstepping boundaries.
Shù Zhēng Yáng (numerous indications of yang),
Liú Xiàng believed, referred to the great drought in the Spring and Autumn period.
When there is drought in summer,
the ceremony for rain (yú)
is called Dà Yú (Grand Rain Ceremony) in the rites.
Not harming the two grains is called "no rain."
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
"When virtue is desired but not employed, this is called Zhāng (expansion);
its calamity is barrenness,
which is drought.
During such a drought, dark clouds do not bring rain,
but turn red,
persisting through the four seasons.
When armies are mobilized out of season, this is called Guǎng (broadening);
its drought prevents growth.
When both superior and inferior are obscured, this is called Gé (separation);
its drought causes the sky to be red for three months,
and sometimes hail kills flying birds.
When those above seek empresses (or consorts) for personal gain, this is called Jiàn (transgression);
its drought lasts three months with great warmth and no clouds.
When the ruler builds high platforms and palaces, this is called Fàn Yīn Qīn Yáng (violating yin and encroaching on yang);
its drought causes the roots of all plants to die,
and frequently leads to fires.
When common officials overstep their bounds, this is called Jiàn (transgression);
its drought causes marsh plants to wither,
and be damaged by fire."
In the second year of Tàihé, the fifth month, during the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
there was a great drought.
This was the consequence of extensive construction of palaces and government offices since the first year.
Furthermore,
in the spring of that year, Emperor Xuān captured Méng Dá in the south,
and established two commanderies.
Zhāng Hé defeated Zhūgě Liàng in the west,
killing Mǎ Sù.
The excessive and severe yang (亢陽自大, overweening yang energy)
was also a corresponding sign.
In the fifth year of Tàihé, the third month,
it had not rained from the tenth month of the previous winter until this month.
On the Xīnsì day,
a Dà Yú ceremony was performed.
In the first year of Zhèngshǐ of King Qí, the second month,
it had not rained from the twelfth month of the previous winter until this month.
In the first month of the previous year,
Emperor Míng had died.
In the second month,
Cáo Shuǎng, on behalf of the successor to the throne,
transferred Emperor Xuān to the position of Grand Tutor (Tài Fù).

At this time, Emperor Xuān's achievements overshadowed the Wèi court,

In the third year of Gānlù of Duke Gāoguìxiāng, the first month,

At this time, Emperor Wén (Sīmǎ Zhāo) besieged Zhūgě Dàn,
which was the consequence of "armies mobilized out of season."
Originally,
Shòuchūn would always have rain in spring and summer that flooded the city,

When the city fell,
it then rained heavily.
Everyone considered Dàn's downfall to be Heaven's will.
In the second year of Wǔfèng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
there was a great drought,
and the common people suffered from famine.
In that year, conscriptions and levies were frequent,
and soldiers resented and rebelled.
This was the punishment for "excessive and severe yang"
and for "labor and toil alienating the populace."
As the conscriptions lasted for a year,
so did the drought.
In the first year of Bǎodǐng of Sūn Hào,
there was a drought in spring and summer.
At this time, Sūn Hào moved the capital to Wǔchāng,

In the seventh year of Tàishǐ, the fifth intercalary month, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ, there was a drought,
and a Dà Yú ceremony was held.
In the eighth year, the fifth month,
there was a drought.
At this time, the emperor listened to Xún Xù's perverse theories,
kept Jiǎ Chōng from returning to garrison the west,
while Rèn Kǎi gradually became estranged.
This was the consequence of "both superior and inferior being obscured."
When Lǐ Xǐ,
Lǔ Zhī, Lǐ Yìn, and others were all in minor positions,
it was close to what is called "virtue desired but not employed."
In the ninth year,
there was a drought from the first month
until the sixth month.
Prayers were offered to the imperial ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the mountains and rivers.
On the Guǐwèi day,
it rained.
In the tenth year, the fourth month,
there was a drought.
In the autumn and winter of the previous year,
daughters of high officials like Qīng Xiào Zhūgě Chōng were selected.
In the spring of this year,
over fifty women entered the palace for selection.
Additionally, several dozen daughters of lower-ranking officers and officials were taken,
and their mothers and children wept aloud in the palace,
their cries heard outside,
causing passersby to feel sorrow.
This was likely the consequence of "accumulated yin giving rise to yang" and
"those above seeking empresses (or consorts) for personal gain."
In the second year of Xiánníng, the fifth month, there was a drought,
and a Dà Yú ceremony was held.
By the sixth month,
heavy rain fell.
In the second year of Tàikāng, there was a drought,
lasting from the previous winter until this spring.
In the third year, the fourth month, there was a drought.

On the Yǐyǒu day, an edict ordered Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Qí Wáng Yōu, along with the Shangshū (Ministers of the Grand Secretariat), Tíngwèi (Grand Judge), and Hénán Yǐn (Governor of Hénán), to investigate and review imprisoned individuals,
and to grant clemency and amnesty.
In the fifth year, the sixth month,
there was a drought.
In the first month of this year, the sky was overcast,

Liú Yì submitted a memorial stating:

The emperor did not respond.
At this time, Xún Xù and Féng Dǎn usurped power and authority,

In the sixth year, the third month,
the commanderies and states of Qīng, Liáng, Yōu, and Jì suffered drought.
In the sixth month,
Jìyīn and Wǔlíng suffered drought,

In the seventh year, summer,
thirteen commanderies and states suffered a great drought.
In the eighth year, the fourth month,
Jìzhōu suffered drought.
In the ninth year, summer,
thirty-three commanderies and states suffered drought.
Fúfēng, Shǐpíng, Jīngzhào, and Āndìng suffered drought,

In the tenth year, the second month,
there was a drought.
In the first year of Tàixī, the second month,
there was a drought.
After Tàikāng,
although upright people filled the court,
they were not trusted or relied upon,
while Jiǎ Chōng, Xún Xù, Yáng Jùn, Féng Dǎn, and others successively held important and crucial positions.
The reason there was no year without drought
was the punishment for "virtue desired but not employed,"
"both superior and inferior being obscured," and

In the seventh year of Yuánkāng, the seventh month, during the reign of Emperor Huì,
Qín and Yōng provinces suffered a great drought and
pestilence.
Guānzhōng experienced famine,
and a bushel of rice cost ten thousand cash.
Because of this, the Dī and Qiāng rebelled,

As famine and pestilence repeatedly occurred,

The imperial court could not provide relief,

In the ninth month of that year,

In the first year of Yǒngníng,
from summer to autumn, Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Bìng provinces suffered drought.
In the twelfth month,
twelve more commanderies and states suffered drought.
In the spring of this year,
the three kings attacked Zhào Wáng Lún,
and in sixty days, there were dozens of battles,

In the fifth month of the third year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
there was a great drought.
The Dàn Pond in Liángshuǐ, Xiāngpíng County, dried up.
The Hé, Luò, Jiāng, and Hàn rivers were all fordable.
In the third month of that year,
Sīmǎ Yuè returned to the capital,

Furthermore, many feudal lords in the four directions harbored intentions of disloyalty to the sovereign.
Liú Yuánhǎi, Shí Lè, Wáng Mí, and Lǐ Xióng and their ilk harmed the common people,
causing blood to flow like mud,
which was also a manifestation of this.
In the fifth year,
the drought lasted from last winter to this spring.
In the eleventh month of the previous year,
Sīmǎ Yuè brought his Xingtái with him,
dismissing palace guards,
showing no respect for the decorum between ruler and minister.
In the sixth month of the first year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Yuán,
Yángzhōu suffered a drought.
In the twelfth month of the previous year,
Chúnyú Bó died unjustly,

In the fifth month of the fourth year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
there was a drought.
At this time, Wáng Dūn's arrogance and usurpation were already apparent.
In the summer of the first year of Yǒngchāng,
there was a great drought.
In the third month of that year,
Wáng Dūn caused the disturbance at Shítóu.
The two palaces were humiliated,
ministers were executed,
and there was unparalleled usurpation and transgression.
Therefore, the drought was particularly severe.
In the intercalary eleventh month,
the capital experienced a great drought,
and all rivers and valleys dried up.
In the third year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
it did not rain from spring
until June.
In the first year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
there was a drought in summer and autumn.

In the summer of the second year,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
there was a great drought.
In the fourth month of the sixth year,
there was a great drought.
In the seventh month of autumn of the eighth year,
there was a drought.

there was a drought.

At that time, there was a widespread drought throughout the land,

In the third month of the second year,
there was a drought.
In the sixth month of the third year,
there was a drought.

In the fifth month of the first year of Jiànwán of Emperor Kāng,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month of the first year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù,
there was a drought.
