and Empress Dowager Chǔ presided over the court,
following the precedent of Empress Dowager Míngmù.
In the seventh month of the fifth year, it did not rain
until October.
In the summer of the sixth year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the eighth year,
there was a drought.
In the spring of the ninth year,
there was a drought.
In the winter of the third year of Shēngpíng,
there was a great drought.
In the winter of the fourth year,
there was a great drought.
In the summer of the first year of Lónghé of Emperor Āi,
there was a drought.
At this time, Huán Wēn was arrogant and tyrannical,
controlling the imperial court,
which was a punishment for usurpation and transgression.
In the summer of the first year of Tàihé of Hǎixī Gōng,
there was a drought.
In the winter of the fourth year,
there was a drought.
Liángzhōu suffered drought from spring to summer.
In the tenth month of the second year of Xián'ān of Emperor Jiǎnwén,
there was a great drought
and famine.
From Yǒnghé until this time,
the succeeding rulers were young and immature,
Huán Wēn was arrogant and usurping,
and military campaigns were frequent.
The common people were resentful and suffering.
In the third month of the first year of Níngkāng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
there was a drought.
At this time, Huán Wēn entered to pay respects at Gāopíng Líng,
and the entire court bowed to him,
which was a consequence of his transgression and usurpation.
In the winter of the third year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the fourth year of Tàiyuán,
there was a great drought.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
there was a drought.
In the seventh month of the tenth year,
there was a drought
and famine.
Initially,
in the eighth year, Fú Jiān was defeated.
In the ninth year, various generals raided territories,
and there were campaigns in Xú and Yù.
Yáng Liàng and Zhào Tǒng attacked Bā and Miǎn.
In the first month of that year,
Xiè Ān was again sent to garrison Guǎnglíng,
and his son Yǎn advanced to Péngchéng.
There were frequent military activities.
In the sixth month of the thirteenth year,
there was a drought.
Last year, the Northern Garrison sent troops to garrison Húlù,
and Jīngzhōu campaigned in Hénán.
In the summer of that year,
Guō Quán established a garrison at Yěwáng,
and also sent troops to defeat Huánghuái.
In the seventh month of the fifteenth year,
there was a drought.
In the seventeenth year,
drought lasted from autumn to winter.
At this time, Emperor Lièzōng was benevolent and lenient,
trusting Wáng Dàozǐ, Prince of Kuàijī,
and political affairs were relaxed.
Furthermore, Rú Qiānqiū, as the Piaoqi Advisory Councilor,
usurped the authority of the sovereign and prime minister.
Moreover, the relatives and servants of the Buddhist nun who was the emperor's wet nurse
gained close access and led groups in various departments.
Also, many localities imprisoned people in spring without due cause.
The prison officials in Jiànkāng
were particularly corrupt and brutal.
This was also a punishment for usurpation, disobedience, injustice, and abuse.
In the winter of the second year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān,
there was a drought
and severe cold.
In the fifth month of the fourth year,
there was a drought.
In the fifth year,
there was a great drought in summer and autumn.
In December,
it did not rain.
At this time, Sūn Ēn was in rebellion,
Huán Xuán was ambivalent,
forcing the death of Yīn Zhòngkān,
and the court immediately appointed him to the post in Jīngzhōu.
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn also subtly instructed all officials to respect him.
The internal and external affairs were in turmoil,
and military conflicts frequently arose.
These were all consequences of arrogance, usurpation, and anxiety.
In the first year of Yuánxīng, in the seventh month,
there was a great famine.
In the ninth and tenth months, there was no rain,
and springs dried up.
In the second year, in the sixth month,
there was no rain.
In winter,
it was again dry.
At this time, Huán Xuán was extravagant and usurping,
and in the twelfth month, he finally usurped the throne.
In the third year, in the eighth month,
there was no rain.
In the winter of Yìxī fourth year,
there was no rain.
In the sixth year, in the ninth month,
there was no rain.
In the eighth year, in the tenth month,
there was no rain.
In the ninth year,
there was no rain in autumn and winter.
In the tenth year, in the ninth month,
there was a drought.
In the twelfth month, there was another drought,
and many wells and ditches dried up.
At this time, military conscriptions were frequent and numerous.
Ominous Poetry
During the Tàihé reign of Wèi Míngdì,
a song about the "Jiàodōulíng" (bellflowers) of Cáo Zǐ was sung in the capital.
Its chorus was,
"What can be done about you, Cáo clan?"
This was an ominous poem.
Later, Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
and the Cáo clan was consequently deposed.
In the early Jǐngchū period,
a children's rhyme went:
"Ah-gōng, Ah-gōng drives a horse-carriage,
unexpectedly Ah-gōng crosses the river eastward.
When Ah-gōng returns, what will happen?"
When Xuāndì returned from Liáodōng,
he reached Báiwū,
and was supposed to return to garrison Cháng'ān.
But the emperor's illness became critical,
and he was urgently summoned.
So he rode a zhuīfēng carriage and crossed the river eastward,
which ultimately matched the children's rhyme.
During the Jiāpíng reign of Qí Wáng,
there was a rhyme:
"A white horse with a plain bridle gallops southwest,
who rides it? It is Zhū Hǔ."
Zhū Hǔ
was the given name of the Chǔ Wáng.
Wáng Líng and Lìnghú Yú heard this rhyme
and plotted to enthrone Biāo.
The plot was discovered,
Líng and others were executed,
and Biāo was granted death.
In the early reign of Wú Sūn Liàng,
a children's rhyme went:
"Alas, you Kè,
why are you so?
Reed single-garment, bamboo hook-net,
where shall I seek you? Chángzǐ Pavilion."
"Chángzǐ Pavilion"
is
a reversal of Shízǐgāng.
Gōuluò means a hook-belt.
When Zhūgě Kè died,
his body was indeed wrapped in a reed mat,
his waist bound with bamboo strips,
and thrown into Shízǐgāng.
Later, Kè's former subordinates were allowed to collect his remains,
and they searched for him in this gāng, it is said.
In the early reign of Sūn Liàng,
a white alligator cried out in Gōng'ān.
A children's rhyme went:
"The white alligator cries,
the turtle's back is flat,
one can live long in Nánjùn City,
to hold to death and not depart brings no success."
"One can live long in Nánjùn City"
means
that in an emergency, it is easy to escape.
The next year,
Zhūgě Kè was defeated.
His younger brother Róng, who garrisoned Gōng'ān,
was also attacked.
Róng scraped off the gold from his seal and donned a turtle shell before he died.
Alligators have scales and armor,
symbolizing soldiers and weapons.
It is also said
that white is an auspicious sign.
In the second year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Xiū,
when the guards of the imperial hostages were playing in a group,
a strange small child suddenly came and said:
"The three gōngs are hoed away,
Sīmǎ will be as it is."
He also said:
"I am not human,
I am the planet Yínghuò (Mars)."
After speaking, he ascended,
looking up as if pulling a bolt of white silk.
After a while, he vanished.
Gān Bǎo said:
"Four years later, Shǔ fell.
Six years later, Wèi was abolished.
Twenty-one years later, Wú was pacified."
Thus, the nine regions returned to Jìn.
Wèi, Wú, and Shǔ were warring states.
This is what "the three gōngs are hoed away,
Sīmǎ will be as it is"
referred to.
Sūn Hào sent an envoy to sacrifice at an ominous shrine at the foot of Shíyìnshān.
The envoy then inscribed on the rock in red:
"Chǔ is the islet of the nine provinces,
Wú is the capital of the nine provinces.
A scholar from Yángzhōu
will become Son of Heaven.
After four generations of rule,
there will be great peace."
[一０]Hào heard this
and his ambition grew.
He said:
"From the Great Emperor to Us, it is four generations.
If We are not the lord of great peace, then who is it?"
His tyranny became even more excessive,
and soon he surrendered and perished,
this was a recent ominous poem.
During the Tiānjì reign of Sūn Hào,
a children's rhyme went:
"Ah-tóng, Ah-tóng again,
holding a knife, swims across the river.
He fears not the beasts on the bank,
but only the dragons in the water."
Wǔdì heard this
and appointed Wáng Jùn as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
When Wú was conquered,
no other army from the west of the river could pass,
but Wáng Jùn first secured Mòlíng.
After Wǔdì pacified Wú in the third year of Tàikāng,
a children's rhyme in Jiāngnán went:
"Shrunken flesh,
many eyes squinting,
the Central Plains will fail, Wú will return."
It also said:
"The palace gate pillars
will soon decay.
Wú will return
after thirty years."
It also said:
"Cocks crow without flapping wings,
Wú will return effortlessly."
At that time, the people of Wú all believed it referred to the descendants of the Sūn clan,
so there was a continuous succession of secret uprisings and rebellions.
Upon examination,
"many eyes squinting"
consists of four characters.
From the fall of Wú to the rise of Yuándì, it was almost forty years.
Yuándì rose in Jiāngdōng,
all as the children's rhyme said.
Yuándì was weak and indecisive,
so "shrunken flesh"
was
a criticism.
At the end of Tàikāng,
the capital Luòyáng had the song of "Folding Willow Branches" (Zhéyángliǔ).
Its melody initially spoke of the hardships of war and conflict,
and concluded with events of capture, execution, and beheading.
At this time, the three Yángs were highly esteemed and prosperous but were exterminated,
the Empress Dowager was deposed,
and died imprisoned in the central palace.
This was the fulfillment of "Folding Willow Branches."
In the Yǒngxī reign of Emperor Huì,
there was a madman from Wēn County, Hénèi
who wrote a book saying:
"Guāngguāng Wéncháng,
a great halberd forms a wall.
Though poison is administered,
the halberd will turn and harm itself."
It also said:
"Two fires disappear into the ground,
alas, Qiūlán!
Her form returns to the jiēyóu,
ultimately sighed over by men."
Later, when Yáng Jùn resided in the inner palace,
he used halberds as guards.
At the time of his death, he was also harmed by halberds.
Empress Yáng was deposed.
Empress Jiǎ cut off her food for eight days, and she collapsed.
She was buried north of the Jiēyóu Pavilion,
and the common people mourned her.
"Two fires"
was Emperor Wǔ's taboo name.
"Lán"
was Empress Yáng's courtesy name.
At that time, there was also a children's rhyme that said:
"At the end of the second month,
the beginning of the third month,
Jīng Bǐ and Yáng Bǎn issue imperial edicts,
the great horses in the palace almost become donkeys."
At this time, Yáng Jùn held exclusive power,
and the King of Chǔ was in charge of affairs.
Therefore, it says,
"Jīng Bǐ and Yáng Bǎn."
If these two individuals were not executed,
then the decorum between ruler and minister would be perverse.
Therefore, it says,
"almost become donkeys."
In the Yuánkāng reign,
there was a children's rhyme in the capital Luòyáng that said:
"The south wind rises,
blowing white sand.
Looking afar at the state of Lǔ, how towering it is!
A thousand-year-old skull grows teeth."
It also said:
"Horses east of the city, do not make noise,
by next year, they will be entangled with women."
"South wind"
was Empress Jiǎ's courtesy name.
"White"
was the color of the Jìn dynasty.
"Shāmén"
was the crown prince's childhood name.
Lǔ was Jiǎ Mì's state.
It means that Empress Jiǎ would cause trouble with Mì,
endangering the crown prince.
Then the King of Zhào would take advantage of the opportunity to chew up powerful and virtuous individuals,
to achieve usurpation,
and the crown prince would not die a natural death.
In the Yuánkāng reign,
merchants and farmers throughout the empire generally wore large hoods.
At that time, a children's rhyme said:
"Túsū hoods cover both ears,
a blind child will be seen becoming emperor."
Later, when King Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
he was indeed blind in one eye.
After King Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
a children's rhyme in Luòyáng said:
"Beasts come from the north, their noses sweating,
dragons come from the south, climbing the city to watch,
water comes from the west, the river gushes."
Several months later, the Kings of Qí, Chéngdū, and Héjiān united their righteous armies to execute Lún.
It is considered that Chéngdū was a western feudal lord but resided in Yè,
hence it says,
"beasts come from the north."
Qí was an eastern feudal lord but resided in Xǔ,
hence it says,
"dragons come from the south."
The source of Héjiān's water was in Guānzhōng,
hence it says,
"water comes from the west."
Qí remained to assist in government,
residing west of the palace,
and also had a desire to usurp the throne.
Hence, it says,
"climbing the city to watch."
In the Tài'ān reign,
a children's rhyme said:
"Five horses cross the river,
one horse transforms into a dragon."
Later, the Central Plains fell into great chaos,
and many imperial clans were cut off.
Only Lángyá, Rǔnán, Xīyáng, Nándùn, and Péngchéng arrived together east of the river,
and Emperor Yuán succeeded to the throne.
When Sīmǎ Yuè returned to Luòyáng,
there was a children's rhyme that said:
"A large rat in Luòyáng, a foot and two inches long,
if you don't leave early, a big dog will arrive."
Later, when Gǒu Xī was about to defeat Jí Sāng,
another rhyme said:
"The Yuánchāo brothers are very extravagant,
climbing mulberry trees, beating mulberries for Gǒu to make."
Because of this, Yuè resented Xī,
took his Yǎn Prefecture,
and a rift and disaster were thus formed.
In the early days of Emperor Mǐn,
there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Where is the Son of Heaven? In the bean fields."
〔一一〕In the fourth year of Jiànxīng,
the emperor surrendered to Liú Yào,
and was in the walls of the bean fields east of the city.
In the Jiànxīng reign,
a folk song in Jiāngnán said:
"Hōng, like a white pit breaking,
gather together to make a wǔ.
Yáng Prefecture is shattered and ruined,
Wúxīng is overturned and broken."
It is considered that "white"
was the color of the Jìn dynasty.
A pit-vessel with a mouth belongs to the category of urns,
earthen urns are hard in quality,
also a type of metal.
"Hōng, like a white pit breaking"
means
that the two capitals were overturned,
and the royal house was greatly ruined.
"Gather together to make a wǔ"
means
that Emperor Yuán gathered the remnants,
to preside over the altars of state.
He was unable to recover the Central Plains,
but only ruled as a regional king in Jiāngnán,
hence this analogy.
Later, at the matter of Shítou,
the six armies were greatly defeated.
Soldiers plundered the capital,
extending to the two palaces.
Three years later,
Qián Fèng again attacked the capital.
They blocked the water and defended,
holding out for more than a month.
The city was burned,
wells were filled, and trees were cut down.
Fèng and others were defeated and retreated.
Shěn Chōng led his party back to Wúxīng.
The government army pursued them,
trampling over prefectures and counties.
Chōng and his son were executed,
and hundreds of their partisans were punished.
This is what is meant by
"Yáng Prefecture is shattered and ruined,
Wúxīng is overturned and broken."
Bùyǒu is an earthen vessel,
and also smaller than a wǔ.
In the early days of Emperor Míng's Tàiníng reign,
a children's rhyme said:
"Cècè lìlì,
letting horses graze on the mountainside.
The large horse dies,
the small horse starves.
High mountains collapse,
stones break themselves."
Later, Emperor Míng died,
and Emperor Chéng was young.
He was forced by Sū Jùn,
and moved to Shítou.
The imperial meals were insufficient.
This is
"the large horse dies,
the small horse starves."
Gāoshān
refers to Jùn,
also saying Jùn would soon die.
Shí
refers to Sū Shí, Jùn's brother.
After Jùn died,
Shí occupied Shítou,
and was soon defeated by the various dukes.
This again corresponds to the collapse of mountains and breaking of stones.
At the end of Emperor Chéng's reign,
there was also a children's rhyme that said:
"Why the rumbling?
The carriage enters the zǐgōng."
A few days later, the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
In the twelfth month of the second year of Xiánkāng,
a rhyme from north of the Yellow River said:
"Wheat enters the soil,
killing Shí Wǔ."
〔一二〕Later, it happened as the rhyme said.
Yǔ Liàng 初鎮 Wǔchāng,
出至 Shítou,
百姓於岸上歌曰：
「Yǔ Gōng 上 Wǔchāng,
翩翩如飛鳥．
Yǔ Gōng 還 Yángzhōu,
白馬牽旒旐． 」
又曰：
「Yǔ Gōng 初上時，
翩翩如飛烏．
Yǔ Gōng 還 Yángzhōu,
白馬牽流蘇． 」
後連徵不入，
及薨於鎮，
以喪還都葬，
皆如謠言．
Mùdì Shēngpíng 中，
童兒輩忽歌於道曰 Āzǐ Wén,
曲終輒云
「Āzǐ Rǔ Wén Bù」 ？
無幾而帝崩，
太后哭之曰：
「Āzǐ Rǔ Wén Bù？ 」
Shēngpíng 末，
俗間忽作 Lián Gē,
有 Hù Qiān 者聞之曰：
「Lián 者，
臨也．
歌云『Báimén Lián,
Gōngtíng Lián』 ，
內外悉臨，
國家其大諱乎！ 」
少時而 Mùdì 晏駕．
Āidì Lónghé 初，
童謠曰：
「Shēngpíng 不滿斗，
Lónghé 那得久！
Huán Gōng 入 Shítou,
Bìxià 徒跣走． 」
朝廷聞 而惡之，
改年曰 Xīngníng．
人復歌曰：
「雖復改 Xīngníng,
亦復無聊生． 」
Āidì 尋崩．
Shēngpíng 五年而 Mùdì 崩，
「不滿斗」 ，
Shēngpíng 不至十年也．
〔一三〕
Hǎixī Gōng Tàihé 中，
百姓歌曰：
「青青御路楊，
白馬紫遊韁．
汝非皇太子，
那得甘露漿？ 」
識者曰：
「白者，
金行．
馬者，
國族．
紫為奪正之色，
明以紫間朱也． 」
Hǎixī Gōng 尋廢，
其三子並非 Hǎixī Gōng 之子，
縊以馬韁．
死之明日，
南方獻甘露焉．
Tàihé 末，
童謠曰：
「犁牛耕御路，
白門種小麥． 」
及 Hǎixī Gōng 被廢，
百姓耕其門以種小麥，
遂如謠言．
Hǎixī Gōng 初生皇子，
百姓歌云：
「鳳皇生一雛，
天下莫不喜．
本言是馬駒，
今定成龍子． 」
其歌甚美，
其旨甚微，
Hǎixī Gōng 不男，
使左右向 Lóng 與內侍接，
生子，
以為己子．
Huán Shímín 為 Jīngzhōu,
鎮上 Míng,
百姓忽歌曰
「Huáng Tánzǐ」 ．
曲中又曰：〔一四〕
「Huáng Tányīng,
Yángzhōu Dàfó 來上 Míng． 」
頃之而 Huán Shímín 死，
Wáng Chén 為 Jīngzhōu．
Huáng Tánzǐ 乃是 Wáng Chén 字也．
Chén 小字 Fódà,
是
「Dàfó 來上 Míng」
也．
Xiàowǔdì Tàiyuán 末，
Jīngkǒu 謠曰：〔一五〕
「黃雌雞，
莫作雄父啼．
一旦去毛衣，
衣被拉栖． 」
尋而 Wáng Gōng 起兵誅 Wáng Guóbǎo,
旋為 Liú Láozhī 所敗，
故言
「拉栖」
也．
Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ 於 Dōngfǔ 造土山，
名曰 Língxiùshān．
無幾而 Sūn Ēn 作亂，
再踐 Kuàijī．
Kuàijī,
Dàozǐ 所 封；
Língxiù,
Sūn Ēn 之字也．
Yǔ Kǎi 鎮 Lìyáng,
百姓歌曰：
「Chóng Luó Lǐ,
Chóng Luó Lǐ,
Shǐjūn 南上無還時． 」
後 Kǎi 南奔 Huán Xuán,
為 Xuán 所誅．
Yīn Zhòngkān 在 Jīngzhōu,
童謠曰：
「Mánglóngmù,
Shéngfùfù．
Yīn Dāng Bài,
Huán Dāng Fù． 」
未幾而 Zhòngkān 敗，
Huán Xuán 遂有 Jīngzhōu．
Wáng Gōng 鎮 Jīngkǒu,
舉兵誅 Wáng Guóbǎo．
百姓謠云：
「昔年食白飯，
今年食麥[⿰酉⿸广⿱⺾糸]．
天公誅讁汝，
教汝捻嚨喉．
嚨喉喝復喝，
Jīngkǒu 敗復敗． 」
識者曰：
「昔年食白飯，
言得志也．
今年食麥[⿰酉⿸广⿱⺾糸]，
[⿰酉⿸广⿱⺾糸]粗穢，
其精已去，
明將敗也．
天公將加譴讁而誅之也．
捻嚨喉，
氣不通，
死之祥也．
敗復敗，
丁寧之辭也． 」
Gōng 尋死，
京師 又大行欬疾，
而喉並喝焉．
Wáng Gōng 在 Jīngkǒu,
百姓間忽云：
「黃頭小兒欲作賊，
Āgōng 在城，
下指縛得． 」
又云：
「黃頭小人欲作亂，
賴得金刀作藩扞． 」
黃字上恭字頭也，
小人恭字下也，
尋如謠言者焉．
Āndì Lóng'ān 中，
百姓忽作 Ào zhī Gē,
其曲曰：
「草生可攬結，
女兒可攬擷． 」
尋而 Huán Xuán 篡位，
義旗以三月二日掃定 京都，
誅之．
Xuán 之宮女及逆黨之家子女妓妾悉為軍賞，
東及 Ōuyuè,
北流 Huái Sī,
皆人有所獲．
故言時則草可結，
事則女可擷也．
Huán Xuán 既篡，
童謠曰：
「草生及馬腹，
烏啄 Huán Xuán 目． 」
及 Xuán 敗，
走至 Jiānglíng,
時正五月中，
誅如 其期焉．
In the early Yìxī reign of Emperor Ān,
a children's rhyme said:
“The official family raises reeds which turn into cogon grass;
The reeds grow without end and form a pile.”
At that time, the government nurtured Lú Lóng,
〔一六〕bestowing upon him golden and purple insignia,
and entrusting him with famous prefectures.
He was cherished to the extreme.
But Lú Lóng was unable to return kind favor,
raised an army for an internal invasion,
and thus became an enemy.
“The reeds grow without end and form a pile”
referred to the defeat of Lú Lóng;
his partisans were cut down
like grass and wood, forming a pile.
Lú Lóng occupied Guǎngzhōu,
and people made a rhyme about him, saying:
“Reeds grow widely, reaching halfway to the sky.”
Later, he controlled several prefectures in the upper reaches of the river,
pressing close to the capital,
which corresponded to
the words
“halfway to the sky.”
In Yìxī second year,
children meeting on the road
would raise both hands and say
“Lú jiànjiàn” (Lú is strong, strong),
then say
“Dòu tàn dòu tàn” (Fight, alas, fight, alas),
and finally say
“Wēng nián lǎo wēng nián lǎo” (Old man is old, old man is old).
At the time, no one understood what it meant.
Later, Lú Lóng pressed internally,
his boats and ships covering the river,
which was the meaning of
“Jiànjiàn.”
When he reached Chápǔ,
he repeatedly set dates to fight the officials,
which was the fulfillment of
“Dòu tàn.”
“Wēng nián lǎo” referred to
the celebration of the centenarian age of the various dukes,
signifying that the rebellious and evil faction would naturally perish.
At that time, there was also a rumor that said:
“Lú chéngchéng (Lú is orange, orange),
flows with the water.
A sudden east wind arises,
how can he enter Shítou!”
Lú Lóng was indeed defeated,
and could not enter Shítou.
Formerly, Wēn Jiào asked Guō Jǐngchún to divine the fortunes of himself and Yǔ Liàng.
Jǐngchún said:
“Supreme auspiciousness.”
Wēn Jiào said to Yǔ Liàng:
“Jǐngchún is always right in his divinations,
but he dares not speak fully.
We share the safety and danger with the state,
and he says ‘supreme auspiciousness,’
meaning that the undertaking will succeed.”
Thereupon, they jointly attacked and annihilated Wáng Dūn.
In the early reign of Fú Jiān,
a children's rhyme said:
“Ā Jiān reigns for thirty years,
if he is to fail later,
it will be by the rivers and lakes.”
Fú Jiān was indeed on the throne for thirty years,
and was defeated at the Féishuǐ,
which was its fulfillment.
Another rumor said:
“The river water is clear again and again,
Fú Jiān dies in Xīnchéng.”
Fú Jiān was later killed by Yáo Cháng,
dying in Xīnchéng.
There was also a song that said:
“Yúyáng Tiánshēng will destroy Qín.”
Those who understood thought:
“Yúyáng (魚羊) forms
Xiān (鮮);
Tiánshēng (田升) forms
Bēi (卑),
Fú Jiān called himself Qín,
so it means those who destroy him will be the Xiānbēi.”
His ministers advised Fú Jiān
to execute all the Xiānbēi,
but Fú Jiān did not follow.
When he returned after being defeated at Huáinán,
he was first attacked by Mùróng Chōng,
and then killed by Yáo Cháng,
dying himself and perishing his state.
Calamity of the hairy beast
In the sixth year of Tàikāng, Emperor Wǔ,
Nányáng presented a two-legged fierce beast.
This was a calamity of the hairy beast.
Those who understood composed a text for it, saying:
“The martial form is deficient,
the metal beast loses its decorum.
The sage ruler corresponds to Heaven,
what is the purpose of this abnormality!”
It spoke of an omen of chaos.
Jīng Fáng's Yìzhuàn says:
“When the feet are few,
the lower ranks are incompetent.”
Gān Bǎo thought:
“獸 (shòu) is the essence of yin,
residing in yang,
a metal beast.
Nányáng is
the name of fire.
When the metal essence enters fire and loses its form,
it is an omen of chaos in the royal court.”
Six
is the number of water,
meaning that when the number of water reaches its extreme,
the evil of fire emerges,
and metal suffers defeat.
By Yuánkāng ninth year,
the crown prince was executed,
fourteen years after this event.
Two sevens are fourteen,
the number of fire from beginning to end multiplied by itself.
From the Emperor's accession to power
until the deposition of Mǐnhuái,
it was thirty-five years in total.
On the Bǐngchén day of the eleventh month of Tàikāng seventh year,
a four-horned beast appeared in Héjiān.
Wáng Yǒng of Héjiān captured it and presented it.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
horns are symbols of warfare,
and four is the symbol of the four directions,
meaning there would be military disturbances arising from the four directions.
Later, Wáng Yǒng of Héjiān indeed gathered troops from the four directions,
causing the initial stage of chaos,
which was likely its fulfillment.
In Yǒngjiā fifth year of Emperor Huái,
geckos appeared in Yánlíng.
Guō Jǐngchún divined it, saying:
“In a county east of this commandery,
there will be an evil person who wants to claim imperial authority,
but will soon die by himself.”
Later, Xú Fù of Wúxīng rebelled,
killing the Grand Administrator Yuán Xiù,
and Xú Fù was also quickly eliminated,
which was its fulfillment.
On the Dīngsì day of the first month of Xiánhé sixth year of Emperor Chéng,
when outstanding talents and filial scholars from various prefectures and commanderies gathered in the Lèxiántáng,
a appeared in front,
and was captured.
Sūn Shèng considered it auspicious.
Now, outstanding talents and filial scholars
〔一七〕are the refined gentlemen of the realm;
Lèxiántáng is a place
for enjoying and nurturing the worthy.
Since the period of chaos and loss,
moral education has declined.
The examinations for outstanding talents and filial scholars
lack the substance of the four categories.
The emergence of this in front
might be due to this reason?
On the Jiǎshēn day of the tenth month of Lónghé first year of Emperor Āi,
a large stag entered the Dōnghǎi Prince's residence.
The common people exclaimed, saying:
“A large stag has entered the Dōnghǎi Prince's residence.”
Those who understood found it strange.
Later, Hǎixī was deposed and became Prince of Dōnghǎi,
then entering his residence.
On the Guǐsì day of the fourth month of Tàiyuán thirteenth year of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
after the ancestral temple sacrifices were completed,
a rabbit walked upon the temple hall.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
a rabbit is a wild creature,
yet it gathered in the hall of the ancestral temple,
there is nothing more inauspicious than this.
Calamity of the dog
In Gōngsūn Wényì's household, there was a dog
that wore a cap and a crimson robe and climbed onto the roof.
This was a calamity of the dog.
The rooftop is a place of extreme yang, high and perilous.
Heaven's warning seemed to say:
Extreme yang with no superior,
usurping high dignity,
like a dog wearing a cap.
When Gōngsūn Wényì proclaimed himself King of Yān,
he was indeed annihilated by Wèi.
Jīng Fáng's Yìzhuàn says:
“If the ruler is not upright,
and the ministers want to usurp,
its omen is a dog coming out of the palace gate.”
Wèi Attendant Officer Yīng Qú was in the duty room
when he suddenly saw a white dog come out of the gate.
He asked the others,
but no one else had seen it.
He died the following year,
which was close to the calamity of the dog.
When Zhūgě Kè
of Wú returned from his campaign in Huáinán,
as he was about to attend court, a dog seized his garment.
Kè said,
"Does the dog not want me to go?"
He returned to his seat.
After a moment, he rose again,
and the dog again seized his garment.
He then ordered the dog to be driven away,
ascended his carriage,
entered the palace, and was murdered.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
in Yōuzhōu, there was a dog
that walked on its nose for over three hundred paces.
A heavenly warning seemed to say that
at this time, the Emperor did not heed the words of Hé Qiáo,
and ultimately enthroned Emperor Huì,
leading to decline and chaos.
This was the punishment for not heeding counsel.
In the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì,
a family in Lóuxiàn, Wú Jùn, heard the sound of puppies underground.
They dug them out
and found one male and one female.
They returned them to their den,
covered them with a millstone,
and overnight they were gone.
A heavenly warning seemed to say that
as the Emperor was already weak,
and the vassal kings slandered each other,
thus there was a dog calamity.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
the family dog of Zhū Kuí, the Internal Historian of Dānyáng, gave birth to three pups,
all headless.
Later, Kuí was killed by Cáo Wǔ, the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái,
a dog belonging to Zhāng Lín in Jiāxīng, Wú Jùn, spoke human words, saying:
"People throughout the world will starve to death."
After this, there indeed occurred the chaos of the two Hú,
and the world suffered famine.
In the first year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
a dog and a pig copulated.
According to the Hàn Shū,
this occurred during the time of Emperor Jǐng,
and was considered an omen of perversion and chaos,
a calamity of dogs and pigs.
Dogs
are an omen of military conflict.
Pigs
are a symbol of the northern Xiōngnú.
When opposing counsel is disregarded,
and different species interbreed,
it inevitably brings harm.
Soon after, the Emperor perished at the hands of the Hú,
which was its fulfillment.
During the Tàixīng era of Emperor Yuán,
Zhāng Mào, the Grand Administrator of Wú Jùn, heard a dog barking under his bed in his study.
[一八]He searched but could not find it.
Shortly after, the ground naturally split open,
revealing two puppies.
He took them and raised them,
but they both died.
Soon after, Mào was killed by Shěn Chōng.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
"If treacherous ministers are at one's side,
then dogs will produce abnormalities."
In the fourth year of Tàixīng,
in the home of Hé Xù in Qiánxiàn, Lújiāng, a sound of puppies was suddenly heard underground.
They dug and found a mother dog,
blue-black in color,
looking very emaciated.
It ran into the grass,
and its whereabouts became unknown.
At the spot, two puppies were found,
one male and one female.
They were suckled and raised;
the female died, but the male lived.
When it grew into a dog,
it was good at biting beasts.
Later, Xù's village was overcome by the Mán.
In the early Lóng'ān era of Emperor Ān,
dogs in the administration of Wú Jùn barked at night,
gathering on a high bridge.
The number of household dogs was limited, but the barking was very numerous.
Some observed at night and said:
"One dog seemed to have two or three heads,
all facing forward and barking chaotically."
Not long after,
Sūn Ēn caused chaos in Wú Huì.
At this time, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Sūn Wúzhōng resided in Jìyáng.
The sound of puppies was heard underground,
and soon the ground split,
revealing two puppies,
both white,
one male and one female.
He took them and raised them,
but they both died.
Later, Wúzhōng was executed by Huán Xuán.
According to Shī Zǐ, it says:
"A dog found underground
is called a 'dìláng' (earth wolf)."
Xià Dǐng Zhì says:
"A dog dug from the ground
is called a 'jiǎ'."
These are naturally occurring phenomena,
but when they appear unexpectedly,
they signify a dog calamity.
When Huán Xuán was about to be appointed Prince of Chǔ,
the ceremonial mat was already set,
and all officials were in attendance.
Before Xuán could come out,
a dog came and defecated on his mat,
to the astonishment of all.
Xuán, being suspicious and violent by nature,
said nothing,
but merely drove the dog away and changed the mat.
A heavenly warning seemed to say that
Huán Xuán, lacking virtue, usurped a great position,
and thus the dog soiled his mat,
showing the extent of his wrongful usurpation.
Eighty days later, Xuán was defeated and perished.
[一九]
White Omens and White Auspices
In the first month of the third year of Qīnglóng of Emperor Míng of Wèi, on the day Yǐhài,
a meteorite fell in Shòuguāng.
According to Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn,
"a falling stone
is a star."
Liú Xīn explained:
"A common star falling in Sòng
symbolizes Duke Xiāng of Sòng about to gain hegemony among the feudal lords but not completing it."
During the reign of Qín Shǐhuáng, there was a meteorite fall.
Bān Gù believed:
"A stone
is of the Yin category.
Also, it is a white omen,
meaning a minister will endanger his lord."
After this, Emperor Xuān gained power.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ, on the day Dīngsì,
two meteorites each fell in Wēn and Héyáng.
In the first month of the sixth year,
three meteorites fell in Wēn.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
one star fell in Féixiāng.
In the first month of the ninth year,
two meteorites fell in Liángzhōu.
In the fifth month of the second year of Wǔfèng of Sūn Liàng of Wú,
a large stone in Lǐlǐshān, Yángxiàn county, stood up by itself.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says
"it is an omen of a common scholar becoming Son of Heaven."
Its explanation states:
"If a stone stands on a mountain, it means someone of the same surname;
if on flat ground, someone of a different surname."
Gān Bǎo believed
"it was the fulfillment of Sūn Hào, succeeding a dethroned former family, gaining power."
Or it is said to be an omen of Sūn Xiū being enthroned.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
a stone grew from the ground in Yíqiūrǐ, west of Luòyáng Palace,
initially three chǐ high,
shaped like an incense burner,
later like a hunchback,
broad and flat, impossible to dig out.
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation,
this was a white omen.
The following year, the imperial carriage stopped permanently (the Emperor died),
and the royal house began to stir,
eventually leading to chaos and ruin.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
"If a stone stands like a person,
a common scholar will be a hero of the world."
This is close.
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
a stone grew in Yíniánlǐ.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
Xiāngyáng Jùn reported
finding a resonant stone;
when struck,
its sound could be heard seven or eight lǐ away.
In the first year of Tài'ān,
in Xiàjiàhú, Húshúxiàn, Dānyáng, there was a large stone
that floated for two hundred paces and then came ashore.
The people were alarmed and shouted to each other,
"The stone is coming!"
Gān Bǎo said:
"Soon after, Shí Bīng entered Jiànyè."
Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn, Dōngyíng Wáng Téng, moved his garrison from Bìngzhōu to Yè.
On his way through Zhēndìng,
there had been a long accumulation of snow,
but in front of his gate, an area several *zhàng* square uniquely melted away.
Téng found this strange and dug there,
discovering a jade horse,
about a foot high,
with broken teeth and mouth.
Téng, believing that horses represented the national surname (Mǎ),
sent it to the emperor,
considering it an auspicious omen.
However, a horse without teeth cannot eat,
a sign of ominous portents,
a harbinger of decline and downfall.
According to divination,
this was a 'white omen'.
Afterward, Téng was killed by Jí Sāng,
and the empire consequently fell into chaos.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Tàishǐ of Wǔdì,
white hair rained down in the land of Shǔ.
This was a 'white omen'.
At that time, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Huángfǔ Yàn campaigned against the Hú of Wènshān.
Aide Hé Lǚ strongly remonstrated,
but Yàn did not listen.
Yámén Zhāng Hóng and others, resentful of the general,
falsely accused Yàn of plotting rebellion,
and killed him.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"Joy in front, sorrow behind,
the omen is rain of feathers from heaven."
It also says:
"Evil people advance,
virtuous people flee,
heaven rains hair."
Its *Yì Yāo* says:
"Heaven rains hair and feathers,
noble persons flee."
All three divinations proved true.
In the first year of Yǒngníng of Huìdì,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng raised an army of righteousness.
In the army, there was a young boy
from Fánchāng Xiàn, Xiāngchéng,
eight years old,
with entirely white hair and body,
and quite skilled at divination.
According to the Hóngfàn,
this was a 'white omen'.
In the early years of Xiánkāng of Chéngdì,
hair grew from the ground.
This was akin to a 'white omen'.
Sūn Shèng considered it an abnormality due to human toil.
Afterward, Shí Jìlóng was destroyed, and the Central Plains began to submit,
with generals and ministers all willingly complying.
Consequently, regional garrisons were frequently changed,
and border outposts were constantly relocated.
All of them gathered their troops and divisions,
with numbers often reaching tens of thousands.
During this time, there were endless campaigns and levies,
with no peaceful year for service,
the empire was agitated and disturbed,
and the common people were exhausted and resentful.
In the sixth month of the third year of Xiánkāng,
hair grew from the ground.
In the fifth month of the second year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔ,
hair grew from the ground in the capital.
By the fourth year, the Dī bandits reached Xiāngguó,
besieged Péngchéng,
and advanced towards Guǎnglíng.
Garrisons were repeatedly dispatched,
and warfare continued for years without cessation.
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán,
hair grew from the ground in the capital.
At this time, after Fú Jiān's destruction,
many strategic matters had to be handled,
which was the manifestation of human toil.
In the fourth month of the seventeenth year,
hair grew from the ground.
On the *yǐwèi* day of the fourth month of the fourth year of Lóng'ān of Āndì,
hair grew from the ground,
some white and some black.
In the fifth month of the third year of Yuánxīng,
hair grew from the ground in Jiānglíng.
Afterward, Jiānglíng was repeatedly attacked,
with numerous battles.
In the third month of the third year of Yìxī,
white hair grew from the ground.
In the third month of the tenth year,
〔二０〕 hair grew from the ground.
The following year,
the royal army campaigned west against Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
The year after that,
they swept north through Guān and Luò.
Wood afflicts Metal
Towards the end of Zhèngshǐ of Wèi Qí Wáng,
Lí Shèng, the Hénán Yǐn, was presiding over a hearing.
A small piece of wood was dislodged and fell,
striking the head of Shí Biāo, the official receiving tallies,
〔二一〕 breaking it.
This was "wood afflicting metal".
Shèng was defeated ten days later.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng of Huìdì,
the stone of the Jiāoméi Altar in the suburbs spontaneously broke into two.
This was "wood afflicting metal".
The Jiāoméi Altar is the divine seat for praying for sons.
Its destruction without cause
was an omen that the crown prince would be in danger.
The following year,
Mǐnhuái was deposed and died.
In the fourth month of the tenth year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔdì,
Xiè Ān moved to garrison Guǎnglíng.
When he first departed from Shítou,
the metal drums and gongs spontaneously broke without cause.
This was an anomaly of "wood afflicting metal",
an intention of Heaven.
The heavenly warning seemed to say that
Ān would merely project a reputation for strategy,
but ultimately achieve nothing substantial,
an omen that the gongs and drums would not be used.
Over a month later,
he returned due to illness and passed away.
The commentary says:
"If vision is unclear,
this is called unintelligence.
Its fault is slowness,
its punishment is warmth,
its ultimate consequence is illness.
Then there are plant anomalies,
then there are insect calamities,
then there-are sheep misfortunes,
then there are eye diseases,
then there are red omens and red auspicious signs.
This means water harms fire."
"If vision is unclear,
this is called unintelligence."
Zhé [哲]
means knowledge.
The Shī [詩] says:
"Your virtue is unclear,
thus you lose your supporters and ministers.
Unclear is your virtue,
thus you lose your allies and retainers."
This means if the ruler is not clear-sighted,
being ignorant, veiled, and deluded,
then they cannot discern good from evil,
cannot bring close the virtuous,
cannot nurture those of their own kind,
and those who have no merit receive rewards,
and those who are guilty are not punished.
The hundred officials become derelict and chaotic,
the fault lies in slowness and laxity,
thus its fault is slowness.
In midsummer, days are long,
and heat nourishes all things.
If governance is lax,
its punishment is prolonged warmth.
If it is warm, then winter is mild,
and spring and summer are disharmonious,
causing injury, sickness, and illness to people.
Its ultimate consequence is illness.
If executions are not carried out, frost does not kill plants.
If ministers and subordinates are left to their own devices, executions are not carried out in due time.
Hence there are plant anomalies.
Generally, anomalies
appear in attire as visual signs,
are expressed in poems as verbal signs,
and are heard in sounds as auditory signs.
Those that are not seen in colors
are the five colors,
which are the great divisions of things.
They appear in omens and auspicious signs.
Hence the Sàngrén [聖人] consider them plant anomalies,
signifying one who loses the clarity of controlling things.
Warmth and heat breed insects,
thus there are insect calamities,
meaning that creatures like míngténg [螟螣] that ought to die do not die,
or that ought to be born are not born,
or that are more numerous than usual and become a disaster.
Liú Xīn [劉歆] believed this pertained to a mind that is not accommodating.
In the Yì [易],
hardness enveloping softness is Lí [離],
Lí [離] represents fire,
and represents the eye.
Sheep have horns above and hooves below,
representing hardness enveloping softness.
Sheep have large eyes but are not clear-sighted.
If their qi [氣] of vision is damaged,
hence there are sheep misfortunes.
Another explanation says that
in hot years, many sheep die from epidemics,
and become strange,
which is also this.
When it affects humans,
many suffer from eye diseases,
hence there are eye diseases.
The color of fire is red,
hence there are red omens and red auspicious signs.
[二二] Generally, those whose vision is harmed
suffer from the qi [氣] of fire;
when the qi [氣] of fire is harmed,
water harms it.
If its ultimate consequence is illness, one should conform to it,
and its blessing is longevity.
Liú Xīn's [劉歆] commentary on "vision" mentions "calamities of feathered insects"
and "chicken misfortunes."
He explained that in astronomy, the southern stars Zhū [朱] and Zhāng [張] are bird stars,
hence representing feathered insects.
Misfortune also follows feathers,
hence representing chickens.
In the Yì [易], chickens are inherently in Xùn [巽],
so his explanation is incorrect.
As for the "warmth" in the "Shù Zhēng" [庶徵],
Liú Xiàng [劉向] believed it meant no ice in spring and autumn.
Minor warmth is not recorded;
only when there is no ice is it recorded,
citing the major cases.
Jīng Fáng's [京房] Yì Zhuàn [易傳] says:
"If emoluments are not properly distributed, this is called deceit;
its fault is warmth.
When it is warm,
clouds and rain arrive from all four directions and it becomes warm.
If ministers are content with their salaries and enjoy idleness, this is called disorder;
warmth then produces insects.
Knowing a crime but not punishing it, this is called slowness;
when it is warm,
in summer the heat kills people,
and in winter plants blossom and bear fruit.
Not punishing repeated transgressions, this is called a sign of doom;
its fault is that it ought to be cold but is warm for six full days."
In the ninth month of Jiànxīng [建興] first year of Wú Sūn Liàng [吳孫亮],
peach and plum trees blossomed.
In the era of Sūn Quán's [孫權] rule, governance was troublesome and taxes heavy,
people were worn out by labor.
At this time, Zhūgě Kè [諸葛恪] first assisted in governance,
stopping recruitment,
pardoning outstanding debts,
removing barriers,
and promoting leniency and generosity.
This was the manifestation of slowness and laxity.
One explanation says that peaches and plums blossoming in cold weather are plant anomalies,
or belong to hua niè [華孼] (flower calamities).
In the tenth month of Jǐngyuán [景元] third year of Wèi Shàodì [魏少帝],
[二三] peach and plum trees blossomed.
At that time, the Young Emperor deeply cultivated kindness and virtue,
and affairs were characterized by extreme leniency and slowness.
This was its manifestation.
In the second month of Yuánkāng [元康] second year of Huìdì [惠帝],
in the commandery of Bāxī [巴西], all grasses blossomed,
bearing seeds like wheat,
which were edible.
At that time, the Emperor had just ascended the throne,
and Chǔ Wáng Wěi [楚王瑋] falsely issued an edict to execute Rǔnán Wáng Liàng [汝南王亮] and Tàibǎo Wèi Guàn [太保衞瓘],
but the Emperor was unable to discern the truth.
Now, grass bearing fruit out of season
is the punishment for warmth, leniency, and slowness.
In the twelfth month of Yǒnghé [永和] ninth year of Mùdì [穆帝],
peach and plum trees blossomed.
At this time, Jiǎnwén [簡文] assisted in governance,
and many affairs were neglected and lax.
This was the manifestation of slowness and laxity.
Plant Anomalies
In the first month of spring, Jiàn'ān [建安] twenty-fifth year of Hàn Xiàndì [漢獻帝],
Wèi Wǔdì [魏武帝] started building the Jiànshǐ [建始] Palace in Luòyáng [洛陽].
When the Zhuólóng [濯龍] tree was cut, blood flowed out.
[二四] Also, when a pear tree was dug up and transplanted,
its roots were injured and blood also flowed out.
The Emperor was troubled by this,
and consequently fell ill,
dying that month.
This was probably a plant anomaly,
and also a red auspicious sign.
That year was Huángchū [黃初] first year of Wèi Wéndì [魏文帝].
In the sixth month of Wǔfèng [五鳳] first year of Wú Sūn Liàng [吳孫亮],
in Jiāozhǐ [交阯], wild rice transformed into cultivated rice.
In ancient times, when Sān Miáo [三苗] was about to perish,
the five grains changed species.
This was a plant anomaly.
Afterwards, Liàng [亮] was deposed.
In Jǐngyào [景耀] fifth year of Shǔ Liú Chán [蜀劉禪],
a large tree in the palace courtyard inexplicably broke by itself.
Qiáo Zhōu [譙周] was worried about it,
having no one to speak to,
so he wrote on a pillar:
"Numerous and great,
their meeting will be.
Fully provided and bestowed,
how can there be another restoration?"
This meant Cáo [曹] (Cáo Wèi [曹魏]) was numerous,
and Wèi [魏] was great.
Numerous and great,
the world would surely gather under them.
Fully provided and bestowed (by Heaven), how could there be another who could establish (a dynasty)?
Shǔ [蜀] indeed perished,
as Zhōu [周] had said.
This was a plant anomaly.
In Tiānxǐ [天璽] first year of Wú Sūn Hào [吳孫晧],
Línpíng Hú [臨平湖] in Wú Jùn [吳郡], which had been choked with weeds since the end of the Hàn [漢] dynasty,
suddenly cleared overnight, becoming free of grass.
The elders passed down that: "When this lake is choked,
the world is in chaos;
when this lake opens,
the world is at peace."
Wú [吳] soon perished, and the nine regions became unified.
In the eighth month of the third year of Tiān Jì,
in Jiànyè, a guǐmù-cài grew at the home of gōng Huáng Gǒu.
〔二五〕It entwined a jujube tree,
measuring over a zhàng in height,
with a stem four cùn wide
and two fēn thick.
Additionally, a bò-cài grew at the home of gōng Wú Píng,
four chǐ tall,
shaped like a loquat,
round at the top,
with a diameter of one chǐ eight cùn,
a stem five cùn wide,
and green leaves growing on both sides.
The Dōngguān referred to diagrams,
naming the guǐmù as zhīcǎo,
and the bò-cài as pínglǜ.
Consequently, Gǒu was appointed Shìzhī Láng,
and Píng was appointed Pínglǜ Láng,
both with silver seals and blue sashes.
Gān Bǎo said: "Next year Wú will be conquered.
Wáng Jùn will moor his ships precisely at Píng Zhǔ.
The names are strikingly evident,
a clear omen pointing to events.
As for Huáng Gǒu,
Wú, by the earth element, succeeded Hàn,
hence initially there was the auspicious sign of a yellow dragon.
But in its last years,
the ominous guǐmù appeared, entrusting itself to the home of Huáng Gǒu.
The ‘yellow’ designation remained unchanged,
yet the status, noble or humble, differed greatly—
an manifestation of the subtle and profound ways of Heaven."
In the spring of the second year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
bamboo flowered in the Bāxī Commandery,
purple in color,
bearing fruit like wheat,
with a green outer skin,
reddish-white inside,
and sweet in taste.
On the gengzǐ day of the sixth month of the ninth year of Yuánkāng,
a mulberry tree grew in the west wing of the Eastern Palace,
growing over one chǐ per day,
but on the jiǎchén day it withered and died.
This was the same omen as that which occurred during the reign of Yīn Tàiwù.
The Crown Prince failed to comprehend it,
and therefore met with deposition and execution.
Bān Gù stated,
"When wild trees grow in court and sprout rapidly,
it signifies that petty individuals will suddenly occupy high ministerial positions,
an omen of national peril and family ruin,
and the court will become a wasteland."
After this, Sūn Xiù and Zhāng Lín held power,
which led to great chaos.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
the imperial grandson Zāng was established as Crown Imperial Grandson.
On the jiǎzǐ day of the fifth month,
he moved into the Eastern Palace,
and a mulberry tree again grew in the west wing.
The next year,
Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne
and poisoned Zāng.
This was the same omen as that which afflicted Mǐnhuái.
In the same month,
in Zhuàngwǔ Guó, a mulberry tree transformed into a cypress,
and Zhāng Huá met his demise.
Zhuàngwǔ
was Huá’s enfeoffment.
In the winter of the second year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái,
a mulberry tree in Xiàng Xiàn made a sound like cutting timber;
people called it the "crying of the mulberry tree."
According to Liú Xiàng's explanation,
"sāng (mulberry) implies sāng (mourning),"
and also the sound of crying,
which was extremely inauspicious.
At this time, the capital was weak,
barbarian invaders encroached repeatedly,
and Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè had no intention of defending the state.
In the winter of the fourth year he moved south,
〔二六〕and in the spring of the fifth year he died in this city.
Shí Lè ambushed his forces,
surrounded and shot them;
over one hundred thousand people, from princes and dukes down to commoners, died.
He also opened Yuè’s coffin
and burned his corpse.
This defeat
left the Central Plains without anyone to appeal to,
and Luòjīng soon fell.
This was the fulfillment of the mulberry's crying.
In the fifth month of the sixth year,
in Wúxī Xiàn, there were four zhūyú trees
that grew intertwined,
resembling conjoint trees.
Before this,
Guō Jǐngchún divined about the yánlíng-yǎnshǔ,
encountering guà Lín turning into guà Yì,
and said:
"Later there will again be ominous trees growing,
appearing auspicious but not so;
they will be pungent and acrid wood.
If this occurs,
there will surely be rebels within several hundred lǐ to the east and west."
When these trees grew,
afterward Xú Fù indeed started a rebellion;
it was also a plant omen.
Guō also believed
"wood should not be bent or straight."
In the seventh month of that year,
in Yùzhāng Commandery, a camphor tree that had been long withered
suddenly flourished again this month,
which had the same prognostic as the withered She tree in Hàn Chāngyì that revived.
This was an omen of Huái and Mǐn's downfall,
and a sign of Emperor Yuán's restoration.
In the ninth month of the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
in Shàn Xiàn of Kuàijī, wood grew resembling a human face.
After this, Wáng Dūn raised troops and rebelled,
but his nefarious plot came to naught.
In ancient times, during the reigns of Emperors Āi and Chéng of Hàn, similar omens occurred,
but the human features were complete,
hence the calamity was also great.
Now, this one merely resembled a human face,
so its change was minor.
On the guǐhài day of the fifth month of the sixth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
in Qǔ'ā, a willow tree that had withered and fallen for six years
suddenly revived and grew on this day.
By the jiǎxū day of the fifth month of the ninth year,
in Wú Xiàn, at the home of Wú Xióng, a dead elm tree
revived due to wind and rain on this day,
which was the same phenomenon as the broken willow tree in Hàn Shànglín that revived.
Initially,
Emperor Kāng was Wú Wáng.
Although he was later enfeoffed as Lángxié,
he still held Wú Jùn as his fief.
This was an omen that the emperor would bypass the legitimate succession and enjoy the nation.
Qǔ'ā was also formerly part of Wú.
The omen appeared in the dwelling of Wú Xióng in Wú Yì;
was it also the will of Heaven?
On the guǐmǎo day of the fifth month of the third year of Xīngníng of Emperor Āi,
at the home of Xiūmíng in Xīchāng Xiàn of Lúlíng, a fallen chestnut tree
suddenly revived and grew on this day.
At that time, Emperor Xiàowǔ was only four years old.
Soon after, Emperor Āi passed away,
Hǎixī ascended the throne,
but was soon deposed.
Jiǎnwén, crossing over from being a vassal prince,
entered to inherit the great enterprise,
and ascended the throne to rule the nation.
Yet, he did not rule for more than two years,
before Xiàowǔ succeeded to the throne.
The emperor's taboo name was Chāngmíng.
Those who knew secretly said that the auspicious omen of Xīchāng Xiūmíng
indeed corresponded to the emperor's taboo name.
This was also the same phenomenon as that of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
In the first year of Tàihé of Hǎixī,
〔二七〕pine trees grew on poplar trees in Liángzhōu.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say:
pine trees do not change their branches or leaves,
while poplar trees are soft and brittle wood.
Now, pine growing on poplar,
is this not a sign that a lasting enterprise will meet with a place of peril and ruin?
At this time, Zhāng Tiānxī reigned supreme in Liángzhōu,
but soon surrendered to Fú Jiān.
In the sixth month of the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
in Tónglè Xiàn of Jiànníng Commandery, a withered tree broke and fell,
but suddenly stood up and reconnected itself.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn says:
"When one abandons uprightness and commits depravity, the omen is a tree that breaks and reconnects itself.
When empresses or consorts hold exclusive power,
a fallen tree stands upright again."
At this time, upright ways were largely deviated from.
Afterward, Lady Zhāng monopolized imperial favor,
and when the emperor passed away,
the common people blamed the Zhāng clan.
In the third year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān,
bamboo bore fruit like wheat
in the border area between Jīng and Jiāng provinces.
In the ninth month of the second year of Yìxī,
at the home of Chén Gài, an army officer of Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn, there was a bitter bò-cài,
four chǐ six cùn tall,
three chǐ two cùn wide,
and three cùn thick.
This was also a plant omen.
This was likely the same phenomenon as the end of Wú.
Those who understood believed that "bitter bò"
meant "to buy suffering."
Afterward, year after year there were punitive expeditions,
the common people suffered hardship,
this was "buying suffering."
Within more than ten years,
Yáo Hóng was extinguished,
and warfare finally ceased.
This was the fulfillment of the bitter bò-cài omen.
During the Yìxī (義熙) reign,
thistles grew all over the palace walls and on both sides of the imperial road.
This was also a plant omen.
Thistles have thorns,
making them impassable.
Their growth on palace walls and imperial roads
was a warning from Heaven, as if to say:
if the sovereign does not attend to governance,
even if there are palaces and imperial roads,
they are as if empty and abandoned,
hence the growth of thistles.
Winged Creature Omens
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Huángchū (黃初) of Emperor Wén (文帝) of Wèi (魏),
pelicans gathered at the Língzhī (靈芝) pond.
According to Liú Xiàng's (劉向) explanation,
this was an omen of winged creatures,
and also a blue omen.
An imperial edict stated:
"These are what the poets called 'foul wetlands'.
Cáo (曹) poetry 'criticizes Duke Gòng (共公) for keeping worthy gentlemen at a distance and associating with petty individuals.'
Are there now wise and virtuous gentlemen in low positions?
Otherwise, why would these birds have arrived?
Let the most eminent and talented gentlemen of exceptional conduct from all under heaven be broadly recommended,
to respond to the criticism of the people of Cáo (曹)."
Thereupon, Yáng Biāo (楊彪), Guǎn Níng (管寧), and their like were all recommended.
This is what is meant by "seeing an omen and knowing fear."
Yet, they still could not fully accommodate the bright and upright, and many succumbed to favoritism.
Jīng Fáng's (京房) Yì Zhuàn (易傳) says:
"If the virtuous are dismissed and retired,
the omen will be water birds gathering in the state."
In the first year of Huángchū (黃初),
a hawk was born from a swallow in the Wèiyāng (未央) Palace,
its beak and claws both red.
This was similar to the omens of Shāng Zhòu (商紂) and Sòng Yǐn (宋隱).
In the first year of Jǐngchū (景初),
a giant chick, resembling a hawk but with a swallow's bill, was born from a swallow in Lǐ Gài's (李蓋) house in the state of Wèi (衞).
Its form was like a hawk's,
its beak like a swallow's.
This was an omen of winged creatures,
and also a red misfortune.
Gāo Tánglóng (高 堂隆) said:
"This is a great anomaly for the Wèi (魏) house;
it is advisable to guard against 'hawk-like' officials within the palace walls."
Later, Emperor Xuān (宣帝) rose and executed Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽),
thus bringing about the Wèi (魏) house's demise.
In the twenty-third year of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Emperor Xiàn (獻帝) of Hàn (漢),
bald storks gathered at the pond behind the Wénchāng (文昌)殿 of the Yè (鄴) Palace.
The next year,
King Wǔ (武王) of Wèi (魏) died.
In the third year of Huángchū (黃初) of Emperor Wén (文帝) of Wèi (魏),
they again gathered at the Fānglín (芳林) Garden pond in Luòyáng (雒陽).
In the seventh year,
they gathered again.
That summer,
Emperor Wén (文帝) died.
At the end of Jǐngchū (景初),
they again gathered at the Fānglín (芳林) Garden pond.
Having appeared twice before,
each time followed by a great death,
the emperor was displeased by it.
That year,
Emperor Míng (明帝) died.
In the tenth month of the ninth year of Jiànxīng (建興) of Liú Chán (劉禪) of Shǔ (蜀),
from Jiāngyáng (江陽) to Jiāngzhōu (江州), birds flew from the south bank across to the north bank of the Jiāng (江) River,
but unable to reach, fell into the water and died by the thousands.
At this time, Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) had repeatedly mobilized his forces for years,
aiming to conquer the central plains,
but ultimately died south of the Wèi (渭) River,
his plans unfulfilled.
Moreover, his generals quarreled and divided,
losing many troops.
The birds flying north, unable to reach and falling into the water to die,
all symbolized this.
Liàng (亮) ultimately could not cross the Wèi (渭) River;
was this also its fulfillment?
This is roughly similar to the incident in the state of Chǔ (楚) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty where crows fought and fell into the Sì (泗) River.
In the first year of Jǐngchū (景chū),
when the Língxiāo (陵霄) gate tower was first constructed, [二八]magpies built nests on top of it.
Magpies have a mix of black and white plumage;
this was an omen of winged creatures,
and also a black-and-white omen.
The emperor asked Gāo Tánglóng (高堂隆) about it,
who replied:
"The Odes say, 'Though the magpie has a nest,
the dove dwells in it.'
Now, as you are building palaces and magpies come to nest,
this symbolizes that the palaces will not be completed and you will not be able to dwell in them.
The warning from Heaven is as if to say:
before the palaces are completed,
another family will control them.
This must not be taken lightly."
Thereupon, the emperor's expression changed.
In the fourth month of the twelfth year of Chìwū (赤烏) of Sūn Quán (孫權) of Wú (吳),
two crows carried a magpie and dropped it at the Dōngguǎn (東館).
Quán (權) ordered the Chief Chancellor Zhū Jù (朱據) to burn the magpie as a sacrifice.
According to Liú Xīn's (劉歆) explanation,
this was an omen of winged creatures,
and also a black omen.
It was a punishment for not seeing clearly and not hearing acutely.
At this time, Quán (權)'s ambition overflowed and his virtue declined;
he believed slander and enjoyed killing.
His two sons were in peril,
and both the chancellor and generals were endangered.
He saw the omen but did not comprehend it,
and even added burning to it—
this was the height of ignorance of the Way.
The next year,
Crown Prince Hé (和) was deposed,
King Bà (霸) of Lǔ (魯) was granted death,
Zhū Jù (朱據) was demoted,
and Lù Yì (陸議) died of grief.
This was its fulfillment.
The Dōngguǎn (東館) was
the office for education;
that the magpie fell at the Dōngguǎn (東館),
was this also Heaven's will?
In the first month of the second year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Sūn Quán (孫權) of Wú (吳),
the former Crown Prince Hé (和) was enfeoffed as King of Nányáng (南陽),
and sent to Chángshā (長沙).
A magpie nested on his mast.
Hé (和)'s former palace officials heard of it
and were all distressed,
believing that the mast's end tilting was precarious,
not a sign of long-term stability.
After this, he indeed did not die a natural death.
In the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng (建xīng) of Sūn Liàng (孫亮),
five large birds appeared at Chūnshēn (春申).
The people of Wú (吳) took them for phoenixes.
The next year,
the reign title was changed to Wǔfèng (五鳳).
During the reign of Emperor Huán (桓帝) of Hàn (漢), there were large five-colored birds.
Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪) said:
"When the Way of government is in decline and deficient,
it cannot attract phoenixes,
these are merely winged creature omens."
Sūn Liàng (孫亮) had no virtuous governance,
and Sūn Jùn (孫峻) was becoming increasingly arrogant and tyrannical.
This was the same situation as Emperor Huán (桓帝)'s time.
According to the Ruìyìng Tú (瑞應圖),
there was more than one instance of large birds resembling phoenixes but being omens;
it is likely that all of these were such.
In the third year of Jiànhéng (建衡) of Sūn Hào (孫晧),
it was reported from the Xīyuàn (西苑) that a phoenix had gathered,
and the reign title was changed accordingly.
The meaning was the same as Liàng (亮)'s case.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
a pheasant flew onto the Chānghé (閶闔) Gate.
Heaven's warning was as if to say:
the Chānghé (閶闔) Gate is not where a pheasant should stop,
similar to the warning of the pheasant climbing to the ear of the cauldron during the Yīn (殷) dynasty.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng (永康) of Emperor Huì (惠帝),
after King Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) had usurped the throne,
an unusual bird was found in the capital,
which no one could name.
Lún (倫) sent someone to carry it out,
circling the city and asking people.
After several days,
a small child by the west of the palace saw it
and spontaneously said:
"It is a 'fúlúniǎo yì' (服留鳥翳)."
The carrier immediately returned and reported to Lún (倫).
Lún (倫) sent him to look for it again,
and the child was seen again.
He was then brought into the palace,
the bird was secretly caged,
and the child was also locked in a room.
The next day, when they looked,
both were gone.
This was an omen of winged creatures.
At that time, King Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) suffered from an eye tumor.
The phrase 'fúliú' (服留) meant that
Lún (倫) would remain to suffer his punishment.
Soon after, Lún (倫) was executed.
When King Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) usurped the throne,
quails entered the Tàijí (太極)殿,
and pheasants gathered in the Dōngtáng (東堂).
Heaven's warning was as if to say:
the Tàijí (太極)殿 and Dōngtáng (東堂) are places for audiences and attending to governance,
and for quails and pheasants to gather there on the same day
meant that King Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) ought not to occupy this position.
The Odes say:
"The magpie is strong,
the quail is swift.
People without goodness,
I take as my lord."
Was it referring to this?
Soon after, Lún (倫) was destroyed.
In the second month of the first year of Yǒngjiā, during the reign of Xiàohuái Dì,
in Luòyáng, northeast of Bùguǎnglǐ, the ground sank,
and two geese, one black and one white, emerged.
The black one flew up into the sky,
while the white one stayed.
This was an omen involving winged creatures,
and also an auspicious sign involving black and white.
Dǒng Yǎng of Chénliú said:
"Bùguǎng
was Díquán of the Zhōu dynasty,
a place of covenants and gatherings.
The white one
represents the color gold,
the current elemental phase of the state.
The black represents the Hú (barbarian) omen.
Can all of this be fully expressed?"
After this,
Liú Yuánhǎi and Shí Lè successively caused chaos in Huá (China).
On the *gēngxū* day of the eighth month of the third year of Tàiníng, during the reign of Míng Dì,
there were two large birds,
blackish in color,
with wings spanning fourteen *chǐ*.
One landed at the Sītú (Minister of Works) office,
was shot and killed.
The other landed at a house north of the market,
and was also captured.
This was an omen involving winged creatures,
and also an auspicious sign involving black.
Then, on the *wùzǐ* day of the intercalary month, the Emperor passed away,
and later there was the rebellion of Sū Jùn and Zǔ Yuē.
In the first month of the second year of Xiánhé, during the reign of Chéng Dì,
five gulls gathered in the palace courtyard.
This was another auspicious sign involving white.
At this time, Yǔ Liàng stubbornly went against the public's advice,
intending to summon Sū Jùn,
and was blamed for not following counsel.
Thus, the white omen appeared first.
In the second month of the third year,
Sū Jùn indeed rebelled,
the palace was burned and destroyed,
turning into ruins and wasteland.
This was its fulfillment.
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Xiánkāng,
white egrets gathered on the palace roof.
At this time, Kāng Dì had just ascended the throne,
this was an omen of a short reign.
After two years, the Emperor passed away.
According to Liú Xiàng, he said:
"When wild birds enter a dwelling,
the palace will soon be empty."
This was its fulfillment.
Hǎixī Dì, upon ascending the throne in the second month of the third year of Xīngníng,
had a wild pheasant gather on the *xiāngfēng* (wind vane).
This was an omen involving winged creatures.
Soon after, he was deposed by Huán Wēn.
In the sixth month of the sixteenth year of Tàiyuán, during the reign of Xiàowǔ Dì,
magpies nested at the eastern end of the Tàijí Hall's owl tail,
and also at the western end of the Guózǐxuétáng (National Academy) hall.
In the eighteenth year, the Eastern Palace was completed.
In the first month of the nineteenth year, magpies again nested at its western gate.
This is likely the same omen as during the Jǐngchū era of Wèi.
The academy hall
is where enlightenment and education gather;
the western end
is also an auspicious sign of the metal element.
After the Emperor passed away,
Ān Huángsì (Emperor Ān) succeeded to the throne,
Huán Xuán then usurped it,
and enlightenment and education then declined.
This was the symbol of the metal element not prevailing.
In the third year of Yìxī, during the reign of Ān Dì,
Zhū Yī, the Longxiáng General, was stationed at Shòuyáng.
When a maid was cooking rice,
a flock of crows suddenly gathered around the stove,
competing to peck and eat.
The maid drove them away but they would not leave.
A hunting dog bit and killed two crows.
The remaining crows then together pecked the dog to death,
and also ate its flesh,
leaving only bones.
This was also an omen involving winged creatures,
and also an auspicious sign involving black.
In the sixth month of the following year,
Zhū Yī died.
This was its fulfillment.
Sheep Omen
In the fifth month of the second year of Xiánhé, during the reign of Chéng Dì,
a sheep in the stable of Sītú Wáng Dǎo was born without hind legs.
This was a sheep omen.
The *Jīngfáng Yìzhuàn* says:
"When there are too few legs,
the subordinates are incompetent."
The following year,
Sū Jùn attacked the capital,
and Wáng Dǎo and the Emperor were both imprisoned at Shítóu,
barely escaping.
This was its fulfillment.
Red Calamity, Red Omen
During the time of Gōngsūn Wényì,
in the northern market of Xiāngpíng, living flesh grew,
each several *chǐ* long and wide,
with heads, eyes, mouths, and beaks,
but no hands or feet, yet it moved.
This was a red omen.
The divination said:
"If there is a form but it is incomplete,
if there is a body but it makes no sound,
then its state will perish."
Gōngsūn Wényì was soon executed by Wèi.
Dèng Xǐ, a Wú garrison commander, killed a pig to sacrifice to the gods.
After preparing it, he hung it up,
and suddenly saw a human head come to eat the meat.
Dèng Xǐ drew his bow and shot it, hitting it.
It made a *zāzā* sound
and circled the house for three days.
This was a close red omen.
Later, someone accused Dèng Xǐ of plotting to defect to the north,
and his whole family was executed.
The *Jīngfáng Yìzhuàn* says:
"Mountains are seen with *bǎo*,
rivers in cities,
cities have soldiers,
shaped like human heads,
red in color."
On the *rénzǐ* day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng, during the reign of Wǔ Dì,
the pool water in Lǔguó turned red like blood.
In the tenth month of the seventh year,
there were two *qǐng* of red snow in Héyīn.
These were red omens.
Four years later, the Emperor passed away,
and the royal house then fell into chaos.
In the third month of the fifth year of Yuánkāng, during the reign of Huì Dì,
blood flowed in Lǚxiàn,
for over a hundred paces east to west.
This was a red omen.
By the end of Yuánkāng,
there was extreme brutality and chaos,
which was the fulfillment of corpses and flowing blood.
Gān Bǎo believed
that "eight years later, Fēng Yún caused chaos in Xúzhōu,
killing tens of thousands of people."
This was its fulfillment.
In the third month of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
it rained blood in Wèishì.
Indeed, when government and punishment are lenient,
there are always omens of persistent warmth and red portents.
In the first month of this year,
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ was sent and imprisoned in Xǔgōng.
The warning from Heaven seemed to say
that it was not appropriate to be lenient and indulge treacherous people,
which would cause the Crown Prince to die unjustly.
Huì Dì was foolish and oblivious,
and in this month, Mǐnhuái indeed died.
Thereupon, conflict arose in the royal house,
and disaster spread throughout the land.
On the day Nàochǐ killed Qí Mǐnwáng,
it rained blood, staining clothes.
Heaven was giving a warning.
Is this what is meant? The *Jīngfáng Yìzhuàn* says:
"If imprisonment is not resolved,
this is called pursuing wrong,
its calamity is blood raining from heaven.
This is called not being close,
if subordinates have evil intentions,
within three years,
their clan will be no more."
It also says:
"When flatterers are rewarded,
and meritorious ministers are executed,
heaven rains blood."
In the twelfth month of the first year of Jìanxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
there was an earthquake in Hédōng,
and it rained flesh.
In the twelfth month, on the day Bǐngyín, of the fourth year,
the Prime Minister's office executed Chúnyú Bó, the Administrator of Transportation.
His blood flowed backward and ascended a pillar two zhàng and three chǐ.
This was an auspicious sign of redness.
At this time,
Chǔ Póu, the General of the Rear, was garrisoned in Guǎnglíng.
[二九]The Prime Minister publicly declared a northern expedition.
Bó was executed according to military law
for delaying transportation and for illicitly employing laborers.
His son appealed, stating:
"The transportation matter was concluded;
there was no delay or shortage.
Although he accepted bribes and employed laborers illicitly,
the crime does not warrant death.
In military strategy,
public declarations precede actual operations.
This was actually a garrison assignment,
not a campaigning army.
Since the fourth year,
all delays in transport have
not been judged according to military emergency law."
The officials did not address this.
When the change occurred,
the Director of Justice impeached various officials,
but Emperor Yuán did not question it,
and consequently, there was a continuous drought for three years.
Gān Bǎo believed this was a response to a wrongful grievance.
Guō Jǐngchún said:
"Blood is a type of water,
both belonging to Kǎn.
Kǎn symbolizes law,
and water naturally flows downward,
it should not flow backward.
This is a sign of faults and errors in governance."
In the first month of the first year of Jiànyuán of the pseudo Liú Cōng,
there was an earthquake in Píngyáng.
His Chóngmíng Temple collapsed into a pond,
the water was red like blood,
red qi ascended to the sky,
and a red dragon struggled and departed.
A shooting star originated from Qiāniú,
entered Zǐwēi,
its form like a winding dragon,
its light illuminated the ground,
and it fell ten lǐ north of Píngyáng.
When inspected, it was flesh,
its stench was smelled in Píngyáng,
thirty steps long,
and twenty-seven steps wide.
Next to the flesh, there was always crying,
day and night without ceasing.
After several days,
Liú Shì, Cōng's empress, gave birth to a snake and a beast,
each harming people and then fleeing.
They were sought but not found,
but soon after, they were seen next to the fallen flesh.
At this time,
Liú Cōng had taken Liú Yīn's three daughters,
and all of them became his empresses.
Heaven's warning seemed to say that
since Cōng had claimed the surname Liú,
and the three empresses were also all of the Liú clan,
this violated the ethical principles of kinship
and disrupted the rules of human relations.
The fallen flesh and various other strange phenomena,
their ominous signs were also great.
Shortly after, the Liú clan died,
and the crying sound ceased by itself.
