there was hail in Guǎnglíng.
In the following year,
Lú Xún reached Càizhōu.
In the first month of the sixth year, on the *bǐngyín* day,
there was snow and also thunder.
In the fifth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
there was hail.
On the *xīnwèi* day of the fourth month, the first day of the month, in the eighth year,
there was hail.
In the sixth month, on the *guǐhài* day,
there was hail
and a strong wind that tore off roofs.
In this autumn,
Liú Fān and others were executed.
In the fourth month of the tenth year, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
there was hail.
Thunder
During the Jǐngchū reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,

the eastern bridge of Luòyáng city, the floating bridge over the Luò River west of the city, and the main pillars of the Hányíng building were all struck by lightning simultaneously in three places on the same day.
Soon after, lightning also struck the weather vane (wooden bird) on the western city wall.
At that time, large labor projects were initiated,
and the Emperor soon passed away.
In the summer of the eighth year of Chìwū of Sūn Quán of Wú,
lightning struck the palace gate pillars,
and also hit the main pillars of the great bridge at Nánjīn.
On the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Jiànxīng of Sūn Liàng,
there was a strong wind, thunder, and lightning.
In this month,
there was also thunder and rain.
The meaning is the same as the previous explanation,
and Liàng was eventually deposed.
On the *jiǎshēn* day of the twelfth month, the first day of the month, in the sixth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
there was thunder and lightning in the commandery of Huáinán.
In the twelfth month of the seventh year, on the *jǐhài* day,
there was thunder and lightning in Pílíng,
and Dài Liàng, the Salt Administrator of Nánshā, reported it.
In the twelfth month of the tenth year, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
there was thunder, lightning, and heavy rain in Lújiāng and Jiàn'ān.
In the sixth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng of Emperor Huì, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
lightning struck the monument of Chóngyáng Mausoleum,
and the monument five hundred *bù* to the southwest was broken into seventy pieces.
At this time,
Empress Jiǎ framed and harmed the chief ministers,
and favored her private relatives,
which was the same event as when lightning struck the imperial mausoleum during Emperor Huán of Hàn's time.
The Empress was eventually executed.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng, on the *dīngchǒu* day of the tenth month,
thunder struck.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiā, during the reign of Emperor Huái, in the tenth month,
thunder and lightning struck.
In the first year of Jiànxīng, during the reign of Emperor Mǐn, on the *wùwǔ* day of the eleventh month,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning in Kuàijī.
On the night of the *jǐsì* day,
red vapor glowed in the northwest.
That evening,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
there was heavy snow.
According to Liú Xiàng’s explanation,
“Thunder emerges in the second month
and withdraws in the eighth month.”
Now, for thunder and lightning to strike in this month
indicates that the *yang* energy is not being contained and stored.
Once it has discharged, the very next day there is heavy snow;
these are all anomalies of misplaced seasons.
At this time,
Liú Zǎi usurped the title in Píngyáng,
Lǐ Xióng claimed imperial rule in Shǔ,
the nine provinces were fragmented,
the Western Capital was isolated and weak;
these are signs of a ruler out of step with the times.
Red vapor
is a red auspicious omen.
In the first year of Tàixīng, during the reign of Emperor Yuán, on the *yǐmǎo* day of the eleventh month,
there was a sudden storm with thunder and lightning.
In the second year of Yǒngchāng, on the *bǐngzǐ* day, the first day of the seventh month,
thunder struck a pillar of the Tàijí Hall.
In the twelfth month,
thunder and lightning struck in Kuàijī and Wújùn.
In the first year of Xiánhé, during the reign of Emperor Chéng, on the *jǐsì* day of the tenth month,
there was heavy rain with thunder and lightning in Kuàijī Commandery.
In the third year, on the *xīnmǎo* day of the sixth month,
destroying ten small house pillars inside the commandery yamen
and killing people.
On the *rénwǔ* day, the second day of the ninth month, which was the beginning of winter,
there was thunder and lightning in Kuàijī.
In the fourth year, in the eleventh month,
Wújùn and Kuàijī again experienced thunder and lightning.
In the seventh year of Yǒnghé, during the reign of Emperor Mù, on the *rénwǔ* day of the tenth month,
there was a thunderstorm with thunder and lightning.
In the first year of Shēngpíng, on the *gēngxū* day of the eleventh month,
there was thunder.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
there was thunder again.
In the fifth year, on the *gēngwǔ* day of the tenth month,
thunder originated from the southeast.
In the fifth year of Tàiyuán, during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ, on the *jiǎyín* day of the sixth month,
thunder struck four pillars of the Hánzhāng Hall,
and killed two palace attendants.
In the tenth year, in the twelfth month,
the sound of thunder was in the south.
In the fourteenth year, on the *jiǎyín* day of the seventh month,
thunder struck,
burning the western pillar of the Xuānyáng Gate.
In the second year of Lóng'ān, during the reign of Emperor Ān, on the *rénchén* day of the ninth month,
there was a thunderstorm.
In the third year of Yuánxīng,
when Empress Yǒng'ān arrived from Bālíng
and was about to be ceremonially led into the palace,
heavenly thunder struck,
killing one person and one horse.
In the fourth year of Yìxī, on the *xīnmǎo* day, the first day of the eleventh month,
a swift wind arose from the northwest.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
there was thunder.
In the fifth year, on the *bǐngyín* day of the sixth month,
breaking the eastern *chīwěi* ornament
and piercing a pillar,
and also struck the combined hall by the Crown Prince’s western pond.
At this time,
the emperor did not personally perform the autumn and spring ancestral sacrifices,
hence heaven struck it with thunder,
to highlight the neglect of the ancestral temple.
The western pond was built when Emperor Míng was crown prince,
hence it was called the Crown Prince's Pond.
And when Emperor Ān was often ill
and worried about not having an heir,
hence heaven struck it with thunder,
to indicate the absence of an heir.
In the sixth year, on the *bǐngyín* day of the first month,
there was thunder
and also snow.
In the twelfth month, on the *rénchén* day,
there was great thunder.
In the ninth year, on the *jiǎxū* day of the eleventh month,
there was thunder.
On the *yǐhài* day,
there was thunder again.
Drum Anomalies
In the ninth year of Yuánkāng, during the reign of Emperor Huì, in the third month,
a sound like that of an ox
emerged from Xǔchāng city.
In the twelfth month,
the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was deposed
and confined in the Xǔ Palace.
The following year,
Empress Jiǎ sent the palace attendant Sūn Lǜ to kill the crown prince,
striking him with a pestle;
the sound was heard outside,
which was the omen's fulfillment.
Sū Jùn, in his outer camp at Lìyáng,
had his general’s drum sound by itself,
as if someone were beating it.
Jùn personally broke it,
saying:
“When I was in my hometown, if this happened,
the city would be emptied.”
Soon after, he rebelled and was annihilated.
This was the punishment for not heeding the warning.
At the end of Shí Jìlóng’s reign,
nine *lǐ* northwest of Luòyáng city,
a stone ox on a bluestone pedestal
suddenly bellowed,
the sound heard forty *lǐ* away.
Jìlóng sent men to chip off its ears and tail
and nail down its four legs with iron spikes.
Soon after, Jìlóng died.
In the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán, during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ, on the *jǐyǒu* day, the first day of the third month,
there was a sound like thunder in the northeast.
According to Liú Xiàng’s explanation,
he believed that
“thunder ought to depend on clouds,
just as a ruler depends on his ministers.
Thunder without clouds
is a sign that the ruler does not care for his subordinates,
and the common people will rebel.”
And when the emperor passed away, the world gradually fell into chaos,
with Sūn Ēn and Huán Xuán successively menacing the capital.
On Mount Xiàjià in Chángchéng, Wúxīng, there was a stone drum,
over a *zhàng* in length,
its face about three *chǐ* in diameter,
with a flat rock beneath it as its base.
When it sounded, its noise was like that of a metal drum,
and there would be soldiers in the Three Wú.
During the Lóng'ān period of Emperor Ān, it boomed loudly,
and afterwards there was Sūn Ēn’s rebellion.
Fish Anomalies
In the fourth year of Jiāpíng, during the reign of Wèi Qíwáng, in the fifth month,
two fish gathered on the roof of the Wǔkù,
this was a fish anomaly.
Wáng Sù said:
“Fish are born in water,
yet they are elevated onto a roof;
creatures with scales have lost their proper place.
Will not the border generals face a rebellion involving [military] armor?”
Later, there was indeed the defeat at Dōngguān.
Gān Bǎo further believed it was the omen for the military disaster of Gāoguìxiāng Gōng.
Both explanations are consistent with Bān Gù’s intent.
During the Tàikāng period of Emperor Wǔ,
two carp were seen on the roof of the Wǔkù.
Gān Bǎo believed:
“The Wǔkù is an armory,
and fish have scales and armor,
also a type of military object.
Fish are extremely *yin*,
while the roof is *yang*.
Fish appearing on the roof
symbolizes the extreme *yin* causing military disaster to affect the *yang*.
At the beginning of Emperor Huì’s reign,
Yáng Jùn was executed,
the empress dowager deposed,
and arrows flew through the halls and pavilions.
At the end of Yuánkāng,
Empress Jiǎ slandered and killed the crown prince,
and was herself executed and deposed soon after.
Within ten years,
the disaster involving empresses and empress dowagers erupted twice;
this was its fulfillment,
and from then on, chaos and rebellion ensued.”
The *Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
“If fish leave the water
and fly onto the road,
war is about to break out.”
Locusts
The *Chūnqiū*
records *zhōng* (locusts).
Liú Xīn considered it an anomaly of armored insects,
sharing the same divination meaning as fish.
In the third year of Huángchū, during the reign of Wèi Wéndì, in the seventh month,
there was a great locust plague in Jìzhōu,
and people suffered hunger.
According to Cài Yōng’s explanation,
“Locusts
are caused by the greed and harshness of those in power.”
At this time,
Sūn Quán submitted,
but the emperor, due to his campaign at Xīlíng,
led a large army to attack him,
and Quán subsequently rebelled.
In the sixth month of the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
there was a locust plague.
At this time,
Xún and Jiǎ held political power,
and harmed the public and the upright.
In the first year of Yǒngníng of Emperor Huì,
there were six locust plagues in the commanderies and kingdoms.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
there was a great locust plague.
From Yōu, Bìng, Sī, and Jì to Qín and Yōng,
the grass, trees, and manes and tails of cattle and horses were all consumed.
At this time,
the world was in military turmoil,
and the common people were hunted like fish,
with the survival of the dynasty dependent
solely on Sīmǎ Yuè and Gǒu Xī.
They competed in their cruelty and harshness,
and their governance was chaotic.
Thus, this calamity occurred.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
there was a great locust plague.
Last year, Liú Yào repeatedly attacked Běidì and Féngyì,
and Qū Yǔn and others led all their forces to resist him.
They were ultimately defeated by Liú Yào,
and the Western capital collapsed.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor was in Píngyáng,
and there were locusts in Sī, Jì, Qīng, and Yōng.
In the sixth month of the first year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
there was a locust plague in Lánlíng’s Héxiāng,
damaging crops.
On the Yǐwèi day,
locusts in Dōngguǎn spread three hundred *lǐ* both vertically and horizontally,
damaging young crops.
In the seventh month,
locusts in the four commanderies of Dōnghǎi, Péngchéng, Xiàpī, and Línhuái damaged grain and beans.
In the eighth month,
locusts in the three provinces of Jì, Qīng, and Xú
consumed all the growing grass,
and this continued for two years.
At this time,
the Central Plain was lost,
and violence and chaos greatly intensified.
In the fifth month of the second year,
locusts in the five commanderies of Huáilíng, Línhuái, Huáinán, Ānfēng, and Lújiāng consumed autumn wheat.
On the Guǐchǒu day of this month,
there were locusts in Xúzhōu and the commanderies west of the Jiāng River in Yángzhōu,
and many people in Wújùn starved to death.
In this year,
Wáng Dūn concurrently governed Jīngzhōu,
and the source of harshness and cruelty arose from this.
In the eighth month of the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
there was a locust plague in Yǎnzhōu.
At this time,
the Muróng clan pressured Hénán,
and military expeditions continued without end.
Thus, this calamity occurred.
In the fifth month of the sixteenth year,
flying locusts came from the south,
gathering in the borders of Dángyì county,
damaging young crops.
In the spring of this year,
two thousand armored soldiers from Jiāngzhōu were mobilized,
with six or seven thousand family members,
and assigned to the Protector-General and the Eastern Palace.
Later, they quickly dispersed and almost all perished.
Also, frontier generals were continuously engaged in expeditions,
thus this calamity occurred.
Calamities from Swine
In the first year of Bǎodǐng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
a wild boar entered the camp of the Grand Marshal of the Right, Dīng Fèng.
This was a calamity from swine.
Later, Dīng Fèng was dispatched to attack Gǔyáng,
but returned without success.
Sūn Hào was enraged
and beheaded his vanguard commander.
When he led a large army north,
Dīng Fèng and Wàn Yù and others said to each other:
“If we reach Huálǐ,
we will have no choice but to return individually.”
This plot was leaked.
Although Dīng Fèng had already died at that time,
Sūn Hào investigated the Gǔyáng incident,
killed his son Wēn,
and all his family members were exiled to distant places.
This was the manifestation of the calamity from swine.
Gōng Suì said,
“If beasts from the mountains and wilds
enter the palace,
the palace will become empty.”
This is also its omen.
During the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái,
a sow in Shòuchūn city gave birth to two-headed piglets that did not survive.
Zhōu Fù took and observed them.
At that time, those who understood said:
“The pig
is an animal of the north,
symbolizing the Hú and Dí peoples.
Two heads means
there will be no supreme ruler.
Born and then dead means
it will not succeed.
Heaven’s warning seems to say,
‘Do not conceive schemes of exclusive self-interest,
for you will bring about your own downfall.’”
Zhōu Fù did not awaken to this,
and then wished to welcome the Son of Heaven and command the feudal lords.
Shortly after, he was defeated by Emperor Yuán.
This was its manifestation.
Shí Lè also soon crossed the Huái River,
and nine out of ten common people died.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Yuán,
a pig was born with eight legs.
This was the punishment for inattentiveness,
and also for employing the wicked.
After this, there was the rebellion of Liú Wǎi.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
in a family in Qiántáng, a boar gave birth to two piglets,
both with human faces,
resembling Hú people,
but their bodies were still like pigs.
Jīng Fáng’s *Yì Yāo* says:
“When a pig is born with a human head and a pig’s body,
there will be danger and chaos.
Now this boar gave birth,
which is an extreme anomaly.”
In the fourth month of the tenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
in the capital, a piglet was born with one head, two spines, and eight legs.
In the thirteenth year,
in a family in the capital, a sow gave birth to piglets,
one with one head, two bodies, and eight legs,
both being the same omen as in Jiànwǔ.
After this,
the prime ministers indulged in excessive drinking,
neglecting state affairs.
Close attendants gained influence,
gradually disrupting the national order,
leading to great ruin.
Black Calamities and Black Omens
In the twelfth month of the fifth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Xiàohuái,
black *qì* filled all directions.
This was a black omen.
The Emperor was soon overthrown,
and the imperial house became a ruin.
This was its manifestation.
On the Jǐsì day, the first day of the first month of the second year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
black fog clung to people like ink,
lasting for nights,
and only stopped after five days.
This was a black omen.
In its fourth year,
the Emperor surrendered to Liú Yào.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán,
there was a great fog in the capital,
with black *qì* obscuring the sky,
and the sun and moon losing their light.
In the eleventh month,
the Emperor passed away.
Fire Afflicting Water
In the sixth month of the fifth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
the waters in the ponds of Rénchéng and Lǔguó all turned red like blood.
According to Liú Xiàng’s explanation,
this is an omen of fire afflicting water,
a punishment for inattentiveness.
Jīng Fáng’s *Yì Zhuàn* says:
“If the ruler is licentious and indulgent in pleasure,
and worthy men are hidden,
the state will be in danger.
Its omen is water flowing red.”
In the second month of the third year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù,
there was fire in the pond east of Liángzhōu city.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
there was again fire in the swamp waters of Gūzàng.
These were omens of fire afflicting water.
The next year,
Zhāng Tiānxī killed the Central Protector-General Zhāng Yōng.
Zhāng Yōng was
a person in power.
In the tenth month of the second year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Ān,
the waters of Línpíng Lake in Qiántáng turned red.
Huán Xuán implicitly encouraged Wújùn to declare it an auspicious sign for himself.
Shortly after, Huán Xuán was defeated.
The commentary says:
"When the 'thinking mind' is not capacious,
this is called 'not sagely.'
Its affliction is dimness,
its punishment is wind,
its ultimate consequence is ill-omened short lives and premature deaths.
At such times, there are omens of 'fat at night,'
at such times there are 'flower anomalies,'
at such times there are 'ox calamities,'
at such times there are 'ailments of the heart and abdomen,'
at such times there are 'yellow blights and yellow omens,'
at such times there are disruptions of earth by metal, wood, water, and fire."
When the 'thinking mind' is not capacious,
this is called 'not sagely.'
'Thinking mind'
means the mind's thoughts and deliberations.
'Capacious'
means broad.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"If one in a high position is not capacious,
how can I observe him!"
This means that if superiors are not broad and inclusive,
then their subordinates cannot occupy sagely positions.
Appearance, speech, sight, and hearing
are all governed by the mind;
if all four are amiss,
then there is dimness and lack of discernment,
hence its affliction is dimness.
Rain, drought, cold, and warmth
also take wind as their basis;
if the four qi are all in disorder,
hence its punishment is wind.
Wind harms things,
hence its ultimate consequence is ill-omened short lives and premature deaths.
Harm to humans is called ill-omened (xiōng),
to birds and beasts it is called short (duǎn),
to plants and trees it is called broken (zhé).
Another explanation says:
Xiōng
means early death;
a younger brother dying before an elder brother is called duǎn,
a father losing a son is called zhé.
In humans,
the fat that covers the heart within the abdomen
is zhī.
If the mind is dim and obscure,
hence there are omens of 'fat at night.'
Another explanation says:
there are greasy substances that cause anomalies at night,
like zhī yè zhē people's clothes,
which is an omen of lewdness.
Another explanation says:
'night anomalies'
are when clouds and wind rise together and become dark and obscure,
hence they have the same omens as ordinary wind.
If it is warm and windy, then mealybugs and planthoppers will be born,
leading to anomalies of naked insects.
Liú Xiàng believed:
"In the Yì,
Xùn is wind,
and is wood.
The hexagram is in the third and fourth months,
following Yáng to govern,
presiding over the flowers and fruits of wood.
When the wind energy is exceedingly strong,
and trees re-blossom in autumn and winter,
hence there are 'flower anomalies.'"
Another explanation says:
if the earth's energy is strong, then it re-blossoms in autumn and winter.
Another explanation says:
huá means color,
earth governs internal affairs,
referring to female anomalies.
In the Yì,
Kūn is earth,
and is an ox.
Oxen have large hearts but cannot think or deliberate,
so the heart's qi is damaged,
hence there are 'ox calamities.'
Another explanation says:
many oxen dying or acting strangely
is also this.
When it affects humans,
many suffer from heart and abdominal illnesses,
hence there are 'ailments of the heart and abdomen.'
The color of earth is yellow,
hence there are 'yellow blights and yellow omens.'
Generally, those whose 'thinking mind' is damaged
suffer from earth qi illness;
if earth qi is ill,
then metal, wood, water, and fire will disrupt it,
hence it is said: "at such times there are disruptions of earth by metal, wood, water, and fire."
Not saying
"wéi"
but only saying
"shí zé yǒu"
indicates
that it is not a disruption caused by a single surge of qi,
making clear its significant difference.
As for its ultimate consequence being ill-omened short lives and premature deaths,
if one conforms to it,
its blessing is called 'dying a full natural life.'
Liú Xīn's 'Thinking Mind Commentary' says:
"At times there are anomalies of naked insects,
referring to creatures like mealybugs and planthoppers."
Various omens: wind
In the eleventh month of the ninth year of Zhèngshǐ of Wèi Qí Wáng,
there was a great wind for several tens of days,
tearing off roofs and breaking trees.
On the Wùmǎo day of the twelfth month, it was especially severe,
shaking the eastern gallery of the Tàijí palace.
On the Rénchén day, the first day of the first month of Jiāpíng year 1,
there was a great wind from the northwest,
tearing off roofs, breaking trees,
and dim dust obscured the sky.
According to Guǎn Lù's explanation,
this was a warning against punishing high officials at the wrong time,
and a cause for concern for those in power.
At this time,
Cáo Shuǎng was dim-witted and acted arbitrarily,
excessively arrogant and presumptuous.
Heavenly warnings appeared repeatedly,
but he ultimately did not reform,
this was the wind's punishment for the 'thinking mind' not being sagacious.
More than ten days later, Shuǎng and others were executed.
Jīng Fáng's 'Yì Zhuàn' says:
"When the multitude acts against common will,
and supreme virtue becomes hidden,
its anomaly is wind.
This wind
blows unceasingly,
things do not grow,
and rain is light but damaging.
When government deviates and virtue is concealed, this is called disorder,
its wind is a preliminary wind without rain,
a great wind rises violently,
tearing off roofs and breaking trees.
When one holds to righteousness but does not advance, this is called mào,
its wind rises together with clouds,
breaking the stalks of the five grains.
When ministers usurp the government of their superiors, this is called insubordination,
its wind is a great whirlwind that tears off roofs.
When levies and taxes are not managed properly, this is called calamity,
its wind severs the threads,
and when it stops, it becomes warm,
and when warm, insects appear.
When marquises monopolize their fiefs, this is called disunity,
its wind is swift but trees do not sway,
and grains do not ripen.
When rulers do not consider the benefits of the Dao, this is called lacking benevolence,
its wind does not sway trees,
there is drought without clouds,
harming grain.
When dukes constantly pursue profit, this is called disorder,
its wind is slight and warm,
giving birth to worms and locusts,
harming the five grains.
When one abandons governance and indulges in lewdness, this is called delusion,
its wind is warm,
mealybugs appear,
harming things beneficial to people.
When feudal lords do not attend court, this is called rebellion,
its wind is absent,
the earth turns red,
and rain kills people."
On the first day of the eighth month of Tàiyuán year 1 of Wú Sūn Quán,
there was a great wind,
the rivers and seas surged and overflowed,
the water on flat ground was eight feet deep,
two thousand trees on high mounds were uprooted,
stone steles moved and shook,
and two gates of Wúchéng flew off.
〔一二〕 According to Huá Hé's reply,
this was the punishment for frequent labor service and heavy taxes, and a dim and uncapacitous mind.
The next year, Quán passed away.
On the Bǐngshēn day of the twelfth month of Jiànxīng year 1 of Sūn Liàng,
there was a great wind and thunder.
In this year,
Wèi dispatched large armies in three routes to attack;
Zhūgě Kè defeated their Dōngxīng army,
and the other two armies also retreated.
The next year,
Kè again attacked Xīnchéng,
losing more than half of his troops.
He returned
and was executed.
In the eleventh month, *jiǎwǔ* day, of the first year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Xiū,
winds shifted four times and returned five times,

Water

The collapse of Mount Liáng in the Spring and Autumn period,

For the three dynasties (Xià, Shāng, Zhōu), when they offered sacrifices,

The *Zhuàn* says:
“When the *huáng* is not extreme,
this is called not establishing.
Its calamity is *mào*,
its punishment is *yīn*,
and its extreme is weakness.
At such times there are shooting portents.
At such times there are misfortunes of dragons and snakes.
At such times there are horse calamities.
At such times there are diseases of inferiors attacking superiors.
At such times the sun and moon travel erratically,
and the stars move retrogradely.”
“When the *huáng* is not extreme,
this is called not establishing.”
*Huáng*
means ruler.
“Extreme”
means central.
“Establishing”
means to set up.
When a ruler loses all five functions of appearance, speech, sight, hearing, and thought,
failing to maintain the mean,
he cannot establish myriad affairs,
and the fault lies in *mào* (dimness) and perversity.
Therefore, its calamity is *mào*.
The king, from below, receives Heaven and governs all things.
Clouds rise from the mountains
and spread across the sky.
The *qi* of Heaven is in disorder,
so its punishment is *yīn* (darkness).
One interpretation says:
When the superior loses the mean,
then inferiors become strong and vigorous, obscuring the ruler's brilliance.
The *Yì* says:
“An arrogant dragon has regrets.”
This means being noble but losing one's position,
being high but losing the people,
and having worthy men in inferior positions without assistance.
If this is the case,
then the ruler possesses the dignity of facing south,
but lacks the help of a single person.
Therefore, his extreme is weakness.
Strong *yáng* moves, advances, is light and swift.
According to the Rites,
in spring, there is a grand archery ceremony
to accord with the *yáng* *qi*.
When the superior is weak and feeble, inferiors become agitated and startled,
hence there are shooting portents.
The *Yì* says:
“Clouds follow the dragon.”
It also says:
“The hibernation of dragons and snakes
is for preserving their lives.”
When *yīn* *qi* moves,
〔三七〕therefore there are misfortunes of dragons and snakes.
In the *Yì*,
the *Qián* trigram represents the ruler
and the horse.
When those employed are strong and powerful,
and the ruler's *qi* is damaged,
then there are horse calamities.
One interpretation says:
Many horses dying or behaving strangely
is also this.
When the ruler is chaotic and weak,
people will rebel against him,
and Heaven will abandon him.
If there is no execution by an enlightened king,
then there will be the calamity of usurpation and murder.
Therefore, there are diseases of inferiors attacking superiors.
In all cases where the Way of the ruler is harmed,
it afflicts the *qi* of Heaven.
It does not say that the Five Phases disrupt Heaven,
but rather says
“the sun and moon travel erratically,
〔三八〕and the stars move retrogradely.”
This is to suggest that inferiors dare not disrupt Heaven,
just as the *Chūnqiū* says,
“The royal army was defeated by the Máoróng,”
not explicitly stating who defeated them,
but framing it as self-defeat
to preserve the dignity of the respected.
Liú Xīn's *Huángjí Zhuàn* says there is the disease of the lower body growing above.
It explains that if inferiors attack superiors,
Heaven's punishment is already complete,
and it cannot again be called a disease.
Yīn
In the third year of Tàipíng of Wú Sūn Liàng (258 CE),
from the eighth month, there was persistent cloudy weather without rain
for over forty days.
At this time,
Sūn Liàng was about to execute Sūn Chén,
but the plot was leaked.
On the *wùxǔ* day of the ninth month,
Sūn Chén surrounded the palace with troops
and deposed Sūn Liàng as the King of Kuàijī.
This was the punishment of *yīn*.
In the first year of Bǎodǐng of Wú Sūn Hào (266 CE), in the twelfth month,
the Grand Astrologer reported prolonged *yīn* without rain,
indicating an impending *yīn* conspiracy.
Sūn Hào was alarmed and frightened.
At that time, Lù Kǎi and others plotted to depose him during his visit to the ancestral temple.
When Sūn Hào emerged,
Liú Píng led the vanguard with troops.
Lù Kǎi first spoke to Liú Píng,
but Liú Píng did not agree,
so the plot did not succeed.
As Sūn Hào indulged in tyranny,
many of his subordinates harbored different plans,
eventually leading to his surrender and downfall.
Shèyāo (Shooting Portent)
Shǔ's General of Chariots and Cavalry, Dèng Zhī, campaigned in Fúlíng.
He saw a black ape climbing a mountain
and shot it with his hand.
The ape pulled out the arrow,
rolled up tree leaves, and plugged its wound.
Dèng Zhī said:
“Alas!
I have violated the nature of creatures,
and I will probably die!”
Soon after, he died.
This was a *shèyāo*.
One interpretation says:
An ape mother was holding her child,
and Dèng Zhī shot it.
The child pulled out the arrow
and took tree leaves to plug the wound.
Dèng Zhī sighed,
threw his crossbow into the water,
and knew he was about to die.
When Gōngdì was the King of Lángyá,
he was fond of curious games.
He once locked a horse inside a gate
and ordered people to shoot it,
wanting to see how many arrows it would take to kill it.
One of his attendants remonstrated, saying:
“The horse
is the imperial surname.
Shooting it now
is inauspicious.”
Thereupon, he stopped,
but the horse had already been hit by about ten arrows.
This was probably a *shèyāo*.
Soon after, he abdicated the throne to the Sòng dynasty.
Lóngshé zhī Niè (Misfortunes of Dragons and Snakes)
In the first month of the first year of Qīnglóng of Wèi Míngdì (233 CE), on the *jiǎshēn* day,
a green dragon appeared in a well in Móbeì, Jiá county.
Generally, when auspicious omens arise out of season,
they become portents or misfortunes,
let alone being trapped in a well,
which is not a good omen.
The Wèi dynasty changed its year title because of this,
which was incorrect.
Gān Bǎo said:
“From Míngdì
to the end of the Wèi dynasty,
the appearances of green and yellow dragons
were all responses to the rise and fall of their rulers.
The Wèi dynasty's *tǔ* element,
while green represents wood,
was not overcome by metal.
Yellow gaining its position and green losing its position is the symbolism.
The frequent appearance of green dragons
means that the ruler's virtue and the dynastic fortune were internally conflicting and destructive.
Thus, Gāoguìxiāng Gōng ultimately perished by military force.”
According to Liú Xiàng's interpretation,
a dragon, being a noble symbol, trapped in a well,
signifies that the feudal lords will suffer the calamity of imprisonment.
Throughout the Wèi dynasty,
dragons were always seen in wells;
this was an omen of those in superior positions being oppressed and controlled.
Gāoguìxiāng Gōng composed the “Qianlong Poem” (*Poem of the Hidden Dragon*),
which refers to this very meaning.
In the tenth month of the first year of Zhèngyuán of Gāoguìxiāng Gōng (254 CE), on the *wùxǔ* day,
〔三九〕a yellow dragon appeared in a well in Yè.
In the first month of the first year of Gānlù (256 CE), on the *xīnchǒu* day,
a green dragon appeared in a well in Zhǐ county.
In the sixth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
a green dragon appeared in a well in the border area of Yuánchéng county.
In the second year (257 CE), in the second month,
a green dragon appeared in a well in Wēn county.
In the third year (258 CE),
yellow and green dragons both appeared in wells in the border areas of Dùnqiū, Guànjūn, and Yángxià counties.
In the first month of the fourth year (259 CE),
two yellow dragons appeared in wells in the border area of Nínglíng county.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Jǐngyuán of Yuándì (260 CE), on the *jiǎshēn* day,
a yellow dragon appeared in a well in Huáyīn county.
〔四０〕In the second month of the third year (262 CE),
a dragon appeared in a well in Zhǐ county.
During the Tiāncè era of Wú Sūn Hào,
a dragon nurtured its young in a private home in Chángshā
and ate chicks.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Yāo* says:
“When a dragon nurtures its young in a private home,
the king will become a commoner.”
Later, Sūn Hào surrendered to the Jìn dynasty.
In the sixth month, on the day *bǐngwǔ*, in the second year of Xiánníng of Emperor Wǔ,
two white dragons were seen in the well of Jiǔyuán.
In the first month, on the day *guǐmǎo*, in the fifth year of Tàikāng,
two dragons were seen in the well of the imperial armory.
The emperor observed them
with a joyful expression.
When the officials were about to offer congratulations,
Liú Yì alone submitted a memorial saying:
"In ancient times, dragon spittle in the courtyard of Xià
led to disaster for the Zhōu dynasty.
When a dragon appeared at the gate of Zhèng,
Zǐchǎn did not offer congratulations."
The emperor replied:
"My virtuous rule is not yet perfected;
I have nothing to deserve such a felicitous omen."
Thus, no congratulations were offered.
Sūn Shèng said:
"Dragons
are creatures of water.
What do they have to do with humans?
What Zǐchǎn said was correct.
However, when they are not in their proper place,
they are truly portents of disaster.
Dragons are considered auspicious when they soar and are clearly visible;
but now they are hidden in a secluded place,
which is not a good omen."
In the second year of Emperor Huì of Hàn,
two dragons were seen in the well of Lánlíng.
The original record considered this a sign that King Zhào would later die imprisoned.
The imperial armory
is where the instruments of imperial authority and control are treasured and stored.
Its buildings are deep and secluded,
not a place for dragons.
Seven years after this,
the feudal princes harmed each other.
Twenty-eight years later,
there were indeed two Hú who usurped the divine instruments of power.
Both of these rebels had the courtesy name Lóng,
thus this strange manifestation
is proven by events.
In the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
a Qiāng dancer in Páohǎn gave birth to a dragon-child,
whose color resembled brocade patterns.
It often suckled its mother,
and a divine light was seen from afar,
but few were able to approach and look.
This also indicated the failure of the emperor to establish himself,
and subsequently, the emperor indeed fell and was lost.
At the end of Lǚ Zuǎn's reign,
a dragon emerged from the well in the eastern annex,
and coiled and lay in front of his palace hall.
It was lost by dawn.
Soon after, a black dragon ascended his palace gate.
Zuǎn and others all considered it an auspicious omen.
Some said:
"Dragons are creatures of *yīn*,
appearing and disappearing at certain times.
Now that they frequently appear,
there must be a change where subordinates plot against their superiors."
Later, Zuǎn was indeed killed by Lǚ Chāo.
During the Xiánníng era of Emperor Wǔ,
in the Sītú mansion, there were two large snakes,
about ten *zhàng* long,
residing on the flat rafters of the reception hall, unknown to people.
For several years, it was only strange that small children, pigs, and dogs frequently went missing from the mansion.
Later, one snake came out at night,
was wounded by a blade and could not leave.
Only then was it discovered.
Servants were dispatched to attack it,
and it died after some time.
The Sītú
is the office for the five teachings.
The fact that the imperial order was not established
is why this snake calamity appeared.
During the time of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
a snake was seen on the imperial throne.
Yáng Cì said it was a sign of the emperor's indulgence in sensuality.
During the Wèi dynasty, palace women were excessively numerous,
and the Jìn surpassed them.
They were addicted to feasting and revelry;
this was the calamity.
The *Shī* says:
"Whether *huǐ* or snake,
they are omens for women."
In the third month, on the day *guǐsì*, in the fifth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
in Línzī, there was a large snake,
over ten *zhàng* long,
carrying two small snakes, which entered the city's north gate,
and directly passed through the market into the temple of King Yáng Jǐng of Chéngyáng of Hàn,
and disappeared.
Heaven's warning seemed to say: In the past, King Jǐng of Hàn had the merit of stabilizing the precarious,
but did not strictly adhere to loyalty and caution,
leading to the humiliation of losing his position and having his merits stripped.
Now, King Qí Jǐong does not awaken to this,
and although he performed the meritorious deed of restoration,
he became arrogant and overbearing, bringing disaster upon himself.
This is the sign.
In the early Tàiníng era of Emperor Míng,
in Wǔchāng, there was a large snake
that often resided in a hollow tree in an old shrine.
It would regularly stick its head out and accept food from people.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Yāo* says:
"When a snake is seen in a city,
within three years there will be a great war,
and the state will face great sorrow."
Soon after, Wáng Dūn's rebellion occurred.
Calamity of Horses
In the first year of Tàixī of Emperor Wǔ,
in Liáodōng, a horse grew horns
below its two ears,
three *cùn* long.
Upon examining Liú Xiàng's commentary, it says:
"This is an omen of war."
After the emperor passed away,
the royal house was severely afflicted by military disasters;
this was its fulfillment.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"When subjects replace their superiors,
and governance is not compliant,
the omen is a horse growing horns.
This indicates a lack of worthy scholars."
It also says:
"When the Son of Heaven personally conducts an expedition,
horses grow horns."
The *Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū* says:
"When a ruler loses the Way,
horses grow horns."
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was dim-witted and lost the Way,
and also personally led expeditions against Chéngdū;
this was its fulfillment.
In the twelfth month of the eighth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì,
when the Crown Prince was about to perform the *shìdiàn* ceremony,
Grand Tutor King Zhào Lún rode alongside him in the imperial carriage.
Upon reaching the south city gate,
the horse stopped,
and strongmen could not move it by pushing.
Lún then entered a small carriage,
and only then did it proceed.
This was a calamity of horses.
Heaven's warning seemed to say: Lún does not know righteous principles,
and will ultimately cause rebellion and disorder.
He is not the right person to guide and perform the rites.
In the eleventh month, on the day *wùyín*, in the ninth year,
a chestnut stallion suddenly galloped in alarm to the interrogation hall of the Grand Judge,
let out a mournful cry, and died.
Heaven's warning seemed to say: This is an omen of Mǐnhuái's unjust death.
That it appeared in the interrogation hall of the Grand Judge,
was that Heaven's will?
In the second month of the sixth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
a divine horse neighed at the south city gate.
In the ninth month of the second year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
in Púzi county, a horse gave birth to a human.
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Zhuàn* says:
"When the Son of Heaven is lost,
and feudal lords fight each other,
the omen is a horse giving birth to a human."
At this time,
the imperial house was in decline,
hanging by a thread.
The Hú and Dí tribes encroached from all sides,
and military conflict pressed closer day by day.
Soon after, the emperor also fell into captivity;
hence this omen appeared.
In the second year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
Púyáng Yǎn, an official in Dānyáng Commandery, had a mare give birth to a foal
with two heads,
separated from the front of the neck.
It died at birth.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
"This is an omen of governance being in private hands,
represented by the two heads."
After this, Wáng Dūn encroached upon the throne.
In the fifth month, on the day *jiǎxū*, in the eighth year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
there was a horse, red as blood,
which ran directly from Xuānyáng Gate into the front of the palace hall,
circled around, and ran out.
It was pursued but its whereabouts remained unknown.
On the day *jǐmǎo*,
the emperor became unwell.
In the sixth month,
he passed away.
This was a calamity of horses,
and also a red omen.
That year,
Zhāng Chónghuá was in Liángzhōu.
When he was about to execute his Grand Administrator of Xīhé, Zhāng Xiáng,
dozens of stable horses
simultaneously lost their tails.
In the tenth month of the fourth year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān,
in Liángzhōu, a horse grew horns.
The Inspector Guō Quán sent it to Huán Xuán.
Upon examining Liú Xiàng's commentary, it says: A horse should not grow horns,
just as Xuán should not have raised troops against his superior.
Xuán did not awaken to this,
leading to his destruction.
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) was in Yè (鄴).
There was a horse with a burnt tail,
which entered the Zhōngyángmén (中陽門),
and exited the Xiǎnyángmén (顯陽門).
It could not enter any of the Eastern Palaces,
and galloped towards the northeast,
soon disappearing.
The diviner Fóyúchēng (佛圖澄) sighed, saying:
“Calamity will surely strike!”
More than a year later, Jìlóng (季龍) died,
and his state was subsequently extinguished.
Human Ailments
At the beginning of the Huángchū (黃初) reign of Emperor Wén (文) of Wèi (魏),
the mother of Sòng Shìzōng (宋士宗) of Qīnghé (清河) transformed into a turtle,
and entered the water.
In the third year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Míng (明),
a daughter of Qiū Xīnóng (丘奚農), a subordinate of Cáo Xiū (曹休), died and was resurrected.
At that time, someone also opened a tomb from the Zhōu (周) era,
and found a buried woman,
who showed signs of life after several days,
and could speak after several months.
Empress Dà (大) Guō (郭) loved and nurtured her.
Moreover,
a person from Tàiyuán (太原) opened a tomb and broke a coffin,
finding a living woman inside.
When asked about her past,
she knew nothing.
Judging by the wood of her tomb,
it seemed to be about thirty years old.
The *Yì Zhuàn* (易傳) by Jīng Fáng (京房) states:
“When extreme yin becomes yang,
the low become the high.”
This was an omen for Emperor Xuān (宣) to rise.
Emperor Píng (平) and Emperor Xiàn (獻) of Hàn (漢) both had such anomalies,
which were interpreted as omens for Wáng Mǎng (王莽) and Cáo Cāo (曹操).
In the fourth year of Yǒng'ān (永安) of Sūn Xiū (孫休),
Chén Jiāo (陳焦), a commoner from Ānwú (安吳), died and was resurrected after seven days,
emerging from his tomb.
Gān Bǎo (干寶) said:
“This is the same event as with Emperor Xuān (宣) of Hàn (漢),
an auspicious sign for Hóu (侯) Hào (晧) of Wūchéng (烏程) to succeed to the throne from a fallen family.”
In the first year of Bǎodǐng (寶鼎) of Sūn Hào (孫晧),
Xuān Qiān (宣騫)’s mother from Dānyáng (丹楊), aged eighty,
transformed into a giant turtle while bathing.
Her brothers closed the door and guarded her.
They dug a large pit in the hall,
filling it with water.
The turtle entered the pit and played.
After a day or two, it stretched its neck out and looked around.
When the door opened slightly,
it spun around and leaped out,
entering a distant pool,
and never returned.
This was the same event as the mother of the Huáng (黃) family during the reign of Emperor Líng (靈) of Hàn (漢),
an omen for the fall of Wú (吳).
In the eighth month of the second year of Xiánxī (咸熙) of Emperor Yuán (元) of Wèi (魏),
Xiāngwǔ (襄武) County reported the sighting of a giant man,
over three *zhàng* (丈) tall,
with footprints three *chǐ* (尺) two *cùn* (寸) long,
white hair,
wearing a yellow turban and a yellow single robe,
leaning on a staff, calling out Wáng Shǐ (王始)’s name and saying:
“Now there will be great peace.”
Jìn (晉) soon replaced Wèi (魏).
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Wǔ (武),
a seventy-year-old man from Yuánchéng (元城) grew horns.
This was probably an omen for the usurpation and chaos of Zhào (趙) Wáng (王) Lún (倫).
In the twelfth month of the second year of Xiánníng (咸寧),
Yán Jī (顏畿) from Lángyé (琅邪) died of illness.
He had been coffined for a long time.
His family all dreamt that Jī (畿) said to them:
“I will be resurrected,
you should open the coffin quickly.”
So they took him out,
and he gradually became able to eat, bend and stretch, and see,
but could not walk or speak.
He died again two years later.
The *Yì Zhuàn* (易傳) by Jīng Fáng (京房) says:
“When extreme yin becomes yang,
the low become the high,
and the omen for this is people dying and being resurrected.”
After this, Liú Yuánhǎi (劉元海) and Shí Lè (石勒) committed usurpation and rebellion,
thereby destroying the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
which was the fulfillment of “the low becoming the high.”
During the Yuánkāng (元康) era of Emperor Huì (惠),
there was a girl named Zhōu Shìníng (周世寧) in Ānfēng (安豐),
aged eight,
who gradually transformed into a boy,
and whose temperament became fully masculine by the age of seventeen or eighteen.
The *Yì Zhuàn* (易傳) by Jīng Fáng (京房) says:
“When a girl transforms into a man,
this is called yin flourishing,
and a humble person becoming king.”
This was also an omen for Liú Yuánhǎi (劉元海) and Shí Lè (石勒) to overthrow the world.
At the beginning of Yǒngníng (永寧),
Qí (齊) Wáng (王) Jiǒng (冏) raised an army of righteousness,
executed the rebellious,
and restored the imperial carriage.
Suddenly, a woman came to the gate of the Grand Marshal’s residence seeking to give birth.
The gatekeepers questioned her,
and the woman said:
“I will leave as soon as the umbilical cord is cut.”
At this time,
Qí (齊) Wáng (王) Jiǒng (冏) restored the royal house,
and the world attributed功績 to him.
Those who understood considered this to be a bad omen for him,
and he was indeed beheaded later.
On the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day of the twelfth month of the first year of Yǒngníng (永寧),
a white-haired old man entered the Grand Marshal’s residence of Qí (齊) Wáng (王) Jiǒng (冏),
and shouted loudly:
“A great army will rise,
not beyond a *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) *xún* (旬) (ten-day period).”
Jiǒng (冏) killed him.
In the twelfth month of the next year, on the *wùchén* (戊辰) day,
Jiǒng (冏) was defeated,
which was indeed within the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) *xún* (旬).
On the *guǐyǒu* (癸酉) day of the fourth month of the first year of Tàiyān (太安),
someone entered the palace gate from Lóngmén (龍門) and stood before the hall,
facing north and bowing twice, saying:
“I am to be the Director of the Imperial Secretariat.”
He was immediately arrested and beheaded.
Gān Bǎo (干寶) believed
that “the imperial court is a place of尊祕 and sanctity.
Now a humble person brazenly entered without the gate guards noticing,
which is an omen that the palace will be empty and the low will usurp the high.”
After this, Emperor Huì (惠) moved north to Yè (鄴),
and then to Cháng'ān (長安),
and the palace indeed became empty.
During the Yuánkāng (元康) era,
a girl from Liángguó (梁國) was betrothed,
and the betrothal gifts had been received.
Soon after, her husband was garrisoned in Cháng'ān (長安),
and did not return for a year.
Her family then married her to another man.
The girl was unhappy about leaving,
but her parents forced her.
She reluctantly departed,
and soon fell ill and died.
Later, her husband returned
and asked about the girl’s whereabouts.
Her family told him everything.
Her husband went straight to the girl’s tomb,
overwhelmed by sorrow,
and opened the tomb and coffin.
The girl then revived,
and he returned home with her.
Later, the second husband heard of this
and went to the authorities to dispute.
The local officials could not decide.
Wáng Dǎo (王導), a Secretariat Imperial Clerk,
discussed the matter, saying:
“This is an extraordinary event,
and cannot be judged by ordinary principles.
She should be returned to her former husband.”
The imperial court followed his advice.
During the reign of Emperor Huì (惠),
Dù Xī (杜錫)’s family buried someone, and a maid was accidentally trapped inside.
Ten years later, when the tomb was opened for a subsequent burial, the maid was still alive.
Initially, she seemed to be in a trance,
but after a while, she gradually regained consciousness.
When asked,
she said she had only been there for two nights.
Initially,
the maid was fifteen or sixteen when buried.
When the tomb was opened and she revived,
she was still fifteen or sixteen,
and she married and had children.
In the first year of Guāngxī (光熙),
Xiè Zhēn (謝真) from Kuàijī (會稽) had a child
with a large head and hair,
both soles of its feet facing upwards,
and both male and female organs.
It made a man’s voice at birth,
and died after one day.
This indicates that the imperial power was not stable,
an ailment of the low attacking the high,
thus there were omens of usurpation and chaos among the various princes.
During the reign of Emperor Huì (惠),
there was a person in Jīngluò (京洛) with both male and female organs,
who could engage in human acts with both,
and whose nature was especially lewd.
This was born of chaotic *qì* (氣).
From after Xiánníng (咸寧) and Tàikāng (太康),
male companionship became very popular,
even more so than female beauty.
No scholar-official failed to admire it,
and the whole world imitated it.
Sometimes couples even separated,
leading to much resentment and loneliness,
thus the *qì* (氣) of male and female was chaotic, and monstrous forms appeared.
In the first year of Emperor Huái's Yǒngjiā reign,
in Wúxiàn, Wújùn, the maid of Wàn Xiáng gave birth to a child,
two horse hooves for feet,
one hand,
no hair,
a yellow tail,
and as large as a pillow.
This was also a human monstrosity,
an omen of chaos.
In the fifth year, in the fifth month,
Yán Gēn, the magistrate of Báohǎn, had a concubine who gave birth to a dragon,
a girl,
and a goose.
The Jīng Fáng Yì Zhuàn says:
"When humans give birth to other creatures,
things not seen among humans,
these are all signs of great warfare in the world."
At that time,
the emperor succeeded Emperor Huì,
the four seas were in turmoil,
and soon he was trapped in Píngyáng,
and killed by the rebellious Hú.
This was its omen.
In the fourth year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng reign,
Rèn Qiáo, an official of Xīncài County, had a wife who gave birth to two girls,
whose abdomens and hearts were joined,
but separated from the chest upwards and from the navel downwards.
This was an evil omen that the empire was not yet unified.
At that time, Lǚ Huì, the Internal Historian, reported:
"According to the Ruìyìng Tú,
different roots on the same body are called 'liánlǐ' (joined trees),
and different stalks with the same ear are called 'jiāhé' (auspicious grain).
Now two people share one heart,
and the Yì says, 'When two people are of one heart,
their sharpness can cut through metal.'
This is an auspicious sign of the four seas being of one mind."
At the time, everyone scoffed at this.
Soon, the four seas split apart,
and the emperor also perished.

Even unusual plants and trees are considered auspicious.

She came from Zhōngguó to Jiāngdōng.
She was promiscuous but could not bear children.
There was also a woman whose vulva was on her head,
who crossed to Yángzhōu.
She was also promiscuous.
Jīng Fáng Yì Yāo says:
"If a human gives birth to a child
with the vulva on the head,
there will be great chaos in the world;
if it is in the abdomen,
there will be trouble in the world;
if it is on the back,
there will be no successor in the world."
At that time, Wáng Dūn occupied the upper reaches [of the river],
and was about to cause rebellion.
This was its omen.
In the third year, in the twelfth month,
Shàngshū Zōu Xiè Píng's wife gave birth to a daughter,
who made a gasping sound upon falling to the ground
and died shortly after.
Her nose and eyes were all on the top of her head,
her face was like her neck,
her mouth had teeth
all fused into one,
her chest was like a turtle's,
and her hands and feet had claws like a bird's,
all hooked downwards.
This was also a human giving birth to another creature,
something not seen among humans.
Two years later,
there was the defeat at Shítóu.
In the second year of Emperor Míng's Tàiníng reign, in the seventh month,
the wife of Jì, Marquis of Jiāngníng, Dānyáng, died,
and revived after three days.
In the fifth year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánkāng reign, in the fourth month,
Wáng Hé, a commoner from Xiàpī, who resided in Jìyáng,
had a daughter named Kě, aged twenty,
who claimed to have returned from Heaven,
having obtained an auspicious seal and ribbon,
and was destined to be the mother of the world.
The Administrator of Jìnlíng considered her a sorceress
and had her arrested and imprisoned.
By the eleventh month,
someone carrying a mulberry staff and wearing a crimson robe went to the Zhǐchē Gate,
claiming to be an envoy of a saint seeking an audience with the Son of Heaven.
The gate guard took down the statement,
which claimed the name Lǚ Cì.
all the stars had hair,
