Upon hearing this report,
he was immediately executed,
and an order was sent to Jìnlíng to execute Kě.
In the second year of Emperor Kāng's Jiànyuán reign, in the tenth month,
Chén Dú, a woman from the guards and soldiers under the command of Wèi Jiāngjūn Yíng Dū Guò Wàng, had a pattern on her foot
"Mother of the World,"
and it became clearer when cauterized.
The capital was in an uproar,
and the authorities arrested her and reported it.
Soon she escaped from the Jiànkāng County prison.
The following year,
the emperor died,
and Empress Xiàn presided over the court.
This was its auspicious sign.
In the early period of Emperor Xiàowǔ's Níngkāng reign,
Ms. Táng from Zhōulíng, Nánjùn, gradually transformed into a man.
In the seventh year of Emperor Ān's Yìxī reign,
Zhào Wèi, an eight-year-old from Wúxī,
with a luxuriant beard and mustache,
and died three days later.
During the Yìxī period,
a woman named Mò from Dōngyáng gave birth to a daughter but did not raise her.
she cried from underground.
She was taken out and raised, and she survived.
Towards the end of Yìxī,
a man from Wúpíng, Yùzhāng, had two male genitals,
In the first year of Emperor Gōng's Yuánxī reign,
a man from Jiàn'ān had no head for his penis,
it was completely flat.
Originally, his lower body was in the shape of a woman.
Collation Notes
Treatise 20: Penal Law
The commentary says:
"Governed by ritual,
they will have a sense of shame and will come to good."
If the inviolability of penal law
is not as good as the insuperability of ritual,
then 昊岁 (hào suì) will compare to 犧年 (xī nián),
and there should be a decline.
As for the time when the heavens and earth first separated,
and light and darkness were distinguished,
when forms flowed, expressing joy and anger,
and innate dispositions revealed good and evil,
then there was a natural principle.
To remember the punishment after the act within one's own chamber,
and to show favor before the wine cup in the public square,
is to ward off disasters,
and lead towards peace and harmony.
Taking the analogy of the zither and se,
not forgetting to hold the reins,
it is to emulate the transformative influence of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
like the mindset of 堯 (Yáo) and 舜 (Shùn).
When the wilds were desolate and grave,
軒皇 (Xuān Huáng) had the army that roamed the fields;
when thunder and lightning displayed their might,
高辛 (Gāo Xīn) had the task of touching the mountains.
To array soldiers and weapons and display them in the markets,
to establish severe heavenly punishments,
to deter the leaders of rebellion,
when examining their original intent,
it was surely something that could not be avoided and thus was employed.
Therefore, at 丹浦 (Dānpǔ), benevolence flourished,
and at 羽山 (Yǔshān), all submitted.
But when the world relies on chance,
and matters involve corruption,
when governance loses ritual and ritual becomes weak,
and prisons are filled and punishments arise,
then Confucius said:
"In hearing lawsuits, I am no different from others.
What is essential is to prevent lawsuits!"
When the Zhōu (Zhōu) clan acted reverently,
they put away their sharp blades,
inheriting the tradition of creation,
and modeling themselves on 堯 (Yáo) and 禹 (Yǔ).
Their government was like nourishing dew,
their authority encompassed ritual and music.
Sometimes they would observe words to understand their meaning,
sometimes they would listen intently to discern their subtleties,
sometimes they would extol goodness to inspire sentiment,
sometimes they would eliminate evil to uphold fundamentals.
As for establishing authority and securing hegemony,
unifying and bringing together the realm,
the allegories of 成 (Chéng) and 康 (Kāng),
did not rely on ensnaring nets.
This is what is called drawing upon their enduring virtues,
and loving the people and governing the country.
If, however, transformation disregards ethical norms,
and the Way deviates from clarity and prudence,
then there was 廈癸 (Xià Guǐ)'s brutal slaughter of the common people,
and 商辛 (Shāng Xīn)'s poisoning of the four seas.
衞鞅 (Wèi Yāng) had nowhere to accommodate himself,
and 韓非 (Hán Fēi) could not overcome his own cruelty,
all these
do not share the same outcome as the enduring praises for 甘棠 (Gāntáng).
秦 (Qín) culture initially created the punishment of参夷 (cānyí),
and 始皇 (Shǐ Huáng) added the "pulling out of ribs" punishment.
Prisons were like markets,
and sorrow filled the roads.
The Hán (Hàn) King used the Three-Chapter Code to comfort them,
and Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) approached with the principle of "placing punishments aside" (刑厝).
At that time, the common people were joyful,
anticipating an era of great harmony.
But judicial cases shifted with personal feelings,
and laws changed with whims.
Presenting jade cups at the palace gate,
and relocating blue-clad maids to the roads of Shǔ (Shǔ),
punishments were determined by mincing meat (覆醢),
and entire clans were overthrown, leading to imprisonment.
Moreover, there were multiple imprisonments in the capital during the night,
and five-day public executions in the markets of Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān).
Those being led away at the northern palace gate and those following at the central capital
were also frequently seen.
And in states on the verge of ruin,
all laws and punishments were abandoned,
edicts were hastily engraved to tighten the laws,
and then relaxed according to whims.
Was it not so during the late years of Huán (Huán) and Líng (Líng)?
During the reign of Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) of Wèi (Wèi),
grand palaces were built,
and deadlines were pressing.
If anyone delayed,
the Emperor himself would summon and question them.
Their words were still on their lips,
when their heads were already separated from their bodies.
Wáng Sù (Wáng Sù) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Those whom Your Majesty executes
are all people who deserve death.
However, the common people do not know this,
and will consider it rashness.
I wish Your Majesty would hand them over to officials and publicly declare their crimes.
Although their death is the same,
it would not stain the imperial palace,
would not alarm or grieve the gentry,
and would not be doubted by those near and far.
Human life is of utmost importance,
difficult to bring forth, easy to extinguish.
Once the breath ceases, it cannot be reconnected.
Therefore, the sagely kings valued it highly.
Mèng Kē (Mèng Kē) said: 'To kill one innocent person to gain the empire,
a benevolent person would not do it.'"
Emperor Shìzǔ Wǔ (Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì) inherited the subtle threads of the three unified traditions,
and drew upon the millennia-old model.
He then commanded the relevant officials
to greatly clarify the penal codes.
At that time, imperial edicts promulgated new laws throughout the empire,
the entire realm followed the same standards,
and the people were greatly at peace.
Although the regulations were established,
they were called simple and benevolent,
reflecting heaven's favor above,
and benefiting the hearts of the people below.
The Way had laws and no failures,
and virtue, relying on punishment, stood firm for a long time.
When the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty moved south,
for one hundred and two years,
they looked to ancient precedents,
and imbibed their flowing beneficence.
To the east of the Jiāng (Jiāng), there were no foreign lands,
and barbarians from distant corners came to submit.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ (Xiàowǔ),
Prince Huìjī (Kuàijī Wáng) Dàozi (Dàozi) manipulated court power,
and his appointed partisans
trafficked in official positions and private lawsuits.
Emperor Lièzǔ (Lièzǔ) was muddled,
unaware of the failures of justice,
and the order of Jìn (Jìn) was greatly disrupted.
The commentary says:
"The Three Sovereigns established words, and the people did not disobey.
The Five Emperors drew symbols, and the people knew what was forbidden."
This is what the Shū (Shū) says:
"Use symbols to set standard punishments,
commute the Five Punishments (五刑) with leniency,
the whip is for official punishment,
and the rod is for educational punishment."
Thus, those who committed the branding punishment wore black scarves,
those who committed the nose-cutting punishment wore red clothes,
those who committed the foot-cutting punishment blackened their bodies,
those who committed the castration punishment wore mismatched shoes.
For the crime of grand execution,
the most extreme of special punishments,
their clothes were spread out without collars or borders,
thrown into the market,
and abandoned with the populace.
Shùn (Shùn) commanded Gāoyáo (Gāoyáo), saying:
"The Five Punishments have distinctive apparel,
the Five Garments have three levels.
The Five Exiles have residences,
the Five Residences have three degrees."
Compared to earlier records,
the matters are three times as numerous.
When the Xiàhòu (Xiàhòu) clan ruled the world,
the categories of the Five Punishments numbered three thousand.
The Yīn (Yīn) dynasty followed the Xià (Xià),
with some additions and subtractions.
The Zhōu (Zhōu) people used the three standard punishments to govern the states,
and the five hearings to discern popular sentiment.
To the left were good deeds, to the right were grave offenses,
matters were equally subjected to refinement,
yet the categories of the Five Punishments still numbered two thousand five hundred.
Then they established the laws of three inquiries, three leniencies, and three pardons: The first inquiry was to interrogate ministers,
the second inquiry was to interrogate officials,
the third inquiry was to interrogate the myriad people;
the first leniency was for ignorance,
the second leniency was for accidental error,
the third leniency was for forgetfulness;
the first pardon was for the young and weak,
the second pardon was for the old and infirm,
the third pardon was for the foolish and ignorant.
The Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ) Law states: Some raise troops and weapons to punish injustice;
if tribute duties are neglected, they are attacked;
if court assemblies are not attended, they are executed;
if the proper order of sons by wife and concubine is disturbed, they are imprisoned;
if ritual and punishment are altered, they are banished.
The tradition says:
"The fundamental nature of the
Yīn and Zhōu dynasties
could not overcome their culture."
When Zhāo Hòu set out on his campaign,
and Mù Wáng was already old,
penal laws were then established
to prosecute offenders in all directions.
As villainy and treachery became widespread,
and chaos and disruption persisted,
this is what is meant by
"When Xià had misgovernment, Yǔ Xíng was created;
when Shāng had misgovernment, Tāng Xíng was created;
when Zhōu had misgovernment, Jiǔ Xíng was created."
In ancient times, for major offenses, weapons were used;
for medium offenses, knives and saws were used;
for minor offenses, whips and sticks were used.
From then on,
treachery and deceit became increasingly frequent.
Wǔ Huángdì
considered the former statutes still dubious
and unfit to govern the state.
Thereupon, he ordered the Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng, Lǔ Gōng to seek out talented individuals
to revise the laws and establish new chapters.
After Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne in the Hàn dynasty,
the old regulations no longer existed.
Guāngwǔ Zhōngxīng,
paid close attention to judicial matters,
often attended court to hear lawsuits,
and personally resolved doubtful cases.
At that time, following a period of chaos and disunity,
the legal net was loose,
and the categories of crimes were lenient,
so there was nothing to deter wrongdoers.
Liáng Tǒng then submitted a memorial, saying: "Your subject humbly observes that in the fifth year of Chūyuán of Yuándì,
thirty-four types of severe punishments were lightened.
From the first to the fourth year of Jiànpíng of Āidì,
eighty-one types of capital punishments were lightened,
of which forty-two types,
where one personally killed another, were all reduced by one degree from the death penalty,
and established as permanent laws.
From then on,
people lightly violated the law,
officials easily killed
people,
and both officials and commoners lost their way,
reaching a state of lawlessness.
Your foolish subject believes that punishments should not merely strive to be lenient,
but to be appropriate.
The way of a ruler
prioritizes benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolent people love others;
righteous people manage affairs.
Since one loves people, one should eliminate harm for them;
since one manages affairs, one should also remove chaos for them.
Therefore, the Wǔ Dì had punishments of exile, extermination, banishment, and execution;
the Sān Wáng had severe penalties
and branding of the flesh,
which served to eliminate cruelty and remove chaos.
Hence Kǒngzǐ said,
'A benevolent person must be brave,'
and also said,
'Managing finances, rectifying speech,
and forbidding people from wrongdoing is called righteousness.'
Gāo
Dì received the mandate,
established restrictive orders,
and settled laws,
which were passed down to later generations,
and could be continuously implemented.
Wén Dì was generous, benevolent, gentle, and humble,
and encountered a peaceful and stable era.
He dispensed favor according to the times,
abolished corporal punishments,
and eliminated the law of collective responsibility.
In other matters, he largely followed the old regulations,
and the empire nearly achieved great peace.
Wǔ Dì lived during a prosperous period in Zhōngguó,
with abundant financial resources.
He dispatched troops and appointed generals,
campaigned in distant lands,
and military expeditions frequently arose,
exhausting the populace.
Powerful individuals violated prohibitions,
and corrupt officials manipulated the law.
Therefore, he established laws against evasion and concealment,
and promulgated
laws against knowingly condoning crimes.
Xuān Dì was intelligent and upright,
adhered to the Dao, and grasped the essentials,
to govern the realm.
His ministers upheld the constitution,
without deviating from the rules.
Yuán Dì's laws
were rarely
changed,
and the empire was called peaceful.
Xiàochéng and Xiào'āi,
inherited the throne during a period of peace,
and had been on the throne for a short time,
so their judgments were still few.
Prime Minister Wáng Jiā and others,
in just a few years,
abolished the old agreements of the former emperors,
and arbitrarily cut laws and statutes,
totaling over one hundred matters.
Some were inconvenient for governance,
and some displeased the people's hearts.
Your subject respectfully selects from them
those that most impede governance and harm good people,
and presents them to Your Majesty as attached on the left.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty embraces the Wǔ Cháng,
practices the Jiǔ Dé,
pushes through the times to rectify chaos,
and widely bestows aid upon the era,
yet you instead follow the degenerate practices of latter ages,
and weakened paths.
This is truly
not the way to return to the beginning and revert to the root,
or to rely on the origin and start anew.
I wish for Your Majesty to issue an edict to the relevant authorities,
to examine all the arbitrary changes made during Chūyuán and Jiànpíng,
assess their lightness
and severity,
observe their impact on customs,
sufficient to understand the proper place of governance and teaching,
choose the good ones and follow them,
and revise the bad ones,
establish unchanging statutes,
and implement them
endlessly.
This would be a great fortune for the empire."
The matter was referred to the Sān Gōng and Tíngwèi for deliberation.
They believed that severe penalties and harsh laws
were not the urgent task of an enlightened ruler,
and could not be permitted.
Tǒng again submitted a memorial, saying:
"The authorities arbitrarily deem what your subject presented as unfeasible.
What your subject says now
is not advocating harsh punishments.
I humbly submit that from Gāo Dì onward,
up to Xuān Dì,
what was implemented,
when compared with classics and commentaries,
and current affairs,
was not severe penalties and harsh laws.
Unable to bear my earnest wish,
I wish to be summoned for an audience,
or to discuss my ideas orally with the Shàngshū and close ministers."
The Emperor ordered the Shàngshū to inquire about the situation,
and Tǒng again responded,
strongly arguing that the system of governance and punishment should be reformed.
However, his proposal was ultimately not adopted.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he often attended to hear lawsuits and reviewed records in the prisons of Luòyáng.
The Emperor's nature was discerning and insightful,
capable of detecting corruption among subordinates,
hence the Shàngshū's reports and judgments of punishments tended to be strict and meticulous.
When Emperor Zhāng's time arrived,
Shàngshū Chén Chǒng submitted a memorial, saying:
“The governance of the former kings
rewarded without excess
and punished without abuse.
If it was absolutely necessary,
they would rather err on the side of excess [in reward] than abuse [in punishment].
Therefore, Táng Yáo inscribed in the canon, ‘Abolish the five punishments with leniency;
pardon inadvertent transgressions and disasters.’
Emperor Shùn commanded Gāo Táo with ‘The five residences and three abodes,
only with enlightenment can one be trustworthy.’
King Wén carefully interpreted the six lines of the Yì,
and instituted the hearing of cases under the thorny bush;
Duke of Zhōu created the Lìzhèng,
admonishing King Chéng not to err in the common lawsuits.
Your Majesty, since ascending the throne,
has followed this principle,
but the officials in charge
have not fully upheld it.
Those who judge cases are eager to inflict severe pain through flogging and instruments of torture;
those who enforce the law multiply deceitful and abusive regulations,
deviating from the root and departing from the reality,
committing evil through flogging and scourging.
Some even use public office for private gain,
to display their power and authority.
Indeed, governing
is like tuning a qín-sè:
if the large strings are too taut, the small strings will break.
Therefore, Zǐgòng criticized Zāngsūn's harsh laws
and praised Zhèng Qiáo's benevolent governance.
Currently, Your Sacred Virtue permeates
both above and below.
It is appropriate at this time
to elevate the tasks of the former sages,
cleanse away vexatious and harsh [laws],
lighten and reduce flogging and scourging,
to benefit the multitudes,
and spread the greatest virtue.”
The Emperor accepted Chǒng’s words,
and in adjudicating crimes and administering punishments,
he aimed for leniency and generosity.
Subsequently, he issued an edict to the officials
to prohibit and abolish all cruel old regulations,
release the prohibitions against evil omens,
remove the requests for elaborate textual interpretations,
and discuss more than fifty matters,
fixing them into law.
After this, the prison laws became harmonious.
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán,
Chǒng again replaced Guō Gōng as Tíngwèi.
He once more reviewed the statutes and ordinances,
and those penal laws that exceeded the Fǔxíng
were proposed for abolition.
He stated:
“Your servant has heard that the Lǐjīng has three hundred [articles],
and the ceremonies have three thousand [rules].
Thus, the Fǔxíng specifies two hundred capital crimes,
and three thousand categories within the five punishments.
What ritual discards,
punishment takes up;
a breach of ritual leads to punishment.
They are like the outer and inner parts of a garment.
Currently, in the statutes and ordinances,
there are six hundred and ten crimes punishable by death,
one thousand six hundred ninety-eight punishable by exile [or hard labor],
and two thousand six hundred eighty-one punishable by redemption or lesser penalties.
This exceeds the Fǔxíng by one thousand nine hundred eighty-nine [articles],
of which four hundred ten are capital crimes,
one thousand five hundred are punishable by exile,
and seventy-nine by redemption.
The Chūnqiū Bǎo Qiántú states: ‘A king revises the laws every three hundred years.’
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
three hundred and two years have passed.
The laws and ordinances have gradually increased,
and the regulations are limitless.
Moreover, there are three schools of law,
each with differing interpretations.
With the penal laws being so numerous and complex,
it is appropriate to order the Sāngōng and Tíngwèi to collectively evaluate the statutes and ordinances.
Those that are in accordance with the classics and principles, and can be implemented,
should total two hundred capital crimes,
and two thousand eight hundred for exile and redemption penalties,
making a total of three thousand,
corresponding to ritual.
The remaining one thousand nine hundred eighty-nine matters
can all be thoroughly abolished.
This will enable the people to change their perceptions and understanding,
to achieve great transformation,
and bring about the beauty of 'no need for punishments,'
to be passed down infinitely.”
Before it could be implemented,
Chǒng was implicated in a crime,
and so it was shelved.
Chǒng’s son was Zhōng.
Later, Zhōng also became Shàngshū,
and largely following Chǒng’s intentions,
he presented thirty-three articles
as a "Comparisons for Deciding Cases,"
to eliminate the abuses of seeking interpretations for judgments.
He also proposed abolishing the Cánshì punishment,
lifting the three-generation ban on corrupt officials,
allowing for lighter sentencing for those who kill in a state of madness,
and granting pardons to those who take the place of their mothers, sons, or brothers in facing death.
All these measures were implemented.
Although there were occasional revisions and reforms,
the old laws were still numerous and disorganized,
and had not been compiled.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān during Emperor Xiàn’s reign,
Yīng Shào again edited and compiled the statutes and ordinances,
considering them as the Hàn’s deliberations.
He presented a memorial, saying:
“Of the great affairs of the state,
none is more important than the written records.
Written records
resolve doubts,
clarify right and wrong,
ensure appropriate rewards and punishments,
and faithfully maintain the mean,
so that future generations may forever have a mirror.
Therefore, when the Chancellor of Jiāodōng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, retired due to old age and illness,
whenever the imperial court had a policy discussion,
it frequently dispatched Tíngwèi Zhāng Tāng personally to his humble alley,
to inquire about its merits and demerits.
Thereupon, Dǒng Zhòngshū wrote two hundred thirty-two cases of ‘Chūnqiū Judgments,’
always responding with classical precedents,
speaking in great detail.
The rebellious minister Dǒng Zhuó
overturned the royal house,
burning the canonical texts and documents,
leaving nothing behind.
Since the beginning of heaven and earth,
no cruelty has been as great as this.
Now the imperial carriage has moved eastward,
inspecting Xǔdū,
rescued from danger and difficulty;
its mandate is new.
Your servant presumptuously,

without measuring himself, has compiled the original chapters and sentences of the laws, old affairs from the Shàngshū, Tíngwèi’s official ordinances, comparisons for deciding cases, the Sītú’s official records, edicts from the Wǔcáo, and the Chūnqiū Judgments,
totaling two hundred fifty chapters.
Repeated and overlapping sections have been removed,
and they have been organized into sections.
He has also compiled thirty chapters of 'Collected Debates and Rebuttals,'
grouped by category,
totaling eighty-two matters.
Twenty-five of these are found in the Hànshū,
and four in the Hànjì,
all of which have been edited and polished
to maintain their original form.
Twenty-six [chapters] extensively gather excellent and unique individuals from ancient and modern times,
whose virtues and righteousness are commendable.
Twenty-seven [chapters] are my own creations.
The Zuǒshì states: ‘Even if there are Jī and Jiāng [noble ladies],
do not abandon the withered and thin;
even if there are silk and hemp,
do not abandon grass and straw.’
This is to make up for what is lacking.
Therefore, I dare to reveal my unpolished talent,
to be placed at the end of the wise.
Although it is not sufficient to govern the state,
or to spread harmony for the present time,
I hope it will be observed
and further enlighten Your Sacred Virtue.
I beg that during Your Majesty’s leisure from myriad state affairs,
You may peruse it.”
Emperor Xiàn approved of it,
and thus the old affairs were preserved.
At that time, the empire was about to fall into chaos,
the common people were in a state of imminent collapse.
Punishments were insufficient to deter evil.
Therefore, renowned scholars and great talents such as the former Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, Cuī Shí;
the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Zhèng Xuán; and the Grand Herald, Chén Jì, and their like,
all believed that corporal punishments should be reinstituted.
The Hàn court, however, did not discuss the matter,
so they were not implemented.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi assisted the Hàn imperial house,
Shàngshūlìng Xún Yù widely consulted the hundred officials,
again desiring to put it into effect.
However, Shǎofǔ Kǒng Róng argued,
"In ancient times, people were simple and honest;
good and evil were clearly distinguished.
Officials were upright, punishments were clear, and government was simple,
without a single transgression.
If the common people committed crimes,
they brought it upon themselves.
In these latter days, morality has declined,
and customs have become corrupted and chaotic.
Government policies distort their customs,
and laws harm their teachings.
Hence it is said, 'When the superior loses their Way,
the people have been scattered for a long time.'
To then try to correct them with ancient punishments,
and inflict upon them mutilation,
is not what is called 'adapting to the times.'
Zhòu cut off the shanks of those crossing the ford in the morning,
and the world called him without the Way.
Now, in the land of the Nine Pastures,
there are eighteen hundred lords.
If each were to mutilate one person,
then the world would constantly have eighteen hundred Zhòu's.
To seek peace and harmony in the world,
it would be impossible to achieve.
Moreover, those who have suffered corporal punishment
do not think of living,
but rather contemplate death.
The majority tend towards evil,
and none return to uprightness.
Sùshā brought chaos to Qí,
Yīlì brought disaster to Sòng,
Zhào Gāo and Yīng Bù
became great scourges to the world.
Such punishments cannot stop people from committing wrongdoing.
Though loyal like Yú Quán,
trustworthy like Biàn Hé,
wise like Sūn Bìn,
wronged like Xiàng Bó,
talented like Shǐ Qiān,
and successful like Zǐ Zhèng,
〔一０〕once they suffer the knife and saw,
they are shunned for life.
Then the reflections of Tàijiǎ,
Duke Mù's achieving hegemony over Qín,
Chén Tāng's establishing authority in Lài,
and Wèi Shàng's governing the border
would have no opportunity to be displayed.
The Hàn dynasty opened the path for correcting evil,
and this was precisely the reason.
Therefore, a ruler of illustrious virtue,
who takes long views and deep considerations,
abandons shortcomings and adopts strengths,
does not rashly change their policies."
The court approved of this,
and so it was not changed.
When the state of Wèi was established,
Chén Jì's son Qún was then Censor-in-Chief.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi issued an order again desiring to reinstitute it,
and instructed Qún to elaborate on his father's arguments.
Qún deeply expounded on its advantages.
At that time, Zhōng Yáo was Grand Councilor,
and also supported it.
However, Fèngcháng Wáng Xiū disagreed with their proposal.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi also found it difficult to alter the Hàn dynasty's system as a vassal state,
and so it was shelved and not implemented.
It was then that the Jiǎzǐ Code was established,
where those who committed offenses requiring cutting off the left or right toes were instead given wooden shackles.
At that time, iron was scarce,
hence wood was used instead.
Also, considering the Hàn laws too severe,
it was ordered that those judged according to the law should be allowed to pay half the fine,
thus enabling a reduction by half.
When Emperor Wén of Wèi received the abdication,
the matter of corporal punishment was again discussed.
The detailed discussions were not finalized,
as there were military affairs to attend to,
so it was again shelved.
At that time, there was an elderly woman, Liú Zhū,
who cruelly beat her daughters-in-law,
leading to three daughters-in-law committing suicide.
Liú Zhū was sentenced to a reduced death penalty, to be sent to work in the Imperial Workshops.
Because of this, an order was issued for reducing the death penalty for those who killed out of resentment.
Emperor Míng of Wèi changed the order for commoners to pay fines;
men were allowed to pay fines,
while women were subjected to flogging and returned to the example of whipping,
because their bodies would be exposed [during flogging].
At this time, the old laws of Qín and Hàn were adopted,
their text originating from Lǐ Kuī, the teacher of Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Kuī compiled and arranged the laws of various states,
and authored the Fǎjīng.
He believed that among a ruler's governance,
nothing was more urgent than bandits and thieves.
Therefore, his laws began with bandits and thieves.
Bandits and thieves needed to be impeached and apprehended,
so he wrote two chapters on netting and apprehending.
〔一一〕He also made one chapter of miscellaneous laws concerning light frivolity, scaling city walls, gambling, borrowing and not returning, licentiousness, and exceeding regulations.
He also included a comprehensive chapter (Jù Lǜ) to detail additions and subtractions.
Thus, only six chapters were written,
but they all constituted the system of criminal charges.
Shāng Jūn adopted them to serve as Prime Minister of Qín.
The Hàn dynasty inherited the Qín system.
Xiāo Hé established the laws,
abolishing the crime of extended family implication and joint responsibility.
He added articles concerning the knowledge and supervision of section heads,
and increased the number of chapters by three: "Matters," "Construction," and "Households,"
making a total of nine chapters.
Shúsūn Tōng supplemented what the laws did not cover,
with eighteen additional chapters.
Zhāng Tāng added twenty-seven chapters to the Palace Laws,
and Zhào Yǔ added six chapters to the Court Laws,
making a total of sixty chapters.
Furthermore, when the Hàn dynasty made judicial decisions,
they were compiled into over three hundred chapters, from Lingjiǎ downwards.
And Sītú Bào Gōng compiled decisions on marriage, disputes, and lawsuits into the Fǎ Bǐ Dū Mù,
totaling nine hundred and six scrolls.
Throughout generations, there were additions and deletions,
mostly compiling categories into chapters,
and summarizing cases into sections.
Within a single section, there might be dozens of cases.
Even if the types of cases were similar,
their severity differed.
Yet, the articles and sentences were interconnected,
with upper and lower parts mutually dependent.
Although broadly distinguished into different chapters,
they in fact drew from one another.
The "Theft Law" had examples of wounding,
and the "Bandit Law" had texts on theft.
The "Construction Law" had methods for prison sentences,
and the "Law" had matters of arrest.
Such instances were
confused and inconsistent.
Later generations developed their own ideas,
each writing their own章句 (zhāngjù).
Scholars like Shúsūn Xuān, Guō Lìngqīng, Mǎ Róng, and Zhèng Xuán had over ten schools of zhāngjù,
each comprising hundreds of thousands of words.
All the articles that ought to be used for judging crimes
totaled twenty-six thousand two hundred and seventy-two articles,
and seven million seven hundred and thirty-two thousand two hundred odd words.
As the number of words grew,
it became increasingly difficult for those consulting them.
The Son of Heaven then issued an edict,
stating that only Zhèng's zhāngjù were to be used,
and no mixing with other schools was allowed.
Wèi Jì then memorialized, saying:
"Criminal law is something
the state values highly,
yet it is despised in private discussions.
Prison officials are those
on whom the lives of the common people depend,
yet they are chosen from among the lowest ranks.
The failings of royal governance
are not necessarily unrelated to this.
I request that Doctors of Law be established,
to mutually transmit their teachings."
The matter was subsequently implemented.
However, the legal texts were voluminous and broad,
and the comparisons of cases were numerous.
Departing from the root and adhering to the branches,
judicial officials like Fàn Hóng, a prison official of the Court of Judicial Review, received two *zhang* of silk from a prisoner,
and judged him according to a lighter law.
Liú Xiàng, a prison official, accepted a bribe to selectively interrogate prisoner Zhāng Mào until he died,
and judged him according to a heavier law.
Although both Hóng and Xiàng were executed in the marketplace,
cases of light judgments and wrongful convictions followed one after another.
At this time, Grand Mentor Zhōng Yáo again submitted a memorial requesting the reinstitution of corporal punishment.
An imperial edict was issued regarding his memorial,
but Sītú Wáng Láng's discussion again differed.
At that time, there were over a hundred debaters,
and many agreed with Láng.
The Emperor, considering Wú and Shǔ not yet pacified,
again shelved it.
After that,
the Son of Heaven again issued an edict to revise and establish the penal system.
He ordered Sīkōng Chén Qún, Sànqí Chángshì Liú Shào, Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Hán Xùn, Yìláng Yú Yí, Zhōngláng Huáng Xiū, Xún Shēn, and others to abridge the old codes,
and also to draw upon the Hàn laws,
to establish the Wèi laws.
Eighteen new chapters of laws were enacted,
forty-five chapters of provincial and commandery ordinances,
and ordinances for the Shàngshū office and military ordinances,
totaling over one hundred and eighty chapters.
Its preface briefly stated: "The reason the old laws were difficult to understand
was due to the scarcity of the six chapters.
When chapters are few, the text is sparse;
when the text is sparse, cases are few;
when cases are few, crimes are omitted.
This"
later generations slightly augmented them,
further diverging from the original body.
Now, in establishing new laws,
it is advisable to comprehensively categorize all matters
and expand their chapters and articles.
The old statutes, following the Qín (秦) laws,
were merely augmented by three chapters,
and the "Complete Statutes" (具律) remained unchanged,
still residing in the sixth position.
The articles concerning crimes (罪條例) were neither at the beginning
nor at the end,
which is inconsistent with the meaning of chapters.
Therefore, the crime articles were collected to form "Criminal Designations" (刑名),
placed at the head of the statutes.
The "Robbery Statutes" (盜律) included seizing, plundering, intimidating, threatening, and illicitly buying and selling people.
The "Regulations" (科) included holding hostages.
These were not matters of ordinary theft.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Seizure and Plunder Statutes" (劫略律).
The "Banditry Statutes" (賊律) included deception,
fraud, transgression of borders, and falsely assuming authority.
The "Prisoner Statutes" (囚律) included falsely claiming life or death.
The "Order B" (令丙) included falsely exempting oneself.
These matters were numerous.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Fraud Statutes" (詐律).
The "Banditry
Statutes" (賊律) included banditry involving cutting down trees, killing or injuring people's livestock, and various instances of lost seals.
The "Gold and Cloth Statutes" (金布律) included destroying, damaging, or losing government property.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Damage and Loss Statutes" (毀亡律).
The "Prisoner Statutes" (囚律) included accusations and repeated investigations.
The "Statutes" (律) included reporting rebellion, arrests, and receiving bribes.
[一二]The "Regulations" (科) included presenting petitions to the emperor.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Accusation Statutes" (告劾律).
The "Prisoner Statutes" (囚律) included laws on detaining prisoners,
interrogating, and sentencing.
The "Initiation Statutes" (興律) included matters of appealing to higher courts.
The "Regulations" (科) included examining cases and reporting verdicts.
These were suitable for separate chapters.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Detention and Interrogation Statutes" (繫訊律) and "Sentencing Statutes" (斷獄律).
The "Robbery
Statutes" (盜律) included supervisors receiving bribes and bending the law.
The "Miscellaneous Statutes" (雜律) included unrighteous borrowing.
The "Order B" (令乙) included reprimanding people for taking money.
The "Regulations" (科) included envoys examining bribes.
These matters were similar.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Bribery Statutes" (請賕律).
The "Robbery Statutes" (盜律) included violating and brutally robbing.
The "Initiation Statutes" (興律) included unauthorized imposition of corvée labor.
The "Complete Statutes" (具律) included selling presentations.
The "Regulations" (科) included unauthorized construction or repair of dwellings.
Therefore, they were separated to form the "Initiation and Unauthorized Action Statutes" (興擅律).
The "Initiation Statutes" (興律) included delays due to lack of corvée labor.
The "Banditry Statutes" (賊律) included failure to prepare stores.
The "Statutes" (律) included initiating military shortages.
And the old canons included showing disrespect in following imperial edicts
and failing to comply with imperial decrees.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty's implementation, there were minor transgressions of not complying with orders.
[一三]These were immediately impeached as "failure to comply with imperial decrees and military shortages, to be executed by beheading" (不承用詔書乏軍要斬).
Furthermore,
this was reduced by the Dīngyǒu (丁酉) imperial edict.
The Dīngyǒu (丁酉) imperial edict
was issued by Hàn Wén Dì (漢文帝).
It was no longer appropriate to use it as law.
Therefore, a separate "Delay Statutes" (留律) was established for it.
During the Qín (秦) era, there were already provisions for courier stations (置),
post-chariots (乘傳), secondary carriages (副車), and travelling kitchens (食廚).
The early Hàn (漢) followed Qín (秦) without changes.
Later, due to high expenses, they were gradually reduced.
Therefore, the Later Hàn (後漢) only established mounted courier stations (騎置) without chariots or horses.
Yet the statutes still contained
these texts,
making them nominal provisions.
Therefore, these statutes were abolished,
and their applicable parts were combined with regulations
to form the "Post and Courier Orders" (郵驛令).
The matters of reporting rebellion, arresting, and verifying
were separately moved into the "Accusation Statutes" (告劾律).
Reporting unusual events
was made into the "Unusual Events Order" (變事令).
Reporting emergencies with alarm,
together with the "Beacon Statutes" (烽燧) in the "Initiation Statutes" (興律) and relevant regulations,
[一四]was made into the "Alarming Events Statutes" (驚事律).
The "Robbery Statutes" (盜律) included
returning stolen goods to the owner.
The "Gold and Cloth Statutes" (金布律) included fines and redemption payments made with gold as value.
[一五]The "Regulations" (科) included cases of ordinary people being implicated for stolen goods.
These were made into the "Compensation for Stolen Goods Statutes" (償贓律).
When the statutes
were first established,
there was no text for "exemption from implication."
Zhāng Tāng (張湯) and Zhào Yǔ (趙禹) first established the rules for "supervising officials" (監臨部主) and "knowingly allowing" (見知故縱).
Those who knew but deliberately did not report or impeach
were
to be punished with the same crime.
Those who failed to report or impeach due to oversight
were to be punished with redemption.
Those who neither saw nor knew
were not to be implicated.
Thus, the text was concise and the rules general.
As for the system of "Regulations" (科),
each article
had a specific violation.
Unaware or unknowing individuals
were exempted from implication.
This was no longer differentiated,
and the exemptions from implication became numerous.
It was appropriate to consolidate them into a general rule of exemption
to simplify the "Regulations" (科) texts.
Therefore, their rules
were re-established and defined
to form the "Exemption from Implication Statutes" (免坐律).
All statutes and orders that contain such instructions,
but whose original articles do not have texts concerning implication,

In total,

Old Hàn (漢) statutes that were not enforced in Wèi (魏) were all abolished.
Instead, the five punishments were re-established according to ancient principles.
There were three types of death penalty,

eleven types of redemption punishment (贖刑),

In total, there were thirty-seven categories,

Also, the "Banditry Statutes" (賊律) were revised.
Merely by speech
and violation of ancestral temples or imperial tombs

As for plotting rebellion or great treason,

immediately.
Some were thrown into muddy pits,

exterminating their three clans.
These were not in the statutes and orders,

For bandits who killed in a fight,

it was permitted, according to ancient principles,

In cases of general amnesty or accidental killing,
revenge was not allowed,

Directly killing a stepmother
was treated the same as killing one's birth mother,
to prevent discord between step-relatives.
The regulation concerning "different children" (異子之科) was abolished,
so that fathers and sons would not have separate property.
Beating elder brothers or sisters was increased to a five-year prison sentence,
to demonstrate
moral education.
Prisoners who falsely accused someone of rebellion,
with the crime extending to their relatives,
were treated differently from good people,
to burden them and make them reflect on their punishment and cease false accusations.
The regulation of "throwing letters and abandoning in the market"
was revised,
to lighten the punishment.
The crime of "usurping prisoners and abandoning in the market"
was rectified, to sever the path of violent and strong individuals acting righteously.
For sentences of two years or more,
the system of household members requesting
an inquiry was abolished,
to reduce burdensome legal cases.
The rule that various commanderies could not choose their own "Fú Rì" (伏日) was changed,
to standardize customs.
These were all changes made during the Wèi (魏) era,
and their general outline is as such.

Your servant believes that women have the principle of 'three obediences,'

Yet, if parents are guilty,

A single person

if she bears children,

This is an oversight for the principal offenders

Sons do not incur guilt from other clans,

Your servant believes that daughters still at home

women who have been wed
should follow their husband's family's punishment.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to revise the law code.

Their laws were temporarily established,

The implemented system

Regular matters of style and procedure

They reduced the articles concerning "exposure of the head" (xiāo), "beheading" (zhǎn), and "clan extermination" (zúzhū) penalties for complicity.
They abolished the provisions where those planning rebellion, adopted mothers, or married daughters were no longer subject to the parents' market execution (qìshì).
They eliminated the articles regarding mutual accusation in confinement.
They removed the system of pursuing fugitives and enslaving absconders as government bondservants.
They lightened the penalties for unintentional offenses by the elderly, young, and women.
For those who should be fined or beaten with a staff,
all penalties were halved.
They strengthened the ordinance against incest with paternal uncles' wives,
making it punishable by market execution.
For adultery with a widow,
the punishment was three years' imprisonment.
They emphasized the importance of marriage,
making the initial betrothal gift the sole legitimate basis,
and not recognizing private agreements.
They tightened the prevention of violations of ritual and moral education,
calibrating punishments according to the five degrees of mourning attire.
In total, the laws and ordinances comprised two thousand nine hundred and twenty-six articles,
one hundred and twenty-six thousand three hundred characters,
sixty scrolls,
and thirty scrolls of precedents.

If corporal punishment is implemented now,

This memorial was submitted,

Eight years ago,

Recently,

The text of the penal code is limited,

As for
these matters,

the system.

Although Wěi submitted this memorial,

At that time, Liú Sòng was the *Sān Gōng Shàngshū* (Minister of Personnel of the Three Ducal Ministries),

Why
Why is this so?
Indeed, a law
[three three] naturally takes the exhaustive pursuit of reason as its principle,
and when one seeks the ultimate good,
then all subordinates twist the text to suit their intentions,
to conform to what the ruler allows.
This means that the law
cannot be complete.
When penal statutes scrutinize the text,
such scrutiny inevitably creates discrepancies with decisions based on emotion and hearing,
and yet the superiors are content with fitting the particulars,
so those who administer justice can twist the text as they see fit,
thus giving rise to
two extremes.
If the law has many avenues,
and its commands are not uniform,
then officials will not know what to uphold,
and the common people will not know what to avoid.
Fraudulent individuals exploit the law's many avenues
to further their
intentions.
Regardless of the depth of their desires,
if judgments are not uniform,
then those in authority will find it difficult to supervise their subordinates.
Consequently, similar cases result in different opinions,
and legal judgments are unfair,
which harms the law.
The ancients had a saying:
"If the ruler is too meticulous,
his administration becomes chaotic;
if the ruler is decisive,
his affairs are well-ordered."
Being meticulous is none other than
seeking the ultimate good, which harms the law,
hence his administration becomes chaotic.
Being decisive means weighing matters appropriately,
and even if it doesn't satisfy emotions,
if it aligns with the text,
then one follows and implements it,
hence his affairs are well-ordered.
Indeed, one who is skilled at applying the law
endures decisions that violate emotions
and do not satisfy hearing.
Even if the severity of punishment does not accord with people's hearts,
when examined generally,
it may seem impractical,
but then the law can be righteous.
Furthermore, the divisions between ruler and minister
each have their
responsibilities.
The law must be obeyed,
so the primary administrators are ordered to adhere to the text;
reason has its limits and obstructions,
so important ministers are made to resolve difficulties;
affairs have their timely expediencies,
so the ruler makes discretionary judgments.
When primary
administrators adhere to the text,
it is like Shìzhī's (釋之) impartial judgment in the case of violating the imperial escort;
when important ministers resolve difficulties,
it is like Gōngsūn Hóng's (公孫弘) judgment in the case of Guō Jiě (郭解);
when the ruler makes discretionary judgments,
it is like Hànzǔ's (漢祖)
execution of Dīng Gōng (丁公).
Of the myriad affairs under Heaven,
unless they are similar to these exceptional and serious matters,

All other matters should be handled
according to statutes and ordinances.
Only then will the law be trusted by the populace,

If the ruler uses these principles to demand accountability from his subordinates,
and his important
ministers and petty officials each uphold their respective duties,

The ancients had a saying:
"One who is skilled at governing
adapts his teachings to the people."
Adapting teachings to the people
refers to the formulation of laws.
It also says,
"According to the exigencies of the time,"
which refers to
attending to urgent matters.
Thus, adapting to people and to time
lies in broad consideration,

Once the legal framework is established, it should be implemented,
implemented as reliably as the four seasons,
and upheld
as firmly as metal and stone.
How could officials, within the established system,
again claim "exigencies of the time,"

Why
is this so?
At the very beginning of its formulation,

Now, if the established law is not entirely appropriate,

But if it is considered good,
it should not be entirely
seen as merely a framework,

What a ruler shares with the world

Once it has been promulgated throughout the
four seas,

In seeking the world's respect,

Moreover, former sages have said:
People are utterly foolish, yet
they cannot be deceived.
This is not to say that ordinary deviations from the spirit of the law, made on personal whim,
do not outweigh the wishes of the common people.
In high antiquity, matters were discussed and enacted,

During the Xià (夏), Yīn (殷), and Zhōu (周) dynasties,
laws were inscribed and displayed at the city gates.
The rulers of the Three Dynasties were wise and sagely,

This is not because the sages were different,

Today, the times are considered simple and honest,
[three four] not reaching the level of the middle antiquity,

to suit their comfortable emotions,

Your servant secretly believes that if one listens to the words, they are beautiful,

However, the world is vast,
and affairs are numerous
and complex,

Therefore, your servant suggests establishing regulations as limits,

system

When a case lacks clear evidence,

As for extraordinary judgments,

perform their duties to imitate or deliberate upon.
Only then will the traces of emotional pleas and personal requests be cut off,

This is indeed the great standard for unifying the law.
The primary administrators and petty
officials
handle affairs inconsistently.
Why is this so?
Without emotion, the law is merely strict,

Accumulated strictness seems selfless,

and also
what one relies on to protect oneself.
When judgments are strictly enforced,

judgments,

This is another aspect of fair law.
Indeed, making discretionary laws

one gains one thing but loses ten.

one who gains in the near

inconvenience

and regulations

An imperial edict was issued concerning this matter,

This minister memorialized with differing opinions on various matters since the eighth year of Tàikāng (太康).
Zhōu (周) displayed the writings on the *xiàngwèi* (象魏),

Thereupon, the *Ménxià* (門下) instructed the *Sāngōng* (三公), saying:

Since the Middle Ages,

The memorial

When it came to the left bank of the Jiāng (江),

the court was just being established,

People established differing opinions,

*Zhǔbù* (主簿) Xióng Yuǎn (熊遠) memorialized, saying:

Thus, Zhōu (周) established the *xiàngwèi* (象魏) system,

The creation of laws and ordinances

Since the military uprisings,

The *fǔ* (府) establishes regulations,

Systems are changed when facing matters,
made in the morning and changed in the evening,

If the local departments handle affairs not in accordance with laws and ordinances,

Laws are but a crude art,

If every time one follows human sentiment,

The inconsistency of law
is called having multiple doors,
opening the path for personal connections

All those who raise objections
— if they violate laws, ordinances, or regulations,

I humbly suggest that the *lùshì* (錄事) be ordered to establish new regulations,

Those in charge should only consult texts and rely on laws
to make judgments."
At that time, the Emperor acted expediently,
and was not yet able to follow this advice.
However, Hé​dōng (河東) Wèi Zhǎn (衞展), as *Jìn Wáng Dàlǐ* (晉王大理),
examined old cases with discrepancies and those not in line with sentiment,

"Currently, some imperial edicts being implemented
involve torturing sons to execute fathers,
or whipping parents to inquire about their children's whereabouts.
Recently, the *gēngyín* (庚寅) edict cited by those in charge states that
if an entire family flees, the head of the household is to be executed.
If the head is indeed the leader of the flight,
his execution, though severe, might be acceptable.
But if a son or grandson commits an offense,
and their grandparents flee to avoid torture,
the fugitives are the descendants,
yet the father and grandfather suffer their cruelty.
Such instances of harming filial piety and disrupting teaching
are numerous.
If the principle of mutual concealment is abandoned,
then the righteousness between ruler and minister is abolished;
if the righteousness between ruler and minister is abolished,
then acts of rebellion against superiors will arise.
Qín (秦) law was intricate and severe.
With the rise of Hàn (漢),
troublesome and harsh regulations were swept away,
customs changed,
almost reaching a state where punishments were rarely used.
A great man revolutionizes
and must sweep away filth
and clear obstructions.
Many of the current imperial edicts should be abolished;
those that are beneficial today

making the law somewhat simpler."
Yuán Dì (元帝) issued an order, saying:
"If *lǐ* (禮) and *yuè* (樂) are not promoted,
then punishments will not be just.
Therefore, clarifying punishments and rectifying laws
was what the former kings valued.
Since Yuánkāng (元康),
incidents have multiplied,
and legal prohibitions have become lax.
What the *Dàlǐ* (大理) has submitted
should be discussed in a court meeting,

This is something I sincerely wish for."
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Zhǎn became the Grand Judge,
and again submitted a memorial, stating:
"In ancient times, corporal punishment
was a matter sanctioned by previous sages.
Emperor Hàn Wén abolished it,
increasing capital punishment instead.
Now, people's households are desolate and withered,
with scarcely one in a hundred surviving,
yet the penal laws are severe and heavy.
This is not in line with the principle of Gōu Jiàn nurturing fetuses.
I humbly suggest that the ancient practice be restored
to promote the transformation of universal peace."
An imperial edict ordered discussions among all officials, both inside and outside the court.

Thereupon, Grand General of Cavalry Wáng Dǎo, Grand Minister of Rites Hé Xún, Palace Attendant Jì Zhān, Palace Attendant Gū Liàng, Grand General's Advisory Staff Officer Méi Táo, and Palace Gentleman-in-Waiting Zhāng Ní, among others, deliberated,
stating:
"The institution of corporal punishment
has a long history.
Originating from remote antiquity,
and continuing through the Three Dynasties,
it was never altered by sages and enlightened kings.
How could it be something that a common ruler like Emperor Hàn Wén could change?
At that time, Xiāo and Cáo were already gone,
and followers like Jiàng and Guàn could not rectify its meaning.
Later, Bān Gù deeply discussed the matter,
believing that it outwardly bore the name of light punishment,
but inwardly actually involved killing.
Moreover, capital punishment was too heavy,
while corporal punishment was too light;
corporal punishment was lenient at the top,
while capital punishment caused resentment below.
The imbalance between heavy and light was inappropriate,
hence the penal administration was not just.
Furthermore, the creation of punishments by the former kings
was not due to excessive anger,
nor was it intended to harm people.
It was to prevent wickedness,
and to ensure that crimes met their due.
Now, thieves steal people's property,
lechers covet people's beauty,
and fugitives evade military service—
none of these involve murder;
yet punishment is inflicted upon them.
If punishment stops them,
but instead they are subjected to decapitation and execution,
the execution exceeds their crime.
The dead cannot be brought back to life,
and this cruelty is rampant,
amounting to a huge number each year.
This is something that benevolent gentlemen cannot bear to hear,
let alone implement in governance!
If one is confused by the name and does not scrutinize the reality,
detesting their lives and hastening their deaths,
this is like fearing water and jumping into a boat,
or avoiding a pit and stepping into a well.
It is worse than a fool,
so what good would it do for governance?
Now, the Great Jìn is undergoing a restoration,
revering and restoring ancient classics,
and following old statutes.
It is reviving long-stagnant principles of a thousand years,
saving the remaining people from countless devastations,
causing imperial institutions, once abandoned, to exist again,
and the common people, once dead, to be reborn.
The ultimate righteousness will spread to the era of the Three Dynasties,
and the lingering custom will be broadcast for a hundred generations thereafter.
Giving flesh to dry bones,
its benevolence rivals creation itself—
how splendid is that!
Some confused people say:
'Even death does not deter,
let alone corporal punishment?'
However, people are deluded;
they are utterly foolish.
Even if subjected to decapitation and execution,
they quickly turn to ashes and dust.
The thought of death fades daily,
while the desire for life persists daily;
they do not consider it a change.
If punishment is inflicted in markets and courts,
serving as a daily warning,
the punished will lament the eternal pain of their wrongdoing,
and wrongdoers will behold the permanent disfigurement of mutilation.
Thus, it is truly fearsome.
Only then will one realize that the former kings' use of light punishments to govern people
and clear warnings to deter fools,
had a profound logic."
Minister of Personnel Diāo Xié, Director of the Palace Secretariat Xuē Jiān, and others deliberated,
believing:
"The Sage Emperor grieves for the desolate and remaining common people,
and is saddened by the multitude of those who commit capital crimes.
He wishes to implement mutilation to replace capital punishment,
allowing those who commit capital crimes to preserve their lives.
Then, all within the realm will receive the grace of new life,
and the myriad people will surely return to transformation with gratitude.
Now that the restoration is flourishing
and the great mandate is renewed,
it is truly appropriate to establish lenient laws to nurture the people.
However, we fear that the ignorant masses,
accustomed to what they see and neglecting unfamiliar doctrines,
may not all readily accept this.
We humbly suggest that at the time of implementing the punishment,
the laws and regulations should first be clearly explained:
those who prefer corporal punishment will be mutilated,
and those who are willing to die will be executed.
Then, people's hearts will surely be convinced.
According to ancient custom, punishment does not extend to high officials.
Now, if scholars commit crimes,
we suggest that it should remain as before,
not falling within the scope of corporal punishment.
This would ensure appropriateness in both advancement and retreat."
Director of the Palace Secretariat Zhōu Yǐ, Aide Cáo Yàn, and Palace Attendant Huán Yí, among others, deliberated,
believing:
"Restoring corporal punishment to replace death
is indeed the utmost virtue of a sage king,
and a grand act of compassion and pity.
However, we humbly believe that the severity of punishments
is implemented according to the times.
If people commit few crimes and are easily deterred,
then a lighter and more lenient approach should be taken;
if people commit many crimes and are difficult to deter,
then a transformative punishment should be used to aid them.
[三六]Corporal punishment is suitable for peaceful times,
not for remedies against current ills.
Currently, the sage's transformation is in its early stages,
and people still harbor wickedness.
Those accustomed to evil
have not ceased their wrongdoings.
Even decapitation and strangulation
cannot restrain them.
If we further amputate feet and cut off noses,
making the punishments lighter,
this would cause those who wish to do evil to lightly commit crimes under lenient punishment,
and the number of offenders would increase.
This would be lightening punishment to lure people into crime,
and mutilating their bodies to inflict harsh suffering.
Those who feared capital punishment in the past and thus became good people
would now all commit light offenses and have their bodies mutilated.
Ordinary people who feared heavy punishment
would instead commit light offenses and become prisoners.
How is this different from mutilating ordinary people in the name of benevolence?
The number of people receiving punishment would increase,
and wrongdoers would become more numerous daily.
Leg prostheses would become expensive, and shoes cheap;
those with noses would be considered ugly.
It would merely have the name of light punishment,
but would actually open a source for the prolonged growth of evil.
It would be better to stop killing with killing,
and use heavy punishment to preserve the light.
Let us temporarily suspend this.
Once the sage's transformation gradually becomes evident,
and the myriad people are easily deterred,
then it can be slowly implemented."
When the deliberations were presented,
Emperor Yuán still wished to adopt what Zhǎn had proposed.
However, Grand General Wáng Dūn believed:
"The common people have been accustomed to the current customs for a long time.
Suddenly reinstating corporal punishment
would surely alarm people far and wide.
Moreover, the rebellious bandits are not yet eradicated,
and it is not appropriate to have the sound of cruelties
heard throughout the realm."
Thereupon, it was stopped.
During the Xiánkāng reign,
Yǔ Bīng was fond of strict scrutiny,
bordering on over-fastidiousness.
Later, he became even more contradictory,
restoring leniency and indulgence.
Strictness and leniency were at his whim,
rendering laws and regulations useless.
Towards the end of Emperor Ān’s Yuánxīng reign,
Huán Xuán was regent.
He again proposed reinstating the corporal punishments of mutilating the left and right feet,
to make death sentences lighter.
He ordered all officials to deliberate.
Cài Kuò submitted his deliberation, saying:
“In establishing a state and enacting laws,
and broadly promoting education and cultivating morality,
it is essential to institute policies according to the times,
applying both virtue and punishment.
Upholding constancy and integrity keeps evil in check,
while teachings and prohibitions curb arrogance.
Scattering refreshing dew brings forth moisture,
and wielding severe frost commands awe.
Though plainness and refinement may be used alternately,
this principle remains unchanged.
The institution of corporal punishment
began with sagacious kings.
This was because in ancient times, customs were simple,
and people were mostly honest and cautious.
Once images [of punishments] were displayed,
scheming thoughts would immediately cease.
When criminals were on the roads,
the ill-behaved would change their ways.
Thus, it was possible to put an end to brutality and eliminate killing,
and transform society through non-action.
In later, decadent ages, deceit became rampant,
and the net of laws became ever denser.
The desire for profit and cunning grew daily,
while feelings of shame and fear diminished.
Lifelong arduous labor
is insufficient to stop their treachery;
how then can tattooing and nose-cutting
turn them to good?
There are only sounds of misery and suffering,
but no benefit to society.
As for the regulation of public execution,
it is truly not a crime that cannot be pardoned.
When the act is not personal killing,
the law considers them similar.
When light and heavy penalties are equally applied,
Zhōng Chén therefore spoke out against it,
and Emperor Yuán showed pity for it.
Now, with the excellent regent providing support,
his virtue far surpasses that of Yī and Zhōu.
It is truly fitting to be clear and cautious in applying punishments,
to cherish people and promote their well-being,
to extend compassion to rectify abuses,
and to replace the death penalty with corporeal mutilation,
preserving the utmost importance of life,
and expanding posterity for the future.”
However, Kǒng Línzhī's deliberation differed,
adopting the views of Wáng Lǎng and Xiàhóu Xuán.
Public opinion at the time largely agreed with Línzhī,
so it was not implemented.
Collated Notes
Biographies, First Section, Empresses and Consorts, Part 1
When Heaven and Earth are set in their positions,
and male and female forms flow forth,
the meaning of partnership is shared,
but the names of noble and humble differ.
If one is to be matched with the imperial apex,
sharing the status of the purple palace,
symbolizing the jade bed connected to the rear star,
likening the golden wave to the conjunction of Xī and Bì.
From ancient times,
this was called the primary consort;
descending to the middle period,
she was then called queen.
Four women standing side by side
brought glory to the palace of Emperor Dìkù;
two consorts descending together
are recorded in the classics of the Yǒu Yú clan.
Before the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
the details of the six palaces system
cannot be fully known.
Since the Jī and Liú dynasties,
the regulations of the five pheasant-patterned robes
can be briefly described.
According to the Rites of Zhōu,
the Son of Heaven establishes one empress, three ladies (fūrén), nine consorts (pín), twenty-seven female officials (shìfù), and eighty-one imperial wives (yùqī),
to oversee the internal affairs of the king.
Thus, the meaning of marriage states:
“The relationship between the Son of Heaven and the empress
is like that between the sun and the moon,
Yīn and Yáng.”
From this perspective,
its origin is ancient.
Therefore, she can be the motherly exemplar of the world,
assisting in promulgating the king's transforming influence,
her virtue equaling that which supports all things,
comparable to the great Kūn axis.
The ancestral temple accepts her offerings,
and Heaven and Earth await their harmonious interaction.
Thus, sagacious kings established legal norms,
especially valuing the rite of building a boat [for marriage];
poets articulated principles,
first praising the teachings of "Gě Tán."
The back-door lamp casts its light,
thereby regulating private entertainment;
the faint sound of chamber music,
is used to restrain movement and posture.
Correcting the beginning and establishing the root –
this is what it means!
If the betrothal and acceptance are proper,
and guarding against impropriety is done with ritual,
maintaining solemn dignity and cultivating the four virtues,
embodying gentle exemplary conduct and promoting the six virtues,
then the Yīn teachings will spread throughout the palace,
and a good reputation will ascend across the land.
Then, dark clouds will enter the household,
and the Lord on High will bestow the omen of motherly growth;
the Yellow Spirit will descend with portents,
and the Earth Spirit will assist the way of Shòuqīu,
ultimately leading to an eternal reign
and prosperous descendants.
However, if the imperial consort falls short in her duties,
and relies on Heaven to commit evil,
reversing her robes on the mat,
and influencing the crescent moon's eclipse and phases.
Then, dragon's phlegm will form a grievance,
and the Zhōu dynasty will be reduced to fields of millet;
swallow's tails will instigate disaster,
and the glorious Hàn dynasty will collapse its ancestral altars.
Since Cáo and Liú elevated inner mistresses,
positions were gained through beauty,
and the families of Zhēn and Wèi
rose to prominence not through virtue.
Promiscuity and wantonness became their nature,
disregarding the ritual conduct of the western suburbs;
graceful and alluring words
created the exotic charms of the southern states.
Flattery and illicit requests thus came from outsiders,
and impure virtues were thereby spread within.
The peppered palace spread the style of morning hens,
and the orchid hall silenced the sounds of "Hé Jū."
Reflecting on the vermilion annals,
the example of Dà Liàn became increasingly faint;
looking back at the green rushes,
the wisdom of removing earrings was lost.
The Jìn inherited its decline,
rising and falling with the world.
Emperor Xuān founded the base,
his achievements great but his methods flawed;
Empress Mù's single act of goodness
equaled the accomplishments of the ten sages.
When it came to Emperor Shìzǔ,
he first personally selected good families,
but then the emperor hid behind a silk fan,
personally engaging in requests and solicitations.
The empress chose Changbai,
thereby clearly revealing her jealousy;
Jiǎ adopted Short-blue,
eventually treading the path of ruin.
The successes and failures left behind
shine brightly in books,
the reasons for rise and fall
are universally the same.
Therefore, their main stories are listed
to form the "Biographies of Empresses and Consorts."
Empress Xuānmù Zhāng
Empress Xuānmù Zhāng, personal name Chūnhuá,
was a native of Píngwú, Hénèi.
Her father, Wāng,
was the Magistrate of Sùyì in Wèi;
her mother was from the Shān clan of Hénèi,
a cousin of Sītú Tāo's grandfather.
The empress, in her youth, possessed virtue
and superior intelligence.
She gave birth to Emperor Jǐng, Emperor Wén, Prince Gàn of Píngyuán, and Princess Nányáng.
Emperor Xuān initially declined the summons of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
feigning paralysis.
Once, he was airing books [in the sun],
and a sudden downpour occurred.
He instinctively rose to collect them.
Only one maid in the household saw this.
The empress feared the matter would be exposed and cause disaster,
so she personally killed the maid to silence her,
and cooked the meals herself.
The emperor esteemed her greatly because of this.
Later, Lady Bó became favored,
and the empress rarely had an audience.
Once, the emperor was ill in bed,
and the empress went to visit him.
The emperor said:
“That old hag is hateful,
why bother coming out!”
The empress was ashamed and angry, refusing to eat
and was about to commit suicide.
Her sons also refused to eat.
The emperor was alarmed and apologized,
whereupon the empress stopped.
The emperor withdrew and said to others:
“That old hag is not worth caring about,
I just worried about troubling my good sons!”
She passed away in the eighth year of [Wèi] Zhèngshǐ,
at the age of fifty-nine.
She was buried in the Gaoyuán mausoleum in Luòyáng.
She was posthumously granted the title of Gǔangpíng Xiànjūn.
In the first year of Xiánxī,
she was posthumously honored as Xuānmù Fēi.
When [Jìn] Wǔdì received the abdication,
she was posthumously honored as Empress.
Empress Jǐnghuái Xiàhóu
Empress Jǐnghuái Xiàhóu, personal name Huī,
courtesy name Yuánróng,
was a native of Qiáo, Pèiguó.
Her father, Shàng,
was the Grand General Conquering the South of Wèi.
Her mother, Lady Cáo,
was the Dèyáng Xiāngzhǔ of Wèi.
The Empress was elegant and perceptive.
Whenever the Emperor was about to undertake something,
she would invariably plan it in advance.
During the reign of Wèi Míngdì,
[Jìn] Xuāndì held the important position of supreme general,
and all his sons possessed outstanding talent and grand strategies.
The Empress knew that the Emperor was not a pure subject of Wèi,
and since the Empress was a maternal niece of the Wèi imperial clan,
the Emperor greatly feared her.
In the second year of Qīnglóng,
she consequently passed away from poison,
at the age of twenty-four.
She was buried in Jùnpíng mausoleum.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
he initially did not posthumously honor her.
However, Hóngxùn Tàihòu repeatedly spoke of it,
and in the second year of Tàishǐ, the honorary title and posthumous name were finally bestowed.
The Empress had no sons,
but bore five daughters.
Empress Jǐngxiàn Yáng
Empress Jǐngxiàn Yáng, personal name Huīyú,
was a native of Nánchéng, Tàishān.
Her father, Dào,
was the Administrator of Shàngdǎng.
Her maternal mother, Lady Cài of Chénliú,
was the daughter of Yōng, the Left Commander of the Gentlemen of the Household of Hàn.
The Empress was intelligent and talented in her conduct.
When Empress Jǐnghuái passed away,
Jǐngdì first married the daughter of Wú Zhì of Púyáng, General Who Guards the North,
but she was deposed.
He then took the Empress,
but they had no son.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
she resided in the Hóngxùn Palace,
and was titled Hóngxùn Tàihòu.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
Lady Cài was posthumously granted the title of Jìyáng Xiànjūn,
with the posthumous name Mù.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng,
the Grand Empress Dowager passed away
at the age of sixty-five,
and was interred with Jùnpíng Mausoleum.
Empress Wénmíng Wáng
Empress Wénmíng Wáng, personal name Yuánjī,
was a native of Tán, Dōnghǎi.
Her father, Sù,
was the Central Leader of the Army and Marquis of Lánlíng in Wèi.
At the age of eight, the Empress
could recite the Shī and Lún,
and was particularly skilled in the rites of mourning.
If there was any written text or meaning,
upon a single glance,
it would invariably be ingrained in her heart.
At the age of nine,
when her mother fell ill,
she attended to her without leaving her side,
and for a long time did not loosen her sash.
She would always anticipate her mother's intentions and gestures,
adapting to her every movement.
Because of this, her parents entrusted her with managing family affairs,
which she always handled with utmost care.
Her grandfather, Láng, loved and admired her greatly,
saying:
"She who will bring prosperity to my family
must be this daughter.
What a pity she is not a boy!"
At the age of twelve,
when Láng passed away,
the Empress mourned and wept
with genuine grief,
which further increased her father's respect and admiration.
After reaching marriageable age,
she married Wéndì,
and bore Wǔdì, as well as Dàowáng Dìngguó of Liáodōng, Xiànwáng Yōu of Qí, Āiwáng Zhào of Chéngyáng, Shāngwáng Guǎngdé of Guǎnghàn, and Princess Jīngzhào.
The Empress fully fulfilled her duties as a daughter-in-law to her parents-in-law,
and humbly treated her inferiors,
with the imperial concubines maintaining proper order.
When she observed her father's mourning,
she was so frail she could not wear heavy clothes,
and her words were always accompanied by tears.
At that time, Zhōng Huì was entrusted with important tasks due to his talent.
The Empress often said to the Emperor:
"Huì forgets righteousness when he sees gain,
and is fond of stirring up trouble.
Excessive favor will surely lead to disorder.
He should not be given great responsibility."
Huì indeed later rebelled.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
she was honored as the Empress Dowager,
and her palace was called Chónghuà.
Initially, palace ministers were appointed,
and their positions were carefully selected.
Zhūgě Xù, the Grand Minister of Sacrifices, was made the Commandant of the Guards;
Liú Yuán, the Grand Coachman, was made the Grand Coachman;
Cáo Kǎi, the Court of the Imperial Clan, was made the Privy Treasurer.
Although the Empress held a revered position,
she did not forget her former simple life.
She personally engaged in spinning and weaving,
her utensils and clothes were unadorned,
she wore washed and mended garments,
and her food was not excessively flavored.
She was kind and harmonious with her nine clans,
and showed concern for all things.
Her words were always in accordance with etiquette,
and she was impervious to insidious influence.
As Wǔdì had not yet bestowed an honorable posthumous title upon his maternal grandmother, Lady Yáng,
in the third year of Tàishǐ, he issued an edict which stated:
"In the past, Hàn Wén posthumously honored the title of Língwén,
and Wǔ and Xuān had the enfeoffments of Píngyuán and Bópíng.
All these were to show reverence to the revered,
and to extend the grace to kin.
The late Lady Yáng, wife of the Grand General who guards the state and Marquis Jǐng of Lánlíng,
possessed inner brilliance and a compliant nature,
complete in benevolence and virtue.
Internally, she carried on the legacy of her noble lineage,
and externally, she married into a great house.
Her conduct according to the 'three obediences'
was always in accordance with the rites.
She then encountered misfortune,
repeatedly losing her successors.
She raised many offspring
and successfully upheld the family's way.
Her maternal instruction
brought glory to the nation and her clan,
giving birth to a sagely and enlightened one,
whose reign flows to all nations.
Yet she passed away early,
not receiving the auspicious honor.
The Empress Dowager's filial thoughts are fervent,
her eternal longing boundless.
I am moved by her surviving teachings,
and my heart is saddened by the remembrance of the distant past.
Therefore, let the Lady be enfeoffed as Xiànjūn,
and let her posthumous name be determined according to her virtue.
Let the responsible officials follow the old precedents in detail."
Thereupon, Hè Róng, the emissary holding a staff of authority and a Gentleman of the Household, was sent to posthumously honor her as Píngyáng Jìngjūn.
In the fourth year,
the Empress passed away
at the age of fifty-two,
and was interred with the Chóngyáng Mausoleum.
When she was to be interred,
the Emperor personally penned the Empress's virtues and conduct,
and ordered the official historian to compose a lamentation edict, which said: Bright and illustrious, the late Empress,
brought forth our Jìn way.
Her shining wisdom and virtue
assisted my imperial father.
Her surpassing virtue and guidance
created a great undertaking.
She bequeathed fortune to this ignorant orphan,
securing
the foundation.
We hoped to rely on her guidance again,
to enjoy eternal longevity.
Yet suddenly she ascended to the heavens,
abandoning us so early!
Deep sorrow without recourse,
how can the vast heavens be thus?
Alas!
How tragic!
In the beginning, when the people were born,
they were given kindness and health.
Heaven bestowed bright virtue,
looking upon my late imperial ancestor.
Heaven established his consort,
bringing glory to my sovereign.
She established the state and formed the pair,
her virtue
and reputation boundless.
Pity me, who is not fortunate,
as Heaven severely sends down calamity.
The sun sets and brightness is obscured,
in middle age she met her demise.
Alone in grief,
forever I carry this grievous wound.
Reflecting on Jǐng
行，
喔！肅穆不絕！
海岱降下靈氣，
世代承受無數福祉．
永遠賜予繼嗣，
厚重地生育了聖母．
她稟受純粹的和諧，
舉止淑雅謹慎．
品
行正直不變，
體現了孝順友愛．
她喜愛《詩經》和《尚書》，
記誦禮儀典籍．
三從之德從無違逆，
內政家事治理得井井有條．
追憶先皇后，
她以勤勞謙遜為
崇尚．
最初未出嫁時，
竭力奉養雙親．
嫁入大國，
輔佐了皇家的基業．
她使國家安寧興盛，
成就了帝王的事業．
她對內嬪妃以禮相待，
對外
符合時人的期望．
她誠信順從，
德行廣布暢達．
她勤勉政事，從不懈怠，
辛勞付出且能謙讓．
她崇尚節儉，抑制奢華，
順應質樸的本性．
雖然享有崇
高的地位，
卻未能盡享歡樂嘉慶．
為何上天要拋棄她？
我將仰賴何人？
嗟乎，我不肖，
大禍接連而至．
先皇駕崩離世，
至今才剛過三年．
本想仰
奉慈母，
希望不再有後來的艱難．
不料凶災又不斷降臨，
究竟對上天有何罪過？
嗚呼哀哉！
她的靈魂過早地駕車離去，
在內宮中設下靈堂．
轀輬車啟動了車輪，
一旦逝去就無法追回．
哀哉我皇妣，
靈光將永遠隱匿．
上前攀扶梓宮，
回望素色的
招魂幡．
驚慌失措，悲痛欲絕，
我該向誰傾訴？向誰依靠？
我將情意寫成祭文，
以抒發我的悲傷．
或許她尚有聽聞，
能顧念我這個孤兒．
嗚呼哀哉！
其後，帝王追慕不已，
又下詔書說：
「外曾祖母，故司徒 Wáng Lǎng 夫人 Yáng Shì，
舅家尊長，
鄭氏、劉氏兩位從母，
都是先皇后至親至愛之人．
每念及她們的聖善之德，
以及先皇后敦厚和睦的遺訓，
那渭陽之感，
讓我永遠懷念，卻無法再見．
特封 Yáng fūrén 及從母為 Xiāngjūn，
各賜食邑五百戶．」
Tàikāng 七年，
追贈繼祖母 Xiàhóu Shì 為 Xíngyáng Xiāngjūn．
Wǔyuán Yáng Huánghòu
Wǔyuán Yáng Huánghòu，諱 Yàn，
字 Qióngzhī，
是 Hóngnóng Huàyīn 人．
其父 Wénzōng，
載於《外戚傳》；
其母 Tiānshuǐ Zhào Shì，
早逝．
皇后寄養在舅家，
舅母仁愛，
親自哺乳撫養皇后，
讓其他人去乳養她的兒子．
長大後，
又隨後母 Duàn Shì，
住在她的家中．
皇后幼年聰慧，
善於書寫，
姿容美麗，
擅長女紅．
有善於相面的人曾為皇后相面，
說她將來必將極其尊貴，
Wéndì 聽聞後便為世子聘娶了她．
她深得寵愛，
生下了 Pílíng Dàowáng Guǐ、Huìdì、Qín Xiànwáng Jiǎn，
以及 Píngyáng、Xīnfēng、Yángpíng 公主．
Wǔdì 即位後，
立她為皇后．
有司奏請依漢朝舊例，
皇后、太子各食湯沐邑四十縣，
但帝王認為這不符合古典，
不允許．
皇后追念舅家之恩，
顯赫提拔 Zhào Jùn 為官，
並將 Zhào Jùn 兄長 Yú 的女兒 Càn 納入後宮為夫人．
帝王因皇太子不堪繼承大統，
便私下將此事告訴皇后．
皇后說：
「立嫡以年長為重，不以賢能為重，
豈能輕易變動呢？ 」
起初，
Jiǎ Chōng 的妻子 Guō Shì 行賄皇后，
請求將女兒嫁給太子為妃．
等到討論太子婚事時，
帝王想娶 Wèi Guàn 的女兒．
然而皇后極力稱讚 Jiǎ Hòu 有淑德，
又暗中指使太子太傅 Xún Yǐ 進言，
帝王才聽從了．
Tàishǐ 年間，
帝王廣泛選取良家女子充實後宮，
先下詔書禁止天下嫁娶，
派宦官乘坐使車，
配給騶騎，
馳驛各州郡，
召集被選中的女子，讓皇后挑選．
皇后性情妒忌，
只選取潔白高大的女子，
那些端正美麗的女子一概不予留下．
當時 Biàn Fān 的女兒姿色美麗，
帝王掩扇對皇后說：
「 Biàn Shì 女子很不錯． 」
皇后說：
「 Biàn Fān 三代都是皇后外戚，
他的女兒不能屈就卑微的位份． 」
帝王於是作罷．
司徒 Lǐ Yìn、鎮軍大將軍 Hú Fèn、廷尉 Zhūgě Chōng、太僕 Zāng Quán、侍中 Féng Sūn、秘書郎 Zuǒ Sī 以及其他世族子女，都被充入三夫人、九嬪之列．
司、冀、兗、豫四州二千石級將領官吏之家，
則補充為良人以下位份．
名門望族的女兒們，
大多穿著破舊，容貌憔悴以避開選徵．
待到皇后有病，
見帝王素來寵幸 Hú fūrén，
恐怕以後會立她為后，
擔心太子不安．
臨終時，
她枕在帝王的膝上說：
「叔父 Jùn 的女兒 Yáng Yìn 有德色，
願陛下將她納入六宮． 」
於是悲泣，
帝王流淚應允了她．
Tàishǐ 十年，
她在 Míngguāng Diàn 駕崩，
在帝王膝上斷氣，
當時她三十七歲．
詔書說：
「皇后生前侍奉先皇后，
我常期望她能始終如一地永奉宗廟，
不料一旦逝世，
令人悲痛傷懷．
我常因自己早年喪失雙親，
對家族親情特別重視．
她又有心想要改葬父祖，
因為近來務求節儉，
最初未曾開口，
近期病危時，
才說出此意，
我心中也憐憫她．
其命令領前軍將軍 Jùn 等人自行決定改葬事宜，
