屆時，
主管官員供給葬禮所需．
追諡其母 Zhào Shì 為 Xiànjūn，
以其繼母 Duàn Shì 為 Xiāngjūn．
《左傳》不是說過嗎，
『慎終追遠，
民德歸厚』 ．
況且如果逝者有知，
或許也會嘉許此事． 」
於是，有司卜得吉日，
下葬日期已定，
便命史官寫哀策文．
其文曰： 天地配合次序，
化育出陰陽兩儀．
君王有家室，
治道在於夫妻和諧．
Jiāng Yuán 輔佐 Kù，
二妃興盛於 Guī 姓．
仰慕古昔，
希望
亦同規.
今胡不然，
景命夙虧.
嗚呼哀哉！
我應圖籙，
統臨萬方.
正位于內，
實在嬪嬙.
天作之合，
駿發之祥.
河嶽降靈，
啟
祚華陽.
奕世豐衍，
朱紼斯煌.
纘女惟行，
受命溥將.
來翼家邦，
憲度是常.
緝熙陰
教，
德聲顯揚.
昔我先妣，
暉曜休光.
后承前訓，
奉述遺芳.
宜嗣徽音，
繼序無荒.
如
何不弔，
背世隕喪.
望齊無主，
長去烝嘗.
追懷永悼，
率土摧傷.
嗚呼哀哉！
陵兆既窆，
將遷幽都.
宵陳夙駕，
元妃其徂.
宮闈遏密，
階庭空虛.
設祖布紼，
告
駕啟塗.
服翬褕狄，
寄象容車.
金路晻藹，
裳帳不舒.
千乘動軫，
六驥躊躇.
銘旌樹
表，
翣柳雲敷.
祁祁同軌，
岌岌烝徒.
孰不云懷，
哀感萬夫.
寧神虞卜，
安體玄廬.
土
房陶簋，
齊制遂初.
依行紀諡，
聲被八區.
雖背明光，
亦歸皇姑.
沒而不朽，
世德作謨.
嗚呼哀哉！
乃葬于峻陽陵.
武悼楊皇后 (左貴嬪 Zuo Guìpín, 胡貴嬪 Hú Guìpín, 諸葛夫人 Zhūgě Fūrén)
武悼楊皇后 Wǔdào Yáng Huánghòu, personal name Zhǐ 芷,
courtesy name Jìlán 季蘭,
milk name Nányìn 男胤,
was the cousin of the former empress.
Her father, Jùn 駿,
has a separate biography.
She was established as empress in the second year of Xiánníng 咸寧 [276 CE].
Gentle and virtuous, possessing the qualities of an empress,
her beauty shone in the imperial harem,
and she was greatly favored.
She gave birth to the deceased Prince of Bóhǎi 渤海,
who died young,
and thus she had no other children.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng 太康 [288 CE],
the empress led the imperial consorts, ladies, and court women to personally gather mulberries in the western suburbs,
and they were all given silk according to their rank.
Crown Princess Jiǎ 賈 was jealous,
and the emperor intended to depose her.
The empress spoke to the emperor, saying:
“Jiǎ Gōnglǘ 賈公閭 rendered great service to the state,
and his family should still be pardoned for several generations.
Crown Princess Jiǎ is his own daughter,
and even if she is jealous,
a single fault is not enough to obscure her great virtues.”
The empress also repeatedly admonished the Crown Princess,
but the Crown Princess was unaware of the empress’s help,
and consequently held a grudge,
believing the empress was slandering her to the emperor,
and her resentment deepened.
When the emperor passed away,
she was honored as Empress Dowager.
Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu was cruel and perverse,
and jealous of the empress dowager’s father, Jùn 駿, holding power.
She thus falsely accused Jùn 駿 of rebellion,
and sent Wěi 瑋, Prince of Chǔ 楚, and Yáo 繇, Prince of Dōng'ān 東安, to issue an imperial edict to execute Jùn 駿.
With the inner and outer palaces cut off,
the empress dowager wrote a message on silk,
and shot it outside the city wall,
saying,
“There will be a reward for those who save the Grand Tutor.”
Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu then publicly declared that the empress dowager was complicit in the rebellion.
After Jùn had died,
an imperial edict ordered Hòujūn Jiāngjūn Xún Kǔ to escort the Empress to Yǒngníng Gōng.
The life of the Empress's mother, Gāodū Jūn Páng Shì, was specially spared,
and she was permitted to reside with the Empress.
Empress Jiǎ hinted to the various dukes and officials to memorialize, saying:
"The Empress Dowager secretly fomented a wicked plot,
scheming to endanger the state.
She flew arrows with letters attached,
soliciting generals and soldiers
to join her in wickedness and assist each other,
thereby cutting herself off from Heaven.
The Lord of Lǔ divorcing Wén Jiāng
was permitted by the Chūnqiū;
this was to uphold and obey the ancestors
and entrust impartiality to all under Heaven.
Although Your Majesty harbors endless affection,
your subjects dare not obey the edict.
It is fitting to declare an imperial order for the kings and dukes to meet in conference in the court hall."
The imperial edict stated:
"This is a major affair,
let us consider it more thoroughly."
The officials then again memorialized:
"Jùn, relying on his status as an external relative,
occupied the position of prime minister.
When Your Majesty was in mourning,
he was entrusted with great power,
yet he secretly plotted treasonous rebellion,
and established his private faction.
The Empress Dowager acted as his close confidante,
collaborating in the rebellious conspiracy.
When the calamity and wrongdoing were exposed,
she resisted and defied imperial edicts,
obstructed forces and turned the masses against them,
shedding blood in the palace,
and moreover circulated letters to recruit the populace
to support her wicked party.
Upwards, she defied the spirits of the ancestors;
downwards, she cut off the hopes of the myriad people.
In ancient times, Wén Jiāng was involved in disorder,
which the Chūnqiū censured.
The Lǚ clan was rebellious and defiant,
and Empress Gāo was demoted.
It is fitting to depose the Empress Dowager as a commoner of Jùnyáng."
Zhōngshū Jiān Zhāng Huá and others believed that
"the Empress Dowager did not offend the former emperor.
Now, siding with wickedness and those close to her,
she acts as not a mother in this sagely era.
It is fitting to follow the precedent of Empress Zhào of Xiào Chéng,
who was called Empress Wǔ Dì and
placed in a detached palace,
to preserve the grace of a noble end."
Shàngshū Lìng, the King of Xiàpí, Huǎng and others deliberated, saying:
"The Empress Dowager and Jùn secretly plotted
to endanger the state.
She cannot again be honored in the ancestral temple
or matched with the former emperor.
It is fitting to demote her esteemed title
and banish her to Jīnyōng Chéng."
Thereupon, the officials memorialized:
"We request to follow the deliberation of Huǎng and others,
deposing the Empress Dowager as a commoner.
An envoy should be sent to announce this with a grand sacrifice at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
to uphold the command of the ancestors
and fulfill the hopes of all nations.
As for all her provisions,
they should follow the imperial grace
and be made bountiful."
The imperial edict did not permit it.
The officials again strongly requested it,
and it was then approved.
They further memorialized:
"Yáng Jùn caused disorder,
and his family members should be punished.
An edict spared the life of his wife, Páng,
to comfort the Empress Dowager's heart.
Now that the Empress Dowager is deposed as a commoner,
we request that Páng be handed over to the Grand Judge for execution."
The imperial edict stated:
"Permit Páng to accompany the commoner."
The officials, desiring Empress Jiǎ's will,
strongly requested it,
and she then consented.
When Páng was about to be executed,
the Empress Dowager embraced and cried out,
cut her hair and kowtowed,
submitting a memorial to Empress Jiǎ, addressing herself as concubine,
pleading for her mother's life to be spared,
but it was not heeded.
Originally,
the Empress Dowager still had more than ten attendants,
but Empress Jiǎ took them away,
and she died of starvation,
at the age of thirty-four,
having been on the throne for fifteen years.
Empress Jiǎ also believed in sorcerers,
who said the Empress Dowager would surely complain of her injustice to the former emperor,
so she was buried face down,
and charms, talismans, and medicines for suppression were placed on her.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
her esteemed title was posthumously restored,
and a separate temple was erected for her,
but her spirit tablet was not matched with Emperor Wǔ.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
an imperial edict was issued, commanding both internal and external officials to deliberate thoroughly.
Wèi Jiāngjūn Yú Tán deliberated, saying:
"Emperor Shìzǔ Wǔ Dì brilliantly possessed all under Heaven,
and Empress Yuán rightfully became his consort.
After Empress Yuán passed away,
Empress Dào succeeded her.
When Yáng Jùn committed outrageous treason,
the calamity extended to the Emperor's mother.
Did Emperor Xiàohuái not posthumously restore her title and posthumous name
because when Gǔn was executed, Yǔ arose,
and the principle was that it should not be replaced?
Moreover, in the second year of Tàiníng,
I held the office of Zōngzhèng.
The imperial genealogy was lost and forgotten,
with no record to follow.
At that time, I consulted widely with elders
to determine the order of generations.
With the late Piàojì Jiāngjūn Huá, Shàngshū Xún Sōng, and Shìzhōng Xún Suì, based on old genealogies, we discussed and compiled it,
and the gravity of esteemed titles
was not altered in any way.
Now, His Majesty's filial piety
reverently and solemnly attends to the ancestral sacrifices,
consulting all officials,
intending to restore and settle the great rites.
I have carefully considered this,
and respectfully refer to the 'Records of the Emperor Huì's Daily Life' and the memorials of the various ministers,
which listed Jùn's treasonous plot
to endanger the state,
citing Lǔ's Wén Jiāng
and Hàn's Empress Lǚ.
I humbly submit that although Wén Jiāng was Duke Zhuāng's mother,
she was truly her father's enemy.
Empress Lǚ promoted her private relatives,
almost endangering the Liú clan.
These two cases are different from the present one.
In ancient times, Empress Dòu of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn killed the mother of Emperor Hé.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne, he executed all the Dòu relatives.
At that time, deliberators wished to demote Empress Dòu,
and after her death, they wanted not to bury her with proper rites.
Emperor Hé, having served her for ten years,
believed it was unethical to transgress this.
The way of a child-subject is to strive for generosity and abundance,
and his reputation for benevolence and wisdom
was manifest in past generations.
I also saw the deliberation of the late Shàngshū Púyè Péi Wěi on the precedent of Empress Dào,
stating that even if a stepmother is divorced,
posthumous mourning should not be altered.
Therefore, Emperor Xiàohuái honored her title and posthumous name
and reburied her at Jùn Líng.
This means the mother-son relationship was fully upheld,
and the deposed status was completely abolished.
At that time, sacrifices were performed in the Hóngxùn Palace,
but she had not entered the Grand Ancestral Temple.
This was likely an incomplete resolution of the matter,
not a matter of ritual principle.
If it is deemed appropriate for Empress Dào to be restored to her position,
then she should be matched with Shìzǔ in sacrifice;
if her restoration is deemed inappropriate,
then her entry in the genealogy and her posthumous name should be omitted.
There is no precedent for someone holding a proper title
yet being solely sacrificed in a separate chamber.
If it is argued that Emperor Xiàohuái privately exalted the mother-son relationship
and specially erected a temple for her,
this would be a mere indulgence of private sentiment,
detrimental to national rites.
In that case, the imperial names in the national genealogy
should all be removed and discarded,
and she should not merely be denied co-sacrifice in Shìzǔ's temple."

The King of Kuàijī, Yù, Zhōngshū Jiān Yǔ Bīng, Zhōngshū Lìng Hé Chōng, Shàngshū Lìng Zhūgě Huī, Shàngshū Xiè Guǎng, Guānglù Xūn Liú Zhuó, Dānyáng Yǐn Yīn Róng, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Féng Huái, Sànqí Chángshì Dèng Yì, and others all agreed with Tán's deliberation.
Thus, the Empress Dowager was matched with Emperor Wǔ in sacrifice.
Zuǒ Guìpín's name was Fēn.
Her brother, Sī,
has a separate biography.
Fēn was fond of learning in her youth
and skilled in literary composition;
her reputation was second only to Sī's.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this and took her into his palace.
In the eighth year of Tàishǐ,
she was appointed Xiūyí.
She received an imperial order to compose a text about sorrowful thoughts,
and consequently wrote the 'Lísī Fù,' which said: Born in a humble and lowly dwelling,
I am not skilled in literary symbols.
I have not seen the wondrous images of paintings,
nor heard the classic advice of ancient sages.
Both foolish and ignorant,
and lacking in knowledge,
I am mistakenly placed
among the purple chambers.
This is not where common grass belongs,
and I am fearful and anxious.
Filled with sorrowful longing
and beginning
to
Myriad worries come to an end.
Alas, the accumulated hidden sorrow,
I am uniquely melancholic and without recourse.
My mind is desolate and restless,
My thoughts are entangled, increasing my longing.
Through the
long, sleepless night,
My soul wanders restlessly until dawn.
The wind rustles and rises from all four directions,
The frost is white and clings to the courtyard.
The sun is dim and without light,
The air
is chilling and crisp.
Harboring much sorrow and sensitivity,
Distressed by tears falling of their own accord.
In the past, Bóyú [伯瑜] was gentle and loving,
Always entertaining his parents in colorful attire.
I lament today's separation and estrangement,
Suddenly, my home and I are like Shēn [參] and Chén [辰] stars.
How can it be said that we are
far apart,
Not even a few *xún* [尋] away?
How secluded and strict are the palace precincts,
I wish to gaze upon them but have no means.
I look up at the moving clouds and sigh,
Tears stream down and
dampen my kerchief.
Only the sorrow and emotion of Qū Yuán [屈原],
Alas, the grief of separation.
He composed poetry at the city gate towers,
Also comparing the day to the moon.
How much more so for blood relations
who are bound to each other,
Forever separated and cut off from each other.
Long I bear sorrow and grief,
Looking up at the azure sky, I weep blood.
The *luàn* [亂] says: Closest kin,
Transformed into strangers,
Forever bidding farewell.
Distressed and sorrowful,
In dreams my soul returns,
To see whom I long for.
Waking up with a cry and
a wail,
My heart is disconsolate,
Tears flow ceaselessly.
Taking up the brush to express my feelings,
Tears flow even more,
As I lament this poem.
Later, she became a noble consort,
Her appearance was plain and she was not favored,
But she was treated with respect for her talent and virtue.
Her body was frail and often ill,
She often resided in a simple chamber.
Whenever the emperor visited Huálín [華林],
He would turn his carriage to pass by her.
When they spoke of literature and meaning,
Her replies were eloquent and brilliant.
The attendants listening on all sides
All praised her.
When Yuán Yáng Huánghòu [元楊皇后] passed away,
Fēn [芬] presented a dirge saying: It was in the seventh month of autumn, on the day *bǐngyín* [丙寅], in the tenth year of Tàishǐ [泰始],
That Jìn Yuán Huánghòu Yáng Shì [晉元皇后楊氏] passed away.
Alas, how mournful!
In ancient times, Yǒuxīn [有莘] went to Yīn [殷],
Jiāng Sì [姜姒] returned to Zhōu [周].
They proclaimed
virtue within the inner court,
Their excellent reputation flows on forever.
The two consorts, Fán [樊] and Wèi [衞],
Assisted Qí [齊] and aided Chǔ [楚];
The two empresses, Mǎ [馬] and Dèng [鄧],
Also helped the Hàn [漢] ruler.
Lofty was the Yuán Hòu [元后],
Gracing the Jìn [晉]
palace.
A consort to the Sagely Emperor,
Her accomplishments matched those of ancient times.
Her destiny was not long,
She turned her back on the sun and entered the shade.
The six palaces wailed,
The four seas mourned in their hearts.
Alas, I, a humble concubine,
Am particularly
deeply indebted to her grace.
In emulation of the three worthies,
I would gladly immerse myself.
What can I use to remember her?
Her virtuous words I shall not forget.
What can I use to record her?
I entrust my words to the forest of brushes.
Thus, I composed
this dirge: Illustrious was the Yuán Hòu [元后],
Originating from the Yáng [楊] clan.
For generations, their vermilion carriages shone,
Radiant in Huáyáng [華陽].
As if a spirit descended from the mountains,
Manifesting auspicious omens.
She was born a brilliant lady,
Blessed
with glorious light.
Endowed with spirit and embracing literary grace,
Different from the common Jiāng [姜].
Gentle and pleasant as a spring day,
But firm in principle as autumn frost.
She abhorred that which was easy to achieve,
And upheld the path of righteousness.
Following the four
teachings,
Neither lazy nor wanton.
Her conduct embraced all six relations,
Her excellent reputation was widely proclaimed.
What was proclaimed?
Her goodness in the imperial household.
Thus, she was betrothed and brought in,
And became consort to the Sagely Emperor.
She occupied the proper position within the inner chambers,
And always upheld virtue.
Her jade pendants jingled with rhythm,
Her words were well-ordered.
Looking up at the displayed diagrams,
And looking down at the written texts.
Consulting the female scribes,
And seeking advice from bamboo
and silk records.
She strove to please the imperial matriarch,
Reverent and diligent day and night.
She competently managed the internal affairs,
Performing her duties with utmost care.
In rites, she was industrious;
In reverence, she was diligent.
Though she was said to be wise and sagely,
Her virtue grew ever new.
How was it ever new?
She was able to greatly extend profound benevolence.
Ultimately gentle and benevolent,
She treated the Emperor's
sisters as kin.
She managed the six palaces,
And none were not thoroughly governed.
The multitude of concubines all looked up to her,
Like the North Star.
When the green spring arrived,
The cuckoos announced the season.
She personally held the mulberry
leaves,
Leading the accompanying consorts.
She cultivated the silkworm cocoons,
Dividing the cocoons and processing the silk.
She inspected the women's work,
And prepared the sacrificial garments.
She reverently served the ancestral temple,
Always thinking of filial piety.
Among
the six virtues,
None did she not follow.
Huángyīng [皇英] assisted Shùn [舜],
Túshān [塗山] aided Yǔ [禹].
Wèi [衞] and Fán [樊],
Helped the two hegemons.
Our bright and clear Empress,
In a different era, followed the same
principles.
She was also capable of governing,
Her counsel reaching the imperial court.
Within, she spread the feminine teachings,
Without, she assisted the masculine transformations.
She meticulously worked with all officials,
Diligently from dawn till night.
Her grace followed the wind
as it soared,
Her benevolence spread with the falling rain.
Both within and without, happiness flourished,
Near and far, songs were sung.
Heaven bestowed purity and auspiciousness,
Allowing her to prosper and thrive.
Hundreds of blessings were hers,
Raising sages and worthies.
Her teachings surpassed Rènsì [妊姒],
Her instructions exceeded Jiāngyuán [姜嫄].
Majestic was the Crown Prince,
The
foundation of the state.
Numerous were the lords of Nányáng [南陽],
Serving as shields and bulwarks.
The main lineage and its branches flourished,
Shading the four seas.
Without this imperial mother,
Who could have achieved this?
It is said that Heaven is
wise,
It is said that the Sage is truly sincere.
The hall of accumulated good deeds,
Where the five blessings gather.
She ought to have enjoyed a long life,
Without falling or inclining.
Like Páng [彭] in age,
Like Dān [聃] in years.
Thus.
did this not happen,
but instead this misfortune and calamity?
Seriously ill and lingering,
sleeping and waking were not peaceful.
Wū Xián displayed his arts,
Hé Què presented his remedies.
Prayers brought no response,
tasting medicine brought no
relief.
Body and spirit about to separate,
sometimes昏, sometimes wild.
Suddenly collapsed and passed away,
essence vanished and light extinguished.
Alas, my beloved crown prince,
from Nányáng Fánchāng.
Clinging and unable to sleep,
beating
the breast and leaping, heart-torn and grieved.
Oh, how sad!
The entire palace wailed and wept,
the whole world was shocked.
Those who rushed filled the streets,
those who came filled the courtyard.
Their grief and sorrow were like thunder,
tears fell like
rain.
Sobbing incessantly,
as if having lost their own parent.
Only the Emperor and the Empress,
were intimately bound in the past.
Like paired wings in a humble cottage,
flying together to a purple pavilion.
Mourning the Empress, grieving for the Empress,
she soon entered her tomb.
As these words were spoken,
tears
streamed down.
Remembering our Empress,
truly intelligent and wise.
Penetrating the mysteries of life and fate,
achieving moderation and frugality.
Her funeral rites,
matched those of the ancient, unadorned era.
The shroud had no precious
jewels,
the mouth no "bright moon" pearl.
Her brilliance concealed in the funerary chamber,
forever turning her back on the light.
Ministers and concubines wailed in sorrow,
sharing this absolute severance.
Courtyards were sealed in silence,
the dark chamber grew even darker.
Curtains
were set up in vain,
clothes and bedding laid out uselessly.
People also say,
the path of the spirits is hard to find.
Wandering spirits,
do they float or sink?
Rich offerings are presented daily,
hoping her soul will come.
Who says the late Empress,
cannot hear their voices?
Thus, virtues were discussed,
virtues already abundant.
Then, turtle shells and divining stalks were consulted,
the divination showed repeated good fortune.
Thus, the burial site was chosen,
and the dark chamber completed.
When her soul departs,
it will be on an auspicious day.
On a morning in mid-autumn,
as the Morning Star first appeared.
Stars arrayed, early carriages were hitched,
the spirit carriage drawn by four horses.
What was that carriage like?
Gold wheels and jade box.
What were its
four horses like?
Two camels, two yellow horses.
Solemnly moved the attendant carriages,
in crimson robes and red insignia.
Slowly moved the mourning carriages,
in mourning caps and sackcloth skirts.
Adorned hubs shone across the fields,
white canopies covered the plains.
The Fāngxiàng stood tall and strong,
banners and streamers fluttered.
Mourning youths sang dirges,
white steeds whinnied at the carriage shafts.
Spectators lined the roads,
men and women shed tears.
A thousand chariots and ten thousand riders,
reached that lofty
mountain.
The lofty mountain, towering,
with stacked peaks and many hills.
Vast, high, and open,
leaning on the Luò River, facing the Yellow River.
To the left, looking at Huánggū,
to the right, gazing at Dìjiā.
Comparing the living and pondering the dead,
it was clearly
blessed by the spirits.
All the imperial aunts and sisters,
younger sisters-in-law, and concubines.
Followed the dusty path,
wailing on the roads.
Kings, marquises, high ministers, and gentry,
gathered like clouds, spread like stars.
All officials and common
clerks,
countless white canopies.
Sighing through the night,
until dawn broke in the east.
All deities reverently welcomed,
our Empress laid to rest.
Both insiders and outsiders were present,
sharing sorrow and admiration.
Tears like continuous clouds,
like dew-soaked drops.
When the gate was closed,
deep and dark.
There was night but no day,
what use was its brightness?
Unsealed and unplanted with trees,
the mountain slopes
remained in their natural form.
When the Empress passed away,
the Great Fire star flowed westward.
Cold departed, heat passed,
now it is also the first month of autumn.
Since I began my mourning,
a year has suddenly passed.
Clothing is about to change,
my heart still aches
as if being torn.
Constrained by the rites,
this only increases my sorrow.
Removing these plain clothes,
my affections remain tied to the spirit mound.
There is a beginning and an end,
this is the constant principle of heaven and earth.
Other than the three
luminaries,
who can avoid fading?
While alive, broadcast good virtues;
after death, portray them in pictures.
This was the ambition of the ancient sages,
considering this their glory.
Gentle was our Empress,
truly benevolent.
Nurturing
all beings,
her grace and kindness flourished.
Her enduring love is ceaseless,
she will be forever remembered.
Her name hung in the sun and moon,
lasting ten thousand springs.
Alas, we concubines,
are moved by the four seasons
indeed.
Speaking of her, thinking of her,
tears stream down.
In the second year of Xiánníng,
commemorating the deceased Empress,
Fēn received an imperial decree in her seat to compose an eulogy.
Its text reads: Majestic Huá Yuè,
its height reaches the ultimate Pure Realm.
Jùlíng guided its waters,
the river course was laid.
The spirit of the river,
the numen of the mountain.
Converged upon the Yáng clan,
giving
birth to a brilliant light.
Solemnly our Empress,
arose at the destined time.
Possessing intelligence and acting with wisdom,
precocious and accomplished from an early age.
Flourishing like an orchid,
glorious like jade.
Even in her tender
youth,
she had an excellent reputation.
Her fame soared to the eight cardinal points,
quietly entering the purple palace.
Surpassing Rèn and excelling Sī,
her virtues comparable to Huáng Yīng.
The imperial house approved,
performing all rites to seek her hand.
On an auspicious
month and lucky day,
all officials reverently welcomed her.
The maiden of Zhōu returned to Hán,
poets sang of this.
Our Empress arrived,
her carriage and attire shining brightly.
Ascending to the position in the Tàiwēi palace,
her brilliant virtue daily
grandly.
The multitude of common people rejoiced in their support,
and the whole of Huáxià celebrated together.
How reverent was the sagely Emperor!
His sagacity and wisdom were exceedingly pure.
He took pity on this reckless wickedness,
and spread benevolence and goodness.
He eliminated sins and cleansed impurities,
renewing everything with the times.
A great amnesty was spontaneously granted,
and his
gracious edicts resounded far and wide.
When the Empress ascended the throne,
the prisons were emptied.
All nations rejoiced,
and the six directions were filled with joy.
The Earth spirit danced and clapped,
and Heaven and humans alike were pleased.
Auspicious omens arose and
propitious signs descended,
manifesting their essence in the sun and moon.
Harmonious qi permeated,
and the three luminaries shone brightly.
Having received this propitious time,
soon sweet snow was spread.
Dark clouds gathered obscurely,
and spiritual dew fell.
It was
stored and accumulated,
awaiting the sun to dry it.
Warm sunshine moistened and permeated,
gently nourishing the central region.
May we long enjoy abundant years,
and may fortune and blessings forever be at peace.
When Dì Nǚ Wànnián Gōngzhǔ died,
the Emperor grieved endlessly,
and ordered Fēn to compose an elegy.
Its text was exceedingly beautiful.
The Emperor highly valued Fēn's literary talent,
and whenever there were rare objects or exotic treasures,
he would order Fēn to compose a rhapsody or eulogy for them.
Because of this, Fēn repeatedly received imperial favors.
His replies to his brother's poems, letters, and various rhapsodies and eulogies, numbering several tens,
were all circulated in the world.
Hú Guìpín's personal name was Fāng.
Her father was Fèn,
whose biography is given elsewhere.
In the 9th year of Tàishǐ (273 CE),
the Emperor selected many daughters from good families to fill inner court positions.
He personally chose the most beautiful ones by tying a red silk ribbon around their arms.
When Fāng was selected,
she cried loudly as she descended the palace steps.
Those around her stopped her, saying:
"His Majesty will hear your voice."
Fāng said:
"I don't even fear death,
why should I fear His Majesty!"
The Emperor sent Luòyáng Lìng Sīmǎ Zhào to present the imperial edict and enfeoff Fāng as a Guìpín.
Whenever the Emperor consulted her,
she did not embellish her words,
but answered straightforwardly,
her demeanor always proper and elegant.
At that time, the Emperor had many imperial consorts.
After the conquest of Wú, he further took in several thousand palace women from Sūn Hào's palace.
From then on, the Yètíng (inner palace) almost reached ten thousand people.
There were many who enjoyed his favor simultaneously,
and the Emperor did not know where to go.
He often rode a sheep carriage,
letting it go wherever it wished,
and then rested where it stopped.
The palace women then took bamboo leaves and stuck them on their doors,
and sprinkled the ground with salt water,
to attract the Emperor's carriage.
However, Fāng was the most favored and beloved,
almost enjoying exclusive access to his chamber,
her attendants' clothing and ornaments second only to the Empress.
The Emperor once played tú pú with her,
and they argued over a dart,
which then injured his upper finger.
The Emperor angrily said:
"This is indeed the offspring of a general!"
Fāng replied:
"Attacking Gōngsūn in the north,
and resisting Zhūgě in the west,
if not the offspring of a general, then what?"
The Emperor showed much shame.
Fāng gave birth to Wǔ'ān Gōngzhǔ.
Zhūgě Fūrén's personal name was Wǎn,
and she was from Lángyé Yángdū.
Her father was Chōng,
courtesy name Mào Zhǎng,
Tíngwèi Qīng.
Wǎn entered the palace in the spring of the 9th year of Tàishǐ (273 CE).
The Emperor, facing the palace entrance,
sent the envoy, bearer of the imperial insignia, Luòyáng Lìng Sīmǎ Zhào, to enfeoff her as Fūrén.
Her elder brother was Quán,
courtesy name Délín,
Sànqí Chángshì.
Quán's younger brother was Méi,
courtesy name Rénlín,
Shìzhōng and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Méi's wife's younger brother was Zhōu Mù,
who was the maternal uncle of Qīnghé Wáng Tán.
In the early Yǒngjiā period,
Mù and Méi persuaded Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè to depose Huái Dì
and enthrone Tán,
but Yuè did not agree.
When they repeatedly pressed him,
Yuè became angry,
and then executed Méi and Mù.
At the execution,
Méi said to Mù:
"What did I tell you?"
Mù said:
"What more can be said today?"
People at the time then realized that the plan originated from Mù,
and was not Méi's intention.
Huì Jiǎ Huánghòu
Huì Jiǎ Huánghòu's personal name was Nánfēng.
She was from Píngyáng.
Her childhood name was Ā.
Her father was Chōng,
whose biography is given elsewhere.
Originally,
Wǔ Dì wanted to take Wèi Guàn's daughter for the Crown Prince.
However, Yuán Hòu accepted the advice of Jiǎ Guō's relatives and partisans,
wishing for a marriage to the Jiǎ family.
The Emperor said:
"Wèi Gōng's daughter has five merits,
while Jiǎ Gōng's daughter has five demerits.
The Wèi family line is virtuous and produces many children,
beautiful and fair-skinned;
the Jiǎ family line is jealous and produces few children,
ugly and dark-skinned."
Yuán Hòu insisted,
and Xún Yǐ and Xún Xù both praised Chōng's daughter's virtue,
so the marriage was decided.
Initially, they intended to betroth the Empress's younger sister, Wǔ.
Wǔ was twelve years old,
one year younger than the Crown Prince,
and too short and small to wear formal attire.
So instead, Nánfēng was taken,
who was fifteen at the time,
two years older than the Crown Prince.
On the Xīnmǎo day of the second month in the 8th year of Tàishǐ (272 CE),
she was enfeoffed as the Crown Princess.
She was jealous, scheming, and manipulative.
The Crown Prince feared and was deluded by her,
and few consorts or palace women had the good fortune of being favored.
The Emperor often suspected the Crown Prince was not intelligent,
and moreover, many court officials like Hé Qiáo often spoke of it,
so he wanted to test him.
He summoned all officials, great and small, from the Eastern Palace,
held a banquet for them,
and sealed controversial matters,
making the Crown Prince decide them,
then waited for the reply.
The Princess was greatly afraid,
and secretly asked an outsider to write the answers.
The answers mostly cited ancient precedents.
The attendant Zhāng Hóng said:
"The Crown Prince is not learned.
If the reply to the edict cites precedents,
the one who drafted it will surely be blamed,
and it will only add to the reprimand and fault.
It is better to respond directly with his own thoughts."
The Princess was greatly pleased,
and told Hóng:
"Please write a good reply for me,
and I will share wealth and honor with you."
Hóng had some minor talent,
so he drafted it,
and had the Crown Prince copy it himself.
The Emperor reviewed it,
and was very pleased.
He first showed it to the Crown Prince's Grand Tutor, Wèi Guàn.
Guàn was greatly embarrassed.
Everyone then knew that Guàn had previously made disparaging remarks,
and all in the hall cheered "Long live!"
Chōng secretly sent a message to the Princess, saying:
"Wèi Guàn, that old slave, almost ruined your family."
The consort's nature was cruel and tyrannical.
She once personally killed several people.
Sometimes she would throw a halberd at a pregnant concubine,
and the fetus would fall to the ground with the blade.
The emperor heard of this
and was greatly enraged.
He had already repaired the Jīnyǒngchéng (Golden Moat City)
and was about to depose her.
Chōnghuá Zhào Càn (Lady of Bright Countenance Zhào Càn) calmly said:
"Jiǎ Fēi (Consort Jiǎ) is young,
and jealousy is merely a woman's emotion.
It will naturally subside with age.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this."
Afterwards, Yáng Yáo (楊珧) also spoke on her behalf, saying:
"Has Your Majesty forgotten Jiǎ Gōnglǘ (賈公閭)?"
Xún Xù (荀勖) strongly pleaded for her,
and so she was spared deposition.
When Huìdì (惠帝) ascended the throne,
she was made empress,
and gave birth to Princess Hédōng (河東), Línhǎi (臨海), Shǐpíng (始平), and the mournfully deceased imperial daughter.
The empress's tyranny grew daily.
Shìzhōng Jiǎ Mó (Attendant Counselor Jiǎ Mó),
a cousin of the empress,
and Yòuwèi Guō Zhāng (Commander of the Right Guards Guō Zhāng),
her maternal cousin,
both held positions due to their talent and reputation,
and along with Chǔ Wáng Wěi (Prince Wěi of Chǔ) and Dōng'ān Gōng Yáo (Duke Yáo of Dōng'ān), they shared control of court affairs.
The empress's mother, Guǎngchéng Jūn (Lady of Guǎngchéng), raised her grandson Jiǎ Mì (賈謐), who interfered in state affairs,
his power rivaling that of the ruler.
Yáo (繇) secretly wished to depose the empress,
and the Jiǎ (賈) clan feared him.
When Tàizǎi Liàng (Grand Tutor Liàng) and Wèi Guàn (衞瓘) and others memorialized to transfer Yáo (繇) to Dàifāng (帶方)
and strip Chǔ Wáng (Prince of Chǔ) of his position as Zhōnghóu (Central Marquis),
the empress, knowing Wěi (瑋) resented them,
made the emperor issue a secret edict ordering Wěi (瑋) to execute Guàn (瓘) and Liàng (亮)
to avenge past grievances.
Mó (模) knew the empress was vicious and violent,
and feared that disaster would befall him,
so he conspired with Péi Wěi (裴頠) and Wáng Yǎn (王衍) to depose her.
Yǎn (衍) later regretted it, and the plan was dropped.
The empress then indulged in debauchery and wanton behavior,
engaging in illicit affairs with Tàiyī Lìng Chéng Jù (Director of Imperial Physicians Chéng Jù) and others, spreading scandal both inside and outside the palace.
In Luò Nán (south of Luò), there was a petty official from the Weìbù (尉部) (Constabulary Bureau)
who was handsome and had a fine demeanor.
After he was assigned to servile duties,
he suddenly acquired extraordinary clothing.
Everyone suspected him of theft,
and the Weì (尉) (Constable) became suspicious and interrogated him.
A distant relative of Empress Jiǎ (賈) wanted to inquire about the stolen goods,
so he went to listen to the testimony.
The petty official said:
"Initially, I met an old woman
who said her family had an illness,
and the diviner said it was advisable to find a young man from south of the city to ward off evil.
She wished to trouble me for a short while,
promising a substantial reward.
So I followed her.
I got into a carriage with closed curtains,
and was placed inside a basket.
After traveling about ten li,
passing six or seven thresholds,
the basket was opened,
and suddenly I saw beautiful pavilions and palaces.
I asked where this was,
and she said it was 'heaven.'
Immediately, I was bathed in perfumed water,
dressed in fine clothes, and served delicious food.
I saw a woman,
about thirty-five or thirty-six years old,
short and dark-skinned,
with a blemish behind her eyebrow.
She kept me for several nights,
and we slept together and enjoyed feasts.
Before I left, she gave me all these things."
Those who heard his description
knew it was Empress Jiǎ (賈).
They departed with shame and laughter,
and the Weì (尉) (Constable) also understood the implication.
At that time, many others who entered died,
but only this petty official,
because the empress favored him,
was able to return safely.
When Princess Hédōng (河東) fell ill,
the masters and shamans thought it advisable to issue a lenient decree.
Thus, an imperial edict was announced, granting a general amnesty to the empire.
Initially,
the empress feigned pregnancy,
placing objects inside her to simulate childbirth.
She then took Wèizǔ (慰祖), the son of her sister's husband Hán Shòu (韓壽), and raised him,
claiming he was born during the period of mourning,
and thus not publicly acknowledged.
She then plotted to depose the crown prince,
and replace him with the one she had adopted.
At that time, a ballad in Luò (洛) went:
"The scorching south wind blows yellow sand,
looking afar, Lǔguó (魯國) stands towering and lofty.
By the third month, your house will be destroyed."
The empress's mother, Guǎngchéng Jūn (Lady of Guǎngchéng), because the empress had no son,
greatly respected and cherished Mǐnhuái (愍懷) (the Crown Prince),
and often urged the empress
to show more maternal love.
Jiǎ Mì (賈謐), relying on his noble status, was arrogant and unrestrained,
and failed to show proper respect to the Crown Prince.
Guǎngchéng Jūn (Lady of Guǎngchéng) sternly admonished him.
When Guǎngchéng Jūn (Lady of Guǎngchéng) became critically ill,
divination indicated it was not auspicious to enfeoff her as Guǎngchéng (廣城).
Thus, her title was changed to Yíchéng (宜城).
The empress went out to attend to her mother for more than ten days.
The Crown Prince often visited the Yíchéng (宜城) residence,
bringing doctors in and out,
acting with utmost respect.
Yíchéng (宜城), before her death, held the empress's hand,
and urged her to devote herself fully to the Crown Prince,
speaking with great earnestness.
She also said:
"Zhào Càn (趙粲) and Wǔ (午) will surely disrupt your affairs.
After I die,
do not let them enter again.
Remember my words deeply."
The empress failed to heed her words
and subsequently monopolized control of the empire,
intimidating all within and without the court.
She further conspired with Càn (粲) and Wǔ (午) in wicked schemes,
falsely accusing the Crown Prince,
and their evil deeds became widely known.
Initially,
the execution of Yáng Jùn (楊駿), Rǔnán Wáng Liàng (Prince Liàng of Rǔnán), Tàibǎo Wèi Guàn (Grand Protector Wèi Guàn), Chǔ Wáng Wěi (Prince Wěi of Chǔ), and others
were all decided on the spot by her.
The eunuch Dǒng Měng (董猛) participated in these affairs.
Měng (猛),
during Wǔdì's (武帝) reign, was a Sìrén Jiān (Director of Eunuchs),
serving in the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince's palace).
He gained the empress's trust and intimacy
and participated in the execution of Yáng Jùn (楊駿).
He was enfeoffed as Wǔ'ān Hóu (Marquis of Wǔ'ān).
All three of Měng's (猛) elder brothers were made Tínghóu (Marquis of a Pavilion).
The empire was filled with resentment.
When the Crown Prince was deposed,
Zhào Wáng Lún (Prince Lún of Zhào) and Sūn Xiù (孫秀) and others, spurred by popular resentment, conspired to depose the empress.
The empress repeatedly sent palace maids in disguise among the people to observe and listen,
and their plot was somewhat leaked.
The empress was greatly frightened,
and so she harmed the Crown Prince
to extinguish public hope.
Zhào Wáng Lún (Prince Lún of Zhào) then led troops into the palace,
ordering Yìjūn Xiàowèi Qí Wáng Jiǒng (Commander of the Elite Army, Prince Jiǒng of Qí) to enter the hall and depose the empress.
The empress and Jiǒng's (冏) mother had a quarrel,
which is why Lún (倫) sent him.
The empress exclaimed in surprise:
"Why have you come, my lord!"
Jiǒng (冏) replied:
"There is an imperial edict to arrest the empress."
The empress said:
"Edicts ought to come from me;
what edict is this?"
The empress reached the upper gate,
and called out to the emperor from afar, saying:
"Your Majesty has a wife,
and you let others depose her.
You are also deposing yourself."
She then asked Jiǒng (冏):
"Who started this affair?"
Jiǒng (冏) replied:
"Liáng (梁) and Zhào (趙)."
The empress said:
"When tying a dog, one should tie its neck.
Now, you have tied its tail instead.
How can it not be so!"
When she reached the west of the palace,
she saw Mì's (謐) corpse,
cried out twice, and then abruptly stopped.
Lún (倫) then fabricated an edict and sent Shàngshū Liú Hóng (Minister Liú Hóng) and others with imperial credentials and gold-powdered wine to grant the empress death.
The empress was in power for eleven years.
Zhào Càn (趙粲), Jiǎ Wǔ (賈午), Hán Shòu (韓壽), Dǒng Měng (董猛), and others were all executed.
Princess Línhǎi (臨海) was first enfeoffed as Qīnghé (清河).
During the chaos of Luòyáng (洛陽),
she was captured by someone
and sold to Qián Wēn (錢溫) of Wúxīng (吳興).
Wēn (溫) gave her to his daughter,
who treated the princess very cruelly.
When Yuándì (元帝) was stationed in Jiànyè (建鄴),
the princess went to the county and revealed her identity.
Yuándì (元帝) executed Wēn (溫) and his daughter,
re-enfeoffed her as Línhǎi (臨海),
and Zōngzhèng Cáo Tǒng (Court of Imperial Clan Affairs Cáo Tǒng) married her.
Huì Yáng Huánghòu (Empress Yáng of Huì) (Lady Xiè)
Empress Yáng of Huì (惠羊皇后), personal name Xiànróng (獻容),
was a native of Nánchéng (南城), Tàishān (泰山).
Her grandfather was Jǐn (瑾),
and her father was Xuánzhī (玄之),
both mentioned in the "Biographies of Imperial Relatives" (Wàiqī Zhuàn 外戚傳).
After Empress Jiǎ (賈) was deposed,
Sūn Xiù (孫秀) proposed establishing a new empress.
The empress's maternal grandfather Sūn Qí (孫旂) was related to Xiù (秀),
and her sons had also formed ties with Xiù (秀).
Thus, in the first year of Tàiyán (太安) (302 CE), she was established as empress.
As she was about to enter the palace, there was fire in her clothes.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (Sīmǎ Yǐng) attacked Chángshā Wáng (Sīmǎ Yì),
using "punishing Xuán" as the pretext.
He was defeated.
Yǐng memorialized to depose the Empress as a commoner,
and she was held in Jīnyōngchéng.
Chén Zhěn and others advocated attacking Chéngdū Wáng,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the Empress was restored to her position.
Zhāng Fāng entered Luò,
and again deposed the Empress.
Fāng coerced the imperial carriage to move to Cháng'ān.
The acting court restored the Empress to her position.
In the early Yǒngxīng era,
Zhāng Fāng again deposed the Empress.
Héjiān Wáng Yóng (Sīmǎ Yóng) falsely issued an edict,
stating that because the Empress had been repeatedly enthroned by treacherous individuals,
he sent Shàngshū Tián Shū to order the acting court to grant the Empress death.
The imperial edicts arrived repeatedly.
Sīlì Xiàowèi Liú Tūn, together with Shàngshū Púyè Xún Fān and Hénán Yǐn Zhōu Fú, rushed to submit a memorial, saying:
"Having received the handwritten edict,
we read it with trepidation and distress.
Your subjects have examined ancient and modern texts;
the ruin of nations and the downfall of families,
the destruction of ancestral temples and altars,
have all been caused by offending the populace and going against the will of the people.
Your Majesty has moved your residence,
the old capital is deserted,
the common people are adrift,
with no one to rely on.
Every household has a longing heart,
everyone imagines the sound of the imperial carriage,
they look forward to Your great virtue,
and wish for peace and return to farming.
But the entanglement of war does not cease,
conflicts arise everywhere;
is this not because good governance has not arrived,
and people's feelings are suspicious and alienated?
Now Shàngguān Sì has violated the palace and raised troops,
burning down the palace quarters.
The common people are clamorous and terrified;
it is proper to pacify them with tranquility.
But the imperial envoy suddenly arrived,
sternly carrying the poison,
to be administered at Jīnyōng;
inside and outside, everyone was shaken,
believing it was not the Saint's intention.
The household of Yáng (Empress Yáng) the commoner is broken and ruined,
she has been cast aside in an empty palace,
the palace gates are strictly guarded,
as if cut off from heaven and earth.
She has no means to conspire with treacherous individuals and cause disorder.
Without exception, intelligent or foolish,
all say it is not so.
The sentence has been hastily issued,
the crime does not merit the punishment.
The indignation of the people,
can easily lead to uprising.
Indeed, to kill one person and have the entire realm rejoice,
that is a blessing for the ancestral temple and the altars of the land and grain.
Now, to kill one destitute and lonely person will cause sorrow throughout the realm.
Your subjects fear that villains will seize the opportunity
and falsely create new incidents.
Your subjects, occupying positions in the capital,
observe the hearts of the people,
and are truly deeply worried;
it is advisable to endure.
Unable to bear what we have witnessed,
we respectfully and secretly report this.
We wish Your Majesty to deliberate more deeply with the Tàizǎi,
so as not to cause doubt among those near and far,
and incur criticism throughout the realm."
Yóng saw the memorial and was greatly enraged.
He then sent Chén Yán and Lǚ Láng eastward to arrest Tūn.
Tūn fled to Qīngzhōu,
and thus the Empress was able to escape.
The Emperor returned to Luò,
and welcomed the Empress back to her position.
Later, Luòyáng Lìng Hé Qiáo again deposed the Empress.
When Zhāng Fāng's head arrived,
on that very day the Empress was restored to her position.
Coincidentally, the Emperor (Huì Dì) died.
The Empress feared that if the Imperial Younger Brother (Huái Dì) was enthroned, he would be a brother-in-law to her,
and she would not be able to be called Empress Dowager.
She urged the former Crown Prince, Qīnghé Wáng Tán (Sīmǎ Tán), to come in,
intending to enthrone him,
but it did not succeed.
Huái Dì ascended the throne,
honored the Empress as Huì Dì Huánghòu,
and she resided in Hóngxùn Gōng.
When Luòyáng fell,
she was captured by Liú Yào.
Yào usurped the throne
and made her his Empress.
He then asked,
"How do I compare to the Sīmǎ family boy?"
The Empress replied,
"How can they be mentioned in the same breath?
Your Majesty is a sagely ruler who founded a new dynasty;
he was an ignorant man who ruined his country,
he had a wife, a son, and three imperial seals,
yet could not protect them.
Though an emperor,
his wife and son were disgraced at the hands of commoners.
At that time, this concubine truly did not wish to live;
how could I have imagined such a day as this?
This concubine was born into a noble family,
and always thought all men in the world were alike.
Only since serving you has this concubine known that there are true men in the world."
Yào greatly loved and favored her.
She bore two sons for Yào and then died.
She was posthumously given the false title Xiànwén Huánghòu.
Xiè Fūrén's given name was Jiǔ.
Her family was originally poor and lowly;
her father made a living as a sheep butcher.
Jiǔ was pure, intelligent, chaste, upright, and possessed a graceful bearing.
She was selected to enter the inner court as a Cairen.
When Huì Dì was in the Eastern Palace,
he was about to take a consort.
Wǔ Dì, concerned that the Crown Prince was still young
and unfamiliar with matters of the bedchamber,
sent her to the Eastern Palace to serve him in bed.
From this, she gained favor and became pregnant.
Jiǎ Hòu was jealous of her.
Jiǔ requested to return to the Western Palace,
and subsequently gave birth to Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ.
When he was three or four years old,
Huì Dì did not know about him.
When he entered the court,
he saw Mǐnhuái playing with the other imperial princes.
Wǔ Dì took his hand and
said,
"This is your son."
When he was established as Crown Prince,
Jiǔ was appointed Shúyuán.
Jiǎ Hòu did not allow the Crown Prince to see Jiǔ,
and confined her to a single room.
When Mǐnhuái met with a cruel fate,
Jiǔ was also killed.
In the early Yǒngkāng era,
an edict ordered the reburial of the Crown Prince,
and consequently bestowed upon Fūrén Jiǔ an official seal and ribbon.
She was buried in Xiǎnpíng Líng.
Huái Wáng Huáng Tàihòu
Huái Wáng Huáng Tàihòu's given name was Yuánjī;
her origin is unknown.
She first entered Wǔ Dì's palace
and was appointed Zhōng Cairen.
She died young.
When Huái Dì ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
Yuán Xiàhóu Tàifēi
Yuán Xiàhóu Tàifēi's given name was Guāngjī.
She was a native of Qiáo, Péiguó.
Her grandfather, Wēi,
was the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Her father, Zhuāng,
courtesy name Zhòngróng,
was the Grand Administrator of Huáinán and Marquis of Qīngmíng Tíng.
The concubine was born of a distinguished lineage,
intelligent and discerning from a young age.
Lángxié Wǔ Wáng (Sīmǎ Zhòu) took her as consort for his heir, Jìn (Sīmǎ Jìn).
She gave birth to Yuán Dì (Sīmǎ Ruì).
When Gōng Wáng (Sīmǎ Jìn) passed away,
Yuán Dì succeeded to the throne,
and she was referred to as Wáng Tàifēi.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
she died south of the Yangtze River
and was buried in Lángxié Guó.
Initially there was a prophecy saying,
"A bronze horse enters the sea; Jiànyè is the destined time."
The Tàifēi's childhood name was Tónghuán (Bronze Ring),
and Yuán Dì indeed revived the dynasty south of the Yangtze.
JIAÒKĀO JÌ
LIÈZHUÀN DI ÈR HÒU FĒI XIÀ YUÁN JÌNG YÚ HUÁNGHÒU (XÚN YÙZHĀNG JŪN)
Yuán Jìng Yú Huánghòu's given name was Mèngmǔ.
She was a native of Wàihuáng, Jìyáng.
Her father, Yù,
is mentioned in the "Biographies of Imperial Relatives."
When the Emperor (Yuán Dì) was Lángxié Wáng,
he took the Empress as his consort;
she had no children.
She died in the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
at the age of thirty-five.
The Emperor was then Prince of Jìn,
and posthumously honored her as Queen.
The officials reported that the Queen should have a separate ancestral temple established for her.
An edict stated:
"The imperial ancestral temple is not yet complete,
so it is not appropriate to undertake new construction.
Let the existing structure over the mausoleum be refurbished to serve as her temple."
In the third year of Tàixīng,
a decree announced:
"The Emperor addresses the former Princess Consort of Lángyá, Lady Yú: I, by reverently following the mandate of August Heaven,
have ascended the imperial throne.
I grieve that the Consort departed prematurely,
her excellent reputation now hidden.
Governing the household and the nation,
there is no one to emulate,
and the female teachings are lacking,
which causes me sorrow.
Bestowing posthumous titles is
a custom of the former kings.
Now, I dispatch an envoy, holding the staff of authority and concurrently serving as Grand Commandant Wàn Shèng, to present the decree bestowing the Empress's seal and ribbon,
and sacrifice with a grand offering.
If her soul has spiritual power,
may it appreciate this honor and glory."
She was then interred in the Grand Ancestral Temple
and buried at Jiànpíng Líng.
During the Tàiníng era,
Emperor Míng, recalling the kindness of her maternal upbringing,
posthumously honored Yù's wife, Lady Wáng, as the Lady of Yáng County,
and his maternal cousin, the wife of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Prince of Xīnyě, Hǎn, as the Lady of Píngyáng Township.
Lady Xún of Yùzhāng Commandery
was a palace woman of Emperor Yuán.
She was initially favored,
giving birth to Emperor Míng and Prince Pú of Lángyá,
which caused the Empress Yú to be jealous of her.
Feeling her own status was low,
she often harbored resentment,
for which she was reprimanded by the Emperor
and gradually became estranged.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Lady of Jiàn'ān
and given a separate residence.
In the first year of Tàiníng,
the Emperor welcomed her back into the palace,
and her provisions and attendance were grand.
When Emperor Chéng ascended,
her respect and status were equal to that of the Empress Dowager.
She passed away in the first year of Xiánkāng.
An edict stated:
"I, as a child, suffered misfortune,
receiving no loving instruction.
The diligence of nurturing me was the benevolence of the Lady of Jiàn'ān.
Her sudden passing
truly makes me think of repaying her;
forever recalling the past,
I feel grief and sorrow.
Let her be posthumously granted the title of Lady of Yùzhāng Commandery,
and a separate temple be established for her in the capital."
Empress Míngmù Yǔ
Empress Míngmù Yǔ, personal name Wénjūn,
was from Yānling, Yǐngchuān.
Her father, Chēn,
is mentioned in the "Biography of Imperial Relatives."
The Empress was benevolent by nature
and had a beautiful appearance.
Emperor Yuán heard of her
and betrothed her as the Crown Prince's consort.
She was highly regarded for her virtuous conduct.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
A decree stated:
"Consort Yǔ, having previously received the imperial command,
became the consort of the Eastern Palace,
reverently and diligently managing the household affairs,
and reflecting on pleasing norms and standards.
She trod in faith and thought of obedience,
thereby accomplishing the way of solemn harmony;
she held the correct position in the inner chambers,
thereby manifesting the beauty of harmonious virtue.
I, from an early age, suffered misfortune,
alone and distressed.
All the dukes and ministers,
after examining past generations,
unanimously agreed that honoring the principal wife clarifies the succession,
as recorded in the classics and counsels,
and it is fitting to establish the Changqiu Palace
to serve the ancestral temple.
Therefore, reiterating the former intention
and not abandoning the old mandate,
I send an envoy, holding the staff of authority and concurrently serving as Grand Commandant, to bestow the Empress's seal and ribbon.
The virtue of earth is to be yielding,
and the way of a wife is to serve her mother-in-law,
to uphold the rites of sacrifice
and emphasize the righteousness of abundance.
Thus, the benefit lies in eternal constancy,
being able to glorify the foundation of the hall,
serving as a maternal model for the world,
and subtly spreading female instruction.
Reflecting on the six female virtues,
and examining the records,
misfortune and fortune have no fixed gate,
rise and fall depend on people.
Though glorious, do not become complacent.
Be reverent!
How can one not be cautious!"
When Emperor Chéng ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress as Empress Dowager.
The ministers reported: The Son of Heaven is young,
so it is appropriate to follow the precedent of Empress Dowager Héxī of Hàn.
She declined several times,
but being unable to refuse, presided over court and managed all affairs.
The Empress's brother, Secretary of the Central Secretariat Liàng, managed the imperial edicts,
and the dukes and ministers addressed her as "Your Majesty the Empress Dowager" when presenting matters.
In the first year of Xiánhé,
the officials requested to posthumously honor the Empress's father and Lady Wúqiū,
his wife. The Empress declined, not allowing it,
and even after three requests, she did not consent.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
and the capital was overthrown,
the Empress was subjected to coercion and humiliation,
and consequently died of sorrow,
at the age of thirty-two.
The Empress had reigned for six years in total.
Afterwards, the Emperor's filial piety was boundless;
he posthumously honored Chēn as General of Agile Cavalry and Minister of the Household of the Three Excellencies,
Lady Wúqiū as Lady of Ānlíng County,
his maternal cousin Lady Xún as Lady of Yǒngníng County,
and Lady Hé as Lady of Jiàn'ān County.
Liàng presented a memorial stating his late father's wishes,
declining to accept.
Empress Chénggōng Dù (Grand Consort Zhōu)
Empress Chénggōng Dù, personal name Língyáng,
was from Jīngzhào,
and the great-granddaughter of General Zhennán, Yù.
Her father
is mentioned in the "Biography of Imperial Relatives."
Because of the Empress's family's generational renown and virtue,
Emperor Chéng, in the second year of Xiánkāng, with full rites, appointed her as Empress,
and she entered the palace that very day.
The Emperor was in the Tàijí Front Hall,
and all the officials offered congratulations.
When the day's clepsydra finished,
the bells were suspended,
and the hundred officials then dispersed.
The Empress was beautiful in her youth,
but still had no teeth as she grew older,
so any suitor would stop pursuing her.
On the day the Emperor made his marriage proposal,
her teeth grew in completely overnight.
Xuānchéng Commandery's Língyáng County was renamed Guǎngyáng County.
In the third month of the seventh year,
the Empress passed away,
at the age of twenty-one.
Outer officials attended for five days,
inner officials entered daily,
stopping after the burial.
The Empress
had been on the throne for six years
and had no children.
Before this,
women in the Three Wú region wore white flowers in their hair,
looking like white pears,
and it was rumored that the Celestial Lord's Weaving Maid had died,
and they were wearing mourning for her;
it was then that she passed away.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Ceremonies for auspicious and inauspicious events
should indeed be fully prepared;
however, the degree of lavishness or frugality
should also adapt to the times,
especially for what lies beneath the heavy earth,
why adorn what is useless!
Now, for the affairs of the imperial mausoleum,
let everything follow frugality.
The interior of the mausoleum should only be clean and swept,
and no clay carriages or straw figures should be placed."
The officials proposed constructing a mournful gate and cypress avenues,
and dispatching pallbearers,
but all were denied.
He also prohibited envoys from near and far.
In the New Year's grand assembly of the following year,
the officials proposed abolishing music.
An edict ordered the abolition of wind and string instruments,
but allowed percussion instruments of metal and stone as before.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended,
in the second year of Níngkāng,
the Empress's mother, Lady Péi, was made Lady of Guǎngdé County.
Lady Péi, personal name Mù,
was the granddaughter of Colonel of Changshui, Chuò,
the daughter of Grand Tutor's Registrar, Xiá,
and the maternal granddaughter of Grand Commandant Wáng Yīfǔ.
Her beauty, both maternal and paternal side,
was unparalleled in her time.
Xiá was killed along with the Prince Yuè of Dōnghǎi
and had no sons.
Only Mù crossed the Yangzi River,
thus enjoying glory and prosperity.
Her residence was established outside the Southern Yè Gate,
Zhāng Tàifēi, née Zhōu, was selected to enter the palace of Chéngdì.
She was favored,
and gave birth to Āidì and Hǎixī Gōng.
Initially, she was appointed as Guìrén.
When Āidì ascended the throne,
an edict instructed the officials to discuss the title for Guìrén.
Tàiwèi Huán Wēn proposed that she should be called Fūrén,
while Shàngshū Púyè Jiāng Bīn proposed that she should be called Tàifūrén.
An imperial edict elevated her to Huáng Tàifēi,
with ceremonial attire and rituals equal to those of the Empress Dowager.
Another edict asked,
"Should court officials not show respect to the Tàifēi,
in accordance with ritual codes?"
Tàicháng Jiāng Yōu argued,
"If her rank is not supreme,
full respect should not be given."
She died in the first year of Xīngníng.
The Emperor wished to observe a heavy period of mourning.
Jiāng Bīn memorialized that three months of sìmá mourning was appropriate.
The Emperor intended to reduce it to one year,
but Bīn again memorialized,
"Suppressing private feelings
is how one shows utmost respect to ancestors."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Kāngxiàn Chǔ Huánghòu
Kāngxiàn Chǔ Huánghòu, personal name Suànzǐ,
was from Yángzhái, Hénán.
Her father, Póu,
is mentioned in the Biographies of Maternal Relatives.
The Empress was intelligent and had discerning judgment.
In her youth, from a distinguished family, she entered the palace as the wife of the King of Lángxié.
When Kāngdì ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress,
and her mother, née Xiè, was enfeoffed as Xúnyáng Xiāngjūn.
When Mùdì ascended the throne,
the Empress was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
At that time, the Emperor was young and immature,
not yet personally managing state affairs.
Lǐng Sītú Cài Mó and others submitted a memorial, stating:
"The heir to the throne is born wise and intelligent,
inheriting the heavenly mandate.
The hearts of all within the four seas are settled,
and the myriad people benefit.
Your Majesty embodies the way of the坤 (earth/female),
and fosters the virtue of a cultured mother.
In ancient times, Túshān brought glory to Xià,
and Jiǎndí brought prosperity to Yīn.
This was truly due to their wisdom and discernment,
which enhanced the glorious fortune.
We humbly consider Your Majesty's virtue to be equal to that of the two Guī [Empresses],
with the beauty and goodness of Guānju.
Please preside over the court and administer the government,
to bring peace to the world.
Now the state is in grave danger,
and the lives of the myriad people hang in the balance.
We, your humble servants, are filled with trepidation,
as affairs of state are countless in a single day.
This is a crucial moment for the nation,
where the blessings of Heaven are concentrated.
It is no longer a time for modest humility and lofty yielding.
Empress Hèxī and Empress Shùnliè of Hàn
both presided over the court,
and the recent precedent of Empress Míngmù
serves as an established rule.
We, your servants, cannot bear our sorrow and fear,
and thus humbly prostrate ourselves to make this request.
We beg Your Majesty to comply with the wishes of your ancestors above,
and consider your officials and people below.
Promote public duty and uphold the Dao,
to harmonize Heaven and man.
Then the myriad states will receive blessings,
and the masses will be reborn."
The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"The Emperor is young and immature;
he must rely on the myriad Dukes, Ministers, and Scholars to guide and assist him,
to fulfill the late Emperor's intention of honoring the worthy.
Moreover, it is the tradition of old virtue passed down through generations.
Thus, the gravest mandate will not fall,
and the foundation of the ancestors will be upheld.
This is why I merely wished to maintain my position within the inner palace.
The memorial submitted is earnest and thorough,
expressed in writing.
Examining it, I am still unresolved,
and filled with sorrow and fear.
I, the former Empress, am truly respectful and humble,
desiring to follow the way of the坤 (earth/female).
Therefore, I will not refuse the sentiments of the multitude,
as it is truly for the sake of the nation.
How dare I cling to my immaturity and ignorance,
thereby going against the former Emperor's will?
I shall respectfully comply with the memorial."
Thereupon, she presided over the court and issued decrees.
Officials memorialized that,
since Lady Xiè had been enfeoffed,
the two ladies Xún and Biàn should also be posthumously granted titles,
as they were both former mothers of the Empress.
The Empress Dowager did not permit this.
Tàicháng Yīn Róng debated, based on Zhèng Xuán's interpretation,
that while Wèi Jiāngjūn Póu, when in the palace, should fully show respect as a minister,
on days when the Empress Dowager visited her family, she should conduct herself according to family rites.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"The rites are indeed unclear on this point.
As stated in the memorial,
this is something my feelings cannot accept.
Investigate it further."
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Yì and Nán Zhōngláng Shàng argued that
"respect for a father is paramount within a family,
while respect for a ruler is paramount throughout the realm.
Zhèng Xuán's interpretation aligns with both sentiment and ritual."
The Empress Dowager followed their advice.
Thereafter, all court officials respected Póu.
When the Emperor came of age,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"In the past, encountering misfortune,
the Emperor was in his tender youth.
The imperial lineage was weak,
as fragile as a dangling tassel.
The numerous officials and ministers followed the precedent of previous dynasties,
urging me to assume regency.
Due to the gravity of the state,
and the established righteousness of past generations,
I reluctantly and respectfully complied,
without time to stubbornly refuse.
Relying on the spiritual power of the Seven Ancestral Temples above,
and leaning on the strength of the many rulers below,
the Emperor has reached adulthood,
with rites completed and virtue fully developed.
He should now personally govern,
and rule over all nations.
Therefore, I now return power and government,
entirely according to old traditions."
Thereupon, she resided in Chóngdé Gōng,
and personally issued a handwritten edict to the Dukes, saying:
"In the past, because the Emperor was young,
I followed the counsel of the Dukes.
Being dim-witted and weak,
and repeatedly experiencing extreme sorrow,
I have borne grief for many years,
steeped in worry and distress.
The Sītú, with his esteemed virtue and weighty influence,
guided and remedied the difficulties.
That the royal house has not perished
is truly due to his reliance.
Now that the Emperor has completed his capping ceremony,
yet the four seas are not unified,
the Wǔ Hú are rebellious,
and wolves are on the path,
expenses and labor increase daily,
and the common people suffer.
I wish for all you gentlemen to contemplate and plan far ahead,
to unite your efforts and minds,
assist the young Emperor,
and rectify his shortcomings.
I, the widowed person, will forever return to my separate palace,
to live out my remaining years.
Thinking of the nation,
I therefore entrust these words of my heart to you."
During the reigns of Āidì and Hǎixī Gōng,
the Empress Dowager again presided over the court and issued decrees.
When Huán Wēn deposed Hǎixī Gōng,
the Empress Dowager was in the Buddhist chamber burning incense.
An inner attendant reported,
"There is an urgent memorial from outside."
The Empress Dowager then came out.
Still leaning against the door, she read several lines of the memorial,
then said,
"I suspected this from the beginning."
She stopped halfway,
asked for a brush, and replied to the memorial, saying:
"I, the widowed person, have suffered these myriad sorrows.
Reflecting on those living and dead,
my heart is as if cut."
When Wēn first presented the draft of the edict,
fearing the Empress Dowager's disagreement,
he was agitated and sweating,
visibly showing it.
When the edict was issued,
Wēn was greatly pleased.
Jiǎnwén Dì (Emperor Jiǎnwén) ascended the throne.
He honored the Empress Dowager as Chóngdé Tàihòu.
When the Emperor passed away,
Xiàowǔ Dì (Emperor Xiàowǔ) was young and immature,
and Huán Wēn had also died.
The assembled officials petitioned, saying:
“The royal house has experienced many misfortunes;
calamities and difficulties have continuously arrived.
The nation’s sorrow had just completed its cycle
when we again lost a great minister.
The world is dismayed,
as if there is no one to save it.
Although the Lord above possesses extraordinary and abundant sagely qualities,
he is indeed divinely bestowed and naturally unrestrained.
Yet his years are still youthful,
like one in mourning;
his sorrowful thoughts
have not yet allowed him to attend to myriad affairs.
We humbly pray that Your Majesty, whose virtue responds to the earth’s 厚 (hòuyá, profundity)
and whose benevolence and sagely goodness are manifest,
has faced many family difficulties,
and personally oversees the court.
The beauty of your great illumination
and the harmony of your transforming influence were evident in the past;
songs of praise and flowing verses
spread boundlessly.
Though there was Shēnyóu (莘有) who flourished in Yīn,
and Rènsì (妊姒) who brought prosperity to Zhōu,
they are not sufficient to compare.
Therefore, the Five Plans are obeyed,
and both humans and spirits are of one mind,
looking up to you for relief,
their hearts suspended on your presence like the sun and moon.
The principle of adapting to the times
is esteemed by the Zhōu Yì (Book of Changes);
to secure the altars of soil and grain is the duty of a great person.
We humbly beseech Your Majesty to manage all affairs of state,
and to bring order and harmony to the government,
in order to comfort the ancestors
and to bring peace to the myriad common people.
We are overwhelmed by our anxious concern for the nation, and offer this most sincere petition.”
The Empress Dowager issued an edict, saying:
“The royal house is unfortunate,
and has continuously encountered hardships and tribulations.
Upon reviewing your petition,
my sorrow and lamentation increase.
All the gentlemen, both inside and outside the court,
agree that because the Lord above is young in years
and his sorrowful longing is profound,
he cannot yet personally oversee affairs;
therefore, orders and decrees ought to have a source.
If it can secure the altars of soil and grain
and benefit the world,
then how could I cling to any personal reservations?
I shall respectfully follow what has been petitioned.
However, as for my shortcomings in obscurity,
I hope you will fully assist me in the path of harmony.”
Thereupon, the Empress Dowager again presided over the court.
When the Emperor was capped,
she then issued an edict, saying:
“The Emperor’s marriage and capping rites are complete;
people near and far are settled in their minds.
It is fitting for him to personally oversee affairs openly
and to initiate brilliant governance.
I now return the affairs of government,
following the old statutes.”
Thereupon, she was again referred to as Chóngdé Tàihòu.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán,
she passed away in the Xiǎnyáng Diàn,
at the age of sixty-one,
having been in her position for a total of forty years.
The Empress Dowager was the Emperor’s paternal cousin’s wife;
the court deliberated on the mourning attire.
Xú Zǎo, a scholar of the Imperial Academy,
argued:
“One serves one’s father and serves one’s lord with equal reverence.
Moreover, the rites say, ‘For one whose husband is associated with the path of the father,
the wife is always associated with the path of the mother’;
thus, if the husband is associated with the path of the lord,
the wife is also associated with the path of the empress.
Mourning the empress with equal reverence is the meaning of a mother.
Lǔ (the state of Lǔ) criticized inverse sacrifices
to clarify status.
Now, the present Emperor personally conducts the sacrifices for Kāng (Kang), Mù (Mu), Āi Huáng (Emperors Ai), and Jìng Hòu (Empress Jing),
showing equal reverence to those regarded as Heaven.
How can one honor her with the path of a lord
but neglect mourning her as a close relative?
It is appropriate to wear qícuī (coarse hemp) for one year.”
This was followed.
Mùzhāng Hé Hòuhòu (Empress Mùzhāng Hé)
Mùzhāng Hé Hòuhòu,
personal name Fǎní,
was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
Her father, Zhǔn,
is found in the biography of external relatives.
She was chosen from a prominent family.
In the eighth month of the first year of Shēngpíng,
an imperial decree was issued, saying:
“The Emperor asks former Grand Commandant Cānjūn (Staff Officer) Hé Qí: The primordial chaos is the source of all things,
and from it human relations were established,
extending to husband and wife,
in order to serve Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain.
I have consulted with the high officials,
and all agree that the old statutes should be followed.
Now I send Jié Tàicháng (Bearer of the Credentials, Grand Minister of Sacrifices) Biāozhī and Zōngzhèng Zōng (Director of the Imperial Clan, Zōng),
to perform the ritual of offering betrothal gifts.”
Qí replied:
“Your humble servant, Hé Qí, former Grand Commandant Cānjūn and Marquis of Dūxiāng, bows his head and prostrates twice.
The Emperor’s auspicious command
seeks a marriage from my humble clan,
completing the number of selections.
The posthumous daughter of my paternal cousin, former Sanjì Shìláng (Palace Attendant), Zhǔn,
is not skilled in education,
and her clothes and shoes are just like any person’s.
I respectfully receive the old statutes
and solemnly comply with the established regulations.”
He also sent acting Grand Protector, Wǔlíng Wáng Xī,
and acting Grand Commandant, Zhōnglǐngjūn Qià,
bearing credentials, to present the imperial scroll and establish her as empress.
The empress had no sons.
When Āi Dì (Emperor Āi) ascended the throne,
she was known as Mù Hòuhòu,
residing in the Yǒng’ān Gōng (Yǒng’ān Palace).
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he moved the empress to the Sītú Fǔ (Ministry of Works).
As her carriage passed the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple),
the empress stopped her carriage and wept bitterly,
her sorrow moving passersby.
Xuán heard of this and angrily said:
“The transfer of the empire is a normal course of affairs;
how does it concern the woman of the Hé clan?!”
He then demoted the empress to Línglíng Xiànjūn (Lady of Línglíng County).
She traveled west with Ān Dì (Emperor Ān)
to Bālíng.
When Liú Yù raised his banner of righteousness,
Yīn Zhòngwén escorted the empress back to the capital,
issuing an order that said:
“Military chariots have been repeatedly alerted,
and the common people are hindered by hunger.
Yet the imperial meals are extravagant;
how can this be congruent with the frugality of the people?
Reduce the provisions,
and do not allow excess.”
At that time, the empress, having returned from afar,
wished to pay respects at the imperial tombs and temples.
The officials, citing that the banditry had not yet been quelled,
petitioned to stop her.
She passed away in the third year of Yuánxīng,
at the age of sixty-six,
having been in her position for a total of forty-eight years.
Āijìng Wáng Hòuhòu (Empress Āijìng Wáng)
Āijìng Wáng Hòuhòu,
personal name Mùzhī,
was a native of Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
She was the daughter of Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ Méng.
The empress was initially the Princess of Lángyá.
When Āi Dì ascended the throne,
she was established as empress,
and her mother, Yuán Shì, was posthumously granted the title of Ānguó Xiāngjūn (Lady of Ānguó Township).
The empress was in her position for three years
and had no sons.
She passed away in the second year of Xīngníng.
Fèi Dì Xiàoyǔ Hòuhòu (Empress Xiàoyǔ, the Deposed Emperor’s Empress)
Fèi Dì Xiàoyǔ Hòuhòu,
personal name Dàolián,
was a native of Líng, Yǐngchuān.
Her father, Bīng,
has his own biography.
She was initially the Princess of Dōnghǎi.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
she was established as empress.
She passed away in the sixth year of Tàihé
and was buried at Jìngpíng Líng.
The Emperor was deposed as Hǎixī Gōng (Duke of Hǎixī),
and the empress was posthumously demoted to Hǎixī Gōng Fūrén (Lady of Hǎixī Duke).
In the eleventh year of Tàiyuán,
Hǎixī Gōng died in Wú,
and she was then reburied with him in Wú Líng.
Jiǎnwén Xuān Zhèng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Xuān Zhèng of Emperor Jiǎnwén)
Jiǎnwén Xuān Zhèng Tàihòu,
personal name Āchūn,
was a native of Xíngyáng, Hénán.
Her family was a prominent clan for generations.
Her grandfather, Hé,
was Línjì Lìng (Magistrate of Línjì).
The empress dowager was orphaned young,
had no brothers,
only four sisters,
and she was the eldest.
She was first married to the Tián clan of Bóhǎi,
gave birth to one son, and then became a widow.
She depended on her maternal uncle, the Wú clan of Púyáng.
When Yuán Dì was chancellor,
Jìng Hòu had died earlier,
and he intended to take a daughter of the Wú clan as his lady.
The empress dowager and the Wú clan daughter were both strolling in the rear garden,
and someone saw them,
and said to the emperor:
“Though the daughter of the Zhèng clan is a widow,
she is far more virtuous than the Wú clan daughter.”
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
she was taken as the Lady of Lángxié Wáng,
and was greatly favored.
Though the empress dowager was honored and favored,
she had a worried expression.
The emperor asked her the reason,
and she replied:
“Your concubine has sisters;
the middle one has already married Wáng Bǎo of Chángshā,
but the other two sisters are not yet married.
I fear that since their elder sister is a concubine,
no one will seek them out anymore.”
The emperor then leisurely said to Liú Wèi:
“For the two younger sisters of the Zhèng clan,
you can find them good matches,
so they do not lose their former standing.”
Wèi recommended his nephew, Yōng, to marry the third sister,
and the youngest was married to the Lǐ clan of Hànzhōng,
all of whom were from old noble families.
The emperor summoned Wáng Bǎo to be Shàngshū Láng,
to please the empress dowager.
The empress dowager gave birth to Lángxié Dào Wáng, Jiǎnwén Dì, and Xúnyáng Gōngzhǔ.
When the emperor assumed the revered title,
although she was a lady,
he decreed that the Crown Prince and the Kings of Dōnghǎi and Wǔlíng should all treat her as their mother.
When the emperor passed away,
the empress dowager was called Jiànpíng Guó Fūrén.
She died in the first year of Xiánhé.
At that time, Jiǎnwén Dì was King of Lángxié,
and he observed the heaviest mourning.
The officials argued that since the king had been adopted out,
he should reduce the mourning for his birth mother.
The national ministers failed to correct this,
and memorialized to dismiss the Chancellor of the State, Zhūgě Yí.
The king submitted a memorial saying:
“My late mother lived in my state when alive,
and after her death, her coffin remained in the state residence.
Although I am an adopted son,
I have no resentment,
and thus my personal feelings are satisfied.
In the past, when Jìng Hòu died,
Xiào Wáng, though adopted out,
also returned to observe the heaviest mourning.
This is a clear precedent,
which I follow.”
Míngmù Huánghòu did not overrule his will,
and so transferred the King of Lángxié to be King of Kuàijī,
and posthumously honored the empress dowager as Kuàijī Tàifēi.
When Jiǎnwén Dì ascended the throne,
he did not have time to posthumously honor her.
Before his death,
he enfeoffed his imperial son Dàozi as King of Lángxié,
to lead the state of Kuàijī,
and maintain the sacrifices for Tàifēi.
In the nineteenth year of Tàiyuán,
Xiàowǔ Dì issued an edict saying:
“Kuàijī Tàifēi possessed the virtue of a cultured mother,
her illustrious reputation was profound,
she gave birth to a sagely and enlightened ruler,
and brilliantly extended the Jìn dynasty.
The late emperor posthumously honored the sagely virtuous,
but the court discussions were not unified,
and the matter was put aside due to doubt.
I, who uphold the aspirations of my predecessor,
am constantly mindful of this.
Now, reverently following the last imperial wishes,
and according to the precedents of Xiàohuái Huángdì of the two Hàn dynasties in the Chūnqiū period,
I confer the revered title of Jiǎnwén Tàihòu upon Tàifēi.”
Thereupon, a temple was erected west of the Tàimiào road,
and her tomb was named Jiāpíng.
At that time, many ministers, hoping to please the emperor,
said that Zhèng Tàihòu should be enshrined alongside Yuán Dì.
The emperor asked the former chief of the Crown Prince’s household, Xú Miǎo,
and Miǎo said:
“I examine the principle of the Chūnqiū,
that a mother is honored by her son.
Lǔ Yǐn honored Huán Mǔ,
and established a separate palace for Zhòng Zǐ’s ancestors without enshrining her alongside Huì Miào.
Furthermore, in her lifetime,
she was not the principal consort of the late emperor.
When it comes to descendants,
how can one establish a consort for an ancestor?
Her high honor and complete rites
are due to her son's devotion,
hence she can be called Tàihòu,
and her tomb and temple are established according to the proper rites.
However, as for burial alongside and joint sacrifices,
that is impermissible by principle.”
The emperor followed this.
Empress Jiǎnwén Shùn Wáng
Empress Jiǎnwén Shùn Wáng, whose personal name was Jiǎnjī,
was from Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
Her father, Xiá,
is seen in the Biography of Imperial Relatives.
The empress, being from a prominent clan,
was initially the consort of the King of Kuàijī,
and gave birth to a son, Dàoshēng,
who became the heir apparent.
In the fourth year of Yǒnghé,
both mother and son lost the emperor's favor,
and were both confined and deposed.
The empress subsequently died of grief.
In the second year of Xián'ān,
Xiàowǔ Dì ascended the throne,
and posthumously honored her as Shùn Huánghòu,
and she was interred with him in Gāopíng Líng.
Her father, Xiá, was posthumously granted the titles of Tèjìn, Guānglù Dàfū,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì.
Empress Dowager Xiàowǔ Wén Lǐ
Empress Dowager Xiàowǔ Wén Lǐ, whose personal name was Língróng,
originally came from humble origins.
