When Jiǎnwén Dì was still King of Kuàijī,
he had three sons,
all of whom died young.
After Dàoshēng was deposed,
and Xiàn Wáng died prematurely,
his concubines remained barren for nearly ten years.
The emperor ordered the diviner Hù Qiān to consult the oracle,
who said:
“Among the ladies in the rear chambers, there is a woman
who will nurture two noble sons,
one of whom will eventually make the Jìn dynasty flourish.”
At that time, Xú Guìrén had given birth to Xīn'ān Gōngzhǔ,
and was favored for her virtue and beauty.
The emperor always hoped she would conceive,
but for years she had no son.
There was also a Daoist, Xǔ Mài,
whom many court officials of the time highly praised as having attained the Way.
The emperor casually asked him about it,
and he replied:
“I am a person who enjoys mountains and rivers;
I possess no Daoist arts.
How could I possibly judge such matters?
However, Your Highness's virtue is profound and fortune deep,
and you should ensure the flourishing of your lineage for generations.
You should follow Hù Qiān's words,
and maintain the method of extensive relations.”
The emperor agreed,
and adopted more widely.
Still having no son for several more years,
he then ordered a skilled physiognomist to summon all his beloved concubines and show them,
but all said they were not the one.
Then all the maidservants and secondary concubines were also shown.
At that time, the empress dowager was a palace attendant,
working in the weaving workshop,
tall in stature and dark-skinned;
the palace attendants all called her Kūnlún.
When she arrived,
the physiognomist exclaimed:
“This is the one!”
The emperor, considering this a major matter,
summoned her to attend him.
The empress dowager frequently dreamt of two dragons resting on her lap,
and the sun and moon entering her bosom.
She considered this auspicious and told her peers,
and the emperor heard and found it extraordinary,
and subsequently she gave birth to Xiàowǔ Dì, Kuàijī Wénxiào Wáng, and Póyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ first ascended the throne,
she was honored as Shūfēi.
In the third year of Tàiyuán (378 CE),
she was promoted to Guìrén.
In the ninth year (384 CE),
she was further promoted to Fūrén.
In the twelfth year (387 CE),
she was further elevated to Huáng Tàifēi,
with ceremonial attire identical to that of an Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
In the nineteenth year (394 CE),
Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ memorialized:
“A mother is ennobled by her son,
with abundant blessings and elevated rites.
We humbly observe that the Huáng Tàifēi's pure virtue is splendid and great,
with auspicious blessings gathered upon her,
initiating a fortunate reign for the sagely emperor,
and continuing a noble reputation among the highest ranks.
Although the hidden and the manifest concur,
her appellation is not yet fully expressive,
which is not how we should convey the emperor's sacred will
and truly respond to heaven and man.
It is fitting to elevate and rectify her title,
after carefully consulting the old statutes.”
On the *xīnsì* day of the eighth month (September 16, 394 CE),
the Emperor presided over a ceremony,
sending the acting Tàibǎo, Liú Dān, to honor her as Huáng Tàihòu,
and her palace was called Chóngxùn Gōng.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
she was honored as Tàihuáng Tàihòu.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān (400 CE),
she passed away in Hánzhāng Diàn.
The court debate concerned her mourning attire.
Zuǒ Púyè Hé Chéng, Yòu Púyè Wáng Yǎ, Shàngshū Chē Yìn, Kǒng Ānguó,
Cíbù Láng Xú Guǎng and others deliberated, saying:
“The Tàihuáng Tàihòu's title and position are truly correct,
her status is equal to the imperial supreme,
the principles of regulations are fully exhausted,
and both emotional and ritual considerations are expressed.
According to the principles of the *Yángqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
a mother is ennobled by her son.
Since she was titled Fūrén,
her ritual attire follows the correct standard.
Thus, Chéng Fēng was made prominent by the title of Fūrén,
and Duke Wén wore three years of mourning.
The son for the one who gave birth to his parents
holds a revered status and a profound obligation.
Moreover, the rites do not weary the grandson (from mourning an ancestor),
so it is certainly appropriate to observe mourning without abatement,
and to establish regulations based on emotion.
If one objects that there is no clear text,
then doubt leads to following the more severe rule.
We believe it should be the same as wearing *zīcuī* for three years for a paternal grandmother.”
This was followed.
The Empress and all officials wore *zīcuī* for one year,
while Empress Yǒng'ān performed mourning rites once.
Thereupon, a mourning hut was set up in Xītáng,
and the funeral rites were held at Shénshòu Mén.
She was buried in Xiūpíng Líng,
and her spirit tablet was enshrined in Xuān Tàihòu Miào.
Empress Xiàowǔ Dìng Wáng Fǎhuì
Empress Xiàowǔ Dìng Wáng Fǎhuì, whose taboo name was Fǎhuì,
was the niece of Empress Āijìng.
Her father was Yùn,
whose biography is found in the "Biographies of Imperial Relatives" (Wàiqī Zhuàn).
Originally,
when the Emperor was about to take an empress,
he consulted the *gōngqīng* (high officials).
At that time, Yùn's son, Gōng, then a young adult (aged twenty), met Púyè Xiè Ān.
Ān deeply respected him.
Later, he said to others:
“In the past, Máo Jiā brought shame upon the Wèi court,
and Yáng Jùn nearly toppled the Jìn dynasty.
If the Emperor takes an empress,
and she has a father,
only one with a respected reputation like Wáng Yùn would be acceptable.”
Subsequently, they sought Yùn's daughter.
She was beautiful, virtuous, elegant, and excellent,
so she was proposed to meet the selection criteria.
In the third year of Níngkāng (375 CE),
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Huán Chōng and others memorialized, saying:
“Your subjects have heard that the Way of Heaven and Earth
is that they depend on each other to form and transform;
and the virtues of the Emperor and Empress
must harmonize to make governance prosperous.
Only then will all things flow into their proper forms,
and constant human relationships be established,
the spiritual root long consolidated,
and the main lineage endure for a hundred generations.
The common goal of Heaven and man,
none is not achieved through this.
Therefore, when Túshān became a companion,
the Xià clan flourished;
and when Rènsì married into Zhōu,
the Jī dynasty prospered.
Now that the Chángqiū (Empress's palace) is to be established,
it is fitting to select [a candidate] in due course.
We humbly hear that the daughter of Wáng Yùn, acting Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
is naturally gentle and compliant,
and possesses all four virtues.
Moreover, she is of a lineage of eminent virtue,
with excellence and goodness accumulated beforehand.
Your subjects have deliberated and agreed,
that she can match the virtue of Qiányuán (Heaven),
reverently uphold the ancestral temple,
spread noble influence throughout the six palaces,
and be a maternal model for all under Heaven.”
Thereupon, the Emperor finally took her as his consort.
Yùn's wife, Lady Liú, was enfeoffed as Lèpíng Xiāngjūn.
The Empress was fond of wine, arrogant, and jealous.
The Emperor was deeply troubled by this.
So he summoned Yùn to Dōngtáng,
fully explained the Empress's faults,
and ordered him to admonish her.
Yùn removed his cap and expressed his apologies.
Thereupon, the Empress slightly reformed her behavior.
In the fifth year of Tàiyuán (380 CE), she passed away,
at the age of twenty-one.
She was buried in Lóngpíng Líng.
Empress Āndé Chén Guīnǚ
Empress Āndé Chén, whose taboo name was Guīnǚ,
was a native of Sōngzī, Xúnyáng.
Her father was Guǎng,
who rose through acting (or singing),
and served as Píngchāng Tàishǒu.
The Empress, with her beauty and skill in singing and playing instruments,
entered the palace as Shūyuàn,
and gave birth to Emperors Ān and Gōng.
In the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán (390 CE), she passed away.
She was posthumously granted the title of Fūrén.
Later, she was posthumously honored as Huáng Tàihòu,
her spirit tablet was enshrined in Xuān Tàihòu Miào,
and her mausoleum was called Xīpíng.
Empress Ānxī Wáng Shén'ài
Empress Ānxī Wáng, whose taboo name was Shén'ài,
was a native of Lángyé, Línyí.
Her father was Xiànzhī,
whose biography is found in a separate record;
her mother was Xīn'ān Mǐn Gōngzhǔ.
In the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán (396 CE), she was taken as the Crown Prince's consort (Tàizǐfēi).
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
She had no sons.
In the eighth year of Yìxī (412 CE), she passed away in Huīyīn Diàn,
at the age of twenty-nine.
She was buried in Xiūpíng Líng.
Empress Gōngsī Chǔ Língyuán
Empress Gōngsī Chǔ, whose taboo name was Língyuán,
was a native of Yángzhái, Hénán,
and the daughter of Yìxīng Tàishǒu Shuǎng.
The Empress was initially the Princess Consort of Lángyé Wáng.
In the first year of Yuánxī (419 CE),
she was established as Empress,
and gave birth to Princess Hǎiyán and Princess Fùyáng.
When the Emperor abdicated in favor of Sòng,
she was demoted to Princess Consort of Línglíng Wáng.
In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng (436 CE), she passed away,
at the age of fifty-three.
She was buried alongside in Chōngpíng Líng.
The official historian says: When Fāng Qí's body is at peace,
it matches the order of qián and aligns with its virtue;
when Yuán Shū follows the sun's path,
it pairs with Xī Yào and shines with equal brilliance.
Therefore, we know that when the yang blazes and the yin congeals,
all things depend on their shaping and molding;
when fire blazes and water moistens,
the six qì rely on their regulation.
Drawing a parallel to virtuous women,
they make a match for refined thought,
and the spiritual root is firmly established,
truly relying on this.
When Xuānmù observed the rites,
she coincidentally possessed the virtue of a潛鱗 (qí lín),
assisting the heavens through difficult times,
and continued the excellent legacy of Túshān.
The precious destiny fell to her descendants;
this was indeed due to the help of a mother's example.
Wǔyuán Yáng Shì prematurely involved herself in court affairs.
Her insight did not reach far,
and she was infatuated by private affection.
She deeply rejected the words of Wèi Guàn
and did not understand the deceit of Zhāng Hóng.
Her ominous influence operated,
eclipsing the clarity of qián.
The decline of the Jìn dynasty
was based on this.
Huì Huáng was endowed with a nature,
and Wáng gave full rein to his foolishness.
His understanding was as dim as a croaking frog,
and his wisdom as confused as a clam.
Nán Fēng, in her cunning,
stirred up disaster that reached the heavens.
First, she trod the pepper palace,
displaying her cruel heart in Chánglè;
then, observing the catalpa trees,
she distributed poisoned feathers in Límíng.
The destruction of Zhōu by Bāo Hòu
was, when compared, small;
the overthrow of Xià by Mèi Fēi
was not even worth mentioning.
The Central Plains falling into the din of war cries
was foreshadowed by this.
In the past, when Gāo Zōng was in mourning,
he entrusted all officials to the elder statesmen;
when Chéng Wáng was young and frail,
he entrusted all state affairs to the dukes.
For empress dowagers to govern the court,
it is known that this is not ancient practice.
However, Míngmù and Kāngxiàn
each ruled the court for generations.
The times demanded the delegation of power,
and they personally governed from behind the screen.
Each avoided the calamity of Huáyáng
and ultimately followed the footsteps of Héxī,
preserving the declining state until the end;
their good fortune was indeed great.
A eulogy says: Two consorts shone for Shùn,
three mothers aided Zhōu.
Mò ascended with Yí Guǐ,
Bāo advanced and caused the ruin of Yōu.
The rise and fall of family and nation,
from this, the cause.
Mù Hòu, with deep resolve,
forgot her emotions while cooking.
The old sword bade farewell to favor,
the pond's reeds evoked sighs.
Promoting transformation and abundant blessings,
she initiated the turmoil of Shāng.
The two Yángs, succeeding in favor,
when fortune reached its peak, disaster arose.
Nán Fēng raged cruelly,
the state was lost, and lives perished.
Xiànróng benefited from the chaos,
living in disgrace yet seeming glorious.
Wielding a pen, she deposed the ruler;
holding a ruler, she intimidated the emperor.
Ultimately, she suffered separation,
and died in deep sorrow.
Fragrant and graceful,
sweet and gentle.
Lǚ Qiè changed Yíng,
Huáng Jī transformed into a trigram.
Shí Wén spread far,
Jīn Xíng secretly shifted.
Feminine virtue overthrew cities,
bewildering zhū and seizing zǐ.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 3: Wáng Xiáng (younger brother Lǎn)
Wáng Xiáng, courtesy name Xiūzhēng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyé.
He was a descendant of Jí, a Han remonstrance official.
His grandfather, Rén,
was the Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
His father, Róng,
was invited to serve in the Duke's office but declined.
Xiáng was supremely filial by nature.
He lost his birth mother early.
His stepmother, Zhū Shì, was not kind,
and frequently slandered him,
causing him to lose his father's affection.
He was often made to sweep the cowshed,
but Xiáng became even more respectful and diligent.
When his parents were ill,
he did not untie his clothes,
and always personally tasted their medicine.
His mother once desired fresh fish when
the weather was freezing cold.
Xiáng took off his clothes and was about to break the ice to search for it,
when the ice suddenly broke by itself,
and two carp leaped out.
He took them home.
His mother also wished for roasted yellow sparrows.
Again, dozens of yellow sparrows flew into his tent,
and he used them to provide for his mother.
The villagers were amazed and exclaimed,
believing it was due to his filial piety.
When a red pear tree bore fruit,
his mother ordered him to guard it.
Whenever there was wind and rain,
Xiáng would embrace the tree and weep.
His profound filial piety was truly like this.
At the end of the Han dynasty, encountering chaos,
he took his mother and his younger brother Lǎn to take refuge in Lújiāng,
living in seclusion for over thirty years,
not answering calls from the prefecture or commandery.
After his mother passed away,
he grieved so much during mourning that he wasted away,
only able to rise with a staff.
Lǚ Qián, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, summoned him to be a biejia.
Xiáng was nearly sixty,
and firmly declined.
Lǎn persuaded him and
prepared a carriage and oxen for him.
Only then did Xiáng accept the summons,
and Qián entrusted him with the affairs of the province.
At that time, bandits were rampant.
Xiáng rallied and encouraged his soldiers,
repeatedly defeating them.
The province became peaceful,
and his governance and reforms were widely implemented.
People at the time sang:
"The peace of Hǎiyí,
is truly thanks to Wáng Xiáng.
The nation is not empty,
it is the achievement of the biejia."
He was recommended as a xiùcái,
appointed as the Magistrate of Wēn,
and successively promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
When Gāo Guì Xiāng Gōng ascended the throne,
he contributed to the strategic planning,
was enfeoffed as an Internal Marquis,
appointed as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and transferred to Commissioner of the Capital.
He participated in the campaign against Wú Qiū Jiǎn,
was granted an additional four hundred households,
promoted to Grand Minister of Sacrifices,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Wànsuìtíng.
When the Son of Heaven visited the Imperial Academy,
he appointed Xiáng as the Sanlǎo.
Xiáng faced south, leaning on a small table and staff,
assuming the role of a teacher.
The Son of Heaven faced north and sought his advice.
Xiáng expounded the essentials of governance for enlightened kings, sagely emperors, and their ministers to instruct him,
and all who heard were inspired.
When Gāo Guì Xiāng Gōng was assassinated,
court officials mourned,
and Xiáng cried out,
"This old minister is unworthy!"
Tears streamed down his face,
and the multitude felt ashamed.
Soon after,
he was appointed as Minister of Works,
transferred to Grand Commandant,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant.
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Suīlíng,
with one thousand six hundred households.
When Wǔdì became the King of Jìn,
Xiáng, along with Xún Yǐ, went to pay their respects.
Yǐ said to Xiáng:
"The King-Chancellor is highly esteemed.
Since Hóu Hé has already shown his full respect,
we should now bow."
Xiáng said:
"The King-Chancellor is indeed noble and respected,
but he is the Chancellor of Wèi.
We are the Three Dukes of Wèi.
Between a Duke and a King,
there is only one rank difference.
Our positions are largely similar.
How can the three highest officials of the Son of Heaven casually bow to others?
This would diminish the prestige of the Wèi court,
and impair the virtue of the King of Jìn.
A junzǐ loves others with propriety,
I will not do it."
Upon entering,
Yǐ then bowed,
but Xiáng alone made a long bow.
The Emperor said:
"Today I truly understand how deeply you value me!"
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Xiáng was appointed Grand Mentor (Tàibǎo),
and his noble title was advanced to Duke,
with the additional appointment to the seven official positions.
The Emperor, newly having received the Mandate,
humbled himself to seek forthright advice.
Xiáng, along with Hé Zēng, Zhèng Chōng, and other venerable elders,
rarely attended court.
The Emperor sent the Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng) Rèn Kǎi to consult them on gains and losses,
and on the priorities of governance and transformation.
Xiáng, due to his old age and debility,
repeatedly requested to retire,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
The Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) Hóu Shǐguāng, on the grounds that Xiáng had been ill for a long time
and neglected court attendance rituals,
requested to dismiss Xiáng from office.
An imperial edict stated:
"The Grand Mentor is a venerable elder of noble conduct,
whom We rely upon to uphold the path of governance.
He has previously offered to resign,
but We have not allowed it.
This is not something for the relevant officials to deliberate upon."
Thus, Guāng's memorial was set aside.
Xiáng earnestly begged to retire,
and an imperial edict allowed him to reside at home as the Duke of Suīlíng,
with a status equivalent to that of the Grand Guardians and Grand Tutors,
ranking above the Three Dukes,
and his emoluments and gifts remained as before.
The imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, those who retired from office
did not serve kings or marquises.
Although he now remains in the capital as a state duke,
it is not appropriate to trouble him with court attendance.
He is granted a couch and a staff,
and is excused from court attendance.
All major affairs shall be consulted with him.
He is granted an elegant carriage drawn by four horses,
a mansion,
one million coins,
five hundred bolts of silk,
a bed with curtains, mats, and cushions,
and six palace attendants to serve as attendants for the Duke of Suīlíng,
along with twenty official cavalry guards.
His son, Zhào, the Cavalry Commandant (Qíjì Dūwèi), is appointed as Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng),
so that he may always enjoy leisure and attend to his parents.
Furthermore, because the Grand Mentor is of high integrity and simple living,
without a family residence,
he shall temporarily remain in his current office,
and move out only when the granted mansion is completed."
When his illness became critical,
he wrote a final instruction to his descendants, saying:
"That life has death
is the natural principle.
I am eighty-five years old;
what regret is there in letting go?
If I leave no last words,
you will have nothing to recount.
I was born in a declining age,
was promoted and tested throughout my career,
but achieved no assisting merits,
and have nothing to repay after my death.
When my breath ceases, just wash my hands and feet,
no need for bathing.
Do not wrap the corpse.
All old clothes should be washed,
whatever was worn in life.
The granted 'mountain Xuan jade pendant,' the Wèi family 'jade jue' earring, and the ribbon case should not be buried with me.
The earth on Mount Xīmáng is naturally firm and pure;
do not use bricks or stones,
and do not raise a tomb mound.
Dig two zhang deep,
and make the outer coffin just large enough for the inner coffin.
Do not build a front hall, arrange tables and mats, or place book boxes and mirror cases;
in front of the coffin, only a bed can be placed.
One plate each of dried rice and dried meat,
and one cup of 'Xuan wine'
shall be offered as morning and evening libations.
Family members, young and old, need not attend the funeral procession.
Only for the small and large mourning rites should a special animal sacrifice be made.
Do not disobey my command!
Gāo Chái wept blood for three years,
and the Master called him foolish.
Mǐn Zǐ, after the mourning period, came out and was seen,
taking up his zither, he played with deep sorrow,
and Zhòngní called him filial.
Therefore, the sorrow of weeping,
the decreasing frequency with the passage of days and months,
and the appropriateness of eating and drinking,
all have their own established regulations.
To ensure one's words and actions are verifiable is the ultimate trustworthiness;
to attribute good to others and take blame oneself
is the ultimate virtue;
to make one's name known and honor one's parents
is the ultimate filial piety;
for brothers to be harmonious,
and the clan joyful,
is the ultimate fraternal love;
when faced with wealth, nothing surpasses yielding: these five
are the foundations for establishing oneself.
Yán Zǐ took these as his destiny,
yet he did not think of them.
What could be so far away!
His sons all respected and followed these instructions.
He died in the fifth year of Tàishǐ.
An imperial edict granted secret artifacts from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
three hundred thousand coins,
and one hundred bolts of cloth and silk.
At that time, it had been just over a month since the passing of the Empress Dowager Wénmíng.
Later, an imperial edict stated:
"Lamenting for the Duke of Suīlíng
has continued until now.
Though We are moved to sorrow each time,
We have not yet been able to express Our grief specifically.
Now We shall weep for him."
The following year,
he was posthumously titled Yuán.
When Xiáng died,
those who rushed to mourn were either worthy officials of the court,
or relatives and former subordinates;
there were no miscellaneous guests at his gate to offer condolences.
His clan grandson, Róng, sighed, saying:
"The Grand Mentor can truly be called pure and eminent!"
He also said:
"In the Zhèngshǐ era, Xiáng was not among those known for their eloquence.
Yet, when one spoke with him,
his reasoning was clear and profound.
Perhaps he veiled his words with his virtue!"
Xiáng had five sons: Zhào, Xià, Fù, Liè, and Fēn.
Zhào was born to a concubine.
Xià died young.
Fù inherited the ducal title.
At the beginning of Xíanníng,
because Xiáng's family was very poor and frugal,
they were granted three hundred bolts of silk,
and Fù was appointed Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Shàngluò.
He died and was posthumously titled Xiào.
His son Gēn inherited the title
and served as a Cavalry Attendant (Sǎnjì Láng).
Zhào served as Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng.
Zhào's son Jùn
served as a Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ Shèrén)
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngshì.
Jùn's son Xiá
served as Grand Administrator of Yùlín.
Liè and Fēn were both famous in their youth
and beloved by Xiáng.
These two sons also died at the same time.
Before their deaths,
Liè wished to be buried back in their old homeland,
while Fēn wished to be buried in the capital.
Xiáng wept and said:
"Not forgetting one's homeland is benevolence;
not clinging to one's native soil is clear understanding.
Both benevolence and clear understanding,
my two sons possessed them."
Lǎn (覽) had the courtesy name Xuántōng (玄通).
His mother, Zhū (朱),
treated Xiáng (祥) without humanity.
When Lǎn (覽) was several years old,
he saw Xiáng (祥) being beaten with a rod
and would weep and hold him.
When he reached adulthood,
he often admonished his mother,
and his mother slightly curtailed her cruelty.
Zhū (朱) repeatedly made Xiáng (祥) do things unreasonably,
and Lǎn (覽) would always be with Xiáng (祥).
She also cruelly made Xiáng's (祥) wife work,
and Lǎn's (覽) wife would also rush to join her.
Zhū (朱) was troubled by this
and then stopped.
After Xiáng (祥) lost his father,
he gradually gained a reputation.
Zhū (朱) deeply resented him
and secretly tried to poison Xiáng (祥).
Lǎn (覽) knew of this
and immediately got up to take the wine.
Xiáng (祥) suspected it was poisoned
and struggled, refusing to give it to her.
Zhū (朱) quickly snatched it back.
Thereafter, when Zhū (朱) gave food to Xiáng (祥),
Lǎn (覽) would always taste it first.
Zhū (朱) feared that Lǎn (覽) would die
and so stopped.
Lǎn (覽) was filial, friendly, respectful, and meticulous;
his reputation was second only to Xiáng's (祥).
When Xiáng (祥) entered officialdom,
Lǎn (覽) also answered the summons of his home commandery,
gradually rising to Sītú Xīcáoyuàn (司徒西曹掾) and Qīnghé Tàishǒu (清河太守).
When the five ranks were established,
he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Jíqiū (即丘子),
with a stipend of six hundred households.
At the end of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he was appointed Hóngxùn Shǎofǔ (弘訓少府).
His position was abolished,
and he was transferred to Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫),
with a salary and emoluments equal to those of a Qīng (卿).
At the beginning of Xiánníng (咸寧),
an imperial edict stated:
"Lǎn (覽) in his youth was devoted to proper conduct,
practiced benevolence and upheld righteousness;
his chaste and unadorned character
became even firmer in adulthood.
Let Lǎn (覽) be Zōngzhèng Qīng (宗正卿)."
After a while,
due to illness, he submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
The emperor granted his request,
allowing him to return home to old age as Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫),
bestowing twenty million coins,
a bed, curtains, mattresses, and blankets,
and sending court physicians to treat his illness and provide medicine.
Later, he was transferred to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
with the privilege of setting up a barrier and allowing horses to pass by his gate.
He died in the fourth year of Xiánníng (咸寧)
at the age of seventy-three,
and was given the posthumous title Zhēn (貞).
He had six sons: Cái (裁), Jī (基), Huì (會), Zhèng (正), Yàn (彥), Chēn (琛).
Cái (裁) had the courtesy name Shìchū (士初), and was Fǔjūn Chángshǐ (撫軍長史).
Jī (基) had the courtesy name Shìxiān (士先), and was Zhìshū Yùshǐ (治書御史).
Huì (會) had the courtesy name Shìhé (士和), and was Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
Zhèng (正) had the courtesy name Shìzé (士則), and was Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
Yàn (彥) had the courtesy name Shìzhì (士治), and was Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍).
Chēn (琛) had the courtesy name Shìwěi (士瑋), and was Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒).
In the beginning,
Lǚ Qián (呂虔) had a treasured sword,
which a skilled physiognomist examined,
saying that one who would surely rise to the rank of Sāngōng (三公) could wear this sword.
Qián (虔) said to Xiáng (祥):
"If it is not the right person,
the sword may even bring harm.
You possess the capacity of a Gōngfǔ (公輔),
thus I give it to you."
Xiáng (祥) firmly declined,
but was compelled to accept.
When Xiáng (祥) was on his deathbed,
he gave the sword to Lǎn (覽),
saying:
"You will surely prosper later,
and be worthy of this sword."
Later, Lǎn's (覽) descendants for generations produced many talented individuals,
and prospered in Jiāngzuǒ (江左).
Cái's (裁) son, Dǎo (導),
has a separate biography.
Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖)
Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖), courtesy name Wénhé (文和),
was a native of Kāifēng (開封), Xíngyáng (滎陽).
He rose from humble beginnings,
distinguishing himself by his character,
being pure, serene, and having few desires.
He delighted in studying the classics and histories,
and thus thoroughly investigated Confucianism and the sayings of the Hundred Schools.
He had a dignified appearance,
and his actions always conformed to ritual.
He maintained his true nature,
not seeking local renown,
and for this reason, the commandery and province long failed to treat him with courtesy.
When Emperor Wén of Wèi (魏文帝) was太子 (tàizǐ),
he sought out humble talents
and appointed Chōng (沖) as Wénxué (文學),
who successively rose to Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎)
and was sent out to serve as Chénliú Tàishǒu (陳留太守).
Chōng (沖) valued refinement as a virtue;
in office, he had no reputation for efficiency,
living on meager fare and wearing a coarse robe,
not managing property.
The world esteemed him for this.
Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) Cái Sǎng (曹爽) enlisted him as Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎),
and he was transferred to Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Guānglùxūn (光祿勳).
In the third year of Jiāpíng (嘉平),
he was appointed Sīkōng (司空).
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng (高貴鄉公) lectured on the Shàngshū (尚書),
Chōng (沖) personally taught the classics,
and he and Shìzhōng (侍中) Zhèng Xiǎotóng (鄭小同) both received rewards.
Soon after, he was transferred to Sītú (司徒).
When Chángdào Xiānggōng (常道鄉公) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tàibǎo (太保),
a position above the Sānsī (三司),
and enfeoffed as Shòuguāng Hóu (壽光侯).
Although Chōng (沖) held the rank of a Tái Fǔ (台輔),
he did not participate in worldly affairs.
At that time, Emperor Wén (文帝) was assisting in governance;
after pacifying Shǔ (蜀),
he ordered Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), Yáng Hù (羊祜), and others to divide the tasks of establishing rituals, laws, and regulations.
All these matters were first consulted with Chōng (沖)
before being implemented.
When the Wèi (魏) emperor announced his abdication,
he made Chōng (沖) present the imperial rescript.
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) ascended the throne,
Chōng (沖) was appointed Tàifù (太傅)
and advanced in peerage to Gōng (公).
After a while,
Sīlì (司隸) Lǐ Xǐ (李憙)
and Zhōngchéng (中丞) Hóu Shǐguāng (侯史光) memorialized that Chōng (沖), Hé Zēng (何曾), Xún Yǐ (荀顗), and others were all ill
and should be relieved of their offices.
The emperor did not permit it.
Chōng (沖) then ceased to attend to affairs
and memorialized, requesting to retire.
A gracious edict refused his request,
and an envoy was sent to convey the imperial message.
Chōng (沖) firmly declined,
submitting his貂蟬 (diāochán) cap and seals of office.
The emperor again refused.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
an imperial edict stated:
"In the past, Hàn Zǔ (漢祖), by knowing people and entrusting them well,
succeeded in pacifying the empire.
He publicly acknowledged their achievements
and attributed merit to the three outstanding individuals.
He then, with his meritorious ministers, broke tallies and made oaths,
depositing them in the ancestral temple,
with copies held by the relevant officials,
thereby illuminating virtue and commemorating service,
and thus safeguarding the royal house.
In ancient times, our ancestors,
faced with a troubled world,
enlisted outstanding heroes
and swore eternal loyalty with them,
thereby resolving the pressing issues of the time
and establishing a great enterprise.
Tàifù (太傅) Shòuguāng Gōng (壽光公) Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖), Tàibǎo (太保) Lánglíng Gōng (朗陵公) Hé Zēng (何曾), Tàiwèi (太尉) Línchuái Gōng (臨淮公) Xún Yǐ (荀顗) each revered virtue and relied on benevolence,
were clear-sighted, sincere, and steadfast,
assisting the former emperor
and glorifying the imperial enterprise.
The late Sīkōng (司空) Bólíng Yuángōng (博陵元公) Wáng Shěn (王沈) and Wèijiāngjūn (衞將軍) Jùpíng Hóu (鉅平侯) Yáng Hù (羊祜) possessed both civil and military talents,
were loyal, solemn, and upright.
We greatly praise them.
Does not the Book of Documents say:
'Heaven has orders with rituals,
the five robes and five patterns!'
Therefore, for the states of Shòuguāng (壽光), Lánglíng (朗陵), Línchuái (臨淮), Bólíng (博陵), and Jùpíng (鉅平), let a Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令) be appointed,
and grant the wives and heirs seals and ribbons,
with a stipend of one-third of their original emolument,
all to be treated as equivalent to Jun Gōnghóu (郡公侯)."
In the ninth year,
Chōng again submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
An imperial edict stated:
"Grand Tutor Wěi Chōng's virtue is profound and pure,
his conduct lofty and unblemished,
serene, distant, clear, and unworldly,
truly exceptional in his generation.
He has served the imperial court
for over sixty years,
loyal and scrupulous in public service,
his thoughts never straying to personal matters.
He responded to public acclaim
and successively rose to the Three Ducal Ministers.
He then bore the heavy responsibility of Grand Mentor,
and the task of discoursing on the Dao,
brilliantly assisting the successive generations,
illuminating the Emperor's work,
proclaiming strategies and plans,
and greatly achieving magnificent feats.
He can be called the eminent elder of the court,
looked up to by all.
I am ignorant in the ways of governance,
and myriad affairs are not yet settled.
I rely on his sagely instructions
to guide and enlighten my ignorance,
hoping to depend on his manifest virtue
to achieve success.
However, the Duke has repeatedly cited his advanced age and severe illness,
requesting to retire from office.
If I follow the Duke's wishes,
then with whom shall I consult and plan?
It would be like crossing a river,
not knowing how to reach the other side.
Therefore, I have not allowed it
for several years.
But his humble refusal is ever more resolute,
his ultimate intention difficult to thwart.
Upon seeing his strong resolve,
it makes me sigh with regret.
To accomplish deeds without claiming them,
is what supreme virtue exalts;
to help others achieve their aspirations,
is what a gentleman does.
How can I insist on my reliance
and thus violate the grand principle of a great sage's advance and retreat!
Now I shall heed his firm resolve,
and allow Shòu-Guāng-Gōng to return to his residence,
his rank equal to that of Grand Mentor,
above the Three Ducal Ministers.
The Duke should nourish his essence and spirit,
preserve his great harmony,
to attain lasting blessings.
He is granted a couch and a staff,
and is not required to attend court.
Ancient wise kings
reverently respected the elders of the state,
and sought their words as a rule,
to mend their shortcomings.
If there are major state affairs at court,
they shall all be consulted with him.
He is also granted an an-chē with four horses,
a first-class residence,
one million cash,
five hundred bolts of silk,
bed curtains, mats, and mattresses.
Six attendants are assigned to him,
and twenty imperial cavalrymen.
His heir, Huī, is appointed Sǎnqí Chángshì,
so he can regularly attend to and inquire after his father's health.
The emoluments and provisions,
as well as the ceremonial regulations for his appointment,
shall all follow the old precedents with additions. "
He died the following year.
The Emperor mourned in the court hall,
posthumously appointing him Grand Tutor,
and bestowing upon him secret artifacts,
court attire,
a set of clothes,
three hundred thousand cash,
and one hundred bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title was Chéng.
At the beginning of the Xiánníng era,
the relevant officials memorialized that
Wèi Chōng and Ānpíng-Wáng Fú, along with twelve other people, should all have their inscriptions preserved in the Tàicháng temple,
and be worshipped with sacrifices in the imperial ancestral temple.
Previously,
Wèi Chōng, along with Sūn Yōng, Cáo Xī, Xún Yǐ, and Hé Yàn, together compiled the best commentaries and annotations from various schools on the Lúnyǔ,
recording the names of their authors,
and following their interpretations.
If anything was unsuitable, they would revise it,
naming it Lúnyǔ Jíjiě.
Once completed,
it was presented to the Wèi court,
and has been transmitted to this day.
Wèi Chōng had no sons, so
he adopted his nephew, Huī, as his heir,
who rose to the position of Píngyuán Nèishǐ.
When Huī died,
his son Jiǎn succeeded him.
Hé Zēng (son Shào, Zūn)
Hé Zēng, courtesy name Yǐngkǎo,
was a native of Yángxià, Chéngguó.
His father, Kuí, was Grand Coachman of Wèi and Marquis of Yángwǔtíng.
Zēng inherited his title at a young age,
was fond of learning and widely knowledgeable,
and was as renowned as Yuán Kǎn from the same commandery.
At the beginning of Emperor Míng of Wèi's reign, when he was still Marquis of Píngyuán,
Zēng served as a literary attendant.
After he ascended the throne,
Zēng successively rose to Sǎnqí Shìláng, Jí Jùn Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng, and Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant has heard that for a state, tranquility and purity are the foundation,
and for the common people, good officials are the root.
Currently, the land within the seas is depleted,
and there are numerous tasks and services.
It is truly fitting to care for and nurture the populace,
and to make them joyful in their service.
Although the authority of a Grand Administrator is slight,
they still have sole responsibility over a thousand li.
Compared to antiquity,
they are like the rulers of feudal states.
Above, they should proclaim imperial benevolence
to bring about benefit and harmony;
below, they should promote advantages and remove harms.
If the right person is obtained, there can be stability;
if not the right person, there will be trouble.
Therefore, Emperor Xuān of Hàn declared: '
The reason why the common people are settled in their fields and homes,
and have no sighs of sorrow or resentment,
is that governance is fair and litigations are justly resolved.
Those who share this with me,
are surely the good two-thousand-shi officials!'
This can truly be said to know the foundation of governance.
Currently, the state is undertaking a great endeavor,
with new levies dispatched.
The armies are campaigning far away,
and both superiors and subordinates toil.
Indeed, the common people can share in the joy of success,
but are difficult to involve in the beginning of plans.
Ignorant people
can dislike the small toil of the present,
and forget the great disaster of rebellion.
Therefore, it is even more imperative that Grand Administrators are the right people.
Though talent is difficult to encompass completely,
they should at least possess some awe-inspiring benevolence,
and be trusted and respected by the common people.
Your servant has heard that among the Grand Administrators,
some are old or ill,
and all delegate governance to their aides and clerks,
not caring for sundry affairs.
Or their temperament is lax and negligent,
and they do not take governance seriously.
They hold office for years,
but their beneficence does not reach the people.
Yet, within the limits of performance evaluation,
their offenses do not lead to dismissal or demotion.
Thus, they are able to prolong their tenure for years
without a date for removal.
Your servant humbly believes that a secret edict should be issued to the relevant authorities,
to secretly investigate and examine the Grand Administrators.
Those who are old or ill and do not personally interact with the people,
or who, as local rulers, lack compassion,
are fond of personal connections,
and harass the common people,
should all be recalled
and replaced with new selections. "
Soon after,
he was promoted to Sǎnqí Chángshì.
When Xuāndì was about to campaign against Liáodōng,
Hé Céng submitted a memorial to the Wèi Emperor, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Former Kings, when establishing laws,
invariably emphasized prudence.
Therefore, when appointing officials and entrusting them with duties,
they would install deputies and assistants;
when deploying armies and commissioning generals,
they would establish supervisors and seconds-in-command;
when proclaiming decrees and dispatching envoys,
they would set up attendants and deputies;
and when facing the enemy in battle,
they would also include an charioteer and a right-hand man.
This was to fully utilize the power of strategic thinking
and guard against changes in security and danger.
Thus, in times of peril and difficulty,
their authority was sufficient to complement each other;
if one faltered or was indisposed,
their talent was sufficient to take over.
As a defense for the state,
this was extremely profound and far-reaching.
When it came to the Hàn dynasty,
they also followed the old regulations.
When Hán Xìn attacked Zhào,
Zhāng Ěr served as his second-in-command;
when Mǎ Yuán suppressed Yuè,
Liú Lóng was his deputy commander.
The precedents of former generations
are clearly recorded in historical annals.
Now, the Grand Commandant is carrying out the mission to punish the guilty,
with elite armor and sharp weapons,
tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
and a long and arduous journey,
indeed four thousand *lǐ*.
Although relying on Heaven's might,
there may be a march without battle,
or the enemy might evade and conceal themselves,
consuming days and months.
Life has no fixed term,
and humans are not made of metal or stone.
For long-term foresight and comprehensive preparation,
it is truly fitting to have a deputy.
Currently, all the generals of the Northern Army and those commanded by the Grand Commandant
are merely colleagues and subordinates;
their ranks and positions are not distinct.
They have never had an established superior authority to command them.
Should a sudden emergency arise,
they would not be able to stabilize and control each other.
To remember danger in times of safety
is the wisdom of sages and accomplished individuals.
Your servant foolishly believes that a great minister or renowned general, respected for their authority and experience, should be selected,
their ceremonial rank established,
and dispatched to the Northern Army,
to participate in strategy when advancing,
and serve as a deputy when retreating.
Even if there were a one-in-ten-thousand unexpected contingency,
with a reserve commander for the army,
there would be no cause for concern."
The Emperor did not follow his advice.
He was appointed as the Administrator of Hénèi,
and during his tenure, he earned a reputation for awe-inspiring strictness.
He was summoned and appointed as a Palace Attendant,
but resigned his office due to his mother's mourning.
In the Jiāpíng era,
he became the Minister of Justice (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
Yǐn Mó, the supervising inspector of the Commander of the Army, relied on imperial favor to act tyrannically,
accumulating ill-gotten gains.
Both court and populace feared him,
and no one dared to speak out.
Hé Céng impeached him,
and the court praised him for it.
At that time, Cáo Shuǎng wielded supreme power,
and Xuāndì claimed illness;
Hé Céng also pleaded illness.
After Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
Hé Céng resumed his duties.
When the Wèi Emperor was deposed,
Hé Céng participated in the plot.
At that time, Ruǎn Jí, the Commander of the Infantry, was arrogant due to his talent and unrestrained in behavior,
showing no decorum during mourning.
Hé Céng directly challenged Ruǎn Jí in the presence of Wén Dì, saying:
"You indulge your passions and disregard propriety,
a person who corrupts customs.
Now, loyal and virtuous officials are in power,
investigating names and realities.
Those like you
should not be tolerated for long."
He then said to the Emperor:
"Your Excellency is about to govern the world with filial piety,
yet you permit Ruǎn Jí to drink wine and eat meat in your presence while in deep mourning.
He should be banished to the four extremities,
not allowed to pollute Huáxià."
The Emperor said:
"This son is so emaciated and ill;
can you not bear with him for my sake?"
Hé Céng reiterated his arguments,
his words and reasoning very sharp.
Although the Emperor did not comply,
people at the time respected and feared him.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn was executed,
his son Diàn and wife Xún were implicated and sentenced to death.
His clan brother Yǐ and clan uncle Yú, both connected to Jǐng Dì by marriage,
jointly memorialized the Wèi Emperor to beg for their lives.
An edict permitted divorce.
Xún's daughter Zhī, wife of Liú Ziyuán, the Administrator of Yǐngchuān,
was also implicated and sentenced to death.
She was imprisoned while pregnant.
Xún went to Hé Céng to plead for mercy, saying:
"Zhī is imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review;
she looks at her reflection and knows her fate,
counting the days until the law is carried out.
I beg to become a government slave
to redeem Zhī's life."
Hé Céng pitied her,
conveyed her plea, and submitted it for deliberation.
The court unanimously agreed it was proper,
and thus the law was changed.
The details are in the "Treatise on Penal Law."
Hé Céng served as Sīlì for many years,
then was promoted to Shàngshū.
In the Zhèngyuán era, he became General Who Guards the North, [一０] Inspector of All Military Affairs in Héběi, and was granted a "staff of authority."
When he was about to depart for his post,
Wén Dì had Wǔ Dì and Qí Wáng Yōu escort him for several tens of *lǐ*.
Hé Céng splendidly hosted them as guests,
preparing a grand feast.
His attendants and charioteers
were all thoroughly drunk and fed.
After the Emperor departed,
he also visited Hé Céng's son, Shào.
Hé Céng had previously instructed Shào, saying:
"The guest will surely visit you;
you should prepare beforehand."
Shào did not wear his cap and sash,
detaining the Emperor for a considerable time.
Hé Céng severely reprimanded Shào for this.
Hé Céng was thus held in such high esteem.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the North
and advanced to the title of Marquis of Yǐngchāng Township.
In the early Xiánxī era,
he was appointed Grand Minister of Education (Sītú)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lánglíng.
When Wén Dì became King of Jìn,
Hé Céng, Gāo Róu, and Zhèng Chōng were all Three Ducal Ministers.
When they were about to enter for an audience,
Hé Céng alone knelt and paid full respects,
while the other two merely bowed.
When Wǔ Dì succeeded to the kingship,
he made Hé Céng the Chancellor of Jìn,
with the additional title of Palace Attendant.
He, along with Péi Xiù, Wáng Shěn, and others, urged the Emperor to ascend the throne.
After ascending,
he was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
advanced to the rank of Duke,
and granted a fief of 1,800 households.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
an edict stated:
"Indeed, insightful and harmonious advisors
ensure the safety of the King's person,
thereby promoting great teachings
and achieving harmony throughout the four seas.
Palace Attendant and Grand Commandant Hé Céng
possesses lofty virtues,
maintains a loyal and upright heart,
is widely learned and well-informed,
clear-sighted and broadly accomplished.
He assisted the late emperor,
and his achievements and contributions are conspicuous.
I have inherited this grand enterprise
and served as the chief minister of the royal house.
I follow the example of previous men,
applying it to myself.
He truly assisted in establishing the mandate and fostering transformation,
brilliantly supporting the path of governance.
The duties of the Three Ducal Ministers,
although they assist in royal affairs,
if I err and you correct me,
encouraging me where I fall short,
then this resides with the Grand Tutor.
Therefore, to illuminate the duties of the Emperor,
nothing compares to utilizing the importance of his sovereign.
Let Hé Céng be made Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo),
with his position as Palace Attendant unchanged."
After a long time,
he concurrently held the position of Grand Minister of Education (Sītú) with his original office.
Hé Céng firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
A Palace Regular Attendant was dispatched to convey the imperial will,
and only then did he assume the duties.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù).

Zǐ Qí sì. Because of his old age,
When Shào had just died,
Yuán Càn went to mourn Qí,
but Qí declined due to illness.
Càn wept alone and, as he left, said,
"This year, I will definitely demote the rank of this servant!"
Wáng Quán said to him,
"Knowing of a death, one mourns the dead;
why must one see the living?
Qí had many faults before,
but you did not demote him then.
Now that Héfū is newly deceased,
you immediately demote Qí's rank.
People will say that the impartial judge fears the strong and bullies the weak."
Zūn, courtesy name Sīzǔ,
was Shào's elder paternal half-brother.
In his youth, he had ability and competence.
He began his career as a Sànqí Huángmén Láng, then Sànqí Chángshì, and Shìzhōng,
successively transferring to Dàhónglú.
His nature was also extravagant,
employing imperial craftsmen to make prohibited items,
and also selling travel equipment.
He was impeached by Sīlì Liú Yì
and removed from office.
At the beginning of Tàikāng,
he was reappointed as the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn,
then promoted to Tàipú Qīng,
but was again removed from office,
and died at home.
He had four sons:
Sōng, Suí, Jī, and Xiàn.
Sōng, courtesy name Tàijī,
was magnanimous and fond of scholars,
widely read in ancient texts,
and particularly skilled in the *Shǐ Jì* and *Hàn Shū*.
He served in clean offices in his youth,
leading the Zuòzhù Láng.
Suí, courtesy name Bówèi,
rose to the position of Shìzhōng Shàngshū.
Believing himself to be from a noble family that held prominent positions for generations,
he was excessively extravagant.
His nature was also contemptuous of others,
and his letters were arrogant.
Chéngyáng Wáng Ní saw Suí's letters
and said to others,
"Bówèi lives in troubled times and is still so arrogant and overbearing.
How can he avoid disaster?"
Liú Yú and Pān Tāo slandered him to Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè,
and Yuè subsequently executed Suí.
Earlier,
Zūn had attended a banquet hosted by Wǔdì.
Upon returning, he told Zūn and others,
"The state received the mandate of Heaven and abdicated,
establishing an enterprise and leaving a legacy.
Every time I attend a banquet,
I never hear about strategies for governing the country or long-term plans,
only talk about ordinary everyday matters.
This is not a sign of providing for one's descendants.
It will only last for this generation;
will the future generations be in peril?
This is a worry for my sons and grandsons.
You can still manage to die naturally."
He pointed to his grandsons and said,
"These ones will surely encounter chaos and perish."
When Suí died,
Sōng cried and said,
"My ancestor was indeed a great sage!"
Jī was the Magistrate of Zōupíng.
His nature was also arrogant,
and he demanded that his local gentry, Xiè Kūn and others, bow to him.
Someone warned him,
"Politeness and respect are based on age and rank,
with virtue as the main principle.
Forcing Kūn to bow out of deference to power
is feared to harm the prevailing customs."
Jī was not ashamed of this.
Xiàn was the Magistrate of Líhú.
He was both arrogant and stingy,
looking down on and oppressing people.
The local community resented him as an enemy.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
the Hé clan was wiped out without any survivors.
Shí Bāo (son Chóng, Ōuyáng Jiàn, grandson Shuò)
Shí Bāo, courtesy name Zhòngróng,
was a native of Nánpí, Bóhǎi.
He was magnanimous and had a discerning intellect,
with a magnificent and handsome appearance,
and did not bother with minor details.
Hence, people at the time had a saying about him:
"Shí Zhòngróng,
matchless in charm."
The county summoned him to be an official,
serving as a Gěi Nóng Sīmǎ.
At that time, the Yèzhě, Guō Xuánxìn of Yángzhái, was on an imperial mission
and sought someone to drive his carriage.
The Sīmǎ assigned Bāo and Dèng Ài to him.
After traveling more than ten *lǐ*,
Xuánxìn said to the two men,
"You will both eventually reach the ranks of ministers and chancellors."
Bāo said,
"We are mere carriage drivers,
how can we become ministers and chancellors?"
Soon after, he was again sent on a mission to Yè.
The matter dragged on,
so he sold iron in the Yè market.
The Market Master, Zhào Yuánrú of Pèiguó, was known for his discernment of people.
He saw Bāo
and was impressed,
subsequently befriending him.
He praised Bāo's far-reaching vision,
predicting he would reach the highest government offices,
and Bāo became known through this.
He met with the Lìbù Láng, Xǔ Yǔn,
and asked to be a magistrate of a small county.
Yǔn said to Bāo,
"You are one of our kind;
I should recommend you for a position at court.
Why do you want a small county?"
Bāo returned, sighing,
not expecting Yǔn to know him so well.
He gradually advanced to Zhōnghùjūn Sīmǎ under Jǐngdì.
Yí Dì heard that Bāo was fond of women and had shallow conduct,
and reproached Jǐngdì about it.
The emperor replied,
"Although Bāo's minor conduct is lacking,
he possesses talent and strategy for governing the country.
Virtuous and honest scholars
may not necessarily be able to manage state affairs.
Therefore, Duke Huán of Qí overlooked Guǎn Zhòng's extravagance and impropriety,
and instead valued his grand strategies for uniting the states;
Emperor Gāo of Hàn abandoned Chén Píng's corrupt conduct,
and instead took his six brilliant stratagems.
Although Bāo cannot be compared to these two figures,
he is also a chosen talent of today."
Yí Dì's concern was then allayed.
Bāo was transferred to Yè as Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng.
At that time, many princes and nobles of the Wèi dynasty resided in Yè.
The Shàngshū, Dīng Mì, was powerful at the time,
and they all competed for profit.
Bāo memorialized these matters,
and thus received even more praise.
He successively served as Grand Administrator of Dōnglái and Lángxié,
and in every place he governed with authority and beneficence.
He was promoted to Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu.
When Wéndì suffered a defeat at Dōngguān,
Bāo alone retreated with his army intact.
The emperor pointed to the staff of authority he held and said to Bāo,
"I regret not entrusting this to you,
to bring about great achievements."
He then promoted Bāo to Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn, acting as a holder of the staff, and Inspector of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu.
When Zhūgě Dàn raised troops in Huáinán,
Bāo commanded the Qīngzhōu armies,
overseeing Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Tài and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Hú Zhì,
selecting elite troops as a mobile force
to guard against external invaders.
Wú dispatched its great generals Zhū Yì and Dīng Fèng to welcome them.
Dàn and others left their baggage at Dūlù
and crossed the Líshuǐ with light troops.
Bāo and others met them in battle
and utterly defeated them.
The Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Hú Liè, used a surprise attack along a deceptive route to assault Dūlù,
burning all their supplies.
Yì and others gathered their remaining troops and retreated.
After Shòuchūn was pacified,
Bāo was appointed Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngguāng, and granted the acting staff of authority.
Soon after,
he replaced Wáng Jī as the Grand Commandant of all military affairs in Yángzhōu.
Bāo then entered the court.
When it was time to return,
he took leave of Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
and they spoke for the entire day.
After leaving,
he reported to Wéndì,
"He is not an ordinary ruler."
A few days later, the incident involving Chéng Jì occurred.
Later, he was promoted to Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn,
and soon after transferred to Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
When Wéndì died,
Jiǎ Chōng and Xún Xù debated the funeral rites without resolution.
Bāo rushed to the mourning,
weeping sorrowfully, saying,
"The foundation of the empire is like this,
yet he ends as a subject!"
The funeral rites were then decided.
Later, he often subtly urged Wèi Dì, together with Chén Qiān, that the imperial mandate had ended,
and that Heaven's will lay elsewhere.
When the abdication took place,
Bāo played a crucial role.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Bāo was promoted to Dàsīmǎ,
further enfeoffed as the Duke of Lèlíng Commandery,
additionally granted the title of Shìzhōng,
with the feather-canopied carriage and drum-and-wind music.
After Zhūgě Dàn's defeat,
Shí Bāo took charge of pacifying Huáinán.
His troops and cavalry were strong,
and there were many duties on the frontier.
Shí Bāo was diligent in various affairs,
and also subdued people with his prestige and virtue.
Wáng Chēn, the Military Supervisor of Huáiběi, lightly regarded Shí Bāo's humble origins,
and also heard a children's rhyme that said:
"The great horse in the palace nearly became a donkey;
a great stone presses it, so it cannot stretch."
Because of this, he secretly memorialized that Shí Bāo was communicating with the Wú people.
Previously, an observer of portents said,
"There will be a great army rising in the southeast."
When Wáng Chēn's memorial arrived,
Emperor Wǔ was very suspicious of it.
At that time, Hú Liè, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, memorialized that the Wú people intended to launch a large offensive as bandits.
Shí Bāo also heard that the Wú army was about to enter,
and so he built fortifications and dammed water to secure himself.
The Emperor heard of this
and said to Yáng Hù,
"When the Wú people come,
they always correspond from east and west;
there's no reason for it to be one-sided like this.
Could Shí Bāo truly be disloyal?"
Yáng Hù thoroughly clarified the matter,
but the Emperor remained suspicious.
At that time, Shí Qiáo, Shí Bāo's son, was a Shàngshū Láng.
The Emperor summoned him,
but he did not arrive for several days.
The Emperor believed that Shí Bāo would certainly rebel,
and wished to punish Shí Bāo but conceal the reason.
So he issued an edict stating that Shí Bāo had misjudged the enemy's strength,
built fortifications, dammed water,
and troubled the common people,
and thus dismissed him from office.
He dispatched Tàiwèi Yìyáng Wáng Wàng to lead a large army to levy him,
in preparation for extraordinary circumstances.
He also commanded Zhèn Dōng Jiāngjūn, Lángxié Wáng Zhòu, to gather at Shòuchūn from Xiàpī.
Shí Bāo followed the advice of his aide Sūn Shuò,
released his troops to march out,
and awaited punishment at the Dūtíng.
The Emperor heard of this,
and his suspicions were relieved.
When Shí Bāo arrived at the imperial court,
he was allowed to return to his residence as a duke.
Shí Bāo was personally ashamed that he had been ineffective in his appointment but showed no resentment.
At that time, Guō Yì, the Supervisor of Xīguān in Yè, submitted a memorial to vindicate Shí Bāo.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"The former Dà Sīmǎ Shí Bāo was loyal, upright, clear-headed,
and capable of managing worldly affairs.
His achievements in administration
are recordable throughout his career.
He ought to manage educational doctrines
to assist in current governance.
Therefore, appoint Shí Bāo as Sītú."
The relevant officials memorialized:
"Shí Bāo previously suffered a setback
and was not equal to his responsibilities.
Allowing him to return to his residence as a duke
was already exceedingly generous;
it is not appropriate to promote and employ him."
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"The Wú people are light and fragile,
and will ultimately achieve nothing.
Therefore, as for frontier affairs,
one merely desires to securely guard and defend,
preventing them from exceeding or escaping, that is all.
Because Shí Bāo's plans differed
and his fear of the enemy was excessive,
he was recalled and given a new appointment.
In ancient times, Dèng Yǔ faltered in Guānzhōng,
but ultimately assisted the Hàn dynasty.
How could one minor fault obscure a great virtue!"
Thereupon, he assumed his post.
Shí Bāo memorialized:
"For the promotion of agriculture and sericulture in the provinces and commanderies, there is currently no system of rewards and punishments.
It is appropriate to dispatch aides to inspect,
all of whom should balance local conditions,
identify the best and the worst,
and then make promotions or demotions accordingly."
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Agriculture
is the foundation of governance
and a great affair for a state.
Although one wishes to bring peace to the times and promote transformation,
if one does not first enrich them and then educate them,
there is no way to achieve it.
Yet to this day, the four seas are troubled,
military and state expenditures are vast,
and moreover, following continuous campaigns,
there have been repeated incidents of floods and droughts,
granaries are not full,
and the common people have no savings.
In ancient times, the cultivation of grains and planting of trees
were managed by the Sītú.
Although now it is about discussing principles,
establishing state policy
is what is urgent for the times.
Therefore, in the era of Táo Táng,
the position of Jì Guān was important.
Now the Sītú holds that responsibility,
devoting his heart to the king's affairs,
having the ambition to sacrifice his family to relieve the state
and tirelessly perform his duties.
Therefore, let the Sītú supervise and inspect the planting and cultivation in the provinces and commanderies;
I will entrust him with the task and expect success,
observing from afar as he accomplishes it.
If it is appropriate to carry out inspections,
then increase the number of aides by ten,
and allow them to select capable officials from the royal bureaucracy who have practical experience."
Shí Bāo was known for his loyalty and diligence in office,
and the Emperor always entrusted him.
He died in the eighth year of Tàishǐ (272 CE).
The Emperor expressed sorrow in the imperial court,
bestowed secret treasures,
one set of court attire,
one suit of clothes,
three hundred thousand cash,
and one hundred bolts of cloth.
At the funeral,
he was provided with a ceremonial banner and standard, a curved canopy, a vanguard carriage, drum and wind music, armored guards, and large carriages,
all in accordance with the precedent of Wèi Sīkōng Chén Tài.
The imperial carriage personally saw him off outside the East Yè Gate.
His posthumous title was Wǔ.
In the early Xiánníng era,
an edict declared Shí Bāo and others to be meritorious ministers of the realm,
and their names were inscribed and honored.
Shí Bāo had previously made a will regarding his funeral, stating:
"Yánlíng was buried simply,
and Confucius considered it to be observing the rites;
Huá Yuán was buried lavishly,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals considered it unfilial,
which is the clear ancient principle.
From now on, those who die
shall all be shrouded in seasonal clothes,
not excessively.
Moreover, no food or jade should be placed in the mouth,
as it is a practice of foolish customs.
Furthermore, no beds, curtains, or burial goods should be set up.
After the burial is completed,
the earth should be filled to level the pit;
no mound should be raised or trees planted.
In the past, Wángsūn was nakedly buried to correct the customs of his time,
and his son followed his command;
a gentleman did not criticize it.
How much more so for those who accord with ritual norms!"
All his sons faithfully obeyed his dying instructions,
and also forbade relatives and former officials from offering sacrifices.
He had six sons: Yuè, Qiáo, Tǒng, Jùn, Jùn, and Chóng.
Tǒng was made his heir.
Shí Tǒng, courtesy name Hóngxù,
held positions such as Shèshēng Xiàowèi and Dà Hónglú.
His son, Shùn,
became a Shàngshū Láng.
Shí Yuè, courtesy name Hónglún,
died early.
Shí Qiáo, courtesy name Hóngzǔ,
held positions such as Shàngshū Láng and Sànqí Shìláng.
The Emperor, unable to summon Shí Qiáo,
deeply suspected Shí Bāo of rebellion.
When Shí Bāo arrived,
the Emperor showed an ashamed expression
and said to him,
"Your son almost ruined your family."
Shí Bāo then disowned him
and he was never allowed to serve in office again for the rest of his life.
Because of his disgraceful conduct,
he was exiled to Dùnqiū,
and was killed along with his younger brother Chóng.
His two sons, Chāo and Xī, escaped and survived.
When Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng raised his righteous army,
he appointed Shí Chāo as Zhé Chōng Jiāngjūn
to attack Sūn Xiù,
and he was enfeoffed as a marquis for his achievements.
He also served as Zhèn Wǔ Jiāngjūn
to campaign against the Jīngzhōu bandit Lǐ Chén.
When Yǐng and Chángshā Wáng Yì attacked each other,
Shí Chāo always served as the vanguard,
and was promoted to Zhōng Hùjūn.
When Chén Zhěn and others escorted Emperor Huì on the northern expedition,
Shí Chāo fled back to Yè.
Yǐng sent Shí Chāo to confront the Emperor at Dàngyīn,
where the imperial army was defeated.
Shí Chāo compelled the Emperor to proceed to the Yè Palace.
When Wáng Jùn attacked Yǐng at Yè,
Yǐng appointed Shí Chāo as Yòu Jiāngjūn to resist Wáng Jùn,
but he was utterly defeated and returned.
He accompanied the imperial cortege to Luòyáng,
and then moved west to Cháng'ān.
Héjiān Wáng Yóng appointed Shí Chāo as Lǐng Běi Zhōng Lángjiāng,
and ordered him and Yǐng to jointly resist Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè.
Shí Chāo recruited soldiers in Xíngyáng.
Yòu Jiāngjūn Wáng Chǎn and Diǎn Bīng Zhōng Láng Zhào Zé both received Shí Chāo's command,
and served as reinforcements for Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Qiáo.
Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo intercepted and killed Shí Chāo,
but Shí Xī managed to escape.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he served as a Cānjūn to Tàifù Yuè.
Jùn, courtesy name Jǐnglún,
was clean-living, modest, and discerning.
He respected and cherished people.
He rose to the position of Huángmén Shìláng,
was a celebrated scholar of his time,
and died young.
Jùn, courtesy name Yànlún,
had a good reputation in his youth.
Commentators called him a "fine vessel" (outstanding talent).
He served as Yángpíng Tàishǒu,
and died young.
Chóng, courtesy name Jìlún,
was born in Qīngzhōu,
hence his childhood nickname Qí Nú.
He was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
courageous and resourceful.
When Bāo was on his deathbed,
he divided his wealth among his sons,
but alone excluded Chóng.
His mother mentioned this to him,
and Bāo said:
"Although this child is young,
he will be able to acquire things himself later."
At over twenty years old,
he served as Xiūwǔ Lìng,
and was known for his ability.
He entered court service as a Sànqí Láng,
then was promoted to Chéngyáng Tàishǒu.
He achieved merit in the campaign against Wú,
and was enfeoffed as Ānyáng Xiānghóu.
Although he had official duties in the commandery,
he studied tirelessly,
and resigned due to illness.
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Huángmén Láng.
His elder brother, Tǒng, offended Fúfēng Wáng Jùn.
The authorities, following instructions, impeached Tǒng,
planning to impose a heavy penalty.
However, he was later pardoned.
Because Chóng did not go to the palace gate to express gratitude for the pardon,
the authorities intended to re-impose charges on Tǒng.
Chóng submitted a memorial himself, stating:
"My elder brother Tǒng, owing to the kindness of our late father,
received preferential treatment early on,
served in prominent positions,
and performed his duties diligently.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty's sagely heart
has given this consideration.
Recently, he was falsely accused and slandered by Fúfēng Wáng Jùn.
The Sīlì Zhōngchéng and others hastily submitted a heavy impeachment,
meticulously drawing up the charges,
repeatedly troubling the imperial ear.
My brothers and I were in extreme distress,
our hearts pounding with anxiety.
Jùn's relatives hold esteemed positions,
and his power and influence are resplendent.
Both internal and external officials,
upon hearing his intentions, immediately complied.
If he disliked someone,
it was easier than throwing an egg.
Since Tǒng's wrongful impeachment,
my brothers and I have not dared to utter a single word in our defense.
We kept our tongues silent and our mouths shut,
merely awaiting the judgment.
The ancients said: 'Glory and splendor come with compliance,
withered decline with disobedience.'
How true these words are,
and how they are proven today.
Therefore, even if an honest officer holds the straight rope,
he cannot but make the charges severe.
Bearing injustice and harboring slander,
one cannot but submit to its logic.
Fortunately, Your Majesty's celestial hearing reaches far and wide,
and your divine discernment shines forth.
Remembering the great meritorious virtue of our late father,
and observing our diligent aspirations,
an imperial edict was issued for re-evaluation,
and the accusations and condemnation were completely cleared.
My brothers and I, even if we were to slice our flesh and shatter our heads,
would not be enough to repay this.
On the fourteenth day of this month,
I, along with my brother Tǒng, Jùn, and others, went to the Gōngchē gate to submit a memorial and express our gratitude.
I humbly believe that on the day it was submitted to Your Majesty,
it briefly reached the imperial ear.
On the twentieth day of this month,
we suddenly received a prohibition order from Lántái,
stating that since Tǒng was pardoned,
an extraordinary grace,
I remained composed in my private home,
never having presented my thanks,
and was again impeached,
with the censure and humiliation being exhaustive.
When I first heard this,
I was terrified and disoriented.
But upon calm reflection,
there is indeed nothing strange about it.
If driven by power and influence,
what is impossible?
To expect the straight rope of the law-enforcer,
is not to be had.
I, with my ordinary talent,
have repeatedly received significant favor,
but have been unable to shoulder the burden and chop the wood (i.e., exert myself),
to repay a myriad of a myriad.
Within a single month,
impeachments have been frequently submitted.
Whether it is right or wrong,
is not for me to calculate.
What I am ashamed of is being unable to serve the relatives of the powerful,
thereby falling into this situation.
Not flattering the stove god,
I am truly ashamed before Wángsūn.
Suícháo Zǐ said: 'The virtue of an enlightened ruler
is best at discerning emotions,
and secondary at discerning affairs.'
My feelings have now been fully heard by Your Majesty,
and I humbly await my punishment and dismissal.
There is nothing more to say."
Thus, the matter was resolved.
He was successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Shìzhōng.
Wǔ Dì, seeing Chóng as the son of a meritorious minister
and capable,
deeply valued him.
In the early Yuánkāng era,
Yáng Jùn assisted in governance,
lavishly bestowed enfeoffments and rewards,
and cultivated many partisans.
Chóng, together with Sànqí Láng Hé Pān from Shǔjùn, jointly drafted a proposal,
which they submitted to Huì Dì, stating:
"Your Majesty's sagely virtue shines forth,
and the imperial spirit has initiated this auspicious reign.
You have rightly occupied the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince)
for over twenty years,
your teachings and transformations have spread,
and myriad nations have given their allegiance.
Now you inherit the great foundation,
this is truly bestowed by Heaven.
As for the distribution of rewards and conferral of ranks,
it is more generous than at the beginning of the Tàishǐ revolution.
This is the first uneasiness.
Wú and Huì usurped power and rebelled
for almost a hundred years.
The borders suffered from their tyranny,
and the court toiled tirelessly because of it.
The late emperor, with his uniquely decisive wisdom,
unleashed his divine martial strategy,
sweeping away the remaining rebels,
as easily as destroying withered things.
Yet, even then, the strategists and brave generals
still exerted their thoughts and efforts.
[一四] But now, the enfeoffments of imperial grace
are more generous than the merits of conquering Wú.
This is the second uneasiness.
Heaven's favor and protection
truly lie with the Great Jìn.
The number of generations (to rule) is
yet unknown.
The regulations established today
should be passed down to future generations.
If there is no distinction between noble and humble,
and everyone with a title must be promoted,
after a few generations,
there will be no one who is not a Duke or a Marquis.
This is the third uneasiness.
We humbly dare to present our thoughts.
We believe that at the beginning of Tàishǐ,
and when merits were assessed after the pacification of Wú,
the systems and lists of names
are all fully preserved.
Even if we cannot strictly follow ancient precedents,
we should still adhere to past practices."
The memorial was submitted,
but not accepted.
He was appointed Nán Zhōngláng Jiàng, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently leading the Nánmán Xiàowèi,
and given the additional title Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn.
While Chóng was in Nánzhōng,
he obtained a chick of a zhèn bird,
and gave it to Hòujūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Kǎi.
At the time, there was a regulation that
zhèn birds were not allowed to cross the river.
He was impeached by Sīlì Xiàowèi Fù Zhī,
but an imperial edict pardoned him,
and the zhèn bird was burned in the capital street.
Shí Chóng 崇 was intelligent and talented,
but he was a swashbuckler without self-restraint.
While in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
he robbed envoys and merchants,
accumulating immeasurable wealth.
He was summoned to be Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng 大司農),
but was dismissed for leaving his post without waiting for the official summons to arrive.
A short while later,
he was appointed Grand Coachman (Tàipú 太僕).
He was then sent out as General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍),
with a staff of authority and supervisory command over all military affairs in Xúzhōu 徐州,
stationed at Xiàpī 下邳.
Shí Chóng had a separate villa at Jīngǔ 金谷 in Héyáng 河陽,
also known as Zǐzé 梓澤.
Those who came to see him off filled the entire capital,
drinking at this place.
Upon reaching his post,
he quarreled with Gāo Dàn 高誕, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, over drinks and insulted him.
He was impeached by the military supervisor
and dismissed from office.
He was again appointed Guard-General (Wèiwèi 衞尉).
He and Pān Yuè 潘岳 fawned upon Jiǎ Mì 賈謐.
Jiǎ Mì was close to them,
and they were known as
the "Twenty-four Friends."
Whenever the Lady of Guǎngchéng 廣城 appeared,
Shí Chóng would dismount his carriage on the left side of the road
and bow at the sight of her dust.
Such was his obsequiousness.
He had immense wealth,
and his residences were grand and beautiful.
His rear chambers housed hundreds of women,
all adorned in silk and embroidery,
wearing gold and jade ornaments.
His musicians were the best of the time,
and his kitchens offered the rarest delicacies from land and sea.
He competed in extravagance with royal relatives like Wáng Kǎi 王愷 and Yáng Xiù 羊琇.
Wáng Kǎi used malt sugar to wash his cooking pots;
Shí Chóng used wax as firewood.
Wáng Kǎi made forty *lǐ* of purple silk screens;
Shí Chóng made fifty *lǐ* of brocade screens to rival him.
Shí Chóng plastered his houses with pepper;
Wáng Kǎi used red ochre.
Such was the rivalry in extravagance between Shí Chóng and Wáng Kǎi.
Emperor Wǔdì 武帝 often helped Wáng Kǎi,
once bestowing upon him a coral tree
about two *chǐ* high,
with sprawling branches
rarely seen in the world.
Wáng Kǎi showed it to Shí Chóng.
Shí Chóng immediately struck it with an iron *rúyì* 如意 scepter,
and it shattered in his hand.
Wáng Kǎi was both regretful
and thought Shí Chóng was jealous of his treasure,
so his expression and tone became severe.
Shí Chóng said:
"No need for much regret;
I will return one to you now."
He then ordered his attendants to bring out all his coral trees.
There were six or seven trees three or four *chǐ* high,
their branches and trunks extraordinary,
their luster dazzling the sun.
There were many comparable to Wáng Kǎi's.
Wáng Kǎi was utterly dumbfounded.
Shí Chóng made bean porridge for his guests,
preparing it instantly.
Every winter,
he obtained fresh scallions.
Once, when out traveling with Wáng Kǎi,
they raced into Luòchéng 洛城.
Shí Chóng's oxen were as swift as flying birds,
and Wáng Kǎi could not catch up at all.
Wáng Kǎi always regretted these three things.
He secretly bribed one of Shí Chóng's retainers to ask how they were done.
The retainer replied:
"Beans are very difficult to cook.
They are prepared in advance as cooked powder.
When a guest arrives,
plain porridge is made and the powder is added.
The scallions are just pounded scallion roots mixed with wheat sprouts.
The oxen are not naturally fast.
[一五] The driver, instead of urging them on when they are slow, controls them.
If you let them run freely, they will be fast."
[一六] Wáng Kǎi then followed all these suggestions,
and consequently gained the upper hand.
Shí Chóng later learned of this
and killed the informer.
Once, with Wáng Dūn 王敦, he entered the Imperial Academy (Tàixué 太學).
Seeing images of Yán Huí 顏回 and Yuán Xiàn 原憲,
he looked around and sighed, saying:
"If I were to ascend Confucius's hall with them,
how could I be any different from them?"
Wáng Dūn said:
"I don't know about others,
but Zǐgòng 子貢 is somewhat closer to you."
Shí Chóng, with a stern expression, said:
"A true scholar should be illustrious in both person and name.
[一七] Why end up in an earthenware pot!"
His aspirations were always like this.
When Liú Yú 劉輿 and his brothers were young, they were envied by Wáng Kǎi.
Wáng Kǎi invited them to stay overnight,
intending to bury them alive.
Shí Chóng had always been friendly with Liú Yú and his group.
Hearing that there was to be trouble,
he galloped to Wáng Kǎi's place that night
and asked where the two Liús were.
Wáng Kǎi, being pressed, could not hide them.
Shí Chóng went straight into the rear study to search them out,
[一八] and left with them in his carriage.
He said:
"Young men, why do you lightly stay overnight at others' homes!"
Liú Yú was deeply grateful to him.
When Jiǎ Mì was executed,
Shí Chóng was dismissed from office due to his association.
At that time, Zhào Wáng Lún 趙王倫 held sole power.
Shí Chóng's nephew, Ōuyáng Jiàn 歐陽建, had a grudge against Zhào Wáng Lún.
Shí Chóng had a concubine named Lǜzhū 綠珠,
who was beautiful and charming,
and skilled at playing the flute.
Sūn Xiù 孫秀 sent someone to request her.
Shí Chóng was at his Jīngǔ 別館 金谷 villa
and was then ascending the cool terrace,
overlooking a clear stream,
with women attending him.
The envoy informed him of the request.
Shí Chóng brought out dozens of his maidservants and concubines to show him,
all fragrant with orchid and musk,
dressed in fine silk gauze,
saying:
"Choose as you please."
The envoy said:
"Your lordship's attendants are indeed beautiful,
but I was instructed to specifically request Lǜzhū.
I don't know which one she is?"
Shí Chóng flared up and said:
"Lǜzhū is my beloved;
she cannot be obtained."
The envoy said:
"Your lordship is learned in antiquity and understands the present,
perceptive of the distant and clear-sighted about the near.
I urge you to reconsider."
Shí Chóng said:
"No."
The envoy left and then returned again,
but Shí Chóng still would not agree.
Sūn Xiù was enraged
and persuaded Zhào Wáng Lún to execute Shí Chóng and Ōuyáng Jiàn.
Shí Chóng and Ōuyáng Jiàn also secretly knew of their plan.
So, with the Palace Attendant (Huángmén Láng 黃門郎) Pān Yuè, they secretly urged Huáinán Wáng Yǔn 淮南王允 and Qí Wáng Jiǒng 齊王冏 to act against Zhào Wáng Lún and Sūn Xiù.
Sūn Xiù discovered this
and falsely issued an imperial edict to arrest Shí Chóng, Pān Yuè, Ōuyáng Jiàn, and others.
Shí Chóng was in the middle of a banquet upstairs when
armed guards arrived at his gate.
Shí Chóng said to Lǜzhū:
"I am now being punished because of you."
Lǜzhū wept and said:
"I shall repay you with my death before the authorities."
She then threw herself from the building and died.
Shí Chóng said:
"I will only be exiled to Jiāozhōu 交州 or Guǎngzhōu 廣州."
When he was loaded onto a cart and taken to the Eastern Market,
Shí Chóng then sighed:
"These scoundrels covet my family wealth."
The arresting officer replied:
"Knowing that wealth brings harm,
why didn't you disperse it earlier?"
Shí Chóng could not answer.
Shí Chóng's mother, brother, wife, and children, young and old, were all killed.
Fifteen people died.
Shí Chóng was fifty-two at the time.
Earlier,
rice from Shí Chóng's house, when left on the ground overnight,
all turned into snails.
People at the time considered this an omen of his family's extinction.
The officials inventoried over thirty water mills belonging to Shí Chóng,
over eight hundred male servants (cāngtóu 蒼頭),
[一九] and other precious treasures, goods, bribes, fields, and residences in proportion.
When Emperor Huìdì 惠帝 was restored to the throne,
an edict ordered him to be buried with the rites befitting a high minister.
Shí Chóng's grandnephew, Shí Yǎn 石演, was enfeoffed as Duke of Lèlíng 樂陵.
Pāo's 苞 great-grandson, Pú 樸, courtesy name Xuánzhēn 玄真,
[二０] was a cautious and honest person,
without other talents or skills.
He perished during the Barbarian (Hú 胡) invasions.
