Shí Lè 石勒, because he shared the same surname as Shí Pú and
both came from Héběi 河北,
adopted Shí Pú into his imperial clan,
giving him special favor and grace.
He rose to the position of Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒).
Ōuyáng Jiàn
had the courtesy name Jiānshí. His family was for generations a prominent clan in the Jì region.
He possessed a refined intellect
and elegant literary talent,
gaining fame in the northern provinces.
People of his time made a saying about him:
“The illustrious Bohǎi,
Ōuyáng Jiānshí.”
He was appointed to a ducal office,
successively serving as the Magistrate of Shānyáng, Secretariat Gentleman, and Administrator of Féngyì,
and garnered considerable contemporary praise.
When he met with disaster,
none did not grieve and regret it.
He was a little over thirty years old.
He composed a poem on his deathbed,
the words of which were exceedingly sorrowful.
Sūn Shuò,
courtesy name Jùyè, was a man from Huái in Hénèi.
In his youth, he enjoyed serving as a county clerk.
〔二一〕Administrator Wú Fèn promoted him to Registrar.
When Shuò rose from his humble origins to a position of authority,
the local gentry still refused to sit with him.
〔二二〕Fèn was greatly angered
and subsequently recommended Shuò to be the Superintendent of Criminal Cases for the Minister of Justice.
The Censor-in-chief, Liú Nà, greatly appreciated and admired him.
At that time, Fèn also recommended Shuò to Grand Marshal Shí Bāo.
Bāo appointed him as his Aide.
As Shuò was about to accept the appointment,
he traveled to Xǔchāng.
It happened that the court had already secretly dispatched light troops to attack Bāo.
At that time, the King of Rǔyīn was garrisoned in Xǔ.
Shuò visited him.
The King, who had known Shuò previously,
privately told Shuò with fellow townsman sentiment:
“Do not get involved in the misfortune.”
After Shuò left,
he immediately rushed to Shòuchūn
to draw up plans for Bāo,
who relied on him and escaped harm.
He was promoted to Secretariat Gentleman.
While in office, he successfully argued against more than ten matters,
earning praise at the time.
The historian states: As for one who served as an imperial tutor,
Zhèng Chōng was indeed worthy of this.
As for filial piety being the root of virtue,
Wáng Xiáng embodied benevolence.
Hé Céng was good to his parents and extended that to his parents' kin.
Yǔ of Xià was reverent and frugal.
The Yīn dynasty built upon the foundations, making additions and subtractions.
Sacrificial animals and clothing
each had their regulations:
feudal lords did not use oxen,
and retainers did not use pigs.
To ride in a carriage and be arrogant and extravagant
is related to governance.
Establishing systems in due course,
none failed to follow this.
Shí Chóng was widely learned,
but his nature was perverse and he had few regrets.
He surpassed the Four Grandees in wealth,
and competed with the Five Marquises in splendor.
His spring fields, adorned with flowing patterns,
were arrayed even on mornings of frozen sleet;
his brocade curtains, long and winding,
stretched beyond mountains and rivers.
With clanging bells and dancing girls,
he indulged to the point of forgetting to return.
Eventually, the Golden Valley harbored sorrow,
and the Blow-Wind Tower was on the verge of collapsing.
This is like the high cicada dwelling in light shade,
unaware that a mantis is stalking it from behind.
A eulogy states: Zhèng Chōng embraced simplicity,
Wáng Xiáng matured late.
All virtues converged,
flying together towards the heavenly path.
Hé and Shí, though differing in conduct,
had remarkable reputations.
The imperial winds flowed decadently,
and Chóng's heart raced.
His boundless extravagance
turned into a source of calamity.
His clan was torn apart and his body fell;
joy departed, and sorrow followed.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 4: Yáng Hù
Yáng Hù,
courtesy name Shūzǐ, was a native of Nánchéng in Tàishān.
For nine generations down to Hù, his family served as officials receiving two thousand dàn of salary,
and were all known for their pure virtue.
His grandfather, Xù,
served Hàn as the Administrator of Nányáng.
His father, Dào,
was the Administrator of Shàngdǎng.
Hù was
the maternal grandson of Cài Yōng
and the full brother of Empress Jǐngxiàn.
At the age of twelve, Hù lost his father;
his filial mourning exceeded the rites.
He served his uncle, Dān, with great diligence.
Once, while traveling by the banks of the Wèn River,
he met an old man who said to him:
“Young man, you have a good countenance.
Before you reach sixty,
you will certainly achieve great deeds in the world.”
After saying this, the old man departed,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and skilled in writing.
He was seven *chǐ* three *cùn* tall,
with a handsome beard and eyebrows,
and was eloquent in discussion.
The Prefect of the commandery, Xiàhóu Wēi, thought him extraordinary
and gave him his elder brother Bā's daughter in marriage.
He was recommended as a Chief Clerk,
the province repeatedly appointed him as Aide and an "Outstanding Talent,"
and the Five Ministries issued successive summons,
but he did not take any of them.
Guō Yì of Tàiyuán, upon seeing him, said:
“This is the Yán Zǐ of our time.”
He and Wáng Shěn were both summoned by Cáo Shuǎng.
Shěn urged him to accept the summons,
but Hù said:
“To dedicate oneself to serving others
is not so easy.”
When Shuǎng was defeated,
Shěn was spared because he was his former subordinate.
He then said to Hù:
“I always remembered your earlier words.”
Hù said:
“This was not something I foresaw from the beginning.”
His foresight and lack of boasting were like this.
When Xiàhóu Bā defected to Shǔ,
many of his in-laws severed ties,
but Hù alone kept his household peaceful,
showing increased kindness and courtesy.
Soon after, he suffered the sorrow of his mother's death,
and his eldest brother Fā also passed away.
He was worn out by mourning and sorrow for over ten years,
living in humble simplicity,
and was modest like a Confucian scholar.
Emperor Wén, as Grand General,
summoned Hù,
but he did not accept.
He was then summoned by imperial carriage to be appointed as Secretariat Gentleman,
and soon promoted to Palace Aide to the Imperial Censor and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
At that time, the Marquis of Gāoguì Township enjoyed composing literature.
Many in office presented poems and rhapsodies.
Hé Yōu of Rǔnán was dismissed for expressing dissenting opinions.
Hù was among them,
unable to be intimate or estranged,
which showed his discerning character.
When the King of Chénliú was established,
he was granted the title Marquis of Guānzhōng,
with an estate of a hundred households.
Because the Young Emperor did not wish to serve as his attendant,
he requested to be appointed as an external official
and was transferred to Director of the Imperial Library.
When the system of Five Ranks was established,
he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Jùpíng,
with an estate of six hundred households.
Zhōng Huì was favored but jealous,
and Hù also feared him.
When Huì was executed,
Hù was appointed Aide-de-camp to the Chancellor
and managed secret affairs with Xún Xù.
He was promoted to Central Army Commander,
commanding all palace guards,
and entered the palace to directly manage affairs within,
holding the vital military power,
with responsibilities both internal and external.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
due to his meritorious service in assisting the mandate,
his title was advanced to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the additional post of Sànqí Chángshì.
He was enfeoffed as a郡公 (Jùn Gōng),
with an estate of three thousand households.
He steadfastly declined the enfeoffment and did not accept it.
So, his original peerage was advanced to Hóu,
and a Lángzhōng Lìng was appointed for him,
completing the functions of the nine offices.
His wife was also granted an official seal and ribbon.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ era,
an imperial edict stated:
"To comprehensively manage the reins of government,
and to justly administer the six offices,
is the foundation of court governance.
Hù possesses a pure and eminent virtue,
loyal, bright, and genuinely excellent.
He is skilled in both civil and military affairs,
and is upright and outspoken.
Although he holds a position of inner trust,
he does not oversee the crucial pivotal affairs.
This is not the intention of ruling by folded hands, doing nothing, and entrusting responsibility for success.
Therefore, Hù is appointed as Shàngshū Yòupúyè
and Wèijiāngjūn,
and his original camp troops are assigned to him."
At that time, Wáng Yòu, Jiǎ Chōng, and Péi Xiù were all renowned figures from the previous dynasty.
Hù always yielded to them,
not taking precedence over them.
The emperor intended to conquer Wú,
and appointed Hù as Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, with a Jiǎjié,
while his Sànqí Chángshì and Wèijiāngjūn titles remained as before.
Hù led his camp troops to garrison Nánxià,
established schools,
and pacified and embraced people far and near,
winning the hearts of the Jiāng-Hàn region.
He established great trust with the Wú people,
allowing those who surrendered to leave if they wished.
At that time, when a chief official lost his position,
successors, disliking him,
often destroyed the old official residences.
Hù, believing that life and death are decreed by fate,
not determined by one's dwelling,
issued orders to garrisons and towns,
universally prohibiting such acts.
The Wú Shíchéng garrison was more than seven hundred *lǐ* from Xiāngyáng.
It constantly caused border troubles.
Hù was troubled by this,
and eventually, through a cunning stratagem, caused Wú to abandon the garrison.
Consequently, the number of border guards was halved,
and the freed personnel were used to cultivate over eight hundred *qǐng* of land,
gaining great profit from it.
When Hù first arrived,
the army had less than a hundred days' provisions.
By his final years,
there was a ten-year accumulation.
An edict abolished the Dūdū of Jiāngběi,
established a Nánzhōnglángjiāng,
and all the troops under his command in Hàndōng and Jiāngxià were added to Hù's command.
While in the army, he often wore light furs and loose belts,
and did not wear armor.
Below the bell gate,
the attendants and guards numbered no more than ten.
However, he somewhat neglected governance for hunting and fishing.
Once, he wanted to go out at night.
The army supervisor, Xú Yìn, held a ceremonial staff and stood at the camp gate, saying:
"General, you oversee thousands of *lǐ*.
How can you be so reckless and casual?
Your safety, General,
is also the safety of the state.
If I, Yìn, die today,
only then will this gate open."
Hù changed his expression, apologized,
and rarely went out after this.
Later, he was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and granted the privilege of establishing an official residence like the Three Ministers.
Hù submitted a memorial steadfastly declining, saying:
"I humbly heard the gracious edict,
exalting me to be equal to the Tái Sī.
Since I first entered public service,
it has been but ten-odd years.
I have been entrusted with duties both internal and external,
always holding positions of extreme prominence and weight.
I constantly felt that my wisdom and ability could not advance so swiftly,
and imperial favor could not be long undeserved.
Morning and night, I trembled with apprehension,
regarding glory as a source of worry.
I have heard the words of the ancients:
if one accepts high titles before one's virtue is acknowledged by others,
it hinders the advancement of talented officials;
if one bears heavy emoluments before one's achievements are recognized by others,
it discourages diligent officials.
Now, I am connected to the imperial family through marriage,
and my affairs are intertwined with the fortunes of the time.
My caution lies in excessive favor,
not in being overlooked.
Yet, an edict from the inner court has been condescendingly issued,
bestowing an unmerited honor.
What merit do I have to bear this,
and what heart can I have to feel at ease with it?
If I disgrace a high position,
overthrow will soon follow.
How can I wish to guard my ancestors' humble abode
if I do not decline?
To defy an order would truly offend celestial majesty,
but to passively comply would lead to such a state.
I have heard that the ancients upheld what they knew.
The principle for a great minister
is to stop if it is impossible to comply.
Although I am a humble person,
I dare, in reliance on what I have received,
to keep this principle in mind.
Now, since the world submitted to transformation,
it has gradually been eight years.
Although we seek out worthy men, even among the obscure and humble,
I have been unable to promote the virtuous
or make known the meritorious,
so that Your Majesty may know that there are many superior to me,
and not a few who have not yet been discovered.
Supposing there are hidden virtues among those who build walls,
and concealed talents among butchers and fishermen,
if the court counsel employs me without considering it wrong,
and I occupy the position without feeling ashamed,
would not the loss be great indeed?
Though I have been an undeserving incumbent for a long time,
it is not like today,
where I concurrently hold the highest civil and military favors,
equal to the exalted position of prime ministers.
Moreover, though my perception is limited,
I observe that currently, Guānglù Dàfū Lǐ Xǐ holds firmly to high principles and brightness,
and is upright and stern in public office;
Guānglù Dàfū Lǔ Zhī keeps himself pure and has few desires,
being amiable but not conforming;
Guānglù Dàfū Lǐ Yìn is pure, bright, simple, and unadorned,
establishing himself in court.
All have served with graying hair,
maintaining propriety from beginning to end.
Though they have held honored positions both inside and outside the court,
they are no different from humble families,
yet they have not received this selection.
If I were to surpass them,
how could I satisfy the expectations of the world,
and bring little benefit for long?
Therefore, I swear with my heart to uphold integrity,
with no ambition for unmerited advancement.
Now, the roads are open,
and there are many affairs in the frontier regions.
I beg to retain my previous grace
and allow me to return to my garrison quickly.
Otherwise, if I linger,
there will surely be shortcomings in external defense.
The will of a common man
cannot be taken away."
He was not heeded.
When he returned to his garrison,
Bù Chǎn, the Dū of Wú Xīlíng, surrendered with his entire city.
Wú general Lù Kàng attacked him very fiercely.
An edict ordered Hù to go to Chǎn's aid.
Hù led fifty thousand troops out of Jiānglíng,
and sent Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Zhào to attack Kàng.
He did not succeed,
and Chǎn was eventually captured by Kàng.
The officials in charge submitted a memorial:
"Hù commanded over eighty thousand men,
while the enemy forces numbered no more than thirty thousand.
Hù stalled his troops at Jiānglíng,
allowing the enemy to prepare their defenses.
Then he sent Yáng Zhào's isolated force into dangerous terrain,
with few soldiers and stretched supply lines,
resulting in the defeat of the army.
He defied imperial orders,
and showed no integrity as a great minister.
He should be dismissed from office
and reside at home as a marquis."
He was ultimately demoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
and Yáng Zhào was dismissed as a commoner.
Hù, seeing that Méng Xiàn (孟獻) had built Wǔláo (武牢) and the people of Zhèng (鄭) were afraid,
and Yàn Ruò (晏弱) had fortified Dōngyáng (東陽) and the Lái (萊) clan submitted,
then advanced to occupy strategic strongholds,
built five new cities,
seized fertile lands,
and took resources from the Wú (吳) people.
West of Shíchéng (石城),
all became territory of Jìn (晉).
From then on, those who surrendered continuously appeared.
He then enhanced his virtue and trustworthiness
to conciliate and pacify the newly attached,
and harbored a keen desire to annex Wú (吳).
Whenever he engaged in battle with the Wú (吳) people,
he would set a specific date for combat,
and would not resort to surprise attacks.
If any of his generals and commanders wished to propose deceptive tactics,
he would always offer them strong wine
to prevent them from speaking.
When someone captured two Wú (吳) children as prisoners,
Hù (祜) sent them back to their homes.
Later, Wú (吳) generals Xià Xiáng (夏詳) and Shào Yǐ (邵顗) came to surrender,
and the father of the two children also led his subordinates with them.
When Wú (吳) generals Chén Shàng (陳尚) and Pān Jǐng (潘景) came to raid,
Hù (祜) pursued and decapitated them,
but admired their sacrifice for their loyalty and gave them a generous funeral.
When Jǐng (景) and Shàng’s (尚) sons and nephews came to retrieve the coffins,
Hù (祜) sent them back with proper rites.
When Wú (吳) general Dèng Xiāng (鄧香) plundered Xiàkǒu (夏口),
Hù (祜) offered a reward for his capture alive.
Once he arrived,
Hù (祜) pardoned him.
Xiāng (香) was deeply moved by his kindness
and led his troops to surrender.
When Hù’s (祜) army marched into Wú (吳) territory,
they cut grain for provisions.
He calculated all that was encroached upon
and sent silk to compensate for it.
Whenever he gathered his troops for hunting expeditions between the Jiāng (江) and Miǎn (沔) rivers,
he always stayed within Jìn (晉) territory.
If any birds or beasts were first wounded by Wú (吳) people but then caught by Jìn (晉) soldiers,
he would return them.
Consequently, the Wú (吳) people were universally pleased and submitted,
calling him Yáng Gōng (羊公),
not daring to use his personal name.
Hù (祜) and Lù Kàng (陸抗) faced each other,
and their envoys traveled between them.
Kàng (抗) praised Hù’s (祜) virtue and magnanimity,
saying that even Yuè Yì (樂毅) and Zhūgě Kǒngmíng (諸葛孔明) could not surpass him.
Kàng (抗) once fell ill,
and Hù (祜) sent him medicine.
Kàng (抗) took it without suspicion.
Many advised Kàng (抗),
but Kàng (抗) said:
“How could Yáng Hù (羊祜) be someone who poisons people!”
People at the time remarked that Huá Yuán (華元) and Zǐ Fǎn (子反) were seen again today.
Kàng (抗) often told his garrison:
“He is entirely devoted to virtue,
while I am entirely devoted to brutality.
This is to submit without fighting.
Each should simply guard their own boundaries,
and not seek small advantages.”
Sūn Hào (孫晧) heard that the two borders were at peace
and questioned Kàng (抗).
Kàng (抗) replied:
“Even a single village or hamlet
cannot be without trust and righteousness,
how much less a great state!
If I do not act like this,
it would only highlight his virtue,
and cause no harm to Hù (祜).”
Hù (祜) was upright and selfless,
and hated evil and sycophancy.
Xún Xù (荀勖), Féng Dǎn (馮紞), and their ilk greatly feared him.
His nephew by marriage, Wáng Yǎn (王衍), once visited Hù (祜) to discuss affairs,
and his words were very eloquent and persuasive.
Hù (祜) did not agree with him,
and Yǎn (衍) left in a huff.
Hù (祜) turned to his guests and said:
“Wáng Yíbǔ (王夷甫) is now holding a high position with great renown,
but the one who will ruin customs and corrupt morals will surely be this man.”
During Bù Chǎn’s (步闡) campaign,
Hù (祜), according to military law, was about to execute Wáng Róng (王戎).
Therefore, Róng (戎) and Yǎn (衍) both resented him,
and often spoke ill of Hù (祜).
People at the time coined a saying:
“With the two Wángs (王) in power,
Yáng Gōng (羊公) has no virtue.”
In the early Xiánníng (咸寧) era,

he was appointed Grand General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, 征南大將軍) and granted the privilege to establish his own staff and the ceremonial distinctions of the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, 開府儀同三司),
thus gaining the authority to exclusively nominate and summon officials.
Previously,
Hù (祜) believed that attacking Wú (吳) would necessarily rely on the advantage of the upstream region.
Moreover, at that time, there was a children’s rhyme in Wú (吳) that went:
“Ā Tóng (阿童) and Ā Tóng (阿童),
holding a knife, float across the river.
They fear not the beasts on the bank,
but only the dragons in the water.”
Hù (祜) heard this and said:
“This must mean that the naval forces will be victorious,
but we must consider who corresponds to that name.”
It happened that Wáng Jùn (王濬), the Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州), was summoned to serve as Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng, 大司農).
Hù (祜) knew he was capable,
and Jùn (濬) also had the child’s name Ā Tóng (阿童).
So, he petitioned to keep Jùn (濬) to supervise the various armies in Yìzhōu (益zhou),
and added the title General of Valiant Dragons (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, 龍驤將軍),
secretly ordering him to repair boats and oars
in preparation for a downstream campaign.
Hù shàn jiǎ xùn zú,
guǎng wéi róng bèi.
Zhì shì shàng shū yuē:
“Xiāndì shùn tiān yìng shí,
xī píng Bā Shǔ,
nán hé Wú Huì,
hǎinèi déyǐ xiūxī,
zhàoshù yǒu lè ān zhī xīn.
Ér Wú fù bèixìn,
shǐ biānshì gēng xīng.
Fū qīyùn suī tiān suǒ shòu,
ér gōngyè bì yóu rén ér chéng,
bù yī dà jǔ sǎomiè,
zé zhòngyì wú shí dé ān.
Yì suǒyǐ lóng xiāndì zhī xūn,
chéng wúwéi zhī huà yě.
Gù Yáo yǒu Dānshuǐ zhī fá,
Shùn yǒu Sānmíáo zhī zhēng,
xián yǐ níngjìng yǔzhòu,
jí bīng hé zhòng zhě yě.
Shǔ píng zhī shí,
tiānxia jiē wèi Wú dāng bìng wáng,
zì cǐ lái shísān nián,
shì wèi yī zhōu,
píngdìng zhī qī fù zài jīn rì yǐ.
Yìzhě cháng yán Wú Chǔ yǒu dào hòufú,
wúlǐ xiān qiáng,
cǐ nǎi wèi hóu zhī shí ěr.
Dāngjīn yī tǒng,
bùdé yǔ gǔ tóng yù.
Fū shì dào zhī lùn,
jiē wèi yìng quán,
shì gù móu zhī suī duō,
ér jué zhī yù dú.
Fán yǐ xiǎnzǔ dé cún zhě,
wèi suǒ dí zhě tóng,
lì zú zì gù.
Gǒu qí qīngzhòng bù qí,
qiángruò yì shì,
zé zhìshì bùnéng móu,
ér xiǎnzǔ bùkě bǎo yě.
Shǔ zhī wéi guó,
fēi bù xiǎn yě,
gāoshān xún yúnní,
shēngǔ sì wú jǐng,
shù mǎ xuán chē,
ránhòu dé jì,
jiē yán yī fū hé jǐ,
qiān rén mò dāng.
Jí jìnbīng zhī rì,
céng wú fānlí zhī xiàn,
zhǎn jiàng qiān qí,
fú shī shù wàn,
chéng shèng xíjuǎn,
jìng zhì Chéngdū,
Hànzhōng zhū chéng,
jiē niǎoqī ér bùgǎn chū.
Fēi jiē wú zhànxīn,
chéng lì bùzú xiāngkàng.
Zhì Líu Chán jiàngfú,
zhū yíngbǎo zhě suǒrán jù sàn.
Jīn Jiāng Huái zhī nán,
bùguò Jiàngé;
shānchuān zhī xiǎn,
bùguò Mín Hàn;
Sūn Hào zhī bào,
chǐ yú Líu Chán;
Wú rén zhī kùn,
shèn yú Bā Shǔ.
Ér Dà Jìn bīng zhòng,
duō yú qiánshì;
zīchú qìxiè,
shèng yú wǎngshí.
Jīn bù yú cǐ píng Wú,
ér gēng zǔ bīng xiāng shǒu,
zhēng fū kǔ yì,
rì xún gāngē,
jīnglì shèng shuāi,
bùkě chángjiǔ,
yí dāngshí dìng,
yǐ yī sìhǎi.
Jīn ruò yǐn Liáng Yì zhī bīng shuǐlù jù xià,
Jīng Chǔ zhī zhòng jìnlín Jiānglíng,
Píng Nán、Yùzhōu,
zhízhǐ Xiàkǒu,
Xú、Yáng、Qīng、Yǎn bìng xiàng Mòlíng,
gǔ pèi yǐ yí zhī,
duōfāng yǐ wù zhī,
yǐ yīyú zhī Wú,
dāng tiānxià zhī zhòng,
shì fēn xíng sàn,
suǒ bèi jiē jí.
Bā Hàn qí bīng chū qí kōngxū,
yī chù qīnghuài,
zé shàngxià zhèndàng.
Wú yuán Jiāng wèi guó,
wú yǒu nèiwài,
dōngxī shù qiānlǐ,
yǐ fānlí zì chí,
suǒ dí zhě dà,
wú yǒu níngxī.
Sūn Hào zìqíng rènyì,
yǔ xià duō jì,
míngchén zhòngjiàng bù fù zìxìn,
shìyǐ Sūn Xìu zhī tú jiē wèibī ér zhì.
Jiāng yí yú cháo,
shì kùn yú yě,
wú yǒu bǎoshì zhī jì,
yīdìng zhī xīn.
Píngcháng zhī rì,
yóu huái qùjiù,
bīng lín zhī jì,
bì yǒu yìng zhě,
zhōng bùnéng qí lì zhì sǐ,
yǐ kě zhī yě.
Qí sú jíshù,
bùnéng chíjiǔ,
gōngnǔ jǐshùn bùrú Zhōngguó,
wéi yǒu shuǐzhàn shì qí suǒ biàn.
Yī rù qí jìng,
zé Cháng Jiāng fēi fù suǒ gù,
huán bǎo chéngchí,
zé qù cháng rù duǎn.
Ér guānjūn xuán jìn,
rén yǒu zhìjié zhī zhì,
Wú rén zhàn yú qí nèi,
yǒu píngchéng zhī xīn.
Rúcǐ,
jūn bù yú shí,
kè kě bì yǐ. ”
Dì shēn nà zhī.
Huì Qín Liáng lǚ bài,
Hù fù biǎo yuē:
“Wú píng zé hú zì dìng,
dàn dāng sù jì dàgōng ěr.”
Ér yìzhě duō bùtóng,
Hù tàn yuē:
“Tiānxià bùrúyì,
shí jū qībā,
gù yǒu dāngduànbùduàn.
Tiān yǔ bù qǔ,
qǐ fēi gèngshì zhě hèn yú hòushí zāi!”
Qí hòu,
zhào yǐ Tàishān zhī nán Wǔyáng, Móu, Nánchéng, Líangfù, Píngyáng wǔ xiàn wèi Nánchéng Jùn,
fēng Hù wèi Nánchéng Hóu,
zhì xiāng,
yǔ Jùn Gōng tóng.
Hù ràng yuē:
“Xī Zhāng Líang qǐng shòu líu wàn hù,
Hàn Zǔ bù duó qí zhì.
Chén shòu Jùpíng yú Xiāndì,
gǎn rǔ zhòngjué,
yǐ sù guānbàng!”
Gùzhí bù bài,
Dì xǔ zhī.
Hù měi bèi dēngjìn,
cháng shǒu chōngtuì,
zhìxīn sù zhù,
gù tè jiàn shēn yú fēliè zhī wài.
Shìyǐ míngdé yuǎnpò,
cháoyě jù zhān,
jìnshēn qiānyì,
dāng jū Táifǔ.
Dì fāng yǒu jiānbìng zhī zhì,
zhàng Hù yǐ dōngnán zhī rèn,
gù qǐn zhī.
Hù lì zhí èr cháo,
rèn diǎn shūyào,
zhèngshì sǔnyì,
jiē zīfǎng yān,
shìlì zhī qíu,
wúsuǒ guānyǔ.
Qí jiāmóu dǎngyì,
jiē fén qí cǎo,
gù shì mò wén.
Fán suǒ jìndá,
rén jiē bùzhī suǒ yóu.
Huò wèi Hù shènmì tàiguò zhě,
Hù yuē:
“Shì hé yán yú!
Fū rù zé zàoxī,
chū zé guǐcí,
jūnchén bùmì zhī jiè,
wú wéi jù qí bù jí.
Bùnéng jǔ xián qǔ yì,
qǐ dé bù kuì zhī rén zhī nán zāi!
Qiě bài jué gōngcháo,
xiè ēn sīmén,
wú suǒ bù qǔ.”
Hù's son-in-law once advised Hù,
"If you were to establish something significant,
so that people would flock to and support it,
wouldn't that be wonderful?"
Hù silently did not respond.
Later, he told his sons,
"This can be described as knowing one thing but not the other.
When a subject establishes private interests, it is disloyal to the public good.
This is a great delusion.
You should understand this intention of mine."
He once wrote a letter to his younger cousin, Xiù, saying:
"Once the border affairs are settled,
I will put on a kerchief and head east,
return to my old village,
and prepare a burial place.
How can a commoner holding a high position
not be blamed for his overwhelming success?
Shūguǎng is my teacher."
Hù loved mountains and rivers.
Whenever the scenery was fine,
he would visit Mount Xiànshān,
set out wine, and recite poems,
never tiring all day long.
He once sighed with emotion,
and turning to his Aide-de-camp Zhōuzhàn and others, said:
"Since the beginning of the universe,
this mountain has existed.
From ancient times, many virtuous and distinguished gentlemen,
climbing here to gaze into the distance,
like me and you, have been numerous!
All have vanished without a trace,
which makes one sad.
If after a hundred years one has awareness,
our souls should still ascend here."
Zhàn said:
"Your Excellency's virtue surpasses the four seas,
and your principles inherit those of former sages.
Your excellent reputation and high standing
will surely be transmitted together with this mountain.
As for people like me,
we will indeed be as Your Excellency said."
When Hù had merit in suppressing the Wú bandits,
and was about to be promoted in rank and enfeoffed,
he begged that it be bestowed upon his maternal cousin, Càixí.
An imperial edict enfeoffed Xí as Guānnèihóu,
with three hundred households.
When the Wú people raided Yìyáng and Jiāngxià,
and plundered households,
an imperial edict was sent by a court attendant to write a letter questioning Hù's reasons for not pursuing and attacking them,
and also suggesting the suitability of moving the province back to its old location.
Hù said:
"Jiāngxià is eight hundred *lǐ* from Xiāngyáng.
By the time news of the bandits arrived,
the bandits had already been gone for a day.
When the infantry arrives,
how can they rescue them?
To exhaust the army to avoid blame,
I fear is not appropriate.
In ancient times, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi established regional commanders (*dūdū*),
who were generally close to the provincial capitals,
because military strength thrives on cohesion and suffers from dispersion.
In border regions,
one moment they are here, the next they are there.
Careful defense is all that is needed;
this was the good teaching of antiquity.
If we were to move the provincial capital at will,
the bandits appear unpredictably,
and it would be unknown where the provincial capital should be located. "
The envoy could not refute him.
Hù fell ill
and requested to enter the court.
When he arrived in Luòyáng,
it happened that Emperor Jǐngxiàn's imperial carriage was in mourning,
and Hù was deeply grieved.
An imperial decree was issued to console him,
and though ill, he was granted an audience.
He was ordered to ride in a litter into the palace
without having to prostrate himself,
showing him great honor.
When he was seated in attendance,
he personally presented his plan for conquering Wú.
The Emperor, considering his illness,
deemed it inappropriate for him to regularly enter the court,
and sent the Grand Secretary Zhānghuà to ask about his strategy.
Hù said:
"Currently, the Emperor possesses the virtue of dynastic transfer,
but his merits and virtues are not yet fully manifest.
The Wú people's tyrannical rule is already extreme,
and they can be conquered without a fight.
Unifying the six directions [China]
and promoting culture and education
will make the Emperor equal to Yáo and Shùn,
and his ministers comparable to Jì and Xiè,
setting a grand example for a hundred generations.
If we abandon this opportunity,
and if Sūn Hào unfortunately dies,
and the Wú people establish another capable ruler,
then even with a million troops,
the Yangtze River may not be crossable,
which will lead to future trouble!"
Huà deeply approved of his plan.
Hù said to Huà:
"The one who will fulfill my ambition
is you."
The Emperor wanted Hù to oversee the generals from his sickbed,
but Hù said:
"To conquer Wú does not necessarily require my personal involvement.
But after it is pacified,
it will trouble Your Majesty's thoughts.
I dare not claim the glory and fame.
If the matter is concluded,
there should be someone entrusted with it.
I hope you will carefully select the person."
His illness gradually worsened,
and he recommended Dùyù to succeed him.
He then passed away,
at the age of fifty-eight.
The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and wept for him,
with great sorrow.
That day was bitterly cold,
and the Emperor's tears soaked his beard and temples,
turning them into ice.
The people of the southern province, upon hearing the news of Hù's death on a market day,
all wailed and grieved,
closing their markets,
and the sounds of people crying in the alleys were continuous.
The Wú border guards and soldiers also wept for him.
Such was the impact of his benevolent virtue.
He was posthumously granted secret funerary objects from the eastern garden,
a set of court robes,
thirty thousand *qián*,
and a hundred bolts of cloth.
An imperial edict proclaimed:
"Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, Nánchénghóu Hù,
trod the path of virtue and was pure and humble,
with a clear and far-reaching mind.
Initially in an internal position,
he met with the great mandate,
and his heart was sincere and devoted.
He assisted in royal affairs,
managing confidential matters internally,
and commanding the regional territories externally.
He should have concluded his glorious achievements
and forever assisted Our Person,
but suddenly he passed away,
causing Us grief and sorrow.
He is posthumously promoted to Shìzhōng and Tàifù,
retaining his staff of authority as before."
Hù conducted himself with purity and frugality,
and his clothing was simple.
All the funds from his salary and emoluments
were used to provide for his nine generations of relatives
and to reward soldiers.
His family had no surplus wealth.
His will stipulated that the seal of Nánchénghóu should not be placed in his coffin.
His younger cousin Xiù and others, carrying out Hù's long-held wish,
requested to bury him near his ancestors' tombs.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but granted an *qǐng* of burial land ten *lǐ* outside the city, near the imperial mausoleum,
and his posthumous name was Chéng.
When Hù's funeral procession began,
the Emperor personally saw him off from the south gate of the Grand Marshal's Residence.
Hù's nephew, Qíwáng Yōu, memorialized the Emperor about Hù's wife's wish not to be buried with the title of marquis.
The Emperor then decreed:
"Hù firmly declined titles for many years,
and his will could not be swayed.
Though his body is gone, his humility remains,
and his legacy of integrity is even stronger.
This is why Yíshū was praised as virtuous,
and Jìzǐ preserved his integrity.
Now, We permit the restoration of his original enfeoffment
to make manifest his lofty excellence."
Initially,
Emperor Wén 帝崩,
Hù 祜 said to Fù Xuán 傅玄:
"The three-year mourning period,
though noble, is observed to its full extent,
from the Son of Heaven downwards;
yet Emperor Wén of Hàn 漢文 abolished it,
destroying ritual and harming righteousness.
I often sigh over this.
Now, the present sovereign is naturally of utmost filial piety,
possessing the nature of Zēng Zǐ 曾子 and Mǐn Zǐ 閔子.
Though he was deprived of the full mourning attire,
he actually performed the mourning rites.
If the mourning rites are actually performed,
what is the purpose of abolishing the mourning attire?
If we could use this opportunity to reform the shallowness of Hàn 漢 and Wèi 魏,
and revive the laws of the ancient kings,
to strengthen customs
and establish beauty for a hundred generations,
would that not be excellent?"
Xuán 玄 said:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn 漢文, seeing the shallowness of later generations,
was unable to observe the mourning rites for a ruler,
and therefore abolished them.
It has been abolished for several hundred years;
to restore it suddenly
would be difficult to implement."
Hù 祜 said:
"If we cannot make everyone in the empire conform to the rites,
at least let the sovereign observe the full mourning.
Would that not be better?"
Xuán 玄 said:
"If the sovereign does not abolish it, but the empire does,
this would mean there are only fathers and sons,
but no longer lords and ministers.
The Way of the Three Bonds would be diminished."
Hù 祜 then stopped.
The essays written by Hù 祜 and his commentary on the Lǎozi 老子 were both circulated in the world.
The common people of Xiāngyáng 襄陽 built a stele and a temple on Xiànshān 峴山, where Hù 祜 used to wander and rest,
and offered sacrifices there seasonally.
No one who gazed at his stele failed to shed tears,
so Dù Yù 杜預 named it the Duòlèi Bēi 墮淚碑 (Tears-Falling Stele).
The people of Jīngzhōu 荊州 avoided Hù's 祜 personal name;
all houses were referred to by 'door',
and Hùcáo 戶曹 (Household Registry) was changed to Cícáo 辭曹 (Registry of Resignations).
Hù 祜 had established his yámen 牙門 for several years,
but was modest and did not recruit officials.
He had just begun to make appointments
when he died,
and so they could not be officially registered.
Thus, his former staff, Liú Kuài 劉儈, Zhào Yín 趙寅, Liú Mí 劉彌, Sūn Bó 孫勃, and others, submitted a memorial to Yù 預, saying:
"Formerly, through mistaken selection,
we were unworthy to be part of the official staff,
each of us having the fortune to assist the former General-in-Chief of the Southern Expedition, Hù 祜, in various matters.
Hù 祜 possessed profound and humble virtue,
and his conduct and aspirations were pure and lofty.
His virtue was high, but his person was humble;
his position was excellent, but his conduct was reverent.
He previously received an illustrious appointment
to pacify the southern lands,
possessing the dignity of the Three Dukes
and further granted the title of General-in-Chief.
Though he held the position,
he did not fully implement its prerogatives.
Even now, the people within the seas thirst and wait,
and numerous elites look up to him.
Those who entered his gate
— the greedy became honest,
the timid became resolute;
even the conduct of Bó Yí 伯夷 and Liǔ Xiàhuì 柳下惠
could not surpass it.
Since taking charge of this region,
his governance and reforms have spread across the Jiāng 江 and Hàn 漢 rivers.
His subtle plans and far-reaching strategies
expanded the state and opened new territories.
All his plans and designs
had a fixed measure.
His ambition lay with the public good,
and he worked diligently until death.
He had just appointed four clerks,
but died before they could arrive.
To recommend the worthy and repay the state is the far-reaching responsibility of the Three Dukes and Ministers;
to seek out and promote the humble and overlooked
is also the long-cherished desire of the Three Dukes and Ministers.
To be interrupted midway
is also their private regret.
He practiced humility for many years,
but his late endeavors were not fulfilled.
This is why both near and far lament him.
Formerly, where Shào Bó 召伯 rested,
love flowed to the sweet pear tree;
where Xuān Zǐ 宣子 wandered,
trees were planted and cultivated.
If one thinks of the person,
one still extends it to their trees;
how much more so for the scholars he recruited while alive,
who should simply be abandoned according to routine?
We beg that you may submit this
so that we may be appointed as clerks,
as they were already designated."
Yù 預 memorialized, saying:
"Although Hù 祜 established his yámen 牙門, he did not fill all the staff positions.
His extreme humility
should be made known.
Furthermore, he recruited scholars while ill,
but died before they arrived.
His family had no direct heir,
and his office had no designated officials.
The people of this region
harbor hidden sorrow.
Indeed, to show fidelity to the end and cherish the distant past
is to return to the essence of human virtue.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn 漢高祖 did not hesitate to grant a fief of four thousand households
to comfort the sons of Zhào 趙.
I request this be discussed."
The emperor's edict did not permit it.
Two years after Hù's 祜 death, Wú 吳 was pacified.
The officials offered congratulations to the emperor,
who held his cup and wept, saying:
"This is the achievement of Grand Tutor Yáng 羊!"
Therefore, with the achievement of conquest and pacification,
an imperial edict was sent to Hù's 祜 temple,
and, following the precedent of Xiāo Hé 蕭何,
his wife was enfeoffed.
The edict stated:
"The Emperor orders the Usher Dù Hóng 杜宏 to announce to the late Attendant Counselor and Grand Tutor, the Marquis of Jùpíng 鉅平, Hù 祜: Formerly, Wú 吳 was disrespectful,
relying on its dangerous terrain and claiming imperial titles.
Our borders were not pacified,
and this lasted for many years.
Hù 祜 was entrusted with the mission in the southern lands,
thinking of pacifying its troubles,
spreading the royal transforming influence externally,
and planning strategies within the temple courts.
He established virtue and extended sincerity,
and the Jiāng 江 and Hàn 漢 rivers returned their loyalty.
His endeavors had established foundations,
and his plans were complete strategies.
Heaven, however, was unkind,
and his aspirations were not fulfilled.
I, therefore, feel deep sorrow and regret in my heart.
Thus, I commanded all the generals
to bring forth Heaven's punishment,
and the army, in less than a season,
conquered and destroyed Wú 吳 in one expedition.
The plans of yesteryear
were like a perfectly matched tally.
Indeed, rewards should not fail to recognize merit,
for the state has established statutes.
It is proper to increase the territory granted
to exalt his previous appointment,
but this would again go against the Marquis's noble modesty.
Therefore, We now enfeoff his wife, Lady Xiàhóu 夏侯, as Wànsuì Xiāngjūn 萬歲鄉君 (Lady of Wànsuì Township),
with an estate of five thousand households,
and further bestow ten thousand bolts of silk
and ten thousand dan 斛 of grain."
When Hù 祜 was five years old,
he told his wet nurse to retrieve a golden ring he played with.
The wet nurse said:
"You never had such a thing before."
Hù 祜 immediately went to a mulberry tree in the eastern wall of his neighbor, the Lǐ 李 family, and found it.
The owner was astonished and said:
"This is something my deceased child lost.
How could you take it away?"
The wet nurse explained everything,
and the Lǐ 李 family was saddened.
People at the time found this unusual,
and said that the Lǐ 李 family's child was Hù's 祜 previous incarnation.
There was also a skilled geomancer of tombs who said
that Hù's 祜 ancestral tomb possessed the aura of an emperor.
If it were dug up, he would have no heirs.
Hù 祜 then dug it up.
The geomancer saw it and said,
"There will still be a Duke who breaks an arm."
And Hù 祜 indeed fell from his horse and broke an arm,
and reached the position of a Duke but had no son.
The emperor designated Hù's 祜 elder brother's son, Jì 暨, as his heir.
Jì 暨, however, could not become another's heir because his own father had died.
The emperor then ordered Jì's 暨 younger brother, Yī 伊, to be Hù's 祜 heir,
but he also did not obey the edict.
The emperor was angered,
and arrested and dismissed them both.
In the second year of Tàikāng 太康 (281 CE),
Yī's 伊 younger brother, Piān 篇, was made Marquis of Jùpíng 鉅平,
to serve as Hù's 祜 heir.
Piān 篇 held various official positions with integrity and caution.
He had a private ox that gave birth to a calf in the official residence,
and when he was transferred, he left it behind.
He rose to the position of Attendant Censor,
and died young.
During the Tài Yuán reign of Emperor Xiào Wǔ,
Fēng Hù's elder brother Xuán Sūn's son, Fǎ Xìng, was enfeoffed as Jù Píng Hóu,
with an estate of five thousand households.
Due to Huán Xuán's faction being purged,
the state was abolished.
Shàng Shū Cí Bù Láng Xún Bó Zǐ submitted a memorial arguing for it, saying:
"I have heard that when Gào Yáo's line died out,
Zāng Wén considered it a deep sorrow;
when Bó Shì's city was taken away,
Guǎn Zhòng called it benevolent.
High merit can be imperishable for a hundred generations,
while excessive rewards cannot last even a morning.
Thus, Grand Tutor, Jù Píng Hóu Yáng Hù, with his luminous virtue and broad wisdom,
was a pillar of the state.
His achievements were instrumental in assisting the ruler,
and his功gōng was completed in pacifying Wú.
Yet his descendants are lacking,
and there is no one to offer ancestral sacrifices.
The Hàn dynasty, recognizing Xiāo Hé's paramount功gōng,
allowed his line to be continued even after it died out.
I believe the enfeoffment of Jù Píng should be treated similarly to the state of Zàn.
The former Grand Commandant, Guǎng Líng Gōng Zhǔn, was a partisan of the rebel Lún,
bringing disaster upon Huái Nán,
and profited from this rebellion,
illicitly enjoying a great state.
At that time, the Western court's government and penal system were out of order,
and the restoration did not revoke it.
Now that the royal way is being renewed,
how can we not make a clear distinction between right and wrong?
I propose that the state of Guǎng Líng should be abolished.
The former Grand Guardian, Wèi Guàn's original title was Zī Yáng Xiàn Gōng.
After he was unjustly killed,
he was advanced to an actual fief,
first posthumously granted Lán Líng,
and then transferred to Jiāng Xià.
Many famous officials of the Central court
met untimely ends,
but Guàn's merits and virtues were no different,
yet he alone received a special reward.
I propose that his commandery enfeoffment be rescinded,
and his estate of Zī Yáng be restored.
Then, there will be order in granting and revoking,
and good and evil will be distinguished."
This was ultimately put aside and not acted upon.
Hù's former mother
was a daughter of Kǒng Róng.
She gave birth to his elder brother Fā,
who reached the office of Dū Dū Huái Běi Hù Jūn.
Initially,
Fā and Hù's full elder brother Chéng both fell ill.
Hù's mother, judging that she could not save both,
concentrated her efforts on nursing Fā,
so he recovered,
while Chéng eventually died.
Fā's eldest son was Lún,
Minister of Gāo Yáng.
Lún's younger brother was Jì,
Administrator of Yáng Píng.
Jì's younger brother was Yī,
who first served as a clerk for Chē Qí Jiāng Jūn Jiǎ Chōng,
and later held positions such as Píng Nán Jiāng Jūn and Dū Dū Jiāng Běi Zhū Jūn Shì.
He was garrisoned at Wǎn,
and was killed by Zhāng Chāng.
He was posthumously granted Zhèn Nán Jiāng Jūn.
Hù's paternal uncle was Mì,
who reached the office of Jīng Zhào Tài Shǒu.
His son was Zhǐ,
Administrator of Wèi Jùn.
Mì's grandson was Liàng,
courtesy name Cháng Xuán,
who possessed talent
and was skilled in stratagem.
Those who interacted with him
always believed he was fully sincere,
everyone thought they had gained his trust,
but this was far from the truth.
He first served as a staff officer for Grand Tutor Yáng Jùn.
At that time, there were many thefts in Jīng Zhào.
Jùn wished to make the laws harsher,
punishing theft of a hundred coins with capital punishment,
and called a meeting of his officials to discuss it.
Liàng said:
"Formerly, the mother of Chǔ Jiāng Yǐ lost cloth,
and believed the theft was due to the Prime Minister.
If you, sir, have no desires,
theft will naturally cease.
Why make the laws harsher?"
Jùn was ashamed and stopped.
He was successively promoted to Dà Hóng Lú.
At that time, Emperor Huì was in Cháng Ān.
Liàng, conspiring with those east of the passes,
felt insecure and
fled to Bìng Zhōu.
He was killed by Liú Yuán Hǎi.
Liàng's younger brother Táo
was the Inspector of Xú Zhōu.
Dù Yù (son of Xī)
Dù Yù, courtesy name Yuán Kǎi,
was a native of Jīng Zhào Dù Líng.
His grandfather, Jī,
was Wèi Shàng Shū Pú Yè.
His father, Shù,
was Inspector of Yōu Zhōu.
Yù was broadly learned and widely informed,
understanding the principles of rise and fall.
He often said:
"Virtue cannot be aspired to; establishing achievements and establishing words can be hoped for."
Initially,
his father and Emperor Xuān were not on good terms,
and he died in Yōu Zhōu,
hence Yù was not appointed to office for a long time.
When Emperor Wén succeeded to the throne,
Yù married the Emperor's younger sister, Gāo Lù Gōng Zhǔ,
and was appointed Shàng Shū Láng,
inheriting his grandfather's title of Fēng Lè Tíng Hóu.
After four years in office,
he was transferred to serve in military affairs in the Prime Minister's residence.
When Zhōng Huì attacked Shǔ,
Yù was made Zhèn Xī Cháng Shǐ.
When Huì rebelled,
his subordinates were all killed,
but Yù alone escaped through his wit.
His enfeoffment was increased by eleven hundred and fifty households.
He, along with Chē Qí Jiāng Jūn Jiǎ Chōng and others, codified the laws and regulations.
Once completed,
Yù provided annotations for them,
and then memorialized, saying:
"Laws
are merely precedents for the application of rules,
not books that exhaust principles and human nature.
Therefore, the text is concise and the precedents are straightforward,
easy to understand and simple to prohibit.
Straightforward precedents are easy to see,
simple prohibitions are difficult to violate.
When it is easy to see, people know what to avoid;
when it is difficult to violate, it approaches a state where punishments are set aside.
The essence of punishment lies in simplicity and straightforwardness,
thus the precise distinctions must be clear.
Those who clarify precise distinctions
must tolerate minor deviations.
Ancient penal codes
were inscribed on bells and tripods,
cast in metal and stone,
to prevent heterodox ideas
and avoid excessive cleverness.
The present annotations encompass the intent of the law,
and standardize them with precise distinctions.
This allows users to grasp the principles and precedents to judge what to take and what to discard,
to uphold the rectitude of the rules,
and to eliminate the complexities of over-analysis."
An imperial edict distributed this throughout the realm.
During the Tàishǐ reign,
he served as the Protector of Hénán-Yǐn.
Yù believed that as the imperial capital was the beginning of kingly transformation,
starting from near and extending to far,
all his policies and discussions
should focus on upholding the grand principles.
He received an imperial edict to formulate an evaluation system for promotion and demotion.
Its summary states:
“Your servant has heard that in the governance of high antiquity,
it followed nature,
emptying oneself and entrusting sincerity,
and the way of trust and obedience responded;
spirits were moved and hearts communicated,
and the principles of the world were attained.
As the primordial simplicity gradually dispersed,
beauty was highlighted and evil exposed,
offices were established and functions divided,
to bestow ranks and emoluments,
and the Six Canons were extensively promulgated
to conduct detailed investigations.
Yet, it still relied on the assistance of sagacious and discerning individuals,
and established loyal and upright officials,
so that reputation could not surpass merit to be uniquely beautiful,
and merit could not be obscured behind reputation.
All were consulted widely,
and advice was presented in words.
However, in later generations,
they could not consider distant matters but sought out minute details;
they doubted their hearts but trusted their ears and eyes;
they doubted their ears and eyes but trusted written records.
The more numerous the written records,
the more deceitful the official conduct became;
the more laws and decrees multiplied,
the more elaborate the deceptions.
In the past, the Cìshǐ of Hàn
also reported their affairs at the end of the year;
no numerical evaluations were imposed,
yet the clear and the corrupt were roughly identified.
The evaluation system of the Wèi dynasty
was the legacy of Jīng Fáng,
and its texts could be called extremely detailed.
However, it accumulated trivialities that violated its essence,
hence it could not be universally applied throughout successive generations.
How could it compare to reviving the old system of Táng Yáo,
abandoning complexity for simplicity,
thus making it simple and easy to follow?
To fully express the principles of things,
and to enlighten them divinely,
depends on the individual.
To remove the individual and rely on law
is to damage principle.
For the current assessment of excellence and inferiority,
nothing is better than entrusting it to high officials,
each evaluating those under their jurisdiction.
After one year in office,
each year one excellent person is designated as 'superior grade',
and one inferior person as 'inferior grade',
reported by name during the annual assembly.
After six such years,
the responsible officials compile and analyze the cases.
Those who have been designated 'superior grade' for six years are promoted exceptionally;
those who have been designated 'inferior grade' for six years are impeached and dismissed;
those with more 'superior' than 'inferior' designations are promoted;
and those with more 'inferior' than 'superior' designations are demoted.
Currently, the categories for evaluation
are not uniform in what they address;
there are indeed difficulties and ease.
If one takes difficulty to achieve excellence,
and ease to be negative,
the responsible officials should certainly weigh the importance,
and slightly adjust the grades,
without needing to fully enforce every intricate law.
The imperial edict of the Jǐchǒu year stated that as evaluations were difficult to complete,
the system of general recommendations was permitted.
The principle of recommendations
is also derived from public opinion.
A single recommendation after six years,
with no gradual promotion or demotion,
is also not the intent of the ancient 'three-year review'.
Now, with an annual evaluation,
accumulated excellence leads to promotion,
and accumulated inferiority leads to demotion.
If gentlemen interact with each other in good faith,
it is impossible for an official to dismiss six competent individuals and promote six incompetent ones over six years.
The supervising censors will also impeach such behavior.
If superiors and subordinates openly tolerate each other's faults,
this would lead to a great decline in public morality,
and there would be no value in promotion or demotion.”
The Prefect of Sīlì, Shí Jiàn, impeached Yù due to a long-standing grudge,
and he was dismissed from office.
At that time, barbarian invaders were plundering Lǒngyòu.
Yù was appointed Anxī Jūnsī,
and given 300 soldiers and 100 cavalry.
Upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
he was further appointed Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
also serving as Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi and Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, with the power of Jíajié.
At that time, the barbarian forces were strong and flourishing.
Shí Jiàn, then Anxī Jiāngjūn,
ordered Yù to lead troops to attack them.
Yù believed that the barbarians, riding on their victory, had fat horses,
while the government troops were depleted.
He argued that it would be advisable to combine forces for a major expedition
and wait until spring to launch an attack,
presenting 'five impossibilities' and 'four unnecessary actions'.
Jiàn was furious,
and again impeached Yù for unauthorized decoration of city gates and official residences,
and for delaying military provisions.
He dispatched an imperial censor to arrest him in a cage cart and bring him to the Grand Judge.
As Yù was related to the imperial family through marriage,
he was among the 'Eight Deliberations',
and was allowed to redeem himself with his marquisate.
Later, the situation in Lǒngyòu turned out exactly as Yù had predicted.
At this time, the imperial court all considered Yù to be skilled in strategy.
Coincidentally, Liú Měng, a Xiongnú chieftain, raised an army in rebellion,
extending from Bìngzhōu westward to Hédōng and Píngyáng.
An edict ordered Yù, as a scattered marquis, to deliberate on plans in the imperial chambers.
Soon after, he was appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Yù then proposed establishing land for imperial plowing,
setting up frontier defenses,
and discussing the crucial matters of the military and the state.
He also created a new device for human-powered irrigation,
established Ever-Normal Granaries,
stabilized grain prices,
regulated salt transportation,
and formulated taxes and levies,
more than fifty articles which benefited the state internally and relieved the frontiers externally.
All were adopted.
Shí Jiàn returned from his military campaign,
and his claims of merit were found to be untrue,
which Yù exposed.
Thus, their enmity grew,
and their public arguments became boisterous.
Both were dismissed from office,
with Yù retaining his marquisate and concurrent original post.
Several years later,
he was again appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū.
The coffin of Empress Yuán was about to be moved to Jùnyánglíng.
According to old regulations,
after the burial,
the Emperor and his officials immediately resumed auspicious attire.
The Shàngshū reported
that the Crown Prince should also be allowed to shed his mourning clothes.
Yù argued,
“The Crown Prince should revert to the ancient system,
observing the full period of silent mourning.”
This was followed.
Yù believed that the current calendar was inaccurate
and did not correspond to celestial measurements.
He presented the Èryuán Qiándù Lì,
which was then adopted throughout the realm.
Yù also noted that the Mèngjīn ferry was perilous
and prone to capsizing.
He requested the construction of a river bridge at Fùpíngjīn.
Debaters believed that as it was the capital of the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
and even sages and worthies throughout history had not built one,
it must be impossible to erect.
Yù said:
“ 'Building boats to make a bridge'
refers to a river bridge.”
When the bridge was completed,
the Emperor, accompanied by all his officials, came to observe it.
He raised a cup and addressed Yù, saying:
“Without you,
this bridge would not have been built.”
Yù replied:
“Without Your Majesty's wisdom,
your servant would also not have been able to apply his humble skill.”
The tilting vessel of the Zhōu temple
was still in the imperial seat until the Eastern Hàn dynasty.
During the chaos at the end of Hàn,
it ceased to exist,
and its form was lost.
Yù ingeniously recreated it
and presented it to the Emperor,
who greatly praised and admired it.
In the autumn of the fourth year of Xiánníng,
there were heavy incessant rains,
and locusts arose.
Yù submitted a memorial extensively detailing important agricultural matters,
which are recorded in the Shíhuò Zhì.
Yù served for seven years in the inner court,
making countless improvements and adjustments to state affairs.
The court and populace praised him,
calling him
“Dù Wǔkù” (Dù the Arsenal),
meaning that he possessed knowledge of everything.
At that time, the Emperor secretly harbored a plan to conquer Wú,
but the court discussions were mostly opposed.
Only Dù Yù, Yáng Hù, and Zhāng Huá were in agreement with the Emperor's intention.
When Yáng Hù fell ill,
he recommended Dù Yù to succeed him.
Consequently, Dù Yù was granted a fictitious command (jiǎ jié) as Pacifying General of the East (píngdōng jiāngjūn) with his original official post,
and concurrently served as Military Superintendent of the Southern Expedition (zhēngnán jūnsī).
When Yáng Hù died,
Dù Yù was appointed General Who Guards the South (zhènnán dàjiāngjūn) and Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Jīngzhōu,
and was granted a vanguard chariot (zhuīfēng chē) and a second imperial horse (fùmǎ).
Once Dù Yù arrived at his post,
he repaired the armor and weapons,
displayed his military might,
and then selected elite troops
to attack Zhāng Zhèng, the Wú governor of Xīlíng.
He utterly defeated him,
and for this achievement, his enfeoffment was increased by 365 households.
Zhāng Zhèng
was a renowned general of Wú.
He held a strategic stronghold,
was ashamed of his defeat due to lack of preparedness,
and did not report the true extent of his losses to Sūn Hào.
Dù Yù wished to sow discord among Wú's border generals,
so he reported to Sūn Hào, requesting the return of the captured troops.
Sūn Hào indeed recalled Zhāng Zhèng
and sent Liú Xiàn, the Supervisor of Wǔchāng, to replace him.
Thus, when the grand army approached,
it caused the transfer of their commanders,
thereby creating a situation conducive to their collapse.
After Dù Yù had settled all arrangements,
he petitioned to set a date for the campaign against Wú.
The Emperor replied that he intended to launch the major offensive next year.
Dù Yù submitted a memorial outlining his best plan, saying:
“Since the intercalary month,
the enemy has only been issuing strict orders;
no troops have been sent from below to above.
Judging by the circumstances and logic,
the enemy's desperate plan
cannot secure both fronts.
They will certainly first protect the upper reaches
and diligently defend the area east of Xiàkǒu
to prolong their existence.
There is no reason for them to send many troops westward
and leave their capital empty.
Yet Your Majesty, by listening to excessive caution,
is about to abandon a great plan
and allow the enemy to cause future trouble.
This is truly a long-term strategy for the state;
if it fails after being launched,
it might as well not be launched.
Matters are to be regulated by circumstances,
and efforts should be made to ensure complete security.
If it succeeds,
it will lay the foundation for great peace.
If it fails,
it will only mean a loss of a few days or months.
Why hesitate and not give it a try?
If we have to wait until the year after next,
the timing and human affairs might not remain constant,
and I fear it will become even more difficult.
Your Majesty’s long-standing plan
is to order your servants to advance according to their respective sectors.
The prohibitions imposed
will be uniformly applied East and West.
This is a plan for complete safety;
there is no concern of failure.
My heart truly understands,
and I dare not invite future trouble by presenting ambiguous views.
I only ask Your Majesty to examine this.”
Within ten days, Dù Yù submitted another memorial, saying:
“Yáng Hù differed greatly from many court officials;
he did not broadly discuss the plan beforehand but secretly implemented it with Your Majesty,
which is why there are more dissenting opinions.
In all matters, one should compare the advantages and disadvantages.
Now, this endeavor has an eighty to ninety percent chance of success;
the one or two percent chance is merely that it yields no results.
The form of failure they speak of is also impossible to achieve.
It is simply that the plan did not originate from them,
the merit will not be theirs,
and each is ashamed of their previous words,
hence they adhere to their positions.
Lately, in the court, regardless of the matter’s importance,
dissenting opinions arise sharply.
Although people’s minds differ,
it is also because they rely on imperial favor and do not consider future difficulties,
thus they lightly agree or disagree.
In ancient times, Emperor Xuān of Hàn, after discussing and seeing the effectiveness of Zhào Chōngguó’s submitted plan,
reprimanded the dissenting officials,
who all bowed their heads and apologized
to suppress heterodox views.
Since autumn,
the intention to attack the enemy has been quite evident.
If we stop now,
Sūn Hào will be frightened and devise plans.
He might move his capital to Wǔchāng,
further reinforce the cities south of the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
relocate their inhabitants,
making the cities impregnable and
the countryside barren of plunder.
If he accumulates large ships at Xiàkǒu,
then next year’s plan might achieve nothing.”
At that time, the Emperor was playing go with Zhōngshū Lìng Zhāng Huá,
and Dù Yù’s memorial happened to arrive.
Zhāng Huá pushed the go board aside, clasped his hands, and said:
“Your Majesty is sagacious and divinely martial,
the court and country are peaceful and serene,
the state is rich, the army strong,
and orders are unified.
The ruler of Wú is licentious and tyrannical,
executing the virtuous and capable.
If we attack him now,
we can pacify him without effort.”
The Emperor then agreed.
In the first month of the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE), Dù Yù
deployed troops at Jiānglíng.
He dispatched his staff officers Fán Xiǎn, Yǐn Lín, Dèng Guī, and the Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Zhōu Qí, and others, to lead their forces upriver along the Jiāng,
giving them strategic instructions.
Within ten days,
they successively captured cities and towns,
all according to Dù Yù’s plan.
He also sent Yámén Guǎn Dìng, Zhōu Zhǐ, Wǔ Cháo, and others to lead 800 elite soldiers,
paddle boats across the river by night
to raid Yuèxiāng.
They displayed many banners and flags,
set fires on Bāshān,
emerged from strategic locations,
to demoralize the enemy.
Wú Grand Supervisor Sūn Xīn was terrified,
and wrote to Wǔ Yán, saying:
“The northern armies
have actually flown across the river!”
More than ten thousand Wú men and women surrendered.
Zhǐ, Cháo, and others lay in ambush outside Yuèxiāng city.
Sūn Xīn sent troops to resist Wáng Jùn,
suffering a great defeat and retreating.
Zhǐ and his men launched their ambush,
following Sūn Xīn’s army inside.
Sūn Xīn did not notice
until they reached his tent,
capturing him and returning.
Thus, the army sang a ballad:
“One strategic move is worth ten thousand battles.”
Thereupon, they pressed on towards Jiānglíng.
Wú Supervising General Wǔ Yán feigned surrender but arrayed his troops on the battlements.
Dù Yù attacked and captured the city.
After the upper reaches were pacified,
then from the south of Yuán and Xiāng
all the way to Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu,
all the Wú provinces and commanderies surrendered at the mere sight of their power,
offering up their seals of office.
Dù Yù, wielding his staff of authority, proclaimed imperial edicts and pacified them.
In total, he executed or captured fourteen Wú Grand Supervisors and Army Supervisors,
and over 120 Yámén officers and Grand Administrators.
Also, leveraging military might,
he resettled the families of officers and soldiers who were stationed there to garrison the north of the Jiāng,
and in the former territories of Nánjùn, he appointed officials.
The Jīng region became orderly,
and the Wú people flocked to him as if returning home.
Wáng Jùn had earlier reported capturing Sūn Xīn’s head,
but Dù Yù later sent Sūn Xīn alive,
which caused great amusement in Luòyáng.
At that time, during a council of the various armies,
some said:
“An enemy of a hundred years
cannot be completely defeated yet.
It is now approaching summer,
the floods are about to descend,
and epidemics will soon arise.
We should wait until next winter
to launch another major offensive.”
Dù Yù said:
“In the past, Yuè Yì relied on one battle at Jìxī to unify strong Qí.
Now our military might is already shaking.
It is like splitting bamboo:
after a few sections,
it will all split along the blade,
with no further effort needed.”
Thereupon, he directed the various commanders
to proceed directly to Mòlíng.
The cities and towns they passed
all surrendered without resistance.
The dissenting officials then wrote to him to apologize.
After Sūn Hào was pacified,
Dù Yù returned triumphantly with his troops.
For his achievements, he was promoted to Marquis of Dāngyáng County,
his enfeoffment, including previous grants, totaled 9,600 households.
His son, Dù Dān, was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu
with 1,000 households,
and he was bestowed 8,000 rolls of silk.
Initially,
when attacking Jiānglíng,
the Wú people knew Dù Yù suffered from a goiter,
and fearing his wisdom and strategy,
they tied gourds to dogs' necks to show him.
Whenever they saw a large tree resembling a goiter,
they would chop it down to make it white,
and inscribed it with
“Dù Yù’s neck.”
When the city was pacified,
all those involved were captured and executed.

Later, he was summoned to be the Grand Administrator of Sīlì,

The Emperor was deeply grieved and saddened,

The design and regulations will follow the example of the Zhèng

His descendants all followed this.
His son, Xī, succeeded him.
Xī, courtesy name Shìgǔ,
was famous in his youth.
He began his career as an Administrator of Literature for Chángshā Wáng Yì,
and was successively promoted to Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén).
He was straightforward, loyal, and ardent by nature,
and repeatedly admonished Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ.
His words were earnest,
which displeased the Crown Prince.
Later, a needle was placed in the seat Xī usually sat on,
which pricked him and drew blood.
Another day,
the Crown Prince asked Xī,
“What did you get stuck on just now?”
Xī replied,
“I was drunk and didn’t notice.”
The Crown Prince pressed him, saying,
“You like to criticize others;
why do you make mistakes yourself?”
Later, he was transferred to Chief Clerk to the General of the Household (Wèijiāngjūn Zhǎngshǐ).
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
Xī was appointed Palace Secretary (Zhìshū Yùshǐ).
Sūn Xiù sought to befriend Xī,
but Xī rejected him.
Although Xiù resented him,
he was deterred by Xī’s high reputation
and dared not harm him.
When Huì Dì regained power,
Xī was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Civil Office (Lìbù Láng) and Governor of Chéngyáng (Chéngyáng Tàishǒu).
He did not take up the latter post,
but was instead promoted to Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng).
He died at the age of forty-eight
and was posthumously granted Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
His son, Yì, inherited his title,
and is mentioned in the "Biographies of Imperial Relatives" (Wàiqī Zhuàn).
The Historian says: In the era of Tàishǐ,
heaven and earth presented auspicious signs.
Gōng Yáng initiated the strategy to pacify Wú,
thereby revealing the mind of heaven and earth.
In the past, Qí had Qiánfū,
and Yān had the Ghost of Běimén;
Zhào had Lǐ Mù,
and Qín Wáng abandoned his ambition to annex the East.
Mulberry branches did not contend;
the melon’s moisture brought only empty shame.
He established great trust in the southern territories,
subduing the Wú people at the Hán River banks.
The river routes were smooth as a whetstone,
and people flocked together.
Yet, after achieving success, he did not dwell on it,
but lived in a simple cloth cap in a poor lane,
distant and dignified.
Dù Yù was not born with innate knowledge,
but acquired it through practice.
He wielded long strategies for conquest,
and combined scholarly demeanor with continuous warfare.
Confucius’s school spoke of four virtues,
and he attained three of them;
the Spring and Autumn Annals has five virtues,
and he uniquely mastered one.
Was he not outstanding!
As for the three-year mourning period,
it is said to apply to all, regardless of status.
That minor omissions were seized upon in those in high positions is regrettable;
that the Crown Prince was exempted from mourning after burial,
how cruel that was.
To conform out of expediency,
not seeking what is right,
treating the enlightened heir of the current age
as a common son of a feudal lord—
Tángōng was skilled in changing rituals,
and Dù Yù was likewise.
A eulogy says: The western precipice of Hán Chí,
the leftward winding of Wú Jiāng.
Yáng Gōng’s grace and trust,

Correction Notes
Biographies, Volume Five: Chén Qiān (Zǐyú)
Chén Qiān
was from Dōngyáng, Lín Huái.
His father, Jiǎo,
was the Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) of Wèi.
Jiǎo was originally of the Liú clan of Guǎnglíng,
but was adopted by his maternal grandfather, of the Chén clan,
and thus changed his surname.
Qiān was profound and resourceful.
Initially,
when Jiǎo was Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Liú Yè, favored by Wèi Míng Dì,
slandered Jiǎo for monopolizing power.
Jiǎo was worried and asked Qiān.
Qiān said,
“The emperor is wise and sagacious.
Even if a great minister like you
does not align with his wishes,
at most you will just not be a duke.”
Later, the emperor’s anger indeed dissipated.
When Qiān was still young,
he was insulted by Xiàhóu Xuán,
but his demeanor remained calm,
which impressed Xuán.
He began his career as a Secretariat Gentleman (Shàngshū Láng),
and was promoted to Governor of Zhōngshān and Ānpíng,
both posts where he achieved notable successes.
He was summoned to be Chief Commandant to the Chancellor (Xiàngguó Sīmǎ), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ), and Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
then promoted to Minister of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānguó Tíng.
When the Shǔ bandits raided Lǒngyòu,
he was appointed Acting General Who Conquers Shǔ (Xíng Zhēngshǔ Jiāngjūn) with a Staff of Authority (Chíjié), while still serving as Minister of State Affairs.
He defeated the bandits and returned.
During Zhūgé Dàn’s rebellion,
he was again appointed Acting General Who Pacifies the East (Xíng Āndōng Jiāngjūn) as Minister of State Affairs.
After Shòuchūn was pacified,
he was appointed Envoy with Staff of Authority, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs North of the Huái River (Dūdū Huáiběi Zhūjūnshì), and General Who Pacifies the East,
and advanced to the title of Marquis of Guǎnglíng.
He was transferred to Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Yùzhōu, and Inspector of Yùzhōu,
retaining his Staff of Authority and generalship.
He was again transferred to Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs South of the Jiāng (Dūdū Jiāngnán Zhūjūnshì),
then moved to Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Jīngzhōu (Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhūjūnshì) and General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Tán.
When Wǔ Dì received the abdication,
for his merits in assisting the new dynasty,
he was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Duke of Gāopíng Commandery,
then promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
He was sent out as Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Yángzhōu (Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhūjūnshì),
with his other titles remaining as before,
and granted the privilege of the Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè).
He attacked and captured the city of Zhǐlǐ in Wú,
and defeated the garrisons at Túzhōng.
Qiān’s elder brother’s son, Kuī, was granted the title Marquis within the Passes (Guānzhōng Hóu).
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
then transferred to Grand Minister of War (Dàsīmǎ).
Qiān used an opportunity during an imperial audience to tell the Emperor,
“Hú Liè and Qiān Hóng are both brave but without strategy,
and too self-reliant.
They are not suitable for pacifying the borders
and will become a national disgrace.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.”
At that time, Hóng was Inspector of Yángzhōu
and did not obey Qiān’s commands.
The Emperor thought they were simply in conflict,
so he summoned Hóng,
and upon his arrival,
soon reappointed him as Inspector of Liángzhōu.
Qiān secretly sighed,
believing they would surely fail.
Later, both men indeed lost the trust of the Qiāng and Róng tribes,
and were killed by invaders.
Campaigns continued for years,
and stability was only barely achieved,
whereupon the Emperor regretted his decision.
Qiān was magnanimous in his youth,
concealing flaws and enduring humiliation,
and achieved success wherever he served.
He, along with Jiǎ Chōng, Shí Bāo, Péi Xiù, and others, were considered confidants,
but Qiān’s wisdom and foresight surpassed theirs,
and Chōng and the others also admitted their inferiority.
He served in various official positions,
and was cherished by both gentry and commoners.
Having reached the highest ministerial office,
and his age exceeding that for retirement,
he wished to withdraw.
In the third year of Xiánníng,
he sought an audience at court,
and thereupon requested to retire and return his bones.
He was granted court robes and a crown,
and an imperial edict stated:
"Qiān has rendered great service and possesses old virtues.
He has governed the eastern realm
and greatly achieved far-reaching merits
by unifying Wúhuì.
However, his ailments have not been removed,
and he has repeatedly expressed his earnest desire
to be relieved from the burden of current affairs.
Now, he is permitted to remain in the capital city.
His former Grand Commandant's Residence is to be made the Grand Marshal's Residence.
Two Libationers are to be added,
and the subordinate Cavalry Commander, official riders, grand chariots,
and drum and fife bands shall all remain as before.
He shall have one hundred personal guards,
ten qǐng of kitchen fields,
fifty mǔ of kitchen gardens,
ten kitchen staff,
and all his implements and expenses shall remain supplied to him.
Furthermore, he shall be granted an imperial sedan chair,
and when entering and exiting the palace, a drum and fife band shall accompany him,
following the precedent of Xiāo Hé of the Hàn dynasty."
Qiān repeatedly cited illness to resign his post.
An imperial edict stated:
"Qiān embodies virtue and discusses the Way,
and is whom We consult.
We still rely on his counsel
to greatly promote the various achievements.
He should attend to his duties at this time.
A Regular Palace Attendant should be dispatched to convey Our intention."
Qiān immediately returned to his residence.
An edict was again sent, dispatching the Palace Attendant Dūn to persuade him to return to his office.
He then firmly requested permission to retire,
which was granted.
His position was equivalent to that of a Grand Tutor,
above the three highest ministers.
He was granted a stool and a staff,
and was not required to attend court.
He was given a comfortable carriage with four horses,
and returned to his residence as the Duke of Gāopíng.
The Emperor, considering his distinguished service and advanced age,
treated him with great honor.
Moreover, as Qiān was ill,
he was permitted to ride in a carriage into the palace hall.
Qiān was not known for blunt and forthright remonstrance,
yet he spoke haughtily to the Emperor.
However, upon seeing the Crown Prince, he showed increased respect,
which people at the time considered flattery.
His younger brother Zhì and his son Yú had a bitter dispute.
Zhì then spoke of the immoral conduct of Qiān's daughters,
and Qiān petitioned to have his brother banished,
which earned him criticism from the world.
In the second year of Yuánkāng, he passed away
at the age of eighty-one.
He was enshrouded in imperial robes,
posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor,
and given the posthumous name Wǔ.
At his burial,
the Emperor mourned at the Grand Marshal's Gate,
weeping as he gazed at the coffin.
The rites followed the precedent of Grand Marshal Shí Bāo.
His son Yú inherited the peerage.
Yú, courtesy name Xiǎnchū,
was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Magistrate of Luòyáng.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and successively served as Left General of the Imperial Army, Grand Minister of Agriculture, and Palace Attendant.
Due to his discord with his uncle,
he was dispatched out of the capital to be Administrator of Hénèi.
Though Yú lacked integrity,
he was effective in his duties.
He soon died.
His son Zhí, courtesy name Hóngxiān, inherited the title
and rose to the official position of Regular Palace Attendant.
He died,
and his son Cuì inherited.
During the Yǒngjiā era, he was murdered.
Emperor Xiàowǔ allowed Qiān's great-grandson to inherit the peerage.
He died,
and his younger brother Hào zhī inherited.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
the state (of Jìn) was abolished.
Péi Xiù (son Wěi; Xiù's cousin Kǎi; Kǎi's son Xiàn)
Péi Xiù, courtesy name Jìyàn,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
His grandfather Máo was Minister of the Imperial Secretariat during the Hàn dynasty.
His father Qián was Minister of the Imperial Secretariat during the Wèi dynasty.
Xiù was studious from a young age
and possessed a distinguished demeanor.
At the age of eight, he could compose essays.
His uncle Huī had a great reputation,
and many guests.
When Xiù was over ten years old,
those who visited Huī,
upon leaving, would stop by to see Xiù.
However, Xiù's mother was of low status,
and his stepmother, Lady Xuān, did not treat her with proper respect.
She once made Xiù's mother serve food to guests.
All who saw this rose in respect for Xiù.
Xiù's mother said:
"Being so humble and lowly,
it must be for the sake of my child."
Lady Xuān, realizing this,
thereafter ceased to do so.
At the time, people said of him:
"Among the rising leaders, there is Péi Xiù."
Wúqiū Jiǎn, General Who Crosses the Liáo, once recommended Xiù to Grand General Cáo Shuǎng,
saying:
"Born with extraordinary intelligence,
he naturally embodies the Way as he grew;
profoundly serene and upholding truth,
his nature delves into the depths of the Way;
widely learned and possessing a strong memory,
there is no text he does not encompass;
filial piety and fraternal love are evident in his local community,
and his high reputation is heard far and wide.
He is indeed fit to assist in wise counsel,
help harmonize the affairs of state,
aid and support the Grand Office,
and brightly illuminate its flourishing transformation.
He is not merely on par with Zǐ Qí or Gān Luó,
but also encompasses the virtues of Yán, Rǎn, Yóu, and Xià."
Shuǎng then appointed him as an aide.
He inherited his father's peerage as Marquis of Qīngyáng Pavilion,
and was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
When Shuǎng was executed,
he was dismissed as an old subordinate.
After a while,
he became Chief Justice,
and successively served as Marshal under Emperor Wén when he was General Who Pacifies the East and General-in-Chief.
In military and state affairs,
he was often trusted and heeded.
He was promoted to Regular Palace Attendant.
When the Emperor campaigned against Zhūgě Dàn,
Xiù, along with Minister Chén Tài and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Zhōng Huì, accompanied him as members of the traveling government,
participating in strategy.
After Dàn was pacified,
he was transferred to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
advanced in peerage to Marquis of Lǔyáng Township,
and his fief was increased by a thousand households.
When the Duke of Chángdào Township was enthroned,
for his participation in the discussions to establish the succession,
he was advanced in peerage to County Marquis,
his fief increased by seven hundred households,
and he was promoted to Minister-Counselor of the Imperial Secretariat.
In the early Xiánxī era of Wèi,
the official system was reformed.
At that time, Xún Yǐ set the rites and ceremonies,
Jiǎ Chōng rectified the laws,
and Xiù reformed the official system.
Xiù proposed the five ranks of nobility,
and over six hundred people from the Cavalry Commander and above were enfeoffed.
Thus, Xiù was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jìchuān,
with a territory of sixty lǐ,
and a fief of fourteen hundred households,
using the Jìchuān Ruins in Gāoyuàn County as his marquisate.
Initially,
Emperor Wén had not yet decided on his successor,
but favored Yōu, Marquis of Wǔyáng.
Emperor Wǔ feared he would not be established,
and asked Xiù:
"Do people have an auspicious physiognomy?"
And then subtly showed his own appearance.
Xiù later told Emperor Wén:
"The Central Army Protector's popular standing is already great,
and his celestial physiognomy is such
