that he is certainly not the physiognomy of a mere minister."
Because of this, the Crown Prince was then decided.
After Emperor Wǔ ascended to the throne,
Xiù was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat and Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
He, along with Censor-in-Chief Wáng Chén and General-in-Chief Jiǎ Chōng, were all granted the privilege of establishing their own offices,
and he was additionally made a Palace Attendant.
When the Emperor received the abdication,
he was additionally made Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
enfeoffed as Duke of Jùlù Commandery,
with a fief of three thousand households.
At that time, Hǎo Xǔ (郝詡), the Protector-General of Ānyuǎn, wrote to an old friend, saying:
"I am acquainted with Péi Xiù (裴秀), the Minister of the Secretariat,
and hope to benefit from him."
The relevant authorities proposed dismissing Xiù from office.
An imperial edict stated:
"Not being able to prevent others from imposing things upon oneself
is something even the ancients found difficult.
The interference in personal matters
is Hǔ's (詡) crime alone,
how could the Minister of the Secretariat prevent it?
Do not question him further."
Lǐ Xǐ (李憙), the Colonel Director of Retainers, again submitted a memorial, stating that
Liú Shàng (劉尚), the Cavalry Commandant, was occupying official rice fields for Péi Xiù (裴秀), the Minister of the Secretariat,
and requested that Xiù (秀) be prohibited from doing so.
An edict again stated that Xiù (秀) had helped and supported the imperial administration,
and had rendered meritorious service to the royal house;
he should not have his great virtue overshadowed by a small flaw.
It ordered that Shàng's (尚) crime be duly investigated and Xiù's (秀) prohibition be lifted.
After a long time,
an imperial edict said:
"The responsibility of the Three Ducal Ministers
is to assist in promoting the imperial standard
and to help achieve the king's affairs.
Therefore, the governance of the state and the discussion of principles
rely on their sagacity.
If they are not the right people,
the office should not be idly filled.
Péi Xiù (裴秀), the Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left,
possesses a broad and generous mind,
and his thoughts are far-reaching.
The late Emperor appointed him,
and he assisted in affairs before the court.
When We received the mandate,
he splendidly aided Our great enterprise,
and his meritorious virtues are widely renowned,
matching those of Yuánkǎi (元凱) [Dù Yù (杜預)].
He should rightly assume a central position
to bring peace to all undertakings.
Let Xiù (秀) be made Minister of Works."
Xiù (秀) was learned in Confucian studies,
and also focused on governmental affairs.
During the transition of imperial power,
he held the crucial role of chief censor.
His decisions
were always in accord with propriety.
Furthermore, since his office was that of the Minister of Works,
he considered that the place names of mountains and rivers in the Yǔgòng (禹貢) [Tribute of Yǔ]
had existed for a long time,
and many had changed.
Later commentators sometimes forcefully misinterpreted them,
gradually leading to obscurity.
Therefore, he scrutinized old texts,
leaving doubtful ones blank.
For names that existed in antiquity but not now,
he noted them down as appropriate,
and compiled eighteen chapters of the "Yǔgòng Region Maps" [Yǔgòng Dìyù Tú (禹貢地域圖)],
which he presented
and stored in the imperial archives.
Its preface states: "The establishment of maps and records
has a long history.
Since ancient times, symbols and systems have been created,
and their utility relied upon.
The Three Dynasties established officials for this purpose,
with the Grand Scribe managing the duty.
When
Hàn (漢) annihilated Xiányáng (咸陽),
Chancellor Xiāo Hé (蕭何) collected all the maps and records of Qín (秦).
Now, the imperial archives have neither ancient maps
nor those acquired by Xiāo Hé (蕭何);
there are only the Hàn (漢) dynasty's
'Maps of the Terrestrial Globe' [Yúdì (輿地)] and various 'Comprehensive Terrestrial Maps' [Kuòdì (括地)].
None of them set forth scale ratios,
nor do they verify accurate bearings,
nor do they fully record famous mountains and great rivers.
Although they have rough shapes,
they
are not precise or accurate,
and cannot be relied upon.
Some contain extravagant and unrealistic statements about distant regions,
not conforming to facts,
and thus without value in meaning.
When the Great Jìn (晉) arose,
uniting the six directions [under heaven],
and clearing the universe,
it began with Yōng (庸) and Shǔ (蜀),
entering their rugged terrains.
Emperor Wén (文皇帝) therefore ordered the relevant authorities
to compile and seek maps of
Wú (吳) and Shǔ (蜀).
Once the land of Shǔ (蜀) was pacified,
the routes taken by the six armies,
the distances of the regions,
the dangers and ease of mountains and rivers,
and the winding or straight paths of expeditions
were all verified with maps and records,
without any discrepancies.
The present Emperor examined the mountains, seas, rivers,
plains, wetlands, and marshes from the Yǔgòng (禹貢),
the Nine Provinces of antiquity,
and the sixteen provinces of today,
as well as the commanderies, kingdoms, counties, cities,
borders, and villages,
and the old
names of ancient states' alliances and gatherings,
and land and water routes,
to create eighteen chapters of maps.
There are six principles in map-making.
First is the 'scale ratio' [fēnlǜ (分率)],
which is used to determine the extent of breadth and width.
Second is 'accurate bearings' [zhǔnwàng (準望)],
which is used to correct the shapes
of locations relative to each other.
Third is 'distances' [dàolǐ (道里)],
which is used to determine the number of units traversed.
Fourth is 'elevation' [gāoxià (高下)],
fifth is 'angles' [fāngxié (方邪)],
and sixth is 'straightness or winding' [yūzhí (迂直)].
These three are adapted to the specific terrain
to suit conditions,
and are used to verify differences in flatness and ruggedness.
If there are images but no scale ratios,
then one cannot discern the differences in distances.
If there are scale ratios but no accurate bearings,
even
if correct in one corner,
it will certainly be wrong in other directions.
If there are accurate bearings but no distances,
then when applied to areas separated by mountains and seas,
they cannot be connected.
If there are
distances but no verification of elevation, angles, or straightness/winding,
then the numerical distances of paths will inevitably deviate from the actual distances,
losing the accuracy of the bearings.
Therefore,
these six are consulted and examined together.
However, the actual distances are determined by the scale ratio;
the actual relative positions are determined by the distances;
and the actual measurements are determined by calculations of elevation,
angles, and straightness/winding.
Therefore, even with the separation of towering mountains and vast seas,
the remoteness of distant regions and different lands,
and the winding ascents and descents,
all can be measured and determined.
Once
the method of accurate bearings is established,
then the winding or straight, and far or near shapes will have nowhere to hide."
Xiù (秀) initiated the establishment of court ceremonies
and extensively presented criminal policies.
The imperial court largely followed and adopted them,
making them standard practice.
He served for four years [as Minister of Works]
and was a renowned statesman of his time.
He took the Cold Food Powder,
and was supposed to drink hot wine but drank cold wine instead.
He died in the seventh year of Tàishǐ (泰始) [271 CE],
at the age of forty-eight.
An imperial edict stated:
"The Minister of Works embodied virtue and followed sagacity,
manifesting refinement and scholarly conduct.
He assisted in the imperial mandate and helped the world,
and his meritorious achievements were grand and abundant.
He was about to promulgate and establish systems
to be a model for the world,
but unfortunately he passed away.
We are deeply grieved by this.
Let him be granted secret artifacts, one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, three hundred thousand cash, and one hundred bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title shall be Yuán (元)."
Initially,
Xiù (秀) believed that the thirty-six bureaus of the Secretariat managed affairs with unclear standards
and that it would be better to have various ministers assume these responsibilities.
He died before he could present this proposal.
His friends sorted through his writings
and found a draft memorial regarding the pacification of Wú (吳).
Its text read:
"Sūn Hào (孫晧) is cruel and tyrannical.
If a sagacious ruler governs the world and attacks the weak and ignorant,
leaving it to his descendants,
they will eventually be unable to become subjects.
Times have their ups and downs;
this is not a position of lasting peace.
Although your servant has repeatedly spoken on this in the past,
no definitive decision has been made.
Now, being gravely ill and unable to recover,
I reverently make this proposal again.
May Your Majesty consider implementing it at the proper time."
It was then sealed and reported to the Emperor.
The imperial reply stated:
"The Minister of Works has passed away,
and the pain and sorrow cannot leave Our heart.
We have also received your draft memorial;
though in critical condition,
you did not forget the royal house,
and showed utmost loyalty and concern for the state.
Reading it increases Our grief and sadness.
We shall discuss it with all the worthy officials."
In the early Xiánníng era,
he, along with Shí Bāo and others, was made a duke,
and his spirit tablet was placed in the ancestral temple for sacrificial offerings.
He had two sons: Jùn and Wěi.
Jùn inherited the title,
and rose to Sànqí Chángshì,
but died young.
Jùn's illegitimate son, Jǐng, was not intelligent,
so he was separately enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāoyáng Tíng.
Jùn's younger brother, Wěi, succeeded him.
Wěi's courtesy name was Yìmín.
He was elegant and had foresight,
was extensively learned, and studied ancient texts,
and was well-known from a young age.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Zhōu Bì saw him and sighed, saying:
"Wěi is like an armory;
all five types of weapons are deployed freely.
He is a hero of his time."
Jiǎ Chōng, who was Wěi's maternal aunt's husband,
memorialized,
"Xiù has performed services worthy of assisting the Mandate.
Unfortunately, his legitimate eldest son passed away,
leaving a young and weak orphan.
Wěi's talent and virtue are outstanding and flourishing,
sufficient to prosper the national succession."
An imperial edict ordered Wěi to succeed to the爵.
Wěi firmly declined,
but was not permitted.
In the second year of Tàikāng,
he was summoned to be the Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
then promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
concurrently serving as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Earlier,
Wěi's nephew Jǐng was a commoner.
Wěi argued for his family's generational achievements,
and Jǐng was granted the title of Marquis of Gāoyáng Tíng.
When Yáng Jùn was about to be executed,
Yáng Jùn's partisan, Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yù, had soldiers arrayed at the gate.
He encountered Wěi
and asked where the Tàifù was.
Wěi deceived him, saying:
"I just met the Duke in a plain carriage at the Xīyè Gate,
and he departed west with two attendants."
Yù asked:
"Where should I go?"
Wěi replied:
"You should go to the Tíngwèi."
Yù followed Wěi's advice
and then left.
Soon after, an edict ordered Wěi to replace Yù as Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
stationed at Wànchūn Gate.
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
Wěi was due to be enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wǔchāng for his merits.
Wěi requested that the enfeoffment be given to Jǐng.
The emperor, however, enfeoffed Wěi's second son, Gāi.
Wěi earnestly argued that Jǐng was originally the legitimate heir
and should succeed to the Jùlù title.
He cited the late emperor's gracious intent,
but his pleas were not accepted.
He stated that the enfeoffment of Wǔchāng
was bestowed upon himself,
and specifically requested it be given to Jǐng.
Gāi was then married to a princess,
so the emperor did not listen.
He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng.
At that time, the empire was temporarily at peace.
Wěi memorialized to repair the national academy
and to engrave scriptures on stone.
After the Crown Prince lectured,
a sacrificial ceremony was offered to Confucius,
followed by feasting and archery,
which proceeded with great ritual and order.
He also had Xún Fān complete the aspirations of his father, Xù.
Bells were cast and stone chimes carved
to be used for the ritual music of the suburban sacrifices, ancestral temple, and court ceremonies.
Wěi was broadly knowledgeable and well-informed,
and also skilled in medicine.
When Xún Xù was rectifying the pitch standards,
he discovered an ancient ruler
that was more than four parts shorter than those currently in use.
Wěi memorialized, saying:
"It is appropriate to change all measures.
If it is not possible to change everything at once,
the weights and measures of the Imperial Medical Bureau should be changed first.
If these are inaccurate,
they will deviate from the correct standards of Shénnóng and Qí Bó.
The varying weights of medicines
and conflicting divisions of dosages
can cause harm and premature death,
which is particularly damaging.
The fact that people in ancient times lived long, but now die young,
may not be unrelated to this."
Ultimately, his advice was not adopted.
Yuè Guǎng once engaged in a pure conversation with Wěi,
intending to convince him with reason,
but Wěi's arguments were extensive and abundant.
Yuè Guǎng smiled and said nothing.
People at the time called Wěi "the forest and marsh of eloquent discourse."
Wěi, concerned that Empress Jiǎ was displeased with the Crown Prince,
submitted a strong memorial requesting an increase in the rank and title of Xiè Shūfēi, the Crown Prince's birth mother.
He also requested an increase in the number of household guards and officers,
and the provision of three thousand soldiers,
whereupon the Eastern Palace's resident guard numbered ten thousand.
He was promoted to Shàngshū,
retained his position as Shìzhōng,
and was awarded Guānglù Dàfū.
Every time he was appointed to a position,
he never failed to earnestly and firmly decline,
submitting over ten memorials
citing numerous examples of success and failure from ancient and modern times as arguments.
Those who read them were all chilled to the bone.
Wěi deeply feared Empress Jiǎ's misrule.
He discussed with Sīkōng Zhāng Huá and Shìzhōng Jiǎ Mó the possibility of deposing her and establishing Xiè Shūfēi.
Both Huá and Mó said:
"The emperor himself has no intention of deposing her.
If we proceed unilaterally,
the emperor will not approve of it.
Moreover, the various princes are strong and active,
forming factions with differing opinions.
We fear that disaster will strike like a triggered mechanism,
resulting in our deaths and danger to the state,
without benefiting the altars of soil and grain."
Wěi said:
"That is truly as you fear.
But a confused and tyrannical person
has no scruples.
Chaos can be expected at any moment.
What then shall we do?"
Huá said:
"You two are still trusted.
You should diligently explain the warnings of misfortune and fortune to those around the emperor,
hoping to avoid major deviations.
Fortunately, the empire is still peaceful,
so we may perhaps leisurely pass the remaining years."
This plan was thus shelved.
Wěi continuously urged his maternal aunt, Lady Guǎngchéng,
to admonish Empress Jiǎ to treat the Crown Prince favorably.
Someone advised Wěi, saying:
"Fortunately, you can speak freely with the empress, both within and outside her circle.
If your words are not heeded,
then you can feign illness and withdraw.
If neither of these options is pursued,
even ten memorials
will hardly save you."
Wěi sighed with emotion for a long time,
but ultimately could not act upon it.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
retaining his position as Shìzhōng.
Although Wěi was a relative of the Empress,
his esteemed reputation was always high;
the empire did not consider his advancement due to kinship,
but rather feared he might not remain in office.
Soon after, Wěi was again solely entrusted with the affairs of the Ménxià.
He firmly declined,
but was not permitted.
Wěi memorialized, saying:
"Jiǎ Mó has just passed away,
and I am appointed to replace him,
thereby elevating the influence of the empress's relatives
and demonstrating a biased appointment.
When have imperial in-laws ever been able to protect themselves?
Everyone knows that those with close kinship cannot escape harm.
However, among the twenty-four Hàn emperors, only Emperor Xiàowén, Emperor Guāngwǔ, and Emperor Míng did not favor their imperial in-laws,
and they all preserved their lineage.
Was it because they were uniquely virtuous?
It was truly because it was a principle for stability.
In the past, Mù Shū did not accept a banquet that violated rites;
I, your subject, also dare not heed an unusual imperial edict."
He further memorialized:
"Gāoyáo advised Yú,
Yī Yǐn assisted Shāng,
Lǚ Wàng supported Zhōu,
Xiāo Hè and Zhāng Liáng aided Hàn.
All spread their achievements and transforming influence,
reaching to the four cardinal points.
Down to their successors,
Gāo Dān, Fù Yuè,
Zǔ Jǐ, Fán Zhòng,
also greatly revitalized their dynasties.
Some raised up the obscure and humble,
others rose from common families.
Were these not acts of valuing virtue,
thereby achieving such excellence!
Observing recent times,
people have failed to emulate the distant past,
indulging in immediate sentiments,
often relying on the empress's relatives,
leading to unrest.
In the past, Shū Guǎng warned the Crown Prince against making his maternal relatives court officials,
and people of later generations considered him to understand ritual.
How much more so for the court, what benefit is there in appointing imperial in-laws?
Even if their talents are equal,
one should still prioritize those who are more distantly related,
to demonstrate ultimate impartiality.
The Hàn dynasty not employing Féng Yěwáng is an example of this principle."
When the memorials were submitted,
all were met with gracious imperial edicts offering gentle persuasion.
At that time, Chén Zhǔn's son Kuāng (陳匡) and Hán Wèi's son Sōng (韓嵩) were both serving in the Eastern Palace.
Wěi (頠) admonished, saying:
"The establishment of the Eastern Palace
is to store up the imperial ultimate.
Those with whom the crown prince associates
must be selected from the heroic and outstanding,
and should be of established virtue.
Kuāng (匡) and Sōng (嵩) are young and weak,
not yet understanding the principles of human conduct and the integrity of self-establishment.
The crown prince, in reality, embodies the outward appearance of early maturity,
yet now there is talk of child attendants,
which is not a grand principle for glorifying and spreading far-reaching customs."
When Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ (愍懷太子) was deposed,
Wěi (頠) and Zhāng Huá (張華) bitterly argued against it, but their advice was not followed.
The details are in Zhāng Huá's biography.
Wěi (頠) deeply lamented that the customs of his time were dissolute,
showing no respect for Confucian doctrines.
Hé Yàn (何晏) and Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) had high reputations in the world,
but they spoke of emptiness and nothingness,
did not abide by rites and laws,
occupied official positions idly, enjoying favor,
and did not attend to affairs in office.
To the extent that followers of Wáng Yǎn (王衍),
whose reputations were exceedingly great,
held high positions and heavy influence,
did not involve themselves in worldly matters.
Consequently, they imitated each other,
and the moral influence declined.
Thus, Wěi (頠) wrote "Chóng Yǒu zhī Lùn" (崇有之論, "Essay on Reverence for Being") to explain its shortcomings, saying: "The ultimate blending of all origins
is the Way of the supreme ultimate.
Distinctions by categories
are the classes of various kinds.
Forms and images mark divisions,
they are the bodies of living beings.
Transformations
and responses, interwoven,
are the origins of principles and traces.
Now, if things are classified into categories,
then what they receive is partial.
The partial cannot be self-sufficient,
therefore it relies on external resources.
Thus, what can be
sought from birth
is called principle (理, lǐ).
What principle embodies
is called being (有, yǒu).
What being requires
is called resource (資, zī).
Where resources meet suitability
is called appropriateness (宜, yí).
Choosing
what is appropriate
is called sentiment (情, qíng).
Once knowledge and wisdom are bestowed,
although their comings and goings differ,
and their silence and speech are on different paths,
the sentiment for preserving life and adhering to appropriateness
is one.
When all
principles coexist without harm,
then noble and base forms appear.
Gain and loss depend on interactions,
thus good and ill omens emerge.
Therefore, the wise and the noble
know that desires cannot be eliminated,
and that interacting with things has its occasions.
Observing what comes and goes,
they assess the mean to set their tasks.
Indeed, by utilizing the way of Heaven,
distributing the benefits of Earth,
personally undertaking their responsibilities,
they enjoy the fruits after toil.
Dwelling in benevolence and compliance,
maintaining with respect and frugality,
leading with loyalty and trustworthiness,
acting with reverence and humility,
having no excessive demands,
and no extravagant uses in affairs,
then success can be achieved!
Thus, establishing the great
ultimate,
pacifying and governing all living beings,
instructing things and setting examples,
all depend on this.
This is the reason why the Sages govern.
If, however, there is indulgence, arrogance, and tyranny,
then harm will begin to sprout.
Thus, excessive desires lead to swift misfortune,
unrestrained sentiments lead to widespread resentment,
arbitrary behavior leads to attacks,
and monopolizing profits leads to
invasion.
This can be called losing life while seeking to enrich it.
The masses,
alarmed by such misfortunes,
seek the origin of hardship and contention.
Observing the flaws in partial qualities,
and seeing the good in simplicity and reduction,
they then expound the doctrine of revering nothingness (貴無, guìwú)
and establish the theory of devaluing being (賤有, jiànyǒu).
Devaluing being inevitably leads to disregarding form;
disregarding form inevitably leads to abandoning regulations;
abandoning
regulations inevitably leads to neglecting precautions;
neglecting precautions inevitably leads to forgetting rites.
If rites and regulations do not exist,
then there will be no means to govern.
The adherence of the multitude to their superiors
is like water residing in a vessel.
Thus,
the sentiments of the common people
are rooted in what they are accustomed to;
when accustomed, their hearts submit to their occupation;
when their occupation is submitted to, they consider it to be natural.
Therefore, rulers must be careful in what they teach,
distributing their government and punishments,
and
all their affairs.
They divide dwellings for the common people,
and assign each to one of the four occupations,
so that those who receive orders are secure without being coerced,
suddenly forgetting differences,
and having no desire to change.
How much more so for
those who hold the dignity of the highest positions,
nurturing feelings of profound esteem,
and diligently using them as instruction!
This is the step that leads to either clarity or confusion,
and it must be carefully considered.
Excessive desires can be reduced but cannot be utterly cut off,
extravagant uses can be regulated but cannot be said to have no value.
Those who possess the means to speak
extensively list the reasons for
visible forms
and greatly praise the beauty of emptiness and nothingness.
The reasons for forms and vessels are verifiable,
but the meaning of emptiness and nothingness is difficult to examine.
Eloquent and skillful writings are pleasing,
and plausible words
are enough to confuse.
The public listens, bewildered,
and becomes immersed in their established theories.
Although there are some whose hearts differ from this,
their words cannot prevail,
and they yield to what they are familiar with,
thus concluding that the principle of emptiness and nothingness
is indeed
undeniable.
One person sings, and others echo;
many go forth and do not return.
Consequently, they disdain the affairs of the world,
undervalue meritorious deeds,
elevate the pursuits of idleness,
and belittle those of practical and substantial virtue.
What human nature pursues
is profoundly fame and profit.
Thus, the eloquent elaborate their words,
and the inarticulate praise their meaning,
infecting the multitude.
Therefore, setting forth theories is based on emptiness and nothingness,
calling it profound and subtle;
holding office without personally attending to duties
is called refined and aloof;
conducting oneself by abandoning integrity
is called broad-minded and unconstrained.
Hence, the spirit of discipline and self-cultivation
becomes increasingly
lax.
The dissolute, taking advantage of this,
sometimes violate the rites of good and ill fortune,
and disregard the outward appearance of deportment,
defiling and abandoning the order of senior and junior,
blurring the distinctions of noble and base.
In extreme cases,
they go so far as to be naked,
speaking and laughing inappropriately,
taking recklessness as magnanimity,
and thus scholarly conduct is further diminished.
Lǎozi (老子) wrote the five thousand characters,
exposing the evils of defilement and chaos,
and distinguishing and promoting the meaning of tranquility and unity,
enabling people to feel relieved and at ease,
conforming to the principles of the Yì (易, *I Ching*)'s
Sǔn (損), Qiān (謙), Gèn (艮), and Jié (節) hexagrams.
Yet tranquility and unity adhere to the root,
without being called nothingness;
categories like Sǔn (損) and Gèn (艮)
are indeed one path for the noble person,
not what the Yì (易)
takes as its essence to uphold nothingness.
Although Lǎozi's (老子) book broadly encompasses many scriptures,
yet it says,
"Being (有, yǒu) is born from nothingness (無, wú),"
taking emptiness as its main principle,
thus establishing a partial school of thought.
discourse,
how could it be without a reason!
When man is born,
he takes preserving life as completeness.
The means to attain this completeness
is to make conforming to sensations one's priority.
If one savors the near and thereby harms one's
endeavors,
then the misfortune of indulgence arises.
If one cherishes the trivial and forgets the fundamental,
then the truth of heavenly principle is extinguished.
Therefore, where actions meet
is the juncture of survival and destruction.
Indeed, that which is
"being" is not truly "being",
and in "non-being" there is not truly "non-being";
in "non-being" there is not truly "non-being",
and in "being" there is not truly "being".
Therefore, it elaborates on the burdens of indulgence and scattering,
and composes the discourse on "valuing non-being" (guìwú).
This is intended to eliminate the excessive errors
of what is wrong,
preserve the moderation of great goodness,
reclaim the errant from past transgressions,
and restore clarity and rectitude to one's heart.
It is appropriate that it uses "non-being" (wú) as its discourse,
but its aim is to preserve
"being" (yǒu) completely.
Therefore, its discourse says,
"considering language to be insufficient."
If this is the case,
then it is merely a way of expression,
a statement from one perspective.
If one claims that ultimate truth truly takes "non-being" (wú) as its
principle,
then it is biased and harmful.
Previous worthies and enlightened thinkers,
considering it something not to be fixated upon,
presented profound arguments against it.
Only Bān Gù (Bān Gù) composed an objection,
but it was not enough to refute its sentiment.
Sūn Qīng (Sūn Qīng)
and Yáng Xióng (Yáng Xióng) largely suppressed it,
yet still partially conceded to it.
But the discourse of "nothingness" (xūwú)
expanded and spread daily.
Various schools fanned it up,
each presenting its own theories.
Reaching up
to creation and transformation,
and down to all affairs,
none failed to value "non-being" (wú),
and what was maintained was universally the same.
This sentiment, solidified by the multitude,
then declared that all principles of "being" (yǒu) were lowly expressions of righteousness,
and treated them lightly and
contemptuously.
Debating human relations and the work of clarifying the classics
consequently changed its focus.
Wěi (Wěi) was thus startled,
expressed what he harbored in his heart,
but attackers gathered in abundance.
Some thought it
a momentary oral statement.
A guest happened to visit,
and was commissioned by all to write a treatise,
enumerating the evidences of "nothingness" (xūwú) being unacceptable.
If one cannot correct every single matter,
then the doctrine of the "non-being school" (wú jiā)
cannot be overturned.
Wěi (Wěi) retired and reflected on this:
although a virtuous person settles in his sentiments
and seeks no prominence,
when it comes to establishing words,
it is simply about conveying the meaning.
However, the sages are
long distant,
and differences and similarities are entangled.
If there is even a slight resemblance
that can elevate and aid the ancient classics,
support and clarify the great undertaking,
and benefit the present time,
then one should only worry about not being able to speak;
how could one remain silent,
and merely briefly indicate what one maintains
without fully expounding it!
Indeed, that which is utterly "non-being" (zhìwú) cannot give birth;
therefore, that which first comes into being is self-generating.
If it is self-generating, it must embody "being" (yǒu);
then "being" would be abandoned and generation would be deficient.
Generation takes "being" (yǒu)
as its inherent part;
then "nothingness" (xūwú) is what "being" (yǒu) calls its abandoned part.
〔一０〕 Therefore, nourishing the "being" (yǒu) that has already transformed
cannot be made complete by that which is useless;
governing the multitude of already existing
things
cannot be followed by "non-action" (wúwéi).
The mind is not an affair,
yet governing affairs must originate from the mind.
However, one cannot, because governing affairs is not an affair itself,
say that the mind is "non-being" (wú).
A craftsman is not a tool,
yet making tools must rely on a craftsman.
However, one cannot, because making tools is not a tool itself,
say that a craftsman does not "exist" (yǒu).
Therefore, if one wishes to catch fish from deep
springs,
〔一一〕it cannot be obtained by merely resting;
to fell birds from high walls,
it cannot be swiftly accomplished by quietly folding one's hands;
to wisely employ hooks and bait,
it cannot be grasped by the
ignorant.
From this perspective,
that which aids "being" (yǒu) is all "being" (yǒu);
what benefit can "nothingness" (xūwú) bring to the existing multitude of living beings!
Wáng Yǎn (Wáng Yǎn) and his followers launched successive attacks and objections,
but none could make him yield.
He also composed the Biàncái Lùn (Biàncái Lùn) [Discourse on Eloquence],
in which all profound principles of ancient and modern times were clarified and explained.
However, before it was completed, he met with disaster.
Initially,
Zhào Wáng Lún (Zhào Wáng Lún) fawned upon Empress Jiǎ (Jiǎ Hòu),
and Wěi (Wěi) greatly detested him.
Lún (Lún) repeatedly sought official positions,
but Wěi (Wěi) and Zhāng Huá (Zhāng Huá) firmly refused again.
Because of this, he was deeply resented by Lún (Lún).
Lún (Lún) also secretly harbored ambitions of usurpation and rebellion,
wishing to first eliminate those esteemed in court.
Taking advantage of the occasion of Empress Jiǎ's (Jiǎ Hòu's) deposition, he then executed him.
He was thirty-four years old at the time.
His two sons, Sōng (Sōng) and Gāi (Gāi),
Lún (Lún) also wished to harm.
Liáng Wáng Róng (Liáng Wáng Róng) and Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè) stated that Wěi's (Wěi's) father Xiù (Xiù) had rendered meritorious service to the imperial house,
and was honored with sacrifices in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
so it was not proper to exterminate his descendants.
Therefore, they were spared death,
and exiled to Dàifāng (Dàifāng).
When Emperor Huì (Huì Dì) restored order,
Wěi's (Wěi's) original official positions were posthumously restored,
he was reburied with the rites of a Minister,
and given the posthumous title Chéng (Chéng).
Sōng (Sōng) inherited his noble rank,
and became a Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng (Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng).
Gāi (Gāi) went out to become the heir of his paternal uncle ☲,
and became a Sànqí Chángshì (Sànqí Chángshì).
Both were harmed by the Qǐhuó (Qǐhuó) bandit Chén Wǔ (Chén Wǔ).
Kǎi (Kǎi), courtesy name Shūzé (Shūzé).
His father was Huī (Huī),
Governor of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu) in Wèi (Wèi).
Kǎi (Kǎi) was intelligent and insightful, with breadth of vision.
He became famous in his youth,
especially skilled in Lǎo (Lǎo) and Yì (Yì).
In his youth, he was equally famous with Wáng Róng (Wáng Róng).
Zhōng Huì (Zhōng Huì) recommended him to Emperor Wén (Wén Dì).
He was appointed Clerk to the Chancellor,
and later promoted to Shàngshū Láng (Shàngshū Láng).
Jiǎ Chōng (Jiǎ Chōng) revised and established the laws and ordinances,
appointing Kǎi (Kǎi) as Dìngkē Láng (Dìngkē Láng).
When the task was completed,
an imperial edict commanded Kǎi (Kǎi) to hold and read them before the emperor,
and openly discuss their appropriateness.
Kǎi (Kǎi) was skilled at clear articulation;
those around him watched intently,
and listeners forgot their weariness.
When Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) was Fǔjūn (Fǔjūn),
he exquisitely selected his staff,
and appointed Kǎi (Kǎi) as Cānjūn Shì (Cānjūn Shì).
When the position of Lìbù Láng (Lìbù Láng) became vacant,
Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) asked Zhōng Huì (Zhōng Huì) about a suitable person for it.
Zhōng Huì (Zhōng Huì) said:
"Péi Kǎi (Péi Kǎi) is pure and perceptive,
Wáng Róng (Wáng Róng) is concise and essential;
both are excellent choices."
Thereupon, Kǎi (Kǎi) was appointed Lìbù Láng (Lìbù Láng).
Péi Kǎi’s (裴楷) demeanor was lofty and uninhibited,
his appearance handsome and clear.
He read widely in all kinds of books,
but especially excelled in the study of principles and righteousness.
People of the time called him
“The Jade Man,”
and also said,
“Seeing Péi Shūzé (裴叔則) is like approaching a jade mountain,
reflecting light onto others.”
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎),
and whenever he entered or exited the palace,
those who saw him would respectfully compose themselves.
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) first ascended the throne,
he drew lots to divine the length of his reign,
and obtained “one.”
The Emperor was displeased.
The assembled officials turned pale,
and no one dared to speak.
Kǎi (楷) straightened his attire and countenance,
and harmonized his tone,
then calmly advanced and said:
“I have heard that Heaven obtains unity to be clear,
Earth obtains unity to be tranquil,
and a king or lord obtains unity to be the stabilizer of the world.”
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) was greatly pleased,
and all the officials exclaimed “Long live the Emperor!”
Soon after, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎),
and successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Hénèi Tàishǒu (河內太守).
He was then recalled to the capital as Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉) and Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍),
then transferred to Shìzhōng (侍中).
Shí Chóng (石崇), as the son of a meritorious official, possessed talent and spirit,
but his aspirations and tastes differed from Kǎi’s (楷),
so he did not associate with him.
The Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (長水校尉) Sūn Jìshū (孫季舒) once feasted and drank heavily with Chóng (崇)
and behaved excessively arrogantly.
Chóng (崇) wanted to memorialize for his dismissal.
Kǎi (楷) heard of this
and said to Chóng (崇):
“You gave people a mad drug to drink,
and then demand proper etiquette from them;
is this not contradictory?”
Chóng (崇) then stopped.
Kǎi (楷) was by nature generous and tolerant,
and never offended others.
He did not uphold frugality,
and whenever he visited the wealthy and powerful,
he would take their precious treasures.
Yet, his chariots, horses, implements, and clothes,
within a single day and night,
he would bestow upon the poor and needy.
Once, he built a new residence,
and his elder cousin Yǎn (衍) saw it and was delighted,
so he immediately gave the residence to Yǎn (衍).
The two princes of Liáng (梁) and Zhào (趙)
were close relatives of the state,
and highly esteemed at the time.
Kǎi (楷) annually requested one million cash in rent from the two states,
to distribute among his relatives.
Some people criticized him,
but Kǎi (楷) said:
“To reduce what is excessive to supplement what is insufficient
is the way of Heaven.”
He was content with both praise and blame,
and his conduct was always spontaneous and unrestrained,
all in this manner.
He, alongside Shān Tāo (山濤) and Hé Qiáo (和嶠), held positions due to their eminent virtues.
The Emperor once asked:
“I have received Heaven’s mandate and followed the times,
the realm within the seas has been renewed.
Regarding the trends and reputation of the world,
what have I gained and what have I lost?”
Kǎi (楷) replied:
“Your Majesty has received the mandate,
and the four seas have submitted to your influence.
The reason you have not yet rivaled Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜)
is simply that people like Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) are still in court.
It is appropriate to invite worthy people from all over the world,
and together promote the upright path.
You should not show favoritism to others.”
At that time, Rèn Kǎi (任愷) and Yú Chún (庾純) also spoke against Chōng (充).
The Emperor then sent Chōng (充) out to be the Dūdū (都督) of Guānzhōng (關中).
Chōng (充) married his daughter to the Crown Prince,
and so the matter stopped.
After the conquest of Wú (吳),
the Emperor planned to cultivate an era of great peace.
He often invited dukes and ministers,
and discussed governance with them.
Kǎi (楷) expounded on the customs of the Sān Wǔ (三五) (Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors),
and then on the rise and fall of the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties.
The Emperor praised him,
and those present were filled with admiration.
Kǎi’s (楷) son Zàn (瓚) married Yáng Jùn’s (楊駿) daughter,
but Kǎi (楷) had always looked down on Jùn (駿)
and was not on good terms with him.
When Jùn (駿) came to power,
he transferred Kǎi (楷) to Wèiwèi (衞尉),
then promoted him to Tàizǐ Shàoshī (太子少師).
He was at leisure with nothing to do,
and remained silent.
When Jùn (駿) was executed,
Kǎi (楷) was arrested due to his marital relation and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) (Minister of Justice),
and was about to be punished by law.
On that day, events occurred suddenly,
with executions everywhere,
and everyone was terrified.
Kǎi’s (楷) expression did not change,
and his actions were self-composed.
He asked for paper and brush to write to his relatives and old friends.
Thanks to the rescue of the Shìzhōng (侍中) Fù Zhī (傅祗), he was spared,
but still lost his official position.
Tàibǎo (太保) Wèi Guàn (衞瓘) and Tàizǎi (太宰) Liàng (亮) praised Kǎi’s (楷) integrity and unwavering character,
saying he deserved a noble title and land.
Thus, he was enfeoffed as Línhǎi Hóu (臨海侯),
with a stipend of two thousand households.
He replaced Prince Wěi (瑋) of Chǔ (楚) as Běijūn Zhōnghóu (北軍中候),
and was additionally granted the title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Wěi (瑋) resented Guàn (瓘) and Liàng (亮) for dismissing him and appointing Kǎi (楷).
Kǎi (楷) heard of this
and did not dare to accept the appointment,
so he was transferred to Shàngshū (尚書).
Kǎi’s (楷) eldest son Yú (輿) had previously married Liàng’s (亮) daughter,
and his daughter had married Wèi Guàn’s (衞瓘) son.
Kǎi (楷) feared that internal strife was not yet over,
and requested to be sent out to command a frontier post.
He was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍), granted the insignia of Jiǎjié (假節), and made Dūdū (都督) of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Just as he was about to depart, Wěi (瑋) indeed forged an imperial edict and executed Liàng (亮) and Guàn (瓘).
Wěi (瑋) resented Kǎi (楷) for previously taking his Zhōnghóu (中候) position,
and also for his marital ties with Liàng (亮) and Guàn (瓘).
He secretly sent men to arrest Kǎi (楷).
Kǎi (楷) had always known that Wěi (瑋) harbored ill will towards him.
Upon hearing of the turmoil,
he entered the city in a single carriage,
and hid in the home of his wife’s father, Wáng Hún (王渾).
He and Liàng’s (亮) young son moved eight times in one night,
and thus escaped the calamity.
After Wěi (瑋) was executed,
Kǎi (楷) was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
with the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
He, along with Zhāng Huá (張華) and Wáng Róng (王戎), managed crucial affairs of state.
Kǎi (楷) suffered from a severe illness (likely diabetes, causing excessive thirst)
and did not enjoy holding high positions.
Wáng Hún (王渾) pleaded on Kǎi’s (楷) behalf, saying:
“Kǎi (楷) received the grace of promotion from the late Emperor,
and now again enjoys Your Majesty’s favor.
This is truly a time to exert his utmost effort.
However, Kǎi (楷)’s nature is not competitive.
In the past, as Chángshì (常侍),
he requested to be sent out as Hénèi Tàishǒu (河內太守);
later, as Shìzhōng (侍中),
he again requested to be sent out as Hénán Yǐn (河南尹).
And he worried deeply about Yáng (楊) [referring to Yáng Jùn (楊駿)].
The position of Guānglùxūn (光祿勳) is vacant,
and I believe he could fill it.
Now Zhāng Huá (張華) is in the Zhōngshū (中書),
and Wáng Róng (王戎) is in the Shàngshū (尚書),
which is sufficient to manage affairs;
there is no need to bring Kǎi (楷) back in.
He was unhappy with Jùn (駿),
and requested to be Wèiwèi (衞尉);
when he was transferred to the Eastern Palace (太子少師),
his rank was below his contemporaries.
He was content with a life of obscurity and retirement,
and discerning people could see his true intentions.
Kǎi (楷) is now ailing and exhausted;
I am deeply worried about him.
The position of Guānglùxūn (光祿勳) is vacant,
and I believe he could fill it.
Now Zhāng Huá (張華) is in the Zhōngshū (中書),
and Wáng Róng (王戎) is in the Shàngshū (尚書),
which is sufficient to manage affairs;
there is no need to bring Kǎi (楷) back in.
There are not many eminent ministers;
they should be looked after and nurtured,
and their wishes not thwarted,
so as to secure their long-term benefits to the state.”
His request was not granted.
Instead, Kǎi (楷) was appointed Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) with the privilege of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
When his illness became critical,
an imperial edict dispatched the Huángmén Láng (黃門郎) Wáng Yǎn (王衍) to visit him.
Kǎi (楷) turned his eyes and looked at him, saying:
“We never really knew each other in the end.”
Yǎn (衍) deeply admired his brilliant spirit.
Kǎi (楷) had a discerning eye for people.
When he was in Hénán (河南),
Lè Guǎng (樂廣) resided as a guest within his jurisdiction,
though not yet famous.
Kǎi (楷) saw him and found him extraordinary,
and brought him into the government office.
He once described Xiàhóu Xuán (夏侯玄) as
“solemn and dignified, like entering a ancestral temple,
seeing only ritual vessels and musical instruments.”
Zhōng Huì (鍾會) as
“like viewing a dense armory,
seeing only spears and halberds in front.”
Fù Gǔ (傅嘏) as
“vast and expansive, seeing everything.”
And Shān Tāo (山濤) as
“like ascending a mountain and looking down,
profoundly deep and distant.”
Initially,
at Péi Kǎi’s (裴楷) home, when millet was steamed in a zèng (甑),
some grains transformed into a fist-like shape,
some turned into blood,
and some became like radish seeds.
That year, he passed away
at the age of fifty-five.
His posthumous name was Yuán (元).
He had five sons: Yú (輿), Zàn (瓚), Xiàn (憲), Lǐ (禮), and Xùn (遜).
Yú’s (輿) courtesy name was Zǔmíng (祖明).
At a young age, he inherited his father’s noble title.
He served as a Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎),
and upon his death, his posthumous name was Jiǎn (簡).
Zàn (瓚)’s courtesy name was Guóbǎo (國寶).
He was a Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎),
possessing a noble and transcendent demeanor,
and all who saw him respected him.
He was especially esteemed by Wáng Suī (王綏),
who often accompanied him in his excursions.
Suī’s (綏) father, Róng (戎), said to him:
“Guóbǎo (國寶) initially didn’t come here.
Why do you frequently go to him?”
He replied:
“Although Guóbǎo (國寶) doesn’t know Suī (綏),
Suī (綏) knows Guóbǎo (國寶).”
When Yáng Jùn (楊駿) was executed,
he was harmed by the rogue soldiers.
Xiàn (憲)’s (憲) courtesy name was Jǐngsī (景思).
He was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
and enjoyed befriending light-hearted and chivalrous individuals.
When he reached the age of twenty,
he changed his ways to be strict and serious,
cultivating Confucian studies,
and for several years, his feet did not cross the threshold [of his home].
Xiè Kūn (謝鯤) of Chénjùn (陳郡) and Yǔ Gāi (庾敳) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) were both brilliant and distinguished scholars.
They met him and found him remarkable,
saying to each other:
“Péi Xiàn (裴憲) is upright, intelligent, and broad-minded,
understanding opportunities and knowing fate.
We don't know how he compares to his father;
but regarding his profound and steadfast preservation of simplicity,
not allowing worldly affairs to trouble his heart,
he likely surpasses him.”
Initially,
he served as a lecturer in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
and successively held positions as Huángmén Lìbù Láng (黃門吏部郎) and Shìzhōng (侍中).
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越), the Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王), appointed him as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史), Běizhōng Lángjiàng (北中郎將), and Gōng Jié (假節).
Wáng Jùn (王浚) issued an imperial decree [on his own authority],
appointing Xiàn (憲) as Shàngshū (尚書).
At the end of the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Wáng Jùn (王浚) was defeated by Shí Lè (石勒).
Zǎo Sōng (棗嵩) and others all apologized at the army gate,
offering bribes in abundance.
Only Xiàn (憲) and Xún Chuò (荀綽) remained tranquil in their private residences.
Lè (勒) had long heard of their reputation,
so he summoned them and said:
“Wáng Jùn (王浚) was tyrannical and cruel in Yōuzhōu (幽州),
resented by both men and spirits.
I respectfully act according to heavenly decrees,
saving these common people,
and all the old and new residents are joyful.
Thanks and celebrations fill the roads.
You two gentlemen equally indulged in wickedness and defied authority,
your sincerity and integrity are utterly obstructed.
Whom should the punishment of Fángfēng (防風) fall upon?”
Xiàn (憲)’s (憲) expression was upright and firm.
He wept and replied:
“Your subjects’ families have for generations received the glory of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
and our imperial favor has been exceptionally profound.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) was brutal and behaved outrageously,
yet he was still a remnant vassal of Jìn (晉).
Although we rejoice in your sagely transformation,
our righteousness obstructs our sincere submission.
Moreover, when King Wǔ (武王) attacked Zhòu (紂),
he honored the village of Shāng Róng (商容);
we have not heard of Shāng Róng (商容) being among those who turned their spears [against Zhòu (紂)].
If your Excellency does not wish to transform people with the Dao (道),
but must govern through cruel punishments,
〔一三〕then the punishment of Fángfēng (防風) is my due.
Please hand me over to the authorities.”
He bowed and left.
Lè (勒) deeply admired him,
treating him with the courtesy due to a guest.
Lè (勒) then inventoried the officials and relatives of Wáng Jùn (王浚),
all of whom possessed immense wealth amounting to millions.
Only Xiàn (憲) and Xún Chuò (荀綽) had merely a hundred or so scrolls of books at home,
and ten-odd hù (斛) each of salt and rice.
Upon hearing this,
Lè (勒) said to his Chángshǐ (長史), Zhāng Bīn (張賓):
“Their reputation is not false.
I am not happy to have obtained Yōuzhōu (幽zhou),
but I am delighted to have acquired these two men.”
He appointed them Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎),
and later dispatched them as Chánglè Tàishǒu (長樂太守).
When Lè (勒) assumed the imperial title,
before he had time to establish institutions,
he collaborated with Wáng Bō (王波) to compile the court rituals.
Thus, regulations and cultural artifacts [of the state] were established,
emulating those of a true king.
Lè (勒) was greatly pleased,
appointing him Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫),
and later promoted him to Sītú (司徒).
During Jìlóng (季龍)’s (季龍) reign,
he was even more highly regarded and respected.
Xiàn (憲) had two sons: Yì (挹) and Jué (瑴),
both known for their literary talent.
Jué (瑴) served Jìlóng (季龍) as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子) and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Yì (挹) and Jué (瑴) were both chivalrous and fond of wine,
enjoying to criticize and praise people.
They had a grudge against Xíng Yú (邢魚) of Héjiān (河間).
Yú (魚) secretly rode Jué (瑴)’s (瑴) horse and fled to Duàn Liáo (段遼),
but was captured.
Yú (魚) falsely accused Jué (瑴) of instructing him to inform the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) that Jìlóng (季龍) was about to attack them,
so they should prepare.
At that time, Jìlóng (季龍) was indeed planning to attack Liáo (遼),
and Yú’s (魚) testimony coincided with this.
Jìlóng (季龍) executed both Yì (挹) and Jué (瑴),
and Xiàn (憲) was also dismissed because of this.
Not long after,
he was reinstated as Yòuguānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫), Sītú (司徒), and Tàifù (太傅),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Āndìng Jùn (安定郡公).
Xiàn (憲) held various official positions,
but was not known for administrative achievements.
However, in court, he was quiet and reserved,
never allowing worldly affairs to trouble his mind.
It was simply due to his profound virtue and high reputation
that he was always treated with respect.
He eventually died during the Shí (石) clan’s rule,
and his clan member Zhì (峙)’s (峙) son, Mài (邁), was made his heir.
Kǎi (楷)’s (楷) eldest brother, Lí (黎),
and second brother, Kāng (康),
were both well-known.
Kāng (康)’s (康) son, Dùn (盾),
held prominent positions from a young age.
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
he served as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史),
entrusting his Chángshǐ (長史) Sīmǎ Ào (司馬奧).
Ào (奧) advised Dùn (盾) to establish authority through harsh punishments and executions,
mobilizing many common people for the army,
and those who did not obey the law were immediately punished with death.
After three years in office,
the common people grumbled and complained.
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越), the Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王),
was Dùn (盾)’s (盾) brother-in-law.
After Yuè (越) died,
the cavalry commander Mǎn Héng (滿衡) led the mobilized common people back east.
Soon after, Liú Yuánhǎi (劉元海) sent his generals Wáng Sāng (王桑) and Zhào Gù (趙固) towards Péngchéng (彭城).
When a few vanguard horsemen reached Xiàpī (下邳),
the civil and military officials, unable to bear the harsh governance,
all scattered and fled.
Dùn (盾) and Ào (奧) fled to Huái’yīn (淮陰),
and their wives and children were captured by the bandits.
Ào (奧) then lured Dùn (盾) to surrender to Zhào Gù (趙固).
Gù (固) had married Dùn (盾)’s (盾) daughter,
who was greatly favored.
Dùn (盾) wept before his daughter,
and Gù (固) subsequently killed him.
Dùn (盾)’s (盾) younger brother, Shào (邵),
courtesy name Dàojī (道期).
When Emperor Yuán (元帝) was Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍),
he appointed Shào (邵) as Chángshǐ (長史),
and Wáng Dǎo (王導) as Sīmǎ (司馬).
The two formed a deep friendship.
He was summoned to serve as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
then transferred to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and appointed as Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Yángzhōu Jiāngxī Huáiběi Zhūjūnshì (都督揚州江西淮北諸軍事), and Dōngzhōng Lángjiàng (東中郎將).
He followed Yuè (越) on an expedition to Xiàng (項),
and died in the army.
When Wáng Dǎo (王導) became Sīkōng (司空),
upon his appointment,
he sighed and said:
“If Péi Dàojī (裴道期) and Liú Wángqiáo (劉王喬) were still alive,
I would not be able to occupy this position alone.”
Dǎo (導)’s (導) son Zhòngyù (仲豫) had the same courtesy name as Kāng (康).
Out of remembrance for his old friend,
Dǎo (導) changed his son’s courtesy name to Jìngyù (敬豫).
Kǎi's
younger brother Chuò,
courtesy name Jìshū,
had a grand and magnanimous disposition. He served as Yellow Gate侍郎 (Shìláng) and Commander of the Long River (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi).
Chuò's son Xiá
was skilled in discussing profound principles.
His voice and manner of speaking were clear and flowing,
as harmonious as a qín or sè.
He once debated with Guō Xiàng from Hénán,
and the entire assembly was filled with admiration.
He also once sat with General of Pacifying the East Zhōu Fù
and played wéi (圍).
Fù's Sīmǎ (司馬) was serving wine,
and Xiá had not yet drunk.
The Sīmǎ, in a drunken rage,
pulled Xiá to the ground.
Xiá slowly rose and returned to his seat,
his expression unchanged,
and he resumed as before.
Such was his serene and composed nature.
Yue, Prince of Dōnghǎi, appointed him as his chief clerk (Zhǔbù).
Later, he was killed by Yuè's son Pí.
Initially,
the Pèi and Wáng clans flourished in the Wèi and Jìn eras.
At the time, people considered "Eight Pèi" to be comparable to "Eight Wáng":
Kǎi (楷) like Wáng Yǎn,
Kāng (康) like Wáng Suī,
Chuò (綽) like Wáng Chéng,
Zàn (瓚) like Wáng Dūn,
Xiá (遐) like Wáng Dǎo,
Wěi (頠) like Wáng Róng,
Miǎo (邈) like Wáng Xuányún.
The historian remarks: Zhōu (周) was praised for its numerous scholars,
Hàn (漢) was said to have obtained the right people.
They were likened to stars and constellations,
their prestige matching like a tally.
When famous figures were scarce,
many were lauded for their outstanding abilities,
bringing glory to their families and the nation.
Was this not what Chén Qiān (陳騫) was referred to as?
Xiù's (秀) reputation overshadowed his peers,
and he was known as a leader.
Kǎi's (楷) brilliant spirit manifested early,
and he was considered clear and penetrating.
Both were renowned ministers of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
and for good reason.
A eulogy says: As the world accommodates talent,
talent arrives to meet the world.
Gāopíng (高平) was profound and perceptive,
embodying such a distinguished capacity.
Jùlù (鉅鹿) was natural,
also known as a repository of classics.
Nǚwā (媧皇) refined stones;
the Jìn (晉) narrative reveals its mysteries.
Wěi (頠) had pure principles,
inheriting a graceful family tradition.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume Six: Wèi Guàn (His sons, his grandsons Zǎo, Jiè)
Wèi Guàn, courtesy name Bóyù,
was from Ānyì, Hédōng.
His great-great-grandfather Gǎo,
during the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
was summoned from Dàijùn for his Confucian scholarship.
He died in Ānyì, Hédōng,
and was granted the land where he died for burial.
His descendants consequently settled there.
His father, Jì,
was a Wèi (魏) Shàngshū (尚書).
Guàn lost his father at the age of ten and
was exceedingly filial.
His nature was chaste and quiet, and he possessed renowned philosophical insight.
He was praised for his clear discernment and uprightness.
He inherited his father's title, Marquis of Wéixiāng.
At twenty, he became a Wèi (魏) Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
At that time, Wèi (魏) laws were severe and harsh.
His mother, Lady Chén, worried about him.
Guàn himself requested to be transferred to Tōngshì Láng (通事郎),
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎).
At that time, powerful ministers monopolized authority.
Guàn navigated their midst with ease,
showing no particular favoritism or aversion.
He was greatly esteemed by Fù Gǔ,
who called him Níng Wǔzǐ.
He served for ten years,
distinguished by his competence in office,
and was repeatedly promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
When the Prince of Chénliú ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中),
holding a staff of authority to comfort and reassure Hébĕi.
For his contribution to settling the deliberations,
his fiefdom was increased.
Several years later, he was transferred to Tíngwèi Qīng (廷尉卿).
Guàn was clear in legal principles.
Whenever he presided over lawsuits,
he handled all matters, great and small, with fairness.
When Déng Ài and Zhōng Huì attacked Shǔ,
Guàn, in his original capacity, held the staff of authority to supervise Ài and Huì's military operations,
acting as the Commander of the General Who Guards the West (Zhèn Xī Jūn Sī),
and was granted a thousand soldiers.
After Shǔ was pacified,
Ài immediately, on his own authority, conferred titles and appointments.
Huì, secretly harboring ulterior motives,
used Ài's unauthorized actions
and secretly memorialized the situation jointly with Guàn.
An imperial edict ordered Ài to be summoned in a caged cart.
Huì sent Guàn to first arrest Ài.
Huì, thinking Guàn had few soldiers,
intended for Ài to kill Guàn,
and then to add this crime to Ài's charges.
Guàn knew Huì intended to endanger him,
but he could not refuse.
So, he went to Chéngdū at night,
issued a declaration to all the generals under Ài's command,
stating that an imperial edict ordered Ài's arrest,
but that nothing else would be investigated.
If they came to join the imperial army,
their ranks and rewards would remain as before;
anyone who dared not come out
would have their three familial generations punished.
By the time the roosters crowed,
all had come to join Guàn,
except for those within Ài's personal tent.
At dawn, the gates were opened.
Guàn rode in the envoy's carriage
directly to the front of the Chéngdū palace.
Ài was still asleep and had not yet risen;
father and son were both captured.
Ài's generals planned to seize Ài by force,
marshaling their weapons and heading towards Guàn's camp.
Guàn calmly went out to meet them,
falsely drafting a memorial
to clarify Ài's situation.
The generals believed him and stopped.
Soon after, Huì arrived.
He then invited all the generals, including Hú Liè,
and consequently arrested them,
imprisoning them in a guesthouse in Yìzhōu,
and then mobilized troops for rebellion.
Thereupon, the soldiers yearned to return home,
and there was unrest both inside and outside;
everyone was anxious and fearful.
Huì kept Guàn to discuss plans.
He then wrote on a tablet,
"I intend to kill Hú Liè and the others,"
and showed it to Guàn.
Guàn disagreed,
which led to mutual suspicion.
Guàn went to the latrine
and saw Hú Liè's former attendant,
whom he sent to spread the word to the three armies
that Huì was rebelling.
Huì pressed Guàn to finalize their plans,
not sleeping for a night,
each with a horizontal sabre across their laps.
The armies outside had already secretly intended to attack Huì,
but since Guàn had not come out,
they dared not initiate the attack.
Huì sent Guàn to comfort and reassure the armies.
Guàn wished to leave,
and also to strengthen his resolve,
saying:
"You are the lord of the three armies;
you should go yourself."
Huì said:
"You are the supervising officer;
you should go first,
and I will follow later."
Guàn then descended from the hall.
Huì regretted sending him away
and sent for Guàn.
Guàn claimed to be dizzy and feeling unwell,
feigning a fall to the ground.
By the time he reached the outer gate,
dozens of messengers were chasing him.
When Guàn reached the outer lodging,
he drank salted soup
and vomited violently.
Guàn was naturally weak,
so he appeared to be severely ill.
Huì sent his close confidants and doctors to check on him;
they all said he would not recover,
so Huì was no longer apprehensive.
By evening,
the gates were closed.
Guàn drafted a declaration and announced it to all the armies.
The armies had already declared righteousness
and jointly attacked Huì the next morning.
Huì led his personal guards to resist,
but the generals defeated them.
Only a few hundred men from his personal tent followed Huì, running around the palace,
and they were all killed.
Guàn then organized the various generals,
and everyone was solemn and orderly.
Dèng Ài's original camp soldiers pursued and broke the caged cart from which Ài was being transported,
returning towards Chéngdū.
Guàn, believing he and Huì had together trapped Ài,
feared a change of plans,
and also wished to monopolize the credit for punishing Huì.
So he dispatched Guard Commander Tián Xù to Miánzhú,
who ambushed Ài at Sānzào Tíng during the night,
and executed Ài and his son Zhōng.
Initially,
when Ài entered Jiāngyóu,
he considered Xù to be hesitant,
and intended to execute him,
but later pardoned him.
When Guàn dispatched Xù,
he said to him:
"Now you can avenge the humiliation at Jiāngyóu."
When the affair was settled,
the imperial court debated ennobling Guàn.
Guàn, considering the achievement of conquering Shǔ,
the efforts of all the commanders,
the rebellious nature of the two generals,
and their self-inflicted demise,
and although he had employed strategy and schemes,
he had no merit in leading charges or planting flags,
firmly declined the offer.
He was appointed Minister-Bearer of the Axe, Area Commander of all military affairs in Guānzhōng, and General of the West-Pacifying Army.
Soon after, he was transferred to Area Commander of all military affairs in Xúzhōu, and General of the East-Pacifying Army,
and his fief was increased to Lord of Zīyáng.
With the remaining ducal rank, his younger brother Shí was enfeoffed as Marquis of Kāiyáng Tíng.
In the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he was transferred to General of the East-Conquering Army,
and his noble rank was advanced to Duke.
He was appointed Area Commander of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu and Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
and was further granted the titles of Grand General of the East-Conquering Army and Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Wherever he served, he achieved good administrative results.
He was appointed Grand General of the North-Conquering Army, Area Commander of all military affairs in Yōuzhōu, Inspector of Yōuzhōu, and Protector of the Wūhuán.
Upon arriving at his post,
he memorialized for the establishment of Píngzhōu,
and later concurrently supervised it.
At that time, in Yōu and Bīng, there were Wùhuán to the east,
and Lìwēi to the west,
both causing trouble on the border.
Guàn sowed discord between the two barbarians,
which eventually led to enmity,
whereupon Wùhuán surrendered and Lìwēi died of anxiety.
The imperial court commended his achievement
and bestowed upon one of his sons the title of Marquis of a Pavilion.
Guàn requested that this be granted to his younger brother.
Before the imperial edict was received, he passed away,
and his son Mì received the title of Marquis of a Pavilion.
Guàn's six sons had no noble titles,
and he yielded all of them to his two younger brothers,
which was praised far and wide.
He repeatedly sought to enter the court.
Upon his arrival,
Emperor Wǔ treated him well,
and soon after ordered him to return to his post.
In the beginning of the Xiánníng era,
he was summoned and appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and was further granted the title of Attendant Censor.
He was severe and orderly by nature,
governing his subordinates with strict laws.
He regarded the Directors of the Imperial Secretariat as his personal staff,
and the Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat as his clerks.
Guàn was deeply learned and widely knowledgeable,
and well-versed in literature and arts.
He and Sǒ Suǒjìng of Dūnhuáng, a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat, were both skilled in cursive script.
People at the time called them
"The Two Excellencies of the Imperial Secretariat."
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, Zhāng Zhī was also skilled in cursive script.
Commentators said that Guàn inherited the "sinews" of Bóyīng,
and Jìng inherited the "flesh" of Bóyīng.
In the beginning of the Tàikāng era,
he was promoted to Minister of Works.
His titles of Attendant Censor and Director of the Imperial Secretariat remained as before.
His administration was clear and simple,
and he gained great renown both at court and among the people.
Emperor Wǔ ordered that Guàn's fourth son, Xuān, marry Princess Fánchāng.
Guàn, considering himself a descendant of ordinary scholars,
and that the marriage match was too humble for his family,
submitted a memorial firmly declining,
but it was not granted.
He also concurrently held the position of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and was granted the establishment of a drum and fife band with a thousand soldiers and a hundred cavalry.
Due to a solar eclipse,
Guàn, along with Grand Commandant Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and Minister of Education Wèi Shū, all offered to resign their posts,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Guàn believed that the Nine-rank System established by the Wèi dynasty
was a temporary measure,
not a permanent and universally applicable system.
He proposed returning to the ancient system of recommendation by the local community and selection from villages.
He and Grand Commandant Liàng and others submitted a memorial stating:
"In ancient times, sagely kings esteemed the worthy,
recommended the good, and instructed them,
thus ensuring that the court was filled with virtue and humility,
and there was no wicked conduct among the populace.
This was truly because the administration of neighborhoods and groups of five households
was sufficient for mutual supervision,
and by inquiring into their actions and examining their words,
their goodness was certainly ascertained.
People knew that fame could not be sought without substance,
and therefore they would cultivate themselves.
Thus, by honoring the worthy, customs became more harmonious,
and by dismissing the wicked, conduct became more upright.
Therefore, the system of recommendation by the local community and selection from villages
was an excellent institution of the former kings.
From then onwards,
this law gradually declined.
The Wèi clan, succeeding to a chaotic era,
and rising after a period of devastation,
saw people migrating and displaced,
making it impossible to thoroughly investigate and examine them.
Therefore, the Nine-rank System was established
merely as a temporary basis for selection and employment.
When it was first created,
the local communities offered pure assessments,
unconstrained by titles,
and the praises and criticisms applied
were sufficient to encourage and admonish,
still retaining some vestiges of local public opinion.
In the interim, it was gradually corrupted,
and eventually, ranks were determined by wealth,
causing everyone to look forward
to only high positions as being noble.
People abandoned virtue and neglected moral cultivation,
contending for petty gains,
damaging customs.
Its弊 (malpractices) were not insignificant.
Now that the nine regions are under a unified rule,
and great transformation is just beginning,
your servants believe it is proper to abolish all these secondary laws,
and uniformly adopt the ancient system,
determining status by land residence.
From the grandees and ministers downwards,
everyone should be officially recognized based on their place of residence,
with no more 'guest households' or those distantly associated with other lands.
In this way,
those of the same locality, neighbors, and groups of five households
will all form a single community.
The administrators of commanderies and counties
will then act as their heads,
and the system of neutral arbiters and Nine-ranks will be completely abolished,
allowing the recommendation of the good and advancement of talent
to be entirely based on local public opinion.
Thus, the lower ranks will respect their superiors,
people will feel secure in their education,
customs and governance will both be purified,
and transformation and law will advance together.
People will know that the teaching of right and wrong
does not depend on social connections,
and then superficial competition will naturally cease,
and each will seek it within themselves.
Now, if the Nine-rank System is abolished,
it should follow the ancient system,
allowing court officials to mutually recommend and appoint.
This would broaden the path for talent to emerge,
and also encourage a public-mindedness in recommending the worthy,
and scrutinize the clarity or obscurity of those in office.
This is truly an excellent institution."
Emperor Wǔ approved of it,
but ultimately could not implement the change.
When Emperor Huì was still the Crown Prince,
all court officials considered him simple-minded
and incapable of managing state affairs.
Guàn often wanted to memorialize for his deposition,
but dared not speak.
Later, during a banquet at Língyún Tái,
Guàn, feigning intoxication,
knelt before the Emperor's couch and said:
"Your servant wishes to submit a proposal."
The Emperor said:
"What is it that you wish to say, Duke?"
Guàn tried to speak but stopped three times.
Then he patted the couch with his hand and said:
"This seat is a pity!"
The Emperor then understood his intention,
and jokingly said:
"Are you truly very drunk, Duke?"
Guàn said nothing further after this.
Empress Jiǎ resented Guàn because of this.
Yuán Xuān
frequently committed excesses due to wine and women. Yáng Jùn
had long been at odds with Yuán Guàn.
Jùn further desired to monopolize power and authority.
If Xuān divorced,
Guàn would surely resign his position.
Therefore, Jùn collaborated with the eunuchs and others to slander him,
hinting to the emperor to have Xuān divorced from the princess.
Guàn was ashamed and fearful,
so he requested retirement, citing old age, and resigned his position.
An imperial edict was then issued, saying:
"Sīkōng Guàn, though not yet of retirement age,
has for years expressed his desire to yield his position,
wishing to fulfill his original intention
while his mind is still sound.
Such utmost sincerity
truly moves Our heart.
We now grant his request,
promoting him to Tàibǎo,
and allow him to reside at his mansion as a duke.
He shall be granted a hundred personal guards,
and retain a Zhǎngshǐ, a Sīmǎ, an Cóngshì Zhōngláng, and clerks;
as well as a grand carriage, imperial cavalry, a feathered banner, and drums and flutes, with all ceremonial regalia,
just as in old precedents.
He shall be granted ten qǐng of kitchen land, fifty mǔ of garden, a million qián, and five hundred bolts of silk;
and bed curtains, mats, and mattresses,
the officials concerned shall ensure they are amply provided,
in accordance with Our intention to honor the worthy."
The appropriate officials further memorialized to arrest Xuān and commit her to the Tíngwèi,
and to dismiss Guàn from his position,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Later, the emperor learned that the eunuchs had fabricated the story,
and wished to reinstate the princess,
but Xuān died of illness.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
he restored Guàn's thousand soldiers.
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
Guàn was made Lù Shàngshūshì,
granted a green ribbon and sash,
allowed to enter the palace with sword and shoes,
and not required to hurry when attending court,
and given a cavalry Sīmǎ,
to assist in governing the court together with Rǔnán Wáng Liàng.
Liàng memorialized to send the various princes back to their fiefs.
When discussed in court with the ministers,
no one dared to agree,
only Guàn supported the matter.
Chǔ Wáng Wěi thus harbored resentment.
Jiǎ Hòu had always resented Guàn,
and moreover feared his uprightness,
which prevented her from indulging in her debauchery and cruelty;
she also heard that Guàn and Wěi had a rift,
so she slandered Guàn and Liàng, accusing them of planning to emulate the deeds of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng.
She prompted the emperor to write a handwritten edict,
ordering Wěi to dismiss Guàn and others from their offices.
A eunuch carried the edict and delivered it to Wěi.
Wěi, being naturally fickle and treacherous,
desired to vent his personal resentment,
and that night sent Qīnghé Wáng Xiá to arrest Guàn.
Guàn's attendants suspected Xiá of having a fabricated edict,
and all advised him, saying:
"According to the Rites and Laws, regarding high-ranking ministers,
there has been no such precedent;
please resist them for now.
Wait until you have reported and received a reply,
it will not be too late to accept execution then."
Guàn did not follow their advice,
and consequently, he, along with his sons Yuè and Yì,
and nine others including his grandsons, were all killed,
at the age of seventy-two.
His two sons, Zǎo and Jiè,
were at a physician's house at the time and thus escaped.
Formerly,
when Dù Yù heard that Guàn had killed Dèng Ài,
he said to the crowd:
"Will Bóyù not escape disaster?
Though he is a famous scholar,
he holds the position of supreme commander,
yet he lacks virtuous reputation,
and does not govern his subordinates with uprightness.
This is a petty man riding in the vehicle of a gentleman,
how can he bear such a responsibility?"
When Guàn heard this,
he immediately went to apologize without waiting for his carriage.
In the end, it was as Yù had predicted.
Initially,
when Guàn's family cooked rice,
some fell to the ground and all turned into snails.
About a year later, the disaster struck.
The Tàibǎo's record keeper, Liú Yáo, and others braved the danger to collect Guàn's body and bury him.
Initially,
when Guàn was Sīkōng,
his camp commander Róng Huì committed a crime,
and Guàn dismissed him.
When the disaster occurred,
Huì joined the soldiers to attack Guàn,
and thus Guàn's sons and grandsons were all caught in the calamity.
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi was executed,
Guàn's daughter wrote to the state officials, saying:
"My late father's name and posthumous title have not been proclaimed,
making him no different from common folk.
I am always surprised that the whole country remains silent.
Where does the fault of the Spring and Autumn period lie?
Filled with grief and indignation,
I thus convey my thoughts."
Thereupon, Yáo and others held yellow banners,
beat the drum of remonstrance,
and memorialized, saying:
"Initially,
when the bearer of the fabricated edict arrived,
the Duke, receiving the edict to be dismissed,
immediately presented his seal and ribbon.
Although there were armed guards,
he did not draw a single blade.
He was further instructed to leave his residence,
and complied, riding in a single carriage.
The text of the fabricated edict merely stated the dismissal of the Duke from office.
However, the Ròujūn and those below immediately acted upon the deception and falsehood,
violating the original text.
They summarily executed the chancellor
without first reporting it,
and arbitrarily arrested his sons and grandsons and immediately executed them,
harming and killing nine people, the minister, his sons, and grandsons.
We humbly observe the imperial edict stating,
'Those who were deceived and misled by the King of Chǔ,
and were not original conspirators, shall all be released.'
The intent of this text,
we believe, refers only to commoners who were driven and coerced to carry white staffs.
According to the law,
those who kill under instruction
cannot be exempted from death.
How much more so for those who personally harmed meritorious officials and
murdered loyal and upright individuals?
Although it is said they were not conspirators,
reason dictates they cannot be pardoned.
Now, although the primary culprit has been executed,
those who carried out the killing still remain.
We fear that the relevant officials have not thoroughly investigated the facts,
and may overlook or fail to exhaust the matter,
allowing the Duke and his sons' enemies and murderers to remain unpunished,
leaving their wronged souls with eternal hatred,
appealing to the heavens,
and causing immense pain to loyal subjects,
a sorrow in this enlightened age.
We ourselves are wounded,
and the funeral arrangements have just been completed.
We respectfully state that when Guàn was previously Sīkōng,
his subordinate aide Róng Huì was unjustly dismissed,
and knew the number of people in Guàn's family and the names of his young grandsons.
Later, Huì was reassigned to the Ròujūn.
That night, Huì stood outside the gate, loudly shouting,
proclaiming an edict to dismiss the Duke and return him to his residence.
When the gate opened,
Huì advanced to the central gate,
again read the false edict he carried,
personally took the Duke's seal, ribbon, and cicada ornaments,
and urged the Duke to leave his residence.
Huì then systematically recorded the members of Guàn's household, including his sons and grandsons,
and had them all taken under armed guard,
besieged north of the East Pavilion road,
and within an instant,
they were all beheaded.
The harm to the Duke's sons and grandsons
was indeed caused by Huì.
Furthermore, leading men to loot the treasury
was also Huì's doing.
If Huì alone is investigated,
all the other conspirators will be exposed.
We beg that the truth be thoroughly investigated
and he be punished by extermination of his clan."
The edict granted this.
The court, considering that Guàn's entire family had suffered undeserved calamity,
posthumously honored Guàn for his meritorious service in conquering Shǔ,
enfeoffed him as Lánlíng Jùn Gōng,
increased his fief by three thousand households,
gave him the posthumous title Chéng,
and granted him the insignia of Jiǎ Huángyuè.
His courtesy name was Jùshān.
In his youth, he was appointed to the Sīkōng Qí Wáng's princely establishment,
then successively served as Tàizǐ Shèrén, Shàngshū Láng, Mìshū Chéng, Tàizǐ Shùzǐ, and Huángmén Láng.
He was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and wrote "Four Forms of Calligraphy":
"In ancient times, during the reign of Huángdì,
he initiated the creation of things.
There were Jǔ Sòng and Cāng Jié,
who first invented written characters and contracts,
to replace knotted ropes.
This was probably inspired by observing bird tracks.
Consequently, they proliferated,
and were called characters,
possessing six principles.
The first is 'indicative characters,'
such as shàng (上) and xià (下).
The second is 'pictographic characters,'
such as rì (日) and yuè (月).
The third is
Xíngshēng.
Jiāng and Hé are examples.
Fourth is Huìyì.
Wǔ and Xìn are examples.
Fifth is Zhuǎnzhu.
Lǎo and Kǎo are examples.
Sixth is Jiǎjiè.
Lìng and Zhǎng are
examples.
As for Zhǐshì,
that which is above is shàng (up),
that which is below is xià (down).
As for Xiàngxíng,
the sun is full, the moon wanes,
imitating their forms.
As for Xíngshēng,
a category forms
the shape,
and a sound is matched to it.
As for Huìyì,
to stop a spear is Wǔ,
human words are Xìn.
As for Zhuǎnzhu,
Lǎo means to live long (shòukǎo).
As for Jiǎjiè,
several
words share the same character.
Though their sounds differ,
the literary meaning is one.
From Huángdì to the Three Dynasties,
their writing did not change.
When Qín adopted Zhuànshū,
and burned the ancient texts,
then
ancient script was lost.
During the reign of Hàn Wǔ,
Lǔ Gōngwáng destroyed Kǒngzǐ's residence,
and obtained the Shàngshū, Chūnqiū, Lúnyǔ, and Xiàojīng.
People at the time, no longer knowing there was ancient
script,
called it Kēdòu Shū.
The Hàn imperial court secretly stored them,
rarely allowing them to be seen.
In early Wèi, the one who transmitted ancient script
was Hándān Chún.
Zǔ Jìnghóu copied Chún's
Shàngshū.
Later, he showed it to Chún,
but Chún could not distinguish it.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
the Sānzì Shíjīng was erected,
and Chún's method was gradually lost.
Because of the name Kēdòu,
people then imitated its
shape.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
a person from Jìxiàn unearthed the tomb of Wèi Xiāngwáng,
obtaining over ten myriad words of bamboo slips.
Examining what Jìnghóu had written,
there was still a semblance.
Ancient
books also had several types;
the one scroll discussing the affairs of Chǔ was the most exquisite.
I secretly delight in it,
thus I have exhausted my foolish thoughts
to praise its beauty.
I am ashamed that I am insufficient to be placed among the works of former
sages,
but hope to preserve the images of the ancients.
Anciently, there was no separate name,
it was called Zìshì (character momentum).
"Huángdì's historians,
Jǔsòng and Cāngjié,
gazed at bird tracks,
and first created writing.
They ordered all things,
established laws and systems,
and imperial canons were promulgated,
with both plain
and ornate aspects manifest in the world.
Then came the tyrannical Qín,
committing monstrous evil.
The Great Way was destroyed,
and ancient script also vanished.
Wèi Wén favored antiquity,
and generations passed down tombs and mounds;
none opened them through the ages,
so truth and falsehood were indistinguishable.
When the Great Jìn began its reign,
it promoted the Dao and spread teachings.
Heaven revealed its images,
and Earth illuminated its writings.
Its writings shone,
brilliant were their patterns.
According to sound, gathering
meaning,
