classifying things methodically: the sun occupies the sovereign's place and fills its measure,
the moon assumes the minister's role and wanes at its side;
clouds gather and spread upwards over the rivers,
stars separate and unfurl their light;
grain and plants flourish and hang their ears,
mountains are lofty and connected by ridges;
insects crawl as if moving,
birds seem to fly but have not yet soared.
Observe their crossed brushes and conjoined ink,
their minds focused
and devoted;
their momentum harmonious and forms balanced,
starting and stopping without gap.
Some maintain rectitude and follow rules,
bending like a carpenter's square and turning like a compass;
others are neither square nor round,
adapting to circumstances and exercising discretion.
Their curves are like bows,
their straight lines like strings.
They rise majestically,
like dragons soaring in the river;
they descend densely,
like rain falling from the sky.
Some wield their brushes with vigor,
like wild geese flying
high,
distant and graceful;
others are unrestrained and elegant,
like hanging tassels or fluttering feathers,
soft and continuous.
Therefore, viewed from afar,
they are like wind sweeping across water,
clear
waves rippling;
observed closely,
they are as if natural.
Truly, they are relics of Huáng and Táng,
a model for the Six Arts.
Zhòuzhuàn is their descendant,
and Lìcǎo is
their great-great-grandchild.
To perceive the images of things and give rise to thought,
this cannot be expressed in words."
In the past, during the reign of Zhōu Xuānwáng,
Shǐ Zhòu first compiled fifteen chapters of Dàzhuàn.
Some parts were the same as ancient script,
some parts were different from ancient script,
and the world called them Zhòushū.
When Píng
wáng moved east,
the feudal lords contended for power,
each family and state being different,
and characters diverged in form.
When Qín Shǐhuángdì first unified the realm,
Chancellor Lǐ Sī then memorialized to supplement them,
abolishing those that did not conform to Qín writing.
Lǐ Sī composed the Cāngjié Piān,
Zhōngchēfǔlì Zhào Gāo composed the Yuánlì Piān,
Tàishǐlìng Húwú Jìng composed the Bóxué Piān.
All of them took
Shǐ Zhòu's Dàzhuàn,
or somewhat simplified and altered it,
which is what is called Xiǎozhuàn.
Some say
that Chéng Miǎo, a minor official from the lower land,
was an official in the imperial prison.
He offended Shǐhuáng,
and was imprisoned in Yúnyáng
for ten years.
From prison, he created a Dàzhuàn,
adding to the fewer strokes,
reducing the more strokes,
making squares round,
and rounds square.
He presented it to Shǐhuáng.
Shǐhuáng approved
of it,
released him, made him an Yùshǐ,
and commanded him to standardize writing.
Some say
that what Miǎo standardized was Lìzì.
Since Qín destroyed ancient script,
there were eight types.
First was Dàzhuàn,
second
was Xiǎozhuàn,
third was Kèfú,
fourth was Chóngshū,
fifth was Móyìn,
sixth was Shǔshū,
seventh was Shūshū,
and eighth was Lìshū.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he ordered
Sīkōng Zhēn Fēng to collate the characters section,
and revise ancient script.
There were again six types of writing.
First was Gǔwén,
the characters from Kǒngzǐ's wall.
Second was Qíjì,
which is ancient
writings which differ.
Third is Zhuànshū,
the Qín Zhuànshū.
Fourth is Zuǒshū,
which is Lìshū.
Fifth is Miùzhuàn,
used for carving seals.
Sixth is Niǎoshū,
used for writing on banners and tallies.
When Xǔ Shèn compiled the Shuōwén,
he used Zhuànshū as the standard,
establishing it as the exemplary style,
which is most suitable for discussion.
In the Qín
era, Lǐ Sī was known for the two Zhuàn styles;
the inscriptions on mountains and bronze figures were all written by Sī.
In the middle of the Jiànchū reign of the Hàn,
Cáo Xǐ of Fúfēng differed slightly from Sī,
but was also called
excellent.
Hándān Chún was his disciple,
and he thoroughly explored its subtleties.
Wéi Dàn was Chún's disciple but did not reach his level.
In the middle of the Tàihé reign,
Dàn served as the Administrator of Wǔdū.
Because of his skill in writing,
he was retained
and appointed as a Shìzhōng.
All the inscriptions on precious artifacts of the Wèi clan were written by Dàn.
In the late Hàn, there was also Cài Yōng,
who adopted the methods of Sī and Xǐ,
creating various ancient and modern forms,
but his precision and elegance
were not as good as Chún's.
Yōng wrote "Zhuànshì" (The Force of Seal Script), saying:
"Bird traces,
Huáng Jié followed.
Sages made rules,
establishing this writing.
There are six forms,
Zhuàn is the true one.
Its form is exquisite,
its skill enters
the divine.
Sometimes like tortoise patterns or needle arrays,
or dragon scales arranged like a comb;
relaxing bodies and releasing tails,
long and short, repeatedly;
drooping like the ears of millet and grain,
densely packed like insects and snakes in burning
hemp;
stirring waves and shaking feathers,
eagles perching, birds trembling;
necks extended, wings pressed,
their momentum seems to pierce the clouds.
Or light strokes cast inward,
thin at the base, thick at the end,
as if broken, as if connected;
like
water dew and green silk,
congealed and hanging at the lower end;
vertical strokes like suspensions,
horizontal strokes like weaving;
subtle and slanting,
neither square nor round;
as if walking, as if flying,
fluttering
and hovering.
Viewed from afar,
it resembles flocks of swans and wild geese playing,
continuously moving and lingering;
observed closely,
its edges and boundaries cannot be seen,
its indications cannot be fully traced.
Yán
Sāng could not count its twists and turns,
Lí Lóu could not perceive its gaps,
Bān and Chuí would bow and yield their cleverness,
Zhòusòng would clasp hands and conceal their writing brushes.
Placed at the head
of books and records,
it shines splendidly, worth admiring.
It displays its brilliant beauty on white silk,
serving as the foremost model for scholarship and art.
We delight in the vast and beautiful virtues of the writing,
yet lament that its creators cannot be completely exhausted.
Considering the ups and downs of the script forms,
I will briefly discuss them."
After Qín adopted Zhuàn,
official reports became numerous,
and Zhuàn characters were difficult to write quickly.
So, Lìrén were ordered to assist with writing,
calling it Lìzì.
The Hàn followed this practice,
using Zhuàn only for tallies, seals,
banners, and inscriptions.
Lìshū is
the faster version of Zhuàn.
Wáng Cìzhòng of Shànggǔ was the first to create the standard script (Kǎifǎ).
When Emperor Líng loved calligraphy,
there were many skilled calligraphers at that time,
but Shī Yíguān was the best.
Large characters were a zhàng in diameter,
small ones could contain a thousand words in a square cùn.
He greatly prided himself on his skill.
Sometimes, when he did not have money to drink at a wine shop,
he would write
on its wall,
letting viewers pay for his wine,
and erasing it when enough money was collected.
Each time he wrote, he would shave and burn his stencils.
Liáng Hú then added boards and treated him to
wine,
waiting for him to get drunk and then stealing his stencils.
Hú eventually reached the position of Shàngshū of the Xuǎnbù through his calligraphy.
Yíguān later became a general under Yuán Shù.
Today, in Sòngzǐ, Jùlù, there is the Gěng Qiú
Stele,
erected by Shù.
Its calligraphy is very skillful,
said to be by Yíguān.
Liáng Hú fled to Liú Biǎo.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi conquered Jīngzhōu,
he sought Hú.
When Hú was
in the Xuǎnbù,
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi wanted to appoint him as the Magistrate of Luòyáng,
but instead made him a Běibù Wèi.
Therefore, he was afraid and bound himself to approach the gate,
where he was appointed Jùn Jiǎ Sīmǎ.
In the Bìshū, he distinguished himself with his diligent
writing,
which is why many of Hú's extant manuscripts exist today.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi hung them in his tent,
and even nailed them to the wall to admire them,
believing them superior to Yíguān's.
Many of the palace
and hall inscriptions today are in Hú's Zhuàn style.
Hú was good at large characters,
Hándān Chún at small characters.
Hú said Chún had obtained Cìzhòng's method,
but Hú's brushwork fully expressed
its potential.
Hú's disciple Máo Hóng taught in the Bìshū,
and today's Bāfēn style all follows Hóng's method.
In the late Hàn, there was Zuǒ Zǐyì,
who differed slightly from Chún and Hú,
but
was also famous.
In the early Wèi, Zhōng and Hú were two families known for Xíngshū,
both having learned from Liú Déshēng,
but the Zhōng family differed slightly.
However, each had their own skill,
and are now widely popular
in the world.
It says in "Lìshì" (The Force of Clerical Script):
"The transformation of bird tracks,
indeed gave rise to Zuǒlì.
Removing those complex characters,
honoring this simplicity and ease.
Its use is already vast,
its forms have
measure.
Radiant like stars arranged,
dense like clouds spread.
The largest are a xún in diameter,
the smallest cannot accommodate a hair.
Adapting to circumstances and suiting convenience,
there is no fixed rule.
Sometimes domed and expansive,
sometimes like comb teeth and needle arrays,
sometimes smooth and straight as a plumb line,
sometimes winding and twisted,
sometimes long, slanted, and angular,
sometimes rotating circularly, sometimes angularly bent.
Long and short complement each other,
different bodies, same
momentum.
The brush is wielded lightly,
separating but not breaking.
Fine waves and thick dots,
scattered between them.
Like bells and stands arranged,
courtyard torches flying smoke.
Towering cliffs, dark and rugged,
high and low, connected.
Like lofty terraces and layered eaves,
rising into clouds and crowning mountains.
Viewed from afar,
like flying dragons in the sky;
observed closely,
the mind is confused, the eyes are dizzy.
Its strange
postures and subtle transformations,
cannot be fully traced.
Yán Sāng could not calculate them,
Zǎi Cì could not describe them.
Why should Cǎozhuàn be worth mentioning,
when this writing remains unproclaimed?"
Is it because of its grand scale that it is difficult to behold,
or because its profundity is not transmitted?
Allow me to observe it closely for a while,
and discuss it in general terms. "
When the Hàn dynasty arose, there was 'Cǎoshū',
but the name of its creator is unknown.
By the time of Emperor Zhāng,
Dù Dù, the Prime Minister of Qí, was renowned for his skill in composing 'Cǎoshū' pieces.
Later, there were Cuī Yuàn and Cuī Shí,
who were also praised for their skill.
Mr. Dù's character endings were very stable,
but his calligraphic style was slightly thin.
Mr. Cuī was very adept at brushwork,
but his character structures were a little sparse.
Zhāng Bóyīng of Hóngnóng,
thereupon refined it further and made it exceedingly ingenious.
Whenever his family had silk cloth,
he would write on it before it was dyed.
He practiced calligraphy by a pond,
until the pond water turned completely black.
Every stroke he made was a model,
and he was so busy that he had no time for 'Cǎoshū'.
Not a single inch of paper was wasted,
and even today, the world treasures his calligraphy,
Wéi Zhòngjiāng called him the 'Cǎoshèng' (Sage of Cursive Script).
Bóyīng's younger brother, Wénshū,
was second only to Bóyīng.
There were also Jiāng Mèngyǐng, Liáng Kǒngdá, Tián Yànhé, and Wéi Zhòngjiāng and their ilk,
all disciples of Bóyīng,
who were famous in the world,
but none
surpassed Wénshū.
Luó Shújǐng and Zhào Yuánsì
were contemporaries of Bóyīng,
praised in Xīzhōu,
and they were proud of their skill and self-satisfied,
which somewhat confused the public.
Therefore,
Bóyīng himself said,
"Compared to Cuī and Dù above, I am insufficient;
compared to Luó and Zhào below, I have more than enough."
Zhāng Chāo of Héjiān was also famous,
but although he was from the same prefecture as Mr. Cuī,
he did not
obtain the method as well as Bóyīng.
Cuī Yuàn wrote 'Cǎoshū Shì' (The Power of Cursive Script), saying:
"The rise of writing
began with Xiéhuáng.
He copied bird tracks
to establish written forms.
By the later ages,
texts
became increasingly numerous.
Times were often difficult,
and governance involved many expedients.
Official duties were neglected,
and writing was simplified.
Only 'Zuǒlì' (clerical script) was created,
and old characters were omitted.
The method of 'Cǎoshū'
is even simpler.
It responds to the moment and conveys meaning,
used in urgency.
It combines efforts and uses them together,
saving time and effort.
This transformation to pure simplicity,
why must it follow ancient styles?
Observe its
form and image:
it bows and rises with grace.
Squares do not conform to the ruler,
circles do not match the compass;
it suppresses to the left and lifts to the right,
looking as if it were rugged.
It stands tall like a bird poised,
its intent to fly and move;
like a cunning
beast startled,
about to gallop but not yet running.
Sometimes it is like cuttlefish or silkworms emitting dots,
resembling a string of pearls,
broken but not separated;
accumulating anger and pent-up emotion,
releasing them to create wonder.
Sometimes it hovers over a deep
ravine, trembling,
as if gripping a dry branch over a precipice;
side dots attach obliquely,
like a cicada gripping a branch.
When the brush stops and the momentum is withdrawn,
the remaining thread entangles,
like Dù Bó carrying poison to climb a perilous cliff,
or a flying
snake entering a hole,
its head submerged and tail drooping.
Therefore, seen from afar,
it is like collapsing peaks and crumbling cliffs;
but observed closely,
not a single stroke can be moved.
Subtle, crucial,
and exquisite,
it adapts to the occasion.
Briefly sketching the general idea,
it is roughly like this."
When Guàn was framed by Chǔwáng Wěi,
upon hearing of the變 (calamity),
he went to Hé Shào,
who was his sister-in-law's father,
through a hole in the wall,
to inquire about the news.
Shào knew but did not tell him.
Upon returning, he passed through the kitchen,
where people were eating,
and was consequently killed.
Later, he was posthumously granted the title of Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and given the posthumous epithet Lánlíng Zhēn Shìzǐ.
He had two sons: Zǎo and Jiè.
Zǎo, courtesy name Zhòngbǎo,
inherited Guàn's noble title.
Later, Dōnghǎiwáng Yuè enlarged his domain with Lánlíng,
and Zǎo was re-enfeoffed as Jiāngxià Jùngōng,
with 8,500 households.
When Emperor Huái ascended the throne,
he served as Sànqí Shìláng.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
he perished in Liú Cōng's rebellion.
Emperor Yuán appointed Guàn's great-grandson Chóng as his successor.
Jiè, courtesy name Shúbǎo.
At five years old,
his demeanor was remarkably refined and unusual.
His grandfather Guàn said:
"This child is different from the crowd;
I am old,
and will not live to see him grow up!"
As a child, he rode a sheep cart into the market,
and those who saw him all thought he was a jade figure;
the entire capital flocked to see him.
Piàojì Jiāngjūn Wáng Jì,
Jiè's maternal uncle,
was handsome and distinguished,
and whenever he saw Jiè,
he would exclaim:
"With pearls and jade beside me,
I feel my own appearance is inferior."
He also once said to others:
"When traveling with Jiè,
it is like having a bright pearl beside one,
radiantly illuminating all."
When he grew up,
he was fond of discussing profound principles.
Later, he was often ill and weak,
and his mother forbade him to speak.
On a propitious day,
when relatives and friends would occasionally ask him for a word,
everyone would sigh with admiration,
believing it to be deeply insightful.
Lángyáwáng Chéng had a high reputation,
and rarely admired anyone,
but whenever he heard Jiè speak,
he would sigh and faint from admiration.
Thus, people of the time created a saying for him:
"When Wèi Jiè discusses the Way,
Píngzǐ faints from admiration."
Chéng, Wáng Xuán, and Wáng Jì all had great reputations,
but all were inferior to Jiè;
the world said,
"The three sons of the Wáng family
are not as good as one child of the Wèi family."
Jiè's father-in-law Lè Guǎng,
had a great reputation throughout the realm;
commentators believed
that "the father-in-law is as pure as ice,
and the son-in-law is as lustrous as jade."
He received numerous invitations to official positions,
but did not accept any.
After a long time,
he became Tàifù Xīgé Jìjiǔ,
and was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
Zǎo served as Sànqí Shìláng,
and attended Emperor Huái within the palace.
Jiè, seeing the great chaos in the world,
wished to move his family south.
His mother said:
"I cannot bear to leave Zhòngbǎo."
Jiè earnestly explained the grave implications
for the family's future,
and his mother tearfully agreed.
At their farewell,
Jiè said to his elder brother:
"The duty of the third son
is highly valued by people.
Now is the day to dedicate yourself;
brother, strive hard!"
Then he helped his mother move to Jiāngxià.
Wèi Jiè's (衛玠) wife had died previously.
The General Who Conquers the South, Shān Jiǎn (山簡), met him
and greatly admired and respected him.
Shān Jiǎn said,
"Formerly, Dài Shūluán (戴叔鸞) married off his daughter,
giving her only to those who were worthy,
without regard for their wealth or status.
How much more so for a person of the Wèi (衛) clan, a powerful and noble household with a distinguished reputation!"
Thereupon, he married his daughter to him.
He then advanced to Yùzhāng (豫章).
At this time, the Grand General Wáng Dūn (王敦) was stationed in Yùzhāng.
His Chief Clerk, Xiè Kūn (謝鯤), had long admired Wèi Jiè.
When they met, they were overjoyed
and conversed for a whole day.
Wáng Dūn said to Xiè Kūn,
"Formerly, Wáng Fǔsì (王輔嗣) uttered 'golden sounds' in the capital.
Now this young man has produced 'jade reverberations' south of the Jiāng (江).
The thread of profound discourse,
though broken, is now reconnected.
I did not expect that at the end of the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
I would again hear the 'sounds of Zhèngshǐ' (正始).
If Hé Píngshū (何平叔) were alive,
he would surely collapse in admiration."
Wèi Jiè (玠) had once remarked that if a person had shortcomings,
one could forgive them out of compassion;
one could dismiss it with reason.
Thus, throughout his life, he never showed signs of joy or anger.
Considering Wáng Dūn's (王敦) unrestrained and unconventional nature,
yet his fondness for asserting dominance over others,
Wèi Jiè feared he might not be a loyal minister to the state,
and requested to return to Jiànyè (建鄴).
Upon hearing of his graceful appearance, the people of the capital
came to gaze upon him in crowds as dense as a wall.
Wèi Jiè's illness, exacerbated by exhaustion, worsened considerably,
and he died in the sixth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉)
at the age of twenty-seven.
People at the time said that Wèi Jiè was "gazed to death."
He was buried in Nánchāng (南昌).
Xiè Kūn (謝鯤) wept for him in profound sorrow.
Someone asked him,
"What sorrow do you feel that causes such grief?"
He replied,
"The main pillar has broken!
I cannot help but grieve!"
During the Xiánhé (咸和) era,
his grave was moved to Jiāngníng (江寧).
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo (王導) issued an instruction saying,
"Wèi Xǐmǎ (衛洗馬) is to be reburied tomorrow.
This gentleman was a distinguished and elegant scholar,
admired by all within the seas.
A modest sacrifice should be prepared
to uphold our old friendship."
Later, Liú Dàn (劉惔) and Xiè Shàng (謝尚) were discussing the prominent figures of the central court.
Someone asked,
"Can Dù Kěfāng (杜可方) be compared to Wèi Xǐmǎ?"
Xiè Shàng replied,
"How can he be compared?
Several people could fit between them."
Liú Dàn also said,
"Dù (杜) has a clear complexion,
but Shūbǎo (叔寶) has a clear spirit."
Such was the esteem in which he was held by discerning people.
At that time, among the famous scholars of the restoration,
only Wáng Chéng (王承) and Wèi Jiè were considered paramount.
His cousin, Wèi Zhǎn (展), whose courtesy name was Dàoshū (道舒),
served successively as Secretarial Court Gentleman and Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
he became Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and was successively promoted to Grand Judge for the Prince of Jìn (晉王).
There were imperial edicts allowing sons to testify against fathers,
or whipping parents to ascertain the whereabouts of their sons.
Wèi Zhǎn considered this to be detrimental to proper moral education,
and memorialized to have them all abolished.
When the restoration began,
he became Court Judge.
He submitted a memorial suggesting the restoration of corporal punishment,
the details of which are in the "Treatise on Penal Law."
He died
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Guanglu.
Zhāng Huá (張華) (son Yī (禕), Wěi (韙), Liú Biàn (劉卞))
Zhāng Huá, courtesy name Màoxiān (茂先),
was a native of Fāngchéng (方城), Fànyáng (范陽).
His father, Zhāng Píng (平), was the Administrator of Yúyáng (漁陽) Commandery under the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
Zhāng Huá was orphaned and poor in his youth,
and herded sheep himself.
Lú Qīn (盧欽) of the same commandery saw him and recognized his talent.
Liú Fàng (劉放), a fellow townsman, also marveled at his ability
and married his daughter to him.
Zhāng Huá's learning was extensive and profound,
his literary compositions elegant and refined.
He was eloquent, knowledgeable, and broadly informed.
There was no book on diagrams, prognostication, or technical arts that he had not thoroughly studied.
In his youth, he was self-disciplined and cautious,
always acting with propriety and decorum.
He was courageous in upholding righteousness
and earnest in assisting those in urgent need.
His capacity and insight were vast and profound;
people of his time
rarely understood him fully.
Initially not well-known,
he composed "Ránjiāo Fù" (鷦鷯賦) to express his sentiments.
Its words are: "How varied are the transformations of creation,
scattering myriad forms among all species!
Among the tiny birds, the wren,
also maintains life and receives vital energy.
It nurtures its humble, fluttering body,
without
yellow or black to elevate its worth;
its feathers are useless for any tool,
its flesh does not grace the sacrificial platter.
Even eagles and hawks pass by with folded wings;
what then should it fear from nets and snares?
In dense thickets and
hidden cages,
there it nests and gathers.
Its flight is not ostentatious,
its soaring not showy.
Its dwelling is easy to find,
its sustenance easy to obtain;
a nest in the forest is but a single branch,
each meal no more than
a few grains.
It roosts without attachment,
it roams without lingering;
it disdains not the lowly bramble,
nor glories in the fragrant orchid.
It takes flight with a movement of its wings,
it finds peace with a settling of its feet.
It commits its life to reason,
and has no trouble with other creatures.
This bird, though lacking intellect,
conducts itself with apparent wisdom.
It does not hoard treasures to invite harm,
nor adorn its exterior to attract burdens.
In stillness, it maintains its nature
without arrogance;
in motion, it follows the course of things with simplicity.
It relies on nature as its resource,
without being enticed or attracted by worldly deceit.
Eagles and vultures wield their beaks and talons,
swans and egrets soar beyond the clouds,
pheasants hide in deep ravines,
peacocks live in distant lands.
Those morning ducks and returning geese,
again
arch their wings and fly further;
all are admired for their fine feathers and plump flesh,
thus they are killed without fault;
they merely carry reeds to avoid snares,
yet ultimately meet their doom in this world.
The fierce goshawk
is tied by a leash,
the clever parrot enters a cage.
Their fierce ambitions are bent to servitude,
they are confined and imprisoned in deep chambers;
they change their voices to please,
thinking to break their wings and become servants.
They yearn for the forests and wilds of Zhōng Dài (鍾岱),
and long for the tall pines of Lǒng Dí (隴坻).
Though they enjoy good fortune today,
it is not like the freedom of old.
The seabirds make their home,
avoiding the wind and
arriving;
the giant cranes of Tiáozhī (條支),
cross mountains to come;
carrying themselves for ten thousand miles,
they drift in fear.
This is because their large bodies obstruct others,
and their extraordinary forms are awe-inspiring.
Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) mold and nourish,
all things in one realm.
Large and small are intertwined,
species numerous and diverse.
The wren nests on a mosquito's eyelash,
the great Peng bird spans the corners of the sky.
This is to say that
what is above is not enough, and what is below has abundance.
Looking broadly across heaven and earth,
how do I truly know the measure of large and small?"
Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) of Chénliú (陳留) saw it
and sighed,
"This is the talent of a king's minister!"
From then on, his fame began to spread.
The Administrator of the Commandery, Xiānyú Sì, recommended Huá as Táicháng Bóshì.
Lú Qīn spoke of him to Emperor Wén,
and he was transferred to Hénán Yǐn Chéng.
Before he took up the post,
he was appointed Zuǒ Zhùzuò Láng.
After a while,
he was promoted to Chángshǐ,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Láng.
Many of the court's deliberative memorials
were adopted,
and he thereby gained full authority.
When the Jìn received the abdication,
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
and enfeoffed as Guānnèi Hóu.
Huá had a powerful memory and photographic recall;
within the four seas,
it was as if he pointed them out on his palm.
Emperor Wǔ once asked about the palace system of the Hàn dynasty and the Jiànzhāng Palace with its thousand gates and myriad households.
Huá answered fluently,
and those who listened never tired.
He drew diagrams on the ground,
captivating everyone around him.
The Emperor was very impressed,
and people at the time compared him to Zǐchǎn.
After several years,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng,
and later given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He suffered the sorrow of his mother's death,
grieving and wasting away beyond the customary rites.
An imperial edict encouraged him,
compelling him to resume his duties.
Initially,
the Emperor secretly plotted with Yáng Hù to attack Wú,
but most of the officials thought it was unfeasible.
Only Huá supported the plan.
Afterwards,
when Hù was critically ill,
the Emperor sent Huá to Hù
to ask about the plan to attack Wú.
The conversation is recorded in Hù's biography.
When the great expedition was about to launch,
Huá was made Dùzhī Shàngshū.
He then calculated the transport and logistics,
and decided the court's strategy.
When the armies had advanced
but had not yet achieved any victories,
Jiǎ Chōng and others memorialized that Huá should be executed to appease the world.
The Emperor said:
"This was my idea,
Huá merely agreed with me."
At that time, all the great ministers thought it was not yet advisable to advance rashly,
but Huá alone firmly insisted,
believing victory was certain.
When Wú was destroyed,
an edict stated:
"Shàngshū and Guānnèi Hóu Zhāng Huá,
previously conspired with the late Tàifù Yáng Hù to devise a grand strategy.
He then presided over military affairs,
allocated forces to various fronts,
calculated strategies and tactics,
and planned to achieve victory.
He has the merit of strategic planning.
He is hereby advanced in enfeoffment to Guǎngwǔ Xiànhóu,
his fief increased by ten thousand households,
one of his sons is enfeoffed as Tínghóu,
with one thousand five hundred households,
and he is granted ten thousand bolts of silk."
Huá's reputation was weighty throughout his generation,
and he was admired and respected by all.
The Jìn historical records and the ceremonial regulations were all entrusted to Huá,
who made many additions and deletions.
Imperial edicts and proclamations of the time were all drafted by him,
and his fame grew even greater,
holding the prospect of becoming a grand councilor.
However, Xún Xù, considering himself from a prominent clan
and relying on the Emperor's deep favor,
resented and disliked him.
He always watched for an opportunity
to send Huá out as a regional governor.
It happened that the Emperor asked Huá:
"Who can be entrusted with matters after my death?"
He replied:
"Among those of illustrious virtue and closest kin,
none is like Qíwáng Yōu."
This was not what the Emperor intended,
slightly offending him,
and so Xù's slanderous words were put into effect.
Huá was then sent out as Chíjié, Dūdū Yōuzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, concurrently Lǐng Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi, Ānběi Jiāngjūn.
He managed and integrated both the new and old populations,
and both the northern tribes and the Huá (Chinese) submitted to him.
The Eastern Yi peoples of Mǎhán and Xīnmí, and other kingdoms, bordering mountains and seas,
more than four thousand *lǐ* from the province,
had for generations remained unsubmissive, over twenty kingdoms,
all sent envoys to pay tribute.
Thus, distant barbarians submitted,
and the four borders were without worry.
Year after year there were abundant harvests,
and the soldiers and horses were strong and flourishing.
The court deliberated on summoning Huá back to serve as Prime Minister,
and also intended to advance his title to Yítóng.
Earlier,
Huá had slandered the recluse Féng Huī to the Emperor.
Dǎn was Huī's younger brother,
and deeply favored by the Emperor.
Dǎn once attended the Emperor,
casually discussing matters of Wèi and Jìn,
and then said:
"Your subject privately believes that the calamity of Zhōng Huì
was somewhat due to Grand Ancestor (Emperor Wén of Wèi, Cáo Pī's father Cáo Cāo)."
The Emperor's countenance changed, and he said:
"What are you saying!"
Dǎn removed his cap and apologized, saying:
"Your subject's words are foolish, ignorant, and blind,
and my crime deserves ten thousand deaths.
However, your subject's humble opinion
still has something to be explained."
The Emperor said:
"How do you explain it?"
Dǎn said:
"Your subject believes that a good charioteer must understand the dynamics of extending and retracting the six reins,
and a good governor must carefully assess the appropriateness of managing officials and controlling them.
Therefore, Zhòng Yóu was suppressed for being overly ambitious,
while Rǎn Qiú was promoted for being humble and yielding.
The eight kings of Hàn Gāo (Emperor Gāozǔ) were annihilated due to excessive favor,
while the generals of Guāngwǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ) ended their lives well due to suppression and moderation.
It is not that superiors differ in benevolence or cruelty,
nor that subordinates differ in foolishness or wisdom.
Rather, it is the acts of elevating, suppressing, granting, and taking away that make it so.
Zhōng Huì's talent and insight were limited,
yet Grand Ancestor praised and lauded him excessively,
commended his strategies,
exalted his fame and status,
placed him in a position of great power,
and entrusted him with a large army.
This caused Huì to believe himself infallible in strategy,
his achievements beyond reward,
and to become arrogant and overbearing,
thus leading to his wicked rebellion.
If Grand Ancestor had merely recognized his minor abilities,
restrained him with great rites,
suppressed him with authority,
and guided him with rules and regulations,
then his rebellious heart would have had no way to arise,
and his rebellious acts no way to succeed."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
Dǎn bowed his head and said:
"Since Your Majesty has affirmed your humble subject's words,
you should consider the gradual formation of firm ice,
and not allow such individuals as Huì to again cause ruin and loss."
The Emperor said:
"Are there any like Huì now?"
Dǎn said:
"Dōngfāng Shuò said, 'How easy is talk?'
And the *Yì* says, 'If a minister is not discreet, he loses his life.'"
The Emperor then dismissed his attendants and said:
"Speak frankly."
Dǎn said:
"Your Majesty's strategizing minister,
who has achieved great merit for the empire,
whose fame is known throughout the realm,
and who holds the responsibility of guarding a frontier region and commanding military forces,
all these are within Your Majesty's sagacious consideration."
The Emperor fell silent.
After a while,
Huá was summoned back to serve as Táicháng.
Due to a broken roof beam in the Ancestral Temple,
he was dismissed from office.
He then lived out the rest of the Emperor's reign,
attending court as a 列侯 (Lièhóu).
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
Huá was made Tàizǐ Shàofù.
He, along with Wáng Róng, Péi Kǎi, and Hé Qiáo, were all feared by Yáng Jùn for their virtue and prestige,
and none were allowed to participate in court politics.
After Jùn was executed,
there was a plan to depose the Empress Dowager.
Officials gathered in the court hall,
and those who deliberated all followed the prevailing sentiment,
believing
that "the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) severed Wén Jiāng,
and now the Empress Dowager has severed herself from the ancestral temple,
so she should also be deposed."
Only Huá argued,
believing that "the way of husband and wife
cannot be obtained by a father from his son,
nor by a son from his father.
The Empress Dowager has not committed an offense against the late Emperor.
Now, she is partial to her kin,
acting not as a mother to the sagely era.
She should be treated according to the precedent of the Hàn dynasty, which demoted Empress Dowager Zhào to Empress Xiàochéng.
Her title as Empress Dowager should be reduced,
and she should revert to being called Empress Wǔ,
residing in a different palace,
to preserve the grace of an honorable end."
This was not followed,
and the Empress Dowager was subsequently deposed as a commoner.
Chǔ Wáng Wěi 楚王瑋, having received a secret imperial edict, killed Tài Zǎi Rǔnán Wáng Liàng 太宰汝南王亮 and Tài Bǎo Wèi Guàn 太保衞瓘, etc.
Internal and external troops were in turmoil,
the imperial court was greatly alarmed,
and no plan could be devised.
Huà Bái Dì 華白帝 said:
"Wěi 瑋 falsely issued an imperial edict and arbitrarily harmed the two dukes.
The generals and soldiers were caught off guard
and thought it was the imperial court's intention,
so they followed him.
Now, if we send a Zōu Yú Fān 騶虞幡 (a banner signifying peace), the external armies will surely lift their siege,
and the principle will undoubtedly spread like wildfire."
The Emperor followed his advice,
and Wěi's 瑋 troops were indeed defeated.
When Wěi 瑋 was executed,
Huà 華, having made the initial plan and rendered meritorious service,
was appointed Yòu Guānglù Dàfū 右光祿大夫, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司, Shìzhōng 侍中, and Zhōngshū Jiān 中書監,
and granted a golden seal and purple ribbon.
He firmly declined the Kāifǔ 開府 appointment.
Jiǎ Mì 賈謐 and the Empress plotted together,
considering Huà 華, though from a common family,
to be cultivated and resourceful,
with no suspicion of overstepping his bounds,
and, when retreating, a figure of hope for the multitude.
They wished to rely on him for the administration of the court
and consult him on matters of government.
Hesitant and undecided,
they consulted Péi Wēi 裴頠.
Wēi 頠 had always highly esteemed Huà 華
and strongly supported the proposal.
Thus, Huà 華 fully devoted himself to assisting and guiding,
mending and supplementing deficiencies.
Although he served under a benighted emperor and a cruel empress,
the realm was peaceful,
which was Huà's 華 achievement.
Huà 華, fearing the empress's family's growing power,
composed "Nǚshǐ Zhēn 女史箴" (Admonitions of the Court Instructress) as a satirical warning.
Though Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu was fierce and jealous,
she knew to respect and value Huà 華.
After a long time,
in recognition of his consistent loyal service,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Zhuàngwǔ Jùn Gōng 壯武郡公.
Huà 華 declined more than ten times,
but an imperial edict strongly urged him,
and he then accepted.
Several years later,
he replaced Xiàpī Wáng Huǎng 下邳王晃 as Sīkōng 司空
and concurrently held the office of Zhùzuò 著作.
When Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu plotted to depose the Crown Prince,
Zuǒ Wèi Shuài Liú Biàn 左衞率劉卞 was greatly trusted and favored by the Crown Prince,
and at every gathering or banquet,
Biàn 卞 was always present.
He frequently witnessed Jiǎ Mì's 賈謐 arrogance,
and the Crown Prince resented it,
expressing it in his words and demeanor;
Mì 謐 also could not tolerate it.
Biàn 卞 questioned Huà 華 about Empress Jiǎ's 賈 Hòu plot.
Huà 華 said:
"I have not heard of it."
Biàn 卞 said:
"I, Biàn 卞, from my humble beginnings,
received your promotion and elevation from a minor official in Xūchāng 須昌
to reach my current position.
A scholar appreciates his confidant,
which is why I speak frankly.
Do you, sir, still doubt me, Biàn 卞?"
Huà 華 said:
"Supposing this were true,
what do you intend to do?"
Biàn 卞 said:
"The Eastern Palace has heroes like a forest,
and the four commanders have ten thousand elite soldiers.
You, sir, hold the position of Āhéng 阿衡.
If we obtain your command,
the Crown Prince could enter the court, assume the duties of Lù Shàngshū Shì 錄尚書事,
and depose Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu in Jīnyǒng Chéng 金墉城.
It would take only the strength of two eunuchs."
Huà 華 said:
"Today, the Son of Heaven is in power.
The Crown Prince
is the son of a man.
Moreover, I have not received the mandate of Āhéng 阿衡.
If we were to suddenly embark on such a course,
it would be to disregard our sovereign and father,
and display unfilial conduct to the world.
Even if it succeeded,
we would still not escape punishment,
let alone with powerful relatives filling the court
and authority not unified.
How could it be peaceful?"
When the Emperor convened his ministers in Shìgān Diàn 式乾殿,
he produced a letter in the Crown Prince's handwriting,
showed it to all the ministers,
and none dared to speak.
Only Huà 華 advised:
"This is a great calamity for the state.
Since the time of Hàn Wǔ 漢武,
every time a legitimate heir has been deposed,
it has led to chaos.
Moreover, the state has held the empire for only a short time;
I beg Your Majesty to consider this carefully."
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Péi Wēi 尚書左僕射裴頠 believed it was appropriate to first investigate the person who delivered the letter,
and also requested to compare it with the Crown Prince's usual handwriting,
otherwise,
he feared there might be fraud.
Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu then brought out more than ten of the Crown Prince's usual petitions,
and the crowd compared them,
but none dared to say they were not genuine.
The discussion continued until sunset without a decision.
The Empress, knowing that Huà's 華 and others' intentions were firm,
then submitted a memorial requesting that the Crown Prince be demoted to a commoner,
and the Emperor approved her request.
Initially,
Zhào Wáng Lún 趙王倫, as Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn 鎮西將軍,
caused chaos in Guānzhōng 關中,
and the Dī Qiāng 氐羌 rebelled.
Thus, Liáng Wáng Róng 梁王肜 was sent to replace him.
Someone advised Huà 華:
"Zhào Wáng 趙王 is greedy and foolish,
trusting Sūn Xiù 孫秀,
causing disorder wherever he goes.
And Xiù 秀 is cunning and deceitful,
a hero among villains.
Now, if we could send Liáng Wáng 梁王 to execute Xiù 秀,
cutting Zhào's 趙 power in half,
and apologize to Guānyòu 關右,
would that not be acceptable?"
Huà 華 agreed,
and Róng 肜 assented.
Xiù's 秀 friend Xīn Rǎn 辛冉 came from the west
and said to Róng 肜:
"The Dī Qiāng 氐羌 rebelled on their own,
it was not Xiù's 秀 doing."
So Xiù 秀 was spared death.
When Lún 倫 returned,
he flattered Empress Jiǎ 賈 Hòu,
and then sought to assume the duties of Lù Shàngshū Shì 錄尚書事.
Later, he also sought to be Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令.
Huà 華 and Péi Wēi 裴頠 both firmly opposed this,
thereby incurring their resentment.
Lún 倫 and Xiù 秀 hated Huà 華 as an enemy.
When the military arsenal caught fire,
Huà 華 feared that this would lead to a rebellion,
so he deployed troops to guard it firmly,
and only then did he send aid.
Consequently, many treasures of successive generations, including Hàn Gāo's 漢高 snake-slaying sword, Wáng Mǎng's 王莽 head, and Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 clogs, were all burned.
At that time, Huà 華 saw a sword fly through the roof,
its destination unknown.
Initially,
in the Zhuàngwǔ Commandery (壯武郡) enfeoffed to Huá (華), a mulberry tree transformed into a cypress.
Those who recognized this deemed it inauspicious.
Furthermore, Huá's (華) residence and his secretariat often experienced strange occurrences.
His youngest son, Wěi (韙), seeing the rupture of the Central Terrace star,
advised Huá (華) to abdicate.
Huá (華) did not comply,
saying:
"The ways of Heaven are profound and distant.
One can only respond by cultivating virtue.
It is better to calmly await it,
and defer to Heaven's decree."
When Lún (倫) and Xiù (秀) were about to depose Empress Jiǎ (賈后),
Xiù (秀) sent Sīmǎ Yǎ (司馬雅) to inform Huá (華) secretly at night, saying:
"Now the state is in peril.
King Zhào (趙王) wishes to jointly rectify the court with you,
and undertake the affairs of a hegemon."
Huá (華) knew that Xiù (秀) and the others would inevitably achieve usurpation,
and thus refused them.
Yǎ (雅) angrily said:
"The blade is about to be placed at your neck,
yet you speak thus!"
He left without looking back.
Huá (華) was then sleeping during the day,
when he suddenly dreamt that his house had collapsed.
He awoke and felt it to be ominous.
That night, the rebellion broke out.
They falsely claimed an imperial edict to summon Huá (華),
and he was subsequently arrested along with Péi Wěi (裴頠).
When Huá (華) was about to die,
he said to Zhāng Lín (張林):
"Do you wish to harm a loyal minister?"
Lín (林) claimed an imperial edict and questioned him, saying:
"As a prime minister,
responsible for the affairs of the realm,
when the Crown Prince was deposed,
why did you not die for your principles?"
Huá (華) replied:
"Regarding the deliberation at Shìqián (式乾),
my remonstrances are fully preserved;
it is not that I did not remonstrate."
Lín (林) said:
"If your remonstrances were not followed,
why did you not resign your position?"
Huá (華) could not answer.
A moment later,
an envoy arrived and said:
"An imperial edict orders the execution of His Excellency."
Huá (華) said:
"I am an old minister of the former emperor;
my heart is as red as cinnabar.
I do not begrudge death;
I fear the difficulties of the royal house,
and the calamity will be immeasurable."
He was then killed south of the horse path in the front hall.
His three familial exterminated.
No one in the court or among the common people did not mourn him.
He was sixty-nine years old at the time.
Huá (華) had a fondness for people,
tirelessly promoting and advancing them.
Even those of impoverished status who knocked at his gate, if they possessed a single virtue,
he would sigh in praise,
and extend their reputation.
He greatly loved books.
On the day of his death,
his household had no surplus wealth,
only literary works overflowing from his desks and chests.
He once moved residences,
transporting thirty cartloads of books.
Zhì Yú (摯虞), the Director of the Imperial Library, compiled and standardized official texts,
all relying on Huá's (華) editions for verification.
All rare and secret items in the world,
those rarely seen by generations,
were all in Huá's (華) possession.
Due to this, he was learned in natural history and widely read,
with no one in his generation comparable to him.
During Emperor Huì's (惠帝) reign,
someone obtained a bird feather three *zhàng* (丈) long
and showed it to Huá (華).
Huá (華) saw it
and said sorrowfully:
"This is called the feather of a sea cormorant;
when it appears, the world will be in chaos."
Lù Jī (陸機) once presented Huá (華) with salted fish.
At that time, guests filled the seats.
Huá (華) opened the container
and immediately said:
"This is dragon meat."
The crowd did not believe him.
Huá (華) said:
"Try washing it with bitter wine;
there will surely be something unusual."
Afterward, a five-colored light arose.
Jī (機) returned and asked the owner of the salted fish,
who indeed said:
"Under a stack of straw in the garden, a white fish was found,
of a very unusual appearance.
It was made into salted fish;
it was exceptionally delicious,
so it was presented to you."
The military arsenal was sealed very tightly,
but suddenly pheasants crowed within it.
Huá (華) said:
"This must be a snake transformed into a pheasant."
They opened it and looked;
indeed, there was a snake slough beside the pheasants.
At Línpíng (臨平) in Wú Commandery (吳郡), the bank collapsed,
uncovering a stone drum.
When struck, it made no sound.
The Emperor asked Huá (華) about it.
Huá (華) said:
"You can take paulownia wood from Shǔ (蜀),
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it; then it will make a sound."
They followed his words,
and indeed, the sound was heard for several *lǐ* (里).
Initially,
before the state of Wú was extinguished,
there was always a purple aura between Dǒu and Niú,
and all practitioners of divination and geomancy believed that Wú was strong and prosperous,
and could not yet be overthrown.
Only Huá thought otherwise.
After Wú was pacified,
the purple aura became even brighter.
Huá heard that Lái Huàn from Yùzhāng was adept at understanding celestial phenomena,
so he invited Huàn to stay the night,
and, dismissing all attendants, said:
"Let us together observe the celestial phenomena
to know the auspicious and inauspicious events of the future."
Thereupon, they ascended a tower and gazed upwards.
Huàn said:
"I have observed this for a long time;
there is indeed a strange aura between Dǒu and Niú."
Huá asked:
"What omen is this?"
Huàn replied:
"It is the essence of a precious sword,
piercing through to heaven."
Huá said:
"Your words are correct.
When I was young, a physiognomist told me
that when I reached over sixty years of age,
and attained the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers,
I would obtain a precious sword to wear.
Could this prophecy be coming true!"
He then asked:
"In what commandery is it located?"
Huàn replied:
"It is in Fēngchéng, Yùzhāng."
Huá said:
"I wish to ask you to serve as its magistrate,
so we can secretly search for it together,
would that be permissible?"
Huàn assented.
Huá was greatly pleased,
and immediately appointed Huàn as the Magistrate of Fēngchéng.
When Huàn arrived at the county,
he excavated the foundations of the prison,
going down over four zhàng into the earth,
and found a stone casket.
Its light and aura were extraordinary.
Inside were two swords,
both inscribed.
One was named Lóngquán,
and the other Tàia.
That evening,
the aura between Dǒu and Niú was no longer seen.
Huàn used soil from beneath the northern cliff of Xīshān in Nánchāng to polish the swords,
and their gleam shone brilliantly.
He filled a large basin with water,
placed the swords upon it,
and those who looked at them found their eyes dazzled by the sharp brilliance.
He sent an envoy to deliver one sword and some soil to Huá,
keeping one for himself.
Someone said to Huàn:
"You found two and sent one;
how can Zhāng Gōng be deceived?"
Huàn replied:
"The present dynasty is about to fall into chaos,
and Zhāng Gōng will suffer its calamity.
This sword is destined to be hung on the tree at Xú Jūn's tomb.
Spirits and wondrous objects
will eventually transform and depart,
not to be possessed by humans forever."
When Huá received the sword,
he treasured it dearly,
always keeping it by his side.
Huá felt that the Nánchāng soil was not as good as the red earth from Huáyīn,
and wrote a letter in reply to Huàn, saying:
"Upon detailed examination of the sword inscription,
it is Gānjiàng;
why then did Mòyé not arrive as well?
Nevertheless,
heaven-born divine objects
will eventually be reunited."
He then sent one jīn of Huáyīn soil to Huàn.
Huàn polished the sword with it again,
and it became even brighter and more brilliant.
When Huá was executed,
the sword's whereabouts were lost.
After Huàn died,
his son, Huá, served as a Commandery Commissioner.
While carrying the sword and passing through Yánpíngjīn,
the sword suddenly leaped out from his waist and fell into the water.
He ordered someone to dive into the water to retrieve it,
but the sword was not seen;
instead, two dragons, each several zhàng long,
were seen coiled and embellished with patterns.
The diver was frightened and returned.
A moment later, a brilliant light illuminated the water,
and the waves surged.
Thus the sword was lost.
Huá sighed and said:
"My late father's words about them transforming and departing,
and Zhāng Gōng's theory of their eventual reunion,
is this not the verification of it!"
Many of Huá's encyclopedic observations were like this,
and cannot be fully recorded.
Later, after Lún and Xiù were executed,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng assisted in the government.
Zhì Yú submitted a memorial to Jiǒng, saying:
"Recently, after Zhāng Huá's death, I entered the Central Secretariat
and obtained a draft of Huá's reply to an imperial edict from the time of the late emperor.
The late emperor asked Huá whom he could entrust with assisting the government and important matters for the future.
Huá replied: 'Among those of clear virtue and closest kin,
none is like the former prince;
he should be retained as a pillar of the state.'
His loyal and good counsel,
his sincere words,
were trusted by the gods;
they became evident after his death.
He cannot be discussed in the same breath as those who merely go along with the times.
Some critics blame Huá for not staunchly opposing the matter of Crown Prince Mǐnhuái in court.
At that time,
any remonstrator would surely have met a disobedient death.
The teachings of the ancient sages state
that one should not blame others
for dying without benefit.
Thus, Yàn Yīng,
the Chief Minister of Qí,
did not die in the calamity of Cuī Zhù;
Jì Zhá,
a clan elder of Wú,
did not contend over the principles of rebellion or loyalty.
When reasons are exhausted and nothing can be done,
it is indeed what the teachings of the sages do not hold accountable."
Jiǒng then memorialized, saying:
"Your servant has heard that reviving what is weak and continuing what is cut off
are the lofty policies of sagely kings;
condemning evil and praising good
are the noble principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, King Wǔ sealed the tomb of Bǐ Gān
and honored the dwelling of Shāng Róng,
truly because the visible and the invisible can communicate with each other.
Sūn Xiù, in his rebellious disorder,
destroyed ministers who aided the founding of the state
and executed honest and upright officials,
thereby harming the royal house;
he indulged in his tyranny and cruelty,
and many descendants of meritorious officials
were wiped out.
Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi were each executed at the time due to being feared;
Xiè Xì and Xiè Jié similarly suffered harm for being 'lambs';
Ōuyáng Jiàn and others died innocently,
and the common people pitied them.
Now, Your Majesty brings forth the light of a new era
and issues decrees for renovation,
yet these various families have not yet received grace and justice.
In the past, Luán and Xì were degraded to servitude,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded their transgressions;
King Yōu cut off the descendants of meritorious officials
and abandoned the children and grandchildren of worthy men,
and poets used this as satire.
Your servant, though unworthy, is in office
and wishes to offer humble sincerity.
If this accords with the sagely intention,
the various officials can be ordered to discuss it thoroughly."
The discussants each held their own views,
but many spoke of their injustice.
Zhú Dào, a minister of Zhuàngwǔ Guó, also went to the King of Chángshā
to request the restoration of Huá's titles and ranks,
and those who prevaricated delayed it for a long time.
In the second year of Tàipíng
an imperial edict stated:
"Indeed, love and hatred attacking each other,
and flattery and evil slandering the upright,
have existed since ancient times.
Therefore, the former Sīkōng and Duke of Zhuàngwǔ, Huá, exhausted his loyalty and integrity,
and sought to assist the court government.
His meritorious counsels and strategies
were relied upon in every matter.
Previously, because of Huá's meritorious assistance,
he should have been enfeoffed equally,
yet Huá firmly declined it eight or nine times,
deeply explaining that the great system could not be like that,
and that there would ultimately be concerns of downfall and disgrace.
His words of refusal were earnest and sincere,
sufficient to encourage those near and far.
Huá's utmost sincerity
was sworn to the gods.
Huá received his title from the late emperor
for his meritorious service in conquering Wú.
Later enfeoffment was neither in line with the state system
nor appropriate for a small achievement to surpass a previous great reward.
Huá's death
was entirely due to traitorous rebels plotting chaos,
and he was wrongfully killed.
Therefore, restore Huá's positions of Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Jiān, Sīkōng, Gōng, and Guǎngwǔ Hóu, along with his confiscated property, official seals, and tally sticks.
Send an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices."
Initially,
Lù Jī and his brothers were high-spirited and proud,
considering themselves to be a prominent family from Wú.
When they first arrived in Luò,
they did not think highly of the gentry of the Central Plains.
However, upon meeting Zhāng Huá, they felt as if they had known him for a long time.
They admired Zhāng Huá's virtuous conduct,
treating him with the respect due to a teacher.
After Zhāng Huá was executed,
Lù Jī composed an elegy for him,
and also wrote "An Ode to Virtue" to mourn him.
Zhāng Huá authored ten scrolls of the Bówù Zhì,
and his literary works circulated widely in the world.
He had two sons: Yī and Wěi.
Yī, whose courtesy name was Yànzhòng,
was studious
and humble, possessing his father's demeanor.
He successively held the position of Sànqí Chángshì.
Wěi was learned in Confucian classics
and understood astronomy,
serving as a Sànqí Shìláng.
Both were killed at the same time.
Yī's son, Yú,
whose courtesy name was Gōng'ān,
inherited Zhāng Huá's noble title.
He crossed the river to escape danger,
and was appointed Céngxiàng Yuàn and Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Liú Biàn, whose courtesy name was Shúlóng,
was a native of Xūchāng, Dōngpíng.
He was originally from a military family,
and was straightforward and a man of few words.
When he was young, he served as a low-ranking county official.
One night, the Gōngcáo, drunk, went to the latrine
and ordered Liú Biàn to hold a torch.
Liú Biàn refused to comply.
The Gōngcáo resented this
and appointed him to a subordinate position at the post station for another matter.
There was a scholar named Zǔ Xiùcai
who was writing a letter to the刺史 (Cìshǐ) at the post station.
He took a long time to complete it.
Liú Biàn instructed him with a few words
that were remarkably insightful and profound.
Zǔ Xiùcai said to the county magistrate:
"Liú Biàn
is an excellent candidate for a staff member in the duke's administration.
How can you make him a subordinate at a post station?"
The magistrate immediately summoned him to be a Ménxià Shǐ.
However, Liú Biàn's handling of affairs was too simple and unrefined,
and he could not be meticulous.
The magistrate asked Liú Biàn:
"Can you study?"
He replied:
"I wish to."
So the magistrate sent him to study.
Not long after,
Liú Biàn's elder brother, who was the Tàizǐ Chángbīng,
died.
According to custom, the position had to be filled by a substitute.
The Gōngcáo requested that Liú Biàn replace his brother in service.
The magistrate said:
"Zǔ Xiùcai has spoken of him."
So he did not consent.
Later, Liú Biàn followed the magistrate to Luò
and was able to enter the Tàixué.
After passing an examination on the classics, he became a fourth-grade official in the bureau.
Fǎngwèn ordered him to copy a cartload of yellow papers.
Liú Biàn said:
"Liú Biàn is not one to copy yellow papers for others."
Fǎngwèn, realizing Liú Biàn's anger,
reported it to the Zhōngzhèng.
Liú Biàn was demoted to Shàngshū Lìshǐ.
Someone said to Liú Biàn:
"Your talent is broad but lacks detail.
You are suited for grand tasks, not petty ones.
It would be better to be a Shǒushèrén."
Liú Biàn followed this advice.
Later, he became Lìbù Lìshǐ,
then was promoted to Sīkōng Zhǔbù for Qí Wáng Yōu,
and subsequently transferred to Tàicháng Céng, Sītú Zuǒ Xīcáo Yuàn, and Shàngshū Láng.
He performed his duties commendably in all these positions.
He was successively promoted to Sànqí Shìláng
and appointed Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He returned to the capital as Zuǒwèilǜ.
He learned of Jiǎ Hòu's plot to depose the crown prince
and was greatly worried by it.
He tried to advise Zhāng Huá with a plan, but it was not adopted,
which made him even more disturbed.
Jiǎ Hòu's relatives and partisans secretly observed outside matters in plain clothes,
and they heard some of Liú Biàn's remarks.
So Liú Biàn was transferred to Qīngchē Jiàngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Liú Biàn, knowing his words had been leaked,
feared execution by Jiǎ Hòu,
and thus drank poison and died.
Initially,
when Liú Biàn was going to Bìngzhōu,
more than ten people who had been his fellow low-ranking officials in Xūchāng years ago held a farewell banquet for him.
One of them slighted Liú Biàn,
who ordered him to be escorted out.
People thought less of him because of this.
The historian remarks: Indeed, loyalty is a noble virtue,
and learning is the glory of the nation,
like the stars having ritual and righteousness,
and human relations having their crowns and caps.
Wèi Guàn stroked the couch of Emperor Wǔ,
and Zhāng Huá resisted Zhào Lún's command.
In giving remonstrance, Bóyù was prominent;
in facing danger, Màoxiān excelled.
Following a treacherous path,
there is reason to say: when chaos begins to solidify,
affairs deviate from their proper course;
when pine and bamboo remain unchanged,
death is preferable to life.
They were determined to rush into action
and did not shrink from ruin.
Both fell into the net of depravity,
and together lamented accepting the sword.
The state and families were destroyed and withered;
is this not grievous!
An encomium says: Worthy men committed themselves,
their principles illuminating the cold heights.
Drawing salaries and witnessing ruin,
my life is not at ease.
Wèi perished due to Jiǎ,
Zhāng was destroyed by Zhào.
To be loyal in a chaotic age
has always been difficult.
Collation Notes

Biographies, Volume 7. Imperial Clan: Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú (Son Yōng; Yōng's younger brother Yìyáng Chéng Wáng Wàng; Wàng's son Héjiān Píng Wáng Hóng; Hóng's son Wēi; Hóng's younger brother Suí Mù Wáng Zhěng; Zhěng's younger brother Jìnglíng Wáng Máo; Wàng's younger brother Tàiyuán Chéng Wáng Fǔ; Fǔ's younger brother Yì; Yì's younger brother Xiàpí Xiàn Wáng Huǎng; Huǎng's younger brother Tàiyuán Liè Wáng Guī; Guī's younger brother Gāoyáng Yuán Wáng Guī; Guī's younger brother Chángshān Xiào Wáng Héng; Héng's younger brother Pèi Shùn Wáng Jǐng)
Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú, whose courtesy name was Shúdá,
was Emperor Xuān's second younger brother.
Initially,
Fú's eldest brother, Lǎng, whose courtesy name was Bódá;
Emperor Xuān, whose courtesy name was Zhòngdá;
Fú's younger brother, Kuí, whose courtesy name was Jìdá;
Xún, whose courtesy name was Xiǎndá;
Jìn, whose courtesy name was Huìdá;
Tōng, whose courtesy name was Yǎdá;
Mǐn, whose courtesy name was Yòudá;
all were renowned.
Therefore, at that time, they were called
"the Eight Dás."
Fú was gentle, generous, honest, and yielding,
and widely studied the classics and histories.
During the chaos and destruction at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
he and his brothers lived amidst danger and ruin,
eating from a bamboo basket and drinking from a gourd,
yet he never tired of reading.
He was tolerant by nature,
and established himself with integrity and purity,
never bearing grudges against others.
Yīn Wǔ of Chénliú was famous throughout the land.
He once suffered a criminal punishment,
and Fú went to visit him.
He then shared his residence and food with him,
a deed praised by commentators.
Chensī Wáng Zhí of Wèi, who possessed outstanding talent,
carefully selected his officials
and appointed Fú as Wénxué Yuàn.
Zhí, relying on his talent, looked down on others.
Fú frequently offered sharp remonstrances,
which initially did not please Zhí,
but later Zhí apologized to him.
Fú was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi died,
the crown prince wailed excessively.
Fú remonstrated, saying:
"The great departed has ascended to heaven,
and the world relies on Your Highness for its life.
You must, above, serve the ancestral temples,
and below, serve the myriad states.
Why should you imitate the filial piety of a common man?"
The crown prince stopped after a long while
and said:
"Your words are correct."
At that time, when the officials first heard of the emperor's death,
they gathered and wailed,
losing all sense of order.
Fú sternly spoke in the court, saying:
"Now that the great departed has ascended to heaven,
the world is shaken.
We should swiftly enthrone the heir to stabilize the realm,
and not just weep!"
Fú, with Shàngshū Hé Qià, dismissed the officials,
prepared the imperial guard,
arranged the funeral rites,
and supported the crown prince in his ascension to the throne.
This was Emperor Wén.
At that time, officials like the Shìzhōng and Chángshì were to be selected.
The crown prince’s old associates from his inner circle somewhat subtly hinted to the authorities,
wishing to promote themselves directly
without allowing other candidates.
Fú said:
“Even if there were Yáo and Shùn,
there would still be Jì and Xiè.
Now that the successor ruler has just ascended,
we should advance and employ the talented and virtuous from all corners of the land.
We still fear we might not find enough,
how then can one wish to seize the opportunity to recommend themselves?
If officials are ill-suited to their posts,
then those who obtain them are not worthy of esteem.”
So, other candidates were chosen.
Fú was transferred to be Zhōngshūláng and Gěishì Chángshì,
lodging within the palace province.
He was appointed Huángmén Shìláng
and granted the rank of Qí Dūwèi.
At this time, Sūn Quán declared himself a vassal
and requested to send a hostage.
Yú Jìn, the former general, was supposed to return,
but he was long overdue.
The Son of Heaven asked Fú about this.
Fú said:
“The former kings established the system of nine zones of dependence,
truly because distant and wild regions are difficult to win over with virtue,
and should not be held to the rites of the central states.
Your Majesty inherits the lineage,
and distant peoples bring tribute.
Although Sūn Quán has not yet sent a hostage
and Yú Jìn has not returned,
it is still proper to treat him leniently.
We should raise and train soldiers and horses
to observe his changes.
We should not demand or blame him based on suspicion,
lest we harm the principle of cherishing distant peoples.
From Sūn Cè to Sūn Quán,
their family has succeeded each other for generations.
The matter of strength and weakness
does not hinge on one Yú Jìn.
Yú Jìn's delay
must be due to other reasons.”
Later, Yú Jìn arrived,
indeed having been delayed by illness,
but the hostage never arrived.
When a large army approached the Jiāng River
and blamed him for breaking his word,
Wú subsequently completely ceased tribute.
Later, Fú was appointed Hénèi Diǎnnóng,
granted the title Guānnèi Hóu,
and then transferred to be Qīnghé Tàishǒu.
Initially,
Emperor Wén of Wèi established the Dùzhī Shàngshū,
solely in charge of military and state expenditures.
The court deliberated that as expeditions had not ceased,
every movement required careful budgeting.
When Emperor Míng succeeded to the throne,
he wished to employ Fú
and asked his attendants:
“Does he have the disposition of his elder brother?”
They replied:
“He resembles his elder brother.”
The Son of Heaven said:
“If I have two Sīmǎ Yìs,
what worries do I have then!”
Fú was transferred to be Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Fú believed that to capture the enemy and achieve victory,
preparations should be made.
Whenever Zhūgě Liàng invaded Guānzhōng,
the border troops were unable to repel the enemy,
and the central army rushed to the scene,
often failing to arrive in time for the critical moment.
He suggested pre-selecting twenty thousand infantry and cavalry,
divided into two units,
as a defense against invaders.
He also noted that Guānzhōng had repeatedly suffered enemy invasions,
leading to a shortage of grain and silk.
He dispatched five thousand peasant households from Jìzhōu to garrison Shàngguī,
where they would train in combat in autumn and winter,
and cultivate fields and mulberry trees in spring and summer.
As a result, Guānzhōng had a surplus in military and state resources,
and was prepared for the enemy.
Later, he was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
advanced to the title Chāngpíng Tínghóu,
and promoted to Shàngshūlìng.
When Dàjiāngjūn Cáo Shuǎng wielded power arbitrarily,
Lǐ Shèng, Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, and others created political disorder,
Fú did not concern himself with mundane affairs,
but merely kept himself upright and avoided harm.
When Xuāndì executed Cáo Shuǎng,
Fú and Jǐngdì garrisoned the Sīmǎ Mén.
For his merits, he was advanced to the title Chángshè Xiànhóu
and granted the additional post of Shìzhōng.
At that time, the Wú general Zhūgě Kè besieged Xīnchéng,
and Fú was promoted to supervise all two hundred thousand troops to defend against him.
Fú arrived at Shòuchūn
and dispatched Wúqiū Jiǎn, Wén Qīn, and others to advance and attack.
The generals wished to strike quickly.
Fú said:
“An attacker
uses the strength of others to achieve success,
and should also employ cunning,
not contend by force.”
Therefore, he delayed for over a month before advancing the army,
and the Wú army retreated at the mere sight of them.
When Empress Míngdào of Wèi died,
there was a discussion about inscribing the funerary banner.
Some wished to omit the surname and simply inscribe Wèi,
while others wished to inscribe both.
Fú believed:
“According to the correct meaning of the classics,
neither should be inscribed.
All emperors and kings used the name of their original state as the designation for the realm
to distinguish themselves from past dynasties,
not to choose a beautiful name to glorify themselves.
Heaven is called Huángtiān,
so the Emperor is called Huángdì;
Earth is called Hòutǔ,
so the Empress is called Huánghòu.
This is how they share the grand titles of heaven and earth,
spreading the unique and esteemed names.
They do not need to use the state name to identify themselves,
nor wait to use their clan name to make themselves known.
Therefore, in the Spring and Autumn Annals, in the third year of Yǐnggōng, the classic text states: 'In the third month, on the day Gēngxū, the Heavenly King died.'
He is honored as 'Heavenly,'
and not called 'King of Zhōu,'
to distinguish him from the rulers of the various states.
'In the eighth month, on the day Gēngchén, Duke Hé of Sòng died.'
The state name and personal name are recorded
to distinguish him from the Heavenly King.
In the fifteenth year of Xiānggōng, the classic text states: 'Liú Xià met the Queen in Qí.'
It does not say 'met Empress Jiāng of Zhōu,'
to distinguish her from the wives of the various states' rulers.
As for the various states,
it says: 'Lady Jiāng arrived from Qí,'
and also 'Jì Bójī died.'
The state name and surname are recorded,
which distinguishes them from the Heavenly King’s empress.
From this, we can deduce,
that when honoring the Emperor,
his majesty is resplendent and unique.
What need is there for 'Wèi'?
When honoring the Empress,
she is distinguished by her posthumous title.
What need is there for a surname?
Those who suggest writing 'Wèi'
believe that the esteemed Heavenly Emperor
is equivalent to the rulers of ancient states.
Or those who suggest writing the surname
believe that the Heavenly Emperor's Empress
is equivalent to the wives of ancient times.
This deviates from the great principles of the classics
and differs from the clear system established by the sages.
This is not how to pass down instructions for the future
or serve as an unchangeable model for all generations.”
So, Fú’s suggestion was adopted.
He was promoted to Sīkōng.
He replaced Wáng Líng as Tàiwèi.
When the Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi invaded Lǒngyòu,
the Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jīng was defeated.
Fú was sent west to garrison Guānzhōng,
overseeing all military affairs.
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Chén Tài and Ānxī Jiāngjūn Dèng Ài attacked Jiāng Wéi,
and Jiāng Wéi retreated.
Fú returned to the capital,
and was transferred to Tàifù.
When Gāoguìxiāng Gōng met with misfortune,
none of the officials dared to rush to him.
Fú pillowed the corpse on his lap
and wept bitterly,
saying:
“That Your Majesty was killed is my crime.”
He then memorialized to investigate the perpetrators.
It happened that the Empress Dowager ordered a commoner's funeral,
but Fú and the various dukes submitted a memorial,
requesting a royal funeral,
which was granted.
Fú was by nature extremely cautious.
When Xuāndì was in power,
he always humbled himself.
Later, during times of deposition and establishment,
he never participated in conspiracies.
Emperors Jǐng and Wén, considering Fú to be of a senior position,
did not dare to pressure him.
Later, he was advanced to be Lánglè Gōng.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
the King of Chénliú went to Jīnyǒngchéng.
Fú bid farewell,
holding the king's hand,
shedding tears and sobbing,
unable to control himself.
He said:
"On the day I die,
I will still be a pure minister of Great Wèi."
An imperial edict stated:
"The Grand Tutor's meritorious virtue is great and abundant,
and I look up to him.
To brightly guide and broadly instruct,
and to pacify the realm,
I wish to honor him with the rites due to one who is not a subject.
He is to be enfeoffed as the King of Ānpíng,
with four hundred thousand households.
He is promoted to Grand Preceptor, holds the imperial credential, and is Superintendent of All Military Affairs, internal and external."
The officials reported that
for those kings who had not yet gone to their states,
the appointed officials
were not yet fully established.
The Emperor considered Fú's bright virtue and esteemed position,
and that he should disseminate civilization and establish teachings
to serve as a model for all lords.
Thus, all official positions were fully established for him.
Moreover, because Fú had relatives on his mother's side
and friends on his father's side,
and the expenses for benefiting his subordinates
were not abundant,
two thousand bolts of silk were granted.
During the New Year's assembly,
an edict commanded Fú to ascend the hall in the imperial carriage,
and the Emperor welcomed and bowed to him at the eastern steps.
Once seated,
the Emperor personally offered a cup of wine to wish him longevity,
like a family member.
Each time the Emperor bowed,
Fú knelt to stop him.
He was also given a mica sedan and a blue-canopied carriage.
Although Fú was highly honored,
he did not consider it glorious,
and often had a worried expression.
At his death,
he left a will saying:
"Sīmǎ Fú, courtesy name Shúdá, a steadfast scholar of Wèi from Wēnxuàn, Hénèi,
was neither Yī nor Zhōu,
neither Yí nor Huì.
He established himself and practiced the Way,
consistent from beginning to end.
He should be laid in a plain coffin and a single outer coffin,
shrouded in everyday clothes."
He passed away in the eighth year of Tàishǐ at the age of ninety-three.
The Emperor mourned for three days at the Eastern Hall of Tàijí.
An edict stated:
"The King's meritorious virtue surpasses the age,
his honor is unparalleled.
At the age of one hundred, he held office,
and was relied upon by Us.
Hoping for a long life of a hundred years,
to consult and look up to his guidance,
his sudden passing
fills Us with sorrow and deep emotion.

Let the eastern garden's 'warm and bright secret vessels,' one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, one hundred bolts of crimson silk, five hundred bolts each of plain silk and linen, one million coins, and one thousand hù of grain be provided for the funeral.
All other arrangements
shall follow the precedent of Prince Xiàn Cāng of Dōngpíng of the Hàn dynasty."
His family followed Fú's dying wishes,
and none of the provided items
were used.
The Emperor visited the mourning again,
personally bowing with profound grief.
At the time of the burial,
he again went to the Dūtíng,
bowed towards the coffin,
and his sorrow moved those around him.
A carriage with bells and a light carriage were provided,
along with one hundred armored guards and brave warriors,
and more than two thousand escorts for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions,
with front and rear drum and wind music.
He was accorded the privilege of being worshipped in the Tàimiào.
He had nine sons: Yōng, Wàng, Fǔ, Yì, Huǎng, Guī, Guī, Héng, Jǐng.
Yōng's courtesy name was Zǐkuí.
Initially, he was the heir apparent,
appointed Commandant of Infantry and Court Attendant.
He died before Fú,
and was posthumously granted the title General Who Aids the State,
with the posthumous name Zhēn.
Yōng's son Chóng became the imperial grandson,
but also died young.
In the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
Chóng's younger brother Lóng, the Marquis of Píngyángtíng, was established as the King of Ānpíng.
He reigned for four years,
and died in the second year of Xiánníng,
with the posthumous name Mù.
He had no sons,
and the state was extinguished.
Wàng, the Accomplished King of Yìyáng, courtesy name Zǐchū,
was adopted by his paternal uncle Lǎng,
and was generous and had his father's demeanor.
He served as a senior clerk in the commandery,
was recommended as Xiàolián,
appointed as a clerk in the Ministry of Works,
and successively served as Administrator of Píngyáng and Colonel of Agricultural Affairs in Luòyáng.
He followed Emperor Xuān in suppressing Wáng Líng,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒng'āntíng for his merits.
He was promoted to General of the Guards,
renamed Marquis of Ānlèxiāng,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant.
At that time, Emperor Gāoguìxiāng of Wèi liked talented people and valued scholars.
Wàng, Pèi Xiù, Wáng Shěn, and Zhōng Huì were all treated with intimacy and trust,
and frequently attended banquets.
The Duke was of an impatient nature,
and Xiù and others held internal positions,
so they arrived quickly when summoned.
As Wàng held an external office,
he was specially given one "pursuing vanguard" carriage
and five brave warriors.
At that time, Jǐng and Wén successively assisted in governance,
but never attended court;
power returned to the Jìn imperial house.
Although Wàng received favor and trust,
he was never at ease,
and therefore requested to be sent out.
He served as General Who Conquers the West, held the imperial credential, and was Superintendent of All Military Affairs in Yōng and Liáng Provinces.
He served for eight years,
and his prestige and transformation were clear and solemn.
Previously, the Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi repeatedly raided Guānzhōng.
When Wàng arrived,
he extensively set up strategies,
and Wéi was unable to raid,
and Guānzhōng relied on him.
He was promoted to Marquis of Shùnyáng.
He was recalled to serve as General of the Guards,
leading the Central Army Commander,
and taking charge of the imperial guards.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of General of Agile Cavalry and established a mansion.
After a short while, he replaced Hé Zēng as Minister of Works.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Yìyáng,
with ten thousand households,
and granted two thousand soldiers.
In the third year of Tàishǐ,
an edict stated:
"Indeed, valuing the worthy, rewarding merit,
honoring the ancestors, and flourishing relatives
are the means by which the state is governed and transformed,
and serve as a model for all officials.
Moreover, the importance of the Three Dukes
lies in the celestial offices.
Thus, Zhōu established six offices,
with the Minister of Works at the head of administration.
The Minister of Works and Central Army Commander,
with bright virtue and close kinship,
have generations who have passed on their excellence.
Their ancestors founded the enterprise,
assisting the great mandate;
they held external responsibilities,
and entered to assist in court administration.
Their civil virtue is already manifest,
and their military achievements are widely known.
When I succeeded to the throne,
they assisted the Way with clarity.
It is fitting for them to ascend to a High Minister position,
and concurrently command the military,
assisting the imperial house internally
and externally enhancing prestige and authority.
Therefore, he is promoted to Grand Commandant,
and his position as Central Army Commander remains as before.
One Military Administrator for the Grand Commandant shall be appointed,
six Councilors,
and five Cavalry Commanders.
Additionally, ten imperial cavalrymen are added,
making a total of thirty,
and he shall be granted a feathered canopy and drum and wind music."
Wú general Shī Jì (施績) invaded Jiāngxià (江夏),
disturbing the border.
Wàng (望) was put in charge of the central army's infantry and cavalry, 20,000 strong,
and stationed at Lóngpí (龍陂),
becoming a major garrison for the two regions,
granted a staff of authority,
and promoted to Grand Chief Controller of All Military Affairs.
At that time, Jīngzhōu (荊州) Inspector Hú Liè (胡烈) resisted Jì (績),
defeating him.
Wàng (望) then withdrew his troops.
Soon after, Wú (吳) general Dīng Fèng (丁奉) invaded Sháopí (芍陂),
and Wàng (望) again led his armies to respond,
but Fèng (奉) retreated before he arrived.
He was appointed Grand Minister of War.
Sūn Hào (孫晧) led his forces towards Shòuchūn (壽春).
An imperial edict ordered Wàng (望) to command the central army of 20,000 men
and 3,000 cavalry,
to hold the area north of the Huái (淮) River.
Hào (晧) retreated,
and the army was disbanded.
He passed away in the seventh year of Tàishǐ (泰始)
at the age of sixty-seven,
with generous posthumous grants.
Wàng (望) was frugal and fond of accumulating wealth;
after his death,
gold and silk overflowed,
for which he was criticized.
He had four sons: Yì (弈), Hóng (洪), Zhěng (整), and Máo (楙).
Yì (弈) reached the rank of Huángménláng (黃門郎)
and died before Wàng (望).
Zhěng (整) also died young.
Yì's (弈) son Qí (奇) inherited the爵.
Qí (奇) was also fond of accumulating wealth,
without restraint.
He sent envoys from three departments to Jiāoguǎng (交廣) for trade,
for which he was impeached by the appropriate authorities.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng (太康),
an imperial edict demoted him to Lord of Sānzòngtíng (三縱亭侯).
Subsequently, Zhāngwǔ (章武) Prince Wēi (威) was established as Wàng's (望) heir.
Later, Wēi (威) was executed,
and Qí (奇) was re-established as Jíyáng (棘陽) Prince to inherit Wàng's (望) title.
Héjiān (河間) Plain Prince Hóng (洪), courtesy name Kǒngyè (孔業),
was adopted as heir to his paternal uncle Chāngwǔ (昌武) Lord Yí (遺).
He served in Wèi (魏),
successively holding positions such as Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng (典農中郎將) and Yuánwǔ (原武) Grand Administrator,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngbēn (襄賁).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Héjiān (河間) Prince.
He reigned for twelve years,
and passed away in the second year of Xiánníng (咸寧).
He had two sons: Wēi (威) and Hùn (混).
Wēi (威) succeeded him,
and his title was transferred to Zhāngwǔ (章武).
Later, after Wēi (威) succeeded Yìyáng (義陽) Prince Wàng (望),
Hùn (混) was established as Hóng's (洪) heir.
Hùn (混) successively held the position of Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
then passed away.
When Luòyáng (洛陽) fell,
all of Hùn's (混) sons perished among the Hú (胡).
His youngest son, Tāo (滔), who had initially succeeded Xīncài (新蔡) Prince Què (確),
also perished along with his brothers.
Later, he managed to return south,
but he disagreed with the Xīncài (新蔡) Grand Consort.
In the second year of Tàixīng (太興), he submitted a memorial,
stating that his brothers had all perished in Liáodōng (遼東),
that the state of Zhāngwǔ (章武) was without heir,
and that he ought to return to his birth family.
The Grand Consort disputed this,
and the matter was referred to the Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Hè Xún (賀循), deliberated:
"Zhāngwǔ (章武) and Xīncài (新蔡) both inherited the lineage of a continuous state.
It is not right to replace their original branch and prioritize collateral relatives.
According to the rules, since Tāo (滔) has already been appointed as an heir to another,
he must have no remaining brothers and his original state must be permanently extinct
