before he can return to his birth family.
Now, his brothers are far away,
but it cannot be said that they are non-existent;
though the journey is difficult,
it is not an entirely inaccessible region.
Furthermore, the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) obey imperial commands,
and communications are uninterrupted.
It is proper to issue an imperial edict to Liáodōng (遼東),
following the examples of Liú Qún (劉羣) and Lú Chén (盧諶) and others,
to send them back
to succeed to their original fiefdoms.
Therefore, Tāo (滔) is not yet permitted to abandon his adopted family."
Emperor Yuán (元帝) decreed:
"Although Tāo (滔) was adopted,
he still has his birth mother.
The Xīncài (新蔡) Grand Consort treats him very poorly,
and Tāo (滔) holds this conviction.
If we do not assent,
there will eventually be disputes,
which would be even less desirable.
Let us now accede to his conviction
and allow him to inherit Zhāngwǔ (章武)."
Tāo (滔) successively held the position of Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
then passed away.
His son Xiū (休) succeeded him.
Xiū (休) and Péngchéng (彭城) Prince Xióng (雄) both fled to Sū Jùn (蘇峻).
When Jùn (峻) was pacified,
Xiū (休) had already died in battle.
His younger brother Zhēn (珍), aged eight,
was not implicated due to his youth.
In the sixth year of Xiánhé (咸和),
he inherited the爵,
rising to the position of Grand宗正.
He passed away
without an heir.
Héjiān (河間) Prince Qīn (欽) adopted his son Fànzhī (範之) as heir,
who rose to the position of Yóují Jiàngjūn (游擊將軍).
He passed away.
His son Xiù (秀) succeeded him.
In the first year of Yìxī (義熙),
he became Guìyáng (桂陽) Grand Administrator.
Xiù's (秀) wife was the sister of Huán Zhèn (桓振).
When Zhèn (振) rebelled,
Xiù (秀) felt insecure,
plotted rebellion,
was executed,
and his state was abolished.
Wēi (威), courtesy name Jǐngyào (景曜),
first succeeded Hóng (洪).
In the third year of Xiánníng (咸寧),
his title was transferred to Zhāngwǔ (章武).
In the ninth year of Tàikāng (太康),
he succeeded Yìyáng (義陽) Prince Wàng (望).
Wēi (威) was brutal and lacking in moral conduct,
fawning over Zhào (趙) Prince Lún (倫).
Towards the end of Yuánkāng (元康) era,
he was Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
When Lún (倫) was about to usurp the throne,
he sent Wēi (威) and Huángménláng (黃門郎) Luò Xiū (駱休) to force the Emperor to surrender the imperial seals and ribbons.
Lún (倫) appointed Wēi (威) as Zhōngshūlìng (中書令).
When Lún (倫) was defeated,
Emperor Huì (惠帝) was restored,
saying:
"Ā Pí (阿皮) twisted my fingers
and took my imperial seals and ribbons;
he must be killed."
Ā Pí (阿皮)
was Wēi's (威) pet name.
Consequently, Wēi (威) was executed.
Suímù (隨穆) Prince Zhěng (整),
after his elder brother Yì (弈) died,
Zhěng (整) was made heir apparent.
He successively held the position of Nánzhōnglángjiàng (南中郎將),
was enfeoffed as Qīngquán (清泉) Marquis,
and passed away before his father Wàng (望).
He was posthumously granted the title of Guànjūn Jiàngjūn (冠軍將軍).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) posthumously enfeoffed him as Suíxiàn (隨縣) Prince using one county from the Yìyáng (義陽) state.
His son Mài (邁) succeeded him.
In the ninth year of Tàikāng (太康),
Pínglín (平林) from Yìyáng (義陽) was added to Mài (邁) as Suíjùn (隨郡) Prince.
Jìnglíng (竟陵) Prince Máo (楙), courtesy name Kǒngwěi (孔偉),
was initially enfeoffed as Lèlíng (樂陵) Lord,
and began his career participating in the Grand Counselor's military affairs.
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Dōngpíng (東平) Prince,
with 3,097 households.
He entered the court as Sanqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Shàngshū (尚書).
Máo (楙) was skilled at flattery
and humbly served Yáng Jùn (楊駿).
When Jùn (駿) was executed,
Máo (楙) was legally liable for death,
but Dōng'ān (東安) Duke Yáo (繇) was on good terms with Máo (楙),
so he escaped implication.
Soon after, he was promoted to Dàhónglú (大鴻臚)
and given the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
Yáo (繇) wanted to monopolize court power
and was at odds with Rǔnán (汝南) Prince Liàng (亮).
Liàng (亮) used the pretext that Yáo (繇) had been hesitant in the campaign against Jùn (駿)
to dismiss Yáo (繇), Máo (楙) and others from their offices,
and sent Máo (楙) to his fiefdom.
Máo (楙) then accumulated wealth
and indulged in extravagance beyond his station.
When Zhào (趙) Prince Lún (倫) usurped the throne,
Máo (楙) was recalled.
When the righteous army arose,
Lún (倫) appointed Máo (楙) as Wèijiàngjūn (衞將軍) and Chief Controller of All Military Affairs.
When Lún (倫) was defeated,
Máo (楙) was dismissed from office.
When Qí (齊) Prince Jiǒng (冏) assisted in governing,
Yáo (繇) again became Púshè (僕射)
and recommended Máo (楙) as Píngdōng Jiàngjūn (平東將軍) and Chief Controller of All Military Affairs of Xúzhōu (徐州),
stationed at Xiàpī (下邳).
When Chéngdū (成都) Prince Yǐng (穎) assisted in governing,
Máo (楙) was promoted to Wèijiàngjūn (衞將軍).
It happened that Huìdì
was on a northern campaign, so Máo was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry,
retaining his former command,
and ordered to lead his troops to Yè.
During the battle of Dàngyīn,
the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, fled to Xiàpéi.
Máo did not admit him,
so Yuè returned to his principality.
When the Emperor then moved west,
Yuè gathered his forces, intending to welcome the imperial carriage.
Máo was very afraid.
His chief clerk, Wáng Xiū, advised him, saying:
“The Prince of Dōnghǎi is a respected member of the imperial clan.
Now that he is raising a righteous army,
Your Grace should hand over Xúzhōu to him.
This would be an act of commendable deference.”
Máo followed his advice,
and then, acting on his own authority, appointed himself Inspector of Yǎnzhōu and General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and memorialized the Son of Heaven.
At that time, the Emperor was in Cháng’ān,
and sent the envoy Liú Qián to immediately bestow the appointment.
Máo worried that Gǒu Xī, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, would not yield to him,
so he gave troops to Qián,
ordering him to claim an imperial edict to execute Xī.
Xī had already relinquished his position at that time.
Máo, in the province, continued to levy taxes and demands relentlessly,
and the commanderies and counties could not bear it.
The Prince of Fányáng, Xiāo, sent Xī back to Yǎnzhōu
and transferred Máo to command the military affairs of Qīngzhōu.
Máo did not accept the order,
and, defying the princes of Shāndōng,
allied himself with Liú Qiáo, the Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Xiāo sent his general Tián Huī to attack Máo,
defeated him,
and Máo fled back to his principality.
When the Emperor returned to Luòyáng,
Máo then went to the palace gate.
When Huáidì ascended the throne,
Máo was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Jìnglíng
and appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
When Yuè went out to govern Yùzhōu,
he left his heir, Pí, and his partisan Hé Lún, to investigate the imperial palace.
Máo memorialized the Emperor to attack Yuè,
then gathered his troops and assaulted Lún,
but did not succeed.
The Emperor blamed Máo,
who fled and escaped harm.
Upon Yuè's death,
he re-emerged.
When Luòyáng fell,
he was killed by mutinous soldiers.
Fǔ, the Prince Chéng of Tàiyuán,
was the Administrator of Yěwáng at the end of the Wèi dynasty.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Bóhǎi,
with an income of 5,379 households.
In the second year of Tàishǐ, he went to his principality.
Later, he served as Commandant of the Guards,
then was sent out as Middle General of the East,
and later transferred to Middle General of the South.
In the third year of Xiánníng,
he was transferred to be Prince of Tàiyuán
and Overseer of all military affairs in Bìngzhōu.
In the fourth year of Tàikāng, he entered court,
and in the fifth year, he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Who Guards the North.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
he was further posthumously granted General of the Guards, with the privilege of establishing a government office equal to the Three Excellencies.
His son Hóng succeeded him.
During the Yuánkāng era, he served as Palace Attendant Consultant,
and later was transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Zhōngqiū.
In the third year, he died,
and his son Shuò succeeded him.
Yì, whose courtesy name was Zǐshì,
held prominent positions from a young age,
eventually reaching the office of Middle General of Valiant Cavalry.
Wǔdì died before receiving the abdication,
and Yì's eldest brother Yōng's collateral son Chéng was made his heir,
enfeoffed as Prince of Nángōng County.
After Yì's death,
his son Yòu succeeded him,
and Chéng thus had no successor.
Huǎng, the Prince Xiàn of Xiàpéi, whose courtesy name was Zǐmíng,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔshǐ Pavilion by Wèi,
appointed Yellow Gate Attendant,
then re-enfeoffed as Baron of Xī'ān.
He was sent out as Administrator of Dōngguǎn.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Xiàpéi,
with an income of 5,176 households.
In the second year of Tàishǐ, he went to his principality.
Huǎng was filial, friendly, upright, and honest,
humble and respectful to scholars,
and highly praised by the imperial clan.
Later, he served as Commandant of the Long Water and Middle General of the South.
In the ninth year,
an imperial edict stated:
“Huǎng, Middle General of the South and Prince of Xiàpéi, is clear-minded and upright,
with a bright and pure character and conduct,
and his talent is comprehensive in governance.
He possesses both civil and military strategy and discernment.
Therefore, let Huǎng be appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Overseer of all military affairs in the two provinces of Níng and Yì, and General Who Guards the West,
also holding the post of Inspector of Yìzhōu.”
Huǎng did not take up the post due to illness.
He was re-appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
then promoted to Right Grandee Secretary.
After a long time,
he was sent out as General Who Guards the East and Overseer of all military affairs in the two provinces of Qīng and Xú.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
he was recalled to serve as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
with the added title of Palace Attendant Consultant.
When Yáng Jùn was to be executed,
Huǎng was made acting Commander of the Imperial Guard,
stationed at the East Yè Gate.
Soon after, he was appointed Prefect of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was promoted to Minister of Works,
with the added title of Palace Attendant,
retaining his former post.
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng, he died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Tutor.
He had two sons: Póu and Chuò.
Póu died young,
and Chuò suffered from a severe illness.
He was separately enfeoffed as Prince of Liángchéng County.
Wěi,
the third son of Fǔ, Prince of Tàiyuán, was made his heir.
Wěi rose to the offices of Palace Attendant and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
but died young,
and his son Sháo succeeded him.
Guī, the Prince Liè of Tàiyuán, whose courtesy name was Zǐquán,
was Marquis of Chánglè Pavilion under Wèi,
then re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Guìshòu Rural District.
He successively served as General Who Manifests Awe and Director of the Imperial Library,
and was enfeoffed as Viscount of Gùshǐ.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán,
with an income of 5,496 households.
In the second year of Tàishǐ, he went to his principality.
In the fourth year, he entered court,
was bestowed with a ceremonial robe and crown,
and promoted to Middle General of the East.
In the tenth year, he died.
An imperial edict stated:
“Guī was loyal and devoted in his heart,
with an elegant and bright intellect.
He served in both civil and military positions,
and had achievements in handling affairs.
When he governed his feudal territory,
both Chinese and non-Chinese were drawn to him,
and in guarding Xǔdū,
his thoughts and strategies were noteworthy.
It is unfortunate that he died so early;
I mourn him greatly.
As his burial place is near,
let him be posthumously granted General of the Vanguard.”
His son Yóng succeeded him.
He was later transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Héjiān,
and has a separate biography.
Guī, the Prince Yuán of Gāoyáng, whose courtesy name was Zǐzhāng,
had talent and reputation from a young age.
He was Marquis of Gāoyáng Rural District under Wèi.
He successively served as Magistrate of Hénán,
was promoted and enfeoffed as Viscount of Zhēnyáng,
and appointed Palace Attendant Yellow Gate Attendant.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Gāoyáng,
with an income of 5,570 households.
He successively served as Middle General of the North and Overseer of all military affairs guarding Yèchéng.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ, he entered court,
and because his father Fú was elderly,
he requested to remain to care for him.
He was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
then promoted to Right Grandee Secretary.
In the tenth year, he died.
An imperial edict sent an acting Grand Herald with credentials to supervise his funeral,
and he was posthumously granted General of Chariots and Cavalry, with the privileges of the Three Excellencies.
Guī had a good reputation in the world,
and the Emperor deeply mourned and regretted his loss.
He had no son,
so an imperial edict designated Jī, the son of Fǔ, Prince of Tàiyuán, to succeed to his title.
Jī reigned for five years.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng, he died,
with the posthumous title of Āi.
He had no son,
so in the second year of Tàikāng, an imperial edict designated Sòng, the son of Yóng, heir to Guī, Prince of Tàiyuán, to be Jī's successor,
and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhēndìng County.
Héng, the Prince Xiào of Chángshān, whose courtesy name was Zǐpíng,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Déyáng Rural District under Wèi.
He was promoted and enfeoffed as Viscount of Rǔyáng,
and served as Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-law.
When Wǔdì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Chángshān,
with an income of 3,790 households.
In the second year, he died.
He had no son,
so Dūn, the fourth son of Yōng, heir to Ānpíng, was designated his successor.
Pèi Shùnwáng Jǐng (沛順王景), whose courtesy name was Zǐwén (子文),
was the Marquis of Lè'ān (樂安) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
He successively held the position of Jiàn yì dàfū (諫議大夫).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Pèi (沛王),
with a household of 3,400 families.
After eleven years,
he passed away in the first year of Xiánníng (咸寧) reign.
His son, Tāo (韜), succeeded him.
Péngchéng Mùwáng Quán (彭城穆王權) (whose great-grandson was Hóng (紘) and Hóng's son was Jùn (俊))
Péngchéng Mùwáng Quán (彭城穆王權), whose courtesy name was Zǐyú (子輿),
was the son of Xuāndì's (宣帝) younger brother, Kuí (馗), who was the Marquis of Dōngwǔchéng (東武城) and Prime Minister of Lǔ (魯) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
Initially, he inherited the enfeoffment
and was appointed Róngcóng Púyè (宂從僕射).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Péngchéng (彭城王),
with a household of 2,900 families.
He was sent out as the Běi zhōnglángjiàng (北中郎將) and supervisor of all military affairs for the defense of Yèchéng (鄴城).
During the Tàishǐ (泰始) reign, he entered the court
and was granted the robes of Gǔnmiǎn (袞冕).
He passed away in the first year of Xiánníng (咸寧) reign.
His son, Yuánwáng Zhí (元王植), succeeded him.
He successively held the position of Hòujiāngjūn (後將軍),
and shortly thereafter was appointed Guózǐ jìjiǔ (國子祭酒), Tàipúqīng (太僕卿), Shìzhōng (侍中), and Shàngshū (尚書).
He was sent out as Āndōngjiāngjūn (安東將軍) and supervisor of all military affairs in Yángzhōu (揚州),
to replace Huáinánwáng Yǔn (淮南王允) in garrisoning Shòuchūn (壽春),
but he had not yet departed.
Some say that Zhí (植) assisted Yǔn (允) in attacking Zhàowáng Lún (趙王倫),
and then died of grief.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chēqíjiāngjūn (車騎將軍)
and his enfeoffment was increased by 15,000 families.
His son, Kāngwáng Shì (康王釋), succeeded him.
He held the official positions of Nánzhōnglángjiàng (南中郎將), Chíjí (持節), and Píngnánjiāngjūn (平南將軍).
The two counties of Fán (蕃) and Xuē (薛) in Lǔ (魯) were partitioned
to augment his kingdom, totaling 23,000 families.
After his death,
his son, Xióng (雄), succeeded him.
Xióng (雄) was executed for participating in Sū Jùn's (蘇峻) rebellion.
Thus, Shì's (釋) son, Hóng (紘), was made his successor.
Hóng (紘), whose courtesy name was Wěidé (偉德),
was initially enfeoffed as the Duke of Tángyì County (堂邑縣公).
At the end of the Jiànxīng (建興) reign,
Emperor Yuán (元帝) assumed imperial authority
and appointed Hóng (紘) to succeed Gāomìwáng Jù (高密王據).
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Sànqíshìláng (散騎侍郎),
then promoted to Yìjūnxiàowèi (翊軍校尉) and Qiánjiāngjūn (前將軍).
When Xióng (雄) was executed,
Hóng (紘) inherited his original lineage.
He was appointed Guózǐ jìjiǔ (國子祭酒),
and additionally Sànqíchángshì (散騎常侍).
Shortly after, he was promoted to Dàzōngzhèng (大宗正) and Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
He suffered from mental illness,
and his temperament was not sound.
Sometimes he wanted to submit memorials to the throne,
and would show them to the high officials.
He also shut himself in, resigning his official seals, the sable cap, and cicada ornaments,
and wrote the "Dùmén fù" (杜門賦) to express his resolve.
Because of this, he was again appointed Guānglùdàfū (光祿大夫)
and made to lead the Dàzōngshī (大宗師),
while retaining his position as Chángshì (常侍).
Later, his illness became severe;
he galloped without restraint,
sometimes attacking and plundering military barracks,
or harming his subordinates,
speaking vulgar and abusive words,
and slandering superiors and inferiors.
He also drove a carriage and burst into the Duānmén (端門),
reaching the front of the Tàijídiàn (太極殿).
Thereupon, Yùshǐzhōngchéng Chē Guàn (御史中丞車灌) impeached him,
requesting that Hóng (紘) be removed from office
and that his kingdom be ordered to strictly guard and record his actions.
Emperor Chéng (成帝) issued an imperial edict saying:
"The king, with his bright virtue and prominent kinship,
holds the weighty position of Dàzōngshī (大宗師).
He should spread the Way, cultivate virtue,
and maintain a calm and unified demeanor.
However, recently he has been moving about too frequently,
and recklessly exposing himself to the dust of the world.
It is proper to order his subordinates and those below them
to each guard him according to their duties,
so that the king no longer has to exert himself in this way.
All internal and external officials
should each be careful in their respective positions.
The king may be relieved of his positions as Chángshì (常侍), Guānglù (光祿), and Zōngshī (宗師).
The carriages and oxen previously provided to him should be taken back.
He shall be granted rice, cloth, beds, and curtains to aid his illness."
He passed away in the eighth year of Xiánkāng (咸康) reign,
and was posthumously granted Sànqíchángshì (散騎常侍) and Jīnzǐguānglùdàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
He had two sons: Xuán (玄) and Jùn (俊).
Xuán (玄) succeeded him.
At that time, the Gēngxū (庚戌) decree prohibited hiding households.
Xuán (玄) hid five households.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) memorialized that Xuán (玄) had violated the prohibition,
and he was arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Later, he was pardoned
and rose to the position of Zhōngshūshìláng (中書侍郎).
After his death,
his son Hóngzhī (弘之) succeeded him,
and rose to the position of Sànqíchángshì (散騎常侍).
After his death,
his son Shàozhī (邵之) succeeded him.
his son Chóngzhī (崇之) succeeded him.
After his death,
his son Jīzhī (緝之) succeeded him.
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty received the abdication,
the kingdom was abolished.
Gōngwáng Jùn (恭王俊), whose courtesy name was Dàodù (道度),
succeeded his uncle Gāomìwáng Lüè (高密王略),
and rose to the official position of Sànqíchángshì (散騎常侍).
After his death,
his son Jìngwáng Chúnzhī (敬王純之) succeeded him,
successively serving as Línchuānnèishǐ (臨川內史), Sīnóngshàofùqīng (司農少府卿), and Tàizǎi Yòuzhǎngshǐ (太宰右長史).
After his death,
his son Huīzhī (恢之) succeeded him.
At the end of the Yìxī (義熙) reign,
he served as Jǐshìzhōng (給事中) concurrently with Tàiwèi (太尉),
and was sent to repair and visit the imperial tombs in Luòyáng (洛陽).
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty received the abdication,
the kingdom was abolished.

Gāomì Wénxiànwáng Tài (高密文獻王泰) (whose son was Xiàowáng Lüè (孝王略); Lüè's (略) elder brother was Xīncài Wǔ'āiwáng Téng (新蔡武哀王騰); Téng's (騰) son was Zhuāngwáng Què (莊王確); Lüè's (略) younger brother was Nányángwáng Mó (南陽王模); Mó's (模) son was Bǎo (保))
Gāomì Wénxiànwáng Tài (高密文獻王泰), whose courtesy name was Zǐshū (子舒),
was the younger brother of Péngchéng Mùwáng Quán (彭城穆王權).
He was the Marquis of Yángtíng (陽亭) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty,
appointed as the Magistrate of Yángdí (陽翟),
and then promoted to Administrator of Fúfēng (扶風).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Lǒngxī (隴西王),
with a household of 3,200 families,
and appointed Yóujījiāngjūn (游擊將軍).
He was sent out as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州)
and additionally Yīngyángjiāngjūn (鷹揚將軍).
He was promoted to Imperial Commissioner (使持節), supervisor of all military affairs in Níng (寧) and Yì (益) provinces, and Ānxījiāngjūn (安西將軍),
leading as Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
but he claimed illness and did not go.
He was transferred to Ānběijiāngjūn (安北將軍),
replacing his elder brother Quán (權) in supervising the defense of Yèchéng (鄴城).
He was then promoted to Ānxījiāngjūn (安西將軍) and supervisor of affairs in Guānzhōng (關中).
he entered the court as Sànqíchángshì (散騎常侍) and Qiánjiāngjūn (前將ūn),
leading the Yèchéngménxiàowèi (鄴城門校尉),
but left office due to illness.
Later, he replaced Xiàpīwáng Huàng (下邳王晃) as Shàngshūzuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射).
He was sent out as Zhènxījiāngjūn (鎮西將軍),
leading the Hùxīróngxiàowèi (護西戎校尉) and acting as commissioner (假節),
replacing Fúfēngwáng Jùn (扶風王駿) in supervising military affairs in Guānzhōng (關中),
but returned to the capital due to illness.
In the early Yǒngxī (永熙) reign,
he replaced Shí Jiàn (石鑒) as Sīkōng (司空),
and shortly after also held the position of Tàizǐtàibǎo (太子太保).
When Yáng Jùn (楊駿) was executed,
Tài (泰) took charge of Jùn's (駿) camp,
was additionally granted Shìzhōng (侍中),
and provided with 2,500 infantry soldiers
and 500 cavalry horses.
Tài (泰) firmly declined,
so he was then provided with 1,000 soldiers and 100 cavalry.
When Chǔwáng Wěi (楚王瑋) was arrested,
Tài (泰) prepared troops to rescue him.
Jìjiǔ Dīng Suī (祭酒丁綏) advised him, saying:
"As a prime minister,
you should not act lightly.
Moreover, it is an urgent matter in the middle of the night.
You should send someone to carefully investigate and confirm."
Tài (泰) followed his advice.
After Wěi (瑋) was executed,
Tài (泰) was appointed Lùshàngshūshì (錄尚書事),
promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉),
and held the position of Shàngshūlìng (尚書令),
re-enfeoffed as the King of Gāomì (高密王),
with a household of 10,000 families.
He passed away in the ninth year of Yuánkāng (元康) reign,
and was posthumously granted Tàifù (太傅).
Tài (泰) was by nature honest and quiet,
not indulging in sensual pleasures.
Although he was a chief minister,
enjoying the revenue of a great kingdom,
his clothing, food, and dishes were like those of a common scholar.
He was genuine and simple in his conduct.
Whenever he attended court,
those who did not know him would not realize he was a king or a duke.
He was respectful and cautious in serving his parents,
and deeply sorrowful during mourning.
Humble and modest towards others,
he was a model for the imperial clan.
Among the kings of his time,
only Tài (泰) and Xiàpīwáng Huàng (下邳王晃) were praised for their self-restraint.
Although neither of them could achieve great accomplishments,
no one else could compare to them.
Tài (泰) had four sons: Yuè (越), Téng (騰), Lüè (略), and Mó (模).
Yuè (越) has his own biography.
Téng (騰) succeeded his uncle.
His younger brother Lüè (略) succeeded him.
Xiào Wáng Lüè (孝王略), courtesy name Yuánjiǎn (元簡),
was filial, respectful, compassionate, and compliant.
He was cautious and humble towards scholars,
and in his youth, he already possessed his father's bearing.
In the early Yuánkāng (元康) period,
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ (愍懷太子) was in the Eastern Palace.
He selected sons of high officials who were well-known to be his companions and friends.
Lüè (略) and Huá (華) and others attended him.
He successively served as Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng (散騎黃門侍郎), Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), and Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
He was sent out as Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍), holding the jié (節), and Dūdū Miǎnnán Zhū Jūnshì (都督沔南諸軍事).
He was promoted to Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍) and Dūdū Qīngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督青州諸軍事).
Lüè (略) pressured Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史) Chéng Mù (程牧).
Mù (牧) avoided him,
and Lüè (略) took charge of the province himself.
In the early Yǒngxīng (永興) period,
Líu Gēn (劉根) was ordered to raise an army in Dōnglái (東萊),
His followers numbered in the tens of thousands.
They attacked and captured Línbó (臨淄).
Lüè (略) could not resist,
and fled to secure Liáochéng (聊城).
When Huái Dì (懷帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督荊州諸軍事), Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn (征南大將軍), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
encamping at Guānjūn (冠軍).
Lüè (略) sent Cānjūn (參軍) Cuī Kuàng (崔曠) to lead Jiāngjūn (將軍) Pí Chū (皮初) and Zhāng Luò (張洛) and others to attack Yóu (逌).
They were deceived by Yóu (逌)
and defeated in battle.
Lüè (略) then sent Zuǒ Sīmǎ (左司馬) Cáo Chū (曹攄) to command Kuàng (曠) and others to advance and pressure Yóu (逌).
As a great battle was about to commence,
Kuàng (曠) secretly retreated from the rear.
Chū's (攄) army had no support,
was defeated in battle,
and he died.
Lüè (略) then pardoned Kuàng's (曠) crime,
and again sent his subordinate general Hán Sōng (韓松) to supervise Kuàng (曠) in attacking Yóu (逌).
Yóu (逌) surrendered.
Soon after, he was promoted to Kāifǔ (開府)
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
He died in the third year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) (309 CE)
and was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Tàiwèi (太尉).
His son Jù (據) succeeded him.
When Jù (據) died
without a son,
Hóng (紘), son of Péngchéng Kāngwáng (彭城康王), was made his heir.
Later, Hóng (紘) returned to his original lineage.
Hóng's (紘) son Jùn (俊) was established to continue his ancestral sacrifices.
Xīncài Wǔ'áiwáng Téng (新蔡武哀王騰), courtesy name Yuánmài (元邁),
was appointed Rǒngcóng Púyè (宂從僕射) in his youth
and enfeoffed as Dōngyíng Gōng (東嬴公).
He successively served as Nányáng (南陽) and Wèijùn (魏郡) Tàishǒu (太守),
performing his duties commendably wherever he was.
He was summoned to be Zōngzhèng (宗正)
and then promoted to Tàicháng (太常).
He was transferred to be Chíjié (持節), Níngběi Jiāngjūn (寧北將軍), Dūdū Bìngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督并州諸軍事), and Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (并州刺史).
When Huì Dì (惠帝) attacked Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎),
the imperial army was defeated.
Téng (騰), together with Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍) Wáng Jùn (王浚), killed Hé Yǎn (和演), whom Yǐng (穎) had appointed as Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (幽州刺史),
and led their forces to attack Yǐng (穎).
Yǐng (穎) sent Běizhōnglángjiāng (北中郎將) Wáng Bīn (王斌) to resist.
Jùn (浚) led Xianbei (鮮卑) cavalry to attack Bīn (斌),
with Téng (騰) acting as the rear guard,
and they thoroughly defeated him.
Yǐng (穎) was afraid,
and escorted the Emperor back to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Téng (騰) was promoted to the position of Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍).
In the early Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
he was promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) and Dūdū Yèchéng Shǒu Zhū Jūnshì (都督鄴城守諸軍事),
garrisoning Yè (鄴).
Furthermore, for his achievement in escorting the emperor,
he was re-enfeoffed as Xīncài Wáng (新蔡王).
Originally,
when Téng (騰) departed from Bìngzhōu (并州),
he stopped at Zhēndìng (真定).
There was a heavy snowfall,
several feet deep on flat ground.
In front of his camp gate, an area several zhang (丈) square had snow that melted and did not accumulate.
Téng (騰) found this strange and dug there,
finding a jade horse,
about a foot high,
which he presented as a tribute.
Thereafter, Gōng Shīpān (公師藩) and Jí Sāng (汲桑) from Píngyáng (平陽) and others formed bandit groups,
rising up in Qīnghé (清河) Yúxiàn (鄃縣),
numbering over a thousand people.
They raided Dùnqíu (頓丘).
Using the pretext of burying Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎),
together with Lǐ Fēng (李豐) and others, former generals of Zhāng Hóng (張泓), to attack Yè (鄴).
Téng (騰) said:
"I have been in Bìngzhōu (并州) for seven years,
and the Hu (胡) surrounded the city but could not capture it.
Jí Sāng (汲桑) is a small bandit, why should I worry about him?"
When Fēng (豐) and others arrived,
Téng (騰) could not defend,
and fled with light cavalry,
and was killed by Fēng (豐).
He had four sons: Yú (虞), Jiǎo (矯), Shào (紹), and Què (確).
Yú (虞) was brave and strong.
When Téng (騰) was killed,
Yú (虞) pursued Fēng (豐).
Fēng (豐) threw himself into the water and died.
On that day,
Yú (虞), Jiǎo (矯), and Shào (紹), along with Jùlù Tàishǒu (鉅鹿太守) Cuī Màn (崔曼), Chēqí Chángshǐ (車騎長史) Yáng (羊),
all perished.
Originally,
although the coffers of Yè (鄴) were depleted,
Téng (騰) had abundant resources.
He was naturally frugal and miserly,
giving no alms or favors.
When in distress,
he only granted his officers and soldiers a few sheng (升) of rice
and a few zhang (丈) of silk each.
Because of this, people did not serve him,
which led to disaster.
When Gǒu Xī (苟晞) rescued Yè (鄴),
Sāng (桑) returned to Píngyáng (平陽).
It was then mid-summer,
and the corpses were so decayed that they could not be recognized.
The bones of Téng (騰) and his three sons could not be recovered.
His illegitimate son Què (確) succeeded him.
Zhuāng Wáng Què (莊王確), courtesy name Sì'ān (嗣安),
successively served as Dōngzhōnglángjiāng (東中郎將) and Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督豫州諸軍事),
garrisoning Xǔchāng (許昌).
At the end of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
he was killed by Shí Lè (石勒).
He had no sons.
Initially, Tāo (滔), son of Zhāngwǔ Wáng Hún (章武王混), was made to continue his sacrifices.
Later, Bì (弼), son of Rǔnán Wēiwáng Yòu (汝南威王祐), was again made Què's (確) successor.
He died in the first year of Tàixīng (太興) (318 CE)
without a son.
Then Bì's (弼) younger brother Miǎo (邈) succeeded Què (確),
reaching the position of Shìzhōng (侍中).
When he died,
his son Huǎng (晃) succeeded him
and was appointed Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎).
Huán Wēn (桓溫) deposed Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王),
and removed Huǎng (晃) to commoner status,
exiling him to Héngyáng (衡陽).
Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝) established Huǎng's (晃) younger brother Chóng (崇) to succeed Miǎo (邈).
Chóng (崇) was killed by a servant.
His son Huì (惠) succeeded him.
When Sòng (宋) received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Nányáng Wáng Mó (南陽王模), courtesy name Yuánbiǎo (元表),
was fond of learning in his youth,
and together with Yuán Dì (元帝) and Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo (范陽王虓), he was well-regarded among the imperial clan.
He was initially enfeoffed as Píngchāng Gōng (平昌公).
At the end of Huì Dì (惠帝)'s reign,
he was appointed Rǒngcóng Púyè (宂從僕射) and successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (太子庶子) and Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) fled to Cháng'ān (長安).
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) appointed Mó (模) as Běizhōnglángjiāng (北中郎將),
garrisoning Yè (鄴).
In the early Yǒngxīng (永興) period,
Gōng Shīpān (公師藩), Lóu Quán (樓權), Hǎo Chāng (郝昌) and others, former commanders under Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎), attacked Yè (鄴).
Mó's (模) attendants conspired to join them.
Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu (廣平太守) Dīng Shào (丁邵) led his forces to rescue Mó (模).
Shīpān (師藩) and the others scattered and fled.
He was promoted to Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn (鎮東大將軍),
garrisoning Xǔchāng (許昌).
He was advanced in peerage to Nányáng Wáng (南陽王).
In the early Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
he was transferred to Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn (征西大將軍), Kāifǔ (開府), and Dūdū Qín Yōng Liáng Yì Zhū Jūnshì (都督秦雍梁益諸軍事),
replacing Héjiān Wáng Yōng (河間王顒) to guard Guānzhōng (關中).
Mó (模) was grateful for Dīng Shào's (丁邵) virtue,
and ordered the people of his state to erect a monument for Shào (邵) during his lifetime.
At that time, Guānzhōng (關中) suffered from famine,
and people cannibalized each other.
Moreover, there were epidemics,
and bandits roamed openly.
Mó (模) was unable to control them
and thus cast bronze figures and bells and tripods into pots and utensils to exchange for grain.
Those who debated this disapproved.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) submitted a memorial requesting Mó (模) to be Sīkōng (司空),
and sent Zhōngshūjiān (中書監) Fù Zhī (傅祗) to replace him.
Mó's (模) advisor Chúnyú Dìng (淳于定) said to Mó (模):
"Guānzhōng (關中) is a heavenly storehouse of a nation,
a place for hegemons and kings.
If you return now due to your inability to pacify and comfort,
your reputation will be damaged.
Furthermore, you and your brothers initiated this great undertaking,
and are all in the imperial court.
If you act strongly, you will be guilty of seizing power;
if you are weak, you will be controlled by others.
This is not to your advantage."
Mó (模) accepted his words
and did not take up the appointment.
He submitted a memorial to send his eldest son Bǎo (保) as Xīzhōnglángjiāng (西中郎將) and Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi (東羌校尉),
garrisoning Shàngguī (上邽).
Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (秦州刺史) Péi Bāo (裴苞) resisted him.
Mó (模) ordered his subordinate commander Chén Ān (陳安) to lead his forces to attack Bāo (苞).
Bāo (苞) fled to Āndìng (安定).
Tàishǒu (太守) Jiǎ Yǎ (賈疋) welcomed Bāo (苞) with his commandery.
Mó (模) sent Jūn Sī (軍司) Xiè Bān (謝班) to attack Yǎ (疋).
Yǎ (疋) retreated and fled to Lúshuǐ (盧水).
In that same year,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉) and Dà Dūdū (大都督).
Luòjīng傾覆,
Mó使牙門 Zhào Rǎn 戍 Púbǎn,
〔一八〕Rǎn 求 Fèngyì 太守不得,
怒,
率衆降于 Liú Cōng.
Cōng 使其子 Càn 及 Rǎn 攻 Cháng'ān,
Mó 使 Chúnyú Dìng 距之,
為 Rǎn 所敗.
士衆離叛,
倉庫虛竭,
軍祭酒 Wéi Fǔ 曰:
「事急矣,
早降可以免. 」
Mó 從之,
遂降于 Rǎn.
Rǎn 箕踞攘袂數 Mó 之罪,
送詣 Càn.
Càn 殺之,
以 Mó 妃 Liú shì 賜 Hú Zhāng Běn 為妻.
子 Bǎo 立.
Bǎo 字 Jǐngdù,
少有文義,
好述作.
初拜 Nányáng Guó 世子.
Mó 遇害,
Bǎo 在 Shàngguī.
其後 Jiǎ Pǐ 死,
Péi Bāo 又為 Zhāng Guǐ 所殺,
Bǎo 全有 Qínzhōu 之地,
自號大司馬,
承制置百官.
Lǒngyòu Dī Qiāng 並從之,
Liángzhōu 刺史 Zhāng Shí 遣使貢獻.
及 Mǐn Dì 即位,
以 Bǎo 為右丞相,
加侍中、都督陝西諸軍事.
尋進位相國.
Mó 之敗也,
都尉 Chén Ān 歸於 Bǎo,
Bǎo 命統精勇千餘人以討 Qiāng,
寵遇甚厚.
Bǎo 將 Zhāng Chūn 等疾之,
譖 Ān 有異志,
請除之,
Bǎo 不許.
Chūn 等輒伏刺客以刺 Ān,
Ān 被創,
馳還 Lǒngchéng,
遣使詣 Bǎo,
貢獻不絕.
Mǐn Dì 之蒙塵也,
Bǎo 自稱 Jìn Wáng.
時 Shàngguī 大饑,
士衆窘困,
Zhāng Chūn 奉 Bǎo 之 Nán'ān.
Chén Ān 自號 Qínzhōu 刺史,
稱藩於 Liú Yào.
Chūn 復奉 Bǎo 奔 Sāngchéng,
將投于 Zhāng Shí.
Shí 使兵迎 Bǎo,
實禦之也.
是歲,
Bǎo 病薨,
時年二十七.
Bǎo 體質豐偉,
嘗自稱重八百斤.
喜睡,
痿疾,
不能御婦人.
無子,
Zhāng Chūn 立宗室 Sīmǎ Zhān 奉 Bǎo 後.
Chén Ān 舉兵攻 Chūn,
Chūn 走,
Zhān 降于 Ān,
Ān 送詣 Liú Yào,
Yào 殺之.
Ān 迎 Bǎo 喪,
以天子禮葬于 Shàngguī,
諡曰 Yuán.
Fànyáng Kāng Wáng Suí (子 Xiāo)
Fànyáng Kāng Wáng Suí, courtesy name Zǐdū,
was the youngest brother of Péngchéng Wáng Quán.
He was initially appointed as Jiànyì Dàfū.
In the first year of Tàishǐ, he received his enfeoffment,
and held office for fifteen years.
In the fifth year of Xiánníng, he passed away,
and his son Xiāo succeeded him.
Xiāo, courtesy name Wǔhuì,
was fond of learning and famous in his youth,
diligently studying classics and records,
and was articulate and eloquent in debate.
As a member of the imperial clan, he was selected and appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and progressively promoted to Shàngshū.
He was sent out as Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Chíjíe,
stationed at Xǔchāng, and was further promoted to Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (河間王顒) memorialized to establish Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) as the Crown Prince,
but he was defeated by Wáng Jùn (王浚),
and escorted the Emperor back to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Xiāo (虓), along with Dōngpíng Wáng Máo (東平王楙) and Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Zhōu Fù (鎮東將軍周馥) and others, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since Mǐnhuái (愍懷) was murdered,
the Imperial Heir has not been established.
The heavy responsibility was entrusted to the former Chancellor,
who then failed in his duty as a subject.
That is why two years ago, the Grand Tutor and your subjects,
ever mindful of the heir to the altars of soil and grain,
and that it could not long remain empty,
together proposed Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎)
to be the assistant to the state.
After receiving this heavy trust,
he was unable to bear the burden.
'Do not employ small men,'
yet he made them his close confidantes.
Kinship should be cherished,
yet suspicion and frivolity frequently arose.
Those who are treacherous and perverse should be kept at a distance,
yet slanderous words ruined good conduct.
All these are due to your subjects' lack of wisdom and discernment,
losing the one they relied upon.
This led Your Majesty to err in bestowing this appointment.
Even if your subjects were executed,
it would not be enough to apologize to the world.
Now that the imperial carriage has returned to the palace,
civil and military affairs are desolate,
institutions are in ruins,
with nothing left.
Although your subjects are inferior,
we are capable of assisting the royal house.
However, there are rumors that
Zhāng Fāng (張方) differs from your subjects.
We regret the conflict arising from his location,
and also believe that the Grand Tutor, with his profound virtue and excellent prime,
is known to all,
and whenever a righteous matter arises,
he is always at the forefront for the altars of soil and grain and the imperial clan.
Zhāng Fāng (張方) received his instructions,
and rendered service to the state.
In the actions of last year,
he was willing to die rather than be disloyal.
This is indeed the Grand Tutor's good general,
and Your Majesty's loyal subject.
However, by nature he is resolute and firm,
and does not adapt to change,
thus clinging to his former resolve,
which has already led to disputes.
Yet, upon reflection,
this is precisely his unyielding principle.
Furthermore, he feared that after the situation was reversed,
he would be condemned by the world,
and therefore did not immediately return west.
Considering his original intentions,
there is truly no deep blame.
Your subject has heard that the enlightened rulers of previous generations
never failed to completely protect meritorious officials,
allowing their blessings to flow to their descendants.
Since the middle period,
none of Your Majesty's meritorious officials have been completely spared.
It is not only that their talents were all inferior,
but their misfortune
was truly due to the court's improper policies,
not allowing for mutual tolerance.
To lose years of accumulated merit due to a single fault,
not only violates the Zhōu (周) rites' standard for evaluating merit,
but also causes no one in the world to dare to exert themselves for Your Majesty again.
Your subjects' words
are not solely for the sake of Zhāng Fāng (張方),
but are truly a long-term plan for the altars of soil and grain,
wishing for meritorious officials to long maintain wealth and honor.
Your ignorant subject believes it appropriate to entrust the Grand Tutor with the responsibility for Guānyòu (關右),
making him solely responsible for important matters in that region,
and from the prefectures and commanderies downwards,
the selection and appointment of officials
should all be submitted to him for approval.
As for major affairs of the court,
such as abolition, establishment, reduction, or increase,
they should always be discussed with him.
This would be the meaning of the two dukes performing their duties,
and Zhōu (周) and Shào (召) dividing their jurisdictions,
which Your Majesty would now revive.
Send Fāng (方) back to his commandery,
allow the various lords to express their will,
and stabilize the royal house in due course.
The offices bestowed upon Fāng (方),
we request that they all be restored as before.
In this way, loyal subjects and righteous gentlemen will be encouraged,
and meritorious officials will surely be spared harm.
Sītú Róng (司徒戎) is a worthy man of a different surname;
Sīkōng Yuè (司空越) is a hope of the imperial clan,
both loyal to the state and devoted to the ruler,
cautious and circumspect.
They are fit to manage important affairs,
and should be entrusted with court governance.
Ānběi Jiāngjūn Wáng Jùn (安北將軍王浚) is a descendant who aided in the founding of the dynasty,
he conducts himself according to the Dao,
is loyal, honest, pure, and upright,
praised by all near and far.
As for the great undertaking of today,
he truly has the merit of stabilizing the altars of soil and grain.
This is why your subjects sigh and commend him highly.
Jùn (浚) should be especially honored and given great responsibility,
to meet the expectations of the masses,
and then govern Yōu (幽) and Shuò (朔),
serving forever as the northern bulwark.
Your subjects will exert all our strength to defend the cities,
protecting the imperial family as a screen.
Your Majesty will rule with folded hands,
and the four seas will naturally be set right.
Then the achievements of the Four Ancestors
will surely flourish in the present time,
and the brilliance of the sun and moon,
though dimmed, will shine again.
We beg Your Majesty to reflect three times,
and consider what your subjects have said.
Furthermore, this memorial from your subject can be shown to the Grand Tutor in the west."
Another memorial said:
"Chéngdū Wáng (成都王) lost his way,
misled by treacherous villains.
Regarding the king himself,
he should not be deeply blamed.
Moreover, he is a descendant of the late emperor,
and one of Your Majesty's younger brothers.
Since Yuánkāng (元康),
crimes and executions have followed one another,
which has indeed caused great turmoil within the seas,
and for which your subjects feel profound pain.
Now to depose Chéngdū (成都),
and re-enfeoff him with a single city,
should surely be granted.
If, after being deposed, he soon suffers misfortune,
it would not only harm Your Majesty's benevolent grace,
but also cause people near and far to believe that the imperial clan no longer has any kinship affection.
This truly makes your subjects feel inwardly sad and ashamed,
unable to face the world.
We beg Your Majesty to discern your subjects' loyal sincerity."
Thereupon, Xiāo (虓) first led his troops from Xǔ (許) to garrison in Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Coincidentally, when Huì Dì (惠帝) moved west,
Xiāo (虓), along with his paternal cousin Píngchāng Gōng Mó (平昌公模) and Chángshǐ Féng Sōng (長史馮嵩) and others, sacrificed a white horse and smeared blood to swear an oath,
electing Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) as the alliance leader.
Xiāo (虓) was appointed Dūdū Héběi Zhū Jūnshì (都督河北諸軍事), Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Chíjié (持節),
and Administrator of Yùzhōu (豫州 Cǐshǐ).
Liú Qiáo (劉喬) did not accept the command of Yuè (越) and others,
and taking advantage of the vacuum, defeated Xǔ (許).
Xiāo (虓) extricated himself and crossed the river.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) memorialized to appoint Xiāo (虓) as Administrator of Jìzhōu (冀州 Cǐshǐ),
and supplied him with troops and horses.
Xiāo (虓) entered Jìzhōu (冀州) and raised an army,
then crossed the river south again,
and defeated Qiáo (喬) and others.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (河間王顒), hearing of Qiáo's (喬) defeat,
executed Zhāng Fāng (張方),
and sent his head to Yuè (越).
Yuè (越) and Xiāo (虓) went west to welcome the Emperor,
and Yǒng (顒) fled.
Thereupon, they escorted the Son of Heaven back to the capital.
Xiāo (虓) was appointed Sītú (司徒).
In Yǒngxīng (永興) 3, he died suddenly of illness,
at the age of thirty-seven.
He had no sons,
and adopted Mó's (模) son Lí (黎) as his heir.
Lí (黎) followed Mó (模) to his state,
and was killed in Cháng'ān (長安).
Jìnán Huì Wáng Suì (濟南惠王遂) (great-grandson Xūn)
Jìnán Huì Wáng Suì (濟南惠王遂), courtesy name Zǐbó (子伯),
was the son of Xuān Dì's (宣帝) younger brother Wèi Hónglú Chéng Xún (魏鴻臚丞恂).
He served as a Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯) in Wèi (魏),
and was promoted to Píngchāng Tínghóu (平昌亭侯),
successively serving as Diǎnjūn Lángjiàng (典軍郎將).
In Jǐngyuán (景元) 2,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Wǔchéng Xiānghóu (武城鄉侯), Dūdū Yèchéng Shǒushǒu Zhū Jūnshì (督鄴城守諸軍事), and Běizhōng Lángjiàng (北中郎將).
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was enfeoffed as Zhù'ā Bó (祝阿伯),
and successively promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍).
When Wǔ Dì (武帝) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Jìnán Wáng (濟南王).
He died in Tàishǐ (泰始) 2.
He had two sons: Dān (耽) and Jī (緝).
Dān (耽) succeeded him,
and in Xiánníng (咸寧) 3, he was moved to become Zhōngshān Wáng (中山王).
He died that year,
having no sons,
so Jī (緝) succeeded.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) appointed Jī (緝) as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍),
and with Shí Xī (石熙) and others, he led troops to resist Wáng Jùn (王浚),
and was lost in battle,
dying.
He had no sons,
and the state was abolished.
Hòusuì's great-grandson, Xūn, courtesy name Wěicháng,
was over ten years old
at the end of Mǐn Dì's reign.
When Cháng'ān fell,
Liú Yào's general, Línghú Ní, adopted him as his son.
When he grew up,
he was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and could shoot from both sides.
In the sixth year of Xiánhé (331 CE),
he returned from Guānyòu
and declared himself, saying:
"I am the great-great-grandson of Dàchángqiū Xún,
the great-grandson of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Jǐnán Huì Wáng Suì,
and the son of Lüèyáng Tàishǒu Guàn."
Consequently, he was appointed Yèzhě Púshè
and was renowned for his bravery.
When Yǔ Yì was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
he heard that Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Huánxuān had died,
〔一九〕and requested Xūn to replace him.
He first garrisoned Xīchéng,
then retreated to defend Wǔdāng.
At that time, Shí Jìlóng died,
and the Central Plains fell into chaos.
The local strongmen of Yǒngzhōu all sent messages to Xūn.
Xūn led his troops out of Luògǔ
and encamped at Xuángōu,
two hundred *lǐ* from Cháng'ān.
He dispatched his subordinate general, Liú Huàn, to attack Cháng'ān
and also captured Hèchéng.
Thereupon, all of Guānzhōng killed Jìlóng's *tàishǒu* and *lìngzhǎng* in response to Xūn.
Xūn's forces were small,
and he was unable to secure his position,
so he returned to Liángzhōu.
During the Yǒnghé era (345-357 CE),
Zhāng Jū occupied Lǒngdōng
and sent an envoy to invite Xūn.
Xūn again entered Cháng'ān.
Initially,
Dù Hóng, a powerful clan member from Jīngzhào, oppressed Jū.
Jū, with his bravery and chivalry, insulted Hóng.
Hóng knew that Xūn feared Jū's strong army,
so he persuaded Xūn, saying:
"If Zhāng Jū is not killed,
Guānzhōng will not belong to the state."
Xūn then feigned an invitation to Jū
and killed him at the feast.
Jū's younger brother fled to Chíyáng,
gathered troops to attack Xūn,
suffered frequent defeats in battle,
sued for peace,
and returned to Liángzhōu.
Later, when Huán Wēn campaigned against Guānzhōng,
he ordered Xūn to march out via Zǐwǔ Dào,
but Xūn was defeated by Fú Xióng
and retreated to garrison Nǚwā Bǎo.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
Supervisor of Military Affairs in Guānzhōng,
and concurrently Xi Róng Xiàowèi,
and was granted the title of Tōngjí Tínghóu.
His administration was cruel and tyrannical;
if any *zhìzhōng*, *biéjià*, or powerful local magnate
spoke against his wishes,
he would immediately execute them on the spot,
or even shoot them himself with an arrow.
The people of the western regions suffered from his savagery.
While in the province, he constantly harbored ambitions to seize Shǔ
and had intentions of usurpation.
Huán Wēn, hearing of this,
endeavored to soothe and conciliate him,
appointing his son Kāng as Hànzhōng Tàishǒu.
Xūn's rebellious plans were already formed,
but he feared Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Fǔ,
and so had not yet acted.
When Fǔ died,
he then led his troops into Jiàngé.
Liángzhōu Biéjià Yōng Duān and Xī Róng Sīmǎ Wěi Cuì both strongly remonstrated,
but Xūn executed them all.
He declared himself牧 Mù of Liáng and Yì provinces, and King of Chéngdū.
Huán Wēn sent Zhū Xù to suppress Xūn.
Xūn's army collapsed
and he was captured by Xù.
Along with his son Lóngzǐ, Chángshǐ Liáng Dàn, and Sīmǎ Jīn Yī, etc., he was sent to Wēn,
who executed them all
and sent their heads to the capital.

Qíao Gāng Wáng Xùn (son Mǐn Wáng Chéng 〔二０〕 Chéng's son Liè Wáng Wújì Wújì's son Jìng Wáng Tián Tián's son Zhōng Wáng Shàngzhī Shàngzhī's younger brothers Huīzhī Xiūzhī Yǔnzhī Hán Yánzhī Tián's younger brother Yīn)
Qíao Gāng Wáng Xùn, courtesy name Zǐtì,
was the son of Xuān Dì's younger brother, Wèi Zhōngláng Jìn.
He served Wèi as Guānnèi Hóu,
was later enfeoffed as Chéngyáng Tínghóu,
participated in the military affairs of Zhèndōng,
and was appointed Qīngchē Jiāngjūn and Yǔlín Zuǒjiān.
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Jīngyáng Nán.
When Wǔ Dì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Qíao Wáng,
with an estate of four thousand four hundred households.
He died in the second year of Tàishǐ (266 CE).
He had two sons: Suí and Chéng.
Dìng Wáng Suí succeeded.
He died,
and his son Suì succeeded,
but was lost to Shí Lè.
Yuán Dì appointed Chéng to succeed Xùn.
Mǐn Wáng Chéng, courtesy name Jìngcái,
was sincere and virtuous in his youth, with high aspirations and conduct.
He was appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi and Fèngcháoqǐng,
gradually promoted to Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn and Ānyí Hùjūn,
and stationed at Āndìng.
He followed Huì Dì back to Luòyáng
and was appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
During the Yǒngjiā era (307-313 CE),
as the world gradually fell into chaos,
he traveled secretly to rely on Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Shān Jiǎn.
When Jiǎn died,
he proceeded to Wǔchāng.
When Yuán Dì first took up station in Yángzhōu,
Chéng returned to Jiànkāng
and was appointed Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
Mǐn Dì summoned him to be Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
but he did not go.
When Yuán Dì became Jìn Wáng,
he, acting on his own authority, re-enfeoffed Chéng as Qíao Wáng.
At the beginning of Tàixīng (318 CE),
he was appointed Túnqí Xiàowèi,
given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently served as Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Chéng was frugal in office;
his household had no separate chambers.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
with Fǔguó and Zuǒjūn as before.
Wáng Dūn had rebellious intentions,
and his memorials showed disrespect.
The emperor summoned Chéng at night,
showed him Dūn's memorial,
and said:
"Wáng Dūn's rank and position in recent years are sufficient,
yet his demands never cease,
and his words have come to this.
What should we do?"
Chéng replied:
"If Your Majesty does not decide early,
trouble will arise."
The emperor wanted to establish藩屏 *fānpíng* (a defensive screen).
It so happened that Dūn memorialized to appoint Shěn Chōng, the Administrator of Xuānchéng, as Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
The emperor said to Chéng:
"Xiāngzhōu, in the south of Chǔ, is a rugged and strategic location,
a vital point in the upper reaches,
controlling the confluence of three provinces.
It is a country for military use.
Now, if my uncle resides there,
what do you think?"
Chéng replied:
"I am fortunate to be counted among the distant relatives,
and my person is responsible for guarding the palace.
I have not yet endured the toil of campaigning,
yet I have repeatedly received excessive favor.
Morning and night, I strive to improve myself,
desiring to repay the emperor's kindness.
What my lord commands,
I shall act according to my ability.
How dare I refuse!
However, Xiāngzhōu is what remains after the Shǔ bandits,
its people and resources completely depleted.
If, relying on celestial might,
I can accomplish what I undertake,
by three years,
I ask to participate in military service.
If it is not achieved by then,
even if I perish,
it will be of no avail."
Thereupon, an imperial edict stated:
"The king governs the world in accordance with heaven's principles;
without a multitude of talents, his affairs cannot be accomplished.
Externally, he establishes the wise and virtuous
to cultivate moral influence;
internally, he strengthens ties with relatives
to expand his defensive screen.
This is why Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and Bóqín resided in Lǔ.
These are the excellent institutions of the former kings,
a universal principle throughout history.
When our Jìn Dynasty was founded,
many states were established,
and Lángyá Wǔ Wáng was granted authority
to govern Dōngxià;
Rǔnán Wénchéng
unified Huái and Xǔ;
Fúfēng and Liáng Wáng
alternately held Guānyòu;
and reaching Dōngyíng,
acted as supervisor of Bìngzhōu.
Although the imperial clan is now small
and cannot compare to former times,
how can we abandon the old regulations?
Sànqí Chángshì, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, Qíao Wáng Chéng is sincere and bright by nature,
devoted to loyalty and diligence,
attentive to the emperor's left and right,
with increasing reverence and solemnity.
Therefore, Chéng is now appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs in Xiāngzhōu, Nán Zhōnglángjiāng, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ."
Initially,
Liú Wèi (劉隗), believing Wáng Dūn's (王敦) power and authority to be excessive
and ultimately uncontrollable,
advised the emperor to dispatch his trusted confidants
to guard the regional frontiers.
Therefore, he first assigned Chéng (承) to Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
and subsequently appointed Wèi (隗) and Dài Ruòsī (戴若思), among others,
as provincial governors.
When Chéng (承) arrived in Wǔchāng (武昌),
he dismissed his military escort to meet Wáng Dūn (王敦).
Dūn (敦) hosted a banquet for him,
wishing to discern his intentions.
He said to Chéng (承):
“Your Highness is a refined and cultured gentleman,
but I fear you lack the talent for a general.”
Chéng (承) replied:
“You just haven't recognized it yet;
can't a lead knife make at least one cut?”
Chéng (承) knew Dūn (敦) wanted to probe his feelings,
hence he made this remark.
Dūn (敦) indeed said to Qián Fèng (錢鳳):
“He knows no fear and speaks bravely,
but he is not martial;
what can he achieve?”
He then allowed Chéng (承) to proceed to his post.
At that time, the land of Xiāng (湘) was desolate and ruined,
and both public and private affairs were in distress.
Chéng (承) personally lived frugally,
riding in a simple reed carriage,
but devoted himself wholeheartedly to pacification,
gaining a great reputation for his abilities.
Dūn (敦), fearing he would become a threat,
falsely claimed to be launching a northern expedition
and summoned all boats and carriages within Chéng's (承) jurisdiction.
Chéng (承) knew his treacherous plan
and gave him half.
Soon after, Dūn (敦) instigated trouble,
sending his参军 (cānjūn) Huán Pí (桓羆) to persuade Chéng (承),
saying that Liú Wèi (劉隗) monopolized the emperor's favor,
and that he would attack him immediately.
He invited Chéng (承) to be his military commander,
requiring him to set out by a military deadline.
Chéng (承) sighed:
“I shall surely die!
The land is desolate, people are few,
my position is isolated, and aid is cut off.
To rush to the sovereign's aid is
loyalty;
to die for the king's cause is
righteousness.
With loyalty and righteousness alone,
what more could one ask for?”
He immediately intended to raise the banner of righteousness,
but the hearts of the multitude were full of doubt.
Chéng (承) said:
“Having received the nation's grace,
my loyalty permits no wavering.”
His府長史 (fǔzhǎngshǐ) Yú Kuī (虞悝) was brave and resolute,
and said to Chéng (承):
“Wáng Dūn (王敦) holds the important post of regional commander,
yet suddenly commits rebellion.
This is unforgivable by Heaven and Earth,
and abhorred by gods and men.
Your Highness is a scion of the imperial house, a bulwark of the realm;
how can you follow his deception?
You should rise up like lightning
for the sake of survival.”

Thereupon, he, along with Kuī (悝), his younger brother, former丞相掾 (chéngxiàng yuàn) Wàng (望), the Administrator of Jiànchāng (建昌), Chángshā Wáng (長沙王) Xún (循), and the Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽), Huáilíng (淮陵) Liú Yì (劉翼) and others, swore an oath of alliance,
imprisoned Huán Pí (桓羆),
and sent urgent proclamations throughout Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
setting a date to reach Bālíng (巴陵).
Yǐn Fèng (尹奉), the Administrator of Línglíng (零陵), was the first to join the righteous cause,
leading his army to Yíngyáng (營陽).
Thus, within the entire province,
all joined the righteous endeavor.
He then sent Yú Wàng (虞望) to subjugate those who did not comply,
and executed Zhèng Dàn (鄭澹), the Administrator of Xiāngdōng (湘東).
Dàn (澹)
was Dūn’s (敦) brother-in-law.
Dūn (敦) dispatched Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉) Wèi (魏), and generals Lǐ (李) and Tián Sōng (田嵩) with two tens of thousands of armored soldiers to attack Chéng (承).
Chéng (承) both fought and defended,
awaiting rescue from Yǐn Fèng (尹奉) and Yú Wàng (虞望),
but the city walls were not strong,
and the people were terrified.
Some advised Chéng (承) to surrender to Táo Kǎn (陶侃) in the south,
while others suggested retreating to Líng (零) and Guì (桂).
Chéng (承) said:
“I raised this righteous army
with the resolve to die for the cause.
How can I steal a life and escape disgrace,
becoming a defeated general on the run?
If the endeavor fails,
let the people know my heart.”
Earlier,
Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍) Gān Zhuó (甘卓) had written to Chéng (承),
advising him to hold his position,
and promising to lead troops out of Miǎnkǒu (沔口)
to cut off Dūn’s (敦) retreat,
which would automatically relieve the siege of Xiāng (湘).
Chéng (承) replied in a letter:
“To Jìsī (季思), my esteemed friend: You labor diligently for the king’s cause.
Heaven’s net is temporarily broken,
the central plains are in ruins.
Righteous men from all four seas
are planning to recover and restore,
rebuilding the dynasty south of the Yangtze.
It is but a fledgling endeavor,
who would have thought such wickedness would sprout from a favored minister?
I, being ignorant and short-sighted,
am entrusted with a position among the imperial clan.
I humbly received the secret mandate
to govern the southern lands,
personally received the imperial edict,
and the established plan is in my heart.
Bó Rén (伯仁) and other virtuous men
are in despair at the crossroads.
My arrival here is still recent,
and the people are utterly bewildered.
Wolves are easily startled,
thus they unleashed their ugly poison.
Upon hearing this, I was horrified and filled with indignation,
my spirit soaring.
Inspired by Zǐ Lái’s (子來) righteousness,
people flocked by the hundreds,
arriving unbidden,
numbering over several thousand.
Truly enough to seize the moment,
and unleash the accumulated resentment of mountains and seas.
However, pressed by urgency,
boats and oars are not yet ready.
Wèi (魏) and Lǐ (李)
soon surrounded and pressed us,
so events ran contrary to my intentions,
and my resolve and strength could not be fully displayed.
I am deeply grateful for your envoy's visit,
and for sharing in this great aspiration;
your excellent counsel and brilliant calculations
come from the depths of your heart.
Reading your letter repeatedly,
my joy is immeasurable.
If you, my friend, can don your armor and rush here like lightning,
there may still be salvation;
but if you hesitate,
you will find me in the fish market, merely dried fish.
It is said that swiftness, even if clumsy, is better than skillful delay.
Jìsī (季思), my esteemed friend,
exert yourself, exert yourself!
My letter cannot fully express my feelings,
I shall end here.”
Zhuó’s (卓) army encamped at [⿰月者]kǒu (𦩨口),
but upon hearing that the imperial army had been defeated,
he halted his troops and did not advance.
As the attacks intensified daily,
Dūn (敦) also sent letters and memorials he had seized from the court
to be shot into the city for Chéng (承) to see.
Those within the city, knowing the imperial court could not hold,
were all filled with sorrow and regret.
Liú Yì (劉翼) died in battle,
and after holding out for over a hundred days,
the city finally fell.
Chéng (承) was escorted in a cage to Jīngzhōu (荊州),
where the governor Wáng Yì (王廙), following Dūn’s (敦) orders, murdered him en route.
He was fifty-nine years old at the time.
After Dūn (敦) was pacified,
an imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍).
His son Wújí (無忌) succeeded him.
Liè Wáng (烈王) Wújí (無忌), courtesy name Gōngshòu (公壽),
was spared during Chéng’s (承) disaster
due to his young age.
During the Xiánhé (咸和) era,
he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎),
and successively promoted to Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉), Zhōngshū (中書), and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎).
When Chǔ Póu (褚裒), the governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州), was about to take up his post,
Wújí (無忌) and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹) Huán Jǐng (桓景) and others saw him off at Bǎnjiáo (版橋).
At that time, Wáng Qí (王耆), the son of Wáng Yì (王廙) and Dānyáng Chéng (丹楊丞), was present.
Wújí (無忌), intent on revenge,
drew his sword, intending to personally kill him.
Póu (裒) and Jǐng (景) ordered their attendants to intervene and save him.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Chē Guàn (車灌) impeached Wújí (無忌) for attempting to commit murder
and referred him to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) for sentencing.
Emperor Chéng (成帝) issued an edict saying:
“Wáng Dūn (王敦) caused chaos,
and Mǐn Wáng (閔王) suffered calamity.
Considering the circumstances and the sentiment,
what blame can be attached to Wáng (王) today?
However, public and private laws
already have established rulings.
Wáng (王) should prioritize the nation’s interests;
how can he dwell on past events
to disrupt the court’s laws?
Let the responsible authorities clarify the laws and regulations;
from now on,
anyone who violates them
shall be punished.”
Thus, he was permitted to redeem himself.
In the early Jiànyuán era, he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì.
He was then transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He was sent out as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Chángshā Xiàng.
He also held the position of Jiāngxià Xiàng.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Nánjùn and Hédōng.
His general rank remained as before.
He followed Huán Wēn on his expedition to Shǔ.
For his meritorious service, his younger son, Yīn, was granted the noble rank of Guǎngjìn Bó.
His title was advanced to Qián Jiāngjūn.
He passed away in the sixth year of Yǒnghé.
He was posthumously granted Wèi Jiāngjūn.
He had two sons: Tián and Yīn.
Tián succeeded him.
Jìng Wáng Tián, courtesy name Yuányú,
was appointed Sànqí Shìláng in his youth.
He successively rose to Sànqí Chángshì, Huángmén Láng, and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Hǎixī was deposed
and Jiǎnwén Dì ascended the throne,
the state of emergency had not yet been lifted.
Dàsīmǎ Huán Wēn was stationed in the central hall,
sounding an alarm horn.
Tián submitted a memorial impeaching Wēn for great disrespect,
requesting that he be punished.
Wēn read the memorial and sighed, saying:
"This boy dares to impeach me;
he is truly formidable."
Tián was loyal, upright, and capable.
The court feared him.
He was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn and Sī Yōng Qín Liáng Sìzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng.
He was appointed Shàngshū.
He was then transferred to Shìzhōng,
and also held the position of Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was appointed Wúgúo Nèishǐ,
and also held the position of Tàizǐ Zhànshì.
As Tián was both a prominent member of the imperial clan and capable,
Emperor Xiàowǔ deeply trusted him.
He was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng provinces, as well as Jìnlíng of Yáng Province and the northern and southern commanderies of Xú Province.
He also held the titles of Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Yǎn and Qīng provinces, and was granted Jiǎjié.
He passed away in the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán.
He was posthumously granted Chējì Jiāngjūn.
He had four sons: Shàngzhī, Huīzhī, Yǔnzhī, and Xiūzhī.
Shàngzhī succeeded him.
Zhōng Wáng Shàngzhī, courtesy name Bódào,
was initially appointed Mìshū Láng.
He was then transferred to Sànqí Shìláng.
When Tián was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
Shàngzhī served as Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and Guǎnglíng Xiàng.
He resigned his post due to his father's mourning.
After the period of mourning ended,
he became Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn.
Within the imperial clan,
there were always distinguished individuals from generation to generation.
When Wáng Guóbǎo was executed,
Sànqí Chángshì Liú Zhènzhī, Péngchéng Nèishǐ Liú Juānzǐ, and Xúzhōu Biéjià Xú Fàng were all arrested as his confederates.
They were about to be severely punished.
Shàngzhī spoke to Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ, saying:
"Criminal cases should not be expanded.
It is fitting to release Zhènzhī and others."
Dàozǐ relied on Shàngzhī and his brothers, who all held high positions, in every matter,
so he followed his advice.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Gōng, fearing their growing influence,
raised an army with Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yǔ Kǎi,
using the pretext of punishing Shàngzhī.
They allied with Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yīn Zhòngkān and Nánjùn Gōng Huán Xuán in the south.
Dàozǐ ordered Qián Jiāngjūn Wáng Xún and Yòujiāngjūn Xiè Yǎn to attack Gōng,
while Shàngzhī resisted Kǎi.
Yǔnzhī fought against Kǎi's son, Hóng, at Dānglì.
Hóng was defeated and fled.
Kǎi's general, Duàn Fāng, was killed.
Kǎi fled alone on horseback to Huán Xuán.
Dàozǐ appointed Shàngzhī as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted him Jiǎjié,
following Kǎi's previous precedent.
Soon after, his title was advanced to Qián Jiāngjūn.
Yǔnzhī was made Wúgúo Nèishǐ.
Huīzhī was made Piàojì Sīmǎ and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Xiūzhī was made Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu.
Each commanded troops and cavalry,
and their power overshadowed the court.
When Hòu Jiāngjūn Yuán Xiǎn was in power,
he also relied on them for support.
Yuán Xiǎn favored Zhāng Fǎshùn,
and in every banquet,
they sat and rose without distinction.
When Shàngzhī attended court,
he sternly said to Yuán Xiǎn:
"Zhāng Fǎshùn is a petty person.
What extraordinary talent does he possess
to be suddenly promoted?
In this enlightened age,
this should not be so."
Yuán Xiǎn remained silent.
Shàngzhī further said:
"Although there are many in the imperial clan,
few dare to offer correction.
Even a king still accepts the words of a commoner.
Moreover, I, your humble subordinate, am not distantly related to you, my lord,
and have been favored for generations.
How can I sit by and watch errors without speaking my mind completely?"
He then shouted at Fǎshùn to descend.
Everyone present turned pale.
Shàngzhī remained composed, speaking and laughing as usual.
Yuán Xiǎn deeply resented this.
Later, an order was sent to the western command to dispatch two thousand able-bodied men.
Shàngzhī refused,
saying:
"The western frontier borders on uncivilized lands.
Bandits and enemies are unpredictable.
With only a few thousand troops,
it is insufficient for defense,
and there are no more to be divided."
Yuán Xiǎn was even more enraged.
However, as he was about to attack Huán Xuán,
he did nothing further.
When Yuán Xiǎn, by imperial edict, launched the western expedition,
he appointed Shàngzhī as the vanguard.
Shàngzhī's son, Wénzhòng, was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
When Huán Xuán reached Gūshú,
he sent Fēng Gāi and others to attack Lìyáng,
block the Dòngpǔ,
and burn Shàngzhī's boats and ships.
Shàngzhī led nine thousand infantry and arrayed them on the riverbank.
He had previously sent Wǔdū Tàishǒu Yáng Qiū to garrison Héngjiāng.
Qiū defected to Huán Xuán's army.
Shàngzhī's forces collapsed.
He escaped and hid on the road for more than ten days.
Hán Lián and Dīng Yuán of Qiáogúo reported this to Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán had him killed in the marketplace of Jiànkāng.
Huán Xuán then submitted a memorial stating that the prince of Mǐn should not be without an heir.
He then re-enfeoffed Shàngzhī's cousin, Kāngzhī, as Qiáoxiàn Wáng.
When Ān Dì was restored to power,
Shàngzhī was posthumously granted Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Xiūzhī's eldest son, Wénsī, was made Shàngzhī's heir
and succeeded to the title of Qiáojùn Wáng.
Wénsī was naturally violent.
He often deviated from proper conduct
and frequently killed innocent people.
He enjoyed hunting,
burning people's graves.
He was repeatedly impeached by officials.
He then plotted rebellion with a group of petty individuals.
When Liú Yù heard of this,
he executed his confederates
and sent Wénsī to his father, Xiūzhī,
ordering him to discipline his son himself.
Later, he and Xiūzhī together harbored resentment and raised troops.
They were defeated and killed by Yù.
His state was abolished.
Huīzhī, courtesy name Jìmíng,
successively served as Piàojì Sīmǎ and Dānyáng Yǐn.
When Shàngzhī was killed by Huán Xuán,
Huīzhī and others were exiled to Guǎngzhōu,
but they were killed en route.
When Ān Dì was restored to power,
Huīzhī was posthumously granted Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn.
Xiūzhī, courtesy name Jìyù.
He began his career in a respectable office.
For his meritorious service in pacifying Wáng Gōng and Yǔ Kǎi,
he was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu,
and stationed at Lìyáng.
When Huán Xuán attacked Lìyáng,
Xiūzhī defended the city resolutely.
When Shàngzhī was defeated in battle,
Xiūzhī led five hundred men out of the city and fought fiercely.
He was unsuccessful.
He then returned to the city
and fled with his sons and nephews to Mùróng Chāo.
Upon hearing of the righteous army's uprising,
he returned to the capital.
Dàjiāngjūn Wǔlíng Wáng issued an order saying:
"The former Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Xiūzhī
is capable, firm, and discerning.
His accomplishments are already established.
In the battle of Lìyáng,
the situation demanded quick action.
When circumstances became unfavorable and his strength was exhausted,
he sought refuge by fleeing.
Yet, he still gathered righteous volunteers,
enduring hardships and dangers.
As he meets the criteria for a worthy official,
he should be entrusted with the important responsibility of governing a region.
He is appointed Jiān of the military affairs of Jīng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Qín, and Yōng six provinces, also holding Hù Nánmán Xiàowèi, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted Jiǎjié."
Not long after arriving at his post,
Huán Zhèn again attacked Jiānglíng.
Xiūzhī was defeated in battle
and fled to Xiāngyáng.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Zhāng Chàngzhī and Gāopíng Xiàng Liú Huáisù attacked Zhèn from Miǎn,
and put him to flight.
Xiūzhī returned to his post.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Wáng Zhēnzhī memorialized that Xiūzhī had lost his garrison,
and he was removed from office.
The court appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Wèi Yǒngzhī to replace him.
Xiūzhī was summoned back to the capital
and appointed Hòu Jiāngjūn and Huìjī Nèishǐ.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Ruǎn Xīnzhī memorialized that Xiūzhī and Shàngshū Yú Xiàofù had violated prohibitions by engaging in leisurely activities.
His title was demoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Hòu Jiāngjūn.
When Lú Xún 盧循 rebelled,
he was additionally appointed Area Commander (dūdū 督) of the military affairs of the five eastern commanderies of Zhèjiāng 浙江.
He was dismissed due to a public matter.
When Liú Yì 劉毅 was executed,

he was reinstated as Area Commander (dūdū 督) of the military affairs of Jīng 荊, Yōng 雍, Liáng 梁, Qín 秦, Níng 寧, and Yì 益 six prefectures, General Who Pacifies the West (píngxī jiāngjūn 平西將軍), Inspector of Jīng Prefecture (Jīngzhōu cìshǐ 荊州刺史), and given the Staff of Authority (jiǎjié 假節).
When his son, Wénsī 文思, caused trouble,
he submitted a memorial apologetically, saying:
“Wénsī 文思 was unable to cultivate himself,
and brought罪 and calamity upon himself.
I am filled with anxiety and trepidation,
and a mixture of regret and shame.
I have been without method in managing my family,
my authority and instruction have not been effective,
resulting in my son and nephew transgressing the law,
and letting down the imperial court.
I am filled with sorrow and shame,
how can I face myself?
I request to resign from my post,
and submit to the court for punishment.”
This was not granted.
Later, due to Wénsī’s 文思 affair, he harbored resentment,
and consequently allied with Rǔ Zōngzhī 魯宗之, the Inspector of Yōng Prefecture (Yōngzhōu cìshǐ 雍州刺史),
intending to jointly execute the powerful ministers.
At that time, Xiūzhī’s 休之 second son Wénbǎo 文寶 and his brother’s son Wénzǔ 文祖 were both in the capital.
They were arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge (tíngwèi 廷尉) and granted death.
Liú Yù 劉裕 personally led an expedition against him,
and secretly sent a letter to Xiūzhī’s 休之 chief clerk (zhìzhōng 治中), Hán Yánzhī 韓延之, saying:
“The matter concerning Wénsī 文思,
is known far and wide.
Last autumn, I sent Kāngzhī 康之 to return Sīmǎ Jūn 司馬君,
pushing to the extreme of ultimate fairness.
Yet there is no sense of shame,
and memorials have long ceased.
This is not tolerated by heaven and earth.
I received the order to campaign in the west,
only targeting his father and son.
The gentry and old families of that land,
who were forced and pressed into service by them,
will not be questioned at all.
In previous years, Xī Sēngshī 郗僧施, Xiè Shào 謝劭, Rèn Jízhī 任集之, and others plotted for years,
specifically devising plans for Liú Yì 劉毅,
which led to this situation.
Now, you gentlemen are all being pressed and forced at once,
though you originally had no minor grievances.
My open-mindedness and expectations of others
have their own origins.
Now that I am close by,
this is the day for you worthies to save yourselves.
If the great army approaches,
and swords clash and blades meet,
orchids and mugwort will be mixed together,
and perhaps indistinguishable.
Therefore, I state this intention,
and you may also show it to others who share your sentiments.”
Yánzhī 延之 replied:
“I hear that you are personally leading an army,
and have traveled far into the western region.
The scholars and commoners throughout the territory
are all alarmed and terrified.
Why?
Because they do not know the reason for the army’s expedition.
Having received your letter,
I finally learned of the previous matter concerning the King of Qiáo 譙.
It truly makes me sigh.
Sīmǎ Píngxī 司馬平西 is loyal and steadfast to the state,
and treats others with sincerity.
Because you have the merit of restoration,
and the family and state rely on it,
he demonstrates virtue and entrusts sincerity,
consulting and looking up to you in every matter.
The King of Qiáo 譙 was impeached for a minor matter in the past,
yet he still modestly resigned his position.
How much more so with a major transgression,
should he remain silent?
However, Kāngzhī’s 康之 previous words
were not exhaustive,
so he again sent Hú Dào 胡道
to fully express his thoughts.
Before Dào 道 could return,
a memorial had already been submitted to depose him.
What was not exhaustive was the order itself.
The trust and reliance between us
should naturally be like this.
What is so objectionable
that it leads to war?
Since the uprising of the righteous army,
which regional governor dared not consult first,
but directly memorialize the Son of Heaven?
This can be called ‘when one wishes to accuse someone, one can always find a pretext’!
Your Excellency Liú Yù 劉裕,
who among the people within the seas
does not see this heart of yours?
And yet you still wish to deceive the men of the state,
‘not tolerated by heaven and earth’
that applies to you, not to us.
Your letter states, ‘open-mindedness and expectations of others,
have their own origins’;
now you attack another’s lord,
and lure people with profit.
Truly, this can be called ‘open-mindedness and expectations of others,
have their own origins’!
Liú Fān 劉藩 died at the gate of the imperial palace,
Zhūgé諸葛 was destroyed by those close to him.
You use sweet words to deceive the regional governors,
〔二一〕and then attack them with light troops.
This leads to a situation where on the mat there are no sincere gentlemen,
and outside the gate there are no feudal lords who trust themselves.
To consider this a good strategy
is truly shameful.
I am truly base and inferior,
but I have learned the Way from gentlemen.
With Píngxī’s 平西 ultimate virtue,
how could there be no minister who would accept his command?
Even if there were eternal chaos in the world,
and the nine streams were turbid,
I would rather wander in the underworld with Zāng Hóng 臧洪.”
Yù 裕 received the letter and sighed,
showing it to his aides, saying:
“One should serve others like this!”
Zōngzhī 宗之 heard that Yù 裕 was heading towards Jīng Prefecture (Jīngzhōu 荊州),
and traveled from Xiāngyáng 襄陽 to join Xiūzhī 休之 to garrison Jiānglíng 江陵 together.
They sent Wénsī 文思 and Zōngzhī’s 宗之 son Guǐ 軌 with troops to resist Yù 裕,
and they fought at Jiāngjīn 江津.
Xiūzhī 休之 suffered a great defeat,
and consequently fled with Zōngzhī 宗之 to Yáo Xīng 姚興.
When Yù 裕 pacified Yáo Hóng 姚泓,
Xiūzhī 休之 intended to flee to Wèi 魏,
but died on the way
before reaching it.
Yǔnzhī 允之, courtesy name Jìdù 季度,
was adopted as heir to his uncle Yīn 愔.
He inherited the title of Count of Guǎngjìn (Guǎngjìn bó 廣晉伯),
and successively held positions such as General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó jiāngjūn 輔國將軍), and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wúguó Xuānchéng Qiáoliáng nèishǐ 吳國宣城譙梁內史).
When Wáng Gōng 王恭, Yǔ Kǎi 庾楷, Huán Xuán 桓玄, and others launched internal attacks,
King Dàozǐ of Kuàijī (Kuàijīwáng Dàozǐ 會稽王道子) ordered Yǔnzhī 允之 and his brothers to resist Kǎi 楷,
and they defeated him.
In the early Yuánxīng 元興 era,
he and his brother Huīzhī 恢之 were exiled to Guǎng Prefecture (Guǎngzhōu 廣州) together,
and were murdered on the way.
When the righteous army rose,
he was posthumously appointed Grand Minister of Sacrifices (tàicháng qīng 太常卿).
His cousin Kāngzhī 康之 succeeded to the title with his son Wénhuì 文惠.
When the Sòng 宋 received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Hán Yánzhī 韓延之, courtesy name Xiǎnzōng 顯宗,
was a native of Zhěyáng 赭陽 in Nányáng 南陽,
a descendant of Wèi 魏 Grand Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) Jì 暨.
In his youth, he was known for his integrity.
During Emperor Ān’s 安帝 reign, he served as General Who Establishes Awe (Jiànwēi jiāngjūn 建威將軍) and Chief Clerk of Jīng Prefecture (Jīngzhōu zhìzhōng 荊州治中),
then transferred to Registrar and Military Advisor (lùshì cānjūn 錄事參軍) of the Pacifying the West regional command (Píngxī fǔ 平西府).
Because Liú Yù’s 劉裕 father’s given name was Qiáo 翹 and courtesy name was Xiǎnzōng 顯宗,
Yánzhī 延之 thereupon adopted the courtesy name Xiǎnzōng 顯宗,
and named his son Qiáo 翹,
to show his defiance towards the Liú 劉 clan.
He fled with Xiūzhī 休之 to Yáo Xīng 姚興.
When Liú Yù 劉裕 entered the pass,
he again fled to Wèi 魏.
Yīn 愔, courtesy name Jìngwáng 敬王,
was initially enfeoffed as Count of Guǎngjìn (Guǎngjìn bó 廣晉伯).
He died young
without a son,
so his elder brother Tián 恬 had his son Yǔnzhī 允之 succeed him.
King Mù of Gāoyáng (Gāoyáng Wáng Mù 高陽王睦)
King Mù of Gāoyáng (Gāoyáng Wáng Mù 高陽王睦),
courtesy name Zǐyǒu 子友,
was the younger brother of King Xùn of Qiáo (Qiáowáng Xùn 譙王遜).
He was Marquis of Ānpíng Tíng (Ānpíngtíng Hóu 安平亭侯) in Wèi 魏,
and successively served as Imperial Censor (shìyùshǐ 侍御史).
When Emperor Wǔ 武帝 received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as King of Zhōngshān (Zhōngshān Wáng 中山王),
with an income of 5200 households.
Mù 睦 memorialized requesting to establish temples for Gāoyáo 臯陶, following the precedent of Liùliáo 六蓼,
and for Xiàng 相, following the precedent of Zēngshí 鄫嵵.
The matter was sent down to the Grand Minister of Sacrifices (tàicháng 太常),
who was to deliberate according to ritual classics.
The Erudite (bóshì 博 士) Libationer (jìjiǔ 祭酒) Liú Xǐ 劉憙 and others debated:
“The ‘Royal Regulations’ (Wángzhì 王制) chapter of the Lǐjì 禮記 states,
feudal lords have five ancestral temples:
two zhāo 昭 and two mù 穆,
plus the grand progenitor, making five.
This means that the temple of the founding ancestor
refers to the heir who inherits the main line,
and only one person is allowed to establish it.
Even if collateral brothers also become feudal lords,
the ruler of the initial enfeoffment is not allowed to establish a temple.
Now, Mù 睦 is not of the legitimate lineage.
If ancestral temples are established,
Zhōngshān 中山 cannot have one concurrently.
Later generations in Zhōngshān 中山 will then be able to establish a temple for Mù 睦,
as the founding ancestor for later generations of his descendants.”
An imperial edict stated:
“The ritual texts are unclear.
This is a matter of great importance for the system.
It should be thoroughly examined,
and sent down to the ritual officials for extensive discussion,
before a decision is made.”
In the third year of Xiánníng,

Mù dispatched envoys to recruit and relocate over seven hundred households from eight counties within the state who were harboring fugitives, occupying private lands, changing names, or fraudulently claiming exemptions.
Dù Yǒu, the Governor of Jìzhōu, memorialized that Mù was enticing fugitives,
which was unfitting for a ruler.
The relevant authorities memorialized,
"The matter occurred before the amnesty,
so it should be pardoned."
An imperial edict stated:
"How could the King of Zhōngshān act to this extent?
Reading the memorial fills me with deep regret.
Establishing numerous relatives
is intended to assist the imperial house from above
and benefit the common people below.
How could it merely be for personal glory and elevation,
leading the people to transgress laws and regulations!
This matter should be thoroughly discussed to determine right and wrong,
and to ascertain where merit or fault lies.
If it is truly unfitting for a ruler,
why discuss it in terms of an amnesty edict?
