Let Mù be demoted to County Marquis."
He was then enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dànshuǐ County.
After the pacification of Wú,
an edict in the early Tàikāng period restored his title.
The relevant authorities memorialized that he should be enfeoffed as the King of Jiāngyáng.
The Emperor said:
"Mù retreated to quietly reflect on his faults
and reform his virtue.
He now has a noble title and territory,
not merely because of an amnesty.
Jiāngyáng is remote and distant;
let him be enfeoffed with Gāoyáng Commandery."
He was then enfeoffed as the King of Gāoyáng.
In the first year of Yuánkāng,
he became Zōngzhèng.
He passed away in office.
His heir-apparent Wèi had died young,
so his grandson Yì succeeded him.
Yì was appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
During the Yǒngjiā period, he perished at the hands of Shí Lè.
In the first year of Lóng'ān,
an edict ordered Wénshēn, the son of Huī (the second son of Tián, the King Jìng of Qiáo), to succeed Yì.
He reigned for five years
and died
without an heir.
Fǎlián, the son of Chún, the King of Gāomì, was again appointed to succeed him.
When the Sòng received the abdication,
his state was abolished.
Líng, the King Jǐng of Rènchéng (brothers Shùn, Bīn)
Líng, the King Jǐng of Rènchéng, styled Zǐshān,
was the son of Tōng, the Marquis of Ānchéng Tíng and Wei Sīlì Cóngshì, who was a younger brother of Emperor Xuān.
He was initially appointed Yìláng.
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Běihǎi,
with four thousand seven hundred households.
In the third year,
he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Rènchéng
and went to his state.
He died in the fifth year of Xiánníng.
His son Jì succeeded him.
Jì was appointed Sànqí Shìláng, Gěishìzhōng, Sànqí Chángshì, and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
He followed Yuè, the King of Dōnghǎi, to Xiàng,
and was killed by Shí Lè.
His two sons also perished.
He had two younger brothers: Shùn and Bīn.
Shùn, styled Zǐsī,
was initially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xíyáng Tíng.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
Shùn sighed, saying:
"This act deviates from that of Táng and Yú,
yet it is falsely called an abdication!"
He then wept sorrowfully.
Because of this, he was dismissed
and exiled to Gūzāng County in Wǔwēi.
Although he was punished with exile,
he maintained his resolve until his death.
Bīn, the King Miù of Xīhé, styled Zǐzhèng,
was a Wei Zhōngláng.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Chén,
with one thousand seven hundred and ten households.
In the third year,
he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Xīhé.
He died in the fourth year of Xiánníng.
His son Yǐn succeeded him.
Yǐn died,
and his son Cuò succeeded him.
[二二]
The historiographer comments: In the early Tàishǐ period,
there were few troubles in the realm.
The remaining evils of Wei were reformed,
and the ancient institutions of Zhōu were followed.
Members of the imperial clan were concurrently established
as bulwarks.
The paternal uncles enjoyed the reverence of Yú and Guó,
and the brothers received the blessings of Lǔ and Wèi,
in the belief that the dynastic reign would be long
and the main and branch lineages would last for a hundred generations.
Ānpíng possessed a grand and distant demeanor,
with a lofty and elegant bearing.
Internally, he promoted righteousness and morality;
externally, he expounded loyalty and integrity.
When Gāoguì passed away,
he wept bitterly beside the body.
When Chénliú went to his state,
he bowed in farewell, shedding tears.
The saying goes,
"Strong winds reveal sturdy grass";
Xiànwáng truly exemplified this.
Thus, he was able to rank among the highest officials,
enjoy a long life,
and with his pure integrity and ultimate example,
he became a hero of the Jìn imperial clan.
His descendants followed his ways,
and their good fortune was firm for generations.
Gāomì's character was pure and far-reaching,
simple and with few desires.
He served his parents with filial piety
and his sovereign with loyalty.
Among all the branch lineages,
he was truly a pillar of the state.
Xīncài and Nányáng
both governed regional commands.
Faced with numerous difficulties for the imperial house
and the desolation of the central plains,
they displayed righteousness and distinguished their integrity,
achieving merit in perilous times.
At that time, numerous vile factions emerged,
and their ferocious power grew daily.
With forces vastly unequal,
they successively perished.
Alas!
Qiáo Mǐn was profound, heroic, strong, and brave,
establishing his authority in the southern territories.
When treacherous villains unleashed chaos
and brazenly used military force internally,
he, filled with loyal indignation, rose up,
initiating a righteous cause in Xiāngzhōu.
Jīng and Miǎn responded,
and many talented individuals exerted their efforts.
Although he did not establish great merits,
his sincere integrity was clearly manifested,
leaving a legacy for future generations,
and his valiant spirit was illustrious for many generations.
How could this not be splendid!
Xūn belonged to a remote branch,
inherently violent and savage.
Yet, he was entrusted with a court commission,
and dispatched to Liáng and Mín.
He then abandoned his kin and betrayed his lord,
ungratefully acting wantonly.
Relying on the abundance of Yōng and Shǔ,
he harbored sinister intentions;
trusting in the fortifications of the rivers and mountains,
his treacherous schemes deepened daily.
Therefore, officials gritted their teeth,
expressing their pent-up indignation;
righteous men thought of rising up,
vowing to sacrifice themselves.
Heaven's way brings disaster upon the wicked,
and he was swiftly pacified.
In the past, while Jí Àn was still alive,
Huáinán suppressed his schemes;
if Zhōu Fǔ had remained,
the fierce bandit would not have risen.
The wicked fear the righteous,
a rule constant across different eras.
The *Shī* says,
"You bring trouble upon yourself,"
which describes Xūn.
Xíyáng, relying on his branch's good fortune,
held to simplicity and harbored a desire for ease.
He settled his emotions outside the dust of the world,
aspiring to transcend worldly affairs.
Considering the solitary virtue of an ordinary man,
he valued the grand principle of achieving his ambition.
That his words were broadcast and he survived
was still fortunate.
The encomium states: Ānpíng established his integrity,
with a refined and loyal character.
Gāomì embraced harmony,
a hope of the imperial clan.
Xīncài met with disaster,
losing his life while fully loyal.
Qiáo Mǐn sacrificed for righteousness,
[二三] his strength failed but his will was acclaimed.
Xūn brought trouble upon himself,
his name and body perished.
Shùn disregarded taboos,
exiled to a distant land.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 8: The Five Kings of Xuān
Emperor Xuān had nine sons.
Empress Mù Zhāng gave birth to Emperor Jǐng, Emperor Wén, and Gàn, the King of Píngyuán.
Consort Fú gave birth to Liàng, the King Wénchéng of Rǔnán; Zhòu, the King Wǔ of Lángyá; Jīng, the Marquis Qīnghuì Tíng; and Jùn, the King Wǔ of Fúfēng.
Consort Zhāng gave birth to Róng, the King of Liáng.
Consort Bǎi gave birth to Lún, the King of Zhào.
Separate biographies exist for Liàng and Lún.
Gàn, the King of Píngyuán
Píngyuán Wáng Gàn (平原王榦), courtesy name Zǐliáng (子良).
When young, as a princely son during the Wèi (魏) period, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānyáng Tíng (安陽亭侯).
He was gradually promoted to Fǔjūn Zhōnglángjiāng (撫軍中郎將),
and his noble title was advanced to Marquis of Píngyáng Xiāng (平陽鄉侯).
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Earl of Dìngtáo (定陶伯).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Píngyuán (平原王),
with an estate of eleven thousand three hundred households.
He was granted a drum and pipe band and two imperial outriders,
and the attire of a Shìzhōng (侍中) was added.
At the beginning of the Xiánníng (咸寧) era,
when the various kings were sent to their states,
Gàn (榦) suffered from a severe illness.
His temperament was abnormal,
yet he was quite pure, detached, and reclusive,
simple in his desires,
so a special edict allowed him to remain.
At the end of the Tàikāng (太康) era,
he was appointed Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
with the added title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was specially granted a gold seal and purple ribbon,
and his rank was placed among the Three Dukes.
When Emperor Huì (惠帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫),
retaining his position as Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was allowed to wear his sword and shoes when ascending the hall,
and not required to hasten when entering court.
Although Gàn (榦) was the king of a great state,
he did not attend to its affairs.
When appointments or reassignments were made,
it was always based on ability.
Although he possessed noble titles and emoluments,
it was as if they were not his own.
His salary in cloth and silk
was all left exposed to rot.
When it rained, he would move the open carts outside and the covered carts inside.
Someone asked him the reason,
and he replied,
"The exposed ones are suitable for being inside."
When court officials visited him,
even if their names were announced,
they were compelled to leave their carriages and horses outside the gate,
and some would not be seen for an entire evening.
Occasionally, when an audience was granted,
he would interact with people
with a sincere and respectful demeanor,
never making any mistakes.
When his beloved concubines died,
after the shrouding,
he would never nail the coffin shut,
but place it in an empty room in the back.
Every few days, he would open it and look,
sometimes engaging in improper acts,
waiting until the corpse decomposed before burying it.
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) assisted in governance,
he made Gàn (榦) a Wèijiāngjūn (衞將軍).
When Emperor Huì (惠帝) was restored to power,
he was again Shìzhōng (侍中),
with the added title of Tàibǎo (太保).
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) suppressed Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫),
all the imperial kinsmen and court officials presented cattle and wine to congratulate Jiǒng (冏).
Gàn (榦) alone brought a hundred coins.
When he saw Jiǒng (冏), he presented them,
saying,
"Zhào Wáng (趙王) was rebellious and chaotic,
and you were able to act righteously.
This is your achievement.
Now I present you with a hundred coins to congratulate you.
However,
great power is difficult to hold;
you must not be careless."
After Jiǒng (冏) began assisting in governance,
Gàn (榦) visited him.
Jiǒng (冏) came out to greet him and bowed.
Gàn (榦) entered,
sat on his bed,
did not order Jiǒng (冏) to sit,
and said to him,
"Do not imitate the daughter of Bái (白女兒)."
His intention referred to Lún (倫).
When Jiǒng (冏) was executed,
Gàn (榦) wept grievously,
saying to his attendants,
"The imperial clan declines daily.
Only this child was most worthy,
yet he too has been harmed.
From now on, it will be dangerous indeed!"
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) raised his army of righteousness
and arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽),
he went to visit Gàn (榦).
Gàn (榦) closed his gate and did not receive him.
Yuè (越) waited in his carriage for a long time.
Only then did Gàn (榦) send someone to apologize and dismiss him,
while he himself peeped through the gate.
At the time, no one could fathom his intention.
Some said he was ill,
others thought he was concealing his traces.
He passed away in the fifth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
at the age of eighty.
At that time, Liú Cōng (劉聰) invaded Luò (洛),
so there was no time for posthumous honors.
He had two sons.
The heir apparent, Guǎng (廣), died young.
His second son, Yǒng (永), was enfeoffed as the Duke of Āndé Xiàn (安德縣公) during the Tàixī (太熙) era,
and held the post of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Both were virtuous men.
They met with disaster,
and their entire household was annihilated.
Lángyá Wáng Zhòu (琅邪王伷) (sons Jìn (覲), Dàn (澹), Yáo (繇), Cuǐ (漼))
Lángyá Wǔ Wáng Zhòu (琅邪武王伷), courtesy name Zǐjiāng (子將).
At the beginning of the Zhèngshǐ (正始) era, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nán'ān Tíng (南安亭侯).
He showed talent and promise early on. He began his career as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
and supervised and guarded Yèchéng (鄴城),
earning a reputation for pacification and conciliation.
He was successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
advanced to Marquis of Dōngwǔ Xiāng (東武鄉侯),
and appointed Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍), Jūn Yǎnzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (監兗州諸軍事), and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史).
When the Five Ranks were first established,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Nánpí (南皮伯).
He was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍) and granted a 'false-jie' (假節).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Dōngguǎn Jùn (東莞郡王),
with an estate of ten thousand six hundred households.
At the initial establishment of the two ministers (卿),
a special edict ordered the various kings to personally select their magistrates (令長).
Zhòu (伷) submitted a memorial declining,
but it was not permitted.
He entered court as Shàngshū Yòu Púyè (尚書右僕射) and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍).
He then left to be Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn (鎮東大將軍),
with a 'false-jie' (假節) and command of Xúzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (徐州諸軍事),
replacing Wèi Guàn (衞瓘) in garrisoning Xiàpí (下邳).
Zhòu (伷)'s garrison management was effective,
winning the utmost loyalty of his officers and soldiers.
The people of Wú (吳) feared him.
He was granted the authority of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and re-enfeoffed as the King of Lángyá (琅邪王),
with Dōngguǎn (東莞) added to his state.
During the campaign to pacify Wú (吳),
he led tens of thousands of troops through Túzhōng (涂中).
Sūn Hào (孫晧) submitted a memorial and sent the imperial seal and ribbon,
appearing before Zhòu (伷) to surrender.
An edict stated:
"Lángyá Wáng Zhòu (琅邪王伷) commanded his forces,
successively holding Túzhōng (涂中),
preventing the rebels from aiding each other.
He also ordered Lángyá Xiàng Liú Hóng (琅邪相劉弘) and others to advance and press upon the Jiāng (江).
The rebels were terrified,
and sent envoys to present the false imperial seal and ribbon.
He also ordered Chángshǐ Wáng Héng (長史王恆) to lead various armies across the Jiāng (江),
breaking the rebel border defenses,
capturing Dū Cài Jī (督蔡機),
beheading and receiving the surrender of fifty to sixty thousand,
and Zhūgě Jìng (諸葛靚) and Sūn Yì (孫奕) and others all pledged their lives and asked for death.
His merits and achievements are outstanding.
Therefore, his two sons are to be enfeoffed as Tinghóu (亭侯),
each with three thousand households,
and awarded six thousand bolts of silk."
Soon after,
he also supervised the military affairs of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and was granted the attire of a Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was advanced to Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
Zhòu (伷) was already respected as an imperial relative,
and furthermore had the merit of pacifying Wú (吳).
He was self-restrained and modest,
showing no arrogance or complacency.
His subordinates exerted their full effort,
and the common people were transformed by his influence.
When his illness became severe,
he was granted a bed curtain, clothes, money, silk, glutinous rice, millet, and other items,
and a Shìzhōng (侍中) was sent to inquire about him.
He passed away in the fourth year of Tàikāng (太康),
at the age of fifty-seven.
Before his death, he submitted a memorial requesting to be buried near his mother, the Grand Consort's tomb,
and also asked to divide his state to enfeoff his four sons.
The emperor granted his request.
His son, Gong Wáng Jìn (恭王覲), succeeded him.
His second son, Dàn (澹), was enfeoffed as Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王).
Yáo (繇) was enfeoffed as Dōng'ān Wáng (東安王).
Cuǐ (漼) was enfeoffed as Huáilíng Wáng (淮陵王).
Jìn (字 Sīzǔ)
was appointed Róngcóng Púshè.
He died in the first year of Tàixī
at the age of thirty-five.
His son, Ruì, succeeded him,
who became Emperor Yuán.
At the beginning of Zhōngxīng,
Prince Póu was enfeoffed as the King of Lángyá,
to continue the sacrifices for King Gōng.
Póu died young,
so Prince Huàn was made King of Lángyá.
He died on the same day,
and again Prince Yù was made King of Lángyá.
At the beginning of Xiánhé,
as he had already been transferred and enfeoffed as the King of Kuàijī,
Emperor Chéng further made Emperor Kāng the King of Lángyá.
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Emperor Chéng's eldest son, Emperor Āi, as the King of Lángyá.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
he made the deposed Emperor the King of Lángyá.
When the deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
the King of Kuàijī was appointed to manage the sacrifices of the state of Lángyá.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
the King of Lángyá had no heir.
Just before the Emperor's death,
he enfeoffed his youngest son, Dàozǐ, as the King of Lángyá.
Dàozǐ later became the King of Kuàijī,
and Emperor Gōng was made King of Lángyá.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the state of Lángyá was abolished.
Wǔlíng Zhuāngwáng Dàn (字 Sīhóng)
was initially appointed Róngcóng Púshè,
and later enfeoffed as the Duke of Dōngwǔ,
with an estate of 5,200 households.
He was then transferred to Qián Jiāngjūn and Zhōng Hùjūn.
He was jealous and harmful by nature,
and lacked filial piety and fraternal affection.
His younger brother, Dōng'ānwáng Yáo, had a good reputation
and was beloved by their parents.
Dàn hated him like an enemy,
and thus slandered Yáo to Rǔnánwáng Liàng.
Liàng already had a rift with Yáo,
and so he memorialized for Yáo to be deposed and exiled.
When Zhàowáng Lún rebelled,
he made Dàn Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Dàn was always close to Guō Chú and Guō Kǎn, brothers from Hénèi.
While drunk,
Chú and others spoke of Zhāng Huá's injustice.
Dàn, being a heavy drinker,
thereupon killed them all,
and sent their heads to Lún.
His drunkenness and cruelty were thus.
Dàn's wife, Lady Guō,
was the younger sister of Empress Jiǎ.
Initially, relying on her influence,
she was disrespectful to Dàn's mother.
When Qíwáng Jiǒng assisted in governance,
Dàn's mother, Grand Consort Zhūgě, memorialized that Dàn was unfilial
and requested Yáo's return.
Because of this, Dàn and his wife and children were exiled to Liáodōng.
His son, Xǐ, who was five years old,
refused to go with them,
saying:
"I must seek my father's return;
I will not be exiled with him."
He pleaded for several years,
and after the Grand Consort died
and Yáo was harmed,
only then was he able to return.
He was appointed Guānglù Dàfū, Shàngshū, and Tàizǐ Tàifù,
and re-enfeoffed as the King of Wǔlíng.
At the end of Yǒngjiā, he was killed by Shí Lè.
His son, Āiwáng Zhé, succeeded him.
Zhé (字 Jǐnglín)
was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and was also killed by Lè.
He had no son.
Thereafter, Emperor Yuán enfeoffed Prince Xī as the King of Wǔlíng
to continue Dàn's sacrifices.
Dōng'ānwáng Yáo (字 Sīxuán).
He was first appointed Duke of Dōng'ān,
and successively served as Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng,
then promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
He had a beautiful beard,
was firm and resolute by nature,
possessed authority,
was learned and talented,
filial to his parents,
and observed mourning rites fully.
During the execution of Yáng Jùn,
Yáo was stationed at Yúnlóngmén
and also commanded various armies.
For his merits, he was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
concurrently holding the position of Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
and advanced in rank to a Commandery King,
with an estate of 20,000 households.
He was given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
concurrently Diǎnjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and retained Yòuwèi as before.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
On that day, over 300 people were punished or rewarded,
all by Yáo's decision.
Wén Chú, the father of Dōngyí Xiàowèi Wén Chú, had been killed by Yáo's maternal grandfather, Zhūgě Dàn.
Yáo feared Chú would become a threat to his mother's family,
and so on that day, he executed Chú without proper cause.
Yáo's elder brother Dàn repeatedly made accusations against Yáo to Rǔnánwáng Liàng,
but Liàng did not accept them.
Now, because Yáo had unilaterally carried out punishments and rewards,
Dàn took advantage of the opportunity to slander him.
Liàng was misled by his words
and consequently dismissed Yáo from office,
sending him to his residence as a duke.
Due to rebellious remarks,
he was deposed and exiled to Dàifāng.
At the beginning of Yǒngkāng,
Yáo was summoned,
re-enfeoffed,
appointed Zōngzhèng Qīng,
promoted to Shàngshū,
and then transferred to Zuǒpúshè.
When Emperor Huì attacked Chéngdūwáng Yǐng,
Yáo was observing mourning for his mother in Yè,
and advised Yǐng to disband his troops and surrender.
When the imperial army was defeated,
Yǐng resented Yáo
and then killed him.
Later, Hún, the Marquis of Chánglè Tíng and son of Lángyáwáng Jìn, was enfeoffed as the King of Dōng'ān
to continue Yáo's sacrifices.
He died soon after,
and the state was abolished.
Huáilíng Yuánwáng Cuǐ (字 Sīchōng).
He was initially enfeoffed as the Duke of Guǎnglíng,
with an estate of 2,900 households.
He successively served as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Sànqí Chángshì.
When Zhàowáng Lún usurped power,
the three kings raised an army.
Cuǐ, along with Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Yú, attacked and killed Sūn Xiù,
and subsequently deposed Lún.
For his merits, he was advanced in rank to the King of Huáilíng,
entered service as Shàngshū,
with the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and then transferred to Zōngzhèng and Guānglù Dàfū.
He died,
and his son, Zhēnwáng Róng, succeeded him.
He died
without a son.
During Emperor Ān's reign, Wǔlíng Wēiwáng Sūn Yùn was enfeoffed as the King of Huáilíng
to continue the sacrifices of Yuánwáng.
He rose to the position of Sànqí Chángshì.
He died
without a son,
so Ānzhī, the son of Línchuānwáng Bǎo, was made his heir.
When Sòng received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Qīnghuì Tínghóu Jīng (字 Zǐzuǒ).
At the end of Wèi, he was granted a noble title as a princely son.
He died at the age of twenty-four.
He was posthumously granted Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
and Jī (字 Tàixuán), the son of Emperor Wén, was made his heir.
In the first year of Tàishǐ,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Yān,
with an estate of 6,663 households.
When Jī went to his state,
he was summoned in the early Xiánníng era to be Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Yúyáng Commandery was added to his state,
and he was given the attire of a Shìzhōng.
He was appointed Qīngzhōu Dūdū, Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, with the provisional authority of Jiǎjié.
Běipíng, Shànggǔ, and Guǎng Commanderies, totaling 10,337 households, were added to the state of Yān, making it 20,000 households.
He died
without a son.
Qíwáng Jiǒng memorialized that his son Jǐ should succeed him.
Later, Jiǒng was defeated,
and the state was abolished.
Fúfēngwáng Jùn (子 Chàng, Xīn)
Fúfēng Wǔwáng Jùn (字 Zǐzāng).
As a child, he was intelligent and wise.
At the age of five or six, he could write memorials
and recite classics.
Those who saw him marvelled at him.
When he grew up,
he was pure, upright, and adhered to the Dao,
and was the most outstanding among the imperial clan.
During the Jǐngchū era of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngyáng Tíng.
When Qíwáng Fāng ascended the throne,
Jùn was eight years old
and served as Sànqí Chángshì and Imperial Lecturer.
He was soon promoted to Bùbīng and Túntúnqí Xiàowèi,
retaining his position as Chángshì.
He was advanced in rank to Marquis of Xiāng,
and then appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Jiǎjié, and Dūdū Huáiběi Zhūjūnsì.
He was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngshòu,
and then transferred to Āndōng Jiāngjūn.
At the beginning of Xiánxī,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngmóu,
then transferred to Āndōng Dàjiāngjūn,
garrisoned at Xǔchāng.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
Jùn was promoted to King of Rǔyīn,
with an estate of ten thousand households,
and was appointed Grand Inspector of all military affairs in Yùzhōu.
When Wú general Dīng Fèng invaded Sháopí,
Jùn commanded the various armies to repel him.
He was then transferred to Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Grand Inspector of all military affairs in Yángzhōu,
replacing Shí Bāo to garrison Shòuchūn.
Soon after, he was again appointed Grand Inspector of Yùzhōu,
returning to garrison Xǔchāng.
He was promoted to General-in-Chief Guarding the West, Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Grand Inspector of all military affairs in Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, and other prefectures,
replacing King Liàng of Rǔnán to garrison Guānzhōng,
and was granted the formal court attire of a gǔnmiǎn robe and a Shìzhōng.
Jùn was skilled at governing and controlling,
possessing both authority and benevolence.
He encouraged and supervised agriculture and sericulture,
and shared work with his soldiers.
He, his aides, and the generals and soldiers were all limited to ten *mǔ* of land.
He reported this fully in a memorial.
An imperial edict was issued to widely disseminate it to the prefectures and counties,
making everyone diligent in agricultural matters.
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
the Qiāng barbarians under Shùjīnéng rebelled,
and Jùn dispatched troops to suppress them,
beheading over three thousand.
He was promoted to General-in-Chief Conquering the West,
granted the privilege of establishing an administration and appointing officials,
with status equal to the Three Excellencies,
and retained his Envoy with Imperial Credentials and Grand Inspector posts.
An edict also ordered Jùn to send seven thousand men to replace the garrison troops in Liángzhōu.
Shùjīnéng, Hóu Dànbó, and others wanted to preemptively attack the tenant soldiers,
so Jùn ordered the Protector of the Army Subduing Barbarians, Wén Shū, to command the armies of Liáng, Qín, and Yōng prefectures to advance and take up positions to overawe them.
Jīnéng then sent his twenty subordinate tribes and Dànbó, with hands tied, to the army gate,
each sending a hostage.
The various Hú tribes of Āndìng, Běidì, Jīnchéng, namely Jí Kēluó, Hóu Jīnduō, and the northern barbarians such as Rè Jiǒng, totaling two hundred thousand people, also came to surrender.
That year, he came to court,
and was transferred to be King of Fúfēng,
with an increased enfeoffment of Dī households within the national borders,
and was granted a feather canopy and military band.
At the beginning of Tàikāng,
he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry,
retaining his privilege of establishing an administration, Envoy with Imperial Credentials, and Grand Inspector posts.
Jùn was known for his filial piety.
When his mother, Consort Fú, was with his elder brother Liàng in office,
Jùn often wept with longing.
If he heard she was ill,
he would immediately worry and refrain from eating,
sometimes abandoning his official duties to visit and pay his respects.
From a young age, he loved learning
and was capable of writing essays.
He debated with Xún Yǐ on the priority of benevolence and filial piety,
and his writing was commendable.
When King Yōu of Qí was dispatched to garrison a region,
Jùn submitted a heartfelt memorial to remonstrate,
but because the Emperor did not comply,
he fell ill and passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Marshal,
and given the additional titles of Shìzhōng and Deputy with Imperial Battle-Axe.
When the people of the Western regions heard of his death,
those weeping filled the roads.
The common people erected a stele for him,
and the elders, upon seeing the stele, all bowed down;
such was the affection he left behind.
He had ten sons,
Chàng and Xīn being the most renowned.
Chàng’s courtesy name was Xuánshū.
He was restyled King of Shùnyáng,
and appointed Attendant-in-ordinary, Colonel of Cavalry, and General of Roving Cavalry.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
Liú Cōng entered Luòyáng,
and his ultimate fate is unknown.
Xīn, King Zhuāng of Xīnyě, had the courtesy name Hóngshū.
After King Wǔ’s death,
his elder brother Chàng, out of generosity, requested to divide his fief to enfeoff Xīn.
During the Tàikāng era,
an edict enfeoffed him as Duke of Xīnyě County,
with an estate of one thousand eight hundred households,
and his ceremonial status was comparable to a county king.
Although Xīn was noble from a young age,
he was cautious and practiced the Way.
When his mother, Consort Zàng, passed away,
he observed mourning rites beyond what was prescribed,
and was known for his filial piety.
He was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
When King Lún of Zhào usurped the throne,
he appointed Xīn as General of the Central Army in the South.
When King Jiǒng of Qí raised an army of righteousness,
and issued a proclamation throughout the realm,
Xīn did not know whom to follow.
His favorite attendant, Wáng Suī, said:
“Zhào is close and strong,
Qí is distant and weak.
Your Grace should follow Zhào.”
His military aide, Sūn Xún, declared loudly to the multitude:
“King Zhào is cruel and rebellious;
the world should jointly attack him.
To uphold righteousness even against one's kin
is a clear ancient principle.”
Xīn followed this advice.
He then sent Xún to see Jiǒng.
Jiǒng welcomed him and clasped his hand, saying:
“It is Duke Xīnyě
who has enabled me to accomplish this great endeavor.”
When Jiǒng entered Luòyáng,
Xīn personally donned armor,
and led his subordinates to join Jiǒng.
For his merits, he was promoted to King of Xīnyě Commandery,
with an estate of twenty thousand households.

He was transferred to Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Grand Inspector of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu, General-in-Chief Guarding the South, and granted the privilege of establishing an administration with status equal to the Three Excellencies.
When Xīn was about to go to his garrison,
he rode in the same carriage as Jiǒng to visit the imperial mausoleum,
and took the opportunity to advise Jiǒng, saying:
“Chéngdū is a close relative,
who jointly achieved great merits.
He should now be kept here to assist in governance.
If that is not possible,
then his military authority should be seized.”
Jiǒng did not follow this advice.
Soon after, Jiǒng was defeated,
and Xīn, in fear,
allied himself with King Yǐng of Chéngdū.
Xīn’s administration was strict and harsh,
and the various barbarians resented him.
When Zhāng Chāng rebelled in Jiāngxià,
Xīn memorialized requesting to suppress him.
At that time, King Chángshā was in charge of government,
and had a rift with King Yǐng of Chéngdū.
Suspecting Xīn was colluding with Yǐng,
he did not allow Xīn to dispatch troops,
and Chāng’s forces grew stronger by the day.
At this time, Sūn Xún was Acting Central Administrator,
and said to Xīn:
“The ancients said,
to give an enemy a day’s leeway
is to invite trouble for generations.
Your Grace bears the responsibility of a feudal lord,
and holds the heavy duty of recommending talent.
To submit a memorial and then proceed
—what is wrong with that?
Instead, you allow villains to spread,
causing unforeseeable disasters.
How can this be called upholding the imperial house
and pacifying the land?!”
Xīn was about to dispatch his army,
but Wáng Suī again said:
“Chāng and his ilk are petty bandits;
subordinate generals are sufficient to control them.
There’s no need to defy imperial orders
and personally face arrows and stones!”
So Xīn stopped.
When Chāng reached Fánchéng,
Xīn went out to resist him.
His forces collapsed,
and he was killed by Chāng.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of Agile Cavalry.
He had no sons,
so his nephew Shào was adopted as his heir.
At the end of Yǒngjiā, Shào perished at the hands of Shí Lè.
King Róng of Liáng
King Róng, King Xiào of Liáng, had the courtesy name Zǐhuī.
He was pure, self-cultivated, respectful, and cautious,
without other notable talents.
As a princely son, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglè Pavilion.
When the five ranks were established,
he was restyled Viscount of Kāipíng.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as King of Liáng,
with an estate of five thousand three hundred fifty-eight households.
When he went to his state,
he was transferred to General of the Central Army in the North,
supervising the defense of Yèchéng.
At that time, the various kings selected their own officials.
Róng appointed Zhāng Fān, a former administrator of Rǔyīn, as Central Grand Master.
Fān had always been without moral conduct.
His original name was Xióng.
His wife, Lady Liú, was skilled in music
and taught performing arts for Cáo Shuǎng.
Fān also frequented Hé Yàn’s residence
and indulged in illicit affairs.
When Yàn was executed,
Fān was exiled to Héjiān,
whereupon he changed his name and allied himself with Róng.
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities,
and an edict ordered the reduction of one county from Róng’s fief.
During the Xiánníng era,
he was again granted Chéngguó and Nándùn of Rǔnán as additional enfeoffments, making it a secondary state.
During the Tàikāng era,
he replaced Kǒng Xún as Supervisor of military affairs in Yùzhōu,
〔一０〕was given the additional title of General Pacifying the East,
and garrisoned Xǔchāng.
Shortly thereafter,
he, in his existing capacity, replaced King Huàng of Xiàpéi as Supervisor of military affairs in Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu,
and was promoted to General Pacifying the East.
In the early Yuánkāng era,
he was transferred to be General of the Punishers of the West,
replacing Qín Wáng Jiǎn as the Area Commander of military affairs in Guānzhōng,
and concurrently serving as Colonel Protector of the Western Róng.
He was appointed Grandee Remonstrant-Consultant [Shìzhōng]
and further commanded military affairs in Liángzhōu.
Soon after, he was summoned to be General of the Guard [Wèijiāngjūn] and concurrently Supervisor of the Masters of Writing [Lù Shàngshūshì],
acting as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince [Tàizǐ Tàibǎo],
and granted one thousand soldiers and one hundred cavalry.
After a long time,
he was again made Grand General of the Punishers of the West,
replacing Zhào Wáng Lún in garrisoning Guānzhōng,
and appointed Area Commander of military affairs in Liáng and Yōng provinces.
He was granted left and right chief clerks [Zhǎngshǐ] and commanders [Sīmǎ].
He also concurrently served as Colonel of the Western Róng,
stationing at Hǎozhì,
and commanded General Jiànwēi Zhōu Chǔ and General Zhènwēi Lú Bō, among others, to attack the Dī bandit Qí Wànnián at Liùmò.
Róng and Chǔ had a grudge.
Róng hastened Chǔ to advance his army and then cut off his rear.
Bō also failed to rescue him,
hence Chǔ was harmed.
The court blamed him for this.
Soon after, he was summoned and appointed Grand General, Master of Writing [Shàngshū Lìng], Commander of the Army [Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn], and concurrently Supervisor of the Masters of Writing.
Róng once held a grand assembly,
and said to his staff officer [Cānjūn] Wáng Quán:
"My cousin [brother of the same generation] is the Master of Writing,
but he cannot eat large chunks of meat.
Large chunks of meat are indeed difficult."
Quán replied:
"Even for you, my lord, to chew alone here,
it is already difficult."
Róng asked:
"Whose large chunk of meat is the Chief Clerk [Zhǎngshǐ]?"
He replied:
"It is Lú Bō."
Róng said:
"He is a household official;
I just hide him."
Quán replied:
"If everyone in the world is a household official,
then the royal law might not be enforceable again."
Róng then asked:
"When I was in Cháng'ān,
what bad things did I do?"
He then pointed to the patched curtain of his single-layer carriage, claiming it showed his integrity.
Quán responded:
"The court and the populace hoped that you, my lord, would recommend worthy talents [Xiáncái]
and send away the inhumane.
Yet, you hold the position of a ducal minister [Gōngfǔ],
and by patching your carriage curtain,
you consider this integrity;
this is not worthy of praise."
Róng showed a look of shame.
In the early Yǒngkāng era,
he, along with Zhào Wáng Lún, deposed Empress Jiǎ.
An imperial edict appointed Róng as Grand Tutor [Tàizǎi] and Acting Master of Writing,
and increased his enfeoffment by twenty thousand households.
When Zhào Wáng Lún was regent,
there was an astral phenomenon.
The divination said,
"It is unfavorable for the Senior Chancellor."
Sūn Xiù, fearing that Lún would suffer misfortune,
therefore abolished the Minister of Education [Sītú] and established the Chancellor [Chéngxiàng] position,
and bestowed it upon Róng,
lavishly promoting him,
hoping to fulfill the prophecy with him.
Someone said:
"Róng has no power,
it will be of no benefit."
Róng firmly declined, refusing to accept it.
When Lún usurped the throne,
he made Róng Chief Minister [Āhéng],
granted him one hundred martial attendants [Wǔbēn],
and ten performers for the suspended bell and chime music [Xuānxuán zhī Yuè].
After Lún's downfall,
an imperial edict appointed Róng as Grand Tutor,
concurrently leading the Minister of Education,
and also replacing Gāomì Wáng Tài as宗師 Zōngshī (Master of the Imperial Clan).
He died in the second year of Yǒngkāng,
Bóshì Cáilǐu Cài Kè deliberated on his posthumous name, saying:
"Róng held the position of Chancellor,
with deep responsibilities and heavy duties.
He was of noble lineage and close to the imperial family,
and furthermore served as Master of the Imperial Clan.
He was looked up to by the court
and regarded by those below.
Yet, when facing great principles,
he lacked the will to be unyielding;
when confronted with dangerous matters,
he was unable to sacrifice his life for righteousness;
during the deposition of the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái,
not a single word of remonstrance was heard from him;
during the disaster of Huáinán,
he was unable to use the situation to assist righteousness;
when Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
he was unable to withdraw himself from court.
During the chaos of the Dàng clan in Sòng,
Huá Yuán considered himself unfit for office,
saying, 'The instruction between ruler and minister
is my responsibility.
The ducal house is weak and not rectified,
my sin is great!'
If even the small state of Sòng
had ministers who would not idly receive their salary,
how much more so an imperial court,
yet it had a chancellor who merely compromised?
If this is not censured,
what will become of the law?
Carefully examining the posthumous naming laws, 'one who does not diligently achieve fame is called Líng,'
Róng saw righteousness but did not act,
thus cannot be called diligent.
He should be posthumously named Líng."
Sūn Lín, an imperial attendant [Chángshì] of Liángguó, and Róng's relatives and party claimed injustice.
The Censorate [Tái] then issued a directive stating:
"The Jiǎ clan monopolized power,
and Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne;
they both forcefully controlled the court and the populace.
Róng was unable to leave due to circumstances,
yet to fault him for not being able to withdraw himself from court,
on what principle is this based?"
Kè re-deliberated, saying:
"Róng was a minister of the imperial clan,
yet when the state was in chaos, he could not rectify it;
when the ruler was imperiled, he could not support him.
This is not how a chancellor should be.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized Huá Yuán for enjoying his position,
calling him un-ministerial.
Moreover, the cruelty of the Jiǎ clan
was not more severe than that of Empress Lǚ,
yet Wáng Líng was still able to shut his door;
the wickedness of Zhào Wáng Lún
was not more severe than that of King Zhòu of Yīn,
yet Wēizǐ was still able to leave him.
More recently, Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi] Chén Zhǔn,
a person of a different surname,
and whose younger brother Huī had a grudge from the 'shot hook' incident,
not involving himself with the usurping court.
How can it be that Róng, the brother of Lún's kin,
alone could not leave?
Zhào Dùn entered to remonstrate but was not heeded;
he fled but did not go far,
yet still could not escape blame.
How much more so Róng, who could not leave his position
and served the usurper facing north?
It is proper to follow the previous deliberation,
to add censure to him,
to broaden the principle of being a minister,
and to clarify the way of serving a ruler."
Thereupon, the court followed Kè's deliberation.
Róng's former officials continued to appeal repeatedly,
so it was changed again.
He had no sons.
Mǔlíng Wáng Dàn's son Xǐ was made his heir,
who was known as Huái Wáng.
He was appointed General of the Punishers of the Lú,
and he and Dàn were both captured and killed by Shí Lè.
During the time of Yuán Dì,
Xīyáng Wáng Yáng's son Kuí was made Róng's successor.
He died young,
and was known as Shāng Wáng.
At this point, Huái Wáng's son Qiáo returned to the state from the Shí clan and was enthroned,
known as Shēng Wáng,
and his highest office was Palace Regular Attendant [Sànqí Chángshì].
He died
without sons.
An imperial edict made Mǔlíng Wēi Wáng's son Zhāng Qiáo's successor.
He successively served as Grand Coachman [Tàipú] of Yǒng'ān,
and he and his father Xī were both deposed and banished to Xīn'ān.
After his death,
the state was restored during the Tàiyuán era,
and his son Hé succeeded.
After his death,
his son Zhēnxī succeeded.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
the state minister Kǒng Pú carried Zhēnxī and fled to Shòuyáng.
In the early Yìxī era, he returned,
and was successively promoted to General of the Left Guard and Minister of the Imperial Clan [Tàicháng Qīng].
When Liú Yù attacked Yáo Hóng,
he requested to be an Advisor to the Army [Zīyì Cānjūn].
He was killed by Yù,
and the state was abolished.
The Six Princes of Wén
Emperor Wén had nine sons.
Empress Wénmíng gave birth to Emperor Wǔ, Qí Xiàn Wáng Yōu, Chéngyáng Āi Wáng Zhào, Liáodōng Dàohuì Wáng Dìngguó, and Guǎnghàn Shāng Wáng Guǎngdé.
The mothers of Lè'ān Píng Wáng Jiàn, Yān Wáng Jī, the imperial prince Yǒngzuò, and Lèpíng Wáng Yánzuò are unknown.
Yān Wáng Jī succeeded Qīnghuì Tínghóu
and has a separate biography.
Yǒngzuò died young
and has no biography.
Qí Wáng Yōu (sons Ruí, Zàn, Shí)
Qí Xiànwáng Yōu 攸, courtesy name Dàyóu 大猷.
From a young age, he was intelligent and astute.
When he grew up,
he was pure, peaceful, and fair-minded.
He befriended the virtuous and was fond of charity,
loved classics and books,
was skilled in writing,
and excelled at letter-writing,
becoming a model for his generation.
His talent and reputation surpassed those of Wǔdì 武帝,
and Xuāndì 宣帝 always held him in high regard.
Jǐngdì 景帝 had no sons,
so he ordered Yōu to be his heir.
He participated in the campaign against Wáng Líng 王淩,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chánglè 長樂 Pavilion.
When Jǐngdì passed away,
Yōu was ten years old.
His grief moved those around him,
and he was greatly praised.
He inherited the title of Marquis of Wǔyáng 舞陽.
〔一四〕He housed Empress Jǐngxiàn Yáng Hòu 景獻羊后 in a separate residence,
and was known for his filial piety towards the empress.
He successively held the posts of Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 and Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉.
At that time, he was eighteen years old,
and he pacified and managed his commandery and troops,
wielding great authority and beneficence.
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānchāng 安昌,
and promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn 衞將軍.
During the mourning period for Wéndì 文帝,
his grief and emaciation exceeded the rites,
and he could only rise with the aid of a staff.
His attendants offered him rice mixed with dried food and the Lǐzhōng Wán 理中丸 medicine,
but Yōu wept and refused to accept it.
The Empress Dowager personally went to persuade him, saying:
“If by any chance another illness befalls you,
what will become of us?
You should consider the long-term and plan deeply;
you cannot solely adhere to one purpose.”
She often sent people to compel him to eat and drink.
Sīmǎ Jī Xǐ 司馬嵇喜 also remonstrated, saying:
“Grief should not destroy one's life—
this is the teaching of the sages.
Moreover, Your Highness holds a position of close kinship
and is a primary assistant.
Even a commoner cherishes his life
for the sake of his ancestors,
how much more so when one bears the great undertaking of the world
and assists in the heavy responsibility of the imperial house?
How can one indulge in endless sorrow
and compete with Yán Mǐn 顏閔 in filial piety!
You must not make the wise laugh
and the foolish rejoice.”
Jī Xǐ personally offered him food.
Yōu, having no choice,
forced himself to eat.
After Jī Xǐ left,
Yōu said to his attendants:
“Sīmǎ Jī intends for me not to forget the etiquette of mourning,
and to preserve my humble self.”
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Yōu was enfeoffed as Qíwáng 齊王.
At that time, the court was in its nascent stages,
and Yōu commanded all military affairs,
pacifying and stabilizing both inside and outside the realm,
so none failed to attach themselves to him.
An imperial edict proposed that vassal kings select their own senior officials within their states.
Yōu submitted a memorial, stating:
“In ancient times, the sagely kings established numerous states
to secure their relatives among the feudal lords.
Their methods have been passed down in succession,
and none have been able to change them.
This is truly because if the ruler does not reside there for generations,
people's hearts become opportunistic;
if people have no constant lord,
customs become superficial and false.
Therefore, the former emperor deeply understood the far-reaching system of governance,
and desired to restore the practices of ancient sages,
dividing territories and delineating boundaries,
establishing noble ranks in five grades,
some for advancing virtue,
others for rewarding merit.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty, responding to the opportune moment, founded this enterprise,
establishing relatives as rulers,
and allowing vassal states to appoint their own senior officials.
However, now that the state is newly established,
and institutions are only beginning to be set up,
although Yōngshǔ 庸蜀 has submitted,
Wú 吳 has not yet pledged allegiance.
It is advisable to wait until there is peace and stability,
then to discuss restoring the ancient system.”
His memorial was submitted three times,
but each time it was rejected.
Later, when the position of Senior Official in his state was vacant,
the Diǎnshū Lìng 典書令 requested to select a candidate.
Yōu issued an order saying:
“I am humbly receiving grace and honor,
and my worry is that I am unworthy.
As for officials and talents,
these are all matters of the imperial court,
not something the state should decide.
Therefore, let the matter be reported to the court for appointment.”
At that time, the clothing and food for the royal family members all came from the imperial treasury.
Yōu memorialized that his rent and salary were sufficient for his own needs,
and requested that the provision be ceased.
He submitted this request more than ten times,
but the emperor again did not grant it.
Although Yōu had not yet gone to his state,
he allocated rent and taxes to provide for his civil and military officials,
down to the soldiers,
and gave them gifts in cases of illness, death, and funerals.
Moreover, when there were floods or droughts,
he would lend assistance to the people in his state,
and collect repayment only in abundant years,
reducing the debt by two-tenths,
which benefited the people of his state.
He was promoted to Piàojí Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍,
granted the authority to establish his own bureau and make appointments,
with courtesies equal to the Three Excellencies.
He humbled himself and emptied his mind,
treating others with sincerity.
He often lamented that public offices did not follow the regulations for officials,
but as he was in charge of military administration,
it was also appropriate to exercise authority and conquest.
Thus, he issued an instruction saying:
“The former kings, in ruling the world,
clarified punishments and rectified laws,
using corporal punishment as a means of instruction
to correct tardiness and negligence.
Even in the courts of Táng Yú 唐虞,
supervision and accountability were necessary.
Previously, I wished to compile and organize these matters
to make them generally consistent.
Fearing the appropriateness of either brevity or complexity,
and unsure of their essentials,
I therefore ordered the two gentlemen Liú 劉 and Chéng 程 to carefully finalize them.
However, reflecting on this,
when Zhèng 鄭 cast penal laws,
Shú Xiàng 叔向 disapproved;
when Fàn Xuān 范宣 debated establishing a system,
Zhòngní 仲尼 criticized it.
Therefore, let everything remain as before,
without any additions or deletions.
Matters not covered by the regular regulations
should be decided on a case-by-case basis.
All officials should exert their utmost effort,
and aspire to the integrity of the ancients who served the public.
If there are any shortcomings,
relying on the supportive and corrective guidance of my trusted aides,
I hope to avoid failures.”
Thereupon, both inside and outside the government were solemn and orderly.
At that time, the Piàojí 驃騎 was to dismiss some troops,
but several thousand soldiers, attached to Yōu’s benevolence and virtue,
refused to leave,
blocking the Jīngzhào Zhǔ 京兆主 to state their case.
The emperor then returned the troops to Yōu.
Yōu每次朝廷有重大議論，
都悉心陳述。
皇帝下詔說近年來飢荒，
議所節省。
Yōu奏議說：
「臣聽聞先王的教化，
無不先端正其根本。
務農重本，
是國家的綱領。
當今四方清靜太平，
武夫釋下盔甲，
廣泛分發休假，
以從事農業。
然而郡守和國相不能勤心恤公，
以盡地利。
從前漢Xuān帝感嘆說：『與朕治理天下者，
唯有賢良的二千石官員啊！』
勤加賞罰，
黜陟幽明，
於是當時普遍響應，
湧現出許多名守。
估計現在土地有餘，
而不從事耕種的人很多，
加上兼營其他行業的人又有虛假，
通天下謀之，
〔一五〕則飢者必不少矣。
現在應當嚴格敕令州郡，
檢查各種虛假詐騙、危害農業的事情，
督促實際耕種南畝，
上上下下共同致力於此。
則天下之穀可復古政，
豈患於暫一水旱，
便憂飢餒哉！
考績黜陟，
務必嚴明，
畏威懷惠，
莫不自厲。
又都邑之內，
游食滋多，
巧伎末業，
服飾奢麗，
富人兼美，
猶有Wèi朝的遺弊，
染化日淺，
靡財害穀，
動輒萬計。
應當申明舊法，
必禁絕之。
使去奢即儉，
不奪農時，
畢力稼穡，
以實倉廩。
則榮辱禮節，
由之而生，
興化反本，
於茲為盛。」
轉任Zhèn Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn，
加Shìzhōng，
享受羽葆、鼓吹的待遇，
行Tàizǐ Shàofù之事。
數年後，
授予Tàizǐ Tàifù，
向太子獻箴說：
「伊昔上皇，
建國立君，
仰觀天文，
俯察地理，
創業恢道，
以安人承祀，
祚延統重，
故援立太子。
尊以弘道，
固以貳己，
儲德既立，
邦有所恃。
夫親仁者功成，
邇佞者國傾，
故保相之材，
必擇賢明。
昔在Zhōu Chéng王，
Dàn Shì作傅，
外以明德自輔，
內以親親立固，
德以義濟，
親則自然。
Yíng氏廢除公族，
其崩如山；
Liú氏建立子弟，
Hàn祚永傳。
Chǔ國因Wújí作亂，
Sòng國因Yī Lì興難。
Zhāng Yǔ佞給，
卒危強漢。
輔弼不忠，
禍及乃躬；
匪徒乃躬，
乃喪乃邦。
無曰父子不間，
昔有Jiāng Chōng；
無曰至親匪貳，
或容Pān Chóng。
諛言亂真，
譖潤離親，
Lí Jī之讒，
Jìn Hóu疑Shēn。
固親以道，
勿固以恩；
修身以敬，
勿託以尊。
自損者有餘，
自益者彌昏。
庶事不可以不恤，
大本不可以不敦。
見亡戒危，
覩安思存。
冢子司義，
敢告在閽。」
世以為工。
Xiánníng二年，
代替Jiǎ Chōng為Sīkōng，
Shìzhōng、Tàifù如故。
起初，
Yōu特為Wén Dì所寵愛，
每次見到Yōu，
輒撫床呼其小字曰
「此桃符座也」，
幾為太子者數矣。
及帝寢疾，
慮Yōu不安，
為Wǔ Dì、Hàn Huáinán Wáng、Wèi Chénsī的故事而泣。
臨崩，
執Yōu手以授帝。
先是太后有疾，
既瘳，
帝與Yōu奉觴上壽，
Yōu以太后前疾危篤，
因歔欷流涕，
帝有愧焉。
Yōu嘗侍帝疾，
有憂戚之容，
時人以此稱歎之。
及太后臨崩，
亦流涕謂帝曰：
「桃符性急，
而汝為兄不慈，
我若遂不起，
恐必不能相容。
以是屬汝，
勿忘我言。」
及帝晚年，
諸子並弱，
而太子不令，
朝臣內外，
皆屬意於Yōu。
Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù、Shìzhōng Féng Dǎn皆諂諛自進，
Yōu素疾之。
Xù等以朝望在Yōu，
恐其為嗣，
禍必及己，
乃從容言於帝曰：
「陛下萬歲之後，
太子不得立也。」
帝曰：
「何故？」
Xù曰：
「百僚內外皆歸心於Qí Wáng，
太子焉得立乎！
陛下試詔Qí Wáng之國，
必舉朝以為不可，
則臣言有徵矣。」
Dǎn又言曰：
「陛下遣諸侯之國，
成五等之制者，
宜先從親始。
親莫若Qí Wáng。」
As the emperor had already believed Xù’s words,
and also accepted Dǎn’s counsel,
in the third year of Tàikāng he issued an edict saying:
“In ancient times, a person appointed to nine ranks became a ‘bó’ (feudal lord),
some entered to assist in court administration,
some went out to govern the regions.
Lǚ Wàng of Zhōu,
the Five Marquises and Nine Earls,
truly obtained this right to command.
The Attendant-in-Chief (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Jì Wáng Yōu,
is of bright and clear virtue,
loyal, just, earnest, and sincere.
By virtue of being a younger brother of the empress,
he received the responsibility of a high official,
assisting in establishing achievements,
toiling diligently for the royal house.
He ought to ascend to a prominent position,
to meet the expectations of all.
He shall be appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) and Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs in Qīngzhōu,
retaining his position as Attendant-in-Chief as before,
granted the power to act by proxy (jiǎjié),
commanding a thousand men from his original camp,
with his personal cavalry, attendants beneath his banner, and grand carriages all as before.
One more set of drum and wind instruments shall be added,
the number of official cavalry shall be increased to twenty men,
and five Cavalry Marshals (Qí Sīmǎ) shall be appointed.
The rest shall be implemented by the responsible officials in accordance with old regulations.”
Yōu was displeased.
His Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù), Dīng Yí, said:
“In the past, when Tài Gōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
he still manifested his power over the Eastern Sea.
Huán Gōng united the feudal lords nine times,
and became the chief of the Five Hegemons.
How much more so, Your Highness, with your expansive virtue and respectful brilliance,
will you broadly assist the great dependencies,
and respectfully settle the eastern regions,
leaving none without their proper place.
Why must it be in the Vermilion Palace (Jiàng Què)
that you expand the imperial enterprise!”
Yōu said:
“I have no ability to rectify the times;
why do you say so much?”
The next year,
an imperial pronouncement was issued to Yōu, saying:
“Alas!
The Mandate (mìng) is not constant;
Heaven has already removed the fortune of Wèi.
Our Jìn has received the bright mandate that accords with Heaven,
gloriously established numerous feudal lords,
and furthermore created a kingdom in the eastern land,
granting this Qīngshè,
to act as a bulwark for our state and family.
Be diligent and not remiss,
to forever protect the ancestral temple.”
An edict was also sent to the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tài Cháng),
to deliberate on the objects of honor to be bestowed,
and to add Jìnán Commandery to the state of Qí.
Furthermore, Yōu’s son, Shí, was made Prince of Běihǎi.
Thereupon, all the ceremonial objects and edicts were prepared,
the Xuān Xuán music and the six-line dance were performed,
and the yellow axe, court carriage, and imperial entourage followed.
Yōu knew that Xù and Dǎn had plotted against him,
and, filled with indignation and resentment, fell ill.
He requested to guard the imperial tombs,
but was refused.
The emperor sent imperial physicians to examine him,
but the physicians, catering to the emperor’s wishes,
all said he had no illness.
His illness worsened,
but he was still urged to set out.
Yōu forced himself to go in and take leave.
He usually maintained a dignified bearing,
and though his illness was severe,
he still composed himself,
and his demeanor was as usual.
The emperor became even more suspicious that he had no illness.
After he took leave and stayed for two nights,
he vomited blood and died,
at the age of thirty-six.
The emperor wept inconsolably.
Féng Dǎn, attending at his side, said:
“Qí Wáng’s reputation exceeded his reality,
and the world honored him.
Now that he has died,
it is a blessing for the state.
Why does Your Majesty grieve so excessively!”
The emperor wiped away his tears and stopped.
An edict commanded that his funeral rites should follow the precedent of Ānpíng Wáng Fú,
that Xuān Xuán music should be performed in his ancestral temple,
and that he should be sacrificed to in the Grand Ancestral Temple.
His son, Jiǒng, succeeded him;
there is a separate biography for him.
Yōu constrained himself with propriety
and rarely committed errors.
When he borrowed books from others,
he would always personally mark out the errors
before returning them.
Moreover, his filial piety surpassed others;
whenever anyone touched upon his taboos,
he would invariably shed tears.
Even Wǔ Dì respected and feared him,
and whenever he invited him to sit together,
he would always choose his words carefully before speaking.
He had three sons: Ruí, Zàn, and Shí.
〔一六〕
Ruí, courtesy name Jǐnghuí,
was adopted as heir to Liáodōng Wáng Dìngguó.
At the beginning of Tàikāng,
he was enfeoffed as Dōnglái Wáng.
During Yuánkāng,
he successively held the posts of Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi) and Colonel of Agile Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi).
Ruí was strong and violent,
and frequently drank to excess.
He often insulted his younger brother Jiǒng,
but Jiǒng tolerated him on account of him being his elder brother.
When Jiǒng raised an army of righteousness,
Zhào Wáng Lún arrested Ruí and his younger brother, Běihǎi Wáng Shí, and imprisoned them in the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi),
sentencing them to execution.
Lún’s Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ), Zǔ Nà, submitted a memorial advising:
“Crimes do not extend to others,
evil stops with the person themselves.
This is the grand principle of ancient sages,
the established system of a hundred kings.
Thus, Gǔn was executed,
but Yǔ then succeeded him.
The Two Uncles were punished and exiled,
but Xíng and Wèi were not held responsible.
Reaching the Warring States period,
and up to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the path of clear leniency was abandoned,
and suspicion and doubt were employed.
Thus, hostages were established to control the masses,
and guilt by association was set up to expose treachery.
The origin of this [practice]
is merely a corrupt law from the Three Dynasties.
Ruí and Shí,
sons of Xiàn Wáng,
descendants of bright virtue,
should receive special pardon,
to preserve the principle of harmonious kinship.”
At this time, Sūn Xiù died,
and Ruí and others were all spared.
When Jiǒng led his army into Luòyáng,
Ruí met him on the road.
Jiǒng did not see him immediately,
but waited for a document to be handed to the former temporary residence.
Ruí, angry, said:
“I almost died because of you,
and yet you show no brotherly affection!”
When Jiǒng became regent,
an edict appointed Ruí as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
with the added title of Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
〔一七〕Commander of the Rear Army (Lǐng Hòujūn), Attendant-in-Chief (Shìzhōng), and Specially Advanced (Tèjìn),
with his fief increased to a full twenty thousand households.
Ruí also requested from Jiǒng to establish a personal administration (kāifǔ).
Jiǒng said:
“The sons of Wǔ Dì, Wú and Yùzhāng, have not yet established their administrations;
it is appropriate to wait a while.”
Because of this, Ruí’s resentment grew.
He secretly memorialized that Jiǒng was usurping power,
and conspired with the Left Guard General (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn), Wáng Yú, to depose Jiǒng together.
The matter was discovered,
and he was dismissed to commoner status.
Soon after, an edict stated:
“The Grand Marshal, with his experienced discernment and clear judgment,
and his high strategy and far-reaching plans,
has humbly led his allies,
and restored the state.
Since the records of writing,
the merits of Zhōu and Shào are not enough to compare with his achievements,
hence he was appointed the Chief Minister (Shàngzǎi).
Dōnglái Wáng Ruí secretly harbored jealousy,
and concealed malicious intent.
He secretly conspired with Wáng Yú,
planning to slander and harm.
On the day Yú was arrested,
Ruí fled in a commoner’s carriage with a servant,
disguised and ran off,
returning only after a night.
His villainy was blatant,
and he deceived both internal and external parties.
Moreover, his previous memorial against Jiǒng contained deeply serious accusations,
even Guǎn and Cài’s deviation from the Way,
and Yá and Qìng’s disruption of the clan,
did not exceed this.
According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
great righteousness may override kinship.
Therefore, Ruí shall be relocated to Shàngyōng.”
Later, he was enfeoffed as Wēiyáng Hóu.
At the beginning of Yǒngníng,
Shàngyōng Internal Historian (Shàngyōng Nèishǐ), Chén Zhōng, acting on Jiǒng’s order, harmed Ruí.
When Jiǒng died,
an edict ordered Zhōng’s execution,
restored Ruí’s enfeoffment,
and reburied him with princely rites.
Zàn, courtesy name Jǐngqī,
was adopted as heir to Guǎnghàn Shāng Wáng Guǎngdé.
At the age of six,
in the first year of Tàikāng, he died,
and was posthumously named Chōng Wáng.
Shí, courtesy name Jǐngshēn,
was initially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chánglè Tíng.
As Yōu had died on account of Zàn,
and Shí was made to succeed to the posthumous title of Shāng Wáng of Guǎnghàn,
he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Běihǎi.
At the beginning of Yǒngníng, he was made Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and granted a jié,
and additionally Sanqí Chángshì.
He replaced Qí Wáng Jiǒng in garrisoning Xǔchāng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Yùzhōu Jūnjì,
and his income fief was increased to a full twenty thousand households.
Before he could depart,
he was retained as Shìzhōng, Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted a thousand soldiers and a hundred cavalry.
Chéngyáng Wáng Zhào
Chéngyáng Āi Wáng Zhào, courtesy name Qiānqiū,
died prematurely at the age of ten.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
an edict stated:
"My late younger brother Qiānqiū was intelligent from a young age,
with a talent for early maturity.
Unfortunately, he died young,
which the previous emperor and empress especially mourned and pitied.
The empress desired to establish an heir for him,
but this was never achieved.
Whenever I recall her last wish,
my heart is filled with sorrow.
Therefore, let the imperial son Jǐngdù be Qiānqiū's heir.
Although this is not in accordance with classical rites,
it has been practiced in recent times,
and also fulfills the empress's original intention."
Thereupon, Zhào was posthumously granted an additional enfeoffment and a posthumous title.
Jǐngdù died in the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
and then the fifth son Xiàn was made to succeed Āi Wáng.
When he died,
the sixth son Zhī was again made King of Dōnghǎi,
succeeding Āi Wáng.
When he died,
at the beginning of Xiánníng, the thirteenth son Xiá was again enfeoffed as King of Qīnghé,
to succeed Zhào.
Liáodōng Wáng Dìngguó
Liáodōng Dàohuì Wáng Dìngguó
died at the age of three.
At the beginning of Xiánníng, he was posthumously granted an additional enfeoffment and a posthumous title.
Qí Wáng Yōu made his eldest son Ruí the heir.
When Ruí died,
his son Zūn inherited.
Guǎnghàn Wáng Guǎngdé
Guǎnghàn Shāng Wáng Guǎngdé
died at the age of two.
At the beginning of Xiánníng, he was posthumously granted an additional enfeoffment and a posthumous title.
Qí Wáng Yōu made his fifth son Zàn inherit the enfeoffment.
When he died,
Yōu again made his second son Shí heir to Guǎngdé.
Lè'ān Wáng Jiàn
Lè'ān Píng Wáng Jiàn, courtesy name Dàmíng,
was initially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Línsì Tíng.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as King of Lè'ān.
The emperor personally selected excellent teachers and friends for Jiàn and Yān Wáng Jī.
An edict stated:
"Lè'ān Wáng Jiàn and Yān Wáng Jī are both grown up,
and ought to have mentors and friends to guide them.
Select those who are learned in the classics and Confucian studies,
possess integrity and frugality,
and are sufficiently respectable and awe-inspiring.
In the past, Hán Qǐ associated with Tián Sū and became fond of goodness;
it is essential to find such people."
In the middle of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
he was granted additional territory from Liángzōu in Qí,
and then proceeded to his state,
wearing the robes of a Shìzhōng.
At the beginning of Yuánkāng,
he was summoned to be Sanqí Chángshì, Shàngjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and concurrently Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yùzhōu Jūnjì, Ānnán Jiāngjūn,
replacing Qīnghé Wáng Xiá in garrisoning Xǔchāng,
but did not go due to illness.
He died in the seventh year.
His son, Shāng Wáng Jí, succeeded.
When he died,
having no son,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng made his son Bīng heir to Jiàn.
The 11,219 households of Jìyīn were changed to Guǎngyáng Guó,
and Bīng was established as King of Guǎngyáng.
When Jiǒng was defeated,
he was deposed.
Lèpíng Wáng Yánzuò
Lèpíng Wáng Yánzuò, courtesy name Dàsī,
suffered from a chronic illness from a young age,
and was unfit for enfeoffment.
At the beginning of Tàikāng,
an edict stated:
"My younger brother Zuò was orphaned early and lacked understanding;
I pity him greatly.
He contracted a chronic illness in childhood,
and I hoped daily for his recovery.
Now, having become permanently debilitated,
there is no hope for his future.
My heart is deeply pained by this.
Therefore, let him be enfeoffed as King of Lèpíng,
so he may have a title,
to console my heart."
He died shortly after,
without a son.
The court historian remarks: The nature and principles of Píngyuán were unfathomable;
no one in his generation could gauge them.
Yet, when he found himself amidst chaos and separation,
and in a time of conflict,
he was able to avert harm and preserve himself,
enjoying this great good fortune.
His "folly" was indeed beyond reach!
The martial achievements of Lángxié were both extensive
and adorned with warmth and reverence.
The cultural education of Fúfēng was greatly proclaimed,
and moreover, supplemented with filial piety.
These were indeed the praiseworthy members of the imperial clan.
The King of Qí, with his kinship to two virtuous offerings,
promoted the civilizing influence of the two "Nán" odes,
his Way enlightened both the refined and the common,
and his prestige outweighed the high officials.
All the hundred officials looked up to him,
and the myriad regions placed their hopes in him.
However, his territory became suspected of encroachment,
and his refinement was criticized.
Dǎn and Xù presented the wicked schemes of "creeping vines,"
and Emperor Wǔ harbored deep, lingering affection for his son.
Consequently, his imperial vestments were stripped from his official duties,
and his marquisal robes were transferred to a lower fief.
Before he could even set out on his journey,
he succumbed to anger and resentment.
What a pity!
If Heaven had granted him more years and removed the harm,
allowing him to receive the mandate of the "embroidered robe"
and assume the trust of the "bearer of the mandate,"
to brilliantly assist the succeeding ruler
and truly rectify national governance,
then seeking the reasons in mysterious portents,
perhaps there would have been a destined time for rise or fall;
and examining human affairs,
it is likely that the "overcoming of savagery" could have been achieved.
How then could the Eight Kings have dared to contend,
or the Five Barbarians been able to compete?
The *Shī* says:
"When the people pass away,
the state is utterly exhausted."
Yōu indeed exemplified this.
"Slanderers are limitless,
sowing discord among the four states."
This refers to Xún and Féng.
Eulogy says: The descendants of Wénxuān,
some worthy, some base.
Fúfēng left behind affection,
Lángxié exercised self-restraint.
Dàn and Chǎn, wicked leaders,
Róng and Cān, the beginning of strife.
Gàn, though quiet and reclusive,
his nature was contrary to reason.
Ah, the beauty of Qí Xiàn,
distinguished and outstanding.
From ordering his family to governing the state,
he wove martial prowess with civil accomplishments.
The tree is broken in its prime,
the orchid burned by its fragrance.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 9: Wáng Shěn (son Jùn)
Wáng Shěn, courtesy name Chǔdào,
was a native of Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
His grandfather, Róu, was the Hàn Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiāng.
His father, Jī, was the Wèi Dōngjùn Tàishǒu.
Shěn was orphaned young,
raised by his paternal uncle Sīkōng Chǎng,
serving Chǎng as if he were his father,
and was praised for his filial piety and righteousness towards his stepmother and widowed sister-in-law.
He was fond of books
and skilled at writing.
Dàjiāngjūn Cáoshuǎng appointed him as a Yuàn,
and he was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Ménxià Shìláng.
When Shuǎng was executed,
he was dismissed as a former subordinate.
Later, he was appointed Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ,
then transferred to Mìshūjiān.
During Zhèngyuán,
he was promoted to Sanqí Chángshì, Shìzhōng,
and was in charge of scholarly works.
He collaborated with Xún Yǐ and Ruǎn Jí in compiling the *Wèi Shū*,
which contained many taboos of the time,
and was not as factual as Chén Shòu's *Shílù*.
At that time, the Wei Gāoguì-xiānggōng 高貴鄉公 was fond of learning and possessed literary talent.
He invited Shěn (Shěn Yóu 沈猶) and Péi Xiù 裴秀 to lecture, feast, and compose literary works frequently in the East Hall.
He styled Shěn as Wénjí Xiānshēng 文籍先生,
and Xiù as Rúlín Zhàngrén 儒林丈人.
When the Gāoguì-xiānggōng was about to attack Wén Dì 文帝,
he summoned Shěn and Wáng Yè 王業 and informed them of his plan.
Shěn and Yè galloped to inform Dì (Sīmǎ Zhāo 司馬昭),
and for this service, Shěn was enfeoffed as Ānpíng-hóu 安平侯,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
As Shěn had been disloyal to his lord,
he was severely criticized by public opinion.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū 尚書,
and appointed as Inspector of the Military Affairs of Yùzhōu 豫州, Fènbǔ Jiāngjūn 奮武將軍, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ 豫州刺史.
Upon arriving at his post,
he issued an order stating:
“From ancient times, the sagely and virtuous
were pleased to hear words of criticism,
and to listen to the opinions of commoners.
This is because even woodcutters can have matters worth recording,
and burden-bearers can speak words worthy of the court.
Since my arrival at this post,
I have not heard any words that are unpleasant to the ear.
Could it be that my openness of mind is not yet clear,
thus causing those who would speak to have doubts?
Therefore, it is hereby proclaimed to all subordinate cities, officials, and common people,
that if anyone can recommend forgotten talents from the wilds,
or dismiss cunning flatterers from the state,
or present the merits and demerits of chief officials,
or explain the grievances of the populace,
or promote benefits and eliminate harms,
with improvements and detriments clearly demonstrated,
they shall be given five hundred hú 斛 of grain.
If anyone can offer a single profound word,
explaining the Cìshǐ’s gains and losses,
and the strictness or leniency of court policies,
so that rigidity and flexibility achieve a proper balance,
they shall be given one thousand hú of grain.
If you think I will not keep my word,
know that it is as clear as the bright sun.”
The Chief Clerks Chén Xūn 陳廞 and Chǔ Sì 褚禩 said:
“We have respectfully perused your instruction,
and are deeply moved and amazed.
You toil diligently from morning till evening,
desiring to hear harsh words.
In our humble opinion, what the superior desires,
the inferiors will never fail to respond to.
However, recently, there have been no words of extreme remonstrance,
nor distant proverbs passed on by word of mouth.
Perhaps it is genuinely because there have been no matters of gain or loss.
Now, if this instruction is promulgated,
displaying rewards and encouragement,
we fear that principled scholars
might perhaps be deterred by the reward and remain silent;
while avaricious persons
might be tempted by profit and make reckless recommendations.
If these are not appropriate,
the rewards will not be granted in vain,
then distant listeners will not know where the right and wrong lie,
and will only see that words are not adopted,
concluding that the offer exists but is not acted upon.
Your humble servants suggest that the matter of announcing this to the public
can wait a little longer.”
Shěn issued another instruction, saying:
“When virtue is slight but position is high,
and merit is minor but emolument is heavy,
these are what greedy people pursue,
but what noble scholars do not inhabit.
If one presents profound words to the Cìshǐ,
brings benefits to this province,
reveals hidden talents,
and removes the sycophancy of Zhù Tuó 祝鮀,
establishes virtue for the superior,
and receives one’s due from the inferior,
this is truly the conduct of a noble person.
Why would one not speak?
To speak truthfully and profoundly is loyalty.
To extend beneficence to an entire province is benevolence.
To accomplish deeds and decline rewards is integrity.
To practice these concurrently
is an act of benevolence and wisdom.
Why then should one conceal one’s principles and cause one’s state to be lost?!”
Chǔ Sì again remonstrated, saying:
“The reason Yáo 堯, Shùn 舜, and Zhōu Gōng 周公 were able to elicit loyal remonstrance
is because their sincere hearts were manifest.
Ice and charcoal do not speak,
yet their cold and hot natures are self-evident
because they possess intrinsic reality.
If one genuinely desires integrity and straightforwardness,
as naturally as ice and charcoal,
then outspoken officials
will be numerous and fill the court;
and words that are unpleasant to the ear
will arrive spontaneously without being sought.
If one’s virtue is insufficient to match Táng Yú 唐虞 (Yáo and Shùn),
one’s insight insufficient to equal Zhōu Gōng,
and one’s sincerity cannot compare to ice and charcoal,
then even if heavy rewards are offered,
words of loyal remonstrance cannot be obtained.”
“In ancient times, Wèi Jiàng 魏絳, through his merit in making peace with the Rong,
received the赐 gift of female musicians.
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲, for his achievement in strengthening Qí 齊,
was accorded the禮 rites of a high minister.
Merits and achievements were clearly manifest,
and only then did rewards and encouragement follow.
We have never heard of setting up heavy rewards to await remonstrating officials,
or offering grain and silk to solicit full disclosure of words.”
Shěn had no means to refute him,
and so followed Sì’s suggestion.
Shěn diligently sought out good governance,
examining the laws, regulations, and prohibitions since Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵,
and of all those implemented,
he chose the good ones to follow.
He also instructed:
“If later generations do not hear the teachings of the former kings,
and yet hope for the daily flourishing of good governance,
it cannot be achieved.
Using both civil and military means
is the path to longevity.
The prevailing customs are in decline,
and must be reformed.
The key to reforming customs
lies in promoting learning.
In the past, Yuán Bólǔ 原伯魯 disliked learning,
and Mǐn Mǎfù 閔馬父 knew he would inevitably perish.
The children of generals and officials,
who live in idleness at home,
if not educated,
will certainly indulge in frivolous pursuits,
damaging and destroying customs.”
Thereupon, the scholars of the nine commanderies
all delighted in his moral teachings,
transforming customs and changing practices.
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍, with a staff of authority,
and Commander of all military affairs north of the Jiāng 江 River.
When the Five Ranks were first established,
he was enfeoffed as Bólíng-hóu 博陵侯,
his rank being among the secondary states.
During the campaign to pacify Shǔ 蜀,
the Wú 吳 people made a large sortie,
claiming to rescue Shǔ,
and unsettling the border regions.
Shěn managed the defense effectively,
and the invaders retreated upon hearing of it.
He was then transferred to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn 鎮南將軍.
When Wǔ Dì 武帝 ascended the throne as king,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū 御史大夫,
acting Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令,
and additionally Gěishì Zhōng 給事中.
Shěn, by virtue of his talent and reputation,
achieved renown in his era.
Therefore, regarding matters of founding the dynasty,
Yáng Hù 羊祜, Xún Xù 荀勖, Péi Xiù 裴秀, Jiǎ Chōng 賈充, and others,
all consulted and strategized with Shěn.
When the Emperor received the abdication,
for his merit in aiding the establishment of the dynasty,
he was promoted to Píqí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事),
given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and put in charge of all military affairs outside the city.
He was enfeoffed as Bólíng Jùngōng (博陵郡公),
but firmly declined the offer.
So his peerage was advanced to Xiàn Gōng (縣公),
with an income of one thousand eight hundred households.
The Emperor was just about to entrust him with all state affairs
when, in the second year of Tàishǐ (泰始) [266 CE],
he passed away.
The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and expressed his grief,
bestowing a set of ceremonial court robes and a suit of clothes, three hundred thousand coins, one hundred bolts of cloth, and one qǐng (頃) of burial land.
His posthumous name was Yuán (元).
The following year,
the Emperor, recalling Shěn's (沈) profound merits,
issued an edict stating:
“To extol past deeds
is to revere the worthy and establish teachings;
to be mindful of the end and record the distant past
is to strengthen virtue and promote education.
The late Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Píqí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), and Bólíng Yuán Gōng (博陵元公), Shěn Táo (沈蹈), observed rites and upheld uprightness,
his heart pure and unblemished.
He was skilled in organizing and managing the classics and ancient texts,
his talent and knowledge were extensive and profound.
Internally, he held positions like Chángbó (常伯) and Nàyán (納言);
externally, he served as Gān Jiānmù Fāngyuè (榦監牧方嶽), fulfilling crucial responsibilities.
Internally, his strategies and plans were evident;
externally, his might and prowess were proclaimed.
In the establishment of the state and appointment of officials,
he was among the first to serve as a ducal mentor,
also commanding the central court
and issuing important decrees,
truly possessing the merit of assisting and supporting the world.
Let Shěn be posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng Gōng (司空公),
to honor and glorify his past,
so that he may be immortalized even in death.
Moreover, previously for his merit in assisting and supporting,
he was due to receive the enfeoffment of Jùngōng (郡公),
but he firmly and earnestly declined.
Admiring his virtue of humility,
we did not override his will.
His funeral may be attended by the officials and staff appropriate for a Jùngōng (郡公).
Shěn was always pure and frugal,
not engaging in accumulating property.
Therefore, his subordinate troops are to build fifty rooms for him.”
His son, Jùn (浚), inherited.
Later, Shěn's wife, Lady Xún (荀), passed away.
When they were to be buried together,
Shěn's coffin and outer casing had already deteriorated,
so new secret artifacts from the Eastern Park were bestowed.
During the Xiánníng (咸寧) reign [275-280 CE],
Shěn was again posthumously enfeoffed as a Jùngōng (郡公).
Jùn's courtesy name was Péngzǔ (彭祖).
His mother, Lady Zhào (趙),
was a daughter from a respectable family,
but was poor and humble.
She frequented the Shěn family home,
and subsequently gave birth to Jùn.
Shěn initially disavowed him.
At the age of fifteen,
when Shěn passed away,
having no other sons,
his relatives collectively established Jùn as the heir,
and he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉).
In the early years of Tàikāng (太康) [280-289 CE],
he, along with other princes and marquises, went to his enfeoffed territory.
In the third year, he came to court,
and was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎).
In the early years of Yuánkāng (元康) [291-300 CE],
he was transferred to Yuánwài Chángshì (員外常侍), then promoted to Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉) and Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (右軍將軍).
He was sent out to serve as Hénèi Tàishǒu (河內太守).
Since a Jùngōng (郡公) could not hold a position with a salary of two thousand dàn (石),
he was transferred to Dōng Zhōnglángjiāng (東中郎將),
stationed at Xǔchāng (許昌).
When Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ (愍懷太子) was imprisoned in Xǔchāng (許昌),
Jùn, following Jiǎ Hòu's (賈后) decree,
collaborated with Huángmén (黃門) Sūn Lǜ (孫慮) to harm the Crown Prince.
He was promoted to Níngběi Jiāngjūn (寧北將軍) and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史).
Soon after, he was transferred to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), given a jié (節) (credentials), and made Dūdū Yōuzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (都督幽州諸軍事).
At that time, the imperial court was in chaos,
and bandits arose everywhere.
Jùn, for his own security,
formed alliances with the Yi and Di (夷狄),
marrying his daughter to the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Wùwùchén (務勿塵),
and another daughter to Sū Shùyán (蘇恕延).
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) usurped the throne,
the three princes raised armies of righteousness.
Jùn, commanding his troops, sided with both parties,
blocking and cutting off their proclamations,
preventing the gentry and commoners within his territory from joining the righteous cause.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) wanted to punish him but had no time.
After Lún (倫) was executed,
Jùn was promoted to Ānběi Jiāngjūn (安北將軍).
When Héjiān Wáng Yóng (河間王顒) and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) raised armies and advanced inward,
harming Chángshā Wáng (長沙王),
Jùn harbored resentment.
Yǐng (穎) submitted a memorial requesting Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (幽州刺史) Shí Kān (石堪) to be his Yòusīmǎ (右司馬),
and Yòusīmǎ (右司馬) Hé Yǎn (和演) to replace Kān (堪),
secretly instructing Yǎn (演) to kill Jùn (浚)
and seize his troops.
Yǎn (演) conspired with Wūhuán Chányú (烏丸單于) Shěn Dēng (審登).
Thereupon, they arranged to meet Jùn (浚) to tour the Qīngquánshuǐ (清泉水) (Clear Spring Water) south of Jìchéng (薊城).
There were two roads leading west from inside Jìchéng (薊城);
Yǎn (演) and Jùn (浚) each took one.
Yǎn (演) intended to combine their imperial escorts with Jùn's (浚)
and then plot against him.
It happened to rain heavily,
wetting their weapons,
so they returned without accomplishing their goal.
The Chányú (單于) then conspired with his people, saying:
“Yǎn (演) plotted to kill Jùn (浚),
