and the matter was about to be concluded when suddenly it rained,
preventing them from succeeding.
This is Heaven helping Jùn (浚).
To defy Heaven is inauspicious;
I cannot remain with Yǎn (演) for long.”
He then informed Jùn (浚) of the plot.
Jùn (浚) secretly readied his troops
and, with the Chányú (單于), surrounded Yǎn (演).
Yǎn (演) came to Jùn (浚) with a white banner to surrender,
but Jùn (浚) beheaded him
and personally took command of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
He greatly expanded his armaments,
summoned Wùwùchén (務勿塵),
and led a combined force of twenty thousand Hu (胡) and Jìn (晉) soldiers.
He advanced to attack Yǐng (穎).
He appointed his principal clerk, Qí Hóng (祁弘), as vanguard.
They encountered Yǐng's (穎) general Shí Chāo (石超) at Píngjí (平棘)
and defeated him.
Jùn (浚) pressed his advantage and captured Yèchéng (鄴城).
His troops plundered violently,
and many died.
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) greatly abducted women.
Jùn (浚) ordered that anyone daring to harbor them would be beheaded,
whereupon eight thousand people drowned in the Yìshuǐ (易水).
The suffering of the common people
began from this point.
Jùn (浚) returned to Jì (薊),
his reputation and power growing even stronger.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) was about to welcome the Emperor,
Jùn (浚) dispatched Qí Hóng (祁弘) to lead the Wūhuán (烏丸) cavalry as the vanguard.
After Huìdì (惠帝) returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
Jùn (浚) was promoted to Píqí Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍), Dūdū Dōngyí Héběi Zhūjūn Shì (都督東夷河北諸軍事),
and concurrently Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (幽州刺史).
The state of Yān (燕) was added to his enfeoffment of Bólíng (博陵).
Upon Huáidì's (懷帝) ascension,
Jùn (浚) was made Sīkōng (司空) and concurrently Wūhuán Xiàowèi (烏丸校尉).
Wùwùchén (務勿塵) was made Dà Chányú (大單于).
Jùn (浚) also memorialized to enfeoff Wùwùchén (務勿塵) as Liáoxī Jùngōng (遼西郡公),
and his separate tribal leaders Dà Piāohuá (大飄滑) and his brother Kěmò Dà Túwèng (渴末大屠瓮), etc., were all made Qīnjìn Wáng (親晉王).
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) reign [307-313 CE],
Shí Lè (石勒) invaded Jìzhōu (冀州).
Jùn (浚) sent the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Wén Yāng (文鴦) to attack Lè (勒),
and Lè (勒) fled to Nányáng (南陽).
The following year,
Lè (勒) again invaded Jìzhōu (冀州),
and Cìshǐ (刺史) Wáng Bīn (王斌) was harmed by Lè (勒).
Jùn (浚) again assumed concurrent charge of Jìzhōu (冀州).
An imperial edict promoted Jùn (浚) to Dàsīmǎ (大司馬),
and added Shìzhōng (侍中) and Dà Dūdū (大都督), Dūdū Yōu Jì Zhūjūn Shì (督幽冀諸軍事).
Before the envoy could even depart,
the capital Luòjīng (洛京) fell.
Jùn (浚) greatly asserted his authority and command,
specializing in military campaigns.
He dispatched Dūhù (督護) Wáng Chāng (王昌), Zhōngshān Tàishǒu (中山太守) Ruǎn Bào (阮豹), etc.,
leading various armies and Wùwùchén's (務勿塵) heir, Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷), along with his brother Wén Yāng (文鴦) and cousin Mòpēi (末柸),
to attack Shí Lè (石勒) at Xiāngguó (襄國).
Lè (勒) led his troops to resist,
and Chāng (昌) met and defeated them.
Mòpēi (末柸) pursued the fleeing enemy into their camp gate,
and was captured by Lè (勒).
Lè (勒) held Mòpēi (末柸) as a hostage,
and sent a secret envoy to seek peace.
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) then ransomed Mòpēi (末柸) with two hundred fifty suits of armor and horses, and one basket each of gold and silver.
They formed an alliance and withdrew.
Thereafter, Shěn Jùn 瀋濬 announced to all under heaven,
claiming to have received a secret imperial edict and to be acting by imperial authority.
He then appointed Sīkōng 司空 Xún Pān 荀藩 as Tàiwèi 太尉,
Guānglù Dàfū 光祿大夫 Xún Zǔ 荀組 as Sīlì 司隸,
Dàsīnóng 大司農 Huá Huì 華薈 as Tàicháng 太常,
and Zhōngshūlìng 中書令 Lǐ Jìn 李絙 as Hénán Yǐn 河南尹.
He also dispatched Qí Hóng 祁弘 to attack Lè 勒,
reaching Guǎngzōng 廣宗.
At that time, there was a heavy fog.
Hóng 弘 led his army along the road
and unexpectedly encountered Lè 勒.
He was killed by Lè 勒.
Because of this, Liú Kūn 劉琨 and Jùn 濬 contended for Jìzhōu 冀州.
Kūn 琨 sent his kinsman Liú Xī 劉希 back to Zhōngshān 中山 to gather troops.
People from Dàijùn 代郡, Shànggǔ 上谷, and Guǎng 廣 three commanderies all submitted to Kūn 琨.
Jùn 濬 was troubled by this,
so he suspended his campaign against Lè 勒
and confronted Kūn 琨.
Jùn 濬 sent Yān Xiàng 燕相 Hú Jǔ 胡矩 to oversee the various armies,
who, with Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷, jointly attacked and defeated Xī 希.
They drove and plundered the men and women of the three commanderies out of the frontier.
Kūn 琨 was no longer able to contend.
Jùn 濬 returned,
intending to attack Lè 勒.
He sent Zǎo Sōng 棗嵩 to supervise the various armies garrisoned at Yìshuǐ 易水,
and summoned Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷,
planning to attack Xiāngguó 襄國 with him.
Jùn’s 濬’s governance was harsh and violent.
His generals and officials were also greedy and cruel,
extensively occupying mountains and wetlands,
diverting water to irrigate fields,
submerging and collapsing tombs.
Conscriptions and levies were frequent and burdensome,
and the common people could not endure their commands.
Many rebelled and defected to the Xiānbēi 鮮卑.
His aide, Hán Xián 韓咸, remonstrated strongly,
but Jùn 濬 was enraged
and killed him.
Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷, considering his previous disobedience to orders,
feared that Jùn 濬 would punish him.
Lè 勒 also sent envoys with lavish bribes.
Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷 and others consequently did not answer the summons.
Jùn 濬 was furious
and used heavy bribes to entice Dānyú Yīlú’s 單于猗盧子 son, the Right Xiánwáng 賢王 Rìlǜsūn 日律孫,
to attack Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷,
but instead, he was defeated.
At that time, Liú Kūn 劉琨 was heavily pressed by Liú Cōng 劉聰.
Many wandering scholars who fled the chaos returned to Jùn 濬.
Jùn 濬 grew stronger day by day.
He then erected an altar and announced to the spirits,
established an imperial crown prince,
and fully appointed all officials.
Jùn 濬 personally took the position of Shàngshūlìng 尚書令,
appointed Zǎo Sōng 棗嵩 and Péi Xiàn 裴憲 jointly as Shàngshū 尚書,
and made his son reside in the royal palace,
holding the jié 節 (imperial insignia),
and leading the Hù Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiàng 護匈奴中郎將.
He appointed his wife's uncle Cuī Bì 崔毖 as Dōngyí Xiàowèi 東夷校尉.
He also made Sōng 嵩 supervise military affairs in Sī 司, Jì 冀, Bìng 并, and Yǎn 兗 provinces, acting as Ānběi Jiāngjūn 安北將軍.
He appointed Tián Huī 田徽 as the governor of Yǎnzhōu 兗州
and Lǐ Yùn 李惲 as the governor of Qīngzhōu 青州.
Yùn 惲 was killed by Shí Lè 石勒,
and Báo Shèng 薄盛 was appointed to replace him.
Jùn 濬 believed that his father's courtesy name, Chǔdào 處道,
corresponded to the prophecy
of "Dāngtú Gāo 當塗高,"
indicating a king.
He planned to usurp the imperial title.
Hú Jǔ 胡矩 admonished Jùn 濬,
elaborating on why it was not permissible.
Jùn 濬 was angry about this
and demoted Jǔ 矩 to Wèijùn Shǒu 魏郡守.
Former Bóhǎi Tàishǒu 渤海太守 Liú Liàng 劉亮, his nephew Běihǎi Tàishǒu 北海太守 Bó 搏,
and Sīkōng Yuàn 司空掾 Gāo Ròu 高柔 all strongly remonstrated.
Jùn 濬 was enraged
and executed them.
Jùn 濬 had always been discontent with his Chángshǐ 長史 (Chief Clerk) from Yānguó 燕國, Wáng Tì 王悌,
and thus used another matter to kill him.
At that time, a children's rhyme said:
"Ten bags, five bags, all go to Lord Zǎo 棗 (Sōng 嵩)."
Zǎo Sōng 棗嵩
was Jùn’s 濬’s son-in-law.
Jùn 濬 heard this
and reprimanded Sōng 嵩 but could not punish him.
Another rhyme said:
"The gate of Yōuzhōu 城門 (Yōuzhōu Chéngmén 幽州城門) is like a hidden door,
inside lies a hidden corpse, Wáng Péngzǔ 王彭祖."
A fox squatted at the mansion gate,
and a long-tailed pheasant entered the reception hall.
At that time, Huò Yuán 霍原 of Yānguó 燕國,
a renowned scholar in the northern region,
Jùn 濬 showed him his plan for usurpation.
Yuán 霍原 did not reply,
so Jùn 濬 harmed him.
Because of this, scholars were indignant and resentful,
and he had no allies inside or outside.
He grew increasingly arrogant and extravagant,
did not personally attend to governance,
and those he appointed were mostly harsh and severe.
Coupled with severe drought and locust plagues,
his soldiers were weak and exhausted.
When Jùn 濬 assumed imperial authority,
all his aides entered the inner court,
only Sīmǎ 司馬 Yóu Tǒng 游統 remained outside.
Tǒng 游統 resented this
and secretly colluded with Shí Lè 石勒.
Lè 勒 then feigned submission to Jùn 濬,
promising to serve Jùn 濬 as his lord.
At that time, the common people rebelled internally,
and Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷 and others encroached.
Jùn 濬 was pleased that Lè 勒 attached himself to him,
and Lè 勒 then used humble words to serve him,
offering treasures and precious items,
with a continuous stream of envoys.
Jùn 濬 believed Lè 勒 was sincere
and no longer prepared defenses.
Lè 勒 then sent an envoy to set a date to present an imperial title to Jùn 濬.
Jùn 濬 agreed.
Lè 勒 stationed his troops at Yìshuǐ 易水.
Dūhù 督護 Sūn Wěi 孫緯 suspected his deception,
urgently informed Jùn 濬,
and led his army to intercept Lè 勒.
Jùn 濬 did not listen
and allowed Lè 勒 to proceed directly.
All his subordinates said,
"The Hu 胡 are greedy and untrustworthy;
there must be a deception.
Please resist them."
Jùn 濬 was angry
and wanted to execute those who spoke,
so the others dared not remonstrate further.
He grandly prepared to await Lè 勒.
When Lè 勒 reached the city,
he immediately let his soldiers plunder extensively.
Jùn's 濬's entourage again requested to attack him,
but he refused.
When Lè 勒 ascended to the reception hall,
Jùn 濬 then ran out of the main hall.
Lè's 勒's troops seized him and brought him before Lè 勒.
Lè 勒 then sat with Jùn's 濬's wife,
and made Jùn 濬 stand before him.
Jùn 濬 cursed, saying,
"You Hu 胡 slave, how dare you provoke your lord!
How can you be so rebellious!"
Lè 勒 enumerated Jùn's 濬's disloyalty to Jìn 晉,
and also reproached him for the people's starvation and destitution,
having accumulated 500,000 hú 斛 (measures) of grain but not distributing it.
He then dispatched 500 cavalry to escort Jùn 濬 to Xiāngguó 襄國 first,
gathered 10,000 elite soldiers under Jùn’s 濬’s command,
and killed them all.
He stayed for two days and then returned.
Sūn Wěi 孫緯 ambushed him,
and Lè 勒 barely escaped.
When Lè 勒 arrived at Xiāngguó 襄國,
he executed Jùn 濬.
Jùn 濬 ultimately did not yield to him,
cursing loudly until his death.
He had no sons.
In the second year of Tàiyuán 太元 (377 CE),
an imperial edict was issued to revive and continue extinct lines,
enfeoffing Shěn 瀋’s great-grandson Dào Sù 道素 as Bólíng Gōng 博陵公.
When he died,
his son Chóngzhī 崇之 succeeded.
In the eleventh year of Yìxī 義熙 (415 CE),
he was restyled Dōngguǎn Jùn Gōng 東莞郡公.
When the Sòng 宋 received the imperial abdication,
his state was abolished.
Xún Yǐ 荀顗
Xún Yǐ 荀顗, courtesy name Jǐngqiàn 景倩,
was from Yǐngchuān 潁川.
He was the sixth son of Wèi Tàiwèi 魏太尉 Yù 彧.
As a child, he was admired by his brother-in-law Chén Qún 陳羣.
He was extremely filial by nature,
known from his youth,
broadly learned and well-informed,
with meticulous reasoning and thought.
During the Wèi 魏 period, due to his father's achievements, he was appointed Zhōngláng 中郎.
When Xuāndì 宣帝 assisted in governance,
he saw Yǐ 顗 and was impressed,
saying,
"He is the son of Lord Xún Lìngjūn 荀令君."
He was promoted to Sànqí Shìláng 散騎侍郎,
and successively transferred to Shìzhōng 侍中.
He lectured on the classics for Wèi Shàodì 魏少帝,
was appointed Qíjūdūwèi 騎都尉,
and granted the title Guānnèihóu 關內侯.
He debated Zhōng Huì 鍾會 on the difficulty of "Yìwú Hùtǐ 易無互體" (the Yì 易 without mutual bodies),
and also discussed with Fúfēng Wáng Jùn 扶風王駿 whether benevolence or filial piety came first,
earning praise from the world.
At that time, Cáo Shuǎng 曹爽 held exclusive power.
Hé Yàn 何晏 and others wanted to harm Tàicháng 太常 Fù Jiǎ 傅嘏,
but Yǐ 顗营 rescued him, and he escaped.
When Gāo Guì Xiāng Gōng 高貴鄉公 was enthroned,
Yǐ 顗 said to Jǐng Dì 景帝:
"Now that the emperor has ascended the throne,
the means of power are extraordinary.
It is appropriate to quickly send envoys to declare his virtue throughout the four directions,
and also to observe the sentiments abroad."
Wú Qiū Jiǎn 毋丘儉 and Wén Qīn 文欽 indeed did not submit,
and raised troops in rebellion.
Yǐ 顗 participated in suppressing Jiǎn 儉 and others, achieving merit.
He was advanced in noble rank to Wànsuì Tíng Hóu 萬歲亭侯,
with an income of four hundred households.
When Wén Dì 文帝 assisted in governance,
he was promoted to Shàngshū 尚書.
When the emperor campaigned against Zhūgě Dàn 諸葛誕,
Yǐ 顗 was left to guard the capital.
Yǐ's 顗甥 (maternal nephew) Chén Tài 陳泰 passed away,
and Yǐ 顗 succeeded Tài 泰 as Púshè 僕射,
concurrently managing Lìbù 吏部.
He declined four times before taking office.
Yǐ 顗, succeeding Tài 泰,
moreover was virtuous and prudent,
scrutinizing names and realities,
thereby clarifying and rectifying customs.
During the Xiánxī 咸熙 era,
he was promoted to Sīkōng 司空,
and advanced in noble rank to Xiāng Hóu 鄉侯.
Yǐ 顗 was over sixty years old,
and his filial piety was increasingly manifest.
He left office due to mourning for his mother,
and his grief was so intense it almost destroyed him.
The whole country praised him.
Wén Dì 文帝 memorialized,
stating that it was appropriate to follow the precedent of Hú Guǎng 胡廣, the Grand Tutor of Han, when he mourned his mother,
granting Sīkōng 司空 official carriages and escorts for auspicious and inauspicious occasions.
When Shǔ 蜀 was pacified,
and the Five Ranks were revived,
Yǐ 顗 was ordered to establish the rites and ceremonies.
Yǐ 顗 memorialized requesting Yáng Hù 羊祜, Rèn Kǎi 任愷, Yǔ Jùn 庾峻, Yīng Zhēn 應貞, and Kǒng Hào 孔顥 to jointly revise the old texts,
and compile the Jìn Lǐ 晉禮 (Rites of Jin).
In the early Xiánxī 咸熙 era,
he was enfeoffed as Lín Huái Hóu 臨淮侯.
When Wǔ Dì 武帝 ascended the throne,
he was advanced in rank to Gōng 公,
with an income of one thousand eight hundred households.
An imperial edict further stated:
"In the past, Yǔ 禹 appointed the Nine Officials,
and Qì 契 spread the Five Teachings,
thereby promoting the royal transformation [through virtue]
and demonstrating standards of conduct to the people.
I have inherited this great enterprise,
but am ignorant of the Great Way.
I desire to instruct in the Five Relationships,
to bring peace to the four seas.
Shìzhōng 侍中, Sīkōng 司空 Yǐ 顗,
is intelligent, trustworthy, and sincere,
with far-reaching thoughts.
He assisted the former emperor,
and now aids me personally,
truly having the merit of assisting the mandate and guiding the state.
He should manage the canon of teachings,
to bring prosperity to the harmonious age.
Therefore, Yǐ 顗 is appointed Sītú 司徒."
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Shìzhōng 侍中,
and promoted to Tàiwèi 太尉, Dūdū Chéngwài Yámén Zhū Jūnshì 都督城外牙門諸軍事 (Commander-in-Chief of all forces outside the city's main gates),
and granted one hundred Sīmǎ Qīnbīng 司馬親兵 (personal guards).
After a while,
another imperial edict stated:
"Shìzhōng 侍中, Tàiwèi 太尉 Yǐ 顗,
is gentle, respectful, loyal, and upright;
his conduct is utterly pure and complete;
he is broadly learned in ancient matters and widely informed,
and though aged, is not infirm.
Therefore, he is to act as Tàizǐ Tàifù 太子太傅,
while his titles of Shìzhōng 侍中 and Tàiwèi 太尉 remain as before."
At that time, as the court believed the elegant songs of Zhèngdé 正德 and Dàyù 大豫 were not yet harmonious,
Yǐ 顗 was ordered to establish the music.
Before the task was completed,
he passed away in the tenth year of Tàishǐ 泰始 (274 CE).
The emperor mourned him,
the Crown Prince attended the funeral,
and the two palaces sent generous gifts,
with added ritual honors.
An imperial edict stated:
"Shìzhōng 侍中, Tàiwèi 太尉, Acting Tàizǐ Tàifù 太子太傅, Lín Huái Gōng 臨淮公 Yǐ 顗,
was pure and embodied the Way,
loyal and upright in court.
Having served both internally and externally,
his great achievements were numerous,
and his instruction and guidance of the Eastern Palace [Crown Prince]
brought forth widely manifest excellent deeds.
He can be said to have 'returned to Zhōu' (acted perfectly in accordance with the Way),
having a beginning and an end (completing his life's work).
His unfortunate death
causes me great pain.
Therefore, he is granted Wēnmíng Mìqì 溫明祕器 (a precious funeral object), one set of court robes, and one suit of clothes.
His posthumous title is Kāng 康."
Another imperial edict stated:
"The Tàiwèi 太尉 did not care for his private household;
he had no mansion to live in.
His aspiration for simplicity [represented by 'plain silk']
becomes even more evident after his death.
Therefore, two million cash are bestowed upon his family,
to enable them to build a residence."
In the early Xiánníng 咸寧 era,
an edict ordered the compilation of meritorious officials
to be honored in the imperial ancestral temple.
The relevant department memorialized that Yǐ 顗 and twelve others should have their achievements inscribed in the Tàicháng 太常 (Grand Temple)
and be honored in the Qīngmiào 清廟 (Pure Temple).
Yǐ 顗 understood the three rites and
knew the grand ceremonies of the court,
but lacked a straightforward and honest character,
only agreeing and accommodating Xún Xù 荀勖 and Jiǎ Chōng 賈充.
Initially,
when the Crown Prince was to take a consort,
Yǐ 顗 memorialized that Jiǎ Chōng's 賈充 daughter had excellent demeanor and virtue,
and could be considered for selection,
for which he was criticized by his contemporaries.
Yǐ 顗 had no son,
so his grandnephew Huī 徽 succeeded him.
In the early Zhōngxīng 中興 era,
Xù 序, a great-grandson of Yǐ's 顗 brother Xuán 玄, was designated Yǐ's 顗 successor,
and enfeoffed as Lín Huái Gōng 臨淮公.
When Xù 序 died,
the line again became extinct.
Xiàowǔ Dì 孝武帝 then enfeoffed Jì 繼, Xù's 序 son, as Yǐ's 顗 successor.
When he died,
his son Lóngfú 龍符 succeeded him.
When Sòng 宋 received the imperial abdication,
the state (and thus the title) was abolished.
Xún Xù 荀勖 (son Fān 藩; Fān's son Suì 邃; Kǎi 闓; Fān's brother Zǔ 組; Zǔ's son Yì 奕)
Xún Xù 荀勖, courtesy name Gōngzēng 公曾,
was a native of Yǐngchuān Yǐngyīn 潁川潁陰.
He was the great-grandson of Húndàn Sīkōng 漢司空 (Han Sīkōng) Shuǎng 爽.
His grandfather, Fěi 棐, was Shèshēng Xiàowèi 射聲校尉.
His father, Xī 肸,
died young.
Xù 勖 lived with his maternal uncle's family.
He was intelligent and mature from a young age,
and at over ten years old, he could compose essays.
His maternal grandfather, Wèi Tàifù 魏太傅 Zhōng Yáo 鍾繇, said:
"This child will reach the level of his great-grandfather."
When he grew up,
he became broadly learned
and skilled in governance.
He served in Wèi 魏,
and was appointed a clerk to Dàjiāngjūn 大將軍 Cáo Shuǎng 曹爽,
then promoted to Zhōngshū Tōngshì Láng 中書通事郎.
When Shuǎng 爽 was executed,
none of his former retainers or officials dared to go to him,
but Xù 勖 alone went to mourn him,
and only then did others follow.
He served as Ānyáng Lìng 安陽令,
then transferred to Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng 驃騎從事中郎.
Xù 勖 left a legacy of love,
and the people of Ānyáng 安陽 built a shrine for him while he was still alive.
He was promoted to Tíngwèi Zhèng 廷尉正,
participated in Wén Dì's 文帝 Dàjiāngjūn 大將軍 military affairs,
and was granted the noble rank of Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯.
He then transferred to Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎,
concurrently serving as Jìshì 記室.
When Gāo Guì Xiāng Gōng 高貴鄉公 planned a coup,
Dàjiāngjūn 閤門 Yuán 掾 Sūn Yòu 孫佑 and others guarded the Chānghé Mén 閶闔門.
The emperor's brother, Ānyáng Hóu 榦 安陽侯 Gàn 榦, heard of the trouble and wanted to enter.
Yòu 佑 told Gàn 榦:
"No one has entered yet;
you can enter through the Dōngyè Mén 東掖門."
When Gàn 榦 arrived,
the emperor delayed him.
Gàn 榦 reported the situation,
and the emperor wanted to execute Yòu's 佑 entire clan.
Xù 勖 admonished, saying:
"Sūn Yòu's 孫佑 refusal to admit Ānyáng 安陽 was indeed deserving of severe blame.
However, matters have their proper order,
and punishment should not be made lighter or heavier based on joy or anger.
Now Chéngcuì's 成倅 punishment stopped at his own person,
but Yòu 佑 is to be executed with his whole clan.
I fear that righteous scholars will privately criticize this."
So, Yòu 佑 was dismissed as a commoner.
At that time, Guāngjì Lù Yí 官騎路遺 requested to become an assassin to enter Shǔ 蜀.
Xù 勖 said to the emperor:
"Your Excellency governs the world with utmost impartiality.
You should rely on righteousness to punish those who rebel and are disloyal.
To gain fame by using an assassin to eliminate a rebel
is not what is meant by 'setting a model for the four seas'
and 'subduing distant lands with virtue'."
The emperor praised this as good.
When Zhōng Huì 鍾會 conspired to rebel,
the interrogation had not yet reached [him],
but outsiders reported it first.
The Emperor had always treated Huì 訓厚,
and did not believe it.
Xùn 勖 said:
“Although Huì 訓 has received favors,
his nature is such that one cannot allow him to prioritize gain over righteousness.
We must not fail to make preparations quickly.”
The Emperor immediately went out to garrison Cháng'ān 長安.
The Chief Clerk, Guō Yì 郭奕, and the Adjutant, Wáng Shēn 王深, believing that Xùn 勖 was Huì's 訓 maternal nephew,
and had grown up in his maternal uncle's household,
advised the Emperor to dismiss him.
The Emperor did not accept this,
but made Xùn 勖 accompany him in the carriage,
treating him as before.
Before this,
Xùn 勖 had memorialized:
“For the campaign against Shǔ 蜀,
Wèi Guàn 衞瓘 should be made Supervisor of the Army.”
When chaos arose in Shǔ 蜀,
it was thanks to Guàn 瓘 that it was settled.
After Huì 訓 was pacified,
[Xùn 勖] returned to Luò 洛,
and jointly managed confidential matters with Péi Xiù 裴秀 and Yáng Hù 羊祜.
At that time, an envoy was about to be dispatched to invite [the ruler of] Wú 吳,
and simultaneously several contemporary literati were sent to write letters to Sūn Hào 孫晧.
The Emperor used the one written by Xùn 勖.
After Hào 晧 responded with an offer of peace and alliance,
the Emperor said to Xùn 勖:
“The letter you wrote previously
made Wú 吳 desire submission,
surpassing an army of one hundred thousand men.”
When the Emperor ascended to the throne as King of Jìn 晉,
he made Xùn 勖 a Shìzhōng 侍中,
enfeoffed him as Ānyáng Zǐ 安陽子,
with a thousand households.
When Emperor Wǔ 武帝 received the abdication,
he was re-enfeoffed as Jìběi Jùn Gōng 濟北郡公.
Xùn 勖, yielding to Yáng Hù 羊祜,
then firmly declined to be a Marquis.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān 中書監,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng 侍中,
and appointed Lǐng Zhùzuò 領著作,
and jointly established the laws and ordinances with Jiǎ Chōng 賈充.
When Chōng 充 was about to take charge of the region west of the passes,
Xùn 勖 said to Féng Dǎn 馮紞:
“Duke Jiǎ 賈 is being sent far away,
and we will lose influence.
The Crown Prince's marriage is not yet settled.
If Chōng's 充 daughter can become the consort,
then he will not leave, but will stay on his own accord.”
Xùn 勖 and Dǎn 紞 seized an opportunity when the Emperor was unoccupied and both stated:
“Chōng's 充 daughter's talent and beauty are unparalleled.
If she is taken into the Eastern Palace,
she will certainly be able to assist the gentleman,
and possess the virtues of the consort in 'Guān Jū' 關雎.”
Thus, the marriage was accomplished.
At the time, this was greatly resented by the upright,
and incurred the criticism of flattery.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū 光祿大夫.
Having taken charge of musical affairs,
he also refined the pitch pipes,
both of which were put into practice throughout the land.
Initially,
Xùn 勖 encountered a cattle bell belonging to a merchant from Zhào 趙 on the road,
and recognized its sound.
When he took charge of music,
the tones and rhythms were not yet harmonious,
so he said:
“If we obtain the cattle bell from Zhào 趙, it will be harmonious.”
Thereupon, he sent orders to the commanderies and states,
requesting all cattle bells be sent,
and indeed, one that was harmonious was found.
Another time, while dining in the Emperor's presence,
he said to those present:
“This was cooked with waste wood.”
No one believed him.
The Emperor sent to ask the imperial chef,
who then said:
“Indeed, old carriage parts were used.”
The whole world admired his clear discernment.
Soon after, he was appointed Lǐng Mìshū Jiān 領祕書監,
and with Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令 Zhāng Huá 張華, based on Liú Xiàng's 劉向 *Biélù* 別錄,
they organized the records and books.
He also established a Book Erudite,
and set up disciples to teach and practice,
taking Zhōng 鍾 and Hú 胡 as models.
In the early Xiánníng 咸寧 era,
he and Shí Bāo 石苞 and others were all meritorious officials who aided in the founding [of the dynasty],
and were listed in the commemorative inscriptions.
When Wáng Jùn 王濬 submitted a memorial requesting to attack Wú 吳,
Xùn 勖 and Jiǎ Chōng 賈充 firmly advised against it,
but the Emperor did not comply,
and Wú 吳 was indeed destroyed.
Because he exclusively managed imperial edicts and commands,
in recognition of his merits, one of his sons was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu 亭侯,
with one thousand households,
and given a thousand rolls of silk.
His grandson Sūn Xiǎn 孫顯 was also enfeoffed as Yǐngyáng Tínghóu 潁陽亭侯.
When ancient bamboo slips with texts were obtained from a tomb in Jí Jùn 汲郡,
an imperial edict commanded Xùn 勖 to compile and arrange them,
making them into the Zhōngjīng 中經,
listed in the imperial library.
At that time, there was a discussion about sending the imperial princes and dukes to their states.
The Emperor asked Xùn 勖 about this.
Xùn 勖 replied:
“The various princes and dukes are already commandants;
if they are sent to their states,
then their regional responsibilities will be neglected.
Moreover, dividing up commanderies and counties will cause
people to cling to their original homes,
and inevitably lead to lamentations.
If each state establishes an army,
the government troops will then have to be provided to the states,
and the border defenses will be weakened.”
The Emperor again asked Xùn 勖 to reconsider,
and Xùn 勖 again stated:
“If the imperial edict aligns with ancient practices of selecting talents as regional commanders,
making each military state a commandant according to its region,
it would indeed be as your enlightened decree states.
As for dividing and rectifying the borders,
making distinctions between close and distant relations,
that would indeed be excellent.
However, splitting up old territories
still risks much instability,
which will surely disturb people's minds.
My humble opinion is that it should be as before.
If circumstances necessitate occasional re-enfeoffments,
but without dividing territories
or causing any loss or seizure,
it can be done as appropriate.
As for the five ranks for governing the country over the long term,
they truly do not form a complete system.
However, they are merely nominal;
in terms of actual affairs,
they are virtually no different from the old commanderies, counties, townships, and pavilions.
If they are abruptly changed or abolished,
I fear it will inevitably cause resentment.
For now, we are dealing with the major issues;
the five ranks can await later deliberation.
Although some things improve with time,
if at the present moment there are aspects that are not understood,
they should not be neglected.”
The Emperor considered Xùn's 勖 words to be reasonable,
and mostly followed his intentions.
At that time, there was also a discussion about reducing half of the officials in the prefectures, commanderies, and counties to send them to agricultural labor.
Xù argued, saying:
“Reducing officials is not as good as reducing offices.
Reducing offices is not as good as reducing affairs.
Reducing affairs is not as good as purifying the mind.
Formerly, Xiāo Cáo assisted the Hàn dynasty,
and their clear and tranquil governance
led to songs of unity.
This is the essence of purifying the mind.
Emperor Hàn Wén, with folded hands,
nearly abolished all punishments.
This is reducing affairs.
Emperor Guāng Wǔ consolidated officials,
and the number of county and state officials was reduced to one-tenth.
This is reducing offices.
During the Tài Hé era of the Wèi dynasty,
envoys were sent out in all four directions
to reduce the number of officials throughout the empire.
In the Zhèng Shǐ era, commanderies and counties were also merged.
This is reducing officials.
If one must now seek the root cause,
then it is appropriate to prioritize reducing affairs.
All those in positions of power
should strive to emulate the minds of Xiāo Cáo,
to assist and support the great transformation.
Be earnest in righteous conduct,
and promote harmony and unity.
Ensure that those who forget their roots for the sake of favor cannot be tolerated,
and false conduct will naturally cease;
the flashy will be afraid.
Emphasize reverence and humility,
and advocate contentment.
Let the lowly not hinder the noble,
the young not insult the old,
the distant not alienate the close,
the new not displace the old,
the small not overwhelm the great,
and indulgence not corrupt righteousness.
Then superiors and subordinates will live in peace,
and those near and far will trust each other.
Positions cannot be gained by aggressive ambition,
and reputation cannot be sought through factionalism.
Then right and wrong will be clear without distortion,
and officials will not be misled by hearsay.
Eliminate strange skills,
suppress heterodox theories,
and those who like to change old ways to seek extraordinary gains must be punished.
Then official work will be stable,
and people’s hearts will not waver.
If affairs are delayed, governance stagnates;
if governance stagnates, achievements fail.
If those in power are diligent and tireless,
and those in charge of their duties work day and night without slack,
then even with a small jar, they will not need to borrow tools.
Let trust be like metal and stone,
and small errors not harm major policies.
Endure anger and resentment to accommodate them.
Simplify documents,
and disregard petty strictures.
Whatever commands are issued
must make it easy for people to understand.
They should be desired like the spring sun,
and feared like thunder.
Do not let trivial regulations bother and disturb,
and be scorned by all officials.
Do not let repeated commands
be tiresome to the common people.
Then officials will exert their sincerity,
and the people will be pleased with the emperor’s commands.
Establish offices and divide responsibilities,
delegating tasks and holding accountable for results.
A _jūnzǐ_ strives in spirit but does not contend aggressively for power,
takes on responsibilities according to his ability,
and does not think beyond his position.
Then offices will have no conflicting duties,
and administrative policies will not be corrupted.
All these are what my foolish mind considers the essence of reducing affairs.
If these faults are absent,
even without reducing officials,
the empire will surely deem it a reduction.
If one wishes to reduce offices,
I privately believe the Jiǔ Sì can be merged into the Shàngshū,
and the Lántái should be abolished and its duties transferred to the Sān Fǔ.
However, these have been in practice for generations,
and are customary.
Therefore, I have long harbored these foolish thoughts but dared not speak them.
As for reducing affairs,
I truly believe it is good.
If a blanket rule is made
to simply reduce everything by half,
I fear that the civil and military officials, the duties of the commanderies and states,
and the establishment and abolition of affairs
cannot all be treated the same.
Whenever orders are issued and policies enacted,
if they are proper and appropriate, there will be peace;
if there are objections,
they may cause obstruction.
For every duty one assumes,
first meticulously examine its merits and demerits.
Let loyal and trustworthy officials,
and clear-sighted and perceptive chiefs,
each assess what is appropriate
and first memorialize their recommendations.
Then, a comprehensive framework can be formulated,
and the suitable reductions can be thoroughly considered.
Then, when the order is issued, it will surely be implemented
and cannot be swayed.
If it is not done this way,
I fear it will only confuse people.
Compared to previous attempts at reduction,
all were restored in a short while,
or even intensified and became more complex.
This must not be taken lightly.”
Xù’s discussions on increasing or decreasing matters were often of this kind.
During the Tài Kāng era, an imperial edict stated:
“Xù is brilliant, sagacious, and astute,
knowledgeable in the natural order,
with the merit of assisting the mandate,
and possesses broad and profound talent.
Having long held inner responsibilities,
he has achieved magnificent accomplishments.
Upon inquiring about affairs and examining his words,
his strategies and plans are truly sincere.
He is fit to ascend to a high position
and assist in court governance.
Therefore, Xù is appointed Guānglù Dàfū, Yítóng Sān Sī, and granted _Kāifǔ Pìzhào_,
retaining his positions as Zhōngshū Jiān, Shìzhōng, and his title of marquis as before.”
At that time, the Tàiwèi Jiǎ Chōng and Sītú Lǐ Yìn had both died,
and the Tàizǐ Tàifù position was also vacant.
Xù memorialized:
“The Sān Gōng and Bǎofù
should be filled by suitable individuals.
If Yáng Yáo assists the Eastern Palace,
he will surely meet the imperial will.
Shàngshū Lìng Wèi Guàn and Lìbù Shàngshū Shān Táo can both serve as Sītú.
If Guàn is deemed too new to the position of _Lìng_ to be moved,
then Táo is the right person.”
The emperor followed both recommendations.
The following autumn,
there were great floods in various prefectures and commanderies,
especially severe in Yǎn soil.
Xù proposed establishing a Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě.
Afterward, the Ménxià proposed appointing Tōngshì Lìngshǐ Yī Xiàn and Zhào Xián as Shèrén,
to jointly manage legal documents.
The emperor asked Xù for his opinion.
Xù said:
“Today, the empire fortunately relies on Your Majesty’s sagely virtue,
and the six directions are united.
It is hoped that the moral transformation will flourish
and be passed down to future generations.
However, the Ménxià first recommended Chéng Xián and Zhāng Yùn,
and now recommends these individuals,
wishing to govern through legal documents.
These are all things that I, your foolish subject, do not understand.
Formerly, Zhāng Shìzhī admonished Emperor Hàn Wén,
saying that a mere animal keeper should not be employed;
Bǐng Jí stopped his carriage,
illustrating the importance of harmonizing _yīn_ and _yáng_.
How could these two not know the kindness to petty officials?
They truly valued and cherished the great transformation.
Formerly, Emperor Wèi Wǔ made Zhōngjūn Sī Xún Yōu manage judicial matters;
during Emperor Míng’s time, it was still entrusted to the Nèi Chángshì.
As far as I know,
during Emperor Míng’s time, there were only officials like Tōngshì Liú Tài,
whose titles were no different from those in the Diànzhōng.
Moreover, recently, all discussions have been about reducing offices and affairs,
yet requests to increase officials have been continuous.
Many say that Shàngshū Láng and Tàilìshǐ do not personally handle documents,
but instead entrust them to Shūlìshǐ and clerks.
Indeed, when there are many officials, they rely on each other.
Adding positions for legal documents
will, I fear, only further burden and disturb the court.
I humbly believe it is not permissible.”
At that time, the Emperor Sù knew that the Crown Prince was dim-witted and weak.
Fearing that he would bring chaos to the state later,
he sent Xù and Hé Qiáo to observe him.
Upon his return, Xù lavishly praised the Crown Prince's virtues,
but Qiáo said the Crown Prince was "as before."
Thereupon, the world esteemed Qiáo and disdained Xù.
When the Emperor was about to depose Empress Jiǎ,
Xù and Fēng Dǎn and others remonstrated,
so she was not deposed.
At that time, opinion considered Xù to be corrupting the state and harming the era,
a peer of Sūn Zī and Liú Fàng.
However, his nature was cautious and discreet.
Whenever there was an imperial edict or a major matter,
even after it had been announced,
he would never speak of it,
not wishing people to know that he had heard it in advance.
His cousin Liáng once advised Xù, saying:
"You greatly displease public sentiment.
Those who have made progress can certainly be told,
and then many will cherish your kindness."
His son-in-law Wǔ Tǒng also urged Xù,
"You should manage and establish some things,
so that you have those who rally to you."
Xù remained silent and did not respond to either,
and upon withdrawing, he told his sons:
"If a subject is not discreet, he loses himself;
if he establishes private interests, he betrays the public.
These are great warnings.
You, too, will rise in officialdom among men;
you should understand this intention of mine."
After a long time,
Xù was made Shàngshū Lìng (Minister of the Imperial Secretariat).
Xù had long served in the Zhōngshū (Central Secretariat),
solely managing confidential affairs.
When he lost that position,
he was very much lost and regretful.
Some congratulated him,
to which Xù said:
"You've taken my Fènghuáng Chí (Phoenix Pool) from me; are you gentlemen congratulating me?!"
When he was in the Shàngshū (Imperial Secretariat),
he tested the clerical officials and below,
assessing their talents.
Those who were ignorant of legal statutes
and unable to resolve doubts or handle affairs
were immediately dismissed.
The Emperor once said to him:
"Emperor Wǔ of Wèi said, 'Xún Wénruò promotes the good
and does not stop until he has promoted;
Xún Gōngdá dismisses the wicked
and does not cease until he has dismissed.'
I also hope for the virtues of those two Lords Lìng from you."
After holding the office for over a month,
he returned his seals and ribbons due to his mother's mourning,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
He sent the Chángshì Zhōu Huī to convey the imperial decree,
and Xù then received the edict and continued his duties.
Xù had long managed confidential matters,
possessed talent and insight,
understood the subtle intentions of the ruler,
and did not offend by arguing face-to-face.
Therefore, he was able to maintain his favor and emolument from beginning to end.
In Tàikāng 10 (289 CE), he died.
An edict posthumously appointed him Sītú (Minister of Works),
bestowed him with secret burial items from the eastern garden, one set of court attire, 500,000 cash, and 100 bolts of cloth.
An official carrying the imperial insignia was sent to oversee the funeral,
and he was given the posthumous name Chéng.
Xù had ten sons;
the notable ones were Jí, Fān, and Zǔ.
Jí inherited his title,
and his highest office was Wèiwèi (Minister of the Guards).
He died,
and was given the posthumous name Jiǎn.
His son Jùn inherited.
He died,
and was given the posthumous name Liè.
Having no legitimate son,
his younger brother's son Shì was made heir.
Jí's son was Chuò.
Chuò, courtesy name Yànshū,
was widely learned and talented.
He compiled fifteen chapters of the Jìn Hòushū (Later Book of Jìn),
which circulated in the world.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
he served as Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Attendant Official to the Minister of Works),
but was captured by Shí Lè,
and became Lè's Cānjūn (Military Advisor).
Fān, courtesy name Dàjiān.
In the middle of Yuánkāng,
he became Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant),
and received an edict to complete the zhong and qing bells that his father had been overseeing.
For his meritorious service in accompanying the expedition against Qí Wáng Jǒng,
he was enfeoffed as Xīhuá Xiàn Gōng (Duke of Xīhuá County).
He successively rose to Shàngshū Lìng.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
he was transferred to Sīkōng,
but before he could take up the post, Luòyáng fell,
and Fān fled to Mì.
Wáng Jùn, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Fān as Liútái Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant of the Interim Court).
When Emperor Mǐn became Crown Prince,
he entrusted Fān with supervising affairs far and near.
In Jiànxīng 1 (313 CE), he died in Kāifēng at the age of sixty-nine,
and was buried where he died.
He was given the posthumous name Chéng,
and posthumously appointed Tàibǎo (Grand Protector).
Fān had two sons: Suì and Kǎi.
Suì, courtesy name Dàoxuán,
understood music
and was skilled in discussion.
As a young man, he was appointed Xiàngguó Yuàn (Secretary to the Chancellor) by Zhào Wáng Lún,
and later moved to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Attendant to the Crown Prince).
Chángshā Wáng appointed him Cānjūn.
After the defeat,
Chéngdū Wáng became Huáng Tàidì (Imperial Younger Brother to the Emperor),
and meticulously selected his staff,
appointing Suì as Zhōngshèrén (Central Palace Clerk).
When Yèchéng could not be defended,
he followed Fān to Mì.
Yuán Dì summoned him as Chéngxiàng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Attendant Official to the Chancellor),
but he did not take up the post due to the dangerous roads.
Emperor Mǐn added the titles Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (General of the Left) and Chénliú Xiàng (Administrator of Chénliú) to him.
He resigned due to his father's mourning;
after the mourning period,
he inherited the enfeoffment.
Emperor Mǐn wanted to take Suì's daughter as consort,
and first summoned Suì as Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant).
Suì feared the precarious situation of the western capital,
and therefore did not respond to the summons,
but crossed the river to the east.
Yuán Dì appointed him Jūnzī Jìjiǔ (Libationer of Military Consultations).
In the early Tàixīng era,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (Attendant).
Suì had a marital connection with Diāo Xié.
At the time, Xié held power
and wished to make Suì Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel),
but Suì strongly refused him.
Soon after, Wáng Dūn attacked Xié,
and Xié's party members were all caught in the disaster.
Only Suì, by his distance from Xié, escaped.
Dūn nominated him as Tíngwèi (Minister of Justice),
but he did not accept due to illness.
He was moved to Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies),
then transferred to Shàngshū.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Suì, along with Wáng Dǎo and Xún Sōng, served the Emperor at Shítóu.
After Jùn was pacified, Suì died.
He was posthumously appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, Gold and Purple)
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
His son Wāng inherited.
Kǎi, courtesy name Dàomíng,
also had a renowned reputation.
In the capital, there was a saying about him:
"The brilliant Xún Dàomíng in Luò."
Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Marshal) Qí Wáng Jǒng appointed him Yuàn.
When Jǒng was defeated,
his body lay exposed for three days,
and no one dared to collect and bury it.
Kǎi, along with Jǒng's former officials Lǐ Shù and Jī Hán and others, submitted a public memorial requesting a burial,
and the court deliberated and granted it.
Those who discussed it praised him.
He served as Tàifù Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor) and Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary of the Central Secretariat).
He crossed the river with Suì,
and was appointed Chéngxiàng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ (Libationer of Military Consultations to the Chancellor).
When the Zhongxing era began,
he was moved to Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Right),
then transferred to Shǎofǔ (Minister of the Lesser Treasury).
Emperor Míng once casually asked Wáng Yì:
"Which of the two Xún brothers is more worthy?"
Yì replied that Kǎi's talent and brilliance surpassed Suì's.
The Emperor told Yǔ Liàng,
and Liàng said:
"Suì's true purity of character
is also beyond Kǎi's reach."
Because of this, those who discussed them could not determine the superiority or inferiority of the brothers.
He successively held the posts of Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Palace Censor), Shìzhōng, and Shàngshū,
and was enfeoffed as Shèyáng Gōng (Duke of Shèyáng).
In Tàiníng 2 (324 CE), he died.
He was posthumously appointed Wèiwèi
and given the posthumous name Dìng.
His son Dá inherited.
Zǔ, courtesy name Dàzhāng.
As a young man,
Tàiwèi Wáng Yǎn saw him and praised him, saying:
"He is refined and talented with insight."
He first served as Sītú Zuǒxīshǔ (Left Secretary to the Minister of Works),
then was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince).
Sītú Wáng Hún invited him to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then transferred him to Zuǒ Chángshǐ (Left Chief Clerk),
and he successively served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Central Gentleman to the Crown Prince) and Xíngyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xíngyáng).
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) was Prime Minister,
desiring to gain great fame.
He selected men of virtue and prestige from within the seas.
He appointed Lǐ Chóng (李重) from Jiāngxià (江夏) and Zǔ (組) as Left and Right Chief Clerks.
Wáng Kān (王堪) from Dōngpíng (東平) and Liú Mó (劉謨) from Pèiguó (沛國) were appointed Left and Right Commandants.
When Lún (倫) usurped the throne,
he appointed Zǔ (組) as Attendant Counselor.
After the defeat of Chángshā Wáng (長沙王),
Huìdì (惠帝) sent Zǔ (組) and Attendant Regular Palace Assistant Lǘqiū Chōng (閭丘沖) to Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎)
to console his army.
When the emperor moved west to Cháng'ān (長安),
he appointed Zǔ (組) as Administrator of Hénán (河南).
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
then transferred to Commandant of the Imperial Guard,
granted the title of Marquis of Chéngyáng (成陽) County,
and given the additional titles of Attendant Regular Palace Assistant and Director of the Central Secretariat.
He was transferred to Colonel Director of the Retainers,
and given the additional titles of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
with his position as Attendant Regular Palace Assistant remaining as before.
At that time, the world was already in chaos.
Zǔ (組) and his brothers were distinguished and powerful,
fearing they would not be tolerated by the world.
Although they held high office,
they merely offered subtle advice.
At the end of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Zǔ (組) was again appointed Attendant Counselor
and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Before he could take up the post,
Liú Yào (劉曜) and Wáng Mí (王彌) pressed towards Luòyáng (洛陽).
Zǔ (組) and Fān (藩) both fled.
Huáidì (懷帝) was captured.
Grand Master of Works Wáng Jùn (王浚) appointed Zǔ (組) as Colonel Director of the Retainers.
Zǔ (組) and Fān (藩) issued a proclamation to the world
to make Lángyá Wáng (琅邪王) the leader of the alliance.
Mǐndì (愍帝) was proclaimed Crown Prince.
Zǔ (組) was the maternal uncle of the Crown Prince,
and also held the post of Colonel Director of the Retainers,
acting as Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州).
He and Fān (藩) together held Kāifēng (開封) in Xíngyáng (滎陽).
In the early Jiànxīng (建興) era,
an imperial edict commanded Fān (藩) to act as Director of the Temporary Secretariat.
Soon after, Fān (藩) died.
The emperor reappointed Zǔ (組) as Grand Master of Works,
concurrently Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
and also Colonel Director of the Retainers,
again acting as Director of the Temporary Secretariat.
Provincial and commandery appointments were all carried out under his authority.
He was advanced to Duke of Línyǐng (臨潁) County,
and given the seals and ribbons for his Grand Mother and heir apparent.
The following year,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant,
concurrently Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州) and granted a temporary staff.
Yuándì (元帝) acting under imperial authority,
appointed Zǔ (組) as Grand Coordinator of all military affairs in Sīzhōu (司州),
with the additional title of Attendant Regular Palace Assistant,
the rest remaining as before.
After a while,
he was again appointed Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He submitted a memorial declining the appointment.
When Xīdū (西都) could no longer be held,
Zǔ (組) sent envoys to issue a proclamation to the world to collectively urge for the enthronement.
The emperor intended to appoint Zǔ (組) as Minister of Education,
and consulted Grand Historian Hè Xún (賀循).
Xún (循) said:
"Zǔ (組)'s long-standing reputation is esteemed and weighty,
his loyalty and diligence are manifest.
His transfer to training the five ranks
truly accords with public expectation."
Thereupon, Zǔ (組) was appointed Minister of Education.
Zǔ (組) was pressed by Shí Lè (石勒)
and could not maintain his position.
In the early Tàixīng (太興) era,
he led his subordinates, several hundred men, from Xǔchāng (許昌) to cross the river.
He was provided with a thousand infantry and a hundred cavalry,
and Zǔ (組)'s previous subordinates were still all under his command.
After a while,
an edict commanded Zǔ (組) and Grand Tutor Xīyáng Wáng Yáng (西陽王羕) to both oversee the affairs of the Department of State Affairs,
each granted an additional sixty guards with ceremonial swords.
In the early Yǒngchāng (永昌) era,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant,
concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Before he could take up the post,
he died
at the age of sixty-five.
His posthumous name was Yuán (元).
His son Yì (奕) succeeded him.
Yì (奕)'s courtesy name was Xuánxīn (玄欣).
In his youth, he was appointed Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince and Cavalry Commandant,
lecturing in the Eastern Palace.
He was sent out as Administrator for the General Who Guards the East,
acting as General Who Commands Martial Prowess and Magistrate of Xīnjí (新汲).
When Mǐndì (愍帝) was Crown Prince,
he was summoned to be Attendant in the Central Secretariat,
and soon appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Palace,
but he did not take up either post.
He followed his father across the river.
When Yuándì (元帝) ascended the throne,
he was appointed Middle Imperial Assistant,
and promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate with Concurrent Service.
He left office due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Attendant Regular Palace Assistant and Attendant Counselor.
At that time, the palace city was to be repaired.
A dispatch from the Department of State Affairs was sent to Chénliú Wáng (陳留王),
ordering him to provide laborers for the city.
Yì (奕) retorted:
"In ancient times, when the guest from Yú (虞) was in office,
the Classic of Documents praised his excellence.
The Odes sang of guests,
recorded in the greater and lesser odes.
Now Chénliú Wáng (陳留王) holds a rank above the Three Dukes,
seated to the right of the Crown Prince.
Therefore, when replying to his memorial, it is called a 'letter' (書);
when bestowing gifts, it is called 'giving' (與).
This has been revered by ancient and modern times,
a high principle for governing the state.
It is appropriate to exempt him from corvée labor."
At that time, Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhāng Kǎi (張闓) and Director of the Department of State Affairs Kǒng Yú (孔愉) challenged Yì (奕),
believing:
"In the past, Sòng (宋) did not build walls for Zhōu (周),
which the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized.
To specifically exempt something inappropriate,
it would be appropriate to reduce the laborers."
Yì (奕) again retorted,
believing:
"At the end of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the way of civil and military affairs was about to fall to the ground.
There had just been the chaos of Zǐcháo (子朝).
At that time, the feudal lords were neglecting their duties,
none willing to perform their responsibilities.
Sòng (宋) held the power of a feudal state over Zhōu (周).
Moreover, Jìn (晉) was the one who led the efforts to support the king,
and it was acceptable to blame the guest who refused the labor.
The current Chénliú (陳留) has no power of a feudal state.
Whether this is done or not,
what difference does it make?
Your servant believes it should be exempted,
which would be complete for the state's duties."
The imperial edict followed his advice.
At that time, there was also a general discussion on the day of the New Year's grand assembly:
should the emperor show respect to Minister of Education Wáng Dǎo (王導)?
Scholars Guō Xī (郭熙) and Dù Yuán (杜援) and others believed that the rites had no text for bowing to a subject,
and deemed it appropriate to omit the sign of respect.
Attendant Counselor Féng Huái (馮懷) argued:
"The grandest ceremony for the Son of Heaven is at the Imperial Academy.
On such a day,
he still bows to the Three Elders.
How much more so for the former Imperial Tutor?
It is appropriate to show complete respect."
The matter was sent to the Imperial Secretariat.
Yì (奕) argued:
"At the beginning of the three courts,
it is appropriate to clarify the distinction between sovereign and subject,
so respect should not be shown.
If there is a small gathering on another day,
then complete courtesy can naturally be shown.
Moreover, when the emperor writes a personal decree to the duke, it says 'I bow my head and speak' (頓首言);
when the Central Secretariat drafts a decree, it says 'respectfully inquire' (敬問);
when the Attendant Gentlemen issue an imperial mandate, it says 'by imperial decree' (制命).
Now the wording of imperial edicts still differs;
how can the principle for a grand assembly and a small gathering be the same?"
The imperial edict followed his advice.
He died in the seventh year of Xiánhé (咸和),
posthumously granted Grand Charioteer,
with the posthumous name Dìng (定).
Féng Dǎn (馮紞)
Féng Dǎn (馮紞), courtesy name Shǎozhòu (少冑),
was from Ānpíng (安平).
His grandfather Fú (浮)
was Colonel Director of the Retainers for Wèi (魏).
His father Yuán (員) was Administrator of Jí (汲) Commandery.
Dǎn (紞) was learned in the classics and histories from a young age,
with a keen intellect and eloquent debate skills.
He successively served as Administrator of Wèi (魏) Commandery,
transferred to Commandant of Infantry,
then transferred to Commandant of Cavalry.
He gained favor with Wǔdì (武帝),
gradually promoted to General of the Left Imperial Guard.
He was skilled at pleasing the emperor,
and his favor and affection grew daily.
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) and Xún Xù (荀勖) were both close to him.
When Chōng (充)'s daughter became empress to the Crown Prince,
Dǎn (紞) was instrumental in this.
When the empress was about to be deposed,
Dǎn (紞) and Xù (勖) secretly exerted themselves to plead for her,
thus she was not deposed.
In the campaign against Wú (吳),
Dǎn (紞) concurrently served as Administrator of Rǔnán (汝南).
He followed Wáng Jùn (王濬) into Mòlíng (秣陵) with his commandery troops.
He was promoted to Imperial Censor,
then transferred to Attendant Counselor.
When the emperor was critically ill and recovered,
Féng Dǎn and Xún Xù saw that the hopes of the court and the common people
rested with Qí Wáng Yōu.
Yōu had always held Xù in low regard.
Xù, believing the crown prince to be foolish and inept,
feared that if Yōu were to be enthroned,
it would be detrimental to himself.
So he sent Dǎn to speak to the emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty, if your recent illness had not improved,
the crown prince would have been deposed.
Qí Wáng is acclaimed by the common people
and looked up to by the high officials.
Even if he wished to humbly decline,
how could he be exempt?
It would be advisable to send him back to his fiefdom
to secure the stability of the state."
The emperor accepted this.
When Yōu died,
the court and the common people mourned with regret.
Initially,
the emperor's affection for his kinsman was extremely strong.
After adopting Dǎn and Xù's insidious advice,
he consequently made provisions for his own succession
to solidify the heir apparent's position.
When he heard of Yōu's death,
his sorrow was particularly profound.
Dǎn, standing by,
then said:
"Qí Wáng's reputation exceeded his actual abilities.
Now that he has met a natural end,
this is indeed a blessing for the great Jìn dynasty.
Why does Your Majesty grieve excessively?"
The emperor wiped away his tears and stopped.
Initially, when the campaign against Wú was proposed,
Dǎn, along with Jiǎ Chōng and Xún Xù, strenuously advised against it.
After Wú was pacified,
Dǎn harbored inner shame and fear,
and hated Zhāng Huá like an enemy.
When Huá was posted to a regional command,
his prestige and virtue became widely manifest,
and court discussions favored recalling him as Shàngshū Lìng.
Dǎn, calmly attending the emperor,
discussed historical events of Jìn and Wèi,
and subtly hinted to the emperor
that Huá should not be entrusted with a heavy responsibility.
The emperor remained silent and dropped the matter.
The details are found in Huá's biography.
In the seventh year of Tàikāng (286 CE),
Dǎn fell ill.
An imperial edict appointed Dǎn as Sànqí Chángshì,
bestowing upon him 200,000 cash and one set of bedding.
He died soon after.
He had two sons: Bō and Xióng.
Bō was
Dàchángqiū.
Xióng, courtesy name Wéipí, was
Zhōngshū Láng.
Dǎn's elder brother, Huī,
has his own biography.
The court historian remarks: The way to establish oneself
is through benevolence and righteousness.
When actions are manifested,
regret and misfortune follow.
The serving girl of Yǒushēn
differed from the sentiment of Běimén;
the old man of Wèibīn
lacked the integrity of Xīshān.
Tāng and Wǔ achieved their accomplishments,
and Xià and Yīn could not criticize their aspirations.
Wáng Shěn, whose talent encompassed both civil and military arts,
early on held official positions;
in Wèi, he was counted among the precious advisors,
and in Jìn, he was a strategist in the inner chambers.
The plot of Tónggōng was quickly leaked,
and the disaster of Wǔwéi consequently arrived.
From this, we know that Tián Guāng's mouth
could not be silenced by Yān Dān;
Yù Ràng's form
could not be altered by Zhì Shì.
In moments of action and inaction,
some cling to thorns,
while the path of benevolence and righteousness
is sought ever more distantly.
Péng Zǔ ascended by presenting pheasants,
and Yù Běn exchanged silk;
finding a master for his impoverished family,
he eventually attained a prominent rank.
Commanding the soldiers and horses of the northern province,
and encountering the chaotic situation in the eastern capital,
he could have rallied the feudal lords
to exert his strength for the royal house.
Instead, he seized opportunities and gaps,
secretly plotted rebellion,
unleashed the Xūn lǔ barbarians,
and caused the emperor's carriage to be relocated.
Consequently, Zhāng and Fú became desolate,
and the common people perished in the mud.
He indulged the greedy in private houses,
and slew noble scholars at the border of Yān.
He hindered Yuè Shí's internal strife
and sought the external command of Shì Lóng.
His accumulated wickedness led to his ruin by fire.
Lending a hand to his enemies,
he then displayed his ferocity.
The execution of Qìng Fēng,
what good was reviling him then?
Gōng Zēng was
the grandson of Címíng;
Jǐng Qiàn was
the son of Wénruò.
They stood in lofty halls and looked down,
matching their outstanding careers and striving for long success.
Their filial piety and reverence were sufficient to serve their parents,
and their prudence and caution were sufficient to serve their lord.
They revised the old institutions of Jī Gōng
and adopted the lingering laws of Xiāo Xiàng.
However, they supported Zhū and Jūn to rival the supreme power,
and incited Bāo and Yán to cause disruption.
Although rise and fall have their timing,
and prosperity and decline are not constant,
judging by human affairs,
it was the power of the two Xùn.
As for a peck of grain inciting rumors,
and a mile becoming a song,
Xù's instigation of disaster
was even more extreme.
Féng Dǎn outwardly displayed humility
but inwardly was full of cunning and deceit.
He brought about Yōu's death and ensured Jiǎ's safety,
allied with Xù and became an enemy of Zhāng.
His heart was as covetous as Chǔ Fèi's,
and his transgressions exceeded those of Jìn Wǔ.
When Yuán Sī offered longevity,
it merely brought comfort to a benevolent heart.
Dǎn's persuasions,
however, cleverly elicited sorrow from a deluded mind.
The punishment of "throwing them to the wolves" was not heard,
and the poem of "green flies" was not composed.
A praise says: Living in the literary forest,
why did Huù betray his heart?
Péng Zǔ's ill fortune,
he brought sorrow upon himself.
Lín Huái was respectful and reverent,
filial piety shown in his countenance.
Ānyáng was illustrious,
diligent in his duties.
Toppling Qí and clinging to Lǔ,
this was a destructive pest.
Dǎn's lack of goodness,
created endless chaos.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter Ten: Jiǎ Chōng (Sūn Mì, Chōng's younger brother Hùn, kinsman Mó, Guō Zhāng)
Jiǎ Chōng, courtesy name Gōnglǘ,
was a native of Xiānglíng, Píngyáng.
His father, Kuí, was
the Inspector of Yùzhōu in Wèi and Marquis of Yánglǐ Tíng.
Kuí was late in having Chōng,
saying that later there would be the good fortune of "filling the gate,"
hence he was given this name.
Chōng was orphaned young,
and was known for his filial piety during mourning.
He inherited his father's noble rank as Marquis.
He was appointed Shàngshū Láng,
responsible for establishing laws and regulations,
and also for auditing finances and evaluating performance.
His clear articulation of rules
was all put into practice.
He was successively promoted to Huángmén Shìláng and Jí Jùn Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng.
He served as a military advisor to the Grand General
and followed Jǐng Dì in suppressing Wúqiū Jiǎn and Wén Qīn at Yuègā.
When the emperor became critically ill,
he returned to Xǔchāng,
leaving Chōng to supervise all military affairs.
For his meritorious service, his fiefdom was increased by 350 households.
Later, he served as Dàjiāngjūn Sīmǎ for Emperor Wén (Wéndì),
then transferred to Yòuchángshǐ.
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) had newly seized control of the court,
fearing dissent from regional governors.
He sent Chōng to Zhūgě Dàn,
planning to attack Wú,
and secretly observe his disposition.
After Chōng discussed current affairs,
he then said to Dàn:
"Everyone in the realm wishes for the abdication and transfer of power.
What do you think of this?"
Dàn sternly replied:
"Are you not the son of Jiǎ Yùzhōu?
Our family has received the grace of Wèi for generations.
How can we desire to hand over the altars of soil and grain to another!
If there is trouble in Luòzhōng,
I shall die for it."
Chōng remained silent.
When he returned,
he reported to Emperor Wén (Wéndì), saying:
"Dàn has served twice in Yángzhōu.
His prestige and reputation are long-standing,
and he can inspire men to fight to the death.
Observing his plans,
he will certainly rebel.
If we summon him now,
the rebellion will be swift and minor;
if we do not summon him,
the matter will be delayed and the disaster great."
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) then summoned Dàn to be Sīkōng,
and Dàn indeed rebelled.
Chōng again followed in the campaign against Dàn.
Chōng offered a strategy, saying:
"The Chu soldiers are lightly equipped and sharp.
If we dig deep moats and build high ramparts to press the enemy city,
we can conquer it without battle."
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) followed his advice.
When the city fell,
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) ascended the ramparts to reward Chōng.
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) returned to Luòyáng first,
and had Chōng oversee the remaining affairs.
He was promoted to the noble rank of Xuānyáng Xiānghóu,
and his stipend increased by a thousand households.
He was transferred to Tíngwèi.
Chōng was skilled in legal principles,
and earned a reputation for correcting miscarriages of justice.
He was transferred to Zhōnghùjūn.
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng attacked the prime minister's residence,
Chōng led his troops to resist the battle at Nánquē.
When the army was about to be defeated,
the cavalry commander Chéng Cù's younger brother, Crown Prince's Retainer Jì, said to Chōng:
"What should be done about today's situation?"
Chōng replied:
"You gentlemen have been trained for this very day;
what is there to hesitate about?"
Jì then drew his spear and violated the imperial entourage.
When Chángdào Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
Chōng was further enfeoffed as Ānyáng Xiānghóu,
his stipend increased by 1,200 households,
he commanded all armies outside the capital,
and was additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
When Zhōng Huì conspired to rebel in Shǔ,
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) granted Chōng a temporary imperial credential,
and with his original office, he oversaw all military affairs in Guānzhōng and Lǒngyòu,
taking a defensive position in Hànzhōng.
He had not yet arrived when Huì died.
At that time, military and state affairs were numerous,
and all confidential matters of the court
were discussed with him.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) greatly trusted and valued Chōng,
and he, along with Péi Xiù, Wáng Shěn, Yáng Hù, and Xún Xù, shared the responsibility of innermost confidants.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) also ordered Chōng to codify the laws.
He was granted a gold seal (Jiā Jīnzhāng),
and bestowed a top-grade mansion.
When the five ranks were first established,
he was enfeoffed as Línyí Hóu,
and was a founding minister of Jìn,
deeply favored and distinguished.
His salary and rewards were always superior to those of other officials.
Chōng possessed literary talent and skill with the pen,
and was able to discern the emperor's intentions.
Initially,
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) intended to pass the throne to Wǔyáng Hóu Yōu,
because Emperor Jǐng (Jǐngdì) had greatly assisted in the royal enterprise.
Chōng argued that Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) was benevolent
and also the eldest,
possessing the virtues of a ruler,
and should therefore be entrusted with the altars of soil and grain.
When Emperor Wén (Wéndì) became ill,
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) inquired about the succession.
Emperor Wén (Wéndì) said:
"The one who truly understands you is Jǐa Gōnglǘ."
When Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) succeeded to the kingship,
Chōng was appointed Jìn Guó Wèijiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī, Gěishìzhōng,
and re-enfeoffed as Línyǐng Hóu.
When Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) received the abdication,
Chōng, for his role in clarifying the great mandate,
was transferred to Chējì Jiāngjūn, Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū Púyè,
and further enfeoffed as Lǔjùn Gōng.
His mother, Lady Liǔ, was made Lǔguó Tàifūrén.
The new laws drafted by Chōng were promulgated throughout the realm,
and the common people found them convenient.
An imperial edict stated:
"Since the Hàn dynasty,
laws have been strict and severe.
Therefore, from the eras of Yuán and Chéng,
and during Jiàn'ān and Jiāpíng,
there was always a desire to clarify the old statutes
and revise the penal code.
However, the scale of such works was grand,
and they were unfinished for years.
The late emperor pitied the lives of the common people trapped in a dense net,
and personally issued virtuous pronouncements
to rectify names and realities.
Chējì Jiāngjūn Jiǎ Chōng,
promoted the sagely intention
and consulted good ways.
Tàifù Zhèng Chōng,
along with Sīkōng Xún Yǐ, Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Yáng Hù, Zhōnghùjūn Wáng Yè,
and Tíngwèi Dù Yǒu, Shǒu Hénán Yǐn Dù Yù, Sànqí Shìláng Péi Kǎi, Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Zhōu Xióng, Qí Xiàng Guō Qí, Qí Dūwèi Chénggōng Suí Xún Huī,
Shàngshū Láng Liǔ Guǐ, and others,
presided over the rectification of this matter.
I have always observed their dedication,
and often felt deeply pleased by it.
Now that the laws are complete,
they are first promulgated throughout the realm.
The punishments are lenient and the prohibitions simple,
sufficient to accord with the former intention.
In the past, Xiāo Hé received enfeoffment for establishing the laws,
and Shūsūn Tōng was made Fèngcháng for formulating the rituals,
receiving five hundred catties of gold,
and all his disciples became Imperial Retainers (Láng).
Indeed, establishing merit and accomplishing deeds
were highly valued in antiquity.
From the Tàifù and Chējì Jiāngjūn downwards,
all shall receive increased salaries and rewards,
the details of which shall follow ancient precedents."
Thereupon, one of Chōng's sons or younger brothers was granted the title of Guānnéi Hóu,
and five hundred rolls of silk.
He firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
Later, he succeeded Péi Xiù as Shàngshū Lìng,
with his positions as Chángshì and Chējì Jiāngjūn remaining unchanged.
Soon after, Chángshì was changed to Shìzhōng,
and he was granted seven hundred rolls of silk.
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
An edict sent a Huángmén Shìláng to express condolences.
Furthermore, due to affairs in the southeast,
Diǎnjūn Jiāngjūn Yáng Xiāo was sent to convey the imperial message,
ordering him to return to court within sixty days.
When Chōng governed,
he focused on promoting agriculture and economizing expenses,
and consolidating offices and streamlining duties.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) approved of this.
He also, recognizing the different roles of civil and military officials,
requested to relinquish his military command.
When Yáng Hù and others were dispatched to border garrisons,
Chōng again submitted a memorial wishing to establish merit on the frontier,
but Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) denied both requests.
He served at ease,
with the power to commend or criticize residing in himself.
He was quite fond of promoting scholars,
and whenever he recommended someone,
he would guide them from beginning to end.
Therefore, many scholars rallied to him.
The emperor's maternal uncle Wáng Xún once slandered Chōng,
but Chōng instead promoted Xún.
Some turned against Chōng to curry favor with the powerful,
but Chōng always pretended to treat them as before.
However, Chōng lacked integrity in public affairs
and could not rectify himself to lead his subordinates,
relying solely on flattery to gain favor.
Shìzhōng Rèn Kǎi, Zhōngshūlìng Yú Chún and others, being upright and adhering to righteousness,
all detested him.
Moreover, his daughter was made Empress to the Prince of Qí,
and they feared his influence would grow even greater later.
When the Dī and Qiāng rebelled,
the Emperor at the time was deeply worried about it.
Kǎi therefore advanced a proposal,
requesting Jǐa Chōng to garrison Guānzhōng.
Thereupon, an edict was issued saying:
“The two regions of Qín and Liáng
have suffered repeated defeats in recent years.
The Hú barbarians are rampant and violent,
and the common people are in distress.
This has allowed foreign tribes to stir up trouble,
and the harm has reached the Central Plains.
Even the invasions of Wú and Shǔ
never reached this extent.
This is truly because the appointed officials are insufficient to pacify the barbarians and Chinese internally,
and to defend against the ugly rebels externally,
rashly employing their troops without being able to exert their full strength.
Unless a trusted confidant is obtained,
who can be fully entrusted and given authority,
to greatly rectify these ills,
I fear the trouble will not cease.
Every time I consider this difficulty,
I forget sleep and food.
Shìzhōng, Shǒu Shàngshūlìng, Chēqí Jiāngjūn Jǐa Chōng
has a refined and magnanimous character,
with clear and far-reaching vision.
In military matters, he possesses the awe of a general who breaks enemy ranks,
and in civil affairs, he harbors thoughts of governing the state.
His trustworthiness binds people's hearts,
and his reputation shakes regions beyond our borders.
If he is given authority to oversee the region
and pacify Xīxià,
then I will have no worries about the west,
and both near and far will achieve peace.”
Therefore, Jǐa Chōng was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Qín Liáng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì,
with his titles of Shìzhōng and Chēqí Jiāngjūn remaining as before.
He was granted the feather canopy and drum music,
and given the privilege of the first imperial son-in-law.
The virtuous and able officials of the court who wished to offer loyal advice and make proposals
all welcomed this appointment for Jǐa Chōng,
hoping for a great and renewed transformation.
After Chōng was ordered to go out,
he considered it a loss of position
and deeply resented Rèn Kǎi,
but had no plan to act.
When he was about to depart for the garrison,
all the officials saw him off at Xīyáng Tíng.
Xún Xù was there privately.
Chōng expressed his worries,
and Xù said:
“You,
as a chief minister of the state,
to be controlled by a single man,
is this not contemptible?
However, this journey,
to decline it is truly difficult.
The only way is to marry into the Crown Prince’s family,
then you will not have to depart and will remain yourself.”
Chōng said:
“Indeed.
Whom can I entrust this to?”
He replied:
“I, Xù, ask to speak of it.”
Shortly thereafter, at an imperial banquet,
when the matter of the Crown Prince’s marriage was discussed,
Xù then spoke of Jǐa Chōng’s daughter, saying her talent and character were excellent and virtuous,
and that she was suitable to marry into the imperial heir’s palace.
Empress Yáng and Xún Yǐ also both praised her.
The Emperor accepted their words.
Coincidentally, there was heavy snow in the capital,
two feet deep on level ground,
and the army could not depart.
Soon after, the imperial heir was to be married,
and so he did not travel west.
An edict commanded Jǐa Chōng to remain in his original post.
Earlier, Yáng Hù had secretly memorialized to keep Chōng,
and when this happened,
the Emperor told Chōng.
Chōng thanked Hù, saying:
“Only now do I know you are a true gentleman.”
At that time, Sūn Xiù, a general from Wú, surrendered,
and was appointed Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn.
The Emperor, considering Chōng an old minister,
wished to rearrange the ranks
so that Chēqí would be superior to Piàojí.
Chōng firmly declined,
and was listened to.
Soon after, he was promoted to Sīkōng,
with Shìzhōng, Shàngshūlìng, and leading the troops remaining as before.
When the Emperor fell ill,
Chōng, along with Qí Wáng Yōu and Xún Xù, consulted on medical treatments.
When the illness recovered,
each was granted five hundred bolts of silk.
Initially,
when the Emperor was gravely ill,
the court's attention was on Yōu.
Hénán Yǐn Xiàhóu Hé said to Chōng:
“Your two sons-in-law,
their closeness and distance are equal;
when establishing a person, one should establish virtue.”
Chōng did not respond.
Later, when the Emperor heard of this,
he transferred Hé to Guānglùxūn,
and then stripped Chōng of his military command,
but his position and favor remained unchanged.
Soon after, he was transferred to Tàiwèi, Xíng Tàizǐ Tàibǎo, Lù Shàngshūshì.
In Xiánníng three years,
there was a solar eclipse on the third morning.
Chōng requested to resign his position,
but it was not granted.
Instead, the Qūqiū of Pèi Guó was added to his enfeoffment,
and his favor became even greater,
to the extent that all court officials looked askance at him.
Hénán Yǐn Wáng Xùn memorialized, saying:
“When Hóngxùn Tàihòu enters the ancestral temple
to share offerings with Jǐng Huángdì,
Qí Wáng Yōu is not permitted to perform the rites of a son.”
Chōng argued, stating:
“According to ritual,
feudal lords are not allowed to worship the Emperor’s ancestors,
and imperial sons are not allowed to worship their former lords.
All this refers to those who inherit the succession and carry on the sacrifices,
not to those who are forbidden to honor their own fathers and grandfathers.
Yōu himself should observe a three-year mourning period,
following the rules for a minister.”
The relevant officials then memorialized:
“If we follow Chōng’s argument,
observing a son’s mourning and following a minister’s rules,
there is no prior precedent.
It is fitting to follow Xùn’s memorial,
and Yōu’s mourning attire should follow the precedent for feudal lords.”
The Emperor followed Chōng’s argument.
During the campaign to conquer Wú,
an edict appointed Chōng as Shǐchíjié, Jiǎ Huángyuè, Dà Dūdū,
to command all six armies,
and he was granted the feather canopy, drum music, crimson banners,
ten thousand soldiers, two thousand cavalry,
and was to establish left and right Chángshǐ, Sīmǎ, Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Ten additional Cānjūn and Qí Sīmǎ were granted,
twenty Zhàngxià Sīmǎ,
and thirty Dàchē and official cavalry each.
Chōng, fearing that the great endeavor would not succeed,
memorialized, stating:
“To the west,
there is the trouble of the Kūnyí;
to the north, there are garrisons in Yōu and Bìng.
The empire is toiling and agitated,
and the harvests are poor.
Raising an army for a punitive expedition
is, I fear, not the right time.
Moreover, I am old and frail,
not capable of such a task.”
The edict stated:
“If you do not go,
I will personally go forth.”
Chōng had no choice
but to accept the staff and axe,
lead the central army,
and act as commander for all armies,
with Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Yáng Jì as his deputy,
stationing them south at Xiāngyáng.
All the garrisons of Jiānglíng in Wú surrendered,
so Chōng then moved his station to Xiàng.
When Wáng Jùn conquered Wǔchāng,
Chōng sent an envoy with a memorial stating:
“Wú cannot be completely pacified yet.
It is approaching summer,
and the areas along the Jiāng and Huái are low and damp;
epidemics are bound to arise.
It is advisable to recall all armies
and make plans for later.
Even if Zhāng Huá were to be cut in half at the waist,
it would not be enough to apologize to the world.”
Huá had previously devised the strategy for pacifying Wú,
which is why Chōng spoke of him.
Zhōngshūjiān Xún Xù memorialized
that it should be as Chōng’s memorial suggested.
The Emperor did not comply.
Dù Yù, hearing of Chōng’s memorial,
rushed a memorial to argue firmly against it,
saying that peace would be achieved at any moment.
The envoy reached Huànyuán
when Sūn Hào had already surrendered.
Wú was pacified,
and the army was disbanded.
The Emperor sent Shìzhōng Chéng Xián to offer congratulations and rewards,
granting Chōng eight thousand bolts of silk,
and increasing his enfeoffment by eight thousand households.
His paternal grandson Chàng was enfeoffed as Xīnchéng Tínghóu,
and Gài as Ānyáng Tínghóu.
His younger brother Hùn, Yánglǐ Tínghóu, and paternal grandson Zhòng, Guānnèi Hóu, had their household and enfeoffment increased.
Chōng originally had no intention of invading the South,
but his earnest remonstrances were not heeded.
When the army marched out and Wú was pacified,
he was greatly ashamed and frightened,
and discussed asking for punishment.
The Emperor heard that Chōng was about to arrive at the palace,
and preemptively went to the East Hall to await him.
His imperial insignia of authority, the jiéyuè, and his subordinate officials were dismissed,
but he was still granted drum-and-horn music and standards.
Chōng and the assembled officials performed the ritual of reporting success,
and requested the officials concerned to arrange the details.
The Emperor humbly declined to permit it.
When his illness became severe,
he surrendered his seals and ribbons, retiring from office.
The Emperor sent a侍臣 shìchén to convey his imperial message and inquire about his illness,
while the Tàiyī of the Diànzhōng dispatched medicines and decoctions.
He was granted a bed curtain, money, and silks,
and the Crown Prince and members of the imperial clan personally visited to inquire about his well-being.
In the fourth month of Tàikāng 3 (282 CE), he passed away,
at the age of sixty-six.
The Emperor wept for him,
and sent an envoy holding the jié, the Tàicháng, to present a posthumous edict, posthumously promoting him to Tàizǎi,
adding a gǔnmiǎn robe and crown, green lǜsòu ribbons, and the imperial sword.
He was granted secret items from Dōngyuán, one set of court attire, and one suit of clothes.
The Dàhónglú was to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and he was granted a jiéyuè, feathered canopies for the front and rear divisions, drum-and-horn music, and crimson banners.
There were to be dàlù, luánlù, wēnlüánchē, and dàchē for the Sīmǎ of the tent,
along with chuífǔ wényī wǔbēn and qīngchē jièshì.
The funeral rites were to follow the precedents of Huò Guāng and Ānpíng Xiànwáng,
and one qǐng of burial land was granted.
He, along with Shí Bāo and others, was to have his accomplishments as a prince honored in the ancestral temple,
and his posthumous title was Wǔ.
Chōng's son, Lí Mín, was posthumously granted the title of Lǔ Shānggōng.
Chōng's wife, Guǎngchéng Jūn Guō Huái,
was of a jealous nature.
Initially,
Lí Mín was three years old,
and his wet nurse was holding him by the door.
Lí Mín saw Chōng enter,
and smiled with joy.
Chōng approached and caressed him.
Huái saw this,
and thinking Chōng was having a private affair with the wet nurse,
immediately whipped her to death.
Lí Mín longed for her,
fell ill, and died.
Later, another son was born,
and after a year,
he was again being held by a wet nurse.
Chōng stroked his head with his hand.
Guō suspected the wet nurse,
and again killed her,
whereupon the child also longed for her and died.
Chōng thus had no surviving heir.
When he passed away,
Huái immediately made her grandson, Hán Mì, Lí Mín's son,
to carry on Chōng's lineage.
Lángzhōng Lìng Hán Xián and Zhōngwèi Cáo Zhěn remonstrated with Huái, saying:
"According to the Rites,
if the main branch has no heir,
a collateral son from a junior branch succeeds them.
There is no provision for someone of a different surname to become an heir.
Do not let the late Duke harbor resentment in the afterlife,
nor let good historians record such a transgression.
Would this not be heartbreaking?"
Huái did not heed them.
Xián and others submitted a memorial requesting a change in the successor,
but the matter was shelved and not acted upon.
