Huái then submitted a memorial stating that this was Chōng's dying wish.
The Emperor then issued an edict saying:
"Tàizǎi and Lǔgōng Chōng,
with his lofty virtue and established achievements,
diligently assisted in the founding of our dynasty.
His passing and demise
always cause me sorrow.
Moreover, his sons died early,
and a successor has not yet been established.
In ancient times, when a vassal state had no heir,
a collateral descendant of the first enfeoffed lord was taken
to continue its lineage.
In recent times, however, such states were abolished.
As for Gōng Dàn of Zhōu,
and Xiāo Hé of Hàn,
some preemptively designated their eldest sons,
while others enfeoffed their eldest consorts.
This was to honor and distinguish their merits,
differing from common practice.
The Tàizǎi had originally taken his grandson, Hán Mì, as successor to his son Lí Mín.
I have deliberated on this matter and decided that
a grandson by marriage is very close kin.
Extending grace and considering the circumstances,
this aligns with human sentiment.
Therefore, Hán Mì shall be the Lǔgōng's grandson,
to succeed to his state.
Unless one's merits are like the Tàizǎi's,
and one's first enfeoffed lineage has no heir like the Tàizǎi's,
and the chosen successor is not one's own offspring, unlike the Tàizǎi,
none of these may be used as precedents."
When the officials of rites were later instructed to deliberate on Chōng's posthumous title,
Bóshì Qín Xiù proposed the posthumous title of Huāng,
but the Emperor did not accept it.
Bóshì Duàn Chàng, seeking to please the Emperor,
suggested the posthumous title of Wǔ,
which the Emperor then adopted.
From Chōng's death to his burial,
funeral gifts amounted to twenty million.
When Huìdì ascended the throne,
Empress Jiǎ monopolized power.
She added the music of six ranks of dancers to Chōng's ancestral temple,
and Chōng's mother Guō was enfeoffed as Yíchéng Jūn.
When Guō Shì died,
she was posthumously titled Xuān,
and given special extraordinary rites.
People at the time criticized this,
but no one dared to speak out.
Originally,
Chōng's former wife, Lǐ Shì, was graceful and talented,
and bore him two daughters, Bāo and Yù.
Bāo was also named Quán, and Yù was also named Jùn.
When her father Fēng was executed,
Lǐ Shì was implicated and exiled.
Later, Chōng married the daughter of Chéngyáng Tàishǒu Guō Pèi,
who was the aforementioned Guǎngchéng Jūn.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Lǐ was able to return due to a general amnesty.
The Emperor specifically decreed that Chōng should have both a Zuo Fūrén and a You Fūrén.
Chōng's mother also ordered Chōng to welcome Lǐ Shì back.
Guō Huái was enraged,
rolled up her sleeves, and confronted Chōng, saying:
"It was I who revised the laws and statutes,
and contributed to the founding of the dynasty;
I have my share in that.
How can Lǐ be my equal!"
Chōng then replied to the edict,
citing humility and modesty as his excuse,
saying he dared not accept the grand rites for two wives,
but in reality, he feared Huái.
Meanwhile, Quán, who was the consort of Qíwáng Yōu,
wished for Chōng to dismiss Guō and bring her mother back.
At that time, the mother of Liú Hán of Pèiguó,
and the former wife of the Emperor's maternal uncle, Yúlín Jiān Wáng Qián,
were both granddaughters of Wúqiū Jiǎn.
Since there were many such cases,
the matter was referred to the officials of rites,
but they could not reach a decision.
Although they did not dismiss their later wives,
many lived separately and had private communications.
Chōng, considering himself a prime minister and a standard for the realm,
then built a house for Lǐ in Yǒngnián Lǐ but did not visit her.
Quán and Jùn repeatedly wept and pleaded with Chōng,
but Chōng never went.
It happened that Chōng was to be stationed in Guānyòu.
The high officials and ministers set up tents for a farewell banquet.
Quán and Jùn feared that Chōng would leave permanently,
so they pushed aside the curtains and emerged from among the guests,
kowtowing until their heads bled,
and presented their case to Chōng and the assembled officials, stating that their mother should be brought back.
The crowd, seeing Quán as a royal consort,
all rose in surprise and dispersed.
Chōng was greatly ashamed and startled,
and sent a Huángmén to escort the court ladies to take them away.
Afterwards, Guō Huái's daughter became the Crown Prince's consort,
and the Emperor then issued an edict decreeing that all cases like Lǐ's were not to be allowed to return.
Later, Quán died from grief and resentment.
Initially,
Huái wanted to visit Lǐ Shì.
Chōng said:
"She has talent and spirit;
it's better if you don't go than if you do."
When her daughter became the consort,
Huái then went with great pomp and ceremony.
As soon as she entered the door,
Lǐ Shì came out to greet her,
and Huái's knees unexpectedly buckled,
causing her to bow twice.
From then on, whenever Chōng went out,
Huái would send someone to follow him,
fearing he might go to Lǐ's place.
Originally,
Chōng's mother Liǔ, seeing the importance of integrity and righteousness in ancient and modern times,
never knew about Chōng's involvement with Chéng Jì's affair.
Believing Jì to be disloyal,
she often cursed him.
Those attending her, hearing this,
all secretly laughed.
When she was about to die,
Chōng asked if she had anything to say.
Liǔ replied:
"I told you to welcome the new daughter-in-law Lǐ, but you wouldn't,
so why ask about anything else!"
She then said no more.
After Chōng passed away,
Lǐ Shì's two daughters wanted their mother to be buried with him,
but Empress Jiǎ did not permit it.
After the Empress was deposed,
Lǐ Shì was finally allowed to be buried with him.
Lǐ Shì wrote "Female Admonitions" which circulated in the world.
Mì's courtesy name was Chángshēn.
His mother was Jiǎ Wǔ,
Jiǎ Chōng's youngest daughter.
His father was Hán Shòu,
courtesy name Dézhēn,
a native of Dǔyáng in Nányáng,
and a great-grandson of Wèi Sītú Jì.
He was handsome in appearance
and graceful in manner.
Jiǎ Chōng appointed him as Sīkōng Yuàn.
Whenever Chōng hosted guests and subordinates,
his daughters would peek at them from behind a green screen.
Seeing Shòu, she was pleased with him.
She asked her attendants if they knew this person.
One maidservant told her Shòu's surname and given name,
saying he was a former master of hers.
The daughter was greatly moved
and thought of him day and night.
Later, the maidservant went to Shòu's house
and fully explained the daughter's feelings,
also saying that the daughter was radiant, beautiful, and exceptionally elegant,
and of unparalleled grace.
Shòu was moved upon hearing this
and immediately had her convey his regards.
The maidservant reported this to the daughter,
who then secretly prepared her appearance,
exchanged many gifts,
and invited Shòu to come that evening.
Shòu was exceptionally agile;
he climbed over the wall and arrived.
No one in the household knew,
only Chōng noticed that his daughter was unusually cheerful that day.
At that time, the Western Regions had offered a rare fragrance as tribute,
which, once applied to a person, would not fade for a month.
The Emperor valued it highly,
giving it only to Chōng and Dàsīmǎ Chén Qiān.
His daughter secretly stole some to give to Shòu.
When Chōng's subordinates socialized with Shòu,
they smelled its fragrance
and mentioned it to Chōng.
From then on, Chōng suspected his daughter and Shòu were having an affair,
but his household was very strict,
and he didn't know how Shòu could have entered.
So, one night he pretended to be alarmed,
claiming there were thieves,
and used this to send people to patrol the walls to observe what happened.
His attendants reported:
"There is nothing unusual,
except the northeast corner looks like a fox had passed there."
Chōng then questioned his daughter's attendants,
who fully confessed the situation.
Chōng kept it a secret
and then married his daughter to Shòu.
Shòu's official career reached Sànqí Chángshì and Hénán Yǐn.
He died at the beginning of Yuánkāng,
and was posthumously granted Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
Mì was fond of learning and
had talent and ideas.
Since he became Chōng's heir
and succeeded the meritorious ministers,
and also because Empress Jiǎ was autocratic,
Mì's power exceeded that of the sovereign,
even to the point of arresting and imprisoning a Huángmén Shìláng.
His display of authority and power was like this.
Relying on his arrogance and imperial favor,
he was excessively luxurious,
his mansions were presumptuously grand,
his utensils and clothes were precious and beautiful,
and his singing boys and dancing girls
were the finest of the era.
When he opened his gates to receive guests,
people from all over the empire flocked to him.
Noble families, powerful relatives, and ambitious adventurers
all paid him full respect.
Some wrote essays praising Mì,
comparing him to Jiǎ Yì.
Bóhǎi Shí Chóng and Ōuyáng Jiàn, Xíngyáng Pān Yuè, Wúguó Lù Jī and Lù Yún, Lánlíng Miào Zhēng,
Jīngzhào Dù Bīn and Zhì Yú, Lángyá Zhūgě Quán,
Hóngnóng Wáng Cuì, Xiāngchéng Dù Yù, Nányáng Zōu Jié, Qíguó Zuǒ Sī, Qīnghé Cuī Jī, Pèiguó Liú Guī, Rǔnán Hé Yù and Zhōu Huī, Ānpíng Qiān Xiù,
Yǐngchuān Chén Zhěn, Tàiyuán Guō Zhāng, Gāoyáng Xǔ Měng, Péngchéng Liú Nà, Zhōngshān Liú Yú and Liú Kūn all gathered around Mì,
and were known as the Twenty-Four Friends;
the others were not included.
He successively held the positions of Sànqí Chángshì and Hòujūn Jiāngjūn.
When Guǎngchéng Jūn died,
he resigned.
Before the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Mìshū Jiān,
in charge of the national history.
Before this,
the court had debated setting a chronological limit for the Jìn Shū.
Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù believed it should begin from the first year of Wèi Zhèngshǐ,
while Zuòzuò Láng Wáng Zàn wanted to include all court officials from Jiāpíng onwards into the Jìn Shǐ.
At that time, no decision had been firmly made.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
the matter was brought up for discussion again.
Mì submitted a memorial,
requesting that the starting point be from Tàishǐ.
Consequently, the matter was sent down to the Three Ducal Offices.
Sītú Wáng Róng, Sīkōng Zhāng Huá, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Yǎn, Shìzhōng Yuè Guǎng, Huángmén Shìláng Jī Shào, and Guózǐ Bóshì Xiè Héng all agreed with Mì's proposal.
Qídūwèi Jìběi Hóu Xún Jùn, Shìzhōng Xún Fān, and Huángmén Shìláng Huá Hùn believed it should begin from Zhèngshǐ.
Bóshì Xún Xī and Diāo Xié thought it should start from Jiāpíng.
Mì repeatedly insisted on the proposal of Róng and Huá,
and the matter was then implemented.
Soon after, he was transferred to Shìzhōng,
retaining his post as Mìshū Jiān.
At that time, Mì accompanied the Emperor to Xuānwǔ Guān for a hunt.
He implicitly urged the Shàngshū to summon Mì during the gathering to receive his appointment,
admonishing his attendants not to let anyone know,
whereupon the multitude suspected he had ulterior motives.
As Mì was a close and noble relative,
he frequently entered the two palaces
and socialized with Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ,
without showing proper deference.
He often argued with the Crown Prince over an弈 game.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng was present
and sternly said:
"The Imperial Crown Prince
is the heir to the nation,
how can Jiǎ Mì be so disrespectful!"
Mì was frightened
and reported it to the Empress,
who then sent Yǐng out as Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
to guard Yè.
When he became Chángshì
and attended to lectures in the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince showed some displeasure,
which Mì worried about.
Moreover, there were frequent omens of misfortune at his house:
a whirlwind blew his court robe several hundred *zhàng* high,
dropping it on the Zhōngchéng Tái;
a snake emerged from his quilt;
and a sudden nighttime thunderstorm shook his room,
causing a pillar to sink into the ground,
crushing and destroying his bed curtains.
Mì became even more afraid.
When he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
taking sole charge of the inner palace,
he conspired with the Empress
to falsely accuse the Crown Prince.
When Zhào Wáng Lún later deposed the Empress,
he summoned Mì to the front of the palace by imperial edict,
intending to execute him.
Mì ran into the area beneath the western bell,
crying out:
"Mother Empress, save me!"
He was then beheaded on the spot.
Hán Shòu's younger brother Wèi had a good reputation and dignity.
Later, Shòu's elder brother Gǒng Lìngbǎo, younger brother Sànqí Shìláng Yù, Wú Wáng Yǒu Jiàn, and Mì's mother Jiǎ Wǔ were all executed.
Initially,
when Chōng campaigned against Wú,
he once camped at Xiàngchéng.
In the camp, Chōng's whereabouts were suddenly unknown.
Chōng's attendant Dūdū Zhōu Qín was napping during the day
and dreamed that over a hundred people were arresting Chōng,
leading him along a small path.
Qín awoke with a start,
heard that Chōng was missing,
and went out to search.
Suddenly, he saw the path he had dreamed of,
and so followed it.
Indeed, he saw Chōng walking to a governmental residence,
where guards were numerous.
The magistrate sat facing south,
his voice and expression very stern.
He said to Chōng:
"You will disrupt my family affairs;
it will surely be you and Xún Xù.
You have already misguided my son
and also corrupted my grandson.
Recently, I sent Rèn Kǎi to dismiss you, but you did not leave.
Then I sent Yú Chún to scold you, but you did not change.
Now the Wú bandits are about to be pacified,
yet you are petitioning to execute Zhāng Huá.
Your foolishness and obstinacy
are all of this kind.
If you do not repent and be careful,
you will be punished morning or evening."
Chōng then kowtowed until his head bled.
The magistrate said:
"The reason you have prolonged your days and achieved such fame and position
is due to Wèi Fǔ's merits.
Eventually, your heir will die between the bell and the stand,
the Crown Prince will perish amidst golden wine,
and your young son will be afflicted beneath withered wood.
Xún Xù should also share this fate,
but his ancestors' virtue was slightly deeper,
so he will be after you;
after several generations,
the national succession will also be replaced."
Having spoken,
he ordered Chōng to leave.
Chōng suddenly returned to his camp,
his face pale and haggard,
his mind confused and lost.
It took a day for him to recover.
As it turned out,
Mì died beneath the bell,
Empress Jiǎ died from drinking golden wine,
and Jiǎ Wǔ was ultimately beaten with a large staff,
all concluding as predicted.
When Zhào Wáng Lún's rebellion failed,
the imperial court sought to commemorate Chōng's achievements,
and debated establishing an heir.
They intended to make Chōng's paternal grand-nephew, Sànqí Shìláng Zhòng, his successor.
Zhòng feigned madness to escape this duty.
Then Chōng's son, Tū, was made his heir,
enfeoffed as Lǔ Gōng,
but he also died of illness.
During the Yǒngxīng era,
Chōng's paternal great-grand-nephew, Zhàn, was established as Lǔ Gōng,
to continue Chōng's lineage.
He died in the chaos,
and the state was abolished.
During the Tàishǐ era,
people composed a rhyme about Chōng and others, saying:
"Jiǎ, Péi, Wáng,
disrupt the fundamental principles.
Wáng, Péi, Jiǎ,
save the empire."
This refers to the fall of Wèi and the establishment of Jìn.
Chōng's younger brother, Hùn, courtesy name Gōngqí,
was sincere and steadfast,
without extraordinary talent.
During the Tàikāng era,
he served as Zōngzhèng Qīng.
He successively held the posts of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Líng Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
was granted Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed as Yǒngpíng Hóu.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī.
Chōng's paternal nephews, Yí and Zūn, both possessed discerning judgment,
and both served as Huángmén Láng.
Zūn's younger brother, Mó, was the most renowned.
Mó, courtesy name Sīfàn,
had high aspirations from a young age.
He read widely in historical records,
and was profound with strategic intelligence,
firm and unyielding.
He was deeply trusted and loved by Chōng,
who consulted him on every matter.
When Chōng was old and critically ill,
he worried about his posthumous title and biography.
Mó said:
"Right and wrong will eventually become clear;
they cannot be concealed."
He began his career as Shàolíng Lìng,
then successively served as Èrgōng Shàngshū Lìbù Láng.
He was dismissed for official reasons,
then reinstated as Chēqí Sīmǎ.
He participated in the execution of Yáng Jùn,
and was enfeoffed as Píngyáng Xiānghóu,
with a thousand households.
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi falsely issued an edict to harm Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and Tàibǎo Wèi Guàn,
an edict ordered Mó to lead two hundred imperial cavalry to rescue them.
At this time, Empress Jiǎ had already become involved in court affairs,
wishing to entrust power to her close relatives.
She appointed Mó as Sànqí Chángshì,
and two days later promoted him to Shìzhōng.
Mó then wholeheartedly offered counsel and assistance,
promoting Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi to jointly assist in governing.
Within a few years,
the court and the countryside were peaceful,
which was due to Mó's efforts.
He was then granted Guānglù Dàfū.
However, Mó secretly wielded power,
while outwardly feigning detachment.
Whenever he had to submit a memorial to Empress Jiǎ,
he would always pretend to be in a hurry to leave,
or feign illness to avoid her.
As for those with whom he had long-standing grudges,
he often implicated and framed many,
and the court greatly feared him.
Moreover, he was greedy and amassed wealth,
comparable to princes and dukes.
But Empress Jiǎ was by nature very strong and violent.
Mó repeatedly spoke frankly about the blessings and misfortunes,
but the empress would not heed him,
and instead thought Mó was slandering her.
Thus, her trust in him gradually waned,
and those who slandered and created discord advanced.
Mó, unable to achieve his ambitions,
became ill from worry and indignation.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and posthumously named Chéng.
His son Yóu, courtesy name Yànjiāng, succeeded him,
and successively held the posts of Tàizǐ Shìjiǎng and Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Guō Zhāng, courtesy name Shúwǔ,
was a native of Tàiyuán,
and Empress Jiǎ's maternal grand-uncle.
He had long been close to Jiǎ Chōng,
and Chōng's wife treated Zhāng as if he were her own brother.
He successively held the posts of Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū, and Wèijiāngjūn,
and was enfeoffed as Guānjūn Xiànhóu.
When Empress Jiǎ monopolized court affairs,
Zhāng participated in the wielding of power,
and public sentiment gravitated towards him,
with guests filling his gate.
People of the time called them
"Jiǎ Guō,"
referring to Mì and Zhāng.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously named Liè.
Yáng Jùn (younger brothers Yáo, Jì)
Yáng Jùn, courtesy name Wéncháng,
was a native of Hóngnóng Huáyīn.
In his youth, he served as Gāolù Lìng and Sīmǎ in the Xiāoqí and Zhènjūn offices through royal appointment.
Later, as the empress's father, he occupied a high position,
progressing from Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn to Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
and was enfeoffed as Línjìn Hóu.
Discerning people debated this, saying:
"Establishing feudal lords
is for shielding the royal house.
Empresses and consorts
are for providing offerings
and promoting internal virtue.
For the empress's father to be initially enfeoffed as a marquis of Línjìn
portends chaos."
Shàngshū Chǔ Sì and Guō Yì both memorialized that Jùn was of shallow character,
and could not be entrusted with the heavy responsibility of the state.
Emperor Wǔ did not heed them.
After the Tàikāng era,
there was peace throughout the empire,
and the emperor no longer focused on state affairs,
but only indulged in wine and women.
He began to favor the empress's faction,
and solicitations were openly conducted.
Jùn, Yáo, and Jì's power was overwhelming,
and people of the time referred to them as
"the Three Yángs."
When the emperor became critically ill,
he had not yet issued a deathbed instruction.
His meritorious officials who helped establish the dynasty
had all passed away.
The court officials were terrified and confused,
at a loss as to what to do.
Jùn dismissed all the high officials,
personally attended the emperor,
and frequently replaced high-ranking officials,
establishing his confidants.
When the emperor temporarily improved,
he saw that the people appointed were inappropriate,
and sternly said to Jùn:
"How can you be like this!"
He then ordered the Zhōngshū
to have Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and Jùn jointly assist the royal house.
Jùn, fearing loss of power and favor,
borrowed the edict from the Zhōngshū to view it,
and then concealed it.
Zhōngshū Jiān Huá Yì was afraid
and personally went to demand it,
but Jùn refused to give it.
Within two days,
the emperor's illness worsened critically.
The empress then memorialized the emperor to let Jùn assist in governing.
The emperor nodded in agreement.
She then summoned Zhōngshū Jiān Huá Yì and Lìng Hé Shào,
orally conveying the emperor's will and instructing them to draft a deathbed edict,
which stated:
"In ancient times, Yī and Wàng served as assistants,
their achievements immortalized;
Zhōu and Huò were appointed,
their names crowned past generations.
Shìzhōng, Chēqí Jiāngjūn, acting Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
concurrently Líng Qiánjiāngjūn Yáng Jùn,
has cultivated virtue and practiced excellence,
with clear and far-reaching discernment,
assisting the two palaces,
his loyalty and solemnity are abundantly manifest.
He is fit to assume the highest position,
emulating the conduct of Āhéng.
Let Jùn be Tàiwèi, Tàizǐ Tàifù, Jiǎjié, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnfù,
with Shìzhōng, Lù Shàngshū, Líng Qiánjiāngjūn as before.
Set up six Cānjūn, three thousand foot soldiers, and one thousand cavalry,
to relocate to the former residence of Qiánwèijiāngjūn Yáo.
If he stays overnight in the palace, he should have a guard.
Select twenty Sīmǎ each from the left and right three divisions of the imperial guards, and ten Dànp Zhōng Dūwèi Sīmǎ to be assigned to Jùn,
allowing him to carry weapons and enter and exit."
When the edict was completed,
the empress presented it to the emperor in front of Yì and Shào.
The emperor personally saw it and said nothing.
Two days later, he passed away.
Jùn thus took on the heavy responsibility entrusted to him,
residing in the Tàijí Diàn.
When the coffin was about to be interred,
the six palaces came out to bid farewell,
but Jùn did not descend from the hall,
protecting himself with a hundred Wǔbēn.
Acts of disrespect began from this point.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
Yáng Jùn was promoted to Grand Tutor (tàifù), Grand Commander (dàdūdū), and granted the authority of the yellow battle-axe (jiǎhuángyuè).
He oversaw court affairs,
and all officials were under his command.
Fearing that his close associates might conspire against him,
he appointed his nephews, Duàn Guǎng and Zhāng Shào, to positions as personal attendants.
Whenever imperial decrees were issued,
the Emperor would review them,
present them to the Empress Dowager (tàihòu),
and only then would they be promulgated.
Yáng Jùn knew that Empress Jiǎ's temperament was difficult to control
and greatly feared her.
He also heavily planted his relatives and party members,
all of whom commanded the imperial guards.
Consequently, the imperial clan harbored resentment,
and the whole realm was indignant.
Yáng Jùn's brothers, Yáng Yáo and Yáng Jì, both possessed outstanding talent
and frequently advised him to desist,
but Yáng Jùn would not heed them,
and they were consequently confined to their homes.
Yáng Jùn was ignorant of ancient principles
and constantly violated old codes.
Emperor Wǔ died less than a year before the reign era was changed,
which commentators all considered to be a violation of the Spring and Autumn Annals' principle of recording accession after a year.
The court regretted this past mistake
and ordered the historians to suppress it,
so the reign year was changed again in the first month of the following year.
Yáng Jùn knew he had always lacked a good reputation
and feared he could not unite those near and far,
so, following the precedent of Emperor Míng of Wèi's accession,
he extensively distributed titles and rewards,
hoping to win over the populace.
His administration was severe and petty;
he was obstinate, rejected counsel, and acted on his own initiative,
failing to win the hearts of the people.
Sūn Chǔ, the Administrator of Féngyì, who had long been close to Yáng Jùn,
advised him, saying:
"As an imperial maternal relative,
you hold the immense power of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
wielding great authority
and assisting a weak ruler.
You should look up to the utmost impartiality, sincerity, humility, and complaisance of the ancients.
In Zhōu, there were Zhōu Gōng and Shào Gōng as chief ministers;
in Hàn, there were Zhūxū Hóu and Dōngmóu Hóu.
Never has a common surname solely controlled the court
and been able to secure their fortune to the end.
Now, the imperial clan is powerful and respected,
and the feudal princes are vigorous,
yet you do not share the myriad affairs of state with them.
You harbor suspicion internally
and establish private intimates externally.
Disaster will strike any day."
Yáng Jùn could not follow his advice.
Kuǎi Qīn, the Prefect of the Bureau of Instruction (Hóngxùn shàofǔ), Yáng Jùn's cousin,
had been close to him since childhood,
was straightforward and unyielding,
and repeatedly offended Yáng Jùn with his upright words,
making Yáng Yáo and Yáng Jì shiver with fear for him.
Kuǎi Qīn said:
"Even if Yáng Wéncháng (Yáng Jùn) is dim-witted,
he still knows that innocent people
should not be arbitrarily killed,
and he will surely distance me.
If I am cast aside,
I can avoid dying with him.
Otherwise,
if the clan is overthrown and exterminated,
how long can it last?"
Méng Guān and Lǐ Zhào, Palace Gentlemen (diànzhōng zhōngláng), who had never been treated with deference by Yáng Jùn,
secretly fabricated a plot that Yáng Jùn intended to seize the throne.
Empress Jiǎ wished to participate in governing affairs,
but she was constrained by Yáng Jùn and could not achieve her desires,
nor would she behave as a proper wife towards the Empress Dowager.
Dǒng Méng, a eunuch (huángmén), had been the eunuch supervisor (sìrénjiān) from the time the Emperor was Crown Prince
and served Empress Jiǎ in the Eastern Palace.
The Empress secretly exchanged messages with Dǒng Méng,
plotting to depose the Empress Dowager.
Dǒng Méng then secretly colluded with Lǐ Zhào and Méng Guān.
Empress Jiǎ also ordered Lǐ Zhào to inform the Grand Commander (dàsīmǎ), Sīmǎ Liàng, Prince of Rǔnán,
to join forces to attack Yáng Jùn.
Sīmǎ Liàng said:
"Yáng Jùn's ferocity and tyranny mean his demise is imminent;
there is no need to worry."
Lǐ Zhào then reported to Sīmǎ Wěi, Prince of Chǔ.
Sīmǎ Wěi agreed with this
and thereupon sought permission to enter the capital.
Yáng Jùn had always feared Sīmǎ Wěi
and had previously intended to summon him
to prevent him from causing trouble,
so he consented.
When Sīmǎ Wěi arrived,
Méng Guān and Lǐ Zhào then reported to the Emperor,
who secretly issued an edict that night,
putting the inner and outer commands on high alert,
and dispatched envoys to present the edict to depose Yáng Jùn,
ordering him to return to his residence as a marquis.
Sīmǎ Yáo, Duke of Dōng'ān, led four hundred men from the palace guard to follow and attack Yáng Jùn.
Duàn Guǎng knelt and said to the Emperor:
"Yáng Jùn received favor from the late Emperor
and wholeheartedly assisted in governing.
Moreover, as a solitary public figure without a son,
how could he possibly rebel?
I beg Your Majesty to investigate this thoroughly."
The Emperor did not respond.
At that time, Yáng Jùn resided in the former mansion of Cáo Shuǎng,
south of the imperial armory.
Hearing of the disturbance within the palace,
he summoned officials to discuss the matter.
Zhū Zhèn, the Grand Tutor's Principal Clerk, advised Yáng Jùn, saying:
"Now that there is a disturbance within the palace,
its intention is clear.
It must be the eunuchs plotting for Empress Jiǎ,
which is not beneficial to you, my lord.
You should burn the Yúnlóng Gate to display your power,
demand the heads of those who initiated this,
open the Wànchūn Gate,
and bring in the troops from the Eastern Palace and outer camps.
You yourself should protect the Crown Prince
and enter the palace to apprehend the treacherous individuals.
Those within the palace, struck with fear,
will surely behead and send them to you,
thus you can escape this calamity."
Yáng Jùn was inherently timid
and indecisive,
so he said:
"Emperor Míng of Wèi accomplished this great work;
how can we burn it down?"
Fù Zhī, the Grandee Secretary (shìzhōng), came to Yáng Jùn at night
and requested to enter the Yúnlóng Gate with Wǔ Mào to observe the situation.
Fù Zhī then said to the assembled officials,
"The palace should not be empty,"
then rose and bowed,
whereupon they all fled.
Soon after, palace troops emerged
and burned Yáng Jùn's mansion.
They also ordered archers on the pavilion to shoot at Yáng Jùn's mansion from above,
preventing Yáng Jùn's troops from sallying forth.
Yáng Jùn fled to his horses
and was killed with a spear.
Méng Guān and others received Empress Jiǎ's secret decree
to execute Yáng Jùn's close relatives,
all of whom had their three kindreds exterminated,
with thousands dying.
Lǐ Zhào was also ordered to burn Yáng Jùn's private letters,
as Empress Jiǎ did not want Emperor Wǔ's deathbed decree
to become known throughout the four seas.
After Yáng Jùn was executed,
no one dared to collect his body;
only Yán Zuǎn of Bāxī, the Grand Tutor's steward (shèréng), gave him a funeral.
Initially,
Yáng Jùn had summoned the recluse Sūn Dēng
and sent him a cloth quilt.
Sūn Dēng cut the quilt at his gate
and loudly cried:
"Chop, chop, stab, stab!"
Within ten days, he feigned illness and death.
Later,
his words indeed proved true.
During the Yǒngxī era,
a man in Wēnxiàn, appearing deranged,
wrote a message saying:
"Bright, bright Wéncháng,
a great halberd for a wall.
Though poison proceeds,
the halberd will wound itself."
Later, when Yáng Jùn resided in the inner mansion,
he indeed used halberds as guards.
In the early Yǒngníng era,
an imperial edict stated:
"The maternal uncle's family lost its way,
and its clan perished.
The sorrow of Wèiyáng (for relatives),
and the feelings of siblings moved me to sadness.
Therefore, let Yáng Chāo, Marquis of Shùtíng, be appointed as Fèngcháoqǐng (an honorary official) and Qí Dūwèi (Commander of Cavalry),
to comfort the sorrow of the bitter artemisia."
Yáng Yáo 字 Wénjū,
successively held the posts of Shàngshūlìng and Wèi Jiāngjūn.
He was known for his reputation
and was favored by Emperor Wǔ.
At the time, his prestige surpassed that of Yáng Jùn.
Because his brother was powerful and prominent,
he knew that holding such power and favor was untenable.
He personally requested to resign from his position,
repeatedly and earnestly,
but was ultimately not granted permission.
Initially,
when the empress was chosen,
Yáo submitted a memorial stating:
"Observing ancient and modern times,
never has a single clan with two empresses
remained intact;
instead, they have suffered the disaster of their entire clan being wiped out.
I beg that this memorial be stored in the ancestral temple,
so that if my words prove true,
we may be spared from disaster."
This was granted.
The Right Army Supervisor Zhào Xiū submitted a memorial, stating:
"Wáng Mǎng had five dukes,
with brothers succeeding each other.
Now the Yáng clan has three dukes,
all holding high positions,
and celestial phenomena have repeatedly appeared.
I secretly worry about this for Your Majesty."
From this, Yáo became even more fearful,
and firmly requested to resign.
This was granted,
and he was given one million coins and five thousand rolls of silk.
Yáo was initially praised for his humility and yielding,
but later he formed cliques
and framed Qí Wáng Yōu for dismissal.
Zhōnghùjūn Yáng Xiù and Běijūn Zhōnghòu Chéng Càn conspired to assassinate Yáo with a knife when they met him.
Yáo, knowing this, feigned illness and did not go out.
He subtly prompted the officials to impeach Xiù,
who was then transferred to Tàipú.
From then on, no one in the court dared to oppose him,
and his initial reputation was completely lost.
When Yáo was about to be executed, he cried out that he was wronged,
saying:
"The matter is in the stone casket;
you can ask Zhāng Huá."
At the time, everyone said that his case should be reviewed,
in accordance with the precedent of Zhōng Yù.
[一０] But the Jiǎ clan and their faction treated the Yángs as enemies,
and hurried the executioner to behead him.
No one at the time failed to sigh in lamentation.
Yáng Jì 字 Wéntōng,
successively held the posts of Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Jì was talented and skilled.
Once, he accompanied Emperor Wǔ on a hunting expedition below Běimáng.
He and Shìzhōng Wáng Jì both wore simple cloth trousers and jackets,
rode horses, and held horn bows in front of the imperial carriage.
A fierce beast suddenly appeared,
and the Emperor ordered Wáng Jì to shoot it.
It fell at the sound of the bowstring.
After a moment, another appeared,
and Jì received the order and shot it dead as well.
The six armies cheered loudly.
The Emperor valued military officials
and often bestowed high and respected military positions upon noble relatives.
Jì was considered competent due to his martial skills.
He and his elder brother Yáo deeply worried about their excessive prominence.
So, he and his nephews Lǐ Bīn and others earnestly remonstrated.
Jùn dismissed Wáng Yòu to be Hédōng Tàishǒu,
and established the imperial heir.
These were all Jì's plans.
Initially,
Jùn was jealous of Dàsīmǎ Rǔnán Wáng Liàng,
and urged him to depart for his fief.
Jì and Bīn repeatedly advised against it,
but Jùn consequently became estranged from Jì.
Jì said to Fù Xián:
"If my elder brother recalls the Dàsīmǎ,
and steps aside for him,
our family might be spared.
Otherwise,
our entire clan will soon be exterminated."
Xián said:
"Just recall him,
and together uphold justice and impartiality.
Then peace will immediately be established;
there is no need to step aside.
Indeed, no subject should monopolize power,
let alone an imperial relative!
Now the imperial clan is weak; they rely on the closeness of the imperial relatives for security.
If the imperial relatives are in danger; they rely on the prestige of the imperial clan for support.
This is what is meant by 'lips and teeth depend on each other';
it is the best strategy."
Jì became even more frightened and asked Shí Chóng:
"What do people think?"
Chóng said:
"Your esteemed brother is in power
and alienates the imperial clan.
He should share power with all under heaven."
Jì said:
"When I see my brother, I will mention this."
Chóng saw Jùn
and did so,
but Jùn did not accept it.
Later, he and his elder brothers were all killed.
On the evening the disaster broke out,
the Eastern Palace summoned Jì.
Jì asked Péi Kǎi:
"Where should I go?"
Kǎi said:
"You are the imperial tutor,
you should go to the Eastern Palace."
Jì was benevolent,
and had long commanded troops.
The more than four hundred men who followed him were all brave warriors from Qínzhōng,
and they all shot with accuracy.
They all wanted to save Jì.
But Jì had already entered the palace,
and they all sighed in regret.
The Grand Historian says:
Jiǎ Chōng, with his obsequious and vulgar character,
and his ordinary talent for writing and law,
was fortunate to live in a prosperous time
and wrongly occupied an undeserved position.
He drew his sword and defied his lord,
without the slightest doubt or hesitation;
he wielded the axe and overthrew the defunct regime,
and quickly requested to withdraw from a dangerous situation.
This was not only a perversion for the Wèi court,
but also a sinner against the Jìn dynasty!
Yet,
he enjoyed extreme imperial favor,
holding both civil and military responsibilities.
In life, he bore the trust of the highest offices,
and after death, he enjoyed the honor of being enshrined with the ancestors.
It can be said that he was without virtue yet enjoyed great fortune,
and disaster would soon reach him.
When it came to his descendants,
they were beggars,
inheriting the accumulated evil of their foundation,
and unleashing wicked and treacherous deeds.
They incited that cunning woman,
and sought to seize the household.
Though they were punished and exterminated,
how can it be said that their responsibilities were met?
In the past, when Dāngtú lacked a successor,
Gōnglǘ indeed exerted himself.
When the Diǎn Wǔ dynasty was collapsing,
Nánfēng also fully exerted his strength.
It can be said,
"A ruler begins with this,
and must end with this."
This is truly so!
Yáng Jùn rose through favor and fortune,
and thus bore the responsibility of a pillar of the state.
Even if he had been respectful, he might have fallen short,
so how could he be spared for his arrogance, extravagance, promiscuity, and indulgence?
Kuò Mǔ saved herself with wisdom and foresight.
Huì Kūn obtained pardon by speaking early.
Wénjū's insight was similar to these past luminaries,
yet his punishment differed from theirs.
Alas!
Eulogy says:
Gōnglǘ was glib and treacherous,
his heart deviated from rectitude.
He met with a timely opportunity,
and thus ascended to a glorious destiny.
His beggar-like descendants inherited his line,
a wicked family that disrupted governance.
The petty Wéncháng
took the position of a pillar of the state.
Occupying a position that was not his,
he thus met destruction.
Although Yáo was prescient,
he also suffered disaster.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 11, Wèi Shū.
Wèi Shū 字 Zì Yángyuán,
a native of Fán, Rènchéng.
He was orphaned young,
and was raised by his maternal relatives, the Níng family.
When the Níng family built a new residence,
the house diviner said:
“A noble nephew will emerge from this house.”
His maternal grandmother, seeing that Wèi Shū, her nephew, was young and intelligent,
thought he was the one being referred to.
Shū said:
“I shall fulfill this prophecy for my maternal family.”
After a long time, he moved out to live separately.
He was eight feet and two inches tall,
with a refined and imposing appearance.
He could drink over one dàn of wine,
but was slow-witted and simple-minded,
and not highly regarded by his fellow villagers.
His paternal uncle, Háng, who was the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Láng),
was famous in his generation,
but did not recognize Shū’s talent either,
and made him manage a watermill.
Háng often sighed, saying:
“Shū is capable of being a village chief (hùzhǎng) for a few hundred households,
and that would fulfill my wish!”
Shū also did not take this to heart.
He did not adhere to the conventions of ordinary people,
nor did he engage in rigorous and competitive endeavors.
He always sought to tolerate talent and foster growth,
and never exposed others’ shortcomings.
He was fond of archery and horse riding by nature,
and would wear leather clothes,
go into the mountains and marshes,
making fishing and hunting his occupation.
Only Wáng from Tàiyuán said to Shū:
“You will eventually become a grand minister (tái fǔ),
but currently you cannot even keep your wife and children from hunger and cold.
I shall help you with their upkeep.”
He often provided for Shū’s needs,
and Shū accepted without demur.
One time, Shū visited Yěwáng.
That night, the host's wife gave birth.
Soon after, the sounds of carriages and horses were heard,
and someone asked:
“Is it a boy
or a girl?”
The answer was:
“A boy.
Record it:
he will die by arms at fifteen.”
They asked again:
“Who is the sleeper?”
The answer was:
“Wèi Gōng Shū.”
Fifteen years later,
Shū visited the host
and asked where the child born that night was.
The host said:
“He died from an axe wound while stripping mulberry bark.”
Shū then knew he would indeed become a duke (gōng).
When he was over forty,
the commander of the commandery (jùn shàngjì yuán) nominated him as Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt).
His clan and relatives, thinking Shū had no academic achievements,
advised him not to accept,
as it would be considered noble.
Shū said:
“If I try and fail,
the fault is mine.
How can I falsely claim the nobility of declining without achieving anything?”
Thereupon, he set himself to study,
mastering one classic in a hundred days,
and subsequently passed the imperial examination, ascending to a higher rank.
He was appointed Magistrate of Miǎnchí,
then promoted to Magistrate of Jùnyí,
and entered the court as Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat).
At that time, there was a desire to purge the Secretarial officials (láng guān),
dismissing those who lacked talent.
Shū said:
“I am precisely such a person.”
He packed his belongings and left.
His colleagues, who had previously lacked integrity, all showed signs of shame,
and those who spoke of it praised him.
He was successively promoted to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) for Hòujiāngjūn Zhōng Yù.
Yù often shot arrows with his aides,
and Shū merely kept score for them.
Later, when there was a shortage of players,
Shū was used to make up the numbers.
Yù initially did not know that Shū was skilled in archery.
Shū, with his composed and elegant demeanor,
hit the target with every shot,
astonishing everyone present,
and no one could match him.
Yù sighed and apologized, saying:
“My inability to fully appreciate your talent
is evident in this archery feat;
how could it be just one matter!”
He was transferred to become Aide to the Chancellor (Xiàngguó Cānjūn),
and enfeoffed as the Earl of Jùyáng (Jùyáng Zǐ).
In the trivial matters of the court,
he was never seen to argue right or wrong.
However, when it came to major issues of rise and fall,
which no one else could decide,
Shū would calmly plan for them,
often proposing solutions beyond common deliberation.
Emperor Wén held him in high regard and deeply valued him.
Whenever a court assembly concluded and he rose from his seat,
the emperor would look at him as he departed, saying:
“Wèi Shū is magnificent,
a leader among men.”
He was promoted to Governor (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Yíyáng and Xíngyáng,
where he earned a great reputation.
He was summoned to be appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
He was then sent out as Inspector of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ),
and for three years in the province,
he was praised for his simplicity and benevolence.
He returned to the court as Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng).
Emperor Wǔ, recognizing Shū’s integrity and simplicity,
specially bestowed upon him a hundred bolts of silk.
He was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū).
He was to be dismissed from office due to official misconduct,
but an imperial edict allowed him to redeem himself.
Shū’s three wives had all died.
That year, he personally petitioned for leave to return to his home commandery to bury his wife.
An imperial edict granted him one qǐng of burial land
and five hundred thousand coins.
In the early years of Tàikāng,
he was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Yòupúyè).
Shū, along with Wèi Guàn, Shān Tāo, Zhāng Huá, and others, considering that the entire realm was unified,
suggested that the ancient rites of Feng and Shan sacrifices on Mount Tài (Dōngyuè) should be performed.
They repeatedly submitted their proposals,
but the emperor, out of modesty, did not permit it.
Shū was made Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zuǒpúyè)
and concurrently in charge of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
Shū submitted a memorial, stating:
“Now, when selecting women for the six palaces,
they are engaged with jade and silk.
However, the old custom of having the Superintendent of the Imperial Wardrobe (Yùfǔ Chéng) present the engagement gifts
to declare the auspicious rites makes the gifts heavy and the envoy light.
I propose that for appointing the Three Ladies (Sānfūrén), a Minister (Qīng) should be sent;
for the Nine Concubines (Jiǔpín), a Colonel-Director of the Palace Gates (Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng) should be sent;
and for the Beautiful Ladies (Měirén) and Virtuous Ladies (Liángrén), an Usher (Yèzhě) should be sent.
This would be grander according to the ceremonial regulations.”
An imperial edict ordered a detailed consideration.
The opinions varied among the officials,
and the matter was dropped.
He was given the additional title of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Right (Yòuguānglù Dàfū)
and bestowed with the honors of the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
When Shān Tāo passed away,
Shū was appointed acting Minister of the Interior (Sītú),
and soon after became the full Minister.
Shū possessed great authority, dignity, and moral prestige.
His stipends and rewards were distributed among his extended family,
leaving no surplus wealth in his household.
Zhōu Zhèn of Chénliú had been repeatedly appointed by various government offices,
but each time an appointment letter was issued,
the appointing duke (gōng) would soon die.
Everyone called Zhèn the “duke-killing clerk” (shā gōng yuán),
and no one dared to appoint him.
Shū, however, summoned him,
and indeed suffered no ill effects.
Knowledgeable people praised his understanding of destiny for this.
Due to his old age,
he often claimed illness and resigned his position.
He temporarily resumed office again,
appointed as the Central Regulator of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Zhōngzhèng),
but soon after again claimed illness.
Xí Shēn, the Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng), wrote to Shū, saying:
“Your Excellency’s long illness has slightly improved,
and attending to duties is appropriate,
especially given the Emperor’s concern.
Why would you get up and then return to bed,
bending your body and evading the law,
thereby greatly disappointing public expectations?
Your Excellency achieved greatness in your youth,
to abandon it all at once,
is it not regrettable?”
Shū continued to feign illness as before.
Later, due to calamities and omens, he offered to resign his position,
but the Emperor did not consent.
Later, after the New Year's Day court session, he returned to his residence
and submitted a memorial offering to return his official seal and ribbons.
The Emperor personally issued an imperial edict earnestly encouraging him
but Shū’s resolve was even firmer.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, saying:
“Sītú, Jùyángzǐ Shū,
embodies profound and pure principles,
his thoughts are far-reaching and well-considered,
he is loyal and upright,
and serves the public with full dedication.
When he managed the selection of officials,
he appointed people fairly and appropriately;
when he assisted in the imperial administration,
he widely promulgated the five teachings.
His benevolent instructions have spread,
and his virtuous reputation is prominently established.
He can be called one of the court’s outstanding figures.
However, he has repeatedly insisted on humility and yielding,
with sincere and earnest words,
and after repeatedly reviewing his request,
We feel saddened and disheartened.
To perfect the good deeds of others
is allowed by ancient precedents,
and it is difficult to go against such sincere feelings.
Therefore, We now grant his insistence,
allowing Jùyángzǐ to retire to his residence,
with a rank equivalent to the Three Dūkès,
and his salary and emoluments as before.
He is exempt from attending court with a stool and staff,
and is granted a million coins,
with his bed curtains, mats, and mattresses supplied.
Four attendants are appointed as Jùyángzǐ’s attendants,
and ten official cavalrymen are provided.
The Guānglùxūn is to present the imperial edict,
and the relevant officials are to meticulously follow the established rites
so that all arrangements are as per old regulations.”
Thereupon, he was granted a comfortable carriage with four horses,
and horses were allowed to pass through his gate.
Shū would always act first and then speak;
at the time of his resignation,
no one knew about it.
At the time, public opinion considered that since the rise of the Jìn dynasty,
none of the Three Gōngs had been able to gracefully resign from honors and die peacefully.
Sīkōng Wèi Guàn wrote a letter to Shū, saying:
“Every time I discussed this matter with you,
it was never resolved on the day.
It can be said that I looked ahead,
and suddenly it was behind me.”
He passed away in the first year of Tàixī,
at the age of eighty-two.
The Emperor was deeply grieved and mourned,
and his funeral and burial expenses were generous.
His posthumous title was Kāng.
His son, Hùn, courtesy name Yán’guǎng,
was pure, benevolent, talented, and virtuous,
serving as a Tàizǐ Shèrén.
At the age of twenty-seven,
he passed away before Shū,
and both court and common people mourned and pitied Shū.
Shū often grieved profoundly,
and upon retiring, sighed, saying:
“I am far inferior to Zhuāngshēng,
how can I harm myself with something useless!”
Thereupon, he ceased weeping for the remainder of the mourning period.
An imperial edict stated:
“Shū had only one son,
who was ill-fated and died young.
In Shū’s old age,
he endures the suffering of loneliness.
Every time We think of this, Our heart aches,
and We sigh in sorrow.
To dispel his sorrow and nourish his spirit,
he may be given more delicacies and provisions.
Furthermore, he is granted a carriage drawn by an ox, with a ‘yángsuì’ mirror, a four-directional viewing screen, and black-wheeled silk curtains,
so that he may go out and look around,
which may help to dissipate his worries.”
His grand-nephew, Róng, succeeded him.
Róng also died young,
so his great-nephew, Huàng, succeeded him.
Lǐ Xǐ
Lǐ Xǐ, courtesy name Jìhé,
was a native of Tóngdī, Shàngdǎng.
His father, Quán,
was the Hàn Dàhónglú.
Xǐ was highly virtuous in his youth,
and deeply learned and refined.
He and Guǎn Níng of Běihǎi were summoned for their virtuous character,
but he did not go.
He was repeatedly invited by the Sānfǔ,
but did not accept.
Xuāndì again invited Xǐ to be a Tàifùshǔ,
but he firmly declined, feigning illness.
The commandery and county officials had to help him onto the road.
At that time, Xǐ’s mother was gravely ill,
so he secretly scaled the walls of Xuánshì city and returned on foot,
thereby experiencing his mother’s funeral.
Commentators praised his integrity and resolve.
Later, he became the Bìngzhōu Biéjià.
At that time, Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Qín Lǎng passed through Bìngzhōu.
The provincial governor, Bì Guǐ, respected him
and ordered that he be driven in a carriage to the palace gate.
Xǐ firmly advised against it, considering it inappropriate.
Guǐ reluctantly followed his advice.
When Jǐngdì assisted in governing,
he appointed Xǐ as Dàjiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When Xǐ arrived,
he was granted an audience.
Jǐngdì said to Xǐ:
“Previously, My late father invited you, but you did not respond.
Now, I summon you, and you have come.
Why is this?”
He replied:
“Your late father treated me with rites,
and I was able to advance or retreat according to rites.
Your Excellency disciplines me with law,
and I fear the law and have come.”
The Emperor greatly respected him.
He was transferred to Sīmǎ,
and soon after appointed Yòu Chángshǐ.
Upon returning from suppressing Wúqiū Jiǎn,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He was upright and principled in office,
not fearing the powerful and overbearing,
and all officials were awed and respectful.
He recommended Sūn Pú from Luò'ān,
who also became prominent for his moral character.
People at the time called him a man who knew others.
He was soon promoted to Dàsīmǎ,
but was dismissed due to a public matter.
Sīmǎ Zhòu became Níngběi Jiāngjūn,
stationed in Yè,
and appointed Xǐ as his Jūnsī.
After a short while,
he was appointed Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added titles of Yángwēi Jiāngjūn and Jiǎjié,
and overseeing Hùqiāng Xiàowèi.
He pacified and governed both Huá and Yí peoples,
achieving great renown and success.
When the Qiāng barbarians invaded the frontier,
Xǐ seized the opportune moment,
without waiting for imperial approval,
and immediately dispatched troops deep into enemy territory.
He achieved a great victory and many captures,
and due to his significant merit, he was exempted from punishment.
People at the time compared him to Fēng and Gān of the Hàn dynasty.
Thereupon, he requested to return,
which was granted.
After residing at home for more than a month,
he was appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and successively promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
When the Wèi Emperor announced his abdication to Jìn,
Xǐ, in his original capacity, acted as Sītú,
assisting Tàiwèi Zhèng Chōng in presenting the imperial edict.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he was enfeoffed as Qíhóu.
Xǐ submitted a memorial, stating:
“The late official Liú Yǒu,
former Shàngshū Shān Táo, Zhōngshān Wáng Mù, and the late Shàngshū Púyè Wǔ Gāi each occupied three Gēng rice fields for their official positions.
I request to dismiss Táo and Mù from their offices.
Gāi has already died,
so I request to demote his posthumous title.”
The imperial edict said:
“Law,
for the whole world to follow justly,
must not avoid relatives or the noble,
only then can it be implemented.
How could We bend or indulge in such matters!
However, this matter was entirely orchestrated by Yǒu,
who exploited the common people
to mislead court officials.
Such treacherous officials dare to do this;
therefore, investigate and punish Yǒu to deter wickedness and sycophancy.
As for Táo and others, who did not repeat their faults,
let no questions be asked of them.
The Yì Jīng says, ‘The king’s ministers are resolute,
not for their own sake.’
Now Xǐ holds firm to his public duty,
acting according to his office.
He can be called ‘the honest official of the state.’
Guāngwǔ once said, ‘Even noble relatives should restrain themselves to avoid the two Bàos.’
Is this not truly the case!
Therefore, instruct all officials
to each be careful in their duties.
The grace of leniency
is not to be frequently encountered.”
Xǐ served as Sīlì for two generations,
and was praised by both court and common people.
He was dismissed due to a public matter.
In that year,
the Crown Prince was established,
and Lǐ Xǐ was made Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Since the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the Eastern Palace had long been vacant,
its system had fallen into disrepair,
and its officials were incomplete.
Posts such as Zhānshì, Zuǒyòushuài, Shùzǐ, and Zhōngshèrén had not yet been established.
Only a Wèishuài was appointed to command the troops,
and the two Grand Tutors jointly managed all affairs.
Lǐ Xǐ was in office for several years,
and his instructions and guidance were utterly meticulous.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Púshè,
and appointed Tèjìn, Guānglù Dàfū,
and then resigned due to old age.
An imperial edict stated:
“Guānglù Dàfū, Tèjìn Lǐ Xǐ,
upholding virtue and residing in righteousness,
should ascend to the ranks of the Grand Ministers,
assisting and illuminating Our person.
Yet, due to his advanced age, he has retired.
Though he may now live in leisurely inactivity,
allowing his spirit to be nourished,
Our longing for his sincerity,
how can We not be filled with regret!
Therefore, in addition to his title of Guānglù,
We bestow upon him the honor of golden and purple robes,
assign him ten mounted guards,
grant him fifty million coins,
and his salary, gifts, and ceremonial privileges
shall be entirely as those of the Sānsī.
Horses shall be permitted to pass through his gate.”
Initially,
when Lǐ Xǐ was Púshè,
the barbarians of Liángzhōu invaded the border.
Lǐ Xǐ advocated sending an army to suppress them.
The court officials believed that deploying troops was not easy,
and that the barbarians were not a sufficient threat,
and ultimately did not follow his advice.
Later, the barbarians indeed broke loose on a large scale,
and Liángzhōu was overthrown.
The court deeply regretted this.
Because Lǐ Xǐ was pure, simple, poor, and frugal,
he was granted one hundred rolls of silk.
When Qíwáng Yōu was sent out to govern a region,
Lǐ Xǐ submitted a memorial to remonstrate,
and his words were extremely earnest.
Throughout Lǐ Xǐ’s career,
although his integrity was not extraordinary,
his family had no savings.
His relatives, old friends, and former associates even had to share clothes and food with him.
He never privately took advantage of his official position.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tàibǎo,
and given the posthumous name Chéng.
His son Zàn succeeded him.
His youngest son, Jiǎn, courtesy name Zhòngyuē,
served successively as Zuǒ Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn and Túnhóu Xiàowèi.
Jiǎn’s son, Hóng, courtesy name Shìyàn,
was known for his integrity from a young age.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
he successively held the posts of Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng and Sànqí Chángshì.
Liú Shí (younger brother Zhì)
Liú Shí, courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
was a native of Gāotáng, Píngyuán.
He was a descendant of Shòu, Prince Huì of Jìběi during the Hàn dynasty.
His father, Guǎng,
was the Magistrate of Chìqiū.
Liú Shí was poor and苦 in his youth,
selling ox-clothes to support himself.
Nevertheless, he loved learning.
He tied a rope to his hand,
recited books aloud,
and was broadly conversant with ancient and modern knowledge.
He kept himself pure and clean,
and his conduct was without blemish.
The commandery investigated him as Xiàolián,
and the province recommended him as Xiùcái,
but he did not accept either.
He entered Luòyáng as an accounts official,
and was appointed Hénán Yǐn Céng,
then promoted to Shàngshū Láng and Tíngwèi Zhèng.
Later, he successively served as Lìbù Láng,
and participated in the military affairs of Emperor Wén’s prime ministership,
being enfeoffed as Xúnyángzǐ.
When Zhōng Huì and Dèng Ài attacked Shǔ,
a guest asked Liú Shí:
“Will the two generals pacify Shǔ?”
Liú Shí said:
“The defeat of Shǔ is certain,
but neither will return.”
The guest asked the reason,
but Liú Shí smiled and did not answer.
It turned out exactly as he had said.
Liú Shí’s foresight
was always of this kind.
Seeing that the world was full of those eager for advancement,
and that the path of humility and yielding was neglected,
he therefore wrote the Chóngràng Lùn to rectify this.
Its words were: Of old, when the sage kings governed the world,
what they valued in yielding was
the desire to bring forth worthy talents
and to put an end to contention.
It is human nature that everyone desires their own worthiness,
therefore, they are encouraged to yield to the worthy to demonstrate their own worthiness.
How could they be asked to yield to the unworthy!
Thus, when the way of yielding flourishes,
worthy and capable persons emerge without seeking,
and appointments of utmost impartiality
establish themselves.
The deputies for all officials are also prepared in advance.
When one office is vacant,
one chooses the person who has yielded the most among the officials, and employs him.
This is indeed the way.
If officials at court yield to each other,
then even commoners in their thatched huts will be transformed by it,
and the custom of recommending the worthy and yielding to the capable will arise from this.
One who is yielded to by an entire state
is a man of that
state;
one who is universally recommended by the world
is a man of the world.
When the custom of recommendation and yielding prevails,
then the worthy and the unworthy will be clearly distinguished.
When this way is practiced,
those in
power need not exert their minds;
an upright public opinion naturally forms,
and they simply follow it.
Thus it is said,
“How great was Yáo as a ruler!
None could find a name for him.”
It means that the world settled itself,
and one did not see how Yáo transformed it,
thus no one could name it.
It is also said,
“Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world and yet did not participate in it.
The one who transformed without acting was perhaps Shùn.”
If worthy men yield to each other at court,
and great talents hold high offices,
and petty men do not contend in the countryside,
then the world will be without trouble.
When worthy talents bring about a state of no
trouble,
the ultimate Way flourishes.
Having received its accomplishment,
what further participation is needed!
Thus, one can sing the poem of Nánfēng [the South Wind]
and play the five-stringed zither.
The one who achieved this accomplishment
was not due to anything else;
it was brought about by promoting yielding.
Confucius said,
“If one can govern a state with ritual and yielding,
it is not difficult.”
For a long time, officials at court have not been diligent in yielding to each other,
and the world has been transformed by this.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
those promoted and appointed,
and officials in office,
upon
being seen and receiving their appointments,
even if they themselves declined due to incapability,
none were ever willing to yield to someone superior to themselves.
Indeed, when the custom of recommendation and yielding ceases,
the heart of contention arises.
Confucius said,
“If those
above encourage yielding, then those below will not contend.”
This clearly indicates that if yielding is not encouraged, those below will certainly contend.
When the way of recommendation and yielding flourishes,
worthy and capable persons are daily recommended;
when the heart of contention arises,
worthy and capable persons are daily slandered and disparaged.
Those who contend desire to be first themselves,
and intensely dislike capable people being first,
so they cannot help but disparage them.
Thus, even Confucius and Mozi could not escape
being slandered by the world,
let alone those who are not as great as Confucius and Mozi!
The discussants all say,
“The world lacks talents of high renown,”
and “The court does not have truly great talents who can
be made high officials.”
People in the mountains and marshes and minor officials also say,
“Although officials at court may hold high offices and have famous virtues,
they are all inferior to the people of former times.”
I believe
that both these statements are mistaken.
It is not that the present age alone lacks worthy people;
it is that the age does not value yielding.
If one person has the reputation of being superior to the masses,
slander will certainly follow,
and their reputation will not
it is due to the current system that this has come to be.
Even if Jì and Qì were to exist again,
they would not be able to fully maintain their reputation.
The capable and the incompetent are mixed,
the superior and the inferior are indistinguishable.
Gentlemen have no fixed
value.
When there is a vacancy in an office,
the selecting official does not know whom to appoint.
They merely follow the official hierarchy and promote accordingly.
Among people of similar talent, those who are appointed first
are either the children of powerful families,
or
must be favored by someone powerful.
Not because they are uniquely virtuous,
but by virtue of their previous appointment,
they are endlessly promoted again.
With endless promotions,
the problem of
being unequal to the task emerges.
Looking at those currently in office,
their political achievements are unheard of.
Unless they are children of powerful families,
most have advanced by virtue of their seniority.
If the world were to value deference,
gentlemen would certainly achieve fame by being deferred to,
and only after achieving fame would officials be appointed.
For all those whose conduct and reputation are not established,
who have no record of political achievement in office,
deference to them would certainly occur,
and officials would not be appointed by chance.
The reason why appointments continue unchecked
is that the way of deference has fallen into disuse,
and the error of
appointing people based on seniority has persisted for a long time.
Therefore, since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
grand recommendations were occasionally initiated,
instructing all officials to recommend those they knew,
appointing only based on talent,
without regard to rank.
Such instances were numerous.
Those recommended must have included suitable candidates,
but we do not hear of immediate promotions,
not knowing who among them was most worthy.
There must have been unsuitable candidates among those recommended,
but
no blame was assigned,
not knowing who was most unworthy.
The reason it could not be known
was that people at the time were unwilling to recommend each other,
and the distinction between the worthy and the foolish was not
made.
This being the case,
recommenders knew that those above could not make accurate observations,
and thus dared to make random recommendations.
Some recommended those they considered worthy,
and also those they favored,
all at once
they were appointed.
The number of people was excessively large,
each claiming that their recommended candidate was worthy;
furthermore, their lofty commendations
were uniformly similar,
making it difficult to distinguish them.
Confusion and disorder,
truth and falsehood
intertwined,
became even worse because of this.
Although the recommenders were not entirely loyal in their duty,
it was also because those above broadly allowed the path of observation and inquiry to become lax,
thus causing this situation.
In ancient times, King Qí
enjoyed listening to the sound of the yú,
always requiring three hundred people to play together before he would listen,
and he paid them the stipends of several individuals.
Nánguō Xiānshēng did not know how to play the yú,
but thinking that with three
hundred people playing together, his lack of skill could be concealed,
he therefore asked to play the yú for the king,
idly receiving the stipends of several people.
The succeeding king, realizing this, changed it,
finding it difficult to expose the errors of the former king.
So
he issued an order saying:
"My fondness for the sound of the yú is even greater than that of the former king.
I wish to hear them one by one."
At this, the gentleman fled.
If the custom of recommending the worthy is not established,
and the practice of indiscriminate recommendations is not reformed,
then the likes of Nánguō Xiānshēng will fill the court.
Those with high talent who uphold the Dao will daily decline,
and those who
rush to powerful
households will daily increase.
Even if the state has laws and penalties,
it will not be able to forbid them.
The ill effects of the non-establishment of the way of deference
are not only that worthy people remain in lower positions
and cannot advance in due course,
but also that the nation's good ministers bearing heavy responsibilities
will gradually
be punished and dismissed.
How do we know this to be so?
Kǒngzǐ believed that Yán Shì's son did not repeat his errors,
clearly implying that non-sages all have faults.
Many desire
positions of honor and wealth,
those who dislike the worthy and capable block their path,
and many also criticize and slander them for their faults.
The emergence of slander
is not merely groundless fabrication;
it must be based on a person's
minor fault and exaggerated.
When words of slander are heard frequently,
those in power, even if they wish not to accept them,
cannot but rely on what they hear,
and consequently investigate
the matter subtly as it arises.
There is no way
to avoid it, as the evidence will eventually emerge.
Once the evidence is obtained,
how can one not address the offense?
If one knows and tolerates it,
the king's authority will daily decline,
and the non-enforcement of his
commands will begin from this.
If one knows and addresses all of them,
those who are punished and dismissed will gradually increase,
and high officials will lose their sense of security.
If worthy talents do not advance,
and honored officials
gradually become alienated,
this is a deep concern for those who govern a nation.
The Shī says:
"Receiving emolument without deference,
it will come to an end with this."
People who do not defer are preoccupied with the worry of ruin,
so how difficult is it to
expect them to benefit the nation and court!
Indeed!
I humbly believe that reforming this custom is very easy.
How do I know this?
For among those currently in office,
though there may be mixed talents of ordinary and vulgar sorts,
there are also many
who are worthy and discerning.
How can it be said that they all do not know the value of deferring to the worthy?
It is simply that everyone at that time did not defer,
having become accustomed to it as a custom,
and so they did not do it.
When a subject
is first appointed,
they all submit memorials to the throne,
known as "thanksgiving memorials," a practice that has existed for a long time.
The origin of the thanksgiving memorial,
its original intention,
was to recommend worthy and capable individuals to express gratitude for the national grace.
In ancient times, when Shùn appointed Yǔ as Sìkōng,
Yǔ bowed his head,
deferring to Jì, Qì, and Gāoyáo.
When Yì was appointed Yúguān,
he deferred to Zhūhǔ, Xióng, and Pí.
When Bó
Yí was appointed to oversee the three rites,
he deferred to Kuí and Lóng.
During the Táng and Yú eras,
when officials were first appointed,
none failed to defer.
The meaning of the thanksgiving memorial
was derived from this.
Those who recorded
it
wished to make it a perpetual model.
In later generations, those appointed,
being unworthy, could not defer to the worthy,
merely expressing empty thanks for being appointed.
This practice continued unchanged,
a failing of
custom.
Hence, for officials who are appointed and allowed to submit memorials,
their deference to the worthy and recommendation of the capable should be approved;
those who cannot defer to anyone and merely waste paper
should all be rejected.
When subjects are first appointed,
each will consider recommending and deferring to the worthy and capable.
The documents of deference shall be entrusted to the responsible officials.
When there is a vacancy in the Sānsī,
the one most deferred to by the Sānsī shall be chosen
and appointed.
This way, for one vacancy in the Gōng,
the Sāngōng would have already pre-selected.
Moreover, the selecting official
does not necessarily appoint a Gōng to select the Sāngōng;
it is better to let the Sāngōng
jointly select one Gōng, which is more thorough.
If there is a vacancy among the Sìzhēng,
the one most deferred to by the Sìzhēng shall be chosen and appointed.
This way, for one vacancy in the Zhēng,
the Sìzhēng would have already pre-selected
it is.
It is certainly detailed in the vacancies and allows the appointing authority to select the four *Zhēng* (征).
When the *Shàngshū* (尚書) position is vacant,
one should choose the person who has been yielded to the most by other *Shàngshū* (尚書) and appoint him.
This is where eight *Shàng*
*shū* (尚書) jointly select one *Shàngshū* (尚書),
detailing how the appointing authority selects eight *Shàngshū* (尚書) when a vacancy occurs.
When the *Jùnshǒu* (郡守) position is vacant,
one should choose the person who has been yielded to the most by other *Jùn* (郡) and appoint him,
detailing
how the appointing authority selects a hundred *Jùnshǒu* (郡守).
However, to compare the yielding of all officials and a hundred *Jùn* (郡)
with that of the appointing authority
cannot be discussed in the same year.
Even if the three *Fǔ* (府) are ordered to jointly recommend officials,
they are fundamentally not
entrusted with the duty of selection,
and each cannot truly discern their intentions.
The matters they focus on are few,
and they merely allow the appointing authority to follow the official sequence and make selections
without
requiring meticulousness.
When both the wise and the foolish yield,
the ears and eyes of the common people become the ears and eyes of the state.
For human nature, when there is contention, one desires to criticize what one does not understand;
when there is yielding,
one competes to recommend those superior to oneself.
Therefore, when the world contends, praise and blame are intertwined,
superiority and inferiority are indistinguishable,
and yielding is hard to achieve.
When the era yields, the wise and intelligent become prominent,
and the virtues of ability
and inability follow clearly, one after another,
and cannot be disordered.
At this time,
those who can withdraw and cultivate themselves
are yielded to by many.
Even if they wish to remain poor and lowly,
it is not
possible.
Rushing forward with ambition and wishing others to yield to oneself
is like walking backward and seeking to go forward.
If this is the case,
both the foolish and the wise will know to advance themselves and seek success;
if it is not cultivated
within oneself, there will be no way.
Those who seek outside themselves
will, in this situation, follow and return to themselves.
Empty fame and baseless discussions
will cease on their own without prohibition.
Everyone will have nothing
to exert their minds on;
they will rely on the opinions of the multitude,
and the world will transform itself.
The transformation without words will prevail,
and the majestic beauty will become evident here.
Yielding can achieve this;
how can one not strive for it!
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* (春秋傳) says:
"When Fàn Xuānzǐ (范宣子) yielded,
all his subordinates yielded.
Although Luán Yǎn (欒黶) was extravagant,
he did not dare to defy it.
The state of Jìn (晉) was thereby pacified,
and several generations relied
on it."
In ancient times, when there was transformation,
gentlemen esteemed ability and yielded to their subordinates,
while common people diligently farmed to serve their superiors.
Superiors and subordinates observed禮 *lǐ*,
and slander and evil were banished far away,
due to not
contending.
But when there was chaos,
the deterioration of the state
invariably resulted from it.
The profound discussion is clear and lucid like this.
If the gentlemen at court who preside over the selection of high officials
can avoid rejecting
good words because of the speaker,
but instead put them into practice,
and each prioritizes yielding to the worthy and promoting the capable,
then talented individuals will emerge in abundance,
and ability and inability will be clearly distinguished.
No accomplishment that transcends generations
is greater
than this.
In the beginning of the *Tàishǐ* (泰始) era,
he was promoted to the rank of *Bó* (伯).
He was successively transferred to *Shǎofǔ* (少府).
In the *Xiánníng* (咸寧) era, he became *Tàicháng* (太常),
and then *Shàngshū* (尚書).
When Dù Yù (杜預) attacked Wú (吳),
Shí (寔) served as *Zhènnán Jūnsī* (鎮南軍司) in his original capacity.
Originally,
Shí’s (寔) wife, Lú Shì (盧氏), died after giving birth to their son Jī (躋).
Huá Shì (華氏) intended to marry her daughter to him.
Shí’s (寔) younger brother, Zhì (智), advised:
"The Huá (華) family is generally greedy;
they will surely ruin our household."
Shí (寔) could not decline and ultimately married into the Huá (華) family, giving birth to his son Xià (夏).
Shí (寔) was eventually implicated by Xià (夏) for accepting bribes
and was dismissed from office.
A short while later, he became *Dàsīnóng* (大司農),
but was again dismissed due to Xià’s (夏) crime.
Whenever Shí (寔) returned to his hometown,
the local people would bring wine and meat to await him.
Shí (寔) found it difficult to refuse their kindness,
so he would always eat with them and return the rest.
Someone once said to Shí (寔):
"Your conduct is exceptional,
yet your sons cannot follow it.
Why do you not admonish them day and night,
so they realize their faults and correct themselves?"
Shí (寔) replied:
"What I practice
is what I have heard and seen;
it is not something passed down or learned through imitation.
How could it be achieved through mere teaching and instruction!"
The world considered Shí’s (寔) words to be correct.
Later, he was reinstated as *Guózǐ Jìjiǔ* (國子祭酒) and *Sànqí Chángshì* (散騎常侍).
When Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ (愍懷太子) was first enfeoffed as *Guǎnglíng Wáng* (廣陵王),
excellent teachers and friends were selected,
and Shí (寔) was appointed as his tutor.
In the beginning of the *Yuánkāng* (元康) era,
he was promoted to the rank of *Hóu* (侯).
He was successively transferred to *Tàizǐ Tàibǎo* (太子太保),
and additionally held the titles of *Shìzhōng* (侍中), *Tèjìn* (特進), *Yòuguānglù Dàfū* (右光祿大夫), and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司),
and concurrently served as *Jìzhōu Dūdū* (冀州都督).
In the ninth year,
he was appointed *Sīkōng* (司空) by imperial edict,
transferred to *Tàibǎo* (太保),
and then *Tàifù* (太傅).
In the beginning of the *Tài'ān* (太安) era,
Shí (寔) resigned due to old age and illness,
and was granted an elegant carriage with four horses and one million cash.
He retired to his residence as a *Hóu* (侯).
When Chángshā (長沙) and Chéngdū (成都) attacked each other,
Shí (寔) was plundered by soldiers
and secretly returned to his hometown.
Upon Emperor Huì’s (惠帝) death,
Shí (寔) attended the imperial funeral.
When Emperor Huái (懷帝) ascended the throne,
Shí (寔) was again appointed *Tàiwèi* (太尉).
Shí (寔) declared his old age
and firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
Zuǒchéng Liú Tǎn (左丞劉坦) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Indeed, a hall is high and far-reaching, and the ruler is esteemed and the minister noble.
Therefore, ancient sagacious kings all honored their chief ministers
and promoted the teaching of caring for the elderly,
instructing and demonstrating to the four seas,
so that young and old
would observe礼 *lǐ*.
Retiring at seventy *zhìshì* (致仕)
was also a way to distinguish and honor those with old merits
and encourage a spirit of integrity and loftiness.
*Tàiwèi* (太尉) Shí (寔) embodies a pure and unadorned character,
upholds an unswerving integrity,
and has hung up his carriage and declared his old age
for over twenty years.
His boundless ambition
has grown even stronger with age.
He can be called a grand elder of the state,
a model for the nation.
I have heard that the elderly are not expected to exert physical strength in ceremonies.
Shí (寔) is over ninety years old,
his life is counted by days,
yet he personally supported himself and came,
braving dangers to arrive,
to express his sorrow at the imperial tomb
and pay his respects at the court.
The duties of a high minister are fully discharged.
The sacred edict is earnest and sincere,
insisting that Shí (寔) preside over the highest platform,
shining like a grand sacrifice,
repeatedly urging and instructing,
which has spanned two years.
Yet Shí (寔) has repeatedly submitted memorials,
with sincere and earnest words of refusal.
I believe that in ancient times, caring for the elderly
meant favoring their non-involvement in affairs,
not valuing their official duties.
Therefore, it is appropriate to permit Shí (寔) to maintain his stance."
In the third year,
an imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, Yú entrusted five ministers,
bringing about a reign of effortless governance.
The Hàn chancellor Xiāo Hé
earned the praise of a unified and peaceful state.
Thus, they were able to shine brightly in their time
and leave a legacy for a hundred generations.
I, having inherited Heaven’s clear mandate
to rule over all states,
rely on my prime ministers and various officials
to uphold and manifest the Way of governance,
exerting their utmost strength and support
to fulfill my greatest hopes.
However, you are advanced in years and have requested retirement,
a request that is truly difficult to refuse.
Therefore, I now grant you permission to return to your residence as a Marquis,
your position ranking above the three highest officials (Sān Sī).
Your salary and emoluments shall be as before.
I bestow upon you a small table and a staff, allowing you not to attend court, and one residential compound.
The great affairs of the state
will still be discussed with you,
to align with my intentions.”
A little over a year later, he passed away
at the age of ninety-one.
His posthumous title was Yuán.
Shí was poor in his youth,
traveling on foot with a staff,
and wherever he stopped to rest,
he never inconvenienced his hosts.
Matters of firewood and water
he always managed himself.
Even when he attained high office and prominence,
he always favored simplicity and frugality,
not valuing extravagance.
Once, he visited Shí Chóng’s house,
and when he went to the latrine,
