he saw crimson-patterned curtains,
and the cushions and bedding were very luxurious,
with two maids holding incense pouches.
Shí immediately withdrew
and smilingly said to Chóng:
“I mistakenly entered your inner quarters.”
Chóng said:
“That is just the latrine.”
Shí replied:
“A poor scholar like me has never encountered such a thing.”
He then went to another latrine.
Though he enjoyed honor and favor,
he had no grand mansion for a residence.
The emoluments he received
he used to assist his relatives and old friends.
Even though the ritual teachings were in decline,
he conducted himself with rectitude.
Upon his wife’s death, he observed the customary three-year mourning period with a mourning hut and a staff,
and did not engage in marital relations throughout the mourning period.
Light-minded people laughed at him,
but Shí did not take it to heart.
From youth to old age,
he was diligent in his studies and never tired,
even while holding office,
books were never out of his hands.
He was particularly skilled in the Three Commentaries (Sān Zhuàn),
correcting and clarifying the Gōng Yáng.
He argued that Wèi Zhé should not have resigned his position citing his grandfather’s (Wáng Fù) command,
and Jì Zhòng failed in the proper conduct of a minister.
He used these two points to illustrate the proper demeanor of a minister or son,
and these views became widely accepted.
He also compiled the Chūnqiū Tiáolì in twenty volumes.
He had two sons,
Jī and Xià.
Jī, courtesy name Jǐngyún,
rose to the office of Sànqí Chángshì.
Xià was cast out for corruption and greed.
His younger brother, Zhì, courtesy name Zǐfáng,
was pure and simple, possessing the demeanor of his elder brother.
Poor in his youth,
he often carried firewood to support himself,
and studied and recited without ceasing,
eventually becoming known for his Confucian conduct.
He successively served as Zhōngshū Huángmén Lìbù Láng
and was dispatched as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
Guǎn Lù of Píngyuán once told people:
“When I converse with Liú Yǐngchuān (Zhì) and his brother,
it makes one’s spirit clear and vibrant,
and prevents sleep even when tired.
Other than that,
I almost want to nap even in broad daylight.”
He returned to serve as Mìshū Jiān,
also holding the post of Nányáng Wáng Shī,
and was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
then transferred to Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, and Tàicháng.
He authored the Sāngfú Shìyí Lùn,
clarifying many points.
He died at the end of Tàikāng.
His posthumous title was Chéng.
Gāo Guāng
Gāo Guāng, courtesy name Xuānmào,
was a native of Yǔchéng, Chénliú,
and the son of Wèi Tàiwèi Ròu.
Guāng studied his family profession from a young age,
excelling in and understanding penal law.
Initially, he served as Tàizǐ Shèrén and was successively promoted to Shàngshū Láng,
then dispatched as Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ and Yǐngzhōu Tàishǒu.
At that time, Emperor Wǔ established the Huángshā Prison
to manage imperial prisoners.
Because Guāng had a family history of understanding the law,
he was appointed Huángshā Yùshǐ,
his rank equivalent to that of Zhōngchéng.
He was promoted to Tíngwèi.
In the Yuánkāng era,
he was appointed Shàngshū,
managing the affairs of the Sān Gōng.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped power,
Guāng, at that critical moment,
upheld his principles and maintained his integrity.
After Lún was ordered to commit suicide,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng assisted in governance,
and Guāng was again appointed Tíngwèi,
then promoted to Shàngshū,
and given the additional title of Fèngchē Dūwèi.
Later, he followed the imperial carriage in the campaign against Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng and rendered meritorious service,
for which he was enfeoffed as Yánlíng Xiàn Gōng,
with a stipend of one thousand eight hundred households.
At that time, the imperial court universally praised Guāng for his clear application of the law,
thus he frequently presided over judicial offices.
When Emperor Huì was coerced by Zhāng Fāng
and sought refuge in Cháng’ān,
the court officials scattered,
with none following him.
Guāng alone attended the emperor to the west.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè,
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
Guāng’s elder brother, Dàn, was employed by Shàngguān Sì and others,
and successively served as Cìshǐ of Xú and Yōng prefectures.
Dàn was unrestrained and unconventional by nature,
but resolute and outstanding,
with a different character from Guāng.
He often considered Guāng to be petty
and treated him with contempt,
but Guāng served Dàn even more respectfully.
After the emperor returned to Luòyáng,
the Crown Prince (Tàidì) had just been established,
and experienced tutors were being sought.
Guāng was appointed Shàofù,
and given the additional title of Guānglù Dàfū,
his Chángshì post remaining as before.
When Emperor Huái ascended the throne,
he was given the additional titles of Guānglù Dàfū with a golden seal and purple ribbon,
and was highly esteemed alongside Fù Zhī.
Soon after, he became Shàngshū Lìng,
his original offices remaining unchanged.
He died of illness
and was posthumously granted the titles Sīkōng and Shìzhōng.
Due to the fall of Jīng Luò,
he was never formally granted a posthumous title.
His son, Tāo, courtesy name Zǐyuǎn,
was dissolute and undisciplined.
When Guāng was Tíngwèi,
Tāo accepted bribes,
and officials impeached him,
but Guāng was unaware.
Although people criticized Guāng for failing to restrain his son,
they did not hold it against him because of his consistently upright character.
He was not burdened by it.
Originally,
when Guāng went to the Liútái in Cháng’ān,
Tāo was concurrently appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Tāo associated with petty individuals in the palace and government offices,
and after Guāng’s death,
he continued to frequent them even during the mourning period.
At that time, Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè was assisting in governance but did not attend court.
Tāo knew that people were hopeful (for a change),
and secretly plotted with Tàifù Cānjūn Jiāng Zé and Jīngzhào Dù Gài and others to attack Yuè.
The plot was exposed,
and he was arrested and executed.
The imperial historian says: Lesser men compete and adorn themselves,
the mediocre are quiet and plain,
but they are not as good as those who, when advancing, find themselves insufficient, and when retreating, find themselves having more than enough.
Wèi Shū and Liú Shí made profound deliberations,
entered officialdom,
and by their mere presence accomplished tasks.
Jì Hé (Gāo Guāng) asked incisive questions and gave prompt responses,
and in office maintained an upright demeanor.
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says,
“A greedy man ruins his kind.”
Is this not referring to Liú Xià!
Eulogy: Shū spoke without boast,
and delighted in conversing with a lord of a thousand chariots.
Zǐzhēn (Liú Shí) and Xuānmào (Gāo Guāng),
their noble aspirations were hard to diminish.
Advancing, they were capable of proposing loyalty;
retreating, their humility emerged.
Like brilliant coral vessels,
they brought light to the celestial rope (the imperial court).

Biographies, Volume Twelve: Wáng Hún (son Jì)
Wáng Hún
was a native of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His father, Chǎng,
was the Sīkōng of Wèi.
Hún was calm, elegant, and had great capacity.
He inherited his father's title of Jīnglíng Hóu,
and was appointed clerk to Grand General Cáo Shuǎng.
When Shuǎng was executed,
he was dismissed in accordance with regulations.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Huái,
and participated in Emperor Wén's military affairs for the Āndōng army.
He was successively promoted to Sànqí Huángmén Shìláng and Sànqí Chángshì.
During the Xiánxī era, he was Yùqí Xiàowèi.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he was given the additional title of Yángliè Jiāngjūn,
and promoted to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, there was a famine,
and Hún opened the granaries to provide relief,
which the common people relied on.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
his enfeoffment was increased by 1,800 households.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Dōngzhōnglángjiàng,
supervising military affairs north of the Huái River,
stationed in Xǔchāng.
He frequently submitted memorials on what was beneficial and what was detrimental,
many of which were adopted.
He was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Supervisor of Military Affairs in Yùzhōu, given the provisional staff (jiǎjié),
and concurrently served as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Hún's territory bordered Wú,
and he promulgated his might and trustworthiness,
leading to many surrenders and affiliations both before and after.
Wú generals Xuē Yíng and Lǔ Shú commanded a force of 100,000 men.
Shú advanced towards Yìyáng,
and Yíng towards Xīnxī.
At that time, the provincial troops had all been released for rest,
numbering only one brigade.
Crossing the Huái River stealthily,
he took them by surprise.
Yíng and others did not anticipate the arrival of the Jìn army.
Hún attacked and defeated them,
and for this merit, his second son, Shàng, was enfeoffed as Guānnèihóu.
He was promoted to Āndōng Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Military Affairs in Yángzhōu,
stationed in Shòuchūn.
The Wú people established large farms in Wǎnchéng,
planning to create border problems.
Hún dispatched Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Yīng Chuò to lead the Huáinán armies to attack and destroy them,
and also broke various other garrisons,
burning over 1.8 million hù of accumulated grain, more than 4,000 qǐng of rice seedlings, and over 600 boats.
Hún then deployed his troops on the eastern frontier,
observing the terrain's dangers and ease,
and examining the enemy's cities,
assessing the feasibility of attack and capture.
When the great expedition to conquer Wú was launched,
Hún led his army out from Héngjiāng.
He sent staff officer Chén Shèn and Colonel Zhāng Qiáo to attack Xúnyáng Lài Xiāng.
He also attacked the Wú gate general Kǒng Zhōng,
defeating them all,
and capturing five Wú generals, including Zhōu Xìng.
He also sent Tǐnwú Hùjūn Lǐ Chún to hold Gāowàng Chéng,
and attack Wú general Yú Gōng,
defeating him,
and achieving many beheadings and captures.
Wú generals Lìwǔ Jiāngjūn Chén Dài and Pínglǔ Jiāngjūn Zhū Míng were afraid and surrendered.
Wú Chancellor Zhāng Tì and Grand General Sūn Zhèn led tens of thousands of troops towards Chéngyáng.
Hún sent Sīmǎ Sūn Chóu and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Jùn to attack and defeat them,
beheading the two generals on the battlefield,
and capturing 7,800 heads and prisoners.
The Wú people were greatly shaken.
Sūn Hào's Sītú Hé Zhí and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Sūn Yàn sent their seals and credentials to Hún to surrender.
Later, Wáng Jùn broke Shítóu,
and received Sūn Hào's surrender,
his prestige greatly increasing.
The next day,
Hún finally crossed the Jiāng River,
ascended the palace in Jiànyè,
and held a grand banquet with wine.
He considered that he had first occupied the area along the river,
defeated Hào's central army,
but had withheld his forces and not advanced,
leading to his coming after Wáng Jùn.
He felt very ashamed and resentful,
showing signs of discontent,
and frequently submitted memorials detailing Jùn's offenses,
which people at the time ridiculed him for.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"His Excellency, with the staff of authority, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs in Yángzhōu, Āndōng Jiāngjūn, and Jīnglíng Hóu Wáng Hún,
commanded his forces,
and successfully pressed upon Mòlíng,
forcing the bandit Sūn Hào to fight for his life to defend himself,
and preventing him from diverting troops to support the west,
thus ensuring the success of the western army.
He also crushed a great enemy,
captured Zhāng Tì,
rendering Hào's path exhausted and his power spent,
forcing him to bind himself and beg for surrender.
He then pacified Mòlíng,
his meritorious achievements being outstanding.
His enfeoffment is increased by 8,000 households,
his peerage advanced to Gōng.
His son Chéng is enfeoffed as Tínghóu, and his younger brother Zhàn as Guānnèihóu,
and 8,000 bolts of silk are bestowed. "
He was transferred to Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn,
and again stationed in Shòuyáng.
Hún did not value harsh punishments,
and his judgments were clear and fair.
At that time, the Wú people had newly submitted,
and were quite fearful.
Hún comforted and guided the itinerants,
and with an open mind, pacified and welcomed them.
His seats were never empty,
and his gate never stopped guests.
Thus, all the scholars of Jiāngdōng were pleased and submitted.
Zhēng was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and was granted Sànqí Chángshì.
When the court officials debated that Qí Wáng Yōu should go to his fiefdom,
Hún submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly learn of the imperial edict,
which, in accordance with classical precedents,
promotes Qí Wáng Yōu to be a senior duke,
exalts his ceremonies,
and sends Yōu to his state.
In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty founded its state,
it extensively enfeoffed members of the Jī clan,
to serve as a bulwark for the imperial house,
establishing an eternal precedent.
As for Gōng Dàn,
King Wǔ's younger brother,
he assisted in royal affairs,
aiding in the great enterprise,
and was not sent to a fiefdom.
This clearly shows that his close kinship and merits were evident,
and he could not be kept far from the court.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhōu was able to, with his sagely virtue, brightly assist the young ruler,
his loyalty and sincerity recorded in the Jīnténg,
gloriously describing the benevolent and sagely virtues of Kings Wén and Wǔ.
Yōu, to the great Jìn,
is kin like Jī Dàn.
He ought to assist the imperial court,
participate in political affairs,
truly serving as His Majesty's most trusted and unwavering minister.
Moreover, Yōu's character is
pure, righteous, and trustworthy;
furthermore, being of esteemed kinship,
his ambition lies in loyalty and integrity.
Now, Your Majesty sends Yōu to his state,
grants him a nominal title of Dūdū,
but without the practical responsibilities of commanding military affairs or managing the region,
separating him from the imperial court,
and preventing him from participating in royal governance.
This wounds the bond of the closest kinship of a younger brother,
and diminishes the profound affection between brothers.
I fear this is not consistent with Your Majesty's original intention of honoring the late emperor and Empress Dowager Wénmíng's treatment of Yōu.
If it is believed that Yōu's prestige is great,
and it is appropriate for him to leave,
then Rǔnán Wáng Liàng could replace Yōu.
Liàng
is the son of Emperor Xuān and
the brother of Emperor Wén.
Zhòu and Jùn each hold important posts,
possessing resources both internal and external.
Considering future concerns,
this is not a trivial matter.
Yōu's departure to his state now
will only serve to foster dissenting opinions,
thus diminishing the beauty of Your Majesty's benevolence and compassion.
And it will make the world perceive that Your Majesty lacks the sentiment of cherishing kin;
I humbly believe this is not advantageous for Your Majesty.
If one relies on the foreign relatives of empresses and consorts
to manage court affairs, then there are the dangers of the Wáng clan usurping the Hàn's power,
and Lǚ Chǎn monopolizing court authority.
If one relies on close kin of the same surname,
then there is the calamity of Wú and Chǔ and the Seven States' rebellion.
Looking through ancient and modern history,
no matter whether the matter is light or grave,
wherever such reliance occurs, it invariably leads to harm.
It is impossible to meticulously guard against every single possibility,
fearing future troubles;
one should only adhere to the righteous path and seek loyal and good individuals.
If one uses cunning and suspicion to distrust others,
even close relatives will be doubted;
how then can distant ones feel secure?
When people harbor fear and insecurity,
it is not a principle for peace.
This is what those who possess a state and a family deeply guard against.
I foolishly believe that since the position of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo is vacant,
it would be appropriate to keep Yōu to occupy it,
and together with Tàiwèi Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and Wèi Jiāngjūn Yáng Yáo,
serve as tutors and assist in managing court affairs.
With the three holding equal rank,
they would be able to uphold righteousness mutually;
in advancement, they would have the benefit of assisting and broadening good counsel,
and in retreat, there would be no tendency for one to become dominant and overpower the others.
This would allow Your Majesty to show profound grace to kin,
and enable Yōu to receive the benefit of benevolent protection.
As your subject, I share in the nation's joys and sorrows,
and it is my duty to speak exhaustively.
What I perceive in my heart,
I cannot keep silent about.
I privately admire the Lǔ maiden's ambition to preserve her state,
and thus dare to present my foolish opinions,
risking offending Your Celestial Majesty.
I wish Your Majesty's actions to always be perfect,
hoping for even a ten-thousandth part of assistance.
If I, your subject, do not speak,
who then will speak?"
The emperor did not accept it.
At the beginning of Tàixī,
he was transferred to Sītú.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was granted Shìzhōng,
and moreover, military officers were stationed in Jīnglíng,
similar to Suīlíng.
After Yáng Jùn was executed,
and old ministers were highly esteemed,
Hún was granted soldiers.
Hún, as a Sītú, was a civil official,
whose main duty was record-keeping and not commanding soldiers.
Those who held soldiers were subordinate officers in crimson robes.
Believing that he had temporarily gained the privilege of commanding soldiers due to imperial favor,
and that this was not an old custom,
he ordered all his soldiers to wear black uniforms.
Commentators praised his humility and understanding of protocol.
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi was about to harm Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and others,
Gōngsūn Hóng advised Wěi, saying:
"In the past, when Emperor Xuān deposed Cáo Shuǎng,
he invited Tàiwèi Jiǎng Jì to ride in his carriage,
to increase his prestige.
Your Highness is now undertaking an extraordinary action;
it is fitting to secure someone of long-standing reputation
to suppress the hearts of the multitude.
Sītú Wáng Hún has long enjoyed prestige,
and is trusted and respected by the three armies.
You can invite him to ride in your carriage,
so that the public will have something to rely on."
Wěi followed this advice.
Hún feigned illness and returned to his residence,
closing his gates and resisting Wěi with over a thousand household soldiers.
Wěi dared not press him.
Soon after, Wěi was executed for issuing a false edict,
and Hún then led his soldiers to the official residence.
The emperor once consulted Hún on the propriety of enquiring about the customs of the commanderies and states from their annual reporting officials during the New Year's court assembly.
Hún memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty is revered, enlightened, and sagacious,
illuminating near and far.
Your enlightened edict, humble and profound,
seeks advice from even the common folk.
This is like King Wén of Zhōu consulting widely,
and Confucius not disdaining to ask questions of inferiors.
In the past, during the New Year's court assembly, before the third audience, the reporting officials would go to the imperial presence,
the Shìzhōng would read the edict,
and the reporting officials would kneel to receive it.
I believe that the text of the edict has been transmitted for a long time,
with no new content,
and does not reflect Your Majesty's intention to pay attention to the various regions.
It would be permissible to have the Zhōngshū publicly announce an enlightened edict,
asking about similarities and differences in local customs,
outstanding talents,
prevailing trends and preferences,
the fundamental matters of agriculture and sericulture,
whether there are any unjust imprisonments in criminal cases,
and whether officials are oppressing the people.
For those who are diligent in governance and transformation, promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
they should be provided with paper and brush,
to fully express their views.
This would show Your Majesty's sagely intention to care for all four directions,
no longer merely following conventional phrases.
Furthermore, by observing their answers and literary style,
one can assess the true talent of the reporting officials.
Also, during the late emperor's time,

after the main assembly, the chief clerks and military advisors of the governors and generals, the ministers of the various kingdoms, and the regional inspectors of the various prefectures were seen in the Eastern Hall.
If it is not possible to see them separately now,
they could come before the imperial presence,
and have the Shìzhōng proclaim questions,
to thoroughly examine the various regions,
which would be convenient for affairs."
The emperor agreed.
He also issued an edict for Hún to oversee the affairs of the Shàngshū.
In all the positions Hún held,
he achieved renown both before and after;
but when he served as a grand assistant, his reputation diminished daily.
He died in the seventh year of Yuánkāng
at the age of seventy-five.
His posthumous title was Yuán.
His eldest son Shàng died young,
and his second son Jì inherited.
Wáng Jì 王濟, courtesy name Wǔzǐ 武子.
In his youth, he possessed exceptional talent,
with a distinguished and heroic demeanor,
and a spirit that outshone his contemporaries.
He excelled in archery and horsemanship,
possessed extraordinary courage and strength,
was skilled in the *Yìjīng* 易經 and the teachings of Zhuāngzǐ 莊子 and Lǎozǐ 老子,
and had outstanding literary talent.
His artistic skills surpassed others.
He was famous in his time,
and was equally renowned with his brother-in-law Hé Qiáo 和嶠 and Péi Kǎi 裴楷.
He married the Chángshān 常山 Princess.
At the age of twenty,
he began his career by being appointed Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎,
but resigned due to his mother's mourning.
He was then appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍,
and successively promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中.
He was ranked alongside Shìzhōng Kǒng Xún 孔恂, Wáng Xún 王恂, and Yáng Jì 楊濟,
and was considered a brilliant figure of his time.
Emperor Wǔ 武dì once gathered the highest officials and regional governors at Shìgān Diàn 式乾殿.
He looked at Jì 濟 and Xún 恂 and said to the assembled officials,
“My left and right attendants can truly be described as `xún xún jí jí 恂恂濟濟`!”
Whenever he attended the emperor,
he never failed to discuss people, events, and the successes and failures of state affairs.
Jì 濟 was skilled in pure conversation (qīngyán 清言),
and polished his rhetoric.
In his admonitions, discussions, and compliance,
no other court official could surpass him.
The emperor increasingly favored and respected him.
Although his advancement was rapid,
critics did not attribute it to his status as the imperial son-in-law,
but all agreed that his talent earned it.
However, though he appeared magnanimous and refined on the outside,
he was often jealous and harsh on the inside,
and liked to hurt others with his words.
His peers consequently thought little of him for this.
Because of his father,
he constantly disparaged Wáng Jùn 王濬,
which was criticized by public opinion at the time.
When Qí Wáng Yōu 齊王攸 was about to depart for his fiefdom,
Jì 濟 not only submitted a petition,
but also repeatedly sent the princess and Zhēn Dé 甄德’s wife, Chángguǎng Gōngzhǔ 長廣公主, to enter together,
bowing and weeping to plead with the emperor to keep Yōu 攸.
The emperor angrily said to Shìzhōng Wáng Róng 王戎,
“Brothers are the closest kin.
Now, sending out the King of Qí 齊 is
my own family matter.
Yet Zhēn Dé 甄德 and Wáng Jì 王濟 repeatedly send their wives to cry loudly!”
For this act of defiance,
he was demoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ 國子祭酒,
but retained his position as Chángshì 常侍.
Several years later,
he re-entered the court as Shìzhōng 侍中.
At that time, Hún 渾 was Púyè 僕射,
and some officials handled matters improperly.
Jì 濟, with his stern and rigorous nature, enforced the law strictly upon them.
He had always been at odds with his cousin, Yòu 佑.
Yòu 佑’s faction often said that Jì 濟 neglected his father,
which led to long-standing disagreements.
He was appointed Hénán Yǐn 河南尹,
but before he could take office,
he was dismissed for whipping a royal official.
At this point, Wáng Yòu 王佑 began to gain trust and appointment.
Jì 濟 was consequently ostracized and banished.
Thus, he moved his residence to the foot of Běimáng Shān 北芒山.
He was extravagant by nature,
wearing splendid clothes and eating luxurious food.
At that time, land in Luòjīng 洛京 was very expensive.
Jì 濟 bought land for a horse-racing track,
and covered it with money.
Contemporaries called it
“Jīngōu 金溝” (Golden Ditch).
Wáng Kǎi 王愷, the emperor's maternal uncle, was also extravagant.
He had an ox named
“Bābǎilǐ Bó 八百里駁,”
whose hooves and horns he constantly polished.
Jì 濟 proposed a bet of ten million coins to shoot arrows against the ox.
Kǎi 愷, confident in his own ability,
told Jì 濟 to shoot first.
With one shot, he hit the target.
He then sat on a folding stool
and ordered his attendants to quickly bring the ox's heart.
It arrived shortly,
and he cut a slice and left.
Hé Qiáo 和嶠 was extremely frugal.
His family had good plums.
When the emperor asked for some,
he gave no more than a few dozen.
Jì 濟 waited until Qiáo 和嶠 was on duty,
then led a group of young men to the orchard,
ate all the plums,
chopped down the trees, and left.
The emperor once visited his residence.
The feast was extremely abundant,
all served in琉璃 liúlí (glazed) vessels.
The steamed pig's trotter was exquisite.
The emperor asked the reason.
He replied,
“It was steamed with human milk.”
The emperor's expression turned very displeased.
He left before finishing the meal.
Jì 濟 was skilled at understanding horses.
He once rode a horse
wearing a continuous protective mud-guard.
There was water ahead,
but the horse refused to cross.
Jì 濟 said,
“This must be because it cherishes the mud-guard.”
He had someone remove it,
and the horse immediately crossed.
Therefore, Dù Yù 杜預 said Jì 濟 had a horse obsession.
The emperor once said to Hé Qiáo 和嶠,
“I will scold Jì 濟 first, then grant him official rank.
What do you think?”
Qiáo 和嶠 said,
“Jì 濟 is sharp and quick-witted,
I'm afraid he cannot be subdued.”
The emperor then summoned Jì 濟
and reprimanded him sternly.
Afterwards, he said,
“Do you feel ashamed?”
Jì 濟 replied,
“The ballad of a `chǐ bù dòu sù 尺布斗粟` (foot of cloth, peck of millet)
has always been a disgrace to Your Majesty.
Others can make kin distant and strangers close,
but I cannot make kin 친 친 (affectionate toward kin).
This is what I am ashamed of before Your Majesty.”
The emperor remained silent.
The emperor once played *yì* 奕 (go) with Jì 濟.
Sūn Hào 孫晧 was at his side.
The emperor said to Hào 晧,
“Why do you like to peel people's faces?”
Hào 晧 replied,
“When I see someone disrespectful to their lord, I peel their face.”
Jì 濟 at that moment stretched his leg under the board,
and Hào 晧 was mocking him.
Soon after, he was appointed Táibó 太僕 in plain clothes.
At forty-six,
he died before Hún 渾.
He was posthumously granted the title Piàojí Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍.
When he was about to be buried,
all the eminent scholars of the time attended.
Sūn Chǔ 孫楚 greatly respected Jì 濟.
When he arrived late,
he wept bitterly,
and all the guests were moved to tears.
After weeping,
he turned to the spirit bed and said,
“You always liked my donkey braying.
I will do it for you.”
His posture and voice were remarkably realistic,
and all the guests laughed.
Chǔ 楚 looked around and said,
“Why do none of you gentlemen die,
but allow Wáng Jì 王濟 to die instead!”
Originally,
when Jì 濟 married the princess,
she was blind in both eyes,
and exceptionally jealous.
However, she bore no sons.
He had two illegitimate sons.
Zhuó 卓, courtesy name Wénxuān 文宣,
inherited Hún 渾’s noble title
and was appointed Jǐshì Zhōng 給事中.
The second son, Yù 聿,
courtesy name Màoxuān 茂宣,
succeeded to the princess's enfeoffment as Mǐnyáng Hóu 敏陽侯.
Jì 濟 had two younger brothers:
Chéng 澄, courtesy name Dàoshēn 道深,
and Wèn 汶, courtesy name Màoshēn 茂深.
Both were eloquent, intelligent, and talented,
and both held prominent official positions.
Wáng Jùn 王濬
Wáng Jùn 王濬, courtesy name Shìzhì 士治,
was a native of Hóngnóng Hú 弘農湖.
His family had held positions of two thousand *shí* 石 for generations.
Jùn 濬 extensively studied the ancient classics,
and had a handsome appearance.
He did not cultivate a reputation for integrity,
and was not praised by his local community.
Later, he changed his ways,
becoming open-minded, clear-sighted, and broad-minded, with great ambitions.
He once built a residence,
and made the road in front of his gate several tens of *bù* 步 wide.
Someone asked him why it was so excessive.
Jùn 濬 replied,
“I want it to accommodate long halberds and banners.”
Everyone laughed at him,
but Jùn 濬 said,
“Chén Shèng 陳勝 had a saying,
‘How can a swallow or sparrow know the ambitions of a swan or goose?’”
The provincial and commandery governments invited Wáng Jùn to serve as an assistant in Hédōng.
If any prefects or magistrates were not incorruptible,
they would, at the mere mention of his reputation, resign and depart.
The Inspector of Yān Guó, Xú Miǎo, had a daughter who was talented and virtuous,
but not yet married.
Xú Miǎo then convened a grand assembly of his subordinates,
and had his daughter observe them from within.
The daughter pointed to Jùn and told her mother,
and Xú Miǎo subsequently married her to him.
Later, he participated in the military affairs of the Commander of the Southern Expedition,
Yáng Hù, who deeply appreciated and respected him.
Yáng Hù's nephew, Jì, reported to Yáng Hù:
"Jùn is too ambitious as a person,
extravagant and unrestrained,
he should not be given sole responsibility;
there should be some means to curb him."
Yáng Hù said:
"Jùn has great talent,
and will achieve what he desires;
he can certainly be employed."
He was transferred to the position of Attendant Officer of Chēqí,
and those who understood the situation said that Yáng Hù could be called one who was capable of promoting the good.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Bā Jùn.
The commandery bordered the territory of Wú,
and the soldiers suffered from arduous labor,
so many male infants were not raised.
Wáng Jùn then strictly enforced regulations,
eased their labor service and taxes,
and granted rest and exemption to those who had births;
several thousand people were thus saved.
He was transferred to become Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn,
where he extended kindness and implemented good governance,
and the common people relied on him.
One night, Wáng Jùn dreamt that three knives were suspended from the beam of his sleeping chamber,
and after a moment, one more knife was added.
Wáng Jùn awoke with a start,
feeling very ill at ease.
His Chief Clerk, Lǐ Yì, bowed twice and congratulated him, saying:
"Three knives form the character '州' (zhōu, meaning province).
With one more added,
will the enlightened lord perhaps preside over Yì Zhōu?"
Soon after, the bandit Zhāng Hóng killed the Inspector of Yì Zhōu, Huángfǔ Yàn,
and Wáng Jùn was indeed transferred to become Inspector of Yì Zhōu.
Wáng Jùn devised strategies,
executed Zhāng Hóng and others,
and for his meritorious service was enfeoffed as Marquis within the Pass.
He conciliated and brought together various ethnic groups,
treating them with both authority and trust,
and many barbarians from beyond the frontier
came to submit.
He was summoned and appointed General of the Right Guard,
then made Grand Minister of Agriculture.
General of Chēqí Yáng Hù, who had always known Wáng Jùn possessed extraordinary strategies,
secretly memorialized to retain Wáng Jùn,
and so he was again appointed Inspector of Yì Zhōu.
Emperor Wǔ planned to attack Wú,
and issued an edict commanding Wáng Jùn to repair warships.
Wáng Jùn then constructed large ships and linked rafts,
each measuring one hundred twenty paces square,
capable of holding over two thousand men.
He used wood to construct city walls,
erected towers and turrets,
and opened four gates,
through which horses could gallop back and forth.
He also painted the heads of éjì birds and monstrous beasts on the prows of the ships,
to intimidate the river gods.
The grandeur of these vessels
was unprecedented in history.
Wáng Jùn built ships in Shǔ,
and the wooden ship-parts floated down the river, blocking it.
Gú Yàn, the Grand Administrator of Wú's Jiànpíng, gathered the floating parts and presented them to Sūn Hào, saying:
"Jìn must have a plan to attack Wú;
we should increase the troops at Jiànpíng.
If Jiànpíng does not fall,
they will ultimately not dare to cross."
Sūn Hào did not heed him.
Soon after, based on a rumor, Wáng Jùn was appointed General of Lóngxiáng and Supervisor of all military affairs in Liáng and Yì.
The account is in the biography of Yáng Hù.
At that time, the court council all advised against attacking Wú,
but Wáng Jùn then submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have repeatedly inquired into the differences between Wú and Chǔ;
Sūn Hào is dissolute, tyrannical, and perverse,
and the wise and foolish alike in Jīng and Yáng all sigh with resentment.
Moreover, observing the current circumstances,
it is advisable to swiftly undertake the expedition.
If we do not attack now,
heavenly changes are difficult to predict.
Should Sūn Hào suddenly die,
and a worthy ruler be established in his place,
with civil and military officials each finding their appropriate positions,
then they would become a formidable enemy.
I have been building ships for seven years,
and they are decaying day by day.
Furthermore, I am already seventy years old,
and my death is not far off.
If any of these three conditions are not met,
then it will be difficult to plan.
I earnestly wish Your Majesty not to miss this opportunity."
The Emperor deeply accepted his advice.
Jiǎ Chōng and Xún Xù repeatedly advised against it, believing it to be impossible,
but only Zhāng Huá strongly urged it.
Also, Dù Yù submitted a memorial requesting it,
and the Emperor then issued an edict,
dispatching various regional commanders to oversee the operations.
Wáng Jùn then commanded the troops.
Those whom he had saved and nurtured earlier in Bā Jùn
were all capable of corvée labor and military service,
and their parents admonished them, saying:
"Lord Wáng Jùn gave you life;
you must strive diligently,
and not fear death!"
In the first month of the first year of Tàikāng,
Wáng Jùn departed from Chéngdū,
leading the Supervising Military Commander of Bādōng and General of Guǎngwǔ, Táng Bīn, to attack Wú's Dānyáng.
They captured it,
and seized its Dānyáng Supervisor, Shèng Jì.
The Wú people, at the dangerous shoals and vital points of the river,
had horizontally blocked it with iron chains,
and also made iron spikes more than ten feet long,
covertly placed them in the river,
to obstruct the ships.
Earlier,
Yáng Hù had captured a Wú spy,
and thus knew all the details of the situation.
Wáng Jùn then constructed dozens of large rafts,
also over one hundred paces square,
tied straw to form effigies of people,
dressed in armor and holding staffs,
and ordered skilled swimmers to lead with the rafts.
When the rafts encountered the iron spikes,
the spikes would get stuck in the rafts and be carried away.
He also made torches,
over ten *zhàng* long,
and dozens of *wéi* in circumference,
doused them with hemp oil,
placed them at the front of the ships,
and when they encountered the chains,
they lit the torches and burned them.
In a moment,
the molten chains broke,
and thus the ships were unobstructed.
On *gēngshēn* day of the second month,
they captured Wú's Xīlíng,
and seized its General of the South, Liú Xiàn, General of the Southern Expedition, Chéng Jù,
and Grand Administrator of Yídū, Yú Zhōng.
On *rénxū* day,
they captured the two cities of Jīngmén and Yídào,
and seized Supervising Military Commander Lù Yàn.
On *yǐchǒu* day,
they captured Lèxiāng,
and seized Naval Commander Lù Jǐng.
General of the Pacifying West, Shī Hóng, and others came to surrender.
On *yǐhài* day,
an edict was issued to promote Wáng Jùn to General of the Pacifying East, with *jiǎjié* authority, and Supervisor of all military affairs in Yì and Liáng.
Jùn, since setting out from Shǔ,
his soldiers had not shed blood,
nor had they encountered any unyielding cities.
Xiàkǒu and Wǔchāng
offered no resistance.
Thereupon, he sailed downstream, beating his oars,
directly reaching Sānshān.
Hào dispatched the Attacking General Zhāng Xiàng with a fleet of ten thousand men to resist Jùn.
Xiàng's army surrendered at the sight of their banners.
Hào heard that Jùn's army's banners, weapons, and armor
filled the sky and covered the river,
their power and might exceedingly great,
and all were struck with terror.
Following the advice of the Grandee Secretary Xuē Yíng and the Chief Secretary Hú Chōng,
he sent a surrender document to Jùn, which read:
"Sūn Hào of Wújùn bows his head in supplication, deserving death.
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty lost control,
the nine provinces were torn apart.
My ancestors, seizing the opportune moment, briefly occupied Jiāngnán,
then relied on mountains and rivers,
remaining separated from Wèi.
Now, the Great Jìn has arisen like a dragon,
its virtue covering the four seas.
I, being ignorant and weak, indulged in temporary peace,
not yet comprehending the mandate of Heaven.
Until today,
I have presumptuously troubled the Six Armies,
whose canopies and chariots have halted in the open,
journeying afar to the riverside.
The entire nation trembles in fear,
living on borrowed time.
Daring to align with the Heavenly Court,
which is broad and magnificent,
I respectfully send my self-appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhāng Kuí and others to present the seals and sashes I wear,
surrendering myself and begging for my life."
On the day Rén Yín,
Jùn entered Shítou.
Hào then prepared the rites of a defeated nation:
a plain carriage and white horse,
baring his torso and binding his face,
holding a jade disc in his mouth and leading a sheep,
with his grand officials in mourning attire
and scholars carrying coffins.
He led his self-styled Crown Prince Jǐn and Jǐn's younger brother, Prince Qí of Lǔ, and twenty-one others,
to the camp gate.
Jùn personally unbound him,
accepted the jade disc, burned the coffin,
and sent him to the capital.
He collected their maps and records,
sealed their treasuries,
and his army took nothing for themselves.
The Emperor sent an envoy to reward Jùn's army.
Originally,
the imperial decree instructed Jùn to descend to Jiànpíng
and be subject to Dù Yù's command,
and upon reaching Mòlíng,
to be subject to Wáng Hún's command.
When Yù reached Jiānglíng,
he said to his generals and commanders:
"If Jùn is able to descend to Jiànpíng,
then he will drive straight downstream,
his renown already established,
and it would be inappropriate to subject him to my command.
If he cannot overcome it,
then there will be no reason for me to issue commands."
When Jùn reached Xīlíng,
Yù wrote to him, saying:
"Since you have crushed their western bulwark,
you should directly seize Mòlíng,
punishing the rebels who have defied us for generations,
and freeing the people of Wú from their misery.
From the Jiāng into the Huái,
passing beyond the Sì and Biàn,
then upstream along the Hé,
and returning to the capital with your troops –
this would be a singular achievement for all time."
Jùn was greatly pleased and
presented Yù's letter to the throne.
When Jùn was about to reach Mòlíng,
Wáng Hún sent a message inviting him to momentarily stop to discuss matters.
Jùn hoisted his sails and headed straight,
replying:
"The wind is favorable;
I cannot anchor."
Wáng Hún had long before defeated Hào's central army,
beheading Zhāng Tì and others,
but had then halted his troops, not daring to advance.
But Jùn, pressing his advantage, accepted the surrender.
Hún felt both shame and resentment,
and so he memorialized that Jùn had defied the imperial decree and refused to accept his command,
falsely accusing him.
The proper authorities then arrested Jùn in a caged cart for an imperial summons.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but issued a decree admonishing Jùn, saying:
"To conquer a state is a weighty matter,
and there should be one clear authority.
The former decree ordered the General to be subject to the command of General of the Pacified East Hún.
Hún, having considered and planned deeply,
waited with his armor donned for the General.
How could you proceed directly,
disobeying Hún's orders,
violating regulations and pursuing personal gain,
thereby greatly losing sight of the greater principle?
The General's merits and achievements
are noted in Our heart,
but you should follow the imperial decrees
and uphold the laws of the state.
Yet, in this matter, you ultimately relied on your achievements to act willfully.
How shall We command the empire?"
Jùn submitted a memorial in his defense, saying: "I previously received an imperial decree on the Gēng Xū day which stated:
'The army, riding on its victories,
its fierce spirit growing stronger,
should press straight downstream,
directly to Mòlíng.'
On the day
I received
this decree, I immediately proceeded eastward.
Furthermore, a previous decree stated
that 'Grand Commandant Jiǎ Chōng oversees all fronts,
and all from the General who Guards the East, Zhòu, and Hún, Jùn, Bīn, etc., are
subject to Chōng's command.'
There was no text ordering me to be separately subject to Hún's command.
From the time I reached Bāqiú,
wherever I went, the enemy fell before me like grass,
knowing that Sūn Hào was in dire straits,
his power at its end.
On the fourteenth day, I reached Niúzhǔ,
two hundred *lǐ* from Mòlíng.
I made arrangements for the night,
in preparation for attacking and seizing it.
When I arrived at Sānshān,
I saw Hún's army on the north bank.
He sent a letter to me,
asking me to briefly come over
to discuss something together.
It also
did not mention that I was to be subject to his command.
My fleet, propelled by the wind,
advanced forcefully towards the enemy city.
Moreover, the arrangements made the previous night were proceeding in order.
There was no way
I could turn my ship in the midst of the long river to pass by Hún,
thereby breaking my formation.
In a short while,
Hào sent an envoy to surrender.
I immediately replied to Hún's letter,
and also copied Hào's memorial,
fully
showing it to Hún,
asking him to come quickly,
as I would await him at Shítou.
My army reached Mòlíng at midday.
It was only in the evening that I received the command from Hún, stating that I was to be subject to his command,
wishing that I
should, on the sixteenth, take all my forces
and return to surround Shítou,
to prevent Hào from escaping.
He also demanded the names of the Shǔ soldiers and all the armies of Zhènnán for inspection.
I believed that since Hào
had already arrived at the capital pavilion,
there was no reason to combine forces for an empty siege.
Moreover, the inspection of soldiers was
not something that could be done hastily,
and none of these were urgent matters at the time,
so they could not be followed.
The imperial decree
states that I suddenly abandoned clear regulations
and acted on my own authority.
Humbly reading the stern decree,
I am greatly alarmed and terrified,
not knowing where my body and life should be placed.
Not only does this old minister alone feel
anxious and burnt,
but all the three armies, high and low, have lost their spirit.
I have received the nation's grace,
my responsibility is heavy and the task great.
I always feared that the trust placed in me would not yield results,
and I would fail the Holy Court.
Therefore, I threw myself
into mortal danger,
fighting for ten thousand *lǐ*.
I received the grace of pardon and leniency,
and was allowed to act appropriately in the circumstances.
Thus, relying on your majestic power,
I fortunately succeeded.
All this is due to Your Majesty's
divine strategy and profound calculations.
I merely followed your instructions,
performing the duty of a hawk or dog.
What merit or achievement do I have to rely on and act willfully?
How would I dare to pursue personal gain and disobey the sacred decree?
I arrived at Mòlíng on the fifteenth,
while the imperial decree departed Luòyáng on the sixteenth.
The distance between them was vast,
so they could not meet.
Therefore, my culpability should be..."
I humbly ask for your understanding and forgiveness.
Supposing Sūn Hào still had the posture of a mantis raising its axe,
and I, your servant, had rashly entered with a small army alone,
and suffered losses,
then it would be permissible to punish me.
I, your servant, commanded
over eighty thousand men,
sweeping forward with victory.
Hào, with his people rebelling and his kin estranged,
had no more wings;
standing alone as an ordinary man,
he could not protect his wife and children.
Like sparrows and rats clinging to life,
he merely begged for survival.
The various armies north of the Jiāngběi, not knowing the true situation,
did not capture him early,
thus making a small error themselves.
When I, your servant, arrived and immediately captured him,
I was met with resentment and anger,
and
they all said they had guarded the bandit for a hundred days,
only for someone else to capture him.
Their words were murmuring and confused,
unfit to be heard.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū,
when a high official travels beyond the border,
he still has the authority to make independent decisions.
Although I, your servant, am foolish,
I believe the way to serve a sovereign is
only to exert myself to the utmost and be completely loyal,
striving
without regard for my own life,
accepting responsibilities according to my ability,
and adapting to circumstances as they arise.
If it benefits the state,
I should embrace it in life or death.
If one were to guard against suspicion,
to avoid blame,
this would be beneficial to
a disloyal official,
but truly not a blessing for an enlightened sovereign or the state.
I, your servant, did not assess myself,
forgetting my humble inadequacies,
but laid bare my sincere heart,
exerting my utmost,
wishing to exhaust
the strength of my limbs and body,
and moreover, with loyalty and integrity,
hoping to surely sweep away the wicked rebels,
unite the realm,
and wish for this holy era to rival the prosperity of Táng Yú.
Your Majesty roughly discerned
my foolish sincerity,
and recognized my genuine desire to serve,
thus bestowing upon me the responsibility of a regional governor,
and entrusting me with matters of conquest and pacification.
Even the trust of the lord of Yān in Yuè
Yì,
or Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn's reliance on Xiāo Hé,
could not surpass this.
Having received such profound grace,
I would not be able to repay it even in death.
Yet, with my stubborn negligence,
my actions and decisions have been inappropriate.
Your Majesty's immense grace,
and yet you have only given a stern rebuke.
I am terrified and distraught,
having no place to settle myself.
I only wish Your Majesty would understand my loyal heart.
Hún also forwarded Zhōu Jùn's letter,
saying Jùn's army obtained treasures from Wú.
Jùn stated in his memorial: "I received the imperial edict of the Rénxū year,
which forwarded the memorial from the Āndōng Jiāngjūn, the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Jùn's letter,
stating that my various armies had obtained Sūn Hào's treasures,
and also stating that my Yámén
Jiāng Lǐ Gāo had set fire to Hào's false palace."
I immediately sent a public document to the Shàngshū,
detailing the full story.
I also heard that Hún has accused and implicated me, your servant.
I, your servant, am by nature foolishly loyal.
In
all my actions and conduct,
I proceed with faith,
hoping only not to betray the spirits and gods.
The matters at Mòlíng
are all as previously reported.
However, those who hate integrity and despise uprightness
are truly numerous.
They wish to fabricate a "Nán Qí"
and weave this "Bèi Jǐn,"
openly, in this holy age,
turning white into black.
Indeed, flattering villains harming the state
has been so since ancient times.
Thus, Wú Jí brought about the downfall of Chǔ,
Zǎi Pǐ caused the ruin of Wú,
and later Shí Xiǎn
disrupted the Hàn court;
all are recorded in historical
texts
as warnings to the world.
Formerly, Yuè Yì attacked Qí,
capturing seventy cities,
yet ultimately fell victim to slander and intrigue,
escaping and fleeing.
When Yuè Yáng returned,
his baskets were filled with slanderous letters.
How much more, then, can I, your servant, with my stubborn negligence,
escape the mouths of slanderers and villains!
However, what I hope for to preserve my life
truly relies on Your Majesty's sagacity, wisdom, and reverence,
so that insidious slanders cannot
take effect.
However, I, your servant, stand alone without foundation,
having no factional support at court,
long abandoned to distant regions,
with human connections severed,
and moreover, I have incurred the hatred of powerful clans
and earned the resentment of influential families.
With a body as precarious as stacked
eggs,
I am in the path of thunder;
with a fragile nature like a silkworm cocoon or a chestnut,
I stand on the road of jackals and wolves.
When I am devoured,
how can I resist with my lips and teeth!
Indeed, to offend a superior or challenge the sovereign,
that crime can be remedied;
but to displease powerful officials,
then disaster is unpredictable.
Thus, Zhū Yún broke the balustrade,
incurring the emperor's wrath,
but Qìng Jì
saved him,
and Emperor Chéng Dì did not pursue the matter.
Wàng Zhī and Zhōu Kān displeased Shí Xiǎn;
although the entire court sighed in lament,
they died without turning back.
This is what I, your servant, greatly fear.
Now, Hún's partisans, relatives by marriage, and kin,
both within and without the court, are all firmly entrenched,
and hold positions of power.
I hear they have sent people to Luòzhōng,
who are solely engaged in forming factions and conspiracies,
whispering extremely sweet slanders,
confusing observers and listeners.
Indeed, that Zēng Shēn did not commit murder
is already clear,
yet when three people reported it,
his mother threw away her shuttle.
Now, my [your servant's] reputation and conduct
are not as established as Zēng
Shēn's;
yet slanders and conspiracies are boiling up,
not just from three men speaking,
but with support from both inside and outside,
creating a widespread clamor.
Indeed, when fierce beasts block the path,
even the Qílín feels fear;
how much more, then, should I, your servant, being fragile,
not tremble with dread!
The former lord and ministers of Wú
are all still alive today;
they can be questioned and verified,
to clarify the truth.
The former false Zhōngláng Jiāng Kǒng Shū said that
in the second month of the previous year, Wǔchāng fell,
and the navy arrived.
When Hào inspected Shítou and returned,
his attendants all brandished their swords and loudly shouted:
"We must fight to the death for Your Majesty to decide this!"
Hào was
greatly pleased,
believing they would surely do so.
He then distributed all his gold and treasures
to them.
The scoundrels, without propriety,
took them and immediately ran off.
Hào was frightened,
and then planned to surrender.
As soon as the envoy of surrender
left,
Hào's attendants looted his valuables,
seized his wives and concubines,
and set fire to the palace.
Hào fled and hid,
fearing he would not escape death.
When I, your servant, arrived,
I dispatched a Cānjūn in charge
to extinguish the fire.
Zhōu Jùn entered Hào's palace sixteen days prior.
At that time, I, your servant, sent a records clerk to inspect the books,
but Jùn had him arrested and bound.
If anything was left
As for the treasures,
Wáng Jùn previously obtained them.
It is inappropriate to shift the blame to later arrivals,
seeking merely to escape punishment.
Previously, when I was in Sānshān, I received a letter from Wáng Jùn saying:
“Sūn Hào distributed all the treasures to his generals and soldiers,
leaving the imperial treasury almost empty.”
Yet now he again says
“chests of gold and silver,
easily
numbering in the tens of thousands,”
suspecting that my army obtained them.
His statements are contradictory,
lacking any consistency.
I, along with the army supervisor Zhāng Mù and the Administrator of Rǔnán, Féng Dǎn, and others, went together to inspect
Sūn Hào’s palace.
There was not even a mat to sit on.
The next day, I again, with Zhāng Mù and others, viewed Sūn Hào’s boats and ships.
Wáng Hún had already boarded the ship a day before me.
All the items on the ship
were
known and seen by Wáng Hún.
My inspections
all followed his;
if there were any treasures,
Wáng Hún should have obtained them.
Furthermore, my generals are usually strict,
and the soldiers are not allowed to leave their formations without authorization.
In Mòlíng, the various armies
totaled two hundred thousand men.
My army arrived first,
becoming
the master of the land.
The hearts of the people
all turned to me,
and I strictly commanded my subordinates
not to take even a single trifle.
For all transactions and exchanges,
there were guarantors and witnesses,
clearly based on contracts.
Thirteen individuals
who violated this
were all executed, which is known to the people of Wú.
Other armies roamed freely,
falsely claiming to be my army.
However, my army was generally
made up of Shuǐ people,
which fortunately served to distinguish ourselves.
Are Wáng Jùn’s generals and soldiers all Bóyí and Shúqí,
while all my armies are a gathering of Dào Zhí?
At one point, more than eight hundred
men
climbed the Shítóu Citadel to loot cloth.
My Subordinate General, Mǎ Qián, immediately captured more than twenty of them
and recorded the names of their supervising generals,
then transferred them to
Wáng Jùn
so he could deal with them himself.
But there was no reply,
leading me to suspect that they were all released,
cutting off any further investigation.
Moreover, I heard from the Wú people that
during Zhāng Tì’s battle,
only about two thousand men were killed,
yet Wáng Hún and Wáng Jùn’s public reports stated tens of thousands.
They appointed Wú Gāngzǐ as
Chief Clerk
and sent Wú Gāngzǐ to Luòyáng,
intending for him to inflate the number of decapitated heads.
You can thoroughly question Sūn Hào and his ministers
to ascertain the truth.
If it is truly as
I have heard,
then Wáng Jùn and his ilk are deceitful.
If they can deceive Your Majesty,
how could they spare me?
They claim that I have gathered Shǔ people,
not sending Sūn Hào promptly,
indicating a rebellious intent.
They also try to alarm
the Wú people,
saying that I intend to execute them all
and take their wives and children,
hoping they will rebel
so they can satisfy their personal grudges.
Since the heinous crime of rebellion
has been attributed to me,
other slanders
are
naturally to be expected.
Wáng Hún claims that I am a
“small vessel, a bottle or a chime,
who has received great imperial favor,
and been repeatedly promoted,
thereby exceeding my capabilities.”
This statement by Wáng Hún is most truthful,
and I feel ashamed and fearful upon self-reflection.
This
year’s pacification of Wú
is truly a great celebration,
but for me personally,
it has brought further blame and burden.
I lack the virtue of Mèng Cè, who tied his horse to a pillar to avoid boasting,
yet I have allowed malicious individuals
into this august court,
damaging its solemn demeanor
and tarnishing the glory of this imperial era.
It is due to my stubbornness and oversight
that this situation has arisen.
I prostrate myself in this memorial, drenched in sweat,
unable to express myself in order.
When Wáng Jùn arrived in the capital,
the relevant officials memorialized that
Wáng Jùn’s memorial failed to list the dates of the seven edicts he had received before and after,
and after the amnesty, he violated the edict by not submitting to Wáng Hún’s command,
which was greatly disrespectful,
and requested he be handed over to the Grand Judge for punishment.
The imperial edict stated:
“Wáng Jùn previously received an edict to proceed directly to Mòlíng,
and only later was he to submit to Wáng Hún’s command.
The edict was delayed,
and what was issued did not reach him,
so to equate him with someone who did not receive the edict is not reasonable.
Wáng Jùn’s failure to immediately report receiving Wáng Hún’s declaration
can be criticized.
However, Wáng Jùn rendered service in the campaign,
and one fault should not overshadow it.”
The officials further memorialized that
Wáng Jùn, after the amnesty, burned one hundred thirty-five enemy ships,
and requested he be immediately handed over to the Grand Judge for interrogation and detention.
The imperial edict stated,
“Do not interrogate.”
Wáng Jùn was appointed Grand General Who Guards the State,
leading the Commandant of Infantry.
There were only five existing commandants; the establishment of this camp began with Wáng Jùn.
The officials again memorialized that
the Grand General Who Guards the State, according to precedent,
was not a high-ranking official,
did not have a Chief Clerk,
and was not provided with official cavalry.
The edict stated that, following the precedent for generals on punitive expeditions and those guarding borders, he would be provided with five hundred large chariots,
an additional five hundred soldiers for the Grand General Who Guards the State’s camp,
one hundred personal cavalry, ten official cavalry,
and a Chief Clerk would be appointed.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xiāngyáng County,
with ten thousand households in his fief.
His son, Wáng Yí, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángxiāng Ting,
with one thousand five hundred households in his fief,
and was granted ten thousand bolts of silk,
as well as a set of clothes, three hundred thousand coins, and food.
Wáng Jùn considered his achievements great,
but he was suppressed by Wáng Hún and his son, as well as powerful magnates,
and was frequently impeached by officials.
Whenever he was granted an audience,
he would recount his efforts in the campaign
and the injustices he suffered.
Sometimes, unable to suppress his indignation,
he would leave abruptly without taking his leave.
The Emperor always tolerated him.
Fàn Tōng, Protector of Yìzhōu,
who was a relative of Wáng Jùn by marriage,
said to Wáng Jùn:
“Your achievements are indeed great,
but I regret that the way you handle these great achievements
is not entirely good.”
Wáng Jùn asked:
“What do you mean?”
Fàn Tōng replied:
“On the day you returned with your banners,
you should have worn a cap and stayed at your private residence,
never mentioning the pacification of Wú.
If anyone asked,
you should have said: ‘It is the virtue of the sagely ruler
and the strength of the many commanders;
what strength could an old man like me have?’
In this way,
even Yán Lǎo’s humility
and Gōng Suì’s elegant replies
would not surpass yours.
How could Lìn Xiàngrú have humbled Lián Pō,
and Wáng Hún not feel ashamed?”
Wáng Jùn said:
“At first, I feared the fate of Dèng Ài,
fearing that disaster would strike,
so I could not remain silent,
nor could I dismiss it from my mind.
This is my narrow-mindedness.”
At the time, everyone felt that Wáng Jùn’s achievements were great but his reward was light.
Doctor Qín Xiù, Equerry to the Crown Prince Mèng Kāng, and former Prefect of Wēn Lǐ Mì, among others, all submitted memorials arguing Wáng Jùn’s case.
The Emperor then promoted Wáng Jùn to General of the Garrison Army,
added Attendant Official,
and put him in charge of the General of the Rear Army.
Wáng Hún went to visit Wáng Jùn,
but Wáng Jùn arranged strict security and guards before receiving him.
Their mutual suspicion and caution were thus.
After Wáng Jùn 平吳 (pacified Wú),
due to his high merit and important position,
he no longer resided in his former humble dwelling,
but ate fine food and wore brocade clothes,
indulging in luxury and ease.
Those he invited and promoted
were mostly people from Shǔ,
showing that he did not forget old acquaintances.
Later, Wáng Jùn was again transferred to General of the Garrison, Kaīfǔ Yìtóng Sānsī,
with the additional title of Tèjìn,
and his positions as Sànqí Chángshì and Hòujūn Jiāngjūn remained as before.
He died in the sixth year of Tàikāng (285 CE),
at the age of eighty.
His posthumous name was Wǔ.
He was buried on Bǎigǔ Shān,
with a grandly constructed burial ground.
The burial enclosure walls were forty-five *lǐ* in circumference,
with one gate opened on each side.
Pine and cypress trees grew luxuriantly.
His son, Jǔ, succeeded him.
Jǔ's younger brother, Chàng, was
Sànqí Láng.
Chàng's son, Cuì, in the
tenth year of Tàikāng (289 CE),
Emperor Wǔ诏 ordered Cuì to marry Princess Yǐngchuān,
and he served up to the position of Wèijùn Tàishǒu.
Wáng Jùn had two grandsons,
who, after crossing the river, were not recorded in the registers.
General of the Pacified West, Huán Wēn, while garrisoned at Jiānglíng,
submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject has heard that exalting virtue and rewarding merit
are the foremost priorities in governance;
reviving the fallen and continuing the severed
are the endeavors of all kings.
Therefore, if virtue is in harmony with the times,
then the ancestral sacrifices are continued for generations;
if merit is illustrious in one era,
then blessings are bestowed upon the descendants forever.
Upon examination, the late General of the Garrison, Wáng Jùn, served in various positions, both civil and military,
combining both civil and military duties.
He assessed the enemy and secured victory,
with keen insight and decisive courage.
His righteousness lay in the benefit of the state,
disregarding the blame for unauthorized action.
He carried his spear and rode swiftly for a long distance,
sweeping across thousands of *lǐ*.
The self-proclaimed state of Wú
was bound and brought before the imperial gates.
Now, the imperial favor covers all nine provinces,
and the profound influence extends beyond the regions.
However, the enfeoffment of Xiāngyáng
has been abolished and not continued;
the titles of imperial favor
have fallen from his recent descendants.
Both far and near feel sorrow,
and your subject secretly mourns this.
Wáng Jùn now has two grandsons,
over sixty years of age,
whose homes are as empty as a hanging *qìng*,
barely making a living by the riverside.
For the four seasonal ancestral offerings,
they cannot even provide vegetable broth.
In ancient times, Emperor Gāo of Hàn, after establishing his dynasty,
sought out the descendants of Yuè Yì;
Emperor Shìzǔ, recognizing worthies,
established the lineage of Zhūgě Liàng.
Even those who demonstrated loyalty in different eras,
and achieved merit in different countries,
still had their goodness made known throughout the realm,
so that it would not be forgotten and discarded.
How much more so Wáng Jùn, who established great merit in his time,
and brought forth auspicious blessings for generations to come!
His spiritual foundation is rooted in the southern border,
and the imperial destiny was revived in the Jiangzuǒ.
The old order was prominently displayed,
and the divine implements shone anew.
Was this not due to the efforts of that man?
It is truly fitting to bestow grace,
to show a little pity and compassion,
to retrospectively recognize his former merits,
and to grant him territory.
Then the grace of the sagely court
will be widely proclaimed above,
and the aspirations of loyal ministers
will not fall to the ground."
In the end, it was not acted upon.
Táng Bīn
Táng Bīn, courtesy name Rúzōng,
was from Zōu in Lǔguó.
His father, Tái, was
Tàishān Tàishǒu.
Táng Bīn possessed great ambition for managing the state,
but was not constrained by conventional conduct.
In his youth, he was skilled with bows and horses,
and enjoyed hunting.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
could run as fast as a galloping deer,
and his strength surpassed that of others.
Later in life, he diligently studied the classics and histories,
especially excelling in the *Yìjīng*.
He studied under a teacher,
and upon returning home, he taught
hundreds of people.
Initially, he served as a clerk in the *jùn* administration,
then was transferred to Zhǔbù.
The Inspector, Wáng Shěn, gathered his advisors,
and thoroughly discussed strategies for resisting Wú,
asking the officials of the nine *jùn*.
Táng Bīn, along with the Zhǔbù of Qiáojùn, Zhāng Yùn, both argued that Wú was vulnerable to conquest.
Wáng Shěn approved of their replies.
He then had Táng Bīn debate against those who said Wú should not yet be attacked,
and all their arguments were defeated.
He returned and was promoted to Gōngcáo,
and then nominated as Xiàolián.
The province appointed him as Zhǔbù,
and he was successively promoted to Biéjià.
Táng Bīn was loyal, solemn, public-spirited, and honest,
fully offering counsel and remedies,
without making his admonitions obvious to draw attention to himself.
He was also dispatched on a mission to the Prime Minister's residence to discuss matters.
At that time, his colleagues were all leading talents of the era.
Upon meeting Táng Bīn, none failed to admire and praise him,
and they recommended him to Emperor Wén,
suggesting he be appointed as an aide.
The Emperor asked his Military Advisor, Kǒng Hào, about him.
Kǒng Hào was jealous of his ability and
did not reply for a long time.
Chén Qiān was present,
and he straightened his tablet and declared:
"Táng Bīn's character
far surpasses mine."
The Emperor smiled and said:
"Even someone like you
is not easy to find,
let alone someone who surpasses you!"
Consequently, he appointed Táng Bīn as Kǎicáo Shǔ.
The Emperor asked:
"How did you come to be appointed?"
He replied:
"I studied in humble alleys,
observing the legacy of ancient people,
who, though their words filled the world, made no errors,
and though their deeds filled the world, bore no resentment or ill will."
The Emperor looked around at those present and said:
"His reputation is not unfounded."
Another day,
he said to Kǒng Hào:
"I recently saw Táng Bīn;
you are to blame for concealing a worthy man."
Originally, when Dèng Ài was executed,
Emperor Wén, knowing that Dèng Ài had been in Lǒngyòu for a long time
and had always won the hearts of the soldiers,
feared that his sudden extermination
might stir unrest in the border regions.
He sent Táng Bīn to investigate secretly.
Upon his return, Táng Bīn reported to the Emperor:
"Dèng Ài was jealous, tyrannical, cunning, and narrow-minded.
He boasted of his ability and talent.
He considered those who followed him to be discerning,
and those who spoke frankly to be defiant.
Even his Chief Clerk, Military Advisor,
and Staff Officers, if their replies missed the point,
were immediately cursed and insulted.
His conduct lacked propriety,
and he greatly lost the support of the people.
Moreover, he was fond of implementing various projects
which frequently exhausted the people's labor.
Lǒngyòu suffered greatly from this
and rejoiced at his misfortune,
unwilling to serve him.
Now, the various armies have arrived,
which is sufficient to suppress both internal and external unrest.
Please do not worry about this."
Soon after, he was dismissed from his post as a Secretary in the Ministry of Waterways (Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng).
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he was granted the title of Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
He was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Yè (Yèlìng).
Táng Bīn's (Táng Bīn) virtue matched the rites,
and within a year, he transformed the people.
He was promoted to Governor of Yìyáng (Yìyáng Tàishǒu).
He clearly established prohibitions and defenses,
and the hundred surnames found peace.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
As Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu) bordered the Wú (Wú) rebels to the east,
the position of Inspector-General (Jiānjūn) was vacant.
The court debated between Yáng Zōng (Yáng Zōng), the Governor of Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng Tàishǒu), and Táng Bīn.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) asked Sànqí Chángshì (Sànqí Chángshì) Wén Lì (Wén Lì) about this.
Wén Lì said:
"Neither Yáng Zōng nor Táng Bīn should be lost.
However, Táng Bīn has many desires for wealth,
while Yáng Zōng is fond of wine.
Your Majesty alone must decide."
The Emperor said:
"Desires for wealth can be satisfied,
but a love for wine is difficult to change."
So, Táng Bīn was appointed.
Soon after, an edict ordered Táng Bīn to oversee all military affairs in Bādōng (Bādōng Zhūjūnshì)
and added the title of General of Guǎngwǔ (Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn).
He presented a strategy for conquering Wú,
which greatly pleased the Emperor.
Later, he joined Wáng Jùn (Wáng Jùn) in attacking Wú.
Táng Bīn garrisoned strategic points
and served as the vanguard for all armies.
He frequently deployed feigned troops,
adapting to circumstances to achieve victory.
He captured Xīlíng (Xīlíng) and Yuèxiāng (Yuèxiāng),
capturing many.
From Bālíng (Bālíng) and Miǎnkǒu (Miǎnkǒu) eastward,
wherever the rebels gathered,
none were not terrified and awe-struck,
throwing down their weapons and baring their torsos.
Táng Bīn knew that the rebel forces were almost wiped out,
and Sūn Hào (Sūn Hào) was about to surrender.
Before reaching Jiànyè (Jiànyè) by two hundred *lǐ*,
he feigned illness and delayed,
to show that he was not competing.
Indeed, those who arrived first contended for spoils,
while those who arrived later contended for merit.
At that time, all discerning people highly praised Táng Bīn's action.
After Wú was pacified,
an edict stated:
"General of Guǎngwǔ Táng Bīn was entrusted with a regional command,
defending against the Wú rebels in the east,
and facing the Mán Yuè (Mán Yuè) in the south.
He pacified and secured the borders,
achieving merits in both pacification and defense.
Moreover, he was always resolute
and determined to establish accomplishments.
During the recent campaign,
he served by imperial command despite illness,
first initiating the military advance,
presenting captives and severed heads.
His meritorious services were outstanding.
Therefore, Táng Bīn is appointed Right General (Yòujiāngjūn) and Supervisor of all military affairs in Bādōng (Dūdū Bādōng Zhūjūnshì)."
He was summoned and appointed Cavalry Commandant of the Exemplary Army (Yìjūn Xiàowèi).
His title was changed to Marquis of Shàngyōng County (Shàngyōng Xiànhóu),
with an enfeoffment of six thousand households,
and bestowed six thousand bolts of silk.
Whenever there was a difficult deliberation at court,
he always participated.
When the northern barbarians invaded Běipíng (Běipíng),

Táng Bīn was appointed Bearer of Imperial Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Inspector of all military affairs in Yōuzhōu (Jiān Yōuzhōu Zhūjūnshì), concurrently leading the Protector of the Wūhuán (Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi), and Right General.
Upon Táng Bīn's arrival at the garrison,
he trained his troops and sharpened their weapons,
promoted agriculture and valued crops,
displayed his awe-inspiring might and martial prowess,
and proclaimed the imperial commands,
showing favor and trustworthiness.
Thereupon, the two Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) tribes, Dàmòkuī (Dàmòkuī) and Zhìhé (Zhìhé), both sent their sons as hostages to offer tribute.
He also repaired schools,
teaching and guiding tirelessly,
and his benevolence and kindness were widely spread.
Consequently, he expanded the old territory,
reclaiming a thousand *lǐ* of land.
He restored the Qin (Qín) Great Wall fortresses,
from Wēnchéng (Wēnchéng) to Jiéshí (Jiéshí),
stretching continuously through mountains and valleys for nearly three thousand *lǐ*.
He divided the army to garrison them,
with beacon towers visible to one another.
Because of this, the border regions enjoyed peace,
without the alarm of a barking dog.
No commander from the Hàn (Hàn) and Wèi (Wèi) dynasties could compare.
The various Xiānbēi tribes became fearful,
and subsequently killed Dàmòkuī.
Táng Bīn wanted to attack them,
but feared that if he reported to the court and waited for a reply,
the barbarians would surely scatter and flee.
So, he mobilized chariots and cattle from Yōu (Yōu) and Jì (Jì) provinces.
His staff officer, Xǔ Zhī (Xǔ Zhī), secretly reported him in a memorial.
An imperial edict then sent an imperial censor in a cage cart to summon Táng Bīn and hand him over to the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi).
He was released because the matter was straightforward.
The hundred surnames cherished Táng Bīn's merits and virtues,
erecting steles and composing encomiums for him while he was alive.
Táng Bīn first studied under Yán Dé (Yán Dé) of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi).
Yán Dé had many disciples,
but uniquely identified Táng Bīn as having the talent for the imperial court.
By the time Táng Bīn achieved high office,
Yán Dé had already passed away,
so Táng Bīn erected a stele for him.
At the beginning of the Yuánkāng era,

he was appointed Bearer of Imperial Credentials, General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn), concurrently leading the Protector of the Western Rong (Lǐng Xīróng Xiàowèi), and Governor of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He issued an instruction stating:
"This province is a famous capital,
a haven for scholars.
Recluses such as Huángfǔ Shēnshú (Huángfǔ Shēnshú), Yán Shūlóng (Yán Shūlóng), Jiāng Màoshí (Jiāng Màoshí), and Liáng Zǐyuǎn (Liáng Zǐyuǎn),
all possess pure and subtle aspirations and conduct,
and their integrity is lofty and clean.
Upon entering this territory and hearing of their reputation,
I am sincerely eager and thirsty
to extend invitations to them,
treating them with the courtesy due to those who do not serve as officials.
I will meet them wearing a simple headscar,
discussing the Way and nothing more.
How can I, with my official duties,
compel and stain their noble principles?
The commanderies and states should prepare the proper etiquette for their dispatch,
to fulfill the hopes of the populace."
Thereupon, all four men arrived,
and Táng Bīn treated them with respect.
He died in office in the fourth year of Yuánkāng,
aged sixty.
He was posthumously granted the epithet Xiāng (Xiāng),
and bestowed two hundred bolts of silk
and two hundred thousand cash.
His eldest son, [name omitted in source] Sī (Sī),
rose to the rank of Governor of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu).
His youngest son, Qí (Qí),
was the Cavalier Commandant Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ).
The史臣 (Shǐchén) (Historian) states: The Sūn (Sūn) clan, relying on the natural barriers of rivers and mountains,
and trusting in the ominous aura of the Niu (Niú) and Dou (Dǒu) constellations,
suddenly occupied the water regions
and contended with the superior state.
The two Wángs (Wáng) were in command of the armies,
received orders and quickly set out.
Wáng Hún (Wáng Hún) presented his victory at Héngjiāng (Héngjiāng),
and Wáng Jùn (Wáng Jùn) also successfully cleared Jiànyè.
At that time, among the campaigns to conquer Wú,
though there were many generals,
the merit of pacifying Wú
was most preeminent here.
If only Wáng Hún had not boasted of his father's achievements,
and Wáng Jùn had emulated the humility of Yáng Xià (Yáng Xià) in attributing merit,
obeying the imperial court above
and relying on his officers and soldiers below,
would they not have been men of great merit and great virtue,
who began well and ended well?
If these principles are not preserved,
then what are those things they strive for?
Some boasted of their achievements and were arrogant,
or relied on their power to bully others,
competing to construct "Nan Ji" (Nán Jī) [a metaphor for empty boasting]
and creating "Bei Jin" (Bèi Jǐn) [a metaphor for internal discord and slander].
They thus disturbed and defiled the imperial court,
and disrupted the natural order of human relations.
This served as a warning to meritorious officials,
and also drew criticism from discerning opinions.
How regrettable!
Wáng Jì (Wáng Jì) indulged in his father's narrow-mindedness,
and strayed from the clear righteousness of a son who contends (for his father's good).
Though there were many talented individuals,
what good did it do?
Táng Bīn, fearing and avoiding contention,
feigned illness and delayed his advance.
This spirit of humility and yielding
was far superior to Wáng Hún and Wáng Jùn.
The biography says,
"he was not restrained by his conduct,"
how could he have the conduct of an elder?
The eulogy says: The two Wángs led the armies,
and all along the Huái (Huái) and the sea were united.
Wáng Hún harmed the good,
and Wáng Jùn boasted of his achievements.
Wǔ Zǐ (Wǔ Zǐ) was a hero,
who early on participated in court affairs.
He indulged his desires like an ox's heart,
and twisted his feelings like a horse track.
The Confucian master knew to retreat,
avoiding fame and preserving his integrity.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 13: Shān Táo (Shān Táo) (Zǐjiǎn (Zǐjiǎn); Zǐjiǎn's son Xiá (Xiá))
Shān Tāo
Zi Jùyuán was a native of Huái in Hénèi.
His father, Yào,
was the Prefect of Wǎnqú.
Shān Tāo was orphaned early
and lived in poverty.
From a young age, he possessed great capacity
and stood out from the crowd.
He had a fondness for Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
often concealing himself and remaining obscure.
He was close with Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān.
Later, he met Ruǎn Jí,
and they became friends of the Bamboo Grove,
forming a bond of "forgetting words."
Later, when Jī Kāng was implicated in an affair
and was about to be executed,
he said to his son, Shào:
"Jùyuán is here;
you will not be alone."
At the age of forty, Shān Tāo
first became the Commandery's Chief Clerk (zhǔbù), meritorious officer (gōngcáo), and clerk for taxation (shàngjì yuàn).
He was recommended as Xiaòlián,
and the province appointed him Supervisor of Hénán.
He once shared a room with Shí Jiàn.
One night, Shān Tāo got up and kicked Shí Jiàn, saying:
"What kind of time is this that you are still sleeping!
Do you know what the Grand Tutor is thinking about?"
Shí Jiàn replied:
"If a Prime Minister fails to attend court three times,
he is ordered by a brief edict to return to his mansion.
What are you worried about?"
Shān Tāo exclaimed:
"Hmph!
Is Shí Shēng idling about at the hooves of horses?!"
He threw down his document and left.
Less than two years later,
the affair of Cái Suǎng indeed occurred,
and Shān Tāo consequently withdrew, no longer involving himself in worldly affairs.
He was related to Empress Xuānmù through her maternal family,
and thus met Emperor Jǐng.
The Emperor said:
"Does Lǚ Wàng wish to serve?"
He commanded the Minister of Justice to recommend talented men (xiùcái),
and Shān Tāo was appointed Gentleman (lángzhōng).
He was transferred to become Aide-de-camp (cóngshì zhōngláng) to the General of Agile Cavalry (piáojì jiàngjūn), Wáng Chǎng.
After a long time,
he was appointed Chancellor of Zhàoguó,
and promoted to Department Director of Personnel (lìbù láng) in the Ministry of Personnel (shàngshū).
Emperor Wén wrote to Shān Tāo, saying:
"Your Excellency has been clear and upright in your duties,
your elegant conduct surpassing your contemporaries.
I consider that you are lacking in many things,
and so I now send you 200,000 cash and 200 hú of grain."
The Wèi Emperor once bestowed spring clothing upon Emperor Jǐng,
who in turn bestowed it upon Shān Tāo.
Also, because his mother was old,
he was given a li-wood staff.
Later, he befriended Shàngshū Hé Yōu,
and also developed a close relationship with Zhōng Huì and Péi Xiù.
As these two held powerful positions and vied for authority,
Shān Tāo maintained a fair and central stance,
allowing each to achieve their aims
without any resentment from either side.
He was promoted to Aide-de-camp (cóngshì zhōngláng) to the General-in-chief.
When Zhōng Huì rebelled in Shǔ,
Emperor Wén was about to march west.
At that time, all the Wèi imperial princes and dukes were in Yè.
The Emperor said to Shān Tāo:
"I will handle the western front myself;
the affairs here I deeply entrust to Your Lordship."
He was appointed Marshal (xíngjūn sīmǎ) with his original office,
given 500 personal guards,
and stationed in Yè.
At the beginning of Xiánxī,
he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Xīntà.
He was transferred to Chief Clerk of the Chancellor of State (xiàngguó zuǒ chángshǐ),
overseeing the detached camps.
At that time, the Emperor considered Shān Tāo a respected elder from his home district,
