and ordered the Crown Prince to bow to him.
The Emperor, having designated Qí Wáng Yōu as successor to Emperor Jǐng,
and also deeply valuing Yōu,
once asked Péi Xiù:
"The General-in-chief's great work was not completed,
and I merely carried on his legacy.
If I establish Yōu,
intending to attribute the merit to my brother, what do you think?"
Péi Xiù deemed it inappropriate.
The Emperor then asked Shān Tāo.
Shān Tāo replied:
"To depose the elder and establish the younger
violates ritual and is inauspicious.
The stability or danger of the state
will certainly be determined by this."
Thereupon, the Crown Prince's position
was settled.
The Crown Prince personally bowed and thanked Shān Tāo.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he appointed Shān Tāo Grand Herald (dà hónglú),
to escort the King of Chénliú to Yè.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he was given the additional title of Cavalry Commandant (fèngchē dūwèi),
and advanced in peerage to Count of Xīntà.
When Yáng Hù was in power,
some people wanted to endanger Péi Xiù.
Shān Tāo, with a stern countenance, protected him.
Because of this, he lost favor with the powerful minister
and was sent out as Inspector of Jìzhōu,
with the added title of General Who Pacifies the Distant (níngyuǎn jiàngjūn).
The customs in Jìzhōu were shallow,
with no mutual recommendation.
Shān Tāo selected and promoted the obscure and overlooked,
sought out and visited talented individuals,
recognizing and commissioning over thirty people,
all of whom became famous at the time.
People admired and respected him,
and the customs were considerably reformed.
He was transferred to Northern Central Commandant (běi zhōngláng jiàng),
supervising the defense of Yè City.
He entered court as Palace Attendant (shìzhōng),
and was promoted to Minister (shàngshū).
He resigned due to his mother's old age.
An imperial edict stated:
"Although you are sincerely devoted to caring for your parent,
yet there are superiors and subordinates in office,
and you should not neglect medicine day and night.
You should put aside your personal feelings
to uphold your public duty."
Shān Tāo wished to retire in his heart,
submitting dozens of memorials.
After a long time,
he was finally granted permission. He was appointed Consultant (yìláng).
The Emperor, considering Shān Tāo's integrity and frugality meant he had no means to provide for himself,
specially granted him a daily stipend,
and additionally bestowed a bed curtain, mattress, and cushion.
His ritual status and respect were exceptionally high,
unrivaled at the time.
Later, he was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (tàicháng qīng),
but did not take office due to illness.
Then his mother passed away,
and he returned to his hometown.
Shān Tāo, being over sixty,
observed mourning rituals beyond what was customary,
carrying earth to build the tomb,
and personally planting pines and cypresses.
An imperial edict stated:
"What I seek to achieve in governing
is the proper administration of officials.
At present, customs are degenerating,
and people's minds are restless.
It is appropriate to clearly distinguish good from bad,
and to stabilize by humility and concession.
Although Grand Master Tāo is still in mourning,
his feelings are difficult to suppress.
However, current affairs are urgent;
how can he be allowed to fulfill his wishes?
Therefore, let Shān Tāo be Minister of Personnel (lìbù shàngshū)."
Shān Tāo declined, citing mourning and illness,
with earnest memorials.
When Empress Yuán died,
he was forced to return to Luòyáng.
Compelled by the imperial command,
he forced himself to take up the post.
In his previous and subsequent elections,
he thoroughly selected officials both inside and outside the court,
and all found their talents well-matched.
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
he was transferred to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎofù),
and was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
He was appointed Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè),
given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and concurrently held the position of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù).
He firmly declined, citing old age and illness,
and submitted a memorial expressing his situation.
He sent up dozens of memorials,
and for a long time did not take up his post,
which led to him being impeached by Left Aide (Zuǒ Chéng) Bái Bāo.
The Emperor said:
"Shān Tāo has informed me himself of his illness,
I merely haven't allowed it.
If Shān Tāo can handle the selection of officials while seated, that would be acceptable;
why must he go up and down (to the court)?
There is no need to question him further."
Shān Tāo felt uneasy,
and memorialized to decline, saying:
"The ancient kingly way
is simply uprightness.
Your Majesty cannot show partiality for one old minister;
what intention do I have to repeatedly present myself month after month?
I beg that my request, as stated in my memorial,
be granted, so as to uphold the laws and penalties."
The Emperor sent two handwritten edicts, saying:
"Bái Bāo's impeachment of you is very misguided.
The reason I did not immediately investigate it
is simply that I do not like ill-omened and aggressive behavior.
With your clear-sightedness and magnanimity,
how could you take it to heart?
You should take up your post at once
and handle the memorials and petitions."
Shān Tāo was determined to retire,
and so, upon the death of his cousin's wife,
he promptly returned to his outer residence.
An imperial edict stated:
"Minister Shān (Shān Púyè) recently left temporarily,
and has not yet returned due to a minor illness.
This is not my expectation, as I anxiously await him.
Let the Censor (Chéngyuàn) be dispatched to convey my imperial decree.
If his physical condition truly has not yet improved,
then let him be brought back to his official residence in a sedan chair."
Shān Tāo, unable to decline further,
then rose and attended to his duties.
Shān Tāo served in the selection office for over ten years.
Whenever an official position was vacant,
he would propose several candidates.
After the imperial decree indicated a preference,
he would then make a formal recommendation,
prioritizing the Emperor's wishes.
Therefore, those whom the Emperor employed
were sometimes not the primary choices;
the public, not discerning the situation,
attributed Shān Tāo's actions to arbitrary favoritism.
Some slandered him to the Emperor,
so the Emperor sent a handwritten edict to caution Shān Tāo, saying:
"Indeed, in employing people, one should only consider their talent,
not neglecting the distant, humble, and low-born;
then the world will be transformed."
Yet Shān Tāo carried out his duties as usual,
and after a year, public sentiment subsided.
The recommendations and selections of individuals made by Shān Tāo
were each given a title,
and at the time were known as "Duke Shān's Memorials" (Shāngōng Qǐshì).
Shān Tāo maintained a neutral stance in court.
In his later years, when the Empress's faction wielded exclusive power,
he did not wish to empower the Yáng (Yáng) clan,
and offered many veiled remonstrances.
Though the Emperor understood, he was unable to change.
Later, as he was old and seriously ill,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement, saying:
"Your servant is nearly eighty years old,
and my life hangs by a thread.
If there were even the slightest benefit,
how could I withhold my strength in this sagely era?
Compelled by extreme old age,
I can no longer handle affairs.
Now the four seas are at peace,
and the world yearns for transformation.
Simply by leaving things be,
the common people will rectify themselves.
It is merely necessary to promote virtuous customs and teachings to cultivate them.
What more does Your Majesty need to do?
Your servant's ears and eyes are dimmed and clouded,
and I cannot rouse myself.
Between ruler and minister, father and son,
there should be no formality;
therefore, I straightforwardly present my foolish thoughts,
begging you to grant my request."
Then he removed his cap and went barefoot,
returning his official seal and sash.
An imperial edict stated:
"The affairs of the world are vast,
and furthermore, the land of Wú (Wú) has just been pacified.
All things are being initiated,
and we must all devote our efforts to transforming them.
You do not deeply understand my past intentions, and yet you seek retirement due to a minor illness.
How can this be what I expect of you?
I still sit anxiously,
unable to fold my hands and rule (meaning, to rule effortlessly).
How can you then claim lofty detachment in this matter?
You should uphold the utmost public spirit,
and no longer trouble yourself with empty pretense."
Shān Tāo earnestly petitioned for retirement,
but the imperial edict again refused.
Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Wèi Guàn memorialized:
"Shān Tāo, due to a minor illness,
has for a long time not attended to his duties.
Imperial edicts have been sent frequently,
yet he still has not complied with the decree.
Councillors are of the opinion that he lacks the virtue of unwavering integrity
and violates the principle of public duty.
If he is truly gravely ill,
it is also inappropriate for him to hold office.
Shān Tāo's official position should be removed."
An imperial edict was issued to Wèi Guàn, saying:
"Shān Tāo, by his virtue and integrity, is the hope of the court,
yet he always deeply retreats and declines,
even to the point of earnestness.
Therefore, there have been repeated edicts
to certainly overcome his will,
so that he may assist in what I lack.
How can the official in charge not consider the clear imperial decree,
but instead deeply criticize and investigate,
diminishing the custom of honoring the worthy,
and compounding my unworthiness?
How can this be shown to those near and far?"
Shān Tāo, having no choice,
again rose and attended to his duties.
At the beginning of Tàikāng,
he was promoted to Right Minister of the Secretariat (Yòu Púyè),
given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
and his positions as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and supervisor of selections remained as before.
Shān Tāo firmly declined due to old age and illness.
A handwritten edict said:
"You, sir, by your virtue and principles, are a model for the world;
moreover, even the late emperor recognized your far-reaching intentions.
I intend to rely on you to harmonize customs.
Why do you wish to abandon the distant court affairs
and maintain your lofty ambition alone?
Is my heartfelt intention truly insufficient to persuade you?
Why are your recent words so earnest?
You should exert yourself in due course
and deeply fulfill my utmost hopes.
If you do not lower your aspirations,
I will not be at peace."
Shān Tāo again submitted a memorial firmly declining,
but it was not granted.
After the pacification of Wú (Wú),
the Emperor decreed that military service be suspended throughout the realm,
to show the great peace within the four seas,
and all provinces and commanderies were to abolish their military forces.
Large commanderies were to retain one hundred military officers,
and small commanderies fifty.
The Emperor once held a military review in Xuānwǔ (Xuānwǔ) Field.
Shān Tāo was ill at the time,
and an edict allowed him to follow in a sedan chair.
He then discussed with Lú Qīn (Lú Qīn) the fundamentals of military deployment,
believing it was inappropriate to abolish military preparations in the provinces and commanderies.
His argument was very insightful.
At that time, everyone thought Shān Tāo had not studied Sūn Wú (Sūn Wú),
yet he coincidentally agreed with him.
The Emperor praised it, saying:
"This is a famous saying in the world!"
But he could not adopt it.
Subsequently, after Yǒngníng,
there were repeated upheavals and difficulties.
Bandits and rebels rose like a whirlwind,
and the commanderies and states, being unprepared, were unable to control them.
The world then fell into great chaos,
just as Shān Tāo had predicted.
Later, he was appointed Sītú,
but Táo again firmly declined.
An imperial edict stated:
"Your Lordship is advanced in years and abundant in virtue,
a venerable elder of the court.
Therefore, I bestow upon Your Lordship the position of a prime minister.
Yet you excessively pursue humility and deference,
even repeatedly doing so,
which truly vexes me.
Your Lordship should consistently participate in court affairs,
assisting my person."
Táo again submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your servant has served the Heavenly Court for over thirty years,
yet has not contributed even a jot to the great transformation.
Your Majesty's private favor for your servant is endless,
unworthily bestowing upon me the Three Ducal posts.
Your servant has heard that where virtue is thin and position high,
or strength little and responsibility heavy,
above there is the misfortune of a broken foot,
and below the calamity of the ancestral temple gate.
I beg Your Majesty to extend the grace of generations
and grant your servant my bones."
An imperial edict stated:
"Your Lordship has assisted in court affairs,
protected and governed the imperial house,
and your achievements in supporting and aiding
are what I rely upon.
The office of Sītú
is truly to manage the state's education,
thus it is respectfully bestowed
to fulfill the expectations of the multitude.
How can one decline and diminish oneself with such humility?"
An order was already issued to cut off his memorials and petitions,
and an envoy then laid the official seal and ribbon upon him while he was lying down.
Táo said:
"How can a dying person
pollute the government offices!"
He was carried home due to his illness.
He passed away in the fourth year of Tàikāng,
at the age of seventy-nine.
An imperial edict granted him East Garden funerary items, one set of court attire, one suit of clothes, five hundred thousand cash, and one hundred bolts of cloth,
to cover the funeral expenses.
A proclamation posthumously appointed him Sītú,
with a cinnabar seal and purple ribbon,
a Shìzhōng's mink and cicada hat,
and as the Count of Xīntà, a cinnabar seal and blue-red ribbon.
He was sacrificed to with a grand offering,
and given the posthumous name Kāng.
Before the burial,
forty thousand cash and one hundred bolts of cloth were bestowed.
The Left Chángshǐ Fàn Guǐ and others memorialized, saying:
"Táo's old residence has ten rooms,
but his sons and grandsons cannot accommodate each other."
The Emperor then had houses built for them.
Initially,
Táo, as a commoner, was poor.
He said to his wife, Hán Shì:
"Endure hunger and cold,
I will later become one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
but I just don't know if you are fit to be a Duchess!"
When he attained glory and eminence,
he was chaste, cautious, and frugal.
Although his rank was equal to one of a thousand chariots,
he had no concubines.
His emoluments, stipends, and salaries
were distributed among his relatives and old acquaintances.
Initially,
Yuán Yì of Chénjùn once served as the Magistrate of Gé.
He was corrupt and bribed high officials
to gain a false reputation.
He also sent Táo one hundred catties of silk.
Táo, not wishing to be different from the times,
accepted it and stored it in an attic.
Later, Yì's corruption was exposed,
and he was sent to the Tíngwèi in a caged cart.
All received bribes
were investigated and recovered.
Táo then took out the silk and handed it to the officials.
It had accumulated years of dust,
and its seal was untouched, just as initially.
Táo could drink eight dou of wine before getting drunk.
The Emperor wanted to test him,
so he made Táo drink eight dou of wine,
and secretly added more wine.
Táo stopped at his usual limit.
He had five sons: Gāi, Chún, Yǔn, Mó, and Jiǎn.
Gāi, whose courtesy name was Bólún,
inherited his father's title.
He rose to the rank of Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ and Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài,
and was posthumously appointed Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
Gāi's son Wěi, courtesy name Yànzǔ,
was Yìjūn Xiàowèi.
His second son, Shìhuí,
was Lìbù Láng and Sànqí Chángshì.
Chún, courtesy name Zǐxuán,
did not serve.
Yǔn, courtesy name Shúzhēn,
was Fèngchē Dūwèi.
Both were sickly from a young age,
and their stature was very short,
but they were remarkably intelligent.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this and wished to see them.
Táo dared not refuse,
and asked Yǔn about it.
Yǔn considered himself unsightly
and refused to go.
Táo thought he was superior to himself,
so he memorialized, saying:
"Your servant's two sons are ill,
and should refrain from social interaction,
thus they dare not accept the imperial summons."
Mó, courtesy name Jìcháng,
was intelligent and talented,
and rose to the official position of Sīkōng Yuàn.
Jiǎn, courtesy name Jìlún.
His nature was gentle and refined,
with his father's demeanor.
At over twenty years old,
Táo did not know him well.
Jiǎn sighed, saying:
"I am almost thirty,
yet I am not known by my family lord!"
Later, he was famous alongside Jī Shào of Qiáoguó, Liú Mó of Pèijùn, and Yáng Zhǔn of Hóngnóng.
Initially, he served as Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shùzǐ and Huángmén Láng,
then sent out as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was recalled to be appointed Shìzhōng,
and shortly thereafter,
transferred to Shàngshū.
He served successively as Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently holding the post of Nánmán Xiàowèi,
but did not take office,
and was again appointed Shàngshū.
At the beginning of Guāngxī,
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
At the beginning of Yǒngjiā,
he was sent out as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ and Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn.
He was recalled to be Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
concurrently leading the Lìbù.
Jiǎn wished to have all court officials recommend those they knew,
to broaden the path for discovering talent.
He submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your servant believes that from ancient times, the rise and fall
truly lies in appointing officials;
if talent is acquired,
then nothing will be ungoverned.
The Book says, 'He who knows men is wise,
but this is what the Emperor finds difficult.'
In the flourishing eras of Táng and Yú,
Yuánkǎi were appointed to office;
during the prosperity of the Zhōu dynasty,
there were numerous scholars.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
elegance and refinement gradually waned.
By the Later Hàn,
female regents governed the court,
and honorable and high positions
came from eunuchs and wet nurses,
this was the beginning of chaos.
Thus, the likes of Guō Tài and Xǔ Shào
clarified public opinion in the countryside;
Chén Fān and Lǐ Gù and their ilk
upheld loyalty and integrity at court.
Only then can the integrity of ruler and minister,
and the ancient and modern traditions,
be discussed.
From the first year of Chūpíng
to the end of Jiàn'ān,
in thirty years,
the myriad people were scattered,
and most died,
this was the extreme of chaos.
Emperor Wǔ, Shìzǔ, responded to Heaven and accorded with man,
receiving the abdication from Wèi.
In the early years of Tàishǐ,
he personally attended to myriad affairs,
and the assisting ministers
all diligently performed their duties.
At that time, Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Xún and Yǔ Chún began to attend court at the East Hall of Tàijí,
commenting on the memorials of the Shàngshū,
mostly discussing criminal cases,
and not discussing appointments.
Your servant believes that one should not prioritize what is difficult
while distinguishing what is easy.
When Your Majesty first governs the myriad states,
people are eager to offer their sincerity.
Therefore, on the days of listening to court affairs,
command the Gōngqīng and great ministers to first discuss appointments,
each speaking of the promising talents they have observed, those particularly outstanding in their hometowns, and those capable of employment.
All should be submitted by name,
and the responsible official shall fill vacancies accordingly.
This is the meaning of conferring ranks at court
and sharing it with the multitude."
The court followed his advice.
In the third year of Yǒngjiā,

he was appointed General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn), Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāo, and Guǎng Prefectures (Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Jiāo Guǎng Sì Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Provisional Staff Holder (Jiǎjié).
He was stationed in Xiāngyáng.
At that time, bandits and rebels plagued all directions,
the empire was disintegrating,
imperial authority was not upheld,
and both court and populace were in peril.
Shān Jiǎn spent his years leisurely,
indulging only in wine.
The Xí clan
was a powerful family in the Jīng region,
possessing beautiful gardens and ponds.
Shān Jiǎn often went there to play and roam,
spending much time by the pond.
He would set out wine and invariably get drunk,
naming it Gāoyáng Chí.
At that time, a child's song went:
“Where does Shān Gōng go?
He goes to Gāoyáng Chí.
At dusk, he rides back reversed,
completely muddled and unaware.
Sometimes he can ride a horse,
wearing his white headscarf backwards.
He raises his whip towards Gě Jiāng,
'How about the boy from Bìngzhōu?' ”
Gě Jiāng’s family was in Bìngzhōu,
and he was Shān Jiǎn's beloved general.
Soon after, he was granted supervisory authority over the military affairs of Níng and Yì Prefectures.
At that time, Liú Cōng invaded,
and the capital was in grave danger.
Shān Jiǎn dispatched Supervising Administrator Wáng Wàn (Dūhù Wáng Wàn) to lead an army to the rescue.
Reaching Nièyáng,
Wáng Wàn was defeated by the bandit Wáng Rú (Wánchéng Zéi Wáng Rú) from Wǎnchéng,
and thus garrisoned the city to defend himself.
When Luòyáng fell,
Shān Jiǎn was also pressed by the bandit Yán Yí,
and consequently moved to Xiàkǒu.
He took in refugees,
and the Jiāng and Hàn river regions pledged allegiance to him.
At that time, Huá Yì stirred up trouble in Jiāngzhōu,
and some advised Shān Jiǎn to attack him.
Shān Jiǎn said:
"I am an old friend of Yànxià.
I feel sorrow for him.
How could I, Shān Jiǎn, take advantage of another's misfortune
to achieve merit and exploits!"
His integrity and magnanimity were like this.
At that time, musicians from the Bureau of Music (Yuèfǔ Língrén) fled the chaos,
many escaping to the Miǎn and Hàn regions.
On days of banquets,
his subordinates sometimes urged him to have them perform.
Shān Jiǎn said:
"The state has collapsed,
and I could not rescue it.
I am a sinner against the Jìn dynasty.
What is there to enjoy about music!"
Thereupon, he shed tears and was filled with righteous indignation,
and all those seated felt ashamed.
He died at the age of sixty,
and was posthumously appointed Grand General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dà Jiāngjūn) and accorded the honor of the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
His son was Xiá.
Xiá, courtesy name Yànlín,
served as Magistrate of Yúyáo.
At that time, the Jīn dynasty was newly established south of the Jiāng,
and laws and prohibitions were lax.
Powerful families often harbored hidden households,
claiming them as their private dependents.
Xiá enforced strict laws.
Eighty days after arriving in the county,
he registered over ten thousand hidden households.
Yú Xǐ, a county resident who had hidden households, was due to be executed in the market.
Xiá intended to punish Yú Xǐ.
All the powerful magnates gnashed their teeth at Xiá,
speaking to the authorities,
saying that Yú Xǐ possessed noble character
and should not be humiliated.
They also accused Xiá of arbitrarily constructing a county office,
thereby entrapping him.
Xiá wrote a memorial to Hé Chōng, the Internal Historian of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Nèi Shǐ Hé Chōng):
"I beg to remain for a hundred days
to thoroughly eliminate the fugitives,
then I will retire and accept my punishment,
with no regrets."
Hé Chōng pleaded on his behalf,
but could not succeed.
He was eventually dismissed from office due to this.
Later, he became the Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
His administration was severe and strict.
Emperor Kāng issued an edict saying:
"In Dōngyáng recently, there have been frequent incarcerations,
and many are sentenced to severe penalties.
Is it that the commandery has many criminals,
or that torture is used to obtain confessions,
such that no one can maintain their integrity?"
Xiá handled it with composure,
and the commandery became orderly.
He died in office.
The court historian says: If an official maintains purity in his duties,
intending to set a standard for the world;
serves his parents throughout his life,
intending to encourage customs throughout the world;
if not for Shān Gōng's (Shān Gōng) complete virtues,
who else could achieve this!
Since the chaos of Dōngjīng,
the personnel office has disappeared.
The Xīyuán had money from the Three Ducal Ministers,
and Pútáo held the appointment of an entire province.
Greed and gluttony rode abreast,
filling the government offices.
Three generations passed,
and nine kings reigned through the ages,
bowing and giving thanks in private courts,
this became the custom.
If the lingering influence gradually diminished,
then the principles might be discussed.
If entrusted with selection and recommendation,
then public sentiment would be naturally suppressed;
if understood like fish and water,
then exclusive use would breed suspicion.
To correct past mistakes,
and return to proper governance,
kindness that transcends the names of ministers,
and grace that spreads from the imperial word,
the world calls it 'Shān Gōng's memorial' (Shān Gōng Qǐshì),
could this be what it refers to!
As for the previous generations of Lú Zǐjiā,
they are hardly worth mentioning.
Wáng Róng (his younger cousin Yǎn, Yǎn's younger brother Chéng, Guō Shū)
Wáng Róng, courtesy name Jùnchōng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángxié.
His grandfather, Xióng,
was the Inspector of Yōuzhōu (Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ).
His father, Hún,
was the Inspector of Liángzhōu (Liángzhōu Cìshǐ) and Marquis of Zhēnlíng Tíng (Zhēnlíng Tíng Hóu).
Wáng Róng was intelligent and quick-witted in childhood,
with brilliant and penetrating spiritual essence.
He could look at the sun without being dazzled.
Péi Kǎi saw him and remarked:
"Wáng Róng's eyes sparkle
like lightning under a cliff."
At the age of six or seven,
he was watching a performance in Xuānwǔ Square.
A fierce beast in a cage roared, shaking the ground.
Everyone fled,
but Wáng Róng stood alone, unmoved,
his expression calm.
Emperor Míng of Wèi saw him from his pavilion and marveled at him.
He also once played with a group of children by the roadside.
Seeing a plum tree laden with fruit,
his peers rushed to pick them,
but Wáng Róng alone did not go.
Someone asked him why,
and Wáng Róng replied:
"A tree by the roadside with many fruits
must surely bear bitter plums."
When picked, they were indeed so.
Ruǎn Jí was friends with Hún.
When Wáng Róng was fifteen,
he accompanied Hún in the official residence.
Wáng Róng was twenty years younger than Ruǎn Jí,
yet Ruǎn Jí befriended him.
Whenever Ruǎn Jí visited Hún,
he would soon leave,
but would pass by to see Wáng Róng,
staying for a long time before departing.
He said to Hún:
"Jùnchōng possesses a refined appreciation
that is not comparable to yours.
Talking with you
is not as good as conversing with Ā Róng."
When Hún died in Liángzhōu,
his former subordinates offered millions in condolence gifts.
Wáng Róng declined them,
thereby establishing his reputation.
He was short,
uninhibited and paid no heed to decorum,
skilled at initiating discussions,
and appreciated their crucial points.
Once, when court officials celebrated the Lustration Festival (Shàngsì Xì Luò) by the Luò River,
someone asked Wáng Jì:
"What discussions were held during yesterday's outing?"
Wáng Jì replied:
"Zhāng Huá was good at expounding on the Shǐ and Hàn;
Péi Wěi discussed ancient words and past deeds,
eloquently and worth listening to;
Wáng Róng discussed the space between Zǐfáng and Jì Zhá,
profoundly and outstandingly."
Such was the admiration he received from discerning critics.
Wáng Róng 戎 once drank with Ruǎn Jí 阮籍.
At that time, Liú Chǎng 劉昶, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu 兗州, whose courtesy name was Gōngróng 公榮, was present.
Ruǎn Jí, finding there was little wine,
did not pour any for Liú Chǎng.
Liú Chǎng showed no resentment.
Wáng Róng found this unusual,
and on another day asked Ruǎn Jí:
"What kind of person is he?"
He replied:
"If he were superior to Gōngróng,
I could not but drink with him;
if he were inferior to Gōngróng,
I would not dare not to drink with him;
only Gōngróng can be someone one does not drink with."
Wáng Róng often went on "Bamboo Grove" excursions with Ruǎn Jí,
and Wáng Róng sometimes arrived late.
Ruǎn Jí said:
"These vulgar fellows have come again to spoil my mood."
Wáng Róng laughed and said:
"Your mood, sirs, is also easily spoiled!"
When Zhōng Huì 鍾會 campaigned against Shǔ 蜀,
he passed by to bid farewell to Wáng Róng,
and asked what strategy he should employ.
Wáng Róng said:
"The Daoists have a saying,
'Act but do not rely on it.'
It is not that success is difficult,
but that maintaining it is difficult."
When Zhōng Huì was later defeated,
commentators considered this a prescient remark.
Wáng Róng inherited his father's peerage,
and was appointed as a Clerk to the Prime Minister.
He successively served as Secretary of the Bureau of Personnel, Palace Attendant, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Administrator of Hédōng 河東, and Governor of Jīngzhōu 荊州.
He was implicated for sending officials to renovate his garden residence,
and was supposed to be dismissed from office;
however, an imperial edict allowed him to commute the punishment with a fine.
He was promoted to Governor of Yùzhōu 豫州,
and given the title General Establishing Might.
He received an imperial order to attack Wú 吳.
Wáng Róng dispatched Staff Officers Luó Shàng 羅尚 and Liú Qiáo 劉喬 to lead the vanguard,
and advanced to attack Wǔchāng 武昌.
Wú generals Yáng Yōng 楊雍 and Sūn Shù 孫述, and Administrator of Jiāngxià 江夏 Liú Lǎng 劉朗, each led their troops to surrender to Wáng Róng.
Wáng Róng commanded the main army to the river,
and Wú Vanguard General Mèng Tài 孟泰 surrendered with the two counties of Qīchūn 蘄春 and Zhū 邾.
After Wú was pacified,
he was promoted in peerage to Marquis of Ānfēng 安豐 County,
his enfeoffment was increased by six thousand households,
and he was bestowed six thousand bolts of silk.
Wáng Róng crossed the Jiāng 江 river,
and pacified and comforted the newly subjugated people,
proclaiming his might and benevolence.
Shí Wěi 石偉, the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of Wú, was upright and frank,
and not tolerated by the court of Sūn Hào 孫晧,
so he claimed illness and returned home.
Wáng Róng praised his integrity
and recommended him in a memorial.
An imperial edict appointed Shí Wěi as a Gentleman-Consultant,
and he received the salary of a two-thousand-piculs official for the rest of his life.
The people of Jīngzhōu were delighted and submitted.
He was summoned to serve as a Palace Attendant.
Liú Zhào 劉肇, the Administrator of Nánjùn 南郡, bribed Wáng Róng with fifty bolts of fine cloth in a bamboo tube.
He was impeached by the Metropolitan Commandant,
but because he knew of it yet had not accepted it,
he was not implicated;
however, commentators still criticized him.
The Emperor said to his ministers:
"Wáng Róng's conduct,
how could it be for private gain or selfish interest?
It must simply be that he does not wish to be different!"
Although the Emperor used these words to excuse him,
he was still scorned by those who valued purity and integrity,
and his reputation suffered as a result.
Although Wáng Róng had no outstanding abilities in office,
all his official duties were properly managed.
Later he was promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Minister of Personnel,
but left office due to his mother's mourning.
He was extremely filial by nature,
not bound by ritual,
drinking wine and eating meat,
or watching chess games,
yet his appearance was emaciated and haggard,
and he needed a staff to rise.
Péi Wěi 裴頠 went to offer condolences,
and said to others:
"If a single wail could hurt a person,
Jùnchōng 濬沖 (Wáng Róng's courtesy name) would not escape the censure of destroying his own nature."
At that time, Hé Qiáo 和嶠 was also in mourning for his father,
and maintained himself strictly according to ritual,
measuring his rice when eating.
His grief and emaciation did not surpass Wáng Róng's.
The Emperor said to Liú Yì 劉毅:
"Hé Qiáo's emaciation is excessive for the rites;
make him stop."
Liú Yì said:
"Although Hé Qiáo sleeps on straw and eats porridge,
that is merely 'living filial piety'.
As for Wáng Róng,
that is 'dead filial piety';
Your Majesty should be concerned about him first."
Wáng Róng had previously suffered from a vomiting illness,
which worsened during his mourning.
The Emperor sent physicians to treat him,
and also bestowed medicines,
and furthermore forbade visitors.
When Yáng Jùn 楊駿 was in power,
Wáng Róng was appointed Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
After Yáng Jùn was executed,
Dōng'ān Gōng Yáo 東安公繇 monopolized judicial and reward powers,
his authority shaking both inside and outside the court.
Wáng Róng warned Yáo:
"After a major event,
one should be deeply cautious and keep a distance."
Yáo did not listen,
and indeed incurred blame.
Wáng Róng was transferred to Central Secretariat Director,
given the title Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
and provided with fifty retainers.
He was promoted to Left Palace Assistant,
and concurrently held the position of Minister of Personnel.
Wáng Róng first established the 'Jiǎwǔ 甲午 System,'
where all candidates for office were first made to govern the common people,
and only then appointed.
The Metropolitan Commandant Fù Xián 傅咸 memorialized against Wáng Róng,
saying:
"The Book of Documents says, 'After three years, their merits are examined;
after three examinations, the obscure and the enlightened are promoted or demoted.'
Now, both internal and external officials,
before completing a full year in office, are recalled by Wáng Róng's proposals.
Their merits and demerits are not yet determined,
and moreover, the old officials depart and new ones arrive,
filling the roads,
giving rise to cunning and deceit,
harming agriculture and damaging governance.
Wáng Róng does not follow the classic models of Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜,
but encourages superficiality and extravagance,
corrupting customs.
Not only is it unhelpful,
but it is greatly damaging.
Wáng Róng should be dismissed from office,
to uphold customs."
Wáng Róng was close to Jiǎ 賈 and Guō 郭,
and ultimately escaped implication.
Soon after, he was transferred to Minister of Works.
As the imperial government was on the verge of collapse,
he merely sought to curry favor,
and when the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái 愍懷 was deposed,
he offered not a single word of remonstrance.
Péi Wěi 裴頠, Wáng Róng's son-in-law,
was executed.
Wáng Róng was dismissed from office due to his implication.
When Qí Wáng Jǒng 齊王冏 raised an army,
Sūn Xiù 孫秀 sheltered Wáng Róng within the city.
The son of Zhào Wáng Lún 趙王倫 wanted to appoint Wáng Róng as his army strategist.
Doctor Wáng Yáo 王繇 said:
"Jùnchōng is full of cunning and tricks;
how could he be used by a youth?"
So the plan was abandoned.
When Emperor Huì 惠帝 returned to the palace,
Wáng Róng was made Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Soon after, Héjiān Wáng Yóng 河間王顒 sent envoys to persuade Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng 成都王穎
to execute Qí Wáng Jǒng.
When the declaration reached him,
Qí Wáng Jǒng said to Wáng Róng:
"Sūn Xiù committed treason,
and the Son of Heaven was confined and oppressed.
I gathered a righteous army
to sweep away the chief evildoers.
The loyalty of a subject
is attested by the gods.
Now the two kings have listened to slander
and created great trouble.
I must rely on loyal counsel
to reconcile the discord.
You must plan well for me."
Wáng Róng said:
"You, sir, were the first to raise a righteous army
and restore the great enterprise.
Since the dawn of time,
nothing like this has happened.
However, when it comes to evaluating merits and rewarding services,
those who labored have not received their due.
The court and the populace are disappointed,
and people harbor disloyal intentions.
Now the two kings command a million armored troops;
their vanguard is irresistible.
If you, Your Highness, were to return to your residence,
you would not lose your former peerage.
To relinquish power and show deference
is a plan for safety."
Qí Wáng Jǒng's advisor Gé Yú 葛旟 angrily said:
"Since the Hán 漢 and Wèi 魏 dynasties,
have any princes who returned to their residences
been able to preserve their wives and children?
The one who proposes this should be executed."
At this, all the officials trembled in fear.
Wáng Róng feigned an attack of his illness and fell into a latrine,
thereby escaping disaster.
Róng, seeing the Jìn household in disarray,
admired Qú Bóyù's way of being,
adapting to the times,
without the rigid integrity of a straightforward remonstrator.
From the selection for official posts,
he never promoted the poor and humble,
nor dismissed those with empty reputations,
but merely drifted with the current,
collecting taxes and selecting officials based on household status.
Soon, he was appointed Sītú.
Although he held a position of great power,
he delegated affairs to his subordinates.
Occasionally, he would ride a small horse,
and go out for excursions through a side gate.
Those who saw him did not know he was one of the Sān Gōng.
Thus, many of his former clerks rose to high offices,
and when they met him on the road, they would always make way for him.
His nature inclined him to seek profit,
widely acquiring gardens, fields, and watermills from all directions,
all over the empire.
He accumulated goods and hoarded money,
without knowing its limits.
Every day, he would personally hold ivory tallies,
calculating day and night,
as if it were not enough.
Moreover, he was frugal and stingy,
not providing for himself adequately.
People throughout the land called this a "mortal illness."
When his daughter married Péi Wěi,
he lent her tens of thousands of coins,
which were not returned for a long time.
When his daughter later returned home to visit her parents,
Róng's expression was displeased.
His daughter immediately returned the money,
and only then did he become cheerful.
When his cousin's son was about to marry,
Róng gave him a single unlined garment as a gift.
After the wedding, he demanded it back.
His family had good plums,
which he always sold.
Fearing that people might get the seeds,
he would bore holes in their pits.
Because of this, he incurred criticism from society.
Later, he followed the Emperor on a northern expedition.
The imperial army suffered a defeat at Dàngyīn.
Róng returned to Yè,
and followed the Emperor back to Luòyáng.
When the imperial carriage moved west,
Róng fled to Jiá.
During times of danger and difficulty,
he personally faced sharp blades,
but talked and laughed as if nothing was wrong,
never showing any sign of fear.
At that time, he would summon relatives and guests,
and enjoy himself all day long.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng (305 CE),
he died in Jiáxiàn,
at the age of seventy-two.
His posthumous title was Yuán.
Róng had a discerning eye for human character.
He once described Shān Tāo as "unhewn jade and unrefined gold,"
saying that everyone admired his preciousness,
but no one knew his capacity.
Wáng Yǎn's divine presence was lofty and clear,
like a grove of precious jade trees,
naturally a being beyond the dust of the world.
He said that Péi Wěi was clumsy in utilizing strengths,
and Xún Xù was skilled in utilizing weaknesses.
He compared Chén Dàoníng to a bundle of long poles.
His cousin Dūn had a high reputation,
but Róng disliked him.
Whenever Dūn called on Róng,
Róng would always feign illness and refuse to see him.
Dūn later indeed committed rebellion.
His discerning foresight was thus.
Once, he passed by the wine shop of Lord Huáng.
He looked back at the guests in his carriage and said:
"I used to drink freely here with Jī Shúyè and Ruǎn Sìzōng,
and was also among the last of the Bamboo Grove gatherings.
Since Jī and Ruǎn passed away,
I have been constrained by the times.
Though it seems near today,
it feels as distant as mountains and rivers!"
Initially,
Sūn Xiù was a clerk in Lángxié Prefecture
and sought an assessment of his character from the local gentry.
Róng's cousin Yǎn was about to refuse,
but Róng persuaded him to approve it.
When Xiù later gained power,
all court officials with old grievances against him were executed,
but Róng and Yǎn were spared.
His son Wàn
had a good reputation.
He was very fat from a young age.
Róng ordered him to eat husks, but he grew even fatter.
He died at the age of nineteen.
He had an illegitimate son, Xīng,
whom Róng disowned.
He adopted his cousin Yángpíng Tàishǒu Yīn's son as his heir.
Yǎn, courtesy name Yífǔ,
had a brilliant and refined spirit,
and an elegant and graceful demeanor.
When he was a young boy, he once visited Shān Tāo.
Tāo sighed and praised him for a long time.
After he left,
Tāo watched him go and said:
"What kind of old woman
gave birth to such a child!
However, the one who will mislead the people of the world,
may very well be this person."
His father, Yì,
was Píngběi Jiāngjūn.
He often had official business
that required couriers to submit reports,
but they were not reported in a timely manner.
Yǎn, at fourteen,
was in the capital at the time.
He visited Púyè Yáng Hù,
explained the situation clearly,
and his words were very articulate and persuasive.
Hù was highly respected for his virtue and prestige,
yet Yǎn, though young, showed no sign of submission,
which greatly impressed everyone.
Yáng Jùn wanted to marry his daughter to him,
but Yǎn found it shameful,
and so feigned madness to avoid it.
Emperor Wǔ heard of his reputation
and asked Róng:
"Who among the present generation compares to Yífǔ?"
Róng replied:
"I have not seen anyone who compares.
One must seek his equal among the ancients."
In the eighth year of Tàishǐ (272 CE),
an edict was issued to recommend extraordinary talents capable of pacifying the borders.
Yǎn initially enjoyed discussing the arts of diplomacy and strategy,
so Shàngshū Lú Qīn recommended him as Liáodōng Tàishǒu.
He did not accept the position.
From then on, he no longer discussed worldly affairs,
but only elegantly recited profound and recondite doctrines.
Once, during a banquet,
he angered a member of his clan,
who threw a fruit-basket at his face.
Yǎn said nothing at first,
but invited Wáng Dǎo to ride with him and left.
However, he could not feel at peace.
In the carriage, he held a mirror to himself
and said to Dǎo:
"Look, my gaze is already on the back of an ox."
When his father died in Běipíng,
he was very generous in providing for the funeral.
He borrowed money from his relatives and acquaintances,
and then gave it away.
Within a few years,
his family fortune was entirely depleted,
and he moved to live in a garden estate west of Luòchéng.
Later, he served as Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and was promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
He was posted out as Yuánchéng Lìng,
and spent his days in pure conversation,
yet the county affairs were also well managed.
He then entered service as Zhōngshùzǐ and Huángmén Shìláng.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign of
Wèi, Hé Yàn, Wáng Bì, and others followed the teachings of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
establishing the theory that:
"Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things all take non-being (wú) as their root.
Non-being it is
that opens up things and accomplishes tasks,
that is nowhere absent.
Yīn and Yáng rely on it to transform and be born,
the myriad things rely on it to take shape,
the wise rely on it to achieve virtue,
and the unworthy rely on it to save themselves.
Therefore, the utility of non-being
is that it is noble without rank."
Wáng Yǎn greatly valued this.
Only Péi Wěi considered it wrong,
writing an essay to criticize it,
but Wáng Yǎn remained composed.
Wáng Yǎn possessed great talent and a handsome appearance,
with an understanding as profound as a deity's.
He often compared himself to Zǐgòng.
His fame was also immense,
swaying the people of his time.
He was exceptionally skilled in xuánxué discourse,
with discussions of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi being his sole preoccupation.
He always held a jade-handled horsetail whisk,
its color matching his hand.
If there was any point in a discussion that caused him unease,
he would immediately change it,
and the world nicknamed him
"Oral Cíhuáng."
The court and the populace enthusiastically
called him
"A Dragon Gate of his age."
He
repeatedly held prominent positions.
Later generations of scholars
all admired and emulated him.
When officials were selected for court,
they all regarded him as their leader.
Arrogance, ostentation, and extravagance
thus became a prevalent custom.
Wáng Yǎn once lost a young son,
and Shān Jiǎn came to condole.
Wáng Yǎn was overcome with grief,
and Shān Jiǎn said:
"A thing that was but an infant in arms,
why grieve to this extent!"
Wáng Yǎn replied:
"Sages forget emotion;
the lowest are not touched by emotion.
But where emotion is most deeply centered,
that is precisely among us."
Shān Jiǎn was convinced by his words,
and then wept with him.
Wáng Yǎn's wife, Madame Guō,
was a relative of Empress Jiǎ.
Leveraging the influence of the central palace,
she was headstrong, greedy, and cruel,
accumulating wealth insatiably.
She loved to interfere in others' affairs.
Wáng Yǎn was troubled by this but could not stop her.
At that time, there was a fellow countryman, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Lǐ Yáng,
a great hero in the capital.
Madame Guō had always feared him.
Wáng Yǎn said to Madame Guō:
"It is not only I who say you cannot do this,
Lǐ Yáng also says you cannot."
Madame Guō then curbed herself slightly.
Wáng Yǎn detested Madame Guō's greed and vulgarity,
and therefore never spoke the word "money."
Madame Guō wanted to test him,
so she ordered a maid to encircle his bed with coins,
preventing him from walking.
Wáng Yǎn rose in the morning, saw the money,
and said to the maid:
"Move this 'ădǔwù' away!"
Such was his careful choice of words.
Later, he successively served as Northern Army Chief Commandant (Běijūn Zhōnghòu), Central Army Protector (Zhōnglǐngjūn), and Minister of Personnel (Shàngshūlìng).
His daughter became the crown princess to Crown Prince Mǐnhuái.
When the Crown Prince was falsely accused by Empress Jiǎ,
Wáng Yǎn, fearing disaster,
personally submitted a petition for divorce.
After Empress Jiǎ was deposed,
the relevant authorities submitted a memorial concerning Wáng Yǎn,
stating:
"Wáng Yǎn wrote a letter to the Grand Minister of Works (Sītú), Prince Róng of Liáng,
enclosing a copy of the Crown Prince's personal letter to his consort and Wáng Yǎn,
explaining the circumstances of the false accusation.
Prince Róng and others read it with reverence;
the words and meaning were sincere and sorrowful.
Wáng Yǎn held a position as a great minister;
he should have been guided by righteousness.
When the Crown Prince was falsely accused and fell into disfavor,
Wáng Yǎn was unable to uphold righteousness to the death,
and instead sought a divorce.
He received the Crown Prince's personal letter
but concealed it and did not reveal it.
His intention was to merely escape harm,
lacking the conduct of loyalty and steadfastness.
He ought to be publicly reproached
to reinforce the integrity of officials.
He should be banned from office for life."
This was approved.
Wáng Yǎn had always looked down upon Zào Wáng Lún's character.
When Lún usurped the throne,
Wáng Yǎn feigned madness and hacked at a maid to save himself.
After Lún was executed,
Wáng Yǎn was appointed Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn),
then transferred to Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū),
and again became Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshūlìng).
At that time, Qí Wáng Jiǒng had accomplished the feat of restoration,
but he seized power and acted arbitrarily.
All the high officials (gōngqīng) bowed before him,
but Wáng Yǎn alone greeted him with a long bow.
He resigned from office due to illness.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng appointed Wáng Yǎn as Army Commander-in-Chief (Zhōngjūnshī),
and he successively rose to Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè),
leading the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù),
and later was appointed Minister of Personnel (Shàngshūlìng), Minister of Works (Sīkōng), and Grand Minister of Works (Sītú).
Although Wáng Yǎn held the important positions of chief minister,
he did not prioritize governing the country,
but rather thought of ways to preserve himself.
He advised Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, saying:
"China is already in chaos;
we must rely on regional governors (fāngbó).
It is imperative to find those who possess both civil and military talents to appoint to these positions."
Thus, he appointed his younger brother Chéng as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and his clansman Dūn as Governor of Qīngzhōu.
He then said to Chéng and Dūn:
"Jīngzhōu has the strong defenses of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and Qīngzhōu has the strategic advantage of facing the sea.
With the two of you outside,
and I remaining here,
it will be enough for three burrows."
Discerning people disdained him for this.
When Shí Lè and Wáng Mí attacked the capital,
Wáng Yǎn was appointed Generalissimo of All Expeditionary Forces (Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhūjūnshì), holding the imperial staff (chíjié) and the imperial axe (jiǎhuángyuè) to resist them.
Wáng Yǎn ordered Former General Cáo Wǔ and Left Guard General Wáng Jǐng and others to attack the bandits,
repelling them and capturing their baggage train.
He was promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
with his position as Minister of Personnel (Shàngshūlìng) remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔlíng,
but he declined the enfeoffment.
At that time, Luòyáng was in grave danger,
and many wished to move the capital to avoid the difficulties,
but Wáng Yǎn alone sold his carriages and oxen to reassure the populace.
When Yuè was campaigning against Gǒu Xī,
Wáng Yǎn, as Grand Commandant, served as the Grand Tutor's Army Superintendent (Tàifù Jūnsī).
After Yuè died,
the multitude jointly nominated him as Commander-in-Chief (Yuánshuài).
Wáng Yǎn, seeing the bandits rising fiercely,
was afraid and dared not accept.
He declined, saying:
"From my youth, I had no ambition for office;
I drifted along with the official assignments,
and thus came to this.
How can I, with my untalented nature,
handle today's affairs?"
Soon after, the entire army was defeated by Shí Lè.
Lè summoned the princely officials
to meet with him,
and questioned Wáng Yǎn about the former Jìn dynasty.
Wáng Yǎn explained the reasons for its downfall,
saying that the plans were not his.
Lè was very pleased,
and spoke with him for a whole day.
Wáng Yǎn claimed he had not been involved in worldly affairs since his youth,
wishing to secure his release,
and then urged Lè to assume the imperial title.
Lè grew angry and said:
"Your name is renowned throughout the four seas,
you hold a position of heavy responsibility,
you entered court in your youth
and served until your hair turned white.
How can you say you were not involved in worldly affairs?
The destruction of the world
is precisely your fault."
He ordered his attendants to escort him out.
He said to his partisan Kǒng Cháng:
"I have traveled widely throughout the world,
and have never seen a man like this.
Should I let him live?"
Kǒng Cháng replied:
"He was a Grandee (Sāngōng) of Jìn;
he will certainly not exert himself for us,
so what value does he have?"
Lè said:
"Still, he must not be killed with a blade."
He ordered men to knock down a wall at night and bury him to death.
As Wáng Yǎn was about to die,
he turned and said:
"Alas!
Though we are not as good as the ancients,
had we not previously exalted the superficial and vain,
and instead exerted our strength to rectify the world,
we would still not have come to this day."
He was fifty-six years old at the time.
Wáng Yǎn was outstandingly talented and had an excellent reputation.
He aspired to the profound and distant,
never speaking of material gain.
When Wáng Dūn crossed the river,
he often praised him, saying:
“Yífǔ among the crowd
is like a pearl or jade among pebbles.”
Gù Kǎizhī, in his praise for painting,
also described Wáng Yǎn as lofty and serenely poised,
standing like a thousand-ren cliff.
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
His son Xuán,
whose courtesy name was Méizǐ,
admired simplicity and broad-mindedness in his youth,
and also possessed outstanding talent,
ranking equally with Wèi Jiè.
Xún Fān employed him as the Grand Administrator of Chénliú,
stationed at Wèishì.
Xuán was originally from a renowned family,
and had a heroic spirit.
During that chaotic and dilapidated time,
people were not loyal to him.
As he was about to join Zǔ Tì,
he was killed by bandits.
Chéng, whose courtesy name was Píngzǐ.
was intelligent and alert from birth.
Though he could not yet speak,
he understood people's intentions
from their gestures.
Wáng Yǎn's wife, Guō, was avaricious and vulgar,
and wanted a maidservant to carry manure on the road.
Chéng, at fourteen,
admonished Guō that this was improper.
Guō was furious,
and said to Chéng:
“When your late mother was dying,
she entrusted the young master to his new wife,
not the new wife to the young master.”
She then grabbed his robe hem,
intending to beat him.
Chéng struggled free,
and fled by climbing out the window.
Wáng Yǎn had a great reputation in the world,
and people at the time considered him an authority on human character.
He especially esteemed Chéng, Wáng Dūn, and Yú Kǎi,
and once evaluated the gentlemen of the realm, saying:
“Āpíng is first,
Zǐsōng is second,
Chùzhòng is third.”
Chéng once said to Wáng Yǎn:
“Your form resembles the Dao,
but your spirit is too sharp.”
Wáng Yǎn replied:
“Indeed, I am not as uninhibited and tranquil as you.”
Chéng thus became famous.
If Chéng had already appraised someone,
Wáng Yǎn would not comment further,
simply saying,
“Píngzǐ has already judged.”
In his youth, he held prominent positions,
progressively rising to the post of Attendant Officer of Chéngdū Prince Yǐng.
Yǐng’s favored eunuch Mèng Jiǔ slandered and killed Lù Jī and his brothers,
causing universal indignation.
Chéng exposed Mèng Jiǔ’s private illicit acts,
and persuaded Yǐng to kill Jiǔ.
Yǐng then executed him,
and all scholars and commoners praised this.
When Yǐng was defeated,
Dōnghǎi Prince Yuè invited Chéng to be his Sīkōng Chief Clerk.
For his merit in welcoming the emperor,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nánxiāng.
He was promoted to General Jiànwēi and Governor of Yōngzhōu,
but did not take up the post.
At that time, Wáng Dūn, Xiè Kūn, Yú Kǎi, and Ruǎn Xiū were all close friends with Wáng Yǎn,
and were known as the “Four Friends.”
Chéng was also intimate with them,
and Guāng Yì, Húmǔ Fǔzhī, and others also participated.
They indulged in drinking and unrestrained behavior,
seeking ultimate pleasure and enjoyment.
At the end of Emperor Huì’s reign,
Wáng Yǎn advised Yuè to appoint Chéng as Governor of Jīngzhōu, with credentials, Supervisor-General,
and concurrently Colonel of the Southern Barbarians,
and Wáng Dūn as Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Wáng Yǎn then asked them about their strategies.
Wáng Dūn said:
“One should adapt to circumstances as they arise;
they cannot be discussed in advance.”
Chéng’s arguments flowed sharply,
and his calculations and strategies were boundless;
everyone present was impressed.
When Chéng was about to depart for his post,
the entire court came to see him off.
Chéng saw a magpie’s nest in a tree,
immediately took off his clothes and climbed the tree,
reaching in and playing with the birds.
His demeanor was carefree and unfazed,
as if no one else was around.
Liú Kūn said to Chéng:
“Although your outward appearance is unrestrained and cheerful,
you are internally impulsive and chivalrous.
If you conduct yourself in this manner in the world,
it will be difficult for you to die a natural death.”
Chéng remained silent.
After Chéng arrived at his post,
he indulged in drinking day and night,
neglecting all official duties.
Even urgent military matters
did not concern him.
He promoted Guō Shū of Shùnyáng from obscurity,
making him a Deputy Governor,
and entrusted the provincial administration to him.
When the capital was in peril,
Chéng led his armies,
intending to respond to the national crisis,
but a whirlwind broke his banner pole.
Coincidentally, Wáng Rú attacked Xiāngyáng.
Chéng’s vanguard reached Yíchéng.
He dispatched an envoy to Shān Jiǎn,
who was captured by Yán Yí, Wáng Rú’s partisan.
Yán Yí pretended to send someone from Xiāngyáng to ask:
“Has Xiāngyáng been taken?”
The envoy replied:
“The city was breached yesterday morning,
and Shān Jiǎn has been captured.”
Yán Yí then secretly released Chéng’s envoy,
allowing him to escape.
Chéng, hearing that Xiāngyáng had fallen,
believed it to be true,
dispersed his troops and returned.
Afterward, he was ashamed of this,
and falsely claimed that provisions were insufficient,
blaming and executing his Chief Clerk Jiǎng Jùn.
He ultimately could not advance.
Displaced people from Bā and Shǔ scattered in Jīng and Xiāng,
quarreled with the local populace,
and subsequently killed a county magistrate,
gathering in Lèxiāng.
Chéng ordered the Grand Administrator of Chéngdū, Wáng Jī, to suppress them.
The rebels requested surrender,
Chéng feigned agreement,
but then attacked them at Chǒngzhōu,
offering their wives and children as rewards,
and drowned over eight thousand people in the river.
Consequently, four to five tens of thousands of displaced families from Liáng rebelled simultaneously,
electing Dù Tāo as their leader.
They attacked Líng and Guì in the south,
and plundered Wǔchāng in the east,
defeating Wáng Jī at Bālíng.
Chéng showed no sign of worry or fear,
but merely continued to drink day and night with Wáng Jī,
playing pitch-pot and dice games,
often starting dozens of rounds.
He killed the wealthy man Lǐ Cái,
and seized his family’s assets to bestow upon Guō Shū.
Nánpíng Grand Administrator Yīng Zhān repeatedly remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Consequently, everyone became disloyal,
and both internal and external factions revolted.
Although Chéng’s reputation and actual power were diminished,
he remained arrogant and self-satisfied.
Later, he led an army to attack Dù Tāo,
stopping at Zuòtáng.
Shān Jiǎn’s Military Advisor Wáng Chōng rebelled in Yùzhōu,
proclaiming himself Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Chéng was afraid,
and sent Dù Ruí to defend Jiānglíng.
Chéng moved to Cánlíng,
and soon fled to Tàzhōng.
Guō Shū remonstrated, saying:
“Even though Your Excellency has not implemented any exceptional policies since taking office,
you have not lost the hearts of the people.
Now, by recruiting the loyal troops from Huáróng in the west,
it would be sufficient to capture this petty villain.
Why abandon yourself?”
Chéng could not follow his advice.
Initially,
Chéng ordered the various commanderies of Wǔlíng to jointly attack Dù Tāo.
Tiānmén Grand Administrator Hù Guī was stationed at Yìyáng.
Wǔlíng Grand Administrator Wǔ Chá was killed by the local barbarians in his commandery,
and Hù Guī returned with his isolated army.
Chéng was enraged,
and replaced Hù Guī with Dù Zēng.
The barbarian Yuán Suì,
an old subordinate of Hù Guī,
used avenging Hù Guī as a pretext
and raised an army to pursue Dù Zēng,
proclaiming himself General Píngjìn.
Chéng sent his Commander Wúqiū Miǎo to suppress him,
but Wúqiū Miǎo was defeated by Yuán Suì.
Meanwhile, Emperor Yuán summoned Chéng to be Libationer of Military Counsel,
whereupon he accepted the summons.
At that time, Wáng Dūn 王敦 was the Grand Governor of Jiāngzhōu 江州,
garrisoned in Yùzhāng 豫章.
Chéng 澄 went to visit Dūn 敦.
Chéng 澄 had long enjoyed a great reputation,
surpassing Dūn 敦.
Both gentry and commoners alike were captivated by him.
He also possessed extraordinary bravery and strength,
and had always been feared by Dūn 敦.
Chéng 澄, still holding to his old impression, slighted Dūn 敦.
Dūn 敦 became even more indignant.
He invited Chéng 澄 to stay for the night,
secretly intending to kill him.
However, Chéng's 澄 twenty attendants
carried iron horsewhips for protection,
and Chéng 澄 himself always held a jade pillow to defend himself.
Therefore, Dūn 敦 had not yet been able to make his move.
Later, Dūn 敦 gave wine to Chéng's 澄 attendants,
who all became drunk.
He then borrowed the jade pillow to observe it.
Thereupon, he got out of bed and said to Chéng 澄:
"Why are you in communication with Dù Tāo 杜弢?"
Chéng 澄 replied:
"The matter can be verified."
Dūn 敦 wanted to go inside (to his quarters),
but Chéng 澄 pulled Dūn's 敦 clothing by hand,
until the sash broke.
Then he climbed onto the beam,
and cursed Dūn 敦, saying:
"If you act like this,
disaster will soon befall you."
Dūn 敦 ordered the strongman Lù Róng 路戎 to strangle him.
Chéng 澄 was forty-four years old at the time.
His body was carried back to his home.
Liú Kūn 劉琨, hearing of Chéng's 澄 death,
sighed and said:
"Chéng 澄 brought it upon himself."
When Dūn 敦 was pacified,
Chéng's 澄 former subordinate, the Gentleman of Letters Huán Zhì 桓稚, submitted a memorial to vindicate Chéng 澄
and request posthumous honors.
An imperial edict reinstated Chéng's 澄 original office
and granted him the posthumous title Xiàn 憲.
His eldest son, Zhān 詹,
died early.
His second son, Huī 徽,
was the Chief Clerk of the Right Army.
Guō Shū 郭舒, courtesy name Zhìxíng 稚行.
As a child, he asked his mother to allow him to study under a teacher.
After about a year, he returned home,
having a rough understanding of the great principles.
The local official, Court Steward Fàn Guǐ 范晷, and his clansman, the Grand Governor of Wǔlíng 武陵, Guō Jǐng 郭景,
all praised Shū 舒, saying he would be a rising talent
and would eventually become a pillar of the state.
He initially served as a Commandant of the Central Army,
but was imprisoned by the Court of the Imperial Censor for unauthorized release of Sīmǎ Biāo 司馬彪.
Many in the world considered this righteous.
The Inspector Xiàhóu Hán 夏侯含 appointed him as Western Bureau Chief,
then promoted him to Chief Clerk.
When Hán 夏侯含 was involved in an incident,
Shū 舒 personally took responsibility to defend Hán 夏侯含,
and the matter was resolved.
The Inspector Zōng Dài 宗岱 appointed him as Chief of Staff,
[一二] but he left office due to his mother's death.
Liú Hóng 劉弘, when governing Jīngzhōu 荊州,
appointed him as Chief of Staff.
After Hóng's 劉弘 death,
Shū 舒 led the officers and soldiers to support Hóng's 劉弘 son, Fán 璠, as their leader,
attacked the rebel Guō Mài 郭勱,
annihilated him,
and preserved the entire province.
Wáng Chéng 王澄, hearing of his reputation,
appointed him as Assistant Governor.
Chéng 澄 indulged in drink all day long,
paying no attention to public affairs.
Shū 舒 often sharply admonished him.
When the world fell into great chaos,
he also urged Chéng 澄 to cultivate virtue and strengthen his authority,
to protect and secure the provincial borders.
Chéng 澄 believed that the chaos originated from the capital,
and that a single province could not rectify or resist it.
Although he did not follow the advice,
he valued Shū's 舒 loyalty and integrity.
A Jīngzhōu 荊州 scholar, Zōng Yīn 宗廞, once offended Chéng 澄 while drunk.
Chéng 澄 grew angry,
and yelled at his attendants to beat Yīn 廞.
Shū 舒 sternly said to the attendants:
"The Governor is overly drunk;
how dare you act recklessly!"
Chéng 澄 angrily said:
"Is the Assistant Governor mad,
falsely claiming I am drunk!"
He then ordered them to pinch Shū's 舒 nose
and cauterize his eyebrows.
Shū 舒 knelt and submitted to it.
Chéng's 澄 anger slightly subsided,
and Yīn 廞 was thus spared.
When Chéng 澄 fled in defeat,
he appointed Shū 舒 to govern Nánjùn 南郡.
Chéng 澄 also wanted to take Shū 舒 eastward downriver.
Shū 舒 said:
"I, Shū 舒, as a chief administrator responsible for thousands of miles,
was unable to rectify matters
and allowed Your Excellency to flee.
I cannot bear to cross the river."
So he remained garrisoned at Dùnkǒu 沌口,
supporting himself by gathering from the lakes and marshes.
A local stole and ate Shū's 舒 ox.
When the incident was discovered,
the person came to apologize.
Shū 舒 said:
"You were hungry,
that's why you ate the ox.
We can share the remaining meat."
The world admired his magnanimity because of this.
Shū 舒 was close to Dù Zēng 杜曾 when young.
Zēng 曾 once summoned him,
but he did not go,
which Zēng 曾 resented.
At this time,
Chéng 澄 again transferred Shū 舒 to be Grand Governor of Shùnyáng 順陽.
Zēng 曾 secretly dispatched troops to ambush Shū 舒,
but he escaped and was spared.
Wáng Dūn 王敦 summoned him to be his military adviser,
and then promoted him to Attendant Official.
When Zhōu Fǎng 周訪, the Regional Commander of Xiāngyáng 襄陽, died,
Dūn 敦 sent Shū 舒 to supervise the army in Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
When Gān Zhuó 甘卓 arrived,
he returned.
The imperial court summoned Shū 舒 to be Right Censor,
but Dūn 敦 detained him and did not send him.
Dūn 敦 plotted rebellion,
but Shū 舒 admonished him without success,
and was made to guard Wǔchāng 武昌.
Zōng Dàn 宗澹, the Assistant Governor of Jīngzhōu 荊州, was jealous of Shū's 舒 talent
and frequently slandered him to Wáng Yì 王廙.
Yì 廙 suspected Shū 舒 of conspiring with Gān Zhuó 甘卓,
and secretly reported this to Dūn 敦,
but Dūn 敦 did not accept it.
Miáo Tǎn 繆坦, a High Official and Supervisor, once requested land west of Wǔchāng 武昌 city for a camp.
The Grand Governor Lè Kǎi 樂凱 said to Dūn 敦:
"The common people have long purchased this land
to grow vegetables for their own sustenance;
it is not right to take it from them."
Dūn 敦 was furious and said:
"If Wáng Chǔzhòng 王處仲 had not come to the rivers and lakes,
would there be any land in Wǔchāng 武昌,
for people to say it is my land?!"
Kǎi 凱 was afraid
and dared not speak.
Shū 舒 said:
"My lord, please listen to a word from me."
Dūn 敦 said:
"Píngzǐ 平子 considered you mad,
which is why he pinched your nose and cauterized your eyebrows.
Is your old ailment recurring?!"
Shū 舒 said:
"The 'madmen' of antiquity were straightforward.
Zhōu Chāng 周昌, Jí Àn 汲黯, and Zhū Yún 朱雲 were not mad.
In the past, Yáo 堯 erected a 'slander wood' (criticism post),
and Shùn 舜 set up a 'drum for daring to admonish',
after which no affairs were unjust or unaddressed.
Are you superior to Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜?
To thus abruptly refuse Shū 舒
and prevent him from speaking,
how far removed you are from the ancients!"
Dūn 敦 said:
"What do you wish to say?"
Shū 舒 said:
"Miáo Tǎn 繆坦 can be called a petty man,
who confuses public perception,
seizes private land from others,
and bullies the weak with strength.
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 said: 'When the ruler says it is acceptable,
the minister presents what is not,
to achieve what is acceptable.'
Therefore, I and others dare not remain silent."
Dūn 敦 then immediately ordered the land to be returned,
and everyone admired his boldness.
Dūn 敦 respected Shū's 舒 integrity and loyalty,
gave him increasingly generous rewards,
and frequently visited his home.
He was memorialized as Inspector of Liángzhōu 梁州.
He died of illness.
Lè Guǎng 樂廣
Yuè Guǎng 字 Yànfǔ,
was a native of Yùyáng, Nányáng.
His father, Fāng,
served as a military advisor to the Wèi General Who Conquers the West, Xiàhóu Xuán.
Guǎng was eight years old at the time.
Xiàhóu Xuán often saw Guǎng on the road,
and so he called him over for a chat.
Upon returning, he said to Fāng:
"I just saw Guǎng; his divine demeanor is bright and clear.
He is destined to be a famous scholar.
Although your family is poor,
you should let him specialize in study.
He will surely bring prosperity to your household."
Fāng died early.
Guǎng was an orphan and poor,
residing as a sojourner in Shānyáng.
He lived a life of poverty and simplicity,
and no one recognized his talent.
He was inherently tranquil and modest,
possessed foresight,
had few desires,
and competed with no one.
He was particularly skilled in discussion,
always using concise language to analyze principles,
thereby satisfying people's minds.
What he did not know,
he remained silent about.
Péi Kǎi once invited Guǎng to talk together.
From dusk until dawn,
he held him in high esteem and admiration,
sighing:
"I am not his equal."
Wáng Róng, as the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
heard that Guǎng was admired by Xiàhóu Xuán,
and thus recommended him as a Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent).
Péi Kǎi again recommended Guǎng to Jiǎ Chōng,
who then appointed him as an aide to the Grand Commandant.
He was subsequently transferred to be a Palace Attendant for the Crown Prince.
The Minister of Personnel, Wèi Guàn,
a venerable elder of the court,
who had conversed with famous scholars during the Zhèngshǐ reign of Wèi,
saw Guǎng and was amazed by him,
saying:
"Since the passing of those former wise men,
I always feared that subtle words would cease.
But now I hear such words from you again."
He commanded his sons to visit him,
saying:
"This man is a 'water mirror,'
seeing him makes one feel clear,
as if parting clouds and mist to behold the blue sky."
Wáng Yǎn himself said:
"When I talk with people, I am very concise and to the point.
But upon seeing Guǎng,
I realize my own verbosity."
Such was the admiration he received from those who recognized talent.
He was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Yuánchéng,
then promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant,
then transferred to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
and progressively promoted to Attendant-in-Chief and Intendant of Hénán.
Guǎng was skilled in pure conversation but not adept at writing.
When he was about to decline the position of Intendant,
he asked Pān Yuè to draft a memorial for him.
Pān Yuè said:
"I need to understand your intentions."
Guǎng then composed two hundred sentences,
expressing his will.
Pān Yuè then arranged them in order,
and it became a famous piece of writing.
People at the time all said:
"If Guǎng had not lent Pān Yuè his thoughts,
and Pān Yuè had not adopted Guǎng's ideas,
this beauty would not have been achieved."
Once, a close friend,
who had been absent for a long time, did not come again.
Guǎng asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"Previously, while sitting here,
I was offered wine.
Just as I was about to drink,
I saw a snake in the cup.
I was very disgusted by it,
and after drinking, I fell ill."
At that time, on the wall of the Hénán Prefectural Office, there was a horn
painted with lacquer to look like a snake.
Guǎng realized that the snake in the cup was the shadow of the horn.
He then placed wine in the same spot as before,
and said to the guest:
"Do you see anything in the wine again?"
He replied:
"I see the same as before."
Guǎng then explained the reason to him.
The guest suddenly understood,
and his chronic illness immediately healed.
When Wèi Jiè was a young boy,
he once asked Guǎng about dreams.
Guǎng said they were thoughts.
Wèi Jiè said:
"If the spirit and body do not interact, and yet one dreams,
how can it be thought?"
Guǎng replied:
"It is caused by circumstances."
Wèi Jiè pondered it for a month without understanding,
and consequently fell ill.
When Guǎng heard about it,
he ordered his carriage to go and explain it to him.
Wèi Jiè's illness immediately recovered.
Guǎng sighed:
"This worthy person's mind will surely have no incurable illness!"
Wherever Guǎng served in government,
he did not seek immediate merit or fame.
However, each time he left office,
the affection he left behind was remembered by people.
Whenever he discussed people,
he would first praise their strengths,
and then their shortcomings would be self-evident without being spoken.
If a person made a mistake,
he would first extend full magnanimity,
and then good and bad would naturally become clear.
Guǎng and Wáng Yǎn both focused on the inner mind and detached themselves from worldly affairs,
and their reputations were highly regarded at the time.
Therefore, when people spoke of "elegant demeanor" in the world,
they referred to Wáng and Yuè as the foremost.
In his youth, he was good friends with Yáng Zhǔn of Hóngnóng.
Yáng Zhǔn's two sons were named Qíao and Máo,
both famous in the world.
Yáng Zhǔn first sent them to visit Péi Wèi.
Péi Wèi was magnanimous and grand,
and admired Qíao for his noble temperament.
He said to Yáng Zhǔn:
"Qíao will be as accomplished as you;
Máo is a little less."
Then he sent them to visit Guǎng.
Guǎng was pure and unadorned,
and admired Máo for his spiritual insight.
He said to Yáng Zhǔn:
"Qíao is indeed as accomplished as you,
but Máo also has a clear and outstanding quality."
Yáng Zhǔn smiled and said:
"The superiority of my two sons
is precisely the difference between Péi and Yuè."
Commentators believed that although Qíao had a noble bearing,
his spiritual insight was insufficient,
and Yuè's assessment was correct.
At that time, Wáng Chéng, Húmǔ Fǔzhī, and others
all acted unrestrainedly as a sign of being accomplished,
some even to the point of nudity.
Guǎng heard of it and laughed, saying:
"Within the teachings of decorum, there is already a place for joy.
Why must it be like this?"
His dwelling on talent and loving things,
every action having inner reason,
were all of this kind.
Living in an era of much trouble in the world,
with court regulations in disorder,
he kept himself pure, remained neutral,
acted sincerely, and preserved his true nature.
People at the time could not perceive his profound understanding.
Previously, the official residences in Hénán were often haunted by strange occurrences.
Former intendants often dared not occupy the main hall,
but Guǎng resided there without doubt.
Once, the outer door closed by itself.
Everyone around him was startled,
but Guǎng remained composed.
He looked and saw a hole in the wall.
He had someone dig into the wall,
found a raccoon dog and killed it,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
When the Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was deposed,
an imperial edict forbade former officials from seeing him off.
All the officials, unable to suppress their indignation and sorrow,
defied the ban and paid their farewells.
The Colonel-Director of Retainers, Mǎn Fèn, ordered the Hénán Zhongbu to arrest those who bowed and send them to prison.
Guǎng immediately released them.
Everyone felt fearful for Guǎng on his behalf.
Sūn Yǎn persuaded Jiǎ Mì, saying:
"Previously, because of the Crown Prince's crimes,
he was deposed.
His officials, not fearing the strict edict,
defied the law to see him off.
If we imprison them now,
it will highlight the Crown Prince's virtues.
It is better to release them."
Jiǎ Mì agreed with his words,
and thus Guǎng avoided punishment.
He was promoted to Minister of Personnel and Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Later, when the Prince of Dōng'ān, Yáo, was to become Assistant Director,
Guǎng was transferred to Right Assistant Director,
overseeing the Ministry of Personnel,
and replaced Wáng Róng as Minister of Personnel.
Wáng Róng had initially recommended Guǎng,
and Guǎng eventually occupied his position,
which people at the time found admirable.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng,
was the son-in-law of Guǎng.
When he encountered trouble with Chángshā Wáng Yì,
and Guǎng was already in a prominent position at court,
a group of petty people slandered him.
Yì questioned Guǎng about this.
Guǎng's expression did not change,
and he slowly replied:
"How could Guǎng exchange five sons for one daughter?"
Yì still had doubts,
and Guǎng eventually died of grief.
Xún Fān, hearing of Guǎng's inevitable fate,
wept for him.
He had three sons: Kǎi, Zhào, and Mó.
Kǎi, courtesy name Hóngxù,
was an aide to the Dà Sīmǎ, Qí Wáng,
and participated in the Piaoqí army's affairs.
Zhào, courtesy name Hóngmào,
was an aide to the Tài Fù, Dōnghǎi Wáng.
When Luòyáng fell,
the brothers carried each other and crossed the Jiāng River southwards.
Mó, courtesy name Hóngfàn,
was the Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Wújùn Nèi Shǐ.
The imperial historians say: The Hàn prime ministers were clear and tranquil,
perceiving opportunities in unburdened affairs;
the Zhōu historians were clear and serene,
not troubled by holding sinecures.
Could it be that the responsibilities of the court's highest offices
were different from those of ordinary officials?
Jùnchōng was good at initiating discussions,
Yífǔ looked up to emulate those beyond the material world,
ascending to a prominent position in the court,
while looking back at Qīyuán with disdain.
Since they relied on emptiness,
the court's order was already in disarray.
Róng ingratiated himself with the world,
privately accumulating wealth;
Yǎn protected himself,
caring little for the ancestral altars or the state?
When the three regions were plunged into chaos,
and the six barbarians gained leverage,
the hordes of dogs and sheep,
their arrows and spears were like clouds.
Yífǔ, so petty,
flattered those fierce leaders,
to seek their indulgence and forgiveness.
The collapse of a crumbling wall
still had its own etiquette.
Píngzǐ indulged his emotions and disdained others,
finding it unbearable to face himself in the mirror,
ultimately losing his life,
bringing about his own ruin.
Moreover, clothing expresses one's appearance,
and jade tablets embody virtue.
Music shifts between gōng and yǔ,
colors illuminate mountain flowers.
One's actions should be orderly,
and one's words should form teachings.
Chéng's sitting in a prone position,
was excessively so.
As for removing one's undergarments and climbing a tree,
[一三] nakedly fondling magpies—
if this is considered unconventional,
called high-minded elegance,
then frivolity is imitated,
how can such refined tastes be achieved?
Their path deviated from the sagely,
their actions were contrary to correct conduct,
clinging to their own unique feelings,
they brought an early end to their own lives.
In the past, Yàn Yīng wept over Duke Zhuāng's corpse;
Lè Lìng dismissed the guests of Mǐnhuái.
Did they hear of Bóyí's character,
the cowardly who could set their will?
A eulogy says: The Jìn house sought scholars,
and thus built the immortal terrace,
reaching the clouds and touching the heavens,
the old man of the mountain knew talent.
Jùnchōng occupied a high position,
eloquent in discussion, deficient in practical affairs.
Yífǔ looked both ways,
retreating to seek three burrows.
His spirit was confused in those years,
his loyalty differed from those of old.
Píngzǐ was contemptuous and insulting,
more often than acting ineptly.
Lè Lìng parted the clouds,
the high heavens were clear and pure.
Textual Notes
Biographies, Chapter 14: Zhèng Mào (His son Mò, Mò's son Qiú)
Zhèng Mào, courtesy name Línshū,
was a native of Kāifēng, Xíngyáng.
His great-grandfather Zhòng
was the Hàn Dà Sī Nóng.
His father, Tài,
was the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and had a high reputation.
Mào became an orphan at a young age,
and early on possessed discernment and judgment.
Xún Yōu saw him and said:
"Zhènggōng Yè will not perish!"
He followed his uncle Hún to take refuge in Jiāngdōng.
At that time, Huá Xīn was the Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
Hún went to rely on him,
and Xīn, who had always been good friends with Tài,
raised Mào as his own son.
At seventeen,
he returned to his hometown.
His nature was pure and upright.
At that time, Wèi Fèng of Jìyīn was the Xiàngguó Yuàn,
highly renowned in his generation.
Mào's fellow townsman Rèn Lǎn befriended him.
Mào considered Fèng a cunning and ambitious man,
who would eventually bring disaster,
and advised Lǎn to distance himself from him.
When Fèng was defeated,
commentators praised Mào.
When Wèi Wǔ Dì first enfeoffed his sons as marquises,
he carefully selected guests and friends.
Mào and Xú Gàn both became literary tutors to the Línzī Hóu,
then transferred to Sīlì Gōngcáo Cóngshì.
Sīkōng Wáng Lǎng appointed him as an aide.
Mào recommended Xǔ Yǔn of Gāoyáng, Lǔ Zhī of Fúfēng, and Wáng Jī of Dōnglái.
Lǎng appointed all of them,
and later they all reached high positions
and had great reputations.
Mào was promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
He was sent out as the Lìyáng Lìng,
and the officials and common people were pleased and submitted to him.
The Tàishǒu, Bān, ranked the subordinate cities,
and Lìyáng was particularly singled out as exceptional,
being the best among all counties.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
He was transferred to Jìyīn Tàishǒu.
