Upon arrival, he conspicuously commended filial piety and fraternal affection,
respectfully treated worthy and capable people,
established schools,
and encouraged junior talents.
He was transferred and appointed as the Dà Jiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and then appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
Coincidentally, the position of Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu was vacant.
Xuāndì said to Mào:
"Your esteemed uncle, the Dà Jiàng, was praised in Yángpíng and Wèijùn,
and the common people benefited from his benevolent governance.
Moreover, Lú Zǐjiā and Wáng Zǐyōng succeeded each other in this prefecture,
ensuring that the world would not lack worthy individuals.
Therefore, I again trouble you."
While in Guǎngpíng, Mào
prioritized virtuous governance,
skillfully established regulations,
and the people of the prefecture loved him.
He was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng,
and the common people missed him so much they
wept at the roadside.
He was promoted to Shǎofù.
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng ascended the throne,
Mào and Hénán Yǐn Wáng Sù prepared the imperial carriage to welcome him at Yuánchéng,
and he was enfeoffed as Guǎngchāng Tínghóu.
He was transferred to Guānglù Xūn,
and concurrently served as Zōngzhèng.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn made trouble,
Emperor Jǐng himself went out to campaign against him.
All the officials saw him off in the east of the city.
Móu was ill and unable to attend.
The Emperor said to the Central Commander Wáng Sù,
"My only regret is not seeing Zhèng Guānglù."
Sù conveyed this to Móu.
Móu had himself carried in a palanquin to pursue the Emperor,
and caught up with him on a nearby road.
The Emperor laughed and said,
"I knew Lord Hóu would come!"
Then he rode with Móu
and said,
"What should be our first strategic priority?"
Móu replied,
"In the past, I was an imperial secretary along with Jiǎn;
I know him particularly well.
He is a man who loves to scheme but does not grasp practical matters.
Since he established his achievements in Yōuzhōu,
his ambitions have been boundless.
Wén Qīn is brave but lacks foresight.
Now our great army will catch them off guard.
The troops from Jiānghuái are sharp but cannot hold their ground firmly.
Dig deep moats and build high ramparts to thwart their morale;
this is the strength of Yàfū."
The Emperor praised this as good.
He was transferred to Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
When Gāoguì Xiānggōng debated establishing the Míngtáng and Pìyōng,
he carefully selected scholars.
Móu recommended Liú Yì, Liú Shí, Chéng Xián, and Yú Jùn,
who later all reached the high positions of Ducal Counselor.
When Chángdào Xiānggōng was enthroned,
Móu participated in discussing and settling the policy,
and was promoted to Marquis of Ānchéng Xiāng,
with an estate of a thousand households.
In the first year of Jǐngyuán,
he became ill and lost his eyesight.
He repeatedly begged to be allowed to retire,
but was not permitted.
He was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
When the five ranks were first established,
he was enfeoffed as Count of Mìlíng.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Marquis.
Although he had been bedridden for over ten years,
contemporary worthies all recommended him.
During the Tàishǐ reign,
an edict stated:
"Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Marquis of Mìlíng, Móu,
conducts himself with purity and integrity,
upholds the Dao with humility and refinement.
When retired, he possesses the air of clarity and harmony;
when advanced, he has the integrity of plain silk.
He is fit to ascend to the brilliance of the Three Ducal Ministers,
and fill the deficiencies in the roles of the highest officials.
Now Móu is appointed Sīkōng."
The Son of Heaven attended the court in person,
and sent the Central Colonel of the Five Offices, Guó Tǎn, to his residence to confer the appointment.
Móu repeatedly declined,
sending his son, Chēng, to return the official seals and ribbons,
doing so over ten times.
He said to Tǎn,
"Wèi appointed Xú Jǐngshān as Sīkōng.
I was then a Grand Palace Secretary,
and received an edict to explain the imperial will.
Duke Xú told me, 'The Three Ducal Ministers must respond to the will of Heaven above.
If one is not the right person,
it truly harms the harmonious energy.
I dare not, in my dying years,
bring repeated disgrace upon the imperial court.'
He ultimately did not accept.
To follow the example of a noble gentleman of great integrity,
how can one not strive for it!"
He firmly declined,
and after a long time, his request was granted.
He remained at his residence as a Marquis,
and was appointed Minister of State with Ceremonial Privileges Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers,
and was provided with staff and cavalry.
He was given a bed, curtains, mat, bedding, and 500,000 cash.
He died in the ninth year,
at the age of eighty-five.
The Emperor mourned in the Eastern Hall,
and bestowed secret artifacts, one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, and 300,000 cash,
and one hundred rolls each of silk and plain cloth,
to cover the funeral expenses.
His posthumous name was Yuán.
He had six sons.
The eldest son, Mò, succeeded him,
followed by Zhì, Shū, Xǔ, Chēng, and Yǔ,
all of whom held positions as high ministers.
Mò's courtesy name was Sīyuán.
He started his career as a Secretary of the Imperial Library,
examining old texts
and deleting superfluous impurities.
The Central Secretariat Director, Yú Sōng, said to him,
"From now on,
red and purple will be distinguished."
He was transferred to Director of the Bureau of Merits in the Ministry of Personnel,
and was solely in charge of the campaign against Shǔ.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis within the Pass,
and promoted to Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he and Guō Yì of Tàiyuán both served as Principal Advisers to the Crown Prince.
The court held that officials of the Crown Prince's establishment should be called "subordinate ministers."
Mò submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Crown Prince embodies the supreme dignity of the Imperial Pole
and has no private interest in the world.
His palace officials all receive their appointments from the imperial court,
and should not be treated the same as those in feudal states."
The matter was subsequently put into effect.
He was appointed Governor of Dōngjùn.
When a famine struck that year,
Mò immediately opened the granaries to distribute provisions,
then abandoned the capital's post house
and personally submitted a memorial to await punishment.
The court praised Mò for his concern for the state,
and an imperial edict lauded him,
comparing him to Jí Àn.
An announcement was made throughout the empire,
stating that if any commandery or county had similar circumstances,
they were all permitted to distribute provisions.
He entered court as a Palace Attendant.
Initially,
the Emperor, considering him a noble son, ranked him,
and no one in his hometown dared to be his peer.
He was sought out within the province,
whereupon the twelve commandery central arbiters unanimously nominated Mò.
Emperor Wén wrote to Móu, saying,
"Your son is able to be counted among the virtuous,
but I am ashamed of the burden of seemingly stealing from the worthy."
When Emperor Wǔ went to sacrifice in the Southern Suburbs,
he ordered Mò to ride in his chariot,
and then said to Mò,
"Do you know why you are permitted to ride with me?
When the province nominated you as a peer,
I was always ashamed of burdening pure discourse."
Then he asked about governance.
Mò replied,
"Encouraging agriculture and promoting farming
is the foundation of the state.
Selecting talented people
is the way to help the world.
Holding office for a long time
is appropriate for government affairs.
Being clear and careful in promotions and demotions
is the means of encouragement and warning.
Promoting Confucian virtues
is the root of transformation and guidance.
That is all."
The Emperor praised him.
Later, he left office due to his father's death.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Grand Judge.
At this time, the Magistrate of Gé, Yuán Yì, was implicated in bribery and corruption,
leading to extensive legal cases.
Many at court were implicated,
but only Mò's brothers remained clean and untainted by the scandal.
He was promoted to Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
At that time, the Executive Assistant, Shān Tāo, wanted to recommend a relative for a Doctor's position.
He said to Mò,
"You are like Yǐn Wēngguī,
making me dare not speak again."
Mò was a dignified and earnest person,
gentle yet capable of maintaining order,
and this was typical of him.
When Qí Wáng Yōu was to go to his feudal state,
the Ministry of Rites discussed the grand ceremonial regulations.
The Grand Scholars and Libationers Cáo Zhì and others all offered dissenting opinions,
but Mò was faulted for his involvement in the matter,
and dismissed.
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Herald.
He suffered his mother's death.
According to the old system,
one would return to office after the burial.
Mò earnestly pleaded his case,
and after a long time, his request was granted.
Consequently, the law was changed,
allowing high officials to complete their mourning period,
starting with Mò.
After the mourning period,
he became Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and then Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
Mò died in the first year of Tàikāng,
aged sixty-eight,
and was posthumously given the epithet Chéng.
The Director of the Secretariat, Wèi Guàn, memorialized:
"Mò's talent, conduct, and reputation
make him suitable for discussing the Way.
He rose through five ranks to the Nine Ministers,
but his position did not match his virtue.
He should be posthumously granted the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers."
However, Yáng Jùn, the emperor's father-in-law, had previously wanted to marry his daughter to Mò's son, Yù.
Mò said:
"Every time I read the biography of Jùn Bùyí,
I often imagine him.
To fear and keep distance from powerful nobles
is what my family has upheld for generations."
Thus, he declined it.
Jùn deeply resented this.
By this time,
Jùn disagreed with the proposal,
and so it was not implemented.
Mò was broad-minded, benevolent,
humble, gentle, and cautious.
He did not boast of his talent or background,
served his superiors with礼 (lǐ),
and treated subordinates with harmony.
Even towards servants and stable boys, he showed no anger or displeasure,
yet he still had detractors and enemies.
Therefore, gentlemen considered his life in the world difficult.
His son was Qiú.
Qiú's courtesy name was Zǐyú.
In his youth, he was appointed to a ducal administration
and served in the two palaces.
When the Prince of Chéngdū became Grand General
and raised an army to suppress the Prince of Zhào, Lún,
Qiú, who was then the Administrator of Dùnqiu, became his Right Chief Clerk.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngshòu.
He successively rose to Attendant, Grand Minister of State, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Central Protector of the Army, Right Assistant Director of the Secretariat,
and concurrently supervised the Ministry of Personnel.
He died in the second year of Yǒngjiā,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal,
and given the posthumous epithet Yuán.
Qiú's younger brother, Yù,
was a Grand Minister of State at the end of Yǒngjiā.
Lǐ Yìn
Lǐ Yìn's courtesy name was Xuānbó.
He was from Xiāngpíng, Liáodōng.
His grandfather, Mǐn,
was a Han Administrator of Hénèi.
After resigning from office and returning to his hometown,
Gōngsūn Dù, the Administrator of Liáodōng, wanted to forcefully employ him.
Mǐn boarded a light boat and sailed the vast sea,
and no one knew his fate.
Yìn's father, Xìn, searched for him for many years,
sailing the sea and crossing the frontier,
but never found him.
He wanted to observe mourning rites, but doubted his father was dead,
so his feelings were like being in mourning, and he did not marry.
Later, an old neighbor, who was the same age as his father, died,
and Xìn observed mourning rites for him.
Xú Miǎo of Yānguó, who was from the same province and district,
argued that there was no greater unfilial act than having no heir,
and persuaded Xìn to marry.
After Yìn was born,
Xìn then ceased marital relations,
observing mourning rites,
and could not bear the sorrow.
He died a few years later.
Yìn was orphaned young,
and his mother remarried.
After he came of age,
he reduced his food and grieved,
also conducting himself with mourning rites.
Furthermore, as he did not know whether his grandfather was alive or dead,
he set up a wooden tablet to serve him.
Because of this,
he became known for his filial piety.
His appearance was plain and unadorned,
appearing somewhat unassuming,
yet his wisdom was profound and insightful,
and his words were always principled.
He first served as a County Auditor,
then was appointed by the province as an Investigator and Chief Clerk,
was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt,
and participated in military affairs for the General Who Guards the North.
He was promoted to Chancellor of Lèpíng Principality,
where his administration was clean and simple.
He entered court as a Gentleman of the Secretariat,
then was promoted to Marshal of the Central Protector of the Army and Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
where he was fair and incorrupt in personnel selection.
He was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass,
and sent out to serve as Administrator of Ānfēng.
Emperor Wén invited him to be a Household Manager for the Grand General,
then promoted him to Imperial Censor.
He was respectful, upright, and just,
and all officials feared him.
During the campaign against Shǔ,
he was appointed General of the Western Central Army and Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Guānzhōng.
Later, he became Governor of Hénán,
and was enfeoffed as Earl of Guǎnglù.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Grand Minister of State
and advanced in peerage to Marquis.
Yìn memorialized, stating:
"In ancient times, the Three Ducal Ministers sat and discussed the Way,
participating in the affairs of the Six Offices internally
and teaching the Six Ministers externally.
Sometimes they sat among the three *Huái* trees,
also hearing legal cases.
The standard for investigating doubts
was to consult with the high ministers.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue is reverent and discerning,
and you devote yourself to myriad affairs.
You have graciously issued a clear edict
to emulate ancient models.
Even the consultations of Táng and Yú,
and the diligence of King Wén of Zhōu,
could not surpass this.
From now on,
when the state has major policies,
Your Majesty should personally invite the ducal ministers
to inquire and accept their upright advice.
As for doubts concerning military or state affairs,
they should be invited to the Secretariat
to have the Attendants and Grand Ministers of State consult on what is appropriate.
If anyone is ill
and unable to attend meetings,
send an attendant to inquire at the time."
The emperor accepted the edict.
He was promoted to Assistant Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and soon after transferred to Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince.
The emperor decreed that Yìn was loyal, just, and of high moral character,
possessing the integrity of one who disregards personal safety,
and made him concurrently Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
Yìn repeatedly submitted memorials declining,
saying he was unfit to be Tutor of the Crown Prince
and should not concurrently hold the office of Supervisor.
Emperor Wǔ, believing both positions required loyal and virtuous individuals,
always refused.
At the beginning of Xiánníng,
the Crown Prince moved to the Eastern Palace.
The emperor believed that the duties of the Prefect of the Masters of Writing were grave and heavy,
while the Junior Tutor had the duty of guiding morning and evening.
Yìn was inherently weak,
and should not be overworked for long.
He was transferred to Attendant,
and granted the additional rank of Special Advanced Official.
Shortly after, he was promoted to Director of the Secretariat,
with his positions of Attendant and Special Advanced Official remaining as before.
Although Yìn held various internal and external positions,
his family was extremely poor and frugal.
When his son fell ill, he had no money to buy medicine.
The emperor heard of this
and bestowed one hundred thousand cash.
Later, the emperor, regarding the position of Minister of Works as the old position of Chancellor,
decreed Yìn to be Minister of Works.
He held the position for five years,
being simple, upright, and serious,
and was praised for his competent administration.
When Wú and Kuàijī were first pacified,
many high ministers had rendered meritorious services
and deserved promotion.
He then submitted a memorial humbly declining his position.
The emperor did not permit it,
and sent an attendant to convey his will,
issuing a gracious edict to exhort him
and stop his memorials.
Yìn had no choice
but to resume his duties.
He died in the third year of Tàikāng.
An edict was issued, sending an Imperial Censor with a *jié* (scepter) to supervise the funeral and offer sacrifices,
and he was posthumously given the epithet Chéng.
The Crown Prince ordered his secretary, Wáng Zàn, to compose a eulogy for him,
which was beautiful in style and meaning.
Later, the emperor, thinking of Yìn's pure integrity,
decreed:
"The late Minister of Works Lǐ Yìn
and Grand Master of Ceremonies Péng Guàn
both lived lives of loyalty, purity, and frugality.
After their deaths,
their families had no remaining savings.
Therefore, I bestow two million cash and one thousand *hú* of grain upon Yìn's family,
and half of that amount upon Guàn's family."
He had three sons:
Gù, Zhēncháng, and Xiū.
Gù, courtesy name Wànjī,
was a Cavalier Gentleman.
He died before Yìn.
Gù's son, Zhì, inherited the peerage.
Zhì, courtesy name Yàndào,
held positions successively as Cavalier Attendant Gentleman, General of Illustrious Might, and Administrator of Yángpíng.
Zhēncháng rose to the position of Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Xiū was a Palace Attendant and Central Gentleman of the Crown Prince's Household.
Lú Qīn (Son Fú, Younger brother Tǐng, Tǐng's son Zhì, Zhì's son Chén)
Lú Qīn, courtesy name Zǐruò,
was a native of Zhuō, Fànyáng.
His grandfather, Zhí,
was a Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) of the Hàn dynasty.
His father, Yù,
was a Grand Minister of Works (Sīkōng) in the Wèi dynasty.
The family was prominent for its Confucian scholarship through generations.
Qīn was pure, indifferent, and had far-sighted wisdom.
He devoted himself to the classics and histories.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián),
but did not take office.
The Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn) Cáo Shuǎng of Wèi appointed him as an aide (yuán).
Shuǎng's younger brother once had a request for a personal favor.
Qīn reported to Shuǎng that his younger brother should not interfere with laws and regulations.
Shuǎng deeply accepted this,
and punished his brother.
He was appointed Palace Aide to the Imperial Censor (Shàngshū Láng).
When Shuǎng was executed,
he was dismissed from office.
Later, he became an Imperial Censor (Shìyùshǐ),
inherited his father's title of Marquis of Dàlìtíng,
and was successively promoted to Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lángxié.
When Emperor Xuān (Sīmǎ Yì) became Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
he was appointed as Attendant in the Bureau of the Aide (Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
He was sent out as Administrator of Yángpíng,
then promoted to Regional Inspector of Huáiběi and General Fúbō (Fúbō Jiāngjūn),
achieving considerable renown for his accomplishments.
He was summoned to be a Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
He was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and advanced in peerage to Marquis of Dàliáng.
When Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he was made Regional Commander of all military affairs north of Miǎn, General Píngnán (Píngnán Jiāngjūn), and granted the Imperial Mace (jiǎjié).

He was bestowed with one chasing-chariot (zhuīfēng yáo) and one sleeping-carriage (wòchē) each, two second-class carriages (dì'èr fùmǎ), all riding equipment and weaponry, imperial armory's human and horse armor, etc.,
and 300,000 cash.
Qīn, in his garrison, maintained a balanced approach of leniency and strictness,
and there were no troubles along the borders.
He entered court as Assistant Minister of the Palace Chancellery (Shàngshū Púyè),
with the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Commandant of Carriages (Fèngchē Dūwèi),
and concurrently led the Ministry of Personnel.
For his integrity and poverty,
he was specially granted one hundred bolts of silk.
Qīn always recommended people based on their talent,
and was praised for being honest and impartial.
He passed away in the fourth year of Xiánníng (278 CE).
An imperial edict stated:
"Qīn followed the Way with purity and uprightness,
and upheld virtue with integrity and simplicity.
His reputation in both civil and military affairs
was renowned throughout the realm.
Within the court, he ascended to positions of power,
ensuring the fairness of all matters.
He diligently served both inside and outside the court,
demonstrating the integrity of selfless devotion.
His unfortunate demise
causes me great sorrow.
He is posthumously granted the title of General of the Guards (Wèijiāngjūn) and given the privilege of establishing an administration ranking with the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He is bestowed with secret ritual objects, one set of court attire, one suit of clothing, fifty bolts of cloth, and 300,000 cash."
His posthumous title was Yuán.
Furthermore, because Qīn was loyal, pure, and noble,
not engaging in accumulating property,
and after his death,
his family had no shelter,
he was specially granted 500,000 cash
to build a residence.
Another imperial edict stated:
"The late Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Wáng Jī, General of the Guards (Wèijiāngjūn) Lú Qīn, and concurrently serving General Supervising the Army (Diǎnjūn Jiāngjūn) Yáng Xiāo,
were all traditionally pure and poor.
After their deaths,
their homes had no private savings.
Recently, due to famine,
it is heard that their families are in great need.
Let each be granted three hundred hú of grain."
Qīn successively governed various prefectures and commanderies,
not pursuing fame and glory,
but solely prioritizing fairness and justice.
His salary and emoluments were distributed among relatives and old friends;
he did not seek to accumulate wealth.
All his actions adhered to ritual norms.
When his wife died,
he constructed a mourning hut and used a mourning staff,
residing outside for the entire mourning period.
His collected poems, rhapsodies, essays, and critiques numbered dozens of pieces,
named "Xiǎodào" (Minor Way).
His son Fú succeeded him.
Fú, courtesy name Zǐyún,
began his career as an Imperial Scribe to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
He suffered from a carbuncle and had his hand amputated,
thus becoming incapacitated.
However, the imperial court highly esteemed him,
appointing him as Erudite of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Bóshì), Libationer (Jìjiǔ), and Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
but he did not accept any of these posts.
Qīn's younger brother, Tǐng, courtesy name Zǐhú,
was the Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
Tǐng's son was Zhì.
Zhì, courtesy name Zǐdào,
was initially appointed as an aide in the Ducal Administrations (Gōngfǔ Yuán) and Palace Aide to the Imperial Censor (Shàngshū Láng).
He was sent out as Magistrate (Lìng) of Yè.
When the King of Chéngdū, Yǐng, garrisoned Yè,
he admired Zhì's talent and capacity,
entrusting him with important matters,
and thus Zhì became his chief strategist.
When the King of Qí, Jiǒng, raised his righteous army,
he sent an envoy to inform Yǐng.
Yǐng summoned Zhì to discuss strategy.
Zhì said:
"The King of Zhào is wicked,
openly engaging in usurpation and rebellion.
Throughout the four seas, both men and gods
are filled with indignation.
Now, Your Highness commands all three armies,
responding to the opportune moment to strike like lightning.
The masses will come to you like children to their parents,
arriving without being summoned.
Sweeping away the wicked rebels
will surely be a campaign without a battle.
However, military affairs are of utmost importance,
something the sages approached with caution.
It is advisable to recognize the worthy and appoint the talented
to garner contemporary esteem."
Yǐng deeply agreed with this,
re-selected his senior subordinates,
and generously appointed aides and officials.
He made Zhì Consultative Army Advisor (Zīyì Cānjūn),
and then appointed him Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Chángshǐ),
specifically managing documents and writings.
When Yǐng's vanguard commander Zhào Xiāng was defeated by Lún,
the soldiers were shaken and terrified,
and many strategists wanted to return and defend Cháogē.
Zhì said:
"Now our army has suffered a defeat,
and the enemy has just won,
they will surely be overconfident and contemptuous.
If we halt our troops and do not advance,
the three armies will be afraid and demoralized,
and might become unusable.
Moreover, how can battles not have victories and defeats?
We should select elite troops again,
travel day and night with double speed,
to catch the enemy by surprise.
This is the unusual strategy of warfare."
Yǐng followed this.
When Lún was defeated,
Zhì advised Yǐng, saying:
"The King of Qí's forces numbered a million,
and he was stalemated with Zhāng Hóng and others, unable to resolve the conflict.
Your Highness directly crossed the Yellow River,
this is a great achievement
beyond compare.
Yet the King of Qí is now to assist in governing the court with Your Highness.
I have heard that two powerful individuals cannot coexist in the same place,
and achievements cannot be equally established.
Now, you should use your mother's slight illness as a pretext,
to request returning to your domain to attend to her,
thereby elevating the King of Qí,
and gradually winning the hearts of the realm.
This is the best strategy."
Yǐng accepted this,
and consequently returned to his feudal domain due to his mother's illness,
entrusting heavy responsibilities to Jiǒng.
Because of this, Yǐng gained renown throughout the realm,
and the hearts of the people turned to him.
The imperial court enfeoffed Zhì as Marquis of Wǔqiáng,
and added the title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
When Héjiān Wáng Yǒng accepted Lǐ Hán's suggestion,
wishing to internally eliminate the two princes [referring to Sīmǎ Yǐng and Sīmǎ Yǒng himself],
and establish Yǐng as heir apparent,
he sent a message to Yǐng.
Yǐng was about to agree,
but Zhì advised against it,
and he did not listen.
After Jiǒng was eliminated,
Yǐng remotely controlled the court,
and thus harbored aspirations of disloyalty.
Because Chángshā Wáng was in the capital,
Yǐng could not act as he pleased,
and secretly wished to remove him.
At that time, there was Zhāng Chāng's rebellion in Jīngzhōu.
Yǐng submitted a memorial requesting to personally lead an expedition,
and the imperial court granted it.
When Chāng and others were pacified,
he turned his troops back to attack.
Zhì advised, saying:
"Your Excellency previously had the great achievement of restoring the imperial succession.
When the matter was settled,
you attributed the success to Qí [Wáng Jiǒng],
declined the rewards of the Nine Bestowals,
and did not assume authority over court affairs.
You succored the starving people of Yángzhái [an area in Yǐng's fief]
and buried the white bones at Huángqiáo [where many died from famine],
all of which are deeds of great virtue.
Everyone within the four seas is indebted to you.
The rebellious bandits have been rampant,
harassing Jīngchǔ.
Now Your Excellency has cleared away all difficulties,
and the southern lands are at peace.
To return with your troops,
station your army outside the pass,
and enter the court in civilian attire,
this is the conduct of a hegemon."
Yǐng did not accept the advice.
When he [Zhì's father] died,
Yǐng appointed Zhì as Zhōngshū Jiān,
and kept him in Yè,
participating in the affairs of the Chancellor's residence.
When the imperial carriage was defeated at Dàngyīn,
Yǐng sent Zhì to lead troops to welcome the emperor.
When Wáng Jùn attacked Yè,
Zhì urged Yǐng to escort the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng.
At that time, there were still 15,000 armored soldiers.
Zhì made arrangements during the night,
and by dawn,
the troops were all arrayed.
However, Consort Tài Chéng was reluctant to leave Yè,
and Yǐng could not make a decision.
Soon after, the troops dispersed,
leaving only Zhì, his son Mì, his nephew Zhēn, and a thousand Imperial Guardsmen.
Zhì again urged Yǐng to depart early.
At that time, there was a Daoist priest named Huáng,
known as the "Sage."
The Grand Consort believed in him.
When he was summoned and entered,
the Daoist priest asked for two cups of wine,
drank them,
threw the cups away, and left.
Only then did Zhì's plan finally solidify.
But the men and horses dispersed again.
Zhì searched among the camps and formations,
and found several deer-carriages.
Sīmǎ Dū Hán Xuán gathered the eunuchs,
obtaining over a hundred people.
Zhì entered,
and the emperor asked Zhì,
"Why have things scattered and failed to this extent?"
Zhì replied,
"The rebels are still eighty *lǐ* from Yè,
yet the people have suddenly scattered in a single morning.
The Crown Prince now wishes to escort Your Majesty back to Luòyáng."
The emperor said,
"That is very good."
Thereupon, the emperor immediately set off in a small carriage.
Túnqí Xiàowèi Hǎo Chāng had previously led 8,000 troops to guard Luòyáng.
The emperor summoned him,
and when they reached Jí Jùn, Chāng arrived,
his troops and weapons very impressive.
Zhì was delighted at the prospect of recovery [of strength],
and memorialized the Son of Heaven that it would be appropriate to issue an amnesty,
to share this joy and celebration with the common people.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
Zhì memorialized to appoint Mǎn Fèn as Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Many who had fled returned,
and the various officials were roughly in place.
The emperor was pleased,
and bestowed upon Zhì 200 bolts of silk, 100 *jīn* of floss, one set of clothes, and one crane-patterned damask robe.
Initially,
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng, hearing that Wáng Jùn had raised an army,
sent the Right General Zhāng Fāng to relieve Yè.
Fāng, hearing that the Chéngdū army had been defeated,
halted his troops at Luòyáng,
not daring to advance.
He let his soldiers plunder,
and secretly wished to move the capital to Cháng'ān,
intending to burn the ancestral temples and palaces,
to cut off people's hopes.
Zhì advised Fāng, saying:
"In the past, Dǒng Zhuó was without principle,
burning Luòyáng,
and the bitter resentment still lingers a hundred years later.
Why would you follow his example!"
Thereupon he stopped.
Fāng then forced the Son of Heaven to move to his encampment.
The emperor wept as he boarded the carriage,
with only Zhì attending by his side,
who said:
"Your Majesty, regarding today's matters,
you must follow the Right General in everything.
Your servant is weak and timid,
and can offer no substantial help,
I only know to exert my meager loyalty,
and not leave your side."
They stayed at Fāng's encampment for three days before heading west.
Zhì again accompanied them to Cháng'ān.
When Yǐng was deposed,
Zhì was also dismissed from office.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè welcomed the imperial carriage,
Yǒng memorialized the emperor to restore Yǐng to Yè,
and appointed Zhì as Wèijùn Tàishǒu,
with the additional title of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
to accompany Yǐng in garrisoning the north.
They reached Luòyáng,
but Píngchāng Gōng Mó sent his vanguard commander Fēng Sōng to intercept Yǐng.
Yǐng returned to Cháng'ān,
and before arriving, heard that Yǒng had executed Zhāng Fāng,
and sought peace with Yuè.
Yǐng stayed at Huáyīn.
Zhì proceeded to Cháng'ān,
went to the imperial court to offer apologies,
and then returned to Yǐng at Wǔguān.
They fled to Nányáng,
were again driven out by Liú Táo,
and returned to Héběi.
When Yǐng died,
his officials and retainers scattered,
only Zhì personally arranged the funeral,
and people at the time praised him for it.
Yuè appointed Zhì as Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
and he was promoted to Wèiwèi.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
he was transferred to Shàngshū.
When Luòyáng fell,
Zhì took his wife and children north to seek refuge with Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Kūn.
Upon reaching Yángyì,
he was captured by Liú Càn,
and he, along with his second son Mì and Shēn, were all killed at Píngyáng.
His eldest son was Chén.
Chén, courtesy name Zǐliàng,
was intelligent, sharp, and thoughtful,
fond of Lǎo-Zhuāng,
and skilled in writing.
He was selected to marry Emperor Wǔ's daughter, Yíngyáng Gōngzhǔ,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
but the princess died before the ceremony.
Later, the province nominated him as Xiùcái,
and he was invited to serve as Tàiwèi Yuàn.
When Luòyáng fell,
he accompanied Zhì north to rely on Liú Kūn,
and was captured along with Zhì by Liú Càn.
Càn occupied Jìnyáng,
and kept Chén as his Cānjūn.
Kūn gathered scattered soldiers,
and led Yīlú cavalry to attack Càn.
Càn was defeated and fled,
and Chén was able to join Kūn.
His parents and brothers who were in Píngyáng
had all been killed by Liú Cōng.
When Kūn became Sīkōng,
he appointed Chén as Zhǔbù,
and he was later promoted to Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Kūn's wife was Chén's paternal aunt,
so he was not only treated with increased affection
but also valued for his talent and background.
At the end of the Jiànxīng period,
he followed Kūn and submitted to Duàn Pǐdī.
Pǐdī himself took control of Yōuzhōu,
and appointed Chén as his Biéjià.
After Pǐdī killed Kūn,
he too soon suffered defeat and loss.
At that time, the southern road was blocked,
and Duàn Mòbō was in Liáoxī,
so Chén went to him.
In the early years of Yuán Dì’s reign,
Mòbō sent envoys to Jiāngzuǒ,
and Chén, through his envoys, submitted a memorial arguing Kūn’s case.
The language and intent were very earnest,
whereupon a memorial ceremony was immediately added.
Chén was repeatedly summoned to be Sànqí Zhōngshū Shìláng,
but was detained by Mòbō,
and thus could not cross south.
After Mòbō died,
his younger brother Liáo succeeded him.
Chén was adrift due to the vicissitudes of life for nearly twenty years.
Shí Jìlóng conquered Liáoxī,
and Chén was again captured by Jìlóng,
who appointed him Zhōngshū Shìláng, Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, Shìzhōng, and Zhōngshū Jiān.
When Rǎn Mǐn executed the Shí clan,
Chén followed Mǐn’s army
and was killed in Xiāngguó,
at the age of sixty-seven.
That year was the sixth year of Yǒnghé.
Chén was from a famous family,
and had an early reputation.
He was highly talented and of pure conduct,
and was acclaimed by his contemporaries.
He lived during a time of chaos in the Central Plains,
and along with Cuī Yuè from Qīnghé, Xún Chuò from Yǐngchuān, Péi Xiàn from Hédōng, and Fù Chàng from Běidì, he was trapped in an inappropriate place.
Although they all achieved prominence under the Shí clan,
they considered it a disgrace.
Chén often told his sons:
“After I die,
just say I was Jìn Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng.”
He compiled the Jìfǎ,
annotated the Zhuāngzǐ,
and his collected essays,
all circulated in the world.
Yuè, courtesy name Dàorú,
was the great-grandson of Wèi Sīkōng Lín,
and the nephew of Liú Kūn’s wife.
He and Chén both served as Kūn’s Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and later became Mòbō’s aide.
After falling into the hands of the Shí clan,
he also held high office.
Separate biographies exist for Chuò, Xiàn, and Chàng.
Huá Biǎo (son Yì, Yì’s son, Yì’s younger brother Jiào)
Huá Biǎo, courtesy name Wěiróng,
was from Gāotáng, Píngyuán.
His father, Xīn,
was of pure character and noble conduct,
and served as Wèi Tàiwèi.
Biǎo, at twenty,
was appointed Sànqí Huángmén Láng,
and was successively promoted to Shìzhōng.
In the early Yuánzhèng period,
Shí Bāo came to court,
and greatly praised Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
considering him a reincarnation of Wèi Wǔ.
At the time, those who heard it were drenched in sweat,
and Biǎo, fearing impending disaster,
frequently claimed illness and returned to his residence,
thus escaping the great calamity.
Later, he was promoted to Shàngshū.
When the Five Ranks were established,
he was enfeoffed as Guānyáng Bó.
He was dismissed for not properly supervising funeral arrangements.
[Dismissed].
In the Tàishǐ period,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shǎofù,
transferred to Guānglù Xūn,
and promoted to Tàicháng Qīng.
After several years,
he requested to retire due to old age and illness.
The imperial edict stated:
“Biǎo is pure, upright, and simple,
possessing the virtues of an elder,
having long managed affairs of state, quietly and diligently without slackness.
Yet he has earnestly declined due to illness,
his memorials being sincere.
We now grant his request,
appointing him Tàizhōng Dàfū,
bestowing twenty thousand cash,
and granting him a bed, tent, mattress, and mat, and a salary equal to a minister,
with a horse allowed to enter his gate.”
Biǎo was renowned for his austere integrity;
Sītú Lǐ Yìn and Sīlì Wáng Hóng, among others,
praised Biǎo’s purity, detachment, reclusiveness, and tranquility,
believing that one should not distinguish between high and low status in their intimacy.
He died in the eighth month of the first year of Xíaníng,
at the age of seventy-two.
His posthumous name was Kāng,
and an imperial edict bestowed a court robe.
He had six sons: Yì, Cén, Jiào, Jiàn, Dàn, and Jiǎn.
Yì, courtesy name Chángjùn,
was brilliant, discerning, talented, and righteous.
His wife’s father, Lú Yù, was in charge of selection,
and found it difficult to promote a relative by marriage.
Thus, Yì was not appointed until he was thirty-five,
later serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Láng.
In the early Tàishǐ period,
he was promoted to Rǒngcóng Púyè.
He was highly regarded by Wǔ Dì from a young age,
and successively served as Huángmén Shìláng, Sànqí Chángshì, Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn, Shìzhōng, Nánzhōngláng Jiāng, and Dūdū Héběi Zhūjūn Shì.
When his father was gravely ill, he returned home;
then he suffered the loss according to old custom,
and resumed his duties after the burial.
Yì firmly declined,
which displeased the emperor.
Earlier,
Biǎo had some personal guests (cìkè) in Gé,
and he had Yì ask the county magistrate Yuán Yì to register their names.
Three of the guests were each replaced by a slave.
When Yì was punished for bribery,
his prison testimony was confusing and contradictory,
no longer clearly stating that slaves replaced guests,
but directly saying he sent three slaves to Yì,
and Yì was also Lú Shì’s son-in-law.
Furthermore, Zhōngshū Jiān Xún Xù had previously sought Yì’s daughter for his middle son,
but Yì refused,
which caused resentment.
Therefore, Xún Xù secretly reported to the emperor
that Yuán Yì had many bribers
and not all could be punished.
It was better to hold the closest person responsible,
and then pointed to Yì.
Moreover, because Yì had committed the offense of disobedience,
his official position was removed during the mourning period,
and his noble rank and fief were stripped.
Dàhónglú Hé Zūn memorialized that since Yì was dismissed as a commoner,
he should not inherit the enfeoffment,
and requested that Biǎo’s great-grandson Hùn succeed Biǎo.
The officials in charge memorialized, saying:
“Yì’s dismissal and stripping of rank was a temporary measure.
Yì is the heir apparent,
recorded in the roster;
not allowing him to inherit is a double punishment.
When feudal lords commit crimes,
and are handled according to the Eight Deliberations,
it is to honor their merits and heavy rank.
An heir by direct lineage should not be condemned for life for an offense;
deposing him would be too severe.
According to the law, he should be allowed to inherit the enfeoffment.”
[This text seems to have a slightly different sentence structure for 149-150, but the meaning is clear: deposing him is too severe, according to the law he should inherit the enfeoffment.]
The edict stated:
“When a feudal lord dies,
his son immediately takes the throne upon reaching age,
this is an ancient system.
If he should take the throne but is deposed,
his noble rank and mandate are all removed.
Why would this be a double punishment?
Moreover, My punishment of Yì
was to maintain strictness against corruption;
it was not based on ordinary law.
The wise officials cannot clearly explain this intention,
but instead pervert rites and laws,
disregarding precedents.
The emperor’s command deposed him,
but the subordinates restore him;
this is for superior and inferior to be completely contradictory.”
[This text seems to have a slightly different sentence structure for 166, but the meaning is clear: this means superior and inferior are completely contradictory.]
Thereupon, the officials in charge memorialized to dismiss the officials who argued this,
and an edict stated that all should be treated as redeemed.
Hùn, as the great-grandson who should receive the enfeoffment,
fled,
cut his hair, feigned madness,
and became mute, unable to speak.
Thus, he avoided being appointed,
and the world praised him.
Yì lived in seclusion in his home for nearly ten years,
teaching his children and grandchildren,
and lecturing on classics.
He compiled important matters from classics,
named it Shànwén,
which circulated in the world.
He and Chén Xié jointly built a pigsty next to his residence.
The Emperor once went to see it,
and asked the reason.
Those around him truthfully answered,
and the Emperor felt pity in his heart.
Later, the Emperor ascended Língyún Tái,
and saw Yì’s alfalfa garden,
with very neat paths and fields,
and felt a sense of nostalgia.
At the beginning of Tàikāng's reign, a general amnesty was declared,
and so he was able to inherit his father's title.
After a long time,
he was appointed City Gate Commandant (Chéngmén Xiàowèi),
then promoted to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
Several years later,
he was made Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiàn).
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was given the additional titles of Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng), Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
and advanced in peerage to Duke (Gōng).
Yì responded to Yáng Jùn's summons
but did not return in time,
so the authorities impeached him, leading to his dismissal from office.
Soon after, he was promoted to Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù),
with the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
He always followed the rituals and canons,
embodying the essence of a tutor and guide.
Later, in his old age, he became seriously ill.
An imperial edict dispatched the imperial physicians to treat his illness,
and he was advanced to the position of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), with the honorific title of Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
At that time, Hán Shòu, the Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn), sought to marry his daughter to Yì's grandson Táo through the Empress Jiǎ.
Yì refused and did not consent.
The Empress deeply resented this,
and thus he was never promoted to the highest offices of state (Táisī).
He died at the age of seventy-five,
and was posthumously granted the title Yuán.
He had three sons: Hùn, Huì, and Huá.
Hùn, styled Jìnglún,
inherited his father's peerage.
He was pure, chaste, simple, and upright.
He held positions such as Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng) and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū),
and died in office.
His son Táo inherited his title,
was appointed Magistrate of Gǒng (Gǒng Lìng),
and perished at the hands of Shí Lè.
Huì, styled Jìngshú,
served as Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn).
He fled from bandits with Xún Pán and Xún Zǔ.
Upon reaching Lín'yǐng,
both he and his son were killed.
Huá, styled Jìngzé,
was widely learned and praised for his purity and simplicity.
He married Emperor Wǔ's daughter, Princess Cháng of Yíngyáng (Yíngyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ),
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Equipage (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
At the beginning of Yuánkāng's reign,
when the Eastern Palace was established,
he was selected to be a friend of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Bīnyǒu),
bestowed the title of Marquis of Guānnèi (Guānnèi Hóu),
and granted an enfeoffment of one hundred households.
He was invited by Minister of Works Wáng Hún (Sītú Wáng Hún) to serve as a clerk in his granary office (Cāngcáo Yuàn).
Subsequently, he was appointed Palace Gentleman (Sànqí Shìláng),
and successively promoted to Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Central Commander of the Northern Army (Běijūn Zhōnghóu).
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn),
with the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
When Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
he was made Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū),
and advanced in peerage to Count of Yuǎnlíng County (Yuǎnlíng Xiàn Gōng).
A short while later,
Liú Cōng pressed on Cháng'ān.
An edict ordered him to go out as General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the position of Administrator of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu),
to serve as an external reinforcement.
He raised a righteous army
of two thousand men,
but before he could hasten west,
Guānzhōng had already fallen.
At that time, numerous bandits were rampant,
and the various prefectures and commanderies successively fell.
Huá also wished to abandon his commandery and cross east,
but his cousin Yì had been executed by Emperor Yuán,
which made him hesitant.
He first wrote to General of Agile Cavalry Wáng Dǎo (Piàojì Jiāngjūn Wáng Dǎo),
and Dǎo spoke to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"The crimes of brothers do not extend to each other,
much less to cousins!"
He was immediately summoned
and appointed Superintendent of the Imperial Clan (Guānglùxūn).
Upon his arrival,
before he could be formally appointed,
he was instead made General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn),
with the additional titles of Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Moderator of his home province (Běnhuā Dàzhōngzhèng).
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
and proposed establishing suburban sacrifices.
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Diāo Xié (Shàngshū Diāo Xié) and Libationer of the Directorate of Education Dù Yí (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Dù Yí) argued
that suburban sacrifices should only be performed upon returning to Luòyáng.
Huá argued
that Emperor Xiàn of Hàn, when residing in Xǔ,
had immediately performed suburban sacrifices;
therefore, it was appropriate to establish them here.
Minister of Works Xún Zǔ (Sītú Xún Zǔ) and General of Agile Cavalry Wáng Dǎo (Piàojì Jiāngjūn Wáng Dǎo) concurred,
and so the suburban sacrifices were decided upon.
Soon after, he requested to be relieved due to illness.
An imperial edict stated:
"The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) is responsible for the ancestral temples,
where the autumn and spring sacrifices are treated with utmost reverence.
However, Huá's illness
prevents him from personally carrying out his duties.
Confucius said, 'If I do not participate in the sacrifice,
it is as if there were no sacrifice.'
How much more so for the duties of the Minister of Ceremonies!
We now transfer him to the position of Grand Judge (Tíngwèi)."
A short while later,
he was granted the additional title of Special Advanced Minister (Tèjìn).
At the beginning of Tàiníng's reign,
he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
with the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
and oversaw all land and water forces at Shítou.
Wáng Dūn memorialized to transfer him to Commander of the Guards (Hùjūn),
but due to illness, he did not accept the appointment.
He was granted the title of Grand Master of Golden and Purple Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and concurrently served as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo).
When Emperor Chéng ascended the throne,
he was granted the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
and concurrently served as Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
At the beginning of Xiánhé's reign,
all titles and advancements in peerage granted during Emperor Mǐn's time were abolished.
He was instead enfeoffed as Marquis of Yuǎnlíng County (Yuǎnlíng Xiàn Hóu) for his merits in suppressing Wáng Dūn,
and again concurrently served as Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
During the Rebellion of Sū Jùn,
he attended the Emperor's side
and followed him to Shítou,
enduring hardship and danger,
suffering for over a year.
Initially,
as Grand Moderator of his province (Zhōu Dàzhōngzhèng),
he had dismissed Rèn Ràng, a villager who was frivolous and without moral conduct.
When Ràng was in Sū Jùn's army,
he used his power to kill many,
but whenever he saw Huá, he would respectfully
refrain from his atrocities.
When Zhōng Yǎ and Liú Chāo died,
Huá was also about to meet the same fate,
but Ràng earnestly saved and protected him,
thus he escaped.
When the Emperor came of age (jiā yuánfú)
and was about to take an empress,
after the troubles of war,
almost no classics remained,
and there was no basis for the rites of marriage and capping.
Huá researched old canons,
compiled and established the rites,
including the rules for suburban temples, the Pìyōng academy, and the imperial court.
All these matters were put into practice.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Left Splendid Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and granted the honorific title of Kaīfǔ,
with his Attendant-in-ordinary (Chángshì) title remaining as before.
He firmly declined the appointment but had not yet accepted it
when he died.
He was sixty-nine years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng), Grand Master of Left Splendid Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū), and Kaīfǔ,
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
He was pure, diligent, frugal, and simple.
Although he held prominent positions,
he always wore plain clothes and ate vegetarian food,
becoming even more devout in his old age.
On the day of his death,
his family had no surplus wealth,
only several hundred scrolls of books.
People of his time valued him for this.
His son Jùn inherited his title
and became a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng).
Jùn's son, Yǎngzhī,
was Grand Chief Supervisor (Dàchángqiū).
Jiào, styled Shú Jùn,
possessed profound and extensive talent and learning,
and gained an excellent reputation in his youth.
When Emperor Wén was General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn),
he was invited to be a clerk (yuánshǔ),
then appointed Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng),
and transferred to Middle Clerk for the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
At the beginning of Tàishǐ's reign,
he was bestowed the title of Marquis of Guānnèi (Guānnèi Hóu).
He was promoted to Central Secretary of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
and then sent out as Administrator of Ānpíng (Ānpíng Tàishǒu).
He declined, citing his elderly parents, and did not go.
Instead, he was appointed Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
overseeing the composition of official documents (zhōngshū zhùzuò),
concurrently serving as Erudite of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Bóshì),
and then promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng).
At the end of Tàikāng,
Emperor Wǔ became quite fond of feasts and entertainment,
and also suffered from frequent illnesses.
When he had a slight recovery,
Jiáo and his attendant officials presented a memorial congratulating him,
and thereupon offered a subtle remonstrance, saying:
"We humbly observe that Your Sacred Body is gradually returning to peace and health.
All rejoice in unison,
and cannot help but clap and dance.
We, your foolish and dull servants,
secretly harbor a humble thought:
that by achieving success in what is overlooked,
affairs will be without regret;
by considering blessings in what is nearing completion,
the Mandate will be renewed daily.
We only wish that Your Majesty would profoundly extend your sagacious wisdom,
deeply contemplate the regrets of what is overlooked,
to achieve the daily renewed blessings.
Cultivate tranquility and harmonious qi,
conserve and nurture your spirit,
nourish your body in the realm of purity and simplicity,
and keep your mind in the domain of emptiness and vastness.
Do not be weary of the common admonitions of the world,
thereby overlooking the words of your subjects,
then abundant good fortune will be prolonged daily,
and the empire will be greatly fortunate!"
The Emperor replied with an imperial handwritten edict, saying:
"I will take care of myself;
there is no need to worry."
At the beginning of Yuánkāng,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xuānchāngtíng.
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
his title was changed to Marquis of Lèxiāng,
and he was promoted to Shàngshū.
Later, because Jiáo was broadly learned and widely knowledgeable,
and his writings were substantial and authentic,
possessing the aspiration of a good historian,
he was transferred to Mìshūjiān,
granted the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and his rank was equal to that of Zhōngshū.
The Secretariat (Mìshūjiàn) was considered the inner court (nèi tái),
and the Zhōngshū, Sànqí, Zhuòzuò, and matters of ritual, music,
astronomy, divination,
writings of the southern ministries,
and compilations of the Ménxià,
were all under its jurisdiction.
Originally,
Jiáo considered the Hàn Jì to be verbose and chaotic,
and deeply harbored the intention to revise it.
At that time, he was a Táiláng,
in charge of official regulations,
and thus he was able to extensively consult secret archives,
which allowed him to pursue his endeavor.
Starting from Guāngwǔ,
and ending with Xiàoxiàn,
covering one hundred and ninety-five years,

he compiled twelve volumes of the Dì Jì (Annals of Emperors), two volumes of the Huánghòu Jì (Annals of Empresses), ten volumes of the Shí Diǎn (Ten Canons), seventy volumes of Biographies (zhuàn), as well as three genealogical tables (sān pǔ), prefaces and biographies (xù zhuàn), and a catalog,
totaling ninety-seven volumes.
Jiáo believed that empresses were matched with Heaven to form a union,
and that previous historians placing their biographies in the Wàiqī Zhuàn (Biographies of Imperial Relatives) at the end of the compilation
was not in accordance with this meaning.
Therefore, he changed it to Huánghòu Jì,
placing it after the Dì Jì.
He also changed Zhì to Diǎn,
because of the precedent of the Yáo Diǎn.
He then renamed it Hàn Hòu Shū and presented it,
and an imperial edict ordered the court officials to hold a conference.
At that time, Zhōngshūjiān Xún Xù, Lìng Hé Jiáo, Tàicháng Zhāng Huá, and Shìzhōng Wáng Jì all agreed that Jiáo's writing was refined yet substantial, the events accurately recorded,
possessing the style of Qiān and Gù,
and the spirit of true historical records,
and should be stored in the imperial archives.
Later, Tàiwèi Rǔnán Wáng Liàng and Sīkōng Wèi Guàn, serving as tutors to the Eastern Palace,
formally presented it for public discourse,
and the matter was thus implemented.
Jiáo's various writings, including discussions, refutations, poems, and rhapsodies, amounted to hundreds of thousands of words.
His memorials on official regulations, the crown prince's proper return to the palace, border pacification, the rain sacrifice, the Míngtáng and Píyǒng, the dredging and guiding of rivers and canals,
the establishment of the Dūshuǐguān following Yǔ's old tracks,
and the revival of sericulture rituals by establishing a Chángqiū,
were mostly put into effect.
He passed away in the third year of Yuánkāng (293 CE),
and was posthumously granted the title of Shàofǔ,
with the posthumous name Jiǎn.
Jiáo was fond of alcohol,
and was often deeply intoxicated.
He passed away before his ten volumes of historical writing (Shí Diǎn) were completed.
Mìshūjiān Hé Shào memorialized to appoint Jiáo's second son, Chè, as Zuǒzhuòzuòláng,
to continue his work,
but he also died before completing it.
Later, Supervisor Miáo Zhēng
again memorialized to appoint Jiáo's youngest son, Chàng, as Zuǒzhuòzuòláng,
who successfully completed the Shí Diǎn,
and also drafted the Wei and Jin annals and biographies,
serving alongside Zhuòzuòláng Zhāng Zài and others as historical officials.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
classics and records were lost,
and over thirty volumes of Jiáo's writings survived.
Jiáo had three sons: Yí, Chè, Chàng.
Yí inherited the title,
and held office up to Chánglè Nèishǐ.
Chàng possessed talent and intellect,
and his written works amounted to tens of thousands of words.
During the bandit uprisings,
he sought refuge in Jīngzhōu,
where he was killed by bandits
at the age of forty.
Shí Jiàn
Shí Jiàn, courtesy name Línbó,
was a native of Yàncí, Lèlíng.
He came from a humble background,
but possessed a refined ambition for public righteousness.
He served in Wei,
successively holding positions such as Shàngshūláng, Shìyùshǐ, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He corrected many errors,
and the court held him in awe.
He was sent out as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ, with the additional titles of Jiǎjié and Hùxiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng.
When Emperor Wǔ accepted the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the Son of Tángyáng.
He entered the court as Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and was then transferred to Shàngshū.
At that time, Qín and Liáng were defeated by the barbarians,
and Jiàn was sent to supervise all military affairs in Lǒngyòu.
He was dismissed from office for making false claims about his achievements.
Later, he became Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and was dismissed for falsely inflating the number of enemy heads taken in a campaign against Wu bandits.
An imperial edict stated:
"Formerly, the Administrator of Yúnzhōng, Wèi Shàng, was punished for inaccurate reporting of decapitations;
General Wǔyá, Tián Shùn, committed suicide for falsely increasing captured spoils.
Deception and violation of the law
have been abhorred throughout history.

Wēn Xiàn, courtesy name Chángqīng,
