restraining selection
and preventing the precise matching of talent to suitability.
What's more, with the current nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
those they dislike have their strengths diminished,
and those they favor have their weaknesses embellished.
They merely compile
empty discussions
to create false reputations.
Thus, if ranks (pǐn) do not measure ability,
how can the hundred offices (bǎikuí) be managed?
How can the myriad affairs (wànjī) be regulated?
This is the seventh detriment to governance.
According to the former imperial edict (zhàoshū) on the nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
good and evil must be recorded
for commendation or censure.
At that time, throughout the land,
there was little to fear.
But with the current nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
those who are demoted have their
crimes not publicized,
and those who are promoted have their good deeds not listed.
This abolishes the principle of commendation and censure,
and relies on personal likes and dislikes for judgment.
The clear and the turbid flow together,
thereby establishing their private interests.
Therefore, it goes against the former system of grades (pǐn),
magnifying its
influence
to manipulate the multitude,
forcing them to side with oneself.
Those who advance have no achievements to encourage them,
and those who retreat have no faults to deter them.
If encouragement and deterrence are unclear,
then customs (fēngsú)
become corrupt.
How can people under heaven not abandon virtue and eagerly pursue personal connections?
This is the eighth detriment to governance.
From this discussion,
it is clear that the impartial and upright (zhōngzhèng) are selected but are not the right people,
authority is granted without rewards or punishments,
or the impartial and upright (zhōngzhèng) are lacking and there are no prohibitions or inspections.
Thus, corrupt factions run rampant,
and injustice and abuses are widespread.
Although the title is impartial and upright (zhōngzhèng),
it is actually a nest of villains.
Although the system is called the nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
it has eight detriments.
Hatred can arise among close relatives,
suspicion can grow between
blood relations,
one can be troubled by enemies in one's lifetime,
and descendants can suffer from its calamities.
These are woes that have plagued successive generations,
not merely a present harm.
Therefore, the ruler of an age observes the times
and enacts laws
to prevent villainy and suppress disorder,
there being no constant system.
Thus, the Zhōu (Zhōu) dynasty followed the Yīn (Yīn) dynasty,
with some additions and subtractions.
As for the impartial and upright (zhōngzhèng) and the nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
the most sagely and ancient worthies never
practiced them.
How could they have been ignorant of this matter or failed to consider it comprehensively?
It must be that the appropriate governance and transformation had no use for this.
Since the establishment of Wèi (Wèi),
it has not been seen to yield the success
of acquiring talent,
but instead has created burdens of enmity and disparagement.
It damages customs and corrupts traditions,
doing no good for transformation.
Of the mistakes, ancient and modern,
none is greater than this.
Your foolish servant believes it is appropriate to abolish the impartial and upright (zhōngzhèng),
do away with the nine grades (jiǔpǐn),
discard the flawed laws of the Wèi (Wèi) house,
and establish an excellent system for our generation.
The memorial was submitted,
and an imperial edict (yōuzhào) responded to it.
Later, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Wèi Guàn (Wèi Guàn) and others also jointly memorialized, advocating for the abolition of the nine grades (jiǔpǐn)
and the restoration of the ancient local recommendations (xiāngyì lǐxuǎn).
The Emperor ultimately did not implement it.
Yì (Yì) worked diligently day and night for the public,
sitting until dawn.
His words and discussions were sharp and direct,
without any bending or deviation,
and he was revered and looked up to by both court and commoners.
He once fell ill during a period of fasting,
and his wife visited him.
Yì (Yì) then memorialized to add a penalty for his wife and requested to end his fasting.
If his wife and children had faults,
he immediately applied a beating,
such was his impartiality.
However, due to his unyielding uprightness,
he did not reach the highest ministerial ranks (gōngfǔ).
The Emperor, seeing Yì (Yì)'s integrity and poverty,
bestowed 300,000 cash upon him
and daily provisions of rice and meat.
At seventy,
he requested retirement.
After a long time,
his request was granted.
He returned to his residence as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
with permission for carriages and horses to enter his gate,
and was again granted 1,000,000 cash.
Later, the Sītú (Grand Minister over the Masses) nominated Yì to be the Dà Zhōngzhèng of Qīngzhōu.
The Shàngshū (Minister of the Secretariat) opined that since Yì had retired from office by "hanging up his carriage,"
he should not be burdened with trivial matters.
Sūn Yǐn (孫尹) of Lè'ān (樂安), the Xiang (Chancellor) of Chénliú (陳留), submitted a memorial, saying:
"According to the Rítuals,
it is proper for the humble to toil,
and the revered to be at ease;
this is in accordance with what is fitting.
Sītú Wèi Shū (魏舒) and Sīlì Xiàowèi (Colonel Director of Retainers) Yán Xún (嚴詢) are close in age to Yì.
Formerly, they all served as Sànqí Chángshì (Regular Palace Attendant).
Later, they were assigned different internal and external posts,
and in the path of their careers,
their beginnings and endings were consistent.
Now, Xún governs a prefecture of 400,000 households,
and also supervises all officials,
managing crucial affairs.
The jurisdiction of Shū is vast and prosperous,
and he also administers the Nine Ranks,
evaluating discussions across sixteen prefectures,
yet the authorities do not consider this arduous.
If Yì is merely to oversee one prefecture,
and it is considered unsuitable to burden him with trivial matters,
then Yì is too favored,
and Xún and Shū are too ill-treated.
If it is because he was previously allowed to retire,
and thus should not be offered new promotions,
then Zhèng Mào (鄭袤), the former Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness), who became Sīkōng (Minister of Works), would be a case in point.
Indeed, to know men is to be wise;
even emperors find this difficult.
To still be entrusted with the responsibility of a chief minister,
yet not be consulted on matters of human relations—
this is what I secretly find unsettling.
In the past, Zhèng Wǔgōng (鄭武公), though over eighty years old,
entered the court to serve as Zhōu Sītú (Minister of the Masses of Zhou).
Even past the age of 'hanging up the carriage,' there
must be occasions when one can still be useful.
Previously, Yì served as Sīlì (Director of Retainers),
upholding the law without compromise,
and impeaching many
of the court officials.
The proverb says: 'One who has suffered the punishment of Yáo (堯)
cannot praise Yáo.'
That upright officials have no party is
known throughout history.
Thus, Jí Àn (汲黯) died in Huáiyáng (淮陽),
and Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒) merely served as a minister to a feudal lord.
Yet Yì alone encountered an enlightened sage ruler,
and remained close to the imperial carriage;
the scholars of his generation all considered this an honor.
Although Yì himself suffers from a partial wind-illness,
his spirit and intellect are keen.
The evaluation of one prefecture
is not enough to burden his thoughts.
Yì's hatred of evil is slightly excessive;
the authorities must suspect that his judgments might harm others.
Therefore, they grant him high courtesies,
keeping him away from actual duties.
This is to corner Yì,
and block his path in human affairs.
In my prefecture, the most virtuous is Yì.
If Yì is not employed,
then clear discussion will be overturned."
Thereupon, the Guānglùxūn (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness) Shí Jiàn (石鑒) and others from Qīngzhōu (青州), from the second rank upwards, jointly memorialized, saying:
"We respectfully note the memorial from Sūn Yǐn (孫尹), Xiang (Chancellor) of Chénliú (陳留), and his letter to us, which are as follows.
Our prefecture borders the sea and Mount Tài (泰),
and participates in the customs of Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯).
Hence, its people are fundamentally practical,
and generations honor virtue and deference.
Although it does not fully match the past,
the inherited teachings still exist.
Therefore, human relations return to practice,
and scholars know what to uphold.
Previously, we received the Sītú's (Grand Minister over the Masses) summons,
to jointly nominate the Dà Zhōngzhèng of the prefecture.
All agreed that Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness) Yì is
of pure filial piety and utmost simplicity,
well-known in his community.
He is loyal, fair, honest, and upright,
devoted to serving his superiors.
He does not seek honor in office,
but only strives to fulfill his duty.
He rectifies himself and leads with principle,
exalting public good and forgetting private interest.
His conduct is noble and his righteousness clear;
his beginnings and endings are consistent.
Thus, he can inspire virtuous scholars to emulate his demeanor,
and his community to return to his clear influence.
Although aged and partially ill,
his spirit is still vigorous.
He is indeed the one whom the people of our prefecture wish to take as their standard and rely upon.
Truly, with Yì's clear integrity,
he can command trust without speaking.
Wherever his influence extends,
the clear and the turbid will surely yield,
thus fulfilling the shared expectation of the entire prefecture.
We secretly believe that honoring the worthy and valuing virtue
is a great principle of teaching.
The king's regulations concerning appointments and dismissals
always serve to open or close paths.
Among those whom scholars respect,
human relations are paramount.
We are humble and unworthy;
though our previous words were rejected,
now, having received Yǐn's letter,
how dare we not present this memorial?
According to Yǐn's argument,
he not only values Yì's reputation,
but also generally presents the court's proper principles of appointment and dismissal.
Whether Yǐn's words are appropriate
should be evaluated."
Consequently, Yì was appointed Dū (Chief) of the prefecture,
evaluating and rectifying the flow of human talent,
distinguishing the clear from the turbid.
Those he impeached and demoted
began with the powerful and noble.
He died in the sixth year of Tàikāng (太康).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) patted his desk and exclaimed in surprise:
"I have lost my renowned minister!
He did not get to live to become one of the Three Ducal Ministers!"
He immediately granted him the posthumous honor of Yítóng Sānsī (Grand Master of Cavalry, Minister over the Masses, Minister of Works),
and dispatched an envoy to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Wáng Gōng (王宮) of Běihǎi (北海), the Yǔlín Zuǒjiān (Left Supervisor of the Feathered Forest), submitted a memorial, saying:
"The imperial edict states that Yì was loyal, fair, and selfless,
and granted him the rank of a Sānsī (Three Ducal Ministers);
this is indeed a fine act of the enlightened court in evaluating merits and recognizing Yì's achievements.
I respectfully note that
a posthumous name (shì) is a record of conduct,
and a title (hào) is a sign of achievement.
Now Yì's achievements and virtues are both established,
yet he has a title but no posthumous name;
this is not consistent with righteousness.
I humbly seek to explain this through the events of the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals).
The system of posthumous names primarily focuses on conduct, not on rank.
However, since Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏),
if one's rank was not that of a Lièhóu (Marquis),
then after death, even if one had noble conduct,
no posthumous name was given.
This led to worthy ministers of the Sānsī (Three Ducal Ministers)
being treated as less than generals in field battles.
Given the discrepancy in inscribed records,
I wish that in this enlightened age, the distant system of the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals) be adopted,
and the old restrictions on titles be changed,
so that the reality of achievements and conduct are not obscured or replaced.
Then all will find reliance.
If it is considered that reforming old customs and destroying established systems
is not something to be done hastily,
then Yì's loyal contributions,
though not involving attacking cities or seizing territory,
should, in terms of recognizing virtue and advancing rank,
also be included in the precedents.
I dare to follow the principle of 'seeking the Zhōu (周) rites for exemplary conduct,'
and respectfully list Yì's achievements and conduct as above."
The Emperor sent out his memorial for the eight chief ministers to discuss,
and many agreed with Gōng's (宮) proposal.
The memorial was shelved and not acted upon.
Yì had two sons: Tūn (暾) and Zǒng (總).
Tūn (暾), courtesy name Chángshēng (長升),
was upright and had his father's demeanor.
In the early Tàikāng (太康) era, he served as a Bóshì (Erudite).
When discussing the transfer of Qí Wáng Yōu (齊王攸) to his feud,
and the augmentation of his ceremonies,
Tūn (暾) and other Bóshì (Erudites) argued against the imperial will.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) was furious
and had Tūn (暾) and others arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (Minister of Justice).
They were released during a general amnesty
and dismissed from office.
Initially,
Tūn's (暾) father, Yì, hated Fēng Dǎn's (馮紞) treachery and sycophancy,
and wanted to impeach him,
but died before he could do so.
By this time,
Dǎn's (紞) official position and influence had grown daily.
Tūn (暾) sighed with emotion and said:
"If my late father were still alive, he would not have allowed Dǎn (紞) to escape trouble."
Later, he became the Magistrate of Suānzhǎo,
then transferred to be a Palace Censor (Shìyùshǐ).
It happened that the Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) Liú Yú of Grand Minister over the Masses (Sītú) Wáng Hún implicated Tūn in his confession during an interrogation,
and Tūn was to be arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Wáng Hún did not want his office to be implicated in wrongdoing,
and intended to resist the impeachment and handle it himself.
He and Tūn argued back and forth over right and wrong,
and Wáng Hún became angry,
so he resigned his position and returned to his residence.
Tūn then impeached Wáng Hún, saying:
"I respectfully submit that Grand Minister over the Masses (Sītú) Wáng Hún,
having received profound grace from the state,
and holding the position of one of the Three Dukes,
is unable to assist the Son of Heaven above,
harmonize Yin and Yang,
or facilitate the proper functioning of all things below,
so that the high ministers and grand officials each obtain their rightful place.
He dared to use Liú Yú to resist and obstruct the imperial envoy,
privately wishing for his great office to initiate protracted litigation.
In the past, Chén Píng did not answer Emperor Wén of Hàn's questions,
and Bǐng Jí did not inquire about the changes surrounding a dead person.
This indeed embodied the deportment of a prime minister.
Having initiated criminal proceedings,
he retreated out of resentment,
acting rashly and impulsively,
without the decorum of a great minister.
I request that Wáng Hún be dismissed from office.
The Right Chief Clerk (Yòuzhǎngshǐ) and Marquis of Yángqiū Tíng (Yángqiū Tíng Hóu) Liú Zhào,
is obsequious and sycophantic,
merely seeking to conform.
I request that the Grand Minister of Rites (Dàhónglú) strip him of his title and fief."
All who heard Tūn's memorial
praised and admired it.
Later, the Imperial Armory (Wǔkù) caught fire.
Shàngshū Guō Zhāng led a hundred men to protect himself but did not help extinguish the fire.
Tūn sternly interrogated him.
Guō Zhāng angrily said:
"I can cut off your horns (i.e., your power)."
Tūn flared up and said to Guō Zhāng:
"How dare you presume upon imperial favor to wield power and influence,
a man wearing the cap of imperial law, and you wish to cut off my horns!"
He asked for paper and brush to impeach him.
Guō Zhāng bowed his head, not daring to speak.
The crowd mediated,
and Tūn stopped.
Guō Zhāng had long been noble and extravagant,
always accompanied by over a hundred people when he went out.
From then on,
he endeavored to be simple and unadorned.
Tūn was promoted to Administrator of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Nèishǐ).
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
he offered Tūn the title of General Who Subdues Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
but Tūn refused,
and joined the Three Princes in raising a righteous army.
When Emperor Huì was restored to the throne,
Tūn became Left Vice Director (Zuǒchéng).
He stood in court with a stern countenance,
and the Three Departments (Sāntái) were clean and solemn.
Soon after, he concurrently held the post of Imperial Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and impeached and dismissed the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè) and Duke of Dōng'ān (Dōng'ān Gōng) Yáo, as well as Wáng Cuì, Dǒng Ài, and more than ten others.
The court commended him,
and he officially assumed the position.
He was promoted to Palace Gentleman (Zhōngshùzǐ), General of the Left Guards (Zuǒwèijiāngjūn), and Colonel Director of the Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
He impeached and dismissed Wǔlíng Wáng Dàn, Hé Suí, Liú Tǎn, Wēn Jī, Lǐ Xuǎn, and others.
When Chángshā Wáng attacked Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
Tūn was involved in the planning.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhūxū County (Zhūxū Xiàn Gōng),
with one thousand eight hundred households.
He died,
and was dismissed for his involvement.
After a while,
he was again made Colonel Director of the Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
When Emperor Huì traveled to Cháng'ān,
Tūn was left to guard Luòyáng.
Hékàn Wáng Yǒng sent an envoy to poison Empress Yáng.
Tūn then, together with the Vice Director of the Temporary Court (Liútái Púyè) Xún Pán and the Governor of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn) Zhōu Fù, submitted a memorial,
arguing for the Empress's innocence.
The details are in the Empress's biography.
When Yǒng saw the memorial,
he was greatly enraged,
and sent Chén Yán and Lǚ Láng with five thousand cavalry to arrest Tūn.
Tūn fled east to Gāomì Wáng Lüè.
It so happened that Liú Gēn rebelled.
Lüè appointed Tūn as Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū),
with the additional title of General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn), to suppress Liú Gēn.
Tūn lost the battle
and returned to Luòyáng.
Arriving at Suānzhǎo,
he met Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, who was escorting the Emperor.
When the Emperor returned to Luòyáng,
Empress Yáng was restored to the palace.
The Empress sent an envoy to thank Tūn, saying:
"It is thanks to the loyal and sincere resolve of Director Liú Sīlì
that I have this day."
For his old merits, his title and fief were restored,
and he was given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
Tūn's wife had died earlier
and was buried in the imperial mausoleum.
His son Gēngshēng was newly married.
According to family custom,
the bride was to pay respects at the grave.
Tūn brought dozens of carriages with guests and relatives,
loaded with wine and food, and set off.
Before this,
Wáng Léng, the Magistrate of Luòyáng, was trusted by Yuè
but disdained Tūn.
Tūn always wanted to discipline him,
which Wáng Léng resented.
At that time, Liú Cōng and Wáng Mí were stationed north of the Yellow River,
and the capital was in peril.
Wáng Léng reported to Yuè,
saying that Tūn was a fellow villager of Wáng Mí and intended to defect to him.
Yuè dispatched elite cavalry to pursue Tūn.
The Right Chief Clerk (Yòuzhǎngshǐ) Fù Xuān clarified that Tūn was not doing so.
Tūn heard of this
and turned back before reaching the tomb,
reproaching Yuè with righteous words.
Yuè was greatly ashamed.
When Liú Yào attacked the capital,
Tūn was appointed General of the Pacifying Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn), given the Axe of Authority (jiǎjié), and made Commander-in-chief of all forces defending the city.
When Liú Yào retreated,
Tūn was promoted to Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè).
Yuè was wary of Tūn having long held supervisory positions
and being highly regarded by the populace.
So he made him Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
concurrently serving as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù),
with the added title of Attendant Censor (Sànqí Chángshì).
This outwardly showed promotion,
but actually stripped him of his power.
Emperor Huái also ordered Tūn to concurrently hold the post of Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi),
and added the title of Special Advanced (Tèjìn).
Later, Tūn was again made Colonel Director of the Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
with the added title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Tūn served as Colonel Director of the Retainers five times,
because he was in harmony with public sentiment.
When Wáng Mí entered Luòyáng,
all officials were slaughtered.
Wáng Mí spared Tūn from the disaster
because he was an old acquaintance from his hometown.
Tūn then persuaded Wáng Mí, saying:
"Now heroes are rising in competition,
and the nine provinces are fractured.
Those who achieve unparalleled feats
will not be tolerated within the realm.
Since the General raised his army,
what attack has he not overcome,
what battle has he not won?
Yet you are at odds with Liú Yào.
You should contemplate the misfortune of Wén Zhǒng
and take Fàn Lí as your teacher.
Moreover, if the General has no imperial aspirations,
you can return to your home province in the East
to observe the situation.
Above, you can unify the world;
below, you can establish a tripod-like (i.e., tripartite) power.
How could this be inferior to Sūn Quán and Liú Bèi?
Kuí Tōng once said something similar.
The General should consider this plan."
Wáng Mí thought this was correct
and sent Tūn to Qīngzhōu
to conspire with Cáo Yì and to recruit him.
When Tūn arrived at Dōng'ē,
he was captured by the scouting cavalry of Shí Lè.
Shí Lè saw the letter from Wáng Mí to Cáo Yì and was greatly enraged,
so he killed Tūn.
Tūn had two sons: Yòu and Bái.
Yòu was an aide to the Grand Tutor (Tàifù Shǔ),
and Bái was a Palace Gentleman for the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
Bái was courageous, resolute, and capable.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè was jealous of him,
and secretly sent the Commander of the Upper Army (Shàngjūn) Hé Lún with over a hundred men to Tūn's residence
to rob him of his property
and kill Bái before leaving.
Zǒng, courtesy name Hóngjì,
was fond of learning, upright and straightforward.
He was the nephew of Biāo,
and his highest position was Central Supervisor of the Northern Army (Běijūn Zhōnghòu).
Chéng Wèi
had the courtesy name Chángxuán and was a native of Qǔzhōu, Guǎngpíng.
From a young age, he established his integrity and conduct,
being strong, upright, and stern.
Liú Yì heard of his reputation
and appointed him as Dūguān Cóngshì.
Yì impeached Zhōnghùjūn Yáng Xiù for violating the law and deserving death.
Emperor Wǔ had an old acquaintance with Xiù,
so he sent Qí Wáng Yōu to persuade Yì,
and Yì agreed.
Wèi sternly declared it unacceptable
and immediately drove his carriage into the Hùjūn camp,
arrested Xiù's subordinates,
interrogated them about their private affairs,
first impeached Xiù for his numerous offenses,
and only then spoke to Yì.
Because of this, his name resonated far and wide,
and all officials were inspired to act rigorously.
He was then appointed as Gōngfǔ Yuàn,
and successively promoted to Shàngshū Láng and Shìyùshǐ.
In all his posts, he distinguished himself through his competent handling of affairs.
He was appointed Luòyáng Lìng,
and subsequently served as Tàishǒu of Āndìng and Dùnqīu,
achieving notable accomplishments in the places he governed.
He died in office.
Hé Qiáo
Hé Qiáo had the courtesy name Chángyú and was a native of Xīpíng, Rǔnán.
His grandfather, Qià,
was Wèi Shàngshū Lìng.
His father, Yōu,
was Wèi Lìbù Shàngshū.
From a young age, Qiáo had an elegant style,
admiring his maternal uncle Xiàhóu Xuán's character,
and held himself in high esteem.
He enjoyed a great reputation in the world,
and both the court and the populace acknowledged his ability to rectify customs
and manage human relations.
He inherited his father's peerage, Shàngcài Bó,
and started his career as Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He was successively promoted to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
His governance was clear and simple,
and he greatly won the people's affection.
Tàifù Cóngshì Zhōngláng Yǔ Yǐ saw him and sighed, saying:
"Qiáo is like a thousand-zhang tall pine,
though rough and knotty,
when used in a grand edifice,
he serves as a ridgepole and beam."
Jiǎ Chōng also valued him highly,
praised him to Emperor Wǔ,
and he entered the court as Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
then was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng.
The Emperor deeply appreciated and favored him.
Traditionally, the Jiān and Lìng rode in the same carriage when entering court.
At that time, Xún Xù was the Jiān.
Qiáo disdained Xù's character,
and out of pride,
whenever they rode together,
he would sit haughtily, taking up the entire carriage.
Thus, the Jiān and Lìng were made to ride in separate carriages,
a practice that began with Qiáo.
When Wú was pacified,
for his meritorious participation in deliberations,
his younger brother Yù was granted the peerage Rǔnán Tínghóu.
Qiáo was transferred to Shìzhōng,
and received increasing intimacy and courtesy.
He was on good terms with Rèn Kǎi and Zhāng Huà.
Qiáo, seeing that the Crown Prince was not well-behaved,
took the opportunity during a shared sitting to say:
"The Imperial Crown Prince possesses the style of ancient simplicity,
but in these degenerate times, there is much deceit.
I fear he may not be able to manage Your Majesty's family affairs well."
The Emperor remained silent and did not respond.
Later, he attended the Emperor with Xún Yǐ and Xún Xù.
The Emperor said:
"The Crown Prince has recently entered court and
shown some improvement.
You may all go to him
and discuss general worldly affairs."
After receiving the imperial edict and returning,
Yǐ and Xù both praised the Crown Prince as intelligent, discerning, and broadly refined,
truly as the imperial edict stated.
Qiáo said:
"His sacred nature is as it was before!"
The Emperor was displeased and rose.
Qiáo retreated to his residence,
filled with sighs of regret,
knowing his advice was not being used,
yet unable to stop himself.
When discussing the state in the imperial presence, he never failed to express concern for the heir apparent.
The Emperor knew his words were loyal,
but never reciprocated.
Later, when speaking with Qiáo,
he avoided future matters.
Someone reported this to Consort Jiǎ,
and she resented him for it.
At the end of Tàikāng,
he became Shàngshū,
but resigned due to his mother's mourning.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shàofù,
with the added titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū.
The Crown Prince went to the Western Palace for audience,
and Qiáo followed him in.
Empress Jiǎ had the Emperor ask Qiáo:
"You once said I could not manage family affairs well.
What do you say today?"
Qiáo replied:
"When I served the late emperor,
I did indeed make such a statement.
That my words did not come to pass
is a blessing for the country.
How dare I evade my fault!"
He died in the second year of Yuánkāng,
and was posthumously granted the title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the addition of a golden seal and purple ribbon.
His original position remained unchanged.
In the early part of Yǒngpíng,
he was posthumously honored with the name Jiǎn.
Qiáo's family wealth was abundant,
comparable to that of a king.
However, he was extremely parsimonious,
which earned him criticism from the world.
Dù Yù considered Qiáo to have a "money obsession."
His brother Yù's son, Jì, succeeded him,
and rose to the position of Zhōngshū Láng.
Yù had the courtesy name Zhòngyú.
His talent and reputation did not match Qiáo's,
but he was known for his integrity and competence.
He successively held the positions of Shàngshū Zuǒyòu Púyè, Zhōngshū Lìng, and Shàngshū Lìng.
When Luòyáng fell,
he fled to Gǒu Xī,
where he died of illness.
Wǔ Gāi
Wǔ Gāi had the courtesy name Yuánxià and was a native of Zhúyì, Pèiguó.
His father, Zhōu,
was Wèi Wèiwèi.
Gāi was profound, astute, and had great capacity,
earning a good reputation early on.
He and his two younger brothers, Sháo (Shúxià) and Mào (Jìxià), were known from childhood for their talent.
Even their paternal uncles, brothers, and respected elders in the community
could not discern their superior or inferior qualities.
Liú Gōngróng of the same commandery, who had a discerning eye for talent,
often visited Zhōu,
and Zhōu introduced his three sons to him.
Gōngróng said:
"They are all men of national caliber.
Yuánxià is the most outstanding,
possessing the talent to assist.
If he exerts his abilities and takes his place in the ranks,
he can become an 'Assistant Duke.'
Shúxià and Jìxià are no less than Chángbó or Nàyán."
From a young age, Gāi delighted in human relations
and was a close friend of Chén Tài of Yǐngchuān.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
he was successively promoted to Xiàpí Tàishǒu.
When Emperor Jǐng became Dàjiāngjūn,
he appointed Gāi as Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He was successively promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi,
then transferred to Tàipú Qīng.
He was initially enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
When the five ranks were established,
he was re-enfeoffed as Xuēxiàn Hóu.
Emperor Wén deeply cherished and valued him,
often discussing and evaluating contemporary figures with him.
He once asked whether Chén Tài was better than his father, Qún.
Gāi praised each for their respective strengths,
believing that Qún and Tài were essentially without superiority or inferiority.
The Emperor agreed.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Shàngshū,
in charge of the personnel bureau,
then promoted to Zuǒ Púyè, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Gāi, being an elder and old minister,
held a high and respected position.
He felt he had no功 of assisting in the founding of the dynasty,
and had already been a senior minister in Wèi.
He reluctantly remained in office,
profoundly humble and deferential,
maintaining his integrity from beginning to end,
which was considered a fine example by his contemporaries.
He died in office
and was posthumously named Dìng.
His son, Fǔ, succeeded him.
Sháo successively served as Lìbù Láng, Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài, and Sànqí Chángshì.
Mào was known for his virtuous character,
his reputation second only to Gāi.
He served as the Administrator of Shàngluò, Cavalry Regular Attendant, Palace Attendant, and Minister of Personnel.
Xún Kǎi of Yǐngchuān, who was younger than Mào,
was Emperor Wǔ's maternal cousin.
Presuming upon his noble lineage,
he wished to associate with Mào,
but Mào rebuffed him without a reply,
which caused resentment.
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
Kǎi was then the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Considering Mào to be Yáng Jùn's maternal cousin,
he implicated him as a rebel,
and Mào was consequently killed.
Mào was pure, upright, and straightforward,
renowned throughout the court and the countryside.
That he was suddenly subjected to such a wrongful and cruel fate
grieved the entire realm.
Palace Attendant Fù Zhī submitted a memorial to clarify the matter,
and later Mào was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
Rèn Kǎi
Rèn Kǎi, courtesy name Yuánbāo,
was from Bóchāng, Lè'ān.
His father, Hào,
was the Grand Master of Ceremonies during the Wèi dynasty.
Kǎi had wisdom and a discerning capacity from a young age.
He married the daughter of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
and successively held the positions of Palace Assistant Secretary and Supernumerary Cavalry Regular Attendant.
When the state of Jìn was established,
he became Palace Attendant
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chāngguó County.
Kǎi possessed the talent for managing state affairs;
he comprehensively oversaw most matters, great and small.
His nature was loyal and upright;
he took the welfare of the state as his personal responsibility.
The Emperor esteemed and favored him,
consulting him frequently on political matters.
In the early years of Tàishǐ,
Zhèng Chōng, Wáng Xiáng, Hé Céng, Xún Yǐ, Péi Xiù, and others, all returned to their residences due to old age and illness.
The Emperor highly favored his great ministers,
not wishing to burden them with physical exertion.
He frequently sent Kǎi to convey his instructions to the various dukes,
consulting them on major contemporary policies,
and discussing their merits and demerits.
Kǎi disliked Jiǎ Chōng's character
and did not wish him to long hold court power,
thus he often curtailed and suppressed him.
Chōng was vexed by this
and did not know what to do.
Later, taking an opportune moment, he said that Kǎi was loyal, upright, and just,
and that he should be in the Eastern Palace
to protect the Heir Apparent.
The Emperor agreed,
appointing him Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
while his position as Palace Attendant remained unchanged,
thus Chōng's plan did not succeed.
At that time, the Qin and Yong regions were troubled by bandits,
which caused the Son of Heaven great concern.
Kǎi then said:
"The collapse and defeat in Qínliáng
and the unrest in Guānyòu
are indeed matters of deep concern for the state.
It is advisable to quickly pacify and stabilize the region
so that the people may have a sense of security.
Without a high-ranking minister of great prestige and strategic ability,
it will be impossible to bring peace to the western lands."
The Emperor said:
"Who is suitable for this responsibility?"
Kǎi replied:
"Jiǎ Chōng is that man."
The Minister of the Secretariat, Yǔ Chún, also suggested him,
whereupon an imperial edict ordered Chōng to go west and pacify Cháng'ān.
Chōng, however, used Xún Xù's plan to remain.
Since Chōng was favored by the Emperor,
he wished to monopolize prestige and influence.
However, Yǔ Chún, Zhāng Huá, Wēn Yǒng, Xiàng Xiù, Hé Qiáo, and others were all friendly with Kǎi,
while Yáng Yáo, Wáng Xún, Huá Yì, and others were close to and respected by Chōng.
Consequently, factions arose in profusion.
The Emperor, aware of this,
summoned Chōng and Kǎi to a banquet at the Shìqián Hall,
and said to Chōng and the others:
"The court should be united,
and the great ministers should be harmonious."
Chōng and Kǎi each bowed in thanks and departed.
Afterwards, Chōng, Kǎi, and the others, knowing that the Emperor was aware but had not reprimanded them,
deepened their enmity even further.
Outwardly, they respected each other greatly,
but inwardly they were very displeased.
Someone advised Chōng:
"Kǎi controls the crucial matters of the Palace Gate,
and has direct access to the Emperor.
You should propose that he be put in charge of selections,
then he will gradually become estranged from the Emperor.
This is merely a matter for a chief clerk.
Moreover, it is difficult to be skilled in the nine classifications of talent,
and gaps are easy to exploit."
Chōng then praised Kǎi's talent,
saying he was suitable for the position of selecting officials.
The Emperor did not doubt this,
believing Chōng had nominated a truly talented person.
On that very day, Kǎi was appointed Minister of Personnel,
and was additionally given the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Once Kǎi was in the Ministry of Personnel,
his selections were fair,
and he devoted himself fully to his duties.
However, his attendance at court audiences became increasingly rare.
Chōng, together with Xún Xù and Féng Dǎn, took advantage of opportunities to spread rumors,
saying that Kǎi was extravagant
and used imperial utensils.
Chōng sent the Minister of Personnel and Grand Minister of Agriculture, Gāo Yáng Wáng Guī, to impeach Kǎi,
who was subsequently dismissed from office.
The authorities arrested the chief cook of the Imperial Granary to investigate,
and it was found that Kǎi's wife, Princess Qízhǎng, had received imperial utensils from the Wèi dynasty as a gift.
After Kǎi was dismissed, slanders against him increased,
and the Emperor gradually held him in low regard.
However, Shān Tāo, knowing Kǎi to be intelligent and prudent with good judgment,
recommended him as Prefect of Hénán.
He was again dismissed from office for failing to capture bandits who had broken out.
He was later promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
Kǎi had always possessed discernment,
and moreover, he was diligent and scrupulous in public service,
earning him great praise from both the court and the common people.
However, Jiǎ Chōng's faction again instigated the relevant authorities to impeach Kǎi, accusing him of illicit dealings with Liú Yǒu, the promulgator of the new regulations.
The matter was sent down to the Ministry of Personnel,
but Kǎi refused to confess.
Minister of Personnel Dù Yǒu and Grand Judge Liú Liáng were both loyal and upright officials;
knowing that Kǎi was being suppressed by Chōng,
they wished to vindicate him.
Therefore, they delayed and did not make a judgment,
and for this, Kǎi, Yǒu, and Liáng were all dismissed from office.
After Kǎi lost his position,
he indulged in wine and pleasure,
living luxuriously to sustain himself.
Initially,
Hé Shào, being a profligate son of a nobleman,
would always eat all sorts of rare delicacies from all regions at every meal.
Kǎi, however, surpassed him,
spending ten thousand cash per meal,
yet still claiming there was nothing good enough to pick up with chopsticks.
When Kǎi occasionally attended court,
the Emperor would sometimes comfort and admonish him.
Kǎi initially made no further comments,
only wept.
Later, he was reinstated as Grand Coachman,
and then transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Initially,
although Wèi Shū had held various positions as Administrator of Commanderies,
he had not yet been appointed to an important post.
When Kǎi was Palace Attendant,
he recommended Shū as Cavalry Regular Attendant.
By this time, Shū was Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, had established a ducal office,
and held the position of Minister of Works.
The Emperor, personally presiding over the court, ordered Kǎi to present the appointment.
Although Shū was praised for his magnanimity and simplicity,
people at the time felt that Kǎi possessed the capacity to assist the world,
yet Shū had ascended to one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
while Kǎi remained a mere Palace Attendant.
No one failed to sigh with indignation for him.
Kǎi, unable to achieve his ambitions,
eventually died of grief,
at the age of sixty-one.
His posthumous name was Yuán,
and his son, Hǎn, succeeded him.
Hǎn, courtesy name Zǐlún,
possessed the family virtues from a young age.
Although his talent and reputation did not equal Kǎi's,
he earned praise for his excellent conduct,
and was considered a pure and outstanding gentleman.
He successively served as Palace Assistant, Cavalry Regular Attendant, Inspector of Yǎnzōu, and Grand Herald.
Cuī Hóng
Cuī Hóng, courtesy name Liángbó,
was from Ānpíng, Bólíng.
His great-grandfather, Shí,
was famous during the Hàn dynasty.
His father, Zàn,
was Minister of Personnel and Grand Minister of Agriculture during the Wèi dynasty,
and was praised for his refined demeanor.
Hóng gained renown in his youth for his purity and sharpness.
He was straightforward and different from others.
Whenever anyone made a mistake,
he would openly admonish them to their face,
but had no further comments afterwards.
Hé Pān, courtesy name Huìxīng,
was a native of Pí, Shǔjùn.
He served the province as a master of records.
When the inspector, Huángfǔ Yàn, was harmed by his cavalry commander, Zhāng Hóng,
he was falsely accused of great treason.
At that time, Pān was observing mourning for his mother,
so he went to Liángzhōu to present a memorial,
attesting that Yàn had not rebelled.
Thus, Yàn's injustice was rectified.
When Wáng Jùn was in Yìzhōu,
he appointed Pān as his attendant official (biéjià).
Jùn planned to attack Wú,
and sent Pān to present a memorial to the court,
verbally explaining the strategic opportunity.
The imperial edict twice summoned him for an audience,
then ordered Zhāng Huá to consult with Pān about the suitability of advancing the attack.
Jùn also sent Pān to visit Yáng Hù,
to personally explain the strategy for attacking Wú.
Pān was skilled at fulfilling his mission,
and the Emperor praised him,
ordering Pān to participate in Jùn's military affairs.
When Sūn Hào surrendered to Jùn,
and Wáng Hún was resentful of the delayed opportunity,
wishing to attack Jùn,
Pān advised Jùn to send Hào to Hún,
whereupon the matter was resolved.
Pān was appointed as Jùn's auxiliary military governor (fǔguó sīmǎ),
and ennobled as a Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
He was transferred to become Magistrate of Xíngyáng,
and submitted ten convenient proposals,
gaining a good reputation.
He was appointed as a Judicial Assistant (Tíngwèi Píng).
At that time, Zhūgě Chōng, the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng), looked down on Pān as a Shǔ scholar.
He slighted him,
but after they jointly judged difficult cases,
Chōng finally expressed his admiration.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng,
but did not take up the post,
and was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Shìláng).
When Yáng Jùn was in power,
he extensively promoted his relatives,
bestowing many enfeoffments and rewards,
hoping to protect himself with imperial favor.
Pān considered this wrong,
and together with Shí Chóng, they jointly drafted a memorial to impeach him.
The details are in the biography of Chóng.
The Emperor did not accept it.
For his pre-emptive meritorious service in executing Jùn,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xichéng,
with an estate of ten thousand households,
and granted ten thousand bolts of silk.
His younger brother Fēng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngxiāng,
and his elder brother's son Kuí as Marquis within the Pass (Guānzhōng Hóu).
Pān firmly declined half of the enfeoffed households and silk,
and distributed the remaining portion he received to his relatives both within and outside the capital,
hardly keeping any for himself.
He was promoted to Colonel of the Yi Army (Yìjūn Xiàowèi).
After a short while,
he was sent out as Colonel of the Eastern Qiāng (Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi).
He was summoned to be Inspector of Yángzhōu.
After three years in office,
he was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng).
He was transferred to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and given the additional title of General Who Spreads Awe (Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn),
but he firmly declined to take the post.
Chéng Càn, the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng), and Biàn Cuì, the General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn), urged Pān to assume his duties.
An imperial edict also added stern exhortations,
but Pān ultimately claimed illness and did not rise.
When King Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
he sent an envoy to summon Pān,
who again claimed severe illness.
Lún was enraged,
and was about to execute him.
Pān had no choice,
and, supporting his illness, rushed to answer the summons.
He died in Luòyáng,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Pān was fair and just in his heart,
and strict and orderly in his official duties.
He loved and cherished people,
and valued scholars and talent.
As the Chief Judge (Zhōngzhèng) for Liáng and Yì provinces,
he attracted and brought forth overlooked talents.
Chén Shòu of Bāxī, Yán and Fèi Lì of Jiànwèi, were all famous scholars from the western region,
and were slandered by their local communities,
suffering from negative public opinion for over ten years.
Pān clarified their cases,
and all were freed from wrongful accusations.
Although Pān held a prominent position,
his family was very poor and simple,
without concubines, maids, or musicians.
His only concern was helping the poor and assisting the needy.
His son, Zhāng, succeeded him,
and also possessed his father's character.
The court historian says: When Yōu and Lì were not proper rulers,
those of high virtue still harbored the desire to promote goodness;
when Gonghuan was in office,
even great sages found it intolerable.
How much more so for noble-minded and benevolent individuals,
who would certainly not seek to merely conform!
To hold their favored positions
was what connected their very existence.
Even if one were to 'dissolve gold with the mouth' (speak persuasively),
or 'cast a gleam and grasp a sword' (display courage),
or 'gallop a message to the Northern Gate' (report quickly to the court),
or 'tread on a broken carriage' (continue despite hardship),
it is still not easy to remonstrate with a ruler,
and it is truly difficult to be a reproving minister.
Liú Yì experienced leniency once,
while Rèn Hé twice suffered superficial wounds;
examining their lingering legacies,
each followed their own heart.
As for Wǔ Gāi harboring the ambition of a Wèi minister,
Cuī Hóng loving the way of Xì Shēn,
Chángshēng urging the veneration of Wáng Mí,
and Hé Pān obeying the command of Zhào Lún—
a true gentleman
is to be judged by how he handles affairs.
The encomium says: Zhòngxióng's initial administration,
loyalty and frankness filled the court.
His person like Zhūgě,
the emperor likened to Huán and Líng.
The great undertaking was not Yáng,
Yuán Bāo criticized Jiǎ.
Hé's regulations were clear and smooth,
fit for building a great mansion.
Cuī did not visit the gate,
his fame spread throughout court and wilderness.
Hóu Shǐ and Wǔ Gāi,
talents for assistance.
Hé Pān was fair and just,
many wrongful accusations were overturned.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter Sixteen: Liú Sòng
Liú Sòng, courtesy name Zǐyǎ,
was a native of Guǎnglíng,
a descendant of Liú Xū, King Lì of Guǎnglíng of the Hàn dynasty.
His family had been a famous clan for generations.
In the same commandery, there were the four clans of Léi, Jiǎng, Gǔ, and Lǔ,
all of whom were beneath his family.
At the time, people had a saying about them:
"Léi, Jiǎng, Gǔ, Lǔ,
Liú is the most ancestral."
His father, Guān,
was the Grand Administrator of Píngyáng.
Sòng was intelligent from a young age and could discern the principles of things,
for which he was praised by his contemporaries.
He was investigated as Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián)
and nominated as Outstanding Talent (xiùcái),
but he did not take up either post.
Emperor Wén appointed him as an aide (yuàn) in the prime minister's office,
and he was sent on a mission to Shǔ.
At that time, Shǔ had just been pacified,
the people were starving and the land desolate.
Sòng memorialized requesting relief and aid,
and acted before awaiting a reply,
which led to his dismissal.
When Emperor Wǔ assumed the throne,
Sòng was appointed Láng in the Department of the Three Dukes,
overseeing laws and regulations,
and redressing grievances.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
During the Xiánníng era,
an imperial edict commanded Sòng and Sànqí Láng Bái Bāo to inspect and pacify Jīng and Yáng provinces.
For their commendable service,
he was transferred to Huángmén Láng.
He was promoted to Yìláng,
and served as Tíngwèi.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìshǐ Hù Yín was unjustly imprisoned.
An edict ordered an investigation into his case,
but Sòng firmly maintained his innocence.
Yín was subsequently acquitted,
and people at the time compared Sòng to Zhāng Shìzhī.
He served for six years,
and was known for his thoroughness and fairness.
When Wú was conquered,
the various generals vied for credit.
Sòng was dispatched to evaluate their achievements.
He ranked Wáng Hún as having the highest merit,
and Wáng Jùn as having medium merit.
The Emperor, believing Sòng had mishandled the law,
demoted him to Jīngzhào Tàishǒu.
He did not take up this post,
but was transferred to Hénèi.
Before departing,
he submitted a memorial on expedient matters,
many of which were adopted.
Within the commandery, there were many imperial princesses' water mills,
which blocked the flowing water,
causing widespread flooding damage.
Sòng memorialized to have them abolished,
and the common people benefited greatly.
Soon after, he left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Huáinán Xiàng.
In office, he was strict and orderly,
achieving significant administrative success.
The Sháopí dam had been repaired in the past,
requiring tens of thousands of laborers annually.
The powerful families seized land,
leaving the poor and isolated jobless.
Sòng made everyone, great and small, contribute their efforts,
and distributed shares based on their work,
prompting the common people to sing praises of his fairness and benevolence.
While in the commandery, Sòng submitted a memorial saying: "I, your servant, was formerly in Hénèi.
Upon my departure, I received an imperial edict:
'All that you say are important matters.
You should frequently report on both major and minor issues.
Should there be many affairs,
I may not be able to
reply to all,
but do not let this cause you doubt.'
On the day I received this edict,
joy and apprehension intertwined within me.
I resolved to exert myself even more,
forgetting my insignificance,
wishing to, like a firefly's gleam,
add a little light.
The matters I had drafted
upon arriving in the commandery are listed below.
Before I could present them in writing,
I, your servant, unfortunately suffered a heavenly affliction,
lying ill for several years.
Now I respectfully seal and present the aforementioned matters.
Although I, your servant, lack the talent to govern
the state,
and my words are shallow and often deviant,
I still wish Your Majesty to consider them,
so that my humble sincerity may be seen by Your sagely gaze,
and not be utterly discarded from the usual records.
If there is anything worthy of adoption,
I hope it may contribute
one in ten thousand.
I humbly observe the imperial edict,
which has opened up the land,
to secure it for a hundred generations,
enfeoffing imperial relatives,
all to become vassals.
How could this not be cherished?
It is a matter of public principle.
The complete system for establishing states
is now fully formed,
surpassing the limitations of Qín, Hàn, and Wèi,
and reviving the lost practices of the Five Emperors and Three Dynasties.
Its achievements cover all within the empire,
its glory flows to future generations.
Such
lofty and magnificent accomplishments
might even put the rulers of the Three Dynasties and Five Emperors to shame.
Why so?
Because they achieved their success by following what was naturally given,
unlike recreating it after its complete loss.
Nevertheless,
enfeoffing young imperial princes in Wú and Shǔ,
in my humble opinion,
is not entirely ideal.
For Wú and Yuè are volatile and restless,
and Yōng and Shǔ are dangerous and remote.
These are precisely the sources of unrest and conflict,
places where turmoil easily arises.
Moreover, since the pacification of Wú,
the generals and soldiers of the six southeastern prefectures have been rotated to guard the Jiāngbiǎo region.
This is a serious problem of the current time.
Furthermore, with internal troops
guarding externally,
the Wú people lack self-confidence.
It is appropriate to have strong rulers to pacify them,
allowing both internal and external populations to return to their former peace.
Also, when the Sūn clan ruled,
their civil and military
officials
were often compared to the imperial court.
Now, they are suddenly overthrown,
becoming mere common households.
They do not recognize the grace of new life they have received,
but rather, distress and hardship beset them,
leading them to feel they have lost their land,
thus harboring
disquiet.
If a mature prince were to govern their state,
assigning responsibilities according to talent,
with both civil and military officials in place,
and soldiers and all laborers not having to leave their hometowns,
those seeking wealth and nobility could find it
within their own region.
The internal troops could be dispersed,
and the new states would also be secure.
Both sides would achieve their objectives,
which would be appropriate for the situation.
It would be advisable to select princes of the imperial clan, aged twenty or above, who are highly talented,
and
divide them to rule Wú and Shǔ.
By moving them from nearby to distant locations,
and partitioning territories,
make the assigned lands double their former size.
Use the former enfeoffed lands
to enthrone the young princes,
and only send them to govern
when the imperial princes are grown.
This would not be too late.
It is urgent to have these lands,
and to secure them with mature rulers.
This matter is appropriate.
Regarding the enfeoffment I have proposed,
the grand principle has already
been established.
However, regarding other numerous matters,
should there be anything worthy of adoption
to complement the established system,
I have included them all as part of this matter.
I have heard that: one who does not shy away from the risk of danger and regret,
but wishes to offer what he sees,
is a loyal minister;
one who listens to unpalatable words,
and is willing to accept bitter counsel,
is a ruler who saves
the world.
I, your servant, by chance of destiny,
am fortunate to live in an era where frankness is tolerated.
Although I have previously submitted memorials and remonstrances,

In the early Yuánkāng [元康] era,

Lǐ Zhòng 李重
Lǐ Zhòng 李重, courtesy name Màozēng 茂曾,

In ancient times, when the feudal lords governed,

officials had no thoughts of exceeding their station,

Qín 秦 reversed this path,

shallow customs

Hàn 漢 reformed its abuses,
