encountered disasters;
the problem lies precisely in emphasizing vast acreage while neglecting proper cultivation.
I humbly observe that the river embankment Yèzhě (謁者) Shí Huī (石恢) is highly skilled in water and land affairs,
and understands their advantages and disadvantages.
I beg that the Zhōngshū (中書) (Secretariat) summon Huī (恢),
and question him thoroughly about what is gained and lost;
he will surely have valuable contributions. The fifth concerns barbarian affairs.
Your humble servant believes that the Hú (胡) and Yí (夷) have animal hearts
and are not like the Huá (華) (Chinese),
with the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) being the worst.
Originally, Dèng Ài (鄧艾) merely sought a temporary advantage,
without considering future
troubles,
allowing tens of thousands of Xiānbēi (鮮卑) to scatter among the populace.
This is bound to become a source of harm.
The governor of Qínzhōu (秦州), Hú Liè (胡烈), has always enjoyed trust and favor in the west.
Now that Liè (烈) has gone there,
although the various Hú (胡) have not yet committed evil,
they will surely be pacified.
However, animal hearts are hard to guarantee,
and it is not certain that peace can be maintained for long.
If there are future disturbances,
Liè (烈) will be able to control them.
I only fear that if the Húlǔ (胡虜) (barbarians) are distressed by attacks,
they will then be able to enter Āndìng (安定) to the east,
and flee to Wǔwēi (武威) to the west.
Outwardly, they may claim to surrender,
but they will act again whenever possible.
These two commanderies are not under Liè’s (烈)
control,
meaning the troublesome Hú (胡) will have places to roam and hide in the east and west,
thus again causing problems,
with no means to restrain them.
It would be advisable to establish another commandery in Gāopíng Chuān (高平川),
and then, through the Àndìng Xīzhōu Dūwèi (安定西州都尉) (Commander of Xīzhōu, Āndìng),
recruit people willing to relocate,
offering them generous tax exemptions to populate it,
to open up the northern road,
and gradually solidify the border.
A detailed discussion should be held concerning these two commanderies and the newly established commandery,
to ensure they all belong to Qínzhōu (秦州),
allowing Liè (烈) to specialize in managing border affairs. The imperial edict stated:
“I have received your memorial on matters of expediency,
discussing the merits and shortcomings of agricultural affairs and the rise and fall of water officials,
as well as the appropriate severity or leniency of policies for stabilizing the border and governing the Hú (胡).
Your thorough and comprehensive presentation
explains everything in detail.
These are indeed the fundamental principles for governing the nation,
and urgent tasks for the present time.
All your arguments are sound.
I deeply understand your sincere intentions,
and appreciate your extensive consideration of all proper measures.
Continue to inform me of your thoughts and actions.”
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Tàipú (太僕) (Grand Coachman).
At that time, years of poor harvests occurred consecutively,
and the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) barbarians disturbed the borders.
An imperial edict summoned the Gōngqīng (公卿) (high officials) for a meeting.
Xuán (玄) answered the questions posed,
presenting his views with incisive honesty.
Although not all of his proposals were implemented,
he was consistently treated with favor and tolerance.
He was then transferred to Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) (Colonel Director of Retainers).
When the Xiànhòuqū (獻皇后) (Empress Xiàn) passed away in the Hóngxùn Gōng (弘訓宮) (Hongxun Palace),
a mourning station was set up.
According to old regulations,
the Sīlì (司隸) would sit outside the Duānmén (端門) (Duānmén Gate),
above all other high officials,
with a separate mat.
However, upon entering the palace hall,
according to his official rank and grade, he was below the other high officials,
and would sit in sequence,
without a separate mat.
But the Yèzhě (謁者) (usher) designated Hóngxùn Gōng (弘訓宮) as part of the inner palace,
and ordered Xuán’s (玄) seat to be below the high officials.
Xuán (玄) became enraged,
and with a stern voice and expression, he reprimanded the Yèzhě (謁者).
The Yèzhě (謁者) falsely claimed that the Shàngshū (尚書) (Secretariat) had ordered it.
Xuán (玄), in front of all the officials, then cursed the Shàngshū (尚書) and those below them.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yú Chún (御史中丞庾純) (Imperial Censor Yú Chún) memorialized that Xuán (玄) had shown disrespect.
Xuán (玄) then submitted his own memorial claiming that the report was untrue,
but he was dismissed from office.
However, Xuán (玄) was by nature severe and impatient,
unable to tolerate anything.
Whenever he had a memorial to impeach someone,
or if it happened to be dusk,
he would hold his white tablet (for notes),
straighten his hairpin and belt,
and anxiously await, unable to sleep,
sitting until dawn.
Because of this, the aristocratic elite were awed and subdued,
and the court became rife with apprehension.
Soon after, he died at home,
at the age of sixty-two,
and was posthumously named Gāng (剛) (Resolute).
Fù Xuán (傅玄) took refuge in Hénèi (河內) when he was young,
devoting himself to recitation and study.
Later, although he became prominent and esteemed,
his writing and publishing never ceased.
He compiled treatises discussing the nine schools of thought concerning statecraft and stories from the three histories,
evaluating their successes and failures,
and categorizing them into distinct sections.
This work was named Fùzǐ (傅子),
comprising the Inner, Outer, and Middle Parts.
In total, there were four divisions and six registers,
amounting to 140 chapters
and several hundred thousand characters.
Additionally, a collection of over one hundred volumes of his essays circulated throughout the world.
When Fù Xuán (傅玄) first completed the Inner Part,
his son Fù Xián (傅咸) showed it to Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Shěn (王沈).
Wáng Shěn (王沈) wrote to Fù Xuán (傅玄), saying:
"I have perused the book you authored;
its words are rich, its principles effective,
its organization of political systems profound,
and its regard for Confucian teachings weighty.
It is sufficient to stem the deviation of Yáng (楊) and Mò (墨),
and to place Sūn (孫) and Mèng (孟) among the ancients.
Every time I open the volume,
I cannot but sigh with admiration.
'Not having seen Jǐa Shēng (賈生),
one might consider oneself superior,
but now one realizes one is not as good' –
this is truly apt!"
Subsequently, he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qīngquán (清泉侯).
Fù Xián (傅咸) succeeded him.
Fù Xián (傅咸), courtesy name Chángyú (長虞),
was resolute and straightforward, possessing great moral integrity.
His demeanor was severe and upright,
his understanding and nature clear and discerning.
He abhorred evil as if it were an enemy,
promoted the worthy, and delighted in goodness,
always aspiring to the ideals of Jì Wénzǐ (季文子) and Zhòngshān Fǔ (仲山甫).
He enjoyed writing essays and treatises;
though they might lack embellishment,
his words formed established precedents and valuable lessons.
Yǐngchuān (潁川) Gǔn Chún (庾純) often sighed, saying:
"Chángyú's (長虞) writing is close to the work of the poets!"
At the beginning of the Xiánníng (咸寧) era,
he inherited his father's peerage
and was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬).
He was successively promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng (尚書右丞).
He was sent out as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jìzhōu (冀州).
His stepmother, Dù (杜) clan, was unwilling to accompany Fù Xián (傅咸) to his post,
so he submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his duties.
Within thirty days,
he was promoted to Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (司徒左長史).
At that time, the emperor was attentive to matters of governance
and issued an edict to solicit opinions from his court officials regarding the advantages and disadvantages of government policies.
Fù Xián (傅咸) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty occupies the most esteemed position,
yet engages in the affairs of a commoner,
personally overseeing all state matters,
toiling until sunset.
Among past emperors and kings,
none have personally practiced such frugality
to benefit the world
as Your Majesty.
However, since the beginning of the Tàishǐ (泰始) era until now,
fifteen years have passed.
Yet the military and the state are not prosperous,
the common people are not self-sufficient,
and if there is one year of poor harvest, people immediately show signs of starvation.
This is truly because officials are numerous and affairs are bustling,
exemptions and dispensations are indiscriminately granted,
those who consume are many, while those who cultivate are few.
As your dull and unrefined servant,
I have wrongly held a close position.
Every time I see Your Majesty's edicts expressing concern for the hunger of the common people,
I am unable to offer any remedy,
and I am humbly ashamed.
How dare I not exert myself
to respond to Your Majesty's inquiry?
There were originally four Dūdū (都督),
but now, including Jiānjūn (監軍),
there are more than ten.
Yǔ (禹) of Xià (夏) demarcated the land,
dividing it into nine provinces;
the number of Cìshǐ (刺史) today
is nearly double that.
The population is one-tenth of that during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
yet more commanderies and counties have been established.
Empty military academies and Yámén (牙門) officials,
which do not benefit the guard,
but military garrisons are uselessly established,
reaching hundreds in number.
The Five Ranks of feudal lords
also appoint their own officials and subordinates.
All those who receive favored provisions
are supported by the common people.
If one man does not farm,
others suffer hunger because of it.
Today, those who do not farm
are countless.
Even if all five grains are universally harvested,
it is barely enough to connect ends meet;
if there is a temporary disaster,
it immediately becomes insufficient.
Therefore, I believe the urgent matter of the present
is first to consolidate officials and reduce affairs,
to quiet matters and cease unnecessary projects,
and for both upper and lower ranks to focus their efforts
solely on agriculture."
While in office, Fù Xián (傅咸) frequently rectified matters.
Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿), the Dà Zhōngzhèng (大中正) of Yùzhōu (豫州), memorialized, saying
that Kǒng Yù (孔毓), the Xiǎo Zhōngzhèng (小中正) of Lǔguó (魯國) and Sīkōng Sīmǎ (司空司馬),
had moved his sick quarters four times and was unable to receive guests,
requesting to replace Kǒng Yù (孔毓) with Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Cáo Fù (曹馥).
Within ten days, he again memorialized to reinstate Kǒng Yù (孔毓) as Zhōngzhèng (中正).
The Sītú (司徒) rejected this three times,
but Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿) insisted on his position.
Fù Xián (傅咸), seeing that Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿) made appointments and dismissals purely based on his own will,
memorialized to dismiss Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿) from his position as Dà Zhōngzhèng (大中正).
Sītú (司徒) Wèi Shū (魏舒)
was a relative by marriage of Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿),
and repeatedly refused to endorse the dismissal.
Fù Xián (傅咸) insisted on the rectification very strenuously.
Wèi Shū (魏舒) ultimately did not comply,
so Fù Xián (傅咸) submitted the memorial alone.
Wèi Shū (魏舒) then impeached Fù Xián (傅咸) for being provocative and unjust,
and an imperial edict transferred Fù Xián (傅咸) to be Chēqí Sīmǎ (車騎司馬).
Fù Xián (傅咸), observing the extravagance of the populace,
again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant believes that grain and silk are hard to produce,
and if they are used without restraint,
there is no way they will not become depleted.
Therefore, when the former kings governed the world,
eating meat and wearing silk
all had their regulations.
I secretly believe that the cost of extravagance
is more severe than natural disasters.
In ancient times, Yáo (堯) had a thatched cottage;
today's common people vie to make their houses grand.
In ancient times, ministers did not eat jade-like food;
today's merchants and servants all tire of fine meats.
In ancient times, only empresses and consorts had distinctive decorations;
today's maids and concubines wear brocade and fine silk.
In ancient times, only grandee officials
did not walk;
today's humble servants ride light carriages and fat horses.
In ancient times, people were numerous and land was scarce, yet there were reserves,
due to frugality;
today, land is vast and people are few, yet there is a problem of insufficiency,
due to extravagance.
If one wishes the times to be frugal,
one must question its extravagance;
if extravagance is not questioned,
people will increasingly emulate it.
In the past, when Máo Jiè (毛玠) was Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
no one at that time dared to dress finely or eat sumptuously.
Wèi Wǔdì (魏武帝) sighed, saying: 'My laws are not as good as Shàngshū (尚書) Máo (毛).'
If all departments are ordered to apply themselves
like Máo Jiè (毛玠),
the shift in customs
will not be difficult."
He also proposed moving county prisons to commanderies and that the two Shè (社) shrines should be established,
which the imperial court adopted.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞).
When Huì-Dì ascended the throne,
Yáng Jùn assisted in governing.
Xián said to Jùn:
"Affairs change with the times,
and rites adapt to circumstances.
That the liàng'àn (mourning period) is not observed has been the case for a long time.
Due to the increasing decline of the world's ways,
power cannot be delegated.
Therefore, even when grieving intensely,
one personally attends to all affairs of state.
By the time of Hàn Wén-Dì,
because the empire was vast,
and the burden of mourning robes was difficult to bear for long,
he decreed that they be removed after the burial.
Shìzǔ Wǔ-Huángdì, though exceptionally filial,
also released his mourning attire in due course,
establishing a three-year period of 'heart mourning.'
As for the myriad affairs of state,
he had no leisure to attend to them.
Now, His Sacred Majesty wishes to delegate governance to you, Sir,
and remain in liàng'àn himself.
While this is a humble and yielding intention,
the empire does not consider it good.
The reason the empire does not consider it good is
that the myriad people look up with reverence,
gazing upon the imperial pinnacle,
listening to the prime minister,
fearing that the light of heaven might be obscured.
Since the hearts of the people are already like this,
it is certainly not an easy position for you, Illustrious Sir, to occupy.
I humbly believe that once the imperial burial is completed,
you, Illustrious Sir, should consider what is appropriate for prosperity or decline.
The Duke of Zhōu, a sage,
still could not escape slander.
Inferring from this,
since the Duke of Zhōu's responsibilities were not easy to manage,
how much more so for His Sacred Majesty, whose spring-autumn years are not those of King Chéng!
When one grasps the meaning, words are forgotten;
yet words are not easily exhausted.
If, Illustrious Sir, you can perceive my sincere intentions,
then words need not be many."
At that time, Sīlì Xún Kǎi was observing mourning for his elder brother.
He memorialized requesting to attend the mourning,
and an imperial edict was issued approving it but had not yet been formally delivered.
Kǎi then went to see Jùn.
Xián thereupon memorialized, saying:
"The sorrow of death and mourning,
especially between brothers, causes profound grief.
That a brother sharing the same hall has passed away,
and he should only now be at the funeral,
His Sacred Majesty's grace and compassion
allow him to attend the mourning.
Yet before the edict was delivered, he immediately went to visit Jùn,
hastily showing deferential flattery,
without any brotherly affection.
He should be severely demoted
to uphold moral instruction."
Since the Emperor had entrusted Jùn with governing the court,
there was an edict not to pursue the matter.
Jùn was very apprehensive of Xián.
Xián again sent Jùn a sharp and critical letter.
Jùn's resolve gradually wavered,
and he became increasingly displeased.
Because of this, he wanted to send Xián out to be the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào or Hóngnóng.
Jùn's nephew Lǐ Bīn persuaded Jùn
that it was not right to banish upright people,
so he stopped.
Jùn's younger brother Jì had always been on good terms with Xián.
He wrote to Xián, saying:
"The waters of rivers and seas flow turbulently,
and thus they achieve their depth and breadth.
The great affairs of the empire
cannot be easily settled in every detail,
yet you seem to want to settle every single matter.
'Giving birth to a foolish son' and
'settling government affairs' —
government affairs are not easily settled.
To settle affairs is truly to act foolishly,
but what a relief it is!
The Left Chancellor oversees the celestial observation platform,
maintaining order among the Eight Ministers;
this is not an easy position.
For you, Sir, to occupy such an uneasy position with your whole nature,
it is even more difficult.
I imagine you are breaking your head over it,
hence I fully inform you."
Xián replied:
"Wèi Gōng said,
'Wine and women kill people' — this is far worse than being upright.
Dying from wine and women,
people do not regret it.
Fearing in advance that uprightness will lead to misfortune —
this comes from a heart that is not truly upright and just,
but wishes to be seen as wise through expediency!
Since ancient times, those who suffered misfortune due to uprightness
were those who overcorrected,
or were disloyal and unjust,
seeking to gain reputation through severity,
and thus incurred resentment.
How could one who sincerely and loyally provides beneficial advice
be disliked?"
Not long after,
Jùn was executed.
Xián was transferred to the position of Crown Prince's Chief of Staff (tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ),
then promoted to Imperial Censor (yùshǐ zhōngchéng).
At that time, the Grand Tutor (tàizǎi), Rǔnán-Wáng Liàng, assisted in governance.
Xián wrote a letter saying:
"Xián believes that Tàijiǎ and King Chéng were young and immature,
hence there were the affairs of Yī and Zhōu.
Even sages could not avoid suspicion,
how much more so when I am not a sage,
and you, Prince, are not a child,
can one undertake the affairs of Yī and Zhōu?
When the Emperor was in liàng'àn,
listening to the prime minister,
Yáng Jùn behaved improperly,
immediately acting as Yī and Zhōu,
placing himself in a position of security over the empire,
which led to his death.
His crimes are too numerous to count,
and are also what Your Highness witnessed.
Jùn's downfall
originated from the Emperor's sagacious discernment,
with Mèng Guān and Lǐ Zhào being privy to the secret imperial decree.
As for discussing merits,
the credit should be given to the Emperor.
Guān and others have already received thousands of households as marquises of counties.
His Sacred Majesty, seeing that no one was unhappy about Jùn's death,
therefore made the awards generous
to ensure their joy.
This is what the subordinates should have accurately weighed,
but instead, they incited agitation,
making Dōng'ān a king,
Mèng and Lǐ dukes of commanderies,
and others marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons.
Not only were these arbitrarily exaggerated,
but they also involved triple promotions in rank.
Such dazzling promotions
shook heaven and earth;
since ancient times,
there have been no such extravagant rewards and enfeoffments.
When there are great rewards without merit,
everyone delights in the country having misfortune,
believing that when misfortune arises,
they will again gain great merit.
If people delight in misfortune,
how can this be controlled?
Those who did this
were all due to the Duke of Dōng'ān.
I had thought that upon Your Highness's arrival,
you would rectify this.
If it were rectified according to the Way,
why would the populace be angry?
What angers the populace
is simply injustice.
But now, everything has been discussed and doubled,
and everyone is disappointed.
I, Xián, in my foolish incompetence,
am not merely disappointed;
I am secretly worried.
Furthermore, at the time of Jùn's suppression,
Your Highness was outside
and did not actually participate.
Now, wishing to entrust you with heavy responsibilities,
the Emperor has ordered Your Highness to assess merits.
The matter of assessing merits
is truly not easy to handle.
It would be better to observe the gains and losses from a distance,
and act as a steady hand."
Xián Fù again, because Sīmǎ Liàng was assisting in governance and monopolizing power,
further remonstrated, saying:
"Yáng Jùn had the awe that shook the lord;
he entrusted power to his relatives.
This is why the world was in an uproar.
Now, holding an important position,
one ought to reverse these errors.
It would be appropriate to remain tranquil, nourishing the spirit,
and only when there are major gains or losses,
then to maintain them.
Unless it is a major affair,
all others should be suppressed and dismissed.
Recently, I have visited four times,
and when passing by your esteemed gate,
the carriages, horses, and officials in their hats
filled the streets and lanes.
This kind of gathering
ought to be stopped immediately.
Furthermore, Xiàhóu Chángróng was sent as an envoy to pray for the life of the late Emperor.
His prayers were not answered,
and the late Emperor passed away.
He should have blamed himself,
yet he sought credit for his efforts in praying for life,
and Your Excellency appointed him as Shǎofǔ.
Private whispers
say that Chángróng is your relative by marriage,
hence this came to be.
When one dog barks at a shadow,
a pack of dogs barks at the sound.
Fearing the barking of the pack,
it becomes unbearable to hear.
As for my character,
I cannot outwardly comply and then speak ill behind one's back.
I once offended Yáng Jùn,
and almost brought disaster upon myself.
How much more so concerning Your Highness,
would I be sparing in my words!
Formerly, when accompanying the imperial carriage,
Your Highness said to me: 'Do you not know Hán Fēi's words about 'touching the dragon's scales' [dangerous advice]?
Yet you suddenly provoke the Son of Heaven's 'reverse scales'!'
I know that what I have presented
indeed touches the whiskers of a fierce beast.
The reason I dare to speak
is to hope that Your Highness will understand my inability to overcome my humble devotion.
Previously, I touched the Son of Heaven's 'reverse scales'
wishing to exhaust my loyalty.
Now, I touch the whiskers of a fierce beast,
not intending to cause harm,
but surely hoping to be pardoned for this."
Sīmǎ Liàng did not accept it.
Chángróng was
Xiàhóu Jùn.
On the day of Bǐngyín,
an imperial edict commanded all officials to nominate suitable persons for county and district positions to fill internal official posts.
Xián Fù again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant Xián believes that the key to promoting transformation
lies in appointing officials.
Talents are not uniform,
and positions differ.
It is like trees in a forest;
whether thick or thin, crooked or straight,
each has its proper use.
Therefore, the worthy should be brought forth even from obscure places,
and inquiries should not be restricted by internal or external divisions.
The responsibilities of internal and external positions,
and whether one serves or withdraws, should be according to what is appropriate.
However, in the selection process,
only internal appointments are favored.
External nominations have declined,
and there are many restrictions.
Competing for internal positions and slighting external ones
has become a custom.
This malpractice truly ought to be promptly reformed,
so that there is no partiality between internal and external channels.
Once there is no partiality between channels,
if the selection and appointment are unfair,
then there should be deep blame.
If the blame is truly deep,
there will be no worry about unfairness.
Moreover, one cannot tune a瑟 (sè) by gluing its bridges;
how much more so for appointing officials, can it be limited!
I humbly think that the reason for these limitations
is to prevent selectors from being unable to pick extraordinary talent.
If one cannot pick extraordinary talent,
it should be dealt with on a case-by-case basis,
and there is no need for restrictive laws.
If laws are limited,
will it not impede reaching distant goals?
It seems like a muddle!
Some might say, 'If there are no laws to regulate,
what will be valued?'
Your servant has heard that punishment corrects the petty person,
while righteousness holds the gentleman accountable.
The accountability of a gentleman
lies in his heart, not in limitations.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign,
Hé Yàn was appointed to oversee selections,
and officials for both internal and external positions each found their suitable talents.
The brilliant beauty of this was evident.
Thus,
this was not merely achieved by control through limitations
or by laws,
but rather by entrusting responsibility.
The fear of entrusting responsibility
is greater than that of restrictive laws.
If it is the fault of the law,
it is not one's own error;
if the fault is not one's own,
there is no fear of blame.
This is what is meant by 'regulating them with punishments,
people will avoid them but have no sense of shame.'
However, if responsibility is truly entrusted,
one would first consider the possibility of being punished,
and second, fear incurring resentment and slander.
If one performs well, the court and commoners will praise it;
if one performs poorly, the blame of the multitude will fall upon one.
This trembling fear,
how can it compare to relying on restrictive laws to escape responsibility opportunistically!"
Xián was again appointed as Zhōngzhèng for his home commandery,
but left office due to mourning his stepmother.
After a short while,
he was summoned to serve as Yìláng,
concurrently holding the position of Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Xián repeatedly declined these appointments,
but he was not listened to.
An imperial edict commanded an envoy to confer the titles upon him.
Xián again sent back the official seals and ribbons.
The imperial carriage office did not accept them and
urged him to take up the post.
Xián, citing that he had no brothers
to oversee the funeral and sacrificial rites,
again humbly pleaded.
It was then ordered that a spirit tablet be set up in the official residence.
Xián again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant is weak and incompetent,
unable to bear such a heavy responsibility.
Moreover, I am in a state of grief and mourning.
Although the period of leave has expired,
Your Majesty, in your excessive kindness,
has bestowed upon me a position I cannot handle.
I have revealed my sincere feelings
and reported my dire circumstances to the throne.
Though the erroneous edict has been issued,
it remains unchanged.
Although your servant cannot sacrifice himself to preserve propriety and instruction,
it is against my principles to brazenly
unworthily accept such great favor.
Previously, upon receiving the solemn edict
to assume my duties,
I secretly swore to myself
to repay this with my life.
As bribery was prevalent and should be thoroughly eradicated,
I sternly commanded the metropolitan officials
to make this their priority.
However, months have passed,
and nothing has been achieved.
This is because Your Majesty encourages and emboldens [officials],
and fears that an ignorant and stubborn person [like me]
might surely be bound to death [for my actions],
so they conceal and restrain themselves to avoid my sharp edge.
I have been in office for some days now,
having made no striking achievements,
nor have I caused fear that makes people 'drop their wings at the sound of a bowstring.'
Who then would still fear me?
Therefore, when Guānglù Dàfū Liú Yì was Sīlì,
his prestige shook both internal and external circles,
and near and far were purified and quieted.
This was not only because Liú Yì possessed the integrity of a loyal minister who would not shirk his duty,
but also because his proposals were adopted,
allowing his authority and prestige to be exercised."
The imperial edict said:
"You should simply strive to be upright and principled,
and your authority and prestige will grow daily.
Why only Liú Yì!"
At that time, the imperial court was lax and
powerful magnates were wanton,
engaging in private entreaties and solicitations,
whereupon the court and the countryside became chaotic.
Xián (咸) memorialized to dismiss Hénán Yǐn (河南尹) Dàn (澹), Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Qiàn (倩), Tíngwèi (廷尉) Gāo Guāng (高光), and concurrent Hénán Yǐn (河南尹) Hé Pān (何攀), among others.
The capital became orderly, and
the noble relatives were awestruck and submissive.
Xián (咸) said,
"The sage remaining long in their office
transforms the world into order.
This is why Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) assessed performance every three years, and
promoted or demoted every nine years.
As for the Zhōu Lǐ (周禮),
there was a grand census every three years.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) also said,
'Three years suffice to achieve success.'
However, since the interim,
when chief officials arrive at their posts,
they are transferred before long,
causing the common people to suffer from instability, and
the officials and soldiers to be exhausted by sending off and welcoming."
At that time, Púyè (僕射) Wáng Róng (王戎) was concurrently Lìbù (吏部).
Xián (咸) memorialized:
"Wáng Róng (王戎) occupies the position of a grand tutor,
and concurrently manages elections.
He is unable to calm the customs
and consolidate the various achievements,
leading to people's hearts being stirred
and contention being encouraged.
Zhōngláng (中郎) Lǐ Chóng (李重) and Lǐ Yì (李義) fail to correct each other.
I request the dismissal of Wáng Róng (王戎)'s and others' offices."
An imperial edict said:
"The foundation of governance
indeed lies in remaining long in one's post;
Xián (咸)'s memorial is correct.
Wáng Róng (王戎)'s duty is to discuss the Way,
which I greatly entrust to him;
let the prohibition be lifted."
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Xiè Jié (解結) deemed Xián (咸)'s impeachment of Wáng Róng (王戎) to be a violation of regulations,
exceeding his jurisdiction and infringing upon another's office,
interfering beyond his authority,
and memorialized to dismiss Xián (咸)'s office.
The imperial edict also did not permit it.
Xián (咸) submitted a memorial, stating:
"According to the regulations,
the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) supervises all officials.
From the crown prince downwards,
those within the 'xingma' (行馬) enclosure
who violate laws and regulations are all to be impeached and investigated.
Even if outside the 'xingma' (行馬) enclosure,
if supervising officials do not correct,
one may also memorialize.
As per the text of the regulations,
'violations within the xingma (行馬) enclosure'
refers to matters of security and prohibition.
Security within the palace
cannot be handled by external offices,
hence it is exclusively assigned to the Zhōngchéng (中丞).
Now, roads and bridges are not repaired,
and disputes among butchers and vendors are unending.
In such cases,
the Zhōngchéng (中丞) holds the prefectural officials responsible,
which is the so-called 'xingma (行馬) nei yu (內語)' applied to security and prohibition.
Since it says the Zhōngchéng (中丞) supervises all officials,
why speak again of 'within the xingma (行馬) enclosure'?
Since it says 'all officials',
and one should not speak again of 'within the xingma (行馬) enclosure',
as internal and external officials are called 'all officials',
then it includes both inside and outside.
The reason why the Sīlì (司隸) does not speak again of 'inside and outside the xingma (行馬) enclosure' is
because matters of security and prohibition have already been spoken of regarding the Zhōngchéng (中丞).
The Zhōngchéng (中丞) and Sīlì (司隸) both impeach from the crown prince downwards,
thus they are jointly responsible for supervising internal and external matters.
It is not that the Zhōngchéng (中丞) exclusively supervises internal officials,
and the Sīlì (司隸) exclusively supervises external officials.
Since the establishment of the Zhōngchéng (中丞) and Sīlì (司隸),
they have alternately impeached internal and external officials,
with no internal or external limit to what they can impeach.
Yet Jié (結) suddenly obstructs me.
The reason I did not elaborate before
was that I hoped to fulfill my private wish through Jié (結)'s memorial.
Now that my wish is not granted,
and the edict says it was merely an oversight,
not beyond my scope,
and I am pardoned for this.
I hold the responsibility of Sīzhí (司直),
and should rectify myself to lead others.
If I had erred,
I would not dare accept the pardon.
Therefore, I reiterate my humble opinion:
The Sīlì (司隸) and Zhōngchéng (中丞) together impeach from the crown prince downwards,
so there is nothing from the crown prince downwards that they do not impeach.
To be able to impeach the crown prince but not the Shàngshū (尚書),
my dullness has not yet grasped this.
Is the crown prince within the 'xingma' (行馬) enclosure?
If the crown prince is within the 'xingma' (行馬) enclosure and can be impeached,
but a Shàngshū (尚書) who is within the 'xingma' (行馬) enclosure cannot be impeached,
there is no such principle.
This principle is crystal clear,
yet Jié (結) uses this to obstruct me.
I have no reason to resent this,
but for those who observe and listen,
is this not strange?
I recall that Mr. Shí (石公) once removed his clothes in the palace hall,
and was impeached by Sīlì (司隸) Xún Kǎi (荀愷).
The former emperor did not deem it wrong,
and at that time no one called it infringing upon another's office;
now I merely impeach a Shàngshū (尚書),
and should I be deemed guilty?"
Xián (咸) repeatedly memorialized, citing historical precedents,
with his reasoning being clear and evident,
and the imperial court had no way to refute him.
Gù Róng (顧榮) of Wú Jùn (吳郡) often wrote to his relatives and friends, saying:
"Fù Chángyú (傅長虞) as Sīlì (司隸) was
forceful, upright, loyal, and resolute,
his impeachments and investigations astonishing people.
Though not a comprehensive talent,
his biased brilliance is commendable."
He died in office in the fourth year of Yuánkāng (元康)
at the age of fifty-six.
An edict posthumously appointed him Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉),
granted one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, and 200,000 coins,
and his posthumous name was Zhēn (貞).
He had three sons: Fū (敷), Xī (晞), and Zuǎn (纂).
His eldest son Fū (敷) inherited.
Fū (敷), courtesy name Yǐnggēn (穎根),
was pure and quiet, possessed the Way,
and was skilled in writing.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
then transferred to Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) and Tàifù Cānjūn (太傅參軍),
but he did not take up any of these posts.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
he sought refuge in Kuàijī (會稽).
Yuándì (元帝) appointed him Zhèndōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (鎮東從事中郎).
He had a long-standing illness,
and was frequently urged to serve,
but could not decline.
He was carried to his post while ill.
He died a few months later
at the age of forty-six.
Xī (晞) also had talent and wit.
He served as Shàngyú Lìng (上虞令),
and had excellent administrative achievements.
He died while serving as Sītú Xīcáo Shǔ (司徒西曹屬).
Zhī (祗), courtesy name Zǐzhuāng (子莊).
His father Gǔ (嘏)
was Wèi Tàicháng (魏太常).
Zhī (祗) was extremely filial by nature
and became well-known early on,
praised for his talent, knowledge, and astuteness.
When Wǔdì (武帝) first established the Eastern Palace,
he began his career as Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
was promoted to Sànqí Huángmén Láng (散騎黃門郎),
granted the title Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯),
and received an enfeoffment of three hundred households.
He resigned due to his mother's mourning.
When his mother was buried,
an edict ordered the provision of Tàicháng (太常)-level ceremonial escorts for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions.
Thereafter, the provision of escorts for the funerals of various ministers' wives
began from this time.
After the mourning period ended,
he became Yíngyáng Tàishǒu (滎陽太守).
Since the great flood of Huángchū (黃初) in Wèi (魏),
the Yellow River and the Jì (濟) River had repeatedly overflowed.
Dèng Ài (鄧艾) once wrote the Jìhé Lùn (濟河論),
opening the Shímén (石門) to connect them,
but by this time it had again been damaged by inundation.
Zhī (祗) then built the Chénlái Yàn (沈萊堰),
and to this day Yǎn (兗) and Yù (豫) have been free from floods,
and the common people erected a stele to praise him.
Soon after, he was concurrently appointed Tíngwèi (廷尉),
and promoted to Chángshì (常侍) and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn (左軍將軍).
When the emperor died,
and the imperial coffin was in the funeral hall,
Grand Tutor Yáng Jùn (楊駿) assisted in governance,
wishing to please the masses,
and discussed universally advancing official ranks and peerages.
Zhī (祗) wrote to Jùn (駿) saying:
"There has never been a time when an emperor had just died
and his ministers discussed their merits."
Jùn (駿) did not heed him.
He was appointed as Shìzhōng (侍中).
At that time, Jùn (駿) was about to be executed,
but Jùn (駿) was unaware of it.
Zhī (祗) was sitting with Jùn (駿),
when the Yúnlóng Mén (雲龍門) was closed,
cutting off communication between inside and outside.
Zhī (祗) requested to hear state news with Shàngshū Wǔ Mào (尚書武茂),
bowed, and descended the steps.
Mào (茂) remained seated.
Zhī (祗) looked back and said:
"Are you not a minister of the Son of Heaven?
Now that inside and outside are cut off,
and we don't know the state of the nation,
how can you sit idly by!"
Mào (茂) then rose in shock.
After Jùn (駿) was executed,
Péi Kǎi's (裴楷) son, Zàn (瓚),
who was Jùn's (駿) son-in-law,
was killed by the mutinous soldiers.
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Xún Kǎi (尚書左僕射荀愷) had a disagreement with Kǎi (楷),
and so he memorialized that Kǎi (楷) was a relative of Jùn (駿),
and had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Zhī (祗) testified that Kǎi (楷) was innocent,
and an imperial edict pardoned him.
At that time, Jùn's (駿) officials were also arrested,
and Zhī (祗) again memorialized:
"In the past, Lǔ Zhī (魯芝) was the Sīmǎ (司馬) of Cáo Shuǎng (曹爽).
He broke through the gates to go to Shuǎng (爽),
and Xuāndì (宣帝) honored him,
even promoting him to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史).
Jùn's (駿) subordinates should not be punished."
An imperial edict again pardoned them.
Zhī (祗) made many such corrections and rectifications.
He was appointed Hénán Yǐn (河南尹),
but before he took office,
he was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉).
For his meritorious service in suppressing Yáng Jùn (楊駿),
he was to be enfeoffed as a Jùngōng (郡公) with 8,000 households.
He firmly declined,
so it was reduced by half,
and he was demoted to Lingchuān Xiàn Gōng (靈川縣公),
with 1,800 households.
The remaining 2,200 households were granted to his younger son Chàng (暢) as Wǔxiāng Tínghóu (武鄉亭侯).
Also, his original enfeoffment was bestowed upon his nephew Jùn (雋) as Dōngmíng Tínghóu (東明亭侯).
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi (楚王瑋) falsely issued an edict,
Zhī's (祗) memorial was delayed in reaching the throne,
and he was dismissed from office.
A year later,
he was promoted to Guānglù Xún (光祿勳),
but was again dismissed due to official matters.
When the Dī (氐) people's Qí Wànnián (齊萬年) raised an army and rebelled,
Zhī (祗) was made Xíng Ānxī Jūnsī (行安西軍司),
with the additional title of Chángshì (常侍).
He led Ānxī Jiāngjūn Xiàhóu Jùn (安西將軍夏侯駿) to suppress the rebellion.
He was promoted to Wèiwèi (衞尉),
but due to a wind ailment, he resigned his position,
and was then appointed Chángshì (常侍),
receiving the salary and rank of a Qīng (卿),
and was granted money and a bed curtain, etc.
Soon after, he was granted Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
with the privilege of horses passing through his gate.
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) assisted in governance,
he appointed Zhī (祗) as Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監),
retaining his Chángshì (常侍) title,
to reassure the masses.
Zhī (祗) declined due to illness,
but Lún (倫) sent an Yùshǐ (御史) to carry Zhī (祗) in a palanquin to take up his post.
Wáng Róng (王戎), Chén Zhǔn (陳準), and others conversed among themselves, saying:
"With Fù Gōng (傅公) in charge,
we have nothing to worry about."
Such was the trust and reliance people placed in him.
When Lún (倫) usurped the throne,
Zhī (祗) was again made Yòu Guānglù (右光祿), Kǎifǔ (開府),
and granted the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
When Huìdì (惠帝) returned to the palace,
Zhī (祗) requested to retire due to having held a false position during the usurpation,
but this was not permitted.
Initially,
when Lún (倫) usurped the throne,
Sūn Xiù (孫秀) and Yìyáng Wáng Wēi (義陽王威) and more than ten others had participated in drafting the ceremonial texts for the abdication.
When Lún (倫) was defeated,

Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) arrested Shìzhōng Liú Kuí (侍中劉逵), Chángshì Zōu Jié Dù Yù (常侍騶捷杜育), Huángmén Láng Lù Jī (黃門郎陸機), Yòuchéng Zhōu Dǎo Wáng Zūn (右丞周導王尊), and others, and handed them over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Since the abdication text came from the Zhōngshū (中書),
they again discussed punishing Zhī (祗).
Fortunately, a general amnesty granted him clemency.
Later, because the draft of the abdication text was not written by Zhī (祗),
an imperial edict restored him to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
His son, Xuān (宣),
married Princess Hóngnóng (弘農公主).
Soon after, he was promoted to Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅),
but he memorialized to resign and return home.
When Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) became Tàifù (太傅),
Zhī (祗) was again appointed Shàofù (少傅),
with the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
When Huáidì (懷帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) and Shìzhōng (侍中).
Before he took office, he was granted the additional titles of Yòu Púyè (右僕射) and Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監).
At that time, Tàifù Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (太傅東海王越) assisted in governance.
Zhī (祗) occupied a prominent position,
and always advocated the virtue of humility between ruler and minister.
Because of this, all levels of society lived in harmony.
Zhī (祗) was discerning and understood the state's structure,
and he managed many court systems and regulations.
He successively served as Zuǒ Guānglù (左光祿), Kǎifǔ (開府),
acting Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅),
retaining his Shìzhōng (侍中) title.
When his illness became severe, he requested to resign,
but was not permitted.
He was promoted to Sītú (司徒).
Due to a foot ailment,
an imperial edict allowed him to be carried in a palanquin into the palace,
but he did not take office.
Dàjiāngjūn Gǒu Xī (大將軍苟晞) memorialized to request a relocation of the capital,
and sent Zhī (祗) to Hényīn (河陰)
to repair boats and oars,
and prepare for water travel.
When Luòyáng (洛陽) fell,
they collectively established a temporary government.
Only Zhī (祗) was made the leader of the alliance,
and as Sītú (司徒), Chíjǐe (持節), and Dà Dūdū Zhū Jūnsī (大都督諸軍事), he issued proclamations to all four directions.
He sent his son Xuān (宣) with the princess and Shàngshū Lìng Hé Yù (尚書令和郁) to inform the regional governors and conscript righteous troops.
Zhī (祗) himself garrisoned the small city of Méngjīn (盟津),
and Xuān's (宣) younger brother Chàng (暢) served as Hényīn Lìng (河陰令),
awaiting Xuān (宣).
Zhī (祗) died suddenly from a severe illness,
at the age of sixty-nine.
Zhī (祗), feeling that his loyalty and integrity were not fully realized,
struggled with his illness to write personal letters of admonition to his two sons, Xuān (宣) and Chàng (暢).
His words were profound and earnest,
and all who read them were moved with emotion.
Zhī (祗) authored more than 100,000 words in essays and驳论 (refutations).
Xuān's (宣) courtesy name was Shìhóng (世弘).
At the age of six, he lost his stepmother,
and wept like an adult,
which his relatives found extraordinary.
When he grew up,
he loved learning.
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) appointed him Xiàngguó Yuàn (相國掾), Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎), and Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人),
then promoted him to Sītú Xīcáo Yuàn (司徒西曹掾).
He resigned from office,
and was successively promoted to Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞) and Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng (驃騎從事中郎).
When Huìdì (惠帝) returned from Cháng'ān (長安),
Xuān (宣) was made Zuǒchéng (左丞),
but he did not take the post,
and was promoted to Huángmén Láng (黃門郎).
When Huáidì (懷帝) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
and then became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
He died at the age of forty-nine,
with no sons,
so Chàng's (暢) son Chōng (沖) was made his heir.
Chàng's (暢) courtesy name was Shìdào (世道).
At the age of five,
a friend of his father saw him and playfully
removed Chàng's (暢) clothes,
took his golden ring, and gave it to a servant.
Chàng (暢) did not regret it,
and was rewarded for this.
Before he reached twenty,
he already had a great reputation.
He was selected to serve as a lecturer in the Eastern Palace
and became Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞).
Soon after, he was captured by Shí Lè (石勒),
who made him Dàjiāngjūn Yòu Sīmǎ (大將軍右司馬).
He was knowledgeable about court ceremonies
and held confidential positions,
and Lè (勒) greatly valued him.
He authored twenty-two volumes of the Jìn Zhū Gōng Zàn (晉諸公讚),
and also nine volumes of Gōngqīng Gùshì (公卿故事).
He died in the fifth year of Xiánhé (咸和)
. His son, Yǒng (詠),
crossed the river and became Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (交州刺史) and Tàizǐ Yòu Shuài (太子右率).
The imperial historian says: Emperor Wǔ viewed the four directions,
judged the common people,
ever spoke of encouragement and admonition,
and deeply valued remonstrating officials.
Fù Xuán possessed a strong and upright demeanor,
held a selfless character,
spoke out with strong words and a serious expression,
corrected deficiencies and assisted against wrongs.
He was outspoken in court,
and did not disgrace his office.
When he attained the position of one of the Three Judges,
and was in charge of impeachments,
he was able to make the imperial court vibrant,
and the imperial relatives restrained themselves.
Even Bào Yǒng and Gé Kōng of previous generations
could not surpass him!
However, he had this narrow-mindedness,
lacked a magnanimous disposition,
and when he suddenly heard of competition,
he was criticized by public opinion.
What a pity!
The ancients took warning from a `wéi` bow and a `xián` string,
and there was indeed a reason for it.
Zhǎng Yú's character was solemn and stern,
not diminishing the family reputation.
When he accepted advice in Rǔnán,
and presented a memorial in Línjìn,
he stood in a position of integrity and uprightness,
and possessed foresight.
Fù Zhī, son of a famous father,
established his reputation early.
In a tumultuous and dangerous court,
he rescued the ruler and his ministers in their hour of need.
He was finally able to preserve his position and emoluments,
which can be called having the Dào within him.
Eulogy: Qúnhú was firm and trustworthy,
truly the hope of the court.
His will was stern and upright,
his nature lacked ease and generosity.
Zhǎng Yú was firm and simple,
without diminishing his integrity.
Zǐzhuāng had talent and discernment,
and thus received the robes of office.
His loyal achievements were not yet realized,
when the path to the underworld suddenly drew near.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 18: Xiàng Xióng
Xiàng Xióng, courtesy name Mào bó,
was a native of Shānyáng, Hénèi.
His father, Sháo,
was the Grand Administrator of Péngchéng.
Xióng first served in the commandery as Chief Clerk,
serving Grand Administrator Wáng Jīng.
When Jīng died,
Xióng mourned him with utmost grief,
and the market people all grieved for him.
Later, Grand Administrator Liú Yì once whipped Xióng for a minor offense.
When Wú Fèn replaced Yì as Grand Administrator,
he again detained Xióng in prison for a slight transgression.
Zhōng Huì, the Colonel Director of Retainers, appointed Xióng as Administrator of the Department of Civil Affairs while he was in prison.
When Huì died, no one collected his body for burial,
so Xióng received his coffin and buried him.
Emperor Wén summoned Xióng and reproached him, saying:
"Previously, when Wáng Jīng died,
you mourned Wáng Jīng in the eastern market.
I did not question it.
Now Zhōng Huì personally committed rebellion,
and you again took it upon yourself to collect and bury him.
If I were to tolerate you again,
what would become of the imperial law!"
Xióng replied:
"In ancient times, the former kings covered skeletons and buried rotting bones.
Their benevolence extended to decaying remains.
At that time, would they first predict their crimes and then bury them?
Now the imperial execution has been carried out,
and the law is already satisfied.
I, Xióng, was moved by righteousness to collect and bury him;
the teachings also have no deficiency.
The law is established above,
the teachings are spread below.
Why must I, Xióng, disregard the living and abandon the dead to establish myself in this era?
Your Highness, to harbor enmity against dry bones and abandon them in the wilds,
for the sake of future benevolent and worthy persons,
is it not a pity?"
The emperor was very pleased,
conversed and dined with him, and then dismissed him.
He was successively promoted to Palace Gentleman.
At that time, Wú Fèn and Liú Yì were both Palace Attendants,
serving together in the palace gate.
Xióng initially did not exchange words with them.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this,
and ordered Xióng to restore the good relationship between ruler and minister.
Xióng, having no choice,
went to Yì,
bowed twice and said:
"I have just received an imperial decree:
'The righteousness between ruler and minister is severed.'
How can this be?"
Then he immediately left.
The emperor heard this and was greatly angered,
asking Xióng:
"I ordered you to restore the good relationship between ruler and minister,
why did you sever it?"
Xióng replied:
"In ancient times, gentlemen advanced people with propriety,
and dismissed people with propriety.
Today, advancing people is like placing them on one's knees,
and dismissing people is like pushing them into a river.

He was then able to repent and return to goodness,
and after three years
and then returned to Bó.
After having been banished and then returning,
the Yīn Way, though it had waned, revived,
and the feudal lords all submitted.
He was known as Tàizōng,
truly relying on the utmost loyalty of Āhéng.
When the Zhōu House declined,
the feudal lords contended,
the King of Heaven became weak,
and governance subsequently languished.
Qí Huán Gōng,
though he was a licentious ruler;
yet the reason he could achieve the merit of
“nine alliances and one unification,”
and gain the name of "honoring Zhōu,"
was truly due to Guǎn Yíwú’s strength.
But when he died,
worms crawled out from his door,
was this not the fault of employing Shùdiāo?
Moreover, in the person
of one Huán Gōng,
when he obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
his achievements were as described;
when he employed Shùdiāo,
his chaos was as such.
Indeed, honor and disgrace, existence and destruction,
truly depend on whom one employs.
How can one not be careful?
Qín
was originally a descendant of Bóyì.
From a tiny, small city,
it only began to grow under Qín Zhòng,
having fine carriages, horses, rites, music, and attendants.
From Mù Gōng to Shǐ Huáng,
all were able to
pay attention to and await worthy men,
seek out extraordinary individuals from afar.
They invited Yóu Yú from the Western Róng,
obtained Wǔgǔ from Wǎncì,
took Pī Bào from Jìnxiāng,
and welcomed Jiǎn Shū from Zōnglǐ.
Because of this, brave and outstanding men from all four directions arrived one after another,
and thus it was able to be a strong state for generations,
swallowing up the feudal lords,
possessing the whole world,
and simultaneously claiming the title of emperor.
This was due to the assistance
of strategists.
But its Way of transformation was not yet pure,
and it collapsed at Shāqiū.
Húhài indulged in cruelty,
deceiving himself with treachery,
unable to uphold the grand lineage,
or complete the grand structure.
Instead, he brutalized
benevolence and righteousness,
and spread poison among the common people.
Thus, Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng
raised their arms and shouted loudly,
and the world responded.
Thereupon, Zhào Gāo rebelled,
Yán Yuè carried out his orders,
the Second Emperor was cornered,
and committed suicide at Wàngyí.
Though Zǐyīng was enthroned,
he dropped the title of emperor for king.
Isolated, imperiled, and without support,
he perished within forty days.
This was due to corrupt ministers usurping authority,
calling
a deer a horse,
which hastened Qín’s disaster.
Qín lost its deer,
and heroes contended for it.
Xiàng Yǔ acquired it but then lost it.
His fault lay in boiling Hán Shēng,
and
not using Fàn Zēng’s strategy.
If Yǔ had rejected Xiàng Bó's misleading words,
executed Pèi Gōng at Hóngmén,
and made Xiányáng his capital to command the feudal lords,
then the world
would have had no equal.
But Yǔ rejected Hán Shēng’s loyal remonstrance,
went against Fàn Zēng’s profound schemes,
believing his hegemonic imperial enterprise was already established.
He made Péngchéng his capital,
returned to his hometown,
and wore
embroidered robes by day.
This was merely the sentiment of worldly children,
yet Yǔ took pride in it.
Therefore, within five years he was captured by Hàn.
Even at this point, he still did not awaken,
but
said,
"Heaven is destroying me,
it is not the fault of war."
How lamentable!
Moreover, when gentlemen return to benevolence,
it is like water returning to a lower place,
or birds running to the open wilderness.
Thus it is said:
"The otter drives fish into the river,
the falcon drives sparrows into the marsh,
and Jié and Zhòu drive people to Tāng and Wǔ."
Hàn Gāozǔ rose from common cloth,
wielding a three-foot
blade to seize the empire.
He used the resources of the Six States,
without the abdication of Táng and Yú.
Was it merely relying on Liáng and Píng's extraordinary strategies,
and exhausting the wisdom and strength of heroes?
It was also because the Xiàng clan drove people away.
His descendants continued the foundation for over two hundred years,
until Chéng Dì delegated power to his maternal relatives,
causing authority to shift outwards.
Ānchāng Hóu Zhāng Yǔ
was
one of the Hàn's Three Excellencies,
and Chéng Dì's tutor.
The emperor personally favored his household,
bowing before Yǔ below the couch,
and deeply questioned him about heavenly disasters and human affairs.
Yǔ should have maintained the integrity of a great minister,
thought deeply for the state,
offered loyal words and excellent counsel,
and presented the disasters and misfortunes.
Then the Wáng clan would not have been able to monopolize power and favor,
Wáng Mǎng would have had no opportunity to seize power and position,
and thus ride the clouds and dragons to
ascend the heavenly path,
causing the Hàn lineage to be interrupted.
Yǔ was flattering and disloyal,
harboring private motives,
merely bowing and scraping among the Five Marquises,
only seeking to gain favor.
For this reason, Zhū Yún stood firm and requested the imperial sword that slays horses,
wishing to execute Yǔ with it,
to warn the others.
This can be called loyal.
But Chéng Dì still did not awaken,
and considered it
speaking ill of superiors from a subordinate position,
publicly insulting his tutor in court,
a capital offense without pardon.
He ordered the censor to take Yún down,
wanting to quickly cook him.
Yún clung to the palace railing and broke it.
Fortunately, the Left General
Xīn Qìngjì kowtowed until his head bled,
contending for him with his life.
If not for that,
Yún would have been crushed.
Although the broken railing was later left unrepaired,
to display the integrity of a righteous
minister,
which was indeed sufficient as a warning for later generations,
what benefit was it to the Hàn house, which perished anyway?
However, those who discuss this era believe that among rebellious ministers, traitorous sons, and those utterly without the Way,
none surpassed Mǎng.
This is also like the evil of Zhòu being not as extreme as this.
Tradition says that Mǎng initially rose as a maternal relative,
humbling himself and striving,
to gain reputation.
His clan called him filial,
and his friends ascribed benevolence to him.
When he assisted in governance during the reigns of Chéng and Āi,
he diligently served the state,
and his actions were always praised.
At that time, the number of people who went to the palace gates to
submit letters recommending Mǎng was countless.
Ministers inside and outside the court all attributed merits and virtues to Mǎng.
He encountered the Hàn house in decline,
with the imperial succession broken three times,
and the Empress Dowager was long-lived,
serving as the clan matriarch.
Thus Mǎng was able to carry out the enthronement of the child emperor and usurp his position.
In ancient times, the rise of Tāng and Wǔ
was also a matter of seizing by unconventional means and holding by conventional means.
If Mǎng had deeply
considered the methods of Yīn and Zhōu in seizing and holding power,
promoted morality,
endeavored in benevolence and righteousness,
acted with sincerity and trustworthiness,
discarded ostentation and falsity,
and bestowed favors upon the world
for eighteen years,
his grace would have been sufficient to move the common
people,
and his righteousness sufficient to bind heroes.
With people cherishing his virtue
and heroes employed together,
in such a case,
the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain ought not to have perished.
Even if Guāngwǔ was wise and talented,
he would
How could one hope for such an undertaking!
After Wáng Mǎng
ascended the throne, he
deemed himself to have received assistance from Heaven and men,
believing his accomplishments surpassed the Sānwáng (Three Sovereigns)
and his virtue outshone Táng Yú (Emperors Yáo and Shùn).
Thus, he grew
arrogant and presumptuous,
brandishing his might and deceit,
issuing proclamations of auspicious omens and prophecies,
and exercising brutal cruelty.
He indulged in extreme wickedness,
causing both men and gods to resent him.
Winter brought thunder and lightning to startle his ears and eyes,
while summer saw earthquakes to alarm his
heart and mind.
Yet Wáng Mǎng remained unaware and unawakened,
instead repeatedly issuing ill-timed edicts,
even enforcing the punishment of collective responsibility (liánwǔ zhī xíng).
Flatterers were favored,
while loyal remonstrators were
executed.
Consequently, the whole empire was filled with indignation,
with unrest breaking out both internally and externally.
The four seas fragmented,
cities and fortifications became indefensible,
and he himself died at the hands of a common man,
becoming a laughingstock for all under Heaven.
Is this not
extraordinary! The reason for this
was not that he erred in taking the throne,
but that he governed without righteousness.
After Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
the whole empire (liùhé) was in turmoil.
Liú Shènggōng
was established as emperor but failed to discern the situation;
Pénzǐ succeeded him but was overthrown;
Gōngsūn Shù also proclaimed himself emperor in Shǔhàn.
Such individuals
were certainly not what one would call those who responded to Heaven's will and accorded with human desires;
they merely served as
expellers for Guāngwǔ.
Indeed, the empire (tiānxià)
is truly the empire of all under Heaven,
not the empire of one person.
“The troops of Yīnshāng
were gathered
like a forest,
arrayed at Mùyě.
Only I, the lord, shall rise.”
It also says:
“The lords served Zhōu,
for Heaven’s mandate is not constant.”
From this, it can be said that
the ruler is not an ordinary person;
if he possesses virtue,
the empire will rally to him;
if he lacks virtue, the empire will rebel against him.
Therefore, the enlightened kings of old,
in their strenuous efforts and far-reaching thoughts,
were always like one standing by a river without a crossing.
Thus, they
modeled themselves on Heaven and Earth,
imitated the four seasons,
magnified their benevolence and virtue,
respected their great ministers,
drew close to the loyal and upright,
and distanced themselves from flatterers.
Benevolence and filial piety were manifest within their palace walls,
and their great transforming influence spread throughout the populace.
They were
fair and upright as a plumb line and arrow,
and their trustworthiness and righteousness moved both men and gods.
Even with the favor of empresses' relatives (jiāofáng wàiqī),
they would not accept their circuitous words.
Even with beloved attendants and favored eunuchs (jìnxí àixìng zhī shù),
they would not
heed their indulgent pleas.
The four gates were solemn and open,
not closed,
welcoming remonstrators without restraint.
Trembling with awe and fear,
they never forgot vigilance and apprehension,
so that they wished
to eternally preserve their heavenly emoluments,
fearing they might become the expellers for future sages.
Moreover, your servant has heard that
those who fear danger
are often secure;
those who worry about perishing
are those who survive.
If a ruler of a state can be secure yet not forget danger,
then his line will continue for a hundred generations,
long preserving his glorious destiny,
his name and position boundless as Heaven and Earth.
Why should he then worry about becoming
an expeller for those to come!
The classics say:
“The words of a madman
are observed by an enlightened ruler.”
The second point is: For gentlemen to establish their careers,
their conduct is not uniform.
Wú Qǐ was greedy for office;
when his mother died, he did not return.
He killed his wife to gain a generalship;
this was extreme unfilial conduct.
Yet in
Wèi,
he made the Qín people dare not look eastward;
in Chǔ,
the Sānjìn states dared not plot southward.
Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Qiān
were truly filial sons,
unable to be separated from their
parents even for a night.
How could they offer their lives and risk dangerous places!
Now, the great Jìn
has received the mandate of the cosmic order,
and its sagely beauty rivals that of Yǒuyú (Shùn).
Yet the Wú people refuse to
submit,
proclaiming themselves emperors and privately allying.
This is also a disgrace to the state.
If Your Majesty sincerely desires to attract brave warriors (xióngpí zhī shì)
and loyal ministers,
to make them display their might on the Huáipǔ
and awe the Southern barbarians (mánjīng) into submission,
then it is fitting to extensively consult and widely gather talents,
broadly opening the path for recommended gentlemen,
recommending recluses (yánxué),
promoting worthy talents,
summoning them for examination.
Only the outstanding should be employed.
Currently, in the selection of officials for the
imperial court (táigé),
the avenues are blocked by private interests,
and when interviewing people for the jiǔpǐn ranks,
only the opinion of the zhòngzhèng is sought.
Thus, those who hold the highest ranks
are either descendants of dukes and marquises
or brothers of powerful officials (dāngtú).
If these two groups are always favored,
how can outstanding individuals from humble backgrounds (bì mén péng hù zhī jùn)
avoid being overlooked and submerged (lùshén)?
The third point is: In the past, Tián Zǐfāng cared for an old horse,
and impoverished scholars knew where to turn.
How much more so for one who resides in the grand dwelling of the world,
occupies the rightful position of the world,
and practices the great
way of the world!
In the past, enlightened kings and sagely rulers
all practiced caring for the elderly.
The elderly are numerous,
not necessarily all worthy,
and cannot all be supported.
Therefore, one treats the Sānlǎo as fathers,
thereby demonstrating filial piety;
one honors the Wǔgēng as clan elders,
thereby demonstrating respect.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Treat my own elderly as the elderly of others,
and my own young as the young of others.”
Today,
although the empire is settled,
on the southern side of Huàshān there are no herds of horses grazing,
and under Táolín there are no resting cattle,
because the Wú people have not yet submitted.
Indeed,
the hungry are easily fed,
and the thirsty are easily given drink;
the common people (yuányuán) of the empire look forward to new governance.
May Your Majesty recall the benevolence of Zǐfāng,
remember the toil of humble servants (quǎnmǎ zhī láo),
think of the recompense for
covering and protection (wéigài zhī bào),
issue benevolent edicts,
and broadly establish the system of caring for the elderly.
The fourth point is: Of all laws, rewards, and punishments,
nothing is greater than trustworthiness.
The ancients said:
“If a person is without trustworthiness,
I do not know what he can do.”
How much more so for one who nourishes people with benevolence
and employs people with righteousness;
how can he act without trustworthiness!
Previously, your servant served as the Administrator of Xījùn,
and received an edict from the province dated Jǐwèi, stating:
“The Qiāng and Hú are far away;
therefore,
only recruit those willing to go,
do not force those unwilling.”
Upon receiving the edict,
your servant immediately proclaimed the grace and widely recruited,
showing trustworthiness with rewards.
The names of those recruited were immediately reported to the Commander of the West.
However,
The Jìn people themselves could be dispatched and strong men conscripted,
taken according to the law.
As for the Qiāng and Hú,
if they were not enlightened through kindness and persuasion,
then none would wish to cross Jīnchéng and Héxī.
Since
whenever an army was raised to cross the river,
there was never any trouble,
thus Governor Guō Suī commended that commander for his effective methods,
greatly praising and encouraging him,
promising him a substantial reward.
Because of this, those who were recruited were grateful
and eager for rewards,
and thus achieved success,
their contributions being paramount.
Now the provincial and commandery governors and generals
have all received enfeoffments,
while the brave warriors of the Qiāng and Hú,
some made kings, some marquises,
have not been granted such consideration
either.
Even Jìn Wén did not covet Yuán to lose trust,
and Qí Huán did not begrudge land to break an alliance,
how much more so a sage ruler!
The fifth point states: In ancient times, when the Zhōu and Hàn arose,
they established kin and built up virtue.
The Zhōu adopted the five ranks of nobility,
and the Hàn had the oaths of rivers and mountains.
But when they declined,
the divine artifact
was seized by powerful ministers,
and the dynasty’s mandate shifted to others.
Thus, the one who destroyed Zhōu was Qín,
not of the Jī surname;
the one who replaced Hàn was Wèi,
not of the Liú clan.
Today, the great
strategy of the state
is to prevent those of different surnames from having territories with exclusive enfeoffment,
and to have those of the same surname jointly hold vast connected lands.
Even if the descendants of these kings were to annex each other again,
this would still be like
the people of Chǔ losing their fánruò bow in Yúnmèng,
which is not yet to say they have lost their bow entirely.
As long as the divine artifact does not pass to another clan,
then the temple of the founder will not be moved,
and for ten thousand years,
for myriad generations, its name will not change.
There are over twenty kings in the Great Jìn,
and over five hundred states of dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons.
If you wish to say all their states are small,
then
when Hàn Zǔ arose,
he had no land of even a foot,
how much more so those who possess states!
Should one claim that the Great Jìn will forever have wise and sagely rulers,
and that the descendants of the feudal lords will always be unworthy?
Then,
Fàng Xūn was wise and enlightened, yet had Dān Zhū;
Gǔ Sǒu was stubborn and wicked, yet had Yú Shùn.
Whenever there is trouble in the world, it is always caused by military force,
and to gratuitously establish many military bases,
widely opening
the source of disorder,
is why I say the five ranks are inconvenient.
I believe it would be advisable, as previously memorialized,
for the kings to have their states enlarged,
their armies increased,
and all of them sent to guard their藩 fiefs,
so that
their strategic positions are sufficient to support each other.
Then Your Majesty can rest peacefully.
I believe the titles of marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons should all be changed,
so that the system of
enfeoffment,
emoluments, and ritual rank
are all consistent with the regulations for all feudal lords under heaven.
I have heard that those who follow the same track as an overturned carriage have never been safe;
those who suffer the same illness as a dead person have never lived;
those who follow the same laws as a perished state have never survived.
How much more so for the majestic Great Jìn,
which is about to ascend Tài Shān,
perform the shàn sacrifice at Liángfù,
engrave its achievements on stone,
and display them for endless generations.
It should draw lessons from the rise and fall of past dynasties,
and establish deep and strict
precautions,
so that those who record events with their pens
will certainly have something to chronicle.
In ancient times, Yī Yǐn was ashamed that his ruler was not like Yáo or Shùn.
This is why I privately harbor such fervent emotion,
forgetting my own humble status.
Yáo
Shū’s memorial was submitted,
and the emperor, upon reading it, was astonished,
promoting him to General of Illuminating Might and Administrator of Wèixīng.
He died in office.
Yán Zuǎn
Yán Zuǎn, courtesy name Xùbó,
was a native of Ānhàn, Bāxī.
His grandfather, Pǔ,
served as Zāng Lǔ’s Grand Clerk (gōngcáo),
persuaded Lǔ to surrender to Wèi,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglè Township.
His father, Pú,
inherited the title,
and served Wú, reaching the position of Administrator of Zāngkē.
Zuǎn lived as an émigré in Xīn’ān, Hénán.
In his youth, he associated with heroes,
making many connections,
and extensively read classical texts,
comprehensively understanding the principles of things.
When his father died,
his stepmother was unkind.
Zuǎn served her with even greater reverence and diligence.
But his mother disliked him even more,
and falsely accused Zuǎn of stealing gold and treasures from his father’s time,
suing him before the authorities.
He was consequently subjected to public condemnation for over ten years,
yet Zuǎn showed no resentment,
maintaining his filial piety and diligence without fail.
Later, his mother changed her mind
and informed the Zhongzhèng (Impartial Judge),
whereupon he regained his official rank.
He served as a Gentleman-in-Waiting (shèrén) to Grand Tutor Yáng Jùn,
then was transferred to be Magistrate of Ānfù.
When Jùn was executed,
Zuǎn abandoned his office and returned,
inviting Jùn’s former Chief Clerk Pān Yuè and clerk Cuī Jī and others to jointly bury him.
Jī and Yuè, fearing punishment,
appointed Zuǎn as the leader.
When the tomb was completed
and it was time for the burial,
Jùn’s cousin Mú informed Wǔlíng Wáng Dàn,
intending to memorialize for the execution of the instigators.
All were terrified,
filled the tomb and fled.
Zuǎn alone used his family wealth to complete the tomb
and buried Jùn before departing.
The Libationer of the Imperial Academy, Zōu Zhàn, considered Zuǎn capable of assisting in scholarly writing,
Qiáo said:
"This position is leisurely and well-paid;
the powerful and influential often compete for it,
so there is no time to seek out talent."
Thus, he was not employed.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng appointed him as Sīmǎ of the Western Regions Protector (xīróng xiàowèi),
and for his achievements,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglè Township.
When Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was deposed,
Zuǎn went to the palace gate with a coffin,
submitting a memorial to argue the Crown Prince’s innocence, saying: I humbly observed the edict of amnesty and the handwritten memorial of the former Crown Prince Yù posted below,
and was astonished.
Since ancient times,
no minister or son has been so rebellious
as this.
Yet,
fortunately, by imperial grace,
his life was spared.
I humbly reflect that Yù, born to a sagely father, came to this state
due to being raised deep in the palace,
immersed in wealth and nobility,
receiving
leniency from the late emperor,
and being indulged by his parents.
Whenever I saw teachers selected, down to the various officials,
they were mostly chosen from families of luxury and opulence,
rarely were there humble and simple scholars like
Wèi Wǎn, Zhōu Wén, Shí Fèn, and Shū Guǎng.
His attendants and gentlemen-in-waiting also had no one comparable to Jí Àn or Zhèng Zhuāng,
which led to him not knowing the way to serve his father and ruler.
I, your subject,
examined the ancient classics,
which state that the Crown Prince should reside according to the rites of a scholar,
and be counted among the common people.
This illustrates that the former kings wished him to know humility first before gaining nobility.
Lately, the Eastern Palace has also been slightly
too extravagant,
which is why it led to ruin.
Not only the Eastern Palace,
but looking back at the teachers, friends, and literati of all the kings,
they were all powerful nobles who could achieve their positions,
rarely like Gōng Suí or Wáng Yáng,
who could instruct with principles.
Friends lacked the integrity of the three beneficial types,
officials held literary titles,
but in reality did not read books;
they merely shared fine clothes and good horses,
indulged in drinking and grand gatherings,
playing and gambling.
How could there be any mutual learning
to help each other improve!
I have always feared that the imperial clan would become arrogant and overbearing,
sighing at this.
Now Yù can serve as a warning,
but I fear that he will be
reprimanded,
cast out and banished to the distant suburbs,
only then will he regret his errors,
but it will be too late to recover.
In the past, Lì Tàizǐ (戾太子) behaved improperly,
raised troops to defy an order,
yet the Sanlǎo (三老) of Húguān (壺關) submitted a memorial,
which contained the words of Tián Qiānqiū (田千秋),
who said:
"A son playing with his father's weapons,
his crime
should only warrant a caning!"
Hàn Wǔ (漢武) was moved and enlightened by this,
and built the Sìzǐtái (思子臺).
Now, Yù (遹) behaves improperly,
his words are rebellious and contrary,
but on the day he receives punishment,
he dares not deviate from the proper path.
This is still
lighter than the case of Lì Tàizǐ (戾太子),
and he can still be restrained
by carefully selecting his tutors and guardians.
For example, Sīkōng (司空) Zhāng Huá (張華),
whose virtue is profound and far-reaching,
and whose heart is loyal and sincere,
should be made his teacher.
Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Liú Shí (劉寔),
who established himself through hardship and poverty,
and whose integrity remained undiminished from beginning to end,
whose age is like that of Lǚ Wàng (呂望),
and who has not abandoned the classics,
should be made his guardian.
Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Péi Wèi (裴頠),
who is discerning,
sincere, and respectful,
embodies the Way and dwells in uprightness,
should be made his friend.
Establish scholars for casual conversation and literature,
all selected from poor families and isolated officials who established themselves through learning and conduct,
as well as those who diligently served and experienced
difficulties, who served their lord and their parents, and whose reputation and conduct are well-known,
and let them reside with him.
Appoint a strict Yùshǐ (御史) to supervise his household,
and cut off contact with sons of noble relatives and
frivolous guests.
If this is done,
those around him, to his left and right, front and back,
will all be upright individuals.
His teachers and scholars
can be ordered to hold discussions once every ten days,
making them debate together in his presence.
Order them
to speak only of filial sons and benevolent parents from ancient and modern times,
loyal ministers serving their lords,
and the principles of contemplating faults and reforming errors,
so that he hears good teachings,
and may perhaps be preserved.
In the past, Tài Jiǎ (太甲) committed a crime,
was banished for three years,
contemplated his errors and reformed,
and became a wise king of Yīn (殷).
Furthermore, Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝) feared being deposed,
and diligently disciplined himself day and night,
and was finally
able to preserve himself.
And down to Míngdì (明帝),
who was implicated by his mother's offense,
and deposed as Píngyuán Hóu (平原侯);
household retainers and concubine's sons were assigned to him,
and teachers, friends, and scholars
were all selected from upright individuals,
to mutually
assist and correct him.
He was scrupulously cautious regarding punishments,
served his father with filial piety,
and after his father's death,
served his mother with reverence,
and his reputation spread throughout the land,
and is still praised today.
Hàn Gāo Huángdì (漢高皇帝) often held feasts
in the courtyard,
intending to depose the crown prince,
but afterwards, with the Sī Hào (四晧) as teachers,
and Zǐfáng (子房) as guardian,
he was ultimately able to succeed.
Past events not forgotten
are a warning for future events.
Mèng Kē (孟軻) said,
"An isolated minister or a concubine's son,
their hearts are dangerously set,
and their contemplation of misfortune is deep,"
thus they often achieve good merits.

Biography 19 Ruǎn Jí (his nephew Xián, Xián's son Zhān, Zhān's younger brother Fú, his cousin Xiū, his clan cousin Fàng, Fàng's younger brother Yù)"
Ruǎn Jí
had the courtesy name Sīzōng and was from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His father, Yǔ,
was a secretary to the Chancellor of Wèi
and was renowned in his generation.
Jí had an extraordinary appearance
and a magnanimous spirit.
He was aloof and self-possessed,
acting on his nature without restraint,
and his joy or anger was never shown on his face.
Sometimes he would close his door and read books,
not coming out for months;
sometimes he would climb mountains and gaze at scenery,
forgetting to return for days.
He read widely from many texts,
especially favoring Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ.
He loved wine and could whistle beautifully,
and he was skilled at playing the qín.
When he was content,
he would suddenly forget himself.
People at the time mostly considered him foolish,
but only his cousin Wényè always praised and admired him,
thinking Jí superior to himself.
From this, everyone acclaimed him as extraordinary.
Jí once accompanied his uncle to Dōngjùn.
Wáng Chǎng, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, invited him for a meeting.
Jí did not utter a single word all day,
and Wáng Chǎng considered him unfathomable.
Tàiwèi Jiǎng Jì heard he possessed exceptional talent and invited him to serve.
Jí went to the capital pavilion and submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly consider that you, Illustrious Duke, with your virtue that embraces all,
occupy the position of the highest office.
Heroes crane their necks,
and eminent worthies raise their feet.
On the day you established your office,
everyone considered themselves your subordinate;
when the invitation was first issued,
I, your humble servant, was the first.
In the past, Zǐxià was on the banks of the Xīhé,
and Marquis Wén would sweep the path for him;
Master Zōu resided in the shade of Shǔgǔ,
and King Zhāo would ride beside him.
The common scholar, simply clad,
living alone and standing apart,
is treated with courtesy by kings, dukes, and great men
because the Way exists in them.
Now, I, Jí, have neither the Way of Zōu nor Bǔ,
but merely their rustic appearance.
To be so unworthily chosen
means I cannot meet expectations.
I shall instead cultivate the southern slopes of Dōnggāo,
paying my surplus tax of millet and grain.
Carrying firewood, I am tired and ill,
my leg strength is not robust.
The summons to become an official
is not something I can handle.
I beg you to withdraw your mistaken favor,
to glorify your pure recommendation."
At first,
Jiǎng Jì feared Jí would not come, but he was delighted to receive the memorial.
He dispatched soldiers to fetch him,
but Jí had already left,
and Jiǎng Jì was greatly angered.
Thereupon, his fellow villagers jointly persuaded him,

He was extremely filial by nature.
When his mother passed away,
he was playing weiqi with someone.
His opponent asked to stop,
but Jí insisted on finishing the game.
Afterwards, he drank two dòu of wine,
let out a loud wail,
and vomited several shēng of blood.
When it was time for the burial,
he ate one steamed pig's trotter
and drank two dòu of wine,
and then, facing the final farewell,
he directly said, "It is over!"
He let out a loud wail,
and again vomited several shēng of blood.
He became emaciated, his bones protruding,
almost to the point of extinction.
Péi Kǎi went to offer condolences to him.
Jí had his hair disheveled, sat with legs spread,
and stared straight ahead while drunk.
Kǎi finished his condolences and left.
Someone asked Kǎi:
