"Generally, when offering condolences,
the host weeps,
and the guest then performs the ritual.
Since Jí did not weep,
why did you weep?"
Kǎi said:
"Ruǎn Jí is a man beyond conventions,
therefore he does not uphold ritual ceremonies.
I am a man of the world,
therefore I conduct myself according to norms."
People at the time praised both as having acted appropriately.
Jí could also use "blue and white eyes."
When he saw conventional scholars,
he would respond with a "white eye."
When Jī Xǐ came to offer condolences,
Jí gave him a "white eye,"
and Xǐ retreated displeased.
Xǐ's younger brother, Kāng, heard about this,
and so brought wine and a qín to visit him.
Jí was greatly pleased
and showed him a "blue eye."
Because of this, scholars of rites and laws hated him as an enemy,
but the emperor always protected him.
Rú Jié's (阮籍) sister-in-law once returned home to visit her parents.
Rú Jié (阮籍) went to see her off and bid her farewell.
Someone criticized this,
to which Rú Jié (阮籍) said:
"How could propriety be established for me!"
A young woman in the neighboring house had a beautiful appearance,
and she tended the counter selling wine.
Rú Jié (阮籍) often went there to drink.
When drunk,
he would simply lie down beside her.
Since Rú Jié (阮籍) himself felt no impropriety,
her husband, observing this,
also harbored no suspicion.
A military family's daughter, possessed of talent and beauty,
died unmarried.
Rú Jié (阮籍) did not know her father or brothers,
yet went directly to weep for her,
expressing his full sorrow before returning.
His outward candor and inner sincerity,
are all of this kind.
Sometimes he would, on a whim, drive alone,
not following established paths.
Wherever his carriage tracks ended,
he would burst into tears and turn back.
He once ascended Guǎngwǔ (廣武),
to observe the battlefield where Chǔ (楚) and Hàn (漢) fought,
sighing,
"At that time there were no heroes,
allowing a mere youth to achieve fame!"
Ascending Wǔláo (武牢) Mountain,
he gazed at the capital city and sighed,
and thereupon composed the "Poem on Heroes."
He died in the winter of Jǐngyuán (景元) 4,
at the age of fifty-four.
Rú Jié (阮籍) was capable of writing,
initially without much deliberation.
He wrote over eighty poems for "Yǒnghuái Shī" (詠懷詩),
which were esteemed by the world.
He authored "Dá Zhuāng Lùn" (達莊論),
valuing non-action.
Many of his writings are not recorded here.
Rú Jié (阮籍) once met Sūn Dēng (孫登) on Sūmén (蘇門) Mountain,
and discussed with him matters of eternity and the art of nurturing spirit and guiding qi.
Sūn Dēng (孫登) did not respond to any of it.
Rú Jié (阮籍) then let out a long whistle and withdrew.
When he reached halfway down the mountain,
he heard a sound like that of a phoenix or a luan,
echoing through the cliffs and valleys;
it was Sūn Dēng's (孫登) whistle.
He then returned and wrote "Dàrén Xiānshēng Zhuàn" (大人先生傳),
which roughly states:
"What the worldly call a gentleman,
only cultivates laws,
only restrains with rituals.
In hand he holds a jade tablet,
underfoot he treads a ruler's line.
His actions aim to be an immediate standard,
his words aim to be an eternal rule.
Young, he is praised by his village,
grown, he is known in neighboring states.
Above, he desires to scheme for the three dukes,
below, he does not fail to be a governor of the nine provinces.
Do they alone not see the cluster of lice living in the trousers,
escaping into deep seams,
hiding in worn out stuffing,
believing it to be a fortunate dwelling?
In movement, they dare not leave the seam edges,
in action, they dare not exit the crotch of the trousers,
believing themselves to have found the rule.
Yet when the fiery hills erupt and fire flows,
charring cities and destroying capitals,
the cluster of lice in the trousers cannot escape.
How is a gentleman dwelling within the world
any different from a louse dwelling in trousers!"
This also represents Rú Jié's (阮籍) fundamental inclination and disposition.
His son, Hún (渾),
courtesy name Chángchéng (長成),
possessed his father's style.
Young, he admired broad-mindedness,
and did not bother with minor details.
Rú Jié (阮籍) told him:
"Zhòngróng (仲容) has already joined my stream;
you must not be like that again!"
In the middle of Tàikāng (太康),
he served as Prince's Secretary.
[Rú] Xián (咸) courtesy name Zhòngróng (仲容).
His father, Xī (熙),
was the Administrator of Wǔdū (武都).
Xián (咸) was unconstrained and broad-minded,
and associated with his uncle Rú Jié (阮籍) in the Bamboo Grove gatherings.
Those who upheld propriety and law at the time criticized his conduct.
Xián (咸) and Rú Jié (阮籍) lived south of the road,
while other Rúans (阮) lived north of the road.
The Northern Rúans (阮) were wealthy, while the Southern Rúans (阮) were poor.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
the Northern Rúans (阮) lavishly displayed their clothes to dry,
all of them dazzling brocades and silks.
Xián (咸), using a pole, hung up a large cloth "ox-nose" (a type of short underwear) in his courtyard.
When someone expressed surprise at this,
he replied:
"I cannot avoid the common custom,
so I'll just do this!"
He successively served as Palace Attendant.
Shān Tāo (山濤) recommended Xián (咸) to take charge of official selection,
saying:
"Rú Xián (阮咸) is chaste and simple, with few desires.
He has deep insight into purity and impurity;
nothing can sway him.
If he were in the post of selecting officials,
he would certainly be unparalleled in his time."
Emperor Wǔ (武帝), however, considered Xián (咸) to be addicted to wine and frivolous,
and thus did not employ him.
Guō Yì (郭奕) of Tàiyuán (太原) was lofty, perceptive, and had a discerning mind,
well-known at the time,
and rarely praised anyone above himself.
Upon seeing Xián (咸), he was deeply impressed,
and could not help but sigh.
Yet, during his mother's mourning,
he indulged his feelings and transgressed ritual.
He had always favored his aunt's maidservant.
When his aunt was to return to her husband's home,
she initially said she would leave the maid,
but then took her along.
At that time, guests were present.
Upon hearing this, Xián (咸)
hastily borrowed a guest's horse to pursue the maid.
When he caught up,
he and the maid rode back together on the same horse.
Commentators greatly condemned this.
Xián (咸) had a subtle understanding of music and rhythm,
and was skilled at playing the pipa.
Although he did not engage in worldly affairs,
he only played string instruments, sang, and feasted with close friends and acquaintances.
He was particularly close with his cousin Xiū (脩),
and they always found joy in their shared understanding.
All the Rúans (阮) drank wine.
When Xián (咸) arrived,
the clansmen would gather.
They no longer used cups and goblets to serve wine;
instead, they filled a large basin with wine,
sat in a circle facing each other,
and drank in large drafts, taking turns.
Once, a group of pigs came to drink their wine.
Xián (咸) directly picked up the basin [after the pigs]
and continued drinking with everyone.
None of his cousins and brothers failed to act in a free and uninhibited manner,
but Rú Jié (阮籍) did not approve of it.
Xún Xù (荀勖) often discussed music and rhythm with Xián (咸),
believing himself to be far inferior to him.
He resented this,
and had him appointed as Administrator of Shǐpíng (始平) and sent out.
He died of old age.
He had two sons: Zhān (瞻) and Fú (孚).
Zhān (瞻), courtesy name Qiānlǐ (千里).
His nature was pure, tranquil, and had few desires,
finding contentment within himself.
He did not meticulously study books,
but silently grasped their essence.
When encountering a principle, he would debate it,
his words being insufficient, but his meaning abundant.
He was skilled at playing the qin.
People who heard of his skill
often came to request to listen,
and regardless of their status, whether noble or common, old or young,
he would play for them.
His spirit was tranquil and harmonious,
and he did not seem to be aware of the presence of others.
His maternal cousin Pān Yuè (潘岳) often asked him to play the qin,
sometimes all day and night,
and he never showed any displeasure.
Because of this, discerning people sighed at his serene indifference,
unconcerned with honor or disgrace.
His demeanor was strikingly clear.
He met Minister of Works Wáng Róng (王戎),
who asked him:
"The sages valued 'name and teaching' (mingjiao),
while Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊) clarified 'nature' (ziran).
Are their essences similar or different?"
Zhān (瞻) replied:
"Perhaps they are not different."
Wáng Róng (王戎) sighed in admiration for a long time,
and immediately ordered him to be appointed.
People at the time called him
"The Three-Word Secretary."
Grand Commandant Wáng Yǎn (王衍) also held him in high regard.
Zhān (瞻) once traveled with a group,
suffering greatly from heat and thirst.
There was a well at an inn,
and everyone rushed to it competitively.
Zhān (瞻) alone lingered behind,
waiting for all those who wished to drink to finish before approaching.
His humility and lack of competitiveness were just like this.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè 東海王越 was stationed in Xǔchāng 許昌.
He appointed Zhān 瞻 as Secretariat Army Advisor.
Zhān 瞻, Wáng Chéng 王承, Xiè Kūn 謝鯤, and Dèng Yōu 鄧攸 were all in Yuè's 越府 residence.
Yuè 越 wrote a letter to Zhān 瞻 and others, saying:
"According to the rites,
at the age of eight, one goes out to study under an external tutor,
indicating that at this age, instruction can begin to be added.
At ten years old, one is called a 'young scholar',
indicating that one can gradually begin to receive the teachings of the former kings.
However, what is learned intellectually is superficial,
while what is internalized and settled is profound.
Therefore, practicing proper conduct in leisure,
is not as good as observing dignified demeanor;
reciting ancient words,
is not as good as personally hearing authoritative pronouncements.
My son Pí 毗 lacks a virtuous and elegant disposition,
and has not heard the wind of morality.
I hope that you gentlemen will occasionally, in your leisure,
interact with him and instruct him."
During the Yǒngjiā 永嘉 era,
he served as an Attendant to the Crown Prince.
Zhān 瞻 had always upheld the theory that there are no ghosts.
No one could refute him,
and he often believed that this principle was sufficient to clarify the realms of the seen and unseen.
Suddenly, a guest announced his name and called upon Zhān 瞻.
After exchanging pleasantries,
they casually discussed profound philosophical principles.
The guest was very talented and articulate.
Zhān 瞻 spoke with him,
and after a long time, the conversation turned to matters of ghosts and spirits.
They argued back and forth with great difficulty.
The guest was finally cornered,
and then changed his expression, saying:
"Ghosts and spirits
have been commonly transmitted by saints and sages throughout history.
How can you alone say they do not exist!
Indeed, I am a ghost."
Thereupon, he transformed into a strange form,
and in a moment, vanished.
Zhān 瞻 was silent,
his face showing great distress.
More than a year later,
he died of illness in Cāngyuán 倉垣,
at the age of thirty.
Fú's 孚 courtesy name was Yáojí 遙集.
His mother
was a Hú 胡 maid.
When Fú 孚 was first born,
his aunt took a line from Wáng Yánshòu's 王延壽 "Rǔ Língguāng Diàn Fù" 魯靈光殿賦 (Rhapsody on the Spirit-Light Palace of Lǔ) which said:
"Hú Rén Yáojí Yú Shàng Yíng 胡人遙集於上楹" (The Hú 胡 people assemble afar at the upper eaves)
and used it for his courtesy name.
Initially appointed to the Grand Tutor's residence,
he was promoted to Clerk of the Cavalry.
He crossed the Yangtze River to escape the chaos.
Emperor Yuán 元 appointed him Army Advisor to the General of the Pacified East.
With disheveled hair, he drank wine and
did not trouble his mind with royal affairs.
At that time, the Emperor was using Shēn Hán 申韓 (Legalist principles) to save the world,
but Fú 孚 and his ilk were unable to abandon their ways.
Nevertheless,
he was not dismissed from his duties.
He was transferred to the position of Attendant Counselor to the Chancellor.
He indulged in drink all day long,
and was impeached by the supervising officials,
but the Emperor always tolerated him.
Lángyá Wáng Póu 琅邪王裒 became General of Chariots and Cavalry,
stationed in Guǎnglíng 廣陵.
He highly selected his staff,
and appointed Fú 孚 as Chief Clerk.
The Emperor said to him:
"Since you are in charge of the military headquarters,
and there are many matters concerning the garrisons and borders,
you should moderate your drinking."
Fú 孚 replied:
"Your Majesty does not consider your servant untalented,
and entrusts him with the heavy responsibility of military affairs.
Your servant diligently attends to his duties,
and dares not speak,
but I secretly believe that with the present king residing in the town,
his prestige is formidable,
the imperial benevolence extends afar,
the bandits have retreated,
the ominous atmosphere has cleared,
and the sun and moon shine brightly on their own.
How can your servant keep a flickering lamp burning?
I should simply sit with folded hands, whistle, and recite poetry, enjoying these times."
He was promoted to Imperial Household Secretary and Palace Attendant.
He once exchanged his golden sable (hat ornament) for wine,
and was again impeached by the supervising officials,
but the Emperor pardoned him.
He was transferred to Crown Prince's Household Commander, Left Guard Commander,
and concurrently held the position of Commander of Tunqi (Cavalry stationed near the capital).
When Emperor Míng 明 ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant.
He participated in the pacification of Wáng Dūn 王敦,
and was granted the title of Marquis of Nán'ān 南安 County.
He was transferred to Minister of Personnel,
and concurrently held the position of Tutor to the Prince of Dōnghǎi 東海.
He pleaded illness and did not accept the appointment.
An imperial edict ordered that he be appointed at home,
but Shàngshū Lìng Xī Jiàn 尚書令郗鑒 considered it improper.
The Emperor said:
"Appointing him at home is indeed not ideal,
but otherwise, his talent would be wasted."
When the Emperor's illness became critical,
Wēn Jiǎo 溫嶠 entered to receive the dying instructions,
and passed by Fú 孚,
inviting him to go together.
Upon ascending the carriage,
he then informed him:
"The Emperor's illness has become critical.
The region east of the Yangtze is weak and precarious,
and truly needs the support of many wise men
to collectively manage the affairs of the world.
You are the one to whom the present age looks up.
Now I wish to ask you to join me in receiving the imperial entrustment."
Fú 孚 did not reply,
and insisted on getting out of the carriage.
Jiǎo 嶠 did not permit it.
When they were nearly at the palace gate,
he told Jiǎo 嶠 that he had an urgent need inside,
asked to temporarily alight,
and then walked home.
Initially,
Zǔ Yuē 祖約 was fond of wealth,
and Fú 孚 was fond of clogs.
Both were burdens, but it was not yet clear whose fault was greater.
Someone visited Yuē 约,
and saw him sorting out his valuables.
When the guest arrived,
he couldn't put everything away,
leaving two small baskets,
which he placed behind his back,
leaning his body to shield them,
his mind unsettled.
Someone else visited Ruǎn 阮,
and saw him personally waxing his clogs.
He then sighed to himself, saying:
"I wonder how many pairs of clogs I will wear in my lifetime!"
His expression was very relaxed and free.
At this point, the winner and loser were finally distinguished.
In the beginning of the Xiánhé 咸和 era,
he was appointed Governor of Dānyáng 丹楊.
At that time, the Empress Dowager was regent,
and governance came from her maternal relatives.
Fú 孚 said to his close associates:
"Although the state in Jiangdong 江東 has been established for generations,
the number of years is actually short.
The young ruler faces difficult times,
and the cycle has reached a critical juncture.
Moreover, Yǔ Liàng 庾亮 is young,
and his virtue and trustworthiness have not yet gained full confidence.
In my opinion,
this will portend chaos."
It so happened that the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu 廣州, Liú Yǐ 劉顗, died,
so he earnestly sought an external posting.
Wáng Dǎo 王導 and others, considering Fú 孚 to be unrestrained
and not suitable for the capital governorship,

appointed him Inspector-General of the Military Affairs of Jiāo, Guǎng, and Níng Provinces (Jiāozhōu 交州, Guǎngzhōu 廣州, Níngzhōu 寧州), General Who Guards the South, concurrently Colonel Who Pacifies Yuè (Yuè 越), Inspector of Guǎngzhōu 廣州, and granted him a staff of authority.
He died before reaching his post,
at the age of forty-nine.
Soon after, Sū Jùn 蘇峻 rebelled,
and those who knew the situation considered Fú 孚 to have foreseen it.
He had no son;
his grand-nephew Guǎng Sī 廣嗣 inherited.
Xīu's 修
courtesy name was Xuānzǐ 宣子.
He was fond of the Yì Jīng 易經 (Book of Changes) and Lǎozi 老子,
and excelled at "pure talk".
There was once a discussion about the existence of ghosts and spirits,
and everyone believed that there were ghosts when people died.
Xīu 修 alone believed there were none,
saying:
"Those who claim to see ghosts today say they are wearing the clothes they wore when alive.
If people have ghosts when they die,
do clothes also have ghosts?"
The debaters were convinced.
Later, he went to cut down a communal shrine tree.
Someone tried to stop him,
but Xīu 修 said:
"If the shrine is the tree,
then cutting down the tree moves the shrine;
if the tree is the shrine,
then cutting down the tree destroys the shrine."
He was simple and unrestrained
and paid no attention to worldly affairs.
He utterly disliked meeting common people;
if he encountered them, he would immediately leave.
When his mind was contemplating something,
he would impulsively lift his robe,
regardless of morning or evening.
Sometimes, he would be silent,
but just happily facing each other.
He often walked,
with a hundred coins hanging from the head of his staff.
When he reached a tavern,
he would indulge in solitary drinking.
Though the wealthy and powerful of his time he would not condescend to notice,
and his family had no store of grain,
he was content.
With his brothers and like-minded friends,
he often found contentment among the forests and hills.
Wáng Yǎn (王衍), then a master of discourse,
believed his discussions on the Yì (易) were nearly exhaustive,
yet there were still points he couldn't fully comprehend.
No matter how he researched them, he could never understand,
and he often said:
"I wonder if after I am gone, there will be anyone who can explain these things."
Wáng Yǎn's (王衍) cousin Dūn (敦) said to Yǎn (衍):
"Ruǎn Xuānzi (阮宣子) is someone you can discuss with."
Yǎn (衍) said:
"I have also heard of him,
but I don't know what his subtle insights are really like!"
When he conversed with Xiū (脩),
the words were few but the meaning profound,
and Yǎn (衍) then marveled and submitted.
Zhāng Wěi (張偉) from Liángguó (梁國) had unusual aspirations;
he lived in seclusion as a butcher and fisherman.
Xiū (脩) admired his talent and beauty,
but knew he was not genuine.
Wěi (偉) later became a Huángmén Láng (黃門郎) and Chénliú Nèi Shǐ (陳留內史),
and indeed suffered setbacks due to worldly affairs.
Xiū (脩) lived in poverty;
at over forty years old, he still had no wife.
Wáng Dūn (王敦) and others collected money for his marriage.
They were all famous scholars,
and those who admired him at the time sought to contribute money but were not allowed.
Xiū's (脩) writings were very few.
He once wrote an encomium on the Great Peng:
"Vast, vast is the Great Peng,
born from the Northern Ocean.
Borrowing the essence of spiritual scales,
it is created through divine transformation.
Its wings like clouds,
its form like mountains.
Carried by the ocean's currents and the water's impact,
it soars upwards on a whirlwind.
Swiftly it rises through the layers,
bearing the vast sky on its back.
Its ambition encompasses heaven and earth,
disdaining the court of Táng (唐).
The sparrows laugh in仰,
scorned by the tiny quail.
Transcending the world, it flies high,
none know its true nature."
Wáng Dūn (王敦) was then Hónglú Qīng (鴻臚卿)
and said to Xiū (脩):
"You are always without food.
Hónglú Céng (鴻臚丞) has a bit of salary;
can you do it?"
Xiū (脩) said:
"It's also acceptable!"
So he took the post.
He then became Tàifù Háng Cānjūn (太傅行參軍) and Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬).
Fleeing the chaos, he traveled south
to Xīyáng Qīsī Xiàn (西陽期思縣),
where he was killed by bandits.
He was forty-two years old at the time.
Fàng (放) had the courtesy name Sīdù (思度).
His grandfather, Lüè (略),
was Qíjùn Tàishǒu (齊郡太守).
His father, Yǐ (顗),
was Huáinán Nèi Shǐ (淮南內史).
Fàng (放), when young, was as famous as Fú (孚).
During the Zhōngxīng (中興) era,
he was appointed Tàixué Bóshì (太學博士), Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人), and Shùzǐ (庶子).
At that time, although military campaigns were frequent,
Fàng (放), serving the crown prince,
always discussed Lǎo Zhuāng (老莊)
and never military or state affairs.
Emperor Míng (明帝) cherished him greatly.
He was transferred to Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
then promoted to Lìbù Láng (吏部郎).
In his post of personnel administration,
he achieved considerable reputation.
At that time, Emperor Chéng (成帝) was young,
and the Yǔ (庾) clan held power.
Fàng (放) requested to be sent to Jiāozhōu (交州),
so he was appointed Jiān Jiāozhōu Jūnjì (監交州軍事), Yángwēi Jiāngjūn (揚威將軍), and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (交州刺史).
When he reached Níngpǔ (寧浦),
he met Táo Kǎn's (陶侃) general Gāo Bǎo (高寶), who was returning from Jiāozhōu (交州) after pacifying Liáng Shuò (梁碩).
Fàng (放) prepared a feast and invited Bǎo (寶),
then ambushed and killed him.
Bǎo's (寶) forces attacked Fàng (放),
who was defeated and fled.
He took refuge in Jiǎnyáng Chéng (簡陽城)
and escaped.
A short while after arriving in the province,
he suddenly developed an insatiable thirst
and saw Bǎo's (寶) ghost haunting him.
He then died.
The imperial court deeply mourned his loss.
He was forty-four years old.
He was posthumously granted the title Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Fàng (放) had always been famous,
and his nature was pure and frugal;
he did not manage property.
Even as Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
he could not avoid hunger and cold.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮), recognizing him as a famous scholar,
often provided him with clothing and food.
His son, Xīzhī (晞之),
was Nándùn Tàishǒu (南頓太守).
Yù (裕) had the courtesy name Sīkuàng (思曠).
He was not as broad-minded as Fàng (放),
but was known for his virtue and achievements.
In his early twenties, he was appointed Tàizǎi Yuàn (太宰掾).
The Grand General Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed him as Zhǔbù (主簿),
and he was greatly appreciated.
Yù (裕) knew that Dūn (敦) had disloyal intentions,
so he spent all day drinking wine,
neglecting his duties due to alcohol.
Dūn (敦) considered Yù (裕) not a truly capable person of the age,
but merely someone with an empty reputation,
so he sent him out as Lìyáng Lìng (溧陽令).
He was again dismissed from office due to official matters.
Because of this, he managed to avoid Dūn's (敦) rebellion,
and commentators valued him for this.
In the early Xiánhé (咸和) era,
he was appointed Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
At that time, after the disturbances,
both public and private affairs were in disarray.
Yù (裕) then resigned his post and returned home,
residing in Kuàijī Shàn Xiàn (會稽剡縣).
Sìtú (司徒) Wáng Dǎo (王導) invited him to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎),
but he firmly declined.
The imperial court was about to summon him,
and Yù (裕), knowing he could not refuse,
requested to be Wáng Shū's (王舒) Fǔjūn Chángshǐ (撫軍長史).
After Shū (舒) died,
he was appointed Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
but did not take the post.
He was then appointed Línhǎi Tàishǒu (臨海太守) at home,
but resigned after a short time.
Sīkōng (司空) Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) invited him to be Chángshǐ (長史),
and an imperial edict summoned him as Mìshū Jiān (祕書監),
but he declined all due to illness.
He was again appointed Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (東陽太守).
Soon after, he was summoned as Shìzhōng (侍中),
but did not accept.
He returned to Shàn Shān (剡山),
with the aspiration of living in seclusion.
Someone asked Wáng Xīzhī (王羲之) about him,
and Xīzhī (羲之) said:
"This gentleman is now unperturbed by favor or disgrace.
Even the reclusive ancients,
how could they surpass this!"
People said that
Yù's (裕) moral fortitude was not equal to Yìshǎo (逸少),
his simplicity and elegance not equal to Zhēncháng (真長),
his brilliance not equal to Zhòngzǔ (仲祖),
and his profound thought not equal to Yīn Hào (殷浩),
yet he possessed the virtues of all these individuals.
When Emperor Chéng (成帝) died,
Yù (裕) attended the imperial funeral,
and returned immediately after the rites were completed.
Others pursued him,
and Yù (裕) also knew that the current trend was to follow him,
but he quickly left,
reaching Fāngshān (方山) before they could catch him.
Liú Tán (劉惔) sighed and said:
"When I go east,
I will just dock below Ānshí Zhǔ (安石渚),
and not dare to approach Sīkuàng's (思曠) side again."
Yù though not extensively learned,
his debates were very profound.
Once, he asked Xiè Wàn, saying:
"I haven't seen the 'Four Theories,'
could you explain them to me?"
After Wàn had finished his explanation,
Yù considered Fù Gǔ's theory superior.
Thereupon, he composed several hundred words,
with subtle and penetrating arguments,
which all who heard praised and savored.
Yù often thought that people do not need extensive learning;
they should primarily prioritize propriety and deference.
Therefore, he remained quiet all day,
not undertaking any studies or compilations,
yet people naturally honored him.
When he was in Shàn, he once had a fine carriage,
and he lent it to everyone who asked.
There was a person burying his mother,
who wished to borrow it but dared not ask.
Later, Yù heard of it,
and sighed, saying:
"I have a carriage, but I make people afraid to borrow it.
What is the point of having a carriage then?"
So he ordered it to be burned.
After staying in Dōngshān for a long time,
he was again summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently Lǐng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Soon after, he was again appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently Lǐng Lángxié Wáng Shī.
For a year, he was urged and pressed,
but achieved nothing.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Zhōu Mǐn impeached Yù and Xiè Ān for repeatedly disobeying imperial edicts for years,
and suggested they both deserved punishment,
to be banished for life,
but an imperial decree pardoned them.
Someone asked Yù, saying:
"You have repeatedly declined imperial summons,
yet you governed two commanderies.
Why is that?"
Yù replied:
"Although I repeatedly declined royal mandates,
I dared not do so out of ambition for fame.
From my youth, I had no desire for officialdom,
and I am moreover clumsy in human affairs.
Since I cannot farm and support myself,
I must rely on something;
thus, I reluctantly served in two commanderies.
It was not to display my abilities,
but for my personal livelihood, that is all."
He died at the age of sixty-two.
He had three sons: Yōng, Níng, Pǔ.
Yōng
died young.
Níng was
Póyáng Tàishǒu.
Pǔ was
Piàojí Zīyì Cānjūn.
Yōng's son Xīnzhī was
Zhōnglǐngjūn.
Níng's son Tiǎn was
Mìshūjiān.
Tiǎn's younger brother Wànlíng and Xīnzhī's son Mízhī
both held prominent positions during the Yuánxī reign.
Jī Kāng
Jī Kāng, courtesy name Shúyè,
was a native of Zhì, Qiáoguó.
His ancestors were surnamed Xī,
from Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
To avoid animosity,
they relocated there.
Zhì has Jī Mountain,
and their family lived by its side,
thus adopting the surname.
His elder brother, Xǐ,
had talent for the era,
and served successively as Tàipú and Zōngzhèng.
Kāng was orphaned early,
possessed extraordinary talent,
far surpassing others and standing out from the crowd.
He was seven feet eight inches tall,
had beautiful speech and temperament,
and a natural, unadorned physique,
not decorating himself.
People considered him to have dragon-like brilliance and phoenix-like grace,
a natural endowment.
He was tranquil and quiet, with few desires,
tolerant of faults and concealing flaws,
broad-minded and generous.
His learning was not acquired from a teacher,
but through extensive reading, there was nothing he did not comprehensively understand.
He particularly loved Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
He married into the royal family of Wèi,
and was appointed Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
He regularly practiced the cultivation of nature and the ingestion of elixirs,
playing the qín and chanting poetry,
content in his heart.
He believed that immortals are endowed by nature,
not achieved through accumulated learning.
As for achieving proper guidance and nourishment,
then figures like Ānqí and Péngzǔ could be emulated.
Thus, he wrote "On Nourishing Life."
He also believed that a gentleman has no self-interest,
and his treatise states:
"Indeed, one who is called a gentleman
does not dwell on right and wrong in his heart,
and his actions do not deviate from the Dao.
How can this be explained?
One whose vital energy is calm and spirit empty
does not harbor pride or ambition in his heart.
One whose body is clear and mind enlightened
is not bound by desires in his emotions.
When pride and ambition are not present in the heart,
one can transcend conventional teachings and act in accordance with nature.
When emotions are not bound by desires,
one can discern the noble and the humble and comprehend the nature of things.
When the nature of things is smoothly understood,
then the Great Dao is not violated.
When one transcends conventional names and acts according to one's heart,
then there is no dwelling on right or wrong.
Therefore, when speaking of a gentleman, not dwelling is taken as primary,
and understanding things is considered admirable.
When speaking of a petty person, concealing emotions is deemed wrong,
and violating the Dao is considered a defect.
Why is this?
Concealing emotions and being stingy are the greatest evils of a petty person.
Having an empty mind and not dwelling on things are the earnest practices of a gentleman.
Therefore, the Great Dao says:
'When I have no self,
what worries do I have?'
Not valuing life as precious
is superior to valuing life.
From this perspective,
the mind of a perfect person
certainly does not dwell on anything.
Therefore it is said:
'A gentleman practices the Dao,
forgetting his own self.' This statement is true.
A gentleman's virtuous conduct
does not examine whether it is within limits before acting.
Acting spontaneously without evil
does not deliberate on good before being correct.
Manifesting emotions without dwelling
does not discuss what is right before acting.
Therefore, he proudly forgets virtue,
and virtue aligns with measure.
He spontaneously acts according to his heart,
and his heart meets with goodness.
He acts indifferently without dwelling,
and his actions are in accord with rightness."
Such is the general idea.
Indeed, the sentiments he harbored
made it difficult to find lofty companions,
and he often thought of the skilled artisan of Yǐng.
Those with whom he shared a spiritual connection were only Ruǎn Jí of Chénliú and Shān Tāo of Hénèi.
Those who belonged to their circle were Xiàng Xiù of Hénèi, Liú Líng of Pèiguó, Jí's nephew Xián, and Wáng Róng of Lángxié.
Thus, they formed the "Bamboo Grove Gathering,"
which the world called
"The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove."
Róng himself said that he lived with Kāng in Shānyáng for twenty years,
and never once saw him express joy or anger.
Kāng once gathered herbs and roamed in the mountains and marshes.
When he found himself deeply absorbed,
he would suddenly forget to return.
At that time, woodcutters and grass-gatherers encountered him,
and all considered him a divine being.
When he went to Jí Jùn in the mountains and saw Sūn Dēng,
Kāng then joined him in his wanderings.
Dēng was silent and self-contained,
speaking nothing.
As Kāng was about to leave,
Dēng said:
"Your nature is fiery and your talent outstanding,
how can you escape misfortune?"
Kāng also met Wáng Liè,
and together they entered the mountains.
Liè once obtained stone marrow like candy;
he immediately ate half himself
and gave the other half to Kāng.
Both portions solidified into stone.
Also, in a stone chamber, he saw a roll of silk books;
he quickly called Kāng to retrieve it,
but it was immediately no longer visible.
Liè then sighed, saying:
"Shúyè's aspirations are extraordinary, yet he constantly encounters no such fortune.
It is fate!"
His spiritual perceptions were such that
he always met with such reclusive and extraordinary things.
When Shān Tāo was about to leave his official post
as a selector, he recommended Kāng to take his place.
Kāng then wrote a letter to Tāo announcing the severance of their friendship,
saying: "I heard that you wish to replace yourself with me.
Although the matter did not proceed,
I know you still do not understand.
I fear that you, like the chef,
would be ashamed of carving alone,
and would drag a corpse
Wishing you self-reliance,
therefore I lay before you what is permissible and what is not.
Lǎozǐ, Zhuāngzhōu,
were my teachers,
who personally held humble positions;
Liǔxiàhuì, Dōngfāngshuò,
were men of understanding,
who found peace in lowly ranks.
How dare I belittle
them!
Moreover, Zhòngní practiced universal love,
and was not ashamed to hold a whip;
Zǐwén had no desire for the rank of minister or prime minister,
yet he thrice served as Lìngyǐn;
this indeed is the gentleman's intention to benefit the world.
It is said that when successful, one can universally benefit without changing (one's principles),
and when poor, one is content and without vexation.
Viewing it this way,
thus one knows that Yáo Shùn dwelling in the world,
Xǔ Yóu residing in cliffs,
Zǐ
fáng assisting the Hàn,
Jiēyú singing on his travels,
their principles are one.
Looking up to these several gentlemen,
it can be said that they were able to fulfill their ambitions.
Therefore, a gentleman's hundred actions,
though by different paths,
reach the same goal;
they act according to their nature,
each attaching to what gives them peace.
Thus there is
"to remain in court without leaving,
and to enter the mountains and forests without returning"
as a doctrine.
Moreover, the character of Yánlíng and Gāo Zǐzāng,
Chángqīng's admiration for Xiāngrú's integrity,
the aspirations they embraced,
could also not be taken away.
Each time I read the biographies of Shàng Zǐpíng and Tái Xiàowēi,
I am deeply moved to admire them,
and imagine their characters.
Furthermore, being orphaned young,
my mother and elder brother were arrogant and willful,
I did not delve into classical studies,
and then read Lǎo Zhuāng,
further increasing my unrestrained nature,
thus causing my desire for glorious advancement to daily decline,
and my inclination for freedom and ease to become more steadfast.
Ruǎn Sìzōng never spoke of others' faults,
I always
took him as my teacher,
but have yet to reach his level.
His nature surpassed others,
harmless to all things,
only his drinking was somewhat excessive;
yet he was admonished by those who upheld ritual law,
who hated him as an
enemy,
fortunately, he was preserved by the Dàjiāngjūn.
I, with talents inferior to Sìzōng,
and with shortcomings of negligence and laxity;
moreover, not understanding human affairs,
ignorant of opportune
moments;
without Wànshí's caution,
but with the burden of wanting to exhaust everything;
having been involved in affairs for a long time,
faults and disputes arise daily,
even if I wish to be without trouble,
how can it be achieved!
I also heard the parting words of a Daoist priest,
that consuming Atractylodes and Solomon's Seal
grants long life,
and I deeply believe it.
Wandering in mountains and marshes,
observing fish and birds,
my heart greatly rejoices in it.
Once
I serve as an official,
these matters would be abandoned,
how can I give up what I enjoy,
and follow what I fear!
Indeed, when people know each other,
it is important to recognize their nature,
and thereby help them.
Yǔ did not force Bóchéng Zǐgāo,
thus preserving his integrity;
Zhòngní did not lend his carriage canopy to
Zǐxià,
thus protecting him from showing his weakness.
Recently, Zhūgě Kǒngmíng did not force Yuánzhí to enter Shǔ,
Huá Zǐyú did not compel Yòu'ān to become a minister or prime minister,
these can be called those who can
remain consistent from beginning to end,
and truly understand each other.
I have already thoroughly divined my own fate;
if my path is exhausted and my journey ended, then so be it.
Your Excellency need not cause me to be unjustly left to perish in a ditch.
I have recently lost the joy of my mother and elder brother,
and my heart is constantly grieved.
My daughter is thirteen,
my son eight years old,
not yet grown,
moreover, often ill;
considering this sorrowful
situation,
how can it be expressed.
Now I only wish to guard my humble lane,
teach and raise my children and grandchildren,
occasionally meet with relatives and old friends,
discuss my life,
with a cup of turbid wine,
play
a piece on the qín;
my ambitions would then be complete.
How could I see a Huángmén and claim integrity!
If you are urgently seeking to jointly ascend the royal path,
hoping to bring me to it,
occasionally enjoying myself would be fine,
but if
forced for a single day,
I will surely go mad.
Unless it is a mortal enemy,
it would not come to this.
Having thus explained to Your Excellency,
I also take this as my farewell.
Once this letter is sent,
I know I cannot be constrained or bent.
His nature was exceptionally skillful and he loved forging.
There was a very luxuriant willow tree in his residence,
so he diverted water to surround it,
and every summer month,
he resided under it to forge.
Lǚ Ān of Dōngpíng admired Kāng's lofty spirit;
whenever he thought of him,
he would immediately order his carriage for a thousand-lǐ journey.
Kāng befriended and treated him well.
Later, Ān was falsely accused by his elder brother,
and imprisoned for the matter.
His testimony implicated Kāng,
and consequently Kāng was also arrested.
Kāng was by nature cautious in his words and actions,
but once imprisoned,
he composed a "Poem of Hidden Indignation,"
which says: Alas, my meager fortune,
young I encountered misfortune,
grieved and desolate, lacking understanding,
even while in swaddling clothes.
My mother and elder brother raised me,
with kindness but no severity;
relying on their love, I acted wantonly,
unreprimanded
and untaught.
Upon reaching adulthood,
I relied on favor and indulged myself,
raising my heart to emulate the ancients,
following my own preferences.
I entrusted my affections to Zhuāng Lǎo,
despising possessions and valuing myself,
my will set on preserving simplicity,
nurturing
my natural self and preserving my true nature.
I say, I am not clever,
loving good but blinding people,
like Zǐyù's defeat,
my faults repeatedly accumulate like dust.
Great men are tolerant and broad-minded,
concealing faults and enduring shame.
People are often perverse,
and government
is not by oneself.
Only this narrow heart of mine,
openly reveals good and bad;
I feel enlightened and ponder my faults,
painfully as if suffering from a fresh wound.
Wishing to reduce my faults,
slander and criticism surge,
my nature does not harm others,
yet frequently causes resentment and hatred.
Formerly I was ashamed before Liǔhuì,
now I am ashamed before Sūn Dēng,
inwardly I have betrayed my long-held aspirations,
outwardly I am ashamed before good friends.
I look up to and admire Yán Zhèng,
delighting in the Dao and quiet dwelling,
unconcerned
with the world,
my spirit calm and tranquil.
Alas, I am not virtuous,
entangled in many troubles.
Not descended from heaven,
but truly due to my stubbornness and heedlessness,
my principles failed and troubles accumulated,
finally leading to prison.
Answering crude interrogations,
imprisoned
This confinement,
in truth, is a shameful grievance.
The times are not with me.
Though my righteousness is straight,
my spirit is humiliated, my will frustrated.
Washing myself in the blue waves,
how could it possibly mend things?
Harmonious, chirping wild geese,
stretch their wings and swim north.
They move with the seasons,
finding joy and forgetting sorrow.
Alas, my indignation and sighs,
I can find no one to match them.
Things go against my wishes,
encountering this prolonged stay.
Success and failure are
destined,
so what more could I seek? The ancients had a saying:
"The good should not seek fame."
Serving the times with respectful silence,
no blame or regret will arise.
Wànshí Zhōushèn
safeguarded his family and preserved his glory.
Worldly affairs are in a muddle,
merely
disturbing my emotions.
Joy and peace must be forewarned against,
then will come lasting benefit and uprightness.
Brilliant, glowing divine ganoderma,
blooms three times a year;
what then am I doing,
having aspirations but not achieving them?
Punished by difficulty, I contemplate recovery,
my heart feeling internal guilt.
I shall strive for the future,
without fragrance or stench.
Picking vetch in the mountain valley,
letting down my hair in the rocky grotto,
forever whistling and sighing,
I shall nourish my spirit and prolong my life.
Initially,
Jī Kāng was poor.
He once forged iron with Xiàng Xiù beneath a great tree,
to support themselves.
Zhōng Huì of Yǐngchuān,
a noble young master,
was refined and talented in debate,
so he went to visit them.
Jī Kāng did not treat him with ceremony,
and continued forging without stopping.
After a long time, Zhōng Huì left.
Jī Kāng said to him:
"What did you hear that made you come? What did you see that made you leave?"
Zhōng Huì said:
"I came having heard what I heard,
and left having seen what I saw."
Zhōng Huì resented him for this.
When the time came,
he spoke to Emperor Wén, saying:
"Jī Kāng
is a crouching dragon;
he cannot be aroused.
Your Majesty should not worry about the world,
but rather be concerned about Jī Kāng."
Then he slandered,
"Jī Kāng wished to assist Wúqiū Jiǎn,
but fortunately Shān Tāo did not listen.
Formerly, Qí executed Huà Shì,
and Lǔ executed Shǎozhèng Mǎo,
truly because they harmed the times and corrupted teachings,
and thus the sages removed them.
Jī Kāng, Ān, and others have wanton discussions,
slandering and destroying the canons and directives,
which should not be tolerated by emperors and kings.
It is fitting to take advantage of this opportune moment to eliminate them,
in order to purify the customs."
The Emperor, having taken a liking to and trusted Zhōng Huì,
then had them both harmed.
When Jī Kāng was about to be executed at the Eastern Marketplace,
three thousand imperial students requested to become his disciples,
but it was not permitted.
Jī Kāng looked at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a qín and played it,
saying:
"In the past, Yuán Xiàoní once learned Guǎnglíng Sàn from me,
but I always guarded it jealously.
Guǎnglíng Sàn is now lost forever!"
He was forty years old at the time.
No scholar within the four seas
was not pained by this.
The Emperor soon realized his mistake and regretted it.
Initially,
Jī Kāng once traveled west of Luò,
and at dusk, lodged at Huáyáng Tíng.
He took out his qín and played.
In the middle of the night,
a guest suddenly visited him,
claiming to be an ancient person.
He discussed music theory with Jī Kāng,
his words clear and articulate.
Then he asked for the qín and played,
performing Guǎnglíng Sàn.
Its melody was unparalleled.
He then imparted it to Jī Kāng,
and swore him not to transmit it to others,
nor to reveal his surname or given name.
Jī Kāng was skilled in discussing principles,
and also capable of writing essays.
His lofty sentiments and profound interests
were naturally abstruse and remote.
He compiled biographies and eulogies for eminent scholars from ancient times,
wishing to befriend these people across a thousand years.
He also composed Tàishī Zhēn,
which was sufficient to elucidate the way of emperors and kings.
He further wrote Shēng Wú Āi Lè Lùn,
which was very well-reasoned.
His son Sháo
has a separate biography.
Xiàng Xiù
Xiàng Xiù, courtesy name Zǐqī,
was a native of Huái in Hénèi.
He was clear-minded and had far-reaching insight,
and in his youth was known by Shān Tāo.
He had a deep fondness for the studies of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
Zhuāng Zhōu wrote dozens of chapters, both inner and outer.
Though talented scholars of successive generations had read them,
none could adequately discuss their main principles.
Xiàng Xiù then provided reclusive interpretations for them,
illuminating their wondrous charm
and reviving the Xuan school of thought.
Those who read them spontaneously achieved profound understanding,
all feeling content for a time.
During the reign of Emperor Huì,
Guō Xiàng further expounded upon and expanded them,
and the traces of Confucianism and Mohism were despised,
while the words of Daoism consequently flourished.
Initially,
Xiàng Xiù wanted to annotate them,
but Jī Kāng said:
"Does this book really need annotations?
It just gets in the way of people enjoying themselves."
When it was finished,
he showed it to Jī Kāng, saying:
"Is it much better now?"
He also debated with Jī Kāng on nourishing life,
exchanging difficult arguments back and forth,
probably wanting to provoke Jī Kāng's lofty spirit.
Jī Kāng was skilled in forging,
and Xiàng Xiù assisted him.
They faced each other with joy,
as if no one else was present.
They also gardened together with Lǚ Ān in Shānyáng.
After Jī Kāng was executed,
Xiàng Xiù responded to his local commandery's summons and went to Luòyáng.
Emperor Wén asked:
"I hear you have the ambition of Jī Shān.
Why are you here?"
Xiàng Xiù said:
"I believe Cháo Fù and Xǔyóu were rigid and aloof individuals,
who did not comprehend the heart of Yáo,
and are hardly worthy of much admiration."
The Emperor was very pleased.
Xiàng Xiù then served in office from this point on.
He composed Sī Jiù Fù, which says: "Jī Kāng, Lǚ Ān, and I lived in close proximity.
They both possessed unconstrained talent.
Jī Kāng's intentions were far-reaching and aloof,
Lǚ Ān's mind was expansive and unrestrained.
Afterward, they were both
punished by the law due to affairs.
Jī Kāng was widely skilled in various arts;
he was especially adept at string and bamboo instruments.
When he was about to meet his fate,
he looked at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a qín, and played it.
I was about to travel west,
passing by their old dwelling.
At that time, the sun was setting over Yú Quán,
and the cold ice felt desolate.
A neighbor was playing the flute,
its sound clear and bright.
I recalled the past joys
of our gatherings,
and was moved by the music to sigh.
Therefore, I composed this fu, which says: About to travel to the distant capital,
I then turned around and journeyed north.
Crossing the Yellow River by boat,
I passed by the old dwellings of Shānyáng.
Gazing at the desolate
and withered wild plains,
I rested my carriage at the city corner.
Treading upon the remnants of the two men,
I passed through empty alleys and vacant homes.
Sighing over the millets of sorrow for Zhōu,
I grieved for the ripening wheat in
Yīnxū.
Alas, I recall the past to contemplate the present,
my heart lingers and hesitates.
The buildings remain, undestroyed,
but where have the forms and spirits gone?
In former times, when Lǐ Sī
was sentenced to punishment,
he sighed for the yellow dog and moaned at length.
Mourning Jī Shēng's eternal farewell,
he looked at the sun's shadow and played the qín.
Entrusting his fate to understanding,
he committed his remaining life
to the shortest moments.
Listening to the passionate sound of the flute,
the wondrous sound ceased and then was sought again.
Standing by, ready to depart,
I therefore take up the brush to express my heart.
Later, he served as Sànqí Shìláng,
then transferred to Huángmén Shìláng and Sànqí Chángshì.
In court, he held no real office,
merely occupying a position.
He died in office.
He had two sons: Chún and Tì.
Liú Líng
Liú Líng, courtesy name Bólún,
was a native of Pèiguó.
He was six chǐ tall,
and his appearance was very uncomely.
He indulged his emotions and gave free rein to his will,
always taking the minimization of the universe and the equalization of all things as his mindset.
He was tranquil, silent, and spoke little,
and did not frivolously engage in social interactions.
When he met Ruǎn Jí and Jī Kāng,
he was joyfully enlightened in spirit
and walked hand-in-hand with them into the forest.
From the outset, he did not care about the presence or absence of family property.
He often rode in a deer cart,
carrying a pot of wine,
and made someone follow him with a spade,
saying:
"When I die, just bury me."
Such was his disregard for his physical form.
Once, being extremely thirsty,
he asked his wife for wine.
His wife poured out the wine and broke the vessels,
advising him tearfully:
"Your drinking is excessive,
it is not the way of nourishing life.
You must cut it off."
Líng said:
"Good!
I cannot restrain myself.
I can only vow before the spirits.
You may prepare wine and meat then."
His wife complied.
Líng knelt and prayed:
"Heaven gave birth to Liú Líng,
whose name is made by wine.
One drink, one hú;
five dǒu to cure the hangover.
The words of wife and child
must not be heeded."
He then drank the wine and ate the meat,
and promptly became drunk again.
Once, while drunk, he offended a commoner.
The man rolled up his sleeves and raised his fist to confront him.
Líng slowly said:
"A chicken rib is not enough to withstand an honorable fist."
The man laughed and stopped.
Although Líng was bewildered, reckless, and uninhibited,
his quick wit was never amiss.
He never devoted his attention to literature,
only composing one essay, the Jiǔdé Sòng.
Its words are:
"There is a great gentleman,
who takes heaven and earth as one morning,
ten thousand ages as a moment,
the sun and moon as gates and windows,
the eight wildernesses as his courtyard and streets.
His travels leave no tracks,
his dwelling has no rooms,
he makes the sky his canopy and the earth his mat,
following his desires wherever they lead.
When he rests, he holds a zhi and grasps a gu;
when he moves, he carries a kē and lifts a hú.
He only cares for wine,
how could he know anything else?
There are noble young lords and gentry scholars,
who, hearing of my reputation,
discuss my ways.
Then they roll up their sleeves and pull back their collars,
staring angrily and gnashing their teeth,
expounding on rites and laws,
with rights and wrongs swarming forth.
At this, the gentleman simply holds an yīng and takes from the trough,
sips from a cup and rinses with fermented liquor,
flaring his beard and sitting with splayed legs,
pillowing on yeast and resting on dregs.
Without thought or worry,
his joy is abundant.
Suddenly he is drunk,
then he wakes up abruptly.
Listening quietly, he hears no sound of thunder;
looking intently, he sees no form of Tài Shān.
He feels not the cold and heat pressing against his skin,
nor the emotions of gain and desire.
Looking down at all things,
they are in turmoil like duckweed floating on rivers and seas.
Two scoundrels attend him,
like a sphecid wasp and its caterpillar."
He once served as Jiànwēi Cānjūn.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ era, when he presented a policy,
he strongly advocated for the transformation through non-action.
His contemporaries were all promoted to high ranks,
but Líng alone was dismissed as useless.
He eventually died of old age.
Xiè Kūn
Xiè Kūn, courtesy name Yòuyú,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénguó.
His grandfather, Zǎn,
was Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng.
His father, Héng,
was renowned for his Confucian simplicity,
and served as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Kūn was famous in his youth,
being open and discerning with high insight.
He did not concern himself with dignified bearing,
was fond of Lǎo-Yì,
and was skilled at singing and playing the qín.
Wáng Yǎn and Jī Shào both regarded him as extraordinary.
During the Yǒngxīng era,
Chángshā Wáng Yì became regent.
At that time, someone who disliked Kūn
reported that he was about to flee.
Yì wanted to flog him.
Kūn took off his clothes and presented himself for punishment,
showing no sign of resentment.
After he was released,
he also showed no sign of joy.
The Grand Tutor Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè heard of his reputation,
and invited him to be an assistant.
Kūn was unrestrained and informal.
Soon, he was stripped of his official position because his family servant stole.
At that time, famous scholars like Wáng Xuán and Ruǎn Xiū
all lamented
that Kūn, upon his first entry into the prime minister's office,
was already humiliated and dismissed.
When Kūn heard this,
he simply sang clearly and played the qín,
not caring in the least.
Everyone admired his far-reaching spirit
and his indifference to honor and disgrace.
A neighboring High family had a beautiful daughter.
Kūn once flirted with her.
The daughter threw a shuttle,
breaking two of his teeth.
People at the time made a saying about it:
"Unrestrained freedom,
Yòuyú broke his teeth."
When Kūn heard this,
he just let out a long whistle, saying:
"It still doesn't stop me from whistling and singing!"
Yuè soon invited him again,
and he became Cānjūn Shì.
Kūn, seeing that the times were fraught with trouble,
feigned illness and resigned from his post,
seeking refuge in Yùzhāng.
He once traveled and spent the night in an empty pavilion.
This pavilion had a history of killing people.
Just before dawn, a yellow-clad person called Kūn's courtesy name and told him to open the door.
Kūn remained calm and fearless,
and reached his hand through the window to pull it.
Its shoulder broke.
Upon inspection,
it was a deer.
He followed the blood and caught it.
After that, the pavilion was free of anomalies.
Zuǒjiāngjūn Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed him as Chángshǐ.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Dù Tāo (杜弢), he was enfeoffed as Xiántínghóu (咸亭侯).
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
When the mourning period ended,
he was promoted to Dūn's Dàjiāngjūn Chángshǐ (大將軍長史).
At that time, Wáng Chéng (王澄) was at Dūn's residence.
Seeing Kūn (鯤) talk tirelessly,
he only sighed, "Xiè Chángshǐ (謝長史) is someone with whom one can converse,"
without even glancing at Dūn.
Such was the admiration he received from others.
Kūn did not strive for fame or glory,
nor did he pursue rigorous conduct.
He positioned himself between affirmation and negation.
Although he seemed to put himself in a "squalid" position,
his actions never diminished his lofty standing.
Dūn displayed signs of disloyalty,
evident to both court and commoners.
Kūn knew he could not rectify or assist him through proper counsel,
so he instead lived a leisurely life, adapting to circumstances,
and showed no interest in political affairs.
He offered gentle criticisms and suggestions,
and merely passed his days.
He often indulged in drinking with Bì Zhuó (畢卓), Wáng Ní (王尼), Ruǎn Fàng (阮放), Yáng Màn (羊曼), Huán Yí (桓彝), Ruǎn Fú (阮孚), and others.
Dūn, valuing his high reputation,
treated him with refined courtesy.
Once, Kūn was sent to the capital.
Míngdì (明帝), then in the Eastern Palace, met him
and held him in high regard and intimacy.
He asked,
"Commentators compare you to Yú Liàng (庾亮).
What do you think of yourself in comparison?"
Kūn replied,
"In managing the court and serving as a model for all officials,
Kūn is inferior to Liàng.
But in a simple, reclusive life,
I consider myself superior."
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) once said to Kūn's son Shàng (尚):
"Your distinguished father is not only immensely perceptive and far-sighted,
but his profound divine insight
even surpasses Zhūgě Jǐn's (諸葛瑾) understanding of Sūn Quán (孫權)."
When Dūn was about to rebel,
he said to Kūn:
"Liú Wěi (劉隗) is treacherous and wicked,
and will endanger the state.
I wish to eliminate the evil at the sovereign's side,
to rectify the ruler and save the times.
What do you think?"
Kūn replied:
"Wěi is indeed the instigator of trouble,
but he is merely a 'fox in the city wall, a rat in the earth shrine' (meaning a minor evil difficult to remove)."
Dūn angrily said:
"You are a mediocre talent;
how can you understand such profound principles!"
He sent Kūn out as the Tàishǒu (太守) of Yùzhāng (豫章),
but then kept him and did not dispatch him,
using his talent and reputation
to force him to accompany him downriver.
When Dūn arrived at Shítou (石頭),
he sighed:
"I can no longer perform acts of great virtue."
Kūn said:
"Why is that?
Just ensure that from now on,
you forget and cast away (these past actions) daily."
Initially,
Dūn had said to Kūn:
"I shall appoint Zhōu Bórén (周伯仁) as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令)
and Dài Ruòsī (戴若思) as Púyè (僕射)."
Upon arriving at the capital,
he again asked:
"How are people's sentiments recently?"
Kūn replied:
"Although your honorable self's undertaking
aims to greatly preserve the state,
the common talk
indeed does not yet comprehend your noble intentions.
Zhōu Yǐ (周顗) and Dài Ruòsī (戴若思) are the hopes of people from both north and south.
If you, Your Excellency,
appoint and employ them,
the masses will be content."
That very day,
Dūn sent soldiers to arrest Zhōu and Dài,
which Kūn did not know.
Dūn angrily said:
"Are you so crude and careless!
Those two are unsuitable;
I have already arrested them."
Kūn and Yǐ had always been close and respected each other.
Hearing this, Kūn was aghast,
as if he had lost a part of himself.
Cānjūn (參軍) Wáng Jiào (王嶠), regarding Dūn's execution of Yǐ,
admonished him very sharply.
Dūn became furious
and ordered Jiào to be beheaded.
At that time, people were fearful,
and no one dared to speak.
Kūn said:
"Your Excellency is undertaking a great enterprise;
you should not execute a single person.
Jiào merely disagreed with your order in offering counsel,
and you would use him to anoint the drum with blood?
Is that not excessive!"
Dūn then stopped.
After Dūn had harmed loyal and virtuous individuals,
he feigned illness and did not attend court,
intending to return to Wǔchāng (武昌).
Kūn advised Dūn, saying:
"You, my lord, have greatly preserved the state,
establishing an unprecedented meritorious deed.
However, the hearts of the people throughout the land still do not truly understand.
If you can attend court and face the Son of Heaven,
allowing both sovereign and minister to be at ease,
then the hearts of all will truly be convinced.
Relying on public trust to comply with popular sentiment,
and fully displaying humility and modesty to serve the Emperor,
if you do so, your achievements will match those of a unifier of the realm,
and your name will be remembered for a thousand years."
Dūn said:
"Can you guarantee that there will be no change (of heart from the emperor)?"
Kūn replied:
"Kūn recently had an audience,
and the Emperor leaned forward in anticipation,
eager to see you, my lord.
The palace is peaceful and calm,
so there will surely be no danger.
If you, my lord, enter the court,
Kūn requests to accompany you."
Dūn suddenly became enraged and said:
"Even if I kill hundreds of you people,
what harm would it do to the times!"
He ultimately did not attend court and departed.
At this time, those of high standing at court who had been harmed
were all worried about him.
Yet Kūn, reasoning logically and acting calmly,
frequently offered righteous counsel.
Dūn, unable to follow it,
was also inwardly displeased.
When the army returned,
he sent Kūn to a commandery.
He governed with purity and strictness,
and the people loved him.
He died in office shortly thereafter,
at the age of forty-three.
After Dūn's death,
Kūn was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng (太常)
and given the posthumous name Kāng (康).
His son Shàng (尚) succeeded him;
his biography is given separately.
Húmǔ Fǔzhī (胡毋輔之) (courtesy name Qiānzhī (謙之))
Húmǔ Fǔzhī (胡毋輔之), courtesy name Yànguó (彥國),
was a native of Fènggāo (奉高), Tàishān (泰山).
His high ancestor, Bān (班), was a Zhí Jīnwú (執金吾) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
His father, Yuán (原),
was skilled in military affairs.
Shān Tāo (山濤) praised his talent as suitable for border assignments
and recommended him as Tàiwèi Chángshǐ (太尉長史).
He ended his career as Hénán Lìng (河南令).
Fǔzhī (輔之) gained high renown in his youth
and possessed a keen eye for discerning people.
He was fond of wine
and was unrestrained, not bothering with minor details.
He, Wáng Chéng (王澄), Wáng Dūn (王敦), and Yǔ Nǐ (庾敳) were all close to Tàiwèi (太尉) Wáng Yǎn (王衍),
and were known as the "Four Friends."
Chéng once wrote in a letter to someone:
"Yànguó (彥國) emits excellent words like sawdust from sawing wood,
continuously and abundantly.
He is truly a leader among the younger generation."
He was invited to serve as Biéjià (別駕) and Tàiwèi Yuàn (太尉掾),
but did not accept either.
Due to family poverty,
he requested to be appointed acting Fánchāng Lìng (繁昌令).
He began to restrain his drinking and disciplined himself,
gaining a reputation for great ability.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
He participated in the campaign against Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏),
and was granted the title of Yīnpíng Nán (陰平男).
He successively became Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (司徒左長史).
He again requested an external posting
and became Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍) and Lè'ān Tàishǒu (樂安太守).
He drank day and night with Guāng Yì (光逸), a local of the commandery,
and neglected his duties.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎), then the crown prince,
summoned him to be Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子).
He then became known for his unrestrained and unconventional lifestyle, along with Xiè Kūn (謝鯤), Wáng Chéng (王澄), Ruǎn Xiū (阮脩), Wáng Ní (王尼), and Bì Zhuó (畢卓).
Once, Húmǔ Fǔzhī 嘗過河南門下飲 was drinking at the gate of Hénán.
A groom from Hénán, Wáng Zǐbó, sat casually beside him.
Fǔzhī shouted at him to fetch a light.
Zǐbó said:
“I am a soldier;
as long as my duties are not neglected, that is enough.
How can I again be at someone else’s beck and call!”
Fǔzhī then went over to talk with him,
and sighed, saying:
“I am not as good as him!”
He recommended him to the Administrator of Hénán, Yuè Guǎng.
Guǎng summoned him,
was very pleased with him,
and promoted him to Gōngcáo.
His discernment and promotion of talent were like this.
The Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, heard of Fǔzhī’s reputation,
and appointed him Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He was later appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Chénliú.
When Wáng Mí passed through his commandery,
Fǔzhī was unable to suppress him,
and was dismissed from office for this.
Soon after, he was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Governor of Yángzhōu,
but he did not take up the post.
Yuè then appointed him Yòusīmǎ and Dàzhōngzhèng of his home province.
When Yuè died,
he fled the chaos and crossed the Jiāng River.
Emperor Yuán appointed him Āndōng Jiāngjūn Cèyì Jìjiǔ,
and he was promoted to Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn, Governor of Xiāngzhōu, and given a provisional seal.
He died shortly after arriving at his province,
at the age of forty-nine.
His son was Qiānzhī.
Qiānzhī’s courtesy name was Zǐguāng.
His talent and learning were not equal to his father’s,
but his arrogance and recklessness surpassed him.
When he was heavily drunk,
he often called his father by his courtesy name.
Fǔzhī also did not take offense,
and those who discussed it considered it madness.
When Fǔzhī was drinking heavily,
Qiānzhī peeped in and said in a harsh voice:
“Yànguó is old,
you shouldn’t be like that!
You’ll make my rear end hit the eastern wall.”
Fǔzhī laughed happily,
called him in and drank with him.
Such was his conduct.
He died before the age of thirty.
Bì Zhuó
Bì Zhuó, courtesy name Màoshì,
was a native of Tóngyáng, Xīncài.
His father, Chén,
was Zhōngshū Láng.
Zhuó, when young, admired freedom and unconventionality,
and was recognized by Húmǔ Fǔzhī.
At the end of Tàixīng,
he served as Lìbù Láng,
often neglecting his duties due to drinking.
When a neighbor’s wine was ripe,
Zhuó, being drunk, went to his vat in the night and stole some to drink.
He was bound by the wine steward.
The next morning, when they saw him,
it was Bì Lìbù,
and they immediately released him.
Zhuó then invited the host to feast by the vat,
got drunk and left.
Zhuó once said to people:
“If I could have a boat filled with several hundred *hú* of wine,
with seasonal delicacies placed at both ends,
holding a wine cup in my right hand,
and a crab claw in my left,
floating in the wine boat,
that would be enough for a lifetime.”
When he crossed the Jiāng River,
he became Wēn Qiáo’s Píngnán Chángshǐ,
and died in office.
Wáng Ní
Wáng Ní, courtesy name Xiàosūn,
was a native of Chéngyáng,
or some say of Hénèi.
Originally the son of a military family,
he resided in Luòyáng, exceptionally unruly.
Initially, he was a soldier in the Hùjūn residence.

Húmǔ Fǔzhī, together with the Prince of Lángyá, Wáng Chéng, Fù Chàng of Běidì, Liú Yú of Zhōngshān, Xún Suì of Yǐngchuān, and Péi Xiá of Hédōng, took turns asking Zhēn Shù, Gōngcáo of Hénán, and Cáo Chè, Magistrate of Luòyáng, to release him.
Chè and the others, fearing it was beyond their authority,
dared not.
Fǔzhī and the others carried sheep and wine to the gate of the Hùjūn,
the gatekeepers listed their names and presented them to the Hùjūn.
The Hùjūn sighed, saying:
“These famous scholars are bringing sheep and wine;
there must be a reason.”
At that time, Ní was in charge of feeding the horses for the residence.
Fǔzhī and the others entered,
and sat down in the stables,
roasted lamb and drank wine with Ní,
then left full and drunk,
without seeing the Hùjūn at all.
The Hùjūn was greatly astonished,
and immediately granted Ní a long leave,
thus releasing him from military service.
Dōngyíng Gōng Téng invited him to be a Shèrén in the Chējì residence,
but he did not accept.
At that time, Shàngshū Hé Suí was excessively extravagant.
Ní said to people:
“Suí lives in a chaotic world,
yet acts so arrogantly and extravagantly.
He will not live long.”
People said:
“Bówèi, hearing these words,
will surely harm you.”
Ní said:
“By the time Bówèi hears my words,
he will already be dead.”
Soon after,
Suí was indeed killed by the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè.
When he first entered Luòyáng,
Ní went to Yuè but did not bow.
Yuè asked him why.
Ní said:
“You lack the ability of a prime minister,
therefore I do not bow.”
Then he counted his faults,
speaking very sharply.
He also said:
“You owe Ní something.”
Yuè was greatly surprised and said:
“How can that be?”
Ní said:
“In the past, a man from Chǔ lost his clothes,
and accused the Lingyǐn of stealing them.
Now, all of Ní’s houses and possessions
have been plundered by your soldiers.
Ní is now hungry and cold,
this is also your debt, Illustrious Sir.”
Yuè laughed heartily,
and immediately bestowed fifty rolls of silk upon him.
When the noblemen heard this,
they competed to send him provisions.
When Luòyáng fell,
he fled the chaos to Jiāngxià.
At that time, Wáng Chéng was Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and treated him very generously.
Ní had lost his wife early,
and had only one son.
He had no dwelling,
only kept an open carriage
and one ox.
Whenever he traveled,
he would have his son drive it,
and they would sleep together in the carriage at night.
He often sighed, saying:
“The azure seas overflow,
nowhere is peaceful.”
Shortly after, Chéng died,
and Jīng land suffered famine.
Ní had no food,
so he killed the ox and dismantled the carriage,
eating the meat.
When it was all gone,
both father and son starved to death.
Yáng Màn (younger brother Dān)
Yáng Màn, courtesy name Zǔyán,
was the grand-nephew of the Grand Tutor Hù.
His father, Jì,
was Administrator of Yángpíng.
Màn was famous when young.
His home province extended invitations,
and the Grand Tutor invited him,
but he declined them all.
Fleeing the chaos, he crossed the Jiāng River.
Emperor Yuán appointed him Zhèndōng Cānjūn,
then transferred him to Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù,
entrusting him with confidential matters.
He successively held positions as Huángmén Shìláng, Shàngshū Lìbù Láng, and Administrator of Jìnlíng,
but was dismissed due to official business.
Màn was unrestrained and indulged himself,
fond of drinking wine.
Wēn Qiáo, Yǔ Liàng, Ruǎn Fàng, and Huán Yí were like-minded and good friends,
all renowned scholars of the restoration.
At that time, people in the province called Ruǎn Fàng of Chénliú Hóngbó,
Xī Jiàn of Gāopíng Fāngbó,
Húmǔ Fǔzhī of Tàishān Dábo,
Biàn Kǔn of Jìyīn Cáibó,
Cài Mó of Chénliú Lǎngbó,
Ruǎn Fú Dànbó,
Liú Suí of Gāopíng Wěibó,
and Màn was Kuòbó.
There were eight people in total,
known as the Eight Bó of Yǎnzhōu,
probably in imitation of the Eight Jùn of antiquity.
Wáng Dūn 王敦, having become disaffected with the imperial court,
imprisoned imperial officials.
Màn 曼 served as his Right Chief Clerk.
Màn 曼 knew Dūn 敦 was disloyal,
and spent his days in drunkenness,
only offering satirical comments.
Dūn 敦, valuing his scholarly reputation,
treated him with great courtesy,
but did not entrust him with affairs.
Thus, Màn 曼 avoided involvement in Dūn's 敦 troubles.
When Dūn 敦 was defeated,
Màn 曼 replaced Ruǎn Fú 阮孚 as Administrator of Dānyáng 丹楊.
At that time, when imperial officials crossed the Jiāng 江 River and received their first appointments,
they adorned themselves and prepared elaborate feasts.
When Màn 曼 was appointed Administrator of Dānyáng 丹楊,
early guests received fine dishes,
but as the day wore on, the food gradually ran out,
and later guests no longer received delicacies.
He treated guests according to their arrival time, regardless of their rank.
Yáng Gù 羊固, upon becoming Administrator of Línhǎi 臨海,
served excellent food all day long;
even latecomers received lavish meals.
Commentators believed that Gù's 固 generosity
was not as genuine and unpretentious as Màn's 曼.
When Sū Jùn 蘇峻 rebelled,
Màn 曼 was appointed General of the Vanguard
and commanded civil and military officials to guard the Yúnlóngmén 雲龍門 Gate.
The imperial army did not prevail.
Some advised Màn 曼 to flee from Jùn 峻.
Màn 曼 said,
“The court is in ruins;
where shall I seek to survive?”
He commanded his troops to stand firm
and was consequently killed by Jùn 峻
at the age of fifty-five.
After Jùn 峻 was pacified,
Màn 曼 was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of Sacrifices.
His son, Bēn 賁, inherited his title.
Bēn 賁 was well-known in his youth
and married Princess Nánjùn Dàogōngzhǔ 南郡悼公主, daughter of Emperor Míng 明.
He was appointed Secretary of the Imperial Library
but died young.
His younger brother was Dān 聃.
Dān's 聃 courtesy name was Péngzǔ 彭祖.
In his youth, he lacked scholarly learning,
and contemporary opinion generally disdained him as common and mediocre.
Previously,
Yǎnzhōu 兗州 had a designation of "Eight Counts" (Bābó 八伯).
Later, there were "Four Counts" (Sìbó 四伯).
Jiāng Quán 江泉 of Chénliú 陳留, Grand Herald, was called the "Grain Count" (Gǔbó 穀伯) for his gluttony;
Shǐ Chóu 史疇, Administrator of Yùzhāng 豫章, was called the "Clumsy Count" (Bènbó 笨伯) for his great corpulence;
Zāng Yí 張嶷 of Gāopíng 高平, Cavalier Attendant, was called the "Sly Count" (Huábó 猾伯) for his cunning and wildness;
and Dān 聃 was called the "Trivial Count" (Suǒbó 瑣伯) for his wolfish cruelty.
These were probably patterned after the ancient Four Felons.
Dān 聃 was initially invited to Emperor Yuán's 元 Chancellor's office,
and successively promoted to Administrator of Lúlíng 廬陵.
He was fierce, cruel, and brutal.
Relying on his connections to the imperial family,
he indulged in excessive wantonness.
Even for minor grievances, he would inflict punishment or death.
He suspected the commoners Jiǎn Liáng 簡良 and others of being bandits,
killed over two hundred people,
including infants,
and imprisoned more than a hundred others.
Yǔ Liàng 庾亮 arrested him
and sent him back to the capital.
The authorities memorialized that Dān's 聃 crime deserved death,
but because Empress Jǐngxiàn 景獻 was his grandaunt,
he should qualify for the Eight Deliberations (Bāyì 八議).
Emperor Chéng 成 decreed,
“This matter is unprecedented in ancient and modern times.
How can there be Eight Deliberations for it!
Yet I cannot bear to execute him publicly in the marketplace.
Let him be granted death in prison.”
His elder brother's son, Bēn 賁, who was married to a princess,
submitted a memorial requesting to dissolve his marriage.
The imperial edict stated,
“Crimes do not extend to others;
this is an ancient and modern legal principle.
Although Dān 聃 faces the ultimate penalty,
what has this to do with Bēn 賁!
Therefore, his request for divorce is not granted.”
The Grand Concubine Shān 山 of Lángxié 琅邪, who was Dān's 聃 niece,
entered the palace and kowtowed, begging for his life.
Wáng Dǎo 王導 also memorialized,
“Dān's 聃 crime is unforgivable
and justly deserves the severest punishment.
However, Grand Concubine Shān 山 is sick with grief.
Given Your Majesty's boundless grace,
she should be granted the favor of his life being spared.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, stating:
“The Grand Concubine has only this one maternal uncle.
Her words are choked with sorrow,
even to the point of spitting blood.
Her feelings are profoundly deep.
When I suffered great misfortune in the past,
I received the Grand Concubine's nurturing grace,
which was like that of a kind mother.
If she cannot endure this unbearable pain
and consequently wastes away,
how can I face her?
Therefore, Dān's 聃 life is now spared
to comfort the Grand Concubine's Wèiyáng 渭陽 sentiments.”
Consequently, he was stripped of his official title.
Shortly after,
he fell ill
and saw Jiǎn Liáng 簡良 and others as vengeful spirits.
He died within ten days.
Guāng Yì 光逸
Guāng Yì's 光逸 courtesy name was Mèngzǔ 孟祖,
and he was a native of Lè'ān 樂安.
Initially, he was a petty official in Bóchāng 博昌 county.
The county magistrate sent Yì 逸 to see off a guest.
He braved the cold and became completely frozen and wet.
When he returned, the magistrate was absent.
Yì 逸 took off his clothes to warm them by the fire
and then lay down in the magistrate's bedding.
When the magistrate returned,
he was furious
and was about to inflict severe punishment.
Yì 逸 said,
“My family is poor and my clothes are thin.
Having gotten wet, I have nothing to change into.
If I do not warm myself for a while,
I will surely freeze to death.
How can you value one blanket so much as to kill a man for it!
A gentleman is benevolent and compassionate;
he would certainly not do so.
Therefore, I lay down without hesitation.”
The magistrate was impressed and released him.
Later, he became a gatekeeper
and escorted the new magistrate to the capital.
Húmǔ Fǔzhī 胡毋輔之 and Xún Suì 荀邃 went together to the magistrate's house.
Seeing Yì 逸 from a distance,
Fǔzhī 輔之 said to Suì 邃,
“That man seems like an extraordinary talent.”
He immediately called him into their carriage
and conversed with him for a long time.
Indeed, he was a brilliant individual.
The magistrate wondered why his guests had not entered,
and his attendant reported that they were talking with Guāng Yì 光逸.
The magistrate was enraged,
removed Yì's 逸 name from the register,
and dismissed him.
Later, he was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
and served as a commandery attendant,
but abandoned his office and went to Fǔzhī 輔之.
Fǔzhī 輔之 was then serving as the Grand Tutor Yuè's 越 Staff Officer,
and recommended Yì 逸 to Yuè 越.
Yuè 越, however, did not summon him due to his humble family background.
Later, during a casual banquet,
Yuè 越 chastised Fǔzhī 輔之 for not recommending anyone.
Fǔzhī 輔之 said,
“Previously, I recommended Guāng Yì 光逸,
but you did not summon him because he was not from a prominent family.
It is not that I made no recommendation.”
Yuè 越 then appointed him.
When the official letter reached the commanderies and counties,
everyone thought it was a mistake.
Only when they confirmed it was indeed Yì 逸
did they prepare full courtesies and send him off.
Soon, due to the chaos of the times,
he fled across the Jiāng 江 River to escape the troubles
and again sought refuge with Fǔzhī 輔之.
When he first arrived,
it happened that Fǔzhī 輔之, Xiè Kūn 謝鯤, Ruǎn Fàng 阮放, Bì Zhuó 畢卓, Yáng Màn 羊曼, Huán Yí 桓彝, and Ruǎn Fú 阮孚
had let down their hair, stripped naked,
closed themselves in a room, and had been drinking for several days.
Yì 逸 was about to force open the door,
but the guard would not allow him.
Yì 逸 then stripped off his clothes outside the door, poked his head through the dog hole, peered in, and let out a loud shout.
Fǔzhī 輔之 exclaimed in surprise,
“No one else could possibly do that;
it must be my Mèngzǔ 孟祖!”
He hurriedly called him in,
and they continued to drink together,
day and night without cessation.
People at the time called them the "Eight Transcendent Ones" (Bādá 八達).
Emperor Yuán 元 appointed Yì 逸 as Libationer of the Military Advisory Board.
When the restoration began,
he served as Attendant Censor
and died in office.
The Grand Scribe says: If learning is not of the constant Way,
then there is nothing that does not become clear;
if principle is to forget words,
then what is in the emotions is thereupon dismissed.
When advancing,
one adapts to customs, mixes with the dust,
and does not reside in fame or profit.
When retreating,
one partakes of harmony and treads in accord,
thereby preserving one's innate purity.
If one unifies their origin,
embodies the function of non-action,
distinguishes their branches and leaves,
and opens the path of parables,
this is why Bóyáng [Lǎozi] set an example,
and Míngqiān [Lǎozi's alleged courtesy name] established a pattern:
wishing to exalt oneself,
one must first humble oneself before others.
It is like the greatest music having no sound,
yet the luan phoenixes still dance in response.
Zhuāngshēng [Zhuāngzi] let his principles roam far and wide,
and his eloquent arguments were inexhaustible.
Discarding worldly glory,
he looked down upon ranks and positions;
cherishing his Daoist arts,
he disdained kings and dukes.
Licking hemorrhoids for a carriage,
a kestrel swallowing carrion.
Using these to express himself,
he thereupon toyed with things,
distinctly different from an empty boat,
yet similar to baring an arm.
Jī [Kāng] and Ruǎn [Jí]'s gathering in the Bamboo Grove,
Liú [Líng] and Bì [Zhuó]'s friendship with fragrant wine vessels,
they galloped through Zhuāng [Zǐ]'s gate,
and climbed into Lǐ [Ěr]'s [Lǎozi's personal name] chamber.
As for those who model themselves on heaven and establish laws,
with all officials following the established tracks,
matters beyond the rituals
are discarded and not preserved.
This is why Emperor Yáo allowed Xǔ Yóu to be beyond the dust and dirt,
and Guāngwǔ left Zǐlíng [Yán Zǐlíng] at the murmuring ford.
Pine and creeping fig vines hang low and are raised,
used to honor the worthy;
rocks and clear waters reflect light,
thereby granting reclusion.
The minister acts on his will,
and the ruler earns a good name.
As for Jī Kāng's letter to Jùyuán [Shān Táo],
and the Ruǎn clan's creation of the "Biography of Mr. X,"
a military counselor letting his hair down,
a Board of Civil Office official stealing a wine vessel—
was it perhaps that they despised the world's pursuit of fame,
and thus defiled themselves? Facing the forging furnace without turning back,
ascending Guǎngwǔ and sighing deeply—
then Jī [Kāng]'s zither lost its sound,
and Ruǎn [Jí]'s spirit merely endured.
Opening their side paths
inevitably corrupts customs;
calling them to serve in office,
they merely fill a sinecure.
Outside the beaten track,
there may be something worth observing.
They were all able to accord with the contract of the spirit and soul,
each upholding their principles from beginning to end,
their spirits grieving in communion with the late flute,
or moving their carriage in yearning for each other.
Therefore, the Grand Scribe gathered their remaining deeds,
and appended them to this chapter.
Encomium: Lǎo [Lǎozi]'s teachings were established,
Kǒng [Confucius]'s teachings held the balance.
Each preserved its own interest;
the Dao values namelessness.
They opposed the improprietous,
and followed the understanding of life.
Autumn waters raise waves,
spring clouds gather reflections.
Excellent wine is their virtue,
their nature relies on emptiness.
If one does not delight in this style,
who would diminish the king's governance?
Biography Twenty: Cáo Zhì
Cáo Zhì, courtesy name Yǔngōng,
was a man from Qiáo in Qiáoguó.
He was the illegitimate son of Wèi Chénsīwáng [Cáo] Zhí.
In his youth, he loved learning,
and was praised for his talent and conduct.
He was simple, easygoing, and had great magnanimity,
