also excelling at horsemanship and archery.
Zhí said:
"This is the one who will preserve my family."
He was established as heir.
Later, his title was changed to Prince of Jìběi.
When Emperor Wǔ [Sīmǎ Yán] was General Who Pacifies the Army,
he welcomed the Prince of Chénliú in Yè.
Zhì visited him at night,
and the Emperor spoke with him
from dusk until dawn,
greatly admiring him.
When the Emperor received the abdication,
Zhì was demoted to Duke of Juànchéng County.
An edict stated:
"In ancient times,
although the mandate changed and dynasties rose and fell,
the descendants of previous dynasties
continued their lineage without being replaced,
or were enfeoffed as princes in the Nine Regions,
orderly arranged in official ranks.
Selecting the multitude and appointing the worthy,
only the virtuous were given positions –
this is truly the Way of ultimate impartiality.
The princes and dukes of the Wèi clan have cultivated their virtue and hidden their talents,
long stagnant and delayed.
Although there was a previous edict
that they should be selectively appointed,
recently few official positions have been vacant,
and thus it has not been possible to do so.
The former Prince of Jìběi, Cáo Zhì, possesses pure and upright virtue,
high talent and clean conduct.
He loves antiquity and is learned in many things,
a hero among the Wèi imperial clan.
I greatly commend him.
Let Zhì be appointed Administrator of Lèpíng."
While in the commandery, Zhì submitted a memorial,
believing it was appropriate to honor Confucianism and value the Dao,
requesting to establish a Doctor of Erudition and attendant officers.
He was promoted to Administrator of Zhāngwǔ and Zhàojùn.
Although he held various commandery posts,
he did not concern himself with administrative matters.
By day he would hunt,
by night he would recite poetry and books,
amusing himself with music and women.
Those who saw him at the time could not fully ascertain his measure.
In the beginning of Xiánníng,
an edict stated:
"The Duke of Juànchéng, Cáo Zhì,
is earnest in his conduct and simple in his ways,
accomplished in learning and widely knowledgeable.
He is fit for the Confucian forest [scholarly circles],
to promote the education of the imperial sons.
Let Zhì be appointed Palace Attendant and Erudite of the Imperial Academy."
The Emperor once reviewed the "Discourse on the Six Dynasties" [Liùdàilùn],
and asked Zhì:
"Was this written by your late king?"
Zhì replied:
"My late king had a catalog written by his own hand.
I request to go home and examine it."
Upon returning, he reported:
"According to the catalog, this is not in it."
The Emperor asked:
"Who wrote it?"
Zhì said:
"From what your servant has heard,
it was written by my paternal cousin Jiǒng.
Because my late king's writings were highly esteemed and his fame was established,
[Jiǒng] wished for the work to be transmitted to later generations,
and thus falsely attributed it."
The Emperor said:
"There have been many such cases since ancient times."
He looked at the high officials and said:
"A father and son bearing witness [to each other]
is sufficient for verification.
From now on,
there need be no further doubt."
Later, he was promoted to Jìjiǔ.
When Qí Wáng Yōu was about to depart for his fiefdom,
the Tàicháng discussed bestowing upon him venerated ceremonial objects.
At the time, Professor Qín Xiù and others believed that Qí Wáng should remain in the capital to assist in court affairs,
and should not go to a藩.
Cáo Zhì had always regretted that his father had not achieved his ambitions in Wèi,
and so, with a sorrowful sigh, he said:
"How can there be such talent,
such close kinship,
yet they are not allowed to establish roots and assist in governance,
but instead are sent far away to the ends of the sea? The prosperity of the Jìn dynasty
is indeed perilous!"
Thereupon, he presented a memorial, saying:
"I humbly hear that the Grand Marshal, Qí Wáng, is to depart for his fiefdom in the Eastern Xià,
with all rituals and provisions complete,
equaling those of the Two Dukes.
Now, Your Majesty is a sagacious ruler,
and Jì and Qì are virtuous ministers;
within, there are relatives as close as those of Lǔ and Wèi,
and without, there are assistants like Qí and Jìn.
To sit and maintain peace—
this is the foundation for myriad generations.
In ancient times, those who supported the royal house—
of the same surname, Dōng Zhōu Gōng was such a person;
of a different surname, Tàigōng was such a person.
Both remained in the capital,
and were buried there after five generations.
Later, although the Five Hegemons successively rose,
and Huán and Wén employed cunning against their lord,
below there was the usurpation of 'requesting a tunnel' (qǐngsuì),
and above there was the rite of the 'nine bestowment' (jiǔxī).
Ultimately, it was cunning and not upright,
proven by the saying 'a tail too large to wag the dog.'
How can this be discussed in the same breath as Shàogōng's song of the Tángdì
or the Zhōu poem praising the Chíxiāo?
Now, in the nascent stage of our sacred dynasty,
if it is not trustworthy from the start,
later affairs will be difficult to accomplish.
If the trunk is not strong,
the branches and leaves will not flourish;
if the bones are not preserved,
the skin will not be full.
Since Xī Huáng,
how could it be exclusively owned by one surname?
Those who wish to bind hearts
must have a foundation as solid as a bedrock.
Indeed, those who wish to enjoy benefits for myriad generations
should discuss it with all under Heaven.
Thus, the sagacity of Heaven
comes from the sagacity of our people.
Qín and Wèi wished to monopolize their authority,
and only achieved the destruction of their own persons;
Zhōu and Hàn were able to share their benefits,
and both close and distant relations were utilized by them.
This is a profound consideration of the sagacious ruler,
illuminated by the sun and moon.
Though the matter is trivial,
it should be deeply contemplated;
though the words are light,
they should be seriously considered.
I, Zhì, hold the position of a Confucian official;
if my words are not in accordance with ritual,
then I, Zhì, am a usurper.
To know loyalty and not speak,
I would not dare to propose it.
I, Zhì, believe it should be as proposed by the professors and others."
When the memorial was completed and about to be presented,
he showed it to his cousin, Gāoyì Gōng Jiā.
Gāoyì Gōng Jiā said:
"Your proposal, elder brother, is very sharp;
a hundred years from now, it will certainly be recorded in the Jìn history,
but for now, you will likely face blame."
The emperor read the memorial,
and was greatly enraged, saying:
"Even Cáo Zhì does not understand my heart,
let alone the four seas!"
Because the memorial did not directly answer the question asked,
but instead created a different argument,
Tàicháng Zhèng Mò was dismissed by imperial edict.
Thereupon, the relevant authorities petitioned for the arrest and conviction of Cáo Zhì and others,
but an imperial edict only dismissed Cáo Zhì from office,
allowing him to return to his residence as a duke;
the rest were handed over to the Tíngwèi.
After a while,
Cáo Zhì was again appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
He suffered the sorrow of his mother's death,
and observed mourning rites beyond what was prescribed,
which led to a serious illness,
causing his moods to become erratic.
He died in the ninth year.
The Tàicháng petitioned for a pejorative posthumous name.
Cuī Bāo sighed and said:
"Wèi Kē did not follow the chaos;
it was due to his illness that he appeared chaotic.
Now, to give Cáo Zhì a posthumous name, and to posthumously name his illness,
does this mean his illness was not chaotic?"
Thereupon, he was given the posthumous name Dìng.
Yǔ Jùn (Zǐmín, Āi)
Yǔ Jùn, courtesy name Shānfǔ,
was a native of Yān líng, Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather, Chéng,
was learned and widely knowledgeable.
He was summoned by the Hàn Sītú
and was called upon for his Dao,
but he declined all appointments.
His paternal uncle, Yì,
was fair, simple, and served Wèi as Tàipú.
His father, Dào,
was incorruptible, modest, and firm in his principles,
cherishing his aspirations without seeking office.
If his cattle or horses would kick or bite,
fearing they might injure someone,
he would not sell them in the market.
When his sons later became distinguished,
he was granted the title of Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Yǔ Jùn was fond of learning in his youth
and possessed talent and insight.
He once traveled to the capital
and heard that Sū Lín, the Wèi Sànqí Chángshì, was old and ill at home,
so he went to visit him.
Sū Lín had studied under Chéng,
and seeing Yǔ Jùn, he shed tears,
and after a long while, said:
"Your grandfather possessed great talent but a modest disposition,
was kind and broadly loving,
pure, tranquil, and had few desires,
not striving for worldly affairs,
but solely cultivating virtue.
Yān líng historically had fifty to sixty thousand households,
but I hear now there are only a few hundred.
Your two fathers, as infants, endured the chaos of war,
and have uniquely reached today.
Your paternal uncle was a capable vessel for his time,
and you and your brothers are also outstanding.
This is all due to your grandfather's accumulated virtue."
He successively served as Jùn Gōngcáo,
was nominated as Jìyuàn,
and was appointed Cóngshì by the province.
Tàicháng Zhèng Mào met Yǔ Jùn
and was greatly impressed by him,
recommending him as Bóshì.
At that time, Zhuāng and Lǎo were highly regarded while the classics and histories were lightly esteemed.
Yǔ Jùn feared that the elegant Way would decline,
so he dedicated himself to Confucian canons.
It happened that Gāoguì Xiānggōng visited the Imperial Academy
and asked Yǔ Jùn about the meaning of the Shàngshū.
Yǔ Jùn cited the teachings of the masters,
illuminated the essence of the classic,
clarified doubts and obscurities,
and his answers were detailed and thorough.
He was promoted to Mìshū Chéng.
There was a major prison case in Cháng'ān
that had long remained undecided.
Yǔ Jùn was appointed Shìyùshǐ
to go and resolve it,
and his judgment was praised as fair by the court and commoners alike.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he was granted the title Guānzhōng Hóu,
promoted to Sīkōng Chángshǐ,
then transferred to Mìshū Jiān and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and appointed Shìzhōng,
with the additional title of Jiànyì Dàfū.
He often attended the emperor's lectures on the Shī;
when Zhōngshùzǐ Hé Shào discussed the meaning of the correct and corrupted styles of Fēng and Yǎ,
Yǔ Jùn rose to challenge and retort,
and no one among the assembled officials could refute him.
At this time, customs were driven by competition,
and etiquette and deference were in decline.
Yǔ Jùn submitted a memorial, saying: "I have heard that the nature of the common people
is such that there are many people but few worthy ones;
when officials are established and duties divided,
then officials are few but worthy ones are many.
If there are many officials for many worthy ones,
then governance is hindered;
if worthy ones are discarded due to lack of official positions,
then the Way is abandoned.
Therefore, when sagacious kings govern the world,
they adapt to human nature,
some serving in office, some living in retirement.
Thus, there are those who serve in court,
and there are also
those who live in the mountains and forests.
Those who serve in court
assist the ruler in accomplishing transformation,
just as a person has limbs and a heart,
all forming one body.
Those who live in the mountains and forests
wear rough clothes but carry
jade,
the highest residing in hills and gardens,
with noble integrity distinguishing them from the common people.
Next, there are those who lightly regard titles and official attire,
shunning disgrace to preserve their aspirations.
The lowest take up official positions,
only without
Though successful, they know when to stop.
Their purity and integrity are enough to suppress greed and corruption,
and their humility and yielding are enough to quell petty matters.
Therefore, officials at court hear of their reputation and are pleased by it;
those
who are about to receive ranks all feel ashamed of their own shortcomings.
This is what the recluses of the mountains and forests and the officials who shun favor consider admirable,
and the former kings commended it.
Although their integrity is detached from the world,
their
virtue accords with the ruler;
although their conduct deviates from the court,
their achievements are the same as good governance.
Therefore, the great ones receive appointments involving jade and silk,
and the lesser ones receive the ceremonies of a stool and staff,
so that their profound virtue carries
all things,
and their engagement and reclusion have their proper place.
Thus, the court is full of worthy talents,
and even commoners do not fail to be gentlemen.
This was the magnanimity of the former kings.
The Qín blocked this path,
making profit issue from a single official.
Though there were recluses by name,
those without official rank at court
were called "six scorpions" by Shāng Jūn,
and "five
parasites" by Hán Fēi.
The times did not value virtue;
only official ranks were esteemed.
Thus, villagers with the rank of gōngchéng insulted their neighbors,
and those above the rank of lángzhōng arrogantly treated their fathers and elder brothers.
Hàn
Zǔ reversed this,
greatly promoting what had been suppressed.
He entrusted Xiāo Cáo with the empire,
and honored the Four Hào on Mount Nán.
Despite Zhāng Liáng's merits,
his rank was behind Shúsūn;
indeed,
though Gài Gōng was humble,
Cáo Càn consulted him on governance.
Emperors valued virtue above,
and society also returned to its roots below.
Thus, Tán Shú and ten others,
among the officials of the Hàn court, none
could surpass them,
yet they never sought official emoluments in their time.
Even with Shì Zhī's high status,
he tied Wáng Shēng's socks at court,
and his reputation only grew.
If not for rulers
and ministers upholding virtue and universal love,
who could have understood the aspirations of the world,
to such a great extent!
Indeed, if one does not reform the弊 of a hundred kings,
but merely strives to save the world with governance,
literati will compete in wisdom and strive to enter office,
while warriors will rely on strength and vie for precedence.
Officials are high,
yet
their ambitions are not satisfied;
their achievements are rewarded,
yet their demands do not cease.
Moreover, the state has no system for appointing officials according to their talents,
and society has no shame in readily advancing and reluctantly withdrawing.
Once a position is high,
even without
merit, one is not looked down upon;
after having failed, one is still employed.
Therefore, if one rises based on previous connections,
the path for recluses is blocked.
Furthermore, the promotion and demotion of officials are without clear regulations,
thus
throughout the world,
people first compete and then yield,
and among all scholars,
there is advancement but no retreat.
Great men are swayed by popular trends,
and those in power are influenced by public opinion.
The scales
lose their balance,
how can clear and turbid be distinguished again? In the past, the former kings worried that what they used to gain the empire
would become a弊 now.
Therefore, when merits were achieved, they would
change their institutions;
when enterprises were established, they would alter their teachings.
Though they used ranks and emoluments to employ their subordinates,
ministers had no greedy and oppressive conduct;
though they used weapons to establish achievements,
rulers had no regrets
of excessive militarism.
I, your foolish servant, believe that in ancient times, grandees retired at seventy by 'hanging up their chariots'.
Now, unless they are great meritorious elders of the state,
or top talents of the Sān Sī,
they should be allowed to retire at seventy.
Then, scholars will have no
suspicion of clinging to office.
If their parents are eighty,
they should be allowed to care for them until their end.
Then, there will be no greater filial piety than serving one's parents.
If an official has repeatedly been tested without achievements,
following ancient custom, he should not
serve again for life.
Then, there will be no bad governance in officialdom.
Those who are capable of small things but not great,
may be demoted to take charge of small matters.
Then, people will be employed according to their capacities.
If rulers promote people with propriety,
and dismiss people
with propriety,
then ministers will also measure their abilities to accept ranks.
Those who are filial like Wáng Yáng,
who left office at a critical juncture,
and pure like Gòng Yǔ,
who would not wear a cap even once removed,
and those who know when to stop like Wáng Sūn,
and are content like Shū Guǎng,
even if they leave high positions and reside in the eastern wilds,
when speaking with a father,
they adhere to kindness;
when speaking with a son,
they adhere to
filial piety.
Their words accord with state regulations,
and their honorable conduct is evident to the imperial court.
They discard power as if kicking off shoes,
and passersby shed tears for them;
they decline favors like gold and stone,
and even common
men are inspired by their actions.
Thus, the former kings approved of them,
and the sages valued them.
Human nature tends to ascend,
just as water flows downward.
If accumulation does not stop, it will surely burst;
if rising does not stop, it will surely lead to distress.
Starting from ordinary men whose righteousness is not
firm,
ending with the imperial carriage suffering defeat,
it is indeed something that cannot but be carefully heeded.
If subordinates are united in striving for advancement,
superiors should use humility and yielding to remove their excesses.
Humility and yielding
cannot be enforced by punishments.
It is best to allow court officials to act according to their aspirations from time to time,
and for recluses to emerge from the mountains and forests occasionally.
Do not make it so that those who enter cannot leave again,
and those who depart cannot
return again.
Only then will engagement and reclusion be mutually beneficial,
standing balanced like scales.
Then there will be no contention,
and the world can be transformed.
He also criticized the superficiality and extravagance of his age,
which did not cultivate true reputation and substance,
writing essays to denounce it.
The text is too extensive to be included.
He died in the ninth year.
An imperial edict granted him one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, and 300,000 coins.
Before his death,
he instructed his son Mín to bury him in the evening if he died in the morning,
wearing a simple cloth turban and plain clothes,
without choosing a specific burial date.
Mín respectfully followed his father's dying wishes,
and laid him to rest in his ordinary clothes.
He had two sons: Mín and Huì.
Mín, courtesy name Zǐjū.
His nature was pure, gentle, and studious;
his conduct was loyal and forgiving.
In his youth, he successively served as Sǎnqí Chángshì, Běnguó Zhōngzhèng, and Shìzhōng,
and was enfeoffed as the Baron of Chángcén.
When Huái Dì was captured by Liú Yuánhǎi,
Mín was with him in Píngyáng.
At a grand gathering held by Yuánhǎi,
he made the emperor serve wine.
Mín, unable to bear his grief and indignation,
prostrated himself twice and presented the wine,
then burst into loud sobs.
The bandit leader disliked him.
Coincidentally, someone accused Mín and Wáng Jùn of plotting to respond to Liú Kūn.
Yuánhǎi then plotted to assassinate the emperor,
and Mín and others were also killed.
Earlier,
before Luòyáng fell,
Mín was a Shìzhōng,
on duty in the palace.
He said to his colleague Xǔ Xiá:
"The ways of the world are like this,
disaster is approaching,
I shall die in this very room!"
And indeed,
he could not escape it.
At the end of the Tàiyuán era,
he was posthumously given the epithet Zhēn.
Yú Ài, courtesy name Zǐsōng.
He was less than seven chí tall,
but his waist measured ten wéi.
He possessed a refined and distant charm.
When he served as the Grand Administrator of Chénliú,
he never let affairs weigh on his mind.
He was at ease, unrestrained,
and simply performed his duties in a perfunctory manner.
Amidst a crowd,
he stood out distinctly.
Once, after reading the works of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
he said:
"They truly accord with my own thoughts."
Grand Commandant Wáng Yǎn held him in high regard.
Yú Ài, seeing the many troubles afflicting the imperial house,
knew that disaster was inevitable.
He then composed a fù to relieve his feelings,
much like Jiǎ Yì did with his "Owl Fù."
Its words are:
"The ultimate truth returns to the undifferentiated One;
Honor and disgrace are indeed of the same thread.
Life and death are already equalized;
Why lament facing death to the fullest?
All things are settled from the very beginning;
One waits for the time to arrive for them to be manifest.
Just as the four seasons naturally cycle,
How could the present situation be far off? And how can there be longevity or an early demise?
Perhaps it is merely that emotions are often entangled in attachment.
The fundamental principles ultimately do not differ at all;
Great virtue is free from desires.
All sentient beings are a manifestation of the spirit;
Foolishness and sagacity are merely built upon inherent qualities.
True men cast off all impurities;
Their nature is vast and boundless.
They roam freely in the vast expanse,
Entrusting their bodies to silent oblivion.
Heaven and Earth are shorter than a morning's life;
A myriad generations are briefer than the first dawn.
Looking upon the universe, it is minute;
Tiny, like half the tip of a hair.
Drifting and soaring in the mysterious and boundless realm,
Deep and serene, free from trivialities.
Immovable, I become one with Nature;
Suddenly, I dissolve and scatter in all directions."
His nephew, Liàng, saw the fù
and asked:
"If you had an intention,
the fù does not fully express it;
If you had no intention,
then what did you compose a fù about?"
He replied:
"It is between having and not having intention!"
He was later promoted to Gentleman of the Department of Personnel.
At that time, the world was fraught with troubles,
and opportunistic changes frequently arose.
Yú Ài always remained quiet and inactive.
He participated in the military affairs of Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, Grand Tutor,
and was transferred to be Libationer for Military Advisers.
At that time, Yuè's establishment had many outstanding talents,
but Yú Ài, among them,
always kept his hands to himself.
Guō Xiàng of Hénán, the Chief Clerk of Yùzhōu Prefecture, was skilled in the works of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi;
contemporaries considered him second only to Wáng Bì.
Yú Ài knew him very well
and often said:
"Why should Guō Zǐxuán necessarily be inferior to Yú Zǐsōng?"
Later, Guō Xiàng became the Grand Tutor's Chief Clerk,
assuming significant power and authority.
Yú Ài said to Guō Xiàng:
"You are truly a great talent of this era;
my intentions from the past are all spent now."
Yú Ài enjoyed great renown
and was highly regarded by the gentry.
However, his accumulation of wealth and property
was criticized by commentators.
Wēn Jiào, the Director of the Department of Criminal Justice, impeached him.
Yú Ài, however, admired Wēn Jiào even more,
describing him as towering like a thousand-zhàng pine tree.
Although it had many gnarled knots,
if used in a grand edifice,
it would serve as a magnificent beam.
At that time, Liú Yú was trusted by Yuè,
and many scholars were implicated by him.
Only Yú Ài detached his mind from worldly affairs,
leaving no trace that could be exploited.
Later, because of Yú Ài's frugal nature and wealthy household,
Liú Yú persuaded Yuè to ask Yú Ài to exchange ten million cash.
He hoped that Yú Ài would be reluctant,
thereby providing an opportunity to exploit him.
Yuè questioned Yú Ài in front of a crowd.
Yú Ài, however, was slumped over, already drunk,
his cè (head covering) having fallen onto the low table.
He put his head through the hole to retrieve it,
and slowly replied:
"Your subordinate has twenty million in his household;
Your Excellency may take as much as you wish."
Liú Yú was then convinced.
Yuè was very pleased
and consequently said:
"One cannot judge the heart of a junzǐ with the thoughts of a xiǎorén."
Wáng Yǎn did not associate with Yú Ài,
but Yú Ài constantly addressed him as 'qīng' (you, familiar).
Wáng Yǎn said:
"You cannot do that."
Yú Ài replied:
"You address me as 'jūn' (lord, respectful),
I address you as 'qīng'.
I use my family's custom,
you use your family's custom."
Wáng Yǎn found this quite remarkable.
During Shí Lè's rebellion,
he was killed along with Wáng Yǎn,
at the age of fifty.
Guō Xiàng
Guō Xiàng, courtesy name Zǐxuán,
showed talent and reason in his youth,
enjoyed Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
and was skilled in qīngtán.
Grand Commandant Wáng Yǎn often said:
"Listening to Guō Xiàng speak
is like water pouring from a hanging river,
it flows continuously and never runs dry."
He was invited by prefectures and commanderies
but did not accept.
He often lived in seclusion,
entertaining himself with essays and discussions.
Later, he was appointed Clerk to the Minister of Works,
and gradually rose to become Yellow Gate Attendant.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè appointed him Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor,
and he was deeply trusted and relied upon,
thus he held office and wielded power,
his influence extending both inside and outside the court.
Consequently, his former reputation declined.
He died of illness at the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
leaving behind twelve chapters of "Bēi Lùn."
Before this, there were dozens of commentators on the Zhuāngzi,
but none could fully grasp its central meaning.
Xiàng Xiù, going beyond the old commentaries, offered his own interpretations,
brilliantly expounding its subtle meanings,
and greatly promoting the xuánxué style.
However, Xiàng Xiù died before completing the chapters "Qiū Shuǐ" and "Zhì Lè."
Xiàng Xiù's son was young,
and his interpretations were scattered,
though there were quite a few alternative versions circulating.
Guō Xiàng's character was rather shallow.
Seeing that Xiàng Xiù's interpretations were not widely known,
he secretly appropriated them as his own commentary.
He then personally annotated the chapters "Qiū Shuǐ" and "Zhì Lè,"
and also revised the "Mǎ Tí" chapter,
while for the other chapters, he merely punctuated and corrected sentences.
Later, alternative versions of Xiàng Xiù's interpretations emerged.
Therefore, today there are two versions of the Zhuāngzi commentary, those of Xiàng and Guō,
but their meanings are identical.
Yú Chún (Zǐfū)
Yú Chún, courtesy name Móufǔ.
He was widely learned and possessed both talent and righteousness,
making him a Confucian master of his time.
He was appointed Chief Clerk by the commandery,
then participated in the staff of the General Who Attacks the South,
and was successively promoted to Yellow Gate Attendant.
He was enfeoffed as an Attendant Marquis,
and successively served as Central Secretariat Director and Administrator of Hénán.
Initially,
Chún considered Jiǎ Chōng to be a treacherous sycophant,
and together with Rèn Kǎi, they advocated sending Chōng to guard Guānzhōng in the west.
Chōng was therefore displeased.
Chōng once hosted a banquet for court officials,
and Chún arrived late.
Chōng said to him,
"You usually lead others,
why are you late today?"
Chún replied,
"This morning there were some small market matters that were not settled,
which is why I am late."
It was said that Chún's ancestors once included a footman,
and Chōng's ancestors included a market rogue.
Chōng and Chún used this to mock each other.
Chōng, believing his position to be high and his reputation weighty,
was very displeased.
When Chún offered wine,
Chōng did not drink promptly.
Chún said,
"As an elder, one should accept a toast;
how dare you refuse!"
Chōng said,
"If an old man does not return to provide for his parents,
what is there to say!"
Chún then grew angry and said,
"Jiǎ Chōng!
The chaos in the world
is due to you alone."
Chōng replied,
"I assisted two emperors,
and pacified Bāshǔ;
what crime have I committed that the world is in chaos because of it?"
Chún said,
"Where is Gāoguì Xiānggōng?"
The company dispersed at once.
Chōng's attendants wanted to seize Chún,
but Zhōnghùjūn Yáng Xiù and Shìzhōng Wáng Jì protected him,
and he was able to leave.
Chōng was ashamed and angry,
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post.
Chún, in fear,
submitted his seals and ribbons as Hénán Yǐn and Guānnéihóu,
and submitted a memorial impeaching himself, saying:
"Sīkōng Gōng Jiǎ Chōng invited various ministers and officials, including myself.
I overestimated myself
and drank too much wine.
In my drunken confusion, I offered wine,
refilling his cup repeatedly;
the Duke refused to drink,
and in the exchange of words,
the Duke reprimanded me, saying that as an old man I did not return to provide for my parents,
and that I was without Heaven and Earth.
I did not confess my fault and withdraw,
but instead became more angry,
and loudly called the Duke by his name,
creating a temporary uproar,
and thus becoming reckless.
According to the Rites,
'at eighty, one is exempt from court duties,'
precisely because in old age,
changes and difficulties are unpredictable.
I did not consider the grace of my birth and upbringing,
to seek to support my elderly father,
but clung to my salary and coveted glory,
being inferior even to birds.
Chōng, as a Sāngōng,
discusses the Dao and promotes transformation,
and reproached me with righteous instruction,
which is correct.
Yet, I wrongly blamed the innocent,
and as a subordinate offended a superior;
drunk and confused,
I behaved in a disorderly manner.
I, with my ordinary talent,
was promoted to an important position.
The Yìjīng warns against 'wetting the head,'
and the Shuōyuàn speaks of the harms of drunkenness,
yet I heard righteousness but did not comply,
my excessive words filled the hall,
defiling and disrespecting the Duke,
violating regulations and norms,
and thus cannot be an example.
I request the court to dismiss me from office,
the Grand Judge to conclude my guilt,
and the Grand Herald to strip me of my title and territory.
I was not careful in controlling myself,
and I await my deserved punishment."
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Kǒng Xún impeached Chún,
requesting his dismissal from office.
The imperial edict stated:
"The former kings upheld the rites of superiority and inferiority,
clarified the order of nobility and lowliness,
established the virtue of gentleness and restraint,
and recorded the calamities of heavy intoxication,
thereby glorifying and proclaiming moral transformation,
and showing people a standard of conduct.
In the past, Guǎnghàn disregarded the prime minister
and incurred the penalty for offending a superior;
Guàn Fū used drunkenness as an excuse to vent his anger
and suffered the crime of execution.
Chún, with his ordinary talent,
occupied the position of minister and magistrate,
but did not consider the virtue of humility and reverence,
nor heed the warning of a capsized cart;
he was disrespectful to his superior,
and uttered perverse words from his mouth.
He ought to be clearly dismissed and demoted,
to rectify the court order."
Thus, Chún was dismissed from office.
Furthermore, concerning Chún's elderly father not being supported,
it was ordered that the matter be formally judged according to the rites and canons.
Tàifù Hé Céng, Tàiwèi Xún Yǐ, and Piàojì Jiāngjūn Qí Wáng Yōu deliberated, saying:
"To judge and rectify right and wrong,
one should first consult the rites and laws.
For those eighty years of age,
one son is exempt from government service;
for those ninety years of age,
their family is exempt from government service.
The new laws also stipulate this.
According to records, Chún's father is eighty-one years old,
and he has six brothers.
Three are at home,
so the duty of serving and supporting him is not neglected.
That Chún did not seek to provide support
is not a violation of the rites or laws.
Sīkōng Gōng considered Chún to be an official holding a position of minister and magistrate,
expecting him to be superior to others.
Yet Chún, in his drunken state,
gave vent to his anger.
We believe that Chún did not exemplify the profound conduct of filial piety,
but rather succumbed to the common failings of ordinary people,
and thus deserves censure and demotion."
Sītú Shí Bāo deliberated:
"Chún, in his pursuit of official glory, forgot his parent,
and was unwilling to hear frank words.
He is disloyal and unfilial,
and should be stripped of his name, title, and territory."
Sītú Xīcáozhuàn Liú Bīn deliberated, believing:
"To strengthen customs,
human relations are primary;
and in the teaching of human relations,
loyalty and filial piety are central.
Loyal, one does not forget one's lord;
filial, one does not forget one's parent.
If filial piety must mean exclusive devotion to caring for one's parents,
then an enlightened ruler would have no ministers;
if loyalty must mean disregard for one's parents,
then parents would have no children.
Therefore, a minister
must use righteousness to temper his affection;
and a son
must use emotion to cut off his righteousness.
At court, one follows the lord's command;
at home, one follows the father's rules.
Only then can both lord and father be satisfied,
and loyalty and filial piety each find their proper place.
Chún's elder brother Jùn requested to return home due to their father's old age.
If Jùn were allowed to return,
Chún would have no reason not to return;
if Jùn were not allowed to return,
Chún would have no reason to return.
Although Chún himself requested it,
it was likewise not granted.
Recently, Sūn Hé, Administrator of Liáodōng, and Dèng Liáng, Administrator of Guǎnghàn, both had elderly mothers.
Liáng had no brothers,
and was appointed to a distant commandery;
he struggled to return home,
but was not granted permission.
Moreover, Chún recently served as Jīngyǐn,
and his father was within the jurisdiction,
so he could regularly request to visit and pay respects.
To singularly apply demotion and dismissal to him outside of ritual and law,
I, Bīn, foolishly believe is unreasonable.
According to the rites,
when one reaches eighty,
one son is exempt from government service.
Chún has two younger brothers at home,
so he did not violate the rites.
Furthermore, the regulation states
that only at ninety
are all permitted to return.
Currently, Chún's father is not yet ninety,
so he did not violate the regulation.
Insulting the prime minister
should warrant dismissal,
to uphold national laws.
The imperial grace is compassionate and generous,
showing demotion as a punishment;
I, your foolish subject, have no further clear opinion."
Hénán Gōngcáoshǐ Páng Zhá and others submitted a memorial, saying: "Your subject's former prefectural magistrate, Guānnéihóu Chún,
lost his composure when drunk.
The imperial edict of Wùshēn already dismissed him from his magistrate post,
and regarding his seriously ill elderly father not being supported,
it was referred to the Five Offices to be deliberated upon according to
The Rites canon corrects their right and wrong.
Your servant humbly observes the system of the Three Kings for supporting the aged:
At eighty,
one son is exempt from public service;
at ninety,
his family is exempt from public service.
This truly enables
people to not neglect the way of filial support,
and ensures that ministers do not violate the principles of public service.
The Former Kings established rites and left instructions,
none more esteemed than those of the Zhōu.
At that time,
Jī Gōng
remained in Zhōu,
Bó Qín went to Lǔ;
filial sons were never lacking,
and rites were without transgression.
Now the ducal administration discusses
a seventy-year-old system,
an eighty-month system,
desiring to annul and revoke the limit
on holding office,
and abolish titles and fiefs.
This is to legislate for Gōng Dàn,
then to violate it himself,
making the Marquis of Lǔ, as his son,
the primary recipient of punishment.
Shí Fèn reached a hundred,
and his four sons
were all appointed to commanderies.
Recently, the Grand Tutor offered his sons to the king,
who also served outside the imperial domain.
Ancient and modern are in accord,
loyalty and filial piety both flourishing.
Your servant has heard that faults of regret and humiliation
are possessed by gentlemen.
Yǐn's nature was to drink little but often,
eventually leading to utter intoxication.
When Yǐn awoke and learned of it,
he grieved and regretted his past error,
humbly admitted
his fault,
and deeply impeached himself in a memorial,
seeking to incur severe penalties.
Now the ducal administration does not investigate the circumstances,
but calls it arrogance and obstinacy.
This is to treat drunkenness as a serious offense,
and obliterate the meaning
of returning to rectitude after error.
Your servant has heard that the relationship between father and son is a natural bond,
love arising spontaneously.
The interaction between ruler and minister
originates from a union of righteousness,
and one seeks loyal ministers primarily among filial sons.
Therefore,
the Former Kings established rites
to show reverence for one's father,
from beginning to end,
equaling one's birth parents.
Even so, they still worried that ministers rarely dedicated themselves fully.
Now the ducal administration discusses and says:
Although ritual
laws have fixed limits,
regarding illness or returning home for care,
one's aspirations should not be taken away.
If this is the case, then rites would forbid uprightness,
and trap people in deceit,
violating the royal
ordinances,
and opening a dangerous source of trouble.
Yǐn has endured hardship since youth,
caring for his parents with cheerful service.
Having served in various internal and external posts,
he has been public-spirited and incorruptible.
This is why His Majesty has repeatedly issued clear edicts,
and why Yǐn has continually been promoted and appointed.
Yǐn conducts himself with humility,
and leads his subordinates with reverence.
Putting the public before himself
has truly been his long-held intention.
Suddenly, due to drunkenness,
he is accused
of violence and disrespect.
The memorial accuses him of disloyalty and unfilial conduct,
and the various dukes propose abolishing his titles and fiefs.
This is why your foolish servant grieves and laments for himself,
clasping his heart and weeping tears of blood.
It is now decreed that if parents are over eighty,
〔一０〕their sons are permitted not to be assigned positions outside the limited period,
truly to allow them the opportunity to return home.
Now Yǐn resides within
the commandery,
and previously often memorialized, receiving repeated permission for visits.
Yǐn has six brothers,
three of whom are at home,
and filial support is not neglected.
His elder brother, Attendant Censor Jùn,
the eldest legitimate son of the family,
previously
memorialized himself,
requesting to return home to provide support,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
The national system and law are the same;
brothers are no different.
To falsely accuse Yǐn of not seeking to provide support in this manner,
your servant fears will enhance the name
of speciousness,
and diminish the reality of loyalty and sincerity.
Indeed, rites
are what govern the state
and secure the altars of soil and grain.
Thus, the flourishing of Táo Táng
followed the ancient canons;
the excellence of Zhōu Chéng
adhered to old regulations.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty, with your sagely and discerning virtue,
upholds rites and promotes education,
consulting the Four Peaks
to examine the canonical system.
Yǐn receives punishment
for his transgression,
but the cause was drunkenness.
The duke receives blame for his doctrines,
but the reason was indignation.
To establish righteousness from accumulated indignation,
to incur guilt from drunkenness,
the ritual laws are no longer
the decisive factor,
but a contrived argument is desired to establish law.
This is why your foolish servant dares to risk the penalty of death,
and is ashamed if I fail to express myself in this enlightened age.
I only ask for your merciful consideration.
The Emperor again issued an edict saying:
“Since the Middle Ages,
many have yielded to the wishes of the honored and powerful,
while the humble have generated feelings.
This is why Shì Zhī and Dìng Guó were able to make their names in previous generations.
Now, when criticizing Yǔ Chún,
one does not consider his gentle and amiable nature.
To blame him for drunkenness and indulgence,
this is to demand sage-like purity from people.
I suspect Jiǎ Gōng was also drunk;
if he were not drunk,
he would certainly not have blamed him among a hundred guests for not resigning from office to provide support.
The Great Jìn relies on the rites of the sages
to regulate the proper conduct of ministers and sons,
and if all those of eighty should return for support,
it is not exclusively Chún.
The ancients said: 'Words spoken due to drunkenness
are like those from a young goat.'
Clearly, one does not blame drunkenness,
lest one err in judgment.
The reason for excusing Chún
should be to serve as a warning for future drunkenness.
Qí Wáng and Liú Yuàn's discussions are appropriate.”
Chún was then made National University Libationer [guó zǐ jì jiǔ],
with the added title of Palace Attendant [sàn qí cháng shí].
Later, General Xún Pān, at a court assembly, memorialized that Chún had previously been dismissed for unfilial conduct,
and should not be promoted.
Attendant Censor Zhēn Dé stepped forward and said:
“Filial piety's greatest manifestation is to make one's parents prominent,
and to provide for them with emoluments is an honor.
The imperial edict pardoned Chún's former transgression,
promoted him to close attendant,
and additionally placed him in charge of teaching officials.
This was the day Chún was summoned without awaiting his carriage.
Yet General Xún Pān dared to use his private opinion to disparage public discourse,
speak out in defiance,
and deceive the imperial court.
He should be demoted and dismissed.”
Pān was dismissed from office for this.
Originally,
Pān and Chún were both invited by the Grand General.
Pān wore splendid carriages and clothes,
while Chún maintained simplicity.
Pān felt ashamed and resentful of this.
At this point,
he slandered Chún.
After Pān was dismissed,
Chún, instead feeling ashamed for him,
frequently went to console and encourage him.
People at the time praised Chún for his magnanimity.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant [shì zhōng],
and resigned from office due to his father's mourning.
He was recalled as Censor-in-Chief [yù shǐ zhōng chéng],
then transferred to Minister of Personnel [shàng shū].
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Wèi Commandery [wèi jūn tài shǒu],
but did not take up the post,
instead being appointed Minister of the Privy Treasury [shǎo fǔ].
He died at the age of sixty-four.
His son was Fū.
Fū, courtesy name Yǔnzāng.
From a young age, he possessed integrity and a clean character.
He successively held the position of Bóshì.
When Qí Wáng Yōu was to go to his state,
the matter was submitted to the officials of rites to deliberate on the objects for his enhanced bestowal.
Fū, along with Bóshì Tàishū Guǎng, Liú Tūn, Miáo Wèi, Guō Yí, Qín Xiù, Fù Zhēn, and others, submitted a memorial, remonstrating: The Shū says,
“Emperor Yáo was able to manifest his eminent virtue,
thereby bringing harmony to the nine clans.”
When King Wǔ brought the world under his rule,
there were sixteen states of his brothers,
and forty
states of his own clan.
The great meritorious ministers and close relatives
were honored with special rites,
and the states of Lǔ, Wèi, Qí, and Jìn were greatly expanded in territory,
and all received distributed ritual vessels.
This is what is meant by "where virtue resides,
kin and stranger
are one."
When the great Jìn arose,
it emulated the distant achievements of Táng and Zhōu.
The royal family's relatives,
and ministers who aided in the founding of the dynasty,
all received titles and lands,
and the four seas were at peace.
Now Wú
and Huì have been pacified.
An imperial edict commands the Dà Sīmǎ, Qí Wáng, to go out and govern the frontier regions.
He should then comfort his state
and prepare to conform to the ancient classics,
to establish a lasting system.
In ancient times, when the Zhōu dynasty selected and established those of illustrious virtue to assist the royal house,
then Zhōu Gōng served as Tàizǎi,
Kāng Shū as Sīkòu,
and Dān Jì as Sīkōng.
And the states of Shào,
Ruì, Bì, Máo, and others
all held positions as Gōngqīng and Dàfū within the court,
clarifying that the responsibility of a trusted minister is heavy,
while the position of guarding a territory is light.
We have never heard of ancient classics dictating that someone holding the important position of "Three Matters"
should be sent out to a state.
Under the Hàn dynasty, the feudal princes and kings held high positions and great power,
above the chéngxiàng and Sān Gōng.
Those who entered to assist in court affairs
then held concurrent offices;
but when
they were sent out to their states,
they were not again granted the empty title of a high official for the sake of elevated favor.
In ancient times, Shēn Wúyǔ said,
“The five great ones should not be on the borders.”
Earlier scholars believed this referred to favored sons and grandsons of nobles,
who held the position of chief minister for generations.
He also said,
“The five small ones should not
be in the court.”
Earlier scholars believed this meant the lowly harming the noble,
the young disrespecting the old,
the distant alienating the close,
the new alienating the old,
and the small overriding the great.
“Not in the court”
means not governing in the imperial court.
He also said:
“Close relatives should not be outside,
and strangers should not be inside.
Now Qìjí is outside,
and Zhèng Dān is inside;
Your Lord should be a little wary of this.”
Shū Xiàng had a saying:
“When the ducal house is about to decline,
its branches and leaves fall first.”
The ducal clan is
the root of the ducal house,
and to abandon it
is what the proverb calls "relying on it while cutting its branches and trunk."
Now, if Qí Wáng is worthy,
then it is not proper for him, with the high status of an imperial younger brother,
to hold the ordinary office of Lǔ and Wèi;
if he is unworthy,
it is not proper to greatly expand his territory
and establish
him in Dōnghǎi.
According to ancient rites,
the Sān Gōng had no specific duties;
they sat and discussed the Way.
We have not heard of them being burdened with regional appointments.
It was only when the Zhōu house suffered great decline,
and King Xuān achieved a revival,
with the four
barbarians repeatedly invading,
and the urgency of the situation was constant,
that Duke Shào Mù was then ordered to campaign against the Huái Yí.
Thus, its poem says,
“When the Xú regions did not return,
the King said, ‘Return swiftly.’”
The prime minister was not permitted
to remain outside for long.
Today, the world is settled,
and the universe is one family.
We should frequently summon the Sān Shì
to discuss the foundations of great peace,
yet instead, he is sent out,
two
thousand *lǐ* away from the royal city,
deviating from ancient precedents.
Fū drafted the memorial,
first showing it to his father, Chún,
who did not forbid it.
Tàicháng Zhèng Mò and Bóshì Jìjiǔ Cáo Zhì both regarded their action as excessive.
Emperor Wǔ was greatly angered that the Bóshì did not answer what was asked
but answered what was not asked.
The matter was referred to the relevant authorities.
Shàngshū Zhū Zhěng, Chǔ Sì, and others memorialized:
“Fū and his colleagues infringed upon officials' duties, abandoned their positions,
confused and misled the court,
embellished malicious words,
and presumptuously spoke without restraint.
We request that Fū and the other eight persons be arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi for sentencing.”
Fū's father, Chún, went to the Tíngwèi to confess:
“Fū showed me the draft memorial,
and in my foolish superficiality, I approved of it.”
An imperial edict absolved Chún of his crime.
Tíngwèi Liú Sòng again memorialized that Fū and his colleagues committed a great disrespect,
deserving execution in the marketplace,
and sought public deliberation.
The Shàngshū again memorialized, requesting approval for the Tíngwèi to carry out the execution.
Shàngshū Xiàhóu Jùn said to Zhū Zhěng:
“The state actually wishes to execute remonstrating ministers!
The Eight Divisions of officials were established
precisely for such times.
You should join me in refuting and correcting this.”
Zhěng did not comply.
Jùn rose in anger,
saying:
“This is not what I expected!”
Then he alone drafted a dissenting opinion.
Zuǒ Púyè Wèi Shū, Yòu Púyè Xiàpéi Wáng Huǎng, and others followed Jùn’s proposal.
The memorial was held in the palace for seven days.
Then an imperial edict stated:
“Fū and others, as scholars,
did not reflect on upholding the imperial regulations,
did not directly answer what was asked,
but dared to spread their deceitful words
to disturb the emperor’s sight and hearing.
Fū, being the principal author of this proposal,
should be punished with death.
However, since Fū and his family all confessed,
great sincerity cannot be denied.
Qín Xiù and Fù Zhēn had previously been presumptuous
and luckily escaped punishment,
but they did not learn from it
and should be punished with death
to expose their wickedness.
Yet, I still cannot bear to do so.
All of them are granted their lives.
Xiù, Zhēn, Fū, and others are all stripped of their titles.”
Several years later,
he was reinstated as Sànqí Shìláng.
He ended his career as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
Qín Xiù.
Qín Xiù,
courtesy name Xuánliáng,
was a native of Yúnzhōng, Xīnxīng.
His father, Lǎng,
was a Wèi Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Xiù was diligent in study and conduct from a young age,
and was known for his loyalty and integrity.
During the Xiánníng era,
he served as Bóshì.
When Hé Zēng died,
the matter was submitted to the officials of rites to deliberate on his posthumous name.
Xiù's deliberation stated: The late Tàizǎi Hé Zēng,
though he ascended through the lineage of an eminent family,
was known from a young age for his lofty and dignified solemnity,
and prominently entered the imperial court.
He had a reputation for showing filial care to his parents,
and in office,
he presented reform policies and model regulations.
These two aspects truly captured the essence of a minister serving his sovereign and a son serving his parents.
However, his disposition was arrogant and extravagant,
and he did not adhere to rules and regulations.
The Shī says:
“Lofty is that Southern Mountain,
with
its rocky peaks so grand;
illustrious is Master Yǐn,
all the people look up to him.”
This speaks of his lofty and eminent virtue and conduct,
acting always in accordance with rites.
Qiū Míng said:
“Frugality
is the reverence of virtue;
Extravagance
is the greatest evil."
When the great Jìn dynasty received the Mandate,
Táng Zēng, despite his modest and humble beginnings,
received favor across two generations,
and became prominent for generations.
By the age of sixty (when his ears were attuned to all sounds),
he held the position of one of the Three
Dukes,
received rent from a large state,
enjoyed the prestige of a guardian and tutor,
and managed the balance of the Sītú.
Both of his sons were high-ranking officials with golden cicada caps,
and were arrayed beside the Emperor.
Compared to the ancients,
his responsibilities were profound and his burdens heavy;
even if his entire family had died,
it still would not have matched his position.
Yet, he was excessively arrogant and extravagant,
his reputation spread across the nine regions,
his conduct did not follow the Way,
yet he enjoyed an extraordinary
position.
From the perspective of ancient righteousness,
not only did he fail in his duty as a chief minister,
but he also violated the benefit of "cutting metal" (i.e., steadfast friendship).
To soil the beauty of the imperial era,
to corrupt the teachings of human relations,
to create the ugliness of the world,
and
to demonstrate arrogance to future generations,
nothing was greater than this.
Since recent times,
no prime minister or chief minister
has ever received such a stained and humiliating reputation,
been impeached by the relevant authorities,
or had father and sons be defiled and burdened, yet still receive grace and leniency as Táng Zēng did.
The Duke of Zhōu mourned the decline of the Two Jì (King Wén and King Wǔ),
and grieved that the great teachings were not practiced,
whereupon he created posthumous titles to record their end.
Zēng Shēn revered this principle;
when he was about to die, he returned his life whole,
changing
his mat before he passed away.
This demonstrates the care taken in one's end,
persisting until death.
The historians of Qí,
mere vassals in a chaotic age,
still recorded their ruler's crimes,
unpunished even unto death.
How much more so should the officials
who uphold the canons of the imperial era
dare not fear the powerful and mighty,
and fully observe propriety?
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are called the Four Pillars;
if the Four Pillars are not upheld,
the state will
perish."
Prime ministers and high officials
are models for the people.
If they live out their desires to the extreme
and suffer no denigration after death,
then the imperial house has no righteous laws.
What then will princes and nobles
fear?
What will the so-called Four Pillars
be founded upon?
Carefully examining the posthumous naming rules:
"When name and reality diverge, it is called 'Móu' (謬);
when one relies on chaos to act recklessly, it is called 'Chǒu' (醜)."
Táng Zēng's conduct,
in all respects,
was in agreement with these.
He should be posthumously titled Móu Chǒu Gōng.
Although the proposal was not adopted at the time,
those who heard it were afraid.
Wáng Xiù's nature abhorred slander and flattery,
and he detested them as enemies.
He had always looked down upon Jiǎ Chōng,
and when the campaign against Wú was launched,
hearing that Jiǎ Chōng was appointed Grand Commander,
he said to his intimates:
"Jiǎ Chōng is a minor talent in paperwork,
yet he is given the great responsibility of attacking a nation.
I shall weep to send off the army."
Someone tried to stop Wáng Xiù, saying:
"In ancient times, Jiǎn Shū knew the Qín army would surely be defeated,
and so he wept when sending off his son.
Now the ruler of Wú is without the Way,
and the state shows signs of self-destruction.
When the various commanders cross the border,
they will rout without a battle.
Your weeping,
being unwise,
will be an unforgivable crime."
Thereupon, Wáng Xiù stopped.
When Sūn Hào surrendered to Wáng Jùn,
Jiǎ Chōng did not yet know of it,
and was still arguing that Wú could not be pacified,
presenting a memorial requesting the army be recalled.
Jiǎ Chōng's memorial arrived at the same time as the victory report.
The court and the populace generally believed that Jiǎ Chōng, whose position was above others,
had wisdom below others,
and all agreed that Wáng Xiù's words were perceptive.
When Jiǎ Chōng died,
Wáng Xiù proposed:
"Jiǎ Chōng did not pass his inheritance to his clansmen,
but took someone of a different surname as his heir,
violating propriety and drowning in emotion,
thus disrupting the great human relations.
In ancient times, the state of Zēng adopted an external grandson, a son of Jǔ, as its heir.
The 'Chūnqiū' records 'The people of Jǔ destroyed Zēng.'
How could the sages not know that an external grandson is kin?
But by reasoning from righteousness,
there is no father-son relationship.
Furthermore, according to the imperial edict, 'Unless one's merit is like that of the Grand Tutor,
or one's enfeoffment had no heir like that of the Grand Tutor,
and the person adopted must be one's own natural child like that of the Grand Tutor,
one cannot be compared to him.'
Thus, to take an external grandson as heir,
unless one has extraordinary merit and prominent virtue,
it is not permissible.
How could the rites for the Son of Heaven
allow this?
It cuts off the blood sacrifices to ancestors,
and opens the gate of calamity for the court.
The posthumous naming rule says, 'Chaotic and confused conduct is called 'Huāng' (荒).'
I request he be posthumously titled Huāng Gōng."
This was not followed.
Wáng Jùn had the merit of pacifying Wú,
but was slandered and disparaged by Wáng Hún.
Although the Emperor did not comply,
he did not clearly reward or punish,
making Wáng Jùn the General Who Guards the State.
The whole world resented this.
Wáng Xiù then submitted a memorial saying:
"Since the great Jìn began its destiny,
the title 'General Who Guards the State'
has generally been granted based on old favors.
This means Wáng Jùn, at a time when he had no merit,
received a prominent position among the nine ranks,
and after achieving merit, he received the humiliating title of a favored person.
How can the four seas view this
without disappointment?
Shǔ was small, Wú was large;
after pacifying Shǔ,
two generals were both promoted to the Three Excellencies.
Now Wáng Jùn returns and is demoted,
how can the world not be confused?
Before Wú was destroyed,
even with the divine martiality of the Three Ancestors,
they personally endured its humiliation.
The empty name of Sūn Hào
was enough to alarm and stir up all of Xià.
Each minor expedition,
even if the sacred heart knew it was on the verge of collapse,
still filled the central states with fear and panic.
At that time,
if someone could lend the Son of Heaven a million troops,
pacify and possess it,
and form a fraternal alliance with the state,
I fear the court and the populace would all gladly accept it.
Now Wáng Jùn led the troops of Shǔ-Hàn,
and pacified Wú in a few tens of days.
Even if all the treasures of Wú were given to him,
it was not originally his to have;
why calculate and quibble over it now?"
Later, he discussed the matter of Qí Wáng Yōu with Liú Tūn and others,
which displeased the Emperor,
and he was removed from office.
Soon after, he was reappointed as a Doctor.
Wáng Xiù was by nature upright and stubborn,
and often clashed with others.
He served as a Doctor for nearly twenty years in total,
and died in office.
The Grand Scribe comments: Qí Xiànwáng, with his illustrious virtue and close familial ties,
managed the state and discussed its governance,
truly rectifying all affairs
and establishing the constant human relationships.
Emperor Wǔ embraced the wicked schemes of treacherous flatterers,
harboring long-term concerns from beginning to end,
and thus made him ruler of this Qīngtǔ [Region],
a shepherd of the eastern fiefdom.
Those near and far were shocked and dismayed,
and the court and common people were disappointed.
Cáo Zhì and others, devoted to their teachings and righteousness,
walked in step with the Confucian school.
They were resolute and selfless,
wholeheartedly serving the state.
Thus, they could speak out at the Phoenix Palace,
offending the Dragon Scales.
Though their persons were temporarily suppressed,
their Way was greatly advanced!
The Yǔ clan, generation after generation, possessed pure virtue,
and were well-regarded by the world.
That Yǐngchuān and Rǔyǐng produced many exceptional scholars,
it is from this that they drew their reputation.
Móu Fǔ inherently detested flattery and wickedness,
yet he spoke out when drunk and full.
To throw a rat yet fear the vessel,
how can such words be easily uttered?
To steal another's property
is still called theft.
Zǐ Xuán, usurping praise and seizing good deeds,
is this not theft?
A eulogy says: Wèi’s ramparts,
Jìběi was renowned.
Yǐngchuān had many scholars,
Jùn also stood out brilliantly.
Chángcén upheld righteousness,
the Libationer relinquished glory.
Móu Fǔ, after three cups,
drunkenness arose.
Xiàng both seized good deeds,
Xiù only hated evil.
Fū offered excellent advice,
almost facing the cauldron.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 21, Huángfǔ Mì (Zǐ Fānghuí)
Huángfǔ Mì, courtesy name Shì'ān,
originally named Jìng,
was a native of Cháonà in Āndìng.
He was the great-grandson of Hàn Grand Commandant Sōng.
He was adopted by his paternal uncle,
and moved to live in Xīn'ān.
At twenty years old,
he disliked studying,
and was dissolute and unrestrained,
some thought him foolish.
Whenever he obtained melons or fruits,
he would offer them to his adoptive paternal aunt, née Rèn.
Née Rèn said:
"The Classic of Filial Piety says: 'Even the sustenance of three animals
is still considered unfilial.'
You are now over twenty years old,
your eyes do not hold to teachings,
your heart does not enter the Way.
You have nothing to comfort me with."
She then sighed and said:
"In the past, Mèng Mǔ moved three times to cultivate benevolence.
Zēng Fù cooked a pig to preserve teaching.
Is it that I did not choose my neighbors well,
or that my teaching was lacking,
that you are so dull and slow?
Cultivating yourself and diligently studying,
that is for you to achieve;
what has it to do with me!"
Then, facing him, she wept.
Mì was thus moved,
and went to the village elder Xí Tǎn to receive instruction,
working diligently without slackening.
Living in poverty,
he personally engaged in farming,
carrying classics while working in the fields,
and thus extensively studied the canons and texts of the Hundred Schools.
He was quiet and had few desires,
and gradually developed a lofty aspiration,
taking writing as his duty.
He styled himself Xuányàn Xiānshēng.
He authored treatises on rites and music, and on the sagely and true.
Later, he contracted a wind-paralysis illness,
yet his hands never ceased holding scrolls.
Some advised Mì to cultivate his reputation and expand his social circle,
but Mì believed:
"Who but a sage can simultaneously uphold both engagement and reclusion?
Dwelling in the countryside, one can also delight in the Way of Yáo and Shùn.
Why must one value connecting with worldly gain,
and be entangled in official duties,
to achieve fame?"
He wrote the Xuánshǒu Lùn to answer them,
saying: Someone said to Mì:
"Wealth and status are what people desire,
poverty and lowliness are what people dislike.
Why do you abandon your body to endure destitution and not change?
Moreover, what the Way
values is managing the world;
what people praise
is acting in a timely manner.
Sir, your years are advanced and your teeth are changing,
you suffer from hunger and cold,
you might die and be abandoned in a ditch—
who would know you?"
Mì said:
"What people most cherish
is life;
what the Way must preserve
is the physical form;
what one's nature and form cannot tolerate
is illness.
If
one disturbs the complete Way to harm one's nature and life,
how can one escape poverty and lowliness to preserve what one desires?
I have heard that those who eat another's emolument harbor another's worries.
Even the strong cannot bear it,
how much less
my weak and ailing self!
Moreover, poverty is common for a scholar,
and lowliness is the reality of the Way.
Dwelling in the common and attaining the real,
one will have no worries until death.
How does that compare to those who seek wealth and status, disturbing their spirit and exhausting their essence?
Furthermore, to live unknown to others,
and to die unmourned by others—
this is the ultimate!
The deaf and mute,
these are the truly enlightened ones in the world.
If one person dies
and the world laments,
it is considered a loss;
if one person lives and the four seas rejoice,
it is considered a gain.
However, lamentation and rejoicing do not truly benefit the dead or harm the living.
Therefore, the ultimate Way
does not diminish,
and ultimate virtue does not increase.
Why?
Because it is complete in itself.
If one were to turn the thoughts of the world
to pursue the misfortune of harming life,
and employ the hearts of the four seas
to expand the illness of non-benefit,
how could that be the pinnacle of morality?
Only by being without diminution
is one ultimately firm;
only by being without increase
is one ultimately profound.
Because it is firm, it will never
diminish;
because it is profound, it will never be superficial.
If one can embody the reality of firmness and profundity,
and dwell in the truth of non-superficiality,
standing beyond gain and loss,
and roaming beyond the physical form,
then my
Way will be complete."
Thus, he did not take office.
He indulged in and delighted in classical texts,
forgetting sleep and food,
and people at the time called him
"Book Glutton."
Someone cautioned him against his excessive devotion,
fearing it would harm and exhaust his spirit.
Mì said:
"If one hears the Way in the morning,
one may die in the evening without regret.
Moreover, the length of one's life is fixed by Heaven!"
His uncle's son had reached manhood,
and Mì, at forty, lost his adoptive mother.
So he returned to his original clan.
Liáng Liǔ, the Administrator of Chéngyáng and Mì's maternal cousin,
was about to take up his post.
People advised Mì to see him off.
Mì said:
"When Liǔ was a commoner and visited me,
I did not go out of the door to welcome or send him off.
My meals consisted of nothing more than salted vegetables.
The poor do not offer wine and meat as a ritual.
Now to see him off because he is taking up a governorship,
would be to value the Administrator of Chéngyáng and despise Liáng Liǔ.
Is this the Way of ancient people?
This is not what my heart finds peace in."
At that time, Wèi Jùn summoned a registrar for the annual report,
and nominated filial and incorrupt officials.
In the early Jiǐngyuán era,
the Chancellor offered him a post,
but he did not accept any of them.
Later, his relatives and friends urged him to accept the invitation,
so Mì composed the "Shì Quàn Lùn" (Discourse on Explaining Persuasion) to make his intentions clear.
Its words were: "The Chancellor, the King of Jìn, summoned thirty-seven of us.
When Tàishǐ ascended the throne,
all those who had received the same summons arrived without exception,
and were all appointed as Jìdūwèi.
Some were granted the noble title of
Guānnèi Hóu,
and were invited to attend court,
with courtesies like those of imperial attendants.
Only I was severely ill,
and could not enjoy the imperial favor.
My kinsmen, elders, and colleagues
all believed that it was a
great celebration for the world,
and all people relied on it.
Although the rites were not yet complete,
it was inappropriate to remain at ease.
Even if my illness was severe,
I should still present myself.
I reflected on the systems of wise kings, ancient and modern,
that for matters,
great or small,
decisions were made based on circumstances.
I am truly incapable due to my health;
how could it be out of disrespect!
So I lay on my pillow and sighed, saying:
'Advancing
is the glory of the person;
retreating
is the
reality of one's fate.
If I were not ill,
and insisted on holding fast to the seclusion of Jīshān,
I should still be tolerated,
let alone when I am truly gravely ill!
Therefore, in the eras of Yáo and Shùn,
some scholars withdrew their footprints into forests and marshes,
or passed by
their own gates without daring to enter.
That those like Gāoyáo fulfilled both their desires
was due to opportune timing.
Thus, the court values ministers who achieve great deeds,
while the wilderness admires scholars who preserve their integrity.
What kind of
people were they?
Now, a sage emperor has arisen,
matching the names of previous wise rulers.
The benevolent Way is not far;
is this not also true now?
Some guests pressed me with conventional remarks,
or worried that my actions were
contrary to the times.
I said that when there is a broad-minded and enlightened ruler above,
there must be people below who listen to their intentions.
Heaven's net is vast;
whether one emerges or withdraws, it is one and the same.
What blame is there in one's course of action?'
Then I elaborated on the guest-host debate
to resolve the difficulties of the questioners,
and named it 'Shì Quàn.'
The guest said:
'I have heard that Heaven establishes its brightness through celestial phenomena,
and Earth reveals its spirituality by embracing and giving forth.
Thus, the Huángzhōng (pitch pipe) follows its sequence,
and the twelve lǜ (pitch standards) are distinct in form.
Therefore, spring blossoms
their buds,
summer flourishes with its fruits,
autumn winds dispel the heat,
and winter ice forms.
Human affairs follow this principle,
responding to the opportune moment.
The three powers (Heaven, Earth, Man) are continuously beneficial,
as clear as a tally and seal.
Thus,
some scholars rose together in the court of Táng,
some had foreknowledge in Yǒushēn,
some inspired their lord through dreams,
some were released from fishing by the Wèibīn,
some knocked on a horn to seek audience with Qí,
some took off their
coarse clothes to become Chancellor of Qín,
some braved slander to bring peace to Zhèng,
some rode in a four-horse carriage to rescue the distressed,
some spread thorny branches to seek friends,
and some borrowed arts from the Yellow Spirit.
Therefore, they were able to ascend like lightning and
stand out,
surpassing their peers and transcending their category,
raising their lofty voices to be heard far and wide,
and upholding the clear music of the universe.
From this perspective,
advancing virtue values timeliness.
Why should you suppress this
and not extend yourself?
Now you, with your brilliant and excellent talent,
have devoted your essence to the repository of the six arts and diffused your thoughts through the gates of myriad wonders for years.
You have encountered the imperial succession
court,
and also arrived at a moment of good fortune and benefit.
You have been entrusted by an enlightened ruler,
and met with like-minded individuals.
The times are clear, the Way is true;
you can advance boldly.
This is truly the autumn for us to cleanse our hair in the clouds and
Milky Way, like a wild goose soaring high.
To conceal your brilliance and hide in the wilderness,
to contain your splendor and not yet shine,
to remain like a dragon latent in the nine springs,
obstinately holding to aloofness,
abandoning the distant path of the Way,
and clinging to the
rigid integrity of a recluse,
is this not contrary to the true spirit of the Way?
Moreover, I have heard that when the celestial pointer (Dipper) turns and returns, the heavenly position is righteous,
and when the five teachings are promulgated, human reason is settled.
Now the King's command is urgent and direct,
entrusting his concerns to the officials.
Above, you risk
incurring the displeasure of the ruler;
below, you cause doubts among the multitude.
The enlightened value conformity;
why must you be uniquely different?
The multitude of wise men can be followed;
why must you cling to your own idea?
At this moment, all those similarly summoned are
arriving,
like the hungry not waiting for a meal,
displaying their brilliance on the imperial road,
all ranked in the heavenly offices.
Why do you alone linger by your humble door,
abandoning your form to the outside world,
retreating to hills and gardens,
not glancing at splendors,
bestowing no benefit upon others,
acting not in accordance with the Way,
afflicted by a great illness,
with your life hard to preserve?
If Xīhé hurries his charioteer,
and the great fire (Antares) declines in the west,
you will regret it by the stream too late;
what
steps will you then take?
To value time over jade is
what the sages counsel;
to invert one's attire is
what the enlightened admonish.
May you learn from the grand paradigm of the former sages,
and live up to the sincere
heart of the sagely dynasty.
Let your pure spirit soar on the cloud road,
and bathe in the heavenly pool to wash your scales.
Pass through the Chānghé Gate,
tread upon the jade peak,
ascend the purple palace,
and serve by the Northern Star,
then suddenly your brilliance will shine,
mingling with the dust of
heroes.
Assist a ruler like Táng and Yú,
transform people into those of Yáo and Shùn,
proclaim policies where punishments are set aside,
and be counted among the ministers of Yīn and Zhōu.
Engrave your merits on grand bells,
and participate in the constant principles.
When alive, you will
eat from tripods;
when deceased, you will be a revered minister.
Is this not glorious?
But to ignore the radiant splendor of gold and white,
to forget the gleam of blue and purple official robes,
to refuse the brilliance of ceremonial attire,
and to embrace coarse clothes
for the whole year,
is this not wearisome?'
The master laughed and responded:
'Alas!
You, my guest, may be said to be accustomed to the outward glitter,
but have not glimpsed the faint presence of the recluse;
you see that ordinary people do not
tolerate such ways,
but have not understood the sage emperor's universal love;
you follow the square and compass for circles and squares,
but do not know that the great form is boundless.
Therefore, it is said,
Heaven is dark and clear,
Earth is tranquil and
Níng,
embracing all myriad categories,
permeating all living beings.
I entrust my body to a sagely era,
and my dao to the spirits.
When spring scatters with the yang,
and winter solidifies with the yin,
the great fluid contains light,
and the primordial qi steams in fusion.
All things look up to transformation,
and the great regulations are revealed with special signs.
Thus, those who advance enjoy heavenly emoluments,
and those who abide find peace in the hills.
Therefore, cold and heat push each other,
and the four seasons
take turns.
Yin and yang do not rule,
and transformation is endless.
Nature is set in its divisions,
and the two both achieve their mean.
When the two things are equally spiritual,
this is called dàtóng;
when neither bears resentment towards the other,
this is called
zhìtōng.
However, at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
cunning was valued and sincerity despised.
People were swayed by power,
seeking honor through profit.
Thus, Sū Zǐ emerged and the six states allied;
Zhāng Yí entered and the "horizontal alliance"
power formed.
When Lián Pō was alive, Zhào was respected;
when Yuè Yì left, Yān became light.
When Gōngshú disappeared, Wèi was defeated;
when Sūn Bìn had his feet amputated, Qí was at peace.
When Lǐ Zhǒng was cherished, Yuè became hegemon;
when Qū
Zǐ was alienated, Chǔ declined.
Hence, rulers had no permanent register,
and ministers no fixed titles.
They sacrificed righteousness and abandoned sincerity,
now empty, now full.
Thus, Féng (Xuān) strummed his sword to move his lord;
a woman had
the saying about reversing a gift.
Xiàng (Yǔ) displayed the strength to pull up mountains;
Kuǎi (Tong) presented the strategy of a tripod's legs.
Dōngguō (Yan) was abducted by Tián Róng;
Yán Hé felt shame at being coerced.
These all abandoned propriety and lost their
true nature,
clinging to the honor of the moment, to urgent matters of the day.
How could this be the root of the dao's transformation!
When the sagely emperors initiated transformation,
they patterned their virtue after the two emperors (Fú Xī and Shén Nóng),
and harmonized their customs with Yú (Shùn) and Xià (Yǔ).
They desired a gentle and harmonious flow,
not a sharp and
cutting clarity;
they desired a turbid, profound flow,
not a vast and prominent reputation;
they desired a disentangling and orderly resolution,
not a binding and knotty entanglement;
they desired a boundless
and infinite expanse,
not a petty and divisive separation;
they desired to be obscure yet daily manifest,
not to display whiteness like ice and snow;
they desired to be pure and rely on virtue,
not to be petty and cling to law.
Therefore, those who saw opportunity succeeded by acting,
and those who loved to withdraw were not pressed.
Thus it is said:
one clear, one obscure,
is the essence of the Dao;
one relaxed, one taut,
is the method of propriety;
one floating, one sinking,
both attain their true nature.
Thus, above there is the love for diligence and humility,
below there are ministers who are not named;
in court there are rites for inviting
the worthy,
in the wilderness there are people who hide away.
Therefore, Zhī Bó resisted Táng with his reclusive illness;
Lǐ Lǎo left his footprints with his western neighbor;
Yán Shì achieved fame by living in humble simplicity;
Yuán
Sī found joy in the Dao amidst extreme poverty;
Róng Qī moved Ní Fù with his three joys;
Qián Lóu's posthumous title was decided by a cloth quilt;
Gàn Mù preserved Wèi by resting in reclusion;
Jīng Lái's aspirations soared beyond the river
peaks;
Jūn Píng became renowned through divination;
the Four Hàos concealed their virtue by the Luò River;
Zhèng Zhēn earned praise by personally tilling the land;
Yòu Ān issued commands to the people of today.
All held an unyielding
integrity,
and an unwavering resolve.
They encountered rulers who rose above the mundane,
and fulfilled their personal aspirations.
Therefore, those who have a uniquely determined plan
do not borrow counsel from the masses;
those who maintain an unmoving
peace
do not rely on the deliberations of many guests.
Thus, they could abandon the splendor of external ties,
and comprehend the truth of the inner Dao;
leave the clear and obvious path,
and enter the obscure dust
and grime;
transform through myriad emotions and outward forms,
rely on emptiness and stillness to dwell,
live in a house of non-action,
and associate with people who relinquish profit.
Light as a goose feather,
heavy as sinking
mud.
If you subtract from it, you cannot;
if you measure it, it becomes deeper.
Truly, these are the teachers and models for my kind,
whom I, pressed by illness, cannot reach.
You criticize me for missing my post and alarming the public;
I, too, find it strange that you compare and discuss without finding a balance.
Indeed, talent not fully utilized

a prolonged illness lasting years

Therefore, when Xū Kè was deposed,

when Bó Niú was
ill,
Kǒng Zǐ sighed over it.
As Huángdì created regulations in the nine classics,

Wén Zhì risked his life for Qí
Wáng;
Yī Hé displayed his skills in Qín and Jìn;

Huà Tuó preserved his essence in unique knowledge;
Zhòng Jǐng bequeathed his marvels in established prescriptions.

seclusion.
Thereafter, Emperor Wǔ frequently issued edicts to repeatedly and relentlessly urge him.
Mì submitted a memorial, calling himself a common subject, saying:
"I, being weary,
lost my way in the paths of life,
and because of illness, I removed my hairpins,
letting my hair loose among the forests and hills.
Unfamiliar with human affairs,
I made birds and beasts my companions.
Your Majesty, you part the thorny bushes to gather orchids,
and also collect mugwort and weeds.
Thus, when Gāoyáo shook his official robes,
the unbenevolent kept their distance.
I am merely a stubborn and ignorant person,
nourished by Jìn's grain,
yet I still recall the joy of the Táng people striking the clods of earth.
I ought to hasten to the capital,
and offer longevity greetings outside the imperial palace.
But this humble person is of no good,
