For a long time, I have been afflicted with a severe illness,
with half my body not functioning,
my right foot being particularly small,
for nineteen years now.
Moreover, I took the 'cold food powder' medicine,
violating the proper regimen,
enduring bitter suffering and torment,
for seven years to date.
In deep winter, I strip naked and eat ice;
in the heat of summer, I suffer from distress and stuffiness,
coupled with coughing and hiccupping,
sometimes resembling a mild malaria,
or like a severe cold.
My qi floats and causes swelling,
and my four limbs are sore and heavy.
To this day, I am weak and frail,
gasping for breath to save my life.
My father and elder brothers have abandoned me,
and my wife and children have bid me a long farewell.
If I were forced by Heaven's majesty
to be carried on a litter to set out on the road,
my suffering would increase,
making me unable to proceed.
I would abandon myself to await punishment,
lying on my pillow, sighing.
I have heard that Sháo and Wèi music are not played together,
and refined music and the songs of Zhèng are not performed concurrently.
Hence, when Xì Zǐ entered Zhōu,
calamity extended to Wáng Shū;
when Yú Qiū praised the worthy,
Fán Jī covered her mouth.
A junzǐ and a common person
do not share the same utensils according to ritual.
How much more so for a humble person like me,
to be mixed with fine rice?
For a common man to wear embroidered clothes
is not befitting his status.
I have secretly heard that all those of similar standing
have already arrived.
Only I, due to my illness,
am confined to my bed with this misfortune.
Although I long for this enlightened era,
I fear I would perish by the roadside.
Even if I were not ill,
having encountered the age of Yáo and Shùn,
I would still hold to my aspirations at Jī Shān,
and ought to be tolerated.
I have heard that when there is an enlightened and sagely ruler above,
there are sincere subjects below;
when there are magnanimous policies above,
there are people who entrust their feelings below.
May Your Majesty pay attention and show clemency,
and further recognize extraordinary talents,
seeking out the reclusive in Fù Yán,
and gathering those who fish by the Wèi River.
Do not let mud and impurities
long pollute the clear stream."
Mì's words were earnest and heartfelt,
and he was thus allowed to decline.
A year later,

He wrote to the emperor requesting to borrow books,
and the emperor sent him a cartload of books.
Although Mì was frail and ill,
he tirelessly pored over them.
He had initially taken the 'cold food powder,'
but his constitution conflicted with it,
often leaving him utterly debilitated and disoriented.
Once, in sorrow and anger,
he struck a blade, intending to commit suicide,

Wén Lì (文立) of Shǔ, the Administrator of Jìyīn,

An imperial edict granted this.
Mì heard of it and sighed, saying:

and to reform the system of previous dynasties,
how can that be right?
The phrase 'bunches of silks, simple and plain,'

the gifts of black and red silks
have been customary since ancient times.
Thus, Kǒng Zǐ said that one should diligently study morning and night to await questions,
and that the treasures on one's mat await an invitation.
A scholar then bows thrice before advancing,

he declines once and withdraws,

As for Yīn Tāng and Yī Yǐn,
and King Wén and Tàigōng,
one personally went to Xīnyě,
and the other was carried home in a carriage.
They only feared that the ceremony was not grand enough,
how could they begrudge its trouble and expense?
Furthermore, if even one ritual is not observed,
a chaste woman would be ashamed,
how much more so a worthy scholar!
Kǒng Zǐ said: 'Cì,
you begrudge the sheep,
I value the ritual.'
How can we abandon it?
The government's failure to secure worthy men
lies precisely here."
In the early years of Xiánníng,
another edict proclaimed:
"The gentleman Huángfǔ Mì is profound and tranquil, upholding simplicity,
devoted to learning and fond of antiquity,
differing from the popular trends.
Appoint Mì as Prince's Household Grandee."
Mì steadfastly declined due to severe illness.
Although the Emperor initially did not override his will,
he soon again issued an edict summoning him as a Consultant,
and then called him to fill the post of Archivist.
Sīlì Jiàowèi Liú Yì requested him as Commander,
but he did not respond to any.
He wrote an essay on the system of burial,
titled 'Dǔ Zhōng' (篤終),
which said: "Xuányàn Xiānshēng believes that existence and non-existence are fixed principles of Heaven and Earth,
and inevitable for human nature.
Therefore, ritual sets the age of sixty as the limit of longevity,
extending to ninety,
with
various distinctions,
to prepare for the end with simplicity.
How could this be due to the many taboos of common customs?
Although my age has not yet reached the set longevity,
I have been afflicted with illness for a full cycle,
and have suffered repeated bereavements and misfortunes.
My spirit
is diminished and weakened,
and I have been in distress many times.
I constantly fear an untimely death,
and worry that my end will lack simplicity.
Therefore, I briefly express my deepest thoughts.
What people covet
is life;
what they hate
is death.
Although one covets,
one cannot exceed one's destined time;
although one hates,
one cannot escape.
When a person dies,
their essence disperses and their form disintegrates,
their soul goes everywhere;
thus, the qi belongs to Heaven.
The borrowed life comes to an end,
the exhausted body returns to its true nature;
thus, the corpse is hidden in the earth.
Therefore, if the spirit does not remain
in the body,
it rises and falls with the qi;
if the corpse is not long entrusted,
it merges with the earth.
The form and spirit are not separated,
this is the nature of Heaven and Earth;
the corpse uniting with the earth
is the principle of returning to true nature.
Now, if one cannot preserve the seven-foot body while alive,
why should one separate it with a coffin after death?
Then, clothes and shrouds only defile the corpse,
and coffins and outer coffins only separate it from its true nature.
Therefore,
Huán Sīmǎ's stone coffin was considered inferior to rapid decay;
Jìsūn compared jade and precious stones to exposing a corpse;
Duke Wén's lavish burial
was regarded by the Spring and Autumn Annals as Huá Yuán's disloyalty;
Yáng Wángsūn's close proximity to the earth
was considered by the Hàn Shū to be more virtuous than Qín Shǐhuáng.
If indeed the soul has consciousness,
then humans and ghosts have different systems.
Among those in the Yellow Springs,
the dead outnumber the living,
and they will certainly be prepared."
Its objects
are used for the deceased.
If one now compares death with life,
this is not the intention of the spirit.
If the deceased is without consciousness,
then it is a futile deprivation of the living's resources,
causing harm without
benefit,
and inciting wicked intentions.
This invites the calamity of exposure
and adds to the distress of the deceased.
Indeed, burial (zàng),
is concealment (cáng);
concealment (cáng) means
desiring that people should not see it.
To construct large coffins and sarcophagi,
and provide abundant grave goods,
is no different from burying gold at a roadside
corner and marking it with a sign.
Even the most foolish person
will surely laugh at this.
Lavish wealth and thick burials incite wicked intentions;
some will split open coffins and sarcophagi,
some will drag
the remains,
some will strip arms to seize gold rings,
or grope in intestines for pearls and jade.
Is the sight of cremation
not less painful than this?
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a person
who did not die,
nor a tomb that was not opened.
Therefore, Zhāng Shìzhī said:
"If there are desires within it,
even if it is as solid as Mount Nánshān, there will still be cracks;
if there are no desires within it,
even
without a stone sarcophagus,
what sorrow is there!"
This saying is profound;
it is my teacher.
Indeed, making lavish provisions for the end of life
is not generosity to the dead,
but for the living themselves.
To pursue
meaning in the useless,
and abandon what belongs to the deceased,
is not what a wise person does.
The Yì Jīng states:
"In ancient times, those who buried
clothed the deceased with brushwood,
and buried them in the middle of the wilderness,
without raising a mound
or planting a tree."
Thus, the dead returned to their true nature,
and the deceased did not harm the living.
Therefore, I wish to be buried in the evening if I die in the morning,
and in the morning if I die in the evening,
without setting up a coffin or sarcophagus,
without adding grave clothes or winding sheets,
without performing ablutions,
without making new clothes.
All items for encoffining
and oral burial
shall be entirely abolished.
Originally, I wished to be exposed and placed into the pit,
with my body directly touching the earth.
But I fear that human sentiments have been long steeped in customs,
making a sudden reform difficult.
Therefore, I now make a rough
regulation:
not as extravagant as a stone sarcophagus,
nor as frugal as exposed remains.
After my breath ceases,
I shall immediately wear the clothes of the time,
a plain headscarf and old clothes,
wrap the body in a rush mat,
tie both ends with hemp rope,
and place the body on a corpse bed.
Choose barren ground,
dig a pit ten chǐ deep,
fifteen chǐ long,
and six chǐ wide.
Once the pit is finished,
carry the bed to the pit,
remove the body
from the bed.
None of my possessions from life
shall accompany me,
only one roll of the Xiàojīng,
to show that I do not forget filial piety.
Beyond the rush mat,
the body shall be in direct contact with the earth.
The earth shall be level
with the ground,
and its original grass returned to it,
allowing it to grow over.
No trees shall be planted or removed,
so that no trace remains,
and it cannot be found even if sought.
If nothing desirable is seen,
then wickedness will not
arise in the heart,
and there will be no fear or anxiety from beginning to end,
no worries for a thousand years.
The remains will be one with the 后土 Hòutǔ (Earth Mother),
the soul will merge with the primordial qi and spirit.
This is the utmost expression of true and profound love.
If deaths occur at different times,
they shall not be moved to be interred together.
Joint burial has existed since the Duke of Zhōu (Zhōugōng),
but it is not an ancient system.
Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
and his two consorts did not follow;
this should be taken as a fixed principle.
Why must one adhere to the Rites of Zhōu?
Do not consult artisans,
do not believe divination,
do not be bound by popular sayings,
do not set up spirit tablets,
do not offer food morning and evening on the fifteenth day.
Rites do not permit
sacrifices at the tomb,
but only monthly offerings at home on the first day,
stopping after one hundred days.
Mourning must be at dusk or dawn,
not at night.
Mourning clothes shall be worn at home,
not by the tomb.
Indeed,
the ancients did not venerate tombs;
that was wisdom.
The mounds and trees of today
are foolishness.
If one does not follow this,
it is like mutilating the corpse underground,
a second injury after death.
If the soul has consciousness,
then
it will suffer endless injustice and sorrow throughout eternity,
and forever be a resentful ghost.
The sons of Wángsūn
can serve as a warning.
A deathbed oath is hard to break;
I hope you will not change it!

He died in the third year of Tàikāng (282 CE),
aged sixty-eight.
His sons, Tóng Líng and Fānghuí, etc., followed his last wishes.
Mì authored many poems, rhapsodies, eulogies, odes, essays, and critiques.

He also compiled the Dìwáng Shìjì (Genealogies of Emperors and Kings), Niánlì (Chronology), biographies of Gāoshì (High-minded Scholars) and Yìshì (Reclusive Scholars), Liènǚ (Exemplary Women), and Xuányàn Chūnqiū.
These were all highly esteemed in the world.
His disciples, Zhì Yú, Zhāng Guǐ, Niú Zōng, and Xí Chún,
all became famous officials of the Jìn dynasty.
Fānghuí adhered to his father's principles from a young age
and also possessed literary talent.
In the early Yǒngjiā era (307-313 CE),
he was summoned by the Erudites,
but did not respond.
He avoided chaos by moving to Jīngzhōu,
living in seclusion behind closed doors,
never entering a city or government office.
He dressed only after raising silkworms,
and ate only after farming.
He prioritized others over himself,
revered the worthy, and cherished all beings.
The people of the southern lands all respected him.
The Inspector Táo Kǎn treated him with great reverence.
Whenever Táo Kǎn visited him,
he would wear plain scholar's clothes,
and dismount from his carriage at the gate before entering.
Wáng Dūn sent his cousin Yì to replace Táo Kǎn
and transferred Táo Kǎn to Guǎngzhōu.
When Táo Kǎn was about to go to Wáng Dūn,
Fānghuí advised him, saying:
"I have heard that when rival states are extinguished,
meritorious officials perish.
You have just defeated Dù Tāo,
and your achievement is unmatched.
Do you wish to avoid danger?
How can that be possible!"
Táo Kǎn did not heed him and departed.
Wáng Dūn indeed intended to kill Táo Kǎn,
but he was saved thanks to Zhōu Fǎng.
After Yì arrived in Jīngzhōu,
he greatly alienated the people,
and the populace rebelled against Yì, welcoming Dù Tāo.
Yì carried out extensive executions to establish his authority.
Knowing that Táo Kǎn respected Fānghuí,
he reproached him for not coming to pay respects to him,
and then arrested and beheaded him.
Both the Chinese and indigenous people of Jīngzhōu
all shed tears.
Zhì Yú
Zhì Yú
had the courtesy name Zhòngqià, and was a native of Cháng'ān in Jīngzhào.
His father, Mú,
was the Grand Coachman (Tàipú Qīng) of Wèi.
Yú served Huángfǔ Mì in his youth,
and his talent and learning were extensive and profound.
He wrote tirelessly.
The commandery summoned him to be Registrar (Zhǔbù).
Yú once said that life and death are destined,
and wealth and honor are in the hands of Heaven.
What Heaven blesses is righteousness,
and what men assist is trustworthiness.
To tread in trustworthiness and contemplate obedience
is the way to extend blessings;
to act contrary to this
is the way to invite calamity.
However, the Way is long and life is short,
and good fortune and misfortune are intertwined.
Those who are pressured and distressed
do not know what to uphold;
they drift aimlessly and accumulate resentment,
some becoming deluded, others dissolute.
Therefore, by borrowing himself as the subject
and using events as the premise,
he first presented the difficulties of encountering no opportunity in life,
then abandoning the constant human relations,
lightly soaring and traveling far,
to fully express the common human feelings of bewilderment and confusion.
Afterward, he led them back to correctness,
returned them to righteousness,
expounded the responses of the spirits and gods beyond sight and hearing,
and elevated the operations of prosperity and adversity beyond human intellect and power,
to clarify that Heaven's decree is irresistible.
Thus, he composed the "Rhapsody on Contemplating Wanderings" (Sī Yóu Fù).
Its words say: There was a distant descendant of Xuānyuán,
whose clan was a grand lineage of Zhòngrèn.
Spreading his brilliant essence in the latter leaves,
he absorbed the spiritual roots of ancient times.
Aligning with Heaven and Earth to wield
the measures,
he modeled Yin and Yang to establish the constant.
Had it not been for the opportune moment, how could he have journeyed forth?
Riding the great void, he drifted and swayed.
Wearing the high crown of the bright moon,
adorned with the
lustrous jade of Tàibái.
He fashioned the colored rainbow as his robe,
and wore the iridescent clouds as his skirt.
He girded himself with the brilliant flashes of lightning,
and wore the tinkling jade of Yùhéng.
The bright sun's light
reflected his form,
truly shining with renewed splendor.
His utmost beauty was strange and good to ordinary eyes,
so profound and rare that it remained unrevealed.
Common stones, adorned in fine silk, graced the nation,
while the uncut jade of Hé was cast far away in Nánjīng.
The summer likeness
was shrouded in dust in the northern market,
while bottles and jars stood tall by the two pillars.
The phoenix, upright and aloof, perched alone,
the orchid and cassia, out of season, blossomed in solitary glory.
Enduring cold and heat to refine
his true nature,
how could he change his appearance or his feelings?
Saddened that Kūnwú is easily crossed,
he mused on the swift dusk of Huīguāng.
Envying a year that becomes three springs,
still holding blossoms, he lingered in ease.
Grieving that the sun's spirit has no
leisure,
constrained by the measured celestial shadow.
Listening to the cicadas' calls marking the seasons,
fearing leaves might fall amidst the congealed dew.
Hoping to follow previous tracks, he hastened his pace,
yet turned his gaze
back to the dust left behind.
The past swiftly vanishes and cannot be overtaken,
the future is obscure and yet to manifest.
The two powers (Heaven and Earth) rest boundlessly,
the four seasons revolve endlessly.
The stars and birds depart, and time reverses,

He beheld the three sovereigns in Heaven,

Indeed, the Way is vast, but destiny
is slight;
who would abandon fullness and gather emptiness?
Holding a Suí pearl and sweet grass,

Why should they who had no time care?
He feared his solitary beauty
might be harmed.
So he profoundly withdrew and hid himself,

Yet fragrance in seclusion grows sweeter,
and treasure in the night shines brighter.
Pressed and constrained
within this realm,

Gazing at the lofty grandeur of the cloud steps,

He went to Páo Xī to ask about images,

He would journey far into the Great Beginning,

The Four Spirits stood solemn as
his guards,

He harnessed white beasts in the autumn wind,

He selected humble servants from the spirit stables,

He summoned Língyáng from Youxī,

His form drifted

He sipped jade dew from Láiyú,

The Grand Norms closed and then reopened,

He gazed at the fluttering Jade Maidens,

He observed the dazzling splendor

He inhaled the morning mists to cure his hunger,

He would release the reins to wander at ease,

short path to the Eastern Zenith.
He commanded Xiān'ē to turn right,

He presided over the gods in the Summer Court,

He harnessed Jiāomíng

He criticized Xīhé in Dānqiū,

He followed the propitious wind and reached the south,
bidding farewell
to the Great Sun in Yánlí.
Distressed by the oppressive heat and humidity,
how could I remain here?
Hearing the Biqi's long morning call,
I shall journey to the west.
He moored the
floating seabirds in Ruòshuǐ,

If purity and essence truly reside there,

Surpassing Wàngshū to soar aloft,

He derided the eclipsed Yin on Wēishān,

examining the
primal talismans of good and ill fortune.

Kǒng (Confucius) shed tears at the Western Hunt,

chuān,

qú,

He recommended virtuous and good men,
and along with Xiàhóu Zhàn and seventeen others, he was ranked in the lowest grade for the policy examination,
and was appointed Zhōngláng.
Emperor Wǔ issued an edict saying:
"Having reviewed the policy responses of the virtuous and good men,
although their words vary in approach,
all are clear on the principles of kingship
and beneficial to the way of governance.
I wish to examine their replies in detail,
to thoroughly understand the intentions of these worthy scholar-officials."
Thereupon, an edict was issued for all virtuous, upright, and outspoken men
to assemble in the eastern hall for a policy question,
which stated:
"Recently, there was a solar eclipse at midday,
and floods and droughts have occurred.
What should be cultivated
to avert these great calamities?
Also, what laws are currently unsuitable,
causing distress to both public and private affairs?
What are these matters?
Generally, a peaceful era depends on obtaining talent,
and obtaining talent also relies on ears and eyes to listen and observe.
If there are individuals with literary or martial abilities beneficial to current affairs who have not yet been promoted,
each should be recommended.
And if there are those who have offended common customs or incurred slander,
who should be cleansed first,
each should also be named."
Yú replied:
"Your servant has heard that the sagely and enlightened rulers of antiquity
traced origins to comprehend outcomes,
and embodied the fundamental to rectify the superficial.
Thus, they worried about inappropriate laws and regulations,
but not about people losing their proper place;
they worried about people losing their proper place,
but not about the widespread occurrence of disasters.
This is sincerely because if the law is attained in this,
then things will be rational in that;
if harmony prevails among the people below,
then calamities will cease above.
If there are celestial anomalies like solar and lunar eclipses,
or disasters of flood and drought,
they would look inward and listen,
seeking their cause,
observing things from afar,
and examining themselves closely.
Could their ears and eyes for listening and observing ever be clouded in their wisdom?
Could their intentions or decrees ever deviate from constant rectitude?
Could major officials in high positions ever be appointed to unsuitable individuals?
Could rewards, punishments, dismissals, and promotions ever fail to be granted appropriately?
Could there be those by riverbanks or in mountain caves,
harboring the Way, fishing or building, yet untouched by dreams or omens?
Could there be exceptional talents in distant, remote regions,
destined to save the age, yet not yet blessed by imperial grace?
By inferring from these categories,
to seek out their reasons,
by inquiring into affairs and examining words,
to fully ascertain their truth,
then the sentiments of Heaven and man can be seen,
and the arrival of ominous signs can be averted.
If, when applying it to things, there is no opposition,
and when seeking it in oneself, there is no fault,
if all things are in natural order,
and internal and external are all appropriate,
if the invocation master speaks truly,
and words are not untrue,
yet the sun and moon move irregularly,
and epidemics occur without warning,
then these are matters of yin and yang,
not indicators of fortune or misfortune.
The destined cycles and numbers
are natural divisions,
which human affairs cannot control.
In such cases, one should merely open granaries to relieve stagnation
and reduce food and expenditure.
Therefore, if one truly encounters a destined cycle,
even Táo Táng and Yīn Tāng would not change it;
but if it is not a destined cycle,
then the rulers of Sòng and Wèi,
and the prime ministers of the feudal lords,
could still evoke a response.
May Your Majesty thoroughly examine the causes
to exhaust their principles,
then the world will be exceedingly fortunate.
Your servant was born and raised in a humble family,
not reaching out to unusual things.
Although there may be worthy talents,
I have not met or known them,
and dare not speak blindly or make rash recommendations,
having nothing with which to answer the sagely inquiry."
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and appointed Wénxǐ Lìng.
At that time, the Son of Heaven kept his mind on the way of governance,
and as the Wu (Wú) rebels had just been pacified,
the world was at peace.
He presented the "Encomium on Tàikāng" to praise the virtues of the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty.
Its words said: "How splendid were the distant ancients,
the progenitors of mankind!
The four corners were all settled,
and myriad states followed the same track.
The Hàn (Hàn) were not competitive,
and chaos knew no end.
The central domains rebelled outwardly,
and the feudal lords
and royal guards collapsed inwardly.
Heaven's calamity had descended,
and the times were fraught with utmost peril.
Dragons fought and beasts contended,
splitting apart distant lands.
Bèi (Bèi) usurped power in Mínshǔ (Mínshǔ),
Dù (Dù) rebelled east of the sea.
Quán (Quán) then took advantage of
the opportunity,
carving out a domain across the Three Rivers.
Bright and manifest was the Lord on High,
looking down with awesome splendor.
He then proclaimed the imperial might,
bringing forth Heaven's decree.
He raised armies at Liáosuì (Liáosuì),
and the guilty were seized.
He pacified
Cháoxiǎn (Cháoxiǎn),
and subjugated Hánmò (Hánmò).
Wén (Wén) indeed met the opportune moment,
sweeping across Liáng (Liáng) and Yì (Yì).
The prime villains surrendered their mandate,
and the Nine Yí (Yí) translated their allegiance again.
Qióng (Qióng), Rǎn (Rǎn), and Āiláo (Āiláo),
it was there
that his achievements were made.
When our August Emperor ascended,
two states were already pacified.
There was no place that was not embraced,
thereby nurturing all living beings.
Wú (Wú) then relied on its strongholds,
defying orders in the Southern Ocean.
His renowned teachings had not yet reached,
and the imperial divine power
had not extended.
The Emperor shook forth his might,
awesome like thunder and lightning.
He cut across the Jiāng (Jiāng) and Miǎn (Miǎn) rivers,
and Jīng (Jīng) and Shū (Shū) were made pure.
How distant and profound was the Sagely Emperor,
matching the two trigrams Qián (Qián) and Lí (Lí).
He transformed with
uprightness,
and overcame chaos with wonder.
He displayed his military might for sixty days,
and his troops were not weary.
He offered sacrifices countless times,
and the ceremonial banners were not diminished.
Vast and boundless were the four seas,
all adhering to propriety and harmony.
Solemn
and majestic were the palace temples,
singing odes of peace and praise.
Under the glorious heaven,
nothing was outside the Emperor's strategy.
Even the barren lands and reflected light
received his righteous calendar and decrees.
Dragon-horses were robust,
and the wind blew towards Huáyáng (Huáyáng).
Bows and arrows were sheathed,
shields and spears put away.
Solemn was the southern gold,
majestic were the remaining emperors.
Valiant swords were presented at court,
and boats were built to form bridges.
The sagely and enlightened one had creative power,
truly
acting as Heaven's artisan.
Heaven and Earth did not violate,
and the common people were thus at peace.
The three duties were thus harmonious,
thereby establishing their merit.
Having extended his traces far,
he will manifest his path.
Mount Qiáo (Qiáo) is the
peak,
the sealed land of the Emperor to be gazed upon.
How majestic, Sagely Emperor,
why not perform the fēng (fēng) sacrifice?!"
He was relieved of his post due to mourning for his mother.
After a long time,
he was summoned to fill the position of Shàngshū Láng (Shàngshū Láng).
Chén Xié (Chén Xié), the Director of Works, dug up an ancient ruler.
The Shàngshū (Shàngshū) reported:
"The current ruler is longer than the ancient ruler;
it is proper to take the ancient one as correct."
Pān Yuè (Pān Yuè) believed that it had been in use for a long time
and should not be changed again.
Yú (Yú) rebutted, saying:
"In ancient times, the sages, having seen the profundity of all under heaven, imitated its forms,
and modeled objects to make instruments
to preserve their utility for the times.
Thus, they referenced Heaven and Earth
to rectify the principles of calculation;
they based divisions on musical pitches
to determine the standards of length.
Their creation had principles,
therefore their use had verification.
By measuring the two cosmic forces,
Heaven and Earth could not conceal their true nature;
by rectifying the three luminaries,
the celestial phenomena could not harbor error;
applied to metals and stones,
the sounds and rhythms were harmonious;
placed against compass and square,
the instruments were suitable.
When the origin is not amiss, all things are correct;
when it is amiss,
all matters are contrary.
The current ruler is nearly half an cùn (cùn) longer than the ancient ruler.
If the Department of Music uses it,
the musical pitches will not align;
if the historians use it,
the celestial observations will lose their accuracy;
if the medical office uses it,
the acupoints will be misplaced.
These three things
are where measurements originate,
and where success or failure is verified.
All are obstructed and cannot be understood,
therefore it is proper to change the current one and follow the ancient one.
The systems of Táng (Táng) and Yú (Yú)
standardized musical pitches, measures, and weights.
The teachings of Zhòngní (Zhòngní)
emphasized careful weighing and precise measurement.
Now with two rulers used in parallel,
it cannot be called standardized;
to know an error and continue to act on it
cannot be called careful.
Neither standardized nor careful,
this is called erroneous law,
not something to guide objects and set standards,
nor to show people the ultimate truth.
Among all things, some are numerous and easily changed,
some are few and hard to alter,
some change and cause trouble,
and some alter and simplify.
Measures and weights are commonly used by people,
and length is not something people cling to and cherish;
thus, it is numerous and easily changed.
Rectifying error with correctness,
reversing deviance to uprightness,
is a temporary change
that will be unrivaled for all ages;
this is altering and simplifying.
To uphold established regulations
and not lose ancient ways;
the arbitrarily agreed-upon systems of later times,
and the mixed, disordered uses of heterodox doctrines,
ought to be revised in due time,
to conform to the singular truth.
Your subject believes it is proper to act as proposed."
He also submitted a memorial discussing the fēng (fēng) and shàn (shàn) sacrifices,
which can be found in the "Records of Rites".
Yú (Yú) observed that during the chaos at the end of the Hàn (Hàn),
many genealogies and family records were lost,
so even their descendants could not speak of their ancestors.
He compiled "Genealogies and Family Names" in ten volumes,
and submitted a memorial presenting it,
believing it was sufficient to provide materials and be useful,
and to broaden the benefits of knowledge.
He was impeached by the Sītú (Sītú) for violating regulations in classifying ranks,
but an imperial edict pardoned him.
At that time, the Imperial Ancestral Temple was newly built,
and an edict ordered a universal increase in rank by one grade.
Later, because the official in charge misunderstood the edict,
it was rescinded.
Yú (Yú) submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your subject has heard that the sagely and enlightened rulers of old
did not begrudge a state of a thousand chariots but cherished the credibility of a paulownia leaf,
thereby emphasizing the command of the supreme sovereign and conveying sincerity to all nations.
The previous amnesty edict of the Yǐsì (Yǐsì) year
referred to the lingering benevolence and favor of the former emperor,
ordering a universal increase in rank by one grade,
to reward the joyful support of the four seas.
The edict was dispatched and circulated,
reaching far and near,
and everyone rejoiced like birds soaring and fish leaping,
grateful for the bestowed favor.
Now, suddenly, because the official in charge did not review the text carefully,
the previous edict is recalled,
and the already conferred favor is revoked.
Your humble subject secretly believes this is improper."
The edict followed his advice.
During the Yuánkāng [reign],
he was transferred to be Prince of Wú Yǒu.
At that time, Xún Yǐ compiled a new code of rituals,
and made Yú discuss its pros and cons before implementation.
When Empress Yuán died,
Dù Yù memorialized:
"The system of liàng'àn [mourning]
originated in high antiquity.
Therefore, Gāozōng had no text on mourning attire,
and only the text mentions 'not speaking.'
Emperor Wén of Hàn limited it to thirty-six days.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
the yúdì ceremony has served as the demarcation.
The Crown Prince, as one body with the state,
should logically remove his mourning attire;
he should do so upon the completion of the cùkū ceremony."
Yú replied to Yù's letter, saying:
"Táng [tradition] speaks of 'èmì' (silence and seclusion),
Yīn [tradition] speaks of 'liàng'àn' (silent seclusion);
each uses an event to name it,
it does not signify a special reduction after the burial.
Since the Zhōu dynasty,
it has been called 'sāngfú' (mourning attire).
Sāngfú
is to express mourning through attire.
Now the Emperor manages myriad affairs in a single day,
and the Crown Prince bears the heavy responsibility of overseeing and consoling;
it is appropriate to suspend the ritual [for them],
to remove mourning attire after the burial.
To change the system and follow reason,
establishing a precedent for the future,
why must we adhere to antiquity
and cause contention among old scholars!"
When the Imperial Grandson Shàng died,
the officials memorialized
that "the imperial attire should be qīcuī for one year."
An imperial edict ordered the academicians to debate this.
Yú said:
"If a Crown Prince is born,
he is treated with the rites of an adult;
thus, the reason for shāng [mourning for a child] is removed.
The Grandson also embodies the ruler and inherits heavy responsibility;
his attire is complete due to his position,
not his age."
This was followed.
Yú also debated the matter of the jade carriage and the two altars to the earth god,
which can be seen in the Yúfú Zhì.
Later, he successively held the posts of Bìshū Jiān and Wèiwèi Qīng.
He followed Emperor Huì to Cháng'ān.
When the eastern army came to welcome them,
the hundred officials dispersed,
and he drifted between Hù and Dù.
He then entered the southern mountains,
where his provisions ran out and he was severely hungry,
picking and eating acorns.
Later, he was able to return to Luò,
successively holding the posts of Guānglù Xūn and Tàicháng Qīng.
At that time, Emperor Huái personally performed the suburban sacrifice.
Since Yuánkāng,
the suburban sacrifices had not been personally performed, and
rituals had fallen into disuse.
Yú corrected the old statutes,
making the ritual objects shine forth.
When the capital Luò was in chaos,
thieves were rampant,
and people ate each other due to hunger.
Yú had always been clean and poor,
and thus died of starvation.
Yú compiled the Wénzhāng Zhì in four scrolls,
annotated the Sānfǔ Juélù,
and also compiled ancient writings,
categorizing them into thirty scrolls,
named Liúbié Jí.
He wrote a commentary for each,
the wording and reasoning were fitting and appropriate,
and it was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
Yú was skilled at observing celestial phenomena,
and once told a friend:
"The world is about to fall into chaos.
Among the countries where one can seek refuge,
will it not be the land of Liáng?"
He loved scholars by nature;
when someone was recommended,
he would draft the memorial for them.
Tàishū Guǎng of Dōngpíng was sharp-witted and eloquent in debate.
When Guǎng spoke extensively,
Yú could not respond;
when Yú wrote,
Guǎng could not answer.
They ridiculed each other,
and this was widely known in the world.
Shù Xī
Shù Xī, courtesy name Guǎngwēi,
was a native of Yuánchéng, Yángpíng.
He was a descendant of Shū Guǎng, Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince of Hàn.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
Guǎng's great-grandson Mèngdá fled for refuge,
moving from Dōnghǎi to reside south of Shālù Shān.
He then removed the radical 'fū' from Shū,
thus changing his surname.
His grandfather, Hùn,
was the Administrator of Lǒngxī.
His father, Kān,
was the Administrator of Féngyì.
Both had good reputations.
Xī was extensively learned and well-informed,
and was well-known along with his elder brother Qiú.
When he was young, he studied at the national academy.
Someone once asked Dr. Cáo Zhì:
"Who among today's scholars is diligent in study?"
Zhì replied:
"Shù Guǎngwēi of Yángpíng is tirelessly diligent in study;
no one can surpass him."
He returned to his hometown,
was investigated as Xiàolián,
and nominated as Màocái,
but declined all posts.
Qiú married a niece of Shí Jiàn,
but then abandoned her.
Jiàn held a grudge,
and hinted to the provincial and commandery governments and ducal mansions not to appoint them,
which is why Xī and others were long without official appointments.
During the Tàikāng reign,
there was a great drought in the commandery.
Xī prayed for rain for the villagers,
and after three days, rain poured down.
The people said Xī's sincerity was effective,
and composed a song for him, saying:
"Master Shù,
communicates with the spirits,
prayed to Heaven for three days, and sweet rain fell.
Our millet is growing,
our broomcorn millet is sprouting.
How shall we repay him?
Repay Shù Chángshēng."
Xī was good friends with Wèi Hòu.
When he heard Wèi Hòu met with disaster,
he went from his own commandery to attend the funeral.
He once wrote essays on encouraging agriculture and various taxes,
but his prose was rather vulgar and common,
and people at the time looked down on it.
Yet, he was reserved and humble by nature,
not aspiring to glory or profit.
He wrote Xuánjū Shì to mimic Kènàn,
its text says: Shù Xī was living in seclusion,
his disciples attending him.
He was drawing the curtains for deep discussion,
leaning on a desk and laughing heartily,
holding a brush and scattering words,
examining and compiling similarities and differences.
Those at his side stepped forward and
asked him:
"We have heard that the Way values adaptability,
and the enlightened are boundless.
When the world is in chaos, they rescue it from disorder;
when the times are peaceful, they support its prosperity.
They uphold the cosmic order to assist in myriad
affairs,
and brighten the imperial reign by fostering the imperial winds.
When alive, the whole land rejoices in their existence;
when dead, the universe grieves their end.
Therefore, a gentleman humbles himself to promote the Way,
not being ashamed
to seek office.
The 'Superior State' has the saying 'If you do not seek, what will you gain?',
and the Zhōu Yì records the phrase 'to leap to seek advancement.'
Shēn Lǎo bore the 'golden cauldron' to present his theories on governance,
and the Guest of Qí
stood at the main thoroughfare singing the 'White Water' poem.
Now, you, Master, indulge in the Way and cultivate arts,
standing majestically like a mountain.
Your hidden brilliance penetrates the subtle,
your broad knowledge and deep insight,
working through the night, forgetting sleep's
toil,
and during the day, pursuing the thought of profound study.
Years accumulate,
yet your ambition does not waver.
Your scales and wings are formed, yet you remain hidden;
your skills and studies are excellent, yet untried.
Instead, you wish to close the box and refuse
to display your worth,
to coil deep in the mud,
forever concealing the brilliance of jade,
hiding your head on the island of cornered fish.
In the age of Táng, you emulate Cháng Jǔ;
when the state has the Way, you turn against Níng Wǔ.
To know
that and ignore this,
this fool dares not accept.
As for scholars being promoted through recommendation,
their advancement must await a request;
if those who cling to power are arbitrarily promoted,
then the talented from the forests and swamps will not be drawn out.
In the vermilion court, silk-clad boys stride,
while the east
the rustic, white-haired old man.
Why not, like Zǐdū, serve Bólù?
Rely on a bird-headed boat to cross the great current,
tread on emerald clouds to startle the swift dragon,
flash radiant light to
frighten the submerged catfish.
Instead, you merely remain confined to a shallow well,
gazing at the heavenly path but not traveling it.
With learning accumulated but your person troubled,
what good is it to hide away in obscure hills?
Moreover, the years do not wait for us;
time is like a galloping steed,
it comes but never returns,
hard to gain, easy to lose.
Sir, you do not know the regret of delay in the prognostication of Xūyù,
and forget the urgent duty of
Pénghé.
Can you ascend to the seashore and hold back the eastward flowing water,
or stand by Yúquán and summon back the westward setting sun?
You merely take biased fear as shackles,
and
scholarship as self-imposed fetters,
imprisoning the great Dao within a small dwelling,
tormenting your body in a humble room.
How can this compare to entrusting oneself to powerful and influential families,
relying on their authority and borrowing their strength,
choosing to nest in fragrant groves,
flying without needing
wings,
sleeping in the chambers of the Seven Maidens in the evening,
and enjoying food from five cauldrons in the morning?
Rectify the Three Norms, and the grand order will be peaceful;
assist the Five Teachings, and the Jade Cord will be straight.
How can this compare to eating wild greens and
vegetables,
hiding oneself for life!”
Shùzǐ said:
“Stay!
I shall guide you with the way of the noble person,
and enlighten you on matters of engagement and withdrawal.
You should clearly receive my instruction,
and carefully listen to
my will.
In ancient times, when the Primal Unity was first opened,
the Two Modes were established.
Radiant light hides at night,
Wàngshū gathers at day.
Birds fly in the forests,
cicadas rush to dampness.
Things follow what their nature
finds peace in,
scholars delight in what their will holds to.
Some turn their backs on glory and dwell in cliffs,
others push open orchid gates to seek entry.
Those in the wild are like soaring dragons,
those at court are like gathering phoenixes.
Though
their paths are different,
the Dao has no nobility or baseness.
They must find peace in their work,
and not envy each other.
Jì and Xiè exerted themselves to promote the Dao,
Cháo and Yóu washed their ears to avoid abdication.
Both
left behind imperishable reputations,
both entered the ranks of the worthy.
Comparing their names and measuring their reputations,
who is inferior, who is superior?
Why must one desire to be among the twenty-eight,
and be ashamed to be among the seven
peers!
Moreover, paths diverge yet lead to the same end;
scholars have different aspirations.
I humbly follow in the footsteps of those who withdraw,
and dare not hear your lofty comparison.
I shall disregard the rush-wheeled carriage and not
look at it;
what powerful and influential families would I attach myself to!
In ancient times, when the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties declined,
it was difficult to entrust oneself to the times.
When the signs of fortune opened,
the beginnings of calamity also arose.
One might roam the lofty palace in the morning,
only to fall into a towering ravine in the evening.
One might laugh by day,
and sigh by night,
flourishing in the morning, decaying in the evening.

Wáng Jiē, courtesy name Zǔyóu,

I secretly observe the recluse Wáng Jiē,

Yuán then called him in and said:

Biographies, Chapter 22: Xì Shēn
Xì Shēn, courtesy name Guǎngjī,
was from Dānfù, Jìyīn.
His father, Xī,
was the Shàngshū Zuǒcéng (Assistant in the Department of State Affairs).
Xì Shēn was widely learned and highly talented,
extraordinary and unconstrained,
not adhering to minor details of conduct.
He did not respond to invitations from the provinces or commanderies.
During the Tàishǐ reign,
an imperial edict ordered the recommendation of worthy and outspoken gentlemen from throughout the realm.
The Tàishǒu Wén Lì recommended Xì Shēn to be selected.
The edict stated:
"The Sages of the highest antiquity governed with virtue,
with simplicity and without elaborate forms.
During the Three Dynasties,
rituals and music were fully developed,
and institutions became increasingly complex.
What was the reason for the transformation from plainness to refinement?
In the eras of Yú and Xià,
sages followed one another,
yet their reforms differed.
When the Zhōu Way declined,
Zhòngní (Confucius) still said to follow Zhōu.
Why were the appropriate reforms
also different?
After the sage kings passed away,
their institutions still existed,
and hegemons rose in succession to assist them.
Could the shortcomings of the kingly way
not be remedied?
Why did decline not reverse itself?
Was it because the hegemonic virtue was shallow?
Or was it that the destined time could not be brought about?
Furthermore, with the wisdom of Yí Wú (Guǎn Zhòng),
his achievements only reached hegemony.
Why?
In the past, those who governed
reformed the abuses of chaos and destruction,
established an eternal order,
changed customs and transformed practices,
so that punishments were laid aside and unused.
Was this not the flourishing of transformation?
How does one cultivate to achieve this?
I have inherited the glorious achievements of my ancestors,
and it has been seven years,
yet the people have not submitted to instruction,
and the way of governance has not been perfected.
Comparing the past to the present,
why is the disparity so great?
Although my enlightenment is lacking,
I still wish to deliberate with all the worthies,
so that we may clarify doubtful and obscure points,
and obtain ultimate truth from honest words.
Moreover, recently, the Róng and Dí have invaded internally,
disasters have occurred repeatedly,
border people have been displaced,
and conscripted laborers suffer hardship.
Is this due to errors in governance and punishment,
or are officials not suited for their posts?
Each of you should fully express your thoughts,
investigate thoroughly, and discuss.
Illustrate ancient systems above,
and address current issues below.
My moral failings
should be rectified and supplemented.
Speak directly and without concealment;
I will respectfully listen."
Xì Shēn replied: "I humbly observe that Your Majesty,
with your sagely virtue, reigns,
yet still deigns to broadly seek advice.
Thus, you summon worthy and upright gentlemen,
but I and others are shallow and humble,
insufficient to answer your great questions.
Therefore, I secretly harbor self-doubt,
and though I present myself at court,
I do so with trepidation.
I humbly read your sagely edict,
and thus know the earnestness of your inquiry.
I have heard that in high antiquity,
the worthy were promoted and yielded their positions,
their teachings unified in virtue,
thus it was simple and the people were transformed.
During the Three Dynasties,
succession was hereditary,
and at their decline, it continued by inheritance,
thus institutions became complex
but later became orderly.
The succession between Yú and Xià,
and the differences in their reforms,
were not due to different ways of emperors and kings,
but to different paths for remedying abuses.
Zhōu came at the end of two previous eras,
inheriting an extreme of decline and artifice.
It perfected the utmost in rites and music,
and exhausted the principles of institutions.
Its texts were detailed and complete.
Zhòngní (Confucius) acted according to the circumstances of the time
when he said to follow Zhōu;
it was not a different theory.
I have heard that the transformations of sage kings
prioritized rites and music;
the rise of the Five Hegemons relied on diligent governance and punishment.
The transformation by rites and music is profound,
the use of governance and punishment is shallow.
If diligently applied, they can bring temporary peace;
if neglected,
they lead to continuous decline.
The path they took was fundamentally short,
thus their corrective achievements were not comparable.
However, Qí Huán (Duke Huan of Qi) failed at Kuíqiū,
and Yí Wú (Guǎn Zhòng) succumbed to petty considerations,
so his achievements
stops at hegemony,
is this not fitting!
The Edict states:
“To establish an eternal governance,
to change customs and transform traditions,
and to make all under Heaven harmonious and peaceful,
by what means should one cultivate to achieve this? ”
Your servant believes that nothing is greater than selecting people and
appointing them to office.
The current system of governance,
is not without a unified structure,
but the talents of the governors and administrators,
vary in quality and achievement.
Some lead to prosperity,
others lead to decline.
This is because people can promote
governance,
not governance promoting people.
To neglect people and focus on governance,
even with diligence, what benefit is there?
Your servant humbly observes ancient and modern times,
and examines their merits and flaws: Ancient people together sought the worthy,
modern people together sought office.
When ancient people appointed officials,
the sovereign held responsibility from above,
the ministers recommended from below.
If the right person was obtained, there was a reward;
if the wrong person was obtained, there was a punishment.
How could they
not seek the worthy!
When modern people become officials,
fathers and elder brothers strive for them,
rel relatives assist them.
If there are personal connections, they succeed;
if there are no personal connections, they are obstructed.
How can they not seek office
If the worthy genuinely seek advancement,
advancement lies in cultivating the Way,
failure lies in losing righteousness.
Therefore, they wait in tranquility.
If office can be sought,
success lies in aggressive pursuit,
failure lies in being late.
Therefore, they act to seize it.
Action leads to contention,
contention leads to factionalism,
factionalism leads to calumny,
calumny leads to the loss of truth in praise and blame,
with truth and falsehood indistinguishably mixed.
The sovereign's
hearing is misled and confused,
this is where treachery gathers.
Tranquility leads to integrity,
integrity leads to uprightness,
uprightness leads to trust and deference,
trust and deference lead to recommending the worthy,
recommending the worthy without boasting,
constantly
yielding to each other with insatiable desire.
The sovereign's hearing is clear and discerning,
this is where virtue tends.
Therefore, if one can make them tranquil,
even if one sleeps soundly all day, people will naturally be upright;
if one cannot prohibit action,
even if one works
day and night,
customs will not be unified.
Moreover, people, whether foolish or wise,
all admire fame and officialdom,
none do not feign righteousness outwardly,
and conceal evil inwardly.
Thus, it is difficult to
know who is evil and who is righteous.
If the appointed are righteous,
then many righteous people will arrive;
if the appointed are evil,
then many evil people will also gather.
When things breed their own kind,
who can stop it!
Therefore, those who lose their
country and their era,
have never failed to be accumulated by many evils.
When it first begins,
it must start subtly,
if subtle things are not eliminated,
they eventually become manifest.
Heaven and Earth cannot
suddenly produce cold and heat;
the sovereign also cannot suddenly cause prosperity or decline.
Therefore, cold and heat gradually emerge in spring and autumn,
prosperity and decline arise from gains and losses.
In the current era,
official careers have no
barriers or checkpoints,
the gate for evil has opened;
the court does not demand the worthy,
the path of righteousness is blocked.
The source of gains and losses,
what could be worse than this!
What is meant by demanding the worthy,
is to make them recommend each
other;
what is meant by barriers and checkpoints,
is to make them vouch for each other.
If the worthy are not recommended, there is blame;
if the guarantee is not trustworthy, there is punishment.
Therefore, in ancient times, feudal lords had to present scholars;
those who did not present
were stripped of territory,
and those who presented but were unsuitable were also stripped.
Now, scholars
are difficult to know;
the unsuitable
are a minor fault.
To have to demand,
is to compel what one does not know;
to punish
for the unsuitable,
is to exaggerate a minor fault,
which is not lenient.
Moreover, for the Son of Heaven towards the feudal lords,
there is the principle of not being purely subjects,
yet they were still held responsible.
The way of implementation,
it is
better to err on the side of leniency rather than abuse.
Now everything is the opposite,
why?
For the worthy are the guidelines of Heaven and Earth,
the pinnacle of all things.
How urgent it is to secure them!
Therefore, it is better to be lenient and obtain
them,
than to be too restrictive and lose them.
Now it is not so;
the people of the world, wandering aimlessly,
each seek only to justify themselves.
Thus, their talents and conduct cannot be relied upon,
resulting in
disorderly governance in public affairs,
and widespread corruption and filth in private life.
Recently, high-ranking officials particularly suffer from this flaw,
some are fugitives with bounties on their heads,
some are bound and
executed.
Greedy and contemptible individuals usurp positions,
who promoted them?
Rhinos and wild beasts escape their enclosures,
who is to blame?
A net so loose that a boat can pass through it,
what can be
worse than this!
People's pursuit of profit
is like treading on water and fire.
Though previous people failed,
later people rise again.
If this continues endlessly,
who will stop it?
Factions compete
daily,
who will worry about it?
Although the sagely thoughts of today's sovereign are tireless day and night,
the people appointed to govern,
being of this kind,
for a sagely era to transform customs into beauty and peace,
is like waiting for the Yellow River to
clear.
If you wish for it to be good,
you should establish a system for recommending the worthy,
and strengthen the defenses of barriers and checkpoints.
Once this system is established,
people will be careful in their recommendations and not be casual,
then the worthy can be
known.
When the worthy are known and tested,
then officials will be appropriately appointed.
When officials are appropriately appointed,
then affairs will be in proper order;
when affairs are in proper order,
then things will be handled appropriately;
when things are
handled appropriately,
then life will be abundant and prosperous,
people will be provided with resources,
and harmony and joy will arise.
Thus, there will be fewer transgressions and distant punishments,
a sense of shame and closeness to propriety.
This is how to establish an eternal
governance,
change customs and transform traditions,
and make punishments unnecessary.
The Edict states:
“Recently, foreign tribes have invaded,
and calamities have repeatedly descended.
Is it that the appointed individuals are not the right people?
How has it come to this? ”
Your servant hears that barbarians confuse
夏,
then Gāo Táo (皋陶) served as the Minister of Justice.
This means that to perfect the minor aspects,
one must first attend to the major ones.
When the virtuous are appointed, governance is benevolent;
when the capable are employed, punishments are lenient.
When governance is benevolent, the people look up to
its beneficence;
when punishments are lenient, people are emboldened.
Beneficence is for enriching their wealth;
boldness is for securing their hearts.
Therefore, when people live, their resources are abundant and they know propriety;
when they act, they are loyal to their superiors
and brave in spirit.
If one considers their benefits and removes their harms,
and benefits them through the way of life,
they will not waver even in death.
If one motivates them to labor through the way of ease,
they will not complain even in hardship.
Therefore,
their lives can be entrusted,
and their strength can be exhausted.
They will be victorious in battle,
and conquer in attack.
Thus, the good admire virtue and submit peacefully,
while the wicked fear and disappear.
To stop war and attain martial prowess,
justice truly lies in culture.
Only by appointing the virtuous can there be no worries.
As for disasters like floods and droughts,
these are natural phenomena.
Therefore, in ancient times, thirty years
of cultivation would surely yield ten years of reserves.
Yáo (堯) and Tāng (湯) encountered such disasters, yet the people did not suffer,
because they were prepared.
Recently, although wind and rain have been somewhat unseasonal,
when examining all nations,
some areas
share contiguous borders,
yet their harvests differ;
or even contiguous plots of land,
yield different successes or failures.
This is certainly not because Heaven is intent on harming people,
but rather that people are unable to equalize their toil
and hardship.
To attribute human failings
to Heaven,
will lead to officials neglecting their duties and not being encouraged,
and the common people becoming disheartened in their work and blaming the times.
This is not the way to stabilize people's will
or bring about
bountiful years.
One should diligently attend to human affairs, and that is all.
Your servant is truly ignorant and humble, insufficient to answer before the sagely court.
Yet, that I still present this to the court,
is it to have me take something from my bosom and offer it?
Your servant fears it is insufficient.
If by accepting unwise words, one can elicit wise words,
then your servant may be useful.
This is why I do not conceal my humble words.
Having placed first in the palace examination,
he was appointed Advisory Gentleman (Yìláng 議郎).
Due to his mother's illness, he resigned his post.
When [Lǐ] Shēn's (李詵) mother was ill,
he suffered from a lack of a carriage.
When she passed away,
he did not want to transport the coffin by carriage,
and being poor, he had no means to buy a horse.
So he temporarily buried her outside the north wall of the hall where he lived,
opened a door,
and bowed and wept morning and evening.
He raised chickens and planted garlic,
exhausting all his methods.
After the three-year mourning period passed,
he acquired eight horses,
and transported the coffin to the tomb,
carrying earth to build the mound.
Before it was finished,
he was summoned to serve as Aide-de-Camp to the Commander of the Eastern Expedition (Zhēngdōng cānjūn 征東參軍).
He was transferred to Secretary in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎),
then became an Aide to the Grand General of Cavalry (Chēqí Cóngshì Zhōngláng 車騎從事中郎).
Minister of Personnel Cuī Hóng (崔洪) recommended Shēn (詵) as Assistant Minister (Zuǒchéng 左丞).
While in office,
he once impeached Hóng (洪) over an matter.
Hóng (洪) resented Shēn (詵),
but Shēn (詵) resisted him with impartiality.
The story is in Hóng's (洪) biography.
Hóng (洪) heard of this and felt ashamed, then submitted.
He was successively promoted to Inspector of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu cìshǐ 雍州刺史).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) held a farewell gathering for him in the Eastern Hall,
and asked Shēn (詵),
"What do you consider yourself to be?"
Shēn (詵) replied,
"Your servant placed first in the examination for 'the worthy and the good and those who offered policy advice' (jǔ xiánliáng duìcè 舉賢良對策),
like a branch from a cassia forest,
or a fragment of jade from Kūnshān (崑山)."
The Emperor laughed.
The Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中) then proposed dismissing Shēn (詵) from office.
The Emperor said,
"I was just joking with him;
there is no need to make a fuss."
Shēn (詵) was majestic, authoritative, and decisive in his post,
and gained great reputation from all quarters.
He died in office.
His son Yán Dēng (延登) served as Prefectural Administrator (Zhōubiéjià 州別駕).
Ruǎn Zhǒng (阮種)
Ruǎn Zhǒng (阮種), courtesy name Déyóu (德猷),
was a native of Wèishì (尉氏) in Chénliú (陳留),
and an eighth-generation descendant of Hàn (漢) Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中) Xū Qīng (胥卿).
At the age of twenty, he possessed extraordinary conduct,
and was highly regarded by Jī Kāng (嵇康).
The "Master Ruǎn (Ruǎnshēng 阮生)" mentioned by Kāng (康) in his "Essay on Nurturing Life" (Yǎngshēng Lùn 養生論)
is indeed Zhǒng (種).
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián 孝廉) candidate,
and served as a Clerk in the Ducal Office (Gōngfǔ yuàn 公府掾).
At this time, the Western barbarians were invading,
calamities were frequently seen,
and the people suffered from famine.
An edict commanded the Three Excellencies (Sān Gōng 三公), Ministers (Qīngyǐn 卿尹), Palace Attendants (Chángbó 常伯), and Governors (Mùshǒu 牧守) to each recommend wise, upright, and outspoken gentlemen.
Thereupon, Grand Tutor Hé Zēng (何曾) recommended Zhǒng (種) as "worthy and good" (xiánliáng 賢良).
The imperial edict for the policy examination read:
"In ancient times, sagely kings,
following the order of Heaven,
brilliantly resided over the universe,
all using the standards of Heaven and Earth,
benefiting and comforting all beings,
with auspicious winds spreading
for a thousand years.
I have ascended to the grand mandate and throne,
and it has been seven years now.
Yet my virtue has not been inherited,
and I am not enlightened in governance.
I rise early, vigilant and diligent,
but have not illuminated my path.
You, gentlemen, possess profound knowledge of the Dao and its arts,
and present yourselves with dignity.
I greatly appreciate this.
Each of you should fully express your hearts
to expound and enlighten my will,
profoundly setting forth the foundation of the kingly way,
concealing nothing.
I shall examine them with an open mind."
Zhǒng (種) replied:
"Heaven and Earth establish their positions,
and the sages perfect their abilities.
The kingly way is profoundly deep,
and thus its transforming influence extends far.
Therefore, it can bring forth things and accomplish tasks,
and its achievements never cease.
Those nearby obey without exception,
and those far away submit without exception.
Its virtue reaches all living beings,
its beneficence covers all lands,
its reputation spreads endlessly,
and its canons endure for a hundred generations.
Hence the classic says: 'The sage endures in his Way,
and the world is transformed and perfected.'
It is fitting to follow the footsteps of past eras,
to emulate the Three Sovereigns (Sān Wǔ 三五),
to correct the age and change customs,
to accord with the hopes of the people.
Let all within the realm shift towards righteousness,
let the common people know where to turn,
spread a pure and beautiful transforming influence,
and block the path of evil and crookedness.
This is truly what the masses long for in great virtue and hope for in auspicious customs."
He was further asked about the unenforced governance and punishments,
and the unestablished rites and music.
He replied:
"The enforcement of governance and punishments
is fundamentally derived from the application of rites and music.
The enlightened kings of the past
devoted themselves solely to this,
thereby preventing arrogance and violence,
moving hearts and minds,
regulating living beings,
and transforming the myriad people.
Rites embody virtue,
and music praises achievements.
Music is founded on harmony,
and rites are based on reverence."
He further asked about the **Róng** and **Mán** barbarians disrupting **Huáxià**.
The reply was:
“When the **Róng** and **Mán** barbarians disrupt **Huáxià**,
invading and ruining the royal domain,
even in ancient prosperous eras,
there was still this concern.
Thus, the **Shī** says, ‘The **Xiǎnyǔn** are fiercely rampant,’
and the **Shū** laments, ‘The **Mán** and **Yí** submissively obey.’
Since the time of the **Wèi** clan,
the barbarians have submitted to the interior,
and there have been few troubles of rebellious audacity or plundering.
Due to this, border defenses have become lax,
and barriers are not established.
Now, ugly barbarians reside within the country,
mingling with the common people,
border officials are accustomed to disturbances,
and people have forgotten how to fight.
Those entrusted with regional responsibilities
are also not of suitable talent,
some, using trickery,
assault and insult the border barbarians;
others, seeking rewards and profits,
wantonly carry out punitive killings.
To use a flimsy bridle to control a wild horse,
and then also to wield a troublesome whip,
that it cannot be controlled
is certainly its natural outcome.
Therefore, the hordes of barbarians are startled and agitated,
and move exploiting the gaps.
Even if three prefectures are overthrown and defeated,
the regional governors do not turn back;
this is not because the **Hú** barbarians are exceedingly strong,
but rather because those who employ them make mistakes.
Your servant has heard that the King’s expeditions
are for chastising, not for fighting;
they pacify distant lands with virtue,
and not, it is heard, with weapons.
Indeed, weapons are instruments of ill omen,
and warfare is a dangerous affair.
When armies rise, farmers are harmed;
when multitudes gather, provisions are wasted.
When farmers are harmed, people are impoverished;
when provisions are wasted, the state is empty.
In the time of **Hàn Wǔdì** in the past,
inheriting the achievements of **Wén Dì**,
relying on the wealth of the realm,
he employed his capable ministers
to satisfy his desire against the **Xiōngnú**,
competing for the merits of victory
and coveting the gains of conquest.
Good generals and strong soldiers
perished in the desert;
victories and defeats were about even,
success was not more than appropriate.
He cut short the lives of the common people
and fed the mouths of hungry wolves.
And when he used his multitude to subdue the few,
making the **Xiōngnú** retreat far away,
achieving success at **Qílián**
and watering horses in the **Hànhǎi**,
the exhaustion of the empire
had already surpassed more than half.
Indeed, to exhaust **Zhōngguó** to serve the barbarians
is truly not a wise plan.
Therefore, bandits rose up like swarms of bees,
and **Shāndōng** did not recover.
By the time of **Xuān** and **Yuán**,
when **Zhào Chōngguó** campaigned against the Western **Líng**
and **Féng Fèngshì** campaigned against the Southern **Qiāng**,
both achieved victory without shedding blood,
crushing the strong and violent,
capturing their ringleaders.
These are examples of averting conflict and suppressing difficulties,
distinguishing victory from defeat,
clear evidence from the middle ages.”
He further asked about inauspicious omens appearing.
The reply was:
“When **Yīn** and **Yáng** are blocked or smooth,
or there are disasters from the six disorders,
the ruler of men must cultivate governance to counter them,
anticipate troubles and prevent them,
establish the foundation of the Imperial Ultimate,
and carefully examine the use of various omens.
The **Shī** says, ‘Be reverent, be reverent,
for Heaven is indeed manifest in thought.’
Heaven’s keenness of hearing and sight comes from the keenness of hearing and sight of our people;
therefore, the ruler of men inherits the Mandate of Heaven,
being cautious day by day.
Thus, he can receive abundant blessings and perpetually establish his reign.
This is how the former kings averted disasters and eliminated calamities.”
He further asked about the essentials of administration and transformation.
The reply was:
“Indeed, the foundation of the Kingly Way,
the essentials of administering the state,
must first be founded on ritual and righteousness,
and lead people to integrity and shame.
When ritual and righteousness are established,
gentlemen will follow the proper path and yield to what is good;
when integrity and shame are established,
petty people will be cautious in their conduct and not transgress the regulations.
Reward is used to encourage the capable,
and authority is used to punish the negligent.
This is how the former kings preserved and stabilized their achievements,
spread their transformation among the common people,
and their merits and deeds endured for generations.
Thus, if there is a custom of humility and yielding among those above,
there will be a custom of non-contention among those below;
if there are officials of integrity in the court,
there will be no greedy people in the countryside.
Indeed, integrity and shame in governance
are like rich soil for cultivation,
or fertile moisture in a good year;
their produce will surely flourish abundantly.
If integrity and shame do not exist,
and only punishment is used to govern,
then customs will decay,
people will lose their nature,
even for the slightest things,
there will be a contentious heart,
and even severe laws and strict punishments
will not suffice.
Its effect on governance
is like a farmer planting in barren land,
or hoping for a rich harvest in a drought year;
it is bound to be unlikely.
This is why the Three Dynasties enjoyed virtue for a long time,
with pure customs and beautiful traditions,
all preserving Heaven’s favor for several hundred years.
But the **Qín** perished in its second generation,
probably because the path it followed was different.”
He further asked:
“To enable the seven virtues of martial accomplishment
and the nine merits of civil administration,
by what path can one achieve this?
Among all these various matters,
what comes last and what comes first?”
The reply was:
“Indeed, for civil and martial virtues
to accomplish great deeds,
and all various achievements to flourish,
nothing is more important than selecting and establishing the wise and discerning,
and entrusting responsibilities to the capable.
If talent matches its office and achievement corresponds to its duty,
then all affairs of state will be managed,
and no officials will be idle.
The **Shū** says: ‘Heaven’s work, let people perform it on its behalf.’
Thus, to carry on Heaven’s work and manage affairs,
to stabilize the state and secure the family,
cannot be accomplished without worthy individuals.
The accumulation of worthy talents in the state
is like a good craftsman needing sharp tools,
or a skilled artisan awaiting ink lines.
If tools are sharp,
cutting is easy and the material is not harmed;
if ink lines are set,
straightness and crookedness are corrected, and all forms are achieved.
Therefore, the ruler of men must diligently seek worthy individuals
and then relax by entrusting them.
Worthy ministers, regarding their lord,
when advancing, are loyal to the state and love the people;
when retreating, they sharpen their integrity and purify their aspirations.
They manage their duties without pursuing private interests,
their intentions always follow the public path,
they clarify standards to demonstrate their abilities,
and meticulously follow regulations to achieve their accomplishments.
This is why the sage kings of old, respectfully facing south,
were able to transform the world as if molding clay, because of the worthy individuals they entrusted and the trust they placed in them.
Currently, all scholars within the realm
look forward to your brilliant glory, hoping to reach the highest authority,
awaiting only the direction you choose.
If you open the four windows of listening,
and broadly seek counsel,
draw out the many heroes,
and invite the distinguished,
assess their work and assign offices,
demonstrate ability and establish positions,
so that there are no idlers in court,
then transformation will flow boundlessly,
and achievements will be immortal.”
At that time, Zhǒng, along with Xì Shēn and Prince Kāng of Dōngpíng, all resided in the imperial mansion.
He was then appointed as Shàngshū Láng.
However, some detractors,
alleged that the respondents had falsely claimed connections.
The Emperor then summoned various scholars again,
and questioned them in court.
The imperial edict stated:
"Previously, in your policy responses,
you each answered the questions directly,
but did not fully express what you, gentlemen, wished to say.
Therefore, I have summoned you again
to fully present your thoughts.
Furthermore, in recent years there have been continuous floods and droughts,
and although I have been greatly apprehensive,
I have not been able to fully comprehend the principles of heaven and humanity.
What measures should be taken to respond to these changes?
How should those who suffer from floods, droughts, and famine
be rescued?
In the interim, there have been many affairs,
and I have not achieved tranquility.
I desire to alleviate burdensome duties
and ensure that the people do not lose their livelihood.
If there are any sufferings or hardships among the people,
or matters that should be improved or reformed
to benefit both public and private interests,
please present them in detail.
Moreover, good governance depends on finding the right people,
but knowing them is extremely difficult;
one can only discern them through others' observations and reports.
If there are reclusive scholars, civil or military,
each of you should recommend those you know.
Even if they are obscure, humble, or unconventional,
do not place any restrictions.
Therefore, I earnestly wish to hear factual accounts,
do not strive for flowery rhetoric,
and do not conceal anything."
Zhǒng responded:
"I humbly reflect that Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom and profound insight,
extends compassion to the common people.
You are about to bring prosperity to all,
equaling the achievements of the Three Dynasties,
and widely seek out talented individuals
to assist in achieving supreme transformation.
This is truly the intention of Yáo and Shùn.
I, an unworthy subject with a dull and slow nature,
responded to the clear and brilliant summons.
My previous policy response
was insufficient to adequately answer the imperial edict.
The matters I presented were not exhaustive.
I am indeed ignorant,
which is my fault.
I have heard that Heaven gives birth to the myriad people
and establishes a ruler to govern them.
When a ruler's Way is pervasive,
the constant human relationships are in order,
and the five blessings arrive in full.
If governance has faults and errors,
and justice is somewhat skewed,
then the various auspicious signs do not appear,
and excessive disasters occur.
This is the principle of Heaven and humanity,
and the reason for rise and fall.
In ancient times, sagely kings,
with a complete political system and well-established institutions,
guided the people in their duties,
ensuring they focused on the fundamentals.
Thus, even if there were floods and droughts,
there was no suffering from famine.
Recently, Yin and Yang have been out of balance,
causing floods and droughts as disasters,
which is perhaps a consequence of cyclical fortune.
Otherwise,
it is due to officials not properly governing,
failing to propagate and uphold Your Majesty's virtue,
and thus not assisting in the great transformation.
Therefore, harmonious qi has not descended, and human affairs are not yet in order.
Currently, the common people are impoverished and exhausted,
and both public and private sectors lack reserves.
The solution truly lies in resting the populace, calming the people,
and encouraging diligence in farming and adhering to their roles.
This is their salvation.
The sufferings of the people
arise from burdensome corvée, dense regulations, and a lack of trust in the Dao.
Burdensome corvée causes the people to lose their livelihoods;
dense regulations make the lower classes betray their honesty;
and a lack of trust in the Dao means people have no firm resolve.
These are the most crucial matters for improvement or reduction,
and the major determinants of security and danger.
The Analects say: 'If one begins with good,
and good progresses,
then evil has no way to arrive.'
Confucius said: 'Look at what he does; observe his motives;
how can a man conceal himself?'
As for reclusive scholars, civil or military,
or talents who are obscure, humble, and unconventional,
these are indeed beyond the recognition of your foolish subject.
I humbly offer this foolish response."
When the policy was submitted,
the Emperor personally reviewed it,
and again ranked him first.
He was then promoted to Zhōngshū Láng.
His conduct was principled,
he disciplined himself and led his subordinates,
and the court officials all respected his dignified presence.
Whenever he offered a counter-argument,
his proposals were always adopted,
thus becoming a model.
He was promoted to the Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
At that time, Wèi Jīng of Xiāngyì, having been transferred from Nányáng Tàishǒu to Hénei,
was appointed together with Zhǒng.
The Emperor looked at them and sighed, saying:
"If all officials holding two thousand dàn salaries were like these,
what worries would I have!"
Zhǒng's governance was simple and benevolent,
and the people praised him.
He died in his commandery.
Huà Tán (Yuán Fǔ)
Huà Tán,
whose courtesy name was Lìngsī,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
His grandfather, Róng,
was the Grand General of the Left and Director of the Department of State Affairs of Wú.
His father, Xū,
was a Palace Attendant of Wú.
Tán became an orphan at the age of one.
His mother, eighteen years old,
remained chaste and raised him,
enduring utmost hardship.
When he grew up,
he was diligent in his studies,
intelligent and eloquent,
and was highly esteemed by his neighbors.
Zhōu Jùn, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, appointed him as a Staff Officer.
He admired Tán's talent and ability,
and treated him with the courtesy due to a guest and friend.
During the Tàikāng period,
Jī Shào, the Inspector, recommended Tán as a Xiùcái.
As he was about to depart,
Chén Zǒng, the Biéjià, saw him off
and asked:
"A ruler who values the worthy makes seeking talent his priority.
Ambitious individuals prioritize achievement and fame.
Why did Hé Zhòngshū not serve in the court of Emperor Wǔ,
and Jiǎ Yì lose favor during the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn?
These are lingering questions from the Wú and Jìn eras.
We can debate this before you depart."
Tán replied:
"When a sage is on the throne,
nothing is left ungoverned,
and the positions of the various ministers
are filled only by the worthy.
Therefore, no talent hides in the mountains,
nor lingers in humble gates.
However, a king who inherits the throne
may be of mediocre talent,
or even an ordinary person.
If such a person occupies the position of a sage
and rules over the myriad people,
then his teachings will decline day by day,
and customs will gradually deteriorate.
Moreover, a ruler of mediocre talent
has limited resources;
things attract their kind,
so he will inevitably rely on his own faction.
Even if his faction's words are wrong,
he will consider them right.
With those he appoints being as wise as Yán and Rǎn,
and those he employs having the caliber of a state minister,
those in office daily hope for the achievements of Yuán and Kǎi,
and those above daily expect the righteousness of Yáo and Shùn.
How could they know that their governance is gradually collapsing?
Although the court has a reputation for seeking the worthy,
it lacks the reality of recognizing talent.
Even if words are correct,
they consider them deceit;
even if strategies are brilliant,
they consider them madness.
Deceit leads to words that disparage oneself,
and madness leads to accusations of disloyalty.
Is this intentional?
Shallow understanding cannot perceive deep principles;
limited talent cannot see distant forms.
Therefore, words are not adopted,
and plans are not implemented.
They fear not having enough time to avoid death,
let alone establishing achievements and fame!
Thus, Shàngguān was favored while Qū Yuán was exiled;
Zǎi Pǐ was honored while Wǔ Yuán was executed.
Is this not lamentable?
As for Zhòngshū being suppressed by Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and Jiǎ Yì losing favor with Emperor Wén of Hàn,
these are perhaps lesser instances.
Thus, Bái Qǐ once said: 'It is not difficult to find the worthy;
it is difficult to employ them.
It is not difficult to employ them;
it is difficult to trust them.'
If one finds the worthy but cannot employ them,
or employs them but cannot trust them,
how can great achievements be accomplished?"
Tán reached Luòyáng.
Emperor Wǔ personally questioned him, saying:
"Now the Four Seas are unified,
and ten thousand *lǐ* share the same customs.
The world is in the Dao,
and none is as prosperous as this era.
However, in the north there are untamed barbarians,
and in the west there are troublesome Dī people.
Therefore, strategists cannot yet rest easy,
and border people have not yet found peace.
How then can we permanently eliminate these troubles
and bring peace and order to the Six Directions?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that when the Sages govern the world,
they follow the principle of Qián to spread their transforming influence,
and conform to the *Gǔfēng* (valley winds) to cultivate benevolence.
They combine the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, Man) to control all things,
