and open the Four Ears to attract the worthy.
Thus, they work diligently from morning till night,
focusing on selecting talent.
They make known the recluses in the mountains and caves,
and cast light upon the hidden and stagnant.
When brilliant dragons leap forth,
the imperial Way shines.
When pure virtues soar like phoenixes,
the royal transformation is achieved.
Therefore, when Gāotáo was appointed,
the inhumane were kept at bay.
When Lù Jiǎ was esteemed by Hàn,
distant barbarians bowed their heads.
Now, the sagely court's virtuous pronouncements issue from the inner chambers,
and pure winds soar to all corners of the world.
When the military banners pointed south,
the Jiāng and Hàn regions were swept up.
When spears and shields marched west,
the Qiāng and Mán yearned for transformation.
This is truly the autumn for opening the Four Gates (i.e., inviting all talents),
and the day for promoting rites and teachings.
Thus, eminent talents hear the call and respond,
and extraordinary individuals gather like clouds when they see the opportunity.
Keep high halls empty to await the worthy,
and establish high ranks to receive scholars.
Be more eager for goodness than for food and drink,
and employ people as swiftly as echo follows sound.
Close the gates to sycophancy,
and abolish the music of Zhèng.
To bring peace and order to the Six Directions
truly depends on these things.
Although in the northwest there are untamed bandits,
and in the distant deserts there are unyielding barbarians,
to conquer them would weary the army,
and to gain them would be of no benefit.
Therefore, Bān Gù said: 'One may possess their land, but it cannot be tilled for food.
One may gain their people, but they cannot be made subjects and kept.
If they come, punish and resist them.
If they leave, prepare and guard against them.'
This is indeed the art of pacifying the borders."
He further questioned:
"Wú and Shǔ relied on their natural defenses,
but now they have been pacified.
The Shǔ people have submitted to transformation,
and harbor no thoughts of disloyalty.
But the Wú people are restless and hesitant,
frequently creating rebellious disturbances.
Is it that the Shǔ people are simple and honest,
and easily influenced and persuaded?
While the Wú people are light and quick,
difficult to settle and prone to agitation?
Now, to tranquilize the newly subjugated,
what should be the priority?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that at the end of the Hàn dynasty, the empire crumbled,
and heroes stood like tripods.
Shǔ resided in Mínlǒng,
and Wú occupied the lands south of the Jiāng.
When the Great Jìn arose like a dragon,
it met the destined moment and received the mandate.
Emperor Wén planned strategically,
and Ānlè (Liú Shàn) followed the path of submission.
The sagely Emperor secretly strategized,
and (Sūn) Hào submitted and turned towards transformation.
Shǔ had been imbued with transforming influence for a long time,
and its customs and teachings were established.
Wú has only recently submitted,
and has not yet changed its customs.
It is not that the Shǔ people are honest and simple, while the Wú people are easily agitated.
However, different customs and distant lands
have dissimilar environments.
Wú is protected by the long Jiāng,
and its old customs are light and fierce.
The strategy for pacifying them
must first involve planning for their eminent individuals.
Let them soar to the imperial gate,
promote their worthy talents,
and treat them with special courtesies.
Clearly select governors and magistrates,
and establish their authority.
Lighten their taxes and levies,
and ensure harmony and joy.
This way, they can be eternally preserved,
and forever be your subjects."
He further questioned:
"The Sage said that if there were a king,
it would take a hundred years for benevolence to prevail.
Now, Heaven and Earth are settled,
and the great transformation knows no bounds.
Although the Xiōngnú are not yet fully bound,
and the Qiāng and Dī are arrogant and cunning,
we shall cultivate civil virtue to pacify them,
and perform dances with shields and axes to attract them.
Thus, weapons of war are sheathed,
and warriors rest.
If this is the case,
can we not yet melt down blades into farming tools,
and decommission the Imperial Armory's military supplies?"
He replied:
"Indeed, it was after Yáo of Táng ruled for many years
that songs of praise arose.
When King Wén and King Wǔ succeeded each other,
rites and music achieved great harmony.
The Eight Directions were brought to peace,
and tranquillity spread everywhere.
All nations followed the path of submission,
and the realm was resplendent.
Even lands of the disheveled-haired
and barefooted nations
all learned to wear formal caps and came to court,
donning robes and bowing respectfully.
Yet, with the virtue of Great Shùn,
there was still the expedition against the Sān Miáo.
At the height of Zhōu's prosperity,
the Xiǎnyǔn were still a menace.
Although there is civil virtue,
military preparedness is still necessary.
To prepare for the unexpected
is an excellent ancient teaching.
Not to forget danger in times of peace
is a constant warning from the Sages.
Do not abolish the regular duties of the armory,
nor melt down blades into farming tools.
One can certainly sheathe weapons,
and wrap them in animal hides.
The generals and commanders
can be made feudal lords.
Amidst joyful relaxation and peaceful customs,
this would not be considered ungenerous."
He further questioned:
"The establishment of laws and regulations
is for adapting to the times.
When times are perilous, strict laws are used to achieve stability.
When times are peaceful, a wide net is cast to foster transformation.
Now the world is at peace,
the four quarters are without incident,
and the people are imbued with virtue.
They are about to achieve a state of non-action.
As for the laws and ordinances,
should there be any reductions or additions?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that the Five Emperors had different rites,
and the Three Kings had different teachings.
Thus, some abdicated to glorify governance,
while others used spears and shields for conquest.
However, as for promoting rites and music to harmonize people,
and spreading pure customs to tranquilize society,
their ultimate goal was one.
Now, truly, customs and teachings are largely unified,
the Four Seas are without worry,
and all people are influenced and transformed,
abandoning evil and following righteousness.
Yet, even at the height of Yáo and Shùn's prosperity,
they still instituted symbolic punishments.
During the flourishing reigns of Yīn and Zhōu,
the Grand Guardian (Bó Hóu) established laws.
The existence of laws and ordinances
does not hinder governance.
If the Great Way extends in all directions,
and rites and music are universally communicated,
ordinary people will practice self-cultivation,
and the common folk will exert themselves in virtue,
so that punishments are suspended and not applied,
and laws and ordinances exist but are not enforced.
This is precisely sufficient to elevate the refined transformation of great peace,
and to spread the wind of benevolence to all corners of the world."
Another edict asked:
"In ancient times, Emperor Shùn achieved success with 'two eights' (sixteen talented individuals),
and King Wén of Zhōu revitalized Zhōu with many scholars.
Indeed, the establishment of civilization depends on obtaining the right people,
but virtuous talents are hard to come by.
Now that the great unity has just been achieved,
it is fitting to seek out substantial talents.
Although the prefectures and commanderies have systems for recommendation,
we have not yet obtained individuals of outstanding and exceptional caliber.
Is it that there are no such people at this time?
Or is it that we have them but have not yet found the right way to bring them forth?"
The reply was:
"Your minister has heard that when establishing civilization and enacting laws,
without the virtuous, its ways cannot be glorified;
when governing a peaceful era or bringing order to chaos,
without talent, its undertakings cannot be proclaimed.
From the exalted Huáng Xī [Fú Xī]
down to the emperors and kings,
none failed to spread the imperial net widely [to gather talents]
and send forth a benevolent wind to envelop all things.
Therefore, when the virtuous are obtained, teaching thrives;
when people are lost, governance fails.
Now, the four seas are unified,
and ten thousand li share the same customs;
prefectures and commanderies recommend Xiùxiào (Filial and Incorrupt),
and the imperial court selects good talents.
With the vastness of the eight directions [of the world]
and the multitude of common people,
how could there be no outstanding, eminent, and exceptional talents!
This is like the South Sea not lacking the treasures of bright pearls,
and Dàyuān (Ferghana) not wanting for thousand-li steeds.
Extraordinary sages are difficult to see,
and distant numbers are hard to behold.
Thus, during the peaceful reign of Yáo and Shùn,
the 'two eights' only became prominent through Shùn;
when Yīn Tāng revolutionized the mandate of the king,
Yī Yǐn was only used after carrying the tripod [as a cook].
In this sacred dynasty,
we treat with courtesy the literati of fallen states,
and welcome people from distant lineages.
Some wear diāochán [official caps] in the imperial strategium,
others are granted insignia of authority over a thousand li.
On imperial tours, there must be encounters like that with Lǚ Gōng;
in nocturnal dreams, there must be inspirations from recluses in caves.
The emergence of virtuous and eminent talents can be anticipated with eagerness."
At that time, among the Xiùxiào candidates from the nine provinces, none could match Tán in the policy questions.
Tán was always highly regarded in the eastern regions for his talent and learning.
Liú Sòng, of the same commandery, then serving as Tíngwèi (Minister of Justice),
saw him and sighed, saying:
"I didn't realize that our local area had such talent!"
Bóshì Wáng Jì, among the crowd, mocked him, saying:
"The Five Bureaus have just opened,
and the high officials are issuing appointments,
gathering extraordinary elites from humble places,
and promoting virtuous and eminent people from secluded caves.
You, a man from Wú and Chǔ, a remnant of a fallen state,
what exceptional quality do you possess to merit this appointment?"
Tán replied:
"Exceptional qualities are indeed born outside the central regions,
not originating from the central domain.
This is why bright pearls and patterned cowries
are born along the banks of the Jiāng and Yù rivers;
and the luminous jade
comes from beneath Jīnglán.
Therefore, if we seek it in people,
King Wén was born in the Eastern Yí,
and Dà Yǔ was born in the Western Qiāng.
Have you not heard, sir?
In ancient times, when King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
he relocated the stubborn people of Yīn to Luòyì.
Are you gentlemen not their descendants?"
Jì then said:
"If one does not uphold the tottering,
nor support the falling,
to the point where ruler and minister lose their positions,
and the state perishes without a master,
what will all those wearing caps and sashes [officials] hold onto then!"
Tán replied:
"Alas!
Survival and demise have their destinies,
rise and fall have their timings.
What Heaven abandons,
man cannot sustain.
Xú Yǎn cultivated benevolence and righteousness but lost his state;
Zhòng Ní (Confucius) was expelled from Lǔ and pressured in Qí;
Duàn Gān Yàn became famous through reclusion.
Indeed, good fortune and ill fortune have their seasons;
how can it be something human effort can accomplish?"
Jì treated him with great respect.
Soon after, he was appointed Lángzhōng,
then promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén (Gentleman of the Crown Prince's Household) and Běnguó Zhōngzhèng (Chief Judge of his native commandery).
He resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he became the Magistrate of Juànchéng.
Passing by the Púshǔi river,
he wrote a eulogy for Zhuāngzǐ and showed it to the Cāncáo (Registrar).
The Tíngyuàn (Court Clerk) Zhāng Yán wrote a response,
the prose of which was very beautiful.
Tán was impressed and recommended him,
and he was subsequently promoted.
By the time Tán was in Lújiāng,
Yán had already become the Grand Administrator of Huáilíng.
He also nominated Zhōu Fǎng, a commoner from a humble family, as Xiàolián.
Fǎng indeed achieved fame and meritorious service,
and Tán was then considered a discerning judge of character.
He resigned from office due to the destruction of his father's tomb.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshūláng (Secretary to the Imperial Secretariat).
In the early Yǒngníng era,
he was dispatched as Magistrate of Jiá.
At that time, after years of warfare,
the region suffered from famine.
Tán devoted himself to providing relief and comfort.
Sītú (Minister of Works) Wáng Róng heard of this and praised him,
donating three hundred hú of grain to assist him.
Tán achieved much in his administration.
He was twice promoted to Lújiāng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Lújiāng),
and given the additional title of Suīyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Distant).
At that time, Shí Bīng's followers, such as Lù Guī, occupied various counties.
Tán dispatched Sīmǎ Chǔ Dūn to suppress and pacify them.
He also sent a separate force to attack Bīng's Dūdū (Commander) Mèng Xú,
capturing his fierce commanders.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu (Marquis of Dūting),
with a stipend of one thousand households,
and was granted one thousand bolts of silk.
During Chén Mǐn's rebellion,
many scholars from Wú were coerced by him.
Gù Róng first accepted Mǐn's official position,
but secretly plotted against him.
Tán, unaware of Róng's true intention,
openly issued proclamations far and wide,
severely criticizing Róng's actions.
Because of this, he incurred Róng's resentment.
Moreover, his administration in the commandery was strict,
and he frequently clashed with his superiors.
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yáng Province) Liú Táo, who had long been on bad terms with Tán,
used the law to arrest Tán
and imprisoned him in Shòuyáng.
Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the East) Zhōu Fù, who had always been close to Tán,
intervened and released him.
When Gān Zhuó attacked Fù,
the populace scattered.
Fù thought Tán had already left,
and sent someone to check,
only to find Tán had moved closer to Fù.
Fù sighed, saying:
"I have always said that Huá Lìngsī is a peer of Zāng Zǐyuán,
and now it is proven true."
Gān Zhuó had once been captured by Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè,
who issued an order that anyone harboring him would be executed.
Zhuó sought refuge with Tán and escaped.
During this campaign,
Zhuó sent someone to inquire, saying:
"Where is Marquis Huá?
I am Gān Yángwēi's envoy."
Tán replied that he did not know,
and gave the envoy two bolts of silk to send him away.
The envoy returned
and reported to Zhuó.
Zhuó said:
"This is Marquis Huá."
He sought him again,
but Tán had already disappeared.
Later, he was recommended by Jì Zhān,
but was hindered and stopped by Gù Róng,
thus he could not be appointed for several years.
In the early Jiànxīng [era],
Emperor Yuán appointed him Zhèndōng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
Tán was learned and widely conversant.
Having nothing to do in the office,
he then wrote a book in thirty volumes,
titled Biàndào.
He submitted a memorial to present it,
and the Emperor personally reviewed it.
He was transferred to Chéngxiàng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
and concurrently held the position of Jùn Dà Zhōngzhèng.
Tán recommended Gàn Bǎo and Fàn Yáo to the court.
Then he submitted a memorial requesting retirement, saying:
"Your servant has heard that enlightened rulers listen widely
and make seeking talent their duty;
officials assess themselves
and make self-examination their lot.
Thus, Shū Guǎng announced his old age,
and Emperor Xuān of Hàn did not thwart his ambition;
Gàn Mù retired to rest,
and Marquis Wén personally sought him in his cottage.
Your servant lacks the virtues of the ancients,
but secretly harbors the aspiration of retirement.
Since ascending to prominent positions,
I have been in and out for two years,
holding a brush without the merit of aiding affairs,
and picking up forgotten matters without achievements in making up for deficiencies;
the fault lies in accepting advice,
being ignorant in promoting the good;
the mad bandits are not yet subdued,
and I am again lacking in strategies.
My age approaches seventy,
my will and strength daily decline,
I consume provisions without labor,
and it is truly fitting for me to resign.
I respectfully return the loaned official tablet of Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ."
This was not granted.
In the early Jiànwǔ [era],
he was appointed Mìshū Jiān,
but he firmly declined the appointment.
In the early Tàixīng [era],
he was appointed Qián Jūn,
but due to illness, he was again transferred to Mìshū Jiān.
He was proud of his long-standing reputation,
but was discontent and did not achieve his ambitions.
At that time, Zhū Fèng of Jìnling and Wú Zhèn of Wújun were both scholarly and upright,
old but not yet appointed.
Tán recommended both of them as Zhùzuò Zuǒláng.
Someone asked Tán, saying:
"The proverb says that the difference between people
is like the hair of nine oxen.
Is there such a principle?"
Tán replied:
"In the past, Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fù yielded the noble position of Son of Heaven,
while common people in the marketplace contend for the profit of half a coin.
The difference between them,
how could it be merely like the hair of nine oxen!"
Those who heard praised his wisdom.
Dài Ruòsī's younger brother Miǎo
was Tán's son-in-law.
Throughout his life, Tán often suppressed Ruòsī and promoted Miǎo,
which Ruòsī resented.
When he came to power,
he slandered Tán to the Emperor,
hence Tán's official career did not progress.
Tán always harbored disappointment,
and once casually said to the Emperor:
"Your servant is already old,
and will await death in the secret archives.
Jí Àn's words
still exist today."
The Emperor was displeased.
After a long time,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
but he repeatedly declined due to illness.
When Wáng Dūn rebelled,
Tán was gravely ill
and unable to enter the palace department,
so he was dismissed from his post.
He died at home.
He was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Dàfū,
with a golden seal and purple ribbon,
and the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
His posthumous name was Hú.
He had two sons: Huà and Mào.
Huà, courtesy name Chángfēng,
was Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ,
and died in battle while suppressing Jí Sāng.
Mào inherited the noble title.
Yuán Fǔ, courtesy name Gōngzhòu, from Huáinán,
was also fond of learning,
and was as renowned as Tán,
known for his eloquence and wit.
He once visited Zhōng Lǐngjūn Hé Xù,
and said he was capable of governing a difficult county.
Xù asked:
"You only wish to govern a county,
not to serve in the offices of the court,
why is that?"
Fǔ replied:
"Each person has what they are capable of and what they are not.
For example, among silks, nothing is better than brocade,
but brocade cannot be used to make sackcloth;
among grains, nothing is better than rice,
but rice cannot be used for porridge.
Therefore, when a sagely king employs people,
he must first consider their aptitude.
If one is not universally talented,
how can one be skilled in everything!
Huáng Bà gained fame in the commanderies and districts,
but his reputation ceased in the capital.
The talent for a Tíngwèi [Minister of Justice]
is not for a Sāngōng [Duke],
this has been so since ancient times."
Xù approved of this,
and appointed him Sōngzī Lìng.
He was then transferred to Huáinán Guó Dànóng and Lángzhōng Lìng.
Shí Héng asked Fǔ:
"You are known for your eloquence.
Do you know why it is dry west of Shòuyáng,
and flooded east of Shòuyáng?"
Fǔ replied:
"East of Shòuyáng are all Wú people.
The music of a vanquished state is mournful and reflective.
Though it was once a strong state standing like a tripod,
it lost its position overnight.
Their indignation and lamentations have greatly accumulated;
accumulated sorrow forms阴 (yin, darkness/gloom),
accumulated yin forms rain,
and prolonged rain forms water.
Therefore, that region is flooded.
West of Shòuyáng are all Central Plains people.
They recently pacified strong Wú,
and all beautiful treasures flowed in.
Their ambitions are fulfilled, their hearts are content,
and they indulge in long festivities.
Gōngyáng has said that
Duke Xī of Lǔ was greatly pleased,
hence it caused a drought in the capital.
If one can suppress the strong and support the weak,
and treat the distant before the close,
then the world will be peaceful,
and disasters will not arise."
Onlookers marveled at his quick wit.
He died at home
at over eighty years of age.
The Imperial Historian comments: To rectify governance and customs,
one must select outstanding talents to accomplish tasks;
to display grandeur and radiate brilliance,
one must await an enlightened ruler to manifest achievements.
In the era of Emperor Wǔ,
the world was at peace,
the court focused on seeking worthies,
and those of great talent harbored the desire to serve.
Xì Shēn and others, though their worth was hidden in their localities,
answered the summons,
and responded to imperial inquiries,
striding high on the path to success.
Compared to past sages,
they are also worthy of praise.
If one were to follow Yì and act for righteousness,
with a steadfast will like Zhōu Gān,
the benevolent must be brave—
this is what is meant!
Although his talents and conduct were renowned early,
he had to await his end in the secret archives.
The regret of piling firewood [without using it]—
is it solely for the ancients?
Eulogy says: Xì and Ruǎn were profoundly learned,
embodying wisdom and political insight.
Huá Shēng cultivated virtue,
and answered the call, discarding his cap.
They once flew on bird paths,
and swam in dragon rivers.
Their inherent achievements are enduring,
their lofty fame flourishes.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 23: Crown Prince Mǐnhuái (Zǐpī, Zāng, Shàng)
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ Yù 愍懷太子遹, courtesy name Xīzǔ 熙祖,
was the eldest son of Huìdì 惠帝.
His mother was Consort Xiè 謝才人.
He was intelligent and astute from childhood.
Wǔdì 武帝 loved him
and kept him by his side.
Once, when he was playing with the other imperial princes in the palace hall,
Huìdì 惠帝 came to court.
Wǔdì 武帝 took the hands of the imperial princes,
and when he reached the Crown Prince,
Wǔdì 武帝 said,
"This is your son."
Huìdì 惠帝 then ceased (his prostrations).
Once, a fire broke out in the palace at night,
and Wǔdì 武帝 ascended a tower to watch it.
The Crown Prince, who was five years old at the time,
pulled Wǔdì's 武帝裾 robe into the darkness.
Wǔdì 武帝 asked him why,
and the Crown Prince said,
"In the suddenness of night,
it is advisable to prepare for the unexpected;
it is not fitting to let the light illuminate the sovereign."
Because of this, Wǔdì 武帝 marveled at him.
Once, when he accompanied Wǔdì 武帝 to observe the pigsty,
he said to Wǔdì 武帝,
"The pigs are very fat.
Why not slaughter them to feast the soldiers,
rather than letting them consume grain for so long?"
Wǔdì 武帝 praised his intention,
and immediately had them cooked.
Then, patting his back,
he said to Tíngwèi Fù Zhī 廷尉傅祗,
"This child will make our family prosper."
He once praised the Crown Prince before his officials, saying he resembled Xuāndì 宣帝,
whereupon his excellent reputation spread throughout the land.
At that time, stargazers said that Guǎnglíng 廣陵 had the qi 氣 of an emperor,
so he was enfeoffed as the King of Guǎnglíng 廣陵王,
with a domain of fifty thousand households.
He took Liú Shí 劉寔 as his teacher,
Mèng Héng 孟珩 as his friend,
Yáng Zhǔn 楊準 and Fény Sūn 馮蓀 as his literary tutors.
When Huìdì 惠帝 ascended the throne,
he was established as the Imperial Crown Prince.
Eminent and virtuous individuals were greatly selected to be his mentors.
Hé Shào 何劭 was appointed Grand Preceptor (tàishī 太師),
Wáng Róng 王戎 Grand Tutor (tàifù 太傅),
Yáng Jì 楊濟 Grand Guardian (tàibǎo 太保),
Péi Kǎi 裴楷 Junior Preceptor (shàoshī 少師),
Zhāng Huá 張華 Junior Tutor (shàofù 少傅),
and Hé Qiáo 和嶠 Junior Guardian (shàobǎo 少保).
In the first year of Yuánkāng 元康 (291 CE),
he moved into the Eastern Palace.
An imperial edict also stated:
"Yù 遹 is still young and ignorant.
Now that he is in the Eastern Palace,
he must rely solely on the instruction of his mentors and worthy gentlemen.
Those who accompany him
should be upright individuals who can associate with him
and mutually improve him."

Thus, the sons of Grand Guardian Wèi Guàn, Wèi Tíng 太保衞瓘息庭; Sikong Tái, Tái Lüè 司空泰息略; Crown Prince's Grand Tutor Yáng Jì, Yáng Bì 太子太傅楊濟息毖; Crown Prince's Junior Preceptor Péi Kǎi, Péi Xiàn 太子少師裴楷息憲; Crown Prince's Junior Tutor Zhāng Huá, Zhāng Yī 太子少傅張華息禕; and Shàngshū Lìng Huá Yì, Huá Yǔ 尚書令華廙息與 were ordered to reside and associate with the Crown Prince,
to assist and guide him.
When he grew up,
he was not fond of studying,
but only played with his attendants,
and failed to respect his mentors.
Empress Jiǎ 賈后, who had always been jealous of the Crown Prince's excellent reputation,
secretly instructed the eunuchs and palace attendants to flatter the Crown Prince, saying:
"Your Highness, it is truly acceptable to fully indulge your desires when you come of age.
Why restrict yourself?"
Whenever they saw him in moments of anger or pleasure,
they would sigh and say,
"Your Highness does not know how to wield authority and punishment.
How can the world then be awed and submit?"
The Crown Prince's favored concubine, Jiǎng Měirén 蔣美人, bore a son.
They also suggested that her rewards and gifts should be increased,
and many toys made for the imperial grandson.
The Crown Prince followed their advice.
Thus, his negligence and laxity became increasingly evident.
Sometimes he neglected court attendance,
playing in the rear garden.
He enjoyed small carriages and ponies,
ordering his attendants to ride them,
cutting their breastplates and reins,
and making them fall to the ground for amusement.
If anyone offended him,
he would personally beat them.
He was constrained by petty superstitions,
not allowing walls to be renovated or repaired,
nor tiles to be adjusted or roofs moved.
However, he set up a market in the palace,
had people slaughter animals and sell liquor,
personally weighing the portions,
ensuring no discrepancy in weight.
His mother was originally a butcher's daughter,
hence the Crown Prince was fond of this.
He also had the Western Garden sell mallow vegetables, indigo, chickens, and the like,
and collected the profits.
According to the old regulations of the Eastern Palace,
500,000 cash were requested monthly
for various expenses.
The Crown Prince preemptively withdrew two months' worth
to support his favorites.
The Xǐmǎ 洗馬, Jiāng Tǒng 江統, presented five points to admonish him,
but the Crown Prince did not accept them.
His words are recorded in Jiāng Tǒng's 江統 biography.
The Shèrén 舍人, Dù Xī 杜錫, knowing that the Crown Prince was not born of Empress Jiǎ 賈后,
and that the Empress was fierce and violent,
was deeply worried.
He always faithfully advised the Crown Prince to cultivate virtue and advance goodness,
and to keep away from slander.
The Crown Prince grew angry,
and ordered someone to place needles in Dù Xī's 杜錫 usual seat to stab him.
The Crown Prince was of a stubborn nature,
and knowing that Jiǎ Mì 賈謐 relied on the Empress's prestige,
he was unwilling to make allowances for him.
When Jiǎ Mì 賈謐 visited the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince would sometimes ignore him and play in the rear gardens.
The Zhānshì 詹事, Péi Quán 裴權, advised him, saying:
"Jiǎ Mì 賈謐 is greatly favored by the Central Palace,
yet you show signs of insubordination.
If, one day, he should stir up trouble,
the great cause will be lost.
You should deeply humble yourself
to guard against such changes,
and widely extend invitations to worthy gentlemen
to assist yourself."
The Crown Prince was unable to follow this advice.
Initially,
Empress Jiǎ's 賈后 mother, Guō Huái 郭槐, wished to make Hán Shòu's 韓壽 daughter the Crown Princess.
The Crown Prince also desired to marry into the Hán 韓 clan to secure his position.
However, Hán Shòu's 韓壽 wife, Jiǎ Wǔ 賈午, and the Empress herself both disagreed,
and instead arranged for the Crown Prince to marry Wáng Yǎn's 王衍 younger daughter, Huìfēng 惠風.
The Crown Prince heard that Wáng Yǎn's 王衍 elder daughter was beautiful,
and that Empress Jiǎ 賈后 had arranged for her to marry Jiǎ Mì 賈謐.
His heart was not at peace,
and he spoke somewhat about it.
Jiǎ Mì 賈謐 once played wei-qi 圍 with the Crown Prince,
and they argued over the board.
The King of Chéngdū 成都王, Sīmǎ Yǐng 司馬穎, saw this and reproached Jiǎ Mì 賈謐.
Jiǎ Mì's 賈謐 mood became even more unsettled.
Because of this, he slandered the Crown Prince to the Empress, saying:
"The Crown Prince is extensively buying up land and property,
and accumulating much private wealth to gather minor figures.
This is for the sake of the Jiǎ 賈 clan.
I secretly heard his words: 'After the Empress lives for ten thousand years (i.e., dies),
I will carve her up like fish and meat.'
It's not just that.
If the Imperial carriage (referring to the Emperor) passes away,
and he assumes the great position,
following the precedent of the Yáng 楊 clan,
he will execute us and imprison the Empress in Jīnyóng 金墉.
It would be as easy as turning over one's hand.
It is better to act early
and establish someone kind and compliant to protect ourselves."
The Empress accepted his words
and further publicized the Crown Prince's shortcomings,
spreading them far and wide.
At that time, everyone in the court and throughout the land knew that Empress Jiǎ 賈后 intended to harm the Crown Prince.
Zhōnghùjūn Zhào Jùn 中護軍趙俊 requested the Crown Prince to depose the Empress,
but the Crown Prince refused.
In the sixth month of the ninth year,
a mulberry tree grew in the west wing of the palace.
It grew over a *chi* a day,
and withered after a few days.
In the twelfth month,
Empress Jiǎ (賈) was about to depose the crown prince.
She falsely claimed that the Emperor was unwell
and summoned the crown prince to court.
Upon his arrival,
the Empress did not see him,
but placed him in a separate room.
She sent her maid Chén Wǔ (陳舞) to give him wine and jujubes,
forcing him to drink until he was intoxicated.
She then had the Palace Gentleman (Huángmén Shìláng) Pān Yuè (潘岳) draft a letter,
like a prayer to the gods,
which was made to seem like the crown prince’s original intention.
While he was drunk, he was to write it.
She ordered the little maid Chéng Fú (承福) to bring paper, brush, and the draft so the crown prince would write it.
The text read:
“Your Majesty should settle matters yourself;
if you do not,
I will settle them for you.
The Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) should also quickly settle matters herself;
if she does not,
I will personally settle them for her.
Together with Consort Xiè (謝), we have agreed on a date to act simultaneously.
Do not hesitate or doubt,
to avoid future trouble.
Eating raw meat and drinking blood under the three celestial bodies,
Heaven (Huángtiān) will surely allow us to sweep away troubles and dangers,
and establish Dào Wén (道文) as king,
and Jiǎng (蔣) as the inner mistress.
If this wish is granted,
we shall sacrifice three animals to the Northern Monarch (Běijūn)
and grant a great amnesty to all under heaven.
The important matters are as prescribed by law.”
The crown prince, confused by drink, was unconscious,
and so he copied it,
but half of his characters were incomplete.
Afterward, they were completed,
and the Empress presented it to the Emperor.
The Emperor proceeded to the Shìgān Diàn (式乾殿),
summoned the high officials (gōngqīng),
and had the Palace Administrator (Huángmén Lìng) Dǒng Měng (董猛) present the crown prince’s letter and a blue paper edict saying:
“Yù’s (遹) letter is as such;
he is now granted death.”
He showed it to all the dukes and kings,
but none spoke,
except Zhāng Huà (張華) and Péi Wěi (裴頠) who testified on behalf of the crown prince.
Empress Jiǎ (賈) had Dǒng Měng (董猛) falsely declare, through the words of Princess Chángguǎng (長廣 Gōngzhǔ), to the Emperor:
“The matter should be decided quickly,
but the various ministers differ.
If anyone disobeys the edict,
they should be dealt with by military law.”
The discussion continued until sunset without a resolution.
The Empress, fearing a change in circumstances,
then submitted a memorial to dismiss the crown prince as a commoner,
and the edict was granted.
Thereupon, she sent Shàngshū Hé Yù (和郁) with a *jié* (節),
Xiè Jié (解結) as his deputy,

along with Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Liáng Wáng Róng (梁王肜), General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn) Huáinán Wáng Yǔn (淮南王允), Former General (Qián Jiāngjūn) Dōngwǔ Gōng Dàn (東武公澹), Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫), and Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo) Hé Shào (何劭) to the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
to depose the crown prince as a commoner.
On that day, the crown prince was strolling in the Xuánpǔ (玄圃).
Hearing that an envoy had arrived,
he changed clothes and came out of the Chóngxián Mén (崇賢門),
bowed twice to receive the edict,
walked out of the Chénghuá Mén (承華門),
and rode in a crude calf-cart.
Dàn (澹) with armed soldiers escorted Crown Princess Wáng (王) and the three imperial grandsons to Jīnyǒng Chéng (金墉城),
and investigated Consort Xiè Shúfēi (謝淑妃) and the crown prince’s governess Jiǎng Jùn (蔣俊).
In the first month of the following year,
Empress Jiǎ (賈) again had a eunuch confess that
he wished to rebel with the crown prince.
An edict displayed the eunuch’s confession to the high officials (gōngqīng).
She also sent Dàn (澹) with a thousand soldiers to escort the crown prince,
and imprisoned him in a separate dwelling of the Xǔchāng Gōng (許昌宮),
ordering the Censor (Zhìshū Yùshǐ) Liú Zhèn (劉振) to guard him with a *jié* (節).
Earlier,
there was a children’s rhyme that said:
“Do not ignore the Eastern Palace’s colt,
by the twelfth month, it will bind you.”
Another said:
“The south wind rises, blowing white sand,
looking afar at Lǔguó (魯國), so towering,
a thousand-year-old skull grows teeth.”
“South wind” (Nánfēng)
was the Empress’s personal name;
“Sand Gate” (Shāmén)
was the crown prince’s nickname.
Initially,
when the crown prince was deposed,
his consort’s father, Wáng Yǎn (王衍), submitted a memorial requesting a divorce.
When the crown prince arrived at Xǔ (許),
he sent a letter to his consort saying:
“Though I am foolish and ignorant,
my heart desires to do good,
wishing to fulfill the duties of loyalty and filial piety,
without any wicked or rebellious intentions.
Although I am not born of the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng),
I served her as if she were my own mother.
Since becoming crown prince,
I have been commanded and restricted,
forbidden from seeing my mother.
Since the death of the Lady Yíchéng (宜城君),
I have not been cared for or comforted,
sitting in an empty room.
Last year in the twelfth month,
Dào Wén (道文) was gravely ill,
and as a father and son,
we truly pitied each other.
At that time, I submitted a memorial to the state, begging for a noble title for him,
but it was not granted.
Since his illness was critical,
I sought blessings and favors for him,
with no malicious intent.
Since Dào Wén (道文) fell ill,
the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) sent her attendants three times to see me,
saying: ‘Heaven instructs you to come.’
By the evening of the twenty-eighth,
a short letter arrived,
titled ‘Issued from the Eastern Palace,’
stating: ‘It is said that Heaven instructs you to be seen.’
I immediately drafted a memorial requesting entry.
Early on the twenty-ninth, I entered to see the Emperor,
and shortly after, I was sent to the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng).
The Central Palace’s (Zhōnggōng) attendant Chén Wǔ (陳舞) met me and said: ‘The Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) has been feeling unwell since morning.’
She had me sit in an empty room.
After a moment, the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) sent Chén Wǔ (陳舞) to tell me: ‘I heard that you memorialized His Majesty to beg for Dào Wén (道文) to be made king,
and not being made king is indeed what happened.’
The Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) then called out to Chén Wǔ (陳舞): ‘Yesterday, Heaven gave the crown prince wine and jujubes.’
She then brought three *sheng* of wine and a large plate of jujubes and gave them to me,
ordering me to drink all the wine and eat all the jujubes.
I usually do not drink alcohol,
so I immediately had Wǔ (舞) report that I could not handle three *sheng*.
The Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) called out from afar: ‘You always hold wine before His Majesty and enjoy it,
why do you not drink?
Heaven gives you wine, and it will make Dào Wén (道文) recover.’
I then replied to the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng): ‘His Majesty also bestowed wine on the same day,
so I dared not refuse,
but I do not drink three *sheng* of wine in a day.
Moreover, I haven’t eaten yet,
and fear I cannot handle it.
And I haven’t seen Your Highness yet,
drinking this might lead to confusion.’
Chén Wǔ (陳舞) then relayed the message again, saying: ‘How unfilial!
Heaven gives you wine to drink,
and you refuse to drink it.
Is there something bad in it?’
So I drank two *sheng*,
and there was one *sheng* left.
I asked to take it back to the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) to finish drinking.
Under duress and with no other option,
I drank another *sheng*.
After drinking,
my body felt confused and dizzy,
and I no longer felt conscious.
After a moment, a little maid brought a sealed box,
saying: ‘An edict orders you to copy this document.’
I was startled and rose,
looked at it,
and there was one white paper and
one blue paper.
She urged me, saying: ‘His Majesty is waiting.’
Then the little maid Chéng Fú (承福) brought a brush, inkstone, and yellow paper,
and had me write.
In my haste, I could not look again,
and truly did not perceive the weight of the words on the paper.
Parents are the closest of kin,
and truly do not doubt each other.
The facts are as such,
I am truly slandered,
I imagine everyone will see clearly.”
Because the Crown Prince was deposed not due to his own fault,
the public sentiment was indignant and resentful.
Sīmǎ Yǎ (司馬雅), the Commandant of the Right Guard,
who was a distant relative of the imperial clan,
along with Xǔ Chāo (許超), the Commandant of the Imperial Retinue, were both favored by the Crown Prince.
The two were deeply saddened by this,
and persuaded Sūn Xiù (孫秀), a strategist for Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫), saying:
"The state has no legitimate heir;
the altars of soil and grain will be in peril,
and a calamity for the high officials is sure to arise.
However, you serve the Empress,
and are close with Empress Jiǎ (賈后).
The deposition of the Crown Prince
is widely believed to have been known to you beforehand.
Once matters come to a head,
disaster will surely befall you.
Why not plan ahead for this!"
Sūn Xiù (孫秀) spoke of this to Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫),
who deeply accepted it.
Once the plan was settled,
Sūn Xiù (孫秀) said to Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫):
"The Crown Prince is a fierce and resolute person.
If he were to achieve his ambition,
he would surely indulge his temperament.
You have always served Empress Jiǎ (賈后),
and common talk in the streets
all considers you a partisan of the Jiǎ (賈) clan.
Even if you now wish to perform a great service for the Crown Prince,
though the Crown Prince might tolerate and suppress his old grievances,
he will certainly not bestow rewards upon you.
He will likely say that you were compelled by the popular sentiment
to reverse your stance simply to escape punishment.
If there were any flaw or misstep,
you would still not escape execution.
It is better to delay the plan;
Empress Jiǎ (賈后) will surely harm the Crown Prince,
and then we can depose Empress Jiǎ (賈后)
to avenge the Crown Prince.
This will still be sufficient as a meritorious deed,
and only then can you achieve your ambition."
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) agreed with this.
Sūn Xiù (孫秀) then sowed discord,
saying that people in the palace intended to depose Empress Jiǎ (賈后)
and welcome back the Crown Prince.
Empress Jiǎ (賈后) heard this and was distressed and fearful,
so she ordered Chéng Jù (程據), the Chief Imperial Physician, to prepare a pill of croton oil and apricot kernels.
In the third month,
she issued a forged imperial edict, ordering Huángmén Sūn Lǜ (黃門孫慮) to take it to Xǔchāng (許昌) to harm the Crown Prince.
Initially,
the Crown Prince feared being poisoned,
so he cooked his own food in front of others.
Sūn Lǜ (孫慮) reported this to Liú Zhèn (劉振).
Liú Zhèn (劉振) then moved the Crown Prince to a small room,
completely cutting off his food.
Yet, people in the palace still passed food to the Crown Prince over the walls.
Sūn Lǜ (孫慮) then pressured the Crown Prince with the medicine.
The Crown Prince refused to take it.
When he went to the latrine,
Sūn Lǜ (孫慮) killed him by striking him with a pestle.
The Crown Prince cried out loudly,
his voice heard outside.
He was twenty-three years old at the time.
He was to be buried with the rites of a commoner.
Empress Jiǎ (賈后) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yù (遹) unfortunately passed away.
I grieve his delusion and perversity,
and also his early demise.
My sorrow and pain
are beyond self-control.
I privately hoped that he would engrave this lesson into his flesh and bones,
to reconsider filial piety,
to respectfully perform kowtows,
and rectify his name and status.
This wish has not been fulfilled,
adding to my bitter regret.
Although Yù's (遹) crime was immense,
he is still a descendant of the King.
To bury him as a mere commoner
is truly pitiable.
I specially beg for heavenly grace
to grant him burial with royal rites.
I am truly ignorant and shallow, unaware of rites and righteousness,
and overcome by extreme emotions,
I presumptuously present this to Your Majesty."
An imperial edict ordered him to be buried with the rites of Guǎnglíng Wáng (廣陵王).
When Jiǎ Shùrén (賈庶人) died,
Liú Zhèn (劉振), Sūn Lǜ (孫慮), Chéng Jù (程據) and others were executed.
The Crown Prince was posthumously reinstated with a pronouncement that said:
"The Emperor dispatches the Imperial Commissioner, concurrently Minister of Works and Grand Commandant of the Guards, Yī Cè (伊策), to the spirit of the late Crown Prince, saying: Alas!
From your youth, you possessed an outstanding and intelligent nature,
and enjoyed the extraordinary favor of the late emperor.
Great territories were opened,
and you swiftly governed Huáilíng (淮陵).
I, following the late emperor's will,
established you as heir apparent
to bring glory to our ancestors.
You respectfully cultivated your virtues
under your tutors,
served your parents with filial piety and respect,
without any violation of rites.
But I, being ignorant of the malicious plot,
brought upon you the calamity of an untimely death,
making Shēn Shēng (申生) and Xiào Jǐ (孝己) reappear in our time.
Thanks to the wise prime ministers
and the indignation of men and gods,
my heart was enlightened,
and the guilty were punished,
all confessing their crimes.
What solace is this for your tormented, wronged, and cruelly pained soul?
Thus, I am deeply grieved and resentful,
shaken within my five viscera.
Now, I posthumously restore the funeral rites of the Crown Prince,
reburying him in the imperial environs,
and sacrificing a grand animal.
If your soul has consciousness,
may it still receive my heart."
The Emperor wore the three-year mourning attire (zhǎncui 斬衰) as for a first son for the Crown Prince,
while the officials wore qiāncui (齊衰).
Shàngshū Hé Yù (尚書和郁) was ordered to lead the Eastern Palace officials to arrange the auspicious and inauspicious rituals,
and to bring the Crown Prince's coffin from Xǔchāng (許昌).
When the coffin set off,
there was a great wind, thunder, and lightning,
and the curtains and canopies were torn and scattered.
An elegy was also composed, saying:
"The Emperor, facing the court,
dispatches Xǐmǎ Liú Wù (洗馬劉務) to address the Crown Prince's coffin, saying: Alas, Yù (遹)!
In youth, you embodied excellence and prominence,
your fragrance and splendor flourished.
Even in childhood,
you showed lofty wisdom and outstanding grace.
Your sagely ancestor of old
admired your pure beauty.
Clear edicts repeatedly exalted you,
your fame resounded among all.
Thus, you were established as heir apparent,
to forever govern the imperial foundation.
How could such malicious plots secretly arise,
leading to such calamity?
Sorrow affects the harmonious qi,
pain pierces through the four seasons.
Alas, how mournful!
Your demotion and deposition
were truly due to my lack of insight.
The hen's disorder caused deep harm,
plots formed, bringing disaster.
Now that you are gone,
who can multiply your form?
Of old, Shēn Shēng (申生)
suffered injustice unspoken.
Now your burden,
you bear your grievance in the East.
All who possess understanding,
who among them does not mourn in agony!
Húguān (壺關) intervened for his lord,
a thousand autumns enlightened himself.
Different eras, same principle;
ancient and modern, one truth.
The imperial grandson is established,
great fortune for your son.
Though you perished prematurely,
may glory begin afterwards.
The tomb is prepared,
to calm your spirit.
Swiftly pass the adorned steeds like lightning,
the war chariots rumble like thunder.
Vast are the feather canopies,
numerous are the officials.
Sharing the same sorrow and pain,
who is not bitter and heartbroken!
May your glory reach future generations,
never to perish through eternity."
He was posthumously given the title Mǐnhuái (愍懷).
On the day Jǐmǎo (己卯) in the sixth month,
he was buried at Xiǎnpínglíng (顯平陵).
The Emperor was moved by Yán Zǎn's (閻纘) words,
and erected the Sīzǐtái (思子臺) (Platform for Remembering the Son).
His former officials, Jiāng Tǒng (江統) and Lù Jī (陸機), both composed elegies and praises.
The Crown Prince had three sons: Bāo (虨), Zāng (臧), and Shàng (尚).
All were imprisoned with their father in Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Bāo (虨), courtesy name Dàowén (道文),
died in the first month of the first year of Yǒngkāng (永康).
In the fourth month,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Nányáng Wáng (南陽王).
Zāng's courtesy name was Jìngwén.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng (300 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Línhuái.
On the day of Jǐsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"Repeated inauspicious signs have occurred,
and treacherous villains have caused a disturbance.
Yù has already been forced into deposition,
and died an unnatural death.
Now, Zāng is established as the Imperial Grandson.
His consort, Lady Wáng, is returned to him to act as his mother,
and is to be called the Grandson Grand Consort.
The officials of the Crown Prince's establishment are immediately transferred to become the Imperial Grandson's officials.
Zhào Wáng Lún will act as the Imperial Grandson's Grand Tutor."
In the fifth month,
Lún and the Imperial Grandson both proceeded to the Eastern Palace.
The Imperial Grandson exited through the Xīyè Gate.
His carriage, attire, and attendants were all those of Mǐnhuái's former establishment.
Upon reaching Tóngtuó Street,
the palace people wept,
and all the attendants choked with sobs,
while passersby wiped away their tears.
A mulberry tree grew again in the west wing,
but when the Imperial Grandson was deposed,
it withered.
In the first month of the first year of Yǒngníng (301 CE),
Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
and Zāng was deposed as the Prince of Púyáng.
He was relocated to Jīnyǒng along with the Emperor,
and soon after, he was murdered.
In the early period of Tài'ān,
he was posthumously granted the谥号 (shìhào) of Āi.
Shàng's courtesy name was Jìngrén.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng (300 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiāngyáng.
In the eighth month of the first year of Yǒngníng (301 CE),
he was established as the Imperial Grandson.
On the day of Guǐmǎo in the third month of the first year of Tài'ān (302 CE),
he died.
The Emperor wore mourning garments of qīcuī for one year.
He was posthumously granted the谥号 (shìhào) of Chōng Tàisūn.
The Historian comments: Mǐnhuái possessed outstanding and brilliant qualities,
manifesting a nature that matured early.
Emperor Wǔ loved him dearly,
having deep plans for his succession;
the world gave him their hearts,
holding considerable hopes for his future.
However, when it came to succeeding to the Imperial position
and guarding the heir apparent's office,
he was not diligent in the four teachings,
and often neglected the three morning audiences.
His leopard-like nature remained unchanged,
and his phoenix-like virtue had already declined.
He believed and was misled by treacherous villains,
and alienated upright scholars.
He indulged in the lowly tasks of slaughtering and brewing,
and immersed himself in the frivolous pleasures of gardens and parks.
It can be said that while there are none who do not have a beginning,
few are able to bring things to a good end.
Subsequently, the Empress was vicious and cruel,
long harboring intentions of harm;
the imperial relatives by marriage were sycophantic,
competing to present treacherous and evil counsel.
The plot of sacrificing animals by burying them was concocted,
and the slander of the dead dog was carried out.
One person lacked the wisdom to perceive hidden truths,
and the hundreds of officials lacked the integrity of remonstrating ministers.
Thus, his injustice surpassed that of Chǔ Jiàn,
and his cruelty was even worse than Lì Yuán.
Though the rites of mourning and glory were observed,
and deep compassion was felt,
what good did it do for the one who suffered such torment!
A eulogy says: Mǐnhuái was intelligent and brilliant,
truly bestowed by heaven.
The Imperial Ancestor cherished him,
and all officials eagerly awaited him.
When the Eastern Palace was first established,
his virtue as heir was not expanded.
Plucking bees created a rift,
returning the sacrificial meat caused disaster.
Having suffered from the vicious and cruel,
he merely hoped for his return.
Textual Notes
Biography Twenty-four: Lù Jī (Sūn Zhěng)
Lù Jī, courtesy name Shìhéng,
was a native of Wújùn.
His grandfather, Sūn Xùn,
was the Chancellor of Wú.
His father, Kàng,
was the Grand Marshal of Wú.
Jī was seven chǐ tall,
and his voice was like a bell.
In his youth, he possessed extraordinary talent,
his writings were unparalleled in the world.
He diligently adhered to Confucian principles,
and did not act contrary to propriety.
When Kàng died,
he took command of his father's troops as a Yámén General.
At the age of twenty, Wú was destroyed,
and he retired to his old hometown,
closed his gate, and diligently studied
for ten years.
Because the Sūn family was in Wú,
and his grandfather and father had been generals and chancellors for generations,
having achieved great accomplishments in the Jiāngbiǎo region,
he deeply lamented Sūn Hào's abandonment of it.
Thus, he discussed the reasons for Quán's success,
and Hào's downfall,
and also wished to narrate his grandfather's and father's achievements.
So he composed the two chapters of the Biàn Wáng Lùn.
The first chapter says: In the past, when the Hàn dynasty lost its rule,
treacherous ministers usurped power,
calamity began in the capital region,
and its poison spread throughout the realm.
The imperial order was slackened and weakened,
and the royal house became lowly.
At this, heroes swarmed
like startled bees,
and righteous armies gathered from all four directions.
Wú Wǔliè Huángdì, with generosity, rose from a lesser state,
rapidly advanced into Jīngnán.
His strategies were numerous and varied,
his loyalty and courage were unmatched in his generation.
His majestic authority caused the Yí and Yì
to tremble,
and when his armies engaged, the ugly foes surrendered their heads.
Thus, he swept clean the imperial ancestral temples,
and offered sacrifices to his imperial ancestors.
At that time, generals rising like clouds covered the provinces,
and armies emerging like whirlwinds spanned the prefectures.
Howling multitudes scattered like the wind,
and bear-like warriors gathered like mist.
Although their armies moved with righteousness,
and allied forces exerted themselves,
they all harbored malicious intentions,
relying on their armies and indulging in chaos.
Some
armies lacked strategy and discipline,
losing prestige and fostering bandits.
Loyal principles and martial integrity
were never as manifest as in him.
After Wǔliè passed away,
Chángshā Huán Wáng, with extraordinary talent, was born into his generation.
At a young age, he displayed outstanding abilities,
recruiting elderly veterans,
and working with them to complete his enterprises.
His divine troops advanced eastward,
valiantly fighting with few
against many.
No fortified city could withstand his assault,
and no enemy could stand against him in battle.
He punished rebels and pacified those who submitted,
and the region beyond the Jiāng was pacified.
He reformed laws and trained his army,
so his prestige and virtue were greatly magnified.
He treated worthy individuals with respect,
and Zhāng Gōng became preeminent among them;
he associated with valiant and talented individuals,
and Zhōu Yú became their hero.
These two gentlemen were both magnanimous, quick-witted, and exceptionally talented,
elegant, perceptive, and
intelligent.
Therefore, those of similar disposition joined by affinity,
and those of equal spirit gathered by inclination.
Jiāngdōng indeed had many talented people.
He was about to launch a northern expedition against the various Huá,
to eliminate those who violated the imperial order,
to restore the imperial
chariot to its original path,
and return the Emperor's seat to the purple palace,
to command the various lords by holding the Son of Heaven,
to clear the imperial path and restore the old order.
When the war chariots had already arrived,
all the evil-doers looked askance.
His great enterprise was not yet accomplished,
and he died in his prime.
Then came our Great Emperor,
who, with extraordinary steps, followed the excellent path,
and with sagacious mind, carried out the brilliant plan.
In governance, he consulted past precedents,
and in promulgating laws, he drew upon ancestral customs;
and he added
to this deep reverence,
and emphasized frugality.
He consulted with talented and outstanding individuals,
was good at planning and decisive in judgment.
Bundles of silk were offered in the fields and gardens,
and imperial decrees reached every street and alley.
Thus, heroes
responded to his call,
and ambitious scholars rushed towards his brilliance like shadows.
Extraordinary people flocked to him,
and brave warriors were like a forest.
Thereupon, Zhāng Gōng became his grand tutor;
Zhōu Yú, Lù Gōng, and Lǔ
Lǔ Sù and Lǚ Méng's
peers became trusted confidants within the court,
and vital aids outside of it.
Gān Níng, Líng Tǒng, Chéng Pǔ, Hè Qí, Zhū Huán, and Zhū Rán's ilk displayed their might.
Hán
Dāng, Pān Zhāng, Huáng Gài, Jiǎng Qīn, and Zhōu Tài's associates exerted their strength.
In refinement and elegance, Zhūgě Jǐn, Zhāng Chéng, and Bù Zhì brought glory to the nation with their reputations.
In governance,
Gù Yōng, Pān Jùn, Lǚ Fàn, and Lǚ Dài managed official duties with their capabilities.
In extraordinary character, Yú Fān, Lù Jì, and Zhāng Dūn upheld justice with their integrity.
In diplomatic missions, Zhào
Zī and Shěn Héng gained renown with their quick perception and understanding.
In divination and numerology, Wú Fàn and Zhào Dá harmonized virtue with auspicious signs.
Dǒng Xí and Chén Wǔ sacrificed their lives to protect their lord.
Luò Tǒng and Liú
Jī offered strong remonstrance to amend errors.
Their plans were without omission,
their actions never missed the mark.
Thus, they managed to seize and hold the mountains and rivers,
control Jīng and Wú,
and contend for supremacy with the world.
The Wèi clan once, relying on the might of their battle victories,
led an army of a million,
launched boats from Dèngsài,
and brought down the forces from Hànyīn.
With tens of thousands of feather-oared boats,
they leaped like dragons downriver,
with a sharp army of
a thousand companies,
marching militarily across plains and lowlands.
Wise ministers filled their chambers,
and martial generals stood shoulder to shoulder.
They sighed with the ambition to swallow the Jianghú region,
and unify the cosmos.
But Zhōu Yú drove our
auxiliary forces,
and routed them at Chìbì.
Their flags were lost, their tracks in disarray,
they barely escaped with their lives,
and fled far away.
The king of Hàn also, relying on his imperial title,
led the people of Bā and Hàn,
took
advantage of peril and pursued change,
building encampments for a thousand *lǐ*.
He was determined to avenge Guān Yǔ's defeat,
and planned to recover the lands of Xiāngxī.
But our Duke Lù also crushed him at Xīlíng,
his army was destroyed and defeated,
he was in distress before being rescued,
and died at Yǒng'ān.
Following this, at the assault on Rúxū,
their vanguard was destroyed on the riverbank.
In the battle of Pénglóng,
not a single chariot returned.
Consequently, the generals of these two nations
lost
morale and their edge was blunted.
Their power waned and resources dwindled,
while Wú complacently reaped their misfortunes.
Thus, the Wèi people sought peace,
and the Hàn clan begged for an alliance.
Then Wú ascended to the imperial title,
standing like a tripod
firmly established.
Its western border reached the suburbs of Yōng and Yì,
its northern border split the banks of Huái and Hàn,
its eastern territory encompassed the land of the Bǎiyuè,
and its southern boundary included the lands beyond the Qúnmán.
Thereupon, they instituted the
rites of the eight dynasties,
collected the music of the Three Kings,
reported to the Supreme帝,
and bowed to the myriad lords.
Martial officials and resolute soldiers
guarded along the river.
Long spears and sturdy halberds
rose in fury at the sight of battle flags.
All
officials offered their best advice to the sovereign,
and the common people pursued their livelihoods below.
Their influence harmonized with distant tribes,
and their customs spread to remote regions.
Thus, a single envoy
could pacify and inspect foreign lands.
Giant elephants and swift
steeds
roamed in the outer stables.
Bright pearls and precious treasures
shone in the inner treasury.
Rare and valuable items arrived continuously,
and exotic curiosities responded to calls.
Light chariots sped through the southern wilderness,
and heavy
chariots rested in the northern wilds.
The common people were free from the calamities of war,
and warhorses had no fear of early morning harness.
Thus, the imperial enterprise was solidified.
After the Great Emperor's demise,
the young lord ascended the throne,
and treacherous villains ran rampant.
Emperor Jǐng arose,
diligently upheld the inherited constitution.
There were no major deficiencies in his governance;
he was a good lord for maintaining tradition.
At the beginning of the reign of Guīmìng,
the laws and institutions had not yet perished,
and old veterans still remained.
Grand Marshal Duke Lù brought prosperity to the court with his civil and military talents.
Left Chancellor Lù Kǎi offered
sincere remonstrance with his bluntness.
Shī Jì and Fàn Shèn were prominent for their authority and gravitas.
Dīng Fèng and Zhōnglí Fěi were known for their martial valor.
Méng Zōng and Dīng Gù and their ilk became high ministers.
Lóu Xuán and Hè Shào
and their associates managed confidential affairs.
Although the head of state was ailing,
the close advisors were still good.
However, in the later years,
the prominent figures had all passed away.
Only then did the common people suffer the calamity of disintegration,
and the imperial
house experienced the crisis of collapse.
The mandate of heaven waned with the changing times,
and the royal army advanced with the turn of fate.
Soldiers scattered in battle,
and the populace fled from the cities.
Cities had no strong defenses,
and mountains
and rivers lacked the strategic advantage of natural barriers.
There were no siege engines like Gōngshū's cloud ladders,
no devastating floods like Zhì Bó's,
no encircling attacks like Chǔ Zǐ's house-building siege,
no ambushes like Yàn Rén's at Jìxī.
The army
had not even spent a full day before the state was destroyed.
Even if loyal ministers were isolated in their indignation,
and valiant warriors died for their principles,
what could save them?
The generals of Cáo and Liú were not chosen in a single generation.
The armies of that time were not as numerous as in earlier days.
The methods of offense and defense also had prior precedents,
and the advantages of strategic terrain remained
unchanged.
Yet, success and failure swapped reasons,
and ancient and modern presented divergent outcomes.
Why is this?
It is because the governance of each side differed,
and the talents entrusted with responsibility were distinct.
The following chapter states: In ancient times, among the three kings,
the Wèi people occupied the Central Plains,
the Hàn clan held Mín and Yì,
and Wú controlled Jīng and Yáng and furthermore possessed Jiāo and Guǎng.
Although Cáo Shì's achievements benefited all
of China,
his cruelty was also profound,
and his people resented him.
Old Man Liú used strategic terrain to embellish his wisdom,
but his achievements were meager,
and his customs were crude.
As for Wú,
King Huán established it with military might,
and Grand
Progenitor completed it with virtue.
He was intelligent and perceptive,
with a grand and far-reaching demeanor.
He sought out worthy individuals as if he could not obtain them fast enough,
and cared for people like infants.
He treated scholars with the utmost virtue,
and gave his wholehearted affection to benevolent people.
He elevated Lǚ Méng from the military ranks,
and tested Pān Jùn among the captives.
He was sincere and trusted scholars,
not worrying about being deceived by others.
He assessed abilities and assigned
positions,
not fearing that power would be usurped.
He held the whip and bowed,
to emphasize Duke Lù's authority.
He completely entrusted the military guard,
to assist Zhōu Yú's army.
He lived in a humble palace and ate simple food,
while generously rewarding meritorious officials.
He opened his heart and emptied himself,
to accept the calculations of strategists.
Thus, Lǔ Sù entrusted himself to him after a single meeting,
and Shì Xiè defied danger to serve him.
He upheld Duke
Zhāng's virtue,
and curtailed the pleasures of hunting.
He valued Zhūgě's words,
and sacrificed the joys of desire.
He was moved by Duke Lù's admonitions,
and abolished burdensome laws.
He admired Liú Jī.
discussion,
and made the oath of the Three Cups;
he held his breath and crouched,
to attend to Zǐmíng's illness;
he shared the tasty and sacrificed the sweet,
to raise Líng Tǒng's orphan;
he ascended the altar with indignation,
attributing the merit to Lǔzǐ;
he erased the resentful words from the memorial,
trusting in Zǐyú's integrity.
Therefore, loyal ministers competed to offer their strategies,
and aspiring gentlemen were all able to exert their strength.
Grand plans and far-reaching strategies
certainly do not disdain the trivial.
Thus, while the hundred officials barely convened,
pressing matters were not yet addressed.
When the capital was first established in Jiànyè,
the ministers requested to prepare the full ceremonial rites,
but the Son of Heaven declined and did not
permit it,
saying:
"What will the world say about Us!"
The palaces and carriages
were indeed modest.
Reaching the middle period,
when the division between heaven and man was settled,
the deficiencies in all systems
were largely rectified.
Although the rich transformation and excellent governance
were not on par with earlier ages,
yet the means for governing the state and administering the realm
were also sufficient for rule.
Its territory spanned tens of thousands of *lǐ*,
it bore
nearly a million armored soldiers,
its fields were fertile,
its troops well-trained,
its weapons sharp,
its wealth abundant;
to the east it bordered the vast sea,
to the west it was blocked by dangerous passes,
the Long River controlled its territory,
lofty mountains
encompassed its borders.
The advantages of the state had never been seen to be greater than this.
If it had been guarded with principle,
governed with skill,
adhering to the ancestral codes,
diligent in managing the people and cautious in
governance,
improving established policies,
and holding constant to its natural defenses,
then it could have endured for generations and enjoyed eternal years,
without the calamity of peril and ruin.
Someone might say:
"Wú and Shǔ were like lips and teeth to each other;
that Shǔ perished and Wú fell,
is therefore logical."
Indeed, Shǔ
was a supporting allied state,
but it was not the determinant of Wú's
existence or demise.
Where their territories met,
there were stacked mountains and perilous heights,
with no long chariot roads by land;
the rivers were narrow and currents swift,
with the difficulty of alarming waves by water.
Even with a hundred thousand elite
troops,
the vanguard could not exceed a thousand men;
with a thousand *lǐ* of wheel tracks,
the advance guard could not exceed a hundred vessels.
Thus, when Liú Shì launched his campaign,
Lù Gōng likened it to a long snake,
its situation
was indeed so.
When Shǔ first fell,
the court ministers had differing opinions;
some wished to pile up stones to obstruct its currents,
others wished to use mechanical devices to counter the changes.
The Son of Heaven gathered all opinions to
consult with Grand Marshal Lù Gōng.
Gōng said that the Four Rivers are how heaven and earth regulate and release their vital energy,
so there is no reason to block them,
and as for mechanical devices, they are common to both sides;
if the enemy were to abandon their strength to exploit their weakness,
and contend for the use of boats and oars in Jīng-Chǔ,
that would be heaven assisting us.
We should carefully guard the峡口 (Xiágkǒu) to await their capture.
When
Bù Chǎn rebelled,
he relied on his strong fortress to draw in powerful invaders,
and used heavy bribes to entice the various barbarians.
At that time, the armies of the great state
swarmed like clouds and struck like lightning,
hanging their banners along the river,
building encampments along the shore,
controlling vital passes,
to stop the Wú people from moving west.
The Bā and Hàn naval forces
descended the river eastward.
Lù Gōng, with a detached force of thirty thousand,
held the northern part of Dōngkēng,
with deep moats and high ramparts,
resting his armor and nurturing his might.
The rebellious captives huddled awaiting execution,
not daring to look north for a way to live,
and the powerful invaders were defeated and fled by night,
losing more than half their army.
He then
sent five thousand elite troops
to defend against the naval forces in the west,
achieving simultaneous victories in the east and west,
presenting tens of thousands of captives.
Truly, the counsel of the wise
does not deceive us!
After this, beacon fires were rarely
alarmed,
and the borders were seldom threatened.
After Lù Gōng's death, secret schemes began to emerge,
Wú's faults deepened, and its armies were terrified.
The campaign of Tàikāng,
its forces were not as numerous as the army of former days;
the rebellion in Guǎngzhōu,
its disaster was greater than the difficulties of previous times,
yet the state was overturned,
and the ancestral temples became ruins.
Alas!
"When a man perishes,
the state is utterly
exhausted,"
is it not so!
The *Yì* says,
"Tāng and Wǔ changed the mandate in accordance with Heaven,"
and some say,
"If chaos does not reach its extreme, order does not manifest,"
speaking of emperors and kings adapting to heavenly timing.
The ancients
said,
"Heavenly timing is not as good as earthly advantage,"
and the *Yì* says,
"Kings and feudal lords establish defenses to guard their states,"
speaking of a state relying on its defenses.
It also says,
"Earthly advantage is not
as good as human harmony,"
"it lies in virtue, not in defenses,"
speaking of maintaining defenses depending on the people.
When Wú rose,
it relied on all three,
which is what Xún Qīng called combining the three.
However,
when it fell,
it relied only on its defenses,
which is what Xún Qīng called abandoning the three.
The four provinces were not without numerous people,
the south of the Great River
was not lacking in outstanding talents,
the mountains and rivers were easy to defend,
the strong and sharp weapons were easy to use,
the policies of previous governments were easy to improve,
yet why did no achievements arise while disaster struck?
It was because those who employed them erred.
Therefore, the former kings comprehended the long-term principles of statecraft,
and discerned the ultimate causes of survival and ruin;
they humbled themselves to bring peace to the common people,
cultivated benevolence to achieve human
harmony,
were broad and accommodating to attract the strategies of talented individuals,
and were kind and amiable to bind the affection of scholars and commoners.
Hence, when it was peaceful,
the populace rejoiced with them;
and when it was in peril,
the common people shared their distress.
If in peace they shared joy with the multitude,
then peril could not befall them;
if in peril they shared distress with their inferiors,
then the hardship was not to be feared.
Because of this,
they were able to preserve their altars of soil and grain and secure their territory,
without the sorrow of Yīn when wheat grew tall,
and without the regret for Zhōu when millet grew wild.
Towards the end of the Tàikāng [reign period],
Lù Jī and his brother Lù Yún both entered Luòyáng.
They went to see Zhāng Huà, the Grand Minister of Sacrifices.
Zhāng Huà had long admired their reputation,
and treated them as old acquaintances,
saying:
“The campaign to conquer Wú
has fortunately brought us these two eminent men.”
Lù Jī once also visited Wáng Jì, the Grandee Secretary.
Wáng Jì pointed to some lamb’s cheese and said to Lù Jī:
“What in your land of Wú can compare to this?”
Lù Jī replied:
“A thousand-lǐ bowl of water shield soup
is not enhanced by salted black beans.”
People at the time called this an excellent retort.
Zhāng Huà recommended Lù Jī to the various high officials.
Later, the Grand Tutor Yáng Jùn appointed him Libationer.
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
he was successively promoted to Palace Guard of the Heir Apparent and Writer in the Imperial Library.
Lú Zhì of Fànyáng asked Lù Jī in a crowd:
“How do Lù Xùn and Lù Kàng relate to you, closely or distantly?”
Lù Jī replied:
“As you relate to Lú Yù and Lú Tǐng.”
Lú Zhì was silent.
After they left,
Lù Yún said to Lù Jī:
“Our homeland is far away,
they might not be familiar with us,
why be so harsh!”
Lù Jī said:
“My father’s and grandfather’s names are broadcast throughout the four seas,
how could he not know them!”
Commentators used this to determine the superiority and inferiority of the two Lùs.
Wú Wáng Yàn went out to govern Huáinán,
appointing Lù Jī as Grand Supervisor of the Palace.
He was promoted to General of the Imperial Guard,
then transferred to Gentleman of the Palace.
When Zhào Wáng Lún was regent,
he was appointed General of the Minister of Works’ Staff.
For his participation in the execution of Jiǎ Mì,
he was granted the title Marquis of the Pass.
When Sīmǎ Lún was about to usurp the throne,
he made Lù Jī a Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat.
When Sīmǎ Lún was executed,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng, because Lù Jī held a position in the Imperial Secretariat,
suspected Lù Jī of being involved in the text of the Nine Bestowals and the abdication edict,
and so arrested Lù Jī and nine others, handing them over to the Grand Judge.
Thanks to Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng and Wú Wáng Yàn who both intervened on his behalf,
his death sentence was commuted to banishment to the frontier.
He was then released by an amnesty.
Initially, Lù Jī had a fine dog
named Huáng'ěr,
which he loved dearly.
Later, when he was living in the capital,
and had long received no news from home,
he laughed and said to the dog:
“I haven’t received any letters from my family for a long time.
Can you take a letter and bring back news?”
The dog wagged its tail and barked.
Lù Jī then wrote a letter, put it in a bamboo tube, and tied it around the dog’s neck.
The dog found its way south,
reached his home,
and returned to Luòyáng with a reply.
Thereafter, this became a regular practice.
At that time, the Central Plains were in turmoil.
Gù Róng, Dài Ruòsī, and others all advised Lù Jī to return to Wú,
but Lù Jī, confident in his talent and prestige,
and aspiring to restore order to the troubled world,
did not follow their advice.
Qí Wáng Jiǒng, being boastful and self-aggrandizing about his achievements,
accepted titles without humility.
Lù Jī disliked this,
and composed the "Rhapsody on a Gallant Scholar" to satirize him.
Its preface states: The foundation of establishing virtue is constant,
but the path to achieving merit is not uniform.
Why is this?
Cultivating the mind to determine one’s capacity lies within oneself,
while accomplishing tasks through external factors
depends on others.
What lies within oneself,
its rise or fall is limited to its own sphere;
what depends on others,
its abundance or scarcity is determined by circumstances.
A falling leaf awaits a gentle breeze to drop,
yet the force of the wind
is indeed minimal;
Mèngcháng cried upon encountering Yōngmén,
yet the emotional power of the qín was secondary.
Why is this?
A leaf about to fall needs no fierce wind,
tears about to drop
need not be troubled by mournful sounds.
Therefore, if the opportunity is granted by Heaven,
and human effort is fully exerted,
an ordinary person can accomplish the work of sages,
and a man of small talent can establish the achievements
of a brave warrior.
Hence it is said,
“Though his talent is not half of the ancients,
his accomplishments are already double theirs,”
which means he achieved it through the times.
Looking through history,
there are those who seized momentary glory and occupied the position of Yī
and Zhōu.
The self existing as self,
even a wise person is entangled by its burdens;
things relating to other things,
all creatures share this sentiment.
Indeed, when one’s own capacity is modest
yet one possesses extraordinary achievements,
divine implements radiate at his gaze,
all things follow his every nod and glance.
His mind delights in the security of his habitual position,
his ears are saturated with flattering words.
How could he know that achievements are external to oneself,
and responsibilities exceed one's talent?
Moreover, loving glory and hating disgrace
is the great expectation of all living beings;
envying abundance and harming superiors,
even gods and spirits cannot avoid it;
the ruler wields his constant
authority,
and the world obeys his great principles,
hence it is said, “Can Heaven be opposed?”
Yet, there are times when one dons a splendid robe and carries a halberd,
standing at the temple gate,
raising banners and rallying the masses,
displaying valor
in the fields;
how much more so for a worldly ruler who controls destiny
and governs others from below!
Extending benevolence widely is insufficient to counter resentment,
diligently promoting benefit is insufficient to compensate for harm,
thus
it is said, “He who carves for the great carpenter will surely injure his hand.”
Furthermore, when the government is run by the Níng family,
loyal ministers feel indignant;
when the sacrifices are performed by the lonely one (meaning the minister usurping authority),
the ruler will not long tolerate it.
Therefore, Jūn Shì was displeased
with Gōng Dàn’s actions;
the officers of Gāopíng were distrustful,
eyeing the power of Bólù.
And Chéng Wáng could not dismiss his suspicion and resentment,
while Xuān Dì
felt as if thorns were pricking his back –
were these not so?
Alas!
To shine across the four quarters,
no one's virtue is richer;
to be called uncle by the king,
no one is closer in kinship;
to ascend to the imperial throne,
no one's merit is greater;
to uphold integrity until one’s teeth
fall out,
no one’s loyalty is more profound.
Yet, to be precarious and stumble,
barely preserving oneself –
then that Yī Shēng who, embracing clarity and fairness, met execution,
and Wén Zǐ who, cherishing loyalty and reverence, faced the sword –
this
is just what happened.
Based on this,
if one possesses profound sagacity and intimate kinship,
as excellent as those examples,
and great virtue and utmost loyalty,
as magnificent as those,
still cannot gain trust in the heart of the ruler,
nor silence the slander from the mouths of the multitude,
then beyond this,
where else can one
find what is right?
The principle of safety and danger
can clearly be understood.
How much more so for those who covet great fame
and thereby transgress the prohibitions of the Daoists,
wielding meager talent to attempt what sages found difficult!
One's person is endangered due to excessive power,
yet one does not know to relinquish power to seek safety;
calamity accumulates
due to excessive favor,
yet one does not know to decline favor to invite blessings.
When one sees the common people plotting against oneself,
one strengthens the palace guard,
thereby increasing an untamed authority;
when one fears that all quarters
will not submit,
one imposes harsh laws and strict controls,
thereby incurring heartbreaking resentment.
Then, authority reaches its limit in awe-inspiring the ruler,
and resentment spreads among all, high and low.
Public sentiment daily erodes,
the crisis
is about to erupt,
yet one still reclines and stares,
believing oneself sufficient to amaze the world,
laughing at the ineptitude of the ancients,
forgetting one's own affairs are already clumsy,
knowing that past achievements can be boasted of,
They obscured the fact that success and failure
have their confluence.
Hence, when affairs are exhausted and fortune is spent,
there must be a downfall.
When the wind rises and dust gathers, misfortune often arrives cruelly.
The Sages feared that their achievements and fame would
exceed what was proper for them,
and detested that their favor and emoluments would surpass their due.
This is why.
Indeed, the great root of desires and cravings
is shared by both the wise and the foolish.
Wanderers sacrifice themselves for high positions in life,
while ambitious scholars seek to leave a name behind them after death.
The lot
received in life
is merely this.
As for achievements that eclipse the age,
no fame is greater;
as for acting according to one's will without hindrance,
no desire is more satisfied.
If that person had somewhat understood the Way of Heaven,
knowing
that the extreme cannot be increased,
and fullness cannot be long sustained,
and had transcendentally withdrawn themselves,
saluting grandly and retiring,
then their magnificent glory
would have looked up to surpass former worthies,
and their expansive influence
would have looked down upon future
records.
Their great desires would not have ceased with their person,
and their supreme joy would have been without fault from old.
Their integrity would have been more effective, and their virtue more extensive;
their person more at ease, and their fame more illustrious.
To not do this,
and to be utterly blind to that,
resulted in the traces of rivers and seas being obliterated into stagnant flows,
and the smallest flaw accumulating into mountains.
Their names were inscribed in the list of the wicked and stubborn,
and their bodies suffered the pain
of bitter poison.
How could this not be a delusion!
Therefore, I have composed this fu,
hoping that a few people in a hundred generations may awaken to it.
Qióng did not awaken to it,
and ultimately failed because of it.
Jī further held that when a Sage King governed the state,
righteousness lay in the enfeoffment system.
Therefore, he adopted its distant implications
and wrote "On the Five Ranks," which states: Now, to embody the state and manage the wilderness,
