the former kings took great care.
They established systems and laid foundations,
thinking to make later generations prosperous.
However, their strategies differed,
and the methods for long-lasting rule varied.
The system of the five ranks
began with Huáng Dáng,
while the administration of commanderies and prefectures
originated with Qín and Hàn.
Their gains and losses, successes and failures,
are all recorded in the canons and counsels.
Therefore, their details can be discussed.
Now, a king knows that the imperial enterprise is supremely heavy,
and the world supremely vast.
The vast cannot be controlled unilaterally,
and the heavy cannot be borne by one person alone.
To bear a heavy burden, one must borrow strength;
to control
the vast, one must ultimately rely on others.
Therefore, offices were established and duties divided,
to lighten their burden.
Vassals were established side by side,
to expand their control.
Thus, the regulations for
establishing territorial
borders were set,
and the appropriateness of kinship and distance was determined,
so that ten thousand states would support each other,
to achieve the stability of a solid rock;
and the imperial clan and commoners would live interspersed,
to establish the enterprise of a bulwark.
Moreover, they
saw the long-term control that stabilizes the world,
and understood the great principle of human nature.
They knew that treating others well is not as good as being generous to oneself,
and benefiting things is not as good as planning for oneself.
Securing the superior lies in pleasing the inferior,
and serving oneself lies in benefiting others.
Hence, the Yì Jīng says,
"By pleasing, one employs people,
and people forget their toil."
Xún Qīng said,
"To benefit them without gaining benefit
is not as good as the benefit
of benefiting them after gaining benefit."
Therefore, by distributing abundant joy throughout the world,
one can share their sorrows.
By feasting the world with abundant benefits,
one can share their harms.
When benefits are extensive
and grace profound,
and joy is far-reaching, then sorrow is deep.
Thus, the feudal lords enjoyed the reality of possessing their lands,
and the myriad states received the inheritance of their fortunes.
If this is so,
then the rulers facing south each devoted themselves to their
governance,
and within the nine domains, it was known that there was a fixed lord.
The affection of the superior for their children was born from this,
and the courtesy and trust of the inferior were established through this.
When the world was peaceful, it was sufficient to strengthen customs;
when the Way
declined, it was sufficient to resist tyranny.
Thus, strong and unyielding states could not monopolize power for a time,
and heroic and outstanding individuals had no place to harbor ambitions of hegemony.
Then, the state was secure thanks to
the aspirations of myriad states for transformation,
and the ruler was honored by relying on the self-preservation of the many princes.
It is like when many eyes guard the direction,
the net of heaven naturally expands;
when the four limbs shirk hardship,
the core of the body is preserved.
This is why the Three Dynasties followed the straight path,
and the Four Kings established their enterprises.
Now, prosperity and decline, rise and fall,
are inherent in the nature of things.
The flourishing or decay of teachings
depends on the people.
The original law was expected to be fully understood,
but the clear Way sometimes becomes obscured.
Thus, the hereditary system was corrupted by the powerful and oppressive,
and the principle of benefiting the lower classes was breached by gradual weakening.
The affliction of erosion and weakening arose from the Three Late Dynasties,
and the calamity of decline culminated in the Seven Hegemons.
In the past, Chéng Tāng personally observed the lessons of the Xià Hòu,
and Gōng Dàn personally experienced the warnings of the Shāng people.
Simplicity and refinement complemented each other,
and additions and subtractions were well-considered.
However, the rites of the five ranks
were not changed in
their time,
and the system of feudal territories
even saw some flourish more than others.
Did they disregard the calamities of the Two Kings and ignore the calculations for governing the world?
They surely knew that a hundred generations could not be governed beforehand,
and that a good
system could not be without flaws.
But the humiliation of being eroded and weakened is worse than the extinction of one's lineage,
and the distress of a collapse is more painful than gradual decline.
Therefore, those who initiate schemes gain many blessings,
and those who consider the end
incur fewer misfortunes.
This does not mean that marquises and earls have no signs of potential chaos,
or that commanderies and prefectures are not tools for promoting transformation.
Hence, when the state is in sorrow, it relies on their relinquishing their positions;
when the ruler is weak, he depends on their support.
When decline accumulated and evils piled up,
and the royal house gradually became humble,
they still preserved their status and position,
and their fortune was passed down to future generations.
The imperial lineage, though obscure, did not cease;
the divine instruments, though adverse, always survived.
Was this not because circumstances
made it so!
Down to the fallen Qín dynasty,
they abandoned the Way and relied on stratagems.
They punished the failures of Zhōu
and boasted of their own gains.
The axe found its beginning where it was sheltered,
and the governance of the state was blinded by weakening the lower ranks.
The state's prosperity
was enjoyed by the ruler alone,
and when the ruler worried, no one shared his harm.
Although swift downfall and descent into chaos
are not necessarily due to a single cause,
the calamity of collapse
was indeed due to isolation.
This was probably due to thinking of the small grievances
of the five ranks,
and forgetting the great virtue of the myriad states.
They knew that gradual decline was a concern,
but were blind to the pain of total collapse.
The weakness of Zhōu
had its origins.
The state lacked
an able ruler
for more than ten generations.
Yet, with a single word to save the king,
the feudal lords would certainly respond.
One morning, when a boast was made,
distant states were the first to rebel.
Thus, the powerful Jìn withdrew its plan for requesting burial tunnels,
and the tyrannical Chǔ abandoned its ambition to observe the tripods.
How could Liú Xiàng have spied on the pass,
or Shèng Guǎng dared to raise a cry in the marsh!
If the Qín people had followed the Zhōu system,
then even without
The Way,
whether it exists or perishes,
the disaster of downfall and destruction,
was it not in earlier days!
The Hàn rectified the 秦's errors,
greatly establishing marquises and kings.
Their territories overflowed,
not complying with the old institutions.
Therefore, Jiǎ Shēng grieved over their danger,
and Cháo Cuò lamented their chaos.
It was for this reason that the various
princes relied on the wealth of their states,
and leveraged the power of their commoners and gentry.
Those with sufficient power rebelled swiftly,
those with smaller territories revolted later.
The six ministers transgressed against its weak principles,
and the seven sons broke through its
leaky net.
The imperial ancestor was humbled by commoners,
and the Western Capital suffered from the Eastern Emperor.
This was a disaster of over-correction,
and not a burden caused by establishing feudal lords.
However, during the calamity of the Lǚ clan,
the court officials looked outwards;
Sòng Chāng, in his strategy for the Hàn,
definitely spoke of the feudal lords.
By the mid-period,
fearing their loss of integrity,
the imperial kinsmen were carved up and diminished,
having the name but no reality.
The world became vast
and empty,
again following the path of the perished Qín.
Therefore, the five marquises wielded power,
disregarding all the states;
Xīn Dū usurped the Hàn,
as easily as picking up something discarded.
Guāngwǔ 中興,
continuing and elevating the imperial lineage,
yet still followed the old tracks of the overturned carriage,
nurturing the chronic illness of a ruined family.
Barely a few generations passed,
and villains and traitors abounded.
Eventually, powerful ministers monopolized the court,
and the world was swept away.
A single man could form alliances or break them,
and cities and walls would crumble on their own.
How could it not be dangerous!
During the decline of Zhōu,
it was difficult to revive the royal house.
Seven ministers issued decrees without authorization,
and three sons seized positions.
The heir king surrendered his Jiǔ Dǐng,
and savage clans occupied his heavenly city.
Gongs
and drums resounded within the palace gates,
and arrows and spears flew within the crimson palace.
However, the disaster was confined to the royal domain,
and the harm did not spread.
The world was peaceful,
waiting out the danger in security.
Thus, Xuān Wáng
rose during the Gònghé Regency,
and Xiāng Huì was revived by Jìn and Zhèng.
How could this be compared to the Hàn dynasties, where a momentary disturbance at the palace gates
caused the four seas to boil,
where favored ministers entered the court in the morning,
and the nine provinces were in chaos by evening!
Thinking back to Wáng Mǎng's usurpation,
and looking at Dǒng Zhuó's seizure of power in recent times,
millions of people were heartbroken,
and the foolish and the wise felt the same pain.
Yet Zhōu survived because of it,
while Hàn
perished.
Why was this?
Was it that the age lacked ministers of former times,
or that scholars lacked the will to restore and unite?
Perhaps distant achievements were diminished by the change of times,
and heroic ambitions were frustrated by humble
circumstances.
Therefore, valiant men clenched their fists,
ultimately surrendering to the hands of their enemies;
ordinary people changed their principles,
thereby aiding the tyrannical Jìe of the oppressive state.
Even if at times there were those who gathered like-minded individuals to
plot for the royal house,
yet the ruler was not an enlightened lord,
and the subordinates were all commoners.
The armies had no pre-established ranks,
and the ruler and ministers had no will to protect each other.
Therefore, righteous armies gathered like clouds,
but could
not save from the disaster of plunder and slaughter.
The hopes of the people had not yet changed,
but the destruction of the Great Hàn was already witnessed.
Some might say,
"The hereditary positions of feudal lords
are not necessarily always secure.
Ignorant rulers and tyrannical kings
sometimes appear consecutively,
which is why the five ranks often led to chaos.
The governors and prefects of today
are all
capable officials chosen by the government.
Though some may fail,
most succeed,
which is why prefectures and counties are easy to govern."
If virtue is resplendent,
and promotion and demotion are applied daily,
and commanders are linked
together,
all fulfilling their duties,
then corrupt and ignorant rulers have no room for error.
Why then would there be no good governance?
Thus, earlier dynasties had reasons for their flourishing.
If, however, they decline,
then all
principles contradict themselves.
Officials who sell offices equate goods with wealth,
then all budding greed and cruelty belong to the powerful chiefs.
How then can there be no chaos?
Therefore, later kings had reasons for their downfall
and destruction.
Furthermore, to put it concisely,
the lords of the five ranks
govern with themselves in mind; the chiefs of prefectures and counties
plan for personal gain as officials.
How can this be proven?
Aspiring to advancement and striving for success
is the common ambition of career officials;
cultivating oneself and bringing peace to the people
is what good scholars rarely achieve.
The desire for advancement is keen,
while the reputation for bringing peace to the people is slow to come.
Therefore, harming the common people to benefit
oneself
is what those in power do not shy away from;
sacrificing practical matters to cultivate one's reputation
is what officials long for.
The ruler has no plans beyond the current year,
and the ministers harbor ambitions only for a short time.
The five ranks are not like this.
They know the state is their own land,
and all the people are their subjects;
if the people are at peace,
they benefit from it;
if the state is harmed,
their family suffers from its illness.
Therefore, predecessors wished to
pass on to descendants,
and future generations thought of continuing their family legacy.
The superiors had no perfunctory intentions,
and the subordinates understood the meaning of loyalty and solidity.
If both are wise in governing,
then their achievements have greater
or lesser weight;
if both are foolish and cause chaos,
then their faults have greater or lesser depth.
Thus, the system of the Eight Dynasties
can almost be understood with a single principle;
the institutions of Qín and Hàn
can perhaps be summarized in a single
statement.
At that time, Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (Sima Ying) attributed success to others and did not claim it for himself,
being modest and humble towards scholars.
Lù Jī, having felt the kindness of being completely saved,
and also seeing the frequent changes and difficulties in the imperial court,
believed that Yǐng would surely be able to restore prosperity to the Jìn dynasty.
So he dedicated himself to him.
Yǐng made Jī participate in the military affairs of the Grand General,
and memorialized him as Prefect of Píngyuán.
At the beginning of Tàiyān,
Yǐng and Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (Sima Yong) raised troops to attack Chángshā Wáng (Sima Ai).
Yǐng temporarily appointed Jī as Posterior General and Grand Commander of Héběi,
overseeing over 200,000 troops, including the Northern Central Protector Wáng Cuì and the Champion General Qiān Xiù.
Jī, considering that three generations of his family had been generals,
which was a taboo in Daoist beliefs,
and also that he had become an official while a sojourner,
suddenly rising above all other scholars,
and that Wáng Cuì, Qiān Xiù and others all harbored resentment,
firmly declined the position of Grand Commander.
Yǐng did not permit it.
Jī's fellow countryman Sūn Huì also advised Jī to cede the Grand Commander position to Cuì.
Jī said:
"They will say I am like a rat peeking out, avoiding danger,
[一０] which is exactly how I would hasten disaster."
So he proceeded.
Yǐng said to Jī:
"If this campaign succeeds and peace is established,
you shall be ennobled as a Duke of a Commandery,
and positioned among the Three Ducal Ministers.
General, strive for it!"
Jī replied:
"In the past, Qí Huán (Duke Huan of Qi) entrusted Yí Wú (Guan Zhong) to achieve the feat of uniting the nine states.
Yān Huì (King Hui of Yan) doubted Yuè Yì and lost an almost-completed enterprise.
The success of today's matter
depends on you, not on me."
Yǐng's Left Chief Clerk Lú Zhì, jealous of Jī's favor,
said to Yǐng:
"Lù Jī compares himself to Guǎn (Zhong) and Yuè (Yì),
likening Your Highness to an ignorant ruler.
Since ancient times, when appointing generals and sending out armies,
there has never been a case where a subject disrespected his lord and was able to succeed."
Yǐng remained silent.
When Jī first took command of the army,
his commander's banner broke,
which he considered a very ill omen.
The army was arrayed from Cháogē to Héquiáo,
and the sound of drums was heard for hundreds of li.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
there had never been such a grand military expedition.
Chángshā Wáng, accompanying the Son of Heaven, fought Jī at Lùyuàn.
Jī's army was greatly defeated,
and those who jumped into Qīlǐ Jiàn (Seven Li Ravine) and died piled up like mountains,
making the water cease to flow.
General Jiǎ Léng also died there.
[一一]
Earlier,
the eunuch Mèng Jiǔ's younger brother, Mèng Chāo, was also favored by Yǐng.
Chāo led 10,000 men as a junior commander.
Before the battle,
he let his troops plunder extensively.
Jī arrested the responsible leaders.
Chāo, with over a hundred iron-clad cavalry,
rode directly into Jī's headquarters and seized them,
then looked at Jī and said:
"Can a Mò slave be a commander?!"
Jī's Military Supervisor Sūn Zhěng advised Jī to kill him,
but Jī did not heed the advice.
Chāo then declared to the multitude:
"Lù Jī is about to rebel!"
He also wrote back to Jiǔ,
saying that Jī was playing both sides and was not acting decisively with the army.
During the battle,
Chāo did not follow Jī's command,
advanced alone with light troops, and was killed.
Jiǔ suspected Jī of killing him,
and so slandered Jī to Yǐng,
saying that he harbored rebellious intentions.
Generals Wáng Chǎn, Háo Chāng, Gōngshī Fān, and others, who were all appointed by Jiǔ,
along with Qiān Xiù and others,
jointly testified against him.
Yǐng was furious and
ordered Xiù to secretly arrest Jī.
That night,
Jī dreamed that a black canopy was wrapped around his carriage,
and he could not open it with his hands.
At dawn, Xiù's soldiers arrived.
Jī removed his military attire,
put on a white cap,
and met Xiù,
his demeanor calm.
He said to Xiù:
"Since the fall of the Wú dynasty,
my brothers and clan have received great imperial favor,
serving in the court,
and being appointed to local offices.
Chéngdū (Wáng Yǐng) entrusted me with a heavy responsibility,
which I could not decline.
To be executed today,
is this not fate?!"
He then wrote a memorial to Yǐng,
the words of which were very mournful.
Afterward, he sighed:
"Can I ever again hear the cry of cranes at Huátíng!"
He was then killed in the army camp,
at the age of forty-three.
His two sons, Lù Wèi and Lù Xià, were also killed.
Jī died unjustly,
and the soldiers grieved for him,
all shedding tears.
That day, a dim fog enveloped the land at midday,
strong winds broke trees,
and a foot of snow fell on flat ground.
Those who discussed it believed it was due to the injustice suffered by the Lù clan.
Jī's talent was outstanding and exceptional,
and his prose was grand and magnificent.
Zhāng Huà once said to him:
"When people write,
they usually lament having too little talent,
but you, on the contrary, worry about having too much."
His younger brother Lù Yún once
wrote in a letter:
"When Jūnmiáo (referring to Lù Yún himself) sees big brother's writing,
he always wants to burn his brush and inkstone."
Later, Gé Hóng wrote a book,
praising
"Jī's writings are like the accumulated jade of Xuánpǔ,
all of which are glowing pearls.
They are like the flowing waters of the Five Rivers,
all from a single source.
Their grandeur, beauty, richness,
sharpness, and elegance are truly unique in their generation!"
Such was the admiration he commanded.
However, he liked to frequent powerful households
and was close to Jiǎ Mì,
which earned him criticism for seeking advancement.
He wrote over three hundred essays,
all of which were circulated in the world.
Sūn Zhěng,
whose courtesy name was Xiǎnshì,
was a native of Fùchūn in Wú Commandery.
He was skilled in writing
and served Wú as a Yellow Gate Attendant.
During the reign of Sūn Hào,
many court officials incurred guilt,
but only Zhěng and Gù Róng preserved themselves with wisdom.
After Wú was pacified,
he became Magistrate of Zhuō,
where he was noted for his accomplishments.
When Jī was framed by Mèng Jiǔ and others,
Zhěng was arrested and tortured,
to the point where his two ankle bones were exposed,
but he never changed his testimony.
His disciples Fèi Cí and Zǎi Yì went to the prison to clear Zhěng's name.
Zhěng persuaded them to leave, saying:
"It is against my principles to falsely accuse an old acquaintance.
Why should you act like this?"
The two men replied:
"How could we betray you, our lord!"
Zhěng then died in prison,
and Cí and Yì also died.
Lù Yún (younger brother Dān, paternal cousin Xǐ)
Yún, courtesy name Shìlóng,
could write at the age of six.
His character was pure and upright,
possessing talent and reason.
In his youth, he was as famous as his elder brother Jī.
Although his writings were not as good as Jī's,
his critical arguments surpassed him,
earning them the title of
"The Two Lùs."
When he was young, Mǐn Hóng of Guǎnglǐng, a Shangshū of Wú, saw him and was impressed,
saying:
"If this child is not a dragon colt,
then he must be a phoenix chick."
Later, Yún was recommended as a Worthy and Filial,
at the age of sixteen.
When Wú was pacified,
Luò Jī entered Luòyáng.
Jī first paid his respects to Zhāng Huá.
Huá asked where [Lù] Yún was.
Jī replied:
“Yún has a laughing sickness,
and does not dare to show himself yet.”
Soon after, Yún arrived.
Huá was a man of many mannerisms,
and also liked to tie his beard with silk cords.
Yún saw this and laughed uncontrollably,
unable to stop himself.
Previously,
he had once worn mourning clothes onto a boat,
and when he looked down and saw his reflection in the water,
he burst out laughing and fell into the water.
People rescued him and he escaped harm.
Yún and Xún Yǐn had never met before.
They once gathered at Huá’s residence.
Huá said:
“Since we meet today,
let us not engage in ordinary conversation.”
Yún then raised his hand and said:
“Lù Shìlóng, from among the clouds.”
Yǐn said:
“Xún Mínghè, from beneath the sun.”
Mínghè
was Yǐn’s courtesy name.
Yún then said:
“Having opened up the blue clouds to behold the white pheasant,
why do you not draw your bow
and notch your arrow?”
Yǐn replied:
“I originally thought it was a cloud-dragon, grand and imposing,
but it turns out to be a mountain deer and a wild elk.
The beast is small and the crossbow strong,
which is why I am slow to shoot.”
Huá clapped his hands and roared with laughter.
Zhōu Jùn, the Inspector, summoned him to be an assistant,
and told people:
“Lù Shìlóng is the Yán Zǐ of our time.”
Soon after, he became a Palace Attendant for the Crown Prince from being a Secretariat Aide,
and was sent out to govern Jùnyí.
The county was located at a vital crossroads,
and was known to be difficult to govern.
When Yún arrived in office, there was a solemn atmosphere,
his subordinates dared not deceive him,
and there were no two prices in the market.
There was a case where a person was murdered,
but the principal culprit could not be identified.
Yún took the victim’s wife into custody,
but questioned her about nothing.
After about ten days, he released her,
and secretly sent someone to follow her.
He instructed:
“When she leaves, if she has not gone ten *lǐ*,
a man will meet her and speak with her.
Then bind him and bring him here.”
And so it happened exactly as he said.
When questioned, he confessed everything,
saying:
“I was having an affair with this woman,
and together we killed her husband.
Hearing that his wife had been released,
I wanted to speak with her,
but I was afraid of being near the county seat,
so I waited for her at a distance.”
Thereupon, the entire county praised his divine sagacity.
The Governor resented his ability,
and repeatedly reprimanded him.
Yún then resigned his office.
The common people missed him,
drew his likeness,
and sacrificed to him at the county shrine.
Soon after, he was appointed Palace Attendant-in-ordinary to Wú Wáng Yàn.
Yàn was extensively building mansions and chambers in the western park.
Yún submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant humbly observes that Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì, when he presided over the court, remained silent and composed,
and instructed the world with frugality.
He reigned for twenty-six years,
and did not undertake any new construction of palaces, towers, or pavilions.
He repeatedly issued clear edicts,
strictly cautioning against extravagance.
The state, inheriting the throne,
is obliged to follow and uphold this.
However, worldly customs have declined,
families compete in excess,
and gradually, this wave has spread,
and thus become a trend.
Although severe edicts are frequently proclaimed,
extravagant customs only proliferate.
Every time the imperial edicts are read,
the populace sighs.
When Qīnghé Wáng was building his tomb residence in the past,
an imperial handwritten edict recounted the former emperor’s teachings on frugality,
the earnestness of which
was manifest throughout the land.
Qīnghé Wáng then demolished the completed residence to comply with the imperial command,
and all within the seas, hearing and witnessing this,
were filled with joy.
Your foolish servant believes that the former emperor’s legacy teachings are daily fading,
and it is truly Your Highness
who can now assist the state in upholding the great transformation and extending the former path.
One must first cultivate simplicity and then one can instruct and rectify the four directions.
As for all that is grand and beautiful,
it should all be appropriately restrained by regulation,
only then will it satisfy the Emperor’s heart above,
and meet the expectations of the time below.
Your servant, with his ordinary talent,
has been specially promoted.
He also wishes to exhaust his loyalty and dedication to repay the kindness he has received,
and therefore, without considering offending,
dares to present his thoughts.
If there is anything commendable in your foolish servant’s words,
I beg Your Highness to consider them thrice.”
At that time, Yàn trusted his military commanders,
and had them audit the money and silk of various officials.
Yún again presented:
“I humbly observe the decree,
appointing the *bùqǔjiàng* Lǐ Xián and Féng Nán, and the *sīmǎ* Wú Dìng and the attendant Xú Tài, to audit the account books of money and silk from purchases made by various officials.
Your foolish servant believes that since the sagely virtue arose like a dragon,
and illuminated this great state,
talented officials have been selected from the multitude,
and all workers have diligently pursued their tasks.
The *Zhōngwèi* Gāi and *Dànóng* Dàn are both incorruptible, virtuous, and prudent,
diligently performing their duties.
Their subordinates, the various officials,
are all humble individuals from their communities.
Although their faults of oversight and ignorance
may be heard daily,
when it comes to upholding righteousness and acting with feeling,
they are likely without major transgressions.
Now, Xián and Nán are lowly military men,
Dìng and Tài are ignoble soldiers.
They are not known for their clear integrity,
nor are their loyalty and public spirit worthy of praise.
What concerns high ministers
is still considered unclear,
yet Xián and others are to supervise and investigate,
only then is it believed?
This is neither the principle of not employing [such people] at the founding of a state,
nor does it reflect Your Highness’s broad-mindedness in trusting sincerity.
Even if Xián and others could exhaust their efforts to benefit the state,
and the gains were a hundredfold,
as for assisting in the glorification of the nation,
it is still not as good as opening one’s heart and trusting worthy scholars without error.
Moreover, the benefit gained is merely a temporary, minor advantage,
while allowing petty men to wield power
and letting the great Way decline.
This is why your servant is deeply concerned.
Your servant holds the position of a high minister,
and his duty is to present what is commendable.
If he has any limited insight,
how would he dare not offer his full counsel?
Your foolish servant believes that a clear order should be issued
to dismiss these audits,
and all matters should be handed over to the *zhìshū* (Chief Clerk).
Then great trust will prevail below, and people will strive to exhaust their efforts.”
Lù Yún loved talent and befriended gentlemen,
making many recommendations and advancements.
He wrote a letter to the Tàicháng Fǔ recommending Zhāng Shàn from his home commandery, saying:
“I have heard that in ancient times, the sagely kings,
receiving Heaven's mandate to rule the world,
earnestly promoted bright virtues
and sought harmony between men and spirits.
None failed to revere the canons and counsels to guide thought,
and promote ritual and learning to refine the distant.
Thus, Emperor Yáo's radiance shone, and his Way aligned with men and Heaven;
Lord Xī's plainness and refinement made Zhōu flourish for two generations.
The great Jìn established its imperial house,
revering and matching Heaven and Earth.
With the lands of Xià now united,
ritual and music are to be implemented.
Your Excellency meets this propitious turn of fate,
assisting the timely confluence of Heaven and man,
widely inviting the outstanding and brilliant,
to gloriously promote the existing canons.
I humbly observe that Zhāng Shàn, a retainer to the Wèi Jiāngjūn and from my home commandery,
possesses abundant virtue and pure clarity,
with profound and penetrating insight.
Initially admiring the sagely gate,
he settled his heart at the double-stacked gate;
he opened the path and ascended the steps,
thus rising to the central profundity.
He extracted the spiritual coffers from the secret palace,
unveiling the metal-bound caskets from the dark summer.
He delighted in studying the Hundred Schools,
widely collecting their treasures.
His prose surpassed that of the Hanlin,
his words eloquently expressed their brilliance.
Exploring the subtle and gathering the excellent,
his thoughts penetrated the divine.
Discussing the Way and composing writings,
his chapters shone brilliantly.
Holding unique talent in the prefectural yamen,
he idled in the public gate.
He dwelt in tranquility, concealing his treasure;
he submerged in emptiness, hiding his vessel.
He wore plain robes over brocade,
and black garments over jade.
The layered springs changed their course,
the suspended carriage was about to depart.
He found comfort in a lowly position,
years passing repeatedly.
The gentry
all harbored resentment and regret.
Currently, the great purity opens its doors,
the four gates unlock their keys;
the dark net encompasses the earth,
Heaven’s net widely gathers.
Auspicious clouds rise to summon dragons,
harmonious winds stir to bring phoenixes.
This is truly an autumn for hidden talents to shine,
a day for crossing the river on a raft.
Yet Zhāng Shàn remains sunken in a lowly position,
causing sorrow in the hearts of many.
If he were allowed to formally serve in the Tàixué,
to synthesize and integrate the ancient canons;
to dangle his cap strings before the jade steps,
and discuss the Way in the purple palace,
he would truly be a rare treasure for the imperial house,
a magnificent vessel for the ancestral temple.
With the nine movements of the grand music,
he would surely ascend to the court of Hào Tiān;
with the six changes of Sháo Xià,
he would surely partake in the sacrifices to Shàngdì.”
Later, he became Shàngshū Láng, Shìyùshǐ, Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén, and Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng appointed him Qīnghé Nèishǐ.
When Yǐng was about to attack Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
he made Lù Yún the Qiánfēng Dūdū.
Upon Jiǒng's execution,
he was transferred to Dàjiāngjūn Yòu Sīmǎ.
In Yǐng's later years, his administration declined,
and Lù Yún often opposed his will with straightforward advice.
Mèng Jiǔ wanted to appoint his father as the Hándān Ling.
Zuǒ Chángshǐ Lú Zhì and others all complied with his wishes,
but Lù Yún firmly refused,
saying:
“This county is a position for officials from the ducal administration.
How can a Huángmén's father hold it?!”
Mèng Jiǔ deeply resented him.
When Zhāng Chāng caused rebellion,
Yǐng appointed Lù Yún as Shǐchíjié, Dàdūdū, Qiánfēng Jiāngjūn to suppress Chāng.
However, he was stopped due to the campaign against Chángshā Wáng.
When Jī was defeated,
Lù Yún was also arrested.
Yǐng's officials Jiāng Tǒng, Cài Kè, Zǎo Sōng, and others submitted a memorial, saying:
“We, your officials, have heard that when the ruler is sagely and discerning,
his subordinates offer all their counsel.
If we have any thoughts,
we dare not withhold them.
Yesterday, we heard the decree that Lù Jī failed to meet the military deadline,
and his army was utterly defeated.
That punishment was applied according to the law
was considered just by all.
It is indeed sufficient to bring order to the three armies,
and to demonstrate authority to those near and far.
This is what is called ‘one man is executed,
and the whole world takes warning.’
However, we also heard a grave decree
that Lù Jī plotted rebellion
and should be punished with extermination of his clan.
Those who do not know the full story
are all perplexed.
Indeed, when a person is honored at court,
it is shared with the multitude;
when a person is executed in the market,
it is an abandonment shared with the multitude.
The careful consideration of punishment
was something the ancients valued.
Now, your Bright Excellency has raised a righteous army
to eliminate the nation's troubles.
The four seas are of one mind,
converging like clouds and responding like echoes.
The lives of the guilty
hang by a thread,
and the era of great peace
is but a morning or evening away.
Lù Jī and his brothers were both elevated
and entrusted with important responsibilities.
They should not betray boundless grace
to side with a dying foe;
nor abandon the security of Mount Tài
to rush into the peril of stacked eggs.
It is simply that Lù Jī's plans and considerations were shallow and shortsighted.
He was unable to manage and control the various commanders,
to achieve decisive results and slay the enemy.
In the ebb and flow of events,
there were matters of doubt and suspicion,
which caused your sagely discernment to not fully ascertain the truth.
Punishment by execution is a serious matter.
If it is said that Lù Jī showed signs of rebellion,
then Wáng Cuì and Qiān Xiù should be ordered to investigate the matter.
Only when the facts are clearly verified
and revealed to the myriad people,
should Lù Yún and others be executed;
it would not be too late.
The present measure
is truly too severe.
If successful, it will make the world willingly submit;
if it fails, it will certainly cause the four quarters to lose heart.
It must not be approached without careful deliberation,
it must not be approached without thorough caution.
We, your humble servants,
are not pleading for Lù Yún's life alone,
but are truly concerned that this action carries the potential for success or failure.
We dare to express our foolish and blunt opinions
to guard against slander.”
Yǐng did not accept it.
Jiāng Tǒng and others repeatedly pleaded,
and Yǐng hesitated for three days.
Lú Zhì then said:
“Formerly, Zhào Wáng killed Zhōnghùjūn Zhào Jùn,
but spared his son Xiáng.
Xiáng went to your Bright Excellency and attacked Zhào;
that is a precedent.”
Cài Kè entered before Yǐng,
knocking his head until it bled,
saying:
“Lù Yún was resented by Mèng Jiǔ;
this is known far and wide.
Now he is indeed to be killed,
without clear evidence of his guilt.
This will cause doubt among the multitude,
and I secretly feel pity for Your Bright Excellency.”
Dozens of officials followed Cài Kè in,
weeping and earnestly pleading.
Yǐng showed a compassionate expression, contemplating pardoning Lù Yún.
But Mèng Jiǔ supported Yǐng and led him inside,
urging him to kill Lù Yún.
He was forty-two years old at the time.
He had two daughters,
but no sons.
His students and former subordinates received his coffin and buried him in Qīnghé,
built a tomb, erected a stele,
and offered sacrifices four times a year.
His collected writings comprised three hundred and forty-nine essays,
and he also compiled ten chapters of a new book,
all circulated in the world.
Initially,
Yún once traveled,
and stopped to lodge at an old friend's house.
At night, he lost his way in the dark,
not knowing where to go.
Suddenly, he saw a firelight in the grass,
so he went towards it.
Reaching a house,
he lodged there,
and saw a young man
of beautiful demeanor,
with whom he discussed Lǎozi,
their conversation profound and far-reaching.
Towards dawn, he took his leave.
After walking about ten *lǐ*,
he reached his old friend's house,
who said that there was no human habitation for several tens of *lǐ* around there.
Yún's mind then began to understand.
He went back to find the place where he had lodged the previous night,
and it was Wáng Bì's tomb.
Yún originally had no knowledge of Xúanxué,
but from then on, his discussions of Lǎozi greatly improved.
Yún's younger brother, Dān, served as Píngdōng Jìjiǔ,
and also had a pure reputation.
He was killed along with Yún.
Sūn Huì, an officer of the Dàjiāngjūn, wrote a letter to Zhū Dàn, the Huáinán Nèishǐ, saying:
"It was unexpected that the three Lùs, serving together in the court,
were suddenly annihilated.
Their achievements in the Way are lost;
the depth of this cruel pain
is unbearable and hard to express.
The state has lost its eminent figures;
this sorrow is not for one person alone!"
Such was the grief and mourning he received from his region.
Later, Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, in campaigning against Yǐng,
issued a proclamation to the whole empire,
also listing the wrongful killing of Jī and Yún as a crime of Yǐng.
Xǐ's courtesy name was Gōngzhòng.
His father, Mào,
was Wú Lìbù Shàngshū.
Xǐ served Wú,
progressively rising to Lìbù Shàngshū.
In his youth, he had a reputation,
was fond of learning, and possessed talent and wisdom.
He once made a preface to his own work,
the gist of which was:
"Liú Xiàng examined the Xīnyǔ and wrote Xīnxù.
Huán Tán recited the Xīnxù and wrote Xīnlùn.
I, not knowing my own measure,
was moved by Zǐyún's Fǎyán and wrote Yándào.
Beholding Jiǎzǐ's splendid talent, I wrote Fǎnglùn.
Observing Zǐzhèng's Hóngfàn, I wrote Gǔjīn Lì.
Perusing Jiǎng Zǐtōng's Wànjī, I wrote Shěnjī.
Reading Yōutōng, Sīxuán, and Sìchóu, I wrote Yúbīn and Jiǔsī.
Truly, I am one who endures shame."
His writings amounted to nearly a hundred chapters.
When Wú was pacified,
he also wrote Xīzhōu Qīnglùn, which was circulated in the world,
attributing it to Zhūgě Kǒngmíng to disseminate his work.
There was a chapter titled "Comparative Discussions on Ranks" which said:
"Someone asked me,
'Is Xuē Yíng truly the foremost among the nation's scholars?'
I replied: 'Judging by reason,
he ranks somewhere between fourth and fifth.'"
The questioner, astonished, pressed for an explanation.
I replied: 'When Sūn Hào was without the Way,
indulging in his tyranny,
those who coiled their bodies like dragons and snakes,
keeping their forms silent,
hiding and not acting,
with intentions unfathomable –
these are the first kind of people.
Those who avoid high positions and dwell in low ones,
whose stipend replaces their farming income,
who maintain profound tranquility and abide by moderation,
who are humble, reclusive, and serene –
these are the second kind of people.
Those who are upright and concerned for the state's governance,
whose hearts do not decline high office,
who are feared for their integrity,
and who govern without apprehension –
these are the third kind of people.
Those who weigh what is appropriate for the times,
who are still prominent in chaos,
whose intentions do not forget loyalty,
and who occasionally offer small benefits –
these are the fourth kind of people.
Those who are gentle, respectful, and cultivatedly cautious,
who do not act as sycophants,
who do not boast of their contributions,
and who calmly maintain their favor –
these are the fifth kind of people.
Beyond these,
they are not worth counting.
Therefore, those of the second rank and above
often remain obscure and far from regret and fault.
Those of the third rank and below
have reputation and position, but are close to blame and entanglement.
Thus, a deeply discerning *jūnzǐ*
conceals his brilliance and acts with gentle compliance.'"
The questioner said: 'Having just heard this profound discourse,
I am enlightened for the rest of my years!'"
During the Tàikāng era,
an imperial edict was issued, stating:
"Lù Xǐ and fourteen other former *shàngshū*,
praised by the southern gentry,
were all, due to their integrity, not tolerated by Hào Cháo.
Some were loyal but incurred punishment,
others withdrew to cultivate their aspirations,
and were cast out into the wilderness.
Let the responsible officials appoint them to their former positions.
Let the local authorities send them forth with due ceremony.
Upon arrival, they shall be employed according to their talents."
So Xǐ was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and soon after, he died.
His son, Yù,
served as Shàngshū Láng and Yìyáng Tàishǒu.
The imperial edict stated: The ancients said:
"Though Chǔ had talent,
Jìn indeed used it."
Observing Lù Jī and Lù Yún,
they were truly the finest timber of Jīnghénɡ,
manifesting the elegance of jade tablets in their brilliance,
and displaying their genius in their early years.
Their discernment was clear and astute,
their spirit distinguished and exceptional.
Their literary style was grand and magnificent,
unmatched in their time;
their discussions were impassioned,
unparalleled throughout history.
Their elevated words resonated far,
like the bright moon hanging luminous;
their layered ideas unfolded gracefully,
like the accumulated beauty of towering peaks.
When analyzing principles into a thousand threads,
it was like lightning rending and frost yielding;
when weaving texts into a single whole,
it was like pearls flowing and jades combining.
Their words were profound and elegant,
their meanings broad and clear,
thus they were truly capable of far surpassing Méi Mǎ,
and loftily treading in the footsteps of Wáng Liú,
becoming the sole literary master
of a hundred generations.
Yet, their ancestors shone brightly,
serving as crucial supports for the Wú dynasty;
generations of their family distinguished themselves in civil and military affairs,
with generals and ministers successively flourishing.
Lù Jī, with his talent fit for court,
and his capacity a model for governance,
should have inherited the blessings of distinction,
and upheld the task of assisting his era,
demonstrating his abilities,
preserving his reputation, and achieving merit.
But the Wú dynasty's foundation tilted,
and Jīnlínɡ's vitality was extinguished.
The ruler was displaced, the state perished,
his family was lost, and his vassals scattered.
Spreading his wings, he departed south,
only to perch in a tree consumed by fire;
with scales flying, he fled north,
only to end up in a scalding pool.
This caused the den of twin dragons to shatter,
and the nest of two phoenixes to collapse.
The ambition to stir up waves remained unfulfilled,
as their bones and long scales swiftly perished;
the will to soar above the clouds was about to take flight,
but their strong wings turned to ash prematurely.
To hope for their soaring and leaping,
how could it be possible!
A worthy person establishes themselves
with accomplishments and reputation as their foundation;
a scholar living in the world
prioritizes wealth and honor.
Therefore, profit and glory are what people crave,
and misfortune and disgrace are what people detest.
Hence, to remain in safety and preserve one's name
is where a jūnzi abides;
to brave danger and pursue high office
is what a zhéshì avoids.
Thus, we know that an orchid planted by the roadside
will certainly not retain its greenness for long;
a cassia growing in a secluded valley
will ultimately preserve its red hue for many years.
It is not that the orchid is resented and the cassia favored,
nor is it that the roadside harms and the valley benefits;
but that their survival and demise differ
due to the distinct circumstances of prominence and obscurity.
Therefore, it is said: flaunting one's beauty in the wrong place
rarely leads to lasting peace;
concealing one's extraordinary talent and choosing one's residence wisely
allows one to preserve one's nature.
Observing the conduct of Jī Yún,
their wisdom fell short of their words.
Seeing the admonitions in their writings,
how is it that understanding is easy, but action is difficult?
They considered their wisdom sufficient to stabilize the times,
and their talent capable of assisting the mandate,
hoping to preserve their rank and position,
and not disgrace their ancestral foundations.
They did not know that the world was still unsettled,
and their fortune was in decline.
Advancing, they could not dispel darkness and rectify chaos;
retreating, they could not withdraw and preserve themselves.
Instead, they exerted themselves for a perilous state,
and devoted their hearts to a mediocre ruler.
Their loyal sincerity was doubted despite being real,
and slanders arose from falsehoods, leading to suspicion.
Life, originating from oneself, was difficult to sustain;
death, due to others, was easily hastened.
The hounds of Shàngcài
were not a warning heeded beforehand;
the cranes of Huátínɡ
were only regretted afterward.
Ultimately, his clan was wiped out and his sacrifices ceased,
which is truly lamentable!
However, three generations served as generals,
and the seeds of calamity fell upon later generations;
executing those who surrendered is inauspicious,
and its ill effects reach one's descendants.
Thus, we know that Xīlínɡ initiated the tragic beginning,
and Héqiáo concluded its disastrous end;
this was the will of Heaven,
how could it be merely human affairs!

Xiàhóu Zhàn, courtesy name Xiàoruò,

His grandfather, Wēi,
was the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu for Wèi.
His father, Zhuānɡ,

Zhàn had exceptional talent in his youth,

He was skilled at coining new phrases,

He was good friends with Pān Yuè,

People in the capital called them

They consider weak judgment important,
and timid words trustworthy.
Those who do not know scholars do not face public censure,
and those who fail to obtain scholars do not feel private shame.
Those in positions of power are all of the caliber of Jì, Qì,
Gāo Yì, Yī Lǚ, Zhōu, and Shào,
or the ilk of Shū Bào and Zhòng Xióng.
When examining antiquity, they surpass Huáng Táng;
when governing, they exceed Yú Xià.
They disdain the
achievements of Kūn Wú,
scoff at the merits of Huán and Wén,
dismiss Cán Guǎn Zhòng,
and ridicule Yàn Yīng.
In the distant future, they aspire to ascend Dǐnghú;
in the near future, they wish to surpass Tàipíng.
They are about to preserve their vital energy and cherish their
spirit,
cultivating their own virtue in solitude.
Profoundly serene and utterly empty,
they vigorously nourish their true nature.
Though they possess the strength to clasp Tài Shān,
they will not lift a single feather;
though they raise waves for ten thousand *lǐ*,
they will not wash a single
scale.
Their coughs and spittle turn into pearls and jade,
and the flick of their sleeves brings forth wind and clouds.
How could they possibly involve themselves in such [⿱⿳一丿⺼夰]㫝 base affairs,
seeking talent and promoting people?
This, again, is a misstatement from you, my son.
Have you not
heard of the divine people?
They inhale the wind and drink the dew,
not eating the five grains.
They ascend to the Grand Purity,
and wander among mountains and peaks,
trampling on spiritual mushrooms,
and playing with white jade.
They are inherently
complete without external means,
and self-sufficient without relying on anything.
They do not share the same tastes and desires as ordinary people,
nor the same honors and disgraces as worldly affairs.
Thus, they can enter the gate of endlessness,
and enjoy years of immortality.
Judging from this,
why wait to promote worthies!”
The guest said:
“The sage said: ‘When the Way prevails in the state,
to be poor and lowly
is a disgrace.’
Now, you live in an age where the Way prevails,
and are in a time of great peace.
Why do you not
roll up your sleeves and rouse your spirit,
devising strategies and performing wonders?
Make the singing cranes harmonize,
and good positions be secured.
Instead, you immerse yourself in the official bureaus,
restraining your ambition and toiling in humble positions—
is this not utterly feeble?
Moreover, Yī Yǐn served Chéng Tāng,
and Nìng Qī encountered Huán Gōng.
One offered himself for the tripod and cutting board,
the other hired himself to feed cattle.
They clarified the opportunities for rise and fall,
and sang of the flowing white water.
Their virtue moved the King of Yīn,
and their righteousness touched the Marquis of Qí.
Thus, Yī Yǐn rose from the kitchen to become Āhéng,
and Nìng Qī emerged from beneath the carriage to step up to the rank of Grand Master.
Externally, they showed no slightness;
internally,
they made no entreaties.
They straightened their bodies and stretched out their hands,
directly attaining prominent positions.
Why do you, my son, not emulate the worthy to spur yourself on,
and aspire to antiquity with fervor?”
Xiàhóu Zǐ said:
“Alas!
What kind of talk is this!
Wealth and nobility are what people desire,
they are not what I dislike.
The sword of Gān Jiàng
could cut through dogs and horses on land,
and sever dragons in water,
yet a lead knife cannot enter mud.
A mount like Qí Jì or Huá Liú
can travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day,
yet a clumsy, lame horse cannot cross a
*mǔ*.
A hundred-times-refined mirror
can distinguish the number of hairs on a beard and eyebrow,
yet a clay wall cannot see Tài Shān.
A swan, with a single flight,
traverses the four seas,
and rises beyond the blue clouds,
yet a tiny wren does not fly over mulberry and elm.
This is the distinction between sharpness and dullness,
the determination of superiority and inferiority.
Those who wish to advance themselves
do so no more than a myriad-chariot state.
Yet, for me to appear in
the imperial court,
and answer the world's questions,
is nothing more than to reveal what I know.
I have exhausted my thoughts and exerted my
talents and learning,
but my ideas lack elegant righteousness to be a standard,
and my arguments have no single word worth adopting.
That is why
I am stuck in my vulgar mediocrity, and no one can uplift me.
Judging from this,
why should I not promote myself?
You do not fault my virtue for being lacking,
but doubt my
position for not being attained.
This is like turning a mirror backward to seek an image,
or climbing a tree to fish downward.
I do not consider myself unworthy for this.
As for Yī Yǐn carrying the tripod to seek Tāng,
Lǚ Shàng hiding and wandering to attract Wén,
Fù Yuè holding a rammer to awaken his lord,
and Nìng Qī striking his horn to summon the ruler,
these are not
things I am capable of.
Zhuāng Zhōu's unrestrained and free talk,
Jūn Píng's fortune-telling to establish his own worth,
Jiē Yú feigning madness to protect himself,
and Méi Fú abandoning his family to seek immortality—
these
are also not what I find comfortable.
As for Jì Zhá upholding his principles in Yánlíng,
Yáng Xióng pondering deeply on the Tàixuán,
Bó Yù being gentle and harmonious among people,
and Liǔ Huì being thrice
dismissed from official posts,
though I am not diligent,
I quietly somewhat resemble their pure example.”
Later, he was selected and appointed Prince’s Chamberlain,

and must be put into practice.
You must concentrate your hearts,
unify your hearing,
and temper your natures,

wise words.”
Chún and the others bowed and kowtowed.

From generation to generation, they expanded upon the previous ways,
and completed their good deeds and beautiful virtues.
The wise and upright succeeded each other,
and official positions were extended to all.
Reaching our Imperial Great-Grandfather, Marquis Mǐn,

will,

Our late father, the Lord Marquis,

respectful, intelligent, cultured, and thoughtful,

Reverently I delve into ancient instructions,
thereby widely expounding on classic texts,
and thus synthesizing their subtle words.
Alas!
From the Sān Fén, Wǔ Diǎn, Bā Suǒ, Jiǔ Qiū,

and the myriad streams of the Hundred Schools,

The Jiǔ Chóu of the Hóng Fàn,

Fù;
this culture rests here.
Moreover, when I was nine years old, my royal mother, Xuē Fēi, passed away.

second wife, Cài Jī,

When Cài Jī passed away,

Therefore,

Since ancient texts contain no such precedent,
my empress,

Therefore,
I, day and night, without slackening,

How can it be that I alone am fearful?
Indeed,
it is the esteemed example I uphold.
Thus, I eat at noon
and sleep at midnight.
How can it be that I fear only the esteemed example?
Indeed, I take your words as my model.
Alas,
I shall be respectful!
Indeed!
I have heard
that Zhōu had a most virtuous person,
a woman.
My mother, Yáng Jī,

When I was a child,

She highly valued benevolence, righteousness, filial piety, and fraternal affection,

generosity.

That my brothers and sisters are disciplined and careful in conduct,

support.
When I govern even a small domain,

If the legal cases are unjust,

Alas!
My mother's sincerity was manifest without words,

clans,

cherish them in my heart, for they are unattainable,

You must remember this!
May my younger brothers be blessed by Heaven in our family,

Chún Yīng, how cultured and gentle you are!

I am veiled in ignorance,

Alas, my six brothers,

I also dare not forget your deficiencies.
Alas!
Young Zhān,
you see my strength in benevolence,

He resided in the district for several years,
and many in the court and countryside lamented his unfulfilled potential.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
then sent out to serve as Nányáng Xiàng.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Pú,
but before he could assume the post,
Emperor Wǔ died.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was made Sànqí Chángshì.
In the early Yuánkāng era,
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
He authored over thirty treatises,
forming a unique school of thought.
Originally,
Zhàn completed his Zhōu Shī and
showed it to Pān Yuè.
Yuè said:
"This work is not only warm and elegant,
but also reveals a distinct nature of filial piety and fraternal love."
Yuè consequently composed his Jiāfēng Shī.
Zhàn's clan was a prominent family,
and he was somewhat extravagant by nature,
wearing splendid robes and eating luxurious food,
indulging in all sorts of rare delicacies.
However, when he was about to die,
he left instructions for a small coffin and simple burial,
without building a burial mound or planting trees.
Commentators say that although Zhàn did not cultivate a reputation for integrity during his life,
his death was marked by frugality and a virtuous end,
showing a deep understanding of the principles of existence and demise.
Chún's courtesy name was Xiàochōng.
He also possessed literary talent
and was famous alongside Zhàn.
He rose to the position of Yìyáng Tàishǒu.
During the upheaval in the Central Plains,
many of his sons and nephews perished at the hands of the barbarian invaders,
and only his son, Chéng, crossed the river.
Chéng's courtesy name was Wénzǐ.
He served as Cān Āndōng Jūnshì,
gradually rising to Nánpíng Tàishǒu.
At the end of the Tàixīng era,
Wáng Dūn raised an army and marched inwards.
Chéng, along with Gān Zhuó, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, Liǔ Chún, the Jiānjūn of Bādōng, Tán Gāi, the Tàishǒu of Yídū, and others,
all issued proclamations to near and far,
listing Dūn's crimes.
However, Gān Zhuó became indecisive and did not advance,
and the imperial army was defeated.
Dūn executed all those who opposed him.
He arrested Chéng
and intended to kill him,
but Chéng's maternal cousin, Wáng Yì, pleaded earnestly and secured his release.
Soon after, he became Sànqí Chángshì.
Pān Yuè (his nephew Ní)
Pān Yuè, courtesy name Ānrén,
was a native of Zhōngmóu, Xíngyáng.
His grandfather, Jǐn,
was Ānpíng Tàishǒu.
His father, Pí,
was Lángyá Nèishǐ.
Yuè was renowned for his talent and intelligence in his youth,
and his hometown called him a "Wunderkind,"
likening him to Zhōng Jiǎ.
He was early appointed to the offices of Sīkōng and Tàiwèi,
and recommended as Xiùcái.
During the Tàishǐ era,
Emperor Wǔ personally ploughed the sacrificial fields.
Yuè composed a rhapsody to praise this event,
saying: "In the fourth year of Jìn, on the Dīngwèi day of the first month,
the Emperor personally led the multitude of nobles to plough the fields of the Qianmǔ domain,
as was the rite.
Thereupon, the Diànshī was commanded to clear
the imperial precinct,
the Yělú to sweep the paths,
the Fēngrén to enclose the palace,
and the Zhǎngshè to set up barriers.
The verdant altar majestically rose like a mountain,
the emerald canopy spread out like dark clouds.
It established the spiritual site of a lofty foundation,
and opened
the broad pathways of the four roads.
The fertile fields were rich,
the rich soil flat and level.
Clear Luò River and turbid canals
diverted and agitated the water.
Distant paths were straight as ropes,
nearby field boundaries straight as arrows.
Lush oxen were harnessed to azure yokes,
dark shafts attached to black ploughshares.
The reserved carriages were solemnly arrayed on the left of the dwellings,
awaiting the emperor's personal presence.
The hundred officials were placed first,
their positions
divided by office,
from top to bottom,
all loyal ministers.
They donned spring robes, lush and splendid,
and rode in carriages, rumbling and rolling.
A gentle breeze arose from the light carriage awnings,
fine dust
rose from the vermilion wheels.
Solemnly holding their jades, they arrayed themselves on the steps,
gazing at the imperial carriage with reverent awe.
It was like the morning sun drying the clear dew,
or the myriad stars orbiting the North Star.
Then, the vanguard formed like a school of fish,
the attendant carriages clustered like scales,
the Chānghé gate opened wide,
four steeds abreast on the three roads.
The Chángbó rode beside him,
the Tàipú held the reins.
The empresses offered early
and late varieties of seeds,
the Sīnóng prepared the planting tools.
The Qièhú managed the rising and falling of the ceremonies,
the Gōngzhèng set up the barriers at the gates.
The Son of Heaven then rode in his jade carriage,
shaded by a magnificent
canopy,
with clanging jade ornaments,
and rustling silk brocades.
The golden chariot shone with dazzling brilliance,
the dragon-like steeds soared and advanced.
Red and black distinguished Líkǎn,
flying
azure and white on Zhènduì.
The central yellow glowed with radiance,
the square colors gathered in profusion.
Luan bells chimed on the five roads,
nine banners fluttered.
Jade dagger-axes entered the buds,
cloud-like standards
were dim and hazy.

speaks only after settling their mind,
seeks only after firming their friendships,

Thus, action

upright;
speech

seeking

action

when he acts,

he does not speak idly;

If

Therefore, if the self is not at peace, there is danger;

The attachment of worries and troubles

Those who are selfish

those who have desires cannot achieve their desires;

If desires are not fulfilled,

If private aims are not followed,
how can there be no aggression?
Everyone is selfish,
every family has desires;
all desires contend in parallel,

Contention

aggression
is the root of resentment.
Once resentment

Can one not be afraid?

tilting

galloping

In the court, there are friends who adjust their caps;
in the wilds, there are friends who knot their sashes;
factions flourish in front,

When misfortune arises,

the lesser are the overthrow of the self and the extinction of the ancestral sacrifices.

Is it not that it begins

The *jūnzǐ* is not like this.
Knowing that selfishness harms the public good,

knowing that having desires injures virtue,

knowing that contention
and rivalry invite disaster,

knowing that loving aggression invites resentment,

He secures himself without being selfish,
therefore his person is upright and
his private aims are complete;
he is cautious in speech and does not indulge desires,
therefore his words are effective and his desires are followed;
he forms associations without seeking advantage,

he is careful in action and does not seek fame,
therefore

things.

he is like all things,

Those who can preserve their peace

they merely do not forget danger.
Those who have a future for advancement

Those who maintain their order

they merely
do not forget chaos.

hide in a humble alley,
wear short coarse clothes,
eat wild herbs,
