Even sitting in a splendid hall,
riding in an ornamented carriage,
wearing embroidered robes,
managing a vast estate,
residing behind multiple gates,
and moving in an orderly procession,
one cannot compare in glory with him.
To utilize
the timing of Heaven,
distribute the advantages of Earth,
be content with plain clothes,
find peace in the swamps,
be soaked in body and muddied in feet,
and eat only after plowing—
if he but exalts virtue,
he is not unadvanced.
Even holding a high position,
enjoying heavy emoluments,
wielding the scales of power,
grasping the secrets of the state,
his achievements covering his era,
his influence rivaling that of the ruler,
one cannot compare in ease with him.
To abandon intentions and calculations,
lose talents and wits,
forget one's inner
feelings,
discard one's physical form,
appear as if incompetent,
and seem to lack ambition—
if he but rectifies his heart,
he is not ungoverned.
Even with complex strategies,
broad arts and skills,
careful attention to names and punishments,
and strict
laws and regulations,
his eloquent arguments flowing like water,
and his discussions peerless in the world,
one cannot contend in merit with him.
Therefore, to be at peace means
to be at peace in the Way.
To advance means
to advance in virtue.
To govern means
to govern the heart.
Never has there been one who secured himself yet could not protect his state,
who advanced in virtue yet could not manage wealth and rank,
or who governed his heart yet could not govern all
things.
However, to contemplate danger is how one seeks peace;
to consider retreat is how one can advance;
to fear chaos is how one preserves order;
to be wary of perishing is how one obtains survival.
As for those who weaken their will and empty
—the heart—
to broaden one's spirit and reach afar,
to lean upon the unshakeable root,
to float and roam beyond the boundless;
not to value oneself above things, yet things venerate it;
not to make oneself esteemed by others,
yet people respect it.
It is approachable but not to be slighted,
honorable but not to be distanced.
Approach it as if it were insufficient,
yet no one in the world can treat it with familiarity;
lift it
as if it were easy to bear,
yet no one in the world can trouble it.
When successful, it aids its path without seeking glory;
when impoverished, it perfects its person without feeling depressed.
When employed, it stands
above without contention;
when retired, it hides below without yielding.
That which glory cannot move,
disgrace cannot inflict;
that which gain
cannot persuade,
harm cannot affect;
that which praise cannot augment,
slander cannot diminish.
If today's scholars can truly abandon self-serving hearts,
block covetous desires,
stop the source of contention,
discard attitudes of boastfulness and self-praise;
when active, walk upon the path
of ultimate accessibility;
when quiet, enter the gate of great harmony;
when prosperous, soar in the vast expanse;
when in adversity, sink into the murky spring;
evil influences cannot infringe upon its measure,
external things cannot disturb its spirit,
sorrow and joy cannot sway its steadfastness,
life and death cannot alter its true nature—
and treat creation as a craftsman,
heaven and earth as a potter's wheel,
fame and position as dregs,
power and profit as dust;
cultivate its inner being without adorning its exterior,
seek within oneself without borrowing from others;
be loyal and reverent in serving superiors,
loving and respectful
in attending to parents—
then one can govern one's body,
one can shepherd the myriad people,
one can dwell in wealth and nobility,
one can be at peace in lowliness and poverty.
To endure rise and fall without change,
then one is almost
able to secure oneself.
Initially, he was appointed to a position in a zhōu,
later, due to his elderly father,
he resigned his post to care for him.
During the Tàikāng period,
he was recommended as a xiùcái
and became a tài cháng bóshì.
He successively held the posts of Gāolù Lìng and Huáinán Wáng Yǔn Zhèndōng Cānjūn.
At the beginning of the Yuánkāng period,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén
and presented the "Shìdiàn Sòng."
Its text reads: In the twelfth month of winter in the first year of Yuánkāng,
His Majesty, seeing that the huáng tàizǐ was in the prime of his youth,
and that among the beginnings of human conduct, nothing precedes filial piety and fraternal love,
first commanded the lecture of the Xiàojīng
in the Chóngzhèng Diàn.
Truly, it corresponded to the Heavenly bestowed measure of innate wisdom;
subtle words and profound meanings
issued from the sagely questions.
The studies concluded, and the understanding was perfected.
In the intercalary month of spring in the third year,
there would be
an event at the shàng xiáng,
a shìdiàn to the former teacher,
which is the proper ritual.
On the twenty-fourth day, bǐngshēn,
those attending the sacrifice were assembled.
The imperial carriage proceeded to the Tàixué.
The Tàifù was
in front,
the Shàofù behind,
dutifully upholding the way of profound instruction and guidance;
palace officials all followed,
the Sānshuài provided guard,
solemnly showing respect for assistance and support.
Then the altar was swept
to form a hall,
and screens were hung to make a palace.
The Master was positioned in the western row,
Yán Huí attended at the northern wall.
The Zōngbó managed the rites,
the Sīyí distinguished the positions.
The Confucian officials of the two academies,
the gentry
and masters,
with flowing sashes and jade pendants,
those whose conduct was exemplary and footsteps precise,
all stood solemnly and reverently below the hall,
awaiting the command of the officiant.
Jùn and fěi were set between the two
pillars,
léi and xǐ were arranged to the left of the eastern steps.
With the tables and mats laid out,
and the bells and suspended chimes arrayed,
our sovereign then personally undertook the diligence of bowing,
embodying the virtue of the threefold.
The beauty of humble radiance was increasingly splendid,
the teachings of Quèlǐ were greatly honored.
How solemn and majestic,
how harmonious and serene!
Truly, it was a glorious institution of the former kings,
an unchangeable and beautiful undertaking,
indeed, it cannot be replaced
or altered.
Thereupon, after the offerings of sacrificial animals were completed,
and the rites of presentation were finished,
the black robes were put aside,
spring attire was donned,
the fasting prohibitions were relaxed,
and the old customs restored.
The Son of Heaven then commanded
all internal and external officials,
the hundred ministers and scholars,
the Fanwáng and the three high officials,
down to the students and sons of the state,
all to come and observe the ritual.
Our sovereign then invited them all to a banquet.
The sounds of metal and stone,
flutes and pipes,
the dances of bāyì and liùdài,
clanged and resonated,
turning and bowing.
Those things that can purify the spirit and cleanse desires,
transform customs and change habits,
were all
performed without exception.
Repressing licentious music,
rejecting the melodies of Zhèng and Wèi,
distancing from flattery and evil,
releasing clever argumentation.
On that day,
people, whether foolish or wise,
from near or far,
leaving their hometowns and crossing states,
supporting the elderly and leading
the young,
converged without prior arrangement.
All craned their necks to see,
inclined their ears to listen,
hoping for the Way and admiring the achievement,
cleansing their hearts and reforming their wills,
imagining the customs of Zhūsì,
singing the praise of the benefit
of coming back to life.
Only then did they know that the goodness of the ruler
was evident a thousand lì away;
the unspoken transformation
overflowed within the nine regions.
Ah, how glorious was this ceremony!
Truly,
it was a grand spectacle of the imperial era,
a unique gathering in ten thousand years.
I, Ní, once held a minor ritual office
and was accustomed to sacrificial vessels.
Now, placed in the last rank,
I personally witnessed this magnificent beauty,
immersed in the splendid
Way,
bathed in its fragrant benevolence.
Unconsciously, I gestured with my hands and recited with my mouth,
secretly composing a sòng.
Its meaning is close, but its wording is crude,
insufficient to describe the form of the great virtue,
or to illuminate the remote wisdom
of the sagely and enlightened.
Its text reads: The Three Primes rotate,
the Five Virtues succeed each other in subtlety.
When the Yellow Essence rises,
the White Spirit shines.
Our Sovereign, receiving Heaven's mandate,
established our Jìn domain.
Bestowed with the great treasure,
he ascended
like a flying dragon.
Xuān Jī broadly initiated the mandate,
Jǐng Xī extended the illustrious lineage.
The division of the realm began with Wén,
the final mandate was received by Wǔ.
Sweeping through the crucial barbarian lands,
pacifying the desolate and rugged;
his Way aided all living beings,
His transforming influence flowed through the entire realm.
Later, the Emperor succeeded to this,
greatly elevating what his ancestors had established.
He possessed all lands,
gloriously residing over the universe.
He begot an eldest heir,
who in due time rose in prominence.
His sagely reverence daily ascended,
his profound wisdom was grand and flourishing.
He devoted his essence to Confucian arts,
and diligently studied ancient teachings.
Following the Way, he yielded to elders,
and humbled himself to seek advice.
He spread forth with a golden voice,
and shone with the luster of jade.
Like the rising sun,
like the movement of the heavens.
Then he invited the Grand Protector,
and commanded the academic officials.
The sagely countenance
was solemn,
the attending lecturers spoke with gentle persuasion.
They drew out and expounded upon subtle words,
enlightening him on the true Way.
Exploring the profound and exhausting the recondite,
reviewing the old to learn the new.
When the lectures were concluded,
and the profound principles had been thoroughly studied.
Esteeming the Sage and honoring the Teacher,
he selected a day to offer a sacrifice.
He arranged the three sacrificial animals,
and led forth the four kinds of suspended meats.
After purification and setting the example,
he then washed his hands and presented the offerings.
How sincere was Kǒng Shèng,
whom a hundred kings admired.
How diligent was Yán Shēng,
who loved learning and never deviated.
It is said of the Imperial Heir,
that he embodies divine spirit and comprehends subtle omens.
He sees auspicious signs in advance,
and knows
the future with profound clarity.
How numerous are the officials of the two palaces,
how abundant are the various ministers.
Talented men gather like scales,
distinguished scholars fill the court.
Like a harmonious market,
none are not precious jades;
like an auspicious phoenix,
delighting in our Yunsháo music.
Who carves the precious jades?
The four gates are wide open;
Why does the Yunsháo delight?
Gods and men truly harmonize.
Cicada caps gleam in the court,
delicate pendants tinkle on the steps.
Virtue shines
with humility,
benevolence cherishes with grace.
Our wine is clear,
our dishes are fragrant.
Dances are performed from the six dynasties,
songs from the nine achievements.
How numerous are the young nobles,
how diligent are the students.
They purify their hearts from all distractions,
and behold the glory of the state.
Learning is like planting seedlings,
transformation is like grass bending to the wind.
Enriching us with culture,
broadening
us with the Way.
All nations shed their old skins,
how much more so the gifted and creative.
Drilling oysters to polish pearls,
splitting stones to reveal their veins.
Silk is not naturally black or yellow,
water has no inherent squareness or roundness.
Draw it and it
flows,
dye it and it acquires brilliance.
Like metal receiving its mold,
like clay in the potter's wheel.
What the superior likes is like clouds,
what the inferiors imitate is like a river.
In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty arose,
and the royal transformation began.
Of Wén and Wǔ,
at that time, they were the Crown Princes.
Now our Imperial Heir,
is as sagely and discerning as they.
His bright glory shines continuously,
how
solemn and unceasing!
How solemn, what is it?
It is the thoughtful and wise Empress.
She charms this one person,
truly assisting the sovereign.
Her filial piety permeates family and state,
her glory illuminates the nine regions.
Pure blessings from
Jìn,
prosperity for eternal generations.
I, a humble minister,
am overly honored to be a close attendant.
Unworthily treading through wind and clouds,
placed among phoenixes and dragons.
My body bathes in the fragrant current,
my eyes delight in these grand events.
I exhaust
my sincerity to compose this ode,
reverently chanting the sagely will.
He went out to be the Magistrate of Wǎn,
where his administration was lenient but not lax,
he sympathized with the hidden suffering and diligently governed,
he strove for fairness and disregarded personal affairs.
He returned to fill the post of Shàngshū Láng,
and soon transferred to Zuòzuò Láng.
He composed an admonition for the imperial carriage,
its words were: The Yì Jīng says:
"Only with heaven and earth did human relations arise;
only with fathers and sons did rulers and ministers arise."
The commentary says:
"The greatest are heaven and earth,
next are rulers and ministers."
However,
the Way of ruler and minister, father and son,
the foundation of heaven, earth, and human relations,
there has never been anything that preceded it.
Therefore, Heaven created the myriad people and established rulers over them,
to oversee and shepherd them,
intending to guide the nature of all living beings,
and order the emotions of all things.
How could it be merely to favor one person's body,
and satisfy limitless desires,
and that's all!
Now, in ancient
times, those who became rulers
were without desire and perfectly impartial,
hence they practiced the frugality of thatched huts and earthen steps;
but later rulers,
having desires and being self-serving,
hence they indulged in the extravagance of jade terraces and
jeweled chambers.
Those without desire
were universally acclaimed by the world;
those with desire
were universally contended with by the world.
When acclamation reaches its peak,
even yielding the throne is like casting off old shoes;
when contention reaches
its peak,
even robbery and murder are not avoided.
Therefore it is said
"the world is not the world of one person,
but the world of all under heaven."
How can it be sought and obtained,
and merely
be refused?
Now, cultivating oneself and transforming others,
what starts near and is seen far away,
refers to words and actions.
Therefore, the ruler's greatest affliction
is nothing more than not knowing
his own faults;
and his greatest virtue
is nothing more than being fond of hearing about his faults.
If there is a ruler here,
who says, "I definitely have no faults,"
and only his words are followed without contradiction,
this is what Kǒngzǐ
called "that which might almost lead to the ruin of a state by a single word."
Indeed, the faults of a noble person
are like eclipses of the sun or moon: when they err,
everyone sees it;
when they correct themselves,
everyone
looks up to them.
Even with the greatness of Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
there were surely trees for criticism,
drums for bold remonstrance,
inscriptions on basins and vessels,
and historians who recorded without concealment,
all designed
to prevent their evil tendencies and guide them to the right path,
their self-maintenance was prepared in this way.
Therefore, the rise of admonitions and criticisms
was to remedy faults and mend deficiencies,
yet they still subtly suggested
and metaphorized,
so that the speaker was blameless,
and the listener was sufficiently warned.
Previous Confucians cited ancient meanings,
and presented the distinction between internal and external,
while Gāozǔ also ordered the six offices,
In discussing the essentials of success and failure,
the principles are just and the words concise,
and they are also perfectly excellent.
From the admonitions of the foresters to those of the hundred officials,
they are not merely meant to regulate their respective departments,
but sincerely to urge the ruler to weigh
their gains and losses.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
"Command the hundred officials to admonish the king regarding his shortcomings."
This, then, is also a matter for the Son of Heaven.
Ní believes that when a king receives the mandate
and holds the reins of divine power,
managing myriad affairs and governing the four seas,
selecting talented individuals and carefully assigning responsibilities,
he should be assiduous in
finding the right people,
and eager to hear of his faults.
Even when there are court disputes and direct remonstrances,
he should still earnestly seek them out.
As for admonitions and regulations,
which are the most compliant forms of remonstrance,
why should he alone neglect
them?
Therefore, without measuring my own shallow learning and thought,
I have, in my spare time,
attempted to compile and narrate this.
I dared not directly use the title of the Most Honored,
so I titled
the
chapter
"Chéngyú."
Indeed, the affairs of emperors and kings are of utmost importance,
and the changes from ancient times to the present are numerous.
The texts are complex and their meanings divergent,
the intentions constrained and the language rustic.
To wish to emulate former
sages
and vaguely follow their lofty paths
is like a small mound looking up at Huádài,
or a star attached to the sun and moon;
its inadequacy is clear.
The Eulogy says:
Vast was the beginning,
immense the great primordial state.
The pure and the turbid flowed together,
heaven and earth stood confused.
Above and below were unformed,
rank and status unestablished.
Hèxū was distant,
Dàtíng
was ancient.
The imperial order was first established,
the two primary forces already separated.
Eternal norms were set in order,
the myriad states became distinct.
States served enlightened kings,
families honored strict lords.
Each had its respected one,
virtue was not forced.
From Xī and Nóng downwards,
reaching Xià and Yīn.
Some abdicated, some transmitted,
some were simple, some refined.
The highest had no name,
the lowest knew of its existence.
When benevolence and righteousness were absent,
people turned to filial piety and compassion.
Without action, without attachment,
what desires, what thoughts?
When loyalty and trust waned,
rites and punishments indeed proliferated.
Praised and feared,
yet also insulted and deceived.
Oaths and covenants were made,
and people began to rebel and doubt.
Glorious were the four seas,
flourishing the myriad chariots,
without oaths,
how could they be relied upon?
Left assistants and right aides,
front advisors and rear ministers.
A myriad affairs in a single day,
anxious and cautious.
If one's words are good,
then a thousand *lǐ* respond;
but if no one
disobeys me,
it is also a sign of a failing state.
The movement of the pivot [of power]
determines rise and fall.
Yīn's lesson is not far off,
how can we not take heed!
Moreover, rich flavors conceal poison,
spacious houses invite disaster.
Xīn built a luxurious palace,
and Xià erected a jade terrace.
Grain-lees hills and wine pools,
ivory chopsticks and jade cups.
What were their
dishes?
Dragon liver and leopard fetus.
It was these clever women,
who primarily caused chaos.
Yīn lost its army,
and Xià also failed to recover.
Therefore, when Dì Yáo was on the throne,
his thatched roof was not
trimmed.
King Wén of Zhōu worked until dusk,
and was greatly illustrious from dawn.
Indeed, virtue is as light as a feather,
yet few are those who can lift it.
Thus, Huò had some regrettable virtue,
and Wǔ was not perfectly good.
In later
ages, the Way declined,
and shallow customs prevailed.
Indulging in pleasure and idle wandering,
abandoned to dissipation and intoxication.
Disregarding ancient teachings,
and favoring glib sophistry;
not following the king's path,
but treading
in the tracks of overturned chariots.
The effects of success and failure
are recorded in ancient texts.
Not only did things decline,
but their generations were extinguished.
Therefore, it is said, "How should a ruler be established?"
He will shepherd the people.
He sees
them as if injured,
and knows their cold and warmth.
Thus, he can soothe them to gentleness,
and strengthen them to harmony;
no distant one will not cherish him,
none will fail to submit.
How could he indulge
himself,
and amuse his eyes and ears;
lost in sights and sounds within,
and wild in pursuit without;
neglecting governance,
and ultimately collapsing?
In the past, Táng (Yáo) entrusted the rule to Shùn,
and Shùn in turn appointed Yǔ.
They received the end of the mandate and adopted the ancestral sacrifices,
greatly inheriting the heavenly order.
It was Tāng who banished Jié,
and Wǔ who conquered Yīn.
Thus, the transfer of power was not
of one family,
nor did the altars of soil and grain have a permanent master.
The Four Peaks and Three Passes,
the barriers of the Nine Provinces.
Pénglǐ, Dòngtíng,
the journey of Yīn and Shāng.
The prosperity of Yú and Xià
did not come from a foot of
land.
Yet Zhòu, with all his victories,
eventually cut off his lineage.
Therefore, a king has no relatives;
it is solely in choosing the right people.
Those who overturn their carriage cover are considered old friends,
while those with white hair are still considered new.
Wàng was a fishing
man,
Yī arose from Yǒuxīn.
Bearing cauldrons and wielding knives,
their counsels aligned with the divine sages.
How could one merely rely on officials to one's left and right,
and take close ministers as intermediaries?
Indeed, those who have states and families,
none should say "I am discerning,"
or "these people merely obey to my face";
none should say "I am wise,"
for listening and accepting is not easy.
Sweet words often conceal faults,
and few are those not burdened by them.
Yóuyí escaped favor,
far like shedding
a sandal.
Why is it that rulers,
when their position is extreme, become extravagant?
To know people is to be sagacious,
this is what even emperors find difficult.
When the Táng dynasty was peaceful,
the Four Clans caused mischief.
When the Zhōu house prospered,
Guǎn and Cài were disloyal.
Were it not for our two sages,
who could have stopped this calamity?
If the nine virtues are all received,
and outstanding talents are in office,
the ruler cannot govern without ministers,
nor can ministers be secure without the ruler.
Therefore, the *Shū* praises "Kāngzāi,"
and the *Yì* values metal
Lán.

Yīn Tāng wú Míngtiáo zhī shì,

chēng,

jié péng
They gather hollow reputations to drive the common people.
Advancing them brings no benefit to the age;
retiring them causes no harm to transformation.
Yet the rulers of the world echo each other with one voice,
blowing and breathing upon them.
Is this not lamentable!
Today, scholars follow routine and cling to the old ways,
behaving strictly and cautiously,
accumulating ranks,
piling up achievements,
and busying themselves to obtain worldly status.
As for those
heroic and outstanding
individuals, those who are extraordinary and unrestrained,
they will simply perish and lie hidden beneath the rugged peaks.
How can they compete for position with those who merely follow the established path!
As for those officials with high positions and adorned robes,
if they cannot rectify transformations and assist government,
benefit the age and help the world,
but merely bow and scrape to gain favor,
seeking honor and pursuing profit,
fattening their own emoluments,
and accumulating private wealth,
this is like
a monkey wearing a hat—
what more is there to say!
Zài also composed the "Fù on Méngsì".
Sīlì Xiàowèi Fù Xuán saw it and sighed in admiration,
welcoming him with a carriage,
conversing all day,
and speaking highly of him,
whereupon he became famous.
He started his career as Zuǒ Zhùzuò Láng,
then was appointed Féixiāng Lìng.
He again served as Zhùzuò Láng,
then transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
and was promoted to Lè’ān Xiàng and Hóngnóng Tàishǒu.
Chángshā Wáng Ài requested him to be Jìshì Dū.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and again led the Zhùzuò department.
Seeing that the world was in turmoil,
Zài no longer had the intention to advance his career.
He then claimed severe illness and requested to return home,
and died at his residence.
Xié, courtesy name Jǐngyáng,
had outstanding talent in his youth,
and was as famous as Zài.
He was recruited as a subordinate in a ducal mansion,
then transferred to Mìshū Láng,
appointed Huáyīn Lìng and Zhēng Běi Dàjiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He transferred to Héjiān Nèishǐ,
and was known for his purity, simplicity, and few desires in the commandery.
At that time, the world was already in chaos,
with bandits everywhere.
Xié thereupon abandoned all worldly affairs,
secluding himself in the wilderness,
upholding the Dao and not contending,
entertaining himself with poetic詠 composition.
He imitated various literary figures and composed "Seven Admonitions".
Its preface states: Chōngmò Gōngzǐ,
contains brilliance and hides his radiance,
happily retired like a coiling dragon,
transcending the world with lofty strides,
his mind wandering in the vastness,
his will delighting in myriad wonders,
his footsteps vanished in the distant,
remote
great wilderness, his voice swallowed in the deep, remote recesses of the secluded mountains.
Thereupon, Xùnhuá Dàfū heard of him and came to visit.
He then adjusted his cloud chariot,
harnessed flying huáng steeds,
crossed the rushing sands,
rolled over
the flowing frost,
climbed the swirling winds,
trod on the solid ice's ford,
his banners brushed the sky's peaks,
his tracks emerged from the azure horizon,
the sky was clear and cool without haze,
the wilderness vast and bright without dust.
He looked down at the layered peaks and reined in,
gazing back at the stone chamber and turning his wheels.
He then arrived at the dwelling of Chōngmò Gōngzǐ.
His dwelling was
towering and secluded,
austere and profound.
The boundless sea surged turbidly behind it,
the Xiè Valley stretched ruggedly before it.
Sprouting bamboos raised their stalks, shading its ravines,
a myriad of sounds in chorus enveloped its mountains.
Torrential waters rushed and turned back
the sun,
flying stones rose and spattered the sky.
Thereupon, he ascended the precipitous peak,
followed the long wind,
presented words of persuasion,
and summoned the Gōngzǐ from within the cliffs.
He said:
"I have heard that the sage
does not abandon the Dao and turn his back on the times,
nor does the wise scholar discard his person and hide his traces.
In life, he must illuminate his splendid name on jade records;
in death, he must engrave his grand achievements on golden tablets.
Now, Gōngzǐ
turns away from the world and sinks into obscurity,
avoiding the world and hiding alone.
The joy of life is extinguished,
the duty of serving one's parents is abandoned.
Sorrow fills a hundred years,
bitterness overflows a thousand generations.
How is this different from a fish with short scales swimming in
muddy shallows,
or a bird with short wings nesting in dense thickets!
Now I will honor you with the great treasures of heaven and man,
and delight you with the utmost pleasure of unrestrained nature.
You will travel to the ends of the earth,
dwell
in the midst of heaven,
enjoy the delights of the four seas,
and exhaust the richness of the nine provinces.
You will bore into the gourds of Qūgǔ,
[one zero] and loosen the bonds of Shūshǔ.
Do you desire this?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"You, Dàfū,
have not forgotten me,
and have come to this desolate outer region.
Though I am not intelligent,
I respectfully listen to your excellent words."
The Dàfū said:
"The phoenix tree of the cold mountains
originates from the Great Darkness,
containing the huángzhōng tone and sprouting its trunk,
standing on the azure peak and growing solitarily.
Then, its jade-like peaks are layered and steep,
its golden
banks are rugged and perilous.
To its right is the wind valley,
to its left is the cloud stream.
Above, there are no nests hovering in the void;
below, there are no paths for treading on fruit.
It sways and stands tall,
distant and lofty.
It absorbs
the overflowing dew of the three springs,
and traces the sounds of the nine autumns.
Falling snow writes on its roots,
[one one] and swirling frost seals its branches.
The trees are verdant only after becoming lush,
the grasses wither
before turning white.
Thereupon, one constructs a cloud ladder,
ascends the perilous heights,
cuts the yang branches for Ruìbīn,
and splits the yin stems for Dàlǚ.
Craftsmen carve its raw wood,
and music masters tune its sounds.
When the instruments
are lifted and the music plays,
the melodies are rapid and the volume high.
The sound is as clear as Hàozhōng,
the rhythm as pure as Ràoliáng.
It pursues lingering echoes among the eight winds,
and gathers strange tunes from Guīchāng.
It opens the wondrous palace of Zhōnghuáng,
and emits the changing shāng notes of Rùshōu.
If, then, the Dragon Fire wanes westward,
and the warm qi initially recedes,
flying frost greets the season,
and high winds send off autumn,
travelers longing for home,
and vagrants suffering myriad hardships,
touching the short zither bridge brings
a sharp pain to the nose,
strumming the perilous strings brings forth tears.
If, then, one pursues clear melodies,
and follows strict rhythms,
playing Lùshuǐ,
and singing Báixuě,
exciting
the Chu迴 melody,
and creating flowing,
coiled harmonies,
mourning the morning fall of the mǐngjiá,
and lamenting the evening wane of Wàngshū.
The lonely widow weeps profusely,
the elderly widow sobs.
The prince brushes
his cap strings and inclines his ear,
the six horses sigh towards heaven and raise their heads to feed.
This is indeed the ultimate wonder of music and melodies.
Would you not come with me to listen to it?"
The Gōngzǐ said:
"I am ill
I am ill and cannot do it.”
The dàfū said:
“In the orchid palaces and secret chambers,
with carved halls and ornate lattices,
cloud-patterned screens shine brilliantly,
and jade-green walls are verdant.
Eight layers of gates guard the entrance,
and the xuán tái rises nine-fold.
It is flanked by a hundred
chí quē,
and encircled by walls of ten thousand zhì.
Then there are the lofty pavilions that greet the wind,
towering high into the sky;
emerald observatories stand majestically green,
and crimson halls connect like rosy clouds.
Long wings touch the clouds,
and flying
stairs ascend the mountains.
They reach their peak, looking up at the Yù Shéng constellation,
and open their windows, receiving the inverted reflections.
Vermilion and white gleam resplendently,
and the fén gǒng are towering.
Dark qíu bear the eaves,
and sun-facing mǎ support the curves.
It is inlaid with beautiful jades,
and carved with golden flowers.
Square latticework holds exquisite beauty,
and round wells sprout blossoms.
Heavy palaces rise one upon another,
with interwoven brocades and facing window frames.
Secluded halls are dim even at midday,
while bright chambers are
luminous at night.
Jiāo Míng flies and the wind arises;
the尺蠖 moves and creates a sound.
If your eyes tire of constant sights,
and your body grows weary of the inner chambers,
take your sons for a dual excursion,
and enjoy the scenery
in the forests and foothills.
Ascend emerald mounds,
and overlook vermilion valleys.
Gorgeous flowers bloom profusely like brocade,
their flying colors sparkling like stars and candles.
Yang leaves are green in spring,
yin branches are green in autumn.
Flowers and fruits are renewed in their seasons,
satisfying your
desire to gaze.
Look up to pluck divine xiāo,
look down to gather morning orchids.
Seek the fragrant breeze in the henglú,
gaze at the peppertree-lined path on the jade altar.
Then, you can float in winged boats,
and sport in the middle of the islet.
Concealed
gills are startled,
startled wings take flight.
Sinking threads entangle,
flying arrows are aimed.
Hung are the returning birds' wings beyond the crimson sky,
and splendid fish scales are brought forth from the depths of the purple pond.
Afterwards, you may let the oars drift with
the wind,
and lay down the paddles to ride the waves.
Play the gūzhú flute,
and strum the Yúnhé zither.
River guests sing the tunes of Huáinán,
and boatmen play the songs of gathering water caltrops.
The song goes: ‘Riding the yìzhōu
for water fun,
approaching the fragrant islet to pluck spiritual zhī.’
Joy makes one forget worries,
recreation fills the time.
The whole night becomes like day,
and the entire year becomes the appointed time.
This, then, is the vast
splendor of leisure,
how can you, young master, not come and dwell here with me?”
The gōngzǐ said:
“I am ill and cannot do it.”
The dàfū said:
“When the white autumn arrives,
and the moon signals the time to don winter clothes,
heaven congeals and earth closes,
the wind is fierce and frost flies.
Tender branches stiffen in the evening,
dense leaves thin out in the morning.
It is then
that, following the season's qi, slaughter is demonstrated,
and instructors are dispatched to the western suburbs.
Then, light chariots are arrayed,
and strong armor is donned.
Feathered banners are raised,
and valiant sharp points are deployed.
Flying swallows of Hóngyáng are harnessed,
and the suōshuāng steeds of Táng Gōng are yoked alongside.
Feathered troops are amassed in the outer woods,
and light-winged archers are unleashed in the central wilderness.
Then, long nets are spread,
and flying snares are laid.
〔一二〕 They ascend yellow ridges,
and hang from green
peaks.
Long ravines are demarcated as boundaries,
and flowing streams serve as passes.
When there are no sparse paths within,
and no escaping tracks outside,
gongs are struck to scatter the prey,
and banners are raised to applaud the catch.
Golden
triggers are drawn,
and whistling arrows are shot.
Fierce beasts are cut down,
and strong wings are severed.
Cavalry charges compete,
their chariots side by side, wheels aligned.
Swiftly and suddenly they strike,
clouds swirl and winds rage.
Sounds echo and reverberate,
forms shift and shadows appear.
Spears rise like a forest,
flashing blades vanish like lightning.
Looking up, cloud nests are toppled;
looking down, earth holes are emptied.
There are boars with round patterns,
and young boars with striped foreheads.
Their bristles
stir the wind,
their angry eyes flash like lightning.
They bite frost-cold blades,
and kick flying spearheads with their feet.
They gnaw at forests and uproot rocks,
stamping through hidden thickets.
Then, Fēi Huáng warriors display their might,
and Bēn Yù fighters show their
skill.
They encircle wild boars,
capture fierce pigs,
tear apart tigers,
and crush wildcats.
Claws are broken,
fangs are shattered.
A messy sprawl,
thickets overturned and ravines filled.
Corpses are scattered and hung on
mountains,
fallen bodies cover the marshes.
The wilderness becomes a forest of fur,
the lowlands become a vermilion-stained expanse.
Then the encirclement is removed and nets are taken down;
banners are furled and kite-like pennants are withdrawn.
Rangers count the beasts,
forest wardens tally the fresh kill.
Merits are judged and the diligent rewarded,
horses are rested and bows are sheathed.
Rich feasts are spread,
wine chariots are drawn forth.
A thousand cups are drained in a flash,
ten thousand torches burn like myriad stars.
Hills and mounds are soaked with rich fat,
streams and valleys are filled with
fragrant smoke.
When joy is extreme and pleasure is exhausted,
the procession turns and returns.
This, too, is a magnificent spectacle of the hunt.
How can you, young master, not come and participate with me?”
The gōngzǐ said:
“I am ill and
cannot do it.”
The dàfū said:
“The Yáng Jiàn of Chǔ,
forged by Ōuyě,
from the ore of Xié Xī,
and the essence of Chì Shān.
It surpasses the melting of Yáng Tóu,
and is wrought by the hammering of yuèduàn.
It is refined
and smelted,
a myriad hammerings and a thousand pourings.
Fēng Lóng wields the hammer,
Fēi Lián fans the coals.
A divine weapon is thus formed,
with bright yang patterns and intricate yin designs.
Then, flowing brocade-like patterns connect like stars,
and floating colors brightly
emerge.
Its light is like scattered lightning,
its substance like shining snow.
The frosty edge congeals like water,
the icy blade is pure like dew.
Its form surpasses that of the most renowned blades,
its name is treasured like Jù Quē.
Point it towards Zhèng and the three armies turn white-haired;
wave it towards Jìn and blood flows for a thousand lǐ.
〔一三〕 How can it merely cut through flood dragons,
or on land fell galloping steeds,
sever flying wings with its skill,
or pierce heavy armor to be called sharp? It is more than that.
“Alas!
As for the spiritual treasures,
they expand and contract boundlessly.
Their strange points and unique forms
make Xūe Zhú tremble,
and their light startles Fēng Hú.
Their value surpasses the three regions,
and their fame is esteemed in the two capitals.
Some gain renown and make Qín tremble,
others fly by night to Wú.
Thus, their achievements crown ten thousand years,
and their might shines eternally.
Those who wield them are unrivaled;
those who possess them are heroic.
They can
subdue the nine states,
and horizontally control the eight barbarian tribes.
Claws and teeth (vassals) attach themselves,
and all of Huáxià submits.
These are indeed rare divine weapons in the world.
How could you not follow me and wield them?”
The young master said:
“I am ill and unable to do so.”
The Grandee said:
“As for the swiftness of heavenly steeds,
their elegant manner transcends all others.
They are endowed with vitality from spiritual streams,
and receive essence from the bright moon.
Their eyes gleam with dark radiance,
their dark coats and manes shimmer.
Their foam is like a splash
of red,
their sweat like gushing blood.
Qín Qīng cannot discern their numerous strides,
and Fāng Yīn cannot perceive their vanishing speed.
Then, with cloud-patterned reins,
they tread on morning mist,
rush to spring paths,
and prepare for autumn rides.
Like hornless dragons leaping and chǐ dragons soaring,
like qílín leaping and true dragons ascending.
They see mountains and gallop,
they see forests and rush.
Their spirits are strong and their anger erupts;
they fly like stars and startle like lightning.
Their ambition surpasses the nine regions,
their power
crosses the four seas.
Their shadows cannot keep up with their forms,
dust has no time to rise.
Before a floating arrow has moved,
they have traversed a thousand *lǐ* again.
Then they cross the roots of heaven,
and transcend the earthly barriers,
passing through where Hànmàn
did not travel,
treading where Zhānghài never set foot.
The sun crow halts its wings for them,
Kuāfù throws down his staff for them.
These are indeed the finest steeds in the world.
How could you not follow
me and ride them?”
The young master said:
“I am ill and unable to do so.”
The Grandee said:
“As for the millet of Dàliáng,
the grain of Qióngshān,
Táng Jì sowed their roots,
and the Divine Farmer tasted their blossoms.
Then, there are six kinds of rare poultry,
and four different
dishes,
all the delicacies of the sea,
and the finest furs of the land.
Yī Gōng cooks in the tripod,
Páodīng wields his knife.
The flavor is deepened by nine boilings,
the harmony enhanced by *sháoyào* (peony root).
Morning wild ducks and dew swans,
frost quails
and yellow sparrows.
The round tables are strewn like stars,
the square mats adorned with flowers.
The paws of a sealed bear,
the trotters of a singing fowl,
sparrow thighs and ape lips,
trimmed yak tails and elephant ivory.
Turtles from spiritual streams,
blowfish from Láihuáng,
larks from Dānxuè,
and fetuses of black leopards.
Warmed with autumn oranges,
served with spring plums.
Accessed with the chopsticks of King Shāng,
held with the cup of Emperor Xīn.
Fàn
Gōng’s scales (fish),
came from the nine ravines,
with crimson tails and cinnabar gills,
purple fins and green scales.
Then, Zhīlí is ordered,
the frost-edged knife flies.
The red flesh scatters like brocade,
the white skin falls like snow.
Even the finest hair of Lóuzǐ cannot match its thinness,
the wings of an autumn cicada are insufficient to compare to its lightness.
After the abundant dishes are finished,
there are also delicious delights.
Fruits of Shāngshān,
hazelnuts of Hàn Gāo.
Breaking open longan pods,
splitting coconut shells.
Ten thousand choices of fragrant delicacies,
presented to please the palate.
Then there are the Wūchéng wine from Jīngnán and Zhúyè wine from Yùběi,
with floating
beetles like shimmering stars,
and flying blossoms like connecting duckweed.
Xuán Shí tasted their flavor,
Yí Shì advanced their methods.
Pouring out a jug in one morning,
one can remain intoxicated for a thousand days.
Pouring a single measure into a river,
can
make three armies declare victory.
These are what gods and humans yearn for,
and what sight and hearing delight in.
How could you not rouse yourself and partake of them?”
The young master said:
“Indulging
in delectable food,
sweetening the taste of deadly poisons,
taking medicines that rot the intestines,
wielding instruments that destroy nations—
though these are glorious to you, Grandee,
they are what we fear.
I am ill and unable to do so.”
The Grandee said:
“Indeed, the Jìn dynasty’s imperial grandeur
began with auspicious signs.
Great men arose,
continuing the bright illumination,
matching Heaven’s glorious dwelling.
Its foundation of virtue
was
more profound than Jī Gōng at Qí;
its manifestation of benevolence
was richer than Yǒuyīn at Bó.
The winds of Nánqí could not spread its transforming influence,
the clouds of Líbì could
not enrich its beneficence.
The imperial way shone brightly,
the emperor’s reign flourished.
Guiding vitality with music,
proclaiming virtue with poetry.
Education was pure as in the age of the Cloud Officials,
governance harmonious as in the time of the Bird Recorders.
The royal domain extended everywhere,
all of Huáxià was peaceful.
The southern barbarians laid down their weapons,
the eastern frontiers released their vigilance.
Horses were turned back from cart shafts,
virtues were inscribed on the tripods of Kūnwú.
All creatures returned to their original simplicity,
the culture of the time flourished.
Farmers yielded their fields,
fishermen ceded their land.
Woodcutters were ashamed of ornate hats,
and servants laughed at short-backed clothes.
The six directions
were in harmony,
majestic and grand.
Children sang in the lanes,
the aged tapped the ground.
They untied the ropes of Xīhuáng,
and rejected the symbols of Táotáng.
As for the barbarians of Huáyì,
the Mò of the remote
wilderness,
whose languages were not transmitted by light chariots,
and whose lands were not reached by the proper calendar,
none failed to hasten forward and kowtow,
offering tribute through multiple interpreters.
At this time, all creatures felt the beneficence,
none felt
disturbed.
Nine-tailed birds played in the parks,
three-legged birds roosted in the preserves.
Singing phoenixes in the forests were
more numerous than in the garden of Huángdì;
dragons swimming in the rivers
were more plentiful than in Kǒngjiǎ’s
of the marsh.
All things are steaming and flourishing,
Heaven and Earth are in harmonious union,
righteous sentiments embrace all within,
transformative influence reaches beyond all boundaries.
In the forests, none wear coarse clothes;
on the mountains, none wear leather belts.
All these are images carved by a hundred
artisans,
omens arising from numinous auspicious plants.
The gentry are numerous and distinguished,
officials with carriages and caps are abundant.
Their achievements contend with creation itself,
their virtue rivals the vastness of the two luminaries (Heaven and Earth)."
Before he finished speaking,
the Young Master Jue
stood up abruptly and said:
"I am a rustic and unrefined fellow,
holding to my wild and unrestrained ways.
Indeed, there is reason to demolish something,
and the dispute over a treasure is resolved;
there is reason to provoke someone with words,
and the sickness of Qí Wáng
is cured.
Previously, you enticed me with the pleasure of deaf ears,
and settled me in a humble shack.
Hunting, roaming, and indulgence,
sharp blades and swift steeds,
are what Lǎo Shì warned against,
and not
what we desire.
Therefore, I could not respond to you.
But hearing that the Imperial influence is auspicious,
the holy Dao of the time is pure,

Therefore, the ruler was able to act without
error,
speak without fault,
and his virtuous reputation spread,
making his name known to later generations.
Your subjects are not as capable,
and are unable to offer much correction.
Thinking of exhausting my humble sincerity,
I respectfully present five matters as
follows,
hoping to receive your consideration, even if only once or twice,
and that you will kindly heed them.
Firstly,
of the six virtues,
filial piety is paramount.
The virtue of Yú Shùn
was celebrated for his filial piety.
Thus, it is the duty of the Crown Prince to inquire about the sovereign's meals morning and evening,
and his
attendants should constantly provide for his needs.
King Wén, as the Crown Prince,
could be said to be devoted in serving his parents,
and thus he was able to embody the virtues of the three dynasties,
and become the model for a hundred kings.
Lately,
Your Sacred Person has frequently suffered from illness,
often missing morning audiences.
Those who observe from near and far cannot fully understand the reasons,
leading to doubt.
I humbly pray, Your Highness, that even with a slight
ailment,
if you are able to be assisted,
you should exert yourself.
The Yì Jīng says:
'The superior man is diligent all day long.'
This means to constantly strive without ceasing.
Secondly,
ancient rulers, though possessing bright intelligence
and sagacious wisdom,
still required the aid of assistants
and the guidance of mentors.
Thus, Yú Shùn prospered with
five ministers,
and King Wén of Zhōu flourished with four friends.
When King Chéng was the Crown Prince,
Zhōu and Zhào served as his tutors and guardians,
and Shǐ Yì elucidated literary works.
Thus, he was able to learn the Way early
and comprehensively,
ascend to great achievements,
render punishment unnecessary,
and spread his fame far and wide.
I humbly believe that Your Highness possesses innate extraordinary talent
and exceptionally penetrating judgment.
Yet, your subject still recommends that you periodically issue sacred
decrees,
proclaim virtuous pronouncements,
consult your tutors and guardians,
seek out your attendant ministers,
meet with guests and visitors,
allowing everyone to express themselves fully,
so that obstructed feelings may flow freely and harmony prevail,
and Your Highness's
virtues may shine brilliantly.
If this is done,
a noble and clear wind
will inspire those who came before;
magnificent examples and excellent rules
will serve as eternal models for posterity.
Thirdly,
ancient sage kings all regarded frugality as a virtue.
Thus, Yáo was praised for his rafters of cut lumber and thatched cottage;
Yǔ for his humble palace and simple clothes;
Emperor Wén of Hàn wore coarse dark silk
and leather sandals,
leading by example,
achieving great peace through his governance,
and was esteemed as a wise king during his life,
and worshipped in ancestral temples after his death.
Among the feudal lords who practiced it,
Duke Xī of Lǔ, by his personal frugality
and economical use of resources,
had his fame listed in the Yǎ and Sòng odes;
Fénmào, by his 'bamboo cart and patched clothes,'
expanded the state of Chǔ.
Among the grandees who practiced it,
Wénzǐ served as prime minister of Lǔ,
and his concubines wore no silk;
Yàn Yīng
served as prime minister of Qí,
and his deer fur robe was not patched,
yet he was able to assist his ruler and benefit society,
strengthening the state and prospering his family.
Among commoners who practiced it,
Yán Huí, with his 'bamboo dish of rice and gourd cup of water,'
spread his reputation for benevolence;
Yuán Xiàn, with his 'thatched door and rope hinge,'
magnified his pure virtue.
These were all the practices of sage rulers, enlightened kings, virtuous ministers, and wise scholars.
Thus, they were able to have their names hung with the sun and moon,
enduring
immortally for all ages;
this was indeed the blessing of frugality.
As for the later generations,
those who fell into ruin through extravagance,
among emperors and kings, had jade towers and coral chambers,
jade cups and ivory chopsticks,
and dishes of
As for delicacies, there were bear paws and leopard fetuses,
wine pools and meat forests.
Among the feudal lords who engaged in this,
they went so far as to paint pillars crimson and carve rafters,
and demand tribute of a hundred sacrificial animals.
High officials had jasper caps and jade tassels,
while commoners struck bells and dined from tripods.
Yet none failed to lose their states and destroy their clans,
break up their families and lose their lives,
their丑名 (chǒumíng) becoming widely known,
serving as a warning for later generations.
I have secretly heard that the rear garden is adorned
with gold and silver,
carved and polished rhinoceros horn and elephant ivory.
The skill of the painting studio
is tested and refined daily.
Your servants believe that with the vastness of the four seas
and the richness of myriad things today,
comparing the present with antiquity,
it
is not extravagance.
However, what the superior likes,
the inferior will surely follow.
Therefore, those in superior positions must be cautious about what they like.
In the past, during the reign of 漢光武皇帝 (Hàn Guāngwǔ Huángdì),
someone
offered a thousand-lǐ horse and a precious sword.
The horse was used to pull a drum chariot,
and the sword was bestowed upon a knight.
世祖武皇帝 (Shìzǔ Wǔhuángdì) had someone present a pheasant-head fur coat,
and immediately ordered the relevant officials
to burn it in the capital street.
Rulers of ancient times
did not value extraordinary objects,
thus they were able to rectify the customs of the world
and influence the practices of the four directions.
Your servants believe that the work of the painting studio
can be temporarily reduced,
and miscellaneous tasks in the rear garden
should all be dismissed,
to achieve solemn quietude,
and leisurely cultivate virtue.
Then the beauty of daily renewal will shine throughout the four seas.
The fourth point is:
the whole world provides for one person,
and a hundred-lǐ territory provides for the feudal lords.
Therefore, kings and marquises eat from their fiefs and dress from taxes,
while dukes, high ministers, and grand masters receive their ranks and
income.
None are left unprovided for.
This is why the four professions—scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant—are not mixed.
Exchanging goods and withdrawing,
to facilitate the circulation of supply and demand,
is the occupation of commoners.
The 《周禮》(Zhōulǐ) describes three markets:
in the morning, for various clans;
at midday, for merchants;
in the evening, for peddlers and hawkers.
Buying cheap and selling dear,
peddling vegetables and fruits,
they earn a hundredfold profit
to
sustain their daily lives.
Thus they are the poor and humble among commoners.
樊遲 (Fán Chí), a common man,
requested to learn how to garden,
but 仲尼 (Zhòngní) did not answer.
魯 (Lǔ) Grand Master 臧文仲 (Zāng Wénzhòng) made
his concubine weave rush mats,
and was criticized for his lack of benevolence.
When 公儀子 (Gōngyí Zǐ) was chancellor of 魯 (Lǔ),
he pulled out the mallows in his garden,
saying that those who receive official salaries should not compete for profit with the poor and humble.
Since 秦漢 (Qín Hàn)
times,
customs have gradually declined.
The esteemed dukes and marquises
all cultivate garden fields
and reap profits from the markets,
gradually imitating each other,
and none consider it shameful.
Judging
by ancient principles,
it is truly regrettable.
Now, the Western Garden sells mallows, plums, chickens, and similar items,
damaging the national dignity
and diminishing its good reputation.
The fifth point is:
I have secretly observed that in the forbidden grounds,
orders were given not to repair walls
or move even a roof tile.
Your servant believes this not only violates traditional norms and old principles,
but also, by adhering to
minor taboos, abandons the broad and great Dao.
It should be abolished,
which would be appropriate for the matter.
The imperial court approved of this.
When the Crown Prince was deposed
and exiled to 許昌 (Xǔchāng),
賈后 (Jiǎ Hòu) subtly instructed officials not to allow palace servants to accompany him.
統 (Tǒng) and other palace servants defied the ban and reached 伊水 (Yīshuǐ),
bidding farewell by the roadside,
weeping sorrowfully.
The capital officials all arrested 統 (Tǒng) and others, sending them to the prisons of 河南 (Hénán) and 洛陽 (Luòyáng).
Those sent to the commandery,
河南尹 (Hénán Yǐn) 樂廣 (Yuè Guǎng), released them all.
Those held in 洛陽 (Luòyáng) were still not released.
都官從事 (Dūguān Cóngshì) 孫琰 (Sūn Yǎn) persuaded 賈謐 (Jiǎ Mì), saying:
"The reason for deposing and exiling the Crown Prince
was because he was deemed evil.
Yet his former Eastern Palace servants defied the law to bid him farewell,
weeping by the roadside,
disregarding severe punishment.
This merely highlights the Crown Prince's virtue.
It would be better to release them."
謐 (Mì) spoke to 洛陽令 (Luòyáng Lìng) 曹攄 (Cáo Chū),
and as a result, they were all pardoned.
When the Crown Prince died
and was reburied,
統 (Tǒng) composed an elegy of grief,
which was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
Later, he became a 博士 (Bóshì) and 尚書郎 (Shàngshū Láng),
and participated in the military affairs of 大司馬 (Dàsīmǎ) and 齊王冏 (Qí Wáng Jiǒng).
When 冏 (Jiǒng) became arrogant and was about to fail,
統 (Tǒng) offered sharp remonstrances,
but the text is too long to include here.
He was promoted to 廷尉正 (Tíngwèi Zhèng).
Whenever there were doubtful cases from provinces and commanderies,
he ruled leniently.
成都王穎 (Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng) invited him to be his 記室 (Jìshì),
and he offered many warnings and remonstrances.
He spoke up for 陸雲 (Lù Yún) and his brothers,
his words being very earnest and direct.
He left office due to mourning his mother.
After the mourning period ended,
he became 司徒左長史 (Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ).
東海王越 (Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè) became 兗州牧 (Yǎnzhōu Mù),
and appointed 統 (Tǒng) as 別駕 (Biéjià),
entrusting him with provincial affairs.
He wrote to 統 (Tǒng) saying:
"In the past, when 王子師 (Wáng Zǐshī) was governor of 豫州 (Yùzhōu),
before he even got out of his carriage,
he invited 荀慈明 (Xún Címíng);
after alighting from his carriage,
he invited 孔文舉 (Kǒng Wénjǔ).
Are there any capable individuals in your honorable province who can respond to this?"
統 (Tǒng) recommended 晉高平 (Jìn Gāopíng) 郗鑒 (Xī Jiàn) as a worthy scholar,
陳留 (Chénliú) 阮脩 (Ruǎn Xiū) for his upright speech,
and 濟北 (Jìběi) 程收 (Chéng Shōu) for his integrity.
At the time, he was regarded as a discerning judge of character.
Soon after, he was promoted to 黃門侍郎 (Huángmén Shìláng) and 散騎常侍 (Sànqí Chángshì),
and concurrently held the position of 國子博士 (Guózǐ Bóshì).
In 永嘉 (Yǒngjiā) fourth year,
he fled from danger to 成臯 (Chénggāo),
where he died of illness.
All the rhapsodies, eulogies, memorials, and petitions he composed were passed down to later generations.
He had two sons: 虨 (Bīn) and 惇 (Dūn).
虨 (Bīn), courtesy name 思玄 (Sīxuán),
was recommended by his home province as a Xiùcaí.
平南將軍 (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) 溫嶠 (Wēn Qiáo) appointed him as his 參軍 (Cānjūn).
He later became 州別駕 (Zhōu Biéjià),
and was invited by 司空 (Sīkōng) 郗鑒 (Xī Jiàn) to be his掾 (Yuàn),
then appointed 長山令 (Chángshān Lìng).
鑒 (Jiàn) again requested him to be his 司馬 (Sīmǎ),
and he was transferred to 黃門郎 (Huángmén Láng).
車騎將軍 (Chēqí Jiāngjūn) 庾冰 (Yǔ Bīng), when stationed in 江州 (Jiāngzhōu),
invited him to be his 長史 (Zhǎngshǐ).
When 冰 (Bīng) died,
庾翼 (Yǔ Yì) appointed him as 諮議參軍 (Zīyì Cānjūn),
and soon after, he was again appointed 長史 (Zhǎngshǐ).
When 翼 (Yì) died,
大將 (Dàjiàng) 干瓚 (Gàn Zàn) caused trouble,
and 虨 (Bīn) suppressed and pacified him.
He was appointed 尚書吏部郎 (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng),
then successively promoted to 御史中丞 (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), 侍中 (Shìzhōng), and 吏部尚書 (Lìbù Shàngshū).
In the 永和 (Yǒnghé) period,
he replaced 桓景 (Huán Jǐng) as 護軍將軍 (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
He was appointed as 會稽內史 (Kuàijī Nèishǐ) and
given the additional title of 右軍將軍 (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn).
He replaced 王彪之 (Wáng Biāozhī) as 尚書僕射 (Shàngshū Púyè).
When 哀帝 (Āidì) ascended the throne,
he was unsure about the proper title for 周貴人 (Zhōu Guìrén).
虨 (Bīn)'s discussion can be found in the Rites Record.
The Emperor wanted to establish a great sacrifice in the palace courtyard,
and also wished to personally perform the plowing ceremony.
虨 (Bīn) argued that both ceremonies had been abandoned for a long time,
the prescribed rituals no longer existed,
and had not been practiced since the restoration of the dynasty.
He suggested they should be stopped.
He served as 僕射 (Púyè) for many years.
When 簡文帝 (Jiǎnwén Dì) was Chancellor,
he often consulted 虨 (Bīn) on matters of government,
and 虨 (Bīn) offered many beneficial suggestions.
He was transferred to 護軍將軍 (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn)
and concurrently held the position of 國子祭酒 (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
and died in office.
Zǐ Ài,
served successively as Administrator of Lángyá and Consultant to the Grand General of Cavalry.
Ài's son
was the Chief Clerk to the General of the Right in the Yuánxī era.
His younger brother, Yí,
was a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Dūn, courtesy name Sīqūn,
was filial and fraternal, pure and refined,
with lofty integrity surpassing the ordinary.
He had a great love for learning,
comprehending both Confucianism and Xuánxué.
He always believed that a junzǐ's conduct
should be guided by ritual,
and although the paths of reclusion and public service differ,
none should deviate from ritual and teaching.
As for those who are uninhibited and unrestrained,
valuing indulgence,
they not only act contrary to ritual and law,
but are also discarded by the Dao.
Thus, he authored the Tōngdào Chóngjiǎn Lùn,
which was widely praised by his contemporaries.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
he sought refuge in Dōngyáng Shān.
Grand Commandant Xī Jiàn appointed him Administrator of Yǎnzhōu,
and later invited him to be a staff officer to the Grand Commandant.
When Emperor Kāng became Grand Minister of Works,
he also invited him.
General of the West Yǔ Liàng requested him as a military advisor in the Ru School.
He was summoned to be an Erudite and a Secretariat Editor,
but he declined all appointments.
The people in his village and clan revered his Dao,
and would always consult him before acting.
Ruǎn Yù, Administrator of Dōngyáng, and Wáng Méng, Magistrate of Chángshān,
were both renowned scholars of their time,
and they associated with Dūn,
holding him in deep respect.
He cultivated his aspirations for over twenty years.
In the ninth year of Yǒnghé, he passed away
at the age of forty-nine.
His friends jointly carved a stone to erect a eulogy,
to commend his virtues.
Sūn Chǔ (Sūn Tǒng and Chuò)
Sūn Chǔ, courtesy name Zǐjīng,
was a native of Zhōngdū, Tàiyuán.
His grandfather, Zī,
was a General of Cavalry for Wèi.
His father, Hóng,
was Administrator of Nányáng.
Chǔ possessed extraordinary literary talent and refined elegance,
was frank and unrestrained,
often arrogant,
and thus lacked local renown.
When he was over forty,
he first served as a military advisor to the General who Guards the East.
Emperor Wén sent Fú Shào and Sūn Yù as envoys to Wú.
General Shí Bāo ordered Chǔ to write a letter to Sūn Hào, which said: "To act upon discerning the opportune moment
is what the Zhōu Yì values;
for the small not to serve the great
is what the Chūnqiū condemns.
These are the initial signs of good and ill fortune,
the origins from which honor and disgrace arise.
Therefore, Xǔ and Zhèng preserved their states by offering their jade disks,
while Cáo and Tán were annihilated for their lack of courtesy.
Since records already document their successes and failures,
and ancient and modern times illustrate their wisdom and folly,
there is no need to extensively
cite examples
or adorn with flowery rhetoric.
To merely boast grandly
would further diminish the substance of loyal counsel.
Now, I shall briefly discuss the essentials,
to awaken your understanding.
In the past, when the fiery essence was dim
and the mandate of heaven was nearing its end,
Huán and Líng lost their virtue,
and disasters and strife arose simultaneously.
Wolves and jackals wielded their poisonous claws and fangs,
and the common people suffered the calamity of being plunged into misery.
Consequently, the nine provinces were severed,
and the imperial order was dismantled.
The four seas were desolate,
no longer belonging to Hàn.
Tàizǔ, receiving the mandate,
with divine might responded to the times.
He suppressed and pacified the rebels,
restoring order to
the central realm.
He harmoniously established divine symbols,
and the heavenly mandate was gathered.
Thus, he expanded his grand foundation,
and held the Wèi territory.
The land included the Central Peaks of the Divine Province,
and the Nine Tripods still existed as artifacts.
Generations carried
beauty and virtue,
with successive periods of brilliance.
Therefore, it is known that the four distant regions were united,
a magnificent spectacle for an emperor.
In the past, the Gōngsūn clan, inheriting from their fathers and brothers,
resided for generations in the eastern borderlands.
They controlled
the Yān and Hú people,
relying on treacherous and distant terrain.
They practiced military arts and roamed freely,
not offering tribute or service.
Internally, they defied imperial commands;
externally, they communicated with the southern states.
They crossed the vast sea on rafts,
exchanging goods and bribes.
Ge and
Yuè cloth spread to the northern lands,
while sable and horses extended to Wú and Kuàijī.
They believed that with ten myriad archers,
their strength could
surely conquer Yān and Qí to the right,
and shake Fúsāng to the left,
crushing
the desert,
and claim kingship in the south.
However, Xuān Wáng led a punitive expedition,
his fierce vanguard driving straight forward.
His army reached Liáoyáng,
but the city walls could not be defended.
The drums merely sounded for a moment,
and the arch-culprit's
head was severed.
Consequently, near and far borders,
and numerous prefectures in the great wilderness,
gathered the dispersed and settled them,
greatly securing their homes.
The populace rejoiced and submitted,
and various foreign tribes pledged allegiance.
Since then,
the nine regions have been clear and peaceful.
The Eastern Yi offered their musical instruments,
and the Sùshèn presented their kǔ arrows.
Those who had been untamed for ages
came in response to transformation.
This grandeur and magnanimity,
I imagine you have already heard
of it.
The ancestors of Wú
originated from Jīng and Chǔ.
Encountering chaotic times,
they secretly scattered across the south of the Yangzi.
Liú Bèi, terrified,
also fled to Bā and Mín.
They then relied on the security of mountains and accumulated rocks,
and the boundless vastness of the Three Rivers and Five Lakes,
borrowing energy and wandering souls,
lasting until these four decades.
The two states formed an alliance,
the east and west responding in harmony,
mutually instigating each other,
to resist
the Central Plains.
They believed that their tripartite division of power
could endure as long as Mount Tàishān.
However, the Chancellor, King of Jìn, assisted the imperial house.
His civil and military officials were mighty,
their spirits
as sharp as autumn frost.
His calculations for victory in the ancestral temple
were inexhaustible in adapting to change.
His unique insight and judgment
surpassed the common understanding.
The sagacious and enlightened emperor
entrusted him with all affairs of state.
With a long rein, he governed from afar,
and secretly imparted brilliant strategies.
His detached forces were united in purpose,
superior and subordinate working together.
They advanced with overwhelming might,
entering their strongholds,
and crushing the enemy in one sweep,
striking terror into their hearts.
A small battle at Jiāng
Yóu,
and Chéngdū collapsed on its own;
displaying military power at Jiànggé,
and Jiāng Wéi was bound with ropes.
They opened up six thousand li of territory,
and gained thirty commanderies.
The military campaign did not last long,
and Liáng and Yì were pacified.
This caused the usurping hero
to bow his head before the vermilion palace gates,
and precious jade and heavy brocade
filled the imperial treasury.
Indeed, Hán was absorbed and Wèi relocated;
Guó was destroyed and Yú perished.
These are all precedents from the past,
and future events
of the outside.
Furthermore, Lǚ Xīng (呂興) of Nánzhōng (南中)
deeply discerned the mandate of Heaven,
shed his skin and attached himself to us internally,
wishing to become a subject.
Externally, we would lose the support of our "gums and teeth" (allies);
internally, there would be a gradual decline of our "feathers and fur" (subordinates)
Yet, to hover over a perilous state,
hoping to prolong its days,
is like Wèi Wǔ Hóu (魏武侯) pointing at the mountains and rivers,
believing himself strong,
not realizing that things rise and fall,
and thus
the beauty is not in its land.
At present, officials are numerous and capable,
talented individuals fill the court,
military officers and fierce generals
deter enemies from afar,
the country is rich and its army strong,
the six armies are well-trained,
eager to soar again,
and water their horses in the Nánhǎi (南海).
Lately, the state has been repairing weapons,
building ships,
and training in naval warfare.
Ten thousand storied ships
stretch for a thousand *lǐ* (里) as far as the eye can see.
Since the carving of wood began,
the use of boats and carriages has never been as extensive and prosperous as it is today.
A million valiant warriors
are storing their strength, awaiting the opportune moment.
A second levy will not be necessary;
this is today's army.
However, the ruler
and prime minister are lingering and have not yet struck like lightning,
still believing that loving the people and governing the country
is what Daoists advocate.
Thus, the grand city was humbled,
King Wén (文王) withdrew his residence.
Therefore, we first extend great sincerity,
explaining
the consequences of survival or extinction.
This earnest intention
is what our envoys are sent to ascertain.
If they can discern the perilous situation,
seek abundant blessings for themselves,
change their demeanor abruptly,
respectfully accept the past grants,
emulate
Nányuè (南越),
with Yīng Qí (嬰齊) entering to serve,
facing north and proclaiming himself a subject,
submissively listening to our instructions,
then his lineage will preside over Jiāngbiǎo (江表),
forever a vassal of Wèi (魏),
and his great achievements and prominent rewards
will be grander than they are today.
If they still insult and neglect us,
not obeying the king's command,
then our forces will gather like clouds,
our commands will be followed like the wind.
The two provinces of Yōng (雍) and Liáng (梁)
will move eastward with the current;
the warriors of Qīng (青) and Xú (徐)
will line the Jiāng (江)
to the west;
Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), Yǎn (兗), and Yù (豫) will
vie to rush through the eight thoroughfares;
the crack troops of Zhēngdōng (征東)
will march on Mòlíng (秣陵).
Then the imperial carriage will be prepared,
the six armies will march slowly,
feathered banners will illuminate the sun,
flags will stream like stars,
the imperial dragon will parade the roads,
songs and music will fill the ears,
soldiers will charge forward,
gathering like a forest,
smoke and dust will rise together,
shaking heaven and startling earth.
Warriors thirsting for rewards
will contend to be first with their arrows and spears.
Suddenly, in one day,
heads and bodies will be severed,
ancestral sacrifices will be overturned,
serving as a warning for ten thousand generations.
Looking south with yearning,
truly it makes one's heart grow cold!
Indeed, to treat a disease
that has reached the vitals,
one must administer bitter medicine;
to resolve a perplexing doubt,
one must also speak unpalatable words.
If one still hesitates,
lost and unwilling to turn back,
I fear Yú Fù (俞附) will see that he is already dead,
and Biǎn Què (扁鵲) will know that his efforts are useless.
Strive to consider a good plan,
and decide what to accept or reject.
Shào (劭) and others will arrive in Wú (吳),
and dare not facilitate this communication.
Chǔ (楚) was later transferred to Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Library,
and again served as Military Advisor to Shí Bāo (石苞), the General of Agile Cavalry.
Chǔ, relying on his talent and spirit,
somewhat disrespected and made light of Bāo (苞).
Upon his arrival,
he saluted with a long bow, saying:
"The Son of Heaven ordered me to serve as your military advisor."
From this, a rift formed.
Bāo (苞) impeached Chǔ (楚), alleging that he and Sūn Shìshān (孫世山) of Wú (吳) together slandered and disparaged current policies.
Chǔ (楚) also submitted a memorial in self-defense.
The dispute lasted for a year,
and before the matter was judged,
he again quarreled with Guō Yì (郭奕), a man from his hometown.
Although Emperor Wǔ (武帝) did not openly declare his guilt,
Chǔ (楚) was reprimanded for his low status,
and thus remained suppressed and废置 for many years.
Previously,
military advisors did not show respect to their commanders.
Chǔ (楚), having slighted Bāo (苞),
then established the rule of showing respect.
This practice began with Chǔ (楚).
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍), King of Fúfēng (扶風) Jùn (駿), who had an old friendship with Chǔ (楚),
appointed him as a military advisor.
He was then transferred to be Prefect of Liáng (梁),
and promoted to Sīmǎ (司馬) for Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍).
At that time, a dragon was seen in the well of the imperial armory.
The officials were about to submit congratulations,
but Chǔ (楚) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Recently I heard there were two dragons in the well of the imperial armory.
Some officials call this an auspicious omen and offer congratulations,
while others call it inauspicious and do not offer congratulations.
It can be said that Chǔ (楚) has lost it,
but Qí (齊) has not necessarily gained it.
Dragons sometimes dive with their scales hidden in deep springs,
or sometimes ascend to grasp the Milky Way and roam the azure heavens.
But now, to be coiled in a shallow well,
akin to frogs and shrimp,
is it not that some capable officials are hidden and unrecognized,
and wise servants are buried among the ranks?
Therefore, the dragon's appearance
should inspire some realization.
I wish that Your Majesty would pardon minor faults,
promote talented individuals,
seek inspiration from Fùyán (傅巖),
and look for talent by the Wèibīn (渭濱).
Restore the academies,
elevate those who are stagnant,
re-issue commands to the dukes and ministers,
to recommend upright gentlemen who can enrich customs and uplift traditions,
and also recommend outstanding and brilliant talents who can resolve difficulties, manage challenges, correct the times, and speak out,
regardless of their family background,
but rather prioritize those of humble origin.
The power of winning battles and conquering,
the might of annexation and unification,
these were the deeds of the Five Hegemons,
and the achievements of Hán (韓) and Bái (白);
as for establishing rites and creating music,
and elucidating the transforming power of the Dao,
this is truly the time for scholars to exert their strength.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will consider the words of a madman."
At the beginning of Emperor Huì's (惠帝) reign,
he became Governor of Féngyì (馮翊).
He died in the third year of Yuánkāng (元康).
Initially,
Chǔ (楚) was close friends with Wáng Jì (王濟) from the same commandery.
Jì was the Grand Moderator for their province.
When interviewing and assessing the character of people in the locality,
he came to Chǔ.
Jì said:
“This man is not someone you can evaluate;
I will do it myself.”
Then he characterized Chǔ, saying:
“His genius is brilliant and extensive,
outstanding and not ordinary.”
When Chǔ was young, he wanted to live as a recluse.
He said to Jì:
“I intend to pillow myself on a stone and rinse my mouth with a stream.”
He mistakenly said
“rinse my mouth with a stone and pillow myself on a stream.”
Jì said:
“A stream cannot be pillowed upon,
and a stone cannot be used to rinse one’s mouth.”
Chǔ said:
“The reason I pillow myself on a stream
is to wash my ears;
the reason I rinse my mouth with a stone
is to sharpen my teeth.”
Chǔ rarely admired anyone,
but he deeply respected Jì.
Initially,
after Chǔ had completed the mourning period for his wife,
he wrote a poem and showed it to Jì.
Jì said:
“I don’t know whether the writing comes from emotion,
or emotion comes from the writing.
Reading it makes me feel sorrow,
and increases the importance of a marital couple.”
He had three sons: Zhòng (衆), Xún (洵), and Zuǎn (纂).
Zhòng and Xún both died young without serving in office,
only Zuǎn’s sons, Tǒng (統) and Chuò (綽), were both well-known.
Tǒng’s courtesy name was Chénggōng (承公).
As a child, he crossed the Yangtze River with Chuò and his cousin Shèng (盛).
He was uninhibited and unrestrained,
but good at writing prose.
People at the time thought he had the style of Chǔ.
Chǔ Pú (禇裒), the General Who Conquers the North, heard of his reputation,
and appointed him as a staff officer,
but he declined the position.
He settled in Kuàijī (會稽).
He loved mountains and waters,
so he requested to be the magistrate of Yín (鄞),
then transferred to Wúníng (吳寧).
While in office, he did not concern himself with trivial matters,
but indulged in excursions,
exploring all famous mountains and scenic rivers
without exception.
Later he became the magistrate of Yúyáo (餘姚),
where he died.
His son Téng (騰) succeeded him,
known for his extensive learning,
and rose to the position of Grand Judge.
Téng’s younger brother, Dēng (登),
was good at logical reasoning when young,
and annotated the Lǎozi (老子),
which circulated widely.
He served as a Secretariat Gentleman,
and died young.
Chuò’s courtesy name was Xīnggōng (興公).
He was widely learned and good at writing prose.
When young, he and Xǔ Xún (許詢) of Gāoyáng (高陽) both shared lofty aspirations.
He lived in Kuàijī,
wandering among mountains and waters
for over ten years.
Then he composed the “Fù (賦) on Seeking the Beginning” to express his sentiments.
He once disdained Shān Tāo (山濤),
and said to people:
“Shān Tāo is someone I don’t understand.
He is neither an official nor
a recluse.
If he considers Yuánlǐ’s (元禮) gate a dragon’s ford,
then he should mark his forehead and expose his scales!”
He planted a pine tree in front of his study,
and guarded it himself.
A neighbor said to him:
“The little tree is indeed charming and lovely,
but I fear it will never become timber for a building.”
Chuò replied:
“Even if maple and willow grow to be a full embrace,
what use are they?”
Chuò and Xún were both famous figures of their time.
Some admired Xún’s lofty detachment
and thus disdained Chuò,
while others admired Chuò’s literary talent
and found Xún uninteresting.
The Buddhist monk Zhī Dùn (支遁) once asked Chuò:
“How do you compare to Xǔ Xún?”
He replied:
“His lofty sentiments and profound demeanor
I have long admired;
however, in terms of writing a single poem or chant,
Xǔ will have to face north (i.e., acknowledge my superiority).”
He greatly valued the Rhapsodies of Zhāng Héng (張衡) and Zuǒ Sī (左思),
often saying:
“The Three Capitals and Two Metropolises Rhapsodies
are the clarion call of the Five Classics.”
He once composed the “Fù on Tiāntái Mountain,”
which was exquisitely crafted.
When it was first completed,
he showed it to his friend Fàn Róngqī (范榮期),
saying:
“You should throw this to the ground;
it will make the sound of metal and stone.”
Róngqī said:
“I fear this metal and stone may not be in harmony with the musical notes.”
Yet, whenever he encountered a fine line,
he would exclaim:
“This must be something we would say!”
He was appointed Auxiliary Scribe,
and inherited the title of Marquis of Chánglè (長樂).
Chuò was unconstrained and frank,
and enjoyed jesting.
Once, while walking with Xí Zuòchǐ (習鑿齒),
Chuò was ahead and
looked back at Zuòchǐ, saying:
“When sand is sifted,
pebbles and stones are left behind.”
Zuòchǐ replied:
“When grain is winnowed and sifted,
chaff and husks are in front.”
Yǔ Liàng (庾亮), the General Who Conquers the West, invited him to be a staff officer.
He was appointed Magistrate of Zhāng'ān (章安),
then summoned to be a Grand Imperial Academician,
and promoted to Secretariat Gentleman.
Yīn Hào (殷浩), the Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州), made him Grand Administrator Who Establishes Might.
Wáng Xīzhī (王羲之), the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, appointed him Grand Administrator of the Right Army.
He was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
then promoted to Palace Attendant,
and concurrently held the position of Director of the Imperial Library.
At that time, Huán Wēn (桓溫), the Grand Marshal, wanted to restore order to China,
and since Hénán (河南) was roughly pacified,
he intended to move the capital to Luòyáng (洛陽).
The court feared Wēn
and dared not voice dissent.
However, the northern lands were desolate,
and people were filled with fear and suspicion.
Although everyone knew it was not feasible,
no one dared to be the first to remonstrate.
Chuò then submitted a memorial, stating: I humbly observe the memorial from the Grand General Who Conquers the West, your servant Wēn,
which says: “I shall personally lead the three armies
to suppress and eliminate the two bandits,
cleanse the Hé (河) and Wèi (渭) rivers,
and purify the old capital.
Then the divine
banners will unfurl like lightning,
and the court attire will cross the Jiāng (江),
restoring the imperial residence to the central plains
and aligning the Jade Scepter with the celestial pole.”
This is a grand plan surpassing all ages,
a glorious event of a thousand years.
However, I
harbor some reservations,
for I believe that when emperors rise,
they all rely on geographical advantage and human harmony to achieve great deeds,
valuing the ability to pacify violence with righteousness
and then to soothe
the people.
When Huái (懷) and Mǐn (愍) failed to establish their rule,
and the capital Qínjīng (秦京) was lost,
it allowed the Hú (胡) barbarians and Róng (戎) tribes to invade,
severing the lifeline of the divine land.
The calamity of collapse
indeed stemmed from the loss of the Way.
However, why did the central plains
fall into such widespread chaos,
with a torrent engulfing everything for a time,
and not a single city among hundreds of prefectures and thousands of cities remaining intact?
It is because
the land could not be defended,
and there was somewhere else to flee to.
Heaven’s mandate had not
yet changed,
and Emperor Zhōng (中宗) rose.
This was not only because his sincerity and compliance accorded with Heaven and man,
but truly relied on the thousands of miles of the Long River (Yangtze) as a natural barrier to defend the land.
The Yì (易) says:
“Kings and dukes establish defenses to
protect their states.”
The significance of strategic defenses in times of need is indeed great!
This is a clear proof of what has already happened.
Now, to make a lofty claim,
one should naturally follow the Way and abandon strategic defenses;
but if one carefully assesses
the situation and measures one’s strength,
one cannot but protect the smaller territory to secure one’s existence.
Since the chaos began over sixty years ago,
the common people have been decimated,
with scarcely one in a hundred surviving.
The Héluò (河洛) region is desolate,
and Huánxià (函夏)
Desolate,
