wells are choked and trees are felled,
fields and paths are leveled and destroyed.
Life is boundless and bleak,
with nowhere to eternally return.
Having been displaced and scattered south of the Yangzi River,
already for several generations,
those who survive are aged sons and grandsons,
and
those who have died form rows of graves.
Although the northern wind stirs thoughts of their original home,
the present sorrow is truly acute and pressing.
If, on the day the capital is moved and the imperial carriage turns,
the
restoration of Wǔlíng
will immediately again become a distant, remote land.
Since the security of Tàishān is difficult to maintain by reason,
how can the yearning thoughts of the populace not trouble the sagely heart?
Huán Wēn’s current endeavor
sincerely seeks a comprehensive view of beginning and end,
to plan for the nation long-term.
Without the urgency of the imperial mausoleums in the past,
he would not have initiated such a grand plan,
undertaking alone the
greatest difficulty in the world.
Now he is so focused that he forgets to eat,
his loyal indignation is manifest and clear.
Among all those with hearts,
who would not be moved?
Yet the common people are shocked and terrified,
all harboring fear and apprehension.
Is this not because
the joy of returning to their old home is far off,
while the sorrow of rushing to their death is imminent?
Why is this?
Their roots have been planted south of the river for several decades;
to pull them out in one morning,
and suddenly drive them to a
barren and desolate land,
carrying their families thousands of *lǐ*,
crossing perilous peaks and deep waters,
leaving their ancestral graves,
abandoning their livelihoods —
the wealthy will have no food for three years,
the poor will have no single meal.
Fields and houses cannot be resold,
boats and carriages cannot be obtained.
They abandon a peaceful and happy country
to go to a land accustomed to chaos,
leaving a place of certain safety
to face a danger like stacked eggs.
They will
suddenly collapse on the roads,
or be swept away and drowned in rivers.
Only a few will reach their destination.
The state takes its people as its foundation.
Calamities and bandits target the people.
If the multitudes perish but the bandits are eliminated,
from whom will
the state draw its resources?
This is what the benevolent should pity and grieve over,
and what the state should deeply consider.
From ancient times to the present, among the capitals of emperors and kings,
how could there be a fixed location?
When times are prosperous, they establish their capital in the center
to plan for greatness;
when their power is constrained, they wait and recuperate for an opportune moment.
It is only when virtue is insurmountable
and the household has three years' worth of provisions
that one can begin to plan for the affairs of great peace.
Today, the conditions of heaven and human affairs
are not yet ripe.
To suddenly desire to unify the universe in one morning,
will it not be difficult to accomplish all at once?
My humble proposal
is that it would be better to send another general, one with renown and practical ability,
to first garrison Luòyáng.
The two fortresses built by the mausoleum should be used to protect the imperial
mausoleums.
Sweep clean Liáng and Xǔ,
and pacify Hénán.
Once the grain transport routes are open,
then exert full effort in cultivation and reclamation,
expanding fields and accumulating grain,
gradually providing resources for the relocated people.
If this is done,
the bandits, seeing signs of their demise,
will certainly flee far away.
If they remain stubborn and unrepentant,
and still wish to court death,
the northern and southern armies will rush like wind and lightning,
like a hand
saving a painful itch,
or a *shuàirán* snake's head and tail responding.
Once the imperial mausoleums are secured,
and the Central Plains enjoy a period of small peace,
Your Majesty can then sit solemnly in the imperial palace,
further cultivate virtuous governance,
personally practice the extreme simplicity of Emperor
Wén of Hàn,
eliminate petty favors,
curtail wasteful expenditures,
scrutinize officials,
and train soldiers and weapons,
making the nurturing of scholars and elimination of bandits the priority.
If this is carried out for ten years
without allowing it to be neglected
or abandoned,
then the poor will prosper their wealth,
the timid will be filled with courage.
People will know Heaven's virtue,
and rush to death as if returning home.
With this to achieve governance,
it will be like moving things within one's grasp.
Why abandon
the long-established principle of a hundred victories,
and stake the whole empire on one throw?
Your Majesty is in the prime of your youth;
Huán Wēn is in his strong years of planning.
If ruler and minister work together,
greatly fostering virtue and enterprise,
containing
ultimate good fortune,
would that not be splendid?
Now Huán Wēn advocates a high-minded proposal,
and the sagely court largely agrees.
I, as a humble and insignificant person,
alone offer my limited view.
The difficulty of speaking out
is truly today,
yet my humble self insists on
making it heard by the Heavenly ear.
I secretly believe that in a court where nothing is concealed,
〔10〕even the blind and ignorant may offer counsel,
and the plans of woodcutters and grass-gatherers
are discerned by sages.
Therefore, unable to bear my extreme sorrow,
I dare to offend and
present my case.
If Your Majesty would bestow your divine attention,
and Huán Wēn would spare a little thought,
would this not be yielding to one person and fulfilling the wishes of billions?
If, however, it is deemed a great crime to contradict,
and I am to be put to public
execution,
let my sincere loyalty reach above,
then I shall retire and accept my punishment.
Even if I die and my body lies in the springs below,
my corpse shall not decay.
Huán Wēn saw Chāo’s memorial,
and was displeased.
He said,
“Convey my regards to Xìnggōng.
Why does he not read Jūnsuì’s 'Chūchū Fù' (Returning to the Beginning Rhapsody) to understand the affairs of people and nation?”
Soon after, he was transferred to become Tíngwèi Qīng,
and concurrently Lǐng Zhùzuò.
Chāo was early praised for his literary talent.
Among the literati of that time,
Chāo was considered their foremost.
When the various lords, Huán, Wáng, Xī, and Yǔ, died,
it was necessary for Chāo to compose their epitaphs
before they were carved in stone.
At the age of fifty-eight,
he passed away.
His son, Sì,
had Chāo’s style,
and their writings were comparable.
He rose to the position of Zhōngjūn Cānjūn,
but died young.
The Grand Scribe commented: Jiāng Tǒng’s
character and conduct were truly praiseworthy;
among the many gentlemen of Chénliú,
he was considered their leader.
His discourse on resettling the Róng people
was indeed a far-reaching strategy for governing the state.
However, the dynasty was nearing its decline,
and its degradation was gradual.
Had his words been put into use,
it might have accelerated disaster and invited resentment,
without saving the impending collapse.
When Mǐnhuái was deposed and exiled,
he defied the prohibition to bid him farewell,
illustrating the saying that life is as light as a goose feather,
but righteousness is as precious as a bear’s paw.
Jiāng Páo held a high position in the government,
and devotedly offered advice and criticism.
Jiāng Dūn overlooked glory and profit,
diligently cultivating his inherent virtue.
Although their paths in life were different,
they were both exceptional brothers.
Sūn Chǔ possessed a brilliant and refined demeanor,
standing out among his peers.
He was recognized by Wǔzǐ,
truly without shame.
Reading his letter to Hàoyǔ,
it is indeed a fine piece of writing from previous generations.
Yet, he was arrogant due to his talent,
dismissive of Bāo and resentful of Yì,
deviating from the path of humility and concession,
and indulging in an overbearing and indignant attitude.
To be sidelined in his prime
was truly his own doing.
Jiāng Chuò’s family was illustrious and prominent,
and his fame was significant during the restoration period,
demonstrating that he did not disgrace his ancestors.
Jiāng Tǒng eventually withdrew to a humble village,
contemplating scenic spots,
and finding contentment in it.
Jiāng Chuò offered straightforward advice and criticisms,
not at all intimidated by Yuánzǐ,
possessing the integrity of selfless devotion—
how could he be merely refined and cultured?
Eulogy: Yìngyuán trod the path of righteousness,
Zǐjīng transcended worldly customs.
Jiāng Tǒng had few regrets or faults,
Sūn Chǔ brought upon himself disgrace.
Jiāng Páo and Jiāng Tǒng were brothers,
their reputations soared in Jiāngzuǒ.
Elegant and refined in thought,
Jiāng Chuò surpassed all heroes.
Collated Notes
Biography Twenty-Seven Luó Xiàn (his nephew, Shàng)
Luó Xiàn, courtesy name Lìngzé,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
His father, Méng,
was the Administrator of Guǎnghàn in Shǔ.
Xiàn, at thirteen,
could compose essays
and gained early recognition.
He studied under Qiáo Zhōu,
and Zhōu's disciples called him Zǐgòng.
He was upright, sincere, and disciplined by nature,
tireless in his treatment of scholars,
light with wealth, generous,
and did not engage in managing property.
He served Shǔ as Crown Prince's Retainer and Xuanxin Commandant.
He was sent twice as an envoy to Wú,
and the people of Wú praised him.
At that time, Huáng Hào was involved in politics,
and many attached themselves to him,
but Xiàn alone remained independent.
Hào resented him,
and demoted him to Administrator of Bādōng.
At that time, Grand General Yán Yǔ was Inspector of Bādōng,
and appointed Xiàn as Commander of the Army,
serving as Yǔ's deputy.
When Wèi attacked Shǔ,
Yǔ was summoned back west,
and Xiàn defended Yǒng'ān city.
When Chéngdū fell,
the city was in turmoil,
and the local officials along the river all abandoned the city and fled.
Xiàn executed one of the rioters,
and the common people then settled down.
Knowing that Liú Shàn had surrendered,
he led his subordinates to mourn at the imperial pavilion for three days.
When Wú heard of Shǔ's defeat,
they dispatched General Shèng Xiàn to ascend west,
outwardly claiming to offer aid,
but inwardly intending to attack Xiàn.
Xiàn said:
"Our imperial court has fallen;
Wú is our lips and teeth.
If they do not pity our difficulties
but instead seek their own advantage,
should I then become a captive?"
So he pledged allegiance [to Wèi].
Thereupon, he repaired armor, gathered provisions,
and spurred his men with integrity and righteousness;
all his soldiers followed his commands.
When Zhōng Huì and Dèng Ài died,
and a hundred cities were without a lord,
Wú again sent Bù Xié to conquer the west,
but Xiàn severely defeated his army.
Sūn Xiū was enraged
and again sent Lù Kàng to assist Xié.
Xiàn defended for a year,
but no reinforcements arrived,
and more than half the city's inhabitants were afflicted by illness and plague.
Some advised him to exit south to Zāngkē,
or flee north to Shàngyōng,
as he could then preserve himself.
Xiàn said:
"As a ruler,
one is relied upon by the common people.
If one cannot preserve [the city],
and abandons it in an emergency,
a gentleman would not do so.
I shall give my life here."
Just then, Hú Liè, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, and others came to his rescue,
and Lù Kàng retreated.
He was promoted to General Línjiāng, Supervisor of the Bādōng Military Affairs, Imperial Commissioner,
and concurrently Administrator of Wǔlíng.
In the early years of Tàishǐ, he came to court,
and an imperial edict declared:
"Xiàn is loyal, resolute, and courageous,
possessing talent, strategy, and capability.
He shall be granted military music."
He was also bestowed with a black jade sword.
He died in the sixth year of Tàishǐ (270 CE),
and was posthumously granted the titles of Imperial Commissioner, General Ānnán, Administrator of Wǔlíng,
and posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Xī'è,
with the posthumous epithet Liè.
Originally,
when Xiàn attended a banquet in the Huálín Garden,
an edict inquired about the sons of Shǔ's high officials.
Later, it asked about worthy elders who should be employed at the time.
Xiàn recommended Cháng Jì, Dù Zhěn, and others from Shǔ,
all of whom were excellent talents from the western region,
and Emperor Wǔ summoned and appointed them all.
His son, Xí,
successively served as Attendant Censor and General Línjiāng,
commanding his father's troops,
and rose to Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
His nephew, Shàng.
Shàng, courtesy name Jìngzhī,
also known as Zhòng.
His father, Shì,
was the Administrator of Zāngkē.
Shàng became an orphan at a young age
and relied on his uncle Xiàn.
He was skilled in writing.
Wáng Róng, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, appointed Shàng and Liú Qiáo as staff officers,
and entrusted them both.
In the late Tàikāng period,
he became Inspector of Liángzhōu.
When Zhào Xīn rebelled in Shǔ,
Shàng reported:
"Xīn is not a man of great talent;
he will surely accomplish nothing.
We can count the days until his defeat."
Thereupon, Shàng was granted the imperial insignia and appointed General Píngxī, Inspector of Yìzhōu, and Commandant of Xīróng.
He was greedy by nature
and indecisive.
The people of Shǔ said:
"Those whom Shàng loves
are either corrupt or sycophantic;
those whom Shàng hates
are either loyal or upright.
His wealth rivals Lǔ and Wèi,
his household became a marketplace;
his greed is like that of a jackal or wolf,
endless and without limit."
They also said:
"The Shǔ bandits were still tolerable,
but Luó Shàng is killing us.
The General Píngxī, on the contrary, brought disaster."
At that time, Lǐ Tè (李特) also rose up in Shǔ (蜀).
He attacked Shǔ (蜀)
and killed Zhào Yīnxún (趙廞).
He then attacked Shàng (尚) in Chéngdū (成都).
Shàng (尚) retreated and held Jiāngyáng (江陽).
Initially,
Shàng (尚) had requested troops from Fāng Yuè (方嶽).
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Zōng Dài (宗岱), along with the Administrator of Jiànpíng (建平), Sūn Fù (孫阜), led forces to relieve him.
They reached Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Dài (岱) and Fù (阜) had strong forces,
and all those who had been oppressed by the bandits
were inspired to fight.
Shàng (尚) then sent his Army Clerk, Rèn Ruì (任銳), to feign surrender.
He then secretly issued a proclamation to the outside,
setting a day for a coordinated attack.
Consequently, they achieved a great victory,
beheading Lǐ Tè (李特)
and sending his head to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Lǐ Tè's (李特) son, Xióng (雄), usurped the imperial title
and made Píchéng (郫城) his capital.
Shàng (尚) dispatched General Wěi Bó (隗伯) to attack him,
but he failed.
Shortly thereafter, Shàng (尚) died,
and Xióng (雄) subsequently occupied the land of Shǔ (蜀).
Téng Xiū (滕脩)
Téng Xiū (滕脩), courtesy name Xiǎnxiān (顯先),
was a native of Xī'è (西鄂) in Nányáng (南陽).
He served Wú (吳) as a general and commander,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xī'è (西鄂).
During Sūn Hào's (孫晧) reign,
he replaced Xióng Mù (熊睦) as Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and was greatly respected and benevolent.
He was summoned to serve as Zhí Jīn Wǔ (執金吾).
When Guō Mǎ (郭馬) and others, who were military superintendents in Guǎngzhōu (廣州), rebelled,
Hào (晧), knowing that Xiū (脩) had long commanded respect and benevolence
and was obeyed by the region south of the mountains,
appointed him as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Guǎngzhōu (廣州) military affairs, General Who Guards the South, and Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州) to suppress the rebellion.
Before he could subdue them, the royal army attacked Wú (吳).
Xiū (脩) led his troops to respond to the crisis.
When he reached Bāqiū (巴丘), Hào (晧) had already surrendered.
He then dressed in white mourning clothes, shed tears, and returned.
Along with Lǘ Fēng (閭豐), Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), and Wáng Yì (王毅), Administrator of Cāngwú (蒼梧), he each sent their seals and sashes.
An imperial edict appointed Xiū (脩) as General Who Stabilizes the South,
with his former titles of Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), Envoy with Credentials, and Area Commander remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔdāng (武當),
given military music,
and entrusted with affairs of the south.
Xiū (脩) resided in the south for many years
and was greatly admired by the border tribes.
He died in the ninth year of Tàikāng (太康)
and requested to be buried in the capital.
The emperor admired his intention,
bestowed upon him one qǐng (頃) of burial land,
and posthumously granted him the name Shēng (聲).
Xiū's (脩) son, Bìng (並), submitted a memorial stating:
"My late father Xiū (脩) was bound and driven in the land of Wú (吳).
He was made to rush about.
Fortunately, he encountered the opening of the country
and was bathed in the ultimate transformation,
allowed to command the crucial military forces as a captive.
Before he could behold the sacred countenance,
he was entrusted with the heavy responsibility of the southern marches.
This was truly due to his merits and achievements being little known to Your Majesty.
As he aged and fell gravely ill,
he repeatedly requested leave to retire due to sickness,
but did not receive Your Majesty's pity
before suddenly passing away.
Your servant, fulfilling his dying wishes,
transported his coffin back to the capital,
gazing towards the imperial palace,
truly feeling heartbroken.
I secretly heard that the court scholars posthumously named Xiū (脩) 'Shēng' (聲),
which merely indicates widespread fame
and does not match his actual deeds.
Unable to suppress my foolish feelings,
I presumptuously venture to appeal to Your Majesty."
The emperor then bestowed the posthumous name Zhōng (忠).
Bìng's (並) son, Hán (含),
initially served Yǔ Bīng (庾冰) as Cavalry Commander's Chief Clerk.
He distinguished himself in suppressing Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
was enfeoffed as Founding Marquis of Xiàyáng (夏陽) County,
with an estate of one thousand six hundred households,
and was appointed General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
He served for many years
and was greatly respected and benevolent.
Upon his death, he was posthumously named Dài (戴).
Hán's (含) younger brother's son, Dùn (遯),
was Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州).
Xiū's (脩) great-grandson, Tiánzhī (恬之),
was General Who Drags the Dragon and Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡).
While garrisoned at Líyáng (黎陽),
he was captured by Zhái Liáo (翟遼)
and died.
Mǎ Lóng (馬隆)
Mǎ Lóng (馬隆), courtesy name Xiàoxīng (孝興),
was a native of Pínglù (平陸) in Dōngpíng (東平).
In his youth, he was intelligent and brave,
and fond of establishing a good reputation and integrity.
When Línghú Yú (令狐愚), Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州) during Wèi (魏), was executed for an offense,
no one in the entire province dared to collect his body.
Lóng (隆), acting as a military officer, claimed to be Yú's (愚) guest,
used his private funds to give him a funeral,
observed mourning for three years,
planted rows of pine and cypress trees,
and only returned after the rites were completed.
The whole province regarded this as a commendable act.
He was appointed Supervisor of Brave Warriors.
In the Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
when the expedition to attack Wú (吳) was about to be launched,
an imperial edict stated:
"As Wú (吳) and Huìjī (會稽) are not yet pacified,
it is necessary to obtain brave warriors to accomplish military achievements.
Although there were existing methods of recommendation,
they were insufficient to discover all extraordinary talents.
Let it be broadly announced to the provinces and commanderies
that those who are valiant, brave, outstanding, and exceptionally talented
should all be reported by name,
so that their most exceptional individuals may be selected
and promoted for use.
If such persons exist,
there should be no limit to their recruitment."
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) recommended Lóng (隆) as capable of being a good general.
He was gradually promoted to Sīmǎ Dū (司馬督).
Initially,
the governor of Liángzhōu, Yáng Xīn, failed to maintain harmony with the Qiāng and Róng tribes.
Lóng stated that Yáng Xīn was sure to be defeated.
Soon after, Yáng Xīn was overwhelmed by the barbarians,
and the Hexi region was cut off.
The emperor frequently worried about the west,
and, presiding over court, sighed, saying:
"Who can campaign against these barbarians for me and reopen Liángzhōu?"
The court officials did not reply.
Lóng stepped forward and said,
"If Your Majesty can entrust this to your servant,
your servant can pacify them."
The emperor said,
"If you can certainly destroy the rebels,
why would I not entrust it to you?
I am just wondering what your strategies are."
Lóng said,
"If Your Majesty can entrust this to your servant,
you must allow your servant to act independently."
The emperor said,
"What do you mean?"
Lóng said,
"Your servant requests to recruit three thousand brave warriors,
no matter their origin,
lead them marching westward with drums beating,
and relying on Your Majesty's might and virtue,
what barbarians would be too difficult to destroy!"
The emperor agreed,
and appointed Lóng as the Administrator of Wǔwēi.
The Dukes and Ministers all said,
"Our six armies are numerous,
and the troops from the various provinces and commanderies are plentiful.
We should just use them;
it is not appropriate to offer special rewards and recruitment, thus disrupting the normal system.
Lóng is a petty general making wild claims,
and should not be listened to."
The emperor did not accept their advice.
Lóng recruited men who could draw a crossbow with a thirty-six jūn draw weight and a bow with a four jūn draw weight,
setting up a target for testing.
From dawn until midday,
he got three thousand five hundred men.
Lóng said,
"That is enough."
He then requested to personally go to the armory to select weapons.
The armory commandant quarreled with Lóng.
The Censorate Investigating Minister impeached Lóng.
Lóng said,
"Your servant is about to risk his life on the battlefield
to repay what he has received.
Yet the armory commandant provides me with rotten weapons from the Wèi era,
which are unusable,
and this is not Your Majesty's intention in having your servant destroy the rebels."
The emperor agreed with him,
and also provided him with three years' military supplies.
Lóng then crossed the Wēnshuǐ westward.
The barbarian leaders, Shùjīnéng and others, with tens of thousands of troops,
either occupied strategic points to block Lóng's advance,
or set ambushes to cut off his rear.
Lóng, relying on the Eight Trigrams Formation, constructed defensive wagons.
Where the terrain was open, he formed wagon camps like deer antlers.
Where the road was narrow, he built wooden houses on top of the wagons.
Fighting as he advanced,
whoever was hit by his arrows
fell at the sound of the bowstring.
His ingenious strategies were launched intermittently,
catching the enemy off guard.
Sometimes he laid magnets along the road.
When the rebels, burdened with iron armor,
could not advance,
Lóng's soldiers, all clad in rhinoceros hide armor,
were unimpeded.
The rebels all thought it was divine intervention.
He fought over a thousand *lǐ*,
killing and wounding thousands.
Since Lóng's departure westward,
all communication had ceased.
The court was worried,
some saying he had already been lost.
Later, Lóng's envoy arrived at night,
and the emperor clapped his hands and laughed with joy.
The next morning,
he summoned his ministers and said,
"If I had followed your advice,
there would be no Qín or Liáng left."
He then issued an edict saying:
"Lóng, with a single, numerically inferior force,
fought fearlessly,
braving dangers and succeeding.
He is hereby granted *jiǎjié*, appointed General Xuānwēi,
and given a red banner, a curved canopy, and drum and wind music."
When Lóng arrived at Wǔwēi,
the barbarian chieftains Cùbá Hán, Qiěwànnéng, and others led over ten thousand households to surrender.
The total number of those executed, killed, or surrendered before and after amounted to tens of thousands.
He also led the loyal Róng tribes, including Mògǔnéng, to engage Shùjīnéng in a great battle,
and beheaded him.
Liángzhōu was thus pacified.
The court debated awarding Lóng's officers and soldiers for their merits.
The relevant officials reported that Lóng's officers and soldiers had all previously been granted high ranks,
and should not be awarded again.
General Wèi, Yáng Yáo, rebutted, saying,
"The previous elite recruitment of officers and soldiers,
where a few were granted noble titles,
was precisely for the purpose of enticement.
Now Lóng has achieved a complete victory with his army alone,
and the western lands have found peace.
We must not use previous grants to block these subsequent achievements.
It is appropriate to agree to all requests,
to demonstrate our solemn commitment."
The emperor then followed Yáo's suggestion,
and awards of titles and promotions were granted according to merit.
In the early years of Tàikāng,
the court, seeing that Xīpíng was desolate and ruined,
decided it should be restored promptly.
Lóng was appointed Protector of the Pacified Barbarians and Administrator of Xīpíng,
leading his elite troops,
and also given one army of *yámén* guards,
to garrison Xīpíng.
At that time, the southern barbarian Chéng Xī frequently caused border troubles.
When Lóng arrived,
he led his army to suppress them.
The barbarians occupied strategic positions and resisted.
Lóng ordered his soldiers to all carry farming tools,
as if they were going to farm.
The barbarians, thinking Lóng had no intention of campaigning,
gradually relaxed their guard.
Lóng took advantage of their unpreparedness,
advanced his troops, and defeated them.
Throughout Lóng's administration,
they dared not act as bandits.
In the early years of Tàixī,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fènggāo County,
and additionally appointed Colonel of the Eastern Qiāng.
For over ten years,
his prestige and trustworthiness resounded throughout Lǒngyòu.
At that time, the Administrator of Luèyáng, Yán Shū of Fēngyì, was closely related to Yáng Jùn,
and secretly plotted to replace Lóng.
He slandered Lóng, saying he was old and senile,
and unfit for military service.
Thus, Lóng was recalled,
and Yán Shū was appointed to govern in his place.
The Dī and Qiāng tribes gathered together,
and the common people were alarmed and frightened.
The court feared that Guānlǒng would again be troubled,
so they dismissed Yán Shū,
and sent Lóng back to his post.
He eventually died in office.
His son, Xián, succeeded him,
and was also brave and fierce.
When the King of Chéngdū, Yǐng, attacked the King of Chángshā,
he appointed Xián as General Yīngyáng,
and ordered him to lead troops to garrison the central islet of the Héqiáo.
He was defeated by General Wáng Hú,
and died in battle.
Hú Fèn
Hú Fèn, courtesy name Xuánwēi,
was from Línjīng, Āndìng. He was the son of Hú Zūn, the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis Yīnmì of Wèi.
Hú Fèn's nature was open and bright,
and he had strategic insight.
In his youth, he enjoyed martial affairs.
When Emperor Xuān campaigned against Liáodōng,
he served by his side as a commoner,
and was greatly received.
Upon his return, he became a colonel,
gradually rising to become the Administrator of Xúzhōu,
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Xiàyáng.
When Liú Měng, the Central Chieftain of the Xiōngnú, rebelled,
General Xiāoqí Lù Fān was sent to suppress him.
Hú Fèn was appointed Supervisor of the Army and *jiǎjié*,
stationing his troops north of Kēng,
to serve as Lù Fān's reserve.
He attacked Liú Měng
and defeated him.
Lǐ Kè, a general under Liú Měng, beheaded Liú Měng and surrendered.
For his achievements, he was successively promoted to General Zhēngnán, *jiǎjié*, and Area Commander of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu.
He was then promoted to Protector of the Army,
and additionally made Regular Mounted Attendant.
Hú Fèn's family had been generals for generations.
In his later years, he became fond of learning,
and was proficient in both literary and martial matters.
Wherever he served, he had notable achievements,
and especially on the border, he displayed great authority and benevolence.
In the final years of the Tàishǐ era,
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn neglected state affairs and indulged in carnal pleasures.
He extensively selected daughters of dukes, ministers, and high officials to fill the imperial harem.
Fèn's daughter was chosen and entered as a guìrén.
Fèn had only one son,
who served as a companion to the Prince of Nányáng,
but he died young.
When Fèn heard that his daughter had become a guìrén,
he wept and said,
"This old slave will not die.
I only had two children:
the son has gone beneath the nine earths,
and the daughter has ascended above the nine heavens."
As Fèn was an old minister,
and also had the support of the imperial family (through his daughter),
he was greatly favored and treated with honor.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Púshè,
and was additionally appointed Zhènqún Dàjiāngjūn with the privilege of kāifǔ yítóng sānsī.
At that time, Yáng Jùn, being the empress's father, was arrogant and self-satisfied.
Fèn said to Jùn,
"Do you rely on your daughter to become even more arrogant?
Looking back through previous dynasties,
those who married into the imperial family
have never failed to have their families destroyed.
It is merely a matter of time.
Looking at your actions,
you are merely hastening disaster."
Jùn replied,
"Is your daughter not also in the imperial family?"
Fèn said,
"My daughter merely serves as a maid for your daughter;
how can she cause harm or benefit?"
At the time, everyone feared for Fèn.
Although Jùn bore a grudge,
he could not harm Fèn.
Fèn later died in office,
and was posthumously granted the title Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Zhuàng.
Fèn had six brothers.
His elder brother was Guǎng,
and his younger brother was Liè;
both were renowned.
Guǎng, courtesy name Xuānzǔ,
reached the positions of Sǎnqí Chángshì and Shǎofǔ.
Guǎng's son, Xǐ,
courtesy name Línfǔ,
was also praised for his ability to achieve and assist.
He rose to the offices of Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, jiǎjié, and Hùqiāng Xiàowèi.
Liè, courtesy name Wǔxuán,
was a general who attacked Shǔ.
When Zhōng Huì rebelled,
Liè and the other generals were all imprisoned.
Liè's son, Shìyuán,
who was eighteen years old at the time,
led the soldiers,
attacked and killed Huì,
and his fame spread far and wide.
Liè served as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Liángzhōu rebelled,
Liè was stationed at Wànzǐduī,
was besieged by the barbarians,
received no reinforcements,
and was killed.
Táo Huáng
Táo Huáng, courtesy name Shìyīng,
was a native of Líng, Dānyáng.
His father, Jī,
was the Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu under Wú.
Huáng served Wú and held prominent positions.
During Sūn Hào's reign,
Sūn Xū, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, was greedy and tyrannical,
and was hated by the populace.
When the inspector of battle, Dèng Xún, arrived,
he arbitrarily requisitioned three thousand peacocks,
and dispatched them to Lǐng.
Suffering from the arduous long-distance task,
everyone thought of rebellion.
The county official Lǚ Xīng killed Xū and Xún,
and brought the commandery over to Jìn.
Emperor Wǔ appointed Xīng as Ānnán Jiāngjūn and Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu.
Soon after, Xīng was killed by his Grand Clerk, Lǐ Tǒng.
The Emperor then appointed Cuàn Gǔ of Jiànníng as Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu.
Gǔ also died,
and Mǎ Róng of Bāxī was sent to replace him.
Róng died of illness.
Huò Yì, the Inspector of the Southern Central Region, then sent Yáng Jì of Jiànwéi to replace Róng.
Jì, along with General Máozǐ,
Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn Dǒng Yuán,
Yámén Mèng Gàn, Mèng Tōng, Lǐ Sōng, Wáng Yè,
and Cuàn Néng,
departed from Shǔ to Jiāozhǐ,
defeated the Wú army at Gǔchéng,
and beheaded the Grand Commander Xiū Zé and Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Liú Jùn.
Wú dispatched Yú Sì as Inspector,
Xuē Xǔ as Wēinán Jiāngjūn and Grand Commander,
and Huáng as Cāngwú Tàishǒu,
to resist Jì.
They fought at Fēnshuǐ.
Huáng was defeated
and retreated to defend Hépǔ,
losing two of his generals.
Xǔ was enraged
and said to Huáng,
"You personally requested to suppress the rebels,
yet you lost two commanders.
Where does the blame lie?"
Huáng replied,
"This humble official could not implement my intentions,
and the various armies did not cooperate,
which is why we suffered defeat."
Xǔ was angry
and intended to withdraw the army.
That night, Huáng, with a few hundred soldiers, raided Dǒng Yuán,
captured his treasures,
loaded them onto boats, and returned.
Xǔ then apologized to him
and appointed Huáng to govern Jiāozhōu
as Qiánbù Dū.
Huáng took the sea route, catching them by surprise,
and directly arrived at Jiāozhǐ.
Yuán resisted him.
As the generals were about to fight,
Huáng suspected there were hidden troops behind a broken wall,
so he arrayed long halberds behind it.
As soon as the troops engaged,
Yuán feigned retreat.
Huáng pursued him,
and indeed the hidden troops emerged.
The long halberds met them,
and Yuán and his forces were utterly defeated.
Huáng sent several thousand bolts of brocade from the treasure ship he had previously captured to Liáng Qí, the bandit leader of Fúyán.
Qí brought over ten thousand men to assist Huáng.
Yuán had a brave general, Xiè Xì, who was also within the city.
Huáng lured Xì's younger brother, Xiàng,
and had him write a letter to Xì.
He also had Xiàng ride in Huáng's chariot,
with music and attendants leading the way.
Yuán and his men said,
"If Xiàng is treated like this,
Xì must surely have intentions to leave."
They then killed him.
Xǔ and Huáng then captured Jiāozhǐ.
Wú consequently appointed Huáng as Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
Huáng was resourceful,
helped the needy, and was generous,
thus gaining popular support.
Téng Xiū repeatedly campaigned against the southern rebels
but could not control them.
Huáng said,
"The people on the south bank rely on our salt and iron.
Cut off trade with them completely,
and melt down all their farm implements.
After two years of this,
they can be destroyed in a single battle."
Xiū followed his advice,
and indeed defeated the rebels.
Initially,
Huò Yìzhī sent Jì, Guì, and others,
and swore an oath with them, saying:
"If the bandits besiege the city for less than one hundred days and you surrender,
your families will be executed.
If more than one hundred days pass and relief troops do not arrive,
I will bear the blame."
Jì and the others defended for less than one hundred days.
Their provisions ran out,
and they begged to surrender.
Huáng did not permit it,
but supplied them with food and ordered them to continue defending.
All the generals remonstrated,
but Huáng said:
"Huò Yì is already dead;
he will surely be unable to rescue Jì and the others.
We can wait until the term is full,
and then accept their surrender,
so that they may be without guilt,
and we may be seen as righteous.
This will instruct our own people
and win over neighboring states.
Is this not acceptable?"
When Jì and the others' term expired and their provisions were exhausted,
and no relief troops arrived,
Huáng then accepted their surrender.
Xiū Zé had already been killed by Máo Guì.
Zé's son Yǔn followed Huáng on the southern campaign.
When the city had surrendered,
Yǔn sought to take revenge,
but Huáng did not permit it.
Guì secretly plotted to attack Huáng.
The plot was discovered,
and Guì was arrested.
Huáng scolded him, saying:
"You Jìn rebel!"
Guì retorted loudly:
"You Wú dog!
Who is the rebel?"
Yǔn sliced open his belly,
saying:
"Can you still make trouble?"
Guì still cursed, saying:
"My ambition was to kill your Sūn Hào.
What kind of dead dog is your father?"
After Huáng captured Jì and the others,
he sent them all away.
When Jì reached Hépǔ,
he fell ill and died.
Méng Gàn, Cuàn Néng, Lǐ Sōng, and others arrived at Jiànyè.
Hào was about to kill them.
Someone advised Hào
that Gàn and the others were loyal to their duties,
and that he should pardon them to encourage his frontier generals.
Hào followed his advice,
intending to relocate them to Línhǎi.
Gàn and the others' ambition was to return north.
Fearing that moving east would take them further away,
and knowing that the Wú people prized the Shǔ-style bamboo crossbows,
they said they could make them.
Hào kept them and assigned them to the manufacturing department.
Later, Gàn escaped to Jīngdū.
Sōng and Néng were killed by Hào.
Gàn presented a plan to attack Wú,
and the Emperor generously rewarded him,
appointing him as Rìnán Tàishǒu.
Before this,
Yáng Jì had been appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and Máo Guì Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu.
Their seals of office had not arrived before their defeat.
The Emperor then posthumously granted Jì the title of Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
and Guì, Sōng, and Néng's sons the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Lǐ Zuò, the Registrar of Jiǔzhēn Commandery, protected the commandery and submitted.
Huáng sent generals to attack him,
but failed.
Zuò's maternal uncle, Lí Huàng, who was with the army,
persuaded Zuò to surrender.
Zuò replied:
"My uncle is a Wú general;
I, Zuò, am a Jìn subject.
We will simply see who is stronger."
After some time, the commandery was captured.
Hào appointed Huáng as Envoy with Imperial Credential, Grand Commandant of All Military Affairs in Jiāozhōu, General of the Vanguard, and Governor of Jiāozhōu.
The lands of Wǔpíng, Jiǔdé, and Xīnchāng were rugged and dangerous,
and their native tribes were fierce and rebellious,
never submitting throughout the generations.
Huáng campaigned and subdued them,
establishing three commanderies,
as well as over thirty counties in the Protectorate of Jiǔzhēn.
Huáng was recalled to be Wǔchāng Dūdū,
and Hépǔ Tàishǒu Xiū Yǔn replaced him.
The people of Jiāozhōu requested that Huáng remain, numbering in the thousands.
Therefore, he was sent back.
After Hào surrendered to Jìn,
he personally wrote a letter and sent Huáng's son Róng to instruct Huáng to submit.
Huáng wept for several days,
then sent an envoy with his seals of office to Luòyáng.
The Emperor decreed that he be restored to his former post,
ennobled as Wǎnlíng Hóu,
and renamed General of Agile Cavalry.
After Wú was pacified,
the imperial court generally reduced the provincial and commandery troops.
Huáng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Jiāozhōu is a desolate frontier region,
isolated on one side,
where people speak through multiple interpreters,
and it is connected by mountains and seas.
Furthermore, Nánjùn is more than a thousand *lǐ* by sea from the provincial capital,
and externally it is only seven hundred *lǐ* from Línyì.
The barbarian chief, Fàn Xióng, has been a persistent bandit for generations,
calling himself king,
and repeatedly attacking the populace.
Moreover, it is connected to Fúnán,
with a great many different tribes,
who form factions and rely on each other,
defying submission due to the dangerous terrain.
In the past, during the Wú period,
they repeatedly committed banditry and rebellion,
attacking and destroying commanderies and counties,
and killing officials.
I, your incapable servant,
was formerly appointed by the former state,
stationed on the southern frontier,
for over ten years.
Although there have been campaigns and punitive expeditions,
and their chieftains have been eliminated,
there are still some fugitives
in the deep mountains and remote caves.
Furthermore, the troops under my command originally numbered over seven thousand.
The southern lands are hot and humid,
with many noxious vapours,
and prolonged campaigns over the years
have led to deaths and depletion.
Those remaining are two thousand four hundred and twenty men.
Now the Four Seas are unified;
there is no one who does not submit,
and we should sheath our armour and put away our weapons,
focusing on rites and music.
However, the people of this province
are few in understanding righteousness;
they are tired of peace and contentment,
and fond of creating chaos.
Also, on the southern bank of Guǎngzhōu,
extending six thousand *lǐ* in circumference,
there are over fifty thousand households who do not submit,
and in Guìlín, those who are unconstrained
number another ten thousand households.
As for those who obey official service,
they are only just over five thousand families.
The two provinces are like lips and teeth,
and only military force can pacify them.
Moreover, Níngzhōu's Xīnggǔ is situated upstream,
one thousand six hundred *lǐ* from Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
with both water and land routes connecting,
mutually defending each other.
The provincial troops should not be reduced
to show weakness.
For changes brought by 'wind and dust' [i.e., warfare]
arise unexpectedly.
I, a remnant of a fallen state,
my counsel is not worthy of being considered.
Yet, Your Sacred Grace is vast and generous,
condescending to adorn and elevate me,
wiping away my guilt and transgressions,
and reassigning me to a regional post.
From disgrace to favor,
I wipe my eyes and look anew,
swearing to devote my life
to repay what I have received.
Based on what I have observed and experienced,
I humbly dare to present this blind appeal."
He also stated:
"The land of Hépǔ Commandery is barren and infertile,
without agriculture.
The people solely rely on pearl fishing for their livelihood,
and merchants come and go,
trading pearls for rice.
However, during the Wú period, the pearl prohibitions were very strict,
fearing that the people would privately disperse good pearls,
and traffic was completely cut off,
leaving people hungry and distressed.
Moreover, the required tribute was excessive,
and quotas were never met.
Now, I request that two-thirds of the finest pearls be submitted,
one-third of the next quality,
and coarse ones be exempted.
From October to February,
which is not the season for collecting the finest pearls,
merchants should be allowed to travel as before."
Both requests were granted.
For thirty years in the south,
his prestige and kindness were renowned among the various peoples.
When he died,
the entire province wept and wailed,
as if they had lost a benevolent parent.
The imperial court then appointed Wú Yàn 吾彥, a Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍, to replace Huáng 黃.
When Yàn 彥 died,
Gù Mì 顧祕, also a Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍, replaced Yàn 彥.
When Mì 祕 died,
the provincial people pressured Mì's 祕 son, Cān 參, to take charge of provincial affairs.
Cān 參 soon died,
and Cān's 參 younger brother, Shòu 壽, sought to lead the province.
The provincial people refused to listen.
He persistently sought it,
and thus gained control of the province.
Shòu 壽 then killed Chángshǐ Hú Zhào 長史胡肇 and others.
He also intended to kill Zhàngxià Dū Liáng Shuò 帳下督梁碩,
but Shuò 碩 fled and escaped.
Shuò 碩 raised an army to attack Shòu 壽,
captured him,
handed him over to Shòu's 壽 mother,
and ordered her to poison him.
Shuò 碩 then welcomed Huáng's 黃 son, Cāngwú Tàishǒu Wēi 蒼梧太守威, to lead as Cìshǐ 刺史.
While in office, he greatly won the hearts of the common people.
He died after three years.
Wēi's 威 younger brother, Shú 淑,
and his son, Suí 綏,
later both served as Jiāozhōu āk刺史.
From Jī āt至 to Suí 綏, across four generations,
five people served as Jiāozhōu āk刺史.
Huáng's 黃 younger brother, Jùn 濬,
was Wú Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Mù 吳鎮南大將軍、荊州牧.
Jùn's 濬 younger brother, Kàng 抗,
was Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子.
Jùn's 濬 son, Yān 湮,
courtesy name Gōngzhī 恭之;
Yān's 湮 younger brother, Yóu 猷,
courtesy name Gōngyù 恭豫,
were both famous.
Yān 湮 rose to Línhǎi Tàishǒu 臨海太守 and Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎.
Yóu 猷 was Xuānchéng Nèishǐ 宣城內史,
and Wáng Dǎo's Yòujūn Chángshǐ 王導右軍長史.
Yān's 湮 son, Fù 馥,
was Yúhú Lìng 于湖令,
killed by Hán Huàng 韓晃,
and posthumously granted the title Lújiāng Tàishǒu 廬江太守.
Kàng's 抗 son, Huí 回,
has his own biography.
Wú Yàn 吾彥
Wú Yàn 吾彥, courtesy name Shìzé 士則,
was a native of Wú 吳 county, Wú 吳 commandery.
He came from humble origins
and possessed both civil and military talents.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
could wrestle fierce beasts with his bare hands,
and his physical strength was unmatched.
He served Wú 吳 as a Tōngjiāng Lì 通江吏.
At that time, General Xuē Xǔ 薛珝, bearing his *jié* 節, marched south,
his army looking very grand.
Yàn 彥 observed it
and sighed with emotion.
A skilled physiognomist, Liú Zhá 劉札, said to him:
"Given your appearance,
you will reach this position later;
there is no need to admire it now."
Initially, he served as a junior officer
under Wú's Dà Sīmǎ Lù Kàng 吳大司馬陸抗.
Kàng 抗 marveled at his bravery and strategy,
and intended to promote him,
but feared that the public sentiment would not agree.
So he gathered all his generals,
and secretly had someone feign madness, drawing a knife and leaping and approaching.
All the generals at the banquet were frightened and fled.
Only Yàn 彥 remained unmoved.
He lifted a small table to defend himself.
Everyone was impressed by his courage,
and he was then promoted.
He gradually became Jiànpíng Tàishǒu 建平太守.
At that time, Wáng Jùn 王濬 was preparing to invade Wú 吳,
building ships in Shǔ 蜀.
Yàn 彥 became aware of this
and requested increased troops for defense.
Hào 晧 did not comply.
Yàn 彥 then immediately made an iron chain
to block the river passage.
When the army reached the border,
all cities along the river surrendered at the mere sight of them,
or were captured after being attacked.
Only Yàn 彥 held firm.
The large army attacked him but could not overcome him.
So they retreated their camp and showed him respect.
When Wú 吳 fell,
Yàn 彥 finally surrendered.
Emperor Wǔ 武 made him Jīnchéng Tàishǒu 金城太守.
The Emperor once casually asked Xuē Yíng 薛瑩:
"Why did Sūn Hào 孫晧's state fall?"
Yíng 瑩 replied:
"Guīmìng Hóu Chén Hào 歸命侯臣晧, when ruling Wú 吳,
kept small-minded people close,
arbitrarily imposed punishments,
did not trust his great ministers and generals,
and everyone was anxious and fearful,
each feeling insecure.
The cause of its downfall
thus arose."
Later, the Emperor again asked Yàn 彥,
who replied:
"The Lord of Wú 吳 was brilliant,
and his chief ministers were wise and enlightened."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"If the ruler was brilliant and the ministers were wise,
why did the state perish?"
Yàn 彥 said:
"Heaven's blessing had come to an end,
and the Mandate of Heaven had shifted.
That is why Your Majesty captured him.
This was the will of Heaven,
how could it be due to human affairs!"
Zhāng Huá 張華 was present at the time
and said to Yàn 彥:
"You served as a general for Wú 吳
for many years,
yet were obscure and unknown.
I am truly puzzled by this."
Yàn 彥 retorted in a stern voice:
"Your Majesty knows me,
but you have not heard of me?"
The Emperor greatly praised him.
He was transferred to Dūnhuáng 敦煌,
where his prestige and kindness were greatly evident.
He was promoted to Yànmén Tàishǒu 雁門太守.
At that time, Shùnyáng Wáng Chàng 順陽王暢 was arrogant and unrestrained.
Previous Nèishǐ 內史 all falsely accused him of crimes.
When Yàn 彥 became Shùnyáng Nèishǐ 順陽內史,
Yàn 彥 conducted himself with integrity and led his subordinates well.
His authority and punishments were strict and solemn,
and everyone was awestruck.
Chàng 暢 could not falsely accuse him,
so he instead recommended him,
hoping he would leave his post.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍.
The Emperor once asked Yàn 彥:
"Who was greater between Lù Xǐ 陸喜 and Lù Kàng 陸抗?"
Yàn 彥 replied:
"In terms of moral virtue and reputation,
Kàng 抗 was not equal to Xǐ 喜;
in terms of achieving merits and accomplishments,
Xǐ 喜 was not equal to Kàng 抗."
Coincidentally, Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Táo Huáng 交州刺史陶璜 died,
and Yàn 彥 was appointed Nánzhōng Dūdū, Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ 南中都督、交州刺史.
He heavily rewarded Lù Jī 陸機 and his brothers.
Jī 機 was about to accept it,
but Yún 雲 said:
"Yàn 彥 was originally of humble status,
and was promoted by our late lord.
However, his reply to the edict was not good.
How can we accept it!"
Jī āt then stopped.
Because of this, they often disparaged him.
Chángshā Xiàolián Yǐn Yú 長沙孝廉尹虞 said to Jī āt and the others:
"Since ancient times, those who rose from humble origins
have even included emperors and kings,
let alone high officials.
For example, Hé Yuángàn 何元幹, Hóu Xiàomíng 侯孝明, Táng Rúzōng 唐儒宗, Zhāng Yìyǔn 張義允, etc.,
all rose from humble backgrounds,
and all served both internally and externally as regional governors,
without anyone criticizing them.
You disparage Shìzé 士則 endlessly
because his reply to the edict was slightly poor.
I fear that all the southerners will leave you,
and you will be left sitting alone."
Thereupon, Jī āt and the others began to understand,
and their disparaging remarks gradually ceased.
Initially,
after Táo Huáng's 陶璜 death,
the garrison troops of Jiǔzhēn 九真 rebelled,
driving away their Tàishǒu 太守.
The bandit leader Zhào Zhǐ 趙祉 besieged the commandery city.
Yàn 彥 completely suppressed them all.
He served in the garrison for over twenty years,
and his prestige and kindness were widely known,
bringing peace and stability to the southern province.
He formally requested to be replaced,
and was summoned to serve as Dàchángqiū 大長秋.
He died in office.
Zhāng Guāng 張光
Zhāng Guāng 張光, courtesy name Jǐngwǔ 景武,
was a native of Zhōngwǔ 鍾武, Jiāngxià 江夏.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
with bright eyebrows and eyes,
and a beautiful voice.
In his youth, he was a commandery official.
His family had hereditary *bùqǔ* 部曲.
He achieved merit as a Yámén Jiàng 牙門將 in the campaign against Wú 吳,
was promoted to Jiāngxià Xībù Dūwèi 江夏西部都尉,
and then transferred to Běidì Dūwèi 北地都尉.
Initially,
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) was the Area Commander of Guānzhōng (關中).
The Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) rebelled.
Tàishǒu (太守) Zhāng Sǔn (張損) was killed in battle,
and few of the county and district officials and soldiers survived.
Guāng (光), with over a hundred men, garrisoned the north of Mǎlánshān (馬蘭山).
The rebels besieged them for over a hundred days.
Guāng (光) encouraged and roused his generals and soldiers,
and repeatedly launched surprise attacks against the rebels,
defeating them.
Guāng (光), due to his small force and distant location,
believed he would be defeated and annihilated.
At that time, Liáng Wáng Róng (梁王肜) sent Sīmǎ (司馬) Suǒ Jìng (索靖) with troops to welcome Guāng (光).
The entire army wept in sorrow,
and then returned to Cháng'ān (長安).
Róng (肜) memorialized about Guāng (光), saying:
"Being in a place of utter siege,
he possessed the loyalty of Gěng Gōng (耿恭).
He should be highly commended and rewarded,
to demonstrate encouragement."
Thereupon, he was promoted to Tàishǒu (太守) of Xīnpíng (新平),
and granted a drum and fife band.
At the time, the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yōngzhōu (雍州), Liú Chén (劉忱), received a secret imperial edict to attack Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (河間王顒).
Guāng (光) raised troops to assist Chén (忱).
Chén (忱) at the time entrusted responsibility to the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qínzhōu (秦州), Huángfǔ Chóng (皇甫重).
Chóng (重), considering himself from a great family in Guānxī (關西),
always slighted Guāng (光) in his heart,
and many of his plans were not adopted.
When the armies of the two prefectures were routed
and captured by Yǒng (顒),
Yǒng (顒) said to Guāng (光):
"When you raised troops earlier, what strategy did you intend to employ?"
Guāng (光), with a solemn expression, replied:
"It was simply that Liú Yōngzhōu (劉雍州) did not adopt my humble plan,
which is why Your Highness is able to have this day."
Yǒng (顒) admired him,
and invited him to a banquet that lasted the entire day,
then memorialized for him to be appointed Yòuwèi Sīmǎ (右衞司馬).
When Chén Mǐn (陳敏) rebelled,
Guāng (光) was appointed Tàishǒu (太守) of Shùnyáng (順陽),
and additionally Lingjiāng Jiāngjūn (陵江將軍),
leading five thousand infantry and cavalry to Jīngzhōu (荊州) to suppress him.
The Cìshǐ (刺史) Liú Hóng (劉弘) respected and highly regarded Guāng (光),
calling him "the outstanding talent of Nánchǔ (南楚)".
At that time, Tàishǒu (太守) Táo Kǎn (陶侃) of Jiāngxià (江夏) was confronting Mǐn's (敏) general Qián Duān (錢端) at Chángqí (長岐).
Before the battle,
Tàishǒu (太守) Pí Chū (皮初) of Xiāngyáng (襄陽) commanded the infantry,
making Guāng (光) set up an ambush to await them.
Tàishǒu (太守) Miáo Guāng (苗光) of Wǔlíng (武陵) commanded the navy,
hiding warships in the Miǎnshuǐ (沔水).
Pí Chū (皮初) and others engaged the rebels,
Guāng (光) launched his ambush troops to respond,
and both land and water forces pressed forward,
the rebel army was utterly defeated.
Hóng (弘) memorialized that Guāng (光) had performed extraordinary meritorious service,
and he was promoted to Cáiguān Jiāngjūn (材官將軍) and Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州).
Before this,
two thousand odd families from Qínzhōu (秦州), including Dèng Dìng (鄧定) and others,
suffering from hunger, fled into Hànzhōng (漢中),
and occupied Chénggù (成固),
gradually becoming bandits and raiders.
The Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州), Zhāng Yīn (張殷), sent Tàishǒu (太守) Zhāng Yàn (張燕) of Bāxī (巴西) to suppress them.
Dìng (定), in distress,
falsely offered to surrender to Yàn (燕),
and also presented Yàn (燕) with gold and silver.
Yàn (燕) was pleased,
and slowed his army for him.
Dìng (定) secretly allied with Lǐ Xióng (李雄).
Xióng (雄) sent troops to rescue Dìng (定).
Yàn (燕) retreated,
and Dìng (定) then advanced to press Hànzhōng (漢中).
Tàishǒu (太守) Dù Zhèngchōng (杜正沖) fled east to Wèixīng (魏興).
Yīn (殷) also abandoned his post and fled.
Guāng (光) was unable to proceed to his prefecture,
and stayed in Wèixīng (魏興).
He then allied with the various Prefects to plan an advance.
Yàn (燕) openly declared:
"Hànzhōng (漢中) is desolate and ruined,
and close to great bandits.
The matter of its recovery
should await a hero."
Zhèngchōng (正沖) said:
"Zhāng Yàn (張燕) accepted gold and silver from the rebels,
did not promptly advance to suppress them,
blocked the army and slowed the enemy,
leading to the loss of Hànzhōng (漢中).
This is truly Yàn's (燕) crime."
Guāng (光) then became angry,
and shouted at Yàn (燕) to come out,
then beheaded him and displayed his head to the public.
He pacified the devastated and ruined areas,
and the common people were pleased and submitted.
Guāng (光) then returned to garrison Hànzhōng (漢中).
At that time, the remnants of the rebel Wáng Rú (王如), Lǐ Yùn (李運) and Yáng Wǔ (楊武) and others,
led over three thousand families from Xiāngyáng (襄陽) into Hànzhōng (漢中).
Guāng (光) sent Cānjūn (參軍) Jìn Miǎo (晉邈) to lead troops to block them at Huángjīn (黃金).
Miǎo (邈) accepted a heavy bribe from Yùn (運),
and advised Guāng (光) to accept Yùn (運).
Guāng (光) followed Miǎo's (邈) advice,
and allowed them to reside in Chénggù (成固).
Later, Miǎo (邈), seeing that Yùn (運) possessed many valuable goods,
and also wishing to seize them,
again spoke to Guāng (光), saying:
"Yùn's (運) followers do not engage in farming,
but only manufacture weapons.
Their intentions are unfathomable;
they can be caught unawares and taken."
Guāng (光) again believed him.
He sent Miǎo's (邈) troops to attack Yùn (運),
but they did not succeed.
Guāng (光) requested troops from the Dī (氐) king Yáng Màosōu (楊茂搜).
Màosōu (茂搜) sent his son Nándí (難敵) to assist him.
Nándí (難敵) demanded goods from Guāng (光),
but Guāng (光) did not give them.
Yáng Wǔ (楊武) then heavily bribed Nándí (難敵),
saying to him:
"All the valuables of the refugees are with Guāng (光).
Now to attack us
is not as good as attacking Guāng (光)."
Nándí (難敵) was greatly pleased,
and openly claimed to assist Guāng (光),
but secretly sided with Yùn (運).
Guāng (光) was unaware of this,
and sent his son Yuán (援) to lead troops to assist Miǎo (邈).
Yùn (運) and Nándí (難敵) jointly attacked Miǎo (邈) and others.
Yuán (援) was struck by a stray arrow and died,
and the rebels then grew greatly in strength.
Guāng (光) fortified the city and held it firmly,
from summer until winter,
becoming enraged and falling ill.
His subordinates and the common people all urged Guāng (光) to retreat to Wèixīng (魏興).
Guāng (光) pressed his sword and said:
"I have received great kindness from the state.
If I cannot eliminate the bandits,
now to die by myself
would be like ascending to immortality.
How can I retreat?"
His voice failed, and he died,
at the age of fifty-five.
The common people wept in sorrow,
and those near and far lamented his passing.
He had two sons: Jiǒng (炅) and Mài (邁).
Jiǒng (炅) was young when he was appointed Táizǎi Yuàn (太宰掾).
Mài (邁) possessed great talent and strategy,
and had the demeanor of his father.
The people of the prefecture supported Mài (邁) to temporarily lead the affairs of the prefecture,
and he died in battle with the rebels.
Biéjià (別駕) Fàn Kuàng (范曠) and Dūhù (督護) Wáng Qiáo (王喬) escorted Guāng's (光) wife and sons,
led his remaining troops,
and returned to occupy Wèixīng (魏興).
Later, Yìyáng Tàishǒu (義陽太守) Rèn Yīn (任愔) became Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州),
and Guāng's (光) wife and sons returned to their home county.
Nánpíng Tàishǒu (南平太守) Yìng Zhān (應詹) reported to Dūdu (都督) Wáng Dūn (王敦),
stating:
"Guāng (光) in Liángzhōu (梁州) was able to revive the fallen and continue the broken,
his prestige shook Bāhàn (巴漢).
At a time when the central plains were overturned,
and frontier garrisons were lost,
with no external assistance,
and lacking internal resources and provisions,
he, with a few against many,
resisted for years,
maintaining his integrity without wavering.
He should be posthumously honored and granted a distinguished title,
to comfort both the living and the dead."
Dūn (敦) was unable to comply.
Zhào Yòu (趙誘)
Zhào Yòu (趙誘), courtesy name Yuánsūn (元孫),
was a native of Huáinán (淮南).
His family was prominent for its generals.
He was appointed Zhǔbù (主簿) by the prefecture.
At that time, the Cìshǐ, Xī Lóng, was summoned by Qí Wáng Jǐong,
who ordered him to raise an army to attack Zhào Wáng Lún.
Lóng wished to obey the summons and raise an army for the righteous cause,
but all his sons and nephews were in Luòyáng.
He considered waiting to see the outcome,
but feared being attacked by Jǐong.
He was hesitant,
and so he gathered his officials for a discussion.
Yòu persuaded Lóng, saying:
"Zhào Wáng has usurped the throne,
a crime that sickens the whole empire.
Now the righteous army has risen like a storm,
and his defeat is certain.
For your sake, my Lord,
it would be best to personally lead elite troops
directly to Xǔchāng.
This is the best strategy.
Otherwise,
you could remain behind
and send a fierce general to lead troops to join the alliance.
This is also a middle strategy.
To merely send a small contingent to follow and assist is
a poor strategy."
Lóng said:
"I have received favors from two emperors,
and I wish to show no partiality.
I merely wish to protect my province."
Yòu, along with Zhìzhōng Liú Bǎo and Zhǔbù Zhāng Bāo, among others, remonstrated with Lóng:
"If you do not assist anyone,
then chaos and difficulty will arise,
and the province cannot be protected."
Lóng remained indecisive,
and was subsequently harmed by his subordinates.
Yòu returned home
and shut his door, not going out.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Wáng Dūn appointed him as Cānjūn,
and promoted him to Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He joined Gān Zhuó and Zhōu Fǎng in attacking Huá Yì,
and defeated him.
He also attacked Dù Tāo at Xīxiāng.
In the early Táixīng era,
he again attacked Tāo with Zhuó,
and destroyed him.
For his accumulated merits, he was granted the title Píng'ā Xiàn Hóu,
and replaced Táo Kǎn as Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
At that time, Dù Zēng welcomed Dìwǔ Yī in Jīngzhōu and rebelled.
Dūn sent Yòu and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu Zhū Guǐ to resist them.
Yī had been dispatched by Mǐn Dì,
and furthermore, had a good reputation at the time,
so the people of Jīngchǔ rallied to him.
Yòu and others fought hard but were all killed.
Dūn greatly mourned and regretted their loss.
He submitted a memorial requesting posthumous titles of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
and a posthumous name of Jìng.
His son Gōng
died with Yòu.
When Yuán Dì became Jìn Wáng,
he issued an order granting Gōng the posthumous title of Xīnchāng Tàishǒu.
Gōng's younger brother was Yìn,
courtesy name Bóshū.
Wáng Dūn sent Zhōu Fǎng to attack Dù Zēng,
and Yìn requested to accompany him.
Fǎng was wary of Zēng's strength
and intended to first use Yìn to bait Zēng,
so that his forces would be exhausted before he attacked them.
Yìn captured many enemy heads.
Wáng Dǎo appointed him as Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When Nándùn Wáng Zōng rebelled,
Yìn killed Zōng.
Thereupon, Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng both relied heavily on him.
He was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to Xīyùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and died in office.
The historian says: Loyalty is an excellent virtue,
and integrity is serving one's lord.
They sacrificed their lives for the state,
maintaining their integrity through danger and ease.
Luó Xiàn and Téng Xiū,
entered officialdom with pure intentions,
took on command at Bādōng,
and raised their banners beyond the mountain passes.
When the imperial destiny declined and fell apart,
and the capital was lost,
they wept at Bāqiū,
and mourned greatly at the capital pavilion.
The loyal and heroic figures of ancient times
are rarely equal to these!
Xiàoxīng's wisdom and courage,
Xuánwēi's martial prowess,
annihilated the vile enemies in Héxī,
and controlled the fierce chieftain north of Kēng.
They foresaw Yáng Xīn's inevitable defeat,
and criticized Yáng Jùn's swift misfortune.
Táo Huáng and Wú Yàn,
advanced with exceptional speed.
Máo Jiǒng respected their profound strategies,
and Lù Kàng marvelled at their excellent plans.
For their crucial roles,
their pure principles are remembered from afar;
as ministers of war,
their reputation is even more esteemed.
Jǐngwǔ
was a distinguished scholar from Nánchǔ;
Yuánsūn
came from a long line of generals.
They faced death as if ascending to immortality,
and expressed their sincerity in the best strategies.
In the end, both perished,
but their integrity endures.
A eulogy says: Xiàn resided in Yùlěi,
his talent and knowledge widely praised.
Xiū went to Shímén,
where his benevolent governance was clearly demonstrated.
Xiàoxīng and Xuánwēi,
their conduct was beyond reproach.
They fulfilled the rites for the common graves,
and criticized the Yáng family.
Huáng's strategies were exceptional,
Yàn's talent was outstanding.
They covertly attacked Dǒng,
and impressed Xuē with their military display.
As for Zhào and Zhāng,
their divine strategies were multifaceted.
They served as officials in Běidì,
and achieved merit in Xīxiāng.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 28: Zhōu Chǔ (son Pǐ; Pǐ's son Xié; Pǐ's younger brother Zhá; Zhá's older brother's son Yán)
Zhōu Chǔ, courtesy name Zǐyǐn,
was a native of Yángxiàn, Yìxīng.
His father, Fáng,
was Wú's Póyáng Tàishǒu.
Chǔ was orphaned young,
and before he reached manhood,
his physical strength was extraordinary.
He loved to ride horses and hunt,
did not cultivate minor virtues,
and indulged his desires,
causing trouble for the local communities.
Chǔ knew that he was disliked by people,
and thus he resolved to reform himself,
saying to the elders:
"Now the weather is mild and the harvest is abundant,
why are you not happy?"
The elders sighed and said:
"With three scourges still present,
what happiness can there be!"
Chǔ asked:
"What do you mean?"
They replied:
"The white-browed fierce beast of South Mountain,
the flood dragon under Long Bridge,
and you, make the three."
Chǔ said:
"If these are the troubles,
I can remove them."
The elders said:
"If you can remove them,
it will be a great celebration for the entire commandery,
not merely the removal of a harm."
Chǔ then entered the mountain and shot the fierce beast,
then plunged into the water to fight the flood dragon.
The dragon sometimes submerged, sometimes surfaced,
traveling for tens of li,
and Chǔ followed it.
After three days and three nights,
people believed him dead
and all congratulated each other.
Chǔ indeed killed the dragon and returned,
and hearing the villagers congratulating each other,
he first realized how deeply he was disliked.
He then went to Wú to seek the two Lùs.
At that time, Jī was not present,
so he met Yún,
and explained his situation in full,
saying:
"I wish to reform myself, but my years have already slipped by,
I fear it will be too late."
Yún said:
"The ancients valued hearing the Way in the morning and changing by evening.
Your future path is still viable;
rather, you should worry about lacking resolve,
why worry about your reputation not being famous!"
Chǔ then resolved to study diligently,
possessing literary talent,
and a spirit for righteousness and heroism.
His words were always faithful, sincere, and self-restrained.
After a year,
he was invited by both the province and the prefecture.
He served Wú as Dōngguān Zuǒchéng.
In the late reign of Sūn Hào,
he served as Wúnán Dū.
When Wú was pacified,
Wáng Hún ascended the palace in Jiànyè to pour wine.
Once he was well into his cups,
he said to the people of Wú:
"You, the remnants of a fallen state,
are you not sorrowful?"
Chǔ replied:
"At the end of Hàn, there was fragmentation and collapse,
and the Three Kingdoms stood in a tripod formation.
Wèi fell earlier,
and Wú perished later.
The sorrow of a fallen state,
how could it be for just one person!"
Hún showed a look of shame.
Upon entering Luò,
he was gradually promoted to Administrator of Xīnpíng.
He pacified and harmonized the Róng and Dí,
and the rebellious Qiāng returned to allegiance.
The people of Yōng admired him for this.
He was transferred to Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
The commandery had many protracted lawsuits,
some remaining undecided for over thirty years.
Chǔ thoroughly investigated their merits and demerits,
and resolved them all in a single day.
He resigned and returned home due to his mother's old age.
Soon after, he was appointed Internal Historian of Chǔ,
but before he took office,
he was summoned to be appointed as Sànqí Chángshì.
Chǔ said:
"Ancient people would decline a major post but not a minor one."
So he first went to Chǔ.
The commandery had just experienced chaos and war,
with old and new inhabitants living mixed together,
and customs were not unified.
Chǔ diligently taught righteousness,
and also collected and buried unowned corpses and bones lying in the fields.
Only then did he proceed with the summons,
and he was praised far and wide.
Upon serving as a close attendant,
he offered much advice and remonstrance.
He was promoted to Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
In all his impeachments,
he did not spare favored relatives.
Liángwáng Róng violated the law,
and Chǔ thoroughly investigated his case.
When the Dī people's Qí Wànnián rebelled,
the court officials, disliking Chǔ's strong integrity,
all said:
"Chǔ
is the son of a famous general of Wú,
loyal, fervent, and resolute."
So he was ordered to serve under Xiàhóu Jùn in the western expedition.
The General Who Pacifies the Waves, Sūn Xiù, knowing that Chǔ was going to die,
said to him:
"You have an elderly mother;
you could use this as a reason to decline."
Chǔ said:
"The way of loyalty and filial piety,
how can both be perfectly achieved?
Having left my parents to serve my lord,
how can my parents then have a son?
Today is where I shall die."
Wànnián heard this and
said:
"Prefect Zhōu once governed Xīnpíng.
I know his character;
he possesses both civil and military talents.
If he comes with his own independent command,
he cannot be resisted.
But if he is subject to others' control,
he will be an easy capture."
Later, Liángwáng Róng became the General-in-Chief of the Western Expedition and Supreme Commander of all military affairs in Guānzhōng.
Chǔ knew that Róng bore a grudge and
would certainly trap him.
Believing that as a subject, he should exhaust his loyalty,
he ought not to shrink back.
So, with sorrow and indignation, he set off,
determined not to return alive.
The Director of the Central Secretariat, Chén Zhǔn, knowing that Róng intended to unleash his long-standing resentment,
spoke to the court, saying:
"Jùn and Liángwáng are both imperial relatives,
not the caliber of generals.
They seek no fame in advancing,
nor fear blame in retreating.
Zhōu Chǔ, a man from Wú,
is loyal, brave, and resolute.
With enemies and no support,
he will surely lose his life.
It is advisable to order Mèng Guān with ten thousand elite soldiers
to serve as Chǔ's vanguard;
he will surely be able to exterminate the bandits.
Otherwise,
Róng will make Chǔ the vanguard,
and his defeat is certain."
The court did not follow this advice.
At that time, the rebels were encamped at Liángshān,
with a force of seventy thousand.
Jùn, however, forced Chǔ to attack them with five thousand soldiers.
Chǔ said:
"Without a rear guard, the army will certainly be annihilated,
even if I die, it will bring shame upon the country."
Róng again ordered Chǔ to advance and attack.
So he, along with General Who Awe-Inspires the Military Lú Bō and Inspector of Yōngzhōu Xiè Xì, attacked Wànnián at Liùmò.
Before the battle,
Chǔ's soldiers had not eaten.
Róng urged them to advance quickly,
and cut off their rear support.
Chǔ knew he would surely be defeated,
and composed a poem, saying:
"Departing, departing, worldly affairs are done.
I spur my horse to observe the western Róng.
Wild herbs and reeds are sweet as fine grain,
I aim to achieve a noble end."
Having spoken, he fought.
From dawn until dusk,
he beheaded tens of thousands.
His bowstrings snapped and arrows ran out.
Bō and Xì did not come to his rescue.
His attendants urged him to retreat.
Chǔ grasped his sword and said:
"This is the day for me to demonstrate my loyalty and give my life.
Why retreat?
Moreover, ancient good generals, when ordered,
would break open the ominous gate to sally forth,
meaning there is only advance, no retreat.
Now, all the armies have betrayed their trust,
and the situation will surely not improve.
As a high minister, for me to sacrifice my life for the country,
is it not proper!"
Thereupon he fought with all his might and perished.
He was posthumously granted the title General Who Pacifies the West,
awarded a million coins,
an acre of burial land,
fifty *mǔ* of land in the capital city for a residence,
and also five *qǐng* of nearby land for his family.
An imperial edict stated:
"Chǔ's mother is old,
and moreover, a person from afar.
I constantly pity and remember her.
Provide her with medicine, wine, and rice,
granted for the rest of her years."
Chǔ authored "Silent Words" in thirty chapters and "Record of Local Customs,"
and also compiled the "Book of Wú."
At that time, Pān Yuè, by imperial decree, composed a poem on Guānzhōng, saying:
"Zhōu carried out his teacher's command,
his body perished by the Qí axe.
Though the man is gone,
his integrity is upheld."
Also, the Colonel of Western Róng, Yán Zǎn, also presented a poem, saying:
"Zhōu completely fulfilled his integrity,
his good name ceaseless.
Though his body has perished,
his name is recorded by good historians."
When Emperor Yuán became the King of Jìn,
and was about to confer a posthumous title upon Chǔ,
the Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Hè Xún, deliberated, saying:
"Chǔ embodied virtue, was pure and upright,
with outstanding talent and magnanimity.
He successively governed four commanderies,
bringing peace to the people and establishing governance.
Upon entering service as an official,
his integrity was unyielding.
In battle, he sacrificed himself,
facing danger and giving his life. These are the eminent achievements of a loyal and virtuous man,
and the profound integrity of a martyr.
According to the rules for posthumous titles, 'unswerving in upholding virtue' is called Xiào (Filial)."
So he was given this posthumous title.
He had three sons: Qǐ, Jìng, and Zhá.
Jìng died young;
Qǐ and Zhá were both renowned.
Qǐ's courtesy name was Xuānpèi.
He was resolute and decisive, having his father's demeanor,
but his literary talent was not equal.
He kept to himself and was pure,
not engaging in frivolous social interactions.
Scholars and friends alike respected and feared him from afar,
hence his renown was great in his region.
When he came of age,
he was invited by the province and commandery,
but did not accept.
When the Inspector first arrived,
he summoned him to be Biejia Congshi.
Humbly and with full ceremony,
only then did he respond to the summons.
He was repeatedly recommended to the prime minister's office,
nominated as Xiùcái,
and appointed Yìláng.
In the beginning of Tàiníng [reign era],
the rebellious brigands Zhāng Chāng and Qiū Shěn, among others, gathered a multitude in Jiāngxià,
and the common people followed them as if returning home.
Emperor Huì sent Supervisor of the Army Huá Hóng to suppress them,
but he was defeated at Zhàngshān.
Zhāng Chāng and his followers became increasingly powerful,
killing the General who Guards the South, Yáng Yī,
the Grand General who Suppresses the South and King of Xīnyě, Xīn, and others;
everywhere they went, garrisons were overrun.
Zhāng Chāng’s separate detachment leader, Fēng Yún, attacked Xúzhōu,
and Shí Bīng attacked Yángzhōu.
The Inspector Chén Huī fled,
and Shí Bīng then seized control of the Yáng territory.
Zhōu Qǐ secretly intended to suppress Shí Bīng,
and covertly allied with the former Administrator of Nánpíng, Wáng Jǔ.
Together, they nominated the Administrator of Wúxīng, Gù Mì, to be the Grand Supervisor of military affairs for the nine commanderies of Yángzhōu,
and with the gentry of Jiāngdōng, they raised a righteous army.
They executed Qū Shān, whom Shí Bīng had appointed as Administrator of Wúxīng, and various Chief Clerks.
Shí Bīng sent his general Qiāng Dú to lead tens of thousands of men to resist Zhōu Qǐ.
Zhōu Qǐ slew Qiāng Dú on the battlefield.
At that time, Right General Chén Mǐn, leading his forces from Guǎnglíng, assisted Zhōu Qǐ,
and slew Shí Bīng’s separate detachment leader, Zhào, at Wúhú.
He then advanced with Zhōu Qǐ to attack Shí Bīng at Jiànkāng.
Shí Bīng fled north and surrendered to Fēng Yún.
Fēng Yún’s Sīmǎ, Zhāng Tǒng, executed Fēng Yún and Shí Bīng, then surrendered,
thus pacifying both Xú and Yáng.
Zhōu Qǐ did not claim credit or reward,
but dispersed his troops and returned home.
Chén Mǐn rebelled in Yángzhōu,
appointing Zhōu Qǐ as Administrator of Ānfēng,
and promoting him to a General of the Fourth Rank.
Zhōu Qǐ claimed illness and did not go.
He secretly sent an envoy to inform the General who Guards the East, Liú Zhǔn,
ordering him to dispatch troops to the river,
while he would act as an internal confederate,
cutting his hair as a token of sincerity.
Liú Zhǔn, who was in Shòuchūn,
sent his Supervising Commandant Héng Yàn to lead troops eastward.
At that time, Chén Mǐn’s younger brother, Chǎng, was General of Guǎngwǔ and Administrator of Lìyáng,
and had appointed Qián Guǎng of Wúxīng as his Sīmǎ.
Zhōu Qǐ secretly encouraged Qián Guǎng to kill Chǎng.
Zhōu Qǐ, along with Gù Róng and Gān Zhuó, among others, attacked Chén Mǐn with their forces.
Chén Mǐn’s troops routed and collapsed,
and he fled north on a single horse.
He was captured in the territory of Jiāngchéng
and executed at Jiànkāng,
his three clans exterminated.
When the King of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, heard of his reputation,
he summoned him to be his Adjutant.
An imperial edict appointed him as a Láng in the Department of the Grand Secretariat and a Láng of the Mounted Retainers,
but he did not take any of these posts.
When Emperor Yuán first settled in the Jiangzuǒ region,
he appointed Zhōu Qǐ as a Clerk in the Granary Department.
Initially,
Qián Zèng, a man from Wúxīng, also raised a righteous army to suppress Chén Mǐn.
Wang Yuè ordered him to be General who Establishes Martial Might,
and sent him to lead his subordinates to gather in the capital.
When Qián Zèng reached Guǎnglíng,
he heard that Liú Cōng was pressing upon Luòyáng,
and, fearing difficulty, dared not advance.
The emperor urged him with military deadlines,
whereupon Qián Zèng planned a rebellion.
At that time, Wáng Dūn was being transferred to the Department of the Grand Secretariat
and was due to be conscripted to go west with Qián Zèng.
Qián Zèng secretly intended to kill Wáng Dūn
and use that as a pretext for his uprising.
When Wáng Dūn heard of this,
he fled to inform the emperor.
Qián Zèng then killed the Colonel in Charge of Expenditure, Chén Fēng,
burned the government storehouses,
and proclaimed himself Grand General who Pacifies the West and Grand Supervisor of Eight Provinces.
He abducted Sūn Hào’s son, Chōng,
and enthroned him as King of Wú,
but shortly thereafter killed him.
He came to raid Zhōu Qǐ’s county.
The emperor sent General Guō Yì and Commandant Sòng Diǎn, among others, to suppress him,
but with too few troops, they dared not advance.
Zhōu Qǐ again rallied his local righteous militia,
and advanced with Guō Yì and others
to suppress Qián Zèng,
executing him
and sending his head to Jiànkāng.
Zhōu Qǐ stabilized Jiāngnán three times,
restoring the imperial strategy.
The emperor commended his achievements,
appointing Zhōu Qǐ as Acting General who Establishes Awe and Administrator of Wúxīng,
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Wúchéng County.
After the disturbances in Wúxīng,
the common people suffered from famine,
and brigands roamed openly.
Zhōu Qǐ possessed great authority and benevolence,
and the common people respected and loved him.
Within a year,
the region was peaceful and tranquil.
The emperor, seeing that Zhōu Qǐ had repeatedly raised righteous armies
and that his achievements and sincerity were both outstanding,
then designated Yángxiàn, the western township of Chángchéng, and Yǒngshì of Dānyáng as a separate Yìxīng Commandery,
to glorify his merits.
Zhōu Qǐ’s clan was powerful and flourishing,
and the people's hearts turned towards them,
which made the emperor suspicious and apprehensive.
At that time, gentry from the Central Plains assisted and supported the imperial enterprise,
but Zhōu Qǐ felt that he was not being properly utilized,
harboring internal resentment and grievances.
Moreover, he was slighted by Diāo Xié,
and his shame and anger intensified.
At that time, Wáng Huī of Dōnglái, Libationer to the General who Guards the East, was also insulted by Zhōu Yǐ.
He then secretly conspired with Zhōu Qǐ to eliminate the powerful officials,
proposing that Zhōu Qǐ and Dài Ruòsī, along with various Southern gentry, jointly support the emperor to manage worldly affairs.
Before this,
the leaders of displaced people, Xià Tiě and others, resided in the Huáishì region.
Wáng Huī secretly wrote to Xià Tiě,
telling him to raise an army,
while he and Zhōu Qǐ would respond from the Sānwú region.
At the beginning of Jiànxīng [reign era],
Xià Tiě had already gathered several hundred men.
The Administrator of Línhuái, Cài Bào, executed Xià Tiě and reported it.
When Wáng Huī heard of Xià Tiě’s death,
he feared punishment
and fled to Zhōu Qǐ.
Zhōu Qǐ killed him
and buried him in a pigsty.
The emperor heard of it but kept it secret,
summoning Zhōu Qǐ to be Sīmǎ to the General who Guards the East.
Before he arrived,
he was again reassigned as General who Establishes Martial Might and Administrator of Nánjùn.
When Zhōu Qǐ departed south,
he reached Wúhú,
and then another order was issued stating:
"Zhōu Qǐ's family has been loyal and distinguished for generations,
and his righteousness and sincerity are evident,
which I admire and delight in.
Now I appoint him as Libationer of Military Counsel,
with his General title remaining as before,
and he is promoted to Duke.
His emoluments, ranks, and subordinates shall all be according to the precedent for founding a state."
Zhōu Qǐ was angered by these changes,
and also knew that his plot had been revealed.
He then died from sorrow and indignation, with a carbuncle on his back,
at the age of fifty-six.
As he was about to die,
he said to his son Xié:
"Those 'cāng' children killed me.
If you can avenge this,
then you are truly my son."
The people of Wú called the people from the Central Plains
"cāng" [a derogatory term],
hence the remark.
He was posthumously granted the title General who Aids the State,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngliè (Loyal and Illustrious).
His son Xié succeeded him.
Xié’s courtesy name was Yànhé.
He often kept his father’s words in mind.
At that time, many officials and gentry from the Central Plains who had lost their posts and territories due to the chaos came to seek refuge,
and many held prominent positions,
governing the Wú people.
The Wú people were quite resentful.
Xié, taking advantage of this, wanted to raise an army,
and secretly allied with Xú Fù, the Administrator of Merit in Wúxīng Commandery.
Xú Fù’s family had private retainers.
