Xié had Xú Fù falsely claim to be acting on the orders of his uncle Zhá to gather troops.
Brave and unruly individuals eagerly joined them,
under the pretext of suppressing Wáng Dǎo and Diāo Xié.
Sūn Bì, a relative of Sūn Hào, also raised an army in Guǎngdé to support them.
Xú Fù killed Yuán Xiù, the Administrator of Wúxīng,
and had several thousand men,
intending to enthrone Zhá as their leader.
At that time, Zhá had returned home due to illness.
When he heard of this, he was greatly alarmed
and reported the rebellion to Kǒng Kǎn, the Administrator of Yìxīng.
Xié knew that Zhá was not in agreement,
and dared not launch his army.
Xú Fù’s followers, fearing,
attacked Xú Fù
and killed him.
Sūn Bì’s forces also dispersed,
and Táo Yóu, the Administrator of Xuānchéng, eliminated them.
Emperor Yuán, considering the Zhōu family’s generations of prestige and influence,
which the Wú people respected,
did not thoroughly investigate the matter,
but treated them as before.
Xié, having been reprimanded by Zhá,
returned home dispirited,
indulging in extravagance and wantonness.
He often said to people:
"How long does a person live?
One should simply do as one pleases."
He died while serving as Administrator of Línhuái.
Xié’s younger brother, Yí,
was renowned in his youth.
Emperor Yuán appointed him as a Clerk in the Chancellor’s office,
but he died young.
Zhā's courtesy name was Xuān Jì.
He was naturally arrogant, treacherous, and fond of profit.
He was outwardly firm but inwardly weak.
In his youth, he regarded himself as a powerful local magnate,
and declined all appointments from the provinces and commanderies.
He was recommended as Xiàolián,
appointed as Lángzhōng, and Dàsīmǎ Qíwáng Jǒng's Cānjūn.
He was then sent out to serve as Jùróng Lìng,
and promoted to Wúguó Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn.
He was invited to be Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè's Cānjūn,
but did not accept.
For his功 in suppressing Qián Zèng,
he was granted the title of Zhāngpǔ Tínghóu.
When Yuán Dì became Chéngxiàng,
he memorialized to appoint Zhā as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Lìyáng Nèishǐ,
but he did not take up the post,
and was transferred to Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
After Xú Fù was pacified,
Zhā was appointed Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Nèishǐ.
Considering his past and present merits,
he was re-enfeoffed as Dōngqiān Xiànhóu,
promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Jiān Yángzhōu Jiāngběi Jūnshì, and Dōngzhōnglángjiàng,
stationed in Túzhōng.
Before taking up this post,
he was transferred to Yòujiāngjūn and Dūdū Shítóu Shuǐlù Jūnshì.
Zhā had a foot ailment
and was unable to perform the obeisance.
He steadfastly declined for a year.
The officials in charge impeached him,
and he reluctantly took up the position.
He was additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
Wáng Dūn raised an army to attack Shítóu,
and Zhā opened the gates to respond to Dūn,
which led to the defeat of the royal army.
Dūn transferred Zhā to Guānglùxūn,
and soon after appointed him Shàngshū.
After a short while,
he was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn and Kuàijī Nèishǐ.
At that time, Zhā's elder brother Jìng's son Mào was Jìnlíng Tàishǒu and Qīngliú Tínghóu.
Mào's younger brother Yán was Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and Wúxīng Nèishǐ.
Yán's younger brother Zàn was Dàjiāngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng and Wǔkāng Xiànhóu.
Zàn's younger brother Jìn was Tàizǐ Wénxué and Dūxiāng Hóu.
His second elder brother's son Xié was Línhuái Tàishǒu and Wūchéng Gōng.
Five nobles from Zhā's family,
all held prominent positions.
Among the gentry of Wú, their prominence
was unrivaled.
Wáng Dūn deeply resented them.
Later, when Yán's mother died,
thousands attended the funeral,
which made Dūn even more apprehensive.
When Dūn fell ill,
Qián Fèng, considering the Zhōu clan to be powerful,
and that their influence was comparable to Shěn Chōng's,
wished to rely on Chōng
and plotted to exterminate the Zhōu clan,
so that Chōng could monopolize power in Yáng.
He then persuaded Dūn, saying:
"For those who rule a state, the greatest concern is powerful coercion;
since ancient times, strife and calamity have always arisen from it.
Now, among the powerful families of Jiāngdōng, none are stronger than Zhōu and Shěn.
After your death,
these two clans will surely not remain peaceful.
The Zhōu clan is powerful and has many talented individuals;
it is advisable to deal with them first,
then your descendants can be secure,
and the state can be preserved."
Dūn accepted this advice.
At that time, there was a Taoist named Lǐ Tuō,
who used sorcery to delude the masses.
He claimed to be eight hundred years old,
and was therefore known as Lǐ Bābǎi.
He came from Zhōngzhōu to Jiànyè,
and used ghostly arts to cure illnesses.
He also bestowed official titles upon people,
and many people at the time believed in and served him.
His disciple Lǐ Hóng gathered followers in Qián Shān,
claiming that he was destined to be king according to a prophecy.
Therefore, Dūn instructed Lújiāng Tàishǒu Lǐ to accuse Zhā and his nephews of conspiring with Tuō to commit treason.
At that time, Yán was Dūn's Cányì Cānjūn.
He immediately killed Yán, Tuō, and Hóng in the camp,
and also sent Cānjūn Hè Luán to Shěn Chōng to completely slaughter Zhā's brothers and sons.
After this, he advanced his army to Kuàijī
and attacked Zhā.
Zhā was initially unaware.
Upon suddenly hearing of the approaching army,
he led several hundred men under his command to resist them,
but his troops scattered and he was killed.
Zhā was greedy for wealth and lustful,
solely focused on his property and business.
On the day the army arrived,
there were excellent weapons in the arsenal.
His subordinates requested to distribute them to the troops,
but Zhā was still reluctant to give them,
instead issuing worn-out ones.
Such was his parsimony,
which is why his soldiers would not fight for him.
When Dūn died,
Zhā and Yán's former subordinates all went to the imperial court to petition for the vindication of the Zhōu clan,
and that they should be granted posthumous honors.
The matter was referred to the Eight Chief Ministers.
Shàngshū Biàn Kǔn deliberated, stating:
“Zhā, during the Battle of Shítou, opened the gates and welcomed the invaders,
thus allowing the rebel Dūn to wreak havoc.
This was Zhā's responsibility.
Granting posthumous honors is not something I feel comfortable with.
Mào and Yán, brothers, should be restored to their original positions.”
Sītú Wáng Dǎo deliberated, stating:
“When Zhā was at Shítou,
his loyalty was to the state,
and his righteousness lay in sacrificing himself.
As for the events of that year,
from those of us who have been aware of things,
how could our sentiments differ from Zhā's!
This statement is truly evident to the Sacred Gaze.
Those who argue, seeing that the treachery and rebellion are now exposed,
then wish to claim that there were already signs of disloyalty in previous years.
Even if that were so,
it was something the masses at the time were not aware of.
Once they became aware of the wicked plot,
Zhā and us pledged our lives to the country,
to cease only after death.
Zhā also was soon executed.
When the imperial edict was issued,
and the great affair was settled,
he was simply considered a rebel.
Right and wrong were misplaced,
and there was no basis for action.
This is truly something the state should deeply regret.
I believe he should be treated in the same manner as Zhōu Yǐ, Dài Ruòsī, and others.”
Shàngshū Lìng Xī Jiàn deliberated, saying:
“In praising or condemning,
it is proper that the principles be clear and the precedents consistent.
Now, Zhōu and Dài were restored to their positions for dying as loyal martyrs,
while Zhōu Zhā is placed in the same category for opening the gates.
The circumstances are different, yet the rewards are the same,
which causes me doubt.
As the Sītú argued,
saying that in the events of that year, all those who were aware had sentiments no different from Zhā's,
this implies that right and wrong clearly existed.
In the past, Sòng Wén violated ritual,
and Huá Yuè suffered punishment for disloyalty;
Qí Líng favored his illegitimate son,
and Gāo Hòu were executed for complicity in his folly.
Comparing ancient times to the present,
Qiáowáng, Zhōu, and Dài should bear such blame.
How can they be granted posthumous honors and restored to their positions!
Now, based on what has already been clearly established,
it is clear that Zhā should be demoted and censured.”
Dǎo deliberated again, saying:
“Having read the Lord Director’s deliberation,
it must be that Zhā's opening of the gates was different from that of Qiáowáng, Zhōu, and Dài.
Now, when Zhā opened the gates,
was it merely a rumor,
or was it truly a fact?
To determine praise and censure based on rumor,
I think it would be better to investigate the circumstances and verify the evidence.
Those who argue say that Zhā knew Kuí and Xié were misgoverning,
and believed Dūn was rectifying the situation.
If he truly believed in the rectification,
and the treacherous ministers were eliminated,
that would be like banishing the Four Evils to elevate the majestic achievements of the ruler.
If this were the case,
then Zhā would have been loyal to the state.
Later, Dūn's depravity emerged unexpectedly,
and Zhā also closed his gates and did not join him,
leading to the extermination of his clan.
This means he died for righteousness.
Believing in Dūn's rectification at the time,
not anticipating his future great rebellion,
hating Kuí and Xié's misgovernment,
and not losing the integrity of a minister —
was Zhōu Zhā the only court official at that time who fit this description!
If everyone were deemed disloyal,
I fear that Qiáowáng, Zhōu, and Dài would be falsely accused.
Each defended the country with their lives,
which is also the integrity of a minister.
However, their views differed,
but they were expected to be loyal,
so this should be clarified.
As for the Lord Director's argument,
Sòng Huá and Qí Gāo were like Kuí and Xié.
In the past, during the turmoil of Zǐ Jiū,
Zhào Hū died for him,
while Guǎn Zhòng did not.
If death is considered virtuous,
then Guǎn Zhòng should be criticized;
if not dying is considered virtuous,
then Zhào Hū's death was a mistake.
How do the ancient canons account for both?
It is clear that the sentiment of loyalty is the same.
While death is one aspect of loyalty,
it is not necessary that all loyal acts must involve death.
The Han founder's dying wish stated:
‘Those who are not of the Liú clan shall not be enthroned;
those who are not meritorious officials shall not be enfeoffed as marquises.’
Whoever violates this command shall be punished by all under heaven.
Later, Empress Lǚ enthroned the Lǚ clan members.
Zhōu Bó complied,
while Wáng Líng openly contended in court.
Can this not be called loyalty?
Zhōu Bó executed the Lǚ clan and honored Wén,
securing the Hàn dynasty.
His loyalty was unsurpassed.
Then what more is there to say about Wáng Líng,
yet previous histories praise both as exemplary.
Thus, it is known that whether one dies or not,
contends or not,
if one examines the circumstances and fully understands the intent,
it cannot be determined by a single standard.
Moreover, Zhā’s posthumous title was decided after his death:
he defied the rebel party and followed the righteous,
suffered execution as a wicked evil,
and did not betray loyalty and righteousness—this is clear.”
Jiàn again rejected this, but
the imperial court ultimately followed Dǎo’s deliberation,
posthumously appointing Zhā as Wèiwèi,
and dispatching an envoy to offer a minor sacrifice with a pig and sheep.
Zhā’s eldest son, Dàn,
was a clerk in the Grand Tutor’s office.
His second son, Zhì,
was nominated as xiàolián but
did not take office.
Yán was outstanding and capable.
He was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
and later promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
During Xú Fù’s rebellion,
Yán’s cousin, Xù, also gathered followers in response.
Yuándì considered launching an expedition against them.
Wáng Dǎo believed:
“If the troops are too few, they won’t be able to control the bandits;
if too many are dispatched, the capital will be empty.
Huángmén Shìláng Zhōu Yán is extremely loyal and courageous,
and respected by the entire commandery.
I suggest simply sending Yán,
which will be enough to kill Xù.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict granted Yán a hundred strong men,
and he set out with light cavalry to return to Yángxiàn.
Yán immediately
took to the road, traveling day and night.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
as he was about to enter,
he met Xù at the gate.
Yán said to Xù:
“We should go together to Prefect Kǒng
to discuss something.”
Xù refused to enter,
but Yán forced him to go along.
Once seated,
Yán said to Tàishǒu Kǒng Kǎn:
“Why does Your Excellency allow a rebel to sit here?”
Xù was wearing a short knife in his belt.
He immediately grasped the blade and threatened Yán.
Yán shouted at the commandery messenger Wú Céng:
“Why don’t you act!”
Céng had courage and strength,
so he struck Xù with the pommel of his knife,
killing him.
Yán then wanted to execute Xié,
but Zhā refused,
laying the blame on his paternal cousin Shào,
who was then executed.
Yán did not return home to see his mother,
but instead rode straight away.
His mother anxiously chased after him.
Such was his public loyalty.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ.
When Wáng Dūn started his rebellion,
he was given the titles Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Dūdū of Kuàijī, Wúxīng, Yìxīng, Jìnlíng, Dōngyáng military affairs,
and led a naval force of three thousand men to attack Shěn Chōng.
But before he set out, the imperial army suffered a defeat.
When Yán heard that Zhā had opened the city gates to admit Dūn,
he expressed his indignation and sorrow through his words and demeanor.
Soon after, he was killed.
After Dūn was pacified,
he and Zhā were both posthumously reinstated to office.
Originally,
Yán built a five-bay house in Gūshú,
and all six beams suddenly sprang out and fell to the ground,
with the crossbeam standing precariously alone on the unjointed top of a pillar.
This was extremely dangerous,
and even with human effort,
it could not have happened.
Later, his clan was indeed destroyed.
Yán’s younger brother, Jìn,
was undisciplined in his youth.
He once encountered a servant girl of the Kǒng clan on Wūyī Dào in Jiànkāng.
At the time, he was riding in a carriage with two colleagues.
He immediately ordered his attendants to seize the servant girl and put her in his carriage.
Such was his violence and arrogance.
Zhōu Fǎng (son Fǔ; Fǔ’s son Chǔ; Chǔ’s son Qióng; Qióng’s son Xiāo; Fǔ’s younger brother Guāng; Guāng’s son Zhòngsūn)
Zhōu Fǎng, courtesy name Shìdá,
was originally from Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he fled to Jiāngnán,
and by Zhōu Fǎng's generation, it had been four generations.
When Wú was pacified,
his family settled in Xúnyáng, Lújiāng.
His grandfather, Zhuǎn,
was the Wēiyuǎn General of Wú.
His father, Mǐn,
was the Zuǒ Zhōngláng General.
Zhōu Fǎng was resolute and steadfast in his youth,
humble and capable of yielding.
He was decisive in action,
aiding the poor and relieving the destitute,
leaving no surplus wealth in his household.
He served as the xiàn Gōngcáo.
At that time, Táo Kǎn was a common official,
and Zhōu Fǎng recommended him as the Zhǔbù.
They became close friends,
and Zhōu Fǎng married his daughter to Kǎn's son, Zhān.
Zhōu Fǎng was investigated as Xiàolián,
and appointed Lángzhōng and Shàngjiǎ Prefect,
he did not take up any of these posts.
Local villagers stole and slaughtered Zhōu Fǎng's ox near his tomb.
When Zhōu Fǎng discovered this,
he secretly buried the meat
without letting anyone know.
When Emperor Yuán crossed the Jiāng,
he ordered Zhōu Fǎng to participate in military affairs of the Zhèndōng Army.
At that time, there was someone with the same name as Zhōu Fǎng,
whose crime deserved death.
An officer mistakenly arrested Zhōu Fǎng.
Zhōu Fǎng bravely fought the arresting officers;
dozens of them scattered and fled.
He then surrendered himself to the emperor,
who did not punish him.
Soon after, he was appointed Yángliè General,
leading 1,200 soldiers,
and stationed at Èlíng, Xúnyáng,
to suppress Huá Yì with Gān Zhuó and Zhào Yòu.
His subordinate Lìwǔ General Dīng Gān conspired with Fēng Yì, the Prefect of Wǔchāng, who was under Huá Yì.
Zhōu Fǎng arrested and executed Dīng Gān.
Fēng Yì came to attack Zhōu Fǎng,
but Zhōu Fǎng led his troops and decisively defeated him.
Fēng Yì fled to defend Cháisāng,
and Zhōu Fǎng pressed his advantage to pursue and attack.
Huá Yì sent his partisans Wáng Yuē and Fù Zhá, numbering over ten thousand, to assist Fēng Yì.
A great battle ensued at Pénkǒu,
and Wáng Yuē and others were again defeated.
Zhōu Fǎng and Gān Zhuó met at Péngzé
and fought with Zhū Jǔ and other naval commanders under Huá Yì,
defeating them again.
Huá Yì's general Zhōu Guǎng set fire to the city in response to Zhōu Fǎng.
Huá Yì's forces collapsed,
and Zhōu Fǎng captured Huá Yì
and executed him,
thus pacifying Jiāngzhōu.
The emperor appointed Zhōu Fǎng as Zhènwǔ General and Prefect of Xúnyáng,
and bestowed upon him drums, pipes, and a curved canopy.
He was again ordered to join other armies in suppressing Dù Tāo.
Dù Tāo used a counter-weighted lever device (júgāo) to attack the imperial fleet.
Zhōu Fǎng constructed long poles (chángqí chéng) to counter it,
rendering the júgāo harmless.
Meanwhile, the bandits secretly ambushed the imperial army from Qīngcǎohú,
and also dispatched their general Zhāng Yàn to seize Yùzhāng,
burning cities and towns.
Wáng Dūn, then stationed at Pénkǒu,
sent his Dūhù Miáo Ruí and Lǐ Shòu to Zhōu Fǎng's command
to jointly attack Zhāng Yàn.
Miáo Ruí engaged Zhāng Yàn in battle
at Shítou in Yùzhāng.
Zhāng Yàn's army retreated and fled.
Zhōu Fǎng led his subordinate general Lǐ Wǔ and others to pursue Zhāng Yàn,
defeating him
and personally beheading Zhāng Yàn on the battlefield.
At that time, Zhōu Fǎng was struck by a stray arrow,
breaking his two front teeth,
but his expression remained unchanged.
By evening,
Zhōu Fǎng and the bandits were separated by water.
The bandit forces were several times larger,
and Zhōu Fǎng knew he could not match them in strength.
So he secretly sent people out as if gathering firewood,
then formed his array, beat drums, and advanced,
shouting loudly,
"The Left Army has arrived!"
The soldiers all cheered "Long live!"
By night,
he ordered his army to spread many fires and eat.
The bandits thought that more imperial troops had arrived,
and retreated before dawn.
Zhōu Fǎng said to his generals,
"The bandits will certainly retreat,
but they will eventually realize that I have no reinforcements
and will return to ambush us.
We should hasten to cross the water to the north."
After crossing,
and breaking the bridge,
the bandits indeed arrived,
but were unable to advance due to the water.
Thus, he returned to Xiāngzhōu.
Zhōu Fǎng again sailed his fleet to Xiāngchéng.
His army reached Fùkǒu,
while Dù Tāo dispatched Dù Hóng to Hǎicūn.
At that time, Pénkǒu was in turmoil.
Zhōu Fǎng marched on foot to Cháisāng,
secretly crossed,
and fought with the bandits,
beheading several hundred.
The bandits retreated to defend Lúlíng.
Zhōu Fǎng pursued and defeated them,
and the bandits barricaded themselves within the city.
Soon after, their military provisions were plundered by the bandits,
so he retreated to Bāqiú.
Once provisions arrived,
he again besieged Dù Hóng in Lúlíng.
Dù Hóng threw many treasures outside the city.
The soldiers vied to pick them up,
and Dù Hóng took advantage of the resulting chaos to break through the encirclement and escape.
Zhōu Fǎng led his army in pursuit,
capturing countless saddles, horses, armor, and weapons.
Dù Hóng entered Nánkāng.
The Grand Administrator led troops to intercept and attack him,
defeating him again.
Dù Hóng fled to Línhè.
The emperor further promoted Zhōu Fǎng to Lóngxiáng General.
Wáng Dūn memorialized for him to be made Prefect of Yùzhāng,
with the additional title of Zhēngtǎo Dūdū,
and bestowed upon him the peerage of Xúnyáng Xiàn Hóu.
At that time, Zhāng Guāng (張光), the Inspector of Liángzhōu, died.
Emperor Mǐn appointed Shìzhōng Dìwǔ Yī (第五猗) as Grand General of the Expedition to the South,
supervising Jīng, Liáng, Yì, and Níng Provinces.
He departed from Wǔguān.
The rebel leaders Dù Zēng (杜曾), Zhì Zhān (摯瞻), Hú Hùn (胡混) and others all welcomed Yī,
pledging allegiance to him.
They amassed several tens of thousands of soldiers,
defeated Táo Kǎn (陶侃) at Shíchéng,
and attacked Píngnán General Xún Sōng (荀崧) at Wǎn.
They failed to capture it,
and led their troops towards Jiānglíng.
Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed his cousin, Yì (廙), as Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and ordered Duūhù (督護) Zhēnglǔ General Zhào Yōu (趙誘), Xiāngyáng Administrator Zhū Guǐ (朱軌), and Língjiāng General Huáng Jùn (黃峻) to attack Zēng.
They were heavily defeated at Nǚguānhú,
and Yōu and Guǐ were both killed.
Zēng then pursued Yì,
directly reaching Miǎnkǒu,
causing great devastation.
His might shook Jiāng and Miǎn.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) commanded Zhōu Fǎng (周訪) to attack him.
Fǎng had eight thousand men,
and advanced to Dùnyáng.
Zēng and his forces were in high spirits.
Fǎng said:
"To seize the enemy's morale first
is a good military strategy."
He ordered General Lǐ Dū (李督) to command the left flank,
Xǔ Cháo (許朝) to command the right flank,
and Fǎng himself led the central army,
raising his banners high.
Zēng, as expected, feared Fǎng and
first attacked the left and right flanks.
Zēng's bravery surpassed that of all three armies.
Fǎng was very displeased by this,
and personally shot pheasants behind the lines to calm his men.
He ordered his troops, saying:
"If one flank is defeated,
beat the drum three times;
if both flanks are defeated,
beat the drum six times."
Zhào Yìn (趙胤) led his father's remaining soldiers, attached to the left flank.
He fought bravely,
was defeated, but then regrouped.
Yìn galloped to inform Fǎng.
Fǎng was furious,
and shouted at him to advance again.
Yìn cried aloud and returned to battle.
From dawn until shēn (申) (3-5 PM),
both flanks were defeated.
When Fǎng heard the drumbeats,
he selected eight hundred elite soldiers,
personally served them wine,
and commanded them not to move rashly,
but to advance only upon hearing the drumbeats.
When the rebels were within thirty paces,
Fǎng personally beat the drum.
The officers and soldiers all leapt forward and charged.
Zēng was then utterly routed,
with over a thousand killed.
Fǎng pursued them at night.
His generals requested to wait until morning.
Fǎng said:
"Zēng is valorous and capable in battle.
His defeat just now
was because they were exhausted and we were fresh.
That is how we overcame them.
We should press the attack while they are weakened,
and we can destroy them."
They advanced with drumbeats,
and thus secured Hàn and Miǎn.
Zēng and his forces fled to fortify Wǔdāng.
For his merits, Fǎng was promoted to Nánzhōngláng General, Supervisor of all military affairs in Liángzhōu, and Inspector of Liángzhōu,
garrisoned at Xiāngyáng.
Fǎng said to his subordinates:
"In the Battle of Chéngpú,
Duke Wén of Jìn (晉文) showed a worried expression because Déchén (得臣) was not killed.
Now, if Zēng is not executed,
the troubles will not cease."
Thereupon, he launched a surprise attack
and again defeated them.
Zēng fled.
Fǎng's subordinate general Sū Wēn (蘇溫) captured Zēng and brought him to the army,
also capturing Dìwǔ Yī (第五猗), Hú Hùn (胡混), Zhì Zhān (摯瞻), and others,
and sent them to Wáng Dūn.
He also informed Dūn,
explaining that Yī had been coerced by Zēng,
and it was not appropriate to kill him.
Dūn did not heed him and executed them.
Fǎng was promoted to Ānnán General, with Imperial Insignia,
and his positions as Commander and Inspector remained as before.
Earlier,
Wáng Dūn, fearing the trouble caused by Dù Zēng,
had said to Fǎng:
"If you capture Zēng,
I will consider appointing you as Inspector of Jīngzhōu."
But by this time, Dūn did not use him.
When Wáng Yì (王廙) left his post,
an imperial edict appointed Fǎng as Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Dūn, seeing Fǎng as a renowned general
with great and significant achievements,
showed signs of doubt.
His Aide-de-camp Guō Shū (郭舒) advised Dūn, saying:
"Although our province has suffered from banditry and devastation,
it is truly a strategic military region.
If it is entrusted to others,
there will be the danger of the tail wagging the dog.
Your Excellency should personally lead it;
Fǎng as Inspector of Liángzhōu is sufficient."
Dūn followed his advice.
Fǎng was greatly enraged.
Dūn personally wrote a letter of explanation and conciliation,
and also sent a jade ring and a jade bowl to express his sincere intentions.
Fǎng threw the bowl to the ground and said:
"Am I a mere peddler
who can be pleased by treasures!"
Secretly, he harbored intentions to scheme against him.
While in Xiāngyáng,
he devoted himself to agriculture and military training,
diligently accepting advice.
Whenever there was a vacancy in a governorship or magistracy, he would fill it,
and only then report it to the court.
Dūn was troubled by this,
but feared Fǎng's strength
and dared not take any different action.
Fǎng's prestige was now established,
and people near and far gladly submitted to him.
His wisdom and courage surpassed others,
making him a famous general of the restoration.
He was humble by nature
and never boasted of his achievements.
Someone once asked Fǎng:
"People with even small merits
rarely fail to boast of themselves.
Your achievements are so great,
yet you have never spoken a word about them. Why is that?"
Fǎng replied:
"It is due to the awe-inspiring might of the court
and the dedication of the officers and soldiers.
What merit do I have!"
The gentry thus esteemed him highly.
Fǎng trained his troops and selected his soldiers,
wishing to exert his power in the Central Plains.
He allied with Lǐ Jǔ (李矩) and Guō Mò (郭默),
and passionately harbored the ambition to pacify the Hélúo region.
He was skilled in winning over and integrating people,
and all his officers and men were willing to die for him.
When he heard that Dūn had disloyal intentions,
Fǎng gnashed his teeth.
Although Dūn harbored rebellious plots,
he dared not act improperly throughout Fǎng's lifetime.
Earlier,
when Fǎng was young, he met Chén Xùn (陳訓) of Lújiāng, a skilled physiognomist,
who told Fǎng and Táo Kǎn:
"Both of you will reach the position of regional governors,
and your achievements and fame will be roughly similar.
However, Táo will enjoy a long life,
while Zhōu will have a shorter life.
The difference lies only in your years."
Fǎng was one year younger than Kǎn.
He died in the third year of Tàixīng (太興) (320 CE),
at the age of sixty-one.
The Emperor wept for him deeply.
An imperial edict posthumously appointed him Zhēngxī General,
and he was given the posthumous name Zhuàng (壯).
A monument was erected in his home commandery.
He had two sons: Fǔ (撫) and Guāng (光).
Fǔ Zì Dàohé.
He was strong and resolute, with his father's demeanor,
but was not as capable in military command.
Yuán Dì appointed him as a clerical assistant to the Chancellor.
When his father died, he resigned from office.
After the mourning period ended,
he inherited the peerage
and was appointed General of Soaring Hawks and Administrator of Wǔchāng.
Wáng Dūn appointed him Aide-de-camp and
he and Dèng Yuè became Dūn's trusted lieutenants.
After Gān Zhuó was killed,
Dūn appointed Fǔ as Commander of the Various Armies North of the Miǎn
and Southern Zhonglang General,
stationed in Miǎnzhōng.
When Dūn rebelled,
Fǔ led two thousand men to follow him.
After Dūn was defeated,
Fǔ and Yuè both fled.
Fǔ's younger brother, Guāng, was about to send provisions to his brother,
but secretly intended to capture Yuè.
Fǔ angrily said,
"I am fleeing with Bóshān (Yuè);
why not behead me first!"
Just then Yuè arrived,
and Fǔ went out the gate and called to him from afar,
"Why don't you leave quickly!
Now even blood relatives want to harm each other,
let alone others!"
Yuè turned his boat and fled.
Fǔ then went with him into the lands of the Xīyáng Mán,
and the Mán chieftain Xiàng Cán sheltered them.
Initially,
when Yuè was Administrator of Xīyáng,
he wanted to attack the various Mán tribes.
By this time, all the Mán resented him
and were planning to kill him.
Cán did not allow it,
saying,
"Administrator Dèng came to me in his distress,
how can I bear to kill him!"
Because of this, both were spared.
The next year,
an imperial edict pardoned Dūn's faction.
Yuè and Fǔ went to the imperial court to plead guilty,
and an edict was issued to banish them.
In the early Xiánhé period,
Sītú Wáng Dǎo appointed Fǔ as Aide-de-camp,
then he was sent out as General of Pacifying Distances and Chancellor of Jiāngxià.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Fǔ led his subordinates to join Wēn Qiáo in suppressing him.
After Jùn was pacified,
Fǔ was promoted to Supervisor of the Armies North of the Miǎn and Southern Zhonglang General,
stationed in Xiāngyáng.
Guō Jìng, a general of Shí Lè, led cavalry to attack Fǔ.
Fǔ could not hold his position
and led his subordinates to flee to Wǔchāng.
He was dismissed from office for this.
Soon after, he was promoted to General of Inspiring Might and Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Later, he replaced Guànqiū Ào as Supervisor of the Various Armies of Bādōng, Inspector of Yìzhōu, and was given the insignia of an imperial envoy,
while retaining his generalship.
Soon after, he was advanced to General of Conquering Barbarians,
and further appointed Superintendent of the Various Armies of Níngzhōu.
In the early Yǒnghé period,
when Huán Wēn campaigned against Shǔ,
Fǔ was promoted to Superintendent of the Armies of the Four Commanderies of Hànzhōng, Bāxī, Zǐtóng, and Yīnpíng in Liángzhōu,
stationed at Péngmó.
Fǔ attacked and defeated the remaining Shǔ rebels, Kuí Wén and Dèng Dìng,
and beheaded the false Secretariat Director Wáng Shì and General Pacifying the South Wáng Rùn.
For his achievements, he was promoted to General Pacifying the West.
Kuí Wén and Dèng Dìng rebelled again,
establishing Fàn Xián's son, Bēn, as emperor.
Initially,
Xián was the National Preceptor of Lǐ Xióng's state,
and misled the common people with heterodox doctrines.
Many people served him,
and Bēn consequently gathered a force of ten thousand.
Fǔ and Longxiang General Zhū Táo attacked, defeated, and beheaded him.
For his achievements, Fǔ was advanced in peerage to Duke of Jiànchéng County.
Commander of the Western Expedition Xiāo Jìngwén rebelled,
killed General Conquering Barbarians Yáng Jǐn,
occupied Fúchéng,
and proclaimed himself Governor of Yìzhōu.
Huán Wēn sent Supervisor Dèng Xiá to assist Fǔ in suppressing him,
but they could not dislodge him
and withdrew.
Wēn then ordered Liángzhōu Inspector Sīmǎ Xūn and others to join Fǔ in attacking him.
Jìngwén held his ground,
from February until August,
before finally surrendering.
Fǔ beheaded him
and sent his head to the capital.
During the Shēngpíng period,
Fǔ was promoted to General Guarding the West.
He served in the province for over thirty years.
He died in the third year of Xīngníng,
and was posthumously granted the title of General Conquering the West,
with the posthumous name Xiāng.
His son, Chǔ, succeeded him.
Chǔ's courtesy name was Yuánsūn.
He began his career as an aide to the General Conquering the West,
and followed his father into Shǔ.
He was appointed General of Soaring Hawks and Administrator of Jiànwéi.
After his father died,
Chǔ was appointed Supervisor of Liáng and Yì Provinces, given the insignia of an imperial envoy,
and inherited the peerage of Duke of Jiànchéng.
His family had been in Liáng and Yì for generations,
and were well-regarded by the populace.
At that time, Liángzhōu Inspector Sīmǎ Xūn rebelled,
and Chǔ and Zhū Xù suppressed him.
He was promoted to General of Championing the Army.
During the Tàihé period,
the Shǔ bandit Lǐ Jīnyín
and the Guǎnghàn sorcerer Lǐ Hóng both gathered followers to form a rebellion.
They falsely claimed to be Lǐ Shì's son,
who was destined to rule by divine power,
and adopted the era name Fènghuáng.
Moreover, Lǐ Gāo from Lǒngxī falsely claimed to be Lǐ Xióng's son
and captured Fúchéng.
Liángzhōu Inspector Yáng Liàng lost the city,
and Chǔ sent his son to suppress the rebels.
That same year,
Chǔ died,
with the posthumous name Dìng.
His son, Qióng, succeeded him.
Qióng was strong and fierce, with military talent.
He successively served in several commanderies,
and replaced Yáng Liàng as Liángzhōu Inspector, General of Establishing Might,
and concurrently Western Rong Colonel.
Initially,
Dī leader Dòu Chōng sought to surrender,
and the court appointed him Eastern Qiāng Colonel.
Later, Chōng rebelled
and wanted to enter Hànzhōng.
Huángfǔ Zhāo from Āndìng and Zhōu Xūn from Jīngzhào plotted to welcome Chōng.
Qióng secretly learned of this,
arrested Zhāo, Xūn, and others, and executed them.
He died soon after.
His son, Xiāo, succeeded him.
Xiāo's courtesy name was Mèngwēi.
From a young age, he possessed integrity.
The province invited him to be Jìjiǔ,
and he later rose through various positions to Western Yí Colonel,
concurrently Administrator of Zǐtóng.
At the beginning of the Níngkāng reign,
Fú Jiān's general Yáng Ān invaded Zǐtóng.
Zhōu Xiāo held Fúchéng firmly,
and dispatched several thousand cavalry and infantry
to escort his mother and wife from the Hànshuǐ River to Jiānglíng.
They were intercepted and captured by Fú Jiān's general Zhū Róng.
Zhōu Xiāo subsequently surrendered to Yáng Ān.
Fú Jiān wanted to appoint him as Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat),
but Zhōu Xiāo said:
"I have received the country's great kindness
until today.
But my old mother has been captured,
causing me to lose my integrity here.
That both mother and son are spared
is the benevolence of Qín.
Even the nobility of a Gōng (Duke) or Hóu (Marquis)
I would not consider an honor,
let alone the post of Láng!"
Fú Jiān then dropped the matter.
From then on, whenever he entered to see Fú Jiān,
he would always sit with his legs splayed out,
and call him "Dī bandit."
Fú Jiān was displeased.
During the Yuánhuì (New Year's court assembly),
the ceremony was extremely solemn.
Fú Jiān then said to Zhōu Xiāo:
"How does the Jìn court's Yuánhuì compare to this?"
Zhōu Xiāo pushed up his sleeves and said in a stern voice:
"Barbarians gathered together
are like dogs and sheep in a flock;
how dare you compare yourselves to the Son of Heaven!"
When Lǚ Guāng was dispatched to conquer Xīyù (the Western Regions),
Fú Jiān went out to bid him farewell.
There were 200,000 soldiers,
and their banners stretched for hundreds of Lǐ.
He again asked Zhōu Xiāo:
"How is Our army's strength?"
Zhōu Xiāo said:
"Since the time of the barbarians,
there has been nothing like it."
Fú Jiān's partisans, angered by Zhōu Xiāo's insolence,
repeatedly asked for him to be executed.
Fú Jiān, however, treated him even more generously.
Zhōu Xiāo then secretly wrote to Huán Chōng,
explaining the bandit's treacherous schemes.
In the third year of Tàiyuán (378 CE),
Zhōu Xiāo secretly went to Hànzhōng.
Fú Jiān pursued and captured him.
Later, he conspired with Fú Jiān's nephew, Fú Bāo, to ambush Fú Jiān.
The plot was exposed.
Fú Jiān brought Zhōu Xiāo in and questioned him about the matter.
Zhōu Xiāo said:
"In ancient times, Jiàn Lí and Yù Ràng,
humble ministers of Yān and Zhì,
still painted their bodies and swallowed charcoal,
not forgetting their loyalty and integrity.
How much more so I, Zhōu Xiāo, who have for generations received Jìn's favor?
How dare I forget it?
Living, I am a Jìn subject;
dead, I am a Jìn ghost.
What more is there to ask?"
Fú Jiān said:
"If I kill him now,
I will merely fulfill his name."
So he had him flogged
and exiled to Tàiyuán.
Later, Fú Jiān again captured Shùnyáng and Wèixīng,
and seized their two governors,
who both held their integrity unyieldingly.
Fú Jiān sighed, saying:
"Zhōu Mèngwēi was unyielding before,
Dīng Yàn yuǎn kept himself pure afterward,
Jí Zǔchōng died from not eating—
all are loyal ministers!"
Zhōu Xiāo eventually died of illness in Tàiyuán.
His son, Zhōu Xīng, brought his coffin back.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Champion Army), Xiè Xuán, personally attended and wept for him,
then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that praising goodness and highlighting achievements,
upholding righteousness and clarifying integrity,
are means to promote moral influence
and leave a legacy for future generations.
Therefore, Zhōu Xiāo, the Xīyí Xiàowèi (Commandant of the Western Barbarians) and Zǐtóng Tàishǒu (Governor of Zǐtóng),
maintained a loyal and ardent heart,
displayed integrity in the enemy's court,
and thus encountered calamity in a desolate region,
sorrowfully interred in the earth.
Your servant often grieves for his ambition,
considering him no less worthy than Sū Wǔ.
Before, a proclamation was sent to Bīngzhōu,
seeking Zhōu Xiāo's coffin
and his family.
After bearing thousands of burdens,
they finally arrived.
Provision was immediately given for their escort,
and they returned to their old burial ground.
Your servant humbly wishes that Your Sacred Dynasty would recall his resolute heart
and make known his exceptional integrity,
so that the ambition of enduring hardship does not fall to the ground,
which would bring honor and comfort to both the living and the dead,
and extend beneficence to both the visible and the hidden realms."
Emperor Xiàowǔ issued an edict saying:
"Zhōu Xiāo showed resolute will and steadfast loyalty,
not shaming ancient heroes.
Before he could extricate himself,
he suddenly met his end.
To recognize and proclaim righteous integrity
is a national institution.
He is posthumously granted the title of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (General of the Dragon Soaring) and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yìzhōu),
with a funeral stipend of 200,000 coins
and 100 bolts of cloth."
His family was also generously endowed.
Zhōu Guāng had his father's demeanor from a young age.
At eleven,
he met Wáng Dūn.
Wáng Dūn asked him:
"Your commandery has no general yet;
who is suitable?"
Guāng replied:
"If the Illustrious Duke is not ashamed to ask a junior,
I privately think there is no one superior to me."
Wáng Dūn laughed and appointed him Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies Afar) and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (Governor of Xúnyáng).
When Wáng Dūn raised troops,
Zhōu Guāng led over a thousand men to join him.
Upon arrival,
Wáng Dūn had already died,
but Zhōu Guāng did not know it.
He requested to see Wáng Dūn.
Wáng Yìng kept it secret
and reported that he was ill.
Zhōu Guāng withdrew and said:
"Now I have come a long way and cannot see Duke Wáng;
has the Duke perhaps died?"
He immediately went to see his elder brother Zhōu Fǔ and said:
"Duke Wáng is dead.
Why are you joining Qián Fèng to commit treason?"
Everyone was astonished.
That night,
the crowd dispersed,
and Qián Fèng fled.
When he reached Hélú Zhōu,
Zhōu Guāng captured Qián Fèng
and brought him to the imperial court to atone for his own sins,
and thus he was not dismissed from office.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Zhōu Guāng followed Wēn Jiǎo and fought bravely, achieving merit.
After Sū Jùn was pacified,
he was granted the title Qǔjiāng Nán (Baron of Qǔjiāng),
and died in office.
His son, Zhōu Zhòngsūn,
at the beginning of Xīngníng, supervised military affairs in Níngzhōu, and was appointed Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Quells the Martial) and Níngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Níngzhōu).
In the province, he was greedy and violent,
and the people could not endure his rule.
Huán Wēn, seeing that Liáng and Yì had many bandits,
and that the Zhōu family had a reputation for might for generations,
reappointed Zhōu Zhòngsūn to oversee the three commanderies of Yì, Yù, and Liángzhōu.
At the beginning of Níngkāng,
Yáng Ān invaded Shǔ.
Zhōu Zhòngsūn lost the defense
and was dismissed from office.
Later, he was summoned to be Guānglù Xūn (Minister of the Imperial Household)
and died.
Originally,
when Táo Kǎn was of humble status,
he suffered the death of a parent.
As he was about to bury him,
his family suddenly lost a ox and did not know its whereabouts.
He met an old man
who told him:
"On the hill ahead, I saw an ox sleeping in a hollow on the mountain.
If you bury [the deceased] there,
you will reach the highest position among officials."
He then pointed to another mountain and said:
"This is also a secondary spot;
it will produce officials receiving two thousand dàn of grain for generations."
After speaking, he disappeared.
Táo Kǎn searched for the ox and found it,
then buried his parent there.
He showed the other mountain he had been pointed to to Zhōu Fǎng.
Zhōu Fǎng's father died and was buried there.
Indeed, Zhōu Fǎng became a Cìshǐ (Governor),
and gained renown in Níng and Yì.
From Zhōu Fǎng downwards,
three generations were Governors of Yìzhōu for forty-one years,
exactly as had been foretold.
The Grand Scribe says: How can benevolence and righteousness be constant?
To tread them is to be a *Jūnzǐ*,
to abandon them is to be a *Xiǎorén*.
Zhōu Zǐyǐn, with his dissolute talent,
harbored untamed conduct.
Compared to fierce *jiāo*-dragons and wild beasts,
he spread poison throughout the villages.
Yet he was ultimately able to overcome himself and strive diligently,
hearing the truth in the morning and changing by evening.
He held life lightly and righteousness heavily,
sacrificing his body for the state.
He can be called a man of resolve and integrity.
Xuān Pèi, spurred by loyalty and courage,
repeatedly extinguished the demonic miasma.
His prestige and strategy surpassed all in the contemporary court,
and his achievements were recorded in the royal archives.
However, he later harbored resentment against the court officials,
secretly plotting a different course.
His anger prevented him from considering the danger,
which was truly narrow-minded.
His end in fury and resentment,
how regrettable was that!
Zhá Yán and others possessed outstanding talent,
holding themselves to be heroic and bold.
Initially suspected by the imperial court,
they ultimately incurred the wrath of those in power.
The strong are not equal to the weak –
this is truly proven.
As for Zhá, entrusted with defending the city,
he opened the gates to invite invaders.
Abandoning the righteous to follow the rebellious,
he truly did so.
Though he later met his end at the hands of villains,
it can be said that the guilty person received his due.
For the imperial court to deliberate bestowing honors upon him,
is that not presumptuous!
The penal administration of the Jìn dynasty declined,
due to this very way.
Zhōu Fǎng's talent encompassed both civil and military arts,
his responsibility lay in warding off invaders.
He pacified Xiāngluó,
and cleared Jiānghàn.
He planned for his grandsons and protected his sons,
bearing the official staff and wielding the *máo* banner.
Western Shǔ looked up to his prestige,
and the Restoration acclaimed him as a renowned general.
His achievements complete, his fame established,
was that not splendid!
Mèng Wēi, though trapped in the barbarian court,
spoke out against the false ruler.
Although recorded in histories,
what could surpass this!
An encomium says: Píngxī was strong and resolute,
starting astray but ending righteous.
His courage was sufficient to eliminate evil,
his loyalty enabled him to sacrifice his life.
Xuān Pèi's great achievements,
thrice secured Jiāngdōng.
Though Zhá opened the way for the enemy,
Yán truly harbored loyalty.
Xúnyáng wielded military might,
bearing the *máo* banner and holding the axe.
For his sons and grandsons,
they followed the rules meticulously.
Mèng Wēi resisted fiercely,
his heart remained with his old lord.
Textual Criticism Notes
Since ancient times, when emperors ruled the world,
they all desired to widely establish their feudal strongholds,
and solidly strengthen their defensive cities.
Before Táng-Yú,
the statutes were perhaps incomplete.
After Xià-Yīn,
their vestiges are discernible.
However, when jade and silks converged at Túshān,
though it was said to be ten thousand states,
as for the division of territories and endowment with lands,
it is still perhaps unclear.
When it reached the Zhōu house,
it was brilliantly observable,
enfeoffing relatives and worthy individuals,
all becoming constituent states.
When it flourished,
Zhōu and Shào assisted its peace and prosperity;
when it declined,
Huán and Wén aided it in times of peril and chaos.
Thus, the blessed longevity of its generations prospered,
and the foundation of its years was eternal.
By the time King Nǎn passed away,
Heaven's blessing had ended.
The vacant position had no master,
for over thirty years.
Then came the tyrannical Qín,
swallowing the whole world.
He warned against the weakening of the declining Zhōu,
but overlooked the far-reaching plan for imperial enterprise.
He believed the decline of the royal house
stemmed from the power of the feudal lords.
Therefore, he abolished the marquises and established commandery governors,
honoring himself alone.
Even his own sons and younger brothers
were all reduced to commoners.
He only desired to indulge in cruelty and assert his might,
disregarding any plans for his grandsons or protection for his sons.
The branches and leaves were weak,
the ancestral altars were isolated and precarious.
Internally, there were no ministers of the state;
externally, there was no assistance from loyal vassals.
Chén Shèng and Xiàng Yǔ raised a call,
and the whole realm erupted.
Qín Èr Shì perished at Wàngyí,
and was bound at Zhīdào.
His actions did not emulate the ancients,
and he perished in the second generation.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn rose vigorously,
and reformed these abuses.
Thereupon, he divided his royal sons and younger brothers,
and established meritorious officials in ranks.
He bestowed upon them mountains and rivers,
and swore oaths with them as enduring as sashes and whetstones.
However, he overcorrected,
blowing on cold soup after burning his mouth with hot,
and the extent of the territories and borders
exceeded those of ancient times.
At first, Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè were minced and pickled;
next, Wú and Chǔ rebelled.
Yet, although he conquered and eliminated the powerful and encroaching,
it was still sufficient to protect the royal domain.
After Chéng and Āi,
the imperial relatives declined.
The monarch and his ministers exploited this gap,
usurping positions and stealing peace.
Guāngwǔ's heroic strategy spanned the heavens,
rising valiantly from the lower ranks.
Thus, he was able to eliminate villains and quell chaos,
restoring the Yǔ family's claim to match Heaven.
Prosperity flourished in the two capitals,
and the dynasty prospered for four hundred years.
The strength of continuing the broken lineage
can be attributed to him.
Wèi Wǔ abandoned the grand strategy of managing the state,
and practiced petty, jealous schemes.
Meritorious officials had no place to stand,
and his own sons and younger brothers were not used as subjects.
They merely received symbolic enfeoffments,
truly holding empty titles.
With no protection for the roots,
the dynasty perished in three generations.
The Jìn dynasty sought to avoid the overturned cart,
and once again strengthened the foundation.
Some were sent out to hold the *máo* banner and official staff,
enjoying the honor of governing regions;
others entered to tread the imperial stairs,
holding the weighty position of prime minister.
However, appointments were misplaced,
and responsibilities were assigned improperly.
Government orders were not clear,
and rewards and punishments were abused.
Some with talent were not employed,
while others were executed without guilt.
In the morning they were like Yī Yǐn and Duke Zhōu,
in the evening they became like Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Zhuó.
Power was lost at the top,
and chaos arose from below.
The princes of Chǔ and Zhào,
successively instigated conflicts.
They merely raised troops in Jìnyáng,
ultimately not acting as forces to aid the emperor.
Initially, they sought benefits for themselves;
before the benefits came, harm befell them.
At first, they had no intention of worrying about the state;
if the state was not worried about, who would save it!
Thus, the rise and fall in Zhāoyáng Palace
was worse than a game of *yì*;
the imperial carriage was imprisoned,
like King Wén in Yǒulǐ.
The Hú and Jié barbarians brought insults,
and the ancestral temples became ruins.
Truly lamentable!
The establishment of feudal lords as bulwarks for the state
is like having boats and oars for crossing a river.
Safety and danger, success and failure,
are truly interdependent.
If the boats and oars are sturdy,
the waves are not enough to make their danger worth mentioning;
if the bulwarks are firm,
how can calamity and disorder ascend to power!
If, among the Eight Princes,
one feudal lord had been relied upon,
like King Liáng [梁王] defending against a great enemy,
or like Zhū Xū [朱虛] eliminating a great villain,
then external invaders would not dare to encroach,
and internal strife would have no way to secretly erupt!
Even if the Son of Heaven were dim-witted and incompetent,
and the high ministers extravagant and unrestrained,
though there might be difficulties,
it would not reach the point of total collapse.
How can this be said?
King Lángyá [琅邪王], compared to those other princes,
had less power and fewer followers;
measuring their strengths,
they could not be compared.
Yet he was able to cross the river with a single horse,
and quickly occupied Wúhuì [吳會],
preserving the important ancestral altars [dynasty] for
over a hundred years.
Though it is attributed to heavenly timing,
it was also due to human effort.
How can it be compared to the likes of Zhào Lún [趙倫] and Qí Jiǒng [齊冏],
or the followers of Héjiān [河間] and Dōnghǎi [東海],
whose families and states both perished,
and whose bodies and reputations were utterly destroyed?
Are these not
the effects of good and evil?
The chaos in government and the peril of the court in the Western Jìn [西晉] dynasty,
though caused by the emperor of the time,
yet those who fanned the flames
and hastened the disaster,
the fault lay with the Eight Princes.
Therefore, I shall arrange and discuss them,
collectively writing their biographies.
Rǔnán Wáng Liàng [汝南王亮] (Sons: Cuì [粹], Jǔ [矩], Yáng [羕], Zōng [宗], Xī [熙]; Grandson: Yòu [祐], son of Jǔ [矩])
Rǔnán Wénchéng Wáng Liàng [汝南文成王亮], courtesy name Zǐyì [子翼],
was the fourth son of Xuāndì [宣帝].
In his youth, he was intelligent, alert, and capable.
He served the Wèi [魏] dynasty as Sànqí Shìláng [散騎侍郎] and Marquis of Wànsuì Tíng [萬歲亭].
He was appointed Dōng Zhōngláng Jiàng [東中郎將],
and advanced to the title Marquis of Guǎngyáng Xiāng [廣陽鄉].
During the campaign against Zhūgě Dàn [諸葛誕] at Shòuchūn [壽春],
he suffered a defeat
and was dismissed from office.
After a short while,
he was appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn [左將軍],
with the additional titles Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍] and Jiǎjié [假節],
and was sent out to supervise military affairs in Yùzhōu [豫州].
When the five ranks were established,
he was re-enfeoffed as Earl of Qíyáng [祁陽伯],
then transferred to Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn [鎮西將軍].
When Wǔdì [武帝] ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as King of Fúfēng Jùn [扶風郡],
with an estate of ten thousand households.
He was given a Qí Sīmǎ [騎司馬],
and his staff of Cānjūn Yuánshǔ [參軍掾屬] was increased.
He held the Jié [節] and was Dūdū Guānzhōng Yōngliáng Zhū Jūnshì [都督關中雍涼諸軍事] (Supervisor of Military Affairs in Guānzhōng, Yōngzhōu, and Liángzhōu).
At that time, Hú Liè [胡烈], the Inspector of Qínzhōu [秦州], was harmed by Qiāng [羌] barbarians.
Liàng [亮] dispatched Generals Liú Qí [劉旂] and Qídū Jìng Yǎn [騎督敬琰] to assist,
but they did not advance.
For this, he was demoted to Píng Xī Jiāngjūn [平西將軍].
Qí [旂] was to be executed.
Liàng [亮] and the military commander Cáo Jiǒng [曹冏] submitted a memorial,
stating that the fault for the lack of coordination lay with Liàng [亮],
and begged for Qí's [旂] life.
An imperial edict stated:
"Gāopíng [高平] was in dire straits.
It was estimated that those in the city and Qí's [旂] forces were sufficient to relieve it.
Even if they couldn't reach it directly,
they should have advanced deeply.
Now, they fled and surrendered
while passively watching the defeat.
Therefore, Qí [旂] is to be severely punished.
If the crime is not Qí's [旂],
then it must be someone else's."
The appropriate officials then proposed to dismiss Liàng [亮] from office
and strip him of his titles and land.
The edict only ordered his dismissal from office.
After a short while,
he was appointed Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn [撫軍將軍].
In that year,
the Wú [吳] general Bù Chǎn [步闡] surrendered.
Liàng [亮] was granted the Jié [節] and made Dūdū Zhū Jūnshì [都督諸軍事] (Supervisor of Military Affairs) to receive him.
Soon after, he was granted the attire of a Shìzhōng [侍中].
In the early years of Xiánníng [咸寧] (275 AD),
four thousand one hundred households from Chíyáng [池陽] in Fúfēng [扶風] were designated as a bath and food allowance fief for Grand Consort Fú [伏氏],
and a household director, assistant, and servants were appointed.
Later, it was changed to Zhījiāng [枝江] in Nánjùn [南郡].
The Grand Consort once had a minor illness,
and performed a purification ritual at the Luò [洛] River.
Liàng [亮] and his two brothers accompanied her,
all holding the Jié [節] with drums and wind instruments,
creating a dazzling display along the bank of the Luò [洛].
Wǔdì [武帝], observing from Lingyún Tái [陵雲臺],
said:
"Consort Fú [伏妃] can truly be called rich and noble."
In that year, he was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn [衞將軍],
and given the additional title Shìzhōng [侍中].
At that time, the imperial clan was numerous and prosperous,
but lacked a unifying leader.
So Liàng [亮] was made Zōngshī [宗師] (Master of the Imperial Clan),
his original post remaining unchanged,
to instruct and observe them.
If any did not conform to ritual and law,
minor offenses were corrected with righteous guidance,
while major ones were reported to the throne as circumstances dictated.
In the third year (277 AD),
he was transferred and enfeoffed as King of Rǔnán [汝南],
and sent out as Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn [鎮南大將軍], Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì [都督豫州諸軍事], Kāifǔ [開府], Jiǎjié [假節],
to his state,
provided with a Chuīfēng Chē [追鋒車], a Zàolún Dúchē [皁輪犢車],
and five hundred thousand cash.
After a short while,
Liàng [亮] was summoned to be Shìzhōng [侍中], Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn [撫軍大將軍],
concurrently serving as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn [後軍將軍],
commanding the Guànjūn [冠軍], Bùbīng [步兵], Shèshēng [射聲], Chángshuǐ [長水] and other camps,
provided with five hundred soldiers
and one hundred horses.
He was promoted to Tàiwèi [太尉], Lù Shàngshūshì [錄尚書事], concurrently serving as Tàizǐ Tàifù [太子太傅],
with Shìzhōng [侍中] as before.
When Wǔdì [武帝] fell ill,
he was obstructed by Yáng Jùn [楊駿],
so Liàng [亮] was appointed Shìzhōng [侍中], Dà Sīmǎ [大司馬], Jiǎ Huángyuè [假黃鉞], Dà Dūdū [大都督], Dū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì [督豫州諸軍事],
to garrison Xǔchāng [許昌],
and granted the privilege of Xuánxuán zhī Yuè [軒懸之樂] (suspended bells and chimes)
and Liùyì zhī Wǔ [六佾之舞] (six-row dance).
His son Yáng [羕] was enfeoffed as Duke of Xīyáng [西陽公].
Before he departed,
the emperor was critically ill,
and issued an edict to keep Liàng [亮] and entrust him with posthumous matters.
Yáng Jùn [楊駿], hearing of this,
demanded the edict from the Zhōngshū Jiān [中書監] Huá Yì [華廙] to inspect it,
and subsequently did not return it.
When the emperor passed away,
Liàng [亮] feared that Jùn [駿] would suspect him,
and declined to enter on grounds of illness,
only grieving outside the Dà Sīmǎ Gate,
and memorialized to be allowed to attend the funeral from afar.
Jùn [駿] wanted to attack Liàng [亮].
Liàng [亮], knowing this,
asked for advice from the Tíngwèi [廷尉] Hé Xù [何勖].
Xù [勖] said:
"Now the court all looks to you, my lord.
Why do you not attack others, but fear being attacked by others?"
Someone also advised Liàng [亮] to lead his troops to depose Jùn [駿],
but Liàng [亮] could not bring himself to do it,
and instead galloped to Xǔchāng [許昌] that night,
thus escaping danger.
When Jùn [駿] was executed,
an edict stated:
"Dà Sīmǎ [大司馬], Rǔnán Wáng Liàng [汝南王亮], embodies pure virtue,
and possesses comprehensive understanding of governance.
His accomplishments in assisting the court are evident,
and the civilizing influence of the 'Two Nans' flows through the land.
We shall rely on his profound strategies
to bring peace to the imperial transformation.
Therefore, Liàng [亮] is appointed Tàizǎi [太宰], Lù Shàngshūshì [錄尚書事],
he may enter court without hurrying,
wear his sword and shoes into the palace,
his staff of Yuánshǔ [掾屬] is increased by ten,
and he is provided with one thousand soldiers and one hundred cavalry.
He shall jointly manage court affairs with Tàibǎo [太保] Wèi Guàn [衞瓘]."
Liàng [亮]'s assessment of the rewards and punishments for the overthrow of Yáng Jùn [楊駿] was excessive,
desiring to please the multitude,
which led to disappointment.
Chǔ Wáng Wěi (楚王瑋) had merits and was fond of establishing his authority.
Liàng (亮) was apprehensive of him
and wanted to seize his military power.
Wěi (瑋) harbored deep resentment,
so, acting on Jiǎ Hòu's (賈后) decree,
he falsely accused Liàng (亮) and Guàn (瓘) of plotting to depose the emperor.
He forged an imperial edict and dispatched his Chief Clerk Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫宏) and General of Arbalests Lǐ Zhào (李肇) to surround Liàng (亮) at night with troops.
Lǐ Lóng (李龍), the Supervisor of the camp, reported that there was a change outside
and requested to resist them,
but Liàng (亮) did not listen.
Soon, Chǔ (楚) soldiers scaled the walls and shouted,
and Liàng (亮) exclaimed in surprise:
"I have no ulterior motives,
how could it come to this!
If there is an imperial edict,
may it be shown?"
Hóng (宏) and others refused,
urging their troops to attack him.
Chief Clerk Liú Zhǔn (劉準) said to Liàng (亮):
"From this, it must be a treacherous plot.
There are as many talented men in the mansion as trees in a forest;
we can still exert our full strength to resist and fight."
He again did not listen,
and was subsequently seized by Zhào (肇),
sighing:
"My loyalty can be broken and shown to all under heaven,
yet how lawless it is
to unjustly kill the innocent!"
It was extremely hot at that time,
and the soldiers made Liàng (亮) sit under a cart.
People at the time pitied him
and fanned him.
As it approached noon,
no one dared to harm him.
Wěi (瑋) issued an order saying:
"Whoever can cut off Liàng's (亮) head
shall be rewarded with a thousand bolts of cloth."
Consequently, he was harmed by the unruly soldiers,
and his body was thrown against the wall of the north gate;
his hair, ears, and nose were all destroyed.
When Wěi (瑋) was executed,
Liàng's (亮) rank and title were posthumously restored.
He was given the Wēnmíng Mìqì (溫明祕器) of the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
three million coins,
and three hundred bolts of plain silk and damask.
His funeral rites were conducted according to the precedent of Ānpíng Xiànwáng Fú (安平獻王孚),
and the Xuānxuán (軒懸) music was performed in his ancestral temple.
He had five sons: Cuì (粹), Jǔ (矩), Yàng (羕), Zōng (宗), and Xī (熙).
Cuì (粹)'s courtesy name was Màohóng (茂弘).
He died young.
Jǔ (矩)'s courtesy name was Yánmíng (延明).
He was appointed heir apparent
and served as Commandant of Cavalry,
suffering harm together with his father Liàng (亮).
He was posthumously granted the title of General Overseeing the Army
and given the posthumous title Huái Wáng (懷王).
His son Yòu (祐) succeeded him,
becoming Wēi Wáng (威王).
Yòu (祐)'s courtesy name was Yǒngyóu (永猷).
During the Yǒng'ān (永安) period,
he followed Huì Dì (惠帝) on the northern expedition.
When the Emperor moved to Cháng'ān (長安),
Yòu (祐) returned to his state.
When the Emperor returned to Luò (洛),
Yòu (祐) was given eight hundred soldiers of the Southern Expeditionary Force,
and four departmental Yámén (牙門) were specially established for him.
In the early Yǒngxīng (永興) period,
he led his forces to join Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越),
achieving merits in suppressing Liú Qiáo (劉喬).
He was appointed General of Martial Might
and additionally enfeoffed with Yúndù (雲杜) in Jiāngxià (江夏),
totaling twenty-five thousand households including previous grants.
When Yuè (越) campaigned against Jí Sāng (汲桑),
he submitted a memorial to leave Yòu (祐) in charge of three thousand soldiers to guard Xǔchāng (許昌),
adding drums and trumpets and military banners to his retinue.
When Yuè (越) returned,
Yòu (祐) went back to his state.
In the late Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
due to the prevalence of bandits and rebels,
he crossed the Yangtze River southwards.
Yuán Dì (元帝) appointed him Libationer of the Military Consultative Staff.
In the early Jiànwǔ (建武) period,
he became General Guarding the Army.
In the late Tàixīng (太興) period,
he assumed command of the Left Army General.
During the Tàiníng (太寧) period,
he was promoted to General-in-Chief of the Guards
and additionally made Attendant at the Imperial Palace.
In the first year of Xiánhé (咸和),
he passed away
and was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Specially Advanced.
His son Gōng Wáng Tǒng (恭王統) succeeded him.
Because Nándùn Wáng Zōng (南頓王宗) plotted rebellion,
Tǒng (統) was deposed.
Later, Chéng Dì (成帝) grieved that Liàng's (亮) entire family line had been exterminated,
so he issued an edict to restore Tǒng's (統) enfeoffment.
Tǒng (統) successively rose to become Director of the Imperial Library and Palace Attendant.
When he passed away,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies.
His son Yì (義) succeeded him,
reaching the office of Attendant at the Imperial Palace.
When he passed away,
his son Zūnzhī (遵之) succeeded him.
In the early Yìxī (義熙) period,
Liángzhōu (梁州) Inspector Liú Zhì (劉稚) plotted rebellion,
proclaiming Zūnzhī (遵之) as their leader.
The plot was exposed,
and they were executed.
Kǎi (楷)'s son Liánfú (蓮扶) then succeeded him.
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Yàng (羕)'s courtesy name was Yánnián (延年).
In the late Tàikāng (太康) period,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Xīyáng (西陽) County
and appointed Attendant at the Imperial Palace.
When Liàng (亮) was harmed,
Yàng (羕) was eight years old.
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Péi Kǎi (鎮南將軍裴楷) was a close relative of his
and secretly took him to escape,
relocating eight times in one night,
thus he was able to be spared.
When Wěi (瑋) was executed,
Yàng (羕)'s rank was advanced to King.
He successively held the posts of Commandant of Infantry and General of the Left Army's Swift Cavalry.
In the early Yuánkāng (元康) period,
he was promoted to an imperial prince with a commandery.
In the early Yǒngxīng (永興) period,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
As a partisan of Chángshā Wáng Yì (長沙王乂),
he was demoted to commoner status.
When Huì Dì (惠帝) returned to Luò (洛),
Yàng's (羕) enfeoffment was restored,
and he was made General Guarding the Army.
His state was further augmented with Qīsī (期思) and Xīlíng (西陵) in Rǔnán (汝南).
In the early Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
he was appointed General Guarding the Army,
additionally made Attendant at the Imperial Palace,
and commanded the Rear Army General.
He was again augmented with Zhū (邾) and Qíchūn (蘄春),
totaling thirty-five thousand households including previous grants.
He followed Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) eastwards out of Juānchéng (鄄城),
and subsequently crossed the Yangtze River southwards.
Yuán Dì (元帝), acting by imperial authority,
reappointed him Grand General Guarding the Army, established his own administration,
and provided him with a thousand soldiers and a hundred horsemen.
An imperial edict commanded him and Nándùn Wáng Zōng (南頓王宗) to lead refugees to populate the central plains.
As the area west of the Yangtze River was barren and obstructed,
he returned.
When Yuán Dì (元帝) ascended the throne,
Yàng (羕) was promoted to Palace Attendant and Grand Tutor.
Due to Yàng's (羕) venerable status,
a special bed was set up for him at the New Year's court assembly.
In the early Tàixīng (太興) period,
he recorded the affairs of the Masters of Writing,
and soon after assumed command as Grand Master of the Clan,
with the addition of feathered parasols and ceremonial axes,
sixty swordsmen for his retinue,
and was promoted to Grand Preceptor.
When Wáng Dūn (王敦) was pacified,
he assumed command as Grand Commandant.
When Míng Dì (明帝) ascended the throne,
due to Yàng's (羕) status as an elder of the imperial clan,
the Emperor specially bowed to him.
Yàng (羕) allowed his soldiers to plunder and loot,
and the relevant department memorialized to dismiss Yàng (羕) from office,
but an edict decreed no investigation.
When the Emperor fell gravely ill,
Yàng (羕) and Wáng Dǎo (王導) together received the deathbed command to assist Chéng Dì (成帝).
As the Emperor was then very young,
an edict commanded Yàng (羕) to follow the precedent of Ānpíng Xiànwáng Fú (安平獻王孚),
setting up a bed with curtains in the palace hall,
and the Emperor personally welcomed and bowed to him.
In the early Xiánhé (咸和) period,
due to his younger brother Nándùn Wáng Zōng (南頓王宗) being dismissed from office,
Yàng (羕) was demoted to King of Yìyáng (弋陽) County.
When Sū Jùn (蘇峻) revolted,
Yàng (羕) went to Jùn (峻) and extolled his achievements,
and Jùn (峻) was greatly pleased,
forging an edict to restore Yàng's (羕) rank and title.
When Jùn (峻) was pacified,
Yàng (羕) was given death.
The heir apparent Bō (播), Bō's (播) younger brother Chōng (充), and his son Sōng (崧) were all executed,
and the state was abolished.
In the early Xiánkāng (咸康) period,
his family's registration was restored,
and Yàng's (羕) grandson Mín (珉) was made Commandant of Chariots and Attendant at Court.
Zōng Zì Yánzuò.
During the Yuánkāng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nándùn County,
and soon after, advanced in peerage to Duke.
For his meritorious service in defeating Liú Qiáo,
he was advanced in enfeoffment to Prince,
with an increase of five thousand households in his territory,
making a total of ten thousand households including the previous ones,
and became General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn).
He and his elder brother Róng both crossed the Yangtze River.
Emperor Yuán, acting as regent,
appointed him Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
When Emperor Mǐn was in the western capital,
he appointed Zōng as General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn).
Upon Emperor Yuán's enthronement,
he was appointed General Who Guards the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Colonel of Chángshuǐ (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi),
and then transferred to Left Guard General (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn).
He and Yú Yìn were both favored by the Emperor,
who entrusted them with the imperial guards.
Zōng's ambitions and interests differed from those of Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng,
and he associated with reckless knights-errant,
treating them as his confidants.
Dǎo and Liàng both spoke against this.
The Emperor, considering Zōng to be a member of the imperial clan,
always tolerated him.
When the Emperor's illness became critical,
Zōng and Yìn secretly plotted rebellion.
Liàng burst through the palace gate,
ascended the imperial couch,
and tearfully spoke of their treachery.
The Emperor then realized the truth.
Zōng was transferred to General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
Yìn became Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan (Dàzōngzhèng).
Zōng's resentment and ill-will became evident in his words and demeanor.
In the early Xiánhé era,
Censor-in-Chief Zhōng Yǎ impeached Zōng for plotting rebellion.
Yǔ Liàng ordered Right Guard General Zhào Yìn to arrest him.
Zōng resisted with his troops,
but was killed by Yìn.
His clan was demoted to the Mǎ family,
and his wife and children were exiled to Jìn'ān,
but later pardoned.
His three sons, Chuò, Chāo, and Yǎn,
were stripped of their status and became commoners.
During the Xiánkāng era,
their family registration was restored.
Chuò became Commandant Who Attends the Chariot (Fèngchē Dūwèi) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Fèngcháoqǐng).
Xī was initially enfeoffed as the Duke of Rǔyáng.
For his meritorious service in defeating Liú Qiáo,
he was advanced in peerage to Prince.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
he was captured by Shí Lè.
Prince Wěi of Chǔ.
Wěi, the Esteemed Prince of Chǔ (Chǔ Yǐnwáng), courtesy name Yàndù,
was the fifth son of Emperor Wǔ.
He was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Shǐpíng,
and successively served as Colonel of Agile Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi).
At the end of the Tàikāng era,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Chǔ,
and went to his state.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Jīngzhōu (Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhū Jūnfàn) and General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn),
then transferred to General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn).
When Emperor Wǔ passed away,
he entered the capital as Guard General (Wèi Jiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the post of Central Supervisor of the Northern Army (Běijūn Zhōnghòu),
and given the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Acting Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Xíng Tàizǐ Shǎofù).
When Yáng Jùn was executed,
Wěi was stationed at the Sīmǎ Gate.
Wěi was young, resolute, and decisive,
and frequently imposed severe punishments,
which made the imperial court apprehensive of him.
Liàng, the Prince of Rǔnán, and Grand Tutor Wèi Guàn, considering Wěi's obstinate and cruel nature,
believed he could not be entrusted with great responsibility.
They proposed that he return to his state along with the other princes.
Wěi was greatly resentful of this.
His Chief Clerk Gōngsūn Hóng and Palace Attendant Qí Shèng were both of poor conduct,
but favored by Wěi.
Guàn and others disliked their character
and feared they would cause trouble and chaos,
intending to arrest Shèng.
Shèng, knowing this,
then plotted with Hóng,
and with the help of General of Massed Crossbows Lǐ Zhào, falsely issued an order in Wěi's name,
slandering Liàng and Guàn to Empress Jiǎ.
The Empress, without investigating,
made Emperor Huì issue an edict saying:
"The Grand Tutor and Grand Protector intend to follow the example of Yī and Huò;
the Prince should proclaim this edict,
and order the Princes of Huáinán, Chángshā, and Chéngdū to garrison the palace gates,
to depose the two dukes."
That night, a Yellow Gate Attendant brought it and handed it to Wěi.
Wěi wanted to submit a memorial to the throne,
but the Yellow Gate Attendant said:
"The matter might leak,
which is not the original intent of the secret edict."
Wěi then stopped.
He then rallied his main army,
and again falsely issued an edict summoning the thirty-six armies,
and personally issued an order to all the armies saying:
"Heaven has brought calamity upon the Jìn imperial house;
disasters and chaos have followed one after another.
Recently, during the difficulty caused by Yáng Jùn,
it truly relied on all of you to pacify the disaster and chaos.
But the two dukes secretly plotted treachery,
wishing to depose His Majesty and cut off the sacrifices to Emperor Wǔ.
I now, in accordance with the edict,
dismiss the two dukes from office.
I now receive the edict to supervise all military affairs, both inside and outside the capital.
All those on duty as imperial guards shall be strictly vigilant;
those in the outer camps,
should lead their men
directly to the provisional headquarters.
Assisting the righteous and punishing the rebellious is blessed by Heaven.
Rewards will be openly offered
to await those who show loyalty.
Heaven and Earth,
truly hear these words."
He also falsely issued an edict ordering Liàng and Guàn to surrender their seals and sashes as Grand Tutor and Grand Protector, and their insignia as Palace Attendants,
and to go to their states,
with all their officials dismissed.
He also falsely issued an edict pardoning Liàng's and Guàn's officials, saying:
"The two dukes secretly plotted
to endanger the state.
They are now dismissed and returned to their residences.
Regarding their officials and subordinates,
none shall be questioned.
If anyone fails to obey the edict,
they will be dealt with according to military law.
Those who can lead their subordinates to surrender first
shall be enfeoffed as marquises and rewarded.
I will not break my word."
He then arrested Liàng and Guàn
and killed them.
Qí Shèng persuaded Wěi
that he could use his military power to execute Jiǎ Mó and Guō Zhāng,
rectify the imperial court,
and bring peace to the world.
Wěi hesitated and was undecided.
At dawn,
the Emperor, following Zhāng Huá's plan,
sent Palace General Wáng Gōng with a Zōuyú banner and waved it to the crowd, saying:
"The Prince of Chǔ has falsely issued an edict!"
The crowd all threw down their weapons and fled.
Wěi had no one left by his side,
and, being in distress and not knowing what to do,
only one fourteen-year-old slave
drove an ox-cart to take him to Kǎn, the Prince of Qín.
The Emperor sent an attendant to summon Wěi back to his camp,
where he was apprehended in the Wǔbēn office,
and then sent to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
An edict stated that Wěi had falsely issued imperial orders to harm the two dukes and their sons,
and also wished to exterminate imperial officials,
plotting treachery.
He was then executed,
at the age of twenty-one.
On that day, there was a strong wind,
thunder, and heavy rain.
An edict stated:
"The Duke of Zhōu decided the execution of the two uncles,
and Emperor Wǔ of Hàn judged the case of Zhāopíng—
these were unavoidable circumstances.
The Grand Judge has reported that Wěi has suffered the law.
I am deeply saddened and pained,
and I shall mourn."
As Wěi was about to die,
he took out a blue paper edict from his bosom,
and, tearfully, showed it to Liú Sòng, the Supervising Secretary of Punishment, saying:
"I received an edict and acted,
thinking it was for the state,
but now it is considered a crime.
Having inherited a body from the late emperor,
to be wronged like this,
I hope my case will be cleared."
Sòng also sighed and could not look up.
Gōngsūn Hóng and Qí Shèng both had their three clans exterminated.
Wěi was open-handed and generous by nature,
and capable of winning the hearts of the people.
At this time, none did not shed tears,
and the common people erected a shrine for him.
Empress Jiǎ had always disliked Guàn and Liàng,
and also feared Wěi,
so she used stratagems to have them executed one after another.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
he was posthumously appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
and his son Fàn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiāngyáng,
and appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Later, he was harmed by Shí Lè.
Lún, the Prince of Zhào.
Lún, the Prince of Zhào, courtesy name Zǐyí,
was the ninth son of Emperor Xuān,
his mother being Lady Bó.
In the early Jiāpíng era of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānlè Pavilion.
When the five ranks were established,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Son of Dōng'ān,
and appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū).
When Wǔ Dì received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángyá Commandery.
For having ordered the Cavalier Attendant Liú Jī to buy an imperial fur stolen by an artisan he brought along,
the Grand Judge Dù Yǒu correctly determined that Jī should be publicly executed,
and Lún ought to share the same crime as Jī.
The relevant authorities memorialized that Lún's rank was high and he was closely related to the imperial family,
and therefore should not be punished.
The Remonstrance Grand Master Liú Yì argued:
"The imperial law in rewarding and punishing
does not favor the noble or the humble.
Only then can the rites and regulations be uniform and the laws and punishments made clear.
Lún knew the fur was extraordinary
but concealed it and did not inform the officials,
sharing the same crime as Jī.
He should be considered for a reduced sentence due to his kinship and nobility,
not simply be exempted from discussion.
He should be judged according to the temporary law
as Dù Yǒu correctly determined."
The Emperor agreed with Yì's rebuttal,
but due to Lún's close kinship,
issued an edict pardoning him.
When he went to his state,
he acted as Eastern Chief Controller and General of Manifested Might.
In the Xiánníng era,
he was re-enfeoffed in Zhào,
and promoted to General Who Pacifies the North and Supervisor of Yèchéng Garrison Affairs,
then advanced to General Who Stabilizes the North.
In the early Yuánkāng era,
he was promoted to General Who Conquers the West and granted the privilege of establishing a staff (kāifǔ yítóng sānsī),
garrisoning Guānzhōng.
As Lún's rewards and punishments were immoderate,
the Dī and Qiāng rebelled,
and he was recalled to the capital.
Soon after, he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
He cultivated deep friendships with Jiǎ and Guō families,
and ingratiated himself with the Empress's palace,
and was greatly trusted and favored by Empress Jiǎ.
He sought the position of Director of the Secretariat,
but Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi firmly opposed it.
He then sought the position of Minister of the Secretariat,
but Huá and Wěi again refused.
When Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was deposed,
Lún was made to lead the General of the Right Army.
At that time, the Right Guard Commander Sīmǎ Yǎ and the Regular Attendant Commander Xǔ Chāo,
both having served in the Eastern Palace,
were distressed that the Crown Prince was innocent.
They conspired with the Palace Attendant Zhōngláng Shì Yī and others to depose Empress Jiǎ
and restore the Crown Prince.
As Huá and Wěi could not be swayed,
it was difficult to plan a coup with them.
Lún held crucial military power,
and was greedy and ambitious,
so he could be used to accomplish the task.
They then persuaded Sūn Xiù, Lún's favorite retainer, saying:
"The Empress is cruel, jealous, and lawless,
and with Jiǎ Mì and others, jointly deposed the Crown Prince.
Now the state lacks a legitimate heir,
the altars of soil and grain are in danger,
and the high ministers are about to undertake a great enterprise.
Yet you publicly serve the Empress,
and are close to the Jiǎ and Guō families.
Regarding the deposition of the Crown Prince,
everyone says you knew about it in advance.
Should something happen one day,
disaster will surely befall you.
Why not plan ahead?"
Xiù agreed,
and spoke to Lún,
who accepted the idea.
They then informed the Chief Clerk of Communications, Zhāng Lín; the Department Clerk, Zhāng Héng; the Palace Investigating Censor, Yīn Hún; and the Right Guard Commander, Lù Shǐ,
to act as internal agents.
When the plot was about to commence,
Xiù realized that the Crown Prince was intelligent,
and if he returned to the Eastern Palace,
he would consult with wise men on governance,
and Xiù himself would certainly not achieve his ambitions.
So he again persuaded Lún, saying:
"The Crown Prince is a fierce and resolute person;
he cannot be privately petitioned.
You have always served Empress Jiǎ,
and public opinion considers you part of the Jiǎ faction.
Even if you wish to perform a great service for the Crown Prince now,
the Crown Prince harbors old grudges
and will surely not reward you.
People will say you were merely forced by the populace's wishes
to reverse the situation and escape punishment.
This is how you would hasten disaster.
Let us delay this matter for now.
Empress Jiǎ will certainly harm the Crown Prince,
and then we can depose the Empress
and avenge the Crown Prince.
That would also be sufficient to establish your merits,
not merely to escape disaster."
Lún followed his advice.
Xiù then subtly leaked their plan,
allowing Jiǎ Mì's faction to hear some of it.
Lún and Xiù then encouraged Jiǎ Mì and others to quickly harm the Crown Prince
to cut off public hope.
After the Crown Prince was harmed,
Lún and Xiù's plot intensified,
but Xǔ Chāo and Yǎ, fearing future difficulties,
wanted to retract their plan,
so they feigned illness.
Xiù again informed the Right Guard Aid-the-Flight Commander Lǘ Hé,
who agreed.
They set the date for the third day of the fourth month, a Bing night, at the first watch,
using drumbeats as a signal.
On the appointed day,
they forged an imperial edict commanding the commanders of the three divisions, saying:
