"The Empress and Jiǎ Mì and others killed Our Crown Prince.
Now We order the General of Chariots and Cavalry to enter and depose the Empress.
All of you must obey this command
and will be granted the title of Marquis of Guānzhōng.
Disobey,
and your three clans will be exterminated."
Thereupon, all of them obeyed.
Lún again forged an edict to open the gates and enter at night,
deploying troops south of the road.
He sent the Commandant of the Valiant Cavalry, Qí Wáng Jiǒng, with a hundred men from the three divisions of commanders,
to force open the palace gates and enter.
The Director of Huálín, Luò Xiū, acted as an internal agent,
welcoming the Emperor to the Eastern Hall.
Then Empress Jiǎ was deposed as a commoner
and imprisoned in Jiànshǐ Hall.
Empress Dowager Wú, Zhào Càn, and Hán Shòu's wife Jiǎ Wǔ, and others were arrested
and handed over to the Punishment Bureau for investigation and conclusion.
An edict instructed the Secretariat to, concerning the matter of the deposed Empress,
arrest Jiǎ Mì and others,
and summon the Supervising Secretary, Attendants, Yellow Gate Attendants, and the Eight Administrators.
All entered the palace at night,
seizing Zhāng Huá, Péi Wěi, Xiè Jié, Dù Bīn, and others,
and executing them in front of the hall.
The Secretariat initially suspected the edict was fraudulent.
The bureaucrat Shī Jǐng submitted a memorial on a bare tablet requesting a handwritten edict.
Lún and others, believing he was hindering the populace,
executed him publicly.
The next day,
Lún sat at the Duānmén Gate,
with troops stationed facing north.
He sent the Minister Wáng Yù, holding the imperial staff, to escort the commoner Jiǎ to Jīnyǒng.
Zhào Càn's uncle, the Protector of the Central Army Zhào Jùn, and the Cavalier Attendant Hán Yù, and others were executed.
Many civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court, were dismissed.
Lún soon forged an edict to appoint himself as Bearer of the Imperial Staff, Grand Chief Controller, Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, and Chancellor.
His titles of Attendant and Prince remained as before.
He entirely followed the precedent of Xuān Wén assisting Wèi,
establishing Left and Right Chief Clerks, Commanders, four Aide-de-camps, ten Attendant Officers,
twenty subordinate clerks, and an army of ten thousand men.
He made his eldest son, the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Sīmǎ Fú, lead the Superintendent of Supernumerary Retainers;
his son Fù, General of the Vanguard,
was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìyáng;
Qián, Yellow Gate Attendant,
was enfeoffed as Prince of Rǔyīn;
Xǔ, Cavalier Attendant,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bàchéng.
Sūn Xiù and others were all enfeoffed with large commanderies
and held military power.
Thousands of civil and military officials were enfeoffed as marquises,
and all officials were subject to Lún.
Lún was originally mediocre
and lacked wisdom or strategy,
and was further controlled by Xiù.
Xiù's power and authority vibrated throughout the court;
the whole empire served Xiù and sought nothing from Lún.
Xiù rose from a minor clerk in Lángyá,
was successively promoted in the state of Zhào,
and achieved prominence through flattery.
Having grasped the reins of power,
he indulged his treacherous schemes,
killing many loyal and upright people
to satisfy his selfish desires.
The Inspector of Sīlì, Yóu Hào, had a grudge against Yīn Hún.
Hún enticed Hào's slave Jìn Xīng
to falsely accuse Hào of harboring ulterior motives.
Xiù did not investigate carefully,
and immediately arrested Hào and the Xiangyáng Central Director Lǐ Mài,
executing them.
He generously treated Jìn Xīng,
making him a commander in his own unit.
The former Commandant of the Guards Shí Chóng and Yellow Gate Attendant Pān Yuè both had grievances with Xiù
and were also executed.
Thus, the gentlemen of the capital no longer enjoyed their lives.
Huáinán Wáng Yǔn and Qí Wáng Jiǒng, because of Lún and Xiù’s arrogance and presumption,
harbored resentment internally.
Xiù and others also deeply feared them,
so Jiǒng was sent out to garrison Xǔ,
and Yǔn was stripped of his position as Protector of the Army.
Yǔn, in a fit of rage,
raised troops to attack Lún.
After Yǔn was defeated and annihilated,
Lún was granted the Nine Bestowals [Jiǔ Xī],
and his enfeoffment was increased by 50,000 households.
Lún falsely made a show of modesty and decline,
so an imperial edict was issued, sending all officials to his residence to urge him to accept.
The attendant-in-ordinary proclaimed the edict,
and only then did he accept it.
Fú was made General Who Pacifies the Army and General of the Central Army;
Fù was made General Who Guards the Army and General Overseeing the Protector of the Army;
Qián was made General of the Central Army and General of the Right Guard;
Xǔ was made attendant-in-ordinary.
Sūn Xiù was also made attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Assists the State, and Administrator of the Chancellor's Office,
with his former position as Right Commander remaining as before.
Zhāng Lín and others all held prominent and important positions.
The chancellor’s office army was increased to 20,000 men,
on par with the palace guards,
and soldiers were also hidden,
bringing the total force to over 30,000.
Three gates and four corner watchtowers were erected for the Eastern Palace,
and the east-west roads of the palace were cut off to form an outer perimeter.
Someone said to Xiù:
“Sanqí Chángshì Yáng Zhǔn and Huángmén Shìláng Liú Kuí intend to support Liáng Wáng Róng to execute Lún.”
There happened to be an unusual celestial phenomenon,
so Róng was transferred to be Chancellor and
resided in the Ministry of the Interior office,
while Zhǔn and Kuí were transferred to external posts.
Lún was unlearned
and illiterate;
Xiù, too, with his cunning and petty talent,
was greedy, licentious, and blinded by profit.
Those who conspired with them to accomplish their goals
were all corrupt and obsequious individuals,
who only vied for glory and profit,
without deep foresight or strategy.
Fú was shallow and vulgar;
Fù and Qián were ignorant, stubborn, and aggressive;
Xǔ was foolish, mute, frivolous, and flippant.
Yet they were all at odds with each other,
mutually hating and slandering one another.
Xiù’s son, Huì,
at twenty years old,
was made Commander of the Archers and
married the emperor's daughter, Hédōng Gōngzhǔ.
The princess's mother's mourning period had not yet completed a year,
when the betrothal gifts were accepted.
Huì was short and homely in appearance;
he was lower than a servant,
initially selling horses with sons of wealthy families in the west of the city.
When the common people suddenly heard that he was marrying the princess,
none were not shocked and astonished.
Lún and Xiù were both obsessed with sorcery and ghosts,
listening to evil and heterodox prophecies.
Xiù had his gate-general Zhào Fèng falsely claim to be the spirit of Xuān Dì,
commanding Lún to quickly enter the Western Palace.
It was also said that Xuān Dì was assisting Zhào Wáng at Běi Máng,
so a separate temple for Xuān Dì was erected on Máng Shān.
They believed that their rebellious plot could succeed.
Péi Shào, the Crown Prince’s Chamberlain, Biàn Cuì, the General of the Left Army, and twenty others were made Attendant Censor,
and another twenty were made clerks.
Xiù and others divided the various armies,
distributing their trusted confidants.
Sanqí Chángshì, Yìyáng Wáng Wēi, was concurrently made attendant-in-ordinary,
to transmit and receive imperial edicts.
A forged edict of abdication was made,
and Shǐ Chíjíe, Shàngshū Lìng Mǎn Fèn,
with Púshè Cuī Suí as his deputy,
was sent to present the emperor's seals and ribbons, ceding the throne to Lún.
Lún feigned refusal.
Thereupon, the imperial princes, the high officials, and ministers all falsely claimed auspicious signs and celestial phenomena to urge him to accept,
and Lún then agreed.
Zuǒ Wèi Wáng Yú, with Qián Jūn Sīmǎ Yǎ and others, led armored soldiers into the palace,
persuading the three marshals [sīmǎ] by analogy,
showing them power and reward,
and none dared to disobey.
That night,
Zhāng Lín and others were ordered to guard the various gates.
Yìyáng Wáng Wēi and Luò Xiū and others forcibly seized the emperor's seals and ribbons.
Before the night watch ended,
all officials, inside and outside, welcomed Lún with the imperial carriage and ceremonial procession.
Huì Dì rode in a mica carriage,
with a ceremonial retinue of several hundred people,
exiting from Húalín Western Gate and residing in Jīnyǒng City.
Shàngshū Hé Yù,
concurrently attendant-in-ordinary, Sanqí Chángshì, Lángxié Wáng Ruì,
and Zhōngshū Shìláng Lù Jī followed,
but turned back upon reaching the city wall.
Zhāng Héng was ordered to guard the emperor,
which was in fact to imprison him.
Lún, with five thousand soldiers,
entered through Duānmén,
ascended Tàijí Diàn,
and Mǎn Fèn, Cuī Suí, and Yuè Guǎng presented the seals and ribbons to Lún.
He then usurped the imperial throne,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title to Jiànshǐ.
That year,
candidates recommended as worthy and upright, those who dared to speak frankly, talented scholars, filial and incorrupt officials, and good generals were all appointed without examination;
accountants and envoys from all four directions who were in the capital,
as well as students of the Imperial Academy aged sixteen and above or who had studied for twenty years,
were all appointed as officials;
governors of commanderies and magistrates of counties with salaries of two thousand piculs who were in office on the day of the amnesty
were all enfeoffed as marquises;
chief clerks of commanderies were all made filial and incorrupt officials,
and chief clerks of counties were made incorrupt officials.
His heir apparent, Fú, was made Crown Prince;
Fù was made attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Minister of Agriculture, General Overseeing the Protector of the Army, and King of Jīngzhào;
Qián was made attendant-in-ordinary, Grand General Overseeing the Army, and King of Guǎngpíng;
Xǔ was made attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Pacifies the Army, and King of Bàchéng;
Sūn Xiù was made attendant-in-ordinary, Director of the Central Secretariat, General of Agile Cavalry, and his status was made equal to the Three Excellencies;
Zhāng Lín and all other partisans were elevated to high ministerial and general ranks,
and all received large enfeoffments.
The rest of the co-conspirators all surpassed their ranks and positions,
too numerous to count,
even servants and menials were given noble titles.
At every court assembly,
sable tails filled the seats.
People at the time had a proverb about it:
“Sable tails are insufficient,
so dog tails are added to make up the number.”
But by using temporary favors to please people,
the stores in the treasury were insufficient for the rewards,
and the smelting and casting of gold and silver could not keep up with the demand for seals.
Thus, there were marquises with blank tablets,
and gentlemen were ashamed to wear their insignia,
while the common people also knew that it would not last.
Lún personally performed sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and on his return,
encountered a strong wind
that blew away and broke his banners and canopies.
Since Sūn Xiù had accomplished an extraordinary feat,
Lún held him in great respect.
Xiù resided in the inner palace that Wén Dì occupied when he was Chancellor.
Nothing, big or small,
was done without consulting him first.
Lún’s edicts
were often altered by Xiù.
He would grant or revoke at will,
personally writing edicts on blue paper.
Sometimes an order issued in the morning would be changed several times by evening,
and officials were replaced as swiftly as flowing water.
At that time, a pheasant entered the palace hall,
ascending the hall from the eastern steps of Tàijí Diàn.
When it was driven away,
it flew under the western bell.
After a moment,
it flew away.
Lún also found a strange bird in the hall,
and when asked, no one knew its name.
For several days, as evening approached,
a small child in white clothes from the west of the palace said it was a Fúl Líu bird.
Lún ordered the child and the bird to be locked in a cell.
The next morning, when they opened it,
the door was as before,
but both the person and the bird were gone.
Lún had a tumor on his eye,
which was considered an ill omen at the time.
At that time, Qí Wáng Jiǒng, Héjiān Wáng Yōng, and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng all commanded strong armies,
each occupying a region.
Xiù knew that Jiǒng and the others would surely have other plans,
so he selected his close associates and Lún's former subordinates to serve as assistants to the three princes and as commandery governors.
Xiù had always had a rift with Zhāng Lín.
Although outwardly they praised each other,
inwardly they truly feared each other.
When Lín became General of the Guards,
he deeply resented not being able to establish his own office.
He secretly sent a letter to Fú,
detailing how Xiù monopolized power,
constantly going against public sentiment,
and how the meritorious officials were all petty men
disrupting the court,
and could be executed all at once.
Fú reported the letter to Lún,
and Lún showed it to Xiù.
Xiù persuaded Lún to execute Lín,
and Lún agreed.
Thereupon, Lún invited the imperial family to a gathering at Huálín Yuán,
summoned Lín, Xiù, and Wáng Yú to enter.
He then arrested Lín,
executed him,
and exterminated his three clans.
When the proclamations of the Three Kings raising armies to campaign against Lún arrived,
Lún and Xiù were finally greatly alarmed.
They dispatched their staunch general Sūn Fǔ as Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Jīně Lǐ Yán as Zhéjǐng Jiāngjūn,
leading seven thousand soldiers to emerge from the Yánshòu Pass.
Zhēnglǔ Zhāng Hóng, Zuǒjūn Cài Huáng, Qiánjūn Lǘ Hé and others led nine thousand men to emerge from the Èbǎn Pass.
Zhènjūn Sīmǎ Yǎ, Yángwēi Mò Yuán and others led eight thousand men to emerge from the Chénggāo Pass.
They summoned Dōngpíng Wáng Máo to be Shǐchíjié, Wèijiāngjūn,
and Dutouchéng Zhūjūn to resist the righteous army.
They sent Yáng Zhēn to go day and night to Xuāndì's detached temple to pray and entreat.
He would always say, "Xuāndì thanks Your Majesty,
on such and such a day the bandits will be broken."
They appointed the Daoist Hú Wò as Tàipíng Jiāngjūn,
to invoke blessings.
Xiù's household daily conducted illicit sacrifices,
and wrote documents for apotropaic magic,
and sent shamans to choose battle days.
He also ordered close relatives to wear feather cloaks on Sōng Shān,
falsely claiming to be the immortal Wáng Qiáo,
and wrote a book of immortals,
describing Lún's long reign to deceive the masses.
Xiù wanted to send Fù and Qián to lead troops to assist the various armies in battle,
but Fù and Qián refused.
Qián had always been close to Liú Yú.
So Xiù sent Yú to persuade Qián.
Qián then led eight thousand men to serve as reinforcements for the three armies.
Although Hóng and Yǎ's forces won consecutive battles,
the righteous army, though dispersed, always regrouped,
and Yǎ's forces could not advance.
Xǔ Chāo and others fought with Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng's army at Huángqiáo,
killing and wounding over ten thousand men.
Hóng went directly to Yángzhái,
and then south of the city, defeated Qí Wáng Jiǒng's baggage train,
killing several thousand men,
and then occupied the city and protected the official residences.
However, Jiǒng's army was already in Yǐngyīn,
forty *lǐ* from Yángzhái.
Jiǒng divided his army and crossed the Yǐng River,
attacking Hóng's forces without success.
Hóng pressed his advantage and reached Yǐngshàng,
arraying his troops facing the Yǐng River at night.
Jiǒng sent light troops to attack them.
The various armies did not move,
but Sūn Fǔ and Xú Jiàn's armies were in disarray at night,
and went directly to Luòyáng to surrender.
When Fǔ and Jiàn fled,
they did not know that the commanders of the various armies were still alive,
and so they said:
"Qí Wáng's army is strong,
irresistible,
and Hóng's forces have already been destroyed."
Lún was greatly shaken,
kept it a secret,
and summoned Qián and Chāo back.
At that time, Hóng's dispatch reporting the defeat of Jiǒng arrived.
Lún was greatly pleased,
and then sent Chāo back again,
but Qián had already returned to Yǔcāng.
Chāo returned and crossed the Hé River,
but his officers and men were suspicious and hesitant,
and their morale was inwardly crushed.
Hóng and all his forces crossed the Yǐng River,
and advanced to attack Jiǒng's camp.
Jiǒng sent out troops to attack his detached commanders Sūn Máo, Sīmǎ Tán, and Sūn Fǔ.
They were all defeated,
and the soldiers scattered back to Luòyáng.
Hóng and his forces gathered their troops and returned to camp.
Xiù and others knew that the situation on the three fronts was becoming critical daily.
They falsely reported that Jiǒng's camp had been broken,
and Jiǒng had been captured,
to deceive and mislead their forces.
They ordered all officials to offer congratulations.
However, Shì Yī, Fú Yìn, and Sūn Huì all held their *jié* (credentials) and refused to comply with each other.
Lún again bestowed a *jié* upon Tàizǐ Zhànshì Liú Kūn,
made him Dū Héběi Jiāngjūn,
and ordered him to lead a thousand infantry and cavalry to urge the various armies to fight.
Huì and others fought the righteous army at Jīshuǐ,
suffered a great defeat,
and retreated to defend the Hé River.
Liú Kūn burned and cut off the river bridge.
Since the righteous army had risen,
all officials and generals wanted to execute Lún and Xiù to appease the world.
Xiù knew that the anger of the masses was difficult to provoke,
and dared not leave the department.
When he heard that the Héběi army was completely defeated,
he was worried and frustrated, not knowing what to do.
Yìyáng Wáng Wēi persuaded Xiù to go to the Shàngshū Shěng to discuss battle preparations with the Eight Dignitaries.
Xiù followed his advice.
He ordered all sons of officials of rank four and below in the capital, aged fifteen and above,
to go to the Sīlì,
to follow Lún out to battle.
The internal and external armies all wanted to seize and kill Xiù.
Wēi was afraid,
and fled from the Chónglǐ Tà to his lower residence.
After Xǔ Chāo, Shì Yī, Sūn Huì and other armies had all returned,
they consulted with Xiù.
Some wanted to gather the remaining troops and go out to battle,
some wanted to burn down the palaces,
and execute those who did not support them,
and take Lún south to join Sūn Qí, Mèng Guān, and others.
Some wanted to take a boat and flee east into the sea.
Their plans were undecided.
Wáng Yú turned against them,
and led over seven hundred camp soldiers to enter through the Nányè Gate.
He ordered the palace guards to defend their respective gates.
The Sīmǎ of the three divisions responded from within.
Yú himself went to attack Xiù.
Xiù closed the southern gate of the Zhōngshū Shěng.
Yú unleashed his soldiers to climb the walls and burn the houses.
Xiù, Chāo, and Yī hurriedly fled out.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Zhào Quán beheaded Xiù and others and displayed their heads.
He arrested Sūn Qí in the Yòuwèi Camp,
and handed him over to the Tíngwèi for execution.
He seized Qiánjiāngjūn Xiè Tán, Huángménlìng Luò Xiū, and Sīmǎ Dū Wáng Qián,
and executed them all in the palace hall.
The Sīmǎ soldiers of the three divisions beheaded Sūn Bì in the Xuānhuà Tà and displayed his head.
At that time, Sīmǎ Fù was sitting with Xiù.
Yú ordered his officers and men to imprison him in the Sànqí Shěng,
and guard the province gate with large halberds.
The Eight Dignitaries all entered the palace hall,
and sat under the trees on the eastern platform.
Wáng Yú garrisoned the Yúnlóng Gate,
and made Lún issue an edict saying:
"I was misled by Sūn Xiù and others,
which angered the Three Kings.
Now that Xiù has been executed,
welcome the Former Emperor back to his position.
I will return to grow old in the fields."
He sent the edict with a Zōuyú banner, ordering the officers and men to disarm.
All civil and military officials fled,
none daring to remain.
The palace eunuch led Lún out of the Huálín East Gate,
and he and Fù both returned to their residence in Wènyáng Lǐ.
Thereupon, several thousand armored soldiers welcomed the Son of Heaven from Jīnyǒng,
and the common people all shouted "Long live!"
The Emperor entered through the Duānmén,
ascended the throne,
and took his seat in the Guǎngshì.
Lún and Fù were sent and handed over to Jīnyǒng Castle.
Initially,
Xiù, fearing the western army's arrival,
again summoned Qián back.
That day, Qián lodged at Jiǔqǔ.
An edict was sent by an envoy to dismiss Qián from office.
Qián was afraid,
abandoned his army, and led several tens of men back to Wènyáng Lǐ.
Liáng Wáng Róng memorialized that Lún and his sons were vicious and rebellious,
and should be executed.
The officials held a joint meeting in the court hall,
and all agreed with Róng's memorial.
Shàngshū Yuán Chǎng was dispatched, holding the *jié*, to grant Lún death,
giving him bitter wine with gold dust to drink.
Lún was ashamed,
covered his face with a cloth,
and said:
"Sūn Xiù misled me!
Sūn Xiù misled me!"
Thereupon, Fù, Qián, Xǔ, and Lún's sons were arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi prison,
and interrogated to their end.
Fù, before his death, said to Qián:
"Because of you, our family is ruined!"
All officials who had been appointed by Lún
were dismissed,
and scarcely any remained in the Censorate, Secretariat, or palace guards.
Since the outbreak of war, over sixty days had passed,
and nearly one hundred thousand people had been killed in battle.
Of those who had joined Lún in rebellion and plotted the grand affair: Zhāng Lín was killed by Xiù;
Xǔ Chāo, Shì Yī, Sūn Bì, Xiè Tán, Yīn Hún, along with Xiù, were executed by Wáng Yú;
Zhāng Héng, Lǘ Hé, Sūn Máo, Gāo Yuè returned from Yángzhái;
Fú Yìn returned to Luòyáng after being defeated in battle;
all were beheaded at the Eastern Market.
Cài Huáng surrendered to Qí Wáng Jiǒng from Yángzhái,
and committed suicide upon returning to Luòyáng.
Wáng Yú was exempted from execution due to his merits,
but later conspired with Dōnglái Wáng Ruí to assassinate Jiǒng,
and was also executed according to law.
Qí Wáng Jiǒng (Zhèng Fāng)
Qí Wǔmǐn Wáng Jiǒng, courtesy name Jǐngzhì,
was the son of Xiàn Wáng Yōu.
From a young age, he was known for his benevolence and kindness,
and enjoyed giving generously,
possessing his father's demeanor.
Initially,
Yōu was ill,
but Wǔdì did not believe it,
and sent imperial physicians to diagnose him.
All said he was not ill.
When Yōu died,
the Emperor went to attend the mourning.
Jiǒng cried out and wept, accusing the physicians of falsely reporting his father's illness.
An edict was issued to execute the physicians immediately.
Because of this, he gained renown,
and thus inherited the title.
During the Yuánkāng era,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
leading the Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn and Yìjūn Xiàowèi.
Zhào Wáng Lún secretly allied with him,
and after deposing Empress Jiǎ,
he was promoted to Yóují Jiāngjūn for his merits.
Qióng was not satisfied with his position,
showing a resentful expression.
Sūn Xiù subtly noticed this,
and also, fearing his presence in the capital,
sent him out as Píngdōng Jiāngjūn, with a provisional authority (Jiǎjié),
to garrison Xǔchāng.
When Lún usurped the throne,
Qióng was promoted to Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn, with the authority to establish his own administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
hoping to placate him with honor.
However, Qióng, seeing the widespread resentment,
secretly conspired with Líhú Wáng Shèng and Yǐngchuān Wáng Chǔmù to raise an army to execute Lún.
Lún sent his confidant Zhāng Wū to spy on him,
but Wū returned,
saying:
"Qí has no ulterior motives."
Qióng, having a well-formed plan yet to be executed,
feared exposure,
so he, along with his army commander Guǎn Xí, killed Chǔmù
and sent his head to Lún,
to reassure him.
Once his plan was set,
he then arrested and killed Xí.
He subsequently raised an army with Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Hé Xù, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Dǒng Ài, and others,
sending envoys to inform the four princes of Chéngdū, Héjiān, Chángshān, and Xīnyě.
They issued a proclamation to all commanders, garrisons, provinces, prefectures, and kingdoms throughout the realm,
making sure everyone was aware.
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Xī Lóng received the proclamation
but hesitated, undecided.
His staff officer, Wáng Suì, beheaded him
and sent his head to Qióng.
Qióng garrisoned his army at Yángzhái.
Lún sent his generals Lǘ Hé, Zhāng Hóng, and Sūn Fǔ to Òbǎn
to engage Qióng in battle.
Qióng's army suffered a defeat
and held its ground by fortifying the camp.
At this time, the Chéngdū army defeated Lún's forces at Huángqiáo,
so Qióng then sallied forth to attack Hé and others,
utterly defeating them.
When Wáng Yú deposed Lún
and Emperor Huì was restored,
Qióng, having finished executing the rebel faction,
led his forces into Luò,
encamping at the Tōngzhāng Bureau.
With hundreds of thousands of armored soldiers,
the magnificence of his banners, flags, and weaponry
shook the capital.
The Son of Heaven personally appointed him Dàsīmǎ,
bestowed upon him the Nine Bestowals,
and accorded him all the regalia and ceremonial documents,
following the precedents of Xuān, Jǐng, Wén, and Wǔ in assisting the Wèi dynasty.
Qióng then assisted in governing,
residing in Yōu's former palace,
and appointing forty clerks and subordinates.
He extensively built residences and mansions,
taking the Wǔgǔ Market in the north
and opening various bureaus in the south,
destroying hundreds of houses
and ordering the Grand Architect to construct them
to be equivalent to the Western Palace.
He excavated the wall of Qiānqiū Gate to connect to the Western Pavilion.
Bells were hung in the back rooms,
and the Bāyì dance was performed in the front courtyard.
He indulged in wine and women,
not attending court.
He sat while receiving officials,
issuing decrees to the Sāntái.
Selections were unfair,
favoring only his relatives and intimates.
He appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn Hé Xù to lead the Zhōnglǐngjūn.
He enfeoffed Gě Yú as Móupíng Gōng,
Lù Xiù as Xiǎohuáng Gōng,
Wèi Yì as Yīnpíng Gōng,
Liú Zhēn as Ānxiāng Gōng,
and Hán Tài as Fēngqiū Gōng,
calling them
"the Five Dukes,"
and entrusted them with his innermost confidence.
When Diànzhōng Yùshǐ Huán Bào presented a report
without first passing through Qióng's mansion,
he was immediately investigated and executed.
At this, the court became wary,
and the realm was disappointed.
The recluse of Nányáng, Zhèng Fāng, openly submitted a memorial with extreme remonstrance,
and the Chief Clerk, Wáng Bào, repeatedly offered advice,
but Qióng could not employ any of it.
He then memorialized for Bào's execution and had him killed.
A white-haired old man entered the Dàsīmǎ's mansion, shouting loudly
that troops would rise
within ten days (Jiǎzǐ xún).
He was immediately arrested and killed.
Qióng's arrogance and indulgence grew daily,
with no intention of changing.
The former Bandit Registrar's subordinate, Sūn Huì, again submitted a remonstrance, saying: "Huì has heard that there are five difficulties and
four impossibilities in the world,
and you, illustrious Duke, embody them all.
To abandon the lord of the ancestral temple,
to disregard the weight of a thousand chariots,
to personally don armor and
helmet,
and to brave the sharp edges of weapons—
this is the first difficulty.
To raise three hundred soldiers,
to devise a strategy for complete victory,
to gather forces from all four directions,
and to attract heroes and talented individuals—
this is the second
difficulty.
To forsake the dignity of the imperial halls,
to reside in humble single tents,
to endure the misery of clamor and dust,
and to share the toil of officers and soldiers—
this is the third difficulty.
To lead a rabble,
to face
a ferocious and powerful enemy,
to rely on divine military strategy,
and to have no fear of doubt or obstruction—
this is the fourth difficulty.
To issue a proclamation within the six directions,
to set forth oaths of alliance and trust,
to elevate the emperor from a secluded
palace,
and to restore the imperial lineage's enterprise—
this is the fifth difficulty.
Great fame cannot be borne for long,
great merit cannot be held for long,
great power cannot be wielded for long,
and great majesty cannot
be maintained for long.
There has never been anyone who accomplished these five difficulties without considering them difficult,
or who neglected the 'impossibilities' and called them 'possibilities.'
This is what makes Huì uneasy.
Since Yǒngxī,
eleven years have passed,
and the people have seen no virtue,
hearing only of executions.
The imperial clan suffered the calamity of usurpation,
kinsmen met with the punishment
of public display of severed heads,
various princes were trapped in imprisonment,
and imperial consorts and princesses endured the sorrow of separation.
Looking back at previous dynasties,
the calamities of the state
and the chaos among close relatives
have never been as severe
as today.
When good historians record these errors,
what will future generations think?
The reason why the world has not turned away from Jìn,
and why the Mandate of Heaven endures in the world, is
that the ruler is free from the tyranny
of severe oppression,
and the court is free from cruel and harsh policies.
Emperor Wǔ's remaining benevolence,
and King Xiàn's lingering affection,
along with the sagely compassion and harmony,
still resonate in people's hearts.
What the four seas depend on
truly lies
in this.
Now, you, illustrious Duke, have established an unprecedented righteousness,
yet you have not made an unprecedented relinquishment.
The world is perplexed by this,
seeking enlightenment.
Chángshā and Chéngdū,
as intimate as Lǔ and Wèi,
are kin of the state,
who count their merits and receive their rewards alongside you, illustrious Duke,
yet they do not put themselves first.
Now, you should emulate the achievements of Huán and Wén,
and surpass the character of Zāng and Zhá.
Treat all
things as straw dogs,
not being inhumane in your transformation.
Exalt your kin and promote those close to you.
After accomplishing your deeds, you should withdraw,
entrusting the myriad affairs of state to the two princes,
and appointing regional governors to the various marquises.
Display the banner of righteousness and humility,
and sound the bells
of returning
home.
Reside in the former territory of Great Qí,
and revive the magnificent spirit.
Rule with folded hands over the regions of Qīng and Xú,
and rest easy as the Marquis of Yíngqiū.
Neither metal nor stone is sufficient to inscribe your loftiness,
nor are the eight musical instruments sufficient to praise your beauty.
King Jī Wén could not exclusively hold sainthood before you,
nor could Tàibó solely be virtuous after you.
Now, you, illustrious Duke, forget the regret of overreaching,
and disregard exhaustion.
Gao’s (高) misfortune:
abandoning the security of the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè)
to reside in the peril of stacked eggs.
Externally, his power and influence drew suspicion;
internally, his multifarious duties damaged his spirit.
Though he dwelled atop a high platform,
roaming
freely beyond the high walls,
his worries of danger and ruin
surpassed the concerns of Yǐng Dì (潁翟).
His subordinates trembled in fear,
none daring to speak.
Huì (惠), in his declining years,
encountered a period of disaster (yángjiǔ zhī yùn),
embraced the calamity of arrows and stones,
and committed to the righteousness of the Great King (Dàwáng).
He shed his coarse clothes and donned a helmet,
joining the army at Xǔ (許).
Having
fought in battles,
with no noteworthy achievements,
he should follow the winds and dust,
awaiting punishment for his initial service.
Qū Yuán (屈原) was exiled,
his heart still with Nányǐng (南郢);
Yuè Yì (樂毅) went to Zhào (趙),
his ambition still yearning for Běiyān (北燕).
How much more so Huì (惠), who received grace
and special nurturing.
Although temporarily separated,
his affection for him surpassed that of those two ministers.
Therefore, he revealed his heartfelt sincerity,
daring to risk offence.
If his words led to his execution,
and his righteousness
brought about success,
then to retreat and face the axe and chopping block,
this death of Huì (惠) would be nobler than his life.
Jiǒng (冏) did not accept it,
nor did he inflict punishment.
The Deputy Commander of the Army (Yìjūn Xiàowèi), Lǐ Hán (李含), fled to Cháng'ān (長安),
falsely claiming to have received a secret imperial edict
ordering the Prince of Héjiān (Héjiān Wáng), Yǒng (顒), to execute Jiǒng (冏),
and then guided him with a profitable scheme.
Yǒng (顒) followed it,
submitting a memorial stating: "The royal house has faced many troubles,
with calamities unending.
Though the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), Jiǒng (冏), initiated the righteous cause and has the merit of restoring the imperial throne,
the establishment of the capital
and the pacification of the altars of soil and grain
were
truly the achievements of the Prince of Chéngdū (Chéngdū Wáng).
Yet Jiǒng (冏) could not firmly uphold the duty of a minister,
instead harbouring deviant ambitions.
In the camp at Xǔchāng (許昌), he established eastern and western outer gates,
officially appointed secretaries and
imperial censors (Yùshǐ),
with chief clerks (zhǎngshǐ) and military governors (sīmǎ) standing directly to his left and right,
in the manner of imperial attendants.
The capital was greatly pacified,
and usurpers were punished and exterminated,
yet he led a million troops to surround Luò
Chéng (洛城).
He held the army in check for a year,
not once presenting himself at court,
while all officials bowed prostrate,
and he sat calmly facing south.
He destroyed the Music Bureau (Yuèguān) and market offices
to expand his own domain.
He arbitrarily took secret
weapons from the armory,
and kept them strictly arrayed without disbanding.
Therefore, Ruí (蕤), the Prince of Dōnglái (Dōnglái Wáng), knowing his rebellious intent,
memorialized the facts,
but was slandered and framed,
punished, and banished.
He established private factions,
and presumptuously
appointed his own officials.
His favoured wife and beloved concubines
were given titles comparable to those of the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng).
He indulged in wine and women,
showing no concern for the common people.
Dǒng (董) and Ài (艾) were unrestrained,
fearing nothing.
When the Imperial Censor (Zhōngchéng)
impeached them,
they were merely dismissed.
Zhāng Wěi (張偉) was arrogant and insolent,
holding up imperial edicts for approval;
Gě Yú (葛旟), a mere lackey,
controlled the fate of the nation.
He manipulated royal titles,
and bribery became rampant.
A gang of villains gathered,
arbitrarily deciding life and death.
He secretly appointed confidantes,
solely for personal gain.
He banished loyal and virtuous officials,
eyeing the sacred imperial regalia.
Your servant, having received a heavy responsibility
to protect the borders,
witnesses Jiǒng's (冏) actions
and feels truly indignant.
On this very day, the Deputy Commander of the Army (Yìjūn Xiàowèi), Lǐ Hán (李含), arrived secretly by post-horse,
delivering the imperial
decree.
Your servant humbly read it, feeling deeply moved,
as if his five viscera were scorched.
According to the righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū),
a minister should not make plans against his lord or parents.
Jiǒng (冏) commands a strong army,
and has established private factions,
with all positions of power and importance
filled by his confidantes.
Even a severe punishment
might not be accepted justly.
Now, I will immediately muster troops,
one hundred thousand elite soldiers,
and together with the provincial expeditionary forces (zhōu zhēng) will uphold loyalty and righteousness,
jointly converging on Luò
Yáng (洛陽).
The General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), the Prince of Chángshā (Chángshā Wáng),
will similarly demonstrate loyalty and sincerity,
to depose Jiǒng (冏) and return him to his residence.
Any who disobey orders
will be dealt with by military law.
Yǐng (穎), the Prince of Chéngdū (Chéngdū Wáng), is of illustrious virtue
and noble lineage,
his merits lofty and achievements weighty.
His conduct in past years
truly conformed to popular expectation,
and he is fit to be the chief minister (zǎifǔ),
replacing Jiǒng (冏) in the role of regent (Āhéng)."
When Yǒng's (顒) memorial arrived,
Jiǒng (冏) was greatly alarmed,
and gathered all officials, saying:
"Formerly, Sūn Xiù (孫秀) acted rebelliously,
usurping and coercing the emperor,
overthrowing the state,
with no one able to resist the calamity.
I assembled a righteous army,
sweeping away the chief villain,
my fidelity as a minister
established before the gods.
Today, the two princes, listening to slander,
have stirred up great trouble.
We must rely on loyal counsel to reconcile these disagreements."
The Minister of Education (Sītú), Wáng Róng (王戎), and the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Yuè (越), Prince of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Wáng), advised Jiǒng (冏) to relinquish power and show humility.
Jiǒng's (冏) Staff Officer (Cóngshì Zhōngláng), Gě Yú (葛旟), angrily said:
"The commoner Zhào (趙 Shùrén) allowed Sūn Xiù (孫秀) to manipulate the heavens and replace the sun (i.e., usurp power),
at that time, there was much chatter,
but no one dared to speak first.
You, my lord, braved arrows and stones,
personally donned armour,
attacked and breached fortifications,
thus achieving success today.
Rewards are being calculated and bestowed,
but matters are too extensive to be fully completed.
The Censors (Sāntái Nàyán) are not concerned with state affairs;
rewards are delayed,
and the blame does not lie with the government.
This slander is rebellious and usurpatory,
and should be jointly punished.
To falsely acknowledge a fabricated letter
and order my lord to return to his residence—
since the Han (Hàn) and Wei (Wèi) dynasties,
has any prince or marquis returning to his residence ever been able to keep his wife and children safe?
Those who propose this should be executed!"
Thereupon, all officials trembled with fear,
none without a change of colour.
Chángshā Wáng (長沙王) directly entered the palace
and dispatched troops to attack Jiǒng's (冏) residence.
Jiǒng (冏) sent Dǒng Ài (董艾) to array troops west of the palace.
He also sent Sòng Hóng (宋洪) and others to set fire to all the pavilions and the Qiānqiū (千秋) and Shénwǔ (神武) gates.
Jiǒng (冏) ordered the Administrator of the Yellow Gates, Wáng Hú (王湖), to steal all the Zōuyú (騶虞) banners,
proclaiming:
"Chángshā Wáng (長沙王) has issued a false edict!"
He also announced:
"The Grand Marshal is plotting rebellion;
those who assist him will have their five kindreds exterminated!"
That night,
a great battle raged within the city;
arrows fell like rain,
and the firelight reached the heavens.
The Emperor went to the Shàngdōng Mén (上東門),
where arrows gathered before his carriage.
His officials fought the fire,
and the dead lay piled upon each other.
The next day,
Jiǒng (冏) was defeated.
He was captured and brought before the palace hall.
The Emperor felt pity
and wished to spare his life.
He shouted at his attendants to quickly drag him out.
Jiǒng (冏) still looked back twice.
He was then beheaded outside the Chānghé Mén (閶闔門),
and his head was displayed to the Six Armies.
All his partisans were exterminated to the third kindred.
His sons, Huáilíng Wáng Chāo (淮陵王超), Lè'ān Wáng Bīng (樂安王冰), and Jìyáng Wáng Yīng (濟陽王英), were imprisoned in Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Jiǒng's (冏) corpse was exposed at Xīmíng Tíng (西明亭)
for three days, and no one dared to collect it for burial.
Jiǒng's (冏) former subordinates, Xún Kǎi (荀闓) and others, submitted a memorial requesting burial,
which was granted.
Initially,
when Jiǒng (冏) was at the height of his power,
a woman came to the Grand Marshal's residence seeking to leave her child there.
The official questioned her.
The woman said:
"I will leave as soon as Qí (齊) is cut off."
Those who understood heard this and were disgusted by it.
At that time, a ballad also circulated:
"Wearing a linen band around the belly,
mourning for Qí (齊)."
Soon after, Jiǒng (冏) was executed.
At the beginning of Yǒngxīng (永興) era,
an edict stated that Jiǒng (冏) had lightly fallen into severe punishment,
but his former meritorious deeds should not be obliterated.
Therefore, his three sons, Chāo (超), Bīng (冰), and Yīng (英), were pardoned and returned to their residences.
Chāo (超) was enfeoffed as a xiànwáng (縣王)
to continue Jiǒng's (冏) sacrifices,
and served as a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
At the beginning of Guāngxī (光熙) era,
Jiǒng (冏) was posthumously honored with an edict that read:
"Alas, former Grand Marshal, Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏)! You, the King, in the past, as a scion of the imperial house, succeeded your generation
and established your lineage in the eastern land.
You served as a bulwark for the capital,
truly stabilizing our imperial house.
You boldly led righteous troops,
allied at Chùzé (觸澤),
achieved great merit,
and greatly rescued Yǐngdōng (潁東).
I responded with commendation for your splendid achievements,
deeming your efforts profound.
I followed former precedents
to reward your illustrious virtue.
You expanded your territory with a special division,
encompassing Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚),
held grand rites and complete regalia,
and enjoyed favor equal to Xiāo (蕭) and Huò (霍).
It was hoped that relying on your weighty support and allegiance,
the aspirations of the state and the royal family would forever flourish.
However, your respectful virtue was not established;
you incurred insult from two sides.
The officials made mistakes
that led to your execution.
The ancients had a saying: 'Even when applying his laws,
one still thinks of the person.'
How much more so, when the King's merits saved my person
and his achievements preserved the altars of soil and grain!
Reflecting on the past,
there is sorrow in my heart!
Now, your original enfeoffment is restored,
and your heir is commanded to return and continue your lineage.
The rites, ranks, and regulations
shall be entirely as the old system.
I dispatch an envoy holding the regalia of authority, the Grand Herald, to your tomb to grant this decree,
and offer sacrifices with a grand victim.
If your spirit has awareness,
humbly accept my command,
thus pacifying your heart
and appreciating this honor and glory."
His son Chāo (超) succeeded to the peerage.
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Emperor Huái (懷帝) issued an edict,
reiterating Jiǒng's (冏) great merit in initiating righteousness,
posthumously granting him the title of Grand Marshal,
adding Attendant-in-Ordinary and the privilege to act independently,
and bestowing a posthumous name.
When Luòyáng (洛陽) fell,
Chāo (超) and his brothers were all lost to Liú Cōng (劉聰),
and thus Jiǒng (冏) had no descendants.
During the Tàiyuán (太元) era,
an edict commanded Róuzhī (柔之), a scion of the former Nándùn Wáng (南頓王) Zōng (宗), to succeed to the title of Qí Wáng (齊王),
and he served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
At the beginning of Yuánxīng (元興) era,
when Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子) was about to attack Huán Xuán (桓玄),
an edict appointed Róuzhī (柔之) concurrently as Attendant-in-Ordinary,
with Zōuyú (騶虞) banners to proclaim the message to Jiāng (江) and Jīng (荊) prefectures.
When he reached Gūshú (姑孰),
he was killed by Xuán's (玄) vanguard.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Imperial Household.
His son Jiànzhī (建之) was established.
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Zhèng Fāng (鄭方),
courtesy name Zǐhuí (子回),
was magnanimous and possessed firm principles.
He was widely read in historical records,
and was exceptional and unconventional.
Those who knew him in his village sighed at his uniqueness,
but were unable to recommend or promote him.
When Jiǒng (冏) monopolized the government and acted arbitrarily,
Fāng (方) indignantly walked to Luòyáng (洛陽),
calling himself a recluse from Jīngchǔ (荊楚),
and presented a letter to Jiǒng (冏) which read:
"I have heard that a sagely and enlightened person assisting the world
is reverent morning and night,
and though at ease, is not arrogant,
thus maintaining his nobility for a long time.
Now, Your Royal Highness, though at peace, does not consider danger,
indulges in wine and women,
and enjoys excessive entertainment – this is your first fault.
Your Royal Highness's proclamations
should make the world peaceful like a clear breeze,
and ensure that the imperial kinsmen have no slightest discord.
But now it is not so –
this is your second fault.
The four barbarian tribes invade frequently,
and the borders are not tranquil.
Your Royal Highness, considering your achievements to be flourishing,
does not give them thought –
this is your third fault.
Your Royal Highness initiated righteousness,
and the common people eagerly responded.
Although the world is now peaceful,
the people are exhausted and suffering.
I have not heard Your Royal Highness's order to rescue them –
this is your fourth fault.
Moreover, you swore a blood oath with the righteous army.
After the matter was settled,
rewards were not given in a timely manner.
Since Qīngtài (清泰),
the merits have not been evaluated and distributed –
this is breaking your word.
This is your fifth fault.
Your Royal Highness has established extraordinary achievements
and holds the responsibility of prime minister,
yet slander fills the roads,
and people harbor resentment.
I, Fāng (方), being foolish and ignorant,
risk death to present my sincerity."
Jiǒng (冏) tolerated it and replied:
"I cannot avoid these five shortcomings.
If I did not have you,
I would not hear of my faults."
Not long after, he was defeated.
Chángshā Wáng (長沙王)
Chángshā Lì Wáng (長沙厲王), courtesy name Shìdù (士度),
was the sixth son of Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
In the tenth year of Tàikāng (太康), he received his enfeoffment
and was appointed Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) died,
he was fifteen years old,
and his mourning exceeded the usual rites.
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi (楚王瑋) rushed to attend the funeral,
all the other princes went near the road to meet him,
but he alone went to the imperial tomb,
wailing loudly to await Wěi (瑋).
He was appointed Commandant of Infantry.
When Wěi (瑋) executed the two Dukes,
he guarded the Eastern Yè Mén (東掖門).
When the Zōuyú (騶虞) banners appeared,
he threw down his bow and wept, saying:
"Chǔ Wáng (楚王) acted on an edict;
that is why I followed him.
How could I know it was not so!"
After Wěi (瑋) was executed,
because they were born of the same mother,
he was demoted to Chángshān Wáng (常山王)
and sent to his domain.
He was seven *chǐ* five *cùn* tall,
open-minded and decisive,
with exceptional talent and strength,
humble towards scholars,
and greatly renowned.
When the Three Princes raised their righteous army,
he led the national army to respond to them.
Passing through the state of Zhào,
the magistrate of Fángzǐ resisted,
so he killed him.
He advanced his army to serve as the rear support for Chéngdū.
Chéng Huī, the Internal Scribe of Chángshān, was about to defect to [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure],
but when he arrived at Yè,
he was executed along with his five sons.
Upon arriving at Luòyáng,
he was appointed Grand General of the Protector Army [Fǔjūn Dàjiàngjūn]
and concurrently General of the Left Army [Zuǒjūn Jiàngjūn].
After a short while,
he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Jiàngjūn] and granted the authority to establish a government [kāifǔ],
and restored to his original state.
Seeing Qí Wáng Jǐong gradually monopolize power,
he once visited the imperial tombs with Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
He then said to Yǐng,
"The empire [tiānxià]
is the legacy of the late emperor.
Your Highness should maintain it."
At that time, all who heard his words feared him.
When Héjiān Wáng Yóng was about to execute Jǐong,
he sent a檄 [letter/proclamation] to act as his internal leader.
Jǐong dispatched his general Dǒng Ài to attack.
Leading about a hundred men on his left and right,
he personally chopped at the carriage curtains,
rode openly and swiftly to the palace,
closed all the gates,
and, supporting the Son of Heaven, attacked Jǐong.
He set fire to Jǐong's mansion.
After three days of continuous fighting,
Jǐong was defeated.
He was executed,
and over two thousand of his associates and partisans were also put to death.
Yóng had initially intended for Jǐong's strength to overwhelm [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure],
hoping that [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] would be captured by Jǐong,
and then he would use that as a pretext
to declare to the four directions that they should jointly attack Jǐong,
and thus depose the emperor and enthrone Chéngdū Wáng,
while he himself would become prime minister [zǎixiàng]
and rule the empire exclusively.
However, after [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] killed Jǐong,
his plan did not materialize.

So he secretly sent Court Attendant [Shìzhōng] Féng Sūn, Governor of Hénán [Hénán Yǐn] Lǐ Hán, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat [Zhōngshū Lìng] Biàn Cuì, among others, to assassinate [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure].
They were all executed.
Yóng then joined Yǐng in attacking the capital [Jīngdū].
Yǐng sent assassins to plot against [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure].
At that time, Wáng Jǔ, the Left Regular Attendant of the State of Chángshā, was on duty.
Seeing the changed expression of the guest,
he killed him.
An imperial edict appointed [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] as Grand Commander [Dà Dūdū] to resist Yóng.
The continuous fighting lasted from August to October.
The court deliberated that [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] and Yǐng were brothers,
and could be reconciled through persuasion.
So they sent Director of the Imperial Secretariat [Zhōngshū Lìng] Wáng Yǎn, acting as Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi],
and Minister of Ceremonies [Guānglùxūn] Shí Lòu, acting as Minister of Works [Sītú],
to persuade Yǐng
to divide the territory and reside separately from [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure].
Yǐng did not comply.
Then [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] wrote a letter to Yǐng, saying:
"The late emperor, in accordance with Heaven, managed the destiny [of the empire],
and united the four seas.
He toiled and suffered
to establish the imperial enterprise,
bringing peace and tranquility to the six directions,
and extended blessings to his descendants.
Sūn Xiù committed rebellion,
overturning the cosmic order.
Your Highness raised a righteous army
to restore the imperial throne.
Qí Wáng, relying on his achievements,
acted unlawfully,
without the heart of a prime minister above,
nor the conduct of a loyal subject below.
He indulged in slander and wickedness,
estranging close kin.
The Emperor was aggrieved and injured,
and he has now been purged.
I and Your Highness
born of the imperial clan,
each enfeoffed in an outer capital.
Neither of us has been able to fully promote the royal teachings
or plan far-reaching strategies for the state.
Now Your Highness has again joined the Grand Commandant to raise a large army,
blocking the way with a million soldiers,
and heavily besieging the imperial city.
The officials are all indignant,
and I have provisionally appointed generals
to demonstrate the national might;
I have not yet intended to destroy [you].
To throw oneself into gullies,
to level mountains and valleys,
with tens of thousands dying daily,
is a cruel pain for the innocent.
Is it that the state's benevolence is unkind,
or that the application of punishment is constant?
Lù Jī, whom Your Highness sent, was unwilling to accept your credentials and authority [jiéyuè],
and led his troops
to secretly communicate with the state.
I imagine those who come against [the state]
will advance one *chǐ*
and retreat one *zhàng*.
Your Highness should return to your post [zhèn]
to bring peace to the four seas,
so that your clan will not be shamed,
which would be a blessing for your descendants.
If not,
considering the pain of kinship division,
I have therefore sent this letter again."
Yǐng replied:
"Wén Dì and Jǐng Dì received the mandate,
Wǔ Dì rode the tide of fortune,
almost like Yáo and Shùn,
together they brought prosperity to the political path.
Their grace nurtured a great enterprise,
their lineage for a hundred generations.
How could we expect that kin would be involved in disaster,
and the empress's relatives would monopolize power?
The Yáng and Jiǎ clans indulged in poison,
while Qí and Zhào usurped internally.
Fortunately, they were exterminated,
but there is still no peace.
I constantly worry about the imperial house,
my heart throbs and liver melts.
Yáng Xuánzhī, Huángfǔ Shāng, and others relied on favor to cause misfortune –
how can one not sigh with emotion!
Therefore, war proclamations from the west
were answered like clouds from the four seas.
I originally thought that my benevolent elder brother shared my sentiments,
and would immediately capture Shāng and others internally,
and send their heads away.
How could you be deluded
and become the chief of the barbarians yourself!
Above, you falsely issue imperial edicts;
below, you alienate your beloved younger brother.
You move the imperial carriage,
recklessly wield military might,
reemploy jackals,
and abandon and execute those close and good.
To commit evil and seek fortune,
how can you justify yourself!
Previously, I sent Lù Jī to oversee with credentials and authority [jiéyuè].
Although Huángqiáo was defeated,
yet Wēnnán secured victory.
One of them for one, the other for another,
it is not enough to increase joy.
Now with a million warriors,
and brave, sharp generals,
I must join my brother to restore order throughout the empire.
If you can follow the Grand Commandant's command,
behead Shāng and others,
throw down your weapons and withdraw,
and seek abundant blessings for yourself,
I, Yǐng, will also return to Yèdū
and join my brother.
I have respectfully read your message,
and feel deeply moved.
Be careful, my elder brother,
and deeply consider your actions!"
He repeatedly defeated Yǐng's army,
killing and capturing sixty to seventy thousand people.
As the war dragged on and provisions ran short,
there was a great famine in the city.
Although they were exhausted,
the generals and soldiers were united in heart,
all wishing to fight to the death.
However, the rites of serving the emperor showed no lapse.
Zhāng Fāng thought it could not yet be overcome [by force]
and wanted to return to Cháng'ān.
But Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, fearing the plan would not succeed,
secretly joined the palace guards to arrest [Pīnyīn for Sīmǎ Yì or another figure] and send him to Jīnyōng Chéng.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"Your Majesty is benevolent and harmonious,
and entrusts me with court affairs.
I am cautious, loyal, and filial;
Heaven and Earth can bear witness.
The princes, holding mistaken views,
led their troops to fault me.
The court officials were not upright,
each fearing their own difficulties,
and arrested me in a separate chamber,
sending me to a secluded palace.
I do not begrudge my life,
but I only worry that the Great Jìn is declining,
that the imperial branches are almost gone,
and that Your Majesty is isolated and in danger.
If my death would bring peace to the state,
it would also be beneficial to my family.
But I fear it would only satisfy the ambitions of wicked people,
and be of no benefit to Your Majesty."
The left and right attendants in the palace resented that the undertaking had almost succeeded but failed.
They plotted to seize and release him,
and then resist Yǐng.
Yuè feared that trouble would arise,
and desired to execute him immediately.
Huángménláng Pān Tāo advised Yuè to secretly inform Zhāng Fāng.
Fāng dispatched his general Zhì Fǔ to lead three thousand soldiers,
to arrest him at Jīnyǒng.
Upon arriving at the camp,
they roasted and killed him.
The sounds of his bitter agony reached everyone around,
and the three armies were all moved to tears.
He was twenty-eight years old at the time.
When he was to be buried east of the city,
none of his officials dared to go,
but his former clerk Liú Yòu alone saw him off.
He walked, holding the funeral carriage,
weeping with such sorrow that his voice broke,
moving the passersby to pity.
Zhāng Fāng, regarding him as a righteous man,
did not question this act.
Initially,
at the beginning of his exercise of power,
a ballad circulated in Luò:
“When plants sprout, Chángshā will be killed.”
He was deposed on the twenty-fifth day of the first month,
and died on the twenty-seventh day,
just as the ballad foretold.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
Emperor Huái had his son, Shuò, inherit his title,
and appointed him Sànqí Chángshì.
Later, Shuò perished at the hands of Liú Cōng.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng, courtesy name Zhāngdù,
was Emperor Wǔ's sixteenth son.
At the end of Tàikāng, he was enfeoffed,
with a household of one hundred thousand households.
Later, he was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì and Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Jiǎ Mì once played *bó* with the Crown Prince,
and they argued over the right-of-way.
Yǐng was present,
and sternly rebuked Mì, saying:
“The Crown Prince
is the nation's heir apparent.
How dare Jiǎ Mì be so disrespectful!”
Mì was frightened,
and consequently had Yǐng appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
and stationed at Yè.
He was then transferred to Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
Yǐng was promoted to Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn,
and given the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng raised a righteous army,
Yǐng dispatched troops to support Jiǒng.
He appointed Yè magistrate Lú Zhì as Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
Dùnqiū Administrator Zhèng Yǎn as Yòu Chángshǐ,
and Yángpíng Administrator Hé Yǎn as Yòu Sīmǎ.
He ordered Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yàn,
Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Yì,
and Dūhù Zhào Xiāng, Shí Chāo, and others to be the vanguard.
Wherever his urgent summons reached,
all responded.
Upon reaching Cháogē,
his forces numbered over two hundred thousand.
Zhào Xiāng reached Huángqiáo,
but was defeated by Lún's generals Shì Yī and Xǔ Chāo,
with over eight thousand casualties,
shaking the morale of his troops.
Yǐng intended to retreat and hold Cháogē,
but adopted the strategies of Lú Zhì and Wáng Yàn,
and again sent Zhào Xiāng to lead eighty thousand troops,
advancing together with Wáng Yàn.
Lún again sent Sūn Huì, Liú Kūn, and others to lead thirty thousand men,
to join Yī and Chāo in resisting Xiāng and others.
Their shining armor glittered in the sun,
and their iron cavalry advanced.
Since Yī had already won a battle,
he underestimated Xiāng.
Before reaching Wēn by more than ten *lǐ*,
they fought another major battle,
and Yī and others fled in disarray.
Yǐng then crossed the river,
and, riding on his victory, advanced rapidly.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Wáng Yú killed Sūn Xiù,
and welcomed the emperor back to his rightful place.
When Yǐng entered the capital,
he executed Lún.
He sent Zhào Xiāng, Shí Chāo, and others to assist Qí Wáng Jiǒng in attacking Zhāng Hóng at Yángdí,
and Hóng and his forces subsequently surrendered.
Jiǒng first led his troops into Luò,
and considering himself the initiator of the great plan,
then monopolized power and authority.
Yǐng camped at the Imperial Academy,
and when he had an audience,
the Son of Heaven personally commended him.
Yǐng bowed and replied:
“This is the merit of Dàsīmǎ Chén Jiǒng;
I had no part in it.”
After the audience,
he immediately excused himself and left,
not returning to his camp,
but instead visited the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
then exited through the Dōngyáng city gate,
and returned to Yè.
He sent a messenger to bid farewell to Jiǒng.
Jiǒng was greatly surprised,
and rushed out to see Yǐng off,
catching up to him at Qīlǐjiàn.
Yǐng stopped his carriage to bid farewell,
shedding tears,
and did not speak of current affairs,
only expressing his concern for his mother, the Grand Consort's, illness and suffering, which was evident in his demeanor.
All the common people watching were deeply moved.
Upon arriving in Yè,
an imperial edict was sent, appointing the acting Tàiwèi Wáng Cuì to confer the nine bestowment ceremonies (Jiǔ Xī) upon him,
promoting him to Dàjiāngjūn, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì, Jiǎjié, with the addition of Huángyuè, and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
allowing him to enter court without rushing,
and to wear swords and shoes on the palace hall.
Yǐng bowed and accepted the honorary titles,
but declined the special honors of the Nine Bestowments.
He submitted a memorial discussing the meritorious officials who initiated the righteous uprising: Lú Zhì, Hé Yǎn, Dǒng Hóng, Wáng Yàn, and Zhào Xiāng, five individuals,
all of whom were enfeoffed as Kāiguó Gōng Hóu.
He also submitted a memorial stating:
“Dàsīmǎ, formerly at Yángdí,
has been engaged in a long confrontation with powerful bandits,
causing the common people to be wounded,
starving and suffering from cold.
It is appropriate to quickly provide relief.
I request that county and prefecture carts be dispatched
to transport one hundred and fifty thousand *hú* of rice from the northern granary of the river in one go,
to relieve the starving people of Yángdí.”
Lú Zhì said to Yǐng:
“Over eight thousand people died in the battle at Huángqiáo;
having passed through the summer heat,
their bones are exposed in the wilderness.
This is truly lamentable.
In ancient times, King Zhōu buried dried bones,
hence the *Shī* says, 'When there are dead people in the road,
they are still sometimes buried.'
How much more so for these individuals who died for the king's cause!”
Yǐng then prepared over eight thousand coffins,
using the stipend of the Chéngdū state for their clothing,
collected and offered sacrifices,
and buried them north of Huángqiáo,
erecting a thorny hedge to form their burial ground.
He also established a general sacrificial hall,
carved a stone and erected a stele,
recording their meritorious deeds in joining the righteous cause,
so that the families of the deceased would have a place for seasonal offerings.
Furthermore, he put up plaques at their gates,
adding two grades above those who died in ordinary battles.
He also ordered Wēn County in Hénèi to bury over fourteen thousand soldiers
Yǐng had a beautiful physique but a dull mind;
he was illiterate.
However, his character was earnest and generous,
and he entrusted matters to Zhì,
thus he achieved his good reputation.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng became arrogant, extravagant, and disrespectful,
public sentiment turned to Yǐng.
An imperial edict was sent, dispatching Shìzhōng Féng Sūn and Zhōngshū Lìng Biàn Cuì to persuade Yǐng to come and assist in governing,
and also to receive the Nine Bestowments.
Yǐng still declined to accept the appointment.
Soon after, he was additionally appointed Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Yǐng's favorite, Mèng Jiǔ, did not wish to return to Luò,
and Grand Consort Chéng was also fond of Yèdū,
due to which this decision was long delayed.
The righteous volunteer soldiers had been kept for a long time,
and all resented their prolonged absence and longed to return home.
Some even left without permission,
and wrote on the gate of Yè city:
“The great matter has dispersed; the silkworms want to hurry.
Please return for now,
to attend to seasonal duties.
Formerly we came for righteousness,
now we leave for righteousness.
If there is another emergency, we will inform each other.”
Yǐng knew he could not keep them,
and so he dismissed them,
whereupon the common people were pacified.
When Jiǒng was defeated,
Yǐng took direct control of court affairs.
Matters, whether big or small,
were all referred to Yè for consultation.
Later, Zhāng Chāng caused chaos in Jīngtǔ,
and Yǐng submitted a memorial to lead a southern expedition,
which was met with widespread support wherever he went.
However, relying on his achievements, he became arrogant and extravagant,
and all regulations became lax and neglected, even more so than during Jiǒng's time.
Yǐng indulged his desires,
but was wary of the King of Chángshā within the capital.
Thus, he and the King of Héjiān, Yóng, submitted a memorial requesting the execution of the Empress's father, Yáng Xuánzhī, Left General Huángfǔ Shāng, and others.
They sent a proclamation for them to be arrested at their residences.
Then, Yǐng and Yóng's general, Zhāng Fāng, attacked the capital.
He appointed Lù Jī, the Administrator of Píngyuán, as Front Vanguard Commandant, Former General, and acting Imperial Envoy.
Yǐng's army encamped at Cháogē.
Every night, the spears and halberds glowed like fire,
and there were dragon and elephant images in the wells of their camp.
They advanced their army and garrisoned Hénán,
building a camp along the Qīngshuǐ river,
and constructing a pontoon bridge to connect with the north of the Yellow River.
They used large wooden boxes filled with stones,
sunk them to secure the bridge,
and called them "stone turtles" (shíbì).
Lù Jī was defeated in battle,
and many died.
Jī was also slandered by Mèng Jiǔ,
so Yǐng arrested Jī and beheaded him,
exterminating his three clans.
The details are in Jī's biography.
Thereupon, they advanced to attack the capital city.
At that time, Wáng Yú, a man from Chángshān, gathered over ten thousand men,
intending to ambush Yǐng.
He was captured,
and his followers beheaded Yú and surrendered.
After Yǐng entered the capital,
he returned to his garrison at Yè,
was granted an additional twenty commanderies,
and appointed Chancellor.
The King of Héjiān, Yóng, memorialized that Yǐng was suitable to be the heir apparent,
and thus deposed Crown Prince Tán,
installing Yǐng as Imperial Younger Brother (Huáng Tàidì),
with the Chancellorship remaining as before.
The institutions were entirely modeled after Wèi Wǔ's precedents,
and the imperial carriage, attire, and regalia were all moved to Yè.
A memorial was submitted to abolish the palace guard troops and place them under the Chancellor's office,
and to instead use royal officials as palace guards.
His extravagance and usurpation grew daily,
and he harbored thoughts of disregarding the emperor.
He entrusted Mèng Jiǔ and others,
greatly losing popular support.
In the early Yǒngxīng era,
Chén Zhěn, the Left Guard General,
Lù Bāo and Chéng Fǔ, Palace Central Cavaliers, and Shàngguān Sì and others, former generals of Chángshā,
supported the great imperial carriage to campaign against Yǐng.
They dispatched proclamations to the four directions,
and respondents gathered like clouds.
The army encamped at Ānyáng,
with over one hundred thousand men.
Yè was greatly shaken and fearful.
Yǐng wanted to flee,
but his aide, Bù Xióng, who had mystical arts,
said:
"Do not move!
The southern army will surely be defeated."
Yǐng assembled his followers to ask for advice.
Then Wáng Yáo, the King of Dōng'ān, said:
"The Son of Heaven is personally leading the campaign;
it is advisable to lay down your arms,
don plain white clothes, go out to welcome him, and beg for pardon."
Simǎ Wáng Hùn and Cānjūn Cuī Kuàng advised Yǐng to resist and fight.
Yǐng followed their advice,
and dispatched Fènwǔ General Shí Chāo to lead fifty thousand men,
who encamped at Dàngyīn.
Zhěn's two younger brothers, Kuāng and Guī, came from Yè to the royal army,
saying:
"Everyone in Yè has already dispersed."
Because of this, they did not make much preparation.
Chāo's forces arrived suddenly,
and the royal army was routed.
Arrows reached the imperial carriage,
and Shìzhōng Jī Shào died by the emperor's side.
All the attendants dispersed,
and the Son of Heaven was abandoned in a ditch.
Chāo then escorted the Emperor to Yè.
Yǐng changed the era name to Jiànwǔ,
killed Wáng Yáo, the King of Dōng'ān,
appointed all officials,
and had the power of life and death himself.
He established an altar for suburban sacrifice south of Yè.
Ānběi General Wáng Jùn and [one-four] Níngběi General, Duke of Dōngyíng, Téng, killed Hé Yǎn, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu appointed by Yǐng.
Yǐng summoned Jùn,
but Jùn garrisoned Jìzhōu and did not advance.
He joined Téng, and the Wūwán and Jié Zhū to attack Yǐng.
[one-five] When the scouts reached Yè,
Yǐng sent Yōuzhōu Inspector Wáng Bīn, and Shí Chāo, Lǐ Yì, and others to resist Jùn.
They were defeated by the Jié Zhū and others.
Yè was greatly shaken,
all officials fled,
and the soldiers dispersed.
Yǐng was fearful,
and with dozens of cavalry from his personal guards,
he escorted the Son of Heaven,
and with Zhōngshū Jiān Lú Zhì, fled in a single carriage.
In five days, they reached Luò.
The Jié Zhū pursued them to Cháogē,
but failed to catch them and returned.
The King of Héjiān, Yóng, sent Zhāng Fāng to lead twenty thousand armored soldiers to rescue Yǐng.
Upon reaching Luò,
Fāng then seized the Emperor,
and escorted Yǐng, Yùzhāng King, as well as Gāo Guāng, Lú Zhì, and others back to Cháng'ān.
Yóng deposed Yǐng and sent him back to his fief,
and appointed Yùzhāng King as Imperial Younger Brother.
After Yǐng was deposed,
the people in Héběi missed him.
Gōng Shīfān and Jí Sāng, former generals in Yè, raised an army to welcome Yǐng,
and public sentiment was unified.
Yóng reappointed Yǐng as Zhèn Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-chief Who Guards the Army), and General Administrator of All Military Affairs in Héběi,
giving him a thousand soldiers,
to garrison Yè.
When Yǐng reached Luò,
the King of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, led his forces to welcome the great imperial carriage,
and uprisings erupted everywhere.
Yǐng, fearing that the north was too strong
to advance,
fled from Luòyáng to Guānzhōng.
When the great imperial carriage returned to Luò,
Yǐng hurried from Huáyīn to Wǔguān,
and emerged at Xīnyě.
The Emperor decreed that Zhènnán General Liú Hóng and Nán Zhōnglángjiàng Liú Táo should arrest Yǐng.
Thereupon, Yǐng abandoned his mother and wife,
and with a single carriage, along with his two sons, Lújiāng King Pǔ and Zhōngdū King Kuò, crossed the Yellow River to Cháogē.
He gathered a few hundred former officers and soldiers,
intending to join Gōng Shīfān.
The Administrator of Dùnqīu, Féng Sōng, seized Yǐng, Pǔ, and Kuò and sent them to Yè.
Fànyáng King Xiāo imprisoned him,
without any other intention.
However, Xiāo suddenly died.
Xiāo's Chief Clerk, Liú Yú, seeing that Yǐng was revered by the capital of Yè,
feared future trouble,
so he secretly did not announce the mourning.
He falsely ordered someone to act as an imperial envoy from the court,
who, claiming an imperial edict, granted Yǐng death that night.
Yǐng asked the guard Tián Huī:
"Has Fànyáng King died?"
Huī replied:
"I do not know."
Yǐng asked:
"How old are you?"
Huī replied:
"Fifty."
Yǐng asked:
"Do you know about the mandate of Heaven?"
Huī replied:
"I do not know."
Yǐng said:
"After I die,
will the world be at peace or not?
I have been in exile
for three years now.
My body, hands, and feet have not been washed.
Bring a few dou of hot water!"
His two sons cried,
and Yǐng ordered someone to take them away.
Then he unbound his hair, lay facing east,
and ordered Huī to strangle him.
He was twenty-eight years old at the time.
His two sons also died.
The people in Yè grieved for him.
When Yǐng was defeated,
his officials and subordinates all fled and dispersed,
only Lú Zhì followed him without fail,
which commentators praised.
Later, Jí Sāng killed Dōngyíng Duke Téng,
claiming it was revenge for Yǐng.
He then exhumed Yǐng's coffin,
carried it with his army,
and consulted the spirit for every matter,
issuing military orders accordingly.
When Sāng was defeated,
he abandoned the coffin in an old well.
Yǐng's former retainers collected it
and reburied it in Luòyáng.
Emperor Huái granted him the rites of a county prince.
Several years after Yǐng's death,
it was rumored in Kāifēng that Yǐng's son, then over ten years old,
was living anonymously among the common people.
The King of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, sent someone to kill him.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
Ruí Zūn, son of Ruí, King of Dōnglái, was established as Yǐng's heir,
and enfeoffed as King of Huáróng County.
Later, he perished at the hands of bandits,
and his state was abolished.
King of Héjiān, Yóng
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng, courtesy name Wénzǎi,
was the grandson of Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú,
and the son of Tàiyuán Liè Wáng Guī.
Initially, he inherited his father's noble title,
and in the second year of Xiánníng, he went to his state.
Three
years later, he was enfeoffed as Héjiān Wáng.
From a young age, he had a reputation for integrity,
valuing scholars lightly over wealth.
When he came to court with the other princes,
Emperor Wǔ sighed, saying Yǒng could be a model for all the states.
In the early Yuánkāng period,
he served as Běizhōngláng Jiāng,
and oversaw Yèchéng.
In the ninth year,
he replaced Liáng Wáng Róng as Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
stationed in Guānzhōng.
According to the "Stone Casket" regulations,
only close relatives could be Dūdū of Guānzhōng.
Yǒng was distantly related to the other princes,
but was specially appointed for his virtue.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
Qí Wáng Jiǒng plotted to attack him.
The former Ānxī Cānjūn Xiàhóu Shì declared himself Shìyùshǐ,
gathered a multitude in Shǐpíng,
numbering several thousand men,
to respond to Jiǒng.
He sent a messenger to Yǒng.
Yǒng sent his Zhǔbù Fáng Yáng and a man from Héjiān Commandery, Zhāng Fāng, to attack and capture Shì,
along with over a dozen of his associates,
and had them waist-chopped in the Cháng'ān market.
When Jiǒng's manifesto arrived,
Yǒng seized Jiǒng's envoy
and sent him to Lún.
Lún requisitioned troops from Yǒng,
and Yǒng sent Fāng to lead elite generals from Guānyòu to assist him.
When Fāng reached Huáyīn,
Yǒng heard that the forces of the two princes were strong,
so he appointed his Chángshǐ Lǐ Hán as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
and had Dūdù Hù Xí Wěi and others recall Fāng's army
to respond to the two princes.
The righteous army reached Tóngguān,
but Lún and Xiù had already been executed,
the Son of Heaven was restored to power,
and Hán and Fāng each led their troops back.
When Jiǒng assessed merits,
although he was angry that Yǒng had not initially joined him,
he ultimately acknowledged his contribution to righteousness,
and Yǒng was promoted to Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi,
and granted the ritual of the three赐 (sāncì).
Later, Hán became Yìjūn Xiàowèi,
and held a grudge against Jiǒng's Cānjūn Huángfǔ Shāng and Sīmǎ Zhào Xiáng and others.
He then fled to Yǒng,
falsely claiming to have received a secret imperial edict to attack Jiǒng,
and persuaded him with arguments about advantages and disadvantages.
Yǒng accepted this,
and immediately raised an army,
sending an envoy to invite Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
He appointed Hán as Dūdū,
leading various armies to garrison Yīnpán,
with the vanguard positioned at Xīn'ān,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* from Luò.
He issued a manifesto to Chángshā Wáng to attack Jiǒng.
When Jiǒng was defeated,
Yǒng appointed Hán as Hénán Yǐn,
and instructed him to secretly plan to harm Fēng Sūn, Biàn Cuì and others.
Shāng knew of Hán's previous deceit and his secret plot with Yǒng,
and reported it fully.
Consequently, Hán and others were executed.
When Yǒng heard of Hán's death,
he immediately raised an army under the pretext of attacking Shāng,
and appointed Zhāng Fāng as Dūdū,
leading seventy thousand elite soldiers towards Luò.
Fāng attacked Shāng,
Shāng resisted but was routed,
and Fāng then advanced to attack Xīmíngmén.
Yǒng led the central army's Left and Right Guards to attack him,
Fāng's forces were greatly defeated,
with over five thousand dead.
Fāng had initially camped west of the Kuàishuǐ Bridge,
and then built several layers of fortifications,
drawing grain from outside
to supply his army.
Yǒng again attacked Fāng with the Son of Heaven,
but was always unsuccessful in battle.
When Yǒng died,
Fāng returned to Cháng'ān.
An imperial edict appointed Yǒng as Tàizǎi, Dà Dūdū, and Yōngzhōu Mù.
Yǒng deposed Crown Prince Tán,
established Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng as Tàidì,
changed the reign title,
and granted a general amnesty.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Chén Zhěn escorted the Son of Heaven to attack Yǐng,
and Yǒng again sent Fāng to lead twenty thousand troops to rescue Yè.
The Son of Heaven had already gone to Yè.
Fāng garrisoned his troops in Luòyáng.
When Wáng Jùn and others attacked Yǐng,
Yǐng took the Son of Heaven and returned to Luòyáng.
Fāng led troops into the palace,
forced the emperor to go to his camp,
looted the imperial treasury,
and was about to burn the ancestral temples to break the spirit of the populace.
Lú Zhì remonstrated,
and he stopped.
Fāng again forced the Son of Heaven to go to Cháng'ān.
Yǒng then selected and appointed officials,
and renamed Qínzhōu to Dìngzhōu.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè raised an army in Xúzhōu,
to escort the imperial carriage westward,
Guānzhōng was greatly alarmed.
Fāng said to Yǒng:
"My forces still number over one hundred thousand men.
We can escort the imperial carriage back to Luòyáng palace,
send Chéngdū Wáng back to Yè,
and you yourself remain to guard Guānzhōng.
I will campaign north to Bólíng.
If we do this,
the empire can achieve a small peace,
and no one will dare to raise a hand again."
Yǒng worried that the undertaking was too difficult to achieve,
and did not agree.
He then granted Liú Qiáo the *jié* (credentials),
promoted him to Zhèndōng Dà Jiāngjūn,
and sent Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng to overall command of Lóu Bāo, Wáng Chǎn, and other armies,
to hold Hèqiáo and resist Yuè.
Wáng Jùn sent Dūdù Hù Liú Gēn,
leading three hundred cavalry to the river.
Chǎn sallied forth to battle,
and was killed by Gēn.
Yǐng garrisoned his troops at Zhāng Fāng's former encampment.
Fányáng Wáng Xiāo sent Xiānbēi cavalry with forces from Píngchāng and Bólíng to raid Hèqiáo.
Lóu Bāo fled west,
the pursuing cavalry reached Xīn'ān,
and the dead along the road were countless.
Initially,
Yuè, angered by Zhāng Fāng's forced removal of the imperial carriage,
which caused widespread resentment,
proclaimed his righteous cause and agreed with the feudal lords east of the mountains to set a date for escorting the emperor.
He first sent someone to persuade Yǒng,
ordering him to send the emperor back to the capital,
and share governing power with Yǒng.
Yǒng wanted to agree,
but Fāng disagreed.
When the eastern army achieved a great victory,
and Chéngdū and others were defeated,
Yǒng then ordered Fāng's trusted general Zhì Fǔ to secretly kill Fāng at night,
and sent his head to show the eastern army.
Soon after, he changed his plan,
and instead sent Diāo Mò to guard Tóngguān.
He then blamed Fǔ for killing Fāng,
and also executed Fǔ.
Yǒng had previously sent General Lǚ Láng and others to hold Xíngyáng.
Fányáng Wáng Xiāo's Sīmǎ Liú Kūn showed Fāng's head to Láng,
whereupon Láng surrendered.
At this time, the eastern army was already strong,
and after defeating Diāo Mò, entered Guān.
Yǒng was afraid,
and again sent Mǎ Zhān and Guō Wěi to resist them at Bàshuǐ.
Zhān and others were defeated and scattered.
Yǒng rode a single horse
and fled to Tàibái Shān.
The eastern army entered Cháng'ān,
the imperial carriage returned.
Tàidì Tàibǎo Liáng Liǔ was appointed Zhènxī Jiāngjūn,
to guard Guānzhōng.
Mǎ Zhān and others went to see Liǔ,
and then conspired to kill Liǔ inside the city.
Zhān and others allied with Shǐpíng Tàishǒu Liáng Mài,
and welcomed Yǒng from Nánshān.
Yǒng initially refused to enter the office.
Cháng'ān Lìng Sū Zhòng and Jìshì Dūdū Zhū Yǒng persuaded Yǒng to submit a memorial claiming Liǔ died of illness,
and to take charge of affairs.
Hóngnóng Tàishǒu Péi Yì, Qín Guónèishǐ Jiǎ Kān, Āndìng Tàishǒu Jiǎ Yà and others raised a righteous army to attack Yǒng,
and executed Mǎ Zhān, Liáng Mài and others.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè sent Dūdù Hù Mí Huǎng to lead the state army to attack Yǒng.
When he reached Zhèng,
Yǒng's general Qiān Xiù resisted Huǎng.
Huǎng killed Xiù,
along with his two sons.
The righteous army held Guānzhōng,
and Yǒng merely protected the city.
In the early Yǒngjiā period,
an imperial edict appointed Yǒng as Sītú,
and he was then summoned.
Nányáng Wáng Mó sent General Liáng Chén to strangle him, along with his three sons, in a carriage in Yōnggǔ, Xīn'ān.
An imperial edict made Róng, the son of Péngchéng Yuán Wáng Zhí, Yǒng's heir,
