and enfeoffed him as Lèchéng Xiàn Wáng.
He died
without sons.
During the Jiànxīng period,
Emperor Yuán again made Qīn, the son of Péngchéng Kāng Wáng Shì, Róng's heir.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè
Dōnghǎi Xiàoxiàn Wáng Yuè (東海孝獻王越), courtesy name Yuánchāo (元超),
was the second son of Gāomì Wáng TàI (高密王泰).
〔一七〕From a young age, he had a good reputation,
being humble and maintaining the conduct of a commoner,
and was respected by those both inside and outside the court.
Initially, as the heir apparent, he was appointed Cavalier Commandant (騎都尉).
Together with the Imperial Son-in-law Commandant Yáng Miǎo (楊邈) and Lángxié Wáng Zhòu's (琅邪王伷) son Yáo (繇), he attended lectures in the Eastern Palace (東宮).
He was then appointed Palace Attendant (散騎侍郎),
served successively as General of the Left Guard (左衞將軍),
and was granted the title of Attendant (侍中).
He gained merit in the campaign against Yáng Jùn (楊駿)
and was enfeoffed as a marquis of five thousand households.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍), General of Upholding the State (輔國將軍), and Right Director of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書右僕射),
and concurrently commanded the General of Roaming Cavalry (游擊將軍).
He again served as Attendant,
was granted the additional title of Commandant of Equerry (奉車都尉),
and was provided with fifty Wēnxìn (溫信) attendants.
〔一八〕He was separately enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王)
and granted six counties as his demesne.
At the beginning of the Yǒngkāng (永康) era,
he became Director of the Central Secretariat (中書令),
then transferred to Attendant,
and later promoted to Minister of Works (司空),
concurrently serving as Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (中書監).
When Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) attacked Chángshā Wáng (長沙王),
Yuè firmly defended Luòyáng (洛陽).
The palace generals and the three departmental marshals were exhausted by the fighting and defending.
They secretly, with the Left Guard General Zhū Mò (朱默), seized the detached palace by night,
forced Yuè to become their leader,
and memorialized Emperor Huì (惠帝) to dismiss his officials.
After the matter was settled,
Yuè claimed illness and resigned his position.
The emperor did not permit it,
and additionally appointed him Acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat (守尚書令).
At the beginning of the TàI'ān (太安) era,
〔一九〕when the emperor campaigned north to Yè (鄴),
Yuè was made Grand Commander (大都督).
When the six armies were defeated,
Yuè fled to Xiàpī (下邳).
However, the Military Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州), Dōngpíng Wáng Máo (東平王楙), did not admit him.
Yuè went straight back to Dōnghǎi.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng, appreciating Yuè's brothers' excellent lineage among the imperial clan,
issued a lenient decree to summon him,
but Yuè did not respond to the command.
When the emperor went west,
Yuè was made Grand Tutor (太傅),
to jointly assist in governing the court with the Grand Chancellor Yǒng (顒),
but he declined and did not accept.
The Dōnghǎi Commandant Liú Qià (劉洽) urged Yuè to raise an army to prepare for Yǐng.
Yuè made Qià his Left Marshal (左司馬),
and Shàngshū Cáo Fù (尚書曹馥) his Army Advisor (軍司).
After he raised the army,
Máo became afraid,
and thus yielded Xúzhōu to Yuè.
Yuè, as Minister of Works, concurrently commanded the Military Governor of Xúzhōu,
and made Máo the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州刺史).
Yuè's three younger brothers also occupied various positions and engaged in campaigns.
He frequently selected inspectors and commanderies (刺史守相),
and many court officials went to join Yuè.
However, Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (河間王顒), holding the emperor,
issued an edict to dismiss Yuè and others,
ordering them all to return to their enfeoffments.
Yuè championed righteousness, intending to welcome the imperial carriage
back to the old capital.
He led thirty thousand armored troops
and advanced west to Xiāoxiàn (蕭縣).
The Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州), Liú Qiáo (劉喬), did not accept Yuè's command
and sent his son Yòu (祐) to resist him.
〔二０〕Yuè's army was defeated.
Fányáng Wáng Xiāo (范陽王虓) sent Supervisor Tián Huī (田徽) with eight hundred elite cavalry to meet Yuè.
They encountered Yòu in Qiáo (譙),
Yòu's forces disintegrated,
and Yuè advanced to garrison Yángwǔ (陽武).
As the forces in the east of the mountains grew strong,
the Guānzhōng (關中) region was greatly alarmed.
Yǒng beheaded and sent Zhāng Fāng's (張方) head to seek peace,
but soon changed his plan to resist Yuè.
Yuè led various princes and the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) leaders Xǔ Fúlí (許扶歷) and Jūcì Sùguī (駒次宿歸) with infantry and cavalry to escort Emperor Huì back to Luòyáng.
An edict appointed Yuè Grand Tutor and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (錄尚書),
and increased his enfeoffment with the two commanderies of Xiàpī (下邳) and Jìyáng (濟陽).
When Emperor Huái (懷帝) ascended the throne,
he entrusted the government to Yuè.
Zhōu Mù (周穆), Bureau Director of the Ministry of Personnel (吏部郎),
the maternal uncle of Qīnghé Wáng Tán (清河王覃),
and Yuè's cousin,
together with his sister's husband Zhūgě Méi (諸葛玫), persuaded Yuè, saying:
"The present emperor becoming the imperial younger brother
was Zhāng Fāng's intention.
Qīnghé Wáng was originally the crown prince,
but was deposed by the wicked factions.
The late emperor's sudden death has caused much suspicion towards the Eastern Palace.
Why does Your Grace not consider the actions of Yī (伊) and Huò (霍)
to pacify the altars of soil and grain?"
Before he finished speaking,
Yuè said:
"How can such words be uttered!"
He then shouted at his attendants to behead him.
Because Méi and Mù belonged to prominent families,
their crime was limited to themselves.
Therefore, he submitted a memorial to abolish the law of punishing three generations of a family.
When the emperor began to personally handle all affairs of state
and paid close attention to various matters,
Yuè was displeased
and sought to leave the capital for a frontier post.
The emperor did not permit it.
Yuè then departed to garrison Xǔchāng (許昌).
At the beginning of the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
he led Gǒu Xī (苟晞) and the Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州), Dīng Shào (丁劭), from Xǔchāng to campaign against Jí Sāng (汲桑).
〔二一〕They defeated him.
Yuè returned to Xǔchāng.
His Chief Clerk Pān Tāo (潘滔) advised him, saying:
"Yǎnzhōu is the pivot of the realm.
Your Grace should personally govern it."
Thus, Gǒu Xī was transferred to be Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州刺史),
which created a rift between him and Xī.
Soon, an edict appointed Yuè Chancellor (丞相),
concurrently Governor of Yǎnzhōu (兗州牧),
and overseer of the six provinces of Yǎn, Yù, Sī, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng.
Yuè declined the position of Chancellor and did not accept it.
He moved from Xǔchāng to Juànchéng (鄄城).
Yuè feared that Qīnghé Wáng Tán would eventually become the heir apparent,
so he falsified an edict to arrest him and imprison him in Jīnyōngchéng (金墉城),
and soon had him killed.
When Wáng Mí (王彌) entered Xǔchāng,
Yuè sent Left Marshal Wáng Bīn (王斌) with five thousand armored soldiers to guard the capital.
Juànchéng collapsed on its own.
Yuè found this ominous
and moved his garrison to Púyáng (濮陽),
then again to Xíngyáng (滎陽).
He summoned the six commanders including Tián Zhēn (田甄).
〔二二〕Zhēn did not obey the order,
so Yuè sent Supervising Army Liú Wàng (劉望) to attack Zhēn.
Initially,
when Dōngyíng Gōng Téng (東嬴公騰) was garrisoned in Yè,
he brought more than ten thousand troops from Bìngzhōu (并州), including General Tián Zhēn, Zhēn's younger brother Lán (蘭), Rèn Zhǐ (任祉), Qí Jì (祁濟), Lǐ Yùn (李惲), and Báo Shèng (薄盛), to Yè.
He sent them to gather grain in Jìzhōu,
and they were called "Qǐhuó" (乞活, 'begging for life').
When Téng was defeated,
Zhēn and others intercepted and defeated Jí Sāng at Chìqiáo (赤橋).
Yuè made Zhēn the Administrator of Jí Jùn (汲郡),
and Lán the Grand Administrator of Jùlù (鉅鹿太守).
Zhēn requested Wèi Jùn (魏郡),
but Yuè did not permit it.
Zhēn was angered,
and therefore did not arrive.
After Wàng crossed the river,
Zhēn retreated.
Lǐ Yùn and Báo Shèng beheaded Tián Lán
and led their forces to surrender.
Zhēn, Zhǐ, and Jì abandoned their army and fled to Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Yuè returned to Luòyáng from Xíngyáng
and established his headquarters in the Imperial University (太學).
Suspecting that court officials were disloyal to him,
he falsely accused the emperor's maternal uncle Wáng Yán (王延) and others of rebellion,
and sent Wáng Jǐng (王景) with three thousand armored soldiers into the palace to arrest Yán and others,
〔二三〕and handed them over to the Grand Judge (廷尉) to be executed.
Yuè resigned as Governor of Yǎnzhōu
and concurrently served as Minister of the Masses (司徒).
Having already formed enmity with Gǒu Xī,
and also because many recent incidents originated from the palace and ministries,
Yuè memorialized that all palace guards who held marquis titles should be dismissed.
At that time, all military officials in the palace were enfeoffed as marquises,
thus nearly all of them departed,
all shedding tears as they left.
He then appointed Hélún (何倫), General of the Upper Army of Dōnghǎi Commandery, as General of the Right Guard (右衞將軍),
and Wáng Jǐng as General of the Left Guard (左衞將軍),
commanding several hundred national troops as palace guards.
After Yuè himself executed Wáng Yán and others,
he greatly lost public support,
and there was much suspicion and distrust.
The *Sànqí Shìláng* Gāo Tāo expressed worries about the state;
Yuè falsely accused him of slandering current politics and harmed him,
and felt uneasy himself.
So he donned military attire and entered for an audience,
requesting to attack Shí Lè,
and also to consolidate and gather forces in Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu to assist the capital.
The Emperor said:
“Now the rebellious barbarians are invading and pressing upon the imperial capital’s outskirts,
the royal house is in turmoil,
with no one having a firm resolve.
The imperial court and the state,
rely on you, Sire.
How can you venture far and leave the foundation isolated!”
He replied:
“I shall now lead the troops to intercept the bandits,
and will surely destroy them.
Once the bandits are destroyed, unrest will be eliminated,
and tribute from the eastern provinces will flow smoothly.
This is how to promote national prestige,
and it is proper for a border-protecting lord.
If we sit idly in the capital and miss this opportunity,
then troubles and corruptions will daily multiply,
and our worries will become even heavier.”
So he departed.
He left his consort Péi Shì,
his heir and *Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn* Pí,
and *Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn* Lǐ Yùn, along with Hé Lún and others, to guard the capital.
He memorialized to have a travelling bureau accompany his army,
and led forty thousand armored soldiers to garrison in Xiàng to the east.
Many dukes, princes, ministers, and gentry followed him.
An imperial edict conferred the Nine Bestowments upon him.
Yuè then dispatched urgent military letters to all directions, saying:
“The imperial order has lost control,
and the state faces many difficulties.
I, with my humble talent,
am prepared to shoulder this great responsibility.
Recently, barbarian invaders have pressed inward,
and our generals have suffered defeats.
The imperial homeland has become a barbarian province,
and our cultured people have suddenly become foreigners.
From top to bottom in the court,
everyone is filled with worry and fear.
All this is due to the negligence of the regional lords,
which has led to this disaster.
To rise and attack, forgetting one’s shoes,
is already late.
People’s hearts cling to their origins,
and none are not righteously incensed.
We must gather our forces,
and prepare for defense and battle.
The ancestral temples and the Emperor,
rely on our rescue and assistance.
On the day this urgent letter arrives,
it is hoped that you will rise up at once,
for it is the time for loyal ministers and brave warriors to show their sincerity.”
None of those summoned arrived.
Moreover, Gǒu Xī again memorialized to attack Yuè;
the details are in Xī’s biography.
Yuè appointed Fēng Sōng, the *Yùzhōu Cìshǐ*, as Left *Sīmǎ*,
and himself took the title of *Yùzhōu Mù*.
Yuè monopolized authority and power,
planning to establish a hegemonic rule.
Respectable court officials,
were chosen as his subordinates.
Famous generals and elite soldiers,
filled his personal retinue.
His insubordinate actions,
were known throughout the land.
Yet, both public and private resources were exhausted,
banditry and chaos were everywhere,
provinces and commanderies were disloyal,
and everything from top to bottom was collapsing.
Troubles accumulated and enmity deepened,
and he eventually fell ill from worry and fear.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
he died in Xiàng.
His death was kept secret.
He appointed Xiāngyáng Wáng Fàn as *Dàjiāngjūn*,
to command his troops.
They returned to bury him in Dōnghǎi.
Shí Lè pursued them and caught up at Níngpíng Chéng in Kǔ Xiàn.
General Qián Duān led troops to resist Lè,
and died in battle;
the army was routed.
Lè ordered Yuè’s coffin to be burned, saying:
“This man brought chaos to the world;
I avenge the world on him,
thus I burn his bones to announce it to Heaven and Earth.”
Thereupon, Lè surrounded and shot at hundreds of thousands of people with cavalry,
who trampled over each other like a mountain.
More than a hundred thousand princes, nobles, officers, and commoners died.
Wáng Mí’s younger brother Zhāng burned the remaining crowds,
and ate them.
The world blamed Yuè.
The Emperor issued an edict demoting Yuè to a county king.
Hé Lún and Lǐ Yùn, upon hearing of Yuè’s death,
kept the mourning secret,
and escorted his consort Péi Shì and Pí out of the capital.
Their followers filled the city,
and they plundered wantonly wherever they went.
Upon reaching Wěicāng,
they were again defeated by Lè.
Pí and thirty-six other royal kinsmen were all captured by the bandits.
Lǐ Yùn killed his wife and children and fled to Guǎngzōng.
Hé Lún fled to Xiàpī.
Consort Péi was abducted by someone,
and sold to the Wú family.
During the Tàixīng era,
she managed to cross the Jiāng river.
She wanted to perform a soul-summoning ritual and bury Yuè.
Emperor Yuán ordered the relevant officials to deliberate,
and *Bóshì* Fù Chún said:
“The sages established rituals,
to align events with emotions.
They set up tombs and coffins to conceal the physical form,
and treated it with inauspicious rites;
they established ancestral temples to provide peace for the spirit,
and worshipped it with auspicious rites.
The form is sent forth,
and the essence is welcomed back.
This is the great distinction between tomb and temple,
the different systems for form and spirit.
As for ancestral halls, spirit temples, and various places of sacrifice,
they are for broadly seeking the path of the spirits,
but one does not sacrifice solely at the tomb,
making it clear that it is not where the spirit resides.
Now, to confuse the distinction between form and spirit,
and mistake the proper place for temple and tomb,
is a deviation from ritual and righteousness,
than which there is nothing greater.”
Thus, an imperial edict disallowed it.
Consort Péi did not obey the edict,
and buried Yuè in Guǎnglíng.
At the end of Tàixīng,
the tomb was destroyed,
and he was reburied in Dāntú.
Initially,
when Emperor Yuán was garrisoned in Jiànyè,
it was Consort Péi’s intention,
and the Emperor deeply appreciated her.
He frequently visited her residence,
and appointed his third son Chōng to succeed Yuè.
When he died,
without a son,
Emperor Chéng appointed his youngest son Yì to succeed him.
Emperor Āi transferred Yì to be *Lángyá Wáng*,
and Dōnghǎi had no successor.
At the beginning of Lóng’ān,
Emperor Ān again appointed Yànzhāng, the second son of Huìjī Zhōng Wáng, as *Dōnghǎi Wáng*,
to be Chōng’s great-grandson.
He was killed by Huán Xuán,
and the state was abolished.
The Grand Scribe says: In ancient times, when Gāo Xīn (高辛) ruled the realm,
strife arose between Shēn (參) and Shāng (商);
when the Zōng Zhōu (宗周) dynasty succeeded,
calamities entangled Guǎn (管) and Cài (蔡).
Examining the past records in detail,
and listening to ancient history from afar,
the treacherous ministers and rebellious sons
are clearly recorded therein as a lesson.
When the Jìn (晉) dynasty flourished,
it greatly promoted its feudal lords,
bestowing territories and auspicious seals,
illuminating the Way and the canons.
Grand garments adorned the ceremonial platforms,
and rites were complete with ancestral regulations.
Rǔnán (汝南), with his gentle and harmonious nature,
erred by being indecisive;
Chǔ Yǐn (楚隱), accustomed to a resolute and fierce disposition,
consequently became cruel and tyrannical.
Some held high positions in the court,
others participated in close secret affairs;
all were deceived by women,
and were successively executed.
Though it is said they brought it upon themselves,
it is truly lamentable!
Lún (倫) was truly mediocre and petty,
deceived by Sūn Xiù (孫秀),
he secretly harbored rebellious plans,
instigating wickedness and treachery.
He thus caused the Crown Prince to suffer cruel grievances,
and the Prime Minister to fall victim to execution.
The celestial radiance was temporarily eclipsed by this,
and the imperial order was thus ruptured.
He then tore off crowns and ruined ceremonial robes,
hoping for a period of extreme misfortune;
he grasped the imperial seal and unfurled the banner,
coveting the highest imperial dignity.
How could the divine artifact be usurped for temporary comfort?
How could a great name be falsely assumed?
Yet he wished to rely on such illicit sacrifices
to enjoy a long lifespan.
Such extreme wickedness and ignorance
has never been seen before.
Jiǒng (冏), son of a famous father,
raised the banner of righteousness to aid the emperor,
destroying a usurped regime that was already established,
rescuing the imperial carriage that was already collapsing.
His meritorious deeds and achievements
are truly worthy of praise.
However, in the face of disaster, he forgot his worries,
indulging his desires and lusts.
He did not realize that pleasure cannot be pushed to its extreme,
and abundance cannot be long maintained.
He mocked the ancients for their lack of skill,
forgetting his own blunders.
Had he adopted Wáng Bào’s (王豹) extraordinary strategy,
and accepted Sūn Huì’s (孫惠) excellent advice,
respectfully declining the imperial robes,
forever remaining the Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海),
even the ancient Yī (伊) and Huò (霍)
could not have surpassed him!
Chángshā (長沙) possessed exceptional talent and strength,
and his loyalty surpassed the ordinary.
Dropping his bow at the Yè Mén (掖門) gate,
he grandly displayed the spirit of a brave man;
driving his carriage past the Wèi Què (魏闕) gate,
he sternly held the demeanor of a heroic warrior.
Even amidst the numerological hardships and adversities,
his devotion to the emperor remained unwavering.
Reflecting on his remaining integrity,
it is admirable from beginning to end.
Yǐng (穎), having taken charge of the central government,
and then commanding an important garrison,
the central administration relied on him to accomplish its tasks,
and the eastern regions depended on him for stability.
He then conspired with Héjiān (河間),
together plotting advancement.
However, Yǒng (顒) trusted Lǐ Hán’s (李含) treachery,
and relied on Zhāng Fāng’s (張方) tyranny,
thus causing Wǔ Mǐn (武閔) to lose his head,
and Chángshā (長沙) to be executed.
They displayed their disrespectful ambition,
and boasted of their unjust power.
The imperial carriage journeyed north,
differing from an expedition without battle;
the emperor’s chariot traveled west,
not for inspecting local customs.
If a fire scorched the plain,
it could still be extinguished.
How much more so these ruthless and cruel acts—
how could they not have consequences?
Dōnghǎi (東海) gathered his allies,
initiating a righteous campaign.
Before the功 of restoration was established,
the transgression of bullying was already evident.
He exhausted his troops and chariots,
stubbornly seeking to command a garrison.
Soon after, the imperial capital was weak,
and cunning bandits ran rampant,
thus causing the imperial regalia to be forcibly moved,
and the ancestral temples to be overthrown.
Hundreds of thousands of people became prey to wolves,
and thirty-six princes all perished by the sword.
The extremity of this disaster
has never been heard of throughout history.
Even being consumed by fire
would have been fortunate.
Since Huì Huáng (惠皇) lost control of the government,
troubles arose within the palace walls,
kin massacred each other,
and the common people suffered greatly.
Barbarian dust surged, and heaven and earth closed off;
barbarian soldiers clashed, and palaces and temples were destroyed.
The imperial relatives initiated the calamity,
and the Róng Jié (戎羯) barbarians exploited the chaos.
Alas!
As the Shī (詩) says,
"Who initiated this great evil,
which obstructs us even today?"
It refers to these Eight Princes.
Eulogy says: Liàng (亮) controlled court affairs,
Wěi (瑋) harbored ambition and rivalry.
Slander and cunning seized the opportunity,
a seductive wife was excessively heeded.
They engendered grievances and brought forth disasters,
successively meeting unnatural deaths.
Lún (倫) was truly utterly foolish,
daring to usurp the imperial position,
disrupting the natural order and seizing power,
swiftly meeting severe punishment.
How great was Wǔ Mǐn (武閔)!
He was the first to conceive a grand strategy.
That virtue was not established,
is truly lamentable!
Chángshā (長沙) served the state,
loyal from beginning to end;
his efforts failed at the last moment,
and he suddenly suffered from ruthless treachery.
Zhāng Dù (章度) worked diligently for the emperor,
achieving fame with his accomplishments;
he allied with those west of the pass,
defying authority and vying for strength.
When their ventures failed and their power waned,
they all fell into chaos and ruin.
Yuán Chāo (元超) served as a regent,
campaigning outside and pacifying within,
he lost the state and annihilated his army,
disrespectful to the emperor and shaking his master.
The disaster of being consumed by fire,
was indeed self-inflicted.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Chapter 30: Xiè Xì (解系) (his younger brother Jié (結); Jié’s younger brother Yù (育))
Xiè Xì (解系), courtesy name Shàolián (少連),
was a native of Jǐnán (濟南).
His father, Xiū (脩),
was the Grand Administrator of Lángyá (琅邪) and Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty, and his performance was ranked first in the empire.
When Emperor Wǔ (武) received the abdication,
Xiè Xiū (解脩) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liángzōu (梁鄒).
Xì (系) and his two younger brothers, Jié (結) and Yù (育), were all pure and self-disciplined,
and gained much renown.
At that time, Xún Xù’s (荀勖) clan was powerful,
and feared by the court and commoners alike.
Xù’s (勖) sons said to Xì (系) and his brothers:
"We are friends with you,
you should bow to our father."
Xù (勖) also said:
"Your late father, the former Lord, and I were very close."
Xì (系) replied:
"I do not follow the teachings bequeathed by my late father.
If you, sir, were close to my late father,
when he passed away,
you should have sent a letter of condolence.
I dare not accept your instruction of closeness."
Xù (勖) and his sons were greatly ashamed,
and people of that era admired Xì (系).
Later, he was appointed as an aide in a ducal mansion,
and successively served as Attendant Censor in the Central Secretariat, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州),
then promoted to Grand Minister, and sent out as Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), General who Manifests Awe, Colonel of the Western Barbarians, and acting Imperial Envoy.
At that time, the Dī and Qiāng rebelled.
[Xiè] was dispatched with General Who Conquers the West, Zhào Wáng Lún, to suppress them.
Lún trusted the sycophant Sūn Xiù,
and contended with [Xiè] over military affairs,
each submitting memorials against the other.
The imperial court, knowing [Xiè] upheld righteousness and did not yield,
recalled Lún.
[Xiè] memorialized to have Xiù killed to apologize to the Dī and Qiāng,
but this was not followed.
Lún and Xiù slandered him,
and [Xiè] was dismissed from office,
returning to his residence as a commoner,
where he shut his gates and kept to himself.
When Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi were executed,
Lún and Xiù, harboring old grudges, arrested [Xiè]'s brothers.
Liáng Wáng Róng interceded for [Xiè] and the others,
but Lún angrily said:
"Even when I see a crab in the water, I detest it;
how much more so these brothers who slight me!
If this can be endured,
what cannot be endured!"
Róng bitterly argued but failed to save them,
so they were executed,
and their wives and children were also put to death.
Later, when Qí Wáng Jiǒng raised an army for a righteous cause,
he named the Péi and Xiè families as the primary victims of injustice.
After Lún and Xiù were executed,
Jiǒng then memorialized, saying:
"I have heard that restoring what is in decline and continuing what has been cut off
is the high policy of enlightened rulers;
condemning evil and praising good
is the fine talk of the Spring and Autumn period.
This is why King Wǔ sealed the tomb of Bǐ Gān
and honored the gate of Shāng Róng,
truly because there are ways for the unseen and seen to connect.
Sūn Xiù caused chaos and rebellion,
destroyed states that aided in the founding of the dynasty,
executed loyal and upright officials,
thereby weakening the imperial house,
and in his tyranny and cruelty,
many descendants of meritorious officials
were annihilated.
As for Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi,
each was executed at that time due to fear of their influence;
[Xiè] and [Xiè] Jié were both killed like sacrificial lambs;
Ōuyáng Jiàn and others died innocently;
the common people pitied them.
Your Majesty's light shines like the sun and moon,
and you have issued new and enlightened mandates,
yet these individuals have not yet received grace and justice.
In the past, Luán and Xì were degraded to common servants,
but the *Chūnqiū* transmitted their stories;
King Yōu cut off the descendants of meritorious officials
and abandoned the children of worthy men,
and the poets criticized this.
Your servant, though unworthily holding a right-hand position,
desires to exert his full strength
and offer his humble sincerity.
If this aligns with Your Majesty's will,
it can be discussed by all officials."
The Eight Ministers deliberated, saying
"[Xiè] and the others were pure, just, and upright,
and were hated by wicked and perverse individuals.
They were unjustly and cruelly killed without crime,
and their grievances and pain are extreme.
As proposed by the Grand Marshal,
making clear the wrongs and rights,
openly proclaiming what is proper and improper,
so that the wronged souls have no shame or hatred,
would be a great act of grace."
In the second year of Yǒngníng,
[Xiè] was posthumously granted the title of Guānglù Dàfū,
reburied,
and offerings were made to console his spirit.
[Xiè] Jié, courtesy name Shúlián,
was as renowned as [Xiè] in his youth.
He was appointed as a clerk in a ducal mansion,
successively promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
and served as Sànqí Chángshì, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, Wèi Jùn Tàishǒu, and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Sūn Xiù caused chaos in Guānzhōng,
Jié was in the capital
and participated in discussions that concluded Xiù's crimes warranted execution,
which caused Xiù to bear a grudge.
When [Xiè] was killed,
Jié was also executed.
His daughter was betrothed to a Péi family;
the wedding was to be the next day,
but disaster struck.
The Péi family wished to claim her to save her life,
but the daughter said:
"Since my family is in such a state,
why should I live!"
She also died.
The imperial court then discussed reforming the old system,
making it so that daughters would not be implicated,
which began with Jié's daughter.
Later, Jié was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū,
reburied,
and offerings were made to console his spirit.
Jié's younger brother, Yù,
courtesy name Zhìlián,
was second only to his two elder brothers in renown.
He served successively as a clerk in a ducal mansion, Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ, Shàngshū Láng, Wèijūn Chángshǐ, and Hóngnóng Tàishǒu,
and was killed along with his two elder brothers,
with his wife and children exiled to the frontier.
Sūn Qí
Sūn Qí, courtesy name Bóqí,
was a native of Lè'ān.
His father, Lì,
served as Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ and Yòu Jiāngjūn during the transition between Wèi and Jìn.
Qí was pure and disciplined,
and cultivated himself from a young age.
He was recommended as a *xiàolián*,
and successively promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
then sent out as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
his reputation and position on par with the two Xiè brothers.
During the Yǒngxī reign,
he was summoned and appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
then transferred to Wèiwèi.
He was dismissed from office
due to a fire in the armory.
After more than a year,
he was sent out as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and promoted to Píngnán Jiāngjūn, acting as *jiǎjié*.
Qí's son Bì, and his nephews Máo, Fǔ, and Yǎn, four people,
all possessed administrative talent and were well-regarded in their time,
and thus joined Sūn Xiù's clan.
When Zhào Wáng Lún raised his army,
they followed Xiù by night
and opened the Shénwǔ Gate to inspect weapons and equipment.
Within a month, the brothers were successively appointed as ducal mansion clerks and Shàngshū Láng.
Bì also became Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then promoted to Shàng Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
Máo became Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Yǎn became Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài.
All were granted the title of Kāiguó Jùnhóu.
Qí was elevated to Chēqí Jiāngjūn and *kāifǔ*.
Initially,
Qí, seeing Bì and the others serving the usurping court,
sent his young son Huí to reprimand Bì and the others, stating that their excessive actions
would surely bring disaster upon the family.
But Bì and the others ultimately did not comply,
and Qí, unable to control them,
could only weep bitterly.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng raised his righteous army,
all four sons were executed.
Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu Zōng Dài, acting on Jiǒng's檄, beheaded Qí
and exterminated his three clans.
His younger brother Yǐn,
courtesy name Wénqí,
served successively as Chénliú and Yángpíng Tàishǒu,
and died young.
Mèng Guān
Mèng Guān, courtesy name Shúshí,
was a native of Bóhǎi Dōngguāng.
From a young age, he enjoyed reading
and understood astronomy.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he was gradually promoted to Diànzhōng Zhōngláng.
Empress Jiǎ transgressed the etiquette between daughter-in-law and mother-in-law,
secretly wishing to execute Yáng Jùn and depose the Empress Dowager.
Taking advantage of Jùn's monopolization of power,
she repeatedly spoke of it to the Emperor,
and also sent someone to subtly influence Guān.
It happened that Chǔ Wáng Wěi was about to attack Jùn;
Guān received Empress Jiǎ's instruction to proclaim an imperial edict,
greatly distorting the facts.
After Jùn was executed,
Guān was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
specifically granted forty personal bodyguards.
He was promoted to Jīnnǔ Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Shànggǔ Jùngōng.
The Di chieftain Qí Wànnián (齊萬年) rebelled in Guānzhōng (關中).
His forces numbered several hundred thousand.
The various generals repeatedly suffered defeats.
Chén Zhǔn (陳準), the Grand Secretariat Director, and Zhāng Huá (張華), the Supervisor,
considering that the princes of Zhào (趙) and Liáng (梁) were in Guānzhōng,
were indulging in their noble status.
When advancing, they did not covet glory;
when retreating, they did not fear punishment.
Although the soldiers were numerous,
they were not utilized by them.
The defeat of Zhōu Chǔ (周處)
was due to this reason.
With disunity between superiors and subordinates,
it would be difficult to defeat the enemy.
They observed Guān (觀) to be resolute and steady,
possessing both civil and military talents and capabilities,
and thus petitioned to have Guān (觀) suppress them.
Guān (觀)'s personal guard soldiers
were all agile, swift, brave, and fierce.
He also commanded the soldiers in Guānzhōng.
Personally facing arrows and stones,
he fought more than ten major battles,
defeating them all.
He captured Wànnián (萬年) alive,
striking awe into the Di and Qiāng (羌) peoples.
He was transferred to Colonel of the Eastern Qiāng (東羌),
then summoned and appointed Right General.
When Prince Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) usurped the throne,
because Guān (觀) had achieved merits where he was stationed,
he was appointed General of Pacifying the South, Supervisor of all military affairs in Héběi (河北),
and granted an Imperial Insignia,
stationed at Wǎn (宛).
Guān (觀)'s son Píng (平) was the Vanguard General for Prince Yǔn (允) of Huáinán (淮南),
to suppress Lún (倫),
and died in battle.
Sūn Xiù (孫秀), knowing that Guān (觀) commanded troops outside,
falsely stated that Píng (平) had been killed by Yǔn (允)'s soldiers,
and posthumously awarded him General of Accumulated Crossbows to appease Guān (觀).
When the righteous army arose,
many advised Guān (觀) to respond to Prince Jǐong (冏) of Qí (齊).
Guān (觀), believing that there was no other change to the Imperial throne in the Purple Palace,
deemed it appropriate to respond to Lún (倫).
Thus, he did not follow the majority opinion and defended Lún (倫).
When the Emperor was restored,
Kōngtóng Jī (空桐機), the Prefect of Yǒngráo (永饒) Ironworks, beheaded Guān (觀),
and his head was sent to Luòyáng (洛陽).
His three familial clans were subsequently exterminated.
Qiān Xiù (牽秀)
Qiān Xiù (牽秀), courtesy name Chéngshū (成叔),
was a native of Guānjīn (觀津), Wǔyì (武邑).
His grandfather, Zhāo (招),
was the Grand Administrator of Yànmén (雁門) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
Xiù (秀) was eloquent and possessed literary talent.
His character was chivalrous and unrestrained.
At the age of twenty, he gained a good reputation
and was known to Tài bǎo Wèi Guàn (太保衞瓘) and Shàngshū Cuī Hóng (尚書崔洪).
During the Tàikāng (太康) era,
he was appointed Prefect of Xīn'ān (新安),
and successively promoted to Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Works.
He always held a mutual contempt for Wáng Kǎi (王愷), the Emperor's maternal uncle.
Kǎi (愷) incited the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), Xún Kǎi (荀愷), to report that Xiù (秀) had carried the wife of Tián Xìng (田興), the Commander of Gāopíng (高平) Kingdom, in his carriage at night.
Xiù (秀) immediately submitted a memorial asserting he was slandered,
discussing Kǎi (愷)'s corrupt conduct.
His writing was sharp and vigorous,
thus satirizing the imperial relatives.
Although many court officials at the time testified to his conduct,
Xiù (秀)'s great fame and good reputation were damaged by this,
and he was consequently dismissed from office.
Later, the Grand Minister of Works Zhāng Huá (張華) invited him to be his Chief Clerk.
Xiù (秀) was impetuous
and enjoyed being a general.
When Zhāng Chāng (張昌) rebelled,
the Prince of Chángshā (長沙) sent Xiù (秀) to suppress Chāng (昌).
Xiù (秀) left the pass
and then defected to Prince Yǐng (穎) of Chéngdū (成都).
When Yǐng (穎) went on campaign,
he appointed Xiù (秀) General of the Champion Army,
and together with Lù Jī (陸機) and Wáng Cuì (王粹), they participated in the battle of Héqiáo (河橋).
After Jī (機)'s defeat,
Xiù (秀) confirmed his guilt.
He also fawned upon the Imperial Attendant Mèng Jiǔ (孟玖),
and thus gained Yǐng (穎)'s favor.
When Emperor Huì (惠) moved west to Cháng'ān (長安),
he appointed Xiù (秀) as Shàngshū (尚書).
When Xiù (秀) was young in the capital,
he saw Liú Yì (劉毅), the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), present a memorial and was moved with indignation,
thinking that if he held the position of Judicial Officer,
he would be able to expose the corrupt and promote the pure.
If he were amidst drums and battle,
he would certainly achieve the merits of a general.
However, when he was in the position of Court Attendant and Chief Minister,
he never offered any extraordinary counsel or opposition.
Prince Yóng (顒) of Héjiān (河間) greatly trusted and employed him.
When the armies east of the pass rallied to welcome the imperial carriage,
Xiù (秀) was appointed General Pacifying the North,
garrisoning Fēngyì (馮翊).
Xiù (秀), along with Yóng (顒)'s generals Mǎ Zhān (馬瞻) and others, intended to assist Yóng (顒) in defending Guānzhōng (關中).
Yóng (顒) secretly sent envoys to Prince Yuè (越) of Dōnghǎi (東海) to request assistance.
Yuè (越) sent generals Mí Huǎng (麋晃) and others to welcome Yóng (顒).
At that time, Xiù (秀) commanded a large force in Fēngyì (馮翊),
and Huǎng (晃) dared not advance.
Yóng (顒)'s Chief Clerk Yáng Téng (楊騰) had previously failed to respond to Yuè (越)'s army,
and fearing Yuè (越)'s retaliation,
he wanted to capture Xiù (秀) to demonstrate his loyalty.
He colluded with the prominent Fēngyì (馮翊) families and various Yán (嚴) clans to falsely claim Yóng (顒)'s order,
instructing Xiù (秀) to disband his troops.
Xiù (秀) believed him.
Téng (騰) then killed Xiù (秀) at Wànnián (萬年).
Miù Bō (繆播) (cousin Yìn (胤))
Miù Bō (繆播), courtesy name Xuānzé (宣則),
was a native of Lánlíng (蘭陵).
His father, Yuè (悅),
was Grand Master of Guanglu.
Bō (播) was talented, thoughtful, clear-spoken,
and insightful.
When Prince TàI (泰) of Gāomì (高密) was Grand Minister of Works,
he appointed Bō (播) as Libationer,
and he was successively promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince.
When Emperor Huì (惠) was in Cháng'ān (長'ān),
Prince Yóng (顒) of Héjiān (河間) wished to control the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords.
Prince Yuè (越) of Dōnghǎi (東海) was about to raise an army to welcome the Emperor.
Because Bō (播)'s father had been an old subordinate,
Yuè (越) entrusted him with important matters.
Bō (播)'s cousin, Yìn (胤), the Right Guard Commander,
was the younger brother of Yóng (顒)'s former consort.
Yuè (越) sent Bō (播) and Yìn (胤) to Cháng'ān (長'ān) to persuade Yóng (顒),
asking him to escort the Emperor back to Luò (洛),
and promising to divide the passes with Yóng (顒) and make him a hegemon.
Bō (播) and Yìn (胤) were always respected and trusted by Yóng (顒),
and after they met,
Yóng (顒) openly listened to them.
Yóng (顒)'s general, Zhāng Fāng (張方), believing his crimes were severe,
feared he would be executed as the primary culprit.
He said to Yóng (顒):
"Now we hold a strategic and advantageous position.
The state is wealthy and the army strong.
We command the Son of Heaven to issue orders.
Who would dare not submit?"
Yóng (顒) was misled by Fāng (方)'s plan
and hesitated, unable to decide.
Fāng (方) disliked Bō (播) and Yìn (胤) for persuading Yuè (越),
and secretly wanted to kill them.
Bō (播) and others also feared Fāng (方) would cause trouble
and dared not speak again.
At that time, Yuè (越)'s military might was very strong,
and Yóng (顒) was deeply worried.
Bō (播) and Yìn (胤) then persuaded Yóng (顒) again,
urging him to execute Fāng (方) immediately as an apology,
which would bring peace without effort.
Yóng (顒) followed this advice,
and thus executed Fāng (方) to apologize to the feudal lords east of the mountains.
Yóng (顒) later regretted this,
and again used troops to resist Yuè (越),
but was repeatedly defeated by Yuè (越).
When the Emperor returned to the old capital,
Bō (播) also followed the Crown Prince back to Luò (洛).
Through difficulties and hardships,
they became deeply intimate.
When the Emperor died,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
known as Emperor Huái (懷).
He appointed Bō (播) as Palace Attendant and Chief of the Imperial Secretariat.
Soon after, he was transferred to Palace Attendant,
then moved to Grand Secretariat Director,
his influence growing daily,
exclusively managing imperial edicts.
At that time, Yuè (越)'s power and authority had become his own,
and the Emperor was unable to suppress him,
deeply disliking him.
Because Bō (播) and Yìn (胤) possessed the capacity of grand ministers
and were utterly loyal to the state,
he entrusted them with important matters.
Yuè (越), fearing harm from them,
entered the court,
and with troops entered the palace,
seizing Bō (播) and others at the Emperor's side.
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"Treacherous ministers and rebellious sons are found in every age.
They were not before me,
nor will they be after me.
How sorrowful!"
He rose and held Bō (播) and the others' hands,
weeping and sighing, unable to control himself.
Yuè (越) then killed them.
The court and common people were indignant,
all saying:
"Good people
are the pillars of the state.
To oppress them thus,
how can it end well?"
When Yuè (越) died,
the Emperor posthumously granted Bō (播) the title of Grand Commandant,
and offered a mid-sized animal sacrifice to him.
Yǐn, courtesy name Xiūzǔ,
was the maternal grandson of Ānpíng Xiànwáng.
His reputation was roughly equal to Bō's.
Initially, he served as Shàngshū Láng.
Later, he was promoted to Tàidì Zuǒwèilǜ,
then transferred to Wèijùn Tàishǒu.
When Wáng Jùn's army pressed towards Yè,
Shí Chāo and others were utterly defeated.
Yǐn fled to Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè in Xúzhōu.
Yuè sent Yǐn and Bō together to enter the pass.
What they advocated was implemented,
and the imperial carriage returned east.
Yuè appointed Yǐn as Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Nányáng Tàishǒu.
Yǐn set out from Lántián, passed through Wǔguān,
and went to Nányáng.
The former administrator Wèi Zhǎn resisted Yǐn and refused to accept him.
Yǐn then returned to Luò.
When Huái Dì ascended the throne,
he appointed Yǐn as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and then transferred him to Sànqí Chángshì and Tàipú Qīng.
Soon after, he, along with Bō, the emperor's maternal uncle Wáng Yán, Shàngshū Hé Suí, and Tàishǐ Lìng Gāotáng Chōng, participated in confidential matters.
He was killed by Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè.
Huángfǔ Chóng
Huángfǔ Chóng, courtesy name Lúnshú,
was a native of Āndìng Cháo.
He was calm and resolute by nature,
and had talent and ability.
He was recognized by Sīkōng Zhāng Huá,
and gradually promoted to Xīnpíng Tàishǒu.
During the Yuánkāng era,
Huá appointed him as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng assisted in governance,
he made Chóng's younger brother Shāng a Cānjūn.
After Jiǒng was executed,
Chángshā Wáng also made him a Cānjūn.
At that time, Héjiān Wáng Yǒng was stationed in Guānzhōng.
His general Lǐ Hán had previously had a grudge with Shāng and Chóng,
and held it against them.
At this point,
he advised Yǒng, saying:
"Shāng is appointed to office,
but Chóng will never be used by others.
It is advisable to quickly eliminate them,
to remove a local threat.
You can memorialize to promote Chóng to an internal position,
and when he passes through Cháng'ān,
then seize him."
Chóng, aware of the plot,
then openly sent a memorial to the Shàngshū,
stating that Yǒng's trust in Lǐ Hán
was leading to rebellion.
He gathered soldiers and commoners from Lǒngshàng,
using "punishing Hán" as a pretext.
As military conflicts had repeatedly arisen,
and had only just settled,
he submitted a memorial requesting an envoy to be sent to issue an imperial edict for Chóng to withdraw his troops
and for Hán to be summoned as Hénán Yǐn.
Once Hán was summoned,
Chóng did not obey the edict.
Yǒng sent Jīnchéng Tàishǒu Yóu Kǎi, Lǒngxī Tàishǒu Hán Zhì, and forces from four commanderies to attack him.
Soon after,
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng and Yǒng raised an army together to attack,
using the pretext of punishing the Empress's father, Shàngshū Púyè Yáng Xuánzhī, and Shāng.
Shāng was appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and Hédōng Tàishǒu,
leading over ten thousand men to resist Zhāng Fāng at Què Mén.
He was defeated by Fāng,
and Yǒng's army advanced.
After repeated defeats,
he sent Shāng to secretly carry an imperial edict written by the Emperor himself,
ordering Yóu Kǎi to completely withdraw his troops
and Chóng to advance his army to attack Yǒng.
Shāng passed through Cháng'ān,
arriving at Xīnpíng,
where he met his maternal nephew.
The maternal nephew had long disliked Shāng
and reported him to Yǒng.
Yǒng captured Shāng
and killed him.
Even after the defeat,
Chóng still held firm,
closing the outer gates,
so those inside the city did not know.
The four commandery armies built earthen mounds to attack the city,
but Chóng consistently shot at them with repeating crossbows.
He dug tunnels everywhere to defend against external attacks,
employing a hundred stratagems.
The besieging army could not get close to the city,
and the officers and soldiers fought to the death for him.
Yǒng knew he could not be dislodged,
so he submitted a memorial requesting an imperial censor be sent to issue an edict to persuade him to surrender.
Chóng knew this was not the true intention of the imperial court
and did not obey the edict.
He captured an imperial censor's attendant and asked:
"Is my younger brother bringing troops here?
Has he arrived yet?"
The attendant said:
"He has already been killed by Héjiān Wáng."
Chóng's face fell,
and he immediately killed the attendant.
Thereupon, the people inside the city knew there was no outside rescue,
and together they killed Chóng.
Previously,
when Chóng was heavily besieged,
he sent his adopted son Chāng to seek help from Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè.
Yuè, because Yǒng had recently deposed Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng
and formed an alliance with Shāndōng,
refused to send troops.
Chāng then, with the former Diànzhōng person Yáng Piān, falsely claimed to have Yuè's order,
welcoming Empress Yáng from Jīnyōng Chéng into the palace,
and using the empress's order to dispatch troops to punish Zhāng Fāng
and escort the Emperor.
The incident arose suddenly,
and initially all officials followed it.
Soon after, they jointly executed Chāng.
Zhāng Fǔ
Zhāng Fǔ, courtesy name Shìwěi,
was from Xī'è, Nányáng,
a descendant of Hàn Hégēnjiāng Xiāng Héng.
From a young age, he had competence and integrity,
and was as renowned as his maternal cousin Liú Qiáo.
Initially appointed Lántián Lìng,
he would not be intimidated by powerful local families.
At that time, Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn Páng Zōng,
a powerful clan in Xīzhōu, and Hùjūn Zhào Jùn,
Zōng's wife's relative,
had their former servants behave wantonly,
which was a problem for the common people.
Fǔ disciplined them,
killing two of their slaves,
and also seized over two hundred qǐng of Zōng's land to give to poor households.
The entire county praised him.
He was transferred to Shānyáng Lìng.
Tàiwèi Chén Zhǔn's household servants also acted tyrannically,
and Fǔ again struck and killed them.
He was successively promoted to Shàngshū Láng,
and enfeoffed as Yíchāng Tínghóu.
He was transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
At that time, Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn Méng Guān was at odds with Míngwēi Jiāngjūn Hǎo Yàn.
Guān used military affairs to harm Yàn.
Also, Jiǎ Mì, Pān Yuè, Shí Chóng, and others mutually supported each other.
And Yìyáng Wáng Wēi had a case of fraud and impersonation.
Fǔ impeached all of them.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Xīn's sister had died,
and less than ten days later,
Chējì Chángshǐ Hán Yù forcibly betrothed his daughter as his wife.
Fǔ, as Zhōngzhèng,
demoted Yù to purify customs,
and commentators praised him.
When Sūn Xiù held power,
Wēi falsely implicated Fǔ to Xiù.
Xiù was deceived
and was about to punish Fǔ according to the law.
Fǔ wrote a letter to Xiù, saying:
"I only know to admire the ancients,
and act according to my office,
no longer knowing how to plan for myself in a small way.
Now, Yìyáng Wáng is indeed magnanimous
and does not take it to heart.
However, my mother, seventy-six years old,
is constantly worried,
fearing that I will be punished due to resentment.
I hope you, Illustrious Duke, will carefully examine my past actions,
I am but a foolish subject of the state."
Though Xiù was fierce and cunning,
he knew Fǔ was upright
and had been slandered by Wēi,
so he stopped.
Later, he was promoted to Féngyì Tàishǒu.
At this time, Chángshā Wáng, seeing Héjiān Wáng Yǒng's exclusive control over Guānzhōng
and his disloyal conduct,
spoke to Huì Dì,
who secretly ordered Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Shěn and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Huángfǔ Chóng to attack Yǒng.
Thereupon, Shěn and others fought Yǒng in Cháng'ān.
Fǔ then led troops to rescue Yǒng,
and Shěn and others were defeated.
Yǒng appreciated this,
and appointed Fǔ to replace Chóng as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
During the time he went to Yǒng's aid,
Jīnchéng Tàishǒu Yóu Kǎi also rendered meritorious service,
and was transferred to Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
but did not proceed to his post.
Kǎi heard of Fǔ's return,
and did not welcome Fǔ promptly,
secretly plotting against him.
He also killed Tiānshuǐ Tàishǒu Fēng Shàng,
wishing to assert his authority in Xītǔ.
He summoned Lǒngxī Tàishǒu Hán Zhì for a meeting,
but no decision was reached.
Zhì's son Pǔ had military talent;
he beheaded those who disagreed,
and immediately gathered troops to attack Fǔ.
Fǔ fought Zhì at Zhēduō Gǔkǒu.
Fǔ's army was defeated
and he was killed by Fù Zhěng, a former aide-de-camp from Tiānshuǐ.
Initially,
Fǔ once authored an essay stating:
"Guǎn Zhòng is not as good as Bào Shū.
Bào Shū knew whom to serve
and whom to commit to.
Guǎn Zhòng served his lord but could not succeed,
and the state he fled to was not one that could accomplish things.
The 'three returns' and 'overturned stands' [incidents]
were all things Bào would not do."
He also discussed Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān, saying:
"Qiān's writings
are concise in wording and comprehensive in events.
Three thousand years of history are covered in only five hundred thousand characters.
Bān Gù covered two hundred years of history in eight hundred thousand characters.
Their verbosity and conciseness differ,
so Bān Gù is inferior to Qiān in this first aspect.
A good historian narrates events
so that the good is sufficient to encourage and admonish,
and the evil is sufficient to deter and warn,
which is the constant way of human affairs.
Minor, commonplace matters
are not worth including,
yet Bān Gù recorded all of them;
this is the second aspect in which he is inferior.
His vilification and denigration of Cháo Cuò
harm the way of loyal ministers;
this is the third aspect in which he is inferior.
Qiān was the pioneer,
while Bān Gù merely followed suit;
the difficulty and ease [of their tasks] were even more different.
Moreover, Qiān wrote biographies for Sū Qín, Zhāng Yí, Fàn Suī, and Cài Zé,
their eloquent and fluid language
is also sufficient to demonstrate his great talent.
Therefore, when narrating rhetoricians, his language is ornate and splendid;
when recording facts, it is profound and precise, adhering to standards.
This is why Qiān is praised as a good historian."
He further argued that Wèi Wǔdì was inferior to Liú Bèi,
and Yuè Yì was inferior to Zhūgě Liàng.
His words are too numerous to be fully recorded.
Lǐ Hán.
Lǐ Hán, courtesy name Shìróng,
was a native of Dídào, Lǒngxī.
He resided in Shǐpíng as an immigrant.
He had talent and capability from a young age,
and was recommended as xiàolián by both commanderies.
Huángfǔ Shāng of Āndìng, a young man from the same province,
relied on his powerful clan in his youth.
Considering Hán's humble family background,
he wished to form an alliance,
but Hán refused him.
Shāng resented this
and consequently influenced the province to summon Hán to be a mén tíngzhǎng through a brief official dispatch.
It happened that the provincial governor Guō Yì had long heard of his virtue,
and upon arrival, promoted Hán to biejia,
placing him above the other officials.
Soon after, he was recommended as xiùcái,
and presented to the Duke's residence.
He transferred from Tài Bǎo Yuàn to Qín Guó Lángzhōnglìng.
The Sītú selected Hán to lead the zhōngzhèng of Shǐpíng.
When Qín Wáng Jiǎn passed away,
Hán, following the imperial court's regulations,
removed his mourning attire after the burial.
Shàngshū Zhào Jùn, who had a favored subordinate,
resented Hán for not serving him,
and thus memorialized that Hán should not have removed his mourning attire.
The Dà Zhōngzhèng of his native province, Fù Zhī, condemned Hán based on moral principles.
Zhōngchéng Fù Xián submitted a memorial to vindicate Hán, saying: "Your minister's Qín Guó Lángzhōnglìng of Shǐpíng, Lǐ Hán,
is loyal, public-spirited, pure, and upright,
with talents capable of managing worldly affairs.
He truly possesses the straightforward integrity of Shǐ Yú.
Although because of this he is unable
to harmonize with common customs,
his character and conduct are severe and strict,
and cannot be concealed.
Both commanderies recommended him as xiàolián for his exceptional conduct.
When Shàngshū Guō Yì arrived in the province,
Hán was a young man from a humble family,
yet
Yì extraordinarily promoted him to biejia.
Tài Bǎo Wèi Guàn appointed Hán as his yuàn,
and often said to your minister:
'Lǐ Shìróng will surely be a loyal and selfless minister of Jìn.'
When the King of Qín passed away,
the grief and sorrow were deeply moving,
and all officials attended the funeral,
which everyone witnessed.
Yet now, because Hán complied with the royal funerary system,
he is accused of 'turning his back on sorrow and dwelling in glory,'
and stripped of his zhōngzhèng position.
In the Imperial Court,
mourning is not removed after burial.
For a feudal state,
mourning is removed after burial.
If a feudal state wished to adopt the custom of not removing mourning,
it would be appropriate to criticize them for elevating the honored and debasing the humble,
which is not what should be said.
Now the Imperial Court
wishes the feudal states to observe the lower [standard],
this would mean the righteousness of the feudal states is emphasized,
while the ritual of the Imperial Court is diminished.
It is also said that all princes and dukes complete their mourning,
and that 'rites are never exhausted,'
implying that mourning rites should be grand,
and the emphasis is on solemnity.
Indeed, 'rites are never exhausted'
implies
grieving the illness.
Different from the Imperial Court,
where the system dictates full mourning,
such writings are not seen.
The national system is to remove mourning after burial,
and after removal, to perform the fù ritual.
From the Hàn and Wèi [dynasties] up
to the Sacred Jìn,
when Emperor Wén ascended to the heavens,
when Emperor Wǔ passed away,
when Shìzǔ was excessively grieved,
and when Your Majesty was devastated,
bearing sorrow and in silent mourning,
to complete three years—
how could the subjects and women throughout the land
not have a yearning desire to follow this observance?
It is truly because the national system cannot be overstepped,
thus they dared not not remove mourning after burial.
For the Imperial Court's mourning,
the removal of mourning is relaxed above,
while the ministers of feudal states
alone fully observe it below;
this cannot be justified.
Furthermore, as the King of Qín had no heir,
Hán should have acted as the chief mourner.
If the King's mourning is removed after burial and the fù ritual performed,
then auspicious sacrifices should follow.
It is then argued that since the King has no temple,
the chief mourner should not remove his mourning attire.
The King of Qín was initially enfeoffed,
with no existing ancestral temple for fù.
Wherever the spirit tablet resides
immediately becomes the temple.
Ignoring what the national system states,
and using the absence of a temple as a reason for demotion.
If Hán's conduct today
were to be presented to erudites to examine ritual texts,
then surely when Fàngxūn passed away,
mourning was observed for three years;
when Shìzǔ passed away,
auspicious rites were performed after several tens of days.
If we use ancient examples to regulate the present,
the whole world would be subject to demotion;
why should only Lǐ Hán not be allowed to remove his mourning attire?
Now there is no demotion;
this is due to the royal system.
When the Sacred Emperor is in silent mourning,
and sounds of sorrow do not cease,
ministers and close attendants
should still mourn in their hearts,
and should not immediately engage in marriages and joyous events.
Yet no one says this;
is it not because
the great system cannot be bent?
Moreover, previously, due to Hán's mourning for the King,
he was assigned a temporary replacement.
The Shàngshū then commanded that the King's burial day was near,
and after the burial,
Hán should resume his duties,
and no replacement would be allowed.
After the burial, Hán still hesitated.
The Sītú repeatedly inquired with penalties,
urging Hán to resume his duties,
and then immediately attacked him.
This means the imperial command and the府's (fǔ) order trapped Hán
in wrongdoing.
If it is believed that the Imperial Court and the府 (fǔ) harmed justice and morality,
then they should be corrected.
If the imperial command and orders are not corrected,
and only Hán is demoted,
is Hán's distress not regrettable enough?
The national system
cannot be partial.
Furthermore, Hán considered himself a person from Lǒngxī;
although his household was registered in Shǐpíng,
it was not his ancestral home.
From the beginning, when he was appointed zhōngzhèng,
he repeatedly expressed
that he was not a native of Shǐpíng
and was not suitable to be zhōngzhèng.
Later, as Lángzhōnglìng,
he again compared himself to an official chosen by the Imperial Court and the府 (fǔ),
and yielded to Sū Sháo, the Prefect of Chángshān,
his words were earnest..."
cut,
expressed in writing.
Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] yielding was firm,
but it was before the King [Zhào Wáng Lún] had died,
and after his burial, he hesitated,
driven by the need to avoid punishment, and thus assumed the position.
My younger cousin, Zhī [Lǐ Zhī],
was the Zhōu Dū [Prefect of the Prefecture].
His intention was to promote moral instruction,
but Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] actions were already excessive.
Bad people then incited each other,
hoping to exploit a pretext,
and brought charges outside the law,
sufficient to
accuse him.
The Zhōngzhèng [Local Administrator] Páng Téng then demoted Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] rank.
Although I do not possess the virtue of Qí Dàfū,
seeing Hán [Lǐ Hán] insulted by Téng [Páng Téng],
I respectfully submit this memorial to be heard,
begging the court to
deliberate broadly in due time,
and not allow Téng [Páng Téng] to wantonly wield his power.
The Emperor did not comply,
and Hán [Lǐ Hán] was subsequently demoted,
his rank reduced to fifth grade.
He returned to Cháng’ān.
After more than a year,
the Guānglù [Court Architect] appointed Hán [Lǐ Hán] as the Dú of the Shòuchéng Dǐgé [Supervisor of the Imperial Granaries at Shòuchéng].
Sītú [Minister of Works] Wáng Róng memorialized that Hán [Lǐ Hán] had once been a great minister,
and although he had been demoted,
he should not be assigned to this position.
An imperial edict suspended the appointment.
Later, he became the Ling [Magistrate] of Shǐpíng.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
someone said to Sūn Xiù:
“Lǐ Hán possesses great civil and military talent,
and should not be unemployed.”
Xiù [Sūn Xiù] made him the Ling [Magistrate] of Dōngwǔyáng.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng memorialized requesting Hán [Lǐ Hán] as his Zhēngxī Sīmǎ [Marshal of the Expedition against the West],
and he was greatly trusted.
Shortly after,
he was transferred to Chángshǐ [Chief Clerk].
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] executed Xiàhóu Shì,
sent Qí Wáng Jiǒng’s messenger to Zhào Wáng Lún,
and dispatched Zhāng Fāng to lead troops to Lún [Zhào Wáng Lún].
All of these were Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] plans.
Later, Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] heard that the armies of the Three Kings were strong,
so he bestowed upon Hán [Lǐ Hán] the title of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn [General of the Dragon Soar],

commanding Xí Wěi’s [Xí Wěi, not a proper noun, but a generic name or possibly an error in the source text, given the context of other names being proper. However, per instructions, I'm treating it as a proper noun to be safe and transliterating it as is.] and other iron cavalry,
and sent Zhāng Fāng’s army back to respond to the righteous army.
When the Son of Heaven returned to the capital,
Hán [Lǐ Hán] reached Tóngguān and returned.
Initially,
Huángfǔ Shāng, the Cìshǐ [Inspector] of Liángzhōu, had been appointed by Zhào Wáng Lún.
When Lún [Zhào Wáng Lún] was defeated,
he resigned his post and went to Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng].
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] consoled and treated him very generously.
Hán [Lǐ Hán] admonished Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng], saying:
“Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] was Lún’s [Zhào Wáng Lún] trusted minister.
Fearing punishment, he came here.
It is not proper to see him frequently.”
Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] knew and resented this.
When Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] was about to return to the capital,
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] hosted a farewell banquet.
Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] then had a heated argument with Hán [Lǐ Hán],
and Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] reconciled them.
Later, Hán [Lǐ Hán] was summoned to be Yìjūn Xiàowèi [Colonel of the Auxiliary Army].
At that time, Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] participated in Qí Wáng Jiǒng’s military affairs,
and Xiàhóu Shì’s brother was in Jiǒng’s [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] residence,
claiming that Shì [Xiàhóu Shì] had risen in righteousness
but was unjustly killed by the western feudal lords.
Hán [Lǐ Hán] felt uneasy.
Jiǒng’s [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] Yòusīmǎ [Right Marshal] Zhào Xiāng also had a grudge against Hán [Lǐ Hán].
When Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] was about to review the troops,
Hán [Lǐ Hán] feared that Xiāng [Zhào Xiāng] would use the troops to attack him,
so he fled alone on horseback to Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng],
falsely claiming to have received a secret edict.
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] saw him that very night,
and Hán [Lǐ Hán] then persuaded Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng], saying:
“Chéngdū Wáng [Sīmǎ Yǐng] is a close relative,
has rendered great service,
and upon returning to his fief,
has gained much popular support.
Qí Wáng [Sīmǎ Jiǒng], a distant relative, has arrogated all power,
and the court watches him with apprehension.
Now, if we issue a proclamation to Chángshā Wáng [Sīmǎ Yì] to attack Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng],
and let Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] hear of it first,
Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] will surely execute Chángshā [Chángshā Wáng Yì].
Then, by transmitting a proclamation to accuse Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] of his crimes,
Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] can be captured.
Once Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] is removed,
and Chéngdū [Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng] is established,
removing the coercion and establishing a close relative,
the state will be at peace.
This would be a great achievement.”
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] followed his advice,
and then memorialized requesting to attack Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng],
appointing Hán [Lǐ Hán] as Dūdū [Commander],
commanding Zhāng Fāng and others to lead all armies towards Luòyáng.
Hán [Lǐ Hán] encamped at Yīnpán,
but Chángshā Wáng [Sīmǎ Yì] executed Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng],
and Hán [Lǐ Hán] and others turned back their armies.
Initially,
Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] original plan was to eliminate both Yì [Chángshā Wáng Yì] and Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng],
so that power would revert to Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng],
and Hán [Lǐ Hán] could then fulfill his long-cherished ambition.
Since Chángshā [Chángshā Wáng Yì] defeated Qí [Qí Wáng Jiǒng],
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] and Yǐng [Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng] still each guarded their fiefs,
and their ambitions were not yet satisfied.
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] memorialized Hán [Lǐ Hán] as Hénán Yǐn [Prefect of Hénán].
At that time, Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] was again appointed and favored.
Shāng’s [Huángfǔ Shāng] elder brother, Zhòng [Huángfǔ Zhòng], was then the Cìshǐ [Inspector] of Qínzhōu.
Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] animosity towards Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] intensified,
and he again stirred up trouble with Zhòng [Huángfǔ Zhòng].
Since Hán [Lǐ Hán] fled back, Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] had entrusted him completely.
He [Yǒng] also feared that Zhòng [Huángfǔ Zhòng] would attack him,
so he sent troops to besiege him,
and they mutually impeached each other for crimes.
Shìzhōng [Palace Attendant] Féng Sūn, who sided with Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng],
requested to recall Zhòng [Huángfǔ Zhòng].
Shāng [Huángfǔ Shāng] said:
“Héjiān’s [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] memorials
are all instigated by Lǐ Hán.
If we do not plan early,
disaster will come.
Moreover, Héjiān’s [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] previous actions
were due to Hán’s [Lǐ Hán] counsel.”
Thereupon, he killed Hán [Lǐ Hán].
Zhāng Fāng
Zhāng Fāng was
a native of Héjiān.
His family was poor and lowly,
but by virtue of his talent and bravery, he gained favor with Héjiān Wáng Yǒng,
and was repeatedly promoted to Jiānzhènwǔ Jiāngjūn [General Overseeing the Pacification of Martial Affairs].
During the Yǒngníng era,
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] memorialized to attack Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
and sent Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] to lead 20,000 troops as the vanguard.
When Jiǒng [Qí Wáng Jiǒng] was killed by Chángshā Wáng [Sīmǎ Yì],
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng again memorialized to attack,
and sent Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] to lead his forces from Hángǔ Pass to encamp in Hénán.
Huì Dì [Emperor Huì] sent Zuǒjiāngjūn [General of the Left] Huángfǔ Shāng to resist him,
but Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] secretly led his army to defeat Shāng’s [Huángfǔ Shāng] forces,
and then entered the city.
The Emperor [Huì Dì] personally attacked Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] within the city.
Fāng’s [Zhāng Fāng] army, seeing the imperial carriage,
then retreated slightly.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] could not stop them,
and his forces were then greatly defeated,
with dead and wounded filling the streets and alleys.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] retreated to his camp at Shísānlǐqiáo.
The morale of the people was shattered,
and they had no will to hold on.
Many advised Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] to flee during the night.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] said:
“The sharpness or bluntness of weapons is common;
what is precious is to use defeat to achieve success.
I will advance further and build a new camp,
catching them off guard.
This is the wonder of military strategy.”
So, he secretly advanced during the night to within seven li of Luòchéng.
Having just achieved a victory,
they [the imperial forces] did not take it seriously.
Suddenly hearing that Fāng’s [Zhāng Fāng] camp was completed,
they then went out to battle,
and were defeated.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè and others captured
and sent him to Jīnyōng Chéng.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] sent Zhì Fǔ to retrieve him to the camp,
and roasted him to death.
Thereupon, he plundered over 10,000 official and private slaves in Luòyáng,
and returned west to Cháng’ān.
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] appointed Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] as Yòujiāngjūn [General of the Right] and Féngyì Tàishǒu [Administrator of Féngyì].
During the Battle of Dàngyīn,
Yǒng [Héjiān Wáng Yǒng] again sent Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] to garrison Luòyáng.
Shàngguān Sì and Miáo Yuàn and others resisted him,
but were greatly defeated and retreated.
Qīnghé Wáng Tán attacked Sì [Shàngguān Sì] and Yuàn [Miáo Yuàn] by night,
and Sì [Shàngguān Sì] and Yuàn [Miáo Yuàn] fled.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] then entered Luòyáng.
Tán [Qīnghé Wáng Tán] welcomed Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] at Guǎngyángmén and bowed.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] swiftly dismounted his carriage to help and stop him.
Thereupon, Empress Yáng [Yáng Xiànróng] was again deposed.
When the Emperor [Huì Dì] returned to Luòyáng from Yè,
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] sent his son Pí [Zhāng Pí] with three thousand cavalry to welcome him.
When about to cross the Héquiáo [River Bridge],
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] also used his own solar-powered carriage and a blue canopy with three hundred attendants as a small ceremonial guard,
welcoming the Emperor to the foot of Mángshān.
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] himself led over 10,000 cavalry, bearing the mica palanquin and adorned with banners and flags,
escorting the Emperor forward.
Initially,
Fāng [Zhāng Fāng] saw the Emperor about to bow,
and the Emperor dismounted his carriage to stop him.
Suǒ Jìng, courtesy name Yòu'ān,
was a native of Dūnhuáng.
His family had been officials for generations;
his father, Zhàn,
was the Administrator of Běidì.
When young, Suǒ Jìng possessed extraordinary qualities,
and with his fellow townsmen Fàn Zhōng, Zhāng Hán, Suǒ Zhěn, and Suǒ Yǒng, he went to the Imperial Academy.
They became renowned throughout the land,
and were
known as the "Five Dragons of Dūnhuáng."
Four of them died young,
leaving only Suǒ Jìng, who was learned in the classics and histories,
and also understood esoteric texts.
The province appointed him as Assistant Administrator,
and the commandery recommended him as "Virtuous and Upright,"
for which he achieved a high rank in the policy examination.
Fù Xuán and Zhāng Huà, having met Suǒ Jìng once,
both formed a close bond with him.
He was appointed as Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Commander of the Imperial Son-in-law Guards),
and then sent out as the Senior Clerk of the Wùjǐ Commandant of the Western Regions.
Zhāng Bó, the Prince's Tutor from the same commandery, specially memorialized,
stating that Suǒ Jìng's talent and skill were unparalleled,
and that he should be in the central government,
not sent far away to the frontier.
Emperor Wǔ accepted this,
and promoted him to Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel).
He served alongside Luó Shàng from Xiāngyáng, Pān Yuè from Hénán, and Gù Róng from Wú Commandery,
all of whom admired and respected him.
Suǒ Jìng and Wèi Guàn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, were both famous for their excellent cursive script,
which the emperor admired.
Wèi Guàn's brushwork surpassed Suǒ Jìng's
in its regular script principles,
but in the distant reach of his cursive, he could not match Suǒ Jìng.
Suǒ Jìng served in the central government for many years,
then was appointed Administrator of Yànmén,
transferred to Prime Minister of Lǔ,
and then appointed Administrator of Jiǔquán.
Upon Emperor Huì's ascension,
he was granted the title of Marquis of Guānnèi.
Suǒ Jìng had foresight and a broad perspective;
knowing that the world was about to fall into chaos,
he pointed to the bronze camels outside the Luòyáng palace gate
and sighed:
"You will soon be seen amidst thorns and brambles!"
During the Yuánkāng era,
when the Western Rong rebelled,
Suǒ Jìng was appointed Left Sīmǎ (Commander of the Army) to the Grand General, Prince Róng of Liáng.
He was also given the title of Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Quells Bandits),
stationed troops at Sùyì,
attacked the rebels,
and defeated them.
He was then transferred to Internal Historian of Shǐpíng.
When Prince Lún of Zhào usurped the throne,
Suǒ Jìng responded to the righteous uprising of the Three Princes
and, as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guards), helped defeat Sūn Xiù, earning merit.
He was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (Attendant-in-ordinary),
and promoted to Hòujiāngjūn (General of the Rear).
At the end of the Tàiyān era,
when Prince Yǒng of Héjiān raised an army against Luòyáng,
Suǒ Jìng was appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of all armies in Luòyáng, and Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Mobile Cavalry).
He led the righteous troops from Yōng, Qín, and Liáng,
fought the rebels,
and severely defeated them.
Suǒ Jìng was also wounded and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies),
at the age of sixty-five.
Later, he was again posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
further enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānlètíng,
and given the posthumous name Zhuāng.
Suǒ Jìng authored the "Lùn on the Correct Verification of the Five Elements and Three Systems,"
which discussed the principles of Yin-Yang and the cycles of cosmic energy.
He also compiled "Master Suǒ" and "Jìn Poetry," each in twenty volumes.
He also wrote an "Essay on Cursive Script,"
the text of which reads: The Sage Emperor governed the world,
adapting to the needs of the times.
When Cāng Jié was born,
writing and contracts came into being.
Tadpole script and bird script,
mimicked objects and their forms.
The wise and sagacious transformed them,
and
skillful ingenuity arose from this.
They were reduced to Clerical and Cursive scripts,
to promote simplicity and ease.
All officials fully cultivated them,
and their works were equally beautiful.
Now, the appearance of cursive script,
is gracefully like a silver hook,
and drifts
like a startled phoenix.
With wings spread but not yet airborne,
as if rising yet settling again;
like worms and snakes coiling,
sometimes going, sometimes returning.
Resembling Āná with her slender form,
suddenly roused to valiant strength.
When it flows freely and widely,
sometimes straight, sometimes crooked.
Like a spirited steed raging and straining its reins,
like the sea swelling and receding, raising its waves.
Like auspicious ganoderma and grapes, following one after another,
like
cherry blossoms blooming in joyful profusion.
Like dark bears sitting opposite each other on mountains,
like flying swallows chasing each other, crisscrossing.
When one observes it closely,
it also seems like a gentle breeze blowing through a forest,
bending
grass and rustling trees.
Branches follow the air currents,
turning and clinging to each other,
gracefully swaying and drooping,
spreading according to their form.
In tumultuous disarray and elegant beauty,
holding in doubt and hesitation.
Black serpents and cunning beasts frolic among them,
leaping monkeys and flying *chēwán* chasing each other.
Leaping fish brandish their tails,
dragons rear back.
Darting into the void, hiding themselves,
spreading out fangs and claws.
Sometimes
as if ascending high to gaze at their kind,
sometimes as if having passed yet looking back,
sometimes as if unconstrained and solitary,
sometimes as if restraining oneself within normal limits.
Thus, the excellent ones of great talent,
the outstanding ones of profound art,
devote their minds to subtle detail,
indulging in this literary paradigm.
Maintaining principles while adapting to circumstances,
generating changes by touching upon categories.
Dissecting the eight
styles,
no form remains unanalyzed.
Removing complexity and preserving the subtle,
the grand design is not confused.
Above, the principles open up the origin;
below, they thoroughly scrutinize.
Unleashing words and freeing the hand,
like rain falling and ice melting.
High
notes soar,
overflowing and spreading.
Suddenly forming patterns into chapters,
truly marvelous and resplendent.
Its structure is rugged and magnificent,
its posture lustrous and brilliant.
Commanding
Dù Dù to move his fingers,
and ordering Bóyīng to turn his wrist.
Creating extraordinary forms on silk,
leaving a unique spectacle for a hundred generations.
Earlier,
Suǒ Jìng saw a stony area south of Gūzāng city,
and said:
"Later, palaces will be built here."
Later, Zhāng Jùn
built the South City on that very spot,
erected ancestral temples,
and constructed palaces.
Suǒ Jìng had five sons: Gěng, Quǎn, Qiú, Yù, and Lín,
all of whom were recommended as Xiùcái (Filial and Incorrupt).
Yù
was the Marquis of Ānchāng Village
and died.
His youngest son, Lín, was the most famous.
Lín, courtesy name Jùxiù,
possessed extraordinary qualities when young.
Suǒ Jìng often said:
"Lín has the talent for the imperial court,
not for simple documents;
provincial and commandery officials are not worthy of my son."
He was recommended as Xiùcái
and appointed Lángzhōng (Gentleman).
He once avenged his elder brother,
personally killing thirty-seven people,
which people at the time admired.
Soon after, he was transferred to Tàizǎi Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Grand Tutor),
appointed Magistrate of Hǎozhì,
entered the court as Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Gentleman),
then left to serve as a Staff Officer in the army of the General Who Attacks the West,
and was transferred to Magistrate of Cháng'ān.
He had a good reputation in office.
When Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng kidnapped and moved Huìdì to Yè,
Yǐng was defeated by Wáng Jùn,
and the emperor was then forced to flee.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng sent Zhāng Fāng and Suǒ Lín eastward to welcome the imperial carriage.
For his merit, he was appointed Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn,
and then transferred to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng for Nányáng Wáng Mó.
When Liú Cōng invaded and plundered Guāndōng,
Suǒ Lín was made Fènwēi Jiāngjūn to resist him.
He beheaded Cōng's general, Lǚ Yì,
and also defeated Cōng's partisan, Liú Fēng.
He was promoted to Xīnpíng Tàishǒu.
When Cōng's generals, Sū Tiě and Liú Wǔdòu, plundered Sānfǔ,
Suǒ Lín was appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn and Féngyì Tàishǒu.
Suǒ Lín possessed both awe and kindness,
and both Chinese and barbarians submitted to him.
The bandits dared not offend him.
When Huáidì was disgraced [lit. covered in dust]
and Cháng'ān also fell,
Mó was killed.
Suǒ Lín wept and said:
"Rather than die with them,
I would prefer to be Wǔ Zǐxū."
He then went to Āndìng
and, with Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Jiǎ Yà, Fúfēng Tàishǒu Liáng Zōng, and Ānyí Hùjūn Qū Yǔn, gathered righteous troops.
They repeatedly defeated the bandit factions,
repaired the old palaces,
and established the ancestral temple.
He then advanced to rescue Xīnpíng,
fighting a hundred battles, great and small.
Suǒ Lín personally captured the bandit leader Lǐ Qiāng,
and, with Yán Dǐng, established the King of Qín as Crown Prince.
When he ascended to the imperial throne,
he was Mǐndì.
Suǒ Lín was promoted to Shìzhōng, Tàipú.
For the merit of being the first to welcome the imperial carriage and ascending the altar to present the imperial seal,
he was enfeoffed as Gēqū Bó.
He was further promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, Líng Lìbù, and Jīngzhào Yǐn,
and given the additional title of Píngdōng Jiāngjūn,
then promoted to Zhēngdōng.
Soon after, an imperial edict stated:
"I formerly encountered a difficult fate,
as my family was unfortunate,
and I fled to Wǎn and Chǔ,
losing the old capital.
Fortunately, with the auspicious spirit of the ancestral temple
and the efforts of the officials,
I was able to be among the protectors,
placed above the dukes.
That the altars of soil and grain have not fallen
is truly dependent on you, my lord.
It is fitting that you assist in all government affairs
and support my person.
Therefore, I grant you Wèi Jiāngjūn,
Líng Tàiwèi,
with the rank of Tèjìn.
All military and national affairs are entrusted to you."
When Liú Yào invaded and pressed upon the imperial city,
Suǒ Lín was made Dūdū Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn
and sent with imperial credentials to suppress him.
He defeated Yào's Hū Rìzhú Wáng Hūyán Mò.
For this merit, he was enfeoffed as Shàngluò Jùn Gōng,
with an income of ten thousand households.
His wife, Lady Xún, was appointed Xīnfēng Jūn,
and his son, Shí Yuán, was made crown prince.
Two of his younger brothers were granted the title of Xiāngtíng Hóu.
When Liú Yào entered Guān to cut down wheat sprouts,
Suǒ Lín again defeated him.
When attacking Liú Cōng from Cháng'ān,
Cōng's general Zhào Rǎn, emboldened by his repeated victories,
showed a proud demeanor.
He led several hundred elite cavalry to fight Suǒ Lín,
and was greatly defeated.
Rǎn fled on a lone horse.
Suǒ Lín was then transferred to Piáojì Dàjiāngjūn, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, and Lù Shàngshū,
acting on imperial authority.
Liú Yào again led his troops into Féngyì.
The emperor repeatedly requested troops from Nányáng Wáng Bǎo.
Bǎo's attendants discussed, saying:
"A poisonous snake is in hand;
a brave man should sever its wrist.
Let us cut off the Lǒng road
to observe the changes."
Cóngshì Zhōngláng Péi Shēn said:
"The snake has already bitten the head;
can the head be cut off?"
Bǎo sent Hú Sōng to act as the vanguard commander,
and intended to set out only after all the armies had gathered.
Qū Yǔn wanted to take the emperor to Bǎo,
but Suǒ Lín believed that Bǎo would certainly indulge his selfish desires,
so he stopped.
West of Cháng'ān,
the people no longer obeyed the imperial court.
Officials were starving
and had to survive on their own.
[一０]At that time, thousands of families, including Yǐn Huán and Xiè Wǔ from Sānqín,
plundered the Hàn tombs of Bà and Dù,
obtaining many treasures.
The emperor asked Suǒ Lín:
"Why is there so much in the Hàn imperial tombs?"
Suǒ Lín replied:
"A Hàn emperor, upon ascending the throne, would begin constructing his tomb a year later.
Of the empire's tribute and taxes,
one-third was for the ancestral temple,
one-third for guests,
and one-third for the mountain tombs.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn lived a long life;
by the time of his death, Máolíng could no longer contain any more objects,
and its trees were already large enough to be embraced.
The Chìméi took less than half of the items from the tomb,
and even now there are still heaps of rotting silks
and inexhaustible pearls and jade.
These two tombs are considered modest,
and they serve as a warning for a hundred generations."
Later, Liú Yào again led his troops to besiege the capital city.
Suǒ Lín and Qū Yǔn held out in Cháng'ān's small city.
Hú Sōng, responding to the urgent summons,
