defeated Yào at Língtái.
Sōng feared that if the state achieved a powerful victory,
the merits of Qū Yǔn and Suǒ Lín would be too great.
So he halted his troops north of the Wèi River
and then returned to Huáilǐ.
Inside the city, there was famine and distress;
people resorted to cannibalism.
Deaths and desertions were uncontrollable.
Only a thousand righteous troops from Liángzhōu held their ground, unyielding unto death.
The emperor sent Shìzhōng Sòng Chǎng with a letter of surrender to Yào.
[一一]Suǒ Lín secretly detained Chǎng
and sent his son to persuade Yào, saying:
"There is still enough food in the city to last a year;
it cannot be easily overcome.
If you promise Suǒ Lín the titles of Chējì, Yítóng, and a ten-thousand-household commandery duke,
I will surrender the city."
Yào beheaded him and sent back his head, saying:
"The army of an emperor
acts on righteousness.
I have been a general for fifteen years,
and have never defeated anyone by cunning.
I must exhaust their troops and resources
before taking them.
Now, what Suǒ Lín has said is the same evil throughout the world;
I have summarily executed him for you.
If it is truly the case that your provisions and troops are not exhausted,
then you may strive to hold out.
But if your provisions are depleted and your forces are weak,
you should also recognize Heaven's mandate early.
I fear that once my frosty might trembles,
both jade and stone will be shattered."
When the emperor surrendered,
Suǒ Lín followed the emperor to Píngyáng.
Liú Cōng, considering him disloyal to his former dynasty,
executed him in the eastern marketplace.
Jiǎ Yà
Jiǎ Yà, courtesy name Yàndù,
was from Wǔwēi.
He was the great-grandson of Wèi Tàiwèi Xǔ.
From a young age, he possessed ambition and strategy.
His bearing and reputation were very grand;
all who saw him were pleased and attached to him,
especially admired by warriors
who were willing to die for him.
Initially invited to a ducal residence,
he subsequently held prominent positions,
and was promoted to Āndìng Tàishǒu.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Dīng Chuò,
being corrupt and tyrannical, lost the hearts of the people,
and thus slandered Jiǎ Yà to Nányáng Wáng Mó.
Mó sent Jūnsī Xiè Bān to attack him.
[一二]Jiǎ Yà fled to Lúshuǐ,
[一三]and there, with Hú Péngdàng Zhòng and the Dī leader Dòu Shǒu, formed a sworn brotherhood.
They gathered a multitude and attacked Bān.
Chuò fled to Wǔdū,
and Jiǎ Yà re-entered Āndìng,
killing Bān.
Mǐndì appointed Jiǎ Yà as Piáojì Jiāngjūn
and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed him as Jiǔquán Gōng.
At that time, the people in all the commanderies suffered from famine;
white bones covered the fields;
not one in a hundred survived.
Pǐ Shuài led over 20,000 soldiers from the Róng and Jìn,
preparing to attack Cháng'ān.
The Administrator of Xīpíng, Zhú Huī, also held firm in defense.
and sent Liú Yào, Liú Yǎ, and Zhào Rǎn to resist Pǐ.
They first attacked Huī,
but failed to overcome him.
Pǐ ambushed and attacked them,
defeating them utterly.
Yào was struck by a stray arrow
and fled.
Liú Càn heard of this
as far as Gānquán.
He then attacked Dàng Zhòng from Wèiqiáo,
killing him.
Subsequently, he welcomed the Prince of Qín
and enthroned him as Crown Prince.
Later, Dàng Zhòng's son, Fū Hù, led a group of Hú to attack Pǐ.
falling into a ravine at night,
where he was killed by Fū Hù.
Pǐ was brave, resourceful, and resolute.
He took it upon himself to restore the Jìn dynasty.
Unfortunately, he met with an untimely end.
People of the time all grieved for him.
The imperial historian says: Since the upheaval of Yǒngjiā,
chaos spread throughout the realm.
Countless people had no one to rely on;
both humans and spirits lacked a lord.
At that time, among the descendants of Emperor Wǔ,
only Jiànxīng remained.
The hopes of the multitude converged upon him;
there was truly no second.
Yán Dǐng and others were loyal to the state
and dedicated to governance.
Thus, despite arduous difficulties,
they supported the young heir,
enabling him to inherit the legacy of Yáo and continue the line.
They offered sacrifices to Xià and honored Heaven.
In terms of their achievements and merits,
there is much to commend.
However, they confronted overwhelming powerful bandits
and inherited a dilapidated foundation.
Their might and strategy had not yet been fully exercised
before they soon met with ruin.
In ancient times, when the Zōngzhōu encountered the Quǎnrong, it moved east.
The Jìn, when faced with the savage Dí, moved west.
The former enjoyed long-lasting auspiciousness,
while the latter swiftly encountered calamity.
Was it that Emperor Mǐn's territory was not a secure place for a ruler,
or that Chén Yǔn lacked the talent for an auxiliary minister?
Why such different paths in terms of longevity
and such varying outcomes of success and failure?
A eulogy says: Huái and Huì were not competitive;
the imperial relatives fiercely vied.
Scheming and deceit entered the counsels,
relying on cruelty to disorder the government.
Their evil knew no end,
and they all met unnatural deaths.
Xiè Miù was loyal and solemn,
but no lasting blessings were heard of.
Emperor Mǐn inherited the throne;
he truly relied on the multitude of nobles.
Dǐng's plans began auspiciously,
while Chén's ended disastrously.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 31: Zhōu Jùn (Zǐsōng, Mó, paternal younger cousin Fù)
Zhōu Jùn, courtesy name Kāilín,
was a native of Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
His father, Péi, was the Shàofǔ Qīng.
Jùn was resolute and fierce by nature.
He was recognized for his talent and discernment
and had a keen eye for character.
His fellow townsman, Shǐ Yào, was originally of humble origins
and unknown to most.
Jùn alone befriended him
and subsequently married his sister to him.
Yào eventually became famous throughout the world.
Jùn initially did not answer the invitations from the province and commanderies,
but later served as Shàngshū Láng in Wèi.
He was successively promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
appointed Zhéchōng Jiāngjūn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shèyáng.
He followed Wáng Hún in attacking Wú,
breaking through the garrisons along the Jiāngxī,
and fought a major battle with Sūn Hào's central army,
beheading several thousand heads, including the spurious Chancellor Zhāng Tì,
and capturing tens of thousands.
He advanced his army and garrisoned at Héngjiāng.
At that time, it was heard that the Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Wáng Jùn had already broken through Shàngfāng.
The Biejia Hé Yùn advised Jùn, saying:
"Zhāng Tì led elite troops,
the entire force of Wú,
and they were annihilated here.
The court and common people of Wú are all shaken and terrified.
Now that Lóngxiáng Wáng has broken through Wǔchāng,
his military might is immense.
Following the current downstream,
he conquers wherever he goes.
The potential for total collapse is evident.
I secretly believe that we should swiftly cross the Jiāng
and head directly for Jiànyè.
When our large army arrives suddenly,
it will strip them of their courage,
and they can be captured without a fight."
Jùn approved of his plan
and immediately sent a report to Hún.
Yùn said:
"Hún is ignorant of military opportunities,
and desires to be cautious to avoid blame.
He will surely not follow my advice."
Jùn insisted on sending the report.
Hún indeed said:
"I received an imperial decree only to confront the Wú army north of the Jiāng,
not to advance lightly.
Although your prefecture is valorous,
how can it alone pacify Jiāngdōng!
If we disobey the order now,
victory is not worth much;
if we do not win,
the crime will be severe.
Moreover, the imperial decree states that Lóngxiáng should be subject to my command.
We only need to prepare our boats
and cross together at the same time."
Yùn said:
"Lóngxiáng conquered an enemy from thousands of miles away,
and comes with the merit of having already succeeded to receive orders –
I have never heard of such a thing.
Furthermore, the essence of wielding troops is that if it is opportune, seize it.
This is what is meant by 'receiving orders but not literal words.'
If we cross the Jiāng now, we will certainly achieve a complete victory.
What worries could there be?
To doubt success is not wisdom;
to know what to do but not act
cannot be called loyalty.
This is truly what causes regret among all in my humble prefecture."
Hún stubbornly refused to listen.
Not long after, Jùn arrived.
Hún summoned him, but he did not come.
Instead, he headed directly for Sānshān,
and Sūn Hào subsequently surrendered to Jùn.
Hún deeply resented this
and wished to dispute the credit with Jùn.
Yùn sent a memorial to Jùn, saying:
"Valuing humility and yielding is noble in writing,
and the 'Great Humility' hexagram of the Yì Jīng shines with light.
These are sung about in ancient texts and revered by Daoists.
Previously, we defeated Zhāng Tì,
and the Wú people lost their spirit.
Lóngxiáng capitalized on this
to conquer their territory.
Considering what happened before and after,
we indeed delayed our army.
Any action would cause harm,
and in terms of timing, we would be too late.
Yet now we are competing for merit.
If he does not swallow his pride,
it will diminish the great harmony
and foster the baseness of contention.
This is what my foolish sentiments reject."
Jùn received the memorial
and immediately advised Hún to desist.
Hún could not accept it,
so they mutually submitted memorials.
After Jùn had crossed the Jiāng,
he and Hún together toured the Wú city walls and ramparts,
soothing and pacifying the newly surrendered.
For his merits, he was promoted to Marquis of Chéngwǔ,
granted an estate of 6,000 households,
and bestowed 6,000 bolts of silk.
The following year,
he moved his garrison to Mòlíng.
At that time, Wú had just been pacified,
and there were frequent fugitives,
whom he repeatedly suppressed.
He treated the old and respected with courtesy,
and sought out talented individuals,
thus possessing great prestige and virtue.
The Wú people were pleased and submitted.
Initially,
before Wú was pacified,
Jùn was in Yìyáng.
The north and south traded with each other,
but many generals frequently attacked and plundered each other to gain merit.
The Wú general, Cài Mǐn, was defending Miǎnzhōng.
His elder brother, Guī, was a general in Mòlíng.
He wrote to Mǐn, saying:
“In ancient times, when armies clashed,
envoys were sent between them.
It is certainly proper for states and armies to uphold sincerity and righteousness to outdo each other.
However, I hear that along the borders,
there are frequent instances of raiding and plundering of mutual markets,
which is highly improper.
Brother, you must be careful not to forget the greater preparations for small gains.”
The scouts obtained Guī’s letter and presented it to Jùn.
Jùn said:
“He is a gentleman.”
When he crossed the Jiāng,
he sought out Guī
and found him.
He asked about his origin,
and Guī replied:
“I am from Rǔnán.”
Jùn joked, saying:
“I always suspected Wú had no gentlemen,
and you are indeed from my home region.”
He was promoted to Shìzhōng.
Emperor Wǔ asked Jùn:
“Among your clan’s younger generation,
who do you recommend?”
He replied:
“My uncle’s son, Huī,
is known as a weighty minister of the clan;
my cousin, Fù,
is known as a pure minister of the clan.”
The emperor summoned and employed them both.
Jùn was transferred to Shǎofǔ,
and concurrently held the position of Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
After the reconstruction of the ancestral temple was completed,
his enfeoffment was increased by five hundred households.
Later, he succeeded Wáng Hún as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
and died in office.
He had three sons: Yǐ, Sōng, and Mó.
Yǐ inherited the peerage;
there is a separate biography for him.
Sōng, courtesy name Zhòngzhì,
was blunt, upright, resolute, and chivalrous.
He often showed contempt for others with his talent and spirit.
When Emperor Yuán served as Chancellor,
he appointed him Cānjūn.
When the emperor became Jìn Wáng,
he was again appointed Fèngcháoqǐng.
Sōng submitted a memorial, saying:
“I have heard that those who seize the empire
always do so when there are no troubles.
When troubles arise,
it is not enough to seize the empire.
Therefore, the ancient kings
would always respond to heaven and conform to the times,
taking power only after righteousness was complete,
and gaining it only after yielding was perfected.
Thus, their reigns were long-lasting,
and their glory shone for myriad generations.
Now, some counselors believe that Your Highness’s influence flows through the Jiāng and Hàn,
your benevolence covers the six prefectures,
and your achievements benefit the common people,
and thus wish to elevate your honorable title.
I submit that at present, the imperial coffin has not yet returned,
the old capital has not yet been cleared;
righteous men weep blood,
and men and women are trembling.
It is fitting to deeply understand the Way of Duke Zhōu,
first cleanse the great shame of the altars of soil and grain,
exhaust the assistance of loyal words and excellent schemes,
and in due time achieve the merits of great benevolence,
exalting the virtue of humility,
and demonstrating the sincerity of putting oneself last.
Then, yielding with bows and apologies to the world,
who would dare not respond,
who would dare not obey!”
Because of this, he displeased the emperor
and was sent out as the Administrator of Xīn'ān.
Sōng was resentful and unhappy.
Just before his departure,
he was with Sǎnqíláng Zhāng Ní at the residence of Shìzhōng Dài Miǎo.
He criticized and praised court officials,
and also slandered Miǎo.
Miǎo secretly reported him.
The emperor summoned Sōng
and reproached him face-to-face, saying:
“You are arrogant and haughty,
daring to slight the imperial court.
This is because of my lack of virtue!”
Sōng knelt and apologized, saying:
“In ancient times, Táng and Yú were supremely sagely,
yet the Four Villains were at court.
Although Your Majesty governs the world with sagely wisdom,
how can you be without incompetent ministers?”
The emperor was enraged
and had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi.
Tíngwèi Huá ruled that Sōng should be executed in the marketplace for gross disrespect,
while Ní’s crime was reduced to dismissal from office for inciting discord.
At that time, Yǐ was highly esteemed,
so the emperor suppressed his anger.
After a long time,
Sōng was appointed Administrator of Lúlíng,
but he did not take up the post
and was instead appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
At this time, the emperor, seeing Wáng Dūn’s growing power,
gradually alienated and became wary of Wáng Dǎo and others.
Sōng submitted a memorial, saying: “I have heard that enlightened rulers seek to promote their Way,
therefore wise and sagely scholars are happy to serve in their court;
loyal ministers will demonstrate their integrity,
therefore they assess the times before taking office.
Being happy to serve
in their court,
there is no criticism of over-appointment;
intending to demonstrate their integrity,
there is no slander of over-favoritism.
Thus, both ruler and minister prosper,
and their achievements reach heaven and earth.
In recent times,
however,
virtue has declined and the Way has waned.
Rulers harbor stratagems to control ministers,
and ministers employ self-interest to serve rulers.
When rulers and ministers mutually seek gain, calamities and chaos follow one after another.
Therefore, the traces of gains and losses are difficult to
explain in detail.
I beg to clarify and distinguish them.
Indeed, Fù Yuè’s assistance to Gāozōng,
Shēn Zhǎo’s aid to Xuānwáng,
Guǎn Zhòng’s support for Qí Huán,
and Suī Fàn’s help for Jìn Wén—
some of them were revered as masters of the Way,
receiving
with folded hands what was achieved,
and entrusted with great power.
Ultimately, they helped their rulers to rectify the state.
There has never been a case where they were worried about being encroached upon,
and thus became a menace to the state.
When the Tián clan initially usurped Qí,
and Wáng Mǎng usurped
Hàn,
they all relied on the strength of their enfeoffments,
presumed upon generations of imperial favor,
exploited weak and dim-witted rulers,
utilized the power of empress dowagers,
established factions of cronies,
and built up a momentum for utter destruction.
Only then were they able to carry out their private schemes
and bring about the disaster of usurpation.
How could they, when encountering a ruler capable of great achievements,
one chosen by heaven and men,
be able to carry out their wicked plans
to
achieve their rebellious aims?
Guāngwǔ, as a member of the imperial clan, rose from the common folk,
seizing the opportune moment,
gathering heroes and extraordinary talents,
and thus restored the Hàn dynasty,
magnifying the merits of the
restoration.
After the empire was settled,
why did he somewhat dismiss and demote meritorious officials?
Because military men do not understand the national system;
though they achieved temporary merits,
they cannot be long entrusted
with power and authority.
The matter of their rise and fall
can thus be seen.
In recent times, the Three Kingdoms stood in rivalry,
all with heroic strategies and talents,
and abilities that shaped their age.
They all entrusted themselves to outstanding
wise men,
eventually achieving their great enterprises
and passing them on to their descendants,
without any faults or regrets left for future generations.
Now, Wáng Dǎo, Wáng Yì, and others,
compared to the former sages,
still fall somewhat short.
However, in terms of unreserved loyalty and utmost sincerity,
and assisting the emperor with righteousness,
collectively promoting the grand foundation
and aiding in the completion of
the great enterprise,
they are indeed like Zhūgé Liàng of old.
Although Your Majesty possesses the virtue of successive generations,
has met with the convergence of heaven and man,
occupies the territory east of the Jiāng,
and possesses the extreme south,
rising like a dragon by the sea,
Restoring old things
is also due to the wisdom of many talented individuals,
how could it be solely Your Majesty's power?
Now, although the imperial enterprise is established,
the Jié bandits are not yet suppressed.
The world is in turmoil,
and those who are not
submissive are numerous.
Both public and private sectors are exhausted,
granaries are not yet full,
the imperial coffin lies neglected,
and the empress and consorts have not returned.
This is precisely the day to rely on the virtuous, appoint the capable, and offer support.
With great achievements about to be made,
and the Jìn dynasty flourishing,
to suddenly listen to the words of isolated ministers,
and be confused by specious arguments,
thereby mistaking danger for safety,
and exchanging distant for close,
banishing old virtues,
and allowing sycophants to
rank among the worthy –
this will gravely diminish past wisdom,
and harm the relationship between Yī and Guǎn,
topple a majestic reputation,
and lose mountain-like accomplishments.
This will cause the wise and intelligent to close their hearts,
and righteous gentlemen to lose
their will,
bringing immediate trouble to the present,
and leaving a laugh for future generations.
Indeed, safety and danger lie in decrees,
survival and demise lie in entrusted responsibilities.
Judging the present by the past,
how can one not feel a chill
in the heart and sigh in sorrow!
My brothers and I have received favors,
without any sense of partiality.
Why then do I dare to violate current taboos
and offend the imperial presence? It is truly out of concern for the nation,
wishing to repay
Your Majesty.
Ancient enlightened kings
desired to hear of their faults,
and awakened to the words of passers-by,
to understand the reasons for success and failure.
Thus, they adopted foolish advice,
to examine truth
and falsehood,
making endless plans for the ancestral temples above,
and gathering the lives of billions of common people below.
Unable to bear my sorrow and indignation,
I exhaust my foolishness in presenting this.
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor was moved and enlightened,
and thus Dǎo and others were spared.
Wáng Dūn, after harming Yǐ, sent someone to console Sōng.
Sōng said:
"My late brother was a man of the world,
killed by men of the world.
What is there to console?"
Dūn deeply resented this,
but feared losing popular support,
so he did not harm him,
and appointed him as an attendant official.
Sōng was
the father of Wáng Yīng's sister-in-law.
Because Yǐ had met with sudden disaster,
he was indignant,
and once said in public:
"Yīng is not fit to command troops."
Dūn secretly sent the sorcerer Lǐ Tuō to falsely accuse Sōng and Zhōu Yán of secretly appointing each other,
and then executed them.
Sōng was devoted to Buddhism,
and even recited scriptures in the marketplace at the time of his execution.
Mó, due to Yǐ,
frequently held prominent positions.
After Wáng Dūn's death,
an imperial edict posthumously honored Dài Ruòsī and Qiáo Wáng Chéng, etc.,
but did not yet include Yǐ.
At that time, Mó was General of the Rear Army,
and he submitted a memorial stating: My late brother Yǐ,
formerly received the favor of the late emperor's attention,
who specifically issued a decree
to include him as a military assistant,
prominently placed among the high-ranking officials,
and he consequently managed court affairs,
together with the various
empresses, jointly promoting the restoration.
He then presided over the selection bureau,
again received generous appointment,
and held the humble position of grand tutor,
being allowed to bow and exchange greetings as equals with Your Majesty.
The grace bestowed was especially profound.
Furthermore, our humble
clan formed a marriage alliance with the imperial house,
deepening our righteous bond and important responsibilities.
We wished to exert ourselves fully
to repay what we had received.
He was resented by the traitorous rebels,
who hated integrity and loathed righteousness.
Though he fell into extreme misfortune,
his loyalty did not
forget his sovereign;
he upheld the good Way unto death,
perishing without wavering.
When Yǐ passed away,
who did not feel heartache?
How much more so for me, his blood brother,
who cannot but be overwhelmed with sorrow!
Wáng Dūn's disloyalty
had long been a reality.
The severity of his wickedness
is unparalleled in ancient and modern times.
Fortunately, with Your Majesty's sagely wisdom and divine martial prowess,
you were able to crush the fierce and strong,
restore order from chaos,
and bring peace to the realm.
During the previous military campaign,
Your sacred grace did not forget,
and took Yǐ's son Mǐn,
allowing him to serve as a close attendant.
At that time, I personally requested,
wishing to let
Mǐn return and inherit the marquisate of my late father.
At that time, Biàn Hú and Yǔ Liàng were both attending Your Majesty,
and Hú said:
"When this matter is resolved, a prominent posthumous honor should be discussed."
Not much time has passed since then,
and the words are still
in my ears.
As for Qiáo Wáng Chéng and Gān Zhuó,
they have already received posthumous rehabilitation,
and even Wáng Chéng, whose case is much older,
is still being discussed.
How much more so Yǐ, who was loyal in defending his lord,
and died in the service of the state!
Even Jī Shào, who did not shun danger,
how could he surpass this!
Yet to this day, I have heard no mention of restoring his enfeoffment, adding posthumous honors, or commendation.
I do not know if Yǐ had some remaining fault,
and alone failed to receive special grace,
or if the court is too preoccupied with current affairs
to discuss it? This is why I feel heartache and severe distress,
and once again sigh in sorrow.
Unable to bear my grief,
I venture to present my humble
feelings.
When the memorial was submitted,
there was no response.
Mó submitted another memorial,
and only then were posthumous official titles granted to Yǐ.
Mó served successively as Shao Fǔ, Dān Yáng Yǐn, Shì Zhōng, and Zhōng Hù Jūn,
and was enfeoffed as Xī Píng Hóu.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Jīn Zǐ Guāng Lù Dà Fū,
and his posthumous name was Zhēn.
Fù, courtesy name Zǔxuān,
was Jùn's paternal cousin.
His father, Ruí,
was Administrator of Ān Píng.
When young, Fù was renowned alongside his friend Chéng Gōngjiǎn,
both initially serving as literary attendants to various princes,
and successively promoted to Zuǒ Xī Shǔ of the Sī Tú.
Sī Tú Wáng Hún memorialized:
"Fù's understanding and judgment are pure and upright,
and he possesses talent and capability.
He presided over the establishment of the nine-rank system,
and his inspections were precise and detailed.
I entrusted him with responsibility,
and his commendations and criticisms were appropriate.
I request that he be appointed as a Shàngshū Láng."
This was granted.
He was gradually promoted to Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ of the Sī Tú, and Lì Bù Láng.
His selections were meticulous,
and his reputation grew finer.
He was transferred to Yù Shǐ Zhōng Chéng, Shì Zhōng,
appointed as Governor of Xú Zhōu,
and given the additional titles of Guàn Jūn Jiāng Jūn and Jiǎ Jié.
He was summoned to serve as Tíng Wèi.
Huìdì幸 Yè,
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng assigned Fù to serve as Hénán Yǐn.
Chén Zhěn, Shàngguān Sì and others enthroned Qīnghé Wáng Tán as Crown Prince.
They further appointed Fù as Wèi Jiāngjūn and Lù Shàngshū,
but Fù declined the appointments.
Tán ordered Fù to combine forces with Shàngguān Sì.
Fù believed that Sì was a petty person, violent and unrestrained,
who would ultimately become a national menace.
Therefore, he conspired with Sīlì Mǎn Fèn and others to eliminate him.
The plot was leaked,
and they were attacked by Sì.
Fèn was killed,
but Fù managed to escape.
When Sì was defeated by Zhāng Fāng,
Fù was recalled to temporarily administer Hénán Yǐn.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè welcomed the emperor’s entourage,
he appointed Fù as Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
Before he could take up the post,
he was transferred to Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and given the additional titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Jiǎjié,
with authority to oversee all military affairs at Miǎnchí.
When the emperor returned to the palace,
Fù was sent out as Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and Dudū Yángzhōu Zhū Jūnshì,
replacing Liú Zhǔn as Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn.
He collaborated with Zhōu Qǐ and others to suppress Chén Mǐn,
and eradicated him.
For this achievement, he was enfeoffed as Yǒngníng Bó.
Having experienced many political upheavals,
Fù always wished to rectify the imperial court,
with sincere and earnest loyalty.
Because Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè did not fully observe the duties of a minister,
Fù’s criticisms were always severe,
and Yuè greatly feared him.
Observing the widespread proliferation of bandits
and the precarious situation of Luòyáng,
Fù proposed a plan to welcome the Son of Heaven and move the capital to Shòuchūn.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiā,
he submitted a memorial with his Chángshǐ Wú Sī and Sīmǎ Yīn Shí, stating:
“We never expected the dire fate to reach such a point!
Barbarians are invading from all sides,
and the imperial domain is in grave danger.
Your ministers, together with Zǔ Nà, Péi Xiàn, Huá Tán, Sūn Huì, and thirty others, have humbly considered the great strategy.
All agree that the Yīn people repeatedly relocated,
and King Zhōu moved to Qíshān.
Currently, the royal capital is utterly depleted
and cannot be long maintained.
Héshuò is desolate,
Xiáohán is rugged and difficult,
Wǎndū has been repeatedly defeated,
and Jiānghàn is fraught with danger.
For now, the east and south
are the most stable.
The region of Huái-Yáng
is blocked to the north by Túshān,
and guarded to the south by Língyuè.
It is surrounded by famous rivers,
possessing natural strongholds.
This is why the people of Chǔ moved east,
eventually settling in Shòuchūn.
Xú, Pī, and Dōnghǎi
are also sufficient for defense.
Furthermore, water transport routes are accessible in all directions,
so there is no fear of scarcity.
Although Your Majesty is divinely intelligent
and your chief ministers are wise and brilliant,
living frugally and adhering to restraint,
this is merely to preserve the ancestral temples.
It is not as good as Xiàng Tǔ relocating the capital
to ensure eternal prosperity.
Your ministers have carefully selected thirty thousand elite soldiers
to respectfully welcome the imperial carriage.
We have already issued a summons to the former Běizhōngláng Jiāng Péi Xiàn to act as Shǐchíjié, Supervisor of military affairs in Yùzhōu, and Dōngzhōngláng Jiāng,
to rush to the road.
Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Yáng are each ordered to first transport 150,000 hú of rice tax and
140,000 bolts of cloth and silk for four years,
to supply the imperial entourage.
Let Wáng Jùn and Gǒu Xī jointly pacify Héshuò,
while your ministers exert our efforts to open the southern route.
Relocating the capital and suppressing the bandits,
both plans will succeed.
When the imperial carriage moves,
your minister should transfer to Jiāngzhōu
to expand the royal strategy.
To do everything one knows without reserve
is what the ancients strived for.
We dare to exhaust our loyalty
in hopes of repaying a millionth part.
Even if we should perish in the evening after achieving this in the morning,
it would still be our wish in life.”
Yuè and Gǒu Xī were not on good terms,
and Fù did not report to Yuè beforehand,
but directly submitted the memorial.
Yuè was furious.
Earlier,
Yuè had summoned Fù and Huáinán Tàishǒu Péi Shuò.
Fù refused to go,
and instead ordered Shuò to lead troops forward.
Shuò, disloyal to Fù,
then raised an army, claiming Fù had acted presumptuously,
and that he had received Yuè’s secret decree to eliminate Fù.
He then attacked Fù,
but was defeated by Fù.
Shuò retreated to defend Dōngchéng
and sought help from Yuándì.
The emperor dispatched Yángwēi Jiāngjūn Gān Zhuó and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Guō Yì to attack Fù at Shòuchūn.
Ānfēng Tàishǒu Sūn Huì led his forces to respond,
and sent Xiè Chī to write a declaration.
Chī
was a former general of Fù.
When Fù saw the declaration,
he shed tears and said:
“This must be Xiè Chī’s writing.”
When Chī heard this,
he immediately destroyed the draft.
Within ten days, Fù’s army disintegrated,
and he fled to Xiàng,
where he was detained by Xīncài Wáng Què.
He died of illness from grief and indignation.
Initially,
when Huá Tán lost Lújiāng,
he went to Shòuchūn to rely on Fù.
When Fù’s army was defeated,
he returned to Yuándì.
The emperor asked:
“How did Zhōu Zǔxuān come to rebel?”
Tán replied:
“Although Zhōu Fù is dead,
there are still upright speakers in the world.
Fù saw the spread of bandits and rebels
and the waning of imperial prestige,
so he wished to move the capital to alleviate the national crisis.
Because the regional commanders disagreed,
it led to his downfall.
Not even a season passed,
and the imperial capital fell.
If Fù’s plan had been followed,
perhaps its destruction could have been delayed.
Considering his true intentions and seeking the facts,
how can he be called a rebel!”
The emperor said:
“Fù held the rank of a commanding general,
wielding military power in a region.
He was summoned but did not come,
and when the country was in danger, he did not uphold it.
He is also a sinner of the world.”
Tán said:
“Indeed.
Fù served in the central court with distinction
and was known for his outstanding talents.
He was dispatched to govern a vital region,
bearing indeed the heavy responsibility of a regional command.
However, his grand strategy was not implemented,
and he often lost harmony.
When the country was in danger, he did not uphold it.
He should share the blame with the world.
However, to call him a rebel,
is that not a slander!”
The emperor’s anger began to subside.
Fù had two sons: Mì and Jiǎo.
Mì, courtesy name Tàixuán,
was simple and unpretentious by nature.
People of his time called him a pure scholar.
He rose to the position of Shàngshū Láng.
Jiǎo, courtesy name Zhèngxuán,
also possessed talent and ability.
Chéng Gōngjiǎn
Chéng Gōngjiǎn, courtesy name Zōngshū,
was from Dōngjùn.
His family had for generations held positions of two thousand piculs.
He was simple and unadorned by nature,
not seeking fame or profit.
He devoted himself to the Way,
and nothing could sway his ambition.
His memory surpassed others.
Zhāng Màoxiān often said:
“Jiǎn’s tranquility is comparable to Yáng Zǐyún,
and his memory to Zhāng Ānshì.”
Later, he became Zhōngshū Láng.
At that time, Fù was already Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and had been promoted to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn.
Jiǎn, feeling that his talent was superior yet he was beneath Fù,
said to Fù:
“Yáng Xióng served as a Láng [official],
unchanged for three generations,
while Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Xián held positions among the Three Excellencies.
The past and present are but one measure.”
Fù was deeply ashamed by this.
His official positions reached Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Sànqí Chángshì.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
he fled to Gǒu Xī
and perished with Xī.
Gǒu Xī
Gǒu Xī (苟晞), courtesy name Dàojiāng (道將),
was a native of Shānyáng (山陽) in Hénèi (河內).
In his youth, he served as a subordinate official (從事) in the Sīlì (司隸) department.
The commandant Shí Jiàn (石鑒) deeply admired him.
When the Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王) Yuè (越) became a palace attendant (侍中),
he appointed Xī as a secretariat clerk (通事令史),
and he was successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Yángpíng (陽平太守).
When the Prince of Qí (齊王) Jiǒng (冏) assisted in governing,
Xī participated in Jiǒng's military affairs
and was appointed Assistant Director of the Right (尚書右丞);
he was then transferred to Assistant Director of the Left (左丞).
He rigorously investigated the various bureaus,
and all officials from the "Eight Seats" (八坐) downward looked askance at him and feared him.
When Jiǒng was executed,
Xī was also dismissed due to his involvement.
The Prince of Chángshā (長沙王) Yì (乂) became General of Cavalry (驃騎將軍),
and appointed Xī as his Staff Officer (從事中郎).
When Emperor Huì (惠帝) campaigned against the Prince of Chéngdū (成都王) Yǐng (穎),
he made Xī the Commandant of the Northern Army (北軍中候).
When the Emperor returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
Xī fled to the Prince of Fànyáng (范陽王) Xiāo (虓),
who, acting on imperial authority, employed Xī as acting Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州刺史).
When Jí Sāng (汲桑) crushed Yè (鄴),
the Prince of Dōnghǎi Yuè stationed his troops at Guāndù (官渡) to suppress him,
ordering Xī to be the vanguard.
Sāng had always feared him,
so he built palisades outside the city to defend himself.
When Xī was about to arrive,
he halted his army to let his soldiers rest,
first sending a lone rider to explain the consequences of their actions.
Sāng's forces were greatly shaken,
abandoned their palisades, and fled during the night,
then fortified themselves within the city walls.
Xī breached their nine encampments,
then pacified Yè and returned.
He then campaigned west to suppress Lǚ Láng (呂朗) and others,
and annihilated them.
Later, the Prince of Gāomì (高密王) Tài (泰) attacked the Qīngzhōu (青州) bandit Liú Gēn (劉根),
defeated Jí Sāng's former general Gōng Shīfān (公師藩),
and routed Shí Lè (石勒) north of the Yellow River.
His fame and power became immense,
and people at the time compared him to Hán Xìn (韓信) and Bái Qǐ (白起).
He was promoted to General of the Army Protecting the State (撫軍將軍), given the symbol of authority (假節), and made Chief Controller of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu (青州) and Yǎnzhōu (兗州) (都督青兗諸軍事).
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngpíng (東平郡侯),
with ten thousand households.
Xī was proficient in official duties;
documents accumulated,
but he made decisions like flowing water,
and no one dared to deceive him.
His maternal cousin relied on him,
and he provided for her very generously.
Her son asked to be a general.
Xī refused, saying:
"I do not leniently apply the royal law to people.
Will you not regret it?"
The son insisted,
so Xī made him a督護 (Dūhù, Inspector-Protector).
Later, he broke the law.
Xī, holding the imperial staff of authority, executed him.
His maternal cousin kowtowed, begging for his life,
but Xī did not listen.
Afterward, he wore plain clothes and wept for him,
shedding tears and saying:
"The one who killed you was the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu;
the one who weeps for his younger brother is Gǒu Dàojiāng."
Such was his adherence to the law.
Xī saw that the court administration was becoming increasingly chaotic
and feared disaster would befall him.
He formed many connections;
whenever he obtained precious objects,
he immediately presented them to influential nobles in the capital.
Yǎnzhōu was five hundred *lǐ* (里) from Luòyáng.
Fearing the gifts might not be fresh,
he recruited swift oxen that could travel a thousand *lǐ* (里) a day,
so whenever he sent a messenger,
they would depart in the morning and return in the evening.
Initially,
the Prince of Dōnghǎi Yuè, seeing that Xī had avenged his humiliation,
was very grateful to him.
He invited him up to the hall
and they became sworn brothers.
Yuè's Marshal (Sīmǎ) Pān Tāo (潘滔) and others advised him, saying:
"Yǎnzhōu is a strategic thoroughfare;
Wèi Wǔ (魏武) used it to assist the Hàn (漢) imperial house.
Gǒu Xī has great ambitions and is not a pure subject.
If he is allowed to remain there for long,
trouble will arise in our heartland.
If he is transferred to Qīngzhōu,
and his titles are enhanced,
Xī will surely be pleased.
You yourself can govern Yǎnzhōu,
manage the entire realm,
and protect the imperial court.
This is what is called 'planning before it exists,
and acting before it is chaotic.'"
Yuè thought this was correct,
so he transferred Xī to General Who Conquers the East (征東大將軍), granting him the privilege of establishing a government (開府儀同三司),
adding the title of Palace Attendant (侍中), granting him the symbol of authority (假節), and making him Chief Controller of all military affairs in Qīngzhōu (都督青州諸軍事).
He was also appointed Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州刺史),
and advanced to Duke of a Commandery (郡公).
Xī then appointed many subordinates
and frequently replaced prefects and magistrates,
establishing his merit through severity and harshness.
Daily, executions increased,
and blood flowed like a river.
People could not endure their lives,
and he was called
"the Butcher."
The Grand Administrator of Dūnqiū (頓丘), Wèi Zhí (魏植), was pressured by displaced people,
who numbered fifty to sixty thousand,
and they extensively plundered Yǎnzhōu.
Xī moved his garrison to Wúyán (無鹽),
appointing his younger brother Chún (純) to govern Qīngzhōu.
Chún's punishments and killings were even more severe than Xī's.
The common people called him
"Little Gǒu (苟) is crueler than Big Gǒu (苟)."
Xī soon defeated Zhí.
At this time, Pān Tāo and Minister (尚書) Liú Wàng (劉望) and others jointly slandered and framed Xī.
Xī was enraged,
and memorialized the throne, requesting the heads of Tāo and others.
He also asked Yuè to appoint his Staff Officer Liú Qià (劉洽) as Army Advisor (軍司).
Yuè refused all these requests.
Xī then openly declared:
"Sīmǎ Yuánchāo (司馬元超) [referring to Yuè] is unjust as a chancellor,
causing chaos throughout the realm.
How can Gǒu Dàojiāng be made to act unjustly?
Hán Xìn (韓信) could not endure the kindness of food and clothing,
and died at the hands of a woman.
Now, I will execute the national traitors
and honor the imperial house.
How can Huán (桓) and Wén (文) be far away!"
He then issued a proclamation to the various provinces,
detailing his achievements
and listing Yuè's crimes.
At that time, Huái Dì detested Yuè's monopolization of power.
He then issued an edict to Xī, saying:
"As I am without virtue,
military campaigns have frequently arisen.
Above, I fear the burden on the ancestral temples,
below, I pity the distress of the myriad common people.
I ought to rely on the regional governors [fāngyuè]
to be the nation's bulwark and support.
Your Excellency's might is awe-inspiring and resounding.
You have slain Fān and Sāng,
routed and forced the surrender of Qiáo and Lǎng.
The likes of Wèi Zhí have also been executed and eliminated.
Is this not due to your profound insight and clear judgment?
I therefore entrust you with this task.
Furthermore, Wáng Mí and Shí Lè pose a threat to the state,
hence the edict entrusting you with command of the six provinces [liùzhōu].
Yet, Your Excellency, out of excessive humility over minor matters,
has delayed in obeying the great command.
This is not what it means to share the nation's sorrow.
Now I again dispatch an edict;
you shall immediately issue a proclamation to the six provinces,
collaborate in a grand undertaking,
eliminate the national calamity,
and fulfill my intent."
Xī then transferred orders to the various garrisons, provinces, and commanderies, saying:
"The Heavenly course is perilous,
disasters and calamities flow abundantly.
Liú Yuánhǎi rebelled at Fén'yīn;
Shí Shìlóng initiated chaos in the Three Wèi.
They have plundered the imperial domain,
devastated Yè Dū,
built encampments near the capital,
and continue to shake Yǎn and Yù.
They harmed three regional inspectors [cìshǐ],
killed two commandants [dūdū],
and dozens of commandery administrators [jùnshǒu] and officials [guānzhǎng]
have been submerged and lost.
The common people are scattered and wandering,
their brains and guts staining the ground.
I, Xī, being weak and insignificant,
bear the heavy burden of the state.
Therefore, I have brought my forces to the coastal regions,
and raised the drumsticks at Cáo and Wèi.
Unexpectedly, I received an imperial edict [zhōngzhào],
entrusting me with Guāndōng,
to supervise all armies.
I reverently obey the imperial decree.
It was decided that on the second day of this month,
I should head west to relieve Líyáng.
On the same day, I received a report from the Administrator of Xíngyáng, Dīng Yí,
stating that Lǐ Yùn, Chén Wǔ, and others, leading troops to relieve Huái, engaged the Jié in a great battle,
and were all broken and scattered.
Huái City has already fallen,
and Péi Zhěng, the Administrator of Hénèi, was captured by the bandits.
The palace guard is depleted,
the Son of Heaven is in distress,
and the danger to the ancestral temples [zōngmiào]
is greater than piled eggs.
On the day I heard this news,
I sighed repeatedly with sorrow.
Xī believes that the former kings selected and established enlightened virtues,
and employed them with proper attire [fúzhāng],
so as to strengthen the royal house,
and prevent the city from falling.
Thus, when the boat was not firm,
Qí Huán held Chǔ accountable;
when Xiāng Wáng was pressed by the Dí,
Jìn Wén launched an expedition.
Indeed, to assist the imperial family [huángjiā]
and exert one's strength for the court,
even if it means falling into boiling water or fire,
is a great principle one should embrace.
Moreover, all regional governors [fāngmù]
have received honor and favor;
it is their shared duty to exert their utmost strength
to repay the nation's grace.
Though I, Xī, am not valorous,
I shall be the first to initiate military action.
My horses are fed and fodder packed,
awaiting the regional commanders [fāngzhèn].
All who are allied with me
should hasten together to the rescue.
To establish a glorious name and integrity [míngjié]
lies in this action."
Coincidentally, Wáng Mí dispatched Cáo Yí to conquer Lángyá,
then attack Qí from the north.
Gǒu Chún defended the city,
and Yí's forces grew stronger,
their camps stretching for dozens of *lǐ*.
When Xī returned,
he ascended the city wall to observe them,
showing fear.
He repeatedly engaged the bandits in battle,
always defeating them.
Later, he selected elite troops [jīngruì]
and fought a great battle with the bandits.
A strong wind raised dust,
and Xī was utterly defeated,
abandoning the city and fleeing by night.
Yí pursued him to Dōngshān,
and Xī's troops all surrendered to Yí.
Xī fled alone on horseback to Gāopíng,
collected supplies,
and managed to recruit several thousand men.
The Emperor again secretly ordered Xī to attack Yuè.
Xī again submitted a memorial, saying:
"When the Palace Colonel [diànzhōng xiàowèi] Lǐ Chū arrived,
bringing the imperial handwritten edict [shǒuzhào],
my heart and liver felt as though they would burst.
Wáng Yuè, Prince of Dōnghǎi, relying on his status as an imperial kinsman [zōngchén], seized control of the court,
appointed wicked and sycophantic individuals,
and favored treacherous factions.
This led to his former Chief Clerk [chángshǐ] Pān Tāo, Attending Cavalier [cóngshì zhōngláng] Bì Miáo, and Chief Clerk [zhǔbù] Guō Xiàng, among others, manipulating imperial authority,
with rewards and punishments determined by themselves.
The Minister of Personnel [shàngshū] Hé Suí, Central Secretariat Director [zhōngshūlìng] Miáo Bō, Grand Coachman [tàipú] Miáo Yìn, and Palace Attendant [huángmén shìláng] Yīng Shào,
were all personally selected and promoted by Your Majesty's sacred edict.
Yet, Tāo and the others falsely framed them,
leading them to severe punishment.
They brought armored troops to the palace,
executed the Empress's younger brother,
eliminated the palace guards,
and privately installed their own men.
They promoted and praised Wèi Zhí,
enticed fugitives,
and brought ruin to provinces and commanderies.
The royal roads are impassable,
regional tributes are disrupted,
the ancestral temples lack the offerings of steamed food and sacrifice,
and Your Majesty suffers from the scarcity of meager meals.
General Who Guards the East [zhèndōng jiāngjūn] Zhōu Fù, Provincial Inspector of Yùzhōu [yùzhōu cìshǐ] Féng Sōng, and former Colonel of the Northern Army [běizhōng lángjiāng] Péi Xiàn,
all recognized the emptiness of the imperial court,
and the monopolistic power of corrupt officials.
Fearing that difficulties would arise
at any moment, they each led their soldiers and horses
to escort the imperial carriage,
desiring to glorify the royal house,
and fulfill their duties as subjects.
However, Tāo, Miáo, and others coerced Yuè to leave the pass,
falsely established a temporary administrative office [xíngtái],
forced the high officials [gōngqīng] to relocate,
usurped the power to issue edicts,
unleashed their troops to plunder,
and devoured the inhabitants.
Corpses blocked the roads,
and bleached bones filled the fields.
This caused regional commanders [fāngzhèn] to lose their positions,
cities and towns to become desolate,
and the people of Huái and Yù
to fall into misery.
Although I am indignant,
I have remained in my position in the eastern corner.
Since receiving the clear edict,
my three armies are invigorated,
they have rolled up their armor and marched swiftly,
reaching Cāngyuán.
On the same day, I received a letter from Sīkōng, the Duke of Bólíng, Jùn,
stating that the Palace Attendant [diànzhōng zhōngláng] Liú Quán brought an edict,
instructing Jùn and me to collaborate in launching a great campaign.
I immediately dispatched the vanguard General Who Conquers the Barbarians [zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn] Wáng Zàn directly to Xiàngchéng,
to make Yuè bow his head and return power to the court,
and send Tāo and others for execution.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will show leniency to the imperial kinsmen [zōngchén],
and permit Yuè to return to the capital.
As for those who were forced,
they should receive broad pardon.
I have already copied the edict and proclaimed it to the regional commanders,
to clearly demonstrate the righteous cause.
I have dispatched General Who Displays Valor [yángliè jiāngjūn] Yán Hóng with five thousand cavalry and infantry,
to guard the ancestral temples."
Five years later,
the Emperor again issued an edict to Xī, saying:
"The Grand Tutor relies on treacherous sycophants,
hoards troops, and usurps power.
Internally, he does not obey the imperial decrees;
externally, he does not cooperate with the provincial governors.
Consequently, the barbarians run rampant,
committing atrocities everywhere.
The troops under Hé Lún plunder palaces and temples,
rob princesses,
kill worthy scholars,
and bring chaos to the world.
This is unbearable to hear.
Although they are close relatives,
the Nine Punishments should be clearly applied.
On the day this edict arrives,
you are to proclaim it to the world,
mobilize all forces for a grand expedition.
The achievements of Huán and Wén
are entirely entrusted to you, Duke.
Please consider all suitable measures
and adeptly formulate grand strategies.
The road is difficult,
so a duplicate has been prepared,
and my handwriting indicates its authenticity."
Xī memorialized, saying:
"I have received your handwritten edict,
entrusting me, your subject, with the punitive expedition,
likening me to Huán and Wén,
with both paper and silk copies available.
I prostrate myself in awe upon reading it,
my five emotions filled with trepidation.
For some time, the prime ministers have exercised autocratic power,
relying on wicked sycophants.
Internally, they usurped court authority;
externally, they brought ruin upon the myriad people.
They forged edicts to launch expeditions,
then plotted rebellion,
allowing their soldiers to plunder,
trampling upon palaces and temples.
Former Sīlì Xiàowèi Liú Tūn, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Wēn Jī, and Yòu Jiāngjūn Dù Yù
were all attacked and robbed.
The princesses of Guǎngpíng and Wǔ'ān,
the Emperor's late father's children,
were all humiliated.
Such rebellious and tyrannical chaos
has never been worse.
I shall respectfully obey the previous edict,
deploying all armies,
and dispatch Wáng Zàn leading Chén Wǔ and others with troops to Xiàng,
to carry out the Heavenly Punishment."
Initially,
Yuè suspected that Xī and the Emperor were conspiring.
He sent cavalry patrols between Chénggāo,
who captured Xī's envoy,
and indeed found the imperial edict and court letters,
thus greatly escalating the suspicion and rift.
Yuè moved to govern Yùzhōu to suppress Xī,
and again issued a proclamation detailing Xī's crimes,
sending Cóngshì Zhōngláng Yáng Mào to Yǎnzhōu
to jointly attack Xī with Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Dùn.
Xī sent cavalry to arrest Hénán Yǐn Pān Tāo,
but Tāo fled by night.
He then seized Shàngshū Liú Zēng and Shìzhōng Chéng Yán,
and executed them.
Coincidentally, Yuè died,
and Dùn was defeated.
The Emperor issued an edict appointing Xī as Dà Jiāngjūn Dà Dūdū, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì of the six provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, Yáng,
increasing his stipend by two thousand households,
adding the yellow yue battle-axe,
with his previous official positions remaining unchanged.
As the capital suffered increasing famine
and a convergence of difficulties,
Xī memorialized requesting a relocation of the capital,
and dispatched Cóngshì Zhōngláng Liú Huì with dozens of boats
and five hundred imperial guards
to offer a thousand *hú* of grain to welcome the Emperor.
Many court officials held differing opinions.
Soon after, the capital fell,
and Xī and Wáng Zàn garrisoned Cāngyuán.
The Prince of Yùzhāng, Duān, and Hé Yù and others fled east to Xī.
Xī, leading the officials, honored Duān as the Imperial Crown Prince,
and established a provisional government (xíngtái).
Duān, acting on imperial authority, appointed Xī as Tàizǐ Tàifù, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūn, and Lù Shàngshū.
They moved from Cāngyuán to garrison Méngchéng,
while Zàn garrisoned Yángxià.
Xī, having risen from humble origins
to the position of supreme general,
became rather arrogant and complacent.
He had nearly a thousand servants and slaves,
and dozens of concubines,
spending days and nights without leaving his inner chambers.
His administration was harsh and cruel,
and he indulged his desires without restraint.
Yán Hēng of Liáoxī earnestly admonished him in a letter,
but Xī was enraged
and killed him.
Xī's Cóngshì Zhōngláng Míng Yù, who was ill at home,
heard of this,
and, carried in a litter despite his illness, admonished Xī, saying:
"The Imperial Jìn faces a calamitous era,
a moment of extreme peril.
You, Illustrious Duke, personally received the court's calculations,
and are to eliminate evildoers for the state.
Yán Hēng was a fine scholar;
how could he be killed innocently and suddenly?"
Xī angrily said:
"I killed Yán Hēng myself;
what business is it of yours
to come here, ill, to scold me?"
His attendants trembled with fear.
Yù said:
"Since you, Illustrious Duke, advanced me with courtesy,
I wish to fulfill my duty with courtesy.
Now you, Illustrious Duke, are angry with me,
but what if those near and far are angry with you, Illustrious Duke?
In ancient times, when Yáo and Shùn ruled,
they prospered through harmony and order;
when Jié and Zhòu ruled,
they perished through wickedness and perversity.
Even Emperors are like this,
how much more so a subject!
I implore you, Illustrious Duke, to set aside your anger for a moment and consider my words."
Xī showed a look of shame.
From then on, popular support gradually waned,
and no one was willing to serve him effectively.
Furthermore, pestilence and famine added to his woes,
and his generals Wēn Jī and Fù Xuān both rebelled against him.
Shí Lè attacked Yángxià,
annihilated Wáng Zàn,
then swiftly attacked Méngchéng,
captured Xī,
appointed him as Sīmǎ,
and killed him after more than a month.
Xī had no sons,
and his younger brother Chún was also killed.
Huá Yì
Huá Yì, courtesy name Yànxià,
was a native of Píngyuán.
He was the great-grandson of Wèi Tàiwèi Xīn.
His grandfather, Biǎo,
was a Tàizhōng Dàfū.
His father, Dàn,
was Hénán Yǐn.
Yì showed talent and spirit from a young age,
and was renowned in his generation.
He was widely loved and embraced,
and public opinion praised him.
Initially, he served as a Bóshì,
and was successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè governed Yǎnzhōu,
he appointed Yì as Liúfǔ Chángshǐ.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he successively held the posts of Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Even amidst chaos and upheaval,
he always upheld rites and ceremonies.
He established the position of Rúlín Jìjiǔ to promote moral education,
and issued an edict stating:
"Now, righteousness has declined,
and ritual codes lack a guiding principle.
Court deliberations are stagnant,
unable to rectify matters.
I have often felt this with regret,
and it is proper to specially establish this office
to promote this cause.
Jūnzī Jìjiǔ Dù Yí,
whose sentiments reside in the profound and distant,
is resolute and aloof from worldly affairs.
His talent and learning are extensive and refined,
and his moral conduct is exemplary.
Let him be appointed Rúlín Jìjiǔ."
Soon after, he received an edict from Yuè, ordering him to assist in suppressing the bandits.
Yì dispatched former Jiāngxià Tàishǒu Táo Kǎn as Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
leading three thousand troops to garrison Xiàkǒu,
as reinforcement.
Yì exercised great authority and benevolence in his province.
He treated the local gentry as friends,
winning the affection of the Jiāngbiǎo region,
and refugees flocked to him as if returning home.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was isolated and imperiled,
and the four quarters were in disarray.
Huà Yì had the ambition to restore order to the realm,
and each time he sent tribute to Luò,
he did not fail in his duty as a subject.
He said to his envoys:
"If the road to the capital Luò is cut off,
you may deliver it to the Prince of Lángxié,
to demonstrate my allegiance to the Sīmǎ clan."
Huà Yì considered himself to have been dispatched by Luòjīng,
and to be supervised by Shòuchūn.
As Luòjīng still existed at that time,
he could not comply with the commands of Yuán Dì.
Many prefectures and counties advised him to do so,
but Huà Yì did not heed them,
saying:
"I only wish to see an imperial edict."
At this time, the Emperor dispatched the General of Yangliè, Zhōu Fǎng, to lead troops and garrison Péngzé to guard against Huà Yì.
When Zhōu Fǎng passed Gūshú,
the Secretary of the Palace Library, Gān Bǎo, saw him and questioned him.
Zhōu Fǎng said:
"The Grand Secretariat has given orders
to garrison Péngzé.
Péngzé
is the western gate of Jiāngzhōu.
Huà Yànxià has a genuine concern for the realm,
but he does not wish to be an ordinary person subject to control by others.
Recently there have been disputes,
and some initial animosity.
Now, without cause, to station troops at his gate
will create a serious conflict.
I should garrison the old county of Xúnyáng.
It is already west of the Jiāng River,
and can defend against the north,
and also avoids the suspicion of pressing too close."
Soon after, Luòdū could not be held.
Sīkōng Xún Pán issued a proclamation,
and proclaimed the Emperor as the alliance leader.
Subsequently, the Emperor, acting under his own authority, changed the senior officials,
but Huà Yì again refused to obey orders.
Thereupon, he dispatched the Left General Wáng Dūn to command Gān Zhuó, Zhōu Fǎng, Sòng Diǎn, Zhào Yòu, and others to attack him.
Huà Yì sent his aide Chén Xióng to garrison Péngzé to resist Wáng Dūn,
and he himself formed a naval force as external support.
The Administrator of Wǔchāng, Féng Yì, was stationed at Pénkǒu.
Zhōu Fǎng attacked Féng Yì,
and defeated him.
The former Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Wèi Zhǎn, had not been treated with courtesy by Huà Yì,
and always harbored resentment.
At this point,
he, together with the Administrator of Yùzhāng, Zhōu Guǎng, acted as an internal response,
secretly leading troops to attack Huà Yì.
Huà Yì's forces disintegrated,
and he fled to Ānchéng.
They pursued and beheaded him,
along with his five sons,
and sent their heads to Jiànyè.
Initially,
Gāo Kuī of Guǎnglíng resided in Jiāngzhōu.
Huà Yì appointed him as Western Bureau Chief.
Soon after, Huà Yì was defeated,
and Gāo Kuī hid Huà Yì's two sons and wife,
enduring hardship for a year.
Subsequently, they received an amnesty.
Gāo Kuī brought them forth to surrender,
and the Emperor commended and pardoned them.
Liú Qiáo (Sūn Dān, Sūn Dān's son Liǔ)
Liú Qiáo, courtesy name Zhòngyàn,
was a native of Nányáng.
His ancestors were of the imperial clan of Hàn,
enfeoffed as Marquises of Ānzhòng,
transmitting the title for three generations.
His grandfather, Yì,
was a Court Attendant during the Wèi dynasty.
His father, Fù,
was the Chancellor of Chénliú.
Liú Qiáo was a Secretary of the Palace Library in his youth.
Wáng Róng, the General of Jianwei, invited him to be his military adviser.
During the campaign to conquer Wú,
Wáng Róng sent Liú Qiáo and military adviser Luó Shàng across the Jiāng River,
where they defeated Wǔchāng.
Upon their return, he was appointed Magistrate of Xíngyáng,
and later promoted to Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent.
For his meritorious service in executing Yáng Jùn,
he was granted the title of Marquis of Guānzhōng,
and appointed Assistant Minister of the Right in the Department of State Affairs.
He participated in the execution of Jiǎ Mì,
and was enfeoffed as Baron of Ānzhòng,
successively promoted to Mounted Regular Attendant.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng became Grand Marshal,
initially, Jī Shào was highly regarded by Jiǒng,
who would always descend the steps to welcome him.
Liú Qiáo said to Jiǒng:
"When Péi and Zhāng were executed,
the court officials feared Sūn Xiù,
and therefore did not dare not accept their property.
What is Jī Shào intimidated by now,
such that he still keeps the Péi family's chariots and oxen, and the Zhāng family's slaves?
When Yuè Yànfǔ came,
Your Excellency never even left your bed,
why do you alone show such respect to Jī Shào?"
Jiǒng then stopped.
Jī Shào said to Liú Qiáo:
"Why does the Grand Marshal no longer welcome guests?"
Liú Qiáo said:
"It seems a righteous person has said
that you are not worthy of being welcomed."
Jī Shào asked:
"Who is this righteous person?"
Liú Qiáo said:
"He is not far off."
Jī Shào fell silent.
After a short while,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
Dǒng Ài, a trusted confidant of Jiǒng, wielded immense power at court,
and no official dared to defy his will.
Within twenty days, Liú Qiáo
submitted six memorials impeaching Dǒng Ài for his crimes.
Dǒng Ài incited Gǒu Xī, Assistant Minister of the Right, to remove Liú Qiáo from office,
and he was reinstated as Colonel of the Cavalry.
During Zhāng Chāng's rebellion,
Liú Qiáo was dispatched as General of Weiyuan and Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and together with the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Liú Hóng, he attacked Zhāng Chāng,
and was promoted to Left General.
When Huì Dì traveled west to Cháng'ān,
Liú Qiáo and various prefectures and commanderies raised troops to welcome the imperial carriage.
The Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, acting under his own authority, transferred Liú Qiáo to General of Anbei and Inspector of Jìzhōu,
and appointed the Prince of Fànyáng, Xiāo, to concurrently hold the post of Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Liú Qiáo believed that Xiāo was not appointed by the Son of Heaven,
and refused to be replaced,
mobilizing troops to resist him.
The Administrator of Yǐngchuān, Liú Yú, was close to Xiāo.
Liú Qiáo submitted a memorial to the Department of State Affairs listing Liú Yú's transgressions.
When the Prince of Héjiān, Yóng, received Liú Qiáo's memorial,

he then proclaimed an imperial edict ordering the General Who Guards the South, Liú Hóng; the Grand General Who Conquers the East, Liú Zhǔn; and the General Who Pacifies the South, Prince of Péngchéng Shì, to join forces with Liú Qiáo in attacking Xiāo at Xǔchāng.
Liú Yú's younger brother, Kūn, led troops to rescue Xiāo,
but before he arrived, Xiāo was defeated.
Xiāo then fled with Kūn to north of the Yellow River.
Soon after,
Kūn led five thousand cavalry across the river to attack Liú Qiáo.
Liú Qiáo seized Kūn's father, Fān,
and transported him in a cage cart,
holding Kǎochéng to resist Xiāo,
but his forces were outnumbered and disintegrated.
Qiáo 復收散卒，
屯于平氏．
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng 進 Qiáo 鎮東將軍、假節，
以其長子 Yòu 為東郡太守，
又遣 Liú Hóng, Liú Zhǔn, Péngchéng Wáng Shì 等率兵援 Qiáo．
Hóng 與 Qiáo 牋曰：
“適承 Fànyáng 欲代明使君．
明使君受命本朝，
列居方伯，
當官而行，
同奬王室，
橫見遷代，
誠為不允．
然古人有言，
牽牛以蹊人之田，
信有罪矣，
而奪之牛，
罰亦重矣．
明使君不忍亮直狷介之忿，
甘為戎首，
竊以為過．
何者﹖ 至人之道，
用行舍藏．
跨下之辱，
猶宜俯就，
況於換代之嫌，
纖介之釁哉！
Fànyáng 國屬，
使君庶姓，
周之宗盟，
疏不間親，
曲直既均，
責有所在．
Lián Lìn 區區戰國之將，
猶能升降以利社稷，
況命世之士哉！
今天下紛紜，
主上播越，
正是忠臣義士同心勠力之時．
Hóng 實闇劣，
過蒙國恩，
願與使君共戴盟主，
雁行下風，
掃除凶寇，
救蒼生之倒懸，
反北辰於太極．
此功未立，
不宜乖離．
備蒙顧遇，
情隆於常，
披露丹誠，
不敢不盡．
春秋之時，
諸侯相伐，
復為和親者多矣．
願明使君迴既往之恨，
追不二之蹤，
解連環之結，
修如初之好．
Fànyáng 亦將悔前之失，
思崇後信矣． ”
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè 將討 Qiáo，
Hóng 又與 Yuè 書曰：
“適聞以吾州將擅舉兵逐 Fànyáng，
當討之，
誠明同異、懲禍亂之宜．
然吾竊謂不可．
何者﹖ 今北辰遷居，
元首移幸，
羣后抗義以謀王室，
吾州將荷國重恩，
列位方伯，
亦伐鼓即戎，
勠力致命之秋也．
而 Fànyáng 代之，
吾州將不從，
由代之不允，
但矯枉過正，
更以為罪耳．
昔 Qí Huán 赦射鉤之讎而相 Guǎn Zhòng，
Jìn Wén 忘斬袪之怨而親 Bó Dī，
方之 於今，
當何有哉！
且君子躬自厚而薄責於人，
今姦臣弄權，
朝廷困逼，
此四海之所危懼，
宜釋私嫌，
共存公義，
含垢匿瑕，
忍所難忍，
以大逆為先，
奉迎為急，
不可思小怨忘大德也．
苟崇忠恕，
共明分局，
連旗推鋒，
各致臣節，
吾州將必輸寫肝膽，
以報所蒙，
實不足計一朝之謬，
發赫然之怒，
使 Hán Lú Dōng Guō 相困而為豺狼之擒也．
吾雖庶姓，
負乘過分，
實願足下率齊內外，
以康王室，
竊恥同儕自為蠹害．
貪獻所懷，
惟足下圖之． ”
又上表曰：
“Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo 欲代 Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáo，
Qiáo 舉兵逐 Xiāo，
Sīkōng, Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè 以 Qiáo 不從命討之．
臣以為 Qiáo 忝受殊恩，
顯居州司，
自欲立功於時，
以徇國難，
無他罪闕，
而 Fànyáng 代之，
代之為非．
然 Qiáo 亦不得以 Xiāo 之非，
專威輒討，
誠應顯戮以懲不恪．
然自頃兵戈紛亂，
猜禍鋒生，
恐疑隙構於羣王，
災難延于宗子，
權柄隆於朝廷，
逆順效於成敗，
今夕為忠，
明旦為逆，
翩其反而，
互為戎首，
載籍以來，
骨肉之禍未有如今者也．
臣竊悲之，
痛心疾首．
今邊陲無備豫之儲，
中華有杼軸之困，
而股肱之臣不惟國體，
職競尋常，
自相楚剝，
為害轉深，
積毀銷骨．
萬一四夷乘虛為變，
此亦猛獸交鬬，
自效於 Biàn Zhuāng 者矣．
臣以為宜速發明詔，
詔 Yuè 等令兩釋猜嫌，
各保分局．
自今以後，
其有不被詔書擅興兵馬者，
天下共伐之．
詩云： 『誰能執熱，
逝不以濯﹖』
若誠濯之，
必無灼爛之患，
永有泰山之固矣． ”
時 Héjiān Wáng Yǒng 方距 Guāndōng，
倚 Qiáo 為助，
不納其言．
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè 移檄天下，
帥甲士三萬，
將入關 迎大駕，
軍次于 Xiāo，
Qiáo 懼，
遣子 Yòu 距 Yuè 於 Xiāoxiàn 之 Língbì．
Liú Kūn 分兵向 Xǔchāng，
Xǔchāng 人納之．
Kūn 自 Xíngyáng 率兵迎 Yuè，
遇 Yòu，
衆潰見殺．
〔一０〕 Qiáo 衆遂散，
與五百騎奔 Píngshì．
Dì 還 Luòyáng，
大赦，
Yuè 復表 Qiáo 為 Tàifù Jūnzī Jìjiǔ．
Yuè hōng，
復以 Qiáo 為 Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ．
Zúyú guān，
shí nián liùshísān．
Mǐndì mò，
zhuī zèng Sīkōng．
Zǐ Tǐng，
Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu．
Tǐng zǐ Dān．
Dān, courtesy name Jìngdào.
In his youth, he had a reputation for good conduct,
and was praised for his uprightness and high principles,
being recommended by his clan.
He was widely learned,
and thoroughly conversant with the Shī, Lǐ, and Sānshǐ.
He successively held the post of Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and was granted the title Sànqí Chángshì.
In office, he was fair, incorruptible, and prudent;
wherever he served, his achievements were noted.
Huán Xuán
was Dān's son-in-law.
When Xuán assisted in governance,
he appointed Dān as Shàngshūlìng,
and granted him the title Shìzhōng,
but Dān did not accept the appointment.
He was then appointed Tèjìn, Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
He died shortly after,
and was posthumously granted the titles Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ.
Dān's son was Liǔ.
Liǔ, courtesy name Shūhuì,
also had a good reputation.
He attained high office at a young age,
and successively held the posts of Shàngshū Zuǒyòu Púshè.
At that time, the Right Censor Fù Dí was fond of reading widely but did not understand their meanings,
whereas Liǔ only read the Lǎozi,
and Dí often belittled him.
Liǔ said:
"Although you read many books,
you understand nothing,
so you can be called a book bag!"
People at the time valued his words.
He was appointed as the Cǐshǐ of the three provinces of Xú, Yǎn, and Jiāng.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the titles Yòu Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Qiáo's younger brother was Yì,
who was Shǐ'ān Tàishǒu.
Yì's son was Chéng,
who was Dānyáng Yǐn.
The historian remarks: Zhōu Jùn's discernment of human character was insightful,
Zhōu Fù's reasoning was precise and detailed,
Huá Yì always referred to the books of rites,
Liú Qiáo's ambition was to be honest and straightforward.
Thus, they were able to serve in various official posts, both internal and external,
and all achieved meritorious service.
However, Zǔ Xuān's proposal to move the capital
was in conflict with Dōnghǎi,
and Yànxià's devotion to the emperor
brought him disfavor with Lángxié.
Consequently, they were branded with ill names
and subjected to public execution.
How lamentable!
If they had gone against the left-collar at Yīchuān,
established the right-altar at Huáifú,
relied on the strategic importance of Fāngchéng,
utilized the resources of the entire Chǔ,
trained and selected the troops of Wú and Yuè,
and transported the grain from Huái and Hǎi,
even if they could not have prayed for eternal heavenly mandate,
they would still have been able to alleviate difficulties and postpone downfall.
Alas!
"Not employing their good men,
but instead making us perverse,"
this is what it refers to.
Gǒu Xī rose from obscurity,
and held the position of supreme general.
Before achieving meritorious service in relinquishing his position,
his greed and tyranny were already manifest.
He used Shìlóng's hand
to bring about slaughter.
This is what is meant by,
"If one kills many,
how can one not come to this?"
The eulogy says: Kāilín's talent and governance,
thereby ascended to high office,
his achievements in military strategy were outstanding,
his civilizing influence spread to the banks of the river.
Yì honored his lord,
Fù also worked diligently for the king;
going against the times brought guilt,
defying heaven was inauspicious.
Qiáo was the leader of the barbarians,
not yet knowing when to act or withdraw.
Dào was about to lead the army,
his prestige and reputation were well established,
his greed and cruelty were known,
his loyalty and diligence were not considered.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 32: Liú Kūn (his son Qún, Kūn's elder brother Yú, Yú's son Yǎn)
Liú Kūn, courtesy name Yuèshí,
was a native of Wèichāng, Zhōngshān,
and a descendant of Liú Shèng, King Jìng of Zhōngshān during the Hàn dynasty.
His grandfather, Mài,
possessed talents for governing the state, and served as Xiàngguó Cānjūn and Sànqí Chángshì.
His father, Fān,
was pure, noble, modest, and frugal,
and reached the position of Guānglù Dàfū.
Kūn was recognized as brilliant and intelligent in his youth,
and was famous for his heroic prowess along with Zǔ Nà of Fànyáng.
At the age of twenty-six,
he became Sīlì Cóngshì.
At that time, the General who Conquers Barbarians, Shí Chóng, had a private residence in Jīngǔjiàn, Hénán,
which surpassed all his contemporaries.
He invited guests
to compose poems daily.
Kūn was among them, and his literary compositions were highly regarded at the time.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Jiǎ Mì, was involved in governing the court,
and all the people in the capital were devoted to him.
Shí Chóng, Ōuyáng Jiàn, Lù Jī, Lù Yún, and others,
all lowered their status due to their literary talent to serve Mì,
and Kūn's brothers were also among them,
being called
"The Twenty-Four Friends."
Tàiwèi Gāomì Wáng Tàipì appointed him as a subordinate,
and he was successively promoted to Zhùzuòláng, Tàixué Bóshì, and Shàngshūláng.
When Zhào Wáng Lún held power,
he appointed Kūn as Jìshì Dū,
and then promoted him to Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Lún's son, Fū,
was Kūn's brother-in-law,
so Kūn's father, sons, and brothers were all trusted by Lún.
When Lún usurped the throne,
Fū became the Crown Prince,
and Kūn became Fū's Zhānshì.
When the Three Princes attacked Lún,
they appointed Kūn as Guānjūn, Jǐajié,
and together with Sūn Xiù's son Huì, led three thousand imperial guards to resist Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
They fought at Huángqiáo,
where Kūn was thoroughly defeated and returned,
burning the Héquiáo to secure himself.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng assisted in governance,
because Kūn's father and elder brother were both figures of renown at the time,
he was specifically pardoned.
His elder brother Yú was appointed Zhōngshūláng,
and Kūn was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
When Jiǒng was defeated,
Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo garrisoned Xǔchāng,
and appointed Kūn as Sīmǎ.
When Huìdì went to Cháng'ān,
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè planned to welcome the emperor,
and appointed Kūn's father Fān as Huáiběi Hùjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Liú Qiáo attacked Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo in Xǔchāng,
Kūn, along with Rǔnán Tàishǒu Dù Yù and others, led troops to rescue him.
Before they arrived, Xiāo was defeated,
and Kūn and Xiāo both fled to Héběi.
Kūn's parents were then captured by Liú Qiáo.
Kūn then persuaded Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Wēn Xiàn
to yield his position to Xiāo.
When Xiāo took charge of Jìzhōu,
he sent Kūn to Yōuzhōu
to request troops from Wáng Jùn.
He obtained eight hundred cavalry,
and with Xiāo, crossed the river
to jointly defeat Dōngpíng Wáng Máo at Lǐnqīu.
They then went south to Liú Qiáo,
and finally recovered his parents.
He also executed Shí Chāo
and forced Lǚ Láng to surrender.
He then led all the armies to welcome the emperor to Cháng'ān.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Guǎngwǔ Hóu,
with an estate of two thousand households.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā (307 CE),
[Zhāng] Kūn was appointed Cìshǐ of Bìngzhōu,
granted the title Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently held the post of Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng.
On the way, Kūn submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant, with my dullness and limited aspirations,
through a stroke of fate,
has humbly taken on a position beyond my capabilities.
I managed to depart at the end of the ninth month.
The roads are treacherous and the mountains steep,
and the Hú bandits block the way.
Repeatedly engaging large numbers with few men,
I pressed forward through danger,
enduring many hardships and perils,
experiencing all manner of suffering.
I reached Húkǒu Pass on that day.
Since your servant entered the provincial boundaries,
I have personally witnessed the destitution.
The displaced people are scattered in all directions,
less than two out of ten remaining.
Carrying the old and supporting the weak,
they endlessly stream along the roads.
As for those who remain,
they sell their wives and children,
abandoning each other while alive,
and when dead, their bodies are left to perish.
White bones litter the fields,
and the sounds of mournful cries
afflict the harmonious atmosphere.
Tens of thousands of Hú surround
the four mountains.
Every step taken risks plunder;
every opening of the eyes sees bandits.
Only Húguān
is a place where provisions can be sought.
But these two routes,
the most perilous in Jǐuzhōu,
when a few men block the path,
a hundred men dare not advance.
Many who travel back and forth, both public and private,
are lost and perish.
Trapped in impoverished cities,
we cannot gather firewood.
The draft oxen are all gone,
and farming tools are also scarce.
With your servant's foolish shortcomings,
facing such extreme difficulties,
my worries circle endlessly,
leaving me no time for sleep or food.
Your servant humbly reflects that although this province is called a border region,
it is actually close to the imperial capital.
To the south, it connects with Hénèi;
to the east, it borders Sī and Jì;
to the north, it defends against foreign tribes;
to the west, it resists powerful invaders.
It is the source of strong bows, good horses, and brave, elite warriors.
It must be supplied,
only then can its life be preserved.
I now appeal to the Shàngshū
to request five million hú of grain,
five million bolts of silk,
and five million jīn of cotton for this province.
I pray Your Majesty will consider my memorial in a timely manner
and grant approval swiftly."
The imperial court granted his request.
At that time, Dōngyíng Gōng Téng had moved from Jìnyáng to Yè.
Bìngzhōu was ravaged by famine,
and the common people followed Téng south.
Fewer than twenty thousand households remained,
and bandits roamed freely,
blocking all roads.
Kūn recruited over a thousand men
and fought his way to Jìnyáng.
The government offices and temples were burned down,
and corpses covered the ground.
Those who survived
were starved and emaciated, no longer resembling humans.
Thorns had grown into forests,
and wolves filled the roads.
Kūn cleared away the thorns,
collected and buried the skeletal remains,
established government offices,
and set up markets and prisons.
Bandits constantly came to raid.
The city gates became battlefields.
The people tilled the fields carrying shields
and hoed with quivers slung over their backs.
Kūn comforted and encouraged them,
winning the hearts of the people greatly.
Liú Yuánhǎi was then in Líshí,
about three hundred lǐ away.
Kūn secretly sent people to sow discord among his various barbarian tribes,
and over ten thousand households surrendered.
Yuánhǎi was very fearful,
and consequently built a city at Púzǐ and resided there.
Before a year had passed in his official capacity,
the displaced people gradually returned,
and the sounds of chickens and dogs were heard again.
Kūn's father, Fān, came from Luò to join him,
and many scattered literati also returned to Kūn.
Kūn was good at comforting and appeasing,
but poor at controlling.
Within a single day,
though several thousand might return,
others would also leave in succession.
However, he was naturally extravagant and indulgent,
fond of music and women.
Although he would temporarily exert himself,
he would often return to his unrestrained ways.
Xú Rùn from Hénán,
who gained favor through his musical talent,
befriended powerful figures.
Kūn greatly cherished him
and appointed him as Jìnyáng Lìng.
Rùn, relying on Kūn's favor, became arrogant and reckless,
interfering in Kūn's governance.
Fènwēi Hùjūn Línghú Shèng, known for his upright and straightforward character,
repeatedly admonished Kūn about this
and also urged Kūn to remove Rùn.
Kūn did not heed him.
Initially,
Dānyú Yīqiū,
for his meritorious service in rescuing Dōngyíng Gōng Téng,
was memorialized by Kūn to have his younger brother, Yīlú, appointed as Dàijùn Gōng.
Yīlú and Liú Xī gathered their forces at Zhōngshān.
Wáng Jùn, believing Kūn had encroached upon his territory,
repeatedly attacked Kūn,
whom Kūn could not resist.
Consequently, Kūn's reputation and strength gradually diminished.
Xú Rùn again slandered Línghú Shèng to Kūn, saying:
"Shèng is going to urge Your Excellency to claim the imperial title."
Kūn did not investigate this
and immediately killed him.
Kūn's mother said:
"You are unable to greatly expand your strategic plans,
or control heroes.
You only wish to eliminate those superior to yourself to secure your own position.
How can you succeed?
If this continues,
disaster will surely befall me."
Kūn did not listen.
Shèng's son, Ní, fled to Liú Cōng
and reported the full situation.
Cōng was greatly pleased
and made Ní his guide.
At that time, Tàishǒu Xí Chún of Shàngdǎng surrendered to Cōng,
and the Wūhuán of Yànmén rebelled again.
Kūn personally led his elite troops to resist them.
Cōng sent his son Càn and Línghú Ní to launch a surprise attack on Jìnyáng, taking advantage of Kūn's absence.
Tàiyuán Tàishǒu Gāo Qiáo surrendered his commandery to Cōng,
and Kūn's parents were both killed.
Kūn led Yīlú to combine forces and attack Càn,
utterly defeating him,
with fifteen or sixteen out of every twenty men killed.
Kūn pursued them, taking advantage of the victory,
but could not overcome them further.
Yīlú believed Cōng could not yet be destroyed,
so he left Kūn cattle, sheep, carriages, and horses and departed,
leaving his generals Jī Dàn
and Duàn Fán to guard Jìnyáng.
Kūn was determined to avenge,
but was constrained by his weakened forces.
Weeping tears of blood, he stood like a corpse,
comforting the wounded and suffering.
He moved his residence to Yángyì City
to gather the scattered people.
When Mǐn Dì ascended the throne,
he appointed Kūn as Dà Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Bìngzhōu Zhū Jūnfàn,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì and Jiǎjié.
Kūn submitted a memorial expressing his gratitude, saying:
"Your Majesty overlooks your servant's great faults
and records your servant's minor virtues.
I have undeservedly received celestial grace
and been granted extraordinary favor,
honored with the glory of a diadem
and elevated to the position of a supreme general.
I humbly examine the imperial edict, and my five emotions soar.
Your servant has heard that Jìn Wén (Duke Wen of Jin) established his hegemony
by appointing Xì Hú as grand marshal,
and Gāozǔ (Emperor Gaozu of Han) accomplished his royal enterprise
by making Hán Xìn his grand general.
Both possessed the virtue of being well-versed in poetry and禮 (rites)
and the awesome might of martial prowess and resolute courage.
Thus, they were able to achieve great exploits in Jīngnán
and expand their grand foundation in Hébĕi.
How much more so for your servant, who is ordinary and crude,
to attempt to emulate these former sages!
I look down in fear of overturning
the tripod, worried about spilling the contents.
In ancient times, Cáo Mò was defeated three times,
yet achieved success at the Covenant of Kē.
Féng Yì had his wings clipped,
yet soared at Mǐnchí.
All were able to turn defeat into success
and compensate for their faults with achievements.
Your Majesty's grace in pardoning my transgressions is already profound,
but your servant's virtue of self-renewal has not yet been established.
Though your servant is not as capable,
I have heard the former teachings,
the principles of humility and deference..."
Your subject still hopes
that the reason I have dared to accept your gracious command
is truly to dedicate my life to repaying the nation,
to die in service,
and to ultimately give my life on the battlefield,
fulfilling my duty as a subject.
As
for the bestowal of honor and glory,
it is beyond words to express my gratitude.
Moreover, the palace attendant Shǐ Lán (史蘭) and Palace Central Attendant Wáng Chūn (王春) and others arrived subsequently,
bearing the imperial decree.
Your subject bowed to discern the imperial will,
and,
prostrate, shed tears on the paper.
Your subject has heard that difficulties and prosperity ebb and flow,
constantly changing through ancient and modern times.
The spirits resent the imperial virtue,
yet have not repented of the calamity.
The ants and barbarians unleashed their poison upon the divine land,
and the foreign tribes wreaked havoc upon the
central state.
The seven ancestral temples lack sacrificial offerings,
the hundred officials have lost the order of their rituals,
the imperial coffin is disgraced and lost,
and the imperial tombs have yet to be established.
The entire realm yearns eternally,
longing for them as for parents.
Your
Majesty's dragon countenance blossoms daily,
and your sagely essence shines ever brighter.
You lift the realm from its fallen state,
and elevate the altars of soil and grain from their collapse.
Within the four seas,
hierarchy has been re-established,
and the people of the nine
provinces
again behold the established system.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty, covered in dust,
