is in the suburbs of Qín (秦),
with reverence for ancestral offerings in your heart,
but unable to return to your homeland.
Your subject has held my position for
many years,
with meager talent and inferior quality.
My great failures are already manifest,
while not an iota of merit has been achieved.
Recently, due to the circumstances,
I was temporarily granted a title,
yet I have accomplished no feat of vanquishing the barbarians,
but rather accumulated the burden of undeserved position.
I ought to suffer the penalties of the law,
to make clear promotions and demotions.
Therefore, your subject previously submitted a memorial,
daring to rely on my foolish sincerity,
begging to retain the rank of the former court,
to
merely hold the office of commander of a detachment,
to be pardoned for my three defeats,
and to have my one achievement put to use,
so that I may fully engage my will on the barbarian battlefield,
and satisfy my desire against the great rebels.
Even if my body becomes fertilizer for wild grasses,
I will have no regret in
the yellow earth.
Your Majesty's special grace is exceedingly profound,
and you have graciously promoted and elevated me,
thus appointing me as supreme general,
with the concurrent rank of a regular minister,
allowing me to manage the affairs of
conquest and suppression as appropriate.
Upon receiving the
command, I was alarmed and
my five senses trembled,
fearing I might stumble and fall,
bringing shame to the court.
In the past, Shēn Xū (申胥) did not follow Bó Jǔ (伯舉) and achieved the merit of Gōng Xù (公壻);
Wǔ Yuán (伍員) did not obey Chéng
Fù (城父) and succeeded in the achievement of entering Yǐng (郢).
Although your subject is foolish and wicked,
I do not aspire to be like the ancients;
however, as for donning armor and grasping weapons,
and devoting myself to the enemy,
it is what is called the beneficence of Heaven and Earth,
which the myriad
creatures cannot but repay.
Having received such deep grace,
I respectfully submit this memorial.
After Qū Yǔn (麴允) was defeated and
Liú Yào (劉曜) executed Zhào Rǎn (趙冉),
Kūn (琨) again memorialized, saying: The rebellious Hu (胡) Liú Cōng (劉聰),
daring to lead his dogs and sheep,
has aggressively encroached upon the imperial capital.
Gods and men are indignant,
and those far and near are roused to fury.
I humbly peruse the imperial decree,
stating that the Grand Chancellor, Prince of Nányáng (南陽)
Bǎo (保),
and the Grand Commandant, Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州) Guǐ (軌),
have gathered the forces of their two provinces,
jointly to care for the royal house;
and that General of the Champions Yǔn (允) and General of the Household Gē (綝)
have commanded the six armies,
exerting their strength for the
national calamity.
The imperial army has achieved a great victory,
capturing thousands of heads.
Banners rise on the Jìn (晉) road,
and drums thunder by the bend of the Hé (河).
Xiáohán (崤函) has no alarm of plunder,
and Qiānlǒng (汧隴) enjoys the blessing of
peace and prosperity.
This truly is due to the divine martial might of the ancestral temples, the altars of soil and grain, and Your Majesty.
Among all living beings,
none do not crane their necks in anticipation.
How could your subject's heart
not be filled with joy?
Your subject previously reported that I would meet with Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Yī Lú (猗盧) in Píngyáng (平陽) this year in the third month.
But the Xiōngjié (匈羯) Shí Lè (石勒) on the third day of the third month directly attacked Jìchéng (薊城).
Grand
Marshal, Duke of Bólíng (博陵) Jùn (浚) accepted his false peace,
and was captured by Lè (勒).
Lè's (勒) power grew,
and he intends to attack your subject.
The walled settlements are terrified,
their will set on self-preservation.
Moreover,
within Yī Lú's (猗盧) state, treacherous plots arose.
Fortunately, Lú (盧) was vigilant and discovered them,
and all were quickly purged.
This caused me to have concerns both north and south,
thus delaying the planned action,
for which your subject weeps tears of blood and
sighs throughout the night,
wringing my hands and sighing deeply.
Lè (勒) occupies Xiāngguó (襄國),
separated from your subject by mountains.
His cavalry can depart in the morning
and reach your subject's city by evening.
Evildoers seek out each other,
and their followers are truly numerous.
Of the eight northeastern provinces,
Lè (勒) has destroyed seven.
Of those granted by the previous court,
only your subject remains.
Therefore, Lè (勒) plots day and night,
making plans to capture your subject.
He spies for
weaknesses,
and raids follow one another.
Our soldiers cannot unbuckle their armor,
and the common people cannot work in the fields.
Though Heaven's net is spread,
its divine favor has not yet reached us;
only your subject stands alone with the enemy as my
neighbors.
If I defend, I delay the execution of Cōng (聰).
If I advance to attack, Lè (勒) will strike from behind.
I am trapped, unable to advance or retreat,
caught between two predicaments.
I am filled with indignation,
but my strength does not match my will.
Ashamed and terrified by the campaign,
my heart aches and my head throbs.
My body remains where it is,
but my spirit flies to the enemy's court.
The autumn grain has been harvested,
and the Hu (胡) horses are fat.
All the vanguards have arrived.
Your subject should be the first to open the military campaign,
leading the soldiers personally.
Between your subject and the two barbarians,
coexistence is impossible.
If Cōng (聰) and Lè (勒) are not destroyed,
your subject will have no intention of returning.
I humbly rely on Your Majesty's
divine power,
to allow my humble wish to be realized,
and then I shall lay down my head to repay the nation,
dying without regret.
In the third year,

the emperor dispatched Zhào Lián (趙廉), concurrently Grand Messenger (Dà Hónglú 大鴻lú), bearing the imperial credentials, to appoint Kūn (琨) as Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空) and Grand Commander (Dūdū 都督) of military affairs in the three provinces of Bìng (并), Jì (冀), and Yōu (幽).
Kūn submitted a memorial declining the post of Minister of Works,
but accepted the Grand Commandership,
and set a date with Yīlú (猗盧) to attack Liú Cōng (劉聰).
Soon after, Yīlú and his son turned against each other;
Yīlú and his nephew Gēn (根) both died of illness,
〔一一〕and their tribes scattered.
Kūn's son Zūn (遵) had previously been a hostage with Yīlú,
and the masses all attached themselves to him.
At this time,
Zūn, together with Jī Dàn (箕澹) and others, led Yīlú's forces of thirty thousand men,
with one hundred thousand horses, cattle, and sheep,
all to surrender to Kūn.
Kūn was thus revived,
and he led several hundred cavalrymen from Píngchéng (平城) to welcome and assimilate them.
At that time, Shí Lè (石勒) attacked Lèpíng (樂平),
and the prefect Hán Jù (韓據) requested aid from Kūn.
However, Kūn considered his troops to be newly gathered,
and wished to use their vigor to intimidate Shí Lè.
Jī Dàn remonstrated, saying:
"Although these are Jìn (晉) people,
they have long lived in a desolate borderland,
are not accustomed to kindness and trust,
and are difficult to control by law.
Now, we should internally gather the remaining grain of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑),
and externally seize the cattle and sheep of the remaining Hú (胡) tribes.
Furthermore, we should close the passes, guard the strategic points,
and focus on agriculture and resting the soldiers.
Once they are civilized and moved by righteousness,
then if we use them,
success can be achieved."
Kūn did not listen,
but mobilized all his troops,
and ordered Dàn to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard,
with Kūn himself following as the rear guard.
Shí Lè had already occupied the strategic points,
and set up an ambush to attack Dàn,
defeating him utterly.
The entire army was lost,
and the whole region was shaken with terror.
Soon after, there was a severe drought,
and Kūn was so hard-pressed that he could no longer hold out.
The Inspector of Yōu Province, the Xiānbēi Duàn Pǐdī (段匹磾), repeatedly sent messengers to invite Kūn,
wishing to jointly support the imperial house.
Kūn thereupon led his forces to him,
entering Jì (薊) via Fēihú (飛狐).
Pǐdī, seeing him,
respected him greatly,
and formed a marriage alliance with Kūn,
agreeing to be sworn brothers.
At this time, the Western Capital (Xīdū 西都) was no longer secure,
and Emperor Yuán (元帝) assumed regency on the south bank of the Yangtze (Jiāngzuǒ 江左).
Kūn then ordered his Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) to urge the emperor to ascend the throne.
Thereupon, one hundred eighty officials and commanders from the region north of the Yellow River (Héshuò 河朔), both Chinese and non-Chinese, jointly submitted a memorial,
the text of which is found in the "Annals of Emperor Yuán" (Yuán Jì 元紀).
The imperial reply stated:
"Wolves and jackals run rampant with poison,
repeatedly overturning the altars of earth and grain.
The myriad common people look up with longing,
stretching their necks, finding no one to rely on.
Therefore, I have taken up the imperial position,
to respond to the world,
hoping to restore the sage lord,
and sweep away the shame of our enemies.
How could I recklessly assume such a lofty position?
This is my utmost sincerity, evident far and wide.
You, Lord, have received generations of imperial favor,
and reached the highest position as a subject.
Your loyalty, integrity, and sincerity
have moved Heaven and Earth.
Indeed, I rely on your far-sighted strategies
to jointly overcome these difficulties.
Though north and south are far apart,
we share the same purpose and aspiration.
From thousands of miles away,
my heart feels you are but a foot away.
May you, Lord, pacify both Chinese and non-Chinese,
and mete out punishment to the ugly lot.
Keep me informed of all your actions."
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
Kūn and Pǐdī set a date to attack Shí Lè.
Pǐdī promoted Kūn to Grand Commander-in-Chief (Dà Dūdū 大都督),
made a blood oath and sealed it with writing,
and issued a proclamation to all regional commanders,
ordering them to gather at Xiāngguó (襄國).
Kūn and Pǐdī advanced and encamped at Gù'ān (固安),
awaiting the arrival of the armies.
Pǐdī's cousin Mòbō (末波) had received a large bribe from Shí Lè,
and alone did not advance,
thereby disrupting their plan.
Kūn and Pǐdī, due to their weakened position, retreated.
In that year,
Emperor Yuán transferred Kūn to Grand Tutor (Tàiwèi 太尉) and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中),
with his other positions remaining as before,
and also presented him with a famous sword.
Kūn replied:
"I shall personally bear it
to behead the two barbarians."
Pǐdī rushed to his elder brother's funeral.
Kūn sent his heir apparent Qún (羣) to escort him.
However, Mòbō led his troops to intercept and attack Pǐdī, who was defeated and fled.
Qún was captured by Mòbō.
Mòbō treated him with great courtesy,
promised to make Kūn Inspector of Yōu Province,
and formed an alliance to attack Pǐdī.
He secretly sent an envoy carrying a letter from Qún to ask Kūn to act as an internal confederate.
However, the letter was seized by Pǐdī's scouts.
At that time, Kūn was separately encamped in a small city at the former Zhēngběi Fǔ (征北府),
unaware of this.
He then came to see Pǐdī.
Pǐdī showed Qún's letter to Kūn and said:
"I do not doubt you,
which is why I am telling you this."
Kūn said:
"I am allied with you,
and my ambition is to assist the imperial house,
relying on your might
to perhaps wipe away the nation's shame.
Even if my son's letter had secretly reached me,
I would still never betray you and forget righteousness for the sake of one son."
Pǐdī deeply respected Kūn,
and initially had no intention of harming him.
He was about to allow him to return to his encampment.
But his younger brother Shūjūn (叔軍), who was studious and resourceful,
and trusted by Pǐdī,
said to Pǐdī:
"We are barbarians.
The reason we can subdue the Jìn people
is because they fear our numbers.
Now, our own flesh and blood are creating trouble;
this is their perfect opportunity.
If someone were to support Kūn and rise up,
our clan would be annihilated."
Pǐdī then detained Kūn.
Kūn's eldest illegitimate son Zūn, fearing execution,
closed the gates and defended himself with Kūn's Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ 左長史) Yáng Qiáo (楊橋) and Bìng Province Administrator (Bìngzhōu Zhìzhōng 并州治中) Rú Suī (如綏).
Pǐdī tried to persuade them without success,
so he unleashed his troops to attack them.
Kūn's general Lóng Jìměng (龍季猛), pressed by lack of food,
then beheaded Qiáo and Suī and surrendered.
Initially,
when Kūn left Jìnyáng (晉陽),
he worried about ruin and failure to avenge the great shame,
and also knew that barbarians were difficult to subdue with righteousness,
but hoped to express his utmost sincerity,
and perhaps succeed by some remote chance.
Whenever he met his generals and aides,
he spoke with impassioned grief,
lamenting the dead end of his path,
wishing to lead his troops to die in the enemy's encampment.
This plan was not realized,
and he was eventually captured by Pǐdī.
Knowing he was certainly going to die,
his demeanor remained calm.
He composed a five-character-line poem and presented it to his Attendant (Biéjià 別駕) Lú Chén (盧諶), saying: "In my grasp is a hanging jade disc,
originally a gem from Jīngshān (荊山).
Only that Tàigōng Wàng (太公望)
was once an old man by the Wèibīn (渭濱).
How spirited was Dèng Shēng (鄧生),
coming a thousand li to seek me!
Báidēng (白登) was saved by Qǔnì (曲逆),
Hóngmén (鴻門) relied on Liú Hóu (留侯).
Chóng'ěr (重耳) depended on five worthies,
Xiǎobái (小白) relied on the one who shot the hook.
They could elevate two great hegemon-lords,
why then ask about allies or foes!
At
midnight I sigh, leaning on my pillow,
imagining wandering with those few worthies.
I have been in decline for a long time,
why do I not dream of Zhōu (周)? Who says the sage comprehends fate's course,
and knowing destiny has no worries?
Confucius
grieved at the capture of the Qílín (獲麟),
the Western Hunt made Kǒng Qiū (孔丘) weep.
My achievements have not yet been built,
the setting sun suddenly flows west.
Time does not wait for me,
it leaves like floating clouds.
Red fruits fall
in the strong wind,
many flowers drop in pale autumn.
On a narrow path, the imperial carriage overturns,
a startled team breaks both shafts.
Who would have thought that hundred-forged steel
would turn into a finger-twisting soft thing?"
Kūn's poem conveyed extraordinary intent,
expressing his deep resentment.
He drew distant parallels to Zhāng (張) and Chén (陳),
and evoked the incidents of Hóngmén and Báidēng,
using them to stir Chén.
Chén, having no extraordinary strategies,
responded with conventional words,
which greatly displeased Kūn's heart.
When Kūn again presented him with a poem,
Chén then said to Kūn:
"Your previous poem expressed the grand aspirations of an emperor;
these are not words to be spoken by a subject."
However, Kūn
was loyal to the Jìn
dynasty and had long commanded great respect.
His detention for a month roused indignation far and wide.
Pìdī's appointee, Pìlú Sōng,
Administrator of Dàijùn, conspired with Kūn's appointees, Wáng Jù,
Administrator of Yànmén, and Hán Jù,
General of the Rear. They secretly prepared siege engines,
intending to attack Pìdī.
However, Hán Jù's daughter was a concubine to Pìdī's son;
she heard of the plot and informed Pìdī.
Thereupon, Wáng Jù, Pìlú Sōng, and their followers were arrested
and all executed.
At this time, Wáng Dūn secretly sent an envoy to Pìdī, ordering him to kill Kūn.
Pìdī also feared that the masses would turn against him,
so he claimed to have an imperial edict
to arrest Kūn.
Initially, when Kūn heard that Dūn's envoy had arrived,
he said to his son,
"Chùzhòng
has sent an envoy but hasn't informed me;
this means he intends to kill me.
Life and death are determined by fate,
but I only regret that my vengeance and shame have not been avenged,
and I will have no way to face my parents below."
With that, he choked with sobs, unable to control himself.
Pìdī then strangled him;
he was forty-eight years old at the time.
Four of his sons and nephews were also killed.
〔一二〕The imperial court, believing Pìdī was still powerful
and needed to fight Shí Lè for the state,
did not mourn Kūn.
Three years later, Lú Chén
and Cuī Yuè,
former Central Clerks to Kūn,
submitted a memorial
to clear Kūn's name, stating:
"Your servants have heard that the essence of governing a state
lies in upholding bright laws and punishments;
the task of establishing governance
lies in firmly securing its passes.
How much more so for a regional official
holding the power of life and death—
how can one not rectify
their right and wrong,
and thereby prevent treachery and evil?
We humbly observe that the late Sīkōng,
Marquis of Guǎngwǔ, Kūn,
during the turbulent times of Huì Dì
and facing the chaos of numerous lords vying for power,
dedicated his efforts to the imperial house,
his righteousness and sincerity ever more resolute.
He personally commanded both Huá
and Yí,
and personally endured arrows and stones.
Shí Chāo
was beheaded,
and Lǚ Lǎng
was bound face-to-face.
The altars of soil and grain were pacified,
and the imperial carriage returned.
Kūn's merit in receiving and escorting the emperor was indeed great;
this is one proof of Kūn's loyalty.
Thereafter, the Provincial Governor of Bīngzhōu,
Duke of Dōngyíng, Téng,
finding Jìnchuān
barren and depleted,
moved his command to Línzhāng.
Tàiyuán
and Xīhé
were completely relocated
to Sānwèi.
Kūn was appointed to Bīngzhōu,
inheriting its ills.
On the day he arrived at his post,
few households remained.
Facing a perilous situation
and in a region difficult to save,
he gathered the wounded,
pacified and harmonized the Róng
and Dí,
and within a few years,
both public and private sectors gradually recovered.
When the capital was lost
and the rebels ran rampant,
the border people were utterly defeated.
Those who harbored thoughts of peace and security
all believed
that Bīngzhōu,
being fortified on all sides,
could be defended by closing its passes,
accumulating resources,
and raising troops.
Kūn, however, spoke out strongly,
his loyalty fervent,
believing that
the Son of Heaven's
humiliation
should not lead him to die without preserving his integrity;
such a thought brought him no peace.
Thus, he traversed mountains and rivers,
campaigning east and west.
When the Tūgē
took advantage of the emptiness,
Jìnyáng
collapsed.
Kūn's parents
suffered the calamity of slaughter,
and his clan endured the disaster of extermination.
Had Kūn followed the will of the provincial people
and adopted a strategy of self-preservation,
then His Sacred Majesty might not have punished him,
and his clan might not have been lost.
When Yīlú
was defeated and in disarray,
Jìn
people sought refuge with Kūn in Píngchéng,
and he accepted their initial allegiance.
General Jī Dàn
further believed that although these were Jìn
people,
having lived long in the wilderness,
they were difficult to discipline by law
and should not be used immediately.
Kūn, however, yielded to them,
his righteousness evident in his expression.
Had he followed Dàn's
counsel,
content to merely survive,
he would have remained secure
in Bīngtǔ
and would not have perished in Yānjì.
Kūn, considering himself to hold a regional office,
and the imperial order not being upheld,
felt he had no reason to falsely bear
great responsibility
and occupy one of the Three
Dignities.
Therefore, when Your Majesty ascended the throne,
he immediately acknowledged his faults and offered to resign,
his memorials both before and after
fully stating his sincere intentions.
Soon after, he ordered his Central Clerk,
your servant Xù Dàn,
to return the official seal and credentials
to the imperial court,
departing at the same time as Pìdī's
envoy Róng Shàoqī.
Furthermore, Pìdī,
considering Kūn an important minister of the imperial house,
feared that Kūn would diminish his own authority and influence.
His jealousy of Kūn
gradually became apparent externally.
Kūn, knowing this,
feared he could not stay long.
He wished to send his wife and children,
both old and young,
to the capital,
entrusting his family entirely to Your Majesty.
If there were a call to arms,
he himself would serve as a soldier;
if Pìdī became violent and malicious,
then his wife and children might be spared.
He fully instructed your servant Dàn
to secretly convey this intention,
requesting an imperial edict
for an escort
along the route.
At that time, Wáng Chéng
fled from Píngyáng
and reported that Nányáng Wáng Bǎo
had proclaimed himself in Lǒngyòu,
with a vast army,
and intended to move into Guānzhōng.
Pìdī,
hearing this,
secretly harbored thoughts of waiting and watching.
He detained Róng Shào,
intending to send his former acting Grand Herald, Biān Miǎo,
as an envoy to Bǎo.
Fearing that Dàn
would go south alone
and reveal this matter,
he refused
to allow him passage.
His utmost sincerity
ultimately did not reach the emperor.
Pìdī's
brother Juàn
had died,
and his heir was young and weak.
Pìdī wished to take advantage of the mourning period
to seize his state.
Furthermore, he himself
had deceived the state and oppressed his family,
Below, I could not devote myself to one region;
above, I could not pledge my loyalty to Your Majesty.”
His words were fervent and righteous,
moving those around him.
Pǐdī (匹磾) had already harmed Kūn (琨),
and then falsely
slandered him,
saying Kūn (琨) wished to usurp the imperial throne
and plotted rebellion.
Kūn (琨) was free from the wild and wicked thoughts of Shùxiāo (述囂),
nor did he possess the fear of execution like Xìnbù (信布).
How could he, amidst the chaos of a collapsing
state,
and caught between different ethnic groups,
harbor such intentions?
Even the most foolish of slaves
or the least intelligent of servants
would not do so,
much less one among the ranks of a national worthy
whose loyalty and integrity
were preeminent!
Pǐdī’s (匹磾) harm to Kūn (琨)
was claimed to be by Your Majesty's secret edict.
If Kūn (琨) were truly guilty,
and Your Majesty had him executed,
he should have been exposed in the market and court,
and abandoned by all.
Not allowing
a common fellow of a different tribe to slay a minister of the imperial court
is already clear.
Therefore, those who usurp edicts are guilty,
and though minor, must be punished;
those who forge decrees and achieve success,
though great, are not considered.
This is
because the roots of rise and fall all lie here,
and the avenues of opening and blocking must therefore be closed.
Yet Pǐdī (匹磾) had no scruples,
relying on chaos to arbitrarily execute,
falsely using the imperial
mandate
to cruelly harm a pillar of the state,
disgracing the hopes of the central states,
and corrupting the laws of the royal house.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be tolerated?
If the Sacred Court continues to endure this,
failing to clarify
the greater principle,
then unscrupulous individuals will follow Pǐdī’s (匹dī) path,
exercising arbitrary power over life and death,
and acting according to their whims.
How then will Your Majesty punish them?
To ward off invaders and overcome difficulties,
only victorious generals are needed;
to eliminate tyranny and quell chaos,
ministers of wisdom and strategy are essential.
Hence, the ancient saying,
“When there are fierce beasts in the mountains,
even the weeds are not gathered,”
is not a hollow
statement.
From the Yellow River northward,
and south of Yōu (幽) and Bīng (并) provinces,
the only one whom the vile hordes feared and respected
was Kūn (琨).
After Kūn (琨) suffered harm,
the numerous villains rejoiced,
all
content.
They marched boldly through the central plain,
meeting no slightest obstacle.
This is why both Chinese and barbarians, great and small, sigh with regret.
We humbly believe that Your Majesty's sagely wisdom is profound,
and the task of restoration has begun.
You are about to establish laws and penal codes
to govern the myriad states.
Yet Kūn (琨) suffered harm unjustly,
his grievance and pain
are extreme,
and we have not heard of the court making any distinction or judgment.
In the past, the three elders of Húguān (壺關) argued the case of Crown Prince Wèi (衛),
and Gǔ Yǒng (谷永) and Liú Xiàng (劉向) clarified the achievements of Chén Tāng (陳湯).
Below, they were sufficient to
clarify the distinction between merits and crimes;
above, they were sufficient to enlighten the sagely ruler's mind.
Since the time of our ancestors,
we, your servants, have generations received exceptional favor,
attending in the imperial presence and holding official posts.
Unable to bear the heavy responsibilities,
we were
dispersed to distant lands,
associating with Kūn (琨)
and witnessing his affairs from beginning to end.
Therefore, admiring the righteousness of the three ministers of old,
we respectfully present the full account
and presumptuously make it
known to Your
Majesty,
humbly hoping the Sacred Court will graciously grant a compassionate investigation.
Crown Prince's Middle Palace Attendant Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) also submitted a memorial to vindicate him.
The Emperor then issued an edict saying:
“The late Grand Commandant and Marquis of Guǎngwǔ (廣武), Liú Kūn (劉琨), was loyal and capable,
sincerely serving the royal house.
Unfortunately, he met with disaster,
and his aspirations and integrity were unfulfilled.
I deeply mourn him.
Previously, due to military affairs,
no condolences or sacrifices were offered.
Let Yōu Zhōu (幽州) be instructed
to proceed with condolences and sacrifices as before.”
He was posthumously granted Attendant-in-ordinary and Grand Commandant,
and given the posthumous name Mǐn (愍).
Kūn (琨) had great ambition and spirit from a young age,
possessing talent for maneuvering.
He was good at associating with those superior to him,
but was somewhat flamboyant.
He was friends with Zǔ Tì (祖逖) of Fànyáng (范陽).
Upon hearing that Zǔ Tì (祖逖) had been employed,
he wrote to his relatives and old friends, saying:
“I sleep on my spear, awaiting dawn,
determined to eradicate the rebel captives.
I constantly fear that Zǔ Shēng (祖生) will reach the goal before me.”
His shared ambition was thus.
In Jìnyáng (晉陽),
he was once besieged by Xiongnú cavalry several layers deep.
The city was in dire straits with no recourse.
Kūn (琨) then ascended a tower under the moonlight and whistled clearly.
When the bandits heard it,
they all sighed with sorrow.
In the middle of the night, he played a Hújiā (胡笳) flute,
and the bandits again shed tears and sighed,
feeling a strong longing for their homeland.
Towards dawn, he played it again,
and the bandits all abandoned the siege and fled.
His son Qún (羣) succeeded him.
Qún (羣), courtesy name Gōngdù (公度),
was granted the title of Hereditary Son of the Marquis of Guǎngwǔ (廣武) when young.
He accompanied his father in Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and encountered bandit uprisings,
often leading partial armies in campaigns.
He was by nature upright and prudent,
with decisiveness,
and won the affection of gentlemen.
When Kūn (琨) was harmed by Pǐdī (匹磾),
Kūn’s (琨) Registrar Lú Chén (盧諶) and others led the remaining followers to take refuge with Mòbō (末波).
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) repeatedly memorialized, stating:
“My maternal cousin Liú Qún (劉羣),
my wife’s younger brother Cuī Yuè (崔悅) and Lú Chén (盧諶), etc.,
are all with Mòbō (末波),
looking south with anticipation.
I humbly believe that these individuals all possess literary talent
and are among the few who deserve compassion.
If they could be summoned and recorded,
continuing their interrupted line and restoring what was lost,
then Your Majesty’s grace of new life
would be unparalleled in ancient times.”
In the second year of Xiánkāng (咸康) (336 CE),
Emperor Chéng (成帝) issued an edict to summon Qún (羣) and others.
But Mòbō’s (末波) brothers, loving their talent,
cited the dangerous roads as a pretext and did not send them.
When Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) destroyed Liáoxī (遼西),
Qún (羣), Chén (諶), and Yuè (悅) all fell into the hands of the Hú (胡).
Jìlóng (季龍) treated them with great courtesy,
making Qún (羣) Zhongshū Lìng (中書令).
After Rǎn Mǐn (冉閔) was defeated,
Qún (羣) was killed.
At that time, Lè (勒) and Jìlóng (季龍) killed many of the high-ranking officials and gentry they captured.
Those who were promoted and eventually
reached high office
were only Péi Xiàn (裴憲) of Hédōng (河東),
Shí Pú (石璞) of Bóhǎi (渤海),
Zhèng Xì (鄭系) of Xíngyáng (滎陽),
Xún Chuò (荀綽) of Yǐngchuān (潁川),
Fù Chàng (傅暢) of Běidì (北地), and Qún (羣), Yuè (悅), Chén (諶) and about ten others.
Yú (輿), courtesy name Qìngsūn (慶孫).
He was intelligent and talented, with a good disposition.
Along with Kūn (琨), he was the nephew of Shàngshū (尚書) Guō Yì (郭奕),
and their names were well-known at the time.
The capital had a saying about them:
“In Luò (洛) (Luòyáng), distinguished and brilliant
are Qìngsūn (慶孫) and Yuèshí (越石).”
He was appointed Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) in a宰府 (zǎifǔ) (high official's residence).
His brothers had always insulted Sūn Xiù (孫秀).
When King Zhào Lún (趙王倫) became regent,
and Sūn Xiù (孫秀) held power,
they were both dismissed from their posts.
His sister married Lún’s (倫) crown prince Fū (荂).
Fū (荂) was not on good terms with Xiù (秀),
so Yú (輿) was again made Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎).
When King Qí Jiǒng (齊王冏) became regent,
Yú (輿) was made Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎).
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè and Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo raised their armies,
they appointed Liú Yú as the Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
When Héjiān Wáng Yǒng issued a檄 to Liú Qiáo to attack Xiāo in Xǔchāng,
he [Yǒng] issued a forged imperial edict saying:
“Liú Yú, Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān, has coerced Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo,
resisting the imperial edict,
establishing many private factions,
unlawfully seizing commanderies and prefectures,
and gathering troops.
In the past, Liú Yú and his brothers, because of their marital ties to Zhào Wáng,
unlawfully wielded power.
They were cruel, cunning, and lawless,
and should have been executed long ago.
However, due to an imperial amnesty,
they were spared their lives.
These vile persons showed no fear,
and their wickedness grew daily.
They arbitrarily appointed Gǒu Xī as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
thereby obstructing the imperial commands.
Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn Hóng,
Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Péngchéng Wáng Shì,
〔一四〕and Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn Zhǔn,
each commanding their respective forces,
are to proceed directly to Xǔchāng
and join forces with Liú Qiáo.
Now, Ròujiāngjūn Zhāng Fāng is dispatched as the Grand Commandant,
to oversee Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Lǚ Lǎng and the Grand Administrator of Yángpíng, Diāo Mò.
They are to lead 100,000 infantry and cavalry
to rendezvous at Xǔchāng
to eliminate Liú Yú and his brothers.
Anyone daring to raise an army to resist the imperial command
will have their five kindreds executed.
Anyone who can kill Liú Yú and his brothers and present their heads
will be enfeoffed as a marquis of a 3,000-household county
and be granted 5,000 bolts of silk.”
After Xiāo’s defeat,
Liú Yú fled with him to north of the Yellow River.
When Xiāo subsequently established himself in Yè,
he appointed Liú Yú as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
When Xiāo died,
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè was about to summon Liú Yú.
Someone said:
“Liú Yú is like grease;
the closer you get, the more he stains people.”
When he arrived,
Yuè was suspicious and treated him with reserve.
Liú Yú secretly observed the empire's military registers, warehouses, cattle, horses, weapons, and land and water formations,
memorizing everything.
At this time, there were many military and national affairs.
During every meeting,
from Pān Tāo downwards,
no one knew how to respond.
When Liú Yú met Yuè,
he responded to the moment and drew plans with eloquence.
Yuè leaned forward to greet him,
and immediately appointed him as Zǒuchángshǐ.
Once Yuè assumed overall command,
he made Liú Yú his chief assistant.
Guests filled the banquets,
and documents piled high on his desk.
Several thousand letters arrived daily from near and far.
He worked tirelessly all day,
sometimes continuing into the night.
Everyone was joyful and harmonious,
and all were pleased to submit to him.
His advice flowed like a stream,
and his replies were comprehensive and fitting.
People of the time admired his ability,
comparing him to Chén Zūn.
At that time, Yuè’s establishment was said to have three talents: Pān Tāo, a great talent;
Liú Yú, a prominent talent;
and Péi Miǎo, a pure talent.
Yuè’s execution of Miào Bō, Wáng Yán, and others
were all at Liú Yú’s instigation.
Wáng Yán’s beloved concubine, Lady Jīng, was skilled in music.
Before Wáng Yán was even encoffined,
Liú Yú proposed to her.
Before he could welcome her,
she was contended for and seized by Tàifù and Cóngshì Zhōngláng Wáng Jùn.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Fù Xuān impeached Wáng Jùn.
Yuè did not question Liú Yú
but dismissed Wáng Jùn from office.
Liú Yú then persuaded Yuè
to send Liú Kūn to garrison Bìngzhōu,
serving as Yuè’s vital northern stronghold.
Before Luòyáng fell,
he died of a carbuncle,
aged forty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title of Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
He had previously been enfeoffed as Dìngxiāng Hóu for his merits,
and given the posthumous name Zhēn.
His son Yǎn succeeded him.
Yǎn’s courtesy name was Shǐrén.
He was first appointed Tàiwèi Yuán,
then promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
He resigned due to his father’s mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he inherited the peerage.
Tàifù Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè invited him to be his Zhǔbù.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ
and then sent out as Grand Administrator of Yángpíng.
From Luòyáng, he fled to Liú Kūn.
Liú Kūn appointed him Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
When Liú Kūn was about to attack Shí Lè,
he appointed Yǎn to lead 1,000 warriors,
acting as Běizhōngláng Jiāng and Cǐshǐ of Yǎnzhōu,
stationed at Lǐnqīu.
Yǎn beheaded Wáng Sāng and
routed Zhào Gù,
gaining 7,000 followers.
He was attacked by Shí Lè,
but Yǎn resisted in battle,
and Shí Lè retreated.
Yuándì appointed him Dūdū and Hòujiāngjūn,
with provisional authority to use the imperial insignia.
Later, he was besieged by Shí Jìlóng.
He sought help from Shào Xù and Duàn Yāng.
Duàn Yāng’s cavalry rescued him,
and Jìlóng fled.
He followed Duàn Yāng to garrison Yàncì,
where he was killed.
His younger brother Yìn led troops for Liú Kūn,
but encountered Wūhuán bandits on the road
and died in battle.
Yìn’s younger brother Yì was initially Tàifù Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè’s Yuán,
and was killed along with Liú Kūn.
Yì’s younger brother Qǐ,
and Qǐ’s younger brother Shù,
along with Liú Kūn’s son Qún, were all caught in the chaos.
Later, they all entered Shí Jìlóng’s service.
Qǐ became Shàngshū Púshè under Jìlóng.
Later, he returned to the state.
Mùdì appointed him Qiánjiāngjūn
and granted him Gěishì Zhōng.
In the ninth year of Yǒnghé [353 CE],
he followed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Yīn Hào on a northern expedition.
He was defeated by Yáo Xiāng,
and Qǐ died in battle.
Shù was Shìzhōng under Jìlóng.
He returned to the state with Qǐ
and was appointed Xiāojí Jiāngjūn.
Zǔ Tiì (Elder brother Nà)
Zǔ Tì, courtesy name Shìzhì,
was a native of Qí in Fànyáng.
For generations, his family had held positions of two thousand piculs [rank],
being an old and prominent clan in the northern provinces.
His father, Wǔ, was Jìn Wáng Yuán and Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ.
Zǔ Tì was orphaned young,
one of six brothers.
His elder brothers Gāi and Nà, among others, were all open-minded and talented.
Zǔ Tì was of a magnanimous and unrestrained nature,
not adhering to formal conduct.
At fourteen or fifteen, he still did not know how to read,
which often worried his brothers.
However, he was generous with wealth and fond of chivalry,
magnanimous and principled.
Whenever he went to a village,
he would often claim to be acting on his brothers' behalf,
distributing grain and silk to aid the poor,
which made his local community and clan hold him in high esteem.
Later, he extensively read books and records,
comprehending ancient and modern affairs.
When he traveled to the capital,
those who met him said he possessed the talent to aid the world.
He resided in Yángpíng.
At twenty-four,
Yángpíng recommended him as Xiàolián,
and Sīlì twice recommended him as Xiùcái,
but he did not accept any of these appointments.
He and Sīkōng Liú Kūn both served as Sīzhōu Zhǔbù.
Their affection for each other was deep and intertwined;
they shared a bed and slept together.
In the middle of the night, upon hearing the crowing of a wild rooster,
he kicked Liú Kūn awake, saying:
“This is not an ominous sound.”
Thereupon, he rose and practiced sword-dancing.
Zǔ Tì and Liú Kūn both possessed heroic spirit.
Whenever they spoke of current affairs,
they would sometimes rise and sit up in the middle of the night,
saying to each other:
“If the four seas boil over [meaning, if the world falls into chaos]
and heroes rise in unison,
you and I should avoid each other in the Central Plains.”
He was appointed Dàsīmǎ Yuán by Qí Wáng Jiǒng, and Piàojí Jìjiǔ by Chángshā Wáng Yì.
He was then transferred to Zhǔbù,
and progressively promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén and Yùzhāng Wáng Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He accompanied Huìdì on a northern expedition,
but the imperial army was defeated at Dàngyīn,
and consequently retreated to Luòyáng.
When the imperial retinue moved west to Cháng'ān,
the feudal lords east of the pass, Fànyáng Wáng Xiāo, Gāomì Wáng Lüè,
Píngchāng Gōng Mó, and others, all vied to recruit him,
but he did not accept any of them.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè appointed Zǔ Tì as Diǎnbīng Cānjūn and Grand Administrator of Jìyīn,
but he did not take up the post due to his mother’s mourning.
When Lǐ Tóu 李頭 was campaigning against Fán Yǎ 樊雅,
he fought valiantly and rendered meritorious service.
At that time, Tì 逖 obtained Yǎ's 雅 excellent horse.
Tóu 頭 greatly desired it but dared not speak.
Tì 逖 understood his intention
and so gave it to him.
Tóu 頭 was touched by Tì's 逖 kindness and favor,
and often sighed, saying:
"If I could have this man as my lord,
I would die without regret."
Chuān 川 heard this and was enraged,
and so killed Tóu 頭.
Tóu's 頭 kinsman Fény Chǒng 馮寵, with his four hundred followers, submitted to Tì 逖.
Chuān 川 became even more enraged,
and sent his general Wèi Shuò 魏碩 to plunder various commanderies in Yùzhōu 豫州,
capturing a great many women, children, carriages, and horses.
Tì 逖 sent his general Wèi Cè 衞策 to intercept them at Gǔshuǐ 谷水,
recovering all that had been plundered.
He ordered all of it returned to its original owners,
and his army took nothing for themselves.
Chuān 川 was greatly terrified,
and so joined Shí Lè 石勒 with his forces.
Tì 逖 led his troops to attack Chuān 川.
Shí Jìlóng 石季龍 led an army of fifty thousand to rescue Chuān 川.
Tì 逖 employed a stratagem to attack them,
and Jìlóng 季龍 was thoroughly defeated.
He withdrew his troops, plundered Yùzhōu 豫州,
and resettled Chén Chuān 陳川 back in Xiāngguó 襄國.
He left Táo Bào 桃豹 and others to guard Chuān's 川 former city,
stationed at the West Terrace.
Tì 逖 sent his general Hán Qián 韓潛 and others to garrison the East Terrace.
It was one large city.
The bandits would go in and out of the south gate to graze their animals.
Tì's 逖 army opened the east gate.
They stood guard against each other for forty days.
Tì 逖 filled cloth sacks with earth to resemble rice,
and had over a thousand men transport them up to the terrace.
He also ordered several men to carry actual rice,
pretending to be exhausted and resting by the roadside.
The bandits indeed pursued them,
and they abandoned their loads and fled.
When the bandits obtained the rice,
they thought Tì's 逖 soldiers and populace were well-fed,
while the Hú 胡 garrison had been hungry for a long time.
They became more afraid
and lost all their courage.
Shí Lè's 石勒 general Liú Yètáng 劉夜堂 transported provisions on a thousand donkeys to supply Táo Bào 桃豹.
Tì 逖 sent Hán Qián 韓潛, Féng Tiě 馮鐵, and others to pursue and attack them at Biànshuǐ 汴水,
capturing all of it.
Bào 豹 fled in the night,
retreating to Dōngyàn Chéng 東燕城.
Tì 逖 ordered Qián 潛 to advance and station his troops at Fēngqiū 封丘 to press them.
Féng Tiě 馮鐵 occupied the Two Terraces.
Tì 逖 garrisoned Yōngqiū 雍丘,
and frequently dispatched troops to intercept Shí Lè 石勒.
Lè's 勒 garrisons and outposts gradually shrank.
His scout cavalry often captured people from Púyáng 濮陽.
Tì 逖 treated them generously and sent them home.
All of them were grateful for Tì's 逖 benevolence,
and led five hundred households from their villages to surrender to Tì 逖.
Lè 勒 again sent ten thousand elite cavalry to resist Tì 逖,
but they were again defeated by Tì 逖.
Many of Lè's 勒 garrisons and outposts defected.
At this time, Zhào Gù 趙固, Shàngguān Sì 上官巳, Lǐ Jǔ 李矩, [一六] Guō Mò 郭默, and others were attacking each other with deceit and force.
Tì 逖 sent envoys to mediate their disputes,
showing them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and they subsequently submitted to Tì's 逖 command.
Tì 逖 loved his people and treated even humble scholars with respect.
Even distant acquaintances and lowly servants
were treated with kindness and courtesy by him.
Because of this, all the land south of the Yellow River became Jìn 晉 territory.
For the fortified settlements along the river that previously had sons serving as hostages among the Hú 胡,
he allowed them to be affiliated with both sides.
Occasionally, he would send a flying column to feign plundering them,
making it clear that they had not yet submitted.
The lords of these forts were grateful and esteemed him.
Whenever there was a suspicious plot among the Hú 胡,
they would secretly report it.
The successes achieved before and after
were also due to this.
If there was even a small achievement,
the reward would not be delayed beyond the day.
He was personally frugal and simple,
and encouraged and supervised agriculture and sericulture.
He was self-sacrificing and devoted to giving,
not accumulating assets.
His sons and younger brothers tilled the fields
and carried firewood.
He also collected and buried dry bones,
offering sacrifices for them.
The common people were moved and pleased.
Once, he hosted a grand feast with wine.
The elders, sitting in the middle, wept, saying:
"We are old!
To gain parents again
— what regret could we have in death!"
Then they sang:
"How fortunate are the remaining people to escape captivity,
The three luminaries shine brightly, and we meet a benevolent father.
Black wine makes us forget toil, sweet gourd and dried meat,
How can we sing of such grace, let us sing and dance!"
Such was the extent to which he won people's hearts.
Therefore, Liú Kūn 劉琨, in a letter to his kinsfolk,
lavishly praised Tì's 逖 prestige and virtue.
An imperial edict promoted Tì 逖 to Zhènxī Jiāngjūn 鎮西將軍 (General Guarding the West).
Shí Lè 石勒 dared not send troops to spy on Hénán 河南.
He had Chénggāo Xiàn 成皋縣 repair Tì's 逖 mother's tomb,
and then sent a letter to Tì 逖,
requesting to open diplomatic relations and trade markets.
Tì 逖 did not reply to the letter,
but allowed mutual trade,
reaping tenfold profits.
Consequently, both public and private resources became abundant,
and his soldiers and horses grew stronger day by day.
Just as he was about to push across the Yellow River with his vanguard
and clear Jìzhōu 冀州 and Shuòfāng 朔方,
the imperial court was about to send Dài Ruòsī 戴若思 as Dūdū 都督 (Grand Governor).
Tì 逖 thought that since Ruòsī 若思 was from Wú 吳,
although he had talent and reputation,
he lacked grand ambition and foresight.
Moreover, Tì 逖 had already cleared the thorns
and recovered the Hénán 河南 territory,
and for Ruòsī 若sī, leisurely
to come and govern it all of a sudden,
he felt quite displeased.
Furthermore, he heard that Wáng Dūn 王敦 was creating discord with Liú Wǎi 劉隗 and others,
and feared there would be internal strife,
preventing his great achievements from being realized.
Moved by emotion, he fell ill,
and then moved his wife and children to the foot of Dàmù Shān 大木山 in Rǔnán 汝南.
At that time, the scholars and common people of the Central Plains all believed Tì 逖 should advance and occupy Wǔláo 武牢,
but instead he moved his family to a dangerous place.
Some advised him against it,
but he did not heed them.
Although Tì 逖 harbored inner worry and indignation,
he did not cease his plans for advancement.
He began building and repairing Wǔláo Chéng 武牢城.
The city bordered the Yellow River to the north,
and adjoined Chénggāo 成皋 to the west,
offering a very distant view in all directions.
Tì 逖 feared that without a strong fortress to the south,
they would surely be attacked by bandits.

So he ordered his nephew Jì 濟, the Administrator of Rǔnán 汝南, to lead Zhāng Chǎng 張敞, the Administrator of Rǔyáng 汝陽, and Zhōu Hóng 周閎, the Prefect of Xīncài 新蔡, with their forces to build a fortress.
Before it was completed,
Tì 逖 became gravely ill.
Earlier,
Huá Tán 華譚 and Yú Chǎn 庾闡 had asked the diviner Dài Yáng 戴洋,
and Yáng 戴洋 said:
"Grand Governor Zǔ 祖 will die in the ninth month."
Originally, a demonic star had appeared in the region of Yùzhōu 豫州.
Chén Xùn 陳訓 of Lìyáng 歷陽 also told people:
"This year, a great general of the northwest will die."
Tì 逖 also saw the star,
and said:
"It is for me!
I am just about to pacify Héběi 河北,
but Heaven wishes to kill me.
This is not to aid the state."
Soon after, he died in Yōngqiū 雍丘,
at the age of fifty-six.
The men and women of Yùzhōu 豫州 grieved as if they had lost their parents.
The common people of Qiáo 譙 and Liáng 梁 erected shrines for him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍 (General of Chariots and Cavalry).
Wáng Dūn 王敦 had long harbored rebellious intentions,
but feared Tì 逖 and dared not act.
Only then was he able to indulge his ambitions.
Soon after, Tì's 逖 younger brother, Yuē 約, was appointed to lead his forces.
Yuē 約 has a separate biography.
Tì's 逖 elder brother was Nà 納.
Nà's 納 courtesy name was Shìyán 士言.
He possessed the utmost integrity,
was skilled in pure conversation (qīngyán 清言),
and his writings were worth reading.
He was extremely filial by nature.
Being orphaned and poor in his youth,
he often cooked himself to support his mother.
Wáng Dūn 王敦, General Guarding the North, heard of this,
[一七] and sent him two maids
and appointed him as Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎 (Attendant-in-ordinary).
Someone joked to him, saying:
"A male slave is worth twice a maid."
Nà 納 replied:
"Why should Bǎilǐ Xī 百里奚 necessarily be cheaper than five sheepskins!"
He was transferred to Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng 尚書三公郎 (Gentleman of the Three Dukes in the Department of State Affairs),
and successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 (Central Gentleman-of-the-Household to the Crown Prince).
Throughout his official career, he corrected many things,
which benefited his time.
When Qí Wáng Jǐong 齊王冏 raised an army for righteousness,
Zhào Wáng Lún 趙王倫 captured Jǐong's 冏 younger brother Běihǎi Wáng Shí 北海王寔 and the former Huángmén Láng 黃門郎 (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate) Dǒng Zuò 董祚 of Hóngnóng 弘農 and his younger brother Ài 艾,
who had risen with Jǐong 冏, and was about to harm them all.
Nà 納 submitted a memorial to rescue them,
and they were all pardoned.
Later, he served as zhōnghùjūn (中護軍) and tàizǐzhànshì (太子詹事),
and was enfeoffed as Jìnchāng Gōng (晉昌公).
Believing that Luò (洛) was about to fall into chaos,
he sought refuge in the southeast.
When Yuán Dì (元帝) became prime minister,
he appointed him jūnzī jìjiǔ (軍諮祭酒).
Nà (納) enjoyed playing yì (弈),
and Wáng Yǐn (王隱) said to him:
“Yǔ (禹) cherished every inch of time;
I have not heard of him playing yì.”
He replied:
“I also forget my worries.”
Yǐn (隱) said:
“I have heard that ancient people, when they encountered favorable circumstances,
achieved their path through merit;
if they did not encounter such circumstances,
they achieved their path through words.
This was certainly true in antiquity,
and it should be so today.
When the Jìn (晉) had no historical records,
and the world was in great chaos,
old events were swept away and obliterated.
You have lived in the five capitals since childhood,
〔一八〕and traveled and served in officialdom across the four directions.
The successes and failures of both Huá (華) and Yì (裔)
must have been seen and heard by you.
Why do you not record them and bring them to completion? Yìng Zhòngyuǎn (應仲遠) wrote Fēngsútōng (風俗通),
Cuī Zǐzhēn (崔子真) wrote Zhènglùn (政論),
Cài Bójiē (蔡伯喈) wrote Quànxuépīan (勸學篇),
and Shǐ Yóu (史游) wrote Jíjiùzhāng (急就章).
They are all still circulated in the world,
and thus they are not forgotten and become immortal.
Although I am untalented,
I am not without ambition.
Therefore, I am distressed at the thought of dying without being known,
which is why I strive unceasingly.
Moreover, the national history clarifies the traces of gains and losses.
Both lead to the dissipation of sorrow;
this can serve both purposes.
Why must one play yì and only then forget worries!”
Nà (納) sighed deeply and said:
“It is not that I do not appreciate your way,
but my strength is insufficient.”
Then he spoke to the emperor, saying:
“Since ancient times, even small states had official historians;
how much more so a great administration,
how can it not establish one?”
He then recommended Yǐn (隱),
praising him as
“clear, pure, bright, and upright,
with profound and keen learning and thought,
comprehending much from the Wǔjīng (五經) and various histories,
and moreover, diligent in study without weariness,
and following good like flowing water.
If he were to compile and write the canon of an era,
to praise, criticize, bestow, and take away,
he would truly be a talent of his time.”
The emperor asked jìshì cānjūn (記室參軍) Zhōng Yǎ (鍾雅) about this.
Yǎ (雅) said:
“Although the one Nà (納) recommended has historical talent,
he is not yet able to establish it now.”
The matter was thus suspended.
However, the establishment of the office of historian
began with Nà (納).
Initially,
his younger brother Yuē (約) was of the same mother as Tì (逖),
and they were especially close and affectionate.
Nà (納) and Yuē (約) were of different mothers,
and there was some displeasure.
So he secretly memorialized the emperor,
stating that
“Yuē (約) harbors a nature that overrides superiors.
It would be acceptable to suppress and employ him.
Now, openly attending by your side,
and wielding his power,
he will become a source of trouble.”
People said that Nà (納) and Yuē (約) were of different mothers,
and that Nà (納) was jealous of Yuē’s (約) favor and prestige.
So the emperor revealed his memorial to Yuē (約).
Yuē (約) hated Nà (納) like an enemy,
and the court consequently abandoned Nà (納).
After Nà (納) was retired,
he merely engaged in pure conversation and read literary and historical texts.
When Yuē (約) later rebelled,
the court and public sighed at Nà’s (納) discerning judgment.
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) respected Nà (納) because he was a senior kinsman from his home province and bowed to him.
When Jiào (嶠) was in power,
he highly praised Nà (納) for his profound understanding of principles,
and Nà (納) was appointed guānglùdàfū (光祿大夫).
Nà (納) once asked Méi Táo (梅陶):
“How is the Yuèdànpíng (月旦評) established in your home county?”
Táo (陶) replied:
“If it praises the good and condemns the bad,
then it is an excellent method.”
Nà (納) said:
“Not beneficial.”
Wáng Yǐn (王隱) was present at the time,
and he said:
“The Shàngshū (尚書) states: ‘After three years of evaluating performance,
after three evaluations, the obscure and the brilliant are promoted or demoted.’
How can one praise or criticize after only one month!”
Táo (陶) said:
“This is the official method.
Yuèdàn (月旦)
is a private method.”
Yǐn (隱) said:
“The Yì (易) states: ‘Families that accumulate good deeds will surely have abundant blessings;
families that accumulate bad deeds will surely have abundant misfortunes.’
Does ‘family’ not refer to officialdom?
It must be accumulated over a long time before good and evil become manifest.
How can public and private be different!
The ancients had a saying:
‘If a chaste and good person perishes,
it is the calamity of their ancestors;
if a cruel and fierce person survives,
it is the merit of their ancestors.’
It takes generations to become manifest,
how can it be just one month!
If it must be Yuèdàn (月旦),
then Yán Huí (顏回), eating dirt,
would not avoid being considered greedy for food;
and Dào Zhí (盜蹠), taking little,
would be considered incorruptible.
Planting in the morning and harvesting in the evening,
good and evil are not yet determined.”
At this time, Méi Táo (梅陶) and Zhōng Yǎ (鍾雅) repeatedly brought up other matters,
and Nà (納) always confounded them,
and then said:
“You are scholars from Rǔyǐng (汝潁),
sharp as an awl;
I am a scholar from Yōujì (幽冀),
dull as a hammer.
Holding my dull hammer,
and striking your sharp awl,
both will surely be broken.”
Táo (陶) and Yǎ (雅) both said,
“There is a divine awl,
which cannot be struck by a hammer.”
Nà (納) said:
“If there is a divine awl,
there must be a divine hammer.”
Yǎ (雅) had no reply.
He died at home.
The historian says: Liú Kūn (劉琨) in his youth
originally had no extraordinary conduct.
Donning ribbons at the mansion of Jiǎ Mì (賈謐),
and borrowing chopsticks in the tent of Mǎ Lún (馬倫),
at that time,
he was indeed a frivolous and cunning person!
Zǔ Tì (祖逖) distributed grain to the poor,
and danced in the dark upon hearing the rooster,
thinking of the beacon fires in the Central Plains,
and hoping for the emperor’s difficult path to continue.
Judging by his original aspirations,
he was indeed one who desired chaos.
However, when the element of metal was damaged in the middle,
and the heavenly order lost its unifying principle,
the three empresses went into exile,
successively suffering the calamity of residing among swine,
and the six barbarians rampaged and devoured,
spreading the poison of the long snake.
Then, the plain silk changed color,
and the unrestrained changed their nature.
Each exerted their extraordinary abilities,
and all displayed their heroic spirit.
They were moved by the difficult times,
and spurred into action by the chaotic world,
exerting their strength in a precarious state,
displaying firmness against the strong wind,
and cultivating their integrity,
establishing their principles like the cold pine.
All were able to achieve the rank of the Three Exalted Ones,
and became famous for a time.
The ancients had a saying:
“In a chaotic world, the loyal and good are recognized.”
This is indeed what it means.
Heaven did not bless the Jìn (晉),
and only then did it stir up the hearts of the barbarians.
Yuèshí (越石) was merely a common man,
yet he alone resisted the sharpness of the whale and the leviathan.
But he put his trust in different kinds,
and ultimately ended up in a dark prison.
How painful!
Shìzhì (士稚) followed the path of the restoration,
and recovered half of the nine provinces,
but then a baleful star announced misfortune,
and his call for assistance was in vain.
What a pity!
A eulogy says: Yuè Shí's talent was mighty;
he showed loyalty in peril.
He slept on his shield for a long time,
threw off his sleeves, and sought功.
He fought fiercely in Fén-Jìn,
and struggled with the Xūn Róng.
He was deceived by the Duàn clan.
Alas, his path was exhausted!
Zǔ Shēng was resolute and spirited,
harboring extraordinary principles from an early age.
He struck his oar in midstream,
swearing to purge the evil.
The neighboring foes attached themselves,
and the remaining populace rejoiced.
Heaven's portents are evident;
how can the national disgrace be wiped away!
Collation Notes
Biography Thirty-Three: Shào Xù
Shào Xù, courtesy name Sìzǔ,
was a native of Ānyáng, Wèijùn.
His father, Chéng,
was a Sànqí Shìláng.
Xù was simple and resolute in ambition,
broadly read in classics and histories,
skilled at discussing principles and righteousness,
and had a profound understanding of astronomy.
Initially, he served as a Cānjūn for Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
When Yǐng was about to attack Chángshā Wáng Yì,
Xù remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant hears that brothers are like left and right hands.
Now, your excellency faces enemies throughout the realm,
yet you wish to cut off a hand?
Your servant is secretly perplexed by this."
Yǐng did not heed him.
Later, he became a Cānjūn for Gǒu Xī,
and was appointed Qìnshuǐ Lìng.
At that time, the world was gradually descending into chaos,
so Xù left the county and returned home,
gathering fugitives,
and obtained several hundred men.
Wáng Jùn provisionally appointed Xù as Suíjí Jiāngjūn and Lèlíng Tàishǒu,
stationing him at Yàncí,
and made Xù's son, Yì, a Dūhù.
Xù pacified and comforted the scattered people,
and many returned to him.
After Shí Lè defeated Jùn,
he sent Yì back to recruit Xù.
Xù, being isolated and without aid,
temporarily submitted to Lè.
Lè also made Yì a Dūhù.
Later, Duàn Pǐdī was in Jì,
and sent a letter inviting Xù to return to Yuán Dì together.
Xù agreed.
His subordinates remonstrated, saying:
"If we abandon Lè and return to Pǐdī now,
your son's life will be in danger."
Xù wept and said:
"I embarked on this path for the country.
How can I consider my son and become a rebel minister!"
Thereupon, he broke off relations with Lè,
and Lè then killed Yì.
Xù feared Lè's attack,
and first sought help from Pǐdī.
Pǐdī sent his younger brother Wén Yāng to rescue Xù.
Before Wén Yāng arrived,
Lè had already led eight thousand cavalry to besiege Xù.
Lè had always feared the Xiānbēi,
and upon hearing of Wén Yāng's arrival,
he abandoned his siege equipment and fled eastward.
Xù and Wén Yāng pursued Lè to Ānlíng,
but did not catch him.
They captured the officials appointed by Lè,
and drove away over three thousand households.
They also sent cavalry to scatter Lè's northern border,
plundering Chángshān,
and returned with two thousand households.
After Pǐdī killed Liú Kūn,
the people of Jìn were mostly resentful and rebellious,
so he led his followers to rely on Xù.
Lè's Nánhé Lìng, Zhào Lǐng, and others led over a thousand households from Guǎngchuān and Bóhǎi to abandon Lè and return to Xù.
The Emperor then appointed Xù as Píngyuán Lè'ān Tàishǒu, Yòu Jiāngjūn, and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
promoted him to Píngběi Jiāngjūn, with provisional authority (jiǎjié),
and enfeoffed him as Zī of Zhù'ā.
Xù sent his elder brother's son, Wǔyì Nèishǐ Cún, with Wén Yāng, leading Pǐdī's forces to forage for food in Píngyuán,
where they were defeated by Shí Jìlóng.
Xù had previously frequently raided Cáo Yí,
and Yí, taking advantage of Cún and the others' defeat,
then broke Xù's military colonies,
and also plundered his households.
Xù rescued them back and forth,
exhausted by rushing to their aid.
In the early years of Tàixīng,
Xù sent Cún and Wén Yāng to garrison Huángjīn Gù in Jìnán,
thereby pressing Yí.
Yí, in fear,
sought peace.
Soon after, Pǐdī led his forces to attack Duàn Mòbēi.
Shí Lè, knowing Xù was isolated and vulnerable,
sent Jìlóng to exploit the weakness and besiege Xù.
Jìlóng's cavalry arrived at the city walls,
and plundered the residents.
Xù led his troops out to rescue them,
but Jìlóng's hidden cavalry cut off his retreat,
and he was consequently captured by Jìlóng,
who ordered Xù to surrender his city.
Xù called out to his elder brother's son, Zhú, and others, saying:
"My ambition was to avenge the national disaster
and repay what I had received,
but unfortunately, I have come to this.
You all must strive diligently,
and serve Pǐdī as your lord;
have no second thoughts."
At that time, when the Emperor heard of Xù's capture,
he issued an edict saying:
"Shào Xù was loyal and resolute in public service,
righteous and sincere, courageous and forthright.
He pacified and gathered the scattered remnants,
and sacrificed himself for the country.
His meritorious achievements were not yet fulfilled,
but he was unfortunately captured.
I grieve and resent this in my heart.
The heavy responsibility he bore
should be replaced in due time.
His military and civil subordinates
have jointly nominated his son, Jī, as camp commander.
Xù's loyalty
is evident in both public and private spheres.
Now, establishing his son
is sufficient to pacify the multitude.
Therefore, bestow upon Jī Xù's former position,
so that he may lead his subordinates,
show loyalty in the national crisis,
and avenge his family's仇."
Jìlóng sent an envoy to deliver Xù to Lè.
Lè ordered his envoy Xú Guāng to reproach him, saying:
"Our state, in response to the divine mandate, restores order from chaos.
The eight directions turn their hearts to us.
The remnants of Jìn, fearful of our might,
fled far to Yáng and Yuè.
Yet you, Xù, like an ant, entrenched yourself by the sea,
and defied the royal mandate.
Do you consider the Yi Di unsuitable to be a ruler?
How utterly disrespectful!
The state has its fixed punishments.
Are you prepared to face them?"
Xù replied:
"At the end of Jìn, there was famine and chaos,
and nowhere to flee.
I gathered my clansmen,
hoping to save the old and young.
When the Great King first ascended to power,
I committed my life and offered a hostage,
but my sincerity was unmoving,
and I did not receive clemency.
Returning to the remnant Jìn,
I continued to receive imperial favor,
and swore to exhaust my loyalty and integrity.
Indeed, I had no second thoughts.
Furthermore, having received such high honor from them,
if I were to be inconsistent in my allegiance,
I fear I would not be tolerated even by your enlightened court.
King Wén of Zhōu was born among the Eastern Yi,
and Great Yǔ emerged from the Western Qiāng.
The rise of emperors and kings
is surely determined by Heaven's mandate,
and attracted by virtue.
How can there be any constancy to it?
I humbly believe that the Great King is divinely martial,
and his Dao is as lofty as Yú and Xià.
Among all living beings,
who would not crane their necks towards your divine transformation,
and be ashamed to be separated from your imperial influence,
let alone a captive!
If this captive were to abandon the true and embrace the false,
and not have been able to knock on Heaven's gate earlier,
the Great King would have failed the captive;
the captive would not have failed the Great King.
The punishment of smearing blood on the drum
is this captive's due,
but I regret that Heaven truly brought this about.
What can be said about it?"
Lè said:
"His words are profound and sincere;
I am greatly ashamed by them.
Indeed, those who are loyal to their lord
are precisely what I seek."
He ordered Zhāng Bīn to invite him to the residence,
treated him generously,
and soon made him a Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He ordered that thereafter, all captured enemies and prominent figures
should be sent to him,
and not be harmed without authorization,
hoping to obtain more individuals like Xù.
Initially,
when Jì Lóng 季龍 attacked Xù 續,
the imperial court was under duress from Wáng Dūn 王敦,
and had no time to provide relief.
After Xù 續 was captured by Lè 勒,
he personally watered gardens and sold vegetables
to provide for his clothing and food.
Lè 勒 repeatedly sent people to observe him,
and sighed, saying:
“This is truly a man of high character!
If he were not like this,
how could he be worthy of respect!”
Admiring his purity and hardship,
he frequently bestowed grain and silk upon him.
Whenever he held court, he would sigh in admiration,
using him to encourage all his officials.
After Xù 續 was captured,
Cún 存 and Zhú 竺, Jī 緝, and others, together with Pǐ Dī 匹磾, defended the city against the invaders,
and the emperor further granted Cún 存 the titles of General of Yangwu and Administrator of Wuyi.
Lè 勒 repeatedly sent Jì Lóng 季龍 to attack them,
and they were exhausted by battle and defense,
unable to maintain their stand.
After a long time,
Pǐ Dī 匹磾 and his younger brother Wén Yāng 文鴦, along with Zhú 竺, Jī 緝, and others, were all captured.
Only Cún 存 managed to break through the encirclement and flee south,
but was killed by bandits on the road.
Xù 續 himself was eventually also killed.
Lǐ Jǔ 李矩
Lǐ Jǔ 李矩, courtesy name Shìhuí 世迴,
was a man from Píngyáng 平陽.
As a child,
when he played with other children,
he would always be their leader,
planning and directing them,
showing the sagacity of an adult.
When he grew up,
he became an official,
and escorted the former county magistrate to Cháng'ān 長安.
The General Who Conquers the West, the Prince of Liáng, Róng 肜, appointed him as a Yámén 牙門 (Gate Guard).
He rendered distinguished service in the campaign against the Dī 氐 people led by Qí Wànnián 齊萬年,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngmíng Tíng 東明亭.
Upon returning, he served as Dūhù 督護 (Commander) of his home commandery.
The Grand Administrator Sòng Zhòu 宋冑 wanted to replace him with his favored relative Wú Jī 吳畿.
Jǔ 矩 feigned illness and left.
Jī 畿 feared Jǔ 矩 would return,
so he secretly sent someone to assassinate Jǔ 矩.
However, someone came to his rescue,
and thus he escaped.
When Liú Yuánhǎi 劉元海 attacked Píngyáng 平陽,
the common people fled.
Jǔ 矩 was always loved by the villagers,
so they elected him as their wǔzhǔ 塢主 (fortress lord),
and he first garrisoned in Xíngyáng 滎陽,
later moving to Xīnzhèng 新鄭.
Jǔ 矩 was brave, resolute, and resourceful,
with an ambition to achieve great deeds.
The Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè 越, appointed him Grand Administrator of Rǔyīn 汝陰.
In the early Yǒngjiā 永嘉 era,
he ordered Jǔ 矩 and the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán 汝南, Yuán Fú 袁孚, to lead troops to repair the Qiānjīn É 千金堨 dam in Luòyáng 洛陽,
to facilitate water transport.
When Luòyáng 洛陽 could not be defended,
the Grand Commandant Xún Fān 荀藩 fled to Yángchéng 陽城,
and the General of the Guards Huá Huì 華薈 fled to Chénggǎo 成皋.
At that time, there was a great famine,
and the bandit leader Hóu Dū 侯都 and others frequently plundered people and ate them.
Many of Fān 藩 and Huì 薈's troops were devoured.
Jǔ 矩 attacked and eliminated Dū 侯都 and others,
then protected Fān 藩 and Huì 薈,
building houses for each of them,
and supplying them with grain.
When Fān 藩 took temporary imperial authority
and established a traveling court,
he provisionally appointed Jǔ 矩 as Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng 滎陽.
Jǔ 矩 attracted and pacified the scattered people,
and many from far and near attached themselves to him.
Shí Lè 石勒 personally led a large army to raid Jǔ 矩.
Jǔ 矩 sent the old and weak into the mountains,
ordered cattle and horses to be scattered everywhere,
and then set up an ambush to await them.
The bandits scrambled to seize the cattle and horses,
the ambush was sprung,
and a unified roar
shook the valleys,
and they were greatly defeated,
with many beheaded and captured.
Lè 勒 then retreated.
Fān 藩 reported to Emperor Yuán 元帝,
who promoted Jǔ 矩 to General of Champiom,
granted him an open carriage and pennant,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yángwǔ Xiàn 陽武縣,
and concurrently appointed him Grand Administrator of Hédōng 河東 and Píngyáng 平陽.
At that time, famine followed famine,
and there were also many epidemics.
Jǔ 矩 dedicated himself to comforting and assisting,
and the common people relied on him.
Just then, bandits from Cháng'ān 長安 moved east,
plundering extensively wherever they went.
Jǔ 矩 sent his generals to attack and defeat them,
recovering over a thousand women who had been plundered by the bandits.
His generals, considering them not part of Jǔ 矩's direct command,
wanted to keep them.
Jǔ 矩 said:
“They are all subjects of the state;
how can there be 'theirs' and 'ours'!”
So he released them all at once.
At that time, Guō Mò 郭默, the Grand Administrator of Hénèi 河內 provisionally appointed by Liú Kūn 劉琨, was besieged by Liú Yuánhǎi 劉元海,
and sought to return to Jǔ 矩.
Jǔ 矩 was about to send his nephew Guō Sòng 郭誦 to welcome him,
but dared not advance.
It happened that Liú Kūn 劉琨 sent his Staff Officer Zhāng Zhào 張肇,
leading over five hundred Xīanbéi 鮮卑 cavalry, including Fàn Shèng 范勝, to Cháng'ān 長安.
As Mò 默 was besieged and
the roads were blocked,
he intended to return and rely on Shào Xù 邵續.
When he reached Jǔ 矩's camp,
Jǔ 矩 said to Zhào 張肇:
“Mò 默 was appointed by Lord Liú 劉,
and for the affairs of the lord,
I will do whatever I know how.”
The Túcāi 屠各 people had long feared the Xiānbēi 鮮卑,
so they invited Zhào 張肇 to provide support,
and Zhào 張肇 agreed.
When the bandits saw the Xiānbēi 鮮卑,
they fled without a fight.
Sòng 誦 secretly dispatched light boats to cross the river,
and sent brave warriors to launch a night attack on Huái Chéng 懷城,
ambushing the bandits' remaining camp,
and again greatly defeated them.
Mò 默 then led his followers to Jǔ 矩.
Later, Liú Cōng 劉聰 sent his cousin Chàng 暢 with thirty thousand cavalry and infantry to attack Jǔ 矩,
who encamped at the former stronghold of King Hán 韓,
seven *lǐ* away.
He sent an envoy to invite Jǔ 矩.
As Chàng 暢 had arrived suddenly,
Jǔ 矩 had no time to prepare.
He sent an envoy to offer cattle and wine, feigning surrender to Chàng 暢,
while secretly concealing his elite and brave troops,
showing only his old and weak.
Chàng 暢 did not suspect him,
and threw a great feast for his chieftains,
everyone becoming drunk and full.
Jǔ 矩 planned a night attack,
but his soldiers, seeing the large number of bandits,
all showed fear.
Jǔ 矩 ordered Guō Sòng 郭誦 to pray at the shrine of Zhèng Zǐchǎn 鄭子產, saying:
“You, sir, once governed Zhèng 鄭,
and ill omens did not appear.
How can these barbaric Hú 胡 and smelly Jié 羯 be allowed to pass through your court!”
He then had a shaman publicly declare:
“Dōnglǐ 東里 has given instructions,
and will send divine troops to assist.”
When the officers and soldiers heard this,
they all eagerly vied to advance.
He then ordered Sòng 誦 and the Dūhù 督護 Yáng Zhāng 楊璋 and others to select a thousand brave men,
and launch a night attack on Chàng 暢's camp,
capturing many armored horses,
and beheading several thousand.
Chàng 暢 barely escaped with his life.
Previously,
Guō Mò 郭默, hearing that Jǔ 矩 was being attacked,
sent his younger brother Zhī 芝 to lead troops to reinforce him.
Upon hearing of the defeat of Chàng 暢,
Zhī 芝 then rushed to Jǔ 矩's aid.
Jǔ 矩 then gave Zhī 芝 five hundred horses,
divided his army into three columns,
and pursued the bandits at night,
again gaining a great victory before returning.
Earlier,
Cōng had sent his general Zhào Gù to garrison Luòyáng.
The Chief Clerk, Zhōu Zhèn, was not on good terms with Gù,
and secretly reported Gù's crimes.
When Jǔ defeated Chàng,
he found a letter from Cōng in the camp,
ordering Chàng, after pacifying Jǔ,
to proceed to Luòyáng,
arrest Gù and execute him,
and then replace Gù with Zhèn.
Jǔ sent the letter to Gù,
who immediately executed Zhèn and his son,
and then led a thousand cavalry to surrender.
Jǔ sent him back to guard Luòyáng.
A few months later,
Cōng dispatched his crown prince Càn, along with Liú Yǎshēng and others, at the head of 100,000 infantry and cavalry, to encamp on the north bank of Méngjīn.
Yǎshēng was separately sent to attack Zhào Gù at Luòyáng.
Gù fled to Yángchéngshān,
and sent his younger brother to report the emergency.
Jǔ sent Guō Sòng to garrison Luòkǒu to relieve him.
Sòng ordered his general Zhāng Pí to select a thousand elite soldiers and cross the river by night.
Càn's scouts reported that troops were arriving,
but Càn, relying on his large numbers,
was not concerned.
Soon, Sòng and the others arrived suddenly,
attacking from ten directions simultaneously.
Càn's forces were startled and thrown into disarray,
and at once collapsed and fled.
More than half were killed or wounded.
They then occupied Càn's camp,
capturing countless weapons, equipment, and military supplies.
When dawn broke,
Càn saw that Pí and his men were few,
and so he and Yǎshēng, with the remaining forces, attacked them again.
After more than twenty days of bitter fighting, they could not overcome them.
Jǔ advanced to relieve them,
sending three thousand brave men by boat to meet Pí.
The bandits arrayed their troops along the river,
using long hooks to grapple the boats.
After several days of continuous fighting, they could not cross.
Jǔ secretly sent his subordinate general Gé Zēng to cross the river at night and enter Pí's camp.
Pí, with over a thousand chosen elite cavalry,
slaughtered the captured cattle and horses,
burned the equipment,
and broke through the encirclement under cover of night,
fleeing to Wǔláo.
Cōng pursued them,
but failed to catch them and withdrew.
Cōng, in his rage and indignation,
fell ill and died.
The Emperor commended his achievements,
appointing Jǔ as Supervisor of Military Affairs of the Three Commanderies of Hénán, General Who Guards the West, and Administrator of Xíngyáng,
and enfeoffing him as Marquis of Xiūwǔ County.
When Liú Càn succeeded to the throne,
his tyranny and cruelty grew daily.
His general Jìn Zhǔn then raised an army and killed Càn,
along with his clan,
opened Cōng's tomb,
and mutilated his corpse.
He sent an envoy to Jǔ,
stating:
"Liú Yuánhǎi, a Xióngnú petty villain,
taking advantage of the great Jìn dynasty's troubles,
caused chaos in Yōu and Bìng provinces,
falsely claiming divine mandate,
leading to the two emperors being trapped and dying in the barbarian court.
I have now led my forces to escort the imperial coffins,
and request to report this to Your Majesty."
Jǔ swiftly submitted a memorial to the Emperor.
The Emperor sent Grand Censor Hán Yìn and others to escort the imperial coffins,
but before they arrived, Zhǔn had already been destroyed by Shí Lè and Liú Yào.
Jǔ, with too few troops to achieve success,
often sighed with indignation.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he appointed Jǔ as Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Sī Province, Inspector of Sī Province,
re-enfeoffed him as Marquis of Píngyáng County,
and his generalship remained as before.
At that time, the Administrator of Hóngnóng, Yǐn Ān, and the General Who Manifests Awe, Sòng Shǐ, along with four other armies, were all garrisoned in Luòyáng,
each suspicious of the others,
none with firm resolve.
Jǔ and Mò each sent a thousand cavalry to Luòyáng to stabilize the situation.
Ān and the others then conspired together and reported to Shí Lè.
Lè sent Shí Shēng with five thousand cavalry to Luòyáng,
and Jǔ and Mò's armies both retreated.
Soon after, the four generals again betrayed Lè,
sending envoys to beg for reception,
and Mò again sent five hundred infantry into Luòyáng.
Shí Shēng, seeing that the four generals were conspiring with each other,
could not feel secure,
and so he captured Sòng Shǐ's army,
crossed the river, and headed south.
The common people, one after another, returned to Jǔ,
and thus Luòyáng was emptied.
Jǔ then memorialized to appoint Guō Sòng as General Who Manifests Martial Might and Magistrate of Yángzhái,
to build a stronghold by the water,
both cultivating and defending,
as a plan to eliminate the bandits.
When Zhào Gù died,
Shí Shēng sent cavalry to raid Sòng.
Sòng had many strategies;
when the bandits arrived,
he invariably set up ambushes and defeated them,
gaining nothing from plunder.
Shēng was enraged,
and again led over four thousand cavalry to violently plunder various counties,
then attacked Sòng's stronghold.
After a brief engagement,
he retreated his army to Èbǎn.
Sòng led five hundred brave and strong men to pursue Shēng to Pánzhī Gùtíng,
and again dealt him a great defeat.
Jǔ, seeing Sòng's many achievements,
memorialized to grant him a vermilion banner and a curved canopy,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Jíyáng Pavilion.
Guō Mò wanted to invade Zǔ Yuē,
but Jǔ forbade it in vain,
and consequently Mò was defeated by Yuē.
Shí Lè sent his adopted son to attack Mò.
Mò feared endless future troubles,
and planned to surrender to Liú Yào.
He sent his military adviser Zhèng Xióng to Jǔ to discuss this,
but Jǔ refused and did not permit it.
Later, Lè sent his general Shí Liáng with five thousand elite soldiers to attack Jǔ.
Jǔ counterattacked but was unsuccessful.
Guō Sòng's younger brother Yuán was again captured by the bandits.
The bandits sent Yuán with a letter to persuade Jǔ, saying:
"Last year, Cáo Yí of Dōngpíng
and Yīlú of the west both became guests.
Jǔ, you are like an ox's horn,
why do you not surrender?"
Jǔ showed it to Sòng.
Sòng said:
"In the past, when Wáng Líng's mother was with the bandits,
he still did not change his mind.
What is my brother to him!"
Lè again sent Sòng a yak-tail whisk and a horse whip,
to show his earnestness,
but Sòng did not reply.
Lè's general Shí Shēng was garrisoned in Luòyáng,
greatly plundering Hénán.
Jǔ and Mò suffered greatly from famine.
Mò again persuaded Jǔ to surrender to Yào.
Jǔ, having been defeated by Shí Liáng,
then followed Mò's plan,
and sent an envoy to Yào.
Yào sent his cousin Yuè to encamp at Héyīn,
intending to conspire with Jǔ to attack Shí Shēng.
Lè sent a general to besiege Yuè,
who closed his gates and dared not venture out.
Mò was later defeated by Shí,
and secretly fled south to Jiànkāng.
Jǔ was greatly enraged upon hearing this,
and sent his general Guō Sòng and others with a letter to Mò.
He also instructed Sòng, saying:
"Do you not know the saying about 'when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold'?
It was entirely due to you that Guō Mò was welcomed.
If he flees in the face of danger,
you must detain him."
Sòng pursued him to Xiāngchéng.
Mò, knowing he had wronged Jǔ,
abandoned his wife and children and fled.
Sòng took his remaining troops and returned.
Jǔ treated Mò's wife and children as before.
Liú Yuè, having no outside reinforcements,
surrendered to Shí Jìlóng.
Among Jǔ's subordinate officers and soldiers, some secretly wished to return to Lè.
Jǔ knew this but could not suppress them,
so he led his forces south,
intending to return to the imperial court.
Most of his men deserted along the way.
Only Guō Sòng and military adviser Guō Fāng,
merits recorder Zhāng Jǐng,
chief clerk Gǒu Yuǎn,
and generals Qiān Tāo, Jiāng Bà, Liáng Zhì, Sīmǎ Shàng, Jì Hóng, Lǐ Guī, Duàn Xiù, and over a hundred others
abandoned their families to escort Jǔ.
When they reached Lǔyáng County,
Jǔ fell from his horse and died.
He was buried on Xiànshān in Xiāngyáng.
Duàn Pǐdī
Duàn Pǐdī was
a Xiānbēi from the Eastern Department.
His clan was strong and valiant,
and they were hereditary tribal chiefs.
His father, Wùwùchén,
sent troops to assist Wáng Yuè, Prince of Dōnghǎi, in campaigns, achieving merit.
Wáng Jùn memorialized to make him a close relative of the Jìn imperial family,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Liáoxī,
and married his daughter to Wùwùchén,
to form a border alliance.
When Emperor Huái ascended the throne,
he appointed Wùwùchén as Grand Chányú,
and Pǐdī as Left Worthy King,
to lead their forces to assist the state in campaigns,
provisionally granting him the title of General-in-chief Who Soothes the Army.
When Wùwùchén died,
his younger brother Shèfùchén allowed Wùwùchén's son Jílùjuàn to succeed to the title.
Liú Yào 逼 Luòyáng,
Wáng Jùn dispatched Dūhù Wáng Chāng and others to lead Jílù Juàn and his younger brother Wén Yāng, along with their cousin Mòbēi, to attack Shí Lè at Xiāngguó.
Lè was defeated and returned to his camp.
Mòbēi pursued him into the camp gate,
and was captured by Lè.
Lè held Mòbēi as hostage
and sent an envoy to seek peace with Jílù Juàn.
Jílù Juàn was about to agree,
but Wén Yāng remonstrated, saying:
“We were ordered to attack Lè.
Should we, for the sake of one Mòbēi,
deliberately release a captured enemy?
Not only would we displease Wáng Jùn,
but we would also have future troubles.
This must not be allowed.”
Jílù Juàn did not listen,
and ransomed Mòbēi with two hundred and fifty sets of armor and horses, and one basket each of gold and silver.
Lè returned him,
and also generously repaid Jílù Juàn with gold, jewels, and colored silk.
Jílù Juàn ordered Wén Yāng to form an alliance with Shí Jìlóng,
pledging to be brothers,
and then led his cavalry back.
Chāng and the others could not hold out alone,
and also returned.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
Pǐdī promoted Liú Kūn to be the Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū),
formed an alliance to attack Lè,
and also sent a proclamation to Shèfù Chén, Jílù Juàn, Mòbēi, and others, instructing them to gather from three sides at Xiāngguó.
Kūn and Pǐdī advanced and garrisoned at Gù'ān,
waiting for the various armies.
Lè was afraid,
and sent a secret envoy to heavily bribe Mòbēi.
Mòbēi, however, not only wished to repay his old favor,
but also, seeing that Pǐdī was out,
desired to raid and seize his state.
