So he secretly sowed discord between Pǐdī and Shèfù Chén and Jílù Juàn, saying:
“Should elder brothers follow their younger brothers?
Even if there is a victory one day,
Pǐdī alone will claim it.”
Shèfù Chén and the others thought this was true,
and led their armies back.
Pǐdī also stopped.
Coincidentally, Jílù Juàn fell ill and died.
Pǐdī rushed from Jì to attend the funeral,
reaching Yòuběipíng.
Mòbēi declared that Pǐdī intended to usurp power,
and sent out his army to defeat him.
Mòbēi then killed Shèfù Chén and his relatives and party members, over two hundred people,
and established himself as Chányú.
When Wáng Jùn was defeated,
Pǐdī assumed the governorship of Yōuzhōu.
Liú Kūn, from Bìngzhōu, sought refuge with him,
and again allied with Pǐdī,
together attacking Shí Lè.
Pǐdī was again defeated by Mòbēi.
His troops scattered,
and fearing Kūn would plot against him,
he then killed him.
Thereupon, the Jìn people dispersed.
Pǐdī could not secure himself,
and sought refuge with Shào Xù to the north.
Mòbēi again attacked and defeated him.
Pǐdī, wounded,
said to Xù:
“I, a barbarian, admired righteousness,
which led to the ruin of my family.
If you do not forget our old bond,
and advance with me to attack,
that would be your kindness.”
Xù replied:
“Relying on your prestige and virtue,
I, Xù, was able to show my loyalty.
Now that you are in trouble,
how dare I not be with you!”
They then combined their forces to pursue Mòbēi,
slaughtering and capturing almost all of them.
He also ordered Wén Yāng to attack Mòbēi’s younger brother in Jìchéng to the north.
When he returned,
eighty *lǐ* from the city,
he heard that Xù had already perished.
His men were afraid and scattered.
They were again intercepted by Shí Jìlóng.
Wén Yāng, with a few hundred of his personal guards, fought fiercely and broke through,
finally managing to enter the city.
Jìlóng again raided below the city.
Wén Yāng ascended the city wall and looked down,
wanting to sally forth and attack him,
but Pǐdī would not allow it.
Wén Yāng said:
“I am known for my bravery,
which is why the common people rely on me.
To see people being plundered and not rescue them
is not the act of a true man.
If the troops are disappointed,
who will again fight to the death for me!”
So he led several tens of valiant horsemen out to battle,
killing many Hu.
His horse became exhausted,
fell, and could not rise.
Jìlóng called out:
“Elder brother, we are both Róngdǐ;
for a long time, I have hoped we could cooperate.
Heaven has not thwarted my wish;
today we meet,
why fight again?
Please lay down your weapon.”
Wén Yāng cursed him, saying:
“You are a bandit and a tyrant;
you should have died long ago.
My elder brother did not follow my advice,
which is why you were able to get this far.
I would rather die
than be captured by you.”
Then he dismounted and fought desperately.
His spear broke,
and he continued fighting fiercely with his sword.
Jìlóng’s army from all four sides dismounted and formed a protective barrier of robes
to seize Wén Yāng.
Wén Yāng fought from *chén* (7-9 AM) to *shēn* (3-5 PM),
and was only captured when his strength was exhausted.
Great fear fell upon the city.
Pǐdī wanted to return to the court alone on horseback,
but Xù’s younger brother, Lè'ān Nèishǐ Jì, stopped him with armed troops.
Jì also wanted to seize the imperial envoy, Wáng Yīng, and send him to Jìlóng.
Pǐdī sternly rebuked him, saying:
“You cannot follow your brother’s will,
and you force me not to return to the court;
this is already too much.
Do you further wish to seize the emperor’s envoy?
Though I am a Húyí,
I have never heard of such a thing.”
He then said to Yīng:
“Pǐdī has received great favor for generations
and does not forget loyalty and filial piety.
Today, circumstances are pressing.
I wish to submit myself to the court,
but I am being forced
and cannot fulfill my loyalty.
If I can get a temporary reprieve,
as long as I am not dead,
my heart will not forget its origin.”
Thereupon, he crossed the Yellow River southwards.
Pǐdī put on court robes,
held the imperial insignia,
and with his retinue, went out to see Jìlóng, saying:
“I received the nation’s grace,
and my ambition was to destroy you.
Unfortunately, my own state fell into chaos,
leading to this.
Since I cannot die,
I also cannot treat you with respect.”
Lè and Jìlóng had always been sworn brothers with Pǐdī.
Jìlóng rose and bowed to him.
When Pǐdī arrived at Xiāngguó,
he again did not pay respects to Lè,
always wearing court robes
and holding the Jìn imperial insignia.
After a year,
there was a conspiracy in the state to make Pǐdī their leader.
The matter was exposed,
and he was killed.
Wén Yāng also died by poison,
only Mòbō survived.
After his death,
his younger brother Yá was established.
After Yá’s death,
his descendant, the grandson of his paternal great-uncle Jiùlù Juàn, Liáo, was established.
After Wùwùchén,
during the chaos and decline of Jìn,
they proclaimed their own titles,
occupied the territory of Liáoxī,
and ruled over the Jìn people.
Their territory extended west to Yōuzhōu,
and bordered the Liáo River to the east.
They ruled over approximately thirty thousand Hú and Jìn households,
and commanded forty to fifty thousand cavalry.
They constantly raided and plundered Shí Jìlóng,
engaging in continuous warfare.
Ultimately, they were defeated by Jìlóng,
who relocated tens of thousands of their remaining people to the Sì and Yōng regions.
Their son Lán again gathered troops
and troubled Jìlóng for a long time.
When the Shí clan fell,
Mòbō’s son Qínjiū gathered over ten thousand Hú and Jié people,
secured Wǎngyīnrén Shān,
proclaimed himself King of Zhào,
and submitted to Mùróng Jùn.
Shortly after, he was defeated by Rǎn Mǐn,
relocated to Yìmù,
and presumptuously assumed the imperial title.
Jùn sent Mùróng Kè to attack him.
Qín, fearing, surrendered.
Wèi Jùn (his clan cousin Gāi)
Wèi Jùn,
a man from Dōng'ā, Dōngjùn,
resided in Guānzhōng.
Initially, he was a minor official in Yōngzhōu.
During the defeat and chaos of King Héjiān Yóng,
he was made General Wǔwēi.
Later, he served as Du zhī Xiàowèi,
and was capable and effective.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
he and several hundred refugee families migrated east to the Xiáshí of Héyīn.
At that time, the capital was desolate and famine-stricken.
Jùn looted and obtained grain and wheat,
which he presented to Emperor Huái.
The Emperor appointed him General Yángwēi and Administrator of Píngyáng,
with his Du zhī position unchanged.
Due to the chaos, he did not take up the official post.
When Luòyáng fell,
he encamped at Shíliángwù north of Luòyáng,
caring for the remaining populace
and gradually repairing military equipment.
To those who had attached themselves to the enemy,
he first reasoned with them,
explaining that the destiny of the Great Jìn was long and prosperous,
and that it would soon be re-established.
Many returned to him.
If there were those who, relying on their distance, did not obey,
he dispatched generals to suppress them,
and they simply submitted,
without suffering further aggression.
Thus, people near and far were moved and pleased,
and those who came carrying their children on their backs gradually increased.
Liú Kūn, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Jùn as Hénán Yǐn.
At that time, Grand Commandant Xún Pān had established a traveling administration in Mìxiàn.
Jùn went to Pān to consult on military matters.
Pān was very pleased,
and invited Lǐ Jǔ to join the meeting.
Jǔ was about to go that night,
but Jǔ's subordinates deemed Jùn untrustworthy
and advised against going at night.
Jǔ said:
"Loyal ministers are of one heart,
what is there to doubt?!"
When they met,
host and guests enjoyed themselves thoroughly.
Jùn then formed an alliance with Jǔ and departed.
Liú Yào, wary of Jùn's growing support,
led his forces to besiege him.
Liú Yǎn and Guō Mò sent troops to his rescue.
Yào divided his forces to intercept them north of the river,
and ambushed them in a hidden location
to waylay Yǎn and Mò's armies.
He greatly defeated them,
capturing all of Yǎn's cavalry.
Jùn escaped by night,
but was captured by Yào,
and consequently died.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Píngxī.
His cousin, Gāi, took command of his forces.
Gāi, also named Hài,
originally resided as a transient in Yīnpán, Jīngzhào.
〔一一〕When King Héjiān Yóng attacked King Zhào Lún,
he made Gāi a Jiāngbīng Dūwèi.
When Liú Yào attacked Luòyáng,
he followed Jùn to the crisis,
first leading troops to guard Jīnyōngchéng,
and thus escaped harm.
When Yào withdrew,
the remaining populace relied on him.
At that time, Dù Yù's son Yǐn was Administrator of Hóngnóng,
stationed at Yīquánwù in Yíyáng county,
and was frequently plundered by various bandits.
Yǐn invited Gāi to jointly resist them.
Gāi dispatched his general Mǎ Zhān with three hundred men to Yǐn.
Zhān, knowing Yǐn was unprepared,
attacked and killed Yǐn by night,
then welcomed Gāi to take over the wù.
The people in the wù were terrified
and all submitted to him.
He then allied with Lǐ Jǔ and Guō Mò to resist the bandits.
Xún Pān then appointed Gāi General Wǔwēi,
to command the Yōngliáng people west of the city,
and tasked him with suppressing Liú Yào.
Emperor Yuán, acting on imperial authority,
added the titles of General Guānjūn and Administrator of Hédōng,
and made him Inspector-General of the three commanderies of Hédōng, Hénán, and Píngyáng.
Yào once attacked Lǐ Jǔ,
and Gāi defeated him.
When Jǔ was about to welcome Guō Mò,
Gāi sent troops to assist him,
and also allied with Rèn Yīn, the Hénán Yǐn.
Later, as famine and hardship grew,
Yào's raids came daily.
Gāi wished to lead his forces south,
but the people did not follow.
Gāi then fled alone on horseback to Nányáng.
The Emperor again appointed him Grand Commander of the Vanguard, General Píngběi, and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Mǎ Zhān led Gāi's remaining forces to surrender to Yào.
As Yào's conscriptions were harsh,
and Zhān was also arrogant and cruel,
Zhān's subordinates sent an envoy to summon Gāi.
Gāi secretly went to them,
and his people killed Zhān and welcomed Gāi.
Gāi moved to Xīnyě,
and led his forces to assist Zhōu Fǎng in suppressing Dù Zēng.
An imperial edict appointed Gāi Administrator of Shùnyáng.
When Wáng Dūn rebelled,
Gān Zhuó, Governor of Liángzhōu, did not comply.
Wishing to see Gāi's stance,
he tested him with Dūn's decree.
Gāi said:
"I originally left the bandits,
and am only loyal to the state.
Now Duke Wáng is raising an army against the Son of Heaven;
this is not something I should be involved with."
He thus resisted and did not respond.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Gāi led his forces to relieve the capital,
and his army was stationed at Shítou,
operating under Táo Kǎn's command.
Before Jùn was pacified,
Gāi fell seriously ill and returned to his camp,
dying on the way.
He was buried in Wǔlíng.
His cousin Xióng took command of his forces.
Guō Mò
Guō Mò,
a man from Huái, Hénèi.
He was humble and lowly in his youth.
With his bravery and strength, he served Administrator Péi Zhěng
as a commanding general.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
Mò led the remaining populace and became a wù owner,
using fishing boats to plunder travelers returning east.
Over the years, he accumulated great wealth,
and the number of refugees who attached themselves to him gradually increased.
He treated his officers and soldiers well,
and greatly won their hearts.
Mò's wife's elder brother, Lù Jiā of the same commandery, took several *shi* of official rice to give to his sister.
Mò considered this a violation of regulations
and was about to kill Jiā.
Jiā, fearing,
fled to Shí Lè.
Mò then shot and killed his own wife
to demonstrate his impartiality.
He sent an envoy to pay respects to Liú Kūn.
Kūn appointed Mò Administrator of Hénèi.
Liú Yuánhǎi dispatched his cousin Yào to attack Mò.
Yào set up three camps to besiege him,
intending to starve him to death.
Mò sent his wife and children as hostages,
and also requested grain.
After the grain was acquired,
he established defenses.
Yào was enraged,
drowned Mò's wife and children in the river, and attacked him.
Mò sent his brother Zhī to seek help from Liú Kūn.
Kūn, knowing Mò was cunning,
detained Zhī and delayed sending aid.
Mò sent another person to report the emergency.
Meanwhile, Zhī went out of the city to bathe his horse,
and Mò forced him to return with the envoy.
Mò then sent Zhī as a hostage to Shí Lè.
Lè, knowing Mò was treacherous,
forwarded Mò's letter to Liú Yào.
Mò had someone secretly obtain Lè's letter,
then broke through the siege and defected to Lǐ Jǔ.
Later, he joined forces with Jǔ to resist Liú and Shí.
Their deeds are recorded in Jǔ's biography.
At the beginning of the Tàixīng era,
he was appointed Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
Mò was defeated in battle against Shí,
and Jǔ's situation became increasingly dire.
Mò was deeply worried and fearful.
He relinquished his seal to his staff officer Yīn Jiào,
saying:
"Administrator Lǐ has treated me very well.
To abandon him now
leaves me no face to apologize.
You may announce my departure in three days."
He then fled to Yángzhái.
When Jǔ heard this,
he was furious.
He sent his general Guō Sòng to pursue Mò.
Sòng reached Xiāngchéng
and caught up with him.
Mò abandoned his family
and rode away alone.
When Mò arrived at the capital,
Emperor Míng appointed him General Zhēnglǔ.
Upon Liú Xiá's death,
Mò was made Northern Middle-ranked General, Supervisor of Huáiběi Military Affairs, and granted a ceremonial axe.
Xiá's former subordinates, Lǐ Lóng and others, plotted rebellion.
An imperial edict ordered Mò and Right Guard General Zhào Yìn to suppress them.
The imperial court was about to levy Sū Jùn,
fearing he would cause trouble.
They summoned Mò, appointed him General of the Rear,
and put him in charge of the Commander of Cavalry.
He achieved success in the initial battle.
When the six armies were defeated,
he fled south.
Xī Jiàn proposed building a fort in Dàyè Lǐ, north of Qǔ'ā,
to divide the rebel forces,
and had Mò guard it.
Jùn sent Hán Huàng and others to attack Mò very urgently.
Water in the fort became quite scarce.
Mò was afraid,
so he sent some men and horses out,
then secretly slipped out through the South Gate,
leaving men to hold the fort resolutely.
When Jùn died,
the siege was lifted,
and he was summoned to be General of the Right Army.
Mò enjoyed being a border general
and did not wish to be a palace guard.
When he went to answer the summons,
he said to General of the Pacified South Liú Yìn:
"I can resist the Hú barbarians but am not being used for it.
The General of the Right Army commands the forbidden troops;
if there's trouble on the frontier,
I would be sent out on an expedition,
only then would provisions be allocated,
the generals and soldiers would have no prior connection,
and trust would not be established.
Facing the enemy with this setup,
it would be rare not to be defeated.
At times like these, the official should choose talent for the court.
If a subject chooses their own official post,
how can there not be chaos!"
Yìn said:
"What you have discussed, though true,
is not something a humble person like me can achieve."
When he was about to depart,
he sought funds from Yìn.
At that time, Yìn had been ordered to be dismissed from office,
but did not immediately confess his guilt,
instead trying to clear himself,
and his extravagance and arrogance became even more pronounced.
People far and near were astonished by this.
Earlier,
when Mò was summoned to resist Sū Jùn,
he stopped at Xúnyáng
and met Yìn.
Yìn's subordinates Zhāng Mǎn and others looked down upon Mò,
treating him with contempt.
Mò always gritted his teeth in resentment.
By this time,
on the Laba Festival, Yìn sent Mò a pot of wine
and a whole duck.
Mò, facing the messenger, threw them into the water,
his indignation growing even greater.
Moreover, the immigrant Gài Zhūn had previously forcibly taken the daughter of Kǒng Wěi, whom Zǔ Huàn had killed, as his wife.
Wěi's family sought her return.
Zhāng Mǎn and others ordered her to be returned to her family,
but Zhūn refused.
Consequently, he had a quarrel with Yìn and Mǎn.
At this point,
Zhūn said to Mò:
"Liú Jiāngzhōu has not accepted his dismissal,
secretly harboring other plans.
He, along with the Chief Clerk and Sīmǎ Zhāng Mǎn and Xún Kǎi, are plotting day and night.
Their rebellion has already taken shape.
They only fear Marquis Guō (Mò himself)
and say they will eliminate Marquis Guō first before starting their uprising.
Disaster is imminent;
you should be deeply prepared."
Mò, already bearing resentment,
then led his followers to wait for the gate to open at dawn and attacked Yìn.
Yìn's officers wanted to resist Mò.
Mò shouted at them, saying:
"I have been ordered to carry out an extermination!
Those who move will have their three kinship groups punished!"
He then entered the inner chambers.
Yìn was still lying with his concubine.
Mò dragged him down and beheaded him.
He then went out and seized Yìn's staff, Zhāng Mǎn, Xún Kǎi, and others,
falsely accusing them of great treason.
He sent Yìn's head to the capital
and forged an imperial edict,
proclaiming it inside and outside.
He plundered Yìn's daughters and concubines, along with gold and jewels, and returned to his boat.
At first, he said he was going down to the capital,
but then he returned
and stayed in Yìn's former residence,
summoning Huán Xuān and Wáng Qiānqī.
Qiānqī feared being coerced
and persuaded Mò to become General of the Pacified South and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
Mò agreed.
Qiānqī then fled to Mount Lú,
while Huán Xuān held his ground and did not respond.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo feared he could not be controlled,
so he issued a general amnesty throughout the realm,
displayed Yìn's head on a large ferry,
and appointed Mò as General of the Western Central Army and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
[一二] Dèng Yuè, the Administrator of Wǔchāng, rushed to inform Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn.
[一三] Kǎn, hearing this,
threw up his sleeves and rose, saying:
"This must be a fraud!"
On that very day, he led his troops to attack Mò
and submitted a memorial detailing Mò's crimes.
Dǎo, hearing this,
then collected Yìn's head
and issued an edict for Yǔ Liàng to assist Kǎn in attacking Mò.
Mò wanted to seize Yùzhāng in the south,
but Kǎn had already arrived at the city walls
and built earthen mounds to overlook it.
All the armies gathered in large numbers,
besieging it in several layers.
Kǎn cherished Mò's valor and bravery
and wanted to spare his life.
He sent Guō Sòng to see Mò.
Mò agreed to surrender,
but Mò's generals Zhāng Chǒu, Sòng Hóu, and others feared Kǎn would kill them,
[一四] which led to their hesitation and inability to come out in time.
The attack grew more urgent.
Sòng Hóu then tied Mò up and sought to surrender,
and Mò was immediately beheaded at the army gate.
Forty of his accomplices died,
and their heads were sent to the capital.
The court historian said: The generals Shào, Lǐ, Wèi, Guō, and others,
during times of separation and chaos,
and while campaigning on horseback,
possessed enough prestige to command a multitude
and enough bravery and strategy to control people.
They defended dangerous cities,
confronted enemies a thousand *lǐ* away,
gathered loyal volunteers,
and resisted their foes.
Although they experienced every hardship,
they were all devoted to the imperial house.
And Jǔ was able to use a small force to defeat a large one,
winning many battles,
thus causing Xuánmíng to be enraged
and Shìlóng to suffer defeat.
It is a pity that he was weak in numbers,
and his achievement fell short by a single basketful of earth.
Compared to these men,
was he not the most outstanding?
As for Mò, he rose from a perilous situation
and joined the ranks of the court.
His resentment led to a petty grudge,
and calamity resulted in his extermination.
If not for his madness and outrageousness,
how could he have reached this point?
Duàn Pǐdī originally came from a distant region,
yet his heart was tied to the imperial court.
At first, he showed utmost loyalty during national crises,
and in the end, he upheld his integrity even in the barbarian court.
Since Sū Zǐqīng,
he is the only one.
Yuèshí's execution by the Duàn clan
was indeed due to his prestige;
Pǐdī's execution by Shìlóng
was also due to popular demand:
how swift are the consequences of fortune and misfortune!
The Odes say:
"No word is unanswered,
no kindness unrequited."
This is what it refers to.
The eulogy says: Shào and Lǐ, these generals,
were truly loyal and strong.
They faced hardships and dangers,
campaigning at outposts.
With limited strength for heavy tasks,
their achievements fell short, and their bodies perished.
Pǐdī was resolute and fierce,
sacrificing his life to preserve his integrity.
Mò was truly cruel and ruthless,
bringing calamity upon himself.
Collations and notes:
Biographies, Chapter 34, Wǔ (Thirteen Kings)
Emperor Wǔ had twenty-six sons: Empress Yáng Yuánhòu gave birth to Pílíng Dàowáng Guǐ, Emperor Huì, and Qín Xiànwáng Jiǎn.
Shěnměi Rén gave birth to Chéngyáng Huáiwáng Jǐng, Chǔ Yǐnwáng Wěi, and Chángshā Lìwáng Ài.
Xú Cáirén gave birth to Chéngyáng Shāngwáng Xiàn.
Kuì Cáirén gave birth to Dōnghǎi Chōngwáng Zhī.
Zhào Cáirén gave birth to Shǐpíng Āiwáng Yù.
Zhào Měirén gave birth to Dài Āiwáng Yǎn.
Consort Lǐ Fūrén gave birth to Huáinán Zhōngzhuàngwáng Yǔn and Wú Xiàowáng Yàn.
Yán Bǎolín gave birth to Xīndū Huáiwáng Gāi.
Chén Měirén gave birth to Qīnghé Kāngwáng Xiá.
Various concubines gave birth to Rǔyīn Āiwáng Mó.
Chéng Cáirén gave birth to Chéngdūwáng Yǐng.
Wáng Cáirén gave birth to Emperor Xiàohuái.
Empress Yáng Dàohòu gave birth to Bóhǎi Shāngwáng Huī.
The remaining eight sons had no mothers specified
and all died young,
nor were they granted enfeoffments or posthumous titles.
Thus, they are all omitted here.
Wěi, Ài, and Yǐng have their own biographies.
Pílíng Dàowáng Guǐ (軌), courtesy name Zhèngzé (正則),
was initially appointed Cavalier Commandant.
He died young at the age of two.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
an additional posthumous封號 (fēng hào) and谥号 (shì hào) were granted,
and he was succeeded by Yì (義), son of Chǔwáng Wěi (楚王瑋).
Qín Xiànwáng Jiǎn (秦獻王柬), courtesy name Hóngdù (弘度),
was deep, perceptive, and had a great capacity for judgment.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
he was enfeoffed as Rǔnánwáng (汝南王).
In the early Xiánníng period,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Nányángwáng (南陽王),
and appointed General of the Left, concurrently Right Army General, and Cavalier Regular Attendant.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) once visited Xuānwǔchǎng (宣武場),
and ordered Jiǎn (柬) to review and correct the military roster of thirty-six armies.
Jiǎn (柬) immediately spotted and removed errors upon a single glance.
The Emperor was impressed,
and he was particularly favored among all the sons.
As General of the Left, he resided in the former mansion of Qí Xiànwáng (齊獻王).
He was held in high esteem and favor,
and was watched by all under heaven.
His nature was benevolent and quiet,
without a reputation for quick wit or eloquence.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Qín (秦),
with eighty thousand households.
At that time, all other princes enfeoffed in the central lands had fifty thousand households;
because Jiǎn (柬) was of the same birth as the Crown Prince,
he was specially granted more.
He was transferred to General Who Guards the West, Western Róng Commandant, and was granted a Staff of Authority.
He went to his state along with the Princes of Chǔ (楚) and Huáinán (淮南).
When Emperor Huì (惠帝) ascended the throne,
Jiǎn (柬) came to court,
and was appointed驃騎將軍 (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), Kaǐfǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
additionally given the titles of Attendant and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and promoted to Grand General.
At that time, Yáng Jùn (楊駿) had been executed.
Jiǎn (柬), deeply pained by the ruin of his maternal clan,
was greatly worried and concerned.
He repeatedly stated Emperor Wǔ's (武帝) wishes,
requesting to return to his fief.
However, Rǔnánwáng Liàng (汝南王亮) kept Jiǎn (柬) to assist in governance.
When Liàng (亮) and Chǔwáng Wěi (楚王瑋) were executed,
people at the time said Jiǎn (柬) had foresight.
He died in the first year of Yuánkāng,
at the age of thirty.
The court and common people grieved for him.
His funeral was conducted according to the precedent of Qí Xiànwénwáng Yōu (齊獻文王攸),
and a軒懸之樂 (xuānxuán zhī yuè) was performed in his temple.
He had no sons,
so Yù (郁), son of Huáinánwáng Yǔn (淮南王允), was made his heir.
Both he and Yǔn (允) were killed.
In the second year of Yǒngníng,
he was posthumously given the epithet Dào (悼).
Later, Yè (鄴), son of Wúwáng Yàn (吳王晏), was made his heir.
When Emperor Huái (懷帝) died,
Yè (鄴) entered and ascended the imperial throne,
and the state was broken.
Chéngyáng Huáiwáng Jǐng (城陽懷王景), courtesy name Jǐngdù (景度),
was adopted as heir to his paternal uncle, Chéngyáng Āiwáng Zhào (城陽哀王兆).
He received his enfeoffment in the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
and died in the sixth year.
Dōnghǎi Chōngwáng Zhī (東海沖王祗), courtesy name Jìngdù (敬度),
received his enfeoffment in the fifth month of the ninth year of Tàishǐ.
After the Shāngwáng (殤王) died,
Zhī (祗) was again made heir to Zhào (兆).
He died that same year,
at the age of three.
Shǐpíng Āiwáng Yù (始平哀王裕), courtesy name Jùndù (濬度),
received his enfeoffment in the third year of Xiánníng,
and died that same year,
at the age of seven.
He had no sons,
so Dí (迪), son of Huáinánwáng Yǔn (淮南王允), was made his heir.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
he was re-enfeoffed as Hànwáng (漢王),
and was killed by Zhàowáng Lún (趙王倫).
Huáinán Zhōngzhuàngwáng Yǔn (淮南忠壯王允), courtesy name Qīndù (欽度),
was enfeoffed as Púyángwáng (濮陽王)
and appointed Yùqí Commandant (越騎校尉)
in the third year of Xiánníng.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Huáinán (淮南),
and went to his state,
overseeing all military affairs of Yáng (揚) and Jiāng (江) two prefectures, General Who Guards the East, and was granted a Staff of Authority.
In the ninth year of Yuánkāng, he came to court.
Originally,
when Mǐnhuái (愍懷) was deposed,
the deliberators intended to establish Yǔn (允) as the younger brother of the Crown Prince.
It happened that Zhàowáng Lún (趙王倫) deposed Empress Jiǎ (賈后),
and an imperial edict then appointed Yǔn (允) as Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Kaǐfǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Attendant,
with his superintendence as before,
and concurrently Central Protector of the Army.
Yǔn (允) was deep and resolute in character;
the palace guards and soldiers all respected and admired him.
Since Lún (倫) harbored ambitions of usurpation,
Yǔn (允) secretly knew of it.
He feigned illness and did not attend court,
secretly gathered loyal warriors,
and clandestinely plotted to execute Lún (倫).
Lún (倫) greatly feared him,
and transferred him to Grand Commandant,
outwardly showing great reverence,
but actually stripping him of his military power.
Yǔn (允) feigned illness and did not accept the appointment.
Lún (倫) sent an Imperial Censor to pressure Yǔn (允),
arresting his subordinates and below,
and impeaching him for high treason.
Yǔn (允) was enraged.
He looked at the edict,
and it was Sūn Xiù's (孫秀) own handwriting.
In a great rage,
he immediately arrested the Imperial Censor,
intending to execute him.
The Imperial Censor fled and escaped,
but Yǔn (允) executed two of his clerks.
He sternly said to his attendants,
"Zhàowáng (趙王) wants to destroy my family!"
He then led his state troops and seven hundred men from his personal guard directly out,
shouting loudly,
"Zhàowáng (趙王) has rebelled!
I am going to attack him!
Those who support Huáinánwáng (淮南王) should bare their left arm!"
Thereupon, many people rallied to him.
Yǔn (允) was about to head to the palace,
but the Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Yú (王輿) closed the Dōngyèmén (東掖門),
preventing Yǔn (允) from entering.
He then surrounded the Chancellor's residence.
The soldiers Yǔn (允) commanded
were all exceptional swordsmen from Huáinán (淮南).
In battle,
they repeatedly defeated Lún's (倫) forces,
killing over a thousand of Lún's (倫) soldiers.
The Crown Prince's Left Captain Chén Huī (陳徽) led the Eastern Palace troops, beating drums and shouting from within in response.
Yǔn (允) arrayed his troops in front of Chénghuámén (承華門),
and bows and crossbows fired simultaneously,
shooting at Lún (倫).
Flying arrows rained down.
The Master Scribe Sīmǎ Qí Mì (司馬畦祕) shielded Lún (倫) with his body,
and was struck by an arrow in his back and died.
All of Lún's (倫) officials stood hidden behind trees;
each tree was hit by hundreds of arrows.
This lasted from chén (辰) to wèi (未) (7-9 AM to 1-3 PM).
Huī's (徽) elder brother Huái (淮), who was then Director of the Central Secretariat,
sent his attendants with a Yúfān (虞幡) banner to break up the fighting.
Lún's (倫) son Qián (虔), who was Attendant,
was in the Dòngxiàshěng (門下省).
He secretly gathered brave men,
promising them wealth and high status.
Thereupon, he sent the Sīmǎ Dūhù (司馬督護) Fú Yìn (伏胤) to lead four hundred cavalry out from the palace,
carrying empty tablets,
falsely claiming to have an imperial edict to assist Huáinánwáng Yǔn (淮南王允).
Yǔn (允) did not realize this,
opened his formation to let them in,
dismounted to receive the edict,
and was killed by Yìn (胤).
He was twenty-nine years old at the time.
Originally,
when Lún's (倫) troops were defeated,
everyone was saying,
"Lún (倫) has been captured!"
The common people rejoiced greatly.
But when they later heard that Yǔn (允) had died,
none refrained from sighing.
All three of Yǔn's (允) sons were killed,
and thousands were implicated and exterminated because of Yǔn (允).
When Lún (倫) was executed,
Qíwáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) submitted a memorial vindicating Yǔn (允), saying:
"The late Huáinánwáng Yǔn (淮南王允) was loyal, filial, and sincerely devoted.
He worried for the state and forgot himself,
fighting bravely to quell the rebellion,
and was close to victory.
He encountered a dire fate from Heaven,
and suddenly met his demise.
The rebel faction committed wickedness,
and also harmed his three sons.
His aggrieved and cruel spirit,
none are not sorrowful for.
When righteous troops were raised,
the people of Huáinán (淮南) spontaneously organized themselves,
numbering over ten thousand,
each filled with indignation,
lamenting the destruction of the imperial lineage,
speaking with tears flowing.
I shall therefore make my son Chāo (超) his heir,
to comfort the living and the dead."
An imperial edict ordered a reburial,
granted him special rites,
and posthumously appointed him Grand Minister of Education.
When Jiǒng (冏) was defeated,
Chāo (超) was imprisoned in Jīnyǒngchéng (金墉城).
Later, Xiáng (祥), son of Wúwáng Yàn (吳王晏), was made his heir,
and appointed Cavalier Regular Attendant.
When Luòjīng (洛京) fell,
he was killed by Liú Cōng (劉聰).
Dài Āiwáng Yǎn
, whose courtesy name was Hóngdù, was enfeoffed in the tenth year of Tàikāng.
He had a debilitating illness in his youth
and did not go to his state.
Yǎn always resided in the palace.
When he died,
he had no sons.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng's son, Kuò, was made his heir
and was enfeoffed as Zhōngdū Wáng.
Later, he died with Yǐng.
Xīndū Wáng Gāi
, whose courtesy name was Xuándù, was enfeoffed in the third year of Xiánníng.
He died in the fourth year of Tàikāng,
aged twelve at the time.
He had no sons,
so his state was abolished.
Qīnghé Kāngwáng Xiá
, whose courtesy name was Shēndù, had a beautiful appearance
and was brilliant.
Emperor Wǔ loved him.
After he was enfeoffed,
he was adopted as the heir of his uncle, Chéngyáng Āiwáng Zhào.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
his fief was increased to include Bóhǎi Commandery.
He successively held the posts of Right General, Cavalry Regular Attendant, and Former General.
In the early Yuánkāng period,
he was promoted to Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn
and granted the additional title of Grandee Remonstrant-and-Consultant.
Xiá was timid and weak as an adult
and did not distinguish between right and wrong.
He was fond of women
and could not connect with scholars and officials.
When Chǔwáng Wěi raised his army,
he sent Xiá to arrest Wèi Guàn.
However, Guàn's former subordinate Róng Huì then killed all of Guàn's sons and grandsons.
Xiá was unable to prevent this
and was criticized by his contemporaries.
He died in the first year of Yǒngkāng,
aged twenty-eight at the time.
He had four sons: Tán, Yuè, Quán, and Duān.
Tán succeeded him.
When Chōng Tàisūn died,
Qíwáng Jiǒng presented a memorial, stating:
"The Eastern Palace is empty,
and there is no successor to the principal heir.
The great enterprise of the empire
and the sacred vessel of the emperor
must have a crown prince established
to secure the grand foundation.
Currently, the imperial harem has no pregnant women,
and it is not advisable to merely hope for future births and leave the imperial line vacant.
This is not the will of our ancestors
nor a long-term plan for the state.
According to ritual,
a brother's son is like one's own son.
Thus, when Hàn Chéng had no heir,
the succession came from Dìngtáo.
When Xiàohé's line was cut off,
Ān continued the succession.
These are the excellent precedents of previous kings
and the established models of past dynasties.
Qīnghé Wáng Tán's divine bearing is outstanding
and his wisdom matured early.
He was born to Kāngwáng's principal consort, Lady Zhōu.
Among the late emperor's numerous grandsons,
he is now the legitimate one.
In the past, Bó Jī was virtuous and intelligent,
and Wén succeeded to the throne.
Tán's maternal grandfather, Huī, has a family history of renowned virtue.
Tán should uphold the weighty responsibilities of the ancestral temple
and lead the endless imperial lineage
to pacify the eager hopes of the four seas.
Although Tán's brothers were all born from adopted lines,
an excellent and virtuous one can be chosen to return as an imperial scion
without changing his succession.
I have consulted with Grand General Yǐng and the various dukes, ministers, and gentry,
and they all share this great wish.
I request that the ceremonies be prepared
and a day chosen to welcome and prostrate before him."
Thus, Tán was established as the Crown Prince.
Soon after, Héjiān Wáng Yǒng forcibly moved the imperial carriage
and memorialized to establish Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng as the Imperial Younger Brother,
deposing Tán and restoring him as Qīnghé Wáng.
Initially,
when Tán was Qīnghé Shìzǐ,
the golden bells he wore suddenly developed raised bumps like sesame seeds.
His grandmother, Grand Consort Chén, considered it inauspicious
and had them destroyed and sold.
Diviners interpreted it as a sign of the great prosperity for Jìn,
and since Tán was an imperial scion,
it was an auspicious omen for him.
Its destruction and sale
symbolized the verification of Tán's deposition and his not completing his destiny.
In the early Yǒngjiā period,
Rènchéng Lǚ Yōng, former Commander of the Northern Army, and Chén Yán, Superintendent of the Household, plotted to establish Tán as Crown Prince.
The plot was discovered,
and he was imprisoned in Jīnyōng City.
Soon after,
he was murdered,
aged fourteen at the time.
He was buried with the rites of a commoner.
Yuè was initially enfeoffed as Xīncài Wáng.
When Tán died,
he was re-enfeoffed as Qīnghé Wáng.
Quán was initially enfeoffed as Shàngyōng Wáng.
When Emperor Huái ascended the throne,
he was re-enfeoffed as Yùzhāng Wáng.
In the second year,
he was established as the Crown Prince.
When Luòjīng fell,
he was captured by Liú Cōng.
Duān was initially enfeoffed as Guǎngchuān Wáng.
When Quán became Crown Prince,
Duān was transferred and enfeoffed as Yùzhāng,
with ceremonial rank equivalent to an imperial son.
He was appointed Cavalry Regular Attendant, Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Supervisor of all military affairs in Jiāngzhōu, and granted credentials.
When he was about to go to his state,
it happened that Luòyáng fell.
Duān fled east to Gǒu Xī in Méng.
Xī established him as Crown Prince.
Seventy days later,
he was captured by Shí Lè.
Rǔyīn Āiwáng Mó
, whose courtesy name was Lìngdù, died in the seventh year of Tàikāng,
aged eleven at the time.
He had no heir,
so his state was abolished.
Wú Jìngwáng Yàn
, whose courtesy name was Píngdù, was enfeoffed in the tenth year of Tàikāng.
He received Dan'yáng, Wúxīng, and Wú three commanderies as his stipend.
He successively held the posts of Shèshēng Jiàowèi and Hòujūn Jiāngjūn.
He and his elder brother Huáinán Wáng Yǔn jointly attacked Zhàowáng Lún.
When Yǔn was defeated,
Yàn was arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge,
who intended to kill him.
Fù Zhī argued with a stern countenance in the imperial court,
and then all the officials remonstrated.
Lún then demoted him to the rank of Bīntú Xiànwáng.
Later, he was transferred and enfeoffed as Dàiwáng.
When Lún was executed,
an edict restored Yàn's original fief,
appointed him as Shàngjūn Dàjiāngjūn, granted him a government office,
and conferred the additional title of Grandee Remonstrant-and-Consultant.
When Chángshā Wáng Yì and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng attacked each other,
Yì made Yàn the Vanguard Commander-in-Chief
and fought several battles.
During the Yǒngjiā period,
he became Grand Tutor and Grand General.
Yàn was humble and sincere by nature,
but his talent was inferior to average people.
Among all the sons of Emperor Wǔ, he was the least capable.
Also, he had a mild "wind illness" from a young age,
causing his gaze to be unsteady.
Later, it worsened,
making him unable to attend imperial audiences.
When Luòjīng fell,
Yàn was also killed,
aged thirty-one at the time.
When Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor.
He had five sons.
The eldest son, whose name is not recorded,
died with Yàn.
The other four sons were Xiáng, Yè, Gù, and Yǎn.
Xiáng succeeded Huáinán Wáng Yǔn.
Yè was Emperor Mǐn.
Gù was initially enfeoffed as Hàn Wáng
and later re-enfeoffed as Jìnán.
Yǎn was initially enfeoffed as Xīndū Wáng
and later re-enfeoffed as Jìyīn,
serving as Cavalry Regular Attendant.
All of them were captured by the rebels.
Bóhǎi Shāngwáng Huī
, whose courtesy name was Sīdù, died in the fifth year of Tàikāng,
aged two at the time.
His enfeoffment and posthumous title were added later.
The Four Kings of Yuán.
Emperor Yuán had six sons: Consort Xún gave birth to Emperor Míng and Lángyá Xiàowáng Póu.
Concubine Shí gave birth to Dōnghǎi Āiwáng Chōng.
Lady Wáng Cáirén gave birth to Wǔlíng Wēiwáng Xī.
Consort Zhèng gave birth to Lángyá Dàowáng Huàn and Emperor Jiǎnwén.
Lángyá Xiàowáng Póu (琅邪孝王裒), courtesy name Dàochéng (道成),
his mother, Lady Xún (荀氏),
entered the palace as a person of humble status.
Yuándì (元帝) ordered Consort Yú (虞妃) to raise him.
Póu (裒) first succeeded his paternal uncle, the Marquis of Chánglè Tíng (長樂亭侯), Hún (渾).
Later, he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Duke of Xuānchéng Jùn (宣城郡公),
and appointed General of the Rear.
When the Emperor became Jìn Wáng (晉王),
the officials proposed establishing a Crown Prince.
The Emperor considered that Póu (裒) had the capacity of a mature man,
surpassing Míngdì (明帝),
and casually said to Wáng Dǎo (王導):
"A son should be established based on virtue, not age."
Dǎo (導) replied:
"Both the Heir Apparent and Xuānchéng (宣城) are considered bright and outstanding;
thus, it should certainly be based on age."
Thereupon, the position of Crown Prince was settled.
Póu (裒) was then enfeoffed as Lángyá (琅邪),
succeeding the late Gōng Wáng (恭王),
and his emolument was changed to Wúhú (會稽) and Xuānchéng (宣城), totaling 52,000 households.
He was appointed Palace Attendant, Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Qīng (青), Xú (徐), and Yǎn (兗) three Prefectures, and General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and recalled to the capital.
He died in the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
at the age of eighteen.
He was posthumously granted General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry,
and additionally Palace Attendant.
When his consort, Lady Shān (山氏), died,
she was interred with him.
Mùdì (穆帝) further posthumously granted Póu (裒) Grand Tutor.
His son, Āi Wáng Ānguó (哀王安國), was enthroned,
but died within a year.
Dōnghǎi Āi Wáng Chōng (東海哀王沖), courtesy name Dàoràng (道讓).
As Yuándì (元帝) thought Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè's (東海王越) heir apparent, Pí (毗), had been lost to Shí Lè (石勒),
and his whereabouts unknown,
he appointed Chōng (沖) to succeed Pí (毗),
calling him the Heir Apparent of Dōnghǎi (東海).
The Commandery of Pílíng (毗陵) was added to his original enfeoffment, increasing it by ten thousand households,
and his emolument was changed to Xiàpī (下邳) and Lánlíng (蘭陵).
Yuè's (越) consort, Lady Péi (裴氏), was made Grand Consort,
and Chōng (沖) was appointed Colonel of Chángshuǐ (長水).
Excellent officials were chosen as his subordinates;
Liú Dān (劉耽) of Pèiguó (沛國) was made his Sīmǎ (司馬),
Yǔ Yì (庾懌) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) his Gōngcáo (功曹),
and Gù Hé (顧和) of Wúchú (吳郡) his Zhǔbù (主簿).
In the early Yǒngchāng (永昌) era,
he was promoted to General of the Central Army,
with the additional title of Palace Attendant.
When the Grand Consort of Dōnghǎi (東海) died,
Pí's (毗) funeral was then held.
Chōng (沖) then acceded to the princely title.
Yíngyáng (滎陽) was added to the state of Dōnghǎi (東海).
He was transferred to General of Chariots and Cavalry,
then moved to General of Agile Cavalry.
He died in the seventh year of Xiánkāng (咸康),
at the age of thirty-one.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, and honored with the ceremonial privilege of the Three Ducal Ministers.
He had no son.
When Chéngdì (成帝) was on his deathbed,
he issued an edict saying:
"Āi Wáng (哀王) has no heir;
the succession of the state is about to be cut off,
which causes me sorrow and distress.
Let the youngest son, Yì (弈), succeed Āi Wáng (哀王) as Dōnghǎi Wáng (東海王)."
Because the distance was too far,
Yíngyáng (滻陽) was removed,
and Líníchuān Jùn (臨川郡) was added to Dōnghǎi (東海) instead.
When Āidì (哀帝), as Lángyá Wáng (琅邪王), ascended the throne,
Yì (弈) was transferred to Lángyá Wáng (琅邪王).
The state of Dōnghǎi (東海) was then without an heir.
Yì (弈) later ascended to the great inheritance,
but Huán Wēn (桓溫) deposed him,
and he was restored as Dōnghǎi Wáng (東海王).
Soon after, he was demoted to Hǎixī Gōng (海西公),
and the state of Dōnghǎi (東海) was again without an heir.
In the third year of Lóng'ān (隆安),
Āndì (安帝) decreed that Yànzhāng (彥璋), the second son of Huìjī Zhōng Wáng (會稽忠王), be made Dōnghǎi Wáng (東海王),
to succeed Āi Wáng (哀王) as his great-grandson,
and his emolument was changed to Wúxīng Jùn (吳興郡).
He was killed by Huán Xuán (桓玄),
and the state was abolished.
Wǔlíng Wēi Wáng Xī (武陵威王晞), courtesy name Dàoshú (道叔),
was adopted to succeed Wǔlíng Wáng Zhé (武陵王喆).
He received his enfeoffment in the first year of Tàixīng (太興).
In the early Xiánhé (咸和) era,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
Later, Xiāngdōng (湘東) was added to the state of Wǔlíng (武陵).
He was appointed General of the Left,
then promoted to General of the Garrison Army,
with the additional title of Palace Attendant.
When Kāngdì (康帝) ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted Palace Attendant and Special Advance.
In the early Jiànyuán (建元) era,
he oversaw the Imperial Library.
When Mùdì (穆帝) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to General-in-Chief of the Garrison Army,
then promoted to Grand Tutor.
In the early Tàihé (太和) era,
he was additionally granted ceremonial feather canopies and military music,
allowed to enter court without rushing,
announced by his title and not his name,
and permitted to wear swords and shoes on the palace hall.
He humbly declined.
Xī (晞) had no academic learning but possessed military talent,
and was thus feared by Huán Wēn (桓溫).
When Jiǎnwéndì (簡文帝) ascended the throne,
Wēn (溫) memorialized about Xī (晞), saying:
"Xī (晞) is of imperial descent,
thus his favor and spiritual influence shine upon the world.
However, he fails to follow the royal norms
and cultivate himself with prudence,
instead gathering frivolous and reckless individuals,
and harboring fugitives.
Furthermore, his son Zǒng (綜) is arrogant and cruel,
〔一０〕tyrannizing others.
Yuán Zhēn's (袁真) rebellion
implicated him.
Recently, he has become suspicious and fearful,
which could lead to further disorder.
I request that Xī (晞) be dismissed from office,
and return to his fief as a prince.
Dismiss his heir Zǒng (綜) from office,
and relieve his son Yǎng (𩼔) of his Palace Attendant post."
Yǎng (𩼔), as Liáng Wáng (梁王), accompanied Xī (晞).
When Xī (晞) was dismissed,
he sent eighty-five horses and three hundred men with staffs back to Wēn (溫).
Wēn (溫) also coerced Xīncài Wáng Huǎng (新蔡王晃) to falsely accuse himself of conspiring with Xī (晞), Zǒng (綜), and the Editor Yīn Juān (殷涓), Grand Tutor's Chief Clerk Yǔ Qiàn (庾倩),
〔一一〕the Aide Cáo Xiù (曹秀), and Chamberlain Liú Qiáng (劉彊) and others in rebellion.
Consequently, they were arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review,
and Wēn (溫) requested their execution.
Jiǎnwéndì (簡文帝) did not consent.
Wēn (溫) then memorialized for Xī (晞) to be exiled to Xīn'ān Jùn (新安郡),
with his family following him entirely.
And Yīn Juān (殷涓) and others were executed by clan,
and Huǎng (晃) was deposed and exiled to Héngyáng Jùn (衡陽郡).
In the sixth year of Tàiyuán (太元),
Xī (晞) died in Xīn'ān (新安),
at the age of sixty-six.
Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝) personally mourned for three days in the West Hall,
and issued an edict saying:
"I am deeply moved and heartbroken.
Let his coffin be escorted back,
and also relocate the funerals of his consort Lady Yīng (應氏) and the late Heir Apparent Liáng Wáng (梁王), and all his family members shall return."
He further issued an edict saying:
"The former Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王), being of imperial descent,
exercised self-restraint and reflected on his faults.
Considering the compassionate and forgiving decree of the former court,
how can his sentiments and rites be left without a place?
Let him be posthumously enfeoffed as Xīnníng Jùn Wáng (新寧郡王),
with an estate of one thousand households."
Xī (晞) had three sons: Zǒng (綜), Yǎng (𩼔), and Zūn (遵).
Zūn (遵) succeeded him.
Zǒng (綜) was posthumously granted Attendant,
and Yǎng (𩼔) Palace Attendant.
In the twelfth year,
Xī's (晞) Wǔlíng (武陵) state was posthumously restored,
Zǒng (綜) and Yǎng (𩼔) each had their former offices restored,
and Yǎng (𩼔) returned to succeed the state of Liáng (梁).
Liáng Wáng Yǎng (梁王𩼔), courtesy name Xiánmíng (賢明),
was adopted to succeed Liáng Wáng Qiáo (梁王翹).
He rose to the office of Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud of Yǒng'ān (永安),
and was deposed together with his father Xī (晞).
He died,
and his son Hé (龢) succeeded.
His state was restored during the Tàiyuán (太元) era.
He died,
and his son Zhēuzhī (珍之) succeeded.
When Huán Xuán (桓玄) usurped the throne,
the people of the state, Kǒng Pú (孔樸), escorted Zhēuzhī (珍之) to flee to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
〔一二〕After Huán Xuán (桓玄) was defeated,
Zhēuzhī (珍之) returned to the court.
The Grand General Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) decreed:
"Liáng Wáng Zhēuzhī (梁王珍之) is wise and upright,
he endured dangers and avoided difficulties,
embraced righteousness and complied with order,
and hastened to the imperial court.
When Shòuyáng (壽陽) was in turmoil,
he remained firm in peril.
He may serve as Palace Attendant, with the title of Assistant."
He was successively promoted to General of Light Cavalry, Left Guard, and Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
When Liú Yù (劉裕) attacked Yáo Hóng (姚泓),
Zhēuzhī (珍之) requested to serve as his Consultant-Participant.
Liú Yù (劉裕) intended to weaken the imperial house,
so he falsely accused Zhēuzhī (珍之) and harmed him.
Zhōngjìng Wáng Zūn, courtesy name Màoyuǎn,
initially succeeded to the title of Xīnníng,
at the age of twelve.
He shed tears when receiving the appointment,
moving all those around him to sorrow.
Right General Huán Yī once visited Zūn,
and Zūn said:
"Why is the gate open to a member of the Huán clan?"
His attendants replied:
"Yī is a distant relative of Huán Wēn;
there is no animosity when they meet."
Zūn said:
"I heard someone's surname had a 'wood' radical,
and I wanted to kill him,
let alone the various Huán members!"
From this, he was praised in his youth for his intelligence.
When Xī was posthumously restored to the title of Wǔlíng Wáng,
Zūn was designated as his successor,
and successively held the positions of Sànqí Chángshì, Mìshū Jiān, Tàicháng, and Zhōnglǐngjūn.
When Huán Xuán came into power,
Zūn was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
Zūn was demoted to Péngzé Hóu
and dispatched to his fiefdom.
As he was traveling through Shítóu,
the night tide waters entered the Huái River,
his boat broke,
and he was unable to depart.
At that time, the righteous army rose,
and he returned to his princely residence.
The imperial court claimed to have received a secret edict,
instructing Zūn to oversee all affairs of state,
and he was given the additional titles of Shìzhōng and Dàjiāngjūn.
He moved into the Eastern Palace,
and was respected by all, both inside and outside the court.
He transferred and appointed many officials,
issuing edicts;
he also issued instructions as decrees.
When Emperor Ān was restored,
Zūn was further appointed Tàibǎo,
with an additional twenty Jian guards.
He died in Yìxī fourth year,
at the age of thirty-five.
An imperial edict granted him grave goods from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court attire,
one set of clothes,
one million cash,
and one thousand bolts of cloth.
He was posthumously appointed Tàifù with a commendation,
and his burial was accorded special rites.
His son, Dìng Wáng Jìdù, succeeded him
and was appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
Upon his death,
his son Qiúzhī succeeded.
When the Sòng dynasty rose,
the state was abolished.
Lángxié Dào Wáng Huàn, courtesy name Yàozǔ.
His mother was favored,
and Emperor Yuán loved him especially.
He first succeeded Hún, the Changlé Tínghóu, the emperor's younger brother,
and was later enfeoffed as Xiǎnyì Tínghóu.
Shàngshū Lìng Diāo Xié memorialized:
"In the past, the Línbò Hóu of Wèi appointed Xíng Yǒng as his household steward and
Liú Zhēn as his shùzǐ (son by a concubine or younger son).
Now the Marquis is young and weak;
it is fitting to select virtuous and enlightened individuals."
The Emperor issued a decree:
"The Línbò Hóu had a fief of ten thousand households,
and Zhí was exceptionally talented in his youth,
able to associate with Yóu Tián Sū.
Now, this late-born child is ignorant and weak;
how can this be compared?
This child was enfeoffed recently,
not out of favoritism for a young son.
My deceased brother should have been succeeded,
so I had no other choice.
A household steward and shùzǐ
are sufficient for managing ancestral sacrifices only;
how can it be appropriate to humble worthy talents to serve someone useless!"
When Huàn became critically ill,
the Emperor ceased his meals for him,
and then issued an edict to enfeoff him as Lángxié Wáng,
to succeed Gōng Wáng.
Shortly thereafter, he died
at the age of two.
The Emperor mourned ceaselessly.
When he was to be buried,
considering that Huàn had been enfeoffed as a princely state,
and adding adult rites,
he decreed the erection of a funeral gate and cypress path,
prepared both auspicious and inauspicious ceremonial attire,
and built a mausoleum park,
with numerous laborers.
Sūn Xiāo of Kuàijī, Right Chángshì of Lángxié State, submitted a memorial advising: "I have heard that laws, regulations, and institutions
were highly valued by the former kings,
and in rites of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
it is important not to exceed what is appropriate.
Therefore, in times of abundance, extravagance is not permitted,
and in times of famine, moderation
and reduction must be sought.
Court visits and joyous gatherings are sufficient to display the grandeur of the academies;
for funerals and accompanying the deceased,
the focus should be on expressing grief and honoring the deceased.
There should be no error of excessive extravagance above,
nor the difficulty of depletion
and exhaustion below.
Therefore, when Huá Yuán practiced lavish burial,
gentlemen considered it disloyal;
when Yíng Bó was extremely frugal,
Zhòngní praised him for adhering to propriety.
It is clear that harming wealth and wasting time
was censured
by the ancients;
while economy and simplicity
were lauded by the sages and worthies.
A saying goes,
'The influence of superiors upon inferiors
is like wind sweeping over grass.'
The capital city is a model,
emulated by the four directions,
which demonstrates
that moral education and legal systems
must be handled with utmost care.
Your Majesty, upon ascending the throne,
revived what was weak and remedied what was ailing.
Your sagely heart is diligent and humble,
striving for simplicity and frugality,
adhering to the old systems,
and still wishing to economize.
Yet for things not found in the rites,
you instead favor embellishment;
this is what my humble feelings find unsettling.
Items such as coffins, outer coffins, carriages, ceremonial flags, and fans
are prescribed by the old
ritual system
and should not be discarded.
However, a funeral gate and cypress path
are not found in the ritual texts.
On clear days, they are unnecessary;
in case of rain, they are useless.
These are things that should be economized to the utmost.
If
the expenses for Lángxié State at this one time
were not great,
I, being close to the inner circle,
would not speak out.
However, where the imperial court is located today,
princes, dukes, and all officials gather in the capital.
For any funeral,
countless pieces of timber and thousands of bamboos must be supplied,
with two funeral gate markers
clothed in fine bamboo and timber.
Their cost is already high,
and
they are not suitable for displaying solemn grief.
Such excessive embellishment
should be made simpler and cruder.
Furthermore, according to the Lǐjì,
for the burial of a ruler of a state,
the space between the coffin and outer coffin accommodates a zhù;
for a dàfū, it accommodates a hú;
for a shì, it accommodates a wǔ.
Since hú and wǔ are differentiated,
it is clear that the zhù is larger
than the hú.
The outer coffin surrounds the inner coffin,
so the outer coffin is not excessively large.
A saying goes,
'Burial means hiding';
'hiding desires depth and firmness.'
If the outer coffin is too large,
it is difficult to make it firm
and secure.
It is useless for the funeral
and harms financial resources.
Reducing rites during times of famine
is a constant national practice.
If, after reduction, it still exceeds the old standards,
this is something the state
should greatly regret.
Moreover, according to the rites,
before burial,
the coffin is moved to the ancestral temple and then proceeds.
Upon reaching the grave, it is interred.
On the day of the burial, one immediately returns to wail and perform the Yú sacrifice.
If so,
the coffin does not
stay overnight above the grave.
It is not that the sages were not saddened by their parents being in the earth or were without feeling for the tomb;
rather, it is because the tomb is not a place for the soul to rest,
hence the Yú sacrifice is performed at the burial.
palaces.
Initially, you built a thatched palace on the mountainside
and moved the divine coffin to the side of the tomb.
This, again, is not in accordance with the classics.
Matters not in accordance with ritual
cannot be used to instruct all nations.
Your servant, being utterly foolish and lowly,
suddenly seeks to reform past wrongs,
which may be called insane and blind, not knowing taboos.
However, today the天下 is in dire straits,
such as has been rare since ancient times.
The宗廟
and社稷
are remotely entrusted to half a prefecture across the Jiāngbiǎo,
and their decline is severe.
Added to this are drought and famine,
and the common people are exhausted and suffering,
not only lacking enough,
but fearing death.
This
is what Your Majesty, with your utmost benevolence, pities and commiserates,
and it is a matter of utmost gravity to worry about.
This is precisely the time to rectify corrupt customs
and change the old ways.
Yet, one is still to exhaust the weary
people
to undertake useless tasks,
and deplete the already distressed wealth
to incur needless expenses.
This is indeed what your servant dares not feel comfortable with.
Now, among the天
下, Lángxié
is the largest state.
If you were to cut off matters that are not in accordance with ritual
and diligently follow classical precedents,
upwards to demonstrate the utmost simplicity and transformative power of the sacred dynasty,
and downwards to establish an eternal
standard for myriad generations,
then these humble words might offer a small contribution,
and this speck of dust and drop of dew might augment the mountains and seas.
The memorial was shelved and not acted upon.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
Huàn's younger brother, Yù, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángxié,
who was later Emperor Jiǎnwén.
In the second year of Xiánhé,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Kuàijī,
and Emperor Kāng was made Prince of Lángxié.
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
Emperor Āi was made Prince of Lángxié.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
the Deposed Emperor was made Prince of Lángxié.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
Emperor Jiǎnwén again acted as regent for the ancestral sacrifices of the Lángxié Kingdom.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
the kingdom thus had no heir.
Before the Emperor's demise,
his youngest son, Dàozǐ, was enfeoffed as Prince of Lángxié.
In the seventeenth year of Tàiyuán,
Dàozǐ became Prince of Kuàijī,
and Emperor Gōng was made Prince of Lángxié instead.
When Emperor Gōng ascended the throne,
the Lángxié Kingdom was abolished.
Emperor Jiǎnwén had three sons:
Emperor Jiǎnwén had seven sons: Empress Wáng gave birth to Dàoshēng, Crown Prince Sī of Kuàijī, and Imperial Prince Yúshēng.
Consort Hú Shúyí gave birth to Yù, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, and Imperial Prince Zhūshēng.
Consort Wáng Shúyí gave birth to Imperial Prince Tiānlíú.
Lady Lǐ Fūrén gave birth to Emperor Xiàowǔ and Dàozǐ, Prince Wénxiào of Kuàijī.
Yúshēng, Zhūshēng, and Tiānlíú all died young,
and are thus omitted here.
Dàoshēng, Crown Prince Sī of Kuàijī, had the courtesy name Yáncháng.
When the Emperor was Prince of Kuàijī,
Dàoshēng was made Crown Prince and appointed Sànqí Shìláng and Jǐshìzhōng.
He was impulsive and restless by nature,
did not cultivate his conduct,
and frequently violated proper decorum.
Ultimately, he was confined and died,
aged twenty-four,
without issue.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
he once saw Dàoshēng and Yù, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, in broad daylight.
Yù said:
"Eldest Brother is hungry, poor, and suffering."
After speaking, they vanished.
The Emperor was grieved and moved,
and thereupon made Xúnzhī, the great-great-grandson of Yáng, Prince of Xīyáng, his heir.
Xúnzhī successively served as Prefect of Wúxīng.
When Líú Yù attacked Guānzhōng,
he appointed Xúnzhī as Cányì Cānjūn.
At that time, the imperial way was declining,
and Xúnzhī, being a distinguished member of the imperial clan,
was killed together with Zhēn, Prince of Liáng.
Yù, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, had the courtesy name Shēnrén.
He was intelligent and keen from a young age.
When Dàoshēng first lost imperial favor due to his lack of decorum,
Yù repeatedly advised him on the path of reverence and caution.
Dàoshēng did not heed him,
and Yù wept for him.
Emperor Jiǎnwén deeply admired and treated him as extraordinary.
He died at the age of seventeen.
After a long time,
he was posthumously granted the title Xiànshìzǐ.
In the early Níngkāng era,
he was posthumously appointed General of the Left,
given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì,
and posthumously enfeoffed as a Commander of a Commandery-Prince.
Bǎo, the great-grandson of Wēi, Prince of Wǔlíng, was made his heir.
〔一三〕His mother, Consort Hú Shúyí, was posthumously honored as Grand Consort of Línchuān.
Bǎo, whose courtesy name was Hóngwén,
successively served as Mìshūjiān, Tàicháng, General of the Left, Sànqí Chángshì, and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the Sòng dynasty was established,
he was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
demoted to Marquis of Xīfēng,
with an allowance of a thousand households.
Dàozǐ, Prince Wénxiào of Kuàijī, had the courtesy name Dàozǐ.
He was adopted as heir to Prince Xiào of Lángxié,
and was praised by Xiè Ān in his youth for his purity and indifference.
At the age of ten,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Lángxié,
with an allowance of 17,651 households,
and acted as regent for the Kuàijī Kingdom, which had 59,140 households.
In the early Tàiyuán era,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
then promoted to Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
Later, the dukes and ministers memorialized:
"Dàozǐ is unrivaled in kinship and virtue,
and ought to be rightly positioned as Sītú."
He firmly declined the appointment.
He was ordered to oversee the six departments of the Shàngshū;
shortly after, he was granted the title Kāifǔ
and concurrently held the position of Sītú.
When Xiè Ān died,
an imperial edict stated:
"With the recent loss of the wise chancellor,
the Huá and Róng tribes are not yet unified.
Unless one possesses brilliant virtue and eminent character,
none can manage and control affairs both internal and external.
Sītú and Prince of Lángxié, Dàozǐ, naturally embodies the Way
and possesses profound and discerning intelligence.
He indeed bears the weighty responsibility of Dàn and Shì
and should command the duties of the two Nán.
He may concurrently serve as Cǐshǐ of Yángzhōu, Lù Shàngshū, Jiǎjié, and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnsì.
All civil and military officials of the Wèifǔ
shall be assigned to the Piàojìfǔ."
He declined and did not accept.
After several years,
he concurrently served as Cǐshǐ of Xúzhōu and Tàizǐ Tàifù.
The dukes and ministers again memorialized:
"He ought to be promoted to Chéngxiàng, Yángzhōu Mù, granted the Jiǎhuángyuè,
with plumes, banners, drums, and trumpets."
He declined all and did not accept.
At that time, Emperor Xiàowǔ did not personally attend to all affairs of state,
but rather made it his business to drink and sing with Dàozǐ.
Wet nurses and Buddhist monks
were particularly close and intimate with them,
and all secretly wielded their power.
All those favored and received
came from the ranks of young eunuchs.
Most of the commandery governors and chief officials
were established by Dàozǐ.
Having concurrently held the general oversight of Yángzhōu,
his influence swayed the whole天下,
and as a result, officials and commoners flocked to him.
Wáng Guóbǎo, Minister of the Central Secretariat, was of a servile and sycophantic nature,
and was particularly favored and indulged by Dàozǐ.
Offices were obtained through bribery,
and governance and punishments were in disarray.
Moreover, he devoutly believed in Buddhist teachings
and spent lavishly,
making it unbearable for those below.
After the Tàiyuán era,
he engaged in prolonged banquets,
with disheveled hair and blurry vision,
and many state affairs were neglected.
Huán Xuán once called upon Dàozǐ
and found him drunk.
With guests filling the seats,
Dàozǐ stared with wide eyes and said to someone:
"Huán Wēn, in his later years, wanted to commit treason,
what do you say?"
Xuán prostrated himself, sweating, unable to rise.
Xiè Chóng, the Chief Clerk, held up his tablet and replied:
"The late Duke Xuānwǔ deposed the unworthy and enthroned the sagacious,
his achievements surpassed those of Yī and Huò.
Conflicting opinions
should be carefully considered."
Dàozǐ nodded and said:
"I know, I know."
Thereupon he raised his cup to Xuán,
and Xuán was then able to rise.
Because of this, Xuán felt increasingly insecure and gnashed his teeth at Dàozǐ.
At that time, the imperial administration was in disarray.
Xǔ Róng of Kuàijī, a general commanding the Left Guard encampment, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Currently, the clerks in the court bureaus, the military officers of the imperial guard, and the servants and maidservants who take their mothers' surnames—
originally slaves—
who have no native places or social ranks,
are all able to make proposals and offer opinions,
and are appointed as prefects and county magistrates.
They also hold positions within the court,
entrusting affairs to the hands of petty officials.
Buddhist monks and nuns and wet nurses
compete to promote their relatives and associates,
and also accept bribes,
then take charge of official positions and lead the populace.
They have none of the talents of Wèi Huò,
yet they are compared to the ancients,
this is the first grievance.
I have heard that the Buddha is a serene, distant, profound, and ethereal deity,
who teaches the Five Precepts,
which forbid alcohol and lust.
But those who now observe them
are impure and disrespectful to Āní,
indulging in alcohol and women;
this is the second transgression.
To cause a person's death
does not necessarily require personally slaying them with a blade.
If governance and teachings are unequal,
and people are brutally and arbitrarily killed without cause,
their heavenly lifespan will surely be cut short;
this is the third transgression.
A thief does not necessarily personally steal another's property.
When Jiāng Yǐ's mother lost her cloth,
the fault lay with the prefect.
Now, prohibitory laws are unclear,
and robberies are openly committed;
this is the fourth transgression.
Those in superior positions, in transforming their subordinates,
must take trustworthiness as their foundation.
Last year, an edict was issued,
commanding everyone to offer their full counsel,
but although numerous opinions were collected,
none were adopted;
this is the fifth transgression.
Nuns and monks form groups,
relying on their religious attire.
Even the basic Five Precepts,
they cannot adhere to,
how much less the subtle and profound teachings!
Yet, the deluded masses
compete to revere and serve them,
and they also exploit the common people,
taking their wealth under the guise of benevolence;
this also does not accord with the Way of giving charity."
He further stated,
"The Crown Prince should go out and supervise the Eastern Palace,
to greatly encourage virtuous conduct."
When the memorial was presented,
it was not attended to.
The Imperial Secretariat Director Fàn Níng also deeply discussed the merits and demerits.
The Emperor was thus gradually displeased with Dàozi,
though outwardly he always highly honored him.
Guó Bǎo was Níng's nephew,
who flattered and served Dàozi.
Níng memorialized requesting his dismissal.
Guó Bǎo was fearful,
and sent Yuán Yuèzhī of Chénjùn, through the nun Miào Yīn, to deliver a letter to the Crown Prince's mother, Chén Shúyuán,
〔一四〕stating that Guó Bǎo was loyal and diligent,
and should be trusted.
The Emperor thereupon became angry
and executed Yuèzhī.
Guó Bǎo was very afraid,
and again slandered Níng to the Emperor.
The Emperor, having no choice,
shed tears and exiled Níng to be the Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Dàozi thus became arrogant and unrestrained.
His favorite, Zhào Yá, came from a theatrical background,
and Rú Qiānqiū was originally a thief-catcher in Qiántáng.
Through bribery and flattery, they gained advancement.
Dàozi appointed Yá as the Administrator of Wèijùn,
and Qiānqiū as Cavalry General's Advisory Military Officer.
Yá built an eastern residence for Dàozi,
constructing mountains and digging ponds,
planting trees and bamboo;
the cost was enormous.
Dàozi had palace women set up a wine shop,
selling wine by the water,
and he and his intimates would board boats to drink and feast there,
finding amusement and pleasure in it.
The Emperor once visited his residence
and said to Dàozi:
"There are mountains within your residence,
allowing you to wander and admire the views;
this is very good.
However, the decorations are too extravagant,
which does not show frugality to the world."
Dàozi had no reply,
only assenting repeatedly,
and the attendants around them dared not speak.
When the Emperor returned to the palace,
Dàozi said to Yá:
"If His Majesty knew that the mountain was made of planks and earth,
you would surely die."
Yá replied:
"With you, Duke, here,
how dare I die!"
The construction became even more extensive.
Qiānqiū sold official positions and noble ranks,
amassing hundreds of millions in wealth.
Furthermore, Dàozi was beloved by the Empress Dowager,
receiving treatment akin to a family member.
Thus, he relied on her favor and, when drunk,
sometimes failed to show proper respect.
The Emperor became increasingly displeased,
yet because of the Empress Dowager,
he further bestowed honors and ranks upon him.
Wénrén Shì of Wúxīng, the Magistrate of Bópíng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Rú Qiānqiū, the Cavalry General's Advisory Military Officer, who assists the Chancellor,
rose from humble origins,
secretly wields power,
and ostentatiously sells imperial offices.
His son, Shòu Líng, was the Magistrate of Lè'ān,
and his corruption was rampant.
Fearing the law, he fled,
yet ultimately faced no punishment,
and arrogantly returned to the county.
Moreover, the families of nuns and wicked women
are swaying and disturbing the times.
Grain is cheap and people are starving,
with continuous streams of corpses,
due to the common people's poverty
and harsh labor demands and taxes.
Also, Yú Míngjué, the General Who Shakes Awe, came to the capital,
and his chief clerk Dài Liángfū was imprisoned for his earnest remonstrance,
nearly losing his life.
Yet, Míngjué was angered by drunkenness,
and Liángfū was dismissed for upholding loyalty.
Furthermore, powerful and favored ministers
each establish their own small offices,
appointing officials and assistants,
which is of no benefit to the government
and harmful to the state."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor became even more displeased,
but constrained by the Empress Dowager,
he could not dismiss anyone.
Instead, he sent Wáng Gōng to Yǎnzhōu,
Yīn Zhòngkān to Jīngzhōu,
Wáng Xún as a Privy Counselor,
and Wáng Yǎ as the Crown Prince's Junior Tutor,
to strengthen the imperial house
and secretly control Dàozi.
Dàozi again entrusted matters to Wáng Xù,
which led to factions competing fiercely,
and brotherly affection was completely lost.
The Empress Dowager often tried to reconcile them,
but Dàozi could not change.
Xú Miǎo, the Imperial Secretariat Director, considering that Dàozi was the closest relative to the state,
and that it was fitting for them to be harmonious,
leisurely spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"In the past, the enlightened ruler of Hàn
still regretted Huáinán;
Emperor Shìzǔ was intelligent and discerning,
yet felt shame for the Prince of Qí.
Between brothers,
it is indeed appropriate to be deeply cautious."
The Emperor accepted his advice
and again entrusted Dàozi as before.
At that time, someone composed a 'Poem from Yúnzhōng' to point out and criticize the imperial court, saying:
"The Chancellor King is deeply intoxicated,
carelessly issuing edicts.
Qiānqiū, the thief-catcher,
interferes with state affairs.
Wáng Kǎi adheres to convention,
Guó Bǎo competes wildly.
Jīngzhōu is magnanimous,
unfettered and difficult to describe;
Among those of great virtue are
Fǎhù and Wáng Níng;
Zhòngkān and Xiānmín
are particularly articulate in their speech;
Āndào of Dōngshān
maintains a noble and unyielding character.
Why is he not summoned
to be a pillar of the court?"
Jīngzhōu
refers to Wáng Chén;
Fǎhù
is Wáng Xún;
Níng
is Wáng Gōng;
Xiānmín
is the courtesy name of Xú Miǎo;
Āndào
is the courtesy name of Dài Kuí.
When Gōngdì was the Prince of Lángxié,
Dàozǐ was enfeoffed with the Commandery of Kuàijī,
and together with Xuānchéng, commanded fifty-nine thousand households.
When Āndì ascended the throne,
the officials presented a memorial:
"Dàozǐ should be promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàifù), Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Mù), Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān), and granted the Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè),
and be given special honors."
He repeatedly declined and would not accept,
and also relinquished the governorship of Xúzhōu.
An imperial edict commanded that all matters, both internal and external,
their every movement, be referred to him.
After the Emperor came of age,
Dàozǐ bowed his head and returned political authority,
and Wáng Guóbǎo then took overall control of state power,
his influence dominating the imperial court.
Wáng Gōng then raised an army to attack him.
Dàozǐ was afraid,
arrested Guóbǎo and handed him over to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi),
and together with his younger cousin, Wáng Xù, the Intendant of Lángxié, had them both executed,
to apologize to Gōng.
Gōng immediately withdrew his troops.

Dàozǐ begged to be relieved of his duties as Grand Commander of Internal and External Military Affairs (Zhōngwài Dūdū) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū) to apologize to the regional commanders,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
Dàozǐ's heir, Yuánxiǎn,
was then sixteen years old,
serving as Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng).
He resented Gōng
and requested Dàozǐ to launch an expedition against him.
Thereupon, Yuánxiǎn was appointed General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and the military and civil officials of the former Guard Headquarters (Wèifǔ) and Xúzhōu were all assigned to him.
At the time, Dàozǐ's consort passed away,
and the Emperor issued an edict saying:
"The consort of the Prince of Kuàijī was uniquely virtuous and worthy;
Our affection for her was like that for a close relative.
Her funeral shall now be given special honors,
entirely following the precedent of Empress Dowager Mù of Lángxié.
Yuánxiǎn has long been remarkably accomplished,
and is someone upon whom Our heart relies;
his sincerity and filial piety are truly profound,
and his extreme grief is difficult to overcome.
However, not to use family matters as an excuse to decline state affairs is
the clear principle of the Spring and Autumn period;
not to violate public regulations due to private mourning restrictions is
the changing ritual of the Middle Ages.
Thus, Mǐn Zǐ wore the waist-cord,
and the Mountain King (Shān Wáng) was forced to yield.
This is truly because deep sorrow comes from within,
while external comportment is demonstrated outwardly.
[一五]Ritual has no fixed time,
and the wise and sagely conform to this.
After the consort's funeral is complete,
he may resume his duties as before."
At this time, Wáng Gōng's power shook both internal and external affairs.
Dàozǐ was very afraid,
and again brought in Prince Shàngzhī of Qiáo as his trusted confidant.
Shàngzhī persuaded Dàozǐ, saying:
"The regional magnates are powerful and strong,
while the prime minister's authority is weak.
It is advisable to secretly establish a force
to protect yourself."
Dàozǐ considered this profoundly true,
and so appointed his Sīmǎ, Wáng Yú, as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu to guard against Gōng.
He and Shàngzhī and others consulted day and night,
watching for opportunities among the four quarters.
Wáng Gōng learned of this
and again raised an army, ostensibly to attack Shàngzhī.
Yīn Zhòngkān, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Yú Kǎi, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, and Huán Xuán, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, all responded to him.
Dàozǐ sent someone to persuade Kǎi, saying:
"Our original relationship was such
that we could be said to cut metal.
The drink in the tent last year,
the words exchanged as we tied our sashes –
how can you forget them?
Now you abandon old friends
and make new alliances;
do you forget the shame of Wáng Gōng's past insults and humiliation?
Are you perhaps willing to submit your person and serve him as a vassal?
If Gōng achieves his ambition,
he will consider you a capricious person
and will certainly not trust you.
How then can your wealth and honor be preserved?
Disaster and ruin will swiftly follow!"
Kǎi angrily replied:
"When Wáng Gōng formerly came for the imperial funeral,
the Prince-Chancellor (Xiàng Wáng) was so worried and helpless,
and I, knowing the urgency of the situation, immediately led my troops there.
Last year's affair
also saw me respond to command and exert myself.
I have served the Prince-Chancellor;
I have never betrayed him.
Since you could not resist Gōng,
you instead killed Guóbǎo.
Since then,
who among us would dare to roll up their sleeves for your affairs again!
Yú Kǎi truly cannot assist in the slaughter of others with a hundred lives;
I shall join the whole world in rising up
to punish and eliminate wicked ministers.
Why should I worry that offices will not open
or that titles will not arrive?"
At that time, Kǎi had already responded to Gōng's manifesto,
and was justly raising troops and horses.
When the messenger returned,
the court was anxious and afraid,
and thereupon, internal and external affairs were put on high alert.
Yuánxiǎn rolled up his sleeves and spoke with great emotion to Dàozǐ, saying:
"Last year we did not attack Wáng Gōng,
leading to this campaign today.
If we again yield to his desires,
then the disaster of the Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi) will be upon us!"
Dàozǐ drank strong wine daily,
and entrusted matters to Yuánxiǎn.
Although Yuánxiǎn was young,
he was intelligent and widely read,
with a resolute and sharp ambition,
taking the safety and danger of the state as his personal responsibility.
Shàngzhī served as his wings.
Those who praised him at the time
all said that Yuánxiǎn possessed the divine martial spirit of Míngdì.
Thereupon, he was made Supreme Commander of Punitive Expeditions (Zhēngtǎo Dūdū), granted an Imperial Insignia (Jiǎjié),
and given command of Wáng Xún, the Former General (Qián Jiāngjūn),
[一六]Xiè Yǎn, the Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn), and generals Huán Zhīcái, Máo Tài, Gāo Sù, and others, to attack Gōng
[一七]and destroy him.
Soon after, Yáng Quánqī, Huán Xuán, Yīn Zhòngkān, and others again arrived at Shítou.
Yuánxiǎn galloped back to the capital from Zhúli,

and dispatched Wáng Kǎi, the Administrator of Dānyáng, Huán Fàngzhī, the Administrator of Póyáng, Hé Sì, the Intendant of Xīncài, Wēn Xiáng, the Administrator of Yǐngchuān, Sūn Tài, the Administrator of Xīn'ān, and others,
mobilized tens of thousands of commoners and gentry from the capital,
and occupied Shítou to resist them.
Dàozǐ was about to go out and set up camp in the central hall,
when suddenly startled horses trampled through the army,
causing disarray,
and many who fled into the Jiāng (Yangtze River) drowned.
Zhòngkān, realizing Wáng Gōng had been defeated and killed,
fled westward in disarray,
and encamped with Huán Xuán at Xúnyáng.
The court maintained strict military defenses,
and there was turmoil both internally and externally.
An edict commanded Yuánxiǎn, with a hundred armored guards, to enter the palace,
and he was soon promoted to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
and also concurrently served as Commander of the Central Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn),
retaining his imperial insignia and superintendence as before.
Huì Dàozǐ (會道子) was ill,
further impaired by drunkenness.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) knew that the imperial court's hopes were turning away from him,
and plotted to seize his power.
He subtly encouraged the Son of Heaven to relieve Dàozǐ of his posts as Grand Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州刺史) and Minister of Works (司徒),
but Dàozǐ remained unaware of it.
Yuánxiǎn, feeling that he had abruptly gained such heavy power at a young age,
feared criticism.
Therefore, he appointed the Prince of Lángxié (琅邪王) to lead as Minister of Works,
while Yuánxiǎn himself became the Grand Governor of Yángzhōu.
Soon after, Dàozǐ sobered up
and only then realized he had lost his position.
He became furious,
but could do nothing about it.
Zhāng Fǎshùn (張法順) of Kuàijī (會稽), the Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江), a man of administrative talent,
became Yuánxiǎn's chief strategist.
He formed alliances with many supporters
and established numerous loyal followers.
From Huán Qiān (桓謙) downwards,
all the noble youths eagerly sought his acquaintance.
Yuánxiǎn's nature was harsh and cruel,
deciding life and death himself.
Fǎshùn repeatedly admonished him,
but he would not listen.
