He also rounded up those in the eastern territories who had been freed from slavery and become tenants,
calling them
"Lèshǔ" (樂屬)
and relocating them to the capital
to fill military service.
The eastern territories were in an uproar,
the people could not endure their plight,
and the whole empire suffered from it.
Soon after, Sūn Ēn (孫恩) took advantage of the opportunity to rebel.
Dàozǐ was granted the Yellow Battle-Axe (黃鉞),
and Yuánxiǎn was made Commander of the Central Army (中軍) to suppress him.
Yuánxiǎn was also granted the title of Overseer of the Affairs of the Secretariat (錄尚書事).
However, Dàozǐ indulged even more in prolonged drinking bouts,
entrusting all matters of government, large or small,
to Yuánxiǎn.
At the time, Dàozǐ was called the Eastern Overseer (東錄),
and Yuánxiǎn the Western Overseer (西錄).
The carriages of the Western Mansion (西府) crowded its gates,
while a sparrow net could be set at the Eastern Residence's (東第) entrance.
Yuánxiǎn had no good teachers or friends;
righteous counsel was unheard.
Flattery and praise arrived daily.
Some considered him a hero of his age,
others a refined and celebrated scholar.
Consequently, he believed himself peerless in the realm,
and so his arrogance and extravagance grew daily.
The Emperor, considering Yuánxiǎn's merits in assisting and upholding,
further elevated his birth mother, Lady Liú (劉氏), to the title of Lady of the Prince of Kuàijī (會稽王夫人),
with a golden seal and purple ribbon.
When Luòyáng (洛陽) fell,
Dàozǐ, lamenting the desecration of the imperial tombs,
submitted a memorial returning his official seals and ribbons,
requesting to return to his fief,
but was not permitted.
When the Grand Empress Dowager died,
an imperial edict allowed Dàozǐ to enter the palace in an imperial carriage.
Yuánxiǎn then subtly prompted the ritual officials to propose an议 (yì),
stating that his virtue was profound and his prestige great,
and since he oversaw all government affairs,
all officials, both inside and outside the court, should show him due respect.
Thus, all the high officials bowed to him.
At that time, military campaigns were frequently launched,
and the national treasury was depleted.
From the Minister of Works downwards,
they were given only seven sheng (升) of rice daily,
yet Yuánxiǎn incessantly amassed wealth,
becoming richer than the imperial house.
When Xiè Yǎn (謝琰) was killed by Sūn Ēn,
Yuánxiǎn sought to lead as Grand Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州刺史),

and was further granted the titles of Palace Attendant (侍中), General of the Rear (後將軍), Established as an Open Mansion with the Dignity of the Three Excellencies (開府儀同三司), and Commander-in-Chief of the Armies of Sixteen Provinces (都督十六州諸軍事).
His son, Yànzhāng (彥璋), was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王).
Soon after, due to a celestial anomaly,
Yuánxiǎn was relieved of his post as Overseer (錄)
and reinstated as Grand Secretary of the Secretariat (尚書令).
When Sūn Ēn reached Jīngkǒu (京口),
Yuánxiǎn barricaded Shítóu (石頭)
and led troops to resist,
but was repeatedly defeated.
Dàozǐ had no other strategies,
only praying daily at the Jiǎnghóu (蔣侯) Temple for protective magic.
Eventually, Sūn Ēn fled to Běihǎi (北海),
and Huán Xuán (桓玄) again occupied the upper reaches of the Yangtze.
He sent a letter to Dàozǐ, saying:
"The rebels reached the nearby suburbs,
and could not advance due to the wind, nor cause fires due to the rain.
They left because their provisions ran out,
not because their strength was exhausted.
After Guóbǎo (國寶) died,
Wáng Gōng (王恭) did not use that might to assume control of court affairs,
which clearly shows his heart did not intend to insult your Excellency.
Yet, you called him disloyal.
Among the current powerful confidants,
who possesses a clear reputation among the contemporary figures?
How can one say there are no good and worthy individuals?
It's simply that they cannot be trusted.
Only men of principle
can be expected to uphold trust and righteousness.
How can those who seek profit
have anything they value that would allow them to be entrusted with confidence?
This daily negligence,
for the past while, has led to today's disaster.
The responsibility of an Àhéng (阿衡) is immense;
words are not to be taken lightly.
Seeking blessings will bring them immediately;
defiance might lead to disaster.
The gentlemen at court,
do they not have their own thoughts?
They merely fear harm to themselves.
I, Xuán, holding a distant post,
therefore openly present the facts."
Yuánxiǎn read it and was greatly alarmed.
Zhāng Fǎshùn said to him:
"Huán Xuán inherits a prominent family background
and has always possessed an imposing spirit.
Having unified Yīn (殷) and Yáng (楊) forces,
he exclusively controls Jīngchǔ (荊楚).
However, the Huán (桓) clan has been in the western border regions for generations,
and some people are used by them,
while the forces under your command
are limited to the Sānwú (三吳) region.
Sūn Ēn's rebellion
devastated the eastern territories.
The registered households are starving,
and both public and private resources are insufficient.
Xuán will surely take advantage of this to unleash his treacherous cruelty.
I am privately worried about this."
Yuánxiǎn asked:
"What should be done about it?"
Fǎshùn replied:
"When Xuán first occupied Jīngzhōu (荊州),
public sentiment was not yet settled.
He is focused on pacifying the region
and has no time for other plans.
When he is in such a state,
we should dispatch troops to punish him.
Let Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) be the vanguard,
and your Excellency follow with the main army.
Huán Xuán's head will surely hang beneath your banner."
Yuánxiǎn thought this was right
and sent Fǎshùn to Jīngkǒu
to strategize with Láozhī.
However, Láozhī showed signs of doubt.
Fǎshùn returned
and advised Yuánxiǎn:
"Observing Láozhī's expression,
he will surely betray us.
It would be better to summon him and kill him.
Otherwise,
he will ruin our great undertaking."
Yuánxiǎn did not follow this advice.
Dàozǐ was soon appointed Palace Attendant (侍中) and Grand Tutor (太傅),
and was granted four aides: Left and Right Chief Clerks (左右長史), Chief of Staff (司馬), and Attendant Gentleman of the Secretariat (從事中郎).
The ceremonies for his exalted status
were meticulously observed.
The civil and military staff of the General of Agile Cavalry (驃騎將軍) were assigned to the Grand Tutor's Mansion.

Yuánxiǎn was additionally granted the titles of Palace Attendant (侍中), Grand General of Agile Cavalry (驃騎大將軍), Established as an Open Mansion (開府), Grand Commander of Punitive Expeditions (征討大都督), Commander-in-Chief of the Armies of Eighteen Provinces (十八州諸軍事),
and the Dignity of the Three Excellencies (儀同三司).
He was also granted the Yellow Battle-Axe (黃鉞)
and twenty swordsmen of the imperial guard
to attack Huán Xuán.
Láozhī was still made the vanguard.
Fǎshùn again spoke to Yuánxiǎn, saying:
"Since undertaking this great enterprise,
there has been no decisive authority.
Huán Qiān and his brothers are constantly the eyes and ears of the upper reaches.
Execute them
to isolate Jīngchǔ's supporters.
Moreover, whether the matter succeeds or not
depends on the vanguard.
But Láozhī is fickle.
Should a change occur,
disaster and defeat will immediately follow.
You should order Láozhī to kill Qiān and his brothers
to demonstrate his loyalty.
If he does not obey,
we should preemptively deal with him."
Yuánxiǎn said:
"Without Láozhī, we cannot stand against Huán Xuán.
Furthermore, to execute a major general at the beginning of an enterprise
would surely alarm people.
This 'two or three' is not acceptable."
At that time, the Yáng (揚) region was suffering from famine and scarcity,
and transport of provisions was disrupted.
Xuán cut off the river route,
stopping all commerce.
Consequently, both public and private resources were depleted,
and soldiers were given only acorns to eat.
The grand army was about to set out,
when Huán Xuán’s paternal cousin, the Cavalry General’s Chief Clerk, Shí Shēng, rode a messenger to inform Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán advanced to Xúnyáng,
then dispatched a proclamation to the capital,
detailing Yuánxiǎn’s crimes.
Shortly thereafter, Huán Xuán arrived at Xīyáng.
The Emperor, in military attire, bade farewell to Yuánxiǎn at Xīchí.
As soon as they boarded the boat, Huán Xuán arrived at Xīntíng.
Yuánxiǎn abandoned the boat and retreated to garrison at the Guózǐ Xuétáng.
The next day,
he arrayed his troops outside Xuānyángmén.
Many of Yuánxiǎn’s subordinate officials scattered and fled.
Some said that Huán Xuán had already reached Dàhéng,
and Liú Láozhī then surrendered to Huán Xuán.
Yuánxiǎn turned back and entered Xuānyángmén.
Láozhī’s Staff Officer, Zhāng Chàngzhī, led his troops in pursuit,
and Yuánxiǎn’s forces collapsed.
Yuánxiǎn fled into the Xiangfǔ,
with only Zhāng Fǎshùn accompanying him.
He asked Dàozǐ for advice,
and Dàozǐ wept in response.
Huán Xuán sent the Grand Tutor’s Attendant Officer, Máo Tài, to apprehend Yuánxiǎn and send him to Xīntíng.
He was bound to the front of a boat and counted his crimes.
Yuánxiǎn replied:
“I was misled by Wáng Dàn and Zhāng Fǎshùn.”
Thereupon, he was delivered to the Tíngwèi,
and he and his six sons were all executed.
Huán Xuán then memorialized:
“Dàozǐ’s excessive indulgence and unfilial conduct
deserve public execution.”
An imperial edict ordered his exile to Ānchéng Jùn,
with Imperial Censor Dù Zhúlín guarding him.
Ultimately, following Huán Xuán’s instructions, he was poisoned to death,
at the age of thirty-nine.
The Emperor mourned in Xītáng for three days.
When Huán Xuán was defeated,
the Grand General, Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn, received an imperial edict which stated:
“The late Grand Tutor, Áhéng for two generations,
was intimately involved with the royal house,
and his closeness to the worthy
was unparalleled in his position.
The Cavalry General-in-Chief managed the affairs of the court internally,
and displayed his might and strategy externally,
intending to quell the world’s troubles
to secure the nation’s destiny.
Heaven has not yet calmed the chaos,
and severe misfortune has befallen us,
stirring grief throughout the realm,
and pain that pierces both men and spirits.
Remembering the past,
our hearts collapse and shatter.
Now that the imperial destiny is restored to its proper course,
and both the visible and invisible realms are at peace,
it is fitting to honor the national framework
and uphold the old institutions.
Therefore, the Grand Tutor should be posthumously elevated to Grand Chancellor,
with special rites,
all in accordance with the precedent of Ānpíng Xiànwáng.
The Cavalry General should be posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant,
with feathered banners and drum music.
The Grand Chancellor’s tomb is now overgrown
and in an unsuitable, desolate state.
Once the southern roads are clear,
his divine coffin should be welcomed back.
The Grand Commandant’s tomb should also be relocated.
The Grand Astrologer should be ordered to find an auspicious day
and determine the site.”
Thereupon, the Palace Regular Attendant, Sīmǎ Xúnzhī, was sent to welcome Dàozǐ’s coffin from Ānchéng.
At that time, the bandits were not yet pacified,
so the funeral could not proceed promptly.
In the first year of Yìxī (405 CE),
he was interred together with the King’s Consort at the royal consort’s mausoleum.
Yuánxiǎn was posthumously granted the谥号 (shìhào) Zhōng.
The son of Línchuān Wáng Bǎozǐ, Xiūzhī, was made Dàozǐ’s heir,
and Consort Wáng was honored as Grand Consort.
During the Yìxī period,
there was someone who claimed to be Yuánxiǎn’s son, Xiùxī, who had fled to the蠻 (mán) tribes and arrived.
The Grand Consort requested that he be made heir,
so Xiūzhī returned to his separate residence.
Liú Yù suspected him of fraud and investigated him,
and indeed he was the Gentleman of the Palace, Téng Xiànnú, a quack physician.
He was eventually executed publicly.
The Grand Consort, unaware,
wept for him greatly.
Xiūzhī again became the heir.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the谥号 (shìhào) Dào Wáng.
He had no son,
and the state was abolished.
The court historian says: When Tàishǐ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he followed the institutions of the past,
and emulated the ancient kings,
making vast oaths across mountains and rivers,
and widely establishing feudal lords.
The sagely and martial,
rivaled those of Lǔ, Wèi, Yīng, and Hán;
as solid as a rock and as interlocking as dog’s teeth,
they formed alliances with Wú, Chǔ, Qí, and Dài.
However, he established laws in a time of chaos,
and entrusted power to the unworthy.
Hé Céng sighed at the lack of strategy in statecraft,
and Guō Qīn perceived the omens of peril and destruction.
When the imperial carriage made its final journey,
and the tomb earth was not yet dry,
national calamities repeatedly befell,
and court regulations relaxed and fell into disuse.
Compounded by the successive chaos of the Eight Princes,
the nine provinces were in turmoil,
the Róng and Jié tribes crisscrossed,
and the imperial carriage was severely constrained.
The jade branches and precious blossoms
vanished with the spears and arrows;
the vermilion canopies and green carriages
withered away with the dust and waves.
This led to the vast territory of Yǔ
being entirely occupied by jackals and wolves;
the diminished remnants of Zhōu
ultimately sank into misery.
Alas!
The ultimate limit of destiny,
it reached such a state!
Examining the records,
never before has such been heard.
Dàozǐ, being a close and worthy kin,
held the responsibility of the prime minister.
He indulged in alcohol,
and believed in slander and flattery.
This allowed the palace maids and old women to usurp court power,
and the treacherous and wicked to control the nation’s fate.
At first, the proper social order was destroyed,
and in the end, the ancestral altars and state collapsed.
Yuánxiǎn, at a young age,
was entrusted with the burden of state,
monopolized the court,
and disrespected his sovereign and kin.
He exerted the ordinary abilities of a mediocre talent,
to resist ruthless and villainous major bandits,
losing his army and destroying the state—
was this not fitting!
Thus, Yuánxiǎn was the Sūn Qiáng of Emperor Ān,
and Dàozǐ was indeed the Zǎi Pǐ of the Jìn dynasty.
Successive dynasties, in establishing their strongholds,
used them to protect the royal house;
but the Jìn dynasty, in enfeoffing its scions,
actually planted the seeds of chaos.
The Odes say:
“By cherishing virtue there is peace,
the sons of the clan are the city walls.
Do not let the walls be destroyed,
do not alone fear this.”
Since the walls were destroyed,
fear is indeed fitting!
The Jìn dynasty’s many disasters and chaos,
indeed stemmed from this.
Eulogy says: Imperial sons enfeoffed,
encountered this great misfortune.
Pestilence followed,
and disasters accumulated.
Qín Xiàn was intelligent and discerning,
Qīnghé cared for the inner court.
Huáinán was loyal and brave,
Xuānchéng possessed discernment.
Dàozǐ was muddled and wicked,
and thus overturned the national destiny.
Collations and Notes
Biographies, Volume 35: Wáng Dǎo (sons Yuè, Tián, Qià, Xié, Shào, Huì; Qià’s sons Xún, Mín; Shào’s son Mì)
Wáng Dǎo, courtesy name Màohóng,
was the grandson of Guānglù Dàfū Lǎn.
His father, Cái, was Zhèn Jūn Sīmǎ.
Dǎo, in his youth, had a discerning perception,
and his judgment was clear and far-reaching.
At fourteen,
the reclusive scholar Zhāng Gōng of Chénliú saw him and was struck by him,
telling his paternal cousin, Dūn:
“This child’s appearance and ambition
are the makings of a general and prime minister.”
He first inherited his grandfather’s title, Jíqiū Zǐ.
Sīkōng Liú Shí soon appointed him as Dōnggé Jìjiǔ,
then transferred him to Mìshū Láng, Tàizǐ Shèrén, and Shàngshū Láng,
but he did not take up any of these positions.
Later, he participated in the military affairs of Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè.
At that time, Yuán Dì was the Prince of Lángxié,
and he and Dǎo were already on very good terms.
Dǎo knew that the world was in chaos,
so he wholeheartedly supported and served him,
secretly harboring the ambition of restoration.
The Emperor also greatly valued and esteemed him,
and they were as close as sworn brothers.
When the Emperor was in Luòyáng,
Dǎo frequently urged him to return to his fiefdom.
It so happened that the Emperor was appointed to garrison Xiàpī,
and he invited Dǎo to be his Āndōng Sīmǎ.
For military strategies and secret plans,
Dǎo spared no effort.
When they moved the garrison to Jiànkāng,
the people of Wú did not submit.
After more than a month,
no gentry or commoner came to visit,
which troubled Dǎo.
When Dūn came to pay respects,
Dǎo said to him:
"Although the Prince of Lángxié is profoundly benevolent and virtuous,
his reputation and influence are still light.
Your prestige has already been established,
so you should do something to assist and save the situation."
It happened to be the third month, the Shangsì festival,
and the Emperor personally attended the lustration ceremony.
He rode in a shoulder-borne palanquin,
with full ceremonial regalia.
Dūn, Dǎo, and other notable figures all followed on horseback.
Jì Zhān and Gù Róng, people of Wú,
were both prominent figures in Jiāngnán.
They secretly observed this,
and seeing him thus,
were all astonished and fearful.
Thereupon, they led each other to bow by the roadside.
Dǎo then put forward a plan, saying:
"Of the ancient kings,
none failed to treat old officials with courtesy,
inquire about customs,
and humble themselves wholeheartedly
to attract talented individuals.
How much more so now, with the world in turmoil,
the nine provinces fragmented,
and a great undertaking just beginning,
when people are urgently needed!
Gù Róng and Hè Xún are
the hopes of this land.
It would be best to draw them in to win the hearts of the people.
Once these two arrive,
then no one will fail to come."
So the Emperor sent Dǎo to personally visit Xún and Róng.
Both men answered the summons and came,
and from then on, the region of Wúhuì was swayed,
and the common people pledged their loyalty.
From this time onward,
they gradually revered and supported him,
and the etiquette between ruler and minister was established.
Soon after, Luòjīng fell,
and sixteen or seventeen out of ten of the gentry and commoners from the Central Plains fled to the south of the Yangzi.
Dǎo urged the Emperor to gather these worthy gentlemen
and consult with them on affairs.
At that time, Jīng and Yáng were peaceful and stable,
with abundant households.
Dǎo's governance emphasized purity and tranquility.
He often urged the Emperor to discipline himself and cultivate virtue,
to assist the ruler and stabilize the state.
Consequently, he was especially trusted and relied upon,
their affection grew daily,
and the court and the public admired him.
He was called
"Zhòngfù."
The Emperor once casually said to Dǎo:
"You,
are my Xiāo Hé."
Dǎo replied:
"In the past, Qín was immoral,
the people were weary of chaos,
great villains ran rampant,
people embraced the Hàn virtue,
revolutionizing and rectifying,
making it easy to achieve success.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
up to the era of Tàikāng,
the high officials and powerful clans
competed in extravagance and luxury,
governance and education declined,
not adhering to laws and regulations.
All the high officials and gentry
were sated with peace and comfort,
thus allowing wicked individuals to exploit opportunities,
causing harm to the supreme Way.
However, difficulty always gives way to prosperity;
this is the constant law of Heaven.
Your Majesty is about to establish world-shaking achievements,
uniting and bringing together all under heaven.
Guǎn Zhòng and Yuè Yì
are in this position;
how can a mere subject of a state compare!
I wish you would profoundly broaden your divine thoughts,
and widely choose talented individuals.
Gù Róng, Hè Xún, Jì Shèn, and Zhōu Qǐ
are all outstanding talents of the southern land.
I wish you would treat them with utmost courtesy,
then the world will be at peace."
The Emperor accepted his advice.
At the end of Yǒngjiā,
Dǎo was transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng,
and additionally appointed as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
Dǎo submitted a memorial saying:
"In the past, Wèi Wǔ,
was a ruler who understood governance;
Xún Wénruò was
the foremost among meritorious ministers,
yet his enfeoffment did not exceed that of a Marquis of a Pavilion.
Cāngshū,
a favored son,
was posthumously granted no more than the rank of a detached commandant.
If we use these to regulate all things,
how can we not be constrained?
Nowadays, when governing a prefecture,
regardless of wisdom or folly, wealth or low status,
all are given heavy titles.
Whenever there are drums and canopies,
they are constantly taken as a standard.
Sometimes those who do not get them
feel shame and disgrace.
Official positions are mixed,
and the dignity of the court is diminished.
I, Dǎo, am burdened with heavy responsibilities,
yet cannot promote the high and profound,
but instead open up sources of disorder,
greedily seizing fame and position,
thereby disturbing established norms.
I respectfully send back the drums, canopies, and other elevated items.
Please let it begin with Dǎo.
May this distinguish the refined from the common,
and leave no confusion among the populace."
The Emperor issued an order saying:
"Dǎo's virtue is profound and his achievements are high,
he is someone I deeply rely on,
and it is indeed fitting to honor him with special ceremonies.
Yet, he restrains himself with a humble heart,
thinks of advancing with utmost sincerity,
and sets an example for the masses.
It is appropriate to follow his refined aspiration,
and thus conform to the principle of opening and closing."
He was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
and soon after, promoted to Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
When Mǐn Dì ascended the throne,
Dǎo was summoned to be Lìbù Láng,
but he did not accept the appointment.
When the State of Jìn was established,
Dǎo was made Céngxiàng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
When Huán Yí first crossed the river,
he saw the court was weak and
said to Zhōu Yǐ:
"Because of the many troubles in the Central Plains,
I came here hoping to survive,
but the court is so weak and isolated,
how can we manage!"
He was worried and unhappy.
He went to see Dǎo,
and they discussed world affairs extensively.
Upon returning,
he said to Yǐ:
"I have just seen Guǎn Yíwú;
I have no more worries."
The gentry who had crossed the river,
whenever they had a leisure day,
would invite each other to Xīntíng for drinks and banquets.
Zhōu Yǐ sighed in the middle of the gathering, saying:
"The scenery is not different,
but looking around, there is the difference of rivers and mountains."
They all looked at each other and wept.
Only Dǎo's expression changed grimly, and he said:
"We should all work together for the royal house,
and recover the divine land.
Why weep together like captives of Chǔ!"
The crowd wiped away their tears and thanked him.
Soon after, he was appointed Yòu Jiāngjūn, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Supervisor of all armies south of the Yangzi.
He was promoted to Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
additionally appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Grand Supervisor of all domestic and foreign armies, concurrently holding the posts of Zhōngshū Jiān and Lù Shàngshū Shì, and granted the Imperial Mace.
His position as Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
Because Dūn commanded six provinces,
Dǎo firmly declined the position of Grand Supervisor of domestic and foreign armies.
Later, he was stripped of the Imperial Mace due to an incident.
At that time, military campaigns were incessant,
and schools were not yet re-established.
Dǎo submitted a memorial saying: "The foundation of moral transformation lies in rectifying human relations,
and the rectification of human relations depends on establishing schools.
When schools are established,
the five teachings become clear,
virtue and rites are universally understood,
and the constant human norms
are upheld.
Then people will have a sense of shame and discipline,
the order of father and son, brothers, husband and wife, and old and young will be harmonious,
and the righteousness between ruler and minister will be firm.

Dì nǎi zhǐ.
Jìn Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī.
Yǐ tǎo Huá Yì gōng,
fēng Wǔgāng Hóu.
Jìnwèi Shìzhōng, Sīkōng, Jiǎjié, Lù Shàngshū,
lǐng Zhōngshū Jiān.
Huì Tàishān Tàishǒu Xú Kān fǎn,
Dì fǎng kěyǐ zhènfǔ Hénán zhě,
Dǎo jǔ Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài Yáng Jiàn.
Jì'ér Jiàn bài,
dǐ zuì.
Dǎo shàngshū yuē:
“Xú Kān pànlì,
jiǔ jī tiānzhū,
chén chuàngyì zhēngtǎo,
diàojǔ Yáng Jiàn.
Jiàn ànnào fù shī,
yǒusī jí fǎ.
Shèng'ēn jiàng tiāndì zhī shī,
quán qí shǒulǐng.
Rán chén shòu zhòngrèn,
zǒnglù jīhéng,
shǐ sānjūn cuò nǜ,
chén zhī zé yě.
Qǐ zì biǎnchù,
yǐ mù cháo lún.”
Zhào bù xǔ.
Xún dài Hè Xún lǐng Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Shí zhōngxīng cǎochuàng,
wèi zhì shǐguān,
Dǎo shǐ qǐ lì,
yúshì diǎnjí pō jù.
Shí Xiàohuái Tàizǐ wèi Hú suǒ hài,
shǐ fèng huì,
yǒusī zòu tiānzǐ sāncáo jǔ'āi,
qúnchén yī kū éryǐ.
Dǎo yǐwéi Huáng Tàizǐ fù'èr chénjí,
pǔtiān yǒu qíng,
yí tóng sāncáo zhī āi.
Cóng zhī.
Jí Liú Wèi yòngshì,
Dǎo jiàn jiàn shūyuǎn,
rènzhēn tuīfēn,
dàn rú yě.
Yǒushí xián chēng Dǎo shàn chǔ xīngfèi yān.
Wáng Dūn zhī fǎn yě,
Liú Wèi quàn Dì xī zhū Wáng shì,
lùnzhě wéi zhī wēixīn.
Dǎo shuài qúncóng kūndì zǐzhí èrshí yú rén,
měi dàn yì tái dàizuì.
Dì yǐ Dǎo zhōngjié yǒusù,
tè huán cháofú,
zhàojiàn zhī.
Dǎo qǐshǒu xiè yuē:
“Nìchén zéizǐ,
héshì wú zhī,
qǐyì jīnzhě jìn chū chénzú!”
Dì xiǎnéi zhí zhī yuē:
“Mào Hóng,
fāng tuō bǎilǐ zhī mìng yú qīng,
shì hé yán yé!”
Nǎi zhào yuē:
“Dǎo yǐ dàyì miè qīn,
kěyǐ wú wéi Āndōng shíjié jiǎ zhī.”
Jí Dūn dézhì,
jiā Dǎo shǒu Shàngshū Lìng.
Chū,
Xīdū fùmò,
hǎinèi sīzhǔ,
qúnchén jí sìfāng bìng quànjìn yú Dì.
Shí Wáng shì qiángshèng,
yǒu zhuān tiānxià zhī xīn,
Dūn dàn Dì xiánmíng,
yù gēngyì suǒlì,
Dǎo gùzhēng nǎi zhǐ.
Jí cǐ yì yě,
Dūn wèi Dǎo yuē:
“Bù cóng wú yán,
jǐ zhì fùzú.”
Dǎo yóu zhí zhèngyì,
Dūn wúyǐ néng duó.
Zì Hàn Wèi yǐlái,
cìshì duō yóu fēngjué,
suī wèi tōng dé zhòng,
xiān wú jué zhě,
lì bù jiā shì.
Dǎo nǎi shàngshū,
chēng
“wǔguān yǒu jué bì shì,
qīngxiào chángbó wú jué bù shì,
shèn shī zhìdù zhī běnyì yě”.
Cóng zhī.
Zì hòu gōngqīng wú jué ér shì,
Dǎo suǒyì yě.
Initially,
Dì loved Lángxié Wáng Pú,
and intended to discuss replacing the heir apparent.
He consulted Dǎo.
Dǎo said:
“Indeed, a son should be established based on seniority,
and Shào is also virtuous;
it is not appropriate to change this.”
Dì was still hesitant.
Dǎo remonstrated day and night,
so the Crown Prince's position was finally settled.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
Dǎo received the dying emperor's edict to assist in governance.
He was relieved of his position in Yángzhōu,
and promoted to Sītú,
entirely in accordance with Chén Qún's precedent in assisting Wèi.
Wáng Dūn again raised troops and advanced inland.
At that time, Dūn had just fallen ill,
and Dǎo immediately led his sons and younger brothers to express mourning.
When the masses heard,
they believed Dūn was dead,
and all became resolute.
When Dì attacked Dūn,
he granted Dǎo a jié (imperial credential),
made him commander-in-chief of all armies,
and concurrently governor of Yángzhōu.
After Dūn was pacified,
Dǎo was promoted to Shǐxīng Jùn Gōng,
with an estate of three thousand households,
and granted nine thousand rolls of silk.
He was promoted to Tàibǎo,
remaining Sītú as before,
with the privilege of wearing swords and shoes to court,
not having to rush when entering court,
and not having his name announced during ceremonies.
He firmly declined.
When Dì passed away,
Dǎo again, along with Yǔ Liàng and others, received the dying emperor's edict,
jointly assisting the young emperor,
who was Chéng Dì.
He was granted the feather canopy and drum and pipe music,
and twenty ceremonial guards.
When Shí Lè invaded Fùlíng,
an imperial edict appointed Dǎo Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) and acting Yellow Battle-axe bearer (jiǎ Huángyuè),
to go and suppress them.
His army reached Jiāngníng,
and the Emperor personally saw him off in the suburbs.
Soon after, the invaders retreated,
and he was relieved of the Grand Marshal position.
Yǔ Liàng intended to summon Sū Jùn,
and consulted Dǎo about it.
Dǎo said:
“Jùn is suspicious and dangerous,
and will surely not obey the edict.
Moreover, he is like a hidden sickness in the mountains and swamps;
it is advisable to tolerate him.”
He firmly argued against it, but was not heeded.
Liàng then summoned Jùn.
Subsequently, rebellion erupted,
and the imperial armies were defeated.
Dǎo entered the palace to attend to the Emperor.
Jùn, respecting Dǎo's virtue and prestige,
dared not harm him,
but still placed him above himself in his original official position.
Jùn also forced the imperial carriage to move to Shítóu,
but Dǎo's opposition was in vain.
Jùn came before the Emperor daily to speak offensively,
and Dǎo greatly feared unforeseen calamity.
At that time, Lù Yǒng, Kuāng Shù, and Jiǎ Níng all urged Jùn
to kill Dǎo,
exterminate all senior ministers,
and establish his own confidantes.
Jùn respected Dǎo and
did not accept their advice,
which caused Yǒng and others to become disloyal to Jùn.
Dǎo sent his staff officer Yuán Dān to subtly persuade and entice Yǒng and others
to plan to help the Emperor flee to the loyalist army.
However, Jùn's guards were extremely strict,
and the plan could not be carried out.
Dǎo then took his two sons and fled with Yǒng to Báishí.
When the rebellion was suppressed,
the imperial ancestral temples and palaces were all reduced to ashes.
Wēn Qiáo proposed moving the capital to Yùzhāng,
while the powerful families of the Sān Wú region requested moving it to Kuàijī.
The two proposals were in contention,
with no decision yet made.
Dǎo said:
“Jiànkāng
is the ancient Jīnlíng,
formerly an imperial city.
Furthermore, Sūn Zhòngmóu and Liú Xuándé both said it was a king's residence.
Ancient emperors did not necessarily move capitals based on abundance or scarcity;
if one can simply uphold the crown of the Wèi king Wén and his simple cloth,
then anywhere is suitable.
If one does not spin one's hemp,
then even a happy land will become desolate.
Moreover, the northern invaders, like wandering spirits,
are watching for our weaknesses.
If we show weakness for a single day
and flee to the southern barbarians,
considering the practicalities and prestige,
I fear it is not a good plan.
Now, it is especially important to calm things down with stillness,
and the public's sentiments will naturally be at ease.”
Because of this, Qiáo's and others' plans were not carried out.
Dǎo was adept at managing affairs,
and although there was no daily benefit,
the annual accounts had a surplus.
At that time, the imperial treasury was empty,
with only several thousand bolts of fine linen (shū) in the storehouse,
which could not be sold,
and national expenditures were insufficient.
Dǎo was concerned about this,
and so he and the court officials all made single garments of fine linen.
Consequently, the gentry eagerly competed to wear them,
and the price of fine linen soared.
He then ordered the officials in charge to sell it,
each bolt reaching one gold piece.
Such was the admiration for him at that time.
In the winter of the sixth year,
during the steamed offerings ceremony,
an imperial edict ordered the sacrificial meat to be given to Dǎo,
saying:
“Do not bow down.”
Dǎo, feigning illness, dared not accept.
Initially,
when the Emperor was young and immature,
he would always bow
when he saw Dǎo.
He also once wrote a personal letter to Dǎo,
which would say
“I humbly speak (huángkǒng yán),”
while official edicts written by the Secretariat
would say
“Respectful greetings (jìngwèn).”
This then became the established custom.
Afterwards, on New Year's Day,
when Dǎo entered,
the Emperor would still rise for him.
At that time, there was a severe drought,
and Dǎo submitted a memorial to resign his position.
The imperial edict said:
“Indeed, when a sagely king governs the world,
his actions align with the supreme Way,
and his influence pervades everything,
thus he can put human relations in order,
and all things find their proper place.
I bear the heavy responsibility of my ancestors,
placed above kings and dukes,
yet I cannot emulate the profound influence from above,
nor spread harmony throughout the universe below.
The persistent drought has lasted beyond its season,
and the multitude of people resent it.
The state's disarray
is solely due to me.
You, Gōng, embody the Way with brilliant wisdom,
your profound plans are far-reaching,
your achievements reach the four seas,
and you have assisted three generations of emperors.
The preservation of the national institutions
is truly like Zhòngshān Fǔ supplementing it.
Yet you humbly display modesty,
taking blame and yielding,
placing the faults of the sovereign
upon the prime minister,
which only increases his shortcomings.
You manage myriad affairs comprehensively;
it is impossible to have a single day without you.
Gōng, you should abandon the immediate virtue of humility
and follow the long-term strategy of governing the state.
Let the palace gate officials immediately dispatch the Imperial Attendants and below to urge him.”
Dǎo firmly declined.
The Emperor repeatedly pressed him,
and only then did he attend to affairs.
Dǎo was simple and moderate in his desires;
his granary had no stored grain,
and his clothes were not of double silk.
The Emperor, knowing this,
granted him ten thousand bolts of cloth
to cover his personal expenses.
Dǎo suffered from a lingering illness
and was unable to attend court meetings,
so the Emperor visited his residence,
indulging in wine and revelry.
Later, he allowed Dǎo's carriage to enter the palace hall,
such was the respect shown to him.
Shí Jìlóng’s raiding cavalry reached Lìyáng.
Dǎo requested to go out and attack them.
He was granted the titles of Grand Marshal (dàsīmǎ), Acting Bearer of the Yellow Battle-axe (jiǎhuángyuè), and Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (zhōngwàizhūjūnshì).
He was assigned Left and Right Chief Clerks (chángshǐ) and Marshals (sīmǎ),
and given ten thousand bolts of silk.
Shortly thereafter, the bandits retreated.
He was relieved of the Grand Marshal position,
but again appointed Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (zhōngwàidàdūdū),
and advanced to the rank of Grand Tutor (tàifù).
He was also appointed Chancellor (chéngxiàng),
and in accordance with Han regulations, the office of Minister of Works (sītú) was abolished and incorporated into his duties.
The imperial edict stated:
“I, having early suffered misfortune,
ascended the imperial throne.
Unable to cope with many difficulties,
disaster and chaos arose all around.
The Duke's civil accomplishments span the Nine Merits,
his military strategies embody the Seven Virtues.
Externally, he has unified the four seas;
internally, he has brought order to the eight policies.
Heaven and earth are thus at peace,
men and spirits are thus in harmony.
His achievements are like those of Yī Yǐn,
his dao as eminent as that of Jī Dàn.
Looking back to Táng Yú,
they promoted the outstanding and talented,
and charged all officials
to truly manage the myriad affairs.
I think of relying on your lofty counsel
to broadly carry out distant plans.
Therefore, drawing upon ancient precedents, I establish you as Grand Duke (shànggōng),
to forever be a pillar of Jìn.
Go and fulfill your office,
reverently propagate your teachings and guidance,
to assist the work of Heaven.
Is this not excellent!
Duke, be diligent!”
That year,
his wife, Lady Cáo, passed away.
She was posthumously awarded a gold seal and purple ribbon.
Originally,
Lady Cáo was jealous by nature,
and Dǎo greatly feared her.
He secretly built a separate residence
to house his many concubines.
When Lady Cáo learned of it,
she was about to go there.
Dǎo, fearing his concubines would be humiliated,
immediately ordered his carriage prepared.
Still fearing delay,
he drove the oxen forward with the handle of the fly whisk he held.
Cài Mó, the Minister of Works, heard of this
and joked to Dǎo,
“The court intends to bestow the Nine Awards (jiǔxī) upon Your Excellency.”
Dǎo did not realize the jest,
but merely modestly declined.
Mó then said,
“I have heard of no other items,
only a short-shafted ox-cart
and a long-handled fly whisk.”
Dǎo became greatly enraged
and said to others,
“When I traveled with many worthies in Luòzhōng,
when did I ever hear of a Cài Kè’ér?”
At that time, Yǔ Liàng, due to his high prestige and influential position,
was sent out to garrison a frontier post.
Táo Chēng, the Commander of the Southern Barbarians (nánmánxiàowèi), secretly suggested that Liàng intended to raise an army and march inward.
Some advised Dǎo to secretly prepare defenses.
Dǎo said,
“Yuánguī and I share the same fate, through good and bad times.
Such idle talk
should be silenced by the wise.
Even if your words were true,
should Yuánguī come,
I would simply don my angled cap and return home.
What is there to fear?”
He also wrote to Chēng,
stating that Duke Yǔ was the Emperor’s maternal uncle,
and ought to be treated well.
Thus, the slanderous rumors ceased.
Although Liàng resided in an outer garrison at the time,
he still wielded power in the court.
As he occupied the upper reaches of the river
and commanded a strong army,
many who sought advancement turned to him.
Dǎo was inwardly displeased.
Whenever the west wind brought up dust,
he would raise his fan to shield himself
and slowly say,
“Yuánguī raises dust to annoy people.”
Since the Han and Wei dynasties,
officials had not bowed at imperial tombs.
Dǎo, considering that Emperor Yuán had regarded him as a close friend from commoner days,
not merely a sovereign and minister,
would bow upon each advancement,
unable to contain his grief and sorrow.
Due to this, an imperial edict commanded all officials to bow at the tombs,
beginning with Dǎo.
This custom started with Dǎo.
He passed away in the fifth year of Xiánkāng,
at the age of sixty-four.
The Emperor mourned in the imperial court for three days,
and dispatched the Grand Herald (dàhónglú) with a tally to oversee the funeral arrangements.
The rites of burial gifts and shrouding
were entirely in accordance with the precedents of the Han Marquis of Bólù and King Xiàn of Ānpíng.

At the time of burial, he was provided with a nine-plume enclosed carriage (jiǔyóuwēnlúchē), a yellow imperial parasol with a left-facing banner (huángwūzuǒdú), feather canopies, drums, and wind instruments both before and after the procession, and a hundred imperial guards (wǔbēnbānjiàn) bearing swords.
No other famous minister of the Eastern Jìn restoration could compare to this.
The imperial edict stated:
“Indeed, high positions reward eminent virtue,
and lavish titles requite great merits.
As for marking one's trace upon closing the coffin,
nothing surpasses an honorific posthumous title.
Lasting renown for a hundred generations
is found therein.
You, Duke, transcended with profound emptiness,
your mysterious insight was noble and lofty.
With an even and detached mind, you constrained your thoughts;
embodying benevolence, you spread your kindness.
When leisurely engaged in external affairs,
your name was eminent throughout China.
When the time came to cleanse your cap-strings and serve,
your subtle calculations were uniquely active.
In the past, when Our Mid-Ancestor (Zhōngzōng) and Reverent Ancestor (Sùzǔ) established the foundation for the restoration,
you withdrew and dedicated your sincerity, and policy was set for the lands south of the river.
You folded your hands and settled your heart, and myriad tasks flourished.
Therefore, where your might was displayed,
bandits and tyrants changed their ways.
Where your civilizing influence was exerted,
the fierce and stubborn transformed their nature.
You harmonized the balance of yin and yang,
and clarified the principles of human relations.
Liáolǒng submitted to your influence,
and Dānxuè adhered to your light.
You achieved the lofty accomplishments of past ages,
and restored the merits of Xuān Wǔ.
The old order was not lost,
and you contributed to its planning.
Furthermore, you bore the burden of the dying Emperor’s charge,
and protected Us, the young Emperor.
Encountering difficulties and decay,
you adapted to both danger and safety with resignation.
You rescued what had fallen and saved it with dao,
supported what was collapsing and broadened it with benevolence.
You governed three reigns, and your profound dao became ever vaster.
We were still relying on your lofty counsel
to bring peace to the four seas.
But compassionate Heaven did not heed,
and you suddenly passed away.
This fills Our heart with shock and sorrow.
Though Yīn lost its Bǎohéng,
and Zhōu lost its Èrnán,
how can that convey this feeling!
Now I send the envoy, bearing a tally, the Palace Attendant (yèzhěpúshè) Rèn Zhān, to bestow the posthumous title Wénxiàn,
and offer a grand sacrifice (tàiláo).
If your soul has spirit,
may you rejoice in this honor and favor!”
His two younger brothers, Yǐng and Chǎng,
were both famous along with Dǎo in their youth.
People at the time compared Yǐng to Wēn Tàizhēn,
and Chǎng to Dèng Bódào,
but they both died young.
Dǎo had six sons: Yuè,
Tián, Qià, Xié, Shào, and Huì.
Yuè, courtesy name Chángyù,
had a great reputation when he reached manhood.
He served his parents with filial piety and tenderness,
and Dǎo loved him very much.
Dǎo once played Go with Yuè,
and they argued over the board.
Dǎo smiled and said,
“We are related by blood;
should it be like this?”
Dǎo was by nature frugal and restrained.
When sweet fruits under his curtain rotted,
he ordered them thrown away,
saying,
“Do not let Eldest Son know.”
Yuè少侍講東宮 (shǎo shìjiǎng Dōnggōng),
歷吳王友 (lì Wúwáng Yǒu)、中書侍郎 (Zhōngshū Shìláng)。
先導 (xiān Dǎo) 卒，
諡貞世子 (shì Zhēn Shìzǐ)。
先是，
導 (Dǎo) 夢人以百萬錢買悅 (mǎi Yuè)，
潛為祈禱者備矣。
尋掘地，
得錢百萬，
意甚惡之，
一皆藏閉。
及悅 (Yuè) 疾篤，
導 (Dǎo) 憂念特至，
不食積日。
忽見一人形狀甚偉，
被甲持刀，
導 (Dǎo) 問：
「君是何人？ 」
曰：
「僕是蔣侯 (Jiǎnghóu) 也。
公兒不佳，
欲為請命，
故來耳。
公勿復憂。」
因求食，
遂噉數升。
食畢，
勃然謂導 (Dǎo) 曰：
「中書 (Zhōngshū) 患，
非可救者。」
言訖不見，
悅 (Yuè) 亦殞絕。
悅 (Yuè) 與導 (Dǎo) 語，
以慎密為端。
導 (Dǎo) 還臺，
及行，
悅 (Yuè) 未嘗不送至車後，
又為母曹氏 (mǔ Cáoshì) 襞斂箱篋中物。
悅 (Yuè) 亡後，
導 (Dǎo) 還臺，
自悅 (Yuè) 常所送處哭至臺門，
其母長封作篋，
不忍復開。
悅 (Yuè) 無子，
以弟恬 (Tián) 子琨 (Kūn) 為嗣，
襲導 (Dǎo) 爵丹楊尹 (Dānyáng Yǐn)，
卒，
贈太常 (Tàicháng)。
子嘏 (Gǔ) 嗣，
尚鄱陽公主 (Shàng Póyáng Gōngzhǔ)，
歷中領軍 (Zhōnglǐngjūn)、尚書 (Shàngshū)。
卒，
子恢 (Huī) 嗣，
義熙 (Yìxī) 末，
為游擊將軍 (Yóují Jiāngjūn)。
恬 (Tián) 字敬豫 (Jìngyù)。
少好武，
不為公門所重。
導 (Dǎo) 見悅 (Yuè) 輒喜，
見恬 (Tián) 便有怒色。
州辟別駕 (biéjià)，
不行，
襲爵即丘子 (jí Qiūzǐ)。
性誕，
不拘禮法。
謝萬 (Xiè Wàn) 嘗造恬 (Tián)，
既坐，
少頃，
恬 (Tián) 便入內。
萬 (Wàn) 以為必厚待己，
殊有喜色。
恬 (Tián) 久之乃沐頭散髮而出，
據胡牀於庭中曬髮，
神氣邁，
竟無賓主之禮。
萬 (Wàn) 悵然而歸。
晚節更好士，
多技藝，
善弈，
為中興第一。
遷中書郎 (Zhōngshū Láng)。
帝欲以為中書令 (Zhōngshū Lìng)，
導 (Dǎo) 固讓，
從之。
除後將軍 (Hòujiāngjūn)、魏郡太守 (Wèijùn Tàishǒu)，
加給事中 (Jǐshìzhōng)，
領兵鎮石頭 (Shítóu)。
導 (Dǎo) 薨，
去官。
俄起為後將軍 (Hòujiāngjūn)，
復鎮石頭 (Shítóu)。
轉吳國 (Wúguó)、會稽內史 (Kuàijī Nèishǐ)，
加散騎常侍 (Sànqí Chángshì)。
卒，
贈中軍將軍 (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn)，
諡曰憲 (shì Yuē Xiàn)。
洽 (Qià) 字敬和 (Jìnghé)，
導 (Dǎo) 諸子中最知名，
與荀羨 (Xún Xiàn) 俱有美稱。
弱冠，
歷散騎 (Sànqí)、中書郎 (Zhōngshū Láng)、中軍長史 (Zhōngjūn Zhǎngshǐ)、司徒左長史 (Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ)、建武將軍 (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn)、吳郡內史 (Wújùn Nèishǐ)。
徵拜領軍 (Lǐngjūn)，
尋加中書令 (Zhōngshū Lìng)，
固讓，
表疏十上。
穆帝 (Mùdì) 詔曰：
「敬和 (Jìnghé) 清裁貴令，
昔為中書郎 (Zhōngshū Láng)，
吾時尚小，
數呼見，
意甚親之。
今所以用為令 (lìng)，
既機任須才，
且欲時時相見，
共講文章，
待以友臣之義。
而累表固讓，
甚違本懷。
其催洽 (Qià) 令拜。」
苦讓，
遂不受。
升平 (Shēngpíng) 二年卒於官，
年三十六。
二子：珣 (Xún)、珉 (Mín)。
珣 (Xún) 字元琳 (Yuánlín)。
弱冠與陳郡謝玄 (Chénjùn Xiè Xuán) 為桓溫 (Huán Wēn) 掾，
俱為溫 (Wēn) 所敬重，
嘗謂之曰：
「謝掾 (Xiè Yuàn) 年四十，
必擁旄杖節。
王掾 (Wáng Yuàn) 當作黑頭公。
皆未易才也。」
珣 (Xún) 轉主簿 (Zhǔbù)。
時溫 (Wēn) 經略中夏 (Zhōngxià)，
竟無寧歲，
軍中機務並委珣 (Xún) 焉。
文武數萬人，
悉識其面。
從討袁真 (Yuán Zhēn)，
封東亭侯 (Dōngtíng Hóu)，
轉大司馬參軍 (Dàsīmǎ Cānjūn)、琅邪王友 (Lángyá Wáng Yǒu)、中軍長史 (Zhōngjūn Zhǎngshǐ)、給事黃門侍郎 (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng)。
珣 (Xún) 兄弟皆謝氏 (Xièshì) 壻，
以猜嫌致隙。
太傅安 (Tàifù Ān) 既與珣 (Xún) 絕婚，
又離珉 (Mín) 妻，
由是二族遂成仇釁。
時希安 (Ān) 旨，
乃出珣 (Xún) 為豫章太守 (Yùzhāng Tàishǒu)，
不之官。
除散騎常侍 (Sànqí Chángshì)，
不拜。
遷祕書監 (Mìshūjiān)。
安 (Ān) 卒後，
遷侍中 (Shìzhōng)，
孝武 (Xiàowǔ) 深杖之。
轉輔國將軍 (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn)、吳國內史 (Wúguó Nèishǐ)，
在郡為士庶所悅。
徵為尚書右僕射 (Shàngshū Yòupúyè)，
領吏部 (Lìbù)，
轉左僕射 (Zuǒpúyè)，
加征虞將軍 (Zhēngyú Jiāngjūn)，
復領太子詹事 (Tàizǐ Zhànshì)。
時帝雅好典籍，
珣 (Xún) 與殷仲堪 (Yīn Zhòngkān)、徐邈 (Xú Miǎo)、王恭 (Wáng Gōng)、郗恢 (Xī Huī) 等並以才學文章見昵於帝。
及王國寶 (Wáng Guóbǎo) 自媚於會稽王道子 (Kuàijīwáng Dàozǐ)，
而與珣 (Xún) 等不協，
帝慮晏駕後怨隙必生，
故出恭 (Gōng)、恢 (Huī) 為方伯，
而委珣 (Xún) 端右。
珣 (Xún) 夢人以大筆如椽與之，
既覺，
語人云：
「此當有大手筆事。」
俄而帝崩，
哀冊諡議，
皆珣 (Xún) 所草。
Early in the Lóng'ān [era],
Guóbǎo was in power.
He planned to dismiss old ministers,
and Xún was transferred to be Shàngshūlìng.
When Wáng Gōng went to the imperial tomb,
he wanted to kill Guóbǎo.
Xún stopped him, saying:
"Although Guóbǎo will eventually cause disaster and chaos,
his crimes are not yet manifest.
If we act now, prematurely,
we will surely greatly lose the trust of both the court and the populace.
Moreover, with strong troops,
if we launch a surprise attack in the capital,
who will not call it rebellion!
If Guóbǎo does not change his ways,
and his evil spreads throughout the land,
then we can eliminate him in accordance with the public's wishes,
and there will be no worry of failure."
Gōng then stopped.
Afterwards, he said to Xún:
"Lately, looking at you,
you are exactly like Hú Guǎng."
Xún replied:
"Wáng Líng openly debated,
Chén Píng was cautious and silent;
just ask how things turn out in the end."
Gōng soon raised an army,
and Guóbǎo was about to kill Xún and others.
They narrowly escaped,
the story is in the Biography of Guóbǎo.
In the second year [of Lóng'ān],
Gōng again raised an army,
granting Xún a ceremonial staff of authority,
and promoting him to Wèijiāngjūn and Dūdū Lángyá Shuǐlù Jūnshì.
When the affair was settled,
he returned the granted staff [to the emperor],
and was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In the fourth year,
he resigned due to illness.
After more than a year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted Chējìjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ,
and given the posthumous name Xiànmù.
Huán Xuán wrote to Kuàijīwáng Dàozǐ, saying:
"Xún's spirit and mind were clear and insightful,
he was thoroughly versed in history and classics.
His elegant charm [and talent] were relied upon by both the public and private spheres.
Although constrained by suspicion and slander, his talent was not fully utilized;
however, when a gentleman is in court,
his beneficial influence is naturally great.
The times are difficult,
and to suddenly lose him,
the depth of my lament and fear
is not merely a sorrow for his elegant charm!
His arduous journey through many twists and turns,
experiencing all kinds of hardships,
though relying on your sagacious discernment,
also demonstrated his understanding of the circumstances.
He died a natural death,
so there is almost nothing to grieve.
But emotions arise at departures and arrivals,
and it is not easy to let go."
When Xuán became regent,
he posthumously re-granted him the title of Sītú.
Initially,
Xún had a rift with Xiè Ān.
When he heard of Ān's death while in the East,
he immediately went to the capital,
and visited his cousin Xiànzhī,
saying:
"I want to weep for Duke Xiè."
Xiànzhī was surprised and said:
"That is what is expected of Fǎhù."
Thereupon, he went straight forward and wept bitterly.
Fǎhù was
Xún's childhood name.
Xún had five sons: Hóng, Yú, Liǔ,
Rú, and Tánshǒu.
During the Sòng dynasty, they all achieved high renown.
Mín, courtesy name Jìyǎn.
He was talented and artistic in his youth,
excelling in running script,
his reputation surpassing Xún.
People at the time had a saying about him:
"Fǎhù is not bad,
but Sēngmí is hard to be a brother to."
Sēngmí was
Mín's childhood name.
At that time, there was a foreign śramaṇa [Buddhist monk],
named Típó,
who was profoundly learned in Buddhist principles.
He lectured on the Pítán Sūtra for the Xún brothers.
Mín was still young at the time,
and before the lecture was halfway through,
he declared he understood,
and immediately went to another room to lecture himself with śramaṇa Fǎgāng and several others.
Fǎgāng sighed and said:
"The main points are all correct,
but it's just not quite refined yet."
He was invited to be a zhǔbù in a province,
and recommended as xiùcái,
but he did not take office.
Later, he served as Zuòzhu, Sànqíláng, Guózǐ Bóshì, Huángmén Shìláng, and Shìzhōng,
succeeding Wáng Xiànzhī as Chángjiān Zhōngshūlìng.
The two had always shared a comparable reputation;
the world referred to Xiànzhī as
"Dàlìng" (Great Lìng),
and Mín as
"Xiǎolìng" (Little Lìng).
He died in the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán,
at the age of thirty-eight,
and was posthumously granted Tàicháng.
He had two sons: Lǎng and Liàn.
During the Yìxī era,
both successively served as Shìzhōng.
Xié, courtesy name Jìngzǔ,
was Fǔjūn Cānjūn under Emperor Yuán.
He inherited the title of Wǔgāng Hóu,
but died young,
without a son.
His brother Shào's son Mì was adopted as his heir.
Mì, courtesy name Zhìyuǎn.
He had a good reputation in his youth,
and was renowned alongside Huán Yìn of Qiáoguó and Wáng Suí of Tàiyuán.
He was appointed Bìshūláng,
inherited his father's title,
and was promoted to Bìshūchéng,
then successively served as Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ, Huángménláng, and Shìzhōng.
When Huán Xuán raised an army,
Mì was ordered to convey a message to Xuán.
Xuán held him in deep respect and affection.
He was appointed Jiànwēijiāngjūn and Wúguó Nèishǐ,
but before he reached his commandery,
Xuán appointed him Zhōngshūlìng, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, and Lìbù Shàngshū,
then promoted him to Zhōngshūjiān,
adding the title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and serving concurrently as Sītú.
When Xuán was about to usurp the throne,
he appointed Mì as concurrent Tàibǎo,
to present the imperial seal and tablets to Xuán.
When Xuán usurped,
he was enfeoffed as Wǔchāng Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng,
and given an additional twenty ceremonial swordsmen.
Initially,
Liú Yù was a commoner,
and the public did not yet recognize him,
but Mì alone held him in high regard,
and once said to Yù:
"You will be a hero of an era."
When Yù defeated Huán Xuán,
Mì was given the additional title of Shìzhōng to his original office,
and concurrently served as Yángzhōu Cìshǐ and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Since Mì had received favor from the Huán clan,
he often felt uneasy.
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yì once asked Mì:
"Where are the imperial seal and ribbons?"
Mì became even more afraid.
At that time, Wáng Suí, suspecting himself because he was a nephew of the Huán clan,
plotted rebellion,
and his father, sons, and brothers were all executed.
Mì's cousin Chén,
who was brave, strong, and fond of chivalry in his youth,
wanted to induce Mì to return to Wú [County],
and raise an army for rebellion.
He then persuaded Mì, saying:
"Wáng Suí committed no crime,
yet the righteous army executed him.
This is to eliminate those held in high regard by the public.
Brother, you established a reputation in your youth,
and your position is now so high.
Do you think you can avoid danger?
You cannot!"
Mì, out of fear, fled.
Liú Yù sent a memorial to the Dàjiāngjūn.
Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn
dispatched people to pursue him.
When Mì returned,
he was reinstated to his former responsibilities,
and given an additional twenty ceremonial swordsmen.
He died in the third year of Yìxī,
at the age of forty-eight.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Sītú,
and given the posthumous name Wéngōng.
He had three sons: Guàn, Qiú, and Xiù.
Upon entering the Sòng dynasty,
they all reached high official positions.
Shào (劭), courtesy name Jìnglún (敬倫),

successively held the posts of Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽 Tàishǒu), Director of the Personnel Bureau (Lìbù Láng), Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Education (Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ), and Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
Shào had a handsome appearance
and elegant demeanor.
Even his close family and attendants
never saw him in a disheveled state.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) greatly esteemed him.
He was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè),
and concurrently served as Commander of the Central Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn).
He was then dispatched as General of Establishing Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wúguó Nèishǐ).
Upon his death,
he was posthumously appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn)
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn (簡).
He had three sons: Mù (穆), Mò (默), and Huī (恢).
Mù was
Administrator of Línhǎi (Línhǎi Tàishǒu).
Mò was
Administrator of Wú Commandery,
with the emolument of 2,000 shí.
Huī was
General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
Mù had three sons: Jiǎn (簡), Zhì (智), and Chāo (超).
Mò had two sons: Jiàn (鑒) and Huì (惠).
During the Yìxī (義熙) era,
they all held prominent official positions.
Huì (薈), courtesy name Jìngwén (敬文).
He was quiet, modest, and upheld tranquility,
not striving for glory or profit.
He held several minor but respected official positions early on,
and was appointed Director of the Personnel Bureau, Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng), General of Establishing Might, and Administrator of Wú Commandery.
At that time, there was a famine and grain was expensive,
and many people starved to death.
Huì used his private rice to make porridge
and fed it to the starving,
saving many lives.
He was summoned and appointed Commander of the Central Army,
but did not accept the post.
He was transferred to Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū),
concurrently serving as Central Protector (Zhōnghùjūn),
and again became General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery.
After a short while,
Huán Chōng (桓沖) submitted a memorial requesting Huì be made Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ),
but he firmly declined to accept.
He was then transferred to Supervisor of the Five Commanderies East of Zhèjiāng (Zhèjiāngdōng Wǔ Jùn Dūdū), Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn), and Administrator of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Nèishǐ),
advanced to the title of General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn),
and additionally appointed Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
He died in office
and was posthumously appointed General of the Guards (Wèijiāngjūn).
His son Yǐn (廞)
successively held the posts of Mid-Palace Clerk to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ) and Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Education.
Due to his mother's mourning,
he resided in Wú.
When Wáng Gōng (王恭) raised an army,
he provisionally appointed Yǐn as General of Establishing Martiality (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery,
ordering him to raise an army
to provide support.
Yǐn immediately donned mourning clothes and assembled a force,
executing those who opposed him.
He then dispatched the former Administrator of Wú Commandery, Yú Xiàofù (虞嘯父), and others to enter Wúxīng (吳興) and Yìxīng (義興) to gather troops.
Tens of thousands of adventurers responded.
Yǐn believed that once his righteous army moved,
the situation would inevitably remain unsettled,
allowing him to seize wealth and honor by exploiting the opportunity.
However, in less than ten days,
Guóbǎo (國寶) was ordered to commit suicide,
Gōng relinquished his military command,
and Yǐn was dismissed from his post.
Yǐn was furious
and turned his forces to attack Gōng.
Gōng sent his Administrator of the Military Affairs, Liú Láozhī (劉牢之), to resist him in battle at Qǔ'ā (曲阿).
Yǐn's forces were routed and fled,
and his whereabouts became unknown.
His eldest son, Tài (泰), was killed by Gōng.
His youngest son, Huá (華), not knowing whether Yǐn was alive or dead,
grieved so much that he lived in seclusion, wearing plain clothes and eating only vegetables.
Later, his cousin Mì (謐) informed him of Yǐn's death.
Huá then began mourning
and entered officialdom.
Initially,
when Dǎo (導) crossed the Huái (淮) River,
he asked Guō Pú (郭璞) to divine his fortune.
After casting the hexagrams,
Pú said:
"Auspicious,
nothing will be unfavorable.
When the Huái River is cut off,
the Wáng (王) clan will perish."
Thereafter, their descendants proliferated,
and it indeed turned out as Pú had said.
The Historian says: When a flying dragon governs the heavens,
it must rely on the power of clouds and rain;
when an emperor rises to power,
he must await the strength of his trusted ministers.
Xuānyuán (軒轅) was a sage,
yet he leaned on his teachers and ministers to receive the mandate;
Shāng Tāng (商湯) was a wise ruler,
who entrusted his state to Yī Yǐn (伊尹) and achieved his enterprise.
From then onward,
none has been able to act otherwise.
As for the Jìn (晉) dynasty's rise to power,
it originated from its weak foundation.
The metal element (Jīn) ruled the age,
but it lacked virtue at the time.
The hearts of the nine provinces were not yet settled,
and the four barbarians had already suffered from its shortcomings.
Then, the Central Plains collapsed,
and the Jiangnan region rose to prominence.
The omen appeared in the diagram of the black stone,
which contradicted Shàokāng's (少康) restoration of Xià (夏).
At that time, there were no men who longed for the Jìn,
which was unlike Wénshú's (文叔) restoration of Liú (劉).
To assist Zhōngzōng (中宗) was truly difficult!
Mào Hóng (茂弘) made a name for himself as a key official,
forming emotional and close friendships.
Relying on his talent and wisdom,
and trusting in the vastness of the land,
he sought to achieve deeds of restoration
to establish the path of Yì and Xuān (翌宣).
Thus, Wáng Dūn (王敦) rebelled internally,
glaring like a wolf from the imperial capital;
Sū Jùn (蘇峻) gathered an army,
striking like a falcon at the imperial residence.
It truly depended on the Grand Minister,
who firmly held a loyal heart;
he secretly implemented loyal strategies,
and ultimately eliminated the ravaging bandits.
His sincerity shone through,
the ruler was able to preserve his dynasty to the end;
his unwavering resolve surpassed the frost,
the state, though in peril, was not extinguished.
Observing his establishment of schools,
amidst a boiling cauldron,
and his creation of regulations,
during a time of hardship;
though the world was full of troubles,
his vision was grand and far-reaching.
Compared to Xiāo (蕭) and Cáo (曹) assisting the Hàn (漢),
making the whole world their home;
or Shì (奭) and Wàng (望) rectifying the Zhōu (周),
making all lands follow the same path,
his achievements were not half of theirs,
and thus not comparable.
As for Yí Wú (夷吾) embodying benevolence,
able to be a minister to a small state;
Kǒng Míng (孔明) upholding righteousness,
skilled at assisting a new state,
considering the facts and discussing the circumstances,
he belongs to this category.
He led three generations,
maintaining a consistent loyalty from beginning to end,
being called
"Grand Protector" (Zhòngfù)
was indeed appropriate.
Tián (恬) and Xún (珣) inherited his virtue,
matching Lǚ Qián's (呂虔) gift of a sword;
Mì (謐), however, sullied his reputation,
shaming Liú Yì's (劉毅) summons by imperial seal.
The saying goes:
"In deep mountains and great marshes,
there are dragons and there are snakes."
This truly describes the situation.
Praise: Fierce as a tiger's roar and a dragon's leap,
a dragon ascends, its glory reflected in the clouds.
Wǔgāng (武岡) was outstanding,
rectifying the times and consolidating governance.
His admirable achievements were proclaimed,
his loyal strategies were unrivaled.
His agreements aligned with three rulers,
his glory surpassed the nine honors.
The gift of a sword foreshadowed auspiciousness,
the divination of water flowed with blessings.
How illustrious was this clan,
its brilliance shining forth in abundance.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 36, Liú Hóng (劉弘)
Liú Hóng, courtesy name Héjì (和季),
was from Pèiguó (沛國).
His grandfather, Fù (馥),
was Inspector of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ) during the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
His father, Jìng (靖),
was General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn).
Hóng possessed talent for strategy, management, and governance.
In his youth, he lived in Luòyáng (洛陽),
residing in Yǒng'ān Lǐ (永安里) with Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
They were also of the same age
and studied together.
Due to their old friendship, he began his official career as Prefect of the Heir Apparent's Gate (Tàizǐ Mén Dàfū),
and was successively promoted to Palace Usher (Shuàigēng Lìng),
then transferred to Chief Clerk to the Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi Chángshǐ).
Zhāng Huá (張華) greatly esteemed him.

Because of this, he was appointed General of Tranquilizing the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), provisionally granted imperial credentials (Jiǎjié), and made Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Yōuzhōu (Jiān Yōuzhōu Zhū Jūnshì),
concurrently serving as Colonel of Wūwán (Wūwán Xiàowèi).
He commanded great authority and beneficence,
and bandits ceased their activities,
earning praise from Yōu (幽) and Shuò (朔).
For his outstanding merits and virtues,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Gōng).
During the Tàipíng
period, Zhāng Chāng rebelled.
[Hóng] was transferred to be an Envoy with Imperial Authority, Colonel of the Southern Barbarians, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He led the former General Zhào Xiāng and others to suppress Chāng.
From Fāngchéng to Wǎn and Xīnyě,
wherever they went, all was pacified.
When Xīnyěwáng Xīn was defeated,
Hóng was appointed in his stead as General Who Suppresses the South and Area Commander of all military affairs in Jīngzhōu.
His other offices remained as before.
Hóng dispatched the Southern Barbarian Chief Clerk Táo Kǎn as Grand Protector,
Staff Officer Kuǎi Wèi as Supervisor of the Righteous Army,
and Yámén General Pí Chū as Commander-in-Chief of battles,
to advance and occupy Xiāngyáng.
Zhāng Chāng massed his troops and besieged Wǎn,
defeating Zhào Xiāng's army.
Hóng retreated and garrisoned Liáng.
Kǎn and Chū repeatedly fought and defeated Chāng,
beheading tens of thousands of heads in total.
Upon their arrival,
Chāng was terrified and fled,
and all his followers surrendered.
Jīngtǔ was pacified.
Previously,
when Hóng retreated,
Fànyángwáng Xiāo had sent Changshuǐ Colonel Zhāng Yì to take charge of Jīngzhōu.
When Hóng arrived,
Yì refused to be relieved,
and raised an army to resist Hóng.
Hóng dispatched troops to attack Yì,
and beheaded him.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"I, your servant, with ordinary talent,
was mistakenly favored with imperial grace,
to govern a provincial region,
and carry out the imperial decree to punish the wicked.
I was unable to thunderously display my might,
and deter enemies from afar.
My army suffered a setback at Wǎn,
and I should have received public execution.
Yet I received your magnanimous forgiveness,
and was appointed to this office,
immediately advancing to take charge of the region.
However, Fànyángwáng Xiāo had previously sent the former Changshuǐ Colonel Zhāng Yì to take charge of Jīngzhōu.
When I arrived,
he refused to submit to my authority,
and presumptuously raised an army to resist me.
Currently, Zhāng Chāng's wicked faction has only just been pacified;
Chāng has not yet been captured and executed.
The displaced people from Yì and Liáng have gathered in disarray,
and desperate individuals are easily incited.
If a whirlwind stirs up trouble,
the vast sea will surge with waves.
If one is worried about losing this opportunity,
there is nothing one will not do.
While awaiting a memorial to be submitted,
fearing to miss the opportune moment,
I immediately dispatched troops to attack Yì,
and instantly beheaded him.
Although Yì was greedy and disruptive,
wishing to cause harm,
it was due to my weakness
and incompetence that
Yì was able to act as he pleased,
thus troubling your majesty with expenses.
I dare to invoke the punishment for overturning the cooking pot
and willingly accept the crime of acting without authorization."
An imperial edict stated:
"General, endowed with both civil and military talents,
was previously entrusted with the governance of a region.
The failure to defend Wǎn city was the fault of Zhào Xiāng.
The armies dispatched by the General
crushed and annihilated the bandits.
Zhāng Yì was greedy for trouble
and defied the imperial decree.
The General's campaign to attack him
and send his head to the court,
though it might incur the suspicion of acting without request,
there is an ancient precedent for such discretionary action.
Therefore, may you expand your grand strategy
and pacify the region south of the mountains,
to fulfill the hopes placed in you."
Zhāng Chāng hid in Xiàjùnshān.
Hóng dispatched troops to attack Chāng,
beheaded him,
and accepted the surrender of all his followers.
At that time, many prefectures and magistracies in Jīng were vacant.
Hóng requested to fill these vacancies through selection,
and the Emperor agreed.
Hóng then evaluated merits and virtues,
appointing individuals according to their talents,
which was highly praised by commentators.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"I received an imperial edict
commanding me to select officials based on their qualifications
to fill the various vacant posts.
However, rewards, punishments, and authority
are not mine to monopolize.
Moreover, 'knowing men is wisdom,'
a task even difficult for sagely emperors,
and not something my dull and ignorant self can deliberate upon.
Nevertheless, all matters have their opportune moments,
and even the slightest detail requires caution.
I respectfully carry out the imperial edict,
and have provisionally appointed those suitable for use.
Indeed, there is nothing better for promoting civilization than honoring virtue,
which is how difficulties are overcome.
Thus, the highest [virtue] is establishing character,
followed by establishing achievements.
Recently, there have been many troubles,
and simplicity has greatly declined.
I have provisionally appointed the reclusive scholar Wǔ Zhāo as Administrator of Línglíng,
hoping thereby to curb the ills of disorder
and cultivate the virtues of humility and yielding.
I, your servant, being unskilled in war,
previously retreated at Wǎn.
Chief Clerk Táo Kǎn, Staff Officer Kuǎi Wèi, and Yámén Pí Chū
united their efforts to campaign,
annihilating the wicked and vicious.
Kǎn handled military affairs from beginning to end,
and Chū served as Commander-in-Chief of battles,
showing loyalty and courage that surpassed the army.
The Hàn and Miǎn regions are now peaceful and orderly,
which is truly the achievement of Chū and others.
The Sīmǎ Fǎ states,
'Rewards should not be delayed beyond the season,'
wishing people to know the swift blessings of doing good.
If they are not rewarded promptly,
there will be no way to encourage those who strive for merit
and comfort the ambitions of brave warriors.
I have provisionally appointed Chū as Administrator of Xiāngyáng,
Kǎn as the Prefectural Sīmǎ,
to oversee the evaluation of merits,
and Wèi as Magistrate of Shāndū.
The imperial edict only permitted me to fill vacancies with common appointments.
However, Yīxiāng Magistrate Yú Tán demonstrated staunch loyalty and rectitude,
being the first to initiate the righteous cause.
To promote good and encourage those who cannot,
I have specially transferred Tán to be Magistrate of Lǐlíng.
Qióu Bó, an honest official from Nánjùn,
whose elderly mother was gravely ill,
did not abandon his post when the bandits arrived,
enduring torture
and nearly losing his life.
Shàngshū Clerk Guō Zhēn,
whom Zhāng Chāng wanted to appoint as Shàngshū Láng
to consult on court matters,
fled and did not appear.
Chāng held his wife and children hostage,
but he avoided him even further.
Bó's filial piety was evident in his moment of peril,
and Zhēn's loyalty was strong in the face of tyranny.
Although both are of the fourth rank,
they can both be used to instruct and encourage officials and subjects,
and to further improve moral conduct.
I have provisionally appointed Bó as Magistrate of Guīxiāng,
and Zhēn as Magistrate of Xìnlíng.
Their achievements and conduct are intertwined,
and their names have been checked against their actual deeds.
Their biographies have been itemized
and submitted with the official documents."
The imperial court held that although Chū had merits,
Xiāngyáng was also a prominent commandery,
and high offices should be filled cautiously,
so it could not be granted to Chū.
Instead, Xiàhóu Zhì, the former Administrator of Dōngpíng, was appointed Administrator of Xiāngyáng,
and the rest were approved.
Zhì was Hóng's son-in-law.
Hóng then issued an instruction saying:
"One who governs the world
should be of one heart with the world;
one who transforms a country
should take responsibility for the country.
If only relatives by marriage can be used,
then how can Jīngzhōu's ten commanderies be governed
unless one has ten sons-in-law?"
He then memorialized,
"Zhì is a relative by marriage,
and old regulations forbid supervising relatives.
Pí Chū's merits should be rewarded."
The emperor granted his request.
Táo Kǎn, courtesy name Shìxíng,
was originally from Póyáng.
When Wú was pacified,
he moved his family to Xúnyáng in Lújiāng.
His father, Dān,
was a Yángwǔ General of Wú.
Kǎn was orphaned early and poor,
serving as a county clerk.
Fàn Kuí, a Xiàolián from Póyáng, once visited Kǎn.
At that time, in a hurry, Kǎn had nothing to entertain his guest with.
His mother then cut her hair to obtain a pair of wigs,
which she exchanged for wine and meat.
They drank and made merry to their hearts' content,
and even the servants were treated beyond their expectations.
When Kuí left,
Kǎn accompanied him for over a hundred *lǐ*.
Kuí said,
“Do you wish to serve in the commandery?”
Kǎn replied,
“I do,
but I am hindered by lacking an avenue!”
Kuí then visited Zhāng Kuí, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng,
and spoke highly of Kǎn.
Kuí summoned him to be Dūyóu,
also leading Cóngyáng county as its Magistrate.
He earned a reputation for competence
and was promoted to Zhǔbù.
When the Zhōu Departmental Attendant came to the commandery,
intending to investigate something,
Kǎn closed the gates and assembled his subordinates.
He said to the Attendant,
“If this humble commandery has committed violations,
it is only right that they be clearly investigated according to law.
There is no need for undue pressure.
If you do not act with propriety,
I am capable of resisting you.”
The Attendant immediately withdrew.
Zhāng Kuí’s wife fell ill,
and a doctor had to be brought from several hundred *lǐ* away.
It was cold and snowy at the time,
and all the officials found it difficult.
Kǎn alone said,
“One who serves his father should serve his lord in the same way.
The lady of the house
is like a mother.
How can one not devote oneself fully when one's parents are ill!”
He then volunteered to go.
Everyone admired his righteousness.
Wàn Sì, the Grand Administrator of Chángshā, passed through Lújiāng,
met Kǎn,
and was deeply impressed and pleased,
saying,
“You will certainly achieve great fame.”
He ordered his son to befriend Kǎn before leaving.
Zhāng Kuí nominated Kǎn as Xiàolián.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
Kǎn frequently visited Zhāng Huá.
At first, Zhāng Huá considered him a man from a distant place
and did not receive him warmly.
Each time Kǎn went,
his demeanor showed no displeasure.
Later, Zhāng Huá conversed with him
and was surprised by him.
Kǎn was appointed Lángzhōng.
Sūn Xiù, the Fúbō General, being a descendant of a fallen kingdom,
his family's standing was not prominent.
Scholars of the Central Plains were ashamed to serve as his subordinates.
Considering Kǎn a common official,
he summoned him to be Shèrén.
At that time, Yáng Mù, the Lángzhōng Lìng of Yùzhāng Commandery,
was Kǎn's fellow provincial
and was highly regarded by local opinion.
Kǎn visited him.
Yáng Mù said,
“The *Yìjīng* says, ‘Perseverance and firmness are sufficient to accomplish great things.’
Táo Shìxíng is such a man.”
He rode with Kǎn to see Gù Róng, the Zhōngshū Láng.
Gù Róng greatly admired him.
Wēn Yǎ, the Lìbù Láng, said to Yáng Mù,
“How can you ride with such an insignificant man?”
Yáng Mù replied,
“This man is no ordinary talent.”
Lè Guǎng, the Shàngshū, wished to gather scholars from Jīng and Yáng provinces.
Huáng Qìng, the Wǔkù Lìng, recommended Kǎn to Lè Guǎng.
Some people disapproved,
but Huáng Qìng said,
“This young man will eventually go far,
what is there to doubt?”
Huáng Qìng later became Lìbù Lìngshǐ
and recommended Kǎn to be appointed Wǔgāng Magistrate.
He had a disagreement with the Grand Administrator Lǚ Yuè,
abandoned his office and returned home,
serving as the Minor Zhōngzhèng for the commandery.
Coincidentally, Liú Hóng became the Inspector of Jīng Province.
As he was heading to his post,
he invited Kǎn to be Nánmán Chángshǐ,
sending him ahead to Xiāngyáng to suppress the bandit Zhāng Chāng,
whom he defeated.
When Liú Hóng arrived,
he said to Kǎn,
“I was once a staff officer for Grand Commandant Yáng,
who said that I would eventually occupy his position.
Now observing you,
you will surely succeed me.”
Later, for his military achievements, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngxiāng,
with a thousand households.
During Chén Mǐn's rebellion,
Liú Hóng appointed Kǎn as Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià,
and added the title Yīngyáng General.
Kǎn prepared the ceremonial regalia,
and welcomed his mother to the official residence,
which brought honor to his hometown.
Chén Mǐn sent his younger brother, Huī, to raid Wǔchāng.
Kǎn led his troops to resist him.
Hù Guī, the Administrator of Suí Commandery, slandered Kǎn to Liú Hóng, saying,
“Kǎn has old ties with Chén Mǐn from their hometown.
He occupies a major commandery
and commands powerful troops.
If he were to harbor different intentions,
then Jīng Province would have no eastern gate.”
Liú Hóng said,
“Kǎn's loyalty and ability,
I have known for a long time.
How could this be true!”
Kǎn secretly heard of this,
and immediately sent his son Hóng and his nephew Zhēn to Liú Hóng to affirm his loyalty.
Liú Hóng appointed them as staff officers,
provided them with resources, and sent them back.
He also promoted Kǎn to Dūhù
and had him join forces with the other armies to resist Huī.
Kǎn then used transport ships as warships.
Some said it was impossible,
but Kǎn said,
“Using official resources to suppress official rebels,
one only needs to record the details.”
Thereupon, he attacked Huī,
and was victorious wherever he went.
Kǎn’s military administration was disciplined and solemn.
Whatever was captured,
he distributed among his soldiers,
keeping nothing for himself.
Later, he left office due to his mother's mourning.
Once, two guests came to offer condolences,
but left without weeping.
They transformed into a pair of cranes
and soared into the sky.
People at the time found this unusual.
When his mourning period ended,
he became an advisor to the military affairs of Dōnghǎi Prince Yuè.
Huá Yì, the Inspector of Jiāng Province, recommended Kǎn as Yángwǔ General,
stationing him at Xiàkǒu,
and also appointed Zhēn as a staff officer.
Huá Yì and Emperor Yuán had long been on bad terms.
Zhēn, fearing that trouble would arise,
feigned illness and returned,
telling Kǎn,
“Huá Yànxià has the ambition to pacify the world,
but lacks the talent,
and furthermore, he is not on good terms with the Prince of Lángxié.
Trouble will soon erupt.”
Kǎn was angry
and sent Zhēn back to Huá Yì.
Zhēn then went east to Emperor Yuán.
The Emperor saw him
and was greatly pleased,
appointing Zhēn as a staff officer
and promoting Kǎn to Fènwēi General,
granting him a red banner, a curved canopy cart, and drum music.
Kǎn then severed ties with Huá Yì.
A little later,
he was promoted to Longxiáng Jiāngjūn (Dragon Soaring General) and Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng.
At that time, the world suffered from famine,
and mountain barbarians frequently cut off the river to plunder.
Kǎn ordered his generals to pretend to be merchant ships to lure them.
The bandits indeed arrived,
and several people were captured alive;
they were attendants of Xīyáng Wáng (Prince of Xīyáng) Yáng.
Kǎn immediately sent troops to press Yáng,
ordering him to send out an attack against the bandits.
Kǎn arranged his formation at Diàotái as a reserve force.
Yáng bound and sent twenty men under Kǎn’s tent,
and Kǎn executed them.
From then on, waterways and land were peaceful,
and refugees returned in droves, filling the roads.
Kǎn exhausted his resources to provide for and relieve them.
He also established a barbarian market east of the commandery,
reaping great profits from it.
Meanwhile, the Emperor ordered Kǎn to attack Dù Tāo,
and ordered Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe) Zhōu Fǎng and Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Expands Martial Power) Zhào Yòu to be under Kǎn’s command.
Kǎn ordered the two generals to be the vanguard,
and his nephew Yú to be the left flank,
to attack the bandits,
and they defeated them.
At that time, Zhōu Yǐ was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
stationed earlier at Xúnshuǐ Chéng.
The bandits plundered his good households.
Kǎn sent his subordinate general Zhū Sì to rescue them,
and the bandits retreated to defend Língkǒu.
Kǎn said to his generals,
"These bandits will surely march towards Wǔchāng again.
We should return to the city.
We can reach it in three days, marching day and night.
Which of you can endure hunger and fight?"
His subordinate general Wú Jì said,
"We are willing to endure hunger for ten days.
By day, we will attack the bandits,
and by night, we will catch fish.
That will be enough to sustain us."
Kǎn said,
"You are a brave general."
The bandits indeed increased their forces and came to attack.
Kǎn sent Zhū Sì and others to counter-attack,
greatly defeating them,
capturing their baggage train,
and killing and wounding many.
He sent his military advisor Wáng Gòng to report the victory to Wáng Dūn.
Dūn said,
"If it weren't for Táo Hóu,
Jīngzhōu would have been lost.
Bó Rén had just entered the border
and was immediately defeated by the bandits.
How did he become an Inspector?"
Gòng replied,
"When our province faced difficulties,
no one but Táo Lóngxiáng could handle it."
Dūn agreed with this,

and immediately submitted a memorial to appoint Kǎn as Shǐchíjié (Envoy with Imperial Credentials), Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies Distant Lands), Nánmán Xiàowèi (Colonel-Protector of the Southern Barbarians), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Jīngzhōu),
with jurisdiction over Xīyáng, Jiāngxià, and Wǔchāng,
stationed at Dùnkǒu,
and then moved to Miǎnjiāng.
He sent Zhū Sì and others to quell the bandits in Jiāngxià,
and killed them.
The bandit Wáng Chōng proclaimed himself Inspector of Jīngzhōu
and occupied Jiānglíng.
When Wáng Gòng returned,
he reached Jìnglín.
He forged Kǎn’s order
to appoint Dù Zēng as the Qiánfēng Dàdūhù (Grand Chief Commandant of the Vanguard),
who advanced and beheaded Chōng,
and captured all his followers.
Kǎn summoned Zēng, but he did not come.
Gòng also feared punishment for forging the order,
so he and Zēng raised an army in rebellion.
They attacked Kǎn’s chief commandant Zhèng Pān at Dùnyáng,
defeating him,
and also defeated Zhū Sì at Miǎnkǒu.
Kǎn wanted to retreat into Yùnzhōng.
His subordinate general Zhāng Yì intended to betray Kǎn,
and deceitfully said,
"If we move when the bandits arrive,
the troops will certainly be unmanageable."
Kǎn was confused by this and did not advance.
Soon after,
the bandits arrived
and indeed defeated him.
The bandits hooked Kǎn’s warship.
Kǎn was in distress
and fled into a small boat.
Zhū Sì fought bravely,
and barely managed to escape.
Zhāng Yì eventually fled to the bandits.
Kǎn was dismissed from office for this.
Wáng Dūn submitted a memorial to reinstate Kǎn as a commoner holding office.
Kǎn again led Zhōu Fǎng and others to advance into Xiāng,
sending Commandant Yáng Jǔ as the vanguard
to attack Dù Tāo,
greatly defeating him,
and garrisoning troops west of the city.
One of Kǎn’s aides went to Wáng Dūn and said,
"Provincial governor Táo Shǐjūn is an upright and independent man,
who rose from obscurity to prominence.
His loyal and just accomplishments
have been effective wherever he served.
He went out to assist in the southern summer,
aiding and supporting Liú Zhēngnán.
First encountering Zhāng Chāng,
then belonging to Chén Mǐn,
Kǎn, with a small force,
alone confronted great bandits.
He conquered every enemy,
