and all the scoundrels were destroyed.
Recently, Wáng Rú brought chaos to the north,
and Dù Tāo straddled the south.
Two generals fled,
and one province scattered like stars.
The remaining commanderies and counties
collapsed everywhere.
Kǎn attracted the displaced with propriety
and embraced the distant with virtue.
The multitudes came to him like children,
arriving repeatedly.
He followed instructions,
alone defending dangerous passes.
When people left, he remained steadfast;
when people scattered, he held firm.
Last year, he supervised [the campaign],
advancing directly to Xiāng Chéng,
his ambition reaching the clouds,
his divine strategy uniquely decisive.
Merely due to insufficient troops and precarious supplies,
he was unable to report a full victory.
Nevertheless, Dù Tāo was intimidated
and returned to Xiàkǒu.
Before two nights had passed,
the displaced people of Jiànpíng rebelled, welcoming the bandits.
Kǎn immediately turned his army upstream,
clearing out the villainous elements,
so much so that the western gate needed no lock,
and Huá Qí was free from danger.
These were Kǎn’s achievements.
The discerning general (Wáng Dūn) pitied Jīngchǔ,
saving lives from misery,
and allowed Kǎn to lead the remnants of the impoverished.
He clothed the cold,
fed the hungry.
Families rejoiced,
as if wearing padded silk.
The riverside is isolated and precarious,
the terrain not heavily fortified.
It cannot be secured by a single army alone.
Therefore, he moved to higher ground
to avoid the main thrust.
The bandits, underestimating him, arrived first,
with their main force following.
Kǎn resisted for days,
killing their famous commander.
The bandits then gathered like dogs and sheep,
attacking with combined strength.
Kǎn, with the integrity of a loyal minister,
felt it was his duty not to retreat.
Wearing armor and wielding weapons,
he personally stood in the battle lines.
His officers and soldiers fought valiantly,
none sparing their lives.
The dead at that time were innumerable.
The bandit forces were mixed,
resting and fighting in turns.
Kǎn, with his single isolated force,
could not resist them alone.
He chose to preserve his forces as appropriate
to await future opportunities.
Yet, the authorities blamed Kǎn,
imposing severe demotions.
Kǎn is humble and modest by nature;
when his task is done, he withdraws.
Now he returns what he received,
only fearing delay.
However, we are anxious,
truly fearing that principles might be lost internally,
and affairs fail externally.
A difference of a hair’s breadth
will lead to a thousand miles of deviation,
causing Jīngmán to become alienated,
and Xīyú to be undefended,
like lips without teeth, a boundless encroachment
will ensue."
Dūn then memorialized to restore Kǎn’s official position.
Táo Kǎn
was intelligent and quick-witted,
diligent in his official duties,
respectful and close to ritual,
and loved good people.
He sat upright with knees drawn in all day long;
there were many matters outside his purview,
a thousand threads and ten thousand ends,
none of which were overlooked.
Letters from far and near,
he answered them all by hand,
his brush flowing like a stream,
never obstructed.
He welcomed those estranged and distant,
with no lingering guests at his gate.
He often said to people:
"Yǔ the Great, a sage,
still cherished every inch of time.
As for ordinary people,
they should cherish every minute.
How can one indulge in idle wandering and reckless drinking,
living without benefit to the age,
and dying without being remembered by posterity?
This is to abandon oneself."
If any of his subordinates neglected their duties for chatter or games,
he would order their wine vessels and gambling equipment
to be thrown into the river.
For his military officers,
he would inflict a flogging,
saying:
"Gambling is merely a game for herdsmen and slaves!
Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi's
frivolous words are not the righteous teachings of the former kings;
they cannot be followed.
A gentleman should straighten his clothes and cap,
and control his demeanor.
How can one have disheveled hair and seek reputation,
calling oneself broad-minded and accomplished?"
When someone offered gifts,
he would always ask how they were obtained.
If they were the result of hard labor,
he would be pleased, even if they were meager,
and would comfort and reward them threefold.
If they were obtained improperly,
he would severely reprimand and humiliate the person,
returning what was offered.
Once, while traveling,
he saw someone holding a handful of unripe rice.
Táo Kǎn asked:
"What are you doing with this?"
The person replied:
"I saw it on the road and just took it."
Táo Kǎn was greatly enraged, saying:
"You do not farm,
yet you playfully harm other people's rice!"
He seized the person and flogged him.
Because of this, the common people were diligent in farming and cultivation,
and every family had enough, and everyone was well-provided for.
At one time, when building ships,
he ordered all the wood chips and bamboo ends
to be collected and stored,
and everyone wondered why.
Later, during the Spring Festival,
after a heavy snowfall had just cleared,
there was still wet residual snow in front of the audience hall,
so he spread the wood chips on the ground.
And when Huán Wēn attacked Shǔ,
he used the bamboo ends stored by Táo Kǎn
to make pegs for fastening ships.
His meticulous management
was all of this kind.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
the capital was not defended.
Táo Kǎn's
son, Zhān,
was harmed by the rebels.
General of the Pacified South, Wēn Qiáo,
urged Táo Kǎn to join the imperial court.
Initially,
when Emperor Míng died,
Táo Kǎn was not among those given the dying imperial command,
which he deeply resented.
He replied to Wēn Qiáo:
"I am a frontier general,
and dare not overstep my bounds."
Wēn Qiáo earnestly pleaded with him,
and consequently proposed him as the leader of the alliance.
Táo Kǎn then dispatched Supervising Officer Gōng Dēng
to lead troops to Wēn Qiáo,
but then recalled them.
Wēn Qiáo, because Sū Jùn had killed his son,
sent another letter to provoke his anger.
Táo Kǎn's
wife, Lady Gōng,
also firmly urged him to go himself.
Thereupon, he donned his military uniform and boarded a boat,
traveling day and night,
not even attending Zhān's
funeral when it arrived.
In the fifth month,
he met with Wēn Qiáo, Yǔ Liàng,
and others at Shítou.
The various armies immediately wanted to engage in a decisive battle.
Táo Kǎn believed that since the rebels were strong,
they should not contend with them directly,
but rather capture them with stratagem over time.
After several battles yielded no success,
the generals requested to build a fortress at Chápǔ.
Military Supervisor Lǐ Gēn, a subordinate general,
suggested building a fortress at Báishí.
Táo Kǎn disagreed,
saying:
"If the fortress is not completed,
you will be held responsible for it."
Lǐ Gēn replied:
"The ground at Chápǔ
is low, and it is south of the water.
Only Báishí is steep and extremely fortified,
able to accommodate several thousand people.
When the rebels attack, it will be inconvenient for them.
This is the method to defeat the rebels."
Táo Kǎn smiled and said:
"You are a good general."
He then followed Lǐ Gēn's
plan,
building through the night until dawn.
The rebels were greatly surprised when they saw the fortress.
When the rebels attacked Dàyè fortress,
Táo Kǎn was about to go to its rescue.
Chief Clerk Yīn Xiàn said:
"If we send aid to Dàyè,
our infantry will be inferior to Sū Jùn's
in battle,
and the great cause will be lost.
We should instead swiftly attack Shítou,
and Sū Jùn will surely come to its rescue,
and Dàyè will be relieved on its own."
Táo Kǎn again followed Yīn Xiàn's
words.
Sū Jùn indeed abandoned Dàyè and went to rescue Shítou.
The various armies battled Sū Jùn
east of Chénlíng.
Táo Kǎn's
Supervising Officer and Administrator of Jìnglíng, Lǐ Yáng's
subordinate general, Péng Shì,
beheaded Sū Jùn
in battle,
and the rebel forces were utterly routed.
Sū Jùn's
younger brother, Yì,
regrouped his forces.
Táo Kǎn and the other armies beheaded Yì at Shítou.
Initially,
Yǔ Liàng had a high reputation from a young age
and, as the brother of Empress Míngmù,
received the heavy responsibility of the dying imperial command.
During the disaster of Sū Jùn,
the blame was laid on Yǔ Liàng.
When Shítou was pacified,
Táo Kǎn
served in the military for forty-one years. He was heroic and resolute,
intelligent and good at making decisions.
From Nánlíng to Báidì, a distance of several thousand *lǐ*,
nothing was lost on the roads.
During the campaign against Sū Jùn,
Yǔ Liàng advanced rashly and suffered a defeat.
Liàng's *Sīmǎ*, Yīn Róng, went to Kǎn to apologize, saying:
"The General's actions
were not something Róng and others could control."
General Wáng Zhāng arrived
and said:
"Zhāng did it himself;
the General was unaware."
Kǎn said:
"In the past, Yīn Róng was a *jūnzǐ* (gentleman),
and Wáng Zhāng was a *xiǎorén* (petty person);
now, Wáng Zhāng is a *jūnzǐ*,
and Yīn Róng is a *xiǎorén*."
Kǎn was meticulous and fond of asking questions,
much like Zhào Guǎnghàn.
Once, he ordered the various camps to plant willows.
The commandant Xià Shī stole official willows and planted them at his own gate.
Kǎn later saw them,
stopped his carriage, and asked:
"These are the willows from outside the west gate of Wǔchāng;
how did they get stolen and planted here?"
Shī was terrified and begged for forgiveness.
At that time, Wǔchāng was known for its many scholars;
Yīn Hào, Yǔ Yì, and others were all his subordinate officials.
Kǎn always had a set limit for drinking alcohol;
he often had remaining cheerfulness but had already reached his limit.
Hào and others would persuade him to drink a little more,
but Kǎn would sigh deeply for a long time, saying:
"When I was young, I once made a mistake with alcohol,
and my deceased mother made me promise
not to exceed the limit, so I dare not."
The strategists believed that since there was Zhū Chéng on the north bank of Wǔchāng,
it would be appropriate to divide forces to garrison it.
Kǎn never responded,
but as the speakers did not cease,
Kǎn then crossed the water to hunt,
and gathered his generals and subordinates to tell them:
"The reason I establish natural barriers to ward off invaders
is precisely the Cháng Jiāng.
Zhū Chéng is separated on the north bank of the river,
with no internal support
and bordering various barbarian tribes externally.
There is deep profit among the barbarians,
and the Jìn people are greedy for profit.
If the barbarians cannot bear the impositions,
they will surely bring in invaders and captives,
thus leading to disaster;
it is not for repelling invaders.
Moreover, during the Wú dynasty, this city was guarded by thirty thousand troops.
Even if it is guarded by troops now,
it will be of no benefit to the south of the river.
If the Jié captives have an opportune moment to strike,
this is also not what we should rely on."
Later, Yǔ Liàng garrisoned it
and indeed suffered a great defeat.
In his later years, he embraced the principle of knowing when to stop,
and did not involve himself in court power.
Less than a year before his death,
he wanted to cede his position and return to his home state,
but his subordinates urged him to stay.
When his illness became critical,
he was about to return to Chángshā.
All the military supplies, weapons, cattle, horses, boats, and ships had fixed registers.
He sealed the warehouses
and personally attached the locks,
entrusting them to Wáng Qiānqī.
Only then did he board the boat.
The court and the public considered this a commendable act.
As he was about to exit the mansion gate,
he looked back and said to Qiānqī:
"This old man is lingering
precisely because of you gentlemen."
The *Shàngshū*, Méi Táo, wrote a letter to his relative Cáo Shí, saying:
"Táo Gōng's discerning spirit and keen judgment are like that of Wèi Wǔ,
and his loyalty, obedience, diligence, and hard work are like that of Kǒng Míng.
Lù Kàng and others cannot compare to him."
Xiè Ān often said:
"Although Táo Gōng used the law,
he grasped its intent beyond the letter of the law."
This is how highly he was regarded by his generation.
However, he had dozens of concubines
and over a thousand household servants.
His rare treasures and precious goods were richer than the imperial treasury.
Some say
"when Kǎn was young, he fished in Léi Zé
and caught a shuttle in his net.
He hung it on the wall.
After a while, there was a thunderstorm,
and it transformed into a dragon and departed."
He also dreamt that he grew eight wings
and flew up to heaven,
seeing nine layers of heavenly gates.
He had already ascended eight of them,
but only one gate he could not enter.
The gatekeeper struck him with a staff,
causing him to fall to the ground,
breaking his left wing.
When he awoke,
his left armpit still hurt.
He also once went to the latrine
and saw a man in a vermillion robe and bound headcloth,
who bowed and said:
"Because you are an elder,
I have come to inform you.
You will later become a *gōng*,
reaching the position of Commander-in-Chief of eight prefectures."
There was a skilled physiognomist, Shī Guī, who told Kǎn:
"Your left middle finger has a vertical line;
you will become a *gōng*.
If it extends to the top,
your nobility will be inexpressible."
Kǎn pricked it with a needle, drew blood,
sprinkled it on the wall, and it formed the character
"公" (*gōng*).
He pressed his hand with paper,
and the character "公" (*gōng*)
became clearer.
When he became Commander-in-Chief of eight prefectures,
holding the upper reaches of the river
and commanding strong armies,
he secretly harbored ambitions of usurpation.
He often thought of the omen of the broken wing,
restraining himself and stopping.
Kǎn had seventeen sons.
Only Hóng, Zhān, Xià, Qí, Qí, Bīn, Chēng, Fàn, and Dài are mentioned in old histories;
the others are not prominent.
Hóng served as a chancellor's subordinate
and died young.
Zhān, courtesy name Dàozhēn,
was talented and capable from a young age.
He successively held the posts of Administrator of Guǎnglíng,
Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Lújiāng and Jiànchāng,
and was promoted to Palace Attendant and Marquis of Dūtíng.
He was harmed by Sū Jùn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of Ceremonies
with the posthumous epithet Mǐndào Shìzǐ.
Xià was made the heir apparent.
When Kǎn's coffin was being sent back to Chángshā,
Xià, Bīn, and Chēng each gathered several thousand troops to plot against each other.
Eventually, they disbanded.
Bīn went to Chángshā first
and took all the weapons and wealth from the state.
When Xià arrived,
he killed Bīn.
Yǔ Liàng submitted a memorial, stating:
"Although Bīn was ugly and evil,
and his crime unbearable,
nevertheless, the royal statutes have decreed that
for close blood relatives,
to personally wield a knife and saw to punish one's own flesh and blood
injures the parents' kindness
and shows no compassion.
He should be banished
to deter such tyranny."
Before Liàng's memorial reached the capital,
Xià died of illness.
An imperial edict reinstated Zhān's son, Hóng, to inherit Kǎn's noble title.
He served as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Upon his death,
his son Chuòzhī succeeded him.
When Chuòzhī died,
his son Yánshòu succeeded him.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
he was demoted to Marquis of Wúchāng,
with five hundred households.
Qí was a *Sīkōng* clerk.
Qí successively held the posts of Palace Attendant and Founding Earl of Chēnxiàn.
At the end of Xiánhé,
he was a Gentleman Attendant at the Palace.
His nature was very fierce and violent.
Upon his death,
his son Dìng succeeded him.
Upon his death,
his son Xízhī succeeded him.
Upon his death,
his son Qiānzhī succeeded him.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Bīn was a Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
He was called Dōng Zhōngláng Jiàng (東中郎將), Nánpíng Tàishǒu (南平太守), Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉), and was granted the authority to act independently (假節).
His nature was ferocious and unruly,
and he was not harmonious with his younger brothers.
Later, he was promoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍).
In the fifth year of Xiánkāng (咸康),

Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) appointed Chēng (稱) as Supervisor of Military Affairs for the three commanderies of Jiāngxià (江夏), Suí (隨), and Yìyáng (義陽), and also Nán Zhōngláng Jiàng (南中郎將) and Jiāngxià Xiàng (江夏相).
He was to take his original two thousand men with him.
When he arrived at Xiàkǒu (夏口),
he lightly took two hundred men to go see Liàng.
〔一五〕Liàng convened a grand assembly of his officials and subordinates,
and reproached Chēng for his past misdeeds and crimes.
Chēng bowed in apology
and then was dismissed and left.
Liàng sent men to arrest him outside the gate,
and he was executed in the marketplace.
Liàng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Based on our investigation, Chēng (稱) was
the illegitimate son of the Grand Marshal Kǎn (侃).
When his father died, he did not observe the mourning rituals.
He was dissolute and indulged in wine,
greedy for profit and stealing glory.
He unauthorizedly managed five commanderies,
called himself a military supervisor,
and arbitrarily summoned court officials
to gather in his military headquarters.
The great-grandson of the former Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) Liú Hóng (劉弘), Ān (安), was residing in Jiāngxià (江夏).
And the generals Yáng Gōng (楊恭) and Zhào Sháo (趙韶),
because their words and expressions were offensive to him,
Chēng (稱) loudly threatened to kill them.
Ān (安) and Gōng (恭), terrified,
threw themselves into the water and died,
while Sháo (韶) committed suicide in prison.
General Guō Kāi (郭開) accompanied Chēng (稱) to Chángshā (長沙) to attend a funeral.
Chēng (稱) suspected Kāi (開) of siding with his brothers,
so he tied Kāi (開)'s hands behind his back and hung him upside down from the mast of a boat,
and shot arrows at him from below.
He then rowed across the river for over twenty *lǐ* (里),
with thousands of spectators,
none of whom were not
shocked and terrified.
He also secretly harbored many palace soldiers,
who were to be arrested and executed.
I could not bear to immediately report him,
and merely dismissed his *Sīmǎ* (司馬).
Chēng (稱) indulged in ugly words,
without any scruples,
and conspired with various generals,
intending to use military force to stir up trouble.
The generals were frightened
and dared not respond,
which prevented his treacherous scheme from being immediately exposed.
I considered Kǎn (侃)'s meritorious service to the imperial court,
and therefore tolerated and covered up for him,
and thus appointed him Nán Zhōngláng Jiàng (南中郎將),
so that he would be close to me,
hoping to be able to guide and save him.
However, Chēng (稱) became even more wolf-like,
speaking provocatively and sharply,
being disloyal and unfilial to an extreme degree.
For the benefit of the state,
I had the righteous authority to make an independent decision,
and thus arrested Chēng (稱) and had him punished by law."
Fàn (範) was the most famous.
In the early years of Tàiyuán (太元),
he served as Guānglù Xūn (光祿勳).
Dài (岱) was Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎).
Zhēn (臻), courtesy name Yànxiá (彥遐),
possessed courage, strategy, and wisdom.
He was bestowed the title of Dāngyáng Tínghóu (當陽亭侯).
In the Xiánhé (咸和) era,
he served as Nánjùn Tàishǒu (南郡太守), concurrently holding the post of Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉), and was granted the authority to act independently (假節).
He died in office
and was posthumously granted the title of Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍),
with the posthumous name Sù (肅).
Zhēn (臻)'s younger brother, Yú (輿),
was resolute and skilled in battle.
For his merits, he was successively promoted to Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn (武威將軍).
Initially,
the bandit Zhāng Yì (張奕), originally from Zhōngzhōu (中州),
was dispatched westward in the Yuánkāng (元康) era.
He encountered the chaos under heaven
and consequently remained in Shǔ (蜀).
At this time,
he led over three hundred families, intending to join Dù Tāo (杜弢),
but was captured by Kǎn (侃).
The generals requested to kill the able-bodied men
and seize their wives and children.
Yú (輿) said:
"These were originally government soldiers,
who have experienced many battles.
They can be pardoned and used."
Kǎn (侃) pardoned them
and assigned them to Yú (輿).
When Kǎn (侃) and Dù Tāo (杜弢) were defeated,
the bandits used *júgāo* (桔橰) (trebuchets) to sink the government army's ships,
causing dismay in the army.
Yú (輿) led light boats upstream to attack them,
and was victorious wherever he went.
The bandits then led their forces to burn Kǎn (侃)'s baggage train.
Yú (輿) again defeated them.
From then on, he was victorious in every battle.
When the bandits saw Yú (輿)'s army,
they said to each other:
"Avoid Táo Wǔwēi (陶武威)."
No one dared to confront him.
Later, in a battle against Dù Tāo (杜弢),
Yú (輿) was severely wounded
and died.
Kǎn (侃) wept for him mournfully,
saying:
"I have lost a treasure of my family!"
The entire army wept for him.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Chángshā Tàishǒu (長沙太守).
The Historian says: In ancient times, when enlightened kings established their states,
they surveyed the vast territories,
divided them into Nine Provinces,
assisted in their profound achievements,
and consulted with the Four Peaks.
This was to aspire to the governance of Qí (齊),
and to spread their influence below.
They established the rituals of commanders-in-chief,
their prestige extending beyond the borders;
they managed the affairs of distributing regulations,
their rites enriching the regions.
When their talent was entrusted to them,
the "Sweet Pear" was sung in praise;
when their virtue was not supported,
enmity and resentment arose with sighs.
In the waning years of the Central Court,
the remote and wild areas were often unruly.
Those who were granted seals and insignia of authority
all disrupted the heavenly order.
Hé Jì (和季), out of a sense of kinship,
renewed the covenant of Lú Wǎn (盧綰),
resided in the position of a regional governor,
and wielded the power of Wú Qǐ (吳起).
From Yōu (幽) to Jīng (荊),
he frequently suppressed the tracks of jackals and wolves;
he elevated the worthy and promoted the good,
gathering the feathers of peacocks and phoenixes.
Because of this, officials and common people exerted their full strength,
and both Chinese and barbarians obeyed his command.
The entire province was tranquil and peaceful,
calm amid a boiling sea;
all cities were safe,
their ominous portents quieted at the edge of the sky.
Still, it is said that good governance was rare!
How few there were!
The *Yì* (易) says:
"Firmness and steadfastness are sufficient for undertaking affairs."
This was seen in the General who Conquered the South.
〔一六〕Shìxíng (士行)'s reputation was not based on a noble lineage,
and his customs differed from the various Chinese.
He rose from among the common folk,
standing shoulder to shoulder with the most outstanding talents.
He rose to a prominent position outside the capital,
presiding over the upper reaches of the river.
When he spread kindness and embraced the frontier,
the fortified cities were peaceful and silent;
when he relinquished his position to assist the ruler,
the fallen dynasty was once again stable.
Yuán Guī (元規), due to his high status as a maternal relative,
bowed to him with respect;
Mào Hóng (茂弘), with the dignity of a grand tutor,
was moved by his words and his countenance changed.
His prestige was great, overseeing a separate region;
this was naturally appropriate.
However, at a time when clouds of discord gathered,
and his wealth surpassed that of the imperial treasury,
he harbored a secret ambition to control everything,
and considered the omen of broken wings –
this was perverse!
Confucius said:
"One should not expect perfection from others."
The truth of this statement
is verified here.
Eulogy: Hé Jì (和季) received imperial favor,
and established his banner in the southern regions.
His might pacified the Jīng (荊) passes,
and his civilizing influence spread to the river estuaries.
He exerted his strength for the imperial court,
never forgetting loyalty and solemnity.
The Chángshā (長沙) man toiled for the king,
waving his banner on the battlefield.
His responsibilities were as great as the three highest ministers,
and his achievements brought about order.
The weight of reliance on him
was not merely that of a boat.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Volume 37, Wēn Jiào (溫嶠)
Wēn Qiáo, courtesy name Tàizhēn,
was the son of Sītú Xiàn's younger brother.
His father, Dàn,
was the Administrator of Hédōng.
Qiáo was intelligent and quick-witted by nature,
possessing discernment and foresight.
He was broadly learned and skilled in composition.
From a young age, he was known for his filial piety and brotherly deference in his clan.
His demeanor was refined and dignified,
and he was eloquent in discussion;
all who met him were delighted by him.
At seventeen,
he was invited by the province and commanderies,
but he did not accept any appointments.
The Sīlì appointed him as Dūguān Cóngshì.
Sànqí Chángshì Yǔ Gāi had a great reputation,
but was quite avaricious.
Qiáo impeached him,
and the capital was shaken into肅.
Later, he was nominated as Xiùcái and Zhuórán.
The Sītú appointed him Dōnggé Jìjiǔ,
and then as Administrator of Lù County in Shàngdǎng.
The wife of Píngběi Dàjiāngjūn Liú Kūn
was Qiáo's maternal aunt.
Kūn treated him with deep respect,
and invited him to be his Cānjūn.
When Kūn was promoted to Dàjiāngjūn,
Qiáo became Cóngshì Zhōngláng and Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
and was additionally granted the title of Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, overseeing the vanguard forces.
He led troops to attack Shí Lè,
and repeatedly achieved military successes.
When Kūn was promoted to Sīkōng,
he made Qiáo his Yòusīmǎ.
At that time, the territory of Bìng Province was devastated and desolate,
with bandits rising up in groups.
Shí Lè and Liú Cōng dominated the borders.
Qiáo became Kūn's chief strategist,
and Kūn relied on him.
When the two capitals fell,
and the ancestral temples lost their sacrifices,
Yuán Dì first established his rule south of the Yangtze.
Kūn was sincerely devoted to the imperial house,
and said to Qiáo:
"In the past, Bān Biāo recognized the restoration of the Liú clan,
and Mǎ Yuán knew that Emperor Guāng of Hàn could be assisted.
Now, although the Jin dynasty is in decline,
Heaven's mandate has not changed.
I wish to establish merits north of the Yellow River,
and send you to spread our reputation south of the Yangtze.
Will you go?"
He replied:
"Although Qiáo lacks the talents of Guǎn Zhāng,
you, Your Grace, have the aspirations of Huán Wén.
Since you wish to achieve the meritorious work of restoring unity,
how dare I decline the mission?"
So, he was appointed Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
and sent out proclamations to both Chinese and "barbarians,"
submitting memorials to urge the emperor's enthronement.
When Qiáo arrived,
he was granted an audience.
He fully expounded Kūn's loyalty and sincerity,
and his determination to serve the nation.
He then spoke of the imperial altars being without a master,
and how both Heaven and man looked with hope.
His words were fervent and impassioned.
The entire court fixed their gaze upon him,
and the Emperor admired and praised him.
Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, Xiè Kūn,
Yǔ Liàng, Huán Yí, and others all became close friends with him.
At that time, the administration south of the Yangtze was just beginning,
and its framework was not yet established.
Qiáo was deeply concerned about this.
When he met Wáng Dǎo and conversed with him,
he joyfully exclaimed:
"Jiangxi has its own Guǎn Yíwú;
what more do I have to worry about!"
He repeatedly requested to return to report,
but was not permitted.
It happened that Kūn was harmed by Duàn Pǐdī.
Qiáo memorialized Kūn's loyalty and sincerity,
stating that although his accomplishments were not realized,
his family was ruined and he himself died.
He ought to be honored and praised
to satisfy the hopes of those within the four seas.
The Emperor agreed with him.
He was appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
Initially,
when Qiáo wished to carry out his mission,
his mother, Lady Cuī, firmly stopped him.
Qiáo tore his robes and left.
Later, when his mother died,
Qiáo was prevented by the chaos from returning to bury her.
Therefore, he resolutely declined the appointment,
earnestly requesting to return north.
An imperial edict ordered the three chief ministers and eight senior officials to discuss the matter.
They all said:
"In the past, Wǔ Yuán was determined to avenge a personal grievance,
first borrowing the power of a feudal lord.
He fled east to Hélǘ,
was appointed a high general,
and then flogged the corpse of King Jǐng.
If Qiáo considers his mother unburied and lost to the northern barbarians,
then he should exhaust his wisdom and strategy,
relying on the imperial divine power,
to make the rebel bandits melt away like ice,
and then return to mourn at her tomb.
How can he slightly discard his grand plan due to personal difficulties?"
Qiáo had no choice
but to accept the appointment.
Later, he served as Chángshǐ to Pàqí Wáng Dǎo,
then was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
While in the Eastern Palace,
he received deep favor and trust.
The Crown Prince treated him as a commoner friend.
He frequently offered counsel and remonstrance,
and also presented a "Zhēn for Attendant Officials,"
which was greatly beneficial.
At that time, the Crown Prince was building a new tower and pavilion at the West Pond,
which was quite costly.
Qiáo submitted a memorial, arguing that the court was newly established,
and the great bandits were not yet eliminated.
It was appropriate to lead by frugality,
and prioritize agriculture and military strength.
The Crown Prince accepted this.
When Wáng Dūn raised troops and advanced inward,
the six armies were defeated.
The Crown Prince was about to lead the battle himself.
Qiáo grasped the reins and remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that a good warrior is not angry,
and a good victor is not belligerent.
How can the heir apparent of ten thousand chariots lightly risk himself in such a way!"
The Crown Prince then stopped.
When Emperor Míng acceded to the throne,
Wēn Qiáo was appointed Shìzhōng.
All major confidential strategies were coordinated and participated in by him,
and imperial edicts and literary compositions also entirely involved him.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng.
Wēn Qiáo had the responsibility of a pillar of the state;
the Emperor held him in high regard and relied on him.
He was greatly feared by Wáng Dūn,
who therefore requested that Wēn Qiáo be made Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
Wáng Dūn, obstructing the Emperor with his military power, did not attend court,
and frequently acted with arrogance and unrestraint.
Wēn Qiáo admonished Wáng Dūn, saying:
"In ancient times, when Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
he toiled diligently and was humble, even spitting out his food to attend to guests.
How could he genuinely enjoy hard work and dislike ease?
It was truly because one who holds a great responsibility must not do otherwise.
Yet, since you returned to the capital
to assist in court affairs,
you have neglected the rituals of paying respects
and simplified the decorum of a subject.
Those who do not understand the Emperor's heart are all dismayed.
In the past, Emperor Shùn served Emperor Yáo,
and Bó Yǔ exhausted himself in the court of Yú.
Even though King Wén was mighty,
his conduct as a subject was never amiss.
Therefore, one who possesses the great virtue of sheltering others
must also possess the humble heart of serving his lord,
so that their glorious reputation may inspire for a hundred generations,
and their excellent influence flow for ten thousand years.
The teachings left by the ultimate sages
should not be overlooked.
I wish you would contemplate the diligence of Shùn, Yǔ, and King Wén in their service,
and consider the matter of Duke of Zhōu spitting out his food to attend to guests;
then the world would be extremely fortunate."
Wáng Dūn did not accept this advice.
Wēn Qiáo knew that Wáng Dūn would ultimately not be awakened,
so he falsely displayed respect,
managed Wáng Dūn's official affairs,
and engaged in secret counsel
to conform to his desires.
He deeply befriended Qián Fèng
and built a reputation for him,
often saying:
"Qián Shìyí is full of spirit and wisdom."
Wēn Qiáo had always been known for his ability to discern people,
and Qián Fèng heard this and was pleased,
forming a deep friendship with Wēn Qiáo.
Coincidentally, the position of Dānyáng Yǐn was vacant.
Wēn Qiáo persuaded Wáng Dūn, saying:
"The 京尹 is the throat and tongue of the imperial capital;
one who is capable in both civil and military affairs should be obtained.
You should personally select such a talent.
If the court appoints someone,
it might not be entirely appropriate."
Wáng Dūn agreed
and asked Wēn Qiáo who would be suitable.
Wēn Qiáo said:
"I believe Qián Fèng could be appointed."
Qián Fèng also recommended Wēn Qiáo,
and Wēn Qiáo feigned a refusal.
Wáng Dūn did not comply
and memorialized to appoint Wēn Qiáo as Dānyáng Yǐn.
Wēn Qiáo still feared Qián Fèng's treacherous schemes.
During Wáng Dūn's farewell banquet for him,
Wēn Qiáo rose to offer wine.
When he reached Qián Fèng,
before Qián Fèng could drink,
Wēn Qiáo feigned drunkenness
and used his tablet to strike Qián Fèng's cap, knocking it off.
He said with a stern expression:
"Who is Qián Fèng,
that Wēn Tàizhēn offers him wine and he dares not drink!"
Wáng Dūn thought he was drunk,
and both were appeased.
As Wēn Qiáo was about to leave, he bid farewell,
with tears streaming down his face.
He went out of the hall and came back in,
doing this two or three times,
and then finally set off.
After he departed,
Qián Fèng entered and persuaded Wáng Dūn, saying:
"Wēn Qiáo is very close to the court,
and deeply friends with Yǔ Liàng;
he may not be trustworthy."
Wáng Dūn said:
"Tàizhēn was drunk yesterday and raised his voice a little;
how can you use this to slander and sow discord between us?"
Thus, Qián Fèng's plan was not implemented,
and Wēn Qiáo was able to return to the capital.
He then fully memorialized Wáng Dūn's rebellious intentions,
requesting that preparations be made in advance.
When Wáng Dūn initiated his rebellion,
Wēn Qiáo was appointed Zhōnglěi Jiāngjūn, with the titles of Chíjíe and Dūdū Dōng'ān Běibù Zhū Jūnjì.
Wáng Dūn wrote to Wáng Dǎo, saying:
"Tàizhēn has been gone for only a few days,
and has done such a thing!"
He memorialized for the execution of treacherous ministers,
with Wēn Qiáo as the leader.
He offered a reward for anyone who could capture Wēn Qiáo alive,
promising to personally rip out his tongue.
When Wáng Hán and Qián Fèng suddenly arrived beneath the capital,
Wēn Qiáo burned the Zhūquè Héng to blunt their attack.
The Emperor was angry about this,
but Wēn Qiáo said:
"Our imperial guards are now few and weak,
and reinforcements have not yet arrived.
If the rebels charge forward like wild boars,
the state will be in danger.
Why does Your Majesty begrudge one bridge?"
The rebels indeed could not cross.
Wēn Qiáo personally led his troops to fight the rebels across the water,
attacking Wáng Hán
and defeating him.
He then ordered Liú Xiá to pursue Qián Fèng in Jiāngníng.
After the matter was settled,
he was enfeoffed as Jiànníng Xiàn Kāiguó Gōng,
awarded five thousand four hundred bolts of silk,
and promoted to the title of Qián Jiāngjūn.
At that time, an edict stipulated that Wáng Dūn's subordinates were to be stripped of their names,
and his staff were to be confined.
Wēn Qiáo submitted a memorial, saying:
"Wáng Dūn was stubborn and unkind,
ruthlessly committing massacres,
trusting petty individuals,
and alienating gentlemen.
The court could not restrain him,
and his own kin could not intervene.
Those who served in his court feared danger and destruction,
thus scholars remained silent,
communicating only with glances on the roads.
This was truly a time when virtuous individuals and gentlemen found their paths blocked and their opportunities exhausted,
and had to endure their obscurity.
Furthermore, on the day Wáng Dūn committed great treason,
he detained scholars.
They had no way to escape on their own.
Considering their private thoughts,
how could they have found peace?
For example, Lù Wán, Yáng Màn, Liú Yìn, Cài Mó, and Guō Pú often spoke with your servant,
and I know this fully.
If they were indeed wicked and perverse,
then the guilty should certainly be punished;
if they were wrongly implicated in the treacherous faction,
they should be treated with leniency.
Moreover, the sincerity of Lù Wán and others
has reached the imperial ears.
To hold them responsible as if they were complicit with the rebels
would truly go against their hearts.
Your Majesty is benevolent, sagacious, and magnanimous,
and seeks to find fairness.
Your servant, by virtue of his broad connections,
has intervened in matters not his own,
but his true intention is to cherish talent
and not forget loyal benefits."
The Emperor followed his advice.
At that time, the empire was in decline and distress,
and the state's resources were insufficient.
An imperial edict commanded the Dukes and Ministers and all below them to gather in the capital to discuss the most urgent matters of governance.
Jiáo then submitted a memorial on vital military and state affairs.
The first point said:
"Zǔ Yuē has withdrawn to Shòuyáng,
and there is a future difficulty to contend with.
Now, defending the two regions [of Xú and Yù]
is still an easy task.
The Grand Administrator of Huái and Sì [Jiāngxī]
should exert himself to support it.
Select worthy and respected gentlemen,
assign them five thousand conscripted soldiers,
and also choose one brigade commander,
to lead two thousand soldiers,
to reinforce Shòuyáng.
This will ensure the security of Xú and Yù,
and provide aid to Sītú."
The second point said:
"If one man does not till,
there will certainly be someone who suffers hunger because of it.
Now, the number of men who do not till
amounts to tens of thousands.
In spring, the system of encouraging agriculture is neglected,
while in winter, the decree for collecting rent is enforced strictly.
Benevolent policies are not seen by the people below,
only taxes are heard of.
Taxes cannot be abolished,
but one should consider how to enable the common people to prosper.
The Sītú used to appoint a Tiáncáo Yuàn,
one in each province,
to encourage farming and sericulture,
and to observe the competence of officials.
It is now fitting to restore this old system.
If we can truly find those who are honest, dedicated to public service,
and capable of proclaiming benevolent reforms,
then the benefits will truly be immense."
The third point said:
"All those commanding troops in outer provinces and commanderies, and non-frontline armies of the Grand Administrator's headquarters,
should both farm and guard.
Furthermore, the previous dynasty had five corps engaged in farming.
Now, among the Four Armies and Five Corps who have soldiers,
and the outer armies supervised by the Hùjūn,
two armies can be dispatched [for farming],
and garrisoned in key locations.
Along the Jiāng river, both upstream and downstream,
there is good farmland.
Clearing it will become easy after one year.
Moreover, it is convenient for the army,
as soldiers with families are outside,
and there are people to gather firewood and vegetables for food."
The fourth point said:
"Officials are established to govern the world,
not for private gain.
If this is the case, then officials will be few and their talents refined.
The Zhōu system had six ministers overseeing affairs;
in the Spring and Autumn period,
they served as ministers and辅佐,
and led the three armies when going out.
Later generations gradually established more officials,
truly because affairs became more complex or simpler.
However, the land in the six provinces south of the Jiāng River
is still desolate and ruined;
compared to peaceful times,
it is but one-tenth or less.
Among the Three Departments' military schools that have no soldiers,
and the Nine Ministries' offices that could be combined under one head,
some could be reduced by half.
Roughly estimate busy and idle tasks,
and reduce them according to the circumstances.
In desolate and ruined counties,
where some are located within the same city,
they can be merged.
In this way, selections can be refined,
salaries and stipends can be generous,
making them sufficient to substitute for farming.
Only then can they be held accountable for honesty and public service."
The fifth point said:
"In ancient times, the ruler personally ploughed the ceremonial field to provide sacrificial grains.
Formerly, officials for the ceremonial field and the sacrificial granary were established.
Now, purchasing them on the market at the last minute
not only defiles the utmost reverence above,
but also wastes resources below,
which is not in line with the purpose of reverently offering sacrifices to the ancestral temple throughout the year.
It is fitting to follow the old system
and establish these two officials."
The sixth point said:
"The further the mission,
the more appropriate it is to select talented individuals
to propagate the Emperor's transforming influence
and extend his reputation in all directions.
When people are unwilling,
and lowly individuals are chosen instead,
it dishonors the national mission
and fosters troubles and harms.
Therefore, the selection should be rigorous;
those with salaries of less than two thousand *dàn* and currently holding a second-rank position should not be chosen."
The seventh point said:
"Punishment should not extend to others,
this is an ancient system.
Recently, cases of high treason
were indeed due to extreme ferocity.
Such extreme ferocity
was handled with temporary expediency.
Now, to continue its enforcement
is not a permanent statute of a sagely dynasty.
It is fitting to revert to the previous dynasty's system of exempting the three kindreds."
This memorial was submitted,
and much of it was adopted.
When the Emperor's illness became critical,
Jiáo, along with Wáng Dǎo, Xī Jiàn, Yǔ Liàng, Lù Yè, Biàn Hú, and others, jointly received the dying imperial charge.
At that time, Sū Jùn, the Grand Administrator of Lìyáng, harbored fugitives,
and the imperial court suspected him.
As General Who Conquers the West, Táo Kǎn, had great prestige in Jīng and Chǔ,
and there was also concern about the west,
Jiáo was therefore made the strategic support for the upper reaches of the river.
In the beginning of Xiánhé,
he replaced Yīng Zhān as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, holding the *jié*, Grand Administrator, and General Who Pacifies the South,
garrisoned at Wǔchāng.
He governed with great beneficence,
discerning and promoting those with unique abilities,
and personally offered sacrifices at Xú Rúzi's tomb.
He also presented [a memorial stating]:
"The vital importance of the ten commanderies of Yùzhāng
suggests that the Inspector should reside there.
Xúnyáng borders the river,
and the Grand Administrator should garrison that place.
Now, with the province subject to the headquarters,
advancement and retreat are inconvenient.
Moreover, ancient garrison commanders often did not simultaneously govern a province,
all because civil and military situations differed.
It is fitting to select an Inspector with a single carriage to separately pacify Yùzhāng,
and specifically govern the common people."
An imperial edict did not permit it.
While at his post, he saw a portrait of Wáng Dūn
and said:
"Wáng Dūn committed high treason;
he should have suffered the punishment of a coffin hewing,
and received the retribution of Cuī Zhù.
Ancient people sealed the coffin before determining the posthumous title,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals emphasized upholding righteousness,
honoring the king's father's command.
There has never been anyone who suffered execution by the Son of Heaven and then had his portrait displayed among the officials."
He ordered it to be removed.
When Jiáo heard of Sū Jùn's conscription,
he worried that there would certainly be a rebellion,
and requested to return to the court to prepare for unforeseen circumstances,
but he was not permitted.
Not long after, Sū Jùn indeed rebelled.

Jiáo garrisoned Xúnyáng and dispatched Supervising Commandant Wáng Qiānqī, Grand Administrator of Xīyáng Dèng Yuè, Internal Administrator of Póyáng Jǐ Zhān, and others to lead a naval force to meet the crisis.
When the capital fell,
Jiáo wept and wailed upon hearing the news.
Those who visited him
mourned and cried with him.
Soon after, Yǔ Liàng came seeking refuge,
proclaiming an imperial edict from the Empress Dowager,
promoting Jiáo to General of Agile Cavalry and granting him the privilege of establishing a personal administration equal to the Three Excellencies.
Jiáo said:
"In this current emergency,
annihilating the rebels is the priority.
To accept such honors before achieving meritorious service
is something I have not heard of.
How can I show this to the world?"
He firmly declined to accept.
Although Yǔ Liàng had fled in defeat at that time,
Jiáo always highly esteemed him
and allocated troops to Liàng.
He sent Wáng Qiānqī and others to urge Táo Kǎn to join in facing the national crisis,
but Kǎn, resentful that he had not been included in the dying imperial charge,
refused.
Jiáo initially complied,
but later, following the advice of his subordinate general Máo Bǎo,
he again firmly requested Kǎn to go.
(The details are in Máo Bǎo's biography.)
Initially,
Jiáo and Yǔ Liàng deferred to each other as the leader of the alliance.
Jiáo's younger cousin, Chōng, said to Jiáo:
"The General Who Conquers the West holds a weighty position and strong forces;
we should jointly defer to him."
Jiáo then sent Wáng Qiānqī to appoint Kǎn as the alliance leader.
Kǎn agreed,
and dispatched Supervising Commandant Gōng Dēng to lead troops to Jiáo.
Jiáo then submitted a memorial to the Shàngshū,
enumerating Sū Jùn's crimes,
with seven thousand troops,
tearfully boarded his boat,
and issued a proclamation to all regional commanders and garrisons: "The treacherous ministers Zǔ Yuē and Sū Jùn, being of the same evil mind, assisted each other,
and thus engendered wicked intentions.
Heaven has taken away their spirit;
their time of death is approaching.
They have violated Heaven and Earth,
and cut themselves off from humanity."
Lún.
The bandits cannot be indulged.
It is fitting to increase the army to suppress them.
I have immediately encamped at Pénkǒu.
On the same day, Grand Warden Yǔ Liàng arrived,
announcing the Empress Dowager's edict:
The bandits are pressing upon the palace city,
the royal
army is defeated and demoralized.
I am issuing this proclamation to my vassal ministers,
to strategize for the peace of the state.
General of the Rear Guō Mò, General of the Champions Zhào Yìn, General Fènwǔ Gōng Bǎo, and Qiáo's overseer Wáng
Qiānqī, along with the Administrator of Xīyáng Dèng Yuè, and the Internal Controller of Póyáng Jì Zhān,
led their subordinates,
and arrived one after another.
The rebel bandits commit atrocities,
treading upon the ancestral temples,
fires spread to the
palace quarters,
arrows fly into the Tàijí Palace.
The two Majesties are confined and pressed,
the prime ministers are trapped and distressed,
courtiers are cruelly abused,
daughters and sons are kidnapped and defiled.
Hearing this news, I am filled with sorrow and fear,
my spirit flies away.
I, Qiáo,
am obscure and weak, not martial,
unable to sacrifice myself in this crisis.
I lament and blame myself,
my five emotions are shattered.
I am ashamed to have failed the heavy trust placed in me by the late Emperor;
my duty dictates that I exert all my strength,
not stopping until death.
Now I personally lead my subordinates,
acting as a vanguard for the soldiers,
urging all armies forward,
to strike like lightning at once.
The Administrator of Xīyáng Dèng Yuè and the Administrator of Xúnyáng Chǔ Dàn, with their banners connected, are arriving
continuously.
The Internal Controller of Xuānchéng Huán Yí has already ordered his subordinates to encamp at a strategic point along the river.
The Commander of Jiāngxià Zhōu Fǔ has sincerely requested to join the expedition,
and his army is already on its way.
In the past, Bāo Xū, a humble minister of the state of Chǔ,
traveled with worn-out feet to convey his sincerity,
and his righteousness moved the feudal lords.
Lìn Xiāngrú, a servant of the state of Zhào,
ashamed of his lord's humiliation,
drew his sword in the Qin
court.
In the late Hán dynasty,
Dǒng Zhuó caused chaos,
kidnapped and relocated Emperor Xiàn,
and cruelly harmed the loyal and good.
The prefectures and commanderies east of the passes united in an alliance.
Zāng Hóng, a judicial clerk of Guǎnglíng,
a minor official of the commandery,
mounted the altar, tasted blood,
his tears flowing across his face,
his heroic spirit
truly inspired the various lords.
How much more so now for those who hold high office,
govern provinces,
are listed among the prominent citizens of the
state,
and have received the nation's grace!
That we should meet without prior arrangement,
and agree without prior consultation,
is it not fitting!
The two bandits have combined their forces,
not exceeding five thousand.
Moreover, externally they fear the Hú barbarians,
and within the city, they suffer from hunger and scarcity.
General of the Rear Guō Mò has already captured and killed a thousand bandits in battle.
Although the bandits have now devastated the capital,
their imperial guard soldiers immediately dispersed,
and are not used by the bandits.
Furthermore, Zǔ Yuē's temperament is narrow and obstructive,
jealous, ruthless, and inhumane.
Sū Jùn
is a mere youth,
who only looks to profit.
Cruel, arrogant, and suspicious,
they have temporarily allied for power.
Righteous forces are rising in the region south of the Yangtze,
to resist them in front,
while strong Hú barbarians are attacking
them from behind.
Shipping
and transport are cut off,
their provisions are depleted.
Lacking support internally and isolated externally,
how can their power last long!
All the Dukes, Generals, and local administrators
have the duty to repel invaders.
General of the West, Duke Táo,
is a venerable figure of the state,
loyal, solemn, and righteous,
his achievements and merits are grand and prominent.
All the regional administrators and commandery governors will
unite like cut metal,
and follow the same strategy,
to wipe away the national shame.
If it benefits the state,
we will dedicate our lives to it.
Although I, Qiáo, am timid and weak,
I have unworthily occupied a regional post.
Relying on the advice of the loyal and wise,
and the assistance of civil and military officials,
gentlemen exert their sincerity,
and commoners exhaust their strength.
Men of noble character, in coarse clothes, join the army,
and those who carry firewood crawl to answer the call.
They lead their
private servants,
and offer their private staffs.
The sincerity of the gentry
cannot be recorded on bamboo or silk.
How could this be due to my lack of virtue?
It is because the gentry are imbued with the spirit of righteousness,
and the people are moved by the Emperor's
grace.
Furthermore, Grand Warden Yǔ,
the Emperor's maternal uncle,
is greatly respected for his virtue and prestige.
He leads General of the Rear Guō, and the three generals Zhào and Gōng,
to work together with me, Qiáo.
With such support and reliance,
I am both
sorrowful and joyful,
as if the imperial court will not perish.
Each of you should clearly lead your subordinates,
and not delay the critical moment.
The promise of rewards and recruitment
is as clear as the sun and moon.
Anyone who can behead
Yuē and Jùn
will be enfeoffed as a marquis of the fifth rank,
and rewarded with ten thousand bolts of cloth.
Indeed, loyalty is a noble virtue,
and benevolence stems from oneself.
A single bond across ten thousand miles,
righteousness needs no words.
At this time, Táo Kǎn, though he had promised to come down, had not yet departed,
and he recalled his overseer Gōng Dēng.
Qiáo wrote another letter to Kǎn, saying: I believe that an army should advance and not retreat;
it should be augmented and not reduced.
I have recently issued proclamations far and wide,
and declared to the alliance headquarters,
that we will launch a major offensive in the latter half of next month.
The armies of the three commanderies of Nán
kāng, Jiàn'ān, and Jìn'ān are all on their way,
to join this assembly.
We only await the arrival of the forces under your command, Benevolent Duke,
then we will advance together.
Now, Benevolent Duke, by recalling the army,
you cause doubt far and wide.
The outcome of success or failure
will hinge on this.
My talent is meager, but my responsibility is heavy.
I truly rely on your deep affection, Benevolent Duke,
and will follow your established plans from afar.
As for taking the lead in the military campaign,
I dare not decline.
You and I, Benevolent Duke, should be like
the serpent of Chángshān,
head and tail defending each other,
or like lips and teeth.
I fear that the confused may not understand your noble intention,
and will say that you, Benevolent Duke, are slow in attacking the bandits.
Such a reputation is hard to
undo.
You and I, Benevolent Duke, both bear the responsibility of governing a region,
so our safety, danger, joy, and sorrow
are naturally intertwined.
Moreover, from our past interactions,
our close ties and exchanges,
our deep affection and heavy
righteousness,
are on the lips of the gentry.
If there were an emergency,
I would also expect you, Benevolent Duke, to bring all your forces to rescue me,
let alone a national crisis!
I alone govern a province,
and all its civil and military officials are eagerly awaiting help.
If this province cannot be defended,
and Yuē and Jùn establish their officials here,
Jīngchǔ will be pressed by strong Hú barbarians in the west,
and bordered by rebel bandits in the east.
Compounded by famine,
the future danger will be even greater than the current situation of this province.
In terms of great righteousness,
then the state...
The altars of soil and grain have been overturned,
the lord has been humiliated, and his ministers have died.
When Gōng Jìn advances, he ought to be a loyal minister of the Great Jìn,
emulating the righteousness of Huán and Wén,
establishing the state and securing the family,
inscribing it in the heavenly records;
when he retreats, he ought
to avenge the pain of his beloved son as a loving father.
Yuē Jùn is utterly evil, lawless,
imprisoning and controlling gentry,
stripping them naked.
Recently, what has transpired
is unbearable to witness.
Kin are separated alive,
their pain reaching Heaven
and Earth,
the hearts of the people are united,
all gnashing their teeth.
To advance and attack now
would be like throwing a stone at an egg!
Now that the army has been delayed in its deployment,
and then recalled,
people's hearts are alienated
and scattered,
this is to fail at the cusp of success.
I wish you would deeply consider what I have presented,
to fulfill the hopes of the three armies.
At that time, Jùn killed Kǎn's son, Zhān.
Because of this, Kǎn was stirred to action,
and then led his forces with Qiáo and Liàng to the capital.
There were sixty thousand soldiers,
banners and flags stretching over seven hundred *lǐ*,
the sound of gongs and drums reverberating for a hundred *lǐ*,
heading straight for Shítou,
and halting at Càizhōu.
Kǎn encamped at Chápǔ,
Qiáo encamped at Shāménpǔ.
At that time, Zǔ Yuē occupied Lìyáng,
forming a front and rear with Jùn.
Seeing Qiáo's army and others so formidable,
he said to his followers:
"I originally knew that Qiáo could accomplish the tasks of the Four Princes,
and now it is indeed so."
When Jùn heard that Qiáo was approaching,
he forced the emperor to Shítou.
At that time, Jùn's army had many horses,
while the southern army relied on boats and rafts,
not daring to engage lightly.
Following General Lǐ Gēn's plan,
they fortified themselves by building a stronghold at Báishí,
and made Yú Liàng defend it.
The rebels' infantry and cavalry, over ten thousand strong, came to attack,
but failed to take it and retreated.
Two hundred-plus heads were pursued and cut off.
Qiáo also built a stronghold at Sìwàngjī to press the rebels,
saying:
"The rebels will surely contend for it.
We will set up an ambush and await the weary with fresh troops;
this is a crucial stratagem to control the rebels."
At this time, the righteous army had repeatedly lost battles,
and Qiáo's army had run out of food.
Táo Kǎn angrily said:
"Your Excellency said before that you were not worried about not having generals and soldiers,
only needing an old servant as leader.
Now, after several battles, all have been defeats.
Where are the good generals?
Jīngzhōu borders the two barbarians, Hú and Shǔ;
its granaries ought to be prepared for contingencies.
If there is again no food,
I will want to return west
and reconsider a better plan.
But for this year's plan,
it is not too late to annihilate the rebels."
Qiáo replied:
"No.
Since ancient times, it has been observed
that victory in war lies in harmony.
Guāngwǔ's success at Kūnyáng,
Cáo Gōng's victory at Guāndù,
pitted few against many,
relying on righteousness.
Jùn and Yuē are mere rascals,
a menace to the entire realm.
Today's undertaking
depends on one decisive battle.
Jùn is brave but without strategy,
relying on his arrogant winning streak,
believing himself invincible.
If we challenge him to battle now,
he can be captured in one swift strike.
Why abandon this imminent success
and devise plans for advance and retreat!
Moreover, the Son of Heaven is confined and oppressed,
the state is in peril,
and the subjects of the four seas
are ready to lay down their lives.
Qiáo and I, together with you, have received the nation's grace,
this is the day to give our lives.
If the mission succeeds,
then minister and lord will share prosperity;
if it does not succeed,
though my body may be reduced to ashes,
it would not be enough to apologize for my failure to the late emperor.
Given the current situation,
there is no turning back.
One who rides a fierce beast
cannot dismount halfway!
If you disregard the consensus and turn back alone,
the morale of the people will surely be dampened.
If the people are disheartened and the mission fails,
the banner of righteousness will turn to point at you!"
Kǎn had no reply,
and so remained.
Qiáo then established a temporary shrine,
widely setting up altars,
reporting to the spirits of Heaven, Earth, and his ancestors,
personally reading the sacrificial text,
his voice stirring and passionate,
tears streaming down his face,
so that none of the three armies could look up at him.
On that day, Kǎn commanded the navy towards Shítou,
while Liàng, Qiáo and others led ten thousand elite brave soldiers from Báishí to challenge.
At that time, Jùn was rewarding his generals and soldiers;
in his drunkenness,
he charged into the formation, his horse stumbling,
and was slain by Kǎn's general.
Jùn's brother Yì and son Shuò defended the city themselves.
Qiáo then established a provisional government,
proclaiming to the world
that all former officials holding two thousand *dàn* salary, and *tái* officials and imperial censors below that rank,
were ordered to report to the government.
Thereupon, those who arrived gathered like clouds.
Minister of Works Wáng Dǎo then recommended Qiáo and Kǎn to be appointed acting *Shàngshū* (Secretaries of the Imperial Secretariat),
and sent a secret envoy to declare the imperial edict,
but they both declined to accept.
Rebel general Kuāng Shù surrendered with Táichéng,
but was attacked by Yì,
and sought help from Qiáo.
Luō Dòng, the assistant governor of Jiāngzhōu, said:
"The waters are rising rapidly now;
it is inconvenient to rescue them.
It would be better to attack Tàháng.
If the Tàháng army is defeated,
Shù's siege will be lifted automatically."
Qiáo followed this advice,
and consequently defeated the rebel army at Shítou.
Ténɡ Hán, the acting General of Inspiring Awe, carried the emperor and fled to Qiáo's boat.
Although Táo Kǎn was the nominal leader at that time,
all the arrangements and strategies came from Qiáo.
After the rebels were eliminated,
he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry, *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*,
additionally given the title of *Sànqí Chángshì*,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Shǐ'ān Commandery,
with a stipend of three thousand households.
Previously,
Jùn's partisans Lù Yǒnɡ, Kuāng Shù, and Jiǎ Nínɡ, all surrendered with their forces midway.
Wáng Dǎo intended to praise and honor them,
but Qiáo said:
"Shù and his ilk initiated the rebellion;
their crime is unsurpassed.
Although they repented late,
it is not enough to compensate for their previous mistakes.
To preserve their lives
is already more fortune than they deserve;
how can they be further favored and granted official positions!"
Dǎo had no counter-argument.
The imperial court debated retaining him to assist in governing,
but Wēn Jiǎo, considering that Dǎo Xiān Dì had appointed him,
resolutely declined and returned to his domain.
Furthermore, as the capital region was desolate and ruined,
and resources were insufficient,
Wēn Jiǎo borrowed provisions and stores,
prepared equipment,
and then returned to Wǔchāng.
Upon reaching Niúzhǔ Jī,
the water was unfathomably deep.
It was commonly said that many monsters resided beneath it.
Wēn Jiǎo then burned a rhinoceros horn and illuminated the water.
After a moment,
he saw aquatic creatures covering the area illuminated by the fire,
with strange shapes and unusual forms,
some riding chariots and wearing red clothing.
That night, Wēn Jiǎo dreamt that a person said to him:
"You and I are separating on the paths of the living and the dead.
Why did you choose to shine a light on me?"
He felt very disturbed by this.
Wēn Jiǎo had previously suffered from a tooth ailment;
at this time, he had it extracted,
and consequently suffered a stroke.
He died within ten days of reaching his post,
at the age of forty-two.
When the scholars and common people of Jiāngzhōu heard of this,
they all looked at each other and wept.
The Emperor issued an imperial edict saying:
"I, with my humble person,
have inherited the great lineage,
yet I have been unable to widely promote the Grand Way,
or bring harmony and prosperity to the age.
Thus, wild rebels have run rampant,
and the altars of soil and grain are in peril.
Only you, Duke, with your clear insight and unique understanding,
and your far-sighted wisdom,
feared that the imperial order would not be maintained,
and were indignant at the violence of the fierce bandits.
You took the lead among the many princes,
and the five provinces responded,
initiating military action,
and the arch-villain was executed.
The royal house, after being in danger, found peace again,
and the three luminaries, after being obscured, shone brightly again.
Your accomplishments reached the universe,
and your merits were renowned in all directions.
Just as we relied on your great strategy to save the land,
Heaven begrudged us,
and you passed away early in life.
I am deeply saddened in my heart.
Indeed, to praise virtue and inscribe merits
is a clear tradition of the former kings.
Now, I posthumously confer upon the Duke the titles of Shìzhōng, Dàjiàngjūn, Chíjíe, Dūdū, and Cìshǐ,
as if he were still alive,
and bestow one million cash,
and one thousand bolts of cloth.
His posthumous name shall be Zhōngwǔ,
and he shall be sacrificed to with a grand offering."
He was initially buried in Yùzhāng.
Later, the imperial court, recalling Wēn Jiǎo's achievements and virtues,
planned to construct a grand tomb for him north of the tombs of Emperors Yuán and Míng.
Táo Kǎn submitted a memorial saying:
"The late Grand General Wēn Jiǎo's loyalty and integrity were renowned in the sacred age,
and his merits and righteousness moved both men and gods;
they are beyond what my pen can praise or express.
At the time of his death,
he wrote a letter to me saying farewell.
I keep it hidden in my casket,
and often review it.
Each time I think of him,
I cannot but press my hand to my chest in the middle of the night,
and feel choked with sorrow at meals.
'When a man passes away,'
Wēn Jiǎo truly embodies this.
I respectfully transcribe Wēn Jiǎo's letter and present it to Your Majesty.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to kindly examine it,
and be moved by its sentiment,
that even in death he did not forget his loyalty.
Even after his body descended to the Yellow Springs,
he still regretted the national disgrace,
and wished to join forces with his subjects
to rescue the country from its difficulties.
If he, though deceased, were conscious,
and harbored resentment that would tie grass,
how could he be pleased with today's expensive undertaking?
I pray for Your Majesty's gracious mercy,
to halt his reburial,
so that Wēn Jiǎo's coffin may be free from the dangers of wind and waves,
and his spirit may rest peacefully in the netherworld."
The Emperor granted this.
Later, Wēn Jiǎo's second wife, Hé Shì, died,
and his son, Fàngzhī, transported her coffin back to the capital.
An edict commanded her burial north of Jiànpíng Líng,
and also posthumously granted Wēn Jiǎo's former wife, Wáng Shì, and Hé Shì the seals and ribbons of Shǐ'ān Fūrén.
Fàngzhī inherited the noble rank,
served in various minor official positions,
and eventually reached the post of Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
Due to poverty,
he sought appointment as the governor of Jiāozhōu,
which the imperial court granted.
Wáng Shù wrote a memorial to the Prince of Huìjī, saying:
"Fàngzhī is the son of Wēn Jiǎo;
he ought to be treated with special distinction.
To cast him out to the Lingnan region,
I am secretly astonished by this.
I hope that the Rites of Zhōu may be remembered from afar,
and human sentiment considered closely,
then reputation and reality will be truly harmonious."
At that time, this was not accepted.
When Fàngzhī arrived in Nánhǎi,
he was very effective and benevolent.
When he was about to campaign against Línyì,
the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, Dù Bǎo, and the Assistant Administrator, Ruǎn Láng, both refused to comply.
Fàngzhī, considering that they were obstructing the army,
executed them,
led his troops forward,
and consequently defeated Línyì and returned.
He died in office.
His younger brother, Shìzhī,
was the Marquis of Xīnjiàn County,
and rose to the position of Sànqí Chángshì.
Xī Jiàn (Son Yīn; Yīn's son Chāo; Yīn's younger brother Tán; Tán's son Huī; Jiàn's uncle Lóng)
Xī Jiàn, courtesy name Dàohuī,
was a native of Jīnxiāng, Gāopíng.
He was the great-great-grandson of Hàn Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǜ.
He was orphaned and poor in his youth,
but extensively read classics,
personally tilled the fields,
and recited poetry tirelessly.
He was renowned for his refined scholarship
and did not answer the provincial summons.
Zhào Wáng Lún appointed him as an aide,
but knowing Lún harbored intentions of usurpation,
he feigned illness and left his post.
When Lún usurped the throne,
all his partisans attained high offices,
but Xī Jiàn remained secluded at home,
not tainted by the rebellion.
When Huì Dì was restored,
he served in the military affairs of Sīkōng,
and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén and Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè appointed him as Master of Records,
and recommended him as a worthy and upright scholar,
but he did not take office.
Zhēngdōng Dàjiàngjūn Gǒu Xī summoned him as Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Gǒu Xī and Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè were at that time contending for power,
but Xī Jiàn did not respond to his summons.
His paternal cousin, Xù,
who was Gǒu Xī's Assistant Administrator,
feared that disaster would befall him,
and urged him to obey the summons,
but Xī Jiàn ultimately did not waver,
nor did Gǒu Xī compel him.
When the capital could no longer be defended,
and bandits and troubles arose everywhere,
Xī Jiàn fell into the hands of the bandit Chén Wǔ.
Zhāng Shí, a local, had previously sought friendship with Xī Jiàn,
but Xī Jiàn had refused.
At this time,
Zhāng Shí came to Chén Wǔ's camp to inquire about Xī Jiàn's illness,
and then paid respects to Xī Jiàn.
Xī Jiàn said to Zhāng Shí:
"We share the same homeland,
but righteousness prevents us from having dealings.
How can you rely on this chaos to such an extent!"
Zhāng Shí was greatly ashamed and withdrew.
Chén Wǔ, knowing Xī Jiàn's reputation,
intended to force him to be their leader,
but Xī Jiàn escaped and was thus spared.
Chén Wǔ soon dispersed,
and Xī Jiàn was able to return to his hometown.
At that time, there was famine everywhere,
and the local gentry, who had always been grateful for his benevolence and righteousness,
helped him with provisions.
Xī Jiàn, in turn, distributed what he received
to assist his relatives and the orphans and elderly in his village.
Many relied on him and were saved,
and they all said to each other:
"Today, the Son of Heaven has been displaced,
and there is no hegemon in the Central Plains.
We should rely on a benevolent and virtuous person,
who can ensure our survival."
So they all jointly acclaimed Xī Jiàn as their leader,
and over a thousand families moved with him to seek refuge in Yìshān in Lǔ.
When Yuán Dì first took up residence east of the Jiāng River,
he appointed Xī Jiàn as Longxiáng Jiāngjūn and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Zōushān.
At that time, Xún Fān used Lǐ Shù,
and Liú Kūn used his nephew Yǎn,
both as Yǎnzhōu governors.
Each garrisoned a commandery,
contending with each other for power.
The entire province's registered households
did not know where to turn.
Furthermore, Xú Kān and Shí Lè attacked from both left and right,
daily engaging in conflict.
With no external relief,
the common people suffered famine.
Some dug up wild mice and hibernating swallows to eat,
yet none rebelled.
Within three years,
his forces grew to several tens of thousands.
The Emperor then promoted him to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Dūdū Yǎnzhōu Zhū Jūnshì.
At the beginning of Yǒngchāng,
he was summoned to be appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Upon his arrival,
he was transferred to Shàngshū,
but did not accept due to illness.
At that time, Míng Dì had just ascended the throne,
and Wáng Dūn wielded sole authority.
With dangers pressing from within and without,
it was planned to rely on Xī Jiàn as external support.
Consequently, he was appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, Dūdū Yángzhōu Jiāngxī Zhū Jūn, and Jiǎ Jié,
stationed at Héfèi.
Wáng Dūn, wary of him,
memorialized to have him appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and summoned him back.
On his way, he passed through Gūshú,
and met with Wáng Dūn.
Wáng Dūn said to him:
"Yuè Yànfǔ was merely a man of short talent.
A later generation of wantonness,
his words going against renowned principles,
if examined by facts,
how could he surpass Mǎn Wǔqiū?"
Xī Jiàn replied:
"One must compare a person to those of their own kind.
Yànfǔ's demeanor was calm and straightforward,
his understanding profound and pure.
In a precarious court,
it was impossible to treat him as close or distant.
As for the deposition of Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ,
he can be called gentle yet upright.
Mǎn Wǔqiū was a man who lost his integrity,
how can they be spoken of on the same day!"
Wáng Dūn said:
"At the time of Mǐnhuái's deposition and exile,
there were critical dangers on all sides.
How could anyone die to protect him!
Comparing them in this way,
it is clear that he was not inferior."
Xī Jiàn said:
"A true man, having purified himself and faced north [pledged allegiance to the emperor],
his duty is the same as being in a state of 'three,'
how can he cowardly cling to life and compromise his integrity,
shamelessly facing heaven and earth!
If his destiny were to end,
he should certainly choose to live or die by it."
Wáng Dūn had long harbored disloyal intentions.
Upon hearing Xī Jiàn's words,
he was greatly indignant,
and they did not meet again.
He detained Xī Jiàn and did not let him leave.
Wáng Dūn's partisans slandered him daily,
but Xī Jiàn remained composed,
showing no fear.
Wáng Dūn said to Qián Fèng:
"Xī Dàohuī is a refined scholar,
and his position and reputation are weighty,
how can he be harmed!"
So he released him back to the capital.
Xī Jiàn then conspired with the Emperor to eliminate Wáng Dūn.
Later, when Qián Fèng attacked and pressed upon the capital,
Xī Jiàn was granted a Jié,
and promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Cóngjià Zhū Jūnshì.
Xī Jiàn, believing it would not be of practical benefit,
firmly declined the military title.
At that time, some deliberated that Wáng Hán and Qián Fèng's forces were a hundred times greater,
and Yuànchéng was small and not secure.
It would be best, while their military power was not yet fully formed,
for the Emperor himself to go out and engage in battle.
Xī Jiàn said:
"The rebels are running wild,
their momentum is irresistible.
They can be overcome by strategy,
but it is difficult to contend with them by force.
Moreover, Hán and others' commands are not unified,
and they are constantly plundering.
The common people, remembering the violence of previous years,
are all defending themselves.
Riding on the momentum of righteousness and rebellion,
where can we go that we will not conquer!
Furthermore, the rebels have no grand strategy or long-term plan,
they merely rely on a single reckless charge.
If we prolong the conflict,
it will surely awaken the hearts of righteous warriors,
allowing our plans to unfold.
To use our current weak forces to contend with their strong enemy,
deciding victory or defeat in a single morning,
determining success or failure in a breath,
even if there are those like Shēn Xū,
whose righteousness prompts them to act immediately,
what good would it do for what has already happened!"
The Emperor followed his advice.
Xī Jiàn, as Shàngshū Lìng, commanded all the encampments.
When Fèng and others were subdued,
Wēn Jiào submitted a memorial,
requesting amnesty for Wáng Dūn's subordinates.
Xī Jiàn believed that the former kings upheld the teachings of loyalty between sovereign and minister,
thus valuing the principle of dying for one's lord;
while for dissolute and lost rulers,
they opened the door to being dismissed.
Although many of Wáng Dūn's subordinates were coerced,
yet living in a rebellious court,
they did not possess the integrity of leaving the passes [refusing to serve].
According to former precedents,
they ought to be morally censured.
He also memorialized that Qián Fèng's mother was eighty years old,
and should be granted full amnesty.
This was then followed.
He was enfeoffed as Gāopíng Hóu,
and granted four thousand eight hundred bolts of silk.
The Emperor, seeing his great ability and reputation,
consulted him on every major and minor matter.
He then decreed that Xī Jiàn should specifically draft memorials and petitions,
for the sake of simplicity.
Wáng Dǎo proposed posthumously honoring Zhōu Zhá with an official position.
Xī Jiàn thought it inappropriate;
the details are in Zhá's biography.
Wáng Dǎo did not follow his advice.
Xī Jiàn then rebutted him, saying:
"Wáng Dūn's rebellious plot
had been brewing for a long time.
Because Zhá opened the gates,
the imperial army was not able to prevail.
If Wáng Dūn's previous actions
were morally equivalent to Huán and Wén,
then could the late Emperor be considered like Yōu and Lì?"
Although the court officials had no way to refute him,
they could not follow his advice.
Shortly after, he was promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Xú Yǎn Qīng Sān Zhōu Jūnshì, Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, and Jiǎ Jié,
stationed at Guǎnglíng.
Soon after, the Emperor passed away.
Xī Jiàn, along with Wáng Dǎo, Biàn Hú, Wēn Jiào, Yǔ Liàng, Lù Yè, and others, received the imperial edict of entrustment,
to assist the young emperor.
He was promoted to Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī,
and also Sanqí Chángshì.
At the beginning of Xiánhé,
he was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu.
When Zǔ Yuē and Sū Jùn rebelled,
Jiàn heard of the trouble
and immediately wanted to lead his forces east to assist.
An imperial edict forbade it, citing the northern invaders.
Thereupon, he dispatched his Sīmǎ, Liú Jǔ, to lead three thousand men to guard the capital.
Soon after, the imperial army was defeated,
and Jǔ consequently retreated.
The Minister of the Central Secretariat, Yǔ Liàng, conveyed the Empress Dowager's oral decree,
promoting Jiàn to Sīkōng.
Jiàn was close to the rebels,
his city was isolated, and supplies were cut off.
The people were apprehensive,
with no firm resolve.
He received the edict with tears,
set up an altar,
sacrificed a white horse,
and made a great oath to the three armies, saying:
"The rebellious ministers Zǔ Yuē and Sū Jùn have defied the mandate of Heaven,
disregarded the imperial execution,
acted with ferocious cruelty and rampant transgression,
violated the principles of the state,
trampled upon the five constant virtues,
and toyed with the sacred implements.
They have thus coerced and threatened the secluded lord,
uprooting the foundation and blocking the source,
harming the loyal and good,
and bringing disaster and tyranny upon the common people,
causing Heaven, Earth, and the spirits to have nowhere to rely upon.
Therefore, the entire land suffers from bitter resentment,
and the myriad commoners weep tears of blood.
All wish to carry out the imperial command and punish the wicked,
to eliminate the prime evil.
In ancient times, when the Róng and Dí annihilated Zhōu,
Qí Huán rallied the alliance;
when Dǒng Zhuó insulted Hàn,
the various lords launched an expedition.
The principle of loyalty to sovereign and kin
is the same throughout ancient and modern times.
Now, our sovereign is in secluded peril,
and the hundred surnames hang upside down.
Loyal ministers and upright scholars are determined to repay the state.
All of us, as allies,
after forming this alliance,
must unite our strength and minds
to save the altars of soil and grain.
If these two rebels are not eliminated,
we have no right to seek temporary peace.
Should anyone violate this oath,
may the bright spirits strike him down!"
Jiàn ascended the altar with fervent emotion,
and the three armies eagerly pledged their lives.
He then dispatched General Xiàhóu Cháng and others to travel secretly,
telling General Píngnán Wēn Qiáo:
"Now the rebels plan to seize the Son of Heaven and enter Huìjī from the east.
It is advisable to first establish camps and fortifications,
occupy strategic points,
both to prevent their escape
and to cut off the rebels' supply lines.
Then, calmly station forces at Jīngkǒu,
clear the walls, and await the rebels.
If the rebels attack the city but cannot take it,
and there is nothing to plunder in the countryside,
with their eastern route cut off,
and their food supplies naturally exhausted,
in no more than a hundred days,
they will inevitably collapse on their own."
Qiáo deeply agreed with this.
When Táo Kǎn became the alliance leader,
he promoted Jiàn to Supervisor of Military Affairs of the eight commanderies of Yángzhōu.
At that time, General Fǔjūn Wáng Shū and General Fǔjūn Yú Tán both received Jiàn's command,
led their troops across the river,
and met Kǎn at Qiézipǔ.
Jiàn built and occupied the Báishí fort.
However, Shū and Tán fought unfavorably,
so Jiàn and General Hòujiāngjūn Guō Mò returned to Dāntú,
establishing three forts at Dàyè, Qǔ'ā, and Chángtíng to resist the rebels.
When the rebel general Zhāng Jiàn came to attack Dàyè,
the city lacked water,
and Guō Mò was in distress.
He then broke through the siege and exited,
causing the three armies to lose morale.
The Staff Officer Cáo Nà believed that Dàyè was the bulwark of Jīngkǒu,
and if it could not be held for a single day,
the rebels would advance unopposed.
He advised Jiàn to retreat to Guǎnglíng to await a later opportunity.
Jiàn then gathered his subordinates,
and rebuked Nà, saying:
"I have received the generous favor of the late emperor
and bear the heavy responsibility of his trust.
Even sacrificing my body to the netherworld would not be enough to repay him.
Now, strong enemies are at the outskirts,
