and the hearts of the multitude are in peril.
You, my trusted aide,
are giving rise to strange ideas.
How can you lead the righteous forces
and stabilize the three armies?!"
He was about to execute him,
but released him after a long while.
When Sū Jùn died,
the siege of Dàyè was lifted.
When Sū Yì and others fled to Wúxīng,
Jiàn dispatched Staff Officer Lǐ Hóng to pursue and behead them,
and over ten thousand men and women surrendered.
He was appointed Sīkōng,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
relieved of the governorship of the eight commanderies,
and newly enfeoffed as the Duke of Nánchāng County,
with his son Tán inheriting his former noble title.
At that time, the rebel leader Liú Zhēng gathered several thousand men,
sailed across the sea, and plundered the southeastern counties.
Jiàn then fortified Jīngkǒu,
was given the additional title of Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jìnliáng and Wújùn in Yángzhōu,
and led his forces to suppress and pacify them.
He was promoted to Tàiwèi.
Initially,
although [Zhōu] Chāo was truly aligned with the Huán clan,
because [Zhōu] Yīn was loyal to the imperial house,
he did not let [Yīn] know of it.
When he was about to die,
he took out a box of books
and entrusted them to a student, saying:
"I originally wanted to burn them, but I fear that since you are old,
you will certainly be overcome with sorrow.
After my death,
if you significantly lose sleep and appetite,
you may present this box.
Otherwise,
burn it."
Later, [Zhōu] Yīn indeed grieved and fell ill,
and the student presented it according to the instructions.
It contained all the secret plans and correspondence between [Zhōu] Chāo and Wēn [Jiàn].
[Zhōu] Yīn was then greatly enraged and said:
"The rascal's death was too late!"
And he no longer wept.
All the friends [Zhōu] Chāo associated with
were at that time outstanding and elegant;
even those from humble families who rose later,
he would elevate and befriend.
On the day of his death,
over forty people, noble and common, took up their brushes to write elegies,
showing how much he was revered and honored by the multitude.
Wáng Xiànzhī and his brothers,
from before [Zhōu] Chāo's death,
whenever they saw [Zhōu] Yīn,
would always wear shoes and inquire after him,
greatly observing the etiquette between maternal uncle and nephew.
After [Zhōu] Chāo died,
when they saw [Zhōu] Yīn, they became disrespectful,
wearing clogs when waiting on him,
and if offered a seat, they would procrastinate and decline.
[Zhōu] Yīn would often exclaim with indignation:
"If Jiābīn hadn't died,
would these little rats dare to act like this?!"
[Zhōu] Chāo's nature was to enjoy hearing of people who lived in seclusion.
If someone could renounce worldly honors and withdraw,
[Zhōu] Chāo would build houses for them,
make clothes and utensils,
and acquire servants for them,
spending a hundred *jīn* without reluctance.
Also, the Śramaṇa Zhī Dùn was famous at the time for his pure conversation;
elegant and noble,
everyone respected him,
considering his profound insights
worthy of comparison with the masters of the Zhèngshǐ era.
And Zhī Dùn always valued [Zhōu] Chāo,
considering him a hero of his time,
and they knew and appreciated each other greatly.
[Zhōu] Chāo had no sons;
his cousin [Zhōu] Jiǎnxī made his son Sēngshī his heir.
Sēngshī, courtesy name Huìtuō,
inherited the title of Duke of Nánchāng.
In his youth,
he was as famous as Wáng Suí and Huán Yìn.
He successively held prominent and important positions,
serving as Administrator of Xuānchéng Commandery,
then entering the court to become the Administrator of Dānyáng.
When Liú Yì was garrisoned at Jiānglíng,
he requested [Sēngshī] to be Southern Man Colonel and granted him the Staff of Authority.
He was executed along with Liú Yì,
and his marquisate was abolished.
[Zhōu] Tán, courtesy name Chóngxī,
was granted the title of Founding Earl of Dōng'ān County in his youth.
The Grand Preceptor Wáng Dǎo appointed him Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat.
Court opinion, considering [Zhōu] Tán the son of a famous official,
often constrained him with regulations,
so at the age of thirty,
he was first appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
then promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén was General of the Expeditionary Army,
he invited [Zhōu] Tán to be his Chief Clerk.
Soon after, he was appointed Bureau Director of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs,
then transferred to Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
At that time, Xún Xiàn, the North Central Army General, was ill,
so the court made [Zhōu] Tán Xiàn's Army Supervisor,
and added Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
After a short while,
Xún Xiàn was recalled. [Zhōu] Tán was then appointed North Central Army General,
overseeing military affairs of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Yōu, and Yáng Provinces in Jìnlíng, and concurrently Governor of Xú and Yǎn Provinces, with the Staff of Authority,
garrisoned at Xiàpī.
Later, he suffered a defeat in battle against the bandit leader Fù Mòbō and others,
and his title was reduced to General Jianwei.
He died soon after,
at the age of forty-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of North Central Army General,
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn.
His son Huī succeeded.
Huī, courtesy name Dàoyìn,
inherited his father's title in his youth,
and served as Cavalier Attendant.
He was successively promoted to Palace Attendant,
and concurrently Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard.
Huī was eight *chǐ* tall,
with a handsome beard,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ greatly esteemed him,
believing him to have the potential of a regional lord.
Coincidentally, Zhū Xù petitioned to resign,
and Huī was promoted to overseeing military affairs of Liáng, Qín, Yōng, Sī, Jīng, Yáng, and Bìng Provinces, General Jianwei, Governor of Yōng Province, with the Staff of Authority,
garrisoned at Xiāngyáng.
Huī was very successful in conciliating the people of Guānlǒng,
with thousands of people surrendering and joining him.
Initially,
Dòu Chōng, a general of Yáo Cháng, surrendered,
and was appointed Eastern Qiāng Colonel.
Chōng later raised an army and rebelled,
entering Hànchuān
and attacking Liáng Province.
At that time, the people of Bá and Shǔ in Guānzhōng
all turned against Yáo Cháng,
occupying Hóngnóng to ally with Fú Dēng.
And Fú Dēng appointed Dòu Chōng as Left Chancellor,
moving his garrison to Huáyīn.
Yáng Quánqī, the Administrator of Hénán, dispatched Xún Jìng, the Administrator of Shàngdǎng, to garrison Huángtiānwù to resist him.
Dòu Chōng repeatedly attacked. [Zhōu] Huī sent General Zhào Mù to defend Jīnyóng City,
while Yáng Quánqī led his troops to Húchéng
to attack Dòu Chōng,
putting him to flight.
Soon after, Mùróng Chuí besieged Mùróng Yǒng at Lùchuān.
Yǒng was in dire straits
and sent his son Hóng to seek aid from [Zhōu] Huī,
offering a jade seal.
[Zhōu] Huī presented the seal to the court,
and also stated,
"If Mùróng Chuí annexes Mùróng Yǒng,
his power will be unfathomable.
From the perspective of national policy now,
I believe we should save Yǒng.
If Yǒng and Chuí both survive,
they will be enemies of each other;
like roosters tied together, they cannot roost,
and will be unable to cause trouble.
Then, seizing the opportunity to defeat both,
the region north of the Yellow River can be pacified."
Emperor Xiàowǔ thought this was correct
and issued an edict to Wáng Gōng and Yú Kǎi to rescue him.
Before they could depart, Mùróng Yǒng was overthrown.
Yáng Quánqī resigned due to illness.
[Zhōu] Huī appointed Xiàhóu Zōngzhī, the Administrator of Suí Commandery, as Administrator of Hénán,
garrisoned at Luòyáng.
Yáo Cháng sent his son Luè to attack Húchéng and Shàngluò,
and also sent his general Yáng Fósōng to besiege Luòyáng.
[Zhōu] Huī sent General Jiànwǔ Xīn Gōngjìng to relieve Luòyáng,
and Wáng Zhèngyìn, the Governor of Liáng Province, led his troops out of Zǐwǔgǔ
as a show of force.
Yáo Luè, fearing, retreated.
For his accomplishments, [Zhōu] Huī was promoted to General Zhenglǔ,
and also concurrently Governor of Qín Province,
with additional command over the forces in Lǒngshàng.
At that time, the Wèi clan (Northern Wèi) was powerful,
and the imperial mausoleums were dangerously close.
[Zhōu] Huī sent Dèng Qǐfāng, the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià, and others with ten thousand men to resist them,
and fought against Wèi ruler Tuòbá Guī at Xíngyáng,
suffering a great defeat and returning.
When Wáng Gōng attacked Wáng Guóbǎo,
Huán Xuán and Yīn Zhòngkān both raised armies to support Wáng Gōng.
[Zhōu] Huī allied with the court to outmaneuver Huán Xuán and others.
Xiàhóu Zōngzhī, the Administrator of Xiāngyáng, and Guō Pí, the Chief Clerk of the Governor's Office, both believed this was not feasible,
and [Zhōu] Huī killed them both.
Afterwards, Huán Xuán and others retreated and garrisoned at Xúnyáng.
[Zhōu] Huī was made a Minister of State Affairs,
and was to bring his family back to the capital.
When he reached Yángkǒu,
Yīn Zhòngkān secretly sent people to kill him on the road,
along with his four sons,
attributing it to killings by various barbarian tribes.
When his coffin returned to the capital,
he was posthumously granted the title of General Zhenjun.
His son Xún succeeded.
[Zhōu] Lóng, courtesy name Hóngshǐ,
was upright and possessed the virtue of selflessness in service.
He first served as an official in the Department of State Affairs,
then transferred to Left Assistant Director,
and in court, he was feared by all officials.
He was dismissed for leaking information.
After a while,
he became Bureau Director of Personnel,
but was dismissed again.
He was then appointed Administrator of Dōng Commandery.
The King of Chángshā [Sīmǎ Yì] served as Commander of Cavalry,
and Gù Róng was again made his Chief Clerk.
When [Sīmǎ Yì] was defeated,
Gù Róng was transferred to be an Attendant Officer in the Chéngxiàng's office for Yǐng, the King of Chéngdū [Sīmǎ Yǐng].
When Emperor Huì [Sīmǎ Zhōng] visited Línzhāng,
Gù Róng was appointed concurrently as Attendant-in-ordinary,
and sent to inspect the imperial gardens and mausoleums.
At that time, Zhāng Fāng occupied Luòyáng,
so [Gù Róng] could not proceed,
and avoided him by going to Chénliú.
When the Emperor later moved west to Cháng'ān,
[Gù Róng] was summoned to be a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
but considering the world was in chaos, he did not respond,
and thus returned to Wú.
When the King of Dōnghǎi [Sīmǎ Yuè] gathered troops in Xúzhōu,
Gù Róng was made Wine Sacrificer and Military Consultant.
At that time, Chén Mǐn, the Administrator of Guǎnglíng, rebelled,
crossed the Jiāng River southwards,
drove away Liú Jī, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, and Wáng Kuàng, the Internal Recorder of Dānyáng,
and, by holding his troops, occupied the province.
He divided and appointed his sons and younger brothers to various commanderies,
and gathered and honored heroes and prominent figures,
having a plan to establish a tripod-like reign similar to the Sūn family.
He provisionally appointed Gù Róng as Right General and Internal Recorder of Dānyáng.
Gù Róng had often been in critical situations,
and he spurred himself on with humility and deference.
At that time, Chén Mǐn wanted to execute all the scholars,
so Gù Róng persuaded him, saying:
"Zhōngguó is in chaos,
and the northern barbarians are invading.
Looking at the Grand Tutor [Sīmǎ Yuè] today, he cannot revive Huáxià,
and the common people will have no descendants left.
Although there are bandits like Shí Bīng in Jiāngnán,
the people and resources are still intact.
I often worry that there is no strategy like that of the Dòu, Sūn, or Liú families
to preserve it.
Now, General, you possess a divine military strategy,
and have the ability of Sūn Wú.
Your achievements are already evident,
and your courage and strategy surpass those of the present age.
With tens of thousands of armored soldiers
and a multitude of stacked ships,
though the imperial court above still has several provinces,
they can also be pacified with a mere proclamation.
If you can trust gentlemen,
allow each to express their thoughts,
dissipate resentment,
and block the mouths of flatterers,
then great things can be planned."
Chén Mǐn accepted his words,
and consequently brought in and entrusted all the powerful clans.
Chén Mǐn then sent Gān Zhuó out to Héngjiāng,
entrusting him with all the strong armor and sharp weapons.
Gù Róng privately said to Gān Zhuó:
"If the affairs of Jiāngdōng can succeed,
we should achieve them together.
However, do you think, considering the circumstances, that they can succeed?
Chén Mǐn is but an ordinary man,
originally without great schemes;
his policies are erratic,
and his plans are undecided.
Moreover, his sons and younger brothers are already arrogant,
so his defeat is inevitable.
If we,
on the day of his defeat,
accept his official salary peacefully,
the armies west of the Jiāng River will send our heads to Luòyáng,
inscribed with 'The heads of the rebels Gù Róng and Gān Zhuó.'
Not only will our own bodies be destroyed,
but we will also bring disgrace upon ten thousand generations.
Should we not plan for this!"
Gān Zhuó agreed.
The following year,
Zhōu Qǐ, together with Gù Róng, Gān Zhuó, and Jì Zhān, secretly plotted to raise an army to attack Chén Mǐn.
Gù Róng dismantled the bridges and collected boats on the south bank.
Chén Mǐn led over ten thousand men out,
but could not cross.
Gù Róng waved his feather fan,
and Chén Mǐn's troops dispersed.
Once the matter was settled,
[Gù Róng] returned to Wú.
In the early Yǒngjiā era,
he was summoned and appointed Attendant-in-ordinary.
When he reached Péngchéng,
he saw that disasters were just beginning,
so he returned in a light boat.
The account is in the Biography of Jì Zhān.
When Emperor Yuán [Sīmǎ Ruì] garrisoned Jiāngdōng,
Gù Róng was made Military Administrator,
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
All plans and strategies
were discussed with him.
Gù Róng was a respected scholar of the southern provinces,
and personally held an important position.
The court and the common people greatly respected him.
At that time, Empress Zhèng Guìpín, favored by the Emperor, was ill.
Due to prayers, many state affairs were neglected.
Gù Róng submitted a memorial, remonstrating:
"In the past, King Wén's father, son, and brothers produced three sages;
they can be said to have thoroughly investigated principles.
Yet King Wén did not have time to eat until sunset,
and Duke Zhōu grasped his hair three times during a single bath.
Why was this?
It was truly because there were myriad state affairs each day
that could not be left unattended;
and a single slip of the tongue
would inevitably lead to trouble.
At this critical end of a decadent era,
amidst a time of chaos and separation,
with the Son of Heaven wandering,
and jackals and wolves blocking the roads,
Your Excellency should camp in the wilderness,
and set out before dawn,
pressing the chariot bar and roaring like a frog to recruit brave warriors,
and hang a gall bladder in the courtyard to signify your hardship.
While the Guìpín is not well,
medicine is indeed urgent;
and sacrificial prayers,
can certainly be performed;
but how can you block the advisors from reporting on affairs,
and refuse guests seeking audience?
Now, powerful bandits are at the border,
and rumors fill the country.
People's minds are in myriad states,
and their decisions to stay or leave are confused.
I wish you would humbly accept suggestions,
widely invite talented individuals,
consider the essentials of the current day,
suppress perverse worship of spirits,
exert diligence in uniting the nine states,
and wash away the shame of All Under Heaven.
Then all living beings will have hope,
and a time of prosperity will be foreseeable."
At that time, the talented scholars of the southern lands had not yet been fully utilized.
Gù Róng also said:
"Lù Shìguāng is upright and pure,
with the quality of jade and gold;
Gān Jìsī is loyal and sincere,
with extraordinary courage;
Yīn Qìngyuán has a discerning mind and clear principles,
and can be employed in both civil and military capacities;
my clan brother, Gù Gōngràng, is enlightened and steadfast,
and does not change his principles in adversity;
Yáng Yànmíng and Xiè Xíngyán of Kuàijī both embrace Confucian teachings,
and are worthy of public esteem;
Hè Shēng is profound and reclusive,
a man of lofty aspirations;
Táo Gōng and his brothers, though of modest talent,
are excellent in practical matters.
All these individuals
are treasures of the south."
His memorial was submitted,
and all his suggestions were accepted.
In the sixth year [of Dàxīng],
he died in office.
The Emperor attended his mourning with full sorrow,
and wished to posthumously honor Gù Róng,
according to the precedent for meritorious officials of the King of Qí.
Yīn Yòu, the Internal Recorder of Wú Commandery, memorialized:
"In the past, the traitorous minister Chén Mǐn, relying on favor and power,
wreaked havoc,
with his brothers and in-laws entrenched in the provinces and commanderies,
coercing scholars and commoners alike into servitude.
At that time,
neither the wise nor the foolish knew what to do.
The late Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Military Administrator of Āndōng, and Earl of Jiāxīng, Gù Róng, embodied virtue and upheld the Dao,
his plans were far-reaching,
and his loyalty and integrity
grew stronger in adversity.
Amidst perilous difficulties,
and under the coercion of traitors,
he always thought of the state,
bursting with indignation.
He secretly gathered trusted confidants,
and together planned to launch
an attack.
His trustworthiness was known to all scholars,
and his renown was preeminent in the east.
Wherever his virtuous reputation spread,
none failed to respond,
carrying spears and rushing forward,
gathering like a forest.
Gù Róng personally faced arrows and stones,
leading
the multitude,
full of loyalty and righteousness,
forgetting his family for the sake of the country.
The bandits, who had evaded capture for years,
collapsed overnight.
With no bloodshed,
six provinces were pacified,
his achievements surpassed those of previous generations,
and his righteousness
illuminated All Under Heaven.
I humbly hear that the merits are to be evaluated according to the precedent of the late Grand Marshal, the King of Qí,
not falling under the category of secret planning and deliberation within the curtains,
nor merely that of provincial expeditions and battlefield combat,
and thus not allowed to be
As titles were advanced and territory expanded,
and his children and younger brothers were granted offices,
everyone, near and far, lamented,
while those south of the Yangtze River were disappointed.
The King of Qí, being a close relative,
held the position of a regional governor,
wielding the imperial staff and commanding troops.
He oversaw
the imperial demesne,
supported externally by five states
and internally by members of the imperial clan.
He waged war for a prolonged period,
his campaign affecting the whole empire.
Although a great achievement was made,
much was also lost.
Róng's
troops were less than a single battalion,
his position was not that of a regional pillar,
he was isolated south of the river,
and imperial edicts could not reach him.
In times of danger, he made his own decisions,
sacrificing himself for the country.
His office incurred not a single ounce of gold in expenses,
and no one expended
a single morning's labor.
After the chief villain was eradicated,
he nobly completed his task,
sealing granaries
to await the main army.
Thus, the old state was secure and its people prosperous,
its customs formed by righteousness.
Today, Kuāngbà's
affairs are accomplished;
it may not be without this that they prospered.
Compared to Qí,
the strength and weakness were different,
and the superiority and inferiority also varied.
As for the advisors and assistants in Qí's
bureaucracy, they supported righteousness and
aided the powerful.
They were not the originators of the plan,
yet all were granted jade tokens and received auspicious signs,
some becoming Dukes, others Marquises.
Róng was the first to lay down the secret plan,
becoming the alliance leader of the region.
His merit surpassed that of a grand marshal,
yet his reward was inferior to that of a
subordinate officer.
This diminished the ranks of those who established national policies and recorded merits
and isolated loyal and righteous men who received their mandate.
Indeed, evaluating achievements, both visible and hidden,
is what imperial governance upholds.
How much more so for one like Róng,
who saved the country from calamity and brought it peace,
acting according to heaven and proactively.
Looking through ancient and modern history,
there has never been one who achieved such merit
yet received such a reward. "
Because of this, Róng was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with the posthumous name Yuán.
When the Emperor became the King of Jìn,
Róng was posthumously enfeoffed as a Gōng,
established his own state,
and received an income fief.
Róng was always fond of the qín;
when he died,
his family always placed a qín on his spirit seat.
Zhāng Hàn of Wú Jùn wept bitterly for him.
Afterward, he sat on the bed and played several pieces on the qín,
then sighed while caressing the instrument:
"Can Gù Yànxiān still appreciate this?"
He then wept bitterly again
and left without condoling with the chief mourner.
His son, Pí, succeeded him
and served as Sànqí Shìláng.
Jǐ Zhān
Jǐ Zhān, courtesy name Sīyuǎn,
was a native of Mòlíng, Dānyáng.
His grandfather, Liàng,
was the Shàngshū Lìng of Wú.
His father, Zhì,
was Guānglù Dàfū.
Zhān was known for his uprightness in his youth.
When Wú was pacified,
his family moved to Lìyáng Jùn.
He was recommended as Xiaolián
but did not take office.
Later, he was nominated as Xiùcái,
and Shàngshū Láng Lù Jī questioned him, saying:
"In ancient times, the enlightened kings of the Three Dynasties
initiated great enterprises.
Their cultures, simple or refined, differed,
yet their good reputations were consistent.
However, the Xià people valued loyalty,
and the drawback of loyalty was rusticity;
to remedy rusticity, nothing is better than reverence.
The Yīn people reformed and refined it,
and the drawback of reverence was superstition;
to remedy superstition, nothing is better than refinement.
The Zhōu people rectified and changed it,
and the drawback of refinement was superficiality;
to remedy superficiality, one must return to loyalty.
So, is the cyclical nature of the kingly way without fixed principles,
or is it that what they inherited differed, leading to different achievements?
Since there have been no sage kings,
people have been scattered for a long time.
Can the reforms and drawbacks of the Three Dynasties,
and the changes among the common people,
be understood?
Now, to revert to antiquity to remedy its flaws,
and clarify customs to purge their impurities,
which system of the Three Dynasties should be followed?
What different path was there in the transformations of remote antiquity?"
Zhān replied:
"I have heard that those who govern states and households
all wish to advance civilization and elevate governance
to bring peace to all undertakings,
leaving behind songs for millions of years,
to be eternally passed down to posterity.
However, customs change and affairs become flawed;
one cannot help but adapt to the times.
Even with sage-like wisdom,
it cannot be altered.
Thus, the flaw of loyalty leads to crudeness,
and the fault of reverence lies in excessive rituals.
Zhōu, observing the flaws of the two kings,
emphasized refinement to distinguish ranks,
but those who drifted away became superficial and lacked sincerity;
when sincerity became superficial,
they then returned to loyalty.
The Three Dynasties followed one another
like water quenching fire.
This is what is meant by adapting to the times
and the art of remedying flaws.
Xīhuáng was simple and rustic,
achieving transformation through non-action;
later sages succeeded him,
their endeavors sometimes differing.
It is not that the worthy and sages were different,
but that the changes of the world made them so.
Now, the Great Jìn elucidates the primal principle,
and its sacred achievements daily ascend.
It follows Heaven and conforms to the times;
the nine regions are unified.
The rulers of distant lands
all come to join.
However, the great Way has passed,
and human changes have long persisted.
It is said that the current governance should shed refinement and preserve simplicity,
to return to its origin.
Then the common people will gradually be transformed,
and great harmony can be achieved. "
Again, he asked:
"In ancient times, the sagely kings designed institutions and prepared all things.
The Míngtáng was for revering the Supreme Lord,
the Qīngmiào was for pacifying the ancestors,
the Bìyōng was for disseminating the rites and teachings,
and the Tàixué was for lecturing on arts and letters.
These were indeed grand ceremonies of a state,
and major administrations for a realm.
The defunct Qín dynasty abolished learning,
and its institutions were desolate and incomplete.
The discussions of various Confucians
on their modifications differed.
The Hàn dynasty inherited these works,
taking them as different things,
yet Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng called them one thing.
What should be followed?"
He replied:
"The Zhōu system's Míngtáng
was for venerating their ancestors to match the Supreme Lord,
reverently and respectfully performing bright sacrifices,
and eternally glorifying filial piety.
Its main aspects were six.
In antiquity, sagely emperors and enlightened kings faced south to govern;
these six aspects took the Míngtáng as their center.
Also, its very center
was called the Tàimiào,
to accord with heavenly timing,
implement laws and decrees,
perform ancestral sacrifices and care for the elderly,
conduct teaching and practice,
hold court for feudal lords and select talented scholars,
prepare rites and distinguish things—
all contributing to a single system of moral transformation.
Therefore, when taking its aspect of ancestral sacrifice,
it was called the Qīngmiào;
when taking its appearance as the main chamber,
it was called the Tàimiào;
when taking its chambers,
it was called the Tàishì;
when taking its hall,
it was called the Míngtáng;
when taking its four-gated schools,
it was called the Tàixué;
when taking its surrounding water, circular like a jade disc,
it was called the Bìyōng.
Different names referred to the same function;
in reality, they were one.
This is why Cài Yōng called them one thing."
Again, he asked:
"When all wise officials brightly shone,
that era was harmonious and tranquil under the Táng;
when the mandate had gathered,
many scholars flourished under the Zhōu.
Thus, the Shū Jīng speaks of the song of enlightened and good officials,
and the Yì Jīng values the beauty of 'golden orchid' friendships.
This is why long-lasting dynasties rise and fall,
and states flourish and decline.
A successful ruler is diligent in seeking talent,
and a reputable scholar is eager to attract the world.
It is not that there is no correspondence in the world,
yet things contradict over a thousand years.
By what path did ancient flourishing kings achieve this?
And by what deficiency did later declining eras become thus?"
He replied:
"The policy of prosperity and flourishing lies in acquiring the virtuous,
and the transformation to peace and purity is urgent in promoting talent.
Therefore, when the 'Two Eights' are employed,
all administrators are in order;
when there are 'ten able ministers',
the world is at peace.
Wǔ Dīng promoted the disciples of Fù Yán,
King Wén of Zhōu took the scholars from the banks of the Wèi River.
They were placed in high positions,
entrusted with state governance,
and thus they could soar like dragons in the heavenly path,
leaving achievements for a hundred generations.
The former kings humbled themselves to the 'white cottages' (commoners),
searching for and promoting the obscure and lowly,
so that there was no Fúsū talent in the mountains,
nor Fátán lament in the wilderness.
Thus, their transforming influence was profound and things responded,
spirits and deities came in response,
phoenixes soared gracefully,
sweet dew abundantly fell,
sweet springs spurted liquid,
crimson grasses grew by themselves,
all things flourished,
the sun and moon shone with renewed brilliance,
harmonious qi filled the four directions,
and the Great Way was established.
They ordered the righteousness between ruler and minister,
strengthened the affection between father and son,
clarified the Way of husband and wife,
and distinguished the proper order of elders and youngsters.
From the nine provinces,
it spread to the eight wildernesses,
peoples overseas changed their minds,
interpreters arrived with tribute,
songs of praise were harmonious,
and the ruler faced south, ruling with folded arms.
Now, the path for recommending the virtuous is open,
but the task of teaching and learning is not widely spread.
This causes the ambition for advancement and competition to be sharp,
but the heart for diligent learning is not cultivated.
If the four gates were opened to welcome talented scholars,
and the five teachings proclaimed to illuminate virtuous conduct,
and performance evaluated and ranked,
their merits and demerits carefully judged,
then they could be placed among all officials,
and appointed to various administrations.
This would enable them to manage affairs appropriately,
and regulate the state's statutes.
This would certainly lead to great prosperity and accord,
matching the former generations.
Enlightened and good officials would respond,
and 'golden orchid' friendships would again exist."
Again, he asked:
"In ancient times, Táng and Yú promulgated the teaching of the five punishments,
and Duke of Zhōu clarified the system of the four crimes.
Therefore, the age praised 'clear inquiries' and the time sang of 'flourishing harmony.'
When treachery and villainy became rampant,
laws and instruments of punishment multiplied.
Later ages revered the writings of the 'Three Punishments,'
and the tyrannical Qín added the law of 'exterminating families.'
Excessive punishments spread extensively,
and cruelty and abuse became extreme.
Hàn and Wèi followed and inherited this,
and did not reform it.
This was also because conditions of danger and peace differed,
and methods for saving the world varied,
so they had no choice but to use them.
Amidst a lenient approach,
what should be established to be acceptable?
Is the law of 'exterminating families' suitable as a permanent system or not?"
He replied:
"When the two fundamental forces separated, all beings were born;
when all beings were born, benefits and harms arose.
The arising of benefits and harms
had its causes.
In primeval times,
they transformed through the teachings of morality and virtue,
disdaining brute force and valuing benevolence and righteousness.
When benevolence and righteousness were valued, the strong did not oppress the weak,
and the many did not brutalize the few.
The Three Sovereigns used knotted cords, and the world was at peace;
this was not merely about figurative punishments and flourishing harmony.
Moreover, in primeval times, knowing the law
was for avoiding imprisonment.
But by later times,
the guilty were not missed,
and thus prisons became increasingly numerous,
and people became increasingly violent,
laws and decrees proliferated,
and robbers became many.
The Shū Jīng says: '
Only reverence the five punishments, to achieve the three virtues.'
In later ages, the Way declined,
and the 'Three Punishments' were instituted.
Then, the abuses of Wén Gōng
further added 'exterminating families.'
Excessive punishments spread extensively,
injuring harmonious qi,
influencing later generations,
and making it impossible to change.
Thus, when Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn commanded, the six directions responded.
Wèi inherited the end of Hàn,
and therefore did not reform it,
probably because the change in customs had been long-standing,
and it was expedient for the time.
Now, the four seas are unified,
people desire to return to fundamentals,
gradually valuing simplicity and plainness,
so greedy individuals will not compete;
honoring the virtuous and dismissing the wicked,
then the inhumane will be far off.
In that case, one can deliberate on the five traditional punishments,
and abolish the law of 'exterminating families.'
All things will each follow their nature,
and flourish in different ages simultaneously."
Again, he asked:
"Indeed, the Five Phases alternate,
Yīn and Yáng mutually depend on each other,
whereby the Two Motes transform,
and the four seasons are generated.
The Yì states: 'In heaven, forms are completed;
on earth, shapes are completed.'
The creation of images and forms
is the way of mutual dependence.
If Yīn and Yáng are not in harmony,
then the great course cannot but be blocked;
if one energy is entirely absent,
then the myriad things cannot achieve completion alone.
This is the ultimate proof of corresponding sameness,
and a clear testament to impartiality.
Now there are hot springs but no cold fires;
what is the reason for this?
I wish to hear your辩論 biànlùn on this,
to resolve this inconsistent principle."
He replied:
"I have heard that Yīn and Yáng rise and fall,
and mountains and lakes share their khí.
The first nine strokes of a pure guà,
like a hidden dragon, should not be used.
Where spring waters are entrusted,
their warmth is appropriate.
As for water, it moistens downwards;
fire, it blazes upwards.
Hardness and softness, dryness and wetness,
are their natural properties.
Thus, Yáng moves and is external,
while Yīn is still and internal.
The internal nature is soft and weak,
taking inclusiveness as its essence;
the external movement is rigid and upright,
taking outward connection as its function.
Therefore, the brightness of metal and water observes internally,
while the light of fire and the sun shines externally.
The rigid acts, the soft receives;
Yáng prevails, Yīn submits.
Water's reception of warmth
is its inclusive nature."
Again, he asked:
"Indeed, comprehending the divine and knowing transformation
is the ultimate praise for talent;
preparing things and putting them to use
is the furthest goal of achievement.
Using this for governance,
the regulations of Huángxī can be followed;
using this to reform chaos,
the customs of Xuángǔ can be continued.
However, Táng Yú tightened the broad net of the Huángrén,
and Xià Yīn multiplied the concise laws of the Dìzhě.
Cunning hearts arose and advanced daily,
and pure virtue departed, never to return.
Could it be that once the Great Simplicity was lost,
the principle could not be restored,
or that the Way of the Sages gradually diminished?"
He replied:
"Governance arises with the times,
and opportunities move with things.
Therefore, the Sagely Kings thoroughly investigated the origins of success and failure,
examined the principles of beginning and end,
adapted to the exigencies of the times,
and aimed at saving the world.
In the age of the Huáng, people were simple and honest,
calamities did not arise,
knotted cords served as trust,
and people knew what to uphold.
Once the Great Way was lost,
wisdom disturbed things;
smooth and perilous differed,
misfortune and prosperity were different fates.
Therefore, Táng Yú tightening the net of the Huángrén,
and Xià Yīn multiplying the laws of the Dìzhě,
all had reasons for their rise and fall,
and their severity was regulated.
This is the Way of comprehending the divine,
the art of knowing transformation,
adapting to the exigencies of the times,
and not a diminution."
At the beginning of Yǒngkāng [year],
the province again nominated for Hánsù,
and the Grand Minister of War appointed him Grand Libationer of the Eastern Pavilion.
In that year,
he was appointed Prime Minister of the State of Yānlíng,
but did not take office.
The following year,
he was demoted to Prime Minister of Marquis of Sōngzī.
During the Tàiaān period,
he abandoned his office and returned home,
and with Gù Róng and others, they together executed Chén Mǐn.
The account is in Róng's biography.
He was summoned and appointed Shàngshū Láng,
and went to Luò together with Róng.
On the journey, they discussed the Grand Ultimate of the Yì.
Róng said:
"The Grand Ultimate
refers to the time of chaos, when it was dim and undivided,
the sun and moon contained their brilliance,
the eight guà concealed their divinity,
heaven and earth mingled their substance,
and the sages hid their bodies.
Then, suddenly, after transformation,
the clear and turbid were arranged,
the Two Motes manifested their forms,
Yīn and Yáng interacted,
the myriad things began to sprout,
and the six directions opened up.
Lǎozǐ said, 'There was something mixed and complete,
born before heaven and earth,'
which is truly the Grand Ultimate of the Yì.
But Wángshì said, 'The Grand Ultimate is heaven and earth,'
which I believe is incorrect.
The term 'Two Motes'
is used to name their substance,
thus it is heaven and earth;
when named by their khí,
it is Yīn and Yáng.
Now if one says the Grand Ultimate is heaven and earth,
then heaven and earth created themselves,
and there is no one who created heaven and earth.
Lǎozǐ also said, 'The reason why heaven and earth can be long-lasting
is that they do not give birth to themselves,
hence they can be long-lasting.'
'One gives birth to two,
two gives birth to three,
three gives birth to the myriad things,'
which originates from the primal khí to achieve harmony.
Tracing the origin of the primal khí,
and seeking the root of heaven and earth,
I fear this should be taken as the standard."
Zhān said:
"In ancient times, Fúxī drew the eight guà,
and the principles of Yīn and Yáng were fully expressed.
Wénwáng and Zhòngní continued his legacy,
the three sages inherited and shared the same understanding,
calling the Yì the standard for heaven,
with nothing beyond it.
Indeed, heaven is clear and earth is flat,
the Two Motes interact,
the four seasons move,
the sun and moon shine between them.
These are natural numbers,
and though experienced by all sages,
who knows their beginning?
My lord says 'dim and undivided,'
how could that be so?
A sage
is a human being;
how could he, at the beginning of chaos, hide his body within the undivided?
Lǎozǐ's words about 'before heaven'
are merely empty and absurd statements,
not the meaning of the Yì.
I also thought that my lord, with your divine comprehension,
would not have such doubts.
I believe that 'Grand Ultimate' simply means the ultimate culmination,
meaning its principle is ultimate,
with no external form beyond it;
once the external form is ultimate,
it gives rise to the Two Motes.
Wángshì's interpretation can be said to be close.
The ancients took the ultimate extreme as proof,
saying that the Two Motes were born from this,
not that they had parents.
If there must be parents,
who else but heaven and earth could they be?"
Róng then stopped.
Upon reaching Xúzhōu,
hearing that the chaos was worsening daily,
he decided not to proceed.
At that time, the Inspector Péi Dùn received a letter from Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè,
stating that if Róng and the others hesitated,
they would be dispatched according to military rites.
So he and Róng and Lù Wán and others each abandoned their boats and carts and oxen,
traveling three hundred lǐ in one day and one night,
and managed to return to Yángzhōu.
When Yuán Dì was the General of Andong,
Zhān was appointed Military Adviser Libationer.
He was then transferred to be Chief Clerk of Zhengdong General.
The Emperor personally visited Zhān's residence,
and returned with him in the same carriage.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Zhōu Fù and Huá Yì,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
When Shí Lè invaded,
he was promoted to General of Yangwei and Area Commander of all military affairs from Jīngkǒu south to Wúhú,
to resist Lè.
When Lè retreated,
he was appointed Administrator of Kuàijī.
At that time, someone fraudulently created a Great General's mansion's tally to arrest the Magistrate of Zhūjì.
The magistrate had already been detained,
but Zhān, realizing the fraud,
immediately broke the enclosure to release him,
and interrogated the envoy.
Indeed, the envoy confessed to the fraud.
Soon after, he was promoted to Prime Minister's Military Adviser Libationer.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Chén Mǐn,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Línxiāng County.
The Western Palace appointed him Court Attendant,
but he did not accept.
When Cháng'ān fell,
he, along with Wáng Dǎo, went to persuade the Emperor to ascend the throne.
The Emperor refused.
Zhān said:
"Your Majesty, your nature aligns with the Way of Heaven.
You still exert your divine intellect in historical records,
observing the successes and failures of ancient people.
Today's affairs are evident at a glance,
not difficult to see.
The two emperors have lost their rule,
the ancestral temples are empty and 폐,
the divine implements have departed from Jìn
for two years now.
The emperor's coffin has not yet been interred,
and both men and spirits have lost their proper order.
Your Majesty has received the mandate and the auspicious omens,
especially bestowed by Heaven.
This will cause the six directions to take on a new appearance,
and distant barbarians to come to court.
Once the ancestral temples are established,
and the spirit tablets are restored to peace,
the myriad people will turn to your influence,
and all foreign customs will arrive,
like the constellations revolving around the North Star,
and all rivers flowing into the great sea.
Yet you still wish to maintain the humility of a common man,
which is not the way to expand the seven ancestral temples
or promote the restoration.
The national traitors ought to be executed,
and you should humble yourself for this and apologize to the world.
But if you wish to defy the heavenly timing,
go against human affairs,
and lose the advantage of the land –
if these three are lost,
even if you try to support the future,
how can you save the ancestors from their peril and urgency?
There are myriad ways to adapt to the times.
What can truly govern and establish a great enterprise
is only reason and appropriateness.
The fortune of Jìn is in decline;
reason dictates action now.
If hastened, it will be obtained,
and the fortune of restoration can be elevated.
If delayed, it will be lost,
thus aiding the power of treacherous bandits.
This is what is meant by 'reason'.
Your Majesty faces a difficult fate,
succeeding to the imperial line.
Looking at the imperial clan,
who else is there to yield to?
You must assume the great position;
this is what is meant by 'appropriateness'.
Our four ancestors greatly expanded the universe,
and the great enterprise was thus.
Now the five capitals are burned,
the ancestral temples are without a master.
Liú Zài illicitly manipulates the divine implements in the northwest,
while Your Majesty wishes to humbly yield in the southeast.
This is like bowing and yielding while trying to put out a fire.
Your humble servants, though insignificant,
would still not permit it.
How much less can a great man, whose virtue accords with Heaven and Earth,
and whose brilliance parallels the sun and moon,
afford to miss the opportunity and be behind the times!"
The Emperor still refused,
and ordered the Palace General Hán Jì to remove the imperial seat.
Zhān shouted at Jì:
"The Emperor's seat corresponds to the constellations above;
whoever dares to move it shall be beheaded!"
The Emperor's expression changed because of this.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Zhān was appointed Court Attendant,
then transferred to Minister of Personnel.
He submitted memorials of remonstrance,
providing many corrections and benefits.
The Emperor greatly praised his loyalty and integrity.
He then suffered a prolonged illness
and was unable to attend court.
He submitted a memorial saying: "My illness is not cured,
and my absence grows longer.
I have repeatedly presented my sincere plea,
but have not seen compassionate consideration.
Moreover, I am a useless occupant of office,
burdened with guilt while confined to my bed.
The weight of worry and responsibility
makes me
not know where to lay my remaining life as I approach death.
Your servant has heard that what is easily lost is time,
and what does not come again is the year.
Therefore, the ambitious scholars and righteous people of old carried cauldrons and rushed about,
singing 'Shāng' songs in
the marketplace,
sincerely wishing to seize the opportunity to offer their loyal counsel,
and have their names passed down for eternity.
However, those who missed it were countless,
while those who succeeded were only one or two.
The common human inclination
is to covet
glory and profit.
I, being ordinary and common,
fortuitously encountered [the opportunity].
I did not labor by carrying a cauldron,
nor did I sing 'Shāng' songs.
I merely encountered a great fortune,
repeatedly and voraciously seizing it.
Although I yearn for the ambition of the ancients
to serve,
I have ultimately rendered not a single hair's breadth of service in return.
My dog-and-horse years are declining,
and all my ailments have incapacitated me.
I lie prostrate, clinging to life,
for over a hundred days,
knocking on my coffin
and pulling my quilt,
worsening day by day.
Even if Heaven grants me more years,
and I receive Your Majesty's favor like the 'Xíng Wěi' poem,
I could at best barely preserve my life,
breathing faintly in a humble alley,
and there would be no way for me to again join
the eight senior officials
or ascend and descend the palace towers.
My eyes are dim, my teeth have fallen out,
my chest and abdomen are cold,
my sores are not improving,
and one foot is again lame.
I am tormented by illness,
which is already agonizingly
bitter.
At seventy years old,
I am left out by ritual codes;
the signs of old age and decrepitude
are clearly manifest.
Although I wish to diligently hide and protect myself,
where can I conceal myself?
My official responsibilities involve
household registration and taxation,
which are of great importance to the state.
Currently, the entire realm is in turmoil,
people have not settled down,
and are only beginning to be transformed by your great influence.
All institutions are in their nascent stages,
and the raising of troops and transportation of supplies
all require manpower.
Even when I was robust,
and worked day and night,
I still could not keep up with affairs.
Now, as I await death, counting the minutes,
and yet am made to long remain in office,
it causes
the affairs of the state to be neglected.
If the court considers this a demonstration of broad grace,
then my worry and responsibility grow daily heavier.
If it considers this a proper sequence of official appointments,
then offices will be vacant and affairs will suffer.
If it awaits my recovery,
then I will only decline
day by day.
Now, by heavenly benevolence,
offices are vacant and affairs are stagnant.
If I receive such partial indulgence,
it will also diminish the great expectations placed upon me.
Now, all nations have reformed,
and worthy talents
are arriving in continuous succession.
Yet to leave an excellent position vacant,
not using it to retain worthy men,
and instead allowing my ailing, diseased self
to hinder office and occupy a position,
is truly not in line with the urgent principles of promotion and demotion, ancient and modern.
I only beg Your Majesty
Hè Xún (循) was young when his family suffered misfortune,
and he was exiled to the seaside.
When Wú (吳) was pacified,
he returned to his home commandery.
Cáo (操) was lofty and severe,
outstanding from childhood.
In his words, actions, advances, and retreats,
he always adhered to propriety and deference.
The Grand Minister Dīng Qǐng (丁請) appointed him Wǔguān Yuàn (五官掾).
The Inspector Jī Xǐ (嵇喜) nominated him as Xiùcái (秀才),
and he was appointed Magistrate of Yángxiàn (陽羨).
He made leniency and benevolence his guiding principles,
not seeking the highest tax quotas.
Later, he became Magistrate of Wǔkāng (武康).
The local custom was to have elaborate burials,
and there were also those who observed taboos and avoided certain months and years,
keeping their deceased unburied.
Hè Xún (循) forbade all of these practices.
His governance and teachings spread widely,
and neighboring cities regarded him as their model.
However, having no connections at court,
he was not promoted for a long time.
The Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎) Lù Jī (陸機) submitted a memorial recommending Hè Xún (循), saying:
“I humbly observe that Hè Xún (賀循), the Magistrate of Wǔkāng (武康), possesses profound and abundant virtue and capacity,
with clear and far-reaching discernment.
He adheres to the fundamental principles of the Dao,
and his character and conduct are firm and majestic.
He has served in two cities,
and his administration of law and government has been solemn and orderly.
The former Magistrate of Zhēngyáng (蒸陽), Guō Nà (郭訥), is broad and unconstrained in demeanor,
with clear and exceptional insight.
He is astute, quick-witted, and capable of handling affairs.
Hè Xún (循) governs a lower-grade county,
his name recorded among the common and humble.
Guō Nà (訥) has returned to his family home,
idling for many years.
Both originate from the newly unified regions,
having no close acquaintances at court.
Residing in distant lands,
they do not seek to promote themselves.
Time passes swiftly,
yet they remain without any path to advancement.
This is indeed a matter of profound regret for both the foolish and wise in their respective provinces and localities.
Your servant and others humbly reflect that the reason the Secretariat officials are sent to the provinces,
and that there are talented people in the provinces,
is not merely to distribute prominent positions equally
or to extend favor to outer provinces.
It is truly because scholars have diverse customs,
and the four regions have different habits.
The harm of obstruction and isolation
is even greater in distant states.
As for Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚) Provinces,
each has hundreds of thousands of households.
Now, Yáng (揚) Province has no Secretariat official,
and in the southern part of Jīng (荊) Province, not a single person holds a position in the capital.
This is truly not the original intention of the sagely court in treating the four regions.
As for their talent, reputation, and qualifications,
Hè Xún (循) is suitable for the post of Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎),
and Guō Nà (訥) for Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬) or Shèrén (舍人).
These are the accumulated expectations of the populace,
not merely an aspiration to achieve high office
or simply to fill a vacancy.
I respectfully list their qualifications
and beg for your discerning examination.”
After a long time,
he was summoned and appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人).
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) usurped the throne,
he was transferred to Shìyùshǐ (侍御史),
but he resigned due to illness.
Later, he was appointed Nán Zhōngláng Chángshǐ (南中郎長史),
but did not take the post.
At that time, the rebel Lǐ Chén (李辰) raised an army in Jiāngxià (江夏),
and the regional commanders were unable to suppress him,
all fleeing at the mere sight of his dust.
Chén (辰)'s subordinate commander Shí Bīng (石冰) seized Yáng (揚) Province,
driving out Zhāng Jǐng (張景), the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
and replacing him with Chéng Chāo (程超), former Níngyuǎn Hùjūn (寧遠護軍).
He then appointed Chéng Chāo (超)'s chief clerk Zǎi Yǔ (宰與) to concurrently serve as Magistrate of Shānyīn (山陰).
The former Grand Administrator of Nánpíng (南平), Wáng Jǔ (王矩), the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興), Gù Mì (顧祕), and the former Xiùcái (秀才) Zhōu Qǐ (周玘) and others, initiated a righteous uprising,
circulating proclamations among the commanderies and prefectures to suppress them.
Hè Xún (循) also gathered forces and responded.
Shí Bīng (冰)'s major general Kàng Chǒng (抗寵) had several thousand troops,
stationed at the commandery's lecture hall.
Hè Xún (循) sent a proclamation to Kàng Chǒng (寵),
explaining the difference between loyalty and rebellion.
Kàng Chǒng (寵) then fled.
Chéng Chāo (超) and Zǎi Yǔ (與) both surrendered,
and the entire commandery was pacified.
Hè Xún (循) welcomed Zhāng Jǐng (景) back to the commandery,
then thanked and dismissed his soldiers,
shutting his door and not going out.
He took no part whatsoever
in the discussions of merit and rewards.
During the rebellion of Chén Mǐn (陳敏),
who falsely claimed to have an imperial edict,
he appointed Hè Xún (循) as Grand Administrator of Dānyáng (丹楊).
Hè Xún (循) declined, citing a foot ailment,
saying his hand could not hold a brush,
and that he had taken hánshísǎn (寒食散),
uncovering his hair and baring his body
to show he was unfit for service.
Chén Mǐn (敏) ultimately dared not compel him.
At this time, all the powerful figures within the province were arrested and imprisoned,
or if they were old and infirm,
they were given honorary titles and appointments.
Only Hè Xún (循) and Zhū Dàn (朱誕) of Wújùn (吳郡) were not involved in the matter.
After Chén Mǐn (敏) was defeated,
Zhōu Fù (周馥), the General Who Attacks the East,
recommended Hè Xún (循) to lead as Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽).
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Administrator of Wúguó (吳國).
He was summoned by public carriage for his virtuous talents,
but did not accept any of these posts.
When Yuán Dì (元帝) was General of the Pacified East,
he again recommended Hè Xún (循) as Grand Administrator of Wúguó (吳國).
Speaking with Hè Xún (循) about affairs during the Wú (吳) era,
he then asked:
“Sūn Hào (孫晧) once had a Hè (賀) family member sawn in half.
Who was that?”
Before Hè Xún (循) could speak,
the Emperor realized and said:
“That was Hè Shào (賀邵).”
Hè Xún (循) wept and said:
“My late father suffered terribly under a merciless ruler.
My wounds are deep, my pain profound,
and I have no way to repay his memory.”
The Emperor was greatly ashamed,
and did not appear for three days.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) ordered him to be a staff officer,
and summoned him to be appointed Bóshì (博士),
but he did not accept either.
When the Emperor was transferred to be Grand General Who Guards the East,
as his Military Commander Gù Róng (顧榮) had died,
he summoned Hè Xún (循) to replace him.
Hè Xún (循) claimed severe illness,
submitting over ten memorials of refusal.
The Emperor sent him a letter saying: “The hundred behaviors are not all the same,
hence the paths of engagement and reclusion differ.
One acts according to one’s nature,
each fulfilling their true self.
When the universe is peaceful and stable,
and the principles of order are well-established,
one may choose
to act or remain silent
according to circumstances.
Some may live in distant seclusion, treading lofty paths,
lightly withdrawing from the mundane world,
living in free and easy harmony,
calm in spirit and content in themselves.
This is surely when the Dao flourishes and people live in ease,
circumstances
making it so.
But if the times are fallen and corrupt,
the sovereign in peril, and the state in crisis,
righteous men save the age,
striving to rescue the world.
Zhú zhī Wǔ (燭之武) descended by rope into Qín (秦),
and Yuán Qǐ (園綺) donned his cap
to assist Hàn (漢).
Are these not actions of great and refined gentlemen, whose engagement and reclusion accord with the Dao?
I am of meager virtue and humble character,
unworthily holding a position among close relatives.
Mistakenly bestowed with high office,
and entrusted with command of a frontier region,
I imbibe the profound wisdom
and admire lofty conduct.
I have always wished to abandon the grandeur of a four-horse carriage
and,
with a humble wattle cart, visit your door.
Yet, I only harbor such sentiments
without actually following the worthy. Why?
It is truly because rebels incessantly disturb,
the various Chinese lands are fragmented,
the imperial residence has lost
its control,
and the common people are suffering profoundly.
Therefore, I worry day and night,
filled with indignation and determination,
my ambition being to dedicate my utmost efforts.
Previously, when Lord Gù (顧) presided over the court,
I deeply relied on his high wisdom.
Once Yuán Kǎi (元凱) ascended,
Cháo Xǔ (巢許) could live in reclusion.
But as for today,
it is what is called ‘the Dao has vanished,’
and the state
is in distress.
The hopes of the multitude are fixed
upon Your Lordship.
If it is a matter of righteousness,
how can one yield from labor and reside in ease?
I trust that an enlightened person will also act consistently with this principle.
May you
embrace noble plans
to broaden your far-reaching strategies.
Now, I have reported to the Secretariat,
humbly requesting you to serve as Military Commander.
I respectfully dispatch Staff Officer Shěn Zhēn (沈禎) with the imperial command to present this to you.
I earnestly hope you will reluctantly accept,
to fulfill
declined and stayed home.
Xún, however, did not rise.
When the Emperor assumed full authority,
he again appointed him Grand Master of Army Consultations (Jūnzī Jìjiǔ).
Xún claimed illness,
but Dūn pressed him, and he had no choice.
So he was carried to the court despite his illness.
The Emperor personally visited his boat,
and consulted him on the principles of governance.
Xún was too frail and ill to perform the full拜謁 (bàiyè) ceremony.
He was merely given court robes to put on,
granted a prime residence,
and provided with a carriage, horses, beds, curtains, clothing, and blankets.
Xún declined and refused,
accepting none of it.
The Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) Zhāng Kāi lived in the small market,
and intended to seize nearby houses to expand his residence.
He privately built a city gate,
which he closed early and opened late.
Many people suffered from this,
and lodged complaints with the provincial government,
but none were heard.
When Xún was traveling,
he reached Pògāng.
People collectively went to Xún to complain about it.
Xún said:
"When I see Grand Judge Zhāng,
I will speak to him about this."
Kāi heard of this and immediately demolished his gate,
then went to Xún to apologize.
Such was the respect he commanded from the world.
At that time, Jiāngdōng was in its initial stages of establishment,
and there were many bandits.
The Emperor pondered how to prevent them,
and asked Xún about it.
Xún replied:
"The Jiāng River spans ten thousand *lǐ*,
traversing five provinces.
It is a route for tribute missions and merchants.
Currently, some propose deploying troops from Xuānchéng to garrison the river islands,
or having various counties raise their own soldiers.
I believe that county magistrates are weak in authority,
and finding capable individuals for both civil and military duties is difficult.
Employing people who resent such service,
and failing to discipline them strictly,
may not prove effective.
From what I have heard,
the only critical strategic location on the river is Hélú,
where the terrain is treacherous and secluded,
a gathering place for fugitives.
It is particularly suitable to guard it with heavy troops,
suppressing and eliminating them as opportunities arise,
cutting off their roots.
As for the various counties along the river, each has its own demarcation.
Within their respective boundaries,
the officials in charge
can assess the land and allocate manpower,
establishing more postal stations and patrols,
making them vigilant,
tightening their oversight,
and strictly enforcing rewards and punishments.
Those who exceed the regular duties
will receive special honors,
while those who slacken will be personally held accountable.
This way, the general order will undoubtedly be maintained.
The assigned personnel should be rotated periodically,
so that the service does not become overwhelming,
and replacements are scheduled.
According to the Hàn system, there was a postal station every ten *lǐ*,
precisely for strict prevention and control.
Even if we cannot achieve that level now,
we should certainly plan carefully
to ensure sufficient resources.
If bandits become too strong and cannot be controlled locally,
their whereabouts can be reported,
and the relevant military governor (Dūdū) will then dispatch troops to suppress them.
Currently, the division of responsibilities is unclear,
causing local commoners and soldiers to share patrol duties indiscriminately,
resulting in both sides neglecting their responsibilities,
with no one truly in charge.
This is why there is only a nominal defense that proves ineffective."
The Emperor followed his advice.
When Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
Xún was summoned to serve as Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng).
When Emperor Yuán was stationed in the provinces,
he again recommended Xún as an Imperial Attendant (Shìzhōng),
but the journey was too dangerous, and he did not go.
For his contributions in suppressing Huá Yì,
he was to be enfeoffed as a Marquis of a District (Xiānghóu).
Xún, however, considering himself bedridden and a private citizen,
firmly declined the offer.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūlìng),
with the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
Again, due to old age and illness, he firmly declined.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"I, with my meager virtue,
have unworthily assumed a great position.
It is like crossing a mighty river,
without knowing what to rely upon.
Xún's words and actions are guided by propriety;
he is the hope of our time
and a model for society.
I truly rely on his counsel
to bring stability to the myriad affairs of state.
Despite his chronic illness,
I still hope he can provide guidance and assistance from his bed.
Yet he firmly adheres to humility
and expresses his heartfelt refusal.
This worthy man acts with integrity and compliance,
regarding yielding as a high virtue.
I shall now follow his wishes."
Thereupon, he was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
with his former title of Palace Attendant remaining.
Xún argued that the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) traditionally did not hold additional offices,
and moreover, being ill,
he was not suited to hold both positions.
He only accepted the appointment as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
At that time, the ancestral temple was newly established,
and many old rituals were lacking.
Some argued that Emperors Huì and Huái should each constitute a generation (shì),
which would make the number of generations for Yǐngchuān exceed seven,
and thus require removal (diéhuǐ) of an ancestor.
The matter was referred to the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Xún deliberated, believing: "According to the Rites,
brothers do not succeed each other,
and therefore succession does not establish a generation.
Bāngēng of the Yīn dynasty did not list Yángjiǎ in his lineage,
and Guāngwǔ of the Hàn dynasty did not succeed Emperor Chéng.
They established separate
ancestral temples
for officials to offer sacrifices.
This is a clear precedent from previous dynasties,
and a well-established principle of succession.
Emperor Huì had no heir,
and Emperor Huái succeeded to the lineage.
Since a younger brother does not succeed
an elder brother,
Emperor Huái directly succeeded the progenitor of the dynasty (Shìzǔ),
not Emperor Huì.
He should be treated similarly to Yángjiǎ of Yīn
and Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
Some argue that given the Emperor's sagely virtue and profound wisdom,
it is not appropriate
to easily change existing customs.
Ritual matters such as these
have not been fully discussed.
This is why Emperor Huì is still in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and Emperor Huái has also entered,
making the number of enshrined ancestors eight.
The reason for having eight
is that Emperor Huì has not been removed,
not that the founding ancestor (Shàngzǔ) should be moved.
When a junior generation ascends,
an senior generation is moved.
Moving and removing ancestors are not interchangeable.
There is no precedent for a junior generation ascending by one
while two senior generations are removed.
Both Emperors Huì and Huái succeeded the dynastic progenitor,
and as brothers and collateral relatives,
they constitute a single generation.
However, two senior generations were removed to make one generation.
Now,
with the demise of Emperor Huì, Yùzhāng has been removed.
With the entry of Emperor Huái, Yǐngchuān is again removed.
In this way, one generation is moved twice,
and the ancestral position is arbitrarily altered.
Searching through ancient principles,
I have not
found such a precedent.
Emperor Huì should be removed,
but this matter should not be lightly discussed.
How much less can one lightly remove an ancestor without ritual justification?
Since there is no reason to remove Yǐngchuān,
the number of
enshrined spirits naturally becomes eight.
This situation arises from specific circumstances,
not as a regular number.
Since there are eight spirits,
it is necessary to temporarily
establish an additional chamber outside the seven chambers.
The present Emperor (Zhìzūn) and Emperors Huì and Huái are all brothers.
The present Emperor directly succeeds the progenitor of the dynasty (Shìzǔ),
not these two emperors.
Therefore, the spirits of these two emperors should be placed elsewhere,
not
as part of an eight-chamber temple.
Furthermore, when Emperor Wǔ first established the Grand Ancestral Temple,
there were only seven principal spirits,
but the spirit of Empress Yáng Yuánhòu was also temporarily placed in a chamber.
During the Yǒngxī
In the first year,
the posthumous title of Shìzǔ was announced at the eight ancestral temples.
This implies that if there are eight deities,
they are not restricted by the old custom of seven.
Furthermore, some debaters held that since Jǐngdì was already in the temple,
Huìhuái should follow the same pattern.
Jǐngdì’s abundant virtue and great merit
were the foundation of the royal house,
his righteousness was evident to the ancestors,
and he would
not be forgotten for a hundred generations.
Therefore, he was specifically in this temple.
Moreover, the generations were still recent,
so it was permissible for them to coexist
to appease the spirits,
without pressing the senior ancestors.
If Wángshì’s zhāomù
was full,
they should ultimately have a separate temple.
Comparing this to the present,
the gravity of the righteousness differs,
and there is the closeness of seven temples for seven generations.
Zhāomù
refers to the positions of father and son.
If, when
the collateral lines of brothers become full,
the senior ancestors are immediately destroyed,
then the ancestral positions would be vacant,
the number of generations insufficient.
How then could one achieve the seven temples comprising three zhāo, three mù, and the temple of the Tàizǔ
ancestor?
Today, the principle of the seven temples
originates from Wángshì.
From the deceased father upwards to the great-great-grandfather (Gāozǔ),
there are four generations of close ancestral temples.
Above the Gāozǔ, there are five or six generations
of ancestors for whom there is no mourning attire.
Thus, it forms seven temples, with three zhāo, three mù, and the Tàizǔ.
Therefore, when Shìzǔ established the temple rites for the suburban sacrifice,
the close relatives in Jīngzhào and Yǐngchuān, up to zēng and gāo,
those in Yùzhāng of the fifth generation,
and the Zhēngxī of the sixth generation,
were to correspond to this principle.
Now, since the current Zūn continues the succession,
it is also appropriate to have ancestors of the fifth and sixth generations.
The Yùzhāng of the sixth generation
and the Yǐngchuān of the fifth generation
should not be destroyed.
Now, since it is said that Yùzhāng was destroyed first,
Yǐngchuān would again be destroyed.
This means that among the close relatives in the temple, only those from Gāozǔ downwards would remain,
without the two generations of ancestors
above Gāozǔ.
According to Wángshì’s principle,
two of the three zhāo and three mù would be abandoned,
which is certainly not what the ancestral temple’s foundation
is based upon.
It also violates Shìzǔ’s intention in sacrificing to
Zhēngxī and Yùzhāng.
Quite a lot would be missing from the rites established by a single king.
At the time, Shàngshū Púyè Diāo Xié held a different opinion from Xún.
Xún’s reply was deeply comprehensive,
much of it not recorded,
but ultimately, Xún’s proposal was followed.
Whenever the court had doubts or difficulties, they consulted Xún.
Xún would answer based on the ritual classics,
becoming the Confucian master of his generation.
Later, the emperor, seeing Xún's integrity and poverty,
issued an edict saying:
"Xún is pure as ice and clean as jade,
his conduct a model for the common people.
Though he holds a high position,
his clothing merely covers his body,
and his house barely shelters him from wind and rain.
I recently visited his humble abode
and felt a sense of sadness.
Therefore, I bestow upon him a six-foot bed with mattress and bedding, along with two hundred thousand coins,
to honor his supreme virtue
and express my sentiments."
Xún declined again,
but it was not permitted.
He had no choice but to accept it,
though he never used it.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
officials proposed that Lángxié Gōngwáng should be referred to as Huángkǎo.
Xún again debated, saying:
"According to the rites,
a son must not elevate his father with his own rank."
The emperor accepted this.
Soon after, Xún was appointed Xíng Tàizǐ Tàifù,
with Tàicháng as before.
Xún considered himself to be infirm with illness and enfeebled,
his duties as a minister neglected.
The principle of elevating the senior and lowering the junior,
and the respect of social interactions, were not maintained.
He feared that this was not a teaching to be passed down as a model.
He repeatedly submitted memorials firmly declining.
The emperor, believing that Xún embodied virtue and guided the people,
providing unspoken benefit,
exhorted him with utmost sincerity,
determined not to permit his resignation,
and ordered the Crown Prince to personally go and pay respects.
Xún suffered from a chronic illness,
yet was reverent in receiving visitors.
An imperial edict prohibited guests,
such was the high esteem he enjoyed.
His illness gradually worsened.
He submitted a memorial begging for his bones to be returned,
returning his seal and sash.
He was instead appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
The emperor personally attended court,
dispatched an envoy with a scepter,
and bestowed the seal and sash.
Although Xún could not speak,
he gestured to his attendants
to push away the official robes.
The imperial carriage personally visited,
holding his hand and shedding tears.
The Crown Prince personally visited three times,
bowing upon arrival and departure.
Confucian scholars considered this an honor.
He died in the second year of Tàixīng,
at the age of sixty.
The emperor wore plain clothes and expressed his grief,
weeping bitterly.
He was posthumously granted Sīkōng
and given the posthumous name Mù.
Before the burial,
the emperor again went out to his coffin,
weeping with full sorrow.
He dispatched a jiān Shìyùshǐ with a scepter to supervise the funeral.
The Crown Prince followed the procession for a short distance,
shedding tears as he watched the boat.
Xún had enjoyed studying books in his youth,
was good at writing,
read extensively,
and was especially skilled in rites and commentaries.
He had an excellent judgment of character,
elevating Yáng Fāng of the same prefecture from obscurity,
who eventually achieved fame in the world.
His son, Xí,
served as Línhǎi Tàishǒu during Kāngdì’s reign.
Yáng Fāng's courtesy name was Gōnghuí.
In his youth, he was fond of learning
and possessed extraordinary talent.
Initially, he served as a bell-bearer and ceremonial attendant for the commandery.
In his free time from official duties,
he would read the Five Classics,
though his hometown did not yet recognize his abilities.
Nèishǐ Zhūgě Huī saw him and found him remarkable,
treating him with the courtesy due to a disciple,
which allowed him to begin associating with the nobility.
At that time, the Yú Xǐ brothers were renowned for their Confucian scholarship,
and they greatly admired Fāng,
extending his reputation.
Huī once asked Fāng to write a document
recommending a merit registrar and chief clerk for the commandery.
Yú Yù praised it highly
and sent it to Xún for his perusal.
Xún replied in a letter:
"This young man has an aspiration to rise and achieve,
I only thought his ideas were somewhat different from the ordinary,
but I did not expect such great talent.
His writing has a truly exceptional quality;
if it flows from his heart,
then he is one whom the entire nation would extol,
how could he merely be distinguished among herdsmen?
I hear he is among the old party members,
and possesses a humble and modest demeanor.
This is also a cornerstone of establishing oneself.
However, with the world in decline and the Way lost,
and people's talents diminished,
whenever I hear of an individual with aspirations toward the Way,
I hope and wish for them.
Someone like Fāng is a special shoot in a desolate field,
an excellent sprout in barren soil.
His inherent quality is already good,
he merely lacks sufficient nourishment.
If transplanted to fertile ground,
he will certainly become fine grain.
Your Excellency’s talent is an outstanding one of the generation,
and your position is among the highest in court.
The Way will flourish and order will be established,
then you will be esteemed.
Formerly, Xǔ Zǐjiāng elevated Fán Zhòngzhāo from a merchant,
and Guō Línzōng established Wèi Dégōng from the fields.
If Your Excellency is dedicated to this endeavor,
the achievements of these two worthies will not be difficult to equal."
Xún then praised Fāng in the capital.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo appointed him as a subordinate,
then he transferred to Dōng'ān Tàishǒu,
and later was promoted to Sītú Cānjūnshì.
While in the capital,
all the officials treated him generously.
He considered his homeland to be a cold and remote place,
and did not wish to stay long in the capital, Jīnghuá.
He requested an appointment to a distant commandery,
desiring a quiet life for writing.
Dǎo followed his wish,
and he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Gāoliáng.
He served in the commandery for many years,
producing Wǔjīng Gōuzhěn
and further compiling Wúyuè Chūnqiū,
along with various essays and writings,
all of which circulated in the world.
Due to old age,
he abandoned his post and returned home.
Dǎo intended to promote him to the court,
but he firmly declined and returned to his hometown,
where he died at home.
Xuē Jiān
Xuē Jiān, courtesy name Lìngcháng,
was a native of Dānyáng.
His grandfather, Zōng,
served Wú as Shàngshū Púyè.
His father, Yíng,
was famous in the Wú court.
When Wú was pacified,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì.
Jiān was pure and upright, possessing great character.
In his youth, he was renowned alongside Jì Zhān from the same commandery, Mǐn Hóng from Guǎnglíng, Gù Róng from Wú Commandery, and Hè Xún from Huìjī,
and they were known as
the "Five Jùn."
When he first entered Luòyáng,
Sīkōng Zhāng Huà saw him and was impressed,
saying:
"They are all 'southern gold'."
He was investigated as an outstanding talent (xiàolián) from Hénán,
and recruited into a ducal residence.
He was appointed as the Chief of Bǐyáng,
and gained a reputation for competence in his post.
He successively served as Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ, Sànqí Chángshì, and Prefect of Huái.
The Sīkōng, Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, appointed him as Cānjūn,
then promoted him to Jìjiǔ,
and bestowed upon him the title of Ānyáng Tínghóu.
When Yuán Dì was Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
he appointed him Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
and he was gradually promoted to Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ.
He was very diligent in royal affairs.
Although his salary as a senior assistant was generous,
he always restrained himself,
taking only what was sufficient.
He was promoted to the title of Ānyáng Xiānghóu
and appointed Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
Upon the establishment of the restoration,
he was transferred to the position of Yǐn,
with an increased rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí,
and then promoted to Shàngshū,
also holding the post of Tàizǐ Shǎofù.
From Zōng to Jiān,
three generations served as tutors to the Crown Prince,
and commentators praised this.
In the early Yǒngchāng period,
Wáng Dūn recommended Jiān as Tàicháng.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
The Emperor, remembering him as his tutor during his time as Crown Prince,
felt it appropriate to show utmost respect,
and thus issued an edict saying:
"I, being unworthy,
suffered misfortune early in life.
Humbly, with my insignificant self,
I am entrusted above kings and dukes.
Grieving and in mourning,
I have no one to consult or look up to,
my heart is filled with anxiety,
as if I were standing on the edge of a valley.
Confucius said: 'Therefore, even the Son of Heaven
must have those he respects.'
I shall respectfully uphold the rites due to former teachers,
and consult those with virtue.
Tàizǎi Xīyáng Wáng is of high rank and great renown,
and in his nobility, he contemplates humility.
Chéngxiàng Wǔchāng Gōng and Sīkōng Jíqiūzǐ embody lofty principles,
possess both merit and virtue,
were trusted friends of the late emperor,
and are my teachers.
Tàicháng Ānyáng Xiānghóu instructed and protected my person,
being loyal, solemn, and sincere.
Indeed, honoring kin and respecting the virtuous
were what the late emperor valued.
When I see the four lords or their written correspondence and deportment,
everything shall be as it was in the Eastern Palace."
That year,
he died.
An edict stated:
"Tàicháng, Ānyáng Xiānghóu Jiān possessed pure virtue
and dedicated himself to loyalty and self-restraint.
We relied on his virtuous guidance
to broadly assist in the path of governance.
His unfortunate demise
pains our heart!
We now dispatch a court censor (chíjié shìyùshǐ) to posthumously grant him the titles of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
If his spirit has consciousness,
may it appreciate this honor and favor."
At his burial,
due to Wáng Dūn's rebellion
and many difficulties at court,
no posthumous title could be deliberated upon.
Instead, an envoy was merely sent to offer a grand sacrifice (tàiláo).
His son, Yǒng,
died before Jiān,
leaving no heir.
The court historian says: Yuán Dì established his foundation in Huáihǎi,
and all systems were beginning.
He longed for talented individuals
to together bring prosperity to the myriad undertakings.
Gù, Jì, Hè, Xuē, and others were all "southern gold" and "eastern arrows,"
from esteemed families of hereditary nobility.
They pledged their allegiance to the sovereign's court
and participated in state governance;
laws and institutions relied on their compilation and editing,
and the court awaited their strategies and plans;
they were highly respected by the officials,
and their responsibilities were like those of Yuánkǎi.
They achieved official success and established their reputations,
bringing glory to the nation and honor to their families.
This was not only due to a confluence of opportune circumstances
but also because their talents and abilities were truly exceptional.
Among them, Hè Xún rose to the position of Bǎofù,
and his prestige at court was especially high,
even leading to the Emperor's imperial carriage (luánbì) visiting his residence,
and the Emperor himself bowing in the Chéngmíng Hall.
Although the honor given to Zhāng Yǔ in the Western Hàn
and the respect shown to Huán Róng in the Eastern capital
were great, they did not surpass this.
Eulogy says: Yànxiān had profound insight,
far-reaching thoughts, and upright character.
Xuē was pure and steadfast,
Hè was learned and principled.
Meeting their time and lord,
they soared on the wind, spreading their wings.
