Biography 39 Líu Wèi (Sūn Bō)
Líu Wèi, courtesy name Dàlián,
was a native of Péngchéng,
a descendant of Chǔ Yuán Wáng Jiāo.
His father, Dǐ, was the Prefect of Dōngguāng.
Wèi showed literary talent in his youth,
and started his career as Mìshū Láng.
He was gradually promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Péngchéng.
Fleeing chaos, he crossed the Yangtze River,
and Yuán Dì appointed him Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would observe from afar the reasons for the decline and fall of the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
and examine closely the collapse of the Western dynasty in recent times.
May you rise above and change your thinking,
acting proactively,
so that the spiritual foundation will be forever secure,
and the altars of grain and soil
will be free from danger.
How could your servant allege that all people of a single dynasty lack loyalty and integrity?
It is merely that talents are not employed in their proper capacities,
and thus desired outcomes are not achieved.
Presently, government is troublesome and levies are heavy,
leading to decay and ruin everywhere.
Granaries are empty,
and national expenditure is depleted.
The common people are exploited and diminished,
with exiles and refugees continually appearing.
A rough calculation of households and population
shows that
since Xián'ān,
three tenths have been lost.
The populace sighs with the lament of the rootless wanderer,
and those in the lower springs stir with thoughts of the Zhōu capital.
In ancient times, Emperor Xuān of Hàn said:
"Those who will govern the empire
with me,
are they not the worthy Erqiānshí (Two Thousand Piculs)!"
Therefore, those who had effective methods for ruling their subordinates were honored with additional seals and awards,
while those who made laws harsh and government chaotic were treated with compassion, not being pardoned from punishment.
Affairs were simple for the superior,
and people rejoiced below.
Today, however, it is not so.
Those who announce the times and beg for positions use family hardship as an excuse,
while those who relieve the poor and assist the stagnant use public office as a means of personal gain.
In ancient times, a ruler was established for the common
people to be their shepherd;
but now, the common people support the ruler,
allowing him to devour them like silkworms.
Indeed, corrupt officials are called pure and diligent,
and those who adhere strictly to the law are called timid
and inferior.
How has the ancient way been reversed to such an extent!
Although Your Majesty personally practices frugality
and shows compassion from above,
the multitude of officials indulge their desires,
giving free rein to their hearts below.
The Six Bureaus (Lìu Sī) hang their wings in despair,
and the Three High Officers (Sān Shì) remain silently inactive.
Therefore, those with insight
sigh at human affairs
and greatly fear when observing ominous portents.
In ancient times, Sòng Jǐng averted the calamity of Yínghuò (Mars);
Yīn Zōng dispelled the strangeness of the Tripod Pheasant (Dǐng Zhì).
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would look up
and contemplate the ambition of Great Yǔ, who passed his own gate without entering,
and look down
and observe the error of Shāng Xīn, who indulged in drunkenness.
Reflect deeply on the satire of Gōng Gōng in the Guófēng (Airs of the States),
and ponder carefully the parable of Xiǎo Chén by Dìng Jiāng.
For a moment, turn back
your sacred grace,
consult broadly with the multitude of high officials,
invite and accept the wisdom of all virtuous individuals,
and inquire about gains and losses.
Let all officials perform their duties,
and let people speak of improvements and detriments.
Investigate their origins,
observe their reasons,
carefully discern all talents,
and assist in harmonizing the flavors in the tripod.
Conquer your thoughts and become a sage,
thereby repaying Heaven's favor.
Then the four seas will be at peace,
and the empire will be greatly fortunate.
Your servant's deceased ancestor, the former minister Kǔi,
once received extraordinary favor.
His integrity, not for personal gain,
still remains in the old histories.
He had aspirations but no opportunity,
carrying his regret to the Yellow Springs.
As for your servant, though mediocre,
I again received boundless kindness.
This grace, accumulated over generations,
cannot truly be repaid by sacrificing my life or ruining my clan.
I submitted this memorial previously,
but it did not reach you in time.
Suddenly afflicted by a severe illness,
I fear my life is fleeting.
Desiring to seize every moment of breath,
I hope my foolish sentiments may be conveyed.
My strength is waning,
and I cannot express myself fully.
(This memorial) was submitted, and then he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Former General.
His son Dàn succeeded.
In the early Yuánxī era,
he served as the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lújiāng.
Kǔi's paternal uncle Nà,
courtesy name Lìngyán,
possessed discernment of human character.
When he first entered Luò,
he saw several famous scholars and sighed, saying:
"Wáng Yíbǔ is too brilliant and clear,
Lè Yànfǔ is whom I respect,
Zhāng Màoxiān is whom I do not understand,
Zhōu Hóngwǔ is clever at using weaknesses,
and Dù Fāngshū is clumsy at using strengths."
He eventually served as the Grand Administrator of the Capital (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
His son Chóu,
courtesy name Wángqiáo,
had an excellent reputation in his youth,
and was skilled in discussing profound principles.
Once, when avoiding chaos in a fortified encampment,
a hundred or so Hu (foreign merchants) wished to harm him.
Chóu showed no fear,
took up a pípa and played it,
producing tunes like "Out of the Fortress" and "Into the Fortress,"
thereby stirring the nostalgic feelings of these travelers.
Thereupon, all the Hu shed tears and left him.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he rose to the position of Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Chángshǐ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú),
but was soon killed by Yán Dǐng.
Cài Mó, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), often sighed and said:
"If Liú Wángqiáo had been able to cross to the south,
he would have been an excellent choice for Minister of Works."
Also, when Wáng Dǎo was first appointed Minister of Works,
he said to others:
"If Liú Wángqiáo had crossed the river,
I would not have been the only one appointed to the ducal office."
Such was the respect he commanded from renowned scholars.
Chóu's elder brother's son Shào
possessed talent and ability.
He was appointed an aide to Chancellor Wáng of Lángyá.
During the Xiánkāng era,
he successively held positions as Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand Minister (Shàngshū), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yùzhāng,
with an emolument of Two Thousand Piculs (Zhōng Èrqiānshí).
Shào's cousin Huánglǎo,
during the Tàiyuán era,
served as a Secretary of the Board (Shàngshū Láng).
He was learned in righteousness,
and annotated the works of Shènzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
both of which are transmitted to this day.
Diāo Xié (Zi Yí; Yí's son Kúi)
Diāo Xié, courtesy name Xuánliàng,
was a native of Ráo'ān, Bóhǎi.
His grandfather Gōng was the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Qíjùn in Wèi.
His father Yōu was the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) during Emperor Wǔ's reign.
In his youth, Xié was fond of classics and records,
having extensive knowledge and a strong memory.
He first entered officialdom as an Erudite (Wénxué) of the Prince of Púyáng,
and successively became Grand Master of Ceremonies Erudite (Tàicháng Bóshì) and Grand Corrector (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of his home commandery.
The Prince of Chéngdū, Yǐng, invited him to be his Commander of the Northern Army (Píngběi Sīmǎ).
Later, he served as Adjutant (Cānjūn) to the Prime Minister (Xiàngguó) of the Prince of Zhào, Lún,
and then as Commander of Cavalry (Piàojì Sīmǎ) to the Prince of Chángshā.
When the Duke of Dōngyíng, Téng, garrisoned Línzhāng,
he appointed Xié as his Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ),
who was later transferred to be the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yǐngchuān.
In the early Yǒngjiā era,
he became the Governor (Yǐn) of Hénán.
Before taking office,
he fled across the Yangzi River (Dù Jiāng) to avoid chaos.
Emperor Yuán made him Libationer (Jìjiǔ) to the General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jūn Sī),
and then promoted him to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ).
When Emperor Mǐn ascended the throne,
he summoned him to be Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
but as was customary, he did not take the post.
When Emperor Yuán became Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
he appointed Xié as his Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Chángshǐ).
With the restoration of the dynasty,
he was appointed Left Vice Director (Zuǒ Púyè) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
At that time, the imperial court was newly established,
and regulations were not yet set.
No court official was familiar with the old ceremonies.
Xié had long served in the central court,
was well-versed in old affairs,
and all regulations and institutions
were based on his advice.
He was highly praised at the time.
In the early Tàixīng era,
he was promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
After several years in office,
he was given the additional title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
retaining his post.
Xié was rigid and fierce by nature,
often at odds with others.
He constantly exalted superiors and suppressed subordinates,
thus incurring the hatred of the Wáng clan.
Moreover, he was intemperate in drink,
insulting and disparaging high officials,
so that all who saw him averted their gaze.
Nevertheless, he devoted all his energy and heart,
aiming to rectify and save the situation.
The Emperor deeply trusted him.
The use of slaves as soldiers,
and compelling generals, officials, and envoys to undertake transport duties,
were all measures Xié proposed.
The common people resented and grumbled about these policies.
When Wáng Dūn 構逆 rebelled,
a memorial was submitted accusing Diāo Xié of crimes.
The Emperor ordered Diāo Xié to lead the Six Armies.
Soon after, the imperial forces suffered a defeat.
Diāo Xié and Liú Wèi both attended the Emperor in the eastern annex of the Tàijí Palace.
The Emperor grasped Diāo Xié's and Liú Wèi's hands,
weeping and choking,
advising them to flee the disaster.
Diāo Xié said:
"Your subject is bound to stand and die;
I dare not be of two minds."
The Emperor said:
"Now the situation is pressing;
how can you not go?"
So he ordered horses and men to be given to Diāo Xié and Liú Wèi,
allowing them to make their own plans.
Diāo Xié was old
and unable to ride.
He had always lacked influence and discipline,
and when he tried to recruit followers,
they all abandoned him and left.
When he reached Jiāngchéng,
he was killed by someone,
who sent his head to Wáng Dūn.
Wáng Dūn permitted the Diāo clan to collect and bury him.
The Emperor grieved that Diāo Xié could not escape,
and secretly captured and executed the person who had delivered Diāo Xié's head.
After Wáng Dūn's rebellion was suppressed,
Zhōu Yǐ, Dài Ruòsī, and others all received prominent posthumous honors,
but Diāo Xié was not included in this category because he had fled.
During the Xiánkāng period,
Diāo Xié's son, Diāo Yí, submitted a memorial pleading his father's case.
Many in power believed that the commendations and criticisms had already been settled during the reign of Emperor Míng,
and that it was not permissible to re-evaluate them.
Furthermore, Diāo Xié had failed to uphold his integrity and die for his country,
but instead fled and met his demise,
so his official rank could not be restored.
Yīn Róng, the Administrator of Dānyáng, deliberated, saying:
"Wáng Dūn's wickedness was such that
his crimes were beyond pardon;
therefore, Diāo Xié's goodness also should not be rewarded.
If one holds that his loyalty was not a good plan,
and his stratagems were miscalculated,
and makes this a point of criticism,
that should merely be a matter for discussion and censure.
If the execution of the brutal and cruel is considered a national punishment,
how then can one deter and encourage?
When Wáng Dūn was exerting pressure,
rewards and punishments, authority and penalties all emanated from him.
For this reason, Emperor Yuán, with deep concern for the foundation,
took Diāo Xié as an example;
the matter arose from national policy,
and was certainly not for private reasons.
In the past, Kǒng Níng and Yí Hángfù followed their lord in his debauchery,
yet Chǔ restored their positions,
because they were the lord's partisans.
How much more so in Diāo Xié's case, whose comparison with the lord
lay in righteousness and obedience.
Moreover, he was one of the Four Assistants of the Restoration,
holding a foremost position in the court.
At that time, the situation was desperate and plans exhausted;
he followed orders to avoid the rebels,
not to escape punishment.
It is proper to grant him prominent posthumous honors,
to clarify his loyalty and righteousness."
At that time, Yǔ Bīng was assisting in government,
and was hesitant, unable to decide.
Cài Mó, the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left, wrote to Yǔ Bīng, saying: "To confer titles upon people,
one should make their achievements manifest;
to punish people,
one should make their crimes clear.
This has always been observed with caution by past and present.
Even for common people, this is still the case.
Diāo Lìng, a senior assistant during the Restoration,
had the reputation of dying in peril,
yet the world did not hear of his crimes,
but only saw his demotion,
causing the Diāo clan to voice grievances.
This is, in effect,
avenging Wáng Dūn.
It internally discourages the integrity of loyal ministers,
and confounds those who discuss it.
If he truly had grave crimes,
it would be proper to make his deeds known,
so that all under heaven would know,
thus making it clear that the sagely court does not demote ministers who die in peril.
The righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is to compensate for faults with merits.
If the fault is light and the merit heavy,
one may receive additional enfeoffment;
if the merit is light and the fault heavy,
one cannot escape execution and annihilation;
if the merit is sufficient
to atone for the crime, there is no demotion.
Even if there was a prior crime of wickedness and flattery,
if in the face of calamity one sided with one's lord,
one is not cut off.
Kǒng Níng and Yí Hángfù
committed adultery with Duke Líng in court.
The lord was killed and the state perished,
due to these two ministers,
yet Chǔ still received them.
The Zuo Zhuan says that those who observe ritual do not cut off their positions,
because they are the lord's partisans.
If Diāo Lìng's crimes were
heavier than Kǒng Níng's and Yí Hángfù's,
then cutting him off would be acceptable.
If he had no such crimes,
then he should be reconsidered.
Some say that since it was already set aside during the reign of Emperor Míng,
it should not be changed now.
I, however, think otherwise.
The Great Way governs the world,
with different paths leading to the same destination.
In the myriad affairs of state,
some are different, some are the same.
Being the same does not mean being superior,
and being different does not mean being criticized.
Thus, Yáo suppressed Yuánkǎi, but Shùn promoted him;
Yáo was not at fault,
nor was Shùn in error.
Why must what was set aside by a former generation necessarily be unchangeable?
Hàn Xiāo Hé's descendants lost their marquisate due to legal transgressions.
Emperor Wén did not enfeoff them, but Emperor Jǐng did.
Later they lost
the marquisate again.
Emperors Wǔ and Zhāo did not enfeoff them, but Emperor Xuān did.
Recently, in the first year [of this reign],
the imperial carriage performed the Shìdiàn ceremony,
bowing to the seat of Kǒngzǐ.
This was also not practiced by Emperors Yuán and Míng.
Moreover, Diāo Lìng was merely not posthumously honored by Emperor Míng;
he was not executed.
Wáng Píngzǐ and Dìwǔ Yī were both executed by Emperor Yuán,
yet today they are
posthumously honored.
Why should changing previous decisions be an issue?
Those who handle affairs
should, above, conform to ancient righteousness,
and below, follow current precedents.
Only then will commentators not be confused,
and those who suffer punishment will have no resentment.
Upon examination, Minister Zhōu [Yǐ] and General-in-chief Dài [Ruòsī] were not targets of Wáng Dūn's initial proclamations;
they were only killed after the situation was settled.
Zhōu Yán and Guō Pú, among others, were also not
defending their lord against calamity;
they were killed in peacetime,
yet all received posthumous honors.
How could Diāo Lìng's case and righteousness be less than theirs?
Recently, even staff attendants without specific appointments have been able to receive posthumous
honors,
let alone Diāo Lìng, whose position was second only to the Three Ducal Ministers.
If he had simply died of old age,
he would not have been excluded from the category of staff attendants without specific appointments.
Even if he had not received posthumous honors,
he would not have been denied burial with his original official rank.
This means that for one person,
if he dies of old age, he receives posthumous honors,
but if he dies in peril, he is cut off.
How can this clarify the way of serving one's lord
and encourage the integrity of ministers?
It is proper to publicly evaluate his case,
to resolve the doubts of the world.
I also hear that many commentators believe he should be posthumously honored.
When a matter is not just,
yet receives widespread support,
it might be due to winning over the masses with kindness and gentleness,
but Diāo Lìng was rough and rigid, often incurring
resentment.
If it is due to nobility,
the Diāo clan is now humble.
If it is due to wealth,
the Diāo clan is now poor.
Why do scholars instead help a humble family and speak thus?

Upon observing this intention,
Bīng rán felt cold.
When the matter was reported,
Emperor Chéng issued an edict saying:
"Diāo Xié's feelings were loyal to his lord,
but he lost the way of a minister.
Therefore, he allowed Wáng Dūn to falsely claim public righteousness,
while in reality indulging his private jealousies,
thereby causing the state to suffer humiliation,
and Emperor Yuán to bear shame, leading to the origin of disaster.
How could this not have a cause!
If we were to thoroughly apply the national statutes,
then the punishment then was not severe.
Now, it is precisely because Xié's diligence is worth recording,
and Dūn's rebellion cannot be prolonged,
that we discuss this matter.
Now, Xié's original position may be restored,
and he shall be granted a sacrificial offering,
to make clear that those loyal to their sovereign, even in the slightest, shall be recognized.
Although the censure and reduction were not entirely just,
this may perhaps serve as a sufficient encouragement."
Thereupon, his original office was posthumously restored,
and he was honored with the grand sacrifice of Tài Láo.
Diāo Yí's courtesy name was Dàlún.
He suffered family misfortunes in his youth.
After Wáng Dūn was executed,
Yí beheaded members of his enemy's faction,
offered their heads at his father's tomb,
and then went to the Tíngwèi to confess his crime.
The imperial court specially pardoned him,
and he became famous thereafter.
He successively served as Shàngshū Lìbù Láng and Wúgúo Nèishǐ,
and was successively promoted to Běizhōngláng Jiàng, Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn two commanderies, and Jiǎjié,
stationed in Guǎnglíng.
He died in office.
His son, Kuí,
courtesy name Bódào;
Kuí's younger brother, Chàng,
courtesy name Zhòngyuǎn;
his next son, Hóng,
courtesy name Shūbi;
all held prominent positions.
During the Lóng'ān period,
Kuí served as Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu,
holding the titles of Píngyuè Zhōngláng Jiàng and Jiǎjié;
Chàng served as Shǐxīng Xiàng;
Hóng served as Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu.
The brothers, sons, and nephews were not constrained by reputation or conduct,
but focused on commerce.
They owned ten thousand qǐng of land,
several thousand slaves,
and their other assets were commensurate.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he appointed Kuí as Xīzhōngláng Jiàng and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed in Lìyáng;
Chàng as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn;
Hóng as Fújun Huán Xiū Sīmǎ.
When Liú Yù launched his uprising,
he executed Huán Xiū.
At that time, Chàng and Hóng plotted to raise troops to attack Yù.
Yù sent Liú Yì to suppress them.
Chàng was executed;
Hóng fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
Kuí, in Lìyáng, seized Liú Yù's Cānjūn Zhūgě Chángmín,
and sent him in a caged cart to Huán Xuán.
When they reached Dānglì, Xuán was defeated,
and the people escorting him broke open the cage to release Chángmín,
who then headed for Lìyáng.
Kuí abandoned the city and fled,
but was captured by his subordinates
and executed at Shítou.
All his sons and nephews, regardless of age, died,
except for his youngest brother, Chěng, who was pardoned
and appointed Gěishìzhōng.
Soon after, he plotted rebellion and was executed,
and the Diāo clan was thus extinguished.
The Diāo clan had always been exceedingly wealthy,
their slaves and retainers ran rampant,
and they were avaricious over mountains and marshes,
acting as a pestilence in Jīngkǒu.
Yù distributed their accumulated wealth,
allowing the common people to take what they could according to their ability,
and it was not exhausted even after a full day.
At that time, the world was suffering from famine and hardship,
and the registered households relied on this to survive.
Dài Ruòsī (younger brother Miǎo)
Dài Ruòsī was
a native of Guǎnglíng.
His given name violated the taboos of Emperor Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His grandfather, Liè,
was Zǔo Jiāngjūn of Wú.
His father, Chāng,
was Huìjī Tàishǒu.
Ruòsī had a dignified bearing
and a calm and straightforward disposition.
In his youth, he enjoyed chivalrous adventures
and was not constrained by moral conduct.
When Lù Jī went to Luò,
his boat was heavily laden,
so Ruòsī and his companions plundered it.
Ruòsī landed,
sat on a camp stool,
and directed his companions,
who all acted appropriately.
Jī observed him,
knew he was no ordinary person,
and from the boat cabin, he called out to him, saying:
"With your talent and capacity,
how can you still be a robber!"
Ruòsī was moved to understanding,
then wept,
threw down his sword, and went to him.
Jī spoke with him,
greatly admired and esteemed him,
and thus they established a friendship.
Later, Ruòsī was recommended as Xiàolián
and entered Luò.
Jī recommended him to Zhào Wáng Lún, saying:
"I have heard that only when the Fán Ruò (bow) is mounted
does the merit of high walls become manifest;
only when the Gūzhú (musical instrument) is played
does the divine melody become complete.
Therefore, a ruler of surpassing age must employ talents from far and near,
and hidden talents must rely on the harmony of grand music.
I have observed the hermit, Dài Ruòsī of Guǎnglíng,
aged thirty.
He is pure and profound, walking the path,
his virtue and capacity are truly full;
his discernment is sufficient to explore the subtle,
and his talent and judgment are sufficient to distinguish things;
he is content in poverty and joyful in his aspirations,
without desire for worldly fame;
he refines his integrity and establishes his conduct,
possessing the purity of a clean well;
he is truly a lost treasure of the southeast,
a rare uncut gem for the court.
If he were to set foot on the public road,
he would be able to follow the path of outstanding steeds;
if he were to display his quality in the imperial court,
he would surely cast a brilliant light like fine jade.
May you, Illustrious Duke, condescend to observe and discern,
and not discard loyal and sincere words because of the person."
Lún then invited him,
and he was appointed Qìnshuǐ Lìng,
but he did not accept it.
He then went to Wǔlíng to visit his father.
At that time, Pān Jīng, a fellow countryman, was known for his discernment
and his ability to judge people.
His father sent Ruòsī to speak with Jīng,
who then praised Ruòsī as having the talent of a prime minister.
He was successively transferred to Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè's Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
and then appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu,
with the additional title of Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Dūdū of the righteous army.
For his meritorious service in suppressing bandits,
he was granted the title of Líng Hóu.
He was promoted to Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ, Piàojì Sīmǎ,
and then appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
Emperor Yuán summoned him to be Zhèndōng Yòusīmǎ.
When about to campaign against Dù Tāo,
Ruòsī was given the additional title of Qián Jiāngjūn,
but Tāo was annihilated before they set out.
When the Emperor became Jìn Wáng,
he appointed him Shàngshū.
When the restoration began,
he served as Zhōnghùjūn,
then transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn and Shàngshū Púyè,
but he declined all these appointments.
He was then appointed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Dūdū of the military affairs of the six provinces of Yǎn, Yù, Yōu, Jì, Yōng, and Bìng, and Jiǎjié,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He recruited a thousand men who offered their resumes to the imperial court to serve as military officers,
and conscripted ten thousand household slaves from Yángzhōu as soldiers to be assigned to them.
He appointed Sànqí Chángshì Wáng Xiá as Jūnsī,
stationed in Shòuyáng,
and set out together with Liú Kuí.
The Emperor personally visited their camp
to encourage the officers and soldiers.
Before their departure, he held a farewell banquet for them,
serving wine and composing poems.
When Dài Ruòsī was about to reach Héféi,
Wáng Dūn raised an army.
An imperial edict recalled Dài Ruòsī to guard the capital.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry (Piāojì Jiāngjūn)
and, together with the Right General of the Imperial Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn) Guō Yì, built fortifications along the road north of Dàhéng.
Soon after, Shítóu fell.
Dài Ruòsī and other generals attacked Shítóu,
but the imperial army was defeated.
Dài Ruòsī led over a hundred of his subordinates to the palace to receive an edict,
and together with the high officials and various bureaucrats, he met Wáng Dūn at Shítóu.
Wáng Dūn asked Dài Ruòsī:
"In the battle the other day, did you have any strength left?"
Dài Ruòsī answered without showing deference:
"How would I dare to have strength left?
It's just that my strength was insufficient."
Wáng Dūn then said:
"How does the world view
this action of mine?"
Dài Ruòsī said:
"Those who see the outward form call it rebellion;
those who understand the true intention call it loyalty."
Wáng Dūn laughed and said:
"You can truly be called eloquent."
Wáng Dūn's staff officer Lǚ Yī had formerly been a clerk in the Imperial Secretariat (Táiláng).
He possessed a talent for writing official documents,
but his nature was especially treacherous and sycophantic.
When Dài Ruòsī was Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū),
he disliked Lǚ Yī's character,
and Lǚ Yī also bore a deep grudge.
At this point,
he persuaded Wáng Dūn, saying:
"Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Ruòsī both have high reputations,
sufficient to mislead the masses.
Their recent words showed no trace of shame.
If Your Excellency does not eliminate them,
I fear there will be the trouble of a renewed uprising,
which will cause future worries."
Wáng Dūn thought this was true,
and he had long been jealous of them.
Shortly after, he sent Dèng Yuè and Miáo Tǎn to arrest Dài Ruòsī and kill him.
Dài Ruòsī had always enjoyed great prestige,
and all scholars across the land grieved for him.
After the rebellion was quelled,
he was posthumously awarded the title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Right (Yòuguānglù Dàfū) with the rank of Yítóng Sānsī,
and his posthumous name was Jiǎn.
Miáo's courtesy name was Wàngzhī.
In his youth, he loved learning,
excelling especially in the histories of the Former and Later Hàn dynasties.
His talent did not match Dài Ruòsī's,
but he surpassed him in classical scholarship.
At the age of twenty, he was recommended as an outstanding talent (xiùcái),
then moved to be an Attendant at the Imperial Academy (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
and later appointed as the Administrator of Xīyáng (Xīyáng Nèishǐ).
During the Yǒngjiā era,
Emperor Yuán appointed him as Administrator of Shàolíng (Shàolíng Nèishǐ) and Libationer of Military Consultations for the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Jūnzī Jìjiǔ),
then sent him out as Army Supervisor for the General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jūnsī).
At that time, everything was just beginning,
and schools had not yet been established.
Miáo submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard that among the great principles of Heaven,
none is greater than Yin and Yang;
among the most important tasks of emperors and kings,
none is more significant than rites and learning.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a state was founded,
there were the systems of the Bright Hall (Míngtáng)
and the Circular Moat (Pìyōng),
and in the villages, there were the institutions of xiáng, xù, hóng, and xiào schools.
All these were for the purpose of drawing out the obscure and stagnant,
and broadening talent and thought.
This is because line six-four has the regret of being 'constrained by ignorance,'
and the noble
man has the merit of greatly nurturing uprightness.
In the past, Kǒngzǐ was merely a high official in a state,
yet he promoted rites and cultivated learning between the Zhū and Sì Rivers,
and outstanding talents from all directions eagerly gravitated towards him,
with over seventy individuals achieving success.
Since then,
a thousand years have passed without comparison.
Is it that the world is smaller than Lǔ and Wèi,
or that wise and sagacious men are lacking compared to earlier times?
It is a matter of whether they are encouraged or not,
that is all.
Recently, the state has suffered unexpected calamity,
and the altars of earth and grain face the danger of hanging by a thread.
Barbarian raiders have watered their horses in the Yangtze River,
and fierce villains are rampant for ten thousand li.
This has caused the Divine
Land to be desolate,
turned into dense weeds,
and within the four seas,
human traces do not intersect.
The hegemon is troubled by late meals,
and the common people suffer the bitterness of oppression.
The barbarian chiefs pay
homage in the Central Plains.
How can we hastily attend to matters of ritual vessels?
However, if rites are not practiced for three years,
rites will certainly decay;
if music is not performed for three years,
music will certainly collapse.
How much more so when it has been neglected for such a long period,
spanning many generations!
Today, the newly advanced young people do not witness the ceremonies of bowing and ascending/descending,
nor do their ears hear the sounds of bells, drums, pipes, and strings.
Literary works are scattered and lost,
and portents are completely gone.
This is deeply lamented by the sages and those of understanding,
and sighed over by the discerning.
Indeed, in times of peace, culture is valued;
in times of chaos, military might is valued.
Culture and military might are used alternately;
this is the path to long-term stability,
like the alternation of darkness and light in Heaven and Earth.
Since ancient times, there has been no one who did not follow this.
Now some argue that since the world is not yet unified,
it is not the time to promote rites and learning.
This statement seems plausible but is not truly so.
The Way of the Confucians is profound and abstruse,
and cannot be accomplished
in a hurry.
An outstanding talent in ancient times took three years to master one classic.
If we wait until the world is peaceful and stable before cultivating it,
then when the work is done and the task is complete,
who will be there to establish rites and create music
then?
Moreover, the sons of noble families may not possess the talent to capture generals and seize banners,
nor may they have the duty of joining the army for expeditions or garrisons.
If they do not, in their prime, study and practice the Way and righteousness,
allowing
a bright pearl to undergo polishing,
and a raw jade to emit the splendor of carving,
would that not be a great pity?
Your servant, in his ignorance and shallowness, believes that the world has lost the Way for a long time,
and people's nature has become accustomed to what they practice;
pure customs are daily fading,
and ostentatious competition is daily increasing,
like fire consuming oil without one's awareness.
Now Heaven and Earth proclaim a new beginning,
and all things are commencing.
The sacred dynasty, with its divine martial virtue,
encounters the destiny of revolution,
sweeping away the corrupt practices of recent times,
and continuing the interrupted path of a thousand years.
It profoundly follows the Way and esteems Confucianism,
establishing a great undertaking.
The enlightened ruler initiates it from above,
and the prime ministers oversee it from below.
What is liked by those above,
those below will certainly exceed in.
Therefore, when the custom of twin swords was esteemed,
the custom of 'flying white' script became common;
when the posture of holding a qín was adorned,
the harmony of accompanying music was created;
the virtue of a noble man is like the wind,
and the virtue of a common
person is like grass,
it is truly a matter of influence.
Your servant, being dim and shallow,
cannot foresee profound principles;
but upon reciting the enlightened decree,
I am filled with emotion and humbly concur,
suggesting that during the leisure of the three seasons,
construction should be gradually undertaken."
The memorial was submitted,
and accepted.
Thus, rites and learning began to be cultivated.
He replaced Liú Wèi as Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
When Wáng Dūn rebelled,
he was given the additional title of General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
When Wáng Dūn achieved his ambitions,
and Dài Ruòsī was killed,
Miáo was dismissed from office.
After Wáng Dūn was executed,
he was appointed Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè).
He died in office
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Guard (Wèi Jiāngjūn),
with the posthumous name Mù.
His son Mì inherited his title and successively served as Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu) and Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
Zhōu Yǐ (Zǐmǐn)
Zhōu Yǐ, courtesy name Bórén,
was the son of General of Andōng, Jùn.
From a young age, he had a great reputation,
with a brilliant and penetrating spirit.
Although his contemporaries were close and familiar with him,
none could slight him.
Bēn Sōng from the same prefecture, a clerk for the Sītú, had a reputation for integrity.
Upon seeing Yǐ,
he sighed,
"Rǔyǐng indeed has many extraordinary gentlemen!
Recently, the refined way has declined,
but now I see Zhōu Bórén again,
who will surely revive the old customs
and purify our people."
Dài Ruòsī of Guǎnglíng, renowned as the beauty of the Southeast,
was nominated as Xiùcái.
Upon entering Luò[yáng],
having heard of Yǐ's fame,
he went to visit him.
He sat through the visit and left
without daring to display his talent for eloquence.
Yǐ's cousin, Mù, also had a good reputation,
and wished to outshine Yǐ.
Yǐ remained placid and did not contend with him,
whereupon scholars increasingly revered and attached themselves to him.
He did not accept any appointments from the prefectures or commanderies.
At the age of twenty,
he inherited his father's title, Marquis of Wǔchéng,
and was appointed Mìshūláng.
He was successively promoted to Shàngshū Lìbùláng.
Pí, son of the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, was General of the Garrison Army,
and appointed Yǐ as his Chángshǐ.
When Emperor Yuán first took up his post south of the Jiāng [River],
he invited Yǐ to be Jūnzhī Jìjiǔ.
He was then dispatched as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, concurrently Protector of the Southern Barbarians, and acting Jié.
Soon after arriving in the province,
rebels from Jiànpíng, such as Fù Mì, defected and welcomed the Shuǐ bandits Dù Tāo.
Yǐ was caught off guard and lost his position.
Táo Kǎn sent his general Wú Jì with troops to rescue him,
thus Yǐ escaped.
He then fled to Wáng Dūn in Yùzhāng.
Dūn kept him there.
Jūnsī Dài Miǎo said,
"Although Yǐ has been defeated,
he has not committed any fault in leading the populace.
His virtue and reputation are highly regarded,
so he should be reinstated."
Dūn did not agree.
The Emperor summoned him to be Yángwēi Jiāngjūn, Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yǐ returned to Jiànkāng,
where the Emperor detained Yǐ and did not send him away.
He was again made Jūnzhī Jìjiǔ,
and soon after transferred to Yòu Chángshǐ.
When Zhōngxīng was established,
he was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Soon after,
he was impeached by the appropriate authorities for being drunk,
and served in his post while wearing plain clothes.
He was again implicated when his disciples injured someone with a club,
and was dismissed from office.
At the beginning of Tàixīng,
he was reappointed Tàizǐ Shǎofù,
while retaining his position as Shàngshū.
Yǐ submitted a memorial declining, saying,
"As your minister reflects upon himself,
my learning does not encompass a single classic,
my wisdom is insufficient for a single office.
Knowing when to stop is truly difficult,
and I have been unable to keep to my station,
thus I have been entrusted with prominent responsibilities,
and my rank exceeds my capacity.
I do not understand why Heaven's discerning gaze overlooked my incompetence and weakness,
intending to make me internally manage appointments
and externally receive the post of Grand Tutor.
My substance is lighter than a cicada's wing,
but the matter is heavier than a thousand jūn.
That this is impossible
is clear without needing further explanation.
If your minister were to bear the responsibility of 'riding a tiger without reins,'
I would certainly bring shame upon this sagely dynasty,
and I am overwhelmed with shame and fear,
knowing not what to do."
An imperial edict stated,
"Although the Crown Prince is young, he holds the noble position of Heir Apparent.
He must rely on skilled instructors to dispel his immaturity.
To be looked upon with solemnity—this is a silent benefit.
How is learning acquired?
It is like the saying, 'associating with Tián Sū makes one forget one's vulgar heart.'
You should therefore fulfill the original intention;
it is not appropriate to decline."
He was transferred to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
concurrently retaining the office of Lìbù as before.
Yú Liàng once said to Yǐ,
"Everyone compares you to Yuè Guǎng."
Yǐ replied,
"How can you carve and paint Wúyán,

An imperial edict stated,

Initially,

When Yǐ was in the central court,

Soon after, the imperial army was defeated.

Dūn was daunted by his righteous words

Hùjūn Chángshǐ Hǎo Gǔ and others advised Yǐ to avoid Dūn.

Before he finished speaking,

Dūn had always been wary of Yǐ;

Dūn sent Miáo Tǎn to confiscate Yǐ's household.

Dàlián (Dàlián) presided over legal matters,

Ruòsī (Ruòsī) and Xiánshuǎng (Xiánshuǎng)

Yǐ (Yǐ) attracted criticism from his contemporaries,
