I, in my inadequacy, was fortunate to be appointed
to this province.
I intended to advance with Your Excellency, together exerting our utmost loyalty to the imperial court,
repaying the young lord's kindness,
and in retirement, to expand upon our lifelong
and enduring old friendship.
How could I have known that time would not wait for me,
and I would soon enter the netherworld?
To forever speak of things I cannot follow through on,
how can I not feel sorrow and regret!
Now, the Divine Land is not yet pacified,
and the four directions face many difficulties.
Your Excellency's age and virtue are both exalted,
your achievements and fame both flourishing.
It is fitting that you strive to establish grand norms;
though you may rest, do not rest,
be utterly impartial and just,
utterly humble and compliant.
Then Heaven itself will bless you,
and all will be auspicious and beneficial.
When a person is about to die,
their words are good.
May Your Excellency discern the sincerity of these words."
He died in the sixth year of Xiánhé (331 CE),
aged fifty-three.
He was posthumously granted the title of Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn (鎮南大將軍) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
given the posthumous name Liè (烈),
and worshipped with a Grand Sacrifice.
His son Xuán (玄) succeeded him,
reaching the position of Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎).
Xuán's younger brother Dàn (誕)
had great talent and ability,
serving successively as Tàishǒu (太守) of six commanderies and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍),
and was posthumously granted the title of Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (冀州刺史).
Initially,
during the chaos of war, Wéi Hóng (韋泓) of Jīngzhào (京兆)
lost all his relatives to famine and plague.
He wandered as a guest to Luòyáng (洛陽),
having long heard of Zhān's reputation,
and thus sought refuge with him.
Zhān shared sweetness and bitterness with him,
their affection like that of brothers.
Wéi Hóng followed him for many years.
Zhān arranged a marriage for him,
provided him with a residence,
and also recommended him to Yuán Dì (元帝), saying:
"Since encountering the chaos,
scholars' principles have easily changed;
few indeed are those who resign themselves to fate and steadfastly endure hardship,
remaining upright and upholding their integrity.
I humbly observe Yìláng (議郎) Wéi Hóng,
aged thirty-eight,
courtesy name Yuánliàng (元量),
whose mind is clear and pure,
whose talent and insight are complete.
He personally tills the fields,
not troubling others for labor.
He lives in quiet solitude,
not participating in government affairs.
In previous years, he migrated
and came to Zhān's territory.
Having lost his assets to bandits,
he stands alone.
His short jacket does not cover his body,
and vegetables do not fill his morning meal,
yet his resolve is even stronger,
and he does not associate with improper types.
Yán Huí (顏回) was praised for not changing his joy,
and Hóng has a share of that quality.
Your sagacious Highness assists and illuminates the imperial house,
restoring and sustaining the universe.
The four gates are opened,
and heroes gather like ducks and water plants,
collecting spring blossoms in the capital,
and gathering autumn fruits from cliffs and wilds.
Yet Hóng holds the unpolished gem of Jīngshān (荊山),
the Hébì (和璧) not yet cut.
If he receives a selection and summons,
and is assigned to one of the various bureaus,
he will surely be able to help enhance the imperial government
and brightly achieve various merits."
The Emperor immediately appointed him.
Thereafter, he reached the position of Shàofǔ Qīng (少府卿).
Having received Zhān's kindness of nurturing and establishing him,
when Zhān died,
Wéi Hóng wore the mourning clothes of a friend,
weeping until the grass grew on the grave.
Following the example of the Zhào (趙) family's worship of Chéng Yīng (程嬰) and Chǔ Jiù (杵臼),
he sacrificed to Zhān for the rest of his life.
Gān Zhuó (Gān Zhuó (鄧騫))
Gān Zhuó, courtesy name Jìsī (季思),
was a native of Dānyáng (丹楊),
a descendant of Qín (秦) Prime Minister Mào (茂).
His great-grandfather Níng (寧)
was a general of Wú (吳).
His grandfather Shù (述) served as Shàngshū (尚書) in Wú.
His father Chāng (昌) was Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅).
When Wú was pacified,
Zhuó retired and lived in self-seclusion.
The commandery appointed him Zhǔbù (主簿) and Gōngcáo (功曹),
and recommended him as Xiàolián (孝廉).
The province nominated him as Xiùcái (秀才),
and he became Chángshì (常侍) to the King of Wú.
He participated in the campaign against Shí Bīng (石冰),
and for his merits, was granted the noble title Dūtíng Hóu (都亭侯).
The King of Dōnghǎi (東海), Yuè (越), invited him to be a Cānjūn (參軍),
and he was sent out to serve as Lìng (令) of Líhú (離狐).
Seeing the great chaos in the world,
Zhuó abandoned his office and returned east.
He arrived at Lìyáng (歷陽),
where he met Chén Mǐn (陳敏).
Mǐn was very pleased,
and they conspired together for ambitious schemes.
Subsequently, Mǐn's son Jǐng (景) married Zhuó's daughter,
and they formed an alliance.
At that time, Zhōu Qǐ (周玘) raised a righteous army,
secretly sending Qián Guǎng (錢廣) to attack Mǐn's younger brother Chǎng (昶).
Mǐn dispatched Zhuó to suppress Guǎng,
and he encamped south of Zhūquè (朱雀) Bridge.
Coincidentally, Guǎng killed Chǎng.
Qǐ informed Gù Róng (顧榮), the Tàishǒu (太守) of Dānyáng, and together they persuaded Zhuó.
Zhuó had always respected and admired Róng,
and also felt fear because of Chǎng's death.
After a long deliberation, he agreed to join them.
He then feigned illness to welcome his daughter,
cut the bridge,
gathered the boats on the south bank,
and together they destroyed Mǐn,
sending his head to the capital.
When Yuán Dì first crossed the Yangtze River,
Zhuó was appointed Qiánfēng Dūdū (前鋒都督), Yángwēi Jiāngjūn (揚威將軍), and Lìyáng Nèishǐ (歷陽內史).
Thereafter, he campaigned against Zhōu Fù (周馥)
and marched against Dù Tāo (杜弢).
He repeatedly engaged in fierce battles
and captured many.
For his successive merits,
he was advanced to the noble title Nánxiāng Hóu (南鄉侯)
and appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守).
Soon after, he was transferred to Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (湘州刺史),
his general title remaining as before.
He was further advanced to the noble title Yúhú Hóu (于湖侯).
In the early period of Zhōngxīng,
because the border incursions were not yet settled
and the schools were in decline,
special permission was granted for Xiàolián not to be tested.
However, Xiùcái still had to undergo the traditional policy examinations.
Zhuó submitted a memorial, arguing:
“To answer questions on gain and loss [in governance]
requires extensive knowledge of ancient and modern times
and a clear understanding of the governmental structure.
One must seek this knowledge from the Fén and Suǒ [books],
only then can one be fit for such an appointment.
The province I, your servant, am associated with has recently suffered from banditry and unrest;
schools have long been neglected,
and scholars have scattered.
It cannot be compared to other provinces.
The reason for policy examinations
is based on academic achievement,
so it would be appropriate to treat them like the Xiàolián [case],
and grant them an extension.”
The memorial was submitted,
but the court council did not approve it.
Zhuó then meticulously prepared and concealed [his plan],
formally nominating Gǔ Jiǎn of Guìyáng as Xiùcái.
Jiǎn declined but was not allowed to refuse,
so the province sent him off with generous gifts.
When Xiùcái from other provinces heard that they would be examined,
they all feared it and did not go.
Only Jiǎn alone arrived at the capital,
and consequently, the policy examination was not conducted again.
Jiǎn was ashamed that his province had few scholars,
so he petitioned to be tested,
and was appointed Zhōngláng with high distinction.
Jiǎn had noble aspirations and conduct from a young age,
establishing himself through hardship and poverty.
He was widely read in the classics and histories.
At that time, the southern lands were desolate and wild,
and the tradition of classical studies had ceased.
Jiǎn could not travel far to seek teachers and friends,
but instead diligently studied at home.
Although his achievements were truly profound,
he had no widespread reputation.
Moreover, he was ashamed to flaunt himself to achieve advancement.
So he returned home
and remained out of office his entire life,
dying at home.
Zhuó was soon promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, granted the Jiǎjié, and overseen all armies north of the Miǎn River,
garrisoned at Xiāngyáng.
Zhuó was outwardly gentle but inwardly firm.
His governance was simple and benevolent,
and he excelled at pacifying and comforting the people.
All tariffs and taxes were abolished,
and there were no two prices in the market.
Regarding all the fishponds in the provincial territory,
which previously had taxes levied,
Zhuó did not collect their profits,
but gave them all to the poor.
The people of the western lands called this benevolent governance.
Wáng Dūn raised an army
and sent an envoy to inform Zhuó.
Zhuó feigned agreement,
but his heart was not with him.
When Dūn embarked,
Zhuó did not go.
He sent his Cānjūn Sūn Shuāng to Wǔchāng to admonish Dūn to stop.
When Dūn heard Shuāng’s words,
he was greatly surprised and said:
“What did Gān Hóu tell me before,
and now he has a different opinion!
Is he perhaps worried that I will endanger the imperial court?
I am now going down [to the capital] only to eliminate corrupt villains.
You return and tell him,
when the matter is settled, I will make Gān Hóu a Gōng.”
Shuāng returned and reported to Zhuó,
who could not make a decision.
Someone advised Zhuó to temporarily pretend to agree with Dūn,
and then attack him when Dūn reached the capital.
Zhuó said:
“During Chén Mǐn’s rebellion,
I also initially complied and later plotted,
but critics said I did it out of fear of coercion.
Although my original intention was not such,
the facts had a semblance of it,
and I felt ashamed.
If I do it again now,
who will be able to understand me!”
At that time, Qiáo Wáng Chéng, the Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu, sent his Zhǔbù Dèng Qiān to persuade Zhuó, saying:
“Liú Dàlián, though holding power and favor,
is not harmful to the empire.
The Grand General [Wáng Dūn], out of personal resentment, raised an army against the imperial palace.
Though he claims to be suppressing rebellion,
he has actually lost the hope of the empire.
This is the time for loyal officials and righteous gentlemen to rescue the situation.
In ancient times, Lǔ Lián, a mere commoner,
still harbored the ambition to leap into the sea [for righteousness],
how much more so one who is appointed a regional governor [fāngbó],
whose position is commensurate with serving the state!
If you now follow the will of heaven and men,
initiate an undertaking like Huán and Wén,
wield great righteousness to sweep away rebellious elements,
and lead a righteous army to serve the imperial house,
this is an opportunity of a thousand years
that must not be missed.”
Zhuó smiled and said:
“The deeds of Huán and Wén
are not something I can achieve.
As for exerting all my strength in national difficulties,
that is indeed my intention.
We should deliberate this together carefully.”
Cānjūn Lǐ Liáng said to Zhuó:
“In the past, when Kuí [Yáo] threw Lǒngyòu into chaos,
Dòu Róng secured Héxī and returned to Guāngwǔ.
Today’s situation
is similar to that.
General, you have a great reputation throughout the empire;
you should merely promote the perishing and consolidate the existing,
and wait passively.
If the Grand General wins,
he will surely elevate you, General, to a position of regional importance;
if he does not win,
the imperial court will certainly replace him with you, General.
Why worry about not being wealthy and noble,
and abandon this assured victory [miàoshèng],
to decide life and death in a single battle!”
Qiān said to Liáng:
“When Guāngwǔ established his enterprise,
China was not yet pacified.
Therefore, Kuí [Yáo] held Lǒngyòu,
and Dòu Róng controlled Héxī.
Each occupied a region,
forming a tripartite power.
Thus, they could outwardly submit to the emperor
and calmly wait and see.
However, once the empire was settled
and the ruler and ministers were in their proper positions,
eventually Lǒngyòu collapsed,
and Héxī submitted to the court.
Why?
Because the outward submission they practiced before
was not tolerated by righteousness.
Now, your position, General, in relation to the imperial court
is not comparable to Dòu Róng’s.
Xiāngyáng’s position in relation to the Grand General’s headquarters
is not as secure as Héxī.
Moreover, it is the duty of a subject
how can one bear to not exert effort in national difficulties,
and then face the Son of Heaven [in court]!
If the Grand General pacifies Liú Kuí,
returns to Wǔchāng,
strengthens the defenses of Shíchéng,
and cuts off grain supplies from Jīng and Xiāng,
where will you, General, go?
The situation will be in his hands,
yet you speak of holding an assured victory;
I have not heard of such a thing.”
Zhuó still hesitated and was undecided.
Qiān further said to Zhuó:
“Now, you have neither made an unrighteous move
nor acknowledged the Grand General’s summons.
This will certainly lead to disaster,
which both the foolish and the wise can see.
Moreover, what critics find difficult
is that they consider him strong and us weak,
which is to not measure the reality.
Now, the Grand General’s army does not exceed ten thousand,
and those he leaves behind cannot be more than five thousand.
Yet, the troops you, General, command are already double that.
Your, General’s, prestigious name is known throughout the empire.
The elite forces of this commandery
are victorious warriors.
Holding strong forces,
relying on your prestigious name,
and advancing with your imperial staff,
how can Wáng Hán be able to resist you!
An army moving against the current [upriver]
cannot save itself.
Your, General’s, advance on Wǔchāng
will be like destroying withered wood and pulling up rotten [material].
What is there to worry about!
Once Wǔchāng is secured,
seizing its military resources,
pacifying and comforting the two provinces,
and bestowing favors upon the soldiers,
making those who return feel as if they are coming home;
this is how Lǚ Méng conquered his enemies.
If this is done,
the Grand General can be defeated without battle.
Now, to abandon a strategy of certain victory,
and sit idly waiting for peril and ruin,
cannot be called wisdom.
I wish you, General, would consider this carefully.”
At that time, Dūn, fearing that Zhuó’s failure to arrive
might lead to trouble later,
sent his Staff Officer, Yuè Dàoróng, to urgently persuade Zhuó to come down with him.
Dàoróng originally intended to betray Dūn,
and so he convinced Zhuó to attack Dūn.
The details are in Róng’s biography.
Since Zhuó had always been unwilling to follow Dūn,
upon hearing Dàoróng’s persuasion,
he firmly declared:
“This was my original intention!”
So he, along with Liǔ Chún, the Administrator of Bādōng, Xiàhóu Chéng, the Grand Administrator of Nánpíng, Tán Gāi, the Grand Administrator of Yídū, and more than ten others,
openly issued a proclamation to all far and near,
enumerating Dūn’s outrageous rebellion,
and led their forces to suppress him.
He dispatched Staff Officers Sīmǎ Zàn and Sūn Shuāng to present a memorial to the court.
Staff Officer Luó Yīng went to Guǎngzhōu
to arrange a date with Táo Kǎn.
Staff Officers Dèng Qiān and Yú Chōng went to Chángshā
to instruct King Qiáo Chéng to hold firm.
General of the Expedition to the West, Dài Ruòsī, who was in Jiāngxī,
had already received Zhuó’s letter,
and memorialized it to the throne.
Everyone in the court cheered, “Long live!”
Wǔchāng was greatly alarmed,
and when news spread that Zhuó’s army was approaching,
people fled in disarray.
An imperial edict promoted Zhuó to Grand General of the Pacified South, Imperial Household Grandee, Area Commander-in-Chief of the armies of Jīng and Liáng provinces, and Governor of Jīng Province.
His position as Inspector of Liáng Province remained unchanged.
Táo Kǎn, upon receiving Zhuó’s letter,
immediately dispatched Staff Officer Gāo Bǎo to lead troops downstream.
Although Zhuó harbored righteous intentions,
his nature was not resolute and decisive.
Moreover, he was old and prone to suspicion,
and his plans were hesitant.
His army encamped at Zhūkǒu
and did not advance for several weeks.
Dūn was greatly frightened.
He sent Zhuó’s nephew and acting Staff Officer, Āng, to sue for peace,
and he apologized to Zhuó, saying:
“Your action truly reflects the duty of a minister,
and I do not blame you for it.
My family’s situation is urgent,
and I could not but act as I did.
I hope you will return your army to Xiāngyáng,
and we can then rebuild our good relations.”
At this time, the imperial army had suffered a defeat,
and Dūn requested a imperial standard with a Zōuyú banner from the court to halt Zhuó.
When Zhuó heard that Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Ruòsī had been killed,
he shed tears and said to Āng:
“My worries
were precisely about a day like this.
Whenever I received letters from people at court,
I always put the Hú bandits first,
and did not realize there would suddenly be internal strife.
Moreover, if His Majesty were in good health,
and the Crown Prince unharmed,
and I were upstream from Dūn,
I would not dare to immediately endanger the state.
If I were to directly occupy Wǔchāng,
Dūn, under duress,
would surely coerce the emperor to extinguish the hopes of all under heaven.
It is better to return to Xiāngyáng
and reconsider our next move.”
He immediately ordered the army to turn back.
Commander Qín Kāng advised Zhuó, saying:
“It is not difficult to divide our troops and seize Dūn now.
If we just cut off Péngzé,
then those above and below cannot support each other,
and they will naturally disperse.
We can capture him in one battle.
Since the General possesses loyalty and integrity,
abandoning the endeavor midway
will only make him a general of a defeated army.
I fear that even your subordinates will then seek to return west,
and you will not be able to hold them.”
Zhuó could not follow this advice.
Yuè Dàoróng also urged Zhuó day and night to advance quickly.
Zhuó’s nature had previously been tolerant and gentle,
but he suddenly became stubborn and obstinate,
and went straight back to Xiāngyáng.
His spirit was disturbed,
and his actions were abnormal.
He looked in a mirror but could not see his head;
he looked at the trees in the courtyard and his head appeared on a tree,
which greatly troubled him.
A golden cabinet in his house began to ring,
sounding like a hammer hitting a mirror,
clear and sorrowful.
A shaman said:
“The golden cabinet is about to be separated,
hence its sorrowful ringing.”
His Chief Clerk, Hé Wújì, and his family all advised him to be vigilant.
Zhuó, however, grew even more stubborn and perverse,
and would get angry whenever he heard advice.
He was scattering his soldiers to cultivate large tracts of land,
and made no preparations for defense.
Róng Jiàn, his Chief of Merit, firmly remonstrated,
but his advice was not accepted.
Zhōu Lǜ, the Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng, and others secretly acting on Dūn’s instructions,
knowing Zhuó was unprepared,
falsely claimed there were many fish in the lake
and urged Zhuó to send all his attendants to catch fish.
They then ambushed and killed Zhuó in his bed,
and sent his head to Dūn.
His four sons, including Sànqíláng Fān, were all killed.
During the Tàiníng era,
he was posthumously granted the title of General of Agile Cavalry,
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
Dèng Qiān, courtesy name Chángzhēn,
was a native of Chángshā.
From a young age, he possessed ambition and spirit,
and was highly regarded by his fellow villagers.
He always acted with sincerity and integrity,
and was able to preserve himself with righteousness during times of great difficulty.
Inspector King Qiáo Chéng appointed him as Chief Clerk,
and he then advised Gān Zhuó.
Zhuó kept him as a Staff Officer and wanted him to accompany him,
but Qiān declined, citing his aged mother, and returned.
Chéng was defeated by Wèi.
As Yú Kuī and his brothers were considered Chéng’s partisans,
they were all executed.
And the search for Qiān was very urgent.
His fellow villagers were all afraid for him,
but Qiān smiled and said:
“They merely want to employ me.
He has just gained control of the province,
and has killed many loyal and good men.
This is the time for him to seek out worthy people;
how could he treat a traveler as a criminal!”
So he went to see him.
The King was delighted and said:
“You are truly an Xiè Yáng of antiquity!”
He made him Assistant Governor.
Qiān possessed integrity, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
combined with broad knowledge and far-reaching discernment.
He was good at interacting with people,
and grew more respected with time.
Grand Commandant Yǔ Liàng praised him
and regarded him as a man of virtue.
He successively served as Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng and Shǐxīng,
was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and died in office.
Biàn Kǔn (cousin of Dūn).
Biàn Kǔn, courtesy name Wàngzhī,
was a native of Yuānqú, Jìyīn.
His grandfather, Tǒng,
was the Internal Scribe of Lángyá.
His father, Cuì,
was known for his clarity of argument and discernment.
His six brothers all rose to high government positions,
and the world called them
“the Six Dragons of the Biàn family,
Xuánrén without peer.”
Xuánrén
was Cuì’s courtesy name.
His younger brother, Póu,
once offended his provincial commander.
The commander, angered, exposed private matters within the Biàn family,
and Cuì was consequently criticized for indiscipline,
declining for many years.
At the beginning of Emperor Huì’s reign,
he became a Department Director of the Secretariat.
When Yáng Jùn held power,
many people attached themselves to him,
but Cuì remained upright and unyielding.
When Jùn was executed,
Cuì was exceptionally appointed Right Assistant,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chéngyáng,
and gradually promoted to General of the Right Army.
When Zhāng Huá was executed,
Cuì was dismissed from office because he was Huá’s son-in-law.
When King Qí Jǐong assisted in governance,
Cuì served as Imperial Household Grandee and Director of the Central Secretariat,
and his noble title was advanced to Duke.
When King Chángshā held exclusive power,
Cuì stood in court with an upright demeanor,
which the King resented and led to Cuì’s harm.
Originally,
when Cuì went to the latrine,
he saw something like two eyes, and soon after, he suffered difficulties.
Kǔn was famous in Sī and Yǎn provinces in his youth.
He declined all invitations from King Qí Jǐong.
Encountering family misfortune,
he returned to his hometown.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he was appointed Writer of the Imperial Secretariat
and inherited his father’s noble title.
General of the Expedition to the East, Zhōu Fù, invited him to be his Assistant Commander,
but he declined.
After his home province was overthrown,
he sought refuge eastward with his wife’s brother, Péi Dùn, the Inspector of Xú Province.
Dùn appointed Kǔn to govern Guǎnglíng.
Hú Gàn (壺榦) genuinely held office,
taking praise and censure as his duty.
He was diligent in official matters,
desiring to rectify and guide the world,
and unwilling to blindly follow popular trends.
However, his nature was not broad and generous,
and his talent did not match his ambitions,
so he was held in low esteem by the various famous scholars,
and lacked outstanding reputation.
Emperor Míng (明帝) deeply valued him,
and among all the great ministers, entrusted him with the most important positions.
Ruǎn Fú (阮孚) often said to him:
"You have no moments of leisure or ease,
always as if you are holding tiles and stones in your mouth;
is it not exhausting?"
Hú Gàn (壺) replied:
"While gentlemen expand their moral virtue
and vie for elegance,
who but I
would hold onto frugality and meanness!"
At that time, many noble young men admired Wáng Chéng (王澄) and Xiè Kūn (謝鯤) for their "enlightened" conduct.
Hú Gàn (壺) sternly declared at court:
"Transgressing propriety and harming teachings—
no crime is worse than this!
The downfall of the central court
was truly due to this."
He wanted to impeach them.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) did not agree,
so he stopped.
However, all who heard him were humbled.
At that time, Wáng Dǎo (王導) assisted in government with his meritorious service and virtue.
Emperor Chéng (成帝) often visited his residence,
and once bowed to Dǎo's (導) wife, Lady Cáo (曹氏).
Shìzhōng (侍中) Kǒng Tǎn (孔坦) secretly memorialized that it was inappropriate to bow.
When Dǎo (導) heard this, he said:
"Wáng Màohóng (王茂弘) is but a worn-out nag.
If it were someone as upright as Biàn Wàngzhī (卞望之),
as discerning as Diāo Xuànliàng (刁玄亮),
or as towering as Dài Ruòsī (戴若思),
would they dare to do such a thing?"
Hú Gàn (壺) was incorruptible, honest, and frugal,
living in great poverty.
When his son was about to marry,
an imperial edict specially bestowed 500,000 cash,
but he firmly declined it.
Later, he suffered from a facial ulcer
and repeatedly requested to resign from his post.
He was appointed Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
At that time, Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) was about to launch an expedition against Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
and he said at court:
"Jùn (峻) has the heart of a wolf cub and is wild;
he will eventually cause rebellion.
If we levy him today,
even if he does not obey orders,
the disaster will still be minor.
If we wait another year,
his wickedness will spread and grow,
and he will be impossible to control.
This is like Cháo Cuò (朝錯) advising Emperor Jǐng (景帝) of Hàn (漢) to promptly reduce the Seven States."
At the time, none of the deliberators could offer a better alternative.
Hú Gàn (壺) vehemently argued,
saying to Liàng (亮):
"Jùn (峻) commands strong troops,
and harbors many scoundrels.
Moreover, he is close to the capital city,
a journey of less than a morning.
Should a sudden change occur,
it would be easy to stumble.
We should consider deeply and far-sightedly;
I fear it is not wise to act rashly."
Liàng (亮) did not accept his advice.
Hú Gàn (壺), knowing it would surely fail,
wrote to General of the Pacified South, Wēn Jiào (溫嶠), saying:
"Yuán Guī's (元規) intention to summon Jùn (峻) is fixed,
and I am filled with anxiety over this.
Wēn Shēng (溫生), my dear friend,
what can be done about this matter!
What I am concerned about now
is a great matter of the state.
Moreover, Jùn (峻) has already conceived mad ideas,
and summoning him will only hasten his advance.
He will surely unleash his host of evildoers against the imperial court.
Although the court's might and power are truly formidable,
it will require clashing swords and treading blades,
and we still don't know if he can be immediately captured.
Wáng Gōng (王公) also shares this sentiment.
I argued with him very earnestly,
but could not prevail.
Originally, you were sent out to be a藩外任 (wài fān rèn, regional governor),
but now I regret that you are outside.
If you were inside and we both remonstrated,
he would surely have followed our advice.
Now that strict precautions are taken both inside and outside the capital,
and the four directions are prepared,
Jùn's (峻) ferocious madness will surely lead him nowhere,
but I fear it will not be without injury.
What can be done?"
Hú Gàn's (壺) Sīmǎ (司馬), Rèn Tái (任台), advised Hú Gàn (壺) to acquire good horses
in preparation for unforeseen events.
Hú Gàn (壺) laughed and said:
"Judging by the principles of顺 (shùn, compliance) and逆 (nì, rebellion),
there is no reason not to succeed.
If, by some remote chance, it does not happen,
why would I need horses!"
Jùn (峻) indeed raised an army.
Hú Gàn (壺) was again appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍), and concurrently Lǐng Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn (領右衞將軍),
with his other offices remaining as before.
When Jùn (峻) reached Dōnglíngkǒu (東陵口),
an imperial edict appointed Hú Gàn (壺) Dūdū Dàhéng Dōng Zhū Jūnjì (都督大桁東諸軍事), granted him Jiǎjié (假節),
and further added the titles of Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍) and Jǐshìzhōng (給事中).
Hú Gàn (壺) led Guō Mò (郭默), Zhào Yǐn (趙胤) and others in a great battle against Jùn (峻) at Xīlíng (西陵),
but was defeated by Jùn (峻).
Hú Gàn (壺) and Zhōng Yǎ (鍾雅) both retreated,
with thousands killed or wounded.
Hú Gàn (壺) and Yǎ (雅) both returned their credentials
and went to the imperial court to apologize for their offense.
Jùn (峻) advanced to attack Qīngxī (青溪).
Hú Gàn (壺) and the various armies resisted,
but could not stop him.
The rebels set fire to the palace temples,
and the imperial armies suffered a crushing defeat.
Hú Gàn (壺) had a back ulcer at the time,
which had not yet healed,
but he fought despite his illness.
He rallied the scattered troops and several hundred personal attendants,
attacked the enemy's banner,
fought bitterly,
and subsequently died,
at the age of forty-eight.
His two sons, Zhěn (眕) and Xū (盱), seeing their father fall,
followed him into battle against the rebels,
and were killed at the same time.
After Sū Jùn (峻) was pacified,
the court deliberated on posthumously bestowing upon Hú Gàn (壺) the title of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫),
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Hóng Nè (弘訥) argued, believing
that "ministers who die for the state are valued by all, ancient and modern.
The loyalty and integrity of Biàn Lìng (卞令) [referring to Hú Gàn (壺)]
should be recorded on bamboo and silk.
The current posthumous bestowal
does not truly meet public expectations.
It is appropriate to add the title of Dǐng Sī (鼎司) [one of the highest ministerial ranks],
to commemorate his loyal and valiant achievements."
Sītú (司徒) Wáng Dǎo (王導) saw the proposal
and advanced the posthumous bestowal to Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍),
with the additional title of Shìzhōng (侍中).
Nè (訥) further argued, saying:
"There is no greater act than filial piety in serving one's parents,
and nothing higher than loyalty in serving one's ruler.
It is only through filial piety
that one can exhaust one's respect and sincerity;
it is only through loyalty
that one can sacrifice one's life when faced with danger.
These are the great virtues of the Three Bonds,
the ultimate conduct of ministers and sons.
Consider Hú Gàn (壺): he dedicated himself to three reigns,
exhausting his counsel and assistance.
When the world faced peril and difficulty,
he stood by it in life and death.
He received the weighty trust of a dying emperor,
held a prime ministerial position,
and protected the supreme ruler,
thus having the grace of a grand tutor.
He maintained a stern demeanor at court,
thus possessing the integrity of self-sacrifice.
When rebel Sū Jùn (峻) instigated rebellion,
he exerted his full strength to suppress him,
personally facing arrows and spears,
clashing with the rebel front twice.
Father and sons perished together,
which can be described as breaking up his family for the state,
and serving diligently unto death.
In ancient times, when Xǔ Nán (許男) died of illness,
he still received a second-grade posthumous honor.
How much more so Hú Gàn (壺), who sacrificed himself in a national crisis!
When there is doubt in rewards, one should err on the side of generosity;
how much more so when there is no doubt!
I believe it is appropriate to set the standard as high as Xǔ Mù (許穆) [Duke Mù of Xu],
and at least equal to Jī Shào (嵇紹),
which would truly conform to the canons and models,
and satisfy the expectations of the multitude."
Thereupon, the posthumous bestowal was changed to Hú Gàn (壺) as Shìzhōng (侍中), Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
with the posthumous name Zhōngzhēn (忠貞),
and he was sacrificed with a grand offering (太牢).
His heir apparent, Zhěn (眕), was posthumously granted Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎),
and Zhěn's (眕) younger brother Xū (盱) as Fèngchē Dūwèi (奉車都尉).
Zhěn's (眕) mother, Lady Péi (裴氏), embracing the bodies of her two sons, cried:
"The father was a loyal minister,
and you were filial sons.
What is there to regret!"
The recluse Zhái Tāng (翟湯) heard of this and sighed:
"The father died for his ruler,
the sons died for their father.
The way of loyalty and filial piety
converged in one family."
Zhěn's (眕) son, Dàn (誕), succeeded.
In the sixth year of Xiánkāng,
Emperor Chéng posthumously recalled Hú [Jù],
and issued an edict saying:
“Hú [Jù] stood in court loyal and diligent,
and died at the hands of fierce bandits.
His enfeoffment was distant and remote,
and his income from taxes and salary was meager,
leaving his wife and children without sufficient support.
This fills me with regret!
He should be given a stipend for the actual number of mouths to feed.”
Later, bandits plundered Hú [Jù]’s tomb.
His corpse was stiff,
his temples and hair were white,
and his face was as if alive.
Both hands were completely clenched,
with fingernails piercing through to the backs of his hands.
Emperor Ān decreed a grant of one hundred thousand coins
to repair the burial site.
Hú [Jù]’s third son, Zhān,
rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Guǎngzhōu.
Zhān’s younger brother, Dān,
was a Shàngshū Láng.
Dùn’s courtesy name was Zhòngrén.
His father, Jùn,
was pure, upright, and discerning,
renowned for his mastery of principles.
His fellow townsman, Xì Shēn, relying on his talent, looked down upon Jùn and his brothers.
Jùn and others, due to their family’s prominence, also disdained Xì Shēn,
viewing each other as enemies.
Xì Shēn was imprisoned as a former subordinate of Yáng Jùn.
Jùn was then a Shàngshū Láng
and investigated his case.
Xì Shēn feared he would not escape.
Jùn impartially judged and rectified the situation,
and Xì Shēn ultimately escaped punishment,
but still did not reform.
Later, as Zuǒchéng,
he again impeached and implicated the Biàn clan.
Jùn successively held the positions of Grand Administrator of Rǔnán and Tíngwèi Qīng.
Dùn, in his youth, served in the provincial and commandery administrations.
He was appointed to the Sīkōng’s office,
gradually rising to Tàizǐ Shèrén and Shàngshū Láng.
Many court officials praised him.
Wáng Yuè, Prince of Dōnghǎi, heard of this
and summoned him to be his Zhǔbù.
When Wáng Mí pressed Lùo,
Dùn and Húmǔ Fǔzhī advised Wáng Yuè to attack Wáng Mí.
However, Wáng Yǎn and Pān Tāo insisted on not listening.
Dùn argued vehemently in court,
and everyone admired his courage.
He was sent out to serve as Internal Administrator of Rǔnán.
When Emperor Yuán was Zhèn Dōng,
he invited Dùn to be Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
but Dùn did not accept.
Shān Jiǎn, the Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn, appointed him Sīmǎ.
Soon after, Wáng Rú and Dù Zēng successively rebelled.
Shān Jiǎn then made Dùn Supervisor of Military Affairs for the seven commanderies north of the Miǎn [River], Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn, and concurrently Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià,
stationed at Xiàkǒu.
Dùn attacked and pacified all areas within the Miǎn.
Afterward, Dù Tāo plundered Xiāngzhōng,
and Dùn was given the additional title of Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū.
He gained merit in subduing Dù Tāo
and was granted the noble title of Ānlíng Tínghóu.
Wáng Dūn, the Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn, invited him to be Jūnsī.
Upon the establishment of the restoration,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài.
At that time, Shí Lè invaded and pressed upon the Huái and Sì [Rivers].
The emperor sought capable generals who could guard the frontiers,
and the high officials recommended Dùn.
He was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Sìkǒu.
When Shí Lè attacked Péngchéng,
Dùn estimated that he could not withstand the force.
He and Wáng Suì, the Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, retreated to defend Xūyí.
The bandit's power then swelled,
and many commanderies north of the Huái [River] were captured by them.
Ultimately, due to his fear and cowardice, his rank was demoted by three grades,
and he became Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn.
He was summoned to be Dàsīnóng.
Wáng Dūn recommended him as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Shítou military affairs.
When Emperor Míng attacked Wáng Dūn,
he appointed Dùn Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, with provisional authority.
After the matter was settled,
he was reappointed Shàngshū,
and enfeoffed as Yìyáng Hóu for his merits.
He was transferred to Guānglùxūn,
then sent out as Dūdū Ānnán Jiāngjūn, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, with provisional authority.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn,
but he firmly declined the appointment.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Wēn Jiào and Yǔ Liàng sent out a manifesto calling for all generals and local administrators to rush to the capital.
Dùn withheld his troops,
and also failed to provide military provisions,
only dispatching Dūhù Xún Suì with a few hundred men to follow the main army.
At that time, no one in the court or countryside was not surprised and dismayed,
and only Táo Kǎn also gnashed his teeth in anger.
After Sū Jùn was pacified,
Táo Kǎn impeached Dùn for obstructing the army and watching from the sidelines,
not responding to the national crisis,
and lacking the integrity of a high official.
He requested that Dùn be arrested in a cage-cart and handed over to the Tíngwèi.
Chéngxiàng Wáng Dǎo believed that after the period of chaos, leniency should be shown,
and Dùn was transferred to Ānnán Jiāngjūn and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He did not take up the post due to illness.
He was summoned to be Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently holding the position of Shàofǔ.
Since Dùn had not attacked Sū Jùn,
he always carried shame and regret,
and his reputation suffered from this point onward.
He soon died of grief.
He was posthumously granted his original official title,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì,
with the posthumous name Jìng.
His son Tāo inherited his title.
Liú Chāo
Liú Chāo, courtesy name Shìyú,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá,
and a descendant of Zhāng, King Jǐng of Chéngyáng in the Hàn dynasty.
Zhāng’s seventh-generation descendant was enfeoffed as Cíxiāng Hóu of Línyí County,
and his descendants subsequently settled there.
His father, Hé,
was the Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn of Lángyá Commandery.
Liú Chāo showed ambition from a young age.
He served as a petty official in the county,
gradually rising to Jìshì Yuàn of Lángyá Commandery.
Due to his loyalty, diligence, purity, and prudence, he was promoted by Emperor Yuán.
He personally served by the emperor’s side,
and thus accompanied him across the Yangtze River,
transferring to Shèrén of the Āndōng government,
exclusively managing documents and dispatches.
When the prime minister’s office was established,
he again served as Shèrén.
At that time, the empire was in turmoil,
with expeditions against rebels and two-faced individuals.
Liú Chāo, considering his close and confidential position,
and that his handwriting resembled the emperor’s own hand,
absolutely ceased exchanging letters with others.
When he was granted leave for rest,
he closed his door and did not receive guests,
thus gradually gaining greater intimacy [with the emperor].
For his diligent service at the emperor’s side,
he was granted the noble title of Yuánxiāng Tínghóu,
with an income of seven hundred households,
and transferred to Xíng Cānjūn.
In the Jiànxīng
period, he became a Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was appointed Qí Dūwèi and Fèng Cháoqǐng.
At that time, the central administration had just been established,
and many tasks were not yet settled.
Cháo took charge of literary matters,
and being cautious, discreet, and reticent,
he was increasingly trusted and favored.
Furthermore, he lived a simple and austere life,
wearing no layered silk,
and his family had no savings of even a dān or shí.
Whenever the emperor bestowed gifts,
he would firmly decline, saying:
“As a humble and insignificant minister,
I improperly receive awards and gifts.
To enjoy emolument without merit
is cause for great fear of calamity and misfortune.”
The emperor praised him
and did not force his will upon him.
Soon after, he was dispatched to serve as the Magistrate of Gōuróng.
He treated people with sincerity
and was cherished by the common folk.
For the annual taxes and levies,
the officials in charge would always personally go out to four different places to assess the assets of the common people.
When it came to Cháo,
he simply made large boxes,
distributed one to each village,
and had them write down their household property themselves.
After throwing it into the box,
they would return it to the county.
The common people reported their assets truthfully,
and the tax revenue received
even exceeded that of previous years.
He entered the capital as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Láng.
Due to his father's mourning, he resigned from office.
After the burial,
when Wáng Dūn raised troops,
an imperial edict ordered Cháo to resume his post,
also commanding him as Āndōng Shàngjiāngjūn.
Soon, the Six Armies were defeated and scattered,
but only Cháo kept his troops in order and guarded the emperor directly.
The emperor was moved by this
and sent him home to complete the mourning rites.
When Qián Fèng caused trouble,
Cháo gathered righteous men
and followed Emperor Míng to suppress Fèng.
After the affair was settled,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Línglíng for his merits.
Cháo was poor,
and his wife and children lacked support.
The emperor personally issued an edict praising him
and bestowed fish and rice upon him.
Cháo declined to accept.
Later, Cháo needed a solid-colored ox,
but could not find one in the market.
He requested to buy an ox from the official imperial stables.
An edict then bestowed it upon him.
He was sent out to serve as the Grand Administrator of Yìxīng.
Not long after,
he was summoned and appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
His appointments and travels
were unknown to anyone in the imperial court.
Coincidentally, when the emperor died,
Empress Mù presided over the court,
and he was promoted to Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
At that time, the military officers had no troops,
but many people from Yìxīng loyally followed Cháo.
He then commanded these troops to guard the palace,
which was known as
the "Jūnzǐ Camp."
At the beginning of the Xiánhé
period, he resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
He did not take off his mourning clothes,
crying day and night.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, he would always walk to the grave,
his sorrow moving passersby.
When Sū Jùn plotted rebellion,
Cháo replaced Zhào Yìn as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
At that time, the capital was in great chaos,
and many court officials sent their families east to avoid disaster.
Former subordinates from Yìxīng wanted to welcome Cháo's family,
but Cháo refused,
placing all his wife and children inside the palace.
When the imperial army was defeated,
Wáng Dǎo appointed Cháo as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
personally attending to Emperor Chéng.
When the Empress Dowager died,
the military guard and ceremonial rituals were incomplete.
Cháo personally led his officers and soldiers to construct the imperial mausoleum.
When Sū Jùn moved the imperial carriage to Shítóu,
it was raining heavily,
and the roads were submerged and muddy.
Cháo and Shìzhōng Zhōng Yǎ walked beside the emperor,
refusing to ride the horses provided by the rebels,
and were sorrowful and full of righteous indignation.
When Sū Jùn heard of this,
he was very displeased,
but dared not harm them yet.
He appointed his trusted associates such as Xǔ Fāng to positions like Sīmǎ Dū and Diànzhōng Jiān,
outwardly claiming they were for palace guard,
but in reality, to defend against Cháo and others.
At that time, there was famine and rice was expensive.
Sū Jùn and others sent gifts,
but he accepted none.
He stayed close day and night,
and his loyalty as a minister grew even more reverent.
The emperor was eight years old at the time,
and even in his dire straits,
Cháo still initiated his instruction in the Xiàojīng and Lúnyǔ.
When Wēn Qiáo and others arrived,
Sū Jùn was suspicious of the court officials,
and because Cháo was favored by the emperor,
his suspicion of him was even greater.
Later, Wáng Dǎo fled.
Cháo secretly conspired with Huáidé Magistrate Kuāng Shù and Jiànkāng Magistrate Guǎn Pèi,
planning to escort the emperor out.
Before the appointed time,
the plot was revealed.
Sū Jùn sent Rèn Ràng with troops to arrest Cháo and Zhōng Yǎ.
The emperor hugged them, crying sadly, saying:
“Give me back my Shìzhōng and Yòuwèi!”
Rèn Ràng did not heed the imperial command
and then killed them.
When Sū Jùn was pacified,
Rèn Ràng had an old acquaintance with Táo Kǎn.
Táo Kǎn wanted to spare him specially,
so he petitioned the emperor.
The emperor said:
“Ràng is the one who killed my Shìzhōng and Yòuwèi;
he cannot be pardoned.”
Thus, Ràng was executed.
When Cháo was to be reburied,
the emperor mourned him ceaselessly.
An edict ordered him to be moved and buried in a prominent, nearby place,
so that the emperor could see his tomb when coming and going.
He was posthumously granted Wèiwèi
and given the posthumous name Zhōng.
Cháo was by nature humble and cautious.
He served three emperors successively,
and in confidential matters,
he was always trusted and favored.
However, he dared not become arrogant or flattering because of favor,
thus scholars all felt at ease with him and respected him.
His son Nè succeeded him.
He was careful and disciplined, having the character of Shí Qìng.
He successively served as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Xiàpī Nèishǐ.
Nè's son Xiǎng
was also pure and cautious,
serving as Sànqí Láng.
Zhōng Yǎ
Zhōng Yǎ, courtesy name Yànzhòu,
was a native of Chángshè, Yǐngchuān.
His father, Niàn,
was a clerk in a ducal mansion,
and died young.
Zhōng Yǎ was orphaned young,
loved learning, and had talent and ambition.
He was recommended for the Four Conducts
and appointed as Magistrate of Rúyáng.
He then entered the capital as Zuǒ Zuòzhù Láng.
He resigned from office for his mother's mourning
and resumed his post after the mourning period.
Wáng Yuè, Prince of Dōnghǎi, invited him to be his Cānjūn,
and he was promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
Fleeing the chaos, he crossed eastward.
Emperor Yuán appointed him as Assistant in the Secretariat for the Chancellor.
He was promoted to Intendant of Línhuái and General Who Guards Awe.
After a short while,
he was summoned and appointed as Mounted Gentleman-in-Attendance.
He was transferred to Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, there was an affair concerning the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Zhōng Yǎ submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty's inherited lineage
traces back to the Administrator of Jīngzhào as a great-great-grandson.
However, the current sacrificial prayer refers to you as a great-grandson.
I fear this is a customary error
that ought to be rectified.
Furthermore, according to the rites,
the brothers of one's grandfather
are treated as one's grandfather.
Emperor Jǐng, considering his own meritorious achievements, was established as Shìzōng,
and was not enshrined in the temple as a paternal grand-uncle.
Thus, the text referring to a paternal grand-uncle should also be removed."
An imperial edict stated:
"According to the rites,
when serving the ancestral temple,
from the great-grandson downwards, all refer to themselves as great-grandsons.
This is not an error due to custom.
The meaning is taken from the 'heavy grandson' (i.e., great-grandson),
allowing it to be a common term for all generations,
with no need for alteration.
The mention of 'paternal grand-uncle' is inappropriate,
as you have suggested in your memorial."
He was transferred to Censor of the Northern Army.
General-in-Chief Wáng Dūn invited him to be an Executive Supervisor.
He was appointed Intendant of Xuānchéng.
When Qián Fèng rebelled,
he was given the additional title of General of Guǎngwǔ,
and led troops to garrison Qīngyì.
At that time, Zhōu Qǐ, a man from Guǎngdé county, raised troops for Fèng and attacked Yǎ.
Yǎ retreated to Jīng county,
gathered gentry and commoners,
attacked Qǐ,
and executed him.
After Fèng was pacified,
he was summoned and appointed Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
Upon the death of Emperor Míng,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
At that time, the national mourning period was not yet a full year,
but Shàngshū Méi Táo privately introduced female entertainers.
Yǎ impeached him, memorializing:
"Your servant has heard that when Fàngxūn passed away,
the eight musical instruments were silenced.
Even among commoners,
this restraint lasts for three years.
Since then,
this has been the same throughout the generations.
The death of Reverent Ancestor Emperor Míng has affected the myriad states,
and the mourning period is nearing one year.
The sagely ruler wears plain white,
weeping tears of blood while presiding over court.
The officials are sorrowful,
their actions devoid of joy.
Méi Táo lacks the loyalty and devotion of a great minister;
his household is extravagant and lavish,
with singers and entertainers in profusion.
The sounds of strings and flutes
are heard flowing out onto the public roads.
He should be dismissed and exiled
to uphold the royal laws.
I request that the Minister of Works be ordered
to discuss and rectify this matter of public integrity."
Empress Mù, presiding over court,
specifically pardoned him and did not pursue the matter.
Yǎ upheld the law and punished transgressions,
and all officials feared him.
When the North Regional Commander Liú Xiá died,
Xiá's troops mutinied.
An edict ordered Guō Mò to suppress them.
Yǎ was appointed Supervisor of the Punitive Expedition and given the Imperial Insignia.
When the affair was settled,
he was appointed General of Spirited Cavalry.
During the rebellion of Sū Jùn,
an edict appointed Yǎ as Front-Line Army Supervisor and gave him the Imperial Insignia,
leading a thousand elite and brave men to resist Jùn.
Yǎ, due to his small force,
dared not attack,
and retreated.
He was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Soon after, the imperial army was defeated.
Yǎ and Liú Chāo jointly guarded the Son of Heaven.
Someone said to Yǎ:
"Advance when it is advantageous,
retreat when it is difficult;
this is the ancient way.
Your nature is honest and straightforward,
you will surely not be tolerated by the rebels.
Why not adapt to the circumstances and await their downfall?"
Yǎ said:

to discern ability or lack thereof,

Now, the various departments of the court consider compliance to be good,
and disagreement results in demotion,
no longer discussing the rightness or wrongness of talent,
or the gains and losses of words.
Whenever someone speaks,
they are
often not used,
which is why the court has few ministers who dare to debate,
and scholars only aspire to salaried positions.
Guō Yì (郭翼) submitted a memorial,
and Emperor Wǔ (武帝) promoted him to Commandant of Túnliú (屯留令),
and also established
admonishing officials,
to allow for direct speech
and encourage future advancements.
Therefore, people could express themselves fully,
and words were not concealed or tabooed.
Appoint to office, then grant noble rank;
stabilize position, then bestow salary.
Present proposals through words,
clearly test through achievements,
and assign carriages and robes according to merit.
Shùn (舜) still underwent trials through various difficulties,
but now people are salaried first without trial,
which greatly violates ancient principles,
and is the source
of chaos.
Seek talent eagerly among the humble and lowly,
apply punishment first to the close and noble,
then orders will be enforced and prohibitions observed,
and none will be overlooked in the wilderness.
Yáo (堯) took Shùn (舜) from obscurity,
Shùn (舜) elevated worthies from
mountain caves.
Jī Gōng (姬公) did not bend the law for his relatives,
Shú Xiàng (叔向) did not violate the law for his brothers.
Now, most of the judicial officials in the court come from humble backgrounds,
which is why official documents are daily
submitted but are insufficient to punish people,
and officials select talents but are insufficient to accomplish affairs.
It is fitting to recruit the worthy and good from among butchers and fishermen,
and invite the upright from villages and gardens.
If this path
is not changed,
even combining offices and reducing positions
will not remedy the abuses and chaos.
If one is wise and benevolent,
what need to worry about Huāndōu (驩兜)?
What need to banish Yǒumiáo (有苗)?
What need to fear the glib and ingratiating Kǒng Rén (孔壬)?
This is the benefit of an office getting the right person.
He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中),
then appointed Nèi Shǐ (內史) of Kuàijī (會稽).
At that time, Wáng Dūn (王敦) rebelled,
and Shěn Chōng (沈充) raised an army to support him.
He was offered the title of Yuǎn Jiāngjūn (遠將軍),
but he resisted and did not accept.
He did not supply military resources to Shěn Chōng (沈充),
making the defense of the border and the security of the populace his priority.
When Wáng Dūn (王敦) reached Shítou (石頭),
he subtly prompted the court to summon Yuǎn (遠),
who was then appointed Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿),
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Wáng Dūn (王敦) deeply feared his uprightness and astuteness,
and appointed him Zhǎngshǐ (長史).
He died of illness a few months later.
Yuǎn’s (遠) younger brother, Jìn (縉),
was second only to Yuǎn (遠) in fame.
He served as Wáng Dūn’s (王敦) Zhǔbù (主簿),
and eventually became Póyáng Tàishǒu (鄱陽太守).
Jìn’s (縉) son, Mínghú (鳴鵠),
rose to the position of Wǔchāng Tàishǒu (武昌太守).
Wáng Jiàn (王鑒)
Wáng Jiàn (王鑒), courtesy name Mào Gāo (茂高),
was a native of Tángyì (堂邑).
His father, Jùn (濬),
was Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
Wáng Jiàn (王鑒) was renowned for his literary skill in his youth.
He first served as Lángyá Guó Shìláng (琅邪國侍郎) under Emperor Yuán (元帝).
At that time, Dù Tāo (杜弢) rebelled,
and the Jiāng (江) and Xiāng (湘) rivers were plagued by his influence.
Wáng Dūn (王敦) could not control it,
and the court was deeply concerned.
Wáng Jiàn (王鑒) submitted a memorial advising the emperor to personally lead an expedition,
saying: "Heaven has brought disaster upon the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
the four seas are overturned,
the extremity of chaos and disorder,
unseen since the dawn of creation.
Your Excellency encounters the misfortune of a changing destiny,
facing the convergence of the 'nine calamities' (yáng jiǔ zhī huì).
Your sacred person
bears the heavy responsibility of Yī (伊) and Zhōu (周),
and the court looks to you for assistance and restoration.
You are about to shake the long reins to control the eight directions,
sweep the Milky Way clear and purify the celestial path.
The resources you rely on,
the land south of the Yangtze,
are merely a corner of the nine provinces,
and the last remnants of people.
Yet, the Bǎiyuè (百越) glare like owls from the Five Ranges,
and the Man (蠻) and Shǔ (蜀) eye the Xiāng (湘) and Hàn (漢) like wolves.
Jiāngzhōu (江州)
is desolate,
white bones cover the ground,
and Yùzhāng (豫章) commandery alone
has lost eight-tenths of its population.
This is followed by years of famine,
public and private resources are depleted,
warehouses lack even a few months' provisions,
and the three armies show
signs of dire want.
Taxes and levies are extorted,
a perpetual cycle,
soldiers scatter, people flee,
filling the roads.
The source of weakness deepens daily,
and the momentum for complete victory has not
yet begun.
I fear that the cloud banners will turn back,
and the general's chariots will enter triumphantly,
not in a matter of days.
In the past, the army of Qí (齊) had not been out for a full year before Shēn Hóu (申侯) feared they would grow old;
how much more so when armor has been worn for three years,
and lice breed in helmets and breastplates?
How can one not deeply consider this!
Jiāng (江) and Yáng (揚) were originally six commanderies,
just one provincial domain.
If the troops are not restrained in time,
and the people cannot endure
their fate,
the Three Rivers will face attack,
Pénglǐ (彭蠡) will tremble,
this is when the bandits will cross inside our walls,
and spy on our homes.
A multitude weary of war is easily stirred,
and birds startled
by a bow are difficult to calm.
This is what I greatly fear.
Since last year,
we have repeatedly lost generals,
and our armies have suffered frequent defeats.
The bandits, in their reckless pursuit of death,
have grown weary of constant campaigns.
The enemy has measured
our strength.
Although we continue to send out subordinate generals,
I fear it will not be enough to achieve success.
Your humble servant believes that Your Majesty should personally visit Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Then the ministers summoned from all directions
will be able
to exert their strength;
the brave warriors,
their valor can be aroused.
Advance the Left Army to Wǔchāng (武昌),
to reinforce Táo Kǎn (陶侃);
establish a famous general in Ānchéng (安成),
to connect the camps of Gān
and Zhuó (卓).
Look south to Jiāo (交) and Guǎng (廣),
pacify the southern barbarians to the west.
Hold strategic locations,
station elite troops to guard them;
deep moats and strong ramparts,
deploy elite armored soldiers to defend them.
Once the six armies are well-supplied,
and the warriors eager to fight,
then seize opportunities and deploy cunning strategies,
harass their strongholds,
display great trustworthiness,
open a path of life,
and Dù Tāo’s (杜弢) neck will surely be bound
beneath your banner.
Some will argue that a major expedition requires heavy labor,
and the people should not be disturbed.
I believe that a temporary disturbance to defeat the enemy
is better than letting the enemy disturb us constantly.
Indeed, the four limbs"
Indeed,
what people cherish most,
if it is fitting to cut out the disease,
then one must cut flesh and scrape bone.
However, the capital must not be empty.
Jiàn recommended that Wáng Dǎo (王導) could be entrusted with the responsibility of Xiāo Hé (蕭何).
Some might say that a small bandit is about to be defeated,
and it is not worth mobilizing the might of a thousand chariots.
Jiàn had seen Wáng Mí (王彌) in the beginning,
who was also a small bandit.
The government forces did not take his power seriously,
allowing the cunning rebel to freely
wreak havoc,
which ultimately led to Wēn Huái (溫懷) not being defended,
the three rivers (Sānhé) falling,
leading to today's calamity.
This is a clear and proven fact.
Even creeping grass should not be allowed to grow long,
how much more
so for the banditry of wolves and rhinoceroses!
During the era of the Five Hegemons (Wǔ Bà),
the generals were not incompetent,
the soldiers were not cowardly.
In campaigns of conquest,
the lord would personally oversee them.
Thus, Qí Huán (齊桓) removed his helmet at
Shàolíng (邵陵),
and Jìn Wén (晉文) donned his armor at Chéngpú (城濮).
In the past, the two emperors, Hàn Gāo (漢高) and Guāngwǔ (光武),
whether the campaigns were near or far,
whether the enemies were great or small,
would personally beat the gongs and drums,
and expose themselves to arrows
and stones,
braving wind and rain,
with not even enough provisions to fill their gourds,
galloping in all directions,
without a moment's rest and peace.
Only then were the imperial foundations established,
and the great achievements completed.
Now, the current great calamity
is more severe than in previous eras.
The fate of prosperity or decline
rests entirely upon us.
To wish for the imperial banners to avoid campaigns in the field,
and the emperor's sacred person to be far from the toil of wind and dust,
while great deeds
are accomplished sitting down,
Jiàn has not seen
how that would be easy.
After Wèi Wǔ (魏武) had pacified the Central Plains,
he personally campaigned at Liǔchéng (柳城),
raising his banners on the ridges of Lúlóng (盧龍),
and halting his reins beyond the layers of passes.
This was not due to
any immediate threat of beacon fires at that time,
but rather because to let an enemy escape for a day
would become a lifelong concern.
Even though the imperial carriage faced danger,
he did not consider it a hardship,
how much more so for a situation more urgent than this!
Liú Xuándé (劉玄德) personally ascended Mt. Hàn (漢山),
and the vanguard of Xiàhóu (夏侯) was crushed.
Wú Wěizǔ (吳偽祖) personally sailed up the Yangtze River,
and the head of Guān Yǔ (關羽) was hung.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) hesitated and missed the opportunity,
crippling his advantage of three
parts of the empire.
Liú Biǎo (劉表) idly guarded his populace,
and ultimately lost the entire territory of Chǔ (楚).
Looking back at all the lords who brought order out of chaos throughout history,
even if they were sages,
there were none who achieved success by sitting idly and doing nothing.
The precedents are not far off,
and can be considered as divine guidance.
Some debaters or advisors suggest that it is currently mid-summer,
not the time for military expeditions.
Jiàn believes that we should now strictly prepare,
and move in autumn.
When the strong winds clear the way,
and the dragon boats swiftly
move like lightning,
in less than ten days,
we can reach Yùzhāng (豫章).
Yùzhāng is still a thousand *lǐ* away from the enemy,
but merely confronting them with awe-inspiring power,
will ensure the success of a hundred victories.
Once the Xiang (Xiāng) plains are swept clean,
and Chǔyǐng (楚郢) is purified,
then ranks and merits can be assigned,
rewarding the efforts of the generals and soldiers;
armor can be rolled up and banners furled,
expanding the tasks of agriculture and sericulture,
spreading benevolent
kindness,
and abolishing burdensome taxes.
In a few years,
the state will be rich and its army strong,
advancing like dragons and tigers,
to awe the world.
What thoughts would not be subdued,
what endeavors would not
succeed?
The achievements of Huán Wén (桓文) would not be difficult to emulate.
Now, to begrudge the effort of a single campaign,
and to delay a dying enemy,
is truly a great disgrace for the state,
and a deep
worry for its ministers and sons.
Jiàn, being of humble talent,
has been mistakenly favored and nurtured.
He wishes to exhaust his foolish loyalty to compensate for even one in ten thousand.
The words of humble woodcutters
are not discarded by sagely kings.
The strategies of garrison soldiers
were adopted by previous
rulers.
I beg Your Majesty to give careful consideration,
and ponder what has been presented.
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor deeply accepted it,
and immediately ordered a general alert throughout the empire,
intending to personally lead a campaign against Tāo (弢).
However, Tāo had already been pacified,
so it was stopped.
At the establishment of the restoration,
he was appointed驸马都尉 (fùmǎ dūwèi), served at court,
and then was transferred to be the magistrate of Yǒngxìng (永興).
Grand General Wáng Dūn (王敦) invited him to be his secretary and staff officer,
but he died before taking up the post,
at the age of forty-one.
His collected works were passed down to posterity.
Jiàn's younger brother Tāo (濤) and his nephew Yǎn (戭),
both possessed literary talent.
Tāo, courtesy name Màolüè (茂略),
successively served as editor in the imperial library (zhùzuò láng) and magistrate of Wúxī (無錫).
Yǎn, courtesy name Tíngjiān (庭堅),
also served as an editor.
Both died early.
Chén Yún (陳頵)
Chén Yún, courtesy name Yánsī (延思),
was a native of Kǔ (苦) in Chén (陳) commandery.
In his youth, he loved learning
and possessed literary acumen.
His father Xīn (訢) built a residence and erected a gate.
Yún said:
"It should be able to accommodate horse-drawn carriages."
Xīn laughed and agreed.
He served as a郡督邮 (jùn dūyóu) (commander of inspection for the commandery),
and apprehended three thousand hidden individuals,
which was the most in the entire province.
Grand Administrator Liú Xiǎng (劉享) promoted him to chief clerk (zhǔbù),
and the province appointed him as a subordinate official (bù cóngshì).
He returned home in a horse-drawn carriage,
and his clan was honored.
The impeachment case against Péi Wáng Tāo
was not yet finished
when Xiè Jié was appointed to replace Yáng Zhǔn as Inspector.
Tāo then placed himself under the patronage of Héjiān Wáng Yǒng, who was connected to Xiè Jié.
When Jié arrived for the grand assembly,
he asked the Chief Clerk, Shǐ Fèng:
“Péi Wáng is a noble prince.
On what legal grounds does the province presume to detain him?”
At that time, Yūn was present,
and replied:
“The edict of the Jiǎwǔ year
states that the Inspector, bearing a mandate,
is an external agent of the state.
Those who are not under his direct jurisdiction but are within his territory,
the Inspector shall also investigate.
The facts are substantiated by written documents,
and have been reported to the throne repeatedly,
receiving seven imperial edicts.
The impeachment by the province,
therefore, contains no error or deviation.”
Jié said:
“One must not heed the words of the multitude rashly;
the matter should be thoroughly investigated according to the law.”
He then asked his subordinates:
“Héběi is fertile land, producing fine grains,
why are there so few prominent individuals there,
and why are they always ranked as third-grade in the nine-rank system?”
They replied:
“The *Shī* (Odes) says, ‘When lofty peaks send down their spirits,
they produce Fǔ and Shēn.’
Indeed, great heroes and eminent sages often emerge from mountains and marshes.
Héběi’s land is flat and its climate uniform;
even the tall reeds are barely three feet high,
insufficient to form a forest, hence this situation.”
Jié said:
“Zhāng Yànzhēn believed that those from Rǔ and Yǐng are skilled in debate,
but perhaps not as refined and elegant as the literati from Qīng and Xú.”
Yūn replied:
“Yànzhēn did not get along with Yuánlǐ,
hence he made such excessive remarks.
Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzhōu were born in Chén and Liáng;
Fúxī, Fù Yuè, Shī Kuàng, and Dà Xiàng came from Yángxià;
the two founding emperors of Hàn and Wèi arose from Pèi and Qiáo.
Compared to these,
no other province can rival them.”
Jié was greatly impressed by this,
and said:
“The literati of Yùzhōu often comprise half the empire;
this statement is not false.”
Soon after, Jié was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
Jié regretted that he could not fully utilize Yūn’s talents.
In the Yuánkāng era,
Yūn was recommended as Xiàolián,
but the provincial governor kept him.
Yūn recommended Jiāo Bǎo, from the same county, saying:
“Bǎo comes from humble origins,
possesses a pure and tranquil disposition.
If he is given a noble appointment,
he will certainly be able to greatly assist in grand policies,
and live up to the court’s expectations,
ensuring that individuals like Huáng Xiàn are not lacking in Yùtǔ,
and sparing Yūn from the blame of Zāng Wén.”
The province then appointed Bǎo.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng raised an army,
the province sent Yūn to lead troops to him,
and he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
He encountered bandits and sought refuge in Jiāngxī.
Lìyáng Internal Historian Zhū Yàn recruited him as a staff officer.
Zhèndōng Aide-de-camp Yuán Xiù recommended Yūn to Yuán Dì,
who then promoted him to Acting Military Advisor to the General of the East,
and he managed the two departments of law and military affairs.
Yūn wrote to Wáng Dǎo, saying:
“The reason why Zhōnghuá is declining and collapsing,
and the four seas are crumbling,
is precisely because the selection of talent is flawed.
People prioritize reputation over actual deeds,
engaging in superficial competition and rushing around,
mutually recommending each other.
Those with influential recommendations are promoted first,
those with less influence later,
thus creating a chain reaction,
leading to gradual decay.
Furthermore, the custom of Zhuāng and Lǎo has misled the court,
where those who cultivate a reputation are considered refined,
and those who attend to practical governance are seen as vulgar.
State affairs are neglected,
and laws and institutions fall into disuse.
Indeed, to control the distant,
one must start from the near.
Thus, if one’s words are good,
they will be echoed a thousand *lǐ* away.
Now, it is necessary to make reforms,
clearly reward and justly punish,
promote Zhuó Mào from Mìxiàn,
and elevate Zhū Yì from Tóngxiāng.
Only then can the great enterprise be achieved,
and a restoration be hoped for.”
At the beginning of the Jiànxīng era,
he was appointed Secretary to the Inspector.
Many assistants and clerks would fabricate excuses to avoid responsibilities.
Yūn argued:
“All officials, influenced by the lingering defects of the former Xītái’s practice of cultivating reputation,
consider carefulness and reverence
as vulgar,
while haughtiness and arrogance
are deemed elegant.
Even now, court officials are dissolute,
procrastinating when faced with tasks.
This gradual decay has not been reformed,
leading to the downfall of the state.
Thus, a hundred-foot high house can be burned down by a protruding beam,
and a thousand-mile dike can be breached by an ant hill.
The ancients guarded against small things to preserve the great,
and were cautious in minute matters to prevent problems.
Henceforth, those who claim illness when assigned a mission
and only act when urged,
shall all be dismissed.”
Initially,
when Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
the three kings raised an army.
They enacted the Jǐhài regulations,
and thereafter, even for minor merits,
these regulations were applied.
Yūn believed that this should not become a permanent system
and refuted it, saying:
“A sagely king offers titles and rewards for meritorious service,
and institutes punishments for transgressions.
If this principle is clear,
people will rush through fire and water.
Moreover, the reality of official positions and honors
must not be conferred carelessly.
To appoint those without talent is to invite disaster,
and excessive favor leads to ruin.
In the past, Sūn Xiù openly advocated usurpation,
and manipulated state affairs.
When Huì Huáng lost control,
the entire empire was without a protector.
The three kings proposed action,
swept across the four seas,
united the armies of righteousness,
and rallied the hearts of the people under heaven.
Therefore, the Jǐhài righteous regulations were established as an expedient measure to overcome the crisis.
This was merely a temporary law,
not a regular system.
Since the uprising,
people have been indiscriminately promoted based on these regulations.
Some became marquises by chance,
others were promoted from military ranks,
or even from servants.
Gold and purple insignia were worn by soldiers,
and official documents were entrusted to common servants,
causing heavenly offices to be debased
and royal titles to be profaned.
This is not what is meant by rectifying the imperial order and valuing official distinctions.
I request that from now on, these practices be ceased.”
As Yūn was of humble origin,
he often submitted memorials,
which many court officials disliked.
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Qiáojùn.
At the beginning of the Tàixīng era,
he was summoned back due to illness.
After some time,
he served as Minister of Personnel in plain clothes,
and then presented proposals on current affairs,
believing that
“In the past, when the area south of the Yangtze was first pacified
and the Central Plains were in chaos,
the system of recommendation and examination was not implemented.
It is appropriate to gradually revert to the old system,
seeking out hidden talents
and testing them with classical texts and strategies.
Furthermore, although Mǎ Lóng and Méng Guān came from humble origins,
their military achievements were great.
However, those who are not accustomed
to commanding military affairs
rarely succeed.
It is advisable to open up channels for recommending those with military strategies suitable for generalship,
interviewing and testing them thoroughly
to ascertain their full capabilities,
and then appointing them according to their talents.
Even if only one out of ten is successful,
it is better than not recommending at all,
let alone if two or three out of ten succeed.
Jì Rìdī, a surrendered barbarian,
served seven generations of emperors as an attendant;
Yóu Yú, a Rong Di,
entered service as Prime Minister of Qín.
Why should we rely solely on noble families
to be distinguished among the competitive crowd?
We should attract outstanding individuals from obscurity,
suppress superficiality and emphasize substance,
then heaven will be clear and earth peaceful,
and humanity and spirits will respond.”
Later, he was appointed the Administrator of Tiānmén,
and the various ethnic groups found peace under him.
He selected trusted subordinates to serve as the Commander of Jīngzhōu,
so that if there were any conscriptions or levies,
all movements and situations would be swiftly reported,
allowing for preparations to be completed in advance.
When Táo Kǎn returned from his campaign,
Yūn arrived first at Bālíng to pay his respects.
Kǎn thought him capable
and memorialized to have him appointed as the Inspector of Liángzhōu.
He pacified and comforted the desolate and impoverished,
and he possessed great prestige and benevolence.
The great families of Liángzhōu, however, were jealous of each other
and spread rumors that Yūn was old and deaf.
Kǎn summoned Yūn back,
and replaced him with Jiǎng Xùn, the Administrator of Xīyáng.
He died at the age of sixty-nine.
Gāo Sōng
Gāo Sōng, courtesy name Màoyǎn,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
His father, Kuī,
was orphaned young,
and was known for his filial piety towards his mother.
At thirteen,
during a famine year,
Kuī would go without enough vegetables to eat,
but always provided sweet and rich food for his mother.
He was praised for his fraternal affection in raising his younger brother.
He resided temporarily in Jiāngzhōu,
and the Inspector Huá Yì invited him to be his Western Office Clerk.
When Yì was defeated,
Kuī hid Yì’s son for over a year,
and only came out when an amnesty was granted.
Emperor Yuán commended and pardoned him,
appointing him as a Staff Officer,
and he subsequently held prominent positions,
reaching the posts of Administrator of Dānyáng and Grand Master of Brightness,
and was ennobled as the Earl of Jiànchāng.
Sōng was fond of learning from a young age
and excelled at historical writings.
When he was a young boy with his hair tied in knots,
Sīkōng Hé Chōng praised his intelligence and discernment.
When Chōng served as the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
he appointed Sōng as his Chief Clerk,
and admired and respected him even more.
He was transferred to be the Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry,
was nominated as a provincial talent (xiùcái),
and appointed as Academician of the Imperial Academy.
He resigned due to his father’s mourning period.
Initially,
Kuī had been dismissed due to a lawsuit caused by taking a concubine.
Upon his death,
Sōng personally bound himself and petitioned the Court of the Grand Judge to redress the injustice,
and thus kept his father’s coffin unburied for five years,
submitting dozens of memorials and petitions.
The Emperor, moved by his plight,
issued an edict stating:
“Kuī, having held the position of a high minister,
was dismissed for violating regulations,
and the matter has long been settled.
His son, Sōng, persistently seeks justice;
therefore, we specially permit the transmission of his father’s marquisate.”
Because of this, he was highly praised.
He was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat and Palace Attendant.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén became regent,
he appointed Sōng as Commander of the Pacifying Army.
At this time, Huán Wēn held absolute power
and led his troops on a northern expedition.
When his army reached Wǔchāng,
Emperor Jiǎnwén was troubled by this.
Sōng said:
“It is advisable to write a letter explaining the potential blessings and misfortunes,
and he will naturally turn back his banners.
If he does not,
then the six armies should be arrayed,
and righteousness and rebellion will be judged at this point.
If there is any other plan,
I request to be the first to stain the drum with blood.”
He then drafted a letter for Emperor Jiǎnwén on the spot, saying:
“The rebellious difficulties should be pacified,
and the opportune moment should be seized.
This is truly a long-term strategy for the country,
a grand calculation for governance.
Who but Your Excellency can achieve this great gathering?
However, to raise an army and mobilize the populace for this purpose
must be founded on resources and provisions.
The difficulty of transportation
was something the ancients found challenging;
it should not be treated lightly at the beginning without careful consideration.
This is why I have been deeply pondering and hesitating recently,
it lies precisely here.
However, such an extraordinary undertaking
is something that startles the populace,
and rumors and whispers spread widely;
I imagine Your Excellency has heard a little of them.
If they are anxious about losing something,
they will stop at nothing.
They might be swayed by rumors and become agitated,
collapsing and scattering in an instant.
If this does not happen,

compared to a grand mansion,
they were like its rafters and purlins!
Sōng’s criticism of Wēn,

frustrated their laborious and troublesome schemes,
and articulated their Rǔ and Yǐng arguments.

Therefore, Huán Wēn abandoned Xǔ Yōu’s plan,

This method was woven into the affairs of the time,

He used a false name to evade prominence,
and presented his writings to Yuè.
Xiàowén was loyal and outspoken,
his wise words were practiced.
Màogāo had great discernment,
and excelled especially in rhetoric.
Sōng inherited the marquisate,
and Yūn brought distinction to his noble family.
