those who are silently enlightened are insufficient to traverse the void.
Therefore, they do not expand their hearts, yet their forms are forgotten;
they are not externally burdened, yet their wisdom is lost.
Without mountain caves, they are
profoundly tranquil;
without rivers and lakes, they wander freely.
Their mysterious enlightenment is not used to respond to opportunities;
their profound insight is not used to illuminate broad vistas.
They do not objectify things as 'things' and 'self' as 'self';
they do not affirm 'right' and deny 'wrong'.
Forgetting
the mind is not my mind;
gaining the mind is not my inclination.
They entrust the myriad sounds to the formless,
and confine all distinctions to a single return.
They do not prolong the life of the prematurely deceased,
nor shorten the life of Péng Juān.
They do not magnify the autumn
finest hair,
nor diminish Mount Tài.
Mosquito tears flow as long as heaven and earth endure;
mayflies share the same age as the great Tūnj.
However, one closing, one opening,
these are the traces of the two cosmic forces;
one emptying, one
overflowing,
these are the rhythms of the celestial phenomena.
Melting and freezing are seasonal appointments of hot and cold;
withering and flourishing are essential to spring and autumn.
The verdant beauty of the spring sun,
the declining vitality of dragons and leopards,
the long splendor of swift wolves,
the brief shadow of the dark earth.
Thus, the wilderness is the abode of joy and sorrow,
and the butterfly is the instrument of transformation.
"Indeed, those who delight in the sounds of the oriole
do not frown at the chirping of the cicada;
those who marvel at the view from Yúntái
must renounce the joy of simple clothing.
Some dance and sing of gathering
shepherd's purse,
while others embrace jade and sigh at guarding the gate.
If one struggles with calculating intentions over external things,
one cannot find satisfaction in a single string.
If one realizes the cycles of regret and lament,
how can one speak of him as someone who
finds joy in heaven?
Thus, Zhuāng Zhōu reclined at Qīyuán;
Lǎo Lái roamed in the forest caves;
Yán Píng remained calm and indifferent in the dusty market;
Méi Zhēn lived hidden among market hawkers.
Liáng
Shēng chanted and whistled, feigning madness;
Jiāo Xiān was simple-minded and still as a tree stump;
Ruǎn Gōng was often drunk and displayed arrogance;
Zhái Sǒu concealed his form and vanished in a flash.
I cannot attain the rhyme
of these few worthies,
so I quietly enjoy this round staff and bone of wisdom."
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
when the imperial grandson was born,
Pú submitted a memorial saying: "A ruler who possesses the Way never fails to hold himself in peril;
a ruler in a chaotic age never fails to consider himself secure.
Therefore, those who exist but do not forget demise,
that is why the Three Dynasties
flourished;
those who perished but believed themselves to exist,
that is why the three later dynasties declined.
For this reason, ancient sagacious rulers welcomed loyal remonstrance
to correct their errors;
they prominently
displayed straightforward and direct advice
to attack their faults.
To the extent that they bowed upon hearing a single good word,
and trembled upon seeing admonition.
Why?
Because they did not privatize their bodies,
but governed the world with utmost
impartiality.
Your servant secretly believes that Your Majesty's heavenly mandate is most manifest,
and your achievements are most great,
yet the prosperity of the restoration is not grand, and the atmosphere of sacred reverence has not ascended.
This is probably due to the laws
being too clear,
and the punishments and teachings too severe.
Therefore, when water is too clear, there are no fish;
when government is too scrutinizing, the people are alienated.
This is the natural course of events.
Last spring, your servant presented a report
stating that the prisons were overflowing,
and yin and yang were out of harmony.
Judging from the principles of divination,
it would be advisable to hold a sacrifice to the suburbs and issue an amnesty
to cleanse away impurities.
Otherwise,
in the future, there will certainly be disasters of excessive sunshine and bitter rain,
calamities of collapses and tremors and solar
eclipses,
and omens of wild, cunning, unruly evils.
A little over a month later,
the sun indeed had an eclipse.
Since
last autumn,
various commanderies have experienced torrential rains,
all waters have become floods,
and the harvest was ruined.
I just heard that Wúxīng again has those who plot rebellion.
Ominous signs are gradually forming,
and your servant
greatly fears this.
Recently,
corvée labor and taxes have become increasingly heavy,
and prisons are filled daily.
The common people are distressed and troubled,
many are willing to cause chaos.
Small-minded, foolish, and dangerous people
incite and mislead each other.
Although their power cannot achieve much,
one must still be vigilant.
According to the commentary on the Hóngfàn,
when the ruler's Way is deficient, there is a solar eclipse;
when the people are indignant and resentful, waters surge and overflow;
when yin energy accumulates, inferiors replace
superiors.
These subtle principles have already manifested as actual events.
Should your servant, by unfortunate chance, be correct in these misguided predictions,
it would certainly cause Your Majesty anxiety.
Now the imperial grandson is growing up,
Heaven has indeed established a spiritual foundation,
and the common people look with eager expectation,
truly hoping for benevolent grace.
Moreover, the year has reached the Wǔ position,
which is avoided by the element of Metal.
It is advisable at this time
to promote grace and spread beneficence,
then the fire energy will quietly dissipate,
and disasters will not arise.
Your Majesty, in accordance with Heaven's will above,
and in compliance with the people's sentiments below,
may take advantage of the imperial grandson's joyous occasion to issue a great amnesty to the
empire.
Thereafter, clarify penalties and rectify laws,
to bring order to officials,
to satisfy Heaven's heart,
and to comfort human affairs.
The myriad commoners would be exceedingly fortunate,
and auspicious omens would surely arrive.
What your servant now presents,
if considered briefly,
may not align with the sacred will;
but if pondered over time,
it will ultimately reveal your servant's sincerity.
If what I have presented is in accordance with the highest principles,
I beg Your Majesty not
to dismiss my words because of my person.
Your servant speaks without concealment,
and Your Majesty accepts it,
this is precisely to demonstrate the principle of a wise ruler and an upright minister."
The memorial was submitted
and accepted,
and a grand amnesty was issued, and the reign year was changed.
At that time, Rèn Gǔ (任谷), a man from Jìyáng (暨陽), was resting under a tree after plowing,
when suddenly a person dressed in feathered clothes came and had intercourse with him.
Afterwards, the person was nowhere to be found,
and Gǔ (谷) subsequently became pregnant.
After months, as he was about to give birth,
the feathered person returned.
He used a knife to pierce Gǔ's (谷) perineum
and pulled out a snake-child before leaving.
Gǔ (谷) then became a eunuch.
Later, he went to the palace gate and presented a memorial,
claiming to possess Daoist arts.
The Emperor kept Gǔ (谷) in the palace.
Puó (璞) again submitted a memorial, saying:
"What Rèn Gǔ (任谷) does is bizarre and uncanny,
without any logical cause.
Your Majesty, with your profound perception and extensive view,
wishes to understand his circumstances,
and so has brought him into the inner palace,
providing for his comfort.
Your servant has heard that a country is governed by proper rites,
not by strange evil.
What is heard depends solely on people,
hence the gods bestow good fortune.
Your Majesty maintains silence and dwells in rectitude,
every action conforming to established laws.
According to the Rites of Zhōu (周禮),
persons with strange attire and bizarre appearance are not admitted to the palace,
much less Gǔ (谷), who is the epitome of the uncanny and grotesque.
Yet he ascends to the hall for lectures
and is close to the side chambers of the palace,
staining the sun and moon,
and defiling the Heavenly audience.
This is what your humble servant privately disapproves of.
If Your Majesty truly believes Gǔ (谷) is possessed by spirits,
then he should be respected but kept at a distance.
For spirits are
intelligent, discerning, and upright,
to be approached with proper human conduct.
If Gǔ (谷) is considered a bewitching fraud,
then he should be banished to distant lands,
and not allowed to profane the purple gates.
If Gǔ (谷) is perhaps a warning from the gods, a harbinger of disaster for the state,
then one should restrain oneself and cultivate rites to dispel the omen,
not allow Gǔ (谷) to comfortably indulge
his evil perversions.
Your foolish servant believes that the harmonious interactions of yin and yang,
producing myriad transformations,
can also be imitated by foxes, weasels, and mountain sprites to cause mischief.
May Your Majesty heed your servant's foolish thoughts
and specifically send Gǔ (谷) away.
Your servant, due to a lack of talent,
has been unworthily entrusted with the duty of a historian.
How could I forget to write truthfully,
guided only by righteousness?"
Afterwards, Yuán Dì (元帝) died,
and Gǔ (谷) consequently fled.
Puó (璞) left his post due to mourning for his mother,
and divined a burial site in Jìyáng (暨陽),
about a hundred paces from the water.
People spoke of its proximity to water,
but Puó (璞) said:
"It will soon become dry land."
Later, sand accumulated,
and areas dozens of miles from the tomb all became mulberry fields.
Less than a year later,
Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed Puó (璞) as his Secretary and Military Advisor.
At this time, Chén Shù (陳述) from Yǐngchuān (潁川) was a clerk for the Grand General,
and had a good reputation,
esteemed by Dūn (敦).
Not long after, he died.
Puó (璞) wept for him very sorrowfully,
exclaiming:
"Sìzǔ (嗣祖),
Sìzǔ (嗣祖),
how do we know this isn't a blessing!"
Not long after, Dūn (敦) rebelled.
At that time, Míng Dì (明帝) had been on the throne for over a year
but had not yet changed the reign title,
and the planet Mars was stationed in Fáng (房).
Puó (璞) was then on leave,
so the Emperor sent an envoy with an imperial handwritten edict to consult Puó (璞).
Coincidentally, Jìyáng (暨陽) county again reported seeing a red crow.
Puó (璞) then submitted a memorial requesting to change the reign year and grant a general amnesty;
the text was too long to be recorded.
Puó (璞) once arranged a burial for someone.
The Emperor, in disguise, went to observe it,
and then asked the owner why he buried it at the 'dragon's horn' –
this method would lead to the extinction of the clan.
The owner said:
"Guō Puó (郭璞) said this is 'burying the dragon's ear',
and within three years it will lead to the arrival of the Son of Heaven."
The Emperor asked:
"Bring forth the Son of Heaven?"
He replied:
"It will bring the Son of Heaven to inquire."
The Emperor was very surprised by this.
Puó (璞) had always been good friends with Huán Yí (桓彝).
Whenever Yí (彝) visited him,
sometimes he found Puó (璞) in his wife's quarters,
and would simply enter.
Puó (璞) said:
"When you come,
you can directly enter other places,
but you must not seek me in the toilet.
Otherwise, both host and guest will suffer calamity."
Later, Yí (彝), while drunk, went to Puó (璞)'s place,
and found him exactly in the toilet.
He covered himself and watched,
seeing Puó (璞) naked, with disheveled hair,
holding a knife in his mouth, performing a libation ceremony.
When Puó (璞) saw Yí (彝),
he clutched his heart in great alarm and said:
"I repeatedly told you not to come,
yet you did this!
Not only will it bring disaster to me,
you too will not escape.
Heaven truly caused this;
whom shall I blame!"
Puó (璞) eventually suffered the calamity from Wáng Dūn (王敦),
and Yí (彝) also died in the rebellion of Sū Jùn (蘇峻).
When Wáng Dūn (王敦) was plotting rebellion,
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) had Puó (璞) divine about it.
Puó (璞) answered indecisively.
Jiào (嶠) and Liàng (亮) then asked him to divine their own fortune.
Puó (璞) said:
"Great fortune."
Jiào (嶠) and others withdrew,
and said to each other:
"Puó (璞)'s indecisive answer
means he dared not speak,
or perhaps Heaven has stripped Dūn (敦)'s courage.
Now we are undertaking a great matter with the state,
and Puó (璞) says 'great fortune',
which means our undertaking will surely succeed."
Thereupon they encouraged the Emperor to attack Dūn (敦).
Originally,
Puó (璞) often said,
"He who kills me is Shān Zōng (山宗)."
At this time, indeed there was a man named Chóng (崇) who slandered Puó (璞) to Dūn (敦).
When Dūn (敦) was about to raise an army,
he again had Puó (璞) divine.
Puó (璞) said:
"No success."
Dūn (敦) was already suspicious of Puó (璞)'s advice to Jiào (嶠) and Liàng (亮),
and upon hearing the ominous divination,
he asked Puó (璞):
"How much longer will Your Excellency live?"
He replied:
"Considering the previous divination,
if your lordship starts this venture,
calamity will certainly come soon.
If you stay in Wǔchāng (武昌),
your lifespan will be immeasurable."
Dūn (敦) was greatly enraged and said:
"How long will you live?"
He replied:
"My life ends today at noon."
Dūn (敦) was furious,
arrested Puó (璞),
and had him executed at Nángāng (南岡).
As Puó (璞) was being led out,
he asked the executioner where he was going.
He replied:
"To the top of Nángāng (南岡)."
Puó (璞) said:
"It must be under the twin cypress trees."
When they arrived,
it was indeed so.
He further said:
"There should be a large magpie's nest in this tree."
The crowd searched but could not find it.
Puó (璞) made them search again,
and indeed they found a large magpie's nest among the branches,
concealed by thick leaves.
Originally,
at the beginning of the restoration, Puó (璞) once traveled through Yuèchéng (越城).
There he encountered a man,
called out his name,
and gave him his trousers and jacket.
The man declined to accept,
but Puó (璞) said:
"Just take them;
you will understand later."
The man then accepted and left.
At this time,
it was indeed this man who carried out the execution.
He was forty-nine years old at the time.
After Wáng Dūn (王敦) was pacified,
Puó (璞) was posthumously granted the title of Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng (弘農).
Initially,
when Yǔ Yì 庾翼 was young, he once asked Pú 璞 to divine for his family and himself.
After the hexagram was formed,
it said:
"At the end of Jiàn Yuán 建元, mountains will collapse;
at the beginning of Cháng Shùn 長順, the son will wither."
When Emperor Kāng 康 ascended the throne,
he was about to change the reign title to Jiàn Yuán 建元.
Someone said to Yǔ Bīng 庾冰:
"Have you forgotten Guō Shēng's 郭生 words?
Qīu Shān 丘山 is a high name;
this title should not be used."
Bīng 冰 sighed with regret.
When the emperor died,
Hé Chōng 何充 changed the reign title to Yǒng Hé 永和.
Yǔ Yì 庾翼 sighed and said:
"The ways of Heaven are subtle and profound,
it must be so.
Cháng Shùn 長順 [meaning 'long duration and smoothness'],
is Yǒng Hé 永和 [meaning 'eternal harmony'],
how can I escape it!"
That same year, Yì 翼 died.
Bīng 冰 again asked for a divination regarding his descendants.
After the hexagram was formed,
it said:
"All your sons will be noble and prosperous;
however, if there is a white dragon,
an ominous omen will arrive.
If a tombstone grows gold,
it will be a great taboo for the Yǔ 庾 clan."
Later, Bīng's 冰 son Yùn 蘊 became the Cì Shǐ 刺史 of Guǎng Zhōu 廣州.
Suddenly, in his concubine's chamber, a newborn white puppy appeared,
and no one knew where it came from.
His concubine secretly cherished it,
not letting Yùn 蘊 know.
The dog grew bigger.
When Yùn 蘊 entered,
he saw the dog's eyebrows and eyes were distinct,
and its body was very long but weak,
different from ordinary dogs.
Yùn 蘊 was very surprised.
He was about to take it out
to show it to everyone,
when it suddenly disappeared.
Yùn 蘊 exclaimed with regret:
"Is it perhaps the white dragon!
Calamity has come to the Yǔ 庾 clan."
And then, his tombstone grew gold.
Soon after, he was annihilated by Huán Wēn 桓溫,
exactly as foretold.
All of Pú's 璞 divinations and verifications
were of this kind.
Pú 璞 compiled more than sixty instances of former and latter divinations and verifications,
naming it Dòng Lín 洞林.
He also copied the essential parts from various schools, such as Jīng 經 and Fèi 費,
and further compiled Xīn Lín Shí Piān 新林十篇 and Bǔ Yùn Yī Piān 卜韵一篇.
He annotated the Ěr Yǎ 爾雅,
separately creating Yīn Yì 音義 and Tú Pǔ 圖譜.
He also annotated Sān Cāng 三蒼, Fāng Yán 方言, Mù Tiān Zǐ Zhuàn 穆天子傳, Shān Hǎi Jīng 山海經, as well as Chǔ Cí 楚辭, Zǐ Xū 子虛, and Shàng Lín Fù 上林賦, amounting to hundreds of thousands of words,
all of which have been passed down to the world.
His poems, rhapsodies, eulogies, and panegyrics also numbered tens of thousands of words.
His son, Ào 驁,
reached the official position of Lín Hè Tài Shǒu 臨賀太守.
Gě Hóng 葛洪
Gě Hóng 葛洪, courtesy name Zhì Chuān 稚川,
was a native of Dān Yáng Jù Róng 丹楊句容.
His grandfather, Xì 系,
was the Dà Hóng Lú 大鴻臚 of Wú 吳.
His father, Tì 悌,
entered Jìn 晉 after Wú 吳 was pacified,
and served as Shào Líng Tài Shǒu 邵陵太守.
Hóng 洪 was fond of learning in his youth.
His family was poor,
so he personally cut firewood to trade for paper and brushes.
At night, he would copy books and recite them,
thus becoming known for his Confucian scholarship.
He had few desires by nature,
and no particular hobbies or amusements.
He did not know the number of moves in a board game,
nor the names of the teeth in a dice game.
He was a taciturn person,
not fond of glory or profit.
He kept his door shut and swept his path clear (of visitors),
never socializing.
In Yú Háng Shān 餘杭山, he saw Hé Yòu Dào 何幼道 and Guō Wén Jǔ 郭文舉,
but merely exchanged glances,
without speaking to each other.
At times, when seeking books or asking about meanings,
he would not hesitate to travel thousands of miles over rugged terrain and dangerous waters,
determined to obtain what he sought.
Thus, he thoroughly examined the classics,
and was particularly fond of the methods of nourishing life for immortals.
His granduncle, Xuán 玄,
learned the Dao and achieved immortality during the Wú 吳 period,
known as Gě Xiān Gōng 葛仙公.
He passed his secret alchemical arts to his disciple Zhèng Yǐn 鄭隱.
Hóng 洪 studied under Yǐn 隱,
and acquired all his methods.
Later, he studied under Bāo Xuán 鮑玄 of Shàng Dǎng 上黨, the Tài Shǒu 太守 of Nán Hǎi 南海.
Xuán 玄 was also skilled in inner arts,
and could predict the future.
Seeing Hóng 洪, he held him in deep regard,
and gave his daughter to Hóng 洪 in marriage.
Hóng 洪 inherited Xuán's 玄 teachings,
and also thoroughly mastered medical arts.
All his writings
were precise in distinguishing right from wrong,
and his literary talent was rich and abundant.
During the Tài Ān 太安 era,
Shí Bīng 石冰 rebelled.
Gù Mì 顧祕, the Tài Shǒu 太守 of Wú Xīng 吳興, became the Dū Dū 都督 of the righteous army,
and, with Zhōu Qǐ 周玘 and others, raised troops to suppress him.
Mì 祕 summoned Hóng 洪 as Jiāng Bīng Dū Wèi 將兵都尉.
He attacked Bīng's 冰 separate commander,
defeated him,
and was promoted to Fú Bō Jiāng Jūn 伏波將軍.
After Bīng 冰 was pacified,
Hóng 洪 did not seek rewards for his merits,
but went directly to Luò Yáng 洛陽,
wanting to search for rare books to broaden his learning.
Hóng 洪 saw that the world was already in chaos,
and wished to flee to the southern lands.
So he joined Jī Hán 嵇含, the Cì Shǐ 刺史 of Guǎng Zhōu 廣州, as a military advisor.
When Hán 含 was killed,
he remained in the southern lands for many years,
declining all summons and proclamations from garrisons and towns.
Later, he returned to his hometown,
and refused all invitations and appointments.
When Emperor Yuán 元 became Chancellor,
he was appointed as a Yuàn 掾.
For his achievements in pacifying bandits,
he was granted the title of Guān Nèi Hóu 關內侯.
At the beginning of Xián Hé 咸和,
Sī Tú Dǎo 司徒導 summoned him to be appointed as Zhōu Zhǔ Bù 州主簿.
He was then transferred to Sī Tú Yuàn 司徒掾,
and promoted to Zī Yì Cān Jūn 諮議參軍.
Gān Bǎo 干寶 was deeply fond of him as a friend,
and recommended Hóng's 洪 talent as suitable for national history.
He was selected as Sàn Qí Cháng Shì 散騎常侍,
and concurrently held the position of Dà Zhù Zuò 大著作.
Hóng 洪 firmly declined the appointment.
Being old,
he wished to refine elixirs to pray for a long life.
Hearing that alchemy ingredients were produced in Jiāo Zhǐ 交阯,
he requested to be appointed as Jù Lóu Lìng 句𧜞令.
The Emperor considered Hóng's 洪 rank too high
and did not grant his request.
Hóng 洪 said:
"It is not for glory,
but because there are alchemy ingredients there."
The Emperor agreed.
Hóng 洪 then traveled with his sons and nephews.
Upon reaching Guǎng Zhōu 廣州,
Cì Shǐ Dèng Yuè 鄧嶽 detained him and would not let him leave.
Hóng 洪 then settled in Luó Fú Shān 羅浮山 to refine elixirs.
Yuè 嶽 memorialized for him to be appointed as Dōng Guān Tài Shǒu 東官太守,
but he again declined.
Yuè 嶽 then appointed Hóng's 洪 nephew, Wàng 望, as Jì Shì Cān Jūn 記室參軍.
He spent many years on the mountain,
living a life of leisure and cultivation,
and writing incessantly.
His self-preface states: "My body lacks the talent for advancement,
and I happen to be fond of the task of non-action.
Even if I could spread my wings to soar to the dark firmament,
or exert my feet to chase the wind and tread on shadows,
I would still wish to fold my mighty wings among the wrens,
and hide my exceptional tracks among the lame donkeys.
How much more so, when the great earth has bestowed upon me short, ordinary wings,
and creation has lent me
the clumsiest of lame feet?
One who knows oneself examines carefully;
one who is incapable stops.
How dare I, with the strength of a common fly, aspire to soar to the heavens,
or, driving a lame turtle, chase the tracks of a flying hare?
To adorn the ugliness of Mó Mǔ 嫫母,
and seek the beautiful praise of Méi Yáng 媒陽?
To offer the base quality of sand and gravel,
and seek a thousand pieces of gold in the market of Hé Shì 和氏?
Indeed, to walk with the steps of Jiāo Yáo 僬僥 [dwarfs]
and hope to reach the footsteps of Kuā Fù 夸父 [a giant]
is why limited talents stumble and are hindered.
To be as frail as Yāo Lí 專離 and forcefully attempt to lift a heavy tripod
is why the man from Qín 秦 broke his sinews.
Therefore, I have cut off all hope from the path of glory and splendor,
and my will finds peace in a realm of poverty and obscurity.
For even wild herbs can be as sweet as rare delicacies,
and a humble dwelling can bring the joy of an ornate hall.
Thus,
I would not follow the powerful and noble,
even if they were a cubit away;
but to a person who knows the Dao,
I would certainly go, no matter how difficult or distant the journey.
I have examined many strange books,
and they are not few,
but most of them contain hidden meanings."
It is not easy to comprehend immediately,
and without utmost precision, one cannot investigate it thoroughly.
Without diligent effort, one cannot grasp it all.
Few Daoist scholars are learned and well-informed,
but many make arbitrary judgments and speak carelessly.
At times, when there are enthusiasts
who wish to cultivate themselves,
they suddenly do not know
where to begin,
and their doubts have no one to consult.
I have compiled this book
to generally expound on the principles of longevity.
Its most profound aspects cannot be expressed in writing;
rather, these rough words and brief explanations are to show one corner,
hoping that those who are frustrated can reflect on them and understand more than half.
How can one expect the ignorant and obtuse to fully grasp the subtle and far-reaching?
I merely
discuss what I have come to know first.
Worldly literati only know how to revere Zhōu Kǒng,
and do not trust the books of Immortals;
not only do they laugh heartily at them,
but they also slander the true teachings.
Therefore, the writings of mine concerning the affairs of yellow and white (alchemy)
are named Nèipiān (Inner Chapters),
while the rest, which refute objections and provide general explanations,
are named Wàipiān (Outer Chapters).
In total, there are one hundred and sixteen
chapters, both inner and outer.
Though they are not worthy of being stored in famous mountains,
I wish to seal them in a golden casket
to show to those who understand.
I call myself Bǎopúzǐ,
and thus named the book.
My other writings include one hundred volumes of steles, eulogies, poems, and rhapsodies;
thirty volumes of memorials, edicts, and petitions;
and ten volumes each of biographies concerning Immortals, virtuous officials, recluses, and collected anomalies.
I also compiled three hundred and ten volumes of excerpts from the Wǔjīng, historical records, Hàn Shū, various philosophical schools, and miscellaneous technical matters;
one hundred volumes of medical prescriptions from the Jīnguì Yàofāng (Golden Casket Prescriptions);
and four volumes of Zhǒuhòu Yàojí Fāng (Emergency Prescriptions Kept in the Elbow).
Hóng was widely read and deeply learned,
unrivaled south of the Jiāng.
His writings and compositions surpassed those of Bān Mǎ,
and he was also skilled at profound debate,
analyzing principles with utmost subtlety.
Later, he suddenly sent a letter to Yuè, saying:
"I shall soon travel far to seek a master;
I will depart on the appointed day."
When Yuè received the letter,
he rushed to bid farewell.
However, Hóng sat until midday,
motionless as if asleep, and then passed away.
When Yuè arrived,
he was unable to see him.
He was eighty-one years old at the time.
His complexion was as lifelike,
and his body was still soft.
When his body was lifted into the coffin,
it was very light,
like an empty garment.
People of the time believed he had attained Immortality through "corpse release."
The historian commented: Jǐngchún was devoted to his studies,
well-read and had a strong memory;
he comprehensively mastered various unusual books,
and resolved all past confusions;
his emotional depth was outstanding,
and his thoughts and achievements were extraordinary;
he inherited refined literature from the Western courts,
and displayed his eloquent sharp wit in the Southern summer,
becoming the patriarch of talent and learning in the restoration.
However, speaking of the strange and invoking spirits,
when the skill is perfected, it becomes disdained.
Previous sages left teachings
that scorned this path.
Jǐngchún's divination and calculation of destiny,
and his ability to know the future by examining the past,
surpassed Jīng Fáng and Guǎn Lù in their previous prognostication,
and excelled over Zǐ Zào in remote inscriptions.
Yet his official career was insignificant in the world,
and he was poorly treated by his contemporaries.
He humbly expressed his feelings through "guests' arrogance" (a literary device),
which was also a burden of his perfected skill.
But as for the great earth forming shapes,
and the dark heavens bestowing life,
good fortune and ill, long life and short,
these are fixed by nature.
Although observing omens might sometimes lead to understanding,
amulets are difficult to rely on;
what is endowed is inherent,
and there will certainly be no deviation.
One can simply live normally and await the end,
relaxing one's heart and submitting to fate.
Why go to the extent of holding a knife, letting one's hair down,
and rushing anxiously in obscure and filthy places?
Later, he offered loyal advice,
but could not save Wáng Dūn from his rebellion;
at first, he was ashamed of having cleverly escaped,
but eventually perished
by the plot of "Shān Zōng."
As Confucius said, "To attack other doctrines,
that is harmful indeed."
Alas!
Zhìchuān, from a young age, followed a master,
and even in old age, he never tired.
He delved into ancient texts,
compiling the remaining writings of a hundred generations;
he documented transformations in the Immortal City,
and exhausted the secret arts of the Nine Elixirs.
He abandoned fleeting glory and discarded miscellaneous skills,
devaluing a foot of jade but valuing an inch of time,
dwelling in virtue and residing in truth,
transcending worldly affairs.
The way of preserving life,
is it not the most excellent?
A eulogy says: Jǐngchún was brilliant and cultivated,
early demonstrating great talent.
He deeply studied bird-script (ancient writing),
and thoroughly understood turtle-shell divination.
It was not the nation's troubles,
but his own actions that brought about personal disaster.
Zhìchuān was gracious and learned,
poor yet content in the Dao.
He established this literature as a model,
and his grand writings will be eternally passed down.

marriage

He was then given his current official title with the additional post of Area Commander of the Expedition,
and led Generals Lù Yǒng (路永), Máō Bǎo (毛寶), Zhào Yìn (趙胤), Kuāng Shù (匡術), Liú Shì (劉仕), and others, with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry,
joining the Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn (陶侃) to jointly attack and defeat him.
Liàng (亮) returned to Wúhú (蕪湖)
and refused any titles or rewards.
Kǎn (侃) sent a letter saying:
"Rewards, punishments, demotions, and promotions
are the great trust of the state.
I am secretly puzzled that you alone so loftily act as a gentleman."
Liàng (亮) replied:
"The marshal gave the commands,
and the military officers carried them out;
what merit do I have?"
He strenuously declined to accept.
He was promoted to General Who Guards the West,
but again firmly declined.
Earlier,
for his merit in executing Wáng Dūn (王敦),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yǒngchāng (永昌) County.
Liàng (亮) repeatedly declined,
presenting dozens of memorials,
until this time he was finally permitted to refuse.
When Táo Kǎn (陶侃) died,
Liàng (亮) was transferred to Area Commander of military affairs in the six provinces of Jiāng (江), Jīng (荊), Yù (豫), Yì (益), Liáng (梁), and Yōng (雍),
concurrently serving as Inspector of the three provinces of Jiāng (江), Jīng (荊), and Yù (豫).
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the West, granted the privilege of establishing a staff office, acting as Governor, and granted the privilege of holding a staff of authority.
Liàng (亮) firmly declined the privilege of establishing a staff office,
and then was transferred to garrison Wǔchāng (武昌).
At that time, Wáng Dǎo (王導) was assisting in governance.
With the emperor young and the times difficult,
Dǎo (導) focused on the major principles,
not being constrained by minor details.
He entrusted responsibilities to generals like Zhào Yìn (趙胤) and Jiǎ Níng (賈寧),
who all failed to uphold the law,
which worried the high officials.
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) had once wanted to raise an army to depose Dǎo (導),
but Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) did not agree,
so he stopped.
At this time,
Liàng (亮) again wanted to lead his troops to remove Dǎo (導).
He consulted Jiàn (鑒) again,
but Jiàn (鑒) again disallowed it.
Liàng (亮) sent a letter to Jiàn (鑒) saying: "Previously in Wúhú (蕪湖), we repeatedly said that although his crimes were serious,
the times were chaotic and the state was in danger,
and for the time being, if the regional governors held superior moral authority,
it would be enough to suppress certain elements.
Therefore, we jointly concealed
and endured,
and explained this to Duke Táo (陶公).
From then until now,
there has been no sign of improvement.
The emperor, from eight or nine years old until adulthood,
when in the palace, was in the hands of palace women,
and when outside, only with military officers and petty men.
He had no one to teach him reading and recitation,
and when
asking questions, he never encountered a gentleman.
Although the attending officials are not outstanding scholars,
they are all good men of their time,
knowledgeable in ancient and modern affairs;
how can they be compared to palace generals and司馬督
in conversation?
Instead of saying that attending officials should be chosen from the best,
it is said that generals and司馬督 should be chosen from the best.
How does this accord with Jiǎ Shēng's (賈生) wish for the ruler to cultivate virtue,
and through practice, achieve
perfection?
Qín Zhèng (秦政) wanted to delude his common people,
and the world still knew it was wrong,
how much more so to delude his lord!
When the lord was young,
no wise and virtuous men were promoted
to assist and guide his sacred person.
Now that his spring and autumn are in their prime,
he should restore governance to the wise ruler.
Instead of bowing and returning power,
he merely occupies the revered position of a grand tutor;
an adult ruler
still receives the perverse
counsel of a teacher-minister.
The emperor knows that the way of ruler and minister should not be like this,
but he cannot but perform the acts of extraordinary deference.
The ruler of ten thousand chariots
is like the 'nine at the top' (上九)
line of 'Arrogant Dragon' (亢龍)
in the Yì Jīng (易經),
having a position but no one in charge.
Wielding the awe-inspiring power that shakes the ruler, he oversees all officials,
and no official dares to oppose him.
This means the former emperor had no minister with a dying injunction,
and power yielded
to the arrogant and treacherous, allowing them to thrive.
Zhào (趙) and Jiǎ (賈) and their ilk harbor disloyal hearts;
if this can be tolerated,
what cannot be tolerated?
Moreover, regarding past events, we tolerated and endured,
believing their crimes might be pardoned,
precisely because the times were chaotic and the state was in danger,
and military action could not be repeatedly taken.
We also hoped they would apologize
for past transgressions,
and out of fear, reform themselves.
But their recent indulgence
means they fear nothing above
and dread nothing below,
believing that fostering many scoundrels is sufficient to maintain control of the realm.
You,
my lord, and I, your humble servant, both received the profound trust of the previous court,
bearing the heavy responsibility entrusted to us.
If this great treachery is not swept away,
how can we face the former emperor in the afterlife?
I hope, my lord, you will deeply consider the long-term plan
for securing the state
and stabilizing the altars of soil and grain,
and then consider the burden of responsibility upon you and me,
assessing what is appropriate."
Jiàn (鑒) again disallowed it,
so the matter was dropped.
At that time, Shí Lè had just died.
Liàng had a plan to recover the Central Plains,
so he relinquished Yùzhōu and granted it to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Máo Bǎo,
sending him and Xīyáng Tàishǒu Fán Jùn with ten thousand elite troops
to garrison Zhūchéng.
He also appointed Táo Chēng as Nán Zhōngláng Jiāng and Jiāngxià Xiāng,
leading five thousand of his personal troops into Miǎnzhōng.
Liàng's younger brother, Yì, was Nánmán Xiàowèi and Nánjùn Tàishǒu,
garrisoned at Jiānglíng.
He appointed Wǔchāng Tàishǒu Chén Xiāo as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
to head towards Zǐwǔ.
He also dispatched a detachment to attack Shǔ,
reaching Jiāngyáng,
capturing the false Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Hóng
and Bājùn Tàishǒu Huáng Zhí,
and sending them to the capital.
Liàng was to lead a great army of one hundred thousand,
occupying Shíchéng,
to provide support for the various armies.
So he submitted a memorial, saying:
"The two enemies, Shǔ and Hú, are increasingly savage and cruel.
They assassinate each other internally,
with the masses rebelling and kinsmen abandoning them.
Shǔ is very weak, but Hú is still strong,
cultivating fields and defending simultaneously,
preparing for offensive advances.
Xiāngyáng borders Wǎn and Xǔ to the north,
and is blocked by the Hànshuǐ to the south.
Its defenses are sufficient for security,
and its land is sufficient for food.
Your servant should move his headquarters to Shíchéng below Xiāngyáng,
and also dispatch various armies to be spread out along the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers.
In a few years,
when the soldiers are well-trained,
we can seize the opportunity and advance simultaneously,
to approach the Hé and Luò rivers.
Once the great momentum is initiated,
the masses will know their survival or destruction,
opening a path for repentance and good deeds,
and pardoning those forced into crimes.
By relying on Heaven's timing,
aligning with human sentiment,
punishing the rebellious,
and avenging the great disgrace,
this is truly the primary task of the sacred court.
I beg Your Majesty to grant what has been stated
and assist in this endeavor.
As for Huáishì and Shòuyáng, which should be advanced upon and occupied,
your servant will immediately select and train forces.
I beg for deliberation among the high officials
to decide on the grand strategy."
The Emperor sent down his proposal for discussion.
At that time, Wáng Dǎo agreed with Liàng's idea,
but Xī Jiàn argued that resources were not yet ready,
and a large-scale expedition was not feasible.
Liàng again submitted a memorial,
intending to move his headquarters immediately.
Coincidentally, the enemy captured Zhūchéng,
and Máo Bǎo drowned himself.
Liàng offered his apologies,
demoted himself three ranks,
and served as Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
An imperial edict ordered his reinstatement.
Soon after, he was appointed Sīkōng,
with his other offices remaining as before,
but he steadfastly declined the appointment.
Since the fall of Zhūchéng, Liàng
fell ill from worry and grief.
When Wáng Dǎo passed away,
Liàng was summoned to be Sītú, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Lù Shàngshūshì,
but he again firmly declined,
and the Emperor permitted it.
In Xiánkāng sixth year (340 CE), he died
at the age of fifty-two.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi,
with the posthumous name Wénkāng.
When his funeral carriage arrived,
the imperial carriage personally attended.
At the burial,
he was again posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Yǒngchāng Gōng.
Liàng's younger brother, Bīng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has carefully considered past events,
and also heard my brother Liàng's words to us,
earnestly speaking on this matter.
That is why he repeatedly pleaded for permission,
for almost ten years.
How could it be merely out of a fondness for declining rather than due deference?
It was considering that past misfortunes nearly arose from Your Majesty's presence,
added to the late emperor's divine martial prowess,
whose calculations and strategies were comprehensive,
hence campaigns did not exceed their time,
and the fierce strong ones were annihilated.
Judging by achievements,
the merit belongs to the sagely ruler;
attributing it to destiny,
victory is not due to human effort.
As for people like Liàng,
relying on the vastness of the sagely strategy,
they were able to perform their duties;
what is there to discuss about deeds?
What is there to reward for merit?
And after suffering setbacks,
the blame exceeded previous achievements.
That is why Your Majesty graciously permitted his requests.
Liàng truly wished to exert himself to repay the divine favor.
How could he have known that his body would vanish in this sagely era,
and his humble aspirations would be forever cut short?
His sorrow over life and death,
his pain penetrates his very core.
I beg Your Majesty to issue a clear edict,
and fulfill your former benevolence,
then your servant Liàng, though dead, will not perish."
The Emperor acceded to it.
When Liàng was about to be buried,
Hé Chōng attended,
and sighed:
"Burying a jade tree in the earth,
how can human sentiment bear it?"
Previously,
Liàng's riding horse had a Dīlú,
and Yīn Hào believed it was unfavorable to the master,
urging Liàng to sell it.
Liàng said:
"How can one transfer one's own misfortune to another!"
Hào was ashamed and withdrew.
When Liàng was in Wǔchāng,
his subordinates, such as Yīn Hào and others,
went up to the South Tower on an autumn night to gather,
and unexpectedly, Liàng arrived.
The others were about to rise and make way for him.
Liàng slowly said:
"Gentlemen, stay a while.
This old man also feels a deep inspiration here."
He then sat on a Húchuáng and talked and recited with Hào and the others until the end of the sitting.
His frank and uninhibited conduct
was often of this kind.
He had three sons: Bīn, Xī, and Hé.
Bīn, at several years old,
had an extraordinary magnanimity.
Wēn Jiào once subtly tested him,
but Bīn's expression remained serene,
and he slowly knelt and said to Jiào:
"How could you be like this, honored sir?"
Those who discussed him said he was no less than Liàng.
During Sū Jùn's Rebellion,
he was killed.
Xī had a good reputation in his youth,
and was initially Wúgúo Nèishǐ.
At that time, Emperor Mù rather liked literature,
and Xī presented poems upon arriving at the commandery,
which contained much satirical admonition.
He then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty possesses sagely and enlightened virtue,
and is poised to bring about the transformations of Táng and Yú.
However, state affairs are vast and prolonged,
and the common people are impoverished and diminished.
To use the resources of a few prefectures
to manage the affairs of the four seas
– how can one fully describe the toil and exhaustion this entails!
In the past, Emperor Wén of Hàn lived in a prosperous era,
personally practicing frugality,
and deciding only four hundred cases,
almost achieving a state where punishments were set aside.
Jiǎ Yì sighed,
still speaking of a pile of firewood (meaning impending danger).
Comparing ancient times to the present,
it only increases my worry and fear.
Your Majesty's discernment is divinely bestowed,
illuminating every hidden corner.
The path of grand salvation
surely does not await blind counsel.
Your servant has received favor for generations,
and wishes to exert himself even slightly.
Having been appointed to the east,
personally witnessing the situation,
I dare, relying on great governance,
to offer my sincere foolishness.
I humbly beg that during your leisure from deciding affairs,
you would cast a brief glance upon this."
Most of his poems and essays are not recorded.
Xī died just as he was about to be given an important appointment.
His son, Zhǔn,
during the Tàiyuán era,
replaced Huán Shíqián as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ and Xī Zhōngláng Jiāng
from his position as Shìzhōng,
garrisoned at Lìyáng,
and died in office.
Zhǔn's son, Yuè,
was Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ during the Yìxī era.
Zhǔn's younger brother, Kǎi,
has his own biography.
Hé, courtesy name Dàojì,
loved learning
and possessed literary talent.
When his uncle Yì was about to move to Xiāngyáng,
Hé, then fifteen years old,
wrote a letter to admonish him, saying:
"I understand that you intend to advance and occupy Xiāngyáng,
displaying your might across Jīngchǔ,
and then both farm and garrison troops,
gradually approaching the Héluò region.
This would cause those inclined to submission to harbor virtue and attach themselves to you,
and the cruel and foolish to fear your power and turn to good.
The foundation of great peace
would then be established in a matter of days.
In ancient times, the Yīn dynasty attacked Guǐfāng,
and conquered it in three years.
Yuè Shēng defended Qí,
and it took many years.
Now, although the imperial court is prosperous,
it does not possess the might of Yīn.
Although the fierce Jié are in decline,
their ugly kind still has followers.
Moreover, the waters of Miǎnhàn
do not offer the defense of ten thousand ren.
Although Fāngchéng is steep,
it does not have the peril of a thousand xún.
Furthermore, the transport of supplies faces the difficulty of ascending against the current,
and the conscripted soldiers suffer from their arduous labor.
If desperate enemies, feeling pressed,
decide to fight to the death,
attacking from both east and west,
advancing simultaneously at head and tail,
then there will be the danger of supply lines being cut off,
and distant strategies will lack the advantage of a 'shuàirán' strike.
Considering this both in advance and retreat,
I see no feasibility.
This is evident to both the wise and the ignorant,
and heard by both the sagacious and the foolish,
let alone by those directly involved!
I wish that you would turn back your army and recall your banners,
carefully choose a strategy for complete victory,
repair city walls,
establish ramparts,
diligently farm,
and train soldiers.
If the evil fortune has a limit,
and Heaven destroys these barbarians,
then you can cross the river by boat to the north,
advance together in parallel,
and gallop by both water and land.
This would not take more than ten days or a month.
I hope you will carefully consider this long-term plan
and calculate what is feasible."
Yì was greatly impressed by him.
During the Shēngpíng era,
he replaced Kǒng Yán as the Administrator of Dānyáng,
and memorialized for the abolition of more than sixty heavy taxes.
At the beginning of the Tàihé era,
he replaced Wáng Kè as Zhōnglǐngjūn
and died in office.
His son,
Shàngshū Púyè,
was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū.
Yì, courtesy name Shūyù,
was praised by his elder brother Liàng in his youth for his broad understanding and straightforwardness.
When he reached manhood,
he was invited by Xīyáng Wáng Yáng,
but did not accept.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Chōng was Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
he carefully selected his staff
and appointed Yì as Gōngcáo.
He was then appointed Jìyáng Lìng,
and later Chōng's Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ,
then transferred to Sànqí Shìláng,
and promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Sū Jùn,
he was enfeoffed as Guǎngráo Nán.
He was then sent out to serve as Línchuān Tàishǒu,
and subsequently oversaw the military affairs of Liáng and Yōng prefectures,
then transferred to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted jiǎjié,
stationed in Wèixīng.
At that time, his elder brother Liàng commanded six prefectures,
and considering Yì's magnanimity and ability to accommodate the masses,
he therefore entrusted him with a distant post
to serve as a strategic support in the east and west.
Soon after, he was promoted to oversee the military affairs of the Qínzhōu Dīqiāng tribes.
Yì sent his Yámén Huò Zuǒ to escort the wives and children of the officers and soldiers,
but Zuǒ led over three hundred people to defect to Shí Jìlóng.
Liàng memorialized this,
and Yì was demoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
The court deliberated recalling him,
but Liàng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Yì governs the populace simply and with kindness.
Although the prefecture is small,
it relies on his lenient governance.
Zuǒ and his accomplices, being evil,
are not a large number.
Moreover, Yì's status is high;
he should not be lightly discussed for advancement or demotion over a minor matter.
The hearts of his civil and military officials have already stabilized,
and the bandit leader Ài Xiù has sent envoys to pledge allegiance.
Over five hundred people from Shàngluò who had surrendered to the bandits
hope for peace and stability,
without further fear."
The court assented to this.
Later, as his garrison was in a dangerous and remote location,
and supplies were difficult to maintain,
an imperial edict ordered Yì to lead his troops back to station at Bànzhōu.
Soon after, he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
then advanced to Xīzhōnglángjiàng, Inspector of the military affairs of Xuānchéng, Lújiāng, Lìyáng, and Ānfēng prefectures, and granted jiǎjié,
stationed in Wúhú.
Yì once presented a white feather fan to Chéngdì.
The emperor disliked it for not being new
and returned it.
Shìzhōng Liú Shào said:
"When the Bólíang Palace is built,
the master craftsman first resides beneath it;
when string and wind instruments play in harmony,
Kuí and Yá first listen to their sounds.
Yì presented the fan
for its quality, not its newness."
Later, Yì heard of this
and said:
"This man should be by the emperor's side."
He also once sent poisoned wine to Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yǔnzhī.
Wáng Yǔnzhī, sensing it was poisoned,
gave it to a dog to drink,
and the dog died.
He then secretly reported it.
The emperor said:
"The elder maternal uncle has already brought chaos to the world,
does the younger maternal uncle wish to do so again!"
Yì heard this
and consequently drank poisoned wine and died,
at the age of fifty.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Wèijiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn.
His son Tǒng succeeded him.
Tǒng, courtesy name Chángrén,
had a good reputation in his youth,
and was invited by Sīkōng and Tàiwèi,
but he declined them all.
He was appointed Fǔjūn, Huìjī Wáng Sīmǎ,
and then served as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Níngyí Hùjūn, and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu.
At the age of twenty-nine,
he died.
People of the time praised his talent and ability
and deeply lamented his death.
His son Xuánzhī
reached the office of Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
Bīng, courtesy name Jìjiān.
His elder brother Liàng was renowned for his virtue and teachings,
while Bīng established a reputation for elegance and simplicity.
All his younger brothers were led to love propriety,
and were highly regarded by public opinion.
Liàng often considered them the treasures of the Yǔ clan.
He was invited by Sītú,
but did not accept,
and was summoned to be Mìshū Láng.
For his participation in suppressing Huá Yì,
he was enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu.
Wáng Dǎo invited him to be Sītú Yòuchángshǐ,
and he was then appointed Wúguó Nèishǐ.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
he sent troops to attack Bīng,
who could not defend against them,
and abandoned the commandery to flee to Huìjī.
Huìjī Nèishǐ Wáng Shū appointed Bīng as Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn
to resist Jùn's separate commander Zhāng Jiàn in Wúzhōng.
At that time, Jiàn's faction was very numerous,
and none of the generals dared to advance first.
Bīng led his troops to attack and rout Jiàn,
then advanced west, taking advantage of the victory,
and proceeded to the capital.
He also sent Sīmǎ Téng Hán to attack the bandit's Shítouchéng,
and captured it.
Bīng's achievements were numerous,
and he was enfeoffed as Xīnwú Xiàn Hóu,
but he firmly declined to accept.
He was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
but again declined the appointment.
Sīkōng Xī Jiàn invited him to be Chángshǐ,
but he did not accept.
He was then appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn, Huìjī Nèishǐ.
He was summoned to be Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
but again declined.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, Dūdū of the military affairs of Yáng, Yù, and Yǎn prefectures, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, and granted jiǎjié.
At this time, Wáng Dǎo had just passed away,
and people's hearts were uneasy.
Since Bīng's elder brother, Liàng, had firmly declined to enter service,
the hopes of the populace turned to Bīng.
As he took on this heavy responsibility,
he managed state affairs
without rest, day or night.
He treated court officials with courtesy
and promoted junior talents.
Because of this, the court and the public focused their attention on him,
all calling him a worthy chancellor.
Initially,
when Dǎo assisted in governance,
he always favored leniency and benevolence,
but Bīng was rather inclined towards severity and punishment.
Yīn Róng remonstrated with him,
and Bīng said:
"The former chancellor was worthy,
yet even he could not endure such magnanimity,
how much less can I!"
Fàn Wāng said to Bīng:
"Recently, celestial phenomena have been anomalous,
Your Excellency should fully implement measures to avert and defend against them."
Bīng said:
"How can I fathom the mysterious celestial phenomena?
One should simply diligently do one's best in human affairs."
He also thoroughly investigated household registrations,
discovering over ten thousand unlisted individuals,
to replenish military resources.
An imperial edict again discussed his previous merits,
and Bīng submitted a memorial, saying:
"My family, unfortunately,
with my humble talent, assisted in state affairs,
causing transgressions to reach the imperial court,
and calamity to afflict my clan.
If the Jin laws were clear and bright,
I would have been executed long ago.
But at that time of upheaval,
the penal code temporarily fell into disuse,
thus allowing your servants to once again exert their efforts for the times.
Ministers devoted to the state
thereby rose up,
achieving merits after great faults,
establishing righteousness after devastation.
This is why your servants are still able to breathe in this world,
and the imperial law does not necessarily clarify past transgressions.
This immense fortune
can be called grand.
How can one again calculate merits and receive enfeoffment,
or accept rewards from the Ministry of Merit!
I wish Your Majesty would graciously bestow your divine favor,
mercifully pardoning from the heart,
issuing a decree to the relevant officials,
granting your servant's request.
Then the wish of your foolish servant will be fulfilled."
The request was granted.
Emperor Chéng was gravely ill.
At that time, someone falsely created an imperial edict
forbidding the chancellor from approaching the palace gate.
All the attendants turned pale.
Bīng remained calm,
saying:
"This must be a fabrication."
An investigation was conducted,
and it was indeed a fraud.
The hearts of the populace then settled.
He was promoted to the title of Left General.
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
he was further promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Fearing his excessive power,
Bīng requested an external posting.
Coincidentally, his younger brother Yì was about to attack Shí Jìlóng,

so Bīng was appointed, with his original title, as Supervisor of Military Affairs of seven prefectures: Jiāng, Jīng, Níng, Yì, Liáng, Jiāo, Guǎng, and four commanderies of Yù prefecture, concurrently Governor of Jiāng Prefecture, and granted a staff of authority,
to garrison Wǔchāng,
as support for Yì.
As Bīng was about to depart,
he submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant, due to family favor,
holds a prominent position in society,
yet has no extraordinary aspirations,
and my capacity does not reach far.
Recently, the imperial house has faced many difficulties,
and troubles have frequently recurred.
Court luminaries and national
talents
have perished with the times,
leading to the imperial favor descending
upon your servant.
I have served humbly
for five years now.
Upwards, I have failed to brilliantly assist the emperor's plans,
and downwards,
I have failed to clarify the principles of governance.
Yet Your Majesty treats me excessively,
and ceaselessly seeks more from me,
again deploying a broken-down carriage's steeds
with the hope of achieving a thousand-mile feat.
If not for the profound
imperial favor,
how could this have happened!
Therefore, I dare to exhaust my foolishness
and present my heartfelt sincerity,
wishing Your Majesty would temporarily put aside the imperial crown
to magnify your acceptance of advice.
Currently, the strong enemies are not yet annihilated,
and the war chariots are not yet sheathed.
Our soldiers are weak in the fields,
and the people are exhausted within.
The extent of enemy incursions
cannot yet be measured;
the distress of the common people
is not
yet appeased;
the utilization of various talents
is not yet exhausted.
Yet Your Majesty is elevated,
and affairs are separated from those below.
Your observation and scrutiny
must be entrusted to your subordinates.
Your subordinates
should be loyal,
not advancing without being drawn forth;
all officials should be diligent,
not striving without supervision or encouragement.
This is why ancient emperors diligently condescended to accept advice.
Even if they managed myriad affairs daily,
they still listened
to generals and chancellors;
sometimes they sought counsel from wagon drivers,
or sought criticism from woodcutters,
there was good reason for this.
How much more so given the current abuses,
the extreme of times of creation.
Yet Your Majesty's reign falls
upon this era,
the difficulties of obstruction and decay afflict Your Sacred Person,
which is why the whole world grieves over the past and looks eagerly towards the future.
We sincerely hope that misfortune will end and prosperity will begin,
and that this era is now.
I sincerely wish Your Majesty to broaden the magnanimity of the heavens,
deepen the benevolence of the earth,
make humility your foundation,
and diligent instruction and supervision your duty.
Widely draw in
the talents of the age,
inquire about the path of governance.
The successes and failures of the court must reach Your Sacred Hearing,
and the true and false sentiments of the people must reach Your Heavenly Understanding.
Then, consider the greater truths,
to manage the national order.
If you personally practice frugality and moderation,
Yáo and Shùn will not be far off!
A simple cloth robe,
what kind of person was Wèi Wén!
Therefore, the ancients said:
'It is not difficult to know,
but difficult to act;
it is not
difficult to act,
but difficult to persevere.'
I wish Your Majesty would consider your daily humility and caution,
and accept the sentiment of 'giving me a start',
then the world will be greatly fortunate."
"Your servant, morning and evening,
holds this to his breast,
yet cannot fully express it.
As I approach this memorial, I hesitate,
unaware that my words are exhausted."
A short while later,
Empress Xiàn took charge of the court,
summoning Bīng to assist in governance.
Bīng declined, citing severe illness.
Soon after, he passed away,
at the age of forty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Sānmù (侍中, Attendant at the Imperial Household) and Sīkōng (司空, Minister of Works),
with the posthumous name Zhōngchéng (忠成, Loyal and Accomplished),
and worshipped with a grand sacrifice.
Bīng was by nature clear-minded and cautious,
always living with frugality.
His second son, Xí, once borrowed ten bolts of official silk.
Bīng was enraged,
beat him,
and had the silk bought and returned to the government.
Before his death,
he said to his Chief Clerk, Jiāng Pī:
"I am about to pass away.
I regret that my ambition to repay the country has not been realized.
Such is fate!
On the day of my death,
shroud me in everyday clothes;
do not use official items."
When he died,
there was no silk to make a quilt.
Moreover, his house had no concubines,
and his family had no private savings.
The world praised him for this.
Bīng had seven sons: Xī, Xí, Yǒu, Yùn, Qiàn, Miǎo, Ròu.
Xī's courtesy name was Shǐyàn.
Initially, he was appointed Mìshū Láng.
He successively rose to Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ, Huángmén Shìláng, and Jiàn'ān Tàishǒu.
Before he could be formally appointed,
he was again made Chángshǐ concurrently Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
then went out as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wúguó Nèishǐ.
Since Xī was related to the empress,
and Bīng's daughter was also the consort of Hǎixī Gōng,
therefore, Xī and his brothers were all prominent and noble.
During the Tàihé reign,
Xī was Běi Zhōngláng Jiāng and the Cǐshǐ of Xú and Yǎn two zhōu,
Yùn was Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
both granted jǐajié.
Yǒu was Dōngyáng Tàishǒu,
Qiàn was Tàizǎi Chángshǐ,
Miáo was Kuàijī Wáng Cānjūn,
Róu was Sànqí Chángshì.
Qiàn had the most talent and capacity,
and Huán Wēn deeply feared him.
Initially,
Mùróng Lì besieged Liángfù,
cutting off the water of the stream.
Tàishān Tàishǒu Zhūgé Yōu fled to Zōushān.
Several commanderies like Lǔ and Gāopíng were all lost.
Xī was dismissed from office because of this.
A short while later,
he was summoned to be Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Xī was angry
and firmly declined.
When Xī was first dismissed,
he had stolen a lot of military supplies from the Běifǔ army.
Wēn subtly prompted the relevant authorities to impeach him,
and he was again dismissed due to this crime.
He then became a guest in Jìyáng, Jìnlíng.
Initially,
Guō Pú had divined for Bīng, saying:
"Your descendants will surely face great disaster.
Only by employing 'Three Yángs' can you have continuity of descendants."
Therefore, Xī sought to be garrisoned at Shānyáng,
Yǒu at Dōngyáng,
and their family settled at Jìyáng.
When Hǎixī Gōng was deposed,
Huán Wēn implicated Qiàn and Róu as partisans of Wǔlíng Wáng
and killed them.
Upon hearing of the trouble, Xī immediately fled with his younger brother Miáo and his son Yōuzhī into the marshlands of Hǎilíng.
Yùn died by drinking poison in Guǎngzhōu.
When Yǒu was about to be executed,
Yǒu's daughter-in-law,
who was Huán Mì's daughter,
pleaded with Wēn,
and thus he was spared.
The former Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Wǔ Shěn,
who was Xī's maternal cousin,
secretly provided Xī with provisions for a year.
Wēn later found out
and sent soldiers to arrest Xī.
Wǔ Shěn's son, Zūn, and Xī gathered a crowd by the seashore,
seized fishermen's boats,
and entered Jīngkǒu city at night.
Píng Běi Sīmǎ Biàn Dān scaled the city wall and fled to Qǔ'ā.
All the officials and soldiers scattered and fled.
Xī released several hundred prisoners in the city,
equipped them with weapons.
Zūn gathered people outside,
proclaiming that the rebel Huán Wēn had deposed the emperor and murdered princes,
and, claiming Hǎixī Gōng's secret edict,
they were executing the evil rebels.
The capital was shaken and disturbed,
with internal and external martial law,
and defensive preparations at the six gates.
Píng Běi Cānjūn Liú Shì, along with Gāopíng Tàishǒu Xī Yìzhī and Yóujūn Dūhù Guō Lóng and others, gathered forces to resist them.
Biàn Dān, along with Hóng Róng of Qǔ'ā, mobilized two thousand soldiers from various counties,
and together they garrisoned Xīnchéng to attack Xī.
Xī was defeated in battle
and closed the city gates to defend himself.
Wēn sent Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu Zhōu Shàosūn to suppress him.
The city fell,
and he was captured.
Xī, Miáo, and five of his sons and nephews were executed in Jiànkāng market.
Zūn and his partisans were all put to death.
Only Yǒu and Yùn's sons were spared.
Yǒu's son, Shúxuān,
was Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Yùn's son, Kuòzhī,
was Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
Tiáo's courtesy name was Yòuxù.
Initially, he was invited to the Tàizǎi Fǔ.
He successively rose to Huángmén Láng and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
He was summoned to be appointed Mìshū Jiān,
and granted the title Xiāngtíng Hóu.
He went out as Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Línchuān Tàishǒu.
Huáng Tāo of Yùzhāng proclaimed himself Xiàoshén Huángdì,
and Lǐ Gāo of Línchuān became his Prime Minister.
They gathered several hundred partisans,
rode in ox-carts,
wore black robes,
and attacked commanderies and counties.
Tiáo suppressed them.
Tiáo was the most mediocre among his brothers,
hence his official emoluments and positions did not reach high.
He died in office
and was posthumously granted Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
Yì's courtesy name was Zhìgōng.
He had a magnificent demeanor and presence,
and from a young age possessed great strategic plans for governing the state.
Dù of Jīngzhào and Yīn Hào of Chénjùn both had talents and reputations that crowned the age,
but Yì did not hold them in high regard.
He often said to people:
"These fellows should be bound and kept in high cabinets,
awaiting the pacification of the world,
only then should their appointments be discussed."
When he saw Huán Wēn in his youth,
he already anticipated his great strategic ability,
and thus spoke to Emperor Chéng, saying:
"Huán Wēn possesses the talent of a hero.
I wish Your Majesty would not treat him as an ordinary person,
nor simply as a son-in-law.
He should be entrusted with important responsibilities as a regional commander,
and he will surely achieve great merit in assisting during difficulties."
When Sū Jùn staged a rebellion,
Yì was twenty-two years old at the time.
His elder brother Liàng made him, as a commoner, lead several hundred men
to defend Shítou.
When Liàng was defeated,
he fled with Yì.
After the matter was settled,
he was first invited to Tàiwèi Táo Kǎn's staff,
then transferred to Cānjūn,
and successively rose to Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
While in public office,
he discussed and advised with composure.
A short while later,
he was appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and Póyáng Tàishǒu.
He was transferred to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
He pacified and harmonized the common people
and gained much popular affection.
He was promoted to Nánmán Xiàowèi,
concurrently Nánjùn Tàishǒu,
and additionally Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and jǐajié.
When Zhūchéng was lost
and Shíchéng was besieged,
Yì repeatedly deployed surprise troops
and secretly delivered provisions and weapons.
Shíchéng was preserved,
which was Yì's achievement.
He was granted the title Dūtíng Hóu.
When Liàng died,
Yì was appointed Dūdū Jiāng Jīng Sī Yōng Liáng Yì Liù Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, and jǐajié,
replacing Liàng to garrison Wǔchāng.
As the emperor's maternal uncle,
Yì was young and held a supernumerary important post,
drawing attention from far and near,
with concerns that he might not be competent.
Yì always exerted his utmost ability and will,
worked diligently and humbly without slackness.
His military administration was strict and clear,
and his strategies were profound and far-reaching.
Within a few years,
both public and private resources were abundant,
and people's sentiments were in accord,
praising his talent and capability.
Because of this, all regions south of the Hé river felt inclined to submit.
Shí Jìlóng's Rǔnán Tàishǒu Dài Kāi led several thousand men to Yì to surrender.
He also sent envoys eastward to Liáodōng
and westward to Liángzhōu,
seeking assistance from both regions,
intending to launch a major joint campaign.
Mùróng Huàng and Zhāng Jùn both responded to his envoys, requesting a date.
Yì naturally possessed great ambition,
desiring to take on the responsibility of eliminating the barbarians and pacifying Shǔ.
His discussions were spirited and profound,
manifesting in his words and expressions.
Jiāngbīng Dūwèi Qián Qí presented matters that aligned with his intentions,
and Yì promoted him to Wǔpǐn Jiāngjūn
and bestowed upon him two hundred hú of grain.
At that time, the eastern territories had many levies and corvées.
The common people thus traveled by sea to Guǎngzhōu.
Cìshǐ Dèng Yuè extensively opened foundries,
and various barbarians consequently learned to manufacture weapons.
Yì submitted a memorial, stating that the eastern border was vital to the state,
but constant harassment led to increasing numbers of fugitives.
The barbarians were always looking for opportunities,
and if they learned the advantages of founding and casting,
it would become uncontrollable.
At that time, Yīn Hào 殷浩 summoned Yú Yì 庾翼 but he did not accept the appointments.
Yú Yì 庾翼 requested to be Sīmǎ 司馬 and Jūnsī 軍司,
but Yīn Hào 殷浩 would not agree.
Yú Yì 庾翼 sent a letter to Yīn Hào 殷浩,
thereby conveying his intentions.
Previously,
Yīn Hào’s 殷浩 father, Yīn Xiàn 殷羨, had been the Administrator of Chángshā 長沙.
While in the commandery, he was greedy and cruel.
His elder brother, Yīn Bīng 殷冰, wrote a letter to Yú Yì 庾翼 about this, entrusting him with the matter.
Yú Yì 庾翼 replied:
“When Mr. Yīn 殷君 first went there,
although he was arrogant and overbearing,
he actually brought beneficial vigor,
and it also seemed to be because he had good sons and younger brothers,
which prevented public sentiment from finding it difficult.
However, for some time now,
his public service has further declined,
while his private burdens have grown daily,
yet he has not been slightly worried by this.
I already deeply respect Hóngyuǎn 洪遠 (Yīn Hào 殷浩’s courtesy name),
and also have a close friendship with Hào 浩.
How can his father and brother's successes and failures
be measured by trivial considerations?
Generally, the administration in Jiāngdōng 江東
favors the powerful and influential,
and regards them as pests to the people.
When laws are enforced,
they are always applied to the poor and weak.
For example, last year, a million *hú* 斛 of grain were stolen from Shítou Cāng 石頭倉,
all by powerful generals,
yet the granary supervisors were simply beaten to death to take the blame.
Shān Xiá 山遐 served as Administrator of Yúyáo 餘姚 for half a year,
and brought out two thousand households for the government.
Although his administration was not flawless,
he was a strong and capable official.
Yet the group jointly drove him away,
preventing him from having a moment’s peace.
Jǐ Mù 紀睦 and Xú Níng 徐寧 were dispatched by the king to investigate criminals.
As their boats reached the shore,
Huán Yì 桓逸 restored order,
and the two envoys were dismissed from office.
Although these were all the folly and mistakes of former ministers,
the decline of Jiāngdōng 江東 was
truly due to these reasons.
My brothers and I are unfortunate
to be caught in this situation.
Since we cannot extricate ourselves from the dusty world,
we must jointly open our eyes and manage it.
Of the twenty commanderies unified by Jīngzhōu 荊州,
only Chángshā 長沙 is the worst.
If it is bad but not removed,
how is that any different from killing the supervisors to take the blame?”
Yú Yì 庾翼 possessed vigor and discernment;
his pronouncements and arguments were always like this.
When Emperor Kāng 康帝 ascended the throne,
Yú Yì 庾翼 wanted to lead his troops on a northern expedition.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
“The bandit Jì Lóng 季龍 (Shí Hǔ 石虎) is already sixty years old.
His extravagance and licentiousness have reached their limit,
and his vile followers resent and rebel against him.
He also intends to fight to the death in Liáodōng 遼東.
Although Guān Huǎng 關皝 (Mùróng Huǎng 慕容皝) is brave and resolute,
he may not be able to hold out.
If there are no northern barbarians to restrain us,
then Jiāngnán 江南 will be no different from Liáozuǒ 遼左.
This is why I boldly mobilize good men,
disregarding indignation and blame.
However, military support from east and west may not be launched simultaneously.
I intend to advance north
and move my garrison to Ānlù 安陸,
entering Miǎnshǔi 沔水 five hundred *lǐ* 里,
where Xùnshuǐ 溳水 flows unimpeded.

I shall lead the thirty thousand elite troops of the Administrator of Nánjùn 南郡, Wáng Qiānqī 王愆期, the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià 江夏, Xiè Shàng 謝尚, the Administrator of Xúnyáng 尋陽, Yuán Zhēn 袁真, and the Administrator of Xīyáng 西陽, Cáo Jù 曹據, etc.
to rush along the road.
At the same time, I shall order General who Pacifies the North, Huán Xuān 桓宣, to attack and seize Huáng Jì 黃季 (Huáng Huáng 黃晃).
I wish to combine the Dānshuǐ 丹水 forces
and shake Qín Yōng 秦雍.
By governing with a long rein
and using rest to await exhaustion,
within several years,
restoration can be hoped for.
Once I am in Xǔluò 許洛,
I humbly suggest that Huán Wēn 桓溫 can cross to garrison Guǎnglíng 廣陵,
Hé Chōng 何充 can move to occupy Huáishǔi 淮水 and Sīshǔi 泗水 at Zhěqí 赭圻,
and Lù Yǒngjìn 路永進 can move his troops to Héféi 合肥.
I earnestly wish that on the day this memorial is presented, Your Sacred Judgment will be made promptly.
One should not extensively inquire about agreements and disagreements,
which would interfere with the opportune moment.
I have heard of the swiftness of clumsy generals,
but never of the prolonged success of skilled ones.”
Thereupon, he mobilized the slaves from the six prefectures under his command, as well as chariots, oxen, donkeys, and horses,
causing the common people to lament and resent.
At the time, he wished to advance towards Xiāngyáng 襄陽,
but fearing the imperial court would not permit it,
he used Ānlù 安陸 as a pretext.
The Emperor and court officials all sent envoys to dissuade him,
and the Chēqí Cānjūn 車騎參軍 Sūn Chuò 孫綽 also sent a letter of remonstrance.
Yú Yì 庾翼 did not comply,
and thus, defying the imperial edict, he proceeded.
Upon reaching Xiàkǒu 夏口, he again submitted a memorial, saying: “Your subject recently observed that the Hu 胡 barbarians showed signs of exhaustion and decline.
I temporarily led my forces
to campaign north of the mountains,
and divided my troops
to recover several cities in Jiāngxià 江夏.
Your subjects, on
the nineteenth day of the ninth month, departed Wǔchāng 武昌,
and on the twenty-fourth day, arrived at Xiàkǒu 夏口.
I immediately selected troops and arranged for transport, preparing to set off.
However, the oxen and horses that were requisitioned
came from
far-off places,
and the common people's
grain and fodder were insufficient.
Most were emaciated and weak,
making it difficult to travel.
Moreover, with winter approaching,
wild grasses are gradually withering.
A round trip of two thousand *lǐ* 里,
might
lead to stumbling and exhaustion.
Therefore, I immediately weighed the circumstances
and temporarily halted this expedition.
Furthermore, in the cities south of the mountains,
every autumn and winter,
the waters often dry up,
making transport of provisions
truly
difficult.
Considering Xiāngyáng 襄陽,
the ancient territory of Jīng Chǔ 荊楚,
it borders Yìliáng 益梁 to the west,
and is but a short distance from Guānlǒng 關隴.
To the north, it is less than a thousand *lǐ* 里
from Luòhé 洛河.
Its soil is fertile and its fields good,
Fāngchéng 方城
is steep and strategically important.
Waterways are unobstructed,
and transportation unimpeded.
Advancing, one can sweep away Qín Zhào 秦趙;
retreating, one can secure the upper reaches of the river.
Although your subject is not martial,
and my intentions and strategies are shallow and short-sighted,
I bear the heavy grace of the state,
and am determined to achieve merit.
Thus, in the four years since receiving my appointment,
I have only focused on military training.
I truly wish to rely on the awe-inspiring divine strategies of the Sacred Court above,
and below, the sincere righteous indignation of the officers and
people,
to take advantage of the enemy's decline
and gradually press upon them.
However, in the spring of the eighth year, I submitted a memorial requesting to occupy Yuèxiāng 樂鄉,
and expand agriculture,
to await the opportune moment of the two bandits’
weakness.
But at that time, the heavens were high and ears far,
and my request was not observed.
Court deliberations were divided,
and thus my humble sincerity could not be expressed.
Since then,
observing the signs from heaven and man above,
and gathering information from defectors and captives below,
the decline and destruction of the Hu 胡 barbarians
is not far off.
Although your subject has not yet been able to drive straight into the Central
Plains,
and behead the vicious villains,
neither can I fail to advance and occupy strategic points,
and consider appropriate tactics for attack and capture.
Therefore, I have immediately assessed the situation and decided to enter Miǎnshuǐ 沔水
and move the garrison to Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
As for Xiè
Shàng 謝尚, Wáng Qiānqī 王愆期, and others,
I have ordered them all to return to their original garrisons.
Upon their arrival at their respective locations,
they shall swiftly dispatch reports to inform you.”
Yǔ Yì at that time had a force of forty thousand men,
an imperial edict added to him the title of Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Jūnfèng.
〔一二〕His army reached Xiāngyáng,
where he gathered all his subordinates,
displayed his banners and armor,
and personally gave a bow and arrow,
saying:
"My expedition
will be like this shot."
He then rose and shot three times, each time hitting the target perfectly;
his troops watched,
and their morale increased tenfold.
Initially,
when Yǔ Yì moved to Xiāngyáng,
the entire court considered it impossible.
Some deliberators said it was to avoid misfortune.
Only his elder brother Yǔ Bīng agreed,
and Huán Wēn and Qiáo Wáng Wújì approved his plan.
By this time,
Yǔ Bīng requested to be stationed at Wǔchāng,
to provide continuous support for Yǔ Yì.
The court deliberations held that Yǔ Bīng should not go,
so Yǔ Bīng ceased.
Furthermore, Yǔ Yì was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently held the post of Nánmán Xiàowèi.
Five to six hundred Xī Hú cavalry emerged from Fánchéng;
Yǔ Yì dispatched Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Cáo Jù to pursue and attack them north of Náogōu.
He defeated them,
nearly half died,
and a hundred horses were captured.
Yǔ Yì pacified the wilderness,
diligently seeking to appropriately attract and gather people,
establishing guest houses,
and setting up Diǎnbīn Cānjūn.
After Huán Xuān died,
Yǔ Yì appointed his eldest son Yǔ Fāngzhī as Yìchéng Tàishǒu,
〔一三〕 to take charge of Huán Xuān's forces.
Yìng Dàn was made Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu.
The Cānjūn Sīmǎ Xūn was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
to garrison Xīchéng.
Emperor Kāng died,
and his elder brother Yǔ Bīng also died.
Due to the circumstances of family and state,
he left Yǔ Fāngzhī to garrison Xiāngyáng,
and returned to guard Xiàkǒu.
He took all the troops previously led by Yǔ Bīng and distributed them himself,
appointing his brother's son Yǔ Tǒng as Xúnyáng Tàishǒu.
An imperial edict ordered Yǔ Yì to return and oversee Jiāngzhōu,
and also concurrently hold the post of Yùzhōu Cìshǐ;
he declined Yùzhōu.
He again wanted to move his garrison to Lèxiāng,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
He repaired military equipment,
extensively cultivated fields and accumulated grain,
intending to plan for a future expedition.
He sent Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Fǔ and Xīyáng Tàishǒu Cáo Jù to attack Shǔ,
where they defeated the Shǔ general Lǐ Huán at Jiāngyáng.
〔一四〕
Yǔ Yì went to the latrine
and saw a creature resembling a Fāngxiāng;
shortly after, a carbuncle erupted on his back.
His illness worsened.
He memorialized to appoint his second son Yǔ Yuánzhī as acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Sīmǎ Zhū Táo as Nánmán Xiàowèi,
with a thousand men to guard Bālíng.
He died in the first year of Yǒnghé (345 CE),
at the age of forty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous name Sù.
Not long after Yǔ Yì's death,
his subordinate generals Gān Zàn, 〔一五〕 Dài Xī, and others rebelled,
killing Jiāngjūn Cáo Jù.
Yǔ Yì's Zhǎngshǐ Jiāng Páo, Sīmǎ Zhū Táo, Jiāngjūn Yuán Zhēn, and others jointly put them down.
Yǔ Yuánzhī possessed Yǔ Yì's demeanor,
but was soon deposed by Huán Wēn.
After Huán Wēn had deposed Yǔ Yuánzhī,
he then appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Tán to oversee the military affairs in Miǎnzhōng,
concurrently holding the post of Yìchéng Tàishǒu,
replacing Yǔ Fāngzhī.
Both Yǔ Fāngzhī and Yǔ Yuánzhī were then moved to Yùzhāng.
The historian comments: Families of imperial relatives by marriage
shine brilliantly in the Jiāoyè;
clans of maternal uncles
share the same spirit in the Lánguī.
None fail to rely on imperial favor and private connections,
ascending through dangerous visits to the emperor.
Their gates conceal a golden abyss,
their status makes them arrogant;
their horses control dragon steeds,
their power becomes oppressive.
In ancient times, the virtuous were honored, and imperial relatives were kept in a secondary position,
thereby blocking the path of excessive private indulgence.
Though loved, their faults were recognized,
and the disaster of overflowing power was deeply guarded against.
Therefore, they were given generous gifts of precious jade,
but rarely promoted to important positions.
The clan of Túshān in Xià
did not share the same drive as Kǎi and Jì;
the Sì Shì in Zhōu
did not participate in the ranks of Yān and Qí.
The sages' foresight
was indeed profound!
The Jìn dynasty favored Yuánguī,
allowing him to participate in hearing the dying emperor's instructions.
Yet, his brush spread out splendid prose,
his lips let loose a torrent of words.
He was on par with the gentry,
fully capable of being an outstanding figure.
But his wisdom was small and his ambitions great,
oblivious to the long-term plans for governing the state;
his talent was high but his insight meager,
lacking a lasting strategy for national security.
When the jade calyxes (Yǔ Yì and his kin) were purged,
public opinion praised the 'uprooting of the root';
when the ivory rule offered guidance,
the emperor's concern was deeper regarding those who bore arms.
This caused Sū Zǔ to seek war,
and the ancestral temple was almost overturned.
Subsequently, he became suspicious of the Shàngzǎi
and plotted to remove the Fùtú.
Had Xī Jiàn collaborated,
surely military chariots would have violated order,
then what difference
〔一六〕 would there have been from those like Tái, Chǎn, Ān, and Jié!
Fortunately, a great peril was averted,
escaping destruction of the imperial statutes.
This was a great blessing for the Yǔ clan,
and it is clear that it was not due to the Jìn zhèng's lack of discipline.
Yǔ Yì indulged his sinister intentions,
poisoning the Liánshuài.
After two generations,
only Sānyáng remained;
the lingering calamity that struck
was probably deserved.
