A eulogy states: Yuánguī feigned his conduct,
and ascended the ladder of favor in the Jiāoyè.
His understanding was dim regarding principle,
and chaos arose from exploiting loopholes.
Bowing low to Chángshā,
he had reason to be ashamed of his loyalty and integrity.
Jìjiān was pure and upright,
cultivating virtue and gaining renown.
In prosperity he was more frugal,
holding power he guarded against excess.
Zhìgōng was spirited and generous,
also possessing a heroic reputation.
Collated Notes

Lièzhuàn Dì Sìshísì: Huán Yí (Huán Yún, Huán Yún's brother Huán Huò, Huán Huò's son Huán Shíqián, Huán Shíqián's son Huán Zhèn, Huán Shíqián's brother Huán Shíxiù, Huán Shímín, Huán Shíshēng, Huán Shísuí, Huán Shíkāng, Huán Huò's brother Huán Bì, Huán Bì's brother Huán Chōng, Huán Chōng's son Huán Sì, Huán Sì's son Huán Yìn, Huán Sì's brother Huán Qiān, Huán Qiān's brother Huán Xiū, Xú Níng)
Huán Yí, courtesy name Màolún,
was a native of Lóngkàng in Qiáoguó.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Wǔ Gēngróng of Hàn.
His father, Huán Hào,
served as a Lángzhōng.
Huán Yí was orphaned and poor in his youth.
Though living on a humble diet,
he accepted it with ease.
He was open and frank by nature,
and gained great renown early.
He had discerning judgment of character,
selecting and promoting talents and scholars.
Some emerged from obscurity,
others were recognized even in childhood.
People of his time compared him to Xǔ Shào and Guō Tài.
In his youth, he formed a deep friendship with Yǔ Liàng,
and was highly esteemed by Zhōu Yǐ.
Zhōu Yǐ once sighed, saying:
"Màolún is rugged and uninhibited,
truly an amusing person."
He began his career as a Zhōuzhǔbù.
He joined the righteous cause of Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
and was appointed Jìdūwèi.
When Emperor Yuán was Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
he issued the Jūnqiú Lìng.
Soon after, he was appointed Chéngxiàng Zhōngbīng Shǔ.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Láng and Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
his name becoming prominent at court.
At that time, Wáng Dūn wielded power arbitrarily,
disliking and fearing esteemed scholars;
Huán Yí resigned from his post due to illness.
He once passed through Yú Xiàn.
The Xiànzǎi Xú Níng, courtesy name Ānqí,
was open, clear, and widely learned.
Huán Yí met him
and happily stayed for several days,
befriending him before departing.
Before this,
Yǔ Liàng had repeatedly asked Huán Yí to find a good Lìbù.
Upon reaching the capital,
he said to Yǔ Liàng:
"I have found a Lìbù for you."
Yǔ Liàng asked where he was.
Huán Yí replied:
"What people should have, they don't necessarily have;
what people shouldn't have, they don't necessarily lack.
Xú Níng is truly a pure scholar from the Hǎidài region."
Consequently, he (Xú Níng) was appointed.
He was immediately promoted to Lìbù Láng,
eventually holding prominent posts.
When Emperor Míng was about to campaign against Wáng Dūn,
Yí was appointed Sanqí Chángshì
and was invited to participate in confidential discussions.
After Dūn was pacified,
Yí was enfeoffed as the Count of Wànníng County for his achievements.
Wēn Jiào, the Administrator of Dānyáng, submitted a memorial saying:
"Xuānchéng, bordered by mountains and rivers,
has frequently experienced upheavals.
It ought to be governed by someone of esteemed reputation and substance.
I humbly submit that Huán Yí is suitable for this selection."
The Emperor issued a handwritten edict saying:
"I have just received Tàizhēn's memorial to this effect.
Now that the great affair has just been settled,
the court requires talent.
If there are no upright gentlemen,
how can the state be governed?
At present, external affairs are somewhat less urgent,
and I wish to postpone this matter."
Yí submitted a memorial deeply declining the offer with humility, stating
that he was unfit for both internal and external responsibilities.
However, as his ancestral tombs were in this commandery,
he wished to temporarily establish a connection there in name,
so Yí was appointed as the Intendant of Xuānchéng.
While in the commandery, he governed with beneficence,
and was cherished by the common people.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
Yí rallied loyal forces,
intending to hasten to the court.
His Chief Clerk, Pí Huì, argued that the commandery's troops were few and weak,
and the mountain people were easily disturbed,
so it would be better to keep the armor sheathed and await a later opportunity.
Yí sternly said:
"When one sees disrespect shown to one's sovereign,
one should be like a hawk pursuing sparrows.
Now the state is in grave danger,
and it is against righteousness to remain peacefully at ease."
He then dispatched General Zhū Chuò to attack a separate rebel leader in Wúhú,
defeating him.
Yí soon moved out to Shígūi.
It happened that the court had sent General Sīmǎ Liú to first occupy Cíhú,
but he was defeated by the rebels,
who then advanced directly and rapidly.
As the commandery had no strong fortifications,
Yí retreated to Guǎngdé.
Soon, the imperial army suffered a major defeat.
Yí heard this and, filled with indignation, wept,
then advanced to station his troops in Jīng County.
At that time, many prefectures and commanderies sent envoys to surrender to Jùn.
Pí Huì again urged Yí to feign alliance and communicate with them
to alleviate the imminent disaster.
Yí said:
"I have received great kindness from the state; my duty lies in giving my life.
How can I endure disgrace and humiliation to communicate with the ugly rebels?
If it does not succeed,
then
this is fate."
He dispatched General Yú Zòng to guard Lánshí.
Jùn sent General Hán Huǎng to attack him.
When Zòng was about to be defeated,
his subordinates urged him to retreat.
Zòng said:
"I have received great kindness from Lord Huán,
and my original intention was to repay it with my life.
That I cannot betray Lord Huán
is just as Lord Huán does not betray the state."
He then fought valiantly and died.
Huǎng then advanced his army to attack Yí.
Yí held out for a year,
but his forces were isolated and his strength exhausted.
The rebels said:
"If Yí surrenders,
we will treat him with great courtesy."
Many officers and soldiers urged Yí to feign surrender
and plan for a later uprising.
Yí refused,
his words and spirit resolute and heroic,
his will and integrity unyielding.
The city fell,
and he was killed by Huǎng
at the age of fifty-three.
At that time, the rebels were not yet pacified,
and his sons were scattered and dispersed.
Jì Shìhé of Xuānchéng led loyal followers to bury him.
After the rebellion was pacified,
he was posthumously granted the title of Tíngwèi,
with the posthumous name Jiǎn.
During the Xián'ān reign,
this was changed to posthumous grant of Tàicháng.
Yú Zòng was also posthumously granted Xīnggǔ Tàishǒu for his loyalty unto death.
Earlier,
Yí was close friends with Guō Pú,
and once asked Pú to perform divination for him.
After the hexagram was formed,
Pú broke it with his hand.
Yí asked him why.
He said:
"The hexagram is the same as mine.
A man facing this is not fated to live long,
what can be done?"
It turned out exactly as he said.
He had five sons: Wēn, Yún, Huò, Mì, and Chōng.
A separate biography for Wēn exists.
Yún's courtesy name was Yúnzǐ.
He was initially appointed Cānjūn to Piàojì Hé Chōng and Shàngshū Láng,
but did not accept.
He inherited the title of Wànníng Nán,
and successively held the positions of Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn and Yìchéng Tàishǒu.
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
After the burial,
he was reappointed as Jīangzhōu Cìshǐ,
but claimed illness
and resided by the tomb.
An imperial edict urgently pressed him,
but he firmly declined to go.
After the mourning period ended,
he then took up his post.
He was also appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Sī and Yù Provinces, concurrently leading Zhènmán Hùjūn, Xīyáng Tàishǒu, and was granted the Jiǎjié.
Yún gathered numerous forces,
aiming to increase his military strength,
and committed many acts of injustice and abuse,
which caused widespread resentment.
At that time, Wēn held power,
so officials did not dare to impeach him.
He died in the fourth year of Shēngpíng,
and was posthumously granted Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous name Zhēn.
His son Xù inherited the title,
and his official post reached Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
Huò's courtesy name was Lángzǐ.
He was initially invited to the Sītú's mansion and as Mìshū Láng,
but declined both.
Emperor Jiǎnwén summoned him as Fǔjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and appointed him Lìbù Láng,
but he resigned due to illness.
He was promoted to Huángmén Láng,
but did not take up the post.
At that time, Xiè Wàn was defeated at Liángpú,
and the cities of Xǔchāng and Yǐngchuān fell one after another,
causing unrest in the western regions.
Wēn ordered Huò to supervise the military affairs of the seven commanderies in Miǎnzhōng, as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Xīnyě and Yìchéng,
to attack Mùróng Qūchén,
defeating him,
and was promoted to the title of Yòujiāngjūn.
After Wēn had established internal control,
he appointed Huò to oversee the military affairs of Jīng, Yáng, and Yōng Provinces, concurrently leading Hù Nánmán Xiàowèi and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, and was granted the Jiǎjié,
with his general's title remaining as before.
At that time, Sīmǎ Xūn, the Cìshǐ of Liáng Province, rebelled with Liáng and Yì Provinces.
Huò sent his Cānjūn Huán Pí to attack him.
Meanwhile, Zhào Hóng and Zhào Yì, the Dūhù of Nányáng, expelled Tàishǒu Huán Dàn,
occupied Wǎnéng, and rebelled.
Huò, along with Luó Chóng, the Tàishǒu of Jìnglín, attacked and defeated them.
He then attacked the pseudo-Nán Zhōnglángjiàng Zhào Pán in Wǎn.
Pán fled,
and Huò pursued him to Lǔyáng,
captured him,
sent him to the capital,
established a garrison, and returned.
He also oversaw the military affairs of Níng and Yì.
After Wēn died,
Huò was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and further oversaw the military affairs of Jiāo and Guǎng, in addition to the previous five provinces.
When Fú Jiān invaded Shǔ,
Huò dispatched Jiāngxià Xiàng Zhú Yáo to resist him.
Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu Zhào Cháng and others died in battle,
and Yáo withdrew his forces.
A short while later,
Jiān again invaded Liáng Province.
His younger brother Chōng dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhū Xù and Huò's son, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Shí Xiù, to proceed upstream to the battle,
to receive orders and instructions.
Huò dispatched Dūhù Huán Pí and Xù to patrol the Miǎnhàn region with their forces
to provide support for Liáng Province.
Soon after, Zhāng Tiānxī was captured,
and an imperial edict sent Zhōngshū Láng Wáng Xúnzhī to Huò
to consult on border affairs.
Huò memorialized to appoint Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Máio Xiànzǔ to oversee the military affairs north of Miǎn,
and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhū Xù as Nán Zhōnglángjiàng and to oversee the military affairs in Miǎnzhōng,
stationed at Xiāngyáng,
to secure the northern frontier.
In the beginning of the Tàiyuán [reign],
he was promoted to Grand General of the West-Conquering Army and granted permission to establish a government.
Huò submitted a memorial firmly declining, saying:
“I have heard that when the three stars of the Sān Tái constellation illuminate the heavens,
the North Star increases its brilliance;
when discoursing on the Way and acting as a pillar of support,
the royal strategies achieve timely harmony.
It is essential to look up and participate in the divine covenant,
to respond and carry out the tasks,
to promote simplicity and ease to assist transformation,
and to spread the profound influence to the utmost.
Thus, it is proper to brightly elevate the humble and obscure,
and appoint the worthy and exceptional,
so that even those who build walls can achieve aspirations that reach the heavens,
and those by the Wèibīn River do not idly cast their fishing rods.
Only then can achievements save the common people,
and the Way shine for a thousand years.
Therefore, if one’s virtue does not meet the expectations of the time,
the established code does not idly bestow positions;
if one’s merits are minor but the rewards are lavish,
the worthy and discerning do not desire them.
I am truly an ordinary person,
my capacity has no far-reaching effect,
I have risen by relying on my family's favor,
and thus presumptuously obtained an unwarranted position.
When advancing, I cannot expound the imperial grandeur
or clarify its political Way;
when retreating, I cannot exert my strength in the place I govern,
nor unify Huá and Róng.
I have idled in office for years,
and no achievements are recorded.
Therefore, I dare to risk defying the imperial decree
and present my sincere plea.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will turn your divine profound gaze,
and retract your mistaken favor,
then those watching will change their expectations,
and I will know myself to be spared.”
Ultimately, it was not permitted.
When Fú Jiān captured Qiúchí,
Huò appointed Jí Yì, the Administrator of Xīnyě, to act as Administrator of Wèixīng and Controller of the military affairs of the five commanderies of Liángzhōu,
to guard Liángzhōu.
When Fú Jiān captured Fúchéng,
Yáng Liàng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, and Zhōu Zhòngsūn, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, both abandoned their posts and fled.
Huò, seeing that military prestige was not maintained,
and that failures occurred everywhere,
again submitted a memorial expressing apologies,
firmly declined,
and did not accept the establishment of a government.
Soon after, he died,
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the title of Sīkōng,
his original official title remaining as before,
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
He was granted fifty million cash,
five hundred bolts of cloth,
and an envoy was dispatched with a staff of authority to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Though Huò's contemporary reputation did not match that of Chōng,
he possessed great capacity and demeanor.
However, he encountered strong invaders,
hence he failed to establish great achievements.
Originally,
Huò heard a rumor in Fú Jiān’s country which said:
“Who says your Jiān (堅, firm) stone will not be broken?”
He had twenty sons,
all of whom he named with the character
“Shí” (石, stone)
to respond to this.
Only Shíqián, Shíxiù, Shímín, Shíshēng, Shísuí, and Shíkāng were renowned.
Shíqián’s courtesy name was Zhèn'è.
He possessed talent and ability,
and was extraordinarily agile and swift.
He followed his father in Jīngzhōu,
and during a hunt, he saw a fierce beast struck by several arrows and collapsed.
The various commanders, who knew his bravery,
jokingly ordered him to pull out the arrows.
Shíqián immediately went forward,
pulled out one arrow,
the fierce beast sprang up,
Shíqián also sprang up,
higher than the beast's body.
The fierce beast lay down,
and he pulled out another arrow and returned.
He followed Wēn into the pass.
When Chōng was besieged by Fú Jiàn
and on the verge of being lost,
Shíqián spurred his horse and rushed in,
rescuing Chōng from amidst tens of thousands of people and returning,
with no one daring to resist.
The entire army sighed in admiration,
and his prestige awed the enemy.
At that time, those suffering from malaria
were told,
“Huán Shíqián is coming!”
to frighten them,
and many of the sick recovered;
such was the extent to which he was feared.
Earlier,
when Yuán Zhēn rebelled at Shòuyáng,
Shíqián, as General Who Keeps the Peace and Administrator of Nándùn, led his generals to attack him,
and captured his southern city.
He also attacked Wáng Jiàn, Fú Jiān’s general, at Shíqiáo,
capturing five hundred horses.
He was appointed Administrator of Jìnglíng,
but resigned due to his father’s mourning.
Soon after, Fú Jiān again invaded Huáinán,
and an imperial edict stated:
“Shíqián has both literary and martial talent and ability,
and a method for controlling the barbarians.
Ancient people ceased mourning
and did not avoid military service;
how much more so in a period of lingering grief,
how can he decline duty!
He may be appointed General Who Rouses Awe and Administrator of Nánpíng.”
Soon after, he was promoted to General Who Commands the Army.
Liáng Chéng, Fú Jiān’s Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and Yán Zhèn, Administrator of Xiāngyáng, led their troops to invade Jìnglíng.
Shíqián and his younger brother Shímín resisted them.
The invaders blocked the Āshuǐ River
and encamped at Guǎnchéng.
Shíqián devised a plan to cross the river at night;
once they had crossed,
the invaders became aware,
and after a fierce battle, he defeated them.
He advanced and captured Guǎnchéng,
captured Zhèn,
beheaded seven thousand,
captured ten thousand people,
several hundred horses,
a thousand cattle and sheep,
and three hundred sets of armored equipment.
Chéng fled with light cavalry to secure Xiāngyáng.
Shíqián again took charge as Administrator of Hédōng,
advanced to occupy Fánchéng,
drove away Zhāng Chóng, Fú Jiān’s Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and returned after accepting the surrender of two thousand households.
When Chōng died,
Shíqián, as General Who Commands the Army, was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for Yùzhōu and the five commanderies of Yángzhōu, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Soon after, he resigned due to his mother’s mourning.
When the mourning period ended,
he resumed his original position.
After a long time,
he was ordered to move his garrison to Mǎtóu,
but Shíqián requested to remain at Lìyáng,
which was granted.
He died in the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Right.
In retrospective recognition of his achievement in defeating Yán Zhèn,
his noble title was advanced to Marquis of Zuòtáng.
His fifth son, Dàn, succeeded him.
Dàn’s eldest brother was Hóng,
Administrator of Xiāngchéng.
Hóng’s younger brother was Zhèn.
Zhèn’s courtesy name was Dàoquán.
He was decisive and sharp in his youth,
but lacked moral conduct.
When Xuán was in Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Zhèn as General Who Manifests Martial Might and Administrator of Huáinán.
He was transferred to Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià,
but was dismissed due to his ferocity and tyranny.
When Xuán was defeated,
Huán Qiān hid in Jǔzhōng,
and Zhèn fled to Yǒngzhōng in Huáróng.
Xuán had previously ordered General Wáng Zhìhuī to garrison Bālíng.
Zhìhuī sent someone to report to Zhèn, saying:
“Huán Qīn has already captured Jīngyì,
Féng Zhì and others have again pacified Xúnyáng,
and the armies of Liú Yì have all been defeated en route.”
Zhèn was greatly delighted.
At that time, Emperor Ān was in Jiānglíng.
Zhèn then gathered several tens of followers and attacked Jiānglíng.
By the time they reached the city,
they had a force of two hundred.
Qiān also gathered his followers and came out,
and consequently captured Jiānglíng,
welcoming the Emperor from his temporary palace.
When Zhèn heard of Huán Shēng’s death,
he was furious
and intended to commit atrocities against the Emperor.
Qiān strenuously restrained him,
and he stopped.
Then he ordered his officials,
declaring that the Chǔ dynasty’s mandate was over,
and the hearts of the people had returned to Jìn.
He again offered the imperial seal and ribbon,
appointing the Prince of Lángyá as Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and Zhèn as Grand Superintendent of Eight Provinces, General Who Guards the West, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Those serving the Emperor on his left and right
were all Zhèn’s confidants.
Then he sighed and said:
“You did not employ me earlier,
which led to this defeat.
If you had been present,
and I had been the vanguard,
the world would not have been difficult to settle.
Now that I am doing this alone,
where can I go?”
He then indulged in wine and women,
and became tyrannical and lawless,
causing much destruction and harm.
Zhèn encamped at Jiāngjīn.
Rú Zōngzhī, the Administrator of Nányáng, broke Zhèn’s general, Wēn Kāi, at Zuòxī from Xiāngyáng,
then advanced and garrisoned Jìnáan.
When Zhèn heard of Kāi’s defeat,
he left his general Fēng Gāi to guard the camp,
and personally led his troops to a major battle with Zōngzhī.
Zhèn’s bravery surpassed all three armies,
and no one could resist him,
so Zōngzhī was defeated.
Zhèn pursued the fleeing forces,
and met Zōngzhī alone on horseback on the road,
but did not recognize him,
so he asked where Zōngzhī was.
He was deceived and told,
“He has already run ahead.”
Zōngzhī then retreated from behind.
Soon after, Liú Yì and others defeated Fēng Gāi
and pacified Jiānglíng.
When Zhèn heard of Gāi’s defeat,
his troops scattered and fled.
Later, he and Gāi’s son Hóng came out of Yúnchéng.
Commander Liú Huáisù led Ningyuan General Suǒ Miáo,
and fought Zhèn at Shāqiáo.
Although Zhèn had few soldiers,
his left and right flanks all fought with might.
Commander Liú Huáisù led Ningyuan General Suǒ Miáo,
and fought Zhèn at Shāqiáo.
Although Zhèn had few soldiers,
his left and right flanks all fought with might.
In every engagement,
Zhèn would glare and strike fiercely,
and no one dared to stand in his way.
Zhèn was drunk at the time,
and was also hit by a stray arrow.
Guǎngwǔ General Táng Xīng cut him down on the battlefield.
Shí Xiù,
from a young age, had a good reputation.
His demeanor was refined and clear,
and he widely read many books,
especially excelling in Lǎo-Zhuāng.
He often stayed alone in a room,
simple in his interactions,
and people of his time compared him to Yǔ Chún.
He was highly esteemed by Emperor Jiǎnwén,
and when Huò became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he was invited to be Eagle-Strife General and Administrator of Jìnglín,
which was not to his liking.
Soon after, he succeeded his uncle Chōng as Ningyuan General, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, concurrently Protector-General to Suppress the Man, and Administrator of Xīyáng,
residing in Xúnyáng.
He had a free and unrestrained nature,
often hunting and fishing in forests and wetlands,
not allowing honor or rank to trouble his mind.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
hitting the target with every shot.
He once accompanied Chōng on a hunt,
ascending Jiǔjǐng Shān.
The entourage was very large,
and spectators filled the area,
but Shí Xiù never even looked at them,
merely whistling and chanting.
Xiè Ān once inquired about worldly affairs,
but he remained silent and did not answer,
which greatly puzzled Ān.
Another day,
Ān spoke of it to his cousin Sì.
When Sì asked him,
Shí Xiù said,
“This gentleman is well-versed in worldly matters,
what more can I say!”
He served in the province for five years,
and left office due to illness.
He died at home at the age of forty-three,
and the court and people mourned his passing.
He was posthumously granted the title of Posterior General,
and later his posthumous grant was changed to Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
His son Zhìyù inherited.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
because of the excellent reputation of Shí Xiù’s family,
he enfeoffed Zhìyù as Prince of Línyuán.
Shí Mín,
was known at the age of twenty.
Guard General Xiè Ān appointed him as his staff officer.
His uncle Chōng submitted a memorial,
and he was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for ten commanderies in the three provinces of Jīng, Jiāng, and Yù, Zhenwu General,
concurrently Administrator of Xiāngchéng,
garrisoning Xiàkǒu,
and with Shí Qián attacked Fú Jiān’s Jīngzhōu Governor Liáng Chéng and others at Jìnglín.
The following year,
he again with Suíjùn Administrator Xiàhóu Chéngzhī defeated Fú Jiān’s generals Mùróng Chuí and Jiāng Chéng and others at Zhāngkǒu.
He was again concurrently Internal Administrator of Qiáoguó and Administrator of Liángjùn.
When Chōng died,
an imperial edict appointed Shí Mín Supervisor of Military Affairs for Jīngzhōu, Western Commander of the Central Army, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
The Huán clan had governed the Jīng region for generations,
and Shí Mín combined this with his talent and reputation,
so he was greatly respected by the people.
Originally,
Chōng had sent Jìnglín Administrator Zhào Tǒng to attack Xiāngyáng.
By this time,
Shí Mín again sent troops to assist him.
Soon after, Fú Jiān was defeated at Huáiféi.
Shí Mín sent Nányáng Administrator Gāo Mào to guard the imperial tombs.
At this time, although Jiān was defeated,
Mùróng Chuí and others had again grown powerful.
Shí Mín sent General Yàn Qiān to attack Hóngnóng,
and the bandit Eastern Commander of the Central Army Mùróng Kuí surrendered to him.
He first established the two garrisons of Hú and Shǎn.
He captured the “carrying banners” performers from Guānzhōng,
to augment the imperial music.
At that time, Fú Jiān’s son Pī proclaimed himself emperor in Héběi,
and plotted to attack Luòyáng.
Shí Mín sent General Fēng Gāi to attack him,
and Pī was cut down on the battlefield,
along with his Left Minister Wáng Fú, Minister of Personnel Gǒu Cāo, and others,
and their heads were sent to the capital.
Then Dīnglíng’s Zhái Liáo again encroached upon the imperial tombs.
[一０] Shí Mín sent Hénán Administrator Fēng Zūn to attack him.
At that time, the Qǐhuó leader Huáng Huái proclaimed himself Governor of Bīngzhōu,
and with Liáo jointly attacked Chángshè,
with several thousand troops.
Shí Mín again sent Nánpíng Administrator Guō Quán and Sōngzī Administrator Wáng Xiázhī to attack Huái,
and cut him down.
Liáo fled to Héběi.
For his accumulated merits,
he was promoted to Left General.
He died,
without a son.
Shí Shēng,
during the Lóng'ān era, was transferred from Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works to Attendant,
and successively held the posts of Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry and Grand Mentor.
When Huìjī世子 Yuánxiǎn was about to attack Huán Xuán,
Shí Shēng quickly sent a letter to inform Xuán,
and Xuán greatly appreciated him.
When Xuán gained power,
he appointed him Anterior General and Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
He died in office shortly thereafter.
Shí Suí,
during Yuánxiǎn’s time, was Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works.
When Xuán gained power,
he was appointed Palace Aide to the Imperial Censor and Left Guard General.
When Xuán was defeated,
Shí Suí fled along the route in Jiāngxī,
[一一] gathered troops and attacked Lìyáng,
but was later killed by Governor of Liángzhōu, Fù Xīnzhī.
[一二]
Shí Kāng,
was particularly favored by Xuán.
When Xuán was Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he appointed him Zhenwei General.
He was successively promoted to Governor of Jīngzhōu.
His merits in suppressing Yǔ Zè,
and suppressing the King of Wǔlíng,
are detailed in Xuán’s biography.
Mì (祕) had the courtesy name Mùzǐ (穆子).
From a young age, he possessed talent and spirit,
and did not conform to common customs.
He was initially appointed as Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
but his elder brother Wēn (溫) suppressed him and did not use him.
After a long time,
he served as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Xuānchéng Nèishǐ (宣城內史).
At that time, Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州), rebelled and joined Shǔ (蜀).
Mì (祕), in his original capacity, was appointed Jiān Liáng Yì Èr Zhōu Zhēngtǎo Jūnjì (監梁益二州征討軍事) and given a Jiǎjié (假節).
After Xūn (勳) was pacified,
he returned to his commandery.
Later, he became Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and was then transferred to Zhōng Lǐngjūn (中領軍).
When Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝) first ascended the throne,
the rebellious bandit Lú Sǒng (盧竦) entered the palace.
Mì (祕), along with Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍) Yīn Kāng (殷康), both entered to attack him.
Wēn (溫) entered court
to thoroughly investigate Sǒng's (竦) affair,
arresting Shàngshū (尚書) Lù Shǐ (陸始) and others,
and a great many people suffered punishment.
Mì (祕) was also dismissed from office
and resided in Wǎnlíng (宛陵).
He often displayed indignation and a sense of injustice.
When Wēn (溫) became gravely ill,
Mì (祕) plotted with Wēn's (溫) sons Xī (熙) and Jì (濟) to depose Chōng (沖).
Chōng (沖) secretly learned of this
and dared not enter.
Shortly after Wēn (溫) died,
Chōng (沖) first sent strongmen to detain Xī (熙) and Jì (濟),
and only then attended the funeral.
Mì (祕) was then abandoned
and lived at his burial ground,
devoting himself to fields and gardens,
and enjoying excursions to mountains and waters.
Later, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and he submitted three memorials to express himself.
An imperial edict stated:
“Mì (祕) was favored by the previous court,
and therefore he was extended [an offer].
However, he repeatedly submitted memorials to decline,
expressing his preference for reclusion and his sincerity,
and also having illness.
We read this with increasing admiration.
His resolve should be respected.”
Mì (祕) had always disdained Chōng (沖).
At that time, Chōng (沖) was powerful and esteemed,
and Mì (祕) was ashamed of the low rank of Chángshì (常侍),
thus he did not respond to the imperial command.
He exchanged ten letters and poems with Xiè Ān (謝安),
the rhetoric of which was admirable.
His writings often cited the benevolent treatment of Jiǎnwén Dì (簡文帝).
He died before Chōng (沖).
His eldest son, Wèi (蔚),
rose to the office of Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Yóujī Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍).
When Xuán (玄) usurped the throne,
he made him Lǐlíng Wáng (醴陵王).
Chōng (沖), courtesy name Yòuzǐ (幼子),
was the most profound and knowledgeable among Wēn's (溫) younger brothers,
and possessed military capability.
Wēn (溫) greatly valued him.
When he reached manhood,
Táizǎi (太宰), Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) Xī (晞) invited him to serve,
but he did not accept.
He was appointed Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn (鷹揚將軍), Zhènmán Hùjūn (鎮蠻護軍), and Xīyáng Tàishǒu (西陽太守).
He participated in Wēn's (溫) campaigns and achieved merit,

and was promoted to Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhī Nányáng Xiāngyáng Xīnyě Yìyáng Shùnyáng Yōngzhōu Zhī Jīngzhào Yángzhōu Zhī Yìchéng Qī Jùn Jūnjì (督荊州之南陽襄陽新野義陽順陽雍州之京兆揚州之義成七郡軍事), Níngsuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), and Yìchéng Xīnyě Èr Jùn Tàishǒu (義成新野二郡太守),
stationed in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
He again accompanied Wēn (溫) in defeating Yáo Xiāng (姚襄).
After capturing Zhōu Chéng (周成),
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍)
and granted the title of Fēngchéng Gōng (豐城公).
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍), Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史), concurrently Lǐng Zhènmán Hùjūn (領鎮蠻護軍), and Xīyáng Qiáo Èr Jùn Tàishǒu (西陽譙二郡太守).
When Wēn (溫) defeated Yáo Xiāng (姚襄),
he captured Xiāng's (襄) generals Zhāng Jùn (張駿) and Yáng Níng (楊凝) and others,
who were exiled to Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Chōng (沖) was in Jiānglíng (江陵),
and had not yet taken up his post,
when Jùn (駿) led his followers, five hundred men, to kill Zhào Pí (趙毗), the Dūhù (督護) of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
plundered the Wǔchāng (武昌) arsenal,
and intended to rebel north with his wife and children.
Chōng (沖) dispatched a general to pursue and capture them,
and then quickly returned to his garrison.
Initially,
after Yí (彝) died,
Chōng's (沖) brothers were all young,
and the family was poor.
His mother was ill
and needed lamb to recover,
but they had no means to obtain it.
Wēn (溫) then used Chōng (沖) as collateral.
The lamb owner was very wealthy
and said he did not want collateral,
but rather wished to adopt Dé Láng (德郎) and purchase merit.
Dé Láng (德郎)
was Chōng's (沖) nickname.
When Chōng (沖) became Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
he went out shooting.
The lamb owner watched from the side of the hall.
Chōng (沖) recognized him
and said,
“I am Dé (德).”
Then he richly rewarded him.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Jiān Jiāng Jīng Yù Sān Zhōu Zhī Liù Jùn Jūnjì (監江荊豫三州之六郡軍事), Nán Zhōnglángjiāng (南中郎將), and Jiǎjié (假節),
while his provincial and commandery posts remained the same.
He served in Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu) for thirteen years until Wēn (溫) passed away.
Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝) decreed Chōng (沖) to be Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍), Dūdū Yáng Jiāng Yù Sān Zhōu Jūnjì (都督揚江豫三州軍事), Yáng Yù Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ (揚豫二州刺史), and Jiǎjié (假節).
At that time, an imperial edict granted mourning gifts of money, cloth, lacquer, and wax to Wēn (溫),
but did not include provisions for the grand burial.
Chōng (沖) submitted a memorial stating that Wēn (溫) had always cherished a simple and frugal disposition,
and that his private belongings were sufficient to manage the funeral rites,
requesting to return the items to the imperial treasury.
The edict did not permit it,
but Chōng (沖) still steadfastly refused to accept them.
Initially,
when Wēn (溫) held power,
all major capital crimes were decided by himself.
After Chōng (沖) took charge of affairs,
he submitted a memorial arguing that the gravity of life and death
has been carefully considered throughout history.
Therefore, all death sentences
should first be reported
and await a reply.
After Chōng (沖) succeeded Wēn (溫) in his responsibilities,
he devoted himself wholeheartedly to the royal house.
Some advised Chōng (沖) to eliminate prominent figures of the time
and solely wield power,
but Chōng (沖) did not follow.
Xiè Ān (謝安) assisted in governance as a prominent figure of the time,
and was the focus of popular sentiment.
Chōng (沖) feared being pressured.
In the third year of Níngkāng (寧康) (375 CE),
he thus resigned from Yángzhōu (揚州)
and sought an external appointment himself.
The Faction of Huán (桓) thought this was not a good plan,
and all wrung their wrists and bitterly advised against it.
Xī Chāo (郗超) also strongly urged him to stop.
Chōng (沖) did not accept any of it,
handling it calmly
without resentment.
He always exerted his full effort
in loyal words and excellent schemes.
Therefore, he was reassigned as Dūdū Xú Yǎn Yù Qīng Yáng Wǔ Zhōu Zhī Liù Jùn Jūnjì (都督徐兗豫青揚五州之六郡軍事), Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍), and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史),
with the Běi Zhōngláng Fǔ (北中郎府) combined with the Zhōngjūn (中軍),
stationed at Jīngkǒu (京口),
and given a Jiǎjié (假節).
An edict also appointed Chōng (沖) and Xiè Ān (謝安) concurrently as Shìzhōng (侍中),
permitting them to enter the palace with fifty armed guards.
At that time, Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹) Wáng Yùn (王蘊), by virtue of being the Empress's father, was close to Ān (安).
Ān (安) wanted to send Yùn (蘊) out as a regional governor,
so he again relieved Chōng (沖) of Xúzhōu (徐州),
making him solely Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) and Dūdū Yù Jiāng Èr Zhōu Zhī Liù Jùn Jūnjì (都督豫江二州之六郡軍事),
transferring his garrison from Jīngkǒu (京口) to Gūshú (姑熟).
Later, Fú Jiān (苻堅) invaded Liángzhōu (涼州).
Chōng (沖) dispatched Xuānchéng Nèishǐ (宣城內史) Zhū Xù (朱序) and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州 Cìshǐ) Huán Yī (桓伊) to lead troops towards Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Huáinán Tàishǒu (淮南太守) Liú Bō (劉波) sailed boats on the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers,
taking advantage of the void to launch an attack
to rescue Liángzhōu (涼zhou),
and then memorialized, saying: "The Dī (氐) bandits have subsumed the Eastern Hú (胡),
and their wicked kind is truly numerous.
However, Shǔhàn (蜀漢) is weak and small,
and Xīliáng (西涼) is unprepared.
This is indeed a sign of their violence and impending downfall,
only hastening their demise.
Yet,
Heaven has not yet utterly destroyed them,
and they repeatedly cause trouble for the state.
I have heard that victory is achieved in the unseen,
and merit is established through manifest deeds.
The way of attacking strategies
is the highest military tactic.
Moreover, these bandits, having seized
Liáng (梁),
will eventually escape and grow.
The Northern Dí (狄) are arrogant and unrestrained,
especially in autumn and winter.
Today, the sun and moon rush by,
and strong winds are beginning to rise.
I have taken the liberty to assess the capital region,
and the defenses are heavy
and manifold.
Furthermore, the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) flow freely,
and the Yangtze River is like the sea.
Jīngchǔ (荊楚) is remote,
and close to the enemy.
Fāngchéng (方城) and the Hànshǔi (漢水) have no inherent natural defenses,
yet the importance of over-preparation
lies in the western gate.
Although I am ordinary,
lacking in military strategy,
I have presumptuously been entrusted with a heavy responsibility,
and my thoughts are on taking up arms.
I request to lead my forces
straight to Nánjùn (南郡),
and with Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍)
Your subject, Huò, participated in the deliberations and strategies.
If the rebels indeed drive their rabble,
sending them to their deaths at Miǎnhàn,
we may rely on righteous compliance,
and thereby gain human advantage.
With one swift move, we shall ride the wind,
sweeping away the
filth,
and the imperial army will not have to toil again.
If there is action in Sānqín,
then the late emperor’s grand achievements will forever prosper in this sacred age,
and Xuānwǔ's posthumous wishes will have no regrets in the past.
If, however, they are intimidated
and daunted by imperial might,
and their plans are thwarted,
then we shall observe their forces and await an opportune moment,
deliberating further on advance and capture.
Whether to withdraw the troops and return the banners,
or to delay, will be determined by what is appropriate.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would review what your subject has presented,
and graciously grant approval.
An imperial edict replied:
"The vile creatures have defied Heaven,
and for years have been unrestrained.
Liángyì is not held,
and Héxī is lost.
Every time I consider that the world is not unified,
indignation and lament fill my heart.
The general’s strategy is profound and far-reaching,
his calculations thorough and meticulous.
His loyalty to the nation
is evident in his righteous intent.
I have not yet finished reading it,
and am already moved and inspired.
Although the bandits have seized opportunities and profited,
they rule with lawlessness.
They are bellicose and extremely vicious,
cruelly employing their populace.
How can their time of destruction
possibly last long!
However, being prepared for the unforeseen
is good military governance.
I shall inquire among the high officials
and respectfully follow your esteemed plan.
I expect you to consult and cooperate with the General Who Conquers the West on the excellent plan,
and your brilliant strategies and far-reaching plans,
whether in action or stillness, shall be reported."
At this time, Zhāng Tiānxī was captured and lost,
so the troops were dismissed.
Soon after, Huò died.

Huò was posthumously made Grand Administrator of the military affairs of seven prefectures: Jiāng, Jīng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Jiāo, Guǎng; Yìchéng of Yáng Prefecture; Jīngzhào of Yōng Prefecture; Hédōng of Sī Prefecture; and concurrently Protector of the Southern Barbarians, Inspector of Jīng Prefecture, and Held the Imperial Staff,
with his generalship and侍zhōng titles remaining as before.
His son, Sì, was also appointed Inspector of Jiāng Prefecture.
When Chōng was about to depart for his post,
the Emperor saw him off at the Western Hall,
and bestowed upon him 500,000 cash.
He also rewarded the civil and military officials with 340 *shi* of wine and 50 oxen.
Xiè Ān accompanied him to Lìzhōu.
Once Chōng arrived at Jiānglíng,
Fú Jiān was strong and powerful at the time.
Chōng wished to move his defenses to the south of the Yangtze River,
so he submitted a memorial, stating:
"Since the Zhongxing era,
the seat of Jīng Prefecture
has been shifted as deemed appropriate.
My deceased elder brother, Wēn, upon the death of Shí Jìlóng,
strategized to pacify the Central Plains.
Taking advantage of the convenient route through Jiānglíng,
he immediately took up residence there.
Circumstances change with time;
the situation is not constant.
Moreover, warfare is a deceptive art; one must display weakness.
It is now appropriate to fully concentrate our strength south of the Yangtze,
and lightly garrison north of the Yangtze.
In the district of Cànlíng County in Nánpíng,
there is a place called Shàngmíng,
where the land is fertile and good,
suitable for provisioning soldiers.
During the Wú dynasty, it was more than forty *li* above Lèxiāng City,
with the great Yangtze River to its north,
and connecting to the Three Gorges to its west.
If the mad barbarians come to their deaths,
then we should build strong defenses north of the old Yǐng and not engage in battle.
The confluence for crossing the Yangtze
is not far.
Taking advantage of their exhaustion and disarray,
it will be easy to defeat and eliminate them.
Your subject, overseeing military affairs,
shall proceed with arrangements as appropriate."
Thus, he moved his headquarters to Shàngmíng,
and dispatched General Who Commands the Army, Liú Bō, to guard Jiānglíng,
and Advisory Counselor, Yáng Liàng, to guard Jiāngxià.
An imperial edict stated that due to drought and famine in Jīng Prefecture,
and Chōng's recent move and initial establishment,
300,000 *hu* of rice would be transported annually to supply military provisions,
until a year of abundant harvest.
Jiān sent his generals Fú Róng to attack Fán and Dèng,
Shí Yuè to attack Lúyáng,
Yáo Cháng to attack Nánxiāng,
and Wéi Zhōng to attack Wèixīng.
All the places they attacked fell.
Chōng dispatched the Administrator of Jiāngxià, Liú Shì, and the Commander of the Central Army of the South, Zhū Xù, to attack them,
but Shì was timid and did not advance,
and Xù was captured by the rebels.
Chōng deeply blamed himself,
submitting a memorial with his seals,
requesting to resign his post,
but this was not allowed.
He sent the General of the Left Guard, Zhāng Xuánzhī, to Chōng to consult on military matters.
Chōng led the Former General Liú Bō, his nephew the General Who Manifests Awe Shí Mín, and the General Who Commands the Army Shí Qián, among others, to attack Fú Jiān,
and captured Jiān's Zhúyáng.
He attacked Wǔdāng,
driving away Jiān's Inspector of Yǎnzōu, Zhāng Chóng.
Jiān sent Mùróng Chuí and Máodàng to attack Dèngchéng,
and Fú Xī and Shí Yuè to attack Xīnyě.
Chōng, fearing Jiān's large forces,
and also due to illness,
returned to garrison Shàngmíng.
He memorialized, stating
that
"Xiàkǒu at the confluence of the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers is a crucial strategic point,
close to a powerful enemy.
My nephew, Shí Mín, is capable of this responsibility,
and I shall provisionally appoint him Supervisor of Military Affairs of ten counties in Jīng and Jiāng, General Who Manifests Valor, and Grand Administrator of Xiāngchéng.
Xúnyáng borders the powerful barbarians to the north
and connects to Jīng and Yǐng to the west;
it is also a crucial post.
Now that the commandery and prefecture are divided,
I request to appoint Wáng Huì as Inspector of Jiāng Prefecture."
The imperial edict approved this.
At this time, Huì had just suffered the loss of his elder brother, Shào,
and was about to bury him,
so he declined to leave his post.
Thereupon, the General of the Guard, Xiè Ān, replaced him with the Commander of the Central Army, Xiè Yóu.
Chōng, hearing this, was angered,
and submitted a memorial stating that Yóu was incompetent in both civil and military matters,
and requested to personally hold the post of Jiāng Prefecture.
The Emperor granted his request.
Chōng sent Shí Qián to attack Jiān's Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Yán Zhèn,
captured him,
along with twenty-nine major and minor chiefs,
and sent them to the capital.
An imperial edict ordered them returned to Chōng's headquarters.
For his achievement in pacifying Zhèn,
his second son, Qiān, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíyáng.
Jiān sent his general Hǎo Guì to guard Xiāngyáng,
Chōng sent the General Who Manifests Awe, Zhū Chuò, to attack him,
and consequently burned the rice fields north of the Miǎn River,
relocating over six hundred households before returning.
He also sent the Grand Administrator of Shàngyōng, Guō Bǎo, to attack Jiān's Grand Administrator of Wèixīng, Chǔ Yuán, and Grand Administrator of Shàngyōng, Duàn Fāng,
both of whom surrendered.
The Grand Administrator of Xīnchéng, Qū Cháng, fled,
and all three commanderies were pacified.
An imperial edict bestowed a million cash
and a thousand bolts of brocade.
Initially,
Huán Chōng was stationed in the west.
As the bandits were then very strong,
he moved his garrison to Shàngmíng.
He believed that the forces in Jiāngdōng were weak,
and that it was only possible to secure the borders
and merely defend oneself.
He also believed that generals and prime ministers had different functions.
He considered his own virtue and prestige inferior to Xiè Ān’s,
and therefore entrusted the internal administration to him,
while taking on the responsibility
of defending the four directions himself.
He was also on intimate terms with Zhū Xù.
Soon after, Xù was captured by the bandits,
and Chōng felt deep regret and shame.
Later, Fú Jiān invaded with his entire nation.
Chōng deeply worried about the foundations of the state,
so he dispatched three thousand elite troops to the capital.
Xiè Ān believed that three thousand men would make no difference,
and wishing to outwardly appear at ease,
upon hearing that the army was nearby,
he firmly refused them.
He replied,
“The court's arrangements are already settled,
and there is no lack of military resources.
The western feudal lords should focus on their own defense.”
At that time, Ān had already sent his nephew Xuán and Huán Yī's armies, among others.
Chōng thought these forces were insufficient to determine success or failure.
He summoned his aides
and sighed to them, saying:
“Xiè Ān has the capacity for the court,
but he is not skilled in military strategy.
Now a great enemy is imminent,
yet he is busy with idle talk.
Even though he has sent inexperienced youths,
and their numbers are few and weak,
the fate of the empire is clear.
I will surely don the left lapel [of a barbarian]!”
Soon after, he heard that Jiān had been defeated,
and a great accomplishment had been achieved.
He also learned that Zhū Xù had consequently returned.
Chōng was already ill,
and this added shame
caused his illness to worsen, and he died
at the age of fifty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi,
with his former official position remaining as before,
and given the posthumous name Xuānmù.
He was given fifty myriad cash in funeral gifts
and five hundred rolls of cloth.
Chōng was naturally frugal
and humble, loving scholars.
Once, after bathing,
his wife sent him new clothes.
Chōng was greatly angered
and quickly ordered them to be taken away.
His wife sent them again,
saying,
“If clothes are never new,
how can they become old!”
Chōng smiled and wore them.
He appointed the recluse Liú Línzhī of Nányáng as his Chángshǐ.
Línzhī did not yield,
so he personally went to welcome him
and treated him with great respect.
He also invited the recluse Dèng Càn of Chángshā to be his Biéjià,
showing full courtesy.
Càn was moved by his appreciation for worthies
and rose to accept the appointment.
Initially,
Xī Jiàn, Yǔ Liàng, and Yǔ Yì all submitted memorials before their deaths,
appointing their relatives.
Only Chōng alone wrote to Xiè Ān, saying:
“Miàolíng and Língbǎo are still young.
My deceased brother’s entrustment was incomplete,
and this I regret!”
His words contained no private matters,
and commentators praised him even more.
When his coffin was brought down to Jiānglíng,
men and women, old and young, all stood by the river to see him off,
wailing with utmost sorrow.
Later, Huán Xuán usurped the throne
and posthumously granted him the titles of Tàifù and Xuānchéng Wáng.
He had seven sons: Sì, Qiān, Xiū, Chóng, Hóng, Xiàn, and Yí.
Sì’s courtesy name was Gōngzǔ.
From a young age, he had a pure reputation,
and he and Huò’s son Shí Xiù were considered the foremost among the Huán clan’s nephews and grandchildren.
After Chōng replaced Huò as the western garrison commander,
an imperial edict appointed Sì as Dūdū of the armies of the three commanderies of Jīngzhōu and the four commanderies of Yùzhōu, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He administered affairs simply and concisely.
When repairing his residence,
which required wooden eaves,
Sì ordered them to be replaced with thatch
and the timber given to the boat officials.
He was transferred to become Tàishǒu of Xīyáng and Xiāngchéng commanderies,
stationed at Xiàkǒu.
Later, he was given the additional title of Jiāngxià Xiàng
and died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title of Nánzhōnglángjiāng
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
His son was Yìn.
Yìn’s courtesy name was Màoyuǎn.
From a young age, he maintained pure conduct.
Although his family had been noble and prominent for generations,
he was highly praised for his tranquility and reclusiveness.
He was first appointed Mìshū Chéng,
and gradually promoted to Zhōngshū Láng and Mìshū Jiān.
Huán Xuán greatly admired and loved him,
promoting him to Zhōngshū Lìng.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
he became Lìbù Shàngshū
and followed Xuán in his westward flight.
After Xuán’s death,
he surrendered.
An imperial edict stated:
“Indeed, when goodness is manifest, one’s blessings are long-lasting;
when merit is evident, one’s story is extraordinary.
Because of Xuānmèng’s loyalty,
he was honored by the Later Jìn state;
because of Zǐwén’s virtue,
his descendants were preserved.
The late Tàiwèi Huán Chōng,
formerly guarding the west,
was loyal to the imperial house.
His sons indulged in villainy
and brought about their own punishment and death.
Thinking of Chōng’s remaining merits,
my heart is filled with sorrow.
His grandson Yìn should be shown compassion and leniency
to encourage good deeds.
He shall be specially spared his life
and exiled to Xīn’ān.”
When the Dōngyáng Tàishǒu Yīn Zhòngwén and Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu Luò Qiú, among others, plotted rebellion,
〔一六〕secretly intending to establish Yìn as Xuán’s successor,
the plot was discovered,
and they were executed.
Qiān’s courtesy name was Jìngzǔ.
He was discerning, upright, and had a dignified reputation.
Initially, due to his father’s merits, he was enfeoffed as Kāiguó Hóu of Yíyáng County.
He was successively promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wúguó Nèishǐ.
During Sūn Ēn’s rebellion,
Qiān fled to Wúxī.
He was summoned and appointed Shàngshū,
and Yuán Xiǎn, the Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, appointed him Cányì Cānjūn,
then transferred him to Sīmǎ.
In the early Yuánxīng era,
the court was preparing to attack Huán Xuán.
As the Huán clan had been in the west for generations,
and Qiān’s father Chōng had left a legacy of kindness in Jīngchǔ,
fearing the sentiments of the people,
they appointed Qiān as Chíjié, Dūdū of the armies of Jīng, Yì, Níng, and Liáng provinces, Xīzhōngláng Jiāng, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Jiǎjié
to pacify Jīngchǔ.
After Xuán took power,
he appointed Qiān as Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
with additional charge of Lìbù,
and added the title of Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Qiān and his brothers held prominent positions,
and Xuán greatly relied on them,
but inwardly, he did not treat them well.
Qiān was re-enfeoffed as Níngdōu Hóu,
appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and additionally given the title Sànqí Chángshì.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng, Wèijiāngjūn, Kāifǔ, and Lùshàngshūshì.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
he again held the additional title of Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his original offices remaining as before,
and was enfeoffed as Xīn’ān Wáng.
When Huán Zhèn (桓振) caused chaos,
Qiān (謙) protected the imperial carriage,
and rendered considerable service.
However, he was obscure
and especially unsuitable for initiating affairs.
Initially,
he advised Zhèn (振) to lead his army to battle,
while he would guard Jiānglíng (江陵).
Since Zhèn (振) slighted Qiān (謙) for his involvement in affairs,
he did not follow the advice.
When Zhèn (振) was defeated,
Qiān (謙) fled to Yáo Xīng (姚興).
Before this,
Qiáo Zòng (譙縱) had pledged allegiance to Yáo Xīng (姚興).
Zòng (縱) and Lú Xún (盧循) exchanged envoys,
secretly influencing each other.
Then Zòng (縱) memorialized Xīng (興), requesting Qiān (謙) to join him in moving eastward downriver.
Xīng (興) asked Qiān (謙),
and Qiān (謙) replied:
"My family has received favor in Jīngchǔ (荊楚).
Although my cousin Xuán (玄) eventually usurped the throne,
it was all due to coercion,
which is clear to both gods and men.
Now if I and Zòng (縱) go eastward,
the common people will surely be alarmed."
Xīng (興) said:
"A small stream cannot accommodate a large boat.
If Zòng's (縱) talent and strength are sufficient to accomplish the task,
he would not need you to be his 'scales and wings.'
You should seek your own good fortune."
So he sent him away.
When Qiān (謙) arrived in Shǔ (蜀),
he wished to embrace a receptive attitude and attract scholars,
but Zòng (縱) suspected him,
and thus placed Qiān (謙) in Lónggé (龍格),
having people guard him.
Qiān (謙) wept to his younger brothers, saying:
"Lord Yáo's (姚) words were divine!"
Later, he and Zòng (縱) brought Qiáo Dàofú (譙道福) down together.
Qiān (謙) recruited on the way,
and the people, moved by Chōng's (沖) lingering benevolence,
had twenty thousand join him.
Liú Dàoguī (劉道規) defeated Qiān (謙),
and executed him.
Xiū (脩), courtesy name Chéngzǔ (承祖).
He married Princess Wǔchāng (武昌公主), daughter of Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝),
served successively as Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
and was gradually promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍).
Wáng Gōng (王恭) was about to attack Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī (譙王尚之),
and first sent Hé Dànzhī (何澹之) and Sūn Wúzhōng (孫無終) towards Jùróng (句容).
Xiū (脩), as Zuǒwèi (左衞), concurrently held the post of Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn (振武將軍),
and, with Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Táo Wújí (陶無忌), resisted them.
Xiū (脩) was stationed in Jùróng (句容).
Soon after, Gōng (恭) was defeated,
and Wúzhōng (無終) sent a letter requesting surrender.
As Xiū (脩) was returning his troops,
Yáng Quánqī (楊佺期) had already reached Shítou (石頭).
At that time, the court was unprepared,
and there was panic both inside and out.
Xiū (脩) advanced a proposal, saying:
"The Yīn (殷) and Huán (桓) relied solely on Wáng Gōng (王恭);
now that Gōng (恭) is defeated and destroyed,
they are all dismayed.
If we now issue a gracious edict to employ Xuán (玄),
Xuán (玄) will be inwardly pleased,
and thus be able to control Zhòngkān (仲堪) and Quánqī (佺期),
making them both obey orders."
The court accepted this.
Xiū (脩) was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍), Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史), with a provisional staff of authority (假節),
and temporarily commanded the civil and military affairs of Zuǒwèi (左衞).
Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) was also ordered to escort him with a thousand men.
Zhòngkān (仲堪) was transferred to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Before Xiū (脩) could depart,
Xuán (玄) and others allied at Xúnyáng (尋陽),
demanding Láozhī's (牢之) execution.
Shàngzhī (尚之) also pleaded that Zhòngkān (仲堪) was innocent,
and had been demoted without cause.
Thereupon, an edict reinstated Zhòngkān (仲堪) as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Jiāng Jì (江績) memorialized that Xiū (脩) had accepted Yáng Quánqī's (楊佺期) words,
exchanged communications,
and not fully conveyed information,
considering his personal interest,
thereby misleading imperial calculations.
He requested that Xiū (脩) be arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
A special edict removed him from office.
Soon after, he replaced Wáng Níngzhī (王凝之) as Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍).
After a while,
Xuán (玄) defeated Zhòngkān (仲堪) and Quánqī (佺期).
An edict appointed Xiū (脩) as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍) and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史).
Soon he was again Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍).
When Xuán (玄) was in power,
he appointed Xiū (脩) Dūdū Liùzhōu (都督六州), Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍), Xú Yǎn Èrzhōu Cìshǐ (徐兗二州刺史), with a provisional staff of authority (假節).
Soon he was promoted to Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍),
and given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
When Xuán (玄) usurped the throne,
he made him Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn (撫軍大將軍),
and enfeoffed him as Ānchéng Wáng (安成王).
Liú Yù's (劉裕) righteous army rose,
and executed him.
Xú Níng (徐寧) was
a native of Tán (郯) in Dōnghǎi (東海).
He was well-known in his youth
and served as magistrate of Yú (輿) county.
At that time, Tíngwèi (廷尉) Huán Yí (桓彝) was renowned for his discerning judgment of character.
Yí (彝) once left his post
and went to Guǎnglíng (廣陵) to visit relatives and old friends.
On his return, he encountered a storm,
and stopped in a harbor.
After several days of worry and dejection,
he went ashore
and saw a building
that resembled a government office.
Upon inquiry,
he was told it was Yú (輿) county.
Yí (彝) then called on him.
Níng (寧) was intelligent, benevolent, and widely learned.
They met with delight,
and Yí (彝) stayed for several nights.
Yí (彝) greatly praised him,
and they became sworn friends before parting.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he said to Yǔ Liàng (庾亮):
"I have found an excellent Lìbù Láng (吏部郎) for you."
The story is in Yí's (彝) biography.
He was immediately promoted to Lìbù Láng (吏部郎), Zuǒjiāngjūn (左將軍), and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史),
and died in office.
The historian says: The decadent wind secretly stirred,
the pure spring gradually dried up.
Morality was abandoned in favor of emotion and nature,
while loyalty and trustworthiness were manifested in official teachings.
The lofty integrity of Shǒuyáng (首陽) – seeking benevolence and attaining it.
The subtle words of Sìshàng (泗上) – hearing the Way in the morning and being able to die content in the evening.
Yuán Zhěn (原軫) removed his helmet,
awe-inspiring in his past strategies.
Jì Lù (季路) severed the cap strings,
far removed from his previous resolve.
Moreover, when frost and snow intertwine in the twilight years,
and wind and rain obscure the approaching dawn,
the clear resonance sometimes changes its tone,
and the upright tree rarely preserves its nature.
Huán Màolún (桓茂倫) embraced a disposition of moderation,
and cherished an unyielding integrity.
He surpassed the pure legacy of Zhōu Yǔ (周庾)
and followed the distant path of Xǔ Guō (許郭).
Fearing to avoid danger by taking the easy way out,
and knowing that facing death was easier,
he spread his fragrance through the ages,
even as his bones sank into the netherworld.
The courage of the benevolent,
is it not so!
As for those whose foundations repeatedly saw rise and fall,
with dragons and snakes coexisting in mountains and marshes:
Chōng (沖) hesitated in internal assistance,
while Huò (豁) acted overbearingly in the upstream regions.
Qián (虔) displayed the might of the northern gate,
and Xiù (秀) calmly handled affairs in Xīyáng (西陽).
Externally, they served as city defenders,
and internally, they avoided suspicion of overstepping their bounds.
Among renowned ministers,
they may also be counted.
However, Wēn (溫) possessed an arrogant disposition,
and Xuán (玄) eventually embarked on the path of ruin.
Thus we know that the excellence of Jì Zhòng (敬仲) could not quell the chaos of Tántái (檀臺),
and the loyalty of Níng Yú (寧俞) could not save from the disaster of Yì (弈).
That Zǐwén (子文) could not receive sacrificial offerings,
how sad!
Appraisal says: How imposing Xuānchéng (宣城),
his chaste heart unyielding.
His body perished like dew,
his name rose with the clouds.
Qián (虔) and Huò (豁) were outstanding through generations,
Chōng (沖) and Xiù (秀) both excellent.
The state relied on loyal ministers,
the family extolled talented sons.
Zhènwǔ (振武), Qiān (謙), and Wén (文),
formed a group in Xúnyì (尋邑).
They returned to usurpation and chaos,
what more is there to say?

Biographies, Chapter 45: Wáng Zhàn (王湛) (His son Chéng (承); Chéng's (承) sons Shù (述), Tǎnzhī (坦之), Yīzhī (禕之); Tǎnzhī's (坦之) sons Kǎi (愷), Yú (愉), Guóbǎo (國寶), Chén (忱); Yú's (愉) son Suí (綏); Chéng's (承) clan cousin Qiáo (嶠); Yuán Yuèzhī (袁悅之); Zǔ Táizhī (祖台之))
Wáng Zhàn
, courtesy name Chǔchōng, was the younger brother of
Sītú Hún.
In his youth, he possessed discernment and bearing.
He was seven chi and eight cùn tall,
with a prominent forehead and large nose,
and spoke little.
Initially, he possessed hidden virtues
that no one could perceive.
His brothers and clansmen all considered him foolish,
but his father, Chǎng, alone thought him exceptional.
When his father died,
he resided by the tomb.
After the mourning period,
he kept his gate closed and maintained quietude,
not associating with contemporary society.
Chōng was always simple and unassuming,
his magnanimity profound,
and he had the potential to be a high minister.
His nephew, Jì, disdained him.
When food was spread out before him,
it filled the table,
but he did not offer any to Zhàn.
Zhàn ordered vegetables to be brought
and ate them opposite him.
Jì once visited Zhàn
and saw the Zhōu Yì by his bed.
He asked,
"Uncle, what do you use this for?"
Zhàn replied,
"When I'm not feeling well,
I sometimes look at it."
Jì requested him to speak about it.
Zhàn then analyzed profound principles,
which were subtly marvelous and uniquely insightful,
all unheard of by Jì.
Jì was talented and spirited,
with little of the respect due from a nephew to an uncle towards Zhàn.
After hearing his words,
he involuntarily trembled,
his mind and body both awed.
Thus, he stayed for an entire day and several nights,
feeling his own inadequacy,
and then sighed,
"My family has a distinguished scholar,
whom I have not known for thirty years.
This is Jì's fault."
Afterwards, he took his leave,
and Zhàn saw him to the gate.
Jì had a difficult-to-ride warhorse.
Jì asked Zhàn,
"Uncle, do you like riding at all?"
Zhàn replied,
"I like it too."
He then rode this horse,
his posture graceful and movements like flowing silk,
such that no skilled rider could surpass him.
Jì also had a horse he rode
which he loved very much.
Zhàn said,
"Although this horse is fast,
its strength is weak and it cannot endure hardship.
I recently saw the dùyóu's horse, which is superior,
but it is simply not fed enough fodder."
Jì tried feeding it,
making it equal to his own horse.
Zhàn again said,
"You will only know this horse's true ability when it bears a heavy load;
on flat ground, there is no way to distinguish it."
Thereupon, they tested it on an anthill-like mound,
and Jì's horse indeed stumbled,
while the dùyóu's horse performed as usual.
Jì was even more astonished,
and returned to report to his father,
saying,
"I have only now gained an uncle;
he is a man superior to me."
Emperor Wǔ also considered Zhàn foolish,
and whenever he saw Jì,
he would tease him, saying,
"Is your family's foolish uncle dead yet?"
Jì usually had no answer.
On this occasion,
the Emperor again asked as before,
and Jì replied,
"My uncle is by no means foolish."
He then praised his virtues.
The Emperor asked,
"Who can he be compared to?"
Jì replied,
"Below Shān Tāo,
and above Wèi Shū."
People at the time said that to rank Zhàn above Shān Tāo was not enough,
and to compare him below Wèi Shū was too much.
Zhàn heard this and said,
"Do they want to place me between Jìmèng?"
Zhàn had a brief official career, serving as Qín Wáng Wénxué, Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ, Shàngshū Láng, and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
then leaving to become Rǔnán Nèishǐ.
He died in the fifth year of Yuánkāng,
at the age of forty-seven.
His son was Chéngsì.
Chéng, courtesy name Ānqī,
was pure and tranquil, with few desires,
and pursued no particular cultivation or aspiration.
When discussing principles and discerning things,
he merely clarified their essential points without embellishing his words,
and those with discernment admired his conciseness yet comprehensiveness.
He became famous in his youth.
Tàiwèi Wáng Yǎn greatly valued and admired him,
comparing him to Nányáng Yuè Guǎng.
In the early Yǒngníng era,
he became Píqí Cānjūn.
At a time when the world was on the verge of chaos,
he fled south to avoid the troubles.
He was promoted to Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He anticipated and welcomed the imperial carriage,
and was granted the title of Lántián Xiàn Hóu.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Láng,
but did not accept.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè, when stationed in Xǔ,
appointed him Jìshì Cānjūn,
and valued him greatly,
instructing his son, Pí,
saying,
"What is gained from learning is shallow;
what is settled by experience is deep.
Practicing etiquette and ceremony
is not as good as observing dignified bearing;
pondering ancient sayings
is not as good as personally receiving instructions.
Wáng Cānjūn is a model for humanity;
you should take him as your teacher."
He served in the prefecture for several years,
and seeing the imperial government gradually decline,
he resigned, citing his mother's old age,
and requested to leave.
Yuè did not permit it.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
His governance emphasized purity and tranquility,
and he was not meticulous in trivial matters.
When a minor official stole fish from a pond,
the disciplinarian officer investigated it.
Chéng asked for the reason,
saying,
"King Wén's park was shared with the people;
what is there to regret about pond fish?"
There was someone who violated the night curfew
and was apprehended by an officer.
Chéng asked his reason,
and he replied,
"I was receiving instruction from my teacher
and did not notice dusk falling."
Chéng said,
"To whip Níng Yuè to establish prestige
is not the foundation of good governance."
He ordered the officer to send him home.
His composure and leniency were like this.
Soon after, he resigned his office
and crossed the river eastward.
At this time, the roads were obstructed,
and people were filled with fear and danger.
Whenever Chéng encountered difficulties and dangers,
he handled them calmly,
and even his family and close attendants
did not see any sign of worry or joy in him.
Upon arriving at Xiàpī,
he climbed a mountain and looked north,
sighing,
"People speak of sorrow;
I am only now about to feel sorrow."
When he arrived in Jiànyè,
he became Yuándì's Zhèndōngfǔ Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and was treated with great courtesy and respect.
Chéng had a high reputation from a young age,
and he treated others with sincerity,
fully embodying the principle of magnanimity,
thus everyone was fond of him.
Among the famous ministers who crossed the river, Wáng Dǎo, Wèi Jiè, Zhōu Yǐ, and Yǔ Liàng
were all inferior to him,
making him the foremost figure in the restoration.
He died at the age of forty-six,
and the court and people mourned him deeply.
From Chǎng to Chéng, the family had high reputations through generations,
Initially,
Wáng Shù’s family was poor.
He sought to serve as the Magistrate of Wǎnlíng.
He received quite a lot of gifts
and renovated his house,
which was investigated by the provincial authorities.
There were 1,300 infractions.
Wáng Dǎo had someone tell him:
“The son of a famous father need not worry about lacking a stipend.
It is very unfitting for you to demean yourself by governing a small county.”
Wáng Shù replied:
“I myself should stop,
but people of the time do not understand it yet.”
Afterward, he repeatedly held positions in commanderies and provinces.
His integrity was unmatched.
He distributed all his stipends and rewards to relatives and old friends.
His residence and old possessions remained unchanged from before.
It was only then that he was admired by people of the time.
However, his quick temper was a burden.
Once, while eating an egg,
he tried to pierce it with his chopsticks,
but failed.
He immediately became furious and threw it on the ground.
The egg rolled around without stopping,
so he got out of bed and tried to crush it with the heel of his clog,
but failed again.
Enraged,
he picked it up and put it in his mouth,
bit it open, and spat it out.
After attaining high positions,
he always practiced gentle overcoming.
Xiè Yì was coarse in nature
and once resented Wáng Shù,
cursing him with extreme words.
Wáng Shù did not respond,
but merely faced the wall.
After half a day,
Xiè Yì left,
and only then did Wáng Shù resume his seat.
People praised him for this.
In the second year of Tàihé
as he was nearing the age for retirement,
he submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
saying:
“My great-grandfather, Wèi Sīkōng Chǎng, wrote a memorial to Emperor Wén, saying: ‘I once served with Zōng Shìlín of Nányáng as officials in the Eastern Palace.
Shìlín gained a good reputation in his youth,
and the people in his locality revered him.
But when he grew old,
he eagerly pushed himself,
fearing he would be discarded,
and people of the time all laughed at him.
If Heaven were to grant him longevity,
at the age of retirement,
he would not engage in such indecisive behavior.’
His sentiment was noble and indignant,
and he held such conduct in deep contempt.
Although it was a memorial,
it was actually an admonition.
I, your subject, hold a high position,
and though my illness causes me to neglect my duties,
I still believe there is a possibility of recovery.
But day by day,
my age and chronic illness advance,
and I will never again have the opportunity to attend the imperial presence.
I beg to follow the admonition of my ancestor
and return to my rural garden to live out my old age.”
The request was not granted.
Wáng Shù ultimately did not rise.
He died in the third year of Tàihé
at the age of sixty-six.
Initially,
when Huán Wēn pacified Luòyáng
and proposed moving the capital,
the court was worried and fearful,
and planned to send a侍中 to stop him.
Wáng Shù said:
“Huán Wēn wishes to intimidate the court with an empty show,
it is not a real intention.
Just agree to it,
and he will naturally not go through with it.”
The matter indeed did not proceed.
He also proposed moving the bells and stands from Luòyáng.
Wáng Shù said:
“During the decline of Yǒngjiā,
we temporarily made the capital south of the Jiāng River.
We are now on the verge of pacifying the realm
and returning to the old capital.
If that is not the case,
it would be better to move the imperial tombs
rather than prioritizing the bells and stands.”
Huán Wēn ultimately could not override him.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ.
His posthumous name was Mù.
To avoid Emperor Mù’s name,
it was changed to Jiǎn.
His son, Tǎnzhī, inherited his title.
Tǎnzhī’s courtesy name was Wéndù.
When he came of age, he and Xī Chāo both had great reputations.
People of the time had a saying about them:
“Xī Jiābīn, with his unmatched virtue,
and Wáng Wéndù, walking alone east of the Jiāng River.”
Jiābīn
was Xī Chāo’s informal name.
Púshè Jiāng Pèi, who was in charge of selections,
intended to nominate him as a Shàngshū Láng.
Tǎnzhī heard of it and said:
“Since crossing the Jiāng,
the position of Shàngshū Láng has only been for the second-best,
how can I be nominated for this?”
Jiāng Pèi then stopped.
Emperor Jiǎnwén, as Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
appointed him as his Yuàn.
He was successively promoted to Cānjūn, Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and then Sīmǎ,
with the added title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He went out to serve as Dà Sīmǎ Huán Wēn’s Chángshǐ.
Soon after, he left office due to his father’s mourning.
When the mourning period ended,
he was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng,
inheriting his father’s title.
At that time, a deceased soldier, Hán Chàng, who had fled, surrendered,
claiming
“he rebelled because he lost his cow.”
The authorities impeached Hán Chàng for stealing a cow
and, through torture, he confessed to the crime.
Tǎnzhī believed that since Hán Chàng had surrendered himself,
it was extra-legal to punish him further. He thought that losing a cow due to negligence
might be forgivable,
and if he was subjected to instruments of torture,
there was a reason for self-incrimination.
Therefore, he should be treated according to the principle of lighter punishment for crimes of doubt.
Thus, he was pardoned.
When Hǎixī Gōng was deposed,
Tǎnzhī was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Tǎnzhī had a noble character,
and particularly disliked the indulgent and unrestrained trends of his time,
which did not uphold Confucian teachings.
He quite esteemed the study of penal philosophy and names,
and wrote “On the Rejection of Zhuāngzǐ,” which stated: Xún Qīng said of Zhuāngzǐ,
“He was obscured by Heaven and did not know humanity.”
Yáng Xióng also said,
“Zhuāng Zhōu was unrestrained and lawless.”
Hé Yàn said,
“He sold his body to Zhuāngzǐ,
indulged in
profound emptiness,
and did not adapt to the changes of the times.”
Are the words of these three sages
not largely true?
Indeed, a solitary pronouncement
sings in emptiness and finds no echo;
a work without inspiration
has a
biased meaning and limited utility.
To move people comes from forgetting oneself,
to respond to things lies in having no mind.
It is not that Confucius did not embody profundity,
but because he embodied profundity, he used what was close at hand.
How could Yán Zǐ not
possess virtue?
It was because his virtue was complete that he accepted instruction.
Why is it so?
It is because there is no choice but for it to be so.
Indeed, those who are self-sufficient are few,
thus principles were distant during the ages of Xī and Nóng;
those who follow instruction are many,
thus righteousness was expanded during the Three Dynasties.
The mind of the Way is subtle,
the human mind is perilous.
With myriad different
voices,
who knows what is truly right!
Even the sentiments of Shǒuyáng,
the wisdom of being thrice dismissed,
the sweetness of wearing out one’s head,
the love of losing one’s hair,
the life of emaciation,
the
death of carrying a stone—
when judged by the doctrine of the Mean,
they do not enter the Way,
let alone those beneath them!
The former kings knew how difficult it was for human emotions to be unfettered,
feared that improper conduct would lead to disputes,
lamented the regrets caused by Sī Chè,
and carefully considered the reasons for removing a sash.
Therefore, they molded all beings,
planned before any signs appeared,
always restrained their urges,
and established regulations.
They made people uphold propriety to honor
transformation.
Daily practices lead to established customs.
Sincerity existing, evil is forgotten.
Gain diminishing, competition ceases.
When achievements are completed and affairs are settled,
the common people all say, "We are naturally so."
Indeed, those who are skilled at obscuring have no
strangeness,
thus they encounter no obstacles.
Adhering to the Way to depart from common customs,
who surpasses those who do not comprehend?
One who speaks of the Way but loses its essence,
that is not the Way.
One who debates virtue yet possesses
that position,
that is not their virtue.
What speech and silence have yet to fully explore,
how much less so to propagate it as a trend!
Moreover, to seek fish by the Háo [River],
imagining their feelings are the same as mine;
to infer the hidden
by seeking the manifest,
the principle is understood but the emotion remains obscure.
As for Zhuāngshēng,
he looked upon the grand courtyard and stroked his agreements,
venerating the ever-higher as insufficient,
entrusting his accumulated thoughts to three chapters,
regretting
that his heart's desires were not fully expressed.
His words are whimsical and deceptive,
his meanings vast and extravagant.
The noble-minded respond inwardly,
following me beyond the mundane world.
The common people rely on it,
making it a resource for
frailty and superficiality.
Therefore, there are few good people in the world,
and many bad people.
Zhuāngzǐ's benefit to the world is little,
his harm to the world is much.
Thus it is said: "The Lǔ wine was thin
and Hándān was besieged;
Zhuāngshēng arose and customs declined."
Propriety departed with the floating clouds,
deceit and the pursuit of gain flourished equally.
People regarded self-restraint as a disgrace,
scholars considered having no fixed position
as broad-minded.
The era lacked praise for walking in virtue,
customs had transgressions for treading on righteousness.
To speak hastily of rewards and punishments is not to be done carelessly;
to repeatedly extol non-action is not suitable for adapting to change.
Though it can be used for the world,
it is insufficient for governing the people of the world.
In the past, the Elder from Hányīn practiced the art of chaos.
Kǒngzǐ believed he knew one aspect but not the other.
Is not the Way of Zhuāngshēng
similar to this?
With that
agreement of the foolish,
what difference is there?
As for benefiting and not harming,
that is the Way of Heaven;
acting and not contending,
that is the virtue of the Sages.
All beings rely on it yet no one
knows its origin;
it is within Confucianism yet not Confucian,
not Daoism yet possessing the Way.
It deeply penetrates the Nine Schools,
mysteriously unifying self and other.
The myriad things use it without exhausting it,
diligently renewing daily yet
never perishing.
Our Kǒng Lǎo of old have already spoken of this.
He was also appointed Grand Moderator of the home province.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén was on his deathbed,
he issued an edict for Grand Marshal Wēn to act as regent following the precedent of the Duke of Zhōu's regency.
Tǎnzhī personally took the edict and entered,
and destroyed it before the emperor.
The emperor said,
"The empire,
it is but a transient fortune.
What do you object to?"
Tǎnzhī said,
"The empire,
it is the empire of Xuān Yuán.
How can Your Majesty monopolize it?"
The emperor then made Tǎnzhī revise the edict.
After Wēn passed away,
Tǎnzhī and Xiè Ān jointly assisted the young emperor.
He was promoted to Grand Secretary,
and concurrently held the post of Administrator of Dānyáng.

Shortly after, he was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xú, Yǎn, and Qīng three provinces, General of the Northern Army of the Central Guard, and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn two provinces,
stationed in Guǎnglǐng.
Before proceeding to his post,
he submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject has heard that the Way of a monarch is founded on filial piety and reverence,
and in ruling the four seas, reliance on trustworthy appointments is paramount.
To be respectful and compliant without meddling,
then great virtue renews daily;
to personally rely on
the worthy and capable,
then the path of governance becomes harmonious.
In the past, Zhōu Chéng and Hàn Zhāo,
both ascended to the great succession in their youth.
At that time, the world was not without difficulties,
yet they were ultimately able to glorify
their ancestors,
and secure the altars of soil and grain.
This was due to honoring the honorable and loving one's kin,
and trusting and accepting great ministers.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty possesses an extraordinary and brilliant disposition,
endowed with inherent wisdom.
Your spring and autumns are still abundant,
your experience of the Way not yet extensive.
You still need guidance to perfect your heavenly virtue.
The Empress
Dowager possesses a benevolent and virtuous character,
surpassing the three mothers.
The late emperor served her for many years,
always praising her sagacity.
Your subject's desire to serve her,
should be likened to serving the revered ancestors;
the Empress Dowager's great loving kindness,
also need not differ from that for her own offspring.
The Prince of Lángyá, the Princess of Yúyáo, and all the imperial princesses,
should pay morning and evening respects,
receive instructions,
and practice proper conduct,
to achieve the beauty of admiration and reverence.
They should not, because they are not direct kin,
treat themselves as distant or suspicious.
When Emperor Sùzǔ passed away,
Chéng and Kāng were young,
and in matters great and small,
they always consulted Chancellor Dǎo.
This is how they achieved sagely virtue,
and this was truly the reason.
Now, Minister Púyè Ān and Minister Zhōngjūn Chōng,
are widely respected and pillars of the state.
They are ministers of the altars of soil and grain.
Moreover, they received kind treatment from the late emperor,
bound to him by close affection,
and both are dedicated to exhausting their loyalty and integrity,
giving their whole heart and strength,
submitting their sincerity to Your Majesty,
to repay the late emperor.
Your foolish
servant believes that all actions and decisions,
should be consulted with these two ministers.
These two ministers to Your Majesty,
are like Dàn and Shì of Zhōu,
Huò Guāng of Hàn,
and Wáng Dǎo to Emperor Xiǎnzōng.
Although Chōng is outside,
the road is not far.
Matters that can wait for a day or two,
must be thoroughly discussed,
only then can feelings be fully expressed,
and all affairs can be completed.
Moreover, though the Heavenly Ear is keen,
it is not enlightened or broad without being opened;
though the sentiments of the multitude are loyal,
they are not fully expressed without being drawn out.
It is fitting to frequently summon attendant ministers,
and seek honest advice.
In times of
peace,
a sagely ruler still takes caution and fear,
not tiring even when the sun begins to set;
how much more so now, in these difficult times where principles are fully tested,
and concerns involve security and danger.
The foundation of the ancestors depends on Your Majesty,
and you must
not fail to diligently pursue the Way,
to extend the Yáo and Shùn style of the late emperor.
How can you not reverently cultivate supreme virtue,
to preserve the destiny of Xuān Yuán, Heaven and Earth?
The memorial was presented,
