and the emperor accepted it."
Initially,
Xiè Ān ài loved music.
During the extreme grief of a one-year mourning period,
he did not give up his entertainers and musicians,
which somewhat became a custom.
Tǎnzhī disapproved and earnestly remonstrated with him.
Ān sent Tǎnzhī a letter saying:
"I know your profound affection and care for me.
What I seek is sound,
which I believe expresses emotion and meaning,
so there is nothing that cannot be done,
I merely amuse myself with it.
As for upholding moral conduct
and promoting worldly teachings,
it is not something I would contemplate,
nor something I would deign to do.
I always thought you somewhat understood my humble tastes,
but have you not yet grasped it, like on the bank of the Háo River?
Thus, I know that true friends,
are not easy to find."
Tǎnzhī replied:
"I fully understand your elegant intention.
This is indeed acting from a sincere heart,
the beauty of independent conduct.
However, I fear it is not what the great and moderate path entails.
My idea is that a person's temperament and rhythm are like the squareness or roundness of an object.
Square and round cannot be used interchangeably;
how can temperament and rhythm be easily altered?
Each should follow its proper path,
to expand their enterprise,
then the efforts of even the harshest times will surely succeed.
My lord, you established your virtuous conduct at a young age,
your discourse is profound and apt,
furthermore, with your esteemed position,
you live in leisurely contentment.
The talks of everyone,
all commend your clarity and remoteness.
Regarding this matter,
I truly have doubts.
In public and private, none can see its suitability.
To regard this as 'on the bank of the Háo River,'
will those who understand it not be few?
Moreover, the treasures of the world
are naturally cherished by the world.
How can one not consider the world's view
for that which the world disapproves of?
I hope
you will reconsider."
Letters went back and forth several times,
but Ān ultimately did not comply.
Tǎnzhī also once wrote to Yīn Kāngzǐ discussing the meaning of public-spiritedness and humility, saying: The Way of Heaven achieves its name through impartiality;
the Two Instruments (Heaven and Earth) establish their virtue through ultimate fairness.
Virtue is established in ultimate fairness,
thus there is no partiality that is not based on principle;
achieving a name lies in
impartiality,
thus one acts appropriately and forgets oneself.
This is how Heaven and Earth achieve success,
and how the Sages accomplish transformation.
From this perspective,
the public way embodies nature,
thus
the more prosperous the principle, the more it descends;
the meaning of humility arises from insufficiency,
thus when the times are corrupt, the meaning becomes prominent.
Therefore, Dà Yǔ and Gāoyáo spoke of their merits and kindness and achieved fame there,
while Mèng
Fǎn and Fàn Xiè guarded the rear and were the last to enter, thereby preserving themselves here.
From this, it can be seen
that the meanings of humility and public-spiritedness are indeed distinct.
That which is praised by things,
one cannot claim for oneself;
that which is valued by people,
one cannot take.
It is truly feared that people dislike those above them,
and the multitude cannot be overshadowed,
therefore the junzǐ
dwells in it,
and constantly adds to his self-restraint.
Great fame lies in correction and reduction,
not in meeting expectations;
concealing one's traces lies in avoiding prominence,
not in seeking what is right.
Thus
the meaning of humble brilliance is born alongside competition,
and the meaning of modest deference advances alongside boasting and arrogance.
Since popular praise arises from insufficiency,
it is not as good as having more
without being known;
good medicine is effective in curing illness,
but it is not as valuable as having no illness.
The Way of Qián is firm and strong,
showing people ease;
the Way of Kūn is yielding and gentle,
showing people simplicity.
The two images are manifest in all things,
the two virtues are evident in all living beings,
how
could they overcorrect and lose their proper place?
From this perspective,
the Way of Great Pervasion is public and vast throughout Heaven and Earth,
while the meaning of humility and boasting is treacherous in human affairs.
Now,
if we uphold public-spiritedness and discard humility,
then those who praise themselves will rely on ultimate fairness to create suspicion,
and those who glorify themselves will use partisanship to cause confusion.
This is what Wáng Shēng called "similar in appearance but
different in reality,"
which must not be overlooked.
However, principles must have a source,
and teachings also have a master.
If one explores their roots,
then the profound meaning will naturally become clear;
if one seeks only their superficial manifestations,
there will be no
end to faults.
How can one doubt ultimate fairness because of apparent similarities,
or forget integrity because of the pitfalls of greed?
Kāngzǐ and Yuán Hóng both had doubts and difficulties.
Tǎnzhī marked chapters and clarified sentences,
explaining and expounding each point,
and all were convinced.
Also, Kǒng Yán wrote the Tōng Gě Lùn,
and Tǎnzhī wrote a letter praising it.
His loyalty, public spirit, and magnanimity,
his clear endorsement of the worthy and superior,
are all of this kind.
Initially,
Tǎnzhī was very close to the monk Zhú Fǎshī.
They often discussed the retribution of the living and the dead,
and agreed that whoever died first should report back on the matter.
After a year,
the Master suddenly came and said:
"This poor monk has died.
Good and evil deeds are indeed not empty.
One must only diligently cultivate virtue and morality,
to uplift and assist the spirit."
After speaking, he disappeared.
Tǎnzhī also died soon after,
at the age of forty-six.
At his deathbed,
he wrote letters to Xiè Ān and Huán Chōng,
not mentioning private matters,
but only worrying about the affairs of the state.
The court and common people greatly mourned him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Ānběi Jiāngjūn,
and his posthumous name was Xiàn.
Yīzhī, courtesy name Wénshào.
He was famous in his youth,
married Princess Xúnyáng,
and served as Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He died before the age of thirty,
and was posthumously granted the title of Sànqí Chángshì.
Tǎnzhī had four sons: Kǎi, Yú, Guóbǎo, Chén.
Kǎi, courtesy name Màorén;
Yú, courtesy name Màohé;
both ascended to high ranks at a young age.
Kǎi inherited his father's noble title,
Yú gradually rose to Piàojí Sīmǎ,
and was granted Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
At the end of the Tàiyuán era, Kǎi served as Shìzhōng,
and concurrently as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
offering many remonstrances and suggestions.
The brothers were eminent and prosperous,
unparalleled at that time.
When Wáng Gōng and others attacked Guóbǎo,
Kǎi and Yú both requested to resign from their posts.
Because they were born of a different mother from Guóbǎo,
and had never gotten along,
they were spared misfortune.
After Guóbǎo's death,
Kǎi was appointed Wújun Nèishǐ,
and Yú was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Dūdū Yùzhōu Sìjùn, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and conferred the privilege of假節 (jiǎjié, acting as imperial envoy).
Not long after,
Kǎi was summoned to serve as Dānyáng Yǐn.
When Huán Xuán and others reached Jiāngníng,
Kǎi led troops to guard Shítou.
Soon after, Xuán and others fled,
and Kǎi again became Wújun.
He died of illness,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng.
Yu arrived at Zhèn.
Not long after,
Yīn Zhòngkān, Huán Xuán, and Yáng Quánqī raised troops in support of Wáng Gōng,
and swiftly arrived by water.
Yu, being unprepared,
fled in panic to Línchuān,
where he was captured by Xuán.
Xuán formed an alliance at Xúnyáng,
and placed Yu at the altar site;
Yu felt greatly disgraced by this.
When the matter was resolved,
he was appointed Huìjī Nèi Shǐ.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
he made Yu Shàngshū Púshè.
When Liú Yù raised his banner of righteousness,
Yu was given the additional title of Qián Jiāngjūn.
Since Yu was Huán's son-in-law,
and both father and son enjoyed favor and wealth,
and he had also once slighted Liú Yù,
he felt uneasy.
He secretly allied with the Sīzhōu Cìshǐ, Wēn Xiáng,
plotting a rebellion.
The plot was exposed,
and he was executed.
More than ten of his descendants also suffered the death penalty.
Guóbǎo, in his youth, lacked gentlemanly conduct
and did not uphold integrity.
His father-in-law, Xiè Ān, disliked his duplicity
and consistently suppressed him, not employing him.
He was appointed Shàngshū Láng.
Guóbǎo, being from a prominent family of the Restoration,
only served as Lìbù,
and would not serve as a Láng in other bureaus.
He harbored deep resentment
and firmly refused the appointment.
His paternal cousin was the consort of the Huìjī Wáng, Dàozǐ.
Through this, he associated with Dàozǐ,
and consequently slandered and disparaged Ān.
When Dàozǐ became regent,
he appointed Guóbǎo Mìshū Chéng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Lángyá Nèi Shǐ,
concurrently holding the position of Tángyì Tàishǒu,
and given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
He entered the court as Shìzhōng,
then was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng and Zhōng Lǐngjūn,
wielding authority and power with Dàozǐ,
stirring up trouble both inside and outside the court.
The Zhōngshū Láng, Fàn Níng,
who was Guóbǎo's maternal uncle,
was refined and upright.
He detested Guóbǎo's flattery
and advised Emperor Xiàowǔ to dismiss him.
Guóbǎo then used Yuán Yuèzhī of Chénjùn, through the nun Miàoyīn, to send a letter to Crown Prince's mother, Chén Shúyuàn,
stating Guóbǎo's loyalty and diligence,
and that he should be trusted.
The Emperor learned of this
and, on the pretext of other crimes, had Yuèzhī executed.
Guóbǎo was greatly alarmed
and subsequently used Dàozǐ to slander Níng.
Níng was consequently sent out as Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
When his younger brother Chén died,
Guóbǎo submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post to welcome his mother
and attend Chén's funeral.
An imperial edict granted him special leave,
but he procrastinated and did not depart promptly.
He was impeached by the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Chǔ Càn.
Guóbǎo, fearing punishment,
dressed in women's clothes,
pretending to be a maid from the royal family,
went to Dàozǐ to report the matter.
Dàozǐ spoke of it to the Emperor,
and thus he was pardoned.
Later, the Piàoqí Cānjūn, Wáng Huī, invited Guóbǎo to a banquet.
Guóbǎo, who was usually arrogant and given to drinking,
became angry at the Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, Zǔ Táizhī.
He rolled up his sleeves and shouted loudly,
throwing plates, cups, and musical instruments at Táizhī.
Táizhī dared not speak.
He was again impeached by Càn.
An imperial edict stated that Guóbǎo's indulgence in his nature
was extremely detrimental to his growth,
and Táizhī's weakness
was unfit for a supervisory official.
Both were dismissed from office.
A short while later,
he was reinstated,
becoming even more arrogant and disregardful of laws and regulations.
He built a study that rivaled the Qīngshǔ Diàn,
and the Emperor disliked his extravagance.
Guóbǎo, fearful,
then fawned upon the Emperor,
and somewhat distanced himself from Dàozǐ.
Dàozǐ was greatly enraged
and once, in the inner palace, openly rebuked Guóbǎo,
throwing a sword at him.
Their old friendship was completely broken.
At this time, Wáng Yǎ also enjoyed favor
and recommended Wáng Xún to the Emperor.
One night, the Emperor held a banquet with Guóbǎo and Yǎ.
The Emperor, slightly intoxicated,
ordered Xún to be summoned.
As Xún was about to arrive,
Guóbǎo, knowing his talent was inferior to Xún's,
feared that Xún's arrival
would diminish his favor.
He then said:
"Wáng Xún is a renowned figure of our time,
and should not be seen in such a state of drink and revelry."
The Emperor then stopped
and considered Guóbǎo loyal.
The Emperor intended to take Guóbǎo's daughter as the Lángyá Wáng's consort,
but before the marriage,
the Emperor died.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
Guóbǎo again served Dàozǐ,
promoting his paternal cousin Xiù to Lángyá Nèi Shǐ,
who also gained recognition for his cunning and wickedness.
Dàozǐ was again swayed by him,
relying on him as a trusted confidant.
Both were despised by the people of the time.
Guóbǎo then participated in managing court affairs,
his power shaking both inside and outside the court.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè,
concurrently overseeing official selection,
and given the additional titles of Hòu Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Dàozǐ assigned all the Eastern Palace troops to him.
At this time, Wáng Gōng and Yīn Zhòngkān, both highly talented,
each held a prestigious regional command.
Gōng detested Dàozǐ and Guóbǎo for disrupting governance
and frequently expressed concern for the state.
Dàozǐ and others also deeply feared them
and plotted to disarm them.
Before they could act,
Gōng's manifesto arrived,
ostensibly to punish Guóbǎo.
Guóbǎo was panic-stricken and did not know what to do.
Xiù advised Guóbǎo
to falsely claim Dàozǐ's order
to summon Wáng Xún and Chē Yìn and kill them,
to eliminate the dissatisfaction of the masses,
and then, with the emperor and prime minister in hand, attack the regional lords.
Guóbǎo agreed.
After Xún and Yìn arrived,
Guóbǎo dared not harm them
and instead asked Xún for advice.
Xún advised Guóbǎo to relinquish his military power to welcome Gōng,
and Guóbǎo believed him.
The account is in Xún's biography.
He also asked Yìn for advice.
Yìn said:
"Both the north and south have risen,
but Jīngzhōu has not yet arrived.
If the imperial court sends troops,
Gōng will surely defend the city.
In the past, Duke Huán besieged Shòuyáng,
and it took a long time to overcome.
If the capital city is not taken,
and the upper stream forces suddenly arrive,
how will you deal with them?"
Guóbǎo became even more frightened,
and so submitted a memorial resigning his post,
proceeding to the palace gate to await punishment.
Afterwards, he regretted it
and falsely claimed an imperial edict reinstated him to his original office,
intending to gather his troops to resist Wáng Gōng.
Dàozǐ, being unable to resist the regional lords,
wanted to shift the blame to Guóbǎo.
He then sent Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī to arrest Guóbǎo,
turn him over to the Tíngwèi,
and grant him death.
Xiù was also executed in the marketplace
to appease Wáng Gōng.
Guóbǎo was greedy and amassed wealth,
knowing no limits.
His inner quarters had hundreds of entertainers and concubines,
and rare treasures from all under heaven filled his rooms.
When Wáng Gōng suffered the death penalty,
an imperial edict posthumously reinstated Guóbǎo to his original office.
In the early Yuánxīng period,
Huán Xuán achieved his ambition
and memorialized to relocate Guóbǎo's family to Jiāozhōu.
Chén, whose courtesy name was Yuándá,
became renowned in his early twenties.
He was acclaimed alongside Wáng Gōng and Wáng Xún for a time.
He successively held the position of Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry.
He once visited his maternal uncle, Fàn Níng,
where he met Zhāng Xuán.
Níng asked them to converse.
Xuán sat upright, adjusted his robes,
and waited for Chén to speak.
Chén, however, did not utter a word,
so Xuán left disappointed.
Níng admonished Chén, saying:
"Zhāng Xuán
is a preeminent figure from Wúzhōng.
Why did you not speak with him?"
Chén smiled and said:
"If Zhāng Zǔxī wishes to make my acquaintance,
he can come to me himself."
Níng said to him:
"Your refined demeanor and distinguished reputation truly mark you as an outstanding talent of the younger generation."
Chén replied:
"Were it not for this uncle,
how could there be this nephew?"
Soon after, Níng sent a messenger to Xuán,
and Xuán, formally dressed, called on Chén.
Only then did they establish a guest-host relationship.
During the Tàiyuán era,
Chén was appointed
Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Area Commander of Jīng, Yì, and Níng Provinces, General of Jianwǔ, and was granted the imperial insignia of "Jiajié" (authorization to execute at will).
Chén relied on his talent and spirit,
indulging in drink and unrestrained conduct,
emulating the character of Wáng Chéng.
Furthermore, being young and holding the responsibility of a provincial governor,
commentators worried about him.
However, when he took charge of Jīngzhōu,
his authority and prestige were solemn and imposing,
and he managed to achieve considerable harmony among the people.
Huán Xuán was then in Jiānglíng.
As it was his native region,
and given his family's long-standing connections,
he often presumed his talent was superior to others.
Chén, however, frequently checked and restrained him.
Huán Xuán once visited Chén.
Before the usher had announced him,
he rode his carriage directly in.
Chén, facing Xuán, whipped the gate post.
Xuán was enraged
and departed,
and Chén did not try to stop him.
On the first day of the lunar month, Chén received guests,
with a large retinue of guards.
Xuán mentioned he wished to hunt
and asked to borrow a few hundred men.
Chén granted them all.
Xuán, awed, was compelled to obey him.
Chén's nature was unrestrained and unconventional.
In his later years, he was particularly fond of wine.
Once he drank for a month without sobering up,
and sometimes roamed about naked.
He often sighed that if he didn't drink for three days,
he felt his body and spirit were estranged.
When his father-in-law once suffered a bereavement,
Chén, in a drunken state, went to offer condolences.
His father-in-law was weeping sorrowfully,
when Chén, along with about ten guests,
linked arms, disheveled their hair, and entered naked,
circled him three times, and exited.
Many of his actions were of this kind.
He died in office a few years later,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Right,
with the posthumous name Mù.
Suí, whose courtesy name was Yànhóu,
was praised for his beauty in his youth
and had a high opinion of himself,
but was actually vulgar and lacked moral conduct.
When Yú was captured by Yīn and Huán,
Suí, unsure of his father's fate,
showed signs of distress in the capital.
In his daily life and diet,
he diminished everything,
which led people at the time to call him
"the filial son on probation."
When Huán Xuán became Grand Commandant,
Suí, being Huán's maternal nephew, was greatly favored and treated well.
He became Chief Clerk of the Right to the Grand Commandant.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
Suí was promoted to Director of the Central Secretariat.
When Liú Yù raised his righteous army,
Suí was appointed General of Champion Cavalry.
One night, in his house, a human head inexplicably fell from the beam onto the bed,
with blood flowing profusely.
Soon after, he was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu and granted the imperial insignia of "Jiajié."
Due to his father Yú's conspiracy,
he and his younger brother Nà were both executed.
Initially,
Suí, along with Wáng Mì and Huán Yìn, were renowned
as outstanding talents of the younger generation.
Mì reached the highest official positions
and preserved himself until the end.
Yìn was executed for involvement in a conspiracy,
but his reputation remained intact.
Suí, however, died a personal death,
and his reputation was almost completely lost,
also due to his shallow conduct, arrogance, and condescending attitude towards others.
From Chǎng's father Zé, the Grand Administrator of Yànmén in the Hàn dynasty, the family had been famous.
Chén was also exceptionally brilliant,
and Suí too achieved renown.
For eight generations, they followed in succession,
with no one comparable to them in terms of official position and prestige.
Jiǎo, whose courtesy name was Kāishān.
His grandfather, Mò,
was Minister of Works in the Wèi dynasty.
His father, Yòu,
was known for his talent and intelligence
and was a close confidant of Yáng Jùn.
Jùn's expulsion of the Prince of Rǔnán, Liàng,
and the retirement of Wèi Guàn,
were all Yòu's schemes.
He rose to the position of Central Commandant of the Northern Army.
Jiǎo was graceful and distinguished in his youth.
He was invited to serve by both Bìng and Sī provinces
but did not accept.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
he brought his two younger brothers to cross the river to escape the chaos.
At that time, Emperor Yuán was stationed in Jiànyè.
He issued an order stating:
"Wáng Yòu's three sons have just arrived.
They are descendants of famous virtue
and all possess integrity.
They should be honored.
They shall be granted three hundred thousand cash,
three hundred bolts of silk,
fifty *hú* of rice,
and twenty personal guards."
Soon after, Jiǎo was asked to serve as Military Advisor to the Crown Prince, General of the Central East,
but he did not accept.
Emperor Mǐn summoned him to be appointed as Scribe of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Prince Bǎo of Nányáng, the Right Chancellor, invited him,
but he declined both due to dangerous roads.
When Emperor Yuán became Chancellor,
he appointed Jiǎo as an aide in the Water Bureau,
then made him Magistrate of Chángshān,
and promoted him to Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince,
but he did not accept due to illness.
Wáng Dūn requested him to be a military advisor,
and he was ennobled as Duke of Jiǔyuán County.
When Dūn was at Shítou,
he wished to prohibit private harvesting of reeds at Càizhōu
and asked his subordinates for their opinions.
At that time, the imperial army had just suffered a defeat,
and officials and commoners were terrified,
no one daring to voice a different opinion.
Jiǎo alone said:
"There are beans in the Central Plains;
the common people gather them.
If the hundred surnames are not sufficient,
how can the lord be sufficient?
If you forbid people from cutting firewood,
I do not know if it is acceptable."
Dūn was displeased.
When Dūn was about to kill Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Ruòsī,
Jiǎo remonstrated from his seat, saying:
"Many accomplished scholars,
King Wén relied on them to achieve peace.
How can you slaughter renowned scholars
to preserve your own life?"
Dūn was furious
and wished to behead Jiǎo,
but he was saved thanks to Xiè Kūn.
Dūn still held a grudge
and sent him out as Chief Clerk of the Commander of the Guards.
After Dūn's rebellion was quelled,
Jiǎo was appointed Secretary of the Central Secretariat
and concurrently Grand Scribe,
but he firmly declined.
He was transferred to Colonel of the Rapid Cavalry,
and frequently promoted to Director of Personnel, Censor-in-Chief, Supervisor of the Imperial Library,
and concurrently Grand Impartial Judge of his home province.
At the beginning of the Xiánhé era,
the court deliberated appointing Jiǎo as Governor of Dānyáng.
Jiǎo, believing the position of Metropolitan Governor was of great importance
and should not be held by someone with his illness,
requested an appointment to Lúlíng Commandery.
Thus, Jiǎo was appointed Administrator of Lúlíng.
As Jiǎo's family was poor
and had no means to travel,
he was granted one hundred bolts of cloth
and one hundred thousand cash.
He died in office shortly after,
and was posthumously named Mù.
His son, Dàn, succeeded him
and successively held the positions of General of the Right Guard, Attendant, Central Protector of the Army, Minister of Works, and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Dàn's son, Dùshì, was General of Agile Cavalry.
Yuán Yuèzhī
had the courtesy name Yuánlǐ, and was from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His father, Lǎng,
was Gěishì Zhōng.
Yuèzhī was skilled at writing both long and short discourses,
which possessed profound logic.
He first served as Xiè Xuán's Cānjūn.
Xuán held him in high regard,
but he left office due to a mourning period.
After the mourning period ended, he returned to the capital,
carrying only Zhànguó Cè,
saying that this book alone contained the essence of governance.
Later, Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ held him in great affection,
and he often advised Dàozǐ to take full control of court power.
Dàozǐ largely accepted his advice.
Soon after, he was executed.
His grandfather, Tái zhī, had the courtesy name Yuánchén,
and was from Fànyáng.
He rose to the office of Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū.
He compiled the collection of zhìguài stories that circulated in the world.
Xún Sōng (Zǐ Ruí, Xiàn)
Xún Sōng had the courtesy name Jǐngyóu,
and was from Línlǐng, Yǐngchuān.
He was the great-great-grandson of Wèi Tàiwèi Yù.
His father, Yūn,
was Yǔlín Yòu Jiān and Ānlíng Xiāng Hóu,
and was a sworn brother to Wáng Jì and Hé Shào.
Sōng's ambition and character were pure and unblemished,
and he had a refined love for literature.
When he was a child,
his great-granduncle Yǐ saw him and was struck by his remarkable qualities,
believing he would surely bring glory to Yūn's family.
Upon reaching manhood,
Tàiyuán Wáng Jì greatly valued him,
comparing him to his maternal uncle, Yuán Kǎn of Chénjùn.
He said to Kǎn's brother, Ào:
"I recently saw Inspector Xún's son.
In his clear and profound reasoning,
he may not surpass his father,
but his moral character is pure and refined,
placing him among the ranks of your venerable brother."
Such was the esteem in which he was held by notable figures.
In the middle of the Tàishǐ era,
an imperial edict ordered Sōng to succeed his brother in inheriting his father's title,
and he was appointed Púyáng Wáng Yǔn Wénxué.
He was on good terms with Wáng Dūn, Gù Róng, Lù Jī, and others.
Zhào Wáng Lún appointed him Xiàngguó Cānjūn.
When Lún usurped the throne,
Sōng was promoted to Hùjūn Sīmǎ and Gěishì Zhōng,
gradually moving to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng and Tàidì Zhōngshùzǐ,
and then successively to Shìzhōng and Zhōnghùjūn.
When Wáng Mí entered Luò,
Sōng fled with the other officials to Mì.
Before he arrived, his mother died.
The bandits were in pursuit and about to catch up.
His companions scattered and fled,
but Sōng, with disheveled hair, followed the carriage,
guarding the corpse and weeping loudly.
When the bandits arrived,
they threw his mother's body to the ground,
seized the carriage, and left.
Sōng sustained four wounds,
and his breath ceased.
He did not revive until nightfall.
He buried his mother on Mìshān.
After the mourning period,
his cousin Fān, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Sōng Jiān Jiāngběi Jūnjì, Nánzhōnglángjiàng, Hòujiāngjūn, Jiǎjié, and Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu.
At that time, the imperial tombs were being excavated.
Sōng sent his Zhǔbù Shí Lǎn with troops to Luò
to repair the imperial tombs.
For his merits, he was advanced to the title of Wǔyáng Xiàn Gōng,
and then promoted to Dūdū Jīngzhōu Jiāngběi Zhū Jūnjì, Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
stationed at Wǎn,
and re-enfeoffed as Qúlǐng Gōng.
He was besieged by the bandit Dù Céng.
Shí Lǎn was then Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu.
Sōng's forces were weak and his provisions exhausted,
so he sent his young daughter Guàn to seek aid from Lǎn and Nánzhōnglángjiàng Zhōu Fǎng.
Fǎng immediately dispatched his son Fǔ to lead three thousand soldiers to rendezvous with Shí Lǎn,
and together they rescued Sōng.
When the bandits heard the troops approaching,
they scattered and fled.
Once Sōng was safe,
he sent Nányáng Zhōngbù Wèi Wáng Guó, Liú Yuàn, and others to secretly lead troops to raid Ráng Xiàn,
capturing Céng's cousin, the fake Xīnyě Tàishǒu Bǎo,
and beheaded him.
When Yuán Dì ascended the throne,
he summoned Sōng and appointed him Shàngshū Púyè,
tasking him and Diāo Xié with jointly establishing the etiquette for the restoration.
His younger cousin Kuí had died young,
leaving two sons, Xù and Xīn,
each several years old.
Sōng welcomed them to live with him,
treating them with the same affection as his own children.
As Tàiwèi and Línhuái Gōng Xún Yǐ's national lineage was cut off,
the court, considering Sōng's close relation,
intended to have Sōng's son inherit the title.
Sōng, pitying Xù's orphaned and humble state,
yielded the enfeoffment to Xù,
which was praised by commentators.
He was then transferred to Tàicháng.
At that time, schools were being renovated,
and the number of Bóshì was being reduced.
One Bóshì each was appointed for Zhōu Yì Wáng Shì, Shàngshū Zhèng Shì, Gǔwén Shàngshū Kǒng Shì, Máoshī Zhèng Shì, Zhōu Guān Lǐjì Zhèng Shì, Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn Dù Shì Fú Shì, Lúnyǔ Xiàojīng Zhèng Shì,
totaling nine people.
The Bóshì for Yílǐ, Gōngyáng, Gǔliáng, and Zhèng Yì were all abolished.
Sōng deemed this unacceptable,
and thus submitted a memorial, stating: "Since the recent chaos,
scholars of Confucianism have become especially few.
To reside in academia means to lack outstanding court officials,
and to serve at court means to neglect the elites of Confucian scholarship.
In the eras of Xiánníng,
Tàikāng, and Yǒngjiā,
Shìzhōng, Chángshì, and Huángmén, who were thoroughly knowledgeable in ancient and modern times and whose conduct served as a model for the world,
led the Guózǐ Bóshì.
Firstly, they would respond in the palace hall,
answering imperial queries;
secondly, they would participate in instructing the Guózǐ,
thereby promoting Confucian teachings;
thirdly, they would clarify doubts regarding the duties of Cí and Yí bureaus, as well as Tàicháng.
Now that the imperial dynasty
is being restored,
it is appropriate to follow the splendid practices of the past,
making regulations and
emulating previous institutions.
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì, in response to fate, ascended to the throne,
highly valuing Confucianism and promoting education.
He initiated the construction of the Míng
Táng,
built the Pìyōng,
announced the calendar and promulgated policies,
and held village drinking ceremonies and grand archery contests.
The Western pavilion and Eastern hall,
the Hétú and esoteric forbidden texts,
the departments and ministries had the precedents of the Zōngmiào Tàifǔ Jīnyǒng,
and the Imperial Academy had the stone classics and ancient texts of former Confucian scholars' teachings.
Scholars such as Jiǎ, Mǎ, Zhèng, Dù, Fú, Kǒng, Wáng, Hé, Yán, Yǐn,
with their detailed commentaries and annotations,
and the schools of many masters,
appointed nineteen Bóshì.
Throughout the nine provinces,
masters and students passed on their traditions,
and scholars were as numerous as a forest.
Yet, Zhāng Huá and Liú Shí were chosen to hold the office of Tàicháng,
to enhance Confucian teaching.
The tradition states:
'When Kǒngzǐ died, subtle teachings ceased;
when the seventy-two disciples passed away, the great principles diverged.'
For some time now, the Central Plains have been devastated,
and recitations have been silenced.
The Way of this culture
is about to fall to the ground.
Your Majesty, with your sagely wisdom, has risen to power like a dragon,
restoring and glorifying the Taoist teachings,
establishing the music master and elegant odes,
which is where it lies.
Jiāng and Yáng provinces
were previously influenced by
teachings,
and the remaining literary works of scholars
are now flourishing.
However, compared to former times,
it is still but one in a thousand.
My scholarship is not in detailed commentaries,
nor is my talent broad and profound.
Compared to Huá
and Shí,
my Confucian style is vastly inferior.
I wish to exert my humble efforts
to add a ten thousandth part.
May this Way flourish for a hundred generations,
and be sung by officials for a thousand years to come.
I have heard that the system of reduction
generally places two out of three.
Previously, nineteen Bóshì were appointed.
Now, the Five Classics combined have nine people,
which, compared to ancient times,
is still less than
half.
It is appropriate to implement the reduction system
in a timely manner.
In addition to the current nine people,
four more should be added.
May Your Majesty, in your leisure from the myriad affairs of state,
occasionally review this."
It is appropriate to establish one Professor for the *Zhèng Yì*,
one Professor for the *Zhèng Yǐlǐ*,
one Professor for the *Chūnqiū Gōngyáng*,
and one Professor for the *Gǔliáng*.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined in ancient times,
the lower encroached upon the upper, and the upper was replaced.
There was no Son of Heaven above,
and no regional lord below.
Who would reward the good?
Who would punish the evil?
Kǒngzǐ feared and composed the *Chūn*
*qiū*.
The feudal lords were secretive and jealous,
fearing to violate the taboos of the time.
Therefore, the subtle words and profound meanings
were not clearly explicit in their righteousness.
Thus it was said,
"Those who understand me, perhaps only the *Chūnqiū*
will know; those who condemn me, perhaps
only the *Chūnqiū* will know."
At that time, Zuǒ Qiūmíng and Zǐxià received direct instruction,
and there was nothing they did not thoroughly research.
After Kǒngzǐ passed away,
the subtle words were about to be lost.
Thereupon, Qiūmíng retired and compiled what he had
heard,
and composed a commentary (*zhuàn*) for it.
His book excels in ritual,
with many rich and beautiful phrases,
establishing the roots and extending the branches
to elucidate the meaning of the classic.
It is indeed full of wonder and grandeur,
and scholars are fond of it.
It is said that Gōngyáng Gāo personally received instruction from Zǐxià,
and it was established in the Hàn court.
Its words and meanings are clear and elegant,
and its judgments are sharp and insightful.
Dǒng Zhòngshū greatly esteemed it.
Gǔliáng Chì's teachings were transmitted
from master to disciple,
and it was temporarily established during the Hàn era.
Xiàng Xīn,
a great scholar of Hàn,
still had father and son each adhering to a different school,
none willing to follow the other.
The text of his book is clear and its meaning concise.
Many of the things
it elucidates
are not recorded in the *Zuǒshì* or *Gōngyáng*,
and it is also sufficient to provide corrections.
Therefore, the three commentaries circulated together in earlier generations,
and even talented individuals could not abandon any one of them.
Now that we are far removed from the sages,
their writings are about to decay.
Rather than excessively discard them,
it is better to excessively establish them.
Your minister believes that although the three commentaries are all called *Chūnqiū*,
their starting points and aims differ.
Considering the arguments about the similarities and differences among the three schools,
this is indeed a battlefield of ideas,
and its words are like the tips of swords and halberds.
It is logically impossible for them to coexist harmoniously.
It is fitting to establish one Professor
for each,
to broaden their learning.
[一０]Emperor Yuán issued an edict saying:
"Sōng's memorial is thus;
these are all matters of governing the state,
and principles for administration.
Even when resting horses and laying down weapons,
one can still discuss arts and skills.
Though we are now too busy to spare a single day,
how can we forget the root and abandon what exists!
Let those who can discuss this extensively deliberate on it."
Most of the deliberators requested to follow what Sōng had proposed.
An edict then stated:
"The *Gǔliáng* is superficial
and not worthy of having a Professor established for it.
The rest is as proposed."
However, due to Wáng Dūn's rebellion,
it was not implemented.
Dūn memorialized to appoint Sōng as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
When the Emperor passed away,
the assembled officials discussed the temple name.
Wáng Dūn sent an envoy to say:
"With jackals and wolves blocking the road,
and the imperial coffin not yet returned,
the ancestral title
should be reconsidered and deliberated upon separately."
Sōng argued:
"According to ritual,
an ancestor is honored for their accomplishments, and a founder for their virtue.
Emperor Yuán, with his heaven-endowed sagely wisdom,
brilliantly initiated the revival.
His benevolent virtue rivaled that of Tàiwù,
and his meritorious kindness surpassed that of Hàn Xuān.
Your minister dares to follow the ancient precedents
and bestow upon him the title of Zhōngzōng."
Immediately after, he wrote to Dūn, saying:
"I have learned that because the 'long serpent' (rebels) has not been eliminated,
the ancestral title is being deliberated upon separately.
The late Emperor responded to heaven's mandate
to bring about a flourishing revival;
how can a ruler of revival
be downgraded or abolished based on worldly circumstances!
I have dared to act with sincere uprightness,
consulting both court and populace,
and bestowed the title Zhōngzōng.
The auspicious day has been set,
leaving no time for repeated requests.
The fault of acting presumptuously
is something I dare not shirk."
Initially,
Dūn treated Sōng very well,
intending to make him Sīkōng.
Because of this, he held a grudge and stopped.
In the early Táiníng period,
he was made Sànqí Chángshì,
and later concurrently Taìzǐ Tàifù.
For his merit in pacifying Wáng Dūn,
he was enfeoffed anew as Pínglè Bó.
He was dismissed from office
for allowing the imperial guard to be eaten by a fierce beast.
Later, he was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
with Sànqí Chángshì as before.
He was promoted to Yòu Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with Lù Shàngshū as before.
He also concurrently held the position of Mìshū Jiān,
and was provided with 120 personal guards.
Although he was old and frail,
he diligently applied himself to classical texts,
and people of the time praised him for this.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
Sōng, Wáng Dǎo, and Lù Yè together ascended the imperial bed to protect the Emperor.
When the Emperor was forced to go to Shítou,
Sōng also attended him, never leaving his side.
After the rebels were pacified,
the Emperor visited Wēn Jiào's boat.
Sōng, though old and severely ill at the time,
still forced himself to walk and follow.
He passed away in the third year of Xiánhé,
[一一]at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
Later, the Zuòzuò Láng Yú Yù sent a memorial to Chancellor Wáng Dǎo, saying:
"I humbly observe that the former Mìshū and Guānglù Dàfū, Lord Xún,
was born into a family of accumulated virtue,
and from a young age was known for his scholarly elegance.
He served in various positions, both inside and outside the court,
and was capable of humility even in high office.
When Sū Jùn raged uncontrollably,
and the imperial carriage suffered misfortune,
Lord Xún was in a position of suspicion and animosity,
facing danger as precarious as a stack of eggs.
Court officials shivered with fear for him,
and commentators believed he could not escape.
Yet, Lord Xún guided himself with wisdom,
undaunted by peril,
assisting and protecting the Emperor,
clinging to him and never departing.
Although he did not have the merit of supporting and welcoming the Emperor,
he ought to receive the reward for upholding his integrity.
Moreover, his benevolent reputation
was manifest far and wide early on.
He was the hope of both court and populace,
who expected him to reach the highest ministerial posts.
Although he did not formally assume such a position,
he had already been granted the rank of Yítóng.
He preserved his pure steadfastness to the end,
his reputation sealed upon his death.
Yet, on the day of his passing,
he was only granted the additional title of Shìzhōng.
While alive, he was hoped to reach the 'three *huái*' (highest ministerial positions),
but after death, he lacked the fame of a 'tripod leg' (one of the three highest ministers).
His favor did not increase beyond his former rank,
and his honor did not match his original expectations.
This was a cause for lamentation among both the foolish and the wise at that time.
Now, after this great decline,
the pure customs have dwindled.
If there is even a shred of goodness,
it should be made an example for commendation,
let alone a venerable elder of the state
whose integrity and resolve were like this!"
It was not followed.
In the fourth year of Shēngpíng,
Sōng was reburied.
An edict granted a million coins
and five thousand bolts of cloth.
He had two sons: Ruí and Xiàn.
Ruí succeeded him.
Nà Zǔyán
was pure and upright from a young age,
resolute and unconventional.
He was first appointed as an aide to the General-in-Chief of the Army (Zhèn Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn), King Wǔlíng,
and was recommended as an outstanding talent by the province.
Wáng Shù of Tàiyuán deeply respected him,
and appointed him as the Chief Clerk of Jianwei (Jiànwēi Zhǎngshǐ).

He was successively promoted to Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng), Provincial Administrator (Běnzhōu Biéjià), and Bureau Director of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng),
then went out to serve as the Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu).
When he was about to go to the commandery,
he first went to Gūshú to bid farewell to Huán Wēn.
He then asked Wēn:
“How much wine can Your Excellency drink before becoming drunk,
and how much meat can you eat?”
Wēn replied:
“As I have grown older, I get drunk on three shēng of wine,
and no more than ten slices of white meat.
What about you, sir?”
Nà replied:
“I have never been a heavy drinker,
I can only drink two shēng,
and my meat consumption is not worth mentioning.”
Later, he found Wēn at leisure
and said to him:
“I have a small gift from outside.
As I am about to govern a distant commandery,
I wish to have one drunk evening with Your Excellency
to express my humble sentiments.”
Wēn joyfully accepted.
At that time, Wáng Tǎnzhī and Diāo Yí were seated.
When the gift was received,
there was only one dòu of wine
and one plate of venison.
The guests were astonished.
Nà slowly said:
“Your Excellency recently said you drink three shēng of wine,
and I can only drink two shēng.
Now there is one dòu,
enough for any spills from cups and ladles.”
Wēn and the guests all admired his simplicity and sincerity.
He then ordered the imperial kitchen to prepare fine dishes,
and they drank heartily and joyfully before dispersing.
When Nà arrived at the commandery,
he refused his salary and emoluments.
Soon after,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Left for the People (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū),
and concurrently Grand Arbiter of the Province (Zhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
When he was about to answer the summons,
an attendant asked how many boats he should prepare.
Nà said:
“My private servants will bring food,
there is nothing else needed.”
When he was about to depart,
he only had his quilt and satchel.
The rest were sealed and returned to the officials.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
then transferred to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and given the additional title of Commandant of Cavalry (Fèngchē Dūwèi) and General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn).
Xiè Ān once wished to visit Nà,
but Nà made no preparations.
His nephew, Chǔ, dared not ask him,
and secretly prepared for him.
When Ān arrived,
Nà only offered tea and fruit.
Chǔ then presented a lavish meal,
with all sorts of delicacies.
When the guests departed,
Nà was furious and said:
“You cannot bring glory to your father’s elder brother;
instead, you corrupt my simple conduct!”
Thereupon, he had him flogged forty times.
Many of his actions were of this kind.
Later, because his beloved son, Chángshēng, was ill,
he sought to resign from office to care for him.
His nephew, Qín, also committed a crime deserving punishment,
and he begged to be relieved of his office to atone for it.
An imperial edict specially permitted a light reduction [in punishment].
Soon, Chángshēng got a little better,
and he was ordered to return to his post.
He was then promoted to Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè),
transferred to Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Púyè),
and given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Soon after, he was appointed Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
with his position as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary remaining the same.
He was diligent, steadfast, and firm,
unchanging from beginning to end.
At that time, Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ, being young, held exclusive power,
and entrusted affairs to petty individuals.
Nà looked towards the palace and sighed, saying:
“This good household,
is it to be ruined by a mere child?!”
The court officials all admired his loyalty and integrity.

Soon after, he was appointed Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and was granted the privilege of establishing an administration equal to that of the Three Excellencies (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He died before being formally invested,
and these titles were conferred posthumously.
Chángshēng died earlier,
without a son,
so his nephew Dàolóng was made his heir.
During the Yuánxī reign,
he became Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Hé Chōng
Hé Chōng, courtesy name Cìdào,
was a native of Qián in Lújiāng.
He was the great-grandson of Zhēn, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū) of the Wèi dynasty.
His grandfather, Yūn,
was the Provincial Governor of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ).
His father, Ruì,
was the Administrator of Ānfēng (Ānfēng Tàishǒu).
Chōng had a refined demeanor and elegant disposition,
and was praised for his literary style and meaning.
He was first appointed as an aide to the Grand General Wáng Dūn,
then transferred to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
Dūn’s elder brother, Hán, was then the Administrator of Lújiāng Commandery (Lújiāng Jùn),
and was notoriously corrupt.
Dūn once praised him at a gathering, saying:
“My elder brother is certainly doing well in the commandery;
the people of Lújiāng all praise him.”
Chōng, with a stern expression, said:
“I am from Lújiāng,
and what I have heard is different from this.”
Dūn fell silent.
Those beside him felt uneasy for Chōng,
but Chōng remained calm and composed.
Because of this, he displeased Dūn
and was demoted to Literary Scholar for the King of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Wáng Wénxué).
Soon after, Dūn was defeated,
and Chōng was successively promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Chōng was the nephew of Wáng Dǎo’s wife.
Chōng’s wife
was the younger sister of Empress Míngmù.
Therefore, he was close to Dǎo from a young age
and held prominent official positions early on.
He once visited Dǎo,
who pointed to a bed with a fly whisk and called Chōng to sit together,
saying:
“This is your seat.”
Dǎo, while repairing his residence in Yángzhōu,
looked around and said:
“This is precisely for Cìdào.”
Emperor Míng also befriended him.
When Emperor Chéng ascended the throne,
Chōng was promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
the capital was overthrown.
Dǎo followed the emperor to Shítóu,
while Chōng fled east to the loyalist army.
Later, Dǎo fled to Báishí,
and Chōng was also able to return.
After the rebels were pacified,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng (Dūxiāng Hóu),
appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
and then served as Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
He was then appointed General of Jianwei (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Nèishǐ).
He governed the commandery with great virtue,
recommending the hermit Yú Xǐ
and promoting local men Xiè Fèng, Wèi Yǐ, and others to be his subordinates.
Later, because his tomb was desecrated, he left the commandery.
An imperial edict summoned him as a Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
but he did not accept the appointment.
After completing the reburial,
he was appointed General of Jianwei (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng both spoke to the emperor, saying:
“Hé Chōng has a broad and resolute character,
and is a man of great public expectation.
He will surely be able to oversee the affairs of the court
and serve as a deputy to the old ministers.
On the day of my death,
I wish for Chōng to be brought into internal service;
then external reputation will be truly consolidated,
and the state will be free from worries.”
Because of this, he was given the additional title of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
promoted to General of the Vanguard (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn),
and also served as Tutor to the King of Kuàijī (Huìjī Wáng Shī).
When Dǎo died,
Chōng was transferred to General of the Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn)
and, along with the Central Secretariat Supervisor Yǔ Bīng, participated in overseeing the affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
An edict ordered Chōng and Bīng to each bring fifty armed guards to the gate where chariots stopped.
Soon after, he was promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
and given the additional title of General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
Chōng believed that as internal and external responsibilities were shared,
it was appropriate to correct each other.
If matters were consolidated under one person,
it would be problematic for reviews and consultations,
so he submitted a memorial firmly declining the appointment.
It was granted.
He was transferred to Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng),
given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
with his position as General of the Guard (Lǐngjūn) remaining the same.
He also served as Grand Arbiter of the Province (Zhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
Because the province had established and virtuous elders, he firmly declined the appointment.
Yǔ Bīng 庾冰 and his brothers, as maternal relatives, assisted the imperial family.
Their power rivaled that of the sovereign.
They worried that after a change of emperor,
their kinship would become more distant,
and they would be attacked by outside forces.
They plotted to enthrone Emperor Kāng 康帝,
who was the emperor's younger brother by the same mother.
They repeatedly told the emperor that the state had powerful enemies
and therefore required a long-reigning ruler.
The emperor agreed.
Chōng 充 suggested,
"The succession of father to son is
an ancient tradition of the former kings.
To suddenly and arbitrarily alter it
is, I fear, not a long-term plan.
Thus, King Wǔ 武王 not granting the throne to his sagely younger brother
is precisely this principle.
In the past, Emperor Jǐng 景 of Hàn 漢 also wished to pass the throne to the Prince of Liáng 梁王,
but the court officials unanimously deemed it a violation and disruption of the established system,
and firmly refused to listen.
Now, with the Prince of Lángxié 琅邪 ascending the throne,
what about the child?
Will the altars of soil and grain, and the ancestral temples,
not be endangered?"
Bīng 冰 and the others did not follow his advice.
Later, Emperor Kāng 康帝 was enthroned.
When the emperor appeared at the court veranda,
Bīng 冰 and Chōng 充 attended him.
The emperor said,
"My succession to this grand enterprise
is due to the efforts of you two gentlemen."
Chōng 充 replied,
"Your Majesty's ascension
is due to the efforts of your servant Bīng 冰.
If my advice had been followed,
we would not have seen an era of peace and prosperity."
The emperor showed a look of shame.
In the early Jiàn yuán 建元 period,

he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piāojì Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xúzhōu 徐州 and Jìnlíng 晉陵 within Yángzhōu 揚州 (Dūdū Xúzhōu Yángzhōu zhī Jìnlíng zhū jūnshì 都督徐州揚州之晉陵諸軍事), and given the Staff of Authority (Jiǎjié 假節).
He concurrently held the position of Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州 (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ 徐州刺史),
stationed at Jīngkǒu 京口,
to avoid the Yǔ 庾 clan.
After a while,
Yǔ Yì 庾翼 was about to launch a northern expedition,
and Yǔ Bīng 庾冰 was sent out to garrison Jiāngzhōu 江州.
Chōng 充 returned to court
and said to the emperor,
"My maternal uncle Bīng 冰 holds a position of great importance;
he should remain as prime minister
and not be sent far away."
The court council did not agree.

Thereupon, Chōng 充 was recalled to serve as Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu 揚zhōu, Yùzhōu 豫zhōu, and Lángxié 琅邪 within Xúzhōu 徐州 (Dūdū Yáng Yù Xúzhōu zhī Lángxié zhū jūnshì 都督揚豫徐州之琅邪諸軍事), given the Staff of Authority (Jiǎjié 假節),
and concurrently held the position of Inspector of Yángzhōu 揚zhōu (Yángzhōu Cìshǐ 揚州刺史),
while his general title remained as before.
Previously,
Yì 翼 had conscripted all registered household slaves from Jiāngzhōu 江zhōu and Jīngzhōu 荊zhōu for military service,
causing widespread outcry among both gentry and commoners.
Chōng 充 again wished to conscript slaves from Yángzhōu 揚zhōu to equalize the criticism.
Later, because the three Wú 吳 regions had already been conscripted during the era of the Restoration,
it was deemed inappropriate to conscript them again, and he stopped.
Soon after, the emperor fell gravely ill.
Bīng 冰 and Yì 翼 intended to enthrone Emperor Jiǎnwén 簡文帝,
but Chōng 充 suggested enthroning the Crown Prince,
which was approved.
When the emperor passed away,
Chōng 充 followed the last wishes
and immediately enthroned the Crown Prince,
who became Emperor Mù 穆帝.
Bīng 冰 and Yì 翼 were greatly displeased by this.
Empress Xiàn 獻 Hòu 獻后 presided over the court.
An edict stated,
"The General of Agile Cavalry (Piāojì 驃騎) holds a heavy responsibility;
he may enter the palace with one hundred armored guards."
He was also given the titles of Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān 中書監) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì 錄尚書事).
Chōng 充 personally stated that since he was Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū 錄尚書),
it was inappropriate to also be Central Secretariat Supervisor (Jiān Zhōngshū 監中書),
and this was granted.
He was again given the title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中)
and ten feather-clad cavalry guards (Yǔlín Qí 羽林騎).
Bīng 冰, Yì 翼, and others soon died,
and Chōng 充 solely assisted the young emperor.
When Yì 翼 was on his deathbed,
he submitted a memorial entrusting his son Yuánzhī 爰之 with his successor's responsibilities.
At that time, commentators all believed that the Yǔ 庾 clan had for generations been in the western region,
and public sentiment favored them.
Therefore, Yì 翼's request should be granted
to soothe public feelings.
Chōng 充 said,
"No.
Jīngchǔ 荊楚 is the western gate of the state,
with a million households.
To the north, it borders the powerful Hú 胡;
to the west, it neighbors the formidable Shǔ 蜀.
Its strategic terrain is rugged and perilous,
extending for ten thousand *lǐ* 里.
If a worthy man is obtained, the Central Plains can be pacified;
if its power weakens, the state will share the sorrow.
This is like Lù Kàng 陸抗 existing meant Wú 吳 existed,
and Kàng's 康 death meant Wú 吳's death.
How can a mere callow youth be appointed to such a position?
Huán Wēn 桓溫's strategic brilliance surpasses others;
he possesses both civil and military wisdom and bearing.
For the responsibility of the western border,
none can surpass Wēn 溫."
The commentators then said,
"Will Yǔ Yuánzhī 庾爰之 be willing to yield to Wēn 溫?
If he were to resist with troops,
the shame and fear would be considerable."
Chōng 充 said,
"Wēn 溫 is fully capable of controlling him;
gentlemen, do not worry."
So he sent Wēn 溫 to the west.
Yuánzhī 爰之 indeed dared not contend.
Chōng 充, considering that General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn 衞將軍) Chǔ Póu 褚裒 was the father of the Empress Dowager,
believed he should oversee the court administration.
He submitted a memorial recommending Póu 裒 to participate in the Directorship of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū 錄尚書).
Póu 裒, due to the close proximity (to the imperial family),
insisted on being sent out (of the capital).
Chōng 充 often said,
"With Huán Wēn 桓溫 and Chǔ Póu 褚裒 as regional governors (Fāngbó 方伯),
and Yīn Hào 殷浩 in the Secretariat (Ménxià 門下),
I can be at ease."
While Chōng 充 held the position of prime minister,
though he lacked the ability to clarify justice or implement reforms,
he was resolute and had a broad capacity.
He maintained a stern demeanor at court,
taking the welfare of the state as his personal responsibility.
All whom he selected and employed
were primarily meritorious officials;
he did not use private favors to elevate relatives.
Those who discussed him valued him for this.
However, his favored associates were common and mixed,
and he entrusted people improperly.
He was also fond of Buddhist scriptures,
and extensively renovated Buddhist temples,
providing for hundreds of Buddhist monks,
spending immense sums without regret.
Yet, when his close friends and relatives fell into poverty,
he offered them nothing,
and for this, he incurred criticism from society.
Ruǎn Yù 阮裕 once teased him, saying,
"Your ambition is as vast as the universe,
and your courage surpasses all antiquity."
Chōng 充 asked him why.
Yù 裕 said,
"I, plotting for a prefecture of several thousand households, have not yet succeeded.
You are plotting to become a Buddha;
is that not grand indeed!"
At that time, Xī Yīn 郗愔 and his younger brother Dān 曇 followed the Daoist Celestial Masters (Tiānshī Dào 天師道),
while Chōng 充 and his younger brother Zhǔn 準 deeply believed in Buddhism (Shìshì 釋氏).
Xiè Wàn 謝萬 mocked them, saying,
"The two Xī 郗 fawn upon Daoism;
the two Hé 何 are sycophantic towards Buddha."
Chōng 充 was a good drinker,
and was greatly esteemed by Liú Dàn 劉惔.
Dàn 惔 often said,
"Seeing Cìdào 次道 (Chōng 充) drink
makes one want to empty one's household wine cellar."
This indicated his gentle and calm disposition.
He died in the second year of Yǒnghé 永和 (346 CE),
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空)
and given the posthumous name Wénmù 文穆.
He had no sons,
so his nephew Fàng 放 succeeded him.
When Fàng 放 died,
he also had no sons,
so his grand-nephew Sōng 松 succeeded him,
reaching the position of Consultant and Adjutant to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piāojì Zīyì Cānjūn 驃騎諮議參軍).
Chōng's 充 younger brother Zhǔn 準
is mentioned in the Biographies of Imperial Relatives by Marriage (Wàiqī Chuán 外戚傳).
Chǔ Sà 褚翜
Chǔ Sà 褚翜, courtesy name Móuyuǎn 謀遠,
was a paternal cousin of Grand Tutor Póu 裒.
His father, Wěi 頠,
was well-known in his youth but died young.
Sà 翜 was praised for his talent, skill, and steadfast character.
He inherited the noble title of Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯)
and was appointed Adjutant to the General Who Manifests Prowess (Guānjūn Cānjūn 冠軍參軍).
At that time, Prince Yì 乂 of Chángshā 長沙 seized power,
while the Princes of Chéngdū 成都 and Héjiān 河間 raised troops externally.
Sà 翜 knew that internal strife was brewing,
so he abandoned his official post and fled to Yōuzhōu 幽州.
Later, when there were bandit troubles north of the Yellow River (Héběi 河北),
he returned to his hometown.
The Prefect of Hénán 河南 (Hénán Yǐn 河南尹) appointed Sà 翜 to manage the affairs of his home county.
When the empire descended into chaos,
Sà 翜 gathered like-minded individuals,
intending to cross the river, and first moved to the area of Yángchéng 陽城.
Yǔ Āi 庾敳 of Yǐngchuān 潁川,
who was Sà's 翜 maternal uncle,
also worried about the world's disorder
and entrusted his family to Sà 翜.
Sà's 翜 path was cut off,
and he could not proceed.
The Prince of Dōnghǎi 東海 (Yuè 越) appointed him as an Adjutant (Cānjūn 參軍),
but he declined due to illness.
Soon after Luòyáng was annihilated,
he joined Guō Xiù, the Administrator of Xíngyáng, to defend Wànshìtái.
Guō Xiù was unable to pacify the masses,
and he incurred resentment from generals Chén Fǔ and Guō Zhòng, among others.
They consequently attacked each other.
Jiá, fearing that disaster would strike him,
said to Fǔ and the others:
"The reason you gentlemen are here
is to escape danger.
Now we should all unite our strength to guard against the enemy.
Fortunately, there is no external threat,
yet we are attacking each other internally.
This is like avoiding a pit only to fall into a well.
Guō Xiù is indeed in the wrong,
but we should tolerate him for now.
If you act on your anger,
the city will collapse from within.
When the Hú bandits hear of this,
they will immediately come and raid us.
Even if you gentlemen succeed in killing Xiù,
it will not save us from the Hú barbarians.
Our dependents are numerous and weak;
you should think deeply about this."
Fǔ and the others repented and understood,
and made peace with Xiù.
At that time, tens of thousands of lives were saved thanks to Jiá.
The following year,
he led several thousand families, intending to move east.
They encountered dangerous roads
and could not advance,
so they remained in Mìxiàn.
Xún Zǔ, the Sīlì Jiàowèi, appointed him as a cānjūn and Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn,
and he was again put in charge of his home county,
leading three thousand local people,
and overseeing the affairs of various camps in the three commanderies of Xīnchéng, Liáng, and Yángchéng.
After a short while,
he was promoted to Sīlì Sīmǎ,
still overseeing the camp affairs.
He led his followers and advanced to Sháiféikǒu on the Rǔshuǐ,
but was again blocked by bandits.
Jiá then rode alone to Xǔchāng,
met Sīkōng Xún Fān,
who appointed him Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and acting Administrator of Liáng Guó.
At the beginning of Jiànxīng,
he was again appointed Yùzhōu Sīmǎ,
and oversaw military affairs in Sīzhōu.
Wáng Xuán, the Tàifù cānjūn, replaced Jiá as Administrator of the commandery.
At that time, Gěng Nú, a commander of troops in Liáng Guó, was very popular with the people
but wielded excessive power.
Jiá always treated him with great courtesy.
Wáng Xuán's administration was strict,
and Jiá knew that he would not tolerate Nú,
so he warned him, saying:
"You have already killed many people through your authority,
and it is difficult to unify public sentiment;
you should be extremely cautious."
Wáng Xuán accepted Jiá's words,
outwardly reining in Nú,
but inwardly harboring resentment.
Coincidentally, he was transferred to Chénliú,
and as he was about to depart,
he arrested Nú and executed him.
Nú's remaining partisans gathered a crowd and killed Wáng Xuán.
Liáng Jùn now faced internal strife,
and Zhāng Píng and other bandits from Xúzhōu intended to launch a surprise attack.
The people of the commandery were confused and panicked,
intending to surrender the commandery to Zhāng Píng.
Xún Zǔ sent Jiá to pacify them,
and the people's morale was then settled.
After a short while,
Xún Zǔ nominated Jiá as Lìbù Láng,
but he did not answer the summons
and instead went east, crossing the Jiāng.
When Yuán Dì became Jìn Wáng,
he appointed Jiá as Sànqí Láng,
then transferred him to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and sent him out as Fènwēi Jiāngjūn and Huáinán Nèishǐ.
At the beginning of Yǒngchāng,
Wáng Dūn instigated rebellion.
Dài Ruòsī, the Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, ordered Jiá to dispatch troops to meet the crisis.
Jiá sent a general with five hundred men to follow him.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
he summoned and appointed Jiá as Túnqí Jiàowèi,
and then promoted him to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài.
At the beginning of Chéng Dì's reign,
he became Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
the imperial court imposed martial law,
appointing Jiá as Shìzhōng
and putting him in charge of the military affairs for the punitive expedition.
After the imperial army was defeated,
Sītú Wáng Dǎo said to Jiá:
"His Majesty should be in the main hall.
You should urge him to come out quickly."
Jiá immediately entered the inner palace,
and personally carried the Emperor to ascend the Tàijí Qiándiàn.
Wáng Dǎo ascended the imperial couch and embraced the Emperor,
while Jiá, Zhōng Yǎ, and Liú Chāo stood by his sides.
At that time, the hundred officials had scattered,
and the palace hall was deserted.
When Sū Jùn's soldiers entered,
they shouted at Jiá to step down.
Jiá stood firm and unmoving,
and sternly rebuked them, saying:
"Sū Chāngjūn has come to pay respects to His Majesty;
how can soldiers invade and press forward!"
Because of this, the soldiers dared not ascend the hall.
When Sū Jùn took power,
he still appointed Jiá as Shìzhōng,
and Jiá followed the imperial carriage to Shítóu.
The following year,
he, along with Guānglù Dàfū Lù Yè and others, went out to hold Yuànchéng.
Sū Yì and Rèn Ràng besieged them,
but Jiá and the others held firm.
After the rebels were pacified,
for his merits, he was enfeoffed as Bó of Chángpíng Xiàn,
and promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn.
At that time, the capital city had been burned and ravaged,
and its people were scattered and withered.
Jiá gathered the scattered and lost,
and implemented many benevolent policies.
He replaced Yǔ Liàng as Zhōnghùjūn,
stationed at Shítóu.
Soon after, he became Lǐngjūn,
then transferred to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and was given the additional title of Fèngchē Dūwèi,
overseeing the affairs of the new palace.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
then transferred to Zuǒpúshè,
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
After a long time,
he replaced Hé Chōng as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his Chángshì position remaining as before.
In Xiánkāng seventh year, he died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the title of Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous name Mù.
His son, Xī, inherited his title,
and rose to the position of Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
Cài Mó
Cài Mó, courtesy name Dàomíng,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Chénliú.
His family had been a prominent surname for generations.
His great-grandfather, Mù,
was a Wèi Shàngshū.
His grandfather, Dé,
was Administrator of Lèpíng.
His father, Kè,
was fond of learning in his youth,
and widely read in books and records,
respected by his county and clan.
He was upright and adhered to justice by nature,
and if someone's conduct did not accord with his own,
he would not associate with them, even if they were wealthy and noble.
Liú Zhěng of Gāopíng, relying on his talent, was unrestrained and extravagant,
with bizarre and unusual attire,
and had no scruples.
Once, when he visited someone,
he found Kè present.
Zhěng felt ashamed and uncomfortable throughout the entire meal.
At that time, Kè was a recluse,
yet he was feared to this extent.
Later, he served as Dàjiāngjūn Jìshì Dū for Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.
When Yǐng became Céngxiàng,
he promoted him to Dōngcáo Yuàn.
Cài Kè
had always possessed great breadth of mind, and when he assumed a position in the Selection Bureau,
sycophants looked upon him with awe and dread.
Initially,
when Kè had not yet entered officialdom,
Shān Jiǎn of Hénèi once wrote to Wáng Yǎn of Lángxié, saying:
"Cài Zǐní is truly a righteous man of today."
Yǎn showed the letter to the crowd and said:
"Master Shān extols a person with just one word,
but it's not so easy to live up to."
Later, Yǎn heard that Kè was in the Selection Bureau
and said:
"Master Shān's words about a righteous man
are now proven true."
Chénliú was at that time a large commandery,
known for its many gentlemen.
Wáng Chéng of Lángxié was passing through its borders,
and the Grand Administrator, Lǚ Yù, sent an official to greet him.
As Chéng entered the commandery,
he asked the official:
"Who are the eminent men of this commandery?"
The official replied:
"There are Cài Zǐní and Jiāng Yìngyuán."
At that time, many people from the commandery held high positions,
so Chéng asked, mentioning their names:
"Are so-and-so
not gentlemen of your commandery?"
The official replied:
"They are."
Chéng then said:
"Why then do you only mention these two?"
The official replied:
"I thought you were asking about people,
not about positions."
Chéng laughed and stopped.
Upon reaching the commandery,
he related the official's words to Yù, saying:
"It was said that this commandery had a particular custom,
and indeed, even a minor official knows it to be so."
As Kè saw the court government deteriorating daily,
he resolutely refused to serve.
Dōngyíng Gōng Téng became Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry,
garrisoned north of the Yellow River.
He appointed Kè as Aide-de-camp of the Secretariat,
knowing he would surely not accept,
so he compelled him with a military summons.
Kè had no choice but to go.
After several tens of days,
Téng was attacked by Jí Sāng.
The city fell,
and Kè was killed.
Cài Mó, at the age of twenty, was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and the province appointed him Aide-de-camp.
He was then nominated as Flourishing Talent,
and Wáng Yuè of Dōnghǎi summoned him as an assistant.
He refused all these appointments.
He crossed the Yangtze River to escape the chaos.
At that time, Emperor Míng was the Grand Administrator of the Eastern Region,
and he invited Mó to be his Army Advisor.
Emperor Yuán was appointed Chancellor,
and again invited him as an assistant,
then transferred him to Army Advisor.
Later, he became Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
served successively as Grand Administrator of Yìxīng, Aide-de-camp of the Secretariat to Grand General Wáng Dūn, and Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education,
and was then promoted to Palace Attendant.
When Sū Jùn staged his rebellion,
Yǔ Bīng, the Internal Administrator of Wú Commandery, fled to Kuàijī.
Thereupon, Mó was appointed Internal Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Upon his arrival,
Mó, together with Zhāng Kǎi, Gù Zhòng, Gù Yáng, and others, raised an army of righteousness
and welcomed Bīng back to the commandery.
After Sū Jùn was pacified,
Mó again became Palace Attendant,
then was promoted to Minister of the Five Bureaus,
concurrently overseeing the tutor of Wáng Lángxié.
Mó submitted a memorial declining, saying:
"The responsibility of the Eight Pillars
is not for the unworthy;
those previously employed
had established reputations.
Kǒng Yú and Zhūgě Huī, both with pure integrity and remarkable talent,
earned fame early.
In the past, when Yú was Censor-in-chief,
I was still a Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education;
when Huī was Grand Administrator of Kuàijī,
I was a Secretariat Director;
when Huī governed Dānyáng,
I was a guardian of a small commandery.
Our reputations were not on par,
and our ranks differed greatly.
Now, for me, a humble and contemptible person,
to presumptuously surpass my peers and transcend my station,
would disrupt the orderly sequence of the sacred court above
and contradict the fair judgment of the gentlemen below.
This is not merely a caution about my own demise,
but truly brings shame upon the sacred administration.
Moreover, a Chief Clerk, leaping directly to attending at the imperial curtain,
and then again ascending to join the censorial officials –
since the restoration,
such an act of promoting virtue has never occurred.
Who am I,
to presumptuously receive such an honor!
Therefore, I reflect on myself with a pounding heart,
and thrice examine my foolish self.
Rather than presumptuously advance and sully the pure path,
I would rather suffer the crime of disobedience and stubbornness."
The memorial was submitted,
but not approved.
He was transferred to oversee the Personnel Bureau.
For his merit in pacifying Sū Jùn,
he was granted the noble title of Baron of Jìyáng.
He again declined,
but it was not approved.
During the winter sacrifice,
Mó oversaw the Bureau of Sacrifices.
The attendant in charge forgot to set up Emperor Míng's tablet.
Mó and Grand Minister of Ceremonies Zhāng Quán were both dismissed,
but continued to hold their posts in plain clothes.
After a while,
he was promoted to Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
concurrently overseeing the Director of the Imperial Library.
Due to illness, he was unable to personally attend to his duties,
and submitted a memorial resigning,
but it was not granted.
When Emperor Chéng presided over the imperial audience,
he sent envoys to appoint Mó as Grand Tutor, Grand Commandant, and Minister of Works.
At that time, music was about to be performed,
with instruments hung overnight in the palace courtyard.
The Imperial Secretariat reported
that there was no regulation for performing music except during sacrifices and banquets.
The matter was referred to the Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Mó argued that music of bronze and stone should be played when the emperor presided over an audience and sent envoys.
This was adopted.
The performance of music at an imperial audience
began from this time.
Wáng Hóng of Péngchéng submitted a memorial, stating
that in the Lèxián Táng, there was a Buddhist image personally painted by the late emperor,
which had survived banditry and hardships,
and this hall still existed.
He proposed that an edict should be issued to compose a eulogy.
The emperor referred the matter for deliberation.
Mó said:
"Buddhism
is a custom of the barbarians,
not a system established by the classics.
The late emperor, with a mind as vast as heaven and earth,
possessed many talents and skills.
He merely painted this image casually for the occasion;
as for genuinely favoring the Buddhist Way,
I have never heard of it.
Bandits rushed about,
and the imperial capital was ruined,
yet this hall stood alone, intact.
This is indeed a sign of divine protection of the dynasty,
but it is not a description of the great virtue of the Great Jìn
that should be glorified in song.
If a subject, seeing something, is moved to write an ode,
composing a private fu or song is acceptable.
But now, to issue an imperial command,
to order the imperial historians,
to praise the late emperor's alleged love for Buddhism above,
and below, to compose a eulogy for a barbarian image,
there is doubt in the righteousness of this."
Thereupon, the proposal was dropped.
At that time, General-in-Chief of the West Yǔ Liàng, seeing that Shí Lè had recently died,
wished to move his garrison to Shíchéng,
as a step towards eliminating the bandits.
The matter was referred to the high officials.
Mó deliberated, saying: "Times have their periods of prosperity and adversity;
the Dao has its moments of expansion and contraction.
Although violent and rebellious bandits are ultimately destined for destruction,
when they are strong and flourishing,
one should yield and avoid them.
Thus, Gāo Zǔ
submitted to being confined to Ba and Han,
and endured humiliation at Píngchéng.
If he had contended for power at Hóngmén,
he would not have survived the day.
Therefore, Xiāo Hé said:
'After a hundred battles and a hundred defeats,
what is there
to wait for
but death?'
Ultimately, the goal is to achieve great salvation.
Why should one contend for a fleeting moment with bandits destined for destruction?
It is precisely because he did not
contend at Hóngmén
that no one could contend with him at Gāixià.
King Wén was imprisoned at Yǒulǐ,
hence his Way flourished at Mùyě;
Gōu Jiàn suffered humiliation at Kuàijī,
hence his might
When Tàiwèi Xī Jiàn was critically ill,
Mó was appointed Tàiwèi Jūnsī,
and granted the additional title of Shìzhōng.
When Jiàn died,
Mó was immediately appointed Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Xú Yǎn Qīng Sān Zhōu Yángzhōu Zhī Jìnlíng Yùzhōu Zhī Pèi Jùn Zhū Jūshì, concurrently Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted Jiǎjié.
At that time, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Chén Guāng submitted a memorial requesting an expedition against the Hú,
and an imperial edict ordered an attack on Shòuyáng.
Mó submitted a memorial saying: "Today Shòuyáng city is small but fortified.
From Shòuyáng to Lángyá,
city walls face each other,
the furthest distance between them being merely a hundred li.
If one city is attacked,
the many cities
will surely come to its aid.
Moreover, the royal army has been on the road for more than fifty days,
Liú Shìyī's army has already entered the Huái River,
and several detachments have been sent north to capture strongholds.
The main army has not yet arrived,
but its approach
has long been known.
And the enemy's postal couriers
travel a thousand li a day,
so the cavalry from north of the Yellow River can arrive quickly.
It's not just neighboring cities that will come to aid.
Even with the bravery of Bái Qǐ, Hán
Xìn, and Xiàng Jí,
they still broke their cooking pots and burned their boats,
and deployed their army with their backs to a river.
Now, to moor boats on a sandbank,
and lead troops to attack the city,
facing a strong enemy in front,
and looking back at the escape
route,
this is what military strategy warns against.
If the offensive does not succeed in capturing the city,
and the Hú cavalry suddenly arrive,
I fear Huán Zǐ will not know what to do,
and the fingers in the boats will be plentiful enough to scoop up.
Currently, the expeditionary army consists of five thousand men,
all elite troops from the imperial capital.
Furthermore, Guāng is the Zuǒwèi,
which is known far and wide.
This is known as the Dìanzhōng army.
It should be ordered that wherever it goes,
there is an expedition without battle.
But to halt it beneath a strong city,
victory would not be glorious,
and defeat would be a laughingstock.
To use the nation's finest steeds to attack a bandit's humble village,
if we gain
it, the profit is meager and insufficient to harm the enemy;
if we lose it, the harm is severe and sufficient to benefit the bandits.
I fear this is not the best strategy.
Your humble servant believes that upon hearing of bandits, we should launch an attack;
when the bandits retreat, we should withdraw our troops.
This would ensure no errors in the matter.
My humble opinion may not be comprehensive,
but I respectfully submit it for your consideration."
Shí Jìlóng built several hundred ships in Qīngzhōu,
plundering the coastal counties,
killing indiscriminately wherever he went.
The imperial court was concerned about this.
Mó dispatched Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Xú Xuán and others to guard Zhōngzhōu,
and also offered rewards:
whoever captured a large enemy white ship would be
rewarded with a thousand bolts of cloth,
and a hundred bolts for a small ship.
At that time, Mó commanded over seven thousand men.
His garrisons extended east to Tǔ Shān,
west to Jiāngchéng,
with eight strongholds under his command,
a total of eleven walled fortifications,
and more than thirty beacon towers and watchtowers.
He made preparations according to the circumstances,
showing great strategic foresight.
Previously,
Xī Jiàn had submitted a list of one hundred and eighty subordinates who had performed meritorious service.
The emperor had agreed to reward their achievements,
but Jiàn died before the rewards were given,
and the decision was made to no longer issue them.
Mó submitted a memorial arguing that since Jiàn had already been promised,
it was inappropriate to cancel it now.
Furthermore, those Jiàn had listed had all accumulated years of meritorious service,
survived numerous battles,
and should not go unrewarded.
An imperial edict approved it.
When Kāngdì ascended the throne,
Mó was summoned and appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī,
and concurrently Sītú.
He replaced Yīn Hào as Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was also appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and concurrently Sītú as before.
Initially,
Mó humbly declined to appoint subordinates (liáozuǒ).
Imperial edicts repeatedly urged him to do so,
and only then did he take on Yuánshǔ.
When Shí Jìlóng died,
China fell into great chaos.
At that time, the court and commoners alike believed that peace would soon be restored,
but Mó alone disagreed,
saying to his close associates:
"The destruction of the Hú
is indeed a great celebration,
but it will bring worries to the royal house."
Someone asked:
"Why is that?"
Mó said:
"Only those who can follow Heaven's will and adapt to the times,
to bring order to the chaos of the realm,
if not supreme sages,
must be heroic figures.
To measure one's virtue and weigh one's strength,
this is beyond what contemporary worthies can achieve.
They will surely strive to expand their territories,
exhausting the people to achieve their ambitions.
If their talent does not match their ambition,
and their strategy does not satisfy their desires,
their resources will be depleted, their strength exhausted,
and both their wisdom and courage will be overcome.
This is why Hán Lú and Dōng Guō both perished."
He was promoted to Shìzhōng, Sītú.
He submitted a memorial declining the appointment, saying:
"I humbly reflect upon myself:
In the past, I ascended through mistaken favor,
undeservedly occupying a position beyond my merits.
My inadequacy accumulated, yet my honor and favor increased,
and as criticism grew, my promotion was further augmented.
This diminishes the Sagely Court's foundational acts of prominence,
and it increases the risk of 'overturning the food cauldron' for this humble minister.
I am full of trepidation and fear,
having no place to put my face.
I beg that Your Heavenly Gaze may turn,
to correct this mistaken favor,
in order to satisfy the hopes of the multitude."
The Empress Dowager issued an edict in reply, refusing his request.
Mó still firmly declined,
saying to his close associates:
"If I were to become Sītú,
I would be ridiculed by future generations.
Righteously, I dare not accept it."
The Empress Dowager sent an envoy to convey her will.
