From the winter of the fourth year to the end of the fifth year,
edicts were repeatedly issued,
but Mó firmly adhered to his refusal.
In the sixth year,
he again submitted a memorial,
requesting to retire due to illness,
and to return the seal and ribbon of the Left Guānglù Dàfū and concurrent Sītú.
He submitted over ten memorials.
Emperor Mù held court,
and sent Shìzhōng Jì Qú
and Huángménláng Dīng Zuǎn to summon Mó.
Mó pleaded severe illness,
and had his chief clerk, Xiè Yōu, reply:
"Your minister Mó is unfortunately afflicted with the illness of Duke Mùzǐ,
and although the imperial presence is but a short distance,
I dare not obey the edict,
but lie prostrate awaiting punishment."
From dawn until shēn (3-5 PM),
the envoys went back and forth over ten times,
but Mó did not arrive.
At that time, the emperor was eight years old,
and very tired.
He asked his attendants:
"Why has the person summoned not come yet?
When will this court session end?"
Both ruler and ministers were exhausted.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict:
"If he absolutely will not come,
the court should be dismissed."
The Central Army General Yīn Hào then impeached and removed Lìbù Shàngshū Jiāng Yǎn from office.
Jiǎnwén, who was then Prince of Kuàijī,
ordered his staff:
"Duke Cài has arrogantly defied the imperial command,
showing no courtesy befitting a minister.
If the ruler must humble himself before his superiors,
and great principles cannot be upheld below,
I do not know how governance can be conducted anymore."
Thereupon, the high officials submitted a memorial, saying:
"Sītú Mó has recently, due to a common illness,
long evaded the imperial command.
When the Emperor held court,
and all officials stood in line,
the respectful bowing
was expected of Mó.
If his intention was to decline and retire,
he should have personally presented his辭 (speech/statement) at the imperial court.
How can a ruler toil all day, while his minister offers not even a single gesture of deference!
His perverse arrogance towards his superior
is a crime akin to disloyalty.
We, your ministers, have deliberated,
and it is appropriate to clarify the national statutes.
We request that he be sent to the Tíngwèi to enforce the penal code."
Mó was afraid,
and led his sons and younger brothers, dressed in plain clothes, to the imperial palace to prostrate themselves,
personally going to the Tíngwèi to await punishment.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict, saying:
"Mó was the teacher of the late emperor,
serving several generations.
Moreover, he has admitted his guilt to the authorities,
and reflects on his transgression internally.
If he were to be dealt with according to law,
my heart cannot bear it.
He may, according to old regulations, be dismissed and reduced to a commoner."
After Mó was deposed,
he shut his door and did not go out,
spending his days lecturing and reciting,
and teaching his sons and younger brothers.
After several years,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict, saying:
"The former Sītú Mó was known for his upright character and virtue,
and his conduct established his reputation.
Therefore, he served in previous courts,
attaining the position of a grand counselor.
Due to last year's transgression,
he was disciplined and reproved.
Since then,
he has closed his doors and reflected on his fault,
truly embodying the principle of a great minister admitting his errors.
Let Mó be appointed Guānglù Dàfū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī."
Thereupon, she sent Yèzhě Púshè Mèng Hóng to confer the appointment.
Mó submitted a memorial expressing his gratitude and declining, saying:
"I, a dull and shallow person,
was in the past undeservedly honored with exceptional favor.
My inadequacy accumulated for many years,
and I further violated and slighted imperial edicts,
deserving to be executed in the marketplace.
Fortunately, I received leniency,
and I did not expect Your Heavenly beneficence to again bestow honor upon me.
This is beyond what my dying efforts can repay.
My illness has not yet subsided,
and I am unable to attend court.
Overwhelmed by Your Sagely Grace,
I respectfully send this memorial of thanks."
Thus, due to his severe illness,
he never again appeared at court.
An edict granted him a stool and a staff,
and allowed horses to pass through his gate.
In the twelfth year,
he died,
at the age of seventy-six.
The rites of mourning and bestowal
were entirely in accordance with the precedent of Grand Commandant Lù Wán.
An edict posthumously appointed him Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
and gave him the posthumous title Wénmù.
Mó was widely learned,
and he settled many discussions regarding rites, ceremonies, and ancestral temple institutions.
His essays and treatises
were compiled and circulated in the world.
He compiled a collected commentary on Bān Gù's Hàn Shū,
incorporating annotations from Yīng Shào onwards.
When Mó first crossed the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
he saw a péngqí (a type of crab-like creature),
and was greatly delighted, saying:
"Crabs have eight legs,
and two additional claws."
He ordered it to be cooked.
After eating it,
he vomited and suffered extreme exhaustion,
only then realizing it was not a crab.
Later, he visited Xiè Shàng and told him about it.
Shàng said:
"You did not study the Éryǎ well enough;
you almost died for the sake of 'encouraging learning'."
Mó's nature was upright and refined.
When Chancellor Wáng Dǎo arranged for female entertainers,
setting up beds and mats,
Mó was already seated,
but was displeased and left,
and Dǎo did not stop him either.
He was especially scrupulous and cautious by nature,
always taking excessive precautions in every matter.
Thus, people at the time said:
"Duke Cài crosses a floating bridge,
untying his belt and wearing it as a life vest."
His eldest son, Shào,
was the Administrator of Yǒngjiā.
His youngest son, Xì,
was talented in learning and literature,
reaching the position of Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ.
Zhūgé Huī
Zhūgé Huī, courtesy name Dàomíng,
was from Yángdū, Lángyé.
His grandfather, Dàn,
was Sīkōng of Wèi,
and was executed by Emperor Wén.
His father, Jìng,
fled to Wú,
and became Dà Sīmǎ.
When Wú was pacified,
he went into hiding and did not emerge.
Emperor Wǔ had an old acquaintance with Jìng,
and Jìng's elder sister was also the Princess of Lángyé.
The Emperor knew Jìng was with his sister,
and so went to see him.
Jìng fled to the latrine,
but the Emperor forced his way in to see him,
saying:
"I did not expect to see you again today."
Jìng shed tears and said:
"I regret that I could not smear myself with lacquer and peel my skin,
to avoid seeing your sagely face again!"
An edict appointed him Shìzhōng,
but he firmly declined to accept it,
returning to his hometown,
and for the rest of his life, he never sat facing the imperial court.
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] became famous at the age of twenty.
He was appointed as the magistrate of Jíqiū [Jíqiū] on probation.
He was then transferred to be the magistrate of Línyí [Línyí].
His governance was peaceful.
When the world fell into great chaos,
he sought refuge south of the Yangtze River,
and his renown was second only to Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] and Yǔ Liàng [Yǔ Liàng].
Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] once said to him:
"My lord, you are destined to be a high official."
When Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] was appointed Sīkōng [Sīkōng],
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] was present.
Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] pointed to his cap and said:
"You will wear this again."
Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] once playfully argued with Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] about their clans' names,
saying:
"People say 'Wáng-Gě' [Wáng-Gě],
not 'Gě-Wáng' [Gě-Wáng]."
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] replied:
"People don't say 'horse-donkey' [mǎ lǘ],
but 'donkey-horse' [lǘ mǎ].
Is the donkey superior to the horse then?"
Such was the familiarity and closeness with which he was regarded.
At that time, Xún Kǎi [Xún Kǎi], courtesy name Dàomíng [Dàomíng], from Yǐngchuān [Yǐngchuān], and Cài Mó [Cài Mó], courtesy name Dàomíng [Dàomíng], from Chénliú [Chénliú],
both enjoyed great fame along with Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī].
They were known as
the "Three Dàmíngs of the Restoration."
People made a saying about them:
"The Three Dàmíngs [Dàmíngs] of the capital each have their fame;
Cài [Cài] is refined, Xún [Xún] and Gě [Gě] are pure."
When Emperor Yuán [Yuán] was General of Andōng [Andōng],
he appointed Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] as his Chief Clerk.
He was twice promoted to be the magistrate of Jiāngníng [Jiāngníng].
He achieved merit in suppressing Zhōu Fù [Zhōu Fù],
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bólíng Tíng [Bólíng Tíng].
He then became an Adjutant to the General of Zhèndōng [Zhèndōng].
Along with Biàn Hú [Biàn Hú], he was promoted to Chief Secretary (Cóngshì Zhōngláng [Cóngshì Zhōngláng]) due to his contemporary reputation,
also overseeing the archives.
At that time, there were many affairs from all directions,
and memorials and reports piled up.
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] would consider and respond,
and all praised his balanced judgment.
At that time, the Wáng [Wáng] clan served as generals,
while Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī]'s brothers and Yán Hán [Yán Hán] all held prominent positions.
Liú Chāo [Liú Chāo] managed official documents with loyalty and diligence.
People at the time believed the emperor was good at employing the talents of the entire state.
When Emperor Mǐn [Mǐn] ascended the throne,
he summoned virtuous and eminent individuals from all corners.
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] was summoned to be a director in the Department of State Affairs.
Emperor Yuán [Yuán], believing he needed his talents for state affairs,
submitted a memorial requesting to retain him.
By imperial decree, he was transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī [Kuàijī].
Before his departure,
the emperor hosted a banquet for him,
and said:
"Today's Kuàijī [Kuàijī] is like Guānzhōng [Guānzhōng] of old.
Abundant in food and soldiers,
its fate lies with a good administrator.
As you possess the methods for governing,
I have asked you to take this position.
With the four quarters in disarray,
you must rectify and restore our crumbling fortunes.
What should be prioritized in governance,
please speak of it."
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] expressed his gratitude,
and then replied:
"Today, the world is in chaos and disorder,
and customs are declining.
It is fitting to honor the five virtues,
discard the four evils,
promote loyalty and sincerity,
and dismiss superficiality."
The emperor deeply accepted his words.
In the early years of Tàixīng [Tàixīng],
he was ranked first in administrative achievements.
An imperial edict stated:
"Recently, there have been many difficulties,
and officials have frequently changed,
which has led to many弊.
Even sages take time to establish their way,
and only then can transformation be achieved.
How much more so for others!
Emperor Xuān [Xuān] of Hàn [Hàn] said, 'Those who can bring peace to the world with me,
are none other than the excellent Two Thousand Piculs.'
This saying is truly valid.
This is why Huáng Bà [Huáng Bà] and others served for ten or even twenty years without transfer,
enabling them to achieve the merits of restoration.
Rewards, punishments, dismissals, and promotions
are used to clarify the path of governance.
The Grand Administrator of Kuàijī [Kuàijī], Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī], has administered his office for three years,
with clear governance and harmonious people,
making him first among all commanderies.
It is fitting to advance his rank and position
to encourage good customs and education.
Now, Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī]'s salary is increased to Two Thousand Piculs."
A short while later,
he resigned his office due to mourning for his mother.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Palace Secretary (Zhōngshū Lìng [Zhōngshū Lìng]).
Wáng Dūn [Wáng Dūn] recommended Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] as the Administrator of Dānyáng [Dānyáng],
but he was excused due to a prolonged illness.
Emperor Míng [Míng] summoned Wáng Dūn [Wáng Dūn],
appointed Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī] as Attendant Official (Shìzhōng [Shìzhōng]),
and added the title of Colonel-Director of Chariots (Fèngchē Dūwèi [Fèngchē Dūwèi]).
He was rewarded for his merits in suppressing Wáng Hán [Wáng Hán],
promoted to Marquis of Jiàn'ān [Jiàn'ān],
and his previous title was bestowed upon his second son, Zhù [Zhù], as a Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu [Guānnèi Hóu]).
He was again appointed General of the Rear and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī [Kuàijī].
He was summoned to be Attendant Official (Shìzhōng [Shìzhōng]),

then promoted to Director of the Left Bureau of Popular Affairs (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū [Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū]), Teacher of Wǔlíng [Wǔlíng] King (Wǔlíng Wáng Shī [Wǔlíng Wáng Shī]), and Director of the Bureau of Appointments (Lìbù Shàngshū [Lìbù Shàngshū]).

He was successively promoted to Right Chief of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè [Shàngshū Yòu Púyè]), additionally serving as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì [Sànqí Chángshì]), Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Silver Seal and Blue Ribbon (Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū [Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū]), overseeing the selection of his home province's Chief Administrator (Dà Zhōngzhèng [Dà Zhōngzhèng]), and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng [Shàngshū Lìng]).
His roles as Attendant-in-Ordinary and Director of the Bureau of Appointments remained unchanged.
When Emperor Chéng [Chéng] ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted the titles of Attendant Official (Shìzhōng [Shìzhōng]) and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold Seal and Purple Ribbon (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū [Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū]).
He died
at the age of sixty-two.

He was posthumously honored as Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū [Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū]) and granted the privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī [Yítóng Sānsī]).
The rites of funeral gifts
followed the precedent of Grand Commandant Xīngpíng Bó [Xīngpíng Bó].
His posthumous title was Jìng [Jìng],
and he was offered sacrifices with a grand ceremony.
His son, Hán [Hán], succeeded him,
reaching the position of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì [Sànqí Chángshì]).
Zhūgě Huī [Zhūgě Huī]'s elder brother, Yí [Yí],
courtesy name Dàohuí [Dàohuí],
was also highly esteemed by Emperor Yuán [Yuán],
and died in the position of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng [Tàicháng]).
Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào] (Gù Yuèzhī [Gù Yuèzhī] Cài Yì [Cài Yì])
Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào], courtesy name Shēnyuán [Shēnyuán],
was a native of Chénjùn Chángpíng [Chénjùn Chángpíng].
His father, Xiàn [Xiàn],
courtesy name Hóngqiáo [Hóngqiáo],
served as the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng [Yùzhāng].
People from the capital entrusted him with over a hundred letters.
When he reached Shítóu [Shítóu],
he threw them all into the water,
saying:
"Those that sink will sink themselves;
those that float will float themselves.
Yīn Hóngqiáo [Yīn Hóngqiáo] does not act as a letter carrier."
Such was his upright and independent nature.
He died in the position of Grand Master of Imperial Sacrifices (Guānglù Xūn [Guānglù Xūn]).
Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào]'s discernment and magnanimity were clear and far-reaching.
He had a good reputation at a young age,
and was particularly skilled in "profound words" (xuányán [xuányán]).
He and his uncle Róng [Róng] both enjoyed Laozi [Lǎozi] and the Yijing [Yìjīng].
When Róng [Róng] and Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào] discussed orally, Róng [Róng] would often be at a loss for words,
but in written works, Róng [Róng] would surpass him.
Because of this, Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào] was revered by those who engaged in refined discussions.
Someone once asked Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào]:
"Why do people dream of coffins when they are about to receive an official position,
and dream of dung when they are about to acquire wealth?"
Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào] replied:
"Official positions are inherently corrupt,
so one dreams of corpses when about to receive an official position.
Money is inherently like dirt,
so one dreams of filth when about to acquire money."
People at the time considered this a famous saying.
He was invited by the Three Palaces,
but all were declined.
General of the West-Conquering, Yǔ Liàng, appointed him as his Secretary (jìshì cānjūn),
and he was successively promoted to Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works (sītú zuǒ chángshǐ).
General of the Pacifying West, Yǔ Yì, again invited him to be his Military Advisor (sīmǎ).
He was then appointed as Palace Attendant (shìzhōng) and Military Advisor to the General of the Pacifying West (ānxī jūn sī),
but he claimed illness and did not take up the posts.
He then secluded himself at his family burial ground,
for nearly ten years.
At that time, people compared him to Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng.
Wáng Méng and Xiè Shàng were still waiting for him to emerge,
to divine the rise and fall of the Jiāngzuǒ region.
They therefore visited him together,
and realized that Hào had a firm resolve.
After they returned,
they said to each other:
“If Shēnyuán does not come forth,
what will become of the common people? ”
Yǔ Yì sent a letter to Hào, saying:
“At present, the safety of the state and dynasty in Jiāngdōng
is entrusted internally to gentlemen like Hé Chōng and Chǔ Pú,
and externally to the Yǔ and Huán clans.
I fear it may not be free from worries for a hundred years,
but will also decline in a matter of days.
From a young age, you have established a good reputation,
and for over ten years,
you have held positions both inside and outside the court.
Yet you wish to live in seclusion, seeking stability and righteousness (lìzhēn).
This principle is difficult to maintain completely.
Moreover, to accomplish the affairs of a time,
one must possess the capabilities of that time.
Why must one’s virtue be equal to that of the ancients,
or one’s charm match that of past luminaries?
Wáng Yífǔ was
a man of refined character in the previous dynasty.
However, I considered his reputation insincere,
and he gained nothing from beginning to end.
If one believes the Dao is not like that of Yú and Xià,
one should naturally remain aloof and solitary.
But if one fails to plan from the beginning,
and greatly accumulates fame and reputation,
reaching the pinnacle of honor and position,
one should properly uphold and promote the norms of governance (míngjiào)
to pacify the source of chaos.
Instead, he engaged in lofty discussions of Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
talking of emptiness all day long.
Although it was called discussing the Dao,
it actually fostered an obsession with empty rhetoric.
By his later years,
people still held expectations of him,
hoping for peace and fearing chaos,
entrusting their lives and duties to him.
But Fǔ merely expressed himself,
pursuing minor interests and seeking fame.
Consequently, he was imprisoned by the Hú barbarians,
and his words became inappropriate.
How could an enlightened and virtuous gentleman,
when encountering such circumstances and opportunities,
act in such a way?
Yet the world approved of him.
This further shows that the distinction between true fame and empty reputation (míngshí) was not yet settled,
and the corrupt trend had not yet been reformed.”
Hào firmly declined and did not take up the post.
In the early Jiànfú era,
Yǔ Bīng and his brothers, along with Hé Chōng and others, died successively.
Emperor Jiǎnwén, then still a prince,
began to oversee all state affairs.
General of the Guard, Chǔ Pú, recommended Hào,
who was summoned to be General of Establishing Martial Might (jiànwǔ jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yángzhōu.
Hào submitted a memorial declining the offer,
and also sent a letter to Emperor Jiǎnwén,
fully explaining his reasons.
Emperor Jiǎnwén replied:
“At this time of adversity,
the state is utterly weak and on the verge of collapse.
It truly relies on individuals with talent emerging at this moment;
we can no longer seek talent from afar like Fù Yuè.
Your profound insight and extensive knowledge,
and your comprehensive and well-practiced thought,
if you would rise and put them to use,
would be sufficient to save the state.
If you persist in your deep desire to withdraw
and merely pursue your original aspirations,
I fear that the affairs of the world will depart from this point.
Now the reins of power are not steady,
and the net of the Jìn dynasty is not taut.
Can we wish to leap into the Eastern Sea
and still achieve our goals?
From this perspective,
your decision to accept or decline is tantamount to the rise or fall of our time.
And the rise or fall of our time is no different from the fate of the nation and the imperial house.
I hope you will consider this deeply,
and calculate carefully.
You will surely have a profound understanding of what is permissible or not.
I hope you will certainly set aside your original aspirations,
and comply with the sentiments of the multitude.”
Hào repeatedly declined,
from March to July,
before finally accepting the appointment.
At that time, Huán Wēn, having conquered Shǔ,
had growing power and prestige,
and the court feared him.
Emperor Jiǎnwén, seeing that Hào had a great reputation
and was respected by both court and commoners,
therefore brought him in as a trusted confidant
to contend with Wēn.
Thus, he and Wēn became somewhat suspicious of and estranged from each other.
When he experienced the sorrow of his father’s death,
he resigned from his post.
At that time, Cài Mó was appointed to temporarily manage Yángzhōu,
awaiting Hào’s return.
After the mourning period ended,
he was summoned to be Minister of Personnel (shàngshū púyè),
but he did not accept.
He was again appointed General of Establishing Martial Might and Governor of Yángzhōu,
and subsequently participated in managing court affairs.
Xún Xiàn of Yǐngchuān, young and with a good reputation,
was promoted by Hào to be Administrator of Yìxīng and Wú Counties,
to serve as his wings.
Wáng Xīzhī secretly advised Hào and Xiàn
to reconcile with Huán Wēn,
and not to create internal friction.
Hào did not follow this advice.
When Shí Jìlóng died
and there was great chaos among the Hú,
the court wished to pacify the entire Guānhé region.

Therefore, Hào was appointed General of the Central Army (zhōngjūn jiāngjūn), given the temporary authority to execute (jiǎjié), and made Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for the Five Provinces of Yáng, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, and Qīng.
Upon receiving the commission, Hào
took the recovery of the Central Plains as his personal responsibility.
He submitted a memorial proposing a northern expedition to Xǔ and Luò.
As he was about to depart,
he fell from his horse,
which was considered an ill omen at the time.
Subsequently, he appointed Chén Kuí, Administrator of Huáinán, and Cài Yì, Governor of Yǎnzhōu, as vanguards.
General of the Pacifying West, Xiè Shàng, and General of the Northern Central Army, Xún Xiàn, were appointed as chief commanders.
He opened up over a thousand qǐng of farmland west of the Jiāng River
to serve as military provisions.
When the army reached Shòuyáng,
he secretly lured Liáng Ān, Léi Ruò'ér, and other ministers of Fú Jiàn,
to persuade them to kill Jiàn,
promising them authority over the Guānyòu region.
Originally,
the surrendered Wei Tuō died.
Yáo Xiāng killed Jǐng
to absorb his troops.
Hào was greatly displeased by this,
and sent General of the Soaring Dragon (lóngxiáng jiāngjūn), Liú Qǐ, to guard Qiáo,
and relocated Xiāng to Liáng.
Thereafter, members of the Wèi clan came and went in Shòuyáng,
and Xiāng became increasingly suspicious and fearful.
Soon, some of Xiāng’s troops wished to return to Hào.
Xiāng killed them,
whereupon Hào plotted to eliminate Xiāng.
It so happened that Fú Jiàn killed his ministers,
and Jiàn’s nephew, Méi, fled west from Luòyáng.
Hào believed that the plot involving Liáng Ān had succeeded,
and that Fú Jiàn was already dead.
He requested to advance and garrison Luòyáng,
restore the imperial mausoleums and gardens,
make Xiāng the vanguard,
station General of the Champions (guànjūn jiāngjūn), Liú Qià, at Lùtái,
and General of Establishing Martial Might, Liú Dùn, at Cāngyuán.
He also requested to be relieved of his duties in Yángzhōu
to solely command Luòyáng.
The imperial edict did not permit this.
Upon Hào’s arrival at Xǔchāng,
Zhāng Yù rebelled,
and Xiè Shàng was also defeated.
Hào returned to Shòuyáng.
Later, he advanced his army again,
reaching Shānsāng,
but Xiāng rebelled.
Hào was afraid,
abandoned his baggage train,
and retreated to defend Qiáochéng.
His weapons and military provisions were all plundered by Xiāng,
and many soldiers deserted.
Hào sent Liú Qǐ and Wáng Bīnzhī to attack Xiāng at Shānsāng,
but both were killed by Xiāng.
Huán Wēn had always been jealous of Hào.
Upon hearing of his defeat,
he submitted a memorial condemning Hào, stating: “It is noted that General of the Central Army, Hào, has been excessively favored by imperial grace,
usurping positions not rightfully his.
His prestige and divine favor are exceptional,
twice holding authority over the capital.
He failed to respectfully and cautiously carry out his duties,
or diligently maintain his official
position.
Instead, he encroached upon other officials’ authority and disrupted the administration,
acting according to his personal whims.
The former Minister of Works, Minister Mó, upheld righteousness and lived simply,
holding a position in the highest ranks of government,
serving as tutor to the late emperor,
and being a venerable elder of the court.
Yet,
When he reached seventy [years of age],
he requested to retire in accordance with the rites.
Although he firmly declined from the imperial court,
disobeying the imperial decree,
this was merely sufficient to demonstrate the custom of yielding and humility
and to promote the rite of honoring the virtuous.
However, [Yǐn] Hào
fabricated cunning theories,
misleading the imperial court;
the officials in charge of justice
were about to inflict the great execution.
Since the death of the Jié Hú [barbarians]
and the annihilation of all the villains,
the common people were suffering terribly,
eagerly awaiting deliverance
and relief.
Hào bore the heavy responsibility of leading a punitive expedition,
but had no will to avenge the disgrace.
He settled down to establish his own power,
and wantonly created disturbances,
thus allowing the enemies to delay their punishment
and treacherous rebels to rise simultaneously.
Huáxià
was in turmoil,
and the common people were in utter distress.
Hào feared that his crimes would catch up to him
and that he would not be tolerated at court,
so he outwardly clamored for an advance expedition
while inwardly seeking a temporary reprieve.
He encamped at Shòuyáng,
stationed his troops for a full year,
exhausted the resources of the imperial treasury,
and depleted the strength of five provinces.
He gathered the unscrupulous
to strengthen his own defense.
His appointments and promotions were chaotic,
and he disregarded the harm caused by suspicion and jealousy.
Thus, Fàn Fēng and his ilk rebelled
at Sháopí,
and Qí Dé and Lóng Huì caused mutinies at his very side.
The Qiāng chieftain Yáo Xiāng led his followers to submit,
sending his younger brother as a hostage to the capital.
Hào was unable to treat
and employ him well,
secretly plotting to kill him,
and twice dispatched assassins,
but was discovered by Xiāng.
Xiāng then became frightened
and consequently rebelled.
The creation of this chaotic situation
began with Hào.
Moreover, he failed to suppress it in time,
allowing a small villain to run rampant,
wielding his poisonous influence,
causing him to be disgraced at Shānshāng,
and his army shattered in Liángguó.
Boats and carts were burned,
and his baggage
train was lost.
The accumulated provisions of the three armies
were instead used to supply the bandits,
and fine armor and sharp weapons
were instead used by the rebels.
Divine wrath and popular resentment
made him abandoned by the multitude,
and the danger of collapse
was about
to reach the state.
Therefore, I, your subject, have forgotten sleep and am anxious,
unable to find peace.
Indeed, upholding righteousness and demonstrating justice
is how instruction is delivered;
clarifying punishments and establishing laws
is how the multitude is regulated.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to recall the punishment of banishment by Táng Yáo
and to observe
the precedent of the stateless in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
If Your Sacred Majesty is magnanimous
and cannot bear to execute him,
then at least he should be banished afar,
exiled to a desolate frontier.
Although this would not be sufficient to fulfill the immense responsibility,
it could roughly serve to proclaim a warning for the future.
He was ultimately dismissed and reduced to a commoner,
and exiled to Xìn'ān County in Dōngyáng.
Hào was as famous as Wēn in his youth,
and they often competed in their hearts.
Wēn once asked Hào:
"How do you compare to me?"
Hào replied:
"I have been acquainted with you for a long time;
I would rather be myself."
Wēn, already considering himself a hero,
often slighted Hào,
but Hào did not fear him.
At this point,
Wēn said to others:
"When I was young, Hào and I rode bamboo horses together.
I threw mine away,
and Hào always picked it up.
Therefore, he must be inferior to me."
He also said to Xī Chāo:
"Hào has virtue and eloquence.
If he had been made a Minister [Lìng] or Grand Master [Pú],
he would have been sufficient to be a model for all officials;
the court simply failed to employ him according to his talent."
Although Hào was dismissed and banished,
he showed no resentment in his speech,
remaining calm and accepting his fate,
and continued to converse and recite without interruption.
Even his family members did not perceive any sadness from his exile.
However, he spent the whole day writing in the air,
the four characters
"Duō Duō Guàishì" (What strange things!)
and nothing else.
Hào's nephew Hán Bó,
whom Hào had always admired and loved,
followed him to his place of exile.
After a year, when Bó returned to the capital,
Hào saw him off at the riverside,
reciting the poem by Cáo Yán Yuǎn:
"The rich and noble are joined by others,
the poor and humble are abandoned by relatives."
He then shed tears.
Later, Wēn intended to make Hào the Shàngshūlìng,
and sent a letter to inform him.
Hào gladly agreed.
When he was about to reply to the letter,
fearing mistakes,
he opened and closed it dozens of times,
and eventually sent an empty envelope,
which greatly displeased Wēn,
and thus their relationship was severed.
He died in the twelfth year of Yǒnghé [357 CE].
His son Juān
also had a good reputation.
At the beginning of Xián'ān [371 CE],
Huán Wēn deposed the Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), Prince Xī of Wǔlíng,
and falsely accused Juān and Yǔ Qiàn of conspiring with Xī in rebellion,
and executed them.
Later, when Hào was to be reburied,

his former subordinate Gù Yuè wrote a memorial defending Hào, saying: I humbly observe that the late General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yángzhōu, Yīn Hào, possessed profound virtue,
extensive and deep understanding of principles,
and refined and superior demeanor,
his fame overshadowing his contemporaries.
He twice oversaw
the divine land,
bringing peace to thousands of miles;
his merits and achievements were prominent,
and the sacred court admired and praised him,
thus entrusting him with the responsibility of regional command.
When the military banner was raised,
he went forth to guard Shòuyáng,
driving away the
jackals and wolves,
clearing the thorns and brambles,
gathering those who embraced righteousness,
and widely establishing military agricultural colonies.
Enduring rain and wind,
he worked as diligently as the court officials.
Relying on imperial might,
the multitude of villains changed their ways,
and he advanced
his army to Héluò,
restoring the imperial tombs.
However, unforeseen changes
caused him to stumble midway,
thus allowing the success of his mountain-building effort to collapse just as it was nearing completion,
and his loyal and sincere aspirations
were thus thwarted.
Having been dismissed and reduced,
he exiled himself to the mountains and seas,
shutting his door for the rest of his life,
completely cut off from the world.
He can be said to have restrained himself and returned to propriety,
and to have been poor without resentment.
Upon examining Hào's transgressions,
they are but the usual penalties for defeat,
not an eternal condemnation based on his true intentions.
If we discuss his famous virtue and deep sincerity, it was as described,
and if we observe his efforts to correct his errors and blame himself,
it was as such.
How can he be abandoned and not cared for,
leaving a lingering injustice in the law?
Presently, his grave site is prepared,
the subterranean passage opened,
and his coffin is suspended for burial,
with rites akin to those of a commoner.
There is an undeserved disparity between his life and death,
and no opportunity for self-vindication in the netherworld.
I am moved by the three loyal ones,
and the vast heaven is boundless.
If a clear edict were issued,
to honor our good man,
to exalt
He was restored to his original office.
This made manifest the obscure and hidden.
Thus, the state’s might and grace exhibited the beauty of comprehensive salvation,
allowing the deceased to be revived,
with no regrets of unfaithfulness.
When the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict ordered Huàn Hào’s original office to be restored.
Gù Yuèzhī, courtesy name Jūnshū,
showed integrity in his youth.
He was the same age as Jiǎnwén Dì,
but his hair turned white early.
The Emperor asked him the reason.
He replied:
“Pines and cypresses,
even through frost, flourish;
willows, of common quality,
wither at the sight of autumn.”
Jiǎnwén Dì was pleased with his reply.
When he first planned to present a memorial to argue on behalf of Huàn Hào,
many of Huàn Hào’s relatives and friends said it was inappropriate.
Gù Yuèzhī was determined to make it known,
and also debated with court officials,
so the crowd could not dissuade him.
People at the time all praised him.
He served as Zhōubiéjià,
and subsequently as Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and died.
His son, Kǎizhī,
[一一]has a separate biography.
Cài Yì had
great courage,
and his voice was like thunder.
Once, two thieves entered his room.
Cài Yì slapped the bed and let out a shout,
and both thieves collapsed.
Thus, Huàn Hào entrusted him with the vanguard of the army.
The historian says: Lù Yè and others were all esteemed figures and national luminaries of their time,
whose achievements were evident through various trials.
They successively held high offices,
participating in managing the affairs of state.
However, they all followed established precedents,
and avoided error and regret.
As for Chōng, he spoke out against a mere boy;
although he was suppressed by powerful ministers,
he supported the Crown Prince,
and ultimately publicized the dying wishes.
He frequently participated in major deliberations,
and repeatedly offered excellent plans.
It can be said that loyalty and integrity resided in him alone.
Yīn Hào, with his pure demeanor and broad-mindedness,
was the object of public approval.
High office and generous stipends
came to him without seeking.
Everyone believed that education and righteousness depended on his rise or fall,
and the fate of the state awaited his handling of its safety or danger.
Yet, when he assumed the reins of national power,
he had no excellent plans or good governance.
When he took command of the military,
one heard only of his country being diminished and his army defeated.
From this, it is known that elegant demeanor is different from steadfast talent,
and discourse is not the essence of strategy.
He deviated from the correct path and misused his appointment,
leading to his downfall.
Alas!
Cài Mó knew his limits and acted accordingly,
practicing the principle of contentment.
His appointment to codify the laws
was, however, a mistake.
A eulogy says: Shìguāng was esteemed in his time,
Shìyáo was appropriate.
Their governance was like brothers,
their responsibilities those of prime ministers.
Zǔyán was concise and direct,
his legacy worthy of respect.
Cài Gě were renowned,
one refined, one pure.
Cìdào was principled,
far-sighted and loyal.
Zhōngjūn surveyed the situation,
his reputation brilliant among all.
He had more than enough ease and magnanimity,
but lacked the ability to manage affairs.
He abandoned his strengths for his weaknesses,
his achievements failed, and his name was disgraced.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 48: Kǒng Yú (son Wāng, Ānguó; younger brother Zhī; paternal cousins Tǎn, Yán; paternal cousin Qún; Qún’s son Chén)
Kǒng Yú, courtesy name Jìngkāng,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His ancestors originally resided in Liángguó.
His great-grandfather, Qián,
was the Táizǐ Shàofù.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he fled to Kuàijī
and settled there.
His grandfather, Zhú,
was the Prefect of Yùzhāng in Wú.
His father, Tián,
was the Prefect of Xiāngdōng.
His paternal cousin, Kǎn,
was the Dàsīnóng.
All were famous south of the Yangtze.
Kǒng Yú was orphaned at thirteen,
and was known for his filial piety in caring for his paternal grandmother.
He was as famous as Zhāng Mào, courtesy name Wěikāng, and Dīng Tán, courtesy name Shìkāng, from the same commandery.
People at the time called them
“The Three Kāngs of Kuàijī.”
After the pacification of Wú,
Kǒng Yú moved to Luò.
At the end of Huì Dì’s reign,
he returned to his hometown.
When he reached the Jiānghuái region,
he encountered Shí Bīng and Fēng Yún causing chaos.
Fēng Yún forced Kǒng Yú to be his Cānjūn.
He refused
and was about to be killed,
but was rescued by Fēng Yún’s Sīmǎ Zhāng Tǒng.
He returned east to Kuàijī,
entered the Xīn’ān Mountains,
changed his surname to Sūn,
and dedicated himself to farming and studying.
His trustworthiness was well-known in the local community.
Later, he suddenly left,
and everyone considered him a divine being,
and established a shrine for him.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
Yuán Dì first took up residence in Yángtǔ as the Āndōng Jiāngjūn,
and appointed Kǒng Yú as Cānjūn.
His relatives and clansmen searched for him,
but no one knew his whereabouts.
In the early Jiànxīng era,
he finally emerged to answer the summons,
serving as Chéngxiàng Yuàn.
He was subsequently appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Cān Chéngxiàng Jūnshì.
At this time, he was already fifty years old.
For his功 in suppressing Huá Yì,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yúbùtíng.
Kǒng Yú once passed by Yúbùtíng
and saw someone holding a caged turtle on the road.
Kǒng Yú bought it and released it into the stream.
The turtle turned its head to the left several times in the middle of the current.
Later,
when the marquis's seal was cast,
the turtle on the seal faced left,
and it did so three times in a row.
The seal-maker reported this,
and Kǒng Yú then understood,
and so wore the seal.
When the Emperor became Jìn Wáng,
he made Kǒng Yú Cháng Jiān Zhōngshū Láng.
At that time, Diāo Xié and Liú Wèi were powerful,
and Wáng Dǎo was rather alienated.
Kǒng Yú argued that Wáng Dǎo was loyal and virtuous,
and had performed meritorious service in aiding the emperor,
and suggested that all matters, big or small, should be discussed with him.
Because of this, his words did not please the emperor,
and he was sent out as Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ,
and successively promoted to Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
When Shěn Chōng rebelled,
Kǒng Yú abandoned his post and returned to the capital,
where he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and then promoted to Shìzhōng and Tàicháng.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Kǒng Yú, in court attire, guarded the ancestral temple.
Initially,
when Kǒng Yú was Sītú Chángshǐ,
due to the death of Píngnán Jiāngjūn Wēn Jiào’s mother and the turmoil preventing her burial,
he did not exceed his rank in offering condolences.
At this time,
after Sū Jùn was suppressed,
and Wēn Jiào had rendered great service,
Kǒng Yú went to Shítóu to visit Wēn Jiào.
Wēn Jiào held Kǒng Yú’s hand and wept, saying:
“The world is in chaos,
and the way of loyalty and filial piety has been abandoned.
Only you, sir,
can uphold the integrity of ancient people,
unfading in the bitter cold.”
People at the time all praised Wēn Jiào for his public-mindedness and Kǒng Yú for upholding righteousness.
Soon after, he was transferred to Dà Shàngshū,
and promoted to Ānnán Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
but he did not take up the post.
He was then transferred to Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
also overseeing the tutor of the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zuǒpúshè.
In the eighth year of Xiánhé,
an imperial edict stated:
“Shàngshū Lìng Wán and Zuǒ Púshè Yú both diligently reside in their official posts,
their emoluments not replacing their cultivation.
The right side of the government holds heavy responsibility,
highly esteemed by the previous court.
Therefore, thirty trusted men shall be granted to Wán,
and twenty to Yú,
for their stipends and rewards.”
Yú submitted a memorial firmly declining,
but a gracious edict did not permit it.
He submitted another memorial, saying:
“I, with my decay and dimness,
am undeservedly placed among the court's right,
and due to my laziness and mediocrity,
I am of no use in assisting.
Currently, strong invaders have not been annihilated,
the frontiers are daily alarmed,
governance is troublesome and burdens are heavy,
the common people are suffering,
corrupt officials wield arbitrary power,
and tyrannical people indulge in oppression.
After great devastation,
granaries and treasuries are empty,
meritorious individuals
are insufficiently rewarded,
and those in distress
have not seen rescue or relief.
The grievances of groans and sighs
move both men and spirits.
It is appropriate to consolidate offices and reduce posts,
cut salaries and economize expenditures,
diligently comfort the people,
to alleviate their hardships.
We, your servants, are unable to promote great reforms
or clarify criminal justice,
yet we selfishly enjoy high positions
and arbitrarily receive favors and provisions.
To have emoluments without virtue,
calamity will surely reach us.
I dare not arbitrarily accept this special favor,
thereby increasing my crimes and transgressions.”
The request was granted.
Wáng Dǎo heard of this and disapproved.
At a meeting in the capital, he said to Yú:
“You say that corrupt officials wield arbitrary power and tyrannical people indulge in oppression.
Who is causing this trouble?”
Yú intended to extensively discuss the court's successes and failures,
but Lù Wán restrained him, and he stopped.
Later, Dǎo was about to appoint Zhào Yìn as Hùjūn.
Yú said to Dǎo:
“Since the Restoration,
those who have held this office
are Zhōu Bórén and Yìng Sīyuǎn only.
Though there is indeed a lack of talent now,
how can Zhào Yìn be placed in it?”
Dǎo did not comply.
His adherence to righteousness was like this.
Because of this, he was resented by Dǎo.
Later, the posts of Zuǒ Yòu Púshè were abolished,
and Yú was appointed Shàngshū Púshè.
Yú was at the age of "hanging up the carriage" (retirement),
and repeatedly requested to resign and return home,
but was not permitted.
He was transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì.
He was again transferred to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
given the additional title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and concurrently held Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
After a while,
he was sent out as Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn and Kuàijī Nèishǐ,
with the additional title Sànqí Chángshì.
In Jùzhāng County, there was an old dike from the Hàn dynasty,
which had been ruined and abandoned for several hundred years.
Yú personally inspected it,
repaired the old weir,
irrigating over two hundred qǐng of fields,
all of which became good farmland.
After three years in the commandery,
he then built a house of several mũ of land at the foot of Hóu Shān, south of Hú Shān in Shānyīn,
with several thatched rooms,
and immediately abandoned his office to reside there.
He was sent several million in assets,
but took nothing at all.
When gravely ill,
he left an instruction to be dressed in ordinary clothes for his burial,
and that not a single offering of condolence from his鄉邑
should be accepted.
He died at the age of seventy-five
in the eighth year of Xiánkāng.
He was posthumously granted Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and given the posthumous name Zhēn.
He had three sons: Yín, Wāng, and Ānguó.
Yín inherited the title,
and his highest position was Jiàn'ān Tàishǒu.
Yín's son, Jìng,
courtesy name Jìgōng,
twice served as Kuàijī Nèishǐ,
and was successively promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè,
with the additional title Hòujiāngjūn.
Wāng, courtesy name Dézé,
was fond of learning and had noble conduct.
During the reign of Xiàowǔ Dì, his highest position was Shìzhōng.
At that time, Rú Qiānqiū was favored by Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ for his flattery.
Wāng repeatedly spoke of this to the Emperor,
but the Emperor did not heed him.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Tàicháng Qīng,
but dissatisfied,
he requested to leave,
and was made Jiǎjié, Dūdū Jiāoguǎng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnmìngshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He had significant administrative achievements,
and was praised by the people of Lǐngbiǎo.
He died in the seventeenth year of Tàiyuán.
Ānguó, courtesy name Ānguó,
was more than thirty years younger than his elder brothers.
All his cousins and elder brothers lacked talent and fame,
establishing themselves through wealth and power.
Only Ānguó and Wāng from a young age upheld the principles of austerity and poverty.
Just as Wāng was known for his uprightness and frankness,
Ānguó was distinguished by his scholarly simplicity.
During the reign of Xiàowǔ Dì, he received much respectful treatment,
serving successively as Shìzhōng and Tàicháng.
When the Emperor passed away,
Ānguó appeared thin and emaciated,
wore mourning clothes,
and wept all day.
Those who saw him believed it to be true filial piety.
He twice served as Kuàijī Nèishǐ and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
During Ān Dì's Lóng'ān reign, an edict stated:
“Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Kǒng Ānguó is steadfast, cautious, pure, and upright,
his reputation spreads whether in or out of office.
He may hold his current office concurrently as the tutor to the King of Dōnghǎi,
and will surely be able to guide him as a bridge and ferry,
to dwell in benevolence and roam in the arts.”
Later, he successively held the posts of Shàngshū Zuǒ Yòu Púshè.
He died in the fourth year of Yìxī,
and was posthumously granted Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Zhī, courtesy name Chéngzǔ.
The Grand Administrator, Zhōu Zhá, appointed him Gōngcáo Shǐ.
When Zhá was killed by Shěn Chōng,
his former associates and officials dared not approach him.
Zhī, braving the blades, wailed and cried,
personally carried out the funeral rites,
and escorted the coffin back to Yìxīng.
People at the time admired his righteousness.
Tǎn, courtesy name Jūnpíng.
His grandfather, Chōng,
was Dānyáng Tàishǒu.
His father, Kǎn,
was Dàsīnóng.
Tǎn was straightforward and upright in his youth,
with a refined reputation.
He was well-versed in the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn
and skilled in literary composition.
When Yuán Dì was King of Jìn,
he appointed Tǎn as Shìzǐ Wénxué.
When the Eastern Palace was established,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and then promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
At that time, new officials in the central administration
were all given a policy test.
The Emperor personally wrote a question:
“Xú Fù of Wúxīng became a rebel,
killing the commandery governor.
Should the commandery now recommend Xiaolián or not?”
Tǎn replied:
“The four crimes are not mutually inclusive.
Gǔn was executed, but Yǔ arose.
Xú Fù's rebellion,
how does it hinder the worthy of a commandery?”
He then asked:
“Corrupt ministers and treacherous sons assassinate their rulers,
destroying palaces and flooding residences—
there is no greater evil.
The old practice of abolishing the selection of the four categories for a xiāng
—what should be relied upon now?”
Tǎn said:
“Jì Píngzǐ drove out Lǔ Zhāogōng,
how can that be a reason to abolish Kǒng Ní?”
Ultimately, he could not be swayed.
When Jùn was pacified,
Tǎn was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Wú County.
He himself stated that Wú was full of talented and prominent figures,
and Tǎn was young,
thus not suitable to oversee it.
Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng both wanted to appoint Tǎn as the Administrator of Dānyáng.
At that time, after a period of chaos and separation,
the common people were desolate and suffering,
so Tǎn firmly declined.
Dǎo and others still did not agree.
Tǎn said with indignation:
"When Sùzǔ was on his deathbed,
all of you personally sat by the imperial couch,
and jointly received his dying edict.
Kǒng Tǎn, being of humble birth,
was not among those entrusted with the deathbed instructions.
Now that there are difficulties,
you put this humble subject forward first.
Today, I am like meat on a chopping board,
to be sliced and diced by others!"
Then he shook out his sleeves and left.
Dǎo and others also ceased their efforts.
Thereupon, he was promoted to Internal Historian of Wúxīng,
enfeoffed as the Baron of Jìnlíng,
and additionally appointed as General Jiànwēi.
As it was a year of famine,
he transported his family's rice to relieve the poor,
and the common people relied on him.
At that time, Tǎn was tasked with recruiting vagrants from the Jiāng and Huái regions for the army.
There were palace guards [Diànzhōng bīng] who,
due to the chaos, had returned eastward,
and came to respond to Tǎn's recruitment.
Tǎn was unaware and accepted them.
Someone then insinuated to the imperial court
that Tǎn was harboring rebellious palace troops,
and he was subsequently dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was appointed as Grandee Remonstrant [Shìzhōng].
In the first year of Xiánkāng,
Shí Cōng raided Lìyáng.
Wáng Dǎo, as Grand Marshal [Dà Sīmǎ],
was ordered to suppress him,
and requested Tǎn to serve as his Marshal [Sīmǎ].
It so happened that Shí Lè had recently died,
and Jìlóng was acting capriciously.
Shí Cōng and Péng Biāo, the Grand Administrator of Qiáo Commandery, among others, each sent envoys to surrender.
Tǎn wrote to Cōng, saying: "The Huá and Dí have different paths,
and the north and south are vastly separated.
Looking towards the Yellow River and longing for Sòng,
I always feel a sense of hunger and thirst.
Repeatedly encountering the Yang Jiu disaster,
Heaven brought calamity upon the Jìn state.
Treacherous villains corrupted Huáxià,
taking advantage of the opportunity
to act tyrannically.
Although our virtue has declined,
Heaven's mandate has not changed.
The auspicious omens foretell the joy of a second gathering,
and the restoration corresponds to the meeting of a spiritual epoch.
The hardship of the 'hundred six' has passed,
and the beauty of renewal
grows daily.
Yet the divine land [Shénzhōu] is in turmoil,
and the remaining populace scattered like waves,
swearing allegiance to the hands of barbarians,
cowering in the dens of jackals and wolves.
The imperial court often sighs endlessly in slumber,
grieving and distressed.
Heaven's punishment has arrived,
the wicked are falling.
Before the imperial army has even arrived,
they are devouring each other.
Is this not the resentment of men and the wrath of gods,
Heaven sending down its disaster?
The burning of both orchids [lán] and mugwort [ài]
is lamented by both wise and foolish.
Pity rather than rejoice;
such is the benevolence of our sovereign.
A grand and vast amnesty has been proclaimed,
and only Jìlóng is to be punished.
The envoy from Péngqiáo arrived,
roughly outlining the situation,
and I learned that the general
is indignant at the vile sort,
and has decisively joined our cause.
Upon hearing this, I am filled with joy and delight,
rejoicing as if it were my own success.
How prescient is your insight,
how easily enlightened
you are to the truth!
We crane our necks, awaiting your arrival,
yet strangely there is no news.
General, you come from a distinguished clan,
born into a great lineage.
Having encountered an age of many troubles,
with your state overthrown and family ruined,
separated from kin in life,
and fostered by a different species.
Though coerced into
false
favor,
what reliance can there truly be?
Even those who hear of it are sometimes saddened,
how much more so for one who experiences it personally—
can one not be indignant?
Those who are not of our kind
must have different hearts.
Indeed, this is the autumn
for turning away from their kind and returning to righteousness,
the day to plan for justice and establish meritorious deeds.
If the general accepts my words,
and proclaims them to your allies,
leading the forces from Guānyòu,
assisting the troops
from Hénán,
displaying your might in Zhào and Wèi,
acting as a vanguard for the state—
even Dòu Róng protecting Xīhé,
or Qíng Bù abandoning Xiàng Yǔ,
compared to these ancient and modern examples,
would not be sufficient metaphors.
His Majesty [Shèngshàng] is
generous and enlightened,
his prime ministers [Zǎifǔ] are broad-minded.
Even for the slight of shooting a hook,
rewards were still bestowed;
for the resentment of Yōng Chǐ,
he was ennobled and granted a state.
How much more so for you, gentlemen, who have no past grievances,
and encounter an opportune moment revealed by Heaven.
You should act as swiftly as a shadow following a form.
Why hesitate?
Now the six armies are strictly prepared,
advancing both by water and land.
Bears and tigers leap forth,
eager to bite and tear.
Once blades clash,
jade and stone will shatter together.
Even if you regret it afterwards,
what
good will lamentation do?
I, though untalented,
have for generations enjoyed imperial favor.
Though truly not sagacious,
I am sincerely the host for envoys.
My humble feelings
are conveyed in the messenger's letter.
Indeed, if a crucial opportunity
is not seized first,
one rarely avoids regret later.
Seek your own good fortune;
it is up to the general to decide."
The imperial court subsequently did not proceed with the northern expedition,
and everyone harbored resentment.
Tǎn served in his position for several years,
then was promoted to Grandee Remonstrant [Shìzhōng].
At that time, Emperor Chéng often visited the residence of Chancellor Wáng Dǎo,
bowing to Dǎo's wife, Madame Cáo,
as if she were a family member.
Tǎn frequently offered urgent remonstrances.
When the Emperor set a date for accepting his empress,
the Left Chief of the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè], Wáng Bīn, died.
Some suggested postponing the date.
Tǎn said:
"The solemnity of a wedding
is more important than saving a solar eclipse.
To save a solar eclipse,
if there is a mourning for an empress,
or if the crown prince falls into a well,
then it is stopped.
How can the grand ceremony of accepting an empress
be postponed due to a minister's death?"
They followed his advice.
When the Emperor came of age [jiā yuánfú],
he still delegated governance to Wáng Dǎo.
Tǎn often felt indignant,
taking the affairs of state as his own concern.
He once spoke to the Emperor at leisure, saying:
"Your Majesty's age is increasing,
and your sagely reverence grows daily.
You should broadly consult with court officials,
and inquire about good governance."
Because of this, he offended Dǎo,
and was sent out as Minister of Justice [Tíngwèi].
Feeling discontent,
he resigned due to illness.
He was given the additional title of Palace Aide to the Emperor [Sànqí Chángshì],
and promoted to Minister [Shàngshū],
but had not yet been formally appointed.
When his illness was severe,
Yǔ Bīng [庾冰] visited him [Tǎn],
and wept.
Tǎn [坦] said cheerfully:
"A great man, at the point of death, should be asked about methods to stabilize the country and pacify the family,
not be questioned like a child or a woman!"
Yǔ Bīng [庾冰] deeply apologized.
Before his death,
he wrote a letter to Yǔ Liàng [庾亮], saying:
"I did not expect the suffering of this illness
to become so debilitating;
I examine myself, frail and fading,
and suddenly there are no more days left.
Long or short, life is fate;
what is there to mourn?
But with my body gone and my name forgotten,
the emperor's kindness unrequited,
my ambitions unfulfilled—
that is the greatest regret of my life!
You, in the esteemed position of a maternal uncle,
hold the weighty responsibility of a regional governor,
wielding formidable power with every glance,
your fame shaking the world.
As a supporting beam and rafter,
I always wished to be beneath your influence.
To bring order to the nine regions,
to unify the four seas,
to erect a 'Jīngguān' [京觀] monument in the Central Plains,
to restore the 'Zǐjí' [紫極] (the imperial court) to the glorious land—
these were my long-cherished aspirations,
the true sincerity of my passionate spirit.
Now to die midway—
is this not regrettable!
If the dead have spirits,
I shall secretly listen to your magnificent deeds."
Soon after, he died,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted the title of Guānglùxūn [光祿勳],
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn [簡].
Yǔ Liàng [庾亮] replied in a letter, saying:
"Chief Justice Kǒng Jūn [孔君] has had his spirit depart from his body—
alas, how sorrowful!
I received your letter of the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
knowing your illness had worsened,
and that you would not recover.
My grief and sorrow are so deep
I cannot bear them.
You were just in your prime,
and had always been free of serious illness.
Though Heaven's decree is immutable,
this calamity was also unforeseen.
Moreover, your talent was recognized by the world,
and the world always needs talent.
How much more so in these present times
do I doubly mourn and cherish you!
I, being inadequate,
have unworthily assumed a great responsibility.
With national shame unavenged,
I am agitated day and night.
I always wished for you to be with me in the outer provinces,
to exert our strength together in current affairs.
This wish was unfulfilled,
and then your letter suddenly arrived.
Rereading it again and again,
I cannot help but shed tears.
I deeply understand your passionate aspirations,
and deeply grieve that your ambitions were not realized.
Separated eternally and distantly,
what more can I say!
I respectfully send this reply,
and also offer a small sacrifice,
hoping your spirit will descend to partake of it."
His son Hùn [混] succeeded him.
Yán [嚴], courtesy name Péngzǔ [彭祖].
His grandfather, Yì [奕],
was the Prefect of Quánjiāo [全椒].
He was remarkably astute.
Once, someone brought him wine as a gift.
As the person began to enter the gate carrying it,
Yì [奕] called out from afar, saying:
"Someone has sent me two jars of wine;
why is one of them not wine?"
When examined,
one jar was indeed water.
Someone asked Yì [奕] how he knew,
and he smiled, saying:
"Wine is heavy, water is light;
the bearer's hands felt different in weight, that's all."
He governed with benevolence and influence,
and when he died,
the people of the market mourned as if they had lost a kind parent.
His father, Lún [倫],
was a Huángménláng [黃門郎].
Yán [嚴], while young, served in the provincial and commandery administrations,
and successively held the positions of Sītú Yuàn [司徒掾] and Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng [尚書殿中郎].
When Yīn Hào [殷浩] took charge of Yángzhōu [揚州],
he invited Yán [嚴] to be his Biéjià [別駕].
Later, he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng [尚書左丞].
At that time, the court highly regarded Yīn Hào [殷浩]
to contend with Huán Wēn [桓溫],
which Huán Wēn [桓溫] deeply resented.
Yīn Hào [殷浩] also welcomed those from desolate areas,
planning to achieve meritorious deeds beyond the borders.
Yán [嚴] said to Yīn Hào [殷浩]:
"Currently, the times are difficult;
it can be called a 'Bǎilù Zhīyùn' [百六之運] (a period of great calamity).
You, Sir, have humbled yourself to respond to the exigencies,
happening to be at this juncture.
The imperial heart, therefore, works tirelessly from dawn till dusk,
meticulous in court,
always wishing to deeply entrench and strengthen the foundation,
to pacify the borders and tranquilize the nation—
how could it be for personal gain?
Yet those holding office have different aspirations,
and varying perspectives.
People's opinions are diverse and ceaseless,
reaching everywhere.
Lately, the state of Heaven and human sentiment
is truly disheartening.
The ancients, in governing,
guarded against people's words more strictly than against a river.
The other day, when attending you,
I already broadly expressed my thoughts;
I wonder how you intend to suppress all this?
Lǎozǐ [老子] said, 'Only by not contending
can one be beyond contention from all things.'
These words must not be overlooked.
My humble opinion is that the court should more clearly define the methods of appointing officials:
Hán [韓] and Péng [彭] can specialize in military campaigns,
Xiāo [蕭] and Cáo [曹] can guard the seals and keys,
so that internal and external responsibilities
each have their designated officials.
Deeply consider the ways of 'lián lìn qū shēn' [廉藺屈申] (Lian Po and Lin Xiangru's flexibility)
and the principles of 'píng bó xiāng hé' [平勃相和] (Zhou Bo and Chen Ping's cooperation),
to ensure harmony and smooth operation,
with no dissenting voices among people.
Only then can one safeguard greatness, establish achievements,
and bring peace to all under Heaven.
Furthermore, observing the recent influx of defectors,
they all have human faces but beastly hearts,
greedy and without loyalty,
difficult to move by righteousness.
Yet they gather in the capital,
mingling among the people.
You, Sir, constantly exhaust your sacred body to receive them,
and empty the state's coffers to aid them,
which is sufficient to cause doubt and confusion among observers."
Yīn Hào [殷浩] deeply accepted his advice.
When Emperor Āi [哀帝] ascended the throne,
the succession line was debated,
and there were many differing opinions.
Yán [嚴] and Dānyáng Yǐn [丹楊尹] Yǔ Hé [庾龢] argued:
"Following the established order and maintaining righteousness, family ties cannot be ignored.
It is proper to succeed Emperor Chéng [成皇帝]."
All the scholars agreed that Yán's [嚴] argument was superior,
and it was ultimately adopted.
In the first year of Lónghé [隆和] (362 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"The celestial phenomena are out of order.
Although the Grand Astrologer has performed rituals to avert disaster,
inauspicious signs frequently appear.
Now, according to the system of 'Hóngsì' [鴻祀] (Grand Sacrifice),
I intend to personally perform solemn rites in front of the Tàijí Diàn [太極殿] (Hall of Supreme Ultimate)."
Yán [嚴] remonstrated, saying:
"Although the 'Hóngsì' [鴻祀] ritual comes from the 'Shàngshū Dàzhuàn' [尚書大傳] (Great Commentary on the Book of Documents),
it was not thoroughly investigated by former Confucians,
and no dynasty in history has ever performed it.
How can one engage in an uncertain ritual to connect with Heaven and spirits?
Heaven's way has no favorites;
it only assists the virtuous.
If Your Majesty respects and reveres,
and dedicates your heart to the myriad common people,
you can dispel disasters and rectify anomalies.
You have already practiced and acted on all these;
your virtue accords with the divine,
and prayers have long been answered.
Why then should you lower the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
and perform such miscellaneous sacrifices?
The actions of the ruler are always recorded;
should one not be cautious?"
The emperor commended him and ceased the plan.
He was appointed Yángzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng [揚州大中正],
but Yán [嚴] did not accept the post.
The relevant authorities impeached him for refusal,
but an imperial edict specifically allowed him to hold the title of Marquis while leading the Shàngshū [尚書] (Secretariat).
At that time, Dōnghǎi Wáng Yì sought to obtain Hǎiyán and Qiántáng to use water buffalo to pull dikes and levy taxes for money.
The Emperor initially agreed to it,
but Yán Jiàn’s stern remonstrance stopped it.
Initially,
the Emperor sometimes bestowed private favors,
giving money and silk to his attendants.
Yán again memorialized that all such separate gifts and provisions for meals
should be reduced and cut.
The Emperor said,
"Many of my attendants are in distress,
which is why I give them gifts.
Now, all such allowances shall be stopped.
Furthermore, kitchen provisions should also be reduced and cut.
I will carefully consider this and expect a detailed report."
Yán provided much guidance and benefit.
During the Tàihé reign,
he was appointed Tàishǒu of Wúxīng,
with an added rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí.
He was skilled in governance and administration,
and greatly enjoyed the support of the people.
A woman from Yúháng, due to a prolonged famine,
sold her child to save her husband's nephew.
In Wǔkāng, there were two brothers.
Their wives were both pregnant.
The younger brother had traveled far and not yet returned.
They encountered a famine year
and could not save both,
so they abandoned their own child to save the younger brother's child.
Yán commended and recommended both cases.
He also selected and rewarded talented individuals,
which commentators praised.
In the fifth year,
he left office due to illness
and died at home.
He had three sons: Dàomín,
who was the Nèishǐ of Xuānchéng;
Jìngmín,
who was a Sànqí Shìláng;
and Fúmín,
who was Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
All were harmed by Sūn Ēn.
Qún, courtesy name Jìnglín,
was Yán’s paternal uncle.
He possessed wisdom and broad-mindedness,
and his aspirations were untrammeled.
When Sū Jùn entered Shítou,
Kūang Shù was favored by Jùn at the time,
and his retinue was very grand.
Qún and his cousin Yú were traveling together at Héngtáng,
when they met him.
Yú stopped to speak with him,
but Qún did not even look at Shù.
Shù became angry
and wanted to kill him with a blade.
Yú dismounted and embraced Shù, saying,
"My brother is having a fit of madness,
please pardon him for my sake."
Thus, he escaped harm.
Later, when Jùn was pacified,
Wáng Dǎo saved Shù.
Once, during a gathering,
Dǎo ordered Shù to offer Qún wine
to release the resentment from Héngtáng.
Qún replied,
"I am not Kǒngzǐ,
but my distress is like that of the people of Kuāng.
Although the vernal warmth spreads its vital energy,
and the hawk transforms into a dove,
those who discern
still detest its eyes."
Dǎo showed a look of shame.
He served successively as Zhōngchéng.
He was fond of alcohol.
Dǎo once warned him, saying,
"When you drink,
do you not see the cloth covering the wine jars at the tavern,
how it rots away after days and months?"
He replied,
"Do you not see how meat soaked in dregs can last even longer?"
He once wrote to a friend, saying,
"This year, my fields yielded seven hundred shí of glutinous rice,
which is not enough for my yeast-making business."
Such was his indulgence.
He died in office.
His heir was Shěn.
Shěn, courtesy name Déduó,
had a good reputation.
Hé Chōng recommended Shěn to Wáng Dǎo, saying,
"His literary thought is clear and perceptive;
he should enter the ministerial gate."
He was invited to serve as Céngxiàng Sītú Yuàn and Lángxié Wáng Wénxué,
but he did not accept either.
His cousin Tǎn gave him a fur coat,
but he refused to accept it.
Tǎn said,
"Yàn Píngzhòng was frugal;
when sacrificing to his ancestors,
a pig's shoulder would not fill the ritual vessel,
yet he wore the same fox fur coat for decades.
What reason do you have to refuse?"
Thereupon, he accepted and wore it.
At this time, Shěn, Wèi Kǎi, Yú Qiú, Yú Cún, and Xiè Fèng were collectively known as the talents of the four clans.
Shěn's son was Xīn,
whose highest office was Wúxīng Tàishǒu and Tíngwèi.
Xīn's son Línzhī
was famous for his cursive script,
and also served as Wúxīng Tàishǒu and Shìzhōng.
Dīng Tán (Zhāng Mào)
Dīng Tán, courtesy name Shìkāng,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His grandfather, Gù,
was Wú Sītú.
His father, Mí,
was the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
Tán initially served as a Gōngcáo of the commandery,
was assessed as Xiaòlián,
appointed Lángzhōng,
and gradually promoted to Céngxiàng Xīgé Jìjiǔ.
At that time, Yuán Dì acted as regent,
and ordered everyone to present their views on the advantages and disadvantages of current affairs.
Tán submitted a memorial saying: "For a state, relying on people requires talent,
and this refers to the Èrqiānshí long officials.
How can one not clearly select their talents
to ensure they are truly suitable?
Once the right people are obtained,
they should be kept in their positions for a long time,
so that those in office do not act carelessly,
and those below have dedication.
This is the essence of governance.
As for the current long officials,
their transfers are frequent,
and there are
expenses for sending off and welcoming.
The ancients evaluated performance every three years,
and promoted or demoted after three evaluations.
Even mediocre talents, when given a stable position,
can hardly achieve success quickly.
As for the military, it is for defense against unforeseen events
and suppressing villains and criminals.
Even though Zhōu had three sages,
its achievements were due to military might.
In this era of warfare,
even more attention should be paid.
Select
elite and sharp forces
to guard against the unexpected.
When there is no business, allow them to rest;
when there is difficulty, demand their strength.
I secretly hear that the current soldiers
are sometimes privately employed,
and the camps
are not adequately staffed.
For a state, it is like managing a household.
Calculate what financial resources can bear,
carefully consider actions of advance and retreat,
do not strive for difficult-to-achieve accomplishments,
and abandon
superfluous
tasks.
Currently, our soldiers are not strong.
We should carefully consider what is appropriate.
Long-distance expeditions
have not yet yielded great victories,
but instead exhaust our strength and resources, and diminish our prestige and power."
When the emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi, Fèng Cháoqǐng, and Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
At that time, Lángxié Wáng Póu had just been enfeoffed.
The emperor wished to draw upon court worthies to serve as the highest ministers of his state,
intending to use Tán.
He consulted Zhōngshū Lìng Hè Xún.
Xún said,
"The position of Lángzhōng Lìng is prestigious and weighty;
it truly requires careful appointment.
Tán is pure, sincere, and upright,
possessing a quiet rectitude.
He has been chosen by the sagacious emperor,
and his talent truly suits the position."
Thus, he became Lángxié Wáng Lángzhōng Lìng.
Coincidentally, Póu died.
Tán submitted a memorial requesting to observe the full mourning rites,
saying:
"Regarding the principle of 'in three generations' (meaning, a limited period),
rites have established regulations.
In recent times,
these have sometimes been reduced or lowered to suit the occasion.
It is fitting that they be rectified
to strengthen the practice for later generations.
I hereby examine the imperial decree:
for the mourning of kings and marquises,
officials wear sackcloth,
which is removed after burial.
Now, the state has no successor,
and the mourning court has no master.
I am truly lowly and insignificant,
unworthy of such a weighty responsibility,
yet I mistakenly bear the primary appointment.
According to ritual, I should observe full mourning."
The imperial edict ordered a broad discussion.
Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Dù Yí deliberated, saying:
"In ancient times, during 'mourning in the dark,'
one did not speak for three years.
Later, in the Zhōu era,
taxes were diminished and allegiance was pledged.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords removed their mourning attire after burial.
This is what is meant by the 'gains and losses of the Three Dynasties,'
where rituals differed.
Hence, the three-year mourning period
was abolished because of this.
Therefore, the edict of Hàn Wén Dì
was in accord with adapting to the times.
All those with states
should likewise follow this,
not only applying to emperors.
According to the Rites,
mourning for those who died young or had no heir
was reduced compared to adults.
If there was an heir,
mourning was removed after burial.
Now, one cannot, due to the absence of an heir, be exempt from removal.
I humbly believe that Dīng Lángzhōng should remove his sackcloth and hemp,
and properly preside over the sacrifices
to complete the three years."
Tàicháng Hè Xún deliberated, saying:
"In the Rites,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords both govern people with supreme honor.
The principles of high and low,
and the rituals between ruler and minister,
have been uniform
since ancient times.
Therefore, when rites are elaborate, their solemnity is fully preserved;
when rites are reduced, they follow the reduction.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords did not observe three years of mourning.
As for a minister observing mourning for his ruler,
it should also be regulated by the ruler's practice.
There has never been a case where the ruler removes mourning but the minister observes it,
or the ruler observes it but the minister removes it.
Now, the laws and decrees state that
the ministers, chancellors, and officials of feudal lords wear sackcloth for their ruler,
and remove it after burial.
From the words of the decree,
it is clear that feudal lords are not subject to the three-year mourning period like the Son of Heaven.
If the ruler were to continue observing mourning,
then no minister or son, regardless of rank, should remove it.
If all are to remove it,
there is no text specifying one person alone should bear greater solemnity.
Ritual provides for a substitute principal mourner but not for a substitute in solemnity.
Hence, if a close relative of 'great mourning' (dàgōng) becomes the principal mourner,
they must offer two further sacrifices for the 'period of training' (liàn) and 'auspicious' (xiáng) rites,
wearing the 'great mourning' attire,
which is for the three-year mourning of the principal mourner.
If it is argued that feudal lords follow the same system as the Son of Heaven,
then if the state has a successor king,
he himself does not observe full mourning.
Yet, if the ruler observes mourning,
he wears plain clothes and presides over sacrifices,
and does not undertake auspicious affairs for three years,
to honor the imperial system.
If we are to trace back to the Three Dynasties
and restore old customs,
not following the current laws,
then the mourning attire of marquises, both noble and humble, should be uniform,
and it cannot be discussed for one person alone."
Thereupon, an imperial edict commanded him to remove his mourning attire,
but observe three years of heart-mourning.
In the third year of Tàixīng,
he was moved to become Wáng Dǎo's Piàojì Sīmǎ,
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng,
and sent out as Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
He was praised for his integrity.
He was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishùai,
but did not accept the appointment.
When Chéng Dì ascended the throne,
he was made Sànqí Chángshì and Shìzhōng.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
the emperor was displaced to Shítou.
Only Tán and Shìzhōng Zhōng Yǎ, Liú Chāo, and others followed closely by the emperor's side.
After Jùn was executed,
he was granted the title Yǒng'ān Bó for his merit,
promoted to Dà Shàngshū,
transferred to Tíngwèi,
and successively promoted to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, concurrently Lǐng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, Běnguó Dà Zhōngzhèng,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì.
When Kāng Dì ascended the throne,
he repeatedly memorialized to request to retire due to old age.
An imperial edict ordered him to return to his residence as Guānglù Dàfū,
horses were allowed to pass through his gate,
his salary and rank remained as before,
he was provided with two imperial decree bearers,
and granted 200,000 cash,
a bed, canopy, mattress, and mat.
He died
at the age of eighty.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng,
Dàfū as before,
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn.
Wáng Dǎo once said that Kǒng Jìngkāng had the talent of a duke but lacked the reputation of a duke,
while Dīng Shìkāng had the reputation of a duke but lacked the talent of a duke.
His son, Huà,
rose to the position of Sànqí Shìláng.
Zhāng Mào, courtesy name Wěikāng,
was poor and humble in his youth,
but had aspirations and good conduct,
and was respected and trusted by his鄉lǐ.
Initially, he raised an army
to suppress the rebel Chén Bīn,
and saved the entire prefecture.
Yuán Dì appointed him as a Yuánshǔ.
The government had dozens of old oxen
that were about to be sold.
Mào said:
"Slaughtering oxen is prohibited.
Those who buy them are not allowed to slaughter them.
Their teeth and strength are old and tired,
and they are no longer fit for plowing or pulling carts.
Thus, they are useless and only serve to profit the common people."
The emperor then stopped the sale.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishùai,
then sent out to serve as Wúxīng Nèishǐ.
When Shěn Chōng rebelled,
Mào and his three sons were all killed.
Mào's younger brother, Àng,
was a general under Zhōu Zhá.
When Chōng attacked Zhá,
Àng also died.
Mào was posthumously granted Tàipú.
When Mào was young, he dreamt of obtaining a large elephant.
He asked Wàn Tuī, a dream interpreter.
Tuī said:
"You will govern a large prefecture,
but it will not end well."
He asked why.
Tuī said:
"An elephant is a large beast,
and 'beast' (shòu) sounds like 'guard' (shǒu).
Therefore, I know you will obtain a large prefecture.
However, elephants are burned for their tusks (teeth),
meaning you will be harmed by others."
It turned out as he said.
Táo Huí
Táo Huí
was from Dānyáng.
His grandfather, Jī,
was the Wú Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
His father, Kàng,
was Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
Huí was summoned by the Sīkōng Fǔzhōngjūn and Zhǔbù,
but did not accept either.
Dà Jiāngjūn Wáng Dūn appointed him as Cānjūn,
then transferred him to Zhōu Biéjià.
After Dūn died,
Sītú Wáng Dǎo appointed him as Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
then promoted him to Sīmǎ.
During the campaign against Sū Jùn,
Táo Huí and Kǒng Tǎn spoke to Wáng Dǎo,
requesting that troops be dispatched early to guard the mouth of the Jiāng River.
Their words are recorded in Tǎn's biography.
When Jùn was about to arrive,
Táo Huí again said to Yú Liàng:
"Jùn knows that Shítóu has a strong garrison
and will not dare to descend directly.
He will certainly come on foot via the southern road of Xiǎodānyáng.
We should lie in ambush to intercept him;
he can be captured in a single battle."
Yú Liàng did not follow this advice.
Jùn indeed passed through Xiǎodānyáng, then through Mòlíng,
lost his way,
encountered a local man,
and seized him to be a guide.
At that time, Jùn was traveling by night,
with very little order.
When Yú Liàng heard this,
he deeply regretted not having followed Táo Huí and the others' advice.
Soon after, when the imperial army suffered a defeat,
Táo Huí returned to his home county,
gathered a volunteer army,
obtaining over a thousand men,
all infantry.
He joined forces with Táo Kǎn and Wēn Jiào to attack Sū Jùn.
He also separately defeated Hán Huǎng,
and for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Kānglè.
At this time, major bandits had just been pacified,
and the governmental framework was slack and neglected.
The Sītú, Wáng Dǎo, seeing Táo Huí's ability and talent,
promoted him to Běijūn Zhōnghóu,
and soon after, he was transferred to Zhōnghùjūn.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
At that time, people were suffering from hunger and grain was expensive,
especially in the Sānwú region.
An imperial edict intended to permit mutual sale and purchase
to alleviate the immediate crisis.
Táo Huí submitted a memorial, stating:
"Currently, the whole world is not universally barren and scarce;
only in the eastern lands are grain prices particularly high.
If mutual sale and purchase are permitted,
the news will certainly spread far.
When the northern bandits hear of it,
they will perhaps spy on our borders.
In your foolish servant's opinion,
it would be better to open the granaries to provide relief."
Therefore, without waiting for a reply,
he immediately opened the granaries,
and also allocated tens of thousands of hu of rice from the treasury and military provisions to relieve the destitute,
whereby the entire region was saved.
Afterward, an imperial edict was issued,
also ordering Kuàijī and Wújùn to follow Táo Huí's example in providing relief;
