the two commanderies benefited from this.
After four years in the commandery,
he was summoned to be appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
while his title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn remained as before.
Táo Huí's character was refined and upright;
he did not fear the powerful.
Huán Jǐng, the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, fawned upon Wáng Dǎo,
and was greatly favored by Dǎo.
Táo Huí often spoke indignantly, saying that Jǐng was not an upright person
and should not be intimately associated with.
It happened that the planet Yínghuò remained in Nándǒu for several days.
Wáng Dǎo said to Táo Huí:
"Nándǒu is
the celestial division of Yángzhōu,
and Yínghuò remaining there means
I should resign my position to avert this calamity."
Táo Huí replied:
"You, Sir, with your illustrious virtue, act as Prime Minister,
assisting the sagacious ruler.
You should be close to the loyal and upright,
and keep away from the wicked and fawning.
Yet you associate intimately with Huán Jǐng;
how can Yínghuò withdraw then!"
Wáng Dǎo was deeply ashamed.
In the second year of Xiánhé (327 CE),
he resigned due to illness,
but the emperor did not permit it.
He was transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
with Chángshì and Lǐngjūn titles remaining as before.
Before he could be formally installed,
he died,
aged fifty-one.
His posthumous name was Wēi.
He had four sons: Wāng, Lòu, Yǐn, and Wújì.
Wāng inherited the peerage,
reaching the position of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
Lòu was Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
Yǐn was Shàofǔ.
Wújì was Guānglùxūn.
All the brothers were capable and useful.
The official historian comments: Kǒng Yú and his son, along with Dīng Tán and others,
all possessed talents like bamboo
and seized the opportunity of founding a new dynasty.
They enrolled their names in the hegemon's administration,
galloped their steeds on the high roads,
were tested through various official ranks,
and thus ascended to prominent positions.
Externally, they publicized their administrative achievements;
internally, they exhausted their strategic wisdom.
They fully devoted their hearts and strength to assist their era,
and exerted their utmost to protect their lord.
They were all able to preserve their reputations and integrity,
making a good start and a good end.
Among them, Kǒng Yú nobly declined wealth worth millions
and refused a grand residence,
embodying the principle of knowing when to stop
and possessing the virtue of humility and yielding.
Táo Huí explained that the wicked and fawning should be kept away
and clarified that mutual sale and purchase were inappropriate.
Both corrected deficiencies and rectified errors,
which is truly commendable.
The encomium says: Kǒng Yú possessed public talent;
Dīng Tán, public prestige.
The Lǐngjūn was refined and elegant;
Píngyuè, loyal and bright.
Jūn Píng estimated the enemy;
Péngzǔ brought great benefits.
Mào was like an elephant on fire;
Qún rectified difficulties.
Táo Huí criticized faults;
his words were like metal and stone.
Correction Notes
Biographies, Chapter 49: Xiè Shàng
Xiè Shàng, courtesy name Rénzǔ,
was the son of Kūn, Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
As a child, he possessed utmost filial piety.
At the age of seven, he lost his elder brother,
and his grief exceeded the proper rites,
which surprised his relatives.
At eight,
he had extraordinary understanding and precocious maturity.
Kūn once took him to see off guests.
Someone said:
"This child is the Yán Huí of the gathering."
Shàng immediately replied:
"If there is no Nífù in the gathering,
how can one distinguish Yán Huí!"
All the guests present marveled at him.
When he was a little over ten years old,
he suffered the loss of his father.
Wēn Jiào, Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, came to condole him.
Shàng wept bitterly with extreme sorrow.
Then, wiping away his tears, he recounted things,
and his demeanor was unusual for a child,
which Wēn Jiào found very remarkable.
When he grew up,
he was open-minded, intelligent, and outstanding,
disregarding minor conduct
and not engaging in common affairs.
He liked to wear embroidered trousers.
His paternal uncles reprimanded him,
and he consequently changed himself,
thus becoming famous.
He was skilled in music
and broadly versed in many arts.
The Sītú, Wáng Dǎo, greatly appreciated him,
comparing him to Wáng Róng,
and often called him
"Little Ānfēng."
He was appointed as an aide.
He inherited his father's peerage, Marquis of Xiántíng.
When he first arrived at the office to pay his respects,
Wáng Dǎo, seeing that he had a superior gathering,
said:
"I heard you can perform the mynah bird dance.
Everyone here is eager to see it.
Is there such a possibility?"
Shàng replied:
"Excellent."
He then put on his cap and danced.
Wáng Dǎo ordered those present to clap their hands and beat time.
Shàng bowed and swayed in the middle,
as if no one else was present;
such was his straightforwardness and naturalness.
He was transferred to the General Affairs Office (Xīcáo) staff.
At that time, there were those who, due to the chaos, had been separated from their parents.
Some councilors argued that advancing in officialdom and managing state affairs,
along with marriage to continue the family line for a hundred generations,
was not objectionable on principle.
Shàng argued:
"The establishment of rites and ceremonies
all follows human sentiment and reason,
broadly facilitating and enhancing life.
If circumstances have their periods of difficulty and ease,
it is essential to decide by great righteousness.
The sin of having no heir,
which even the three thousand crimes do not surpass,
is now to be countered by marriage to continue the family line for a hundred generations,
exalting the ancestral lineage.
This certainly cannot be obstructed.
However, as for the sorrow of natural relatives separated by life,
and the pain of father and son cut off from each other,
of deep pains,
none is deeper than this.
If even a minor ailment of one's own body
can cause one to forget thought and worry,
and impair hearing and observation,
how much more so for one bearing the immense pain of a wounded heart,
and harboring the deepest sorrow and grief?
With one's mind already in disarray,
how can one manage current affairs comprehensively?
A person with a heart
would never recklessly seek glory and undeserved advancement.
Those who recklessly seek glory and undeserved advancement
are certainly not the kind of people we seek,
and merely open the door to superficiality and perpetuate the path of malpractice.
If there are those who hold firm to their aspirations in seclusion and whose hearts remain unchanged,
they should still have their integrity and conduct honored to promote good customs.
How much less should we encourage with glory and nobility
those who are enduring hardship and suffering?"
He was promoted to Companion (Yǒu) to the Prince of Kuàijī.
Later, he was appointed Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
He was sent out as General of Pacifying Martials (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lìyáng.
He was then transferred to supervise the military affairs of the three commanderies of Jiāngxià, Yìyáng, and Suí, and became Chancellor (Xiàng) of Jiāngxià.
His general title remained as before.
At that time, General of the Pacifying West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) Yǔ Yì was stationed at Wǔchāng.
Shàng frequently visited Yǔ Yì to consult on military matters.
Once, when they were shooting arrows together,
Yǔ Yì said:
"If you hit the target,
I will reward you with a military band."
Shàng immediately hit it,
and Yǔ Yì gave him his auxiliary military band.
Shàng's governance was clear and simple.
When he first arrived at his post,
the commandery office made a black cloth tent for Shàng using forty rolls of cloth.
Shàng dismantled it
and made tunics and trousers for the soldiers.
In the second year of Jiàn yuán (344 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"Previously, Shàng, due to the critical nature of military defense,
was relieved of his civilian posts
and assigned to the army.
As he is stationed in a strategic location,
his prestige should be enhanced.
He is now appointed General of the South-Central Region (Nánzhōngláng Jiāngjūn),
with his other offices remaining as before."
When Yǔ Bīng died,
he was again appointed with his original title to supervise the four commanderies of Yùzhōu and lead as Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu.

Shortly after, he was again transferred to General of the West-Central Region (Xīzhōngláng Jiāngjūn), supervising the military affairs of six commanderies of Yángzhōu, Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu, and granted imperial authority (jiǎjié),
stationed at Lìyáng.
Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) Huán Wēn wanted to campaign in the Central Plains.
He ordered Shàng to lead troops towards Shòuchūn
and promoted his title to General of the Pacifying West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn).
Earlier,
Fú Jiàn's general Zhāng Yù surrendered to Shàng.
Shàng was unable to placate and win him over.
Zhāng Yù became angry
and rebelled, holding Xǔchāng.
Shàng attacked him
but was defeated by Zhāng Yù,
and then arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
At that time, Empress Kāngxiàn was presiding over court affairs.
She was Shàng's nephew by marriage,
and specially ordered his title to be downgraded to General of Establishing Martials (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn).
Earlier,
when Shàng was setting out,
he sent General of Establishing Martials (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Púyáng, Dài Shī, to hold Fāngtóu.
Rǎn Mǐn's son, Zhì, and his great general, Jiǎng Gàn, came to surrender,
and then sent an envoy, Liú Yī, to Shàng to request aid.
Dài Shī stopped Liú Yī
and demanded the Imperial Seal.
Liú Yī returned
and informed Jiǎng Gàn.
Jiǎng Gàn believed that Shàng had already been defeated
and feared he could not rescue him,
so he hesitated and did not agree.
Dài Shī sent his staff officer (cānjūn) Hé Róng to lead a hundred brave men into Yè
to ascend the Three Terraces (Sāntái) and assist in its defense.
He tricked them, saying:
"For now, you can hand over the Seal to me.
The ferocious bandits are outside,
and the roads are blocked and difficult.
I also dare not send the Seal yet.
I will send a single envoy to report to the Emperor.
When the Emperor hears that the Seal is already in our possession,
he will know your sincerity
and will certainly send a large army to rescue you,
and also provide generous provisions."
Jiǎng Gàn then handed the Seal to Hé Róng.
Hé Róng carried the Seal and rushed back to Fāngtóu.
Shàng sent General of Manifesting Martials (Zhènnwǔ Jiāngjūn) Hú Bīn to lead three hundred cavalry to receive the Seal
and deliver it to the capital (Jīngshī).
At that time, Fú Jiàn's general Yáng Píng was garrisoning Xǔchāng.
Shàng sent troops to attack and defeat him.
He was summoned and appointed Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng),
awarded a light carriage (yáochē) and a military band,
and stationed at Shítou.
During the Yǒnghé era (345-356 CE),
he was appointed Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Púyè).
He was sent out as Supervisor of all military affairs of Jiangxi and Huáinán, General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu.
His titles of Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng) and Minister of Personnel (Púyè) remained as before.
He was stationed at Lìyáng,
and additionally appointed Supervisor of the military affairs of five commanderies in Yùzhōu and Yángzhōu.
He achieved good administrative results during his tenure.
He submitted a memorial requesting to return to court,
and consequently remained in the capital (Jīngshī),
acting as Minister of Personnel (Púyè).
Soon after, he was promoted to General of Pacifying the West (Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn),
stationed at Shòuyáng.
Shàng then gathered musicians
and commissioned stone chimes (shíqìng)
to be used for the Imperial Music (Tàiyùè).
The music of bells and chimes (zhōngshí zhī yuè) in the Jiāngbiǎo region
began with Shàng.
When Huán Wēn pacified Luòyáng in the north,
he submitted a memorial requesting Shàng to be appointed Supervisor of all military affairs of Sīzhōu.
He was about to be stationed at Luòyáng,
but due to illness, he did not go.
In the early Shēngpíng era (357 CE),
he was again promoted to Supervisor of Yù, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng four provinces.
His illness became critical.
He was summoned and appointed General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn)
and additionally Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Before he arrived,
he died in Lìyáng
at the age of fifty.

An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì), General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), and Minister with Powers Equal to the Three Excellencies (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
with the posthumous name Jiǎn.
He had no sons.
His younger cousin, Yì, used his son Kāng to inherit the title,
but he died young.
Kāng's younger brother, Jìng, again used his son Sù to succeed,
but he also had no sons.
Jìng's son, Qián, used his son Língyòu to succeed Kūn.
Xiè Ān (son Yǎn, Yǎn's son Hùn, Ān's elder brother Yì, Yì's son Xuán, Ān's younger brother Wàn, Wàn's younger brother Shí, Shí's elder brother's son Láng, Láng's nephew Miǎo)
Xiè Ān, courtesy name Ānshí,
was Shàng's younger cousin.
His father, Póu, was Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng).
When Ān was four years old,
Huán Yí of Qiáojùn saw him and sighed:
"This child has a remarkably refined spirit and penetrating intelligence.
In the future, he will be no less than Wáng Dōnghǎi."
When he was a young boy (zǒngjiǎo),
his mind was profound and astute,
his bearing was open and elegant,
and he was skilled in running script.
As a young man (ruòguàn),
he visited Wáng Méng and engaged in pure conversation for a long time.
After he left,
Wáng Méng's son, Xiū, asked:
"How was that guest compared to you, father?"
Wáng Méng replied:
"This guest was subtly profound,
he came to press upon others."
Wáng Dǎo also highly esteemed him.
From then on, he had a great reputation at a young age.
Initially, he was invited to serve in the household of the Sītú (Grand Minister over the Masses),
and was appointed Assistant in the Bureau of Authorship,
but he declined both due to illness.
He lived in Kuàijī,
and associated with Wáng Xīzhī, Xǔ Xún of Gāoyáng, and the Sāngmén Zhī Dùn.
When out, he would fish and hunt in the mountains and rivers;
when in, he would recite poetry and compose essays.
He had no ambition to engage in worldly affairs.
The Inspector of Yángzhōu, Yǔ Bīng, knowing that Ān enjoyed a great reputation,
was determined to bring him into service.
He repeatedly sent messages to the local prefectures to urge and compel Ān,
who, having no choice, answered the summons.
After a little over a month, he announced his return home.
He was again appointed Shàngshū Láng (Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat) and Lángyá Wáng Yǒu (Companion to the Prince of Lángyá),
but he did not take either office.
The Minister of Personnel, Fàn Wāng, recommended Ān to be a Lìbù Láng (Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel),
but Ān wrote a letter refusing it.
The authorities reported that Ān, having been summoned,
had not appeared for years,
and thus he was banned from public service for life.
Consequently, he idled away his time in the eastern lands.
He once visited a mountain in Lín'ān,
sat in a stone chamber,
overlooking a deep valley,
and sighed contentedly, saying:
"How far is this from Bó Yí!"
He once sailed the sea with Sūn Chuò and others.
When the wind rose and waves surged,
everyone else was terrified,
but Ān remained composed, chanting and whistling.
The boatmen, seeing Ān's delight,
continued without stopping.
When the wind grew fiercer,
Ān slowly said:
"If it continues like this, how will we return?"
The boatmen, taking his words, immediately turned back.
Everyone admired his refined demeanor.
Although Ān indulged his passions in nature,
whenever he went out to enjoy the scenery,
he always brought along female entertainers.
Having repeatedly refused official appointments,
when Emperor Jiǎnwén was prime minister,
he said:
"Since Ānshí enjoys himself with others,
he will surely have to share worries with others.
If we summon him, he will surely come."
At that time, Ān's younger brother, Wàn, was the Xī Zhōngláng Jiàng (General of the Western Gentlemen-of-the-Household),
holding a critical frontier command.
Although Ān lived in humble circumstances,
his reputation still surpassed Wàn's,
and he naturally harbored hopes of becoming a high official.
At home, he always guided his children and younger brothers with exemplary conduct.
Ān's wife,
who was Liú Tán's younger sister,
seeing her family grow wealthy and prominent,
while Ān alone remained quiet and withdrawn,
said to him:
"How can a husband not be like this (i.e., seek wealth and status)?"
Ān covered his nose and said:
"I'm afraid I cannot avoid it (i.e., taking office)."
After Wàn was dismissed and disgraced,
Ān first developed ambitions for official advancement.
By then, he was already over forty years old.
Huán Wēn, the Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West), invited him to be his Sīmǎ (Chief of Staff).
As he was about to depart for Xīntíng,
all the court officials came to bid him farewell.
The Grandee Censor Gāo Sōng jokingly said to him:
"You have repeatedly defied imperial decrees,
and dwelled in lofty seclusion on Dōngshān.
Everyone often said to each other,
'If Ānshí refuses to come out,
what will become of the common people!'
Now, what will the common people do with you!"
Ān showed considerable embarrassment.
Upon his arrival,
Huán Wēn was very pleased,
and they talked about their lives,
laughing and enjoying themselves all day.
After Ān left,
Wēn asked his attendants:
"Have you ever seen me have such a guest before?"
Later, Wēn visited Ān,
and found him having his hair dressed.
Ān was naturally slow,
and it took him a long time to finish.
He asked for his cap.
Wēn saw this and
detained him, saying:
"Let the Sīmǎ wear his hat and come in."
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
When Wēn was about to embark on a northern expedition,
Wàn unfortunately died of illness,
and Ān submitted a memorial requesting to return home.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Wúxīng.
While in office, he did not gain immediate fame,
but after his departure, he was missed by the people.
A short while later,
he was summoned to be a Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
then promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) and Zhōnghùjūn (Central Protector of the Army).
When Emperor Jiǎnwén was critically ill,
Wēn submitted a memorial recommending Ān to receive the imperial deathbed commission.
When the emperor died,
Wēn entered to attend the imperial funeral at the mausoleum,
stopping at Xīntíng.
He deployed a large military guard,
intending to usurp the Jìn dynasty.
He summoned Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī,
planning to kill them at the gathering.
Tǎnzhī was very frightened
and asked Ān for advice.
Ān's expression remained unchanged,
saying:
"The fate of the Jìn dynasty,
whether it survives or perishes, depends on this trip."
When they met Wēn,
Tǎnzhī was sweating so much his clothes were drenched,
and he held his tablet upside down.
Ān calmly took his seat,
and once settled,
said to Wēn:
"I have heard that when a feudal lord governs righteously,
his security lies with his neighbors.
Why must your Excellency place men behind the screen?"
Wēn laughed and said:
"I simply cannot help but do so."
They then conversed and laughed the entire day.
Tǎnzhī and Ān were initially equally famous,
but by this point, Tǎnzhī's inferiority was apparent.
Wēn once showed the guests at a gathering Ān's memorial on the posthumous title of Emperor Jiǎnwén,
saying:
"This is Xiè Ānshí's 'shattered gold' (i.e., brilliant fragments of wisdom)."
At that time, Emperor Xiàowǔ was young,
and the government was not in his own hands.
Wēn's power shook both within and outside the court,
and people whispered
with varying opinions.
Ān and Tǎnzhī devotedly assisted and supported the emperor,
and ultimately managed to maintain peace and harmony.
When Wēn was critically ill,
he hinted to the court to grant him the Nine Dignities,
and had Yuán Hóng draft the decree.
When Ān saw it,
he repeatedly revised it,
thus it remained unfinished for weeks.
When Wēn died,
the decree for the Nine Dignities was consequently shelved.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Púyè (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs),
concurrently holding the office of Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel),
and was given the additional title of Hòujiāngjūn (General of the Rear).
When the Grandee Secretary Wáng Tǎnzhī was sent out as Inspector of Xúzhōu,
an imperial edict commanded Ān to take overall charge of the affairs of the Central Secretariat.
Ān loyally assisted and guided the government,
and even Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ benefited from his counsel.
At that time, powerful enemies encroached upon the borders,
and reports from the frontier arrived continuously.
Liáng and Yì were lost,
Fán and Dèng fell.
Ān always maintained calm and composure,
and dealt with matters with farsighted planning.
With his virtuous governance implemented,
civil and military officials followed his commands.
He did not dwell on minor details,
but upheld broad principles.
His prestige and benevolence were evident externally,
and people all compared him to Wáng Dǎo,
saying his refinement surpassed him.
He once ascended Yěchéng with Wáng Xīzhī,
and envisioned distant thoughts contentedly,
possessing an ambition to transcend the mundane world.
Xīzhī said to him:
"Yǔ the Great toiled for the state,
his hands and feet calloused;
King Wén ate late,
having no time to spare during the day.
Now, with many forts in the four outskirts,
one should consider exerting oneself for the state,
but empty talk wastes effort,
and flowery prose obstructs important matters.
I fear this is not suitable for the present time."
Ān replied:
"Qín employed Shāng Yāng,
and perished after two generations.
Was it pure discourse that caused the calamity?"
At this time, the palace buildings were ruined,
and Ān desired to renovate them.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Biāozhī and others advised against it due to foreign invaders,
but Ān did not heed them,
and ultimately decided it himself.
The palace buildings were completed,
all modeled after the celestial phenomena,
matching the celestial pole,
yet the laborers had no complaints.
He also held the post of Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and an imperial edict granted him one hundred armored guards to enter the palace.
At this time, the Emperor began to personally manage all affairs of state.
Ān was promoted to Zhōngshū Jiān,
Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Lù Shàngshū Shì.
He firmly declined the military titles.
At that time, the celestial phenomena were out of order,
and a severe drought lasted for a year.
Ān memorialized to revive what was extinguished and continue what was broken,
seeking out and enfeoffing the descendants of meritorious officials who assisted in the founding of the Jìn dynasty.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Sītú.
All the military and civil officials of the rear army were assigned to the grand administration.
He again declined to accept it.
He was again made Shìzhōng, Dūdū of the military affairs of the five prefectures of Yáng, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Yānguó of Yōuzhōu, and Jiǎjié.
At this time, Fú Jiān was powerful,
and the borders were frequently troubled,
with generals suffering continuous defeats.
Ān dispatched his younger brother Shí and his nephew Xuán and others to campaign and suppress them as opportunities arose,
achieving victories wherever they went.
He was appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and enfeoffed as Jiànchāng Xiàn Gōng.
Fú Jiān later led his troops,
numbering a million,
and encamped at Huáiféi.
The capital was shaken with fear.
Ān was promoted to Zhēngtǎo Dà Dūdū.
Xuán entered to ask for a plan.
Ān remained calm, showing no fear,
and replied:
"There is already a separate imperial decree."
Then he fell silent.
Xuán dared not speak again,
and so ordered Zhāng Xuán to make another request.
Ān then ordered his carriage and went out to his mountain villa.
Relatives and friends all gathered.
He then played Go with Xuán in the villa.
Ān was usually inferior to Xuán,
but on this day, Xuán was fearful,
and thus became an inferior opponent and still did not win.
Ān looked at his nephew Yáng Tán and said,
"I give this villa to you."
Ān then went on excursions,
returning only at night.
He then instructed his generals and commanders,
each performing their duties.
When Xuán and the others had already defeated Fú Jiān,
a dispatch arrived.
Ān was still playing Go with guests.
After reading the letter,
he casually put it on the bed,
showing no sign of joy,
as usual.
The guest asked about it.
He slowly replied,
"My little lads have indeed defeated the bandits."
After the game concluded,
he returned inside.
Passing the threshold,
he was extremely joyful,
and unconsciously broke the heel of his clogs.
Such was his ability to conceal his emotions and maintain composure.
For his overall leadership,
he was promoted to Tàibǎo.
Ān then wished to unify the writing system and regulations.
He submitted a memorial requesting to lead the northern expedition himself,
and was thus promoted to Dūdū of the military affairs of the fifteen prefectures of Yáng, Jiāng, Jīng, Sī, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, Níng, Yì, Yōng, and Liáng.
He was granted the yellow axe,
and his original official posts remained as before.
Two Cóngshì Zhōngláng were appointed.
Ān submitted a memorial declining the Tàibǎo and the title,
but it was not permitted.
At this time, Huán Chōng had just died,
and the two prefectures of Jīng and Jiāng were both vacant.
Public opinion held that Xuán, due to his merits and prestige,
should be granted them.
Ān considered that both father and son had achieved great merits,
fearing suspicion from the imperial court.
He also feared that the Huán clan would lose their positions.
Huán Shíqián also had the merit of Miànyáng,
and he worried that if his fierce bravery
was in a strategically important location,
he might eventually be difficult to control.
So he appointed Huán Shímín as Jīngzhōu,
and moved Huán Yī to Zhōngliú,
and Shíqián as Yùzhōu.
Thus, with the three Huán clan members holding the three prefectures,
there was no resentment between them,
and each obtained their suitable posts.
His far-reaching and uncontested wisdom
was generally like this.
He had a fondness for music.
Since his younger brother Wàn's death,
he did not listen to music for ten years.
But upon reaching the highest ministerial posts,
he did not abandon music during the period of mourning for one year.
Wáng Tǎnzhī wrote to persuade him,
but he did not comply.
Officials followed his example,
and it consequently became a custom.
He also built a villa on an earthen hill,
with magnificent towers, pavilions, forests, and bamboo.
He often brought his inner and outer nephews and nieces to gather and roam there.
The food and drink often cost hundreds of gold.
The world somewhat criticized him for this,
but Ān paid no mind to it.
He often suspected that Liú Láozhī could not be solely trusted,
and also knew that Wáng Wèizhī was not suitable to govern a city independently.
Láozhī indeed met a chaotic end,
and Wèizhī also failed due to greed.
Because of this, discerning people admired his knowledge of human nature.
At that time, Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ held sole power,
and treacherous flatterers somewhat stirred up trouble.
Ān moved to govern Bùqiū in Guǎnglíng,
building a fortress called Xīnchéng to avoid them.
The Emperor saw him off at Xīchí,
offering wine and composing poetry.
Although Ān accepted the imperial commission,
his aspiration for Dōngshān remained unchanged from beginning to end,
often expressed in his words and demeanor.
When he garrisoned Xīnchéng,
he traveled with his whole family,
preparing for a voyage across the sea,
wishing to return eastward from the Jiāng River
after the overall strategy was roughly settled.
His noble ambition was not realized,
and he encountered a severe illness.
He submitted a memorial requesting to turn back his banner as appropriate,
and also summoned his son, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yǎn, to disarm and cease marching.
He ordered Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zhū Xù to advance and occupy Luòyáng,
and the vanguard Dūdū Xuán to assert his might in Péngpèi,
entrusting them with supervision.
If the two bandits were to prolong their existence,
and the waters rose next year,
they would attack simultaneously from east and west.
An imperial edict sent a Shìzhōng to convey greetings and comfort.
He then returned to the capital.
When he heard that his carriage was about to enter the Xīzhōumén,
he considered that his original ambition was unfulfilled,
and deeply lamented his failure.
He then sadly said to his close associates:
"When Huán Wēn was alive,
I often feared for my safety.
Suddenly, I dreamed I rode in Wēn's carriage for sixteen li,
and stopped upon seeing a white rooster.
Riding in Wēn's carriage means
taking his position.
Sixteen li
is exactly sixteen years until now.
A white rooster represents Yǒu,
and this year's Tàisuì is in Yǒu.
Perhaps my illness will not allow me to recover!"
He then submitted a memorial resigning his position.
The imperial edict sent a Shìzhōng and a Shàngshū to convey the Emperor's will.
Previously,
when Ān set off from Shítóu,
the gongs and drums suddenly broke.
Also, his words had never been mistaken,
but he suddenly made one error.
The crowd also found it strange.
Soon after, he passed away,
at the age of sixty-six.
The Emperor mourned for him for three days in the imperial court,
bestowed secret items from the Eastern Garden, one set of court robes, one suit of clothes, one million cash, one thousand bolts of cloth, and five hundred catties of wax.
He was posthumously granted the title Tàifù,
and his posthumous name was Wénjìng.
As there was no lower residence,
an imperial edict instructed the administration to prepare the funeral rites.
At the burial,
special rites were added,
following the precedent of Dàsīmǎ Huán Wēn.
Furthermore, for his merit in pacifying Fú Jiān,
he was re-enfeoffed as Lúlíng Jùn Gōng.
Xiè Hùn (謝混), courtesy name Shúyuán (叔源).
In his youth, he had a fine reputation
and was skilled at writing.
Initially,
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) sought a husband for Princess Jìnlíng (晉陵公主).
He said to Wáng Xún (王珣):
“The princess’s husband need only be like Liú Zhēncháng (劉真長) or Wáng Zǐjìng (王子敬); that would be sufficient.
If he were like Wáng Chǔzhòng (王處仲) or Huán Yuánzǐ (桓元子), it would indeed be good,
but if he merely gains a little wealth and status,
he then meddles in other people’s affairs.”
Xún (珣) replied:
“Xiè Hùn (謝混), though not quite equal to Zhēncháng (真長),
is no less than Zǐjìng (子敬).”
The Emperor said:
“That would be sufficient.”
Not long after,
the Emperor passed away.
Yuán Shānsōng (袁山松) wished to marry his daughter to him.
Xún (珣) said:
“Do not approach a forbidden morsel.”
In the beginning,
when Emperor Yuán (元帝) first took charge in Jiànyè (建業),
both public and private resources were scarce.
Each time he obtained a pig,
it was considered a delicacy.
A piece of meat from the pig’s neck was especially delicious.
He would always present it to the Emperor.
None of his subordinates ever dared to eat it.
At that time, it was called
“Jìnluán” (禁臠, 'forbidden morsel').
Thus, Xún (珣) used it as a jest.
Hùn (混) eventually married the princess
and inherited his father’s title.
Huán Xuán (桓玄) once wanted to make Ānzhái (安宅) his camp.
Hùn (混) said:
“Zhào Bó’s (召伯) benevolence
still extended to the sweet pear tree.
Could Wénjìng’s (文靖) virtue
not even protect a five-mǔ residence?”
When Xuán (玄) heard this,
he was ashamed and stopped.
He successively held the posts of Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令), Zhōnglǐng Jūn (中領軍), Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射), and Lǐngxuǎn (領選).
He was executed for his involvement with Liú Yì’s (劉毅) faction,
and his state title was abolished.
When the Sòng (宋) dynasty received the abdication,
Xiè Huì (謝晦) said to Liú Yù (劉裕):
“Your Majesty, in response to Heaven’s mandate,
on the day you ascend the altar, it is regrettable that Xiè Yìshòu (謝益壽) is not here to present the imperial seals and ribbons.”
Yù (裕) also sighed and said:
“I deeply regret it.
It prevents later generations from witnessing his elegance!”
Yìshòu (益壽)
was Hùn’s (混) childhood name.
Xiè Yì (謝奕), courtesy name Wúyì (無奕),
had a good reputation in his youth.
Initially, he served as the Magistrate of Shàn (剡).
There was an old man who broke the law.
Yì (奕) gave him strong wine to drink.
Even when drunk, he did not stop.
Ān (安), who was then seven or eight years old,
was by Yì’s (奕) knee
and advised him to stop.
Yì (奕) changed his demeanor
and dismissed the old man.
He was good friends with Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Wēn (溫) appointed him Ānxī Sīmǎ (安西司馬),
but still treated him as a close friend from his days as a commoner.
While in Wēn’s (溫) presence,
he would tilt his head covering and sing,
as if it were any ordinary day.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) said:
“He is my unconventional Sīmǎ (司馬).”
Whenever Yì (奕) was drunk,
he disregarded court etiquette.
He once pressed Wēn (溫) to drink.
Wēn (溫) fled into Princess Nánkāng’s (南康主) gate to avoid him.
The Princess said:
“If you didn’t have such a wild Sīmǎ (司馬),
how would I ever get to see you!”
Yì (奕) then carried his wine to the reception hall,
pulled one of Wēn’s (溫) military commanders to drink with him,
and said:
“Losing one old soldier
and gaining one old soldier,
what is there to be surprised about?”
Wēn (溫) did not blame him.
His cousin Shàng (尚) had excellent governance.
After his death,
he was missed by the western border regions.
The court deliberated and, noting Yì’s (奕) consistent virtuous conduct,
believed he would surely be able to continue Shàng’s (尚) work.
Therefore, he was promoted to Dūdū Yù Sī Jì Bìng Sì Zhōu Jūnjì (都督豫司冀并四州軍事), Ānxī Jiāngjūn (安西將軍), Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史), and Jiǎjié (假節).
Not long after,
he died in office
and was posthumously granted the title Zhènxī Jiāngjūn (鎮西將軍).
He had three sons: Quán (泉),
Jìng (靖), and Xuán (玄).
Quán (泉) had a good reputation early on
and successively served as Yìxīng Tàishǒu (義興太守).
Jìng (靖) reached the office of Tàicháng (太常).
Xiè Xuán (謝玄), courtesy name Yòudù (幼度).
He was intelligent and perceptive in his youth.
He and his cousin Lǎng (朗) were both highly esteemed by their uncle Ān (安).
Ān (安) once admonished his nephews and nieces,
saying:
“What do sons and nephews have to do with human affairs
that one should want them to be good?”
No one among them responded.
Xuán (玄) replied:
“It is like wishing for orchids, irises, and jade trees
to grow in one’s courtyard.”
Ān (安) was pleased.
In his youth, Xuán (玄) was fond of wearing a purple silk perfumed sachet.
Ān (安) was bothered by it,
but did not want to hurt his feelings.
So, he playfully gambled for it and,
upon winning, immediately burned it.
Thereafter, Xuán (玄) stopped wearing it.
As he grew older,
he possessed talent and strategy for governing the state
and was repeatedly invited to serve but declined.
Later, he and Wáng Xún (王珣) were both appointed Yuàn (掾) by Huán Wēn (桓溫),
who treated them with equal respect.
He was transferred to be Sīmǎ (司馬) for Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Huán Huò (桓豁), concurrently holding the positions of Nánjùn Xiàng (南郡相) and Jiān Běizhēng Zhū Jūnjì (監北征諸軍事).
At that time, Fú Jiān (苻堅) was powerful,
and the border regions were frequently invaded.
The court sought able civil and military commanders who could defend the north.
Ān (安) then recommended Xuán (玄) for the position.
Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) Xī Chāo (郗超), though previously on bad terms with Xuán (玄),
sighed upon hearing this
and said:
“Ān (安) went against the public opinion to recommend his relative,
which shows his insight.
Xuán (玄) will certainly not disappoint,
which shows his talent.”
At the time, everyone thought otherwise.
Chāo (超) said:
“I once served with Xuán (玄) in Duke Huán’s (桓公) mansion.
I saw him employ his talent,
even in trivial matters, he was always competent.
That is how I know.”
Thereupon, he was summoned back
and appointed Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍), Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史), concurrently holding Guǎnglíng Xiàng (廣陵相) and Jiān Jiāngběi Zhū Jūnjì (監江北諸軍事).
At that time, Fú Jiān 苻堅 dispatched troops to besiege Xiāngyáng 襄陽.
The General of Chariots and Cavalry, Huán Chōng 桓沖, resisted them.
An imperial edict ordered Xuán 玄 to raise able-bodied men from three prefectures,
and dispatched Hé Qiān 何謙, the Administrator of Péngchéng 彭城, to lead a flying column in the Huái-Sì 淮泗 region,
as a strategic reinforcement.
After Xiāngyáng 襄陽 fell,
Fú Jiān's 苻堅 general Péng Chāo 彭超 attacked Dài [⿱丄卜?] 戴[⿱丄卜?], the General of Dragon Might, at Péngchéng 彭城.
Xuán 玄 led Gāo Héng 高衡, the Administrator of Dōngguǎn 東莞, and Hé Qiān 何謙, the General of the Rear Army, to take position at Sìkǒu 泗口.
He wanted to send a secret messenger to inform Dài [⿱丄卜?] 戴[⿱丄卜?],
letting him know that relief was coming,
but there was no way to do so.
A minor officer, Tián Hóng 田泓, requested to go.
He submerged himself in the water and proceeded stealthily.
As he was about to reach the city,
he was captured by the enemy.
The enemy heavily bribed Hóng 泓,
telling him to say
"The southern army has already been defeated."
Hóng 泓 pretended to agree.
Soon after,
he told those in the city:
"The southern army is about to arrive!
I came alone to report,
but was captured by the enemy.
Strive on!"
He was then killed.
At that time, Péng Chāo 彭超 had placed his baggage train at Liúchéng 留城.
Xuán 玄 then publicly announced that he was sending Qiān 謙 and others towards Liúchéng 留城.
When Chāo 彭超 heard this,
he returned to secure his baggage train.
Qiān 謙 advanced rapidly
and lifted the siege of Péngchéng 彭城.
Péng Chāo 彭超 again advanced southwards,
and Fú Jiān's 苻堅 generals Jù Nán 句難
and Máo Dāng 毛當 came from Xiāngyáng 襄陽 to join him.
Péng Chāo 彭超 besieged Tián Luò 田洛, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu 幽州, at Sān'ē 三阿,
with a force of sixty thousand.
An imperial edict ordered Xiè Shí 謝石, the General Who Subdues Rebels, to lead his navy to Túzhōng 涂中.

Máo Ānzhī 毛安之, the General of the Right Guard, Tán Zhī 曇之, the Prince of Héjiān 河間 and General of Mobile Cavalry, Yáng Guǎng 楊廣, the Administrator of Huáinán 淮南, and Qiū Zhǔn 丘準, the Administrator of Xuānchéng 宣城, took position at Tángyì 堂邑.
Soon after, Xūyí 盱眙 city fell,
Máo Zǎo 毛藻, the Administrator of Gāomì 高密, was lost,
and consequently scattered and retreated.
The imperial court was shaken.
Xuán 玄 thereupon personally led a western campaign from Guǎnglíng 廣陵 against Nán 難 and the others.
Hé Qiān 何謙 lifted the siege of Tián Luò 田洛,
advanced to take Báimǎ 白馬,
fought a great battle with the enemy,
and defeated them,
beheading their pseudo-general Dū Yán 都顏.
and defeated them once more,
beheading their pseudo-general Shào Bǎo 邵保.
Chāo 彭超 and Nán 難 retreated.
Xuán 玄 led Hé Qiān 何謙, Dài [⿱丄卜?] 戴[⿱丄卜?], and Tián Luò 田洛 in pursuit,
and fought at Jūnchuān 君川,
again greatly defeating them.
Xuán's 玄 military advisor Liú Láozhī 劉牢之 attacked and broke through the pontoon bridge and the white boats.
Dū Hù Zhūgě Kǎn 諸葛侃 and Lǐ Dū 李都, the Magistrate of Dānfù 單父, also destroyed their transport ships.
Nán 難 and the others fled northwards,
barely escaping with their lives.
Thereupon, the two garrisons of Péngchéng 彭城 and Xiàpī 下邳 were abolished.
An imperial edict sent a Palace General to express commendation,
and he was promoted to the title of General Who Quells Armies,
additionally given command as Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州,
and returned to Guǎnglíng 廣陵.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxīng 東興 County.
When Fú Jiān 苻堅 personally led his troops to Xiàngchéng 項城,
with a host numbering a million,
the army from Liángzhōu 涼州 had just reached Xiányáng 咸陽,
those from Shǔ-Hàn 蜀漢 flowed downstream,
and those from Yōu-Bìng 幽并 were arriving in succession.
He first dispatched Fú Róng 苻融, Mùróng Wěi 慕容暐, Zhāng Háoz 張蚝, and Fú Fāng 苻方 to Yǐngkǒu 潁口.
Liáng Chéng 梁成 and Wáng Xiǎn 王顯 and others were stationed at Luòjiàn 洛澗.

He was to resist them with his uncle Shí 石, the General Who Subdues Rebels, his cousin Yǎn 琰, the General Who Assists the State, Huán Yī 桓伊, the General of Western Central Cavalry, Tán Xuán 檀玄, the General of Dragon Might, Dài Xī 戴熙, the General Who Establishes Might, Táo Yǐn 陶隱, the General Who Displays Martial Prowess, and others,
a total force of eighty thousand.
Xuán 玄 first sent Liú Láozhī 劉牢之, the Prime Minister of Guǎnglíng 廣陵, with five thousand men directly to Luòjiàn 洛澗.
He immediately beheaded Liáng Chéng 梁成 and Chéng's 成 brother Yún 雲.
The infantry and cavalry collapsed,
scrambling to throw themselves into the Huái River.
Láozhī 劉牢之 unleashed his troops in pursuit,
capturing alive Fú Jiān's 苻堅 pseudo-generals Liáng Tā 梁他, Wáng Xiǎn 王顯, Liáng Tì 梁悌, Mùróng Qū Shì 慕容屈氏, and others,
and seizing their military supplies.
Fú Jiān 苻堅 advanced to Shòuyáng 壽陽,
arraying his forces along the Féi River 肥水.
Xuán's 玄 army could not cross.
Xuán 玄 sent a message to Fú Róng 苻融, saying:
"You have traveled far into our territory,
and arrayed your forces facing the river;
this indicates you do not wish for a swift battle.
If you gentlemen would retreat slightly,
allowing our officers and soldiers room to maneuver,
then I and you gentlemen could loosely rein our horses and observe the situation –
would that not be delightful?"
All of Fú Jiān's 苻堅 forces said:
"We should block the Féi River 肥水,
not allowing them to cross.
Our forces are numerous, theirs are few;
victory is assured."
Fú Jiān 苻堅 said:
"Just retreat the army,
let them cross,
and then I will lead several hundred thousand iron cavalry towards the river,
press in and kill them."
Róng 融 also thought this was a good idea,
so he waved his banner to order the army to retreat.
The troops, in their confusion, could not stop.
Thereupon, Xuán 玄, with Yǎn 琰, Yī 伊, and others, led eight thousand elite troops across the Féi River 肥水.
Shí's 石 army engaged Zhāng Háoz 張蚝,
and retreated slightly.
Xuán 玄 and Yǎn 琰 continued to advance,
fighting a decisive battle south of the Féi River 肥水.
Fú Jiān 苻堅 was struck by a stray arrow,
and Róng 融 was beheaded on the battlefield.
Fú Jiān's 苻堅 forces collapsed and fled.
Those who trampled each other and threw themselves into the water to die were countless,
so much so that the Féi River 肥水 ceased to flow.
The remaining troops abandoned their armor and fled by night.
Hearing the sound of wind and the cries of cranes,
they all thought the king's army had arrived.
Traveling through tall grass and sleeping in the open,
further burdened by hunger and cold,
seventeen or eighteen out of ten died.
They captured Fú Jiān's 苻堅 imperial carriage, a mica chariot,
and official regalia, weapons, military supplies, and treasures piled up like mountains,
as well as over one hundred thousand cattle, horses, donkeys, mules, and camels.
An imperial edict sent a Palace General to express commendation,
and he was promoted to General of the Vanguard, and given a temporary imperial staff,
but he firmly declined it.
He was granted a million coins
and a thousand bolts of silk.
Soon after, Ān 安 reported that Fú Jiān 苻堅 had suffered a defeat,
and that they should seize this opportunity.
Xuán 玄 was appointed Vanguard Commander-in-Chief,
to lead Huán Shíqián 桓石虔, the General Who Quells Armies, directly to Wō-Yǐng 渦潁,
to plan the recovery of the former capital.
Xuán 玄 again led his troops to Péngchéng 彭城,
and dispatched his military advisor Liú Xí 劉襲 to attack Zhāng Chóng 張崇, Fú Jiān's 苻堅 Inspector of Yǎnzhōu 兗州, at Juànchéng 鄄城,
and routed him.
He had Liú Láozhī 劉牢之 guard Juànchéng 鄄城.
After Yǎnzhōu 兗州 was pacified,
Xuán 玄 was concerned about the dangerous and difficult waterways
and the arduous supply transport.
Following the advice of Supervising Officer Wénrén Shì 聞人奭,
he dammed the Lǚliáng Lüliang River,
erected palisades,
and built seven weirs to create channels,
confining the flow of both banks,
to facilitate transport,
which benefited both public and private matters thereafter.
He also advanced to attack Qīngzhōu 青州,
hence it was called the Qīngzhōu 青州 Channel.
He sent Gāo Sù 高素, the Administrator of Huáilíng 淮陵, with three thousand men towards Guǎnggù 廣固,
where Fú Lǎng 苻朗, Fú Jiān's 苻堅 Inspector of Qīngzhōu 青州, surrendered.
He also advanced to attack Jìzhōu 冀州,
sending Liú Láozhī 劉牢之, the General of Dragon Might, and Dīng Kuāng 丁匡, the Administrator of Jìběi 濟北, to hold Què'áo 碻磝,
Guō Mǎn 郭滿, the Administrator of Jìyáng 濟陽, to hold Huátái 滑臺,
and Yán Xióng 顏雄, the General Who Incites Martial Prowess, to cross the river and establish camps.
Xuán 玄 ordered Liú Xí 劉襲 to attack Jù 據 by night,
and routed him.
Pī 丕 was panicked and wanted to surrender.
Xuán 玄 accepted.
Pī 丕 reported hunger,
and Xuán 玄 supplied Pī 丕 with two thousand *hú* 斛 of rice.
The three Wèi 魏 regions all surrendered.
With the pacification of Yǎn 兗, Qīng 青, Sī 司, and Yù 豫,
Xuán 玄 was additionally appointed Supervisor-General of the military affairs of Xú 徐, Yǎn 兗, Qīng 青, Sī 司, Jì 冀, Yōu 幽, and Bìng 并 seven prefectures.
Xuán 玄 submitted a memorial stating that with the Hébĕi 河北 region newly pacified,
Yōu 幽 and Jì 冀 should have a unified command,
while Sīzhōu 司州, being distant,
should be under the command of Yùzhōu 豫州.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Kānglè 康樂 County.
Xuán 玄 requested that his former enfeoffment as Marquis of Dōngxīng 東興 be bestowed upon his nephew Wán 玩,
and an imperial edict granted this,
Wán 玩 being re-enfeoffed as the Earl of Yùníng 豫寧.
He again sent Huāng Yǎn 昋演, the General Who Pacifies the Distant, to attack Shēn Kǎi 申凱 in Wèijùn 魏郡,
and defeated him.
Xuán 玄 wanted Zhū Xù 朱序, the Inspector of Yùzhōu 豫州, to garrison Liángguó 梁國,
while Xuán 玄 himself would reside in Péngchéng 彭城,
securing the northern bank of the river,
assisting Luòyáng 洛陽 from the west,
and forming an inner defense for the imperial court.
The court discussion was that since the military campaigns had been long,
garrisons should be set up and the armies returned.
Xuán 玄 was ordered to return and garrison Huáinán 淮陰,
and Xù 朱序 to garrison Shòuyáng 壽陽.
At that time, Zhái Liáo 翟遼 occupied Líyáng 黎陽 and rebelled,
Also, Zhāng Yuàn 張願, the Administrator of Tàishān 泰山, rebelled with his entire prefecture.
Hébĕi 河北 was in turmoil.
Xuán 玄, believing his dispositions were misplaced,
submitted a memorial, returning his imperial staff
and requesting to be relieved of all his positions.
An imperial edict offered him comfort,
ordering him to temporarily return and garrison Huáinán 淮陰,
and appointing Zhū Xù 朱序 to replace him in garrisoning Péngchéng 彭城.
Xuán 既還,
遇疾,
上疏解職,
詔書不許.
Xuán 又自陳,
既不堪攝職,
慮有曠廢.
詔又使移鎮東陽城.
Xuán 即路,
於道疾篤,
上疏曰： 臣以常人,
才不佐世,
忽蒙殊遇,
不復自量,
遂從戎政.
驅馳十載,
不辭鳴鏑之險,
每有征事,
輒請為軍鋒,
由恩厚忘軀,
甘死若生也.
冀有毫釐,
上報榮寵.
天祚大晉,
王威屢舉,
實由陛下神武英斷,
無思不服.
亡叔臣 Ān Xié 贊雍熙,
以成天工.
而雰霧尚
翳,
六合未朗,
遺黎塗炭,
巢窟宜除,
復命臣荷戈前驅,
董司戎首.
冀仰憑皇威,
宇宙寧
一,
陛下致太平之化,
庸臣以塵露報恩,
然後從亡叔臣 Ān 退身東山,
以道養壽.
此誠以
形于文旨,
達于聖聽矣.
臣所以區區家國,
實在於此.
不謂臣愆咎夙積,
罪鍾中年,
上
延亡叔臣 Ān, 亡兄臣 Jìng,
數月之間,
相係殂背,
下逮稚子,
尋復夭昏.
哀毒兼纏,
痛百常
情.
臣不勝禍酷暴集,
每一慟殆弊.
所以含哀忍悲,
期之必存者,
雖哲輔傾落,
聖明方
融,
伊周嗣作,
人懷自厲,
猶欲申臣本志,
隆國保家,
故能豁其情滯,
同之無心耳.
去冬奉司徒 Dàozi 告括囊遠圖,
逮問臣進止之宜.
臣進不達事機,
以蹙境為恥,
退
不自揆,
故欲順其宿心.
豈謂經略不振,
自貽斯戾.
是以奉送章節,
待罪有司,
執徇常
儀,
實有愧心.
而聖恩赦過,
黷法垂宥,
使抱罪之臣復得更名於所司.
木石猶感,
而況
臣乎！
顧將身不良,
動與釁會,
謙德不著,
害盈是荷,
先疾既動,
便至委篤.
陛下體臣
疢重,
使還藩淮側.
甫欲休兵靜衆,
綏懷善撫,
兼苦自療,
冀日月漸瘳,
繕甲俟會,
思更
奮迅.
而所患沈頓,
有增無損.
今者惙惙,
救命朝夕.
臣之平日,
率其常矩,
加以匪懈,
猶不能令政理弘宣,
況今內外天隔,
永不復接,
寧可臥居重任,
以招患慮！
追尋前事,
可為寒心.
臣之微身,
復何足惜,
區區血誠,
憂國實深.
謹遣兼長史 Liú
Jì 重奉送節蓋章傳.
伏願陛下垂天地之仁,
拯將絕之氣,
時遣軍司鎮慰荒雜,
聽臣所
乞,
盡醫藥消息,
歸誠道門,
冀神祇之祐.
若此而不差,
修短命也.
使臣得及視息,
瞻
覩墳柏,
以此之盡,
公私真無恨矣.
伏枕悲慨,
不覺流涕.
詔遣高手醫一人,
令自消息,
又使還京口療疾.
Xuán 奉詔便還,
病久不差,
又上疏曰：
「臣同生七人,
凋落相繼,
惟臣一己,
孑然獨存.
在生荼酷,
無如臣比.
所以含哀忍痛,
希延視息者,
欲報之德,
實懷罔極,
庶蒙一瘳,
申其此志.
且臣孤遺滿目,
顧之惻然,
為欲極其求生之心,
未能自分於灰土.
慺慺之情,
可哀可愍.
伏願陛下矜其所訴,
霈然垂恕,
不令微臣銜恨泉壤. 」
表寢不報.
前後表疏十餘上,
久之,
乃轉授散騎常侍、左將軍、會稽內史.
時吳興太守晉寧侯 Zhāng Xuánzhī 亦以才學顯,
自吏部尚書與 Xuán 同年之郡,
而 Xuánzhī 名亞於 Xuán,
時人稱為
「南北二玄」 ,
論者美之.
Xuán 既輿疾之郡,
十三年,
卒于官,
時年四十六.
追贈車騎將軍、開府儀同三司,
諡曰獻武.
子 Huán 嗣,
祕書郎,
早卒.
子 Língyùn 嗣.
Huán 少不惠,
而 Língyùn 文藻艷逸,
Xuán 嘗稱曰：
「我尚生 Huán,
Huán 那得生 Língyùn! 」
〔十六〕Yǒngxī 中,
為 Liú Yù 世子左衞率.
Those who first followed [Xiè] Xuán (謝玄) in his campaigns
were Hé Qiān (何謙), courtesy name Gōngzǐ (恭子),
a native of Dōnghǎi (東海), and
Dài Bǔ (戴卜), courtesy name Ānqīu (安丘).
Dài Bǔ (戴卜) was the younger brother of the recluse Dài Kuí (戴逵).
Both were brave and resourceful.
Dài Kuí (戴逵) cultivated his character in Dōngshān (東山),
while Dài Bǔ (戴卜) distinguished himself through his martial valor.
Xiè Ān (謝安) once said to Dài Bǔ (戴卜):
"How different are the aspirations and occupations of you brothers?"
Dài Bǔ (戴卜) replied:
"Your humble servant cannot bear its sorrow,
while my elder brother does not change his joy."
Dài Bǔ (戴卜) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Guǎngxìn (廣信) for his military merits,
and rose to the position of Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī nóng).
[Xiè] Wàn (萬), courtesy name Wànshí (萬石),
was talented and outstanding.
Although his breadth of mind was not equal to [Xiè] Ān (安),
he was good at promoting himself,
and thus early on enjoyed a good reputation.
He was skilled in discourse
and good at writing.

He wrote the "Eight Worthies Discourse" (Bā Xián Lùn) on the Fisherman (Yúfù), Qū Yuán (屈原), Jì Zhǔ (季主), Jiǎ Yì (賈誼), the Old Man of Chǔ (Chǔ Lǎo), Gōng Shèng (龔勝), Sūn Dēng (孫登), and Jī Kāng (嵇康), four recluses and four officials,
the main point of which was that those who lived in seclusion were superior
and those who served in office were inferior.
He showed it to Sūn Chuò (孫綽).
Sūn Chuò (孫綽) debated with him,
arguing that for those with public spirit and far-reaching insight, serving or withdrawing ultimately led to the same end.
[一七] Once, while sending off a guest with Cài Xì (蔡系) at the Zhēnglǔ Pavilion (征虜亭),
he argued with Cài Xì (蔡系).
Cài Xì (蔡 Xì) pushed [Xiè] Wàn (萬) off the couch,
causing his hat to fall off.
[Xiè] Wàn (萬) slowly brushed his clothes and returned to his seat,
his demeanor completely natural.
Once seated,
he said to Cài Xì (蔡 Xì):
"You almost disfigured my face."
Cài Xì (蔡 Xì) replied:
"I wasn't thinking of your face to begin with."
However, neither of them took it to heart,
and people at the time praised them for this.
At twenty,
he was appointed as an aide (yuàn) to the Minister of Works (Sītú),
then promoted to Right Assistant (Yòu Xīshǔ),
but he did not accept.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) became chancellor,
he heard of [Xiè] Wàn's (萬) name
and summoned him to be an attendant official (cóngshì zhōngláng) in the Protector-General's (Fǔjūn) office.
[Xiè] Wàn (萬) wore a white silk cap
and a crane-feather cloak,
and advanced by treading on a board.
[一八] Upon meeting,
he talked with the emperor for an entire day.
Wáng Shù (王述) of Tàiyuán (太原),
[Xiè] Wàn's (萬) father-in-law,
was the Governor (Cǐshǐ) of Yángzhōu (揚州).
[Xiè] Wàn (萬) once wore a white silk cap
and rode in a flat sedan chair
directly to the front of the audience hall,
saying to Wáng Shù (王述):
"People say you are foolish,
and indeed you are foolish."
Wáng Shù (王述) replied:
"It's not that there isn't such an opinion,
but it's only recently become true."
[一九]

[Xiè] Wàn (萬) was twice promoted to Governor (Cǐshǐ) of Yùzhōu (豫州), concurrently Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Huáinán (淮南), Supervisor of Military Affairs for Sī (司), Yù (豫), Jì (冀), and Bìng (并) four prefectures, and was granted a marshal's staff (jiǎjié).
Wáng Xīzhī (王羲之) wrote a memorial to Huán Wēn (桓溫), saying:
"[Xiè] Wàn's (謝萬) talent is profound and thorough.
Placed in the imperial court
to participate in discussions and remonstrances,
he is indeed a capable man for the future.
But now to curb his soaring ambition
and make him submit to a desolate and barren region
is certainly to misapply his talent and mishandle affairs."
Huán Wēn (桓溫) did not comply.
After [Xiè] Wàn (萬) received the appointment for the northern expedition,
he was arrogant and boastful,
often indulging in whistling and chanting to show his superiority,
and never bothered to console his troops.
His elder brother [Xiè] Ān (安) was deeply worried about this.
From the squad leaders (duìzhǔ) and commanders (jiàngshuài) downward,
[Xiè] Ān (安) comforted and encouraged everyone.
He said to [Xiè] Wàn (萬):
"You are the commander-in-chief.
The generals should be frequently received and interviewed
to gladden their hearts.
How can you be so arrogant and still succeed?"
[Xiè] Wàn (萬) then summoned the generals,
but said nothing.
He merely pointed his ruyi scepter at all those present, saying:
"All you generals are strong soldiers."
The generals resented him even more.
Later, he first dispatched the General of the Vanguards (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), Líu Jiàn (劉建), to repair the defenses of Mǎtóu City (馬頭城池),
and then personally led his troops into the Guō (渦) and Yǐng (潁) rivers
to aid Luòyáng (洛陽).
When the Northern Commander (Běizhōngláng Jiāng), Xī Tán (郗曇), retreated to Péngchéng (彭城) due to illness,
[Xiè] Wàn (萬) thought it was because the enemy was too strong,
so he withdrew his army.
His troops then dispersed and scattered,
and he returned alone in disarray.
He was stripped of his commoner status.
Later, he was reinstated as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
He died soon after,
at the age of forty-two,
and was posthumously honored for his service.
His son, Sháo (韶),
courtesy name Mùdù (穆度),
was famous in his youth.
At the time, the most outstanding young men of the Xiè (謝) clan
were referred to as Fēng (封), Hú (胡), Jié (羯), and Mò (末).
Fēng (封) referred to Sháo (韶),
Hú (胡) referred to Lǎng (朗),
Jié (羯) referred to Xuán (玄),
and Mò (末) referred to Chuān (川).
[二０] These were all their informal names.
Sháo (韶), Lǎng (朗), and Chuān (川) all died early,
only Xuán (玄) concluded his life with great achievements.
Sháo (韶) rose to the rank of Cavalier Grand Marshal (Chējì Sīmǎ).
Sháo's (韶) son, Ēn (恩),
courtesy name Jǐngbó (景伯),
was broad-minded and had far-reaching strategies.
[Sháo (韶)] was a Yellow Gate Attendant (Huángménláng) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wǔchāng (武昌).
Ēn (恩) had three sons: Yào (曜), Hóng (弘), and Wēi (微),
all of whom held prominent positions.
Lǎng (朗), courtesy name Chángdù (長度).
His father, Jù (據),
died early.
Lǎng (朗) was skilled in discussing profound philosophy,
and his writings were brilliant and insightful.
His fame was second only to [Xiè] Xuán (玄).
When he was a boy (zǒngjiǎo),
having just recovered from an illness,
his body was very frail
and not yet able to endure exertion.
In the presence of his uncle [Xiè] Ān (安), he debated with the Buddhist monk Zhī Dùn (支遁),
and it became a heated argument.
His mother, Lady Wáng (王氏), sent messengers twice to tell him to return,
but [Xiè] Ān (安) wanted him to stay
and finish the debate.
Lady Wáng (王氏) then came out and said:
"This daughter-in-law suffered hardships at a young age,
and all my hopes in life are placed on this child."
She then tearfully led Lǎng (朗) away.
[Xiè] Ān (安) said to his guests:
"My sister-in-law's words and emotions are so stirring;
it's a pity that court officials couldn't see it."
Lǎng (朗) eventually died as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Dōngyáng (東陽).
His son, Chóng (重),
courtesy name Jǐngchóng (景重),
was intelligent and talented,
and served as Chief Clerk (Piàojì Chángshǐ) to Wáng Dàozǐ (王道子), the King of Huìjī (會稽).
Once, while attending the king,
the moonlit night was clear and bright.
Wáng Dàozǐ (王道子) sighed, thinking it beautiful.
Chóng (重) blurted out:
"I think it's not as good as being dotted with faint clouds."
Wáng Dàozǐ (王道子) then playfully said to Chóng (重):
"Your heart is not pure,
so you insist on wanting to defile the pure sky!"
His son, Xuàn (絢),
courtesy name Xuānyìng (宣映),
once made a playful remark in a public gathering,
being disrespectful to his maternal uncle Yuán Zhàn (袁湛).
Yuán Zhàn (袁湛) found it unbearable
and said:
"Your father already treated his maternal uncle lightly in the past;
now you come to add to it.
One might say there is no longer any affection for maternal relatives in this generation."
Xuàn's (絢) father, Chóng (重),
was the maternal grandson of Wáng Hú (王胡),
and there were also discussions about his discord with his maternal uncle,
hence Yuán Zhàn (袁湛) made that remark.
Xiè Shí, courtesy name Shínú.
Initially appointed as Mìshū Láng,
he was successively promoted to Shàngshū Púyè.
He campaigned against Gōunán,
and for his achievements was enfeoffed as Xīngpíng Xiàn Bó.
During the campaign of Huáiféi,
an imperial edict dismissed Xiè Shí from Púyè,
and appointed him Jiāngjūn Jiǎjié Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū.
With his nephews Xiè Xuán and Xiè Yǎn, he defeated Fú Jiān.
Prior to this,
a children's rhyme said:
"Who says you're tough? Rocks shatter!"
Therefore, Huán Huò and others all named their sons
"Shí" (rock)
to invite success.
Thus they sought merit.
When Fú Jiān was defeated,
although the merit began with Liú Láozhī,
and was completed by Xiè Xuán and Xiè Yǎn,
Xiè Shí was indeed the Dūdū at that time.
He was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Shàngshū Lìng,
and re-enfeoffed as Nánkāng Jùn Gōng.
At that time, schools were in decline.
Xiè Shí submitted a memorial requesting the restoration of the Guóxué,
to educate the sons of nobles,
and that orders be sent down to the zhōu and jùn,
to universally repair the xiāngxiào.
When the memorial was presented,
Emperor Xiàowǔ accepted it.
When his elder brother Xiè Ān died,
Xiè Shí was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and given the additional title Sànqí Chángshì.
Due to a public matter, he had a dispute with Lìbù Láng Wáng Gōng,
and Wáng Gōng was very resentful.
He personally declared his narrow-mindedness unacceptable,
and that his illness was deeply rooted,
requesting to return to his private home.
Xiè Shí also submitted a memorial to resign.
The relevant officials reported that
Xiè Shí had immediately left his post,
and should be dismissed.
An imperial edict stated:
"Xiè Shí seeks to retire due to illness;
how can this be judged by ordinary regulations!
Order him to return."
For over a year, he did not rise.
He submitted more than ten memorials,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Xiè Shí requested to follow the precedent of the former Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Biāozhī,
to manage affairs from his residence.
An edict granted this.
As his illness worsened,
he was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and granted drums and pipes.
Before he could be formally invested,
he died,
at the age of sixty-two.
When Xiè Shí was young, he suffered from a facial ulcer.
No remedies cured it,
so he hid himself.
One night, something came and licked his sore.
As it licked, it healed,
and the licked area became very white.
Thus, the world called him Xiè Báimiàn.
In office, Xiè Shí focused on documentation and trivial matters.
Having no other talent or reputation,
he merely held a prominent position due to being the prime minister's brother and having great achievements,
thus occupying a high and esteemed office,
but his avarice was insatiable,
earning him ridicule from his contemporaries.
He was posthumously granted the title Sīkōng.
The ritual officials debated his posthumous name.
Doctor Fàn Hóngzhī proposed the posthumous name Xiāngmò Gōng,
the details of which are in Fàn Hóngzhī's biography.
The court discussion did not follow this,
and he was simply given the posthumous name Xiāng.
His son, Xiè Wāng, succeeded him,
but died young.
Xiè Wāng's cousin, Xiè Chōng, succeeded him with his intelligent son, Xiè Mínghuì.
Xiè Mínghuì was harmed by Sūn ēn.
Xiè Mínghuì's cousin, Xiè Yù, again succeeded him with his son, Xiè Gǎo.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
the peerage was abolished.
Xiè Miǎo, courtesy name Màodù.
His father, Xiè Tiě, was Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu.
Xiè Miǎo was firm and unyielding by nature,
never bowing down,
and possessed considerable insight.
He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng.
At that time, after drinking parties, Emperor Xiàowǔ often bestowed written edicts upon his attendant ministers.
If the words and meanings were not elegant,
Xiè Miǎo would promptly burn them.
Other attendant ministers who received such edicts would sometimes publicize them,
thus commentators often praised Xiè Miǎo for this.
Later, he became Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
During Sūn ēn's rebellion,
he was captured by the bandits Hú Jié, Gāo Piào, and others,
and killed.
The bandits forced him to face north,
〔二二〕but Xiè Miǎo sternly declared:
"I have committed no offense against the Son of Heaven,
why should I face north!"
Thereupon, they killed him.
Xiè Miǎo's wife, Lady Xī,
was very jealous.
Xiè Miǎo had previously taken a concubine,
and Lady Xī resented it,
writing to Xiè Miǎo to break off their relationship.
Xiè Miǎo suspected that the letter's language was not that of a woman,
and believed his retainer Qiú Xuándá had written it for her,
so he dismissed Qiú Xuándá.
Qiú Xuándá, angered,
then defected to Sūn ēn,
and caused the deaths of Xiè Miǎo and his brothers,
ultimately leading to the extermination of their family.
The court historian says: After Jiànyuán,
the affairs of state were fraught with perils,
great villains ran rampant,
and powerful ministers acted wantonly.
Those who held both general and prime ministerial power internally and externally,
and on whom the survival of the state depended,
whom the emperor relied upon to govern peacefully,
and whom the common people depended upon for peace and tranquility,
were perhaps only the Xiè clan!
Xiè Jiǎnhóu assumed overall command of the central administration,
his achievements were manifest in governing the regions.
When Zheng Yì proclaimed,
the ritual for mourning, which had fallen into disuse, was again promoted.
When the lost melodies were restored,
the court music, which had been incomplete, was again made whole.
What a nobleman,
this man was!
Xiè Wénjìng initially lived outside the mundane world,
distancing himself from human affairs,
singing and chanting in the mountains and forests,
drifting on rivers and seas.
At this time,
he possessed a transcendent, ethereal spirit.
Yet he cast off his hermit's robes and donned the red sashes of office,
leaving his humble dwelling to tread the vermilion steps of the court.
All affairs were thus made prosperous,
and moral principles were restored to harmony.
When Fú Jiān's million-strong army had already gazed upon the Wú River,
and Huán Wēn's ambition for supreme power threatened to usurp the Jìn throne,
the gentry changed their minds,
and people near and far were disheartened.
He calmly thwarted treacherous plots,
and cheerfully pacified the numerous bandits.
The imperial residence achieved the stability of Mount Tài,
and the Wéiyáng region was saved from the danger of stacked eggs.
This was truly magnificent.
However, he gathered a large crowd during a period of mourning,
indulged in a single lavish celebration costing a hundred pieces of gold,
discarded rituals in a frivolous age,
and promoted extravagance during a time of agriculture and warfare.
Although he wished to blend sorrow and joy into one,
and equalize luxury and frugality,
he did not realize that a decadent trend had already spread,
and the elegant way was daily decaying.
How could the state's exemplary conduct
have reached such a state!
Xiè Yǎn was praised for his integrity,
and ultimately earned fame for his loyalty and courage.
Xiè Hùn was called elegant and refined,
and ultimately won renown for his literary talent.
Both reached the rank of prime minister,
without disgracing their family's reputation.
Xiè Yìwàn was esteemed for his uninhibitedness,
and Xiè Shínú incurred blame for his narrow-mindedness and impurity.
Though there were minor flaws,
they still lived up to their names and reputations.
Xiè Kānglè possessed both literary and martial talents,
and was dedicated to assisting the state.
During the campaign of Huáiféi,
the powerful enemy collapsed at the sight of him.
During the campaign of Guō and Yǐng,
the Central Plains responded and were swept clean.
Just as he intended to pacify the west at Gǒngluò,
and stabilize the north at Yōuyàn,
the court's calculations had oversights,
and his excellent plans were not realized.
Why was his lifespan so short?
His achievements failed when victory was almost at hand.
Examining his posthumous writings,
his strategies were far-reaching indeed.
I fear that among the assembled worthies of the entire court, there are none who would share this calumny with me.
If I were to now diligently cultivate virtue and mend my shortcomings,
and widely extend invitations to all the worthies
to share in the responsibility with me,
I still do not know if I could achieve what
is expected.
If one were to still regard the past efforts as insufficient,
and thus seek beyond one’s proper place,
though the universe is vast,
where could one find a place for oneself?
I know that my words may not necessarily be heeded,
and I might incur the displeasure of
those in power.
However, when deeply moved by emotion,
I simply cannot but speak my mind completely and frankly.
If there must be a personal expedition,
and this principle is not understood,
then its execution
is incomprehensible to both the foolish and the
wise.
I wish to discuss this again with the multitude.
Again, I received a provincial order
to increase transport by a thousand *shí*,
with levies and conscription arriving concurrently,
all due to military deadlines.
Upon facing this, my spirits sank,
and I knew not what to do.
For some time now, the common people have been exploited and
impoverished,
with convicts filling the roads,
almost akin to Qín's governance,
only lacking the punishment of extermination of three generations.
I fear that the worries of Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng
will not be far off.
I also sent a memorial to Huìjī Wáng, stating that Yīn Hào should not campaign in the north,
and discussing current affairs, saying: Ancient people were ashamed if their lord was not like Yáo or Shùn.
As subjects,
how could one not wish to honor one’s sovereign
and make him comparable to past eras,
especially when encountering a once-in-a-thousand-year
opportunity?
But if one’s wisdom and strength are insufficient for the current times,
how can one not weigh the pros and cons before acting?
Although there are currently reasons for joy,
when looking within myself,
my worries
outweigh my joys.
A proverb says,
“Unless one is a sage,
external tranquility surely brings internal worries.”
Now, externally there is no tranquility,
and internal worries are already profound.
Those of old who accomplished great
endeavors
sometimes did not consult the masses;
those who risked the entire nation to achieve a temporary success
were also common.
If indeed one’s singular wisdom is sufficient to surpass the multitude,
and a temporary hardship
ultimately leads to lasting peace, then it is acceptable.
But when we look at the present,
can this be deliberated upon?
Indeed, for strategic planning to ensure victory,
one must carefully assess both oneself and the enemy,
and act only when absolutely certain of success.
When success is achieved,
one should then rely on the people and fulfill their needs.
Now,
success is uncertain,
while the common people are being exterminated,
with scarcely one in ten thousand remaining.
Moreover, transporting provisions a thousand *lǐ*
has always been difficult since ancient times.
How much more so now, with transport and supply
going west to Xǔluò,
and north into the Yellow River.
Even the abuses of Qín’s governance
did not reach this extent,
yet the anxieties of every household
are now prevalent.
Now, the transport has no end in sight,
and demands are daily increasing.
With the small regions of Wú and Yuè sustaining nine-tenths of the empire,
what else can await but ruin?
Yet, without measuring virtue or assessing strength,
one does not cease until ruin.
This is what grieves
and saddens the people within the borders, yet they dare not speak their minds.
What is past cannot be mended,
but what is to come can still be pursued.
I wish Your Highness would reconsider,
undo what has been done and reform,
allowing Yīn Hào and Xún Xiàn to return and hold Héféi and Guǎng
líng,
and all the armies from Xǔchāng, Qiáojùn, Liáng, and Péngchéng to return and guard the Huái River,
establishing an impregnable foundation.
When roots are firm and power established,
it will not be too late to plan.
This is truly the
best strategy for the present.
If this is not done,
the anxieties for the state can be counted day by day.
The turning point between safety and danger
is as easy as turning one's palm.
When assessing the reality,
it is clear
before our eyes.
I wish Your Highness would exercise your unique discerning wisdom
and make a decision in a single morning.
My position is humble, but my words are profound;
how could I not know that this is not easy?
However, ancient people, even in their common homes or amidst military formations,
still sometimes offered advice on current affairs and state policies,
and critics did not
consider it a fault.
How much more so for one placed in the last rank of ministers—
how can I remain silent?
The survival or ruin of the state depends
on this decision.
One must not again hesitate and miss the opportunity.
If it is not
resolved now,
and one wishes to regret it later,
it will be too late.
Your Highness's virtue crowns the universe.
You assist the court as a member of the imperial clan;
you are most able to act with integrity
to achieve the prosperity of these times.
Yet, you have not met the expectations of the people.
This is why those who have received special favor
sigh constantly, awake and asleep,
and I truly lament this for Your Highness.
The concerns for the state are profound.
I often fear that Wǔ Yuán’s worries are not merely a thing of the past,
and that deer roaming free will not
be confined to forests and swamps alone.
I wish Your Highness would momentarily set aside distant and impractical thoughts
to rescue us from this dire predicament.
This could be called turning ruin into survival,
and transforming disaster into fortune.
Then the blessings for the ancestral
temples
would be relied upon by all within the four seas.
At that time, there was famine in the eastern region.
Xīzhī promptly opened granaries to provide relief.
However, imperial taxes and labor services were heavy,
especially in Wú and Huìjī.
Xīzhī often submitted memorials to argue against them,
and many of his proposals were adopted.
He also sent a letter to the Minister of Personnel, Xiè Ān, saying:
Recently, my previous arguments
have always been accepted,
thereby allowing the common people to obtain some relief
and each to settle in their livelihoods.
If not,
this entire commandery would have long ago plunged into the Eastern
Sea.
Now, the greatest matter has not been settled,
which is grain transport.
My wish is that the imperial court can issue a fixed deadline,
entrusting it to the responsible officials,
and not press for it repeatedly.
Instead,
at the end of the year, their performance should be evaluated.
If a chief magistrate's performance is notably poor,
he should be ordered to be sent to Tiāntái in a caged cart.
If three counties fail to collect,
the governor (two thousand *shí* official) must be dismissed,
or perhaps demoted
to serve in
the most difficult border regions.
Also, since I arrived here,
there have always been four or five subordinates,
along with official documents from the central administration and the Director of River Conservancy's traveling office arriving like rain,
often contradictory and confusing,
no longer
understandable.
I also blindly follow the old routine,
prioritizing major matters and essential regulations,
with minor ones handled by the five departments.
The responsible officials are in charge of affairs
for less than ten days,
while clerks and common people
rush about,
spending tens of thousands.
You are now taking on this heavy responsibility;
you may gradually examine what I have said.
In the ordinary times south of the Yangtze,
one good provincial governor of Yángzhōu would be sufficient to govern it,
let alone
Xìng ài é,
Kuàijī yǒu gū jū mǔ yǎng yī é,
shàn míng,
qiú shì wèi néng dé,
suì xié qīnyǒu mìng jià jiù guān.
Mǔ wén Xīzhī jiāng zhì,
pēng yǐ dài zhī,
Xīzhī tàn xī mí rì.
Yòu Shānyīn yǒu yī dàoshì,
yǎng hǎo é,
Xīzhī wǎng guān yān,
yì shèn yuè,
gù qiú shì zhī.
Dàoshì yún:
“Wèi xiě Dàodé Jīng,
dāng jǔ qún xiāng zèng ěr.”
Xīzhī xīnrán xiě bì,
lóng é ér guī,
shèn yǐwéi lè.
Qí rènshuài rúcǐ.
Cháng yì ménshēng jiā,
jiàn fěijǐ huá jìng,
yīn shū zhī,
zhēncǎo xiāngbàn.
Hòu wèi qí fù wù guā qù zhī,
ménshēng jīng'ào zhě lěi rì.
Yòu cháng zài Jíshān jiàn yī lǎomǔ,
chí liùjiǎo zhú shàn mài zhī.
Xīzhī shū qí shàn,
gè wèi wǔ zì.
Mǔ chū yǒu yùn sè.
Yīn wèi mǔ yuē:
“Dàn yán shì Wáng Yòujūn shū,
yǐ qiú bǎiqián xié.”
Mǔ rú qí yán.
Rén jìng mǎi zhī.
Tārì,
mǔ yòu chí shàn lái,
Xīzhī xiào ér bù dá.
Qí shū wèi shì suǒ zhòng,
jiē cǐ lèi yě.
Měi zìchēng
“wǒ shū bǐ Zhōng Yáo,
dāng kàngxíng;
bǐ Zhāng Zhī cǎo,
yóu dāng yànxíng yě”.
Céng yǔ rén shū yún:
“Zhāng Zhī lín chí xué shū,
chíshuǐ jìn hēi,
shǐ rén dān zhī ruò shì,
wèi bì hòu zhī yě.”
Xīzhī shū chū bù shèng Yǔ Yì, Xī Yīn,
jí qí mùnián fāng miào,
cháng yǐ zhāngcǎo dá Yǔ Liàng,
ér Yì shēn tànfú,
yīn yǔ Xīzhī shū yún:
“Wú xī yǒu Bóyīng zhāngcǎo shí zhǐ,
guò Jiāng diānbèi,
suì nǎi wángshī,
cháng tàn miàojì yǒng jué.
Hū jiàn zúxià dá jiāxiōng shū,
huàn ruò shénmíng,
dùn huán jiùguān.”
Shí Piàojì Jiāngjūn Wáng Shù shào yǒu míngyù,
yǔ Xīzhī qí míng,
ér Xīzhī shèn qīng zhī,
yóu shì qínghǎo bù xié.
Shù xiān wèi Kuàijī,
yǐ mǔsāng jū jùn jìng,
Xīzhī dài Shù,
zhǐ yī diào,
suì bù chóng yì.
Shù měi wén juéshēng,
wèi Xīzhī dāng hòu jǐ,
zhé sǎsǎo ér dài zhī.
Rúcǐ zhě lěinián,
ér Xīzhī jìng bù gù,
Shù shēn yǐwéi hèn.
Jí Shù wèi Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
jiāng jiù zhēng,
Zhōuxíng jùn jiè,
ér bù guò Xīzhī,
lín fā,
yī bié ér qù.
Xiān shì,
Xīzhī cháng wèi bīn yǒuyuē:
“Huáizǔ zhèng dāng zuò Shàngshū ěr,
tóu lǎo kě dé Púshè.
Gèng qiú Kuàijī,
biàn zì miǎorán.”
Jí Shù méng xiǎn shòu,
Xīzhī chǐ wéi zhī xià,
qiǎn shǐ yì cháotíng,
qiú fēn Kuàijī wèi Yuèzhōu.
Xíngrén shī cí,
dà wéi shíxián suǒ xiào.
Jì'ér nèi huái kuìtàn,
wèi qí zhū zǐyuē:
“Wú bù jiǎn Huáizǔ,
ér wèiyù xuánmiǎo,
dāng yóu rǔ děng bù jí Tǎnzhī gù xié!”
Shù hòu jiǎnchá Kuàijī Jùn,
biàn qí xíngzhèng,
zhǔzhě pí yú jiǎnduì.
Xīzhī shēn chǐ zhī,
suì chēng bìng qù jùn,
yú fùmǔ mù qián zìshì yuē:
“Wéi Yǒnghé shíyī nián sān yuè guǐmǎo suò,
jiǔ rì xīnhài,
xiǎozǐ Xīzhī gǎn gào èrzūn zhī líng.
Xīzhī bù tiān,
sù zāo mǐnxíong,
bù méng guòtíng zhī xùn.
Mǔ xiōng jūyù,
dé jiàn shùjī,
suì yīn rén fá,
méng guó chǒngróng.
Jìn wú zhōngxiào zhī jié,
tuì wéi tuī xián zhī yì,
měi yǎngyǒng Lǎoshì, Zhōu Rèn zhī jiè,
cháng kǒng sǐwáng wú rì,
yōu jí zōngsì,
qǐ zài wēishēn éryǐ!
Shìyòng wùmèi yǒngtàn,
ruò duò shēgǔ.
Zhǐzú zhī fèn,
dìng zhī yú jīn.
Jǐn yǐ jīn yuè jí chén sìyán shèxí,
jīgǎo guīchéng,
gàoshì xiānlíng.
Zì jīn zhī hòu,
gǎn yú cǐ xīn.
Tānmào gǒujìn,
shì yǒu wú zūn zhī xīn ér bù zǐ yě.
Zǐ ér bù zǐ,
tiāndì suǒ bù fùzài,
míngjiào suǒ bù dé róng.
Xìnshì zhī chéng,
yǒu rú jiǎorì!”
Xīzhī jì qù guān,
yǔ Dōngtǔ rénshì jǐn shānshuǐ zhī yóu,
yì diào wéi yú.
Yòu yǔ dàoshì Xǔ Mài gòng xiū fúshí,
cǎi yàoshí bù yuǎn qiānlǐ,
biàn yóu Dōngzhōng zhū jùn,
qióng zhū míngshān,
fàn cānghǎi,
tàn yuē:
“Wǒ zú dāng yǐ lè sǐ.”
Xiè Ān cháng wèi Xīzhī yuē:
“Zhōngnián yǐlái,
shāng yú āilè,
yǔ qīnyǒu bié,
zhé zuò shù rì è.”
Xīzhī yuē:
“Nián zài sāngyú,
zìrán zhì cǐ.
Qǐng zhèng lài sīzhú táoxiě,
kǒng ér bèi jué,
sǔn qí huānlè zhī qù.”
Cháotíng yǐ qí shì kǔ,
yì bù fù zhēng zhī.
Shí Liú Tán wèi Dānyáng Yǐn,
Xǔ Xún cháng jiù Tán sù,
chuángwéi xīnlì,
yǐnshí fēnggān.
Xún yuē:
“Ruò cǐ bǎoquán,
shū shèng Dōngshān.”
Tán yuē:
“Qīng ruò zhī jíxiōng yóu rén,
wú ān dé bǎo cǐ.”
Xīzhī zài zuò,
yuē:
“Lìng Cháo Xǔ yù Jì Qì,
dāng wú cǐ yán.”
Èr rén bìng yǒu kuìsè.
Chū,
Xīzhī jì yōuyóu wúshì,
yǔ Lìbù Láng Xiè Wàn shū yuē: Gǔ zhī cí shì zhě huò bèi fà yáng kuáng,
huò zhèshen wèijì,
kěwèi jiān yǐ.
Jīn pú zuò ér huò yì,
suí qí sù xīn,
qí wèi
qìngxìng,
qǐ fēi tiāncì!
Wéi tiān bù xiáng.
Qǐng Dōng yóu huán,
xiū zhí sāngguǒ,
jīn shèng fūróng,
shuài zhū zǐ,
bào ruò sūn,
yóuguān qí jiān,
yǒu yī wèi zhī gān,
gē ér fēn
it,
to amuse myself at present.
Although planting virtue does not differ greatly,
one still wishes to teach and nurture descendants to be earnest and yielding.
Or if one is frivolous,
one hopes to make them count the horses by raising a whip,
resembling the style of Wànshí.
What do you think of this, sir?
Soon I will travel east with Ānshí to the mountains and seas,
simultaneously inspecting the land and its advantages for cultivation,
nurturing leisure.
After food and clothing are provided for,
I wish to frequently enjoy banquets with relatives and friends;
although I cannot utter lofty verses,
holding a cup and drinking deeply,
recounting what has happened in the fields and villages,
will thus serve as material for clapping hands in delight;
as for the satisfaction it brings,
how can it be fully expressed!
I
often model my life on Lù Jiǎ, Bān Sì, and Yáng Wángsūn,
and greatly wish to emulate these several gentlemen;
the old man's aspirations end here.
Wàn later became the Dūdū of Yùzhōu,
and also sent Wàn a letter cautioning him, saying:
"With your extraordinary and disdaining temperament,
to stoop to conform with the multitude of regional governors,
is truly difficult to accept.
However, what is called 'broad understanding'
is precisely to adapt one's actions and retirement to circumstances,
only then can it be far-reaching.
I wish you would always be on par with those of lower status among scholars;
then it will be perfect.
Not eating two dishes,
not sitting on double mats—
what is so special about this?
Yet the ancients considered it a commendable practice.
The success or failure of affairs
truly lies in accumulating small things to achieve great ones;
you should keep this in mind."
Wàn could not follow this advice,
and indeed failed.
He died at the age of fifty-nine,
and was posthumously granted the title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His sons followed their father's prior instructions,
firmly declining the honor.
He had seven sons,
five of whom were well-known.
Xuánzhī died young.
The next was Níngzhī,
who was also skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.
His official career included Jiangzhōu Cìshǐ, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, and Kuàijī Nèishǐ.
The Wáng family had for generations served Zhāng family's Wǔdǒumǐ Dào,
and Níngzhī was even more devout.
When Sūn Ēn attacked Kuàijī,
his subordinates requested preparations be made.
Níngzhī did not comply,
but instead entered the quiet chamber to pray,
then emerged and told his generals and subordinates:
"I have already prayed to the Great Dao,
and it has promised ghost soldiers to assist;
the rebels will defeat themselves."
Since he made no preparations,
he was consequently harmed by Sūn Ēn.
Huīzhī, courtesy name Zǐyóu.
His nature was extraordinary and unrestrained.
He served as Cānjūn to Dà Sīmǎ Huán Wēn;
with disheveled hair and loose belt,
he did not concern himself with the affairs of the office.
He also served as Qíbīng Cānjūn to Chēqí Huán Chōng.
Chōng asked:
"What department do you belong to, sir?"
He replied:
"It seems to be the horse department."
Chōng again asked:
"How many horses do you manage?"
He said:
"If I don't know the horses,
how can I know their number!"
Chōng again asked:
"How many horses have died recently?"
He said:
"If I don't know the living,
how can I know the dead!"
Once, when traveling with Chōng,
they encountered a sudden downpour.
Huīzhī thereupon dismounted and pushed his way into Chōng's carriage,
saying:
"How can Your Excellency monopolize a carriage!"
Chōng once said to Huīzhī:
"You have been in the office for a long time,
it's time to arrange something for you."
Huīzhī initially did not respond,
but simply looked upwards,
propping his cheek with a hand-tablet, saying:
"The western mountains brought some refreshing air this morning."
At that time, there was a scholar-official family in Wúzhōng that had good bamboo.
Desiring to see it,
he went out, sat in his sedan chair, and went under the bamboo,
singing and whistling for a long time.
