The host swept and invited him to sit,
but Huīzhī ignored him.
As he was about to leave,
the host then closed the gate;
Huīzhī then appreciated it this way,
and left in high spirits.
Once, he lived in an empty house,
and immediately ordered bamboo to be planted.
Someone asked him the reason,
Huīzhī merely whistled and sang,
pointing to the bamboo and saying:
"How can one go a day without this gentleman!"
Once, while living in Shānyīn,
after a fresh snowfall,
the moonlight was clear and bright,
and everything visible was a brilliant white.
He drank wine alone and recited Zuǒ Sī's "Zhāo Yǐn Shī",
when he suddenly remembered Dài Kuí.
Kuí was then in Shàn,
so he immediately took a small boat by night to visit him,
arriving after a night's journey.
Upon reaching the gate, he did not enter but turned back.
People asked him the reason,
Huīzhī said:
"I originally went on an impulse,
and when the impulse was gone, I returned.
Why must I see Āndào!"
His nature was elegant and unrestrained,
fond of music and beautiful women.
Once, at night, he and his brother Xiànzhī together read the "Gāoshì Zhuàn Zàn".
Xiànzhī admired Jǐng Dān's noble purity,
but Huīzhī said:
"He is not as good as Chángqīng, who disdained the world."
Such was his broad-mindedness.
People of his time all admired his talent but disliked his conduct.
Later, he served as Huángmén Shìláng,
abandoned his office, and returned east,
falling gravely ill along with Xiànzhī.
At that time, a diviner said:
"If a person's life is destined to end,
but there is a living person willing to substitute,
then the dying person can live."
Huīzhī said to him:
"My talent and position are inferior to my brother's;
please let me substitute with my remaining years."
The diviner said:
"To substitute for the dead,
one must have surplus years of one's own
to make up for the deceased.
Now, both your and your brother's lifespans are exhausted;
how can there be a substitute!"
Not long after,
Xiànzhī died.
Huīzhī rushed to the funeral but did not weep.
He went straight to the spirit bed and sat down,
took Xiànzhī's qín and played it.
After a long time, it was out of tune,
and he sighed:
"Alas, Zǐjìng,
both the person and the qín are gone!"
Thereupon, he fainted.
He had a pre-existing back ailment,
which then worsened and ruptured,
and he too died about a month later.
His son was Zhēnhzhī.
Zhēnhzhī, courtesy name Gōnggàn,
successively held positions such as Shìzhōng and Dà Sīmǎ Chángshǐ.
When Huán Xuán became Tàiwèi,
all the court officials gathered.
He asked Zhēnhzhī:
"How do I compare to your deceased uncle?"
Those present were all stifled with anxiety.
Zhēnhzhī said:
"My deceased uncle was a standard of his time,
Your Excellency is a hero of a thousand years."
Everyone present was pleased.
Cāozhī, courtesy name Zǐzhòng,
successively held positions such as Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, and Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
Xiànzhī’s courtesy name was Zǐjìng.
In his youth, he had a great reputation,
and was lofty and unconstrained.
Even when at leisure all day long,
his demeanor was never negligent.
His elegant style was unmatched at the time.
When he was several years old,
he once observed his retainers playing chūpú,
and said:
“The south wind is not competing.”
A retainer said:
“This young gentleman is also viewing a leopard through a tube,
seeing only a single spot.”
Xiànzhī angrily said:
“I am ashamed to be far inferior to Xún Fèngqiàn,
and recently embarrassed by Liú Zhēncháng.”
Then he brushed his sleeves and left.
He once went with his elder brothers Huīzhī and Cāozhī to visit Xiè Ān.
His two brothers spoke much of worldly affairs,
while Xiànzhī only exchanged greetings.
After they left,
a guest asked Ān about the relative merits of the Wáng family brothers.
Ān said:
“The younger one is superior.”
The guest asked the reason.
Ān said:
“The words of a propitious man are few;
because he spoke little,
I know it.”
He once shared a room with Huīzhī.
Suddenly a fire broke out.
Huīzhī hastily fled,
without time to grab his shoes.
Xiànzhī remained calm in expression,
and slowly called for his attendants to help him out.
One night, as he slept in his study,
a thief entered his room
and stole everything.
Xiànzhī slowly said:
“Thief,
the blue felt mat is an old family possession of mine,
you may specifically leave it.”
The thieves were startled and fled.
He was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and good at painting.
When he was seven or eight years old learning calligraphy,
Xīzhī secretly tried to pull his brush from behind but could not,
and sighed:
“This child will certainly have a great reputation later.”
He once wrote characters on a wall, a square *zhàng* in size.
Xīzhī thought it was very skillful,
and hundreds of people came to see it.
Huán Wēn once asked him to write on a fan.
His brush accidentally slipped,
so he drew a piebald ox,
which was very exquisite.
He started his career as a state chief clerk and secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
then transferred to Assistant,
and was chosen to marry Princess Xīn’ān.
He once passed through Wú Jùn.
Hearing that Gù Pìqiáng had a famous garden,
though previously unacquainted,
he rode a flat-shoulder sedan chair directly inside.
At that time, Pìqiáng was gathering guests and friends.
After Xiànzhī finished touring,
he acted as if no one else was present.
Pìqiáng angrily rebuked him, saying:
“As a host,
this is impolite.
To be arrogant towards scholars based on one’s noble status is
not the proper way.
Lacking these two,
you are not worth mentioning, just a barbarian!”
He then drove him out the gate.
Xiànzhī simply accepted it,
not taking it to heart.
Xiè Ān greatly admired and loved him,
and invited him to be his Chief Clerk.
When Ān was promoted to General Wèi,
he again served as Chief Clerk.
During the Tàiyuán era,
the Tàijí Hall was newly built.
Ān wanted Xiànzhī to inscribe the plaque,
considering it a treasure for ten thousand generations,
but found it difficult to say.
He tentatively said:
“During the Wèi dynasty, the plaque for the Língyún Hall was not yet inscribed,
but the craftsmen mistakenly nailed it up,
and it could not be lowered.
So Wéi Zhòngjiāng was made to hang from a plank to write it.
By the time he finished,
his beard and hair were all white,
and he barely had any breath left.
He returned and told his sons and nephews
that this method should be absolutely forbidden.”
Xiànzhī understood his meaning
and sternly said:
“Zhòngjiāng was
a great minister of Wèi;
how could such a thing happen!
If it were true,
it would be a reason to know that Wèi’s virtue would not last long.”
Ān then did not press him.
Ān also asked:
“How does your calligraphy compare to your honorable father’s?”
He replied:
“They are naturally different.”
Ān said:
“Public opinion does not think so.”
He replied:
“How can people know!”
Soon after, he was appointed General Jiànwēi and Administrator of Wúxīng,
then summoned and appointed Central Secretariat Director.
When Ān died,
there was debate regarding the appropriateness of the posthumous honors.
Only Xiànzhī and Xú Mò jointly affirmed Ān’s loyalty and merit.
Xiànzhī then submitted a memorial, saying:
“The late Grand Tutor, your servant Ān, in his youth promoted the profound philosophy,
and his virtuous reputation spread widely.
In his early twenties, he lived in seclusion,
his resolve matching that of Jī and Hào.
When the time came, he entered officialdom,
and his imperial plans were truly fulfilled.
When he projected his awe-inspiring power,
the powerful and cunning were eliminated.
Once his great merits were established,
he humbly resigned from his post.
Moreover, he served the late emperor,
who held him in high regard even as a commoner.
When Your Majesty ascended the throne,
still young and vigorous,
he dedicated his heart and wisdom to assist the sagely ruler.
Examining his actions from obscurity to prominence, from beginning to end,
his sincere emotions and deep attachment,
he was truly an outstanding assistant to the great Jìn,
his righteousness more profound than that of former ministers.
I humbly ask Your Majesty to pay attention to your eminent ministers,
and clear your mind in scrutiny.”
Emperor Xiàowǔ then bestowed extraordinary honors upon Ān.
Not long after,
Xiànzhī fell ill.
His family performed a Daoist ritual (shàng zhāng),
which required him to confess his faults.
They asked him what mistakes he had made.
He replied:
“I don’t recall anything else,
only remember divorcing the Xī family.”
Xiànzhī’s former wife
was Xī Tán’s daughter.
Soon after, he died in office.
When Empress Ānxī was established,
as her father, he was posthumously granted Attendant-in-ordinary, Special Advanced, Grand Master of Guanglu, Grand Preceptor,
with the posthumous title Xiàn.
He had no son,
so his nephew Jìngzhī succeeded him,
reaching the position of Administrator of Yìxīng.
At the time, commentators believed that no one in the Jiāngzuǒ central court
could surpass Xīzhī’s cursive and clerical scripts,
and that Xiànzhī’s bone structure was far inferior to his father’s,
though he possessed a certain charming appeal.
Huán Xuán was very fond of the father and son’s calligraphy,
making a scroll for each,
and keeping them by his side to admire.
Initially, Xīzhī’s companion in travels was Xǔ Mài.
Xǔ Mài’s courtesy name was Shūxuán,
also named Yìng.
He was from Dānyáng Jùróng.
His family had been scholarly for generations,
but Mài was quiet and calm from a young age,
and had no ambition for official career.
Before reaching twenty,
he once visited Guō Pú.
Pú cast a divination for him,
receiving *Tài* changing to *Dàxù*,
with its top six lines activated.
Pú said:
“Your great auspiciousness comes from heaven;
you should learn the way of ascending to immortality.”
At that time, the Administrator of Nánhǎi, Bào Jìng, was living in seclusion,
and no one knew his whereabouts.
Mài then went to visit him,
and explored his most essential teachings.
His parents were still alive,
and he was reluctant to abandon them.
He believed that Xuánliú Mountain in Yúháng, being close to Máoshān in Yánlíng,
was the western gate of Dòngtíng,
secretly connected to the Five Sacred Mountains.
Chén Ānshì and Máo Jìwěi often frequented it.
So he built a hermitage at Xuánliú,
and traveled to and from the cave chambers of Máolǐng.
He abandoned worldly affairs
to seek the path of immortality,
only returning home on the first and fifteenth of the lunar month to pay respects to his parents.
After his parents passed away,
he sent his wife Sūn back to her family,
and then traveled with like-minded companions to tour famous mountains.
Initially, while gathering herbs on Huánshān in Tónglú County,
he consumed 'zhú' for three years,
intending to abstain from grains.
Since this mountain was close to people,
he could not concentrate.
He fenced off all four sides.
Those who loved the Way and wished to see him
would ascend a tower and speak with him,
taking pleasure in this.
He regularly practiced breath control,
one breath lasting over a thousand exhalations.
In the second year of Yǒnghé (346 CE),
he moved to Xīshān in Lín'ān,
climbing cliffs and eating 'zhī'.
He felt utterly content and free,
with the ambition to remain there permanently.
So he changed his name to Xuán,
and his courtesy name to Yuǎnyóu.
He wrote a farewell letter to his wife,
and also composed twelve poems,
discussing matters of immortals.
Wáng Xīzhī visited him,
never failing to forget to return home for entire days,
and they formed a friendship transcending the mundane world.
Xuán sent a letter to Xīzhī saying:
"From the south of Shānyīn to Lín'ān,
there are many golden halls and jade chambers,
immortals and 'zhī' herbs.
The likes of Zuǒ Yuánfàng
and all the Daoist practitioners of the late Hàn dynasty are all there."
Xīzhī personally wrote a biography for him,
recounting many miraculous deeds,
too numerous to detail.
After this, no one knew Xuán's final whereabouts,
and all who loved the Way said he had 'feathered and ascended' (become an immortal).
The edict states: The rise of writing
began in the middle antiquity.
Rope patterns and bird tracks
are not worth much observation.
In later generations, people abandoned simplicity for embellishment,
unfurling scrolls and dipping brushes,
competing to boast and praise each other,
contending in their skill or clumsiness.
Bóyīng's marvelous calligraphy by the pond
left no remaining traces;
Shīyí's wondrous hanging curtain
rarely left relics.
It is only from Zhōng and Wáng onwards
that we can speak of it.
Although Zhōng excelled in his time,
he was also exceptionally brilliant.
However, regarding his absolute perfection,
there might be some doubts.
As for distributing thick and thin strokes,
and differentiating sparse and dense,
like rosy clouds unfurling and swirling,
there was nothing amiss.
But his style was ancient rather than modern,
and his characters were long and exceeded the standard.
Speaking of his overall stature,
this is considered a flaw.
Xiànzhī, though inheriting his father's style,
was far from novel or ingenious.
Observing his calligraphic posture, it is sparse and thin,
like a withered tree in deep winter;
examining his brushwork, it is constrained,
like a starved slave in a strict household.
His withered tree,
though gnarled, lacks pliability;
his starved slave
is bound and weak, not unrestrained.
Combining these two,
are these not the ailments of his calligraphy!
Zǐyún, a recent talent,
gained fame south of the Yangtze,
yet he merely achieved legibility in writing,
lacking the spirit of a true man.
His lines are like wriggling spring earthworms,
his characters like coiled autumn snakes;
Wáng Méng lies dormant within his paper,
Xú Yǎn sits beneath his brush;
even if a thousand rabbit hairs were worn bald,
there would be not a single sinew;
even if ten thousand valleys of animal skin were exhausted,
there would be not half a bone;
to spread fame with this,
is it not an undeserved reputation!
These several individuals
all have reputations exceeding their reality.
Therefore, after careful observation of ancient and modern,
and meticulous study of seals and plain silk,
the one who achieved utmost perfection and beauty
is none other than Wáng Yìshǎo!
Observing the skill of his dots and strokes,
the marvelousness of his composition,
like misty clouds and dewdrops congealing,
appearing broken yet connected;
phoenixes soaring and dragons coiling,
their force seeming oblique yet turning straight.
Playing with it, one never tires;
gazing at it, one cannot discern its beginning or end.
To admire it in one's heart and pursue it with one's hand,
this person alone is worthy.
As for the rest of those insignificant individuals,
what are they worth discussing!
Collation Notes
Biography 51 Wáng Xùn
Wáng Xùn, courtesy name Shàobó,
was a native of Wèixīng.
He served in the commandery, was selected as Xiàolián,
became the director of the Bureau of Personnel,
then was promoted to General of the Palace Guard,
and successively rose to Administrator of Shàngluò.
He had private cattle and horses that produced colts and calves in the commandery;
when his term of office expired, he handed them all over to the government,
saying they were produced within the commandery.
He was then transferred to become Administrator of Wèixīng.
At the end of Emperor Huì's reign,
the southwestern Yi tribes rebelled.
The Inspector of Níngzhōu, Lǐ Yì, died,
and over a hundred people in the city defended it with Yì's daughter for more than a year.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (310 CE),
Zhìzhōng Máomèng went to the capital to seek an Inspector,
but was not acknowledged.
Mèng earnestly pleaded:
"Your lord has died, your kinsman is dead,
imprisoned in a desolate city.
Crying out in sorrow from ten thousand li,
you show no pity or rescue.
I am ashamed to lack Bāo Xú's feeling of weeping to Qín,
and also regretful to lack Liáng Qī's proof of the city collapsing.
To exist is worse than to perish,
I beg you to grant me death."
The court pitied him,
and appointed Xùn as Commandant of the Southern Yi and Inspector of Níngzhōu,
ordering him to proceed to the garrison from his commandery.
Xùn and Mèng traveled together,
encountered bandits on the way,
and arrived only after more than a year.
Externally besieged by Lǐ Xióng,
and internally by Yi bandits,
officials and soldiers scattered and perished,
cities and towns lay in ruins.
Xùn cleared the wilderness, rallied the scattered,
relied solely on his power and severe penalties,
whipping people of different customs.
Before Xùn arrived in the province,
he remotely nominated Dǒng Lián as Xiùcái (Filial and Incorrupt).
The Commander of Jiànníng, Zhōu Yuè, said Lián was not talented,
and refused to issue the official announcement.
Once Xùn arrived,
he arrested Yuè and killed him.
Yuè's younger brother secretly plotted to kill Xùn,
and install Zhào Hùn's son Táo, the former Administrator of Jiànníng, as Inspector in his place.
The matter was discovered,
and they were all executed.
He also executed dozens of prominent families who did not adhere to the law.
He campaigned against various Yi tribes,
capturing and beheading thousands,
and acquiring tens of thousands of horses, cattle, and sheep.
Consequently, no one failed to submit,
and his authority spread throughout the Níng territory.
He also sent his son Chéng to present a memorial advising Emperor Yuán to ascend the throne.
The Emperor praised him,
and successively promoted him to Palace Attendant, General Who Pacifies the South, with honorary 'jié' authority,
his titles of Commandant and Inspector remaining as before,
and granted him the peerage of Duke of Bāozhōng County.
Xùn, deeming the terrain strategically convenient,
petitioned to divide Zāngkē into Píngyí Commandery,
Zhūtí into Nánguǎng Commandery,
Jiànníng into Yèláng Commandery,
and Yǒngchāng into Liángshuǐ Commandery.
He also renamed Yìzhōu Commandery to Jìnnníng Commandery,
and all these measures were implemented.
Previously,
the Administrator of Yuèkuì, Lǐ Zhāo, had been captured by Lǐ Xióng.
After escaping from Shǔ, he returned,
and Xùn reinstated Zhāo as Administrator of Yuèkuì.
Lǐ Xióng sent Lǐ Xiāng and Rèn Huí to attack Zhāo.
Zhāo and Wáng Zài, Administrator of Hànjiā, resisted them from Nánqín.
They fought at Wēnshuǐ,
and Zhāo was defeated.
Zài then surrendered his two commanderies to Xióng.
Later, Xiāng and others again crossed the Lúshuǐ to raid Níngzhōu.
Xùn sent Generals Yáo Chóng
and Cuàn Chēn to resist them.
They fought at Tángláng,
and severely defeated Xiāng and his forces.
Chóng pursued them to the Lúshuǐ,
where over a thousand people drowned.
Chóng, fearing the distance, did not dare to cross the water.
Xùn, believing Chóng had not pursued far enough,
angrily imprisoned the commanders,
seized Chóng,
and whipped him.
His rage was so intense
that his hair stood on end, piercing his cap,
and the cap split.
He died that night.
Sùn was in the province for fourteen years.
The people of the province again established Sùn's middle son, Jiān, to manage provincial affairs.
An imperial edict appointed Jiān as Nányí Xiàowèi and Níngzhōu Cìshǐ, with the authority to "hold a marshal's staff" (jiǎjié).
Sùn was posthumously given the epithet Zhuàng.
Táo Kǎn feared that Jiān would not be able to contend with the people of Shǔ.
Towards the end of Tàiníng,
he submitted a memorial recommending Yǐn Fèng, the Prefect of Línglíng, as the Prefect of Níngzhōu,
and summoned Jiān back to the capital.
Jiān died of illness.
His elder brother, Chéng, inherited the title.
He successively served as Prefect of Wèixīng and Sànqí Chángshì.
Cài Bào.
Cài Bào, courtesy name Shìxuān,
was a native of Yǔchéng, Chénliú.
His great-grandfather, Zhì,
was a Wèi Wèiwèi during the Hàn dynasty,
and an uncle of Zuǒzhōnglángjiàng Yōng.
His grandfather, Mù,
was a Wèi Shàngshū.
His father, Hóng,
was Prefect of Yīnpíng.
Bào possessed spirit and capability.
He successively served as Hénán Chéng,
and Prefect of Chánglè and Qīnghé.
Fleeing the chaos, he crossed south.
Yuándì appointed him Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn and Prefect of Línchuái,
then promoted him to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Originally,
when Zǔ Tì was Xúzhōu,
Bào was his Sīmǎ,
and Zǔ Tì had always held Bào in low regard.
Now,
Zǔ Tì was Yùzhōu,
and Bào was Xúzhōu,
both entrusted with military campaigns.
Zǔ Tì felt greatly ashamed of this.
At this time, Xú Kān, the Prefect of Tàishān, and Líu Xiá, the Interior Scribe of Péngchéng, together attacked the rebel Zhou Fǔ at Hánshān.
Kān's general Yú Yào beheaded Fǔ.
When merits were discussed,
Xiá was placed first.
Kān was enraged
and rebelled from Tàishān,
styling himself Ānběi Jiāngjūn and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
He attacked and captured Hóu Shǐmáo, the Prefect of Dōngguǎn, and occupied his fortified camp.
Shí Jìlóng attacked him.
Kān, in fear,
sought to surrender.
Yuándì granted his request.
Soon after, he rebelled again and returned to Shí Lè.
Lè dispatched his generals Wáng Fúdū
and Zhāng Jǐng, with several hundred cavalry, to assist Kān.
An imperial edict ordered Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yáng Jiàn, Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn Hóu Lǐ, Línchuái Tàishǒu Líu Xiá, the Xiānbēi Duàn Wényāng, and others to jointly attack him with Bào.
The generals feared the difficulty
and halted their troops at Xiàpī,
not daring to advance.
Bào wanted to advance,
but Jiàn firmly refused.
Kān sent envoys to request aid from Lè.
Lè declined, citing external difficulties,
and demanded many things from Kān.
Furthermore, Wáng Fúdū and others molested his household.
Kān knew Lè would not rescue him,
and also suffered from the rampant violence of Fúdū and others.
He then killed them
and again sought to surrender.
Yuándì detested his repeated vacillation
and did not accept.
He ordered Bào and Jiàn to promptly advance and attack.
Jiàn, Líu Xiá, and others were all suspicious and hesitant, not listening to each other,
and each submitted memorials.
Therefore, Bào was unable to advance for a long time.
Shàngshūlìng Diāo Xié presented a memorial, stating:
"We, your subjects, humbly believe that the Huáiběi campaign has already lost the advantage of speed.
Now it is the height of summer,
and to brave crossing mountains and dangers,
where the mountain people are skilled with bows and arrows
and familiar with the terrain,
one person guarding a pass
cannot be matched by a hundred men.
Moreover, transport and supply are extremely difficult.
If provisions run out one morning,
it will no longer be something that can be defended by wisdom or strength.
The Shu says, 'It is better to lead people
than to be led by people.'
It is advisable to halt the troops where they are,
build strong fortifications,
and if the situation is not resolved by autumn,
then advance with the main army."
The imperial edict stated:
"To retreat when one knows the difficulty
certainly accords with the words of military strategists.
However, although the minor rebels are cunning,
they are still easy to capture.
To retreat before fighting
and to destroy one's own morale first
is also something forbidden in ancient times.
Moreover, Shào Cún has already occupied the rebel's stronghold,
and his prestige and power are already established;
he cannot retreat even one step."
Thereupon, Zhìshū Yùshǐ Hǎo Gǔ was sent as an acting governor (xíngtái)
to urge and supervise them to advance and attack.
Bào wanted to advance directly,
but Jiàn firmly refused to allow it.
Xié again memorialized to dismiss Jiàn from office,
entrusting Bào to be the vanguard,
assigning Jiàn's troops to him,
and demoting Jiàn's title to Zhéichōng Jiāngjūn,
to hold him accountable for future performance.
Bào advanced to occupy Biànchéng,
intending to pressure Kān.
At that time, Shí Jìlóng was stationed at Jùpíng
and was about to attack Bào.
Bào fled during the night
and retreated to guard Xiàpī.
Xú Kān attacked and seized Bào's baggage train at Tánqiū.
Generals Líu Chǒng and Lù Dǎng fought bravely
and died.
After Bào's defeat,
he intended to return to apologize for his crime.
Běizhōngláng Wáng Shū stopped him,
saying:
"The Hu barbarians are about to arrive.
Sir, you should temporarily take charge of your duties
to protect the common people.
It will not be too late
to apologize after the bandits retreat."
Bào followed his advice.
Yuándì heard of Bào's retreat
and sent an order to apprehend him.
When the envoy arrived,
Wáng Shū, at night, surrounded Bào with troops.
Bào thought it was another difficulty
and led his subordinates to attack them.
He stopped only when he heard there was an imperial edict.
Shū seized Bào
and sent him to Jiànkāng,
where he was beheaded,
and his corpse was displayed in the marketplace for three days.
He was fifty-two years old at the time.
While Bào was in Xú land,
he internally pacified his officers and soldiers
and externally embraced all the people.
He gained the affection of both near and far,
and many lamented and regretted his death
upon hearing of it.
He had no sons.
His elder brother's son, Yì, courtesy name Yuánzǐ,
served as Sànqí Chángshì, Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, and Gāoyáng Xiānghóu.
Yīn Hào launched a northern expedition
and ordered Yì to lead troops out of Péngchéng.
He died in the army.
Yáng Jiàn.
Yáng Jiàn, courtesy name Jǐngqī,
was a native of Tàishān.
His father, Jì,
was Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng.
His elder brother, Wěi,
successively served as Tàipú and Cìshǐ of Yǎn and Xú provinces.
Jiàn served as Prefect of Dōngyáng,
and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ.
At that time, Xú Kān rebelled.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo, believing Jiàn was a prominent figure from Kān's home province
and would surely be able to control him,
requested to send him on a northern campaign.
Jiàn strongly declined, saying his talent was not for a general.
Tàiwèi Xī Jiàn also memorialized, stating that Jiàn was not capable
and should not be recklessly employed.
Wáng Dǎo did not accept this
and forcefully memorialized to grant him the command of the Zhēngtǎo Dūdū.
Indeed, he suffered a defeat.
Wáng Dǎo, having recommended an incapable person,
requested to demote himself,
but the Emperor did not comply.
The judicial authorities sought to impose the death penalty on Jiàn.
Yuándì decreed that because Jiàn was related to the Grand Consort's family,
he was specially pardoned from death
and stripped of his name.
After a long time,
he became Shàofǔ.
When Wáng Dùn rebelled,
Míngdì, knowing Jiàn was Dùn's maternal uncle
and had always been closely associated with him,
subtly held him accountable.
When Chéngdì ascended the throne,
Jiàn participated in the suppression of Sū Jùn.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Xiànhóu,
transferred to Guānglùxūn,
and died.
Líu Yìn.
Líu Yìn, courtesy name Chéngyìn,
was a native of Yè, Dōnglái,
and a descendant of Hán Qí Dàohuì Wáng Féi.
He had a handsome appearance,
was good at self-promotion and seeking favorable treatment,
and formed connections with the powerful figures of his time.
His name was renowned throughout the Hǎidài region,
and all scholars admired him.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng
and invited to be a Sīkōng Yuàn,
but did not accept either.
At this time, the world was in great chaos.
Liú Yìn carried his mother, intending to flee to Liáodōng to escape the troubles.
Passing through Yōuzhōu on the way,
the Inspector Wáng Jùn retained Yìn,
and memorialized to have him appointed as Administrator of Bóhǎi.
When Jùn was defeated,
Yìn went to rely on Shào Xù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Xù's followers were few and weak,
and he considered surrendering to Shí Lè.
Yìn spoke to Xù, saying:
“Tán Dān and Bāo Xú
were mere minor officials of Qí and Chǔ,
yet they were able to preserve states that had been extinguished
and restore kingdoms that had been lost.
Now, general, you wield a force of elite troops,
and occupy a completely victorious city.
How can you throw away a success on the verge of achievement for the sake of a single basketful,
and abandon loyal and trustworthy people to jackals and wolves?
Moreover, Xiàng Yǔ and Yuán Shào were not weak,
yet Gāozǔ wore a plain white cap,
and people responded like an echo;
Cáo Gōng supported the emperor,
and the regional lords were pacified and harmonious.
Why is this?
It is because the principles of rectitude and rebellion differ,
and the natural course of events is fixed.
Furthermore, these barbarian and Rong ugly creatures,
a gathering of ruffians,
though they may have the multitude of dogs and sheep,
will ultimately face the calamity of the butcher's block.
To wish to take root and form alliances with them,
is it not indeed perilous!”
Xù said:
“If it is as you say,
what plan should we adopt then?”
Yìn said:
“King Lángxié, with his sagely virtue and brilliant clarity,
has established his foundation south of the Yangtze.
The flourishing restoration of the dynasty can be awaited with eager anticipation.
Now, for your plan, general,
there is nothing better than to uphold the great principle of rectitude to stir the hearts of righteous gentlemen,
and to serve the loyal and upright to inspire the will of the soldiers.
Matters of strategy should be kept secret,
and when the time comes, it is difficult to go against it.
Survival or ruin, rise or fall,
depends on this single action.”
Xù followed his advice,
and thereupon killed several dissenters,
and dispatched envoys to Jiangnán.
The imperial court praised this.
Yìn then requested to go himself,
and Xù generously sent him off.
Upon his arrival,
Emperor Yuán appointed him as Aide to the Chancellor,
and he was successively promoted to Secretariat Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
Yìn heard that Shí Jìlóng was attacking Yàncì,
and spoke to Emperor Yuán, saying:
“All the northern regional commanders have fallen,
only Shào Xù remains.
If this gentleman is controlled by Jìlóng,
it will isolate the hearts of righteous gentlemen,
and block the path to return to the homeland.
I humbly suggest that we should preserve and rescue him.”
Emperor Yuán was about to send aid,
but then Xù had already fallen, and so it stopped.
Wáng Dūn had always been close with Yìn,
and greatly admired and valued him,
and invited him to be Right Chief Clerk.
Yìn knew that Dūn harbored disloyal intentions,
and feigned illness to avoid official duties.
Because of this, he offended Dūn,
and was sent out as Administrator of Yùzhāng.
He declined, citing illness,
and an imperial edict allowed him to receive the seal and ribbon at home.
Mò Hóng, a man from the commandery,
was a powerful local clan leader in the southern region.
Taking advantage of the chaos,
he killed his local magistrate,
and acted with unrestrained arrogance and lawlessness.
The common people suffered greatly from him.
Upon Yìn's arrival,
he executed Hóng and other influential local tyrants,
and the region became orderly.
At the beginning of Xiánhé,
he was appointed Army Commander of Píngnán,
and additionally granted Palace Attendant.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Wēn Jiǎo led his forces down,
leaving Yìn and others to guard Pénkǒu.
When the rebellion was suppressed,
he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Fēngchéng for his meritorious service.
Soon after, he replaced Jiǎo as General of Píngnán, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Jiāngzhōu, concurrently Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, and was granted a symbol of imperial authority.
Yìn's position and responsibility grew higher,
and his arrogance and extravagance increased daily.
He indulged in wine and pleasure,
neglecting official duties,
and accumulated vast wealth,
with commercial ventures worth millions.
Initially,
when Yìn replaced Jiǎo,
everyone far and near considered it an unsuitable choice.
Táo Kǎn and Xī Jiàn both said that Yìn was not a talent for a regional governor,
but the imperial court did not listen.
Someone asked Wáng Yuè:
“Now, after this great calamity,
the discipline and order are lax.
From Jiānglíng to Jiànkāng, over three thousand lí,
tens of thousands of displaced people
are scattered in Jiāngzhōu.
Jiāngzhōu
is the southern frontier of the state,
a strategically vital area.
Yet Yìn, with his extravagant nature,
lies dormant facing it.
If there is no external change,
there will certainly be internal trouble.”
Yuè said:
“I heard that Wēn Píngnán told our family's Duke,
that he repeatedly had bad dreams,
and wished to see a replacement.
Soon after, he said that Liú Yìn could be used.
This was Wēn's intention,
not our family's Duke's.”
At this time, the imperial court was empty and depleted,
and officials received no salaries.
They relied solely on the grain transport from Jiāngzhōu.
However, Yìn's commercial caravans lined the roads,
sacrificing public good for private gain.
The relevant authorities memorialized to dismiss Yìn from office.
The imperial decree had just been issued,
when Yìn was murdered by Guō Mò,
at the age of forty-nine.
His son, Chìsōng, inherited his title,
married Princess Nánpíng,
and reached the positions of Court Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and Administrator of Yìxīng.
Huán Xuān (clan nephew Yī)
Huán Xuān was
a native of Zhì, Qiáoguó.
His grandfather, Xǔ, was Administrator of Yìyáng.
His father, Bì, was Chief Clerk of Champion General.
Xuān was open, helpful, sincere, and simple,
and served as Aide to the Chancellor for Emperor Yuán.
At that time, Zhāng Píng, a commander of fortified villages, proclaimed himself Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and Fán Yǎ styled himself Administrator of Qiáojùn.
Each occupied a city,
with several thousand followers.
The emperor, considering Xuān to be trustworthy,
and also that he was from the same commandery as Píng and Yǎ,
transferred Xuān to be a Staff Officer,
and sent him to see
Píng and Yǎ.
Píng and Yǎ sent their army commander and registrar to follow Xuān to the Chancellor's residence to receive instructions.
The emperor
appointed them all as Generals of the Fourth Rank,
and assigned them to their respective areas
to defend against the north.
Wáng Hán, General of Nánzhōng, invited Xuān to be his Staff Officer.
A short while later,
the Inspector of Yùzhōu, Zǔ Tì, moved his garrison to Lúzhōu.
He sent his Staff Officer Yīn Yì to pacify Píng and Yǎ.
Yì slighted Píng,
looked at his house,
and said he would take it to make a stable.
Seeing a large cauldron,
he wanted to melt it down to make iron tools.
Píng said:
"This is a great cauldron for emperors.
It should only be used after the world is settled.
How can you smash it!"
Yì said:
"Can you even keep your head?
Yet you pity a great cauldron!"
Píng was greatly enraged,
and executed Yì on the spot.
He then relied on his army to hold out in defense.
More than a year later,
Zǔ Tì attacked and killed Píng.
Yǎ, meanwhile, occupied Qiáochéng.
Zǔ Tì, whose forces were weak,
sought help from Hán.
Hán sent Xuān with five hundred soldiers to assist Zǔ Tì.
Zǔ Tì said to Xuān:
"You have already spoken to Píng and Yǎ previously,
and your trustworthiness and righteousness are well-known to them.
Now, please speak to Yǎ again for me.
If Yǎ surrenders,
I will promote him,
not just spare his life."
Xuān again went alone on horseback with two men to see Yǎ.
He said:
"Zǔ Tì is determined to pacify and eliminate these two rebels,
and he always relies on you for support.
The previous incident with Yīn's insolence
was not the intention of the Inspector of Yùzhōu.
If you reconcile now,
you can establish loyal service,
and wealth and honor can be preserved.
If you remain stubborn,
the Eastern Government will ferociously dispatch a fierce general.
With your motley crew,
relying on a desperate city,
strong bandits will spy on you from the north,
and the state will attack you from the south.
There is no chance of survival.
I urge you to consider this carefully."
Yǎ and Xuān shared wine and formed a friendship,
and Yǎ sent his son with Xuān to see Zǔ Tì.
A few days later,
Yǎ himself went to see Zǔ Tì.
Zǔ Tì sent Yǎ back to pacify his troops.
The people under Yǎ all said that they had previously cursed and insulted Zǔ Tì many times,
and feared punishment, so they dared not surrender.
Yǎ again closed the city and defended himself.
Zǔ Tì went to attack him,
and again sent Xuān to persuade Yǎ.
Yǎ immediately executed those who disagreed with him,
and then surrendered.
Not long after,
Shí Lè's detached general besieged Qiáochéng.
Hán again sent Xuān to lead troops to rescue Zǔ Tì,
but the bandits retreated before he arrived.
Zǔ Tì kept Xuān to subdue the unyielding,
and he defeated them all.
He was promoted to Internal Administrator of Qiáoguó.
When Zǔ Yuē abandoned Qiáochéng,
Xuān submitted a memorial in remonstrance,
but it was not followed.
Because of this, Shí Lè then took Chénliú.
When Zǔ Yuē rebelled with Sū Jùn,
Xuān said to Zǔ Zhì:
"Now the powerful Hu barbarians have not been eliminated,
and we should unite our strength to suppress them.
Instead, you rebel with Sū Jùn.
How can this last long!
If you, my lord, wish to be a hegemon,
why not assist the state in suppressing Sū Jùn,
and your prestige and fame will naturally rise."
Zǔ Zhì and others could not adopt his advice.
Xuān wanted to remonstrate with Zǔ Yuē,
and sent his son Róng to request an audience with Zǔ Yuē.
Zǔ Yuē knew that Xuān would surely remonstrate,
and refused to see him.
Xuān then resisted Zǔ Yuē,
and did not join him.
Chén Guāng, a man from Shàolíng, led several hundred households of his tribe to surrender to Xuān.
Xuān comforted and settled them all.
When Zǔ Yuē returned to Lìyáng,
Xuān, with several thousand households, intended to move south to Xúnyáng,
and encamped at Mǎtóushān.
At this time, Zǔ Huàn intended to raid Pénkǒu,
and Táo Kǎn sent Máo Bǎo to rescue it.
Zǔ Huàn sent his troops to attack Xuān.
Xuān sent Róng to seek help from Máo Bǎo.
Máo Bǎo attacked Zǔ Huàn
and defeated him.
Xuān then submitted to Wēn Jiǎo.
Wēn Jiǎo appointed Róng as a Staff Officer.
When the rebellion was pacified,
Xuān resided in Wǔchāng,
and Róng again served as Staff Officer to Liú Yìn.
Guō Mò harmed Liú Yìn,
and again appointed Róng as Staff Officer.
When Táo Kǎn attacked Guō Mò,
Guō Mò sent Róng to seek help from Xuān.
Xuān pretended to agree.
Guō Yuè, the Administrator of Xīyáng, and Liú Xǔ, the Administrator of Wǔchāng, both suspected Xuān of colluding with Guō Mò.
Wáng Suí, the Western Chief Clerk of Yùzhōu, said:
"Xuān even betrayed Zǔ Yuē,
how could he collude with Guō Mò!"
Guō Yuè and Liú Xǔ then sent Wáng Suí to Xuān to observe him.
Wáng Suí said to Xuān:
"Although your excellency's intentions are not so,
there is no way to prove yourself
other than by entrusting Róng to me."
Xuān then sent Róng to go with Wáng Suí to welcome Táo Kǎn.
Táo Kǎn appointed Róng as an Aide,
and recommended Xuān as Administrator of Wǔchāng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Supervisor of the Mianzhong Military Affairs, Vice General of the South, and Governor of Jiāngxià.
Shí Lè's Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Guō Jìng, garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Táo Kǎn sent his son, Píngxī Staff Officer Bīn, with Xuān to attack Fánchéng,
and they captured it.
Lǐ Yáng, the Administrator of Jìnglíng, also defeated Xīnyě.
Guō Jìng was frightened
and fled.
Xuān and Lǐ Yáng then pacified Xiāngyáng.
Táo Kǎn made Xuān garrison it,
and established Yìchéng Commandery with his troops from the southern Huáinán region.
Xuān recruited and appeased the newly surrendered,
encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
simplified punishments,
and minimized formalities.
Sometimes he carried hoes and plows in his small carriage,
and sometimes personally weeded and harvested in the fields.
Over ten years,
Shí Jìlóng twice sent cavalry to attack him.
Xuān was able to win the hearts of the people,
and each time defended with outnumbered forces.
Commentators considered him second only to Zǔ Tì and Zhōu Fǎng.
Táo Kǎn was about to send Xuān north to serve in the Central Plains,
but Táo Kǎn died.
Later, Yú Liàng became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and planned a northern expedition.
He appointed Xuān as Supervisor of the Miǎnběi Vanguard Expeditionary Military Affairs, General Who Pacifies the North, Inspector of Sīzhōu, with temporary imperial authority,
garrisoned at Xiāngyáng.
Shí Jìlóng sent seven thousand cavalry to cross the Miǎn River and attack him.
Yú Liàng sent his Sīmǎ Wáng Qiānqī and General Who Assists the State Máo Bǎo to rescue Xuān.
The bandits dug tunnels on three sides to attack the city.
Xuān recruited brave elites,
caught them by surprise,
killed and wounded several hundred,
and captured many armors and horses.
The bandits lifted the siege and fled.
After a long time,
Xuān sent infantry and cavalry to collect over eight thousand people from the Nányáng commanderies who had been captured by the bandits, and returned them.
Yú Yì replaced Yú Liàng,
and intended to commit all national forces to a northern expedition.

He again appointed Xuān as Supervisor of the Military Affairs of the three prefectures of Sī, Liáng, and Yōng, and the four commanderies of Nányáng, Xiāngyáng, Xīnyě, and Nánxiāng in Jīngzhōu, Inspector of Liángzhōu, with imperial credentials,
and his general rank remained unchanged.
For his cumulative merits,
he was enfeoffed as a male of Jìnglíng County.
Xuān had long been in Xiāngyáng,
and his pacification and appeasement of both migrants and locals
were highly praised.
When Yú Yì moved his garrison to Xiāngyáng,
he ordered Xuān to advance and attack Shí Jìlóng's general Lǐ Pí.
His army reached Dānshuǐ,
and was defeated by the bandits.
Yú Yì was angry
and demoted Xuān to General Who Establishes Might,
ordering him to move his garrison to Xiànshān.
Xuān lost both his reputation and real power,
and moreover, was old and ill.
At that time, Wáng Qiānqī, the Colonel of the Southern Man, was guarding Jiānglíng,
and requested to be replaced due to illness.
Yú Yì appointed Xuān as General Who Guards the South and Administrator of Nánjùn,
to replace Wáng Qiānqī.
Xuān was discontented,
and before taking up his post,
he died of vexation.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Who Guards the South.
Róng rose to the office of Administrator of Xīnyě.
Yī's courtesy name was Shūxià.
His father, Jǐng,
had talents and capabilities fit for his age,
and served as Attendant, Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, General of the Central Army, Protector-General, and Marquis of Chángshè.
Afterwards, Chén Mǐn (陳敏) started a rebellion.
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) was then stationed in Jiāngxià (江夏).
Sī (伺) was good at naval warfare
and skilled in building ships.
So Kǎn (侃) sent Sī (伺) to build large ships.
Sī (伺) was appointed commander of the Left Vanguard.
He positioned himself at the mouth of the river
and crushed Mǐn's (敏) vanguard.
Mǐn's (敏) younger brother Huī (恢) proclaimed himself Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州)
and was in Wǔchāng (武昌).
Kǎn (侃) led Sī (伺) and other armies to advance and attack him,
defeating him.
After Mǐn (敏) and Huī (恢) were pacified,
Sī (伺) was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu (亭侯) for his meritorious service
and appointed as the Commander of Cavalry.
At that time, barbarian bandits from Xīyáng (西陽) plundered Jiāngxià (江夏).
The Administrator Yáng Mín (楊珉) often invited commanders to discuss strategies to repel the bandits,
but Sī (伺) alone remained silent.
Mín (珉) said:
"Why does General Zhū (朱) not speak?"
Sī (伺) replied:
"Others fight bandits with their tongues,
but Sī (伺) fights only with strength."
Mín (珉) again asked:
"General, in your previous engagements with bandits,
why have you always been victorious?"
Sī (伺) said:
"When two enemies confront each other,
one must simply endure.
If they cannot endure,
but I can,
that is why I win."
Mín (珉) laughed heartily.
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Shí Lè (石勒) captured Jiāngxià (江夏).
Sī (伺) and Yáng Mín (楊珉) fled to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
When Táo Kǎn (陶侃) came to garrison Xiàkǒu (夏口),
Sī (伺) joined him
and was promoted to General of Inspiring Awe.
He followed Kǎn (侃) in campaigning against Dù Tāo (杜弢)
and performed exceptional service.
The details are in Kǎn's (侃) biography.
In the Battle of Xiàkǒu (夏口),
Sī (伺) wore an iron mask for self-protection
and used a crossbow to shoot several bandit chieftains,
killing them all.
The bandits pulled their boats ashore
and formed a battle array by the water.
Sī (伺) pursued them up and down the water to intercept them.
An arrow struck his shin,
but his expression did not change.
Soon, the other armies arrived,
and the bandits scattered.
They were pursued and attacked,
abandoning their boats and throwing themselves into the water.
More than half of them died.
The bandits returned to Chángshā (長沙) by night.
Sī (伺) pursued them to Púqí (蒲圻)
but failed to catch them and returned.
He was promoted to General of Inspiring Distant Awe
and granted red banners and curved canopies.
During the Jiànxīng (建興) era,
Chén Shēng (陳聲) led more than two thousand rogue families to block the river and plunder.
Kǎn (侃) sent Sī (伺) as the Dūhù (督護) to attack Shēng (聲).
Although Shēng's (聲) forces were few,
Sī (伺) tolerated them without attacking,
requesting that Shēng (聲) send his younger brother to Kǎn (侃) to surrender.
Sī (伺) outwardly agreed.
When Shēng's (聲) brother left,
Sī (伺) then sent elite warriors to ambush and execute Shēng's (聲) brother,
then secretly moved his army to attack Shēng (聲).
On New Year's Day, Shēng (聲) and his men were all out offering sacrifices and feasting.
Sī's (伺) army entered their gates
before they realized it.
Shēng's (聲) generals Yán Jìn (閻晉) and Zhèng Jìn (鄭進) both fought to the death.
Many of Sī's (伺) soldiers were wounded,
so he returned to his camp.
Shēng (聲) fled east,
securing Dǒngchéng (董城).
Sī (伺) again led his armies to besiege and guard it,
then heavily fortified the area around the city with stakes
and built high watchtowers.
He used strong crossbows to shoot down into the city,
and also cut off its water supply.
There was no water in the city,
so they killed oxen and drank their blood.
Yán Jìn (閻晉),
Shēng's (聲) wife's younger brother, then beheaded Shēng (聲) and surrendered.
For his achievements in pacifying the Shǔ (蜀) bandits and attacking Gāo (高),
Sī (伺) was promoted to General of Vast Awe
and appointed Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng (竟陵).
At that time, Wáng Dūn (王敦) wanted to use his cousin Yì (廙) to replace Kǎn (侃) as Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Kǎn's (侃) former generals Zhèng Pān (鄭攀) and Mǎ Jùn (馬儁) pleaded with Dūn (敦) on Kǎn's (侃) behalf,
but Dūn (敦) did not agree.
Pān (攀) and others, knowing that Kǎn (侃) had just suppressed a great bandit and that everyone was happy to follow him,
and also knowing that Yì (廙) was jealous, cruel, and difficult to serve,
planned to resist him together.
So they gathered their forces at Yǐnkǒu (溳口)
and sent an envoy to inform Sī (伺).
Sī (伺) outwardly agreed
but claimed illness and did not go.
Pān (攀) and others then advanced to resist Yì (廙).
Soon after, the officers and men became suspicious and obstructed,
then dispersed and returned to Héngsāngkǒu (橫桑口),
intending to join Dù Zēng (杜曾).
At that time, Zhū Guǐ (朱軌), Zhào Yòu (趙誘), and Lǐ Huán (李桓) led their troops to attack them.
Pān (攀) and others feared execution,
so they executed their Sīmǎ (司馬) Sūn Jǐng (孫景), who had plotted to resist Yì (廙),
and surrendered to Guǐ (軌) and the others.
When Yì (廙) was about to head west,
he sent his Chief Clerk Liú Jùn (劉浚) to remain stationed at Yángkǒulěi (揚口壘).
At that time, Dù Zēng (杜曾) requested to attack Dìwǔ Yī (第五猗) in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Sī (伺) said to Yì (廙):
"Zēng (曾) is a cunning bandit.
He pretends to return west
to make the masses suspicious,
intending to lure the government army to the west,
and then swiftly attack Yángkǒu (揚口).
You should divide your forces.
You cannot just head west immediately."
Yì (廙) was arrogant, severe, and self-willed by nature,
and moreover, he considered Sī (伺) old, timid, and unreliable,
so he proceeded west.
Zēng (曾) and others indeed rushed back.
Yì (廙) then sent Sī (伺) back.
As soon as he reached the fort,
he was besieged by Zēng (曾) and others.
Liú Jùn (劉浚), seeing that the north gate of the fort was vulnerable,
wanted Sī (伺) to defend it.
Someone persuaded Jùn (浚), saying:
"Sī (伺) is allied with Zhèng Pān (鄭攀)."
So he was reassigned to defend the south gate.
The bandits knew this
and attacked the north gate.
At that time, Mǎ Jùn (馬儁) and others, members of Zhèng Pān's (鄭攀) faction, also came to attack the fort.
Jùn's (儁) wife and children were already inside the fort.
Someone suggested flaying their faces to show Jùn (儁).
Sī (伺) said:
"Killing his wife and children
will not lift the siege,
but only increase his anger."
So he stopped them.
Sī's (伺) habitually used crossbow suddenly jammed and would not fire.
Sī (伺) was greatly displeased by this.
When the bandits captured the north gate,
Sī (伺) was wounded and retreated into a boat.
Initially,
Jùn (浚) had opened holes in the bottom of various boats
and covered them with wood,
calling them "boat mechanisms."
After Sī (伺) entered,
the bandits used their spears to thrust at Sī (伺).
Sī (伺) caught a spear
and used it to thrust back at the bandits.
The bandits climbed onto the boat's roof,
shouting loudly:
"The bandit leader is here!"
Sī (伺) sank and moved underwater for fifty paces from the bottom of the boat,
thus escaping.
He received medical treatment,
and his wound slightly improved.
Dù Zēng (杜曾) sent a messenger to Sī (伺), saying:
"Mǎ Jùn (馬儁) and others are grateful for your kindness;
their wives and children are alive.
I have entrusted all hundred members of your household, both inside and outside, to Jùn (儁).
Jùn (儁) has taken utmost care of them.
You can come here."
Sī (伺) replied:
"There are no white-haired bandits.
I am now over sixty,
and I cannot be a bandit with you again.
When I die,
I will return south;
I entrust my wife and children to you."
Then he returned to Zèngshān (甑山).
At that time, Wáng Yì (王廙) was in a standoff with Lǐ Huán (李桓) and Dù Zēng (杜曾),
with repeated battles below Zèngshān (甑山).
The soldiers often cried out in alarm:
"The bandits are coming!"
Sī (伺) was startled by his wound and died.
He was then buried on Zèngshān (甑山).
Máo Bǎo (毛寶) (son Mùzhī (穆之) grandson Qú (璩), Ānzhī (安之) clan member Dézǔ (德祖))
Máo Bǎo (毛寶), courtesy name Shuòzhēn (碩真),
was a man from Yángwǔ (陽武), Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Wáng Dùn (王敦) made him Magistrate of Línxiāng (臨湘).
When Dùn (敦) died,
he became Wēn Jiào's (溫嶠) Pingnán Cānjūn (平南參軍).
When Sū Jùn (蘇峻) rebelled,
Jiào (嶠) was about to rush to the rescue,
but General Zhengxī Táo Kǎn (陶侃) was suspicious and would not follow.
Jiào (嶠) repeatedly tried to persuade him but could not change his mind,
so he sent an envoy again to humor Kǎn's (侃) intentions, saying:
"My lord should hold his ground for now;
I should go down first."
Two days after the message was sent,
it happened that Bǎo's (寶) other envoy returned.
Hearing of this,
he advised Jiào (嶠), saying:
"Whenever a great undertaking is launched,
it should be done jointly with all under heaven.
Success for the multitude lies in harmony;
I have never heard of anything different.
Even if there were grounds for suspicion,
one should still outwardly show no awareness of it,
let alone create suspicion oneself!
It would be advisable to quickly recall the messenger,
amend the previous letter,
and state that both must surely set out together.
If you cannot catch the previous message,
you should send another envoy."
Jiào (嶠) understood,
immediately recalled the messenger and revised the letter,
and Kǎn (侃) indeed marched together to attack Jùn (峻).
Bǎo (寶) led a thousand men as Jiào's (嶠) vanguard,
and they both reached Qiézipǔ (茄子浦).
Initially,
Jiào (嶠) considered that his southern army was skilled in water warfare
while Jùn's (峻) army was adept at land combat.
He wished to use his strength to control them,
and issued an order to the three armies:
"Those who go ashore shall die."
At this time, Sū Jùn (蘇峻) sent ten thousand *hú* of rice to supply Zǔ Yuē (祖約),
and Yuē (約) dispatched his Sīmǎ (司馬) Huán Fǔ (桓撫) and others to receive it.
Bǎo (寶) told his troops:
"In military strategy,
if a military order is not to be followed,
how can one not go ashore?"
He then employed a stratagem and fought valiantly,
seizing all the rice,
and capturing or killing tens of thousands.
Yuē (約) consequently suffered a great famine.
Jiào (嶠) commended his meritorious service
and recommended him as Grand Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江).
Yuē (約) sent Zǔ Huàn (祖煥) and Huán Fǔ (桓撫) to attempt a raid on Pénkǒu (湓口).
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) was about to personally attack them,
but Bǎo (寶) said:
"The righteous army relies on you, my lord;
you must not move.
I request to campaign against them."
Kǎn (侃) looked at his guests and said:
"This young man's words are usable."
He then sent Bǎo (寶) to go.
Previously,
Huán Xuān (桓宣) had betrayed Yuē (約)
and encamped at Mătóu Shān (馬頭山).
He was attacked by Huàn (煥) and Fǔ (撫)
and sought rescue from Bǎo (寶).
Bǎo's (寶) troops, knowing Xuān (宣) was originally a partisan of Yuē (約),
were suspicious.
Xuān (宣) sent his son Róng (戎) to plead again,
and Bǎo (寶) immediately followed Róng (戎) to his aid.
Before they arrived,
the bandits had already engaged Xuān (宣) in battle.
Bǎo's (寶) army was outnumbered and exposed,
their weapons and equipment were poor,
and they were greatly defeated by Huàn (煥) and Fǔ (撫).
Bǎo (寶) was struck by an arrow
which pierced his thigh and went through his saddle.
He had someone step on his saddle to pull out the arrow,
and blood filled his boots.
He galloped over a hundred *lǐ* to the ships by night,
navigating by the stars.
Upon arrival,
he first wept for the fallen generals and soldiers.
After cleaning his wound,
he returned that night to rescue Xuān (宣).
By the time Bǎo (寶) reached Xuān's (宣) camp,
Huàn (煥) and Fǔ (撫) had also retreated.
Bǎo (寶) advanced to attack Zǔ Yuē (祖約),
his army encamping at Dōngguān (東關),
and defeated Héféi (合肥).
Soon after, he was recalled to Shítóu (石頭).
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) and Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) had not yet been able to defeat the bandits,
and Kǎn (侃) wanted to lead his troops back south.
Bǎo (寶) told Jiào (嶠):
"Your subordinate can keep him here."
He then went to persuade Kǎn (侃), saying:
"You should have originally commanded Wúhú (蕪湖)
to provide strategic support to both north and south.
Since you have already come down,
you cannot return.
Moreover, military discipline dictates advance, not retreat.
This is not merely about maintaining order in the three armies
and showing the troops their determination to die,
but also because retreating means having no support
and ultimately leads to destruction.
In the past, Dù Tāo (杜弢) was certainly not weak or feeble,
yet you eventually annihilated him.
Why should Jùn (峻) alone be unbreakable?
The bandits are also afraid of death;
they are not all brave and strong.
You can try giving me troops,
and I will go ashore to cut off the bandits' supplies,
catching them by surprise
and causing them distress.
If I do not achieve results,
then you may leave,
and people will have no regrets."
Kǎn (侃) agreed,
and promoted Bǎo (寶) to Dūhù (督護).
Bǎo (寶) burned Jùn's (峻) accumulated provisions in Gòuróng (句容) and Húshú (湖孰),
and Jùn (峻) suffered some food shortages.
Kǎn (侃) then stayed and did not leave.
After Jùn (峻) died,
Kuāng Shù (匡術) surrendered Yuànchéng (苑城).
Kǎn (侃) ordered Bǎo (寶) to guard the South City,
and Dèng Yuè (鄧嶽) to guard the West City.
The bandits sent Hán Huàng (韓晃) to attack them.
Bǎo (寶) ascended the wall and shot down dozens of people.
Huàng (晃) asked Bǎo (寶):
"Are you Máo Lújiāng (毛廬江)?"
Bǎo (寶) said:
"I am."
Huàng (晃) said:
"You are renowned for your bravery,
why don't you come out and fight?"
Bǎo (寶) said:
"If you are a capable general,
why don't you come in and fight?"
Huàng (晃) laughed and withdrew.
When the rebellion was pacified,
he was enfeoffed as an open-territory Marquis of Zhōulíng (州陵) County,
with sixteen hundred households.
When Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) took command in the west,
he requested Bǎo (寶) as Auxiliary General, Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏), and Supervisor of Suí (隨) and Yìyáng (義陽) two commanderies,
stationed at Shàngmíng (上明).
He was further promoted to Zhongláng (中郎) of the South.
He followed Liàng (亮) to campaign against Guō Mò (郭默).
After Mò (默) was pacified,
he, along with Liàng's (亮) Sīmǎ (司馬) Wáng Qiānqī (王愆期) and others, rescued Huán Xuān (桓宣) at Zhāngshān (章山),
attacked the bandit general Shí Yù (石遇),
defeated him,
and was promoted to General Zhenglǔ (征虜).
Liàng (亮) planned a northern expedition,
memorialized to relinquish his post as Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州),
and requested it be given to Bǎo (寶).
Thus, an imperial edict appointed Bǎo (寶) as Supervisor of all military affairs west of the Jiāng (江) in Yángzhōu (揚州) and Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州),
with his general title remaining unchanged.
He, along with Fán Jùn (樊峻), Grand Administrator of Xīyáng (西陽), defended Zhūchéng (邾城) with ten thousand men.
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) resented this,
and thus sent his son Jiàn (鑒) and his generals Kuí Ān (夔安), Lǐ Tú (李菟), and others with fifty thousand men to invade,
and Zhāng Dù (張渡) with twenty thousand cavalry to attack Zhūchéng (邾城).
〔一０〕Bǎo (寶) sought rescue from Liàng (亮),
but Liàng (亮), considering the city well-fortified,
did not send troops in time,
and the city consequently fell.
Bǎo (寶), Jùn (峻), and others led their retainers to break through the encirclement,
but six thousand people perished in the river,
and Bǎo (寶) also drowned.
Liàng (亮) wept bitterly for him,
contracted an illness as a result,
and subsequently died.
An imperial edict stated:
"While Bǎo's (寶) defeat
warrants demotion and censure,
during the rebellion of Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
he dedicated his efforts to the imperial house.
Now, blaming him for his mistakes,
we will not bestow posthumous honors,
but a sacrifice is permissible."
Afterward, the high officials argued that Bǎo (寶) had rendered great service,
and moreover died for the imperial cause,
and that it was inappropriate to revoke his title.
In the third year of Shēngpíng (升平) (359 CE),
an edict was issued to restore his original enfeoffment.
Initially,
when Bǎo (寶) was in Wǔchāng (武昌),
a soldier bought a white turtle in the market.
It was four or five *cùn* long.
He raised it until it gradually grew larger,
then released it into the Jiāng (江) River.
During the defeat at Zhūchéng (邾城),
the man who had raised the turtle, wearing armor and holding a saber,
threw himself into the water.
He felt as if he had landed on a rock.
Looking,
he saw it was the white turtle he had previously raised,
now five or six *chǐ* long.
It carried him to the east bank,
and he thus escaped.
Máo Bǎo had two sons: Mùzhī and Ānzhī.
Mùzhī’s courtesy name was Xiànzǔ.
His childhood name was Wǔshēng.
〔一一〕As his formal name violated the taboo of Empress Wáng Jìng’s name,
he used his courtesy name.
Later, because Huán Wēn’s mother’s name was Xiàn,
he then used his childhood name instead.
Mùzhī was resolute and had his father’s demeanor.
Yú Yì, the General of the Pacified West, appointed him as a staff officer.
He inherited the title of Marquis of Zhōulíng.
Yì and others wielded supreme power in Shǎnxī.
He made his son Fāngzhī the General of Martial Establishment
and garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Fāngzhī was young,
so Yì selected trustworthy military commanders to assist him.
He thus appointed Mùzhī as the Commandant of the General of Martial Establishment.
Soon after, Yì passed away.
The generals Gān Zàn and Dài Xī, among others, rebelled.
Mùzhī, along with Jiāng Pī, the Chief Clerk of the Pacified West, Zhū Táo, the Commandant, and others, jointly suppressed them.
Huán Wēn replaced Yì
and again recruited Mùzhī as a staff officer.
He followed Wēn to pacify Shǔ.
For his achievements, his second son was granted the title of Marquis of Dūxiāng.
Soon after, he was appointed General Who Displays Awe and [一二]Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
He followed Wēn to pacify Luò
and enter the pass.
As Wēn was about to withdraw his troops,
and Xiè Shàng was not yet arrived,
he left Mùzhī with two thousand men to guard the imperial tombs.
In the beginning of Shēngpíng,
he was promoted to Inspector-General of All Military Affairs in Níngzhōu, General Who Displays Awe, and Governor of Níngzhōu.
Since Huán Wēn was enfeoffed as Prince of Nánjùn,
Mùzhī was transferred to Marquis of Jiàn’ān.
He again served as a staff officer for Wēn, the Grand Commandant.
He was given the additional title of General Who Commands the Army
and was assigned the soldiers he had recruited.
When Wēn campaigned against Mùróng Wěi,
he ordered Mùzhī to supervise the digging of the Jùyě Canal for over a hundred *li*,
diverting the Wèn River to meet the Jì River.
When Wēn later burned his boats and returned on foot,
he ordered Mùzhī to supervise military affairs in the four commanderies of Dōngyàn
and concurrently serve as Grand Administrator of Dōngyàn.
His previous official posts remained unchanged.
When Yuán Zhēn rebelled at Shòuyáng,
Wēn intended to campaign against him.
Mùzhī, as General Who Commands the Army, concurrently held the post of Grand Administrator of Huáinán
and garrisoned Lìyáng.
After Zhēn was pacified,
his remaining followers scattered.
Mùzhī was then appointed Inspector-General of Military Affairs west of the Jiāng in Yángzhōu
and again concurrently held the post of Grand Administrator of Chénjùn.

Soon after, he was transferred to Inspector-General of Military Affairs of Yìchéng in Yángzhōu, five commanderies in Jīngzhōu, and Jīngzhào in Yōngzhōu, and Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Yìchéng, and Hénán three commanderies.
His general title remained unchanged.
He was soon promoted to concurrently hold the post of Governor of Liángzhōu.
After a while,
he resigned due to illness.
An imperial edict ordered him to return as General Who Commands the Army.
When Fú Jiān’s detached force attacked Péngchéng,
he was again made General, granted the imperial standard, and Inspector-General of Military Affairs north of the Jiāng,
garrisoning Guǎnglíng.
He was promoted to Right General and Internal Scribe of Xuānchéng, and granted the imperial standard,
garrisoning Gūshú.
Mùzhī believed that since the garrison was in the near capital region,
there would be no more military alerts.
It was inappropriate to be granted the imperial standard.
He submitted a memorial declining the honor,
which was granted.
When Fú Jiān’s detached force besieged Xiāngyáng,
an imperial edict ordered Mùzhī to proceed to Shàngmíng and take orders from Huán Chōng.
Chōng ordered Mùzhī to conduct roving patrols in Miǎnzhōng.
As Mùzhī had just arrived,
Zhū Xù was captured.
He withdrew his troops back to the commandery.
Fú Jiān’s forces then attacked Shǔhàn.
Yáng Liàng, the Governor of Liángzhōu, and Zhōu Zhòngsūn, the Governor of Yìzhōu, fled.

Chōng ordered Mùzhī to supervise the military affairs of three commanderies in Liángzhōu, Right General, Colonel of the Western Barbarians, Governor of Yìzhōu, concurrently Grand Administrator of Jiànpíng, and granted the imperial standard,
garrisoning Bājùn.
He made his son Qiú the Grand Administrator of Zìtóng.
Mùzhī and Qiú campaigned against Fú Jiān,
reaching Bāxī Commandery.
Due to a shortage of grain transport,
they retreated and encamped at Bādōng,
where he died of illness.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Central Army
and given the posthumous name Liè.
His son Zhēn inherited the title
and reached the position of Grand Administrator of Tiānmén.
Zhēn’s younger brothers were Qú, Qiú, Fán, Jǐn, and Yuàn.
〔一三〕Qú was the most famous.
Qú’s courtesy name was Shúliǎn.
When he came of age,
Huán Huò, the Right General, appointed him as a staff officer.
Soon after, he mourned his father.
After the mourning period,
he became a staff officer for Xiè Ān, the General of the Guards.
He was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Ān again requested him to be a staff officer,
and he was transferred to Commandant of the General Who Conquers Barbarians for Ān’s son Yǎn.
During the battle of Huáiféi,
Fú Jiān fled in disarray.
Qú and Tián Cìzhī jointly pursued Fú Jiān,
reaching Zhōngyáng,
but failed to catch him and returned.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North and Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
Soon after, he was appointed Commandant for Tián, the General Who Guards the North and Prince of Qiáo.
In Hǎilíng County, there was a place called Qīngpú,
surrounded by lakes and swamps,
all covered with wild rice and dense vegetation.
It was a gathering place for fugitives,
beyond the reach of official authority.
Qú proposed leading a thousand men to suppress them.
At that time, there was a severe drought.
Qú took advantage of this to set fire,
and all the wild rice and vegetation burned.
The fugitive households were in distress
and all came out to surrender to Qú.
There were nearly ten thousand households,
all of whom were recruited into the army.
The imperial court praised this.
He was transferred to Commandant of the General of the Western Central Army, General of the Dragon Stratagem, and Internal Scribe of Qiáo and Liáng two commanderies.
Soon after, he replaced Guō Quán as General of Martial Establishment and Governor of Yìzhōu.
In the early years of Emperor Ān’s reign,
he was promoted to General Who Conquers Barbarians.
When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he sent an envoy to add the titles of Palace Attendant and Left General to Qú.
Qú detained Xuán’s envoy
and refused to accept the order.
Xuán made Huán Xī the Governor of Liángzhōu,
Wáng Yì occupied Fú,
Guō Fǎ garrisoned Dàngqú,
Shī Jì garrisoned Bājùn,
and Zhōu Dàozǐ garrisoned Báidì to defend against him.
Qú circulated a manifesto far and wide,
listing Xuán’s crimes.
He sent Liǔ Yuēzhī, the Grand Administrator of Bādōng, Luó Shù, the Grand Administrator of Jiànpíng, and Zhēn Jìzhī, the Commandant of the General Who Conquers Barbarians, to defeat Xī and others.
He then led his troops to Báidì.
The Prince of Wǔlíng issued an order saying:
“Máo Qú, the Governor of Yìzhōu, is loyal and sincere.
Since Huán Xuán instigated disaster,
he has always thought of pursuing him.
If he can now eliminate
the treacherous rebels and clear Jīng and Yǐng,
he shall immediately be entrusted with the responsibilities of the upper reaches.”
Initially,
Qú’s younger brother Fán, the Governor of Níngzhōu, died in office.
Qú’s elder brother Qiú’s grandson Yòuzhī and staff officer Fèi Tián escorted the funeral with several hundred men
and buried him in Jiānglíng.
Coincidentally, when Xuán was defeated,
they planned to flee to Liángzhōu.
Qú’s younger brother Jǐn’s son Xiūzhī, who was then Xuán’s Colonel of Cavalry,
lured Xuán’s envoy into Shǔ.
Soon after, Xiūzhī, along with Yòuzhī, Fèi Tián, and Fēng Qiān from Hàngjiā, jointly killed Xuán.
Yuēzhī and others, hearing of Xuán’s death,
advanced their troops to Zhījiāng.
However, Huán Zhèn recaptured Jiānglíng.
Liú Yì and others returned to Xúnyáng.
Yuēzhī also retreated.
Soon after, Jìzhī and Shù both fell ill.
〔一四〕Yuēzhī went to Zhèn and pretended to surrender,
intending to attack Zhèn by surprise.
The plot was discovered,
and he was killed.
Yuēzhī’s Commandant Shí Yánzǔ and Wén Chǔmào, the Grand Administrator of Fúlíng, among others, rallied the remaining troops
and secured Fúlíng.
Zhèn sent Huán Fàngzhī as Governor of Yìzhōu,
stationed at Xīlíng.
Chǔmào resisted and attacked,
defeating him.
When Zhèn died,
Emperor Ān was restored to power.
An edict stated:
“Indeed, a steadfast pine stands out in the cold of winter,
and loyal ministers shine brightly in times of national crisis.
Máo Qú, the Governor of Yìzhōu, possesses extensive and upright knowledge.
He sincerely pledged allegiance to the righteous cause.
He received orders as a detached force
and reached the vicinity of the capital.
His meritorious service in assisting the state
truly touched Our heart.
He shall be promoted to General Who Conquers the West,
granted the additional title of Palace Attendant,
Inspector-General of Military Affairs of Yì, Liáng, Qín, Liáng, and Níng five provinces,
and acting Grand Administrator of Yídū and Níngshǔ.
Wén Chǔmào proclaimed and praised the provincial shepherd,
enduring dangers and overcoming difficulties.
He shall be made General Who Assists the State, Colonel of the Western Barbarians, and Grand Administrator of Bāxī and Zìtóng two commanderies.”

Another edict ordered Jǐn, the Colonel of the Western Barbarians, to be granted the imperial standard, Inspector-General of Military Affairs of Liáng and Qín two provinces, General Who Conquers Barbarians, Governor of Liáng and Qín two provinces, and Grand Administrator of Luèyáng and Wǔdū.
Jǐn’s younger brother Yuàn, the Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn, was made General Who Assists the State and Governor of Níngzhōu.
Initially,
Qú heard that Zhèn had been trapped in Jiānglíng,
so he led his forces to the rescue.
He ordered Jǐn and Yuán to proceed down the outer river,
and dispatched staff officer Qiáo Zòng to lead the armies from Bāxī and Zǐtóng Commanderies down the Fúshuǐ River,
intending for them to rendezvous with Qú’s army in Bā Jùn.
The people of Shǔ were not keen on an eastern expedition.
Zòng, taking advantage of the general desire to return home,
rebelled at the mouth of the Wǔchéng River.
He returned to attack Fú,
and killed Jǐn.
Zhèng Chúnzhī, the Chief Clerk of Jǐn’s residence who had remained in Chéngdū, swiftly sent a messenger to inform Qú.
Qú was at Lu:èchéng at the time,
four hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
He dispatched staff officer Wáng Qióng to suppress the rebels,
and they engaged in battle at Guǎnghàn.
Hé Lín, the magistrate of Bódào, gathered a party to assist Zòng,
and Qú's own men, enticed by Zòng’s persuasion,
then jointly killed Qú and Yuán,
along with his sons and nephews who were in Shǔ.
All were annihilated at once.
Qú’s son Hóngzhī succeeded him.
In the Yìxī reign,
Shí Yánzǔ, then the Administrator of Shǐkāng,
submitted a memorial arguing on behalf of Qú and his brothers.
Thereupon, an imperial edict stated:
"The former Inspector of Yìzhōu, Qú, the Colonel of Xīyí, Jǐn, and the Administrator of Shǔ Jùn, Yuán, were loyal and valiant in their service to the emperor,
but their fate turned out unexpectedly.
As the day of their burial approaches,
our sorrow grows deeper.
They shall all be posthumously granted the offices they previously held,
and provided with three hundred thousand cash and three hundred bolts of cloth."
In recognition of Qú's efforts in suppressing Huán Xuán,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Guīxiāng,
with an estate of fifteen hundred households.
Furthermore, in recognition of Yòuzhī’s achievement in beheading Huán Xuán,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yídào County.
From Bǎo to Qú, across three generations,
four individuals held high office and founded states.
They were a family of generals and commanders,
comparable to the Zhōu clan of Xúnyáng,
but their individual talents were not as great.
Jǐn’s son, Xiūzhī,
frequently held prominent and distinguished positions,
reaching the rank of Right General of the Palace Guard.
He followed Liú Yù in pacifying Yáo Hóng.
Later, he became the Chief Clerk for the General Who Pacifies the West,
but perished in the Wei campaign.
Ānzhī, courtesy name Zhòngzǔ,
also possessed military capability.
He successively rose through the ranks to Army Advisor to the General Who Guards the Army and Administrator of Wèijùn.
When Jiǎnwén Fú came to power,
he entrusted Ānzhī with critical military responsibilities.
Upon ascending the throne,
Ānzhī commanded troops and accompanied the emperor,
being permitted to lodge within the palace.
Soon after, he was appointed General of Mobile Cavalry.
When Yǔ Xī entered Jīngkǒu,
the court was shaken.
Ānzhī was ordered to oversee the various troops at the city gates.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
the rebel Lú Sǒng burst into the palace halls.
[一五] Ānzhī, hearing of the danger,
led his men directly into the Yúnlóng Gate,
personally fighting with valor.
Soon after, Left General of the Palace Guard Yīn Kāng, General of the Guard Huán Mì, and others arrived,
joining forces with Ānzhī.
Sǒng was consequently annihilated.
He was promoted to Right General of the Palace Guard.
When Empress Dìng died,
he was appointed Grand Master of Works.
He died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
He had four sons: Tán, Tài, Suì, and Dùn.
Tán inherited the peerage
and his highest office was Prime Minister of Jiāngxià.
Tài successively served as Assistant Officer to the Grand Tutor and Military Advisor to the Rear Army.
Both he and Suì were favored by the Prince of Kuàijī and his son.
Thus, recognizing Ānzhī's achievement in suppressing Lú Sǒng,
Tài was granted the peerage of Viscount of Píngdū,
and Tán was ordered to inherit the original peerage.
Yuánxiǎn once hosted a banquet at Tài’s house.
When he was about to leave,
Tài insisted he stay, saying:
"If Your Excellency leaves now,
I will take your beard."
Yuánxiǎn was greatly angered,
and left in a huff.
Thus, he and Yuánxiǎn had a falling out.
When Yuánxiǎn was defeated,
Tài was then General of Champion Army and Administrator of Tángyì and Tàishān Commanderies.
Suì was General of Mobile Cavalry,
and Dùn was Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor.
When Huán Xuán gained control,
he ordered Tài to arrest Yuánxiǎn
and send him to Xīntíng.
Tài, holding a grudge,
personally beat and humiliated him.
Soon after, both were killed by Huán Xuán.
Only Dùn was exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
In the early Yìxī reign,
he was able to return,
and became Administrator of Yídū.
Dézǔ was
a member of Qú's clan.
Both his father and grandfather perished among the rebels.
Dézǔ and his four brothers
fled south together,
all possessing military capability.
Liú Dàoguī, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, appointed Dézǔ as General Who Establishes Martial Power and Administrator of Shǐpíng,
and later transferred him to Administrator of Fúlíng.
During Lú Xún's rebellion,
Dàoguī again made him an Army Advisor
to attack Xú Dàofù at Shǐxīng.
Soon after, he suffered the loss of his mother.
When Liú Yù attacked Sīmǎ Xiūzhī,
Dézǔ was assigned as Army Advisor to the Grand尉, Administrator of Yìyáng,
granted the peerage of Marquis of Qiānlíng County,
and then transferred to Administrator of Nányáng.
He followed Liú Yù in attacking Yáo Hóng,
repeatedly attacking the commanderies of Xíngyáng, Fúfēng, Nán'ān, and Féngyì,
achieving victories everywhere.
Yù praised him
and made him General Who Guards the Dragon and Inspector of Qínzhōu.
Yù left his second son Yìzhēn as General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
He appointed Dézǔ as Chief Military Advisor,
concurrently Administrator of Tiānshuǐ,
to return with Yìzhēn.
Yù appointed Dézǔ as Superintendent of Military Affairs for Hédōng and Píngyáng Commanderies, General Who Assists the State, and Administrator of Hédōng,
replacing Liú Zūnkǎo in defending Púbǎn.
When the army in Hébèi was defeated,
Dézǔ returned with his entire force.
Yù was planning to pacify Guānluò,
and first appointed Dézǔ as Superintendent of Military Affairs for Nine Commanderies, General of Champion Army, and Administrator of Xíngyáng and Jīngzhào.
For his previous and subsequent merits,
he was granted the peerage of Baron of Guànyáng County.
[一六] Soon after, he was promoted to Superintendent of Military Affairs for Sī, Yōng, and Bìng Provinces, General of Champion Army, and Inspector of Sīzhōu,
garrisoning Wǔláo.
He was captured by Wei.
Dézǔ’s second younger brother, Ní,
and Ní’s younger brother, Biàn,
both possessed integrity and ambition.
Ní died in the disaster of Lú Xún's rebellion,
and Biàn perished in the campaign against Lǔ Zōng.
[一七] Both fought bravely, disregarding their lives,
and were praised by their generation.
Liú Xiá
Liú Xiá, courtesy name Zhèngcháng,
was a native of Yìyáng, Guǎngpíng.
He was resolute and decisive by nature, adept at archery and horsemanship,
open-minded and courageous.
When the world fell into great chaos,
Xiá became a wǔzhǔ (fortress master).
Whenever he attacked bandits,
he led his strong warriors to break through defenses and spearhead assaults.
The people of Jìfāng compared him to Zhāng Fēi and Guān Yǔ.
Shào Xù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu from his hometown, deeply esteemed him
and married his daughter to him.
He then established a stronghold between the Hé and Jì rivers,
and bandits dared not approach.
Xiá sent envoys through secret paths to accept the orders of Emperor Yuán.
The imperial court praised him,
sending him an imperial letter of commendation and encouragement,
and appointing him General Who Guards the Dragon and Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
In the early Jiànwǔ reign,
Emperor Yuán issued an edict saying:
"Xiá is loyal, courageous, resolute, and decisive;
his integrity and sincerity are commendable.
Xiá is to be appointed Grand Administrator of Xiàpí,
with his general's rank unchanged."
Earlier,
Zhōu Jiān of Pèi,
also named Fú,
and Zhōu Mò of the same commandery,
taking advantage of the world’s chaos,
each became a wǔzhǔ (fortress master)
and engaged in banditry and plunder.
Mò surrendered to Zǔ Tì,
but Fú was angered,
and consequently attacked and killed Mò.
He then rebelled at Péngchéng,
and Shí Lè sent cavalry to aid him.
Xiá was ordered to take charge as Grand Administrator of Péngchéng
and, along with Cài Bào, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, and Xú Kān, the Administrator of Tàishān, jointly attack Fú.
They fought at Hánshān,
and Fú was defeated and fled.
Xiá was ordered to be transferred to Administrator of Línhuái.
Xú Kān rebelled again,
but after the matter was settled,
Xiá was appointed General of the Northern Central Army and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
In the early years of the Tàiníng era,
he moved his garrison from Péngchéng to Sìkǒu.
When Wáng Hán rebelled,
Xiá and Sū Jùn both hurried to the capital.
After Hán's defeat,
Xiá followed Dānyáng Yǐn Wēn Jiào in pursuing Hán as far as Huáinán.
Xiá quite unrestrainedly allowed his soldiers to plunder.
Jiào said:
“Heaven's way aids righteousness,
which is why Wáng Hán was annihilated.
One should not cause disorder because of existing disorder.”
Xiá deeply expressed his self-reproach and bowed in apology.
When the matter was settled,
he was enfeoffed as Quánlíng Gōng for his merits,
and promoted to Sànqí Chángshì, Jiān Huáiběi Jūnshì, Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng, [一八]Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted the Jiǎjié,
replacing Wáng Suì to guard Huáiyīn.
He died in the first year of the Xiánhé era,
and was posthumously granted Ānběi Jiāngjūn.
His son, Zhào, was young,
so Emperor Chéng entrusted Xúzhōu to Xī Jiàn,
and appointed Guō Mò as Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng,
to command Xiá's former troops.
Xiá's brother-in-law Tián Fáng, and Xiá's former generals Shǐ Dié, Biàn Xián, Lǐ Lóng, and others were unwilling to be subordinate to others.
They collectively enthroned Zhào,
who inherited Xiá's former position, and rebelled.
Emperor Chéng dispatched Guō Mò and others to lead the various commanderies to suppress them.
As Mò and others were just setting out,
Liú Jiǎo, the Tàishǒu of Línchuái, led several hundred officers and soldiers to ambush Xiá's camp.
Dié and the others fled.
Tián Fáng and the Dūhù Biàn Xián, and others were beheaded.
Dié and Lóng were pursued and beheaded in Xiàpī,
their heads sent to the imperial court.
Xiá's mother, wife, children, subordinates, officers, and soldiers all returned to Jiànkāng.
Xiá's wife was fierce and decisive, inheriting her father's demeanor.
Once, when Xiá was besieged by Shí Jìlóng,
his wife, leading only a few cavalry,
rescued Xiá from among tens of thousands of enemy soldiers.
When Tián Fáng and others intended to rebel,
Xiá's wife tried to stop them,
but they did not listen.
So, she secretly started a fire and burned all their armor and weapons.
Zhào inherited the noble rank,
and his official position reached Sànqí Shìláng.
After Zhào died,
his son Jǔ succeeded.
After he died,
his son Zūnzhī succeeded.
After he died,
his son Bólíng succeeded.
When the Sòng dynasty received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Dèng Yuè (Zi Xiá)
Dèng Yuè, whose courtesy name was Bóshān,
was a native of Chénjùn.
His original name was Yuè,
but because it infringed upon Emperor Kāng's personal name,
it was changed to Yuè.
Later, his name was ultimately changed to Dài.
In his youth, he possessed the talent and strategy of a general.
