He served as Wáng Dùn's Cānjūn,
then transferred to Cóngshì Zhōngláng and Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
When Wáng Hán plotted rebellion,
Yuè led troops to follow Hán towards the capital.
After Hán's defeat,
Yuè and Zhōu Fǔ both fled to the barbarian king Xiàng Cán.
Later, they encountered an amnesty,
and came out with Fǔ.
After a long time,
Sītú Wáng Dǎo appointed him Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Later, he again became Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
Píngnán Jiāngjūn Wēn Jiào dispatched Yuè along with Dūhù Wáng Qiānqī, Póyáng Tàishǒu Jǐ Mù, and others to lead naval forces to aid in the crisis.
After Jùn was pacified,
he returned to his commandery.
When Guō Mò killed Liú Yìn,
Dàsīmǎ Táo Kǎn sent Yuè to lead the troops from Xīyáng to suppress him.
After Mò was pacified,
he was promoted to Dū Jiāo Guǎng Èrzhōu Jūnshì, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, Líng Píngyuè Zhōngláng Jiàng, Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted the Jiǎjié.
For his cumulative past and present merits,
he was enfeoffed as Yíchéng Xiàn Bó.
In the third year of Xiánkāng,
[一九]Yuè dispatched troops to attack Yèláng,
and defeated them.
He was additionally made Dū Níngzhōu,
promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and then to Píngnán Jiāngjūn.
After he died,
his son Xiá succeeded.
Xiá, whose courtesy name was Yìngyuǎn,
possessed extraordinary bravery and strength.
His spirit was preeminent in his time,
and people then compared him to Fán Kuài.
Huán Wēn appointed him Cānjūn,
and he frequently followed Wēn on military expeditions.
He successively held the post of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn
and Tàishǒu of several commanderies,
and was renowned as a famous general.
In the Miǎnshuǐ river north of Xiāngyáng city, there was a蛟 (jiāo, a mythical dragon-like creature)
that frequently harmed people.
Xiá then drew his sword and entered the water.
The jiāo coiled around his leg,
but Xiá swung his sword, cutting the jiāo into several pieces before emerging.
During the battle of Fāngtóu,
Wēn, already feeling shame and resentment,
and also wary of Xiá's bravery and decisiveness,
therefore dismissed Xiá from office.
He died shortly thereafter.
During the Níngkāng era,
he was posthumously granted Lúlíng Tàishǒu.
Yuè's younger brother, Yì,
whose courtesy name was Màoshān,
also possessed military ability.
After Yuè died,
Yì was appointed Jiān Jiāo Guǎngzhōu, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōngláng Jiàng, Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ, and granted the Jiǎjié.
Zhū Xù
Zhū Xù, whose courtesy name was Cìlún,
was a native of Yìyáng.
His father, Táo,
served as Xīmán Xiàowèi and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ due to his talent and ability.
Xù's family had been famous generals for generations.
He was successively promoted to Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn and Jiāngxià Xiàng.
Towards the end of Xīngníng,
when Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Xūn rebelled,
Huán Wēn memorialized to appoint Xù as Zhēngtǎo Dūhù to suppress him.
For his merits, he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Xiāngpíng Zǐ.
During the Tàihé era,
he was promoted to Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, Qián Hóng from Chángchéng gathered over a hundred followers,
hiding them in Yuánxiāng Shān.
Xù was appointed Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
Xù attacked and captured them.
After the matter was concluded,
he returned to Yǎnzhōu.
In the early Níngkāng era,
he was appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Jiān Miǎnzhōng Zhūjūnshì, Nán Zhōngláng Jiàng, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
In that year,
Fú Jiān dispatched his general Fú Pī and others to lead troops to besiege Xù.
Xù held fast to his defense.
The enemy's provisions were nearly exhausted,
so they led their troops in a fierce assault.
Initially,
when Fú Pī came to attack,
Xù's mother Hán personally climbed the city wall and inspected it,
saying that the northwest corner would likely be the first to suffer.
She then led over a hundred maidservants and women from the city to build a sloped wall over twenty *zhàng* long at that corner.
When the bandits attacked the northwest corner,
it indeed collapsed,
but the troops then firmly held the newly built wall.
Pī then withdrew.
The people of Xiāngyáng called this wall 'Fūrén Chéng' (Lady's Wall).
Xù repeatedly fought and defeated the bandits,
but the morale of his troops became weary and lax.
Furthermore, as the bandits had retreated somewhat far,
they doubted they would return soon,
and their defenses became careless.
Dūhù Lǐ Bóhù secretly collaborated with the bandits,
and Xiāngyáng consequently fell,
Xù was captured by Fú Jiān.
Jiān killed Bóhù and displayed his head as a warning,
because of his disloyalty.
Xù wished to escape and return,
and secretly reached Yíyáng,
hiding in Xià Kuí's house.
Jiān suspected Kuí
and arrested him.
Xù then went to Fú Huī to surrender himself.
Jiān commended him and did not question him,
appointing him Shàngshū.
During the Tàiyuán era,
Fú Jiān invaded the south.
Xiè Shí led troops to resist him.
At that time, Jiān's main army was still at Xiàng,
while Fú Róng arrived first with 300,000 troops.
Jiān sent Xù to persuade Xiè Shí,
extolling his military might.
Xù, however, said to Shí:
“If Jiān's million troops all arrive,
they will be invincible.
But before they gather,
attack them,
and you can achieve your objective.”
Thereupon, Shí sent Xiè Yǎn to select 8,000 brave warriors to cross the Féishuǐ river and challenge them to battle.
Jiān's troops slightly recoiled.
Xù, who was then behind their army,
shouted:
“Jiān is defeated!”
The troops then fled in a great rout,
and Xù was able to return.
He was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Lángyá Nèishǐ,
then transferred to Yángzhōu Yùzhōu Wǔjùn Jūnshì, [二０]Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and garrisoned Luòyáng.
Later, Dí Liáo (翟遼) of Dīnglíng (丁零) rebelled.
Xù (序) sent generals Qín Yīng (秦膺) and Tóng Bīn (童斌) to jointly suppress him with the various commanderies of Huái (淮) and Sì (泗).
He was also appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yǎn (兗) and Qīng (青) two provinces, and Inspector of the two provinces.
His general's rank remained as before.
He advanced to garrison Péngchéng (彭城).
Xù (序) requested to garrison Huáiyīn (淮陰).
The Emperor granted it.
Dí Liáo (翟遼) again sent his son Zhāo (釗) to raid Chén (陳) and Yǐng (潁).
Xù (序) sent Qín Yīng (秦膺) back to attack Zhāo (釗),
who fled.
He was appointed General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, 征虜將軍).
He memorialized to request 100,000 hú (斛) of rice and 5,000 pǐ (匹) of cloth from Jiāngzhōu (江州) to fund military expenses.
An imperial edict permitted it.
He was additionally appointed Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of Sì (司), Yōng (雍), Liáng (梁), and Qín (秦) four provinces.
The Emperor sent General Guǎngwēi (廣威), Administrator of Hénán (河南) Yáng Quánqī (楊佺期),
and Administrator of Nányáng (南陽) Zhào Mù (趙睦),
each leading a thousand soldiers, to serve under Xù (序).
Xù (序) also memorialized to request a hundred qǐng (頃) of land from the estate of the former Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Huán Shíshēng (桓石生),
and 80,000 hú (斛) of grain.
These were granted.
He then garrisoned Luòyáng (洛陽)
to guard the imperial tombs.
Afterwards, Mùróng Yǒng (慕容永) led his troops towards Luòyáng (洛陽).
Xù (序) crossed the Yellow River north from Héyīn (河陰),
and encountered Yǒng's (永) false general Wáng Cì (王次) and others.
They then fought at Qìnshuǐ (沁水).
Cì (次) was defeated and fled.
He (Xù) beheaded his (Yong's) subordinate general Wùzhī (勿支).
Advisor Zhào Mù (趙睦) and Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏) Huán Bùcái (桓不才) pursued Yǒng (永),
defeating him at Tàiháng (太行).
Yǒng (永) returned to Shàngdǎng (上黨).
At this time, Yáng Kǎi (楊楷) had gathered several thousand men
in Húshǎn (湖陝).
Hearing of Yǒng's (永) defeat,
he sent his son to Xù (序) to beg for surrender.
Xù (序) pursued Yǒng (永) to Báishuǐ (白水) in Shàngdǎng (上黨),
and they were in a standoff for two旬.
Hearing that Dí Liáo (翟遼) intended to head for Jīnyǒng (金墉),
he then returned.
He then attacked Dí Zhāo (翟釗) at Shímén (石門).
He sent Advisor Zhào Fān (趙蕃) to defeat Dí Liáo (翟遼) at Huáixiàn (懷縣).
Liáo (遼) fled during the night.
Xù (序) retreated and encamped at Luòyáng (洛陽),
leaving General Yīngyáng (鷹揚將軍) Zhū Dǎng (朱黨) to garrison Shímén (石門).
Xù (序) then made his son Lǜe (略) Supervisor of Luòchéng (洛城),
with Zhào Fān (趙蕃) as his assistant.
Xù (序) returned to Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
King Kuàijī (會稽王) Dàozǐ (道子), seeing that Xù's (序) victories and defeats balanced each other out,
neither praised nor criticized him.
Afterwards, Dòu Chōng (竇衝), Commandant of the Eastern Qiāng (東羌), wanted to enter Hànchuān (漢川).
Huángfǔ Zhāo (皇甫釗) from Āndìng (安定) and Zhōu Xūn (周勳) from Jīngzhào (京兆) and others plotted to admit him.
Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州) Zhōu Qióng (周瓊) had lost the three commanderies of Bāxī (巴西),
and his forces were few and weak.
He sent an urgent appeal to Xù (序).
Xù (序) sent General Huángfǔ Zhēn (皇甫貞) to lead troops to his aid.
Chōng (衝) occupied the east of Cháng'ān (長安).
Zhāo (釗) and Xūn (勳) scattered and fled.
Xù (序), due to old age and illness,
repeatedly memorialized to resign his post,
but it was not permitted.
An imperial edict ordered his memorials to be blocked,
so he simply left his post.
After several旬,
he submitted himself to the Court of the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi, 廷尉) for punishment.
An imperial edict pardoned him and did not question him.
He died in the eighteenth year of Tàiyuán (太元)
and was posthumously appointed Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, 左將軍) and Mounted Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì, 散騎常侍).
The historian says: When the Jìn (晉) clan was lost
and moved across the Yangtze River,
internal troubles frequently arose,
and external threats never ceased.
The way of strategizing
was not greatly expanded,
and the merits of generals and commanders
were not heard of.
Xùn (遜), Bào (豹), Xuān (宣), and Yìn (胤) served diligently during the Tàixīng (太興) era.
Máo (毛), Dèng (鄧), Liú (劉), and Zhū (朱) galloped across the land after Xiánhé (咸和).
Although their abilities did not match those of antiquity,
they were still sufficient to be listed among their contemporaries.
An encomium says: Energy divided the Huái (淮) and Hǎi (海),
calamity flowed through Chán (瀍) and Jiàn (澗).
It overturned creatures like black vipers,
and arose from humble wild geese.
Drums and pipes were heard,
rabbit snares were laid.
How mighty were the heroes,
diligent in this royal strategy!
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 52: Chén Shòu (陳壽)
Chén Shòu (陳壽), courtesy name Chéngzuò (承祚),
was a native of Ānhàn (安漢) in Bāxī (巴西).
In his youth, he loved learning
and studied under Qiáo Zhōu (譙周) from the same commandery.
He served in Shǔ (蜀) as an Official of the Imperial Library (Guāngé Lìshǐ, 觀閣令史).
When the eunuch Huáng Hào (黃皓) monopolized power,
all the high officials bent their will to curry favor with him.
Shòu (壽) alone refused to submit to him,
and because of this, he was repeatedly censured and demoted.
When his father died,
he fell ill
and had a maid prepare medicine.
When guests visited and saw this,
the local community criticized it.
When Shǔ (蜀) was pacified,
he was stuck in obscurity for several years because of this.
Minister of Works (Sīkōng, 司空) Zhāng Huá (張華) admired his talent.
Although Shòu (壽) did not avoid suspicion,
given the circumstances, he was not considered worthy of demotion or dismissal.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián, 孝廉) candidate
and appointed Assistant to the Director of Literary Works (Zuòzhù Zuòláng, 佐著作郎),
then transferred to serve as Magistrate of Yángpíng (陽平).
He compiled the collected works of Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮), Prime Minister of Shǔ (蜀),
and presented it.
He was appointed Director of Literary Works (Zuòzhù Láng, 著作郎)
and concurrently held the position of Central Corrector (Zhōngzhèng, 中正) for his home commandery.
He compiled the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sānguó Zhì, 三國志) of Wèi (魏), Wú (吳), and Shǔ (蜀),
totaling sixty-five chapters.
People of the time praised him for his excellent work
and recognized his talent as a fine historian.
Xiàhóu Zhàn (夏侯湛) was at that time writing the Book of Wèi (Wèishū, 魏書),
but upon seeing Shòu's (壽) work,
he abandoned his own book and stopped.
Zhāng Huá (張華) greatly praised him
and said to Shòu (壽):
"The Book of Jìn (Jìnshū, 晉書) will be entrusted to you!"
Such was the esteem in which he was held at the time.
Some say that Dīng Yí (丁儀) and Dīng Yì (丁廙) had great reputations in Wèi (魏).
Shòu (壽) said to their sons:
"If you can give me a thousand hú (斛) of rice,
I will write a good biography for your respected fathers."
The Dīng (丁) family did not give it to him,
and so he ultimately did not write their biographies.
Shòu's (壽) father was an advisor to Mǎ Sù (馬謖).
Mǎ Sù (馬謖) was executed by Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮),
and Shòu's (壽) father was also implicated and had his head shaved.
Zhūgě Zhān (諸葛瞻) also looked down on Shòu (壽).
When Shòu (壽) wrote Zhūgě Liàng's (諸葛亮) biography,
he said that Liàng's (亮) military strategy was not his strong suit
and that he lacked the talent to counter enemies.
He said that Zhān (瞻) was only good at calligraphy,
and his fame exceeded his actual abilities.
Debaters criticized him for this.
Zhāng Huá (張華) was about to recommend Shòu (壽) as a Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng, 中書郎).
Xún Xù (荀勖) resented Huá (華) and disliked Shòu (壽),
so he subtly influenced the Ministry of Personnel to transfer Shòu (壽) to be Administrator of Chángguǎng (長廣).
He declined, citing his mother's old age.
When Dù Yù (杜預) was about to take up his garrison post,
he again recommended him to the Emperor,
suggesting he be appointed to a Scriptorium position (Huángsǎn, 黃散).
Because of this, he was appointed Imperial Household Scribe (Yùshǐ Zhìshū, 御史治書).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
His mother left instructions to be buried in Luòyáng (洛陽).
Shòu (壽) followed her wishes.
He was again criticized
for not returning his mother's remains for burial in his hometown.
Earlier,
Qiáo Zhōu (譙周) once said to Shòu (壽):
"You will certainly achieve fame through your talent and learning,
but you will suffer setbacks;
this is not misfortune.
You should be very careful."
When Shòu (壽) reached this point,
he was twice subjected to dismissal and disgrace,
all as Zhōu (周) had predicted.
A few years later,
he was appointed Palace Manager of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ, 太子中庶子),
but was not yet installed.
In the seventh year of Yuánkāng (元康),
he died of illness,
at the age of sixty-five.
Grand Central Corrector of Liángzhōu (梁州) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng, 尚書郎) Fàn Yūn (范頵) and others memorialized, saying:
"In ancient times, Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢) decreed: 'Sīmǎ Xiāngrú (司馬相如) is very ill;
send someone to collect all his writings.'
The envoy obtained his posthumous writings, which discussed the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
The Son of Heaven was surprised by them.
We, your servants, note that the late Imperial Household Scribe (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ, 治書侍御史) Chén Shòu (陳壽) composed the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sānguó Zhì, 三國志).
His words often offer admonition
and clarify success and failure,
which benefits moral transformation.
Although his literary elegance does not match Xiāngrú (相如),
his sincerity and straightforwardness surpass him.
We wish for your majesty to consider and adopt it."
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to the Administrator of Hénán (河南 Yǐn, 尹) and the Magistrate of Luòyáng (洛陽 Lìng, 令)
to transcribe his works from his home.
Shòu (壽) also compiled Fifty Chapters of Records of Ancient States (Gǔguó Zhì, 古國志) and Ten Chapters of Biographies of Elders of Yìdū (Yìdū Qíjiù Zhuàn, 益都耆舊傳).
His other writings are also transmitted to the world.
Wáng Chángwén (王長文)
Wáng Chángwén, courtesy name Déruì,
was a man from Qī, Guǎnghàn.
In his youth, he was renowned for his talent and learning,
but he was unconventional and unrestrained.
He refused all invitations for official positions from the provincial administration.
When the province invited him to be *biéjià*,
he stealthily left in plain clothes,
and no one in the entire province knew where he had gone.
Later, he was seen squatting in the market of Chéngdū, gnawing on *húbǐng*.
The Inspector knew of his unyielding nature
and respectfully sent him away.
He shut himself in,
avoiding social interaction.
He wrote four volumes of books,
modeled on the *Yìjīng*,
named *Tōngxuán Jīng*.
It contained texts and hexagrams,
which could be used for divination.
People of his time compared it to Yáng Xióng’s *Tàixuán Jīng*.
Mǎ Xiù, from the same commandery, said:
"When Yáng Xióng wrote the *Tàixuán Jīng*,
only Huán Tán believed it would be transmitted to later generations.
Later, it encountered Lù Jì,
and the profundity of the *Xuánjīng* became clear.
Chángwén’s *Tōngxuán Jīng* has not yet encountered a Lù Jì or a Jūnshān."
During the Tàikāng period,
the land of Shǔ suffered from famine.
Granaries were opened to provide relief and loans.
Chángwén, being poor,
borrowed much,
and later had no means to repay.
The commandery and county severely reproached him,
and sent Chángwén to the province.
The Inspector, Xú Gàn, let him go,
and he departed without thanking him.
Later, Wáng Yǐng, King of Chéngdū, appointed him as the Magistrate of Jiāngyuán.
Someone asked:
"Previously you did not lower your aspirations,
why do you yield now?"
Chángwén replied:
"Salary is for supporting my parents,
not for myself."
Liáng Wáng Róng became Chancellor
and appointed him as *Cóngshì Zhōngláng*.
When traveling in Luòyáng,
he always used a small white felt screen to cover his carriage,
which was considered unusual at the time.
He eventually died in Luòyáng.
Yú Pǔ.
Yú Pǔ, courtesy name Yǔnyuán,
was a man from Chāngyì, Gāopíng.
His father, Mì,
was a *piānjiāngjūn*,
stationed in Lǒngxī.
Pǔ followed his father to his post
and dedicated himself to ancient books.
At that time, there were military reviews on the border,
and people vied to watch,
but Pǔ never cast a glance.
He was selected as *xiàolián* by the commandery,
appointed as a *lángzhōng*,
and then as *Shàngshū Dūlìshǐ*.
The *Shàngshū Lìng* Wèi Guàn and *Shàngshū* Chǔ Sì both highly esteemed him.
Pǔ said to Guàn:
"Previously, the Golden Horse revealed the auspicious sign,
and the Great Jìn responded to Heaven.
It is fitting to restore the Five Ranks system of the former kings
to ensure long-term stability.
We should not follow the laws of the tyrannical Qín
and perpetuate the errors of Hàn and Wèi."
Guàn said:
"Successive generations have lamented this,
but ultimately none could change it."
He was gradually promoted to *Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng*,
then appointed *Póyáng Nèishǐ*.
He greatly repaired the schools,
widely recruited students,
and issued a proclamation to the subordinate counties, saying:
"Learning is that by which one settles emotions and perfects nature and principles, and accumulates numerous virtues.
When emotions are settled within, conduct is formed without; when virtue is accumulated in the heart, reputation becomes manifest through teaching.
Thus, the nature of ordinary people changes with teaching;
when virtue is accumulated, habit and nature become one.
In the time of Táng and Yú,
every household could be ennobled;
when it fell into disuse,
it was said that they could be punished.
Is this not because transformation forms customs,
and teaching changes people's hearts?
Since the Hàn dynasty lost control,
the empire disintegrated,
and the regions south of the Yangzi River were cut off by rebels,
long neglecting the kingly teachings.
The instruction of schools
was abandoned and not restored.
Now the four seas are united,
and thousands of miles share the same track.
The myriad common people, in joy and harmony,
all rest in the midst of great peace.
It is fitting to uphold the fundamental Way,
and widely open up learning,
to assist in the harmony of the times
and glorify this flourishing transformation."
Then he meticulously established regulations.
Consequently, over seven hundred people came.
Pǔ then wrote a proclamation to encourage and instruct them,
saying: "All students of literature are among the cultured elite,
vigorous in age and beautiful in aspiration.
They have just entered the halls of learning,
to lecture on and cultivate the classics and precepts.
This is the great accomplishment of a career,
the foundation of establishing virtue.
The Way of the sages is bland and insipid;
thus, beginners do not like it.
But after a month or a year,
what one observes becomes increasingly broad,
and what one practices becomes increasingly abundant.
Each day one hears what one had not
heard,
and sees what one had not seen.
Then the mind opens and the intellect brightens,
one respects one's profession and enjoys one's company.
Unconsciously, one does not perceive how the great transformation molds oneself,
or how the ultimate Way enters one's spirit.
Therefore,
the influence of learning on a person
is more profound than that of painting.
I have seen paintings fade over time,
but I have never seen long-term learning fade.
A craftsman who dyes
first prepares the material,
then applies the color.
When the material is prepared and the color applied,
the dyeing process is complete.
Learning also has its material basis:
filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness
are these.
A *jūnzǐ* rectifies his mind internally
and cultivates his conduct externally.
When he has surplus energy from his conduct,
he then uses it to study literature.
When culture and substance are in perfect balance,
only then is it called virtue.
Scholars
do not worry about lack of talent,
but about lack of resolve.
Therefore, it is said that a horse that aspires to be *Jì* [a famous horse]
is also a mount of *Jì*'s caliber.
Those who aspire to be like Yán [Huí]
are also of Yán's kind.
It is also said:
If you carve and then abandon it,
even rotten wood will not know it;
if you carve and do not abandon it,
gold and stone can be worn away.
Is this not its proof!
Now, if you students recite the classics of the sages
and embody the teachings of the schools,
by the time three years have passed,
you can achieve minor accomplishments.
Then your good name will spread,
and your refined reputation will daily
renew.
Friends will admire and enjoy your company,
and court officials will respect and praise you.
Then the provincial and commandery administrations will repeatedly invite you,
and you can choose an office and serve.
Is this not beautiful!
As for containing brilliance and spreading
literary adornment,
wielding the brush to produce fluent prose,
expounding on worldly affairs,
and delving into mysteries and exploring wonders,
making Yáng [Xióng] and Bān [Gù] sheathe their brushes,
and Zhòngshū [Dǒng Zhòngshū] speechless,
that depends on where talent resides;
there are indeed no fixed individuals.
However, accumulating one spoonful makes a river,
and piling up specks of dust builds a towering peak.
Without resolve and diligence,
there is logically no way to succeed.
If you students abandon worldly affairs,
concentrate your
hearts solely on learning,
string everything together with one principle,
and progress gradually,
then some may be slow or fast,
or first or last.
What could obstruct and not connect,
what could be far and not
reached?
At that time, the libationer requested to rebuild houses for performing rites.
Pǔ said:
"A *jūnzǐ* performs rites
without a fixed location.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ shot arrows in the garden of Juéxiàng
and performed rites under a large tree.
How much more so now, with the academic halls and schools,
which are lofty and spacious!"
Pú's administration was strict but not harsh.
Moral transformation greatly prevailed,
and white crows gathered in the commandery court.
He annotated the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) classics and commentaries,
and authored the *Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn* (Records of Areas East of the Yangtze River) and dozens of essays, poems, and rhapsodies.
He died in Luò,
at the age of sixty-two.
His son, Bó,
crossed the river and presented the *Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn* to Emperor Yuán,
who issued an edict to store it in the Imperial Library.
Sīmǎ Biāo
Sīmǎ Biāo, courtesy name Shàotǒng,
was the eldest son of Mù, Prince of Gāoyáng.
He was adopted as an heir to Mǐn, Emperor Xuān's younger brother.
In his youth, he was assiduous in his studies and never tired,
yet he was fond of women and had poor conduct.
He was reprimanded by Mù,
and thus was not allowed to be the heir.
Although he was nominally adopted as an heir,
he was in fact disinherited.
Because of this, Biāo did not engage in social interaction,
but devoted himself entirely to study.
Thus, he gained extensive knowledge of many books,
completing his task of compilation.
He was first appointed as Cavalry Commandant.
During the Tàishǐ era,
he served as Secretary of the Imperial Library,
and later promoted to Aide.
He annotated *Zhuāngzǐ*
and wrote *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals of the Nine Provinces).
He believed that
"the former kings established historians to record current events,
documenting good and evil to deter and encourage,
which is the essence of educating the world.
Therefore, when the *Chūnqiū* was not compiled,
Zhòngní (Confucius) ordered it;
when the *Guānjū* was in disorder,
Master Zhì corrected it.
Did ancient sages truly enjoy being troubled?
It was truly out of necessity.
Since the restoration of the Hàn dynasty,
up to Jiàn'ān,
loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen were indeed prominent,
yet there were no good historians at the time,
and their records were chaotic and numerous.
Although Qiáo Zhōu had already abridged them,
it was still not exhaustive.
From Ānshùn downwards,
many parts were missing."
Biāo then discussed many books,
compiling what he heard,
starting from Shìzǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ)
and ending with Xiàoxiàn (Emperor Xiàn),
spanning two hundred years,
recording twelve generations.
He comprehensively synthesized the past and present,
and broadly covered various affairs,
comprising annals, treatises, and biographies, totaling eighty chapters,
titled *Xù Hànshū* (Continuation of the Book of Hàn).
In the early Tàishǐ era,
Emperor Wǔ personally performed sacrifices in the southern suburb.
Biāo submitted a memorial to establish the protocol,
the details of which are in the *Jiāosì Zhì* (Treatise on Suburban Sacrifices).
Later, he was appointed as Gentleman-in-Waiting.
He died in the last years of Emperor Huì's reign,
at the age of over sixty.
Originally,
Qiáo Zhōu believed that Sīmǎ Qiān's *Shǐjì* (Records of the Grand Historian), in writing about periods before the Zhōu and Qín dynasties,
sometimes adopted popular sayings and words from various schools,
not solely relying on orthodox classics.
Thus, Zhōu wrote *Gǔshǐ Kǎo* (Investigation of Ancient History) in twenty-five chapters,
all based on old texts,
to correct Qiān's errors.
Biāo, however, considered Zhōu's work still not entirely perfect.
He listed one hundred and twenty-two points in *Gǔshǐ Kǎo* as inappropriate,
largely based on the interpretations of the *Jízhǒng Jìnián* (Annals of Jízhǒng),
which also circulated in the world.
Wáng Yǐn
Wáng Yǐn, courtesy name Chùshū,
was a native of Chén county, Chén commandery.
His family was of humble means.
His father, Quán,
was the Prefect of Lìyáng.
In his youth, he loved learning
and had ambitions of writing.
He often privately recorded Jin affairs and the conduct of meritorious officials,
but died before completing it.
Yǐn maintained his scholarly simplicity,
did not associate with influential figures,
was widely learned and well-informed.
He inherited his father's unfinished work
and was thoroughly familiar with many old affairs of the Western Capital.
During the Jiànxīng era,
he crossed the river.
The Chancellor's Army Advisor and Libationer, Zǔ Nà of Zhuó commandery, held him in high regard.
Nà was fond of playing board games,
and Yǐn often advised him to stop.
Nà said:
"I just use it to forget my worries."
Yǐn replied:
"The ancients, when they encountered favorable times,
achieved their way through accomplishments;
when not,
they expressed their talent through words.
Thus, their success or failure was never limited.
Currently, the Jìn dynasty has no official history,
the world is in great chaos,
and old records are lost.
This is not something ordinary talents can establish.
You grew up in the five capitals
and traveled as an official in all directions.
The successes and failures of both Chinese and barbarians are within your sight and hearing.
Why not narrate and compile them!
Yīng Zhòngyuǎn wrote *Fēngsú Tōng*,
Cuī Zǐzhēn wrote *Zhènglùn*,
Cài Bójī wrote *Quànxué Piān*,
and Shǐ Yóu wrote *Jíjiù Zhāng*.
These still circulate in the world,
becoming immortal even after death.
At that time,
were there few people?
Yet they are completely unknown,
all because they did not write anything.
Therefore, a noble person worries about dying without being known.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says to strive tirelessly.
Moreover, a national history clearly shows the traces of gain and loss.
Why must one play board games to forget worries?"
Nà sighed deeply and said:
"It's not that I don't appreciate your path,
but my strength is insufficient."
He then submitted a memorial recommending Yǐn.
Emperor Yuán, being busy with the initial establishment of the state,
had no time for a historiography office,
and so the matter was dropped without a reply.
In the early Tàixīng era,
as institutions and regulations were gradually established,
Yǐn and Guō Pú were both summoned to be Secretaries for Historiography,
and ordered to compile the history of the Jìn dynasty.
For his participation in pacifying Wáng Dūn,
he was granted the title of Marquis of Pínglíng鄉.
At that time, Yú Yù, another Secretary for Historiography, privately compiled a *Jìnshū* (Book of Jìn).
However, having grown up in the southeast,
he was unaware of affairs in the central court.
He frequently consulted Yǐn,
and also borrowed and secretly copied Yǐn's writings,
gradually broadening his knowledge.
Afterwards, he became increasingly hostile towards Yǐn,
showing it in his words and demeanor.
Yù was a powerful clan member,
who allied with powerful nobles,
forming a faction
to ostracize Yǐn.
Yǐn was eventually dismissed due to slander
and sent back to his home.
Being poor and without resources,
his book remained unfinished.
He then sought refuge with General of the West-Pacifying Army Yú Liàng in Wǔchāng.
Liàng supplied him with paper and brushes,
and thus the book was completed.
He then presented it to the emperor.
Although Yǐn enjoyed writing,
his prose was crude and clumsy,
disorderly and incoherent.
The readable parts of his book, in terms of structure,
were all compiled by his father;
the parts with muddled style and incomprehensible meaning
were Yǐn's own work.
He died at home
at the age of over seventy.
Yǐn's elder brother, Hú,
courtesy name Chùzhòng.
In his youth, he valued military prowess.
When Yǐng, Prince of Chéngdū, raised an army to march on Luò,
he was appointed as Champion Army Adjutant.
Through accumulated merit,
he was successively promoted to Touring General,
and together with Sīlì Mǎn Fèn and Hénán Yǐn Zhōu Fù, he was stationed at the Dàsīmǎ Gate
to guard the palace.
At that time, Shàngguān Sì was violent and lawless.
Hú conspired with Fèn and others to eliminate him,
but was instead killed by him.
Yú Yù
Yú Yù 字 Shūníng,
was the younger brother of the recluse Xǐ.
His original name was Mào,
but because it violated the taboo of the birth mother of Empress Míngmù,
it was changed.
Yù was orphaned at twelve,
and in his youth, he loved learning
and had literary talent.
In the customs of Yúyáo,
each had their own factions.
His clansmen jointly recommended Yù to be the county Gōngcáo,
wishing to use him to purge the corrupt.
Yù wrote to his paternal cousin, saying:
"Recently, I have heard that various gentlemen wish for me to enter the government office.
If I were to dedicate myself,
then I would have to be personally involved in affairs,
and not merely observe.
However, I am extremely foolish,
and have some reservations.
Wicked factions watch each other,
and differing opinions swarm in.
If I were to stumble once,
all drums would sound together.
A tiny mistake
can lead to a deviation of a thousand *lǐ*.
This is the clear warning of the ancients,
and what I greatly fear."
It turned out as Yù had said;
before half a year passed,
he was dismissed.
Grand Administrator Yú Chēn appointed him as Zhǔbù.
Yù presented a memorial listing the shortcomings of the current administration,
saying:
"Since the military incursions,
taxes and corvée have been numerous,
and coinciding with famine years,
the common people have lost their livelihoods.
This is a time for light corvée and thin levies,
for lenient punishments and reduced labor.
Recently, senior officials have frequently come and gone,
sending off the old and welcoming the new,
filling the roads.
Those being welcomed fear only that there are not enough boats and horses,
and those sending off regret only that there are always too few officials and attendants.
To exhaust extravagance and expense is called loyalty and righteousness;
to simplify and reduce is called vulgarity.
They mutually imitate each other,
and the trend flows without return.
Even if there are standing regulations,
none are willing to follow them.
Moreover, the imperial roads are not yet pacified,
and there are stoppages everywhere.
Those sending off spend years,
and permanently lose out on sowing and planting.
If one man does not farm,
ten men will have no food.
What if hundreds are involved?
The hindrance is inestimable.
I foolishly suggest that the subordinate counties should be ordered,
that if a Wèi is ordered to leave office,
the number of people, boats, officials, and attendants should all be itemized,
and upon arrival, they should be reduced according to law,
to make things fair for both public and private.
Also, currently, there are many administrative tasks,
and heavy regulations are always added.
Whenever there is a special urgency,
a Dūyóu is immediately appointed.
By my count, there are over thirty such temporary officials now,
and their people, boats, officials, and attendants all must come from government resources,
which further makes it unbearable.
It is appropriate to reduce them again,
and strictly guard against this."
Chēn approved of it,
and immediately implemented all of it.
When Grand Administrator Jì Zhān arrived,
Yù was again appointed Zhǔbù,
and then transferred to Gōngcáoshǐ.
He was recommended as Xiaolián,
but did not take office.
Āndōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng Zhūgě Huī and Cānjūn Yǔ Liàng and others recommended Yù,
and he was summoned to be Chéngxiàng Xíng Cānjūn concurrently Jìshì.
He suffered mourning for his mother,
and after the mourning period,
he was appointed Zuǒ Zhùzuòláng.
In the second year of Tàixīng (319 CE),
there was a great drought,
and an imperial edict sought forthright and honest speakers.
Yù submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying: "The Great Jìn received the Mandate,
and it has been over fifty years now.
Since Yuánkāng,
the imperial virtue began to wane,
the Róng and Dí reached the Central Plains,
the ancestral temples were burned to ashes,
a thousand *lǐ* had no smoke from cooking,
and Huáxià had no men in caps and belts.
Since the creation of heaven and earth,
and what is recorded in books,
never has there been such an extreme of great chaos as this.
Your Majesty, with sagely virtue and prior enlightenment,
transcendently and foresightedly,
established yourself as the protector in the southeast,
and your fame and teachings spread far and wide.
Heaven regarded you with favor,
and men and spirits assisted your plans.
Although it is called a restoration,
in reality, it is receiving the Mandate.
Shàokāng and King Xuān are truly not sufficient comparisons.
However, the songs of the southern wind can be composed,
but why are the declining customs still unchanged?
I, your
foolish
servant, believe that the essence of governing a state lies in obtaining talent,
and the method of obtaining talent lies in drawing it out.
If they are usable,
even if they are enemies or of low birth, they must be promoted.
Gāozōng and King Wén, in their thoughts of assistants,
had dreams,
and elevated recluses from the cliffs to be prime ministers,
and carried a fishing elder to be their teacher.
Down to the various states,
such things also occurred.
Thus, Yān valued Guō Kuí, and three *shì* vied to arrive.
Wèi honored Gān Mù, and Qín's troops retreated.
Although the empire is now dilapidated,
and talented people are few,
a village of ten households
must have loyal and trustworthy individuals.
The world does not lack fine steeds;
if sought,
they can be found.
Yet, bolts of silk are not bestowed upon those in the hills and gardens,
and carriages with padded wheels are left unhitched.
This is why great reforms are not widespread, and peace and prosperity are lacking."
Yù, believing that the bandits were not yet pacified,
and good generals were needed,
further submitted a memorial, saying: "I, your servant, have heard that in times of peace,
education first emphasizes culture,
but in times of chaos,
it cannot be overcome without military might.
Therefore, in the Battle of Mùyě,
Lǚ Wàng wielded the battle-axe;
when the Huái Yí caused
trouble,
Zhào Bó led the campaign;
when the Xiǎnyǔn were violent,
Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbì drove them back.
Thus, when Yin and Yang are not in harmony,
scholars are promoted to prime ministers;
when the three armies are not victorious,
soldiers are elevated to generals.
The Hàn
emperors, after pacifying the empire,
still sought fierce warriors to guard the four directions.
Emperor Xiàowén was determined to rescue Jùlù,
and Fēng Táng offered advice,
whereupon Wèi Shàng was reinstated as governor.
The *Shī* says,
'Valiant
warriors
are the bulwark of dukes and marquises.'
How can such strategists
be overlooked!
Moreover, now the Central Plains are devastated,
a mere one in a hundred survives.
The regional governors and officials are either not of the Róng or Mò
tribes,
or are lucky survivors of banditry.
Upon Your Majesty's ascension,
your prestige spread far and wide,
thus causing these individuals to return to goodness and embrace civilization.
However, a wolf's cub has a beast's heart,
fickle and easily
swayed.
With the Jié barbarians not yet exterminated,
it makes things even harder to secure.
Zhōu Fǔ and Chén Chuān successively betrayed us;
Xú Kān is arrogant and cunning,
unrestrained by anything,
unleashing his troops to plunder.
His crimes are already
manifest.
In the past, when Gě Bó deviated from the Dao,
Tāng offered him cattle;
when Wú Bì showed disrespect,
he was granted a stool and staff.
Only when their wickedness was complete and their crimes manifest
were they punished.
Kān's insignificance
is not
worth exterminating.
However, preparing for the unforeseen
is the good teaching of the ancients.
How much more so when there is danger,
can we not guard against it!
The method of guarding against it
is to obtain good generals.
Generals are not
lacking
it is difficult to resist the enemy.
Shòuchūn has no garrison,
Zǔ Tì stands isolated.
Before him are powerful invaders,
behind him no support.
Though he possesses wisdom and strength,
he cannot endure for long.
I wish Your
Majesty would consult with the multitude of officials
and broadly seek out opinions from the populace.
If a talent suitable for the current situation
is indeed appointed,
then they should be encouraged and rewarded,
so they disregard their lives.
Looking broadly among the obscure and humble,
if
there is someone capable,
grant them generous favor and treatment,
enough to make them forget themselves.
Formerly, Yīng Bù felt slighted
and was so angry he wanted to kill himself,
but after seeing the provisions and arrangements prepared for him,
he then exerted himself.
The
grace of courteous treatment
should indeed be great!
I sincerely know that the capacity of mountains and rivers cannot be augmented by dust and dew,
and the deliberations of a divine mirror cannot be fathomed by the foolish and shallow;
however, even common men and widows still voice concerns for the nation,
how much
more so for a subject who has obtained a place at the end of the imperial court,
enjoying the honor of wearing cap and sash!
He was transferred to be a Regular Attendant of Lángyá Commandery,
then promoted to Secretary of the Palace Library and Drafting Editor.
At the beginning of Xiánhé,
there was a summer drought.
An imperial edict commanded all officials to present their views on causing rain.
Yù's deliberation stated: "I have heard that the Way of Heaven values trustworthiness,
and the Way of Earth values sincerity.
Trustworthiness and sincerity
are the means by which the two cosmic forces generate and nurture all things,
and by which rulers protect the common people.
Therefore, killing and striking are likened to thunder and lightning,
and extending grace is symbolized by clouds and rain.
Punishments must be unfailingly reliable,
and rewards must be impartially distributed.
I have heard that since a certain time,
legal cases have become increasingly numerous.
Those with influence involve many others,
delaying proceedings for months and years;
those without support are subjected to harsh torture,
with the expectation of severe imprisonment.
Therefore, the people are clamorous
and distressed,
harming the harmonious energy.
I, your foolish subject, believe that for minor offenses and those whose crimes are tolerable,
decisions should be made quickly.
For capital crimes and serious offenders,
further deliberation should be requested.
lighten labor duties and cease forced labor,
diligently adhere to
frugality,
discipline court officials,
so that each knows their prohibitions.
An old ox is not sacrificed;
rituals have constant regulations.
However, recently, when many officials are appointed, granted titles, or awarded posthumous honors,
they boast and show off to each other,
slaughtering oxen and calves,
often in the tens,
and indulging
in excessive drinking,
with no limits,
wasting wealth and corrupting customs,
causing no small loss.
In ancient times, the Yin sovereign cultivated virtue to dispel the anomaly of the mulberry and grain;
Sòng Jǐng's good words averted the change of the Mars planet;
Chǔ suffered no disasters because
King Zhuāng was fearful.
Even the most virtuous
rulers
have not been without calamities.
By responding with trustworthiness and obedience,
Heaven's blessings will be abundant.
My learning and insight are shallow and obscure;
my words are not worth adopting."
He followed Píng Wánghán,
and was granted the title Marquis of Xīxiāng.
When Sū Jùn caused unrest,
Yù had previously been granted leave to return home.
The Grand Administrator Wáng Shū requested him to serve as a Consulting Army Advisor.
After Jùn was pacified,
he was promoted to Marquis of Píngkāng County,
then transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
with his duties as Drafting Editor remaining as before.
He was appointed Cavalier Regular Attendant,
still overseeing the Drafting Bureau.
Due to old age, he retired
and died at home.
Yù was fond of the classics and history,
and detested the profound and mysterious.
His critique of Ruǎn Jí's nakedness
compared him to Yī Chuān with disheveled hair,
believing that the widespread presence of "Hu" barbarians in the Central Plains
surpassed the decline of the Zhōu dynasty.
He authored over forty chapters of the Jìn Shū, twenty chapters of Kuàijī Diǎnlù, and twelve chapters of Zhū Yú Zhuàn,
all circulated in the world.
He also authored dozens of essays, poems, odes, epitaphs, and difficult discussions.
Sūn Shèng
Sūn Shèng, courtesy name Ānguó,
was a native of Zhōngdū, Tàiyuán.
His grandfather, Chǔ,
was the Grand Administrator of Féngyì.
His father, Xún,
was the Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
When Xún was in the commandery, he encountered bandits
and was killed.
Shèng was ten years old
when he fled the disaster and crossed the Yangtze River.
When he grew up,
he was widely learned
and skilled in discussing profound principles.
At that time, Yīn Hào was renowned for a period,
and the only one who could debate with him
was Shèng.
Shèng once visited Hào for a discussion.
While eating,
he furiously brandished his fly-whisk,
causing all the hairs to fall into the food.
The food cooled and was reheated several times.
By evening, they forgot to eat,
and the principle was still not settled.
Shèng also authored works on medicine, divination, and the principles of the Yì Jīng in his Miào Yú Jiàn Xíng Lùn.
Hào and others ultimately could not refute him,
and thus he became famous.
He started his career as an Assistant Drafting Editor,
but due to his family's poverty and his parents' old age,
he sought a position in a small county,
and was appointed Magistrate of Liúyáng.
Grand Administrator Táo Kǎn invited him to be an Army Advisor.
When Yú Liàng replaced Kǎn,
he appointed Shèng as Chief Clerk of the General Who Conquers the West,
and later promoted him to Army Advisor.
At that time, Chancellor Wáng Dǎo held power.
Liàng, as a maternal uncle of the emperor, was stationed outside the capital.
Táo Chēng, the Southern Man Commander, slandered and created discord between them,
causing Dǎo and Liàng to harbor suspicions.
Shèng secretly advised Liàng, saying:
"Duke Wáng's spirit and mind are clear and broad,
always harboring thoughts beyond the mundane world.
How could he engage in ordinary human affairs?
This must be the doing of sycophants who wish to sow discord between the inner and outer circles."
Liàng accepted his advice.
When Yú Yì succeeded Liàng,
he appointed Shèng as Consulting Army Advisor of the General Who Pacifies the West,
and soon promoted him to Rectifier of the Imperial Court.
When Huán Wēn replaced Yì,
he kept Shèng as an Army Advisor
and they went together to conquer Shǔ.
When the army reached Péngmó,
Wēn, with light troops, entered Shǔ himself.
Shèng led the weak and old with the baggage train behind.
Several thousand bandits suddenly arrived,
and everyone was in a panic.
Shèng organized the various generals,
and they resisted with combined strength,
causing the bandits to flee immediately.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he was granted the title Marquis of Ānhuái County,
and successively promoted to Attendant-in-Ordinary to Wēn.
He followed Wēn into the pass to pacify Luò,
and for his achievements, was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Wúchāng County,
and then appointed Grand Administrator of Chángshā.
Due to his family's poverty,
he engaged somewhat in business and trade.
The provincial inspector came to the commandery and discovered this,
but respected his high reputation and did not impeach him.
Shèng wrote a letter to Wēn,
in which the language and intent were unrestrained.
He mentioned that the province sent an inspector to observe customs,
but the inspector "neither had the beauty of an auspicious phoenix arriving,
nor the utility of an eagle or hawk striking its prey,
wandering in the Xiāng River,
he will become a strange bird."
When Wēn received Shèng's letter,
he again sent an inspector to thoroughly investigate the matter.
Shèng's corruption was extensive.
He was arrested in a cage cart and brought to the province,
but Wēn released him without punishment.
He was successively promoted to Supervisor of the Palace Library
and given the additional title of Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
small,
and what is preserved is great!
What has been compiled today,
if it has been inherited from previous records,
then it is not my fault.
If, however, in compiling events of recent times,
there are errors or inaccuracies,
I wish to share the criticism and blame with the former worthies and scholars.
And with regard to their writings,
they are also sufficient to prove that the way of the spirits is not deceptive.
The multitude of sayings and myriad schools are too numerous to examine thoroughly,
and what the ears and eyes have received is too much to record fully.
Now, I have merely selected what is sufficient to expound the gist of the "Eight Strategies" [Bā Lüè],
completing its subtle discussions.
I hope that future enthusiasts will record its root essence,
finding something in it to occupy their minds and eyes without fault.
Bǎo also wrote the *Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì Yì Wài Zhuàn* and
annotations for the *Zhōu Yì* and *Zhōu Guān*, totaling several tens of chapters,
as well as miscellaneous essays, all circulating in the world.
Dèng Càn
Dèng Càn,
a native of Chángshā.
From a young age, he was known for his lofty integrity,
and he was like-minded and friendly with Liú Línzhī of Nányáng and Liú Shànggōng of Nánjùn,
none of whom responded to summonses from prefectures or commanderies.
Huán Chōng, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, humbly and generously invited Càn to be a biéjià,
and Càn, admiring his esteem for worthies,
then rose and answered the call.
Línzhī and Shànggōng said to him:
"Your way is broad and your learning deep,
respected by all.
To suddenly change your principles
is truly disappointing."
Càn laughed and replied:
"You gentlemen may be said to have the aspiration to be a recluse but do not know what reclusion is.
For reclusion as a way,
one can be a recluse in court,
and one can be a recluse in the marketplace.
Reclusion fundamentally resides in me,
not in external things."
Shànggōng and the others had no way to refute him,
but Càn's reputation was halved by this.
Later, he suffered from a foot ailment
and could not attend court,
so he requested to leave his post,
but he was not permitted;
he was ordered to conduct affairs while lying down.
Later, as his illness worsened,
he begged for his bones to be returned,
and it was granted.
Càn believed that his father, Qiān, had spoken loyal and trustworthy words but that no one in the world knew of them,
so he wrote the *Yuán Míng Jì* in ten chapters,
and annotated the *Lǎozi*,
both of which circulated in the world.
Xiè Shěn
Xiè Shěn, courtesy name Xíngsī,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His great-grandfather, Fěi,
was the Administrator of Yùzhāng in Wú.
His father, Xiù, was the Winged Right Commandant of Wú.
Shěn was orphaned young,
served his mother
with extreme filial piety,
was broadly learned and widely knowledgeable,
and was clear and skilled in the classics and histories.
The commandery appointed him as Registrar and Merits Officer,
and recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt,
and Grand Commandant Xī Jiàn invited him,
but he did not accept any of these.
Hé Chōng, the Administrator of Kuàijī, recruited him as a staff officer,
but he resigned due to his mother's old age.
Yǔ Liàng, the General Who Pacifies the West, appointed him as Merits Officer,
and Cài Mó, the General Who Conquers the North, appointed him as a staff officer,
but he did not accept any of these either.
He lived in seclusion, caring for his mother,
not engaging in worldly affairs.
In his leisure from plowing and weeding,
he devoted himself to studying the ancient texts.
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
the court debated the question of the periodic destruction of the seven ancestral temples,
so he was summoned as an academician of the Imperial University
to clarify the doubtful points.
He resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed as Director of the Dùzhī Bureau of the Department of State Affairs.
Hé Chōng and Yǔ Bīng both praised Shěn as having talent for history,
and he was promoted to Drafting Officer,
compiling over thirty chapters of the *Jìn Shū*.
He died shortly thereafter,
at the age of fifty-two.
Shěn had previously written one hundred chapters of the *Hòu Hàn Shū* and the *Máo Shī* and *Hàn Shū Wài Zhuàn*.
All his writings, as well as his poems, rhapsodies, essays, and treatises, circulated in the world.
His talent and learning were said to be superior to Yú Yù's.
Xí Zuòchǐ
Xí Zuòchǐ, courtesy name Yànwēi,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
His clan was wealthy and prominent,
and they were locally powerful for generations.
Zuòchǐ was ambitious from a young age,
broadly learned and widely informed,
and known for his literary skills.
Huán Wēn, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, appointed him as an attendant,
and Yuán Qiáo, the Chancellor of Jiāngxià, deeply esteemed him,
often praising his talent to Wēn,
who then transferred him to become Registrar of the Western Bureau,
treating him with great intimacy and trust.
At that time, Wēn had great ambitions.
He summoned an astrologer from Shǔ
and, holding his hand at night, asked about the duration of the state's fortune.
The astrologer replied:
"The dynastic sacrifices will last forever."
Wēn suspected he was reluctant to speak,
so he embellished his words, saying:
"If, as you say,
it is not only my good fortune but
also the happiness of the common people.
However, what you say today can be fully disclosed.
If there are any minor misfortunes,
you should also speak of them."
The astrologer said:
"The atmospheric conditions of the three palaces—Tàiwēi, Zǐwēi, and Wénchāng—are thus;
there are definitely no worries.
Beyond fifty years, I cannot speak of it."
Wēn was displeased
and stopped.
Another day,
he sent a bolt of silk and five thousand coins to him.
The astrologer then rushed to Zuòchǐ and said:
"My home is in Yìzhōu,
and I was ordered to come down from afar.
Now, I have received an order to take my own life,
and have no means to send my bones home.
Because of your benevolence,
I beg you to make a monument and a coffin for me."
Zuòchǐ asked for the reason,
and the astrologer said:
"The gift of one bolt of silk
is to make me take my own life,
and the five thousand coins
are to buy a coffin."
Zuòchǐ said:
"You were almost wrongly killed!
Have you never heard the principle that a diviner who knows the constellations cannot be covered up?
This silk is to tease you,
and the money is for your travel expenses;
it means he is letting you go."
The astrologer was greatly delighted,
and the next morning he went to bid farewell to Wēn.
Wēn asked his reason for leaving,
and he answered with Zuòchǐ's words.
Wēn laughed and said:
"Zuòchǐ feared you would die by mistake,
but you definitely lived by mistake.
However, thirty years of reading Confucian books
is not as good as one visit to Registrar Xí."
He was successively promoted to biéjià.
When Wēn went on military campaigns,
Zuòchǐ sometimes followed and sometimes remained behind,
serving in his assigned posts,
always holding key positions,
achieving success in his duties.
He was skilled in writing letters and discussions,
and Wēn greatly esteemed and favored him.
At that time, scholars known for their "pure conversation" and literary talent, such as Hán Bó and Fú Tāo, were all close friends with him.
Later, when he went to the capital,
Emperor Jiǎnwén also highly respected him.
Upon his return,
Wēn asked:
"How was the Prince Regent?"
He replied:
"Someone I have never seen in my life."
This greatly displeased Wēn,
and he was demoted to Staff Officer of the Hùcáo Bureau.
At that time, there was a Buddhist monk, Shì Dào'ān,
who was brilliant in debate and highly talented.

then white twisted pearls can be used."
Emperor Chéng
then ordered the Grand Master of Ceremonies to change them.
Before this,
the Emperor, valuing his wet nurse Madame Zhōu
for her maternal care,
wished to bestow a noble title upon her.
Both internal and external officials obeyed the decree.
Hé
alone submitted a memorial arguing
that "Madame Zhōu
protected His Sacred Person,
and her merits are not forgotten.
Her residence and provisions are comparable to those of royal relatives,
and the favors bestowed upon her are already excessively grand.
If a noble title were granted,
there is no clear precedent recorded in the annals.
Only Emperor Líng
of Han
made his wet nurse Zhào Ráo
the Lady of Píngshì.
This was a private favor of a decadent era,
not an excellent precedent from earlier times.
Moreover, the ruler's actions must be recorded,
to set a standard and establish a model.
If recorded actions are not exemplary,
what will future generations look to?"
The Emperor followed his advice.
He was transferred to Minister of Personnel,
and frequently moved to General of the Palace Guard, Grand Master of Ceremonies, and Libationer of the Imperial Academy.
When Emperor Kāng
ascended the throne,
he was about to offer sacrifices at the northern and southern suburbs.
Hé
argued that the imperial carriage should personally attend.
The Emperor followed his advice,
and personally performed the rites.
He was promoted to Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Due to his mother's old age, he firmly declined,
but an imperial decree commanded him to accept,
specifically allowing him to leave court in the evening and return home.
Such was the exceptional favor he received.
Soon after, the court deliberated that the assistant to the highest officials should not hold an external post,
so he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
concurrently Libationer of the Imperial Academy.
After a while,
he left office due to his mother's mourning.
During his period of mourning, he was renowned for his filial piety.
After the mourning period was completed,
General of the Guards Chǔ Póu
submitted a memorial recommending Hé.
He was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and a Cavalier Attendant was sent to convey the imperial decree.
Hé,
whenever pressed,
would wail and faint in sorrow,
saying to his confidants:
"In ancient times, some would set aside their mourning clothes to obey the king's command,
probably because their talents were sufficient to assist the times,
At that time, Xiè Shàng (謝尚), the Zhongláng Jiāng (中郎將) of the South, also held the title of Xuānchéng Nèishǐ (宣城內史).
He arrested and executed Chén Gàn (陳幹), the magistrate of Jīng (涇).
The relevant authorities impeached and dismissed Xiè Shàng for violating the law,
but an imperial edict pardoned him.
Hé Chóng (和重) then submitted another memorial, saying:
"Previously, Xiè Shàng impeached Chén Gàn for embezzlement,
which was covered by the Jiǎxū (甲戌) amnesty,
allowing those who confessed to have their death penalty commuted.
However, Xiè Shàng recently reported that Chén Gàn concealed treachery and cunning,
and he immediately arrested and executed him.
Chén Gàn's case originated in the commandery,
it was not a military offense,
nor was it handled by the Dūdū (都督).
It is observed that Xiè Shàng, having been promoted by esteemed relatives
and entrusted with both civil and military responsibilities,
was unable to uphold the nation's integrity,
judge with impartiality,
but instead harbored personal grudges,
unleashed his cruel authority,
causing dismay far and wide,
and disheartening everyone.
Xiè Shàng is a member of the imperial clan by marriage;
there is precedent for leniency towards him.
However, as for his subordinates,
they should be subject to the full force of the law."
Xiè Shàng
was the maternal uncle of the Empress Dowager,
so the memorial was shelved.
At that time, Rǔnán Wáng Tǒng (汝南王統) and Jiāngxià Gōng Wèi Chóng (江夏公衞崇) both observed a three-year mourning period for their stepmothers.
Hé Chóng then memorialized, saying:
"Ritual is what guides all things and establishes teachings.
Therefore, those who govern a nation invariably uphold righteousness and clarify fundamentals
to unify their rule.
This is the essence of human relations
and an unvarying principle.
Those who are adopted as heirs
must diminish the status of their birth mother,
suppress natural family affection,
and manifest the ultimate principle of public justice.
The regulations for reducing mourning observance
are clearly set forth in the Rites of Zhōu (周典).
It is observed that Rǔnán Wáng Tǒng lived in a mourning hut and observed full mourning for his stepmother.
Jiāngxià Gōng Wèi Chóng, originally from a distant branch of the family
who established the dukedom,
recently lost his birth mother
and again observed full mourning.
Both violated and disregarded the rites and regulations,
indulging their private sentiments.
The common people praise their excessive devotion,
and commentators do not consider it wrong.
If this is the case, then the decline of governance stems from the abandonment of rites,
and the decay of institutions begins with tolerating such transgressions.
If these are not corrected,
it will be impossible to regulate all things.
All should be sent to the Tàicháng (太常) to have their mourning removed.
If they do not comply with the imperial decree,
they should be demoted and dismissed."
An imperial edict approved this.
While in office, Hé Chóng made many valuable contributions,
and he would not arbitrarily bend to powerful officials.
In the seventh year of Yǒnghé (永和, 351 CE), he resigned due to severe illness,
and was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫) with the honors of Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
while his position as Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) remained as before.
He died that same year
at the age of sixty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sīkōng (司空),
and given the posthumous name Mù (穆).
His son, Chún (淳),
served successively as Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎), Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎), and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍).
Yuán Guī (袁瓌) (Zǐqiáo [子喬]; Zǐqiáo's grandson Shānsōng [山松]; Guī's younger brother Yóu [猷]; his paternal cousin Zhǔn [準]; Zhǔn's grandson Dān [耽]; Dān's son Zhì [質]; Zhì's son Zhàn [湛]; Bào [豹])
Yuán Guī (袁瓌), courtesy name Shānpǔ (山甫),
was a native of Yángxià (陽夏), Chénjùn (陳郡).
He was the great-grandson of Huàn (渙), the Lángzhōng Lìng (郎中令) of Wèi (魏).
His grandfather and father both died early.
Guī and his younger brother Yóu (猷) wished to take their mother to avoid the chaos,
so they sought appointment as magistrates in counties between the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers.
He was appointed magistrate of Lǚ (呂),
then transferred to Jiāngdū (江都),
and consequently crossed south.
Yuán Dì (元帝) appointed him Dānyáng Lìng (丹楊令).
When the Central Revival began,
he was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and then promoted to Zhìshū Yùshǐ (治書御史).
At that time, the corpse of Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) had been burned by Shí Lè (石勒),
and his consort, Lady Péi (裴), sought to perform a 'calling of the soul' burial for Yuè.
The court was uncertain about this.
Guī and the academician Fù Chún (傅純) debated the matter,
believing that a 'calling of the soul' burial was tantamount to burying the spirit,
and should not be permitted.
The emperor agreed.
Although he initially granted Lady Péi permission for a 'calling of the soul' burial for Yuè,
he subsequently issued an edict prohibiting it.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江).
Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) Wáng Dūn (王敦) then brought him in as Cányì Cānjūn (諮議參軍).
Shortly thereafter, he became Administrator of Línchuān (臨川).
After Wáng Dūn was pacified,
he became Jūnsī (軍司) for Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍) Biàn Dūn (卞敦).
Soon after, he resigned and returned to the capital,
and traveled to Kuàijī (會稽).
During the calamity of Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
he and Wáng Shū (王舒) raised an army of righteousness together.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chánghé Xiāng (長合鄉),
summoned and appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and then transferred to Dàsīnóng (大司農).
Soon after, he was appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒).
After a while,
he was additionally granted Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
At that time, following years of chaos,
ritual and teaching were in decline.
Guī submitted a memorial, stating: "I have heard that the teachings of the former kings
exalted classical texts to broaden knowledge for distant generations,
and elucidated rites and music to influence future generations,
thereby guiding the nature of all beings
and promoting the path
to goodness.
When the imperial Zhōu (周) dynasty flourished,
its literary and historical records shone brightly,
its institutions extended to the southern barbarians,
and songs of praise filled the four seas.
Therefore, when Yánzhōu (延州) visited Lǔ (魯),
he heard elegant music and sighed;
when Hán
Qǐ (韓起) traveled to Lǔ,
he observed its customs and praised them.
Why is this?
The way of establishing humanity
begins here.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) earnestly taught in the area of Zhūsì (洙泗),
and Mèng Kē (孟軻) continued his work,
teaching and guiding
tirelessly.
This is why the fame of benevolence and righteousness endures to this day,
and principles of propriety and deference are occasionally practiced.
In recent times, the imperial destiny has declined,
and chaos has repeatedly occurred.
The teachings of the Confucian scholars have gradually deteriorated,
and the rites of schools have been neglected.
The national academy is desolate,
and ancient texts are unopened,
leaving
those with aspirations without a means to fulfill them.
In the past, Wèi Wǔ Dì (魏武帝), personally clad in armor
and devoted to military achievements,
still dismounted to read,
and put down his spear to recite poetry.
How much more so now, Your Majesty,
who presides over the court with sagacity and wisdom,
with all officials diligently attending to their duties,
the court and country free from worries,
and the land south of the Jiāng (江) river tranquil?
How can the grand and expansive atmosphere be unheard,
and the magnificent
beauty be lost in a glorious age?
The ancients said,
'The Odes and Documents are the treasury of righteousness;
rites and music are the standard of virtue.'
It is truly fitting to focus on the classics,
elucidate academic principles,
so that the sound of recitation fills the imperial capital,
and worthy individuals who appreciate the Dao emulate and praise them.
Would this not be magnificent!
If residences are provided for them,
and a sufficient number of students are enrolled,
with the positions of academicians
and their staff roughly established,
then that would be my wish."
After the memorial was submitted,
Chéng Dì (成帝) followed it.
The revival of the national academy
began with Guī.
As he was of an age to retire,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to old age.
He died shortly thereafter.
He was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
and given the posthumous name Gōng (恭).
His son, Qiáo (喬), succeeded him.
Qiáo, courtesy name Yànshū,
was initially appointed Zuǒ Zhùzuò Láng.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Huán Wēn invited him to be his Sīmǎ.
He was offered the post of Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ,
but did not accept it.
He was then appointed Shàngshū Láng.
When Huán Wēn was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu,
he again invited Qiáo to be his Sīmǎ
and concurrently Liǎnguǎnglíng Xiàng.
Previously,
Qiáo and Chǔ Póu were close friends.
When Empress Kāngxiàn presided over the court,
Qiáo wrote a letter to Póu, saying:
"Her Majesty the Empress Dowager has ascended to the throne
and governs the imperial court.
As for the general's relationship with the state,
he is an 'external surname' Grand Emperor.
Regarding the imperial sons and close relatives,
all observe the rites of humility and deference,
how much more so for a notable official,
to intimately associate with the emperor's father?
Heaven's nature holds this in high esteem,
and it is also appropriate to consider the state and give it weight.
Therefore, regarding our old friendship,
I beg to withdraw from it at this point.
The change of dyed silk moved Mò Dí to reflection;
the crossroads aroused Yáng Zhū's sighs.
How much more so with the general,
with whom I have associated from youth to old age,
though our worldly reputations vary, our sentiments have converged.
The familiarity of old
must now be lowered with respect to propriety.
The joy of unrestrained intimacy
must be set aside according to the times.
Even if one wished to idly sing in the marketplace,
casting off all formality,
how could one achieve it!
Incoming things do not halt,
change and shift with time;
how could it be merely a matter of a brief moment?
Circumstances also dictate this.
Indeed, he who controls implements is divine,
governing the masses with restraint.
I wish the general to soothe his feelings and remain unburdened,
taking the triumph of reason as his duty,
relying on the wise and eminent,
and valuing the acceptance of good counsel above all.
Holding my brush, I feel melancholy
and cannot fully express myself."
Commentators considered this to be in accordance with ritual.
He was promoted to Ānxī Zīyì Cānjūn and Chángshā Xiàng,
but did not accept the appointments.
Soon after, he was appointed Dū Miǎno Zhōng Zhū Shù Jiāngxià Suíyìyáng Sān Jùn Jūnshì, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngxià Xiàng.
At that time, Huán Wēn planned to attack Shǔ,
but the consensus was that it was unfeasible.
Qiáo advised Wēn, saying:
"Indeed, strategizing major undertakings
is not something ordinary thinking can encompass.
A wise person understands it clearly in his heart
before acting, leaving no miscalculation.
Today, the difficulties for the empire are merely two foes.
Though Shǔ is treacherous and strong,
compared to Hú it is weak.
If one intends to eliminate them,
one should start with the easier one.
Now, to go upriver for ten thousand *lǐ*,
passing through natural strongholds,
if they are prepared,
it may not necessarily be conquerable.
However, the people of Shǔ consider themselves isolated in one corner,
relying on their completeness and solidity,
not cultivating means of attack and defense.
If we take ten thousand elite soldiers,
and with light forces advance swiftly,
by the time they hear of it,
we will have already entered their strategic points.
Lǐ Shì and his ministers will have no choice but to fight one battle with all their might,
and capturing them will be certain.
Commentators fear that once the main army goes west,
the Hú will surely spy upon us.
This, again, seems right but is actually wrong.
Why?
When the Hú hear of a ten-thousand-lǐ expedition,
they will assume that we have strong defenses internally,
and will surely not dare to move.
Even if they were to cross the river and enter our territory,
our various armies would be sufficient to defend the borders.
There is no worry about this.
The land of Shǔ is rich and fertile,
known as a heavenly granary.
In the past, Zhūgě Wǔhóu wished to use it to contend with the Central Plains.
Although it cannot cause harm now,
its strategic position upstream
makes it easy for it to become a bandit's lair.
If we can surprise and take it,
possessing its populace,
this would be a great benefit to the state."
Wēn agreed
and sent Qiáo, as Jiāngxià Xiàng, to lead two thousand men as the vanguard.
The army reached Péngmó;
they were already close to the enemy.
Some suggested advancing by two routes simultaneously
to divide the enemy's forces.
Qiáo said:
"Now we are deep into enemy territory, ten thousand *lǐ* away,
placed in a position of certain death.
The soldiers have no thought of retreat;
this is what is called 'people fighting for themselves.'
If we now divide into two armies,
our military strength will not be unified.
If one flank should happen to be defeated,
then the great undertaking would be lost.
It is better to advance with the entire army,
abandon our cooking pots,
and carry three days' rations.
Victory will then be assured."
Wēn thought this was correct
and immediately advanced with the entire army at once.
Ten *lǐ* from Chéngdū,
they fought a great battle with the enemy.
The vanguard suffered a setback,
and Qiáo's army also retreated.
Arrows reached his horse's head,
and his attendants turned pale.
Qiáo, however, waved his hand and advanced,
his morale becoming even more resolute.
He then thoroughly routed them,
driving straight to Chéngdū.
After Lǐ Shì surrendered,
his generals Dèng Dìng and Wěi Wén rebelled with their subordinates,
each commanding over ten thousand troops.
Wēn personally attacked Dìng,
and Qiáo attacked Wén,
defeating him.
He was promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Xiāngxī Bó.
Soon after, he died
at the age of thirty-six.
Wēn deeply mourned his loss.
He was posthumously granted the title Yìzhōu Cìshǐ
and given the posthumous name Jiǎn.
Qiáo was widely learned and possessed literary talent.
He annotated the *Lúnyǔ* and the *Shī*,
and all his essays and writings circulated in the world.
His son Fāngpíng succeeded him.
Fāngpíng also established himself through his upright conduct,
was appointed Dàsīmǎ Yuàn,
and successively served as Yìxīng and Lángyé Tàishǒu.
Upon his death,
his son Shānsōng succeeded him.
Shānsōng showed talent and renown from a young age,
was widely learned, and possessed literary skill.
He authored one hundred chapters of the *Hòuhàn Shū*.
His sentiments were refined and profound,
and he excelled at music.
There was an old song called "Xínglù Nán Qǔ,"
whose lyrics were rather plain and simple.
Shānsōng liked it,
so he refined its lyrics and phrases
and made its rhythm and control more graceful.
Whenever he was deeply intoxicated, he would sing it freely,
and those who listened could not help but shed tears.
Previously,
Yáng Tán was good at singing popular songs,
and Huán Yī was skilled at elegies.
When Shānsōng's "Xínglù Nán" followed,
people of the time called them
the "Three Uniques."
At that time, Zhāng Zhàn liked to plant pine and cypress trees in front of his study.
And whenever Shānsōng went out,
he liked to have his attendants sing elegies.
People said,
"Zhàn has corpses displayed under his house,
and Shānsōng carries a funeral procession on the road."
Shānsōng held prominent positions,
serving as Wú Jùn Tàishǒu.
When Sūn Ēn instigated a rebellion,
Shānsōng defended Hùdú.
The city fell, and he was killed.
Yóu, courtesy name Shēnfǔ,
was renowned alongside Guī from a young age.
He replaced Guī as Lǚ Lìng,
and then they successively became Jiāngdū.
Thus, they both crossed the Jiāng River.
Guī became Dānyáng,
and Yóu became Wǔkāng.
The brothers served as governors in famous districts,
which commentators praised.
He successively held the positions of Shìzhōng and Wèiwèi Qīng.
Yóu's grandson, Hóng,
is mentioned in the *Wényuàn Zhuàn*.
Zhǔn, courtesy name Xiàoní,
was renowned for his Confucian scholarship,
and annotated the *Sāngfú Jīng*.
He rose to the rank of Gěishìzhōng.
Zhǔn's son, Chōng,
courtesy name Jǐngxuán,
was the Guānglùxūn.
Chōng's son was Dān.
Dān, courtesy name Yàndào,
showed talent in his youth,
was unconventional and unrestrained,
and was praised by scholars.
Huán Wēn, when young, frequented gamblers,
exhausting all his assets,
and still incurred debts.
He sought a way to redeem himself,
but knew not what to do.
He wished to seek help from Dān,
but Dān was in mourning.
He tried telling him his predicament.
Dān showed hardly any difficulty,
and so changed his clothes, donned a cloth cap,
and accompanied Wēn to gamble with his creditors.
Dān had a long-standing reputation for skill (in games),
but the creditors, having heard of him but not knowing him personally,
said to him:
"You surely aren't capable of being Yuán Yàndào."
So they started the game.
Ten myriad (coins) per throw,
straight up to a million.
Dān threw his dice, gave a great shout,
pulled off his cloth cap and threw it to the ground,
saying:
"Do you recognize Yuán Yàndào now?"
Such was his open-mindedness.
During the campaign of Sū Jùn,
Wáng Dǎo appointed him Cānjūn,
and he followed Dǎo to Shítóu.
Initially,
Lù Yǒng, Kuāng Shù, Jiǎ Níng, and others were Sū Jùn's confidants.
Hearing that Zǔ Yuē had fled in defeat,
fearing their cause would fail,
they successively urged Sū Jùn to execute the high officials.
As Sū Jùn did not comply,
Yǒng and the others, fearing inevitable defeat,
secretly allied with Dǎo.
Dǎo sent Dān to secretly persuade Lù Yǒng
to return to allegiance.
After Sū Jùn was pacified,
Dān was enfeoffed as the Earl of Zǐguī,
appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Líyáng Tàishǒu.
In the early Xiánkāng period,
Shí Jìlóng's cavalry, numbering just over ten riders, reached Líyáng.
Dān's memorial to the throne did not mention the small number of riders.
At that time, the Hú barbarians were strong and powerful,
and the court and people were gripped by fear.
Wáng Dǎo, in his capacity as prime minister, requested to personally lead an expedition against them.
However, the enemy cavalry was not numerous
and had already retreated,
so Dǎo stayed put.
The imperial court, deeming Dān to have been reckless and frivolous,
demoted him.
Soon after, he was again appointed Dǎo's Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Just as he was about to be given a great responsibility,
he died,
at the age of twenty-five.
His son was Zhì.
Zhì, courtesy name Dàohé.
From Huàn to Zhì, for five generations,
they all succeeded in their careers through their integrity,
except for his father Dān, who was noted for his boldness and heroism.
By Zhì's time,
he was again known for his filial conduct.
He successively held offices such as Lángyá Nèishǐ and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
Zhì's son was Zhàn.
Zhàn, courtesy name Shìshēn.
In his youth, he possessed integrity and resolve,
establishing himself through his purity and sincerity,
but lacked literary flourish.
Therefore, he was not highly regarded by conventional society.
At that time, Xiè Hùn was the Púyè.
Fàn Tài presented a poem to Zhàn and Hùn, saying:
"There are also outstanding talents appearing later,
leaving the flock, soaring high."
Zhàn resented this and did not reply.
From Zhōngshūlìng, he became Púyè, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Earl of Jìnníng.
He died in office.
Zhàn's younger brother was Bào.
Bào, courtesy name Shìwèi.
He was widely learned and skilled in literary arts,
possessing talent for governing the state,
and was recognized by Liú Yù.
Later, he became Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ and Dānyáng Yǐn,
and then died.
Jiāng Yōu (His cousin Guàn. Guàn's son Jì.)
Jiāng Yōu, courtesy name Dàozài,
was a native of Yǔ, Chénliú.
His great-grandfather, Ruí,
was Qiáojùn Tàishǒu.
His grandfather, Yǔn,
was Wúhú Lìng.
His father, Jì,
was Āndōng Cānjūn.
Yōu was orphaned young,
and lived with his cousin Guàn.
They were very friendly and fraternal,
thus gaining a good reputation at the time.
To avoid the chaos of Sū Jùn,
he secluded himself in Línhǎi,
abandoning all worldly affairs,
cutting reeds to build a hut,
and indulging in books and records,
with the intention of living out his life there.
The local province invited him to be a Cóngshì,
and he was appointed Zuǒ Zhùzuòláng,
but he did not accept either position.
Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Cài Mó appointed him Cānjūn,
and Hé Chōng again invited him to be Piàojì Gōngcáo.
Due to family poverty,
he requested a temporary appointment,
and became Tàimò Lìng.
Within the county's deep mountains,
there were several hundred families of fugitives,
who relied on the dangerous terrain for protection.
Previous magistrates and governors had been unable to pacify them.
When Yōu arrived in office,
he summoned their leaders,
treated them kindly and engaged them warmly,
explaining the consequences of both good and bad actions.
Within ten days or a month,
they came, carrying their children on their backs,
which the imperial court commended.
The province then appointed him Zhìzhōng,
then transferred him to Biéjià,
and promoted him to Wú Lìng.
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Yīn Hào planned a northern expedition,
and requested Yōu to be Cányì Cānjūn.
Hào greatly esteemed him,
and promoted him to Zhǎngshǐ.
Hào was then restoring Luòyáng
and developing the wild and neglected areas.
Yōu, as his chief assistant,
provided great help in advising and correcting,
and all military dispatches and memorials were entrusted to Yōu.
At that time, the Qiāng and Dīnglíng rebelled,
causing panic in Hào's army.
Yáo Xiāng set up camp ten *lǐ* from Hào, pressing him.
Hào ordered Yōu to attack him.
Yōu advanced his troops to Xiāng's camp,
and said to his officers:
"Our troops are not unrefined,
but our numbers are fewer than the Qiāng.
Moreover, their trenches and palisades are very strong,
making it difficult to compete in brute force.
I shall break them with a stratagem."
Thereupon, he took several hundred chickens, tied them with long ropes,
and attached fire to their feet.
The flock of chickens scattered in fright,
flying into Xiāng's camp.
Fire broke out in Xiāng's camp.
Taking advantage of their confusion,
he attacked them,
and Xiāng suffered a minor defeat.
