When Huán Wēn memorialized for the dismissal of Hào's subordinates,
Yōu was consequently discharged.
Soon after,
he was appointed Zhōngshūláng.
During the Shēngpíng era,
he was promoted to Lìbù Láng,
and concurrently held the position of Shìzhōng.
Emperor Mù was about to renovate the imperial pond and
build a covered walkway. Yōu submitted a memorial, saying: Your subject has heard that a king, occupying the supreme position of ten thousand chariots
and enjoying immense wealth,
must clearly establish systems to demonstrate his eminence,
and magnify his culture and achievements to distinguish between noble and base.
Erecting the Lingtai,
dredging the Bìyōng,
establishing palaces and halls,
and setting up parks and preserves,
these are all to promote the emperor's dignity
and manifest the principle of governing the people.
The ancient sages initiated these rituals,
and later generations followed
their rules.
Rulers of every age have engaged in these undertakings.
King Xuān of Zhōu initiated the construction of numerous walls,
and the *Hóngyàn* (wild geese) ode sang of the joy of a peaceful home;
Duke Xī of Lǔ repaired the palace by the Pànshǔi,
and the gathering of water celery
was sung of with praise for happiness.
Truly, when those above act, it is not merely to satisfy their own desires;
and when those below serve their superiors, they do not consider hard work laborious.
These are the excellent ancient institutions,
the models
of the great model.
Indeed, principles are not constant;
the Three Rectifications differ from each other.
The system of governance
shifts with the times.
If one seeks ornament, simplicity is preferred,
hence embellishment reverts to plainness.
If there is greatness, it must be full,
so it is received with humility.
Diminishing the high to benefit the low
pleases the masses.
Offering two *guǐ*
exemplifies the meaning of utmost frugality.
This is why Táng-Yú's (堯 Yáo and 舜 Shùn) influence spread from thatched huts,
and Xià-Yǔ's beauty was manifested in humble dwellings.
The meanness of excessive frugality
is not the mean of the Middle Way,
yet the three sages practiced it to achieve the ultimate Dao.
Hàn Gāozǔ, at the
beginning of his construction projects,
was angered by the grandeur of the palaces and treasuries.
Xiào Wén, living in an era of accumulated wealth,
cherished the property of ten families,
thereby spreading benevolence in his time
and earning renown for future generations.
Presently, the two barbarian enemies are not yet eliminated,
and the divine land is desolate.
Mobilizing the forces from Jiāngzuǒ,
strategic planning is difficult.
Transporting grain from Yángyuè
to provision Hélǔo in the north,
the troops cannot be
mustered,
and supply lines are long and distant.
Storehouses are empty,
and the common people are exhausted.
Furthermore, since spring and summer,
floods and droughts have caused harm.
Harvests near and far have universally decreased from normal years.
Resources are depleted,
people are distressed,
and great labor has not ceased.
Military and national expenditures have no source of supply.
Compared to past eras,
prosperity and decline are vastly different.
To reduce again and again
is truly for today.
We
humbly consider that Your Majesty's sagely nature is Heaven-sent,
serene, expansive, pure, and profound.
You elucidate the splendor of daily renewal
and cultivate a disposition of reverence and wisdom.
Your lack of desire embodies naturalness,
and your humility and simplicity serve as a model for all nations.
Since the *sháo* music is utterly beautiful,
it must also be utterly good.
It is fitting to nourish it with profound emptiness
and uphold it with non-action.
Observing views should not be from high terraces or pavilions,
nor should recreation be in parks or ponds.
Resting should be entirely
in benevolence and righteousness,
and striving should culminate in the Six Arts.
Contemplate the grandeur of the towering (sages),
examine the culture of the two dynasties (Xià and Shāng),
reflect on Xī-Nóng (伏羲 Fú Xī and 神農 Shén Nóng),
and seek out Zhōu-Kǒng (周公 Zhōu Gōng and 孔子 Kǒng Zǐ).
Such freedom and ease
is
sufficient to honor the upholders of morality,
and befriend the elite officials.
Seek counsel in due season,
and consult tirelessly.
Accept or reject suggestions and remonstrances,
hearing them daily.
Then all achievements will be solidified,
the entire realm will flourish,
the splendor of this restoration will surpass that of Yīn-Zōng (殷高宗 Yīn Gāozōng),
and the blessings of auspiciousness will flow endlessly.
In the past, when Hàn built Déyáng Palace,
Zhōnglí expressed strong opposition.
When Wèi constructed palaces,
Chén Qún spoke with righteous words.
Although your minister’s talent is not like these men,
yet my office disgraces that of a close attendant.
My words may not
be worth adopting,
but it is my duty to make them known.
The Emperor praised his words and stopped.
He again held the position of Grand Justice of his native prefecture.
At the end of the Shēngpíng era,
he was promoted to Tàicháng,
but Yóu repeatedly declined, which was not permitted.
When Mù Dì died,
precious artifacts were about to be used for his imperial tomb.
Yóu remonstrated, saying:
"According to Xuānhuáng's dying instructions,
no spirit articles were to be placed in the imperial tomb,
to serve as a future precedent.
Jǐng Dì respectfully followed these遗制 (last wishes).
When Empress Wénmíng died,
Emperor Wǔ also adhered to the former regulations,
providing nothing,
except for offerings of dried meat and cooked rice,
and pottery vessels.
Previously, in Emperor Kāng's Xuan Palace,
precious swords and golden slippers were first used.
This was probably due to the Empress Dowager Wǎngyǐ's feelings,
truly violating the former edicts and ancestral laws of many generations.
Now, if outsiders wish to make this a precedent,
your minister requests to state the former edicts and halt these two items."
The memorial was submitted,
and it was followed.
Emperor Āi, due to anomalies in astronomical phenomena,
wished to follow the system of the Grand Sacrifice in the Shàngshū,
personally conducting a solemn ceremony in the front hall of Tàijí Palace,
hoping to avert calamity.
He ordered the Tàicháng to gather scholars to draft the ceremony.
Yóu submitted a memorial remonstrating: "Your minister has examined the old affairs in the *Shǐ Hàn*,
the *Yìwén Zhì* and Liú Xiàng's *Wǔxíng Zhuàn*,
and the Grand Sacrifice originates from them.
However, since previous generations,
no one has used it.
Moreover, its text only speaks of conducting a sacrifice
but does not record the ceremonial procedures.
This is an event that has not been practiced for a long time,
not something ordinary people can consult and verify.
According to Hàn rituals,
the sacrifices personally
performed by the Son of Heaven
are only those in the ancestral temple.
Sacrificing to Heaven at Yúnyáng,
and sacrificing to Earth at Fényīn,
were done by remote obeisance in separate palaces,
not by proceeding to the altars.
The places for other
group sacrifices
must be secluded and quiet,
which is why the round altar for Heaven and the square altar for Earth are located in the suburbs.
If now, in the court of Chéngmíng,
in front of the main hall,
seats for all gods are set up,
and a personal ceremony is performed,
according to old traditions,
it deviates from the usual norms.
Your minister has heard that the manifestation of omens and calamities
serves to awaken the ruler of the time.
Therefore, if awe and reverence reach above,
then Sòng's disasters receded;
if virtue and propriety are cultivated,
then Yīn's Way flourished.
These are proven experiences of past generations,
unchangeable principles.
Recently, celestial bodies have shown considerable anomalies.
Your Majesty's sincerity in reverence and caution reaches Heaven and man.
The fear of 'in Me' (the Emperor's own responsibility)
has caused you to forget sleep and food.
You reverently look up at the celestial phenomena
and attentively manage all affairs.
The response of auspicious blessings
is truly for today.
Yet you still diligently and vigilantly
seek to expand this Way,
which is truly
the utmost earnestness of a sagely heart.
However, the Grand Sacrifice has texts but no rituals,
and is not practiced in the world.
Inquiring among contemporary scholars,
none know its rites.
Moreover, its text says:
"The Grand Sacrifice
is a great sacrifice.
Yang is called *shén*,
yin is called *líng*.
The whole country leads each other to perform the sacrifice,
following the order of the four seasons,
without allowing any error."
Now, looking at the text,
it is all
vague and without clear direction,
impossible to detail.
If performed without detail,
the error will not be small.
The Emperor did not accept it.
Yóu again submitted a memorial, saying: "Your minister has carefully reconsidered
and compared it with current affairs.
Now, powerful barbarians occupy Guān and Yōng,
and the savage Di tribes run rampant north of the Yellow River.
The 'wild boars' (enemies) rampage in all four directions,
ravaging the divine land.
The long banners are not furled,
and gongs and drums warn daily.
Soldiers are weary, people are exhausted,
and there is no respite throughout the year.
When human affairs are corrupt below,
then the seven luminaries (sun, moon, five planets) are disordered above.
The occurrence of calamities
is indeed
it is fitting.
Moreover, for some time now,
it has perhaps become greatly different.
As for the eclipses of the moon,
their meaning is seen by poets;
as the stars are not alike,
recorded in the Wǔxíng (五行),
therefore the Hóngfàn (洪範)
does not consider them calamities.
Your Majesty now equates the deviation in gǔdù (晷度) with the "six calamities" (liùhù lìu hù 六沴),
drawing a parallel between a minor change and a major misfortune,
seeking self-reflection more earnestly than Yǔ (禹) and Tāng (湯),
toiling with more worry than if the sun were at its zenith,
intending to perform great sacrifices
to ritualistically honor the gods.
The tradition states:
"Externally conform to the times and qi (氣) of Heaven and Earth to sacrifice to their gods and spirits."
If so, then the spirits must have titles,
and the sacrifices must have meaning.
Examining the text of the great sacrifices (hóngsì 洪祀),
it only mentions the "divine spirits" (shénlíng 神靈) in a general sense without specific names for what is sacrificed,
stating that "the whole country performs sacrifices" without distinguishing between noble and lowly,
mentions an abundance of red millet but without
the offering of sacrificial animals and wine.
The rites and methods used
are incomplete in more than one respect.
If one were to follow the text strictly,
then all the meanings would be obstructed;
if one were to add or supplement,
then it would not derive from its origin.
Lú Zhí (盧植), a Chamberlain (Shìzhōng 侍中) of Hàn (漢),
was a learned scholar of his time;
if he did not thoroughly investigate the method he received,
then he would not dare to apply his mind to it.
Truly, the Wǔxíng (五行) are profound and far-reaching,
and the way of the spirits is recondite and obscure.
The search for profundities
is difficult by ordinary thought,
and the principles of combination and permutation cannot be enumerated one by one.
"I am not perfectly skilled,
who then can help with this!"
The Emperor still ordered him to compile and finalize it.
Yóu (逌) again presented ancient interpretations,
and the Emperor then ceased.
Yóu (逌) offered much correction and advice during his tenure.
His works, including Ruan Jí (阮籍)'s preface and eulogy, admonitions for recluses, and several tens of poems, rhapsodies, memorials, and discussions, were circulated in the world.
He died of illness
at the age of fifty-eight.
His son, Wèi (蔚),
was Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
Guàn (灌), courtesy name Dàoqún (道羣).
His father, Méng (瞢), was Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎).
Guàn (灌) was famous in his youth,
his talent and insight second only to Yóu (逌).
The province appointed him Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿),
he was recommended as Xiùcái (秀才),
became Administrator of Justice (Zhìzhōng 治中),
transferred to Assistant Administrator (Biéjià 別駕),
successively served as an aide to the Minister of Works (Sītú shǔ 司徒屬), Chief Clerk to the General of the North (Běizhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ 北中郎長史),
and held the post of Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng (晉陵).
Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) appointed him Aide to the General who Soothes the Army (Fǔjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng 撫軍從事中郎),
and later promoted him to Director of the Bureau of Personnel (Lìbù Láng 吏部郎).
At that time, Xiè Yì (謝奕) was Minister (Shàngshū 尚書),
and his selections were not always fair.
Guàn (灌) always upheld rectitude and did not comply.
Yì (奕) used other pretexts to dismiss him,
and he showed no resentment at his demotion.
A short while later,
Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) again made him Commandant for the General who Soothes the Army (Fǔjūn Sīmǎ 撫軍司馬),
treating him with great respect as a guest.
He was promoted to Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞),
then transferred to Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
Guàn (灌) was upright by nature,
viewing powerful nobles with disdain,
and was hated by Grand Marshal Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Wēn (溫) wanted to harm him;
he was summoned and appointed Chamberlain (Shìzhōng 侍中),
but because of alleged mistakes in public affairs during his time as Grand Administrator,
he was subsequently dismissed.
Later, he became Director of the Imperial Library (Bìshū Jiān 祕書監),
but was soon relieved of that post again.
At that time, Wēn (溫) wielded power,
and the court sought to please him,
so Guàn (灌) remained unappointed for years.
In Wēn (溫)'s final years,
he was made Consultant to the Minister (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍).
Coincidentally, Wēn (溫) died.
He was promoted to Minister (Shàngshū 尚書) and Protector-General of the Army (Zhōnghùjūn 中護軍),
then again sent out as Grand Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡),
with an additional rank of "Middle Two Thousand Piculs" (zhōng èrqiānshí 中二千石).
Before he could take up the post,
he died.
His son, Jī (績).
Jī (績), courtesy name Zhòngyuán (仲元),
had ambition and spirit.
He was appointed Palace Secretary (Bìshū Láng 祕書郎).
Because his father was not on good terms with the Xiè (謝) clan,
in Xiè Ān (謝安)'s (謝安) era, he refused all invitations for appointments,
which was widely praised by commentators.
After Ān (安) died,
he first became Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) to Hùikuài (會稽) Prince Dàozǐ (道子), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍),
offering much advice and remonstrance.
He successively served as Consultant to the Minister (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍),
and was sent out as Chancellor of Nánjùn (南郡).
Coincidentally, Yīn Zhòngkān (殷仲堪), Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), raised troops to respond to Wáng Gōng (王恭).
Zhòngkān (仲堪) wanted Jī (績) to go with Yīn Yǐ (殷顗), Commandant of Southern Man (Nánmán Xiàowèi 南蠻校尉),
but neither agreed.
Zhòngkān (仲kān) and others repeatedly spoke about it,
but Jī (績) ultimately would not yield.
Yǐ (顗) feared that Jī (績) would suffer calamity,
so he reconciled them at Zhòngkān (仲kān)'s banquet.
Jī (績) said:
"How can a great man be threatened with death!
Jiāng Zhòngyuán (江仲元) is sixty years old;
he just doesn't know where he will die."
Everyone present was afraid for him.
Zhòngkān (仲kān) was awed by his firm uprightness
and replaced him with Yáng Quánqī (楊佺期).
The court heard of this and summoned Jī (績) to be Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞),
where he impeached without yielding.
When Yuánxiǎn (元顯), the heir apparent of Huìkuài (會稽), seized sole power,
opening the six gates at night,
Jī (績) secretly memorialized Prince Dàozǐ (道子) of Huìkuài (會稽),
intending to report it to the emperor,
but Dàozǐ (道子) did not permit it.
Chē Yìn (車胤) also said:
"Yuánxiǎn (元顯) is arrogant and unrestrained;
he should be restrained."
Dàozǐ (道子) remained silent.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) heard of this and said to the multitude:
"Jiāng Jī (江績) and Chē Yìn (車胤) are alienating my father and me."
He sent people to secretly reprimand them.
Soon after, Jī (績) died,
and both court and public mourned him.
Chē Yìn (車胤).
Chē Yìn (車胤), courtesy name Wǔzǐ (武子),
was a native of Nánpíng (南平).
His great-grandfather, Jùn (浚),
was Grand Administrator of Wúqī (吳稽).
His father, Yù (育),
was Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) of the commandery.
The Grand Administrator Wáng Húzhī (王胡之), famous for his discernment of people,
saw Yìn (胤) as a young child
and said to Yìn (胤)'s father:
"This child will greatly glorify your family;
you should let him specialize in study."
Yìn (胤) was diligent and tireless,
widely learned and well-versed.
His family was poor and could not always afford lamp oil.
In the summer months, he would put dozens of fireflies in a gauze bag to illuminate his books,
thus making night into day.
When he grew up,
his demeanor was beautiful and refined,
his wit quick and sharp,
and he had a great reputation in his hometown.
When Huán Wēn (桓溫) was in Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he appointed him as an aide (Cóngshì 從事),
greatly valuing his eloquent discernment of principles.
He appointed him Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿),
gradually promoting him to Assistant Administrator (Biéjià 別駕) and Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Zhǎngshǐ 征西長史),
and thus he became prominent in the imperial court.
At that time, only Yìn (胤) and Wú Yǐnzhī (吳隱之) were known in the world for their humble origins and extensive learning.
He was also good at social gatherings;
whenever there was a grand banquet and Yìn (胤) was not present,
everyone would say:
"It's not enjoyable without Master Chē (Chē Gōng 車公)."
On days when Xiè Ān (謝安) held gatherings,
he would always set up a banquet and wait for him.
In the early Níngkāng reign,
Yǐn was made Central Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Shìláng) and Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu).
Emperor Xiàowǔ once lectured on the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng).
Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Púshè) Xiè Ān attended,
Minister (Shàngshū) Lù Nà lectured,
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Biàn Dān held the text,
Yellow Gate Attendant Gentleman (Huángmén Shìláng) Xiè Shí and Bureau Director of Personnel (Lìbù Láng) Yuán Hóng held the classics,
and Yǐn, along with Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn) Wáng Hùn, punctuated the sentences.
The public opinion at the time considered this an honor.
He was successively promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the Tàiyuán reign,
the number of imperial academy students (tàixuéshēng) was increased by a hundred,
and Yǐn was appointed Chief Instructor of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Bóshì).
The following year,
when the matters of the suburban altars, ancestral temples, and Bright Hall (Míngtáng) were deliberated,
Yǐn stated
that "the regulations for the Bright Hall are indeed very difficult to ascertain in detail,
and moreover, music focuses on harmony,
while ritual focuses on reverence.
Therefore, their simplicity and refinement differ,
and their sounds and instruments are also distinct.
Since thatched huts and grand mansions do not share the same standards,
why must we adhere to their forms and models without broadly following the fundamental principles and adapting to the times!
When the nine regions are all peaceful,
and the four wilds are free of dust,
then the Bright Hall and Bi Yong can be gloriously repaired."
At the time, his proposal was adopted.
He was again promoted to Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojí Zhǎngshǐ) and Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
and advanced in peerage to Marquis of Línxiāng.
Due to illness, he left office.
Soon after, he became General of the Palace Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
At that time, Wáng Guóbǎo flattered Scribe of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Wáng) Dàozǐ,
and hinted to the eight ministers (bā zuò) to propose Dàozǐ as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
with special courtesies added.
Yǐn said:
"This is how King Chéng honored the Duke of Zhōu.
Now the emperor is in power,
which is not the position of King Chéng;
the Prince-Chancellor (Xiàng Wáng) is in office,
how can he be the Duke of Zhōu!
The expectations and reality differ greatly,
and this is utterly inappropriate.
It will certainly greatly displease the emperor."
He then claimed illness and did not sign the matter.
After his memorial was submitted,
the emperor was furious,
but greatly admired Yǐn.
In the early Lóng'ān reign,
he was made Grand Administrator of Wúxīng,
with a salary of two thousand piculs (zhì zhōng èr qiān shí),
but declined due to illness.
He was made General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Yuánxiǎn made a mistake,
and Yǐn and Jiāng Jì secretly spoke to Dàozǐ,
intending to report him.
The matter was leaked,
and Yuánxiǎn forced him to commit suicide.
Soon after, Yǐn died,
and the court mourned him.
Yīn Yǐ.
Yīn Yǐ, courtesy name Bótōng,
was a native of Chénjùn.
His grandfather, Róng, was Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng).
His father, Kāng, was Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Yǐ was frank and straightforward by nature,
with talent and spirit.
In his youth, he and his cousin Zhòngkān were both renowned.
In the Tàiyuán reign,
he was promoted from Central Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Láng) to Colonel Protector of the Southern Barbarians (Nánmán Xiàowèi).
He was clear and honest in his duties,
and his administration was orderly and effective.
When Zhòngkān received Wáng Gōng's letter
and intended to raise troops to attack internally,
he informed Yǐ,
wishing to join forces.
Yǐ disapproved,
saying:
"It is the duty of a minister
to carefully guard what he holds.
The right and wrong of the court
are the concerns of the chief ministers (zǎifǔ),
how can they be schemes for a regional protector (fānpíng)!
The affairs of Jìnyáng [Zhōngkān's base] are matters in which one ought not to participate."
Zhòngkān pressed him more urgently,
and Yǐ angrily said:
"I dare not join on advancement,
nor dare I differ on retreat."
Zhòngkān greatly resented this.
Still, he secretly admonished Zhòngkān,
his words being very earnest and sincere.
As Zhòngkān became prominent,
his original disposition also changed,
and his ambitions were insatiable,
considering Yǐ's words to be wrong.
Yǐ saw that Jiāng Jì was also rejected by Zhòngkān for his uprightness,
and knew that Zhòngkān would drive away those who differed from him
and appoint his intimates.
He then went out for a stroll,
claiming illness and not returning.
Zhòngkān heard of his illness
and went to visit him.
He said to Yǐ:
"Brother's illness is indeed worrying."
Yǐ said:
"My illness is no more than death,
but your illness is the destruction of your family.
Please consider this carefully,
do not worry about me."
Zhòngkān did not heed him,
and eventually joined Yáng Quánqí and Huán Xuán in their downfall.
Yǐ then died of grief.
In the Lóng'ān reign,
an imperial edict stated:
"The former Colonel Protector of the Southern Barbarians (Nánmán Xiàowèi) Yīn Yǐ's loyal service had not yet blossomed,
and he suddenly met his demise.
He is granted the posthumous title of General Who Quells the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn)."
His younger brothers, Zhòngwén and Shúxiàn, have separate biographies.
Wáng Yǎ.
Wáng Yǎ, courtesy name Màodá,
was a native of Tán, Dōnghǎi.
He was the great-grandson of Wèi General Who Guards the Army (Wèi Wèijiāngjūn) Sù.
His grandfather, Lóng, was General of the Rear (Hòujiāngjūn).
His father, Jǐng, was Grand Master of the Ceremonies (Dàhónglú).
Yǎ was renowned in his youth.
The province summoned him as Chief Clerk (zhǔbù),
he was recommended as Xùcái,
appointed Gentleman (lángzhōng),
and then assigned as Magistrate of Yǒngxīng,
where he was known for his capable administration.
He was successively promoted to Left and Right Assistant Ministers (Shàngshū Zuǒyòu Chéng),
and held positions as Chief Justice (Tíngwèi), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn), and Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn),
also serving as Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài).
Yǎ was by nature fond of receiving subordinates
and diligently served the public.
Emperor Xiàowǔ treated him with profound courtesy.
Even when he held external posts,
he was frequently summoned for audiences,
and he often participated in deliberations on major court affairs.
Whenever the emperor held banquets and gatherings,
if Yǎ had not arrived,
he would not raise his cup first.
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
However, his appointments and treatment exceeded his talent,
and people at the time labeled him as a flattering favorite.
The emperor built the Qīngshǔ Diàn in the rear palace,
opened the northern upper gate,
and went out to the Huálín Garden
to live and wander with his concubine Lady Zhāng.
Only Yǎ was present.
Scribe of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Wáng) Dàozǐ served as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàifù),
and appointed Yǎ as Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
At that time, Wáng Xún's son was getting married,
and there were many guests, carriages, and riders.
It happened that when they heard Yǎ was appointed Junior Tutor,
more than half of them turned to visit Yǎ.
At that time, customs were decadent
and there was no sense of integrity or shame.
However, for the post of Junior Tutor,
the court's expectation was Xún,
and Xún also somewhat expected it for himself.
But when the imperial edict appointed Yǎ,
the crowd then rushed to Yǎ.
As he was about to accept the appointment,
it rained,
and he requested to enter with an umbrella.
Wáng Xún did not permit it,
so he accepted the appointment in the rain.
Yǎ, being powerful and favored,
his authority was greatly felt.
There were often hundreds of carriages and riders at his gate,
and he was skilled at receiving them,
greeting them with utmost sincerity.
The Emperor, considering that Dàozǐ lacked the caliber for governing the state,
feared that after his demise, the imperial house would be in peril.
Thus, he selected respected figures of the time to serve as its bulwark.
He intended to promote Wáng Gōng and Yīn Zhòngkān, among others,
and first consulted Gù Yǎ.
Gù Yǎ believed that Wáng Gōng and the others lacked the talent for the current era
and could not be entrusted with great responsibility.
So he calmly said:
"Wáng Gōng's demeanor is refined and noble,
and his spirit is upright and severe.
As he holds the significant position of an imperial relative by marriage,
he should be entrusted with duties involving worthy individuals.
However, his nature is stern and narrow-minded,
without any capacity for tolerance.
He holds onto his own self-righteous views
and lacks the will to uphold principles.
Though Yīn Zhòngkān is cautious in minor conduct
and is renowned for his literary and ethical attainments,
he also lacks broadmindedness,
and moreover, is not adept in strategy and leadership.
If entrusted with the heavy responsibility of commanding a large force
and holding strategically important territories,
then with peace throughout the land today,
they would be able to perform their duties.
But if the imperial fortunes are not always prosperous,
they will certainly become the cause of chaos."
The Emperor, considering Wáng Gōng and the others to be the prominent figures of the time,
believed that Gù Yǎ was jealous of their superiority
and therefore did not follow his advice.
Both men were promoted to office,
and later they indeed failed.
Those with discernment praised Gù Yǎ for his judgment of character.
He was promoted to Commander of the Army, Minister of the Department of State Affairs, and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and was being greatly advanced,
about to assume the important position of Vice-Chancellor,
when the Emperor passed away.
In the sudden crisis, he did not receive a dying charge.
Gù Yǎ had always been treated favorably,
but suddenly lost power.
Moreover, as the court was in chaos
and internal and external factions were estranged,
he merely remained cautious and silent,
not daring to speak out or correct anything.
Even during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
he was unable to openly remonstrate in court,
and in all his deliberations,
he merely assented.
Soon after, he was transferred to Left Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān, he died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of Remonstrance and Acting Grand Preceptor.
His eldest son, Gù Zhǔnzhī,
was a Cavalier Attendant.
His second son, Gù Xiézhī,
was a Yellow Gate attendant.
His third son, Gù Shàofqīng,
was a Palace Attendant.
All of them possessed scholarly conduct
and established their reputations in the world.
The historiographer remarks: In the midst of the restoration,
the profound trend (of quietism) spread vigorously,
submerging the imperial order in silent assent,
and disrupting the national progress with empty rhetoric.
The spirit of outspoken and unyielding remonstrance had indeed become faint.
Yet Gù Jūxiào adhered to sentiment and propriety, even defying explicit imperial commands;
Zhōu Shānfǔ offered sincere and direct advice, thereby reviving the declining trend;
Guó Yànshū's military strategies;
Líu Dàozài's righteous remonstrances –
these resound in our ears,
and are truly worthy of praise.
Hú Guàn did not compromise his integrity before powerful officials;
Líu Jī dared to speak dangerous words to a rebel general;
as for Dàozǐ's unusual ceremonies,
Chē Yìn fearlessly thwarted them;
and regarding Yīn Zhòngkān's aberrant actions,
Yīn Yǐ corrected him with a stern expression.
If we seek among ancient heroes,
how could anything surpass these!
Huáng Shānsōng enjoyed mournful laments during his time in high office;
Wáng Yàndào rejoiced with gamblers on the day of mourning.
If the heavenly will is already lost,
how can they succeed!
They soon met an early demise,
and swiftly came to an unnatural end.
How fitting!
Eulogy says: Master Gù set the standards,
repeatedly offering sincere and direct advice.
Master Yuán esteemed Confucianism,
saving it from decline.
Yōu Jī was steadfast and unyielding;
Chē Yìn and Yīn Yǐ were loyal and strong.
Looking back at these upright individuals,
none can surpass them.
Collated Notes
Biography Fifty-four: Wáng Gōng
Wáng Gōng, courtesy name Xiàobó,
was the son of Grand Master of Remonstrance Wáng Yùn,
and the elder brother of Empress Dìng.
In his youth, he had a good reputation,
and his upright conduct surpassed others.
He prided himself on his noble talent and background,
constantly harboring aspirations of becoming a prime minister.
He was equally famous as Wáng Chén and good friends with him,
and admired Líu Tán's character.
Xiè Ān often said:
"Wáng Gōng's character and background are such that he could be a future maternal uncle (of an emperor)."
Once, he followed his father from Kuàijī to the capital.
Wáng Chén visited him
and saw the six-foot bamboo mat Wáng Gōng was sitting on.
Wáng Chén thought it was more than sufficient
and asked for it.
Wáng Gōng immediately sent it to him,
and then sat on a straw mat.
Wáng Chén was greatly surprised upon hearing this.
Wáng Gōng said:
"I have never kept superfluous things in my life."
His simplicity and straightforwardness were like this.
He began his career as Assistant Writer,
and sighed:
"If one does not become a prime minister in an official career,
how can one's talent and ambition be fully realized!"
He then resigned due to illness.
Soon after, he became Secretary,
then transferred to Gentlemen of the Central Secretariat.
Before he could take office,
he suffered the grief of his father's death.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Minister of Personnel,
and successively held the title of General Who Establishes Martial Might.
During the Tàiyuán era,
he replaced Shěn Jiā as Administrator of Dānyáng,
and was promoted to Director of the Central Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Emperor Xiàowǔ, considering Wáng Gōng to be the Empress's elder brother,
deeply respected him.
At that time, Yuán Yuèzhī of Chénjùn used his cunning to serve Prince Dàozǐ of Kuàijī.
Wáng Gōng reported this to the Emperor,
and Yuán Yuèzhī was subsequently executed.
Dàozǐ once gathered court officials
and held a banquet at the Eastern Residence.
Minister of the Department of State Affairs Xiè Shí, in his drunkenness, sang a vulgar street song.
Wáng Gōng sternly said:
"Holding a high position at court,
gathered at a princely residence,
yet indulging in lewd songs,
how do you expect your subordinates to take example?"
Xiè Shí deeply resented this.
Lady Péi, the wife of Internal Scribe of Huáilíng Yú Yáo's son, possessed skills in "food and medicine" (Daoist practices),
and often wore yellow robes,
resembling a Celestial Master.
Dàozǐ was very pleased with her,
and ordered her to discuss with guests.
People at the time all lowered themselves for her.
Wáng Gōng spoke out firmly:
"I have never heard of a promiscuous woman being present in a prime minister's seat."
All the guests were uneasy,
and Dàozǐ was greatly ashamed.
Afterwards, the Emperor intended to promote respected figures of the time to serve as its bulwark.

Thus, Wáng Gōng was appointed Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, Xú, and Jìnlíng Prefectures, General Who Pacifies the North, Governors of Yǎn and Qīng Prefectures, and Bearer of Imperial Credentials,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
Initially,
overall supervisors who
used "North"
in their titles
had repeatedly experienced misfortune.
Therefore, Huán Chōng, Wáng Tǎnzhī, and Diāo Yí, among others, refused the title of General Who Guards the North.
Wáng Gōng submitted a memorial declining the military title,
citing that it was an excessive appointment,
but in reality, he disliked its connotation.
Thus, his title was changed to General of the Vanguard.
When Mùróng Chuí entered Qīngzhōu,
Wáng Gōng dispatched a detachment to resist him,
but suffered a defeat.
His title was downgraded to General Who Assists the State.
When the Emperor collapsed,
Sì-mǎ Dào-zi (會稽王道子), the Prince of Kuài-jī, took charge of the government.
He doted on Wáng Guó-bǎo (王國寶)
and entrusted him with vital authority.
However, Gōng (恭) always spoke with a stern countenance and direct words,
which Dào-zi deeply feared and resented.
When Gōng attended the imperial funeral,
and after the court was dismissed,
he sighed, saying:
"Although the rafters and pillars are new,
there is already a lament for 'millet and sorrow'."
At that time, Guó-bǎo's (國寶) younger cousin, Xù (緒), persuaded Guó-bǎo
to ambush and kill Gōng (恭) when he entered the court to see the Prince.
But Guó-bǎo did not agree.
Dào-zi also wanted to reconcile internal and external factions,
and deeply confided in Gōng,
hoping to erase past animosity.
However, Gōng was often uncooperative;
whenever the current government was mentioned,
his voice and expression would become stern.
Dào-zi knew that Gōng could not be reconciled,
and so Wáng Xù's (王緒) suggestion was finally carried out.
Thus, the national crisis began.
Someone advised Gōng to use his entrance into court to execute Guó-bǎo with soldiers.
However, Yǔ Kǎi (庾楷) was allied with Guó-bǎo,
and his troops were very strong,
so Gōng feared him
and dared not act,
thus returning to his garrison.
When departing,
he said to Dào-zi:
"The Emperor is in mourning.
The responsibility of the Chief Minister
was difficult even for Yī (伊) and Zhōu (周).
I hope that Your Highness will personally attend to all affairs of state,
accept honest advice,
keep distant from 'Zheng' music,
and dismiss flattering people."
His words and demeanor were very stern,
which made Guó-bǎo and others even more frightened.
Gōng was appointed General of the Pacified North (安北將軍),
but he did not accept the post.
He then plotted to execute Guó-bǎo,
sending envoys to form an alliance with Yīn Zhòng-kān (殷仲堪) and Huán Xuán (桓玄).
Zhòng-kān pretended to agree.
Gōng received the letter
and was greatly pleased,
so he submitted a memorial to the capital, saying:
"General of the Rear, Guó-bǎo, has, through marriage ties, repeatedly risen to prominent positions,
but he has not been able to express gratitude or exert effort
to repay the favors of the time.
Instead, he has abused his favor and exercised tyranny,
endangering the state.
When the late Emperor passed away,
he dared to violate the palace gates at night
to forge an imperial edict.
Thanks to the sagacity of the Empress Dowager
and the divine might of the Prince,
his rebellious plot did not succeed.
Furthermore, he carved out the Eastern Palace's existing troops for his own command,
and slandered and envied his two elder brothers worse than enemies.
He formed a faction of villains and cunning individuals with his younger cousin Xù,
inciting each other.
This is clear disloyalty and injustice.
Because of my loyalty and integrity,
I will surely sacrifice myself for the country;
therefore, there has been no end to slanders against me.
Thanks to the clear discernment of the late Emperor,
insidious rumors did not prevail.
In the past, Zhào Yāng (趙鞅) raised an army
to execute the wicked elements around the ruler.
Though I am dull and inferior,
how dare I forget this principle!"
When the memorial arrived,
both inside and outside the capital were placed on high alert.
Guó-bǎo and Xù were terrified and did not know what to do.
Following Wáng Xún's (王珣) plan,
they requested to resign their posts.
Dào-zi arrested Guó-bǎo,
granted him death,
and executed Xù in the marketplace.
He deeply apologized for his errors,
and Gōng then returned to Jīng-kǒu (京口).
When Gōng first submitted his memorial,
fearing that the matter might not succeed,
he appointed Wáng Xùn (王廞), former Chief Clerk (左長史) to the Minister of Works (司徒), as Administrator of Wú-guó (吳國內史),
ordering him to raise an army in the east.
When Guó-bǎo died,
he ordered Xùn to disband his army and resign his post.
Xùn was enraged
and attacked Gōng with his troops.
Gōng sent Liú Láo-zhī (劉牢之) to defeat and destroy him.
Gōng submitted a memorial to demote himself,
but an imperial edict did not permit it.
Qiáo (譙) Prince Shàng-zhī (尚之) again persuaded Dào-zi that the regional lords were too powerful
and the Prime Minister's authority was weak,
so it was advisable to appoint more people to protect himself.
Dào-zi agreed.
He then appointed his Staff Officer (司馬) Wáng Yú (王愉) as Governor (刺史) of Jiāng-zhōu (江州),
and carved out four prefectures from Yǔ Kǎi's Yù-zhōu (豫州) to be supervised by Yú.
Because of this, Kǎi was enraged
and sent his son Hóng (鴻) to persuade Gōng, saying:
"Shàng-zhī and his brothers monopolize the Prime Minister's authority,
desiring to use imperial prestige to degrade and diminish regional governors,
as a warning against past events.
Their influence is becoming increasingly unpredictable.
Before their plans are complete,
we should act swiftly."
Gōng agreed,
and again informed Yīn Zhòng-kān and Huán Xuán of his plans.
Xuán and others followed him,
naming Gōng as their盟主 (leader of the alliance),
and set a date to march together to the capital.
At that time, there was suspicion and obstruction both inside and outside the capital,
and surveillance was extremely strict.
Zhòng-kān's message was delivered through Yǔ Kǎi;
it was written on a piece of slanted silk,
inserted into an arrow shaft,
and the fletching was lacquered over.
Kǎi sent it to Gōng.
When Gōng opened the letter,
the silk characters were crumpled and distorted,
making them unreadable.
He thought Kǎi was playing a trick.
He also figured that Zhòng-kān had not joined the alliance the previous year,
so there was no reason for him to move now.
Thus, Gōng raised his army before the agreed date.
Staff Officer Liú Láo-zhī (劉牢之) advised him, saying:
"General, if you move now, with the great weight of being the maternal uncle [of the Emperor],
and upholding the virtue of loyalty and integrity,
and the Prince, with the尊 (honor) of a Jī Dàn (姬旦),
is what the public hopes for –
last year he already executed Bǎo (寶) and Xù (緒),
and sent a letter to Wáng Xùn (王廞),
which shows he deeply respects you.
Although what he has granted and appointed recently
is not all fitting,
it is not a great error.
What harm is it to you
to carve out four prefectures from Yǔ Kǎi to assign to Wáng Yú?
Can the 'army of Jìn-yáng' (晉陽之師) be raised a second time?"
Gōng did not heed him,
and submitted a memorial with the pretext of attacking Wáng Yú and the Shàng-zhī brothers.
The court ordered Yuán Xiǎn (元顯) and Wáng Xún, Xiè Yǎn (謝琰), and others to resist him.
Gōng dreamed that Láo-zhī was sitting in his place.
The next morning, he told Láo-zhī:
"If we succeed,
I will make you Governor of Běi-fǔ (北府)."
He sent Láo-zhī to lead his subordinates Yán Yán (顏延) to first occupy Zhú-lǐ (竹里).
Yuán Xiǎn sent someone to persuade Láo-zhī,
tempting him with great rewards,
and Láo-zhī then beheaded Yán Yán and surrendered.
On that day,
Láo-zhī sent his son-in-law Gāo Yǎ-zhī (高雅之) and his son Jìng-xuān (敬宣)
to feign parading the army for Gōng,
and then attack Gōng with light cavalry.
Gōng was defeated
and was about to return,
but Yǎ-zhī had already closed the city gates.
Gōng, with his brother Lǚ (履), fled alone on horseback to Qǔ-ē (曲阿).
Gōng had not ridden for a long time,
and developed a sore on his thigh,
making him unable to continue.
A man from Qǔ-ē, Yīn Què (殷確), who was Gōng's former staff officer,
carried him on a boat,
hid him under reed mats,
and was attempting to flee to Huán Xuán.
When they reached Cháng-táng Hú (長塘湖),
they encountered the merchant Qián Qiáng (錢強).
Qiáng harbored an old grudge against Què,
and reported them to the Hú-pǔ Lieutenant (湖浦尉).
The Lieutenant arrested them
and sent them to the capital.
Dào-zi, hearing that he was about to arrive,
wanted to go out and speak with him,
rebuke him face-to-face,
but had not yet killed him.
At that time, Huán Xuán and others had already reached Shí-tóu (石頭),
and fearing that there might be a change,
they immediately executed him at Ní-táng (倪塘) in Jiàn-kāng (建康).
Gōng's five sons, his brother Shuǎng (爽), Shuǎng's nephew Secretary Láng Hé (祕書郎和), and his followers Mèng Pú (孟璞) and Zhāng Kè (張恪) were all killed.
At that time, Fú Pi, the son of Fú Jiān, occupied Yè,
and was besieged by Mùróng Chuí.
He requested surrender,
so Láo Zhī led troops to rescue him.
Chuí heard that an army had arrived,
and fled north from Xīnchéng.
Láo Zhī and Tián Cìzhī, the Administrator of Pèijùn, pursued him,
marching two hundred *lǐ*,
until they reached the midst of Wǔqiáozé.
They vied to seize the baggage train,
gradually fell into disarray,
and were attacked by Chuí.
Láo Zhī suffered a crushing defeat,
and his soldiers were annihilated.
Láo Zhī galloped his horse across Wǔzhàngjiàn
and escaped.
Coincidentally, Pí's relief force arrived,
and thereupon entered Línzhāng,
gathered the dispersed survivors,
and the army was somewhat revitalized.
Láo Zhī was recalled due to the military defeat.
After a short while,
he was again made General Longxiáng,
and garrisoned Huái'yīn.
Later, he advanced to garrison Péngchéng,
and again held the post of Administrator.
The demonic bandit Liú Lí usurped the imperial title at Huángqiū,
and Láo Zhī attacked and exterminated him.
Fú Jiān's general Zhāng Yù dispatched troops to break through Jīnxiāng,
and besieged Yáng Mài, the Administrator of Tàishān.
Láo Zhī sent his staff officer Xiàng Qīnzhī to attack and drive him away.
Coincidentally, Mùróng Chuí's rebellious general Zhái Zhāo came to Yù's rescue,
so Láo Zhī withdrew.
When Zhāo returned,
Láo Zhī advanced and pacified Tàishān,
pursuing Zhāo to Juànchéng.
Zhāo fled north of the Yellow River,
and Láo Zhī then captured Zhāng Yù and returned to Péngchéng.
The demonic bandit Sīmǎ Huī gathered his followers at Mǎtóushān,
and Láo Zhī sent his staff officer Zhú Lǎngzhī to attack and exterminate him.
At that time, the Mùróng clan plundered Jiànqiū,
and Xú Hányuǎn, the Administrator of Gāopíng, sent an urgent report.
Láo Zhī was unable to rescue him,
and was dismissed for cowardice.
When Wáng Gōng was about to attack Wáng Guóbǎo,
he appointed Láo Zhī as Registrar of his headquarters,
concurrently serving as Prefect of Nánpéngchéng,
and also as General Fuguo.
Gōng ordered Láo Zhī to attack and defeat Wáng Xīn,
and appointed Láo Zhī as Administrator of Jìnlíng.
Gōng originally looked down on others based on his talent and status,
and when his manifesto reached the capital,
the court executed Guóbǎo and Wáng Xù.
He believed his prestige and virtue were already established,
and although he relied on Láo Zhī as his claws and teeth,
he treated him merely as a military general in the ranks,
with very scant courtesy.
Láo Zhī, confident in his abilities,
felt deeply ashamed and resentful.
When Gōng later launched another campaign,
Yuán Xiǎn sent Gāo Sù, the Administrator of Lújiāng, to persuade Láo Zhī to betray Gōng.
He promised that if the matter succeeded,
Láo Zhī would immediately assume Gōng's position and title.
Láo Zhī agreed.
Gōng's staff officer Hé Dànzhī reported the plan to Gōng.
Láo Zhī and Dànzhī had a grudge,
so Gōng was suspicious and did not accept the report.
Instead, he hosted a banquet and invited Láo Zhī among the assembled officials,
bowed to Láo Zhī as his elder brother,
and entrusted all his elite troops and sharp weapons to him,
making him the vanguard.
When they reached Zhúlǐ,
Láo Zhī turned his back on Gōng and sided with the court.
After Gōng's death,
Láo Zhī succeeded him as Supreme Commander of the military affairs of Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, Xú, and Yáng Prefectures, and Jìnlíng.
Láo Zhī was originally a minor general,
and suddenly occupied Gōng's position,
which displeased the populace.
So he promoted trusted associates like Xú Qiānzhī to strengthen himself.
At that time, Yáng Quánqī and Huán Xuán led troops to pressure the capital,
submitting memorials to vindicate Wáng Gōng
and demanding Láo Zhī's execution.
Láo Zhī led the troops from Běifǔ and rushed to the capital,
stopping at Xīntíng.
Xuán and others received the imperial edict and withdrew their troops,
and Láo Zhī returned to garrison Jīngkǒu.
When Sūn Ēn captured Kuàijī,
Láo Zhī dispatched general Huán Bǎo to lead forces to rescue Sānwú,
and then sent his son Jìngxúan to reinforce Bǎo.
By the time they reached Qǔ'ē,
Huán Qiān, the Prefect of Wújùn, had already abandoned the commandery and fled.
Láo Zhī then led his forces on an eastern campaign,
submitting his memorial as he marched.
Upon reaching Wú,
he and General Wèi Xiè Yǎn attacked the bandits,
winning repeatedly,
killing and wounding many,
and directly approaching the Zhèjiāng River.
He was promoted to General Qián and Supreme Commander of all military affairs in Wújùn.
At that time, Xiè Yǎn was stationed at Wūchéng,
and sent his Registrar Gāo Sù to assist Láo Zhī.
Láo Zhī led his forces across the Zhèjiāng River,
Ēn was frightened
and fled to the sea.
Láo Zhī returned to his garrison,
and Ēn re-entered Kuàijī,
killing Xiè Yǎn.
Láo Zhī was promoted to General Zhènběi and Supreme Commander of the five commanderies of Kuàijī,
led his forces on an eastern expedition,
garrisoned Shàngyú,
and divided his army to guard the various counties.
Ēn again attacked and broke through Wúguó,
killing the Prefect Yuán Shānsōng.
Láo Zhī sent his staff officer Liú Yù to attack him,
and Ēn again fled to the sea.
After a short while,
Ēn sailed across the sea and suddenly arrived at Jīngkǒu,
with a hundred thousand warriors
and over a thousand turreted ships.
Láo Zhī was at Shānyīn,
and sent Liú Yù from Hǎiyán to meet the crisis,
while Láo Zhī led the main force back.
Yù's army was less than a thousand men,
but he fought the bandits
and defeated them.
Ēn heard that Láo Zhī had returned to Jīngkǒu,
so he fled to Yùzhōu,
and was again defeated by Jìngxúan, Liú Yù, and others.
After Ēn's death,
Láo Zhī's prestige and fame grew.
In the beginning of Yuánxīng era,
the court was about to attack Huán Xuán,
and appointed Láo Zhī as Vanguard Commander and General Zhēngxī,
concurrently in charge of Jiāngzhōu affairs.
Yuán Xiǎn sent an envoy to consult Láo Zhī about attacking Xuán.
Láo Zhī considered that Xuán had a reputation for heroism since youth,
and commanded the forces of the entire Chu region,
fearing he could not control him.
He also worried that after pacifying Xuán, his accomplishments would overshadow all others,
and he would certainly not be tolerated by Yuán Xiǎn.
He was deeply conflicted and suspicious,
but had no choice but to lead the civil and military officials of Běifǔ to garrison Lièzhōu.
Huán Xuán sent Hé Mù to persuade Láo Zhī, saying:
"Throughout history, among rulers and ministers who trusted each other in times of chaos, there were King Zhāo of Yān and Yuè Yì, and Xuándé and Kǒngmíng.
However, their achievements were not completed and both rulers died early.
Even if their accomplishments had been successful, it is not guaranteed that these two ministers would have escaped misfortune.
There is a common saying: 'When the high-flying birds are gone,
the good bows are put away;
when the cunning rabbits are exhausted,
the hunting dogs are cooked.'
Thus, Wén Zhǒng was executed by Gōu Jiàn,
and Hán [Xìn] and Bái [Qǐ] were slaughtered by Qín and Hàn.
Those were all heroic and hegemon kings,
yet they still dared not trust their meritorious ministers,
let alone a foolish and mediocre commoner!
Since the beginning of the world,
who has ever wielded the might of a truly powerful ruler
and achieved unrewardable feats,
yet been tolerated by a dark age?
There are, however, occasional instances like Guǎn Zhòng serving Qí,
or Yǒng Chǐ being ennobled by Hàn.
But how can you, who have twice incurred the deep hatred of a crossbow-hooked enemy, expect the same?
If you lose this battle now, your clan will be annihilated;
if you win, your family will also be destroyed.
To what security do you wish to return?
How much better to turn around and change your plan,
preserving your wealth and honor,
so that your person will be as firm as metal and stone,
and your name as endless as heaven and earth,
rather than having your head and feet separated,
your person and name both obliterated,
becoming a laughingstock to all under heaven!
I urge you to consider this."
Láo Zhī believed he commanded a strong army
and that his talent and strategies were sufficient to govern the Jiāngbiǎo region.
At that time, Qíao Wáng Shàngzhī had already been defeated,
and morale was low,
so he largely accepted Mù's persuasion,
and sent envoys to communicate with Xuán.
His nephew Hé Wújì and Liú Yù strongly admonished him against this.
He ignored them both.
Soon after, he ordered Jìngxúan to surrender to Xuán.
Xuán was overjoyed
and hosted a banquet with Jìngxúan,
secretly planning to execute him.
He displayed legal documents and maps for Jìngxúan to view together,
to reassure and please him.
Jìngxúan did not realize this,
but none of Xuán's subordinate officials could help but exchange glances and smile.
After Yuánxiǎn was defeated,
Xuán appointed Láozhī as General Pacifying the East and Administrator of Kuàijī.
Láozhī then sighed, saying:
"Just now,
he took away my troops;
calamity is approaching!"
At that time, Xuán was garrisoned at the prime minister's residence.
Jìngxūan urged Láozhī to attack Xuán,
but he hesitated.
He moved his garrison to Bāndú,
intending to flee north to Guǎnglíng to join Gāo Yǎzhī,
wishing to hold the north bank of the Yangzi to resist Xuán.
He gathered his troops for a grand deliberation.
His Staff Officer Liú Xí said:
"There is no greater unacceptable act than rebellion.
Yet, last year, the general rebelled against Wáng Yǎnzhōu;
recently, he rebelled against Sīmǎ Lángjūn;
now, he again wishes to rebel against Huán Gōng.
How can one rebel three times
and still stand?"
After speaking,
he rushed out,
and many of the subordinate officials scattered and fled.
Jìngxūan had already returned to Jīngkǒu to retrieve his family,
missing the appointed time.
Láozhī thought he had been killed by Liú Xí,
and so he hanged himself.
Soon after, Jìngxūan arrived;
without time to mourn,
he fled to Gāo Yǎzhī.
The generals and officials jointly encoffined Láozhī,
and the funeral returned to Dāntú.
Huán Xuán ordered the coffin to be opened and his head cut off,
exposing the corpse in the marketplace.
When Liú Yù raised his banner of righteousness,
he posthumously reinstated Láozhī,
restoring him to his original office.
Jìngxūan was
Láozhī's eldest son.
His wisdom and strategy were not equal to his father's,
but his martial skills surpassed him.
During Sūn Ēn's rebellion,
he followed his father on campaigns,
achieving success wherever he went.
He served as Attendant Censor for Yuánxiǎn,
and later as Counselor to Huán Xuán.
After Láozhī's defeat,
he fled with Gāo Yǎzhī, Administrator of Guǎnglíng, to Mùróng Chāo.
He dreamed of swallowing a clay pellet,
and upon waking,
he joyfully said:
"'Wán' (丸) means 'Huán' (桓);
since 'wán' has been swallowed,
I shall return to my homeland."
Within ten days, Xuán was defeated,
and he consequently returned to the capital with Sīmǎ Xiūzhī.
He was appointed General Supporting the State and Administrator of Jìnlíng.
He and Zhūgě Chángmín defeated Huán Xīn at Sháopí,
and he was promoted to General Establishing Martial Prowess and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
stationed at Xúnyáng.
He also attacked Huán Liàng and Fú Hóng in Xiāngzhōng,
achieving merits everywhere.
When Emperor Ān regained power,
he was summoned and appointed General Champion and Internal Administrator of Xuānchéng,
also serving as Administrator of Xiāngchéng.
When Qiáo Zòng rebelled,
Jìngxūan was appointed Supervisor of All Military Affairs for the Expedition to Shǔ and granted a staff of authority,
and he campaigned westward with General Guarding the North Zāng Xǐ.
〔一０〕Jìngxūan entered from Báidì,
capturing all that he attacked.
His army reached Huángshòu,
〔一一〕and he was in a stalemate with the pseudo-general Qiáo Dàofú for over sixty days.
He encountered an epidemic,
and with provisions exhausted,
he withdrew his army.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities
and dismissed from office.
Shortly thereafter,
he became Counselor to the Central Army,
with the additional title of General Champion.
Soon he was promoted to Protector-General to Pacify the Barbarians, Administrator of Ānfēng, and Internal Administrator of Liáng Commandery.
At the time of Lú Xún's rebellion,
he joined the main army as General Champion for the southern campaign.
After Lú Xún was pacified,
he was promoted to General of the Left Guard and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and then to General Who Conquers Barbarians and Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Soon he was reassigned to Jìzhōu,
and was murdered by his staff officer Sīmǎ Dàocì.
Yīn Zhòngkān
Yīn Zhòngkān was
a native of Chénjùn.
His grandfather, Róng, served as Grand Master of Ceremonies and Minister of Personnel.
His father, Shī, served as Counselor to the General of Agile Cavalry, Administrator of Jìnlíng, and Baron of Shāyáng.
Zhòngkān was skilled in pure conversation
and good at composing literary works.
He often said,
"If I don't read the Dàodélùn for three days,
I feel a stiffness at the root of my tongue."
His discussions of philosophy were as renowned as Hán Kāngbó's,
and scholars admired him.
He was appointed Assistant Compiler.
When General Champion Xiè Xuán was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
he invited him to be his Staff Officer.
He was offered the post of Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
but he did not accept.
Xuán appointed him Chief Clerk
and treated him with great trust and respect.
Zhòngkān wrote a letter to Xuán, saying: "After the collapse of the Hú,
the Han children sold into Jiangdong are countless.
Families are scattered like stars,
suffering year after year.
The air of resentment and bitterness
affects
harmony and order.
This is indeed common in times of chaos,
sufficient to serve as a warning.
Moreover, it is not the intention of the royal benevolence to spread widely
and nurture the common people.
If the great men of our time sincerely plan
to rescue them from their misery,
yet allow things to reach this state,
it is truly lamentable!
I wish that Your Excellency would broaden this with virtue,
and operate it with divine wisdom,
to apply your heart
to all beings,
and manifest principles to prohibit violence,
so that those who tread Jin territory will surely harbor no sorrow,
and the withered and parched will all receive the dew of Heaven.
May benevolence and righteousness be
exercised alongside military force,
and virtuous intent flourish with achievements and merits.
This is truly what is expected of an enlightened virtuous one.
Recently, I heard that much of what was obtained through looting
were people scavenging for reeds and suffering from hunger.
The strong wished to save their children,
the young were intent on preserving their parents.
Those traveling emptied their baskets to look after them,
those staying behind sighed and awaited their return.
But then, they were suddenly imprisoned,
separated in life and cut off in death.
To consider this emotionally,
it is extremely heartbreaking.
In the past, Mèngsūn hunted and caught a fawn.
He ordered
Qín Xī to take it home.
Its mother followed and cried mournfully.
Unable to bear it, he released it,
and Mèngsūn pardoned Qín Xī's offense and made him the fawn's foster father.
If even animals cannot be separated,
how much less
can humans!
Even the flying owl,
an ill-omened bird,
when it eats mulberries,
still emits beautiful sounds.
Even if they are called Rong-Di,
can they be without emotion?
If they are moved by something,
it is not difficult
to transform them.
It is essential to ensure that border areas do not covet small gains,
and that the strong do not oppress the weak.
Once the virtuous sound is emitted,
it will surely resonate through the desert,
and the followers of the two enemies
will flock
to our influence.
Why worry that the Yellow River cannot be crossed,
or Hángǔ Pass cannot be opened?"
Xuán deeply agreed with him.
Huán Xuán (桓玄) was in Nánjùn (南郡).
He discussed how the Sì Hào (四晧) came to the Hàn (漢) court to provide guidance,
and Emperor Xiàohuì (孝惠) was established through their efforts.
However, Emperor Huì (惠) was weak,
and Empress Lǚ (呂) was cruel and suspicious.
These several gentlemen,
coming into contact with that dust and grime,
wished to remedy the situation.
Between the two families,
each had its own faction.
To take from one and give to the other,
their animosity would surely arise.
He wondered, with the aspirations of common men,
how could the four lords escape calamity?
If one walks in purity and ends well,
and remains hidden to preserve life,
is that not the way?
He sent this essay to Zhòngkān (仲堪).
Zhòngkān (仲堪) then replied, saying: Whether one is hidden or manifest, silent or speaking,
is not the concern of a wise and discerning person.
Rather, it is because the times one encounters are different,
and therefore the paths one takes must differ.
If the Dao (道) is not compromised, and the world thereby
attains peace,
the heart of a benevolent person cannot but be moved.
As for those four lords,
they nurtured their aspirations in the rocky mountains,
their Dao (道) was lofty throughout the world.
Though Qín’s (秦) net was cruel,
they wandered without
fear.
Though the Hàn (漢) founder was mighty,
he invited them but they did not turn back.
It was merely because a single principle moved them,
and they responded spontaneously.
Their actions were like the rites of guests,
their words contained no right or wrong disputes.
Emperor Xiàohuì (孝惠) thereby attained peace,
and had no way to repay their kindness.
Rúyì (如意) thereby secured his domain,
leaving no room for resentment.
Moreover, when strife and contention arise,
and the ruler is not of a single surname,
the hundred surnames conceive intentions.
If the throne has no constant occupant,
then everyone considers themselves worthy.
What’s more, Hàn (漢) arose by the sword,
people did not yet know righteousness.
To suppress wickedness and evil,
it was especially appropriate to take uprightness and compliance as a
treasure.
The world [tiānxià (天下)]
is a great vessel.
If disorder and destruction are feared,
then the blue seas will overflow.
How could the strategizing of such men
be merely for the rise or fall of one person?
If they could thereby fulfill their benevolence and righteousness,
compared to those who bend their principles and commit themselves to honor or disgrace,
their paths are vastly different,
their principles and circumstances are not the same.
Why do you doubt this, my lord?
You also said that the Zhū Lǚ (諸呂) grew powerful,
almost endangering the Liú (劉) clan.
If Rúyì (如意) had been established,
this calamity would surely not have occurred.
However, fortune and misfortune come from the same gate,
and are intertwined in myriad ways.
It cannot yet
be definitively concluded.
At that time, the world was newly settled,
power was controlled from above.
Gāozǔ (高祖) had enfeoffed his sons and brothers as princes,
with the solidity of bedrock.
Ministers with deep foresight for the state
stood shoulder
to shoulder.
How could trivial officials like Lù Chǎn (祿產) be able to usurp and overturn it?
Perhaps this was what the four lords foresaw,
and even now we have no way to prove it.
But in seeking the hearts of ancient sages,
it is proper
to preserve their far-reaching perspective.
Those who address the root and correct the source,
though they cannot be without danger,
their danger is easy to manage.
If one instead opens the path to contention,
though one may not necessarily be insecure,
that security is difficult
to maintain.
This is the most crucial principle for governing a state,
cherished by ancient and modern sages alike.
Huán Xuán (桓玄) was convinced.
When Zhòngkān (仲堪) was in Jīngzhōu (荊州),
for years there were floods and droughts.
The common people suffered from famine.
Zhòngkān (仲堪) always ate five bowls of food,
with no leftover dishes on his plate.
If a grain of rice fell on the mat,
he would pick it up and eat it.
Although he wished to lead by example,
it was also due to his naturally simple character.
He often told his nephews and disciples:
“People see that I have been appointed to a provincial post
and think I have abandoned my former aspirations.
But it is not easy for me to be in this position now.
Poverty is common for a scholar.
How can one climb the branches and abandon the root?
You should remember this!”
Afterward, the Shǔ (蜀) River overflowed greatly,
floating away thousands of households in Jiānglíng (江陵).
Due to inadequate dikes, he was again demoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍).
When Emperor Ān (安) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍),
but he firmly declined to accept it.
Initially,
Huán Xuán (桓玄) was about to join Wáng Gōng (王恭),
so he persuaded Zhòngkān (仲堪)
to nominate Gōng (恭) as their leader,
and together launch the Jìnyáng (晉陽) campaign,
achieving the merits of Huán Wén (桓文).
Zhòngkān (仲kān) agreed.
Zhòngkān (仲kān) considered that Wáng Gōng (王恭) was in Jīngkǒu (京口),
less than two hundred *lǐ* (里) from the capital.
To connect forces from Jīngzhōu (荊州) was too far,
and their positions would not align.
So he feigned agreement with Gōng (恭),
but in reality did not intend to obey.
When he heard that Gōng (恭) had already executed Wáng Guóbǎo (王國寶) and others,
he then sent a memorial to raise an army,
dispatching Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Yáng Quánqí (楊佺期) to Bālíng (巴陵).
Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子) sent a letter to stop him,
so Zhòngkān (仲kān) returned.
Initially,
Huán Xuán (桓玄) had resigned his official post and returned to his home region.
Zhòngkān (仲kān) respected his talent and background,
and formed a deep alliance with him.
Xuán (玄) also wanted to use his military power,
and so enticed and pleased him.
During the campaign against Guóbǎo (國寶),
Zhòngkān (仲kān) had indeed accepted Xuán’s (玄) persuasion,
and so externally allied with the governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州), Xī Huī (郗恢),
and internally sought the support of his cousin Nánmán Xiàowèi (南蠻校尉) Yǐ (顗) and the grand administrator of Nánjùn (南郡), Jiāng Jì (江績), among others.
Huī (恢), Yǐ (顗), and Jì (績) did not agree with him.
So Yáng Quánqí (楊佺期) was substituted for Jì (績),
and Yǐ (顗) voluntarily resigned his position.
[一二]

Coincidentally, Wáng Gōng (王恭) again joined with the governor of Yùzhōu (豫州), Yǔ Kǎi (庾楷), to raise an army to attack the governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州), Wáng Yú (王愉), and Prince Qióng Shàngzhī (譙王尚之), among others.
Zhòngkān (仲kān) then convened a discussion,
believing that since the imperial court had executed Guóbǎo (國寶) last year,
Wáng Gōng’s (王恭) prestige and renown were already established.
Now that he was raising an army again,
there was no doubt he would succeed.
“Last year, we delayed our army,
and have already lost trust with them.
Now we should prepare our boats and march at dawn,
to participate in his hegemonic achievements.”
Thereupon, he sent Quánqí (佺期) with five thousand marines as the vanguard,
followed by Huán Xuán (桓玄),
and Zhòngkān (仲kān) led twenty thousand troops,
following one after another downriver.
Quánqí (佺期) and Xuán (玄) arrived at Pénkǒu (湓口).
Wáng Yú (王愉) fled to Línchuān (臨川).
Xuán (玄) sent a detachment to pursue and capture him.
Quánqí (佺期) and others advanced to Héngjiāng (橫江).
Yǔ Kǎi (庾楷) was defeated and fled to Xuán (玄).
Prince Qióng Shàngzhī (譙王尚之) and others retreated,
and all the naval forces led by Shàngzhī’s (尚之) younger brother, Huīzhī (恢之), were lost.
Xuán (玄) and others arrived at Shítóu (石頭),
Zhòngkān (仲kān) arrived at Wúhú (蕪湖),
when suddenly they heard that Wáng Gōng (王恭) had died,
and Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) had turned against Gōng (恭),
leading the Beǐfǔ (北府) army to Xīntíng (新亭).
Xuán (玄) and the other three armies lost color,
no longer having firm resolve.
So they turned their armies back and garrisoned at Càizhōu (蔡洲).
[一三]
At that time, the imperial court had just pacified Gōng and Kǎi,
and was unsure of the sentiments of the people in the west.
Zhòngkān and others commanded tens of thousands of troops,
who filled the suburbs and capital region.
Internal and external anxieties pressed in.
Xuán's elder cousin, Xiū, informed Prince Dàozǐ of Huìjī:
"The western army can be persuaded to disperse.
Xiū knows their true feelings.
If Quánqī is promised great rewards,
there will be none who will not turn their spears against Zhòngkān."
Dàozǐ accepted this,
and thus appointed Xuán as the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
Quánqī as the governor of Yōngzhōu,
demoted Zhòngkān to Gǔangzhōu,
and appointed Huán Xiū as the governor of Jīngzhōu.
He then dispatched Zhòngkān's uncle, Tài Cháng Mào, to proclaim the imperial edict and order the army to withdraw.
Zhòngkān was enraged by his demotion,
thinking that although Wáng Gōng had been defeated,
his own forces were still sufficient to achieve something,
and ordered Xuán and the others to advance rapidly.
Xuán and the others were pleased with their new appointments,
and all wished to obey the imperial decree,
thus they hesitated and could not decide.
At this time, Zhòngkān's younger brother Yù, who was Quánqī's Sīmǎ,
fled to Zhòngkān by night,
persuading him to accept the imperial decree
and receive Huán Xiū.
Zhòngkān, in a panic,
immediately retreated south from Wúhú,
sending a message to Xuán and the other armies, saying:
"If you do not all disperse and return,
when the main army reaches Jiānglíng,
all your remaining kin will be slaughtered."
Zhòngkān's general Liú Xìxiān, who commanded two thousand men under Quánqī,
immediately led his troops back.
Xuán and the others were greatly frightened,
and frantically pursued Zhòngkān,
catching up with him at Xúnyáng.
Thereupon,
Zhòngkān lost his position
and relied on Xuán for support.
Xuán and the others, in turn, relied on Zhòngkān's troops.
Although they were mutually suspicious and obstructed each other,
they could not act otherwise.
Zhòngkān and Quánqī exchanged sons and nephews as hostages,
and then formed an alliance at Xúnyáng.
Xuán became the leader of the alliance,
taking an oath and performing a blood sacrifice at the altar.
They all refused to accept the imperial edict,
appealed for the vindication of Wáng Gōng,
and demanded the execution of Liú Láozhī, Prince Shàngzhī of Qiáo, and others.
The imperial court was deeply apprehensive of them.
Thereupon, an edict was sent to Zhòngkān, stating:
"Recently, the general's reliance on others has caused him to lose his position,
and both court and populace are worried.
However, what is past should be forgotten by both sides,
so if you now lead your troops back
and respectfully obey the imperial command,
the change in your appointment
is merely a matter of adapting to the times.
The general's great righteousness
has truly touched Our heart.
Now We restore you to your original position.
Immediately take charge of your garrison,
lay down your arms, and rest your soldiers;
then internal and external peace will be unified.
Therefore, We have dispatched Tài Cháng Mào to fully convey Our sentiments."
Zhòngkān and the others all obeyed the edict
and returned to their respective garrisons.
A short while later,
Huán Xuán was about to attack Quánqī.
He first informed Zhòngkān, saying:
"I am now going to enter Miǎn to attack and eliminate Quánqī.
I have already stationed troops at Jiāngkǒu.
If you stand with me without wavering,
you should kill Yáng Guǎng.
If not,
I will lead my army into the Jiāng."
Zhòngkān then arrested Xuán's elder brother Wěi,
and sent his cousin Yù and others with seven thousand naval troops to Jiāngxīkǒu.
〔一四〕Xuán dispatched Guō Quán and Fú Hóng to attack them,
and Yù and his forces were defeated and fled.
Xuán encamped at Bālíng
and appropriated its grain.
Xuán also defeated Yáng Guǎng at Xiàkǒu.
Having lost the stores at Bālíng,
and with all his generals defeated,
Jiānglíng was shaken with fear.
There was a great famine within the city,
and sesame seeds were used as provisions.
Zhòngkān urgently summoned Quánqī.
Quánqī led his forces to him,
crossed the Jiāng directly to attack Xuán,
but was defeated by Xuán
and fled back to Xiāngyáng.
Zhòngkān fled to Cuōchéng,
where he was captured by Xuán's pursuing troops
and forced to commit suicide.
He died at Zuòxī.
His nephew Dàohù, advisor Luó Qǐshēng, and others were all killed.
In his youth, Zhòngkān followed the Tiānshīdào,
and also served spirits with great devotion,
not begrudging wealth and bribes.
However, he neglected acts of benevolence and righteousness
and was miserly in helping those in need.
When Xuán attacked,
he was still diligently offering prayers.
Nevertheless, he was good at winning people's hearts;
for the sick, he would personally diagnose their pulse and dispense medicine.
But his strategies involving hidden maneuvers were too complex and numerous,
and he lacked foresight,
which led to his defeat.
His son, Jiǎnzhī,
carried his coffin to the lower capital
and buried him at Dāntú,
then resided by the tomb.
When the Yi Banner was raised,
he led his private servants and retainers to follow the righteous army and pursue Huán Xuán.
When Xuán died,
Jiǎnzhī ate his flesh.
During the campaign of Huán Zhèn,
the righteous army suffered a defeat,
and Jiǎnzhi perished in battle.
His younger brother, Kuàngzhī,
resembled his father in character
and served as magistrate of Shàn.
Yáng Quánqī
Yáng Quánqī,
a native of Huáyīn in Hóngnóng,
was a descendant of Hàn Tàiwèi Zhèn.
His great-grandfather, Zhǔn,
was a Tài Cháng.
From Zhèn to Zhǔn,
seven generations were renowned for their virtue.
His grandfather, Lín,
had talent and renown in his youth,
but was lost among the Hu during a period of chaos.
His father, Liàng,
served a false court in his youth,
but later returned to the country
and ended his career as the governor of Liángzhōu,
known for his integrity and competence.
Quánqī was deep, brave, resolute, and vigorous,
while his elder brother Guǎng and younger brothers Sīpíng and others were all strong, fierce, and violent.
He claimed his family's lineage
was unmatched in the region south of the Jiāng,
and when someone compared his family background to Wáng Xún's,
he still felt resentful.
But at the time, people considered him to have crossed the Jiāng too late,
and his marriages and official appointments were out of his class,
so they often suppressed him.
He was constantly indignant and gnashed his teeth,
wishing to seize an opportunity to realize his ambitions.
Quánqī served in military headquarters in his youth.
During the Xiánkāng era,
he led troops to garrison Chénggù.
Fú Jiān's general Pān Měng defended Kānghuí Lěi,
but Quánqī attacked and routed him.
All his troops surrendered,
and Quánqī was appointed General Guǎngwēi and Governor of Hénán,
garrisoning Luòyáng.
Fú Jiān's general Dòu Chōng led troops to attack Zhāng Yuánxī, the governor of Píngyáng, at Huángtiān Wù.
Quánqī attacked and routed him.
Quánqī entered Tóngguān from Húchéng,
winning every battle in a series of engagements.
He captured and killed thousands,
received the surrender of over nine hundred families,
and returned to Luòyáng,
being promoted to General Lóngxiáng.
Due to illness,
he was reappointed as Governor of Xīnyě
and concurrently served as Jiànwēi Sīmǎ.
He was transferred to be Governor of Tángyì,
〔一六〕and supervised military affairs at Shítou,
but resigned due to illness.
Yīn Zhòngkān, the governor of Jīngzhōu, appointed him as his Sīmǎ,
replacing Jiāng Jì as Administrator of Nánjùn.
Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán raised troops to support Wáng Gōng and Yú Kǎi.
Zhòngkān, being naturally unskilled in military strategy,
entrusted all military matters to Quánqī and his brothers.
With five thousand soldiers as the vanguard,
they followed Huán Xuán downriver.
Upon reaching Shítou,
Gōng was dead and
Kǎi defeated.
The imperial court, unsure of Xuán's army,
then appointed Quánqī to replace Xī Huī as the Area Commander of the military affairs of Liáng, Yōng, and Qín three prefectures and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Zhòngkān and Xuán were both transferred.
Thereupon, they both returned to Xúnyáng
and formed an alliance, refusing to obey the imperial edict.
Soon after, the imperial court restored Zhòngkān to his original post,
and they each returned to their garrisons.
Xuán had already fled west.
Yù appointed Yì as Grand General of the Champions and Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
and along with Hé Wújì and Liú Dàoguī, pursued Xuán.
Xuán compelled the Emperor and the Prince of Lángxié to go west.
Yì, Dàoguī, and Mèng Huáiyù, the Administrator of Xiàpī, amongst others, caught up with Xuán,
and fought at Zhēngróngzhōu.
Yì, taking advantage of the wind, unleashed fire,
and exerted his full strength to be first,
causing Xuán's forces to suffer a great defeat.
They burned their baggage train and fled by night.
Xuán's generals Guō Quán and Liú Yǎ, among others, attacked and captured Xúnyáng.
Yì dispatched General Wǔwēi Liú Huáisù to suppress them.
When Xuán died,
Huán Zhèn and Huán Qiān again gathered troops to resist Yì at Língxī.
Xuán's general Féng Gāi brought his troops to join Zhèn.
Yì advanced to attack,
but was defeated by Zhèn.
He retreated to Xúnyáng,
and was dismissed from office for this,
but was soon reinstated.
Liú Yù ordered Hé Wújì to follow Yì's command.
Wújì found the supervision cumbersome,
and immediately dissolved the command.
Yì was angry at Wújì's self-assertion,
and dismissed him as Administrator of Lángxié,
appointing him as General Fǔguó to oversee military affairs.
Wújì then harbored ill will towards Yì.
Yì merely took the blame himself,
and contemporary opinion approved of it.
Yì again set out from Xúnyáng with Dàoguī.
Huán Liàng styled himself Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
and Yì dispatched Liú Jìngxuan to attack and drive him away.
Yì's army encamped at Xiàkǒu.
At that time, Zhèn's partisan Féng Gāi garrisoned Dà'àn,
Mèng Shāntú occupied Lǔchéng,
and Huán Shānkè defended Yǎnyuè Lěi.
Their combined forces numbered ten thousand men,
with ships linked across both banks,
supporting each other by land and water.
Yì led the various armies in an offensive,
but before reaching Xiàkǒu,
they encountered a storm and lost over a thousand men.
Yì, along with Liú Huáisù and Suǒ Miǎo, attacked Lǔchéng;
Dàoguī attacked Yǎnyuè Lěi;
Hé Wújì and Tán Zhǐ arrayed their ships in the middle of the river,
to prevent any escape.
Yì personally donned armor and helmet,
and after half a day of assaulting the city, both fortresses collapsed.
Shānkè was captured alive,
while Féng Gāi fled.
Yì then pacified Bālíng.
Yì was appointed Bearer of Credential, Inspector of Yànzhōu,
his generalship remaining as before.
Yì's orders were strict and orderly,
and wherever he passed through towns and villages,
the common people felt secure and joyful.
Rǔ Zōngzhī, the Administrator of Nányáng, raised a righteous army,
attacked Xiāngyáng,
and defeated Huán Wèi.
Yì and the other armies encamped at Mǎtóu in Jiānglíng.
Zhèn embraced the imperial carriage,
and left the camp for Jiāngjīn.
Zōngzhī again defeated the pseudo-general Wēn Kǎi.
Zhèn personally attacked Zōngzhī.
Yì then led Wújì, Dàoguī, and other armies to defeat Féng Gāi at Yùzhāngkǒu,
pushing forward with great momentum,
and then entered Jiānglíng.
Zhèn heard that the city had fallen,
and fled north with Qiān.
The imperial carriage was restored to its proper place.
Yì captured Xuán's partisans Biàn Fànzhī, Yáng Sēngshòu, Xiàhóu Chóngzhī, Huán Dàogōng, and others,
and executed them all.
Huán Zhèn, along with Fú Hóng, again attacked and captured Jiānglíng from Yúnchéng,
and engaged in a standoff with Liú Huáisù.
Yì dispatched his subordinate generals to attack Zhèn,
killing him,
and also beheading the pseudo-General Fǔguó Huán Zhēn.
Yì also attacked and captured Qiānlíng,
beheading Xuán's Administrator Liú Shūzǔ at Línzhàng.
The remaining tens of those who gathered crowds and assumed false titles,
were all suppressed.
Once the two provinces were pacified,
Yì was appointed General Fǔjūn.
At that time, Diāo Yù and others raised a rebellion,
and were stationed in Xiāngzhōng.
Yì dispatched generals to suppress them separately,
and all were annihilated.
Originally,
Yì was at home observing mourning for his parent.
When the righteous banner was first raised,
he continued to serve in mourning clothes.
Now,
as the military campaigns gradually subsided,
he submitted a memorial requesting to return to Jīngkǒu,
to complete his mourning rites,
saying:
"For those who promote the Way and govern the state,
the principles culminate in benevolence and filial piety.
For those who are in extreme distress and appeal to Heaven,
nothing is more profound than the loss of a parent.
But I am a mediocre person,
fundamentally lacking in deep emotion,
unable to fall down in grief,
which is perhaps fitting for me.
In past years, the nation's calamity was overwhelming,
so I dedicated my foolish loyalty,
shamelessly surviving.
Last spring, the imperial carriage returned,
but the crazy villains were not yet exterminated.
Although some treacherous villains were executed,
the remaining embers were hidden,
and our awe-inspiring benevolence was lacking,
the civil and military officials exhausted.
My humble feelings have not been expressed,
and I look at my shadow with grief and indignation.
Now the imperial majesty has pacified far and wide,
and the land within the seas is clean and clear.
My extreme suffering and impurity
have also been fully heard by Your Sacred Majesty.
Moreover, my weakness and illness have become severe,
and various ailments afflict me,
so much so that now I lie prostrate with no human reason left.
My feeling is,
I never clung to life;
speaking of the matter,
it is also time for me to die.
I beg that my remaining body be granted,
to complete my funeral rites at the tomb,
hoping that the way of loyalty and filial piety may be pardoned in this sacred era."
This was not granted.
