An edict appointed Yì as Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Yùzhōu and the five commanderies of Huáinán, Líyáng, Lújiāng, Ānfēng, and Tángyì in Yángzhōu,
and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
His status as Bearer of Credential, General, and Palace Attendant remained as before,
and all civil and military officials of his original staff were ordered to be assigned to the west.
For his achievements in restoration,
he was enfeoffed as Founding Duke of Nánpíng Commandery,
and also Area Commander of Xuānchéng military affairs,
and granted one set of drums and pipes.
Liú Yǎ, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, rebelled.
Yì dispatched generals to suppress and capture him.
Originally,
Huán Xuán built a study in Nánzhōu,
and had coiling dragons painted all over it.
It was called the Coiling Dragon Study.
Yì's courtesy name was Pánlóng (Coiling Dragon).
By this time,
he then resided there.
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Guards and Administrator Overseeing the Three Ducal Offices.
When Hé Wújì was defeated by Lú Xún,
the rebel army advanced victoriously,
and the court was terrified.
Yì prepared boats and ships to attack them.
As he was about to set out,
his illness became severe,
and everyone inside and outside the court was dismayed.
The court deliberated wanting to escort the imperial carriage north to join the central army under Liú Yù.
But Yì's illness recovered,
and he was about to lead the army in a southern campaign.
Yù wrote to Yì, saying:
"When I fought against the demon rebels,
I understood their changing tactics.
Now the ship repairs are almost complete,
and I will go ahead to strike them.
On the day of pacification,
all responsibilities in the upstream region will be entrusted to you."
He also sent Yì's cousin Fān to dissuade him.
Yì was greatly enraged,
and said to Fān:
"I merely elevated him for a temporary achievement,
and you immediately assume I am inferior to Liú Yù!"
He threw the letter to the ground.
Then he set out with a fleet of twenty thousand troops from Gūshú.
Xú Dàofù heard that Yì was approaching Jiànyè,
and reported to Lú Xún, saying:
"Liú Yì's army is strong,
success or failure hinges on this one battle.
We should combine our forces to resist him."
Xún then led his troops from Bālíng,
and descended with Dàofù in a continuous line of banners.
Yì encamped at Sāngluòzhōu,
and fought against the rebels.
He was defeated,
abandoned his ships,
and fled on foot with several hundred men.
The remaining forces were all captured by the rebels,
and the immense amount of baggage was all abandoned.
Yì fled,
traveling through Man and Jìn territories,
suffering from hunger and exhaustion, with many dying.
Only two or three out of ten reached safety.
His aide Yáng Suì exerted himself to protect him,
and he barely escaped.
Liú Yù greatly comforted and encouraged him,
and reinstated him to his original post.
Yì then appointed Suì as his Consultative Aide.
When Liú Yù marched to suppress Xún Xún,
an edict appointed Yì to manage all internal and external affairs in his absence.
Yì, having suffered a defeat,
requested to be relieved of his post,
and was demoted to Hòu Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Wèi Jiāngjūn, Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Jiāngzhōu Dūdū.
Yì submitted a memorial, saying: "Your subject has heard that Heaven operates by waxing and waning,
and government functions by adjusting for gain and loss.
If the times are adverse yet policies are not reformed,
and the people are suffering yet measures are not reduced,
then there will be no way to rescue the critically
ill from their perilous state,
or to save those on the verge of total destruction.
In recent times, military chariots have frequently been agitated,
and weapons of war have flooded the borders.
The Jiāngzhōu region under my command,
as a single corner of territory, bore the brunt of both rebellion and
loyalty.
Since Huán Xuán's time,
it has been continuously harassed, pressed, and devastated,
to the extent that men are not provided for,
and women have no partners.
People flee and scatter,
seeking refuge even in remote and hidden places,
and only those whose wealth is exhausted
and strength depleted
reach such a state.
If we do not compassionately govern with care,
and make some adjustments,
then the lament of utter desolation will soon arrive.
Setting up offices and dividing responsibilities,
with military and state functions serving distinct purposes,
the priority for governance is to reduce burdens, while
for military strategy it is to accomplish tasks.
To hold both responsibilities simultaneously
was merely a temporary
measure born of expediency.
Because this arrangement has been relied upon for a long time,
it has come to seem like a normal state of affairs.
Jiāngzhōu is located in the heartland,
bordering Yángzhōu and Yùzhōu,
serving as a crucial screen and shield,
truly a vital and repeatedly stressed area.
In the past, when the barbarian bandits
ran rampant,
and northern cavalry reached the Jiāng,
the need for defense
was indeed a temporary exigency.
Now, the small region of Jiāngzuǒ,
with fewer than several hundred thousand households,
and territory not exceeding several thousand *lǐ*,
yet
its military forces are arrayed one after another,
without any reduction,
broadly speaking,
this is truly a national disgrace.
Moreover, the area is free from danger,
yet military headquarters with civil and military officials and aides are still maintained,
incurring
unnecessary expenses.
How can this be called a grand strategic policy for governing the country,
or 'ladling out hot water to put out a fire'?
Since the prefectures and commanderies border the Jiāng,
the common people are scattered and remote.
Added to this, the post stations are perilous and obstructed,
fearing
wind and waves,
transport back and forth
is often delayed and abandoned.
This is also not what is meant by utilizing natural advantages to remedy disadvantages.
Your foolish subject suggests that the military headquarters should be dissolved,
and the garrison moved to
Yùzhāng.
Located in the midst of ten commanderies,
by implementing simple and benevolent governance,
within a few years,
vitality can be restored.
Furthermore, the dependent counties are sparse and scattered,
showing signs of what remains,
yet corvée duties for sending and receiving continue without respite.
It is also suggested that these should be merged as appropriate to simplify public expenses.
The Inspector, Yǔ Yuè,
since his arrival in office,
has shown great sincerity in his concern for the suffering,
but
the administrative structure has not been reformed,
as it falls outside the scope of his specific duties.
Xúnyáng borders the barbarians,
and should show signs of defense and prevention.
One thousand soldiers from the provincial headquarters can be sent to assist the commandery garrison there."
Thereupon, Yuè was dismissed,
and Yì moved his garrison to Yùzhāng,
sending his trusted general Zhào Huī to lead one thousand soldiers to guard Xúnyáng.
Soon after, Yì was promoted to Dūdū of the armies of the four commanderies of Hédōng, Hénán, Guǎngpíng, and Yìchéng in Jīngzhōu, Níngzhōu, Qínzhōu, Yōngzhōu, and Yángzhōu;
Wèi Jiāngjūn, Kǎifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
retaining his *jí* (credentials) and ducal title as before.
Yì memorialized that Jīngzhōu had fewer than one hundred thousand registered households,
and its armaments were desolate.
Although Guǎngzhōu was also devastated,
it still produced cinnabar and lacquer.
He requested to follow the previous standard.
Thereupon, he was also given command over Jiāo and Guǎng two provinces.
When Yì arrived at Jiānglíng,
he arbitrarily took more than ten thousand civil and military personnel from Jiāngzhōu and the Western Command of Yùzhōu,
detaining them and not sending them on.
He also claimed severe illness,
and requested Fán as his deputy.
Liú Yù, considering Yì to be disloyal to him,
then impeached him.
Emperor Ān issued an edict saying:
"Liú Yì is arrogant, fierce, and cruel,
having trampled on frost for a long time.
After his previous defeat,
he deserved immediate execution.
Yet, the tolerant laws of the Jìn
allowed him to receive another privileged appointment.
He never reflected on his transgressions or reproached himself,
but his resentment and discontent grew even stronger.
Fortunately, the prime ministers concealed his faults,
and specially nurtured and supported him,
even entrusting him with command west of the mountains,
granting him great honor and prosperity,
hoping that he would cleanse his heart, be moved by this kindness,
and change his tone and intentions.
Yet, he persisted in his evil ways,
determined to commit treachery,
oppressing superiors and abusing subordinates,
indulging in excess without restraint.
Although relieved of the Dūdū appointment,
and Jiāngzhōu was no longer under his jurisdiction,
he arbitrarily moved troops,
seized military supplies,
expelled former garrisons,
and heavily promoted his close associates.
The two bureaus of the Western Command,
with over ten thousand civil and military personnel,
were all cut off and retained,
without even a single word [of report].
He indulged his heart and desires,
disregarding the imperial court.
Moreover, he and his younger cousin Fán secretly influenced each other from afar,
gathered rogues and villains,
repaired armor, and mustered troops,
outwardly claiming to visit the sick,
but in reality plotting to seize an opportunity,
working together in evil,
planning to control Jīngzhōu and Yǐngzhōu.
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Xiè Hùn, relying on his family's prestige,
received extraordinary favor,
yet he was frivolous and impulsive,
serving as a cause of disorder,
stirring up trouble internally and externally,
conspiring across ten thousand *lǐ*.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be endured!"
Thereupon, Fán and Hùn were executed.
Liú Yù personally led his forces to suppress Yì,
ordering Wáng Hóng, Wáng Zhèn'è, Kuǎi Ēn, and others to lead troops to Yùzhāngkǒu,
where they burned their boats at Jiāngjīn and advanced.
Yì's staff officer, Zhū Xiǎnzī, encountered Zhèn'è
and, with the thousand men under his command, went over to Yì.
Zhèn'è and the others captured the outer city,
while Yì defended the inner city,
still having several thousand elite soldiers.
The battle lasted until late afternoon.
Zhèn'è showed Yù's letter to those within the city.
Yì, angered,
did not open the letter but burned it.
Yì hoped for external relief
and urged his officers and soldiers to fight fiercely.
But when the troops knew Yù had arrived,
none had the will to fight.
At dusk,
Zhèn'è burned all the gates
and attacked with full force.
Yì's troops then scattered.
Yì fled alone on horseback from the north gate,
and hanged himself twenty *lǐ* from Jiānglíng.
After a night,
the local residents reported it,
and he was then beheaded in the marketplace.
His sons and nephews were all executed.
Yì's elder brother Mó fled to Xiāngyáng,
and Lǔ Zōngzhī beheaded him and sent his head in.
Yì was firm, fierce, decisive,
but also willfully stubborn and arrogant.
He assisted Liú Yù in achieving great deeds,
but his accomplishments ranked second.
He was deeply conceited,
and refused to defer to Liú Yù.
When he governed the regional command,
he often felt frustrated and discontented.
Liú Yù always appeased and humored him.
Yì grew increasingly arrogant and presumptuous.
Whenever he read historical records,
especially the part where Lìn Xiāngrú humbled himself before Lián Pō,
he would invariably exclaim that it was impossible.
He once said,
“I regret not having met Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ,
to contend with them for the Central Plain.”
He also said to Xī Sēngshī,
“In the past, Liú Bèi had Kǒngmíng,
like a fish having water.
Now, although you and I are not as talented as the ancient sages,
our situation is similar to that saying.”
Everyone disliked his overbearing and insolent manner.
After his defeat at Sāngluò,
he realized that popular sentiment had turned against him,
and he became even more agitated.
Initially,
when Liú Yù campaigned against Lú Xún,
and returned victorious,
the emperor held a grand banquet at Xīchí,
and issued an edict for composing poems.
Yì’s poem read:
“The Six States had many heroes;
Zhèngshǐ produced the refined.”
He knew his military achievements were not outstanding,
so he displayed his excess of literary elegance.
Later, at Dōngfǔ, they gathered to play *chūpú* and gambled heavily.
One throw could be worth hundreds of thousands.
The others were all “black calves” (lost everything) and returned,
leaving only Liú Yù and Yì.
Yì’s turn came, and he threw a “pheasant” (a high score).
He was overjoyed,
lifted his robe, walked around the bed,
and shouted to those present,
“It’s not that I can’t throw a ‘deer’ (the highest score),
I just don’t bother!”
Liú Yù disliked this.
He then rolled the five dice for a long time,
and said,
“Let your humble servant try to answer for you, my elder brother.”
Afterward, four dice turned black (lowest score),
one die spun and had not yet settled.
Liú Yù shouted at it,
and it immediately became a “deer.”
Yì was very displeased,
but he was usually dark-complexioned,
his face like the color of iron.
Yet he said gently,
“I also know that you cannot be swayed by this!”
After being dispatched to the western region,
although he held a major provincial command,
he completely lost his power in the capital.
He also harbored suspicions about his own position and plans,
so he sought to assert his might and strength,
waiting for an opportunity to scheme against Liú Yù,
which led to his defeat.
Initially,
Yǔ Yuè, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
served as Sītú Zhǎngshǐ during the Lóng'ān period,
and once visited Jīngkǒu.
Yì was then very impoverished.
He had first borrowed the East Hall of the headquarters to practice archery with his relatives and friends.
But Yǔ Yuè later came directly to the hall with his subordinates.
Yì told him,
“We, the impoverished sort, find it very difficult to gather for a single archery session.
You may use any other hall,
and I hope you will yield this one today.”
Yǔ Yuè refused.
All the archers dispersed,
only Yì remained to shoot as before.
Later, when Yǔ Yuè was eating goose,
Yì asked for the leftovers,
but Yǔ Yuè again did not respond.
Yì always held a grudge about this.
In the Yìxī period,
he consequently seized Yǔ Yuè’s Yùzhāng commandery,
and stripped him of his military office,
sending someone to subtly convey his intention.
Yǔ Yuè died of anger and fear.
Yì’s narrow-mindedness and impetuosity were thus.
Mài’s courtesy name was Bóqún.
From a young age, he had talent and ability,
and served as Yīn Zhòngkān’s Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Huán Xuán, while in Jiānglíng,
was very arrogant and overbearing.
Scholars and commoners feared him
more than Yīn Zhòngkān.
Huán Xuán once played horse in front of Yīn Zhòngkān’s main hall,
and aimed a spear at Yīn Zhòngkān.
Mài was present at the time,
and said to Huán Xuán,
“The horse and spear have more than enough,
but the subtle principles are lacking.”
Huán Xuán considered himself the most talented in the world,
but he knew in his heart that others did not agree.
Yīn Zhòngkān turned pale.
When Huán Xuán left,
Yīn Zhòngkān said to Mài,
“You are a madman!
If Huán Xuán sent someone to kill you tonight,
how could I save you!”
Mài refuted Yīn Zhòngkān with righteous words,
and felt no regret.
Yīn Zhòngkān sent Mài to the capital to avoid trouble.
Huán Xuán indeed ordered a pursuit,
and Mài barely escaped disaster.
Later, when Huán Xuán achieved his ambition,
Mài went to his gate to request an audience.
Huán Xuán said to Mài,
“How do you know you won’t die, yet dare to meet me?”
Mài replied,
“Shè Gōu (shooting the hook) and Zhǎn Qū (cutting off the sleeve)
make three with Mài,
thus I know I will not die.”
Huán Xuán was very pleased,
and appointed him Xíngyù Cānjūn.
Later, he became Jìnglíng Tàishǒu.
When Yì and Liú Yù and others conspired to raise an army,
Mài intended to join them.
The matter was leaked,
and he was killed by Huán Xuán.
Zhūgé Chángmín
Zhūgé Chángmín
was a native of Yángdū, Lángxié.
He had both literary and military talents and capabilities,
but lacked moral conduct
and had no good reputation in his hometown.
Huán Xuán appointed him Cānjūn Píngxī Jūnshì,
but he was soon dismissed due to his greed and harshness.
When Liú Yù raised his army,
Zhūgé Chángmín conspired with him
and was appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He followed Liú Yù to attack Huán Xuán,
and for his achievements, he was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
At that time, Huán Xīn gathered troops and advanced towards Lìyáng.
Zhūgé Chángmín attacked and repelled him.
He also, with Liú Jìngxuan, defeated Huán Xīn at Sháopí,
and was enfeoffed as Xīngàn Xiàn Gōng,
with an income fief of two thousand five hundred households,
and was appointed Dū Huáinán Zhūjūnshì in his original office,
stationed at Shānyáng.
At the beginning of Yìxī,
Mùróng Chāo invaded Xiàpī.
Zhūgé Chángmín dispatched his subordinate general Xú Yǎn to attack and repel him.
He was promoted to Shǐchíjié, Dū Qīng Yáng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Qīngzhōu Císhǐ,
additionally serving as Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
stationed at Dāntú,
with his original title and ducal rank remaining as before.
When Hé Wújì was killed by Xú Dàofù,
the bandits pressed on, emboldened by their victory, towards the capital.
The court was shocked and terrified.
Zhūgé Chángmín led his troops to defend the capital,
and subsequently memorialized, saying:
“The demonic bandits gathered boats and cut wood,
yet Guō Chéngzhī, the Minister of Nánkāng, concealed this for an entire year,
and furthermore vouched for them deeply,
repeatedly deceiving Hé Wújì.
His crime deserves execution.”
An imperial edict pardoned Guō Chéngzhī.
When Lú Xún defeated Liú Yì,
Lú Xún and Xú Dàofù advanced with linked banners.
The capital was in peril and fear.
Zhūgé Chángmín urged Liú Yù to temporarily move the emperor across the river.
Liú Yù did not agree,
and ordered Zhūgé Chángmín and Liú Yì to garrison at Běilíng,
to defend Shítou.
After the matter was settled,
he was transferred to Dū Yùzhōu Yángzhōu Zhī Liùjùn Zhūjūnshì, Yùzhōu Císhǐ,
additionally serving as Huáinán Tàishǒu.
When Yù campaigned against Yì,
he appointed Chángmín to oversee the affairs of the Grand Commandant's residence.
An imperial edict granted him fifty armed men to enter the palace.
Chángmín was arrogant, unrestrained, greedy, and extravagant,
paying no attention to political affairs.
He amassed a large collection of treasures and beautiful women,
and constructed residences
without limit,
causing cruelty wherever he went.
He was a source of suffering for the common people.
He knew he had often acted without禮 (lǐ),
and feared the national laws.
When Líu Yì was executed,
Chángmín said to his intimates:
“In yesteryear, Péng Yuè was minced;
the year before last, Hán Xìn was killed.
Calamity must be approaching!”
He plotted to instigate a rebellion,
and asked Líu Mùzhī:
“People say that the Grand Commandant and I are not on equal terms;
why is this?”
Mùzhī replied:
“Your Excellency campaigned in the west,
entrusting his elderly mother and young brother to you, General.
How can you say you are not on equal terms!”
Chángmín’s younger brother, Límín, was frivolous, cunning, and fond of gain.
He strongly urged him, saying:
“Qíng and Péng had different bodies, but their power was not entirely preserved.
The execution of Líu Yì
also struck fear into the Zhūgě clan.
You can make your move before Yù returns.”
Chángmín hesitated and did not act.
Afterward, he sighed:
“When poor and humble, one always thinks of wealth and nobility;
when wealthy and noble, one inevitably faces danger.
To wish to be a commoner of Dāntú today,
how could that be possible!”
Yù deeply suspected him.
He continuously dispatched supply convoys that traveled quickly,
but changed the expected arrival date
when officials waited for him on the road.
He constantly varied the timing.
Then, his light boat advanced directly,
secretly entering Dōngfǔ.
The next morning,
when Chángmín heard of it,
he rushed to the gate in surprise.
Yù concealed the strong man Dīng Wǔ behind a curtain,
and invited Chángmín in to speak,
saying everything that he had previously held back.
Chángmín was pleased.
Wǔ then pulled him from behind and killed him,
and his corpse was delivered to the Ministry of Justice.
An order was given to arrest Límín.
Límín was exceptionally brave and fierce,
and died fighting desperately against his captors.
His youngest brother, Yòumín, who was a staff officer for the Grand Marshal,
fled into the mountains,
but was pursued, captured, and executed.
At the execution of the Zhūgě clan,
both gentry and commoners alike regretted that the righteous punishment came so late,
as if they had been released from shackles.
Previously,
after Chángmín became wealthy and noble,
he would often be startled awake from sleep ten or more nights a month,
leaping and
as if fighting with someone.
Máo Xiūzhī once shared a room with him
and was shocked to see this,
asking the reason.
Chángmín replied:
“I simply see a creature,
very black and hairy,
with indistinct feet,
extraordinarily strong.
No one but I can control it.”
Later, this occurrence became more frequent.
In the house, between the pillars and rafters,
he saw numerous snake heads.
He ordered people to chop them with a hanging knife,
but they would hide at the blade's touch,
only to reappear when it was gone.
Moreover, laundry pounders spoke to each other like human voices,
which was inexplicable.
On the wall, he saw a giant hand,
seven or eight feet long,
with an arm several spans in circumference.
When he ordered it to be chopped,
it suddenly disappeared.
Not long after, he was executed.
Hé Wújì
Hé Wújì was
from Tán in Dōnghǎi.
In his youth, he possessed great ambition,
was loyal, honest, and spirited.
If anyone did not meet his expectations,
it would immediately show in his words and expressions.
The province appointed him as an aide,
and he was later transferred to be a Taìxué Bóshì.
The General Guarding the North, Líu Láozhī,
was his maternal uncle.
At that time, Láozhī was stationed in Jīngkǒu,
and whenever there were major affairs,
he would often consult with Wújì.
When Yuánxiǎn, the heir apparent of Kuàijī, and his son Yànzhāng were enfeoffed as the King of Dōnghǎi,
〔一一〕Wújì was made the kingdom's Commandant,
and granted the title of Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn.
When Huán Xuán killed Yànzhāng in the marketplace,
Wújì entered the marketplace, wailed, and departed.
People at the time considered it righteous.
He followed Láozhī in campaigning south against Huán Xuán.
When Láozhī was about to surrender to Xuán,
Wújì repeatedly admonished him,
his words and intent very earnest,
but Láozhī did not comply.
When Xuán usurped the throne,
Wújì, having a prior acquaintance with Cáoxìngzhī, Xuán's Minister of Personnel,
requested to preside over a small county.
Xìngzhī reported this to Xuán,
but Xuán did not permit it.
Wújì then returned to Jīngkǒu.
Initially,
Líu Yù had once been a staff officer under Líu Láozhī,
and he and Wújì had always been close.
At this point,
they secretly conspired together against Xuán.
Líu Yì's family was in Jīngkǒu,
and he was already on good terms with Wújì.
When they spoke of the matter of restoration,
Wújì said:
“The Huán clan is strong and flourishing;
can they be overthrown?”
Yì replied:
“In the world, there are naturally strong and weak.
Even the strong can become weak.
The only worry is finding a suitable leader!”
Wújì said:
“Among the common people, there are no lack of heroes.”
Yì said:
“The only one I've seen is Líu Xiàpī.”
Wújì smiled and did not answer.
He returned and told Yù,
and then they jointly invited Yì,
and together they supported each other,
subsequently raising an army of righteousness,
and attacked Jīngkǒu.
Wújì falsely donned the attire of an imperial envoy,
claiming to be an imperial messenger,
and no one in the city dared to make a move.
Initially,
Huán Xuán heard that Liú Yù and others, including Hé Wújì, had raised an army,
and was greatly alarmed.
His partisans said:
"Liú Yù's rabble,
will certainly achieve nothing.
We beg you not to worry about it."
Xuán said:
"Liú Yù's bravery is unmatched in the three armies;
he has no equal today.
Liú Yì has no more than a *dan* or *shi* of grain stored at home,
yet gambles millions away with a single throw of the dice.
Hé Wújì
is Liú Láozhī's nephew,
and greatly resembles his uncle.
They are jointly undertaking a great enterprise;
how can you say they will achieve nothing!"
Such was the extent to which he feared them.
When Xuán was defeated and fled,
Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn, acting on his own authority, appointed Wújì as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Lángyá Nèishǐ.
He assigned all the elite troops from Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ's command to him,
to pursue Huán Xuán southwards.
He and Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Dàoguī were both placed under the command of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yì.
Xuán left his Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Hé Tànzhī, Qián Jiāngjūn Guō Quán, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Guō Chǎngzhī to defend Pénkǒu.
Wújì and the others reached Sāngluòzhōu,
and Tànzhī and his forces came to do battle.
Tànzhī's customary boat was adorned with very splendid banners and flags,
and Wújì said:
"The bandit leader certainly won't be in this one;
he wants to trick us.
We should attack it quickly."
The crowd all said:
"If Tànzhī is not in it,
his followers getting it will be of no benefit."
Wújì said to Dàoguī:
"Now, our numbers are unevenly matched;
we cannot win a complete victory in battle.
Although Tànzhī is not in this boat,
it will be easy to capture.
If we let our soldiers rush it,
we can defeat them in one drumbeat."
Dàoguī followed him,
and they consequently captured the bandit boat.
They then shouted:
"We have captured Hé Tànzhī!"
The bandits were thrown into disarray,
and Wújì's troops also believed it to be true.
Dàoguī pressed forward, taking advantage of the victory,
and Wújì also charged with drums and shouts.
Tànzhī's forces then disintegrated.
They advanced and occupied Xúnyáng,
and sent envoys to respectfully escort the ancestral tablets of the imperial temple, as well as Wǔkāng Gōngzhǔ and Lángyá Wángfēi, back to the capital.
He also, with Yì and Dàoguī, defeated and routed Xuán at Zhēngróngzhōu.
Wújì advanced to occupy Bālíng.
Xuán's cousin Qiān and nephew Zhèn seized the opportunity to capture Jiānglíng.
Wújì and Dàoguī advanced to attack Qiān at Mǎtóu,
and attacked Huán Wèi at Lóngquán;
they defeated them all.
Shortly thereafter, they were defeated by Huán Zhèn
and retreated to Xúnyáng.
Wújì, with Yì and Dàoguī, again advanced to suppress Zhèn,
capturing the three cities of Xiàkǒu,
and then pacified Bālíng,
advancing to Mǎtóu.
Huán Qiān requested to cede Jīng and Jiāng prefectures
and respectfully return the Emperor.
Wújì did not permit it.
The army advanced and captured Jiānglíng,
and Qiān and others were defeated and fled.
Wújì escorted Emperor Ān back to the capital.
Wújì was appointed Dūd Yùzhōu Yángzhōu Huáinán Lújiāng Ānfēng Lìyáng Tángyì Wǔjùn Jūnshì, Yòujiāngjūn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, with the additional title of Jiājié.
He was granted fifty armed guards to enter the palace,
but had not yet taken up the post.
He was then transferred to Huìjī Nèishǐ, Dūd Jiāngdōng Wǔjùn Jūnshì,
with his titles of Chíjié and Jiāngjūn remaining as before,
and was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
In the second year of Yìxī (406 CE),
he was transferred to Dūd Jiāng Jīng Èrzhōu Jiāngxià Suí Yìyáng Suīān Yùzhōu Xīyáng Xīncài Rǔnán Yǐngchuān Bājùn Jūnshì, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his titles of Jiāngjūn and Chíjié remaining as before.
For his merits in the restoration,
he was enfeoffed as Ānchéng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng,
〔一二〕with a fief of three thousand households.
He was additionally made Dūd Sīzhōu zhī Hóngnóng Yángzhōu zhī Sōngzī,
and was promoted to Sànqí Shìláng,
and then to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn.
Lú Xún sent his subordinate commander Xú Dàofù downstream,
with all his ships having multiple decks.
Wújì was about to lead his troops to resist them.
The Registrar, Dèng Qiánzhī, remonstrated, saying:
"Now, with our divine and mighty army, we face these rebellious masses;
it is like a mountain pressing an egg,
an insufficient analogy.
However, the nation's fate rests on this one move.
I hear their fleet is mighty,
and they hold the advantage of the upstream position.
The sting of a wasp or scorpion,
as the states of Zhū and Lǔ demonstrated,
is something to be wary of. It would be better to breach the Southern Dike,
hold the two cities, and await them.
They will certainly not dare to bypass us and proceed further downstream.
We should conserve our strength and wait until they are exhausted and weakened,
and then attack them.
If we abandon this perfectly safe long-term strategy,
and decide success or failure in a single battle,
should we suffer a defeat,
regret will be too late."
Wújì did not heed him,
and so he proceeded to meet them with his fleet.
When they met,
the bandits ordered several hundred strong archers to ascend a small hill on the west bank to intercept and shoot at them,
while closing in on the side of the hill.
Soon after, a strong westerly wind suddenly arose,
and Wújì's small vessel was blown to the east bank.
The bandits used the wind to press upon him with their large vessels.
His troops then broke and fled.
Wújì still shouted loudly:
"Bring me my Sū Wǔ staff!"
When the staff arrived,
he personally held it to supervise the battle.
The bandits swarmed around,
and dozens boarded his vessel.
Wújì showed no fear in his words or expression,
and, gripping the staff, died in battle.
An imperial edict stated:
"Wújì possessed wisdom and upheld righteousness,
was loyal, honest, and discerning.
He sacrificed himself for the state,
which aligns with heroic strategies.
When affairs were in gloom,
he dispersed the heavy clouds.
When he spread governance across the land,
he truly disseminated a benevolent influence.
When the demonic rebels stirred up chaos,
disturbing the capital region,
he threw off his robes to chastise them,
determined to pacify the royal domain.
But matters went beyond expectation,
and he became even more resolute in danger,
grasping his staff and falling in battle.
His sincerity penetrates ancient worthies.
We are deeply grieved in our heart.
He is posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Sīkōng,
his original offices remaining as before,
with the posthumous title Zhōngsù."
His son Yōng succeeded him.
Initially,
when Huán Xuán captured Jīngyì,
Liú Yù launched his eastern campaign.
Wújì secretly came to Yù's army,
secretly plotted to raise a righteous army,
and urged Yù to raise troops in Shānyīn.
Yù believed that Xuán's great rebellion was not yet manifest,
and feared that an uprising from afar
would be difficult to accomplish.
If Xuán were to usurp the imperial throne,
it would not be too late to plot against him at Jīngkǒu.
Wújì then returned.
When the righteous army was raised,
he participated and advised in the great undertaking,
achieving success through strategy and conquest.
However, this particular campaign failed due to impetuosity,
which was lamented by both court and commoners.
Tán Píngzhī
Tán Píngzhī, courtesy name Qìngzǐ,
was a native of Gāopíng.
From a young age, he possessed ambition and determination.
His household was harmonious and orderly,
and was praised by the world.
His cousin's son Zhāosháo and his four brothers,
were all young and orphaned.
Píngzhī raised them as if they were his own children.
Initially, he served as Huìjī Wáng Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn,
then transferred to Huán Xiū Chángliú Cānjūn,
and was appointed Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu,
with the additional title of Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
He had an old acquaintance with Liú Yù from their hometown,
and had also frequently participated in eastern expeditions with him,
so their relationship was very close.
When the righteous banner was raised,
Píngzhī, along with Liú Yì, both wore mourning attire due to private bereavement
and rushed to join.
Although his talent and reputation were inferior to Yì's,
his official rank and prestige surpassed him,
thus Yù appointed him Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
When Liú Yù
was about to initiate his righteous uprising, he once met with Hé Wújì and Wèi Yǒngzhī at Tán Píngzhī's residence.
A skilled physiognomist, the elder Wéi from Jìnlíng, saw Tán Píngzhī
and was greatly astonished, saying:
"You face the calamity of sudden military action,
the signs of which will appear in no more than three or four days.
You should hide deeply to avoid it,
and not venture out lightly."
When Huán Xuán's general Huángfǔ Fū arrived at Luóluòqiáo,
Tán Píngzhī and Liú Yù each led a contingent to fight.
Their army was defeated,
and Tán Píngzhī was killed by Fū's army.
He was posthumously granted the title of Inspector of Jìzhōu.
In the early years of Yìxī,
an imperial edict stated:
"Indeed, to commend good deeds and record merits
is a universal principle of nations,
and to remain imperishable after death
is a firm practice of integrity and righteousness.
The former Inspector of Jìzhōu, Tán Píngzhī, was loyal, fervent, resolute,
and sacrificed himself for the state.
Since his righteousness was profoundly rooted in his feelings,
he faced danger and offered his life.
Examining his intentions and actions,
the ancients could not have surpassed him by much,
and the recent posthumous grants
still leave a sense of regret.
He is hereby granted the additional title of Palace Attendant,
with his original office remaining as before.
Having sacrificed his life in royal service,
he should also be posthumously granted a enfeoffment and rewards.
He is to be enfeoffed as the Duke of Qǔ'ā County,
with a stipend of three thousand households."
Wèi Yǒngzhī
Wèi Yǒngzhī, courtesy name Chángdào,
was a native of Rènéng.
His family was poor and humble,
and he personally engaged in farming,
studying diligently without tiring.
He was born with a harelip.
A skilled physiognomist told him:
"You will become rich and noble."
At the age of eighteen,
he heard that the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Yīn Zhòngkān, had a famous physician under his command who could cure it.
Being poor and having no travel expenses,
he said to his family:
"With such a disability and ugliness,
what is the point of living!"
So, he carried several *hú* of rice westwards,
to present to Yīn Zhòngkān.
Upon arrival,
he announced himself at the gate.
Yīn Zhòngkān conversed with him,
admired his earnest intention,
and summoned the physician to examine him.
The physician said:
"It can be cut and mended,
but you must consume only porridge for a hundred days,
and refrain from speaking or laughing."
Wèi Yǒngzhī said:
"To live half a life without speaking, but still have half a life,
I would still seek treatment for it,
let alone for just a hundred days!"
Yīn Zhòngkān then housed him in a separate room,
and instructed the physician to treat him well.
Wèi Yǒngzhī then closed his mouth and did not speak,
eating only thin porridge;
such was his rigorous determination.
When he recovered,
Yīn Zhòngkān generously provided for him and sent him away.
Initially, he served as the Chief Clerk of the prefecture,
and once met Huán Xuán.
After he left,
Huán Xuán disdained his unrefined spirit,
and said to his guests:
"A common spirit inhabiting a great physique
does not make a fine talent."
He was ultimately not appointed and was sent away.
Wèi Yǒngzhī had early on formed a close friendship with Liú Yù,
and when Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he assisted in the righteous plan.
After Huán Xuán's defeat,
he was appointed General Establishing Might and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
When Huán Xīn attacked Lìyáng,
Wèi Yǒngzhī led his troops to defeat and drive him away.
In the early years of Yìxī,
he was promoted to General Exterminating Bandits and Administrator of Wú County.
Soon after, he was transferred to Inspector of Jīngzhōu, holding the imperial credential, Commander of Six Prefectures,
and also served as Southern Barbarian Commandant.
When Wèi Yǒngzhī was still a commoner,
he was not ashamed of his poverty and low status;
and when he held high office,
he also did not pride himself on his wealth and nobility.
Initially, he was a retainer of Yīn Zhòngkān,
but not long after, he actually occupied his position,
which commentators praised.
He died in office shortly thereafter.
An imperial edict stated:
"Wèi Yǒngzhī possessed a magnanimous disposition,
and his discernment and integrity were profound.
His sincerity in supporting the cause
is indeed inscribed in the royal archives;
the efficacy of his achievements
has brought benefit to the people.
His sudden demise
fills my heart with sorrow.
He is hereby granted the title of Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and additionally, Palace Attendant."
Later, in recognition of his meritorious service in supporting the righteous cause,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiānglíng County,
with a stipend of two thousand five hundred households,
and given the posthumous name Huán.
His younger brother, Shùnzhī, reached the position of Administrator of Lángyá.
The historian remarks: Your servant observes that from ancient times, the transformation of peaceful reigns
must rely on righteous people;
extraordinary achievements
are not possible without exceptional individuals.
During the decline and decay of the Jìn dynasty,
and the time when the rebellious Huán Xuán usurped power,
there was a lack of Huán Gōng and Wén Gōng externally,
and no Píng and Bó internally.
If there were no heroic figures,
how could salvation be achieved?
These several individuals
had spirit sufficient to lead their generation,
and talent sufficient to manage the world.
They belonged to a time when great fortune was exhausted,
and seized the opportunity granted by heaven in Yìxī.
They accomplished great deeds as easily as turning a circle,
and eliminated numerous villains like pulling up rotten wood.
Their power swayed all officials,
and their emoluments reached the highest levels.
This was indeed the zenith of a man's life.
However, Xī Lè was arrogant and thereby hastened disaster,
and Zhūgě Cháng was proud and indulgent, causing conflict.
They established Sòng but diverged from those of shared virtue,
and restored Jìn but differed from pure loyal ministers.
Their plans were not good,
and they brought about their own destruction.
Hé Wújì harbored great ambitions for fame and merit,
and possessed outstanding civil and military talents.
Mourning the past, he deeply moved the people of his time,
and leading the righteous, he shook powerful enemies with his reverberating call.
He seized opportunities for swift victory,
and faced death without fear.
Compared to the people of that era,
how can they be spoken of on the same day!
A eulogy says: Liú Bō was rigid and headstrong,
Lord Zhūgě was fierce and unrestrained.
Trouble arose from their over-fullness,
disaster from their suspicion and duplicity.
Tán Píngzhī was heroic and mighty,
embodying loyalty and fervor.
He abandoned his family to die for righteousness,
forgetting life to preserve his integrity.
Tán Píngzhī was truly awe-inspiring,
his body perished, but his name soared.
Wèi Yǒngzhī ultimately cooperated
and displayed his achievements with brilliance.

Biographies, Chapter 56: Zhāng Guǐ (His son Shí, Shí's brother Mào, Shí's son Jùn, Jùn's son Chónghuá, Chónghuá's son Yàolíng, Yàolíng's paternal uncle Zuò, Yàolíng's younger brother Xuánjìng, Xuánjìng's paternal uncle Tiānxī)
Zhāng Guǐ, courtesy name Shìyàn,
was a native of Wūshì, Āndìng, and the seventeenth-generation descendant of Zhāng Ěr, King Jǐng of Chángshān of the Hàn dynasty.
His family was esteemed for filial piety and integrity for generations,
and renowned for classical scholarship.
His father Wēn
was the Grand Provisioner.
Zhāng Guǐ was intelligent and eager to learn in his youth,
possessed great character and prestige,
and his demeanor was exemplary.
He was close with Huángfǔ Mì from the same commandery
and lived as a recluse on Nǚjǐ Shān in Yíyáng.
In the early years of Tàishǐ,
he accepted a fifth-rank official position from his paternal uncle Xī.
Zhāng Huá, the Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, discussed classical doctrines and the advantages and disadvantages of government with Zhāng Guǐ,
and greatly esteemed him,
believing that the Zhongzheng of Āndìng had obscured his goodness and suppressed his talent.
Thus, he praised Zhāng Guǐ in a discourse,
considering him to be an elite of the second rank.
General of the Guards Yáng Yáo appointed him as a subordinate,
he was then appointed as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
and successively rose to Palace Attendant, and Military Commander of the General Who Attacks the West.
Zhāng Guǐ, seeing that the times were fraught with difficulty,
secretly plotted to seize control of Héxī.
He performed a divination,
obtaining the hexagram Tài (Peace) changing to Guān (Contemplation).
Thereupon, he threw down the divining sticks and joyfully exclaimed:
"This is an omen of a hegemon!"
Consequently, he sought to be appointed as the Governor of Liángzhōu.
The high officials also recommended Zhāng Guǐ, deeming his talent capable of governing distant regions.
In the early Yuǒngníng era,
he was appointed as Hùqiāng Xiàowèi (Colonel Protector of the Qiāng) and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Liángzhōu).
At that time, the Xiānbēi had rebelled,
and bandits were rampant.
Upon arriving at his post, Zhāng Guǐ
immediately attacked and defeated them,
beheading over ten thousand enemies.
His prestige thus became established in Xīzhōu,
and his transforming influence spread throughout Hényòu.
He appointed Sòng Pèi, Yīn Chōng, Fàn Yuàn, and Yīn Dàn as his trusted advisors and strategists.
He summoned five hundred promising youths from the nine commanderies,
established schools,
and for the first time appointed a Chóngwén Jìjiǔ (Libationer of Promoting Culture),
whose rank was equal to that of a Biéjià (Vice Administrator).
In spring and autumn, the ceremony of Xiāngshè (Village Archery) was performed.
Mìshūjiān (Director of the Imperial Secretariat) Miáo Shìzhēng and Shàofǔ (Minister of the Lesser Treasury) Zhì Yú observed the celestial phenomena at night
and spoke to each other, saying:
"The world is in turmoil,
and the only safe haven is the land of Liángzhōu.
Zhāng, the Governor of Liángzhōu, possesses immeasurable virtue;
is he not the one?"
When the troubles of the two kings, Héjiān and Chéngdū, arose,
he dispatched three thousand soldiers
to the capital in the east.
Previously,
at the end of the Hàn dynasty, Yáng Chéngyuǎn of Jīnchéng killed the Grand Administrator and rebelled.
A local man, Féng Zhōng, rushed to the corpse and wept aloud,
spitting blood until he died.
Wú Yǒng of Zhāngyè was recruited by Hùqiāng Xiàowèi (Colonel Protector of the Qiāng) Mǎ Xián,
and later became an aide to Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Páng Cān.
Páng Cān and Mǎ Xián falsely accused each other,
and the crime warranted death.
Each called Wú Yǒng as a witness.
Wú Yǒng reasoned that both could not be right,
and so he slit his own throat and died.
Páng Cān and Mǎ Xián were ashamed and remorseful,
and reconciled with each other.
Zhāng Guǐ offered sacrifices at all their tombs and honored their descendants.
In the Yǒngxīng era,
the Xiānbēi Ruòluóbánnéng and others became bandits.
Zhāng Guǐ dispatched his Sīmǎ (Major), Sòng Pèi, to attack them,
who beheaded Ruòluóbánnéng
and captured over one hundred thousand people.
His formidable reputation greatly resonated.
Emperor Huì dispatched an envoy to promote him to Ānxī Jiāngjūn (General Pacifying the West)
and enfeoffed him as Ānlèxiāng Hóu (Marquis of Ānlè Township),
with a thousand households.
Thereupon, he greatly expanded the city of Gūzāng.
This city was originally built by the Xiōngnú,
seven *lǐ* from north to south,
and three *lǐ* from east to west.
The land had the shape of a dragon,
hence it was named Wòlóngchéng (Reclining Dragon City).
Earlier,
at the end of the Hàn dynasty, Bóshì (Erudite) Hóu Jǐn of Dūnhuáng told his disciples:
"Later, the spring water west of the city will dry up,
and a pair of watchtowers will rise above it,
facing the east gate.
From within them, a hegemon will emerge."
By the Jiāpíng era of the Wèi dynasty,
the commandery officials indeed established a school
and built twin watchtowers over the spring,
which precisely faced the east gate.
By this time,
the Zhāng clan indeed became hegemons of Héxī.
In the early Yǒngjiā era,
when Hán Zhì, the East Qiāng Xiàowèi (Colonel of the East Qiāng), killed Zhāng Fǔ, the Governor of Qínzhōu,
Zhāng Guǐ's Shàofǔ (Minister of the Lesser Treasury) Sīmǎ (Major), Yáng Yìn, spoke to Zhāng Guǐ, saying:
"Now Hán Zhì has defied orders
and presumptuously killed Zhāng Fǔ.
My lord, wielding authority over a region,
should punish such insubordination.
This is also in accordance with the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals:
if feudal lords are destroyed by others,
and Duke Huán cannot save them,
then Duke Huán is ashamed of it."
Zhāng Guǐ followed this advice,
and dispatched Zhōngdūhù (Central Supervising Commandant) Fàn Yuàn to lead twenty thousand troops to punish him.
He first sent a letter to Hán Zhì, stating:
"Currently, the imperial order is in disarray,
and regional governors should unite their efforts to serve the emperor.
I have just received a dispatch from Yōngzhōu
stating that you are raising troops to commit internal aggression.
As I am in charge of a region,
it is my duty to suppress rebels.
My thirty thousand warriors
are continuously being dispatched.
The emotion evoked by 'Fá Mù' (Cutting Wood) —
how can my feelings be expressed!
In ancient times, when an army marched,
preserving the state was paramount.
If you come alone to my army camp,
I will work with you to pacify the world's difficulties."
Hán Zhì received the letter and surrendered.
He dispatched his Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk) Línghú Yà to visit Wáng Mó, Prince of Nányáng.
Wáng Mó was very pleased
and presented Zhāng Guǐ with the sword bestowed by the Emperor,
saying to Zhāng Guǐ:
"From Lǒng westwards,
all military campaigns and divisions of territory are entrusted to you,
just like this sword."
Soon after, Wáng Mí attacked Luòyáng.
Zhāng Guǐ dispatched Běigōng Chún, Zhāng Zuǎn, Mǎ Fáng, Yīn Jùn, and others to lead the provincial army to defeat him.
He also defeated Liú Cōng at Hédōng.
The capital sang a song about him:
"The great horses of Liángzhōu
march unopposed across the world.
The *chītiáo* (kite) of Liángzhōu
makes bandits disappear;
the *chītiáo* flutters,
terrifying people to death."
The Emperor praised his loyalty
and advanced his title to Xīpíng Jùngōng (Duke of Xīpíng Commandery),
but he declined it.
On Línsōng Shān (Mount Línsōng) in Zhāngyè, there were characters
"Jīn Mǎ" (Golden Horse)
carved in the stone,
which were worn but still barely discernible,
while the character
"Zhāng"
was clear.
There was also an inscription that read:
"When the first reign begins in the world,
the West will be peaceful for ten thousand years."
In Gūzāng, there was also a black stone
with white dots forming the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
At that time, as the world was in chaos,
no envoys from other places could reach the capital.
Zhāng Guǐ, however, sent envoys to pay tribute,
without fail every year.
The imperial court praised him
and repeatedly sent imperial decrees to commend him.
Later, Zhāng Guǐ suffered from a stroke
and could not speak.
He had his son Zhāng Mào oversee provincial affairs.
Jiǔquán Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator of Jiǔquán) Zhāng Zhènqián intended to bring in Jiǎ Kān, the Governor of Qínzhōu, to replace Zhāng Guǐ.
He secretly sent an envoy to the capital
to request Shàngshū Shìláng (Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat) Cáo Qū to be appointed as Xīpíng Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator of Xīpíng),
planning to form a mutually supportive alliance.
Zhāng Guǐ's Biéjià (Vice Administrator) Qú Cháo, desiring to wield exclusive power and influence,
also sent an envoy to Cháng'ān
to inform Wáng Mó, Prince of Nányáng,
stating that Zhāng Guǐ was disabled by illness,
and requested Jiǎ Kān,
and Jiǎ Kān was about to accept it.
His elder brother, Ràng Kān, said to him:
"Zhāng, the Governor of Liángzhōu, is a distinguished figure of his time,
whose prestige is established in Xīzhōu.
What virtue do you possess to replace him!"
Jiǎ Kān then stopped.
Instead, Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Yuán Yú was appointed as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Liángzhōu).
Zhìzhōng (Chief Clerk) Yáng Dàn galloped to Cháng'ān,
cut off his ear and placed it on a tray,
to protest the false accusations against Zhāng Guǐ.
Wáng Mó then submitted a memorial to halt the appointment.
Zhāng Yuè of Jìnchāng,
a prominent clan in Liángzhōu,
believed that the prophecy "the Zhāng clan will dominate Liángzhōu"
applied to him due to his talent and strength.
He was transferred from Administrator of Lǒngxī to Inspector of Liángzhōu.
Yuè’s ambition was in Liángzhōu,
so he feigned illness and returned to Héxī,
secretly planning to replace Guǐ.
He then sent his elder brother Zhèn, along with Cáo Qū and Qū Pèi, to issue a proclamation to depose Guǐ,
and appointed Army Commandant Dù Dān to act as the Inspector of the province,
instructing Dān to memorialize for Yuè to be appointed Inspector.
Guǐ issued an order saying:
"I have been in this province for eight years,
but have been unable to pacify the region.
Furthermore, I have experienced military chaos in the central plains,
with Qín and Lǒng in turmoil.
Added to this, I have been seriously ill and bedridden,
and truly wish to withdraw and yield to the virtuous.
However, the burden of responsibility is heavy,
and I cannot simply leave.
I did not expect these people to suddenly stir up this rebellion;
this shows they do not understand my heart.
I view leaving this esteemed province as shedding a worn shoe!"
He intended to send the Chief Clerk, Wèi Máo, to present a memorial to the Emperor,
and quickly prepare his carriage
to return to Yíyáng to live out his old age.
The Chief Administrator, Wáng Róng, and Army Advisor, Mèng Chàng, tore up Zhèn's proclamation,
forced their way into Guǐ's chambers, and remonstrated, saying:
"The Jìn dynasty is in great peril,
and both men and gods are suffering.
It truly depends on your excellence to pacify the western regions.
Zhāng Zhèn and his brothers dare to unleash such malicious rebellion.
It is appropriate to declare their crimes and execute them,
and not allow them to achieve their ambition."
Guǐ remained silent.
Róng and others left and put the city on high alert.
The Administrator of Wǔwēi, Zhāng Tián, sent his son Tǎn to rush to the capital,
and memorialized, saying:
"Wèi Shàng pacified the borders but incurred blame,
and Chōngguó served with utmost loyalty but was censured.
These are both subjects of criticism by previous historians,
and clear lessons for today.
When Shùnyáng thought of Liú Táo,
a thousand people stood guard at the palace gate.
The Inspector's administration of our province
is like a loving mother to her infant,
and the people's love for your servant Guǐ
is like drought-stricken seedlings receiving rich rain.
We humbly hear that you are swayed by rumors
and that there will be a transfer of power.
The people are distressed,
as if they have lost their parents.
Now, barbarians are ravaging Xià;
it is not appropriate to disturb this region."
Soon after, Guǐ appointed his son Shí as Zhōng Dūhù (Central Commander),
and led troops to attack Zhèn.
He sent Zhèn's nephew, the Grand Steward's Chief Clerk Lìnghú Yà, to first reason with Zhèn, saying:
"Uncle, why do you not consider the safety and danger,
and clearly discern success from failure?
Your lord has established virtue in Xīhé,
and his troops are like clouds.
This is like a raging fire already burning;
waiting for the waters of the Jiāng and Hàn to extinguish it,
or being submerged in a great flood
and hoping for help from Yuè people –
how can it be sufficient?
Now, tens of thousands of troops are already approaching the border.
Now, the only way is to preserve your aged parents,
save your household,
and sincerely submit to the government.
You will surely be guaranteed complete safety and blessings."
Zhèn wept, saying:
"People have misled me!"
He then laid the blame on the Commandant of Merit Lǔ Lián and executed him,
then went to Shí to confess his crimes.
Guǐ marched south to attack Cáo Qū,
who fled.
When Zhāng Tǎn returned from the capital,
the Emperor issued a generous imperial edict to commend Guǐ,
and, following Máo's memorial,
ordered the execution of Cáo Qū.
Guǐ was greatly pleased
and pardoned all capital offenses and lesser crimes within the province.
He ordered Shí to lead Yǐn Yuán and Sòng Pèi with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Qū,
and separately dispatched Attendants Tián Jiǒng and Wáng Fēng with eight hundred cavalry to go southwest from Gūzāng to Shílǘ,
to occupy Chángníng.
Qū sent Qū Cháo to resist the battle at Huángbǎn.
Shí took a deceptive route out of Hàowěi
and fought at Pòqiāng.
Guǐ executed Qū and his Yámén officer Tián Xiāo.

He sent Secretary Zhāng Làng to deliver five thousand "righteous soldiers" and various tribute items such as outstanding scholars and filial children, memorials, and weapons from the commanderies and states to the capital.
He ordered officials to thoroughly investigate those who, since the establishment of the province, had been pure and virtuous,
or who had chosen reclusion and abandoned worldly glory;
those with great talent and profound learning,
who authored classics and histories;
those who sacrificed themselves for righteousness in times of danger,
giving their lives for their lord;
those who offered loyal remonstrance and suffered misfortune,
or who single-handedly handled diplomatic missions and resolved crises;
those with strategic wisdom and heroic courage,
who eliminated difficulties for their time;
those who flattered and misled their lord,
harming and entrapping loyal and virtuous individuals;
to fully report their situations.
Among the elders of the province, none failed to congratulate each other.
Guānglù Fù Zhī and Tàicháng Zhì Yú sent a letter to Guǐ,
informing him of the famine and scarcity in the capital.
Guǐ immediately sent Army Advisor Dù Xūn to present five hundred horses and thirty thousand bolts of silk.
The Emperor sent an envoy to promote him to General Who Guards the West, Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Lǒngyòu,

enfeoffed him as Marquis of Bàchéng, and further promoted him to General of Chariots and Cavalry, granted him the authority to establish his own staff, and accorded him the same ceremonial status as the Three Dukes.
Before the imperial mandate arrived,
Wáng Mí had already pressed on Luòyáng.
Guǐ dispatched generals Zhāng Fěi, Běigōng Chún, Guō Fū, and others to lead five thousand elite cavalry to guard the capital.
When the capital fell,
Fěi and the others were all lost to the rebels.
Those fleeing the chaos from the central plains arrived continuously, day and night.
Guǐ divided Wǔwēi to establish Wǔxīng Commandery to house them.
The Grand Steward's Chief Clerk Mǎ Fáng spoke to Guǐ, saying:
"The four seas are overturned,
and the Emperor has not yet returned.
Your Excellency, with the strength of the entire province, can advance directly to Píngyáng,
and you will surely sweep through thousands of li,
encountering campaigns but no battles.
I wonder why you hesitate to undertake this endeavor?"
Guǐ said:
"This is my intention."
He also heard that the King of Qín had entered the pass,
so he quickly sent a proclamation throughout Guānzhōng, saying:
"Our Lord has encountered danger,
and has been relocated to an unsuitable place.
The whole world is fragmented,
and all within the realm are disheartened.
The King of Qín is divinely endowed with sagely virtue,
and his martial prowess aligns with the times.
As the grandson of Shìzǔ,
the King is now the eldest.
All of us Jìn people,
those who live on this land,
divination has confirmed,
and both the living and the dead agree.
It is fitting to choose an auspicious day
to enthrone him as Emperor.
Now I dispatch Vanguard Commander Sòng Pèi with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry,
directly to Cháng'ān,
to protect the Emperor and repel threats.
Western Chief Commandant Shí's central army of thirty thousand,
and Wǔwēi Administrator Zhāng Tián's twenty thousand Hu cavalry,
will follow in succession,
gathering at Línjìn in the middle ten days of the eighth month."
Soon after, the King of Qín became the Crown Prince,
and sent an envoy to appoint Guǐ as Grand General of Cavalry, with ceremonial status equal to the Three Dukes.
Guǐ firmly declined.
Pínzhōu Inspector Péi Bāo and Eastern Qiāng Colonel Guàn Yǔ occupied strategic positions and blocked the envoy.
Guǐ ordered Sòng Pèi to attack them.
Xīpíng Prince Shú, along with Cáo Qū's remaining partisans Qū Rú and others, coerced the former Magistrate of Fúlù, Qū Kè, to be their leader,
seized Administrator Zhào Yí,
and responded to Péi Bāo in the east.
Shí turned his troops to attack them
and executed Rú and others.
Left Commander Yīn Yù fought Bāo in Xiázī,
severely defeating him.
Bāo fled to Sāngxiōng Wù.
That year,
Běigōng Chún surrendered to Liú Cōng.
The Crown Prince sent an envoy to reiterate the previous appointment,
but Guǐ firmly declined.
Left Sīmǎ Dòu Táo spoke to Guǐ, saying:
"Zhōu Dàn of Qūfù did not decline,
and Qí Wàng of Yíngqiū accepted the mandate,
thereby clarifying the national laws
and inspiring extraordinary achievements.
The world is in chaos,
and the imperial carriage has been moved.
Although our province is remote,
we have not forgotten to support and protect the court.
Therefore, the court wholeheartedly
repeatedly bestows gracious appointments.
It is appropriate to comply with the imperial decree
to satisfy the hearts of the people."
Guǐ did not comply.
Initially,
when Shí pacified Qū Rú,
he relocated over six hundred households of the main culprits.
Secretary Lìnghú Liú said:
"Removing evil people is
like a farmer removing weeds –
their roots must be completely eradicated
to prevent them from growing again.
Now, all should be relocated
to eliminate future troubles."
Shí did not accept this.
Qū Rú's partisans indeed rebelled,
and Shí advanced to pacify them.
Mào, whose courtesy name was Chéngxùn,
was tranquil and fond of learning,
not letting worldly gains or losses trouble his heart.
At the beginning of the Jiànxīng reign,
Sūn Bǎo, Prince of Nányáng, appointed him Assistant Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
He also recommended him for Gentleman of the Palace, and General of the Central Army,
but he declined all these positions.
In the second year,
he was summoned to be a Grandee Remonstrant,
but he firmly declined on account of his aged father.
Soon after, he was appointed General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Qínzhōu.
In the third year of Tàixīng,
after Shí was harmed,
the people of the province nominated Mào as Grand Commandant, Grand Minister of War, and Governor of Liángzhōu.
Mào did not accept,
but only received the title of Bearer of the Imperial Seal, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Liángzhōu.
He then executed Yán Shā and several hundred of his partisans,
and granted amnesty throughout his territory.
He again appointed his elder brother's son, Jùn, as General Who Guards the Army, Administrator of Wǔwēi, and Duke of Xīpíng.
After more than a year,
Mào constructed the Língjūn Platform,
which had a circumference of over eighty *du*,
and a base nine *rèn* high.
Yán Zēng, a man from Wǔlíng, knocked on the gate at night and shouted:
"Duke Wǔ sent me here to say: 'Why do you toil the people to build a platform?'"
Xīn Yán, the Magistrate of Gūzāng, considered Zēng to be a sorcerer and deluded,
and requested to have him killed.
Mào said:
"I truly am toiling the people.
Zēng spoke on behalf of the late lord's command,
how can that be sorcery!"
Mǎ Fáng, the Chief Clerk of the Ministry of the Privy Treasury, remonstrated, saying:
"Currently, the difficulties of the world have not yet been pacified.
We should only uphold simplicity and virtue,
and should not toil the people with ostentatious construction of platforms and pavilions.
Moreover, in recent years,
it has become increasingly clear that public affairs are more extravagant than in the past,
and every undertaking,
lightly deviates from proper standards,
which is truly not what the gentlemen and ladies expect from you, my lord."
Mào said:
"It is my fault,
it is my fault!"
He ordered the work to stop.
The next year,
Liú Yào sent his general Liú Xián to attack Hán Pú at Jìchéng,
and Hūyán Shí attacked Yīn Jiàn, the Protector of the Qiāng, at Sāngbì.
Zhái Kǎi and Shí Cóng, people from Líntáo, drove out their magistrates,
and offered their counties to Yào,
causing a great shock west of the Hé.
The Military Advisor Mǎ Jí urged Mào to personally lead a campaign,
but Fàn Yī, the Chief Clerk, angrily said:
"These men of a fallen state again wish to meddle and disturb important affairs!
Jí should be executed to pacify the people."
Jí said:
"Lord Fàn is a bookish pedant,
a mediocre talent for censuring and impeaching,
who does not consider the grand strategy of the state.
Moreover, the court has been troubled for many years.
Now that a great bandit has arrived on his own,
there is no need for distant armies.
The sentiments of those near and far
are truly tied to this province,
and by circumstances, we cannot but go out.
Moreover, we should establish a reputation for trustworthiness and courage,
to live up to the expectations of Qín and Lǒng."
Mào said:
"Mr. Mǎ's words are correct."
He then went out to station at Shítou.
Mào said to his Military Advisor Chén Zhēn:
"Liú Yào, with his reputation for victory, commands the elite of the Three Qíns.
He has been training his army for years,
and his soldiers are accustomed to battle.
If he were to swiftly conquer Nán'ān with elite cavalry,
sweep across beyond the Hé,
and then march straight here,
what plan should we adopt?"
Zhēn replied:
"Although Yào is relying on his might and his numerous forces,
his benevolence and virtue have not yet bound the people below.
Moreover, his territories east of the pass are divided,
his internal troubles are not yet removed,
and his elite soldiers are few,
mostly a motley collection of Dī and Qiāng people.
He will ultimately not be able to neglect the troubles east of the pass,
increase his garrisons on Lǒng,
and prolong the stalemate to contend with us.
If he does not retreat within twenty days,
Zhēn requests to lead a few thousand exhausted soldiers for your lordship to capture him."
Mào was greatly pleased,
and appointed Zhēn as Protector of the Pacified Barbarians,
leading one thousand eight hundred soldiers and cavalry to rescue Hán Pú.
Yào secretly intended to withdraw,
but publicly declared he would first take Lǒngxī,
then turn back to destroy Sāngbì.
Zhēn mustered Dī and Qiāng forces,
attacked Yào and put him to flight,
recovering Nán'ān.
Mào greatly praised him,
and appointed him General Who Crushes the Vanguard.
Not long after,
Mào again greatly fortified Gūzāng,
and repaired the Língjūn Platform.
Wú Shào, the Adjutant, remonstrated, saying:
"I humbly submit that repairing the city and building the platform
is a lesson from past events.
I believe that benevolence and virtue have not yet permeated among the close attendants;
even residing in a multistory building
would only arouse suspicion among those below,
merely demonstrating an uneasy state of mind and losing the fundamental trust of the soldiers and people.
It shows a sign of weakness,
and goes against the momentum of establishing dominance.
Distant regions and foreign territories will observe our anxiety,
and will certainly have designs to take advantage of us.
I have always wished for the cessation of labor and reduction of hardship,
to allow the people to rest.
Yet, to restart construction and mobilize the masses,
is this what the common people expect from an enlightened ruler?"
Mào said:
"My late elder brother suddenly lost his life to external forces.
Princes and dukes establish defenses,
and warriors strongly fortify;
these are also the ultimate warnings for clear-sighted people.
Moreover, would not loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen wish to fully demonstrate their integrity and righteousness to my late elder brother?
It was precisely because the crisis arose swiftly
that even with the bravery of Bēn and Yù,
there was nowhere to apply it.
Now that affairs are not yet settled,
we cannot be constrained by conventional wisdom,
and demand the principles of peace from people in an era of distress."
Shào had no reply.
Mào was naturally ambitious and resolute,
and capable of decisive actions in major affairs.
Jiǎ Mó, a prominent family head in Liángzhōu,
and his elder brother Shí's wife's brother,
wielded immense influence in the western region.
Earlier,
a rhyme went:
"Do not lay hands on your head,
or schemes for Liángzhōu."
Mào believed it,
lured and killed him,
whereupon the powerful families retreated,
and his authority extended throughout Liángzhōu.
At the beginning of Yǒngchāng,
Mào sent General Hán Pú to lead forces to capture the lands of Lǒngxī and Nán'ān,
and establish Qínzhōu there.
He died in the third year of Tàiníng,
and on his deathbed,
holding Jùn's hand, he wept and said:
"In the past, our ancestors were renowned for their filial piety and brotherly affection.
Since the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
they have generation after generation upheld loyalty and obedience.
Though now the Central Plains are in great chaos,
and the imperial carriage has been displaced,
you must carefully observe the principles of a subject,
and not fail or fall.
I encountered a turbulent era,
and inherited the remaining virtues of my ancestors.
I temporarily governed this province,
to preserve lives,
and wished, on the one hand, not to betray the Jìn dynasty,
and on the other hand, to protect the common people.
However, my official position was not by royal decree,
and my rank was by private consensus.
If it was merely to get things done,
how could I consider it an honor!
On the day I draw my last breath,
put a white headscarf into my coffin,
without court robes,
to show my resolve."
He was forty-eight years old.
He was in office for five years.
He was privately given the posthumous name Chéng.
Mào had no sons,
so Jùn succeeded him.
Jùn, whose courtesy name was Gōngtíng,
was remarkable and extraordinary in his youth.
In the fourth year of Jiànxīng,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bàchéng.
At the age of ten, he could compose literature,
outstanding and unrestrained,
but he was excessively dissolute and unrestrained,
often traveling secretly through the towns and villages at night,
and the state was influenced by him.
When he assumed control,
he was eighteen years old.
Earlier,
Emperor Mǐn had sent the Gentleman of the Yellow Gates, Shǐ Shú, to Gūzāng.
The Left Chief Clerk Fàn Yī, Right Chief Clerk Mǎ Mó, and others, prompted Shú
to appoint Jùn as Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Grand Commandant, Grand General, Governor of Liángzhōu, concurrently Protector of the Qiāng, and Duke of Xīpíng.
He granted amnesty throughout his territory,
established four commandants for the left, right, front, and rear,
and repaired the Southern Palace.
Liú Yào also sent someone to appoint Jùn as Governor of Liángzhōu and King of Liáng.
At that time, Xīn Yàn (辛晏) was holding up troops at Fúhǎn (枹罕).
Zhùn (駿) hosted a banquet for his officials in Xányù Táng (閑豫堂),
and ordered Dòu Táo (竇濤) and others to march against Xīn Yàn (辛晏).
Attendant Líu Qìng (劉慶) remonstrated, saying:
"A hegemon-king does not raise armies out of joy or anger,
nor does he seek victory through underhanded means.
He must have the right timing (heaven's will) and human affairs (people's support),
and only then does he act.
Xīn Yàn (辛晏) and his son are cruel, merciless, and mad.
Their downfall is to be expected.
Why then should we launch a major campaign in a year of famine,
attacking a city in severe cold?
In the past, King Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周) turned back his spears to await the fall of the Yīn (殷) dynasty.
Cáo Gōng (曹公) gave Yuán (袁) clan time to destroy themselves.
Why is Your Highness alone ashamed to turn back your troops?"
Zhùn (駿) accepted this advice.
He dispatched Cānjūn (參軍) Wáng Zhì (王騭) as an envoy to Líu Yào (劉曜).
Yào (曜) said to him:
"If your state truly wishes to follow in the footsteps of Dòu Róng (竇融),
and sincerely seeks harmony and good relations,
can you guarantee this?"
Zhì (騭) replied:
"I cannot."
Yào's (曜) Shìzhōng (侍中) Xú Mò (徐邈) said:
"You come to establish harmony,
yet you say you cannot.
Why is that?"
Zhì (騭) said:
"At the alliance of Guànzé (貫澤) under Qí Huán (齊桓),
his heart was filled with trepidation,
and the feudal lords came without being summoned.
At the assembly of Kuíqiū (葵丘),
he became arrogant and boastful,
and nine states rebelled.
If the transformation of Zhào (趙) state
could always be like it is today, then it would be fine.
But if governance and teachings decline,
you will not even be able to discern the changes in those nearby,
let alone our humble state!"
Yào (曜) looked to his attendants and said:
"This is a lofty scholar from Liángzhōu (涼州)!
The envoy was well-chosen!"
He treated him with courtesy and sent him back.
In the first year of Tàiníng (太寧) (323 CE),
Zhùn (駿) still used Jiànxīng (建興) twelfth year (324 CE).
Zhùn (駿) personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
Soon after, he received news of Emperor Yuán's (元帝) death.
Zhùn (駿) mourned greatly for three days.
Coincidentally, a yellow dragon appeared in the Jiāquán (嘉泉) spring at Xūcì (揟次).
Right Chángshǐ (長史) Fàn Yī (氾禕) said to Zhùn (駿):
"According to our records, the Jiànxīng (建興) era
was the reign title initiated by the Young Emperor.
The emperor met a tragic end,
so it is reasonable to change the era name.
The court is far away in Jiāngnán (江南),
and communications are cut off.
We should seize this opportunity of the dragon's appearance to change the era name,
to signify this auspicious omen."
Zhùn (駿) did not follow.
Originally,
when Zhùn (駿) ascended,
a folk song in Gūzāng (姑臧) went:
"A swan flies from the south, but sparrows are not alarmed.
Who says the lonely chick has grown tail feathers and wings?
Raising its six pinions high, a phoenix calls."
By this time, he had recovered the lands south of the Yellow River.
In the early Xiánhé (咸和) era (326 CE),

Zhùn (駿) dispatched Wǔwēi Tàishǒu (武威太守) Dòu Táo (竇濤), Jīnchéng Tàishǒu (金城太守) Zhāng Làng (張閬), Wǔxīng Tàishǒu (武興太守) Xīn Yán (辛巖), Yángliè Jiāngjūn (揚烈將軍) Sòng Jí (宋輯) and others to lead troops eastward to join Hán Pú (韓璞),
and attack the various commanderies of Qínzhōu (秦州).
Yào (曜) sent his general Líu Yìn (劉胤) to resist them,
who encamped at Díndào (狄道) city.
Hán Pú (韓璞) advanced and crossed Wògàn Lǐng (沃干嶺).
Xīn Yán (辛巖) said:
"We command tens of thousands of troops,
and rely on the fierce Di (氐) and Qiāng (羌).
We should fight quickly to annihilate them,
and not prolong this.
If prolonged, changes will arise."
Pú (璞) said:
"Since late summer,
Tài Bái (太白) (Venus) has offended the moon,
Chénxīng (辰星) (Mercury) has moved in retrograde,
and a white rainbow has pierced the sun.
These are all major omens of change.
We must not act rashly.
If we act rashly and fail,
the disaster will be even deeper.
I will wear them down over time.
Moreover, Yào (曜) and Shí Lè (石勒) are fighting each other,
so Yìn (胤) cannot stay here for long either."
After more than seventy days,
the army's provisions ran out.
Xīn Yán (辛巖) was sent to supervise the transport of supplies from Jīnchéng (金城).
When Yìn (胤) heard this,
he was greatly pleased,
and said to his officers and soldiers:
"Hán Pú's (韓璞) forces are ten times ours.
The Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) have all rebelled,
and are not working for them.
Our granaries are almost empty,
and we cannot hold out for long.
Now the enemy has divided their forces to transport provisions.
This can be called a gift from heaven to us.
If we defeat Xīn Yán (辛巖),
Pú (璞) and the others will collapse on their own.
They are numerous, we are few;
we must fight to the death.
If we do not achieve victory,
not a single horse will return.
Sharpen your spears and halberds,
and exhaust your wisdom and strength."
All were encouraged.
Thereupon, he led three thousand cavalry,
attacked Yán (巖) at Wògàn Lǐng (沃干嶺),
and defeated him.
Pú's (璞) army subsequently collapsed,
with over twenty thousand dead.
Pú (璞) bound himself with ropes and returned to confess his crime.
Zhùn (駿) said:
"It is my fault.
Why should the general be humiliated?"
He pardoned them all.
Yìn (胤) pursued the fleeing enemy, taking advantage of his victory.
He crossed the river,
attacked and captured Língjū (令居),
and occupied Zhènwǔ (振武).
Héxī (河西) was greatly shaken.
Zhùn (駿) dispatched Huángfǔ Gāi (皇甫該) to defend against him,
and granted a general amnesty throughout his territory.
Coincidentally, Líu Yào (劉曜) marched eastward to attack Shí Shēng (石生),
leaving Cháng'ān (長安) empty.
Zhùn (駿) held a grand military review and training exercise,
intending to attack Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) provinces.
Lǐcáo Lángzhōng (理曹郎中) Suǒ Xún (索詢) remonstrated, saying:
"Although Yào (曜) has gone on an eastern campaign,
Yìn (胤) still guards his base.
The terrain is treacherous and the road long;
it is very easy for the home defender.
If Yìn (胤) uses light cavalry and relies on the Di (氐) and Qiāng (羌) to resist us,
then his sudden attacks will be unpredictable.
If he stops his eastern consolidation and meets us in battle,
then our raiding will be endless.
In recent years, we have frequently campaigned,
and war horses are born in the countryside.
Externally, there is hunger and exhaustion,
and internally, resources are depleted.
How can this be called Your Highness cherishing your people?"
Zhùn (駿) said:
"I always worry that loyal words are not offered,
that people feign compliance but secretly oppose,
and that my governance and teachings are flawed, yet no one corrects me.
You have spoken frankly in your remonstrance.
This deeply fulfills my hopes."
He rewarded him with sheep and wine.
The various Xīyù (Western Regions) states offered sweat-blooded horses, fire-washing cloth, humped cattle, peacocks, giant elephants, and over two hundred other rare and precious items.
Lǐ Bó, the Grand Administrator of Xīyù, requested to attack the rebellious general Zhào Zhēn,
but was defeated by Zhēn.
Discussants held that Bó's strategizing had led to the defeat,
and requested his execution.
Jùn said:
"I have always felt that Emperor Shìzōng of Hàn killing Wáng Huī
was not as good as Duke Mù of Qín pardoning Mèng Míng."
In the end, he was sentenced to a lesser punishment than death,
and all hearts were pleased.
Jùn reviewed his troops in Xīnxiāng,
and hunted in Běiyě.
Subsequently, he attacked Kē-mòlǔ,
and defeated them.
He issued an order within his territory saying:
"In ancient times, Gǔn was executed and Yǔ arose;
Ruì was punished and Quē advanced.
This is how the Táng Emperor eradicated the great flood disaster,
and how the Jìn Marquis achieved the Five Hegemons.
If one commits a capital crime under the law,
their close relatives are not permitted to serve at court.
Now, all are permitted,
only they are not suitable to participate in the imperial guard."
Thereupon, punishments were light and the state was rich.
All the officials urged Jùn to claim the title of King of Liáng,
and concurrently serve as the Governor of Qín and Liáng provinces,
and establish dukes, ministers, and a hundred officials,
following the precedents of Wèi Wǔ and Jìn Wén.
Jùn said:
"This is not what a subject should say.
Whoever dares to say this
shall be unforgiven."
Nevertheless, within his territory, everyone called him king.
The officials again requested Jùn to establish a heir apparent,
but Jùn did not comply.
General of Firm Resolve Sòng Jí spoke to Jùn, saying:
"The rites emphasize the heir apparent
because of the importance of the ancestral temple.
King Chéng of Zhōu and Emperor Zhāo of Hàn were established while still in swaddling clothes,
truly because the succession of the state could not be left vacant,
and the Eastern Palace ought to be established early.
In the past, when King Wǔ first founded the state,
King Yuán was made the heir apparent.
At the beginning of Jiànxīng,
the former king was on the throne,
and Your Highness correctly established the succession.
How much more so now that the altars of soil and grain are flourishing,
Your Sacred Person stands firm,
and the great undertaking is prosperous,
yet the second in line is absent!
Your subject secretly believes that the state is in a precarious situation, like piled eggs,
but Your Highness considers it more secure than Mount Tài,
which is not what should be said."
Jùn accepted this,
and thereupon established his son Chónghuá as the heir apparent.
Earlier,
Jùn had dispatched Fù Yǐng to request passage through Shǔ
to send a memorial to the capital.
Lǐ Xióng did not permit it.
Jùn again dispatched Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Zhāng Chún to declare himself a vassal to Shǔ,
on the pretext of requesting passage.
Xióng was greatly pleased.
Xióng also held a grudge against the Southern Dī, Yáng Chū.
Chún then persuaded him, saying:
"The Southern Dī are outrageous,
repeatedly causing border troubles.
It is advisable to first attack Bǎiqǐng,
then pacify Shàngguī.
With these two states united in power,
sweeping across the Sānqín,
clearing Xǔ and Luò in the east,
and sweeping away the miasma from Yān and Zhào,
rescuing the imperial coffins of the two emperors from Píngyáng,
and returning the imperial chariot to Luòyì—
this would be the act of an heroic hegemon,
a chance in a thousand years.
My humble lord sent this humble subject to brave dangers and communicate sincerity,
traveling ten thousand Lǐ,
because Your Majesty's righteous fame has spread far and wide,
and you will surely pity my humble lord's ambition to assist the emperor.
The good of the world is one,
Your Majesty, please consider this."
Xióng was enraged,
but pretended to agree,
intending to ambush Chún at Dōngxiá.
A man from Shǔ, Qiáo Zàn, secretly informed Chún.
Chún then spoke to Xióng, saying:
"My humble lord sent this humble servant to travel through trackless lands, traverse the territories of a hundred barbarian tribes, and express his sincerity across ten thousand Lǐ,
precisely because Your Majesty's righteousness extends to diligent subjects,
and you are able to perfect the noble integrity of others.
If you wish to kill your subject,
you should do so openly in the city,
proclaiming it to all eyes,
saying that Liángzhōu, not forgetting old righteousness,
sent an envoy to Lángyá,
to express loyalty,
and requested passage through us.
The lord is wise and the minister is discerning,
so it was discovered and he was killed.
This would make your righteous fame spread far,
and the world would fear your might.
But to secretly kill him in the middle of the river,
where your powerful punishment is not evident,
how can this sufficiently proclaim your glorious achievements
and show them to the world!"
Xióng was greatly astonished and said:
"How could there be such a thing!
I shall send you back to Héyòu."
Xióng's Sīlì Xiàowèi Jǐng Qiān spoke to Xióng, saying:
"Zhāng Chún is a brave man,
you should keep and employ him."
Xióng said:
"How could a brave man be kept by others?
And you can observe him with your own intentions."
Qiān said to Chún:
"You are of large build,
and the heat is intense.
You may send your subordinate officials ahead
and wait a little until it gets cooler."
Chún said:
"My humble lord believes that the imperial chariot is disgraced,
the imperial coffins have not returned,
the shame of the world has not been avenged,
and the lives of the common people hang upside down.
Therefore, he sent Chún here
to express sincerity to the great state.
The matters discussed are important,
not something a subordinate official can convey.
If a subordinate official could handle them,
