then Chún would not have come in the first place.
Even if there were mountains of fire or seas of boiling water,
I would not refuse the difficulty.
How could I avoid the cold or heat!"
Xióng said:
"This man is extraordinary,
he cannot be employed."
He treated him with generous gifts and sent him away.
He said to Chún:
"Your esteemed lord's heroic fame covers the world,
his land is perilous and his army strong,
why does he not claim emperorship and enjoy his own region?"
Chún said:
"My humble lord believes that his ancestors and fathers have for generations passed on loyalty and goodness,
but he has not yet avenged the great shame of heaven and man,
nor relieved the inverted suffering of the common people.
From noon till evening, he forgets to eat;
he rests on his weapon awaiting dawn.
Because Lángyá is restoring the dynasty in Jiāngdōng,
he supports him from ten thousand Lǐ away,
intending to achieve the deeds of Huán and Wén.
Why speak of enjoying oneself!"
Xióng showed a look of shame,
and said:
"My ancestors and fathers were also subjects of Jìn.
In the past, they came with the six commanderies to seek refuge in this capital,
and were chosen by their allies,
thus arriving at today.
If Lángyá can indeed restore the great Jìn in Zhōngzhōu,
I too shall lead my troops to assist him."
Chún returned to Lónghè,
recruited soldiers, and sent memorials,
which later all reached the capital.
The imperial court praised him.
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) desired to enforce strict laws and harsh regulations,
and everyone agreed that it was appropriate.
Staff officer Huáng Bīn (黃斌) stepped forward and said:
"Your servant does not see the merit in it."
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) asked him why.
Huáng Bīn (黃斌) replied:
"Laws and regulations are for managing the state,
solidifying customs and unifying things.
Once established, they must be enforced,
without variations or exceptions.
If those in high positions violate the law,
then the law will not be effective."
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) pushed aside his desk and changed his expression, saying:
"Indeed, laws are only effective when applied to superiors,
and regulations know no high or low.
Moreover, were it not for you, Master Huáng (黃君),
I would not have heard of my faults.
Master Huáng (黃君) can be called supremely loyal."
He immediately promoted him at the gathering to Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) possessed stratagems,
and thereupon he refined his conduct and reformed his principles,
diligently attending to all government affairs,
overseeing both civil and military officials.
All were able to serve their purpose,
and he was praised far and wide,
earning the title "Lord of Accumulated Worthies" (Jīxián Jūn, 積賢君).
Since Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) established himself in Liángzhōu (涼州),
coinciding with the chaos under Heaven,
there were campaigns and expeditions everywhere,
and the army had no peaceful year.
By Zhāng Jùn's (張駿) time,
the territory gradually became peaceful.
He also sent his general Yáng Xuān (楊宣) to lead troops across the Liúshā (流沙) desert,
to attack Qiūcí (龜茲) and Shànshàn (鄯善).
Thereupon, the Western Regions all submitted.
Yuán Mèng (元孟), the King of Shànshàn (鄯善), offered his daughter,
who was called "Beauty,"
and he built the Bīnxia Guān (賓遐觀) to house her.
The kings of Yānqí Qiánbù (焉耆前部) and Yútián (于窴) both sent envoys to present local products.
A jade seal was found in the river,
its inscription read:
"Command the myriad states,
establish the boundless."
At that time, Zhāng Jùn (張駿) fully possessed the lands of Lǒngxī (隴西),
and his soldiers and horses were strong and prosperous.
Although he nominally submitted to the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
he did not implement the calendar and decrees of the "Middle Restoration" (Zhōngxīng, 中興).
He performed the dance of six ranks (liùyì, 六佾),
and displayed leopard-tail banners (bàowěi, 豹尾).
The officials and government offices he established were modeled after those of a king,
but with slightly different names.
He also divided the three commanderies in the western part of the province to establish Shāzhōu (沙州),
and the six commanderies in the eastern part to establish Hézhōu (河州).
All the officials in these two administrations referred to themselves as his subjects.
He also built a city south of Gūzāng (姑臧) city,
and erected the Qiānguāng Diàn (謙光殿),
painted with five colors,
adorned with gold and jade,
exhausting all precious and ingenious craftsmanship.
On each of the four sides of the main hall, a subsidiary hall was built:
the eastern one was called Yíyáng Qīngdiàn (宜陽青殿),
and he resided there during the three months of spring;
his robes, attire, and artifacts all corresponded to the color of that direction.
The southern one was called Zhūyáng Chìdiàn (朱陽赤殿),
and he resided there during the three months of summer.
The western one was called Zhèngxíng Báidiàn (政刑白殿),
and he resided there during the three months of autumn.
The northern one was called Xuánwǔ Hēidiàn (玄武黑殿),
and he resided there during the three months of winter.
Beside them were the bureaus and offices for imperial guards and palace staff,
all matching the respective directional colors.
In his later years,
he resided wherever he pleased,
no longer following the seasonal residences.
At the beginning of the Xiánhé (咸和) era,
fearing being pressed by Liú Yào (劉曜),
he sent generals Sòng Jí (宋輯) and Wèi Zuǎn (魏纂) with troops to move over two thousand families of Nán'ān (南安) people from Lǒngxī (隴西) to Gūzāng (姑臧).
He also sent an envoy to Lǐ Xióng (李雄)
to cultivate good neighborly relations.
When Liú Yào (劉曜) attacked Páohǎn (枹罕),
Commandant Sīn Yàn (辛晏) urgently reported,
and Zhāng Jùn (張駿) sent Hán Pú (韓璞) and Sīn Yán (辛巖) to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack him.
They fought at Líntáo (臨洮),
and were greatly defeated by Liú Yào's (劉曜) army.
Hán Pú (韓璞) and the others retreated,
pursued as far as Língjū (令居),
and Zhāng Jùn (張駿) consequently lost the land south of the Yellow River.
Originally,
the Supervisor of the Army for Wùjǐ (Wùjǐ Xiàowèi, 戊己校尉), Zhào Zhēn (趙貞), did not attach himself to Zhāng Jùn (張駿).
By this time,
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) attacked and captured him,
establishing Gāochāng (高昌) Commandery in his territory.
When Shí Lè (石勒) killed Liú Yào (劉曜),
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) took advantage of the chaos in Cháng'ān (長安),
and re-occupied the land south of the Yellow River,
extending to Dí Dào (狄道).
He established five garrison commanderies (túnhùjūn, 屯護軍) at Wǔwèi (武衞),
Shímén (石門), Hòuhé (候和), Qiāngchuān (漒川), and Gānsōng (甘松),
and divided the border with Shí Lè (石勒).
Shí Lè (石勒) sent an envoy to confer official titles and ranks upon Zhāng Jùn (張駿),
but Zhāng Jùn (張駿) refused them,
detaining Shí Lè's (石勒) envoy.
Later, fearing Shí Lè's (石勒) strength,
he sent an envoy to acknowledge himself as Shí Lè's (石勒) subject,
and also presented local products,
sending Shí Lè's (石勒) envoy back.
There was once a great famine in Zhāng Jùn's (張駿) territory,
and grain prices soared.
The market chief Tán Xiáng (譚詳) requested to release grain from the granaries to the common people,
and to collect three times the amount at the autumn harvest.
Assistant Yīn Jù (陰據) remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Xīmén Bào (西門豹) governed Yè (鄴),
and stored up provisions for the people.
Xiè Biǎn (解扁) governed the city of Dōngfēng (東封),
and calculated to collect three times the amount.
Lord Wén (Wénhóu, 文侯) considered Xīmén Bào (西門豹) guilty yet deserving of reward,
and Xiè Biǎn (解扁) meritorious yet deserving of punishment.
Now Tán Xiáng (譚詳) wishes to take advantage of people's hunger
to demand three times the amount,
which is like reversing a fur coat and damaging the hide,
an insufficient analogy."
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) adopted his advice.
Previously,
during the Jiànxīng (建興) era,
Gěng Fǎng (耿訪), a clerk from Dūnhuáng (敦煌), arrived in Cháng'ān (長安).
He then encountered bandits,
and could not return.
He fled to Hànzhōng (漢中),
and then crossed the Yangtze River eastward.
In the second year of Tàixīng (太興, 319 CE), he reached the capital,
repeatedly submitting memorials,
stating that his home province was unaware of the "Middle Restoration,"
and that an ambassador should be sent,
offering himself as a guide.
At that time, there were continuous internal troubles,
and permission was given but not acted upon.
By this time,
Gěng Fǎng (耿訪) was finally appointed Chief Scrutinizer of Official Documents (Zhìshū Yùshǐ, 治書御史),
and Zhāng Jùn (張駿) was appointed General Who Guards the West (Zhèn Xī Dàjiāngjūn, 鎮西大將軍).
His titles of Commandant (Xiàowèi, 校尉), Inspector (Cìshǐ, 刺史), and Duke (Gōng, 公) remained as before.
Twelve people from the western regions, including Jiǎ Líng (賈陵) from Lǒngxī (隴西), were assigned to him.
Gěng Fǎng (耿訪) stayed in Liángzhōu (梁州) for seven years,
and was recalled because the post roads were impassable.
Gěng Fǎng (耿訪) entrusted the imperial edict to Jiǎ Líng (賈陵),
who pretended to be a merchant.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān (長'ān),
he dared not proceed,
and only reached Liángzhōu (涼州) in the eighth year of Xiánhé (咸和, 333 CE).
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) received the edict,
and sent his部曲督 (Bùqǔ Dū, 部曲督) Wáng Fēng (王豐) and others to report his gratitude,
and also sent Jiǎ Líng (賈陵) back.
He submitted a memorial declaring himself a subject,
but did not adopt the "Middle Restoration" calendar,
still using "Jiànxīng (建興) twenty-first year."
In the ninth year,
Gěng Fǎng (耿訪) was again sent with Wáng Fēng (王豐) and others, carrying an official seal and tablet, to present Zhāng Jùn (張駿) with the title of Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn, 大將軍).
From then on, missions were sent every year without interruption.
Later, Zhāng Jùn (張駿) sent staff officer Qū Hù (麴護) to submit a memorial which said:
"East and west are separated and blocked,
having passed many years.
We have long acknowledged your sagely virtue,
and our hearts are tied to the imperial court.
However, Jiāng (江) and Wú (吳) are isolated and distant,
so your influence cannot reach us.
Although we exert ourselves to repair the roads,
our allies are not spared.
On the day we received the edict,
sorrow and joy were intertwined.
Your heavenly grace broadly covers us,
bestowing glorious honors.
You appointed your servant as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn, 大將軍) and Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Shǎnxī (陝西), Yōng (雍),
Qín (秦), and Liángzhōu (涼州).
This immense favor shines brightly,
and all within ten thousand li embrace and support it.
The auspicious decree has manifestly arrived,
filling us with gratitude and anxiety.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty is naturally gifted and brilliant,
establishing the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Encountering a time when the family fortunes were not prosperous,
you were forced to migrate to Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚).
The ancestral temples suffer the sorrow of 'millet growing in the fields' (shǔlí, 黍離),
and the imperial tombs suffer the pain of ruin
and abandonment.
All under Heaven sigh,
and all sentient beings grieve.
Your servant is solely charged with governing one region,
holding the authority of the axe.
This distant region is remote and humble,
its power limited to Qín (秦) and Lǒng (隴).
Since Lè (勒) and Xióng (雄) are
dead,
people desire to return to righteousness.
It is said that the reigns of Jì Lóng (季龍) and Lǐ Qī (李期) did not last even a full morning,
yet they both usurped and succeeded in their wicked ways,
like glaring owls for years.
The east and west are vast and distant,
and support
not connected,
then it would cause Táo Chóng to beat his wings,
and the four barbarians to clamor.
Those who inclined towards righteousness would turn to betray and rebel.
Lead knives would harbor the ambition of Gān Jiàng swords,
and fireflies would hope for the
light of the sun and moon.
This is why Your Servant's previous memorial was so earnest,
wishing for a concerted effort to chastise them at that time.
Yet Your Majesty idles by the Jiāngbiǎo,
watching the disaster and ruin,
cherishing present comfort,
and neglecting the enterprises of the Four Ancestors
Issuing urgent proclamations
is merely setting up empty words.
This is why Your Servant sighs at night in the wilderness
and suffers heartache on the long journey.
Moreover, the common people have been separated from their lord,
gradually over the ages.
The old have perished,
and the young are ignorant.
The loyal and good suffer the punishment of being hung,
while the numerous villains greedily seize rampant profits.
Those who cherish their lord and yearn for the past
see days and months flow by.
Though
there are occasionally righteous gentlemen,
they fear being coerced by their superiors,
and sigh in their humble dwellings.
Your Servant heard that Shào Kāng's restoration
originated from a single army,
and Guāng Wǔ succeeded the Hàn,
with fewer than a hundred men.
They offered sacrifices to Xià and matched Heaven,
not losing their old possessions.
How much more so with the brave
and fierce troops of Jīng and Yáng,
and Your Servant's provincial cavalry,
to devour the remaining Jié
within our grasp!
May Your Majesty widely spread Your Servant's considerations,
and always remember the achievements of the ancestors.
Order Sīkōng Jiàn and Zhēngxī Liàng
to set sail on the Jiāng and Miǎn,
so that they arrive simultaneously.
After this, Jùn's envoys were often captured by Shí Jìlóng
and failed to reach their destination.
Later, Jùn again sent Hùqiāng Cānjūn Chén Yù, Cóngshì Xú Xiāo, Huá Yù, and others to the capital.
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Liàng memorialized, saying that Chén Yù and others ventured afar at great risk,
and ought to be appointed to office.
An imperial edict appointed Yù as Xīpíng Prime Minister,
and Xiāo and others as county magistrates.
In the first year of Yǒnghé,
his heir apparent Zhònghuá was made Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiǔquán Tàishǒu Mǎ Jí memorialized, saying:
"The southern mountains of Jiǔquán
are the very body of Kūnlún.
When King Mù of Zhōu saw the Queen Mother of the West,
he was so delighted that he forgot to return—
this refers to this mountain.
This mountain has stone chambers and jade halls,
adorned with pearls and gems,
shining like a divine palace.
It is fitting to establish a temple to the Queen Mother of the West,
to aid the court with boundless blessings."
Jùn agreed.
Jùn died in office after twenty-two years,
at the age of forty.
Privately, he was posthumously honored as Wén Gōng,
and Emperor Mù later posthumously honored him as Zhōngchéng Gōng.
Zhònghuá, courtesy name Tàilín,
was Jùn's second son.
He was lenient, gentle, and highly esteemed,
resolute and spoke little.
When his father died,
he was sixteen years old.
In the second year of Yǒnghé, he proclaimed himself Chíjé, Dàdūdū, Tàiwèi, Hùqiāng Xiàowèi, Liángzhōu Mù, Xīpíng Gōng, and acting King of Liáng,
and granted amnesty within his territory.
He honored his mother, Lady Yán, as Tàiwáng Tàihòu,
residing in Yǒngxùn Gōng;
and his birth mother, Lady Mǎ, as Wáng Tàihòu,
residing in Yǒngshòu Gōng.
He lightened taxes and levies,
abolished customs duties,
and reduced imperial gardens
to relieve the poor.
He sent an envoy to deliver a memorial to Shí Jìlóng.
Jìlóng sent Wáng Zhuó, Má Qiū, Sūn Fúdū, and others to invade and raid ceaselessly.
Jīnchéng Tàishǒu Zhāng Chōng surrendered to Qiū.
Thereupon, Liángzhōu was shaken.
Zhònghuá swept his territory clean
and ordered his Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Péi Yù to resist them.
He fortified at Guǎngwǔ,
intending to exhaust them through prolonged resistance.
Mùfǔ Xiàng Sīmǎ Zhāng Dān addressed Zhònghuá, saying:
"Your Servant hears that a state is strong through its army,
and led by its generals.
The chief general
is the pivot of survival or destruction,
and on whom fortune or misfortune depend.
Thus, when Yān employed Yuè Yì,
they conquered all of Qí;
but when they employed Qí Jié,
they lost seventy cities.
Therefore, ancient enlightened rulers never failed to be cautious with their generals and ministers.
What is currently needed
lies in the military commanders.
However, those who deliberate often recommend seasoned veterans as generals,
who may not necessarily be exquisitely talented.
Moreover, Hán Xìn's rise
was not due to old fame;
Ráng Jū's trustworthiness
was not due to being an old general;
Lǚ Méng's advancement
was not due to old merits;
Wèi Yán's appointment
was not due to old virtue.
Indeed, when an enlightened king makes appointments,
he does not appoint ordinary people;
anyone who possesses the talent
is entrusted with important affairs.
Now the strong enemy is at our borders,
but the generals do not advance.
The people's hearts are agitated,
and the crisis draws near.
Zhǔbù Xiè Ài
possesses both literary and martial talents,
and is insightful in military strategy.
If he were granted the axe and banner [symbols of military authority],
and entrusted with exclusive command,
he would surely be able to repel aggression,
and annihilate the brutal forces."
Zhònghuá summoned Ài
and asked him about the strategy for suppressing the bandits.
Ài said:
"Gěng Yǎn in the past did not wish to leave enemies for his lord and father,
and Huáng Quán wished to face the enemy with ten thousand men.
I beg you to lend me seven thousand troops
to devour Wáng Zhuó, Má Qiū, and others for Your Highness."
Zhònghuá was greatly pleased,
and appointed Ài as Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn,
assigning him five thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Qiū.
He led his army out to Zhènwǔ.
At night, two owls hooted within the central tent.
Ài said:
"Owl (xiāo)
is similar to 'invite' (yāo),
and in liùbó, one who gets an owl wins.
Now owls hooting in the central tent
is a sign of victory over the enemy."
Thereupon, they advanced to battle,
greatly defeated them,
and decapitated five thousand heads.
Zhònghuá enfeoffed Ài as Fúlù Bó
and treated him well.
However, his favored courtiers, envious of his ability,
collectively slandered him,
so he was sent out as Jiǔquán Tàishǒu.
Jìlóng again ordered Má Qiū to advance and capture Dàxià.
Dàxià Hùjūn Liáng Shì seized Tàishǒu Sòng Yàn
and surrendered the city to Qiū.
Qiū sent Yàn with a letter to entice Wǎnshù Dūwèi Sòng Jǔ.
Sòng Jǔ said to Qiū:
"When one leaves one's father to serve a lord,
one should establish merit and righteousness;
if merit and righteousness cannot be established,
one should uphold one's integrity.
Jǔ will never betray his lord and steal a life in this world."
Thereupon, he first killed his wife and children,
then slit his own throat and died.
In this month,
the relevant authorities deliberated on sending Sī Bīng Zhào Cháng to welcome autumn in the western suburbs.
Xiè Aǐ argued that according to the principles of the *Chūnqiū*,
when the state has a major mourning,
the ritual of hunting should be suspended,
and it should wait until the following year.
Biéjià Cóngshì Suǒ Xiá debated, saying:
"According to the *Lǐ*,
when the Son of Heaven dies,
or a feudal lord dies,
and the body has not yet been interred,
the five sacrifices are not performed;
but once interred, they are performed.
In the third year of Duke Xuān of Lǔ,
when the Son of Heaven died,
the suburban sacrifice was not abolished.
Now, His Majesty has inherited the great throne,
and all affairs are renewed;
it is appropriate to align the 'seven regulators' using the *xuánjī* and *yùhéng*.
The beginning of autumn,
when all things are about to mature,
is the beginning of the 'killing energy'.
Regarding the affairs of the king,
wielding banners to swear in the multitude,
and consecrating drums to sacrifice to the gods,
these are for punishing rebels and eliminating oppressors,
achieving success and accomplishing tasks,
pacifying the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
and bringing prosperity to all under heaven.
They cannot be abolished."
Zhòng Huá followed his advice.
Soon after, Má Qiū advanced to attack Fúhǎn.
At that time, Jìnyáng Tàishǒu Láng Tǎn thought the city was too large and difficult to defend,
and suggested abandoning the outer city.
Wǔchéng Tàishǒu Zhāng Quān said:
"Abandoning the outer city would mean losing the great cause,
and should not be done to disturb the hearts of the people."
Níngróng Xiàowèi Zhāng Qú followed his advice
and firmly defended the great city.
Má Qiū led a force of eighty thousand,
surrounding and digging multiple trenches,
using cloud ladders and hail carts,
and digging a hundred tunnels,
all leading into the city.
The city responded in kind,
killing and wounding tens of thousands of Má Qiū's troops.
Jì Lóng again sent his generals Liú Hún and others to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join them.
Láng Tǎn resented that his advice was not followed,
and instructed the soldier Lǐ Jiā to secretly communicate with Má Qiū,
leading over a thousand bandits onto the city's northwest corner.
Zhāng Qú sent Sòng Xiū, Zhāng Hóng, Xīn Yì, and Guō Pǔ to resist them.
They engaged in close combat,
beheading over two hundred men,
and the bandits retreated.
Zhāng Qú executed Lǐ Jiā and displayed his body,
and burned the siege equipment.
Má Qiū retreated to secure Dàxià,
and said to his generals:
"I have campaigned in the region of the five capitals,
capturing cities and territories,
and never failed.
When I ascended Qínlǒng,
I thought it would be a campaign without a battle.
How could I have known that when I attacked Chóuchí to the south,
my army would be defeated and generals killed;
when building the city of Chángzuì,
not a single horse returned;
and when attacking this city,
my soldiers were wounded and morale crushed?
This must be heaven's aid,
not human effort."
Jì Lóng heard this and sighed:
"I pacified the nine provinces with a single division,
but now, with the strength of the nine provinces, I am bogged down at Fúhǎn.
It is truly as they say: 'they have men there,
and cannot be schemed against yet.'"
Zhòng Huá appointed Xiè Aǐ as Shǐ Chíjié, Jūnshī Jiāngjūn,
and ordered him to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry
to advance to the Lín Hé.
Má Qiū resisted him with thirty thousand troops.
Xiè Aǐ rode in a small carriage,
wearing a white cap,
beating drums as he advanced.
Má Qiū looked on and angrily said:
"Xiè Aǐ is a young scholar,
dressed like this,
he despises me!"
He ordered three thousand of his Hēiguǐ Lóngxiáng troops to charge and attack.
Xiè Aǐ's left and right flanks were in great disorder.
The Left Battle Commander Lǐ Wěi advised Xiè Aǐ to mount a horse,
but Xiè Aǐ refused,
instead dismounting and sitting on a folding stool,
directing and deploying his forces.
The bandits thought hidden troops were being unleashed,
and were afraid to advance.
Zhāng Mào came from the left, following the river south, and cut off their rear,
whereupon Má Qiū's army retreated.
Xiè Aǐ seized the advantage and fiercely pursued,
then utterly defeated them,
beheading Má Qiū's generals Dù Xūn and Jí Yú,
capturing and beheading thirteen thousand ranks,
and Má Qiū fled alone on horseback to Dàxià.
Zhòng Huá, in assessing their merits,
appointed Xiè Aǐ as Tàifǔ Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
and advanced his enfeoffment to Fúlù Xiàn Bó,
[一０]with five thousand households as his stipend,
and eight thousand bolts of silk.
Má Qiū again occupied Fúhǎn,
with a force of one hundred and twenty thousand,
and advanced to屯Hénèi.
He sent Wáng Zhuó to raid Jìnxīng and Guǎngwǔ,
crossing the Hóngchí Lǐng,
reaching Qǔliǔ.
Gūzāng was greatly shaken.
Zhòng Huá deliberated on personally going out to resist him,
but Xiè Aǐ earnestly advised against it, considering it inappropriate.
Biéjià Cóngshì Suǒ Xiá stepped forward and said:
"The bandit forces are very strong,
and are gradually approaching the capital region.
The ruler
is the bulwark of the state;
he should not personally move.
The Zuǒ Chángshǐ Xiè Aǐ
possesses both civil and military talents,
and is the state's Fāng Shào;
he should be entrusted with the responsibility of leadership.
Your Highness should remain in the center as a bulwark,
and bestow upon him strategy and tactics;
then these minor bandits will be insufficient to pacify."
Zhòng Huá accepted his advice,
and thereupon appointed Xiè Aǐ as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì, Xíng Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and Suǒ Xiá as Jūnzhèng Jiāngjūn,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to resist him.
Xiè Aǐ set up the *yáqí* (commander's banner)
and swore in his officers and men.
A northwest wind blew, causing the banners to point southeast.
Suǒ Xiá said:
"The wind is a command.
Now it can make the banners point in that direction;
this is heaven's support,
and we are sure to defeat them."
The army arrived at Shénniǎo.
Wáng Zhuó fought with the vanguard
and was defeated,
fleeing back to Hénán.
They returned to attack the rebellious tribes of Sīgǔzhēn, over ten thousand households.
They defeated them,
beheading over a thousand,
capturing two thousand eight hundred,
and seizing over one hundred thousand cattle and sheep.
Zhòng Huá, considering himself to have repeatedly defeated strong enemies,
became somewhat negligent in governance
and rarely received guests.
Sī Zhí Suǒ Xiá advised, saying:
"Your Highness inherited the foundation of four sages,
is in a time of peace and prosperity,
and bears the present responsibility,
worrying about the suffering of all within the four seas.
You should personally attend to all affairs,
openly welcome heroic and talented individuals,
and diligently strive day and night
in various governmental matters.
Recently, there has been clamor both inside and outside the court,
all saying that those who abandon the bandits and surrender should be immediately pacified,
yet days pass without them being received.
State elders and court worthies
should be received with humility and openness,
and consulted on governmental affairs,
but for many weeks and months,
you have not paid attention to receiving them.
Memorials submitted to the interior
remain unexamined for months,
neglecting current duties
and focusing attention on chess and board games,
indulging in the entertainment of petty attendants,
without considering the grand strategies of generals and ministers.
This has led to trusted ministers not speaking,
and court officials keeping silent.
This humble minister is therefore agitated to the point of forgetting sleep and food.
Now, the royal house is like a burning fire,
and the people are in dire straits;
this is precisely the day for Your Highness to endure hardships and steel your resolve.
I deeply wish for you to devote your heart to court affairs,
welcome honest advice,
thoroughly practice the five virtues,
to achieve the six virtues,
abandon those close attendants,
silence external voices,
reform governance, and attend court,
so that those below may observe and be transformed."
Zhòng Huá read it with great pleasure,
and replied with a gracious text of thanks,
but did not change his ways.
In the tenth year of Yǒnghé [350 CE],
Zhāng Zuò adopted the counsel of Wèi Jī, Zhào Cháng, and others,
and presumptuously assumed the imperial throne.
He established ancestral temples,
performed the Bāyì dance,
appointed all government officials,
and issued an edict which stated:
"In ancient times, when the Golden Virtue lost its mandate,
the Róng and Dí tribes plunged Huáxià into chaos.
The Hú, Jié, Dī, and Qiāng all harbored intentions of seizing the imperial seal.
Our Duke Wǔ, with divine martial prowess, quelled the disturbances,
brought peace to Xīxià,
and diligently offered tribute and served the emperor,
without interruption for months.
Our four ancestors continued this legacy,
their loyalty becoming ever more evident.
That we received the abdication from Jìn is
known to all under Heaven;
we have been humble, modest, and yielding
for forty years now.
Currently, the Central Plains are in chaos,
and both Chinese and barbarians are without a ruler.
All the nobles unanimously believe that the hopes of Jiǔzhōu have no one to rely on,
and the deities of Heaven and Earth, and the mountains and rivers, have no one to whom they are connected.
They have compelled this solitary one to assume the great unified rule
to unite the hearts of the Four Seas.
Unable to decline,
I reluctantly accede to the collective will.
After sweeping away the filth from the two capitals,
and clearing out Zhōu and Wèi,
then I shall welcome the emperor back to the old capital,
and apologize at the Heavenly Gate.
I wish to join the myriad common people in this new beginning."
He changed the 42nd year of Jiànxīng to the 1st year of Hépíng.
He pardoned those deserving of death,
bestowed silk upon the widowed and solitary,
and promoted all civil and military officials by one rank.
He posthumously honored his great-grandfather, Zhāng Guǐ, as King Wǔ (武王);
his grandfather, Zhāng Shí, as King Zhāo (昭王);
his paternal granduncle, Zhāng Máo, as King Chéng (成王);
his father, Zhāng Jùn, as King Wén (文王);
and his younger brother, Zhāng Chónghuá, as King Míng (明王).
He established his wife, Lady Xīn, as Empress;
his younger brother, Zhāng Tiānxī, as King Chángníng (長寧王);
his son, Zhāng Tàihé, as Crown Prince;
Zhāng Tíngjiān as King Jiànkāng (建康王);
and Yàolíng's younger brother, Zhāng Xuánjìng, as Marquis Wǔ of Liáng (涼武侯).
That night,
there was a light in the sky like a carriage canopy,
and a sound like thunder,
shaking the city and its environs.
The next day,
a great wind uprooted trees.
Disasters and anomalies appeared frequently,
but Zuò's cruelty and tyranny only grew worse.
His Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, Mǎ Jí, was dismissed from office for his urgent remonstrance.
The Lángzhōng, Dīng Qí, also remonstrated, saying:
"Your late father consistently upheld loyalty and integrity,
tracing his distant lineage to Wúhuì.
He maintained his prosperity with modesty and humility
for over fifty years.

The reason the common people eagerly looked westward, the reason the Four Seas focused their attention on Dàliáng, the reason Heaven bestowed its aid, and the reason officials and commoners sacrificed their lives,
was precisely because your late father's virtue surpassed that of Péng and Kūn,
and his loyalty exceeded that of the Duke of Xī.
He communicated devoutly for ten thousand *lǐ*,
and his integrity was unwavering.
He was able to resist a devastating barbarian horde with the forces of a single province;
campaigns were launched year after year,
yet no one complained of fatigue.
Although Your Majesty, with your great sagely and heroic demeanor, has inherited the grand legacy,
your achievements and virtue have not yet surpassed those of your late father.
Yet you are undertaking a revolution,
which your servant secretly believes is not advisable.
The reason both Chinese and barbarians pledged allegiance to Dàliáng, and the reason righteous armies responded from a thousand *lǐ* away,
was because Your Majesty belonged to the original dynasty.
Now that you have exalted yourself,
people will compete for higher positions.
How can a corner of the land withstand the armies of the Central Plains!
If the city walls are high, conflicts arise; if one rides on a carriage but carries a load, bandits will come.
Your Majesty, please consider this."
Zuò was greatly enraged
and had him executed at the palace gate.
He dispatched his general Hé Hào to lead troops to attack the Líqián Róng in Nánshān,
but they were utterly defeated and returned.
When Grand Marshal Huán Wēn entered the pass,
Wáng Zhuó, who was then garrisoned in Lǒngxī,
urgently sent an envoy to Zuò,
stating that Wēn was skilled in military strategy,
and his power was unfathomable.
Zuò, already fearful,
also worried that Zhuó would betray him.
He immediately recalled Mǎ Jí to his post and consulted with him.
He secretly sent trusted men to assassinate Zhuó,
but the plot was discovered
and failed.
Zuò grew even more fearful,
gathered a large army,
and openly declared an eastern expedition,
but in reality intended to seek refuge in Dūnhuáng to the west.
It happened that Wēn returned, and so he stopped.
He then sent his General of Pacifying the East and Governor of Qín Province, Niú Bà, and the Commander of Military Affairs, Zhāng Fāng, to lead three thousand men to attack Zhuó,
and they defeated him.
Zhuó fled to Fú Jiàn.
In Zuò's state, frost fell in the fifth month,
killing crops and fruits.
Zuò's kinsman, Zhāng Guàn, was then garrisoned in Páohǎn.
Zuò resented his strength,
and sent his generals Yì Chuǎi and Zhāng Líng to lead thirteen thousand infantry and cavalry to attack him.
At that time, Wáng Luán, a man from Zhāngyè, was somewhat skilled in divination,
and told Zuò:
"The army will depart and not return;
the state of Liáng will face misfortune."
Zuò was greatly enraged,
and considering Luán's words to be ominous talk disheartening the troops,
he executed him publicly.
Only then did the three armies depart.
As Luán faced execution, he said:
"Within twenty days of my death,
the army will surely be defeated."
At this time, a spirit descended upon Xuánwǔ Hall,
identifying itself as Xuánmíng,
and conversed with people.
Zuò prayed to it day and night,
and the spirit promised him blessings.
Zuò greatly believed it.
Zuò also sent Sǒu Fú, the Administrator of Zhāngyè, to replace Guàn in garrisoning Páohǎn,
but Sǒu Fú was killed by Guàn.
Before Líng and others had finished crossing the river,
they were again defeated by Guàn's forces.
Chuǎi fled alone on horseback,
pursued by Guàn's army.
Zuò's troops were greatly terrified.
Sòng Hún from Dūnhuáng, along with his younger brother Chéng and others, gathered troops to support Guàn.
Zhào Cháng, Zhāng Shú, and others, fearing punishment,
entered the inner palace, called out Zhāng Chónghuá's mother, Lady Mǎ, and brought her to the hall to declare Yàolíng's younger half-brother, Zhāng Xuánjìng, as ruler.
Chuǎi and others led their troops into the palace to attack Zhào Cháng
and killed him.
Guàn's younger brother, Zhāng Jū, and his son, Zhāng Sōng, recruited several hundred market people,
and loudly proclaimed,
"Zhāng Zuò is without principle!
My elder brother's great army has already reached the east of the city!
Anyone who dares to raise a hand will have their three familial generations exterminated!"
Zuò's troops dispersed.
Jū and Sōng led their forces into the city.
Zuò, clutching his sword in the palace hall,
shouted loudly,
ordering his retainers to fight to the death.
Since Zuò had lost the hearts of his people,
no one had the will to fight.
Thereupon, he was killed.
His head was impaled and displayed to all inside and outside,
and his body was exposed by the roadside.
Everyone in the state cheered "Long live!"
Zuò usurped the throne for three years before his demise.
Xuánjìng's courtesy name was Yuán'ān.
Upon his establishment,
he styled himself Grand Chief Controller, Grand General, Colonel, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Xīpíng.
He issued a general pardon throughout his state,
abolished the Hépíng era name,
and reverted to the 43rd year of Jiànxīng.
He executed Zuò's two sons,
appointed Zhāng Guàn as General of the Guards,
commanded an army of ten thousand men,
acted as Grand General,
and reorganized the officials.
Since Zhāng Tiānxī 張天錫 succeeded to the throne,
there were successive years of earthquakes and landslides.
Springs gushed forth,
willows transformed into pines,
and fire emerged from mud.
Yet Zhāng Tiānxī was engrossed in music and women,
and paid no attention to state affairs.
Initially,
Liáng Jǐng 梁景 from Āndìng 安定 and Liú Sù 劉肅 from Dūnhuáng 敦煌, both from prominent families,
had been close friends with Zhāng Tiānxī since childhood.
When Zhāng Yōng 章邕 was executed,
Liú Sù 劉肅 and Liáng Jǐng 梁景 rendered meritorious service,
and Zhāng Tiānxī deeply appreciated them.
He bestowed upon them the surname Zhāng 張,
and also changed their given names,
adopting them as his own sons.
All of Zhāng Tiānxī's sons had
the character
“Dà 大” in their given names,
so Liáng Jǐng 梁景 was named Dàyì 大奕,
and Liú Sù 劉肅 was named Dàchéng 大誠.
He deposed Dàhuái 大懷 as Duke of Gāochāng 高昌,
and instead established his favored son Dàyù 大豫 as Crown Prince.
Liáng Jǐng 梁景, Liú Sù 劉肅, and others all participated in state affairs.
People were resentful and fearful.
His cousin, the Attendant Cóngshì Zhōngláng 従事中郎 Xiàn 憲, offered stern remonstrance,
but it was not accepted.
At that time, Fú Jiān 苻堅 was powerful,
and attacked them repeatedly,
so the land had no peace from warfare.
Zhāng Tiānxī was very afraid,
and so he erected an altar and sacrificed animals.
He led the Dianjun Jiangjun 典軍將軍 Zhāng Níng 張寧 and Zhongjian Jiangjun 中堅將軍 Mǎ Ruì 馬芮, among others,
from afar to swear an oath with the Three Ducal Ministers of Jìn 晉,
and sent a letter to the Grand Marshal Huán Wēn 桓溫,
agreeing to launch a joint great expedition in the summer of the sixth year.
He dispatched Attendant Cóngshì Zhōngláng 従事中郎 Hán Bó 韓博 and Fènjié Jiāngjūn 奮節將軍 Kāng Miào 康妙 to present a memorial,
along with the text of the alliance.
Hán Bó 韓博 was eloquent,
and Huán Wēn 桓溫 greatly praised him.
Once, during a grand gathering,
Huán Wēn 桓溫 ordered his Sīmǎ 司馬 Diāo Yí 刁彝 to tease him.
Diāo Yí 刁彝 said to Hán Bó 韓博:
“Are you a descendant of Hán Lú 韓盧 (a famous swift dog)?”
Hán Bó 韓博 replied:
“You are a descendant of Hán Lú 韓盧.”
Huán Wēn 桓溫 laughed and said:
“Diāo Yí 刁彝 asked because your surname is Hán 韓.
He was simply asking.
His own surname is Diāo 刁,
how could he be a descendant of Hán Lú 韓盧?”
Hán Bó 韓博 replied:
“Perhaps Your Excellency has not considered it yet,
but those with short tails are called Diāo 刁.”
The entire assembly praised and sighed in admiration.
In the first year of Tàiyuán 太元 (376 CE),
Fú Jiān 苻堅 dispatched his generals Gǒu Cháng 苟萇, Máo Dāng 毛當, [一七] Liáng Xī 梁熙, and Yáo Cháng 姚萇 to invade,
crossing the Shíchéng Jīn 石城津 ford.
Zhāng Tiānxī convened a meeting.
Zhōng Lùshì 中錄事 Xí Lè 席仂 said:
“Our late dukes had a precedent;
we should calmly consider future changes.
This is Sūn Zhòngmóu's 孫仲謀 strategy of yielding and extending.”
The assembled regarded Xí Lè 席仂 as old and timid,
and all said:
“Longxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 Mǎ Dá 馬達,
with ten thousand elite soldiers, will resist them;
they will certainly not dare to advance.”
Guǎngwǔ Tàishǒu 廣武太守 Xīn Zhāng 辛章 secured the city and held firm.
Xīn Zhāng 辛章, along with Jìnxīng Xiàng 晉興相 Péng Zhīzhèng 彭知正 [一九] and Xīpíng Xiàng 西平相 Zhào Yí 趙疑, conspired, saying:
“Mǎ Dá 馬達 came from the ranks;
he will certainly not be effective,
and then the Qín 秦 army will penetrate deep.
Let us jointly lead the elite soldiers of the three commanderies,
cut off their food supply,
and stake our lives on a single morning.”
Zhēngdōng Cháng Jù 征東常據 also wished to attack Yáo Cháng 姚萇 first,
awaiting Zhāng Tiānxī's orders.
Zhāng Tiānxī led ten thousand men and encamped at Jīnchāng Chéng 金昌城.
Mǎ Dá 馬達 led ten thousand men to oppose Yáo Cháng 姚萇 and others,
then surrendered, and his soldiers scattered and fled.
Cháng Jù 常據 and Xí Lè 席仂 both died in battle.
Sībīng 司兵 Zhào Chōngzhé 趙充哲 fought fiercely with Yáo Cháng 姚萇
and also died.
Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn 中衞將軍 Shǐ Jǐng 史景 also perished on the battlefield.
Zhāng Tiānxī was greatly afraid,
came out of the city to fight himself,
but an uprising occurred inside the city.
Zhāng Tiānxī, in distress,
surrendered to Yáo Cháng 姚萇 and others.
Initially,
the Ānchāng Mén 安昌門 gate and Píngzhāng Diàn 平章殿 hall where Zhāng Tiānxī resided collapsed without cause,
[二０] and within ten days, the state perished.
He had been on the throne for a total of thirteen years.
From Zhāng Guǐ 張軌 becoming Governor of Liángzhōu 涼州
to Zhāng Tiānxī,
there were nine generations in total,
lasting seventy-six years.
Fú Jiān 苻堅 had previously built a residence for Zhāng Tiānxī.
When he arrived,
he appointed him as Shàngshū 尚書
and enfeoffed him as Guīyì Hóu 歸義侯.
When Fú Jiān 苻堅 was utterly defeated at Huáiféi 淮肥,
Zhāng Tiānxī served as the Zhēngnán Sīmǎ 征南司馬 for Fú Róng 苻融,
and returned to Jìn 晉 during the battle.
An imperial edict stated:
“In ancient times, Méng Míng 孟明 was not dismissed,
and ultimately demonstrated his merits.
How can one fault negate talent and usefulness!
Let Zhāng Tiānxī be appointed Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 and Zuǒ Yuánwài 左員外.”
Another imperial edict stated:
“The late Grand Commandant and Duke of Xīpíng 西平, Zhāng Guǐ 張軌, established virtue in distant regions,
and his lineage inherited previous meritorious service.
Powerful armies wantonly caused harm,
leading to the loss of his domain.
Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 Zhāng Tiānxī made his way to court,
while his ancestral sacrifices fell into disuse.
This greatly increases our pity and lamentation;
Zhāng Tiānxī's title as Duke of Xīpíng Jùn 西平郡 may be restored.”
Soon after, he was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫.
Zhāng Tiānxī had literary talent in his youth,
and his reputation spread far and wide.
Upon returning to court,
he received great favor and treatment.
Court officials, considering his state had been destroyed and he himself captured,
often criticized him.
Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ 會稽王道子 once asked about the products of his western land.
Zhāng Tiānxī immediately replied:
“Mulberries are sweet and delicious,
owls' calls resound,
dairy products nourish the constitution,
and people are without jealousy.”
Later, his spirit and vitality became dim and lost;
though he held an official position,
he was no longer treated with respect.
During the Lóng'ān 隆安 period (397–401 CE),
Kuàijī Shìzǐ Yuánxiǎn 會稽世子元顯 gained power,
and often invited him,
treating him as a plaything.
Because his family was poor,
he was appointed Lújiāng Tàishǒu 廬江太守,
while retaining his original office.
During Huán Xuán's 桓玄 time,
wishing to attract and pacify people from all directions,
he appointed Zhāng Tiānxī as Hùqiāng Xiàowèi 護羌校尉 and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ 涼州刺史.
He died soon after,
at the age of sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫.
The historian remarks:
Beyond the Long River,
the moving sands form a boundary;
the Jade Gate hangs precariously,
the Golden City is fortified.
The Miáo 苗 tribe fled there,
and Emperor Shùn 帝舜 cast them out without restraint;
the Qúsōu 渠搜 resided there,
and Great Yǔ 大禹 approached them and pacified them.
In times of many difficulties,
who could control the five commanderies?
In times of military ferocity,
one stood high and overlooked from the three borders.
Although it was not a place of lasting peace,
it was sufficient as a place for temporary survival!
Zhōu Gōng 周公 protected it and established merits,
and Shì Yàn 士彥 embraced it and extended his lineage.
Zhì Yú 摯虞 observed the celestial phenomena,
and recorded that great floods would not flow there;
Hóu Jǐn 侯瑾 observed the springs,
and knew that hegemons would reside there.
This was not only due to the terrain,
but also perhaps to the Way of Heaven!
Mào 茂, Jùn 駿, and Chónghuá 重華 (referring to Zhāng Mào 張茂, Zhāng Jùn 張駿, Zhāng Chónghuá 張重華) possessed loyalty and followed in their footsteps.
Even in their remote and humble position,
they did not forget the central court,
thus they were able to control various Rong 戎 tribes in the west,
and repel great villains in the east,
binding together generations of noble titles,
and offering tribute from distant lands,
displaying their brilliance in remote wildernesses.
This was truly the effect of upholding rectitude.
Zhāng Tiānxī's 祚 (referring to Zhāng Tiānxī) relied on a humble concubine's son,
secretly overthrowing the legitimate heir,
sowing thorns in the crimson tube (i.e., stirring up trouble in government),
and comparing his imperial residence to the Black Mountain.
Dīng Qí 丁琪 was executed for his stern remonstrance,
and Wáng Luán 王鸞 was conspicuously killed for his frank words.
The territory was in turmoil,
hating his usurpation of the name,
ultimately leading to his public display of defeat.
This is the natural course of events.
Chúnxiá 純嘏 (referring to Zhāng Tiānxī's posthumous name, although not explicitly stated, the context suggests this is still about him) was weak,
and ultimately lost his forces.
He presented himself at the Wei Que 魏闕 (imperial court),
and his footsteps joined the court currents,
twice inheriting the silver-and-gold insignia.
This was the extended blessing of his ancestors' virtue.
A eulogy states: The three heavenly bodies formed a miasma,
and the nine regions were divided like a melon.
The imperial cauldron moved to the area between the rivers,
and the land was cut off by the riverbanks.
Sincere allegiance was given to the Jìn dynasty –
how admirable was Lord Zhāng!
Internally, he pacified the remnant populace;
externally, he repelled invading bandits.
His lineage was extended for generations,
and the state was made complete and prosperous.
Relying on righteousness as its foundation,
it was surely blessed by Heaven.
Collational Notes
Biography Fifty-seven: Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng Lǐ Xuánshèng (son Shìyè)
Wǔzhāo Wáng, whose taboo name was Gǎo,
courtesy name Xuánshèng,
and childhood name Chángshēng,
was a native of Chéngjì in Lǒngxī.
His surname was Lǐ.
He was the sixteenth-generation descendant of Lǐ Guǎng, the former general of the Hàn dynasty.
Guǎng’s great-grandfather, Zhòngxiáng,
served as a general in the early Hàn dynasty.
He fought rebellious Qiāng tribes in Sùchāng.
Sùchāng is present-day Díddào.
Outnumbered,
he died there.
Zhòngxiáng’s son, Bókǎo, rushed to attend the funeral
and subsequently buried him in the eastern plains of Díddào,
where he then settled.
His family was for generations a prominent family in Xīzhōu.
His great-great-grandfather, Yōng,
and great-grandfather, Róu,
both served the Jìn dynasty, holding positions as prefectural governors.
His grandfather, Yǎn,
served Zhāng Guǐ as Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn and Ānshì Tínghóu.
His father, Chǎng,
had an excellent reputation in his youth
but died young,
leaving Xuánshèng to be born posthumously.
From a young age, he was fond of learning,
had a profound, quick, tolerant, and gentle nature,
possessed fine deportment,
and was widely conversant in the Classics and histories,
excelling particularly in literary composition.
When he grew up,
he practiced martial arts considerably
and recited Sūn and Wú's military treatises.
He once lodged with Lǚ Guāng’s grand astrologer Guō Nún and his maternal younger brother Sòng Yáo.
Nún rose and said to Yáo:
"You will attain the highest position among officials,
and Lord Lǐ will have a share of the land.
When a dapple-gray horse in his family gives birth to a white-forehead foal,
that will be the time."
In the final years of Lǚ Guāng’s reign,
Duàn Yè from Jīngzhào proclaimed himself the governor of Liángzhōu.
He appointed Mèng Mǐn of Zhàojùn, the administrator of Dūnhuáng, as the Inspector of Shāzhōu,
and designated Xuánshèng as the magistrate of Xiàogǔ.
Mǐn soon died.
Féngyì Guō Qiān, the Dūnhuáng defender, and Dūnhuáng Suǒ Xiān, the chief administrator of Shāzhōu, among others, seeing Xuánshèng's gentle steadfastness and benevolent governance,
supported him as Níngsuò Jiāngjūn and administrator of Dūnhuáng.
Xuánshèng initially found this difficult.
At this time, Sòng Yáo, who was serving under Yè,
returned to Dūnhuáng
and said to Xuánshèng:
"Brother, have you forgotten Guō Nún’s words?
The white-forehead foal has already been born."
Xuánshèng then agreed.
Soon after, he was advanced to the title of Guànjūn
and declared himself a vassal to Yè.
Yè appointed Xuánshèng as Ānxī Jiāngjūn, administrator of Dūnhuáng,
and concurrently Protector of the Western Hú.
When Yè presumptuously proclaimed himself King of Liáng,
his right guard general Suǒ Sì framed Xuánshèng to Yè.
So Yè appointed Sì as administrator of Dūnhuáng
and dispatched him with five hundred cavalry westward.
Before arriving, at twenty *lǐ* away,
he sent a message to Xuánshèng to come out and welcome him.
Xuánshèng was surprised and doubtful.
He was about to go out to greet him,
but Xiàogǔ magistrate Zhāng Miǎo and Sòng Yáo stopped him, saying:
"The Lǚ family's government is in decline,
and Duàn Yè is ignorant and weak.
This is precisely the time for heroes to act.
General, you possess the resources of an entire state,
why would you surrender yourself to others?
Suǒ Sì, presuming upon his own region,
believes people will attach themselves to him.
He does not expect the General to suddenly resist him.
He can be captured in a single battle."
Sòng Yáo also said:
"A great man, already acclaimed by the world,
if he were to surrender to Sì today,
would he not be ridiculed by all under Heaven?
Elder brother, your heroic bearing is outstanding,
possessing the demeanor of a hegemon.
The achievements of the Zhāng kings are not unattainable for you."
Xuánshèng said:
"In my youth, I had no ambition for great deeds.
I came to this position through official service.
I did not expect the literati of this prefecture to suddenly support me.
My previous suggestion of going out to greet him was because I did not know the intentions of the gentry."
Thereupon, he sent Yáo to reconnoiter Sì.
Yáo met Sì
and enticed him with sweet words.
Returning, he told Xuánshèng:
"Sì is arrogant and his troops are weak;
he can be easily captured."
Consequently, he sent his two sons Shìyè and Ràng, along with Miǎo, Yáo, and Sīmǎ Yǐn Jiànxīng, among others, to engage in battle.
They defeated him,
and Sì fled back to Zhāngyè.
Xuánshèng had always been on good terms with Sì,
having sworn an oath of brotherhood.
Yet he was framed by him,
so he deeply resented him.
He then enumerated Sì's crimes to Duàn Yè.
Yè's general Qú Nán also disliked Sì.
At this point,
he advised Yè to eliminate him.
Yè then killed Sì
and sent an envoy to apologize to Xuánshèng.
He divided the three counties of Liángxīng and Wūzé from Dūnhuáng and Yíhé from Jìnchāng into Liángxīng Commandery
and promoted Xuánshèng to Chíjié, Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs West of Liángxīng, Zhènxi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Protector of the Western Yí.
At that time, a red aura rose from Xuánshèng's backyard,
and dragon tracks appeared in the small city.
In the fourth year of Lóng'ān (400 CE),
Táng Yáo, the administrator of Jìnchāng, issued a proclamation to the six commanderies,
recommending Xuánshèng as Grand Commander-in-Chief, Grand General, Duke of Liáng, and concurrently Governor of Qín and Liáng Provinces, and Protector of the Qiāng.
Xuánshèng then granted amnesty throughout his territory,
declared the year Gēngzǐ as the beginning of his reign,
posthumously honored his grandfather Yǎn as Liáng Jǐnggōng,
and his father Chǎng as Liáng Jiǎngōng.
He appointed Táng Yáo as Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn,
Guō Qiān as Jūnzī Jìjiǔ,
Suǒ Xiān as Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
Zhāng Miǎo as Yòu Chángshǐ,
Yǐn Jiànxīng as Zuǒ Sīmǎ,
Zhāng Tǐshùn as Yòu Sīmǎ,
Zhāng Tiáo as Mùfǔ Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
Lìnghú Yì as Yòu Chángshǐ,
Zhāng Lín as Tàifǔ Zhǔbù,
Sòng Yáo and Zhāng Sù as Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
Yáo was additionally appointed Zhéhchōng Jiāngjūn,
Sù was additionally appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
Suǒ Chéngmíng as Mùfǔ Yòu Sīmǎ,
Lìnghú Qiān as Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn and administrator of Jìnxīng,
Fàn Déyú as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and administrator of Xījùn,
Zhāng Jìng as Zhéhchōng Jiāngjūn and administrator of Hélǎng,
Suǒ Xùn as Wēiyuǎn Jiāngjūn and administrator of Xīpíng,
Zhào Kāi as Xīngmǎ Hùjūn and administrator of Dàxià,
Suǒ Cí as administrator of Guǎngwǔ,
Yīn Liàng as administrator of Xī'ān,
Lìnghú Hè as administrator of Wǔwēi,
and Suǒ Shù as administrator of Wǔxīng,
to attract and appease the eastern Xìa.
He also dispatched Sòng Yáo to march east against Liángxīng
and attack the various cities west of Yùmén,
all of which surrendered.
He then garrisoned Yùmén and Yángguān,
expanded agricultural land, accumulated grain,
and prepared resources for an eastern campaign.
Initially,
when Lǚ Guāng proclaimed himself king,
he sent envoys to Yútián to purchase six imperial seals of jade.
By this time,
the jade arrived in Dūnhuáng
and was received into the prefectural treasury.
Subsequently, he erected a hall outside the south gate, by the water,
named the Jìnggōng Zhī Táng,
where he deliberated on court affairs
and reviewed military matters.
He commissioned illustrations and eulogies of ancient sagely emperors and enlightened kings, loyal officials and filial sons, heroic warriors and chaste women.
Xuánshèng personally composed prefaces and eulogies for them
to illuminate the meaning of guidance and admonition.
At that time, all the civil and military officials also had their portraits drawn.
White sparrows flew over the Jìnggōng Táng,
and Xuánshèng was greatly pleased by the sight.
He also established a Bàn Palace
and increased the number of students in the Gaōmén Academy by five hundred.
He erected the Jiānà Táng in his backyard
to commemorate the illustrated eulogies.
In the first year of Yìxī (405 CE),
Xuánshèng changed the era name to Jiànchū.
He dispatched his attendant Huáng Shǐ and Liáng Xīng to secretly deliver a memorial to the imperial court, stating: "In the past, as the Hàn dynasty's fortune was nearing its end,
the Three Kingdoms stood in tripod formation.
Heaven's mandate,
by destiny, fell to the imperial Jìn.
Our great ancestor established the grand foundation,
Jǐng Wén expanded the imperial enterprise,
and their successors received
my wish.
However, as circumstances compelled me,
I have taken on the responsibilities of the province,
with serious duties and burdens.
The matters of the household are weighty.
Although I understand human affairs in detail,
I do not know the will of Heaven.
Mounting the carriage and managing the reins,
a hundred anxieties fill my breast.
Future matters are entrusted to you all.
I will briefly mention a few immediate and pressing matters,
speaking as ideas occur to me,
unable to arrange them in order.
As for nipping evil in the bud and preventing its growth,
and deeply
understanding changes in circumstances,
this must depend on the depth of your own insight,
and is not something my instructions can improve.
Although you are not yet of great age,
if you can curb yourselves and diligently cultivate yourselves,
compared to
the ancients,
you may also achieve great things.
If you do not,
even if you live to old age,
what will you accomplish?
You must all be mindful and cautious.
Be moderate in drinking and cautious in speech,
always consider before expressing joy or anger,
love wisely and know what to dislike,
hate wisely and know what to appreciate.
Let your thoughts be merciful and forgiving,
and act only after careful deliberation.
Do not lightly
believe
what the crowd dislikes;
carefully examine people,
verify truth from falsehood,
keep away from flatterers,
and draw near to the loyal and upright.
Abolish cruel punishments,
endure annoyances,
care for the elderly,
relieve the bereaved and sick,
diligently review cases,
and listen
to petitions.
In matters requiring punishment,
maintain a gentle countenance and act according to reason,
never lightly showing emotion or anger.
Do not let rewards be overlooked,
and do not allow relatives to escape punishment.
Keep your ears and eyes open to the world,
and understand
the suffering of external troubles;
restrain those around you,
and do not let them wield power arbitrarily.
Do not boast of good deeds or claim credit for others' labor,
nor try to anticipate treachery and guess its nature
to show your own cleverness.
Broadly seek advice,
do not act
on your own authority.
Follow goodness as smoothly as a flowing stream,
and shun evil as if touching boiling water.
To be wealthy and noble yet not arrogant is extremely difficult.
Keep this in mind,
and never forget it for a moment.
Treat your subordinates and local
elders
with utmost courtesy and respect.
In banquets and meals,
pay attention to every detail.
You must know
the successes and failures of past and present.
In your leisure after court,
remember to read classics and books.
Standing facing a wall
makes one no
man.
This commandery has long been known for its loyalty and integrity,
and its people are refined and cultured.
Even during times of national prosperity,
it was praised throughout the land.
How much more so today,
it is truly a famous region.
It is precisely because
for five hundred years, local families have been connected by marriage,
that sometimes in public affairs,
there are minor deviations.
You must adapt and consider things appropriately.
I have governed for five years,
during which there have been military difficulties and disturbances,
and I have not been able to give the people rest from service
and bestow favor and peace upon the officials and commoners.
As for concealing flaws and hiding weaknesses,
cleansing blemishes and stains,
treating former enemies
in the morning
as trusted confidants in the evening,
although it is not enough
to compare to the ancients,
it is roughly without fault towards both new and old.
In matters of justice,
I have been open and impartial,
never holding grudges
that would cause harm or benefit.
If the immediate benefits were few,
the long-term gains were more than sufficient,
so I have no shame concerning my previous aspirations.
Initially,
when Xuánshèng [玄盛] went west,
he left his daughter Jìng'ài [敬愛] to be cared for by her maternal grandfather Yǐn Wén [尹文].
After Yǐn Wén [尹文] moved east,
Jìng'ài [敬愛] was raised by Xuánshèng’s [玄盛] paternal aunt, Liáng Bāo's [梁褒] mother.
Later, Tūfà Tán [禿髮檀] sought passage through Běishān [北山],
and the Xiānbēi [鮮卑] sent Bāo [褒] to escort Jìng'ài [敬愛] to Jiǔquán [酒泉],
and also established friendly relations.
Xuánshèng [玄盛] sent an envoy to return the courtesy,
presenting local products.
Xuánshèng [玄盛] personally led two myriad cavalry,
sweeping the land as far as Jiàndōng [建東].
The king of the former part of Shànshàn [鄯善] sent an envoy to offer its local products.
Jūqú Méngxùn [且渠蒙遜] came to invade,
reaching Jiànkāng [建康],
plundering over three thousand households before returning.
Xuánshèng [玄盛] was greatly enraged,
and led his cavalry in pursuit,
reaching Mí'ān [彌安],
where he soundly defeated them,
recovering all the plundered households.
Initially,
at the end of Fú Jiān's [苻堅] Jiànyuán [建元] reign,
over ten thousand households from the Jiānghàn [江漢] region were relocated to Dūnhuáng [敦煌].
Among the people of Zhōngzhōu [中州] whose fields were uncultivated,
over seven thousand households were also relocated.
When Guō Nán [郭黁] attacked Wǔwēi [武威],
several thousand households from Wǔwēi [武威] and east of Zhāngyè [張掖] fled west to Dūnhuáng [敦煌] and Jìnchāng [晉昌].
When Xuánshèng [玄盛] moved east,
he relocated all of them to Jiǔquán [酒泉].
He divided five thousand households of southerners to establish Huìjī Jùn [會稽郡],
five thousand households of Zhōngzhōu [中州] people to establish Guǎngxià Jùn [廣夏郡],
and the remaining thirteen thousand households were divided to establish Wǔwēi [武威], Wǔxìng [武興], and Zhāngyè [張掖] three commanderies.
He built a city at Nánzǐ Tíng [南子亭] south of Dūnhuáng [敦煌],
to awe the southern barbarians.
Moreover, as his previous memorial had not been answered,
he again sent the Buddhist monk Fǎquán [法泉] to secretly convey a memorial,
which read: "Rivers and mountains widely separate us,
I have no means to pay homage at court.
My head stretches to the cloudy peak,
eagerly gazing towards the distant land.
I humbly believe Your Majesty ascended the throne at the opportune moment,
with great fortune bestowed by Heaven.
In the year Guǐsì
(405 CE), I obeyed the unanimous opinion
and temporarily took charge of Fāngchéng [方城].
At that time, I sent the court attendant Huáng Shǐ [黃始] to present a memorial expressing my sincerity.
The remote journey is arduous and vast,
I do not know if it reached you.
Wú [吳] and Liáng [涼] are far
apart,
and bandits fill the roads.
Envoys bearing precious tributes
have no way to reach Your Majesty.
I respectfully enclose a copy of the previous memorial,
hoping it may perhaps reach you easily.
In that year, I advanced my troops to Jiǔquán [酒泉],
and deployed my army at Guǎngpíng [廣平],
hoping to eradicate the thorns and weeds.
However, the cunning barbarians acted wantonly,
not submitting to my authority and teachings,
relying on their lairs,
obstructing my
path forward.
I humbly believe that as everything was in its initial stages,
our granaries were not yet full,
so I halted military operations and focused on agriculture and training soldiers.
Time passed and seasons changed,
three years slipped by.
I grasped my sword
and sighed with anger,
each day feeling like a year.
Now our resources are sufficient,
and our armaments are complete.
I have summoned troops from the western cities,
and brought in the masses of the Dīnglíng [丁零] from the north.
I hope to rely on the nation's prestige,
sweep
through the Hélǒng [河隴] region,
raise our banners in Qínchuān [秦川],
await Your Majesty's decree,
exert my utmost loyalty and sincerity,
and make my efforts even if it means my downfall.
Furthermore, my province is vast and remote,
and powerful enemies have not yet been eliminated.
I must appoint deputies to oversee the deployment and retention of troops.
I hereby provisionally appoint my heir, Shìyè [士業], as Supervisor of the Vanguard Armies,
As Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army) and Hùqiāng Xiàowèi (Colonel Protector of the Qiāng),
he supervises the vanguard,
serving as my (your minister's) pioneer.
Moreover, the great populace of Dūnhuáng Commandery is prosperous,
controlling the Western Regions,
governing ten thousand *lǐ*.
It is the
foundation of the military state.

Therefore, I have immediately appointed my second son, Ràng, as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Xīyí Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Western Yi), and Dūnhuáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dūnhuáng),
to oversee the Kūnyì people
and bring peace and stability to distant lands.
As for my
other sons,
all are serving in the army,
leading the soldiers.
I (your minister) oversee the general strategy,
fully committed to exerting my strength.
I respond to situations as they arise and issue commands,
and news of movements and pacification continues to arrive.
When Xuánshèng was transferred to Jiǔquán,
he earnestly encouraged farming.
The officials, seeing that the harvests were consistently abundant
and the people enjoyed their livelihoods,
requested an inscription to be carved in Jiǔquán.
Xuánshèng consented.
Thereupon, he had Liú Yànmíng, the Jìjiǔ (Libationer) of the Rúlín (Confucian Academy), compose the text,
which was carved on stone to praise his virtues.
Later, Méngxùn's annual incursions did not cease,
but Xuánshèng's ambition was to pacify his territory with virtue.
He merely established peace and an alliance with him,
and did not dispute it.
At this time, white wolves, white rabbits, white sparrows, white pheasants, and white doves all nested in his gardens and parks.
His subordinates believed these were auspicious white signs, born of the essence of metal,
all arriving spontaneously at the opportune moment.
There were also divine lights, sweet dew, conjoined trees, auspicious grains, and numerous other auspicious omens.
They requested the historian to record these events,
and Xuánshèng complied.
Soon after, Méngxùn broke the alliance and invaded.
Xuánshèng dispatched his heir, Shìyè, to intercept and defeat him,
capturing his general, Qú Bǎinián.
On the Shàngsì day, Xuánshèng held a banquet by the winding stream (Qūshuǐ),
commanding his officials to compose poems,
and personally wrote the preface for them.
Thereupon, he transcribed Zhūgě Liàng's admonitions to encourage his sons, saying:
"I bear a heavy burden of difficulties,
and the merit of achieving peace and stability has not yet been established.
Although outwardly I gather talented individuals
and rely on the strength of my trusted aides,
military affairs are extremely urgent,
and I sit awaiting dawn.
Given the stability of the protective wall (of the state),
it is appropriate to engage both kin and worthy individuals.
Therefore, before you could receive instruction from your teachers and guardians,
you all assumed responsibilities at a young age.
I often fear that you might fail,
thereby incurring blame and regret.
One cannot be ignorant of the events of ancient and modern times.
If something close at hand can serve as a teacher,
why must it be distant?
Review Zhūgě Liàng's exhortations
and Yīng Qú's memorialized remonstrances.
Examining their beginnings and ends,
the teachings of Zhōu and Kǒng are fully contained within them.
For governing the state, they are sufficient to achieve peace;
for establishing oneself, they are sufficient to achieve fame.
Their essence is simple and easy to understand;
a mere glance makes them clear.
Although the words come from people of the past,
the principles are taught here.
Moreover, the classics, histories, morality, and virtues are like gathering beans in the central plains;
those who are diligent will achieve much.
How can you not exert yourselves!"
Xuánshèng then repaired the old eastern and western outer walls of Dūnhuáng
to guard against the threat from the northern barbarians.
He also built the old southwestern outer walls of Dūnhuáng
to assert power over the southern barbarians.
With the capacity to govern the world,
Xuánshèng, at the end of the Lǚ clan's rule,
was supported by the various heroes,
thus embarking on his hegemonic plan.
Without bloodshed,
he settled a thousand *lǐ* while sitting,
asserting that Zhāng's enterprise would be completed in due time,
and the ten commanderies west of the river would be unified within a few months.
Later, Tūfà Tán took residence in Gūzāng,
and Qú Méngxùn's territory gradually expanded.
Thereupon, Xuánshèng, filled with emotion, composed a "Zhì Fù" (Ode of Ambition).
Its verses say: Stepping into the ultimate void with vast carriage,
riding what exists upon what is nothingness,
receiving the profound primal essence and being molded and extended,
inheriting the numinous essence in obscure accord.
Shaded by morning clouds, dense and widespread,
looking up at the
bright sun's warm radiance.
Both spread and carried,
to nurture and to complete.
In youth, I aspired to Yán Zǐ's honor of bending his arm as a pillow,
my heart wandering in the lofty classics,
delighting in rites and delving into scriptures.
Disdaining the dark
caps (of officials) for scarlet gates,
envying the arrogant life of Qīyuán;
esteeming the fisherman of Cānglàng,
admiring Jǔ and Nì's paired plowing.
Loathing the cowering of owls and kites,
revering the flying phoenix in the great
azure;
blocking worldly competition within an inch (of my heart),
cutting off praises for temporary fame.
Soaring with sky-songs above lofty peaks,
marveling at the splendid trees that defy frost;
their tall trunks verdant and lush,
passing
through the bitter cold to become even more fragrant.
My feelings far-off, distantly entrusted,
imagining the radiant light of the Four Elders;
about to gather the flourishing prosperity along the common road,
reining in cloud-bridles and soaring high;
climbing jade branches
in Xuánpǔ,
sipping the emerald liquid of exquisite springs;
harmonizing with the ethereal calls of singing phoenixes,
responding to the chiming of phoenixes on the southern slope.
When the time for retreat was not granted,
my heart yearned but my body remained,
turning to the Yang Woods,
looking back at a single mound;
battered by wind and bathed in rain,
now sinking, now floating.
Advantages and disadvantages mingled in confusion,
intertwined,
joy and sorrow cycled and sought each other.
The door to heaven was silently and heavily shut,
heaven and earth devoid of a ferry or boat;
grieving that the way of integrity and trust had thinned,
apologizing for lost virtue to the circling
current.
Thereupon, I abandoned profound contemplation,
responding to worldly guests,
first donning the weak kerchief (of a prince) in the Eastern Palace,
alongside heroes and talents in feathered array,
treading the secret court of宣德 (Xuāndé),
assisting the enlightened sovereign in the purple
firmament.
Radiant in modesty,
resplendent and illustrious,
the royal abode towering,
the hundred officials thronging,
the ruler aspiring to Yú and Xià,
the ministers and populace to Kuí and Yì.
Zhāng Wáng's (King Zhāng) cliff collapsed,
Queen Liáng fell into the ravine.
The pure customs were utterly lost forever,
scholars and officials sank and drowned.
Lǚ's troubles originated within the household,
its structure
shattered and overturned;
fierce winds swept through tall trees,
whirling currents boiled in deep springs;
flying dust gathered, obscuring the sun,
great fires blazed, scorching the plains;
famous cities were silently
extinguished,
a thousand townships desolate and smokeless.
These were the calamities of the cycles of sixty years,
arising and perishing in succession.
Thereupon, people yearned for the pursuit of the deer (emperorship),
each household harbored
thoughts of hegemony,
ignoring the royal decree and not seeking it,
inviting disproportionate desires into the formless.
Thus, overturned chariots lined the road, one after another,
the lives of the people were sacrificed to the soil.
Mourning my kind's
bewilderment,
far-flung, without reliance or support;
the more one sought to monopolize, the further one strayed,
entrusting the profound pearl to the罔象 (wǎngxiàng).
Vast and distant Liang,
utterly desolate and violent,
my humble self, far-off,
in the distant Western land,
not meeting by prior appointment,
but truly united by a mysterious pact.
Crossing the weak
water to establish a foundation,
treading the ruins of Kūn to form a rampart,
controlling the startled reins of galloping steeds,
connecting shattered axles on steep peaks.
Lofty cliffs rise ruggedly,
with heavy dangers ten thousand *xún* deep,
profound and
remote, winding and precipitous,
twisting and towering,
thickets of thorns crisscrossing,
rivers wide and waters deep,
foxes and badgers line the path,
owls hoot in chorus.
Standing firm, not for my own use,
but entrusted with what is most fitting, as
influence.
He held a united heart to manage affairs,
and embraced what was from others in his grasp.
He did not feign feelings or act wildly,
but rather achieved a mystical harmony and proceeded straightforwardly.
Exemplary virtues thus came to his court,
and wild
hermits hence submitted to his rule.
How excellent are the heroes of the time!
How splendid are the brilliant and wise!
They sought to gather widely with nets,
not merely to shoot a hook or cut a sleeve!
Some were freed from shackles and adorned with tassels,
while others, though arriving later,
were ranked first.
He gathered extraordinary talents from mountains and lands,
and promoted outstanding luminaries from the boundless.
He recalled Zhāng Liú’s divine encounter,
which raised high waves to cleanse impurities.
He thought of Kǒng Míng in his thatched hut,
who executed profound strategies without hindrance.
Hóng Cāo Pán was magnanimous and bold,
raising three armies to inspire their sharp edge.
He praised the noble paths of the heroes,
and admired Guān and Zhāng’s outstanding bravery.
They swore to repay Cáo
and return to Liú—
how extraordinary their righteousness and courage!
Holding a spear across the broken bridge—
what a grand display of heroic姿!
Brilliant were the southern treasures,
illustrious were Zhōu and Lǔ.
Extraordinary figures emerged from Jīng
and Wú,
brightly civil and fiercely martial.
They proposed strategies at Wūlín,
and advanced majestically along the Jiāng Pǔ.
They shattered mighty formations,
like swirling wind and rising clouds.
They continued the distant legacy of Fán and Hán,
and equaled
the splendid achievements of Zhào Wǔ.
Without Liú and Sūn’s magnanimous spirit,
who could have achieved such great fortune!
Truly, heaven and earth complement each other,
and all beings yearn for the wind and moistening rain.
When Mǐn and Yì were pacified,
the Three Rivers were cleared.
How solemn their great accomplishments,
how numerous the flourishing peace!
They drove myriad dragons with their strategies,
and spread their glory for ten thousand years.
We admire their enduring legacy
from distant ages,
and aspire to their towering example.
They will raise a vermilion banner to open the way,
and drive long chariots for a swift campaign.
They will wave the autumn wind to lift their pennants,
and brush against the splendid
flags of Zhāoyáo.
They draw divine omens from the imperial ultimate,
and align with the tranquility of the Five Planets.
Valiant are the shields and walls,
orderly are the high advisors.
They wantonly slaughter fleeing whales,
and cut down those ugly hordes.
They sprinkle
floating dust at Dāngyáng,
and rescue the failing virtue from its fall.
They occasionally rode as outriders for Chāngyú,
and reined in their horses at Xiāngchéng.
Knowing that eliminating harm lay in this,
they embodied what the shepherd boy
had described.
They carefully observed the minutest movements of opportunity,
and thought of missing meals and forgetting sleep.
They expressed their broad aspirations on plain silk,
and entrusted their sincerity to the bright sun.
Xuánshèng fell gravely ill.
He gave his dying instructions to Sòng Yáo, saying:
“I have endured bitter suffering since my youth,
and experienced all kinds of hardships.
During times of chaos and war,
I was chosen by this region.
My talent is weak and my wisdom shallow,
unable to unify with Héyòu.
Now my strength is failing,
and I will probably not recover.
Death is a great principle;
I am not saddened by it.
What I regret is that my ambition has not been realized.
Those who hold the position of leader
should deeply guard against the critical moments of danger.
After my death,
my heir is like your son.
Assist him well,
and convey my lifelong wishes:
Do not let him reside above others,
or be arrogant and self-important.
Matters of the military and state
are entrusted to you,
so do not let your strategies deviate from the right path,
and lose the key to success or failure.”
In the thirteenth year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
His countrymen posthumously honored him as Wǔzhāo Wáng,
his tomb as Jiànshì Líng,
and his temple name as Tàizǔ.
Before this,
paulownia, pagoda trees, cypress, and lacquer trees did not grow in Héyòu.
During Zhāng Jùn’s reign,
they were brought from Qínlǒng and planted,
but eventually all died.
However, in the northwest corner of the Jiǔquán Palace, a pagoda tree grew.
Xuánshèng also composed an “Ode to the Pagoda Tree” to express his feelings,
probably lamenting that his achievements in this remote and isolated region
were not in the right place.
He also ordered the Chief Clerk Liáng Zhōngyōng and Liú Yànmíng and others to compose essays.
Moved by the frequent outbreaks of war
and the noisy competition of the times,
he wrote “Ode to Great Wine Capacity” to express his serene and open mind.
He was close friends with Xīn Jǐng and Xīn Gōngjìng, sharing their aspirations.
Jǐng and others returned to Jìn,
and were killed south of the Yangtze.
Xuánshèng heard of it and mourned them.
Xuánshèng’s former wife,
the daughter of Xīn Nà from the same prefecture,
was chaste, compliant, and had the demeanor of a virtuous woman.
She died first,
and Xuánshèng personally composed a eulogy for her.
He also left dozens of other poems and rhapsodies.
His heir, Tán, died young.
His second son, Shìyè, succeeded him.
The later ruler of Liáng, whose taboo name was Xīn,
had the courtesy name Shìyè.
When Xuánshèng died,
his officials respectfully appointed Shìyè as Grand Commandant, Grand General, Duke of Liáng, concurrently Governor of Liángzhōu, and Protector-General of the Qiāng.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the territory,
and the era name was changed to Jiāxīng.
His mother, Lady Yǐn, was honored as Empress Dowager.
Sòng Yáo was made General of the Martial Guard, Administrator of Guǎngxià, Libationer of Military Counsel, and Supervisor of the Affairs of the Three Bureaus.
Suǒ Xiān was made General Who Conquers Barbarians, and Administrator of Zhāngyè.
Qiěqú Méngxùn sent his Administrator of Zhāngyè, Qiěqú Guǎngzōng, to feign surrender and entice Shìyè.
Shìyè sent Wēn Yí of the Martial Guard and others to meet him,
personally leading a large army to follow as reinforcements.
Méngxùn led thirty thousand troops,
setting an ambush at Liǎoquán.
When Shìyè heard this,
he led his troops back,
but was pressed by Méngxùn.
Shìyè personally donned armor and charged first,
greatly defeating them.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for over a hundred *lǐ*,
capturing and beheading more than seven thousand.
The next year,
Méngxùn again attacked Shìyè.
Shìyè was about to go out to resist him,
but the Left Chief Clerk Zhāng Tǐshùn strongly advised against it,
so he stopped.
Méngxùn greatly reaped the autumn harvest and returned.
That year,

the imperial court appointed Shìyè as Bearer of Credentials, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of the Seven Commanderies, General Who Guards the West, Protector-General of the Qiāng, and Duke of Jiǔquán.
Shìyè was quite severe in his punishments,
and also incessantly repaired and built.
The Attendant-in-ordinary Zhāng Xiǎn submitted a memorial admonishing him, saying:
“Since the beginning of the year,
the *yīn* and *yáng* have been out of order,
and there have been frequent destructive winds and violent rains,
harming the harmonious *qì*.
Now the region is divided into three,
and the situation will not remain unified for long.
The basis for unification and expansion
truly lies in agriculture and warfare.
The strategy for pacifying distant lands
should prioritize leniency and simplicity.
Yet you further implement severe punishments and harsh laws,
and focus on palaces and buildings.
Manpower is depleted,
and the common people are distressed.
The cause of these disasters
is indeed due to this.”
The Chief Clerk Fàn Chēng also submitted a memorial admonishing him, saying: “I have heard that Heaven’s affection for the human ruler
is exceedingly diligent.
Therefore, when government is not rectified,
it sends down calamities and warnings to admonish.
Those who change, though in danger, will surely prosper;
Sòng Jǐng is an example.
Those who do not change,
though secure, will surely perish;
Duke Guó is an example.
In the third month of the *guǐmǎo* day of the first year,
the Qiāndé Hall in Dūnhuáng collapsed.
In the eighth month,
Xiàogǔ
the earth cracked;
on the first day of the second year,
dark fog filled the four directions;
in the fourth month,
the sun was red and without light,
and it was not restored for two decans;
in the eleventh month,
a fox ascended the southern gate.
This spring and summer, the earth
has frequently shaken five times;
in the sixth month,
a meteor fell in Jiànkāng.
Although your subject's learning does not delve into antiquity,
and my quickness is inferior to Zhòngshū,
I have also heard the Way from my former teacher.
And since I am fifty-
nine years old,
I beg to briefly speak to Your Highness of what I have seen and heard with my own eyes and ears,
and am no longer able to discuss distant matters from books and commentaries.
Previously, at the beginning of Xián'ān,
the earth cracked in Xīpíng,
and a fox entered before the Qiānguāng Hall;
soon after, the Qín army suddenly arrived,
and the capital could not be defended.
When Liáng Xī became the governor of Liáng
Zhōu,
taking advantage of the Qín clan's military turmoil,
he aimed to possess the entire Liáng region.
Externally, he did not care for the common people;
internally, he accumulated much wealth.
In the nineteenth year of Jiànzhāng, the southern gate of Gūzāng collapsed,
and a meteorite fell
at the Xiányù Hall.
Twenty years later, Lǚ Guāng rebelled in the east,
his sons were defeated first,
and he himself was slain later.
Duàn Yè, relying on the chaos created by the various Hú tribes,
then claimed imperial authority in this region.
Within three years,
there were more than fifty earthquakes.
Soon after, the former king ascended to power in Guāzhōu,
but Méngxùn killed him in Zhāngyè.
These are all established facts before your eyes,
and also known
to Your Highness.
Xiàogǔ,
the beginning of the former king's ascent;
Qiāndé,
the hall of his enthronement—
their foundations collapsed and the earth cracked,
which are omens of great misfortune.
The sun is the essence
of the Great Yang,
and the symbol of the Central Plains.
To be red and without light means
the Central Plains will be overrun and destroyed by the Húyí.
