The proverb says:
"When wild beasts enter a house,
its master will depart."
Now a fox has ascended the southern gate,
which is also a great calamity.
Moreover, "hú" (fox) is "hú" (barbarian);
heaven's will seems to say that Hú people will inhabit this city,
and rule from the south-facing seat.
In ancient Spring and Autumn period,
a star fell in Sòng,
and Duke Xiāng was eventually captured by Chǔ.
Earth is the ultimate Yīn,
an emblem of the Húyí.
It should be still but it moves,
disrupting the heavenly constant.
Heaven's will seems to say that the Húyí will shake the Central Plains,
and if the Central Plains does not cultivate virtue,
it will suffer the disaster of Sòng Xiāng.
Your subject, having received the favor of the former court while still a commoner,
has presumed to treat myself as a son or younger brother,
and therefore does not fear the punishment of offending the superior,
and risks death to present my foolish humble thoughts.
May Your
Highness draw close to the benevolent and make good neighbors,
cultivate your might and observe opportunities,
cease the construction of palaces,
and stop the pleasure of hunting.
Let the concubines and foreign women of the harem
personally receive land allocations,
and personally
encourage sericulture and weaving,
taking pride in pure frugality and simple virtue,
to stop these extravagant expenses.
Let the taxes from the common people
be solely allocated to the military and state.
Humbly welcome scholars,
widely recruit heroes and outstanding talents,
and practice the methods of the Qín clan,
to strengthen the state and enrich the populace.
Wait until the state has accumulated reserves for several years,
and the court is full of civil and military officials,
then order Hán and Bái as vanguards,
and adopt Zǐ
fáng's brilliant strategies.
With one drumbeat, Gūzāng can be pacified,
and a swift advance can lead to watering horses in Jīng and Wèi.
Then, turning eastward to contend for the world,
how could Méngxùn be a cause for worry!
Otherwise,
your subject fears that the peril to the ancestral temple will not be beyond this era.
Shìyè did not accept any of it.
Shìyè ruled for four years when Sòng received the abdication.
Shìyè was planning an eastern expedition,
but Zhāng Tǐshùn strongly admonished him,
so he stopped.
Shìyè heard that Méngxùn was attacking Tūfà Tán in the south,
and ordered internal and external forces to be on high alert,
intending to attack Zhāngyè.
Yǐn Shì strongly remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
Sòng Yáo also strongly remonstrated,
but Shìyè did not heed any of them.
Yáo retreated and sighed:
"The great task is gone!
I see the army depart,
but I will not see the army return!"
Shìyè then led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry on an eastern expedition,
stopping at Dūdújiàn.
Méngxùn came from Hàowèi,
and engaged him in battle at Huáichéng,
where Shìyè was defeated by Méngxùn.
Those around Shìyè urged him to return to Jiǔquán,
but Shìyè said:
"I have disobeyed the Empress Dowager's clear instructions,
and suffered distant defeat and humiliation.
If I do not kill these Hú,
what face will I have to see my mother again!"
He rallied his troops to fight again,
but was defeated at Liáoyuán,
and killed by Méngxùn.

Shìyè's younger brothers: Fān, Administrator of Jiǔquán; Yù, Administrator of Xīnchéng; Mì, Supervisor of the Right Imperial Guard; Tiào, General of the Left; and Liàng, General of the Right, all fled west to Dūnhuáng.
Méngxùn then entered Jiǔquán.
Before Shìyè's defeat,
a large snake entered from the southern gate,
reaching before the Gōngdé Hall;
a pair of pheasants flew out of the palace;
on a large tree on the main street, magpies and crows fought over a nest,
and the magpie was killed by the crow.
Moreover, an elder from Dūnhuáng, Línghú Chì, dreamt of a white-haired old man wearing a cap who said to Chì:
"The south wind blows,
it blows the long wood,
the Hútóng wedge,
does not fit the hub."
After speaking, he suddenly disappeared.
Shìyè's childhood name was Tóngchuí (wedge),
and at this time he died.
Fān and his younger brother Xún, Administrator of Dūnhuáng, along with their sons, abandoned Dūnhuáng
and fled to the Northern Mountains.
Méngxùn appointed Suǒ Sì's son Yuánxù to act as Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
Yuánxù was rough, dangerous, and fond of killing,
losing the support of the people.
The people of the commandery, Sòng Chéng and Zhāng Hóng, knowing that Xún had governed with benevolence in the commandery,
secretly sent a letter to invite Xún.
Xún led several tens of cavalry into Dūnhuáng,
and Yuánxù fled east to Liángxìng.
Sòng Chéng and others acclaimed Xún as General of the Champion Army and Governor of Liángzhōu.
Méngxùn dispatched his heir Dèzhèng to lead troops to attack Xún,
but Xún closed the gates and did not fight.
Méngxùn himself led twenty thousand troops to attack,
building dikes on three sides,
and flooding the city with water.
Xún sent a thousand brave men,
who linked planks to form a bridge,
secretly intending to breach the dikes.
Méngxùn rallied his troops to meet them in battle,
and slaughtered the city.
Shìyè's son Zhòng'ěr
escaped and fled to the east of the Jiāng,
serving the Sòng dynasty.
Later he returned to Wèi,
serving as Administrator of Nóng.
Méngxùn relocated Fān's sons, including Bǎo, to Gūzāng.
After more than a year,
they fled north to Yīwú.
Later they returned to Wèi,
but only Yǐn Shì and the various daughters died in Yīwú.
Xuánshèng was established in the fourth year of Āndì's Lóng'ān reign,
and was extinguished in the first year of Sòng Shàodì's Jǐngpíng reign,
holding the region west of the Yellow River for a total of twenty-four years.
The historian comments: When kings receive the mandate
to rule, they all rely on their accumulated generational virtue.
It is like the unformed chaos preceding the Great Emperor,
or the undivided primordial energy giving birth to the two opposing forces.
Thus, when Zhōngyáng rose powerfully,
he relied on the qīnlóng to form his lineage.
When Jǐngbó established his rule,
it originated from the swallow-swallowing myth that founded his line.
Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng, with his outstanding heroic spirit,
managed yin and yang to weave military might,
his adaptability was godlike.
He devoured the sun and moon to govern the heavens,
his achievements in bringing forth life were like the passage of years.
Therefore, he was able to win over the wild regions and quell brutality,
found a state and transform households.
He occupied five commanderies and declared himself a vassal,
submitting his one-third of the realm in deference.
As for the *Shī* praising Qín Zhòng,
his descendants established the work of unification.
And the *Sòng* lauding Gōng Liú,
his last heir initiated a reign worthy of heaven.
Some started their fortunes in the Qiān and Wèi rivers,
some spread their influence in Bīn and Qí.
They began with a basketful of earth to lay the foundation of the state,
and through diligent effort opened up a realm encompassing the seas.
Since they gradually achieved this,
this ruler also followed the same pattern.
Thus, it is known that where heaven's mandate rests,
it cannot be achieved in a single morning.
The accumulation of merits and blessings,
its origin is indeed ancient.
Eulogy says: Wǔzhāo, heroic and sagacious,
loyal and brave, dominated the era.
Though the royal house was in decline,
his sincerity never wavered.
The surviving populace drank of his virtue,
and distant lands received his benevolence.
Accumulated blessings and a grand foundation
enabled his future descendants to flourish.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 58: Filial Piety and Fraternity
How great it is,
the virtue of filial piety!
It divides the primordial chaos to establish form,
its Dao penetrates the three spirits.
It relies on all things to accord with their names,
its merit encompasses myriad phenomena.
Applied to the state,
it moves heaven and earth to bring down auspicious omens.
Practiced in the family,
it touches spirits and gods to manifest great blessings.
As for extensive generosity and complete provision,
honoring benevolence and securing righteousness,
gentle countenance and pleasing expressions,
joyfully exerting oneself to the utmost,
hunting fresh game for nourishment,
diligently forgetting toil,
gathering bundles of firewood in remembrance of the toil of planting millet,
and walking through the mounded paths with the ode of gathering orchids –
these are the ways of serving one's parents.
Constantly as if they were present,
grieving immensely without end,
gathering firewood and weeping profusely,
holding the halter and sighing,
facing the wind-swept trees with a desolate heart,
and gazing at the cold springs while wiping away tears –
these are the emotions of remembering the distant past.
Carefully evaluating virtue before entering officialdom,
and correcting one's duties to change positions,
being in a high position without danger,
and among the common people without contention,
assisting in cultivation and advancement to rectify transformation,
harboring the caution of treading on thin ice and tempering one's integrity –
these are the actions of establishing oneself.
Therefore, Mǐn Zēng was reverent and respectful,
following the six teachings to weave together upright principles.
Cài and Dǒng were sincere and earnest,
propagating the seven forms of conduct and leaving behind excellent examples.
There were also those whose utmost sincerity moved above,
and whose clear spirits assisted below.
Guō Jù achieved the blessing of receiving bestowed gold,
and Yáng Yōng manifested the auspiciousness of planting jade.
Crows tamed their red feathers,
nesting in Shū Hé's dwelling,
deer presented white fur,
tamed around Gōng Wén's cottage.
However, from filial piety and compassion, fraternity arises,
the principle lies in comprehensive integration,
and the meaning converges to a single standard.
The importance of heavenly bonds,
sharing the same breath and divided form,
if hearts are estranged, then the leaves of the thorny branch wither,
if natures are harmonious, then the flowers of the cherry plum blossom together.
There are those who give the fattier portions in exchange for the leaner,
yielding to the urgency of distress;
sharing fruit and sleeping under the same quilt,
exhausting the utmost of joy: if one looks into the yellowed silk texts,
these are the dusty footprints that have been left behind!
The Jìn dynasty, starting from the central court,
down to the Jiangzǒ,
though the disaster of the "hundred six" quickly arrived,
the Way of the gentleman had not vanished.
Famous figures of filial piety and fraternity
still continued one after another.
Wáng Wěiyuán's conduct,
Xǔ Jìyì's establishment of integrity,
Xià Fāng and Shèng Yàn embodying the utmost nature to spread their renown,
Yǔ Gǔn and Yán Hán earnestly valuing fraternity and proclaiming their example.
Among the rest of the gentry,
all manifested admirable virtue.
Gathering their lingering splendor,
it is enough to motivate a degenerate age,
thus, this chapter on filial piety and fraternity is written to continue the previous histories.
Lǐ Mì
Lǐ Mì, courtesy name Lìngbó,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Jiānwéi,
also known as Qián.
His father died young,
and his mother, née Hé, remarried.
Mì was only a few years old at the time,
and his longing and attachment were intense.
His sincere nature
thus caused him to fall ill.
His paternal grandmother, née Liú,
personally raised him.
Mì became known for his filial piety and reverence in serving her.
When Lady Liú was ill,
he would weep and sigh softly,
never undressing.
He would always taste her food, drink, and medicine before presenting them.
When he had leisure, he would study tirelessly,
and he became a student of Qiáo Zhōu.
Zhōu's disciples compared him to Yóu and Xià.
He served in Shǔ when young,
as a gentleman.
He was sent to Wú several times,
and his talent and eloquence were praised by the Wú people.
After Shǔ was pacified,
in the early years of Tàishǐ,
an imperial edict summoned him to be Crown Prince's Remonstrating Gentleman.
Because his grandmother was elderly
and had no one to care for her,
Mì did not answer the summons.
He then submitted a memorial, saying: "I, your subject, due to unfortunate circumstances,
suffered early misfortunes.
When I was six months old,
my loving father passed away.
At the age of four,
my maternal uncle compelled my mother to remarry.
My grandmother, Lady Liú, pitied my orphaned
and weak state,
and personally raised me.
I was frequently ill when young,
and could not walk until I was nine.
Lonely and suffering,
I reached adulthood.
Having no paternal uncles
and ultimately no brothers,
my family declined and my fortunes were meager,
and I had children late in life.
Outwardly, I have no close relatives for whom to observe mourning for one year;
inwardly, I have no young child of five *chǐ* to answer the door.
I stand alone, a solitary figure,
my body and shadow comforting each other.
Lady Liú, however, was afflicted with illness early on,
and is constantly confined to her bed.
I, your subject, attend to her medicine and soup,
never having neglected her.
Since receiving the grace of the sagely court,
and being bathed in its pure transformative influence,
the former Administrator, your subject Kuí, observed my filial piety and recommended me as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
Later, the Provincial Governor, your subject Róng, nominated me as a Talented Scholar.
I, your subject, declined to accept the appointments
because there was no one
to care for my grandmother.
A clear imperial edict was specially issued,
appointing me as a Gentleman of the Palace.
Soon after, I received imperial favor,
being appointed as Crown Prince's Remonstrating Gentleman.
Humbly, as a person of low status,
I was to serve in the Eastern Palace,
which is beyond what I, your subject,
could repay even by sacrificing my life.
I, your subject, reported everything in a memorial,
declining to take up the post.
The imperial edict was stern and severe,
accusing me of neglect and disobedience.
The commandery and county authorities pressured me,
urging me to set out.
The provincial office's delegate arrived at my door,
with the urgency of a shooting star.
If I, your subject, were to obey the edict and rush to the capital,
Lady Liú's illness would worsen daily.
If I were to follow my private feelings,
my plea would not be granted.
My advancement
To retreat,
was truly a sorry state.
I humbly reflect that the sagely court governs the world with filiality;
all the old and infirm,
still receive compassion and care,
how much more so I, who am utterly desolate, suffering, and frail.
Moreover, I served the false dynasty in my youth,
and held various posts in the departments;
my original aim was merely career advancement,
not to uphold my name and integrity.
Now, I am a humble captive of a fallen state,
of the lowest and most common status,
yet I have been unexpectedly promoted,
and granted a special imperial favor.
How could I
hesitate or harbor any further hopes!
It is merely that Liú [劉] is like the setting sun in the west,
her breath is faint and weakening,
her life is precarious and short,
she cannot foresee the morrow.
Without my grandmother,
I would not have reached
this day;
without me, my grandmother
cannot live out her remaining years.
Grandmother and grandson, we depend on each other for our lives,
thus, out of private affection, I am humbly unwilling to abandon her and go far away.
I, Lǐ Mì [李密], am
forty-four this year,
and my grandmother, Liú [劉], is ninety-six this year.
The days for me to serve Your Majesty with utmost loyalty are long,
while the days to repay and care for Liú [劉] are short.
Like the
private affection of a crow for its mother,
I beg to be allowed to care for her until her end.
My hardships
are not only known to the people of Shǔ [蜀] and the governors of the two provinces,
but Heaven and Earth truly witness them.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will pity
my foolish sincerity,
and grant my humble wish,
so that Liú [劉] may, by good fortune,
live out her remaining years.
When I live, I shall devote my life;
when I die, I shall tie grass into knots (to repay your kindness).
The emperor read it and said:
"The fame of this scholar [Lǐ Mì]
is not baseless!"
Then he rescinded the summons.
Later, after Liú [劉] died,
and the mourning period was over,
he was again summoned to Luò [洛] as a Xǐmǎ [洗馬].
Sīkōng [司空] Zhāng Huà [張華] asked him:
"How was the Duke of Ānlè [安樂公]?"
Mì [密] said:
"He can be ranked after Qí Huán [齊桓]."
Huà [華] asked for the reason,
to which he replied:
"Qí Huán [齊桓] gained Guǎn Zhòng [管仲] and became a hegemon,
but employed Shù Diāo [豎刁] and ended up in turmoil.
The Duke of Ānlè [安樂公] gained Zhūgě Liàng [諸葛亮] and resisted Wèi [魏],
but relied on Huáng Hào [黃皓] and lost his state.
From this, we know that success and failure are but one."
Next he asked:
"Why were Kǒngmíng's [孔明] instructions so fragmented?"
Mì [密] said:
"In ancient times, Shùn [舜], Yǔ [禹], and Gāo Táo [皋陶] conversed with each other,
and thus their words were concise and elegant;
the Great Announcement spoke to common people,
so it ought to be fragmented.
Kǒngmíng [孔明] had no equals among those he spoke with,
hence his instructions were fragmented."
Huà [華] praised him.
He was appointed as the magistrate of Wēn [溫],
but disliked the provincial clerk (Cóngshì [從事]).
He once wrote to someone, saying:
"If Qìngfù [慶父] does not die,
the troubles of Lǔ [魯] will not cease."
The Cóngshì [從事] reported his letter to the Sīlì [司隸],
but the Sīlì [司隸], knowing Mì [密] was honest and upright in the county,
did not impeach him.
Mì [密] possessed talent and always hoped for an internal promotion,
but lacking support in court,
he was instead transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng [漢中].
He felt he had been unfairly treated and harbored resentment.
When a farewell banquet was held in the Eastern Hall,
the imperial edict ordered Mì [密] to compose a poem.
The last stanza read:
"People also have a saying,
there are causes and conditions.
If there is no intermediary in officialdom,
it is better to return to the fields.
The enlightened one is above,
is this saying really so!"
Emperor Wǔ [武帝] was angered by this,
and so the Dūguān Cóngshì [都官從事] memorialized to dismiss Mì [密] from office.
Later, he died at home.
He had two sons: Cì [賜] and Xìng [興].
Cì [賜], courtesy name Zōngshí [宗石],
was capable of writing in his youth,
and once composed a 'Riddle of the Swallows',
the words of which were very beautiful.
The province invited him as Biéjià [別駕],
and he was nominated as Xiùcái [秀才],
but he died before taking office.
Xìng [興], courtesy name Jùnshí [雋石],
also possessed literary talent.
The Inspector Luó Shàng [羅尚] invited him as Biéjià [別駕].
When Shàng [尚] was attacked by Lǐ Xióng [李雄],
he sent Xìng [興] to the General Who Guards the South, Liú Hóng [劉弘], to seek help.
Xìng [興] then wished to stay,
serving as Hóng's [弘] Cānjūn [參軍] and did not return.
Shàng [尚] reported this to Hóng [弘],
who immediately took his ceremonial tablet and sent him away.
When Xìng [興] was in Hóng's [弘] residence,
Hóng [弘] erected steles for Zhūgě Kǒngmíng [諸葛孔明] and Yáng Shūzǐ [羊叔子],
and had Xìng [興] compose the inscriptions for both,
which possessed great literary merit and reason.
Shèng Yàn [盛彥]
Shèng Yàn's [盛彥] courtesy name was Wēngzǐ [翁子],
he was a native of Guǎnglíng [廣陵].
He showed extraordinary talent in his youth.
At the age of eight,
he visited the Grand Commandant of Wú [吳], Dài Chāng [戴昌].
Chāng [昌] presented him with a poem to observe him,
and Yàn [彥] replied in verse on the spot,
his words were very spirited.
His mother, Lady Wáng [王], lost her sight due to illness,
and whenever Yàn [彥] spoke of it,
he never failed to shed tears.
Therefore, he did not respond to invitations for official service,
and personally attended to her care,
always feeding his mother himself.
As his mother had been ill for a long time,
she often beat the maids.
The maids were resentful
and, when Yàn [彥] was briefly away,
they took roasted grubs
and fed them to her.
His mother ate them, finding them delicious,
but suspected they were something unusual,
so she secretly hid some to show Yàn [彥].
When Yàn [彥] saw them,
he embraced his mother and cried heartbrokenly,
fainting and then regaining consciousness.
His mother's eyes immediately opened brightly,
and from then on, she recovered.
Yàn [彥] served Wú [吳]
and reached the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng [中書侍郎].
When Wú [吳] was pacified,
Lù Yún [陸雲] recommended him to the Inspector Zhōu Jùn [周浚],
and Liú Sòng [劉頌], the Grand Zhongzheng [大中正] of his native district, also nominated Yàn [彥] as Xiǎo Zhōngzhèng [小中正].
He died during the Tàikāng [太康] era.
Xià Fāng [夏方]
Xià Fāng's [夏方] courtesy name was Wénzhèng [文正],
he was a native of Yǒngxīng [永興], Kuàijī [會稽].
His family suffered an epidemic,
and thirteen people, including his parents, uncles, and cousins, died.
Fāng [方] was fourteen,
and at night he would wail,
and by day he would carry earth (for burial).
After seventeen years,
the burials were finally completed.
He then built a hut by the graves,
planted pine and cypress trees,
and crows, birds, and fierce beasts became tame around him.
During the Wú [吳] period, he was appointed Rén Yì Dūwèi [仁義都尉],
and successively promoted to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng [五官中郎將].
He never rode in a carriage when attending court assemblies,
and always yielded the path when walking.
When Wú [吳] was pacified,
he was appointed as the magistrate of Gāoshān [高山].
When the common people committed crimes that warranted beating,
Fāng [方] would face them and weep without punishing them,
and no one, great or small, dared to offend.
After three years in office,
the province nominated him as Xiùcái [秀才].
He returned home,
and died
at the age of eighty-seven.
Wáng Póu [王裒]
Wáng Póu's [王裒] courtesy name was Wěiyuán [偉元],
he was a native of Yínglíng [營陵], Chéngyáng [城陽].
His grandfather, Xiū [修],
was famous in the Wèi [魏] era.
His father, Yí [儀],
was lofty, discerning, and upright,
and served as the Sīmǎ [司馬] for Emperor Wén [文帝].
During the battle of Dōngguān [東關],
the emperor asked the assembly:
"Who is to blame for the recent events?"
Yí [儀] replied:
"The blame lies with the commander-in-chief."
The emperor angrily said:
"Does the Sīmǎ [司馬] wish to shift the blame to me?!"
He then ordered him to be led out and executed.
Póu, when young, established his lofty principles.
He conducted himself with propriety.
His body was eight *chǐ* and four *cùn* tall,
his appearance was exceptionally unusual,
his voice was clear and resonant,
and his words and demeanor were refined and upright.
He was broadly learned and multitalented.
Grieved by his father's unnatural death,
he never sat facing west,
demonstrating his refusal to serve the imperial court.
Thereupon, he lived in seclusion, teaching,
and declined three summonses and seven invitations to office.
He built a hut beside his parents' tomb.
Morning and evening, he would always go to the tomb to bow and kneel,
clinging to the cypresses and weeping mournfully,
his tears wetting the trees,
causing the trees to wither.
His mother was afraid of thunder by nature.
After his mother's death,
whenever there was thunder,
he would go to the tomb and say:
"Póu is here."
And when he read the *Shī* to
"Alas, my parents,
who bore me with toil and labor,"
he never failed to repeat it three times and shed tears.
His disciples and students all abandoned the chapter of *Liáo'é*.
His family was poor,
so he personally tilled the land,
calculating the land needed for each mouth to eat,
and raising silkworms according to his own needs.
If anyone offered to help him,
he would not accept.
When his students secretly harvested wheat for him,
Póu then abandoned it.
If old acquaintances sent him gifts,
he would not accept them either.
When his students were conscripted for labor by the local county,
they asked Póu to appeal to the magistrate.
Póu said:
"Your learning is not enough to protect yourselves,
and my virtue is too meager to shelter you.
What good would appealing do?
Moreover, I have not held a writing brush for forty years."
So he walked, carrying dry rice on his shoulders,
while his children carried salted beans, fermented beans, and straw sandals,
to escort the conscripted students to the county.
More than a thousand disciples followed him.
The Magistrate of Ānqiū thought he was coming to see him,
so he straightened his clothes and went out to welcome him.
Póu then descended from the road to the side of a clay ox statue,
bowed deeply and stood,
saying:
"My students have been conscripted by the county,
so I have come to see them off."
Then he clasped their hands, wept, and departed.
The magistrate immediately released them,
and the whole county regarded it as a shame.
A fellow villager, Guǎn Yàn, was talented when young but not yet famous.
Póu alone believed that he would certainly achieve prominence,
and he singled him out and befriended him.
When their children were born,
they promised them in marriage to each other.
Later, Yàn became the Commandant of the Western Barbarians,
and when he died, he was buried in Luòyáng.
Póu later remarried his daughter.
Yàn's younger brother, Fù, asked Póu about it.
Póu said:
"My humble ambition and ultimate wish are for mountains and wilderness.
In the past, when my sisters were married, they all went far away,
and good fortune and bad were cut off.
I always swore this to myself.
Now, your esteemed brother's son buried his father in Luòyáng,
thus he is a person of the capital city.
How can this be the original intention of my forming this bond?"
Fù said:
"His mother,
being a person of Qí,
will return to Línzī."
Póu said:
"How can one bury one's father in Hénán and then follow one's mother back to Qí?
If one's intention is like this,
what marriage can there be?"
Bǐng Chūn of Běihǎi had set his aspirations high when young,
living in hardship.
He traveled with his satchel to study.
The villagers unanimously believed that Bǐng Yuán had reappeared.
Póu, however, thought that Chūn's nature was treacherous and narrow-minded, and that he merely sought fame,
and would ultimately achieve nothing.
Later, Chūn indeed lacked moral conduct
and did not complete his studies.
Those with discernment attributed this to Póu's foresight.
Póu always believed that one's actions should ultimately lead to the good path.
Why must one demand from others what they cannot do, based on what one can?
When Luòjīng fell into ruin,
and bandits rose up everywhere,
all his relatives wanted to move across the Jiāng Dōng.
Póu, however, lingered by his ancestral graves and refused to leave.
When the bandits became very powerful,
he was about to leave,
but still yearned for his home and could not proceed.
He was then killed by the bandits.
Xǔ Zī
Xǔ Zī, courtesy name Jìyì,
was a native of Wúníng, Dōngyáng.
He was filial, friendly, respectful, and yielding,
intelligent and fond of learning.
At the age of twenty,
he became a student of Kǒng Chōng of Kuàijī, the Administrator of Yùzhāng,
and studied the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, *Yì*, as well as the *Xiàojīng* and *Lúnyǔ*.
After completing his studies,
he returned to his hometown.
When Chōng died in his prefecture,
Zī, upon hearing the news, grieved deeply,
and carrying his belongings, rushed to him,
escorting the funeral procession back to Kuàijī,
eating vegetables and performing duties,
and wearing mourning clothes for three years.
Soon after, his two parents died,
and he became emaciated and skeletal from grief,
only able to rise with a staff.
He built a tomb on the East Mountain of the county,
personally carrying earth,
and refusing help from his fellow villagers.
Some people pitied Zī for his exhaustion and weakness,
and earnestly sought to help him.
Zī would not refuse them during the day,
but would remove their contributions at night.
Each time he wailed mournfully,
birds and beasts would gather and hover.
As Zī was undertaking this great task,
he abandoned his wife
and resided permanently at the tomb site,
planting pines and cypresses extending five or six *lǐ*.
At one time, a deer damaged his young pine saplings.
Zī sighed with sorrow, saying:
"Does the deer alone not think of me?"
The next day,
he suddenly saw the deer killed by a fierce beast,
placed beneath the damaged saplings.
Zī was filled with regret and sadness,
so he made a mound for it
and buried it by the side of the tomb passage.
The fierce beast then threw itself down and died in front of Zī.
Zī sighed even more,
and also took it and buried it.
From then on, the trees grew luxuriantly,
and none were damaged.
After more than twenty years,
Zī then married again,
and built a residence near the tomb.
Morning and evening, he sincerely
served the deceased as if they were alive.
Hawks and pheasants nested on his beams,
and deer from the eaves and fierce beasts roamed his courtyard and garden,
intertwining necks and playing together,
without fighting or preying on each other.
During the Yuánkāng era,
the prefecture observed and recommended him as *xiàolián*,
but he did not take office,
wearing coarse clothes his entire life.
At over eighty years old,
he died at home.
The people of the county named his residence "Xiàoshùn Lǐ".
During the Xiánkāng
period, Tài shǒu Zhāng Yú submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that the sagely and virtuous teachings depend on promoting goodness,
and the commendations and censures that arise from them
do not fade even after a thousand years.
I respectfully observe that within the territory I govern, in Wúníng
County, the deceased Xu Zī was of utmost filial and fraternal nature,
established a pure and lofty character,
was humble and deferential in his dealings with others,
and his words and actions were unwavering.
When he served his teacher,
he fulfilled the duty of ‘once, twice, thrice’;
and when he mourned his parents,
it was truly something difficult to achieve in ancient and modern times.
Everyone says that even different species were moved by him,
and fierce beasts ceased their harm.
Although your servant did not personally see him,
I have fully heard these accounts,
and I humbly believe that Cài Shùn and Dǒng Àn could not have surpassed him.
Zī has been dead for many years,
but his son is still alive,
pure and sincere in character and conduct.
He now lives by his father’s tomb.
Your servant believes that Zī’s conduct and principles
are rarely matched in the world,
and it is fitting to mark his excellent deeds
and distinguish his descendants,
to reward the past
and encourage the future.
The Chūnqiū [zhuàn] says: ‘Extend goodness to his descendants.’
Your servant does not fully comprehend the larger principles;
I request the court to deliberate on this.”
When the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict was issued to erect a commendatory marker at his gate
and exempt his descendants from labor.
His son, Shēng, also had filial conduct;
he painted Zī’s portrait in the hall
and bowed to it morning and evening.
Yǔ Gǔn
Yǔ Gǔn, courtesy name Shūbāo,
was the paternal uncle of Empress Míngmù.
From a young age, he practiced diligence and frugality,
was devoted to learning, and loved to ask questions,
and was known for his filial piety in serving his parents.
During the Xiánníng
period, there was a great plague.
His two elder brothers both died,
and his second elder brother, Pí, was also in danger.
As the plague was raging,
his parents and younger brothers all moved out to stay elsewhere,
but Gǔn alone remained and did not leave.
His paternal uncles and elder brothers urged him strongly,
but he said:
“My nature is not to fear illness.”
Thereupon, he personally tended to Pí,
staying awake day and night,
and during that time, he also continued to caress the coffins and mourn incessantly.
After more than ten ten-day periods like this,
the plague subsided,
and his family returned.
Pí recovered from his illness,
and Gǔn also remained unharmed.
The elders all said:
“How extraordinary this young man is!
He guards what others cannot guard,
and practices what others cannot practice.
Only when the year turns cold do we realize that the pine and cypress are the last to wither.
We now doubt that the plague is contagious.”
Initially,
all of Gǔn’s paternal uncles were wealthy and prominent,
but only his father remained poor and humble.
Gǔn personally engaged in farming,
to provide for his parents’ needs,
and was diligent and meticulous in his duties.
When building a fence with his younger brothers,
he would kneel to hand them the branches.
Someone asked:
“You are now in seclusion;
why such excessive deference, Sir?”
Gǔn replied:
“To change one’s conduct whether in public or private
is not the aspiration of a jūnzi.”
After his father died,
he made bamboo baskets and sold them to support his mother.
His mother, seeing his diligence,
said:
“I have nothing to eat.”
He replied:
“If Mother’s food is not sweet,
where shall Gǔn reside!”
His mother was moved and felt at peace.
Gǔn’s former wife, Lady Xún,
and his second wife, Lady Yuè,
were both from official families and wealthy households.
When they married Gǔn,
they both abandoned their luxuries,
distributed their wealth,
and shared his poverty and hardship,
treating each other with mutual respect like guests.
After his mother passed away,
he observed mourning and lived by her tomb.
There was a great famine that year,
and his wild herb soup was not even mixed with grain.
His disciples wanted to offer him food,
but Gǔn always said he had already eaten,
so no one dared to set food for him.
When the wheat ripened,
the reapers had finished,
but there was still much gleaning to be done.
Gǔn then led his children away,
saying:
“Wait for their turn.”
When it was their turn to glean,
he did not stoop low,
nor did he pick from the sides;
he knelt and gathered,
and still had a great harvest.
He also went into the mountains with the villagers to gather acorns,
dividing the easy and difficult paths,
ordering by seniority,
and yielding the easy to take the difficult,
without any breach of propriety.
Someone had cut down a cypress from his tomb,
but no one knew who it was.
He then summoned his neighbors to gather at the tomb and blamed himself,
then prostrated himself, weeping and shedding tears,
apologizing to his ancestors, saying:
“My virtue is not cultivated,
so I cannot protect the trees of my ancestors;
this is Gǔn’s fault.”
The elders all shed tears for him,
and thereafter, no one dared to offend them.
He treated the orphans with kindness,
and served the widows with benevolence,
showing extra generosity and teaching them righteous principles,
so that the elders emulated his conduct,
and the young forgot their orphaned status.
His orphaned nephew, Guō Xiù,
was treated like his own sons and nephews,
and was always given food and clothing first.
His orphaned elder brother’s daughter, Fāng,
was about to be married.
Beautiful clothes had been prepared,
but Gǔn cut thorns and reeds to make a winnowing basket and a broom,
summoned all his children to gather in the hall,
men and women by their ranks,
and ordered Fāng, saying:
“Fāng!
You were orphaned young,
and you were pampered and indulged;
we did not find fault with you.
Now you are marrying,
and you will serve your parents-in-law.
Sweeping and cleaning the inner court
is the way of a wife;
therefore, I bestow these upon you.
It is not for the beauty of the tools,
but I wish for you to be warm and respectful morning and evening,
and even if you have leisure, do not rest.”
He also gave his old residence to his eldest brother’s sons, Gēng and Xī.
When Xī died,
Gǔn grieved his early orphanage,
and was pained that he grew up but was not yet married.
He then caressed the coffin and cried out in a long lament,
his sorrow moving passersby,
and all who heard could not help but shed tears.
Initially,
Gǔn's father admonished Gǔn about alcohol.
Each time he got drunk,
he would blame himself, saying:
"I have abandoned my late father's admonition,
how can I instruct others!"
Then he would cane himself thirty times before his father's tomb.
A neighbor, Chǔ Déyì,
was skilled at serving his parents,
old but never weary;
Gǔn always bowed to him.
Once, with his elder brothers, he visited the local men Chén Zhǔn and his brothers.
His elder brothers were friendly with them
and all bowed to their mother,
but Gǔn alone did not bow.
Zhǔn's younger brother Huī said:
"Why do you not bow to my parent?"
Gǔn replied:
"I do not know the reason to bow.
Indeed, one who bows to another's parent
is effectively equating himself with that person's child;
its meaning is extremely grave,
how dare Gǔn treat it lightly!"
Thus, he did not bow.
Zhǔn and Huī sighed, saying:
"In ancient times, there were men who were bright and upright,
and you, sir, are close to them.
If you, sir, were to serve at court,
you would be a minister of the state!
If you, sir, were to hold military power
and face a great crisis,
who could sway you!
At present, with calls for recruitment,
you, sir, are truly suited for it."
Consequently, the local communities recommended him,
and provinces and commanderies repeatedly summoned him,
recommending him as 'Filial and Incorruptible',
and nominating him as 'Outstanding Talent' and 'Pure and Singular in Conduct'.
He never lowered his aspirations.
The world then referred to him as Yìxíng.
At the end of Yuánkāng,
the Administrator of Yǐngchuān summoned him to be Gōngcáo.
Gǔn wore the clothes of a laborer,
carried a spade and a hoe,
and set off without waiting for a carriage,
saying:
"Please allow me to undertake the labor of a common man."
The Administrator decorated a carriage to welcome him,
but Gǔn hesitated and declined,
asking to enter the commandery on foot.
The messengers then forced him onto the carriage
and escorted him to the Gōngcáo's residence.
Afterward, Gǔn took his own cart and slept there,
his demeanor, though respectful, showed a spirit that could not be moved.
The Administrator, knowing he would not yield,
sighed and said:
"He is no ordinary man;
how can I degrade him!"
He treated him with great courtesy and sent him away.
When Qíwáng Jǐng initiated his righteous cause,
Zhāng Hóng and others plundered Yángzhái,
so Gǔn led his clansmen and other families to seek refuge on Yǔshān.
At that time, the common people were peaceful
and knew nothing of war and defense.
Gǔn said:
"Confucius said: 'To lead the people to war without instructing them
is to throw them away.'"
Then he gathered all the gentlemen and deliberated, saying:
"You, gentlemen, are dwelling together in danger,
intending to keep your esteemed kin safe
and protect your wives and children.
The ancients said: 'A thousand people gathered without one leader,
if they do not disperse, will fall into chaos.'
What shall we do?"
The crowd said:
"Excellent.
Who but you, sir, can be the leader today!"
Gǔn was silent for a while,
then said:
"The ancients, in times of urgent peril, yielded to others and did not dare to shirk
danger.
However, when people establish a leader,
they value obedience to his commands."
Then he swore to them, saying:
"Do not rely on natural defenses,
do not exploit the chaos,
do not harm your neighbors,
do not dismantle houses,
do not cut down trees planted by others,
do not scheme unvirtuous acts,
do not commit unrighteous deeds,
but work together with one heart
to face the dangers and difficulties together."
The crowd all followed him.
Thereupon, he fortified the dangerous passes,
blocked side paths,
repaired defensive walls,
erected barriers,
evaluated contributions,
measured distances,
equalized labor and rest,
facilitated the exchange of goods,
repaired equipment,
assigned tasks according to ability,
ensured everything was appropriate for its purpose,
had each township recommend its capable men,
and each village its worthy men,
and he himself led them.
Once the divisions were clear,
commands were unambiguous,
superiors and subordinates observed etiquette,
and young and old maintained decorum.
He would promote their good qualities
and rectify their faults.
When the bandits arrived,
Gǔn arrayed his troops,
organized his ranks,
and had them all keep their bows fully drawn but not fire.
When the bandits challenged them to battle,
he remained calm and motionless,
and declined.
The bandits respected his caution and feared his orderliness,
so they all retreated.
This happened three times.
People at the time said:
"The one who 'fears when faced with a task, and succeeds through good planning'
must be Yǔ Yìxíng!"
When Jǐng returned to the capital,
and for over a year did not attend court,
Gǔn said:
"The Jìn imperial house is in decline,
and rebellion and disaster are arising!"
So he took his wife and children to Línlǜshān.
He served his new home as he had his old home,
speaking with loyalty and trustworthiness,
and acting with earnest respect.
After about a year,
the people of Línlǜ gathered around him,
all calling him Yǔ Xián.
When Shí Lè attacked Línlǜ,
the elders consulted, saying:
"Here is Dàtóushān,
the most dangerous mountain in Jiǔzhōu.
On it are traces left by ancient people;
we can hold it together."
When Huìdì moved to Cháng'ān,
Gǔn and the others ascended Dàtóushān and farmed below it.
When the year's grains were not yet ripe,
they ate wild fruits
and ingested stone marrow,
securely guarding it together,
with the intention of staying there permanently.
When it was time for harvest,
he ordered his son Yóu to descend the mountain with him.
Midway, his vision blurred,
he fell from a cliff and died.
His fellow guardians rushed to weep, saying:
"Heaven!
Can you not spare our worthy man!"
People at the time mourned him, saying:
"Yǔ Xián cut off from the dust of the world and avoided strife,
soaring high and distancing himself,
content in poverty and humble circumstances,
eating wild fruits and dwelling in the mountains.
He did not share in the world's glory,
nor compete with others for profit,
yet he could not escape fate.
Alas!"
Gǔn was learned in the Shījīng and Shūjīng;
he spoke nothing unlawful,
and did nothing unrighteous.
He revered and served the elderly,
and kindly instructed the young and ignorant.
When attending others' funerals, he always grieved deeply;
when attending others' burials, he always personally helped with the construction.
He was always first in labor,
and last in rest.
What he said, he would certainly do;
what he did, he would certainly carry out well.
Therefore, his clan and local community all respected and admired him,
and his disciples, moved by admiration,
erected a stele for him.
He had four sons: Yóu, Miè, Zé, and Jùn.
He was born in the marshes (zé),
hence named Zé;
because he was born while foraging (jùn),
he was named Jùn.
Miè later crossed the Yangtze River southwards.
At the beginning of the Restoration,
he became Shìzhōng.
Miè had a son, Yuàn,
who was the Administrator of Ānchéng.
His grandson was Guǐ.
Sūn Guǐ, courtesy name Wéndù,
was a man from Fùchūn, Wú State.
He was the great-grandson of Wú's General Fúbō, Xiùzhī.
When Guǐ was a child,
he was never scolded or angered.
Gù Róng saw him and praised him,
telling his maternal grandfather Xuē Jiān,
"This child's spirit is clear and discerning,
his resolve and disposition are upright and firm;
he is no ordinary child."
When he grew up,
he was respectful, filial, pure, and restrained.
His learning and knowledge were based on principles and righteousness.
Whenever he was alone in a secluded and dark place,
his demeanor and gaze never showed any impropriety.
Although his family was wealthy,
Guǐ always wore plain clothes, ate vegetarian food,
personally toiled in the fields,
and recited and chanted without cessation,
finding joy and contentment in his solitude.
His parents pitied him for this
and wished to grant him more ease and comfort,
but he rose early and slept late,
never slackening for a moment.
When his parents were up and ate their meals,
even though his elder brothers personally offered food,
Guǐ would not leave their side.
As carriage roads were scarce in Fùchūn
and journeys often involved crossing rivers,
his father found the wind and waves difficult.
Whenever he traveled, he rode in a basket palanquin.
Guǐ personally supported and attended him.
Upon reaching their destination,
he would rest hidden among the trees or behind a fence outside the gate,
never letting the host know.
His elder brother once suffered a severe illness for a year.
Guǐ personally supported and attended him,
carefully noting the sweetness and bitterness of his medicines.
He personally focused on the details.
He traveled through mountains and waters,
praying with utmost sincerity.
When he heard of people's good deeds,
he rejoiced as if he himself had gained something;
when he heard of people's evil deeds,
he felt sorrow as if he had lost something.
When he saw people suffering from hunger and cold,
he always provided for them.
He received no gifts or offerings from the local community.
He accepted nothing.
There were several poor and elderly relatives and acquaintances
who frequently came to beg.
Many people treated them with disdain,
but when Guǐ saw them,
his respect and joy were even greater.
In cold weather, he shared his quilt with them;
for meals, he shared his utensils,
or even removed his clothes and pushed his quilt to comfort them.
During a time of famine and high grain prices,
someone was cutting his rice stalks while they were still green.
Guǐ saw him and avoided him,
waiting until he had left before coming out.
Afterward, he harvested his own rice and sent it to the person.
His neighbors felt touched and ashamed,
and none dared to encroach upon him.
Yú Xǐ of Kuàijī lived as a recluse by the sea,
possessing a noble character that transcended the world.
Guǐ admired his virtue
and engaged Xǐ's younger brother Yù's daughter as his wife.
Xǐ admonished his daughter to abandon extravagance and embrace simplicity,
to share Guǐ's aspirations.
People at the time called them the Liáng Hóng couple.
Jièyáng's Jiāng Dūn had a noble character from a young age.
Hearing that Guǐ's learning and conduct surpassed others,
he traveled from Dōngyáng to visit him.
Upon their first meeting,
they talked and feasted all day,
parting as firm friends.
Sīkōng Hé Chōng, when he was Governor of Yángzhōu,
summoned Guǐ to be his Master of Records,
and Sītú Cài Mó appointed him as a subordinate official;
he accepted neither.
Shàngshū Zhāng Guómíng,
a prominent figure in the region,
recommended Guǐ in a memorial,
and the Public Coach Office specially summoned him.
He died shortly after,
at the age of thirty-eight.
Both court and commoners lamented his death.
Before Guǐ's formal encoffining,
an old man, wearing a coarse gown and straw sandals,
without giving his name,
went directly to touch the coffin and wept.
His cries were mournful and impassioned,
moving those around him.
After he stopped weeping, he left immediately.
His appearance was very clear,
and his pupils were square.
The gatekeeper told the family of the deceased,
who, surprised, pursued him.
He went straight on without looking back.
Gù Hé and over a hundred others from the same commandery marveled at his unusual divine appearance,
but none could comprehend him.
Yán Hán
Yán Hán, courtesy name Hóngdū,
was a man from Shēn, Lángxié.
His grandfather, Qīn,
was a Gěishìzhōng.
His father, Mò,
was the Administrator of Rǔyīn.
Hán had a noble character and conduct from a young age,
and was renowned for his filial piety.
His elder brother, Jī,
fell ill during the Xiánníng era.
He sought a doctor and treated himself,
but subsequently died at the doctor's house.
When the family brought the coffin home,
the funeral banner always wrapped around trees and could not be untangled.
Those pulling the coffin stumbled,
and Jī's voice spoke, saying:
"My lifespan has not yet ended;
I simply took too much medicine,
which harmed my five viscera.
I am about to revive;
be sure not to bury me."
His father prayed, saying:
"If you are destined to be reborn,
how could it not be what your flesh and blood desire!
For now, we only wish to return home;
we will not bury you."
The banner then untangled.
Upon their return,
his wife dreamt of him saying:
"I am about to revive;
you must open the coffin quickly."
His wife was quite alarmed and told others.
That evening,
his mother and other family members also dreamt of him.
They immediately wanted to open the coffin,
but his father refused.
Hán was still young at the time,
but he resolutely said:
"Extraordinary events
have occurred in ancient times.
Now that such a spiritual marvel has appeared,
the pain of opening the coffin,
how does it compare to the regret of not opening it and failing him?"
His parents followed his advice.
They then opened the coffin together,
and indeed there were signs of life.
He had scratched the coffin with his hands,
his fingernails were all injured,
but his breath was extremely faint,
making it impossible to tell if he was alive or dead.
They gave him drinks and food and nursed him,
but for several months he still could not speak.
His needs for food and drink
were communicated through dreams.
The whole family devoted themselves to caring for him,
completely abandoning their livelihoods.
Even his mother and wife
could not avoid feeling weary.
Hán then completely abandoned worldly affairs,
personally attending and caring for him,
not leaving the house for thirteen years.
Shí Chóng valued Hán's pure conduct
and sent him sweet and delicious provisions.
Hán declined and did not accept.
Someone asked him why,
and he replied:
"The patient is muddled,
his vital functions not fully restored.
He cannot eat,
nor does he recognize human kindness.
If I were to wrongly keep these,
would it be the giver's intention?"
Jī ultimately did not recover.
Yán Hán’s parents both passed away;
his two elder brothers died successively.
His second sister-in-law, Fán Shì, lost her sight due to illness.
Yán Hán diligently encouraged his household,
devoting himself to supporting her.
Each day, he personally tasted her medicines and food,
inquiring about her state of being.
He would always wear his hairpins and shoes, and tie his belt.
A physician prescribed a formula
that required snake gall,
but despite extensive searching,
there was no way to obtain it.
Yán Hán sighed with worry for a long time.
One day, while sitting alone during the daytime,
a green-clad youth, about thirteen or fourteen years old,
suddenly appeared, holding a green pouch, which he handed to Yán Hán.
Yán Hán opened it and looked;
it was indeed snake gall.
The youth lingered for a moment, then went out the door,
transformed into a green bird, and flew away.
Having obtained the gall,
the medicine was prepared,
and his sister-in-law’s illness immediately recovered.
From this, he became well-known.
His home prefecture invited him,
but he did not accept.
Sīmǎ Yuè, Prince of Dōnghǎi, appointed him as a Staff Officer to the Grand Tutor.
He was then transferred to serve as Magistrate of Kāiyáng.
When Yuándì first garrisoned Xiàpī,
he again appointed him as a Staff Officer.
After crossing the Jiāng,
Yán Hán was made Magistrate of Shàngyú,
then transferred to Langzhong of the Royal Domain,
and Sacrificial Libation Officer of the Chancellor’s Eastern Office.
He was then assigned as Administrator of Dōngyáng.
When the Eastern Palace was first established,
Yán Hán, for his scholarly purity and steadfast conduct, was appointed Central Secretariat Officer to the Crown Prince.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Grand Arbiter of his home prefecture,
and successively served as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Minister of Agriculture.
For his merit in suppressing Sū Jùn,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīpíng County,
appointed Chamberlain,
and then made Administrator of Wújùn.
Wáng Dǎo asked Yán Hán,
"Now that you are overseeing a famous commandery,
what will be your priority in governance?"
He replied,
"The royal army moves annually,
leaving registered households empty and depleted.
Powerful families, both north and south, vie to attract wandering laborers,
making the state impoverished and individual families rich—this is the concern of those in office.
Therefore, we should primarily conscript people from powerful households,
making them return to farming and sericulture.
Within a few years,
I wish to ensure that every household has enough, and every person is sufficient,
as for ritual and music,
I will await an enlightened administrator for that."
Yán Hán was simple and benevolent in his various posts,
perceptive and decisive,
yet he governed his subordinates with authority.
Wáng Dǎo sighed, saying,
"With Lord Yán in office,
the people of Wú will rein themselves in!"
Before taking up his new post,
he was again made Chamberlain.
Soon after, he was appointed Libationer of the National University,
with the added title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and promoted to Minister of the Palace Gate.
Due to old age, he resigned his position.
Chéngdì admired his pure conduct
and personally bestowed upon him the title of Grand Master of Guanglu on the Right,
allowing horses to enter his gate,
and gifted him a bed, curtains, quilts, and blankets.
He also ordered the Grand Provisioner to deliver food seasonally,
but Yán Hán firmly declined to accept.
At that time, commentators believed that since Wáng Dǎo was the Emperor’s tutor,
his status was exceptionally high,
and all officials should show him greater deference.
Tàicháng Féng Huái asked Yán Hán about this.
Yán Hán said,
"Although Lord Wáng is distinguished,
there is no reason for preferential respect.
Talk of showing greater deference
might be appropriate for others.
As for this old man,
I do not understand the current affairs."
Afterwards, he told someone,
"I have heard that when attacking a state, one does not consult benevolent people.
Just now, Féng Zǔsī asked me to flatter,
do I possess a wicked virtue?"
Someone once debated whether Shàozhèng Mǎo or Dàozhí was more wicked.
One person said,
"Although Shàozhèng Mǎo was treacherous,
he did not go so far as to carve people up for food.
Dàozhí was more extreme."
Yán Hán said,
"When evil is manifest and exposed,
people desire to inflict punishment;
hidden treachery,
cannot be eliminated except by a sage.
From this perspective,
Shàozhèng Mǎo was more extreme."
The multitude was all convinced.
Guō Pú once met Yán Hán
and wished to divine for him.
Yán Hán said,
"One's lifespan is determined by Heaven,
one's position by men.
To cultivate oneself yet Heaven does not grant it,
is destiny;
to uphold the Way yet people do not recognize it,
is nature.
I have my own nature and destiny;
there is no need for milfoil or tortoise shell."
Huán Wēn sought a marriage alliance with Yán Hán,
but Yán Hán, considering Huán Wēn's excessive success,
did not agree.
He only had a deep friendship with Dèng Yōu.
Someone asked about the relative merits of the scholars south of the Jiāng.
He replied,
"Zhōu Bórén’s uprightness,
Dèng Bódào’s purity,
Biàn Wàngzhī’s integrity,
as for the rest, I do not know."
His refined respect for deeds and sincerity,
and his suppression of frivolous fakery, were like this.
He retired from office for over twenty years
and died at the age of ninety-three.
His dying wish was for a plain coffin and simple burial.
He was posthumously given the epithet Jìng.
While his coffin was awaiting burial, a fire broke out in a neighboring house.
As they moved the coffin, the ropes broke.
The fire was about to reach them but then extinguished.
Everyone believed this was due to his pure sincerity.
He had three sons: Máo, Qiān, and Yuē.
Yán Máo successively served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Chamberlain, and Minister of the Palace Gate.
Yán Qiān reached the position of Administrator of Ānchéng.
Yán Yuē was Administrator of Línglíng.
All had good reputations.
Liú Yīn
Liú Yīn, courtesy name Zhǎngshèng,
was a native of Xīnxīng.
His great-grandfather, Líng,
was a Grand Master of Guanglu in the Hàn dynasty.
Liú Yīn lost his father at the age of seven,
grieving and emaciated beyond customary rites.
During his three years of mourning,
he never once showed his teeth (in a smile).
His great-grandmother, Wáng Shì, craved mallow in the dead of winter but did not speak of it,
and had not eaten her fill for ten days.
Liú Yīn, finding this strange, asked her,
and Wáng Shì explained the reason.
Liú Yīn, then nine years old,
cried bitterly in the marshes,
saying,
"My sins are deep and grave;
in my youth, I suffer hardship and punishment.
My great-grandmother is in the hall,
yet I cannot provide for her for even a month.
As a son,
I cannot obtain what she desires.
Oh, August Heaven and Sovereign Earth,
I pray for your pity and compassion."
His crying did not cease for half a day.
Then, suddenly, someone seemed to say,
"Stop,
stop crying."
Liú Yīn wiped away his tears and looked at the ground;
mallow had sprouted there.
He thus gathered over a *hu* (bushel) and returned home.
They ate from it without diminishing its supply,
until the season for mallow to grow naturally ended.
Another time, he dreamt at night that someone told him,
"There is millet under the western fence."
He awoke and dug there,
finding fifteen *zhōng* (bells/measures) of millet.
The inscription read:
"Seven years' supply of a hundred *dan* of millet,
bestowed upon the filial son Liú Yīn."
From then on, they ate from it,
and it lasted for seven years.
People at the time praised his extreme sincerity that moved Heaven and Earth,
and competed to give him grain and silk.
Liú Yīn accepted them without expressing gratitude,
simply saying, "I will repay you when I achieve nobility."
When he reached manhood,
he was extensively learned in the classics and histories,
comprehensively examining all sayings.
There was no essay, poem, or rhymed prose he did not widely read.
His nature was unconventional and unrestrained,
with an ambition to save the world.
He was frugal without being uncouth,
and pure without being aloof.
When one looked at him, he appeared relaxed yet inviolable.
His village, relatives, and clan all praised him.
The commandery appointed him Main Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and the province invited him as a Manager (Cóngshì).
He declined both, citing that
his mother had no one to support her.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Prince of Qí, Sīmǎ Yōu (Sīmǎ Yōu), invited him to be a Retainer (Yuán),
and General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn), Yáng Hù (Yáng Hù), summoned him to be a Military Advisor (Cānjūnshì).
He declined both due to illness.
Zhāng Xuānzǐ (Zhāng Xuānzǐ) from the same commandery,
a discerning and perceptive scholar,
urged Yīn (Yīn) to accept the summons.
Yīn (Yīn) said:
"The two lords today
are the pillars and beams of Jìn (Jìn).
I aspire to be merely a rafter or beam;
if I do not rely on them,
how can I stand?
My royal mother is now in the hall;
if I were to accept other commands,
I would be unable to exhaust my duty as a minister,
and thus would not be able to provide for her.
The reason Zǐyú (Zǐyú) declined the Grandee (Dàfū) position in Qí (Qí)
was truly because his parents had no one to attend to them."
Xuānzǐ (Xuānzǐ) said:
"What you say,
how can an ordinary person understand it?
From now on,
you shall be my teacher."
He then gave his daughter to him in marriage.
Xuānzǐ (Xuānzǐ)
was a prominent family in Bìngzhōu (Bìngzhōu),
wealthy in possessions.
His wife angrily said:
"Our daughter is only fourteen years old.
With such looks and intelligence,
what worry is there that she would not become a consort to a duke or marquis?
Why hastily marry her to Liú Yīn (Liú Yīn)?"
Xuānzǐ (Xuānzǐ) said:
"This is beyond your understanding."
He admonished his daughter, saying:
"Liú Yīn (Liú Yīn)'s utmost filial piety deeply moves the heavens,
and his talent and insight surpass the age.
This man will eventually achieve great distinction
and become a renowned duke in the world.
You must serve him carefully."
Zhāng Shì (Zhāng Shì)'s nature was also gentle and compliant.
She was known for her filial piety in serving the royal mother,
and attended to Yīn (Yīn) as if he were a sovereign or father.
When Queen Wáng (Wáng) passed away,
Yīn (Yīn) and his wife wasted away from grief,
nearly to the point of extinction of life.
At that time, the coffin was in mourning, and a fire broke out in the western neighbor's house.
The wind was very strong.
Yīn (Yīn) and his wife knocked on the coffin and cried out,
and the fire then skipped over and burned the eastern house instead.
Later, two white doves nested in their courtyard tree.
From then on, his reputation became even more prominent.
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Yáng Jùn (Yáng Jùn), while regent,
formally invited Yīn (Yīn),
but Yīn (Yīn) firmly declined, citing his aged mother.
Jùn (Jùn) then memorialized about him,
and a gracious imperial edict allowed him to fulfill his noble aspiration,
permitting him to continue supporting his parents until the end.
It ordered the local authorities to provide him with clothing and food,
exempt him from labor services and taxes,
and bestowed upon him two hundred bolts of silk
and five hundred *hú* of grain.
When Prince of Zhào, Sīmǎ Lún (Sīmǎ Lún), usurped the throne,
Sūn Xiù (Sūn Xiù), who had long esteemed Yīn (Yīn)'s reputation,
summoned him as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì).
Yīn (Yīn) fled to Yànmén (Yànmén).
When Prince of Qí, Sīmǎ Jiǒng (Sīmǎ Jiǒng), became regent,
he was appointed Wine Libationer for the Grand Marshal's (Dà Sīmǎ) Military Council (Jūnzī Jìjiǔ).
Upon his arrival,
Jiǒng (Jiǒng) said to Yīn (Yīn):
"The late king (Sīmǎ Yōu) sincerely invited you,
but you did not come.
Now I invite you,
how is it that you can condescend to come?"
Yīn (Yīn) replied:
"Emperor Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) corresponded to the era as a great sage,
and the late king assisted the world with his utmost virtue.
With Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn) as rulers,
and Jì (Jì) and Xiè (Xiè) as assistants,
therefore, I hoped to resist a thousand chariots as a single commoner,
making an unalterable plan,
and fortunately to encounter the age of Táng (Táng) and Yú (Yú) (Yáo and Shùn).
Thus, I did not fear execution by axe.
Now Your Highness, with your divine martial prowess and sagacious disposition,
has eliminated the wicked and restored proper governance.
However, the traces of sageliness are somewhat rough,
and strict majesty is growing stern.
If I were to act as before,
I fear I would incur the punishment of Huá Shì (Huá Shì) (referring to criticism and execution for inappropriate advice),
so I dared not not come."
Jiǒng (Jiǒng) was impressed by him,
and transferred him to be Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xīnxīng (Xīnxīng).
He clarified laws and commended the good,
showing great administrative ability.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā (Yǒngjiā),
he was captured by Liú Cōng (Liú Cōng).
〔一０〕Cōng (Cōng) was impressed by his talent and promoted him,
eventually reaching the positions of Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng), Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo), and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
Yīn (Yīn) admonished his children and grandchildren, saying:
"The method of serving one's ruler
should prioritize subtle admonition.
Even ordinary people should not be openly criticized for their faults,
let alone the Son of Heaven!
The calamity of offending the ruler's dignity
will only expose the ruler's faults.
One should reflect on the example of Shào Gōng (Shào Gōng) consulting and discussing with the king (Wǔ Wáng),
and below, remember Bào Xūn (Bào Xūn)'s punishment for touching the dragon's scales (offending the emperor)."
In Cōng (Cōng)'s court,
he was always humble and deferential with the high officials,
always appearing to put himself last.
Scholars who did not cultivate their conduct
were not allowed to enter his gate.
However, those whose just arguments were not advanced,
and who succeeded through Yīn (Yīn)'s help,
also numbered in the hundreds.
He had seven sons.
Five sons were taught one classic each,
one son was taught the *Shǐ Jì* (Tàishǐ Gōng),
and one son was taught the *Hàn Shū*.
Within one family,
seven scholarly pursuits flourished together.
Among the scholars of the northern provinces,
Yīn (Yīn)'s family was the most prominent.
He eventually died of old age.
Wáng Yán
Wáng Yán (Wáng Yán), courtesy name Yányuán (Yányuán),
was a person from Xīhé (Xīhé).
At nine years old, he lost his mother.
He wept blood for three years,
nearly to the point of extinction of life.
Whenever the anniversary of her death arrived,
he would weep sorrowfully for ten days.
〔一一〕His stepmother, Bǔ Shì (Bǔ Shì), treated him cruelly.
She gave Yán (Yán) rushes and old hemp scraps to pad his clothes.
His aunt heard of this and asked him,
but Yán (Yán), knowing the situation, did not speak of it,
and served his mother even more diligently.
Bǔ Shì (Bǔ Shì) once craved fresh fish in the deep winter.
She ordered Yán (Yán) to find some, but he could not,
so she beat him until he bled.
Yán (Yán) then sought the Fén (Fén) River, knocked on the ice, and wept.
Suddenly, a fish, five feet long,
leapt out of the water.
Yán (Yán) took it and presented it to his mother.
Bǔ Shì (Bǔ Shì) ate it,
and it lasted for many days.
Thereupon, her heart was enlightened,
and she treated Yán (Yán) as if he were her own son.
Yán (Yán) served his parents with filial care.
In summer, he fanned their pillows and mats;
in winter, he warmed their quilt with his body.
In the severe cold of deep winter,
he himself had no complete clothing,
yet his parents enjoyed the finest delicacies.
By day he worked as a laborer,
by night he recited books.
He eventually thoroughly read the classics and histories,
understanding all their great principles.
The province and commandery invited him with courtesy,
but he valued providing for his parents and did not rise to office.
After his parents passed away,
he built a hut by their grave.
He would not wear silk unless he himself raised the silkworms,
nor eat grain unless he himself cultivated it.
During the chaos and disintegration of the world,
he followed Liú Yuánhǎi (Liú Yuánhǎi) and relocated to Píngyáng (Píngyáng).
In his leisure from farming and silkworm raising,
he instructed and guided his clan,
speaking earnestly and tirelessly.
His family cow gave birth to a calf.
Another person claimed it.
Yán (Yán) led the calf and gave it to him,
showing no sign of reluctance.
The person later realized his mistaken claim,
returned the calf to Yán (Yán),
and prostrated himself to apologize.
Yán (Yán) still gave it to him,
and did not take it back.
When he was sixty,
Fāng served Liú Cōng,
gradually rising to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
and then to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
After Cōng died,
Jìn Zhǔn was about to rebel.
He consulted Yán,
but Yán refused to follow.
After Zhǔn executed the Liú clan,
he proclaimed himself Hàn Tiānwáng,
and appointed Yán as Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Yán again vehemently refused to accept,
so Zhǔn killed him.
Wáng Tán
Wáng Tán
was a native of Wūchéng, Wúxīng.
When he was ten years old,
his father was killed by a neighbor, Dòu Dù.
Tán secretly harbored a desire for revenge,
but feared Dù would suspect him,
so he kept no blade of any size.
He watched Dù day and night,
but never found an opportunity.
When he reached eighteen,
he secretly bought a sharp spade,
pretending to be a farmer cultivating the land.
Dù often traveled by boat,
passing under a certain bridge.
Tán waited for Dù to return,
hiding in the grass.
Once Dù had passed,
Tán, from on the bridge, struck him with the spade,
and he died instantly.
Afterward, he surrendered to the authorities.
The Grand Administrator Kǒng Yán considered his filial piety and courage righteous,
〔一二〕and submitted a memorial to pardon him.
Yán’s sons were killed by Sūn Ēn,
leaving no heir.
Tán then moved to Kuàijī
and repaired the tombs of Yán and his sons,
devoting all his strength.
Later, the Grand Administrator Kǒng Xìn investigated his righteous conduct.
In the third year of Yuánxīng (404 CE),
he recommended Tán as Xiaolián.
People at the time praised the excellent choice of person.
Tán did not answer the summons
and died at home.
Sāng Yú
Sāng Yú, courtesy name Zǐshēn,
was a native of Líyáng, Wèijùn.
His father, Chōng,
possessed profound insight and farsighted judgment.
During Emperor Huì's reign, he served as Huángmén Láng.
When Hékàn Wáng Yóng held power,
he invited Chōng to be Sīmǎ.
Chōng knew Yóng would inevitably fail,
so after holding the post for ten days,
he feigned illness and requested to retire.
Yú was naturally benevolent and filial.
He lost his father at fourteen,
and his grief and emaciation exceeded the rites.
He ate a hundred grains of rice daily mixed with wild greens.
His elder sister admonished him, saying:
"If you emaciate yourself like this,
you will surely destroy your life.
Destroying your life is unfilial.
You should restrain yourself."
Yú replied:
"Wild greens mixed with rice
are sufficient to overcome my sorrow."
Yú had a garden several miles north of his residence.
When the melons and fruits were first ripe,
someone climbed over the wall to steal them.
Yú considered that the garden fence had many thorny brambles,
and feared that if the thief saw people and fled in surprise, he would get injured.
So he ordered his servant to clear a path for them.
When the thief was carrying the stolen melons out,
he saw the path was open and clear.
Realizing Yú had cleared it,
he returned the stolen melons
and kowtowed to beg for forgiveness.
Yú was delighted
and gave all the melons to him.
Once, while traveling,
he lodged at an inn.
A fellow guest lost some dried meat
and suspected Yú of stealing it.
Yú remained silent,
then took off his clothes to compensate him.
The innkeeper said:
"This inn often loses fish, meat, chickens, and ducks;
it's mostly foxes or badgers that steal them.
Why do you suspect a person?"
Then he led the owner of the dried meat to search among the mountain tombs
and indeed found it.
The guest asked for his clothes back,
but Yú threw them away without looking.
Yú's elder brothers served during the era of Shí Lè,
all attaining prominent positions.
Only Yú felt ashamed to serve non-Han rulers
and secretly wished to relocate to the east of the sea.
However, he encountered his mother's mourning,
and so he stayed.
His grief and emaciation reduced him to skin and bones,
and he built a hut by the tomb.
Five years later,
Shí Lè appointed him as Wǔchéng Magistrate.
Yú, considering Wǔchéng to be close to the Yellow River
and slightly near the sea,
intended to fulfill his earlier ambition,
and gladly took up the post.
Shí Jìlóng's Grand Administrator Liú Zhēng highly esteemed him.
When Zhēng was promoted to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he invited Yú to be his Chángshǐ,
also holding the title for Zhù'ā Jùn.
When Zhēng fell ill and returned to Yè,
he ordered Yú to oversee the provincial administration.
After Jìlóng died,
the country fell into great chaos.
The imperial court, considering Yú to be the son of a famous father,
believed he could certainly achieve great deeds in Hǎidài,
and secretly sent Huá Tǐng, a man from Dōngguǎn, to appoint Yú as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yú said:
"Fame and achievement are not my aspirations."
So he attached a memorial to the envoy to decline the Cìshǐ position,
and lived peacefully in Hǎiyòu,
not interacting with the outside world.
Although he lived through a 'pretender' dynasty,
he did not participate in its troubles,
and the world held him in high regard for this.
He died in office.
Yú lived with five generations under one roof,
and his household was harmonious.
Fú Jiān's Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Fú Lǎng highly respected him.
He once visited Yú's home,
ascended the hall, and bowed to his mother.
People at the time considered this an honor.
Hé Qí
Hé Qí, courtesy name Wànlún,
was the paternal cousin of Sīkōng Chōng.
His grandfather, Kān,
was Hòujiāngjūn.
His father, Fù,
was Huáinán Nèishǐ.
Qí lost his father at fourteen,
and his grief and emaciation exceeded the rites.
He was profound and perceptive by nature, possessing good judgment,
fond of ancient learning and extensively knowledgeable.
He resided in Yánggǔ County, Xuānchéng,
serving his mother diligently,
caring for her morning and evening.
He often worried that he couldn't provide enough sweet and fresh food,
so he became a Jùn Zhǔbù,
was selected as Xiaolián,
appointed as Lángzhōng,
and then chosen to serve as Magistrate of Jīng County, Xuānchéng.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo invited him to be his Cānjūn,
but he did not accept.
When he encountered his mother's mourning,
he wept blood during the period of mourning,
and could only rise with the aid of a staff.
His mother's coffin was placed in the temporary burial hall,
when it was threatened by a neighbor's fire.
Smoke and flames were already intertwined,
and his household lacked servants.
He had no plan to escape the situation,
so he crawled forward, embracing the coffin and wailing.
Suddenly, the wind stopped and the fire subsided,
and one room of the main hall was spared from burning.
Such was the power of his sincere devotion.
When the mourning period ended,
he sighed with emotion and said:
"The reason I embarked on an official career
was not because I possessed extraordinary ability to offer wisdom and strength,
but truly to seek a meager salary
to support my parents privately.
Now, suddenly, I am solitary,
without anyone to rely on or depend on.
How can I, with my decaying and dull nature, again defile the pure court?"
Thereupon, he nurtured his aspirations behind a humble gate,
not engaging in worldly affairs.
He devoted himself to studying classics,
finding joy in zither and books.
He did not manage property,
was frugal and had few desires,
sharing abundance and scarcity with his neighbors.
When his village suffered from chaos,
his elder sister was lost to another family.
Qí had only one maidservant,
whom he sold to redeem his sister.
However, he was not overly modest;
whenever he received gifts,
he did not decline them casually.
But if he had more than enough for himself,
he would readily distribute it.
He acted according to his heart,
and moved as his will dictated.
He did not practice divination,
nor did he consult anyone.
Sīkōng Lù Wán and Tàiwèi Huán Wēn both invited him to serve,
but he declined all offers.
An imperial edict summoned him as a Bóshì,
but he still did not respond.
During the reign of Emperor Jiǎnwén, who was then Fǔjūn,
he admired Qí's reputation and conduct,
and summoned him to be Cānjūn,
but he firmly declined, citing illness.
The imperial carriage made a second summons for Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng and Sànqí Chángshì,
but he did not go.
Because of this, gentlemen revered his virtue,
and none could compel him.
Huán Wēn once ascended the mountain on the border of Qí's county,
and sighed deeply, saying:
"On the south side of this mountain lives a man!
What a truly content person Hé Qí is!"
Qí was skilled in self-cultivation,
and did not decline with age.
He wore coarse clothes and ate plain food,
devoting himself to writing.
He authored "Sānguó Pínglùn,"
[一三] and all his compiled works amounted to about a hundred essays,
all circulating in the world.
He died at the age of eighty-two.
Wú Kuí
Wú Kuí
was from Wúxīng.
After experiencing famine and illness,
thirteen members of his household died.
Kuí himself was also critically ill at the time,
and all their bodies were wrapped in straw mats by neighbors and buried.
Kuí and his wife survived,
but their family was extremely poor and distressed.
In winter, they had no clothes or bedding.
During the day, he worked as a laborer;
at night, he burned bricks.
He was in the mountains day and night,
never resting.
When he encountered venomous insects or fierce beasts,
he would make way for them.
Within a year,
he completed seven graves and thirteen coffins.
At that time, there were offers of funeral contributions,
but he accepted none.
Tàishǒu Zhāng Chóng admired his righteousness,
and treated him with the courtesy due to a man of integrity.
He died at home.
The historian says: The way of honoring parents
is a clear teaching in the Rítuál classics;
the virtue of filial piety and brotherly love
is a beautiful tale among poets.
From this, one knows that the foundation of human relations
is nothing other than what these uphold.
Shèng Wēngzǐ's conduct was pure and profound,
he naturally possessed extraordinary talent.
His heartfelt grief brought about empathetic response,
and his nurturing care fulfilled his duty to his parents.
Dài Chāng praised his pure elegance,
Lù Yún admired his flourishing virtue.
Wáng Póu lived in reclusion and did not accept summons,
his conduct never exceeded the bounds of propriety.
The withered cypress responded to his sincerity,
and startling thunder threatened his concern.
Forever we speak of Dǒng Cài,
who in different times were equally excellent.
Xǔ Zī was keen in learning from a young age,
his rituals were fully observed.
Tame pheasants perched on his beams and pillars,
and fierce beasts disturbed his courtyard and garden.
His observance of mourning rituals
was truly difficult for both ancient and modern times.
Yú Shūbāo's diligence did not fail in his duties,
and his generosity existed in his reverence for his profession.
His integrity did not change whether in obscurity or prominence,
and plague did not disturb his heart.
His rule of giving way to the sick and injured
possessed the noble spirit of ancient people.
Sūn Guǐ's tireless effort,
Wáng Tán's revenge,
gods and men mourned their passing,
and good governors pardoned their crimes.
Liú Yīn, afflicted by harsh grief in his youth,
wasted away beyond customary limits.
He picked violets in three winters,
and was granted grain for seven years.
The bond of utmost sincerity
was manifested here in righteousness.
Wáng Yán broke ice to summon fish,
and fanned mats to cool the summer heat.
Even Huáng Xiāng and Mèng Zōng
were considered his peers.
The rest of the gentlemen
were all worthy of respect for their filial piety and nurturing.
Their pure conduct and noble examples
are like high mountains and grand deeds,
converging into a common stream,
sharing this same aspiration.
A eulogy says: Where virtue reaches,
there must be a response.
How filial were Wáng and Xǔ,
their everlasting longing ever so profound.
Tears flowed, withering the cypress;
facing the coffin, eagles nested.
Mì, Yàn, Xià, Yú,
early displayed their ultimate nature.
Wéndù, Hóngdū,
diligently cultivated admirable conduct.
They upheld filial piety and brotherly love,
shining forth in songs and praises.
Tame doves for Chángshèng,
fish offered for Yányuán.
Tán's mulberry, Yì's elucidation,
Qí's and Wú's principles preserved.
The virtue of Zhāndòng
is all illuminated in the words to the left.
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 59: Loyal and Righteous
An ancient saying goes:
"A junzǐ sacrifices his life to achieve benevolence,
not seeking life by harming benevolence."
It also says:
"It is not difficult to die,
but difficult to face death."
These words are truly trustworthy!
Therefore, one knows that if sacrificing one's integrity aligns with what is proper,
a righteous man will not regret his demise;
if giving up one's body is for a worthy cause,
a heroic person will not begrudge his existence.
Thus, they were able to maintain profound iron-and-stone determination,
and refine the noble character of pine and bamboo.
They showed their steadfast hearts at the year's end,
and displayed their unyielding integrity against fierce winds.
They faced the cauldron as if returning home,
and trod through peril and ruin without looking back.
Their names were inscribed on bamboo and silk,
and their images painted in vivid colors.
Previous historians considered them beautiful tales,
and later generations look up to their glorious deeds.
After the Yuánkāng reign, the [Jìn] Dynasty
experienced political turmoil and a chaotic court.
Calamities and difficulties arose successively,
and distress became widespread.
This allowed villains and evildoers to run rampant,
