while the Róng and Dí tribes launched repeated invasions,
causing the whole of Huáxià to boil over,
and the common people to suffer greatly.
Warfare was daily,
and battles frequently erupted.
Although those who abandoned kindness and forgot righteousness were innumerable,
there was no shortage of those who upheld principles and sacrificed their lives in those times.
Such as Jī Shào, who protected the imperial carriage during danger;
Biàn Hú, who died on the battlefield;
Huán Xióng, whose righteousness surpassed that of Tián Shú;
Zhōu Qí, whose integrity exceeded that of Xiè Yáng;
Luó Dīng, who gave his life for his former lord;
Xīn Jí, who was ashamed to serve the Róng and Lǔ barbarians;
Zhāng Yī, who took poison to preserve his integrity;
and Wáng Liàng, who cut off his arm to demonstrate his loyalty.
All of them displayed spirits as fervent as autumn frost,
and their essence pierced the bright sun.
They were sufficient to inspire a pure spirit for ten thousand ages,
and to invigorate the decadent customs of their own time!
As the saying goes, "In a chaotic world, loyal ministers are known"—
this is what it refers to.
Biàn Hú, Liú Chāo, Zhōng Yǎ, Zhōu Xiāo, and others have already been included in the collective biographies.
The remaining individuals, based on their deeds, are compiled into the "Biographies of Loyal and Righteous Men,"
to commemorate the fact that the Jìn clan had such people.
Jī Shào (cousin Hán)
Jī Shào, courtesy name Yánzǔ,
was the son of Kāng, the Wèi Dynasty's Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
He was orphaned at the age of ten
and served his mother with filial piety and diligence.
Because his father had incurred a transgression,
he lived quietly in a private residence.
Shān Tāo, who was in charge of selections,
reported to Emperor Wǔ:
"The 'Kāng Gào' states: 'Fathers and sons are not punished for each other's crimes.'
Jī Shào's virtue is comparable to that of Xì Quē;
he should be honored with an appointment.
I request that he be made Mìshū Láng."
The Emperor said to Tāo:
"According to what you say,
he is capable of being a丞 (Céng),
why only a Láng?"
Then an imperial edict was issued to summon him,
and he was appointed Mìshū Céng from his private residence.
When Shào first arrived in Luò,
someone said to Wáng Róng:
"Yesterday, in a large crowd, I first saw Jī Shào.
He stood out majestically, like a wild crane among a flock of chickens."
Róng said:
"You have not yet seen his father."
He was successively promoted to Rǔyīn Tàishǒu.
Péi Wèi, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, also esteemed him deeply,
and often said:
"If Yánzǔ were appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
there would be no forgotten talents in the world."
Dài Xī of Pèiguó, who possessed talent and intelligence from a young age,
was on good terms with Shào's cousin Hán.
People at the time expected him to achieve great things,
but Shào believed he would never amount to anything.
Later, Xī became Sīzhōu Zhǔbù,
but was dismissed for his misconduct.
The provincial locals praised Shào for his discerning eye for people.
He was transferred to Yùzhāng Nèishǐ.
Due to his mother's mourning,
he did not take up the post.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, Shí Chóng was the Dūdū.
Though Shí Chóng was arrogant and violent by nature,
Shào governed him with principle,
and Shí Chóng respected him greatly.
Later, he left office due to the death of his eldest son.
In the early Yuánkāng period,
he became Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
At that time, Shìzhōng Jiǎ Mì, due to his status as a maternal relative,
held a high position at a young age,
and Pān Yuè, Dù Bīn, and others all attached themselves to him.
Mì sought to establish a relationship with Shào,
but Shào refused to respond.
When Mì was executed,
Shào was in the department at the time.
Because he had not flattered the treacherous clan,
he was enfeoffed as Yìyáng Zǐ,
and promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
also holding the position of Guózǐ Bóshì.
When Tàiwèi, Guǎnglíng Gōng Chén Zhǔn passed away,
the Tàicháng proposed an posthumous title.
Shào countered, saying:
"Posthumous titles are meant to endure forever.
Great deeds receive great names,
and minor deeds receive minor names.
'Wén' and 'Wǔ' are evident in achievements and virtues;
'Líng' and 'Lì' signify darkness and obscurity.
Recently, the officials of rites have conformed to personal feelings,
and posthumous titles have not been based on reality.
Zhǔn's proposed title is excessive;
he should be posthumously titled Miù."
The matter was referred to the Tàicháng.
Although it was not followed at the time,
the court feared him.
When Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
Shào was appointed Shìzhōng.
When Emperor Huì was restored to the throne,
he retained his position.
Sīkōng Zhāng Huá had been executed by Lún.
Debaters later reviewed his case,
wishing to restore his rank.
Shào again countered, saying:
"A minister serving his lord
should remove troubles and dispel doubts.
Huá held various positions, both inside and outside the court.
Although he had some good deeds,
the blame after his death
is well-known far and wide.
The origin of the calamity and the beginning of the chaos
were indeed caused by Huá.
Therefore, when Zhèng punished the chaos of Yōu Gōng,
they chopped down Zǐ Jiā's coffin;
when Lǔ punished hidden transgressions,
it criticized Huī at the end of the chapter.
Not daring to inflict a second punishment,
the matter is already magnanimous enough.
I say it is inappropriate to restore his rank and position,
and to argue that he was innocent."
At that time, the Emperor had just been restored,
and Shào again submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that those who change previous tracks will not overturn their carriages,
and those who reform past evils will not go astray in their governance.
The Great Unity is led by the sovereign,
and all officials are served by many talented individuals.
Thus, King Wén of Zhōu flourished above,
and Kings Chéng and Kāng brought peace below.
To remember danger in times of safety is a good principle from the 'Yì' [Book of Changes];
I wish that Your Majesty would not forget Jīnyǒng,
that the Dà Sīmǎ would not forget Yǐngshàng,
and that the Dà Jiàngjūn would not forget Huángqiáo,
then the seeds of calamity and chaos will have no way to sprout."
Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) having assisted in governance,
greatly expanded his residences,
and his arrogance and extravagance grew excessive.
Shào (紹) wrote a letter of remonstrance, saying:
"Yǔ (禹) of Xià (夏) was praised for his humble dwelling;
Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) demonstrated virtue with thatched roofs.
Luxurious houses that cover the whole family
are of no benefit in times of peril and ruin.
I secretly heard that you demolished the Grand Music offices to enlarge your residences,
and exerted labor to construct houses for the Three Kings.
How can this be today's most urgent priority?
Now that the great matter is just settled,
the myriad people look up with eager anticipation,
all awaiting renewed nourishment.
It is fitting to reduce the burden of construction
and deeply ponder the principle of humility and restraint.
The merit of restoring the sovereign must not be discarded,
and the dangers of arrows and stones must not be forgotten."
Though Jiǒng (冏) replied with humility and deference,
he ultimately could not put the advice into practice.
Shào (紹) once went to see Jiǒng (冏) to discuss affairs,
and found Jiǒng (冏) holding a banquet.
He summoned Dǒng Ài (董艾), Gě Yú (葛旟) and others to discuss current affairs together.
Ài (艾) said to Jiǒng (冏):
"Jī (嵇) the Palace Attendant is skilled in string and wind instruments,
Your Grace can order him to play."
Attendants presented a qín (琴),
but Shào (紹) pushed it away and did not accept.
Jiǒng (冏) said:
"Today we are making merry,
why are you so stingy about this?"
Shào (紹) replied:
"Your Grace has restored the state,
and should set standards and models,
to be passed down to later generations.
Although I, Shào (紹), am humble and crude,
I am privileged to serve as a high official,
with sash and cap of office,
and jingling jade in the palace chambers.
How can I play string and wind instruments,
and engage in the affairs of entertainers?
If I were to take off my official attire and attend a private banquet,
that I would not dare to decline."
Jiǒng (冏) was greatly ashamed.
Ài (艾) and others retreated, feeling discomfited.
A short while later,
Shào (紹) was dismissed for official reasons,
and Jiǒng (冏) appointed him Left Sīmǎ (司馬).
Ten days later,
Jiǒng (冏) was executed.
Initially,
when the armies engaged,
Shào (紹) rushed dispersedly towards the palace.
There was a man holding a crossbow under the eastern corridor,
about to shoot him.
He encountered Xiāo Lóng (蕭隆), a general of the palace guard,
who, seeing Shào's (紹) dignified appearance,
suspected he was no ordinary person,
and quickly stepped forward to remove the arrow.
Thus, Shào (紹) escaped.
He then returned to his old residence in Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Soon after, he was summoned to be Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
Before he was formally appointed,
he was again made Shìzhōng (侍中).
Héjiān Wáng Yōng (河間王顒) and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎) raised troops and marched towards the capital,
to punish Chángshā Wáng Ài (長沙王乂).
The imperial carriage stopped east of the city.
Ài (乂) declared to the multitude, saying:
"Today we march west,
who do you wish to be the commander-in-chief?"
The soldiers of the six armies all said:
"We wish Jī (嵇) the Palace Attendant to exert his strength and lead the charge;
death would be as good as life."
Thereupon, Shào (紹) was appointed Envoy with Staff, General who Pacifies the West.
When Ài (乂) was captured,
Shào (紹) was again made Shìzhōng (侍中).
All dukes and kings below went to Yè (鄴) to apologize to Yǐng (穎).
Shào (紹) and others were all dismissed and demoted to commoners.
Soon after, the imperial court again had a northern expedition,
and Shào (紹) was summoned and
his noble rank was restored.
Seeing that the Son of Heaven was in distress,
Shào (紹) accepted the order and rushed to the imperial traveling residence.
He arrived when the imperial army was defeated at Dàngyīn (蕩陰).
Officials and guards alike all scattered and fled,
only Shào (紹) stood upright with his cap and robe,
defending the emperor with his body.
The battle reached the imperial carriage,
and arrows fell like rain.
Shào (紹) was then killed beside the emperor,
his blood splattering the imperial robes.
The Son of Heaven deeply grieved and sighed over this.
After the situation settled,
the attendants wished to wash the robes,
but the Emperor said:
"This is Jī (嵇) the Palace Attendant's blood;
do not remove it."
Earlier,
when Shào (紹) was about to depart,
Shìzhōng Qín Zhǔn (秦準) asked him:
"Today you are facing danger,
do you have a good horse?"
Shào (紹) replied with a stern expression:
"The imperial carriage is personally on campaign,
to justly punish rebels.
It is logical that there will be a campaign but no battle.
If, however, the imperial carriage were to be lost,
the duty of a minister remains.
What need is there for a fine horse!"
Those who heard him all sighed in admiration.
When Zhāng Fāng (張方) forced the Emperor to move to Cháng'ān (長安),
Héjiān Wáng Yōng (河間王顒) memorialized to posthumously grant Shào (紹) the title of Sīkōng (司空),
and advance his peerage to Duke.
At that time, the Emperor returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and the matter was not carried out.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) was stationed at Xǔ (許),
and his route passed through Xíngyáng (滎陽).
He visited Shào's (紹) tomb,
and wept bitterly.
He had a stone inscribed and a stele erected.
He also memorialized to posthumously grant official titles and peerage.
The Emperor then sent an envoy to posthumously grant him the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
added a golden seal and purple ribbon,
advanced his peerage to Marquis,
bestowed one qǐng (頃) of tomb land,
and ten households of retainers,
and sacrificed to him with a shàoláo (少牢) (minor sacrifice).
When Yuán Dì (元帝) was Left Chancellor,
he, by imperial authority,
considered Shào's (紹) death in loyalty a grave matter,
and that the posthumous honors did not match his meritorious virtue.
He again memorialized to posthumously grant him Tàiwèi (太尉),
and sacrifice with a tàiláo (太牢) (grand sacrifice).
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he bestowed the posthumous name Zhōngmù (忠穆),
and again added the tàiláo (太牢) sacrifice.
Shào (紹) was broad-minded in his conduct,
and did not bother with minor details,
yet he was magnanimous but disciplined,
and broad-minded but not disorderly.
He lived with five others, including his cousin Hán (含),
and cared for them as if they were his own siblings.
His disciples and former subordinates cherished his memory and kindness,
and observed mourning by his tomb,
over thirty of them completing three years.
His eldest son Zhěn (眕)
had his father's demeanor,
but died young.
His grand-nephew Hàn (翰) inherited the peerage.
During the reign of Chéng Dì (成帝), recalling Shào's (紹) loyalty,
Hàn (翰) was made Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請).
Hàn (翰), having no brothers,
memorialized to return to his original clan.
During the Tàiyuán (太元) era,
Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝) issued an edict, saying:
"Commending virtue and manifesting benevolence
is a wise king's excellent tradition.
The late Tàiwèi (太尉) and Zhōngmù Gōng (忠穆公) held lofty virtues,
which became even more manifest in adversity.
His integrity and purity
are a righteous example for a thousand years.
Whenever I think of his deeds,
my heart aches with sadness.
The descendant of such loyalty and integrity
should continue the ancestral sacrifices for generations.
This is to greatly illuminate his supreme integrity
and uphold the teachings of proper conduct.
Therefore, let his clan be sought out,
to inherit the peerage and preside over the sacrifices."
Thereupon, Hàn's (翰) grandson Kuàng (曠) was again made Marquis of Yìyáng (弋陽).
Hán (含), courtesy name Jūndào (君道).
His grandfather Xǐ (喜)
was the Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州).
His father Fán (蕃)
was a Crown Prince's Shèrén (舍人).
Hán (含) was fond of learning and skilled in writing.
His family lived in Bóqiū (亳丘), Gǒng Xiàn (鞏縣).
He called himself Bóqiū Zǐ (亳丘子),
named his gate 'Gate of Returning to Generosity',
and his room 'Room of Prudent Endings'.
Chǔ Wáng Wěi (楚王瑋) appointed him as a clerk.
When Wěi (瑋) was executed,
Hán (含) was dismissed due to implication.
He was nominated as Xiùcái (秀才),
and appointed Lángzhōng (郎中).
At that time, Hóngnóngwáng Cuì (弘農王粹), being a nobleman's son who married a princess,
had a very magnificent mansion.
He had Zhūang Zhōu (莊周) painted in a room,
and gathered many court officials,
asking Hán (含) to write a eulogy for it.
Hán (含) took up his brush and wrote a lamentation,
without making any corrections.
Its preface said:
"The imperial son-in-law Wáng Hóngyuǎn (王弘遠), with his grand ponds and opulent houses,
extensively invited virtuous gentlemen.
He depicted the image of Zhuāng Shēng (莊生) fishing,
and recorded the story of an eminent man declining an appointment.
He painted a True Man in a room with carved rafters,
and placed a retired scholar in a hall of advancement.
This can be called placing him where he does not belong,
worthy of lament, not eulogy."
Its verse said:
"How mighty is Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周)!
Heaven-sent and exceptionally free,
the Great Clod bestowed his life,
nature endowed his measure.
His vessel was empty, his spirit pure,
reaching the profound and the vast.
When human artifice and vulgarity reached their decline,
the true spirit was scattered.
There were no more sounds of grievance in the wilderness,
but sighs of contention for favor in court.
Superiors and inferiors vied with each other,
the order between elder and younger was lost.
Thus, people borrowed profundity and emptiness to aid their drowning,
and invoked morality to praise themselves.
Every household chanted phrases of tranquility and vastness,
every family painted images of Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊).
Now, Master Wáng (王生), steeped in fame and profit,
is married to an imperial princess.
His brilliance is linked to the three luminaries,
he has an exit but no place to go.
His pond is not a stream from rocky mountains,
his mansion is not a humble thatched dwelling.
He rides fine horses on the imperial road;
where did he get the idea to paint this image?
Alas, Master!
How confined are your lofty footprints!
You lived in a mountain cave,
yet you are placed in a house with carved pillars after death.
Placed where you don't belong,
your disgrace is not yet over.
Mourning the obscurity of the Great Dao,
I therefore pour out my sorrow in this song."
Cuì (粹) showed shame.
Qíwáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) appointed him Cóngxī Cānjūn (征西參軍),
and he inherited the title of Wǔchāng Xiānghóu (武昌鄉侯).
Chángshāwáng Ài (長沙王乂) summoned him to be Piàojì Jìshìdū (驃騎記室督) and Shàngshūláng (尚書郎).
When Ài (乂) and Chéngdūwáng Yǐng (成都王穎) were fighting,
Yǐng's (穎) army grew stronger.
The Shàngshūláng (尚書郎) went out to supervise the battle during the day
and returned at night to manage affairs.
Hán (含) spoke to Ài (乂) saying:
"In the past, whenever Wèiwǔ (魏武) had military matters,
he increased the number of his assistants.
In the second year of Qīnglóng (青龍),
Shàngshūlìng Chén Jiǎo (尚書令陳矯), due to military affairs,
also requested to increase the number of Láng (郎).
Now, the traitors press on all sides,
the royal road is blocked,
the urgency of being in a precarious situation
cannot be greater than this.
Simply managing affairs in the office
still requires an increase in Láng (郎);
how much more so now, when the capital's central cavalry and the three departments go out during the day to supervise the battle,
and return at night to manage affairs?
One person performs two duties,
leading to internal and external neglect.
Hán (含) suggests that if there are 100,000 men,
each commander should have his own chief,
allowing them to push forward and guide,
entrusting matters to the great generals.
It is not appropriate for court officials to interfere among them."
Ài (乂) agreed with him,
and so increased the number of Láng (郎) and clerks.
Huáidì (懷帝) was Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍),
and appointed Hán (含) as Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
When Huìdì (惠帝) went on the northern campaign,
he was transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎).
After the defeat at Dàngyīn (蕩陰),
Hán (含) fled back to Xíngyáng (滎陽).
At the beginning of Yǒngxīng (永興),
he was appointed Tàidì Zhōngshùzǐ (太弟中庶子).
The western road was blocked,
so he could not respond to the summons.
Fànyángwáng Xiāo (范陽王虓) was Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (征南將軍),
stationed in Xǔchāng (許昌),
and again appointed Hán (含) as Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
Soon after, he was granted the titles Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍) and Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu (襄城太守).
When Xiāo (虓) was defeated by Liú Qiáo (劉喬),
Hán (含) fled to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Liú Hóng (鎮南將軍劉弘) in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
who treated him with the courtesy due to a distinguished guest.
Hán (含) was insightful and quick-witted,
and enjoyed recommending talented and virtuous people.
He often wished to elevate Zhào Wǔ's (趙武) posthumous title,
and add to Zāng Wén's (臧文) crimes.
At that time, Chén Mǐn (陳敏) started a rebellion,
shaking Jiāngyáng (江揚).
Nányuè (南越) was perilous and distant,
and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yì (廣州刺史王毅) died of illness.
Hóng (弘) memorialized to appoint Hán (含) as Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng (平越中郎將), Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (廣州刺史), and Jiǎjié (假節).
Before he departed,
Hóng (弘) died.
At the time, some wanted to keep Hán (含) to govern Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Hán (含) was naturally upright and irritable,
and had long-standing animosity with Hóng's (弘) Sīmǎ Guō Mài (司馬郭勱).
Mài (勱) suspected Hán (含) intended to harm him,
and killed him under cover of night.
He was forty-four years old at the time.
When Huáidì (懷帝) ascended the throne,
he was given the posthumous title Xiàn (憲).
Wáng Bào (王豹)
Wáng Bào (王豹),
was a native of Shùnyáng (順陽).
From a young age, he was upright and straightforward.
Initially, he served as Yùzhōu Biéjià (豫州別駕).
When Qíwáng Jiǒng (齊王冏) was Dàsīmǎ (大司馬),
he appointed Bào (豹) as Zhǔbù (主簿).
Jiǒng (冏) was arrogant and indulgent,
losing the hearts of the people.
Bào (豹) sent a memorial to Jiǒng (冏), saying: "Bào (豹) has heard that royal ministers are firm and unyielding,
not for their own sake,
but to secure their lord, stabilize the times,
and preserve the state.
Therefore, for a minister who deceives his ruler,
punishment is not enough to execute him;
for a ruler who rejects remonstrance,
auspicious and grand are not enough for a posthumous title.
I humbly observe that your enlightened Duke is humble towards scholars,
open-minded
to accepting good advice,
and sincere in his manifestation,
yet unpalatable words have not reached his ears.
Bào (豹) humbly reflects that the decline of the Jìn (晉) government
began from Yuánkāng (元康) onward.
Among the prime ministers in office,
not one has achieved a peaceful end.
This is due to the circumstances,
not necessarily because they were inherently bad.
Now, your Grace has successfully quelled chaos,
secured the state, and stabilized the family.
Yet you are again following the previous patterns of downfall
and ruin,
seeking the tracks of overturned carriages in the interim.
To hope for long-term existence by this,
is something I dare not hear.
Currently, Héjiān (河間) has established his roots in Guān Yòu (關右),
Chéngdū (成都) lingers in the old
Wèi (魏) territory,
Xīnyě (新野) holds a large fief in Jiānghàn (江漢).
These three noble princes,
each strong and vigorous,
all command military forces
and occupy strategically dangerous lands.
Moreover, your Grace raised the standard of righteousness
to suppress rebellion,
your achievements overshadow the world.
Your sacred virtue shines brightly,
your fame shakes the present age.
Now, with achievements difficult to reward,
and wielding power that shakes the ruler,
you single-handedly control the capital,
and exclusively hold great
authority.
Advancing, you risk the 'soaring dragon having regrets';
retreating, 'thorns grow in the courtyard'.
To hope for peace by this,
I do not know if it will bring good fortune.
I dare to express my shallow views,
and lay bare my foolish sentiments.
In ancient times, King Wǔ (武王) attacked Zhòu (紂),
and enfeoffed the feudal lords as two Bó (伯).
East of Shǎn (陝),
Duke Zhōu (周公) governed;
west of Shǎn (陝),
Duke Zhào (召公) governed.
By
their end,
in the era of hegemonic states,
they held no more than a few prefectures of land.
The powerful armies of the four seas dared not invade to covet the Nine Tripods.
The reason for this
was that the world was accustomed to what it served.
Now, if you can truly honor the Zhōu (周) methods,
make Chéngdū (成都) the Běizhōubó (北州伯) [Lord of the Northern Provinces],
to command the kings and marquises north of the Yellow River;
and your Grace the Nánzhōubó (南州伯) [Lord of the Southern Provinces],
to oversee the officials in the southern lands..."
chiefs
each according to their original duties,
depart and reside in their respective regions,
establish virtue externally,
and devote loyalty internally.
At year's end, they would lead their subordinates to present tribute to the court,
select talented individuals,
and appoint worthy and eminent persons
to serve as the Son of Heaven's numerous officials.
Then the four seas would enjoy lasting peace,
and all nations would be greatly fortunate.
Your Excellency's virtue would then be on par with that of Zhōu Gōng and Shào Gōng in its utmost beauty.
The path of danger and defeat would be blocked,
and the altars of soil and grain
could be preserved.
I pray, Your Excellency, consider Gāo Zǔ's acceptance of Lóu Jìng's strategy,
and comprehend Zhāng Liáng's profound foresight.
Distance yourself from the peril of standing on the edge of a deep abyss,
and secure the stability of Tài Shān.
If this aligns
with your sagely thoughts,
Wǎn may indeed be made the capital.
The memorial was submitted,
but there was no reply.
Bào wrote another memorial, saying: "My memorial was submitted twelve days ago,
but Your Sagely Wisdom is lofty and distant,
and has not yet deigned to consider it.
No order of a single character has been granted,
nor has the appropriateness of acceptance or rejection been commanded.
This
is the divine treasure of a hegemon,
the secret art of safety and danger,
which cannot be neglected for a moment.
I humbly believe that Your Excellency holds great merit,
possesses great fame,
harbors great virtue,
and wields
great power.
These four great things
cannot be contained within the realm.
This is why the worthy and sagely are ever vigilant and fearful,
not even taking time to eat when the sun is at its zenith,
and not resting even when they should.
In the past,
Zhōu Gōng, with Wǔ Wáng as his elder brother
and Chéng Wáng as his lord,
had rendered meritorious service in defeating Zhòu,
and assisted in governance due to his kinship.
His hold on virtue was profound,
and the sagely grace was vast and far-reaching.
He was supremely loyal, supremely benevolent,
supremely filial, and supremely respectful.
Yet, on the day he took charge of affairs,
rumors spread among the four states,
causing him to be alienated from his lord and flee.
He resided in the east for three years,
and it was only thanks to the change in wind and rain
that Chéng Wáng was moved to understanding.
Had he
not encountered the response of august heaven
and the discernment of divine beings,
the extent of Gōng Dàn's misfortune would have been unknown.
Even when he held the reins of government,
he still shared authority with Shào Gōng, becoming a伯 (bó) in his own domain.
Now, Your Excellency, how do you view your own merits and virtue compared to Zhōu Gōng?
Moreover, since Yuán Kāng,
the suffering of prime ministers,
without time for thought,
and whose hidden calamities arose subtly,
were always imminent,
how could they possibly live out their lives peacefully?
Previous lessons are not far off;
Your Excellency has witnessed them personally.
If a gentleman does not have foresight,
he will surely have immediate worries.
When worries
arrive, then to realize them
will be too late for regret.
Now, if you follow Bào's strategy,
and send all the vassal kings to their states,
and in the north, share authority with Chéng Dū as equals across the river,
with Chéng Dū in Yè and
Your Excellency in Wǎn,
a vast area of a thousand
lǐ,
and with the marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons within the royal domain, great and small, all following suit,
forming alliances and solemn covenants,
jointly assisting the imperial house;
the system of tribute and submission
would be entirely according to the Zhōu典 (diǎn) (ritual/canon).
If this aligns with your sagely
principles,
you may first issue an order to discuss it with Chéng Dū.
Though I possess but meager talent,
I wish to serve as an envoy.
In the past, Sī Yǎng
was but a humble person from Yān and Zhào,
and Bǎi Lǐ Xī
was a merchant from Qín and Chǔ;
when their words were heard,
both states achieved peace.
How much more so for Bào, who, though plain,
is the administrator of a great province,
and furthermore, was Your Excellency's registrar when you embarked on your difficult undertaking.
Therefore, though my person is insignificant,
my words may not necessarily be wrong."
Jiǒng issued an order saying:
"I have received both your memorials,
understand your intentions,
and am considering them separately."
It happened that Chángshā Wáng Yì arrived.
He saw Bào's memorial on Jiǒng's desk
and said to Jiǒng:
"This young fellow is alienating kinsmen.
Why not beat him to death under the bronze camel?"
Jiǒng, being unable to approve of Bào's strategy,
then accepted Yì's words,
and impeached Bào, saying:
"I was enraged by the rampant wickedness of the treacherous,
and the collapse of the imperial succession.
Together with Chéng Dū, Cháng Shā, and Xīnyě, I raised an army of righteousness
to restore the altars of soil and grain,
only wishing to wholeheartedly serve the imperial house,
and deal with intimate relatives and close kinsmen from the宗室 (zōngshì) (imperial clan).
This is what I have sworn to myself day and night,
to never betray the gods.
Yet, registrar Wáng Bào recently submitted memorials,
daring to invent heterodox ideas,
saying that since I undeservedly hold the position of prime minister,
I will surely encounter harm,
with danger possibly arising overnight,
and ill omens awaiting discovery on tiptoe.
He wants me to share authority with Chéng Dū as equals,
and send out all the vassal kings.
Upwards, he slanders the awe of the sagely court's governance;
downwards, he encourages evil delusions,
sows doubt among the people,
spreads rumors and backbiting,
deftly plays both sides,
slanders superiors and denounces inferiors,
maligns those within and alienates those without,
instigates evil and leads to treachery,
thus creating suspicion for no reason.
In the past, Kǒng Qiū, when rectifying Lǔ,
executed Shǎo Zhèng Máo;
Zǐ Chǎn, when serving as prime minister of Zhèng,
first executed Dèng Xī.
This was truly because they confused names and realities,
like the bizarre types such as Zhào Gāo.
Bào is disloyal, disobedient, and unjust to me.
I immediately ordered the metropolitan police to investigate and execute him,
to clarify right from wrong."
As Bào was about to die,
he said:
"Hang my head at the gate of the Grand Marshal,
and you will see the soldiers attacking Qí."
The common people felt he was wronged.
Soon after, Jiǒng was defeated.
Liú Shěn,
whose courtesy name was Dào Zhēn,
was a native of Jì in Yān Guó.
His family had for generations been a prominent clan in the northern provinces.
In his youth, he served in the provincial and commandery governments,
and was widely learned and fond of antiquity.
Grand Preceptor Wèi Guàn appointed him as an aide,
and he also served as the Grand Rectifier for his home district.
He upheld Confucian principles,
cherished the worthy and capable,
promoted Huò Yuán to the second rank,
and advocated for Zhāng Huá.
In both cases, his pronouncements were clear and severe,
earning him praise at the time.
When Qí Wáng Jiǒng assisted in governance,
he appointed him Left Chief Clerk,
then promoted him to Imperial Household Grandee.
At that time, Lǐ Liú caused chaos in Shǔ.
Shěn was ordered, as Imperial Household Grandee and acting Commissioner with Imperial Authority,
to lead the Inspector of Yì Zhōu, Luó Shàng, the Inspector of Liáng Zhōu, Xǔ Xióng, and others to suppress Lǐ Liú.
On his way to Cháng'ān,
Héjiān Wáng Yōng requested Shěn to stay as his military supervisor,
sending Xí Wěi to replace him.
Later, he served as the Inspector of Yōng Zhōu.
When Zhāng Chāng rebelled,
Yōng was ordered to send Shěn with ten thousand provincial troops, along with five thousand from the Western Expeditionary Headquarters,
to suppress him from Lántián Pass.
Yōng did not obey the imperial order.
Shěn led his provincial troops to Lántián,
but Yōng again forcibly seized his forces.
Chángshā Wáng Yì ordered Shěn to return to his province with four hundred military officers.
As Zhāng Fāng (張方) pressed upon the capital,
the imperial army repeatedly suffered defeats.
Wáng Hú (王瑚) and
Zǔ Tì (祖逖) said to Yì (乂):
"Liú Shěn (劉沈) is loyal, righteous, resolute, and brave.
The military strength of Yōngzhōu (雍州) is sufficient to control Héjiān (河間).
It would be appropriate to request an imperial edict for Shěn (沈),
so that he may raise troops to attack Yóng (顒).
Yóng (顒), in distress,
will surely summon Zhāng Fāng (張方) to rescue himself.
This is an excellent plan."
Yì (乂) followed it.
Shěn (沈), receiving the edict, dispatched urgent manifestos to the four borders,
assembling the forces of seven commanderies, along with various defending armies and armed guards from fortified villages, totaling over ten thousand men.
With Wèi Bó (衞博), Administrator of Āndìng (安定),
Zhāng Guāng (張光), Administrator of Xīnpíng (新平), and Huángfǔ Dàn (皇甫澹), Registrar of Āndìng (安定), as vanguards,
he attacked Cháng'ān (長安).
Yóng (顒) was at that time stationed at Gāopíng Tíng (高平亭) in Zhèngxiàn (鄭縣),
acting as a reinforcement for the eastern army.
Hearing of Shěn's (沈) army rising,
he returned to garrison Wèichéng (渭城),
and sent Dūhù (督護) Yú Kuí (虞夔) to lead over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to intercept Shěn (沈) at Hǎozhì (好畤).
In the ensuing battle,
Kuí's (夔) forces were defeated.
Yóng (顒) was greatly alarmed,
retreated into Cháng'ān (長安),
and indeed urgently called for Zhāng Fāng (張方).
Shěn (沈) crossed the Wèi (渭) River and encamped.
Yóng (顒) frequently sent out troops to fight,
but always without success.
Shěn (沈), taking advantage of his victories, attacked him,
sending Dàn (澹) and Bó (博) with five thousand elite armored soldiers
to enter through the Cháng'ān (長安) gate,
fighting fiercely all the way to Yóng's (顒) tent.
Shěn's (沈) main army was slow to arrive.
Yóng's (顒) army, seeing that Dàn (澹) and others had no reinforcements,
felt their spirits redoubled.
Zhāng Fǔ (張輔), Administrator of Féngyì (馮翊), led his troops to rescue Yóng (顒),
attacking them from the flank.
A great battle ensued at the palace gate.
Bó (博) and his son both died,
and Dàn (澹) was also captured.
Yóng (顒), impressed by Dàn's (澹) bravery,
intended to spare him.
Dàn (澹) refused to submit,
and was consequently killed.
Shěn's (沈) army then suffered defeat,
and he led the remaining soldiers to encamp in the old camp.
Zhāng Fāng (張方) sent his general Dūn Wěi (敦偉) to arrive during the night.
Shěn's (沈) army was greatly alarmed and disintegrated.
He fled south with over a hundred of his subordinates,
and was captured by the Magistrate of Chéncāng (陳倉).
Shěn (沈) said to Yóng (顒):
"The consideration for oneself is light,
but the integrity of a minister is weighty.
One cannot violate the edicts of one's lord and father,
or weigh strength and weakness to preserve one's life.
The day I left,
I expected certain death.
The punishment of mincing and pickling,
I will accept as readily as eating water chestnuts."
His words were heroic and impassioned,
and those who heard them grieved for him.
Yóng (顒) was enraged,
whipped him, and then cut him in two at the waist.
Discerning people considered Yóng (顒) to be defying his superior and violating order,
cruelly harming loyalty and righteousness,
and knew that his downfall was not far off.
Qū Yǔn (麴允)
Qū Yǔn (麴允) was
a man from Jīnchéng (金城).
His family, along with the Yóu (游) clan, had for generations been powerful families.
The people of Xīzhōu (西州) had a saying for them:
"Qū (麴) and Yóu (游)
count not a few sheep and cattle.
They open vermilion gates to the south,
and look north to green mansions."
When Luòyáng (洛陽) fell,
Yán Dǐng (閻鼎) and others established the Prince of Qín (秦王) as the Imperial Crown Prince in Cháng'ān (長安).
Dǐng (鼎) took overall charge of all governmental affairs.
Yǔn (允) was then Ānyí Hùjūn (安夷護軍) and Administrator of Shǐpíng (始平).
He felt resentment towards Dǐng's (鼎) achievements
and also coveted power and influence.
When Dǐng (鼎) killed Liáng Zōng (梁綜), Administrator of Jīngzhào (京兆),
Yǔn (允) then, along with Zōng's (綜) younger brother Wěi (緯), Administrator of Féngyì (馮翊), and others, attacked Dǐng (鼎),
forcing him to flee.
At that time, Jiǎ Pǐ (賈疋), the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), was killed by the Túcè (屠各),
and Yǔn (允) took his place.
When Emperor Mǐn (愍帝) ascended the throne,
he appointed Yǔn (允) as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射), Lǐngjūn (領軍), Chíjì (持節), Xīróng Xiàowèi (西戎校尉), and Lù Shàngshūshì (錄尚書事),
with his position in Yōngzhōu (雍州) unchanged.
At that time, Liú Yào (劉曜), Yīn Kǎi (殷凱), and Zhào Rǎn (趙染) with tens of thousands of troops approached Cháng'ān (長'ān).
Yǔn (允) defeated them,
capturing Kǎi (凱) on the battlefield.
Yào (曜) again attacked Běidì (北地).
Yǔn (允) was made Dà Dūdū (大都督) and Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍),
and advanced to Qīngbái Chéng (青白城) to relieve it.
Yào (曜), hearing this, turned to raid Shàngjùn (上郡).
Yǔn (允) encamped at Língwǔ (靈武),
but, due to his weak forces, dared not advance.
Later, Yào (曜) again besieged Běidì (北地).
Qū Chāng (麴昌), Administrator of Běidì (北地), sent an envoy to request help.
Yǔn (允) led his infantry and cavalry to assist him.
Dozens of *lǐ* (里) from the city,
the bandits surrounded the city and set fires,
smoke and dust obscured the sky.
They employed a counter-espionage tactic to deceive Yǔn (允), saying:
"The commandery city has already fallen,
it is almost completely burned down;
it's too late!"
Yǔn (允) believed it,
and his troops, terrified, dispersed.
A few days later,
Qū Chāng (麴昌) broke through the siege and went to Cháng'ān (長'ān),
and Běidì (北地) subsequently fell.
Yǔn (允) was by nature benevolent and kind,
but lacked authority and decisiveness.
Wú Pí (吳皮), Wáng Yǐn (王隱), and other
rogue villains
were all given high titles.
Zhú Huī (竺恢), Administrator of Xīnpíng (新平), Yáng Xiàng (楊像), Administrator of Shǐpíng (始平), Zhú Shuǎng (竺爽), Administrator of Fúfēng (扶風), and Jiāo Sōng (焦嵩), Administrator of Āndìng (安定),
were all summoned to garrison important posts and given imperial credentials,
and appointed as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Chángshì (常侍).
Even the minor chiefs of villages and fortified settlements
were granted the titles of Yínqīng (銀青) and Jiāngjūn (將軍),
hoping to win over the hearts of the people.
However, the generals were arrogant and indulgent,
and their benevolence did not extend to their subordinates.
People's loyalty became somewhat fragmented.
Because of this, the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) became rebellious,
Guānzhōng (關中) fell into chaos.
Liú Yào (劉曜) again attacked Cháng'ān (長'ān).
The common people suffered severe famine,
and more than half died.
After a long time,
the city was in dire straits.
The Emperor was about to surrender,
and sighed, saying:
"It is the two dukes Qū (麴) and Suǒ (索) who have ruined my affairs!"
When the Emperor arrived in Píngyáng (平陽),
and was humiliated and imprisoned by Liú Cōng (劉聰),
Yǔn (允) fell to the ground, wailing, unable to rise.
Cōng (聰) was greatly enraged
and imprisoned him.
Yǔn (允), in despair, committed suicide.
Cōng (聰), commending his loyalty and integrity,
posthumously granted him the title Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍)
and the posthumous name Jiémǐn Hóu (節愍侯).
Jiāo Sōng (焦嵩) was
a man from Āndìng (安定).
Initially, he led his troops to occupy Yōng (雍).
When Yào (曜) pressed upon the capital,
Yǔn (允) informed Sōng (嵩) of the danger.
Sōng (嵩) had always disdained Yǔn (允),
and said:
"I will save him when Yǔn (允) is in distress."
By the time the capital fell,
Sōng (嵩) was also soon destroyed by the bandits.
Jiǎ Hún (賈渾)
Jiǎ Hún (賈渾)
was from an unknown commandery.
During the Tàiyuán (太安) era,
he served as Magistrate of Jièxiū (介休).
When Liú Yuánhǎi (劉元海) rebelled,
he sent his general Qiáo Xī (喬晞) to attack and capture it.
Hún (渾) upheld his integrity and refused to surrender,
saying:
"I guarded it for Jìn (晉) but
could not preserve it.
How could I cowardly seek to survive by serving the enemy bandits?
How could I face the world then?"
Xī (晞) was enraged,
seized him, and was about to kill him.
Xī's (晞) general Yǐn Sōng (尹崧) said:
"General, spare him
to encourage loyalty to one's lord."
Xī (晞) did not listen
and consequently killed him.
Wáng Yù (王育)
Wáng Yù, styled Bóhchūn,
was a native of Jīngzhào.
Young, orphaned, and poor,
he worked as a hired shepherd.
Every time he passed a small school,
he would sigh and shed tears.
When he had free time,
he would twist reeds to practice writing.
Forgetting himself, he lost a sheep,
for which he was blamed by the sheep owner.
Yù was about to sell himself to repay the owner.
Xǔ Zǐzhāng of the same commandery,
a perceptive and intelligent gentleman,
heard of this and praised him.
He repaid the owner on Yù's behalf,
provided him with clothes and food,
and had him study with his own son.
Consequently, Yù became extensively learned in the Classics and histories.
He was over eight *chǐ* tall,
with a beard three *chǐ* long,
an extraordinary appearance,
and a voice that moved people.
Zǐzhāng married his brother's daughter to him,
built a separate residence for them,
and gave them a share of his property.
Yù accepted it without a trace of shame.
However, his conduct was self-willed
and quite out of step with popular custom.
When his wife died,
no more than four or five people came to condole,
but all of them were renowned local gentry.
The Grand Administrator Dù Xuān appointed him as Chief Clerk.
Soon after, Xuān was demoted to Magistrate of Wànnián.
Dù, Magistrate Wáng Yōu, went to visit Xuān.
Xuān did not go out to welcome him.
Yōu became angry and said:
"You were once a Two Thousand *Shí* official,
whom I respected.
Now we are peers,
why do you not welcome me?
Do you mean to treat me as a small sparrow
and make me fear a deadly hawk?"
Yù grasped his sword and rebuked Yōu, saying:
"When the lord is disgraced, the minister dies –
it has been so since ancient times.
My lord has been dismissed and demoted for no crime,
like an eclipse of the sun or moon.
How dare a magistrate of a small county lightly insult my lord!
Do you think my sword is dull,
that you dare to speak like this?!"
He stepped forward, intending to kill him.
Xuān, fearing for his life,
came down barefoot and embraced Yù,
who then stopped.
From then on, he became famous.
Sītú Wáng Hún invited him to be a staff officer,
and he was appointed Magistrate of Nánwǔyáng.
His governance was clear and restrained,
and entrenched bandits fled to other commanderies.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Bìngzhōu.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng was in Yè,
and he further appointed Yù as Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn.
When Liú Yuánhǎi became Běi Chányú,
Yù advised Yǐng, saying:
"Yuánhǎi is leaving now.
Yù requests to hasten him for Your Highness.
Otherwise,
I fear he may not reach his destination."
Yǐng agreed
and appointed Yù as Pòlǔ Jiāngjūn.
Yuánhǎi then detained him,
and later made him Grand Tutor.
Wéi Zhōng
Wéi Zhōng, styled Zǐjié,
was a native of Píngyáng.
Young, he was generous and righteous,
with an unyielding will.
He loved learning and was broadly knowledgeable,
his nature was never to make empty promises.
He kept his gate shut and cultivated himself,
not associating with contemporary society.
Whenever there were auspicious or inauspicious occasions,
though relatives and acquaintances offered gifts,
he accepted none.
At the age of twelve,
he lost his father and
was so grief-stricken and wasted away that
he could only rise with the aid of a staff.
Sīkōng Péi Xiù went to condole him.
He crawled and wept aloud, his profound grief moving everyone.
Xiù left and told others:
"This child, when he grows up, will surely be a fine talent."
Upon returning, he ordered his son Péi Wěi to visit him.
After the mourning period,
he built a hut by the grave.
Wěi admired him and went to visit,
but Zhōng always claimed to be out and refused to see him.
His family was poor,
barely having enough wild vegetables and coarse food.
Others could not bear such hardship,
but Zhōng did not change his joy.
When Wěi became Púshè,
he repeatedly spoke of Zhōng to Sīkōng Zhāng Huá.
Huá invited him to serve,
but he declined, feigning illness, and did not arise.
When people asked him why,
Zhōng said:
"I am a humble scholar with a thatched roof,
originally having no ambition for officialdom.
Furthermore, Mào Xiān (Zhāng Huá) is outwardly brilliant but inwardly barren,
and Péi Wěi is greedy and insatiable.
They have abandoned the rites and attached themselves to the usurping empress.
If this is the case,
how could a true gentleman act thus!
Péi often had a mind to rely on me,
and I constantly feared that a great tide might sweep away the mountains,
and I might be carried away by the residual waves.
How much more so should I not stand at the tail-water [the mythical drain of the ocean] and peer into Wòjiāo [the mythical boiling abyss]!"
The Grand Administrator Chén Chǔ compelled him to serve as Gōngcáo.
At that time, the mountain Qiāng sacked the commandery.
Chǔ fled with his son,
and the bandits shot at them,
hitting Chǔ three times.
Zhōng rushed forward, braving the blades, and shielded Chǔ with his body,
crying:
"Wéi Zhōng is willing to die in place of my lord!
I beg all of you gentlemen to have mercy!"
He also suffered five arrow wounds.
The bandits said to each other:
"He is a righteous man!"
and spared him.
Zhōng then carried Chǔ back home.
Later, he served Liú Cōng
as Zhènxi Dàjiāngjūn and Píngqiāng Xiàowèi.
While suppressing rebellious Qiāng,
he ran out of arrows
but did not yield, and died upholding his integrity.
Xīn Miǎn
Xīn Miǎn, styled Bólì,
was a native of Dídào, Lǒngxī.
His father Hóng
was the Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Miǎn was broadly learned
and possessed steadfast integrity.
During Huái Dì's reign,
he was repeatedly promoted to Shìzhōng.
When Luòyáng fell,
he followed the emperor to Píngyáng.
Liú Cōng was about to appoint him as Guānglù Dàfū,
but Miǎn firmly refused the offer.
Cōng sent his Huángmén Shìláng Qiáo Dù to compel him with medicated wine.
Miǎn said:
"How can a true man compromise his lofty principles for a few years of life,
serve two dynasties,
and then face Emperor Wǔ [Sīmǎ Yán] in the underworld?"
He took the medicine, intending to drink it.
Dù hastily stopped him, saying:
"The emperor was merely testing you;
you truly are a lofty scholar!"
He sighed and left.
Cōng praised his integrity,
deeply respected and admired him,
built a house for him on the west mountain of Píngyáng,
and monthly sent him wine and rice.
Miǎn also refused to accept them.
At the age of eighty,
he died.
Miǎn's clan cousin Bīn
was Shàngshū Láng during Mǐn Dì's time.
When the emperor was disgraced in Píngyáng,
Liú Cōng made the emperor serve wine and wash cups,
wishing to observe the reactions of the Jìn officials present.
Bīn rose and embraced the emperor, weeping loudly.
Cōng said:
"Was killing Yǔ Mín and others before
not enough of a warning?!"
He ordered him removed
and subsequently put him to death.
Liú Mǐnyuán
Liú Mǐnyuán, styled Dàoguāng,
was a native of Běihǎi.
He disciplined himself and pursued learning,
not allowing dangers and difficulties to change his resolve.
He loved astrology, calendrical calculations, Yīnyáng, and numerical arts.
He delved deeply into the *Yì* and *Tàixuán*,
but disliked reading history.
He often told his comrades:
"When reciting books, one should savor the root of the meaning.
Why waste effort on texts of superfluous rhetoric?
The *Yì*
is the source of meaning,
*Tàixuán*
is the gate to principles.
He who can comprehend these
is my teacher."
During the Disorder of Yǒngjiā,
Mǐnyuán fled west from Qí.
Guǎn Píng, a man from the same county, over seventy years old,
followed Mǐnyuán west.
When they reached Xíngyáng,
they were robbed by bandits.
Mǐnyuán had already been released,
but he returned and said to the bandits:
"This elder is an orphan and old,
with not many years left.
Mǐnyuán requests to take his place;
I beg you gentlemen to release him."
The bandits said:
"What relation is this elder to you?"
Mǐnyuán said:
"He is a fellow townsman.
He is poor and without a son,
and depends on Mǐnyuán for his livelihood.
If you gentlemen wish to employ him,
he is too old to be useful.
If you wish to feed him,
he is also not as good as Mǐnyuán.
I beg for your pity."
One bandit glared and shouted at Mǐnyuán:
"If I don't release this elder,
do you think I can't get you?!"
Mǐnyuán brandished his sword and said:
"How can I hope to live?!
I will kill you first and then die.
This elder is poor and old;
even the gods should pity him.
I am not his blood kin,
nor is he my teacher or friend by righteousness.
But because he sought refuge with me,
I beg to take his place.
You gentlemen are benevolent and kind;
you all show signs of listening to me.
How dare you show such brazenness and utter such words!"
He turned to the bandit chief and said:
"What is constant about benevolence and righteousness?
How can they be lost among gentlemen?
Above, one should emulate the deeds of Gāo Huáng and Guāng Wǔ;
below, how can one not emulate Chén and Xiàng?
One should acquire things through the proper way,
so that one's passing is praised and one's might and virtue are sung.
How can you tolerate this person and thereby damage your great reputation?
I will eliminate this person for you gentlemen,
to accomplish your hegemonic and kingly aspirations."
He then proceeded to cut him down.
The bandit chief quickly stopped him
and said to each other:
"He is a righteous man!
Harming him would be a violation of righteousness."
So they released them all.
Later, he served Liú Yào,
as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ.
Zhōu Gāi
Zhōu Gāi was
a native of Tiānmén.
He was resolute and fierce by nature,
and known for his righteousness and bravery.
Although he was not fond of learning,
he always acted according to the teachings of famous scholars.
His uncle, Jí, was the Yídū Nèishǐ,
and also a loyal and principled scholar.
Hearing that King Qiáo, Chéng, had raised a righteous army in Xiāngzhōu,
and that Gān Zhuó also did not agree with Wáng Dūn's actions,
but no letters or proclamations had arrived,
Jí said to Gāi:
"I have long disliked Wáng Dūn's ambition to usurp the throne.
Now he has raised an army and is plotting rebellion,
threatening the stability of the state.
King Qiáo, a hope of the imperial clan,
holds an important regional command,
has raised his banner and sworn in his forces,
planning to attack Wǔchāng.
Gān Ānnán has long been known for his bravery,
and his soldiers, horses, and weapons are the strongest of today.
I hear he has agreed with King Qiáo on a date to raise a righteous army.
This is a crucial time for a valiant man in urgent distress;
it is the time for me to die.
Will you fulfill my aspiration
by expressing our sincerity to King Qiáo?"
Gāi joyfully accepted the command,
secretly went to Xiāngzhōu,
met with Chéng,
and verbally expressed his utmost sincerity.
Chéng was greatly pleased.
At that time, Wáng Dūn had sent his general Wèi Ài to besiege Chéng very tightly.
Gāi then, with Zhōu Qí, an attendant from Xiāngzhōu, secretly went out to report back.
They were both captured by Ài,
and tortured to death,
but they never revealed the reason for their mission.
Jí was thus spared from Wáng Dūn's disaster.
Huán Xióng
Huán Xióng was
a native of Chángshā.
In his youth, he served in the prefecture and county.
When King Qiáo, Chéng, became the governor of Xiāngzhōu,
he appointed him as Zhǔbù.
During Wáng Dūn's rebellion,
Chéng was captured by Wáng Dūn's general Wèi Ài.
His subordinate officials fled and scattered,
but Xióng, along with Xīcáo Hán Jiē and Attendant Wǔ Yán, disguised themselves as servants
and followed Chéng to Wǔchāng.
Ài saw Xióng's dignified appearance
and his polite demeanor,
knew he was no ordinary man,
and felt apprehension.
Thus, he had him killed.
Hán Jiē
Hán Jiē was
a native of Chángshā.
He was known for his integrity, caution, and trustworthiness,
and was respected and loved by his community.
The governor, King Qiáo Chéng, appointed him as Yìcáo Jìjiǔ,
and he was later transferred to Xīcáo Shūzuǒ.
When Chéng was captured by Wèi Ài
and sent to Wǔchāng,
Jiē, along with Wǔ Yán and others, steadfastly followed him,
staying by Chéng's side.
After Huán Xióng was killed,
the two of them became even more determined.
When Chéng met his demise,
Jiē and Yán personally arranged his funeral and coffin,
escorted his coffin back to the capital,
and mourned and offered sacrifices day and night.
They only returned after the burial was complete.
Zhōu Qí
Zhōu Qí was
a native of Shàolíng.
He served as an attendant in Xiāngzhōu.
During Wáng Dūn's disaster,
King Qiáo Chéng sent Qí to seek outside help.
He and Zhōu Gāi were both captured by Wèi Ài's scouts.
Ài demanded an explanation from Qí,
threatening him with a drawn blade.
Qí said:
"The provincial governor sent me to seek external assistance;
there was no fixed destination,
I was merely to adapt to circumstances."
Ài then said to Qí:
"You go tell those in the city
that the Grand General has already defeated Liú Wèi and Dài Ruòsī,
and Gān Zhuó is staying in Xiāngyáng with no further dissent.
The prefectures and counties of the Three Jiāng are
completely pacified for thousands of miles,
and external aid is absolutely cut off.
If you do this,
I will spare your life."
Qí falsely agreed.
Once he reached the city wall,
he shouted loudly:
"Wáng Dūn's army has been defeated at Yúhú!
Gān Ānnán has already captured Wǔchāng
and will immediately dispatch a large force to relieve this urgent situation!
Hold firm with all your might;
the bandits are scattering now!"
Ài then counted his men and killed Qí.
Yì Xióng
Yì Xióng,
courtesy name Xīngcháng,
was a native of Liúyáng, Chángshā.
In his youth, he was a county clerk.
Feeling his humble status
offered no path to self-advancement,
he took off his cap, hung it on the county gate, and left.
He then studied laws and regulations and practiced old customs,
befriending powerful local gentry,
and gradually gained recognition in the province.
He served in the commandery
as Zhǔbù.
During Zhāng Chāng's rebellion,
the rebels captured the Grand Administrator Wàn Sì
and were about to execute him.
Xióng debated the right and wrong with the rebels.
The rebels were enraged and
shouted for someone to drag Xióng away and behead him.
Xióng calmly walked out.
The rebels then called him back and questioned him again.
Xióng answered as before.
This happened three times,
and the rebels finally released him.
Sì was thus spared,
and Xióng became famous.
He was nominated as Xiàolián
and served as Zhōu Zhǔbù,
then promoted to Biéjià.
Feeling that his family was of humble origin
and that he should not remain in a high position for long,
he resigned and returned home.
Later, he served as the Magistrate of Chōnglíng.
Cìshǐ, Qiáowáng Chéng, having already resisted Wáng Dūn,
planned to raise an army to go to the imperial court.
Xióng Chéngfú quickly dispatched proclamations far and wide,
listing Wáng Dūn’s crimes,
and announcing recruitment within the county.
Within a few days,
he had a thousand men,
carrying provisions and bearing spears, following him.
Chéngfú firmly held his ground,
but after Xiāngzhōng had been devastated and left desolate,
the city walls were not complete,
and military supplies were also lacking.
Wáng Dūn sent Wèi Ài and Lǐ Gōng to attack him.
Xióng Chéngfú vigorously led his troops,
defending for several weeks,
until the dead and wounded soldiers lay piled upon each other.
His strength exhausted and the city fallen,
he was captured by Wèi Ài.
His spirit was undaunted,
and his face showed no fear.
He was sent to Wǔchāng,
where Wáng Dūn sent someone to show him the proclamation and enumerate his offenses.
Xióng Chéngfú said:
“This is indeed true.
I regret that my position was humble and my strength weak,
unable to save the country from its difficulties.
The royal house is like a burning fire;
what use is it for me to live?
If I am executed today,
to become a loyal ghost,
that is my wish.”
Wáng Dūn feared his righteous words
and released him.
Everyone congratulated him,
but Xióng Chéngfú smiled and said:
“Last night I dreamt I was riding in a carriage,
with meat hanging by its side.
Now, meat must have sinews,
and sinews (jīn) sound like an axe (jīn).
With an axe by the carriage,
I will surely be executed!”
Soon after, Wáng Dūn sent someone to kill him.
Those who witnessed it at the time
were all moved to sorrow and lamentation.
Yuè Dàoróng
Yuè Dàoróng
was a native of Dānyáng.
From a young age, he had great ambitions,
was tireless in his studies,
and was trustworthy with friends.
He always restrained himself and strove to be generous,
possessing the demeanor of a national scholar.
He served as Wáng Dūn’s Cānjūn.
When Wáng Dūn was planning a rebellion
and plotting to harm loyal court officials,
he informed Gān Zhuó.
Gān Zhuó thought it was unacceptable
and delayed in responding.
Wáng Dūn sent Yuè Dàoróng to summon him.
Although Yuè Dàoróng was Wáng Dūn’s aide,
he resented Wáng Dūn’s rebellious intentions,
and thus persuaded Gān Zhuó, saying:
“The emperor personally oversees myriad affairs;
he does not rely solely on Liú Kuí.
Now, fearing the disaster of the Seven Kingdoms,
he therefore cedes Xiāngzhōu to weaken the feudal lords.
But the Wáng clan has held power for a long time,
and suddenly seeing their authority divided,
they consider it being stripped away.
Wáng Dūn, ungrateful and wantonly rebellious,
raises an army to attack the emperor.
The state has treated your lordship with utmost kindness;
if you join him now,
would you not betray righteousness?
To live as a rebellious minister
and die as a foolish ghost,
forever bringing shame upon your clan and party – how could that be!
Your lordship should pretend to agree to his command,
but then quickly attack Wǔchāng.
When Wáng Dūn’s forces hear of it,
they will surely disperse without a fight,
and a great achievement can be accomplished.”
Gān Zhuó greatly assented to this.
Thereupon, together with Bādōng Jiānjūn Liǔ Chún and others, he openly issued a proclamation detailing Wáng Dūn’s crimes and rebellion,
and led his troops to suppress him.
He also sent a memorial to the court.
However, Gān Zhuó was indecisive by nature,
and being old, he was also prone to suspicion.
Thus, he waited for all parties to advance together,
and his army’s departure was delayed.
When they reached Zhū Kǒu,
Wáng Dūn heard that Gān Zhuó had already deployed troops.
Gān Zhuó’s nephew, Āng, who was then Wáng Dūn’s Cānjūn,
was sent by Wáng Dūn to seek peace with Gān Zhuó,
ordering him to withdraw his army.
Gān Zhuó believed him
and was about to withdraw.
His Zhǔbù Dèng Qiān and Yuè Dàoróng advised Gān Zhuó, saying:
“The general has raised a righteous army and abandoned it midway,
becoming a general of a defeated army.
I secretly believe this is not acceptable for the general.
Now, among the general’s subordinates,
each soldier seeks his own advantage.
If you return all at once,
I fear it may not be possible.”
Gān Zhuó did not heed them.
Yuè Dàoróng wept day and night, admonishing Gān Zhuó,
and died of grief and indignation.
Yú Kuī
Yú Kuī
was a native of Chángshā.
His younger brother was Wàng,
whose courtesy name was Zǐdū.
Both possessed scholarly integrity;
their filial piety, fraternal devotion, integrity, and trustworthiness were praised by their local community,
and both were fond of criticizing and appraising people,
considering human morality their personal responsibility.
In their youth, they served in the prefecture and commandery,
the brothers successively holding the positions of Zhìzhōng and Biéjià.
When Yuán Dì was chancellor,
he recruited scholars from all directions,
and many were appointed to his staff,
which people at the time called
“the hundred and six aides.”
Wàng was also summoned,
but he was ashamed and did not respond.
When Qiáowáng Chéng assumed governorship of the province,
he knew of their reputation,
and summoned Yú Kuī to be his Chángshǐ.
Before he arrived,
he suffered the loss of his mother.
When Wáng Dūn rebelled,
Chéng went to console Yú Kuī,
and stayed to talk with him, saying:
“I was previously decreed
to govern this province,
precisely because Wáng Dūn was acting autocratically,
to prevent him from causing trouble.
Now Wáng Dūn has indeed planned rebellion.
I, having been entrusted with a region,
wish to lead my subordinates to rush to the imperial court,
but my forces are few and provisions scarce,
and I have only just arrived in your province,
so my benevolence and trustworthiness are not yet established.
You, brothers, are the outstanding talents of the southern summer,
and your wisdom and courage are widely renowned.
The ancients wore mourning clothes and went to war;
how much more so now that whales and leviathans block the roads,
and the royal house is in peril!
How can you indulge in boundless grief
and forget the principles of loyalty and righteousness!
If we start now,
can the officers, soldiers, and equipment be sufficient?”
Yú Kuī and Yú Wàng replied:
“Wáng Dūn holds the responsibility of dividing the imperial authority;
yet he suddenly plots rebellion,
scheming to endanger the state.
This is something that heaven and earth cannot tolerate,
and which men and gods resent.
Your Highness, not considering us humble and inferior,
has graciously visited us and inquired.
We brothers have both received state grace,
how dare we not exert ourselves!
Today, the imperial court is undergoing a restoration;
people long for the virtue of the Jìn dynasty.
Your Highness, as a close relative of the imperial clan,
upholds loyalty and obedience to punish the guilty;
who would not bear arms and give their lives!
However, our humble province is desolate and impoverished,
provisions and equipment are exhausted,
and ships are few,
making it difficult to advance and suppress.
It would be advisable to first gather forces and consolidate defenses,
and dispatch proclamations to all four directions.
His forces will surely be divided;
then, if we plan our attack,
the matter can be successful.”
Chéng considered this to be so,
and thus appointed Yú Kuī as Chángshǐ
and Yú Wàng as Sīmǎ,
to oversee all the armies.
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Huán Chōng memorialized, saying:
"The former Qīngchē Jiāngjūn and Wèixīng Tàishǒu, Jí Yì, styled Zǔlǎng,
when the Western Court collapsed,
sacrificed his life to uphold his integrity.
Yì was deeply loyal and filial to his family for generations,
devoting his heart to the imperial court.
My deceased elder brother, Wēn, when he formerly campaigned against Xiányáng,
and his army reached the Bàshuǐ,
Yì brought his two younger brothers,
and came alone on horseback to defect,
acknowledging his sincerity,
he was subsequently promoted and appointed,
transferring from Xīnyě Tàishǒu to Wèixīng.
He long held military posts,
entrusted with border defenses,
the frontier regions submitted to his care,
and he gained renown in the places he administered.
The year before last, the cunning Dǐ ran rampant,
descending the river,
Yì, with his isolated city standing alone,
with no more than a single company of troops,
externally repelled the fierce invaders,
and internally secured crucial strongholds,
capturing enemy boats and ships,
and taking thousands of captives.
However, the bandits exerted all their strength in besieging him,
over a period of months.
When Xiāngyáng fell,
the border situation was disheartening,
moreover, the disparity in strength between few and many,
led to his downfall.
Yì's words and demeanor were resolute,
his ambition was not to be humiliated,
he brandished his blade and pushed away his spear,
resolved to perish.
His officers and men held him back,
preventing him from dying immediately.
He then sealed his mouth and said nothing,
and starved himself to death.
Yì's Cānjūn, Shǐ Yǐng,
recently returned from the enemy's midst,
〔一二〕 bringing Yì's handwritten memorial from his deathbed,
and fully explaining the situation.
Yì's loyal spirit
is still worthy of record.
If he can receive the grace of the heavens and earth to pardon and forgive,
then honor will be bestowed upon the withered,
and favor will extend to the springs and earth."
The Emperor praised him,
posthumously granting him the title of Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wáng Liàng
Wáng Liàng, styled Yòuchéng,
was a native of Dānyáng.
In his youth, he possessed strategy and capability,
and was promoted by Wáng Dūn,
participating in his staff affairs,
gradually rising to Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
Initially,
Xīnchāng Tàishǒu Liáng Shuò wielded sole authority in the Jiāo region,
welcoming and establishing Táo Xián as Cìshǐ.
After Xián's death,
Wáng Dūn appointed Wáng Jī as Cìshǐ,
but Shuò raised troops to resist Jī,
taking the title of Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu himself,
then welcomed Xiū Zé's son, Zhàn, the son of the former Cìshǐ, to govern the province.
In the third year of Yǒngxīng,
Dūn appointed Liàng as Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
As Liàng was about to depart for his post,
Dūn told him:
"Xiū Zhàn and Liáng Shuò are both traitors to the state.
When you arrive,
arrest and execute them."
Upon Liàng's arrival in the territory,
Zhàn retreated to Jiǔzhēn.
Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Táo Kǎn sent someone to entice Zhàn to come to Liàng's place.
Liàng ordered his attendants not to enter the inner chamber.
Once Zhàn came forward,
he seized him.
Shuò was present at the time,
and said:
"Zhàn is the son of the former provincial governor;
if he has committed a crime, he can be sent away,
there is no need to kill him."
Liàng said:
"He is your old acquaintance,
it has nothing to do with me."
And immediately executed him.
Shuò, enraged, left.
Liàng secretly plotted to kill Shuò,
sending an assassin to stab him,
but it failed.
Shuò then led his troops to besiege Liàng at Lóngbiān.
Táo Kǎn sent an army to rescue him,
but Liàng was defeated before they arrived.
Shuò forced Liàng to surrender his credentials (jié),
but Liàng stubbornly refused to give them up,
so Shuò cut off Liàng's right arm.
Liàng, with an unwavering expression, said:
"I do not even fear death,
what is the loss of an arm!"
Ten odd days later,
he died of indignation and resentment.
Shuò occupied Jiāozhōu,
acting ferociously and cruelly,
causing suffering throughout the region.
He was eventually destroyed by Kǎn's army,
and his head was sent to the capital.
Sòng Jǔ
Sòng Jǔ, styled Chǔguī,
was a native of Dūnhuáng.
He was resolute and had a strong sense of integrity.
Zhāng Chónghuá occupied the Liángzhōu territory,
and appointed Jǔ as Wǎnxù Dūwèi.
Shí Jìlóng sent his general Má Qiū to attack Dàxià,
and Hùjūn Liáng Shì 〔一三〕 seized Tàishǒu Sòng Yàn,
surrendering the city to Qiū.
Qiū sent Yàn with a letter to Jǔ.
When Jǔ arrived,
he said to Qiū:
"Leaving one's father to serve a lord,
one should establish merit and righteousness;
if merit and righteousness cannot be established,
one should uphold one's name and integrity.
I will never betray my lord and bring ruin to my clan,
living a stolen life in this world."
He first killed his wife and children,
then committed suicide by slitting his own throat.
Qiū said:
"He is a righteous warrior!"
and ordered him to be buried.
Chónghuá praised his sincerity and integrity,
posthumously granting him the title of Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
Chē Jì
Chē Jì, styled Wàndù,
was a native of Dūnhuáng.
He was resolute and magnanimous.
Zhāng Chónghuá appointed him as Jīnchéng Lìng.
He was captured by Shí Jìlóng's general Má Qiū,
but Jì refused to yield to Qiū.
Qiū was determined to make him surrender,
so he confronted him with soldiers.
Jì's expression and demeanor did not waver,
and he said:
"Although my talent is not that of Páng Dé,
my appointment is the same.
My body can be killed,
but my will cannot be moved."
Then he fell on his sword and died.
Qiū sighed at his loyalty and integrity,
and buried him with full rites.
Later, Chónghuá brought his coffin back,
personally attended and wept bitterly,
posthumously granting him the title of Yíhé Dūwèi.
Dīng Mù
Dīng Mù, styled Yàn Yuǎn,
was a native of Qiáoguó.
He accumulated merit and achievements,
was enfeoffed as Zhēndìng Hóu,
and successively promoted to Shùnyáng Tàishǒu.
In the fourth year of Tàiyuán,
he was appointed Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
He had not yet departed after receiving the imperial edict
when Fú Jiān sent troops to raid Shùnyáng.
Mù was defeated in battle,
captured and taken to Cháng'ān,
where he feigned illness and refused to serve the illegitimate court.
Jiān then mobilized his entire country to invade the south.
Mù, along with prominent figures in Guānzhōng, initiated a righteous uprising,
plotting to launch a surprise attack on Cháng'ān.
The plot was discovered,
and he was killed.
Before his death, he wrote a memorial and entrusted it to his wife, Zhōu.
Afterward, Zhōu managed to reach the capital,
and submitted it to the imperial court.
Emperor Xiàowǔ issued an imperial edict stating:
"The former Shùnyáng Tàishǒu and Zhēndìng Hóu, Dīng Mù, though his strength failed and his person was captured,
his sincerity and integrity became even stronger.
His straightforwardness, honesty, and robust determination
matched the heroic martyrs of antiquity.
His coffin has just returned,
and the news brings grief.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and the burial gifts shall follow the precedent of Zhōu Xiāo.
A residence shall be built for him,
and his wife shall be provided with clothing and food,
for the rest of her life."
Xīn Gōngjìng
Xīn Gōngjìng,
was a man from Dídào, Lǒngxī.
From a young age, he possessed capabilities and talent;
his capacity and measure surpassed others.
During the Lóng'ān period,
he served as the Grand Administrator of Hénán.
When Yáo Xīng came to invade,
Gōngjìng defended resolutely for over a hundred days,
but was overwhelmed due to lack of relief,
and was captured and taken to Cháng'ān.
Xīng said to him,
"I intend to entrust you with the affairs of the Southeast,
would that be acceptable?"
Gōngjìng, with a stern expression, replied,
"I would rather be a ghost for my state
than a minister to a Qiāng rebel."
Xīng was enraged,
and imprisoned him in a separate room.
After three years,
during the Yuánxīng period,
he tricked his guards,
then scaled the wall and escaped,
returning to Jiāngdōng.
Emperor Ān commended him for this.
Huán Xuán invited him to be a Cányì Cānjūn (Consultative Army Advisor),
placing him at the head of the court officials.
Soon after, he died of illness.
Luó Qǐshēng
Luó Qǐshēng, courtesy name Zōngbó,
was a man from Yùzhāng.
He possessed many talents and skills.
Initially appointed Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Library,
due to his family's poverty and his parents' advanced age,
he requested to be appointed Magistrate of Línrǔ.
The Inspector Wáng Níngzhī invited him to be a Biéjià (Special Aide).
When Yīn Zhòngkān garrisoned Jiānglíng,
he recruited him as Gōngcáo (Merit Officer).
He was successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng.
Before he could reach his commandery, Huán Xuán attacked Zhòngkān,
and Zhòngkān reassigned Qǐshēng as Cányì Cānjūn (Consultative Army Advisor).
Zhòngkān was often suspicious and slow to decide,
which Qǐshēng deeply worried about.
He said to his younger brother Zūnshēng,
"Lord Yīn is benevolent but indecisive;
his endeavors will surely fail.
Success or failure
is destiny,
but I shall live or die with him."
Zhòngkān indeed fled,
and among his civil and military officials, none escorted him;
only Qǐshēng followed.
Passing by his family's gate,
Zūnshēng said,
"With such a separation impending,
how can we not clasp hands?"
Qǐshēng turned his horse and offered his hand.
Zūnshēng, who possessed great strength,
pulled him down,
and said,
"We have an old mother at home,
where are you going?"
Qǐshēng, wiping away tears, said,
"Today's events mean
I must surely die.
If you all serve and support her without failing in filial piety,
and our family has both loyalty and filial piety,
then what more regret can there be?"
Zūnshēng embraced him even tighter.
Zhòngkān waited for him on the road,
and Qǐshēng called out from afar,
"Life and death are one;
please wait a little longer."
Zhòngkān, seeing that Qǐshēng had no way to escape,
spurred his horse and left.
When Xuán arrived in Jīngzhōu,
all the gentry went to visit him,
but Qǐshēng alone did not go,
and instead busied himself with Zhòngkān's family affairs.
Someone said to him,
"Xuán's suspicious and ruthless nature
will not appreciate your sincerity and integrity.
If you persist in not going,
disaster will surely strike."
Qǐshēng, with a solemn expression, replied,
"I was Lord Yīn's official,
and he treated me as a national worthy.
Though I was restrained by my brother's strength
and thus could not follow him,
and could not join him in eliminating the vile rebels,
leading to this defeat,
what face do I have to seek life from Huán?"
Xuán heard this and was greatly enraged.
However, he had always treated Qǐshēng generously,
so he first sent someone to say,
"If you apologize to me,
I will release you."
Qǐshēng replied,
"As an official of Yīn of Jīngzhōu,
and with Jīngzhōu having fallen and fled,
and his fate in life or death still undecided,
what face do I have to apologize?"
Xuán immediately arrested Qǐshēng
and sent someone to ask what he wanted to say.
He replied,
"Emperor Wén killed Jī Kāng,
but Jī Shào became a loyal minister of the Jìn.
I beg you, sir, for one brother
to support my old mother."
Xuán granted it.
He then brought Qǐshēng before him
and said,
"I treated you very generously,
why did you betray me?
Now you will die!"
Qǐshēng replied,
"When your excellency raised the army at Jìnyáng,
and your troops were stationed at Xúnyáng,
we both received the royal command
to return to our respective posts.
We ascended the altar and swore an oath,
with the blood from our lips not yet dry,
yet you conceived a treacherous plan.
I lament my lack of strength
to eradicate this heinous rebel,
and regret that I die too late."
Xuán then had him executed.
He was thirty-seven years old at the time,
and everyone mourned him.
Earlier,
Xuán had given a lambskin robe to Qǐshēng's mother, Hú Shì.
When Qǐshēng was killed,
she burned the robe that very day.
Zhāng Yī
Zhāng Yī,
[一四] was a man from Wú County.
From a young age, he possessed integrity.
When Emperor Gōng was Prince of Lángxié,
he appointed Yī as Lángzhōnglìng (Prefect of the Palace Writers).
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Liú Yù, considering Yī to be a former official of the emperor
whom he had always trusted,
sealed a jug of medicinal wine and gave it to Yī,
secretly ordering him to poison the emperor.
Yī, having received the order, sighed,
"To poison one's lord and seek to live,
what face would I have to breathe in this world?
It is better to die!"
Thereupon, he drank it himself and died.
The Historian says: The Cán Sàn was executed for merely accepting a gift,
Wáng Yí incurred blame for speaking out.
At that time, both could be said to have died for no crime.
Wěiyuán was ashamed to serve the Jìn court,
Yánzǔ was willing to face peril and ruin.
Though the principles that guided them were similar,
the paths they chose were different,
yet both were praised in their time
and their fragrance preserved in historical records.
Is this not because the ruler and father hold the ultimate position in society,
and loyalty and filial piety are foremost among all virtues?
Moreover, Póu cultivated his virtue in solitude,
and thus preserved his filial piety;
while Shào also benefited others,
and so it was proper for him to exhaust his loyalty.
One could say that orchids and osmanthus have different qualities but share the same fragrance,
and the music of Sháo and Wǔ have different sounds but are equally beautiful.
Some who discuss Shào censure him for his death in a difficult situation;
to casually comment thus
is not a profound judgment.
Indeed, the ruler
is like Heaven.
How can Heaven be opposed?
If one enjoys prosperity,
but then avoids calamity in times of danger,
with no basis for advancement or retreat,
how can one establish oneself as a person?
Jī Shēng sacrificing himself to preserve his integrity
was precisely based on this principle.
Eulogy says: Valuing righteousness over life,
sacrificing the body for integrity.
Like the strong pine in character,
like severe frost in intensity.
Sharp blades can be endured,
but a chaste heart is hard to break.
Their virtue shines throughout antiquity,
their fragrance flows to future generations.
Collations
Biographies, Chapter 60: Good Officials
Emperor Xuān of Hàn
once said: “The reason the common people are at peace in their homes and fields, without sighs of grief or resentment,
is that the administration is just and disputes are resolved fairly.
Who can share this with me
but the excellent two-thousand-dàn officials!”
This shows that the offices of senior administrators are truly the foundation of governance and guidance.
Thus, Zhèng, the Prime Minister of Dōnglǐ,
Yè, the Magistrate of Xīmén,
Huáng Bà of Yǐngchuān,
and Wén Wēng of Shǔjùn—
some were feared by officials who dared not deceive them,
some were cherished for their benevolence by the people,
some caused their teachings to transform Qí and Lǔ,
and some made broad-minded and harmonious governance their priority.
These were all esteemed by historians who spread their admirable reputations,
and served as standards for upright officials.
When the Jìn dynasty first established its royal enterprise,
it gloriously initiated its hegemonic project,
assigning territories and employing the capable,
managing civil and military affairs.
Upon accepting the abdication in the Tàishǐ era,
it brought new order and ruled the realm,
continuing the grand foundation of three generations,
and receiving the great treasure of all kings.
The emperor toiled for various achievements,
and devoted his attention to the common people,
issuing repeated edicts to governors and magistrates,
and frequently publishing declarations of concern and sympathy.
His words and intentions were earnest and sincere,
his admonitions diligent,
wishing to make them follow the upright path and cultivate integrity,
suppressing the trivial and upholding the fundamental.
At this time,
it could be said that farmers were secure in their livelihoods,
and officials fully exerted their abilities!
However, the emperor's magnanimity, while sufficient to rule men,
and his clear majesty, could not reform customs.
Administration and punishments became subject to private influence,
and bribery became openly practiced.
Those who received official positions considered laxity and corruption to be the norm,
and those who rose in rank valued illicit gain.
They strayed from the path and forgot to return,
gradually making this a common practice.
Liú Yì spoke out against the selling of offices,
which was then considered an overcorrection.
But observing the customs of the time,
how could it have been an empty charge!
Later, by the time of Emperors Huì and Huái,
the Central Plain was in turmoil.
When it reached the east of the Jiāng River,
Jìn governance had many factions.
Emperor Yuán was compared to Shàokāng's resurgence,
yet Chǔ Zhòng became an obstruction.
Emperor Hǎixī's crimes were slight compared to Chāngyì's,
yet Yuánzǐ brought chaos to order.
Since the imperial power was under duress,
a policy of appeasement became the norm.
Those who took office sought benefits for themselves,
and those who selected officials chose offices for others.
While many lower officials possessed outstanding talent,
positions of power were inevitably held by scions of noble families.
This resulted in only a few accomplishments by truly capable individuals.
Although Mào Hóng, with his clear understanding, assisted in governance,
and Ānshí, as the leading figure of his time, stabilized both refined and common society,
nevertheless, external threats were rampant,
and internal difficulties were pressing.
Their efforts to rectify and mend the situation
barely averted collapse.
As for promoting upright customs and reforming abuses,
they did not have the leisure for that.
Now we collect their commendable administrative achievements
to compile this Record of Good Officials.
Lǔ Zhī
Lǔ Zhī, courtesy name Shìyīng,
was a native of Méi in Fúfēng.
His family had a renowned reputation for virtue
and was a prominent clan in Xīzhōu.
His father was killed by Guō Fàn.
Lǔ Zhī, while still an infant, was displaced.
At seventeen,
he moved to Yōng,
and immersed himself in classical texts.
The commandery recommended him as an accountant,
and the province appointed him as a Biejia.
Guō Huái, the General of Chariots and Cavalry of Wèi, serving as Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
deeply respected him.
He was recommended as Xiaolian [filial and incorrupt]
and appointed Langzhong.
When Zhūgě Liàng, the Chancellor of Shǔ, invaded Lǒngyòu,
Guō Huái again requested Lǔ Zhī to be Biejia.
After the conflict subsided,
he recommended him to the Grand Commandant's office,
which appointed him as an aide to Cáo Zhēn, the Grand Marshal,
and then transferred him to be the Literary Officer for the Marquis of Línzī.
Zhèng Mào recommended him to the Minister of Works Wáng Lǎng,
who immediately treated him with ceremony and summoned him.
