Later, he was appointed Cavalier Commandant, Participant in Military Affairs, acting Administrator of Ānnán,
and promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
Cáo Zhēn went out to supervise Guānyòu,
and Lǔ Zhī again participated in the Grand Marshal's military affairs.
After Cáo Zhēn's death,
Emperor Xuān replaced him,
and then invited Lǔ Zhī to participate in the Cavalry General's military affairs,
and transferred him to be the Administrator of Tiānshuǐ.
The commandery bordered Shǔ,
and was frequently invaded and plundered,
its population diminished,
and bandits were rampant.
Lǔ Zhī devoted himself to pacification and defense,
rebuilding cities and towns.
Within a few years, the former [destroyed settlements] were all restored.
He was promoted to Administrator of Guǎngpíng.
The Yi and Hua people of Tiānshuǐ admired his virtue,
and old and young went to the imperial court to present petitions,
begging for Lǔ Zhī to be retained.
Emperor Míng of Wèi granted their request,
and furthermore, issued an imperial edict commending him,
encouraging him with the example of Huáng Bà’s excellence,
and adding the title of General Who Quells Bandits.
When Cáo Shuǎng assisted in governance,
he appointed Lǔ Zhī as Sīmǎ.
Lǔ Zhī repeatedly offered candid advice and excellent strategies,
but Cáo Shuǎng could not accept them.
When Emperor Xuān raised troops to execute Cáo Shuǎng,
Lǔ Zhī led the remaining forces, broke through the gate and cut through the barriers,
galloping to Cáo Shuǎng,
and urged him, saying:
“You hold the position of Yī and Zhōu.
If you are once dismissed for a crime,
even if you wish to lead a yellow dog again,
how could you succeed!
If you hold the Son of Heaven and secure Xǔchāng,
wielding great authority and summoning troops from all four directions with urgent dispatches,
who would dare not follow!
To abandon this and leave,
wishing to go to the eastern market (to be executed),
is this not painful!”
Cáo Shuǎng was confused and could not use his advice,
and thus surrendered himself to be executed.
Lǔ Zhī was imprisoned for his association with Cáo Shuǎng
and was sentenced to death.
Yet, he did not plead his innocence,
nor did he seek to escape death dishonorably.
Emperor Xuān admired him,
pardoning him and not executing him.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Envoy with Credentials, concurrently Commander of the Southern Xiongnu, General Who Manifests Awe, and Inspector of Bìngzhōu.
For his effective pacification and control,
he was promoted to Grand Messenger.
When the High-Noble Duke of Xiāng took the throne,
he was granted the title Marquis of Guānnèi,
with two hundred households in his fief.
After Wúqiū Jiǎn was pacified,
his fief was increased by two hundred households according to precedent,
and he was appointed General Who Displays Martial Prowess and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
When Zhūgě Dàn rebelled in Shòuchūn,
Emperor Wén escorted Emperor Wèi on the expedition,
mobilizing troops from all directions.
Lǔ Zhī led the civil and military officials of Jīngzhōu as the vanguard.
After Zhūgě Dàn was pacified,
he was advanced to the title Marquis of Wǔjìn Pavilion,
and his fief was further increased by nine hundred households.
He was promoted to Grand Minister of the Interior,
in charge of justice.
When the Duke of Chángdào Xiāng took the throne,
he was advanced to the title Marquis of Táichéng Xiāng,
and his fief was again increased by eight hundred households.
He was promoted to Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Qīngzhōu, General Who Manifests Martial Prowess, and Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
then transferred to General Who Pacifies the East.
When the five ranks of nobility were established,
he was enfeoffed as Earl of Yīnpíng.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to General Who Guards the East,
and his noble rank was advanced to Marquis.
The emperor, considering Lǔ Zhī's integrity and upright conduct,
and that he had no private residence,
ordered military personnel to build him fifty rooms.
Lǔ Zhī, having reached the age for retirement,
requested to retire and resign his position,
submitting over ten memorials.
Thereupon, he was summoned as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
given the special rank of Tèjìn,
provided with officials and attendants,
and permitted to have horses run past his gate.
Yáng Hù, then General of Chariots and Cavalry,
offered his position to Lǔ Zhī,
saying:
“Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Lǔ Zhī, pure in conduct and moderate in desires,
harmonious but not conforming,
served in office until his hair turned white,
maintaining propriety from beginning to end.
He has not yet received this selection,
and I am promoted ahead of him.
How can I satisfy the expectations of the world!”
The emperor did not agree.
Such was the respect he commanded.
He died in the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
aged eighty-four.
The Emperor held a mourning ceremony for him,
bestowing generous funeral gifts.
He was posthumously granted the title Zhēn,
and a burial ground of one hundred *mǔ* was bestowed.
Hú Wēi
Hú Wēi, courtesy name Bówǔ,
also named Pí,
was a native of Shòuchūn, Huáinán.
His father, Zhì,
was renowned for his loyalty and integrity.
In his youth, he and his fellow provincials Jiǎng Jì and Zhū Jì were all famous in the Jiānghuái region.
He served the Wèi dynasty, reaching the positions of Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wēi developed high aspirations early on.
When Zhì was the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
Wēi traveled from the capital to visit his parents.
His family was poor,
having no carriage, horses, or servants.
He personally drove a donkey and traveled alone.
Whenever he arrived at an inn,
he personally unburdened the donkey,
gathered firewood, and cooked.
After eating,
he continued his journey with his companions.
Upon arrival,
he saw his father,
and stayed in the stables for more than ten days.
When he announced his departure,
his father gave him a roll of silk for his travel expenses.
Wēi asked:
"Father, you are so upright and pure;
I wonder where you obtained this silk?"
Zhì replied:
"This is what remains of my salary,
for your provisions."
Wēi accepted it and
took his leave.
A Dūdū from Zhì's retinue, who had not yet departed before Wēi,
requested leave to return home.
He secretly prepared provisions about a hundred *lǐ* away,
intending to meet Wēi and travel with him,
assisting him in every matter.
After traveling several hundred *lǐ*,
Wēi grew suspicious and cleverly questioned him.
Once he knew the truth,
he gave the Dūdū the silk he had received,
thanked him, and sent him away.
Later, through another messenger, he informed Zhì.
Zhì flogged the Dūdū one hundred times
and dismissed him from official service.
Such was the integrity and prudence of this father and son.
Thereupon, their reputation became widely known.
He was appointed Shìyùshǐ,
and successively held the posts of Nánxiāng Hóu and Ānfēng Tàishǒu,
then promoted to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was diligent in governance,
and his virtuous influence became widespread.
Later, when he came to court,
Emperor Wǔ spoke of his life,
and sighed about his father's integrity,
saying to Wēi:
"How does your integrity compare to your father's?"
He replied:
"I am not as good."
The Emperor asked:
"In what way is your father superior?"
He replied:
"My father's integrity was such that he feared others would know,
while my integrity is such that I fear others will not know.
In this, I am far inferior."
The Emperor found Wēi's words direct yet tactful,
humble yet compliant.
He was successively promoted to Jiān Yùzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Yòujiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
He then entered court as Shàngshū,
and was additionally granted Fèngchē Dūwèi.
Wēi once advised that the current government's policies were too lenient.
The Emperor said:
"For officials below Shàngshū Láng,
I show no favoritism."
Wēi replied:
"What I submit,
is not about the Chéngláng or Lìshǐ.
It is precisely about those of us of equal rank,
who should be the first to enforce laws and clarify governance."
He was appointed Qiánjiāngjūn, Jiān Qīngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Píngchūn Hóu.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
he died in office.
He was posthumously granted Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Qīngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
with other honors as before,
and given the posthumous title Liè.
His son Yì succeeded him.
Yì, courtesy name Cìsūn,
rose to the position of Píngdōng Jiāngjūn.
Wēi's younger brother Pí,
courtesy name Jìxiàng,
also had administrative abilities,
and rose to the positions of Yìzhōu Cìshǐ and Āndōng Jiāngjūn.
Dù Zhěn
Dù Zhěn, courtesy name Chāozōng,
was a native of Chéngdū, Shǔjùn.
His father, Xióng,
was the Miánzhú Lìng.
Zhěn studied under Qiáo Zhōu,
and was widely read in the Classics.
He declined an appointment from the province
and served as the Gōngcáo Shǐ of the commandery.
When Dèng Ài arrived in Chéngdū,
Zhěn said to the Tàishǒu:
"Now that a large army has come to conquer,
they will surely remove the old and establish the new.
It is appropriate for you, Your Excellency, to yield to them.
This is the path to complete good fortune."
The Tàishǒu then departed.
Dèng Ài indeed sent his Cānjūn, Qiān Hóng, to the commandery.
Hóng asked Zhěn where the former governor was.
Zhěn replied with a stern expression:
"The former governor understood the opportune moment to stay or leave,
and thus left the official residence to await the arrival of a noble man."
Hóng admired him,
and ordered him to resume his post as Gōngcáo.
Zhěn firmly declined.
He was recommended as Xiàolián,
and appointed Jiànníng Lìng.
He governed with virtue,
and his transforming influence became widespread.
Both the native and foreign peoples were pleased and submitted.
When his term was complete and he was about to return,
the various barbarian tribes followed him to see him off,
offering many bribes and gifts.
Zhěn accepted none of them,
leaving as purely as he had arrived.
He was then appointed Chíyáng Lìng,
and was ranked first among the eleven commanderies of Yōngzhōu.
The people erected a shrine for him while he was still alive,
and those who were punished bore no resentment.
He was successively promoted to Shàngshū Láng.
Zhěn was widely learned and well-read,
and many of his memorials and dissenting arguments were adopted.
At that time, Lǐ Xiāng of Fú also served as Shàngshū Láng,
and was as famous as Zhěn.
Whenever there were discussions or debates,
no one in the court could surpass them.
They were known as the "Two Lángs of Shǔ."
Zhěn was later appointed Jiānwéi Tàishǒu,
and had a great reputation.
He was about to be promoted
when he fell ill and died,
aged fifty-one.
His son was Pí.
Pí, courtesy name Chángjī.
He was recommended as Xiùcái by the province,
appointed Dàjiāngjūn Yuàn by Wáng Yǐng, King of Chéngdū,
then promoted to Shàngshū Láng,
and participated in the military affairs of the Tàifù.
When Luòyáng fell,
Pí crossed the Jiāng to the south.
Wáng Dūn appointed him Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
planning to jointly secure Báidì with Liǔ Chún, the Tàishǒu of Yídū.
Dù Tāo sent troops to intercept Pí,
and he was subsequently killed.
Pí's younger brother Xiù,
courtesy name Yàn Yǐng,
served as Luó Shàng's Zhǔbù.
When the province fell,
he was captured by the Dí bandit Lǐ Xiāng,
who wanted to employ him as Sīmǎ.
Xiù refused
and was killed.
Pí's second son, Xīn,
was recommended as Xiùcái.
Zhěn's younger brother Liè
was skilled in governance.
He was recommended as Xiàolián
and successively served as Píngkāng Lìng and Ānyáng Lìng.
In every place he served, he achieved extraordinary results,
and was promoted to Héngyáng Tàishǒu.
Upon hearing of Zhěn's death,
he personally submitted a memorial, stating that his nephew was young and weak,
and requested to resign his post.
An imperial edict transferred him to Jiānwéi Tàishǒu,
which brought glory to the land of Shǔ.
Later, he was promoted to Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu,
and served as Lángzhōng Lìng for Wáng Yǐng, King of Chéngdū,
where he died of illness.
Liè's younger brother Liáng
was recommended as Xiùcái,
and appointed Xīndū Lìng and Fúlíng Tàishǒu.
He did not take office,
but was instead appointed Zhōu Dàzhōngzhèng,
and then died.
Dòu Yǔn
When Qí Wáng Jǐng (齊王冏) assisted in governing,
Chē (攄) and Zuǒ Sī (左思) were both appointed as Secretaries-General.
Jǐng (冏) once casually asked Chē (攄):
“The Son of Heaven was coerced by traitorous ministers,
and no one was able to rise up.
I led the righteous armies of the four seas to restore the royal house.
Now I have entered the court to assist in governing,
to rectify and revitalize in these difficult times.
Some advise me to return to my domain;
what do you think of this, Sir?”
Chē (攄) replied:
“To quell the national traitors
and restore the imperial throne—
the achievements of ministers throughout history have not been as great as Your Highness’s.
However, no Dao (道) is so lofty that it does not also involve destruction;
no thing is so flourishing that it does not also decline.
This is not only true of human affairs,
but also a principle of Heaven.
I humbly presume to answer your question,
and would not dare to hold back my true feelings.
I wish that Your Highness, being in a high position, would consider the dangers,
and in times of abundance, reflect on moderation.
Carefully select all officials,
uphold public interest and eliminate personal desires,
promote the worthy and advance the good,
and strive to find those with true talent.
Then, grease your carriage and feed your horses,
and with a respectful bow, return to your domain.
Then, all above and below will rejoice,
and Chē (攄) and others will be most fortunate.”
Jǐng (冏) did not accept this.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and Chángshā Wáng Yì (長沙王乂) appointed him as Piàojì Sīmǎ (驃騎司馬).
When Yì (乂) was defeated,
he was dismissed from office.
He then observed mourning for his mother.
At the end of Huì Dì’s (惠帝) reign,
he was appointed Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu (襄城太守).
At that time, Xiāngchéng (襄城) had repeatedly suffered from banditry and hardship.
Chē (攄) pacified, comforted, and restored order,
and within a month, it was brought back to normal.
In the second year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
Gāomì Wáng Jiǎn (高密王簡) was stationed in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and appointed Chē (攄) as Zhēngnán Sīmǎ (征南司馬).
In that year, vagrants like Wáng Yóu (王逌) gathered a multitude and encamped at Guānjūn (冠軍),
plundering cities and towns.
Jiǎn (簡) dispatched his Cānjūn (參軍) Cuī Kuàng (崔曠) to suppress them,
ordering Chē (攄) to oversee Kuàng (曠).
Kuàng (曠) was a treacherous and malicious person.
He cunningly urged Chē (攄) to engage in battle first,
promising to follow as a reinforcement,
but then did not arrive.
Chē (攄) fought Wáng Yóu (王逌) alone in Lìxiàn (酈縣),
and his army was defeated, leading to his death.
His former subordinates and the common people all rushed to his funeral to mourn,
wailing on the roads,
as if attending the funeral of their own parents.
Pān Jīng (潘京)
Pān Jīng (潘京), courtesy name Shìcháng (世長),
was from Hànshòu (漢壽), Wǔlíng (武陵).
At a young age,
the commandery appointed him Zhǔbù (主簿).
The Tàishǒu (太守), Zhào Yīn (趙廞), greatly esteemed him.
He once asked,
“Why is your commandery named Wǔlíng (武陵)?”
Jīng (京) replied,
“Our humble commandery was originally named Yìlíng (義陵),
located in the territory of Chényáng (辰陽) County.
It bordered the Yi (夷) people,
and was frequently attacked by them.
During the time of Guāngwǔ (光武), it was moved eastward,
thus achieving complete safety.
Everyone discussed changing its name.
The tradition says ‘stopping a spear makes for martial prowess’ (止戈為武),
and the Odes refer to high plains as ‘líng’ (陵).
Hence, it was named as such.”
He was appointed by the province,
and upon presenting himself and being asked for a plan,
he drew the character
‘bù xiào’ (不孝)
“unfilial.”
The Cìshǐ (刺史) jokingly said to Jīng (京),
“Are we appointing a scholar to be unfilial?”
Jīng (京) held up his tablet and replied,
“Now that I am a loyal minister,
I cannot continue to be a filial son.”
His quick wit was always of this sort.
Later, when the Grand Ancestral Temple was established,
provinces and commanderies all sent envoys to congratulate.
Jīng (京) reported to the Tàishǒu (太守) saying,
“When the Grand Ancestral Temple is established,
and the spirit tablets are moved,
one should inquire about their well-being,
not offer congratulations.”
So, Jīng (京) was sent to compose a text,
and dispatched to the capital,
which became an eternal standard.
Jīng (京) then passed the Xiùcái (秀才) examination
and arrived in Luò (洛).
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Yuè Guǎng (樂廣),
a fellow provincial of Jīng (京),
conversed with him for several days,
deeply praising his talent.
He said to Jīng (京),
“Your innate talent surpasses others,
it is only a pity that you have not studied enough.
If you were to study,
you would surely become a master of discourse for your generation.”
Jīng (京) was touched by his words,
and thereafter diligently studied without weariness.
At that time, the Wǔlíng Tàishǒu (武陵太守) Dài Chāng (戴昌) was also skilled in discussion.
When he conversed with Jīng (京),
Jīng (京) feigned ignorance,
and Chāng (昌) thought he was inferior to himself.
He laughed and dismissed him,
telling him to visit his son Ruòsī (若思).
Jīng (京) then fully expressed his views.
Chāng (昌) secretly listened,
and then sighed in admiration, saying,
“Talent cannot be feigned.”
Thus, both father and son were humbled.
He successively served as the Magistrate of Bāqiú (巴丘), Shàolíng (邵陵), and Quánlíng (泉陵),
three counties.
Jīng (京) was clear-sighted in governance,
and valuables were not picked up from the road.
He was promoted to Guìlín Tàishǒu (桂林太守),
but did not take office.
He returned home
and died at the age of fifty.
Fàn Guǐ (范晷)
Fàn Guǐ (范晷), courtesy name Yàncháng (彥長),
was from Shùnyáng (順陽), Nányáng (南陽).
In his youth, he traveled to Qīnghé (清河) for studies,
and subsequently moved his family and settled there temporarily.
The commandery appointed him Wǔguān Yuàn (五官掾),
and he successively served as Hénèi Jùnchéng (河內郡丞).
The Tàishǒu (太守) Péi Kǎi (裴楷) knew him well,
and recommended him as Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
He was then appointed as Shànggǔ Tàishǒu (上谷太守),
but due to mourning,
he did not take up the post.
Later, he became Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史),
then transferred to Féngyì Tàishǒu (馮翊太守).
He had great administrative ability,
and was skilled at pacification and comforting,
which endeared him to the common people.
He was summoned to be appointed Shǎofǔ (少府),
and then went out to serve as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (涼州刺史),
and then Yōngzhōu (雍州).
At that time, the western lands were devastated,
the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) peoples trod upon them,
fields and mulberry trees yielded no harvest,
and the common people were impoverished.
Guǐ (晷) devoted himself to transforming and guiding them,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
and those under his jurisdiction greatly relied on him.
During the Yuánkāng (元康) period,
he was given the additional title of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍),
and died in office.
He had two sons: Guǎng (廣) and Zhì (稚).
Guǎng (廣), courtesy name Zhòngjiāng (仲將).
He was recommended as Xiàolián (孝廉),
and appointed Língshòu Lìng (靈壽令),
but did not take up the post.
His elder sister married into the Sūn (孫) family,
and died young.
She had a grandson named Mài (邁).
Guǎng (廣) carried him and fled south.
Although bandits caused urgent hardships,
he never abandoned him.
Yuán Dì (元帝), acting provisionally,
appointed him Tángyì Lìng (堂邑令).
His Chéng (丞) Liú Róng (劉榮) was condemned to death for a crime.
The commandery impeached him and handed him over to the county.
Róng (榮) was a local,
and had an elderly mother at home.
At festivals,
Guǎng (廣) would always allow him to return home temporarily,
and Róng (榮) would always return on schedule.
The county court was caught in a wildfire.
Róng (榮) took off his shackles to fight the fire.
When the task was complete,
he put his shackles back on himself.
Later, there was a great drought,
and rice was expensive.
Guǎng (廣) distributed his private grain to feed the starving people,
totaling several thousand hú (斛).
Wanderers from near and far came to him,
and the household population increased tenfold.
He died in office.
Zhì (稚) was renowned from a young age.
He was appointed Dà Jiāngjūn Yuàn (大將軍掾),
but died early.
His son Wāng (汪)
has a separate biography.
Dīng Shào (丁紹)
Dīng Shào, courtesy name Shúlún,
was a man from Qiáoguó.
From a young age, he was open-minded and just,
and served as a pure official early in his career.
When he was the Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng,
his governance was fair and lawsuits were handled properly,
and the Way of transformation greatly prevailed.
At that time, Héběi was in turmoil,
with no intact city,
yet the single commandery of Guǎngpíng was at peace within its four borders.
Therefore, everyone was pleased with his laws and followed his commands.
When Línzhāng was besieged,
Southeastern King Mó of Nányáng was in dire straits.
Shào led the commandery troops to his aid,
and Mó relied on him to survive.
Mó was grateful for Shào's kindness,
and erected a stele for him during his lifetime.
He was promoted to Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and the officials and common people were attached to him with longing,
clinging to him as if returning home.
Before he could take up this post,
he was again transferred to Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He traveled with a thousand carriages,
crossing the Hé River southwards to Xǔ.
At that time, Southeastern King Mó of Nányáng was the Grand Commandant.
He detained Shào
and requested his transfer to Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Upon arriving at his post,
he led the provincial troops to attack and defeat Jí Sāng with meritorious service.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North, granted a symbolic axe, and supervised all military affairs in Jìzhōu.
At that time, the Jié bandits were causing trouble within the borders.
Shào captured and executed them,
and was known for his strictness.
The people of Héběi feared and loved him.
Shào considered himself talented enough to be a hero of the age,
and when he held office and administered government,
he successfully accomplished every task.
He viewed the affairs of the world as if they were within his grasp,
and thus he was filled with the ambition to rectify the four seas.
At this time, Wáng Jùn was flourishing in Yōuzhōu,
and Gǒu Xī was flourishing in Qīngzhōu.
However, Shào regarded the two men with contempt.
In the third year of Yǒngjiā,
he died suddenly of an illness.
On his deathbed, he sighed,
"This is Heaven destroying Jìzhōu,
how can it be my fate!"
Emperor Huái posthumously granted him the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Qiáo Zhìmíng
Qiáo Zhìmíng, courtesy name Yuándá,
was a man from the Former Division of the Xiānbēi.
He lost both parents young,
and mourned to an extent exceeding the rites.
When he grew up, he was renowned for his virtuous conduct.
King Yǐng of Chéngdū appointed him General Who Assists the State.
When Yǐng defeated King Lún of Zhào,
he memorialized Zhìmíng as General Who Destroys Bandits and Magistrate of the two counties of Lónglǜ and Gòng.
The people of the two counties loved him,
calling him
"Divine Lord."
A local man, Zhāng Duì, sought revenge for his father.
His mother was old and living alone,
and he had a wife but no son.
Zhìmíng pitied him
and suspended his imprisonment.
More than a year later,
he allowed Duì to bring his wife into prison,
and secretly released him.
Someone advised Duì to escape,
but Duì said,
"With such a lord,
how can I bear to implicate him!
Even if I were to escape,
what face would I have to live in this world!"
A son was born in prison.
A general amnesty was declared,
and he was pardoned.
His benevolence moved people in this way.
When Emperor Huì attacked Yè,
Yǐng made Zhìmíng General of Valiant Attack and Participator in the Prime Minister's Vanguard Military Affairs.
Zhìmíng advised Yǐng to welcome the imperial carriage,
but Yǐng was furious and said,
"You claim to understand affairs,
and have dedicated yourself to serving me.
The emperor is pressured by small-minded men,
and intends to inflict an unjust punishment upon me.
How can you want me to tie my hands and submit to execution!
Is this the meaning of sharing service?"
Zhìmíng then stopped.
Soon after, during the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he served Liú Yào.
Dèng Yōu
Dèng Yōu, courtesy name Bódào,
was a man from Xiānglíng, Píngyáng.
His grandfather Yīn was upright and resolute.
When Zhōng Huì attacked Shǔ,
he admired his talent
and summoned him from Magistrate of Mǐnchí to be his Chief Clerk.
When Jiǎ Chōng attacked Wú,
he invited Yīn to be his Chief Secretary.
Later, he was assigned to teach poetry to the Crown Prince
and became the Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
He dreamt of walking by the water
and seeing a woman,
when a fierce beast from behind severed her waist-pouch.
A diviner said that the woman by the water was your courtesy name (Rǔ),
and the severing of the waist-pouch
meant a new beast's head replacing the old beast's head,
so it would not be Rǔyīn,
but Rǔnán.
Indeed, he was transferred to Grand Administrator of Rǔyīn.
Later, he became Middle Palace Attendant.
Yōu lost his father at seven years old,
and soon after lost his mother and grandmother.
He observed mourning for nine years,
and was renowned for his filial piety.
He was pure and peaceful, simple and straightforward,
chaste and upright, with few desires.
Being an orphan in his youth,
he lived with his younger brother.
Initially,
his grandfather Yīn had been granted an official post,
and Yōu was ordered to accept it.
Later, the Grand Administrator advised Yōu to resign from the royal office
and wished to recommend him as an Exemplary Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
Yōu said,
"What my ancestors were granted
cannot be changed."
He once visited General of the Garrison Jiǎ Hùn,
who showed Yōu a lawsuit brought by someone
and asked him to decide it.
Yōu did not look at it,
saying,
"Confucius said, 'In hearing lawsuits, I am no different from others;
what is essential is to make it so that there are no lawsuits!'"
Hùn was surprised by this
and married his daughter to him.
He was rated as an outstanding second-rank official,
became Literary Advisor to the King of Wú,
and successively served as Equerry to the Crown Prince and Military Advisor to King Yuè of Dōnghǎi.
Yuè admired his character
and transferred him to Literary Advisor to the Heir Apparent and Bureau Director of Personnel.
Yuè's younger brother Téng was General of the Central East,
and invited Yōu to be his Chief Secretary.
He was sent out as Grand Administrator of Hédōng.
In the late Yǒngjiā period,
he was captured by Shí Lè.
However, Lè had long resented officials above two thousand dàn [shi],
and hearing that Yōu was in the camp,
he sent for him in haste,
intending to kill him.
When Yōu reached the gate,
the gatekeeper had been a retainer of Yōu’s when Yōu was a Láng,
and recognized Yōu.
Yōu asked for paper and brush to compose a farewell statement.
The gatekeeper, observing that Lè was in a good mood,
presented it to him.
Lè valued the statement,
and thus did not kill him.
Lè’s Chángshǐ, Zhāng Bīn, had previously been Yōu’s neighbor,
and admired Yōu’s reputation and integrity.
He then praised Yōu to Lè.
Lè summoned him to his tent,
spoke with him,
and was pleased.
He appointed him Cānjūn [Staff Officer],
and provided him with a carriage and horses.
Whenever Lè moved,
he placed Yōu’s carriage in the camp.
One night, Lè forbade fires;
violators would be put to death.
Yōu was neighbors with a Hú man,
who accidentally set fire to his carriage at night.
The officials investigated,
and the Hú man falsely accused Yōu.
Yōu realized he could not argue with him,
and so replied that his younger brother’s wife had let down her hair to warm wine.
Lè pardoned him.
Soon after, the Hú man was deeply moved,
and tied himself up to go to Lè to clear Yōu’s name,
and secretly gave Yōu horses and donkeys.
All the Hú people sighed in admiration and respect for him.
When Shí Lè crossed the Sìshǔi River,
Yōu chopped up his carriage,
and used oxen and horses to carry his wife and children to escape.
He again encountered bandits,
who plundered his oxen and horses.
He walked,
carrying his own son and his younger brother’s son, Suī.
Judging that he could not save both,
he said to his wife:
“My younger brother died early,
leaving only one descendant;
it is right that his line should not be cut off.
We should just abandon my own son.
If he is fortunate enough to survive,
I will have other sons later.”
His wife wept but followed his instruction,
and so they abandoned him.
His son, abandoned in the morning, caught up in the evening.
The next day,
Yōu tied him to a tree and left.
Upon arriving in Xīnzhèng,
he took refuge with Lǐ Jǔ.
After three years,
he intended to leave,
but Jǔ would not permit it.
Xún Zǔ appointed him Táishǒu of Chénjùn and Rǔnán,
and Emperor Mǐn summoned him to be Shàngshū Zuǒchéng and Chángshǔi Xiàowèi,
but he did not take up any of these positions.
Later, he secretly left Jǔ,
and went to Xún Zǔ in Xǔchāng.
Jǔ deeply resented this,
but after a long time,
he sent Yōu’s family back to him.
Yōu had long been close with Diāo Xié and Zhōu Yǐ,
and so he went to Jiāngdōng.
Emperor Yuán appointed Yōu as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
At that time, the position of Gùnshǒu of Wúchùn was vacant,
and many desired it.
The Emperor bestowed it upon Yōu.
Yōu carried rice to the commandery,
and accepted no salary,
only drinking the water of Wú.
At that time, there was a great famine in the commandery.
Yōu memorialized to distribute relief,
but before a reply came,
he immediately opened the granaries to save the people.
The court dispatched Sànqí Chángshì Huán Yí and Yú to console the starving people,
and to observe their well-being.
They then impeached Yōu for unauthorized grain distribution.
Soon after, an imperial edict pardoned him.
In the commandery, Yōu’s administration and laws were clear and just,
and the people were joyful;
he was considered a good governor of the Zhongxing era.
Later, he claimed illness and resigned from his post.
The commandery traditionally offered millions in welcoming and farewell money;
when Yōu left the commandery,
he did not accept a single coin.
Thousands of people held onto Yōu’s boat,
preventing it from moving forward.
Yōu then stopped for a short while,
and departed in the middle of the night.
The people of Wú sang:
“The drum beats for the fifth watch,
the rooster crows, the sky is about to dawn.
Lord Dèng cannot be held back,
Governor Xiè cannot be pushed away.”
The people went to the court to beg him to stay for one more year,
but it was not permitted.
He was appointed Shìzhōng.
After more than a year,
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
He ate simple food and wore worn clothes,
and helped those in need and relieved the destitute.
His nature was humble and gentle,
and he was good at interacting with people.
Guests, regardless of their status,
were treated equally,
but he was somewhat deferential to the powerful and noble.
During the Yǒngchāng period,
he replaced Zhōu Yǐ as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Tàiníng (324 CE),
Wáng Dūn rebelled.
Emperor Míng secretly plotted to raise an army,
and so transferred Yōu to be Huìjī Tàishǒu.
Initially,
after Wáng Dūn attacked the capital,
the numbers of troops inside and outside the capital were reported to Dūn monthly.
Yōu had already left and was at home,
no longer privy to Hùjūn affairs.
There was someone who hated Yōu,
and falsely accused Yōu of still reporting troop numbers to Dūn.
The Emperor heard this but did not believe it,
and transferred Yōu to be Tàicháng.
At that time, the Emperor performed the Southern Sacrifice,
but Yōu was ill and could not attend.
The imperial carriage passed by Yōu to inquire about his illness,
and Yōu, despite his weakness, came out to bow.
The officials memorialized that Yōu, unable to attend the sacrifice, had bowed by the roadside,
and he was dismissed due to this.
Whenever Yōu was promoted or demoted,
he showed no signs of joy or resentment.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
He died in the first year of Xiánhé (326 CE),
and was posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū,
awarded the golden seal and purple ribbon,
and sacrificed with a shàoláo.
After Yōu abandoned his son,
his wife never conceived again.
Upon crossing the Yangtze River,
he took a concubine
and favored her greatly.
He inquired about her family,
and she said she was a person from the North who had suffered in the chaos.
She recalled her parents’ names,
and it turned out she was Yōu’s niece.
Yōu had always possessed virtue,
and upon hearing this, he was filled with sorrow and regret,
and never kept a concubine again,
thus dying without an heir.
People at the time admired his righteousness and pitied him,
and a saying arose:
“The way of Heaven is without knowledge,
to leave Dèng Bódào without a son.”
His younger brother’s son, Shòu, observed Yōu’s mourning for three years.
Wú Yǐnzhī
Wú Yǐnzhī, courtesy name Chǔmò,
was from Juānchéng, Púyáng,
and a sixth-generation descendant of Wèi Shìzhōng Zhì.
Yǐnzhī was handsome in appearance,
skilled in discussion,
and widely read in literature and history,
distinguishing himself with his refined elegance.
At twenty, he was resolute and independent,
possessing pure integrity.
Even when it was late in the day and he drank only water with beans,
he would not consume grain that was not rightfully his.
Without even a single dàn [shi] of stored grain,
he would not acquire it through improper means.
When he was a little over ten,
he suffered the death of his father.
He wept so frequently
that passersby shed tears for him.
He served his mother with filial piety and reverence,
and when he observed her mourning,
his grief and emaciation exceeded proper bounds.
His family was poor,
and there was no one to beat the drum.
Whenever it was time to weep by the coffin,
a pair of cranes would cry out.
And on the evening of the xiángliàn [ceremony],
a flock of geese gathered.
People at the time all believed it was due to his filial piety.
He once ate salted pickles,
and finding their taste exquisite,
he picked them up and threw them away.
The historian says: Lǔ Zhī and others established their banners and administered justice,
spreading their governance and proclaiming their regulations,
preserving their might and grace during their lives,
and leaving behind affection after their deaths.
All were recognized by enlightened rulers
and lauded in their time.
Like Bówǔ's integrity and diligence,
Yán Yuǎn's rectifying grievances and easing prisons,
Dèng Yōu's carrying provisions to perform his duties,
and Wú Yǐn's drinking water to temper his spirit,
the capable and good officials of the Jìn dynasty,
these were the foremost.
Yet Yōu abandoned his son to save his nephew,
severing affection for righteousness.
If it was beyond his power,
he could have cut off his feelings and endured the pain.
Why did he go so far as to tie a rope around him in advance,
cutting off his chance to escape?
How could this be the intention of a kind father and benevolent person?
He ultimately died without an heir;
this is fitting!
Do not say that the Way of Heaven is unknowing;
indeed, it is knowing.
Shìyīng displayed his loyalty to the Cáo clan,
assailing the gate and cleaving the barriers.
Emperor Xuān accepted his thunderous might
and rewarded his loyal and upright spirit.
Was it not because he was already in our grasp
that we wanted him to curse others?
A eulogy says: Oh, what excellent ministers,
whose virtues succeeded those of earlier worthies.
Their authority was like reining in the unruly,
their tranquility like cooking a small fish.
They only tasted Wú water,
merely scooped from the Greedy Spring.
The people's customs were suppressed,
and societal transformation thus occurred.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 61: The Forest of Scholars
When the virtue of Zhōu had declined,
the feudal lords contended for power.
The Rites and Classics were neglected and incomplete,
the Yǎ and Sòng deteriorated.
The Master, possessing sagely wisdom and manifold abilities,
was indeed sent by Heaven.
He sighed that the phoenix did not arrive,
and was pained that the qílín appeared at the wrong time.
Thereupon, he abridged the Shī and Shū,
established the Lǐ and Yuè,
praised the Yì Dào,
and revised the Chūnqiū.
Lost records were restored,
and the Fēng and Yǎ, though altered, returned to their proper form.
Afterwards, disciples like Bǔ Shāng, Wèi Cì, Tián, Wú, Sūn, and Mèng,
some personally received subtle teachings,
others heard the great principles transmitted.
They were still able to strengthen Jìn and preserve Lǔ,
to protect Wèi and repel Qín,
both maintaining their dignity before rulers
and spreading their fame throughout the realm.
When the Yíng clan became cruel and tyrannical,
abandoning virtue and relying on punishment,
they burned books and records to ashes,
and buried scholars in pits.
They enforced ancient laws strictly
and penalized those who possessed books.
The glorious achievements of the former kings
left not a single trace.
When Hàn Zǔ rose mightily,
saving those in peril and rescuing those drowning,
he roughly reformed rites and laws,
but had no leisure for sacrificial vessels.
It was not until Emperor Xiàowǔ
that he esteemed scholars and culture.
And when it came to the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng),
this trend did not falter.
Thereupon, tattered bamboo slips were widely sought,
and lost books extensively inquired about.
The system of first- and second-class scholars was established,
and meritorious talents were promoted.
All without exception wore green and purple robes,
donned ceremonial caps, and rode in carriages.
Some rose from humble beginnings to become high officials,
others ascended to the highest positions in a matter of weeks.
Thus, the gentry enthusiastically gravitated towards this trend,
and their lasting reputation and glorious deeds
shine brightly and are worthy of record.
When Dāngtú was founded,
it was deeply committed to military power.
Yet the ruler cherished this culture,
and the court had many gentlemen.
Great scholars and erudite masters
were not lacking at the time.
Emperor Wǔ, receiving the Mandate,
was worried and toiled for the military and state.
At that time, having just annexed Yōng and Shǔ,
and preparing for campaigns in Jiānghú,
training soldiers, sharpening weapons,
and diligently promoting agriculture to accumulate grain,
he still repaired and established schools
and personally visited Bìyōng.
Sún Yǐ assisted in the new regulations,
Zhèng Chōng ascended to the position of grand tutor based on his Confucian scholarship,
Màoxiān participated in court politics with his extensive knowledge,
and Zǐzhēn held the position of minister of rites due to his adherence to propriety.
Although they were somewhat ashamed of their fame,
they were certainly not cast aside.
Subsequently, Jīng and Yáng were pacified,
and the regions enjoyed peace.
The high officials drafted the rituals for the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
and the Son of Heaven issued humble edicts.
Though not comparable to the three dynasties (Sān Dài),
it indeed excelled for a time.
Emperor Huì inherited the throne amidst turmoil,
and the court became chaotic and governance lax.
Strife arose within the imperial palace,
and disaster was fueled by the regional princes.
Through Huái and Mǐn,
there was much loss and chaos.
Clothing, rites, and music
were swept away completely.
Emperor Yuán encountered the "hundred-six" cycle of misfortune,
and brilliantly initiated the restoration.
Worthies such as Hè, Xún, Diāo, and Dù all studied the classics and were broadly learned,
creating and perfecting the rites and regulations.
Although decrees encouraging Confucianism and learning were frequently issued,
the sounds of string and recitation were not heard in the Eastern and Western schools.
Emperor Míng was intelligent and wise,
and particularly fond of literary accomplishments.
Emperor Jiǎnwén was profound and quiet,
delighting in ancient books.
They recruited students
and greatly encouraged their virtuous conduct.
However, due to the difficulties of the time and their short reigns,
they were unable to implement everything thoroughly.
From the beginning of the Jìn dynasty in the central court
until its move to the south of the Yangtze (Jiāngzuǒ),
all without exception pursued elaborate competition
and advocated for abstruse metaphysics.
They rejected the classical canons of Qùlǐ
and practiced the remaining doctrines of Zhèngshǐ.
They dismissed rites and laws as common and vulgar,
and regarded unrestrained indulgence as pure and lofty.
Consequently, statutes and regulations became lax and abandoned,
and the moral teachings declined and were ruined.
The Five Hú took advantage of the opportunity to contend for power,
and the two capitals (Èr Jīng) successively fell into ruin.
The fortunes reached their extreme, and the Way disappeared;
this is truly cause for a long sigh.
As Zhèng Chōng and others held prominent positions,
they have their own biographies.
The rest are compiled below,
to continue the previous histories' section on scholars.
Fàn Píng
Fàn Píng, courtesy name Zǐ'ān,
was a native of Qiántáng, Wújùn.
His ancestor, Zhìhóu Fù,
fled the chaos of Wáng Mǎng and moved to Wú,
where his family settled.
Píng extensively studied ancient texts and
was thoroughly versed in all schools of thought.
Yáo Xìn and Hè Shào and their ilk all studied under him.
During the Wú period, he was recommended as Màocái
and was repeatedly promoted to Prefect of Línhǎi,
where his governance showed unusual ability.
In the early reign of Sūn Hào,
he pleaded illness and returned home,
delighting in Confucian studies.
After Wú was pacified,
during the Tàikāng era,
he was repeatedly summoned but did not respond.
He died at the age of sixty-nine.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the honorific title of Wénzhēn Xiānshēng.
Hè Xún engraved a stele to record his virtues and conduct.
He had three sons: Shì, Xián, and Quán,
all of whom achieved high official positions through their Confucian scholarship.
Quán's son, Wèi,
was a Guānnèihóu.
His family had a long tradition of scholarship,
possessing over seven thousand scrolls of books.
Over a hundred people came from near and far to read them,
and Wèi provided them with food and clothing.
Wèi's son, Wéncái,
was also renowned from a young age.
Wénlì
Wén Lì 文立, courtesy name Guǎngxiū 廣休,
was from Língjiāng 臨江, Bā Jùn 巴郡.
During the Shǔ 蜀 era, he traveled to the Imperial Academy,
specializing in the Maó Shī 詩 (Mao Commentary on the Classic of Poetry) and Sān Lǐ 三禮 (Three Rites).
He studied under Qiáo Zhōu 譙周.
His fellow students regarded Lì 立 as Yán Huí 顏回,
Chén Shòu 陳壽 and Lǐ Qián 李虔 as Yóu Xià 游夏,
and Luó Xiàn 羅憲 as Zǐgòng 子貢.
He served as Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister of the Imperial Secretariat).
After the pacification of Shǔ 蜀,
he was recommended as Xiùcái 秀才 (Filial and Incorrupt)
and appointed Lángzhōng 郎中 (Gentleman of the Palace).
In the early Tàishǐ 泰始 period,
he was appointed Jìyīn Tàishǒu 濟陰太守 (Administrator of Jìyīn).
Later, he entered the court as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 (Internal Registrar to the Crown Prince).
He submitted a memorial requesting that the descendants of Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮, Jiǎng Wǎn 蔣琬, Fèi Yī 費禕, and others be relocated to the central domain.
He argued that they ought to be employed,
firstly, to comfort the hearts of Bāshǔ 巴蜀 people,
and secondly, to dampen the hopes of the Wú 吳 people.
All his proposals were implemented.
An imperial edict stated:
"The Crown Prince's Internal Registrar, Wén Lì 文立, is loyal, upright, clear-minded, and honest,
possessing thoughtfulness, intelligence, and organizational ability.
Previously in Jìyīn 濟陰,
his administration was well-ordered and enlightened.
Later, serving in the Eastern Palace (of the Crown Prince),
he fulfilled his duties of assistance and guidance.
In the past, Guāngwǔ 光武, upon pacifying Lǒngshǔ 隴蜀,
gathered all its talented individuals and used them;
this was indeed to uplift the obscure and neglected and to aid distant regions.
Therefore, Wén Lì 文立 is appointed Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 (Palace Attendant Consultant)."
Chéng Qióng 程瓊 of Jiànwéi 犍為, a former Shàngshū 尚書 of Shǔ 蜀, possessed refined virtues and achievements,
and had a deep friendship with Lì 立.
Wǔdì 武帝 (Emperor Wu) heard of his name
and asked Lì 立 about him.
He replied:
"Your servant knows the man very well,
but he is nearly eighty years old,
and his nature is humble and retiring.
He no longer possesses the same aspirations as before,
so I have not reported him to Your Majesty."
When Qióng 瓊 heard of this, he said:
"Guǎngxiū 廣休 can truly be called impartial;
thus, I value that gentleman."
At that time, the Western Regions presented horses as tribute.
The Emperor asked Lì 立:
"What do you think of the horses?"
He replied:
"I beg to refer the question to the Tàipú 太僕 (Grand Coachman)."
The Emperor approved of this.
He was promoted to Wèiwèi 衞尉 (Commander of the Guards).
At the end of the Xiánníng 咸寧 era,
he passed away.
His written memorials, poems, and rhapsodies, numbering dozens of pieces, circulated in the world.
Chén Shào 陳邵
Chén Shào 陳邵, courtesy name Jiéliáng 節良,
was from Xiāngbēn 襄賁, Dōnghǎi 東海.
He was nominated as Xiàolián 孝廉 (Filial and Incorrupt) by the commandery but did not take the post.
He was summoned for his Confucian scholarship to serve as Chénliú Nèishǐ 陳留內史 (Administrator of Chénliú).
He was successively promoted to Yānwáng Shī 燕王師 (Tutor to the King of Yān).
He authored the Zhōu Lǐ Píng 周禮評 (Critique of the Rites of Zhou),
which was very well-structured
and circulated in the world.
In the Tàishǐ 泰始 period,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Tutor to the King of Yān, Chén Shào 陳邵, is pure, upright, and clean,
his conduct is renowned among the populace.
He is devoted to antiquity,
broadly versed in the Six Classics,
delights in ancient texts,
and is untiring in his old age.
He is fit to be by Our side to strengthen Confucian teachings.
He may be appointed Gěishìzhōng 給事中 (Gentleman of the Palace)."
He died in office.
Yú Xǐ 虞喜
Yú Xǐ 虞喜, courtesy name Zhòngníng 仲寧,
was from Yúyáo 餘姚, Kuàijī 會稽,
a relative of Guānglù Tán 光祿潭.
His father, Chá 察,
was Wú Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 吳征虜將軍 (General who Conquers the North for Wú).
Xǐ 喜, from a young age, established his integrity and conduct,
and was broadly learned and fond of antiquity.
When Zhūgě Huī 諸葛恢 governed the commandery,
he humbly appointed Xǐ 喜 as Gōngcáo 功曹 (Merit Officer).
He was nominated as Xiàolián 孝廉,
recommended as Xiùcái 秀才 by the province,
and appointed by the Sītú 司徒 (Minister of Works),
but he declined all appointments.
In the early Yuándì 元帝 era, when the emperor first established his authority south of the Yangtze,
a memorial was submitted recommending Xǐ 喜.
Upon Huáidì’s 懷帝 (Emperor Huai) ascension,
he was summoned by public carriage to be appointed Bóshì 博士 (Erudite),
but he declined.
Hè Xún 賀循, a native of Xǐ’s 喜 hometown, who was Sīkōng 司空 (Minister of Works) and an esteemed and prominent figure,
would often visit Xǐ 喜,
staying for days, forgetting to return,
and saying that he could not fathom him.
In the Tàiníng 太寧 period,
he was summoned as Bóshì 博士 along with Rèn Xù 任旭 from Línghǎi 臨海,
but he declined.
Another imperial edict was issued, stating:
"For promoting reform and achieving good governance,
nothing is more important than revering the Way and teaching,
and clarifying the virtue of reclusion.
Since the time of chaos and unrest,
refined culture has declined.
Whenever We read the poem 'Zǐ Jīn' 子衿 (My Collar),
We are never without a sigh of regret.
Rèn Xù 任旭 from Línghǎi 臨海 and Yú Xǐ 虞喜 from Kuàijī 會稽 both maintain pure and untainted conduct,
unwavering in the face of hardship.
They diligently study the classics and ancient texts,
living by ancient principles in the present.
Their aspirations and integrity are sufficient to inspire the populace,
and their extensive learning is sufficient to elucidate the Way.
Although they did not respond to the previous summons,
they shall again be summoned as Bóshì 博士."
Xǐ 喜 declined, citing illness, and did not go.
At the end of the Xiánhé 咸和 era,
an edict instructed the high officials to recommend virtuous, upright, and outspoken gentlemen.
Tàicháng Huá 太常華 (Grand Minister of Ceremonies Huá) recommended Xǐ 喜 as Xiánliáng 賢良 (Virtuous and Good).
However, due to military affairs in the state,
the appointment did not proceed.
In the early Xiánkāng 咸康 period,
Nèishǐ Hé Chōng 內史何充 submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that when eight times two are appointed, the four gates become serene;
when ten virtuous men are employed, the world is at peace.
Eminent principles are thus unfolded,
this has always been the case.
At present, Your Majesty's sagely virtue is revered and enlightened;
You wish to restore the great achievements of the past.
Your imperial carriage is prepared,
awaiting worthy men before moving.
I respectfully observe that the former Xiánliáng 賢良, Yú Xǐ 虞喜, is endowed by Heaven with integrity and purity,
lofty and distant from the world.
He cultivated virtue from a young age,
and is untiring in his old age.
Moreover, he comprehensively surveys a vast and profound range of knowledge,
is widely learned and has a strong memory,
diligently studying profound and subtle matters with unparalleled effort.
Living in tranquility and savoring the Way, he has no worldly ambitions.
He rests easy behind his wicker gate,
content and self-sufficient.
It is fitting to send a carriage with rush wheels to fetch him,
to honor his extraordinary conduct,
firstly, to assist and support great transformations,
and secondly, to inspire and encourage the declining customs."
When the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict stated:
"We find that Xúnyáng Zhái Tāng 尋陽翟湯 and Kuàijī Yú Xǐ 會稽虞喜 both adhere to the Way with purity and integrity,
not engaging in worldly affairs.
They are devoted to learning, highly esteemed,
and their conduct emulates the ancients.
Although they were previously summoned, they did not accept the appointments.
How could it be that plain silk is difficult to dye, yet Our invitations are too simple?
The path of governance requires worthy men,
and they ought to be brought into the court.
They shall both be summoned as Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍."
Yet, he did not respond.
In the early Yǒnghé 永和 period,
the relevant authorities proposed that for the殷祭 Yīnjì (Grand Imperial Sacrifice) in the tenth month,
the tomb tablet of Jīngzhào Fǔjūn 京兆府君 (Lord Administrator of Jīngzhào) should be moved to another ancestral hall,
while the tomb tablets of Zhēngxī 征西 (Generalissimo of the West), Yùzhāng 豫章, and Yǐngchuān 潁川 Fǔjūn 府君 (Lord Administrators) should be newly destroyed.
There was extensive debate inside and outside the court, and no decision could be reached.
At that time, Xǐ 喜 was in Kuàijī 會稽,
and the imperial court sent envoys to consult him.
Such was the respect he commanded.
Xǐ 喜 focused his mind on the classics and commentaries,
and also read prognostications and apocrypha.
He then wrote Āntiān Lùn 安天論 (Treatise on Tranquil Heaven) to refute Hún and Gài (the celestial sphere and domed heaven theories),
and also compiled a concise explanation of the Maó Shī Lǜe 毛詩略 (Outline of Mao's Classic of Poetry),
annotated the Xiàojīng 孝經 (Classic of Filial Piety),
and authored Zhìlín 志林 (Forest of Aspiration) in thirty chapters.
All his annotations and writings amounted to several hundred thousand words,
and circulated in the world.
He died at the age of seventy-six,
without sons.
His younger brother Yù 豫 has his own biography.
Liú Zhào 劉兆
Liú Zhào, courtesy name Yánshì,
was a native of Dōngpíng, Jìnán.
He was a descendant of the Hàn king, Guǎngchuān Huìwáng.
Zhào was broadly learned and widely informed,
warm, sincere, and good at guiding others.
Several thousand people came to him for instruction.
During the reign of Wǔdì, he was invited five times to serve in the ducal government,
and summoned three times to be a bóshì,
but he accepted none of these offers.
He was content in poverty and delighted in the Way,
devoting himself to writing and scholarship.
For several decades, he did not step outside his gate.
Observing that the one classic of the Chūnqiū was interpreted in three different schools,
and that the discussions of right and wrong among various Confucians were contentious,
with them becoming rivals,
he therefore contemplated the differences among the three schools,
and sought to combine and reconcile them.
The Zhōulǐ has an official called the Tiáorén.
He wrote the Chūnqiū Tiáorén in over seventy thousand words,
discussing all its beginnings and ends,
to ensure that the main principles were not contradictory.
When there were inconsistencies,
he would discuss their strengths and weaknesses to reconcile them.
He also wrote a commentary on the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì,
titled Quánzōng,
which incorporated the interpretations of Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng into the classic text and its commentary.
He used red ink to differentiate them.
He also compiled a commentary on the Zhōuyì Xùnzhù,
reconciling the texts through the interpenetration of the fixed and moving two forms.
All his writings amounted to over a million words.
Once, someone wearing boots and riding a donkey arrived outside Zhào's gate,
and said:
"I wish to see Liú Yánshì."
Zhào was known for his Confucian virtue and simple lifestyle;
in Qīngzhōu, no one referred to him by his courtesy name.
His students were greatly angered.
Zhào said:
"Let him in."
When the guest entered,
he sat on the bed and asked Zhào:
"I hear you are a great scholar.
What have you been working on recently?"
Zhào answered as above,
concluding with:
"I have many doubts."
The guest asked about them.
After Zhào had explained his doubts,
the guest said:
"These are easily explained."
Then he proceeded to clarify the right and wrong of the doubtful points.
Zhào then proposed a new idea,
and the guest challenged it once,
Zhào could not respond.
When the guest left,
having already exited the gate,
Zhào wanted to detain him
and sent someone to call him back.
The guest said:
"My kin are here to arrange a burial,
I must attend to it;
I will come again later."
After he left,
Zhào sent someone to check on the burial family,
but did not find this guest,
and ultimately did not know his name.
Zhào died at the age of sixty-six.
He had five sons: Zhuó, Zhào, Yào, Yù, and Qí.
Fàn Yù
Fàn Yù, courtesy name Zhìchūn,
was a native of Lú, Jìběi.
His family had been Confucian scholars for generations,
and were diligent and harmonious with their extended kin.
They had resided in Qīngzhōu as sojourners
for seven generations by Yù's time.
People at the time called his family
"children without a constant father,
clothes without a constant owner."
From a young age, Yù upheld lofty principles,
content in poverty and having ambition in his work.
When his father died,
he lived by the tomb for over thirty years.
On the first and last days of the month,
he personally swept the graves,
and walked around the tomb mound and planted trees.
When he returned home, he would not step out of his gate.
Someone recommended him to Wǔdì,
who summoned him to be the Nányángwáng Wénxué, Mìshūláng, and Tàifù Cānjūn,
but he accepted none of these.
At that time, the reclusive scholars of Qīngtǔ, Liú Zhào, Xú Miáo, and others, all engaged in teaching,
but Yù alone did not keep students,
maintaining his purity and self-restraint.
When there were those who admired antiquity and virtue and sought his advice,
he would also open his heart and guide them,
showing them one corner (of the truth).
He combined the three commentaries to write a comprehensive commentary,
and compiled Chūnqiū Shìyí and Ròuxíng Lùn.
All his writings amounted to over seventy thousand words.
He died at the age of seventy-one.
Xú Miáo
Xú Miáo, courtesy name Shúzhòu,
was a native of Chúnyú, Gāomì.
His family had for generations succeeded one another,
all serving as bóshì and then as Jùnshǒu.
His great-grandfather, Huá,
had exceptional conduct.
Once, when he was staying in a pavilion,
a divine being told him at night
that "the pavilion is about to collapse."
He immediately went out
and was saved.
His grandfather, Shào,
served as a Wèi Shàngshūláng,
and was praised for his integrity and uprightness.
Miáo was poor in his youth.
By day, he wielded a hoe and plow;
by night, he recited texts.
At the age of twenty,
he and his younger brother, Jiǎ, went to Jìnán to study under the bóshì Sòng Jūn,
and thus became a Confucian master.
He wrote Wǔjīng Tóngyì Píng,
and also, based on Daoist principles, wrote Xuánwēi Lùn.
His total writings amounted to tens of thousands of words,
all with profound meaning and flavor.
He was assertive and unyielding by nature,
lightly regarding wealth and valuing righteousness,
and also possessed the ability to discern people.
When his younger brother suffered from a mouth ailment
with a bursting abscess,
Miáo sucked the pus out for him.
Both of his brothers died young,
so he raised their orphans,
and his compassion was renowned throughout the province and local communities.
He gave all his fields, houses, slaves, and maids to them.
When a neighbor died,
he would stop plowing to help prepare the coffin,
and if a student died at his home,
he would enshroud them in the lecture hall.
His personal conduct was pure and sincere,
and all his actions were like this.
People near and far all ascribed to his righteousness
and emulated his conduct.
The commandery investigated him as Xiàolián;
the province appointed him as Cóngshì, Zhìzhōng, and Biéjià;
he was nominated for exceptional conduct;
the ducal government invited him five times to be a bóshì;
and he was summoned twice,
but he accepted none of these.
During the reign of Wǔhuìdì, when officials reported to the court,
the Emperor would invariably ask about his well-being.
He died in the second year of Yǒngníng.
His dying wish was to wash his headscarf and clothes,
use a simple elm coffin and mixed bricks,
carry his body on an open cart,
with only a reed mat and earthenware.
Cuī Yóu
Cuī Yóu, courtesy name Zǐxiàng,
was a native of Shàngdǎng.
From a young age, he loved learning,
and his Confucian scholarship was clear and bright.
He was tranquil, modest, and self-effacing.
From youth to old age,
he never spoke of wealth or profit.
In the late Wèi dynasty,
he was investigated as Xiàolián,
appointed as a Shèrén in the Chancellor's office,
and then sent out as the chief of Dǐchí,
where he governed with great benevolence.
He was dismissed due to illness,
which rendered him permanently disabled.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
Wǔdì, remembering the former officials of Wéndì's household,
appointed him Lángzhōng at his home.
At over seventy years old,
he still diligently pursued learning without fatigue,
and compiled the Sāngfú Tú,
which circulated in the world.
When Liú Yuánhǎi usurped the throne,
he appointed Yóu as Yùshǐ Dàfū,
but Yóu firmly declined.
He died at home,
at the age of ninety-three.
Fàn Lóng
Fàn Lóng 字 Xuánsōng,
a native of Yànmén.
His father, Fāng,
was the Grand Administrator of Yànmén for Wèi.
Lóng was in the womb for fifteen months,
and his father died when he was born.
At four years old,
he lost his mother again.
His mournful wails
moved passers-by to tears.
Being an orphan without close kin of the sisu (mourning attire) degree,
a distant relative, Fàn Guǎng, took pity on him and raised him,
bringing him home to teach him and
establishing an ancestral hall for him.
Lóng was fond of learning and meticulous in his conduct,
serving Guǎng as if he were his father.
He was widely versed in the classics and other writings,
leaving nothing unread.
He authored a "Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals in Three Traditions"
and compiled "A Record of Auspicious and Inauspicious Rites of the Three Rites,"
which was very well-structured and insightful.
During the reign of Huìdì,
when the world was on the verge of chaos,
Lóng hid his traces and did not respond to calls from provinces and commanderies.
He diligently farmed by day
and recited classics by night.
He was quite skilled in esoteric calendrical and Yīnyáng studies,
knowing that Bìngzhōu would soon experience portents of disaster,
thus he even more resolutely refrained from taking office.
He was good friends with Zhū Jì of Shàngdǎng.
Once, he and Jì traveled in the mountains together,
and saw an old man by the edge of a deep ravine.
The old man said,
"What are you two gentlemen doing here?"
Lóng and the others bowed to him,
but when they looked up, he was gone.
Later, he and Jì sought refuge with Liú Yuánhǎi.
Yuánhǎi appointed Lóng as Grand Minister of the Court (Dà Hónglú),
and Jì as Grand Usher (Tàicháng),
and both were ennobled as dukes.
Lóng died during the reign of Liú Cōng.
Cōng posthumously granted him the title of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Dù Yí
Dù Yí, 字 Xíngqí,
was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
His family was known for its Confucian scholarship
and was a prominent clan in the commandery.
Yí was quiet and unassuming from a young age,
maintaining integrity and simplicity in his conduct.
He lived in extreme poverty,
not managing any property.
He extensively read the classics and various schools of thought,
and exhaustively studied calendrical calculations, diagrams, and weft texts.
He lived between Rǔ and Yǐng,
not leaving his home for ten years.
At over forty years old,
he finally returned to his hometown,
closed his doors to teach,
and had a thousand students.
During Huìdì's reign, he was thrice examined as Xiàolián,
and the province appointed him Biéjià.
In the early Yǒngjiā era,
the imperial carriage summoned him to be a Boshi (Erudite).
The Grand Tutor (Tàifù), the Prince of Dōnghǎi Yuè, also invited him,
but he did not accept any of these.
Huáidì issued an edict for princes and dukes to recommend xianliang (virtuous and good) and fangzheng (upright and honest) individuals.
The Inspector (Cìshǐ) Wáng Dūn recommended Hè Xún as xianliang
and Yí as fangzheng,
then submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant has heard that when Táng inquired broadly,
Yuánkǎi ascended in due time;
when Hàn Wǔdì revered the worthy,
talented individuals responded,
thus enabling harmony in the state
and promoting great civilization.
I observe that Hè Xún of Kuàijī, Grandson-Heir's Retainer, and Dù Yí of Lújiāng, a recluse, walk an increasingly noble path,
their pure conduct transcends the mundane.
Their thought and learning are profound,
their talent suitable for royal affairs.
Xún governed two counties,
both with famous achievements,
and served as an officer in the Eastern Palace (heir apparent's residence),
where his loyalty and diligence were evident.
Yí is clear, profound, and detached,
following a different path from the common folk,
dwelling in a quiet valley,
happily withdrawing and concealing his traces.
He is indeed a rare treasure for governing the nation,
urgently needed to be invited.
If he could be summoned by the imperial carriage
and respond to imperial questions,
he would surely offer loyal and good strategies,
greatly benefiting the way of government."
Wáng Dūn then pressed Yí to go to Luòyáng.
Yí fled to Shòuyáng.
The General who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn) Zhōu Fù sincerely received him with courtesy,
inviting him to be an assistant officer.
Yí declined due to illness.
Zhōu Fù, knowing he could not be compelled,
personally visited Yí,
built a residence for him,
and provided him with medicine.
After Zhōu Fù's defeat,
Yí returned to his old residence.
On the way, he encountered soldiers and bandits.
Inspector Liú Táo announced to Lújiāng Commandery:
"In the past, Wèi Wénhóu bowed by Gān Mù's door,
and Qi's Chancellor Cáo Cān honored Gài Gōng,
all to honor the worthy and display virtue,
and to encourage later generations.
The reclusive scholar Dù Jūn possesses profound virtue and pure conduct,
upholding noble aspirations.
Recently, he has been wandering on the roads,
and I hear of his hardships.
I, the Inspector, holding an unworthy position,
have been unable to honor and adorn those of the Way,
and instead, a man of such lofty conduct suffers these difficulties.
Now I send an official to express my condolences.
The commandery should send one official,
and the county five officials,
to care for him,
and regularly supply his family with grain from market taxes,
lest they lack anything."
Soon after, due to barbarian incursions,
he again moved across the Jiāng River.
Wáng Dǎo sent officials to assist him thoroughly.
Yuándì, as Chancellor,
issued an instruction saying:
"Now the great principles are decaying,
and the rites and classics lack a common standard.
The court is bogged down in disputes and cannot rectify them.
It is fitting to specially establish the office of Libationer of the Confucian Academy (Rúlín Jìjiǔ)
to promote this matter.
The recluse Dù Yí has set his heart on detachment and distance,
firmly separated from the mundane.
His talent and learning are profound and extensive,
his conduct exemplary.
Let Yí be the Libationer."
Yí declined due to illness
and never attended court.
The Emperor often wished to visit Yí.
Yí remonstrated that a ruler of ten thousand chariots should not go to the home of a commoner.
The Emperor then wrote to Yí, saying:
"Although our bond is beyond words,
I have sincerely esteemed you for many years.
Precisely because of your frail health,
I wish to visit you.
How can ordinary protocol matter?"
He was also appointed Libationer of the National University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
During the Jiànwǔ era,
an edict stated:
"The Libationer of the National University Dù Yí finds joy in poverty and the Way,
maintaining a tranquil mind in his humble abode,
so busy that he has no time for himself.
Even Yuán Xiàn could not surpass him.
Therefore, grant him two hundred hu of grain."
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) visited Yí's residence three times,
holding classics to ask about their meaning.
Although Yí was constrained by the times and commands,
he never attended court.
When the state had major policies,
they would consult Yí.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
Yí personally submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
An imperial edict said:
"The way of the former kings is about to fall to the ground.
You study in seclusion and ponder deeply,
like Liú and Yáng of today.
Officials and gentry look up to your conduct and teachings.
How can you retire,
leaving Us with no one to emulate?"
He died in the first year of Tàiníng (323 CE)
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of the Court (Dà Hónglú)
and given the posthumous name Zhēnzǐ.
On his deathbed, Yí
left instructions to his son Yàn, saying:
"I did not go out into the world much in my youth.
Although I have recently been restrained by office,
I have never worn the formal attire of caps and shoes.
Therefore, wrap me in a horned turban and plain clothes,
and bury me in ordinary attire.
For the funeral arrangements,
be sure to be simple and economical,
and do not seek to be ostentatiously unconventional."
Yí's twenty chapters of "Yōuqiúzǐ"
circulated in the world.
Yàn served as Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.
Yí had three brothers.
His elder brother, Sōng,
字 Xínggāo,
also had aspirations and integrity.
During Huìdì's time,
the customs were often superficial and deceitful,
so he wrote "Rènzǐ Chūnqiū" to satirize them.
His younger brother, Yuán,
was the Chancellor of Gāopíng.
Yuán's son, Qián,
was Right General of the Guards (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
Dǒng Jǐngdào
Dǒng Jǐngdào
zì Wénbó, a native of Hóngnóng.
From a young age, he loved learning,
traveling a thousand *lǐ* to pursue teachers.
Wherever he was, he only read and recited day and night,
scarcely interacting with others.
He mastered the *Sān Zhuàn* of the *Chūnqiū*, Jīng Shì's *Yì*, Mǎ Shì's *Shàngshū*, and Hán Shī's poetry,
all with profound understanding of their essential meaning.
Regarding the principles of the *Sān Lǐ*,
he exclusively followed Zhèng Shì's interpretations,
writing *Lǐ Tōng Lùn* to refute other scholars
and elaborate on Zhèng Shì's ideas.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
knowing that the world would soon descend into chaos,
he secluded himself in Shāngluò Shān,
dressing in leaves,
eating tree fruits,
and amusing himself by playing the *qín* and singing with laughter.
Poisonous insects and fierce beasts all gathered around him.
Thus, despite repeated summons from Liú Yuánhǎi and Cōng,
he was hindered from reaching them.
It was not until Liú Yào's time that he emerged from the mountains
and built a hermitage by the Wèi River bend.
Yào summoned him to be Crown Prince's Junior Tutor (tàizǐ shàofù) and Mounted Regular Cavalier (sànqí chángshì),
but he firmly declined both,
and ultimately died of old age.
Xù Xián
Xù Xián,
zì Xiàozōng, was a native of Shàngdǎng.
He was by nature filial, careful, and steadfast,
and his conduct was upright and simple.
He loved learning
and studied under Dù Yù of Jīngzhào,
specializing in the *Chūnqiū* and Zhèng Shì's *Yì*.
He often taught several tens of students,
had extensive knowledge of various writings,
and possessed great talent in writing essays.
He also revised Chén and Dù's laws,
and was well-versed in legal texts.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he successively held the positions of Judge of the Ministry of Justice (tíngwèi píng) and Administrator of Dōng'ān (Dōng'ān tàishǒu).
When Liú Kūn established his authority in Bīngzhōu,
he appointed Xù Xián as Attendant Censor (cóngshì zhōngláng).
Later, he was captured by Shí Lè,
who made him Staff Officer in charge of Judicial Affairs (lǐcáo cānjūn).
He administered justice fairly and meticulously;
at the time, he was praised for his integrity and generosity,
and compared to Gōng Yú.
He authored *Yuǎnyóu Zhì*, *Yìwù Zhì*, and *Jízhǒng Gǔwén Shì*,
each in ten scrolls,
which circulated in the world.
At the age of ninety-seven,
he died during the reign of Shí Jìlóng.
Jìlóng posthumously granted him the title of Administrator-in-Chief (yítóng sānsī).
Xú Máo
Xú Máo,
was a native of Gūmù, Dōngguǎn.
His grandfather, Chéngzhī, was a Provisional Governor of the Prefecture (zhōu zhìzhōng).
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he, along with his fellow villager Zāng Kūn and others, led their sons, younger brothers, and over a thousand families of local gentry and commoners,
to cross the Yangtze River southwards
and settle in Jīngkǒu.
His father, Zǎo,
was Superintendent of Waterways (dūshuǐ shǐzhě).
Máo had a dignified and refined character,
was diligent in his conduct and devoted to learning.
He was widely read and knowledgeable,
and maintained a cautious and discreet demeanor.
When young, he was as famous as his fellow villager Zāng Shòu.
He studied behind closed curtains,
and did not frequent cities.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ first began to read classical texts
and invited scholars,
Máo, being an upright scholar from the eastern regions,
was recommended by Grand Tutor Xiè Ān to be selected.
At forty-four,
he was first appointed Editorial Assistant (zhōngshū shèrén),
serving the emperor in the Western Office.
Though he did not verbally transmit chapters and verses,
he would elucidate the meaning of the texts
and clarify their main points,
compiling and correcting the pronunciation and exegesis of the Five Classics,
which scholars revered.
He was promoted to Mounted Regular Cavalier (sànqí chángshì),
still serving in the Western Office.
For ten years,
whenever he was consulted,
he always offered suggestions,
providing much assistance and benefit,
and was greatly favored.
After the emperor's banquets ended in high spirits,
he liked to write imperial edicts and poems to bestow upon his attendants.
Sometimes the wording was impromptu,
and what was said was vulgar and mixed.
Máo would always collect them promptly,
return to his office, and revise and edit them,
making them all presentable.
After the emperor re-examined them,
they were then released.
At that time, attendants who received edicts
would sometimes publicize them,
so public opinion at the time greatly praised Máo for this.
When Xiè Ān died,
some commentators had differing views
on the proper mourning rites. Máo firmly advised Grand Secretary Wáng Xiànzhī to request the addition of special rites.
He also promoted Xiè Shí to Minister of the Secretariat (shàngshū lìng)
and Xuán to Governor of Xúzhōu.
Máo was transferred to Bureau Director of Rituals (cíbo bùláng),
and presented the rites for the alternating destruction and reconstruction of the imperial ancestral temples in the northern and southern suburbs,
all supported by evidence.
Fàn Níng, the Administrator of Yùzhāng, wanted to send fifteen councillors (yìcáo) to various subordinate counties to collect information on customs and governance,
and also to have officials on leave return
to inquire about the successes and failures of local administrators.
Máo wrote to Níng, saying: "I understand that you are sending fifteen councillors, each to one county,
and also having officials on leave return
to report what they have heard and seen.
This truly shows your concern for the common people,
and thus you are broadening their sight
and hearing.
I believe that guidance should be based on substance, not on formality.
What exactly do these fifteen councillors intend to proclaim?
In various matters of litigation,
if your judgments are fair and conclusive,
then the principles of governance
will be sufficient.
If the superiors have a mind to manage affairs well,
then those below seeking good governance will come.
If you review matters from dusk until dawn,
and no affairs are left pending,
then officials will be cautious in their responsibilities and the people will not be
confused.
How can there be a need to visit every town and village,
and adorn these superficial inspections?
Not only will it not bring benefit,
but it will also provide an opportunity for exploitation and plunder.
Furthermore, one should not allow minor officials to be one's
eyes and ears.
How can there be good and honorable gentlemen who meddle in matters not their own
and make many reports?
As for the mind of a gentleman,
who does he slander, who does he praise?
If he has any
praise,
it must be based on long-term observation.
If he has any criticism,
it must be clear and evident.
Rats that take refuge in the altar (託社之鼠)
are a great harm to governance.
Since ancient times,
those who wished to be the eyes and ears
of the ruler
were invariably petty individuals.
They first used minor loyalty to achieve great disloyalty,
and first used minor trustworthiness to achieve great untrustworthiness,
thereby causing the way of the gentleman to decline
and good
people to be treated like corpses.
What is recorded in previous histories
can serve as a profound warning.
If you select your chief administrators (gāngjì) and obtain men of national caliber,
they will be sufficient to manage all departments.
If all department officials are good administrators,
they will be sufficient to handle documents.
Moreover, if you choose impartial individuals
to be supervising officials,
then their integrity, competence, or lack thereof
will become clear through their work.
You only need to maintain an impartial heart and remain at the center of authority.
Why do you need eyes and ears?
In the past, the virtuous Empress Mǎ
never spoke to her attendants without purpose,
which can be called farsightedness.
How much more should a great man not be unable to avoid this!"
He was promoted to Imperial Secretary (zhōngshū shìláng),
exclusively managing imperial edicts,
and the emperor was very close to him.
Initially,
Fàn Níng and Miǎo were both entrusted by the Emperor,
and together they filled the deficiencies in the imperial court.
Níng was naturally talented and upright in his intentions,
but he was slandered by Wáng Guóbǎo,
and sent out to govern a distant commandery.
Miǎo, as an official from a humble background, was easily vulnerable,
and dared not oppose powerful clans.
So he devised a plan for his own security.
It happened that the Emperor had grown somewhat distant from Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ.
Miǎo wished to reconcile them,
and so he spoke leisurely to the Emperor, saying:
"In the past, the kings of Huáinán and Qí
served as warnings for the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
Although Kuàijī Wáng has indulged in excesses,
his devotion to Your Majesty is pure and singular.
It is advisable to show him greater generosity,
to dispel disagreements,
which would be for the benefit of the state externally,
and to comfort the Empress Dowager internally."
The Emperor accepted his advice.
Miǎo once visited the Eastern Mansion,
where he encountered many guests thoroughly intoxicated,
drinking deeply and making a clamor.
Dàozǐ said:
"Do you ever indulge yourself, Sir?"
Miǎo replied:
"I, Miǎo, am a scholar from a humble lane;
I find my indulgence only in frugality, purity, and cultivation."
Dàozǐ, seeing that Miǎo valued the Dao and simplicity in his conduct,
smiled and was not offended.
Dàozǐ intended to appoint him as Administrator of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Láng),
but Miǎo believed that contention had become customary
and was not something he could regulate,
so he vehemently declined, and the appointment was dropped.
At that time, the Crown Prince was still young,
and the Emperor doted on him greatly.
The selected civil and military officials were all outstanding talents of their time.
Miǎo was appointed as Commander of the Imperial Vanguard (Qiánwèi Shuài),
concurrently Grand Censor for his home commandery (Běnjùn Dà Zhōngzhèng),
and instructor of classics to the Crown Prince.
The Emperor said to Miǎo:
"Although I have not yet decreed that you be treated with the courtesy due to a teacher,
you are certainly not to be treated merely as a 'Doctor' (bóshì)."
Ancient emperors,
when receiving instruction in classics, always showed respect.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
it became common to have minor figures teach,
who were called "Doctors" (bóshì),
and were no longer honored as teachers.
Thus, the Emperor spoke as he did.
Although Miǎo was in the Eastern Palace,
he still attended court daily,
participated in and managed state affairs,
refined imperial edicts,
and offered suggestions and made up for deficiencies,
toiling diligently by the Emperor's side.
The Emperor admired his prudence and discretion,
comparing him to Jīn Hò,
and had the intention of entrusting him with great responsibilities,
planning to promote him to a high position.
But before this could happen, the Emperor suddenly died.
When Ān Dì ascended the throne,
Miǎo was appointed General of Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Lóng'ān,
he suffered the bereavement of his father.
Miǎo had already been ill,
and the grief and emaciation worsened his condition,
and he died within a year,
at the age of fifty-four.
His home region mourned him,
and those who knew him were saddened.
Miǎo was simple and benevolent in his official duties,
and adept at governance.
His discussions and opinions were precise,
and many consulted him at the time.
He could explain things by analogy,
and always had an answer to questions.
There was an old doubt regarding the year's zodiac sign being "Mǎo" (Rabbit):
if the left side of one house is the right side of another,
how could both be taboo towards the East?
Miǎo believed that the influences of the Grand Commander of the Year (Tàisuì)
were merely wandering spirits,
just as when the sun rises,
facing East is considered inauspicious,
which does not mean the sun's body is hidden underground.
His commentary on the Gǔliáng Zhuàn
was highly valued at the time.
Miǎo's eldest son, Huò,
had his father's demeanor
and was known for his filial piety.
He served as Erudite of the Grand Court (Tàicháng Bóshì) and Palace Secretary (Mìshū Láng).
Huò's younger brother, Hào,
was a Cavalier Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng).
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Hé Wú-jì invited him to serve as Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo),
then he was appointed Administrator of Xīyáng,
and was killed along with Wú-jì by Lú Xún.
Miǎo's younger brother, Guǎng,
has a separate biography.
Kǒng Yǎn
