Kǒng Yǎn, courtesy name Shūyuán,
was a native of Lǔguó.
He was the twenty-second generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ.
His grandfather, Wén,
was Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Dà Hónglú) during the Wèi dynasty.
His father, Yù,
was Military Supervisor for the Pacifier of the South (Zhēngnán Jūnsī).
Yǎn was fond of learning from a young age.
At twelve,
he could understand the Shī and Shū.
Upon reaching manhood,
he was invited by the Ducal Administration
and recommended by his home province for his exceptional conduct and outspokenness,
but he declined all appointments.
He sought refuge in Jiāngdōng,
where Yuán Dì appointed him as Staff Officer to the General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Cānjūn),
exclusively managing the secretarial duties.
The official documents were numerous,
yet Yǎn was always recognized for his competence.
In the early years of the restoration,
he was appointed Middle Secretary (Zhōngshū Láng) along with Yǔ Liàng.
When Míng Dì was in the Eastern Palace,
Yǎn served as Principal Secretary to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ).
At that time, various matters were in their initial stages,
and Yǎn's knowledge of the classics was profound and extensive.
He was also well-versed in old institutions,
so court rituals and regulations were often rectified according to his advice.
Because of this, Emperors Yuán and Míng both loved and respected him.
When Wáng Dūn held exclusive power,
Yǎn privately told the Crown Prince:
"Your Highness should extensively invite court luminaries,
seek out and promote talented individuals,
and consult them on current policies,
to broaden your sagacious hearing."
Dūn heard this and disliked him,
so he petitioned to have Yǎn sent out as Administrator of Guǎnglíng Commandery.
People at the time felt a chill for him,
but Yǎn showed no change in his expression.
Although the commandery bordered the western rebels,
he still taught and guided the younger generation,
not letting military affairs interrupt his studies.
Shí Lè once rode to Shānyáng,
and ordered his followers that because Yǎn was a refined scholar,
they were not to arbitrarily enter the commandery territory.
He held the post for about a year,
and died in office in the third year of Tàixīng,
at the age of fifty-three.
Although Yǎn was not renowned for his literary talent,
his extensive reading surpassed that of Hè Xún.
All his writings
amounted to over a million characters.
His son, Qǐ,
was Administrator of Lúlíng.
A clan member, Yíwú, had a good reputation,
though his scholarship was not as extensive as Yǎn's,
his reputation in worldly affairs surpassed him.
Emperor Yuán appointed him as Principal Clerk (Zhǔbù),
then transferred him to Staff Officer (Cānjūn),
and gradually promoted him to Imperial Attendant (Shìzhōng),
then moved him to Commander of the Left Guard of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài).
He died,
and was posthumously granted Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú).
Fàn Xuān
Fàn Xuān, courtesy name Xuānzǐ,
was a native of Chénliú.
At the age of ten,
he could recite the Shī and Shū.
Once, he injured his hand with a knife,
and held his hand with a changed expression.
When asked if it hurt,
he replied:
"It is not enough to be called pain,
but to damage a body received in its entirety,
that is unacceptable."
His family considered him extraordinary for his young age.
From youth, he cherished reclusion,
and in addition, he loved learning.
He never let go of a book,
continuing from night to day.
Thus, he extensively studied many books,
and was especially skilled in the Three Rites (Sān Lǐ).
His family was extremely poor,
and he personally farmed to support his parents.
After his parents' death,
he carried earth to build their grave,
and built a hut by the tomb.
Grand Commandant Xī Jiàn ordered him to be Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and an imperial edict summoned him as Erudite of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì) and Cavalier Attendant (Sànqí Láng),
but he declined all.
He made his home in Yùzhāng.
The Grand Administrator, Yīn Xiàn, saw that Xuān's thatched hut was not complete,
and wished to rebuild his dwelling.
Xuān steadfastly declined.
Yǔ Yuánzhī, knowing Xuān was always poor,
and furthermore that it was a year of famine and plague,
generously supplied him with provisions.
Xuān again refused to accept.
Yuánzhī asked Xuān,
"You are learned and comprehensive in your studies,
why are you too Confucian?"
Xuān replied,
"When the Hàn dynasty arose,
they valued classical scholarship.
As for the discussions at Shíqú,
it was indeed considered that Confucianism had its弊 (disadvantages).
Since the Zhèngshǐ reign,
the world has esteemed Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
By the beginning of the Jìn dynasty,
people competed in exposing their nakedness to be considered superior.
I am indeed too Confucian,
but 'Qiū does not participate in change.'"
Xuān's conversations never touched upon Lǎozi or Zhuāngzi.
A visitor once asked about the saying, "Life is born with sorrow,"
not knowing where this saying originated.
Xuān said,
"It comes from the 'Zhìlè' chapter of Zhuāngzi."
The visitor said,
"You said you do not read Lǎozi or Zhuāngzi,
how then do you know this?"
Xuān smiled and said,
"I glanced at it once when I was young."
The people of the time could not fathom him.
Although Xuān lived in reclusion and was often destitute,
he always made lecturing and reciting his profession.
Dài Kuí of Qiáoguó and others, hearing of his reputation, revered him,
coming from afar.
The sound of their chanting and reciting
was like that in Qí and Lǔ.
During the Tàiyuán era,
Fàn Níng of Shùnyáng became the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Níng was also learned in Confucianism and comprehensive in his studies.
In the commandery, he established local schools,
teaching several hundred people.
Because of this, the scholars of Jiāngzhōu all became fond of classical studies,
influenced by the style of the two Fàns.
He died at the age of fifty-four.
His treatises on ritual and his discussions on the Yì Jīng were both circulated in the world.
His son, Jí,
successively served as Grand Administrator, Erudite of the Directorate of Education, and Central Aide-de-camp to the Grand General.
After resigning and returning home,
he also engaged in lecturing and teaching.
During the Yìxī era,
he was repeatedly summoned but did not go.
Wéi Suǒ
Wéi Suǒ, courtesy name Xiàndào,
was a native of Jīngzhào.
He had an elegant fondness for Confucian studies,
and was skilled in writing.
He comprehensively studied
all the meanings of various sayings and secret essentials.
He served Liú Yào,
as a Palace Gentleman.
Later, he also joined Shí Jìlóng,
and was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
He successively governed seven commanderies,
and was renowned for his clean administration.
He was also summoned to be Grand Judge.
Discerning people compared him to and Zhāng.
He ascended to the Nine Dignitaries four times in total,
was in the Department of State Affairs six times,
served as Attendant-in-ordinary twice,
and as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince twice.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jīngzhào.
He was fond of direct remonstrance,
and many of his proposals concerning military and state affairs
were accepted.
He authored *Fú Lín* in over three thousand words,
which he then expanded into *Diǎn Lín* in twenty-three chapters.
All his writings and collected records of contemporary events amounted to hundreds of thousands of words,
all profound, extensive, talented, and righteous.
Under Rǎn Mǐn,
he was again appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
At that time, Mǐn appointed his son Yìn as Grand Chányú,
and placed a thousand surrendered Hú under his banner.
Suǒ remonstrated, saying:
"Now that several thousand surrendered Hú have been received
and treated as before,
this is indeed an act of gracious inducement.
However, the Hú and Jié were originally enemies,
and their current allegiance
is merely to preserve their lives.
Should there be assassins,
a disturbance could arise in an instant.
If we regret it after defeat,
what good will it do?
The ancients had a saying,
'One man is not to be trifled with,'
how much more so a thousand!
I beg you to execute and banish the surrendered Hú,
remove the title of Chányú,
and deeply reflect on the holy kings' admonition of 'wrapping the mulberry tree.'"
Mǐn's ambition was to pacify and soothe,
and he was keen on clarifying and stabilizing.
Upon hearing his words,
he was greatly angered,
and consequently executed him,
and also killed his son Bóyáng.
Suǒ's character was not serious,
and he was fond of boasting about his own achievements,
which critics found fault with.
He once said to Bóyáng,
"My high ancestors and my great ancestors brought splendor and accumulated virtue;
my grandfathers and my fathers, generation after generation of fathers and sons.
You, in response to me,
are just an evil obstruction."
Bóyáng replied,
"Bóyáng's unworthiness
is indeed as your honored teaching states,
but you, honored one, are also just a soft obstruction."
Suǒ was ashamed and speechless.
People at the time spread this story as a joke.
Fàn Hóngzhī
Fàn Hóngzhī, courtesy name Chángwén,
was the grandson of the General Who Guards the North, Wāng.
He inherited the title of Marquis of Wǔxīng.
He had an elegant fondness for learning,
and because of his comprehensive understanding of Confucian scholarship,
he became an Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
At that time, the General of the Guards, Xiè Shí, passed away.
A request for his posthumous title was made,
and it was sent down to the ritual officials for deliberation.
Hóngzhī's deliberation stated: "Xiè Shí, relying on his family's influence,
repeatedly rose to high prominence,
supervised all affairs of state,
and assisted in the three departments.
He was skilled in various matters
and worked diligently without slackness.
Both internal and external opinions
all
said he was capable.
During the victory at Huáiféi,
his meritorious service rescued the state from peril.
Although the imperial might resounded far and wide,
and the treacherous rebels perished by heaven's will,
Xiè Shí also contributed
to the achievements made at that time.
Moreover, he established
schools,
to attract the sons of nobles.
Although the grand transformation was not fully realized,
he still cherished ritual and preserved the sheep (i.e., preserved the outward forms).
However, the virtuous ministers of antiquity,
at best, served their ruler with the Way,
speaking with integrity all day long;
next, they disciplined themselves and served the country,
working tirelessly day and night;
and at worst, they loved the people and spared their labor,
to facilitate the affairs of the time.
Only by these few points
could one avoid the criticism of being merely a hanger-on
and stop the reproach of eating without working.
Now, Xiè Shí held a position at the imperial court,
his duty was to discuss the Way,
but his pronouncements lacked loyal counsel for the state.
He merely protected his own position,
so he cannot be said to have
served his ruler.
He bought and sold corruptly in the capital,
accumulating wealth insatiably,
so he cannot be said to have disciplined himself.
He sat with vast numbers of retainers,
infringing upon and consuming the people's resources.
Great evils flowed far and wide,
and resentment and bitterness gathered
in the hearts of the multitude,
so he cannot be said to have loved the people.
Artisans toiled in construction,
thoughts were exhausted in schemes and contrivances,
fine silks were squandered on maids and concubines,
and financial resources were consumed by music and instruments,
so he cannot
be said to have spared labor.
These are great harms for a minister,
and things that a state should discard.
The former kings, in rectifying customs
and managing human relations,
valued nothing more than frugality.
Therefore, Yí Wú was slandered for his 'three returns,'
while Píng Zhòng gained renown for his self-restraint.
Since recent times, morality has declined,
extravagance and usurpation have known no bounds,
shame has not risen,
and competition for profit has spread.
One cannot but deeply guard against the root cause
to cut off its flow.
Hàn Wén adopted
The clothing made of fine silk
was still considered extravagant by the feudal lords.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) burned a pheasant-head fur robe,
but extravagance did not cease.
This was truly because although the virtue of frugality was manifest,
the prohibitions enforced with authority were not strict;
the Way was
established by us,
but punishment did not reach the objects of offense.
If we maintain punishment for transgressions
and disparage evil,
then the four principles [of propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame] will certainly be upheld,
and ritual and righteousness will prevail.
According to the rules of posthumous titles,
one who accomplished meritorious deeds based on circumstances is called
“Xiāng” (襄),
and one who was greedy and ruined their office is called
Therefore, it is appropriate to posthumously title him Lord Xiāngmò (襄墨公).
Furthermore, it was argued that Yīn Hào (殷浩) should be given an additional posthumous title,
and that Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) demotion should not be treated as a national precedent,
as there were many signs of Huán Wēn (桓溫) attempting to usurp power.
At that time, the Xiè (謝) clan was prominent,
and Huán Zōng (桓宗) (likely referring to Huán Wēn's clan) was still powerful.
Wáng Xún (王珣), the Director of the Department of State Affairs,
was a former subordinate of Huán Wēn (桓溫),
and had always been favored by Huán Wēn (桓溫).
With these three grievances converging,
Hóng (弘) was sent out to be the Magistrate of Yúháng (餘杭).
Before his departure,
he wrote a memorial to Prince Huìjī Dàozǐ (會稽王道子), saying: "Your humble official is a person of humble origins and low status,
who has wrongly been allowed to participate in state affairs.
I truly fear that I might disgrace the pure stream [of virtuous officials]
and merely create dust in this sagely era.
I humbly believe that a ruler dwelling in the imperial court,
whose wisdom encompasses the four seas and beyond,
not only relies on their own inner enlightenment,
but also on the assistance of many voices.
Thus, when Shùn (舜) assisted Yáo (堯),
he prioritized opening up [avenues for remonstrance];
when Gāoyáo (咎繇)
advised Yǔ (禹),
he put forth frank and straightforward speech first.
Therefore, there were no hidden feelings among those below,
and those above achieved the merits of divine wisdom.
I dare to follow this principle,
with the intention of expressing everything fully.
I have always believed that Xiè Shí (謝石)
brought disgrace upon himself
and should be rectified,
while Yīn Hào (殷浩) was loyal and faithful
and should be honored and distinguished.
Therefore, disregarding my own insignificance,
I spoke before the multitude.
However, those who detest uprightness and condemn righteousness
are truly
numerous.
Although I rely on the sagely and enlightened disposition of the Emperor above,
and depend on the profound love for all beings from Your Excellency below,
the troubles that converge [upon me]
are truly unavoidable.
Your humble official and Xiè Shí (謝石) originally
held no grudges or animosity;
we never knew each other during our lives,
and our affairs were unrelated.
It is precisely because the national system should be clear
that one should not consider strengths and weaknesses.
My age is vastly different from Yīn Hào’s (殷浩),
and our eras do not
overlap.
There is no need for me to hear [about him] again;
it is merely old men recounting his past deeds.
What pain or itch does this cause to your humble official,
that I should offend the times and provoke the ruler for it?
Whenever I examine historical records,
there are men of lofty aspirations and benevolence who speak from their hearts and act according to the straight path,
and there are those who, knowing what is right, feign ignorance and conform to distortion.
Though their methods differ,
both are transmitted to later generations.
Thus, Bǐ Gān (比干) is among the "three benevolent ones,"
and Jīzǐ (箕子) is counted among the foremost virtuous sages.
How later generations accept or reject them
varies differently;
each believes what they see,
and acts accordingly.
Some achieve glorious and prominent fame,
while others suffer misfortune and failure one after another.
These are all cases of not judging the trends of the times,
and bringing disaster upon themselves.
Although they may be praised for their firmness of character,
this
is not the attainment of a true gentleman.
This is also what your humble official would not do.
People of the world say that your humble official is upright
and capable of facing difficulties;
this statement is truly an exaggeration.
Your humble official knows
that the Emperor above is sagely and enlightened,
and Your Excellency is humble,
seeking honest counsel,
and will certainly not allow loyal ministers to be oppressed by perverse and crooked factions.
Therefore, I dare to offer my foolish sincerity,
and present
it to the authorities.
How can this be compared in importance to the people of old?
Moreover, a minister's service to his lord
is solely to exhaust his loyalty.
He should not consider gain or loss.
If an matter does not accord with
his heart, then upright words enlighten the lord.
If righteousness moves his feelings, then he will present his remonstrance without regret.
If one conceals feelings and hides intentions,
harboring them without speaking,
this is why the ancients offended
enlightened rulers,
and why enlightened rulers brought laws upon their subordinates.
Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) deeds
are spread throughout the imperial court,
and the nature of his rebellion or loyalty
is revealed throughout the four seas.
Among all subjects and sons,
how could their feelings differ?
Among all common people,
who among them lacks a heart?
The entire court is silent,
with no one yet speaking out.
Therefore, I put down my brush and suppress my emotions,
not daring to say more.
Regarding Huán Wēn (桓溫) and my late grandfather,
though his intentions were difficult to
discern,
judging by the events,
my grandfather merely avoided demotion;
there was no extreme enmity.
My late father was formerly Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) subordinate.
Judging by the circumstances and etiquette,
my duty is no different from anyone else's.
The reason I always feel
indignant and outraged,
pained as if it were my own body,
Your Excellency can understand.
Wáng Xún (王珣) believed that my discussion of Yīn Hào’s (殷浩) posthumous title
should not openly expose Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) evil deeds.
Wáng Xún (王珣) was moved by
the favor of his promotion,
and cherished his appointment to Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) staff.
He claimed that by deposing the ignorant and dark ruler
and establishing the sagely and enlightened one,
this matter alone was sufficient to demonstrate his loyalty and integrity.
Your Excellency, please observe this from another event.
In ancient times, when Duke of Zhōu (周公) acted as regent,
he brought about an era of peace and prosperity.
Ritual, music, law, and government all originated from him.
In terms of virtue,
the Duke of Zhōu (周公) was a great
sage.
In terms of age,
King Chéng (成王) was young and weak.
Yet, the Duke immediately relinquished the sovereign's position,
restoring the enlightened ruler to his rightful place.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, Huò Guāng (霍光) achieved outstanding and brilliant merits.
Emperor Xuān (宣帝) was not yet
twenty years old,
but Huò Guāng (霍光) also returned all affairs of state.
Thus, both ruler and minister flourished,
and their Way transcended a thousand years.
If Huán Wēn (桓溫) was loyal to the state
and his sincerity lay with the imperial court,
he should have immediately followed the example of these two
dukes,
and emulated their excellent conduct.
Why did he not return all affairs of state
and retreat to his role as a protector of the realm?
Instead, he led and controlled the princes and dukes,
and took charge of the imperial court.
Was it because the former emperor was young and weak,
and not yet capable of
governing personally?
Or was it that Emperor Dé (德) was Huán Wēn (桓溫) and unable to govern?
Furthermore, he coerced Yuán Hóng (袁宏)
to compose the "Nine Bestowals" text,
describing magnificent and complete regalia.
The text still exists in full.
The court
was terrified,
and everyone followed his lead,
except for Xiè Ān (謝安) and Wáng Tǎnzhī (王坦之), who defended it with their lives.
Thus, the process was delayed.
Then, Heaven sent down its wrath,
and the wicked perished on their own.
The state
precarious and then stable again,
the spiritual mandate having fallen, then re-established.
Since the Restoration of the Jìn,
orders and authority have largely come from powerful ministers.
Zhōngzōng and Sùzǔ bowed to Wáng Dūn;
the late emperor suffered humiliation from the Huán clan.
Now
His Majesty personally oversees myriad affairs,
and your Excellency brilliantly assists in all government matters.
Policy issues from the royal house,
and people have no other expectations.
If we do not now greatly clarify the national statutes
and establish a system for a hundred generations,
I
do not know whom we are waiting for.
The former kings, in governing all things,
would certainly clarify their ordinances and proclamations,
leaving plans for their descendants.
Thus, their good reputation and auspiciousness endured,
and for a thousand years, people followed their example.
I wish that your Excellency would look far back to
Yīn and Zhōu,
and closely examine Hàn and Wèi;
consider what caused their peril,
and seek what led to their security.
This is all.
He also wrote to Wáng Xún, saying: I have seen your reply to Zhòngkān's letter,
which fully expresses a sense of righteous indignation.
Among the things valued in human conduct,
none surpass ruler and parents.
What pertains to ruler and parents
is loyalty and filial piety, nothing more.
Filial piety prioritizes exalting one's parents;
loyalty puts integrity and righteousness first.
Yīn Hóu was loyal and upright, residing in righteousness,
his heart piercing through men and gods.
Moreover, he cultivated a deep friendship with the late emperor as commoners,
establishing
a bond of profound intimacy.
Through thick and thin,
he endured smooth and rough paths with him.
Although he suffered humiliation from a treacherous hero,
his ambition reached through a thousand years.
This is why loyal and upright individuals, driven by righteousness,
cannot cease.
Not only was this thoroughly understood by the chaste and resolute people of that time,
but it is also fully heard by later generations.
How dare I evade the mad and cunning,
thereby deceiving the sagacious and enlightened?
Your Excellency fails to appreciate the great righteousness of Jūzhèng,
but cherishes the small kindness of a confidant.
You wish to supplant the weighty righteousness of orthodox teachings with the minor etiquette of the headquarters.
In the relationship between ruler and minister,
this is already a failing.
Exalting the great ruler, Yīn Hóu collaborated with him in loyal plans,
together supporting the royal house.
His resolve was as sharp as autumn frost,
his sincerity penetrated his era.
The reason Yīn Hóu was able to proclaim his
righteous reputation
was truly due to the great ruler's cooperative support.
Your Excellency is unable to glorify the great ruler's straightforward ambition in this matter.
Instead, you are moved by Wēn's petty regard
and harbor his twisted intentions.
While publicly in a
sagacious age,
you deceive the world,
causing the Prime Minister's virtue not to last three generations,
and the Commander's foundation, once established, to collapse.
This is why loyal ministers are disheartened,
and filial sons
lose morale.
Is the way of father and son truly like this?
Your Excellency's words as a minister are not loyal,
and as a son are not filial.
Since both are absent,
whom do I fear?
When I was young, I often passed by the courtyard,
and fully heard the words of my ancestors.
I never failed to feel indignant to the point of my hair bristling,
my emotions evident in my words.
At that time,
I only feared
utter ruin.
How could I have time to plan for the state?
I did not expect that today I would be able to wield the pen for this matter.
Therefore, I am indignant that the court lacks ministers of righteousness,
and secondarily I reflect that my ancestors had a lifelong
regret.
How could I share the same feelings as your Excellency?
My late father also once served as his official.
At that time, he was in peril and fear,
unable to protect himself.
He looked up to the sagacious court,
expressing indignation and sighing in his heart and mouth.
How could he have plotted and sought fame in the past,
equating himself with those three?
In the past, Zǐzhèng was a pure minister for five generations,
while Zǐjùn and others pledged allegiance to Wáng Mǎng.
Former records have already judged their right and wrong,
and later generations have also learned from their successes and failures.
Every time I read these accounts,
I cannot but lament with deep sorrow while reading the text,
filled with indignation.
Comparing
the present with the past,
I then realize they are one and the same.
Hóng's words, though candid and upright,
ultimately led to his not being promoted due to Huán and Xiè,
and he died as Magistrate of Yúháng
at the age of forty-seven.
Wáng Huān
Wáng Huān, courtesy name Jūnhòu,
was a native of Lèlíng.
Content in poverty and joyful in the Way,
he devoted himself to studies.
He did not manage property,
often begging for food while reciting poetry.
Even if his home had no provisions,
he was at ease.
His wife worried about this,
sometimes burning his books and seeking to remarry.
Huān smiled and said to her:
"Have you not heard of Zhū Mǎichén's wife?"
At the time, many who heard this laughed at him.
Huān's resolve grew firmer,
and he eventually became a renowned scholar.
When Mùróng Wěi assumed the false title,
he appointed him Guózǐ Bóshì (Imperial University Erudite),
and personally received instruction in the classics from him.
He was promoted to Jìjiǔ (Libationer).
When Wěi was vanquished by Fú Jiān,
Huān died in Cháng'ān.
The historian says: Fàn Píng and others were Confucian masters in the academies,
renowned and respected.
Some raised doubts, belonging to this faction,
or were exemplars to whom others looked.
Although they did not equal the ancients,
they were indeed talents of their time.
Such as Zhòngníng, who was pure and chaste, upholding the Way,
maintaining his integrity within his humble abode;
Xíng Qí, whose living quarters were often empty,
his heart residing in a humble alley;
Wén Bó, who rinsed his mouth with stream water and used a stone as a pillow,
erasing his tracks and silencing his name;
Xuānzǐ, who found joy in the Way and peace in poverty,
promoting and elucidating the teachings: these were all highly esteemed among accomplished scholars.
As for Miǎo, he harmonized with the ruler and prime minister,
cutting superfluous words.
It can be said he followed and supported their good,
and rectified and saved their errors.
Shū Yuán entered to participate in state affairs,
and the enlightened ruler admired his extensive knowledge;
when he went out to govern the frontier,
the fierce barbarians revered his enlightened virtue.
Hóng's outspoken arguments and propositions,
not shying away from court power,
criticizing Shí and resisting Wēn,
were indeed appropriate.
Yet he was consequently trapped by three enmities,
leading to his decline.
Alas!
Eulogy says: Lush was King Wén of Zhōu,
vast were the Hàn classics.
Their excellence was widely praised,
their brilliant arguments brought joy.
The elegant pronouncements did not fade,
the subtle words reappeared.
Arriving at the Jìn dynasty,
this tradition became even more widespread.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 62, Literati
That culture transforms and completes,
is the high righteousness of the sages;
that it does not go far if not practiced,
is a maxim from previous historians.
Therefore, the auspicious diagrams of the Wēn and Luò Rivers,
and the green tallies completed the great achievements of Yú;
the spiritual inscriptions of Yuán Mountain,
and the golden tablets accomplished the imperial rule of Huángdì.
Thereafter, the way of writing and contracts flourished,
and the writings on bells and stones became even more extensive.
They transformed customs through royal governance,
and promoted filial piety and respect among human relations.
They wove the fabric of heaven and earth,
encompassing inside and outside.
Thus, one knows that the contemporary significance of culture is great and far-reaching!
When the era of Jī Lì
approached its twilight, songs and odes became increasingly abundant.
The lineage of Xún and Sòng
traced its origins far back,
like yoked golden steeds galloping in unison,
or jade chariots racing side by side.
Their words flowed like springs converging into nine streams,
and their literary rhythms harmonized with the six variations.
From that time onward,
their paths converged.
In the Western Capital, Jiǎ Yí and Mǎ Róng displayed spiritual serpents in their grasp;
in the Eastern Hàn, Bān Gù and Zhāng Hé carved dragons onto silk scrolls and bamboo slips.
Both were hailed as foremost,
and universally regarded as preeminent.
When the Tuó dynasty founded its mandate,
literary masters flourished.
The Three Zǔ harmonized their lofty rhymes,
and the Seven Zǐ shared their brilliant rules.
The Hán Lín collected their essence,
and the Diǎn Lùn detailed their ornate beauty.
The splendor of their literary grace
competed in excellence in those years.
Yet, uniquely, King Chén,
with his forceful and elevated thought,
mastered the classical and profound,
lofty as the sun and moon.
When the Jìn dynasty succeeded to power,
literary refinement greatly flourished.
Zhāng Zài excelled in the beauty of "Inscription on a Mountain,"
while Lù Jī exhibited the marvel of "Burning the Inkstone."
Pān and Xià shone together,
rivaling their peers.
They both gathered
intricate and beautiful works, crafting pure and excellent pieces.
They thoroughly explored the green books of the imperial library,
and compiled the exquisite melodies of the Píng Tái.
Their excellent reputation and rich achievements
are recorded in their separate biographies.
As for Jí Fǔ and Tài Chōng,
they were literary heroes from the region east of the Jiāng;
Cáo Pí and Yǔ Chǎn,
were outstanding talents of the Restoration era.
Truly, they possessed the luster of gold and jade,
their talents converging like forests and rivers.
They equaled the beauty of their predecessors,
and left a rich legacy for future generations.
Now, I compile the eminent scholars of grand writing
and record them in the Wén Yuàn.
Yìng Zhēn
Yìng Zhēn, courtesy name Jí Fǔ,
was a native of Nándùn, Rǔnán.
He was the son of Yìng Qú, a Wèi Shìzhōng.
From Hàn to Wèi,
his family was renowned for its literary accomplishments,
with officials succeeding one another, establishing them as a prominent clan in the commandery.
Zhēn was skilled in discussion and debate,
and known for his talent and learning.
Xiàhóu Xuán had a great reputation;
Zhēn visited Xuán,
who highly esteemed him.
He was appointed to a high position,
and frequently held prominent offices.
When Emperor Wǔ was Fǔjūn Dàjiàngjūn,
he appointed Zhēn as his Cānjūn.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he was promoted to Gěishìzhōng.
When the Emperor held a banquet and archery contest in Huálín Yuán,
Zhēn's poem was the most excellent.
Its verses said:
Vast and distant is the Supreme One,
the origin of humankind.
The imperial standard was first established,
and the constant norms were thus spread.
The Five Virtues alternated in their course,
responding to the records and receiving the talismans.
When Táo Táng passed away,
Heaven's calendar was with Yú.
At that time, the August Lord
looked upon and showed favor.
Glorifying our Jìn fortune,
it responded to the timing and received the abdication.
The throne ascended like a soaring dragon,
and culture transformed like a leopard's spots.
Profound
beneficence flowed broadly,
and benevolent winds quietly spread.
The people within the realm settled their minds,
and all regions turned their faces.
Heaven displayed its signs,
and Earth revealed its patterns.
Phoenixes sang in the morning sun,
and dragons soared amid propitious clouds.
Auspicious grain yielded double ears,
and málíng plants bore fragrance.
The entire land was peaceful,
and all people were joyful and pleased.
Vast, vast is the imperial standard,
solemn, solemn is the sacred countenance.
His words are considered sincere,
his demeanor is considered respectful.
In seeing, he is discerning;
in hearing, he is acute.
He appoints to office by virtue,
and clearly
tests by merit.
What of his reverence?
He shines forth mightily from dawn.
No principle is not followed,
no reason is not practiced.
In action, he discards ostentation;
in speech, he avoids sophistry.
His mind
roves in ultimate emptiness,
his principles align with ease and simplicity.
The Six Treasuries are greatly cultivated,
and the Nine Regions come to him.
No beneficence is unbestowed,
no transformation is unadded.
His teachings reach the south,
and spread west to the Moving Sands.
The remote
people abandon their danger,
distant nations forget their remoteness;
Yuècháng sends interpreters repeatedly,
filling the imperial court.
Lofty, lofty are the feudal lords,
resplendent, resplendent are the military officials.
Internally, they harmonize the Five Grades;
externally, they awe the Four Guests.
They contribute their duties according to the season,
and enter to pay homage to the Son of Heaven.
They are fully granted imperial appointments,
with feather canopies and vermilion wheels.
They bestow banquets and good gatherings,
their number not constant.
What the divine heart bestows
is understood without words.
At this time, for the archery contest,
bows and arrows are prepared.
They shoot at the alternating
targets,
and there is wine for all to be sated.
The Way of culture and military,
its principles have not fallen.
In ancient times, the former kings
used this archery implement.
They demonstrated martial prowess to deter chaos,
but excess leads to error.
All their multitudinous lords
were not lax in their positions.
When the office of Tài Zǐ Zhōng Shù Zǐ was first established,
Zhēn and Hùjūn Chángshǐ Kǒng Xún both held it.
Later, he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
As a scholar, he collaborated with Tàiwèi Xún Yǐ in compiling and revising the new rituals,
which were not yet implemented.
He died in the fifth year of Tàishǐ (269 CE),
and his collected works circulated in the world.
His younger brother was Chún.
Chún's son, Shào,
during the Yǒngjiā era,
reached the position of Huángmén Láng,
but was killed by Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè.
Chún's younger brother was Xiù.
Xiù's son, Zhān,
has his own biography.
Chéng Gōngsuí
Chéng Gōngsuí, courtesy name Zǐ'ān,
was a native of Bǎimǎ, Dōngjùn.
He was intelligent and keen from childhood,
and widely read in the Classics and commentaries.
He had few desires by nature,
and did not manage assets;
though his family was poor and years were lean,
he was always at ease.
In his youth, he had outstanding talent,
and his prose and rhapsodies were very beautiful.
He remained quiet and self-composed,
not seeking fame or advancement.
At that time, there were filial crows
that often gathered at his dwelling.
Suí considered them to have the virtue of filial regurgitation,
and regarded them as auspicious birds.
He then composed a rhapsody to praise them,
much of the text is not recorded here.
He also said,
"For a rhapsody, the valuable thing is to be able to describe the myriad phenomena,
expounding without limit.
The grandeur of Heaven and Earth
can thus inspire thought.
Reviewing the ancients, none have composed a rhapsody on this;
could it be because its ultimate beauty is without specific form,
making it difficult to praise with words?
Otherwise,
why is it missing?"
Thereupon, he composed the "Rhapsody on Heaven and Earth," saying:
Oh, in the primordial beginning of nature,
the Dao was void and profoundly clear.
The Great Simplicity was chaotically indistinct,
and then things first came into being and were blended.
Ah!
The cosmos opened up and took shape.
Then the clear and the turbid were separated,
The black and the yellow were distinguished.
Once the tài jí was differentiated,
The liǎng yí were born.
The stars shone in array,
The sun and moon
followed their orbits,
Heaven moved with dignity,
Earth remained still in humility.
Day and night alternated their illumination,
Sometimes waxing, sometimes waning.
Yīn and yáng cooperated their qi to interchange,
Cold and heat shifted with the seasons.
The three
realms had distinct natures,
The five phases occupied different positions.
A myriad changes and transformations,
Proliferating all kinds of creatures,
Bestowing them with forms,
Endowing them with qi.
Colors displayed their hues,
Sounds possessed their melodies.
Covering
and supporting without boundaries,
Shaping all things.
It beats with thunder,
It moistens with auspicious clouds.
The eight winds soar,
The six qì are dense and moist.
Creeping and wriggling creatures,
Gather in groups and divide into kinds.
Scaled
creatures of different tribes,
Feathered creatures of various flocks.
Each contains its essence and is refined,
All are molded by the potter’s wheel.
How boundless is the nurturing and growth!
How great and divine is the creative transformation!
As for the celestial phenomena forming patterns,
The constellations arranged in order,
The three luminaries shine brightly,
The five planets radiate their light.
The Milky Way stretches like a belt across the sky,
Rainbows curve gracefully in the vast
blue firmament.
Wàngshū extends its course through the nine paths,
Xīhé straightens its reins in the central yellow.
The myriad stars revolve around the pole,
Zhāoyáo moves and points to the directions.
The White Beast stands guard in Cān
and Fá,
The Azure Dragon lowers its tail in Xīnfáng,
The Sombre Tortoise hides its head in Nǚ and Xū,
The Vermilion Bird flaps its wings in Zhù and Zhāng.
The Emperor sits majestically in the Zǐgōng,
His辅臣 are arrayed
in Wénchāng.
The enclosing walls are continuous like strung pearls,
The Sāntái are scattered like flying geese.
Xuānyuán is spread out in a curved array,
Shètí stands like a tripod, facing each other.
As for
auspicious signs indicating fortune,
And calamitous changes displaying anomalies:
Conjunctions and eclipses,
Halos and solar ears,
Retrograde movements and transgressions,
Warnings symbolized by events.
When péng róng appears, disasters arise,
When a lao
rén appears, the ruler receives joy.
When a yellow sky arrow appears, the country is auspicious,
When comets appear, they are feared by the world.
Then, observing the four cardinal points,
And looking down upon the geography:
Rivers and streams flow mightily and diverge,
Mountains and peaks rise majestically and are arrayed.
The vast blue ocean surrounds them on all sides,
Xuánpǔ rises lofty and unique.
Kūnwú is magnificent in the south pole,
Zhúlóng shines in the northern foothills.
Fúsāng is tall, ten thousand rén high,
Xúnmù is long, a thousand lǐ in length.
Kūnlún
stands guard in the yīn corner,
Chìxiàn occupies the chén and sì directions.
Thus, eighty-one regions,
Are divided and distinct;
Customs differ,
Dangerous barriers obstruct.
Ten thousand states are
spread out,
The nine provinces are arrayed side by side.
Qīng and Jì have white soil,
Jīng and Héng have muddy earth.
Hǎi and Dài have red clay,
Huá and Liáng have black loam.
Yǎn has the Hé and Luò rivers,
Yáng has the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Distinguishing directions
and rectifying the land,
Planning and establishing states.
The royal domain and the nine services,
All the states are unified.
Connected cities and adjacent towns,
Deep moats and high walls.
Broad roads intersect,
Reaching in four directions and connecting five ways.
East
to Yánggǔ,
West to Tàiméng,
South to Dānpáo,
North to Kōngtóng.
Distant regions and outer areas,
Remote lands with unique neighbors,
Human heads and serpent bodies,
Bird wings and dragon forms,
Clad in fur, covered in feathers,
Some armored, some scaled,
Dwelling in forests, floating on water,
Like beasts, like humans.
Residing beyond the Great Wilderness,
Living by the shore of the vast sea.
Thus the six directions are unified and share a dwelling,
The universe forms a body and encompasses all.
The primordial qi circulates endlessly,
Yīn and yáng follow their courses and are constant.
Turning and moving
intricately and diligently,
The Way of Heaven is unceasing and self-strengthening.
It commands all beings and nourishes them,
Humans entrust their lives to what sustains them.
Honoring Tài Yī as the Supreme Sovereign,
Serving myriad deities
among the Wǔ Dì.
Therefore, what all things ultimately rely on,
Must be revering Heaven and serving Earth.
If Gònggōng raged furiously,
And the pillar of Heaven was broken,
The southeast tilted suddenly,
The northwest gaped and split open.
Cutting off the tortoise’s feet to mend the damage,
Refining jade and stone
to patch the holes.
Is there evidence for this event,
Or is it merely a fabrication of storytellers?
How unfathomable are yīn and yáng,
How grand and expansive are the liǎng yí!
Kūn, with its profound virtue, bears all things,
Qián, as the origin, is supremely great.
Looking down, it observes all forms,
Looking up, it is veiled by what it covers.
It wanders among all things and thinks deeply,
Therefore
I speak a word from beyond the heavens.
Suī Yǎ, who loved music,
Once, in the heat of summer, faced the wind and whistled,
A clear melody formed,
And so he composed the "Whistling Rhapsody" saying: The distinguished young master,
Possessed of unique temperament and fond of the extraordinary,
Disdained the world and forgot glory,
Completely abandoned human affairs,
Aspired to loftiness and admired antiquity,
Longed for distant thoughts.
He would ascend Jī Shān to uphold his integrity,
And float upon the vast sea to wander with his aspirations.
Thereupon, he invited his friends,
Gathered those of like mind,
Probing the ultimate mysteries of life and nature,
Studying the profound intricacies of morality.
Pitying the unenlightened common folk,
He alone stood aloof and was the first to awaken.
Finding the worldly path narrow and cramped,
He looked up to the celestial highway and strode loftily,
Transcending the common world and forgetting his body,
And then he whistled long and with fervor.
At that time, the sun’s
splendor was setting,
Its light flowing towards Míngsì.
Wandering freely, hand in hand,
Pausing with hesitant steps.
He emitted wondrous sounds from his cinnabar lips,
Stirring mournful tones from his white teeth.
The echoes rose and fell, then subtly
turned,
The qi surged forth intensely and rose like sparks.
Harmonizing the huánggōng with the qīngjiǎo,
Mixing shāng and yǔ with the liúzhǐ.
Causing light clouds to drift in the Tàiqīng,
Gathering the long wind from ten thousand lǐ.
The melody
ended and the sound ceased,
But the lingering enjoyment was not yet over.
Truly it was a sound of ultimate naturalness,
Not to be compared with strings and flutes.
Therefore, the sound does not rely on instruments,
Its use does not borrow
things,
drawing closely from one's own body,
directing the mind and controlling the vital energy.
Moving the lips, there are tunes;
opening the mouth, sounds are produced.
Responding to categories and feeling things,
following songs and accompanying chants.
Grand yet not turbid,
subtle yet
not sinking.
Clear and sharp like the yú and shēng,
gentle and harmonious like the sè and qín.
Profound and marvelous enough to communicate with spirits and enlighten souls,
refined and subtle enough to explore the hidden and plumb the deep.
Gathering the sorrowful desolation
of Jīchǔ,
regulating the extravagance and decadence of Běilǐ.
Rescuing from great disaster in scorching drought,
turning back the intense yang in heavy yin.
With myriad changes in leading chants,
the application of tunes is boundless.
Harmonious and joyful,
content,
sorrowful and heart-rending.
Sometimes reclusive and about to cease,
then suddenly vigorous and慷慨 (kǎigǎnɡ),
slowly gentle and leisurely,
then bustling and impetuous and rousing.
Feelings, having contemplated,
can then revert;
the heart, though sorrowful, is not broken.
Encompassing the ultimate harmony of the eight tones,
it is truly supreme joy without excess.
As for ascending a high terrace to gaze into the distance,
or opening a decorated chamber and letting one's gaze roam,
sighing, looking up, clapping one's hands, and raising one's head,
the long-drawn out sound is clear and bright.
Sometimes spreading out freely and then
reverting,
sometimes lingering and then releasing again.
Sometimes soft and pliant,
sometimes surging and vigorous.
Suppressing a mournful cry that becomes choked,
then unfurling into a distant, clear, and spacious sound.
Unrestrained
spirit surges forth,
intertwining in colorful profusion.
Fierce winds sweep up,
chirping sounds arise.
Playing the longings of a Húmǎ,
recalling the cold wind in Běishuò.
Or like wild geese
leading their young,
crying out in flocks in the desert.
Thus it can create sounds based on form,
compose tunes according to events.
Responding to things endlessly,
the mechanism activates, and sounds are swift.
Depressed emotions surge forth,
intertwining
like clouds.
Sometimes separating, sometimes joining,
about to cease, then resuming.
Fēilián beats in the deep abyss,
fierce beasts respond in the middle valley;
the Nánjī constellation moves in the vast sky,
clear winds sway
tall trees;
dispersing accumulated stagnation and spreading it forth,
washing away the turbidity of dust and haze,
transforming yin and yang into ultimate harmony,
changing the vulgar customs of decadent trends.
As for roaming high ridges,
ascending Jǐngshān,
approaching a cliff side,
gazing at flowing streams,
sitting on a large rock,
rinsing the mouth with clear springs,
leaning on the trailing Gāolán,
shaded by tall bamboo
that sways gently,
then chanting and sighing,
the sounds follow one after another, resonating continuously.
Unveiling accumulated thoughts of frustration,
releasing long-held, intertwined emotions.
The heart is cleansed and unburdened,
the will
leaves worldly concerns and floats freely.
As for borrowing the imagery of metal and leather (bells and drums),
imitating the principles of pottery and gourds (flutes and stringed instruments),
many sounds play in profusion,
like the jiā and the xiāo;
booming, crashing, rumbling,
thundering, noisy.
When the zhēng tone is produced,
winter is warm and steamy;
when the yǔ tone is played, severe frost withers in summer;
when the shāng tone moves, autumn rains fall in spring;
when the jué tone is sounded, valley winds rustle the branches.
The musical intervals are not uniform,
the tunes have no fixed pattern.
It flows without deviation,
it stops without stagnation.
It expresses itself through the mouth and lips,
it borrows fragrant air to drift far away.
The sounds are subtle and echo,
the voice is sharp and clear.
Truly it is the ultimate beauty of nature,
indeed, it is exceptionally unique and incomparable.
Surpassing Sháoxià and Xiánchí,
why merely seek difference from Zhèng and Wèi!
At this time, Miánjū was tongued-tied and lost his spirit,
Wángbào closed his mouth and lost his color,
Gōnggōng stopped his voice and ceased to sing,
Níngzǐ clasped his hands and sighed,
Zhōng
Qí abandoned his qín and changed his listening,
Nífù forgot the taste of food and did not eat.
All beasts led the way, clapping their feet,
phoenixes came to perform their dance and flap their wings.
Then one realizes the wondrous
mystery of the long shout,
this is the ultimate of sounds and music.
Zhāng Huà deeply valued Suí,
every time he saw his writings,
he admired them, considering them unparalleled,
and recommended him to the Tàicháng,
who appointed him as Bóshì.
He successively served as Mìshū Láng,
then transferred to Chéng,
and was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng.
He often received imperial decrees with Huà and composed poetry and rhapsodies together,
and also participated with Jiǎ Chōng and others in revising the laws.
He died in the ninth year of Tàishǐ,
at the age of forty-three.
His collected poems, rhapsodies, and miscellaneous writings, over ten volumes, circulated in the world.
Zuǒ Sī
Zuǒ Sī, courtesy name Tàichōng,
was a native of Línzī, Qí state.
His ancestors were a princely clan of Qí who had Zǔoyòu Gōngzǐ,
and thus took the surname.
His family had been Confucian scholars for generations.
His father, Yōng,
started as a minor official,
and was promoted for his ability to Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ.
In his youth, Sī studied the calligraphy of Zhōng and Hú, and also played the qín,
but did not achieve mastery in either.
Yōng told a friend:
“What Sī understands
is less than what I knew in my youth.”
Sī was thus moved to study diligently,
and also excelled in the art of Yīnyáng.
He was unattractive in appearance,
and spoke with difficulty,
but his literary style was grand and magnificent.
He did not enjoy socializing,
but only considered quiet contemplation as his primary pursuit.
He composed the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Qí,"
which took him a year to complete.
He then wanted to compose the "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals."
Coincidentally, his sister, Fēn, entered the palace,
and his family moved to the capital, Jīngshī.
So, he visited the Gentleman of the Palace Library, Zhāng Zài, to inquire about affairs in Mínqióng.
He then conceptualized for ten years,
covering every part of his home, from the gate to the privies, with writing brushes and paper,
and whenever he got a line,
he would immediately write it down.
Believing his own observations to be insufficiently broad,
he sought to become a Secretary of the Imperial Library.
When the rhapsody was completed,
people at the time did not value it highly.
Sī himself felt that his work was no inferior to those of Bān Gù and Zhāng Héng,
and feared that his work might be dismissed due to his low status.
Huángfǔ Mì of Āndìng had a high reputation,
so Sī visited him and showed him the work.
Mì praised it,
and wrote a preface for his rhapsody.
Zhāng Zài annotated the Wèi Capital,
and Liú Kuí annotated the Wú and Shǔ Capitals, prefacing it thus:
"Observing those who have composed rhapsodies since ancient times, there are many.
Xiāngrú's 'Zǐxū' dominated in earlier times,
Bān Gù's 'Two Capitals' surpassed it in reason,
and Zhāng Héng's 'Two Metropolises' exceeded its intent in literary quality.
As for this rhapsody,
it imitates and discusses several schools;
its choice of words and convergence of meanings
are often exquisite.
Without diligent researchers, one cannot discern its essence;
without those with extensive knowledge, one cannot systematize its peculiarities.
The world commonly values the distant and disparages the near,
unwilling to apply their minds to understanding current matters.
To this work, I have a different view,
and so I have, with some leftover thought, provided an interpretation for it,
just as Hú Guǎng did for the 'Guānzhēn' (Admonitions for Officials),
and Cài Yōng did for the 'Diǎnyǐn' (Guiding Principles)."
Wèi Quán of Chénliú also wrote a brief commentary on Sī's rhapsody,
with a preface stating:
"I observe the 'Rhapsody on the Three Capitals';
its words are not idly ornate but
are certainly classical and essential.
The various types of objects it describes
are derived from maps and records.
Its diction and meaning are extraordinary and beautiful,
truly worthy of esteem.
The recluse of Jìn, the former Middle Gentleman of the Crown Prince's Household, Huángfǔ Mì of Āndìng,
an exceptional scholar of the western region,
who immersed himself in books and delighted in the Way,
held his affairs in high regard,
read this work with deep emotion,
and composed a preface for its capitals.
The Gentleman of the Palace Library in the Central Secretariat, Zhāng Zài of Ānpíng, and the Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, Liú Kuí of Jìnán,
both renowned for their profound knowledge of the classics
and beautiful, flourishing literary talent,
all admired and enjoyed it,
and provided annotations for it.
As for its mountains, rivers, territories,
plants, trees, birds, and beasts,
and strange and precious rarities,
all were thoroughly investigated to understand their origins,
explaining their meanings in detail.
I admire this work,
and cannot remain silent.
Borrowing from the omissions of these two gentlemen,
I have also made a brief commentary,
merely adding to its cumbersome nature;
readers may disregard it."
After this,
it was highly esteemed at the time,
and many literary works were not recorded.
Sīkōng Zhāng Huà saw it and sighed, saying:
"He is in the same class as Bān Gù and Zhāng Héng!
It makes readers feel that they have read their fill and yet there is still more,
and the longer they read it, the fresher it becomes."
Thereupon, families of the rich and powerful competed to copy it,
making paper expensive in Luòyáng.
Initially,
Lù Jī entered Luòyáng
and intended to compose this rhapsody.
Hearing that Sī was writing it,
he clapped his hands and laughed,
writing to his younger brother Yún:
"There's a rustic here
who wants to write the 'Rhapsody on the Three Capitals';
when he finishes it,
it will just be good for covering wine jars."
But when Sī's rhapsody came out,
Jī praised it profusely and submitted to it,
believing he could not surpass it,
and so he stopped writing.
Jǐa Mì, the Director of the Imperial Library, invited him to lecture on the Hànshū.
When Mì was executed,
he retired to Yíchūn Lǐ and
dedicated himself to classical texts.
Qí Wáng Jǒng ordered him to be Record-keeper Supervisor,
but he declined due to illness
and did not accept.
When Zhāng Fāng rampaged through the capital,
his entire family moved to Jìzhōu.
After several years,
he died of illness.
Zhào Zhì
Zhào Zhì, courtesy name Jǐngzhēn,
was a native of Dàijùn.
He resided in Luòyáng.
When the magistrate of Gōushì first arrived at his post,
Zhì, then thirteen years old,
watched with his mother.
His mother said:
"Your ancestors were originally not of humble status;
due to the chaos of the world and displacement,
they became mere soldiers.
Can you become like this in the future?"
Zhì was moved by his mother's words
and went to a teacher to study.
Hearing his father's shouts as he tilled the fields,
he threw down his books and wept.
His teacher asked him, surprised,
and Zhì said:
"I am too young to bring glory and support to my parents,
making my old father suffer and toil."
His teacher found this very unusual.
At fourteen,
he went to Luòyáng
and studied at the Imperial Academy.
He encountered Jī Kāng there, writing on stone classics,
and lingered, unable to leave,
asking his name.
Kāng said:
"Why does a young man ask?"
He replied:
"I observe your extraordinary demeanor,
which is why I ask."
Kāng, surprised, told him.
Later, he went missing to Shānyáng,
but could not find Kāng and returned.
He then wanted to go far away to study,
but his mother forbade him,
so Zhì feigned madness,
running for three to five *lǐ*,
only to be caught and brought back.
At sixteen,
he traveled to Yè,
and again met Kāng.
He followed Kāng back to Shānyáng,
changing his given name to Jùn,
and courtesy name to Yǔnyuán.
Kāng often said:
"Your head is small and sharp,
your pupils distinct in black and white;
you have the air of Bái Qǐ."
When Kāng died,
Zhì visited the Grand Administrator Zhāng Sìzōng in Wèixīng
and was treated with great favor.
Sìzōng was promoted to Chancellor of Jiāngxià,
and Zhì followed him to Yǐnchuān.
He intended to enter Wú from there,
but Sìzōng died,
so he headed to Liáoxī and registered his household there.
Earlier,
Zhì was good friends with Kāng's nephew, Fān.
When he was about to depart far away,
he wrote a farewell letter to Fān,
also expressing his aspirations: "In ancient times, old man Lǐ entered Qín
and sighed at the pass.
Liang Sheng went to Yuè
and sang a long song on the mountain.
Even with the act of glorious seclusion,
one still harbors lingering regret,
how much more so
for those who have no choice!
After our parting,
I shall leave the group and depart alone,
turning my back on glorious banquets,
bidding farewell to dear friends,
traversing distant roads,
and reaching the desert.
At cockcrow, announcing dawn,
I shall embark on
my morning journey;
when the sun dips below the western mountains,
there will be no place for my horse's head to rest.
Whenever I trace the winding and treacherous paths,
my thoughts become entangled and deep;
when I ascend high and gaze afar,
mountains and rivers separate us.
Sometimes,
swirling winds rage violently,
the bright sun loses its light,
I pace back and forth, confused,
hills and lowlands facing each other,
lingering within the nine marshes,
sighing on the peak of stacked mountains.
There is no way forward,
When retreating, there is nowhere to rely on.
Wading through marshes to find a path,
parting thorny bushes to seek a road,
singing and chanting in ditches –
truly unfathomable.
This is indeed the hardship of travel,
yet it is not what my heart
fears.
As for _Lánzhǐ_ leaning and falling,
_Guìlín_ being transplanted,
their roots not yet established, but their shoots shallow and their strings taut,
I constantly fear hidden turmoil and
secretly emerging crises.
This is why I am apprehensive on the long road.
Moreover, the nature of the northern lands
makes it difficult to take root.
If one offers a night-shining jewel to someone,
few will not grasp their sword.
Now, to plant tangerines and pomelos in the
_Xuánshuò_,
to cultivate lotus flowers in _Xiūlíng_,
to display dragon patterns in barren lands,
and to perform _Sháowǔ_ for deaf customs –
it is certainly difficult to gain honor.
If things do not value me, then no one will associate with me.
If no one associates with me, then those who harm me will arrive.
A wandering traveler,
entrusting his body to a desolate land,
reining his horse on distant roads,
faces the difficulties of the aforementioned words;
hanging his saddle in a humble dwelling,
he has the warnings of future worries;
when the morning glow illuminates,
his body is weary, and he must hurry on;
when the sun withdraws its light,
his spirit is toiled, and he is vigilant at dusk;
gazing across the
_Píngxí_,
it is vast and empty, with nothing to see;
listening intently on _Xiūyuán_,
it is silent and unheard.
Alas, how sorrowful!
My heart is deeply pained!
Only then do I know that a man of mere
steps is not to be valued.
Looking back at the Central Plains,
indignation surges like clouds.
Mourning things and lamenting the age,
passion is fierce like the wind.
Dragons roar in the great wilderness,
beasts gaze across the six directions.
Mighty aspirations are confused,
heroic ambitions
are everywhere.
I wish to ascend the cloud ladder,
to contend across the eight extremes,
to overcome hardships and sweep away filth,
to quell the seas and level the mountains,
to kick _Kūnlún_ so it topples westward,
to stomp _Tàishān_ so it overturns eastward,
to flatten and cleanse
the nine regions,
and to restore the universe.
This is my humble wish.
Time does not favor me;
my wings hang, and I fly far away.
My sharp claws are useless;
my six feathers are broken.
If not for one who
understands destiny,
who could not be indignant and dejected?!
My son, you have rooted in a fragrant garden,
washed your elegance in clear streams,
dried your leaves on a splendid cliff,
and flown your literary talent to the cloud's expanse.
You crouch on the islet of a hidden dragon,
and are sheltered by the forest of a roaming phoenix.
Glory and splendor dazzle before you;
alluring beauty entices behind you.
Fertile fields intersect on your left;
fame spreads to your right.
Soaring among your peers,
displaying your
grace in inner chambers,
calmly looking around,
you have ample leisure.
Bowing and rising, chanting and singing,
you consider yourself to have achieved your ambition.
How can you share the
joys and sorrows of a true man with us?!
Go, _Jīshēng_!
We are far separated!
Lonely and adrift,
facing the desert!
Three thousand _lǐ_ stretch far,
the road is difficult to cross!
The time to hold hands
is remotely
without a date!
My longing heart is deeply bound;
who says it can be released!
I do not have your golden jade-like voice, but I have a distant heart.
Though our bodies are like _Hú_ and _Yuè_,
our intentions cut metal.
Each respect your
demeanor,
adhere to the unpolished gem.
Fleeting luxury and extravagance,
the noble man does not admire.
My thoughts are tied when I face this paper;
what more can I say?
_Zhì_ was seven _chǐ_ four _cùn_ tall,
eloquent and skilled in argument,
with a talent for political strategy.
He was appointed county clerk in _Liáoxī_.
Upon arriving in _Luò_,
he met his father.
At that time, his mother had already died,
but his father wanted him to establish a career,
so he did not tell him.
Instead, he warned him not to return,
and _Zhì_ went back to _Liáoxī_.
He was appointed three times as an inspector in _Yōuzhōu_,
resolved nine prison cases,
and was praised for his meticulousness.
In the _Tàikāng_ era,
he was summoned to _Luò_ as a good official,
and only then learned of his mother's death.
Initially,
_Zhì_ was ashamed of his humble background,
and wished to establish his name through official service and scholarship,
hoping to provide for his parents.
However, his ambition was not realized,
and he cried out in grief and indignation,
vomited blood, and died,
at the age of thirty-seven.
_Zōu Zhàn_
_Zōu Zhàn_, courtesy name _Rùnfǔ_,
was from _Xīnyě_, _Nányáng_.
His father, _Guǐ_,
was General of the Left of _Wèi_.
_Zhàn_ was known for his talent and learning in his youth.
He served _Wèi_ successively as _Tōngshìláng_ and _Tàixué Bóshì_.
At the beginning of the _Tàishǐ_ era,
he was transferred to _Shàngshūláng_, _Tíngwèipíng_, and _Zhēngnán Cóngshì Zhōngláng_.
_Yáng Hù_ highly esteemed him.
He entered the court as _Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ_.
In the _Tàikāng_ era,
he was appointed _Sànqí Chángshì_,
then sent out to be _Bóhǎi Tàishǒu_,
and then transferred to _Tàifù Yáng Jùn_’s _Zhǎngshǐ_,
and promoted to _Shìzhōng_.
After _Jùn_ was executed,
he was dismissed from office as a subordinate.
Soon after, he was reinstated as _Sànqí Chángshì_ and _Guózǐ Jìjiǔ_,
then transferred to _Shǎofǔ_.
He died at the end of the _Yuánkāng_ era.
His collected poems and twenty-five essays on state affairs
were highly valued at the time.
Initially,
_Zhàn_ once dreamed of a man
who called himself _Zhēn Shūzhòng_,
saying nothing else.
This happened more than once.
After a long time,
he suddenly realized:
"To the west of my house there is accumulated earth and broken tiles.
There must be a dead person inside.
_Zhēn Shūzhòng_ is
the person in the earth and tiles west of my dwelling."
Upon inspection,
it was indeed so,
and he gave the remains a lavish burial.
After the burial,
he dreamed of the man coming to thank him.
His son, _Jié_,
courtesy name _Tàiyīng_,
also had literary talent.
In the _Yǒngkāng_ era,
he served as _Sànqí Shìláng_.
When King _Zhào Lún_ usurped the throne,
_Jié_ and _Lù Jī_ both composed texts of abdication.
When _Lún_ was executed,
_Jié_ was imprisoned in the _Tíngwèi_,
but was pardoned.
Later, he became _Tàifù Cānjūn_.
He died at the end of the _Yǒngjiā_ era.
_Zǎo Jù_
Zǎo Jù
, whose courtesy name was Dào-yàn, was a native of Cháng-shè
in Yǐng-chuān. His original surname was Jí,
but his ancestors changed it to avoid an enemy.
His father, Shū-yī,
was the Administrator of Jù-lù
in Wèi. Jù
had a beautiful appearance and was skilled in literature.
At the age of twenty (literally, "weak cap"),
he was invited to serve in the Grand General's office,
then sent out to be the Magistrate of Shān-yáng,
where he achieved political success.
He was promoted to Shàng-shū Láng,
then transferred to Yòu-chéng.
When Jiǎ Chōng campaigned against Wú,
Jù was invited to be his Cóng-shì Zhōng-láng.
After the army returned,
he was transferred to Huáng-mén Shì-láng, Jì-zhōu Cì-shǐ, and Tàizǐ Zhōng-shūzǐ.
He died during the Tài-kāng era,
at the age of over fifty.
His forty-five poems, fu, and treatises
were mostly lost during times of chaos.
His son, Tiǎn,
whose courtesy name was Xuán-fāng,
also became prominent for his literary talent.
During the Yǒng-jiā era, he served as the Administrator of Xiāng-chéng.
His younger brother, Sōng,
whose courtesy name was Tái-chǎn,
was especially gifted in talent and art.
He served as Tàizǐ Zhōng-shūzǐ and Sàn-qí Cháng-shì,
and was killed by Shí Lè.
Chǔ Táo
Chǔ Táo, whose courtesy name was Jì-yǎ,
was a native of Qián-táng
in Wú-jùn. As a youth, he did not enjoy playing,
and was intelligent from an early age.
He was pure, calm, and silent,
finding pleasure in the classics (fén and diǎn).
At thirteen,
he composed two fu, "Ōu-niǎo" (Seagull) and "Shuǐ-wèi" (Water Mill),
which those who saw them found extraordinary.
Táo once said to a close friend:
"The sages and worthies are all found within the yellow scrolls;
what else could one seek beyond them!"
He was invited by the prefecture and commandery,
but did not accept.
After Wú was pacified,
he was summoned to serve as Shàng-shū Láng.
Zhāng Huá, upon seeing him,
said to Lù Jī:
"Your brothers soar like dragons through the clouds,
and Gù Yàn-xiān crows like a phoenix facing the morning sun.
We thought the treasures of the Southeast were exhausted,
but did not expect to see Master Chǔ again."
Jī replied:
"You just haven't seen those who neither crow nor soar."
Huá said:
"Thus I know that the virtue of Yán-zhōu is not isolated,
and the treasures of the rivers and mountains are not depleted."
He was promoted to Administrator of Jiǔ-zhēn,
then transferred to Zhōng-wèi.
He died at the age of fifty-five.
Wáng Shěn
Wáng Shěn, whose courtesy name was Yàn-bó,
was a native of Gāo-píng.
From a young age, he possessed outstanding talent,
coming from humble origins.
Unable to conform to the ways of the world,
he was suppressed by the powerful families of the time.
He served as Wén-xué Yuàn in the commandery,
but felt frustrated and unfulfilled.
So he composed "Shì-shí Lùn" (Discourse on Explaining the Times),
whose text goes: An old man from Dōng-yě
observed the times and settled,
living hidden, cultivating a fertile land.
There was a son of the Bīng clan,
who came from a frozen, cold valley.
He passed by and asked for directions.
The old
man said:
"Where do you come from?"
He replied:
"From a land of dry yin."
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"I wish to go to the illustrious hall."
The old man said:
"Those who enter the illustrious
hall must possess a radiant brilliance.
Now you are distressed by the cold, yet wish to seek warmth,
but you have no means of acquiring warmth."
The son of Bīng looked startled and said:
"Why should it be
so?"
The old man said:
"Those who are warm and genial are all men who gravitate towards warmth.
Of those who gain access to the furnace gates,
only the sons who carry charcoal succeed.
If you are not such a person,
it is better
to desist."
The son of Bīng said:
"I have heard that the vessels of the ancestral temple do not necessarily require wood from beautiful forests,
and the guests at the four gates need not be from families of high officialdom.
Former worthies have untied ropes of hemp
and worn crimson knee-pads,
abandoned mere carrying poles and ridden in red carriages.
Judging from this,
why should one worry about having no emolument!
I only ask you, sir, to tell me the fastest path."
The old man said:
"Alas!
You hear of success thus,
but you do not know the times are against it.
I shall explain to you.
Indeed, there are safe and perilous paths,
and the times have difficult
and easy phases.
Talent has what it should correspond to,
and conduct has what it should adapt to.
Extraordinary heroes emerge in an era of vertical and horizontal alliances,
and the wise and intelligent become prominent at the beginning of a hegemon's or king's rule.
When faced with difficulties, they employ strategic cunning
to devise good plans.
When encountering a new creation, they display Confucian principles to expound them.
Thus, embroidered dragons emerge from humble clothes,
and ministers and prime ministers arise from commoners.
Hence, there are those who are lowly in the morning and noble in the evening,
first suppressed and then thriving.
At such times,
who considers the high or low status of family background,
or discusses the importance of position and power!
But it is not so now.
The sage above and the enlightened below rule,
the times
are prosperous, and the Way is tranquil.
All the lords live in ease and pleasure,
content and maintaining peace.
All the officials and gentlemen,
generation after generation,
public households have public officials,
ministerial households have ministers.
They point to rotten bones with bald fingers,
not distinguishing the foolish from the weak.
Many scholars are abundant among the noble families,
and appointments do not leave the inner courtyards.
The four gates are solemn,
filled with children from wealthy families,
sons of Rén-shū
are all
accomplished elders.
The lowly suffer constant humiliation,
the noble enjoy constant glory.
Meat-eaters follow one another into grand houses,
while those who eat coarse food continue their farming.
Those who speak of status and position attach themselves to power with flattery,
and those who raise high reputations follow appearance based on wealth.
So much so that the empty and noisy
consider their booming voices as elegant measure,
the petty and clever consider their shallow shrewdness as brilliance,
the sluggish
consider their lack of restraint as magnanimity,
the stooping and dirty consider their adherence to their own ideas as firmness and integrity,
the jeering and roaring consider their coarse outbursts as nobility and brightness,
the timid
consider their thick-skinnedness as sincerity,
the greedy consider their broad acceptance as generosity,
the narrow-minded consider their inaccessibility as pure stillness,
the slack and unkempt acquire a reputation for gravity,
the stingy and petty gain a reputation for integrity,
the fearful are timid in their humility,
while the vulgar and mean are bold in their contention for gain.
These are all the mortal ailments of the humble,
and the glorious names of the successful.
All these types,
observing their intentions,
examining
what they are comfortable with,
are quick to blame others,
but lenient with themselves.
They have no great virtue, yet deem themselves noble;
their position is not high, yet they deem themselves venerable.
Their eyes look in no particular direction, yet they see far;
their noses
point towards heaven.
They detest gentlemen,
and delight in flattering small-minded people.
They disdain the pure and simple,
and bow to powerful figures.
Their hearts are swayed by profit,
their wisdom clouded by power.
Relatives and factions incite each other,
praise and slander are intertwined.
Those in power are confused by what they receive,
and their decisions are misled by what they hear.
In the capital, there are countless scholars,
crowded and bustling,
rushing to influential families,
seeking office and buying
職，
童僕闚其車乘，
閽寺相其服飾，
親客陰參於靖室，
疏賓徙倚於門側．
時因接見，
矜
厲容色，
心懷內荏，
外詐剛直，
譚道義謂之俗生，
論政刑以為鄙極．
高會曲宴，
惟言遷
除消息，
官無大小，
問是誰力．
今以子孤寒，
懷真抱素，
志陵雲霄，
偶景獨步，
直順常
道，
關津難渡，
欲騁韓盧，
時無狡兔，
衆塗圮塞，
投足何錯！ ”
於是 Bīngzǐ 釋然乃悟曰：
“富貴人之所欲，
貧賤人之所惡．
僕少長於孔顏之門，
久處
於清寒之路，
不謂熱勢自共遮錮．
敬承明誨，
服我初素，
彈琴詠典，
以保年祚．
Bóchéng、
Yánlíng，
高節可慕．
Dāngǔ 滅族，
Lǚhuò 哀吟，
朝榮夕滅，
旦飛暮沈．
Dānzhōu 道師，
Cháoyóu 德林，
豐
屋蔀家，
易著明箴．
人薄位尊，
積罰難任，
三 Xì 尸晉，
宋 Huá 咎深，
投扃正幅，
實獲我心． ”
是時王政陵遲，
官才失實，
君子多退而窮處，
遂終于里閭．
Yuánkāng 初，
Sōngzī 令吳郡 Cài Hóng 字 Shūkāi，
有才名，
作《孤奮論》，
與釋時意同，
讀之者莫不歎息焉．
Zhāng Hàn
Zhāng Hàn 字 Jìyīng，
吳郡吳人也．
父 Yǎn，
吳大鴻臚．
Hàn 有清才，
善屬文，
而縱任不拘，
時人號為
“江東步兵” ．
Kuàijī Hè Xún 赴命入洛，
經吳 Chāngmén，
於船中彈琴．
Hàn 初不相識，
乃就 Xún 言譚，
便大相欽悅．
問 Xún，
知其入洛，
Hàn 曰：
“吾亦有事北京． ”
便同載即去，
而不告家人．
Qí Wáng Jiǒng 辟為大司馬東曹掾．
Jiǒng 時執權，
Hàn 謂同郡 Gù Róng 曰：
“天下紛紛，
禍難未已．
夫有四海之名者，
求退良難．
吾本山林間人，
無望於時．
子善以明防前，
以智慮後． ”
Róng 執其手，
愴然曰：
“吾亦與子採南山蕨，
飲三江水耳． ”
Hàn 因見秋風起，
乃思吳中菰菜、蓴羹、鱸魚膾，
曰：
“人生貴得適志，
何能羈宦數千里以要名爵乎！ ”
遂命駕而歸．
著《首丘賦》，
文多不載．
俄而 Jiǒng 敗，
人皆謂之見機．
然府以其輒去，
除吏名．
Hàn 任心自適，
不求當世．
或謂之曰：
“卿乃可縱適一時，
獨不為身後名邪？ ”
答曰：
“使我有身後名，
不如即時一杯酒． ”
時人貴其曠達．
性至孝，
遭母憂，
哀毀過禮．
年五十七卒．
其文筆數十篇行於世．
Yǔ Chǎn
Yǔ Chǎn 字 Zhòngchū，
Yǐngchuān Yānlíng 人也．
祖 Huī，
Ānběi 長史．
父 Dōng，
以勇力聞．
武帝時，
有西域健胡趫捷無敵，
晉人莫敢與校．
帝募勇士，
惟 Dōng 應選，
遂撲殺之，
名震殊俗．
Chǎn 好學，
九歲能屬文．
少隨舅 Sūn shì 過江．
母隨兄 Zhào 為 Lè'ān 長史，
在 Xiàngchéng．
Yǒngjiā 末，
為 Shí Lè 所陷，
Chǎn 母亦沒．
Chǎn 不櫛沐，
不婚宦，
絕酒肉，
垂二十年，
鄉親稱之．
州舉秀才，
Yuándì 為 Jìn Wáng，
辟之，
皆不行．
後為太宰、西陽王 Ráng 掾，
累遷尚書郎．
Sū Jùn 之難，
Chǎn 出奔 Xī Jiàn，
為司空參軍．
Jùn 平，
以功賜爵 Jíyáng Xiànnán，
拜 Péngchéng Nèishǐ．
Jiàn 復請為從事中郎．
尋召為散騎侍郎，
領大著作．
頃之，
出補 Línglíng Tàishǒu，
入 Xiāngchuān，
弔 Jiǎ Yì．
其辭曰： “中興二十三載，
余忝守衡南，
鼓觵三江，
路次 Bālíng，
望 Jūnshān 而過 Dòngtíng，
涉 Xiāngchuān 而觀
Mìshuǐ，
臨 Jiǎshēng 投書之川，
慨以永懷矣．
及造 Chángshā，
觀其遺象，
喟然有感，
乃弔之云．
偉哉蘭生而芳，
玉產而潔，
陽葩熙冰，
寒松負雪，
莫邪挺鍔，
天驥汗血，
苟云其雋，
Who can compare with Jié!
Thus, with lofty brilliance and grand splendor,
he alone manifested exceptional grace.
His Dao followed true nature,
not debating the world's ills.
Resplendent, like Wàngshū illuminating the landscape and outshining the myriad stars;
soaring, like a phoenix beating its wings and escaping the cosmos.
His glory flew to Luòruì,
his talent emerged in Shāndōng.
His character was as pure as a floating qìng,
his voice like an isolated tóng tree.
Resounding like unpolished jade,
towering like a mountain peak.
He believed in the Dao and maintained righteousness,
holding that all under Heaven was public.
He drove his chariot and strode forth,
not seeking passage through winding paths.
Thus, Zhāng Gāoxián's strings played sadly,
his voice
shook the bridge and made the zither pegs fall.
The pure songs were not harmonized,
but Sāngpú tunes arose in their place.
Though there were beautiful sounds,
none surpassed Sháohù.
Though there were soaring scales,
they ultimately fell into one gully.
Alas!
The Great Court
is already distant,
the profound wind far-off and remote.
The imperial Dao is not exalted by wisdom,
supreme virtue is not manifested by benevolence.
The esteemed reputation of the Sānwǔ
— their paths can be looked up to and marked;
the achievements of the hegemons, though outstanding,
— their ways can be assisted and elucidated.
How sorrowful for this gentleman,
how unfortunate his destiny!
He held a treasure like jade,
yet his life's fortune was shallow!
In the past, Gāoyáo assisted Yú,
Lǚshàng returned to Chāng;
their virtues accorded with the auspicious signs,
and thus they responded to emperors and kings.
Yíwú assisted Huán,
Xiāo and Zhāng were raised to power by Hàn;
the thatched cottage was visited thrice,
its fragrance
like that of orchids.
Thus, when the Dao is hidden, one retracts like a silkworm;
when the time is ripe, a phoenix is seen.
If one perches without choosing the tree,
and flies not in the jiǔwǔ position,
though one speaks of jade breaking,
what good is
outstanding talent?
For if the mind is not dead ash,
wisdom must preserve its form.
When form relies on the spirit-king,
it can preserve its life.
How is it that the orchid ointment,
which diffused its fragrance in the Hàn court,
was shattered by the fierce
wind,
and alone lost its brilliance?
Vast and ancient Primal Simplicity,
existence and extinction are but a single thought.
When the Dao comes, it penetrates;
when the world passes, it crumbles.
I mourn his life,
not having witnessed his death.
How dare I not
respectfully offer condolences,
and entrust them to the clear water.
Later, due to illness,
he was summoned and appointed Gěishìzhōng,
and again led the editing of texts.
Yú Tán, the Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery, erected a stele for Tàibó,
and 闡製 composed its inscription.
He also wrote the Yángdū Fù,
which was highly valued by the world.
He died at the age of fifty-four,
and was given the posthumous name Zhēn.
His collected poems, rhymed prose, inscriptions, and eulogies in ten volumes circulated in the world.
His son Sùzhī
was also renowned for his literary talent,
serving successively as Gěishìzhōng, Records Officer in the Prime Minister's residence, and Grand Administrator of Xiāngdōng.
He died during the Tàiyuán period.
Cáo Pí
Cáo Pí, courtesy name Fǔzuǒ,
was a native of Qiáoguó.
His great-grandfather Xiū was
Grand Minister of War of Wèi.
His father Shí was
General of the Right Army.
Pí was fond of literature from a young age
and excelled at composing rhymed prose.
The commandery recommended him as a Xiàolián,
and he was appointed Lángzhōng.
Cài Mó recommended him as Assistant Editor-in-chief.
He resigned his post due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Jùzhāng
and then summoned and appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
At that time, Zhāng Shuò of Guìyáng was possessed by the divine maiden Dù Lánxiāng.
Pí consequently composed two poems to mock him,
and also continued the Lánxiāng Gēshī with ten poems,
which were very eloquent.
He also wrote the Yángdū Fù,
which was second only to Yǔ Chǎn's.
He was successively promoted to Shàngshū Láng, Aide-de-camp to the General Who Guards the Army, and Grand Administrator of Xiàpī.
Because his position and reputation did not match his ambitions,
he wrote the Duì Rú to express his self-vindication.
Its text says: Someone asked Master Cáo:
"Indeed, a treasure is valued for containing gems,
a scholar is esteemed for concealing his abilities,
the qílín is distinguished by its unique tracks,
and the pine is praised for bearing frost.
Thus,
orchids grow in secluded valleys,
and jade shines from a thousand-rèn height.
Hence, Master Zǐzhōu floated on the azure waves and coiled like a dragon,
Jì Wú suddenly abandoned the myriad chariots and shed his seal,
Duke Yú hid in lofty peaks to nourish
his spirit,
and Master Liáng went to Nányuè to preserve his integrity.
Indeed, they were able to preserve their true nature, nourish harmony,
smooth their tracks, and live in seclusion,
spreading their fragrance through winter,
and standing firm alone amidst the snow.
"Now, you admired the profound wind in your youth,
and stood out with graceful appearance in your weakness.
Your extraordinary talents emerged in childhood,
your literary brilliance unfolded as a mere boy.
When you uttered words, your eloquence rivaled Yáng Xiōng and Bān Gù;
when you set your heart, your aspirations matched
lofty wild geese.
When you tasted the Dao, your reasoning pierced through Zhuāngzǐ and Sīmǎ Xiāngrú;
when you delved into the subtle, your sharpness surpassed the most skilled writers.
Indeed, you already soared across the vast expanse, lush and vibrant,
and pushed through the white silk, verdant and fresh.
Why
must you take penal laws and rites as your personal responsibility,
and Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi as your grand masters?
You ascended to the Eastern Conservatory,
and handled the historian's brush;
then you held office in the Imperial Academy,
and managed the Confucian tasks.
Yet you never cultivated profound tranquility and detachment,
nor a transcendent spirit in empty vastness,
nor nourished your essence in deep obscurity,
nor concealed your brightness in twilight mist.
You did not pursue the path of dwelling in forests,
nor aspired to the dragon that hides its scales,
nor engaged in arts of refining truth,
nor yearned for the inner
hearing.
Instead, you occupied ordinary positions to assess things,
and spread dusty doctrines to obscure yourself,
carrying salt carts to display your ability,
and adorning yourself to seek deference.
In retirement, you did not reside in the Lìyuán's
grounds;
when you emerged, you did not tread the perilous passes of Céngchéng;
in leisure, you did not frequent the elegant chambers;
