when you sprinted, you did not aspire to the tracks of Lù'ěr.
You merely, with a petty mind, organized the canons of
names and titles,
and with the capacity of an overturned basket, sought to block the great floods of the northern rivers,
examining names and realities in a fleeting moment,
and determining gain and loss at the tip of a single brush.
"If you say that I am indeed right,
then you need not conform to the common ways.
If you say that the common ways are indeed wrong,
then the common ways should not be followed indiscriminately.
The common ways and I dispute in contention,
benefits and harms are muddled and grow heavier.
How is this different from holding rotten reins to drive a runaway steed,
or grasping autumn mugwort in a strong wind,
or forcing a tranquil nature to fill a toilsome
office,
or facing all things as a pair of resentful adversaries?
Have you not heard of Zhōng Jūn's brilliance,
and Jiǎ Shēng's talent,
who stood out in Shāndōng,
their jade-like splendor shining on the Hàn terrace,
whose fame
resounded throughout the six directions,
and whose voices startled infants,
yet were slandered by the mouths of Jiàng and Guàn,
and suffered dire calamities?
From this, it can be said that
fame is the guest of reality,
and blessings foster disaster.
fetal,
blooming with splendor in the morning,
returning to dust in the evening,
is not as good as having a clear and empty mind in Xuánpǔ,
shading the jade trees in Pénglái,
forsaking worldly affairs and excelling the Huáng and Qǐ,
stirring the vast rivers
and churning the dragon's gills.
I am secretly perplexed by this.”
The host brightened his ears and laughed,
and spoke with joy:
“When the two elemental forces were first opened,
Yīn and Yáng expanded boundlessly,
the five elements were used in succession,
and transformations brought forth a multitude of beings.
The myriad creatures
are countless;
who can fathom their origin?
Therefore, if one does not ascend Làngfēng,
how can one behold the forms of extraordinary sights?
If one does not tread the luminous stars,
how can one observe the grandeur of the cosmos?
Thus,
those who are deluded by the crude follow a singular wisdom,
and those who are stubborn adhere to a rigid principle.
How can they know that a forest of fire nourishes the blazing branches,
and a glacial spring nurtures the vital grasses?
Therefore, the great person
has a broad perspective,
allowing transformations to govern day and night,
not exerting oneself to the extreme when active,
and not dwelling in isolation when withdrawn.
Among Ruists, they are Ruists;
among Daoists, they are Daoists.
When the times are constrained, they conceal their pure radiance;
when the times are favorable,
they display their magnificent talents.
This is the circular motion of engagement and withdrawal,
not something cherished by ordinary people.
“Now, the three luminaries illuminate each other,
the two energies are widely proclaimed,
the profound teachings condense in the evening,
and the bright winds are fresh in the morning.
The Way flourishes with talent,
and transformation is perfected according to principle.
Thus, the Five Canons are clearly understood
by all officials,
and the music of Yú resonates harmoniously with the five strings.
Ānqī sheds his coarse clothing in the beautiful forest,
and the fisherman casts his hook into the long river.
In this way, there is no transformation that does not merge,
no Way that
does not extend.
The wind purifies the customs,
and the waves clarify the river.
Soon, golden dragons will dance in auspicious clouds,
and auspicious phoenixes will be summoned to numinous mountains.
Jade wine will flow into grand palaces,
and
crimson grasses will bloom before the courtyard.
How can there be worries of violating principle,
or suspicions of harming one’s true nature?
You only know how to debate its theory but have not fathomed its source.
The morning mushroom cannot be compared to the dark
new moon,
and the cicada cannot comprehend a great year.
Indeed, these are not things that can be described by a pen,
but I respectfully respond to conclude this chapter.”
He was successively promoted to Guānglùxūn,
and then died.
All his written works amounted to fifteen scrolls,
which were transmitted to the world.
Lǐ Chōng
Lǐ Chōng, courtesy name Hóngdù,
was from Jiāngxià.
His father, Jǔ,
was the Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Chōng was orphaned young.
The cypress trees in his father’s tomb were once cut down by thieves.
Chōng personally killed them,
and thereby became famous.
He was skilled in standard script,
masterfully emulating Zhōng and Suǒ,
and was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
He was appointed an aide to Chancellor Wáng Dǎo,
then transferred to Recorder and Staff Officer.
In his youth, he enjoyed the study of names and forms (legalism)
and deeply suppressed those who were superficial and ostentatious.
He once wrote a “Scholar’s Admonition,”
stating: Lǎozi said:
“Abandon benevolence and forsake righteousness,
and the people will return to filial piety and compassion.”
Is it that the way of benevolence and righteousness must be forsaken
before filial piety and compassion can arise?
Perhaps it is due to the problem that those who genuinely possess benevolence and righteousness
are few, while those who profit from benevolence and righteousness are many.
When morality is lost, benevolence and righteousness become prominent;
when benevolence and righteousness become prominent, fame and profit arise.
The abuses of ritual teachings
lie precisely in this.
The former
kings, seeing that the Way of morality was not practiced,
therefore transformed people with benevolence and righteousness.
When the practice of benevolence and righteousness was not earnest,
they then regulated it with rituals and laws.
The more frequent the regulation,
the more widespread
the hypocrisy became.
Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi thus elucidated the benefits of non-action,
blocking the gate of competitive desires.
Now, he who attains the utmost subtlety of spiritual wisdom and embodies the harmony of universal understanding,
none surpasses the sage.
To reform the grand system of an era
and bequeath a legacy for a thousand years
is impossible without a sage.
Thus, when the sage is in the world,
their words become instructions,
and their actions
become models for all things.
When the times are prosperous, they thrive with the age;
when principles are lost, they decline with the world.
Therefore, profound arguments are made to delineate their essence.
Things must have a root,
and affairs must
have a master.
Responsibility is entrusted to the sage, while the burden is left to old traces.
Therefore, they are transformed by abandoning sageliness and casting off wisdom,
and kept stable by the uncarved block of namelessness.
The teachings of the sages rescue the
end,
while Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi clarify the root.
The paths of the root and the end are different, but their teaching is one.
Human delusion,
it has been long-standing!
Many see the forms,
but few reach
the Way.
They do not perceive the gate of a thousand ren but pursue the traces of superficial things.
The more diligently they pursue traces,
the further they depart from the root,
thus causing elaborate artifices and vulgar customs to flourish together,
while profound principles and
pure customs are simultaneously extinguished.
This is why the sage remains hidden for a long time, yet their traces never perish.
Fearing that later generations might be confused by this,
and thus abandon rituals and neglect learning to aspire to the spirit of non-action,
seeing the decline of righteous teachings
but not observing their flourishing,
I briefly state what I hold in mind
to supplement its deficiencies.
By citing the profound principles of Daoism
and integrating them with the appropriate teachings of the world,
so that meaning does not deviate from the root,
and words are not unbridled,
perhaps this can remove the veil of ignorance
and awaken those deluded by singular views!
His verses say: Vast, vast, the Great Beginning,
distant, distant, the primal wilderness.
Ignorant, ignorant, the myriad creatures,
forgetting the Way along with all else.
The sage's traces not yet manifest,
the worthies' names not yet illustrious.
Contentedly, they rub their bellies,
letting me
run wild.
When life's provisions became abundant,
the multitude of paths sought connection.
Obscurity indeed took clarity as its teacher,
not seeking my ignorance,
sacrificing oneself to benefit others, and the world became public.
Dàtíng initiated the foundation,
Xī
and Nóng greatly assisted.
The six positions were established in due course,
the radiant splendor was grandly observed.
Favor spread like soaking rain,
transformation flowed like scattering wind.
Houses shared the same dust, and no one dared to transgress or cause disorder.
Then came the Middle Ages,
when wise kings succeeded each other.
Simplicity and refinement appeared in alternation,
and ritual systems rose one after another.
Affairs became complex due to utilization,
and transformation solidified due to obstruction.
Motion was not inherently agitated,
nor stillness inherently serene!
Where fame
was made manifest,
there the Way declined.
Then what was exalted was diminished,
and what was superseded was revered.
Punishment arose from the decay of virtue,
and the three punishments appeared in later generations.
Both encouraged and guided,
they were then rectified
Then [it] became harsh.
厚 (hòu) had already been fully prepared,
矯 (jiǎo) had already become deeply entrenched.
Carving and polishing produced patterns;
modulations created sounds.
All skills were unleashed;
all ingenious minds exhausted themselves.
There were no land-horses in the wilds;
mountains
had no scattered forests.
No wind failed to stir;
no transformation failed to shift.
People lost their virtue,
turning right into strange.
Then indulgence in desire transgressed propriety,
unaware that seeking competition was
a malady.
They abandoned that easy path and followed this dangerous trail.
Cunning rabbits scaled the ridges;
swimming fish hid in the rivers.
Reaching the most profound and subtle,
the great images obscure and mysterious.
They discarded bait and collected traps, yet demanded
credit for hoof-marks and fish-traps.
First lost the way home, then entrusted their meaning to forgetting words.
Policies diverged from principle;
they uprooted the foundation and blocked the source.
Hiding their traces for a long day;
chasing echoes for a full year.
They deliberately departed from nature
and lost their natural state.
The world has its dangers and ease;
destiny has its prosperity and decline.
To diminish or augment is timely;
to rise or fall is merely rational.
The Way cannot be abandoned for a single day,
nor can it be
imitated for a single morning.
Rites cannot be established for a thousand years,
nor can they be stopped in that very year.
Without benevolence, one cannot nurture things;
without righteousness, one cannot eliminate shame.
Benevolence and righteousness are indeed not
to be distant;
just remove what harms benevolence and righteousness.
Even diligently practicing, one fears not reaching [it];
aspiring to it is vastly distant!
If a room has good words,
the response reaches a thousand *lǐ*.
How much more so
if one's actions and conduct return to propriety and overcome oneself!
The poet supervises admonitions,
respectfully presenting them to noble personages (jūnzǐ).
General Zhengbei Chǔ Póu (褚裒) again invited him to be an assistant (cānjūn).
Chōng (充) pleaded poverty,
earnestly requesting an external appointment.
Póu (裒) was about to appoint him as a county magistrate,
and asked him,
Chōng (充) said:
"A poor ape seeking a forest,
how can it have time to choose a tree!"
Thereupon, he was appointed Magistrate of Shàn County (剡縣).
He suffered the sorrow of his mother's death.
After the mourning period,
he was made Grand Administrator of Writings (Dà Zhùzuò Láng).
At that time, the imperial archives were in disarray.
Chōng (充) deleted the cumbersome and redundant,
grouped them by category,
divided them into four sections,
which had excellent order.
The Imperial Library (Mì Gé) adopted it as a permanent system.
He was successively promoted to Zhongshu Shìláng (中書侍郎),
and died in office.

Chōng (充) annotated the *Shàngshū* (尚書) and wrote six chapters on the principles of the *Zhōu Yì* (周易), two chapters, upper and lower, on expounding *Zhuāngzi* (莊子), and two hundred forty miscellaneous pieces of poetry, *fù*, memorials, and eulogies (shīfù biǎosòng),
which circulated in the world.
His son Yǒng (顒)
also had literary talent and righteousness,
wrote many works,
and was nominated as Xiaolián (孝廉) by the commandery.
Chōng's (充) cousin Shì (式) was known for his balanced and gentle character,
and was skilled in regular and clerical scripts (kǎilì).
In the early years of the Central Revival (Zhōngxīng),
he rose to the position of Shìzhōng (侍中).
Yuán Hóng (袁宏)
Yuán Hóng (袁宏), courtesy name Yànbó (彥伯),
was the grandson of Shìzhōng Yóu (猷).
His father Xù (勖) was the Magistrate of Línrǔ (臨汝).
Hóng (宏) had exceptional talent,
and his writings were exquisitely beautiful.
He once wrote "Yǒngshǐ Shī" (詠史詩, Poems on History),
which conveyed his sentiments.
Young and an orphan, he was poor.
He made a living by transporting grain.
Xiè Shàng (謝尚) was then stationed at Niúzhǔ (牛渚).
On an autumn night, riding the moonlight,
he spontaneously went out with his attendants in disguise to boat on the river.
It happened that Hóng (宏) was in a boat reciting and chanting;
his voice was clear and melodious,
and his words were elegant and distinguished.
So Xiè Shàng (謝尚) stopped and listened for a long time,
then sent someone to inquire.
The reply was:
"It is young Master Yuán Línrǔ (袁臨汝) reciting poetry."
It was indeed his "Poems on History" (Yǒngshǐ zhī Zuò).
Shàng (尚) was greatly moved and deeply charmed.
He immediately welcomed Hóng (宏) onto his boat,
and discussed with him
until dawn without sleeping.
From then on, Hóng's (宏) reputation grew daily.
Shàng (尚) was appointed General Anxi (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Yù Prefecture (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ),
and he invited Hóng (宏) to serve in his military staff.
Hóng (宏) was successively promoted to Recorder (Jìshì) in the office of Grand Marshal Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Wēn (溫) highly valued his writing skills,
and exclusively entrusted him with secretarial duties.
Later, Hóng (宏) composed the "Dōngzhēng Fù" (東征賦, Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition).
At the end of the *fù*, he listed many famous virtuous individuals who had crossed the Yangtze River (Guòjiāng),
but omitted Huán Yí (桓彝).
At that time, Fú Tāo (伏滔) was already in Wēn's (溫) office,
and also had a good relationship with Hóng (宏),
so he strenuously advised against it.
Hóng (宏) smiled and did not reply.
Wēn (溫) knew of this and was greatly indignant,
but he feared Hóng (宏) was the literary master of the time,
and did not want anyone to openly question him.
Later, when they returned from drinking at Mount Qīngshān (青山),
Wēn (溫) ordered Hóng (宏) to ride in the same carriage.
Everyone was afraid for Hóng (宏).
After traveling several *lǐ*,
Wēn (溫) asked Hóng (宏):
"I heard you composed the 'Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition' (Dōngzhēng Fù),
praising many former worthies.
Why did you not mention my late father?"
Hóng (宏) replied:
"Your esteemed father's title is not something this humble official dares to assume for himself.
As I had no time to consult you,
I dared not reveal it."
Wēn (溫) suspected this was not true,
so he said:
"What words would you wish to use?"
Hóng (宏) immediately replied:
"His discerning gaze was broad and clear,
sometimes exploring, sometimes guiding.
Though the body may perish,
the Way cannot be lost.
The integrity of Xuānchéng (宣城)
was indeed in his faithfulness and trustworthiness."
Wēn (溫) wept and stopped the discussion.
Hóng's (宏) *fù* also omitted Táo Kǎn (陶侃).
Kǎn's (侃) son Húnú (胡奴) once drew a blade in a private room and asked Hóng (宏):
"My late father's achievements are so great,
how could your *fù* neglect him?"
Hóng (宏) was in a desperate situation,
and replied:
"I have already greatly praised your esteemed father,
how can you say there is nothing?"
Then he said:
"Refined gold, hammered a hundred times,
when cut, it can sever.
His achievements helped his era;
his duty was to calm chaos.
The merits of Chángshā (長沙)
are lauded by historians."
Húnú (胡奴) then stopped.
Later, he composed "Sānguó Míngchén Sòng" (三國名臣頌, Eulogy for Famous Officials of the Three Kingdoms), which states: People cannot govern themselves,
therefore rulers are established to govern them.
Enlightened rulers cannot govern alone,
so officials are made to assist them.
Thus, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors (Sānwǔ) successively
flourished;
successive dynasties inherited the foundation.
Whether abdication or warfare,
civilian virtue or military achievement,
none failed to serve as masters and molds, and all talents were perfected.
The sovereign planned and managed, and
the trusted ministers exerted their strength.
Although they encountered different circumstances,
and their achievements had superior and inferior points,
as for their fundamental nature being firm and steadfast,
and their adherence to the Way not falling into disuse,
the beautiful customs they inspired,
and the reforms they taught lasting for a thousand years,
their guiding principle was one.
Thus, the two and eight (i.e., the capable ministers) rose, and the Táng (唐) dynasty flourished.
Yī (伊) and Lǚ (呂) were employed, and Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武) achieved peace.
The three worthies advanced, and Xiǎobái (小白) rose to power.
The five ministers became prominent, and Chóng'ěr (重耳) became hegemon.
In the Middle Ages, decline set in,
and this Way was abandoned.
Those above did not govern things with utmost impartiality;
those below inevitably sought glory through private channels.
Those in command did not lead the masses with sincerity and trustworthiness;
those in authority
inevitably sought self-promotion through schemes and stratagems.
Consequently, the relationship between ruler and minister became estranged, and moral teachings (míngjiào) became thin.
The world became chaotic, and the times were not well governed.
Therefore, Qú Níng (蘧甯) consequently withdrew.
Shū,
Liǔxià was thrice dismissed because of it;
Jiēyú sang songs because of it;
Lǔlián went to the sea because of it.
In times of decline,
to maintain one’s integrity,
with sovereign and minister perfectly attuned,
like
halves of a tally fitting together,
is to be like Yān Zhāo and Yuè Yì of old.
If one does not meet Bólè,
then there will not be a single thoroughbred in a thousand years;
when the time meets with the Dragon Face (an enlightened ruler),
then in that very year, one can control three
heroes.
The excellence of the Hàn dynasty in obtaining worthy men
is to be cherished in this regard.
Although Gāozǔ did not govern things by the Way,
his subordinates were able to fully express their loyalty;
although Xiāo and Cáo did not serve
their lord as in the Three Dynasties,
the common people did not lose their livelihoods.
Bringing order to chaos and protecting the people,
this is also secondary.
When the times are in turmoil,
then prominence is not as good as reclusion;
when all things yearn for order,
then silence
is not as good as speaking.
Therefore, the junzǐ of old did not worry about the difficulty of promoting the Way,
but worried about the difficulty of encountering the right time;
to encounter the right time is not difficult,
but to meet the right ruler is.
Thus, having the Way but not the time
is why Mèngzǐ
sighed;
having the time but not the ruler
is why Jiǎshēng wept.
A lifespan of ten thousand years is but a single cycle,
the common path of all living things;
a meeting once in a thousand years
is a grand
opportunity for the wise and sagacious.
How can one not rejoice upon meeting it,
and how can one not lament upon losing it?
The words of the ancients
are indeed full of emotion!
In my leisure, I often peruse the Guó Zhì,
examining its
rulers and ministers,
and comparing their actions.
Although their Way falls short of earlier generations,
they too represent their own era in a different age.
Wénruò possessed a unique insight
and had a heart to save the world.
When discussing the times, people were in great suffering;
when assessing abilities, none surpassed Wèiwǔ.
Therefore, he committed his plans to the hegemonic
court,
and preemptively planned world affairs.
He recommended talent not by outward appearance,
thus people became prominent only after his death;
he strategized not for personal gain,
thus matters were settled only after they arose.
Although he died
in accordance with the clear principles,
his insight was also profound.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
the divine instruments (imperial authority) were seized and threatened.
Gōngdá, filled with emotion,
was determined to dedicate his life.
From this perspective,
he thus greatly preserved his integrity.
As for him being a
Hàn official yet his traces entering the Wèi camp,
the origin and development of his choices,
this also applies to Wénruò.
The reasons for differing outcomes of survival and demise,
and different beginnings and ends,
might it be because Wénruò was both enlightened
and wise,
and the principles of moral teaching were entrusted to him?
Benevolence and righteousness must be made clear,
so the eminent of the time upheld their essence;
life must be preserved completely,
so the enlightened took hold of its principles.
To jointly promote the Way,
is this not far-reaching?
Cuīshēng was noble and upright,
bending but not breaking.
The reason he was registered with Wèiwǔ and held the tablet at the hegemonic court
was likely because the Hàn emperor was still on the throne,
and the Wèi empress was facing north.
Indeed!
If, however, the imperial seal were one day presented,
and sovereign and minister exchanged positions,
then Cuīshēng would not have participated,
and the Wèi clan would not have tolerated him.
The rivers and lakes that enable boats to cross,
are
also what overturns boats;
benevolence and righteousness that allow one to preserve oneself,
are also what can cause one to lose oneself.
Yet, the former sages were crushed like jade in the front,
and later wise men rolled up their sleeves at the back.
Could it be that their innate disposition
arose from within,
and the moral teachings bound them?
Kǒngmíng lingered,
waiting for the right time to act.
He yearned for Guǎn and Yuè,
and far-reachingly illuminated their style.
He governed the state with ritual,
and the people had no complaints;
punishments were not excessive,
there was not
leftover weeping.
Even the ancient benevolent rulers,
how could they surpass this!
When he was near death, he entrusted his affairs,
received the charge and became prime minister.
Liúhòu entrusted him without suspicion,
Wǔhóu received it
without fear,
the successor accepted it without hesitation,
the common people believed him without dissent.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is truly praiseworthy!
Gōngjǐn was outstanding,
with lofty aspirations that transcended the common.
As a youth, he assessed his lord,
in his later years, he displayed extraordinary brilliance,
and divided the realm into three at Chìbì.
It is a pity
his life was short,
his ambition immeasurable.
Zǐbù assisted Cè,
achieving the beauty of extending his fame,
stopping tears and calming sorrow,
performing the service of supporting and protecting.
His spiritual engagement
was not merely outspokenness!
However,
he kept his door shut and was not employed,
and was ridiculed when he ascended the altar.
The insight of one person may not differ,
but the difference in being employed or rejected can be sudden,
let alone those who remain hidden in valleys,
and those who meet
or do not meet opportunities!
The composition of odes and eulogies
has a long history.
Some are for expressing emotions and nature,
others for recording virtues and displaying merits.
Although the main objectives converge,
the subjects to which they are entrusted may differ.
However, if one's actions are aligned with the Way,
and one's reputation and integrity are not tarnished,
one's conduct and virtuous voice
serve as models for the world,
and cannot be abandoned.
Again, I append this preface expressing my thoughts,
to serve as its eulogy: The Fire Virtue (Hàn dynasty) has waned,
fate is entangled in great adversity.
A great gale fans the sea,
the two oceans raise waves.
Though dragons and beasts are startled,
Hidden fish choose
their streams,
high-flying birds wait for branches.
Resplendent are the three heroes,
together they turn the axis of heaven.
Competing to gather qǐzǐ (talented people),
contending to pluck pine and bamboo.
The phoenix has no place to perch,
the dragon has no time to hide.
The valley
is without secluded orchids,
the ridge is without lingering chrysanthemums.
Brilliant Wénruò,
whose spiritual insight penetrates all.
Responding to change and knowing the subtle,
calmly appreciating the essential.
The sun and moon are in his person,
the more he conceals them, the more they shine.
Enlightenment illuminates his heart,
the more he delves
into it, the more wondrous it becomes.
When the vast sea overflows,
jade and stone are crushed together.
The enlightened person benefits both himself and others,
abandoning self to preserve love.
Planning to resolve the chaos of the times,
his accomplishments saved the world.

The upright Zǐjìng [Yuán Zhǒng],
rose from obscurity.
Bearing responsibility and offering brilliant insights,
he then constructed the Cloud Terrace.
Zǐyú [Yú Hóng], the governor,
had a pure and virtuous nature.
He admonished without offending,
and was upright but not harsh.
He carried out his duties in the public court,
and upon retirement, forgot his private position.
How could he not be like the wagtail,
but
cautious with reputation and position?
Bóyán [Lù Xùn] spoke forthrightly,
assisting the world with the Dao.
When he went out, he could diligently serve,
and when he came in, he also offered criticisms.
He planned for the peace of the state,
resolved disputes, and blunted sharp edges.
His rectitude invited suspicion,
and his loyalty
earned him blame.
Yuántàn [Rǔ Xuán] was profound and far-reaching,
with a harmonious spirit and restrained form.
Like that white jade,
his substance was without a speck of dust.
He established his conduct with [propriety],
and corrected his lord gradually.
Purity did not make him cleaner,
and turbidity
did not add stain.
Zhòngxiáng [Wèi Qí] was noble and bright,
his nature did not blend with others.
He delighted in standing apart,
and would bend but not break.
He repeatedly challenged the dragon's scales,
and was dismissed for his uprightness.
He sighed more than Sūn Yáng,
and was exiled
like Jiǎ Yí and Qū Yuán.
These numerous wise individuals,
are met only once in a thousand years.
They reined in their horses on the high road,
and raised their heads towards the heavenly path.
They looked up and saluted the profound flow,

Their reputations and integrity followed different paths,
but their elegant
aspirations shared the same goal.
The sun and moon adorn the sky,

Benevolence and righteousness are embodied,

Later generations clap their
hands,

His "Northern Expedition Ode," written when he accompanied Huán Wēn on his northern campaign,
and the "Northern Expedition Ode" itself,
are among the loftiest of his writings.
Once, he, Wáng Xún, and Fú Tāo were all sitting with Huán Wēn.
Huán Wēn ordered Fú Tāo to read his "Northern Expedition Ode."
When he reached
"I heard what was passed down through generations,
that a qílín was found in this wilderness.
A divine creature born to signify virtue,
why was its form bestowed upon Yú's descendants?
The deep sorrow of Confucius [for the qílín's demise],
seemed to be genuine grief, not feigned.
How could one nature be enough to wound,
but rather cause injury to all under heaven?"
The original text changed rhyme here.
Wáng Xún said:
"This ode will be transmitted for a thousand years;
it must not be composed carelessly.
Now, after 'all under heaven,'
the rhyme is changed and the topic shifted,
but the expression of the sentiment
seems incomplete."
Fú Tāo said:
"If we could add one line to the rhyme,
it might be a small improvement."
Huán Wēn said:
"You two think about adding to it."
Yuán Hóng immediately replied:
"Feelings are inexhaustible in my heart,
I complain to the prevailing winds and express myself alone."
Wáng Xún savored it for a long time,
and said to Fú Tāo:
"Regarding the excellence of literature today,
we should certainly collectively acclaim this man."
He was strong, upright, and honest by nature.
Although Huán Wēn treated him with courtesy,
when it came to debate,
he never yielded obsequiously,
thus his promotion to high office did not materialize.
He and Fú Tāo were both in Huán Wēn's mansion,
and the household called them
"Yuán-Fú."
Yuán Hóng felt ashamed of this in his heart,
and often sighed:
"The Duke's great kindness is not sufficient for a national scholar,
to be placed shoulder-to-shoulder with Fú Tāo,
what an immense humiliation!"
Xiè Ān often admired his quick wit and debating speed.
Later, when Xiè Ān became the Governor of Yángzhōu,
Yuán Hóng, having left his post as Clerk of the Ministry of Personnel, became the Administrator of Dōngyáng Commandery.
He then performed the ancestral sacrifice at Yětíng.
All the worthies of the time gathered.
Xiè Ān wanted to test him with a sudden challenge,
so at their farewell, he held Yuán Hóng's hand,
and looking around, picked up a fan from those nearby
and handed it to him, saying:
"This is merely a gift for your journey."
Yuán Hóng immediately replied:
"I shall certainly endeavor to spread benevolent influence,
and comfort the common people."
People at the time admired his spontaneity and conciseness.
Yuán Hóng saw that Fù Yì of the Hàn dynasty had composed the "Encomium of Emperor Xiǎozōng,"
whose diction was very elegant and classical.
So he composed nine chapters of encomiums,
praising the virtues of Emperor Jiǎnwén,
and presented them to Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the early years of Tàiyuán,
he died in Dōngyáng,
at the age of forty-nine.

He compiled "History of the Later Hàn Dynasty" in thirty volumes, "Biographies of the Zhúlín Scholars" in three volumes, and three hundred miscellaneous pieces of poetry, odes, elegies, memorials, etc.,
which were transmitted to the world.
He had three sons: the eldest Chāozǐ,
the second Chéngzǐ,
and the youngest Míngzǐ.
Míngzǐ possessed his father's style,
and was the most famous,
reaching the official post of Administrator of Línhè.
Fú Tāo.
Fú Tāo, courtesy name Xuándù,
was a native of Ānqiū, Píngchāng.
He had talent and learning,
and was famous in his youth.
The province nominated him as Xiùcái,
and appointed him as Secretary,
but he did not accept either.
The Grand Marshal Huán Wēn invited him to be his Adjutant,
and treated him with deep respect.
At every banquet or gathering,
he would certainly invite Fú Tāo to join.
He followed Huán Wēn in the campaign against Yuán Zhēn,
and when they reached Shòuyáng,
because Huáinán had repeatedly rebelled,
he wrote two essays,
titled "Rectifying Huái."
The first essay stated: Huáinán
was a division of Yángzhōu in the Three Dynasties period.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
it was the territory of Wú, Chǔ, Chén, and Cài.
Chǔ
completely possessed it,
and King Kǎoliè established his capital there.
Qín unified all under heaven,
established commanderies and counties,
and this was Jiǔjiāng.
During the time of Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ,
it was called Dōngchǔ.
From
the Warring States period until the revival of Jìn,
over six hundred years,
nine clans held Huáinán,
and eleven individuals raised armies,
all of whom perished swiftly,
their misfortune
overflowing into the world,
yet none ever learned from it.
Was it due to heaven's timing,
the geographical advantage,
or human affairs?
Why was the disorder so great?
Let us try to analyze
and discuss it.
Indeed, celestial phenomena are clearly manifest,
and auspicious signs appear among the constellations;
mountains and rivers act as girdles,
and strategic terrain is evident in hills;
the rise and fall of order shift,
and prosperity and decline are seen
in human affairs.
From this perspective,
then a combination of factors must be certain.

a comet streaked across the Milky Way, and Liú Ān
Alas!
The Yì Jīng
states: "Treading on frost, solid ice arrives.
This is the way of gradual development."
This speaks of gradualism.
Alas!
Is this why treacherous ministers and rebel sons, who brought ruin to their states and destruction to their families, have continued
throughout generations without cease?
In antiquity, when the former kings governed the realm,
they selected those with virtue,
consulted the three officials,
rectified their ranks,
clarified their grades,
marked their borders,
and proclaimed their decrees.
Thus,
there was order between superiors and inferiors,
with no suspicion of transgression or disparity.
The common people were secure in their livelihoods,
and there were no states that merged and annexed others.
Every three years, officials were evaluated and promoted or demoted,
and their merits and faults could not escape scrutiny.
Punishments and rewards were
timely administered through the nine expeditions,
without any deviation from their true purpose.
Their commands were gradual,
their regulations measured,
their favors restrained,
authority was not delegated externally,
and prestige was not debased below.
This was how they prevented
the sprouting of evil,
valued official titles and insignia,
deepened their roots and strengthened their foundations,
passing them down for a hundred generations.
Though times might wax and wane,
the weak had nothing to fear for their destruction;
though the Way might flourish or decline,
the strong
could not exploit its weaknesses.
If this were so,
it would cause the Son of Heaven to lead by example,
to serenely follow the proper path,
with blessings originating from him alone,
and benevolence flowing to all nations.
How could there be the troubles
of the past?

for his achievements, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wénxǐ County
and appointed Magistrate of Yǒngshì.

He was promoted to Yóují Jiāngjūn,

He died in office.

Luó Hán.
Luó Hán, courtesy name Jūnzhāng,
was a native of Léiyáng, Guìyáng.
His great-grandfather, Yàn,
was the Grand Administrator of Línhǎi.
His father, Suī,
was the Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng.
Hán was orphaned young
and raised by his aunt, Lady Zhū.
In his youth, he had noble aspirations.
Once, while sleeping during the day,
he dreamt of a bird with extraordinary markings and colors,
which flew into his mouth.
He woke up in surprise and told his aunt.
Lady Zhū said:
"A bird with such markings and colors means
you will certainly have literary talent in the future."
From then on, his literary thoughts grew day by day.
When he reached manhood,
the province invited him three times,
but he did not accept.
Hán's father had once governed Xīngàn.
A man from Xīngàn, Yáng Xiàn, later became Hán's provincial general,
and invited Hán to be his principal clerk.
Hán was arrogant and paid no heed,
but Xiàn's persistent invitations
made it impossible for him to refuse, so he accepted.
When Xiàn left office,
Hán escorted him to the county border.
The people of Xīngàn, considering Hán to be the son of their former magistrate,
all offered him gifts.
Hán found it difficult to decline and accepted them.
Upon returning,
he sealed and set them aside before leaving.
Because of this, people near and far respected and admired him.
Later, he became the Commander of Merit for the commandery.
Governor Yǔ Liàng appointed him as an aide for Jiāngxià.
Grand Administrator Xiè Shàng formed a friendship with Hán that transcended ordinary bounds,
and thus praised him, saying:
"Luó Jūnzhāng can be called the 'linlang' of Xiāngzhōng."
Soon after, he was transferred to provincial principal clerk.
Later, Huán Wēn came to the province
and again appointed him as Zhēngxī Cānjūn.
Wēn once sent Hán to Shàng
to investigate and impeach something.
Hán arrived,
did not inquire about commandery affairs,
but drank heartily with Shàng for several days before returning.
Wēn asked about the impeachment matter.
Hán said:
"What do you think of Shàng as a person?"
Wēn replied:
"He is better than I am."
Hán said:
"How could someone better than you act improperly?
Therefore, I asked nothing at all."
Wēn admired his insight and did not blame him.
He was transferred to provincial 別駕 (Biéjià).
Finding the official residence noisy,
he built a thatched hut on a small island in a pond west of the city,
felled trees for timber, [一四]
wove reeds into mats, and resided there,
wearing simple clothes and eating vegetables,
content and peaceful.
Wēn once held a banquet with his subordinates.
Hán arrived late.
Wēn asked those present:
"What kind of person is this?"
Someone replied:
"He can be called a talent of Jīngchǔ."
Wēn said:
"This is truly an outstanding figure from Jiāngzuǒ,
not just Jīngchǔ."
He was summoned to be Shàngshū Láng.
Wēn deeply esteemed his talent
and further recommended him to be transferred to Zhēngxī Hùcáo Cānjūn.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Yídū.
When Wēn was enfeoffed as Duke of Nánjùn,
he appointed Hán as Lángzhōng Lìng.
He was soon summoned to be Zhèngyuán Láng,
and successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Shìzhōng,
then transferred to Tíngwèi and Chancellor of Chángshā.
In his old age, he retired from office,
was granted the title of Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
and carriages were allowed to pass through his gate.
Initially,
when Hán was in his official residence,
a white sparrow roosted in his hall.
When he retired and returned home,
chrysanthemums suddenly grew in clusters on his steps and courtyard,
which was believed to be a manifestation of his virtuous conduct.
He died at the age of seventy-seven,
and his writings circulated in the world.
Gù Kǎizhī.
Gù Kǎizhī, courtesy name Chángkāng,
was a native of Wúxī, Jìnlíng.
His father, Yuèzhī,
was Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Kǎizhī was broadly learned and possessed great talent.
Once, after completing a rhapsody on the zheng,
he said to people:
"My rhapsody, compared to Jī Kāng's rhapsody on the qín,
those who do not appreciate it will certainly dismiss it as a later work,
but those with profound insight will value it for its lofty uniqueness."
Huán Wēn invited him to be his Dà Sīmǎ Cānjūn
and held him in great affection and intimacy.
After Wēn passed away,
Kǎizhī visited Wēn's tomb
and composed a poem, saying:
"Mountains collapse, the dark seas dry up;
where will fish and birds find refuge?"
Someone asked him:
"You relied so heavily on Lord Huán, to what extent was your crying visible?"
He replied:
"My voice was like thunder shaking mountains,
my tears like a river pouring into the sea."
The imperial historian says:
while strength and gentleness are rooted in nature.
What emotion finds fitting
expresses itself in songs and verses.
Yet, the power of evocation is formless,
and poetic styles are diverse.
As for Yìng Zhēn’s banquet archery composition,
it fully expresses the beauty of language,
rarely matched by the numerous ornate pieces in the Huálín garden.
Zǐ’ān displayed brilliance and sensitivity from a young age,
and accumulated pure thoughts in his youth.
He embraced the vastness of heaven and earth,
and composed what other poets had overlooked.
He specially created new sentiments;
how could common mediocrity aspire to such heights!
Tài Chōng held his brush for years,
to compose “Sān Dū Fù”.
Shì’ān saw it and praised it as excellent,
while Píng Yuán saw it and put away his writing brush.
Not only did he stand tall in his own time,
but he also achieved lasting glory for all ages.
Zōu Zhàn’s critical discourse
and Zǎo Jù’s connection to emotion
were truly outstanding talents from Nányáng,
and indeed, exceptional figures from Yǐngchuān.
Jì Yǎ’s compositions were robust and vigorous,
and he had long possessed accomplished virtues.
To be called a treasure of Quán Dài
was indeed fitting.
Yàn Bó was unable to merge his traces with the dust and light
and was constrained to a humble position.
However, his profound discussions of the times
are sufficient to reveal his ambition.
Jì Yīng was unrestrained and unconventional in his time,
not seeking fame or rank.
His “Huáng Huā zhī Shí”
deeply revealed his divine talent.
Zhòng Chū’s writings
were admirable for their elegance.
He excelled among scholars,
and the beauty of Yáng Dū
was particularly valued by the literati of the time.
Cáo Pí deeply studied secret texts,
but was confined to a lower position.
His elaborate "Songs of Divine Descent"
and his clear, fluent "Discourses with Confucian Scholars" were notable.
Lǐ Chōng’s scholarly admonitions
were truly pure and vigorous.
Yuán Hóng’s "Dōng Zhēng Fù" and "Míng Chén Lùn"
were second only to those of Pān [Yuè] and Lù [Jī].
Xuán Dù was abundantly skilled in learning and arts,
and excelled remarkably in writing and editing.
He brought forth imperial inquiries in the western hall,
which was indeed his glorious spectacle.
Jūn Zhāng illuminated the treasures of Xiāngzhōng,
and brought forth the talents of Jīngchǔ.
His dream of a bird arose from his sincerity;
why should it be limited to the geomancer’s dragon or phoenix!
Cháng Kāng boasted of his abilities beyond reality,
and indulged in jests to curry favor.
Yet, his talent possessed an unrestrained spirit,
hence he earned the title of “Three Perfections.”
Zhòng Jìng’s thoughts were acute and perceptive,
earning him praise from the pure stream of society.
Dé Yú’s plan for the western campaign
was determined by his subtle indications.
A eulogy says:
Gōng and Zhǐ flow as melodies.
How beautiful are these many talents,
flourishing in the Forest of Brushes.
All in harmony, jingling like jade,
each excelling, clanging like gold.
Zǐ’ān and Tài Chōng,
their vigorous writings are splendid.
Yuán, Yǔ, Chōng, and Kǎi,
their ornate phrases shine like clouds.
They transcend those poets,
together soaring above the clear standard.
COLLATED NOTES
Biographies, Chapter 63: Empress’s Kin
Upon careful examination of past edicts,
and listening afar to former accounts,
those who rose to prominence and honor through their connections as empress’s kin
have a long history.
Yet, why is it that many met with disaster and ruin,
and few ended well?
Is it not
because their emoluments were increased by favor,
and their positions were not granted based on virtue;
their understanding was ashamed of clear wisdom,
and their talent lacked comprehensive knowledge;
they relied on the emperor’s favored consort’s prestige and spiritual power,
and controlled the crucial affairs of the military and state?
Some wielded power that shook the sovereign,
or their influence overturned the court;
they resided in peace without foreseeing danger,
and were intent on advancement without knowing when to retreat;
when arrogance and extravagance reached their peak,
faults and cracks followed?
This is why the families of Lǚ and Huò were exterminated in the Western Hàn,
and the clans of Liáng and Dèng were annihilated in the Eastern Dū.
The rest who violated discipline, disturbed norms, harmed the times, and corrupted government,
are too numerous to recount.
As for Fán Mǐqīng’s father and son,
Dòu Guǎngguó’s brothers,
Yīn Xīng’s adherence to restraint and avoidance of extravagance,
and Shǐ Dān’s concealing of faults and promoting of good deeds—
these are all considered virtuous among the empress’s kin.
From this perspective,
those who unrestrainedly indulged in the affairs of the time inevitably met a disastrous end,
while those who adhered to the Dao with humility and moderation forever preserved their integrity and auspiciousness.
As the ancients said, "Calamity and blessing have no gate,
they are only summoned by people."
Is this not its manifestation!
Reaching the calamities of the Jìn,
they began from within the palace.
Yáng Jùn, relying on Emperor Wǔ’s personal favor,
usurped power unjustly.
Jiǎ Mì, taking advantage of Emperor Huì’s mental incapacity,
created this dangerous situation.
Consequently, the Dào Empress met with the disaster of the Yúnlín,
and the Mǐnhuái Empress suffered the cruel fate of Húchéng.
The ways of heaven and man were exhausted,
and chaos and disorder proliferated.
The ancestral temples were overthrown because of this,
and the common people suffered and perished.
The *Shī* says:
"Resplendent was the royal Zhōu,
but Bāo Sì destroyed it."
This is what it refers to.
When it came to the Jiāngzuǒ,
they did not change the overturned cart.
Yǔ Liàng was an exemplar of an aristocratic clan,
and Wáng Gōng was a leader among the high-ranking families.
Thereafter, they held concurrent roles in issuing and receiving documents,
and their responsibilities were crucial as trusted advisors.
Xiàobó ultimately perished,
and Yuánguī nearly brought the state to ruin.
Is this not lamentable!
As for Chǔ Jìyě’s avoidance and fear of court power,
and Wáng Shūrén’s firm request to be appointed to a frontier post—
by these means, they were able to preserve themselves and avoid harm,
which is commendable.
Jiǎ Chōng, Yáng Jùn, Yǔ Liàng, Wáng Xiànzhī, and Wáng Gōng, etc., have already been included in the *Liezhuan*.
The others, according to their success or failure,
are included in the "Empress’s Kin" chapter.
Yáng Xiù
Yáng Xiù, courtesy name Zhìshū,
was the paternal cousin of Empress Jǐngxiàn.
His father, Dān,
reached the office of Grand Minister of Sacrifices (Tàicháng).
His elder brother, Jǐn,
was the Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè).
Xiù, while young, was recommended by the commandery [for service],
and participated in military affairs under Zhōng Huì, the General Who Guards the West.
He followed him in the pacification of Shǔ.
When Huì plotted rebellion,
Xiù spoke frankly and earnestly admonished him.
Upon his return,
he was granted the noble title of Marquis within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
Xiù was learned and had strategic intelligence.
From a young age, he had an open relationship with Emperor Wǔ,
and they were very close.
Whenever they shared a banquet or sat together,
he once said to the Emperor:
"If I gain wealth and honor and am put to use,
I should be in charge of the guards for ten years each."
The Emperor playfully agreed.
Initially,
before the Emperor was established as Crown Prince,
his reputation was not as good as that of his younger brother Yōu.
Emperor Wén always thought highly of Yōu,
and there was a discussion of replacing the heir.
Xiù secretly devised a strategy for Emperor Wǔ,
which provided great assistance and salvation.
He also observed the pros and cons of Emperor Wén’s governance,
and estimated what to say when consulted,
all of which he made Emperor Wǔ silently remember.
Later, when Emperor Wén discussed the affairs of the time and the suitability of people with Emperor Wǔ,
Emperor Wǔ’s answers were always agreeable,
and thus, his position as heir was settled.
When the Emperor became General Who Guards the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
he appointed Xiù as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn Shì).
After the Emperor ascended to the throne as King,
he promoted Xiù to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Gānlù Tíng.
When the Emperor ascended the imperial throne,
Xiù was successively promoted to Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn),
and given the additional title of Attendant Censor (Sànqí Chángshì).
Xiù served in office for thirteen years,
commanding the imperial guard,
and participating in confidential matters.
His favor and treatment were exceedingly generous.
Initially,
Dù Yù was appointed Grand General Pacifying the South.
All the court officials offered their congratulations,
and they sat with their couches joined together.
Wáng Xiù and Péi Kǎi arrived later
and said,
“How could Dù Yuánkǎi seat his guests with joined couches?”
Then they left without sitting.
Wáng Xiù's nature was extravagant and opulent;
his expenses knew no bounds.
He would crush charcoal and mix it to form animal shapes to warm wine,
and all the wealthy nobles in Luòxià competed to emulate him.
He also loved banquets,
continuing day into night.
There was no distinction between males and females among his five degrees of relatives, both inside and outside the family,
for which people at the time criticized him.
However, he admired and was drawn to those superior to himself;
when he promoted and honored someone,
he would dedicate himself wholeheartedly and without reservation.
For those who were impoverished and distressed,
he was especially able to relieve and aid them.
In selecting and appointing officials, he often prioritized those whom he favored,
not fully adhering to the principles of orderly promotion.
Generals and officers who risked their official positions
to serve his interests
would not hesitate to sacrifice their lives.
Yet, his unrestrained and law-breaking conduct
was often forgiven by the authorities.
Later, Liú Yì, the Colonel Director of Retainers, impeached him,
and he deserved a severe punishment.
However, Emperor Wǔ, on account of their old friendship,
simply dismissed him from office.
Soon after, he was appointed Protector-General with the title of Marquis, wearing plain clothes.
After a while,
he was reinstated.
When Qí Wáng Yōu was sent out to govern,
Wáng Xiù's frank remonstrance displeased the emperor,
and he was demoted to Grand Coachman.
Having lost favor, he felt resentful and frustrated,
which led him to fall ill.
Due to the severity of his illness, he requested to retire.
He was appointed Special Advanced Official [Tèjìn],
and additionally made Regular Mounted Attendant [Sànqí Chángshì].
He returned to his residence
and died.
The emperor personally issued an edict saying:
“Wáng Xiù and I shared the bond of relatives by marriage
and the kindness of childhood.
Having served in various positions, both inside and outside the court,
his loyalty and uprightness were amply manifest.
His unfortunate early demise
causes me great sorrow.
He is posthumously granted the titles of Grand General Assisting the State [Fǔguó Dàjiāngjūn] and Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
bestowed with secret treasures from the Eastern Garden [Dōngyuán Mìqì],
one set of court robes,
and 100 bolts of cloth.”
His posthumous name was Wēi.
Wáng Xún (brothers Qián, Kǎi)
Wáng Xún, courtesy name Liángfū,
was the younger brother of Empress Wénmíng.
His father, Sù,
was the Marquis of Lánlíng in Wèi.
Wáng Xún was well-versed in literature and extensive in his learning.
In court, he was loyal and upright.
He successively rose to Governor of Hénán [Hénán Yǐn],
established two academies,
and promoted the Five Classics.
Yuán Yì, the Prefect of Gé, once gifted him a fine horse,
but Wáng Xún did not accept it.
When Yuán Yì was later defeated,
all those who had accepted bribes were dismissed.
The Wèi dynasty allocated tenant farmers with oxen to officials from dukes down, each with a different quota.
Afterward, common people, fearing labor,
were often happy to become such tenants,
and powerful and influential families often had hundreds of them.
Moreover, various tribes in Tàiyuán also used Xiōngnú and Hú people as agricultural tenants,
some numbering several thousand.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he issued an edict prohibiting the recruitment of tenants.
Wáng Xún strictly enforced this prohibition,
and no one in his jurisdiction dared to violate it.
He died in the fourth year of Xiánníng,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Wáng Xún's brothers were Qián and Kǎi.
Qián, courtesy name Gōngzǔ,
was known for his meritorious service and competence.
He successively rose to Commandant of the Guards,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānshòu Pavilion,
and appointed General Pacifying the East, acting as Imperial Commissioner and overseeing military affairs in Qīngzhōu.
He was summoned to serve as Minister of the Grand Sacrifices,
then transferred to Grand Minister of Works,
and died.
His son, Shìwén, succeeded him.
Shìwén successively served as General of the Right Guard and General of the Southern Gentlemen-of-the-Household,
and was stationed in Xǔchāng,
where he was killed by Liú Cōng.
Kǎi, courtesy name Jūnfū,
possessed talent and ability from a young age.
He held various prominent and important positions.
Although he lacked minor virtues,
he was praised for his public service.
For his meritorious service in suppressing Yáng Jùn,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Shāndū County,
with a stipend of 1,800 households.
He was promoted to General Soaring Dragon,
also holding the position of General of Valiant Cavalry,
and additionally made Regular Mounted Attendant.
Soon after, he was dismissed from office due to an incident.
He was reappointed as Colonel of the Archers,
and after a long time,
he was transferred to General of the Rear.
As Wáng Kǎi belonged to a prominent clan and was a relative of the imperial family,
and his nature was also extravagant and opulent,
he used red ochre to plaster his walls.
Shí Chóng and Wáng Kǎi were about to engage in a treacherous plot,
and Fù Zhī, the Colonel Director of Retainers, impeached them.
The authorities all determined they deserved severe punishment,
but an imperial edict specially pardoned them.
Because of this, everyone feared Wáng Kǎi,
and thus he dared to act as he pleased,
without any scruples regarding his desires.
When he died,
his posthumous name was Chǒu.
Yáng Wénzōng
Yáng Wénzōng
was the father of Empress Wǔyuán.
His ancestors served the Hàn dynasty,
with four generations serving as the Three Dukes.
Yáng Wénzōng served as Grandee of Communication in Wèi [Wèi Tōngshì Láng]
and inherited the title of Marquis of Rúxù Pavilion.
He died early.
As the empress's father,
he was posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry [Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn]
and given the posthumous name Mù.
Yáng Xuánzhī
Yáng Xuánzhī
was the father of Empress Huì and
the son of Jǐn, the Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
Yáng Xuánzhī initially served as a Department Secretary.
As the empress's father,
he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness [Guānglù Dàfū], Special Advanced Official [Tèjìn], and Regular Mounted Attendant [Sànqí Chángshì],
and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīngjìn.
He was promoted to Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Yòupúyè],
additionally made Imperial Household Grandee [Shìzhōng],
and advanced to the rank of Duke.
When Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng attacked Chángshā Wáng Yì,
he used "punishing Yáng Xuánzhī" as a pretext.
Consequently, Yáng Xuánzhī died of worry and fear.
He was posthumously granted the titles of General of Chariots and Cavalry [Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn] and Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Yú Yù (son Yìn)
Yú Yù
was the father of Empress Yuánjìng.
From a young age, he had an excellent reputation.
Though invited by provinces and commanderies,
he did not accept.
He was appointed Erudite of Nányáng Prince.
He died early.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Regular Mounted Attendant [Sànqí Chángshì], Grand General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn], Kaīfǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Marquis of Píngshān County.
His son Yìn succeeded him.
Yìn
was the younger brother of Empress Jìng.
He was initially appointed Regular Mounted Attendant,
and then promoted to Colonel of Infantry.
At the end of Tàiníng,
Yú Yù's official positions were posthumously granted to Yìn,
and Yìn inherited the marquisate,
and was transferred to General of the Right Guard.
He and Nándùn Wáng Zōng were both favored by Emperor Míng
and jointly commanded the imperial guard.
When the emperor fell ill,
Zōng's conspiracy was discovered,
and the matter implicated Yìn.
The emperor, enduring in silence, did not inquire into it,
but moved Yìn to Minister of the Imperial Clan [Zōngzhèng Qīng],
and additionally made him Regular Mounted Attendant.
In the second year of Xiánhé,
Zōng was executed,
and Yìn was demoted to Administrator of Guìyáng,
with a salary of two thousand piculs.
He was frequently transferred to Administrator of Lángyá and Lúlíng.
He died in the first year of Xiánkāng,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Guards [Wèijiāngjūn],
and additionally made Regular Mounted Attendant.
His son Hóng inherited the marquisate.
Yǔ Chēn
Yǔ Chēn, styled Zǐměi,
was the father of Empress Mù.
His elder brother, Gǔn,
is in the Biography of Filial Piety.
In the early Yǒngjiā era, Chēn served as General Jiànwēi.
After crossing the Jiāng,
he became the Administrator of Kuàijī.
He was summoned to serve as Aide to the Chancellor's Military Advisor.
He died in office.
As he was the father of the Empress, he was posthumously granted the title of General Zuǒ.
His wife, Lady Wúqiū, was posthumously enfeoffed as Xiāngjūn.
His son, Liàng, following Chén Xiānzhì's example, refused the honors.
In the Xiánhé era,
Emperor Chéng again issued an edict posthumously granting Chēn the titles of General Piàojì and Yítóng Sānsī.
Liàng again declined.
Liàng is in the Biographies.
Dù Ài
Dù Ài, styled Hónglǐ,
was the father of Empress Chénggōng,
grandson of General Zhènnán Yù,
and son of the Minister Left Assistant Xī.
He was naturally pure and gentle,
with a beautiful appearance,
and enjoyed a great reputation in Jiāngzuǒ.
Wáng Xīzhī saw him and remarked:
"His skin is like congealed fat,
his eyes like dotted lacquer;
this is a celestial being."
Huán Yí also said:
"Wèi Jiè is spiritually clear,
Dù Ài is physically clear."
He inherited the title of Marquis of Dāngyáng,
was appointed as a clerk in the ducal residence,
and served as the Administrator of Dānyáng.
He died young,
without a son.
He died after the Empress was born.
His wife, Lady Péi, lived as a widow, raising the Empress,
and guarded herself with propriety,
possessing a reputation for great virtue.
In the early Xiánkāng era,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal,
and given the posthumous name Mù.
Lady Péi was enfeoffed as Xiāngjūn of Gāo'ān,
with an estate of five hundred households.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
she was further elevated to Jùnjūn of Guǎngdé County.
Lady Péi lived to an old age,
and the common people called her Dù Lǎo.
Initially,
Minister of Works Cài Mó greatly esteemed Ài,
and once said to the court:
"I regret that you gentlemen have not seen Dù Ài."
Such was the regard in which he was held by famous figures.
Chú Póu
Chú Póu, styled Jìyě,
was the father of Empress Kāngxiàn.
His grandfather, Sì,
possessed great capacity and judgment,
and was renowned for his competence.
Once, when he was a county clerk,
there was a matter in which he disagreed with the magistrate,
and the magistrate wished to whip him.
Sì said:
"Every object has its proper use;
rafters are not suitable for making fences.
I hope your honor will observe this."
Thereupon, he was spared.
His family was poor,
so he resigned from his post.
When he was nearly fifty,
General Zhènnán Yáng Hù, who had an old acquaintance with Sì,
spoke to Emperor Wǔ,
and Sì was first promoted and employed,
rising to the rank of General Āndōng.
His father, Qià,
was the Administrator of Wǔchāng.
Póu, from a young age, possessed a refined and noble demeanor,
and together with Dù Ài of Jīngzhào, he enjoyed a great reputation,
surpassing all others in the Restoration.
Huán Yí of Qiáoguó saw him and remarked:
"Jìyě has the 'skin and bones of Spring and Autumn Annals'."
This meant that outwardly he showed no approval or disapproval,
but inwardly he had his commendations and criticisms.
Xiè Ān also deeply respected him,
saying:
"Though Póu does not speak,
the 'air of the four seasons' is complete within him."
He was initially appointed Clerk to the Prince of Xīyáng and Literary Tutor to the Prince of Wú.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
General of Chariots Xī Jiàn appointed Póu as his military advisor.
After Jùn was pacified,
Póu was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāngtíng for his功績,
and gradually rose to become Minister of Works, Administrator of the Central Bureau,
and then was appointed Yellow Gate Attendant.
When Emperor Kāng was Prince of Lángyá,
he was about to take a consort.
After a careful selection of those with high reputation,
an edict was issued to betroth Póu's daughter as consort.
Thereupon, he was sent out to serve as Administrator of Yùzhāng.
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be appointed Attendant,
and then promoted to Minister of Works.
As he was the father of the Empress,
he earnestly requested an outside appointment,
and was appointed General Jiànwēi and Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
stationed at Bànzhōu.
In office, he was incorruptible and frugal;
though he held the position of a regional commander,
he had his private servants gather firewood.
Soon after,
he was summoned to be General Wèi,
concurrently holding the post of Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Póu believed that the Central Secretariat managed imperial decrees,
and it was improper for an in-law to hold such a position,
so he firmly declined.
An edict then appointed him General Zuǒ, Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Regional Commander of the various military forces of Lángyá in Yǎnzhōu and Xúzhōu, holding a temporary imperial tally,
stationed at Jīnchéng,
and also concurrently holding the post of Administrator of Lángyá.
Initially,
when Póu was a young boy, he visited Yǔ Liàng.
Liàng had Guō Pú divine for him.
When the hexagram was formed,
Pú was astonished.
Liàng asked:
"Is there anything inauspicious?"
Pú replied:
"This is not a hexagram for a subject.
I don't know why this young man shows such an auspicious sign.
In twenty years or more,
my words will be proven true."
Twenty-nine years later, Empress Dowager Kāngxiàn assumed regency.
The officials, considering Póu to be the father of the Empress Dowager,
deliberated on granting him extraordinary honors,
appointing him Attendant, General Wèi, and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
with his imperial tally, regional command, and governorship remaining as before.
Póu,
as a close relative, feared incurring criticism and suspicion,
so he submitted a memorial firmly requesting to remain in the provinces,
saying:
"I, being humble and untalented,
with abilities insufficient for service,
have excessively received imperial favor,
and repeatedly held positions I did not deserve.
Having done no meritorious service to receive such favor,
I am deeply ashamed.
How can I further accept extraordinary appointments
and have exalted titles multiplied?
What merits do I possess to be capable of bearing them?
How can I brazenly advance?
Having entrusted myself to this sacred era,
how can I not exert my utmost effort?
I truly fear a fall,
and the error would be great.
Now, the imperial strategy has not yet fully flourished,
and the myriad affairs of state are extremely numerous.
Your Majesty should sincerely entrust affairs to your chief ministers,
and consistently follow the late emperor's way of employing the virtuous,
humbly accepting their accomplishments,
and openly displaying impartiality to the world.
You should not outwardly show favoritism to private relatives,
causing disappointment among the court and the populace,
which would be a significant loss!"

Thereupon, he was reassigned as Regional Commander of the various military forces of Jìnlíng and Wúguó in Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Yáng Prefectures, General Wèi, Governor of Xú and Yǎn Prefectures, and granted a temporary imperial tally,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
In the early Yǒnghé era,
Póu was again summoned,
and was to be appointed Governor of Yángzhōu and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Minister of Personnel Liú Xiá advised Póu, saying:
"The Prince of Kuàijī possesses great virtue;
he is the Duke of Zhōu of our state.
Your Excellency should entrust the major affairs of state to him."
Póu's chief clerk Wáng Húzhī also urged him,
so he firmly declined and returned to his provincial post,
which was admired and praised by both court and commoners.
He was promoted to General Zhēngběi Dà, and granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
but he firmly declined the Kāifǔ.
Póu also believed that the way of governance lay in obtaining talent,
and that it was proper to entrust capable individuals and promote respected elders,
so he recommended former Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Gù Hé and Attendant Yīn Hào.
When the memorial was submitted,
Hé was immediately appointed Minister of Works, and Hào was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
When Shí Jìlóng died,
Póu submitted a memorial requesting to attack him.
On that very day, a state of emergency was declared,
and they marched directly to Sìkǒu.
The court deliberated that Póu's responsibilities were too weighty
for him to penetrate deeply;
a detachment should be sent first.
Póu reiterated that previously, the vanguard supervisor Wáng Yízhī and others, whom he had dispatched, had marched directly to Péngchéng,
demonstrating their power and trustworthiness.
Later, supervisor Mí Yì was sent to advance to Xiàpī,
and the bandits immediately fled and collapsed.
Yì led his troops to occupy their cities and fortifications.
Therefore, he argued, they should now act swiftly
to establish their influence and prestige.
Consequently, he was appointed Grand Military Governor for Punitive Expeditions and Supervisor of all military affairs for the five provinces of Qīng, Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù.
Póu led a host of thirty thousand directly to Péngchéng.
From Héshuò, thousands of gentry and commoners surrendered daily.
Póu pacified and accepted them,
greatly winning their hearts.
He first dispatched supervisor Xú Kān to attack Pèi,
capturing the puppet minister Zhī Chóng.
Over two thousand people in the commandery surrendered.
In the mountains of Lǔjùn, there were over five hundred families
who also raised a righteous banner and requested aid.
Póu sent Kān to lead three thousand elite soldiers to meet them.
Kān disobeyed Póu's command.
His army, while encamped at Dàipī,
was defeated by Lǐ Tú, a general of Shí Zūn.
More than half were killed or wounded.
Kān, holding his standard, did not waver,
but was slain by the bandits.
Póu, applying the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals where the commander takes responsibility,
and recognizing his failure in assigning the task,
which resulted in a loss of prestige and strategy,
submitted a memorial to demote himself.
He requested to act as General Who Conquers the North
and be stationed at Guǎnglíng.
An imperial edict stated that the responsibility lay with the subordinate commander
and Póu should not blame himself.
As the fleeing rebels had not yet been annihilated,
and his role as a regional commander was important,
it was inappropriate to demote him.
He was ordered to return to his post at Jīngkǒu
and relieved of the title of Military Governor for Punitive Expeditions.
At that time, Shí Jìlóng had just died,
and his state was in great chaos.
Two hundred thousand households of his remnants crossed the river,
intending to surrender,
and pleaded for military aid.
But Póu had already returned,
and his power and influence could not reach them.
Unable to extricate themselves,
they were all plundered by the forces of Mùróng Huàng and Fú Jiàn,
and all perished.
Póu, disappointed that his long-term plans had not been realized,
fell ill from sorrow and indignation.
When he arrived at Jīngkǒu,
he heard many sounds of weeping.
Póu asked:
"Why are there so many crying?"
His attendants replied:
"It is because of the battle at Dàipī."
Póu felt even more ashamed and regretful.
He died in the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
aged forty-seven.
People far and near lamented his passing,
and officials and soldiers mourned him.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Grand Tutor,
his original office remaining unchanged,
and was given the posthumous name Yuánmù.
His son, Xīn,
courtesy name Yòu'ān,
was renowned for his learning and conduct.
He successively held the posts of Palace Regular Attendant and Director of the Imperial Library.
Hé Zhǔn (Zǐ Chéng)
Hé Zhǔn, courtesy name Yòudào,
was the father of Empress Mùzhāng.
He was noble-minded and had few desires.
He was well-known by the time he reached manhood (around twenty),
and various provincial and prefectural offices invited him to serve,
but he did not accept any of them.
His elder brother Chōng became General of Agile Cavalry
and urged him to take office.
Zhǔn said:
"How is the name 'Fifth' inferior to General of Agile Cavalry?"
Zhǔn was the fifth among his brothers,
hence this remark.
Chōng held a heavy position as a chief minister,
and his power overshadowed his era.
However, Zhǔn remained a recluse,
not engaging in worldly affairs,
but only reciting Buddhist scriptures
and building stupas and temples.
He was summoned and appointed Gentleman Attendant at the Palace,
but did not take office.
He died at forty-seven.
In the first year of Shēngpíng,
he was posthumously granted the title Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jìnxīng County.
His son Tán, considering his father's consistently noble and pure conduct,
submitted a memorial to decline the posthumous honors.
He had three sons: Fàng, Tán, and Chéng.
Fàng succeeded Chōng (as his heir).
Tán held office up to Administrator of Nánkāng,
but died young.
Tán's son Yuándù was
Administrator of Xīyáng;
his second son Shúdù was
Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Minister.
Chéng, courtesy name Jìxuán,
began his career as a Secretary,
then became an Assistant.
He was upright and highly respected,
and was successively promoted to Director of the Imperial Library, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Central Protector of the Army.
Emperor Xiàowǔ deeply cherished him,
appointing him General Who Leads the Army and Administrator of Wú Commandery.
At the end of the Tàiyuán era,
the Prince of Lángxié moved to an external residence.
A distinguished teacher was sought,
and Chéng was summoned and appointed Minister,
also serving as Preceptor to the Prince of Lángxié.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
Chéng was promoted to Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs,
retaining his duties in selection and as the Prince's Preceptor.
At that time, Chéng suffered from a foot ailment,
and firmly declined (to attend court).
He was specially permitted not to attend court
and managed affairs from home.
He also held the position of Grand Impartial Judge for his home province.
When Huán Xuán took power,
Chéng was dismissed from office due to illness, as he had requested,
and died at home.
When Emperor Ān was restored,
Chéng was posthumously granted the title Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal.
His eldest son Jí
died young.
His second son Róng,
during the Yuánxī era,
became Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Wáng Méng (Zǐ Xiū)
Wáng Méng, courtesy name Zhòngzǔ,
was the father of Empress Āijìng.
His great-grandfather Àn
successively held the post of Minister.
His grandfather Yòu was
Central Supervisor of the Northern Army.
His father Nà was
Magistrate of Xīngàn.
When Méng was young, he was unrestrained and undisciplined,
and not respected by his local community.
In his later years, he began to control himself and discipline his conduct,
earning a reputation for elegance and charm.
He emptied himself to respond to things (was open-minded and adaptable),
and acted with forgiveness,
so everyone respected and loved him.
He served his various stepmothers with great care.
Regarding his salary and assets, he always pushed for others to take more and himself to take less.
His joy and anger were not shown on his face.
He did not bother with minor neatness,
but was praised for his purity and frugality.
He was skilled in clerical script.
He had a handsome appearance,
and once, looking at himself in a mirror,
he referred to his father's courtesy name and said:
"Did Wáng Wénkāi really beget such a son!"
He lived in poverty,
and when his hat was worn out,
he went to the market himself to buy one.
An old woman, pleased with his appearance,
gave him a new hat.
People at the time considered him enlightened.
He was equally renowned and good friends with Liú Tán of Pèiguó.
Tán often said that Méng's nature was utterly open-minded,
yet naturally disciplined.
Méng often said:
"Lord Liú knows me
better than I know myself."
People at the time compared Tán to Xún Fèngqiàn,
and Méng to Yuán Yàoqīng.
Indeed, whoever spoke of elegance and charm
would name Méng and Tán as their exemplars.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo (王導) appointed him as an aide.
Dǎo (導) also brought in Kuāng Shù's (匡術) younger brother Xiào (孝).
Méng (濛) sent a memorial to Dǎo (導), saying:
"To establish a state and maintain a family,
small-minded people should not be employed.
To rule the world by virtue and righteousness,
one must clarify the eternal norms
and revere titles and honors.
Military and civil affairs have distinct uses,
and civil and martial have different appearances.
How can one allow the Jīng (涺) and Wèi (渭) rivers to mix their currents,
diminishing the pure and tranquil customs,
in order to meet universal expectations
and serve as a model for the whole land!"
Dǎo (導) did not respond.
Later, he was assigned as the Magistrate of Chángshān (長山),
and then again as Sītú (司徒) Zuǒ Xīshǔ (左西屬).
Méng (濛) knew that this position entailed corporal punishment for transgressions,
and firmly declined it.
An imperial edict suspended the punishment,
but he still would not take the post.
He was transferred to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎).
When Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) was still the Prince of Kuàijī (會稽),
he once discussed various cultured figures with Sūn Chuò (孫綽).
Chuò (綽) said:
"Liú Tàn (劉惔) is clear, elegant, concise, and upright;
Wáng Méng (王濛) is gentle, warm, tranquil, and harmonious;
Huán Wēn (桓溫) is lofty, straightforward, and outstanding;
Xiè Shàng (謝尚) is pure, easygoing, orderly, and perceptive.
But Méng's (濛) nature is amiable and smooth,
he is good at discussing principles,
and his words are concise yet insightful."
When Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) became regent,
he valued and favored him even more,
and he and Liú Tàn (劉惔) were known as his "in-chamber guests."
He was transferred to Sītú (司徒) Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史).
Late in his career, he requested to be the Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽),
but was not allowed.
When Méng (濛) fell ill,
the emperor regretted not having appointed him.
When Méng (濛) heard of this, he said:
"People say the Prince of Kuàijī (會稽) is foolish,
and indeed he is!"
His illness gradually worsened.
By lamplight, he turned his deer-tail whisk over and looked at it,
sighing:
"Such a man as this will not even reach forty!"
He died at the age of thirty-nine.
At his funeral,
Liú Tàn (劉惔) placed a rhinoceros-horn-handled deer-tail whisk in his coffin,
and then fainted from grief for a long time.
Xiè Ān (謝安) also often praised Méng (濛), saying:
"Wáng Chángshǐ (王長史) did not say much,
but his words can be called excellent."
He had two sons: Xiū (脩) and Yùn (蘊).
Xiū (脩), courtesy name Jìngrén (敬仁), childhood name Gǒuzi (苟子).
He was intelligent and handsome, and well-regarded.
He was skilled in clerical script,
known as "flowing and splendid, clear and elevated."
At the age of twelve,
he wrote "Xián Quán Lùn" (賢全論).
Méng (濛) showed it to Liú Tàn (劉惔) and said:
"Jìngrén's (敬仁) essay
is sufficient to be compared with profound words."
He began his career as Zuòzuò Láng (著作郎) and Lángxié Wáng Wénxué (琅邪王文學),
then transferred to Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ (中軍司馬),
but died before taking office,
at the age of twenty-four.
At his death,
he sighed:
"I am not ashamed before the ancients;
my age is on par with theirs."
Wáng Xiá (王遐)
Wáng Xiá (王遐), courtesy name Huánzǐ (桓子),
was the father of Empress Jiǎnshùn (簡順皇后),
and the paternal uncle of Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) Shù (述).
From a young age, being from an illustrious clan,
he rose to the position of Guānglù Xūn (光祿勳).
In the early Níngkāng (寧康) era,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Tèjìn (特進) and Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
additionally Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and his posthumous name was Jìng (靖).
His eldest son, Kè (恪),
was Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
Kè's (恪) son, Xīnzhī (欣之),
was Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (豫章太守),
with a salary of two thousand stones.
Xīnzhī's (欣之) younger brother, Huānzhī (歡之),
was Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (廣州刺史).
Xiá's (遐) youngest son, Zhēn (臻),
was Chóngdé Wèiwèi (崇德衞尉).
Wáng Yùn (王蘊)
Wáng Yùn (王蘊), courtesy name Shūrén (叔仁),
was the father of Empress Xiàowǔ Dìng (孝武定皇后),
and the son of Sītú (司徒) Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史) Méng (濛).
He began his career as Zuòzuò Láng (佐著作郎),
and gradually rose to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎).
His nature was peaceful and harmonious,
and he did not suppress the humble.
Whenever there was an official vacancy,
ten groups of people would seek it,
but Yùn (蘊) did not express approval or disapproval of any.
At that time, Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) was the Prince of Kuàijī (會稽),
and acted as regent.
Yùn (蘊) would then report them all on a single memorial,
saying:
"So-and-so has the right background,
so-and-so has the talent."
He made an effort to promote and advance them,
each according to their suitability,
so those who did not get a post had no complaints.
He was appointed Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守),
and governed with great virtue.
When the affiliated commanderies suffered from famine and their people were starving,
he would immediately open granaries to provide relief.
His chief clerk, holding a remonstrance,
requested to first submit a list to the court and await a response.
Yùn (蘊) said:
"Now the common people are wailing,
with famine along the roads.
If we submit a memorial and await a response,
how can we save those on the verge of death?
The fault of acting on my own
rests with the Grand Administrator.
Even if I fail while performing righteousness,
I will have no regrets."
Thereupon, he greatly distributed aid,
and seventeen or eighteen out of ten were saved through Yùn's (蘊) efforts.
The imperial court dismissed Yùn (蘊) from office for violating regulations,
but officials and commoners alike pleaded on his behalf at the palace gate.
An imperial edict specially demoted him to Jìnlíng Tàishǒu (晉陵太守).
He again brought about beneficial reforms,
and the people sang his praises.
When Empress Dìng (定后) was established,
as the empress's father,
he was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
concurrently Lǐng Wǔbīng Shàngshū (領五兵尚書) and Běnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng (本州大中正),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiànchāng (建昌縣).
Yùn (蘊), considering the title was granted as a favor
rather than through the excellent ancient systems of the Three Dynasties,
firmly declined to accept it.
The imperial court urged him,
but he ultimately refused to accept,
so he was appointed Dūdū Jīngkǒu Zhūjūn Shì (都督京口諸軍事), Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍), Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史), and given the temporary credentials of Jiǎjié (假節).
He again firmly declined.
Xiè Ān (謝安) said to Yùn (蘊):
"You hold the important position of the empress's father.
You should not unnecessarily belittle yourself
and thereby miss this opportune moment.
You should follow Chǔ Gōng's (褚公) precedent:
just let the authority be there but not be used in practice.
You may temporarily assume this office
to ease the burden on the imperial in-laws."
Thereupon, he accepted the appointment
and garrisoned at Jīngkǒu (京口).
After a while,
he was summoned and appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射),
his general title remaining as before.
He was transferred to Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹),
with his original military title plus Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Yùn (蘊), being an imperial in-law,
did not wish to serve in the capital.
He earnestly requested an outside post,
and was again appointed Dūdū Zhèjiāng Dōng Wǔ Jùn (都督浙江東五郡), Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍), and Kuàijī Nèishǐ (會稽內史),
his Chángshì (常侍) title remaining as before.
Yùn (蘊) had always been fond of wine,
