and it was especially pronounced in his later years.
When he was in Kuàijī (會稽),
he was rarely sober,
yet his amiable and simple nature still made him beloved by the people.
At that time, Wáng Yuè (王悅) came to visit a tomb.
Yùn's (蘊) son Gōng (恭) went to visit him.
They had always been on good terms,
so Gōng (恭) stayed for more than ten days before returning.
Yùn (蘊) asked him the reason,
and Gōng (恭) said:
"I was talking with Ā Tài (阿太),
and I couldn't get away."
Yùn (蘊) said:
"I'm afraid Ā Tài (阿太) is not your friend."
Ā Tài (阿太)
was Yuè's (悅) childhood name.
Later, their initial good relationship indeed soured,
and people at the time considered Yùn (蘊) to be a good judge of character.
He died in the ninth year of Tàiyuán (太元)
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
His eldest son, Chǔ Huá,
died young.
His second son, Chǔ Gōng,
is in the biographies.
Chǔ Gōng's younger brother, Chǔ Shuǎng,
whose courtesy name was Jìmíng,
was resolute and strong-willed, with a sense of purpose and capability.
He successively served as Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng and Shìzhōng.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
Wáng Guóbǎo wanted to open the palace gate at night to enter and forge an imperial edict.
Chǔ Shuǎng stopped him,
saying:
"The Great Emperor has passed away,
and the Crown Prince has not yet arrived.
Those who dare enter will be executed!"
So, Wáng Guóbǎo stopped.
Chǔ Shuǎng once drank with Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ.
Dàozǐ, in his drunkenness, called Chǔ Shuǎng a "little fellow."
Chǔ Shuǎng replied:
"My late grandfather, the Grand Historian, was a commoner friend of Emperor Jiǎnwén.
My late aunt and late elder sister were consorts in the two palaces.
How can I be a 'little fellow'!"
When Wáng Guóbǎo gained power,
he dismissed Chǔ Shuǎng from office.
Later, his elder brother Chǔ Gōng rose again in rebellion,
and also appointed Chǔ Shuǎng as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
participating in military affairs.
When Chǔ Gōng was defeated,
he was executed.
Chǔ Shuǎng
Chǔ Shuǎng, whose courtesy name was Hóngmào,
and childhood name was Qīshēng,
was the father of Empress Gōngsī.
His grandfather was Chǔ Póu,
and his father was Chǔ Xīn.
Chǔ Shuǎng was well-regarded from a young age.
Xiè Ān thought highly of him,
once saying:
"If Qīshēng doesn't turn out well,
I will no longer comment on scholars."
He served as Yìxīng Tàishǒu,
but died young.
As the empress's father,
he was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Chǔ Shuǎng's sons, Chǔ Xiùzhī, Chǔ Yánzhī, and Chǔ Yùzhī,
during the Yìxī reign,
all served in high offices.
The historian says: Yáng Xiù relied on his close familial ties,
benefited from extensive knowledge,
encountered opportunities during times of obscurity and prominence,
and participated in the initial planning.
Thus, he enjoyed deep favor and private affection,
and was frequently appointed to important positions.
He indulged his desires by relying on imperial favor and spiritual power,
and behaved arrogantly and overbearingly by relying on his status and position.
He repeatedly violated laws and regulations,
and frequently interfered with state affairs.
Fortunately, he encountered a lenient government,
and was spared from legal punishment.
Wáng Kǎi's land was near Wèiyáng,
and his family inherited hereditary stipends.
He was never known for his modesty or frugality,
but only for his indulgence in luxury and excess.
He competed for extravagance with Shí Lún,
and vied for precedence with Wǔzǐ.
He not only sullied honorable reputations,
but also marred the king's governance.
Even if there was a discussion to change his posthumous name,
it would not be enough to admonish evil and encourage good.
Hónglǐ's outward appearance was bright and dignified,
Jìyě's inner discernment was profound,
Zhòngzǔ was gentle, refined, and elegant,
and Yòudào was pure, detached, and had few desires.
All of them were renowned south of the Yangtze,
and respected in their time.
Were they merely the cream of the empress's family,
or also esteemed figures among the gentry?
A eulogy says: Relying on connections in the Inner Palace,
reflecting the brilliance of the Imperial Palace.
Their position afforded power and favor,
their responsibility was to wield authority.
Moderation led to few errors,
arrogance led to bullying others.
The overturned chariot serves as a lasting warning,
truly worthy of inscription on one's belt.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 64: Recluses
When the vast heavens cast down their light,
the Lesser Bright Star occupies its position in the sky;
when the Yì Jīng explores the obscure,
steadfast reclusion perfects its image.
Thus, there are those who avoid speech and demeanor,
their way is heard through Kǒng Gōng;
and those who are proud of wealth and nobility,
whose principles are detailed by Sūnzi.
Therefore, dwelling in gentleness leads to preservation,
this is the nature of living beings;
while being full leads to harm,
this is the constant way of the spirits.
Ancient wise scholars understood this to be so,
and thus stood aloof from the common world,
cultivating their true nature with expansive minds,
hiding their renown above rivers and seas,
withdrawing their traces beyond the dusty world.
They rinsed their mouths with streams to sharpen their purity,
slept in nests to conceal their brilliance.
Excellent strategies matched their aspirations,
and they severed all worldly connections to empty their minds.
Their purity was like shining jade and clear ice,
their steadfastness like a still river and a towering mountain.
They cultivated the path of ultimate joy,
securing boundless blessings.
They departed far away and were not pursued,
arranging themselves in solitude without regret.
Cultivating themselves for self-preservation,
regret and vexation did not arise.
The poet's song of "building a hut"
is also found here.
As for the time after the heavens established the system,
when lawsuits ceased and punishments were clear,
people still seated reclusive and chaste individuals to stabilize spiritual transformation.
The rites of summoning and inviting enriched the mountain caves,
and gifts of jade and silk were sent to humble abodes.
Thus, the Yuè Lìng says:
"In the month of late spring, invite renowned scholars,
and treat worthy people with courtesy."
Is this not what it means!
Since the Dǐanjǐn dynasty began,
it sought out recluses everywhere.
Qiáo Yuán'yàn cut off human affairs,
and Jiāng Sīqūn sang and chanted in the forests.
They established a noble and pure path,
and achieved a detached existence.
Although they did not respond to the grand invitations,
they were sufficient to inspire those who were greedy and competitive.
Now, their lofty virtues are praised,
and compiled into this chapter.
Sūn Dēng
Sūn Dēng, whose courtesy name was Gōnghé,
was a native of Gòng County, Jí Commandery.
He had no family,
and lived in an earthen cave on the mountain north of the commandery.
In summer, he wove grass into clothes;
in winter, he covered himself with his hair.
He loved to read the Yì Jīng,
and played a one-stringed zither.
All who saw him felt affection and joy towards him.
He was naturally free from anger.
Sometimes people would throw him into the water,
wanting to see him get angry.
After Sūn Dēng emerged,
he would simply laugh heartily.
Occasionally he would wander among people.
If a household he passed through offered him clothes and food,
he would accept everything without refusal,
but would abandon it all when he left.
He once stayed on Yíyáng Mountain.
A charcoal burner saw him,
knew he was no ordinary person,
and spoke with him.
Sūn Dēng did not respond.
Emperor Wén heard of him,
and sent Ruǎn Jí to observe him.
When Ruǎn Jí met him,
he spoke with him,
but Sūn Dēng also did not respond.
Jī Kāng then spent three years traveling with him,
asking about his intentions,
but Sūn Dēng never answered.
Jī Kāng often sighed in admiration.
As they were about to part,
Jī Kāng said:
"Sir, will you truly say nothing?"
Sūn Dēng then said:
"Do you know about fire?
Fire is born with light,
but it does not use its light;
its purpose lies in using light.
A person is born with talent,
but does not use their talent;
their purpose lies in using talent.
Therefore, using light depends on obtaining firewood,
which is how its brilliance is preserved;
using talent depends on discerning truth,
which is how one completes one's years.
Now you have much talent but little discernment,
it will be difficult for you to escape the troubles of this age!
Do you seek nothing?"
Jī Kāng could not follow his advice,
and indeed met an untimely end.
He then wrote the "Poem of Hidden Indignation," saying:
"Formerly I was ashamed of Liǔ Xià,
now I am ashamed of Sūn Dēng."
Some say Sūn Dēng's silence was because the transition between the Wèi and Jìn dynasties
could easily lead to suspicion,
hence his silence.
His ultimate fate is unknown.
Dǒng Jīng
Dǒng Jīng, courtesy name Wēiliǎn,
was from an unknown commandery.
Initially, he arrived in Luòyáng with the accounts clerk from Lǒngxī,
his hair unbound as he walked,
wandering and chanting,
often sleeping in the Bái Shè.
Sometimes he begged in the market,
and when he received torn fragments of silk and cotton batting,
he would tie them together to cover himself.
He would not accept whole bolts of fine silk or cotton.
If he was pushed, shoved, cursed, or insulted,
he never showed any sign of anger.
Sūn Chǔ, who was then a Zhùzuò Láng,
often visited the Shè to converse with him.
Eventually, he took Dǒng Jīng with him back home,
but Jīng refused to sit.
Chǔ then presented him with a letter,
urging him, since it was an era like that of Yáo and Shùn,
why did he cling to his Dao and lose his way in the country?
Jīng replied with a poem, saying:
"The Zhōu Way is ruined, and the eulogies are gone,
The Xià government wanes, and the Wǔcháng are submerged.
The eminent gentlemen,
Look around and depart,
Vast and overflowing to the eye,
And the authors are seven.
Is it not joyful to experience the transformations of heaven and earth?
Alas, the times cannot be engaged with,
I confront them by dwelling in solitude.
Let nothing entertain me as joy,
Pure streams are for drinking,
The ultimate Dao is for sustenance,
Why busy myself to and fro,
Making myself weary and exhausted?
Fish suspended in cages, beasts in traps,
Even a common fellow knows this.
Indeed, the ultimate sages of old,
Concealed their vessels within their spirit.
A tattered robe could not make them warm,
Noble carriages and caps could not make them glorious;
In motion, like the flow of a river,
In stillness, like the calm of a river.
Parrots can speak,
The floating chimes by the Sì River,
Are all admired by the multitudes,
But how can they conform to the true nature of things?
The dark swallow entwines itself in the curtain,
Yet suffers no harm?
The fish hawk nests far away,
All are eager to die.
Look at that fish on the bridge,
Hesitating and turning its tail,
Pondering indecisively,
Suddenly it loses the water.
Alas!
Fish and birds interact,
For ten thousand generations they do not awaken;
From my perspective,
Their reasons become clear.
How do I know there isn't an enlightened person,
Profound and serene in their demeanor,
Who will also gaze at me,
Frown and depart?
All things are lowly,
Only humans are noble.
In action, they find the nine provinces too narrow,
In stillness, they find a humble dwelling vast."
Several years later,
he absconded,
and no one knew where he went.
In the place where he had slept, there was only a stone bamboo shoot and two poems.
One read:
"The Way of Qián is strong and simple,
The body of Kūn is thick and dense,
Vast and boundless primordial essence,
Is what is affirmed and followed.
In later generations, people rush about,
Replacing substance with superficiality,
The eyes of the world are distant and unfocused,
Who knows the truth of it!
I shall depart from this ultimate void,
And return to my natural abode."
Another said:
"Kǒngzǐ did not meet his time,
Then he was moved by the Qílín.
Qílín, Qílín!
Why do you not escape the world to preserve your true nature?"
Xià Tǒng.
Xià Tǒng, courtesy name Zhòngyù,
was from Yǒngxīng, Kuàijī.
Orphaned and poor in youth,
he was known for his filial piety in raising his parents,
and was harmonious with his siblings.
He often gathered firewood for food,
traveling at dawn and returning at night,
sometimes going to the seaside
to gather barnacles and cuttlefish to support his parents.
He was inherently skilled in discourse.
His clan urged him to enter officialdom,
saying to him:
"You are clear-minded and upright,
you could serve as a supervisor in the commandery,
connecting with the prefectural court,
and naturally rise to prominence.
Why endure hardship in the mountains
and end your life by the sea?"
Tǒng flared up in anger and said:
"Do you gentlemen regard me in such a way!
If Tǒng lived in a time of great peace,
I would discuss my choices of engagement or withdrawal with Yuánkǎi;
If I encountered a corrupt era,
I would consider sharing the same defilement and mud with Qū Shēng;
If it were a time between purity and corruption,
I would naturally join Jǔnì in plowing the fields.
How could I disgrace myself and bend my will in the commandery government!
Hearing your words,
I can't help but feel all my hairs stand on end,
cold sweat covers my body,
my face is flushed red,
my heart burns like charcoal,
my tongue shrinks and my mouth hangs open,
and both my ears are completely blocked."
Those who spoke were greatly ashamed.
From then on, Tǒng no longer met with his clan.
When his mother fell ill,
Tǒng attended to her medicine,
and his relatives thus had a chance to see him.
His paternal cousin Jìngníng was offering sacrifices to his ancestors,
and invited two female shamans, Zhāng Dān and Chén Zhū,
both of whom possessed national beauty,
were exquisitely dressed,
and skilled in singing,
and could also become invisible and hide their shadows.
At the beginning of the first watch of the night,
bells were struck and drums beaten,
interspersed with strings and flutes.
Dān and Zhū then drew knives to cut their tongues,
swallowed knives and spat fire,
while clouds and mist became dark and obscure,
and light flashed like lightning.
Tǒng's cousins wanted to go and watch,
but found it difficult because of Tǒng.
So they conspired to deceive him, saying:
"Our cousin has recently recovered from an illness,
and everyone is celebrating.
We wish to take advantage of his ancestral sacrifice
to go and congratulate him.
Would you like to come along?"
Tǒng agreed.
Upon entering the gate,
he suddenly saw Dān and Zhū in the central courtyard,
moving lightly and circling,
speaking with spiritual voices and laughing like ghosts,
flying and touching plates,
responding to challenges with graceful turns.
Tǒng was astonished and fled,
not through the gate,
but breaking through the fence directly.
Returning, he rebuked the others, saying:
"In ancient times, when customs of debauchery arose,
Wèi Wéngōng grieved over them;
When the qi of the rainbow appeared,
a gentleman dared not even point at it;
When Jì Huán took in the Qí women,
Zhòngní departed in his carriage;
When Zǐlù saw Xià Nán,
he was filled with righteous indignation.
I often regret that I could not smash Shúxiàng's head,
and blind Huáfù's eyes.
How could you gentlemen invite these demonic creatures,
play with them at night,
indulge in unrestrained passions,
give rein to extravagant and licentious behavior,
disrupt the rites between men and women,
and destroy the virtue of integrity and loftiness?
Why?"
Thereupon, he hid on his bed,
lying down with unbound hair,
and spoke no more.
The relatives were embarrassed and uneasy,
and immediately dismissed Dān and Zhū,
sending them each on their way.
Later, his mother fell gravely ill,
so he went to Luò City to buy medicine.
It happened to be the third month, the third day of the third lunar month (Shàngsì Festival),
and the princes and dukes of Luò, down to the commoners, all went to the floating bridge.
Gentlemen and ladies crowded together,
their carriages and clothes illuminating the road.
Tǒng was at the time on a boat, drying the medicine he had bought.
The carriages of the various nobles came like clouds,
but Tǒng paid them no attention.
Grand Commandant Jiǎ Chōng found this strange and asked about him.
Tǒng at first did not respond.
When asked again,
he slowly replied:
“I am Xià Zhòngyù of Kuàijī.”
Jiǎ Chōng had someone ask about the customs of his land.
Tǒng said:
“Its people are upright and orderly,
still possessing the residual customs of Dà Yǔ,
the righteous humility of Tàibó,
the resolute ambition of Yán Zūn,
and the noble integrity of Huáng Gōng.”
Then he asked:
“Since you live by the sea,
are you quite skilled at playing with water?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
Tǒng then grasped the rudder and adjusted the oar,
turning and circling in the middle of the stream.
First, he performed the leap of the mú [zā] fish,
then the pull of the pú fish,
making the prow soar like a swift crane,
and the stern dip like a beast's tail.
He wielded the long pole, and the boat shot straight forward three times.
At this, the wind and waves were violently stirred,
and clouds and mists became dark and vast.
Suddenly, eight or nine white fish leaped into the boat.
All the spectators were startled and fearful.
Jiǎ Chōng found him especially extraordinary in his heart,
so he went to the boat to speak with him.
His responses were like echoes.
When Jiǎ Chōng wanted him to take office,
he bowed his head and did not reply.
Jiǎ Chōng then said:
“In the past, Yáo sang,
Shùn sang.
You, when singing with others and doing it well,
must harmonize only after returning.
This shows that there were no ancient sages or former wise men who did not sing.
Can you make a song from your land?”
Tǒng said:
“My ancestor resided only in Kuàijī Mountain.
At court, he met with all nations,
imparted his civilizing influence to my humble region,
and was buried after his death.
His benevolence spread like clouds,
and his sage-like transformation still remains.
The common people, moved, sang praises,
thus composing the ‘Mùgē’ (Song of Admiration).
Also, the filial daughter Cáo É,
only fourteen years old,
whose virtue of chastity and obedience surpassed even Liáng and Sòng.
Her father fell into the river, and his body could not be recovered.
É looked up to the sky and cried mournfully,
lamenting sadly in the middle of the river.
Then she threw herself into the water and died.
Both father and daughter were lost.
Later, their bodies emerged together.
The people of the state grieved their filial piety and righteousness,
and composed the ‘Hénǚ zhī Zhāng’ (Chapter of the River Girl) for her.
Wǔ Zǐxū advised the King of Wú,
but his words were not heeded.
He was executed and thrown into the sea.
The people of the state grieved his loyalty and heroism,
and composed the ‘Xiǎohǎi Chàng’ (Song of the Small Sea) for him.
Today, I wish to sing them.”
Everyone unanimously said:
“Excellent.”
Tǒng then tapped the boat with his foot,
and his voice trilled,
clear, stirring, and impassioned.
A great wind responded and arrived,
carrying water, splashing the sky.
Clouds and rain gathered with a roar,
shouts and cheers,
thunder and lightning darkened the day.
He gathered his qi and let out a long howl,
and sand and dust rose like smoke.
The princes and dukes and all below were afraid,
and only stopped him when he finished.
The people looked at each other and said:
“If we had not journeyed to the Luò River,
how would we have seen such a person!
Listening to the sound of the ‘Mùgē’,
we seemed to behold the countenance of Dà Yǔ.
Hearing the melody of the ‘Hénǚ’,
tears flowed unconsciously,
as if Bójī’s noble conduct were right before our eyes.
Listening to the ‘Xiǎohǎi Chàng’,
we felt Wǔ Zǐxū and Qū Píng standing by our side.”
Jiǎ Chōng wanted to impress him with his civil and military processions,
hoping he would come to watch,
and then offer his respects.
So he ordered red banners to be erected,
pennants and standards to be raised,
and feathered cavalry to be divided into formations.
The military ranks were solemn.
In a moment,
drums and pipes played riotously,
foreign horns blared loudly,
carriages intermingled chaotically,
galloping crisscross on the road.
He also had female entertainers wear fancy dresses,
displaying gold and jade,
circling his boat three times.
Tǒng sat upright as before,
as if he heard nothing.
Jiǎ Chōng and others dispersed, saying:
“This Wú fellow has a wooden man’s body and a stone heart.”
Tǒng returned to Kuàijī,
and his end was never known.
Zhū Chōng
Zhū Chōng, courtesy name Jùróng,
was a native of Nán'ān.
In his youth, he had utmost integrity,
was quiet and had few desires.
He loved learning but was poor,
often engaged in farming as his occupation.
A neighbor lost a calf,
mistook Zhōng’s calf for his own, and took it home.
Later, he found his own calf under a tree,
was greatly ashamed,
and returned the calf to Zhōng,
but Zhōng utterly refused to accept it.
When an ox damaged his crops,
Zhōng repeatedly carried fodder to feed the ox without showing any resentment.
The owner was ashamed of this,
and thereafter stopped being violent.
In the fourth year of Xiánníng (278 CE),
an imperial edict appointed him as a Boshi (Erudite),
but Zhōng declined, claiming illness.
Soon after, another imperial edict stated:
“The officials of the Eastern Palace should also include those who embody utmost integrity and are devoted to classical texts.
Therefore, Zhōng is to be appointed as Crown Prince’s Right Shùzǐ.”
Whenever Zhōng heard that a summons had arrived,
he would escape into the deep mountains.
People at the time considered him a man of the same caliber as Liáng and Guǎn.
Zhōng lived near barbarian customs,
and the Qiāng and Róng revered him as their lord.
Zhōng also instructed them with rites and humility,
and his village was transformed.
Nothing was picked up from the road,
there were no wicked people in the village,
and venomous insects and fierce beasts did no harm.
He eventually died of old age.
Fàn Càn (Zǐqiáo)
Fàn Càn, courtesy name Chéngmíng,
was a native of Wàihuáng, Chénliú, and a grandson of Dān, the Prefect of Láiwú in the Hàn dynasty.
Càn was noble, bright, chaste, and upright,
possessing the character of Dān.
He was widely learned and had a strong memory;
all his learning could serve as a teacher.
Many people from far and near sought his instruction.
By nature, he was not arrogant or formal,
yet everyone felt awe in his presence.
During the Wèi period, provincial and prefectural administrations repeatedly invited him,
but he accepted none.
After a long time,
he eventually accepted an appointment as Zhìzhōng,
then transferred to Biéjià.
He was appointed as Grand Commandant’s Yuàn and Shàngshū Láng,
and later served as Sīmǎ of the General Who Conquers the West.
In all the positions he held, he gained renown.
When Emperor Xuān (Sīmǎ Yì) assisted in governance,
he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
he selected good officials,
established schools,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
At this time, the Róng and Yí barbarians frequently encroached upon the borders.
Càn clearly established defenses,
and the enemy dared not invade.
Trade with the Western Regions flowed freely,
without the alarm of beacon fires.
Furthermore, the commandery’s land was rich and fertile,
accumulating many precious and rare goods.
Càn controlled this,
stopping its extravagance.
He resigned from office due to his mother’s old age.
As the commandery was close to the enemy,
the court found fault with Càn for suddenly leaving such an important post,
and demoted him to Magistrate of Lèguǎn.
After a short while,
he was transferred to be Tài zǎi Cóng shì Zhōng láng.
He experienced the grief of his mother’s death,
and was known for his extreme filial piety.
When the mourning period ended,
he again served as Tài zǎi Zhōng láng.
When Qí Wáng Fāng was deposed
and moved to Jīn yōng Chéng,
Càn wore plain clothes to bid him farewell,
grieving profoundly, moving those around him.
At that time, Jǐng Dì was assisting in governance,
and summoned officials for a meeting.
Càn again did not attend.
The imperial court, given his reputation at the time,
tolerated him.
Càn again feigned illness
and shut his door, not going out.
Thereupon, a special edict appointed him Shì zhōng,
holding the staff of authority as envoy to Yōng zhōu.
Càn then feigned madness and did not speak,
sleeping in his carriage,
his feet never touching the ground.
His sons and grandsons attended him,
and when there were major matters concerning marriage or official appointments,
they would secretly consult him.
If he approved, his expression would not change;
if he disapproved, he would sleep restlessly.
His wife and children thus understood his intentions.
When Wǔ Dì ascended the throne,
during the Tàishǐ reign,
Sūn Hé, Càn’s fellow townsman, was then Tài zǐ Zhōng shù zǐ.
He submitted a memorial recommending Càn,
praising his noble conduct
and stating that, though long afflicted by illness,
he could be brought to the capital by carriage from his commandery and county,
and with imperial grace
be granted medicine.
If he were to recover,
he would certainly benefit the government.
An edict was then issued for commanderies and counties to provide medicine,
and he was given a salary of two thousand dàn for his illness,
which became a regular annual stipend,
plus a special gift of a hundred bolts of silk.
His son Qiáo, fearing his father’s illness was critical,
declined to accept,
but the edict did not permit it.
He died in the sixth year of Tàikāng,
at the age of eighty-four.
He had not spoken for thirty-six years,
and died in the carriage where he slept.
His eldest son was Qiáo.
Qiáo’s courtesy name was Bó sūn.
When he was two years old,
his grandfather Xīn, on his deathbed,
stroked Qiáo’s head and said:
"I regret not seeing you grow up!"
He then gave him his inkstone.
At five years old,
his grandmother told Qiáo about it,
and Qiáo immediately held the inkstone and wept.
At nine, he requested to study,
and among his peers,
his words were never disrespectful.
Upon reaching adulthood,
he studied under Jiǎng Guó míng of Lè’ān.
Liú Gōng róng of Jìyīn, who had a reputation for judging people,
upon seeing Qiáo,
greatly admired him.
His friend Liú Yàn qiū, who had long been renowned,
once told people:
"Fàn Bó sūn's nature is pure and harmonious,
his reasoning thorough and meticulous.
I have often tried to find fault with him in one matter, but ultimately could not."
Guāng lù Dà fū Lǐ Quán once argued that Yáng Xióng’s talent and learning surpassed Liú Xiàng’s.
Qiáo believed that Xiàng established the writings of an entire era
and rectified the chapters of numerous classics.
If Xióng had been tasked with this,
it would not have been his strong suit.
He then wrote the Liú Yáng Yōu liè Lùn,
much of which is not recorded here.
Qiáo was fond of learning and never tired.
When his father Càn feigned madness and did not speak,
Qiáo and his two younger brothers both abandoned their studies,
eschewed social interaction,
and attended to their father’s illness at home.
Until Càn’s death,
they did not step out of their neighborhood.
Sī lì Xiào wèi Liú Yì once argued before the court, saying:
"If Fàn Wǔ wēi’s illness were not severe,
it would mean Bó Yí and Shú Qí live again today.
If it is indeed severe,
it is even more reason for the sagely ruler to show pity.
His son has long attended his father’s illness,
and his virtuous character is prominently established.
Not to employ him
is a deep criticism of the court for neglecting a worthy talent."
During the Yuánkāng reign,
an edict sought those who were modest, yielding, unassuming, who upheld the Way, and were of humble background,
regardless of their qualifications,
to be considered for selection.
Shàng shū Láng Wáng Kūn then recommended Qiáo, saying:
"Qiáo’s character is truly pure,
his integrity noble and undefiled,
his Confucian scholarship profound,
containing inner brilliance.
He is content in poverty and rejoices in the Way,
dedicating his aspirations to a humble alley.
With a single bamboo basket and gourd, he chants his works,
growing firmer with age.
He is truly a humble scholar of our time,
a clear talent who inspires and rectifies society."
At that time, Zhāng Huà was leading the Sī tú,
and among the seventeen individuals recommended from across the empire,
he gave a particularly favorable evaluation of Qiáo.
Moreover, Lì bù Láng Xī Lóng also sought reclusive gentlemen from within the seas,
and Qiáo had supported his family behind his humble gate
until his hair turned white.
Thereupon, he was appointed Magistrate of Lè’ān.
He declined, feigning illness, and did not accept.
Qiáo was recommended once as Xiào lián,
eight times to the ducal palaces,
twice as a pure and exceptional individual,
and again as a humble scholar,
but he accepted no appointments.
Initially,
on a lunar New Year's Eve, a person from Qiáo’s village secretly chopped down his tree.
Someone reported it,
but Qiáo feigned not hearing,
and the villager, ashamed, returned it.
Qiáo went to explain, saying:
"You took the firewood for the festival,
wishing to enjoy yourselves with your parents,
why should you be ashamed!"
His broad-mindedness and skill in guidance
were all of this kind.
Wài huáng Lìng Gāo Yūn sighed and said:
"Among the many scholar-officials, none have been free from self-interest,
yet Fàn Bó sūn diligently follows the Way.
His name has never appeared in official records due to any wrongdoing.
The nobility and uniqueness of a scholar
are seen in him today.
When the Great Way is abandoned, benevolence and righteousness arise –
this is truly so!"
His conduct, unblemished,
was admired and praised by others in this way.
He died in the eighth year of Yuánkāng,
aged seventy-eight.
Lǔ Shèng
Lǔ Shèng, courtesy name Shú shí,
was a native of Dài jùn.
In his youth, he possessed talent and integrity,
and served as Zuǒ Zhù zuò Láng.
In the early Yuánkāng period,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
Upon arriving at his post,
he wrote the Zhèng Tiān Lùn, saying:
"After the winter solstice, one should erect a gnomon to measure shadows,
and precisely determine the degrees of the sun, moon, and stars.
Your subject observes that the diameters of the sun and moon are merely a hundred *lǐ*,
not a thousand *lǐ*;
stars are ten *lǐ*,
not a hundred *lǐ*."
He then submitted a memorial requesting all high officials and scholars to examine and discuss it.
"If your subject's words are reasonable,
we should be able to correct the errors of previous generations
and rectify the order of heaven and earth.
If there is no verifiable evidence,
I willingly accept punishment,
to make known the crime of falsehood."
The matter was not reported back on.
He once observed atmospheric phenomena on New Year's Day,
and knowing that many troubles were coming,
he feigned illness and left his official post.
Zhōng shū Lìng Zhāng Huà sent his son to persuade him to re-enter service,
and he was twice summoned as Bó shì
and nominated as Zhōng shū Láng,
but he accepted none of these.
His writings were praised by his generation,
but were lost during the chaos.
Only his commentary on the Mò Biàn
survives, in which he states: "Names are used to distinguish similarities and differences,
to clarify right and wrong,
the gateway to morality,
and the standard for political transformation.
Confucius said:
'It is imperative to rectify names.
If names are not rectified,
then affairs will not be accomplished.'
Mò Zǐ wrote books,
composing the Biàn Jīng to establish the foundation of names.
Huì Shī and Gōng sūn Lóng inherited and developed his scholarship,
and became famous in the world for rectifying and distinguishing names.
Mèng
Zhū Fēi Mòzǐ,
his arguments and correct rhetoric were identical to those of Mò.
Xún Qīng, Zhuāng Zhōu, and others all disparaged and condemned the School of Names,
but they could not alter its theories.
Names must have form;
to examine form, nothing is better than distinguishing colors.
Hence, there was the debate on "hardness and whiteness."
Names must have clarity;
to achieve clarity, nothing is better than "being and non-being."
Hence, there was
the debate on "order and disorder."
"This is so, this is not so";
"can be, cannot be"—
this is called "ambiguous naming."
"Same yet different,"
"different yet same"—
this is called "debating sameness and difference."
"Reaching
ultimate sameness without anything being different,"
"reaching ultimate difference without anything being non-different"—
this is called "debating sameness and debating difference."
Sameness and difference give rise to right and wrong;
right and wrong give rise to fortune and misfortune.
To take an argument from a single object and trace it to the extreme
of the rise and fall of all under Heaven—
this is the ultimate of names.
From Dèng Xī to the School of Names thinkers of the Qín period,
there were compiled works in each generation,
but they were generally quite difficult to understand.
Later scholars no longer passed on and practiced them,
and now, after more than five hundred years,
they have been
completely lost.
The Mò辯 (Mò Biàn) has two parts, the Upper Jīng and the Lower Jīng.
Each Jīng has its explanations,
totaling four chapters.
They were arranged consecutively with other chapters in his book,
and thus they alone survived.
Now, the explanations are cited and aligned with the Jīng,
each appended
to its respective section.
Those that are doubtful are omitted.
Furthermore, two chapters, Xíngmíng (刑名), have been compiled from various miscellaneous collections,
briefly explaining their meaning and purpose,
awaiting discerning gentlemen.
Should anyone revive them or continue what was lost,
they
too would find joy in this!
Dǒng Yǎng
Dǒng Yǎng, courtesy name Zhòngdào,
was a native of Jùnyí in Chénliú.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he arrived at Luòxià,
but did not seek official position or honor.
When Empress Yáng was deposed,
Dǒng Yǎng went to the Imperial Academy,
ascended the hall, and sighed, saying:
"Why was this hall built?
What purpose will it serve?
Each time I read the imperial amnesty decrees,
all those who committed rebellion and high treason are pardoned,
but those who killed their grandparents or parents are not pardoned.
This is considered intolerable by royal law.
How can the high officials deliberate,
embellishing the codes of ritual,
to reach such a state!
When the principles of Heaven and man are extinguished,
great chaos will ensue."
Thereupon, he wrote the Wúhuà Lùn to criticize it.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
the ground collapsed in the Bùguǎnglǐ district northeast of Luòchéng.
Two geese emerged from it;
the grey one flew away,
but the white one could not fly.
Dǒng Yǎng heard of it and sighed, saying:
"The place where the Zhou dynasty once held an alliance at Díquán
is this very spot.
Now there are two geese;
the grey one symbolizes the Hú,
and the white one symbolizes the state.
How can one fully express it!"
He turned to Xiè Kūn and Ruǎn Fú and said:
"The Yì Jīng says, 'He who knows the subtle spring of action is divine indeed!'
You gentlemen should hide yourselves deeply."
Then he and his wife took up their burdens and entered Shǔ,
and no one knew their ultimate fate.
Huò Yuán
Huò Yuán, courtesy name Xiūmíng,
was a native of Guǎngyáng in Yān kingdom.
In his youth, he possessed ambition and strength.
When his uncle was sentenced to death for violating the law,
Huò Yuán entered prison to argue his case.
Despite enduring all manner of torture,
he ultimately secured his uncle's release.
At eighteen,
he observed the rituals at the Imperial Academy
and subsequently stayed to study them.
Noble youths heard of him and esteemed him,
wishing to meet him.
Considering his humble renown,
they did not wish to go by day,
so they collectively visited him at night.
His father's friend, Liú Dài from the same commandery, intended to recommend him,
but before he could, he fell gravely ill.
On his deathbed,
he instructed his son Shěn, saying:
"Huò Yuán admires the Dao, pure and empty;
he is destined to become an extraordinary talent.
You must recommend him later."
Later, Huò Yuán returned to his hometown.
Xǔ Měng of Gāoyáng had long admired his reputation.
When he became the Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
he intended to visit Huò Yuán,
but his chief clerk blocked his carriage, advising him not to leave the border.
Xǔ Měng sighed with regret and stopped.
Huò Yuán lived in the mountains for many years,
with hundreds of disciples.
The King of Yān sent him sheep and wine monthly.
When Liú Shěn became the Grand Central Censor of the state,
in the Yuánkāng era,
he advanced Huò Yuán to the second rank.
The Grand Tutor disagreed,
so Liú Shěn submitted a memorial to argue his case.
An imperial edict was issued for the Grand Tutor to discuss it.
Zhāng Huá, the Director of the Central Secretariat, ordered Chén Zhǔn to memorialize for him to be made a first-rank official,
and the edict was approved.
At the end of the Yuánkāng era,
Huò Yuán, along with Wáng Bāo and others, were summoned as Worthy and Excellent.
The summons was repeatedly sent down to the commanderies and districts,
and they were courteously dispatched,
but none arrived.
Later, Wáng Jùn proclaimed himself emperor and planned usurpation.
He sent someone to ask Huò Yuán,
but Huò Yuán did not reply.
Wáng Jùn bore a grudge against him in his heart.
There were also more than three hundred prisoners from Liáodōng
who had become bandits in the mountains,
intending to abduct Huò Yuán to be their leader,
but they had not yet acted.
At that time, there was a folk song that said:
"Where is the Son of Heaven?
Close by, in the bean fields."
Wáng Jùn interpreted "bean" (豆, dòu) as "Huò" (霍),
arrested Huò Yuán, and beheaded him,
hanging his head.
His students wept in sorrow,
secretly burying his body at night.
People far and near were shocked and dismayed,
and all grieved his injustice.
Guō Qí
Guō Qí, courtesy name Gōngwěi,
was a native of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
In his youth, he was straightforward
and possessed a refined character.
He was broadly learned
and skilled in the Wǔxíng (Five Phases).
He authored the Tiānwén Zhì and Wǔxíng Zhuàn,
and annotated the Gǔliáng Zhuàn and the Jīng Shì Yì, comprising one hundred volumes.
His fellow villagers, such as Wáng Yóu, all studied under Guō Qí.
Emperor Wǔ wished to appoint Guō Qí as Assistant to the Imperial Historiographer
and asked Guō Zhāng, a high official and relative of Guō Qí.
Guō Zhāng had always disliked Guō Qí
and replied:
"I do not know him."
The Emperor said:
"If what you say is true,
then a child from the Wūhuán tribe who serves you
would be qualified to be an official."
He then firmly decided to employ him.
When King Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
he also wished to employ Guō Qí.
Guō Qí said:
"I have already served as an official for Emperor Wǔ;
I cannot again serve as an official for the present age."
He remained at home for the rest of his life.
Wǔ Cháo
Wǔ Cháo 伍朝, courtesy name Shìmíng 世明,
was a native of Hànshòu 漢壽, Wǔlíng 武陵.
From a young age, he possessed refined conduct,
found joy in the Way while living in seclusion,
and did not involve himself in worldly affairs.
He was fond of learning by nature;
he was summoned as a Bóshì 博士 (Erudite),
but did not accept.
The Cìshǐ 刺史 (Inspector) Liú Hóng 劉弘 recommended Cháo 朝 to be the Tàishǒu 太守 (Grand Administrator) of Línglíng 零陵,
but the officials in charge refused,
citing it as contrary to selection regulations.
The Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎 (Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat) Hú Jì 胡濟 then memorialized, saying:
“Your servant believes that the current era, inheriting the remnants of chaos and disorder,
and the accumulated abuses of a hundred kings,
sees those who aggressively advance seizing national opportunities for their own gain,
while those who adhere to the Way keep their virtues hidden and live out their lives in obscurity.
This has diminished the culture of honor and commendation
and weakened the custom of modesty and deference.
Upon examination, Cháo 朝 dedicates his mind to matters beyond this world,
cares not for current affairs,
lives quietly behind his humble gate,
and his aspiration for the Way grows daily.
He is over sixty years old, yet his high ideals remain undiminished.
He is truly an exceptional talent from Jiāngnán 江南
and a reclusive elder from the countryside.
If we do not promote such individuals,
how can we encourage good?
Moreover, for a commoner to become a commander of a commandery
has precedents in the Former Hàn 前漢 dynasty.
It is fitting to allow him to be distinguished,
to encourage such a noble custom.”
The memorial was approved,
but Cháo 朝 did not accept the position,
and died at home.
Lǔ Bāo 魯褒
Lǔ Bāo 魯褒, courtesy name Yuándào 元道,
was a native of Nányáng 南陽.
He loved learning and was widely read,
establishing himself through poverty and simplicity.
After the Yuánkāng 元康 era,
the social order greatly deteriorated.
Bāo 褒 grieved over the greed and baseness of the times,
so he concealed his name
and wrote the *Qián Shén Lùn* 錢神論 (Discourse on the Spirit of Money) to criticize it.
Its summary states: The form of money
resembles that of Heaven and Earth;
its interior is square,
its exterior is round.
Its accumulation is like a mountain,
its flow like a river.
It has its times for motion and stillness,
and its measures for activity and concealment.
It is convenient for markets,
and not susceptible to damage or wear.
Not easily broken symbolizes longevity,
not depleted symbolizes the Way;
thus it can last long,
and is considered a divine treasure by the world.
We treat it as a
brother,
calling it
“Kǒng Fāng 孔方” (Square Hole).
To lose it is to be poor and weak;
to gain it is to be rich and prosperous.
It flies without wings,
it walks without feet.
It softens stern and severe faces,
and opens difficult-to-open
mouths.
Those with much money are at the forefront;
those with little money are at the rear.
Those at the forefront are rulers and lords;
those at the rear are ministers and servants.
Rulers and lords are abundant and have
surplus;
ministers and servants are impoverished and insufficient.
The *Shī Jīng* 詩經 (Classic of Poetry) says:
“Ah, the rich man is well off!
Pity this solitary one!”
The word 'qián 錢' (money) means 'quán 泉' (spring);
there is no distant place it does not reach,
no hidden place it does not arrive.
The officials in the capital,
weary from lectures and studies,
tired of hearing pure conversation,
fall asleep when facing it;
but upon seeing our brother,
none fail to look up in surprise.
Where money bestows its blessing,
all is auspicious and beneficial.
Why must one read books
to achieve wealth and nobility?
In the past, Lǚ Gōng 呂公 rejoiced at an empty
account;
the Hànzǔ 漢祖 (Emperor Gāozǔ 高祖 of Hàn) conquered with a mere two coins.
Wén Jūn 文君 exchanged her cotton dress for brocade and embroidery;
Xiāngrú 相如 rode in a grand carriage and discarded his calf-nose trousers.
Honored office and distinguished fame
are all achieved
by money.
An empty account is utterly hollow,
how much more so if it were substantial!
Even two small coins,
can lead to intimacy.
From this perspective,
it is called a divine object.
It is honored without virtue,
and popular
without power.
It can push through golden gates and enter purple palaces.
It can make the dangerous safe,
and the dead live.
It can make the noble base,
and the living killed.
Therefore, disputes cannot be won
without money;
obscurity cannot be removed without money;
enmity cannot be resolved without money;
a good reputation cannot be spread without money.
The red-robed officials in Luòyáng 洛陽,
the powerful figures of the day,
all love our brother
without end.
They hold my hand,
embrace me from beginning to end,
without considering superiority or inferiority,
without discussing
age.
Guests flock to their doors,
which are constantly like a marketplace.
A proverb says:
“Money has no ears,
yet it can make ghosts work.”
All people today
care only for money.
Therefore it is said: If an army has no
wealth,
soldiers will not come;
if an army has no rewards,
soldiers will not go.
If one has no intermediary in officialdom,
it is better to return to farming.
Even if one has an intermediary,
but not our brother,
it is no different from wanting to fly
without wings,
or wanting to walk without feet.
Those who detested the times widely circulated his work.
Bāo 褒 did not serve in office;
the manner of his end is unknown.
Fàn Téng 氾騰
Fàn Téng 氾騰, courtesy name Wújì 無忌,
was a native of Dūnhuáng 敦煌.
He was nominated as Xiàolián 孝廉 (Filial and Incorrupt),
and appointed Lángzhōng 郎中 (Gentleman).
When great disorder broke out across the land,
he resigned his post and returned home.
The Tàishǒu 太守 (Grand Administrator) Zhāng Bì 張閟 visited him,
but he kept his gate closed and refused to see him,
accepting none of his gifts.
He sighed, saying:
“Born in a time of chaos,
only by being noble yet able to live in poverty
can one escape harm.”
He distributed fifty million of his family wealth
to his relatives,
and lived contentedly with his simple brushwood gate, tending his garden,
playing the qín 琴, and reading books.
Zhāng Guǐ 張軌 summoned him to be his Fǔ Sīmǎ 府司馬 (Chief Clerk of the Administrator's Office),
but Téng 騰 said:
“Once a gate is closed,
how can it be opened again!”
He firmly declined.
He fell ill for over two months and then passed away.
Rèn Xù 任旭
Rèn Xù
zì Cìlóng, was a native of Zhāng'ān, Línghǎi.
His father, Fǎng,
was the Grand Protector of Nánhǎi for the Wú dynasty.
Xù was orphaned and weak in his youth,
and diligent in study as a child.
When he grew up,
he established a pure conduct and cultivated himself,
untainted by worldly customs,
and the people of his乡曲 esteemed and loved him.
The Commander of the commandery, Jiǎng Xiù, admired his reputation,
and invited him to serve as Gōngcáo.
Xiù was greedy and corrupt in office,
often disregarding the law,
and Xù, with a serious demeanor, earnestly remonstrated with him.
Since Xiù did not accept his advice,
Xù resigned and left,
closing his door to teach and study,
merely cultivating his aspirations.
After a long time,
Xiù was arrested for his misdeeds.
Xù, in distress, attended to his affairs and provided for him.
Xiù sighed with emotion and said:
"Gōngcáo Rèn is truly a man of character.
I disregarded his upright words,
which led me to this.
What more can I say!"
Soon after, he was selected as Xiàolián
and appointed Lángzhōng.
The province and commandery repeatedly nominated him as the Zhōngzhèng of the commandery,
but he firmly declined and returned home.
In the early years of Yǒngkāng,
Emperor Huì extensively sought out men of pure character and exceptional talent.
Grand Protector Qiú Fù recommended Xù as pure, upright, and unblemished,
with extensive and profound learning.
An imperial edict was issued to the province and commandery to send for him with proper ceremony.
Xù, considering the many troubles at court,
and aspiring to a life of reclusion,
declined on grounds of illness and did not go.
Soon the world fell into great chaos.
Chén Mǐn rebelled,
and the prominent figures of Jiāngdōng were all imprisoned.
Only Xù and Hè Xún held firm to death and did not yield.
Mǐn was ultimately unable to subdue them.
When Emperor Yuán first took up residence in Jiāngdōng,
he heard of Xù's reputation
and summoned him to be a Cānjūn.
He personally wrote to Xù,
desiring his sure arrival,
but Xù firmly declined due to illness.
Later, when the Emperor was promoted to Zhèndōng Dàjiàngjūn,
he summoned him again;
and when he became Zuǒ Chéngxiàng,
he appointed him Jìjiǔ,
but Xù did not accept any of these positions.
When the Zhōngxīng era began,
he was summoned by Gōngchē,
but happened to be mourning his mother.
At that time, Sīkōng Wáng Dǎo proposed the establishment of schools,
selecting scholars skilled in the classics from throughout the realm.
Xù, along with Yú Xǐ of Kuàijī, were summoned for their reclusive scholarship.
Before the matter could proceed,
the disturbance of Wáng Dūn occurred.
Soon after, the Emperor died,
and the matter was dropped.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he again summoned him and appointed him Gěishìzhōng.
Xù claimed severe illness,
and did not arrive for a year.
The Shàngshū decided to remove him from office for delaying,
but Púyè Xún Sōng argued that it was improper.
At the end of Tàiníng,
Emperor Míng again issued an edict, fully equipping the ceremony to summon Xù.
But just as the edict was issued, the Emperor died.
He passed away in the second year of Xiánhé (327 CE).
Grand Protector Féng Huái submitted a memorial suggesting he should be posthumously granted the rank of Jiǔliè,
but due to the rebellion of Sū Jùn,
the matter was never carried out.
His son, Jū,
reached the position of Dàzōngzhèng,
and died at home.
Guō Wén
Guō Wén, zì Wénjǔ,
was a native of Zhǐ, Hénèi.
From a young age, he loved mountains and rivers,
and favored a life of reclusion.
At thirteen,
he would often wander in the mountains and forests,
forgetting to return for ten days.
When his parents died,
after completing the mourning period,
he did not marry,
left home, and roamed famous mountains,
traveling to the cliffs of Huá Yīn
to observe the stone caskets in the stone chamber.
When Luòyáng fell,
he then walked, carrying his belongings, into a remote, uninhabited valley in Dàpì Shān, Yúháng, Wúxīng.
He leaned wood against a tree,
covered it with thatch, and lived there,
without any walls.
At that time, fierce beasts were rampant,
entering houses and harming people,
yet Wén slept alone for over ten years,
and was never harmed.
He wore a deerskin cloak and a kudzu-fiber turban,
did not drink wine or eat meat,
cultivated soybeans and wheat in small plots,
gathered bamboo shoots and wild fruits,
and traded for salt to support himself.
If people offered a low price,
he would still give it to them.
Later, people recognized Wén,
and no longer offered cheap prices.
If he had surplus grain,
he would always help the poor and needy.
If someone offered him gifts,
he would take only the coarse ones,
showing that he did not refuse outright.
Once, a fierce beast killed a large doe near his hermitage.
Wén told people about it,
and they took and sold it,
sharing the money with Wén.
Wén said:
"If I needed this,
I would have sold it myself.
The reason I told you
is precisely because I don't need it."
Those who heard him all sighed in admiration.
Once, a fierce beast suddenly opened its mouth towards Wén.
Wén saw a transverse bone in its mouth,
so he reached in with his hand and removed it.
The next morning, the fierce beast brought a deer to the front of his dwelling.
Hunters sometimes stayed with him,
and Wén would carry water for them at night without showing any sign of fatigue.
The magistrate of Yúháng, Gù Yáng, and Gě Hóng together visited him,
and took him to return with them.
Yáng thought Wén might need leather clothing for mountain travel,
and presented him with a set of leather leggings and jacket.
Wén did not accept it,
and declined to return to the mountains.
Yáng sent an envoy to place the clothing in his dwelling and depart.
Wén also said nothing,
and the leather clothing eventually rotted inside his door,
as he never wore it.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) heard of his name,
and sent men to welcome him.
Wén (文) refused to take the boat or carriage,
but carried his burden and walked.
When he arrived,
Dǎo (導) placed him in the West Garden.
The garden was full of fruit trees forming a forest,
and there were also birds, beasts, and deer.
Wén (文) was thus lodged there.
Thereupon, all the court officials came to observe him.
Wén (文) sat slumped and sprawling,
as if there were no one else around.
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) once asked Wén (文),
“Everyone has six kinds of relatives to enjoy.
What pleasure do you find in abandoning them, Sir?”
Wén (文) replied,
“I originally pursued the Dao (道) through study.
I did not expect to encounter a chaotic world.
With no path to return home,
this is why I came.”
He asked again,
“Hunger leads to thoughts of food,
and vigor leads to thoughts of a spouse.
These are natural inclinations.
How can you alone, Sir, be without feelings?”
Wén (文) replied,
“Feelings arise from memory.
Without memory, there are no feelings.”
He asked again,
“Sir, you live alone in the desolate mountains.
If you were to fall ill or meet your end,
you would be devoured by crows and other birds.
Do you not consider this cruel?”
Wén (文) replied,
“Those who are buried are also eaten by ants and other insects.
How is that any different!”
He asked again,
“Fierce beasts harm people,
which is something people fear.
But why do you alone, Sir, not fear them?”
Wén (文) replied,
“If people have no intention to harm beasts,
then beasts will also not harm people.”
He asked again,
“If the world is not peaceful,
one’s person cannot be at ease.
Now, if we were to use your life to save the times,
what would you say?”
Wén (文) replied,
“A person of mountain grass [i.e., a recluse]
how can he assist the world!”
Dǎo (導) once gathered many guests,
with strings and flutes playing in unison,
and tried to call for Wén (文).
Wén (文) stared with unmoving eyes,
and strode through the splendid hall as if walking in a wilderness.
At that time, those seated all uttered profound and far-reaching words,
but Wén (文) always claimed not to understand what was said.
His divine essence was profound and echoing,
and no one could glimpse its gate.
Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) once praised him, saying,
“Wén (文) has the nature of a worthy man,
but not the talent of a worthy man,
perhaps a junior to Liǔxià (柳下) and Liáng Yǐ (梁踦)!”
During the Yǒngchāng (永昌) era,
there was a great plague,
and Wén (文) was also critically ill.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) sent medicine,
Wén (文) said,
“Life is in heaven,
not in medicine.
Longevity or brevity,
is a matter of time.”
He lived in Dǎo’s (導) garden for seven years,
and never went in or out.
One day, he suddenly asked to return to the mountains,
but Dǎo (導) did not allow it.
Later, he escaped and returned to Lín’ān (臨安),
building a hut in the mountains.
Wàn Chǒng (萬寵), the Magistrate of Lín’ān (臨安), welcomed him and lodged him in the county seat.
When Sū Jùn (蘇峻) rebelled,
he devastated Yúháng (餘杭),
but Lín’ān (臨安) alone remained intact.
Everyone was surprised by this,
believing he understood the opportune moment.
Thereafter, he no longer spoke,
but only gestured with his hands,
to convey his meaning.
When his illness became severe,
he asked to return to the mountains,
wishing to rest his body on a stone and not be buried by others.
Chǒng (寵) did not allow it.
He did not eat for more than twenty days,
and also did not grow thin.
Chǒng (寵) asked,
“Sir, how many more days can you last?”
Wén (文) raised his hands three times,
and indeed died fifteen days later.
Chǒng (寵) buried him at the place where he lived and offered sacrifices and wept for him.
Gě Hóng (葛洪) and Yǔ Chǎn (庾闡) both wrote biographies for him,
eulogizing his virtues.
Gōng Zhuàng (龔壯)
Gōng Zhuàng (龔壯),
courtesy name Zǐwěi (子瑋),
was a native of Bāxī (巴西).
He maintained his integrity and self-discipline,
and was as renowned as Qiáo Xiù (譙秀) in his native place.
His father, Shū (叔), was killed by Lǐ Tè (李特).
Zhuàng (壯) did not remove his mourning clothes for many years,
but was too weak to avenge him.
When Lǐ Shòu (李壽) garrisoned Hànzhōng (漢中),
he had a grudge against Lǐ Qī (李期).
Qī (期)
was Tè’s (特) grandson.
Zhuàng (壯) wanted to use Shòu (壽) to exact revenge,
so he persuaded Shòu (壽), saying:
“If Your Excellency can annex the Western lands,
and become a vassal to Jìn (晉),
the people will surely happily follow.
Moreover, to abandon the small for the great,
and exchange danger for security,
is the greatest strategy.”
Shòu (壽) agreed with him,
and thereupon led his troops to attack Qī (期),
and indeed conquered him.
Shòu (壽) still assumed the false title,
and wanted to appoint Zhuàng (壯) to office,
but Zhuàng (壯) vowed not to serve,
and took absolutely nothing from the bribes and gifts.
It happened that there was prolonged rain,
and the people suffered from hunger and inundation.
Zhuàng (壯) submitted a memorial persuading Shòu (壽) to surrender to the court,
to accord with Heaven’s will,
and respond to the people’s hopes,
to be a perpetual bulwark for the state,
and for blessings to flow to his descendants.
Shòu (壽) read the letter and felt inward shame,
but kept it secret and did not publicize it.
Then he sent envoys to the Hu (胡),
and Zhuàng (壯) again remonstrated against it,
but Shòu (壽) again did not accept it.
Zhuàng (壯) believed that among all actions, loyalty and filial piety were the greatest.
Having used Shòu (壽) to kill Qī (期),
his private vendetta was avenged,
and he also wanted to make him return to the court,
to demonstrate the integrity of a minister.
Since Shòu (壽) did not comply,
Zhuàng (壯) then pretended to be deaf,
and also said his hands could not control objects,
and would never again go to Chéngdū (成都) in his lifetime.
He only devoted himself to studying the classics,
and contemplating literature.
Initially,
Zhuàng (壯) often lamented that Central China had many scholars of classics,
while Bā Shǔ (巴蜀) was crude and unrefined,
and also suffered the calamity of the Lǐ (李) family,
with no more students.
So he wrote the *Màidé Lùn* (邁德論),
much of the text of which is not recorded.
Mèng Lòu (孟陋)
Mèng Lòu (孟陋),
courtesy name Shǎogū (少孤),
was a native of Wǔchāng (武昌).
He was the great-grandson of Wú Sīkōng Zōng (吳司空宗).
His elder brother, Jiā (嘉),
was the Western Expedition Chief Clerk for Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Lòu (陋) was chaste and upright in his youth,
his pure conduct incomparable.
Wearing plain clothes and eating simple food,
he found enjoyment in literary works.
He did not speak of worldly affairs,
and never socialized.
Sometimes he would hunt or fish,
going alone with solitary pleasure;
When his mother died,
he grieved and wasted away almost to the point of losing his life,
not drinking wine or eating meat for more than ten years.
His relatives took turns saying to him,
“Shǎogū (少孤)!
Who is without parents?
Who has parents [forever]?
The sages established rituals,
allowing the worthy to comply humbly,
and the unworthy to strive to reach them.
If you destroy your nature and leave no heirs,
that would be even more unfilial.”
Lòu (陋) was moved by these words,
and only then followed the auspicious [customs].
Guō Fān 字 Chángxiáng,
was a native of Wǔchāng.
His paternal uncle, Nà,
was the Prefect of Guǎngzhōu.
His father, Chá,
was the Administrator of Ānchéng.
Fān was ambitious and principled from a young age,
declining invitations from the provinces and commanderies, as well as recommendations for "worthy and good" men.
He made his home in Línchuān,
not involving himself in worldly affairs,
finding enjoyment only in fishing, hunting, and fowling.
Living in poverty and without an occupation,
he wished to cultivate wasteland.
He would first erect a marker,
and if it remained unclaimed for a year,
then he would proceed with the cultivation.
When the rice was about to ripen,
if someone claimed it,
he would completely yield it to them.
The county magistrate heard of this and questioned him,
returning the rice to Fān,
but Fān firmly refused to accept it.
Once, when hunting by carriage,
he was over a hundred *lǐ* from home.
He encountered a sick person on the road,
and gave them his carriage to send them home,
while he walked back himself.
Whatever he obtained from fishing or hunting,
if someone wanted to buy it,
he would give it to them without taking payment,
nor would he reveal his name.
Because of this, scholars and commoners alike respected and esteemed him.
He and Zhái Tāng were both recommended by Yǔ Liàng.
He was summoned by the "Public Carriage Scholar" (Gōngchē Bóshì),
but did not accept the appointment.
At the end of Xiánkāng (咸康) era,
he briefly returned to Wǔchāng in a small boat to visit his ancestral tombs.
The General of the West-Pacifying Army, Yǔ Yì, despite the great importance of being the emperor's maternal uncle,
personally went to visit Fān,
intending to force him to take office.
Fān said:
"Every person has their shortcomings;
how can one be forced!"
Yì then, seeing his boat was small and narrow,
wished to invite him to a larger vessel.
Fān said:
"That you, Sir, do not disdain my humbleness and condescend to visit me,
this is indeed the boat of a rustic."
Yì bent down and entered his boat,
staying the whole day before leaving.
Once, he dropped his knife into the water,
and a passerby retrieved it for him.
He then offered it to the passerby.
The passerby would not take it,
firmly refusing.
Fān said:
"If you hadn't retrieved it just now,
how could I have gotten it back?"
The passerby said:
"If I were to take this,
I would surely be blamed by Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits."
Fān knew he would ultimately not accept it,
so he again sank the knife into the water.
The passerby sighed regretfully,
and then dove in again to retrieve it.
Fān then, not going against his wishes,
gave him ten times the knife's value.
His incorruptibility and refusal of favors
were all of this kind.
He died at home.
Xīn Mì
Xīn Mì, 字 Shúzhòng,
was a native of Dídào, Lǒngxī.
His father, Yí,
was the Prefect of Yōuzhōu,
and the family was known as a prominent clan.
Mì had lofty aspirations from a young age,
was widely learned and skilled at writing prose,
and excelled in *cǎo* (cursive) and *lì* (clerical) script,
serving as a calligraphic model for his time.
He was tranquil by nature
and did not associate lightly with others.
He was summoned to be appointed as a Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ Shèrén) and Royal Literary Scholar (Zhūwáng Wénxué),
but repeatedly declined the summons.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) era,
Mì was appointed as an Attendant Censor (Sànqí Chángshì) to pacify Guānzhōng.
Mì, seeing that Luòyáng was about to fall,
therefore accepted.
When Cháng'ān fell to Liú Cōng,
Cōng appointed him Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
but he firmly refused the appointment.
He also lived through the eras of Shí Lè and Jìlóng (石勒, 季龍),
but did not accept any invitations for appointment.
Although living amidst chaos and upheaval,
he remained aloof and refined,
regarding honor and profit as nothing.
When Rǎn Mǐn usurped the throne,
he was again summoned with full ceremony to be Grand Sacrificer (Tàicháng).
Mì sent a letter to Mǐn, saying:
"In ancient times, Xǔ Yóu declined Yáo's (堯) offer,
yielding the empire to him,
thereby preserving his pure and lofty integrity.
Bó Yí left his state,
and Zǐ Tuī fled from rewards;
all are prominently recorded in history,
transmitted endlessly.
These are those who left and did not return.
However, worthy men and gentlemen, even when dwelling in the imperial court,
are no different than when in the mountains and forests.
This is the subtlety of exhaustively investigating principles and fully realizing one's nature;
how could there be those who truly understand it!
Therefore, those who are not entangled in misfortune and calamity
do not avoid them;
they merely align their minds with the ultimate truth and thus meet with auspiciousness.
I have heard that when things reach their extreme, they change,
as with winter and summer;
when one attains the highest position, one is in peril,
as with a stack of chess pieces.
Your Majesty's accomplishments are already complete,
but to remain in that position for too long
is not the way to ensure complete safety and distance oneself from the calamity of ruin.
It would be fitting, after this great victory,
to return yourself to the proper court (Běncháo).
You would surely possess the incorruptibility of Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yí,
enjoy the longevity of Sōng Qiáo (松喬),
and forever be an aid to the world.
Would this not be excellent?"
Thereupon he stopped eating and died.
Liú Línzhī
Liú Línzhī, 字 Zǐjì,
was a native of Nányáng,
and a member of the clan of the Grand Master of Guanglù, Dān (耽).
Línzhī was simple and unadorned from a young age,
humble, retiring, and had few desires.
He did not cultivate proper demeanor,
and people did not know him.
He enjoyed wandering in mountains and marshes,
with a mind set on reclusion and escape.
Once, while gathering herbs, he reached Héngshān,
penetrating so deeply that he forgot to return.
He saw a stream,
and south of the stream were two stone granaries (quán),
one closed,
one open.
The water was too deep and wide to cross.
Wishing to return,
he lost his way.
He met a man cutting bows,
asked for directions,
and barely managed to return home.
Some said that inside the granaries were immortal elixirs and various other items.
Línzhī wished to search for them again,
but never found the place again.
The General of Chariots and Cavalry, Huán Chōng, heard of his reputation
and invited him to be his Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).
Línzhī firmly refused to accept.
Once, Chōng visited his home.
Línzhī was grafting mulberry trees on a branch.
The envoy delivered the message.
Línzhī said:
"Since you, Sir, have troubled yourself to honor us with your presence,
you should first visit my father."
Chōng heard this and was greatly ashamed,
so he then went to visit his father.
His father summoned Línzhī,
and only then did he return.
He brushed his coarse hemp garment and conversed with Chōng.
His father had Línzhī personally bring cloudy wine and vegetables from inside to serve the guest.
Chōng ordered his attendants to pour the wine and serve the dishes in Línzhī's place.
His father declined, saying:
"If you use attendants,
it is not the intention of a rustic."
Chōng felt a deep emotion, and did not leave until dusk.
Lín Zhī, though from a family of high-ranking officials,
his trustworthiness was well-known even among the common people.
For any family, be they commoners or servants,
he personally attended their weddings, funerals, and burials.
He lived in Yángqí,
by the side of the official road.
People passing by,
none failed to stop at his place.
Lín Zhī personally provided for them all,
which the gentry found quite burdensome,
and they therefore hesitated to pass by his home.
He accepted nothing from people who offered him gifts.
He received absolutely nothing.
About a hundred *lǐ* away from Lín Zhī's home,
there lived an old solitary woman
who was critically ill.
She sighed and said to people,
"Who will bury me?
Only Liú Chángshǐ will!
How can I let him know?"
Lín Zhī, having heard in advance of her illness,
went to visit her.
He arrived just as she was passing away,
so he personally arranged for her coffin and burial.
His compassion and sympathy were like this.
He eventually died of old age.
Suǒ Xí
Suǒ Xí, courtesy name Wěi Zǔ,
was a native of Dūnhuáng.
He was tranquil and studious,
and did not respond to invitations from prefectures or commanderies.
He declined all nominations for Filial and Incorrupt, Worthy and Upright,
citing illness.
He delved into the arts of *yīn* and *yáng*,
and authored over ten chapters on astronomy and geography,
which were very insightful.
He did not socialize with his contemporaries.
Sometimes he would talk to himself or laugh to himself,
sometimes he would sigh deeply and weep,
or sometimes he would ask questions but then not speak.
During Zhāng Mào's time,
Yīn Dàn, the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng, found him extraordinary and went to visit him.
He stayed for a whole day, forgetting to return,
and upon leaving, he sighed,
"Master Suǒ is a scholar of profound virtue and renown,
truly one with whom to consult on great matters of principle."
Dàn wished to perform the *xiāngshè* ritual
and asked Xí to serve as the Three Elders.
He said,
"Now the four directions are peaceful and united.
I plan to perform the *xiāngshè* ritual.
Sir, your advanced age and esteemed reputation,
your wisdom surpasses your time.
The duty of caring for the elderly
is truly tied to scholarly worthies.
To plant not a *wútóng* tree,
yet hope for the *luánfèng* to descend;
to lack the capacity of Cáo Gōng,
yet hope for Gài Gōng to grace us with his presence—
this is truly not what I mean.
However, the Master (Confucius) was a supreme sage,
yet he responded to summons;
Mèng Kē (Mencius) was of great virtue,
and never failed to attend when invited.
This was presumably to promote and spread the Great Way
and enlighten the teachings.
My current invitation to you,
to follow the Way and revere the teachings,
is not for any official position.
Perhaps this may be acceptable!"
Soon after, he fell ill and died,
at the age of seventy-nine.
Dàn wore plain clothes to attend the funeral
and offered twenty thousand coins.
Dàn said,
"What common people have in abundance
is wealth and nobility;
what their eyes delight in
are the five colors;
what their ears enjoy
are the five sounds.
Yet the Master abandoned what the masses collect,
and collected what the masses discard.
He tasted the tasteless amid the vague and indistinct,
and embraced the profound mystery within all wonders.
His dwelling did not exceed an *mǔ*, yet his ambition transcended the Nine Provinces;
his body resided in the mundane world, yet his heart dwelled beyond the heavens.
Even Qián Lóu's loftiness
and Zhuāng Shēng's detachment
cannot surpass him."
He was then given the posthumous title Xuán Jū Xiānshēng.
Yáng Kē
Yáng Kē was
a native of Tiānshuǐ.
In his youth, he loved the *Yì Jīng*.
He grew old without marrying.
His scholarship was profound and subtle.
He gathered hundreds of disciples.
He constantly ate coarse food and drank water,
wearing coarse linen and patched robes.
Others could not bear his hardships,
but Kē was perfectly content.
With ordinary guests and unusual visitors,
he never exchanged words.
Even among his disciples,
only the inner-chamber disciples
were allowed to speak intimately with him.
When he wished to discuss or teach something,
there had to be no other people present.
He would teach his inner-chamber disciples,
who would then relay the teachings to each other.
When Liú Yào usurped the throne,
he summoned Kē and appointed him Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Kē firmly declined and did not report for duty.
Yào also respected him and did not force him,
so Kē withdrew into Lǒng Shān.
Later, when Yào was captured by Shí Lè,
and the people of Qín moved east,
Kē remained in Cháng'ān.
When Shí Jìlóng succeeded to the usurped throne,
he prepared black and crimson silks, bolts of fabric, and an imperial carriage to summon him.
Kē declined due to illness.
When he was pressed,
he finally set out.
Upon seeing Jìlóng,
he did not bow
and did not speak when addressed.
He was ordered to be housed in the second residence of Yǒngchāng.
His officials, considering Kē arrogant,
requested that he be charged with gross disrespect.
Jìlóng did not comply,
and issued an order allowing Kē to follow his own preferences.
While Kē was in Yǒngchāng,
whenever Jìlóng sent provisions,
Kē would verbally instruct his disciples
to write memorials of thanks.
Their writings were very beautiful,
and those who read them praised their profound meaning.
Jìlóng wished to observe his true nature,
so he secretly ordered beautiful women
to try to tempt him at night,
but Kē remained calm and ignored them.
He also had people take all of Kē's disciples away,
and sent burly Jié soldiers, clad in armor and bearing swords,
to confront him with weapons,
and also secretly carried away the clothes he had been given.
Kē looked at them and spoke,
showing no fear whatsoever.
He often slept on the bare earth,
covered with a cloth quilt,
sleeping naked beneath it,
with no mattress or cushion below.
Xún Pù of Yǐngchuān,
a man fond of curiosities,
came to him to discuss the classics.
Kē closed his eyes and did not respond.
Pù pulled off Kē's quilt,
exposing his body,
and laughed loudly at him.
Kē's spirit and body remained relaxed,
showing no signs of shock or anger.
At that time, everyone considered him a follower of Jiāo Xiān,
and no one could fathom his depth.
Later, he submitted a memorial expressing his homesickness
and requested to return.
Jìlóng sent him back with an imperial carriage with rush wheels,
and exempted ten households to provide for him.
After returning to Qín Zhōu,
he continued teaching without interruption.
Later, when the people of Qín fled west to Liáng Zhōu,
Kē's disciples carried him on an ox.
They were pursued and captured by the garrison army,
and both were killed.
Gōngsūn Fèng
Gōngsūn Fèng, courtesy name Zǐ Luán,
was a native of Shànggǔ.
He lived in reclusion in the Jiǔchéng mountain valley of Chānglí.
In winter, he wore a single layer of coarse cloth;
he slept on an earthen bed.
In summer, he would eat all his meals from a single vessel,
allowing the food to spoil
before consuming it.
He played the *qín* and chanted poetry,
contented and at ease.
Everyone found him strange,
and no one could understand him.
Mùróng Wěi summoned him with an imperial carriage to Yè.
Upon seeing Wěi,
he neither spoke nor bowed.
His clothing, food, and demeanor were as they were in Jiǔchéng.
When guests came to visit and request an audience,
few were able to speak with him.
He died of illness after several years.
Gōngsūn Yǒng
Gōngsūn Yǒng
zì Zǐyáng, a native of Xiāngpíng.
While young, he loved learning and was tranquil and humble.
He lived as a recluse on the Southern Mountain of Píngguō,
taking no wife or concubine.
Unless he himself cultivated it,
he would not eat or wear it.
He recited poetry among the cliffs,
joyfully content.
When over ninety years old,
his integrity and aspirations remained undiminished.
He and Gōngsūn Fèng were both summoned by Mùróng Wěi to Yè.
When he saw Wěi,
he did not bow.
Princes, dukes, and those below them who visited him
were not spoken to.
Even through severe winter and scorching summer,
he remained composed.
After more than a year,
he feigned madness,
and Wěi sent him back to Píngguō.
Later, Fú Jiān again intended to summon him with complete禮,
but finding him advanced in age and the journey long,
he sent an envoy to inquire after him.
Yǒng died before the envoy arrived.
Jiān deeply lamented his passing
and posthumously honored him with the title "Chóngxū Xiānshēng."
Zhāng Zhōng
Zhāng Zhōng
zì Jùhé, a native of Zhōngshān.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he lived as a recluse on Tài Shān.
He was tranquil and quiet, with few desires,
pure and ethereal, practicing "qì-breathing,"
eating ganoderma and mineral elixirs,
and cultivating methods of self-nurturing.
In winter, he wore a simple padded robe;
in summer, a rope belt.
He sat upright as if a corpse.
He had no interest in zither or books,
nor did he study the classics.
His teachings were based solely on the ultimate Dao and emptiness.
He resided in remote cliffs and secluded valleys,
carving a cave dwelling into the earth.
His disciples also lived in caves,
more than sixty paces from Zhōng,
visiting him once every five days.
His teaching was through form, not words.
Disciples, upon receiving instruction,
would observe his form and then withdraw.
He erected a Daoist altar above his cave,
worshiping it every morning.
He used earthenware for food,
and carved a cauldron from stone.
Local residents offered him clothing and food,
but he accepted none.
Some curious youths occasionally asked him about omens of flood or drought.
Zhōng said:
"Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons proceed
and all things are born.
Matters of Yin and Yang are not for a hermit in a remote mountain to know."
His dismissal of all external matters
was always of this kind.
He was over one hundred years old,
yet his sight and hearing were unimpaired.
Fú Jiān sent an envoy to summon him.
When the envoy arrived,
Zhōng bathed and arose,
saying to his disciples:
"I have few years left;
I cannot go against the will of the present ruler."
After bathing, he got into the carriage.
Upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
Jiān bestowed a hat and robe upon him.
He declined, saying:
"My hair is falling out with age;
I am not suited for official attire.
Please allow me to appear in my rustic clothes."
Jiān agreed.
When they met,
Jiān said to him:
"Sir has lived peacefully in the mountains and forests,
〔一三〕delving deeply into the essence of the Dao.
The beauty of self-perfection is abundant,
but the merit of benefiting others is yet to come.
Therefore, I have troubled you from afar,
intending to entrust you with the role of Qí Shàngfù."
Zhōng replied:
"In former times, due to chaos and disorder,
I sought refuge on Tài Shān,
living among birds and beasts
to preserve my meager life.
In this era of Yáo and Shùn,
I wish to behold the sacred countenance.
However, my years are declining, and my aspirations have waned;
I am unable to display my abilities.
The comparison to Shàngfù
is not something I dare to appropriate.
My nature is to dwell in the mountains;
my heart remains in the rocky caves.
I beg to be allowed to return for my remaining years,
to die at Dài Zōng."
Jiān sent him off in a comfortable carriage.
When he reached Huà Shān,
he sighed:
"I am a Daoist from the Eastern Peak;
to die at the Western Peak
is my fate.
What can be done!"
He traveled fifty *lǐ*,
and died upon reaching the pass.
An envoy swiftly reported this.
Jiān sent Huángménláng Wéi Huá with a ceremonial staff to offer condolences,
sacrificing a grand offering,
and bestowing honorary garments,
posthumously honoring him with the title "Āndào Xiānshēng."
Shí Yuán
Shí Yuán
zì Hóngsūn, claimed to be from Jù, Běihǎi.
He had no fixed abode,
took no wife or concubine,
and did not engage in property management.
He did not seek fine food,
and his clothes were always coarse and worn.
If someone gave him clothes,
he would accept them and then give them to others.
When people had funerals,
he would always take his staff and go to offer condolences.
Regardless of the distance
or the season,
he would always be there.
Sometimes, he was seen
in multiple places at the same time on the same day.
He could also retrieve objects in the dark
as clearly as in daylight.
During the chaos of Yáo Cháng,
no one knew what became of him.
Sòng Xiān
Sòng Xiān
zì Lìng'ài, a native of Xiàogǔ, Dūnhuáng.
From a young age, he had lofty aspirations
and was serene and not involved with the world.
He lived as a recluse on the Southern Mountain of Jiǔquán.
He deeply understood the classics and historical records.
More than three thousand disciples received instruction from him.
He did not respond to invitations from prefectures or commanderies,
only maintaining a good friendship with Yīn Yōng and Qí Hǎo.
During Zhāng Zuò's time,
Táishǒu Yáng Xuān painted his image on the cabinet door,
looking at it whenever he went in or out,
and composed a eulogy that said:
"What stone serves as his pillow?
What stream does he rinse with?
His person cannot be seen,
his name cannot be sought."
Mǎ Jí, the Táishǒu of Jiǔquán,
a man of high character,
came with full retinue,
beating gongs and drums,
to visit him.
Xiān, from his high tower and multiple pavilions,
refused to see him.
Jí sighed:
"His fame can be heard, but his person cannot be seen;
his virtue can be admired, but his form cannot be perceived.
From now on, I know Mr. is a dragon among men."
He inscribed a poem on the stone cliff that said:
"Crimson cliffs a hundred *zhàng* high,
azure walls ten thousand *xún* deep.
Strange trees lush and dense,
like the vibrant Dènglín forest.
The man is like jade,
a treasure of the state.
The dwelling is near, but the man is distant,
truly vexing my heart."
Xiān annotated the *Lúnyǔ*,
and composed tens of thousands of words in poetry and eulogies.
At eighty years old,
he remained diligent in his studies without weariness.
Later, Zhāng Zuò sent the envoy Zhāng Xīng with full ceremonial courtesy to summon him as Prince's Companion (Tài Zǐ Yǒu).
Xīng pressed and urged him very earnestly.
Xiān sighed regretfully, saying:
"My virtue is not like Zhuāng Shēng's,
my talent is not like Gān Mù's,
how dare I delay a clear command!"
So he followed Xīng to Gūzāng.
