Zhāng Zuò sent his son, Prince Tàihé, to visit him with the courtesy due to a friend.
〔一五〕Xiān claimed illness and refused to see him,
and rejected all gifts and offerings.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Prince (Tài Zǐ Tài Fù).
A short while later,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject was born outside the common world,
my heart yearns for the primeval past.
I do not delight in life,
nor do I grieve at death.
I have a long-standing will,
entrusted to my acquaintances:
if in the mountains, bury me in the mountains;
if by water, cast me into the water;
if in a marsh, leave my body exposed;
if among people, bury me near the earth.
〔一六〕Let no news or letters
reach my family.
Now that my life is nearing its end,
I beg that my long-cherished wish be granted."
Thereupon he stopped eating and died,
at the age of eighty-two.
He was posthumously titled Master Xuánxū.
Guō Hé
Guō Hé, courtesy name Chéngxīu,
was a native of Lüèyáng.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Zhěng,
during the Ānshùn era of the Hàn dynasty,
was summoned eight times by the ducal administrations
and five times by the imperial carriage,
but he declined them all.
From Zhěng to Hé,
the family gained positions through classical scholarship for generations.
Guō Hé thoroughly mastered numerous texts,
and was particularly skilled in historical writings.
He did not respond to summons from the provinces or commanderies.
Zhāng Zuò sent an envoy with an comfortable carriage and bundles of silk to summon him as Libationer of Academicians (Bó Shì Jì Jiǔ).
The envoy compelled him to come.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Prince's Companion (Tài Zǐ Yǒu).
Guō Hé submitted a memorial requesting to return home.
Zhāng Zuò granted his request,
and sent him back to the eastern mountains of Zhāngyè with an comfortable carriage and rush-wrapped wheels.
He died at the age of eighty-four,
and was posthumously titled Master Xuándé.
Guō Yǔ
Guō Yǔ, courtesy name Yuányú,
was a native of Dūnhuáng.
In his youth, he possessed an extraordinary character,
traveled east to Zhāngyè,
studied under Guō Hé as his teacher,
and inherited all his learning.
He was proficient in the meaning of the Classics,
eloquent in debate,
talented in many arts,
and skilled in writing.
When Guō Hé died,
Guō Yǔ believed that a father gives life,
a teacher brings accomplishment,
and a lord grants rank;
yet according to the system of five mourning rites,
one does not wear heavy mourning for a teacher.
This, he thought, was the humility of the sages.
Thus, he wore the deepest mourning (zhǎncuī),
and lived in a hut by his teacher's grave for three years.
After the rites were completed,
he secluded himself in Línsōng Xiègǔ,
carved out a stone grotto to live in,
ate cypress seeds to lighten his body,
wrote *Chūnqiū Mòshuō* and *Xiàojīng Cuòwěi*,
and had over a thousand registered disciples.
Zhāng Tiānxī sent the envoy Mèng Gōngmíng with an imperial credential,
and with a rush-wrapped carriage, dark red and black silks, and full ceremonial courtesy, summoned him,
sending Guō Yǔ a letter which said:
"Master, you hide your brilliance in the depths of the marsh,
clinging to your truth and keeping yourself aloof.
Your heart profoundly aligns with the ultimate realm,
and your will waxes and wanes with the four seasons.
How can you know that the common people are hanging upside down,
and that all within the four seas await rescue?
I, though unworthy, have received the mandate of the times,
and bear a great responsibility.
I wish to jointly assist the imperial Way with the wise and enlightened.
In the past, Fù Yuè soared like a dragon in the Yīn court,
Shàngfǔ (Jiāng Zǐyá) soared like a hawk in the Zhōu house.
Confucius's carriage never stopped,
and Mòzǐ would not wait until dawn to harness his.
All were because the calamity of the common people could not be left unrescued,
and because the lord does not stand alone,
but the Way is spread by men.
How much more so now, when the nine provinces are divided into barbarian lands,
and the two capitals are entirely barbarian lairs!
The Son of Heaven is secluded in Jiāngdōng,
and orthodox teachings are degenerating into barbarian customs (zuǒrèn).
Such extreme wounds and poisons
have been unheard of since the creation of the world.
Master, possessing talent to save the world,
to merely sit and observe without rescuing them,
as to your benevolence and wisdom,
I am secretly puzzled.
Therefore, I send this envoy, leaving an empty seat by my side and offering the carriage rein,
eagerly hoping, Master,
you will bestow your presence upon my humble state."
When Gōngmíng arrived at the mountain,
Guō Yǔ pointed to a soaring swan to show him, saying:
"This bird,
how can it be caged?"
Thereupon he deeply fled and vanished without a trace.
Gōngmíng detained his disciples.
Guō Yǔ sighed, saying:
"I fled from emolument,
not from crime.
How can I, by living in seclusion and acting righteously,
bring harm to my disciples?"
So he came out and submitted to the summons.
Upon arriving in Gūzāng,
it happened that Tiānxī's mother had died.
Guō Yǔ tied up his hair (as a sign of respect and mourning) and entered to offer condolences,
performed three leaps of grief, and then left,
returning to Nánshān.
When Tiānxī was overthrown,
Fú Jiān again summoned Guō Yǔ with an comfortable carriage to determine rites and ceremonies.
However, he happened to be mourning his father, so he stopped.
The Grand Administrator (Tài Shǒu) Xīn Zhāng sent three hundred scholars to receive instruction from him.
Towards the end of the Fú clan's rule,
Wáng Mù, Prince of Lüèyáng, raised an army in Jiǔquán
in response to Zhāng Dàyù,
and sent an envoy to invite Guō Yǔ.
Guō Yǔ sighed, saying:
"When approaching a river to save someone drowning,
one does not predict the length of their life;
when treating an illness of three years,
one does not preemptively cut off their food;
Lǔ Lián in Zhào,
for righteousness' sake, did not hold his tongue.
How much less so when people are about to adopt barbarian customs (zuǒrèn) and I do not rescue them!"
So he and Sǒ Gǔ of Dūnhuáng raised an army of five thousand,
transported thirty thousand *shí* of grain,
and went east to respond to Wáng Mù.
Wáng Mù appointed Guō Yǔ as Left Chief Clerk of the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Tài Fǔ Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ) and General of the Military Strategists (Jūn Shī Jiāng Jūn).
Although he held a prime ministerial position,
he orally recited the works of Huáng Lǎo,
hoping that once the task was accomplished and the world settled,
he could follow the path of Bó Chéng.
Wáng Mù was misled by slander
and attacked Sǒ Gǔ in the west.
Guō Yǔ admonished him, saying:
"In the past, the Hàn dynasty first pacified the realm,
and then executed meritorious officials.
Now, your enterprise is not yet established, and you execute him;
you will immediately see deer roaming in this court."
Wáng Mù did not listen.
Guō Yǔ went out of the city and wept loudly,
raising his hands to bid farewell to the city, saying:
"I shall not see you again!"
He returned and pulled his quilt over his face,
spoke to no one,
did not eat for seven days,
and was carried away sick to return home,
praying for death day and night.
At night, he dreamed he rode a green dragon to ascend to heaven,
but it stopped at a house.
Awakening, he sighed and said:
"A dragon flying in the sky
now stops at a house.
The character for 'house' (屋, wū)
is 'corpse' (尸, shī) beneath 'to arrive' (至, zhì).
A dragon flying to a corpse—
I must be about to die.
In ancient times, a gentleman would not die in his inner chamber;
how much less so should I, an upright scholar!"
So he returned to Chìyágé in Nánshān, Jiǔquán,
held his breath and died.
Qí Jiā
Qí Jiā
with the courtesy name Kǒngbīn, was a native of
Jiǔquán.
In his youth, he was pure and impoverished,
and loved learning.
When he was a little over twenty,
one night a voice suddenly called from his window, saying:
"Qí Kǒngbīn,
Qí Kǒngbīn!
Go into hiding,
go into hiding!
Adorning the human world
is so bitter and cannot be harmonized.
What is gained is not a single hair or speck,
what is lost is like a mountain cliff."
The next morning, he fled
west to Dūnhuáng,
where he relied on the academy to recite books.
Being poor and without clothes or food,
he was supported by all the students to sustain himself.
〔一七〕He then became extensively learned in the classics and commentaries,
and profoundly investigated their great principles.
He traveled west to the islands,
teaching over a hundred disciples.
Zhāng Chónghuá summoned him to be the Jìjiǔ of the Rúlín.
His nature was harmonious and generous,
and he taught tirelessly.
Based on the Xiàojīng, he composed the Èrjiǔ Shénjīng.
Among the ministers in court and the governors of commanderies and counties, Péng Hézhèng and others who received instruction and knelt alone at his bedside numbered over two thousand.
Tiānxī referred to him as "Xiānshēng" without using his given name.
He ultimately died of old age.
Qúxíng Xiānshēng
Qúxíng Xiānshēng –
his given name is unknown,
nor is it known where he was from.
At the end of the Tàihé era,
he often lived in Wénjǐshān in the territory of Xuānchéng Commandery.
The mountain had a Qúxíng,
so he took it as his name.
The Grand Marshal Huán Wēn once went to visit him.
Upon arrival,
he saw the Xiānshēng wearing a deerskin cloak,
sitting in a stone chamber.
His demeanor showed no displeasure.
Huán Wēn and his dozens of subordinates were all unable to fathom him,
so he ordered Fú Tāo to compose an inscription and eulogy for him.
He eventually died in the mountains.
Xiè Fū
Xiè Fū,
with the courtesy name Qìngxù, was a native of Kuàijī.
His nature was clear, tranquil, and had few desires.
He entered Tàipíngshān for over ten years.
Zhèn Jūn Xī Yīn summoned him to be a Chief Clerk,
and the court summoned him as a Scholar.
He did not accept any of these positions.
Initially,
the moon encroached upon Shǎowēi.
Shǎowēi is also called the "Scholar's Star";
diviners considered it to refer to a recluse.
Dài Kuí of Qiáoguó had great talent,
and some worried for him.
Soon after, Xiè Fū died,
so the scholars of Kuàijī
joked about the people of Wú, saying:
"The noble scholars of Wú
are simply those who seek death but cannot die."
Dài Kuí
Dài Kuí,
with the courtesy name Āndào, was a native of Qiáoguó.
In his youth, he was broadly learned,
enjoyed discussions,
was skilled at writing essays,
could play the qín,
and excelled in calligraphy and painting;
there was no other delicate art in which he was not thoroughly proficient.
When he was a child,
he used egg white to mix with white tile shards to make a stele for Zhèng Xuán,
and also composed the text and personally carved it.
The words were beautiful and the craftsmanship exquisite,
and people of the time were all amazed and praised it.
By nature, he did not enjoy engaging with contemporary society,
and often entertained himself with the qín and books.
He studied under the geomancer Fàn Xuān in Yùzhāng.
Fàn Xuān regarded him as extraordinary
and gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
The Grand Tutor, Wǔlíng Wáng Xī, heard that he was skilled at playing the qín,
and sent someone to summon him.
Dài Kuí broke his qín in front of the envoy, saying:
"Dài Āndào does not become a musician for the prince's gate!"
Wáng Xī was angry,
and instead summoned his elder brother, Dài Shù.
Dài Shù heard the order with joy,
and went with his qín.
Dài Kuí later moved to Yǎn Xiàn in Kuàijī.
His nature was noble and pure;
he always conducted himself with propriety and decorum,
and deeply regarded unconstrained behavior as contrary to the Dao.
So he wrote an essay, saying:
"If parents die and one does not return after gathering herbs,
that is an unfilial son.
If the ruler is in danger and one frequently leaves to go near the border,
that is a minister who seeks merely to escape.
Yet why did the ancients
never consider these as harming the essence of the name-and-teaching system?
Because they understood their underlying purpose.
Because they understood their underlying purpose,
they were not confused by their superficial actions.
If we speak of the people of the Yuánkāng era,
they can be said to have liked
to hide their tracks without seeking their root,
hence there was the fault of abandoning the root to pursue the trivial,
and the conduct of forsaking substance to chase reputation.
This is like admiring Xī Shī and imitating her frown,
or revering a man of the Dao
and tearing off the corner of his headscarf.
What they admired was not what made her beautiful,
but merely valued superficial resemblance.
The confusion of purple with crimson
is because it resembles crimson.
Therefore, the village worthy resembles moderation,
which is why he corrupts virtue.
The unrestrained person resembles the unhindered,
which is why he corrupts the Dao.
However, the unrestrainedness of the Bamboo Grove Seven
was like a person with an illness frowning;
the unrestrainedness of the Yuánkāng era
was like a person without virtue tearing off his headscarf.
How can one not discern this?
Moreover, the Confucians who valued reputation
originally did so to promote the worthy.
Once they lost this root,
there was the conduct of merely taking a pleasing appearance.
Harboring ulterior motives and losing sincerity,
deceiving each other with outward appearance,
its弊必至於末偽．
The Daoists who renounced names
wished to be earnest and sincere.
If they lost this root,
there was also the conduct of exceeding proper limits.
When both emotion and propriety are deficient,
then
both lofty singing and forgetfulness are practiced;
its弊必至於本薄．
Falsehood and shallowness
are not faults of the two roots,
but those who fall into these faults must rely on the two roots to justify themselves.
The Dao
has constant principles,
but faults have no constant nature.
Therefore, the Six Classics have their failings,
and royal governance has its弊．
〔一八〕If it deviates from its root,
even the sages and worthies can do nothing about it.
Alas!
Among those who practice the Dao, if they are not by nature fully endowed and complete,
acting instinctively and appropriately,
how can they not dwell their feelings on the ancients' lofty deeds,
and emulate the former worthies?
〔一九〕
If one acts only after confused emulation,
and speaks only after deliberation,
one must first distinguish the extreme points of what to take and what to abandon,
seek the root of their intentions,
understand the meaning of bending a foot to straighten a fathom,
and grasp the reason for wearing coarse clothes while cherishing jade.
If so,
though the paths differ,
their destination can be observed;
though the traces are chaotic,
their agreement is not divergent.
Otherwise,
they will drift away and forget to return,
acting like wind and waves,
driving themselves by external things,
deceiving themselves with falsity,
outwardly dazzled by superficial splendor,
inwardly losing the substance of the Dao,
allowing conceit to usurp their true
master,
and dust to obscure their inherent uprightness.
They will be laughed at for a thousand generations.
Can one not be careful?"
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Dài Kuí was repeatedly summoned to serve as Sànqí Chángshì and Guózǐ Bóshì.
He declined, citing his father's illness.
As the commanderies and counties pressed him incessantly,
he fled to Wú.
Wú Guó Nèishǐ Wáng Xún had a separate residence on Wǔqiūshān.
Kuí secretly went there,
and he and Xún spent more than ten days together.
Huìjī Nèishǐ Xiè Xuán, fearing that Kuí had fled far away and would not return,
submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that Dài Kuí of Qiáoguó sets his heart above worldly affairs,
does not involve himself in mundane matters,
resides in a humble dwelling,
and takes zither and books as his companions.
Although imperial commands have been repeatedly issued,
his reclusive integrity remains unchanged.
He has completely withdrawn from the world,
seeking to fulfill his own aspirations.
Moreover, he is nearing sixty years of age,
and constantly suffers from a debilitating illness.
Sometimes, when he is unwell,
it escalates to a serious condition.
Now, with the imperial command yet to be withdrawn,
he will suffer the hardship of wind and frost.
Since Your Majesty already cherishes and values him,
it is also proper to allow his person and reputation to coexist.
I request that the summons be ceased."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor granted his request,
and Kuí returned to Shàn.
Later, Wáng Xún became Shàngshū Púyè
and again submitted a memorial requesting that Kuí be summoned to serve as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
When summoned,
he again did not come.
In the twentieth year of Tàiyuán,
when the Crown Prince first left the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince's Grand Tutor Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ, Junior Tutor Wáng Yǎ, and Chamberlain Wáng Xún again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Kuí maintains a firm and severe integrity,
relishes solitary wandering.
Advanced in years,
his pure reputation shines ever brighter.
The Eastern Palace, lacking virtue,
extends an invitation to one beyond worldly affairs.
It is fitting to bestow an imperial command
to include him among the attendant officials.
Since Kuí highly values his reclusive integrity,
he will surely consider it honorable to be difficult to advance.
It is proper to instruct the local authorities to prepare the full rites for his dispatch."
He died shortly thereafter from illness.
His eldest son, Bó,
possessed his father's demeanor.
In the early years of Yìxī,
he was summoned as Sànqí Shìláng,
but did not respond,
and soon died.
Gōng Xuánzhī
Gōng Xuánzhī, courtesy name Dàoxuán,
[二０] was a native of Hànshòu in Wǔlíng.
His father, Dēng,
successively held the positions of Chángshā Xiàng and Sànqí Chángshì.
Xuánzhī was fond of learning, quiet and reserved,
content in his humble dwelling.
The province recommended him as Xiùcái,
and the ducal mansion invited him,
but he did not accept.
Emperor Xiàowǔ issued an edict saying:
"When a wise king governs the world,
he must search out and bring forth the reclusive and hidden.
Thus, there are songs of empty valleys and tethered carriages,
and observations of humble gardens and bundles of silk.
Dài Kuí of Qiáoguó and Gōng Xuánzhī of Wǔlíng both uphold their lofty integrity,
abide in benevolence and delight in the arts,
keep themselves pure and untainted,
and have profound scholarship in Confucian studies.
We have long held an open mind.
How could these gentlemen
conceal their talents within their bosoms!
We desire to hear their elegant words,
and humbly seek their sincere counsel.
They can both be appointed as Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently serving as Guózǐ Bóshì.
The local authorities are to be instructed to prepare the full rites for their dispatch.
They are not to follow routine procedures,
lest they delay Our expectation of their presence by Our side."
The commanderies and counties pressed him,
but he earnestly declined, citing severe illness,
and did not go.
He died shortly thereafter,
at the age of fifty-eight.
His disciple, Yuánshòu,
also possessed virtuous conduct.
He was lofty and did not serve in office.
When recommended as Xiùcái and invited by the province,
he likewise claimed illness and did not accept.
Emperor Xiàowǔ repeatedly summoned him as Tàixué Bóshì, Sànqí Shìláng, and Gěishìzhōng,
but he ultimately did not respond.
He died at home.
Táo Dàn
Táo Dàn, courtesy name Chùjìng,
was the grandson of Grand Commandant Kǎn.
His father, Xià,
was deposed for misconduct.
Dàn was orphaned young.
He was fond of the art of self-cultivation,
believing that immortality could be sought.
At fifteen or sixteen,
he began consuming elixirs and abstaining from grain,
and did not marry.
His family possessed thousands of gold,
and hundreds of servants and retainers,
but Dàn sat upright all day,
never bothering to inquire about them.
He was quite fond of reading the Yì,
and skilled in divination.
He built a hut in the mountains of Línxiāng, Chángshā, and lived there,
keeping a white deer as his companion.
When relatives or old friends came to visit him,
he would always move across the stream,
so no one could approach him.
When the province recommended him as Xiùcái,
Dàn heard of it,
and thereupon fled to Píshān in Luóxiàn,
never returning for the rest of his life.
No one knew his ultimate fate.
Táo Qián
Táo Qián, courtesy name Yuánliàng,
was the great-grandson of Grand Marshal Kǎn.
His grandfather, Máo,
was Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
Qián harbored lofty aspirations from a young age,
was widely learned and skilled in writing.
He was outstanding and unrestrained,
true to his nature and self-content,
and was valued by his neighbors.
He once wrote "Biography of Mr. Five Willows" to describe himself, saying:
"Mr. Five Willows, I do not know where he came from,
nor his family name or given name.
By his dwelling were five willow trees,
and so he was given this appellation.
He was quiet and spoke little,
and did not covet fame or profit.
He was fond of reading,
but did not seek meticulous understanding.
Whenever he grasped the meaning,
he was so joyful he would forget to eat.
By nature, he loved wine,
but his family was poor and he could not obtain it.
Relatives and old friends, knowing this about him,
would sometimes prepare wine and invite him.
When he went to drink, he would always finish it,
determined to get drunk.
Once drunk, he would leave,
never begrudging his feelings.
His four bare walls were desolate,
offering no shelter from wind or sun.
His short coarse clothes were torn and patched,
his bamboo basket and gourd often empty,
yet he was content.
He often wrote essays to entertain himself,
somewhat expressing his aspirations,
forgetting concerns of gain or loss,
and thus lived out his days."
This was his self-introduction,
and people of his time called it a truthful record.
Because his parents were old and his family was poor,
he was appointed as a Jìjiǔ of the prefecture.
Being unsuited for official duties,
he resigned himself after a few days and returned home.
The prefecture summoned him to be the Zhǔbù,
but he did not accept.
He personally tilled the land to support himself,
and consequently suffered from a debilitating illness.
He was again appointed as Cānjūn to the Zhènjūn and Jiànwēi generals.
He said to his relatives and friends:
“I merely wish to sing for a while,
would it be acceptable to use this as funds for my three paths? ”
Those in charge heard of this
and appointed him as Píngzé Magistrate.
In the county, he ordered all the public fields to be planted with glutinous millet,
saying:
“It is enough for me to be constantly drunk on wine. ”
His wife repeatedly requested that ordinary rice be planted,
so he then had one qǐng and fifty mù planted with glutinous millet,
and fifty mù with ordinary rice.
He was always humble and valued integrity,
and did not privately serve his superiors.
When the Commander of the Inspectorate sent an Inspector to the county,
his subordinates reported that he should don his official robes and sash to meet him.
Táo Qián sighed and said:
“I cannot bend my waist for five dòu of rice,
and servilely attend to a minor person from the countryside! ”
In the second year of Yìxī,
he resigned his seal and left the county,
and then composed “Guī Qùlái Cí” (The Return).
Its lyrics say: “Return home!
My garden and fields are about to become overgrown,
why not return?
Since I have already let my mind be enslaved by my body,
why should I feel disheartened and sorrowful alone?
I realize that what is past cannot be mended,
but I know that what is to come can still be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far from the right path,
and now I perceive that this is right and yesterday was wrong.
My boat sways lightly and gently,
the wind gently blows and rustles my clothes.
I ask the traveler
about the road ahead,
and regret the faintness of the morning light.
Then I behold my humble dwelling,
joyfully rushing home.
My boy servants come to welcome me,
my young children wait at the gate.
The three paths are overgrown,
but the pine
and chrysanthemums still remain.
I lead my children into the room,
where there is wine filling the goblet.
I take the jug and cup to pour for myself,
my eyes fall on the garden trees with a cheerful countenance.
Leaning against the south window to give vent to my pride,
I realize how easily
a small space brings peace.
I stroll through the garden daily, finding pleasure in it,
the gate, though set up, is always closed.
I lean on my staff to rest as I wander,
at times raising my head to gaze into the distance.
Clouds emerge from the
peaks without intention,
birds, weary of flying, know to return.
The sun dims, about to set,
I stroke the solitary pine and linger.
Return home!
Let me cease all social contact and abandon my travels.
The world and I have abandoned each other,
what more should I seek by yoking my carriage again!
I delight in the heartfelt talks with relatives and friends,
and find joy in music and books
to dispel my sorrows.
The farmers tell me it is late spring,
and there will be work in the western fields.
Perhaps I will order a covered cart,
or paddle a lone boat.
I will delve deep to find the valleys,
and also traverse
rugged hills.
The trees eagerly grow towards prosperity,
the springs trickle and begin to flow.
I admire how all things embrace their season,
and feel that my life is nearing its end.
So be it!
How much longer shall I lodge my form in this universe?
Why not let my heart freely decide whether to stay or go,
why wander anxiously, where do I wish to go?
Wealth and nobility are not my desire,
the imperial court is not what I anticipate.
Cherishing fine mornings, I go out alone,
sometimes planting my staff to weed,
climbing the eastern hill to let out a long cry,
or facing the clear stream to compose poetry.
Let me simply follow transformation
until my end,
and be content with fate, what more doubts could there be! ”
A short while later,
he was summoned to be Zuòzuò Láng,
but did not accept.
Having already severed all visits to prefecture and county officials,
his relatives Zhāng Yě and his associates Yáng Sōnglíng, Chǒng Zūn, etc., would sometimes invite him for wine,
or invite him to join a drinking gathering.
Even if he did not know the host,
he would happily and without objection partake,
and return home when thoroughly drunk.
He never initiated a visit anywhere,
his only destinations were his farm and excursions to Lúshān.
When Cìshǐ Wáng Hóng took office in the prefecture during the Yuánxī reign,
he greatly admired and yearned to meet Táo Qián.
Later, he went to visit him himself.
Táo Qián claimed illness and refused to see him,
but later told people:
“My nature is not to be familiar with the world.
Because of illness, I maintain my reclusion.
Fortunately, it is not out of a desire for purity or fame.
How dare I take pride in making a duke or minister inconvenience himself!
Indeed, to be wrongly considered unworthy,
this is why Liú Gōnggàn incurred the criticism of gentlemen;
his fault was not small. ”
Wáng Hóng often sent people to inquire about him,
and secretly learned that Táo Qián was going to Lúshān.
So he sent his old acquaintance Páng Tōngzhī and others with wine,
to intercept him halfway.
When Táo Qián encountered the wine,
he immediately sat down in a roadside pavilion to drink,
happily forgetting to proceed.
Wáng Hóng then appeared and met him,
and they joyfully feasted for the entire day.
Táo Qián had no shoes,
so Wáng Hóng looked to his attendants and ordered them to make shoes for him.
The attendants asked for his shoe size,
and Táo Qián stretched out his foot from his seat for them to measure.
Wáng Hóng urged him to return to the prefecture.
When asked what he would ride,
he replied:
“I have always had a leg ailment;
I rode in a basket palanquin just now,
which is enough for me to return by myself. ”
So Wáng Hóng ordered one of his students and two children to carry him to the prefecture together,
and he laughed and talked, enjoying himself,
not feeling any envy for splendid carriages.
Later, when Wáng Hóng wanted to see him,
he would always wait for him in the forests and marshes.
When Táo Qián was short of wine and rice,
Wáng Hóng would also provide for him from time to time.
His relatives and friends who enjoyed good company
would sometimes bring wine and food to him,
and Táo Qián would not decline.
Each time he got drunk,
he would feel perfectly content and at ease.
He also did not manage his livelihood,
leaving all household chores to his children and servants.
He never showed signs of joy or anger;
he only drank when there was wine,
and sometimes when there was no wine,
he would still recite poetry elegantly without interruption.
He once said that in the quiet leisure of summer,
he would lie high beneath the north window,
and when the cool breeze rustled in,
he considered himself a person from the age of Xīhuáng.
He had no understanding of music,
but kept a plain qín,
without strings or frets.
Whenever there was a gathering of friends and wine,
he would strum it and accompany the others,
saying:
“As long as I understand the meaning within the qín,
why bother with the sound of the strings! ”
He died during the Yuánjiā reign of the Sòng dynasty,
at the age of sixty-three.
All his collected works are still in circulation.
The imperial historian says: The paths of noble persons vary,
referring to their prominence or obscurity.
When they serve, they faithfully manage myriad affairs
to save the times with the Way;
when they reside in seclusion, they extricate themselves from the clamor and dust,
cultivating themselves with humility.
A detailed examination of their principles
shows their long-standing origins.
Gōnghé [Gōnghé] resided in a cave dwelling,
his lower garment merely woven grass,
admonishing Shūyè [Shūyè] to focus his spirit and discern;
Wēilián [Wēilián] dwelled in a cluster of shrines,
his clothes without whole silk,
facing Zǐjīng [Zǐjīng] and setting forth virtuous principles: both hid their tracks and were not pursued,
being peers of Liǔqín [Liǔqín] and Shàngpíng [Shàngpíng].
Xià Tǒng [Xià Tǒng] was acclaimed far and wide for his filial piety and fraternal love,
his clan and community esteemed his honesty and uprightness.
When he sang the melody of Xiǎohǎi [Xiǎohǎi],
Wǔ Xū [Wǔ Xū] still seemed present;
when he solidified the heart of a chaste stone,
Gōnglǘ [Gōnglǘ] felt even more ashamed.
At that time, those who were fortunate enough to witness him at Luòbīn [Luòbīn]
would confirm these words.
Sòng Xiān [Sòng Xiān] cherished lofty principles from youth,
his pure conduct shining forth.
Yáng Xuān [Yáng Xuān] praised his portrait,
Mǎ Jí [Mǎ Jí] lauded him as a human dragon.
The epithet Xuánxū [Xuánxū]
was truly a commendation for him.
As for the other gentlemen,
some left office due to illness,
some wrote treatises to correct customs,
some sat cross-legged facing their contemporaries,
or fished and hunted while dwelling in mountains and marshes,
containing their harmony and hiding their unpolished jade,
concealing their brilliance by following the Way,
not bending their will,
and stirring a pure wind for future generations.
A eulogy says: High office invites burdens,
a good name follows one's desires.
Resolute among the scholars,
they transcended the mundane.
Nourishing their essence in rocky valleys,
silencing their names in forest nooks.
They stirred the greedy and stopped contention,
leaving behind noble footsteps forever.
Collation Notes
Biography Sixty-Five: Arts
The rise of arts
has a long history.
Ancient kings used them to resolve doubts,
determine fortune and misfortune,
discern survival and destruction,
and examine calamity and blessing.
They are called divine and wise,
hiding the past and knowing the future;
covertly assisting and mysteriously aligning,
they aid in the completion of human affairs;
they both generate benefit and remove harm,
and also awe the multitude to establish authority.
What is called establishing teachings through divine ways
largely stems from this.
However, strange deceptions border on the bizarre and delusive,
and circuitous tales are difficult to trace to their source.
Methods and techniques are diverse and numerous,
and their variations are truly not uniform.
Although truth exists,
falsehood also relies upon it.
The sages did not speak of strange phenomena, violence, disorder, or spirits,
and there was truly a reason for this.
When Qiūmíng [Qiūmíng] first championed it,
using auspicious dreams to create writings,
Zǐcháng [Zǐcháng] followed,
citing tortoise shells and milfoil stalks to compile biographies.
Since then,
historians have never ceased writing about them.
Emperor Wǔ [Wǔ] of Hàn [Hàn] was particularly fond of immortals,
and Emperor Shìzǔ [Shìzǔ] was especially devoted to prophetic arts.
This caused Wénchéng [Wénchéng] and Wǔlì [Wǔlì] to use their cunning and deceit to gain favor and glory,
while Yǐn Mǐn [Yǐn Mǐn] and Huán Tán [Huán Tán] incurred blame and punishment for opposing the times.
This was indeed an oversight for even well-informed persons,
one mistake among a thousand considerations!
Upon detailed observation of the various arts,
they are indeed but minor paths.
To discard them might be regrettable,
yet to preserve them risks being deemed uncanonical.
Since records must be broadly knowledgeable,
editing and selection should logically be detailed and comprehensive.
The Jìn [Jìn] called it *chéng* [chéng],
and its meaning lies herein.
Now, we record those whose calculations are especially precise and whose skills are notable,
to form the Biographies of Arts,
as a complement to previous histories.
Chén Xùn [Chén Xùn]
Chén Xùn [Chén Xùn], courtesy name Dàoyuán [Dàoyuán],
was a native of Lìyáng [Lìyáng].
In his youth, he enjoyed esoteric studies,
mastering astronomy, calendrical calculations, yin and yang, and prognostication without exception,
and was especially skilled in *fēngjiǎo* [fēngjiǎo] (wind-angle divination).
Sūn Hào [Sūn Hào] appointed him Fèngjìn Dūwèi [Fèngjìn Dūwèi],
tasking him with prognostication.
Hào’s [Hào] governance was harsh and cruel,
and Xùn [Xùn] knew it would surely fail but dared not speak.
At that time, Qiántáng [Qiántáng] Lake opened,
and some said that the world would be at peace,
and a blue carriage would enter Luòyáng [Luòyáng].
Hào [Hào] asked Xùn [Xùn] about it.
Xùn [Xùn] replied:
“Your minister can only observe *qì* [qì],
and cannot comprehend the opening and closing of the lake.”
He retreated and told his friend:
“The blue carriage entering Luòyáng [Luòyáng]
will involve carrying a coffin and holding a jade disk,
which is not auspicious.”
Soon after, Wú [Wú] perished.
Xùn [Xùn] was moved inland according to regulations
and appointed Jiànyì Dàfū [Jiànyì Dàfū].
Shortly after, he resigned and returned to his hometown.
When Chén Mǐn [Chén Mǐn] rebelled,
he sent his younger brother Hóng [Hóng] to be Lìyáng [Lìyáng] Grand Administrator.
Xùn [Xùn] told the local people:
“The Chén [Chén] family has no kingly *qì* [qì];
they will soon be destroyed.”
Hóng [Hóng] heard this
and was about to execute him.
Xùn’s [Xùn] fellow townsman Qín Qú [Qín Qú], who was Hóng’s [Hóng] staff officer,
then persuaded Hóng [Hóng] saying:
“Xùn [Xùn] is skilled in *fēngjiǎo* [fēngjiǎo];
you can test him.
If he is not accurate,
it will not be too late to execute him later.”
So, he was pardoned.
At that time, Hóng [Hóng] was attacking Héng Yàn [Héng Yàn], the commander of the Eastern Expedition, at Lìyáng [Lìyáng],
and asked Xùn [Xùn]:
“How many thousands of men are in the city?
Can it be taken by assault?”
Xùn [Xùn] ascended Niúzhǔ [Niúzhǔ] Mountain to observe the *qì* [qì],
saying:
“No more than five hundred men,
but it cannot be attacked.
If you attack, you will surely be defeated.”
Hóng [Hóng] again grew furious and said:
“How can five thousand men attack five hundred and not succeed?”
He ordered his officers and soldiers to attack,
and indeed they were defeated by Yàn [Yàn].
Only then did Hóng [Hóng] believe Xùn [Xùn] had magical arts
and treated him with great respect.
Zhōu Kàng [Zhōu Kàng] of Huáinán [Huáinán], a Duóshuǐ Cānjūn [Duóshuǐ Cānjūn], once asked Xùn [Xùn] about his official position.
Xùn [Xùn] said:
“You will receive a seal of office for a nearby commandery in the *mǎo* [mǎo] year,
and have a curved carriage in the *yǒu* [yǒu] year.”
Kàng [Kàng] said:
“If your words come true,
I will recommend and promote you.”
Xùn [Xùn] said:
“My nature is not fond of officialdom;
I only wish to obtain rice.”
Later, Kàng [Kàng] indeed became Yìxīng [Yìxīng] Grand Administrator and Jīnzǐ Jiāngjūn [Jīnzǐ Jiāngjūn].
At that time, Liú Cōng [Liú Cōng] and Wáng Mí [Wáng Mí] raided Luòyáng [Luòyáng].
Wǔ Xiá [Wǔ Xiá], the Lìyáng [Lìyáng] Grand Administrator, asked Xùn [Xùn]:
“What is the state of the imperial court’s affairs?”
Xùn [Xùn] replied:
“The barbarian bandits will press three times,
the state will be defeated,
and the emperor will die in the wilderness.
This has not happened yet.”
Afterwards, the cruelty of Píngyáng [Píngyáng] indeed befell Emperors Huái [Huái] and Mǐn [Mǐn].
Someone asked him about the fortune and misfortune of the next year.
Xùn [Xùn] said:
“The Yángzhōu [Yángzhōu] Inspector will die,
Wǔchāng [Wǔchāng] will suffer a great fire,
and a general from the imperial court will also die.”
At that time,
Liú Táo [Liú Táo] and Zhōu Fǎng [Zhōu Fǎng] both died,
and Wǔchāng [Wǔchāng] experienced a great fire,
burning several thousand households.
At that time, Gān Zhuó [Gān Zhuó] was Lìyáng [Lìyáng] Grand Administrator.
Xùn [Xùn] privately told his intimates:
“Lord Gān’s [Gān] head is low and his gaze is upward,
which in physiognomy is called ‘glancing at a blade.’
Moreover, his eyes have red veins
entering from the outside.
Within ten years,
he will surely die by military means.
If he does not command troops, he can avoid it.”
Zhuó [Zhuó] was indeed harmed by Wáng Dūn [Wáng Dūn].
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo [Wáng Dǎo] was frequently ill
and often worried about himself,
so he consulted Xùn [Xùn].
Xùn [Xùn] said:
“Your ears are upright and hang to your shoulders;
you will surely live long,
and also be greatly noble.
Your descendants will prosper in Jiāngdōng [Jiāngdōng].”
Everything happened as he said.
Xùn [Xùn] died at over eighty years old.
Dài Yáng [Dài Yáng]
Dài Yáng
had the courtesy name Guóliú. He was from Chángchéng, Wúxīng.
When he was twelve,
he fell ill and died.
He revived five days later.
He said that when he died, a celestial official had made him a wine cellar administrator,
giving him talismans and records,
and providing him with banners and flags for his retinue.
He was to ascend various mountains, including Pénglái, Kūnlún, Jīshí, Tàishì, Héng, Lú, and Héng.
Later, he was sent back.
He met an old man
who told him:
“You will attain the Way later
and be recognized by noble people.”
When he grew up,
he became skilled in geomancy.
He was short and plain in appearance,
lacking impressive bearing,
but he was fond of Daoist arts
and had a marvelous understanding of divination and numerology.
In the late Wú period, he served as a Tái official.
Knowing that Wú was about to fall,
he feigned illness and did not serve.
When Wú was pacified,
he returned to his hometown.
Later, when he traveled to Lài Xiāng
and passed the Lǎozi Temple,
all these places were where Yáng had been sent during his death, as he had seen.
However, he no longer saw the old objects.
He then asked the storehouse keeper, Yīng Fèng,
“More than twenty years ago,
did anyone riding a horse eastward,
pass Lǎo Jūn without dismounting,
and before reaching the bridge,
fall from his horse and die?”
Fèng said there was such a case.
Many of the things Yáng asked about
matched his experience.
The Prefect of Yángzhōu once asked Yáng about good and bad fortune.
He replied:
“Yínghuò (Mars) has entered the Nándǒu (Southern Dipper).
There will be a sudden flood in the eighth month,
and in the ninth month, an invading army will come from the southwest.”
As predicted, there was a great flood,
and Shí Bīng rebelled.
After Bīng occupied Yángzhōu,
Yáng told people:
“Looking at the bandit’s aura,
they will be defeated in the fourth month.”
It happened exactly as he said.
Shī Chén Mǐn became the Right General.
Sūn Hùn, the Prefect of Tángyì, saw this and envied him.
Yáng said:
“Mǐn is about to become a bandit and have his family annihilated.
What is there to desire?”
Not long after,
Mǐn indeed rebelled and was executed.
Initially,
Hùn wanted to bring his family over.
Yáng said:
“This place will be defeated.
You will get through the twelfth month (làyuè) but not the first month (zhēngyuè).
How can you move your family into a bandit-occupied area?”
Hùn then stopped.
At the end of the year,
Mǐn’s brother, Chǎng, attacked Tángyì.
Hùn then escaped alone.
Later, Má Wǔ, the Chief of Waterways, recommended Yáng as a Clerk of Waterways.
Yáng requested urgent leave to return home.
When he was about to go to Luòyáng,
he dreamt that a divine being told him:
“Luòyáng will be defeated.
Everyone will cross to the south.
Five years from now, there will certainly be an Emperor in Yángzhōu.”
Yáng believed this
and thus did not go.
Later, everything happened as in his dream.
Huà Tán, the Administrator of Lújiāng, asked Yáng:
“Who among the people will rebel again?”
Yáng said:
“Wáng Jī.”
Soon after, Jī rebelled.
Chén Zhěn asked Yáng:
“People say there will be noble people in Jiāngnán.
Are Gù Yànxiān and Zhōu Xuānpèi them?”
Yáng said:
“Gù will not last past the twelfth month (làyuè).
Zhōu will not see August of next year.”
Yànxiān (Gù Róng) indeed died on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month.
The twentieth day was là.
Xuānpèi (Zhōu Qǐ) died on the last day of the seventh month of the next year.
Wáng Dǎo fell ill
and summoned Yáng to ask about it.
Yáng said:
“Your Lordship’s natal sign is Shēn (Monkey).
Metal is subject to Earth.
Yet you have established a forge on a stone in Shēn.
The firelight illuminates the sky.
This signifies Metal and Fire clashing,
and Water and Fire boiling each other.
That is why you are suffering.”
Dǎo immediately moved to the Eastern Palace,
and his illness recovered.
Zhāng Kǎi, the Acting Cavalry Commander of the General Who Guards the East, recommended Yáng as a Chancellor’s Clerk.
At that time, Sīmǎ Yáng was the Magistrate of Wūchéng.
When he was about to take office,
Yáng said:
“Your Lordship should be very careful with your subordinates.”
Later, Yáng was indeed dismissed from office due to his subordinates.
Yáng then told him:
“Although you are dismissed,
you will become a governor in the eleventh month
and be promoted to general.”
At the appointed time,
he became the Administrator of Tàishān and General Who Guards the Military.
Yáng was selling his house and about to leave,
but Dài Yáng stopped him, saying:
“You will not reach there;
you will return,
so you cannot be without a house.”
Yáng was indeed forced by Xú Kān
and could not reach his commandery.
Emperor Yuán increased Yáng’s troops by two thousand
and sent him to assist Zǔ Tì.
Dài Yáng advised Yáng not to go.
Yáng then claimed illness.
He was arrested and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review,
but soon after, he was released due to a general amnesty.
When Emperor Yuán was about to ascend the throne,
he had Dài Yáng choose a date.
Dài Yáng thought it was suitable to use the twenty-fourth day of the third month, which was a bǐngwǔ day.
Chén Zhuō, the Grand Astrologer, proposed the twenty-second day,
saying:
“In the past, the King of Yuè used the third month, jiǎchén day, to restore his state.
Fàn Lǐ said that it was before yáng,
when the ruler would leave entirely,
and both high and low would be completely empty,
virtue would travel out,
and punishment would enter the central palace.
This is the same as now.”
Dài Yáng said:
“The King of Yuè was imprisoned by Wú.
Although he acted submissive and flattering at the time,
he harbored resentment.
Lǐ therefore used jiǎchén,
riding on virtue to return,
leaving punishment in the Wú palace.
Now, His Majesty has no internal faults
and no external resentments.
He is about to receive the great mandate from Heaven
and enjoy endless blessings.
Why should we follow the story of the King of Yuè leaving his state and leaving behind calamity?”
The Emperor then followed Dài Yáng’s advice.
When Zǔ Yuē 代 his brother to garrison Qiáo,
he invited Yáng to be the Zhōngdiǎnjūn,
and then promoted him to Dūhù.
In the fourth month, Gēngchén day of Yǒngchāng first year
at midday, there was a great wind
that rose from the southeast,
breaking trees.
Yáng said to Yuē:
“In the tenth month, bandits will surely arrive east of Qiáochéng,
reaching Lìyáng,
and there will be rebels in the south.”
The Registrar Wáng Zhèn considered Yáng to be a sorcerer,
and reported to Yuē to arrest Yáng,
handing him over to the interrogators and cutting off his food for fifty days,
but his speech remained unchanged.
Yuē knew he possessed divine techniques,
so he pardoned him and reproached Zhèn.
Later, Zhèn committed a crime and was arrested,
and Yáng saved him.
Yuē said:
“Zhèn imprisoned you in the past;
why do you save him now?”
Yáng said:
“Zhèn did not understand fengjiao;
it was not due to an old grudge.
Zhèn was about to starve to death in the past,
and I kept him alive;
yet Zhèn still forgot this.
Indeed, it is very difficult for those in wealth and high position not to abandon the poor and humble.”
Yuē admired his righteousness,
and immediately pardoned Zhèn,
and bestowed thirty dàn of rice upon Yáng.
On the third day of the tenth month,
Shí Lè’s cavalry indeed arrived east of Qiáochéng.
Yáng said to Yuē:
“The bandits will surely head towards Chéngfù.
You can send cavalry to pursue them south of the river,
and infantry to block the main road north of the river;
the bandits will surely be defeated.”
Yuē ultimately did not pursue them,
so the bandits plundered women and baggage from Chéngfù and departed.
Yuē’s general Lǔ Yán sought to pursue the bandits,
Yáng said:
“You must not.”
Yuē did not heed him,
and sent his nephew Zhì with Yán to pursue them.
The bandits feigned abandoning women and baggage and fled.
Zhì and Yán and others vied for the goods,
and the bandits returned and ambushed them.
Zhì and Yán barely escaped with their lives,
and all the soldiers died.
Yuē memorialized Yáng to be Xiàyì Zhǎng.
At that time, people from Liángguó rebelled,
expelling the Grand Administrator Yuán Yàn.
Liángchéng was steep and perilous.
Yuē wanted to suppress them but had not yet decided.
Yáng said:
“The bandits rebelled on the Xīnyǒu day of the eighth month.
Both the day and the zodiac branch are in ascendancy.
The virtue of Xīn is in the south,
and Yǒu suffers self-punishment.
Liáng is north of Qiáo.
Riding on virtue to strike at punishment,
the bandits will surely be annihilated.
Moreover, on the Jiǎzǐ day, an east wind and thunder went west.
Qiáo is in the southeast,
and the thunder is before the army,
clearing the way for the army.
In the past, when Wú attacked Guān Yǔ,
heavenly thunder was ahead,
and Zhōu Yú bowed in congratulations.
Now it is the same as then,
thus I know you will surely conquer.”
Yuē followed him,
and indeed pacified Liángchéng.
In the first month of Tàiníng third year,
there was a large meteor travelling southeast.
Yáng said:
“By autumn,
the headquarters will have to move to Shòuyáng.”
When Wáng Dūn rebelled,
Yuē asked about victory or defeat.
Yáng said:
“Tàibái is in the east,
and Chénxīng does not appear.
In military strategy, the one who initiates is the host,
and the one who responds is the guest.
If Chénxīng appears,
Tàibái is the host,
and Chénxīng is the guest.
If Chénxīng does not appear,
Tàibái is the guest,
and the one who initiates the army will fail.
Now there is a guest but no host,
a front but no rear.
You should issue a proclamation to your subordinates,
and respond to the imperial edict to attack him.”
Yuē then led his troops towards Héféi.
Soon after, Dūn died and his forces were defeated,
and so they settled in Shòuyáng.
Yáng also said:
“There will be military affairs between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Qiáochéng is empty and vast;
it is advisable to return and fortify it.
Otherwise,
Yōngqiū and Pèi will both no longer be under official control.”
Yuē did not heed him,
and the land of Yù was then lost to the bandits.
In the spring of Xiánhé first year,
Yuē travelled south to farm,
and encountered a great thunderstorm coming from the southwest.
Yáng said:
“On Jiǎzǐ day, thunder from the southwest,
in that summer a great general will surely be lost.”
By summer,
people from Rǔnán rebelled,
seized Yuē’s nephew Jì,
and sent him to Shí Lè.
Inside Yuē’s residence, the ground suddenly turned red like cinnabar.
Yáng said:
“According to the Hétú Zhēngyún, ‘When the ground is red like cinnabar and blood is like pellets,
there will be subordinates rebelling against superiors.’
I fear that on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month, Hú horses will come to drink the Huái river water.”
At that time,
Shí Lè’s cavalry arrived in great numbers,
attacking the city in a major battle.
On that day, there was a west wind,
and both soldiers and fire were unleashed.
Yuē was greatly alarmed.
Then the wind shifted,
and the bandits retreated.
At that time, it was rumored that Lè had sent cavalry towards Shòuyáng.
Yuē wanted to send his family back to Jiāngdōng.
Yáng said:
“There will certainly be no such event.”
Soon after, the rumor indeed proved false.
In the early Xiánhé period,
a halo appeared around the moon, touching the left corner,
with red and white appendages.
Yuē asked Yáng,
and Yáng said:
"The horn (Jiǎo) is the celestial gate;
when it opens and the yang path is revealed,
there will be a great war at the official gates."
Soon after, Sū Jùn sent an envoy to invite Yuē to revolt together.
Yáng said to Yuē:
"Sū Jùn will surely fail,
but at the beginning of his uprising,
his military might will be irresistible.
You should maintain external peace and internal strictness,
and await the change."
Yuē did not listen,
and consequently revolted with Jùn.
By the fifth month of the third year,
a great storm with thunder and rain came from the northwest,
and the city became dark.
Yáng said to Yuē:
"Thunder above people
indicates that the illustrious lord should keep flatterers away and draw honest people near,
and love his subordinates and help the poor.
In the past, Qín experienced such a change,
and ultimately met with chaos and destruction."
Yuē was greatly angered
and had Yáng arrested and imprisoned.
He sent his subordinate Lǐ Gài with troops to Lújiāng,
but all his forces dispersed.
Yuē summoned Yáng out
and asked him:
"Is it better for me to return east or stay in Shòuyáng?
If I stay in Shòuyáng,
is it better than entering Hú (barbarian territory)?"
Yáng said:
"Going east will result in losing half;
entering Hú will lead to the extinction of your family.
Staying in Shòuyáng is still acceptable."
Yuē wanted to head east to Lìyáng,
but his followers were not happy about going east.
kidnapped Yuē's elder sister and sister-in-law, and fled to Shí Lè.
All rebelled against Yuē,
Zǔ Huàn asked Yáng:
"You once said that the Pingxi General could stay in Shòuyáng for five years,
and it turned out exactly as you said.
Now that he is in Lìyáng,
how long can he stay?"
Yáng replied:
"Only six months."
Yuē asked Yáng:
"How are the atmospheric conditions in the capital and here?"
Yáng said:
"Here, there will be another rebellion.
The capital will achieve great peace by the third month of next year,
and Jiāngzhōu will experience a great mourning.
Later, there will be military affairs again in the south,
a thousand *lǐ* from here."
Soon after, Qiān Téng rebelled against Yuē.
Yuē led his close associates and family to flee to Shí Lè.
In the second month, the Son of Heaven returned to power;
in the fourth month, Wēn Jiǎo died;
Guō Mò occupied Pénkǒu and rebelled.
Later, Lè executed Yuē and all his relatives,
all as Yáng had predicted.
After Yuē's defeat,
Yáng went to Xúnyáng.
At that time, Liú Yìn was garrisoned in Xúnyáng.
Yìn asked Yáng:
"Will my illness get better?"
Yáng said:
"I am not worried about your illness not getting better,
I am worried that you will face a great misfortune this year.
You are forty-seven years old,
and your current year enters *Gēngyín*.
The Grand Duke's 'Secret Schemes' says: '
The six *Gēng* (days) are the White Beast; above, it is the Guest Star;
below, it is harmful energy.'
When the year and destiny combine,
it will surely be ominous and must be avoided.
On the *Gēngyín* day of the twelfth month, the twenty-second day, do not see guests."
Yìn said:
"I should resign my post
and take you back to the countryside to treat my illness."
Yáng said:
"You will become the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and cannot resign."
Yìn asked:
"Is Grand Master Wēn not returning?"
Yáng said:
"Even if Grand Master Wēn returns,
you will still be the governor of Jiāngzhōu."
Soon it was as he said.
In the ninth month, on the *Jiǎyín* day, during the *shēn* hour,
a whirlwind came from the east,
entered Yìn's son's boat,
passed westwards,
resembling a piece of white silk,
fifty or sixty *chǐ* long.
Yáng said:
"The wind comes down from Xiánchí
and goes down to Shèdí.
Xiánchí signifies weapons and warfare,
great slaughter and death.
By the *Jiǎzǐ* day, *shēn* hour,
a large pile of bones will be buried within the prefecture."
Yìn asked where,
Yáng said:
"It will not be outside the gates of the provincial office."
Yìn had a gate built to the east of the office.
Yáng also said:
"The east is the celestial prison;
if a gate is opened beneath the prison,
I fear a heavenly prison will arrive."
On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month,
Yáng again said:
"As *là* (the twelfth lunar month) approaches, you can close the gates,
and station fifty men to guard them,
and also a hundred men to guard the northeast direction (*yín* position)
to ward off harmful energy."
Yìn did not comply.
On the twenty-fourth day, *Rénchén*,
Yìn was harmed by Guō Mò.
Huán Xuān, the Central Protector General of the South, appointed Yáng as a staff officer.
Yáng was to accompany Xuān to Xiāngyáng,
but Grand Commandant Táo Kǎn kept him in Wǔchāng.
At that time, Kǎn was planning a northern expedition.
Yáng said:
"In the eleventh month of the year before last, Yínghuò (Mars) remained in Wèi and Mǎo (constellations),
until the fourth month of this year,
for over five hundred days.
Mǎo
is the region of Zhào,
so Shí Lè died.
Yínghuò retreated in the seventh month,
moving clockwise from Bì (constellation) into the ecliptic,
but before reaching Tiānguān,
on the twenty-second day of the eighth month, it moved retrogradely back to Gōu,
circling Bì towards Mǎo.
Mǎo and Bì represent border troops
and govern the Hú and Yí (barbarians),
hence the placement of the celestial bow to shoot them.
Yínghuò's retrograde motion
governs a country without virtue,
which is the case with Shí Lè's death.
The remnants of Lè's regime
will self-destruct.
This year, Guān (the official star) conjoins the Grand Cycle (Tàisuì) and the Grand Yin (Tàiyīn) in a triple conjunction at Guǐsì.
Guǐ is the north,
so the north will suffer disaster.
The *Suì* and *Zhèn* (Jupiter and Saturn) stars have conjoined in Yì and Zhěn (constellations),
from *zǐ* to *sì*,
lingering for six years.
The region of Jīngchǔ,
guarded by *Suì* and *Zhèn*,
will see its country flourish.
Is this not a sign of merit and virtue!
In the sixth month of this year,
Zhèn Xīng (Saturn) will be ahead of Jiǎo and Kàng (constellations).
Jiǎo and Kàng
are the region of Zhèng.
Suì Xīng (Jupiter) will move into Fáng (constellation),
and Tàibái (Venus) will be in Xīn (constellation).
Xīn and Fáng
are the region of Sòng.
Those who follow them will prosper;
those who defy them will perish.
If Shí Jìlóng raises troops towards the southeast,
this will be his moment of death.
If you respond to Heaven and execute punishment,
directly occupying Sòng and Zhèng,
you will be invincible.
If Heaven offers but you do not take,
you will in turn suffer its blame."
Kǎn was intent on the Central Plains
and was greatly pleased upon hearing this.
However, he became gravely ill
and could not proceed with the expedition.
Kǎn died.
General of the Western Expedition, Yǔ Liàng, took his place to guard Wǔchāng.
Again he invited Yáng to inquire about the atmospheric omens.
Yáng said:
"The heavens show a white vapor;
the funeral procession will surely go east,
and it will be fulfilled within a few years."
Soon, a large deer appeared heading towards the west city gate.
Yáng said:
"Wild beasts approaching the city
indicate the master will depart."
A family east of the city saw several torches inside the city at midnight,
emerging from atop the city wall,
resembling a large chariot,
covered with white cloth canopies,
moving northeast out of the city with the torches,
and disappearing upon reaching the river.
Yáng heard of this and sighed, saying:
"This is the same as the previous white vapor."
At this time, Liàng wished to move west to guard Shíchéng.
Someone asked Yáng:
"Is this western move sufficient to counter the desired eastern move?"
Yáng said:
"It is not sufficient."
In the third year of Xiánkāng,
Yáng said to Liàng:
"The land of Wǔchāng has mountains but no forests;
it is suitable for beginnings,
but not for remaining to the end.
The mountains form an 'eight' character (八),
the number does not reach nine.
In the past, Wú ascended in the Rén'yín year,
establishing the palace city,
and by the Jǐyǒu year,
it returned down to Mòlíng.
Duke Táo also spent eight years there.
The prosperity and decline of the land have their cycles,
and the movement of people has its timing;
these cannot be changed.
Your Excellency should choose another auspicious place;
Wǔchāng is not a place to stay long."
In the fifth year,
Liàng ordered Máo Bǎo to garrison Zhūchéng.
In the ninth month,
Yáng said to Liàng:
"Máo, the Prefect of Yùzhōu, will face a death omen this year.
Yesterday morning, there was a great fog and a calm wind,
indicating vengeful bandits will seek retribution,
attacking and besieging the feudal lords,
so it is truly advisable to scout far."
Bǎo asked when this would happen.
He replied:
"Within fifty days."
That evening,
he also said:
"In the ninth month, Jiànxū,
the Vermilion Bird flies alarmed,
the expeditionary army returns home,
carrying a fiery glow.
Heaven provides a sign,
disaster erupts in Dōngfáng,
leaves return to their roots,
beware of future troubles."
The next day,
he further said:
"Last night's fire disaster
is not a national blessing.
Building houses this year
will cause Your Lord to fall ill.
You can use the burning of the house
to move your family south across the river;
there will be no ill omens."
Bǎo immediately sent his daughter-in-law back to Wǔchāng.
Soon, news arrived that bandits were about to attack the city.
Yáng said:
"The omen of the bandits will be received at midnight on the Dīnghài day of the tenth month.
Gān represents the lord,
zhī represents the minister,
Dīng represents the General of the Western Expedition's headquarters,
Hài represents Zhūchéng.
Gōngcáo is the bandit's deity.
Adding the Zǐ hour, and in the tenth month, water flourishes and wood is ascendant.
The flourishing and ascendant energies combine,
so bandits will certainly come.
Yín corresponds to the number seven,
Zǐ to the number nine.
The maximum number of bandits will be nine thousand,
the minimum seven thousand.
Cóngkuí is the noble person added to Dīng,
indicating the lower overcoming the upper,
with matters of emptiness and void,
so they will not dare advance to Wǔchāng."
The bandits indeed captured Zhūchéng and left.
Liàng asked Yáng:
"Will Shíchéng then not be lost?"
Yáng said:
"The bandits are going from Ānlù towards Shíchéng,
going against Tàibái,
they will harm themselves;
there is no need to worry."
Liàng said:
"Why does Heaven favor the Hú and afflict us?"
Yáng said:
"Heaven's symbols have good and ill fortune,
and lands have their periods of prosperity and decline.
This year's harmful energy combines with Jǐhài.
Jǐ represents all under Heaven,
Hài represents the Rónghú.
Jìlóng will also suffer death.
Now, I am not worried about the bandits,
but only about Your Lord's illness."
Liàng said:
"What method can save me from my illness?"
Yáng said:
"Jīngzhōu will suffer military action,
Jiāngzhōu will suffer disaster.
Your Lord can leave these two prefectures."
Liàng said:
"If so,
will there be a resolution?"
Yáng said:
"It's regrettable that it's late.
Still, it might make a difference."
Liàng ultimately could not leave the two prefectures,
and consequently fell into great distress.
Yáng said:
"During the time of Sū Jùn,
Your Lord prayed for blessings at Báishí Temple,
promising to sacrifice a cow,
but this has not yet been fulfilled,
therefore you are troubled by this ghost."
Liàng said:
"That is true.
You are a divine person."
Someone asked Yáng:
"How much longer will Duke Yǔ live?"
Yáng said:
"He will see next year."
At that time, Liàng no longer recognized people,
and everyone thought this was nonsense,
but he indeed died on the first day of the first month.
Yǔ Yì replaced Liàng,
and Yáng again performed divinations.
A short while later, he died,
at over eighty years old.
The verified predictions are too numerous to count.
Hán Yǒu
Hán Yǒu, courtesy name Jǐngxiān,
was a man from Shū, Lújiāng.
As a scholar,
he studied the *Yì* from Wǔ Zhèn of Kuàijī,
was skilled in divination,
and capable of interpreting house plans and tomb locations,
also practicing the methods of Jīng Fèi's 'yànshèng' (warding off evil).
Dèng Lín, the magistrate of Lóngshū, had a wife who had been ill for years,
on the verge of death;
doctors and shamans had all given up hope.
Yǒu divined for her,
and had a wild boar drawn and placed on the screen by her bed.
After one night, she felt better,
and then she recovered completely.
Wáng Mù, a clerk of Shū County, died of illness,
but his soul returned.
Yǒu divined for him,
and ordered red paint to be used to draw the sun and moon on a board and place it by the bed,
and also to place leopard skin and a horse's mud-guard over him.
He immediately recovered.
Liú Shìzé's daughter had been ill with possession for years.
Shamans had attacked and prayed,
felling trees between empty tombs and old city walls,
obtaining dozens of civets and alligators,
but the illness still did not get better.
Yǒu divined for her,
and ordered a cloth bag to be made.
According to the time of the girl's attacks,
he hung the bag by the window.
Yǒu closed the door and performed a ritual, as if driving something out.
In a short while,
the bag was seen to swell greatly as if inflated.
He then decided to destroy it,
and the girl then suffered a major relapse.
Yǒu then made two more leather bags,
stacked them,
and hung them as before.
The bags again swelled full.
He then quickly tied the mouths of the bags,
and hung them on a tree for about twenty days.
They gradually deflated.
When opened, there were two *jīn* of fox fur inside,
and the girl then recovered.
In the fourth month, Biān Hóng of Xuānchéng consulted Yǒu regarding his family’s well-being.
Yǒu said:
“Your household faces a military calamity,
and the disaster is extremely severe.
You should cut seventy bundles of firewood,
pile them in the Gēng direction,
and on the Dīngyǒu day of the seventh month, set them ablaze.
The misfortune may then be averted.
Otherwise,
its ill-omen is unspeakable.”
Hóng immediately gathered the firewood.
On the appointed day,
a strong wind blew,
and he dared not light the fire.
Later, Hóng became a commander (lǐngxiào) in Guǎngyáng,
and returned home for his mother's funeral.
Yǒu came to stay with him.
By then, it was already dusk.
Yǒu went out and told his attendant,
“Quickly pack up;
I must leave tonight.”
The attendant said,
“It’s already dark today,
and it's dozens of *lǐ* through the wilderness.
Why the rush to leave again?”
Yǒu replied,
“This is not something you would understand.
Blood will cover the ground here;
how can I possibly stay?”
Despite being urged to stay,
he left without waiting to eat.
That night, Hóng suddenly went mad,
strangled his two sons,
and also killed his wife.
He also slashed two of his father's concubines,
who were both wounded.
He then fled and went missing.
The next day,
his clan went to collect and inter the deceased.
They searched for Hóng
for several days
and found him in the woods in front of his residence,
having hanged himself.
The Grand Administrator (tàishǒu) of Xuānchéng, Yīn Yòu, was ill.
Yǒu divined for him
and said:
“On the last day of the seventh month,
a large grackle will come and perch on the main hall.
You should diligently watch for and catch it.
If you succeed, it will be good;
if not, it will lead to disaster.”
Yòu then carefully made preparations.
On the appointed day,
indeed, a large grackle with a tail nine *chǐ* long
came and perched on the main hall.
They ambushed and caught it.
Yòu was then promoted to Supervisor of Shítóu,
and later became the Grand Administrator of Wújùn.
Yǒu’s divinations and predictions were remarkably effective,
and in averting calamity and transforming misfortune,
none ever failed to come true.
Gān Bǎo asked him why.
Yǒu replied,
“Divining hexagrams uses the mutual generation and destruction of the Five Phases,
just like prescribing medicine according to a formula to treat illness,
using hot and cold to counteract each other.
Whether it works or not
cannot be certain.”
Yǒu was nominated as a “Worthy and Filial” candidate in the sixth year of Yuánkāng.
When Emperor Yuán crossed the Jiāng River,
he appointed Yǒu as General of Guǎngwǔ.
He died at the end of Yǒngjiā.
Chúnyú Zhì
Chúnyú Zhì, courtesy name Shúpíng,
was a native of Fāgàn, Jìběi.
He was thoughtful and righteous,
skillful in the *Yì* divination,
and adept at the art of sympathetic magic.
When Líu Róu of Gāopíng was sleeping one night,
a rat bit his left middle finger.
He asked Zhì about it.
Zhì said,
“It wants to kill you but cannot.
I will make it die instead.”
He then used vermilion ink to draw a ‘田’ (tián) character on his wrist, three *cùn* after the transverse line,
a square of one *cùn* and two *fēn*,
and told him to sleep with his hand exposed.
The next morning,
a large rat was found dead, lying in front of his hand.
When Xiàhóu Zǎo of Qiáo's mother was gravely ill,
he went to Zhì for a divination.
Suddenly, a fox howled at him from the doorway.
Zǎo was terrified and amazed,
and rushed to see Zhì.
Zhì said,
“The calamity is extremely urgent.
You must return quickly.
At the place where the fox howled, beat your chest and weep loudly,
so that your family will be startled.
Everyone, young and old, must come out.
If even one person does not come out,
do not stop crying.
Only then can the disaster be averted.”
Zǎo returned
and did as he was told.
His mother also, though ill, came out.
As soon as the family had gathered,
the five rooms of the main hall collapsed with a crash.
When Zhāng Shào, the Protector of the Army (hùjūn), had a gravely ill mother,
Zhì divined for him
and told him to go west to the market to buy a macaque,
tie it to his mother’s arm,
have bystanders beat it,
making it cry out,
and release it after three days.
Shào followed his instructions.
As soon as the monkey left the gate, it was bitten to death by a dog,
and his mother's illness was cured.
Bāo Yuàn of Shàngdǎng experienced many deaths, illnesses, and poverty in his family.
Someone told him,
“Chúnyú Shúpíng is a divine person.
Why don't you try consulting him
to find out the source of your misfortune?”
Yuàn was by nature straightforward
and did not believe in divination,
saying,
“Life has its destiny;
how can divination change it?”
Just then, Zhì arrived.
Yīng Zhān said to him,
“This gentleman is a poor scholar
who often encounters difficulties.
You have a penetrating spiritual insight;
could you perform a divination for him?”
Zhì then performed a divination.
When the hexagram was complete,
he said to Yuàn,
“Your residence is unsuitably situated,
which is why you are in distress.
To the northeast of your house there is a large mulberry tree.
Go directly to the market.
Within dozens of steps of the entrance,
you will encounter a person holding a荆 (jīng) horsewhip.
Buy it from him and hang it on this tree.
In three years, you will suddenly become wealthy.”
Yuàn followed his words and went to the market.
Indeed, he found the horsewhip.
He hung it for three years.
When he dug a well,
he found hundreds of thousands of coins
and over two hundred thousand units of copper and iron implements.
From then on, he became prosperous,
and the sick among his family also recovered.
His ability to dispel disasters and transform misfortunes
was innumerable,
and his divinations
were accurate in hundreds of thousands of cases.
Yīng Zhān was also sickly in his youth.
Zhì then made an amulet and had Zhān wear it,
reciting its text.
Afterward, they all came true,
but no one could learn it.
He was profound and reserved by nature.
He often spoke of his short life,
saying,
“In the Xīnhài year, there will be trouble under heaven,
and geomancers and doctors who possess Daoist arts will die.
I uphold the principles of the *Yì* and act accordingly;
should I not be exempt from this?”
At the end of Tàikāng,
he served as a Commandant (sīmǎ dū)
and was favored by Yáng Jùn.
Therefore, he was killed.
Bù Xióng
Bù Xióng, courtesy name Shú Pí,
was a native of Fāgàn, Yángpíng.
In his youth, he loved divination and numerology,
and had a large following of disciples.
One day, a person burned to death next to Xióng’s schoolhouse.
Officials arrested Xióng’s students,
thinking it was their fault for starting the fire.
Xióng said,
“I have divined and found the person responsible.
Have someone go south along the road.
When a person comes and asks if the fire-starter has been found,
immediately arrest him.”
The official did as Xióng said,
and indeed, it was a farmer
who admitted that the weeds were bad and hard to plow,
so he had burned them.
Suddenly, the wind rose and spread the fire far and wide.
He truly did not know there was someone in the weeds.
Another time, a neighbor’s child traveled far away,
and someone reported he had died.
His parents wept and put on mourning clothes.
Xióng divined for them
and set a date for his return.
He arrived exactly as predicted.
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) heard of his reputation,
and summoned him.
Xióng (熊) said to his students:
“Lún (倫) will die soon;
he is not worth responding to.”
Lún (倫) was enraged,
and dispatched soldiers to besiege him repeatedly.
Xióng (熊) then instructed his students to put on their fur coats and flee south.
Lún’s (倫) soldiers all rushed to seize them,
while Xióng (熊) secretly exited from the north
and escaped.
Later, he was recruited by Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng (成都王穎).
Yǐng (穎) had Xióng (熊) perform *shèfù* (射覆),
and he made no mistakes regarding the objects.
Later, when Yǐng (穎) fled to Guānzhōng (關中),
Píngchāng Gōng Mó (平昌公模) garrisoned Yè (鄴).
Considering Xióng (熊) a member of Yǐng’s (穎) faction,
he executed him.
Dù Bùqiān (杜不愆)
Dù Bùqiān (杜不愆)
was a man from Lújiāng (廬江).
In his youth, he studied divination by the *Yì* (易) with his maternal grandfather, Guō Pú (郭璞),
and frequently proved accurate.
Xī Chāo (郗超) of Gāopíng (高平), in his early twenties,
contracted a severe illness.
He requested Bùqiān (不愆) to divine for him.
Bùqiān (不愆) said:
“Judging from the hexagram,
your suffering will soon be removed.
However, you should go northeast, thirty *lǐ* (里) away, to a family surnamed Gōng (宮) and obtain a male pheasant they keep,
cage it, and place it under the east eaves.
Nine days later, on a *bǐngwǔ* (丙午) day at noon,
a female pheasant will surely fly in to mate with it,
and then they will fly away together.
If this happens,
within twenty days, your illness will be completely cured,
and this is also an auspicious sign:
you will live to nearly eighty years old,
and reach the highest position among officials.
If the female merely departs and the male remains,
your illness will only abate after a full cycle (of the illness),
you will live to half eighty,
and your fame and position will also be lost.”
Chāo (超) was at that time extremely weak
and feared his life was on the brink.
He laughed and replied:
“If I can preserve half of eighty,
that would be more than enough!
An illness cured in one cycle
is hardly a delay!”
However, he did not believe it.
Someone persuaded him to follow the advice,
and a pheasant was indeed found as prescribed.
On the *bǐngwǔ* (丙午) day,
Chāo (超) lay under the south veranda to watch it.
Late in the day,
a female pheasant indeed flew into the cage,
mated with the male pheasant, and departed,
while the male pheasant remained still.
Chāo (超) sighed and said:
“Even the wonders of Guǎn (管) and Guō (郭)
cannot surpass this!”
Chāo’s (超) illness lasted a full year before he recovered.
At the age of forty,
he died as a zhōngshūláng (中書郎).
Bùqiān’s (不愆) subsequent divinations became less accurate,
without similar instances.
Later, he became the jiànwēi cānjūn (建威參軍) for Huán Sì (桓嗣).
Yán Qīng (嚴卿)
Yán Qīng (嚴卿)
was a man from Kuàijī (會稽).
He was skilled in divination.
His fellow villager, Wèi Xù (魏序), wished to travel east for a short while.
It was a year of famine with many bandits,
so he asked Qīng (卿) to divine for him.
Qīng (卿) divined and said:
“You must not travel east;
you will certainly encounter violent and harmful *qì* (氣),
but it will not be a robbery.”
Xù (序) did not believe him.
Qīng (卿) said:
“Since you are determined to go,
it is advisable to avert it.
You can find a white male dog from a single mother’s house outside the west city wall and tie it to the front of your boat.”
He searched but only found a pied dog;
there was no white one.
Qīng (卿) said:
“A pied one will also suffice,
but I still regret its color is not pure,
so there will be a minor residual harm,
affecting only livestock,
nothing more to worry about.”
When Xù (序) was halfway on his journey,
the dog suddenly cried out very urgently,
as if someone was hitting it.
By the time they looked,
it was already dead,
having vomited over a *dǒu* (斗) of black blood.
That evening,
several white geese at Xù’s (序) villa died without cause,
but Xù’s (序) family remained unharmed.
Wěi Zhào (隗炤)
Wěi Zhào (隗炤)
was a man from Rǔyīn (汝陰).
He was skilled in the *Yì* (易).
At his deathbed,
he wrote on a wooden tablet and gave it to his wife, saying:
“After my death, you will face great poverty and destitution.
Even so,
be sure not to sell the house.
Five years from now, in spring,
an imperial envoy will arrive and stop at this pavilion.
His surname will be Gōng (龔).
This man owes me money.
You should take this tablet and demand it from him;
do not disobey my words.”
After Zhào (炤) died,
his family fell into severe destitution.
They wanted to sell the house,
but remembered her husband’s words and always stopped.
On the appointed day,
an envoy named Gōng (龔) stopped at the pavilion.
The wife then brought the tablet and demanded the money from him.
The envoy held the tablet, looking bewildered,
not knowing why.
The wife said:
“My husband, on his deathbed,
personally wrote this tablet and instructed me thus;
I dare not be mistaken.”
The envoy pondered for a long time and then understood.
He asked her:
“What was your worthy husband good at?”
The wife said:
“My husband was skilled in the *Yì* (易),
but he never divined for others.”
The envoy said:
“Aha,
now I understand!”
He then ordered to fetch yarrow stalks and divined.
When the hexagram was formed,
he clapped his hands and sighed, saying:
“How marvelous, Master Wěi (隗)!
He concealed his brilliance and hid his tracks,
truly one who could mirror success and failure, and penetrate fortune and misfortune.”
Thereupon, he told Zhào’s (炤) wife:
“I do not owe you money.
Your worthy husband himself had money.
He knew that after his death, you would temporarily face hardship,
so he hid the money to await times of peace.
The reason he did not tell his children and wife was
that he feared the money would be spent, and your destitution would be endless.
Knowing that I was skilled in the *Yì* (易),
he therefore wrote the tablet to convey his meaning.
There are five hundred *jīn* (斤) of gold,
contained in a green urn,
covered by a bronze plate,
buried at the east end of the main hall,
ten *chǐ* (尺) from the wall,
and nine *chǐ* (尺) deep in the ground.”
The wife returned and dug,
and everything was as predicted.
Bǔ Xǔ (卜珝)
Bǔ Xǔ (卜珝), courtesy name Zǐyù (子玉),
was from the rear section of the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
In his youth, he enjoyed reading the *Yì* (易).
Guō Pú (郭璞) saw him and sighed, saying:
“I am not his equal,
but why can he not escape military hardship?”
Xǔ (珝) said:
“Indeed.
My great misfortune will be at forty-one,
when I will hold the position of a *qīngjiāng* (卿將) and suffer disaster.
Otherwise,
I would also be harmed by a fierce beast.
I also do not foresee your good end.”
Pú (璞) said:
“My misfortune is in Jiāngnán (江南).
I have indeed made preparations,
but I do not see a sign of escape.
However,
in the south, I might still prolong my life,
but staying here, it would not be more than a month or so.”
Xǔ (珝) said:
“If you do not become a government official,
you can escape it.”
Pú (璞) said:
“I cannot avoid being a government official,
just as you cannot avoid being a *qīngjiāng* (卿將).”
Xǔ (珝) said:
“Although there will be an imperial prince here,
I will ultimately no longer serve the two capitals.
Lángyé (琅邪) can be served.
You should diligently serve him;
the one who will continue the sacrifices of Jìn (晉) must be this person.”
Xǔ (珝) then retired to Lóngmén Shān (龍門山).
Liú Yuánhǎi 僭號 (usurped the imperial title).
Bǔ Xǔ was summoned to be Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī nóng) and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
He firmly declined due to illness.
Yuánhǎi said:
"Each person has their own aspirations.
Bǔ Xǔ's unwillingness to serve in my court
is no different from Gāozǔ's Four Whiteheads (Sì Gōng)!
Let him pursue his noble aspirations."
Later, he was again summoned to be Grand Master of Bright Radiance (Guānglù Dàfū).
Xǔ said to the envoy:
"This is not where I am meant to die."
When Liú Cōng succeeded to the false throne,
Xǔ was summoned to be Grand Supplicator (Tàicháng).
At that time, Liú Kūn held Bìngzhōu.
Cōng asked when it could be pacified.
Xǔ replied:
"Bìngzhōu is rightfully Your Majesty's territory.
It will surely be conquered this year."
Cōng jested:
"I wish to reward you, sir, with a journey; would that be acceptable?"
Xǔ said:
"The reason I came without making preparations
was precisely for this journey."
Cōng was greatly pleased
and appointed Xǔ as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe) and General Who Pacifies the North (Píng Běi Jiāngjūn).
As he was about to depart,
he said to his sister:
"On this journey,
death is my lot;
afterward, be sure not to cause trouble."
When they attacked Jìnyáng,
they were defeated by Kūn.
Xǔ fled first
and was killed by his own commander.
Bāo Jìng
Bāo Jìng, courtesy name Tàixuán,
was a native of Dōnghǎi.
At the age of five,
he told his parents:
"I was originally the child of the Lí family in Qǔyáng,
and died by falling into a well at the age of nine."
His parents sought out and found the Lí clan,
and their inquiries matched all the details.
Jìng studied both inner and outer (Daoist and Confucian) teachings,
and was versed in astronomy and the Hétú and Luòshū.
He was gradually promoted to Central Commandant of Nányáng (Nányáng Zhōngbù Dūwèi),
and became Administrator of Nánhǎi (Nánhǎi Tàishǒu).
Once, while inspecting his district and entering the sea,
he encountered a storm
and became extremely hungry.
He took white stones and ate them to sustain himself.
Wáng Jī, then Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu,
entered the latrine
and suddenly saw two men dressed in black clothes
grappling with him.
After a long time, he captured them,
obtaining two creatures resembling black ducks.
Jìng said:
"These creatures are inauspicious."
Jī burned them,
