and they flew directly up to heaven.
Jī was soon executed.
Jìng once met the immortal Yīn Jūn,
who imparted Daoist techniques to him.
He died at over a hundred years old.
Wú Měng
Wú Měng
was a native of Yùzhāng.
When young, he was known for his filial piety.
In summer, he often did not wave away mosquitoes with his hands,
fearing that if they left him, they would bite his parents.
At forty,
Dīng Yì, a local from his district, first taught him divine methods.
Later, returning to Yùzhāng,
the river waves were very swift.
Měng did not use a boat,
but drew on the water with a white feather fan and crossed.
Onlookers found it extraordinary.
Yǔ Liàng, when Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu,
once fell ill.
Hearing of Měng's divine powers,
he invited him,
asking about his illness.
Měng declined, saying his lifespan was exhausted,
and requested a coffin and burial clothes be prepared.
He died within ten days,
his form appearing as if alive.
Before the grand embalming,
his corpse was lost.
Those who knew considered it an inauspicious omen for Liàng.
Liàng's illness indeed proved fatal.
Xìng Líng
Xìng Líng
was a native of Jiànchāng, Yùzhāng.
He was taciturn by nature.
When living among commoners,
he showed no resentment when insulted,
so his village called him "the fool."
Even his parents and siblings considered him foolish.
Once, when assigned to guard rice,
a herd of cattle came to eat it.
Líng saw them but did not drive them away,
waiting for the cattle to leave before tidying up the ravaged plants.
His parents saw this and were angry.
Líng said:
"All creatures living between heaven and earth
desire food.
If the cattle are eating,
why should I drive them away?"
His father grew even angrier and said:
"If that is what you say,
then why bother tidying up the ruined plants?"
Líng said:
"This rice also wishes to fulfill its natural course.
Since the cattle themselves infringed upon it,
how can Líng not gather it?"
At that time, Fán Chángbīn of Shùnyáng was Magistrate (Lìng) of Jiànchāng.
He conscripted the common people to build official boats in Jiànchéng mountain,
and the officials ordered each person to make a pair of chopsticks.
Líng made them but had not yet submitted them,
when someone stole them.
Soon after, the thief suffered from severe heart pain, wanting to die.
Líng said to him:
"Did you perhaps steal my chopsticks?"
The thief did not answer.
A moment later,
the pain became more acute.
Líng said:
"If you do not tell me the truth,
you will truly die now."
The thief, in desperation,
confessed and produced them.
Líng then gave him water to drink,
and the illness immediately disappeared.
Travelers thenceforth respected and feared him.
When the boats were finished
and about to be launched,
the officials used two hundred men to pull one vessel,
but it could not be moved,
and they were about to request more men.
Líng said:
"This is more than enough;
it is just that the method has not been applied correctly.
Líng requests to pull it himself."
So he took hold of the ropes with his hands,
used only a hundred men,
and the boat moved like flowing water.
The crowd was greatly astonished,
all proclaiming his divinity,
and thus he became famous.
There was a woman, the daughter of Gōng Zhòngrú, who had been ill for many years,
her breath barely clinging to her.
Líng told her to hold water in her mouth,
and soon after, she was able to rise strongly,
recovering completely at once.
Also, Lǚ Yī's mother, Lady Huáng, suffered from paralysis,
for more than ten years.
Líng treated her,
sitting a few feet away from Lady Huáng,
closing his eyes in silence.
After a while,
he looked at Yī and said:
"Help your mother to stand up."
Yī said:
"The old lady has been ill for years;
how can she suddenly stand up?"
Líng said:
"Just try to help her up."
So two people supported her to stand.
A short while later,
Líng told them to remove their support,
and she was able to walk by herself,
thus recovering completely.
Then the common people rushed,
converging from land and water,
following him like clouds.
Lady Huáng, considering her long illness,
feared a relapse.
Líng then left a vessel of water for her to drink.
Each time she took water,
he would replenish the spot with fresh water.
For over twenty years, the water remained as clear as new,
untouched by dust or dirt.
At that time, Gāo Lǐ's
house had a ghost that spoke and scolded,
throwing things inside and outside,
yet no human form was seen.
Sometimes objects moved on their own,
and fire broke out repeatedly.
Shamans and exorcists were unable to stop it.
It happened that Líng was passing by,
so Gāo Lǐ invited him.
Líng looked at his house from the end of the road,
and said to Gāo Lǐ,
"Is this your residence?"
Gāo Lǐ said,
"It is."
Líng said,
"Knowing this is enough."
Gāo Lǐ insisted on inviting him,
so Líng, having no choice,
arrived at the gate.
Seeing many talismans and cords,
he said to Gāo Lǐ,
"One should stop evil with righteousness,
but you are trying to cure evil with evil.
How can it possibly cease?"
He then had them all burned,
and merely sat for a short while on the porch before leaving.
That evening, the ghost ceased immediately.
Many of those Líng healed were of this kind,
yet he took no rewards or thanks.
He did not ride in conveyances when traveling,
nor did he take a wife in old age.
His nature was extremely deferential;
whenever he saw someone, he would bow first,
and when speaking, he would always refer to himself by name.
Any plant or tree damaged in the mountains and forests,
he would certainly rise to tend to it.
Any object overturned on the road,
he would certainly pick it up and set it right.
He traveled around Jiāngzhōu
and said to its scholars:
"Heaven and Earth regard all beings,
human and otherwise, as one.
All desire not to lose their nature and disposition.
How can you subjugate people and make them slaves?
If you gentlemen wish to enjoy abundant blessings and preserve your lives,
you should release all of them."
For over ten years,
an extremely large number of people benefited from his techniques.
Later, he married a wife,
acquired carriages, horses, and slaves,
and accepted bribes and gifts.
Thereupon, his art gradually declined,
and in his treatments, success and failure were equally divided.
Fótiúdēng
Fótiúdēng was
a man from Tiānzhú.
His original surname was Bái.
He studied the Dao in his youth
and was wonderfully skilled in mysterious arts.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiā,
he came to Luòyáng.
He claimed to be over a hundred years old,
constantly nourishing himself by breath-holding techniques,
and was able to go without food for many days.
He was skilled at reciting divine incantations
and could command ghosts and spirits.
He had a hole in his side,
which he usually plugged with cotton.
Every night when he read,
he would remove the cotton,
and light would emanate from the hole,
illuminating the entire room.
Also, during a fast,
he once went to the side of a flowing stream at dawn,
and from the hole in his side, he drew out his five *zàng* and six *fǔ* to wash them.
Afterwards,
he put them back into his abdomen.
He could also tell good and bad fortune by listening to the sound of bells,
and none of his predictions failed to be confirmed.
When the disturbances broke out in Luò,
he hid in the wilderness to observe the changes.
Shí Lè's troops were encamped at Gěpí,
and he carried out mass killings.
Many *shāmén* were among those killed.
Fótiúdēng went to the home of Shí Lè's great general, Guō Hēilüè.
Whenever Guō Hēilüè accompanied Shí Lè on campaigns,
he would predict victory or defeat in advance.
Shí Lè grew suspicious and asked,
"I am not aware of any extraordinary wisdom or strategy you possess,
so how is it that you always know the fortune of military expeditions?"
Guō Hēilüè said,
"General, your divine martial prowess is heaven-endowed,
aided by unseen spirits.
There is a *shāmén* whose wisdom and art are extraordinary.
He says that you, General, are destined to conquer the whole of China,
and he should be your teacher.
All the reports I have made previously
are his words."
Shí Lè summoned Fótiúdēng
and tested him with his magical arts.
Fótiúdēng immediately took a bowl, filled it with water,
burned incense, and chanted incantations over it.
In a moment, a green lotus flower grew in the bowl,
its brilliance shining brighter than the sun.
Shí Lè believed in him from then on.
When Shí Lè returned from Gěpí to Héběi,
passing through Fāngtóu,
the people of Fāngtóu wanted to attack his camp at night.
Fótiúdēng said to Guō Hēilüè,
"The bandits will arrive shortly;
you can let the Duke know."
It happened exactly as he said;
they were prepared,
and thus not defeated.
Shí Lè wanted to test Fótiúdēng.
At night, he donned his helmet and armor,
holding a sword, and sat down.
He sent someone to tell Fótiúdēng,
"Last night, I don't know where the Great General is."
When the messenger arrived,
before he could speak,
Fótiúdēng preemptively asked,
"In peacetime without bandits,
why are you so heavily armored tonight?"
Shí Lè believed in him even more.
Later, Shí Lè, in a fit of anger,
wanted to harm all the Daoists,
and also wanted to inflict suffering upon Fótiúdēng.
Fótiúdēng then secretly went to Guō Hēilüè's residence
and told his disciples,
"If the General's messenger arrives
and asks where I am,
report that you do not know where I have gone."
Presently, Shí Lè's messenger arrived,
but could not find Fótiúdēng.
When the messenger returned and reported to Shí Lè,
Shí Lè exclaimed in alarm,
"I had evil intentions towards Fótiúdēng,
and Fótiúdēng has left me!"
He did not sleep all night,
desiring to see Fótiúdēng.
Fótiúdēng knew Shí Lè had repented,
so the next morning he went to see Shí Lè.
Shí Lè asked,
"Where did you go last night?"
Fótiúdēng said,
"You had anger in your heart,
so I temporarily avoided you last night.
Now that you have changed your mind,
I therefore dare to come."
Shí Lè laughed heartily and said,
"You, Daoist, are mistaken!"
The source of the moat water for Xiāngguó city was five *lǐ* northwest of the city,
but its source suddenly dried up.
Shí Lè asked Fótiúdēng how to get water.
Fótiúdēng said,
"I will now command the dragon to bring water."
So he went with several disciples, including Fǎshǒu, to the old spring source,
sat on a rope bed,
burned benzoin incense,
and recited prayers for several hundred words.
After three days of this,
water emerged faintly,
and a small dragon, about five or six inches long,
came with the water.
All the Daoists eagerly went to see it.
A moment later,
a great flow of water arrived,
filling the moats and trenches.
The Xiānbēi Duàn Mòbō attacked Shí Lè,
and his forces were very strong.
Shí Lè was frightened and
asked Fótiúdēng.
Fótiúdēng said,
"Yesterday, the temple bell rang, saying,
'Tomorrow morning at mealtime,
Duàn Mòbō will be captured.'"
Shí Lè ascended the city wall to look at Duàn Mòbō's army,
but could not see its beginning or end.
He paled and said, "If Mòbō is like this,
how can he be captured?"
He sent Kuí Ān again to ask Fótiúdēng.
Fótiúdēng said,
"Mòbō has already been captured."
At that moment, the hidden troops north of the city came out,
encountered Mòbō,
and seized him.
Fótiúdēng advised Shí Lè to pardon Mòbō
and send him back to his native country.
Shí Lè followed this advice
and eventually gained his service.
Liú Yào sent his cousin Yuè to attack Lè.
Lè sent Shí Jìlóng to resist him.
Yuè was defeated
and retreated to defend Shíliáng Wù.
Jìlóng firmly fortified and guarded it.
Chéng was in Xiāngguó
when he suddenly sighed,
"Liú Yuè is to be pitied!"
His disciple Fǎzuò asked him why.
Chéng said,
"Yesterday, at the Hài hour (9-11 PM),
Yuè was already defeated and captured."
It turned out exactly as he had said.
When Yào personally attacked Luòyáng,
Lè was about to go to its rescue,
but his subordinates all advised against it, deeming it impossible.
Lè consulted Chéng about this.
Chéng said,
"The bell sound from the Xianglún Pagoda says: 'Xiùzhī tìlìgāng,
púgǔ qútūdāng.'
This is the Jié language.
Xiùzhī
means 'army.'
Tìlìgāng
means 'to go out.'
Púgǔ
is Liú Yào's Hú official title.
Qútūdāng
means 'to capture.'
This means 'the army goes out and captures Yào.'"
He also instructed a young boy to cleanse himself for seven days,
take sesame oil and mix it with rouge,
and personally grind it in his palm.
He raised his hand and showed it to the boy,
who saw a brilliant glow.
The boy exclaimed in surprise,
"There are many soldiers and horses,
and I see a tall, large, white man
whose elbows are bound with red silk."
Chéng said,
"This is Yào himself."
Lè was greatly pleased,
and so he went to Luòyáng to resist Yào
and captured him alive.
Lè usurped the title of King of Zhào,
exercising the duties of an emperor,
and his reverence for Chéng became even deeper.
At that time, Shí Cōng was about to rebel.
Chéng warned Lè, saying,
"This year, there are worms in the scallions.
Eating them will surely harm people.
You should order the common people not to eat scallions."
Lè issued a proclamation throughout his territory,
cautioning everyone not to eat scallions.
Soon after, Shí Cōng indeed fled.
Lè esteemed him even more,
always consulting him before acting,
and called him Dà Héshàng (Great Monk).
Lè's beloved son Bīn died suddenly from illness.
As they were about to arrange the funeral,
Lè sighed,
"I have heard that when the Crown Prince of Guó died,
Biǎn Què was able to revive him.
Can we achieve a similar effect now?"
He then ordered someone to inform Chéng.
Chéng took a willow branch, dipped it in water,
sprinkled it, and chanted a spell.
Then he grasped Bīn's hand and said,
"Rise up!"
Consequently, he revived
and, after a while,
fully recovered.
From then on, many of Lè's sons were raised in Chéng's temple.
In the year Lè died,
the sky was still and windless,
yet a single bell on the pagoda rang by itself.
Chéng told the multitude,
"The bell sound says
there will be a great national mourning,
and it will happen within this year."
Soon after, Lè indeed died.
When Jìlóng usurped the throne,
he moved the capital to Yè.
He devoted himself to serving Chéng
even more than Lè had.
He issued a decree to clothe Chéng in silk brocade,
and had him ride in an ornate carriage.
On days of court assembly,
he would be led to ascend the hall.
All officials from the Chángshì downwards helped carry the palanquin,
and the Crown Prince and other princes supported him as he ascended.
The attendant would call out "Dà Héshàng,"
and all those seated would rise,
to show their respect.
He also had Sīkōng Lǐ Nóng personally inquire after him morning and evening,
and the Crown Prince and other princes paid their respects every five days.
His respect was unparalleled.
Zhī Dàolín, who was in the capital,
heard that Chéng associated with the Shí family,
and said,
"Master Chéng must regard Jìlóng as a mere seagull."
Because of Chéng, many common people embraced Buddhism,
all constructing temples and monasteries,
and competing to become monastics.
The genuine and the fake became mixed,
leading to many transgressions.
Jìlóng issued a decree to sort them out.
His Zuòshùláng Wáng Dù memorialized, saying,
"Buddha
is a deity from a foreign land,
not one that the people of Huá should worship.
When his doctrine was first transmitted in the Hàn dynasty,
only Western Region people were allowed to establish temples in cities
to worship their deity,
and no Hàn people became monastics.
The Wèi dynasty continued the Hàn system
and also followed the former practice.
Now, we should prohibit all Zhào people from going to temples to burn incense and prostrate themselves,
in order to follow the established rites.
All officials, from the highest ministers to the lowest servants,
should be forbidden without exception.
Those who violate this
will be punished with the same crime as illicit worship.
Zhào people who are Shāmen
should return to lay life."
Many court officials agreed with Dù's memorial.
Because of Chéng, Jìlóng
issued a decree saying,
"I originate from the border tribes
and am unworthily ruling Zhū Xià.
Regarding sacrifices and worship,
I should follow my original customs.
Buddha is a tribal deity,
who should also be worshipped.
Therefore, I specially permit those amongst the Í (barbarians) and Zhào common people who wish to practice Buddhism
to do so."
Chéng at that time resided in a temple in Yèchéng.
His disciples were spread throughout the commanderies and states.
He once sent his disciple Fǎcháng north to Xiāngguó.
His disciple Fǎzuǒ returned from Xiāngguó,
and they met under the walls of Liángjīchéng.
They talked through the night, sitting in their carriages,
mentioning their Master.
At dawn, they each departed.
As Zuǒ first entered,
Chéng laughed and said to him,
"Last night, you and Fǎcháng met in your carriages and spoke about your Master, didn't you?"
Zuǒ was astonished and ashamed, confessing.
Hence, people in the country often said to each other,
"Don't harbor evil thoughts,
the Master knows you."
And wherever Chéng was located,
no one dared to spit or blow their nose in his direction.
Jìlóng's Crown Prince Suì had two sons
in Xiāngguó.
Chéng told Suì,
"Little Āmí will soon fall ill.
You should go and see him."
Suì immediately dispatched a messenger to go and see,
and indeed, he had already fallen ill.
The imperial physician Yīn Téng and foreign Daoists claimed they could cure him.
Chéng told his disciple Fǎyá,
"Even if a sage were to reappear,
he could not cure this illness,
let alone these people!"
Three days later, he indeed died.
Suì intended to plot a rebellion
and told his palace attendants,
"The Master has supernatural powers;
he might reveal my plan.
Tomorrow, if he comes,
I must eliminate him first."
Chéng, on the fifteenth day of the lunar month, was about to enter the palace to pay respects to Jìlóng.
He told his disciple Sēnghuì,
"Last night, a heavenly deity called out to me, saying: 'If you enter tomorrow,
do not visit anyone on your way back.'
If I should happen to visit someone,
you must stop me."
Chéng, when entering,
always visited Suì.
Suì knew Chéng was coming
and waited for him anxiously.
As Chéng was about to ascend the Southern Terrace,
Sēnghuì pulled his robe.
Chéng said,
"I cannot stop now."
He barely sat down before getting up again.
Suì tried to keep him, but he did not stay,
and thus Suì's plot was thwarted.
Returning to the temple,
he sighed,
"The Crown Prince is plotting rebellion;
its form is almost complete.
I want to speak but it's hard to speak;
I want to bear it but it's hard to bear."
So, he seized an opportunity to subtly advise Jìlóng,
but Jìlóng ultimately failed to understand.
Soon after, the incident occurred,
and only then did he realize Chéng's words.
Later, Guō Hēiluè 將兵 (jiāngbīng) marched troops to conquer the Qiāng in the northern mountains of Cháng'ān.
He fell into a Qiāng ambush.
At that time, Chéng was seated in the hall,
and with a sorrowful change of expression, he said:
"Lord Guō is now in peril."
He then announced:
"All monks, offer prayers!"
Chéng also prayed himself.
After a moment,
he further said:
"If he heads southeast, he will live;
if he heads in any other direction, he will be in distress."
He again offered prayers.
After a while,
he said:
"He has escaped."
More than a month later,
Hēiluè returned,
and recounted how he had fallen into a Qiāng encirclement.
He fled southeast,
but his horse became exhausted.
He just happened to encounter one of his subordinates,
who pushed his own horse to him and said:
"My lord, ride this horse.
I, your humble servant, will ride your horse.
Whether we are saved or not,
it is fate."
Hēiluè obtained his horse,
and thus managed to escape.
When the time and date were checked,
it was precisely the time when Chéng had offered his prayers.
At that time, there was a drought.
Jìlóng sent his crown prince to Línzhāng (臨漳) to Fúkǒu (滏口) in the west to pray for rain.
For a long time, no rain fell.
So, he ordered Chéng to go himself.
Immediately, two white dragons descended at the shrine.
That day, heavy rain fell over several thousand *lǐ*.
Chéng once sent a disciple to the Western Regions to buy incense.
After the disciple had left,
Chéng told his other disciples:
"I see in my palm that the disciple buying incense is in a certain place, robbed and on the verge of death."
Thereupon, he burned incense and offered prayers,
remotely saving and protecting him.
Later, the disciple returned
and said that on a certain month, a certain day, in a certain place, he had been robbed by bandits,
and was about to be killed,
when he suddenly smelled a fragrant aroma.
The bandits, without any apparent reason, cried out in alarm:
"Rescue troops have arrived!"
And abandoned him and fled.
Yellow River (Huánghé) had never before produced soft-shelled turtles (yuán).
At this time, someone found one
and presented it to Jìlóng.
Chéng saw it and sighed, saying:
"Huán Wēn will enter the river.
Will it not be long?"
Wēn's courtesy name was Yuánzǐ (元子).
Later, it indeed happened as he had said.
Jìlóng once took a daytime nap
and dreamt of a flock of sheep carrying fish coming from the northeast.
Upon waking, he consulted Chéng about it.
Chéng said:
"This is inauspicious.
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) will perhaps possess the Central Plains!"
Later, this also all came true.
Chéng once ascended the central terrace (Zhōngtái) with Jìlóng.
Chéng suddenly exclaimed in alarm:
"Disaster!
Disaster!
Yōuzhōu (幽州) will suffer a fire."
He then took wine and spurted it out.
After a long while, he smiled and said:
"The rescue has been achieved."
Jìlóng sent someone to verify in Yōuzhōu.
They reported that on that day, fires broke out from the four gates,
but black clouds came from the southwest,
and a sudden rain extinguished them.
The rain also had a rather strong smell of wine.
Shí Xuān (石宣) was about to kill Shí Tāo (石韜).
Xuān arrived at the temple first and sat with Chéng.
A single bell of the Buddhist (Fútú) temple rang by itself.
Chéng said to him:
"Do you understand the sound of the bell?
The bell says, 'The Huzi (胡子) have lost their way (Luòdù - 洛度).'"
Xuān's expression changed, and he said:
"What kind of talk is this?"
Chéng pretended to mistake it and said:
"The old Hu (胡) cultivates the Way,
unable to live in the mountains without speaking.
With thick cushions and beautiful clothes,
how can this not be losing the Way?"
Shí Tāo arrived later.
Chéng stared at him intently for a long time.
Tāo was afraid and asked Chéng.
Chéng said:
"I find your blood to have a foul smell,
that is why I looked at you."
Jìlóng dreamt of a dragon flying southwest,
falling from the sky.
In the morning, he asked Chéng about it.
Chéng said:
"Calamity is about to arise.
It is advisable for father and son to be loving and harmonious,
and to be deeply cautious about it."
Jìlóng led Chéng into the eastern wing (Dōnggé),
and inquired about it with his empress, Dù Shì (杜氏).
Chéng said:
"There is a bandit at your side.
Within ten days,
from the Buddhist temple westward,
and this palace eastward,
there will be a flow of blood.
Be careful not to go east."
Empress Dù said:
"Is the monk senile?
Where are there any bandits?"
Chéng immediately changed his words and said:
"All that is received by the six senses
are all bandits.
It is natural for the old to be senile,
but it is good as long as the young are not confused."
He then spoke metaphorically,
no longer explicitly.
Two days later,
Xuān indeed sent people to harm Tāo in the Buddhist temple,
intending to kill Jìlóng when he came to mourn.
Jìlóng, due to Chéng's prior warning,
thus escaped.
When Xuān was arrested,
Chéng advised Jìlóng:
"They are all your Majesty's sons.
Why commit such a grave calamity?
If your Majesty can swallow your anger and show mercy,
you still have over sixty years of life.
If you must execute him,
Xuān will become a comet sweeping down over Yè Gōng (鄴宮)."
Jìlóng did not listen.
More than a month later,
there was a demonic horse,
its mane and tail all appearing burnt.
It entered the Zhōngyáng Mén (中陽門),
exited the Xiǎnyáng Mén (顯陽門),
headed east toward the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
but could not enter any.
It galloped toward the northeast
and soon disappeared.
Chéng heard about it and sighed:
"Calamity is upon us!"
Jìlóng gave a grand feast for his officials in the front hall of the Tàiwǔ Diàn (太武殿).
Chéng recited:
"Oh hall,
oh hall!
Thorns will form a forest,
and tear people's clothes."
Jìlóng ordered the floor stones of the hall to be opened and looked underneath.
There were thorns growing there.
Rǎn Mǐn's (冉閔) small name was Jǐnú (棘奴, meaning 'thorn slave').
When Jìlóng's construction of the Tàiwǔ Diàn was first completed,
the murals depicted ancient sages, loyal ministers, filial sons, virtuous martyrs, and chaste women,
but they all transformed into Barbarian (Hú) appearances.
After more than ten days,
all their heads shrank into their shoulders,
only their caps and headbands faintly protruding.
Jìlóng found this extremely unsettling
and kept it secret, not speaking of it.
Chéng wept as he looked at them,
then personally announced his intention to prepare his tomb (yíngmù) at Zǐmò (紫陌) west of Yè.
Returning to the temple,
he spoke to himself:
"Will I get three years?"
He answered himself:
"No."
He then said:
"Will I get two years, one year, a hundred days, a month?"
He answered himself:
"No."
Then he spoke no more.
He told his disciple Fǎzuò (法祚):
"In the year of Wùshēn (戊申), chaos will gradually emerge.
In the year of Jǐyǒu (己酉), the Shí (石) clan will be destroyed.
I will pass away before the chaos begins."
He died in the Yè Gōng Temple (Yè Gōng Sì - 鄴宮寺).
Later, a Shāmen (沙門) came from Yōngzhōu (雍州)
claiming to have seen Chéng entering Guān (關) in the west.
Jìlóng dug up the tomb to check,
and found only a stone, with no corpse.
Jìlóng was displeased and said:
"Stone (Shí)
is me.
He buried me and then left.
I am going to die."
Thereupon, he fell ill.
The next year,
Jìlóng died,
and great chaos ensued.
(This is the end of the text, "麻襦" is a final term in the original document, not part of the narrative and not to be translated as narrative.)
Márú,
it is not known from where he came,
nor could his name be ascertained.
During the time of Shí Jìlóng,
he begged in the markets of Wèixiàn,
wearing a hemp jacket and cloth skirt,
hence people at the time called him Márú.
His words were profound,
and he appeared like a madman.
The rice and grain he received from begging he would not eat,
but scattered it on the main road,
saying it was to feed the "Heavenly Horses."
Zhào Xìng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Zhào Xìng) Jí Zhuàng arrested him and sent him to Jìlóng.
Before this,
Fótúchéng had told Jìlóng:
“Two hundred *lǐ* east of the capital, on a certain month and day, an extraordinary person will be sent.
Do not kill him.”
As scheduled, he indeed arrived.
Jìlóng spoke with him,
but he said nothing out of the ordinary,
except to say,
“Your Majesty will end up beneath a single pillar in a hall.”
Jìlóng did not understand,
and sent him to Chéng.
Márú said to Chéng:
“Once, during the Guānghé era, we met,
and suddenly it is today.
The western *Róng* have received the dark mandate,
〔一０〕the end of their calendar is imminent.
Gold and separation vanish into the earth,
the border wilderness cannot be followed,
expelling the traces of spiritual eras,
none can achieve such excellence.
Descendant sprouts flourish,
their coming is accumulating.
When will the time of rest be?
I sigh eternally over this.”
Chéng said:
“Heaven’s rotation has reached its limit,
misfortune will not be sustained.
The difficulty of the nine woods and water,
there is no technique to pacify it.
Although the profound sages exist in the world,
none can establish and none can certainly stop the decline.
〔一一〕Long have I wandered in Yánfúlì,
troubled by these many woes.
I ascend to the cloud-reaching abode,
to meet in the ethereal expanse.”
What he said, no one could understand.
Jìlóng dispatched an express horse to send him back to his original county.
As soon as they left the city,
Márú asked to walk,
saying:
“I have somewhere to pass through;
you wait for me at Hékǒuqíao.”
The envoy rode as instructed,
and upon reaching the bridge,
Márú had already arrived.
Later, Mùróng Jùn threw Jìlóng’s corpse into the Zhāngshuǐ,
where it leaned against a bridge pillar and did not float away.
People at the time believed
that “beneath a single pillar in a hall”
referred to this.
When Yuán Dì succeeded to the throne in Jiāngzuǒ,
it was also thought
to be an omen for the “Heavenly Horses.”
So it is said.
Shàn Dàokāi
Shàn Dàokāi
was from Dūnhuáng.
He always wore coarse hemp clothing.
If given silk garments,
he would not wear them.
He feared neither cold nor heat,
and did not sleep day or night.
He ingested small stones,
swallowing several at a time,
once a day,
sometimes more, sometimes less.
He liked living in the mountains.
When the mountain trees and various spirits appeared in strange forms to test him,
he showed no fear.
During the time of Shí Jìlóng,
he came from Xīpíng,
traveling seven hundred *lǐ* in a single day.
A fourteen-year-old *shāmí* accompanying him
also matched his pace.
Upon reaching Qínzhōu,
he was reported and sent to Yè.
Jìlóng ordered Fótúchéng to speak with him,
but could not subdue him.
Initially, he resided in the temple of the *Shāmén* Fǎlín west of Yèchéng.
Later, he moved to Zhāodé Sì in Línzhāng.
Inside his room, he built a double-layered partition,
eight or nine *chǐ* high,
and on top of it, he wove straw to make a meditation cell,
where he often sat.
Jìlóng provided him generously,
but Dàokāi gave everything to others.
If people came to consult him,
Dàokāi would not answer.
Daily, he would take several pills of a stabilizing medicine,
the size of *wútóng* seeds.
The medicine had the scent of pine, honey, ginger, cinnamon, and *fúlíng*.
Occasionally, he would drink one or two *shēng* of tea.
He claimed he could cure eye diseases,
and those who sought treatment were often cured.
Observing his actions,
he seemed divinely inspired.
Fótúchéng said:
“This Daoist observes the rise and fall of nations.
If he leaves,
there will be great chaos.”
Towards the end of Jìlóng’s reign,
Dàokāi crossed south to Xǔchāng,
and soon after, there was great chaos in Yè.
In the third year of Shēngpíng, he arrived at the capital,
and later went to Nánhǎi,
entering Luófú Shān,
dwelling alone in a thatched hut,
detached from worldly affairs.
He was over a hundred years old
when he died in his mountain dwelling.
He instructed his disciples to place his body in a stone cave.
His disciples then moved it into a stone chamber.
Yuán Hóng of Chénjùn, who was the Administrator of Nánhǎi,
along with his younger brother Yǐngshū and the *shāmén* Zhī Fǎfáng, ascended Luófú Shān.
Upon reaching the entrance of the stone chamber,
they saw Dàokāi’s remains as if alive,
with incense, ashes, and earthenware still present.
Hóng said:
“The Dharma Master’s practice and conduct were extraordinary,
just like a cicada shedding its skin.”
He then composed an encomium for him.
Huáng Hóng
Huáng Hóng, courtesy name Shǐcháng,
was from Chìqiū, Wèijùn.
His father, Shěn,
was skilled in astronomy and secret arts.
Hóng inherited his father’s profession,
surpassing him in subtlety and depth.
He also extensively read classics and histories,
and was particularly clear on rites and the *Yìjīng*.
His nature was loyal and diligent;
he would not act contrary to rites.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he and Gāo Zhān of Bóhǎi sought refuge in Yōuzhōu.
He advised Zhān, saying:
“Wáng Jùn is dim-witted and violent,
and will ultimately accomplish nothing.
You should consider departing or staying to plan for long-term security.
Mùróng Kuì’s laws and governance are clear and enlightened,
and he has an open mind to attract people.
Moreover, the prophecies say a true man will emerge from the northeast;
could it perhaps be he?
We should go and pledge allegiance to him,
and together establish a great undertaking.”
Zhān did not follow.
Hóng then led his clan to surrender to Kuì.
Kuì treated him with the courtesy due to a guest,
and appointed him as *Cānjūn*,
consulting him on all military and state affairs.
Hóng pointed out successes and failures,
and everything happened as he predicted.
Kuì often said:
“*Cānjūn* Huáng
is my Zhòngxiáng.”
When Guǎng succeeded to the throne,
Hóng was promoted to Zuǒ Chángshì,
and oversaw the historical records,
being greatly valued.
When Shí Jìlóng attacked Guǎng,
Guǎng intended to flee to Liáodōng.
Hóng said:
“The bandits show signs of defeat;
there is nothing to worry about.
In no more than two days,
they will certainly collapse and flee.
You should strictly command your soldiers and horses,
and prepare for a counter-attack.”
Guǎng said:
“Now the enemy is so formidable;
you say they will surely flee,
but I dare not believe it.”
Hóng said:
“Your Highness says they are formidable;
that is human affairs.
I say they will surely flee;
that is the opportune moment.
Why should there be any doubt?”
At the appointed time,
Jìlóng indeed retreated,
and Guǎng admired him even more.
When Mùróng Jùn 慕容儁 ascended the throne as king,
he was promoted to Clerk and Central Secretary (Cóngshì Zhōngláng 從事中郎).
Jùn 儁 heard of Rǎn Mǐn's 冉閔 rebellion
and planned to conquer the Central Plains.
He consulted Hóng 泓.
Hóng 泓 advised him to proceed,
and Jùn 儁 followed his advice.
When Jùn 儁 usurped the imperial title,
he appointed Hóng 泓 as General Who Advances Strategy (Jìnmóu Jiāngjūn 進謀將軍), Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng 太史令), and Marquis within the Passes (Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯).

Soon after, he was further granted the titles of Mounted Escort Commander (Fèngchē Dūwèi 奉車都尉), Administrator of Xīhǎi 西海 (Xīhǎi Tàishǒu 西海太守), concurrently holding the position of Grand Astrologer, and Marquis of Kāiyáng Tíng 開陽亭.
He was also ennobled as a fifth-rank伯 (bó 伯) of Píngshū Xiàn 平舒縣.
He was constantly by the king's side,
consulted on major decisions.
Xǔ Dūn 許敦, the Director of the Astronomical Observatory (Língtái Lìng 靈臺令), resented Hóng's 泓 favor
and flattered Mùróng Píng 慕容評.
He raised dissenting opinions to slander Hóng 泓.
Consequently, Hóng 泓 was appointed Superintendent of all offices of the Grand Astrologer and Astronomical Observatory (Tàishǐ Língtái Zhūshǔ Tǒng 太史靈臺諸署統),
and further granted the title of Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng 給事中).
Hóng 泓 treated Dūn 敦 with even greater generosity,
not letting the slander change his heart.
When Mùróng Wěi 慕容暐 was defeated,
Hóng 泓 retired home due to old age.
He sighed,
"Yàn 燕 will surely experience a restoration.
It will be achieved by the King of Wú 吳.
I only regret that I am too old to witness it."
He died at the age of ninety-seven.
Three years after his death,
the pretender King of Wú 吳, Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂, rose to power.
Suǒ Dǎn 索紞
Suǒ Dǎn 索紞, courtesy name Shúchè 叔徹,
was a native of Dūnhuáng 敦煌.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital
and studied at the Imperial Academy.
He was broadly versed in the classics
and became a profound scholar.
He understood yin and yang, astronomy,
and was skilled in numerology and prognostication.
The Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) invited him,
and he was appointed Gentleman (Lángzhōng 郎中).
Knowing that China was about to fall into chaos,
he withdrew from the world and returned home.
His fellow villagers came to Dǎn 紞 to ask about good and ill fortune,
and his gate was like a marketplace.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"Attacking heterodox doctrines
is to be warned against as it harms oneself;
do not involve yourself in many affairs,
for many affairs lead to many troubles."
Thus, he deliberately spoke deceptive and empty words,
and only stopped when there was no verification.
Only in interpreting dreams did he feel no regret or remorse,
and thus he did not turn away those who sought answers.
The Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián 孝廉) Línghú Cè 令狐策 dreamed he stood on ice
and spoke with a person beneath the ice.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"Above the ice is yang,
below the ice is yin;
this is an affair of yin and yang.
If a gentleman marries a wife
before the ice melts,
it is a matter of marriage.
You stand on the ice and speak with a person beneath the ice,
which is yang speaking to yin;
this is a matter of mediation.
You will act as a matchmaker for someone,
and when the ice melts, the marriage will be complete."
Cè 策 said,
"I am old and decrepit,
I will not be a matchmaker."
Soon after, the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) Tián Bào 田豹, through Cè 策, sought the daughter of his fellow villager Zhāng Gōngzhēng 張公徵 for his son,
and the marriage was completed in mid-spring.
The Commandery Chief Clerk (Jùn Gōngcáo 郡主簿) Zhāng Zhái 張宅 dreamed he galloped a horse up a mountain,
then circled his dwelling three times,
seeing only pines and cypresses,
not knowing where the gate was.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"A horse belongs to Lǐ 離 [the trigram],
and Lǐ 離 represents fire.
Fire
means disaster (huò 禍).
A person going up a mountain
forms the character for 'fierce' or 'ominous' (xiōng 凶).
Seeing only pines and cypresses
is the image of a tomb gate.
Not knowing where the gate is
means there is no gate.
Three circles
mean three years.
After three years, there will surely be a great disaster."
Zhái 宅 was indeed executed for plotting rebellion.
Suǒ Chōng 索充 initially dreamed that two coffins fell from the sky before him.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"A coffin (guān 棺) represents an office (guān 官);
you will be recommended by a nobleman from the capital.
Two offices
mean two successive promotions."
Soon after, Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) Wáng Róng 王戎 wrote to the Administrator to recommend Chōng 充.
The Administrator first appointed Chōng 充 as Supervisor of Merit (Gōngcáo 功曹) and then recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt.
Later, Chōng 充 dreamed he saw a barbarian,
who took off his upper garment and came to Chōng 充.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"Remove the top part of the character 'lǔ' 虜 (barbarian),
and the lower part is the character for 'male' (nán 男).
Barbarians are associated with the yin category.
Your wife will give birth to a son."
It ultimately came true as he said.
Sòng Jué 宋桷 dreamed there was a person in the inner chamber wearing red clothes,
and Jué 桷 held two sticks
and beat him severely.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"A person in the inner chamber (nèi zhōng yǒu rén 內中有人) forms the character for 'meat' (ròu 肉).
The color of meat
is red.
Two sticks
resemble chopsticks (zhù 箸).
Beating severely
means eating one's fill of meat."
Soon after, this also came true.
Huáng Píng 黃平 asked Dǎn 紞,
"Last night I dreamed the horses in my house were dancing,
and dozens of people clapped their hands towards the horses.
What does this omen mean?"
Dǎn 紞 said,
"A horse (mǎ 馬) is fire (huǒ 火),
and dancing represents fire starting.
Clapping hands towards the horses
means people putting out the fire."
Before Píng 評 returned home, a fire broke out.
Suǒ Suí 索綏 dreamed that from the east, two horn-shaped documents came to Suí 綏.
The large horn was decayed and rotten,
the small horn had an inscription on a leather bag with a horn pendant,
one in front,
one behind.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"The large horn decayed and rotten
means a rotten coffin.
The small horn with an inscription
means a question or inquiry.
One in front
means in front is ominous (xiōng 凶).
One behind
means behind is a betrayal (bèi 背).
There will be a question of ominous betrayal."
At that time, Suí's 綏 father was in the east.
Three days later, news of misfortune arrived.
The Commandery Supervisor of Merit (Jùn Gōngcáo 郡功曹) Zhāng Miǎo 張邈 once served on a mission to the province.
One night he dreamed a wolf bit off one of his legs.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"Flesh of the leg being eaten
forms the character 'quē' 卻 (to withdraw or refuse)."
At that time, the Eastern Barbarians rebelled,
so he did not proceed.
All his predictions were unfailingly accurate.
The Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) Yīn Dàn 陰澹 asked him for his book on prognostication.
Dǎn 紞 said,
"When I entered the Imperial Academy,
I met an old man who became my host.
This person knew everything
and concealed his name,
resembling a recluse.
I then learned the art of dream interpretation from this old man.
I thoroughly analyze and explain;
there is actually no book."
Dàn 澹 appointed him Libationer of the Western Gallery (Xīgé Jìjiǔ 西閤祭酒),
but Dǎn 紞 declined, saying,
"In my youth, I lacked the ambition of a hermit.
I traveled and studied in the capital,
associating with the wise of the time,
hoping to display my humble skills.
But then China became unsettled,
and I wished to cultivate my ambition for the rest of my years.
Old age has also arrived,
and I do not seek fame or advancement.
Moreover, I was not accustomed to diligence in my youth,
and in old age, I have no administrative ability.
At the age of Měngsì 濛汜 (approaching the end of life),
I dare not accept the command."
Dàn 澹 presented him with silk as a禮 (lǐ 禮)
and sent him sheep and wine monthly.
At seventy-five,
he died at home.
Mèng Qīn 孟欽
Mèng Qīn
was a man from Luòyáng.
He possessed the arts of Zuǒ Cí and Liú Gēn,
and the common people were deceived and flocked to him.
Fú Jiān summoned him to Cháng'ān,
but disliking his deceiving the masses,
ordered Fú Róng to execute him.
Soon after, Qīn arrived,
and Róng detained him.
He then hosted a grand banquet for his subordinate officials in the commandery.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he signaled his attendants to seize Qīn.
Qīn transformed into a whirlwind
and flew out of the residence.
A short while later,
someone reported he was in the eastern part of the city.
Róng dispatched cavalry to pursue him.
As they were about to catch him,
he suddenly became distant.
Sometimes there were troops fighting them off,
and sometimes there were streams and ravines ahead,
preventing the cavalry from passing.
Thus, his whereabouts became unknown.
In Fú Jiān's later years,
he was again seen in Qīngzhōu.
Fú Láng sought him out,
and he entered a sea island.
Wáng Jiā,
whose courtesy name was Zǐnián,
was a man from Ānyáng, Lǒngxī.
He was light in his demeanor
and ugly in appearance.
Outwardly, he seemed deficient,
but inwardly he was intelligent and discerning.
He was humorous and fond of talking and laughing.
He did not eat the five grains
and did not wear beautiful clothes.
He purified himself, consumed *qì*,
and did not associate with worldly people.
He lived as a recluse in Dōngyáng Gǔ,
carving cliffs to make cave dwellings.
Hundreds of disciples received his teachings,
and they also lived in caves.
In the later years of Shí Jìlóng,
he abandoned his followers
and went to Cháng'ān,
secretly hiding in Zhōngnán Shān,
where he built an hermitage and stayed.
When his disciples heard, they followed him again,
so he moved to Dǎoshòu Shān.
Fú Jiān repeatedly summoned him, but he did not respond.
Dukes and marquises and those below them all personally went to visit him.
There was no refined scholar who did not take him as their master.
When asked about current affairs,
he would answer according to the question.
He was fond of using metaphors,
which resembled humorous remarks;
when speaking of future events,
his words were like prophecies,
which few at the time could understand,
but all were proven true after the events.
When Fú Jiān was about to campaign south,
he sent an envoy to ask him.
Wáng Jiā said:
"Jīngāng huǒ qiáng" (Diamond fire strong).
Then he rode the envoy's horse,
adjusted his clothes and hat,
and slowly walked several hundred paces eastward.
Then he spurred the horse back,
took off his clothes,
discarded his hat and shoes, and returned.
He dismounted and sat cross-legged on his couch,
saying nothing.
When the envoy returned and reported this,
Fú Jiān did not understand.
He sent another envoy to ask him,
saying:
"What about the fate of my dynasty?"
Wáng Jiā said:
"Wèiyāng" (Not yet ended).
Everyone thought it was auspicious.
The next year, *guǐwèi*,
he was defeated at Huáinán.
This was what was meant by "wèi nián ér yǒu yāng" (the year of *wèi* and calamity).
Those who sought him,
if their hearts were sincere, would see him;
if not sincere, he would become invisible.
His clothes were on the rack,
his shoes and staff still there.
If someone wanted to take his clothes,
they could not reach them.
If they stood on tiptoe to reach them,
the clothes rack would become even higher,
though the room was not large.
His shoes, staff, and other items were also like this.
When Yáo Cháng entered Cháng'ān,
he treated Wáng Jiā with the same respect as Fú Jiān had,
compelling him to stay by his side,
and consulting him on every matter.
When Yáo Cháng was in a standoff with Fú Dēng,
he asked Wáng Jiā:
"Can I kill Fú Dēng and pacify the world?"
Wáng Jiā said:
"Luè dé zhī" (You will vaguely obtain it).
Yáo Cháng became angry and said:
"If I obtain it, I should say 'obtain,'
what is this 'vaguely' about?"
So, he executed him.
Before this,
Shì Dào'ān had said to Wáng Jiā:
"The world is in turmoil,
you can leave now."
Wáng Jiā replied:
"You go first;
I have not yet settled my debts, so I cannot leave."
Soon after, Dào'ān died,
and now Wáng Jiā was executed,
which was what he meant by
"settling debts."
When Fú Dēng heard of Wáng Jiā's death,
he set up an altar and wept for him,
posthumously granting him the title of Tàishī
and the谥号 (shìhào) Wén.
When Yáo Cháng died,
Yáo Cháng's son Yáo Xīng, whose courtesy name was Zǐlüè, then killed Fú Dēng.
This was the meaning of "luè dé."
On the day Wáng Jiā died,
some people saw him in Lǒngshàng.
The *Qiān Sān Gē Chèn* he composed,
all its prophecies were proven true after the events,
and it has been passed down for generations.
He also authored *Shíyí Lù* in ten scrolls,
which records many strange and bizarre events,
and is still circulated in the world today.
Sēng Shè
Sēng Shè
was a man from the Western Regions,
his surname is unknown.
He became a *shāmén* at a young age,
and entered Cháng'ān during Fú Jiān's time.
He was serene and practiced *qì* cultivation,
did not eat the five grains,
and could travel five hundred *lǐ* a day.
He spoke of future events,
and his predictions were as clear as pointing to one's palm.
He could use secret incantations to summon divine dragons.
Whenever there was a drought,
Fú Jiān often made him invoke dragons to ask for rain.
Soon after, a dragon would descend into his bowl,
and the heavens would then bring heavy rain.
Fú Jiān and his officials personally went to the bowl to observe it.
He died in Cháng'ān.
Later, when there was a great drought for a long time,
Fú Jiān sighed and said:
"If Master Shè were alive,
how could I worry about this!"
Guō Xún
Guō Xún
was a man from Xīpíng.
From a young age, he was skilled in *shìyì* divination,
and served as the chief clerk of the commandery.
In the final years of Zhāng Tiānxī,
whenever the Fú clan had questions about western campaigns,
the Grand Administrator Zhào Níng would have Guō Xún divine for them.
Guō Xún said:
"If, on the fifteenth day of the second month, a prisoner escapes from within the commandery,
the eastern army will arrive,
and Liáng's mandate will surely end."
Zhào Níng then sent orders to the subordinate counties.
On the fifteenth day,
a Xiānbēi man named Zhéjué sent a horse to Zhào Níng.
Zhào Níng was angry that it was not a fine steed
and imprisoned him.
The Xiānbēi man was frightened and fled during the night.
Zhào Níng reported this to Guō Xún.
Guō Xún said:
"This is it.
The state is about to perish,
and cannot be saved."
In the later years of Fú Jiān,
the Dāngyáng Mén trembled.
The Inspector Liáng Xī asked Guō Xún:
"What does this omen signify?"
Guō Xún said:
"It concerns the four barbarian tribes.
There will be two foreign kings who come to pay homage to the sovereign.
One will return to his country,
and one will die in this city."
More than a year later, the kings of Shànshàn and Qiánbù paid homage to Fú Jiān.
Upon returning west,
the King of Shànshàn died in Gūzāng.
When Lǚ Guāng ruled Hexi,
Wáng Zhēn, the Grand Administrator of Xihai, rebelled.
Yún exhorted Guāng to attack him.
Guāng’s Assistant Minister, Lǚ Bǎo, said:
“Attacking someone a thousand li away
has always been difficult since ancient times.
Moreover, a king’s army is known throughout the realm;
how can one rely on luck to achieve success?
Yún should not be followed;
he will ruin a great undertaking.”
Yún said:
“If it is not victorious,
I myself will submit to execution by axe.
If it is victorious,
the Assistant Minister will be shown to be without strategy.”
Guāng followed him and was victorious.
Guāng compared Yún to Jīng Guǎn and
he often participated in secret council meetings.
When Guāng was about to attack Qǐfú Gānguī,
Yún admonished him, saying:
“Today, the planet Venus has not yet appeared;
it is not suitable to move troops.
Going forth will surely yield no success
and will ultimately end in defeat.”
The Grand Astrologer, Jiǎ Yào, believed that he would certainly gain Qin and Long territories.
When Jīnchéng was conquered,
Guāng had Yào question Yún.
Yún secretly said to Guāng:
“Yesterday, a meteor fell to the east.
There will be dead generals lying in ambush.
Although this city has been gained,
the worry is that it cannot be held.
In the first ten days of the first month,
the river ice will break.
If you do not cross early,
I fear there will be a great disaster.”
Two days later, news of defeat arrived.
After Guāng led his army across the river,
the ice melted.
People at the time admired his divine accuracy.
Guāng appointed Yún as Sanqí Chángshì and Tàicháng.
Later, Yún, knowing that Guāng was old
and that he would soon fail,
then, with Guāng’s Púshè Wáng Xiáng, raised an army and started a rebellion.
〔一三〕When the common people heard that Yún had raised an army,
they all believed that a sage was undertaking a matter,
and that no matter would fail.
Therefore, they rushed to follow him as if they were unable to catch up.
Yún believed that the one who replaced Lǚ would be king,
so he enthroned Wáng Qǐjī as their lord.
〔一四〕Later, Lǚ Lóng surrendered to Yáo Xīng.
Xīng appointed Wáng Shàng as the Inspector of Liángzhōu,
which ultimately came true just as Yún had said.
When Yún and Guāng were at a stalemate,
a fugitive reported that Lǚ Tǒng had died of illness.
Yún said:
“Not yet.
The lives of Guāng and Tǒng will end at the same time.”
Three days after Tǒng died, Guāng died.
Yún once said:
“Later, the Qiānguāng Palace in Liángzhōu will be occupied by Suǒtóu Xiānbēi.”
Eventually, Tūfà Tán and Júqú Méngxùn successively occupied Gūzāng.
Yún was narrow-minded and cruel by nature,
and was not supported by either scholars or commoners.
After being defeated in battle,
he fled to Qǐfú Gānguī.
When Gānguī was defeated,
he entered Yáo Xīng’s domain.
Yún believed that it would be Jìn who would destroy Yáo,
so he took his wife and children and fled south,
but was killed by pursuing soldiers.
Jiūmó Luóshí
Jiūmó Luóshí was
a native of Tiānzhú.
His family served as prime ministers for generations.
His father, Jiūmó Luóyán,
was intelligent, virtuous, and of great character.
He was about to inherit the prime minister’s position,
but declined it and became a monk,
crossing the Cōnglíng mountains to the east.
The King of Qiūcí heard of his fame,
went out to the suburbs to welcome him,
and invited him to be the national preceptor.
The king had a sister,
aged twenty,
who was talented, discerning, and intelligent.
Various states proposed marriage,
but she refused them all.
When she saw Luóyán,
she wished to marry him.
So the king forced her to become his wife.
After Luóshí was conceived,
his mother’s wisdom and understanding became many times greater than usual.
When he was seven years old,
his mother then became a nun with him.
Luóshí studied scriptures under a master,
reciting a thousand verses daily.
Each verse had thirty-two characters,
totaling thirty-two thousand words,
and he understood their meaning by himself.
At the age of twelve,
his mother took him to Shālè.
The king greatly respected him,
so they stayed in Shālè for one year.
He extensively read various treatises on the Five Sciences, as well as on yin and yang, stars, and calculations,
mastering them all.
He profoundly understood good and bad omens,
and his words were like prophecies.
He was by nature straightforward and unrestrained,
not adhering to minor conventions.
Practitioners often doubted him.
However, Luóshí was content in his heart,
never taking it to mind,
and devoted himself to propagating Mahāyāna Buddhism.
All scholars considered him their master.
At the age of twenty,
the King of Qiūcí welcomed him back to the country,
where he extensively expounded on various scriptures.
Scholars from all directions could not rival him.
A short while later,
Luóshí’s mother bade farewell to the King of Qiūcí and went to Tiānzhú,
leaving Luóshí behind.
She said to him:
“The profound teachings of Vaipulya (Fangdeng)
are inconceivable.
Their transmission to the Eastern Lands
depends solely on your power.
However, it will be of no benefit to you;
what can be done about that?”
Shí said:
“If it ensures the widespread transmission of the Great Teaching,
then even if it brings hardship, I will have no regrets.”
His mother arrived in Tiānzhú,
achieved enlightenment,
and ascended to the third fruit.
All the Western Regions admired Luóshí’s divine brilliance.
Whenever he lectured,
the kings would all kneel beside him,
allowing Luóshí to step on them to ascend.
Fú Jiān heard of this
and secretly intended to welcome Luóshí.
It happened that the Grand Astrologer reported:
“A star has been seen in the foreign sector,
indicating that a great sage will come to assist China.”
Jiān said:
“I have heard of Jiūmó Luóshí in the Western Regions;
could it be he?”
Thereupon, he dispatched the Valiant Cavalry General Lǚ Guāng and others, leading an army of seventy thousand,
to march west and attack Qiūcí.
He said to Guāng:
“If you capture Luóshí,
immediately send him by swift post-horse.”
Before Guāng’s army arrived,
Luóshí said to Bái Chún, the King of Qiūcí:
“The destiny of the kingdom is in decline.
A powerful enemy will come from the direction of the sun.
You should respectfully submit to them;
do not resist their advance.”
Chún did not follow this advice
and sent out troops to resist and fight.
Guāng then defeated him
and captured Luóshí.
Guāng saw that he was still young
and treated him like an ordinary person, joking with him.
He forced him to marry the daughter of the King of Qiūcí.
Luóshí resisted and refused,
his pleas were very bitter and sincere.
Guāng said:
“A Daoist’s integrity is no greater than his late father’s;
why such firm refusal?”
Then he made him drink strong wine
and locked them together in a secret room.
Luóshí, being forced,
then married her.
When Guāng was returning,
he stationed his army at the foot of a mountain halfway.
The officers and soldiers had already rested,
when Luóshí said:
“Staying here will certainly lead to trouble.
It is advisable to move the army to the ridge.”
Guāng did not heed him.
That night,
it indeed rained heavily,
and a sudden flood rose rapidly.
The water was several zhang deep,
and thousands of people died.
Guāng secretly found this extraordinary.
Lu_3 Guāng wanted to keep Wáng Róng in the western country.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí said to Lu_3 Guāng:
"This is a land of misfortune and doom.
It is not advisable to stay long.
Along the way, there will be a blessed land suitable for dwelling."
When Lu_3 Guāng returned to Liángzhōu,
he heard that Fú Jiān had already been harmed by Yáo Cháng.
Thereupon, he secretly claimed the title 'He_2 Yòu'.
There was a great wind in Gūzāng.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí said:
"This inauspicious wind indicates treachery and rebellion,
but it will settle itself without effort."
Soon after, there were rebels,
who were all annihilated quickly.
Jǔ_3 Qú_2 Méng_2 Xùn first promoted Jiànkāng Tàishǒu Duàn Yè as leader.
Lu_3 Guāng sent his son Lu_3 Zuǎn to lead troops to attack them.
At that time, public opinion held that Duàn Yè and his group were a rabble,
while Lu_3 Zuǎn had a formidable reputation,
so it was certain he would achieve a complete victory.
Lu_3 Guāng consulted Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí about this.
He replied:
"This expedition will not see its benefit."
Soon after, Lu_3 Zuǎn was defeated at Hélí.
〔一五〕Shortly thereafter, Guō Nún raised an army.
Lu_3 Zuǎn abandoned his main force and returned lightly,
and was again defeated by Guō Nún,
barely escaping with his life.
Zhōngshū Jiān Zhāng Zī fell ill.
Lu_3 Guāng extensively sought cures.
There was a foreign dào_4 rén Luó_2 Chā,
who claimed he could cure Zhāng Zī's illness.
Lu_3 Guāng was pleased
and gave him very generous rewards.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí knew Luó_2 Chā was a fraud
and told Zhāng Zī:
"Luó_2 Chā cannot help you;
he will only cause unnecessary expense.
Though the workings of fate are hidden,
they can be tested by events."
So he took five-colored threads, made a rope knot,
burned it to ash,
and threw it into the water.
He said if the ash came out of the water and reformed into a rope,
the illness could not be cured.
In a moment,
the ash gathered and floated up,
becoming a rope again.
Luó_2 Chā's treatment indeed had no effect,
and Zhāng Zī died a few days later.
After a short while,
Lu_3 Guāng died,
and Lu_3 Zuǎn ascended the throne.
A pig gave birth to offspring,
with one body and three heads.
A dragon emerged from a well in the eastern chamber,
coiled and lay down in front of the palace hall.
By dawn, it was gone.
Lu_3 Zuǎn considered it an auspicious sign
and named his hall Lóngxiáng Diàn.
Soon after, a black dragon ascended to the Dāngyáng Jiǔgōng Mén.
Lu_3 Zuǎn renamed Jiǔgōng Mén to Lóngxīng Mén.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí said:
"Recently, hidden dragons have been appearing and roaming,
and a pig monster has displayed an unusual sign.
Dragons are yin creatures,
with a time for their appearance and disappearance.
To see them repeatedly now
is a sign of disaster.
There will surely be an uprising where a subordinate plots against a superior.
It is advisable to restrain oneself and cultivate virtue
to respond to Heaven's warning."
Lu_3 Zuǎn did not heed this,
and later was indeed killed by Lǚ Chāo.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí had been in Liángzhōu for many years.
Since Lu_3 Guāng and his son did not promote the Dharma,
he kept his profound understanding hidden,
without proclaiming or transforming.
Yáo Xīng dispatched Yáo Shuòdé to campaign westward,
defeating Lǚ Lóng.
Thereupon, he welcomed Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí,
treating him with the rites due a National Preceptor,
and then had him enter Xīmíng Gé and Xiāoyáo Yuán
to translate numerous sūtras.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí had memorized much by heart,
and thoroughly understood the meaning and purpose of everything.
Having reviewed the old sūtras and found many errors,
Yáo Xīng then sent the shā_1 mén Sēng Ruì, Sēng Zhào, and more than eight hundred other people to transmit and receive his teachings,
and re-edited the sūtras and treatises,
totaling over three hundred scrolls.
The shā_1 mén Huì Ruì possessed lofty talent and insight,
and often followed Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí to transcribe.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí often discussed the style of Western texts with Huì Ruì,
comparing their similarities and differences,
saying:
"The customs of Tiānzhú highly value literary composition.
Their gōng_1 shāng_1 rhythms
are best when played on pipes and strings.
Whenever one appears before a king,
there must be praises of his virtue.
The verses and odes in the sūtras
are all in this style."
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí profoundly loved Mahāyāna Buddhism,
and was devoted to its propagation.
He often sighed, saying:
"If I were to take up my brush and write a Mahāyāna Abhidharma,
it would be incomparable to Kā_1 Zhān_1 Zǐ.
But now, profound scholars are few,
so what can I discuss!"
He only wrote two scrolls of the Shíxiàng Lùn for Yáo Xīng,
who revered him as a god.
Once, when he was lecturing on the sūtras at Cǎotáng Sì,
Yáo Xīng, the court officials, and over a thousand eminent shā_1 mén observed and listened with solemn expressions.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí suddenly descended from his high seat
and said to Yáo Xīng:
"Two small children are climbing on my shoulders,
desiring to block (my view of) a woman."
Yáo Xīng then summoned palace women to present to him,
and with one union, two sons were born.
Yáo Xīng once said to Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí:
"Great Master, your intelligence and enlightenment are unparalleled in the world.
How can the lineage of the Dharma lack successors?"
Thereupon, he compelled him to accept ten courtesans.
After this, he no longer resided in the monastic quarters,
but lived in a separate dwelling.
Many monks imitated him.
Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí then gathered a bowl full of needles
and, calling the monks to him, said:
"If you can imitate me and eat this,
then you may keep wives."
Thereupon, he picked up a spoon and ate the needles
as if they were ordinary food.
The monks were ashamed and convinced,
and ceased their conduct.
Bēi_1 Dù Bǐ_3 Qiū was in Péngchéng.
Hearing that Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí was in Cháng'ān,
he sighed and said:
"I played with this child.
We have been separated for over three hundred years.
A reunion is still distant and uncertain.
I expect to meet him in a future life."
A few days before Jiū_1 Mó_2 Luó_2 Shí's death,
he felt his four elements were unwell.
He then uttered three divine incantations
and had his foreign disciples recite them to save himself.
Before they could fully exert themselves,
he felt his condition worsen.
Thereupon, he forced himself to bid farewell to the assembled monks, saying:
"We met because of the Dharma,
but I have not fully exhausted my efforts.
To meet again in a future life
is truly sorrowful to speak of."
He died in Cháng'ān.
Yáo Xīng, in Xiāoyáo Yuán, cremated his body according to foreign rites.
When the firewood burned out, the body was disintegrated,
but only his tongue remained unburnt.
Tán_2 Huò_4
The shā_1 mén Tán_2 Huò_4 –
no one knew where he was from.
Tū_1 Fǎ_3 Tán_2 came from Hénán at the time,
carrying a tin staff.
He told people to kneel and said:
"This is the eye of Prajñā.
If you revere it, you can attain the Dao."
People at the time all found him unusual.
Sometimes, when given clothes,
he would accept them and throw them into the river.
The next day, they would be returned to their original owner,
the clothes unstained.
He walked like wind and clouds,
and predicted people's life, death, nobility, and lowliness with not a hair's breadth of error.
If someone hid his tin staff,
Tán_2 Huò_4 would cry loudly several times,
close his eyes for a moment,
then rise and retrieve it.
Everyone marveled at his divine strangeness,
none able to fathom him.
He often said to Tū_1 Fǎ_3 Tán_2:
"If you can sit peacefully and do nothing,
then the world can be settled,
and your lineage will prosper.
If you exhaust your troops and delight in killing,
calamity will befall you."
Tū_1 Fǎ_3 Tán_2 could not follow this advice.
Her younger brother, Chǎng, served as a staff officer to the Grand General Cáo Shuǎng.
When Xuāndì was about to execute Shuǎng,
he took advantage of the Wèi Emperor leaving the city to close the city gates.
Shuǎng’s Sīmǎ, Lǔ Zhī, led his personal troops, cut through the barriers, and rushed to Shuǎng.
He called out to Chǎng to go with him.
Chǎng, afraid,
asked Xiànyīng,
“The Son of Heaven is outside,
and the Grand Tutor has closed the city gates.
People say this will be detrimental to the state.
Can things truly be like this?”
Xiànyīng said,
“Some things are unknowable,
but in my estimation,
the Grand Tutor had no choice but to do this.
When Emperor Míng was on his deathbed,
he grasped the Grand Tutor’s arm
and entrusted him with the affairs of state.
These words are still in the ears of the court officials.
Moreover, Cáo Shuǎng and the Grand Tutor both received the trust of that appointment,
yet Shuǎng monopolized power and influence.
This is disloyal to the royal house
and unjust in human relations.
This action is nothing more than to execute Shuǎng.”
Chǎng said,
“If so, then should I not go out?”
Xiànyīng said,
“How can you not go out!
One’s duty
is a great principle for a person.
When people are in distress,
one still sympathizes with them;
to be a whip-holder for someone and abandon one’s duty
is inauspicious.
Moreover, to be entrusted by someone,
and to die for that person,
is the duty of intimacy.
You should just follow the multitude.”
Chǎng then went out.
Xuāndì indeed executed Shuǎng.
After the matter was settled,
Chǎng sighed,
“Had I not consulted my elder sister,
I almost would not have acted righteously!”
Later, Zhōng Huì became the General Who Guards the West.
Xiànyīng said to Dān’s nephew, Hù,
“Why is Zhōng Shìjì going west?”
Hù replied,
“He is going to conquer Shǔ.”
Xiànyīng said,
“Huì acts recklessly in affairs,
which is not the way of one who can long remain subordinate.
I fear he has other ambitions.”
When Huì was about to depart,
he asked Xiù, her son, to be his staff officer.
Xiànyīng worried, saying,
“Other days I worried for the state;
today, trouble has come to my family.”
Xiù earnestly pleaded with Emperor Wén,
but the Emperor did not agree.
Xiànyīng said to Xiù,
“Go then,
but be warned!
The gentlemen of old, when at home, showed filial piety to their parents;
when outside, they showed integrity to the state.
In office, they considered their responsibilities;
in righteousness, they considered their stance,
and did not leave their parents with worry.
Among military affairs, what can be beneficial
is perhaps only benevolence and magnanimity!”
Huì indeed rebelled upon reaching Shǔ,
but Xiù ultimately returned unharmed.
Hù once sent a brocade quilt,
but Xiànyīng disliked its extravagance
and turned it over to use the reverse side.
Her clear judgment and frugality were like this.
She died in the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
at the age of seventy-nine.
Dù Yǒudào’s wife, Lady Yán
Dù Yǒudào’s wife, Lady Yán,
courtesy name Xiàn,
was from Jīngzhào.
She was chaste, virtuous, discerning, and magnanimous.
At thirteen,
she married into the Dù family,
and at eighteen, she became a widow.
Her son, Zhí, and daughter, Wěi, were both orphaned and young.
Although Xiàn was young,
she vowed not to remarry,
raising her two children
and educating them in ritual and proper conduct.
Zhí subsequently achieved renown at the time,
and Wěi also possessed virtuous character.
Fù Xuán sought her to be his second wife,
and Xiàn readily agreed.
At that time, Xuán was not on good terms with Hé Yàn and Dèng Yáng,
and Yàn and others constantly sought to harm him.
People at the time were unwilling to marry into his family.
When Xiàn agreed to Xuán,
those within and without felt worried and fearful.
Someone said,
“Hé and Dèng hold power and will surely harm Xuán.
It’s like pushing a mountain to crush an egg,
or pouring boiling water on snow.
Why become kin with him?”
Xiàn said,
“You know one aspect,
but not the other.
Yàn and his ilk are arrogant and extravagant,
and will certainly bring about their own downfall.
Grand Tutor Sīmǎ merely feigns sleep.
I fear that even if the eggs are crushed and snow melts,
there will still be someone to answer for it.”
So she married Xuán.
Yàn and his group were indeed soon executed by Xuāndì.
Zhí later became the Administrator of Nán’ān.
Zhí’s cousin, Yù, was the Inspector of Qínzhōu
and was falsely accused.
When he was recalled,
Xiàn wrote a letter to Yù, warning him,
saying,
“The proverb says, ‘Endure humiliation and reach the rank of Grand Commandant.’
You can now be said to be humiliated.
If you can endure it,
the rank of Grand Commandant will be yours.”
Yù later indeed became Yítóng Sānsī.
Xuán’s son from his previous wife, Xián, was six years old
and once accompanied his stepmother to visit Xiàn.
She said to Xián,
“You are a colt that can travel a thousand li,
and will surely achieve great things.”
She married her sister’s daughter to him.
Xián later also gained renown throughout the land.
Her discernment of people was like this.
She died at the age of sixty-six.
Wáng Hún’s wife, Lady Zhōng
Wáng Hún’s wife, Lady Zhōng,
courtesy name Yǎn,
was from Yǐngchuān,
and was the great-granddaughter of Wèi Grand Tutor Yóu.
Her father, Huī, was a Yellow Gate Lang.
Yǎn could compose prose at several years old,
and when she grew up,
she was intelligent, elegant,
and widely read in records.
She had a beautiful demeanor,
was skilled in whistling and reciting,
and her etiquette and proper conduct were emulated by her relatives.
After marrying Hún,
she gave birth to Jì.
Hún once sat with Yǎn,
and Jì passed through the courtyard.
Hún delightedly said,
“To have a son like this
is enough to comfort one’s heart.”
Yǎn smiled and said,
“If our daughter-in-law had been matched with the Staff Officer,
the son born would certainly be no less than this.”
The Staff Officer
referred to Hún’s middle younger brother, Lún.
Yǎn’s daughter also possessed talent and virtue,
and Yǎn sought a worthy husband for her.
At that time, there was a son of a military family who was very handsome.
Jì wanted to marry his daughter to him
and informed Yǎn.
Yǎn said,
“I must see him.”
Jì had this soldier mingle with other young men.
Yǎn observed him from behind a curtain,
and then said to Jì,
“Is the one in the scarlet robe not the one you selected?”
Jì said,
“He is.”
Yǎn said,
“This man’s talent is indeed outstanding,
but his constitution is weak and his lifespan short.
He is not suited to fully display his abilities,
so he cannot be wed.”
So the marriage was stopped.
That man indeed died a few years later.
Yǎn’s clear judgment and foresight
were all of this kind.
Hún’s younger brother Zhàn’s wife, Lady Hǎo, also possessed virtue and conduct.
Although Yǎn came from a noble family,
she and Hǎo were elegantly close and respected each other.
Hǎo did not humble herself before Yǎn due to her lower status,
and Yǎn did not lord over Hǎo due to her noble status.
People at the time praised the etiquette of Lady Zhōng
and the principles of Lady Hǎo.
Zhèng Mào’s wife, Lady Cáo
Zhèng Mào's wife, Cáo Shì,
was a person from Xuē in Lǔguó.
Zhèng Mào had first married Sūn Shì,
who died young,
and he then betrothed Cáo Shì to be his second wife.
She served her parents-in-law with great filial piety,
personally performing the diligent work of spinning and weaving
to provide for their upkeep.
As for her younger brothers' wives and younger sisters,
she fulfilled all the courtesies
and won everyone's affection.
When Zhèng Mào became Sīkōng,
and his son Mò and others also became prominent in court,
people at the time acclaimed their glory and prestige.
Cáo Shì deeply feared excess in prosperity;
whenever Mò and the others were promoted,
her worry would show in her voice and expression.
Her food lacked rich flavors,
and she wore washed and simple clothes.
The salaries and official emoluments Zhèng Mào and the others received,
Cáo Shì would always distribute among relatives and in-laws,
ensuring everyone was well provided for,
leaving no surplus wealth in the household.
Initially,
Sūn Shì had been buried in Líyáng.
When Zhèng Mào passed away,
some argued that it would be difficult to move a long-deceased person,
and suggested not burying them together.
Cáo Shì said:
"Sūn Shì was his first wife;
it is right that she be buried with him.
How can we allow her lonely spirit to be without a resting place?"
Thereupon, she prepared ceremonial rites for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions, with a retinue, to welcome her,
equipped clothing, shrouds, and a ritual table,
and personally performed the "goose formation" ritual.
All who heard of it could not but sigh in admiration,
believing that Zhào Jī's treatment of Shú Wěi
was not worth mentioning in comparison.
She passed away in the first year of Tàikāng,
at the age of eighty-three.
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ Fēi Wáng Shì
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ Fēi Wáng Shì
was the daughter of Grand Commandant Yǎn.
Her courtesy name was Huìfēng.
She was chaste, gentle, and principled.
After the Crown Prince was deposed and resided in Jīnyǒng,
Yǎn requested to sever the marriage.
Huìfēng cried loudly and returned home,
and passersby shed tears for her.
When Liú Yào captured Luòyáng,
he bestowed Huìfēng upon his general Qiáo Shǔ.
Shǔ intended to make her his wife.
Huìfēng drew a sword and resisted Shǔ, saying:
"I am the daughter of the Grand Commandant and
the Crown Princess.
It is my duty not to be disgraced by a rebellious barbarian."
Shǔ then killed her.
Zhèng Xiū's wife, Shí Shì
Zhèng Xiū's wife, Shí Shì,
her origins are unknown.
She possessed virtuous conduct from a young age,
and when she was a little over ten years old,
the local community praised her.
After marrying into the Zhèng family,
she was respected by all her relatives.
Zhèng Xiū's former wife's daughter was still young,
and when Zhèng Xiū's father, Bù, was on his deathbed,
he had a concubine's son named Shěn
whom he ordered to be abandoned.
Shí Shì said:
"How can we allow my father-in-law's lineage to perish!"
So, she raised Shěn and his former wife's daughter.
Unable to support both (her own children and these two) at the same time,
within nine years,
she did not raise a child three times.
Táo Kǎn's mother, Zhàn Shì
Táo Kǎn's mother, Zhàn Shì,
was a person from Xīngàn, Yùzhāng.
Initially,
Kǎn's father, Dān, betrothed her as a concubine.
She gave birth to Kǎn.
As the Táo family was poor and lowly,
Zhàn Shì always provided for him by spinning and weaving,
so that he could make friends with people superior to himself.
When Kǎn was young, he served as a clerk in Xúnyáng County.
He once supervised the fish weirs
and sent his mother a pot of pickled fish.
Zhàn Shì sealed the pickled fish and sent a letter,
reprimanding Kǎn, saying:
"You are an official,
yet you send me official property.
Not only does it not benefit me,
but it increases my worry."
Fàn Kuí, a Xiàolián from Póyáng, lodged at Kǎn's place.
It was snowing heavily at the time.
Zhàn Shì then took apart the new mat from her bed
and personally cut it up to feed his horse.
She also secretly cut her hair and sold it to a neighbor
to provide food and drink.
When Fàn Kuí heard of this,
he sighed, saying:
"Without such a mother, such a son would not be born!"
Kǎn eventually became famous for his achievements.
Jiǎ Hún's wife, Zōng Shì
Jiǎ Hún's wife, Zōng Shì,
her origins are unknown.
Jiǎ Hún was the Magistrate of Jièxiū.
He was attacked and defeated by Liú Yuánhǎi's general, Qiáo Xī,
and died.
Zōng Shì had a beautiful appearance,
and Qiáo Xī wanted to take her as his wife.
Zōng Shì cursed, saying:
"Túgè slave!
How can you harm a man's husband and then wish to act indecently (towards his wife)?
How can you find peace in that?
Why don't you quickly kill me!"
Then she cried loudly to the heavens.
Qiáo Xī then killed her.
She was then a little over twenty years old.
Liáng Wěi's wife, Xīn Shì
Liáng Wěi's wife, Xīn Shì,
was a person from Dídào, Lǒngxī.
Liáng Wěi was a Sànqí Chángshì.
When the Western Capital fell,
he was killed by Liú Yào.
Xīn Shì had extraordinary beauty,
and Liú Yào intended to make her his wife.
Xīn Shì sat on the ground and cried loudly,
looking up and saying to Liú Yào:
"I have heard that men are valued for their righteousness and valor,
and women do not remarry.
My husband is dead;
it is illogical for me to live on alone.
Moreover, for a woman to be shamed twice,
of what use would such a woman be to Your Excellency!
I beg to die immediately
and serve my parents-in-law below (in the afterlife)."
She continued to cry loudly without stopping.
Liú Yào said:
"She is a chaste woman;
let her be."
Then she hanged herself and died.
Liú Yào buried her with proper rites.
Xǔ Yán's wife, Dù Shì
Xǔ Yán's wife, Dù Shì,
her origins are unknown.
Xǔ Yán was the Assistant Governor of Yìzhōu
and was killed by Lǐ Xiāng.
Lǐ Xiāng wanted to take Dù Shì as his wife.
Dù Shì cried loudly and guarded her husband's corpse,
cursing Lǐ Xiāng, saying:
"You rebellious bandits are without principle!
Death comes to all, sooner or later;
how can you expect to live long!
I am a daughter of the Dù family;
how could I become a bandit's wife!"
Lǐ Xiāng became angry
and then killed her.
Yú Tán's mother, Sūn Shì
Yú Tán's mother, Sūn Shì,
was a person from Fùchūn, Wú Jùn,
and also a grand-niece of Sūn Quán's clan.
She first married Tán's father, Zhōng.
She was respectful, compliant, chaste, and harmonious,
and possessed great wifely virtues.
When Zhōng passed away,
leaving behind a young orphan,
although Sūn Shì was young,
she swore not to change her principles (i.e., remarry).
She personally raised and nurtured him,
her arduous efforts were utterly complete.
Her nature was intelligent and quick-witted,
and her judgment surpassed others.
From Tán's early childhood,
she instructed him in loyalty and righteousness.
Thus, he gained widespread excellent reputation
and was praised by the imperial court.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā
period, Tán served as the Grand Administrator of Nánkāng.
When Dù Tāo instigated a rebellion,
she led a multitude to suppress him.
Sūn-shì encouraged Tán with the principle of fighting to the death,
and together they poured out their assets to provision the warriors.
Tán then achieved victory.
When Sū Jùn caused unrest,
Tán was at that time defending Wúxīng.
She was again granted the jié (imperial staff of authority) to lead an expedition against Jùn.
Sūn-shì admonished her, saying:
"I have heard that loyal ministers emerge from the homes of filial children.
You must sacrifice your life for righteousness.
Do not let my old age be a burden."
She then sent all her household servants
to follow Tán and assist in the battle,
and traded the jade ornaments she wore for military funds.
At that time, Wáng Shū, the Internal Historian of Kuàijī, sent his son Yǔnzhī to be a Commander.
Sūn-shì again said to Tán:
"Lord Wáng has sent his son to lead the expedition,
why should you not do the same?"
Tán immediately appointed her son Chǔ as a Commander,
and he joined forces with Yǔnzhī.
Her sincerity in worrying for the state was thus.
She was appointed Grand Lady of Wǔchāng Hóu,
and given a golden seal and purple ribbon.
Tán established a "Hall of Nurturing" at home,
and Wáng Dǎo and others all came to pay their respects.
She died at the end of the Xiánhé period,
aged ninety-five.
Emperor Chéng sent an envoy to mourn and offer sacrifices,
and she was posthumously named Dìng Fūrén.
Zhōu Yǐ's mother, Lǐ-shì
Zhōu Yǐ's mother, Lǐ-shì,
whose courtesy name was Luòxiù,
was from Rǔnán.
When she was young and unmarried,
Yǐ's father, Jùn, was the General Who Guards the East.
One time, he went hunting,
and encountered rain,
so he stopped at Luòxiù's home.
Her father and elder brothers happened to be absent.
Luòxiù, hearing that Jùn had arrived,
and with one maidservant, slaughtered pigs and sheep inside,
preparing a feast for dozens of people,
very meticulously and efficiently, yet no human sound was heard.
Jùn, finding it strange, sent someone to spy on her.
He saw only a single, very beautiful woman.
Jùn then asked for her to be his concubine.
Her father and elder brothers did not agree.
Luòxiù said:
"Our family is in decline;
why be so reluctant about one daughter?
If we form a marriage alliance with an aristocratic family,
it may bring great benefits in the future."
Her father and elder brothers agreed.
She then gave birth to Yǐ, Sōng, and Mó.
When Yǐ and the others had grown,
Luòxiù said to them:
"I humbled myself to become a concubine in your family;
it was for the sake of our household.
If you do not treat my family as close kin,
what care do I have for my remaining years?"
Yǐ and the others obeyed,
and thus the Lǐ clan was able to become a distinguished and prominent family.
During the Zhōngxīng period,
Yǐ and the others were all appointed to high positions.
Once, on the winter solstice, she held a banquet.
Luòxiù raised her cup and offered it to her three sons, saying:
"When I first crossed the river,
I had no place to settle.
I did not expect that you would all become noble,
arrayed before my eyes.
What more worries do I have?"
Sōng rose and said:
"I fear it may not be as Your Esteemed Wisdom intends.
Bórén (Yǐ) has great ambition but limited talent,
