a weighty reputation but dim perception.
He likes to take advantage of others' weaknesses;
this is not the way to preserve oneself.
My nature is straightforward and unyielding,
and I, too, am not tolerated by the world.
Only Ānú (Mó), being ordinary,
will remain under Mother's eyes."
Ānú
was Mó's childhood name.
Later, it indeed turned out as he had said.
Zhāng Mào's wife, Lù-shì
Zhāng Mào's wife, Lù-shì,
was from Wú Jùn.
When Mào was the Grand Administrator of Wú Jùn,
he was killed by Shěn Chōng.
Lù-shì spent her family assets,
and led Mào's troops as the vanguard to suppress Chōng.
When Chōng was defeated,
Lù-shì went to the imperial court and submitted a memorial,
apologizing on Mào's behalf for his failure to succeed.
An imperial edict stated:
"Mào and his wife were loyal and sincere,
and their entire household was righteous and heroic.
Mào shall be posthumously granted the title of Grand Coachman."
Yǐn Yú's two daughters
Yǐn Yú's two daughters
were from Chángshā.
Yú, formerly the Grand Administrator of Shǐxīng,
raised an army to suppress Dù Tāo.
He was defeated in battle,
and his two daughters were captured by Tāo.
Both possessed peerless beauty,
and Tāo intended to marry them.
The daughters said:
"Our father was a two-thousand-shi official;
we can never be the wives of a bandit.
There is only death!"
Tāo then killed them both.
Xún Sōng's youngest daughter, Guàn
Xún Sōng's youngest daughter, Guàn,
showed extraordinary integrity even in her youth.
When Sōng was the Grand Administrator of Xiāngchéng,
he was besieged by Dù Céng.
His forces were weak and food ran out.
He wished to seek aid from his former subordinate, the General Who Pacifies the South, Shí Lǎn,
but had no way to get a message out.
Guàn, then thirteen years old,
led dozens of brave warriors,
scaled the city walls, broke through the encirclement, and departed at night.
The bandits pursued them very closely.
Guàn encouraged and exhorted her soldiers,
fighting as they advanced,
and managed to enter Lǔyáng Shān, thus escaping.
She personally went to Lǎn to beg for troops,
and also wrote a letter for Sōng to Zhōu Fǎng, the General of the Central Army, requesting aid.
She even formed a sworn brotherhood with him.
Fǎng immediately dispatched his son Fǔ, leading three thousand men, to join Shí Lǎn in rescuing Sōng.
When the bandits heard that troops were approaching,
they scattered and fled.
This was all due to Guàn's efforts.
Wáng Níngzhī's wife, Xiè-shì
Wáng Níngzhī's wife, Xiè-shì,
courtesy name Dàoyùn,
was the daughter of Xiè Yì, General Who Guards the West.
She was intelligent, discerning, and eloquent.
Her uncle Ān once asked:
"Which line from the Shī Jīng (Classic of Poetry) is the best?"
Dàoyùn recited:
"Jífǔ composed the eulogy,
serene as a gentle breeze.
Zhòngshān Fǔ harbored eternal thoughts,
thereby comforting his heart."
Ān found it to possess an elegant and profound meaning.
Another time, during a family gathering,
snow suddenly fell heavily.
Ān asked:
"What does it resemble?"
Ān's elder brother's son, Lǎng, said:
"Scattering salt in the air is somewhat comparable."
Dàoyùn said:
"It is not as good as willow catkins rising with the wind."
Ān was greatly pleased.
When she first married Níngzhī,
she returned [home]
and was very unhappy.
Ān asked:
"Wáng Láng (Níngzhī)
is Yìshǎo's son;
he is not bad.
What do you regret?"
She replied:
"Among my paternal uncles, there are Ādà (Xiè Ān) and Zhōngláng (Xiè Wàn).
Among my cousins, there are Fēng, Hú, Jié, and Mò.
I never expected that in this world there could be such a Wáng Láng!"
Fēng referred to Xiè Sháo,
Hú to Xiè Lǎng,
Jié to Xiè Xuán,
and Mò to Xiè Chuān.
These were all their childhood names.
She also once criticized Xuán for not progressing in his studies,
saying:
"Is it because worldly affairs occupy your mind,
or because your natural endowments are limited?"
Níngzhī's younger brother Xiànzhī was once discussing with guests,
and his arguments were about to be refuted.
Dàoyùn sent a maidservant to tell Xiànzhī:
"I wish to rescue the young master from this predicament."
She then set up a screen of green brocade to conceal herself,
and elaborated on Xiànzhī's previous arguments,
and the guests could not refute her.
When she encountered the disaster of Sūn Ēn,
she behaved with composure.
When she heard that her husband and sons had already been harmed by the rebels,
she immediately ordered a maid to carry her in a palanquin, drew a sword, and went out the gate.
As the chaotic soldiers approached,
she personally killed several people,
and then was captured.
Her external grandson, Liú Táo, was then several years old,
and the rebels also wanted to harm him.
Dào Yùn said:
"The matter is with the Wáng family;
what concern is it of other clans?
If it must be so,
I would rather be killed first."
Although Ēn was cruel and tyrannical,
he changed his expression for her,
and thus did not harm Táo.
From then on, she lived as a widow in Kuàijī;
in her household, no one was not solemn.
The Grand Administrator, Liú Liǔ, heard of her reputation
and invited her to converse and discuss.
Dào Yùn had long known of Liǔ's reputation
and did not refuse him.
So she wore a hair bun and plain bedding, sitting inside the curtain.
Liǔ, with his sash fastened and belt straightened, called on a separate couch.
Dào Yùn's demeanor was lofty and outstanding,
attaining purity and elegance.
She first spoke of family matters,
with emotion and flowing tears,
then gradually answered the questions' purport,
her words and reasoning without hindrance.
Liǔ withdrew and sighed, saying:
"This is truly something I have not seen before;
observing her speech and aura,
it makes one's heart and form both submit."
Dào Yùn also said:
"My close relatives have passed away,
and only now have I met this gentleman.
Listening to his questions
truly opens up one's mind."
Originally,
Zhāng Xuán's sister from the same commandery also possessed talent and quality,
and married into the Gù family.
Xuán often praised her,
comparing her to Dào Yùn.
There was a nun named Jì Ní,
who frequented both families.
Someone asked her,
and Jì Ní replied:
"Wáng Fūrén's spirit is open and expansive,
thus possessing a 'forest-dweller's' charm.
The Gù family's wife has a pure heart and jade-like brilliance,
she is naturally an outstanding talent of the women's quarters."
Dào Yùn's composed poems, rhapsodies, eulogies, and panegyrics are all transmitted to the world.
Liú Zhēn's wife, Chén Shì.
Liú Zhēn's wife, Chén Shì,
was also intelligent, articulate, and capable of writing.
She once presented a "Pepper Flower Ode" on New Year's Day,
its words being:
"The revolving heavens encircle,
the three dawns begin to establish.
The verdant yang scatters its radiance,
the clear scenery is renewed.
Embellishing beautiful spiritual blooms,
they are gathered and presented.
The sacred countenance reflects them,
eternal longevity for ten thousand years."
She also compiled the ceremonies for New Year's Day and Winter Solstice audiences,
which circulated in the world.
Pí Jīng's wife, Lóng Shì.
Pí Jīng's wife, Lóng Shì,
courtesy name Lián,
was a person from Xīdào County.
At age thirteen, she married Jīng.
Less than a year passed before Jīng died,
and Jīng's two younger brothers also successively perished.
Having no descendants,
and also no relatives within the mourning period of one year.
Lián sold her dowry possessions
and personally spun and wove.
Within a few years, all three funerals were held.
After the burials and interments were completed,
she never failed in her regular offerings and sacrifices.
The province and village heard of her virtue,
and many sought to marry her.
Lián vowed not to remarry,
maintaining her integrity and living in poverty for over fifty years until her death.
Mèng Chǎng's wife, Zhōu Shì.
Mèng Chǎng's wife, Zhōu Shì,
and Chǎng's younger brother Yǐ's wife, was also her paternal cousin.
Both families were rich in property.
Initially,
Huán Xuán deeply respected Chǎng, but Liú Mài slandered him.
Chǎng knew this
and was deeply distressed.
When Liú Yù was about to launch the uprising,
he consulted Chǎng,
and Chǎng wanted to entirely disperse his wealth to supply military provisions.
He thought his wife was an extraordinary woman,
with whom great matters could be discussed,
so he said to her:
"Liú Mài slandered me to Duke Huán;
this means a lifelong downfall.
I will definitely become a rebel.
You should fortunately separate from me early.
If I attain wealth and status,
it will not be too late to welcome you back."
Zhōu Shì said:
"Your parents are alive in the hall;
do you want to undertake an extraordinary plot?
How can this be something a woman should advise upon?
If the matter does not succeed,
I will serve and care for the elders in the women's quarters;
I have no intention of returning home."
Chǎng was saddened for a long time before getting up.
Zhōu Shì called Chǎng to sit down,
saying:
"Observing your actions,
you are not someone who discusses plans with women;
you merely want to obtain wealth."
At that time, her infant daughter was in her arms;
she pushed her and showed her, saying:
"If even this could be sold,
I would not hesitate,
let alone possessions!"
So she emptied her assets to provide for him,
and entrusted them under another pretense.
When the matter was about to be launched,
Zhōu Shì said to Yǐ's wife:
"Last night I had a very bad dream.
The household should wash and bathe to cleanse it,
and it's not suitable to wear red.
I will collect all red items for a seven-day purification ritual."
Yǐ's wife believed her,
and gathered all her crimson-colored items and handed them over.
She then placed them inside the curtain,
secretly removed the cotton,
and gave the crimson cloth to Chǎng,
thus obtaining several tens of people brightly clothed,
all provided by Zhōu Shì,
without her family knowing.
Hé Wújì's mother, Liú Shì.
Hé Wújì's mother, Liú Shì,
was the daughter of General Zhēnglǔ Jiàn.
In her youth, she possessed ambition and integrity.
Her younger brother, Láo Zhī, was harmed by Huán Xuán,
and Liú Shì always resented this,
constantly thinking of revenge.
When Wújì consulted with Liú Yù about the plan,
Liú Shì observed that his actions were unusual,
and was happy but said nothing.
One night, Wújì was drafting a manifesto behind a screen,
and Liú Shì secretly covered the candle with a utensil,
then slowly climbed onto a stool to peek over the screen.
Having understood,
she wept and caressed him, saying:
"I am clearly not as enlightened as Mother Lǚ of Dōnghǎi!
Having been isolated in my sincerity,
I always feared a short life.
Since you can be like this,
my vengeance and shame will be avenged."
She then asked about his co-conspirators,
and knowing the matter involved Yù,
she was even happier.
She then explained the reasons why Huán Xuán would surely fail and the righteous army would surely succeed, to encourage him.
Later, it indeed happened as she said.
Liú Cōng's wife, Liú Shì.
Liú Cōng's wife, Liú Shì,
personal name É,
courtesy name Lìhuá,
was the daughter of the false Grand Preceptor Yīn.
From childhood, she was intelligent and astute.
During the day, she engaged in women's work;
at night, she recited books.
Her nurse tried to stop her,
but É practiced even more diligently.
Whenever she discussed scriptural meanings with her brothers,
her reasoning and insight were far-reaching,
and her brothers deeply admired and submitted to her.
She was filial and fraternal by nature,
and good at decorum and comportment.
Cōng having usurped the throne,
summoned É to be the Right Guìpín,
and greatly favored her.
Soon after, she was appointed Empress.
He was about to build the Yíbì Hall for her residence.
His Grand Judge, Chén Yuándá, earnestly remonstrated.
Cōng was furious,
and intended to execute him.
É, at that time in the rear hall,
secretly ordered her attendants to stop the execution,
and personally wrote a memorial, saying:
“I humbly hear that Your Majesty is about to construct a hall for your concubine.
Currently, Zhāodé Hall is sufficient for residence;
Yíbì Hall is not urgent.
The Four Seas are not yet unified,
and calamities and difficulties are still numerous.
Every action requires manpower and resources,
and thus great caution is especially needed.
The Grand Judge's words
concern the great policies of the state.
The remonstrance of a loyal minister,
how could it be for his own person?
An emperor rejecting it
is also not for his own person.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty should look up to the prosperity of enlightened rulers who accepted remonstrances,
and look down upon the calamity of benighted rulers who rejected remonstrances.
You should reward the Grand Judge with a noble title,
and recompense the Grand Judge with enfeoffment.
How can it be that not only do you not accept,
but instead wish to execute him?
Your Majesty's anger arose because of your concubine,
and the Grand Judge's misfortune was invited by your concubine.
The people will resent and the state will be exhausted,
and the blame will fall upon your concubine.
Rejecting remonstrance and harming the loyal
is also due to your concubine.
From ancient times, states were ruined and families were destroyed,
never without women being the cause.
Whenever I review ancient history,
I am so indignant that I forget to eat.
How can I today become such a one myself!
When future generations view your concubine,
it will be just as your concubine views those of the past.
What face will I have left to serve Your Majesty by your side?
I beg to return to this hall and die,
to atone for Your Majesty's error and delusion.”
Cōng, upon reading it, changed color,
and said to his subordinates:
“I have recently suffered from a wind-illness,
and my joys and angers are beyond the norm.
Yuándá
is a loyal minister.
I am deeply ashamed.”
He pointed to É and said to Yuándá:
“With an external assistant like you,
and an internal assistant like this Empress,
I have no worries!”
When É died,
she was posthumously granted the fraudulent title of Empress Wǔxuān.
Her elder sister Yīng,
whose courtesy name was Lìfāng,
was also intelligent and well-read,
and her literary style and quick wit
understood and mastered state affairs
even better than É.
Initially, she was summoned with É and appointed Left Guìpín.
She died soon after
and was posthumously granted the fraudulent title of Empress Wǔdé.
Wáng Guǎng Nǚ.
Wáng Guǎng Nǚ was
of unknown origin.
She was very beautiful in appearance
and possessed the resolute spirit of a man.
Guǎng served Liú Cōng
as Inspector of Xīyáng Prefecture.
The barbarian chieftain Méi Fāng attacked and captured Yáng Prefecture,
and Guǎng was killed.
Wáng, then fifteen years old,
was taken by Fāng.
Soon after, in a dark room, she struck Fāng,
but missed.
Fāng, startled, rose and said:
“Why this rebellion?”
Wáng cursed, saying:
“Barbarian beast!
I wish to execute the rebel,
what do you mean 'rebellion'?
I have heard that a father's enemy cannot share the same sky,
and a mother's enemy cannot share the same earth.
You are lawless and rebellious,
harming people's parents,
and furthermore insult others without propriety.
The reason I have not died yet
is that I wished to execute you!
Now death is my lot;
I will not wait for you to kill me.
My only regret is that I cannot hang your head in the public thoroughfare,
to assuage this great shame.”
Her words were fierce and sharp.
As soon as she finished speaking, she committed suicide.
Fāng tried to stop her but could not.
The woman from Shǎn.
The woman from Shǎn,
whose surname and given name are unknown,
was nineteen years old.
During Liú Yào’s time, she lived as a widow in Shǎn County.
She served her paternal aunt-in-law very diligently.
Her family wished to marry her off,
but this woman disfigured her face and swore an oath.
Later, her paternal aunt-in-law fell ill and died.
Her paternal aunt-in-law had a daughter who was at her husband’s home,
and had previously begged this woman for leave but was refused.
Therefore, she falsely accused this woman of killing her mother.
The officials, unable to ascertain the truth, executed her.
At that time, flocks of birds sorrowfully cried over her corpse,
their sounds extremely mournful.
In the height of summer, the corpse lay exposed for ten days,
but did not decay,
nor was it damaged by insects or beasts.
The surrounding area then suffered a drought for a whole year.
Yào dispatched Hūyán Mó as Administrator.
When he learned of her injustice,
he executed this daughter,
and offered a lesser animal sacrifice at her tomb,
posthumously titling her Filial and Ardent Chaste Woman.
On that day, there was heavy rain.
Jìn Kāng Nǚ.
Jìn Kāng Nǚ was
of unknown origin.
She was beautiful in appearance
and possessed strong will and integrity.
When Liú Yào executed the Jìn clan,
he intended to take Jìn Nǚ as his concubine.
Jìn said:
“Your Majesty has already exterminated her parents and brothers,
what further use is your concubine to you!
I have heard that when rebellious people are executed,
even their palaces are destroyed and trees cut down,
let alone their sons and daughters!”
Thereupon, she wept bitterly and pleaded for death.
Yào pitied her,
and spared one son of Kāng.
Wéi Chěng Mǔ Sòng Shì.
Wéi Chěng Mǔ Sòng Shì was
of unknown commandery,
her family was known for its generations of Confucian scholarship.
Sòng Shì lost her mother in childhood,
and her father personally raised her.
When she grew up,
he taught her the pronunciation and meaning of the Zhōu Guān,
and said to her:
“Our family has studied the Zhōu Guān for generations,
transmitting the learning in succession.
This was also compiled by the Duke of Zhōu,
recording the principles and canons,
the myriad officials and all things,
all are contained herein.
I now have no son to transmit it to.
You may receive it,
do not let it be lost to this generation.”
Amidst the chaos and disorder in the realm,
Sòng Shì recited it without cease.
Thereafter, Shí Jìlóng moved them to Shāndōng.
Sòng Shì and her husband were among those moved.
They pushed a deer cart,
and she carried on her back the books her father had given her.
When they arrived in Jìzhōu,
they relied on Chéng Ānshòu, a wealthy man from Jiāodōng.
Shòu protected and supported them.
Chěng was young at the time.
Sòng Shì would gather firewood and forage during the day,
and teach Chěng at night,
yet her spinning and weaving were never neglected.
Shòu often sighed, saying:
"Among scholars and high officials,
is there anyone else like this!"
Chěng thus completed his studies and made a name for himself,
serving Fú Jiān as Tàicháng.
Jiān once visited his Grand Academy,
questioned the doctors on the classics,
and then lamented the omissions in rites and music.
At that time, Doctor Lú Hú replied:
"Learning has been neglected for a long time,
and books and transmissions are scattered.
In recent years, compilation has been attempted,
and the main classics have been roughly collected.
Only the annotations to the Rites of Zhōu have no master.
I humbly observe that Wéi Chěng's mother, Sòng Shì, comes from a family of scholars for generations,
and has inherited her father's learning.
She possesses the pronunciations and meanings of the Rites of Zhōu.
This year she is eighty,
her sight and hearing are unimpaired.
Without this mother, there is no one who can transmit it to the next generation."
Thereupon, a lecture hall was set up at Sòng Shì's home,
with one hundred and twenty students.
They received instruction separated by a crimson gauze curtain.
Sòng Shì was honored with the title Xuānwén Jūn,
and granted ten serving maids.
The study of the Rites of Zhōu was again propagated in the world,
and at that time, she was known as Wéi Shì Sòng Mǔ.
Zhāng Tiānxī's concubines, Yán Shì and Xuē Shì.
Zhāng Tiānxī's concubines, Yán Shì and Xuē Shì,
neither knew where they were from,
but both were favored by Tiānxī.
When Tiānxī fell ill,
he said to them:
"How will you two repay me?
After I die,
how can you become another's wife!"
They both said:
"If Your Honor does not consider it inauspicious,
your concubines request to offer our lives,
to serve by sweeping below ground,
swearing to have no other ambition."
When his illness became critical,
both concubines committed suicide by cutting their own throats.
When Tiānxī recovered from his illness,
he grieved for them,
and buried them with the rites of a lady.
Fú Jiān's concubine, Zhāng Shì.
Fú Jiān's concubine, Zhāng Shì,
it is unknown where she was from,
but she was articulate and insightful.
When Jiān was about to invade the territory south of the Yangtze,
his officials earnestly advised against it, but he did not listen.
Zhāng Shì stepped forward and said:
"Your concubine has heard that in the creation of myriad things by Heaven and Earth,
and the governance of the world by sagely kings,
none fail to follow their nature and give them full play.
Thus, the Yellow Emperor harnessed oxen and rode horses,
because he followed their nature;
Yǔ dredged the Dragon Gate and channeled the great rivers,
because he followed the force of water;
Hòujì sowed and cultivated the hundred grains,
because he followed the qi of the earth;
Tāng and Wǔ overthrew Xià and Shāng,
because they followed the desires of the people.
Therefore,
with reliance comes success,
without reliance comes failure.
Now, all your officials, from top to bottom, say it cannot be done.
Upon what does Your Majesty rely?
The Book of Documents says: 'Heaven's discernment and wisdom are from the discernment and wisdom of my people.'
If Heaven is like this,
how much more so for a human ruler!
Your concubine has heard that when a ruler has the ambition to conquer a state,
he must observe the heavenly phenomena above,
and gather all auspicious signs below.
The way of Heaven is lofty and distant,
not what your concubine understands.
Speaking from human affairs,
I do not see its feasibility.
The proverb says: 'Roosters crowing at night are unfavorable for military campaigns;
dogs howling in groups mean palaces will surely be empty;
troops moving and horses startled,
means the army will be defeated and not return.'
Since autumn and winter,
every night dogs have howled in groups,
and many roosters have crowed at night.
I have humbly heard that stable horses are startled and flee,
and weapons in the military arsenal make sounds.
The principles of good and ill fortune
are indeed not for your humble concubine to discuss,
but I wish Your Majesty to consider them carefully."
Jiān said:
"Matters of military campaigns are not for women to be involved in."
Thereupon, he raised an army.
Zhāng Shì requested to follow.
Jiān indeed suffered a great defeat at Shòuchūn,
and Zhāng Shì then committed suicide.
Dòu Tāo's wife, Sū Shì.
Dòu Tāo's wife, Sū Shì,
was from Shǐpíng,
her given name was Huì,
and her courtesy name was Ruòlán.
She was skilled in writing.
Tāo,
during Fú Jiān's time, served as the governor of Qínzhōu,
and was exiled to Liúshā.
Sū Shì missed him,
and wove a brocade palindrome poetic diagram as a gift to Tāo.
Read by turning and circulating,
the words were very sorrowful and poignant.
It contained a total of eight hundred and forty characters,
but the text is not fully recorded due to its length.
Fú Dēng's wife, Máo Shì.
Fú Dēng's wife, Máo Shì,
it is unknown where she was from,
but she was brave and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
When Dēng was attacked by Yáo Cháng,
and his camps were breached,
Máo Shì still drew her bow and rode her horse,
leading several hundred brave warriors,
and fought with Cháng,
inflicting many casualties.
Outnumbered,
she was captured by Cháng.
Cháng wished to take her as his wife,
but Máo Shì cursed him, saying:
"I am the Empress of the Son of Heaven,
how can I be defiled by a thieving Qiāng?
Why do you not kill me quickly!"
Thereupon, she looked up to heaven and wept loudly, saying:
"Yáo Cháng is without the Way!
Before, he harmed the Son of Heaven,
now he defiles the Empress!
Imperial Heaven and Sovereign Earth,
will you not witness this!"
Cháng became enraged,
and killed her.
Mùróng Chuí's wife, Duàn Shì.
Mùróng Chuí's wife, Duàn Shì,
courtesy name Yuánfēi,
was the daughter of the false Right Guānglù Dàfū Yí.
From a young age, she was gentle and intelligent,
and possessed integrity.
She often said to her younger sister, Jìfēi:
"I will never be the wife of an ordinary man."
Jìfēi also said:
"My sister will also not be the wife of a common man."
Their neighbors heard this and laughed at them.
When Chuí was proclaimed King of Yān,
he took Yuánfēi as his second wife,
and she thus received exceptional favor.
The false King of Fányáng, Dé, also betrothed Jìfēi.
Both sisters became the wives of Chuí and Dé,
thus fulfilling their ambition.
After Chuí usurped the throne,
she was appointed Empress.
Yǐn Shì arrived in Gūzāng.
Méngxùn received her and expressed condolences.
She replied,
"The Lǐ clan was destroyed by the Hú.
What more is there to say!"
Someone remonstrated with her, saying,
"Mother and child's lives hang in another's hands,
how can you be so arrogant!
Moreover, the state has fallen, and your descendants have been slaughtered.
Why are you not sorrowful?"
Yǐn Shì said,
"Rise and fall, life and death,
these are the great divisions of principle.
Why should I behave like common people,
and show the sorrow of children!
I am a mere woman.
If I cannot die,
do you think I fear the calamity of the axe and battle-axe
and seek to become a concubine?
If they kill me,
that would be my wish."
Méngxùn admired her,
did not execute her,
and betrothed her daughter to his son Màoqián.
When the Wèi clan married Princess Wǔwēi to Màoqián,
Yǐn Shì and her daughter were moved to live in Jiǔquán.
Later, her daughter died.
She caressed her but did not weep,
saying,
"You died too late!"
Jǔqú Wúhuì was then garrisoned in Jiǔquán.
He often said to Yǐn Shì,
"The empress's grandsons are in Yīwú.
Can the empress go there?"
Yǐn Shì did not understand his words,
and replied,
"My descendants are scattered,
entrusting themselves to ugly barbarians.
With the remaining years of my old age,
I should die here,
I cannot become a ghost of Qíu."
Soon after, she secretly fled to Yīwú.
Wúhuì sent cavalry to pursue and overtake her.
Yǐn Shì said to the envoy,
"Jǔqú of Jiǔquán promised to let me return north,
why have you come to pursue me?
You may cut off my head and return,
I will never turn back."
The envoy dared not press her and returned.
She died in Yīwú
at the age of seventy-five.
The historian says: When heavy frost descends in season,
it reveals the resolute heart of that which withers late;
when floods prevail in their time,
they show the steadfast integrity of supreme virtue,
not only in gentlemen,
but also in women.
Since the Jìn government declined,
few established moral standards,
losing integrity and abandoning principles,
vying with each other to form a custom,
which was further exacerbated by Liú and Shí,
and swept away by Fú and Yáo.
For three months, they sang Hú songs,
only seeing newfangled adornments;
one morning they abandoned Hàn,
without even a hint of longing for the old.
They galloped through dust and wind,
discarding traditional teachings,
indulging in decay and forgetting to repent,
reaching an extreme in this.
As for the numerous female relatives of Huìfēng,
Dàoyùn's confrontation with Sūn'ēn,
Lady Xún's deliverance from severe siege,
Lady Zhāng's revenge against powerful bandits,
the empresses of usurpers
who faced death without turning back,
the consorts of pseudo-rulers
who sacrificed their lives without regret,
Zōng Xīn who resisted emotionally and met an early death,
and Wáng Jìn who upheld her integrity until the end,
these all secretly followed the path of righteousness,
not by teaching.
They elevate the lofty leaves of the clear Hàn,
with abundant excellent reputation;
they shake the steadfast tassels of the secluded valley,
without shame to elegant models,
compared to those who hung themselves without looking back,
and bit swords as if returning home,
differing like Qí Fēng.
They can inspire thousands of years.
Eulogy says: Composed in yin rites,
gentle and yielding in principle.
Following the six virtues,
manifesting the four excellences.
Her integrity pure as frost,
her reputation flowing throughout the land.
The red brush leaves instructions,
her pure fragrance never failing.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 67: Four Barbarians
Indeed, the vast and expansive virtue of heaven
is the origin of all myriad things;
the grand and magnificent order of earth
is what equally supports the nine regions.
Examining Fúxī and Xuānyuán in past reigns,
they began by receiving heaven's mandate and ordering creation;
consulting Yándì and Hàotài,
they then set up boundaries on earth.
Donning caps and girdles to distinguish the Huá,
and setting limits on the remote and wild to differentiate distant descendants,
the division between inner and outer
has a long history.
The Nine Yí and Eight Dí,
covered the green wilderness and extended to the dark north;
the Seven Róng and Six Mán,
spread across the western regions and traversed the far south.
Numerous tribes,
with different chiefs,
when encountering a virtuous ruler, sometimes followed his teachings,
but when falling into misfortune, they fiercely engaged in plunder and massacre,
stirring up dust and wind,
which was their usual nature.
Carefully examining distant discussions,
and reviewing profound strategies,
none failed to manage them with loose reins,
to prevent their disturbance of China.
Emperor Wǔ received the mandate after the decline of Wèi,
and expanded his territory to include all of Wú.
With his strategic might asserted,
he extensively invited and gathered.
He disdained the idea of mixing with the Huá,
but valued the reputation of attracting distant visitors.
He comforted the old and embraced the new,
never neglecting the annual tributes.
In total, twenty-three states
from the four barbarians submitted tribute.
Later, Emperor Huì lost his virtue,
and Emperor Zhōngzōng was displaced.
Wicked factions divided and occupied the land,
and the imperial city fell.
The influence of the court
only extended south of the Jiāng River.
The rites of tribute
almost ceased at this point,
and the different customs and practices
could not be fully detailed.
Therefore, we have collected what is known
to compile this biography.
As for the Northern Dí who usurped titles in the central plains,
they are thoroughly recorded in the chronicles;
their various tribes and types
are now briefly noted here.
Eastern Yí (Fúyúguó, Mǎhán, Chénhán, Sùshènshì, Wōrén, Bīlí, and ten other states) Fúyúguó
Fúyúguó is located over a thousand *lǐ* north of Xuántú,
bordering Xiānbēi to the south,
and having the Ruòshuǐ to its north.
Its territory spans two thousand *lǐ*,
with eighty thousand households.
It has walled cities and palaces,
and its land is suitable for growing five grains.
Its people are strong and brave,
and their ceremonies of assembly and deference resemble those of China.
When they send envoys,
they wear brocade and fine wool,
and adorn their waists with gold and silver.
According to their law,
those who kill are put to death,
and their families are confiscated;
thieves are punished by twelvefold restitution;
men and women who commit adultery,
and women who are jealous,
are all put to death.
If there is a military campaign,
they sacrifice cattle to heaven,
and divine good or ill fortune from their hooves:
a cloven hoof means ill fortune,
and an intact hoof means good fortune.
The deceased are buried with living people,
with an outer coffin but no inner coffin.
During mourning,
both men and women wear plain white,
women wear cloth face-coverings,
and remove jade pendants.
They produce good horses, sable, weasels, and beautiful pearls,
some pearls as large as sour dates.
Their country is prosperous and wealthy.
Since ancient times,
it has never been defeated.
The inscription on their king's seal reads
"Seal of the King of Huì."
Within the country, there is an ancient Huì city,
which was originally the city of Huì.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
Fúyú frequently sent tribute.
By the sixth year of Tàikāng,
it was attacked and defeated by Mùróng Cuī.
Its king, Yīlǜ, committed suicide,
and his sons and brothers fled to protect Wòjū.
The Emperor thereupon issued an edict saying:
“The king of Fúyú has for generations maintained loyalty and filial piety.
To be annihilated by a wicked barbarian
is most lamentable.
If any of his remaining kin are capable of restoring the kingdom,
we should devise a plan for them
to survive.”
The relevant authorities memorialized that Xiānyú Yīng, the Protector-General of the Eastern Barbarians, had failed to rescue Fúyú
and had been deficient in strategy.
An edict dismissed Yīng,
and Hén Kān was appointed to replace him.
The following year,
Yīluó, the later king of Fúyú, sent an envoy to Hén Kān,
requesting to lead his remaining people back to restore their old country,
and also asked for assistance.
Kān reported this,
and sent the inspector Jiǎ Shěn with troops to escort them.
Cuī again waylaid them on the road.
Shěn fought with him
and soundly defeated him.
Cuī’s forces retreated,
and Luó was able to restore his kingdom.
Thereafter, Cuī frequently plundered their people
and sold them in the Central Plains.
The Emperor pitied them,
and again issued an edict to redeem them with official funds,
ordering the two provinces of Sī and Jì
to prohibit the market for Fúyú captives.
Mǎhán
There were three kinds of Hán people: one was Mǎhán,
two was Chénhán,
and three was Biànhán.
Chénhán was south of Dàifāng,
bordered by the sea to the east and west.
Mǎhán lived between the mountains and the sea,
without walled cities.
There were fifty-six small states in total,
the largest having ten thousand households,
the smallest several thousand families.
Each had its own chieftain.
Their customs lacked order,
and they had no rituals of kneeling or bowing.
They lived in earth chambers,
shaped like tombs.
Their doors faced upward,
and the whole family lived together inside,
without distinction of old or young, male or female.
They did not know how to ride cattle or horses;
those they raised were only for funeral purposes.
Their customs did not value gold, silver, brocade, or fine wool,
but they prized glass beads,
which they used to adorn clothing or to decorate their hair and hang from their ears.
Their men went bareheaded with exposed topknots,
wore cloth robes,
and straw sandals.
Their nature was brave and fierce.
When the state imposed levies or labor,
such as building city walls and moats,
the young and strong men would all pierce the skin of their backs,
pass a large rope through it,
and shake the rope with a staff,
working strenuously and loudly all day,
without feeling pain.
They were skilled in using bows, shields, spears, and large shields.
Although they had disputes, attacks, and battles,
they valued mutual submission.
Their customs believed in spirits and gods.
They always gathered to sing and dance to worship the gods
after the spring planting in the fifth month;
and likewise
after the autumn harvest in the tenth month.
Each state and settlement appointed one person to preside over the worship of the celestial gods,
calling him Tiānjūn.
They also established separate settlements
called Sūtú,
where they erected large wooden poles
and hung bells and drums.
The meaning of their Sūtú
was similar to the Fútú (Buddhism) of the Western Regions,
but their practices of good and evil differed.
In the first and second years of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
their ruler frequently sent envoys to present local products as tribute.
In the seventh, eighth, and tenth years,
they again came frequently.
In the first year of Tàixī,
they presented offerings to Hén Kān, the Protector-General of the Eastern Barbarians.
In the third year of Xiánníng, they came again,
and the following year again requested to become internal subjects.
Chénhán
Chénhán was east of Mǎhán.
They claimed to be fugitives from Qín who had fled conscription and entered Hán.
Hán ceded its eastern border for them to settle,
where they built walled enclosures.
Their language was similar to that of the Qín people,
which is why they were sometimes called Qínhán.
Initially, there were six states,
which later gradually divided into twelve.
There was also Biànchén,
also twelve states,
totaling forty to fifty thousand households.
Each had its own chieftain,
all subordinate to Chénhán.
Chénhán usually employed Mǎhán people as their rulers.
Although they succeeded each other through generations,
they were not allowed to establish themselves independently,
indicating that they were people who had moved there,
and thus were controlled by Mǎhán.
The land was suitable for five grains,
and their customs were rich in sericulture.
They were skilled at making thin silk and cloth
and used oxen for plowing and horses for riding.
Their customs were similar to Mǎhán,
and their weapons were also the same.
When a child was born,
they would immediately press its head with a stone to flatten it.
They enjoyed dancing
and were skilled at playing the sè,
a zither-like instrument.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
their king sent an envoy to offer local products.
In the second year, they again came to pay tribute,
and in the seventh year, they came again.
Sùshèn Shì
Sùshèn Shì was also called Yìlóu.
It was north of Bùxián Shān,
about sixty days’ journey from Fúyú.
To the east, it bordered the great sea;
to the west, it adjoined Kòumànhàn Guó;
to the north, it reached Ruò Shuǐ.
Its territory stretched for thousands of *lǐ* in breadth and length,
dwelling in deep mountains and remote valleys.
Its paths were steep and treacherous,
impassable for chariots and horses.
In summer, they nested in trees;
in winter, they dwelled in caves.
Father and son succeeded each other as rulers.
They had no writing,
using spoken words as agreements.
They had horses but did not ride them,
only keeping them as property.
They had no cattle or sheep,
but raised many pigs.
They ate their meat,
wore their skins,
and spun their wool into cloth.
There was a tree called Luòcháng.
If a sage emperor were to arise and take the throne in China,
then its bark would grow suitable for clothing.
They had no wells or stoves.
They made earthenware pots
holding four or five *shēng* for cooking.
When sitting, they squatted with legs splayed,
holding meat between their feet to eat it.
If they obtained frozen meat,
they would sit on it to warm it.
The land had no salt or iron.
They burned wood to make ash,
poured water over it to extract the juice, and ate it.
Their customs were all to braid their hair.
They made an apron from cloth,
about a *chǐ* in length,
to cover front and back.
When marrying,
the man would insert feathers into the woman's hair.
If the woman agreed, she would take them home,
and then the betrothal rituals would be performed.
Wives were chaste, but daughters were promiscuous.
They valued the strong and despised the old.
The dead were buried on the same day in the wilderness.
They crossed wood to make a small coffin,
killed pigs and piled them on top,
as food for the deceased.
Their nature was fierce and aggressive.
They prided themselves on having no worries or sorrow.
When parents died,
men did not weep.
Those who wept were considered unmanly.
For theft,
whether minor or major, they were all killed.
Therefore, even though they lived in the wilderness, they did not commit mutual offenses.
They had stone arrowheads,
armor of hide and bone,
sandalwood bows three *chǐ* and five *cùn* long,
and kǔ wood arrows one *chǐ* and one *zhǐ* long.
To the northeast of their country, there was a mountain that produced stone.
Its sharpness was comparable to iron.
Before extracting it,
they must first pray to the gods.
In the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
they presented their _hú_ arrows and stone arrowheads.
Later, when the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
they again sent envoys to offer congratulations.
Thereafter, for over a thousand years,
even during the height of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
none were able to attract them.
When Emperor Wén became chancellor,
at the end of the Jǐngyuán era of Wèi,
they came to offer tribute of _hú_ arrows, stone arrowheads, bows and armor, and sable pelts, among other things.
The Wèi emperor issued an edict to send them to the chancellor's residence
and bestowed upon their king chickens, brocade blankets, and silk cloth.
In the early Yuánkāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
they again came to offer tribute.
During the restoration of Emperor Yuán,
they again went to Jiāngzuǒ to present their stone arrowheads.
In the time of Emperor Chéng,
they offered tribute to Shí Jìlóng,
taking four years to arrive.
Shí Jìlóng asked them about it,
and they replied,
"For three years we have observed the cattle and horses sleeping facing southwest;
from this, we knew there was a great nation there,
so we came."
Thus it was said.
The Wōrén
The Wōrén are in the great sea southeast of Dàifāng,
forming their nation on mountainous islands.
Their land has many mountains and forests,
no fertile fields,
and they eat seafood.
Previously there were over a hundred small states connected to each other;
by the time of Wèi,
thirty states were in friendly communication.
They had seventy thousand households.
Males, regardless of age,
all tattooed their faces and bodies.
They called themselves descendants of Tàibó,
and also said that in ancient times, when envoys went to Zhōngguó,
they all called themselves Dàfū.
Formerly, Shào Kāng's son was enfeoffed in Kuàijī;
he cut his hair and tattooed his body to avoid harm from dragons.
Now, the Wōrén enjoy diving into the water to catch fish,
and also tattoo their bodies to ward off aquatic birds.
Calculating the distance,
they are to the east of Dōngyě in Kuàijī.
Their men wear clothes made of horizontal strips of cloth,
simply tied together,
with almost no sewing.
Women's clothes are like a single quilt,
with a hole cut in the center to put their head through,
and they all wear their hair loose and go barefoot.
Their land is warm,
and it is customary to plant rice, ramie, and also raise silkworms and weave.
The land has no cattle or horses,
but they have swords, shields, bows and arrows,
with iron arrowheads.
They have houses;
parents and siblings sleep in separate places.
They use ritual vessels (_zǔdòu_) for eating and drinking.
For marriage, they do not offer money or silk,
but present clothes to welcome the bride.
For death, there is a coffin but no outer coffin,
and a mound of earth is raised as a tomb.
At the beginning of mourning,
they weep
and do not eat meat.
After burial,
the whole family enters the water to bathe and purify themselves,
to ward off misfortune.
When undertaking important matters,
they always scorch bones to divine good or ill fortune.
They do not know the correct year or the four seasons,
but simply count the time of the autumn harvest as a year.
Many people live to a hundred years,
or eighty or ninety.
The country has many women,
who are not licentious or jealous.
There are no disputes or lawsuits;
those who commit minor crimes have their wives and children confiscated,
while serious offenders have their families exterminated.
Formerly, men were the rulers.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
the Wōrén were in chaos,
with constant attacks and fighting,
so they established a woman as king,
named Bēimíhū.
When Emperor Xuān pacified the Gōngsūn clan,
their queen sent envoys to Dàifāng to pay homage,
and thereafter tribute and formal visits were continuous.
When Emperor Wén became chancellor,
they came several more times.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
they sent envoys who used multiple interpreters to offer tribute.
The countries of Bìlí and ten others
The country of Bìlí is northwest of Sùshèn,
about two hundred days' journey by horse,
governing twenty thousand households.
The country of Yǎngyún is another fifty days' journey by horse from Bìlí,
governing twenty thousand households.
The country of Kòumòhàn is another hundred days' journey from Yǎngyún,
governing over fifty thousand households.
The country of Yīqún is another one hundred fifty days' journey from Mòhàn,
totaling over fifty thousand _lǐ_ from Sùshèn.
Their customs and soil are not detailed.
In the third year of Tàishǐ,
each sent small tribal leaders to present their local products.
By the early Tàixī era,

there were again Múnúguo Commander Yìzhīwéilí, Mólúguo Commander Shāzhīchénzhī, Yúlí Mòlìguo Commander Jiāmóuchénzhī, Púdùguo Commander Yīnmò, Shéngyúguo Commander Mǎlù, and Shālóuguo Commander Shàngā,
each sending chief and deputy envoys to the Eastern Barbarian Colonel Hé Kān to declare their allegiance.
Western Rong (Tǔyùhún, Yānqíguó, Qiūcíguó, Dàyuánguó, Kāngjūguó, Dàqínguó) Tǔyùhún (Tǔyán, Yèyán, Pìxī, Shìlián, Shìpí, Shùluògān)
Tǔyùhún was
Mùróng Kuí's eldest half-brother.
His father, Shèguī, divided seventeen hundred households from his tribe to be under Tǔyùhún.
When Shèguī died,
Kuí succeeded to the position,
and the horses of their two tribes fought.
Kuí angrily said:
"Our late father separated and established us individually;
why are you not keeping a distance,
allowing the horses to fight!"
Tǔyùhún said:
"Horses are but animals;
fighting is their nature.
Why be angry at people!
It is very easy to separate.
I shall go ten thousand _lǐ_ away from you."
Thereupon, he left.
Kuí regretted it,
and sent his Chief Scribe, Shǐ Nàlóuféng, and the elders from his father's time to bring him back.
Tǔyùhún said:
"Our late father mentioned the words of divination,
that there would be two sons who would prosper
and whose blessings would flow to their descendants.
I am of low birth;
it is not reasonable for us to both become great.
Now, we separate because of horses;
perhaps this is Heaven's will!
Gentlemen, try to drive the horses eastward.
If the horses return eastward,
I will follow you."
Nàlóuféng sent two thousand cavalrymen as followers
to drive the horses eastward for several hundred paces,
but they would always neigh sadly and run westward.
After this happened more than ten times,
Nàlóuféng knelt and said:
"This is not a human affair."
So he stopped.
The Xiānbēi call an elder brother Āgān.
Kuí remembered him with longing,
and composed the "Song of Āgān."
At the end of the year, when filled with deep thoughts,
he would often sing it.
Tǔyùhún said to his tribe:
"My brother and I are both destined to enjoy ruling a state.
Kuí's rule will only last a little over a hundred years, down to his great-great-grandchildren.
After my great-great-grandchildren,
perhaps it will prosper!"
Thereupon, he went west and attached himself to the Yīnshān mountains.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he first crossed the Lǒng mountains to the west.
Thereafter, his descendants held the territory west of Xīlíng up to the border of Gānsōng,
extending thousands of _lǐ_ to Báilán.
However, they had walled cities but did not reside in them,
following water and grass,
using tents as houses,
and relying on meat and dairy products for sustenance.
Their officials included Chief Scribes, Marshals, and Generals,
and they were quite literate.
Their men generally wore long skirts,
and their hats sometimes resembled those of the Xià.
Women used gold flowers as head ornaments,
braided their hair and coiled it at the back,
adorning it with pearls and shells.
For their marriages,
wealthy families would offer a large bride price,
and then abduct the girl and leave.
When a father died,
his son would marry his stepmothers;
when an elder brother died,
his younger brother would marry his sisters-in-law.
Mourning rites were observed,
and removed after burial.
The country had no regular taxes;
if contributions were insufficient,
they would levy from wealthy households and merchants,
taking only what was needed.
Murderers and horse thieves were punished with death;
other offenses were redeemed with goods.
The land was suitable for barley,
and had many turnips,
and some beans and grains.
They produced Shu horses and yaks.
The mixed tribes in the northwest called them Ācháilǔ,
or sometimes Yělǔ.
Tǔyùhún died at the age of seventy-two,
having sixty sons.
The eldest was Tǔyán,
who succeeded him.
Tùyán was seven _chǐ_ eight _cùn_ tall,
a commanding and outstanding figure.
The Qiāng barbarians feared him,
calling him Xiàng Yǔ.
His nature was magnanimous and unconventional.
He once passionately said to his subordinates:
“As a great man, if one is not born in the Central Plains
during the era of Gāo and Guāng,
and cannot contend with Hán, Péng, Wú, and Dèng in the Central Plains,
to determine the victor of the empire,
and have one’s name inscribed on bamboo and silk,
but instead hides in remote mountains,
separated by strange customs,
unable to hear the rites and teachings from the Imperial Capital,
and unable to make a name for oneself in the Imperial Archives,
living among deer and elk,
and dying as a ghost of a fur coat,
even if one steals a glimpse of the sun and moon,
does one not feel ashamed in one’s heart? ”
He was cruel and unforgiving by nature,
and relied on his intelligence,
but could not care for his subordinates,
and was assassinated by the Qiāng chieftain Jiāng Cōng.
With the sword still in his body,
he said to his general Hébání:
“This lad stabbed me;
it is my fault.
Above, I have let down my ancestors;
below, I have shamed my officials and people.
The reason I controlled the various Qiāng
was because of me.
After my death,
take good care of Yèyán,
and quickly secure Báilán.”
Having spoken, he died.
He was on the throne for thirteen years,
and had twelve sons.
His eldest son, Yèyán, succeeded him.
Yèyán was ten years old
when his father was killed by the Qiāng chieftain Jiāng Cōng.
Every morning, he would bind grass to make an effigy of Jiāng Cōng,
weep and shoot at it.
If he hit it, he would wail and cry;
if he missed, he would glare and shout loudly.
His mother said to him:
“Jiāng Cōng
has already been slaughtered by the generals;
why do you do this? ”
Yèyán wept and said:
“I truly know that shooting a grass figure does not benefit my former enemy,
but it expresses my boundless determination.”
He was extremely filial.
When his mother was ill
and did not eat for five days,
Yèyán also did not eat.
As he grew up, he was resolute and steady,
and liked to inquire about the creation of heaven and earth, and the chronology of emperors and kings.
Sīmǎ Bóluòlín said:
“We, your subjects, are unlearned,
and truly do not know whose sons the Three Sovereigns were,
or whose mothers gave birth to the Five Emperors.”
Yán said:
“Since the time of Xīhuáng,
the auspicious omens and mysterious celestial phenomena have been clearly manifested and seen,
yet you gentlemen face the wall.
How ignorant you are!
The saying ‘a summer insect knows not winter ice’
is indeed not false.”
He also said:
“The _Lǐ_ says that the son of a _Gōngsūn_ may take the ancestral name as his surname.
Our ancestor first came from Chānglí to settle here,
and now we take Tǔyùhún as our surname.
This is the meaning of honoring our ancestor.”
He died after reigning for twenty-three years,
at the age of thirty-three.
He had four sons;
his eldest son, Pìxī, succeeded him.
Pìxī was benevolent, kind, and compassionate by nature.
When he first heard of Fú Jiān’s prosperity,
he sent an envoy to offer fifty horses
and five hundred _jīn_ of gold and silver.
Jiān was greatly pleased
and appointed him General Ānyuǎn.
At that time, Pìxī’s three younger brothers were all arrogant and self-willed.
Chángshǐ Zhōng Èdì feared they would harm the state,
and said to Sīmǎ Qǐsùyún:
“In the past, Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng and King Zhāo of Qín, due to the favor shown to a single brother,
nearly caused their ancestral sacrifices to collapse.
How much more so now, with three illegitimate sons all arrogant,
they will surely become a disaster for the state.
You and I are undeservedly holding the positions of chief ministers.
If we manage to preserve our lives and die in our beds,
when our former lord questions us,
what will we say?
I will now execute them.”
Sùyún requested to inform Pìxī,
but Èdì said:
“Our King is indecisive;
he cannot be told.”
Thereupon, taking advantage of the subordinates entering to pay respects,
he seized the three brothers and executed them.
Pìxī threw himself onto his bed.
Èdì and the others rushed to help him up,
saying:
“Your subjects dreamt last night that the former king told us: ‘Your three brothers will cause rebellion;
you must quickly eliminate them.’
Your subjects respectfully obeyed the command of the former king.”
Pìxī had always been friendly and affectionate towards his siblings,
and became ill with a distraught mind.
He said to Crown Prince Shìlián:
“I have caused the destruction of my blood relatives.
How can I face them in the underworld?
You should take charge of all state affairs, big and small.
My remaining years and fading life
are merely to sustain myself.”
He then died of grief.
He reigned for twenty-five years,
at the age of forty-two.
He had six sons;
Shìlián succeeded him.
After Shìlián ascended the throne,
he established friendly relations with Qǐfú Gānkuī,
and was appointed King of Báilán.
Shìlián was cautious and had aspirations from a young age.
Due to his father’s sorrowful death,
he was ignorant of government affairs,
and had not drunk wine or gone hunting for seven years.
Zhōng Èdì stepped forward and said:
“A ruler
governs the world with virtue
and unifies the populace with authority.
They are nourished with the five flavors
and entertained with music and beauty.
These four
are prioritized by sagely emperors and enlightened kings,
yet Your Grace neglects them all.
In the past, Duke Zhāo was frugal and lost his state,
and King Yǎn was benevolent and righteous, yet perished.
Thus, benevolence and righteousness can preserve oneself,
but can also destroy oneself.
That which governs a state
is virtue and propriety;
that which saves the world
is criminal law.
If these two deviate,
then the order will be lost.
Your illustrious Grace, your generations shine brightly,
and your kindness is extended to the Western Xià.
Although your benevolence and filial piety stem from your nature,
you should still follow the precedents of Zhōu and Kǒng.
You should not solely pursue the benevolence of Xú Yǎn,
allowing punitive measures and virtue to be neglected and unestablished.”
Shìlián wept and said:
“The former king, grieving the pain of brotherhood,
ascended to heaven in sorrow and indignation.
Although I have inherited the enterprise,
I am but a corpse existing.
How can I find joy in music, beauty, and hunting?
The governance of state and the rites and laws
will be entrusted to the future.”
At his deathbed,
he said to his son Shìpí:
“My great ancestor, Duke Tǔyùhún, often said that his descendants would surely rise
and forever be the western vassal of the Central Plains,
with blessings flowing for a hundred generations.
I can no longer see it,
and neither will you.
It will happen in the generation of your descendants.”
He died after reigning for fifteen years.
He had two sons:
the elder was Shìpí,
the younger was Wūhédī.
Shìpí was courageous, resolute, and had grand strategies.
He once casually said to the scholar Jīnchéng Qiānbāo:
“The _Yì_ says: ‘
Movement and stillness have regularity,
and the firm and soft are differentiated.’
The former kings governed the world with benevolence,
not relying on severe punishments,
thus the firm and soft were not differentiated,
and they were lightly regarded by neighboring enemies.
When faced with benevolence, one should not yield.
How can one merely remain silent?
Now I shall feed my horses and sharpen my weapons,
to contend for supremacy in the Central Plains.
What do you think, Master?”
Bāo replied:
“Your Majesty’s words
are strategies that surpass the age,
which the heroes of Qín and Lǒng wish to hear.”
Thereupon, he opened his heart and welcomed them,
and the masses flocked to him as if returning home.
Qífú Gān’guī sent an envoy to appoint him as an Imperial Commissioner with credentials, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs West of Lónghè, Governor of Shāzhōu, and King of Báilán.
Shì Pí did not accept,
and said to the envoy:
"Since the Jìn dynasty's principles became disordered,
cunning heroes have competed for power.
Liú and Shí brought tyranny and chaos,
while Qín and Yān acted arrogantly.
The King of Hénán occupies a strategically superior land;
he ought to gather a righteous army
to punish the disobedient.
How can he privately bestow titles upon each other,
imitating and usurping the various villains!
I, the寡人, inherit the glorious achievements of five ancestors,
and command twenty thousand armed horsemen.
I intend to sweep away the miasma from Qínlǒng,
and pacify Shā-Liáng.
Thereafter, I will water my horses in the Jīng and Wèi Rivers,
slay those who dare 'inquire about the tripods,'
seal the eastern passes with a single lump of mud,
close the roads of Yān and Zhào,
welcome the Son of Heaven to the Western Capital,
and fulfill the duties of a distant vassal.
I will never be like Jì Mèng and Zǐ Yáng, who vainly exalted themselves.
Tell the King of Hénán for me,
why does he not establish meritorious deeds for the imperial house,
register his name in the royal court,
achieve glory in his time,
and leave a fragrant reputation for future generations! "
Gān’guī was greatly enraged,
but feared his strength.
At first, they still maintained friendly relations,
but later he eventually sent troops to attack him.
Shì Pí was greatly defeated
and retreated to defend Báilán.
He reigned for eleven years,
and died at the age of thirty-three.
His son, Shùluògān, was young,
so he passed the throne to Wūhétí.
Wūhétí, also named Dàhái,
was weak by nature,
indulged in wine and lust,
and neglected state affairs.
When Qífú Gān’guī entered Cháng’ān,
Wūhétí repeatedly raided his territory.
Gān’guī was angered,
and led his cavalry to attack him.
Wūhétí was greatly defeated,
losing over ten thousand people,
and sought refuge in Nánliáng,
where he subsequently died in the Hú state.
He reigned for eight years,
and was thirty-five years old at the time.
Shì Pí's son, Shùluògān, then ascended.
Shùluògān was orphaned at nine,
and his mother, of the Niàn clan, was intelligent, wise, and beautiful.
Wūhétí took her as his wife,
and she was favored,
thus she monopolized state affairs.
At ten, Luògān proclaimed himself Crown Prince.
At sixteen, he succeeded to the throne,
and led several thousand households of his部 to flee to Mòhéchuān.
He proclaimed himself Grand Commander, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Chán Yú, and King of Tǔyùhún.
His governance spread throughout his domain,
and the populace enjoyed their livelihoods.
He was called Wùyín Kèhán,
and all the various Qiāng tribes of Shā-Qiāng pledged allegiance.
He then declared:
"My ancestors sought refuge here,
and now I am the seventh generation.
I wish to revive the glorious legacy with all the worthy.
Now my soldiers and horses are strong and numerous,
with tens of thousands of archers.
I will display my might in Liáng and Yì,
dominate the Western Róng,
parade my troops in the Three Qín,
and pay distant respects to the Son of Heaven.
What do you all think? "
The assembly all replied:
"This is a matter of great virtue;
may Your Majesty exert yourself! "
Qífú Gān’guī greatly feared him,
and led twenty thousand cavalry
to attack him at Chìshuǐ.
Shùluògān was greatly defeated
and subsequently surrendered to Gān’guī.
Gān’guī appointed him General Who Pacifies the Di, and Governor of Chìshuǐ.
He also appointed his younger brother Tǔhùzhēn as General Who Captures the Captured, and Commandant of Céngchéng.
Afterwards, he was repeatedly defeated by Qífú Chìpán,
and again took refuge in Báilán.
Ashamed and indignant, he fell ill and died.
He reigned for nine years,
and was twenty-four years old at the time.
Chìpán, upon hearing of his death,
rejoiced and said:
"This barbarian was indeed extraordinary,
a 'pig with white hooves' as they say."
He had four sons;
his heir, Shíqián, succeeded.
Thereafter, his lineage continued unbroken.
Kingdom of Yānqí
The Kingdom of Yānqí is eight thousand two hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
Its territory extends south to Wèilí,
and borders Wūsūn to the north,
measuring four hundred *lǐ* square.
It is surrounded by great mountains on four sides,
with dangerous and narrow paths.
A hundred men can guard them,
and a thousand cannot pass.
Their custom is for men to cut their hair,
and women wear short jackets
and large trousers.
Marriages are the same as in Huáxià.
They are fond of wealth and profit,
and prone to cunning and deceit.
The king has several tens of attendants and guards,
all arrogant and disrespectful of hierarchy.
During the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
their king Lóng’ān sent his son to serve at court.
Ān's wife was the daughter of Kuàihú.
She was pregnant for twelve months,
and gave birth to a son by cutting her side.
He was named Huì,
and was established as the Crown Prince.
Huì was courageous and heroic from a young age.
When Ān was gravely ill,
he said to Huì:
"I was once humiliated by Báishān, King of Qiūcí,
and have not forgotten it.
If you can avenge this,
you are truly my son."
When Huì ascended the throne,
he attacked and destroyed Báishān,
and then occupied his kingdom.
He sent his son Xī back to his own country to be king.
Huì had courage and strategic acumen,
and thus dominated the Western Hú.
All regions east of the Cōnglíng Mountains submitted to him.
However, he relied on his bravery and was reckless,
once spending the night outside,
and was killed by Luóyún, a person from the Kingdom of Qiūcí.
Afterwards, Zhāng Jùn sent Yáng Xuān, the Governor of Shāzhōu, to lead troops to manage the Western Regions.
Xuān appointed his subordinate general Zhāng Zhí as the vanguard,
who swept all before him wherever he went.
When the army reached his kingdom,
Xī resisted in battle at Bēnlúnchéng,
but was defeated by Zhí.
Zhí advanced and camped at Tiěmén.
When he was still more than ten *lǐ* away,
Xī again led his troops to ambush him first in Zhēliúgǔ.
When Zhí was about to arrive,
someone said:
"Hàn Zǔ was fearful at Bǎirén,
and Cén Péng died at Péngwáng.
Now the valley is named Zhēliú ('Obstruct and Detain'),
perhaps there is an ambush?"
Zhí rode ahead alone to scout,
and indeed an ambush was sprung.
Zhí swiftly attacked and defeated them,
then advanced and occupied Wèilí.
Xī, with forty thousand of his subordinates, surrendered to Xuān, baring their upper bodies.
When Lǚ Guāng campaigned in the Western Regions,
he surrendered to Guāng again.
When Guāng usurped the throne,
Xī again sent his son to serve at court.
Kingdom of Qiūcí
The Kingdom of Qiūcí is eight thousand two hundred and eighty *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
Its customs include walled cities.
Its city has three walls,
with a thousand Buddhist pagodas and temples inside.
The people engage in farming, planting, and animal husbandry.
Both men and women cut their hair to neck-length.
The royal palace is magnificent,
shining like a divine dwelling.
During the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
their king sent his son to serve at court.
Towards the end of the Huì-Huái period,
due to the chaos in China,
he sent envoys to offer local products as tribute to Zhāng Chónghuá.
During Fú Jiān's time,
Jiān sent his general Lǚ Guāng to lead seventy thousand troops to attack it.
Its king, Bái Chún, resisted at the border and did not surrender.
Guāng advanced his army and pacified it.
Kingdom of Dàyuān
Dàyuān is 13,350 *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
To its south is Dàyuèzhī,
and to its north, it borders Kāngjū.
There are over seventy cities, large and small.
The soil is suitable for rice and wheat,
and there is grape wine.
Many excellent horses are found there,
and their horses sweat blood.
The people all have deep-set eyes and abundant beards.
It is their custom that when marrying a woman, they first use a golden concentric ring as a betrothal gift.
They also test her with three female slaves;
if she is not fertile (unable to bear male children), the marriage is dissolved.
If children result from adultery,
they are all held in contempt by their mother.
If a person falls from a horse and dies because the horse is untamed,
the horse owner must provide the burial implements.
They are good merchants,
爭 striving for profit down to the smallest fraction.
When they obtain gold and silver from the Central Plains,
they immediately fashion them into artifacts,
not using them as currency.
In the sixth year of Tàikāng (285 CE),
Emperor Wǔ sent an envoy, Yáng Hào, to enfeoff Lányǔ, their king, as the King of Dàyuān.
When Lányǔ died,
his son Mózhī succeeded him
and sent envoys to offer blood-sweating horses as tribute.
The State of Kāngjū
The State of Kāngjū is about two thousand *lǐ* northwest of Dàyuān,
bordering Sùyì and Yīliè.
Its king resides in Sūxiè City.
Their customs, appearance, and clothing are generally similar to those of Dàyuān.
The land is mild and warm,
abundant in *tóng* trees, willows, and grapes,
with many cattle and sheep,
and produces good horses.
In the Tàishǐ period (265-274 CE),
Nàbí, their king, sent an envoy to present a sealed memorial
and also offered excellent horses.
The State of Dàqín
The State of Dàqín, also known as Líjiān,
is west of the Western Sea.
Its territory extends several thousand *lǐ* in each of the four directions.
It has walled cities,
with some city walls measuring over a hundred *lǐ* in circumference.
Houses are all built with coral beams and rafters,
lapis lazuli walls,
and crystal pillars.
Their king has five palaces,
each palace ten *lǐ* apart from the next.
Every morning, he holds court in one palace,
and then the cycle repeats.
If the country experiences disasters or anomalies,
they immediately establish a virtuous person as king,
exiling the former king,
who dares not complain even when exiled.
They have official bureaus and registers,
and their writing is akin to Hú script.
They also have small white-canopied carriages, banners, and the like,
as well as a postal system,
all exactly like those in the Central Plains.
Their people are tall,
resembling Central Plains people in appearance but dressed in Hú attire.
Their land produces much gold, jade, precious treasures, bright pearls, and large cowrie shells.
They have luminous jade discs, rhinoceros horns that frighten chickens, and fire-resistant cloth.
They can also embroider with gold thread and weave brocade and fine woolens.
They use gold and silver for money,
with ten silver coins equivalent to one gold coin.
The people of Ānxī and Tiānzhú trade with them by sea,
profiting a hundredfold.
When envoys from neighboring countries arrive,
they are always supplied with gold coins.
The journey involves crossing a vast sea,
whose saltwater is bitter and undrinkable.
Merchants traveling there carry three years' worth of provisions,
which is why few reach it.
During the Hàn dynasty, the Protector-General Bān Chāo sent his subordinate Gān Yīng as an envoy to their country.
Upon entering the sea,
the boatmen said:
"There is a substance in the sea that causes homesickness;
all who go there are filled with sorrow.
If a Hàn envoy does not long for his parents, wife, and children,
he may proceed."
Gān Yīng could not cross.
In the Tàikāng period of Emperor Wǔ,
their king sent envoys to offer tribute.
Southern Barbarians (Línyì, Fúnán) The State of Línyì
The State of Línyì was originally Xiànglín County during the Hàn dynasty,
the place where Mǎ Yuán cast pillars,
three thousand *lǐ* from Nánhǎi.
Towards the end of the Later Hàn dynasty,
a county administrator surnamed Qū
had a son named Lián,
who killed the magistrate and established himself as king.
His descendants succeeded him.
Later, when a king had no heir,
his maternal grandson, Fàn Xióng, took his place.
When Fàn Xióng died,
his son Yì succeeded him.
It is their custom to open north-facing doors to face the sun,
while their residences
may be oriented east or west without fixed rules.
Their people are fierce and violent,
resolute in battle,
adept in mountains and water,
but not skilled on flat ground.
The four seasons are warm and mild,
without frost or snow.
The people are all naked and barefoot,
considering blackness to be beautiful.
They value women and despise men;
marriage is allowed between people of the same surname,
and the woman first proposes to the man.
When a woman marries,
she wears a *jiāpán* garment,
a horizontal strip of cloth sewn together like a well-curb,
and wears precious flowers on her head.
During mourning, they cut their sideburns, calling it filial piety.
Burning corpses in the wilderness is considered burial.
Their king wears a celestial crown
and an adorned necklace.
Whenever he holds court,
his sons, younger brothers, and attendant officials are not allowed to approach him.
Since Sūn Quán's time,
they had not paid homage to the Central Plains.
It was not until Emperor Wǔ's Tàikāng period
that they began to offer tribute.
In the second year of Xiánkāng (327 CE),
Fàn Yì died,
and his slave Wén usurped the throne.
Wén was
an Yi chieftain, Fàn Chuí's slave, from Xījuǎn County in Rìnán.
He once herded cattle in a ravine
and caught two carp,
which transformed into iron.
He used this to make a knife.
When the knife was finished,
he stood before a large stone cliff and cursed it, saying:
"Carp transform,
forged into twin knives.
If the stone cliff breaks,
there is a divine spirit."
He advanced and chopped it,
and the stone immediately shattered.
Wén knew
of its divine power, so he kept it.
He traveled with merchants,
observed the institutions of the superior country,
and upon reaching Línyì,
he taught Yì to construct palaces, cities, and weapons.
Yì greatly cherished and trusted him,
making him a general.
Wén then slandered Yì's sons,
some of whom were exiled or fled.
When Yì died
without an heir,
Wén then established himself as king.
He placed all of Yì's wives and concubines in a high tower;
those who followed him were taken in,
and those who refused were starved.
Thereupon, he attacked the various states of Dàqíjiè, Xiǎoqíjiè, Shìpú, Xúláng, Qūdū, Gānlǔ, Fúdān, and others,
annexing them,
and had a force of forty to fifty thousand people.
He sent envoys to present a memorial and tribute to the Emperor,
his letters all in Hú script.
In the third year of Yǒnghé (347 CE),
Wén led his forces to attack and capture Rìnán,
killing the Administrator Xiàhóu Lǎn,
and slaying five or six thousand people.
The rest fled to Jiǔzhēn.
He used Xiàhóu Lǎn's corpse as a sacrifice to heaven,
leveled Xījuǎn County city,
and then occupied Rìnán.
He announced to Zhū Fán, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
that he sought to establish the Heng Mountain, the northern frontier of Rìnán, as the border.
Initially,
the various states beyond the frontier often brought treasures by sea to trade,
but the Inspector of Jiāozhōu and the Administrator of Rìnán, being greedy and oppressive,
took two or three tenths of the goods.
When Jiāng Zhuàng became Inspector,
he sent Hán Jí to be Administrator of Rìnán.
Hán Jí estimated and seized more than half,
and also felled ships and prepared oars,
claiming to be preparing for a punitive expedition.
Because of this, the various states were resentful.
Moreover, Línyì had little arable land
and coveted the territory of Rìnán.
Hán Jí died and was succeeded by Xiè Zhuó,
who continued to exploit them as before.
When Xiàhóu Lǎn arrived in the commandery,
he was also devoted to drink,
and his administration became even more chaotic,
which led to his defeat and destruction.
The Běidí classify themselves by their tribes.

Among those who settled within the passes are the Túgè種, Xiānzhī種, Kòutóu種, Wūtán種, Chìlè種, Hàndì種, Hēiláng種, Chìshā種, Yùpí種, Wēisuō種, Tútóng種, Bómì種, Qiāngqú種, Hèlái種, Zhōngqí種, Dàlóu種, Yōngqū種, Zhēnshù種, and Lìjié種.
There are altogether nineteen types,
each with its own tribe,
not intermingling.
The Túgè were the most powerful and noble,
and therefore held the title of Chányú,
leading all the tribes.

Their state titles included Zuǒxián Wáng, Yòuxián Wáng, Zuǒyìlí Wáng, Yòuyìlí Wáng, Zuǒyú Lù Wáng, Yòuyú Lù Wáng, Zuǒjiànshàng Wáng, Yòujiànshàng Wáng, Zuǒshuòfāng Wáng, Yòushuòfāng Wáng, Zuǒdúlù Wáng, Yòudúlù Wáng, Zuǒxiǎnlù Wáng, Yòuxiǎnlù Wáng, Zuǒānlè Wáng, and Yòumānlè Wáng.
There were sixteen such ranks in total,
all held by the sons and younger brothers of the Chányú.
Among them, the Zuǒxián Wáng was the most honored,
a position reserved solely for the crown prince.
Their four prominent clans were Hūyán氏, Bǔ氏, Lán氏, and Qiáo氏.
The Hūyán氏 was the most esteemed,
holding the positions of Zuǒrìzhú and Yòurìzhú,
serving as hereditary prime ministers.
The Bǔ氏 held the Zuǒjùqú and Yòujùqú.
The Lán氏 held the Zuǒdānghù and Yòudānghù.
The Qiáo氏 held the Zuǒdūhóu and Yòudūhóu.
There were also other miscellaneous titles such as Chēyáng, Jùqú, and Yúdì,
which were like the various officials in Zhōngguó.
Among their people, there were the Qímú氏 and Lè氏,
both courageous and strong,
and prone to rebellion.
During the reign of Wǔdì,
a cavalry commander, Qímú Xiánxié, rendered meritorious service in an expedition against Wú,
and was promoted to Chìshā Dūwèi.
In the Yuánkāng era of Huìdì,
the Xīongnú Hǎo Sàn attacked Shàngdǎng,
killed the chief officials,
and then entered and guarded Shàngjùn.
The following year,
Sàn's younger brother Dù Yuán again led the Qiāng and Hú from Féngyì and Běidì to attack and conquer the two commanderies.
From this time onward,
the Běidí gradually grew stronger,
and the Central Plains fell into chaos.
The historian says: Those who take form in the dark and receive vital energy
are called the noblest of all beings;
tied to the earth and following their regions,
they then have differences in groups.
Those who tread the path of benevolence and righteousness are the Zhōnghuá,
while those who indulge in ferocity and brutality are the Wàiyí.
Comparing them to plants and trees,
they are distinguished by their categories.
The Yi and Di tribes,
beyond the reach of moral teaching,
peeking at the borders and seeking opportunities,
have been a problem since ancient times.
Examining previous histories,
their aggressions have been numerous.
Xuānhuáng drove them north,
Tángdì campaigned south,
Yīn Hòu conquered east,
and Zhōu Wáng hunted west;
all these actions were to resist their invasions and disturbances.
At the time of Yíng and Liú,
the Xīongnú were at their strongest.
Between the Yuán and Chéng eras,
Hūhán submitted,
and the Hàn commended his loyalty,
settling him in the middle lands.
As years passed,
their types grew more numerous,
with confused names and different appellations,
too many to enumerate.
By the time of Tàishǐ,
not having corrected past mistakes,
the border walls were extensively opened,
and more tribes were recruited,
accepting the newly attached Wēisuō,
and welcoming the recently surrendered Yùjū,
their tents connecting and covering
the countryside and fields.
Soon, their barbaric customs spread,
and their whistling arrows gathered into hordes,
spreading disaster with their owl-like cries,
and indulging in violence with their wolfish hearts.
Hé Zhēng's strategy,
could not stop the wicked sprouts;
Guō Qīn's urgent memorial,
could not save from the ominous spread.
Before a full year had passed,
the capital city was overthrown,
the common people lay dead,
and the wicked tribes ran rampant.
Tracing its origins,
this was indeed the fault of Wǔhuáng.
Tǔyùhún branched off from the pseudo-Yàn,
distancing himself from the true lineage,
leading the remnants of the Dōnghú,
and occupying the old territory of the Xīqiāng.
With relaxed regulations and ample leisure,
vast territory and complete military strength,
he laid the foundation for ten thousand *lǐ*,
and left behind instructions for unifying the realm.
He never forgot loyalty and righteousness;
truly he is commendable.
Tǔyán distinguished himself early with his grandeur,
compared to Xiàng Jí.
He began to follow the court's civilization,
but was quickly cut short by Jiāng Cōng.
His noble character was unmatched,
also a talent among the border lords.
Yèyán was utterly filial,
mourning his new grief by shooting at grass.
Pìxī had deep friendship,
surpassing ancient heroes by sharing a thorn.
Shìlián was vigorous,
bringing glory to the righteousness of honoring ancestors.
Shìpí was magnificent,
possessing strategies for a long time.
Luògān was young,
but early excelled in brilliant plans.
Before he could unleash his ambition,
he was prematurely killed by a wicked hand.
Those who submit must fail;
did Heaven destroy Jìn?
Furthermore, Húnhuì were connected by kinship,
born on the very frontiers.
Each planned for their grandsons and protected their sons,
all changing their barbarian ways to aspire to Huá culture.
Huì's descendants were treacherous and wicked,
usurping titles with false imperial aspirations.
Hún's heir was loyal and diligent,
resisting Lónghè and returning his allegiance.
Those who harbor treachery perish after a few generations,
while those who possess loyalty become more esteemed with successive generations.
The saying that accumulated good brings lasting blessings
is indeed true.
Eulogy: Far back, ancient kings,
distinguished all regions.
Rebellion arose when virtue declined,
the court flourished when civilization spread.
After Wǔ elevated the imperial design,
his wisdom dimmed, moving the Hú in.
Swiftly the family and state collapsed,
many wise plans were lost.
Gǔhún bravely rose,
desiring to rectify the declining fate;
he managed to make his line prosperous,
truly relying on loyal instruction.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 68: Wáng Dūn (Shěn Chōng)
Wáng Dūn, courtesy name Chùzhòng,
was the paternal cousin of Sītú Dǎo.
His father, Jī, was Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
Dūn was considered an extraordinary person from a young age.
He married Princess Xiāngchéng, daughter of Wǔdì,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
then Prince's Attendant.
At that time, Wáng Kǎi and Shí Chóng competed in extravagance.
Kǎi once hosted a banquet,
where Dūn and Dǎo were both present.
A female musician made a slight error in her flute playing,
and Kǎi immediately had her beaten to death.
Everyone present changed their expression,
but Dūn remained composed.
Another day,
he visited Kǎi again.
Kǎi had a beautiful woman serve wine,
and if a guest did not finish their drink,
she would be killed.
When the wine reached Dūn and Dǎo,
Dūn deliberately refused to drink it.
The beauty, in fear, turned pale,
but Dūn did not even look at her.
Dǎo, who normally could not drink much,
feared that the wine-server would be punished,
and so forced himself to empty his cup.
When Dǎo returned,
he sighed and said:
"If Chùzhòng were to govern the world,
his heart is so resolute and cruel,
he would not come to a good end."
The Prince's Advisor Pān Tāo saw Dūn and remarked:
"Chùzhòng's 'bee eyes' are already apparent,
but his 'jackal voice' has not yet rung out.
If he doesn't devour others,
he will surely be devoured by others."
When the crown prince was moved to Xǔchāng,
an imperial edict forbade officials of the Eastern Palace from seeing him off.
Dūn, along with the Prince's Advisors Jiāng Tǒng and Pān Tāo,
and Attendants Dù Ruí and Lǔ Yáo, defied the prohibition and tearfully bowed from the roadside.
Public opinion at the time praised them.
He was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) usurped the throne.
Dūn’s (敦) uncle Yán (彥) was the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Lún (倫) sent Dūn (敦) to convey greetings and comfort him.
Coincidentally, the various princes raised armies of righteousness.
Yán (彥) received a summons from Qí Wáng Jiǒng (齊王冏).
Fearing Lún’s (倫) military strength,
he dared not respond to the call.
Dūn (敦) persuaded Yán (彥) to raise troops and respond to the various princes.
Thus, Yán (彥) achieved distinguished service.
When Huì Dì (惠帝) restored order,
