Dūn (敦) was promoted to Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍), General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍), Grand Herald (Dàhónglú 大鴻臚), and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中).
He was then appointed as General of Guǎngwǔ (廣武將軍) and Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Qīngzhōu (青州).
At the beginning of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
he was summoned to be Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān 中書監).
At that time, the empire was in great chaos.
Dūn (敦) distributed over a hundred palace maids and attendants to the officers and soldiers,
and scattered gold, silver, and treasures among the multitude.
He returned to Luò (洛) in a single carriage.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) came from Xíngyáng (滎陽) to pay court.
Dūn (敦) said to his confidants:
“Now all authority resides with the Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅).
Yet, when selecting and requesting appointments,
the Secretariat (Shàngshū 尚書) still judges them by old regulations.
When the Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅) arrives now,
there will surely be executions and punishments.”
Soon after, Yuè (越) arrested more than ten people, including Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令) Miáo Bō (繆播), and executed them.
Yuè (越) appointed Dūn (敦) as Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yángzhōu (揚州).
Pān Tāo (潘滔) advised Yuè (越):
“To establish Chǔzhòng (處仲) outside the Jiāng (江),
allowing him to indulge his overbearing ambitions,
is to invite disaster.”
Yuè (越) did not listen.
Later, he was summoned to be appointed as Minister (Shàngshū 尚書),
but he did not accept.
Yuán Dì (元帝) summoned him to be Libationer (Jìjiǔ 祭酒) of the Military Adviser (Jūnshī 軍諮) of Āndōng (安東).
Coincidentally, the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yángzhōu (揚州), Liú Táo (劉陶), died.
The Emperor again appointed Dūn (敦) as Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yángzhōu (揚州),
and added the title General of Guǎngwǔ (廣武將軍).

Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn 左將軍), Area Commander (Dūdū 督) of All Expeditions (Zhēngtǎo 征討) and Military Affairs (Jūnjì 軍事), and given the Implied Grant of Authority (Jiǎjié 假節).
When the Emperor first took up residence in Jiāngdōng (江東),
his prestige was not yet established.
Dūn (敦), together with his cousin Dǎo (導) and others, united their efforts to support him,
thereby bringing about the revival of the dynasty.
People at the time had a saying:
“The Wángs (王), along with the Mǎ (馬),
rule the empire together.”
Soon after, he and Gān Zhuó (甘卓) and others suppressed Huá Yì (華軼), the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and beheaded him.
When the Shǔ (蜀) bandit Dù Tāo (杜弢) rebelled,
Zhōu Yí (周顗), the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺ǐ) of Jīngzhōu (荊州), retreated.
Dūn (敦) sent Táo Kǎn (陶侃), the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Wǔchāng (武昌), and Zhōu Fǎng (周訪), the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Yùzhāng (豫章), and others to suppress Tāo (弢).
Dūn (敦) then advanced to Yùzhāng (豫章)
to provide continuous support for the various armies.
After Kǎn (侃) defeated Tāo (弢),
Dūn (敦) recommended Kǎn (侃) as Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Later, Kǎn (侃) was defeated by Tāo’s (弢) general Dù Zēng (杜曾).
Dūn (敦), considering his arrangements flawed,
demoted himself to General of Guǎngwǔ (廣武將軍).
The Emperor did not permit it.
When Kǎn (侃) annihilated Tāo (弢),

Dūn (敦), as the supreme commander, was promoted to Grand General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn 鎮東大將軍) and granted the privilege of establishing an administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司).

He was additionally made Area Commander (Dūdū 督) of All Military Affairs (Jūnjì 軍事) of the Six Provinces (Liù Zhōu 六州) of Jiāng (江), Yáng (揚), Jīng (荊), Xiāng (湘), Jiāo (交), and Guǎng (廣), and Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Hàn’ān (漢安侯).
Dūn (敦) began to appoint his own officials
and concurrently control provinces and commanderies.
After a while,
Dù Tāo’s (杜弢) general Dù Hóng (杜弘) fled south to Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
seeking to prove his worth by suppressing the bandits of Guìlín (桂林).
Dūn (敦) permitted it.
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) blocked Hóng (弘) from advancing.
Hóng (弘) then went to Yǐn Fèng (尹奉), the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Línglíng (零陵), and surrendered.
Fèng (奉) sent Hóng (弘) to Dūn (敦).
Dūn (敦) made him a general
and subsequently treated him with favor.
Hé Qīn (何欽), a native of Nánkāng (南康), occupied a strategic and fortified position,
gathering several thousand followers.
Dūn (敦) immediately appointed him a fourth-rank general.
Thus, the signs of his autocratic power gradually became apparent.
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ (建武),
he was again promoted to Grand General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn 征南大將軍),
retaining the privilege of establishing an administration as before.
When the restoration began,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中), Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn 大將軍), and Governor (Mù 牧) of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
He sent his subordinate generals Zhū Guǐ (朱軌) and Zhào Yòu (趙誘) to attack Dù Zēng (杜曾),
but they were killed by Zēng (曾).
Dūn (敦) demoted himself,
relinquished the title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中),
and also declined the governorship.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Governor (Mù 牧) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Dūn (敦) submitted a memorial, saying: “In the past, Hàn Zǔ (漢祖), with divine martial prowess, revolutionized the state
and established the imperial enterprise.
He was succeeded by the virtuous Wén Dì (文帝),
who inherited the great legacy.
He was pure, calm, and profound,
emulating the achievements of Chéng (成) and Kāng (康) [of the Zhōu (周) dynasty].
Jiǎ Yì (賈誼) sighed
and believed the empire was in dire peril.
Although his words had both praise and criticism,
they did not lose sight of the essence of the matter.
Now, the sacred dynasty has just been established,
gradually revitalizing the great framework.
Previously, Duàn Pǐdī (段匹磾)
sent envoys to pledge loyalty and devotion.
Without yet having rendered service,
he was given a regional province.
Now, Jīn Míng (靳明) and others wish to wipe away the nation’s shame
and eliminate the great rebels.
Their aspirations and hopes
are all to attach themselves to the emperor and ascend.
Although great merits deserve reward,
they should also be constrained.
It is important to prevent nascent problems and nip them in the bud;
caution is paramount at the beginning.
In the intervening period, unruly individuals
repeatedly caused
troubles and changes,
all without loyalty or righteousness,
driven by temporary glory.
The gradual decline of the empire
is indeed due to this.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Son of Heaven was weak,
and the feudal lords were extravagant
and luxurious.
Jìn Wén (晉文) desired to uphold the Zhōu (周) house,
even requesting a passage for his carriage.
Xiāng Wáng (襄王) yielded to him with courtesy,
and upon hearing righteousness, submitted.
From then on, the feudal lords dared not overstep their bounds.
Your servant
believes that previously, when the bandits were not yet annihilated,
to merely resolve matters,
the various appointments bestowed by the court
often involved excessive titles and positions.
Now, from your servant downwards,
all these should be abolished,
if only to curb the ambitions of minor officials who boast of their achievements,
and the unrestrained demands of barbarians.
If we further delay,
looking to prevailing customs,
allowing cunning individuals to harbor ill intentions,
leading to mutual slander,
pointing fingers at the imperial court,
and sycophancy to rise like a swarm of bees,
your servant knows Your Majesty will be unable to rectify it.
This is a crucial moment for security or danger,
and the hope of the empire.
My family has received special honor and responsibility,
possessing great power,
with exceptional grace bestowed upon us,
and favor surpassing even the imperial clan.
Even commoners on the road deem this unacceptable;
how can your servant alone
feel at ease with it?
If my clan misleads Your Majesty,
ruin will soon follow;
even if I were to be burned to ashes and my heart torn out,
what good would Your Majesty’s regret then do!
I humbly pray
that Your Majesty will understand your servant’s sincere intention,
and at this critical juncture,
slightly disperse these powers,
and bestow positions upon the worthy and talented.
This will slightly comfort those with discerning minds,
allowing each to fully express their thoughts,
and then people will be eager to exert themselves.
The title of Governor (Zhōu Mù 州牧)
is something I dare not accept.
I therefore send back the sable tail and cicada ornaments of the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中) that I was granted.
Furthermore, offices should be consolidated and positions reduced,
to curb the covetous desires of minor officials.”
The Emperor issued a gracious edict, refusing his request.
He again firmly declined the governorship,
and was permitted to serve as Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史).
At that time, Liú Wèi (劉隗) held power,
and somewhat alienated the Wáng (王) family.
Dǎo (導) and others were very displeased with this.
Dūn (敦) submitted a memorial, saying: “Dǎo (導) formerly received extraordinary favor,
entrusted with important affairs of state.
He emptied himself to seek out the worthy,
and served the nation with utmost sincerity.
He thus relied on imperial grace
to hold the heavy responsibility of assisting in government.
The imperial system is profound and distant,
and matters of righteousness are different.
Although the imperial foundation has just been established,
and the teachings are being expounded,
the beauty of renewal
still has shortcomings.
Your servant often feels indignant about the distant future,
and ashamed and angry at my family
and clan.
This is why in my previous memorials,
I have always mentioned this.
Your Majesty has not yet deigned to give it a little thought
to express my humble feelings.
It is said that Dǎo (導) has recently been alienated...”
What was stated then is as clear as yesterday,
but its signs are already manifest.
The blame for it
will not merely fall upon my person.
My kinsmen and followers,
all have received more than their due share.
I, Dǎo, truly cannot properly
measure myself,
and Your Majesty, out of love, forgets my shortcomings.
It is common human nature,
relying on favor to advance blindly,
to alone transgress against the dragon's scales,
and be unaware of one's own delusion.
What I secretly worry about,
I have not
fully understood the reason for,
and I am fearful and ashamed,
my spirits like ashes and dust.
Affairs of state are vast,
and it is truly difficult to manage everything.
Though Dǎo is ordinary and common,
he has not incurred the burden of corruption.
His past
merits,
and Your Majesty's former care,
the closeness of our affection,
are sufficient to inspire a shallow age,
enlighten the relationship between ruler and minister,
unite virtue and righteousness,
and emulate the ancient sages.
In the past, I personally received a gracious command,
which said:
"I, you, and Mào Hóng shall have a friendship like that of Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shú."
I was unworthily appointed to an external post,
and ten years have gradually passed.
The teachings and instructions
have been forgotten day by day;
but as for this command,
I engrave
it in my heart,
and still cherish it,
believing that former grace cannot be extinguished in a single day.
I humbly observe that Your Majesty's sagely wisdom renews daily,
broadly extending to outstanding talents,
governing them with administration,
and regulating them with ritual.
Recently, Your Majesty ordered Dǎo to secretly manage confidential affairs within the court,
and externally to oversee the Secretariat
of the Imperial Household,
wielding the imperial staff in the capital,
and also commanding the Six Armies.
Having already been appointed Governor,
he also holds weighty titles,
which is truly inappropriate for a subject.
The superficial praise of the common folk
will certainly lead to criticism and slander.
It is advisable to relieve him of the oversight of the Secretariat, the imperial staff, and the governorship.
Moreover, for a truly capable assistant to the king,
one should find someone with broad understanding and far-sightedness, uprightness and clear judgment, and complete moral virtue.
With my
dim perception,
I have not seen such a talent.
However, among the people I have seen,
none surpasses Dǎo;
and he has assisted and supported for many years,
truly exerting his utmost effort.
Which hegemonic ruler
has never employed
the worthy and capable,
to jointly see things through from beginning to end!
Guǎn Zhòng was criticized for his 'three palaces and inverted altars,'
Zǐ Fàn was blamed for 'meeting the ruler by the river,'
and Xiāo Hé and Zhōu Bó were imprisoned,
yet they ultimately remained excellent assistants.
Given Dǎo's talent,
how could he be without fault!
He should be appointed to duties that are not excessive,
employing his strengths,
to compensate for his faults with his achievements,
and to secure his
future.
Dǎo's nature is prudent and discreet,
and he is particularly capable of enduring hardship.
He is good at deliberation,
possesses literary talent and righteousness,
and in both activity and stillness, when consulted,
he inspires Your Majesty's sagely thoughts.
Externally, he has not been overly favored,
and both public
and private matters are well-managed.
Now that the imperial reign has just been established,
the whole world looks up to Your Majesty's influence;
if the sagely favor does not endure,
then near and far will be disappointed.
The empire is desolate and impoverished,
and people's hearts are easily swayed;
if public opinion
shifts,
it will lead to doubt and suspicion.
I dare not be selfishly biased towards my kin,
but only wish to be loyal to the state.
When the memorial arrived,
Dǎo sealed it and sent it back to Dūn.
Dūn then dispatched it again for presentation.
Initially,
Dūn made an effort to rectify himself,
elegantly valuing pure conversation,
and never spoke of wealth or women.
Since he already had a high reputation,
and had achieved great merits south of the Yangtze,
he solely held command outside the court,
controlling powerful troops with his own hand.
His kinsmen were influential,
and his authority was unrivaled.
Thus, he desired to control the court entirely,
and had ambitions for the throne.
The Emperor feared and disliked him,
and consequently drew Líu Wǎi and Dīao Xié and others to be his trusted confidants.
Dūn became even more indignant,
and thus the rift began to form.
After drinking, he would often recite the lyrics from Emperor Wèi Wǔ's yuefǔ poem:
"An old warhorse in the stable,
its ambition is a thousand lǐ.
A valiant warrior in his twilight years,
his heroic spirit never ceases."
He would use his ruyí scepter to beat the spittoon as a rhythm,
and the edges of the spittoon were all chipped.
When Gān Zhuó, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, was transferred to Liángzhōu,
Dūn wanted to replace Zhuó with Chén Bān, his Attendant-in-ordinary.
The Emperor disagreed,
and instead appointed Qíao Wáng Chéng to govern Xiāngzhōu.
Dūn again submitted a memorial, recounting ancient and modern loyal ministers who were suspected by their rulers,
and how "blueflies" (slanderers) created discord among them,
hoping to move the Emperor.
The Emperor became even more wary of him.
Soon, Dūn was granted feathered canopies and ceremonial music,
and an additional two Attendants-in-ordinary, two clerks, and two palace attendants.
The Emperor appointed Líu Wǎi as General Who Guards the North,
and Dài Ruòsī as General Who Conquers the West,
mobilizing all the slaves from Yángzhōu as soldiers,
ostensibly to suppress the barbarians,
but actually to defend against Dūn.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
Dūn led his troops towards the capital,
using the execution of Wǎi as his pretext, and memorialized: Líu Wǎi, formerly in the Imperial Secretariat,
was wicked and sycophantic,
slandering loyal and good men,
confusing Your Majesty's sagely hearing,
and thus gaining powerful favor,
disrupting the heavenly order,
wielding power and authority at will,
causing all discerning people to remain silent.
He initiated numerous grand projects,
troubling and burdening soldiers and commoners;
outwardly claiming to uphold righteousness,
inwardly he enriched himself;
his extravagance exceeded regulations,
even appointing commoners to positions like Staff Officer,
something unheard of since
the Jìn and
Wèi dynasties.
He emptied the imperial treasury
to enrich himself;
taxes and labor were unequally distributed,
causing the common people to lament;
he released slaves of good people,
claiming it as his own beneficence.
It would be proper to have them cultivate large fields to fill the granaries,
but now they are immediately allocated
to fill Wǎi's army.
I previously requested to welcome the wives and children of various generals,
and Your Majesty graciously assented,
but Wǎi obstructed
it,
causing all the soldiers of the three armies to resent him.
Furthermore, the refugees from Xúzhōu had endured hardship for years,
and their households had just begun to be established.
Wǎi forcibly drove them all away,
to fill his own coffers.
When
Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
you presented official appointments,
originally as an extraordinary blessing, allowing them to share in the honor.
But instead, they were conscripted for military service,
reverting to their old status.
All the foreign
residents were expelled,
having been here for a long time,
spanning many years,
some having died out,
some having bought their freedom,
some having been released,
some whose fathers and elder brothers were involved in affairs which they themselves were not,
If something was unobtainable,
they would immediately blame the local officials,
and the common people were grieved and indignant,
their complaints filling the roads.
He (Wáng Dūn) intended to cross north (of the Yangtze),
using the excuse of being far from the imperial court,
but secretly getting to know important secrets,
covertly
engaging in treacherous and wicked acts,
promoting some people and dismissing others,
elevating or demoting according to his whims.
His cunning and rapacity
had no one to match Wěi,
and even Wú Jì, Zǎi Pěi, Hóng Gōng, and Shí Xiǎn were not
enough to compare.
Thus, those near and far were enraged,
and all the lords were disappointed.
I (Wáng Dūn) hold the position of prime minister,
sharing the fate of the nation.
Though I truly lack the strategies of Píng and Bó to save the age,
I have forgotten my own mediocrity,
and my ambition lies in the altars of soil and grain.
How could I bear to sit idly by and watch success
or failure,
thereby diminishing Your Majesty's supreme virtue?
Since circumstances leave me no choice,
I will now advance my army
to jointly suppress the treacherous scoundrel (Liú Wěi).
I implore Your Majesty to deeply consider and examine,
and quickly execute Wěi's head.
Then the masses will be appeased
and submissive,
and the imperial throne will again flourish.
If Wěi's head is displayed in the morning,
all armies will retreat by evening.
In the past, Tài Jiǎ could not follow the clear ordinances of Tāng,
overthrowing his principles.
Fortunately, he accepted the merits of Yī Yǐn,
and the Yīn dynasty's way prospered again.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, with his heroic strategies,
was also misled by the slanderous and wicked words of Jiāng Chōng,
leading to a father and son slaughtering each other,
blood staining the ground.
Yet in the end, he was able to awaken,
and did not
lose the main principle.
Today's affairs
are even more critical than this.
I implore Your Majesty to deeply deliberate thrice,
and consult virtuous ways.
Then the four seas will be well-governed and peaceful,
and the altars of soil and grain will be eternally secure.
He (Wáng Dūn) also said: "Your Majesty, when you formerly governed Yángzhōu,
you humbly welcomed scholars,
valued the worthy and appointed the capable,
and gained the masses through leniency.
Therefore, gentlemen gave their utmost,
and common people exerted all their strength.
Although I (Wáng Dūn) am
obscure and ignorant,
I participated in your splendid endeavors.
Thus, those far and near responded to your reputation,
and discerning individuals exhausted themselves.
The imperial enterprise then flourished,
and a new beginning was successfully established.
All within the four seas craned their necks,
all hoping for great peace.
Since trusting Wěi (Liú Wěi),
punishments have been unjust.
Street talks and lane discussions
all say it is like the coming demise of Wú.
Hearing this, I am terrified and confused,
my spirit scattered.
I cannot
but feel my chest torn apart,
and weep tears of blood.
Your Majesty should preserve the ancestral heritage,
and uphold the importance of the divine artifacts (imperial authority).
Consider the memorials I have submitted before and after.
How could you abandon and neglect loyal
words,
and instead trust treacherous sycophants?
Who would not feel pain in their heart!
I wish for my memorial to be issued,
and for Your Majesty to consult the court officials.
The critical moment is imminent,
not even waiting for the end of the day.
Order all armies to return early,
so as not
to cause futile disturbance."
Dūn's partisan, Shěn Chōng from Wúxīng, raised an army in support of Dūn.
When Dūn reached Wúhú,
he again submitted a memorial detailing the crimes of Diāo Xié.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and issued an edict saying:
"Wáng Dūn, relying on his favor and spiritual power,
dares to commit mad rebellion,
equating me to Tài Jiǎ,
wishing to see me imprisoned.
If this can be endured,
what cannot be endured!
Now I will personally lead the six armies
to punish this great rebel.
Whoever kills Dūn
shall be enfeoffed as a Marquis of five thousand households."
He summoned Dài Ruòsī and Liú Wěi to gather in the capital.
Dūn's elder brother, Hán, who was then Grand Master of Ceremonies,
rebelled and fled to Dūn.
Dūn arrived at Shítou,
intending to attack Liú Wěi.
His general Dù Hóng said:
"Liú Wěi has many loyal fighters,
and cannot be easily overcome.
It's better to attack Shítou.
Zhōu Zhá has little benevolence,
and his soldiers will not fight for him.
Attacking him will surely lead to victory.
If Zhá is defeated,
then Wěi will flee on his own."
Dūn followed his advice.
Zhá indeed opened the city gates to admit Hóng.
The generals fought Dūn,
but the imperial army was defeated.
After entering Shítou,
he (Wáng Dūn) held his troops and did not attend court,
allowing his soldiers to freely plunder inside and outside.
Government offices dispersed,
with only two Palace Attendants remaining to serve the Emperor.
The Emperor removed his military uniform,
put on court robes,
looked around and said:
"If you want my position,
just say so early.
I will return to Lángyé myself.
Why torment the common people like this!"
Dūn arrested Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Ruòsī and executed them.
He (the Emperor) appointed Dūn as Chancellor and Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
advanced his peerage to Duke of Wǔchāng Commandery,
with an estate of ten thousand households,
and sent Grand Master of Ceremonies Xún Sōng to confer the appointment.
He was also given feathered banners and drum music,
but he (Wáng Dūn) falsely declined them.
He returned to garrison Wǔchāng,
harming many loyal and good people,
and favoring his relatives.

He appointed his elder brother Hán as General of the Guards, Area Commander of the military affairs of Miǎnnán, concurrently holding the post of Colonel of the Southern Barbarians, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He appointed Rèn Yīn, the Administrator of Yìyáng, as Area Commander of the military affairs north of the Yellow River, and General of the Southern Central Army.
Dūn also personally supervised Níng and Yì two prefectures.
When the Emperor died,
in the first year of Tàiníng,
Dūn hinted to the imperial court to summon him.
Emperor Míng then personally issued an edict to summon him;
the details are in the biography of Emperor Míng.
He (the Emperor) also sent concurrent Grand Master of Ceremonies Yìng Zhān to confer upon him the Yellow Axe,
twenty palace guards with drawn swords,
permission to report to the throne without using his personal name,
to enter court without hurrying,
and to wear swords and shoes on the palace hall.
Dūn moved his garrison to Gūshú.
The Emperor sent Palace Attendant Ruǎn Fú with cattle and wine to reward and comfort him.
Dūn claimed illness and did not appear,
sending his Chief Clerk to receive the edict.
Wáng Dǎo was made Minister of Education,
and Dūn himself became Governor of Yángzhōu.
Once Dùn had achieved his ambitions,
his arrogance and cruelty became even more severe.
Most of the tribute from the four directions entered his private coffers,
and all the generals, ministers, and provincial governors came from his faction.
He transferred Hán to be General of the Punishers of the East and Grand Administrator of military affairs in Yángzhōu and the region west of the Jiāng River.
His younger cousin Shū was made governor of Jīngzhōu,
Bīn of Jiāngzhōu,
and Suì of Xúzhōu.
Hán, courtesy name Chǔhóng,
was vicious, stubborn, and brutal,
and despised by his contemporaries.
Because of Dùn's high status,
he consequently held prominent positions.
Dùn regarded Shěn Chōng and Qián Fèng as his chief strategists,
and Zhūgě Yáo, Dèng Yuè, Zhōu Fǔ, Lǐ, and Xiè Yōng as his henchmen.
Chōng and the others were all cruel, dangerous, arrogant, and unrestrained.
They incited each other,
killing and massacring for their own gain.
They also extensively built camps and mansions,
encroaching on people's fields and homes,
excavating ancient tombs,
and plundering markets and roads.
Both scholars and commoners were dismayed,
and all foresaw his downfall and ruin.
Dùn's younger cousin, Lěng, the Administrator of Yùzhāng, remonstrated with him day and night.
Dùn grew angry
and secretly had him killed.
Dùn had no sons,
so he adopted Hán's son, Yìng.
When Dùn's illness became severe,
he appointed Yìng as General of the Martial Guard to assist him.
Qián Fèng said to Dùn:
"Should the worst happen,
you should entrust future affairs to Yìng."
Dùn replied:
"Extraordinary matters
are not something an ordinary person can handle!
Moreover, Yìng is young;
how can he manage important affairs?
After I die,
it would be best to disband the troops, release the soldiers,
surrender to the court,
and preserve the family.
This is the best plan.
Retreating to Wǔchāng,
holding the soldiers for self-defense,
and not ceasing tribute
is also a middle-tier plan.
While I am still alive,
to gather all forces and descend [on the capital],
and by some remote chance succeed,
is the worst plan."
Fèng said to his confederates:
"His Lord's 'worst plan'
is actually the best strategy."
So he and Shěn Chōng settled on a plan
to start trouble after Dùn's death.
Dùn also resented Zhōu Zhá,
killed him, and completely exterminated his clan.
The attendants Dú Rǎn Zēng, Gōngchéng Xióng, and others were the inner circle of Emperor Yuán.
Dùn also harmed them.
Because there were still many palace guards,
he memorialized to have them rotate, with two-thirds resting at any given time.
When Dùn's illness became critical,
an imperial edict dispatched Attendant Counselor Chén Guǐ and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yú to inquire about his illness.
At that time, the Emperor was about to campaign against Dùn.
He traveled incognito to Wúhú
to inspect his encampments,
and also repeatedly sent high officials to inquire about his daily life.
Hán was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and granted the ritual privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers;
Hán's son Yú was made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Dùn appointed Wēn Jiǎo as Administrator of Dānyáng,
intending him to spy on the court.
When Jiǎo arrived,
he fully reported Dùn's rebellious intentions.
The Emperor wanted to suppress him,
but knowing that Dùn was feared and obeyed by the populace,
he then falsely declared Dùn dead.
Thereupon, an imperial edict stated: "The late Emperor, by his sagely virtue, responded to the times
and founded the enterprise in Jiāngdōng.
Minister of Works Dǎo first served as a trusted confidant,
assisting with virtue.
Therefore, Grand General Dùn served as a limb and joint;
whether inside or outside,
his efforts in assisting [the throne]
contributed significantly.
Through opportune circumstances,
he came to occupy the highest ministerial position,
wielding the staff of authority and commanding independent campaigns,
entrusted with five provinces.
Diāo Xié and Liú
Wěi, in their disagreements at court,
Dùn raised a righteous banner to punish them.
His sentiment was to emulate Yùquán;
although his troops violated loyalty,
we still lauded his sincerity,
and his official rank and treatment were exceptionally high,
unparalleled by any subject.
After the matter was
resolved,
he plundered cities,
allowed his soldiers to act without restraint,
and encroached upon the palace.
He violated the terms of the amnesty,
executed high officials,
indulged in extreme violence and rebellion,
and retreated without coming to court.
The six
directions turned against him,
and the people shared a common indignation.
The late Emperor endured humiliation and shame,
tolerating him without rebuke,
trusting him as before,
and even adding to his official rank and treatment.
I, being unworthy of Heaven,
soon suffered
a cruel affliction,
lonely in my grief,
with nowhere to express my sorrow.
Yet Dùn showed no filial piety or mourning,
nor did he possess the integrity to assist the orphaned and uphold the good.
Instead, he repaired armor and gathered troops,
arriving in mid-summer.
He arbitrarily bestowed official positions upon his private associates,
intending to intimidate the court
and endanger the imperial altars.
I pitied his madness and hoped for his awakening,
thus
I temporarily concealed [his transgressions] to observe his ultimate actions.
But Dùn, proud of his unrighteous might,
had the ambition to insult and weaken the court,
abandoning relatives to use strangers,
and turning his back on the worthy to appoint the wicked.
Qián Fèng,
that mere youth,
served exclusively as his chief strategist,
indulging his ferocity and wickedness,
and slandering loyal and good people.
Zhōu Sōng, being honest and upright,
incurred disaster for his frank words.
Zhōu Zhá and Zhōu Yán, loyal and righteous for generations,
were listened
to slanders and fabrications,
and their clan was utterly destroyed.
The cruelty of the Qín people,
their punishments did not exceed five.
Dùn's executions
indiscriminately harmed the innocent,
exterminating people's clans,
with no one knowing their crimes.
The world was shocked,
people exchanged glances on the roads.
Heaven was enraged, and people resented;
afflicted by a severe illness,
he became increasingly muddled, perverse, and rebellious day by day.
He arbitrarily installed his brother's son to succeed himself,
and established many private factions,
all of whom were equally evil.
Never before has a minister succeeded to office without an imperial command.
The stubborn and vicious praised each other,
having no scruples.
They arbitrarily recruited
artisans,
and arbitrarily diverted transport revenues,
eager to achieve their wicked ambitions
and usurp the imperial regalia.
The danger to the state
was imminent,
whether morning or evening.
Heaven does not permit long-lasting evil,
and Dùn has perished.
Fèng, inheriting his vicious lawlessness,
further incites rebellion.
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot be tolerated?
Now I send Minister of Works Dǎo,
General Who Guards the South and Administrator of Dānyáng Jiǎo,
and General Who Establishes Might Zhào Yìn, with an army of thirty thousand,
advancing along ten routes simultaneously.
General Who Pacifies the West
Suì will lead Yánzhōu Inspector Xiá, General Who Manifests Martial Power Jùn, and General Who Displays Awe Zhān, with thirty thousand elite troops,
advancing by both land and water.
I will personally command the six armies,
with Left Guard General
Liàng,
Right Guard General Yìn,
Protector-General Zhān,
General of the Central Army Zhān,
General of the Central Army Hú,
General of Swift Cavalry Ài,
General of Agile Cavalry and King
Zōng of Nándùn,
General Who Guards the Army and King Yòu of Rǔnán,
Grand Tutor and King Yáng of Xīyáng, with three thousand armored soldiers
and thirty thousand soldiers in chainmail,
to command all armies
and punish Fèng's
crimes.
Only one person is guilty of these crimes;
We will not inflict punishment indiscriminately.
Anyone who can kill Fèng and present his head
will be enfeoffed as a Marquis of Five Thousand Households
and rewarded with five thousand bolts of cloth.
General of Agile Cavalry Dèng Yuè's 鄧嶽 spirit is steady and upright,
and he understands right and wrong.
Former General Zhōu Fǔ's 周撫 character is both thorough and straightforward,
and his integrity and sincerity have always been prominent.
As for the descendants of meritorious officials,
their loyalty and righteousness are constant.
In previous years, when they followed Dūn 敦,
their true feelings were not expressed;
they were pressured by their superiors
and could not refuse.
Considering their true intentions,
they bear no disloyalty to the imperial house.
We commend their sincerity
and shall now appoint them to various affairs.
As for the rest of the civil and military officials,
all those who were appointed by Dūn
shall not be questioned in the slightest.
Prefects and officials earning two thousand *shí* shall not arbitrarily leave their posts.
When this document
arrives, comply with it
and seek your own good fortune.
Do not harbor suspicions
lest you bring about your own destruction.
As for Dūn's officers and soldiers,
who have followed Dūn for many years,
their long-standing grievances and prolonged separation,
with some having lost parents
and others
having lost wives and children,
prevented them from attending to these matters.
They endured their sorrow while serving;
We deeply pity them.
Who among them is not heartbroken?
Those who are single men in the army and have no other responsibilities
shall all be sent home
and never again be conscripted.
The rest shall all be granted three years' leave.
After their leave, they shall return to the palace
and serve in the imperial guard, rotating three times, just like the regular guards.
Clearly abide by this imperial edict;
We
will not go back on Our word.
Another edict stated:
"Anyone who dares to discard Wáng Dūn's 王敦 name and refer to himself as the Grand General
will be dealt with according to military law."
Dūn's 敦 illness became more severe,
and he could not command the troops.
He sent Qián Fèng 錢鳳, Dèng Yuè 鄧嶽, Zhōu Fǔ 周撫, and others to lead an army of thirty thousand towards the capital.
Hán 函 said to Dūn:
"This is a family matter;
I ought to go."
Thus, Hán was made the commander-in-chief.
Fèng 鳳 and others asked Dūn:
"On the day of victory,
what about the Son of Heaven?"
Dūn replied:
"He has not yet performed the southern suburban sacrifice;
how can he be called the Son of Heaven?
Just exert your full military might
to protect the Prince of Dōnghǎi 東海 and Consort Péi 裴, and nothing more."
Then, he submitted a memorial listing Wēn Jiǎo's 溫嶠 crimes,
using the pretext of executing a treacherous minister.
When Hán arrived in Jiāngníng 江寧,
Grand Minister Sītú Dǎo 司徒導 sent a letter to Hán, saying: "Recently, I heard that the Grand General is gravely ill and has been in a prolonged state of decline.
Some even say he has passed away,
and the grief and sorrow
are unbearable.
Soon I learned that Qián Fèng 錢鳳 is making extensive preparations,
intending to carry out
treacherous rebellion.
The court officials are indignant,
and all wring their hands.
On the twenty-third day of last month,
I received a report from the General Who Conquers the North, saying that
Liú Xiá 劉遐, Táo Zhān 陶瞻, Sū Jùn 蘇峻, and others are deeply worried
and, without prior consultation, expressed the same sentiments.
All, from the capital's common people to the imperial household and the guards of the two palaces, fear a repeat of last year's plundering
and can no longer guarantee the safety of their wives and children.
Therefore, the Sacred Lord has issued a solemn
command,
just as stated in the proclamation.
Recently, there was a gracious edict
elevating your eight commissions,
hoping that you would encourage the loyal and righteous hearts of the wise
and suppress the schemes of the wicked and discontented.
You should return to Wǔchāng 武昌
and
exert yourself in your regional duties.
When I suddenly received your recent message,
I learned that you are descending with those 'dogs and sheep.'
Though it must be due to coercion,
it still fills me with dismay.
Brother, your conduct has always been upright and simple,
and your trustworthiness
is well-known within your clan.
You are over sixty,
and your position is supreme among officials.
Zhòngyù 仲玉 and Ānqī 安期 are also not suitable for being 'fine young men.'
This family's legacy
is truly lamentable!
Brother, do you think this action of yours
can achieve what the Grand General did in past years?
In past years, treacherous ministers corrupted the court,
and people were uneasy;
those like me, Dǎo,
desired
to bring peace from the outside.
But now it is different.
When the Grand General came and garrisoned at the lake,
he gradually lost the people's hearts.
Gentlemen are in peril and fear,
and the common people are exhausted and suffering.
On his dying day,
he entrusted
heavy responsibilities to Ānqī 安期.
Ānqī had barely been weaned a few days
and also lacks current prestige;
can he then inherit the position of prime minister?
Since the beginning of time,
have there ever been
child prime ministers?
All who have ears know that this implies an intention to usurp the throne;
it is not the duty of a subject.
The late emperor restored the dynasty,
and his love remains in the hearts of the people.
The Sacred Lord
is intelligent,
and his virtue permeates the court and the land.
He desires to work with the wise and virtuous to overcome difficulties.
Instead of facing north and upholding the duty of a subject,
you privately establish and appoint,
arbitrarily wielding power and bestowing favors.
Among all
subjects,
who is not indignant and sighing?
This is simply Qián Fèng's wicked heart, known far and wide.
Knowing he has no place,
he then incites rebellion.
As for Dèng Bóshān 鄧伯山 and Zhōu
Dàohé 周道和, they have good intentions,
as all who have dealings with them clearly know.
We are about to entrust them with responsibilities
and work together with them,
not just to alleviate our worries.
My family, Dǎo 導, regardless of status, has received abundant imperial grace,
and my brothers have been honored;
this can be called truly great.
Though Dǎo is not martial,
his sentiment is to pacify the nation.
Today's matter demands
that I, with clear
eyes and bold heart, lead the six armies,
preferring to die as a loyal minister
than to live as a scoundrel.
I only regret that the Grand General's achievements, like those of Huán 桓 and Wén 文, were not fulfilled,
and that you, Brother, in a single
day, become a rebellious subject,
betraying the upright aspirations of your ancestors.
On the day of your death,
how will you have the face to see your elders in the netherworld
and greet the late emperor beneath the earth?
Upon reading
your message,
I feel ashamed for you, Brother,
and am both saddened and embarrassed.
I wish you would quickly make a great plan,
and merely seize Qián Fèng 錢鳳 alone,
so that the empire may find peace,
and the family and nation may be blessed.
This
is a matter worthy of being recorded in history,
not merely escaping disaster.
Indeed, good fortune is as easy as turning your hand;
if you seize it, it is yours.
The six armies under my command, Dǎo,
are fifteen thousand men at Shítou 石頭;
the imperial guards in the palace's rear garden are twenty thousand men;
the protectors of the army stationed at Jīnchéng 金城 are six thousand men.
Liú Xiá 劉遐 has already arrived,
and the General Who Conquers the North crossed the Jiāng 江 yesterday with fifteen thousand men.
With the Son of Heaven's might
and the full efforts of civil and military officials,
how can you be withstood?
This matter
can still be
remedied;
Brother, think early about it.
Once our great army is unleashed,
Dǎo believes it will be a decisive victory."
Hán did not reply.
The Emperor dispatched the Central Army Marshal, Cáo Hún [Cáo Hún] and others, to attack Hán [Hán] at Yuèchéng [Yuèchéng].
Hán's [Hán] army was defeated.
Dùn [Dùn] heard this,
and angrily said:
"My elder brother is merely an old servant woman!
Our house is in decline!
Among my brothers, those with both civil and military talent,
Shìjiāng [Shìjiāng] and Chǔjì [Chǔjì], both died young.
Now, the affairs of the world are gone [from us]."
He said to his参軍 [cānjūn] Lǚ Bǎo [Lǚ Bǎo]:
"I must exert myself."
Thereupon, he made an effort to rise,
but, exhausted, lay down again.
Fèng [Fèng] and others arrived at the capital,
and encamped south of the Shuǐ [Shuǐ] River.
The Emperor personally led the six armies to resist Fèng [Fèng],
and after several battles, defeated him.
Dùn [Dùn] said to Yáng Jiàn [Yáng Jiàn] and his son Yīng [Yīng]:
"After I die,
Yīng [Yīng] should immediately ascend the throne,
first establishing the court officials,
and only then attend to the funeral arrangements."
Initially,
when Dùn [Dùn] first fell ill,
he dreamt of a white dog descending from heaven and biting him.
He also saw Diāo Xié [Diāo Xié] riding in a light carriage, escorted by attendants,
glaring and ordering his左右 [zuǒyòu] to seize him.
Soon after, Dùn [Dùn] died,
at the age of fifty-nine.
Yīng [Yīng] secretly withheld the news of his death,
wrapped the body in a mat,
coated its exterior with wax,
and buried it in the central hall.
He and Zhūgě Yáo [Zhūgě Yáo] and others indulged in wine and revelry.
Shěn Chōng [Shěn Chōng] arrived from Wú [Wú] with over ten thousand troops,
and joined Hán [Hán] and others.
Chōng's [Chōng] Marshal, Gù Yáng [Gù Yáng], advised Chōng [Chōng], saying:
"Now that we are undertaking a great endeavor,
the Son of Heaven has already seized its throat.
Morale is divided and the masses are disheartened,
our vanguard is shattered and our momentum broken.
Hesitation and indecision
will surely lead to disaster and defeat.
If we now decide to breach the Zhàtáng [Zhàtáng],
and use the lake water to flood the capital,
unleashing the power of our warships
and making full use of our naval forces,
this is what is called 'subduing the enemy without fighting,'
the best strategy.
Relying on the initial sharpness of our forces
and combining the strength of the southeastern armies,
advancing along ten routes simultaneously,
our numbers more than double theirs,
and we are bound to break through.
This is the middling strategy.
To turn disaster into fortune,
and failure into success,
we should summon Qián Fèng [Qián Fèng] to discuss matters,
then immediately execute him and surrender.
This is the inferior strategy."
Chōng [Chōng] could not adopt it,
so Yáng [Yáng] fled back to Wú [Wú].
Hán [Hán] again led his troops across the Huái [Huái] River,
but Sū Jùn [Sū Jùn] and others met and attacked him,
greatly defeating him.
Chōng [Chōng] also burned his camp and retreated.
Soon after, Zhōu Guāng [Zhōu Guāng] beheaded Qián Fèng [Qián Fèng],
and Wú Rú [Wú Rú] beheaded Shěn Chōng [Shěn Chōng],
and both their heads were sent to the capital.
The officials deliberated, saying:
"Wáng Dùn [Wáng Dùn] committed monstrous rebellion
and had a disloyal heart.
It is fitting to follow the precedents of Cuī Zhù [Cuī Zhù] and Wáng Líng [Wáng Líng],
open his coffin and defile his corpse,
to make known his primary evil."
Thereupon, his burial was excavated, and the corpse exhumed.
His clothes and cap were burned,
and he was knelt and executed.
The heads of Dùn [Dùn] and Chōng [Chōng] were hung on the southern gallows on the same day,
and all who witnessed it celebrated.
Once Dùn's [Dùn] head was hung,
no one dared to collect it for burial.
The Grand Secretary, Xī Jiàn [Xī Jiàn], spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"In the past, Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng] lacquered the head [of his enemy] and attached it to a carriage,
Dǒng Zhuó [Dǒng Zhuó] burned the belly [of his enemy] to illuminate the market.
Wáng Líng [Wáng Líng] was buried in bare earth,
Xú Fù [Xú Fù] had his head burned.
The former dynasty executed Yáng Jùn [Yáng Jùn] and others,
all first subjected them to official punishments,
then allowed private funerals.
However, the Spring and Autumn Annals permitted Qí Xiāng [Qí Xiāng] to bury Marquis Jì [Jì Hóu],
and Wèi Wǔ [Wèi Wǔ] righteously allowed Wáng Xiū [Wáng Xiū] to mourn Yuán Tán [Yuán Tán].
From this, it can be said:
the imperial punishment is applied from above,
while private righteousness is practiced below.
Your servant believes that private burial may be permitted,
which would be magnanimous in its righteousness."
The imperial edict granted permission,
whereupon Dùn's [Dùn] family collected and buried him.
Hán [Hán] and his son fled in a single boat to the Inspector of Jīngzhōu [Jīngzhōu], Wáng Shū [Wáng Shū].
Shū [Shū] ordered his men to drown them in the river,
and the remaining rebels were all pacified.
Dùn [Dùn]'s eyebrows and eyes were open and clear;
he was straightforward and unconstrained by nature,
with keen discernment.
His learning encompassed the Zuǒ Shì [Zuǒ Shì].
He never spoke of wealth or profit,
and especially enjoyed pure conversation.
People of his time did not understand him,
except for his cousin Róng [Róng], who thought him extraordinary.
His strategizing and command were such that
those a thousand *lǐ* away were awed,
yet his immediate subordinates were disorderly and he could not keep them in order.
Emperor Wǔ [Wǔdì] once summoned contemporary worthies to discuss artistic skills.
Everyone had something to say,
but Dùn [Dùn] was completely uninterested,
and his expression was exceptionally sullen.
He then claimed to know how to beat a drum,
and proceeded to raise his sleeves and brandish the drumstick,
the rhythm and tones harmonious,
his spirit self-content,
as if no one else were present.
The entire company admired his heroic boldness.
Shí Chóng [Shí Chóng] boasted of his extravagance and luxury;
in his latrine, there were always more than ten maidservants attending,
all beautiful.
Perfumery powders and aloeswood juice were provided,
and those who used the latrine
were given new clothes to wear when they emerged.
Many guests were too ashamed to undress,
but Dùn [Dùn] took off his old clothes and put on new ones,
his expression showing no shame.
The maidservants said to each other:
"This guest will surely become a rebel."
He also once indulged excessively in sexual pleasure,
to the detriment of his health.
His attendants admonished him,
but Dùn [Dùn] said:
"This is very easy."
Thereupon, he opened the back chambers
and drove out dozens of his concubines and maidservants, releasing them all.
People of the time admired his uniqueness.
Shěn Chōng [Shěn Chōng], courtesy name Shìjū [Shìjū].
From a young age, he loved military treatises,
and was widely known in his hometown for his heroism and boldness.
Dùn [Dùn] enlisted him as a参军 [cānjūn].
Chōng [Chōng] then recommended Qián Fèng [Qián Fèng] from the same prefecture.
Fèng [Fèng], courtesy name Shìyí [Shìyí],
was appointed by Dùn [Dùn] as Armorer参军 [cānjūn],
and frequently gained audiences with him.
Knowing that Dùn [Dùn] harbored disloyal intentions,
he offered perverse advice,
whereupon they conspired together,
monopolizing power and authority,
their words determining misfortune or fortune.
When his father died,
he outwardly claimed to return for the burial,
but secretly served as Dùn's [Dùn] envoy,
conspiring with Chōng [Chōng].
Initially,
Dùn's [Dùn]參軍 [cānjūn] Xióng Fǔ [Xióng Fǔ], seeing Dùn [Dùn] entrusting Fèng [Fèng] and intending to act differently,
said to Dùn [Dùn] while tipsy:
"To found a state and manage a family,
small men should not be employed.
If sycophants are in office,
rarely does an enterprise not fail."
Dùn [Dùn] changed color and said:
"Who are you calling a small man?"
Fǔ [Fǔ] showed no fear,
and thereupon announced his return home.
Before parting with Dùn [Dùn],
he sang:
"The fierce wind rises over mountains and hills,
mist obscures the sun, jade and stone burn.
Past events are gone, forever to be sighed over,
sad at parting, it is hard to meet again."
Dùn [Dùn] knew he was satirizing him but did not heed it.
Míngdì was about to attack Dūn,
and sent his fellow townsman Shěn Zhēn to persuade Chōng,
promising to make him Sīkōng.
Chōng said to Zhēn:
“The grave responsibility of the Three Chancellors,
how can it be something I am capable of taking on!
Rich gifts and sweet words,
are what the ancients feared.
Moreover, when men serve together,
they should remain consistent from beginning to end.
How can one change midway,
who would tolerate me then! ”
Zhēn said:
“Not so.
Whoever abandons loyalty and obedience,
none have failed to perish.
The Grand General obstructs the army and does not attend court;
he bestows titles and rewards upon himself.
Even a five-foot tall child knows his different intentions.
Now, this action of his,
is to commit usurpation and regicide,
how can it be the same as in previous years?
Therefore, the generals on the borders all rush to return to the imperial court,
and officials both inside and outside are willing to lay down their lives,
precisely because he is moving to change the state and replace the ruler;
it is against righteousness to serve him by facing north.
How can you participate in this rebellious scheme,
and bear the responsibility for such unrighteousness!
The court is open and honest,
as I know.
Even for the rebels' associates,
it pardons their crimes
and grants them a fresh start,
how much more so for those who act when they see the opportunity! ”
Chōng did not accept.
Leading his troops, just before setting off,
he said to his wife and children:
“A man will not return
until he has erected the leopard-tail banner.”
When he was defeated and returned to Wúxīng,
he lost his way
and accidentally entered the home of his former general Wú Rú.
Rú lured Chōng into a fortified room,
then laughed and said to Chōng:
“A marquis of three thousand households!”
Chōng said:
“Being enfeoffed as a marquis is not worth coveting.
If you spare me for the sake of great righteousness,
my clan will surely repay you generously.
If you insist on killing me,
your clan will be exterminated.”
Rú then killed him.
Chōng’s son, Jìng, eventually exterminated the Wú clan.
Jìng's biography is found in the Zhuāngyì Zhuàn.
The historian says: When Lángyá first garrisoned Jiànyè,
his dragon virtue was still latent.
Though the imperial destiny was predetermined by a hidden omen,
his great achievements and bountiful benefits had not yet reached the common people.
Wáng Dūn held various offices in the central court,
his prestige and reputation were established early.
When he became governor of Huáihǎi,
his reputation and power grew even stronger.
Thus, he was able to make a deep promise of fish-and-water intimacy,
and establish a close bond of golden-orchid friendship.
He assisted in perfecting the king's rule,
and shone as a supporter of the restoration.
The prognostication for the dynasty extended to a period of one hundred and two years,
and the establishment of the capital founded the enterprise of three parts.
These achievements were certainly not small.
But then, relying on his high achievements, he coveted what was beyond his ambition;
and presuming on his overwhelming power, he indulged in arrogance and oppression.
The rift began with Diāo and Liú,
and the disaster was brought about by Qián and Shěn.
He raised the army of Jìnyáng,
and entangled the troops around Xiàngwèi.
His waspish eyes were revealed,
and his wolfish voice was heard again.
He usurped the national mandate,
and murdered loyal and virtuous officials,
eventually wishing to usurp the imperial carriage
and force the relocation of the imperial regalia.
Thanks to the sagacious strategies of the heir apparent,
the Jìn dynasty's fortune was long-lasting.
The regional lords relinquished their positions,
and the high officials exerted their utmost strength.
Thus, they were able to implement these strategic calculations,
annihilate those wicked rebels,
firmly secure the grand design,
and purify the heavenly path.
Huán Wēn (Méng Jiā)
Huán Wēn, courtesy name Yuánzǐ,
was the son of Huán Yí, the Administrator of Xuānchéng.
He was less than a year old when Wēn Qiáo of Tàiyuán saw him
and said:
“This child has unusual bones;
try making him cry.”
Upon hearing his voice,
he said:
“Truly an extraordinary person!”
Because Yí was admired by Qiáo,
he thus named him Wēn.
Qiáo laughed and said:
“If so,
later he will change my surname.”
Yí was murdered by Hán Huǎng,
and Jiāng Bō, the magistrate of Jīng, was involved.
Wēn was fifteen at the time.
He slept on a spear and wept blood,
determined to seek revenge.
When he reached eighteen,
it happened that Bō had already died.
His three sons, including Biāo, were in mourning,
and kept blades in their staffs
as a precaution against Wēn.
Wēn deceptively claimed to be a condolence visitor,
gained entry,
and stabbed Biāo in the mourning hut,
then pursued and killed his two younger brothers.
People at the time praised him for this.
Wēn was bold and unrestrained, with a grand demeanor.
His appearance was very imposing,
and he had seven "stars" on his face.
In his youth, he was close friends with Liú Dàn of Pèiguó.
Dàn once praised him, saying:
“Wēn’s eyes are like purple stone prisms,
his beard bristles like hedgehog quills;
he is in the same league as Sūn Zhòngmóu and Jìn Xuānwáng.”
He was chosen to marry Princess Nánkāng,
appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
inherited the title of Marquis of Wànníng,
appointed Administrator of Lángyá,
and successively promoted to Governor of Xúzhōu.
Wēn was good friends with Yǔ Yì,
and they promised each other to achieve the pacification and relief of the empire.
Yì once recommended Wēn to Míngdì, saying:
“Huán Wēn has had heroic strategies since his youth.
I hope Your Majesty will not treat him as an ordinary person,
nor merely as a son-in-law.
He should be entrusted with responsibilities like Fāng and Shào,
and given the task of saving the empire from hardship.”
When Yì died,
Wēn was appointed Dūdū Jīng Liáng Sìzhōu Zhūjūn Shì, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Lǐng Hù Nánmán Xiàowèi, and Jiǎjié.
At that time, Lǐ Shì was weak.
Wēn was determined to establish achievements in Shǔ.
In the second year of Yǒnghé,
he led his forces westward.
At that time, Empress Dowager Kāngxiàn presided over the court.
When Wēn was about to depart,
he submitted a memorial and left.
The court was very worried,
because Shǔ was distant and perilous,
and Wēn’s forces were few,
penetrating deep into enemy territory.
Initially,
Zhūgě Liàng had created the Eight Trigram Formation (Bāzhèntú) on the flat sands of Yúfù,
piling stones into eight rows,
each row two zhàng apart.
When Wēn saw it,
he said:
“This is the snake formation of Chángshān.”
None of the civil or military officials could recognize it.
When the army reached Péngmó,
he ordered Staff Officer Zhōu Chǔ and Sūn Shèng to guard the baggage train,
and personally led the infantry directly to Chéngdū.
Shì ordered his uncle Fú and cousin Quán to attack Péngmó.
Chǔ and others resisted them,
and Fú retreated.
Wēn also attacked Quán and others,
winning three battles in three engagements.
The rebel forces dispersed
and returned to Chéngdū via mountain paths.
Shì then gathered all his forces to fight Wēn at Zuóqiáo.
Staff Officer Gōng Hù was killed in battle.
The troops were afraid and wanted to retreat,
but the drum officer mistakenly beat the advance drum.
Thus, they attacked,
and Shì’s forces were utterly routed.
Wēn pressed on with his victory,
burning their small city.
Shì then fled ninety lǐ overnight,
reaching the city of Jiāmáng in Jìnshòu.
His generals Dèng Sōng and Zǎn Jiān persuaded Shì to surrender,
so he came with his hands tied and carrying a coffin, begging for his life.
Wēn untied him and burned the coffin,
sending him to the capital.
Wēn stayed in Shǔ for three decades,
promoting the worthy and commending the good.
The former President of the Board of Civil Office, Wáng Shì, Palace Administrator, Wáng Yú,
General Who Guards the East, Dèng Dìng, and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Cháng Qú, etc.,
who were all excellent people of Shǔ,
were all appointed as staff officers.
The common people were all pleased.
Before the army returned, Wáng Shì, Dèng Dìng, Wěi Wén, and others rebelled.
Wēn again campaigned and pacified them.
He returned with his troops to Jiānglíng,
was promoted to Grand General Who Conquers the West and granted a staff,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Línhè Commandery.
After Shí Jìlóng died,
Huán Wēn wished to lead his forces in a northern expedition.
He first submitted a memorial requesting the court to deliberate on the advisability of a land and water campaign,
but received no reply for a long time.
At that time, he knew the court was relying on Yīn Hào and others to resist him,
and Huán Wēn was greatly indignant.
However, he had always known Yīn Hào
and was not afraid of him.
As the state had no other internal troubles,
they were able to maintain a standoff for a full year.
Although there were traces of a lord-subject relationship,
it was merely a matter of mutual restraint.
The resources and levies from the eight provinces,
were almost not used for the state.
He declared a northern expedition,
submitted his memorial, and immediately departed.
He sailed downstream,
reaching Wǔchāng.
His forces numbered forty to fifty thousand.
Yīn Hào feared he would be deposed by Huán Wēn,
and intended to avoid him.
He also wished to use the Zōuyú banner to halt Huán Wēn's army.
There was murmuring inside and outside,
and people's hearts were shocked and dismayed.
Emperor Jiǎnwén, then Fǔjūn,
wrote to Huán Wēn, explaining the great plans for the altars of soil and grain,
and the source of his doubts.
Huán Wēn immediately turned his army back to his garrison,
and submitted a memorial which read: "Your servant recently personally led his forces,
intending to sweep northwards through Zhào and Wèi.
When the army reached Wǔchāng,
I received a letter from Fǔjūn Dàjiàngjūn, King Yù of Kuàijī,
stating that 'the dust and winds are in commotion,
giving rise to baseless doubts,
and the words and intent are critical and urgent,
causing concern for the altars of soil and grain.'
Reading it, I was surprised and shocked,
unable to understand the reason,
my body and shadow looking at each other,
with no place to fall.
Your servant, due to his ignorance
and obscurity,
unworthily bears a heavy responsibility.
Although my talent is not equal to the man,
my duty is to quell disorder.
If the enemies are not annihilated,
and the national shame not yet avenged,
should I be fortunate enough to encounter a period of prosperity
and a favorable
opportunity,
even a common man with ambition
would still feel indignation.
What heart do I have
to sit and watch its ruin!
Therefore, bearing my halberd, I have campaigned tirelessly,
without leisure for rest.
My memorials and submissions,
have
continued for years now.
My loyal sincerity is clear
and evident to both public and private scrutiny.
What trifling matter
could give rise to such suspicion and apprehension?
Could it be that those who hate the upright are harboring fear in their hearts,
and are manipulating false
stories
to mislead the court's ears?
In the past, Yuè Yì exhausted his sincerity,
and fled with tears flowing;
Huò Guāng devoted his loyalty,
yet Shangguān reported a betrayal.
Slanderous talk destroys conduct,
and treachery corrupts virtue.
This has been a constant
calamity throughout the ages,
and the cause of rise and fall.
Now, the Sovereign is in the prime of his youth,
Your Majesty presides over the court with sagacity and virtue,
reverently delegating authority,
and holding all subordinates accountable.
He is now entrusting the gathering
and communication to all talents,
and extending virtue and trust to distant wildlands.
Moreover, your servant has for generations received exceptional grace,
and served three reigns.
My person is not that of a wandering guest,
nor are my actions tainted by the flaws of Hán Xìn or Péng Yuè.
Yet, counter-intelligence arises from within my heart,
and the confusion exceeds that of the four states.
This is why ancient sages sighed over the past,
and your servant is also greatly fearful in this very year.
Now,
the bandits are melting away like ice,
and the great task is nearing completion.
The remaining people of Jìn stand on tiptoe, looking south,
and those who rally to righteousness eagerly take to the road.
The life of the arch-villain hangs by a thread,
yet
erroneous discussions arise,
forming this brocade of slander,
allowing the doomed bandits to revive.
This causes deep pain and despair,
and profound sorrow.
Although your servant's concern
is public,
and his endeavor is for the state,
if external troubles are not quelled,
and internal ills arise together,
then my original intention of exerting my strength will be lost."
He was promoted to Tàiwèi,
but firmly declined the appointment.
At this time, Yīn Hào reached Luòyáng to repair the imperial tombs.
This took several years,
and he repeatedly fought and was repeatedly defeated,
his weapons and equipment completely exhausted.
Huán Wēn was again promoted to commander of Sīzhōu.
Taking advantage of the resentment from the court and public,
he then impeached and deposed Yīn Hào.
From this, all great power, both internal and external, fell to Huán Wēn.
Huán Wēn then led forty thousand infantry and cavalry from Jiānglíng.
The naval forces entered Jūn kǒu from Xiāngyáng,
and reached Nánxiāng.
The infantry marched from Xīchuān to conquer Guānzhōng,
ordering Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Xūn to exit via the Zǐwǔ Dào.
A separate force attacked Shàngluò,
capturing Fú Jiàn's Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Guō Jìng,
and advanced to attack Qīngní,
which they defeated.
Fú Jiàn again sent his son Fú Shēng and his brother Fú Xióng with tens of thousands of troops to garrison Yáoliǔ and Chóusīduī to resist Huán Wēn.
A great battle ensued.
Fú Shēng personally charged into the enemy lines,
killing Huán Wēn's generals Yīng Dàn and Liú Hóng,
and causing thousands of casualties.
Huán Wēn's army fought bravely,
and Fú Shēng's troops then scattered.
Fú Xióng also fought against General Huán Chōng at Báilù Yuán,
and was again defeated by Huán Chōng.
Fú Xióng then swiftly attacked Sīmǎ Xūn.
Sīmǎ Xūn retreated to Nǚwābǎo.
Huán Wēn advanced to Bàshàng.
Fú Jiàn fortified himself with five thousand men in deep trenches.
The local residents all settled down and resumed their livelihoods,
eight or nine out of ten brought cattle and wine to welcome Huán Wēn on the road.
The elders wept with emotion, saying:
"We never expected to see the imperial army again today!"
Initially,
Huán Wēn relied on the ripe wheat,
taking it as military provisions.
However, Fú Jiàn cut down the crops and cleared the fields,
so military supplies were not forthcoming.
He collected over three thousand people and returned.
The Emperor sent Shìzhōng Huángmén to console Huán Wēn at Xiāngyáng.
Initially,
Huán Wēn considered his heroic bearing and temperament to be on par with Xuān Dì and Liú Kūn.
When some compared him to Wáng Dūn,
he was very displeased.
Now, returning from this expedition,
he found a skilled old maid in the north.
Upon inquiring,
she turned out to be Liú Kūn's concubine-musician.
As soon as she saw Huán Wēn,
she burst into tears.
Huán Wēn asked her why,
and she replied:
"You greatly resemble Sīkōng Liú."
Huán Wēn was greatly pleased.
He went outside to tidy his clothes and cap,
and then called the maid again to ask.
The maid said:
"Your face is very similar,
but unfortunately thin;
〔一０〕your eyes are very similar,
but unfortunately small;
your beard is very similar,
but unfortunately reddish;
your physique is very similar,
but unfortunately short;
your voice is very similar,
but unfortunately feminine."
Huán Wēn then removed his cap and loosened his belt,
and fell into a daze,
unhappy for several days.
His mother, Lady Kǒng, passed away.
He submitted a memorial resigning from his post,
wishing to transport her coffin to Wǎnlíng.
An imperial edict forbade it.
She was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Línhè Tàifūrén,
with the posthumous name Jìng.
Shìzhōng was dispatched to offer condolences,
and Yèzhě to supervise the funeral arrangements.
Within a month,
envoys arrived eight times,
their carriages visible along the road.
After Huán Wēn completed the funeral, he resumed his duties,
wishing to repair the imperial tombs
and move the capital to Luòyáng.
He submitted over ten memorials,
but they were not approved.
Huán Wēn was promoted to Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū and Dūdū Sī Jì Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì,
entrusting him with the sole responsibility of campaigns.
Huán Wēn dispatched his supervisor, Gāo Wǔ, to hold Lǔyáng.
The Auxiliary General of the State, Dài Shī, garrisoned the area north of the Yellow River.
He ordered his naval forces to advance and pressure Xǔluò.
Since the waterway between Qiáo and Liáng was now open,
he requested that troops from Xú and Yù provinces use the Huái and Sì rivers to enter the Yellow River.
Huán Wēn himself launched a northern expedition from Jiānglíng.
As he passed through Jīnchéng,
he saw that the willows he had planted when he was young in Lángyé had all grown to ten arm-spans in circumference.
He sighed with emotion, saying:
“Even trees are like this;
how can humans bear it!”
He grasped a branch and held a twig,
and tears flowed profusely.
Subsequently, he crossed the Huái and Sì rivers,
trod upon the northern border,
and ascended Píngchéng Tower with his staff and subordinates.
Gazing out at the Central Plains,
he sighed with emotion, saying:
“To think that the Divine Land has sunk,
and for a hundred years has been reduced to ruins!
Wáng Yífǔ and others cannot but bear the responsibility for this!”
Yuán Hóng said:
“Fortune has its rise and fall;
how can it necessarily be the fault of these individuals!”
Huán Wēn, his expression changing, said to all present:
“I once heard that Liú Jǐngshēng had a thousand-catties ox
that consumed ten times more fodder and beans than a normal ox,
yet in bearing heavy loads and traveling far,
it was not even equal to one lean cow.
When Wèi Wǔ entered Jīngzhōu,
he offered it to his soldiers.”
His intention was to allude to Yuán Hóng,
and everyone present turned pale.
The army then reached the Yī River.
Yáo Xiāng was encamped north of the river,
and they fought across the water.
Huán Wēn formed his ranks and advanced,
personally donning armor and supervising his younger brother Chōng and other generals in a fierce attack.
Yáo Xiāng was utterly defeated,
with several thousand of his own men killing each other.
He fled west, crossing Mount Běimáng,
but was not overtaken.
He then escaped to Píngyáng.
Huán Wēn encamped in front of the former Tàijí Hall,
then moved into Jīnyōng City.
He visited the tombs of the former emperors;
those tombs that had been violated or damaged were all repaired,
and tomb prefects were appointed.
He then turned his army back,
capturing and bringing back the surrendered rebel Zhōu Chéng.
He resettled over three thousand surrendered households between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
He dispatched the Administrator of Xīyáng, Téng Jùn, to lead forces out of Huángchéng
to suppress the indigenous bandit Wén Lú and others.
He also dispatched the Chancellor of Jiāngxià, Liú Hù, and the Administrator of Yìyáng, Hú Jì, to suppress the rebel wizard Lǐ Hóng.
Both groups were defeated,
and their heads were sent to the capital.
After Huán Wēn’s army returned,
Sī, Yù, Qīng, and Yǎn provinces again fell to the bandits.
During the Shēngpíng era,
his title was changed to Duke of Nánjùn,
and Línhè was reduced to a county dukedom,
which was bestowed upon his second son, Jì.
At the beginning of the Lónghé era,
bandits threatened Hénán,
and the Administrator Dài Shī fled.
The General of Champiom Might, Chén Yòu, reported an emergency.
Huán Wēn sent the Administrator of Jìnglíng, Dèng Xiá, to lead three thousand men to assist Chén Yòu,
and also wished to return the capital to Luòyáng.
He submitted a memorial, saying: “Now that Bāshǔ has been pacified
and the invading Hú barbarians eliminated,
the opportune moment has arrived,
and the blessings of peace and prosperity are manifest.
Yet, human affairs have gone awry,
repeatedly losing royal strategies,
and
allowing two bandits to rise simultaneously,
causing the realm to crumble and tear apart.
The Hénán and Luòyáng regions are desolate,
and the mountains and imperial tombs are perilously close to danger.
This is why people far and near are anxious and fearful,
grieving over the past.
I humbly submit that
Your Majesty possesses the innate qualities of Heaven and Earth,
and embodies the profound and brilliant virtues of Fúxī and Shénnóng.
Like a phoenix nesting in an outer fief,
and a dragon soaring to the imperial zenith,
the urgent matters of the time have been neglected,
but are fully heard by Heaven,
and the
true and false in human nature
are all known to You.
Therefore, the hearts of the nine regions are settled,
and those in distant lands crane their necks
with anticipation, hoping that Your influence will extend like a net
to encompass all four barbarian lands.
It is indeed fitting to plan far-sightedly with imperial calculations,
to greatly preserve and implement strategies,
to restore the old capital to glory,
and to manage the territory of Huáxià,
so that benevolent winds and generous favors may spread to the eight directions,
and Your awe-inspiring majesty may awe without limits.
Would this not perfectly fulfill
auspicious fortune,
and unite Heaven and man in agreement!
Now, the rivers are vast and wide,
and the lands are far apart.
Thus, those who incline towards righteousness repeatedly face ruin,
yet those who establish their banners continue to follow one after another without
regret.
Moreover, when the imperial star turns,
all other stars look up to it.
When the root source moves,
the branches and tributaries naturally shift.
Then, the remaining people of Jìn will rejoice in the imperial virtue they rely upon,
and the rebellious and wicked hordes
will know that their demise is imminent.
If we unleash the desire for compliance
and beat the drums with the force of thunder,
then the lives of the two bandits will be extinguished without the need for execution.
Thus, perfect strategy is valued for
its unimpeded flow,
and the wise and discerning value seizing the opportune moment.
Solid as a rock,
this is how achievements are made.
If, however, the tide of fortune has shifted,
but the wings of the great bird do not lift,
and one forever takes root in the southern
border,
abandoning the Divine Land to the deserts,
it will make even five-foot-tall children cover their mouths and sigh.
The ancient kings laid the foundations,
and the sagely wise settled their hearts
by dividing the land into nine regions
and establishing nine subservient territories.
They valued the central region and internalized all Huáxià states,
precisely because the sun’s shadow naturally centers there,
and frost
and dew are uniformly distributed,
crowning all nations
and drawing the four seas into submission.
Ever since the fierce Hú barbarians plundered,
and Huáxià was overturned,
we have been in distress and lost our foundation,
and have temporarily moved south of the Yangtze River,
contracting
like a silkworm awaiting the moment of a dragon’s stretch,
and lying dormant awaiting the time of wind and clouds.
This is due to the accumulation of calamity and ruin,
not because of superior reason.
Yet, the chaos and disorder are distant,
over fifty
years have passed,
the old generations have died off,
and the later generations are young.
They sit on mats and cease their laments,
and accumulated habits have become customs,
thus abandoning hope for their original homeland,
and finding peace in their adopted place.
When I recall
this,
I cannot help but sigh with sorrow!
Although I am mediocre and incompetent,
my talent is insufficient for these duties,
yet I have taken office to fill a vacancy
and bear a heavy responsibility.
I wish to exert all my strength,
and deploy my power as the vanguard,
to cut
away the thorns
and drive out these jackals and wolves.
All those who, since the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
were scattered and flowed into the Jiāngbiǎo region,
I request that they all be resettled northwards
to populate Hénán,
providing them with their former livelihoods,
returning them to their
homelands,
encouraging them in agriculture and sericulture,
making full use of the benefits of the three seasons,
guiding them with righteousness,
and regulating them with propriety,
so that both civil and military virtues are proclaimed,
and trust and obedience flourish.
Once the communities are
restored
and the general order is established,
then Your Majesty can raise the banners of the three luminaries,
wave the flags of command,
with crown and pendants, bells and ornaments,
in court robes, cross the Yangtze River.
Then, within the universe,
who would not be extremely fortunate!
People are accustomed to security and comfort,
and it is difficult to plan a new beginning with them;
extraordinary undertakings
are doubted by the multitude.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to make a clear decision with profound insight,
and to resolve the matter of fairness and equality."
Outside,
he tasked this minister with the effect of restoration,
and entrusted this minister with the accomplishment of ultimate success.
When this matter is settled,
and this achievement is made,
then Your Majesty's great merits will rival those of previous generations,
and the restoration lauded during the reign of Zhōu Xuān will return in our time.
If it is not effective,
it is this minister's fault,
and I shall lift my skirt and jump into the cauldron,
finding it as sweet as water caltrop.
The imperial edict stated:
"In the past, during times of chaos and war,
five *jì* have swiftly passed.
The Róng and Dí have rampaged,
their evil deeds continuing.
Looking back towards the west,
sorrowful sighs fill my heart!
I know that you wish to personally lead the three armies,
to cleanse the filth,
clear the central region,
and restore the old capital.
Unless one is willing to sacrifice oneself for the country,
who could achieve this!
All arrangements
are entrusted to your profound judgment.
However, Hélòu is a ruin,
and what needs to be managed is vast.
The efforts of initiation
have caused you much fatigue."
Thereupon, he was reassigned as the governor of the three prefectures of Bìng, Sī, and Jì,
and because Jiāo and Guǎng were far away,
the position of Grand Inspector (Dūdū) was abolished. [Wēn] expressed his refusal to accept this in a memorial.
He was also appointed Shìzhōng, Dàsīmǎ, Grand Inspector of all internal and external military affairs (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì), and granted the仮黃鉞 (Jiǎ Huángyuè) axe.
Wēn, believing that since he was already the overall commander of internal and external affairs,
he should not be far away,
again submitted a memorial detailing seven expedient matters: First,
factions collude,
and private discussions are rampant.
It is advisable to suppress frivolous competition,
and prevent it from taking root.
Second,
the population is diminished,
not even as much as one Hàng郡 (Jùn).
It is advisable to merge offices and streamline positions,
and allow people to serve longer in their roles.
Third,
urgent affairs cannot be suspended,
and routine documents should have a deadline.
Fourth,
it is advisable to clarify the rites between elders and juniors,
and commend loyal and impartial officials.
Fifth,
praise, censure, reward, and punishment
should be in accordance with the truth.
Sixth,
it is advisable to follow previous precedents
and diligently promote learning.
Seventh,
it is advisable to select and appoint historians
to complete the Jìnshū.
All relevant authorities presented their memorials to implement these.
Soon after, he was granted the feather canopy and drum and pipe music (Yǔbǎo Gǔchuī),
and appointed a Left and Right Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ), a Chief Commandant (Sīmǎ), and four Attendant Military Advisors (Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
He accepted the drum and pipe music,
but declined all the other appointments.
He then led a naval force to advance on Héféi.
He was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu and Recorder of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
The Shìzhōng Yán Máo was sent to convey the imperial decree,
summoning Wēn to participate in court administration.
Wēn submitted a memorial saying: "I am now eradicating the various villains
and pacifying the chaos.
We should exhaust the wisdom and strength of the whole realm
and cooperate with everyone to achieve success.
However, the court opinions are all doubtful,
and the imperial edict is becoming increasingly firm.
The matter deviates from the original
plan;
how dare I insist on it!
As for participating in court administration,
it is not something I dare to hear of.
This minister has been absent from the palace for over twenty years,
burdened by military duties,
and toiled with bitter
thoughts.
If I could unburden myself and roam freely,
ringing my jade pendants at the palace gates,
participating in the agreement of non-action,
and hearing of the transformation that brings all things to completion,
though I am truly not clever,
would this not be my wish!
However,
considering the difficulties of Jiānghàn,
which are unlike former days,
and that Yì and Liáng have just been pacified,
and Níngzhōu has just submitted,
with troops deployed along the Hàn River,
and the defense greatly extended,
furthermore, the strong barbarians are entrenched
and hold the upper reaches of the river,
and the rivers and lakes are vast and distant.
We must command the marquises and counts;
without a person of esteemed reputation and great authority,
there is no way to镇禦 (zhènyù) the distant regions.
This minister knows the difficulties and dangers of abandoning this,
and dares to go against it without resentment.
That I wish to raise my arm and throw myself into the affairs of the Central Plains
is truly because I am ashamed that the imperial Way and the imperial residence are confined to the southeast,
and grieved that the spiritual land of our ancestors (Shénhuá Sāngzǐ) is buried
among the Róng and Dí.
If we rely on the spirit of the ancestral temples,
then we will clear them away like clouds and sweep them up like mats,
cleansing them in a breath.
If we are to allow for a temporary respite,
then this minister will occupy Hélòu,
personally face the two
enemies,
widely proclaim the imperial spirit,
and control Qín and Zhào.
In no more than five years,
the great task will certainly be accomplished.
Now, Your Majesty's humble servant Yù is assisting the country with his kin and worthies,
brilliantly aiding two generations.
There is no need for this humble and dull minister
to also intervene in state affairs.
Moreover, if there are no travelers (those who go out),
who will guard the herds
and fences?
The inner and outer (表裡 biǎolǐ) complement each other,
which is truly deep and important.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to consider what this minister has stated,
and also consult both internal and external opinions.
I request to return to my encampment at this time,
to pacify the border regions."
The edict did not allow it,
and again summoned Wēn.
When Wēn reached Zhèqí,
the edict again sent Shàngshū Chē Guàn to stop him.
Wēn then fortified Zhèqí,
firmly declined the internal appointment,
and remotely held the position of Governor of Yángzhōu.
At this time, the Xiānbēi attacked Luòyáng,
and Chén Yòu fled.
Jiǎnwén Dì was assisting in government at the time.
He met Wēn at Lièzhōu,
