to discuss matters of expedition and suppression.
Wēn moved his garrison to Gūshú.
Coinciding with the death of Āi Dì,
the matter was then dropped.
Wēn was frugal by nature;
whenever he hosted a banquet, he would only serve seven plates of tea and fruit.
However, being militarily powerful and monopolizing court affairs,
he harbored inappropriate ambitions.
Sometimes, when reclining, he would say to his trusted aides:
"If I remain so obscure,
I will be laughed at by Wén and Jǐng."
No one dared to reply.
Presently, he sat up, leaning on his pillow, and said:
"Since I cannot leave a good reputation for posterity,
is it not enough to leave a bad reputation for ten thousand generations!"
Once, passing by Wáng Dūn's tomb,
he looked at it and said:
"A capable man,
a capable man!"
Such were his thoughts and actions.
At that time, there was a Buddhist nun from a distant land named Yǒu Dàoshù,
who bathed in a separate room.
Wēn secretly spied on her.
The nun, naked, first used a knife to cut open her own belly,
then cut off both her legs.
After bathing, she came out.
Wēn asked about the fortune.
The nun said:
"If you become the Son of Heaven,
it will also be like this."
In the fourth year of Tàihé,
Húan Wēn again submitted a memorial requesting to lead all troops in a northern expedition.
General Píngběi, Xī Yīn, resigned due to illness.
Húan Wēn was then appointed General Píngběi and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn prefectures.
He led his younger brother, Nán Zhōngláng Húan Chōng, and Xī Zhōngláng Yuán Zhēn, with fifty thousand infantry and cavalry, on a northern expedition.
All officials saw him off in Nánzhōu,
and the capital city was completely deserted.
The army reached Húlù,
and attacked Mùróng Wěi's general, Mùróng Zhōng.
They captured him,
and advanced to Jīnxiāng.
At that time, there was a severe drought,
and the waterways were impassable.
So they dug a canal over three hundred *lǐ* through Jùyě to facilitate boat transport,
entering the Yellow River from Qīngshuǐ.
Mùróng Wěi's generals Mùróng Chuí and Fù Mòbō, leading eighty thousand troops, resisted Húan Wēn,
and fought at Línzhǔ.
Húan Wēn decisively defeated them,
and then reached Fāngtóu.
He had previously sent Yuán Zhēn to attack Qiáoliáng,
and open Shímén to secure supply lines.
Yuán Zhēn pacified Qiáoliáng,
but was unable to open Shímén,
and the army's provisions were exhausted.
Húan Wēn burned his boats and retreated on foot,
departing from Dōngyàn and passing through Cāngyuán,
then Chénliú.
They dug wells for water,
traveling over seven hundred *lǐ*.
Mùróng Chuí pursued him with eight thousand cavalry,
and they fought at Xiāngyì.
Húan Wēn's army was defeated,
with thirty thousand casualties.
Húan Wēn was deeply ashamed of this,
and blamed Yuán Zhēn,
submitting a memorial to have him demoted to a commoner.
Yuán Zhēn resented Húan Wēn for falsely accusing him,
and fortified himself in Shòuyáng,
secretly communicating with Fú Jiān and Mùróng Wěi.
The Emperor sent Attendant Counselor Luó Hán to reward Húan Wēn with cattle and wine in Shānyáng.
He also had King of Kuàijī, Yù, meet with Húan Wēn in Túzhōng.
An imperial edict appointed Húan Wēn's heir apparent, Xī, as General Zhēnglǔ, Inspector of Yù Prefecture, and granted him *jiǎjié*.
When Princess Nánkāng passed away,
an edict granted a posthumous gift of one thousand bolts of cloth
and one million cash.
Húan Wēn declined to accept it.
He also stated that Xī, an orphan of three years,
was too young to hold such a critical position.
The imperial edict did not permit this.
He mobilized people from the prefecture to build Guǎnglíng city,
and moved his garrison there.
At that time, Húan Wēn's campaigns had been long,
and a plague had also struck.
Four or five tenths of his men died,
and the common people complained and resented him.
Yuán Zhēn died of illness.
His general Zhū Fǔ enthroned his son, Jǐn, to succeed him.
Mùróng Wěi and Fú Jiān both sent armies to assist Jǐn.
Húan Wēn sent Supervisors Zhú Yáo and Jiǎo Yángzhī, among others, with a naval force to attack them.
At that time, Mùróng Wěi's army had already arrived.
Yáo and others fought them at Wǔqiū,
and defeated them.
Húan Wēn led twenty thousand men from Guǎnglíng and arrived again.
Jǐn fortified himself within the city and held firm.
Húan Wēn built a long siege-wall around it.
Fú Jiān then sent his generals Wáng Jiàn and Zhāng Háoo, among others, with troops to relieve Jǐn.
They encamped at Luòjiàn,
first sending five thousand elite cavalry to the north of the Féishuǐ.
Húan Wēn sent Huán Yī and his nephew Shíqián, among others, to intercept and attack them.
They utterly routed them.
Jǐn's forces then collapsed.
They captured Jǐn alive,
along with dozens of his clan members and Zhū Fǔ, and sent them to the capital city where they were executed.
Hundreds of *qǐhuó* (beggar-survivors) whom Jǐn had kept were all buried alive,
and their wives and children were distributed as rewards.
For Húan Wēn's achievements,
an edict granted him ten additional *jiànbǐ*.
The army was rewarded along the way,
and civil and military officials received various rewards for their merits.
Húan Wēn, already confident in his talent and strength,
had long harbored ambitions.
He wished to first establish achievements north of the Yellow River,
and then receive the Nine Marks of Favor.
After suffering a defeat,
his reputation and prestige greatly diminished.
Thereupon, his參軍 (aide-de-camp) Xī Chāo proposed the plan of deposing and establishing an emperor.
Húan Wēn then deposed the Emperor and enthroned Emperor Jiǎnwén.
An edict commanded Húan Wēn to follow the precedent of Zhūgě Liàng,
entering the palace with one hundred armed guards,
and bestowed upon him fifty million cash,
twenty thousand bolts of silk,
and one hundred thousand bolts of cloth.
Húan Wēn deposed and exiled many people,
executing Yú Qiàn, Yīn Juān, Cáo Xiù, and others.
At this time, Húan Wēn's power and influence were overwhelming.
Attendant Counselor Xiè Ān saw him and bowed from a distance.
Húan Wēn, surprised, said:
"Ānshí,
why are you doing this?!"
Ān replied:
"There has never been a ruler bowing in front
and a minister making a salutation from behind."
At that time, Húan Wēn suffered from a foot ailment.
An imperial edict permitted him to ride in a carriage to court.
When he had an audience,
he intended to explain his original intention for the deposition and establishment,
but the Emperor immediately shed dozens of lines of tears.
Húan Wēn, awestruck and intimidated, left without saying a word.
Initially,
during the reign of Yuán Míng,
Guō Pú made a prophecy which said:
"The lord will not be without heirs,
but brothers will alternate in succession."
This meant that Emperor Chéng had sons,
but the throne would be passed to his younger brother.
It also said:
"There is a person named Lǐ,
whose son specializes in warfare.
Like a chariot axle,
detached on one side."
The character *ér* (兒) [son]
is a component of the character *zǐ* (子).
Removing *zǐ* (子) from *lǐ* (李) leaves *mù* (木).
Removing *zhóu* (軸) [axle] from *chē* (車) leaves *gèn* (亘).
Combining these
forms the character "Huán" (桓).
It also said:
"*Ěr lái*, *ěr lái*,
a great county in Hénèi."
*Ěr lái* refers to Yuánzǐ as the beginning of an era,
and Wēn's courtesy name was Yuánzǐ.
Therefore, "a great county in Hénèi"
refers to Wēn.
After Chéng and Kāng died,
the Huán clan began to grow powerful,
thus they were mentioned together.
It also said:
"The death of Zǐ will prolong our dynasty.
The demise of Zǐ will bring the imperial fortune to its twilight."
These two *zǐ* refer to
Yuánzǐ (Húan Wēn) and Dàozǐ (King of Kuàijī).
Húan Wēn intended to usurp the throne,
but died before his plan succeeded,
which was fortunate.
Although King of Kuàijī, Dàozǐ, initiated chaos in the Jìn state,
his death was also a cause for Jìn's decline,
hence the mention of "pain."
Húan Wēn returned to Báishí
and submitted a memorial requesting to return to Gūshú.
The edict stated:
"Heaven and Earth combine in essence,
and thereby transform to create all things;
when two people are of one mind,
they need not speak of their benefits.
Ancient sagely kings all relied on prime ministers.
Jī Dàn's brilliance extended to the four quarters,
and thus the Zhōu Way flourished;
Yī Yǐn's virtue reached High Heaven,
and thus the Yīn transformation was harmonized.
The Grand Marshal's illustrious virtue meets the opportune moment,
its brilliance is profound and far-reaching.
It accords with the heart of Heaven above,
its inner splendor manifests in due time.
Therefore, it gathers the great mandate,
resting with me alone.
His merits surpass those of Bólù,
his Way is solid for ten thousand generations.
Now, I promote you, Lord, to Chancellor,
and your original post as Grand Marshal remains as before.
Stay, Lord, in the capital city,
to stabilize the state."
Húan Wēn firmly declined,
still requesting to return to his garrison.
The Emperor sent Attendant Counselor Wáng Tǎnzhī to summon Húan Wēn to become Chancellor,
and increased his fief to ten thousand households,
but he again declined.
An edict stated that due to the incident involving Yuán Zhēn in the Western Commandery,
military supplies were insufficient.
It granted Húan Xī, the heir apparent, thirty thousand bolts of cloth
and sixty thousand *hú* of rice.
Additionally, Xī's younger brother Jì was appointed Attendant Counselor.
When the Emperor fell ill,
he issued an edict to Huán Wēn, saying:
“I am gravely ill.
You must come in at once.
I hope to see you.
Come immediately,
come immediately!”
Thus, in one day and one night, four edicts were repeatedly issued.
Huán Wēn submitted a memorial stating:
“The Saintly Body has been unwell
for many days.
My foolish heart is fearful
and has nowhere to place its feelings.
Indeed, flourishing and decline are constant principles;
excessive preparations cause no harm.
Thus, Gāo Zǔ of Hàn was ill in bed,
and Empress Lǚ inquired about the succession;
Wǔ Dì was unwell,
and Huò Guāng established the successor.
To sorrowfully inquire about matters after one's demise
is because what is at stake is great.
Now, the Imperial Princes are young,
and among the worthy officials of the court, only Xiè Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī possess talent, knowledge, and wisdom that are all deeply appreciated by Your Sagely Majesty.
To assist the young sovereign internally
and guard against powerful enemies externally,
this is indeed the great fear of all sentiments,
yet the solution lies here.
Your Majesty should immediately grant them high authority,
so that the populace knows where to place its trust,
and Ān and others can obey the command, exert their efforts,
and make it appropriate for both public and private matters.
As for this servant Wēn, my position combines both general and prime minister.
Furthermore, Your Majesty has shown me the regard of a commoner.
However, I am decaying and ill,
fearing I cannot last long,
and am incapable of being entrusted with matters after your passing.”
Before the memorial could be presented, the Emperor passed away.
The dying edict stated that matters of the family and state should entirely be handled by Huán Wēn,
following the precedents of Zhūgé Wǔhóu and Prime Minister Wáng.
Initially, Huán Wēn had hoped that Jiǎnwén Dì would abdicate the throne to him on his deathbed.
Failing that, he expected to act as Regent Gōng.
Since matters did not turn out as he had hoped,
he was very resentful and angry.
He wrote to his younger brother Chōng, saying:
“The dying edict only makes me follow the precedents of Wǔhóu and Duke Wáng.”
Wáng and Xiè managed the great affairs,
and for days, Huán Wēn felt indignant and little comforted.
When Xiàowǔ Dì ascended the throne,
an edict stated:
“The late Emperor's dying instruction said: ‘Serve the Grand Marshal as you would serve me.’
Let the reply to his memorial be made with utmost respect.”
Another edict said:
“The Grand Marshal is entrusted with the altars of soil and grain.
The late Emperor entrusted him with the family and state.
All internal and external matters should be carried out by Duke Huán.”
Xiè Ān was again sent to summon Huán Wēn to assist the government,
with the addition of a vanguard with feather canopies and drum music,
and sixty martial retainers.
Huán Wēn declined to accept.
When Huán Wēn arrived at court
to attend the imperial burial,
an edict stated:
“The Duke's merits and virtues are highly esteemed.
He is the teacher and guardian of Our Person.
Furthermore, he suffers from a wind-illness.
Therefore, there is no need for him to perform rituals of respect.”
It was also decreed that the Grand Secretaries Ān and others should greet him at Xīntíng,
and all officials bowed by the roadside.
At that time, all those with prominent positions were trembling and losing color,
some saying that Huán Wēn would use this opportunity to kill Wáng and Xiè;
both inside and outside the court, there was fear.
When Huán Wēn arrived,
he sent Lú Sǒng into the palace,
then arrested Grand Secretary Lù Shǐ and handed him over to the Grand Judge,
accusing him of the crime of contempt and negligence.
Then, he bowed at Gāopíng Líng.
Those around him noticed something unusual.
After getting into the carriage,
he said to his attendants:
“The late Emperor just manifested his spirit.”
Since he did not recount what the Emperor said,
the crowd did not know,
but only saw that when he was about to bow, he repeatedly said,
“I dare not,”
and that was all.
He also asked his attendants about Yīn Juān's appearance,
and the respondent said he was fat and short.
Huán Wēn said:
“I also just saw him beside the Emperor.”
Initially,
after Yīn Hào had been deposed and died by Huán Wēn,
Juān had quite some spirit and integrity,
and thus did not visit Huán Wēn,
but associated with Wǔlíng Wáng Xī.
Therefore, Huán Wēn suspected and sought to harm him,
but never actually met him.
At this time,
he also saw Juān as an apparition,
and consequently fell ill.
He stayed in the capital for fourteen days,
then returned to Gūshú,
where he became bedridden and never recovered.
He implicitly urged the court to grant him the Nine Bestowals,
repeatedly pressing the matter.
Xiè Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī, hearing of his grave illness,
secretly delayed the matter.
Before the document of bestowal was completed, he passed away,
aged sixty-two.
The Empress Dowager and the Emperor mourned him in the imperial hall for three days.
An edict bestowed upon him the Nine Commands and court robes,
one set of court attire,
one suit of clothes,
secret instruments from the Eastern Garden,
two million cash,
two thousand bolts of cloth,
and five hundred catties of dried meat,
to be used for the funeral.
At his burial,
everything followed the precedents of Grand Tutor Ānpíng Xiànwáng and Hàn Grand General Huò Guāng,
bestowing a carriage with nine streamers and phoenix-shaped decorations,
a yellow canopy and left banner,
a hearse,
two groups of funeral songs,
feather canopies and drum music,
and one hundred martial retainers with ceremonial swords.
The special imperial decree increased his former title of Duke of Nánjùn by seven thousand five hundred households,
advanced his territory by three hundred *lǐ*,
granted fifty million cash,
twenty thousand bolts of silk,
and one hundred thousand bolts of cloth,
and posthumously appointed him Prime Minister.
Initially,
Chōng asked Huán Wēn about the appointments of Xiè Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī.
Huán Wēn said:
“They will not be managed by you.”
Huán Wēn knew that while he was alive, they would not dare to act differently.
Harming them would not benefit Chōng,
but would instead lose popular support,
which is why he ceased his plans.
Huán Wēn had six sons: Xī, Jì, Xīn, Yī, Wěi, Xuán.
Xī, courtesy name Bódào,
was initially the heir apparent,
but later, due to his weak talent,
Chōng was made to lead his troops.
When Huán Wēn was ill,
Xī conspired with his uncle (Shū, referring to Huán Mì) to kill Chōng.
Chōng learned of this
and moved him to Chángshā.
Jì, courtesy name Zhòngdào,
conspired with Xī and was also moved to Chángshā.
Xīn, courtesy name Shúdào,
was granted the title of Duke of Línghè.
Yī was the most foolish,
unable to distinguish beans from wheat.
Wěi, courtesy name Yòudào,
was gentle, honest, and earnest,
and while serving as a regional official, was cherished by both gentry and commoners.

He successively held the titles of Imperial Commissioner, General-in-Chief supervising military affairs of the five provinces of Jīng, Yì, Níng, Qín, and Liáng, General Pacifying the West, Administrator of Southern Barbarians, Inspector of Jīng Province, and Marquis of Xīchāng.
He was posthumously granted the titles of General of Agile Cavalry and bestowed with the ceremonial rights of the Three Dukes.
Xuán inherited the ducal title;
his biography is separately recorded.
Mèng Jiā, courtesy name Wànnián,
was from Méng, Jiāngxià.
He was the great-grandson of Wú's Grand Chancellor Zōng.
Jiā was well-known in his youth.
When Grand Commandant Yǔ Liàng governed Jiāng Province,
he appointed him as an attendant official for Lúlíng.
When Jiā returned to the capital,
Liàng invited him to inquire about the customs and their advantages and disadvantages.
He replied:
“When I return, I will ask the officials.”
Liàng raised his deer-tail whisk to cover his mouth and laughed,
saying to his younger brother Yì:
“Mèng Jiā is truly a man of great virtue.”
He was then transferred to be an attendant official for promoting learning.
When Chǔ Póu was Governor of Yùzhāng,
he paid respects to Liàng on New Year's Day.
Póu had great discernment.
Liàng hosted a large gathering of provincial officials and gentry.
Jiā was seated quite far away.
Póu asked Liàng:
“I heard there is a Mèng Jiā in Jiāng Province.
Where is that man?”
Liàng said:
“He is seated here.
You may find him yourself.”
Póu looked around
and pointed to Jiā, saying to Liàng:
“This gentleman is a little different.
Might it be him?”
Liàng smiled delightedly,
pleased that Póu had recognized Jiā,
and amazed that Jiā had been recognized by Póu.
Thus, he esteemed him even more.
Later, he became an aide (cānjūn) to Huán Wēn, who was the Generalissimo who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī).
Wēn greatly esteemed him.
On the ninth day of the ninth month,
Wēn held a banquet at Lóngshān.
All his staff and subordinates were assembled.
At that time, the attending officials were all wearing military attire.
A wind came,
blowing Jiā's hat off.
Jiā did not notice it.
Wēn told his attendants not to speak,
wishing to observe his demeanor.
Jiā went to the latrine after a long while.
Wēn ordered it to be retrieved and returned to him,
and commanded Sūn Shèng to write an essay mocking Jiā,
placing it at Jiā's seat.
When Jiā returned and saw it,
he immediately replied to it.
His essay was exceedingly beautiful,
and all present sighed in admiration.
Jiā was fond of heavy drinking;
the more he drank, the less confused he became.
Wēn asked Jiā:
"What is so good about wine,
that you are so addicted to it?"
Jiā replied:
"You, my lord, have not yet grasped the true essence of wine."
He further asked:
"When listening to performers,
strings are not as good as flutes,
and flutes are not as good as voices.
What is the meaning of this?"
Jiā replied:
"It is because they gradually approach the original (nature)."
[一三]All present sighed in wonder.
He was successively transferred to Attendant Gentleman of the Masters of Records (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
and then promoted to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ).
He died at home at the age of fifty-three.
The historian says: Huán Wēn possessed an extraordinary spirit of heroism and power,
and harbored remarkable talents in both civil and military arts.
He was appreciated by discerning people,
and had long earned a good reputation.
At a time when 'wolves and jackals' (rebels) were rampant,
and the borders were filled with anxieties,
he was entrusted with defending the cities,
and used his power and strategy to expand territory.
He then traversed treacherous obstacles,
subdued and pacified Mín'é.
His unique accomplishments
are indeed commendable.
When he advanced his troops to Luòruì,
restored the Five Mausoleums (Wǔ Líng),
led his banners into the suburbs of Qín,
and pacified the Three Auxiliary Regions (Sānfǔ) with his might—
though he could not completely eliminate the fierce rebels,
it was sufficient to demonstrate the sovereign's majesty.
Afterward, he took command of all military power,
and occupied strategically important territories.
He considered his heroic wisdom unparalleled,
and his achievements unsurpassed in his time.
He wielded power that intimidated the sovereign,
and harbored ambitions of disrespecting the ruler.
He longed for Jǐngwén and sighed with emotion,
and thought of Chǔzhòng and wished to emulate him.
He cast a disdainful eye upon the Hàn court,
and coveted the Zhōu tripod (throne).
He further desired to achieve extraordinary merits in Zhào and Wèi,
to truly gain the hopes of both heaven and man;
and then to follow in the footsteps of previous kings,
and emulate Yú and Xià.
But then the Shímén road was blocked,
and his army at Xiāngyì was crushed.
He resented the failure of his strategies,
and was ashamed of his army's defeat.
He vented his anger on the imperial court,
and blamed his subordinate generals.
He deposed the emperor to establish his authority,
and killed people to satisfy his desires.
He did not even know that a precious mandate (for the throne) cannot be sought by force,
and the divine implement (the empire) cannot be seized by strength.
Is this not perverse!
Is this not perverse!
This indeed is what the executioner's axe (fǔyuè) should be applied to,
and what both men and gods abandon.
Yet, he lived to enjoy extreme favor and honor,
and after death received mournful glory.
From this, one knows that the imperial administration was without order,
and the emperor's authority was not established.
The encomium says: Spreading out along the Jiāngfén,
the government was weak and power divided.
Yuánzǐ relied on strength,
Chǔzhòng boasted of achievements.
His conduct was defiant towards superiors,
and his ambition was to disregard the ruler.
His crimes surpassed those of Zhuó[gē],
his heart coveted Shùn and Yǔ.
He established his authority through foreign conquest,
and waged war and insulted internally.
Both he and his descendants,
ultimately suffered the 'Qí axe' (execution).
Collation Notes
Biography Sixty-Nine: Huán Xuán
Huán Xuán, courtesy name Jìngdào,
also known as Língbǎo, was the illegitimate son of Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) Wēn.
His mother, Lady Mǎ, once sat at night with her peers.
Under the moonlight, they saw a meteor fall into a bronze basin of water,
suddenly appearing like a two-inch fire pearl,
glowing brightly and clearly.
They competed to scoop it up with gourds.
Lady Mǎ obtained it and swallowed it,
feeling as if she had conceived.
She then became pregnant.
When Xuán was born,
a light shone in the room.
The diviner found it extraordinary,
hence his infant name was Língbǎo.
The nursemaid always brought him to Wēn,
but would always change to a different person before arriving,
claiming that he was unusually heavy for a child.
Wēn greatly loved and marveled at him.
Before his death,
Wēn designated him as his heir,
and he inherited the title of Duke of Nánjùn.
When he was seven years old,
Wēn's mourning period ended.
The civil and military officials of the government and prefecture bade farewell to his uncle, Chōng.
Chōng patted Xuán's head and said:
"These are your family's former officials."
Xuán then shed tears that covered his face,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
When he grew up,
his appearance was remarkable,
and his demeanor was open and grand.
He was extensively knowledgeable in various arts,
and skilled at writing essays.
He often prided himself on his talent and background,
considering himself a powerful hero.
Everyone feared him,
and the imperial court was also suspicious and had not yet employed him.
At the age of twenty-three,
he was first appointed Crown Prince's Household Administrator (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
At the time, public opinion held that Wēn had rebellious tendencies,
hence Xuán and his brothers were demoted to ordinary officials.
At the end of the Tàiyuán era,
he was sent out to serve as Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu),
feeling dejected and unsuccessful.
He once ascended a height and gazed upon Zhènzé,
sighing:
"My father was the Hegemon of the Nine Provinces,
my son is a 'chief' (long) of the Five Lakes!"
He abandoned his office and returned home.
Considering himself from a family of great merits yet slandered by the world,
he then submitted a memorial stating: Your servant has heard that Dùkegōng, though a great sage, was slandered by the Four States;
Yuè Yì, though a king's assistant, was slandered by Qíjié.
Hàngbó had the sorrow of being like a jackal,
Sūgōng stirred up 'whirlwind'
satires.
Hating the upright and reviling the righteous—
which era has been without it!
My late father received extraordinary favor from the state,
and was related by marriage to the imperial family.
He always wished to repay this kindness with his life,
seizing opportunities to act.
He pacified Bashǔ in the west,
and cleared Yīluò in the north,
causing the usurping rebels to be executed at the Northern Gate (Běi Què),
the imperial tombs to be restored,
and great shame to be washed away.
He watered his horses at Bà and Chǎn,
and displayed his banners in Zhào and Wèi.
His efforts
to support the king
were not just a single victory.
At the end of the Tàihé era,
the imperial foundation faced the fear of being secretly shifted.
He then respectfully followed Heaven and men,
and assisted in establishing the holy dynasty.
When the bright separation (of chaos and order) became clear,
the Four Villains (Sì Xiōng) were also pacified.
Had this achievement not been made,
and this matter not been accomplished,
how could the affairs of the imperial ancestral temple (Zōngmiào) have been considered (safe)!
In the past, although Tàijiǎ was deluded,
the Shāng dynasty's fate was not imperiled;
though Chāng[yì] was ignorant,
the harm (to the Hàn) was not as severe as the three usurpations.
From this perspective,
the Jìn dynasty's crisis was more perilous than those of Yīn and Hàn,
and my late father's achievements were greater than those of Yī and Huò.
Yet, after undertaking such a heavy responsibility,
he incurred slander in a clear era.
The way of promoting and demoting in a holy age and by enlightened kings
does not involve discarding and neglecting obvious achievements,
probing hidden motives,
opening the path to suspicion and slander,
and starting
or the path of wickedness and perversion.
My late father's arduous and difficult efforts in supporting the emperor,
and his achievements in restoring and pacifying the realm,
if the imperial court should forget them,
I, your subject, will not count them again either.
As for the late emperor ascending to the throne,
and Your Majesty's succession to rule as emperor,
I ask those who speak,
by whose doing was this?
By whose virtue was this?
It is not only that the Jìn
house would enjoy eternal peace,
and the ancestors would continue to receive sacrifices,
but for Your Majesty's family,
it was truly an extraordinary achievement.
Recently, powerful families have grown daily,
and ugly policies have truly proliferated.
All praise and endorse the current imperial will,
mutually fanning and attaching themselves to each other.
They say that my brothers are all criminals of Jìn,
so how can I
and my like still have any reason to barely survive in this sacred era?
What face can we have to occupy and enjoy official salaries and emoluments?
If Your Majesty forgets the great achievements of my late father,
and believes the slanderous
words,
I and my like will naturally return our three封 (fēng, a type of official remuneration)
and be executed in the market or court,
and then follow our late father,
returning the late emperor to the dark palace.
If Your Majesty follows and observes the former
imperial decrees,
and recalls old merits,
I secretly hope you will extend a little kindness and protective grace.
The memorial was sent but not answered.
Huán Xuán stayed in Jīngchǔ for many years,
living a leisurely and uneventful life.
Yīn Zhòngkān, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, greatly respected and feared him.
When Wáng Guóbǎo, the Minister of the Central Secretariat, gained power,
and plotted to weaken the regional commanders,
the interior and exterior were disturbed.
Knowing that Wáng Gōng had expressed concern for the state,
Huán Xuán secretly harbored ambitions for achievements,
and so he persuaded Zhòngkān, saying:
"Guóbǎo and you and your associates have long been rivals,
fearing only that you would not be harmed quickly enough.
Now that he holds crucial power,
and is aligned with Wáng Xù as his inner and outer support,
whatever he changes,
nothing fails to go as he wishes.
Xiàobó occupies the position of the emperor's maternal uncle,
and his uprightness is valued by both court and commoners,
so he will certainly not be moved immediately.
You alone will be made the primary target.
You were promoted by the late emperor,
soaring into a regional post,
but people are not convinced,
all saying that although you have profound thoughts,
you are not a man for a regional governorship.
If an imperial edict is issued to summon you as Minister of the Central Secretariat,
and Yīn Yǐ is appointed as Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
how will you deal with it?"
Zhòngkān said:
"I have been worried about this for a long time.
What do you think is the best plan?"
Huán Xuán said:
"Guóbǎo's treachery and villainy
are known throughout the realm.
Xiàobó's righteous indignation against evil is always timely and accurate.
In this present situation,
reasoning from principle,
he will certainly surpass others.
If you secretly send someone,
with a letter persuading Wáng Gōng,
that it is fitting to raise the army of Jìnyáng,
to rectify the imperial court from within,
then I will lead all the troops of Jīngchǔ downstream,
proclaim Wáng Gōng as the alliance leader,
and we and others will also throw up our sleeves in support.
There will be no one who does not respond.
If this matter is carried out,
it will be an achievement like that of Huán Wén."
Zhòngkān was hesitant and undecided.
Shortly after, Wáng Gōng's letter arrived,
inviting Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán to rectify the imperial court.
After Guóbǎo's death,
the armies were then disbanded.
Huán Xuán then sought to be appointed as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Wáng Dàozǐ, Prince of Kuàijī, also feared him,
and did not want him to be in Jīngchǔ,
so he complied with his wish.
In the early years of Lóng'ān,
an edict appointed Huán Xuán as Supervisor of Jiāo and Guǎng two prefectures, General Who Establishes Might, Commander of the Southern Man, Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, and Granted Imperial Authority.
Huán Xuán accepted the appointment but did not go.
In that year,
Wáng Gōng again raised an army with Yǔ Kǎi to attack Wáng Yú, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, and the brothers Wáng Shàngzhī, Prince of Qiáo.
Huán Xuán and Zhòngkān believed that Gōng's endeavor would certainly succeed,
and they responded at once.
Zhòngkān gave Huán Xuán five thousand men,
and he and Yáng Quánqī together served as the vanguard.
When the army reached Pénkǒu,
Wáng Yú fled to Línchuān.
Huán Xuán sent a partial general to pursue and capture him.
Huán Xuán and Quánqī reached Shítou,
and Zhòngkān reached Wúhú.
Gōng's general, Liú Láozhī, betrayed Gōng and defected.
After Gōng's death,
Yǔ Kǎi was defeated in battle
and fled to Huán Xuán's army.
Afterwards, an edict appointed Huán Xuán as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
and Zhòngkān and others were all replaced.
So they each returned their boats westward,
garrisoned at Xúnyáng,
made a pact together,
and proclaimed Huán Xuán as their alliance leader.
Huán Xuán finally achieved his ambition,
and then jointly memorialized to vindicate Wáng Gōng,
requesting the execution of Shàngzhī, Láozhī, and others.
The imperial court deeply feared him,
and so dismissed Huán Xiū and reinstated Zhòngkān to reconcile.
Previously,
when Huán Xuán was in Jīngzhōu, he was arrogant and unrestrained.
The gentry and commoners feared him
even more than the provincial governor.
Zhòngkān's close associates urged him to kill Huán Xuán,
but Zhòngkān did not listen.
Upon returning to Xúnyáng,
relying on his reputation and status,
they therefore proclaimed him alliance leader.
Huán Xuán became even more self-important.
Quánqī was arrogant and fierce,
often considering himself to be of noble lineage,
unmatched in the Jiāngbiǎo region.
But Huán Xuán always treated him as a humble scholar,
which Quánqī greatly resented.
He immediately wanted to ambush Huán Xuán at the altar.
Zhòngkān feared the fierceness of Quánqī and his brothers,
and was concerned that after overcoming Huán Xuán, they would again harm him,
so he strenuously forbade it.
Thereupon, each returned to their garrisons according to the imperial edict.
Huán Xuán also knew that Quánqī had other intentions,
and secretly harbored a plan of annexation.
So he garrisoned at Xiàkǒu.
During the Lóng'ān period,
an edict added Huán Xuán as Supervisor of the four prefectures of Jīngzhōu,
and his elder brother Wěi as General Who Aids the State and Commander of the Southern Man.
Zhòngkān feared Huán Xuán's unruliness,
and so married his daughter to Quánqī's son as an alliance.
Previously,
Huán Xuán, having already had a rift with Zhòngkān and Quánqī,
feared a surprise attack, and sought to expand his jurisdiction.
The imperial court also wished to exacerbate their conflict,
so they divided the four prefectures supervised by Quánqī and gave them to Huán Xuán,
which greatly angered and frightened Quánqī.
It happened that Yáo Xīng invaded Luòyáng.
Quánqī then set up his battle flag,
claiming to be reinforcing Luòyáng,
but secretly intending to attack Huán Xuán with Zhòngkān.
Although Zhòngkān outwardly allied with Quánqī, he doubted his intentions,
resisted and did not consent.
Still fearing he could not restrain him,
he again sent his cousin Yù to garrison the northern border to block Quánqī.
Since Quánqī could not act alone,
and did not understand Zhòngkān's true intentions,
he consequently ceased military action.
Yáng Guǎng, Commander of the Southern Man,
who was Quánqī's elder brother,
wanted to resist Huán Wěi,
but Zhòngkān did not permit it.
So he sent Guǎng out as Administrator of Yídu and Jiànpíng two prefectures,
and added General Who Conquers Barbarians.
Quánqī's younger brother, Zījìng, was formerly the Chancellor of Jiāngxià.
Huán Xuán attacked him with troops and summoned him.
When he arrived,
he made him Consultant Aide-de-camp.
Huán Xuán then raised an army for a western expedition,
also claiming to be rescuing Luòyáng.
He wrote to Zhòngkān,
stating that Quánqī had received imperial favor but abandoned the imperial tombs,
and they should jointly condemn him.
He was now personally leading his army,
proceeding directly to Jīnyōng,
and asked Zhòngkān to arrest Yáng Guǎng.
If not,
there would be no way for them to trust each other.
Zhòngkān's original plan was to keep both sides intact.
After receiving Huán Xuán's letter,
he knew he could not forbid him,
so he said:
"You may travel from Miǎn,
but not a single person is allowed to enter the Jiāng River."
Huán Xuán then stopped.
Later, a great flood occurred in Jīngzhōu.
Zhòngkān distributed relief to the starving,
emptying the granaries.
Xuán took advantage of this weakness and attacked him,
first sending troops to raid Bālíng.
The governor of Liángzhōu, Guō Quán, was to hold the place he was garrisoned at.
Passing through Xiàkǒu,
Xuán proclaimed that the imperial court had sent Quán to be his vanguard.
He then entrusted him with the forces of Jiāngxià,
ordering him to lead the various armies and advance together.
He secretly informed his elder brother Wěi to act as an inside supporter.
Wěi, in a panic, did not know what to do,
so he personally took the secret message and showed it to Zhòngkān.
Zhòngkān seized Wěi as a hostage,
and made him write a letter to Xuán,
the words of which were very bitter and heartfelt.
Xuán said:
"Zhòngkān is a person who cannot make decisive judgments,
always harboring thoughts of success or failure,
and worrying for his son.
My brother will certainly be safe."
When Xuán reached Bālíng,
Zhòngkān sent troops to resist him,
but they were defeated by Xuán.
Xuán advanced to Yángkǒu,
and again defeated Zhòngkān's nephew, Dàohù.
Riding on his victory, he reached Língkǒu,
twenty *lǐ* from Jiānglíng.
Zhòngkān dispatched troops along several routes to resist him.
Quánqī came from Xiāngyáng to assist,
and together with his elder brother Guǎng, attacked Xuán.
Xuán, fearing their sharpness,
withdrew his army to Mǎtóu.
Quánqī and others then pursued Xuán and fought fiercely.
Quánqī was defeated
and fled back to Xiāngyáng.
Zhòngkān fled to Cuōchéng.
Xuán sent his general Féng Gāi to pursue Quánqī,
and captured him.
Guǎng was captured by someone,
sent to Xuán,
and both were killed.
Zhòngkān heard of Quánqī's death,
and with a few hundred men, fled to Yáo Xīng.
Upon reaching Guānjūnchéng,
he was captured by Gāi.
Xuán ordered him killed.
Thus, he pacified Jīng and Yōng.
He then submitted a memorial requesting to govern Jiāng and Jīng prefectures.

An imperial edict appointed Xuán as Grand Administrator of the seven prefectures of Jīng, Sī, Yōng, Qín, Liáng, Yì, and Níng, General of the Rear, Governor of Jīngzhōu, and Bearer of the Imperial Staff.
Huán Xiū was made Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Xuán sent a memorial firmly arguing for Jiāngzhōu.
Thereupon, he was promoted to Grand Administrator of eight prefectures and eight commanderies of Yáng and Yù,
and again held the post of Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Xuán also unilaterally appointed Wěi as General of the Guards and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
At that time, bandits had not yet been pacified,
and the court found it difficult to go against his wishes,
so they permitted it.
Xuán then promoted his confidants,
and his military strength grew daily.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to suppress Sūn Ēn,
but the imperial edicts consistently refused.
Later, Ēn threatened the capital.
Xuán established his banner and gathered troops,
outwardly claiming to support the emperor,
but in reality wishing to observe the opportune moment to advance.
He again submitted a memorial requesting to suppress him.
By then, Ēn had already fled.
Xuán again received an imperial edict to lift the alert.
He appointed Wěi as Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
stationed at Xiàkǒu;
his Administrator Diāo Chàng as General Who Guards the State,
overseeing eight commanderies,
stationed at Xiāngyáng;
and sent Huán Zhèn, Huángfǔ Fū, Féng Gāi, and others to garrison Pénkǒu.
He moved two thousand households of Jǔzhāng Mán to the south of the Yangtze River,
and established Wǔníng Commandery.
He further recruited and gathered displaced people,
establishing Suī'ān Commandery.
He also established commandery assistant posts.
Imperial edicts summoned the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Diāo Kuí, and the Administrator of Yùzhāng, Guō Chǎngzhī.
Xuán kept them both and did not send them.
He considered himself to possess two-thirds of the realm,
knowing where the mandate of heaven lay,
and repeatedly presented auspicious signs as omens for himself.
Originally,
after Yǔ Kǎi had fled to Xuán,
when Xuán sought to suppress Sūn Ēn,
he made Kǎi General of the Right.
After Xuán lifted the alert,
Kǎi also resigned his post.
Kǎi believed that Xuán was now in conflict with the imperial court,
and feared that if the undertaking failed, disaster would befall him.
So he secretly colluded with the General of the Rear, Yuán Xiǎn,
promising to be an inside supporter.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
Yuán Xiǎn, claiming an imperial edict, attacked Xuán.
Xuán's cousin, Shí Shēng, who was then Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor,
secretly sent a letter to Xuán to inform him.
Xuán originally thought that with famine in Yángtǔ,
and Sūn Ēn not yet suppressed,
they would certainly not have time to attack him.
He could accumulate strength and gather troops,
and act when the opportunity arose.
When he heard that Yuán Xiǎn was going to attack him,
he was very afraid
and wanted to secure Jiānglíng.
His Chief Clerk, Biàn Fànzhī, advised Xuán:
"Your Excellency's heroic strategy and formidable reputation shake the world.
Yuán Xiǎn still has milk on his breath,
and Liú Láozhī has greatly lost public support.
If your army approaches the capital,
and you display your might and offer rewards,
then the collapse of the enemy can be awaited on tiptoe.
Why invite the enemy into your territory and weaken yourself?"
Xuán was greatly pleased,
and so he left his elder brother Wěi to guard Jiānglíng,
submitted a memorial, and led his troops
down to Xúnyáng.
He sent a manifesto to the capital,
denouncing Yuán Xiǎn's crimes.
When the manifesto arrived,
Yuán Xiǎn was greatly frightened
and boarded a ship but could not set off.
Xuán had lost popular support,
and by raising an army against the legitimate government,
he feared his troops would not be used,
and considered turning back.
However, after passing Xúnyáng
and seeing no imperial army,
he was very pleased,
and his generals and officials also took heart.
Yǔ Kǎi's plot was exposed,
and he was arrested and imprisoned.
Upon reaching Gūshú,
he ordered his generals Féng Gāi, Fú Hóng, Huángfǔ Fū, Suǒ Yuán, and others to first attack Prince Shàngzhī of Qiáo.
Shàngzhī was defeated.
Liú Láozhī sent his son, Jìngxuān, to Xuán to surrender.
When Xuán reached Xīntíng,
Yuán Xiǎn's forces disintegrated on their own.
Xuán entered the capital
and issued a forged imperial edict saying:
"The righteous banners have gathered like clouds;
the fault lies with Yuán Xiǎn.
The Grand Tutor has already issued a separate instruction;
you should lift the alert and sheathe your weapons,
to align with the righteous cause."
He also issued a forged imperial edict adding himself to oversee all state affairs,
as Imperial Household Grandee, Grand Administrator of all military affairs at home and abroad, Chancellor, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Governor of Yángzhōu,
and concurrently Governor of Xúzhōu.
He was also granted the Yellow Battle-axe, Feathered Canopy and Military Band, twenty Swordsmen-in-Attendance,
and was allowed to appoint Left and Right Chief Clerks, Administrators, and four Palace Gentlemen Attendants,
with two hundred armed guards allowed to ascend the hall.
Xuán listed the wickedness of Grand Tutor Dàozǐ and Yuán Xiǎn in a memorial,
exiled Dàozǐ to Ānchéng Commandery,
and executed Yuán Xiǎn in the marketplace.
Thereupon, Xuán moved into the Grand Tutor's mansion
and killed the Grand Tutor's Chief Clerk Máo Tài,

Tài's younger brother, the General of the Elite Cavalry Suì, Grand Tutor's Military Advisor Xún Xùn, former Governor of Yùzhōu Yǔ Kǎi and his son, Ministry of Personnel Director Yuán Zūn, Prince Shàngzhī of Qiáo, and others.

He exiled Shàngzhī's younger brother, the Administrator of Dānyáng Huīzhī, the Earl of Guǎngjìn Yǔnzhī, the Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry Wáng Dàn, and the Grand Tutor's Registrar Máo Dùn, and others to various commanderies in Jiāo and Guǎng.
Soon after, Huīzhī and Yǔnzhī were pursued and killed on the road.
He appointed his elder brother Wěi as General of the Pacified West and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and concurrently Colonel of the Southern Man.
His cousin Qiān was made Left Director of the Imperial Secretariat, additionally General of the Central Army, and concurrently Director of Elections.
Xiū was made General of the Right and Governor of Xú and Yǎn prefectures.
Shí Shēng was made General of the Vanguard and Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Chief Clerk Biàn Fànzhī was made General Who Establishes Might and Administrator of Dānyáng.
Wáng Mì was made Minister of the Central Secretariat and General of the Army.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Dàhēng.
Xuán declined the position of Chancellor,
and appointed himself Grand Commandant, concurrently General Who Pacifies the West and Governor of Yùzhōu.
He was also granted the ceremonial robes and crown,
a green sash,
increased the Swordsmen-in-Attendance to sixty,
was allowed to wear swords and shoes into the palace,
not required to hurry when entering court,
and his name was not to be uttered when announcing memorials.
Xuán was about to move out to Gūshú
and consulted with his officials.
Wáng Mì replied:
"The *Gōngyáng Commentary* says,
'Why did Duke Zhōu not go to Lǔ?
He wished the world to be unified under Zhōu.'
I wish you to stabilize the foundation
and take Duke Dàn as your model."
Xuán approved of his reply but could not follow it.
He then undertook large-scale construction of his mansion,
with pavilions, towers, mountains, and ponds, all magnificent.
Then he moved his garrison there.
Upon arriving at Gūshú,
he firmly declined the position of Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
The imperial edict granted his request,
but all major state affairs were still referred to him,
while minor matters were decided by Huán Qiān and Biàn Fànzhī.
Initially,
Huán Xuán feared that the Emperor would not be willing to issue a handwritten edict,
and also worried that the imperial seal could not be obtained.
He coerced Línchuān Wáng Bǎo to ask the Emperor to personally write a decree,
and then seized the seal.
By the time he approached the main hall,
the seal had already been taken out a long time ago.
Huán Xuán was greatly pleased.
All the officials went to Gūshú to persuade Huán Xuán to usurp the throne.
Huán Xuán feigned refusal,
but the court officials insisted.
Huán Xuán then established a suburban altar seven *lǐ* south of the city,
ascended the altar, and usurped the throne,
announcing it to Heaven with a black ox.
All the officials were present,
but the ceremonial procedures were incomplete;
they forgot to shout "Long live the Emperor!"
and did not change the Emperor's taboo name.
The proclamation he issued to Heaven and the Empress Dowager stated:
"The Jìn Emperor, reverently complying with the auspicious destiny,
respectfully follows the bright mandate,
thereby bestowing it upon Huán Xuán.
Indeed, Heaven works through human agents,
which is why emperors arise.
Without a ruler, there can be no governance;
only virtue presides over the beginning.
Therefore, to receive Heaven's will and manage all things,
there must be a unified rule.
Two saints cannot coexist as two rulers,
nor can a state be without a wise lord.
Thus, the ages saw five emperors change,
and the cauldrons shift for three dynasties.
Coming down to the Hàn and Wèi,
all returned to those of merit and renown.
Since the middle period of the Jìn,
generations have been fraught with trouble.
During the chaos of Hǎixī,
the imperial lineage was almost overthrown.
The achievements of restoring peace for nine generations,
and the merits of elevating the enlightened and demoting the unworthy,
without the virtue of Yǔ,
we would soon be wearing the lapel to the left (barbarian dress).
At the end of Tàiyuán,
the way of the noble declined,
accumulating grievances and founding chaos.
Culminating in Lóng'ān,
disaster spread to scholars and commoners,
and human relations were utterly severed.
Though Huán Xuán was in the wilderness,
rejected by the ranks of the time,
his righteous feelings were stirred;
how could he not lament?
The effort of rising to quell the unrest,
the achievement of Áhéng in restoring order,
all relied on the benefit of the former virtuous ones' lingering love.
What merit did Huán Xuán have?
It happened to be a convergence of destined rule,
and the multitude of willingly supportive people gathered.
With my humble and ignorant self, I follow the weighty responsibility of the later martial kings,
receiving the beginning of change and renewal,
placed above kings and dukes.
Indeed, I rely on a grand foundation,
and the spread of virtue has its reasons.
I am mindful with trepidation from dawn till dusk,
knowing not where to place myself.
The position of ruler cannot be long vacant,
nor can the gods and people lack sacrifices.
Therefore, I dare not but respectfully accept with great ceremony,
and reverently choose an auspicious day
to ascend the altar and receive the abdication,
announcing and sacrificing to the Supreme Emperor,
to eternally pacify the hopes of the multitude,
and thereby gain the trust of all nations.
May the bright spirits accept this sacrifice."
Then he issued a decree saying:
"Indeed, the three powers (Heaven, Earth, Man) mutually assist each other;
this is how Heaven and Man achieve success.
Reason proceeds from a unified system;
this is how the *zhēnfū* presides over the contracts.
The rise of emperors,
its source is profound.
Since the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
generations have varied,
though the paths taken may differ,
their ultimate destination is one.
My imperial father, Xuānwǔ Wáng, possessed lofty sacred virtue,
and grandly initiated a great foundation.
The auspicious mandate converged,
and the principle has been consistent since ancient times.
In the interim, through difficulties and perils,
I was unable to bear the burden.
Looking up at the grand undertaking,
it was almost like a hanging banner about to fall.
By virtue of the turning point of misfortune,
I encountered the opportune moment,
thus able to eliminate villains and save the drowning,
rescuing human relations.
The Jìn clan, with numerous difficulties successively arriving,
its cosmic number was exhausted.
Following the standards of Táng and Yú in statutes and regulations,
and adhering to the precedents of Hàn and Wèi,
Heaven's bounty has been gathered upon my person.
Though my virtue is not keen,
I cannot decline the mandate.
Consulting the excellent precedents,
I thereupon ascended the altar and offered burnt offerings in the southern suburb,
receiving the end of the dynasty from Wénzǔ.
I desire to extend this joy widely,
and wish to begin anew with the myriad people."
Thereupon, a great amnesty was proclaimed,
the era name was changed to Yǒngshǐ,
two ranks of nobility were bestowed upon all under Heaven,
three ranks upon filial, fraternal, and industrious farmers,
and five *hú* of grain upon the widowed, solitary, orphaned, and infirm who could not support themselves.
However, the system of rewards and gifts
was merely an empty formality,
without actual implementation.
When the false edict was first issued,
the year was changed to Jiànshǐ.
The Right Chancellor Wáng Yōuzhī said:
"Jiànshǐ
was the false reign title of Zhào Wáng Lún."
It was then changed to Yǒngshǐ,
which again was the year Wáng Mǎng first seized power.
Its initial reign title was inauspicious,
thus perfectly matching the usurpation.
He further issued a decree saying:
"Indeed, the 'three reverent guests' serving as vassals
has a long history.
Coming down to the Hàn and Wèi,
they all established their territories.
The Jìn clan, reverently complying with the cosmic number,
has abdicated the throne to my person.
It is fitting to follow ancient teachings
and bestow upon them this territory.
The county of Pínggù in Nánkāng was offered to the Jìn Emperor, who was enfeoffed as Pínggù Wáng.
His carriages, banners, and calendar were all to be as in the old system."
He moved the Emperor to reside in Xúnyáng,
following the precedent of Chénliú Wáng in Yègōng.
Empress Yǒng'ān was demoted to Línglíng Jūn,
Lángyá Wáng to Shíyáng Xiàn Gōng,
and Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn to Péngzé Xiàn Hóu.
He posthumously honored his father Wēn as Xuānwǔ Huángdì,
his ancestral temple was called Tàimiào,
and Princess Nánkāng as Xuān Huánghòu.
He enfeoffed his son Shēng as Yùzhāng Jùn Wáng,
his paternal uncle Yún Sūn Fàngzhī as Níngdū Xiàn Wáng,
Hūo Sūn Zhìyù as Línyuán Xiàn Wáng,
Hūo's second son Shíkāng as Right General and Wǔlíng Jùn Wáng,
Mì's son Wèi as Lǐlíng Xiàn Wáng.
He posthumously appointed Chōng as Grand Tutor and Xuānchéng Jùn Wáng,
with special funerary rites,
following the precedent of Jìn's Ānpíng Wáng.
His grandson Yìn succeeded to the title
and was made Minister of Personnel.
Chōng's second son Qiān was made Governor of Yángzhōu and Xīn'ān Jùn Wáng.
Qiān's younger brother Xiū was made Grand General of the Garrison and Ānchéng Jùn Wáng.
His older brother Xīn was made Línhé Xiàn Wáng,
Yī was made Fùyáng Xiàn Wáng.
He posthumously appointed Wěi as Attendant-in-Chief, Grand General, and Yìxīng Jùn Wáng,
with his son Jùn succeeding to the title
and made General Who Upholds the State.
Jùn's younger brother Miǎo was made Xīchāng Xiàn Wáng.
He enfeoffed Wáng Mì as Wǔchāng Gōng,
with twenty armed guards,
Biàn Fànzhī as Línrǔ Gōng,
Yīn Zhòngwén as Dōngxīng Gōng,
and Féng Gāi as Yúfù Hóu.
He also demoted Shǐ'ān Jùn Gōng to Xiàn Gōng,
Chángshā to Línxiāng Xiàn Gōng,
Lúlín to Bāqiū Xiàn Gōng,
each with a thousand households.
Kānglè, Wǔchāng, Nánchāng, Wàngcài, Jiànxīng, Yǒngxiū, and Guānyáng were all demoted to enfeoffments of one hundred households,
but their titles of Duke and Marquis remained unchanged.
He also generally promoted the military titles of various commanders, with varying degrees.
He appointed the Grand Chancellor's Left Chief Clerk, Wáng Suí, as Central Secretariat Director.
He honored Huán Qiān's mother, Lady Yǔ, as Grand Consort of Xuānchéng,
bestowing special rites
and providing her with a carriage.
Wēn's tomb was named Yǒngchóng Líng,
and forty guards were stationed there.
Huán Xuán entered the Jiànkāng Palace.
A headwind blew fiercely,
causing all the banners and ceremonial decorations to lean and fall.
When he held a small gathering at the Western Hall,
entertainers and musicians were arranged.
Scarlet silk curtains were hung in the hall,
with gold threads woven into facial features,
and golden dragons at the four corners.
Their heads bore five-colored feathered canopies and streamers.
The officials whispered among themselves, saying:
"This somewhat resembles a carriage;
it's in the same vein as Wáng Mǎng's Immortal Canopies.
Dragon horns
are what is meant by 'the arrogant dragon has regrets'."
He also had a golden-wheeled carriage made,
drawn by six horses.
That month,
Huán Xuán personally oversaw judicial hearings and inspected prisoners.
Regardless of the severity of their crimes,
many were pardoned and released.
If there were those who begged from palanquins,
he would sometimes show them compassion.
His habit of performing such small acts of kindness was like this.
Believing himself to be of Water virtue,
on the *rénchén* day,
he performed the Lâ ceremony to his ancestors.
He changed the title of the Director of the Dūguān Department of the Imperial Secretariat to 'Thief Officer',
and also increased the number of Five Commanders, Three Generals, and the officers of the Strong Crossbowmen and Massed Archers Imperial Guards.
In the third year of Yuánxīng,
which was the second year of Huán Xuán's Yǒngshǐ era,
the Imperial Secretariat replied
with the character "蒐" (*sōu*, hunt)
mistakenly written as "菟" (*tú*, rabbit),
for "Spring Hunt".
All those involved in the signature were demoted.
Huán Xuán failed to manage major affairs,
yet he meticulously scrutinized minute details,
all of which were of this nature.
He appointed his wife, Lady Liú, as empress.
Intending to renovate the palace buildings,
he then moved into the Eastern Palace.
He also opened the Dōngyè, Píngchāng, Guǎngmò gates and other palace gates,
all of which had three passages.
He further constructed a grand palanquin
that could seat thirty people,
and required two hundred men to carry it.
He was fond of hunting and excursions,
but his large physique prevented him from riding horses.
So he also created a 'wandering palanquin' (*páihuái yú*)
with revolving mechanisms,
allowing it to turn without obstruction.
Since he had not posthumously honored his great-grandparents and grandparents,
he questioned the proper rituals
among his officials.
Xú Guǎng, the Palace Attendant, citing the Jin Dynasty's precedents, suggested that seven ancestral temples should be established,
and that honoring one's father brings joy to the son;
the higher one's position, the more one's feelings can be expressed,
and the wider one's influence, the more universal the reverence received.
Huán Xuán said:
"The Rites say 'three zhāo, three mù',
which, with the Grand Ancestor, makes seven.
Then the Grand Ancestor must occupy the main position in the temple.
Zhāo and mù are both terms for those of lower status,
so it is clear that they do not count in reverse order.
According to the Rites,
the Grand Ancestor faces east, with zhāo on the left and mù on the right.
If, in the temples of the Jìn imperial house,
Emperor Xuān were among the zhāo-mù ranks,
he could not be in the position of Grand Ancestor.
If zhāo and mù are thus confused,
and the Grand Ancestor has no place,
the error is profound."
Huán Xuán's great-grandparents and earlier ancestors did not have prominent positions,
so he did not wish to list them.
Moreover, as Wáng Mǎng's nine temples had been criticized by previous historians,
he therefore countered it with a single temple,
and the suburban and ancestral temple fasts lasted only two days.
Biàn Chéngzhī, the Director of the Imperial Library, said:
"Failing to offer sacrifices up to one's ancestors,
one knows that the virtue of Chǔ will not last long."
He also demolished the small Jìn temples to expand his terraces.
His sacrifices to his secondary mother had no fixed place.
On the death anniversary, he received guests and indulged in feasts,
only weeping once at the moment of death.
Within the year of mourning,
music was not abandoned.
When Huán Xuán went out to visit the Shuǐmén,
a strong gust of wind blew away his ceremonial canopy.
That night,
tidal waters entered Shítou,
the Dàhéng Bridge was swept away and damaged,
killing many people.
A great wind blew down the Zhūquè Gate tower,
its upper level crashing to the ground.
Since Huán Xuán's usurpation,
he became arrogant, extravagant, and wasteful.
His hunting and excursions were limitless,
continuing from night into day.
On the day of his brother Wěi's funeral,
he wept in the morning and roamed in the evening,
sometimes galloping out several times within a single day.
His temperament was also quick-tempered and violent;
his summons were strict and urgent.
Officials on duty all tied their horses in front of the provincial office.
Inside the forbidden palace, there was noisy disorder,
and no longer the decorum of a court.
Consequently, the common people were weary and suffering,
the court and country exhausted,
and eight or nine out of ten households were resentful and longing for rebellion.
Thereupon, Liú Yù, Liú Yì, Hé Wúgì, and others conspired together to launch a restoration.
Yù and his group executed Huán Xiū at Jīngkǒu,
and Huán Hóng at Guǎnglín.
Xīn Hùxīng, Administrator of Hénèi, Wáng Yuándé, Administrator of Hóngnóng, Tóng Hòuzhī, General Manifesting Awe, and Liú Mài, Administrator of Jìnglíng, planned to act as internal supporters.
At the appointed time,
Yù dispatched Zhōu Ānmù to inform them.
However, Mài became flustered
and consequently reported it to Huán Xuán.
Huán Xuán was shocked and terrified,
and immediately executed Hùxīng and others.
Ānmù galloped away and escaped.
Mài was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chóng'ān,
but was killed after only one night.
Yù led the righteous army to Zhúlǐ.
Huán Xuán moved back to the Upper Palace,
with all officials following on foot,
and summoned all court attendants to stay in the provincial office.
He issued a general amnesty for the six provinces of Yáng, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì.
He promoted Huán Qiān to Commander-in-Chief of Expeditions and granted him *jiǎjié* authority.
He replaced Huán Xiū with Yīn Zhòngwén,
and dispatched Wú Fǔzhī, Administrator of Dùnqiu, and Huángfǔ Fū, Right Guard General, to confront the righteous army in the north.
Yù and his group engaged them in battle at Jiāngchéng,
beheading Fǔzhī on the battlefield.
They advanced to Luóluò Bridge
and battled Fū,
again capturing his head.
Huán Xuán heard of this and was greatly alarmed.
He then summoned various Daoist practitioners to calculate omens and perform rituals for averting evil.
He then asked the assembly:
"Will I be defeated?"
Cáo Jìngzhī replied:
"The gods are angry, and the people are resentful.
Your subject is truly afraid."
Huán Xuán said:
"People may be resentful,
but why would the gods be angry?"
He replied:
"The Jìn imperial ancestral temples were moved,
left to drift without a proper place.
The sacrifices of Great Chǔ
do not reach the ancestors.
This is why they are angry."
Huán Xuán said:
"Why did you not remonstrate?"
He replied:
"All the gentlemen in the imperial carriage
believed it to be like the era of Yáo and Shùn.
How dared your subject speak!"
Huán Xuán became even more furious and fearful.
He ordered Huán Qiān and Hé Dànzhī to station at Dōnglíng,
and Biàn Fànzhī to station west of Fùzhōushān,
with a combined force of twenty thousand
to resist the righteous army.
When Yù reached Jiǎngshān,
he sent the weaker soldiers, clad in oilskin cloaks, to climb the mountains,
spreading out flags and banners,
advancing along several routes simultaneously.
Huán Xuán's scouts returned, saying:
"Yù's army is everywhere,
their numbers unknown."
Huán Xuán became even more anxious and fearful.
He dispatched Yǔ Yízhī, General of the Imperial Guard, with elite soldiers
to reinforce the various armies.
At that time, the northeast wind was strong.
The righteous army set fires,
smoke and dust filled the sky,
and the sound of drums and shouts shook the capital.
Liú Yù, wielding an axe, led the charge,
and Qiān's and the other armies immediately collapsed.
Huán Xuán, with several thousand of his close associates, claimed to be heading to battle,
but instead took his son Shēng and his nephew Jùn out of the Nányè Gate,
west to Shítou.
He ordered Yīn Zhòngwén to prepare boats,
and they fled south together.
Initially,
Huán Xuán was in Gūshú.
The stars of generals and prime ministers frequently changed.
On the evening of his usurpation,
the moon and Tàibái (Venus)
entered Yǔlín again.
Huán Xuán greatly disliked this.
When he fled in defeat,
his confidants urged him to fight.
Huán Xuán had no time to answer;
he merely pointed to the sky with his whip.
He went days without food.
Those around him offered coarse rice,
but he could not swallow it.
Shēng (his son) was a few years old at the time;
he embraced Huán Xuán's chest and comforted him.
Huán Xuán was overcome with grief.
Liú Yù appointed Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn to oversee all affairs,
established a traveling office (xíngtái),
and managed all officials.
He sent Liú Yì and Liú Dàoguī to pursue Huán Xuán,
and executed Huán Xuán's nephews, as well as Shí Kāng's elder brother Quán and Zhèn's elder brother Hóng, among others.
Huán Xuán reached Xúnyáng,
where Guō Chǎngzhī, the Governor (Cǐshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu, provided him with equipment and troops.
Yīn Zhòngwén arrived later,
and from a distance saw Huán Xuán's boats,
with flags, banners, chariots, and attire all matching the imperial regalia.
He sighed and said,
"To rally again after defeat,
this is indeed possible."
Huán Xuán then forced the emperor's carriage to travel west.
Huán Xīn gathered his partisans and headed towards Lìyáng;
Zhūgě Chángmín, the Internal Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Xuānchéng, defeated him.
Along the way, Huán Xuán compiled the Records of Imperial Daily Life (Qǐjūzhù).
Regarding the matters of his resistance against the Righteous Army,
he claimed that his strategies and directives
were flawless,
but the generals had disregarded his orders,
leading to losses;
it was not the fault of the battle itself.
Thus, he did not bother to discuss with his subordinates,
but only indulged in contemplating and narrating,
and proclaiming this far and wide.
Huán Xuán arrived at Jiānglíng,
where Shí Kāng welcomed him.
He set up a tented residence south of the city,
appointed officials,
making Biàn Fànzhī the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Púyè),
while many other positions were filled by those of lesser rank.
He then greatly repaired the navy.
Within less than thirty days,
his forces numbered nearly twenty thousand,
and the tower ships and weaponry were very formidable.
He told his partisans:
"You all have cleared the path and served in my entourage.
Those who have usurped positions in the capital should now apologize at the army gates.
When I see you enter Shítou,
it will be no different from people in the clouds and sky."
After his defeat and flight,
Huán Xuán feared that laws and orders would not be strict,
so he became quick to anger and executed wantonly,
causing many to become alienated and resentful.
Yīn Zhòngwén remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty gained a splendid reputation in your youth,
respected by those near and far.
You swept clean Jīng and Yōng,
and rectified the imperial household.
Your fame spread across the eight directions.
Having attained the highest position,
you then encountered this ruinous fate,
which was not due to a lack of prestige.
The common people eagerly
look forward to imperial grace.
It is fitting to promote benevolence,
to win over the hearts of the people."
Huán Xuán angrily said:
"Hàn Gāo and Wèi Wǔ nearly suffered defeat,
but it was just that their generals lost!
Because of the inauspicious astronomy,
I returned to the old Chu capital.
But the common folk are foolish and deluded,
arbitrarily creating right and wrong.
I should now rectify them with severity,
it is not yet appropriate to show them kindness."
Huán Xuán's entourage called him
"Huán Zhào."
Huán Yìn remonstrated, saying:
"Zhào (edict)
is used in pronouncements,
not as a form of address.
The rulers of Hàn and Wèi never used this term.
We only hear the northern barbarians refer to Fú Jiān as 'Fú Zhào'.
I wish Your Majesty would emulate the ancient imperial principles,
so that they may serve as a model for ten thousand generations."
Huán Xuán said:
"This matter has already been implemented.
If I now issue an edict to abolish it,
it would be even more inauspicious.
If it truly needs to be changed,
it can wait until affairs are settled."
Because Huán Xuán was in exile, the commandery governors (Jùnshǒu) of Jīngzhōu
either sent envoys to submit memorials
containing words of disquiet.
Huán Xuán refused them all,
and then ordered all localities to submit congratulatory memorials on the relocation of the capital.

Huán Xuán sent General of Roaming Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn) Hé Dànzhī, General of Martial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) Yǔ Zhìzǔ, and Jiangxià Administrator (Tàishǒu) Huán Dàogōng to join Guō Quán with several thousand men to guard Pénkǒu.
He also sent General Who Aids the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) Huán Zhèn to Yìyáng to gather troops.
Upon reaching Yìyáng,
he was defeated by General of Dragon Charge (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) Hú Huá,
and Zhèn fled back alone on horseback.
Hé Wúji, Liú Dàoguī, and others defeated Guō Quán, Hé Dànzhī, and Guō Chǎngzhī at Sāngluòzhōu,
and advanced their army to Xúnyáng.
Huán Xuán led two hundred ships and vessels from Jiānglíng,
making Fú Hóng and Yáng Sēngshòu his vanguard.
He appointed Xú Fàng, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Póyáng, as Attendant Official (Sànqí Chángshì),
intending to send him to persuade the Righteous Army.
He told Fàng:
"These people do not recognize the Mandate of Heaven,
leading to this foolish action.
Thus, fearing disaster, they have banded together
and cannot turn back.
You are trusted in the three commanderies,
so you can clearly convey my intentions.
If they withdraw their troops and disband their armor,
I will make a fresh start with them,
assigning each their positions and duties,
so that they do not lose their share.
The Jiāng River is here (as a witness);
I will not break my word."
Fàng replied:
"Liú Yù is the leader of this initiative,
and Liú Yì's elder brother was executed by Your Majesty.
Neither can be persuaded.
I will instead convey the imperial will to Hé Wúji."
Huán Xuán said:
"If your mission is successful,
I will appoint you as the Administrator (Xiàng) of Wúxīng."
Fàng then accepted the mission
and entered Hé Wúji's army.
Wèi Yǒngzhī defeated Huán Xīn at Lìyáng,
and Zhūgě Chángmín again defeated Xīn at Sháopí.
Xīn crossed the Huái River alone on horseback.
Yì led Dàoguī and Mèng Huáiyù, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xiàpī, to battle Huán Xuán at Zhēngróngzhōu.
At that time, the Righteous Army numbered several thousand,
and Huán Xuán's troops were very numerous.
However, Huán Xuán feared defeat,
and always kept a light boat floating beside his flagship.
Thus, his troops had no will to fight.
The Righteous Army took advantage of the wind to set fires,
fighting with all their might for the vanguard.
Huán Xuán's forces suffered a great rout,
burning their baggage and fleeing by night,
and Guō Quán surrendered.
Huán Xuán's former generals Liú Tǒng and Féng Zhì, among others, gathered four hundred partisans,
and attacked and captured Xúnyáng City.
Yì sent General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) Liú Huáisù to quell them.
Huán Xuán left Empress Yǒng'ān and the empress at Bālíng.
Yīn Zhòngwén, who was then on Huán Xuán's flagship,
requested to move to a separate boat to gather scattered troops.
He then betrayed Huán Xuán,
and escorted the two empresses to Xiàkǒu.
Huán Xuán entered Jiānglíng City.
Féng Gāi urged him to go down and fight again,
but Huán Xuán did not comply.
He wanted to exit into Hànchuān
and seek refuge with Huán Xī, the Governor (Cǐshǐ) of Liángzhōu.
However, the people were disloyal and obstructed him,
so his orders were not carried out.
Huán Xuán rode out of the city.
When he reached the gate,
his attendants hacked at him in the dark,
but missed.
Those in front and behind him fought and killed each other in confusion.
Huán Xuán barely managed to reach a boat.
At this, Wáng Kāngchǎn, the Assistant Administrator (Biéjià) of Jīngzhōu, escorted the emperor into the Nánjùn government office,
and Administrator (Tàishǒu) Wáng Téngzhī led civil and military officials to guard him.
At that time, Máo Qú (毛璩), the Inspector of Yìzhōu, sent his grandnephew Yòuzhī (祐之) and his staff officer Fèi Tián (費恬) to escort his younger brother Fán's (璠) coffin for burial in Jiānglíng.
They had a retinue of two hundred men.
Qú's (璩) younger brother Xiūzhī (修之) was Xuán's (玄) General of Agile Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi).
He lured Xuán (玄) into entering Shǔ.
Xuán (玄) followed him.
When they reached Méihuízhōu (枚回洲),
Tián (恬) and Yòuzhī (祐之) ambushed and attacked Xuán (玄).
Arrows fell like rain.
Xuán's (玄) favored attendants Dīng Xiānqī (丁仙期), Wàn Gài (萬蓋), and others shielded Xuán (玄) with their bodies,
and were all struck by dozens of arrows and died.
Xuán (玄) was hit by an arrow,
which his son Shēng (昇) immediately pulled out.
Féng Qiān (馮遷), the Commander of Yìzhōu, drew his sword and advanced.
Xuán (玄) pulled off the jade ornament from his head and gave it to him,
then said:
"Who is this person?
How dare you kill the Son of Heaven!"
Qiān (遷) replied:
"Just a bandit who wants to kill the Son of Heaven."
Then he decapitated him.
He was thirty-six years old at the time.
Shí Kāng (石康) and Jùn (濬) and five others were also decapitated.
Yǔ Yízhī (庾頤之) died in battle.
Shēng (昇) said:
"I am the King of Yùzhāng (豫章),
gentlemen, do not kill me."
He was sent to the Jiānglíng market and decapitated.
Initially,
when Xuán (玄) was in the palace,
he felt uneasy,
as if he were disturbed by ghosts and spirits.
He told his close associates:
"I fear I am about to die,
hence I am racing against time."
During the Yuánxīng (元興) era,
in Héngyáng (衡陽), a hen transformed into a rooster,
and after eighty days its comb withered.
〔一一〕When Xuán (玄) established his state in Chǔ,
Héngyáng (衡陽) was part of it.
From his usurpation until his defeat,
exactly eighty days passed.
At that time, there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Chánggān (長干) alley,
alley of Chánggān (長干),
this year the young master is killed,
the year after next all the Huán (桓) will be beheaded."
Such were the ominous omens that converged.
The "young master" (lángjūn 郎君)
referred to Yuánxiǎn (元顯).
In this month,
Wáng Téngzhī (王騰之) escorted the Emperor to reside in the Grand Treasury (Tàifǔ).
Huán Qiān (桓謙) also gathered a crowd in Jǔzhōng (沮中),
mourned Xuán (玄),
set up a funeral hall,
and posthumously bestowed upon him the false title of Emperor Wǔdào (武悼皇帝).
Yì (毅) and others sent Xuán's (玄) head,
which was displayed at the Dàhéng (大桁).
All the common people who witnessed it were overjoyed.
Hé Wújì (何無忌) and others attacked Huán Qiān (桓謙) at Mǎtóu (馬頭),
and Huán Wèi (桓蔚) at Lóngzhōu (龍洲),
and defeated them all.
The righteous army pressed forward with their victories.
Zhèn (振), Gāi (該), and others resisted them at Língxī (靈溪).
Dàoguī (道規) and others were defeated,
with over a thousand killed or lost.
The righteous army retreated to Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and re-equipped their ships and armor.
Máo Qú (毛璩) personally took charge of Liángzhōu (梁州),
and sent generals to attack Hànzhōng (漢中),
killing Huán Xī (桓希).
Zhāng Chàngzhī (張暢之), Chancellor of Jiāngxià (江夏), and Liú Huáisù (劉懷肅), Administrator of Gāopíng (高平), attacked Hé Dànzhī (何澹之) at Xīsàijī (西塞磯),
and defeated him.
Zhèn (振) sent Huán Wèi (桓蔚) to replace Wáng Kuàng (王曠) in defending Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Dàoguī (道規) advanced to attack Wǔchāng (武昌),
defeating the false Administrator Wáng Mǐn (王旻).
Wèi Yǒngzhī (魏詠之) and Liú Fān (劉藩) defeated Huán Shísuí (桓石綏) at Báimáo (白茅).
The righteous army departed Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Huán Liàng (桓亮) styled himself Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and invaded Yùzhāng (豫章).
Liú Jìngxūan (劉敬宣), Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州), attacked and drove him away.
The righteous army advanced to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
The false General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn) Féng Gāi (馮該) and others defended Xiàkǒu (夏口).
Méng Shāntú (孟山圖), General Who Manifests Martial Might (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn), occupied Lǔchéng (魯城),
and Huán Shānkè (桓山客), General Who Protects the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), defended Yǎnyuè Lěi (偃月壘).
〔一二〕Liú Yì (劉毅) attacked Lǔchéng (魯城),
Dàoguī (道規) attacked Yǎnyuè Lěi (偃月壘),
and Wújì (無忌) and Tán Zhī (檀祗) arrayed their ships in the middle of the river,
to prevent escape.
The righteous army surged forward,
their shouts shaking the valleys.
From dawn to noon,
both cities collapsed.
Féng Gāi (馮該) dispersed and fled,
and Shānkè (山客) was captured alive.
Yì (毅) and others pacified Bālíng (巴陵).
Máo Qú (毛璩) sent Wén Chǔmào (文處茂), Administrator of Fúlíng (涪陵), eastward.
Zhèn (振) sent Huán Fàngzhī (桓放之) to Yìzhōu (益州),
to garrison Yílíng (夷陵).
Chǔmào (處茂) resisted him in battle,
Fàngzhī (放之) was defeated and fled,
returning to Jiānglíng (江陵).
In the first month of the first year of Yìxī (義熙),
Lǔ Zōngzhī (魯宗之), Administrator of Nányáng (南陽), raised a righteous army and attacked Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
defeating the false Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), Huán Wèi (桓蔚).
Wújì's (無忌) forces reached Mǎtóu (馬頭) near Jiānglíng (江陵).
Zhèn (振) took the Emperor out of the camp to Jiāngjīn (江津).
Lǔ Zōngzhī (魯宗之) led his forces at Zuòxī (柞溪),
defeating the false General of Martial Might of the Guard (Wǔbēn Zhōngláng) Wēn Kǎi (溫楷),
and advanced to Jìnán (紀南).
Zhèn (振) personally attacked Zōngzhī (宗之),
and Zōngzhī (宗之) suffered a defeat.
At this time, the Shǔ army occupied Língxī (靈溪).
Yì (毅) led Wújì (無忌), Dàoguī (道規), and others to defeat Féng Gāi's (馮該) army,
and pushed forward,
immediately pacifying Jiānglíng (江陵).
When Zhèn (振) saw the fires rising,
he knew the city had fallen,
so he and Qiān (謙) and others fled north.
On that day,
Emperor Ān (安) was restored to power.
A general amnesty was declared throughout the realm,
except for the rebel partisans who were executed.
An imperial edict specifically pardoned only Huán Yìn (桓胤).
Huán Liàng (桓亮) from Yùzhāng (豫章)
styled himself General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
Fú Hóng (苻宏) raided Ānchéng (安成) and Lúlíng (廬陵).
Liú Jìngxūan (劉敬宣) sent generals to attack him.
Hóng (宏) fled into Xiāngzhōng (湘中).
In the second month,
Huán Qiān (桓謙), Hé Dànzhī (何澹之), Wēn Kǎi (溫楷), and others fled to Yáo Xìng (姚興).
Huán Zhèn (桓振) and Hóng (宏) emerged from Yínchéng (溳城),
and attacked and captured Jiānglíng (江陵).
Liú Huáisù (劉懷肅) from Yúndù (雲杜) attacked Zhèn (振) and others,
and defeated them.
Táng Xīng (唐興), General of Broad Martial Might (Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn), decapitated Zhèn (振) and the false General Who Protects the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) Huán Zhēn (桓珍).
Yì (毅) decapitated the false Administrator of Línglíng (零陵) Liú Shúzǔ (劉叔祖) at Línzhāng (臨鄣).
〔一三〕Huán Liàng (桓亮) and Fú Hóng (苻宏) again emerged and raided Xiāngzhōng (湘中),
harming the local administrators.
Tán Zhī (檀祗) attacked Hóng (宏) at Xiāngdōng (湘東),
and decapitated him.
Guō Mí (郭彌), General of Broad Martial Might (Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn), decapitated Liàng (亮) at Yìyáng (益陽).
The rest who gathered crowds and assumed false titles were all attacked and pacified.
An imperial edict ordered Huán Yìn (桓胤) and other partisans to be exiled to the various commanderies of Xīn'ān (新安).
In the third year,
Yīn Zhòngwén (殷仲文), Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽), and Luò Qiú (駱球), Administrator of Yǒngjiā (永嘉), plotted rebellion,
intending to establish Huán Yìn (桓胤) as heir.
Cáo Jìngzhī (曹靖之), Huán Shísōng (桓石松), Biàn Chéngzhī (卞承之), Liú Yánzǔ (劉延祖), and others secretly formed alliances.
Liú Yù (劉裕) arrested and executed them one by one,
and also punished their family members.
Later, Huán Qiān (桓謙) fled into Shǔ.
The Shǔ bandit Qiáo Zòng (譙縱) appointed Qiān (謙) as Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and sent him to lead troops down.
Many from Jīngchǔ (荊楚) responded to him.
When Qiān (謙) reached Zhījiāng (枝江),
Liú Dàoguī (劉道規), Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), decapitated him.
Fù Xīn (傅歆), Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州), also decapitated Huán Shísuí (桓石綏).
Thus, the Huán (桓) clan was extinguished.
Biàn Fànzhī (卞範之)
Biàn Fànzhī (卞範之), courtesy name Jìngzǔ (敬祖),
was from Wǎnjù (宛句) in Jìyīn (濟陰).
〔一四〕He was insightful and intelligent,
and highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
During the Tàiyuán (太元) era,
he went from Assistant in Dānyáng (丹楊丞) to Administrator of Shǐ'ān (始安).
Huán Xuán (桓玄) had befriended him in his youth.
When Xuán (玄) became Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
he appointed him as Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ),
and entrusted him with vital responsibilities.
All secret plans and schemes
were decided by him.
Later, when Xuán (玄) was about to usurp and cause chaos,
he appointed Fànzhī (範之) as Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
Fànzhī (範之) and Yīn Zhòngwén (殷仲文) secretly drafted the imperial mandate for abdication.
Fànzhī (範之) was promoted to General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
When Xuán (玄) usurped the throne,
he appointed Fànzhī (範之) as Court Gentleman (Shìzhōng),
with twenty sword-wielding guards,
and promoted him to General of the Rear (Hòujiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Línrǔ County (Línrǔ Xiàn Gōng).
The abdication edict
was Fànzhī's (範之) writing.
As Xuán (玄) was extravagant and unrestrained,
Fànzhī (範之) also extensively built mansions.
Considering himself a founding minister,
he harbored deep pride and boastfulness.
He flaunted his wealth and status,
and his children and younger relatives were arrogant,
so everyone feared and resented him.
When the righteous army rose,
Fànzhī (範之) garrisoned troops west of Fùzhōushān (覆舟山),
was defeated by Liú Yì (劉毅),
and fled west with Xuán (玄).
Xuán (玄) again appointed Fànzhī (範之) as Grand Secretariat Assistant (Shàngshū Púshè).
When Xuán (玄) was defeated by Liú Yì (劉毅) and others,
his attendants scattered,
only Fànzhī (範之) remained by his side.
When Xuán (玄) was pacified,
Fànzhī (範之) was decapitated in Jiānglíng (江陵).
Yīn Zhòngwén (殷仲文)
Yīn Zhòngwén
was the younger brother of Yīn Jī, the Nánmán Xiàowèi.
From a young age, he possessed talent and literary skill,
and a handsome appearance.
His cousin Yīn Zhòngkān recommended him to Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ,
who immediately appointed him Pìqí Cānjūn,
