and greatly appreciated and treated him well.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zīyì Cānjūn,
and later served as Yuán Xiǎn’s Zhēnglǔ Chángshǐ.
At that time, Huán Xuán had a rift with the imperial court.
Xuán’s elder sister,
who was Zhòngwén’s wife,
grew suspicious and sowed discord,
leading to his demotion to Xīn’ān Tàishǒu.
Although Zhòngwén was Xuán’s relative by marriage,
they were not close friends.
When he heard that Xuán had pacified the capital,
he abandoned his commandery and joined him.
Xuán was very pleased with this,
and made him Zīyì Cānjūn.
At that time, Wáng Mì was treated with礼 (lǐ) but not intimacy,
while Biàn Fànzhī was treated with intimacy but little 礼 (lǐ).
However, Zhòngwén’s favor and treatment were more profound
than both Wáng and Biàn.
When Xuán was about to cause rebellion,
he ordered Zhòngwén to take charge of all imperial edicts,
and appointed him Shìzhōng,
also holding the position of Zuǒwèi Jiàngjūn.
Xuán’s Nine Bestowals were
Zhòngwén’s composition.
Initially,
when Xuán usurped the throne and entered the palace,
his bed suddenly collapsed.
His subordinates lost color,
but Zhòngwén said:
“This must be because of your profound sagely virtue,
which the earth cannot bear.”
Xuán was greatly pleased.
As a close and esteemed helper in the usurpation,
he greatly enriched himself,
his carriages, horses, utensils, and clothing
were of the utmost splendor and luxury.
His rear chambers housed dozens of female musicians and concubines,
with strings and flutes playing ceaselessly.
He was by nature greedy and parsimonious,
accumulating much wealth and bribes.
His family accumulated thousands of gold,
yet he always felt it was not enough.
When Xuán was defeated by Liú Yù,
he fled west with Xuán.
All his treasures and valuables, which were hidden underground,
turned into earth.
Upon reaching Bālíng,
he then presented the two empresses to the righteous army,
and became Zhènzhūn Chángshǐ,
then transferred to Shàngshū.
When the emperor first restored the rightful government,
he submitted a memorial to resign, saying:
“Your servant has heard that when great waves shake the valleys,
the rivers have no calm scales;
when a strong gale sweeps the plains,
the forests have no still branches.
Why is this?
When one’s power is weak, one is controlled by great force;
when one’s substance is small, one cannot protect oneself.
Though this may be spoken of in principle,
it is truly not something your servant dares to compare himself to.
During the time of Huán Xuán,
it is true that many were compelled and coerced.
However, as for your humble servant,
my crime is truly deep.
I could not advance to face danger and offer my life,
sacrificing myself for the country;
nor could I retreat to refuse grain like those at Shǒuyáng,
shaking off my robes and withdrawing in noble reclusion.
Instead, I indulged in peace and imperial favor,
greedily accepting false appointments.
I drafted documents for the usurpation,
yet had no firm resolve.
My reputation and integrity thus both collapsed,
and my principles were simultaneously compromised.
It is fitting that I should face the extreme penalty,
to distinguish loyalty from treachery.
It so happened that Zhènzhūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yù restored the imperial altars,
and greatly extended benevolence and leniency.
He paused at the single execution of a humble life,
and extended the three chases of great trustworthiness.
Not only did he bestow upon me my head,
but he also bound me with ties.
At that time, the imperial carriage was obstructed and separated,
and heaven and humanity were not yet settled.
I forgot about advancing or retreating,
and therefore reluctantly engaged in affairs,
identifying myself with the common people.
Now that the imperial peak has been restored,
and a new beginning announced,
the laws are clear,
and all things long for the old order.
How can your servant, with such a thick face,
still conspicuously occupy an honored position!
I beg to resign from my post,
and await punishment at my private residence.
Though I depart from the imperial court,
my heart yearns for it.”
The imperial edict did not permit it.
On the first day of the month, Zhòngwén went with the crowd to the Grand Marshal’s residence.
There was an old scholar tree in the residence.
He looked at it for a long time and sighed, saying:
“This tree is sprawling,
with no more signs of life!”
Zhòngwén had always enjoyed a good reputation,
and believed he would certainly participate in government affairs.
Moreover, those he had previously slighted, like Xiè Hùn and his ilk,
were now all his peers.
He was often discontent and unsatisfied.
Suddenly, he was transferred to Dōngyáng Tàishǒu,
and his mood became even more unbalanced.
Liú Yì loved talent and respected scholars,
and treated him with deep courtesy.
Before Zhòngwén departed for his commandery, they feasted for an entire day.
Upon arriving at Fùyáng,
he sighed with emotion, saying:
“Looking at the lie of these mountains and rivers,
another Bófú
is bound to emerge.”
Hé Wújì greatly admired him.
Dōngyáng
was under Wújì’s jurisdiction.
Zhòngwén promised to pay him a visit along the way.
Wújì therefore looked forward to him even more,
ordering the literary men in his residence, such as Yīn Chǎn and Kǒng Níngzǐ, to compose essays
to await his arrival.
Zhòngwén, being dejected and disoriented,
did not visit the residence after all.
Wújì suspected he was looking down on him,
and was greatly enraged,
thinking of harming him.
At that time, Mùróng Chāo was invading from the south.
Wújì spoke to Liú Yù, saying:
“Huán Yìn and Yīn Zhòngwén are a disease of the heart;
the northern barbarians are not worth worrying about.”
In Yìxī third year,
Zhòngwén, along with Luò Qiú and others, was also accused of plotting rebellion,
and he and his younger brother, Nánmán Xiàowèi Shúwén, were both executed.
At that time, Zhòngwén looked into a mirror but could not see his face,
and a few days later met with disaster.
Zhòngwén was skilled in writing,
and was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
Xiè Língyù once said:
“If Yīn Zhòngwén had read half as many books as Yuán Bào,
his literary talent would be no less than Bān Gù.”
This meant that his writing was abundant but his reading was limited.
The imperial historian said: Huán Xuán
usurped the foundations left by his father.
With a treacherous and perverse nature,
he harbored resentment for having lost his position.
He concealed his porcine heart,
then presented a memorial to lament his supposed wrongs.
He ascended a height to vent his frustration,
observed the opportune moment to act,
and secretly plotted for an undeserved prize.
At first, he feigned favor with Zhòngkān,
but soon after, he executed Yīn to satisfy his desires.
Thus, he gained control of the entire territory of Chǔ,
commanding strong and brave soldiers.
Taking advantage of the Jin dynasty's decline,
and relying on the dissipated nature of Huìjī,
he unleashed his cunning schemes
and fanned his arrogant and aggressive ambitions.
Daring to lead a multitude of base followers,
he raised an army to invade and insult the imperial court.
Heaven had long suffered from disorder and chaos,
and his destructive power was truly immense.
Within a year,
he suddenly overthrew the Jin dynasty's mandate.
He believed himself to be like Yáo abdicating to Shùn,
changing the order of things and ruling as monarch,
that his imperial enterprise would flourish,
and his reign would last forever.
Soon after, the righteous banner was unfurled like lightning,
and loyal and brave men rushed forth like thunder.
In half a day, the capital was cleared,
and within a month, the evil ringleader was executed.
The fallen imperial lineage was prolonged,
and the decaying order was restored.
From this, one knows that the divine implements of state cannot be clandestinely usurped,
and Heaven's bounty cannot be presumptuously held.
A true emperor or king
has accomplishments that extend throughout the world,
and his Way benefits all living beings.
Dragon palaces and phoenix calendars display their auspicious signs,
and crimson clouds and black stones present their omens.
Only then can one majestically ascend to the great throne,
and enjoy a grand reputation,
genuinely fulfilling the hopes of the empress,
and satisfying the expectation of joyous support.
As for the likes of Huán Xuán, with his twisted and treacherous ways,
how can he be worth mentioning?
He merely disrupted the fundamental principles and violated the normal order,
overthrowing his clan and ending its lineage,
initiating the calamity of the element Metal,
and becoming one of those purged by the Sòng clan!
Encomium: Lǐngbǎo, a hidden villain,
inherited wicked virtues across generations.
His trustworthiness was not sufficient,
and treachery was his rule.
He committed rebellion, usurped the throne,
relied on power, and indulged in wickedness.
He defied Heaven and oppressed the people,
bringing ruin to his clan and annihilating his state.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 70: Wáng Mí
Wáng Mí
was a native of Dōnglái.
His family had been officials holding a salary of two thousand *shí* for generations.
His grandfather, Qí,
was the Administrator of Xuánfén during the Wèi dynasty.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
he became the Administrator of Rǔnán.
Mí possessed talent and ability,
and was widely read in historical records.
When he was young, he was a knight-errant in the capital.
The hermit Dǒng Zhòngdào saw him and said,
"Sir, you have the voice of a jackal and the gaze of a leopard,
you love chaos and delight in misfortune.
If the world were to become turbulent,
you would not remain a mere scholar-official."
Towards the end of Emperor Huì's reign,
the demon bandit Liú Bó'gēn rose up in a county of Dōnglái.
Mí led his household retainers to follow him.
Bó'gēn made him his Chief Clerk.
After Bó'gēn died,
Mí gathered followers on an island in the sea.
He was defeated by Gǒu Chún,
and fled into Chángguǎng Shān to become a bandit leader.
Mí had many stratagems.
Whatever he plundered,
he would always plan for success or failure in advance.
He never had a failed strategy.
He was swift with bow and horse,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
In Qīngtǔ, he was known as
"Flying Leopard."
Later, he led his troops to invade Qīng and Xú.
Gǒu Xī, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, intercepted and attacked him,
thoroughly defeating him.
Mí retreated and gathered his scattered forces.
His army greatly revived.
Xī fought several battles with him,
but could not defeat him.
Mí advanced his troops and attacked the commanderies of Tàishān, Lǔguó, Qiáo, Liáng, Chén, Rǔnán, Yǐngchuān, and Xiāngchéng.
He entered Xǔchāng,
opened the armories,
took weapons and equipment.
Wherever he went, cities fell,
and he killed many administrators and magistrates.
He had tens of thousands of followers,
and the imperial court could not control him.
Just then, the world fell into great chaos.
He advanced to threaten Luòyáng.
The capital was greatly shaken,
and the palace gates were closed during the day.
Sītú Wáng Yǎn and others led all the officials to defend against him.
Mí was encamped at Qīlǐ Jiàn.
The imperial army advanced and attacked,
greatly defeating him.
Mí said to his comrade Liú Líng,
"The Jin army is still strong,
and we have nowhere to return.
Liú Yuánhǎi was once a hostage.
I associated with him in the capital,
and we had a deep bond.
Now he claims to be the King of Hàn.
Should I go to him?
Is it permissible?"
Líng agreed.
So he crossed the Yellow River and went to Yuánhǎi.
Yuánhǎi was very pleased to hear this,
and sent his Palace Attendant concurrently Grandee Remonstrant Yùshǐ Dàfū to welcome him outside the city,
sending a letter to Mí which said:
"It is because General has unparalleled achievements,
and virtues that transcend the age,
that I have extended this welcome.
Eagerly awaiting General's arrival,
I will personally go to General's residence
to sweep the mat and wash the cups,
respectfully awaiting General."
When Mí met Yuánhǎi,
he urged him to assume the imperial title.
Yuánhǎi said to Mí,
"I originally thought General was like Dòu Zhōugōng,
but now you are truly my Kǒngmíng and Zhònghuá.
Our Illustrious Ancestor once said, 'My having General
is like a fish having water.'"
Thereupon, Mí was appointed Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Tèjìn.
Mí firmly declined.
He was sent to follow Liú Yào to invade Hénèi,
and also attacked Línzhāng with Shí Lè.
At the beginning of Yǒngjiā,
he invaded Shàngdǎng and besieged Húguān.
Wáng Yuè, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, sent Wáng Kuàng, the Administrator of Huáinán, and Wèi Gān, the Administrator of Ānfēng, and others to suppress him.
They fought Mí between Gāodū and Chángpíng,
and thoroughly defeated him,
with sixteen or seventeen out of ten killed.
Yuánhǎi promoted Mí to Grand General of the Pacification of the East,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Dōnglái.
He joined Liú Yào and Shí Lè in attacking Wèijùn, Jíjùn, and Dùnqíu,
capturing over fifty fortified villages,
all of whose inhabitants were conscripted as soldiers.
He also attacked Yè with Lè.
Hé Yù, the General Who Pacifies the North, abandoned the city and fled.
Emperor Huái sent Péi Xiàn, the Central Protector-General of the North, to Bái Mǎ to suppress Mí.
Wáng Kān, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, went to Dōngyàn to suppress Lè.
Cáo Wǔ, the General Who Pacifies the North, went to Dàyáng to suppress Yuánhǎi.
Péng Mò, a general under Wǔ, was defeated by Liú Cōng
and killed.
All the imperial armies retreated.
Cōng crossed the Yellow River.
The Emperor sent Liú Tūn, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, and Sòng Chōu, the General, and others to resist him,
but they could not withstand him.
Mí and Cōng arrived at the capital with ten thousand cavalry,
and burned the two academies.
Wáng Yuè, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, engaged them in battle at Xīmíng Mén.
Mí and his forces were defeated and fled.
Mí then led two thousand cavalry to invade the various counties of Xiāngchéng.
Tens of thousands of refugee families from Hédōng, Píngyáng, Hóngnóng, and Shàngdǎng who were in Yǐngchuān, Xiāngchéng, Rǔnán, Nányáng, and Hénán,
were not treated courteously by the local inhabitants.
They all burned cities and towns,
and killed two-thousand-shí officials and chief magistrates to respond to Mí.
Mí then joined Shí Lè with twenty thousand men to invade Chénjùn and Yǐngchuān,
encamping at Yángzhái.
He sent his younger brother Zhāng to join Shí Lè in invading Xú and Yǎn,
thereby defeating Yuè's army.
Later, Mí fought with Yào, invading Xiāngchéng,
and then pressed close to the capital.
At this time, the capital suffered a great famine;
people ate each other,
the common people fled,
and the dukes and ministers fled to Héyīn.
Yào, Mí, and others then breached the palace city,
reached the Tàijí Qiándiàn,
and let their soldiers plunder freely.
They imprisoned the Emperor (Yōu Dì) at Duānmén,
humiliated Empress Yáng,
killed Crown Prince Quán,
excavated tombs,
burned palaces and temples.
The cities and treasuries were completely emptied,
and over thirty thousand officials, men and women, were killed.
They then moved the Emperor to Píngyáng.
During Mí's plundering,
Yào forbade it,
but Mí did not comply.
Yào executed his vanguard general Wáng Yán as a public example,
which enraged Mí.
He and Yào raised their troops and attacked each other,
resulting in over a thousand deaths.
Mí's Chief Clerk, Zhāng Sōng, advised him, saying:
"My lord and the state are jointly embarking on a great enterprise;
the work has just begun,
yet you are already attacking each other.
How will you face His Majesty?
The merit of pacifying Luò is indeed with the general,
but Liú Yào is of the imperial clan;
it is fitting to yield a little to him.
The lesson of the two Jìn princes pacifying Wú
is not far off;
I hope, my general, you will consider this.
Even if the general raises troops and does not return,
what about your sons, brothers, and clan members?"
Mí said:
"Excellent.
If not for you,
I would not have heard of this fault."
Thereupon, he went to Yào to apologize,
and their bond was restored as before.
Mí said:
"This subordinate hearing his fault
is the achievement of Chief Clerk Zhāng."
Yào said to Sōng:
"You are Zhū Jiàn,
let alone Fàn Shēng!"
They each bestowed upon Sōng a hundred catties of gold.
Mí said to Yào:
"Luòyáng is the center of the world,
with four strategic mountain and river defenses,
and its city walls and palaces require no new construction.
We can move the capital from Píngyáng here."
Yào did not agree,
burned it, and departed.
Mí angrily said:
"This Túgē fellow,
how can he have the ambition of an emperor?
What will you do for the world?"
Then he led his troops east to garrison Xiàngguān.
Initially,
Yào resented Mí for entering Luò first
without waiting for him,
and now the rift was formed.
Liú Tūn persuaded Mí to return and occupy Qīngzhōu.
Mí agreed,
and appointed his Left Chief Clerk Cáo Yì as Commander of the East (Zhèn Dōng Jiāngjūn),
gave him five thousand soldiers,
and many treasures to return to his homeland,
to recruit fugitives,
and also to bring back his family.
Mí's generals Xú Miǎo and Gāo Liáng immediately led several thousand of their troops to follow Yì,
which further weakened Mí.
Initially,
Shí Lè disliked Mí's bravery
and always secretly prepared for him.
When Mí breached Luòyáng,
he sent Lè many beautiful women and treasures to establish good relations.
At this time, Lè captured Gǒu Xī
and made him Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Sīmǎ).
Mí said to Lè:
"You captured Gǒu Xī and employed him;
how divine and marvelous!
If Xī is your left hand
and Mí is your right,
the world will not be difficult to pacify!"
Lè became even more wary of Mí
and secretly plotted against him.
Liú Tūn again advised Mí to summon Cáo Yì
and use his forces to execute Lè.
Thereupon, Mí sent Tūn to Qīngzhōu,
ordering Cáo Yì to lead his troops to join him,
while falsely pretending with Lè to attack Qīngzhōu together.
When Tūn reached Dōng'ē,
he was captured by Lè's cavalry scouts.
Lè saw the letter from Mí to Yì,
was greatly enraged,
and then killed Tūn.
Mí did not know this;
Lè ambushed and attacked Mí,
killed him,
and assimilated his forces.
Zhāng Chāng
Zhāng Chāng
was originally a Mán from Yìyáng.
When he was young, he was a county official in Píngshì county.
His martial strength surpassed others;
he often performed divination for himself,
saying he was destined for wealth and nobility.
He enjoyed discussing warfare;
his peers all laughed at him.
When Lǐ Liú invaded Shǔ,
Chāng secretly absconded for half a year,
gathered several thousand followers,
stole a banner,
and falsely claimed that the court had dispatched him to recruit people to suppress Liú.
It happened that an imperial edict (rénwǔ zhàoshū) ordered the recruitment of brave men to proceed to Yìtǔ,
dubbed
"Rénwǔ troops."
Since the world was in great turmoil,
diviners said there would be an emperor arising in Jiāngzuǒ.
When this recruitment was initiated,
people were all unwilling to go on the western expedition.
Chāng's followers then used this to mislead them,
and the common people each refused to go.
However, the imperial edict urged dispatch with severe speed,
stating that any place through which they passed that delayed for five days
would result in the dismissal of officials holding salaries of two thousand dàn.
Because of this, the county officials all personally went out to drive them on,
but they did not travel far,
instead gathering and engaging in robbery.
That year, Jiāngxià had a great harvest,
and several thousand displaced people came to eat there.
In the second year of Tàiaān,
Chāng gathered his forces at Shíyán Shān in Ānlù county,
eighty *lǐ* from the commandery.
Many displaced people and those avoiding military service joined him.
Chāng then changed his name to Lǐ Chén.
The Grand Administrator Gōng Qīn dispatched troops to suppress him,
but they were repeatedly defeated.
Chāng's followers increased daily,
and he then came to attack the commandery.
Qīn went out to battle
but was greatly defeated,
and then took his family and fled south to Miǎnkǒu.
The Grand General of the South (Zhèn Nán Dàjiāngjūn) and Prince of Xīnyě, Xīn, sent cavalry commander Jìn Mǎn to suppress Chāng west of Suíjùn.
In a great battle,
Mǎn was defeated and fled.
Chāng obtained his weapons
and occupied Jiāngxià,
seizing its treasury.
He created a false prophecy, saying:
"A sage is about to appear."
Shāndū Xiàn county official Qiū Shěn (丘沈) met [Zhāng] Chāng (張昌) in Jiāngxià (江夏).
Chāng (昌) proclaimed him a sage,
prepared carriages and robes, and went out to welcome him.
He was established as the Son of Heaven,
and officials were appointed.
Shěn (沈) changed his name to Liú Ní (劉尼),
claiming to be a descendant of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
He made Chāng (昌) Prime Minister (相國),
Chāng’s (昌) elder brother Wèi (味) General of Cavalry and Chariots (車騎將軍),
and his younger brother Fàng (放) General of Guǎngwǔ (廣武將軍),
each leading troops.
They built palaces in the rock caves,
and on the rocks above, they wove bamboo into bird shapes,
clothed them with five colors,
and gathered meat beside them.
When numerous birds gathered,
they falsely claimed that phoenixes had descended.
They also said that pearl robes, jade seals, iron credentials, and golden drums had arrived naturally.
Then they issued a general amnesty,
established the era name Shénfèng (神鳳),
and conducted suburban sacrifices and adopted vestment colors according to Hàn (漢) precedents.
Those who did not respond to their summons
were exterminated with their clans.
They also spread rumors, saying:
"South of the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers, there will be a great rebellion.
The imperial army will rise in great numbers
and exterminate them all."
The common people incited each other,
and people were terrified.
In the region between the Jiāng (江) and Miǎn (沔) rivers, a sudden uprising occurred.
They raised牙旗 yáfāng (牙旗) (banners with tusks),
beat drums, and blew horns
in response to Chāng (昌).
Within a month,
their numbers reached thirty thousand.
They all wore crimson turbans,
adorned with fur.
Among the gentry and commoners of Jiāngxià (江夏) and Yìyáng (義陽), none failed to join them,
except for Wáng Yǔ (王傴), the former Jiāng'ān (江安) county magistrate, and the Xiùcái (秀才) Lǚ Ruí (呂蕤), both from old families in Jiāngxià (江夏).
Chāng (昌) summoned them with offers of the Three Ducal (三公) positions.
Yǔ (傴) and Ruí (蕤) secretly led their clans north to Rǔnán (汝南),
throwing themselves upon Liú Qiáo (劉喬), the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州).
Their fellow villagers Lǐ Quán (李權), the magistrate of Qīxī (期思), Wú Fèng (吳鳳), the magistrate of Cháng'ān (常安), and Wú Chàng (吳暢), a Xiàolián (孝廉), gathered benevolent gentlemen,
amounting to over five hundred families,
and followed Yǔ (傴) and others,
not participating in the evil rebellion.
Xīnyě Wáng Xīn (新野王歆) submitted a memorial, saying:
"The demonic bandits Zhāng Chāng (張昌) and Liú Ní (劉尼) falsely claim divinity,
with tens of thousands of their dog-like and sheep-like followers,
with crimson turbans and furry faces,
brandishing swords and wielding halberds.
Their advance cannot be resisted.
I request that the imperial court order all armies
to provide aid from three routes."
Thereupon, Liú Qiáo (劉喬) led his armies to hold Rǔnán (汝南) to defend against the bandits.
Former General Zhào Xiāng (趙驤) led eight thousand elite troops to hold Wǎn (宛),
assisting General Píngnán (平南將軍) Yáng Yī (羊伊) in defense.
Chāng (昌) dispatched his general Huáng Lín (黃林) as Grand Commander (大都督),
leading twenty thousand men towards Yùzhōu (豫州).
His vanguard Lǐ Gōng (李宮) intended to plunder the residents along the Rǔ Shuǐ (汝水).
Qiáo (喬) sent General Lǐ Yáng (李楊) to intercept and attack them,
inflicting a great defeat.
Lín (林) and others then attacked Yìyáng (弋陽) to the east.
The Administrator Liáng Huán (梁桓) fortified the city and held firm.
Chāng (昌) also dispatched his general Mǎ Wǔ (馬武) to defeat Wǔchāng (武昌),
killing the Administrator.
Chāng (昌) personally led his troops
to attack Wǎn (宛) to the west,
defeated Zhào Xiāng (趙驤),
and killed Yáng Yī (羊伊).
He then advanced to attack Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
killing Xīnyě Wáng Xīn (新野王歆).
Chāng (昌) separately dispatched Shí Bīng (石冰) to the east to defeat Jiāng (江) and Yáng (揚) two Prefectures,
and falsely appointed administrators and governors.
At that time, the borders of five prefectures were all intimidated and joined the rebellion.
He also sent his generals Chén Zhēn (陳貞), Chén Lán (陳蘭), and Zhāng Fǔ (張甫) to attack Chángshā (長沙), Xiāngdōng (湘東), Línglíng (零陵) and other commanderies.
Although Chāng (昌) controlled five prefectures
and established governors and magistrates,
they were all cruel bandits and petty individuals without restraint,
whose only task was plunder.
People's loyalty gradually alienated.
In this year,
an imperial edict appointed Liú Hóng (劉弘), General of Níngshuò (寧朔將軍) and Acting Commandant of the Southern Barbarians (領南蠻校尉), to garrison Wǎn (宛).
Hóng (弘) sent Commandant Táo Kǎn (陶侃), Aide-de-camp Kuǎi Huán (蒯桓), Pí Chū (皮初), and others to lead troops to attack Chāng (昌) in Jìnglǐng (竟陵).
Liú Qiáo (劉喬) also sent General Lǐ Yáng (李楊) and Overseer Yǐn Fèng (尹奉) to lead troops towards Jiāngxià (江夏).
Kǎn (侃) and others fought fiercely against Chāng (昌) for several days,
inflicting a great defeat.
Tens of thousands surrendered.
Chāng (昌) then fled and hid in Xiàjùn Shān (下儁山).
In the autumn of the following year,
he was captured
and his head was sent to the capital.
All his confederates were exterminated with their three clans.
Chén Mǐn (陳敏)
Chén Mǐn (陳敏), courtesy name Lìngtōng (令通),
was a native of Lújiāng (廬江).
In his youth, he possessed competence and ability.
As an incorruptible official of the commandery, he was appointed Secretary of the Granary Department of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書倉部令史).
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) usurped the throne,
the Three Princes raised armies of righteousness,
and were long encamped without dispersing.
The granaries in the capital were empty.
Mǐn (敏) suggested:
"The rice and grains in the south have been accumulated for decades;
they are about to spoil.
Yet they are not transported to aid the central regions.
This is not how to relieve distress and help the needy."
The imperial court followed his advice
and appointed Mǐn (敏) Controller of Finances for Héféi (合肥度支),
and later promoted him to Controller of Finances for Guǎnglíng (廣陵度支).
During Zhāng Chāng's (張昌) rebellion,
he sent his general Shí Bīng (石冰) and others towards Shòuchūn (壽春).
Commander Liú Zhǔn (劉準) was anxious and at a loss for a plan.
At that time, Mǐn (敏) commanded a large army in Shòuchūn (壽春).
He said to Zhǔn (準):
"These people originally did not enjoy being stationed far away,
and thus were forced to become bandits.
A motley crowd,
their unity is easily broken.
I request to combine and lead the transport troops,
and openly distribute the collective strength.
We will surely defeat them."
Thereupon, Zhǔn (準) reinforced Mǐn (敏) with troops to attack them.
He defeated Wú Hóng (吳弘), Shí Bīng (石冰) and others.
Mǐn (敏) then pursued the defeated enemy, taking advantage of his victory,
fighting dozens of engagements.
At that time, Bīng's (冰) forces were ten times larger,
but Mǐn (敏) attacked the many with few,
winning every battle,
and thus reached Yángzhōu (揚州).
He turned back to suppress the Xúzhōu (徐州) bandit Fēng Yún (封雲).
Yún's (雲) general Zhāng Tǒng (張統) beheaded Yún (雲) and surrendered.
Mǐn (敏) was appointed Chancellor of Guǎnglíng (廣陵相) for his merits.
At that time, Emperor Huì (惠帝) resided in Cháng'ān (長安),
and the four quarters were in contention.
Mǐn (敏) then harbored the ambition of occupying Jiāngdōng (江東).
His father, upon hearing this,
angrily said:
"The one who will destroy my family
must be this child!"
After his father passed away,
Mǐn (敏) resigned from his post.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè (東海王越) was about to go west to welcome the Emperor.
He, acting on imperial authority, appointed Mǐn (敏) as Right General (右將軍), acting as Jí (假節), and Vanguard Commander (前鋒都督).
He wrote a letter to Mǐn (敏), saying: "General, in devising strategies to enrich the state,
you accomplished the great feat of transport.
When encountering the chaos of Bīng (冰) and Chāng (昌),
you were the first to lead righteous volunteers,
to pit few against many.
With no strong
military aid from outside,
and no companions for strategizing within,
you stood alone and firm.
Your heroic strategies spread far and wide,
producing extraordinary schemes on horseback,
and displaying divine plans in times of peril.
Your golden voice resonated beyond
the Jiāng (江) river,
and your brilliant light shone brightly in Yáng (揚) and Chǔ (楚).
Attacking fortified positions and overcoming dangers,
you fought over thirty battles,
without losing troops.
The formidable enemies destroyed themselves.
The five prefectures were restored to integrity,
and the fragrant grasses were sent as
tribute.
Was this not the General's merit and effort!
Now, the Jié (羯) bandits gather,
their wandering souls roam the Hé (河) and Jì (濟) rivers.
Like rats they hide, like pheasants they flee,
concealing themselves in Chénliú (陳留).
They first intend to commit villainy and theft,
and ultimately plot rebellion.
General, your art of Sūn (孫) and Wú (吳)
is already clear,
and your tested merits are established.
My feelings and relationship with the General are especially deep.
I hope you will suppress your grief of mourning,
and restrain the thought of retreating from your difficult position,
cast aside your mourning clothes and grasp your spear,
to come and
relieve the national crisis.
The Son of Heaven is on a distant tour,
and the imperial carriage has not yet returned.
He yearns for the East and
thinks of the imperial tombs.
We must rely on the General's concerted efforts,
so that the royal carriage may return.
General,
lead your subordinates.
Upon receiving this letter, rise swiftly.
As for provisions for the army,
the General shall manage them."
At that time, Yuè (越) was attacking Liú Qiáo (劉喬), Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州).
Mǐn (敏) led his troops to join him,
and both Yuè (越) and Mǐn (敏) were defeated at Xiāo (蕭).
Mǐn, due to the great chaos in Zhōngguó,
then requested to return east,
and gathered troops to occupy Lìyáng.
At this time, Gān Zhuó, the royal attendant of Wú Wáng, arrived from Luò.
He instructed Zhuó to falsely claim an imperial younger brother's (huángtàidì) command,
appointing Mǐn as Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and also falsely appointed Gù Róng and over forty other prominent figures from Jiāngdōng as jiāngjūn and jùnshǒu.
Róng and the others feigned compliance.
Mǐn married Zhuó's daughter for his son,
and they thus became allies through marriage.
Liú Jī, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, Wáng Guǎng, Dānyáng Tàishǒu, and others all abandoned their posts and fled.
Mǐn's younger brother Chǎng knew that Gù Róng and the others had ulterior motives,
and urged Mǐn to kill them,
but Mǐn refused.
Chǎng led tens of thousands of elite troops to occupy Wūjiāng.
His younger brother Huī, with Qián Duān and others, raided Jiāngzhōu to the south,
causing Cìshǐ Yīng Miáo to flee.
His younger brother Bīn campaigned in the eastern commanderies,
and thus occupied the territory of Wúyuè.
Mǐn ordered his staff to declare him Dūdū Jiāngdōng Jūnshì, Dàsīmǎ, and Chǔ Gōng,
enfeoffing ten commanderies,
and granting him the Jiǔ Xī,
which he submitted to the Shàngshū,
claiming he would enter the Hé from the Jiāng,
to welcome the imperial chariot.
Huá Tán, Jūnzī Jìjiǔ to Dōnghǎi Wáng, heard that Mǐn had self-appointed,
and that Gù Róng and the others, who were prominent figures of Jiāngdōng,
had all accepted Mǐn's official titles and ranks.
Thereupon, he sent a letter to Róng and the others, saying: "During the chaos of Shí Bīng,
the imperial court recognized Mǐn's minor achievements,
and therefore granted him an exceptional honor,
entrusting him with the responsibility of a supreme general,
hoping for the effectiveness of a 'Hán Lú's single bite'.
However,
his nature is cruel and cunning,
and he has always lacked discernment.
He is greedy for honor and seeks to usurp power,
acting against the will of Heaven.
He resists with troops and exerts his might,
usurping and occupying Wúhuì.
Internally, he uses his cruel younger brothers;
externally, he entrusts military officials.
Above, he has betrayed the honor of the imperial court's favor and appointment;
below, he has let down the extraordinary generosity of the prime ministers.
Heaven's way punishes evil,
and neither men nor gods will protect him.
Though he is protected by the long Jiāng,
his life is as precarious as morning
dew.
Loyalty and integrity lead to strategic plans;
a junzi upholds noble conduct.
To lower one's dignity and join a rebel,
is what a righteous warrior would be ashamed of.
Wáng Zhú, a common man,
could not be coerced;
Yú Qī admired righteousness,
and offered his head in the court of
Yān.
How much more so for the benevolent people of Wúhuì, who have all received the nation's favor,
some appointed to commanderies with imperial seals,
others listed as close ministers,
yet you debase yourselves in the court of a treacherous man,
lowering your dignity to join a rebellious
faction,
bowing your heads and bending your knees?
Is this not shameful?
In the past, Gōng Shèng starved himself,
refusing to eat under Mǎng's court;
Lǔ Lián plunged into the sea,
ashamed to be a Qín subject.
The righteous actions of junzi
are consistent through a thousand generations.
I estimate your noble character from afar,
and surely you would not tolerate this!
In the past, the Martial Emperor of Wú
was praised throughout an era.
Though he achieved extraordinary feats in Wǎnyè,
he was also defeated in Xiāngyáng.
The Valiant Destroyer's imposing spirit
aimed at the Central Plains,
but when he arrived at the Jiāng, he became
enraged,
and his life ended at Dāntú.
Fortunately, the Former Lord inherited the Mandate,
with heaven-bestowed grand strategies.
He relied internally on the benevolent and enlightened teachings of his kind mother,
and externally on the loyal remonstrances of Zǐ Bù in court.
Moreover,
he had the clans of Zhūgě, Gù, Bù, Zhāng, Zhū, Lù, and Quán.
Thus, he was able to control the Baiyuè
and rule over Nánzhōu.
However, the rise of a military house
does not last beyond three generations.
Its
fortune did not endure a full century
before it surrendered and became subjects.
Now, Chén Mǐn, a mere Cāngbù Lìshǐ,
a seven-ranked stubborn ignoramus,
a sixth-grade low talent,
wishes to follow the lofty path of Huán Wáng
and tread
the supreme track of Dà Huáng.
Judging from afar, even the wise would
surely not permit this.
You gentlemen lower your heads,
unable to execute the plans of Zhái Yì;
and Master Gù bows his brows,
having already suffered the humiliation of
being bound.
The imperial chariot is heading east,
and will soon reach the Zǐguǎn.
All officials will hang their sashes,
soaring like clouds to the Fèngquē.
The strategies for victory in the temple
are secretly planned in the camp.
Then,
the elite troops from Jīngzhōu will be dispatched,
moving downstream to the east.
The sharp vanguard from Xúzhōu
will occupy Tángyì to the south.
The powerful soldiers of Zhēngdōng
will display their might at Lìyáng.
Flying bridges will cross the ferry at Héngjiāng,
and boats will
traverse the sandbars of Guābù.
Their might will shake Dānyáng,
capturing the bandit at Jiànyè.
How then will you gentlemen have the face to meet the scholars of Zhōngzhōu?
The petty bandit is separated by the ferry,
our messages are few and the path is wide.
I stretch my neck, looking south,
my heart filled with old affections.
Loyal and righteous people,
which era has been without them?
If one is in danger and cannot bring
peace,
or facing ruin and cannot preserve,
what then is one valued for?
Yǒngcháng's long-standing virtue,
I have always highly esteemed;
Yànxiān's youthful integrity,
is engraved in gold and stone;
Gōngzhòu's early friendship,
his kindness
and discipline are exceptionally profound;
Lìngbó's righteous reputation,
our close friendship is firmly established.
Above, I wish to serve with you gentlemen by the Zǐchén,
to achieve great deeds in the imperial records.
If not so,
you could also paddle boats on
the Hé and Wèi,
striking oars and singing clear songs.
Why debase yourselves at the hands of a petty bandit,
and fall into the calamity of rebellion?
Formerly, we were comrades;
now we are in different realms.
In the past, we were of one
body;
now we have become separate individuals.
Gazing at the Jiāng, I sigh deeply,
whom do I think of but you?
I hope you will devise a good strategy,
to preserve your excellent reputation."
Mǐn was of mediocre talent and lacked long-term strategy.
Once he occupied Jiāngdōng,
his administration was disorderly,
and he was not obeyed by the outstanding figures.
Moreover, his sons and younger brothers were brutal,
causing trouble wherever they went.
Zhōu Qǐ, Gù Róng, and their ilk constantly feared disaster.
Upon receiving Tán’s letter,
they all showed shame.
Qǐ and Róng secretly sent envoys to report to General Zhēngdōng Liú Zhǔn, urging him to send troops to the Jiāng River,
and they would act as internal allies.
Zhǔn sent Governor of Yángzhōu Liú Jī and General Níngyuǎn Héng Yàn, among others, to depart from Lìyáng.
Mǐn sent his younger brother Chǎng and General Qián Guǎng to Ujiāng to resist them.
He also sent his younger brother Hóng to be the Administrator of Lìyáng,
to garrison Niúzhǔ.
Qián Guǎng's family was in Chángchéng,
and he was Qǐ's fellow villager.
Qǐ secretly conspired to eliminate Chǎng.
Guǎng sent his subordinates Hé Kāng and Qián Xiàng to feign joining the army and deliver a secret message to Chǎng.
When Chǎng lowered his head to read the letter,
Kāng swung his sword and beheaded him,
proclaiming that the prefecture had already killed Mǐn,
and anyone who dared to move would have their three kinship groups executed.
They blew horns as an internal signal.
Guǎng had already ordered his troops to be at Zhūquèqiáo,
arraying them south of the river.
Qǐ and Róng also persuaded Gān Zhuó,
and Zhuó consequently turned against Mǐn.
Mǐn led over ten thousand men to battle Zhuó,
but before he could cross the river,
Róng waved a white feather fan at them,
and Mǐn’s forces scattered.
Mǐn fled eastward alone on horseback to Jiāngchéng,
where he was killed by a righteous army.
His mother, wife, and children were all executed.
Consequently, all the commanderies in Kuàijī killed Mǐn’s younger brothers, leaving none alive.
Wáng Rú
Wáng Rú
was a native of Xīnfēng, Jīngzhào.
He initially served as a military officer in the prefecture.
During the chaos, he migrated to Wǎn.
At that time, there was an imperial edict that all displaced people should be sent back to their hometowns.
Rú, seeing that Guānzhōng was desolate and ruined,
was unwilling to return.
General Zhēngnán Shān Jiǎn and General Nánzhōngláng Dù Ruí each sent troops to escort him,
and urged them to depart by a fixed date.
Rú then secretly gathered a group of lawless youths,
attacked the two armies by night,
and defeated them.
Dù Ruí led all his troops to attack Rú,
fighting at Nièyáng.
Ruí’s army suffered a great defeat.
Shān Jiǎn was unable to resist
and moved his camp to Xiàkǒu.
Rú then also captured Xiāngchéng.
Thereupon, Páng Shí of Nán'ān,
Yán Yí of Féngyì, Hóu Tuō of Cháng'ān, and others each led their factions to attack various cities and towns,
killing many magistrates and chiefs to support him.
Soon after,
his forces reached forty to fifty thousand men.
He proclaimed himself Grand General
and oversaw the two prefectures of Sī and Yōng.
Rú, fearing Shí Lè would attack him,
bribed Lè heavily
and became sworn brothers with him.
Lè also acknowledged his strength and accepted him.
At that time, Hóu Tuō occupied Wǎn
and was not in agreement with Rú.
Rú persuaded Lè, saying:
“Although Hóu Tuō is nominally a Han official,
he is in fact a Han rebel.
I constantly fear he will attack.
Brother, you should prepare for him.”
Lè had long been angry that Tuō was disloyal to him,
but he was wary of Rú as a vital ally,
so he did not attack Tuō.
When he heard Rú’s words,
he was very pleased.
He then secretly ordered his three armies to eat their rations and await orders that night.
They were to harness their chariots at cockcrow,
and those who departed late would be beheaded.
At dawn, they pressed against the gates of Wǎn and attacked it.
In twelve days, they captured it,
and Lè then beheaded Tuō.
Rú then extensively plundered Miǎnhàn
and advanced to threaten Xiāngyáng.
General Zhēngnán Shān Jiǎn sent his general Zhào Tóng to lead an army to attack him,
but for a year, they could not overcome him.
Their wisdom and strength were exhausted,
so they merely held the city defensively.
Wáng Chéng led an army to rush to the capital,
but Rú intercepted and defeated him.
For consecutive years, all the grain Rú planted turned into weeds.
There was a great famine in his army.
His followers attacked and plundered each other.
When the government army advanced to suppress them,
they all led their groups to surrender.
Rú, having no other recourse,
returned to Wáng Dūn.
Dūn’s cousin Lèng admired Rú’s bravery and martial skill,
and requested Dūn to assign him to his command.
Dūn said:
“People like him are fierce and dangerous, difficult to keep.
Your temper is impatient and hasty;
you cannot tolerate and nurture him.
He will only become a source of trouble.”
Lèng insisted,
and Dūn granted him the request.
Lèng kept him by his side
and treated him with great favor.
Rú frequently competed in archery with Dūn’s generals,
and repeatedly engaged in disputes and committed transgressions.
Lèng indeed could not tolerate him and flogged him with a staff.
Rú was greatly shamed by this.
Initially,
Dūn showed signs of disloyalty,
and Lèng often admonished him.
Dūn was always angry that he differed from him.
When Dūn heard that Rú had been humiliated by Lèng,
he secretly sent someone to provoke Rú’s anger
and urged him to kill Lèng.
Rú went to Lèng
and, during a private banquet,
requested to perform a sword dance for entertainment.
Lèng agreed.
Rú then danced with a saber as if playing,
gradually moving forward.
Lèng disliked this and repeatedly admonished him,
shouting at his attendants to drag him away.
Rú moved directly forward and harmed Lèng.
Dūn feigned surprise when he heard of it
and also arrested Rú and executed him.
Dù Zēng
Dù Zēng
was a native of Xīnyě,
and a cousin of General Nánzhōngláng Ruí.
In his youth, he was exceptionally brave and fierce,
able to swim in water while wearing armor.
He first served as a military advisor to Xīnyě Prince Xīn, General Zhènnán,
then became Magistrate of Huáróng,
and later South Barbarian Sīmǎ.
In every battle,
his bravery surpassed that of all three armies.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
Jīngzhōu became desolate and obstructed.
The former Yajmén general Hú Kàng gathered a multitude in Jìnglíng,
proclaimed himself Duke of Chǔ,
and falsely appointed Zēng as Administrator of Jìnglíng.
Kàng later became suspicious of his own partisans,
executing dozens of his brave generals.
Zēng felt insecure
and secretly plotted against him.
He humbled himself and bowed to serve Kàng,
who did not perceive it
and greatly trusted him.
At that time, Wáng Chōng, a bandit in Jīngzhōu, proclaimed himself Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and his forces were also strong.
He repeatedly sent troops to plunder the territory Kàng controlled.
Kàng was troubled by this
and asked Zēng for advice.
Zēng advised him to attack Chōng,
and Kàng thought it was a good idea.
Zēng reported to Kàng that he would take the sabers and halberds from beneath the tent to give to craftsmen for sharpening.
He then secretly led Wáng Chōng’s troops.
Kàng sent elite cavalry to confront Chōng,
leaving the city empty.
Zēng then beheaded Kàng and assimilated his forces,
proclaiming himself General Nánzhōngláng
and Administrator of Jìnglíng.
Zēng sought the daughter of Liú Wù, Administrator of Nánjùn, but failed to obtain her,
so he annihilated her entire family.
At that time, Emperor Mǐn sent Dìwǔ Yī as General Ānnán and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Zēng welcomed Yī in Xiāngyáng,
married Yī’s daughter to his elder brother’s son,
and then divided and occupied Miǎnhàn.
Soon after, Táo Kǎn was made the governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Upon reaching Shǐxīng,
the people of the province all advised him not to advance lightly.
Kǎn did not listen.
When he arrived at the provincial capital,
all the prefectures and counties had already welcomed Jī.
Kǎn first attacked Wēn Shào and Liú Shěn,
killing them both.
Jī sent his yámén Qū Lán back to the provincial capital,
falsely claiming to increase provisions,
secretly enticing his subordinates,
hoping to resist Kǎn.
Kǎn immediately arrested Lán and executed him,
then sent Dūhù Xǔ Gāo to attack Jī, who fled
and died of illness on the way.
Gāo dug up his corpse, beheaded it,
and also killed his two sons.
Jī's elder brother, Jǔ,
courtesy name Lìngshì.
He had a beautiful appearance,
and whenever he went out,
observers filled the road.
He was initially the Administrator of Nánpíng,
and gained merit by participating in the suppression of Chén Huī,
so he was promoted to Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
As he was about to take up his post,
he suddenly saw a man carrying a memorial and seeking an audience with Jǔ,
who introduced himself as Dù Língzhī from Jīngzhào.
Jǔ questioned him,
and he replied,
"The Jīngzhào from Heaven
has sent me to summon you to be a Master of Records."
Jǔ felt great displeasure about this.
A little over a month after arriving at the provincial capital, he died.
Zǔ Yuē
Zǔ Yuē, courtesy name Shìshǎo,
was the younger brother of Zǔ Tì, the Governor of Yùzhōu.
Initially, he was appointed Magistrate of Chénggāo due to his filiality and integrity,
and he and Tì were very close and affectionate.
Towards the end of Yǒngjiā,
he followed Tì across the river.
When Yuán Dì took control of the government,
he appointed him as a subordinate official,
and he was as renowned as Ruǎn Fú of Chénliú.
Later, he was transferred to Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
overseeing elections.
Yuē's wife had no sons and was jealous by nature,
and Yuē also dared not disobey her.
Once, he slept outside at night,
and was suddenly injured by someone.
He suspected his wife was responsible,
so Yuē requested to resign.
The Emperor did not permit it,
so Yuē privately left from the east gate of the encampment of the Right Sīmǎ.
Sīzhí Liú Wèi impeached him, saying:
"Yuē was fortunate to receive special favor,
holding a prominent position in the selection office,
evaluating people,
and was looked up to by all.
He should have been reverent and upright within,
righteous and proper externally,
preventing evil in its infancy,
and curbing harm.
Instead, conflict arose within his household,
trouble came from his maids and concubines,
and he himself suffered injury,
harming his body and hair.
The small-minded gossiped,
rumors spread far and wide,
defiling the pure transformation,
and burdening the enlightened era.
Heavenly grace endured his disgrace,
still comforting and soothing him,
yet Yuē disobeyed orders and left lightly.
Having neither clear wisdom to protect himself,
nor gratitude to uphold his duty,
he should be demoted and dismissed,
to silence public criticism."
The Emperor did not punish him for this.
Wèi repeatedly insisted on his accusation,
but ultimately was not granted permission.
When Tì gained merit in Qiáopèi,
Yuē gradually received important appointments.
After Tì died,
Yuē, from being a Shìzhōng, replaced Tì as Píngxī Jiāngjūn and Governor of Yùzhōu,
taking command of Tì's troops.
Yuē's half-brother, Guānglù Dàfū Nà, secretly told the Emperor:
"Yuē harbors a desire to usurp authority.
It would be acceptable to suppress and employ him.
Now, to openly serve at your side,
granting him power,
will lead to the root of rebellion."
The Emperor did not accept this.
People at the time also believed that Nà and Yuē, being born of different mothers,
were jealous of his favor and prominence,
hence Nà made these remarks.
However, Yuē ultimately lacked the talent to govern and control,
and was not supported by his officers and soldiers.
When Wáng Dūn raised an army,
Yuē returned to defend the capital,
leading his troops to Shòuyáng,
driving away Rèn Tái, the Administrator of Huáinán appointed by Dūn.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as a Marquis of the Fifth Rank,
promoted to Zhènxī Jiāngjūn,
and stationed at Shòuyáng
to serve as a barrier in the northern border.
He considered his status and generation to be no less than Xī and Biàn,
but was not included in Míng Dì's deathbed instructions,
and also hoped for the establishment of a mansion (kāifǔ).
Many of his requests and petitions were also not granted,
leading to resentment and disappointment.
Shí Cōng once pressed him with a large force,
and Yuē repeatedly memorialized requesting aid,
but the imperial army did not arrive.
After Cōng retreated,
the court council also wanted to build Tútáng to block the Hú invaders.
Yuē considered this to be abandoning him,
and his indignation grew.
Earlier,
the Empress Dowager sent Cài Mó to console him.
Yuē, upon seeing Mó,
glared and rolled up his sleeves,
criticizing and slandering the court administration.
When Sū Jùn raised an army,
he therefore promoted Yuē and blamed the current administration.
Yuē was overjoyed upon hearing this.
His nephews Zhì and Yǎn were both treacherous and fond of chaos,
and also supported his actions.
So, he ordered Tì's son, Pèi Grand Administrator Huàn,
and his son-in-law, Huáinán Grand Administrator Xǔ Liǔ, to join Jùn with their troops.
His wife,
who was Liǔ's elder sister, vehemently advised against it, but he did not listen.
When Jùn conquered the capital,
he forged an imperial edict making Yuē Shìzhōng, Tàiwèi, and Shàngshū Lìng.
Chén Guāng from Yǐngchuān led his subordinates to attack him.
One of Yuē's attendants, Yán Tū, resembled Yuē in appearance.
Guāng mistook him for Yuē and captured him.
Yuē scaled a wall and escaped.
Guāng fled to Shí Lè,
and Yuē's generals secretly colluded with Lè,
asking to be his internal support.
Lè sent Shí Cōng to attack him.
Yuē's troops disintegrated,
and he fled to Lìyáng.
He sent his nephew Huàn to attack Huán Xuān at Wǎncchéng.
Máo Bǎo reinforced Xuān,
attacked Huàn,
and defeated him.
Zhào Yìn then sent General Gān Miáo from Sānjiāo to Lìyáng.
Yuē, frightened, fled at night.
His general Qiān Téng led his troops and surrendered.
Yuē fled with several hundred personal retainers to Shí Lè.
Lè disdained his character
and did not grant him an audience for a long time.
Lè's general Chéng Xiá persuaded Lè, saying:
"The world is roughly settled.
We should clearly distinguish between loyalty and rebellion.
This is why Hàn Gāozǔ executed Dīng Gōng.
Now, those loyal to their lord are all promoted,
and those who betray and are disloyal are all exterminated.
This is why the world submits to Your Majesty.
Zǔ Yuē is still alive,
and I am truly perplexed by this.
[一０] Moreover, Yuē extensively invited guests
and seized the ancestral lands of his fellow villagers,
causing much resentment among the landowners."
Thereupon, Lè deceitfully told Yuē:
"Marquis Zǔ has come from afar,
and we have not yet fully enjoyed ourselves.
You can gather your sons and younger brothers for a simultaneous gathering."
On the appointed day,
Lè excused himself due to illness,
and ordered Xiá to invite Yuē and his clan members.
Yuē knew that disaster was at hand
and drank heavily to get drunk.
When he arrived at the marketplace,
he embraced his maternal grandson and wept.
Then, he was killed,
and over a hundred of his relatives, both immediate and extended, were all exterminated.
The women, entertainers, and concubines were distributed among the Hú people.
Initially,
Tì had a Hú slave named Wáng Ān,
whom he treated very kindly.
When he was in Yōngqiū,
he told Ān:
"Shí Lè is of your kind,
and I am not concerned with you alone."
So, he generously provided for Ān and sent him away.
Ān subsequently became a general for Lè.
When the Zǔ clan was exterminated,
Ān brought many followers to the marketplace to observe,
and secretly took Tì's illegitimate son Dàozhòng,
hid him as a Buddhist monk.
He was ten years old at the time.
After the Shí clan was destroyed, Dàozhòng returned.
Sū Jùn
In ancient times, emperors and kings often gave birth to extraordinary beings.
Were the descendants of Chúnwéi and Bóyǔ
any different?
They wore animal skins turned inside out,
ate rank meat and drank milk,
yet they shook the central regions
and came from afar.
Heaven had not yet repented of the calamity,
and their tribes proliferated.
Their customs were treacherous and depraved,
their nature wild and impulsive.
Previous histories record this
in great detail.
Xuāndì was troubled by their transgressions against the imperial order,
and therefore launched punitive expeditions.
Wǔwáng exiled them to the desolate frontier,
treating them like beasts.
Yet in the cold, exposed wilderness,
they watched the moon and observed the winds,
saw opportunities and raised dust,
seized chances to act violently.
The border towns could not relax their guard,
and the common people had no stable homes.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If not for Guǎn Zhòng,
we would have our hair unbound and our clothes buttoned on the left."
This statement means that he could instruct soldiers,
organize chariots and armor,
and once the border areas were subdued,
the interior would be secure.
Therefore, Yān built fortifications in the suburbs of Zàoyáng,
and Qín dug trenches along the dangers of Líntáo,
ascended Tiānshān,
cut across the earth's veins,
encompassed Xuántú,
and connected to the Huánghé.
This was all to prevent the barbarians from disrupting Zhōnghuá,
and their preparations were like this.
In the early reign of Hàn Xuāndì, Hūhán was first admitted,
settled in watchtowers and fortresses,
and entrusted with guard duties,
thus beginning to show leniency towards the Róngdí.
Guāngwǔ also moved tens of thousands from the Southern Court to Xīhé,
and later they were further relocated to Wǔyuán,
stretching across seven commanderies.
During the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
the suburbs of Fén and Jìn became desolate.
Guō Qīn submitted a memorial to Wǔdì,
and Jiāng Tǒng presented a strategy to Huìhuáng.
Both believed that Wèi had settled the Róngyí,
and they were interspersed among the towns and villages.
They requested to move them beyond the desert frontiers,
and establish a uniform system like in Yīn and Zhōu.
Tǒng worried about the Bìng department,
while Qīn was concerned about Méngjīn.
While their words were still on their lips,
Yuánhǎi had already arrived.
The saying goes,
"a miss by a hair's breadth,"
which was the humiliation of the Jìn ministers and grandees.
Cōng swore his army,
and in the east, he annexed Qí territory.
Yào's banners galloped,
and in the west, he crossed Lǒngshān,
overrunning the two capitals,
and slaughtering millions of common people.
The Son of Heaven crossed the river to command affairs,
occupying strategic strongholds.
Looking back at the Central Plains,
he was powerless to save it.
The area north of the Huái River
was largely abandoned.
The Hú people took advantage of our difficulties and troubles,
dividing their forces to stir up rebellion.
Some Jìn officials also obstructed military efforts from afar,
following suit and imitating them.
In general, Liú Yuánhǎi occupied Líshí in the first year of Yǒngxīng during Huìdì's reign and proclaimed himself Hàn.
Nine years later,
Shí Lè occupied Xiāngguó and proclaimed himself Zhào.
The Zhāng clan first occupied Hexī;
this year,
thirty-six years after Shí Lè,
Zhònghuá proclaimed himself King of Liáng.
One year later,
Rǎn Mǐn occupied Yè and proclaimed himself Wèi.
One year later,
Fú Jiàn occupied Cháng'ān and proclaimed himself Qín.
The Mùróng clan first occupied Liáodōng and proclaimed themselves Yān;
this year,
one year after Fú Jiàn,
Jùn first usurped the title.
Thirty-one years later,
Hòu Yān's Mùróng Chuí occupied Yè.
Two years later,
Xī Yān's Mùróng Chōng occupied Épáng.
This same year,
Qǐfú Guórén occupied Páohǎn and proclaimed himself Qín.
One year later,
Mùróng Yǒng occupied Shàngdǎng.
This same year,
Lǚ Guāng occupied Gūzāng and proclaimed himself Liáng.
Twelve years later,
Mùróng Dé occupied Huátái and proclaimed himself Nán Yān.
This same year,
Tūfà Wūgū occupied Liánchuān and proclaimed himself Nán Liáng,
and Duàn Yè occupied Zhāngyè and proclaimed himself Běi Liáng.
Three years later,
Lǐ Xuánshèng occupied Dūnhuáng and proclaimed himself Xī Liáng.
One year later,
Júqú Méngxùn killed Duàn Yè
and proclaimed himself Liáng.
Four years later,
Qiáo Zòng occupied Shǔ and proclaimed himself King of Chéngdū.
Two years later,
Hèlián Bóbó occupied Shuòfāng and proclaimed himself Dàxià.
Two years later,
Féng Bá killed Lí Bān
and occupied Hélóng and proclaimed himself Běi Yān.
Of all the land under heaven,
eight tenths were lost,
and there was none who did not display dragon banners and imperial robes,
establish altars to the land and grain,
with both Huá and Yí peoples gathered,
and all sorts of people present.
Some usurped prosperous market towns,
some controlled territories of several prefectures.
Their grand ambitions were contained internally,
their armies waged war externally,
exhausting their military might in victory and defeat,
and sacrificing human lives to the spears and arrows.
This period of warring states lasted one hundred and thirty-six years,
and Yuánhǎi is said to have been the instigator of this calamity.
Liú Yuánhǎi (Zǐhé, Liú Xuān)
Liú Yuánhǎi was
a Xīnxīng Xiōngnú person,
a descendant of Mòdú.
His given name violated the taboo of Gāozǔ's ancestral temple,
thus he was referred to by his courtesy name.
Initially,
Hàn Gāozǔ gave a woman of the imperial clan as a princess
to marry Mòdú,
and they pledged to be brothers.
Therefore, his descendants subsequently adopted the surname Liú.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
Wūzhūliú Ruòdī Chányú's son, the Right Àojiān Rìzhúwáng Bǐ, established himself as the Nán Chányú,
and moved to reside in Měijì, Xīhé.
Today's Líshí Zuǒguóchéng is the court to which the Chányú moved.
In the middle of the Zhōngpíng era,
Chányú Qiāngqú sent his son Yúfúluó to lead troops to assist Hàn
in suppressing the Yellow Turban rebels.
Coincidentally, Qiāngqú was killed by his own people,
so Yúfúluó remained with his forces in Hàn
and established himself as Chányú.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
he plundered Tàiyuán and Hédōng,
and encamped in Hénèi.
After Yúfúluó died,
his brother Hūchúquán succeeded him,
and made Yúfúluó's son Bào the Zuǒxiánwáng,
who was Yuánhǎi's father.
Wèi Wǔ divided his forces into five sections,
making Bào the commander of the Left Section,
and all the other section commanders were also of the Liú clan.
In the Tàikāng era,
Dūwèi were re-established:
the Left Section resided in Zīshì, Tàiyuán;
the Right Section in Qí;
the Southern Section in Púzi;
the Northern Section in Xīnxīng;
and the Central Section in Dàlíng.
Although the Liú clan was divided into five sections, they all resided along the Fén River in Jìnyáng.
Liú Cōng (劉聰), courtesy name Xuánmén (玄門),
also named Zǎi (載),
was Yuán Hǎi's (元海) fourth son.
His mother was Lady Zhāng (張夫人).
Initially,
when Cōng (聰) was in his mother's womb,
Lady Zhāng (張氏) dreamed that the sun entered her bosom.
When she awoke, she told Yuán Hǎi (元海),
who said:
"This is an auspicious omen;
you must not speak of it."
Fifteen months later, Cōng (聰) was born,
and there was an unusual white light at night.
His physique was extraordinary;
he had a white hair on his left ear,
more than two *chǐ* (尺) long,
and very lustrous.
From a young age, he was intelligent, astute, and fond of learning.
Doctor Zhū Jì (朱紀) was greatly amazed by him.
At fourteen,
he had thoroughly mastered the classics and histories,
and was conversant with the teachings of a hundred schools.
There was nothing of Sūn Wú's (孫吳) art of war that he did not recite.
He was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and adept at writing,
authoring over a hundred *huái* (懷) poems and more than fifty *fù* (賦) and encomiums.
At fifteen, he practiced combat techniques;
with ape-like arms, he was a good archer,
able to draw a bow of three hundred *jīn* (斤).
His physical strength was valiant and agile,
surpassing all others of his time.
Wáng Hún (王渾) of Tàiyuán (太原) saw him and was pleased,
saying to Yuán Hǎi (元海):
"This child is beyond my comprehension."
As a young man, he traveled to the capital,
where he befriended all the famous scholars.
Yuè Guǎng (樂廣) and Zhāng Huá (張華) found him especially remarkable.
Guō Yí (郭頤), the Administrator of Xīnxīng (新興), appointed him as Chief Clerk,
and he was recommended as a good general.
He entered service as Commandant of Cavalry, Separate Command,
and was successively promoted to Commandant of the Right Division.
He was skilled at management and reception,
and all the powerful families of the five divisions pledged allegiance to him.
Wáng Yóng (王顒) of Héjiān (河間) memorialized to appoint him as Chief Commandant of Chìshā (赤沙).
Cōng (聰), fearing that Yuán Hǎi (元海) in Yè (鄴)
might be harmed by Wáng Yǐng (王穎) of Chéngdū (成都),
then fled to Wáng Yǐng (王穎) of Chéngdū (成都),
and was appointed Right General of Accumulated Crossbows,
participating in the vanguard's military affairs.
When Yuán Hǎi (元海) became Northern Chányú (單于),
Cōng (聰) was made Right Wise King,
and followed him back to the Right Division.
When Yuán Hǎi (元海) assumed the position of Great Chányú (大單于),
Cōng (聰) was reappointed Lùlí Wáng (鹿蠡王).
After Yuán Hǎi (元海) killed his elder brother Hé (和),
the officials urged him to assume the imperial throne.
Cōng (聰) initially yielded to his younger brother, Wáng Yì (王乂) of Běihǎi (北海).
Yì (乂) and the dukes and ministers tearfully and earnestly entreated him.
Cōng (聰) eventually agreed,
saying:
"Yì (乂) and the dukes and ministers truly believe that the four seas are not yet settled,
and disasters and difficulties are still rampant,
so they prefer this aged, solitary one.
This is an affair of the state;
how dare this solitary one not comply?
Now I wish to follow the example of Rǔ Yǐn (魯隱) from afar,
and when Yì (乂) comes of age,
restore the bright ruler to him."
Thereupon, in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉), he usurped the imperial throne,
granted a general amnesty within the borders,
and changed the era name to Guāngxīng (光興).
He honored Yuán Hǎi's (元海) wife, Lady Shàn (單氏), as Empress Dowager.
His mother, Lady Zhāng (張氏), became the Emperor's Empress Dowager.
Yì (乂) was made Imperial Younger Brother,
holding the titles of Great Chányú (大單于) and Grand Chancellor.
He established his wife, Lady Hūyán (呼延氏), as empress.
He enfeoffed his son Càn (粲) as Wáng (王) of Hénèi (河內),
and appointed him as Commander with Imperial Insignia, General of the Guarding Army, and Overseer of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital.
He enfeoffed Yì (易) as Wáng (王) of Héjiān (河間),
Yì (翼) as Wáng (王) of Péngchéng (彭城),
and Kuí (悝) as Wáng (王) of Gāopíng (高平).
He dispatched Càn (粲) and his Eastern Expeditionary Wáng Mí (王彌), Longxiang General Liú Yào (劉曜), and others, leading forty thousand troops,
to drive deep into Luòchuān (洛川),
then exit Húanyuan (轘轅),
maneuvering between Liáng (梁), Chén (陳), Rǔ (汝), and Yǐng (潁),
capturing over a hundred camps and strongholds.
He appointed his Grand Minister of Works Liú Jǐng (劉景) as Grand Marshal,
Left Grandee Remonstrant Liú Yīn (劉殷) as Grand Chancellor,
and Right Grandee Remonstrant Wáng Yù (王育) as Grand Minister of Works.
The false Empress Dowager Shàn (單氏) was exquisitely beautiful,
and Cōng (聰) had incestuous relations with her.
Shàn (單) was Yì's (乂) mother.
Yì (乂) repeatedly spoke of this,
and Lady Shàn (單氏) died of shame and resentment.
Cōng (聰) grieved for her endlessly.
Later, he knew the reason for her death,
and Yì's (乂) favor gradually declined thereafter.
However, he still remembered Lady Shàn (單氏),
and did not immediately depose Yì (乂).
He also honored his mother as Empress Dowager.
He appointed his Commandant of the Guards Hūyán Yàn (呼延晏) as Commander with Imperial Insignia, Grand Commander of the Vanguard, and General of the Vanguard,
assigning him twenty-seven thousand elite troops.
He entered Luòchuān (洛川) from Yíyáng (宜陽),
ordering Wáng Mí (王彌), Liú Yào (劉曜), and General of the Guarding Army Shí Lè (石勒) to advance and join him.
Before Yàn (晏) reached Hénán (河南),
the imperial army suffered twelve defeats,
with over thirty thousand killed.
Mí (彌) and the others had not yet arrived,
so Yàn (晏) left his baggage train at Zhāng Fāng's (張方) old stronghold,
then attacked Luòyáng (洛陽),
capturing Píngchāng Gate,
and burning Dōngyáng (東陽), Xuānyáng (宣陽), and other gates, as well as various official residences and temples.
Emperor Huái (懷帝) dispatched Liú Mò (劉默), the Administrator of Hénán (河南), to resist him.
The imperial army was defeated at Shèmén (社門).
As Yàn (晏) lacked external support,
he exited Dōngyáng Gate,
plundering over two hundred daughters of princes and nobles before leaving.
At this time, the Emperor intended to cross the Hé (河) and flee east,
preparing boats on the Luò Shuǐ (洛水).
Yàn (晏) burned them all,
and returned to Zhāng Fāng's (張方) old stronghold.
Wáng Mí (王彌) and Liú Yào (劉曜) arrived,
and again joined Yàn (晏) to besiege Luòyáng (洛陽).
At that time, there was severe famine within the city;
people resorted to cannibalism.
Officials dispersed,
none maintaining their resolve.
Xuānyáng Gate fell,
and Mí (彌) and Yàn (晏) entered the Southern Palace,
ascended the front hall of Tàijí (太極),
and unleashed their troops to plunder extensively,
seizing all palace women and treasures.
Yào (曜) then killed over thirty thousand princes, nobles, and officials,
and built a Jingguan (京觀) [mound of skulls] north of the Luò Shuǐ (洛水).
He moved the Emperor, Empress Yáng (羊后) of Emperor Huì (惠帝), and the six imperial seals to Píngyáng (平陽).
Cōng (聰) granted a general amnesty,
changed the era name to Jiāpíng (嘉平),
and appointed the Emperor as Special Advance, Left Grandee Remonstrant, and Duke of Píng'ā (平阿).
He dispatched his General Who Pacifies the West Zhào Rǎn (趙染) and General Who Pacifies the West Liú Yǎ (劉雅), leading twenty thousand cavalry, to attack Wáng Mó (王模) of Nányáng (南陽) in Cháng'ān (長安).
Càn (粲) and Yào (曜) followed with a large army.
Rǎn (染) defeated the imperial army at Tóngguān (潼關),
and General Lǚ Yì (呂毅) died.
When the army reached Xiàguī (下邽),
Mó (模) surrendered to Rǎn (染).
Rǎn (染) sent Mó (模) to Càn (粲).
Càn (粲) killed Mó (模) and his son, Wáng Lǐ (王黎) of Fànyáng (范陽),
and sent General of the Guards Liáng Fēn (梁芬), Mó's (模) Chief Clerk Lǔ Yáo (魯繇), concurrent Palace Attendants Dù Ào (杜驁) and Xīn Mì (辛謐), and Běigōng Chún (北宮純) and others to Píngyáng (平陽).
Cōng (聰) was greatly enraged by Càn's (粲) killing of Mó (模).
Càn (粲) said:
"Your servant killed Mó (模) not because he was late in recognizing Heaven's will,
but because he was a close relative of the Jìn (晉) clan,
and could not die in loyalty during the calamity of Luòyáng (洛陽).
This is a great evil in the world,
so I executed him."
Cōng (聰) said:
"Even so,
I fear you will not escape the disaster of executing those who surrendered.
The Way of Heaven is most divine;
there is no principle without retribution."
He appointed Liú Yào (劉曜) as General of Chariots and Cavalry, Open-Palace with the Three Ducal Ministers, and Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州),
re-enfeoffing him as Wáng (王) of Zhōngshān (中山),
to guard Cháng'ān (長安).
Wáng Mí (王彌) was made Grand General,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Qí (齊).
Soon after, Shí Lè (石勒) and others killed Mí (彌) at Jǐwú (己吾) and annexed his troops,
reporting Mí's (彌) rebellion.
Cōng (聰) was greatly angered,
dispatching an envoy to reproach Lè (勒) for unilaterally harming a duke and minister,
accusing him of having an ambition for supreme power.
Fearing that Lè (勒) had ulterior motives,
he assigned Mí's (彌) troops to him.
After Liú Yào (劉曜) occupied Cháng'ān (長安),
Jiǎ Pǐ (賈疋), Administrator of Āndìng (安定), and all the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) submitted hostages.
Only Qū Tè (麴特), Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), and Zhú Huī (竺恢), Administrator of Xīnpíng (新平), held fast and did not surrender.
Protector of the Army Qū Yǔn (麴允) and Magistrate of Pínyáng (頻陽) Liáng Sù (梁肅), from the Nánshān (南山) of Jīngzhào (京兆), were about to flee to Āndìng (安定),
when they met Pǐ's (疋) hostage son in Yīnmì (陰密).
They escorted him back to Línjīng (臨涇),
and acclaimed Pǐ (疋) as General Who Pacifies the South,
leading fifty thousand troops
to attack Yào (曜) in Cháng'ān (長安).
Liáng Zōng (梁綜), Administrator of Fúfēng (扶風), and Qū Tè (麴特), Zhú Huī (竺恢) and others also led one hundred thousand troops to join them.
Yào (曜) dispatched Liú Yǎ (劉雅) and Zhào Rǎn (趙染) to resist,
but they were defeated and returned.
Yào (曜) then led all the elite troops of Cháng'ān (長安) to battle with the various armies at Huángqiū (黃丘).
Yào's (曜) army was utterly defeated,
and he was struck by a stray arrow,
retreating to Gānqú (甘渠).
Wáng Tū (王禿) and Jì Tè (紀特) of Dùrén (杜人) attacked Liú Càn (劉粲) in Xīnfēng (新豐).
Càn (粲) returned to Píngyáng (平陽).
Yào (曜) captured Chíyáng (池陽),
plundering over ten thousand people and returning to Cháng'ān (長安).
At this time, Yán Dǐng (閻鼎) and others enthroned the King of Qín (秦王) as Imperial Crown Prince,
entering Yōngchéng (雍城).
None of the Róng (戎) and Jìn (晉) in Guānzhōng (關中) failed to respond.
At that time, a shooting star rose from Niú (Altair),
entered Zǐwēi (Purple Forbidden Enclosure),
its dragon-like form winding and extending,
its light illuminating the ground,
and fell ten *lǐ* north of Píngyáng.
Upon inspection,
there was a piece of flesh thirty *bù* long
and twenty-seven *bù* wide.
Its stench was perceptible in Píngyáng.
Beside the flesh, there was always a sound of crying,
which did not cease day or night.
Cōng was deeply disgusted by it,
and summoned his ministers and dukes to ask:
"My lack of virtue
has caused this anomaly.
Each of you should speak your mind fully,
without any reservations."
Chén Yuándá and the academician Zhāng Shī and others stepped forward and replied:
"The anomaly of the changing star
portends impending disaster.
Your servants fear that there will be a matter of 'three empresses' in the imperial harem,
and the downfall of the state and ruin of the family
never fails to stem from this.
We pray that Your Majesty exercises caution."
Cōng said:
"This is a principle of *yīn* and *yáng*;
how does it concern human affairs!"
Soon after, Lady Liú gave birth to a snake and a fierce beast,
each harming people and then running away.
They were sought but not found.
After a short while,
they were seen beside the fallen flesh.
Shortly thereafter, Lady Liú died,
and then this flesh disappeared,
and the sound of crying also ceased.
From then on, the imperial harem became chaotic with favoritism,
and there was no order in who was admitted to the emperor's chambers.
Cōng appointed Liú Yì as Tàiwèi.
Initially, the position of Xiàngguó was established,
a rank of Shànggōng,
bestowed only posthumously upon those with exceptional merit and virtue.
Thereupon, he greatly reorganized the officialdom,
establishing Tàishī and Chéngxiàng.
From Dàsīmǎ upwards, the seven dukes
all held the rank of Shànggōng,
wearing green silk ribbons
and *yuǎnyóu guān* (distant journey hats).
He established Fǔhàn,
Dūhù,
Zhōngjūn,
Shàngjūn,
Fǔjūn,
〔一０〕Zhèn, Wèi, Jīng,
Qián, Hòu, Zuǒ, Yòu, Shàng, Xià Jūn,
Fǔguó,
Guānjūn,
Lóngxiáng,
Wǔyá Dàjiāngjūn.
Each camp was allotted two thousand soldiers,
and all these positions were given to his sons.
He established Zuǒ-Yòu Sīlì,
each governing over two hundred thousand households.
For every ten thousand households, an Nèishǐ was established,
making a total of forty-three Nèishǐ.
The Zuǒ-Yòu Fǔ of the Chányú
each governed one hundred thousand barbarian settlements,
with a Dūwèi appointed for every ten thousand settlements.
The Lìbù was abolished,
and Zuǒ-Yòu Xuǎncáo Shàngshū were established.
From Sīlì downwards, the six officials
all ranked below Púyè.
He established Yùshǐ Dàfū and Zhōumù,
all ranking as Yàgōng.
He made his son Càn the Chéngxiàng, concurrently Dàjiāngjūn, and Lùshàngshūshì,
and elevated him to be Jìn Wáng,
with an income from five prefectures.
〔一一〕Liú Yánnián was Lùshàngshū Liùtiáoshì,
Liú Jǐng was Tàishī,
Wáng Yù was Tàifù,
Rèn Yǐ was Tàibǎo,
Mǎ Jǐng was Dàsītú,
Zhū Jì was Dàsīkōng,
Liú Yào was Dàsīmǎ.
Yào again encamped at Wèiruì,
and Zhào Rǎn encamped at Xīnfēng.
Suǒ Qín marched eastward from Cháng'ān to attack Rǎn.
Rǎn, emboldened by repeated victories,
showed contempt for Qín.
His chief clerk, Lǔ Huī, said:
"Now Sīmǎ Yè and his ministers consider themselves to be in close proximity to the usurped royal domain.
Their strength and weakness are not the same,
so they will surely fight us to the death.
The general should arrange the formation and hold back troops to attack them;
they should not be taken lightly.
A cornered beast still fights,
let alone a state!"
Rǎn said:
"With the strength of Sīmǎ Mó,
I took him as easily as pulling apart rotten wood.
How can the young punk Suǒ Qín
stop my horse's hooves and sword's edge!
I will capture him before I eat."
In the morning, he led several hundred elite cavalry,
raced out to meet them,
fought west of the city,
suffered a defeat and returned.
He regretted, saying:
"I did not heed Lǔ Huī's words,
and thus came to this.
How can I face him!"
Thereupon, he executed Huī.
Before his execution, Huī said to Rǎn:
"General, you have stubbornly rejected advice and defied counsel,
foolishly incurring defeat.
Then you resent previous successes and harm the victorious,
executing the loyal and good,
to satisfy your ignorant anger.
What face do you have to live in this world for even a moment!
Yuán Shào did this before you,
and you follow in his footsteps.
Overthrow, defeat, and ruin
will surely follow for you as well.
My only regret is not being able to see Dàsīmǎ once before I die.
If the dead are unknowing, so be it;
but if they are knowing,
I shall descend to join Tián Fēng,
and I will surely accuse you to the Yellow Springs,
so that you cannot die in your bed."
He then shouted at the executioner:
"Let me face east."
Dàsīmǎ Yào, upon hearing this, said:
"A small puddle cannot hold a foot-long carp;
that describes Rǎn."
Yào returned his army to attack Guō Mò at Huáichéng,
seized eighty thousand *hú* of his rice and grain,
and established three garrisons to guard it.
Cōng sent an envoy to say to Yào:
"Now Cháng'ān barely breathes,
Liú Kūn's spirit wanders.
These are what the state should especially eliminate first.
Guō Mò is a petty villain,
how can he be worth troubling your divine strategy?
You can leave the Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Bèiqiū Wáng Yìguāng, to guard it.
You should return."
Thereupon, Yào returned to Púbǎn.
Soon after, Yào was summoned to assist in governing.
Zhào Rǎn raided Běidì.
He dreamt that Lǔ Huī was enraged,
drew his bow and shot him.
Rǎn awoke in shock and fright.
The next morning, as he was about to attack the city,
he was struck by a crossbow bolt and died.
Liú Cōng made Liú Càn the Prime Minister,
to manage all affairs of state.
He abolished the position of Chancellor and merged it with that of Prime Minister.
In Píngyáng, there was an earthquake,
and violent winds uprooted trees and unroofed houses.
In Guāngyì, a man named Yáng Chōng and his wife gave birth to a child with two heads.
His elder brother secretly ate it,
and died three days later.
Because his Imperial Ancestral Temple was newly completed,
Liú Cōng granted a great amnesty within the realm,
and changed the year name, establishing a new era.
Blood rained in his Eastern Palace's Yánmíng Hall,
penetrating the tiles on the ground to a depth of five inches.
Liú Yì disliked this,
and consulted his Grand Tutor Lú Zhì, Grand Mentor Cuī Wěi, and Grand Guardian Xǔ Xiá.
Zhì and the others said:
"The sovereign previously made Your Highness the Imperial Younger Brother
to appease public sentiment.
His true intention has long been for the Prince of Jìn.
From the princes and dukes downwards, none fail to discern his will and align themselves with him.
The position of Prime Minister,
since Cáo Cāo of Wèi,
is no longer an office for a mere subject.
The sovereign originally issued a clear edict
to make it an honorary post.
Now, he has suddenly bestowed it upon the Prince of Jìn,
whose ceremonial pomp and prestige surpass those of the Eastern Palace.
All affairs of state pass through him.
He has appointed a Grand Preceptor, a Grand General, and established various princely camps as his wings.
The momentum has shifted;
Your Highness cannot possibly be enthroned.
Moreover, it's not merely that you cannot be enthroned;
unforeseen dangers and calamities lie imminent.
You should make plans early.
The elite troops of the four guards number no less than five thousand.
The remaining princely camps are all still young in age,
and can be seized and taken.
The Prime Minister is frivolous;
a single assassin would suffice to trouble him.
The Grand General is out almost every day;
his camp can be attacked and taken.
Your Highness only needs to have the intention,
and twenty thousand elite troops can be immediately obtained.
March with drums towards the Yúnlóng Gate;
which of the imperial guards would not turn their spears and welcome you?
There is no need to worry about the Grand Marshal becoming an adversary."
Liú Yì did not follow their advice,
and thus stopped.
Liú Cōng visited the residence of Zhīnt Zhǔn, the Central Protector of the Army,
and took his two daughters as left and right Noble Consorts.
The elder was named Yuèguāng,
the younger Yuèhuá;
both were beauties of the realm.
Several months later,
Yuèguāng was made Empress.
Xún Yù, a palace attendant of the Eastern Palace, accused Lú Zhì and others of urging Liú Yì to rebel,
and how Liú Yì had refused them.
Liú Cōng then arrested Zhì, Wěi, and Xiá and imprisoned them in the imperial dungeons,
fabricating other charges to kill them.
He ordered Guàn Wēi to divine and oversee the Eastern Palace,
forbidding Liú Yì from attending court or offering congratulations.
Liú Yì, anxious and not knowing what to do,
then submitted a memorial to declare his innocence,
begging to become a commoner,
and to have his sons' enfeoffments revoked.
He praised the Prince of Jìn, Liú Càn, as suitable for the heir apparent position.
However, Guàn Wēi suppressed it and did not transmit it.
His Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Cáo Yì, attacked the Wènyáng Pass and Gōngqiū,
capturing them.
He killed Xú Fú, the Administrator of Qí Commandery,
and captured Liú Xuān, the Commander who upheld prestige.
More than forty commanderies, counties, and fortified walls between Qí and Lǔ surrendered.
Cáo Yì then seized territory,
marching west to Zhù'ā and Píngyīn.
His forces numbered over a hundred thousand.
He established garrisons along the Yellow River,
and then returned to Línzī.
Cáo Yì thus conceived the ambition to seize and hold all of Qí.
Shí Lè, seeing Cáo Yì's divided loyalty,
requested to attack him.
Liú Cōng, however, feared Shí Lè's annexation of Qí,
and thus shelved the request, not permitting it.
Liú Yào crossed from Méngjīn,
intending to attack Hénán.
General Wèi Gāi fled to Yīquán Wù.
Lǐ Jǔ dispatched General Lǐ Píng to garrison Chénggāo.
Liú Yào routed and destroyed them.
Lǐ Jǔ, fearful,
sent a hostage and requested to surrender.
At this time, Liú Cōng made his Empress Jìn an Empress Dowager,
established Noble Consort Liú as the Left Empress,
and Right Noble Consort Jìn as the Right Empress.
strongly remonstrated against the establishment of three empresses.
Liú Cōng did not accept it.
Instead, he made Chén Yuándá Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness,
outwardly showing favor to a worthy man,
but in reality seizing his power.
