Thereupon, Grand Commandant Fàn Lóng, Grand Marshal Liú Dān, Grand Minister of Works Hūyán Yàn, Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Jiàn, and others all submitted memorials to resign their posts,
yielding them to Chén Yuándá.
Liú Cōng then appointed Chén Yuándá Grand Censor and Administrator with the Ranks of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Liú Yào attacked Cháng'ān,
but was repeatedly defeated by the imperial army.
Liú Yào said:
"They are still strong;
they cannot be overcome."
He withdrew his troops and returned.
In Liú Cōng's palace, ghosts cried at night;
after three days, the sound moved to the Right Director of the Imperial Secretariat's office,
and then stopped.
His Empress Dowager Jìn engaged in licentious conduct.
Chén Yuándá reported it in a memorial.
Liú Cōng deposed Jìn,
and Jìn, ashamed and angry, committed suicide.
Jìn had received exceptional favor,
but Liú Cōng was pressured by Chén Yuándá's influence,
hence he deposed her.
Afterward, recalling her beauty,
he deeply resented Chén Yuándá.
Liú Yào advanced his troops to Shàngdǎng,
intending to attack Yángqǔ.
Liú Cōng sent an envoy to Liú Yào, saying:
"Cháng'ān usurping authority
is a deep shame for the state.
You should prioritize Cháng'ān.
Leave Yángqǔ entirely to the General of Agile Cavalry.
The opportune moment, in heaven and among men,
should be at hand.
You should return quickly."
Liú Yào turned back and destroyed Guō Mài,
then paid homage to Liú Cōng,
and then proceeded to Púbǎn.
Píngyáng experienced an earthquake,
and blood rained in the Eastern Palace,
covering an area of over a qǐng.
Liú Yào again advanced his army,
stationing it at Sùyì.
Qū Yǔn was severely short of supplies.
He abandoned Huángbái and encamped at Língwǔ.
Liú Yào advanced to attack Shàngjùn.
Administrator Zhāng Yǔ and Administrator of Fēngyì Liáng Sù fled to Yǔnwú.
Thereupon, the area west of the pass unanimously
responded to Liú Yào.
Liú Yào advanced to occupy Huángfù.
Liú Cōng's arsenal sank one zàng and five chǐ into the ground.
At this time, Liú Cōng's Palace Regular Attendants Wáng Shěn, Xuān Huái, Yú Róng,
Palace Aide-de-camp Guō Yī,
Central Yellow Gate Líng Xiū, and others were all favored and held power.
Liú Cōng indulged in feasts in the rear palace,
sometimes not emerging for a hundred days.
All officials had to convey their reports through Shěn and the others,
many of which were not presented to Liú Cōng.
They mostly decided matters based on their own likes and dislikes.
Thus, some old and meritorious officials were not rewarded,
while cunning and corrupt minor officials reached the rank of Two Thousand Piculs in a few days.
Military campaigns were launched every year,
but the generals and soldiers received no rewards of money or silk.
Yet, the families of the rear palace received enormous gifts and endowments, extending even to their servants,
often amounting to tens of millions.
The carriages, clothing, and residences of Shěn and others surpassed those of the princes.
Their sons, younger brothers, and maternal and paternal relatives who were commoners became Commanders or Prefects in the interior, numbering over thirty.
All were extravagant, corrupt, and cruel,
harming good people.
Zhīnt Zhǔn and his entire clan, both inner and outer members, flattered them and served them.
Guō Yī 郭猗 harbored resentment against Liú Yì 劉乂,
and said to Liú Càn 劉粲:
"The Grand Heir Apparent, even during His Majesty's reign, harbors ambitions of unruliness.
This is a deep enmity to Your Highness's father and son,
and a grave grievance to the common people of the four seas.
Yet His Majesty has shown excessive lenience,
not even replacing the positions of the two venerated ones.
Should a sudden upheaval arise,
I secretly fear for Your Highness.
Moreover, Your Highness is a descendant in the line of the High Ancestor,
and the legitimate heir of His Majesty.
All living beings
look up to you.
Affairs of state are momentous;
how can they be entrusted to others?
I heard yesterday that the Grand Heir Apparent met with the Grand General,
and spoke at length.
If their plan succeeds,
they promise to make His Majesty the Grand Supreme Emperor,
and the Grand General the Crown Prince.
Yì 乂 also promised the Army Protector the title of Grand Chányú 大單于,
and the two princes have already agreed to it.
The two princes reside in an unquestionable position,
and both wield heavy military power.
With this, they can launch their endeavor,
and what can prevent it from succeeding?
I say that this action by the two princes
is worse than that of beasts.
To betray one's father and kin—
how can others trust them?
Now they are merely coveting their immediate strength.
After the plan succeeds,
how can His Majesty remain unharmed?
Your Highness's brothers are indeed beyond words;
the Eastern Palace, the Chancellor, and the Chányú in Wǔlíng 武陵 are brothers;
how could they give way to others?
They promised to make trouble on the Shangsì 上巳 day of the third month, during a banquet.
If the matter is delayed, complications will arise,
so it is advisable to act early.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* 春秋傳 says: 'Even creeping grass cannot be completely removed,
let alone the lord's favored younger brother!'
I have repeatedly petitioned His Majesty,
but His Majesty's nature is kind towards his relatives,
and he considers my words untrue.
I am a survivor of punishment by blade and saw,
and have received the grace of His Majesty and Your Highness for my creation and upbringing.
Therefore, I do not fear the punishment for offending the dragon's scales,
and always speak what I hear,
hoping it will be accepted.
I will go in and speak of this.
I hope Your Highness will not reveal it,
but will secretly memorialize the situation."
"If you do not believe my words,
you may summon Wáng Pí 王皮, the Director of Works of the Grand General, and Liú Dūn 劉惇, the Sīmǎ 司馬 of the Army Protector.
Bestow favor and care upon them,
open the path for them to return to goodness, and question them,
and you will surely know."
Càn 粲 deeply agreed with him.
Yī 猗 secretly said to Pí 皮 and Dūn 惇:
"The rebellious acts of the two princes
are already fully known to His Majesty and the Chancellor.
Are you complicit?"
The two men were startled and said:
"No."
Yī 猗 said:
"This matter is certainly beyond doubt.
I pity your relatives and old friends who will all be exterminated."
Thereupon, he sighed and shed tears.
Pí 皮 and Dūn 惇 were greatly frightened,
and prostrated themselves, begging for mercy.
Yī 猗 said:
"I will make a plan for you.
Can you use it?"
Both men said:
"We respectfully obey the adult's instruction."
Yī 猗 said:
"The Chancellor will surely question you.
You just say that it is true.
If he reproaches you for not reporting it earlier,
you immediately answer:
'I am truly guilty of a capital crime.
However, I reverently reflected that His Majesty's sacred nature is generous and compassionate,
and Your Highness is devoted to your kin,
fearing that my words might lead to false accusations.'"
Pí 皮 and Dūn 惇 agreed.
Càn 粲 soon summoned and questioned the two men,
though not at the same time,
yet their testimonies were identical,
and Càn 粲 believed it to be true.
Earlier,
Jìn Zhǔn's 靳準 younger sister was a rúzǐ 孺子 (lady) to Yì 乂.
She committed adultery with a servant,
and Yì 乂, in anger, killed him,
and repeatedly mocked Zhǔn 準 with it.
Zhǔn 準 felt deep shame and resentment.
He persuaded Càn 粲, saying:
"The Eastern Palace is the deputy of all state affairs;
Your Highness should occupy it yourself,
and lead the Chancellery,
so that the world knows there is an early object of hope and reliance."
At this point,
Zhǔn 準 again persuaded Càn 粲, saying:
"In the past, Emperor Xiàochéng 孝成 disregarded Zǐzhèng's 子政 words,
allowing the Wáng 王 family to ultimately usurp power.
Is that acceptable?"
Càn 粲 said:
"How could it be acceptable!"
Zhǔn 準 said:
"Indeed,
as Your Sacred Majesty says.
This humble official has long wished to say something,
but being neither of the virtue of a 'reborn' person,
nor of imperial lineage,
I feared that as soon as loyal words were uttered,
the frost-like might would already have arrived,
and so I dared not."
Càn 粲 said:
"Just speak."
Zhǔn 準 said:
"I heard rumors of upheaval,
saying that the Grand General, Army Protector, and the Right and Left Assistants all plan to support the Grand Heir Apparent,
and are scheduled to foment rebellion in late spring.
Your Highness should prepare for this.
Otherwise,
I fear there will be the calamity of Shāngchén 商臣."
Càn 粲 said:
"What should be done?"
Zhǔn 準 said:
"His Majesty trusts and loves the Grand Heir Apparent,
and may not believe it if he hears of it suddenly.
In my humble opinion,
it would be advisable to relax the restrictions on the Eastern Palace,
and not cut off the Grand Heir Apparent's guests,
allowing frivolous individuals to associate with him.
Since the Grand Heir Apparent has always liked to treat scholars well,
he will surely not think of guarding against this suspicion.
Frivolous small men cannot but have rebellious intentions to encourage the Grand Heir Apparent.
Small men have beginnings but no ends,
and cannot be like those of Guàn Gāo 貫高's ilk.
Then, this humble official will openly memorialize his crimes for Your Highness,
and Your Highness and the Grand Tutor will detain and interrogate those with whom the Grand Heir Apparent has associated,
to uncover the origin of the matter.
His Majesty will surely punish him for the crime of 'lack of loyalty to the sovereign.'
Otherwise,
many in the court currently favor the Grand Heir Apparent.
Should His Majesty suddenly pass away,
I fear that Bǔ Chōu 卜抽 will seize the opportunity to be enthroned."
Thereupon, Càn 粲 ordered Bǔ Chōu 卜抽 to lead troops away from the Eastern Palace.
From the previous winter until this time, Sōng 聰
had ceased to receive court greetings,
and all military and state affairs were decided by Càn 粲.
He merely issued imperial decrees for killing, granting life, and appointing or dismissing officials,
and whatever Wáng Zhěn 王枕, Guō Yī 郭猗, and others desired was granted.
He also set up a market in the rear garden,
and held banquets and games with palace women,
sometimes remaining intoxicated for three days.
Sōng 聰 ascended the Qiū Gé 秋閤,
and executed Qíwú Dá 綦毋達, his Grandee of Advanced Rank,
Gōngshī Yù 公師彧, Grandee of the Grand Palace,
Wáng Yǎn 王琰 and Tián Xīn 田歆, Shàngshū 尚書,
Chén Xiū 陳休, Lesser Steward,
Bǔ Chóng 卜崇, Left Protector,
and Zhū Dàn 朱誕, Grand Minister of Agriculture, etc.,
all of whom were disliked by the eunuch faction.
Shìzhōng 侍中 Bǔ Gàn 卜榦 tearfully admonished Sōng 聰, saying:
"Your Majesty is currently promoting the governance of Wǔxuān 武宣,
wishing that there would be no hermit in the secluded valley.
How can you suddenly execute loyal and good men first,
and how will you leave a legacy for posterity?
In ancient times, Qín 秦 loved three good men but executed them,
and gentlemen knew that it would not achieve hegemony.
Despite Jìn Lì's 晉厲 wickedness,
after executing three ministers,
he still had a heart that could not bear it.
How can Your Majesty suddenly believe the words of those around you who love and hate,
and wish to execute seven ministers in one day!
The edict is still with your servant,
not yet proclaimed.
I beg you to bestow the benevolence of Heaven,
and withdraw the might of thunder.
Moreover, if Your Majesty merely wishes to execute them,
and does not reveal their crimes,
how will you demonstrate this to the four seas?
Is this the three-interrogation method of emperors and kings?"
Thereupon, he kowtowed until his head bled.
Wáng Shěn 王沈 shouted at Gàn 榦:
"Does Bǔ Shìzhōng 卜侍中 wish to oppose the edict?"
Sōng 聰 flicked his robes and entered,
and dismissed Gàn 榦 to commoner status.
At this time, Liú Yuè (劉岳) was locked in a standoff with the Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州), Zhāng Mào (張茂), on the Héshàng (河上).
Yào (曜) marched swiftly from Lǒng (隴) to Xīhé (西河).
His barbarian troops numbered 285,000.
They lined the riverbank with their camps,
stretching over a hundred *lǐ*.
The sound of bells and drums echoed, making the river boil and the earth tremble.
Never before in history had there been such a mighty army.
All of Mào's (茂) garrisons along the river fled at the sight of them.
Yào (曜) loudly declared his intention to cross the river by a hundred routes simultaneously
and proceed directly to Gūzāng (姑臧).
Liángzhōu (涼州) was greatly terrified,
and its people lost all will to resist.
All the generals wanted to cross quickly,
but Yào (曜) said:
"Although my army is mighty,
it does not surpass that of Wèi Wǔ (魏武) in his eastern campaign.
Those who have come out of fear of my might
are two-thirds of the total.
My central army's palace guards are already old and weary,
and cannot be used.
The Zhāng (張) clan knows that I have just pacified Chén Ān (陳安),
and my forces are abundant.
Judging by appearances and reputation,
they are not something that the armies of their five commanderies can withstand.
They will certainly be afraid and surrender,
submit to my control, and declare themselves my vassals.
What more could I ask for!
You can test this;
within ten days,
if Zhāng Mào's (張茂) memorial does not arrive,
then I will have failed you."
Mào (茂) was indeed terrified,
and sent an envoy to declare himself a vassal,
offering 1,500 horses,
3,000 cattle,
380 *jīn* of gold,
700 *jīn* of silver,
twenty female entertainers,
and countless other precious treasures, pearls, jade, and fine goods from various regions.
Yào (曜) was greatly pleased,

and through his Grand Minister of the Court, Tián Sōng (田崧), he appointed Mào (茂) as Commissioner with Imperial Authority (使持節), Acting Grand Axe-bearer (假黃鉞), Palace Attendant (侍中), Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Palace (都督中外諸軍事), Grand Preceptor (太師), concurrently Grand Marshal (領大司馬), Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州 Mù 牧), concurrently Grand Protector of the Western Regions (領西域大都護), Protector of the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) Tribes (護氐羌校尉), and King of Liáng (涼王).
Yào (曜) returned from west of the river
and sent Hú Yuán (胡元) to raise his father's and wife's tombs to a height of ninety *chǐ*.
Yáng Nándí (楊難敵), fearing for himself after Chén Ān (陳安) had been pacified,
fled to Hànzhōng (漢中).
The General Who Guards the West, Liú Hòu (劉厚), pursued him,
capturing over a thousand carts of his baggage
and more than 6,000 men and women,
and returned them to Qiúchí (仇池).
Yào (曜) appointed the Grand Minister of the Court, Tián Sōng (田崧), as General Who Guards the South (鎮南大將軍) and Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
stationed at Qiúchí (仇池).
He appointed Liú Yuè (劉岳) as Palace Attendant (侍中), Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Palace (都督中外諸軍事),
and advanced his title to King of Zhōngshān (中山王).
Originally,
during Jìn Zhǔn's (靳準) rebellion,
Yào's (曜) heir apparent Yìn (胤) was lost among the Hēinì Yùjú (黑匿郁鞠) tribe.
By this time,
Yìn (胤) revealed his identity.
Yùjú (郁鞠) was greatly astonished,
provided him with clothes and a horse,
and sent his son to escort him.
Yào (曜) wept sadly upon seeing Yìn (胤),
praised Yùjú's (郁鞠) loyalty and sincerity,
and appointed him Commissioner with Imperial Authority (使持節), Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍), General of Loyal Righteousness (忠義大將軍), and Left Worthy King (左賢王).
Yìn's (胤) courtesy name was Yìsūn (義孫).
He had a handsome appearance
and was skilled in witty repartee.
At ten years old,
he was seven *chǐ* five *cùn* tall,
with eyebrows and sideburns like a painting.
Cōng (聰) considered him extraordinary
and said to Yào (曜):
"How can this child's spirit and aura be the same as Yìzhēn's (義真)!
He should certainly be your eldest legitimate son.
You should consider King Wén's (文王) intention to set aside Bóyìkǎo (伯邑考) and establish King Wǔ (武)."
Yào (曜) replied:
"My feudal state
is barely sufficient to maintain ancestral sacrifices, and that is enough.
One cannot disrupt the order of seniority."
Cōng (聰) said:
"Your achievements reach heaven and earth,
and your state encompasses a hundred cities.
You are destined to inherit the position of Grand Preceptor (太師) and be entrusted with the authority to command expeditions.
Of the five marquises and nine earls who possess the authority to command expeditions,
your descendants,
how can you say they are like other feudal states!
Since Yìzhēn (義真) cannot emulate the noble humility of Tàibó (太伯),
I will simply grant him a state."
Yìzhēn (義真) was Yào's (曜) son Jiǎn's (儉) courtesy name.
Thereupon, Jiǎn (儉) was enfeoffed as King of Línhǎi (臨海王),
and Yìn (胤) was established as heir apparent.
Although Yìn (胤) had been separated from his family and endured hardships at a young age,
wandering through remote and difficult lands,
he possessed a distinguished bearing and handsome features,
bright and outstanding.
He was eight *chǐ* three *cùn* tall,
his hair was as long as his body,
he was strong and skilled in archery,
swift and agile like wind and clouds.
Yào (曜) consequently held him in high regard,
and his court officials also favored him.
Yào (曜) then looked at his subordinates and said:
"Yìsūn (義孫) can be said to be one who does not wither in the cold of winter
and is not stained by dirt.
Although Yìguāng (義光) was established earlier,
he is young and overly cautious,
which I fear makes him ill-suited to be the heir apparent in these times.
I worry that this would not secure the altars of soil and grain above,
nor show love to Yìguāng (義光) below.
Yìsūn (義孫) is older and possesses bright virtue,
and he is also the former heir apparent.
I wish to emulate King Wén of Zhōu (周文) in the distant past
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) in more recent times,
so that the ancestral temple may enjoy the security of Mount Tài (泰),
and Yìguāng (義光) may enjoy boundless blessings.
What are your thoughts, gentlemen?"
His Grand Tutor Hūyán Yàn (呼延晏) and others all said:
"Your Majesty's distant emulation of Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢)
is an immeasurable plan for the state.
Not only will we, your subjects, rely on it,
but it is also truly a blessing for the ancestral temple and all under heaven."
The Left Grandee of Light, Bǔ Tài (卜泰), the Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince, Hán Guǎng (韓廣), and others stepped forward and said:
"If Your Majesty believes that deposition and establishment is correct,
then you should not obscure the brightness of the sun and moon
by seeking opinions from your subordinates.
If you have doubts,
then you must desire to hear our differing opinions.
We humbly believe that to sincerely depose the Crown Prince is wrong.
Why?
In ancient times, before King Wén of Zhōu (周文) had established an heir,
it was acceptable for him to choose a sage and elevate him.
Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) deposed and established heirs based on the beauty of their mothers.
How can this be a model for a sagely dynasty!
If Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) truly wished for Dōnghǎi (東海) to inherit the succession,
why could he not be like Emperor Míng (明帝)?
Imperial Son Yìn (胤) possesses martial and civil talents,
and his divine bearing is profound and far-reaching.
He is indeed uniquely outstanding for his time,
sufficient to emulate Zhōu Fā (周發);
however, the Crown Prince is filial, friendly, benevolent, and compassionate,
with noble and refined aspirations,
also sufficient to uphold the sacred foundation of the state
and be a virtuous ruler in times of peace.
Moreover, the position of heir apparent
is where the hopes of all humanity and spirits are placed.
It cannot be lightly deposed or changed.
If Your Majesty truly insists on this,
we, your subjects, can only die,
and would not dare to obey the decree."
Yào (曜) fell silent.
Yìn (胤) stepped forward, weeping, and said:
"A benevolent father to his son
should strive to embody the kindness of the *shījīu* (尸鳩, a kind of dove),
how can you replace Xī (熙) and establish me!
If Your Majesty's misplaced kindness is such,
I request to die here
to show my true heart.
Furthermore, if Your Majesty loves and overlooks my inadequacy,
considering me barely capable of guidance,
I should also be able to assist Yìguāng (義光)
and respectfully follow the sacred path."
He then sighed and shed tears,
moving the court officials to sorrow.
Yào (曜) also considered that the Crown Prince was born to the Yáng (羊) clan,
and Yáng (羊) was favored,
so he felt pity and could not bear to depose him,
and thus stopped the matter.
He posthumously honored his former wife Bǔ (卜) clan as Empress Yuándào (元悼皇后),
who was Yìn's (胤) mother.
Bǔ Tài (卜泰) was Yìn's (胤) maternal uncle.
Yào (曜) commended him
and appointed him Upper Grandee of Light (上光祿大夫), Acting Grand Minister Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (儀同三司), and concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (領太子太傅).
Yìn (胤) was enfeoffed as King of Yǒng'ān (永安王),

appointed Palace Attendant (侍中), Grand General of the Guards (衞大將軍), Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs of the Two Palaces' Guards (都督二宮禁衞諸軍事), Established a Department with Authority Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (開府儀同三司), and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat (錄尚書事),
concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (領太子太傅),
and given the title Imperial Son (皇子).
He commanded Xī (熙) to treat Yìn (胤) with the respect due to a family elder.
At this time, a phoenix with five chicks soared above the former Wèiyáng (未央) Palace for five days.
They wailed mournfully, ate nothing, and all died.
Yào (曜) established Empress Liú (劉) as empress.
Yào dispatched his military attendant, Liú Lǎng (劉朗), leading thirty thousand cavalry, to attack Yáng Nándí (楊難敵) at Chóuchí (仇池).
They were unsuccessful,
but plundered over three thousand households before returning.
Zhāng Jùn (張駿), hearing that Yào's (曜) army had been defeated by the Shí (石) clan,
then renounced Yào's (曜) official titles,
and again claimed the title of Grand General of Jìn (晉) and Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州).
He dispatched the Administrator of Jīnchéng (金城), Zhāng Làng (張閬), along with the Protector of Páohǎn (枹罕), Xīn Yàn (辛晏), and General Hán Pú (韓璞), among others, leading tens of thousands of troops,
to attack and plunder the various commanderies of Qínzhōu (秦州) from Dàxià (大夏).
Yào (曜) dispatched Liú Yìn (劉胤), leading forty thousand infantry and cavalry, to strike them.
They were stalemated across the Táo (洮) River for over seventy days.
The Champion General, Hūyán Nàjī (呼延那雞), led two thousand cavalry of the imperial guard,
cutting off their supply route.
Yìn (胤) led his army across the river and pressed them.
Pú's (璞) army was greatly defeated
and fled back to Liángzhōu (涼州).
Yìn (胤) pursued them,
caught up with them at Lìngjū (令居),
and beheaded twenty thousand.
Zhāng Làng (張閬) and Xīn Yàn (辛晏), leading tens of thousands of troops, surrendered to Yào (曜).
They were all appointed generals
and enfeoffed as marquises.
Shí Lè (石勒) dispatched Shí Jìlóng (石季龍), leading forty thousand troops,
to march west from Zhǐguān (軹關) to attack Yào (曜).
Over fifty counties in Hédōng (河東) responded to him.
He then advanced to attack Púbǎn (蒲坂).
Yào (曜) was about to go east to save Púbǎn (蒲坂),
but feared that Zhāng Jùn (張駿) and Yáng Nándí (楊難敵) would take advantage of the void to attack Cháng'ān (長安).
He dispatched his Prince of Héjiān (河間), Shù (述), to mobilize the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) peoples to garrison Qínzhōu (秦州).
Yào (曜) brought all his elite forces, both naval and land, to confront them,
crossing the river north of Wèiguān (衞關).
Jìlóng (季龍) was afraid
and withdrew his army.
Yào (曜) pursued him,
caught up at Gāohòu (高候),
fought a great battle,
and defeated him.
He beheaded Shí Zhān (石瞻), one of his generals,
with bodies strewn for over two hundred *lǐ*,
and captured countless stores of equipment.
Jìlóng (季龍) fled to Cháogē (朝歌).
Yào (曜) then crossed the river from Dàyáng (大陽)
and attacked Shí Shēng (石生) at Jīnyǒng (金墉),
breaching the Qiānjīn (千金) Dam to flood it.
Yào (曜) did not comfort his officers and men,
but indulged solely in drinking and gambling with his favored ministers.
Some of his attendants tried to remonstrate,
but Yào (曜) grew angry,
considering it "ominous speech,"
and executed them.
Great winds uprooted trees,
and dense fog filled all four directions.
Hearing that Jìlóng (季龍) had advanced to Shímén (石門),
and then learning that Lè (勒) himself had led a large army across the river,
he finally began to discuss reinforcing the garrison at Xíngyáng (滎陽)
and blocking Huángmǎguān (黃馬關).
Soon after, the scouts at Luòshuǐ (洛水) engaged Lè's (勒) vanguard,
captured a Jié (羯) soldier,
and sent him to Yào (曜).
Yào (曜) asked:
"Did the 'Big Barbarian' come himself?
How large or small is his army?"
The Jié (羯) soldier replied:
"The 'Big Barbarian' came himself;
his army is so mighty it cannot be resisted."
Yào's (曜) expression changed.
He ordered the siege of Jīnyǒng (金墉) to be lifted
and arrayed his forces west of Luò (洛) River,
stretching over ten *lǐ* north to south.
Yào (曜) had been given to excessive drinking since youth,
and it became especially severe in his later years.
When Lè (勒) arrived,
Yào (曜) was about to go to battle,
having drunk several *dǒu* of wine.
His usual red horse inexplicably stumbled and fell,
so he rode a smaller horse.
Before going out,
he again drank over a *dǒu* of wine.
When he reached the Xīyáng Mén (西陽門),
he pointed to the formation and straightened it.
Lè's (勒) general, Shí Kān (石堪), took advantage of this to charge,
and Yào's (曜) army was utterly routed.
Yào (曜), in a drunken stupor, fled,
his horse stumbled into a stone ditch,
and he fell onto the ice.
He suffered over ten wounds,
three of which penetrated his body,
and was captured by Kān (堪),
who sent him to Lè (勒).
Yào (曜) said:
"King Shí (石)!
Do you remember the covenant at Chóngmén (重門)?"
Lè (勒) had Xú Guāng (徐光) tell Yào (曜):
"Today's events
are ordained by Heaven;
what more can be said!"
Yào (曜) was imprisoned in the office of the Hénán (河南) Assistant,
and the wound surgeon, Lǐ Yǒng (李永), was ordered to treat him,
before he was sent back to Xiāngguó (襄國).
Yào's (曜) wounds were severe.
Lè (勒) had him carried in a horse-drawn carriage,
and ordered Lǐ Yǒng (李永) to ride with him.
Sūn Jī (孫機), an elder of Běiyuàn Shì (北苑市), presented gifts and requested to see Yào (曜).
Lè (勒) granted permission.
Jī (機) offered wine to Yào (曜) and said:
"My Lord Púgǔ (僕谷),
you claimed emperorship west of the passes.
You ought to have held your ground,
and protected your territory.
You lightly used your army,
and were defeated at Luòyáng (洛陽).
Your fortune is exhausted,
destroyed by Heaven.
Open a great portion,
and hold a cup."
Yào (曜) said:
"Why are you so strong?
I will drink for this old man."
Lè (勒), hearing this,
his expression changed to one of sorrow, and he said:
"A man whose kingdom is lost is still able to criticize this old man."
Yào (曜) was housed in the small city of Yǒngfēng (永豐) in Xiāngguó (襄國),
provided with his concubines,
and strictly guarded.
Liú Yuè (劉岳) and Liú Zhèn (劉震), among others, were dispatched on horseback,
accompanied by men and women,
dressed, to see Yào (曜).
Yào (曜) said:
"I long thought you all were dust and ashes.
King Shí (石) is benevolent and generous,
pardoning you all until now.
But I killed Shí Tuō (石他),
Today's disaster
is my due."
They feasted all day and then departed.
Lè (勒) ordered Yào (曜) to write a letter to his crown prince Xī (熙),
Yào (曜) only ordered Xī (熙),
"Work with the various ministers to maintain the state;
do not change your mind because of me."
Lè (勒) read it and disliked it,
and Yào (曜) was later killed by Lè (勒).
Xī (熙), along with Liú Yìn (劉胤) and Liú Xián (劉咸), debated whether to retreat to Qínzhōu (秦州).
The Grand Secretariat Hú Xūn (胡勳) said:
"Although we have lost our lord,
the state is still complete.
The generals and soldiers are united in spirit,
and there has been no defection.
We can join forces to hold the difficult passes;
it is not too late to flee."
Yìn (胤) disagreed,
was angered by his disheartening the troops,
and executed him.
He then led all the officials to flee to Shàngguī (上邽).
Liú Hòu (劉厚) and Liú Cè (劉策) both abandoned their posts and fled to him.
Guānzhōng (關中) was in turmoil.
Generals Jiǎng Yīng (蔣英) and Xīn Shù (辛恕), leading several hundred thousand troops,
held Cháng'ān (長安),
and sent envoys to invite Lè (勒).
Lè (勒) dispatched Shí Shēng (石生) with the army from Luòyáng (洛陽) to assist them.
Yìn (胤) and Liú Zūn (劉遵), leading tens of thousands of troops,
advanced from Shàngguī (上邽) to attack Shí Shēng (石生) at Cháng'ān (長安).
The various commanderies of Lǒngdōng (隴東), Wǔdū (武都), Āndìng (安定), Xīnpíng (新平), Běidì (北地), Fúfēng (扶風), and Shǐpíng (始平), both Rong (戎) and Xia (夏) peoples, all raised armies to support Yìn (胤).
Yìn (胤) encamped at Zhòngqiáo (仲橋),
while Shí Shēng (石生) strongly defended Cháng'ān (長ān).
Lè (勒) ordered Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) to lead twenty thousand cavalry to resist Yìn (胤).
They fought at Yìqú (義渠),
and Yìn (胤) was defeated by Jìlóng (季龍),
with over five thousand killed.
Yìn (胤) fled to Shàngguī (上邽).
Jìlóng (季龍) pursued the fleeing army,
with bodies strewn for a thousand *lǐ*,
and Shàngguī (上邽) was routed.

Jìlóng (季Lóng) captured the false crown prince Xī (熙), King of Nányáng (南陽) Liú Yìn (劉胤), along with their generals, ministers, various princes, and their high-ranking officials, marshals, dukes, and marquises, numbering over three thousand,
and killed them all.

He moved their palace officials, civil and military, the displaced people from east of the passes, and the prominent families of Qín (秦) and Yǒng (雍), totaling over nine thousand people, to Xiāngguó (襄國).
He also buried alive their princes and dukes, along with over five thousand Túcá (屠各) people from five commanderies, at Luòyáng (洛陽).
Yào (曜) reigned for ten years before his defeat.
Initially,
Yuánhǎi (元海) usurped the throne in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) of Emperor Huái (懷),
and through Yào (曜)'s three generations,
a total of twenty-seven years passed,
until their destruction in the fourth year of Xiánhé (咸和) of Emperor Chéng (成).
Yóu Lún (游綸) and Zhāng Chái (張豺) of Guǎngpíng (廣平) gathered tens of thousands of men,
received provisional appointments from Wáng Jùn (王浚),
and occupied Yuànxiāng (苑鄉).
Lè (勒) dispatched Qú Ān (夔安), Zhī Xióng (支雄) and other seven generals to attack them,
and they broke through their outer fortifications.

Wáng Jùn (王浚) sent his military supervisor Wáng Chāng (王昌) and the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) contingents of Duàn Jiùliùjuàn (段就六眷), Mòbēi (末柸), Pǐdī (匹磾) and others, numbering over fifty thousand, to suppress Lè (勒).
At this time, the city walls had not yet been repaired,
so Lè (勒) built an internal wall and multiple fences in Xiāngguó (襄國),
setting up barriers to await them.
Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) encamped at Zhǔyáng (渚陽).
Lè (勒) repeatedly sent his generals out to challenge them,
but they were frequently defeated by Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷).
Upon hearing that the enemy was extensively building siege equipment,
Lè (勒) turned to his generals and advisors and said:
"Now the bandits are pressing closer,
their forces are numerous while ours are few.
I fear that if the siege is not broken,
external relief will not arrive,
and our internal provisions will be exhausted.
Even if Sūn Wú (孫吳) were reborn,
he would not be able to hold out.
I intend to select and train my officers and soldiers,
then deploy a large formation in the open field to decide this.
What do you think?"
All the generals replied:
"It is advisable to hold firm and wear out the enemy.
When their army is exhausted, they will retreat on their own.
If we pursue and attack them then,
there will be nothing we cannot overcome."
Lè (勒) turned to Zhāng Bīn (張賓) and Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) and said:
"What do you two think?"
Bīn (賓) and Cháng (萇) both said:
"We hear that Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) has scheduled his 'sending of the dead to the northern wall' for the first ten days of next month.
His large army has come from afar,
fighting and defending for many days.
Believing our forces to be few and weak,
they will assume we dare not sally forth,
and their vigilance will surely slacken.
Among the fierce warriors of the Duàn (段) clan,
Mòbēi (末柸) is the most prominent.
His soldiers are the most elite and brave,
and all of them are under Mòbēi's (末柸) command.
We should stop sending out challenges,
showing them weakness.
Quickly dig over twenty sally ports in the northern rampart.
When the enemy's formations are not yet stable,
take them by surprise,
directly charging Mòbēi's (末柸) camp.
The enemy will surely be shocked and panic-stricken,
unable to devise a plan in time.
This is what is meant by 'swift thunder leaves no time to cover the ears.'
Once Mòbēi's (末柸) forces flee,
the rest will naturally collapse and disperse.
After capturing Mòbēi (末柸),
Péngzǔ (彭祖) can be secured by pointing to the hour."
Lè (勒) smiled and adopted their suggestion.
He immediately appointed Cháng (萇) as Commander-in-Chief for Attacks and Battles,
and sally ports were built on the north wall.
When the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) encamped in the northern rampart,
Lè (勒) waited until their formation was not yet stable, then
personally led his officers and soldiers in a drum-beating uproar from atop the city.
At the same moment, Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) led all the hidden troops from the sally ports to attack them,
capturing Mòbēi (末柸) alive.
Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) and his forces then fled and scattered.
Cháng (萇) pursued them, taking advantage of the victory,
leaving bodies strewn for over thirty *lǐ*,
and capturing five thousand armored horses.
Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) gathered his remaining forces
and encamped at Zhǔyáng (渚陽).
He sent an envoy to sue for peace,
offering armored horses, gold, and silver,
and also presented Mòbēi's (末柸) three younger brothers as hostages, requesting Mòbēi's (末柸) return.
All the generals advised Lè (勒) to kill Mòbēi (末柸) to demoralize the enemy.
Lè (勒) said:
"The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) of Liáoxī (遼西) are a strong nation,
and have always had no enmity with us;
they were merely employed by Wáng Jùn (王浚).
If we kill one person now,
we will incur the hatred of an entire nation.
This is not a good plan.
If we release him, they will surely be pleased,
and will no longer serve Wáng Jùn (王浚)."
Thereupon, Lè (勒) accepted their hostages
and sent Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) to ally with Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) at Zhǔyáng (渚陽),
forming a brotherhood.
Jiùliùjuàn (就六眷) and others then withdrew.
Lè (勒) sent his military advisor Yán Zōng (閻綜) to present the victory report to Liú Cōng (劉聰).
Thereupon, Yóu Lún (游綸) and Zhāng Chái (張豺) requested to surrender and become vassals.
Lè (勒) intended to attack Yōuzhōu (幽州) and needed to preserve his officers and soldiers,
so he granted their request for the time being,
appointing them both as generals.
Subsequently, he dispatched his forces to raid Xìndū (信都),
killing Wáng Xiàng (王象), the Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州).
Wáng Jùn (王浚) again appointed Shào Xíng (邵行) as Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州),
who took refuge in Xìndū (信都).
In the first year of Jiànxīng (建興) [313 CE],
Shí Jìlóng (石季龍) attacked the Three Terraces of Yè (鄴).
Yè (鄴) fell,
and Liú Yǎn (劉演) fled to Lǐnqīu (廩丘).
Generals Xiè Xū (謝胥), Tián Qīng (田青), Láng Mù (郎牧) and others led the displaced people from the Three Terraces to surrender to Lè (勒).
Lè (勒) appointed Táo Bào (桃豹) as the Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡) to pacify them.
He adopted Duàn Mòbēi (段末柸) as his son,
appointed him as an Imperial Envoy, General who Guards the North, and Duke of Běipíng (北平),
and sent him back to Liáoxī (遼西).
Mòbēi (末柸), grateful for Lè's (勒) great kindness,
bowed three times facing south each day during his journey.
The Duàn (段) clan thus wholeheartedly submitted,
and from then on, Wáng Jùn's (王浚) authority gradually waned.
Lè (勒) attacked Yuànxiāng (苑鄉),
capturing Yóu Lún (游綸) and making him his chief clerk.
He attacked the Qǐhuó (乞活) leader Lǐ Yùn (李惲) at Shàngbái (上白),
beheading him.
When he was about to bury the surrendered soldiers alive,
he saw Guō Jìng (郭敬) and recognized him,
saying:
"Are you Guō Jìzǐ (郭季子)?"
Jìng (敬) prostrated himself and said:
"Yes, I am."
Lè (勒) dismounted, clasped his hand,
and wept, saying:
"For us to meet today,
is this not fate?"
He bestowed clothes, chariots, and horses upon him,
appointed Jìng (敬) as Supreme General,
and released all the surrendered men to be assigned to him.
His general Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) raided Dìnglíng (定陵),
killing Tián Huī (田徽), the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Wūhuán (烏丸) Báo Shèng (薄盛) seized Liú Jì (劉既), the Administrator of Bóhǎi (渤海),
and, leading five thousand households, surrendered to Lè (勒).
Liú Cōng (劉聰) bestowed upon Lè (勒) the titles of Attendant Censor and Grand General Who Conquers the East,
with other titles remaining as before.
He appointed Lè's (勒) mother, Lady Wáng (王), as Grand Madam of Shàngdǎng (上黨) Commandery,
and his wife, Lady Liú (劉), as Lady of Shàngdǎng (上黨) Commandery,
with the ceremonial ornaments and headwear identical to those of a royal consort.
Duàn Mòbēi (段末柸) allowed his younger brother to escape back to Liáoxī (遼西).
Lè (勒) was greatly enraged
and ordered the killing of all local officials in the areas the brother passed through.
Wūhuán (烏丸) Shěn Guǎng (審廣), Jiàn Cháng (漸裳), and Hǎo Xí (郝襲) rebelled against Wáng Jùn (王浚),
secretly sending envoys to surrender to Lè (勒).
Lè (勒) treated them generously and accepted them.
Sī (司) and Jì (冀) provinces gradually became peaceful,
and people began to pay taxes and tributes.
He established a Grand Academy,
selected capable and well-versed officials who were skilled in writing and appointed them as literary clerks,
and chose three hundred sons of his generals and advisors to teach them.
Lè's (勒) mother, Lady Wáng (王), died.
She was secretly buried in a mountain valley,
her exact location unknown.
Later, the rites of the nine imperial appointments were observed, and a ceremonial funeral was held south of Xiāngguó (襄國) city.
Liú Kūn sent Wáng Dàn to attack Zhōngshān,
driving out Qín Gù, the Administrator appointed by Lè.
Lè's general, Liú Miǎn, resisted Dàn,
defeated him,
and captured Dàn at Wàngdūguān.
Lè attacked Shào Xù at Lèlíng.
Xù, with all his troops, met him in battle,
was greatly defeated, and returned.
Wáng Qǐ of Zhāngwǔ raised an army at Kēdòulěi,
disturbing Lè's various commanderies in Héjiān and Bóhǎi.
Lè appointed Yángwǔ Zhāng Yí as Administrator of Héjiān,
and Staff Officer Lín Shēn as Administrator of Bóhǎi,
each leading three thousand infantry and cavalry to pacify them.
He also had Chánglè Administrator Chéng Xiá garrison Chāngtíng to create a show of force.
He relocated over thirty thousand households of Wūwán, including Zhǎn Guǎng and Liú Duō, from Píngyuán to Xiāngguó.
He sent Shí Jìlóng to attack Qǐhuó King Wáng Píng at Liángchéng,
but was defeated and returned.
He also attacked Liú Yǎn at Lǐnqīu.
Zhī Xióng and Lù Míng attacked Níng Hēi at Dōngwǔyáng,
captured it,
and Hēi drowned himself in the river.
Over ten thousand of his followers were relocated to Xiāngguó.
Shào Xù sent Wén Yāng to rescue Yǎn.
Jìlóng retreated to Lúguānjīn to avoid him.
Wén Yāng was unable to advance,
and garrisoned Jǐngtíng.
The powerful local gentry of Yǎnzōu and Yùzhōu, including Zhāng Píng, raised troops to rescue Yǎn.
Jìlóng abandoned his camp by night and set up an ambush outside,
spreading word that he was returning to Héběi.
Píng and others believed it to be true
and entered the empty camp.
Jìlóng turned back and defeated them,
then captured Lǐnqīu.
Yǎn fled to Wén Yāng's army.
Yǎn's younger brother Qǐ was captured
and sent to Xiāngguó.
Yǎn was Liú Kūn's elder brother's son.
Lè, because Kūn had taken care of his mother,
was grateful to him.
He bestowed Qǐ with land and dwellings,
and ordered scholarly officials to teach him the classics.
At this time, there was a great locust plague,
especially severe in Zhōngshān and Chángshān.
Zhāi Shǔ, a Dīnglíng from Zhōngshān, rebelled against Lè,
attacking Zhōngshān and Chángshān.
Lè led cavalry to suppress him,
capturing his mother and wife and returning.
Shǔ defended Xūguān,
then fled to Dàijùn.
Lè attacked Lèpíng Administrator Hán Jù at Diànchéng.
Liú Kūn sent General Jī Dàn to lead over a hundred thousand troops to attack Lè.
Kūn stationed himself at Guǎngmù
to support Dàn.
Lè was about to resist him.
Someone advised him, saying:
"Dàn's army is strong and spirited,
its vanguard is irresistible.
It is advisable to dig deep moats and build high ramparts to blunt their edge.
The advantages of offense and defense are different;
this will surely ensure complete safety."
Lè said:
"Dàn's large army has come from afar,
they are tired and exhausted.
They are a motley crowd, like dogs and sheep,
their commands are not unified.
They can be captured in one battle.
What strength do they have?
The enemy has already arrived.
How can we abandon them and leave?
Once a large army moves,
how can it easily turn back midway?
If Dàn were to take advantage of our retreat,
we would not even have time to look back,
how could we dig deep moats and build high ramparts?
This is a path to self-destruction without fighting."
He immediately beheaded the advisor.
He appointed Kǒng Cháng as Vanguard Commander
and ordered that anyone from the three armies who lagged behind should be executed.
He set up a feigned army on the mountain
and divided his forces into two ambushes.
Lè, with light cavalry, fought Dàn,
feigning a retreat of his troops to the north.
Dàn unleashed his troops in pursuit.
Lè's front and rear ambushes launched,
attacking from both sides.
Dàn's army was greatly defeated.
Ten thousand sets of armor and horses were captured.
Dàn fled to Dàijùn.
Jù fled to Liú Kūn.
Kūn's Chief Clerk, Lǐ Hóng, surrendered Bìngzhōu to Lè.
Kūn then fled to Duàn Pǐdī.
Lè moved the households of Yángqǔ and Lèpíng to Xiāngguó,
appointed governors and magistrates, and then withdrew.
Kǒng Cháng pursued Jī Dàn to Sānggān.
Lè sent Acting Left Chief Clerk Zhāng Fū to present the victory to Liú Cōng.
When Lè was campaigning in Lèpíng,
his Nánhé Magistrate Zhào Lǐng gathered several thousand households from Guǎngchuān, Píngyuán, and Bóhǎi to rebel against Lè
and flee to Shào Xù.
Xíng Gǔ of Héjiān, having been repeatedly summoned but not arriving,
also gathered several hundred men to rebel.
Lè toured the various counties of Jìzhōu.
He appointed Right Sīmǎ Chéng Xiá as Níngshuò General and Supervisor of Military Affairs for the seven commanderies of Jìzhōu.
Lè's brother-in-law, Guǎngwēi Zhāng Yuè, was playing dice with the generals.
Lè personally came to watch.
Yuè's casual remark offended Lè.
Lè was furious,
shouting for strongmen to break his shins and kill him.
Kǒng Cháng attacked Dàijùn,
and Dàn died there.
At this time, tens of thousands of displaced households from Sī, Jì, Bìng, and Yǎnzōu were in Liáoxī,
recruiting each other,
with no one settled in their occupation.
Kǒng Cháng and others attacked Mǎ Yán and Féng Zhě,
but were unsuccessful for a long time.
Lè asked Zhāng Bīn for advice.
Bīn replied:
"Féng Zhě and others are not truly deep enemies of your Excellency.
The displaced people of Liáoxī all yearn to return to their homeland.
Now, it is appropriate to withdraw the army and rest our weapons,
select good administrators,
entrust them with the affairs of Gōng Suì,
without adhering to conventional rules,
to proclaim benevolence and kindness,
and display military might.
The bandits of Yōuzhōu and Jìzhōu can be pacified instantly,
and the displaced people of Liáoxī can be made to arrive at a specified time."
Lè said:
"Right Marquis's plan is correct."
He recalled Cháng and others,
and appointed Wǔsuì Magistrate Lǐ Huí as Yìběi Commander, Zhènwǔ General, and Gāoyáng Administrator.
Mǎ Yán's troops were mostly Lǐ Qián's soldiers.
Huí had previously been Qián's Chief Clerk.
They had always respected Huí's authority and virtue,
and many deserted Yán to join him.
Yán, seeing his troops divided,
was afraid
and fled to Yōuzhōu,
where he drowned.
Féng Zhě led his troops to surrender to Lè.
Huí moved to Yìjīng.
Lè greatly praised him,
enfeoffed Huí as Viscount Yìyáng,
with an estate of three hundred households.
Bīn was granted an additional thousand households
and promoted to the position of Former General,
but he firmly declined it.
There was a great locust plague north of the Yellow River.
They first burrowed into the ground to be born,
transformed into silkworm-like shapes after twenty days,
lay dormant for seven or eight days,
then molted and flew after four days.
They spread across all plants,
except for the three beans and hemp.
Bìngzhōu and Jìzhōu were especially severe.
Shí Jìlóng crossed from Chángshòujīn,
invaded Liángguó,
and harmed Internal Historian Xún Hé.
Liú Kūn met with Duàn Pǐdī, Shè Fùchén, Jílìu Juàn, Duàn Mòbēi, and others at Gù'ān,
planning to attack Lè.
Lè sent Staff Officer Wáng Xù to deliver gold and treasures to Mòbēi to sow discord.
Mòbēi, both wishing to repay Lè's kindness
and delighted by the generous bribe,
persuaded Chén Juàn and others to withdraw.
Kūn and Pǐdī also retreated to Jìchéng.
Shào Xù sent his elder brother's son Jì to attack Lè's Bóhǎi,
capturing over three thousand people and returning.
Liú Cōng's general Zhào Gù submitted Luòyáng.
Fearing Lè would attack him,
he sent Staff Officer Gāo Shǎo with a letter to extol Lè
and request an army to attack Cōng.
Lè, based on righteousness, declined his offer.
Gù harbored deep resentment
and, with Guō Mò, plundered Hénei and Jíjùn.
Duàn Mòbēi killed the Xiānbēi Chányú Jiéfùzhēn
and installed Hūbālín as Chányú.
Duàn Pǐdī attacked Mòbēi from Yōuzhōu.
Mòbēi met and defeated him.
Pǐdī fled back to Yōuzhōu,
and subsequently harmed Grand Commandant Liú Kūn.
Kūn's generals and staff successively surrendered to Lè.
Mòbēi sent his younger brother, the Cavalry Commander, to attack Pǐdī at Yōuzhōu.
Pǐdī, with several thousand of his followers,
was about to flee to Shào Xù.
Lè's general Shí Yuè intercepted him at Yánshān
and greatly defeated him.
Pǐdī retreated to defend Yōuzhōu.
Yuè was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Lè mourned for him, suspending music for three months,
and posthumously granted him the title of Píngnán General.
Lè usurped the throne,
and established [Shí] Hóng as crown prince.
He was open-minded and fond of scholars,
enjoying literature and poetry.
Those he was close to
were all cultured and unassuming.
Lè said to Xú Guāng:
"[Shí] Dàyǎ is so quiet and refined,
quite unlike the son of a general."
Guāng replied:
"The Han progenitor (Gāo Zǔ) seized the empire on horseback,
while Emperor Xiào Wén preserved it through quiet governance.
After a sage,
his descendants will surely overcome brutality in subsequent generations;
this is the Way of Heaven."
Lè was greatly pleased.
Guāng then said:
"The Crown Prince is benevolent, filial, gentle, and respectful,
whereas the Prince of Zhōngshān (Shí Jìlóng) is violent and deceitful.
Should Your Majesty suddenly pass away,
your servant fears that the altars of soil and grain will surely be in peril.
It would be advisable to gradually strip the Prince of Zhōngshān of his power and authority,
and allow the Crown Prince to participate in court administration early."
Lè accepted this.
Chéng Xiá also spoke to Lè, saying:
"The Prince of Zhōngshān is valiant, martial, and shrewd;
among the numerous officials, none can equal him.
Observing his ambition,
apart from Your Majesty,
he regards all others as insignificant.
Moreover, he has been entrusted with sole military command for many years,
his prestige shaking both inside and outside the court.
His nature is also unkind,
cruel, and unscrupulous.
His sons are all grown,
and all participate in military authority.
While Your Majesty is alive,
there will naturally be no trouble,
but I fear that he will be discontent and unable to assist the young lord.
It would be advisable to eliminate him early,
to facilitate the grand plan."
Lè said:
"Today, the world is not yet pacified,
and military difficulties have not ceased.
Dàyǎ is young and immature,
and needs strong assistance.
The Prince of Zhōngshān is a meritorious official who aided in establishing the dynasty,
his relationship is as close as Lǔ and Wèi.
He is currently entrusted with the responsibilities of Yī [Yǐn] and Huò [Guāng];
how can it come to what you say?
You must be afraid that on the day you assist the young lord,
you will not be able to exclusively wield the power of the emperor's maternal uncle, that's all.
I will also include you in the dying testament;
do not be overly fearful."
Xiá wept and said:
"What your servant says is most impartial.
Your Majesty rejects it with private favoritism;
how can this be the principle of an enlightened ruler opening his heart to accept advice,
and a loyal minister exerting his utmost?
Although Zhōngshān was raised by the Empress Dowager,
he is not Your Majesty's blood relative;
one cannot expect family loyalty from him.
Relying on Your Majesty's divine strategy,
he rendered the service of a hawk or hound,
and Your Majesty has rewarded him and his sons with favor and honor,
which is already sufficient.
Wèi entrusted the father and son of Sīmǎ Yì,
which ultimately led to the shifting of the imperial fortune.
Viewing it this way,
how can Zhōngshān be beneficial in the future?
Your servant, by fortunate circumstance,
is related to the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince);
if your servant does not speak his mind to Your Majesty,
then to whom shall I speak?
If Your Majesty does not eliminate Zhōngshān,
your servant already foresees that the altars of soil and grain will no longer receive blood sacrifices."
Lè did not listen.
Xiá retired and told Xú Guāng:
"The sovereign just spoke like that;
the Crown Prince will surely be in peril.
What shall we do?"
Guāng said:
"Zhōngshān constantly grinds his teeth at the two of us;
I fear it's not just a national crisis,
but also a family calamity.
We must devise a plan to secure the state and pacify our families;
we cannot sit and await disaster."
Guāng again seized an opportunity to speak to Lè, saying:
"Your Majesty has pacified the eight provinces [regions] and
become the emperor of all within the seas,
yet why is your countenance displeased?"
Lè said:
"Wú and Shǔ are not yet pacified,
and written decrees are not unified.
The Sīmǎ family still has descendants in Dānyáng,
and I fear that future generations will say I did not conform to the divine mandate.
Each time I think of this,
it involuntarily shows on my face."
Guāng said:
"Your servant thought Your Majesty was worried about an affliction in your heart and abdomen,
so how could you have leisure to worry about your limbs?
Why so?
Wèi inherited the Han destiny,
and was the legitimate imperial dynasty.
Although Liú Bèi revived [the Han] in Bā and Shǔ,
it cannot be said that Han was not destroyed.
Although Wú spanned east of the Jiāng River,
how could it diminish Wèi's glory?
Since Your Majesty has encompassed the two capitals [Luòyáng and Cháng'ān]
and become the emperor of the Central Plains,
what difference is that Sīmǎ family child from Xuándé [Liú Bèi],
and the Lǐ family is just like Sūn Quán.
If the divine mandate is not with Your Majesty,
where else could it possibly go?
These are merely minor troubles of the limbs.
Prince Zhōngshān, relying on Your Majesty's guidance and divine strategy,
is spoken of by all in the world as heroic and martial, second only to Your Majesty.
Moreover, he is cruel, violent, and highly treacherous,
forgetting righteousness when he sees profit,
without the loyalty of Yī [Yǐn] and Huò [Guāng].
The high ranks of him and his son,
their influence overshadows the imperial house.
Observing his resentment,
he constantly harbors discontent.
Recently, at a private banquet in the Eastern Palace,
he showed disrespect towards the Crown Prince.
If Your Majesty tolerates and endures this,
your servant fears that after Your Majesty's passing,
thorns will surely grow in the ancestral temples.
This is a serious affliction of the heart and abdomen;
may Your Majesty consider it."
Lè was silent,
but ultimately did not comply.
When Lè died,
Jìlóng seized Hóng and made him preside over the court,
ordering the arrest of Chéng Xiá and Xú Guāng and sending them to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
He summoned his son Suì to lead troops to garrison the palace,
and all civil and military officials scattered.
Hóng was greatly frightened,
and ceded the throne to Jìlóng.
Jìlóng said:
"When the ruler dies and the heir apparent is established,
how dare a minister cause disorder!"
Hóng wept and insisted on abdicating,
Jìlóng angrily said:
"If you are truly incapable,
the world will naturally have a great debate;
why bother discussing it now?"
Thus, in the seventh year of Xiánhé (332 AD), he forced Hóng to ascend the throne,
〔一六〕 changed the regnal year to Yánxī,
and all civil and military officials were promoted one rank.
Chéng Xiá and Xú Guāng were executed.
Hóng issued an edict appointing Jìlóng as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), King of Wèi, Grand Chányú,
and bestowed upon him the Nine Bestowals.
Thirteen commanderies, including Wèi Jùn, were granted as his domain,
and he was to oversee all government affairs.
Jìlóng feigned refusal for a long time before accepting the appointment.
He pardoned all prisoners within his territory from capital punishment downwards.
He established Jìlóng's wife, Lady Zhèng, as Queen of Wèi,
and his son Suì as Crown Prince of Wèi,

adding the titles of Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dà Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūshì), Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn), and Superintendent of the Palace Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì);
Xuān was made Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ),
and enfeoffed as King of Héjiān;
Tāo was made Vanguard General (Qiánfēng Jiāngjūn) and Director of the Masters of Writing (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
and enfeoffed as King of Yuè'ān;
Zūn as King of Qí,
Jiàn as King of Dài,
Bāo as King of Lèpíng;
and Bīn, the King of Tàiyuán, was transferred to be King of Zhāngwǔ.
All of Lè's former civil and military officials were appointed to minor positions between the Left and Right Chancellors,
while all of Jìlóng's personal staff and old confidants were assigned to key positions in the Central Secretariat and Imperial Chancellery.
He ordered the Crown Prince's palace to be called Chóngxùn Palace,
and Lè's wife Lady Liú and others were all moved to reside there.
He selected the most beautiful and virtuous women, as well as Lè's chariots, horses, treasures, and the finest articles for personal use,
all of which were brought into his own residence.
Zhèn Jūn Kuí Ān was made Left Grandee Secretary (Zuǒ Púshè),
and Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū) Guō Yīn was made Right Grandee Secretary (Yòu Púshè).
Shí Jìlóng
was Shí Lè's
paternal cousin. His given name violated the taboos of the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ,
so he was referred to by his courtesy name.
His grandfather was named Táo Xié,
and his father was named Kòumì.
Shí Lè's father, Zhū Yòu, adopted Jìlóng as a child,
so some called him Shí Lè's younger brother.
At six or seven years old,
a skilled physiognomist said:
"This child has an extraordinary appearance and strong bones;
his nobility is beyond words."
During the Yǒngxīng era,
he was separated from Shí Lè.
Later, Liú Kūn sent Shí Lè's mother, Wáng, and Jìlóng to Gěpí.
At that time, he was seventeen.
He was cruel and ruthless by nature,
fond of riding and hunting,
and indulged in excesses.
He was particularly skilled with a slingshot,
often shooting people,
which the army considered a harmful menace.
Shí Lè reported to Wáng that he intended to kill him,
but Wáng said:
"A swift ox, when it is a calf,
can often break a cart.
You should tolerate him a little longer."
At eighteen,
he gradually curbed his behavior.
He was seven feet five inches tall,
swift and agile with a bow and horse,
and his bravery surpassed all others of his time.
Generals, aides, and relatives all revered and feared him.
Shí Lè greatly admired him,
and appointed him as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
He was betrothed to General Guō Róng's younger sister as his wife.
Jìlóng was infatuated with and misled by his male concubine Zhèng Yīngtáo, and killed Lady Guō,
then took a daughter of the Cuī clan of Qīnghé as his wife.
Yīngtáo again slandered her and had her killed.
His actions were brutal and abusive.
If there was anyone in the army whose courage, ability, and strategy matched his own,
he would cunningly find a way to harm them,
and the number of those he killed both before and after was considerable.
As for captured cities and fallen strongholds,
he no longer distinguished between good and bad,
but buried or beheaded men and women,
with few survivors.
Although Shí Lè repeatedly admonished and tried to persuade him,
his conduct remained unchanged.
However, his command of the troops was strict but not vexing,
and no one dared to offend him.
When he directed attacks and campaigns,
he was unstoppable.
Therefore, Shí Lè favored him,
and his trust in him grew immensely,
relying on him for independent military commands.
When Shí Lè resided in Xiāngguó,
he appointed him as Wèijùn Tàishǒu,
garrisoning Yè Sāntái.
Later, he was enfeoffed as Fányáng Hóu.
When Shí Lè assumed the title of Dà Chányú and Zhào Wáng,
he appointed him as Chányú Yuánfǔ and Dūdū Jīn Wèi Zhū Jūnshì,
promoting him to Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ,
and further enfeoffing him as Zhōngshān Gōng.
When Shí Lè usurped the imperial title,
he was granted the titles of Tàiwèi and Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng,
and further enfeoffed as a King,
with an estate of ten thousand households.
Jìlóng considered his achievements to be the highest of his time,
and believed that after Shí Lè ascended the throne,
the title of Dà Chányú would certainly belong to him.
Instead, it was conferred upon Shí Hóng, Shí Lè's son.
Jìlóng resented this deeply,
and privately said to his son, Shí Suì:
"Since His Majesty made Xiāngguó his capital,
he has merely sat idly and given orders,
while I have personally faced arrows and stones.
For over twenty years,
I captured Liú Yuè in the south,
drove Sǒutóu to the north,
pacified Qí and Lǔ in the east,
and stabilized Qín and Yōng in the west,
conquering and annihilating thirteen prefectures.
It is I
who established the great state of Zhào.
The hope and reality of the Dà Chányú title belonged to me,
but it was given to that yellow-mouthed slave boy.
Every time I think of this,
it makes me unable to sleep or eat.
After His Majesty passes away,
there will be no need to keep his seed."
In the first year of Xiánkāng,
Jìlóng deposed Shí Hóng, Shí Lè's son.
All the officials and those below urged him to assume the exalted title.
Jìlóng issued a decree saying:
"The royal house faces many difficulties,
and Hǎiyáng has abandoned himself.
The burden of the realm is heavy,
so I reluctantly yield to the pressure.
I have heard that those whose Way aligns with Heaven and Earth are called Huáng,
and those whose virtue harmonizes with humans and gods are called Dì.
The title of Huángdì is not one I dare to hear.
For now, I shall be called Jūshè Zhào Tiānwáng,
to fulfill the expectations of Heaven and mankind."
Thereupon, he pardoned everyone within his territory
and changed the era name to Jiànwǔ.
He appointed Kuí Ān as Shìzhōng, Tàiwèi, and Shǒu Shàngshū Lìng;
Guō Yīn as Sīkōng;
Hán Xī as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè;
Wèi Gài, Féng Mò, Zhāng Chóng, and Cáo Xiǎn as Shàngshū;
Shēn Zhōng as Shìzhōng;
Láng Kǎi as Guānglù Dàfū;
and Wáng Bō as Zhōngshū Lìng.
Civil and military officials were enfeoffed and appointed according to their ranks.
He established his son, Shí Suì, as the Crown Prince.
Jìlóng believed that a prophecy stated the Son of Heaven would come from the northeast,
so he prepared the imperial carriage and drove from Xìndū and returned to fulfill this.
He divided the Liǔ Xiāng of Yǐngtáo to establish Tíngjià County.
Jìlóng's Xúzhōu Cóngshì, Zhū Zòng, killed the Cìshǐ Guō Xiáng
and offered Péngchéng in surrender.
Jìlóng dispatched his general Wáng Lǎng to attack him,
and Zòng fled to Huáinán.
Jìlóng indulged in frivolous activities and neglected governance,
undertaking many construction projects.
He made Shí Suì review and approve memorials to the throne from the Shàngshū,
select governors,
and offer sacrifices at the suburban and ancestral temples;
only matters of conquest, punishment, and judgment he personally oversaw.
The Guānquè Tái collapsed,
and he killed the Diǎnjiàng Shàofǔ, Rèn Wāng.
He then ordered its reconstruction,
to twice the usual scale.
Jìlóng personally led his troops to raid Lìyáng in the south,
and turned back upon reaching the Jiāng river,
causing great alarm in the capital.
He sent his Zhēnglǔ, Shí Yù, to raid Zhōnglú,
and then besieged the Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Huán Xuān, at Xiāngyáng.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Máo Bǎo, Nán Zhōngláng Jiāng Wáng Guó, Zhēngxī Sīmǎ Wáng Qiānqī, and others led the forces of Jīngzhōu to relieve him,
stationing themselves at Zhāngshān.
Shí Yù attacked for two weeks,
but his army suffered from hunger and plague and returned.
Jìlóng, seeing that tax revenues were abundant
and transportation arduous,
ordered the central granaries to receive one million hu of grain annually,
storing the rest near rivers.
The Jìn general Chúnyú Ān attacked his Fèi County in Lángyé,
capturing and returning with captives.
Shí Suì's wet nurse, Liú Zhī, initially rose through witchcraft.
After nursing Shí Suì,
she gained deep favor,
accepted bribes,
and interfered in discussions.
Her power overshadowed the imperial court,
and many nobles and high-ranking officials came through her door.
She was then enfeoffed as Yíchéng Jūn.
Jìlóng issued a decree allowing those who had to pay fines for crimes to substitute money for silk,
and if they had no money, they could use grain or wheat,
all to be delivered to the riverside granaries at market price.
Hail fell in eight counties of Jìzhōu,
severely damaging the autumn harvest.
He issued a decree deeply blaming himself.
He sent imperial censors to all locations to distribute wheat from the riverside granaries
for autumn planting,
and in the most severe areas, taxes were remitted for a year.
When Jìlóng was about to move to Yè,
the Shàngshū requested the Tàicháng to announce it to the ancestral temple.
Jìlóng said:
"In ancient times, when there was a major event,
it was always announced to the ancestral temple,
but not to the altars of the land and grain.
The Shàngshū should deliberate carefully and report."
The high officials then requested that the Tàiwèi announce it to the altars of the land and grain,
which he accepted.
When he entered the Yè Palace,
a timely and widespread rain fell.
Jìlóng was greatly pleased
and pardoned all criminals down to those sentenced to death.
The Shàngfāng Lìng, Xiè Fēi, completed a south-pointing chariot.
Jìlóng, impressed by its ingenious design,
bestowed upon him the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
and generously rewarded him.
He first decreed that Shànqí Chángshì and above could ride in light carriages,
while kings and dukes, when performing suburban sacrifices, could use secondary carriages,
drawn by four horses,
with dragon banners having eight streamers.
For court assemblies on the first and fifteenth days of the month, they could ride in light carriages.
At that time, the Qiāng Báo Jù Dà still held strongholds and had not submitted.
He sent his son, Zhāngwǔ Wáng Bīn, leading twenty thousand elite cavalry,
along with troops from Qín and Yōng prefectures, to subjugate them.
Jìlóng traveled to Chánglè and Wèiguó.
If there were uncultivated fields or unmaintained mulberry industries,
he demoted their local administrators before returning.
In the second year of Xiánkāng,

Shǐ Jiélóng ordered the commander of the Yámén, Zhāng Mí, to relocate the bells and stands (zhōngjù), the nine dragons (jiǔlóng), the Wēngzhòng statues, bronze camels, and Fēilián statues from Luòyáng to Yè.
One bell sank into the river.
Three hundred men skilled in diving were recruited to enter the river,
tie it with bamboo ropes,
and then a hundred oxen
and a lùlú machine were used to pull it out.
A boat capable of carrying ten thousand hú was built to transport it across the river.
Using four-wheeled chariots with reinforced rims,
with tracks four chí wide
and two chí deep,
it was transported to Yè.
Jìlóng was greatly pleased,
pardoned criminals sentenced to two years or less,
bestowed grain and silk upon all officials,
and granted one rank of nobility to the common people.
He issued an edict saying:
"Evaluating performance every three years
to promote the capable and dismiss the incompetent
is a standing regulation of the former kings,
and the basis for the smooth or obstructed flow of governance.
Wèi first established the nine-rank system,
clarifying and fixing it every three years.
Although not entirely comprehensive and excellent,
it was still a pure and clear law for the gentry
and a bright mirror for human relations.
Since then,
it has been followed without change.
The late emperor, when he first assumed rule over the world,
re-established it twice with yellow edicts.
As for appointments and selections,
evaluation (quán) was the primary standard.
It has not been clarified and fixed for three years now.
It has been three years since then.
Let the officials responsible re-evaluate and re-discuss,
striving to promote the pure and suppress the corrupt,
so that all nine streams (of talent) are justly served.
For selections by the Ministry of Personnel,
the Jìn dynasty's nine-grade selection system may be followed,
to be a permanent standard.
Once selections are complete,
they shall be submitted to the Zhōngshū and Ménxià for proclamation to the three provinces,
and only then implemented.
This edict shall be recorded in the statutes.
If those responsible for evaluation and selection fail to comply,
the Censorate shall impeach and report them."
Suǒtóu Yùjū led a host of thirty thousand and surrendered to Jìlóng.
Yùjū and thirteen others were appointed to have direct access to the King of Zhào,
and all were enfeoffed as Lièhóu.
Their troops were dispersed among six provinces, including Jì and Qīng.
At this time, numerous construction projects were underway,
and military campaigns were unceasing.
Furthermore, there was a prolonged drought and high grain prices,
with one jīn of gold being worth only two dǒu of rice,
leaving the common people lamenting and without means of livelihood.
He also adopted Jiě Fēi's suggestion
to throw stones into the river directly south of Yè
to build a pontoon bridge.
The cost amounted to several hundred thousand million,
but the bridge was ultimately not completed.
The laborers suffered severe hunger,
so the project was stopped.
He ordered magistrates and chiefs to lead able-bodied men to gather acorns and catch fish in mountains and swamps to relieve the elderly and weak,
but these resources were again seized by powerful magnates,
leaving the people with nothing.
He also assessed wealthy families
and allocated hungry people to them to be fed.
Officials from the Gōngqīng downwards contributed grain to assist in relief,
but corrupt officials used this as an opportunity to endlessly extort and seize,
so that while there was the name of lending and assistance, there was no reality to it.
He changed the Zhídàng to Lóngténg,
and adorned them with crimson turbans.
He began building the Tàiwǔ Hall in Xiāngguó,
and constructed the East and West Palaces in Yè,
all of which were completed by this time.
The foundation of the Tàiwǔ Hall was two zhàng and eight chí high,
decorated with patterned stones.
A hidden chamber was dug underneath,
where five hundred guards were stationed.
It measured seventy-five bù from east to west,
and sixty-five bù from north to south.
All featured lacquered tiles, golden caissons, silver eaves, golden pillars, pearl curtains, and jade walls,
exhausting the limits of craftsmanship.
He also built the Língfēng Terrace with nine halls behind the Xiǎnyáng Hall,
selecting women from both scholarly and common families to populate it.
There were over ten thousand women in the rear palace wearing fine silks, brocades, and precious jewels.
Eighteen grades of female officials were established internally,
teaching palace women astrology and horseback archery.
Female Grand Scribes were stationed at the Língtái,
to observe omens and calamities,
and to verify the accuracy of the external Grand Scribes.
Female drummers and pipers with ceremonial feathered staffs were also established,
along with various artisans and craftsmen,
all matching their male counterparts.
It was forbidden for commanderies and kingdoms to privately study astrology or prognostication;
anyone daring to violate this would be executed.
The director of the Left Corps, Chénggōng Duàn, created a courtyard torch at the top of a towering pole,
over ten zhàng high.
The upper platform held the torch,
and the lower platform held people,
with ropes to go up and down.
Jìlóng tested it and was pleased.
His Grand Guardian Kuí Ān and five hundred nine other civil and military officials urged Jìlóng to assume a more honorable title.
As Ān and others were about to enter, the oil from the courtyard torch poured onto the lower platform,
killing seven people.
Jìlóng was disgusted by this,
became furious,
and executed Chénggōng Duàn at the Chānghé Gate.
Thereupon, following the systems of Yīn and Zhōu,
in the third year of Xiánkāng, he presumptuously declared himself the Grand King of Zhào (Dà Zhào Tiānwáng),
ascended the throne in the southern suburbs,
and granted a general amnesty for all crimes down to capital punishment.
He posthumously honored his ancestor Tāoxié as Wǔ Huángdì,
and his father Kòumì as Tàizōng Xiàohuángdì.
He established his concubine Zhèng as the Tiānwáng Huánghòu,
and made his son Suì the Tiānwáng Huángtàizǐ.
All princely kings were demoted to commandery dukes,
and tributary kings to county marquises.
All officials were enfeoffed and appointed with varying ranks.
Over five hundred households of relocated people from Tàiyuán rebelled and joined the Hēi Qiāng.
Hán Qiáng, a relocated person from Chángchéng in Wǔxiāng, found a black jade seal,
measuring four cùn and seven fēn square,
with a turtle knob and golden inscriptions.
He went to Yè to present it.
Qiáng was appointed Qí Dūwèi,
and his entire family was exempted from duties.
Kuí Ān and others again urged him to advance, saying:
"We respectfully observe that the Grand Zhào possesses the virtue of water.
The black turtle is
the essence of water;
jade is
the treasure of stones.
Its division in number symbolizes the Seven Luminaries,
and its measurement in cùn aligns with the Four Extremes.
Heaven has established this decree,
and it cannot be long delayed.
We have thus instructed the historians to select an auspicious day,
prepare the ceremonies,
and respectfully, risking death, present the title of Emperor (Huángdì)."
Jìlóng issued an edict saying:
"You have overly praised and
inappropriately urged me;
upon reading this, I am even more ashamed,
as this is not what I desire.
This discussion should be stopped immediately.
Now that spring plowing has begun,
outside the capital city,
no one is permitted to present congratulations."
The director of the Zhōngshū, Wáng Bō, presented a eulogy for the black seal to praise it.
Jìlóng considered that this seal had been made during Shí Hóng's time,
and Qiáng had merely chanced upon it and presented it.
Shí Zūn (石遵) heard of Jìlóng's (季龍) death.
He garrisoned at Hénèi (河內).

Yáo Yìzhòng (姚弋仲), Fú Hóng (苻洪), Shí Mǐn (石閔), Liú Níng (劉寧), and Wǔwèi Wáng Luán (武衞王鸞), Níngxī Wáng Wǔ (寧西王午), Shí Róng (石榮), Wáng Tiě (王鐵), and the Lìyì General Duàn Qín (段勤) and others, having pacified Qín (秦) and Luò (洛),
returned their armies.
They met Zūn (遵) at Lǐchéng (李城),
and advised Zūn (遵), saying:
"Your Highness is both grown and virtuous.
The former emperor also had intentions for Your Highness.
But in his later years, he was confused and deluded,
and misled by Zhāng Chái (張豺).
The current emperor and Shàngbái (上白) are still at a standoff.
The capital guards are empty.
If you declare Zhāng Chái's (張豺) crimes,
and march forth with drums beating to punish him,
who would not turn their weapons and open the gates to welcome Your Highness!"
Zūn (遵) followed this advice.
The Governor of Luòzhōu (洛州), Liú Guó (劉國) and others also led the forces from Luòyáng (洛陽) to Lǐchéng (李城).
Zūn's (遵) proclamation reached Yè (鄴).
Zhāng Chái (張豺) was greatly frightened,
and hastily summoned the army from Shàngbái (上白).
Zūn (遵) encamped at Dàngyīn (蕩陰),
with ninety thousand soldiers.
Shí Mǐn (石閔) was the vanguard.
Chái (豺) was about to go out to resist him,
when the elders and Jié (羯) soldiers all said:
"The Son of Heaven's child comes to mourn;
we should go out to welcome him.
We cannot guard the city for Zhāng Chái (張豺)."
They climbed over the city walls and went out.
Chái (豺) beheaded them but could not stop them.
Zhāng Lí (張離) led two thousand Longténg (龍騰) troops, broke through the gate, and welcomed Zūn (遵).
Lady Liú (劉氏) was afraid.
She led Zhāng Chái (張豺) in,
and wept bitterly to him, saying:
"The former emperor's coffin has not yet been interred,
and misfortune and chaos are rampant.
Now the imperial heir is young and immature.
I entrust him to the general.
How can the general rectify and save the situation?
If we bestow a heavy office upon Zūn (遵),
can it not pacify things?"
Chái (豺) was terrified and lost his composure,
unable to devise any plans.
He merely said, "Yes, yes."
Lady Liú (劉氏) ordered Zūn (遵) to be made Chancellor, Grand Marshal, Grand Commander of all armies inside and outside, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
with the addition of the Yellow Axe and Nine Bestowals,
and an increase of ten counties to his fief,
entrusting him with the responsibility of Āhéng (阿衡).
When Zūn (遵) reached Ānyángtíng (安陽亭),
Zhāng Chái (張豺) fearfully went out to welcome him.
Zūn (遵) ordered him seized.
Thereupon, donning armor and displaying weapons,
Zūn (遵) entered through Fèngyáng Mén (鳳陽門),
ascended to the Tàiwǔ Qiándiàn (太武前殿),
mourned with great sorrow,
then retired to the Dōnggé (東閤).
He beheaded Zhāng Chái (張豺) at Pínglè Shì (平樂市)
and exterminated his three clans.
He issued a false decree in Lady Liú's (劉氏) name, saying:
"The heir is young and immature,
appointed by the late emperor's private favor.
The imperial enterprise is of utmost importance,
which he is not capable of bearing.
Therefore, Zūn (遵) shall succeed to the throne."
Zūn (遵) feigned refusal repeatedly,
but his officials earnestly urged him.
Then he accepted it,
usurping the revered position in the Tàiwǔ Qiándiàn (太武前殿).
He issued a general amnesty for all crimes down to capital offenses,
and lifted the siege of Shàngbái (上白).
He enfeoffed Shì (世) as Qiáowáng (譙王),
with ten thousand households,
and treated him with the ceremony of one not a subject.
He demoted Lady Liú (劉氏) to Grand Concubine,
and soon after killed them both.
Shì (世) reigned for only thirty-three days.
Thereupon, Lǐ Nóng (李農) returned to beg for punishment.
Zūn (遵) restored him to his position,
treating him as before.
He honored his mother, Lady Zhèng (鄭氏), as Empress Dowager,
his wife, Lady Zhāng (張氏), as Empress,
made Shí Bīn's (石斌) son, Yǎn (衍), the Crown Prince,
Shí Jiàn (石鑒) the Palace Attendant,
Shí Chōng (石沖) the Grand Tutor,
Shí Bāo (石苞) the Grand Marshal,
Shí Kūn (石琨) the Grand General,
and Shí Mǐn (石閔) the Commander of all armies inside and outside, Auxiliary General-in-Chief, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
assisting in governance.
A violent storm uprooted trees.
Thunder rumbled,
and hail as large as bowls and pints fell.
The Tàiwǔ (太武) and Huīhuá (暉華) palaces caught fire.
All gates, towers, and pavilions were completely destroyed.
More than half of the imperial carriages and regalia were burned.
The flames illuminated the sky.
Gold and stone were all consumed.
The fire was extinguished after more than a month.
Blood rained all over Yèchéng (鄴城).
Shí Chōng (石沖), who was then garrisoned at Jì (薊),
heard that Zūn (遵) had killed Shì (世) and enthroned himself.
He then said to his staff:
"Shì (世) received the command of the former emperor.
Zūn (遵) has brazenly deposed and killed him.
His crime is immense and most rebellious.
Therefore, order the internal and external forces to be on alert.
I will personally lead an expedition against him."
Thereupon, he left Níngběi Shù Jiān (寧北沭堅) to guard Yōuzhōu (幽州),
and led fifty thousand troops
from Jì (薊) to attack Zūn (遵).
He sent proclamations to Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙),
and forces gathered like clouds everywhere.
By the time they reached Chángshān (常山),
the army numbered over one hundred thousand.
When they encamped at Yuànxiāng (苑鄉),
they encountered Zūn's (遵) amnesty edict.
He said to his attendants:
"We are brothers.
The dead cannot be brought back.
Why should we continue to fight each other?
I shall return."
His general Chén Xiān (陳暹) stepped forward and said:
"Péngchéng (彭城) usurped and murdered to enthrone himself;
his crime is great.
Although Your Highness may turn north,
your servant will turn south,
pacify the capital,
capture Péngchéng (彭城),
and then welcome the Grand Imperial Carriage."
Chōng (沖) agreed.
Zūn (遵) hastily dispatched Wáng Zhuó (王擢) with a letter to persuade Chōng (沖),
but Chōng (沖) did not listen.
Zūn (遵) granted Shí Mǐn (石閔) the Yellow Axe and Golden Gong,
and with Lǐ Nóng (李農) and others, led one hundred thousand elite troops to attack him.
They fought at Píngjí (平棘).
Chōng's (沖) army was utterly defeated.
Chōng (沖) was captured at Yuánshì (元氏),
and granted death.
Over thirty thousand of his soldiers were buried alive.
Zūn (遵) then buried Jìlóng (季龍),
naming his tomb Xiǎnyuán Líng (顯原陵),
and giving him the posthumous title of Wǔ Huángdì (武皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
Zūn's (遵) Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州), Wáng Jiá (王浹), surrendered Huáinán (淮南) to the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
The Jìn (晉) Central General of the West, Chén Kuí (陳逵), advanced and occupied Shòuchūn (壽春).
The General-in-Chief of the North, Chǔ Póu (褚裒), led his army to attack Zūn (遵),
and encamped at Xiàpī (下邳).
Zūn (遵) made Lǐ Nóng (李農) the Grand Commander of the Southern Expedition,
and he led twenty thousand cavalry to resist.
Póu (裒) could not advance
and retreated to garrison at Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
Chén Kuí (陳逵) heard of this,
and was afraid.
He then burned the accumulated supplies at Shòuchūn (壽春),
destroyed the city, and returned.
Shí Bāo (石苞), then garrisoned at Cháng'ān (長安),
planned to lead the forces from Guānzhōng (關中) to attack Yè (鄴).
His Left Chief Clerk Shí Guāng (石光), Grand Administrator Cáo Yào (曹曜) and others strongly remonstrated.
Bāo (苞) was enraged,
and executed Guāng (光) and over a hundred others.
Bāo (苞) was greedy and lacked strategy.
The local magnates of Yōngzhōu (雍州), knowing he would not succeed,
all sent envoys to inform Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳), the Jìn (晉) Governor of Liángzhōu (梁州).
Xūn (勳) then led his troops to him,
encamping at Xuángōu (懸鉤),
over two hundred *li* from Cháng'ān (長安).
He ordered his Administrator Liú Huàn (劉煥) to attack Liú Xiùlí (劉秀離), the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào (京兆),
and beheaded him.
Many local magnates in the Sānfǔ (三輔) killed their prefects and chiefs,
rallied over thirty strongholds,
and had fifty thousand troops to respond to Xūn (勳).
Bāo (苞) abandoned his plan to attack Yè (鄴),
and ordered Má Qiū (麻秋), Yáo Guó (姚國) and others to lead cavalry to resist Xūn (勳).
Zūn (遵) dispatched the Chariot and Cavalry General Wáng Lǎng (王朗) with twenty thousand elite cavalry,
ostensibly to attack Xūn (勳),
but actually to abduct Bāo (苞)
and send him to Yè (鄴).
Xūn (勳) was again resisted by Lǎng (朗).
He abandoned Xuángōu (懸鉤),
captured Wǎnchéng (宛城),
killed Zūn's (遵) Grand Administrator of Nányáng (南陽), Yuán Jǐng (袁景), and returned.
Initially,
when Shí Zūn set out from Lǐchéng,
he said to Shí Mǐn:
"Exert yourself!
If the undertaking succeeds,
I will make you heir apparent."
However, he subsequently established Yǎn,
and Mǐn was greatly disappointed.
Considering his own achievements to be unmatched at the time,
