he planned to control the court,
but Zūn was wary and could not trust him with authority.
After Mǐn became Dūdū,
commanding all military power, both internal and external,
he appeased the palace guards and the more than ten thousand former Crown Prince's elite soldiers,
all of whom he recommended to be appointed as Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Guānwài Hóu,
and bestowed with palace women,
thereby cultivating his own influence.
Zūn did not suspect this,
but instead marked names as good or bad to suppress them,
and everyone resented it.
Furthermore, he adopted the counsel of Zhōngshū Lìng Mèng Zhǔn and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Luán,
and grew somewhat suspicious and apprehensive of Mǐn,
gradually stripping him of his military authority.
Mǐn became even more resentful,
and Zhǔn and others all urged Zūn to execute him.
Zūn summoned Shí Jiàn and others to enter,
and discussed the matter before his Empress Dowager Zhèng,
all of whom requested to execute Mǐn.
Empress Zhèng said:
"When we returned from Lǐchéng,
how could we have reached this day without Jí Nú (Mǐn)?
A little indulgence is fine;
he should not be killed immediately."
Jiàn left,
and dispatched the eunuch Yáng Huán to quickly inform Mǐn.
Mǐn then seized Lǐ Nóng and Yòuwèi Wáng Jī,
secretly plotting to depose Zūn.
He ordered generals Sū Hài and Zhōu Chéng to lead thirty armored soldiers to capture Zūn at Rúyì Guān.
Zūn was at that time playing a board game with women,
and asked Chéng and the others:
"Who is the rebel?"
Chéng replied:
"Yìyáng Wáng Jiàn is to be enthroned."
Zūn said:
"If I am like this,
how long will you last if you enthrone Jiàn?!"
Then he killed him at Kūnhuá Diàn,
and executed Empress Zhèng, his Crown Prince Yǎn, Shàngguānglù Zhāng Fēi, Zhōngshū Lìng Mèng Zhǔn, Zuǒwèi Wáng Luán, and others.
Zūn was in power for a total of one hundred eighty-three days.
Jiàn then usurped the throne,
and granted a general amnesty from capital offenses downwards.
He appointed Shí Mǐn as Dàjiāngjūn,
enfeoffed him as Wǔdé Wáng,
and Lǐ Nóng as Dàsīmǎ,
both overseeing the affairs of the Shàngshū.
Láng Kǎi was appointed Sīkōng,
Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Qún as Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
and Shìzhōng Lú Chén as Zhōngshū Jiān.
Jiàn ordered Shí Bāo, Zhōngshū Lìng Lǐ Sōng, and Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Zhāng Cái and others to secretly assassinate Mǐn and Nóng at Kūnhuá Diàn during the night.
They failed,
and the palace was thrown into chaos.
Fearing that Mǐn would revolt,
Jiàn feigned ignorance,
and that night executed Sōng and Cái at Xīzhōnghuámén,
and also killed Shí Bāo.
At that time, Shí Zhī was in Xiāngguó,
and communicated with Yáo Yìzhòng, Fú Hóng, and others,
forming an alliance and issuing a manifesto to punish Mǐn and Nóng.
Jiàn dispatched Shí Kūn as Dàdūdū,
with Zhāng Jǔ and Shìzhōng Hūyán Shèng, leading seventy thousand infantry and cavalry to separately attack Zhī and the others.
Zhōnglǐngjūn Shí Chéng, Shìzhōng Shí Qǐ, and former Hédōng Tàishǒu Shí Huī plotted to assassinate Mǐn and Nóng.
Mǐn and Nóng killed them.
Lóngxiáng Sūn Fúdū and Liú Zhū and others, with three thousand Jié warriors, ambushed them at Hútiān,
also intending to kill Mǐn and the others.
At this time, Jiàn was at Zhōngtái.
Fúdū led over thirty people, intending to ascend the platform to hold Jiàn hostage and attack Mǐn.
Jiàn saw Fúdū destroying the elevated walkway,
and asked him the reason from above.
Fúdū said:
"Lǐ Nóng and others are rebelling,
they are already at Dōngyèmén.
Your subject has strictly ordered the guards and respectfully wishes to inform you first."
Jiàn said:
"You are a meritorious official,
you serve the court well.
I will watch you from the platform,
do not worry about not being rewarded."
Thereupon, Fúdū and Zhū led their forces to attack Mǐn and Nóng,
but failed,
and entrenched themselves at Fèngyángmén.
Mǐn and Nóng led several thousand men, destroyed Jīnmíngmén, and entered.
Jiàn, fearing that Mǐn would kill him,
quickly summoned Mǐn and Nóng,
opened the gates to let them in,
and said:
"Sūn Fúdū has rebelled,
you should quickly suppress him."
Mǐn and Nóng attacked and beheaded Fúdū and others.
From Fèngyáng to Kūnhuá,
corpses piled up,
and blood flowed into channels.
They issued an order that any of the six barbarian tribes, inside or outside, who dared to bear arms would be executed.
Innumerable Hu people either broke through the gates
or scaled the city walls to escape.
He ordered Shàngshū Wáng Jiǎn and Shàofǔ Wáng Yù to lead several thousand men
to guard Jiàn at Yùlóng Guān,
providing him with suspended food.
He announced within the city:
"Those who are loyal to the government shall stay;
those who are not, may go wherever they wish."
He ordered the city gates to no longer restrict movement.
Thereupon, all Zhào people within a hundred *lǐ* entered the city,
while Hu and Jié people who left filled the gates.
Mǐn knew that the Hu people would not serve him,
so he issued an order to all Zhào people, internal and external,
that whoever presented a Hu head at Fèngyángmén,
civil officials would be promoted three ranks,
and military officers would all be appointed to the Yámén.
Within a single day,
tens of thousands of heads were severed.
Mǐn personally led the Zhào people to execute all Hu and Jié,
regardless of noble or common, male or female, young or old, all were beheaded.
Over two hundred thousand people died,
their bodies were piled outside the city gates,
all eaten by wild dogs, jackals, and wolves.
Those who were entrenched in the four directions,
wherever they were, followed Mǐn's orders to execute them.
At that time, half of those with prominent noses and full beards were unjustly killed.
Tàizǎi Zhào Lù,
Tàiwèi Zhāng Jǔ, Zhōngjūn Zhāng Chūn, Guānglù Shí Yuè, Fǔjūn Shí Níng, Wǔwèi Zhāng Jì, and over ten thousand dukes, marquises, ministers, and commanders like Lóngténg, fled to Xiāngguó.
Shí Kūn fled to and held Jìzhōu.
Fǔjūn Zhāng Shěn garrisoned Fúkǒu.
Zhāng Hèdù held Shídú.
Jiànyì Duàn Qín held Líyáng.
Níngnán Yáng Qún garrisoned Sāngbì.
Liú Guó held Yángchéng.
Duàn Kān held Chénliú.
Yáo Yìzhòng held Húnqiáo.
Fú Hóng held Fāngtóu,
each with tens of thousands of followers.
Wáng Láng and Má Qiū fled from Cháng'ān to Luòyáng.
Qiū, acting on Mǐn's orders,
executed over a thousand Hu people from Láng's unit.
Láng fled to Xiāngguó.
Má Qiū led his forces to Fú Hóng.
Shí Kūn, Zhāng Jǔ, and Wáng Láng led seventy thousand men to attack Yè.
Shí Mǐn led over a thousand cavalry
to resist them north of the city.
Mǐn wielded a double-edged spear,
charged on horseback and attacked them.
They all crumbled before his onslaught,
and three thousand heads were taken.
Kūn and the others suffered a great defeat,
and then returned to Jìzhōu.
Mǐn and Lǐ Nóng led thirty thousand cavalry to attack Zhāng Hèdù at Shídú.
Jiàn secretly dispatched a eunuch with a letter to summon Zhāng Shěn and others,
ordering them to seize Yè while it was undefended.
The eunuch informed Mǐn and Nóng.
Mǐn and Nóng hurried back,
deposed Jiàn and killed him,
executed thirty-eight grandsons of Jìlóng,
and exterminated the Shí clan.
Jiàn was in power for one hundred three days.
Jìlóng's youngest son, Hùn,
in the eighth year of Yǒnghé, fled to the capital with several wives and concubines.
An imperial edict ordered his arrest and delivery to the Tíngwèi.
Shortly after, he was executed in Jiànkāng market.
Of Jìlóng's thirteen sons,
five were killed by Rǎn Mǐn,
eight mutually destroyed each other,
and Hùn now also died.
Originally,
a prophecy stated that "Líng will destroy Shí".
Soon after, Shí Mǐn was enfeoffed as Lánlíng Gōng.
Jìlóng disliked this,
and changed Lánlíng to Wǔxīng Jùn.
By this time, he was ultimately destroyed by Mǐn.
Shǐ Lè usurped the throne in the third year of Chéngdì Xiánhé (328 AD).
Two rulers and four sons (successors),
a total of twenty-three years,
were extinguished in the fifth year of Mùdì Yǒnghé (345 AD).
to arrange the capital region.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
among those who reached the pinnacle of glory,
has there ever been anyone like this?
In my opinion,
if his achievements are realized and his enterprises succeed,
he will surely enjoy the
fame of Shēn Bó;
but if they do not materialize,
he will not escape the fate of Liáng and Dòu.
Whenever I read historical accounts,
I have never failed to see how the mother's clan was favored and indulged,
allowed to wield power and disturb the court,
first enjoying extraordinary glory,
then quickly suffering the burden of "riding on a cart without knowing how to drive it" (i.e., being incompetent and bringing disaster),
which is what is meant by
"loving them is precisely what brings them harm."
I often resent the rulers of past dynasties
for not fully employing the methods to prevent initial problems and control favored individuals,
why not grant them land as a fief,
allowing the vassal states to
be passed down,
like Qí and Chén in the Zhōu dynasty?
If this were done, then the dignity of facing south (i.e., being a sovereign) would be forever preserved,
and what worry of demotion or humiliation would there be?
Dòu Wǔ and Hé Jìn were fond of goodness and humble,
attracting worthy men
to their cause.
Although they were endangered by the eunuchs,
and the world lamented their fate,
they still managed to conduct themselves without arrogance,
planning for the state even at the cost of their own lives.
Currently, the four seas suffer from extreme distress,
and the central plains are plagued by usurping rebels.
Every family has grievances of bloodshed,
and every person harbors thoughts of revenge.
How can one possibly sleep
soundly and carefree,
engaging in elegant discussions to pass the year?
Although I lack virtue,
I was undeservedly granted the title of a leading general by the late emperor.
With the people of a few commanderies,
I still desire to annex the powerful barbarians.
That is why
from then until now,
engaging in battles and clashing weapons,
one season for farming,
three seasons for military endeavors,
yet my troops are not exhausted,
our granaries have surplus grain,
the enemy fears us daily,
and our territory
expands daily.
How much more so the majesty of a king,
with his imposing power,
how can that be spoken of in the same breath?
Bīng (Liú Bīng) saw the memorial and letter and was greatly alarmed,
considering him too distant
to be controlled.
So, he and Hé Chōng and others memorialized to permit Mùróng Huǎng to claim the title of King of Yān.
In that year, Huǎng attacked Gāogōulí,
and King Zhāo (Gāo Zhāo) begged for an alliance, whereupon Huǎng returned.
The following year,
Zhāo sent his heir apparent to pay homage to Huǎng.
Initially,
when Duàn Liáo was defeated,
Jiànwēi Hán (Mùróng Hán) fled to Yǔwén Guī.
Believing that his prestige and renown had long been established,
he would ultimately not be spared.
So, he feigned madness and indulged in alcohol,
letting his hair down and singing loudly.
Guī believed him and did not restrain him,
thus Hán was able to travel freely and act as he pleased,
thoroughly familiarizing himself with the advantageous terrain of mountains and rivers,
and crucial routes for attack and defense.
Huǎng sent a merchant, Wáng Chē, to secretly observe Hán.
Hán saw Chē but said nothing,
merely patted his chest.
Chē returned and reported this,
and Huǎng said:
"Hán wants to come."
Then he sent Chē to give Hán a bow and arrows.
Hán then secretly acquired a fine horse,
took his two sons, and returned.
Huǎng planned to attack the Shí clan (Later Zhào).
He calmly said to his generals:
"Shí Jìlóng believes that the defenses of his cities, such as Ānlè, are severe,
so the north and south of the cities will certainly not be fortified.
Now if we take a circuitous route and strike when they least expect it,
the entire northern part of Jì Province can be conquered."
Thereupon, he led two thousand cavalry out of the Yē'ōng Pass,
drove straight to Jìchéng,
advanced across the Wǔsuì Ford,
and entered Gāoyáng.
Wherever they passed, they burned accumulated supplies,
and plundered and relocated over thirty thousand households from Yōu and Jì provinces.
He ordered Yáng Yù and Táng Zhù and others to build Lóngchéng,
construct palaces and temples,
and rename Liǔchéng to Lóngchéng Xiàn.

Thereupon, Emperor Chéng sent Guō Xī, acting as Grand Herald, with imperial credentials, to appoint Mùróng Huǎng as Grand Master of Remonstrance, Grand Commander of all military affairs north of the Yellow River, Grand General, and King of Yān.
All his other offices remained as before.
He enfeoffed over a hundred meritorious officials.
In the seventh year of Xiánkāng (341 CE),
Huǎng moved his capital to Lóngchéng.
He led forty thousand elite troops,
entering from the Southern Shǎnxī,
to attack Yǔwén and Gāogōulí.
He also made Hán and his son Chuí the vanguard,
and dispatched Chief Clerk Wáng Yí and others to lead fifteen thousand troops,
advancing from Běizhì.
King Zhāo of Gāogōulí, thinking Huǎng's army would come from the northern route,
sent his younger brother Wǔ to command fifty thousand elite troops to resist at Běizhì,
while he personally led weaker troops to guard the Southern Shǎnxī.
Hán fought Zhāo at Mùdǐ,
heavily defeating him.
Riding on their victory, they then entered Wándū,
and Zhāo fled alone on horseback.
Huǎng dug up the tomb of Zhāo's father, Lì,
loaded his corpse, along with his mother, wife, and treasures,
plundered over fifty thousand men and women,
burned their palaces and houses,
destroyed Wándū, and returned.
The following year,
Zhāo sent envoys to declare submission to Huǎng,
offering local products.
Huǎng then returned his father's corpse.
Yǔwén Guī sent his prime minister, Mòqiǎn Hún, to attack Huǎng.
The generals requested to fight,
but Huǎng refused.
Hún thought Huǎng feared him,
so he indulged in alcohol and hunting,
no longer setting up defenses.
Huǎng said:
"Hún is excessively extravagant and negligent;
now we can fight him."
He sent Hán to lead cavalry to attack him.
Hún was greatly defeated,
barely escaping with his life,
and all his troops were captured.
Huǎng personally toured the commanderies and counties,
encouraging and instructing agriculture and sericulture,
and began constructing palaces in Lóngchéng.
Soon after, he again led twenty thousand cavalry to personally attack Yǔwén Guī,
with Hán and Chuí as the vanguard.
Guī sent his cavalry general Shè Yìyú with all his troops to resist Hán.
Huǎng galloped to send a message to Hán, saying:
"Yìyú is brave and fierce,
you should slightly avoid him,
wait until the enemy becomes arrogant,
and then capture him."
Hán said:
"Guī's elite forces
are all here.
If we can defeat them now,
then Guī can be eliminated without further military effort.
Yìyú merely has an empty reputation;
in reality, he is easy to deal with.
We should not let the enemy go and dampen our morale."
Thereupon, he engaged in battle,
beheaded Yìyú,
captured all his troops,
and Guī fled far to the north of the desert.
Huǎng expanded his territory by over a thousand *lǐ*,
relocating over fifty thousand households of their people to Chānglí,
and renamed Shè Yìyú City to Wēidé City.
He held the ritual of "drinking to achievement,"
and distributed rewards according to merit, each varying.
He gave cattle to poor families,
who cultivated land in the imperial park.
The government collected eight-tenths (of the harvest),
and two-tenths went to the private families.
Those who had cattle but no land
also cultivated land in the imperial park.
The government collected seven-tenths (of the harvest),
and three-tenths went to the private families.
Huǎng's Record Keeper and Military Adviser, Fēng Yù, admonished him, saying: "I have heard that when sagely kings govern a state,
they levy light taxes and store (wealth) among the common people.
They divide the land into three grades,
and tax it at one-tenth;
they clothe the cold,
feed the hungry,
ensuring that every family has enough and every person is well-fed.
Even during floods and droughts, these do not become disasters;
why is this?
They select high-ranking agricultural officials,
dedicated to urging and instructing (the people to farm).
Each person cultivates a hundred *mǔ* of well-managed fields,
without even needing cattle power.
Diligent farmers receive commendations and rewards,
while lazy farmers incur penalties that exclude them from society.
Furthermore, they establish officials according to the task,
and appoint people according to the official positions,
enabling them to..."
Wáng Xiàn and Liú Míng
are loyal ministers.
I wish to pardon their offense of opposing the sovereign
and accept the efficacy of their corrective advice.
Mùróng Huǎng then issued an order, saying:
"Having read Fēng Jìshì's remonstrance,
I am truly fearful.
The sovereign relies on the common people for the state,
and the common people rely on grain for their lives.
Therefore, agriculture
is the foundation of the state.
However, the Erqiānshí (Two-Thousand-Picul) Prefects and Magistrates do not observe the regulations of early spring,
discouraging diligent farming.
It is appropriate to subject those who are most negligent in cultivation to the law,
strictly disciplining their subordinate cities.
The responsible officials shall thoroughly investigate and examine,
and report the full details.
All imperial parks and preserves shall be abolished
to be distributed to the common people who have no land.
The poor who are entirely without assets
and cannot sustain themselves
shall each be granted one ox for plowing.
If anyone privately has surplus labor
and is willing to take official oxen to cultivate official land,
they shall follow the old laws of Wèi and Jìn.
The construction of canals and irrigation systems
benefits both official and private interests.
The responsible officials shall estimate and construct them,
making full use of the potential of both land and water.
The Central Plains are not yet pacified,
and military difficulties are ceaseless.
As meritorious deeds are numerous,
the number of officials cannot be reduced.
We shall wait until the fierce rebels are subdued and pacified,
then discuss it again.
Regarding the number of various artisans and merchants,
the Sizuǒ (Four Assistants) and the Liejiàng (Ranked Generals) shall swiftly determine the major positions,
and the rest shall return to farming.
Students who are not fit for training and teaching
shall also be removed from the roster.
It is extremely difficult
for a minister to speak to the sovereign.
All matters that are wild, baseless, and unfounded should be completely disregarded,
and only the good ones should be followed.
Although Wáng Xiàn and Liú Míng's offenses warrant their removal and expulsion,
it would also indicate my own lack of magnanimity.
They may all be restored to their original official posts,
and continue to serve in the remonstrance office.
Fēng Shēng is upright and steadfast,
deeply embodying the spirit of a royal minister.
Does the Shījīng not say: 'No word goes unreturned'?
He shall be granted fifty thousand coins.
Let this be clearly proclaimed both within and without,
that anyone wishing to express my faults,
regardless of their status,
should hide nothing."
At that time, there was one black dragon and one white dragon
seen at Lóngshān.
Mùróng Huǎng personally led his officials to observe them.
Two hundred paces from the dragons,
he offered a Grand Sacrifice (tàiláo).
The two dragons intertwined their necks and soared playfully,
then shed their horns and departed.
Mùróng Huǎng was greatly pleased.
Upon returning to the palace,
he issued an amnesty throughout his territory.
He named the new palace Hélóng
and built the Lóngxiáng Buddhist Temple on the mountain.
He granted the children of his high ministers who were official students the title Gāoménshēng (Students of Noble Families).
He established the Dōngxiáng (Eastern School) at the old palace,
where the archery ritual (xiāngshè zhī lǐ) was performed.
He personally observed it monthly
to examine their performance.
Mùróng Huǎng was fond of literature
and diligent in lecturing and teaching.
His students were very numerous,
reaching over a thousand people.
He personally composed the Tàishàng Zhāng to replace the Jíjiù Zhāng,
and also wrote fifteen chapters of Diǎnjiè (Canonical Admonitions)
to instruct his heirs.
Mùróng Kè attacked Nánsū in Gāogōulì,
conquered it,
established a garrison, and returned.
In the third year,
he dispatched his heir apparent, Mùróng Jùn, and Mùróng Kè, leading seventeen thousand cavalry to raid Fúyú in the east.
They conquered it,
capturing its king and over fifty thousand people, and returned.
Mùróng Huǎng personally visited the Dōngxiáng to examine the students.
Those who were outstanding in their mastery of the classics
were promoted to serve as close attendants.
Due to a prolonged drought,
he remitted the land taxes for the common people.
He abolished the commanderies of Chéngzhōu, Jìyáng, Yíngqiū, and others.
People from Bóhǎi were designated as Xīngjí County,
people from Héjiān as Níngjí County,
people from Guǎngpíng and Wèi Commandery as Xīngpíng County,
people from Dōnglái and Běihǎi as Yùlí County,
and Wú people as Wú County,
all subordinate to the state of Yàn.
Mùróng Huǎng once hunted in the western frontier.
As he was about to cross the river,
he saw an old man
dressed in red clothes
riding a white horse.
The old man raised his hand and waved at Mùróng Huǎng, saying:
"This is not a hunting ground;
the King should return."
Mùróng Huǎng kept it secret and did not speak of it,
then crossed the river,
making great gains for several consecutive days.
Later, he saw a white rabbit,
galloped to shoot it,
his horse stumbled, and he was injured.
He then recounted what he had seen.
He was carried back to the palace
and summoned Mùróng Jùn to entrust him with future affairs.
He died in the fourth year of Yǒnghé,
having reigned for fifteen years,
at the age of fifty-two.
Mùróng Jùn usurped the title
and posthumously honored him as Wénmíng Huángdì.
Mùróng Hàn, courtesy name Yuán Yōng,
was Mùróng Huì's eldest illegitimate son.
He was brave and daring by nature,
with many strategies.
He had long arms and was skilled in archery,
with extraordinary physical strength.
Mùróng Huì greatly admired him
and entrusted him with military command.
Wherever he led his troops on campaigns,
he achieved success,
and his prestige greatly spread,
making him feared by both near and far.
When he was garrisoned in Liáodōng,
Gāogōulì dared not commit depredations.
He was good at dealing with people and befriending them,
and cherished classical learning.
From scholars and officials to soldiers,
everyone was happy to follow him.
When he fled to Duàn Liáo,
he was deeply respected and loved by Duàn Liáo.
During the defeat at Liǔchéng,
Duàn Lán wanted to take advantage of the victory and advance deep into enemy territory.
Mùróng Hàn feared that this would harm his native country,
so he tricked Duàn Lán with a deceptive argument,
and Duàn Lán consequently did not advance.
Later, Shí Jìlóng attacked Liáo,
and Mùróng Huǎng personally led the main army to occupy the area north of Lìngzhī.
Duàn Liáo debated whether to pursue them.
Mùróng Hàn knew that Mùróng Huǎng was personally leading the army
and would surely win the battle.
So he said to Duàn Liáo:
"Now the Shí clan is approaching;
we are facing a formidable enemy,
and it is not appropriate to concern ourselves with minor matters again.
The King of Yàn has come himself,
with elite soldiers and horses.
Weapons are instruments of ill omen;
there is risk in battle.
If we suffer a defeat,
how can we defend against the south?"
Duàn Lán angrily said:
"I listened to your deceitful words before,
which led to the current trouble.
I will not fall for your schemes again."
He then led his troops to pursue Mùróng Huǎng,
and Duàn Lán was indeed greatly defeated.
Although Mùróng Hàn was in an enemy country,
he seized opportunities to demonstrate loyalty,
and all were of this kind.
When Duàn Liáo fled,
Mùróng Hàn again defected north to Yǔwén Guī.
Soon after, he escaped,
so Yǔwén Guī sent over a hundred elite cavalry to pursue him.
Mùróng Hàn called out to the pursuers from afar, saying:
"Since I have returned due to longing for home,
there is no reason for me to turn back.
You all know my archery well enough.
Do not press me;
you will only bring death upon yourselves.
I have been in your country for a long time,
and I regret not killing you.
You may set up a saber one hundred paces away.
If I hit it,
you should turn back;
if I do not hit it,
you may come forward."
The cavalry dismounted their sabers and set them up.
Mùróng Hàn shot once and hit the saber's ring,
whereupon the pursuing cavalry scattered.
Fú Jiān’s general, Fú Suǒ, seized Shǎn,
and surrendered to Wěi.
At the time, there was a prophecy which said:
“Yan horses will drink the Wèi River.”
Jiān feared that Wěi would take advantage of the opportunity to enter Guān,
and was greatly alarmed.
So he mobilized all his elite troops to defend Huáyīn.
Wěi’s subordinates discussed sending troops to rescue Suǒ,
and then taking Guānyòu.
Mùróng Píng, who had always lacked strategic vision,
and had also received bribes from Fú Jiān,
discouraged the plan, saying:
“Although Qín is in trouble,
it is not easy to seize.
Although the imperial court is wise,
how can it compare to the late emperor?
Our strategic abilities
also do not match those of the Grand Tutor.
We will ultimately be unable to conquer Qín.
We should just close the passes and rest our troops,
securing our borders; that will be sufficient.”
Wěi’s Wèiyǐn, Mùróng Dé, submitted a memorial, saying:
“The late emperor responded to Heaven and conformed to the times,
receiving the mandate to reform the age.
He was about to pacify distant lands with civil virtue,
and unify the six directions.
His divine accomplishments were not yet complete
when he suddenly ascended to Heaven.
After King Wén of Zhōu passed away,
King Wǔ succeeded him and rose to power.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty emulates Heaven in virtue,
and matches the Sages in achievement.
You are about to expand the great foundation
and complete the former aspirations.
The rebellious Dī have usurped control of Guānlǒng,
and assumed the title of king.
Their wickedness has accumulated and their misfortunes have overflowed.
They are suspicious of and slaughter each other.
Trouble has arisen within their own ranks,
and their power is split into four states.
They have sworn allegiance and requested aid,
one after another within days.
Is this not because their ill fortune is about to end,
and the mandate is returning to the virtuous?
To attack the weak and assault the confused,
to exploit chaos and insult the fallen,
this is the highest opportunity.
Now Qín’s territory is divided into four;
it can be called weak.
The time has come, the opportunity has gathered,
Heaven assists us.
If Heaven grants it and we do not take it,
we will instead suffer misfortune.
The lesson of Wú and Yuè
is our teacher.
It is fitting to respond to the convergence of Heaven and man,
and raise the banner of Mùyě.
Order Huángfǔ Zhēn to lead the troops from Bìng and Jì
straight to Púbǎn;
let your servant Chuí lead the soldiers from Xǔ and Luò
to swiftly relieve Suǒ’s siege;
let the Grand Tutor command the capital’s martial forces
as a follow-up for the two armies.
Issue flying proclamations throughout Sānfǔ,
let benevolent fame precede our arrival.
Those who capture a city will be ennobled,
even small merits will be rewarded.
Then those heroes who have been waiting for their time,
and exceptional individuals whose ambitions are yet unfulfilled,
will surely stand like mountains at Bàshàng,
and gather like clouds beneath Lǒng.
With the heavenly net cast,
and external and internal forces united,
those petty usurpers
will either flee or surrender.
The time for the great unification
is now.
I wish Your Majesty would make a decisive judgment,
and not consult benevolent men.”
Wěi read the memorial with great joy,
and intended to follow it.
Píng adamantly refused to allow it,
so he stopped.
Fú Suǒ, knowing Píng and Wěi lacked foresight,
and fearing that the rescue army would not arrive,
then wrote to Mùróng Chuí and Huángfǔ Zhēn, saying:
“Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng are both outstanding individuals.
They have been plotting to harm Yàn
for a long time.
If we do not seize this opportunity and act now,
I fear that the ruler and ministers of Yàn will have the regret of Yǒngdōng.”
Chuí received the letter,
and privately said to Zhēn:
“The one who will bring harm to others will certainly be in Qín.
Our lord is young,
and cannot yet focus on state affairs.
Looking at the Grand Tutor’s strategic ability,
how can he resist Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng?”
Zhēn said:
“Indeed.
Ràocháo said,
‘If a plan is not followed, what can one do!’”
Wěi’s Púyè, Yuè Wǎn, spoke to Wěi, saying:
“The Grand Tutor’s administration has always been lenient and mild,
and many common people secretly attach themselves to him.
It is said,
‘Only the virtuous can rule the multitude with leniency;
the next best is fierceness.’
Now, the households of the various military camps
are divided into three, sharing common registries.
Morale and discipline are declining,
and authority is not upheld.
It is fitting to abolish all military enfeoffments
to enrich the imperial treasury,
and to rigorously enforce laws and decrees
to bring order to the entire realm.”
Wěi accepted this.
Once Wǎn had established the new regulations,
the court and country were shocked.
More than two hundred thousand households were displaced.
Mùróng Píng was greatly displeased.
He soon sought out Wǎn,
and killed him.
Jìn’s Dàsīmǎ, Huán Wēn, along with Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Huán Chōng, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, Yuán Zhēn, led a force of fifty thousand to attack Wěi.
Former Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ, Sūn Yuán, raised an army to support them.
Wēn’s subordinate, Tán Xuán, attacked Húlù,
and captured Wěi’s Níngdōng, Mùróng Zhōng.
Wěi dispatched his general, Mùróng Lì, to battle Wēn at Huángxū.
Lì’s army was greatly defeated,
and he fled back on a single horse.
Gāopíng Tàishǒu, Xú Fān, surrendered his command.
Wēn’s vanguard, Zhū Xù, again defeated Wěi’s general, Fù Yán, at Línzhǔ.
Wēn’s army was greatly encouraged,
and advanced to Fāngtóu.
Wěi was frightened,
and considered fleeing to Hélóng.
Mùróng Chuí said:
“Not so.
I request to attack them.
If the battle is not victorious,
it will not be too late to flee.”
Thereupon, Chuí was made Shǐchíjié, Nántǎo Dàdūdū;
Mùróng Dé was made Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn.
They led a force of fifty thousand to confront Wēn.
He sent his Sànqí Shìláng, Yuè Sōng, to request aid from Fú Jiān.
Jiān dispatched General Gǒu Chí with a force of twenty thousand,
marching from Luòyáng,
and encamping at Yǐngchuān.
Outwardly, they were there to reinforce,
but inwardly, they were watching for an opportunity,
with aspirations of annexation.
Mùróng Dé camped at Shímén,
cutting off Wēn’s supply lines.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, Lǐ Bāng,
led five thousand provincial troops to cut off Wēn’s provisions.
Wēn repeatedly fought without success,
and his supplies were again cut off.
Upon hearing of Jiān’s army’s arrival,
he burned his boats, abandoned his armor, and retreated.
Dé led four thousand elite cavalry,
arriving east of Xiāngyì before Wēn,
and lay in ambush in the valley.
Together with Chuí, they attacked from front and rear,
and the royal army was greatly defeated,
with over thirty thousand killed.
Gǒu Chí, hearing of Wēn’s retreat,
ambushed him at Qiáo.
Wēn’s forces were again defeated,
with tens of thousands killed.
Since Chuí had achieved great merit,
his prestige and power grew even stronger.
Mùróng Píng had always been displeased with him.
Chuí also stated that his generals, Sūn Gài and others, had bravely charged into battle,
and ought to be rewarded with promotions.
Píng suppressed this and did not record it.
Chuí repeatedly brought it up,
and often argued with Píng in court.
The Kěsúhún clan had always disliked Chuí,
and disparaged his military achievements.
They then conspired with Píng to kill Chuí.
Chuí, in fear,
fled to Fú Jiān.
That year,
Fú Shuāng (苻雙) rebelled against Jiān (堅) by occupying Shàngguī (上邽), and Fú Liǔ (苻柳) by occupying Púbǎn (蒲坂).
Fú Yǔ (苻庾) held Shǎnchéng (陝城),
and Fú Wǔ (苻武) held Āndìng (安定); both responded to them,
planning to jointly attack Cháng'ān (長安).
Jiān sent an envoy to reason with them,
and they each bit a pear as a sign of trust,
but all refused Jiān's command,
blocking his forces and defending themselves.
Jiān sent General of the Rear Guard Yáng Chéngshì (楊成世) and General of the Left Máo Sōng (毛嵩) and others to suppress Shuāng (雙) and Wǔ (武).
Wáng Měng (王猛) and Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌) attacked Púbǎn (蒲坂).
Yáng Ān (楊安) and Zhāng Háo (張蚝) attacked Shǎnchéng (陝城).
Chéngshì (成世) and Máo Sōng (毛嵩) were defeated by Shuāng (雙) and Wǔ (武).
Jiān then sent his Martial Guard Wáng Jiàn (王鑒) and Níngshuò (寧朔) Lǚ Guāng (呂光) and others, leading elite troops from within and without the capital, to suppress them.
Left Guard Fú Yǎ (苻雅) and Left prohibitor Dòu Chōng (竇衝) led seven thousand Yǔlín (羽林) cavalry as a follow-up force.
Shuāng (雙) and Wǔ (武), emboldened by their victory, reached Yúméi (榆眉).
Jiàn (鑒) and others attacked and defeated them,
slaying and capturing fifteen thousand men.
Wǔ (武) abandoned Āndìng (安定)
and fled with Shuāng (雙) to Shàngguī (上邽).
Jiàn (鑒) and others attacked them.
Fú Liǔ (苻柳) rode out to challenge,
but Měng (猛) kept his troops within the camp and did not respond.
Liǔ (柳) thought Měng (猛) feared him,
so he left his heir, Liáng (良), to guard Púbǎn (蒲坂),
and led twenty thousand troops,
intending to attack Cháng'ān (長安).
Cháng'ān (長安) was over a hundred *lǐ* from Púbǎn (蒲坂).
Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌) led seven thousand elite cavalry in a night raid and defeated him.
Liǔ (柳) withdrew his army.
Měng (猛) then led all his troops to intercept and attack,
capturing all of Liǔ's (柳) soldiers.
Liǔ (柳) entered Púbǎn (蒲坂) with a few hundred cavalry.
Jiàn (鑒) and others attacked Shàngguī (上邽),
conquered it,
and beheaded Shuāng (雙) and Wǔ (武).
Měng (猛) soon after broke Púbǎn (蒲坂),
beheaded Liǔ (柳) and his wife and children,
and sent their heads to Cháng'ān (長安).
Měng (猛) garrisoned Púbǎn (蒲坂),
and sent Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌) with Wáng Jiàn (王鑒) and others to capture Shǎnchéng (陝城),
which they conquered.
They sent Yǔ (庾) to Cháng'ān (長安)
and killed him.
In the fourth year of Tàihé (太和),
Jìn (晉) Grand Marshal Huán Wēn (桓溫) attacked Mùróng Wěi (慕容暐),
reaching Fāngtóu (枋頭).
Wěi's (暐) forces were repeatedly defeated,
so he sent an envoy to request aid from Jiān (堅),
offering to cede the land west of Wǔláo (武牢).
Jiān (堅) also wanted to form an alliance with Wěi (暐),
so he sent his general Gǒu Chí (苟池) and others, leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, to aid Wěi (暐).
The royal army soon suffered a defeat,
and retreated.
Chí (池) then returned.
At this time, Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂), fleeing danger, sought refuge with Jiān (堅).
Wáng Měng (王猛) spoke to Jiān (堅), saying:
"Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂)
is a relative of Yān (燕),
whose family has been powerful in the eastern Xīa (夏) for generations.
He is magnanimous and benevolent towards his subordinates,
and has won the favor of both gentry and commoners.
People throughout Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙) harbor intentions to support and embrace him.
Observing his talent and strategy,
his resourcefulness is boundless.
Moreover, his sons are intelligent, resolute, and capable—
they are all outstanding men.
A flood dragon or fierce beast
is not something that can be tamed;
it would be better to eliminate him."
Jiān (堅) said:
"I am just now gathering heroes through righteousness
to achieve unprecedented accomplishments.
Furthermore, when he first arrived,
I declared my utmost sincerity to him.
If I harm him now,
what will people say of me?"
After the royal army returned,
Mùróng Wěi (慕容暐) regretted ceding the land of Wǔláo (武牢),
and sent an envoy to tell Jiān (堅):
"The envoy who negotiated the land cession earlier
misspoke.
For states and families
to share misfortunes and relieve distress
is a constant principle."
Jiān (堅) was greatly angered.
He sent Wáng Měng (王猛) with Jiànwēi (建威) Liáng Chéng (梁成) and Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌), leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry.
He appointed Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂) as General of the Champion Army (冠軍將軍),
to serve as a local guide,
to attack Wěi's (暐) Governor of Luòzhōu (洛州), Mùróng Zhù (慕容筑), in Luòyáng (洛陽).
Wěi (暐) sent his general Mùróng Zāng (慕容臧), leading a hundred thousand elite soldiers,
to relieve Zhù's (筑) siege.
Měng (猛) ordered Liáng Chéng (梁成) and others to lead ten thousand elite troops, covering their armor, to rush to meet him.
They greatly defeated Zāng (臧) at Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Zhù (筑), terrified, requested to surrender.
Měng (猛) arrayed his army to receive his surrender.
He left Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌) to guard Jīnyǒng (金墉),
and Měng (猛) triumphantly returned.
He established the spirit tablet of Fú Jiān in the army,
carrying it on a baggage carriage.
It had feathered canopies and a blue parasol,
and the carriage flew a yellow banner.
Three hundred brave warriors guarded it.
Before battle, they would always report to it,
and for anything they wished to do,
they would inform the spirit lord before proceeding.
Having repaired armor and gathered troops,
he was about to lead his army eastward,
and so he announced to Fú Jiān's spirit tablet, saying:
"Your great-grandson, Emperor Fú Dēng,
by the spiritual power of the Great Emperor, respectfully ascends the treasured throne.
Formerly, during the calamity of the Five Generals,
the rebellious Qiāng wrought havoc upon your sacred person.
This was truly Dēng's sin.
Now, having assembled a righteous army,
with over fifty thousand troops,
well-armored and strong,
sufficient to achieve merit,
and with abundant harvests,
sufficient for provisions.
Today, like stars and lightning, we shall march,
directly attacking the rebels' court.
Fighting without regard for life,
death is our only objective,
hoping to avenge the Emperor's cruel wrong
and wash away the great shame of your servants and sons.
O, spirit of the Emperor,
look down upon our sincerity."
Thereupon, he sighed and shed tears.
None of the generals and soldiers were not overcome with grief,
and all carved the characters
"死休" (death or rest)
onto their lances and armor,
indicating their resolve to fight to the death.
In every battle, they used long spears with hooked blades to form a large square and circular formation,
knowing where it was strong and where it was weak,
and distributing forces accordingly.
Thus, each person fought for themselves,
and they were unstoppable.
Initially,
when Cháng'ān was about to fall, Fú Jiān's Middle Army General Xú Sōng and Cavalry Commandant Hú Kōng each gathered five thousand followers,
fortified strongholds in strategic locations to secure themselves,
and accepted official titles from Yáo Cháng.
When Yáo Cháng harmed Fú Jiān,
Xú Sōng and others buried Fú Jiān with royal rites between their two strongholds.
By this time,
they each led their followers to surrender to Fú Dēng.
Fú Dēng appointed Xú Sōng as General Who Guards the Army and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
and Hú Kōng as General Who Assists the State and Governor of Jīngzhàoyǐn.
Fú Dēng then reburied Fú Jiān with imperial rites.
He also presumptuously established his wife, Lady Máos, as Empress,
and his younger brother Yǐ as Crown Prince.
He sent an envoy to appoint Fú Zuǎn as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Palace Attendant, Grand Inspector-General of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, and Grand Tutor,
also holding the title of Grand Marshal,
and advanced his peerage to Prince of Lǔ.
Fú Zuǎn's younger brother Shīnú was appointed General-in-Chief Who Protects the Army, Governor of Bīngzhōu, and Duke of Shuòfāng.
Fú Zuǎn angrily said to the envoy:
"The Prince of Bóhǎi is a grandson of Emperor Shìzǔ,
a son of the late emperor.
How can the Prince of Nán'ān not be established and exalt himself?"
Fú Zuǎn's Chief Clerk, Wáng Lǚ, advised him, saying:
"Nán'ān has already been established;
it is unreasonable to change that midway.
The barbarian rebels are not yet pacified;
we cannot become enemies among ourselves within the imperial clan.
I wish Your Highness would follow the example of Emperor Guāngwǔ from afar, upholding the righteousness of the Holy Lord,
and after decapitating the two barbarians,
then plan anew."
Fú Zuǎn then accepted the appointment.
Thereupon, the barbarian chieftains Péng Pèigǔ from Èrxiàn, Dǒng Chéng of the Túcá, Zhāng Lóngshì, Lái Èdì of the Xīnpíng Qiāng, and others all responded,
with a total of over one hundred thousand followers.
Fú Zuǎn sent Shīnú to attack the Qiāng chieftains Jīn Dàhēi and Jīn Luòshēng in Shàngjùn.
Jīn Dàhēi and others met them in battle and were greatly defeated,
with five thousand eight hundred heads captured.
Fú Dēng appointed Dòu Chōng as General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry and Inspector of Nánqínzhōu,
Yáng Dìng as Grand General and Inspector of Yìzhōu,
and Yáng Bì as Minister of Works and Inspector of Liángzhōu.
Fú Zuǎn defeated Yáo Shuòdé at Jīngyáng.
Yáo Cháng himself resisted Fú Zuǎn from Yīnmì,
and Fú Zuǎn retreated to garrison at Fūlù.
Dòu Chōng attacked Yáo Cháng's two cities of Qiān and Yōng,
capturing them and beheading his generals Yáo Yuánpíng and Zhāng Luè.
He also fought Yáo Cháng east of Qiān
but was defeated by Yáo Cháng.
Fú Dēng encamped at Wǎtíng.
Yáo Cháng attacked Péng Pèigǔ's stronghold,
capturing it.
Péng Pèigǔ fled to Xìngchéng,
and Yáo Cháng moved to Yīnmì.
Fú Dēng's General Who Conquers Barbarians and Prefect of Féngyì, Lán Dú, led twenty thousand followers from Pínyáng into Héníng,
to coordinate with Fú Zuǎn,
intending to attack Cháng'ān.
Shīnú urged his elder brother Fú Zuǎn to claim the imperial title,
but Fú Zuǎn refused.
So, Shīnú killed Fú Zuǎn
and established himself as Duke of Qín.
Lán Dú cut ties with him,
and both were defeated by Yáo Cháng.
Fú Dēng advanced and occupied Hú Kōng's stronghold,
and over one hundred thousand people, both barbarians and Chinese, submitted to him.
Yáo Cháng sent his general Yáo Fāngchéng to attack and capture Xú Sōng's stronghold.
Xú Sōng was killed,
and all the barbarian soldiers were buried alive.
Fú Dēng led his forces down Lǒng and entered Cháonà.
Yáo Cháng occupied Wǔdū, and they were in a standoff,
with several battles having alternating victories and defeats.
There was a great famine in Fú Dēng's army,
and they collected mulberries to feed the soldiers.
He established his son Chóng as Crown Prince,
Biàn as Prince of Nán'ān,
and Shàng as Prince of Běihǎi.
Yáo Cháng retreated to Āndìng.
Fú Dēng moved to Xīnpíng for provisions,
leaving his main army at Hú Kōng's stronghold.
He led over ten thousand cavalry to surround Yáo Cháng's camp,
weeping loudly on all four sides,
their mournful cries moving people.
Yáo Cháng disliked this,
and ordered his entire army to cry in response to Fú Dēng,
whereupon Fú Dēng withdrew.
Yáo Cháng, seeing that Fú Dēng frequently won battles,
believed Fú Jiān had divine power,
and also established Fú Jiān's spirit tablet in his army,
praying:
"Last year's disaster at Xīnpíng
was not Cháng's fault.
My elder brother Xiāng crossed from north of Shǎn,
seeking passage westward.
Like a fox dying with its head towards its mound,
he wanted to briefly see his homeland.
Your Majesty and Fú Méi blocked his path and attacked him,
and he died without fulfilling his wish.
Xiāng ordered your servant to carry out the killing;
it was not your servant's fault.
Fú Dēng is a distant relative of Your Majesty;
he still wants revenge.
Your servant avenges his elder brother's humiliation;
how does this go against reason and sentiment?
Formerly, Your Majesty granted your servant the title of Lóngxiáng,
saying to your servant: 'I established my enterprise with Lóngxiáng;
you should strive diligently!'
Your clear decree is evident,
and your words still echo in my ears.
Although Your Majesty has passed away and become a god,
how can you use Fú Dēng to plot against your servant,
forgetting your words from the previous campaign?
Now I establish a divine image for Your Majesty.
You may rest here.
Do not hold my transgressions against me,
but listen to my sincere heart."
Fú Dēng advanced his army to attack Yáo Cháng.
Afterward, he ascended a tower and said to Yáo Cháng:
"From ancient times to the present,
how can one who kills his lord then establish a divine image to pray for blessings
and expect any benefit?"
He loudly shouted:
"Yáo Cháng, the regicide, come out!
I will settle this with you!
Why do you wrongly harm the innocent?"
Yáo Cháng was intimidated and did not respond.
Since Yáo Cháng had established Fú Jiān's divine image,
the battles had not been favorable,
and the army was startled and afraid every night.
So, he beat the drums sternly and decapitated the image, sending the head to Fú Dēng.
Fú Dēng's generals Dòu Luò and Dòu Yú conspired to rebel, but their plot was discovered,
and they fled to Yáo Cháng.
Fú Dēng advanced to attack Péngchí but failed.
He attacked Míjiě's camp and the various strongholds at Fánchuān,
all of which he captured.
Yáo Cháng suffered repeated defeats in consecutive battles,
so he sent his Central Army General Yáo Chóng to raid Dàjiè.
Fú Dēng led his army to intercept him,
greatly defeating Yáo Chóng at Ānqíu,
capturing and beheading twenty-five thousand.
He then attacked Yáo Cháng's generals Wú Zhōng and Táng Kuāng at Píngliáng,
capturing them.
He appointed Minister Fú Shuòyuán as General of the Former Forbidden Army and Commandant Who Destroys Qiāng,
to garrison Píngliáng.
Fú Dēng advanced and occupied Gǒutóuyuán to threaten Āndìng.
Yáo Cháng led thirty thousand cavalry to launch a night attack on Dàjiè camp,
capturing it.
He killed Fú Dēng's wife, Lady Máos, and his sons Biàn and Shàng,
captured dozens of famous generals,
and carried off over fifty thousand men and women before leaving.
The Jin Dynasty's General Who Conquers the West, Huán Wēn, marched from Jiānglíng to attack Yáo Xiāng.
They battled north of the Yīshǔi River,
where Xiāng was defeated by Wēn,
and fled with several thousand cavalry under his command to Běishān.
That night,
over five thousand common people abandoned their wives and children to follow Xiāng,
and encamped at Yángxiāng.
Another four thousand odd households came to join them.
Xiāng had been defeated and suffered losses many times before this,
yet when the masses learned of Xiāng's whereabouts,
they would always rush to him, supporting the old and leading the young.
At times, when it was rumored that Xiāng was gravely wounded and beyond recovery,
the men and women captured by Wēn's army would all look north and weep.
His popularity was truly remarkable.
Earlier,
Yáng Liàng of Hóngnóng had submitted to Xiāng,
and Xiāng treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
Later, he fled to Huán Wēn.
Wēn asked Liàng about Xiāng.
Liàng replied,
"He possesses a divine and noble demeanor,
on par with Sūn Cè,
but his martial prowess surpasses him."
Such was the high regard in which he was held.
Xiāng soon moved to Běiqū,
intending to conquer Guānzhōng.
He advanced and encamped at Xìngchéng,
sending his cousin, Fǔguó Yáo Lán, to seize territory in Fūchéng.
He also sent his elder brother, Yì, and General Wáng Qīnlú to recruit the Róng and Xià peoples in Běidì,
and over fifty thousand households submitted to them.
Fú Shēng dispatched his general, Fú Fēi, to resist the attack.
Lán was defeated
and captured by Fēi.
Xiāng led his troops westward.
Shēng again sent Fú Jiān and Dèng Qiāng to intercept him.
When Xiāng was about to engage in battle,
the Buddhist monk Zhìtōng strongly advised Xiāng
to sharpen his weapons, gather his forces,
and reconsider his next move.
Xiāng said,
"Two heroes cannot stand together.
I hope Heaven will not abandon my virtue to save the common people.
My plan is decided."
Just then, Qiāng's army pressed close.
Xiāng, enraged,
charged forward directly,
and battled at Sānyuán.
Xiāng was defeated
and killed by Jiān.
He was twenty-seven years old at the time.
This year was the first year of Shēngpíng of the Jìn Dynasty.
Fú Shēng buried him with ducal rites.
Cháng usurped the imperial title,
posthumously honored him as Wèi Wǔ Wáng,
and enfeoffed Xiāng's grandson, Yán Dìng, as Dōngchéng Hóu.
Yáo Cháng
Cháng, courtesy name Jǐngmào,
was Yì Zhòng's twenty-fourth son.
As a youth, he was intelligent and wise,
with many stratagems and schemes.
He was open-minded and spontaneous,
not adhering to conventional conduct,
and all his elder brothers admired him.
He followed Xiāng in campaigns,
always participating in major councils.
When Xiāng attacked Luòyáng,
he dreamt that Cháng was wearing an imperial robe,
ascending the imperial throne,
with all the chieftains standing by his side.
In the morning, he said to his generals and advisors,
"I had such a dream.
This boy's ambition and bearing are extraordinary,
perhaps he can greatly elevate our clan."
When Xiāng was defeated at Mátǐán,
his horse was struck by an arrow and died.
Cháng dismounted and offered his horse to Xiāng.
Xiāng asked,
"How will you escape?"
Cháng replied,
"As long as my brother is safe,
how dare those lads harm Cháng!"
Just then, reinforcements arrived,
and both escaped.
After Xiāng died,
Cháng led his younger brothers to surrender to Fú Shēng.
Fú Jiān appointed Cháng as Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
successively serving as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
Administrator of Lǒngdōng, Jíjun, Hédōng, Wǔdū, Wǔwēi, Bāxī, and Fúfēng,
Inspector of Níng, Yōu, and Yǎn three provinces,
and again as Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
Colonel of Infantry,
and was enfeoffed as Yìdū Hóu.
As Jiān's general,
he repeatedly achieved great merits.
Initially,
Cháng followed Yáng Ān in attacking Shǔ.
He once slept by a stream in the daytime,
and above him, a divine light shone brightly,
which his attendants all found extraordinary.
When Fú Jiān attacked Jìn,
he appointed Cháng as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Supervisor of all military affairs in Yì and Liáng provinces,
saying to Cháng,
"I originally founded my enterprise with the title of Lóngxiáng,
and the title of Lóngxiáng has never been bestowed upon anyone else.
Now I specially grant it to you,
and all matters south of the mountains are entrusted to you."
Jiān's Left General Dòu Chōng stepped forward and said,
"Kings do not joke lightly.
This general's title is an ominous sign.
I humbly request Your Majesty to consider it."
Jiān remained silent.
After Jiān's defeat at Huáinán,
he returned to Cháng'ān.
Mùróng Hóng raised an army and rebelled against Jiān.
Jiān sent his son, Ruì, to suppress him,
with Cháng as his Sīmǎ.
They were defeated by Hóng,
and Ruì died.
Cháng sent Lóngxiáng Chief Clerk Zhào Dū to Jiān to apologize,
but Jiān was enraged
and killed him.
Cháng was afraid
and fled to Wèiběi,
then went to Mǎmù.
The powerful families of Xīzhōu, such as Yǐn Xiáng, Zhào Yáo, Wáng Qīnlú, Niú Shuāng, Dí Guǎng, Zhāng Qián, and others, totaling over fifty thousand households,
all acclaimed Cháng as their盟主 (méngzhǔ).
Cháng was about to refuse them when
Yǐn Wěi of Tiānshuǐ persuaded Cháng, saying,
"Now that the era of great calamity has arrived,
and the omen of Qín's downfall has appeared,
with your general's awe-inspiring spirit, you are destined to rule,
and will surely be able to rectify the difficulties of the time.
Therefore, the heroes flock to you,
all unanimously looking up to you.
My lord should humble himself and accept their counsel,
to fulfill the hopes of the masses.
You cannot sit idly by and watch them drown without rescuing them."
Cháng then followed Wěi's advice.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán, he proclaimed himself Grand General, Grand Chányú, and King of Wànnián Qín,
granted a general amnesty within his territory,
adopted the era name Báiquè,
and began to issue decrees and conduct affairs.
He appointed Yǐn Xiáng of Tiānshuǐ and Páng Yǎn of Nán'ān as Left and Right Chief Clerks,
Yáo Huǎng and Yǐn Wěi of Nán'ān as Left and Right Sīmǎ,
Dí Bózhī, Jiāo Qián, Liáng Xī, Páng Wèi, and Rén Qiān of Tiānshuǐ as Attendant Censor,
Jiāng Xùn,
and Yán Zūn as clerks and subordinates.
Wáng Jù, Jiāo Shì, Jiǎng Xiù, Yǐn Yánnián, Niú Shuāng, and Zhāng Qián were appointed as Military Advisors.
Wáng Qīnlú, Yáo Fāngchéng, Wáng Pòlǔ, Yáng Nán, Yǐn Sōng, Péi Qí, Zhào Yáo, Dí Guǎng, Dǎng Shān, and others were appointed as commanders.
At this time, Mùróng Chōng and Fú Jiān were attacking each other,
and Chōng's forces were very strong.
Cháng intended to move westward,
fearing that Chōng would block him.
So he sent an envoy to inform Chōng,
offered his son Chóng as a hostage to Chōng,
then advanced and encamped at Běidì,
sharpening his weapons and accumulating provisions,
to observe the changing situation.
Fú Jiān had earlier relocated several thousand households of Jìn people, including Lǐ Xiáng, to Fūlù.
At this time,
they surrendered to Cháng.
Over one hundred thousand households of Qiāng and Hú from Běidì, Xīnpíng, and Āndìng also surrendered.
Jiān led his generals to attack,
but could not overcome them.
Cháng heard that Mùróng Chōng was attacking Cháng'ān,
and discussed plans for advancement.
His subordinates all said,
"It is advisable to first occupy Xiányáng to control the world."
Cháng said,
"Yān arose because of those who cherished old loyalties.
If they succeed and achieve victory,
they will all desire to return east.
How can they long hold Guānchuān?
I wish to move my troops to Lǐngběi,
extensively gather resources,
wait until Qín is exhausted and Yān returns,
and then take it with folded arms.
Without shedding a drop of blood,
we will pacify the world while sitting.
This is the meaning of Biàn Zhuāng acquiring two."
Jiān's Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Sòng Fāng led three thousand cavalry from Yúnzhōng to proceed to Cháng'ān.
Cháng intercepted and defeated them at Èrxiàn.
Fāng escaped on a single horse,
and his Sīmǎ Tián Huàng led his troops to surrender to Cháng.
Cháng sent his generals to attack Xīnpíng,
captured it,
and then seized territory reaching Āndìng.
All the cities north of the岭 (lǐng) surrendered to him.
At this time, Fú Jiān was pressed by Mùróng Chōng
and fled into Wǔjiàng Shān.
Chōng entered Cháng'ān.
Jiān's Sīlì Xiàowèi Quán Yì, Shàngshū Zhào Qiān, Dàhónglú Huángfǔ Fù, Guānglù Dàfū Xuē Zàn, Fúfēng Tàishǒu Duàn Kēng, and several hundred other civil and military officials fled to Cháng.
Cháng sent Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Wú Zhōng to lead cavalry to besiege Jiān,
and Cháng went to Xīnpíng.
Soon after, Zhōng captured Jiān and sent him.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) secretly attacked Fú Dēng (苻登).
He commanded his crown prince, Yáo Xīng (姚興), saying:
"Gǒu Yào (苟曜) is fond of treachery and change.
He will be a menace to the state.
When he hears I have returned north,
he will surely come to see you.
You must arrest him."
Gǒu Yào (苟曜) indeed went to see Yáo Xīng (姚興) in Cháng'ān (長安).
Yáo Xīng (姚興) sent Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) to reproach him and then execute him.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) utterly defeated Fú Dēng (苻登) east of Āndìng (安定).
He held a grand feast with wine.
All the generals said:
"If we had met Wèi Wǔ Wáng (魏武王) (Cao Cao),
this villain would not have lasted until now.
Your Majesty is too lenient!"
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) laughed and said:
"I am inferior to my deceased elder brother (Yáo Xiāng (姚襄)) in four respects: his height of eight feet five inches,
his arms reaching below his knees,
which made people fear him at sight –
that is one;
when facing a host of 100,000,
contending for supremacy with all under heaven,
advancing at the sight of his banner,
with no opposing ranks before him –
that is two;
being learned in antiquity and understanding the present,
discussing the Way and arts,
managing heroes,
and gathering exceptional talents –
that is three;
leading large armies,
treating danger as ease,
with harmony between superiors and subordinates,
and everyone exerting their utmost strength –
that is four.
The reason I have been able to establish achievements
and appoint numerous worthy men
is precisely due to a fragment of my strategic calculations."
All the ministers cheered, "Long live!"
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) issued a decree ordering the various garrisons of the central administration to establish schools,
without neglecting any,
to examine their excellence and inferiority,
and promote them according to their talents.
Fú Dēng's (苻登) Pìqí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Mò Yìyú (沒奕于), led six thousand households in surrender.
He was appointed Shǐchíjié (使持節), Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍), and Gāopíng Gōng (高平公).
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) fell ill.
He sent Yáo Shuòdé (姚碩德) to garrison Lǐrùn (李潤)
and Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) to defend Cháng'ān (長安).
He summoned his crown prince, Yáo Xīng (姚興), to the traveling camp.
Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (征南將軍) Yáo Fāngchéng (姚方成) said to Yáo Xīng (姚興):
"Now the rebels are not yet subdued,
and His Majesty is again ill.
Wáng Tǒng (王統), Fú Yìn (苻胤), and others all have their own troops
and will eventually cause harm.
It is advisable to eliminate them all."
Yáo Xīng (姚興) then executed Fú Yìn (苻胤), Wáng Tǒng (王統), Wáng Guǎng (王廣), Xú Chéng (徐成), and Máo Shèng (毛盛),
and then answered the summons.
When Yáo Xīng (姚興) arrived,
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) angrily said:
"Wáng Tǒng (王統) and his brothers are from our home region
and have no other ambitious designs.
Xú Chéng (徐成) and others were formerly famous generals in the Qín (秦) court.
The world is just beginning to settle,
and I was about to employ them.
Why did you arbitrarily execute them,
causing people to lose heart!"
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) issued a decree that for soldiers and officials who participated in campaigns,
and whose households were in the grand camp,
their families would be exempt from corvée labor for generations,
without any involvement.
Fú Dēng (苻登) and Dòu Chōng (竇衝) were in a standoff.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) discussed attacking them.
Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) said to Yáo Cháng (姚萇):
"The Crown Prince has a reputation for purity and generosity
that is known far and wide,
but his military brilliance
is not yet known to those near and far.
It would be appropriate to send the Crown Prince to lead personally,
which can gradually extend his prestige and power,
and prevent the origin of covert designs."
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) agreed and
admonished Yáo Xīng (姚興), saying:
"The rebels, knowing you are approaching,
will surely drive themselves into the strongholds.
Gather and ambush them,
and none will fail to be overcome."
By the time he reached Húkōngbǎo (胡空堡),
Dòu Chōng's (竇衝) siege had lifted itself.
Fú Dēng (苻登), hearing that Yáo Xīng (姚興) was heading to Húkōngbǎo (胡空堡),
withdrew.
Yáo Xīng (姚興) then raided Píngliáng (平涼),
gained a great victory, and returned,
all according to Yáo Cháng's (姚萇) plan.
He sent Yáo Xīng (姚興) back to garrison Cháng'ān (長安).
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) issued a decree to eliminate slanderous rumors and previous illicit acts.
Those who impeached or accused others
would all be punished with the same crime.
Jìn (晉) Píngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (平遠將軍) and Hù Dī Xiàowèi (護氐校尉) Yáng FóSōng (楊佛嵩) led over three thousand Hú (胡) and Shǔ (蜀) households in surrender to Yáo Cháng (姚萇).
Jìn (晉) generals Yáng Quánqī (楊佺期) and Zhào Mù (趙睦) pursued them.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) sent Yáo Chóng (姚崇) to relieve them,
who greatly defeated the Jìn (晉) army
and beheaded Zhào Mù (趙睦).
He appointed Yáng FóSōng (楊佛嵩) as Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (鎮東將軍).
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) went to Cháng'ān (長安).
When he reached Xīnzhībǎo (新支堡),
his illness became critical,
and he advanced, carried on a litter.
He dreamed that Fú Jiān (苻堅), leading a celestial envoy and hundreds of ghost soldiers, burst into his camp.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) was terrified
and ran into his palace.
His palace attendants, welcoming Yáo Cháng (姚萇), stabbed the ghosts,
but accidentally struck Yáo Cháng's (姚萇) groin.
The ghosts said to each other:
"Right in the spot of death."
They pulled out the spears,
and over one *shí* (石) of blood flowed out.
He woke up startled and agitated,
and then suffered from a swollen groin.
A doctor lanced it,
and blood flowed out as in the dream.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) then spoke wildly,
sometimes saying:
"I, your servant Cháng (萇),
the one who killed Your Majesty was my brother Xiāng (襄),
not my fault.
I beg you not to wrong me."
Upon reaching Cháng'ān (長安),
he summoned Tàiwèi (太尉) Yáo Mín (姚旻), Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Yǐn Wěi (尹緯), Yòupúyè (右僕射) Yáo Huǎng (姚晃), Shàngshū (尚書) Dí Bózhī (狄伯支), and others to enter
and receive his last will to assist in governance.
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) said to Yáo Xīng (姚興):
"If anyone slanders these men,
be careful not to believe them.
You must treat your family with benevolence,
receive great ministers with courtesy,
deal with affairs with integrity,
and treat the common people with kindness.
If these four are complete,
I will have no worries."
He died in the eighteenth year of Tàiyuán (太元) (393 CE),
at the age of sixty-four,
having reigned for eight years.
His posthumous title was Wǔzhāo Huángdì (武昭皇帝),
his temple name was Tàizǔ (太祖),
and his tomb was called Yuánlíng (原陵).
COLLATIONS
RECORD OF EVENTS, VOLUME 17, Yáo Xīng (姚興) Part 1
Yáo Xīng (姚興), courtesy name Zǐlüè (子略),
was Yáo Cháng's (姚萇) eldest son.
During Fú Jiān's (苻堅) time, he was a Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人).
When Yáo Cháng (姚萇) was at Mǎmù (馬牧),
Yáo Xīng (姚興) ran from Mǎ'ān (馬安), risking danger, to Yáo Cháng (姚萇).
Yáo Cháng (姚 Cháng) established him as Crown Prince.
When Yáo Cháng (姚 Cháng) went out on campaigns,
he often left Yáo Xīng (姚 Xīng) to manage affairs.
When he later garrisoned Cháng'ān (長安),
he possessed great authority and benevolence.
He discussed classics and literature with his zhōngshèrén (中舍人) Liáng Xǐ (梁喜), xǐmǎ (洗馬) Fàn Xù (范勖), and others.
He did not abandon his studies because of military difficulties,
and the people of his time were all influenced by him.
When Yáo Cháng (姚 Cháng) died,
Yáo Xīng (姚 Xīng) secretly kept the mourning undisclosed.
He sent his uncle Yáo Xù (姚緒) to garrison Āndìng (安定),
Yáo Shuòdé (姚碩德) to garrison Yīnmì (陰密),
and his younger brother Yáo Chóng (姚崇) to guard Cháng'ān (長安).
Yáo Shuòdé's (姚碩德) subordinate officers said to him:
"Your Excellency's prestige and reputation are long-standing and heavy,
and your troops are the strongest.
Now, at the time of succession,
the court will certainly be suspicious and jealous of each other.
This is not the way to lasting peace.
It is advisable to flee to Qínzhōu (秦州)
and observe the situation."
Yáo Shuòdé (姚碩德) said:
"The Crown Prince's ambition and disposition are broad and enlightened;
he will certainly have no doubts or suspicions.
Now Fú Dēng (苻登) is not yet eliminated, and we are already seeking internal conflict.
This is what is called following the footsteps of the two Yuáns (袁紹 and 袁術),
handing over one's head to others.
I would rather die
than ever do such a thing."
When he arrived,
Yáo Xīng (姚 Xīng) treated him with great courtesy and dismissed him.
Xīng set out from Píngliáng, like going to Cháonà.
Hearing that Chōng was plotting rebellion,
and because he was the youngest among his brothers,
and singularly brave and strong,
Xīng still wished to endure and tolerate him.
Liǎnchéng wept and said to Xīng:
“Chōng is fierce, dangerous, and inhumane.
Whenever he attends your左右
I can never sleep soundly.
I wish you would deal with him soon.”
Xīng said:
“What can Chōng do?
He merely lightly harmed a famous general.
I want to declare his crime to all under heaven.”
Then he issued a decree granting Chōng death,
and buried him with the rites of a commoner.
Jìn princes Guó Fán of Héjiān and Shū Dào of Zhāngwǔ came to surrender.
Xīng said to them:
“Liú Yù is restoring the Jìn dynasty.
Why have you gentlemen come?”
Guó Fán and others said:
“Yù, with unscrupulous characters, has weakened the royal house.
Among the imperial clan, those who can establish themselves are all harmed by him.
We have come to flee him.
It is not out of sincere loyalty;
it is simply to escape death.”
Xīng praised them,
and appointed Guó Fán as Jiànyì Jiāngjūn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shū Dào as Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and bestowed upon them grand mansions.
Xīng went to Èrchéng,
intending to attack Hèlián Bóbó.
He dispatched Ānyuǎn Yáo Xiáng, Liǎn Mànwěi, and Zhènjūn Péng Báiláng to jointly oversee grain transport.
Before the armies were assembled, Bóbó's cavalry arrived in great numbers.
Xīng wanted to leave the infantry
and lightly proceed to Wěi's camp.
Everyone was terrified,
and the officials unanimously insisted that it was not permissible.
Xīng did not heed them.
Shàngshū Láng Wéi Zōng, discerning Xīng's wishes, encouraged him to go.
Lántái Shìyùshǐ Jiāng Léng stepped forward out of turn and said:
“Wéi Zōng is treacherous and disloyal,
sabotaging national plans.
He should be cut in half at the waist first to apologize to all under heaven.
If your imperial carriage moves lightly,
the six armies will be alarmed and terrified,
and the men will lose their resolve.
This is the way to invite danger.
It is advisable to send a single envoy to summon Xiáng and others.”
Xīng remained silent.
Yòu Púshè Wéi Huá and others remonstrated, saying:
“If the cavalry moves lightly,
it will surely collapse without a fight,
and Wěi's camp may not even be reached.
Only Your Majesty should consider this carefully.”
Xīng then dispatched Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Yáo Wénzōng to lead the imperial guards to resist in battle,
and Zhōnglěi Qí Mò led the Dī troops to reinforce them.
Wénzōng and Mò were both exceptionally brave and resolute.
They fought with all their might,
and Bóbó then retreated.
Xīng left five thousand imperial guards to Yáo Xiáng to defend Èrchéng,
and returned to Cháng'ān.
Qiáo Zòng dispatched his Shìzhōng Qiáo Liáng and Tàicháng Yáng Guǐ to pay court to Xīng,
requesting a large-scale invasion of Jiāngdōng.
He sent his Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Qiān and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáo Dàofú to lead twenty thousand troops to invade Jiānglíng to the east.
Xīng then dispatched Qián Jiāngjūn Gǒu Lín to lead cavalry to join them.
Qiān encamped at Zhījiāng,
and Lín encamped at Jiāngjīn.
Qiān,
a noble of the Jiāngzuǒ,
had private troops in Jīngchǔ.
The Jìn generals and soldiers all harbored rebellious intentions.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Dàoguī was greatly alarmed
and fortified the city.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǔ Zōngzhī led the troops from Xiāngyáng to rescue them.
Dàoguī then left Zōngzhī to defend Jiānglíng
and led his army to meet the enemy in battle.
Qiān and others had a powerful fleet of ships,
and also arrayed infantry and cavalry to await them.
In a great battle at Zhījiāng,
Qiān was defeated.
He fled in a light boat to Gǒu Lín.
The Jìn people captured and beheaded him.
Gǒu Lín was afraid and withdrew.
As national resources were insufficient,
Xīng increased taxes on passes and ferries.
Salt, bamboo, and mountain timber were all taxed.
The officials all remonstrated,
believing that Heaven bestows various products to nourish all living beings,
and that a king should nurture all nations.
It was not appropriate to restrict and seize their benefits.
Xīng said:
“Those who can cross passes and ferries and profit from mountains and rivers
are all wealthy families.
I am taking from those who have in excess to supplement those who are lacking.
What is wrong with that?”
Thus, he proceeded with it.
Xīng traveled from the Cháomén gate to the Wénwǔ Yuàn.
As it grew dark, he returned,
intending to enter through the Píngshuòmén gate.
When his vanguard arrived,
Chéngmén Jiàowèi Wáng Mǎncōng, clad in armor and holding a staff,
closed the gate and resisted,
saying:
“It is now dark.
The good and the wicked cannot be distinguished.
I would rather die,
but the gate cannot be opened.”
Xīng then turned back and entered through the Cháomén gate.
The next morning, he summoned Mǎncōng
and promoted him two ranks.
Qǐfú Gān Guī rebelled with his troops,
attacked and captured Jīnchéng,
and seized the Grand Administrator Rèn Lán.
Lán, with a stern expression, reproached Gān Guī for betraying kindness and violating righteousness.
Gān Guī was enraged and imprisoned him.
Lán then refused to eat and died.
Hèlián Bóbó sent his general Hú Jīnzuǎn to lead over ten thousand cavalry to attack Píngliáng.
Xīng went to Èrchéng,
and then relieved Píngliáng.
Jīnzuǎn’s troops were utterly defeated,
and Jīnzuǎn was captured alive.
Bóbó sent his nephew Tí to attack and capture Dìngyáng,
and seized the Northern Zhōngláng Jiāng Yáo Guǎngdū.
Xīng’s generals Cáo Chì, Cáo Yún, and Wáng Sìfó, each with several thousand households, moved inward to avoid Bóbó.
Xīng settled Sìfó at Huángshān Zé,
and Chì and Yún at Chéncāng.
Bóbó raided Lǒngyòu,
attacked Báiyá Bǎo,
and broke it.
Then he advanced towards Qīngshuǐ.
Lüèyáng Tàishǒu Yáo Shòudū abandoned his post and fled to Qínzhōu.
Bóbó then gathered his troops and returned.
Xīng pursued him from Āndìng,
reaching Shòuqú Chuān,
but could not catch him and returned.
Previously,
Jiāng Jì, a man from Tiānshuǐ,
was a treacherous official of the Lǚ clan.
He was obsequious, cunning, and deceitful,
and enjoyed creating discord among people's relatives.
Xīng's son Bì was favored by Xīng,
and Jì wholeheartedly attached himself to him.
At that time, Bì was Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Āndìng.
They secretly plotted to return to court,
making it their intention to serve Chángshān Gōng Xiǎn wholeheartedly
and establish a faction around them.
At this time,
Xīng appointed Bì as Shàngshū Lìng, Shìzhōng, and Dà Jiāngjūn.
Having assumed the positions of general and minister,
he openly welcomed and attracted people,
and formed connections with court officials.
His influence overshadowed the Eastern Palace,
and he thus conceived the plot to usurp the heir apparent.
All the generals earnestly requested Lǐ Xióng to assume the throne.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng, he presumptuously declared himself King of Chéngdū,
pardoned those within his territory,
established the era name Jiànxīng,
abolished the Jìn laws,
and promulgated seven chapters of laws.
He appointed his uncle Lǐ Xiāng as Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
his elder brother Lǐ Shǐ as Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo),
Zhéchōng Lǐ Lí as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
Jiànwēi Lǐ Yún as Minister of Education (Sītú),
Yìjūn Lǐ Huáng as Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Cáiguān Lǐ Guó as Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi),
and the rest were appointed to various ranks accordingly.
He posthumously honored his great-grandfather Lǐ Wǔ as Duke Huán of Bājùn,
his grandfather Lǐ Mù as Prince Xiāng of Lǒngxī,
his father Lǐ Tè as Prince Jǐng of Chéngdū,
and his mother, Lady Luó, as the Queen Dowager.
Fàn Chángshēng traveled from Xīshān in a plain carriage to Chéngdū.
Lǐ Xióng welcomed him at the gate,
held a tablet, and invited him to sit.
He appointed him Chancellor (Chéngxiàng)
and honored him as Fàn Xián.
Fàn Chángshēng advised Lǐ Xióng to assume the imperial title.
Lǐ Xióng then presumptuously ascended the imperial throne,
pardoned those within his territory,
and changed the era name to Tàiwǔ.
He posthumously honored his father Lǐ Tè as Emperor Jǐng,
with the temple name Shǐzǔ,
and his mother, Lady Luó, as Empress Dowager.
He promoted Fàn Chángshēng to Grand Master of Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì Tàishī),
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xīshān,
exempted his personal troops from military conscription,
and all their taxes went directly to his household.
At that time, Lǐ Xióng’s state was newly founded and in its initial stages,
lacking established regulations.
The generals, relying on imperial favor,
each vied for rank and position.
His Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshūlìng) Yán Shì submitted a memorial, saying:
"When establishing laws for a state,
merit should still adhere to old customs.
According to the precedents of Hàn and Jìn,
only the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) commanded troops;
the Grand Tutor (Tàifù) and Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) were offices for paternal uncles and elder brothers,
responsible for discussing doctrine;
the Minister of Education (Sītú) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng) managed the Five Teachings and the differences in the Nine Regions.
Qín established the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng)
to manage all affairs.
Towards the end of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's reign,
the Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn) was used to preside over government.
Now that the state enterprise is newly established,
all things are yet to be prepared.
The ranks of the dukes and grand generals differ.
Inferiors compete to request appointments,
which does not conform to precedents.
It is proper to establish a system to serve as a model."
Lǐ Xióng adopted this.
He dispatched Lǐ Guó, Lǐ Yún, and others to lead an army of 20,000 to invade Hànzhōng.
The Inspector of Liángzhōu, Zhāng Yīn, fled to Cháng'ān.
Lǐ Guó and the others captured Nánzhèng
and relocated all the people of Hànzhōng to Shǔ.
Before this,
the southern region had suffered from years of famine and pestilence,
with deaths numbering in the tens of thousands.
The Southern Yi Commandant, Lǐ Yì, held out firmly and did not surrender.
Lǐ Xióng enticed the Jiànníng Yi to attack him.
Lǐ Yì died of illness,
the city fell,
over three thousand strong men were killed,
and a thousand women were sent to Chéngdū.
At that time, Lǐ Lí occupied Zǐtóng.
His subordinate generals, Luó Yàng and Zhāng Jīngǒu, killed Lǐ Lí and Yán Shì,
and surrendered Zǐtóng to Luó Shàng.
Luó Shàng sent his general Xiàng Fèn to garrison Yífú in Ānhàn to pressure Lǐ Xióng.
Lǐ Xióng led his troops to attack Xiàng Fèn
but failed to overcome him.
At that time, Lǐ Guó was stationed in Bāxī.
His subordinate Wén Shuò again killed Lǐ Guó
and surrendered Bāxī to Luó Shàng.
Lǐ Xióng then withdrew
and sent his general Zhāng Bǎo to raid Zǐtóng,
capturing it.
Just then, Luó Shàng died,
Bājùn fell into chaos,
Lǐ Xiāng attacked Fú,
and captured it as well.
He seized the Administrator of Zǐtóng, Qiáo Dēng,
and then, riding on his victory, advanced to attack Wén Shuò,
killing him.
Lǐ Xióng was greatly pleased,
pardoned those within his territory,
and changed the era name to Yùhéng.
Lǐ Xióng’s mother, Lady Luó, died.
Lǐ Xióng, trusting the words of shamans,
had many taboos
and even wished not to bury her.
His Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Zhào Sù, remonstrated,
and Lǐ Xióng then yielded to him.
Lǐ Xióng wished to observe the three-year mourning ritual.
His officials earnestly remonstrated,
but Lǐ Xióng refused.
Lǐ Xiāng said to Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Shàngguān Dūn:
"The current difficulties are not yet resolved.
I wish to earnestly remonstrate
against allowing the Lord to observe the full period of mourning in seclusion.
What do you think?"
Shàngguān Dūn said:
"The three-year mourning period,
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
is established. Therefore Confucius said: 'Why only Gāozōng?
The ancients all did so.'
However, since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
there have been many difficulties in the realm,
and the ancestral temples are of utmost importance
and cannot be left empty for long.
Therefore, they laid aside the coarse mourning garments
and observed only the deepest sorrow."
Lǐ Xiāng said:
"Rèn Huí is about to arrive.
This man is decisive in his actions,
and the Lord often finds it difficult to go against his words.
When he arrives,
we should request together."
When Rèn Huí arrived,
Lǐ Xiāng and Rèn Huí both met Lǐ Xióng.
Lǐ Xiāng removed his cap and shed tears,
earnestly requesting a public observance.
Lǐ Xióng wept aloud but refused.
Rèn Huí knelt and stepped forward, saying:
"Now the royal enterprise is newly established,
and everything is in its initial stages.
One day without a ruler
would cause widespread panic in the realm.
In the past, King Wǔ wore plain armor to review his troops,
and Duke Xiāng of Jìn wore black mourning clothes to go to war.
How could they have wished to do so?
It was for the sake of the realm that they humbled themselves.
I beg Your Majesty to put aside personal feelings and adapt to circumstances,
thereby forever securing the celestial mandate."
Then they forcefully helped Lǐ Xióng to his feet,
had him change out of mourning clothes, and attend to government.
At this time, Hànjiā and Fúlíng to the south were gained,
and people from distant lands continued to arrive.
Lǐ Xióng then issued a lenient decree,
granting all who surrendered and submitted special exemptions.
He emptied himself for the love of the people,
and those he appointed and employed all achieved their talents,
and thus Yìzhōu was pacified.
He falsely installed his wife, Lady Rèn, as empress.
The Dī kings, Yáng Nándí and his brothers, were defeated by Liú Yào
and fled to Jiāmáng,
sending their son as a hostage.
The Lǒngxī bandit chief Chén Ān also allied with him.
He sent Lǐ Xiāng to conquer Yuèsuī,
and its Administrator, Lǐ Zhāo, surrendered.
Lǐ Xiāng advanced his army via Xiǎohuì to attack the Inspector of Níngzhōu, Wáng Xùn.
Wáng Xùn sent his general Yáo Yuè with all his troops to engage in battle.
Lǐ Xiāng’s army was at a disadvantage,
and then encountered continuous rain.
Lǐ Xiāng withdrew his army,
and during the struggle to cross the Lúshuǐ River,
many soldiers died.
When Lǐ Zhāo arrived in Chéngdū,
Lǐ Xióng treated him very generously.
The court rituals
and mourning rites
were all decided by Lǐ Zhāo.
When Yáng Nándí fled to Jiāmáng,
Lǐ Xióng’s Protector-General of the North (Ānběi) Lǐ Zhì treated him kindly.
He allowed Yáng Nándí and his brothers to return to Wǔdū.
Yáng Nándí then, relying on the treacherous terrain, committed many illegal acts.
Lǐ Zhì requested to attack him.
Lǐ Xióng sent his Central Leader of the Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn) Lǐ Hàn and generals Lè Cì, Fèi Tā, Lǐ Gān, and others to attack Xiàbiàn via Báishuǐqiáo.
Lǐ Shòu, Commander of the East (Zhēngdōng), supervised Lǐ Hàn’s younger brother Lǐ Wǔ in attacking Yīnpíng.
Yáng Nándí sent troops to resist them,
and Lǐ Shòu could not advance.
However, Lǐ Hàn and Lǐ Zhì advanced swiftly to Wǔjiē.
Yáng Nándí sent troops to cut off their retreat path
and attacked them from four sides,
capturing Lǐ Hàn and Lǐ Zhì.
Several thousand men died.
Lǐ Hàn and Lǐ Zhì
were the sons of Lǐ Dàng, Lǐ Xióng's elder brother.
Lǐ Xióng deeply grieved for them,
did not eat for several days,
and wept whenever he spoke,
deeply blaming himself.
Thereafter, when Lǐ Xióng was about to establish Dàngzǐ Bān as his heir,
Xióng had over ten sons,
and all his officials wished to establish a son born to Xióng.
Xióng said:
"When I first raised an army,
I put my hand to my head,
never expecting the enterprise of an emperor.
It so happened that the world was in chaos and turmoil,
and the Jìn clan was scattered and in disarray.
The masses righteously rose up,
determined to rescue those suffering.
Then you, gentlemen, pushed and compelled me
to a position above kings and dukes.
The foundation of this enterprise
was due to the former emperor.
My elder brother was the rightful successor,
to whom the great mandate belonged.
He was grand, virtuous, intelligent, and sagacious,
probably destined by Heaven.
The great task was on the verge of completion
when he died in battle.
Bān is by nature benevolent and filial,
studious, and accomplished early.
He will surely be a vessel of renown."
Lǐ Xiāng and Sītú Wáng Dá remonstrated, saying:
"The former kings established the legitimate eldest son
to prevent the budding of usurpation,
which must not be taken lightly.
Wú Zǐ set aside his own son to establish his younger brother,
which led to the disaster of Zhuān Zhū.
Sòng Xuān did not establish Yǔyí but established Mùgōng,
which ultimately led to the upheaval of Sòng Dū.
Are the words of a nephew
comparable to those of a son?
We deeply wish Your Majesty to consider this."
Xióng did not comply,
and indeed established Bān.
Xiāng retired and wept, saying:
"Chaos will begin from this!"
Zhāng Jùn sent an envoy to send a letter to Xióng,
advising him to relinquish his imperial title
and declare himself a vassal to Jìn.
Xióng replied in a letter:
"I was wrongly pushed into this position by the scholar-officials,
but I originally had no desire for the imperial throne.
When I advance, I think of becoming a meritorious minister of the Jìn court;
when I retreat, I think of being a general guarding the frontier together,
sweeping away the dust and chaos
to restore peace to the imperial domain.
But the Jìn court has declined,
