its virtuous reputation not rising.
I have yearned to look eastward
for years and months.
I happen to receive your kind gift,
my feelings are in a dark room;
how can I stop now?
I know you wish to follow the distant example of Chǔ and Hàn,
honoring the Righteous Emperor.
In the righteousness of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
nothing is greater than this."
Jùn valued his words,
and his envoys continued to visit.
The Bā Jùn once reported an emergency,
saying there was an eastern army.
Xióng said:
"I have always worried that Shí Lè would be tyrannical
and invade Lángyá,
which troubled me greatly.
I didn't expect him to actually field an army,
which makes one happy."
Many of Xióng's noble remarks
were of this kind.
As the Central Plains were in chaos,
Xióng frequently sent envoys to pay tribute,
and divided the world with Jìn Mùdì.
Zhāng Jùn governed Qín and Liáng.
Before this,
he sent Fù Yǐng to request passage through Shǔ
to submit a memorial to the capital,
but Xióng did not allow it.
Jùn then sent Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Zhāng Chún to declare vassalage to Shǔ,
under the pretext of requesting passage.
Xióng was greatly pleased,
and said to Chún:
"Your lord's heroic name covers the world,
his land is perilous and his army strong.
Why does he not declare himself emperor in one region?"
Chún replied:
"Our humble lord, whose ancestors have generations of loyalty and integrity,
has not yet been able to wash away the shame of the world
and relieve the people from their distress.
He forgets food at dusk
and waits for dawn with his weapon as a pillow.
Since Lángyá is restoring the Jìn dynasty in Jiāngdōng,
he supports it from thousands of miles away,
intending to achieve the feats of Huán and Wén.
How can he speak of taking it for himself!"
Xióng showed a look of shame,
and said:
"My ancestors and father were also Jìn subjects.
Formerly, I and the six commanderies sought refuge here,
and were supported by our allies,
thus we have today.
If Lángyá can restore the Great Jìn in Zhōngxià,
I will also lead my forces to assist it."
Chún returned,
and submitted the memorial to the capital.
The Son of Heaven praised him.
At this time, Lǐ Xiāng died.
His son, Lǐ Shòu, was appointed Great General and Colonel of the Western Yi,
overseeing Marshal of the South Fèi Hēi and Marshal of the East Rèn Shuāng in attacking and capturing Bādōng.
Governor Yáng Qiān retreated and held Jiànpíng.
Shòu separately dispatched Fèi Hēi to raid Jiànpíng.
Jìn Supervisor of Bādōng Wúqiū Ào retreated and held Yídū.
Xióng sent Lǐ Shòu to attack Zhūtí,
with Fèi Hēi and Áng Pān as vanguards.
He also sent General Zàngnán Rèn Huí to campaign against Mùluò,
to divide the reinforcements for Níngzhōu.
The Governor of Níngzhōu, Yǐn Fèng, surrendered,
and thus they possessed the land of Nánzhōng.
Xióng then granted a general amnesty within his territory,
and sent Bān to subdue the Yi in Níngzhōu,
appointing Bān as Fǔjūn.
In the eighth year of Xiánhé,
Xióng developed a carbuncle on his head,
and died six days later,
at the age of sixty-one,
after reigning for thirty years.
his temple name Tàizōng,
and his tomb was named Āndū Líng.
Xióng was broad-minded and generous,
simplified punishments and restricted laws,
and had a very good reputation.
The Dī Fú Chéng and Kuí Wén, who had surrendered and then rebelled,
were all pardoned of their crimes
upon their return
and treated with great kindness and acceptance.
Because of this, both Yi and Xia found peace with him,
and his prestige shook the western lands.
At that time, there was great chaos within the seas,
but Shǔ alone was peaceful,
so those who came to him followed one another.
Xióng then established schools,
appointed historians,
and in his leisure from governing,
never let a book leave his hand.
He taxed male adults three *hú* of grain annually,
and female adults half of that.
Household taxes in silk did not exceed several *zhàng*,
and cotton several *liǎng*.
There were few incidents and rare corvée labor,
the people were prosperous and well-off,
their doors were not closed,
and there was no mutual invasion or theft.
However, Xióng's intention was to attract people from afar,
and the state's expenditure was insufficient.
Therefore, when his generals presented gold, silver, and treasures,
many obtained official positions by doing so.
Chancellor Yáng Bāo remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty is the lord of the world;
you should encompass the four seas.
How can you buy offices with gold!"
Xióng humbly thanked him.
Later, Xióng, when drunk, once pushed the Director of the Central Secretariat
and struck the Director of the Imperial Kitchen.
Bāo came forward and said:
"The Son of Heaven is solemn and dignified,
the feudal lords are majestic.
How can the Son of Heaven be a drunkard!"
Xióng immediately stopped.
When Xióng went out briefly without incident,
Bāo followed behind, holding a spear and riding a horse past Xióng.
Xióng was surprised and asked him.
He replied:
"Indeed, governing the heavy burden of the world
is like your servant riding a wild horse and holding a spear.
If I rein it in tightly, I fear injuring myself;
if I loosen the reins, I fear losing control.
Therefore, the horse gallops without being restrained."
Xióng was awakened,
and immediately returned.
Xióng had no proper decorum for his state,
officials had no fixed salaries or ranks,
the order of precedence was not distinguished,
and noblemen and commoners wore indistinguishable attire.
His army had no clear commands,
his military operations had no organized units,
they did not yield to each other in victory,
nor rescue each other in defeat.
When attacking cities and capturing towns, they always prioritized plunder.
This was why he failed.
Lǐ Bān
Bān (班), courtesy name Shìwén (世文),
was initially appointed General Who Pacifies the South.
Later, he was established as the Crown Prince.
Bān was humble and open-minded,
respecting and loving scholars and virtuous people.
From Hé Diǎn (何點) and Lǐ Zhāo (李釗),
Bān treated them all as his teachers.
He also invited renowned scholars Wáng Gǔ (王嘏), Dǒng Róng (董融) from Lǒngxī (隴西), and Wén Kuí (文夔) from Tiānshuǐ (天水), among others, to be his friends.
He often said to Róng and the others:
“When I observe Crown Prince Jìn (晉) of King Jǐng (景) of Zhōu (周), Crown Prince Pī (丕) of Wèi (魏), and Crown Prince Sūn Dēng (孫登) of Wú (吳),
their literary talent and discernment
are extraordinarily outstanding,
and I never fail to feel ashamed.
How could the ancients be so noble and radiant,
while later generations cannot catch up!”
He was by nature universally benevolent,
and his every action adhered to rules and regulations.
At that time, the younger generation of the Lǐ (李) clan all indulged in extravagance,
but Bān constantly admonished them.
Whenever there was a major discussion in court,
Xióng (雄) would always let him participate.
Bān held that in ancient times, cultivated land was evenly distributed,
and the poor and rich alike found their place.
Now, the wealthy extensively occupy uncultivated land,
the poor have no land to farm,
and the rich sell their surplus.
How can this be the principle of great equalization for a king!
Xióng adopted his suggestion.
When Xióng fell ill,
Bān attended to him day and night.
Xióng had fought in many battles in his youth
and suffered many injuries.
By this time, his illness was severe,
and all his wounds festered with pus.
Xióng’s son Yuè (越) and others were disgusted and kept their distance.
Bān sucked out the pus for him,
showing no sign of difficulty.
He often tasted the medicine and shed tears,
never taking off his clothes and cap.
His filial piety and sincerity were thus.
After Xióng died,
Bān succeeded to the usurped throne,
and appointed Lǐ Shòu (李壽) to record the affairs of the Secretariat to assist in governance.
Bān remained in the central palace to observe the mourning rites,
entrusting all governmental affairs to Shòu, as well as Sìtú (司徒) Hé Diǎn (何點) and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Wáng Guī (王瓌).
At that time, Yuè (越) was stationed in Jiāngyáng (江陽).
Since Bān was not Xióng's biological son,
Yuè felt very resentful.
At this point,
he hurried back for the funeral
and secretly plotted with his younger brother Qī (期).
Lǐ Wǔ (李玝) advised Bān to send Yuè back to Jiāngyáng
and appoint Qī as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州),
stationing him in Jiāmáng (葭萌).
Bān, because the funeral had not yet taken place,
could not bear to send them away.
He acted with sincere generosity,
with no trace of ill will in his heart.
At that time, there were two streaks of white qi stretching across the sky.
Tàishǐ Lìng (太史令) Hán Bào (韓豹) reported:
“There is a military conspiracy in the palace,
a warning for close relatives.”
Bān did not understand.
In the ninth year of Xiánhé (咸和)
Bān cried at night.
Yuè killed Bān in the funeral palace
at the age of forty-seven.
He had been on the throne for one year.
Then Xióng's son Qī (期) was installed to succeed to the throne.
Lǐ Qī (李期)
Qī (期), courtesy name Shìyùn (世運),
was Xióng’s fourth son.
He was intelligent, fond of learning,
and able to compose essays in his youth.
He was generous with wealth and liked to bestow gifts,
and was open-minded in recruiting talent.
Initially, he was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍).
Xióng ordered his sons and clan members to gather followers through kindness and trust.
Most only managed a few hundred at most,
but Qī alone attracted over a thousand people.
Xióng often adopted those whom Qī recommended,
so many officials in the Chángshǐ (長史) and various departments came from his recommendations.
After killing Bān,
he wanted to establish Yuè as the ruler.
Yuè, considering that Qī was adopted by Xióng’s wife Rèn (任) and
also possessed many talents,
yielded the throne to Qī.
Thereupon,
he usurped the imperial throne,
granted a general amnesty throughout the realm,
and changed the era name to Yùhéng (玉恆).
He executed Bān’s younger brother Dū (都).
He sent Lǐ Shòu (李壽) to attack Dū’s younger brother Wǔ (玝) in Fú (涪).
Wǔ abandoned the city and surrendered to Jìn (晉).
Shòu was enfeoffed as King of Hàn (漢),
and appointed Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州), Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi (東羌校尉), Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍), and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事).
His elder brother Yuè was enfeoffed as King of Jiànníng (建寧),
and appointed Xiàngguó (相國), Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍), and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事).
He made his wife, Lady Yán (閻), Empress.
He appointed his Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍) Yǐn Fèng (尹奉) as Yòuchéngxiàng (右丞相), Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
and Wáng Guī (王瓌) as Sìtú (司徒).
Qī, believing that he had successfully accomplished a great undertaking,
thought little of the old ministers.
Outwardly, he trusted Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Jǐng Qiān (景騫), Shàngshū (尚書) Yáo Huá (姚華), and Tián Bāo (田褒).
Bāo had no other talents,
but Xióng had once advocated for Qī’s establishment,
so he was highly favored.
Inwardly, he trusted the eunuch Xǔ Fú (許涪) and others.
The nation's criminal and administrative affairs
seldom involved the ministers and chancellors again.
Rewards, punishments, and displays of power
were all decided by a few individuals,
whereupon the fundamental order was disrupted.
Then he falsely accused his Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射), Duke Wǔlíng (武陵公) Lǐ Zài (李載) of plotting rebellion,
and he was imprisoned and died.
Before this,
Jìn’s Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳) was stationed in Hànzhōng (漢中).
Qī sent Lǐ Shòu (李壽) to attack and conquer it.
Subsequently, he established officials and administrators
and garrisoned Nánzhèng (南鄭).
Xióng’s sons Bà (霸) and Bǎo (保) both died without illness.
Everyone said that Qī poisoned them,
whereupon the high ministers harbored fear,
and no one felt safe.
It rained large yellow fish in the palace.
Its color was yellow.
Also, pigs and dogs copulated in the palace.
Qī executed and exterminated many people,
confiscating women and wealth to fill his inner court.
Inside and outside, there was turmoil;
people communicated by glances on the roads.
Those who admonished incurred punishment,
and everyone sought to merely escape harm.
Qī also poisoned his Ānběi (安北) Lǐ Yōu (李攸).
Yōu (攸)
was Shòu’s adopted younger brother.
Thereupon, he conspired with Yuè (越), Jǐng Qiān (景騫), Tián Bāo (田褒), and Yáo Huá (姚華) to launch a surprise attack on Shòu (壽) and others,
intending to burn Shìqiáo (市橋) and then mobilize troops.
Qī also repeatedly sent Zhōngchángshì (中常侍) Xǔ Fú (許涪) to Shòu’s residence
to observe his movements.
After Yōu (攸) was killed,
Shòu (壽) was greatly frightened,
and also suspected Xǔ Fú’s frequent comings and goings.
So he led ten thousand infantry and cavalry
from Fú (涪) towards Chéngdū (成都),
presenting a memorial accusing Jǐng Qiān (景騫) and Tián Bāo (田褒) of disrupting governance,
and mobilizing the army of Jìnyáng (晉陽)
to eliminate the wicked elements surrounding the ruler.
He appointed Lǐ Yì (李奕) as the vanguard.
When Shòu arrived in Chéngdū,
Qī (期) and Yuè (越) did not anticipate his arrival
and were unprepared.
Shòu then seized the city
and stationed his troops at the gates.
Qī sent his Shìzhōng (侍中) to comfort Shòu.
Shòu memorialized that Xiàngguó (相國), King of Jiànníng (建寧) Yuè (越),
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Duke of Hénán (河南公) Jǐng Qiān (景騫),
Shàngshū (尚書) Tián Bāo (田褒) and Yáo Huá (姚華),
Zhōngchángshì (中常侍) Xǔ Fú (許涪),
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Lǐ Xiá (李遐) and Jiāngjūn (將軍) Lǐ Xī (李西), etc.,
all harbored treachery and disrupted governance,
conspiring to overthrow the state and its altars,
which was utterly lawless and rebellious,
a crime deserving of extermination.
Qī agreed.
Thereupon, Yuè (越), Qiān (騫), and the others were executed.
Shòu (壽) forged an order from Lady Rèn (任)
to depose Qī as Duke of Qióngdū County (邛都縣公)
and confined him in a separate palace.
Qī sighed:
“The ruler of all under Heaven has come to be a duke of a small county;
it is better to die!”
In the third year of Xiánkāng (咸康),
he hanged himself.
〔一二〕He was twenty-five years old at the time
and had reigned for three years.
〔一三〕His posthumous title was Duke Yōu (幽公).
At his funeral,
he was granted a imperial chariot with nine streamers,
with other arrangements as per a prince's rites.
All of Xióng’s sons were killed by Shòu.
Lǐ Shòu (李壽)
His general, Xú Guǐng (徐炅), conspired with Zhāngyè (張掖) Grand Administrator Péng Huàng (彭晃) to rebel.
Guāng (光) dispatched an army to attack Guǐng (炅).
Guǐng (炅) fled to Huàng (晃).
Huàng (晃) allied with Kāng Níng (康寧) in the east,
and communicated with Wáng Mù (王穆) in the west.
Guāng (光) deliberated on attacking them.
All the generals said:
“Kāng Níng (康寧) is now in the south,
blocking our forces and awaiting a weakness.
If the imperial carriage heads west,
Níng (寧) will surely take advantage of our absence and emerge from the east side of the mountains.
If Huàng (晃) and Mù (穆) are not yet pacified,
and Kāng Níng (康寧) arrives again,
we will be caught in a dilemma,
and the situation will be extremely perilous.”
Guāng (光) said:
“The situation is indeed as you say.
But if we do not go now,
we will have to sit and wait for them to come to us.
Huàng (晃) and Mù (穆) are allies, like lips and teeth,
and Níng (寧) will also come to their aid as a fellow evildoer.
If they arrive from both east and west,
the area outside the city will not be ours.
If that happens,
the great enterprise will be lost.
Huàng’s (晃) rebellion has only just begun;
Níng (寧) and Mù’s (穆) alliance with him is not yet firm.
While they are caught unawares,
it will be easy to capture them.
Moreover, prosperity and decline are matters of destiny.
You need not say more.”
Thereupon, Guāng (光) personally led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
marching day and night at double speed.
Upon arrival,
he attacked for two *xún* (旬) [twenty days].
Huàng’s (晃) general Kòu Yǐ (寇顗) cut open the gate and admitted Guāng (光).
Thereupon, Péng Huàng (彭晃) was executed.
Wáng Mù (王穆) appointed Suǒ Gǔ (索嘏), a member of his faction, as the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
Later, he grew wary of Gǔ’s (嘏) prestige and fame,
and led his forces to attack Gǔ (嘏).
Guāng (光) heard of this
and said to his generals:
“These two enemies are attacking each other;
this is an easy capture.”
Guāng (光) was about to attack them,
but the multitude all thought it was not feasible.
Guāng (光) said:
“To exploit chaos and insult the defeated is a good principle of military strategy.
We cannot lose the opportunity for lasting peace
due to the toil of repeated campaigns.”
He led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Jiǔquán (酒泉),
conquered it,
and advanced to Liángxīng (涼興).
Mù (穆) led his army back east,
but his forces dispersed on the way.
Mù (穆) fled alone on horseback to Xīngmǎ (騂馬).
Guō Wén (郭文), the magistrate of Xīngmǎ (騂馬), had him beheaded and sent his head.
At this time, a *lín* (麟) [kylin] was seen in Jīnzé (金澤) County,
with hundreds of beasts following it.
Guāng (光) considered it his auspicious omen,
and in the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Xiàowǔ (孝武), he proclaimed himself King of Sānhé (三河),
established all officials from Cíngláng (丞郎) downwards,
granted a general amnesty within his territory,
and changed the era name to Língjiā (麟嘉).
Guāng’s (光) wife Shí (石) and son Shào (紹), and younger brother Déshì (德世) arrived from Qiúchí (仇池).
Guāng (光) welcomed them east of the city,
and held a grand banquet for all his officials.
He sent his son, Left General Tā (他), and Commandant of the Martial Retainers Lǚ Zuǎn (呂纂), to attack Pǐqín (匹勤) of the Northern Hú (胡) at Sānyán (三巖) Mountain,
and they greatly defeated him.
He established his wife, Lady Shí (石), as Queen Consort,
and his son Shào (紹) as Heir Apparent.
He feasted his officials in the new hall of the inner garden.
The Grand Ancestral Temple was newly completed,
and he posthumously honored his great-great-grandfather as Jìng Gōng (敬公),
his great-grandfather as Gōng Gōng (恭公),
his grandfather as Xuān Gōng (宣公),
his father as Jǐngzhāo Wáng (景昭王),
and his mother as Zhāoliè Fēi (昭烈妃).
His Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat Yáng Yǐng (楊穎) submitted a memorial,
requesting to follow the precedents of the Three Dynasties,
and posthumously honor Lǚ Wàng (呂望) as the founding ancestor,
to be enshrined in a temple that would never be moved.
Guāng (光) assented to this.
That year,
Fù Yào (傅曜), the Inspector of Zhāngyè (張掖), investigated the subordinate counties.
Yǐn Xìng (尹興), the magistrate of Qiúchí (丘池), killed him
and threw him into an empty well.
Yào (曜) appeared in Guāng’s (光) dream and said:
“I am a minor official of Zhāngyè (張掖) Commandery,
who was inspecting the various counties.
Yǐn Xìng (尹興), the magistrate of Qiúchí (丘池), had abundant evidence of corruption,
and fearing I would report it,
killed me and threw me into an empty well in Nántíng (南亭).
My clothes and appearance are thus.”
Guāng (光) awoke and still saw him,
and only after a long time did he vanish.
He sent an envoy to investigate, and it was exactly as in the dream.
Guāng (光) was enraged
and killed Xìng (興).
Duàn Yè (段業), a Compiler, feeling that Guāng (光) had not yet clearly distinguished the pure from the turbid,
nor separated the wise from the foolish,
took advantage of treating an illness at Tiāntī (天梯) Mountain
to compose a memorial, a chronicle poem, nine lamentations, and sixteen remonstrances to subtly criticize him.
Guāng (光) read them and was pleased.
Péng Xīniàn (彭奚念) of the Southern Qiāng (羌) invaded and attacked Báitǔ (白土).
Commandant Sūn Zhì (孫峙) retreated and fled to Xìngchéng (興城).

Guāng (光) sent his Southern Commandant Lǚ Fāng (呂方), along with his younger brother Right General Lǚ Bǎo (呂寶), Zhènwēi (振威) Yáng Fàn (楊範), and Qiángnǔ (強弩) Dòu Gǒu (竇苟) to attack Qǐfú Gān Guī (乞伏乾歸) at Jīnchéng (金城).
Fāng (方) garrisoned north of the river,
while Bǎo (寶) advanced his forces across the river,
but was defeated by Gān Guī (乾歸).
Bǎo (寶) died there.
Martial Retainer Lǚ Zuǎn (呂纂) and Qiángnǔ (強弩) Dòu Gǒu (竇苟) led five thousand infantry and cavalry south to attack Péng Xīniàn (彭奚念),
fought at Pányí (盤夷),
and returned after a great defeat.
Guāng (光) personally led a campaign against Gān Guī (乾歸) and Xīniàn (奚念).
He sent Zuǎn (纂), along with Yángwǔ (揚武) Yáng Guǐ (楊軌), Jiànzhōng (建忠) Jǔqú Luóchóu (沮渠羅仇), and Jiànwǔ (建武) Liáng Gōng (梁恭), to encamp at Zuǒ Nán (左南).
Xīniàn (奚念) was greatly alarmed.
At Báitǔjīn (白土津), he piled stones to form a dam,
using the water to secure himself,
and sent ten thousand elite troops to defend the river crossing.
Guāng (光) sent General Wáng Bǎo (王寶) to secretly make for Shàngjīn (上津) [the upper ford],
and cross the Huáng Hé (湟河) by night.
Guāng (光) himself crossed at the stone dam,
attacked and conquered Fáohǎn (枹罕).
Xīniàn (奚念) fled alone on horseback to Gānsōng (甘松),
and Guāng (光) returned triumphantly with his troops.
Initially,
Guāng (光) had relocated people from Xīhǎi (西海) Commandery to other commanderies.
At this point,
a popular rhyme said:
“Why is the northern horse so sad?
Thinking of the old home tires its heart.
Why do the swallows and sparrows linger?
They wish to return to their old nests.”
Soon after,
they incited each other,
and were again relocated to Xīhé Yuèlì (西河樂都).
The assembly deliberated that although Gāochāng (高昌) was on the western frontier,
its terrain was strategically advantageous.
It bordered the Hú (胡) barbarians externally,
and was prone to instability,
so it was advisable to send a son or younger brother to garrison it.

Guāng (光) appointed his son Fù (覆) as Envoy with Credentials, General Who Guards the West, Overall Superintendent of All Military Affairs west of Yùmén (玉門), and Grand Protector of the Western Regions,
to garrison Gāochāng (高昌),
and ordered sons and younger brothers of high-ranking officials to accompany him.
Guāng (光) then, in the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán (太元), proclaimed himself Heavenly King,
granted a general amnesty within his territory,
and changed the era name to Lóngfēi (龍飛).
He established his Heir Apparent Shào (紹) as Crown Prince,
and twenty of his sons and younger brothers as Dukes and Marquises.
Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Xiáng (王詳) was appointed Left Grandee Secretary,
and Duàn Yè (段業) and four others were appointed Grandee Secretaries.
When Jiān captured Wěi,
Chuí followed Jiān into Yè.
He gathered his children,
and wept over them in sorrow.
When he saw his former subordinates,
he showed signs of displeasure.
The former palace attendant, Gāo Bì, privately said to Chuí:
"Your Majesty, with your heaven-ordained talents,
have encountered undeserved misfortune,
wandering and hiding,
your difficulties have reached their peak.
Heaven has revealed a propitious gathering,
and the spiritual mandate has temporarily shifted.
This is the beginning of a grand ascent,
the start of a dragon's transformation.
I deeply wish that your benevolence and compassion can console him.
Moreover, a high-minded strategy must embrace rules that transcend common customs.
One should now cast a net wide enough to let even a boat pass through,
to uphold the principle of broad embrace;
and gather the descendants of former officials,
to achieve the merit of building a mountain.
How can you abandon them out of a moment's anger?
I secretly find this unacceptable for Your Majesty."
Chuí deeply accepted this.
While Chuí served in Jiān's court,
he successively held the position of Jīngzhàoyǐn,
and was promoted to be enfeoffed as the Marquis of Quánzhōu.
Wherever he campaigned,
he achieved great merit.
When Jiān was defeated at Huáinán,
Chuí's army alone remained intact.
Jiān, with over a thousand cavalry, fled to Chuí.
Chuí's heir apparent, Bǎo, said to Chuí:
"Our family and state are in ruins,
the imperial order is in disarray.
The Supreme One's mandate is clearly recorded in prophecies,
and you should establish the enterprise of a restoration,
and achieve the merits of Shàokāng.
It is just that the opportune time has not yet arrived,
hence you hide your brilliance and await your moment to act.
Now, Heaven abhors chaotic virtue,
and the wicked multitude has collapsed.
This can be said to be Heaven opening a divine opportunity,
bestowing it upon us.
A thousand years' chance in one moment,
this is that occasion!
You should respectfully accept the will of August Heaven,
and take advantage of it.
Moreover, those who achieve great merits do not concern themselves with minor details,
and those who practice great benevolence do not dwell on small favors.
Qín has already overthrown the three capitals,
secretly defiling the divine vessels.
The depth of this hatred and shame
is unparalleled.
I hope you will not forget the importance of the state and its altars for the sake of momentary sentiment or minor kindness.
The auspicious sign of the five woods
has now arrived."
Chuí said:
"Your words are correct.
However, he entrusted his life to me with a loyal heart;
how can I harm him?
If Heaven truly abandons him,
then devising a plan will be easy.
Moreover, even if I let him return north,
and wait for another opportunity,
I will not have betrayed my original intention,
and I can righteously take over the world."
Chuí's younger brother, Déjìn, said:
"The swallowing of neighboring states
has been common throughout history.
When Qín was strong, it annexed Yān;
when Qín is weak, we should plot against it.
This is to avenge and wipe away shame,
how can it be called betraying one's original intention?
In the past, Dèng Qíhóu did not heed the words of his three nephews,
and was ultimately destroyed by Chǔ;
King Fūchā of Wú disregarded Wǔ Zǐxū's remonstrance,
and brought disaster upon himself from Gōujiàn.
Past events, when not forgotten,
serve as a lesson for future generations.
I hope you will not abandon the accomplished paths of Tāng and Wǔ,
or pursue the failed footsteps of Hán Xìn.
Take advantage of their collapse,
and respectfully carry out Heaven's punishment,
slaughter the rebellious Dī,
restore the ancestral sacrifices,
establish a restoration,
and continue the grand achievements.
This great opportunity for the world
should not be missed.
If you release tens of thousands of troops,
and hand over the hilt of a sharp sword,
this is to reject the opportune moment and await future harm,
which is not the best strategy.
The saying goes: 'If you hesitate when you should decide,
you will invite disaster upon yourself.'
I hope my brother will not waver."
Chuí said:
"In the past, I was not tolerated by the Grand Tutor,
and I surrendered myself to the Qín ruler.
I was also slandered by Wáng Měng,
but then I saw Zhāo Liàng,
who always treated me with profound respect as a national talent,
yet my debt of gratitude remains unsettled.
If Qín's destiny is indeed exhausted,
and the mandate is to return to me,
why worry about not having an opportunity to strike?
The land west of the pass,
Guānxī, will not be mine eventually.
There will naturally be those who disturb it.
I can simply sit idly and secure Guāndōng.
A gentleman does not rely on chaos,
nor does he initiate misfortune.
Let us observe for now."
Then he handed over his troops to Jiān.
Initially,
Bǎo was in Cháng'ān.
Together with Hán Huáng, Lǐ Gēn, and others,
he played chūpú at a banquet.
Bǎo sat upright, his demeanor solemn,
and swore, saying:
"People say that chūpú has a spirit,
how can it be false?
If prosperity and high rank are to be expected,
let me repeatedly get three lú."
Thereupon, he threw three lú in a row.
Bǎo bowed and accepted the omen,
hence it was called the auspicious sign of the five woods.
When Jiān reached Miǎnchí,
Chuí requested to go to Yè to pay respects at the ancestral tombs,
and then display the state's military might
to pacify the Róng and Dí.
Jiān agreed.
Quán Yì admonished, saying:
"Chuí is a fierce and famous general,
the Hán and Bái of today.
He is a formidable figure in the eastern region,
and his ambition is not to serve others.
Recently, he returned to us to escape disaster,
not because he admired our virtue.
Even ruling a thousand cities cannot satisfy his ambition,
how can the title of 'Champion General' be enough to please his heart?
Moreover, Chuí is like a hawk;
when hungry, it attaches itself to people;
when full, it soars high.
Should he encounter a time of upheaval,
he will surely have the ambition to reach the heavens.
It is imperative to tighten his reins,
and not allow him to do as he pleases."
Jiān did not listen.
He dispatched his generals Lǐ Mán, Mǐn Liàng, and Yǐn Guó to lead three thousand troops to escort Chuí,
and also sent Shí Yuè to garrison Yè
and Zhāng Háo to garrison Bìngzhōu.
Jiān reported,
“I, due to my unworthiness,
have humbly received the celestial mandate,
ruling over myriad states,
for thirty years now.
Distant regions and remote frontiers,
none failed to come to court.
Only one corner in the southeast
dared to defy the royal decree.
So I roused my six armies,
to恭行 Tiānfá,
but the celestial mechanism was unpropitious,
and the royal army was defeated.
It is due to your utmost loyalty and sincerity,
that you supported me,
and the ancestral shrines did not fall;
this is your strength.
The *Shī* says: ‘
Hidden in the heart, when shall it be forgotten?’
I was about to appoint you as Prime Minister,
and enfeoff you as a commandery marquis,
hoping to broadly overcome difficulties,
and honor your great achievements.
How could I have imagined Bóyí suddenly destroying his pure integrity,
and Liǔhuì abruptly becoming an adulterous husband!
Reading your memorial, I am saddened,
and ashamed before my court officials.
Since you were not tolerated in your original court,
you came alone to seek refuge.
I then honored you with a general's rank,
and treated you as a distinguished guest,
giving you the same responsibilities as old ministers,
and a rank equal to meritorious輔.
We sealed our bond with blood,
and I entrusted my heart to you.
I thought you would cherish our bond,
and we would grow old together.
How could I have expected to keep a creature that overturns boats,
or raise a beast that turns around and harms one!
Regretting it only when biting the navel,
what good will it do!
Your outrageous words shock the multitude,
your comparisons are extraordinary.
The matter of Zhōu Wǔ,
how can an ordinary person like you discuss it!
A bird that has escaped its cage,
cannot be restrained by a net;
a whale that has broken through the net,
how can it be controlled by a fish trap!
Your ambitions are high and far-reaching,
why bother to speak of them.
I think of you in your old age,
old and becoming a rebel,
living as a traitorous subject,
dying as a rebellious ghost.
Spreading your poison in the visible and invisible worlds,
among the living and the dead,
the men and women of the Central Plains,
what pain could be like this!
The rise and fall of my dynasty’s destiny,
how can it still be up to you!
But Chánglè and Píngyuán, in their youth,
met you in the two capitals.
I fear their strategies did not meet my expectations.
This is my only regret.”
Chuí attacked and captured Yèfú,
Pī stubbornly defended the inner city.
Chuí dug trenches and surrounded it,
and sent the old and weak to Wèijùn and Féixiāng,
building Xīnxīngchéng to store supplies,
and diverted the Zhāng River to flood it.
Zhái Bīn secretly incited the Dīnglíng and Western people,
requesting Bīn to be Shàngshūlìng.
Chuí consulted his officials;
his Āndōng Jiāngjūn Fēng Héng sternly said:
“A horse can travel a thousand *lǐ*,
but cannot escape its bridle and reins,
clearly, animals cannot be governed by humans.
Bīn is a barbarian commoner,
who seized the opportune moment.
His brothers were enfeoffed as kings,
a blessing unseen since Huāndōu.
Suddenly he forgot to stop when full,
and again has such a demand.
His soul is disturbed and confused,
he will surely die before the year is out.”
Chuí still tolerated him with forbearance,
and issued a decree saying:
“The merits of Zhái Wáng deserve the position of senior assistant,
but since the court has not yet been established,
this office cannot be immediately set up.
Once the whole world is pacified,
we will discuss it again.”
Bīn was enraged,
and secretly conspired with Fú Pī,
covertly ordering the Dīnglíng to breach the dam and release the water.
The plot was discovered,
and Chuí executed him.
Bīn’s nephew, Zhēn, led his troops north to Hándān,
and marched towards Yè,
intending to form an inside-outside alliance with Pī.
Chuí ordered his Taìzǐ Bǎo and Guànjūn Mùróng Lóng to defeat him.
Zhēn fled north from Hándān,
and Chuí also sent Mùróng Kǎi with cavalry to pursue him.
They fought at Xiàyì,
but were defeated by Zhēn.
Zhēn then encamped at Chéngyíng.
Chuí said to his generals:
“Fú Pī is a cornered foe,
he will surely fight to the death and not surrender.
The Dīnglíng rebellion is a threat to our very heart.
I want to move our army to Xīnxīngchéng,
open an escape route for them,
and in doing so, repay the former kindness of the Qín ruler,
and prepare for a vigorous attack on Zhēn.”
Thereupon, he withdrew his army from Yè,
and encamped north at Xīnxīngchéng.
Mùróng Nóng attacked Zhái Sōng at Huángní,
and defeated him.
Chuí said to his Fànyáng Wáng Dé:
“Fú Pī, even if I let him go,
he will surely lead the Jìn army to secure Yèdū,
he cannot be left alone.”
He advanced his army and again attacked Yè,
opening a path for them to flee west.
Chuí had the intention of making Zhōngshān his northern capital.
Nóng led tens of thousands of troops to welcome him.
Upon hearing that Mùróng Wěi had been killed by Fú Jiān,
the officials urged Chuí to usurp the throne.
Chuí, because Mùróng Chōng had already claimed a title in Guānzhōng,
did not agree.
Jìn Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Liú Láozhī led his troops to relieve Fú Pī,
and reached Yè.
Chuí met him in battle
and was defeated.
He then lifted the siege of Yè,
and retreated to Xīnxīngchéng.
Chuí fled north from Xīnxīngchéng,
and Láozhī pursued Chuí,
defeating him in successive battles.
They fought again at Wǔqiáozé,
and the royal army was defeated.
Dé and Lóng led their troops to intercept him at Wǔzhàngqiáo,
but Láozhī galloped his horse and leaped across Wǔzhàngjiàn,
and was saved by the timely arrival of Fú Pī's reinforcements.
Zhái Zhēn left Chéngyíng,
and moved his encampment to Hángtáng.
Zhēn’s Sīmǎ Xiānyú Qǐ killed Zhēn,
and massacred the entire Zhái clan,
proclaiming himself Zhào Wáng.
The camp followers attacked and killed Qǐ,
and welcomed Zhēn’s cousin, Chéng, as their leader.
Zhēn’s son Liáo fled to Líyáng.
Gāogōulí raided Liáodōng,
and Chuí’s Píngběi Mùróng Zuǒ dispatched Sīmǎ Hǎo Jǐng with troops to relieve it,
but they were defeated by Gāogōulí,
and Liáodōng and Xuántú were lost.
Jiànjié Jiāngjūn Xú Yán rebelled in Wǔyì,
plundering over four thousand people,
and fleeing north to Yōuzhōu.
Chuí urgently ordered his general Píng Guī:
“Just hold your ground and do not fight.
When the Dīnglíng are defeated,
I will personally deal with him.”
Guī defied the order and engaged in battle,
and was defeated by Yán.
Yán, taking advantage of his victory, entered Jì,
plundered over a thousand households, and then departed,
ravaging and plundering wherever he went,
and then occupied Lìzhī.
Zhái Chángshǐ Xiānyú Dé killed Chéng and surrendered.
Chuí entered Hángtáng,
and buried all his troops alive.
Fú Pī abandoned Yèchéng,
and fled to Bìngzhōu.
Mùróng Nóng attacked and captured Lìzhī,
executing Xú Yán and his brothers.
He then marched against Gāogōulí,
recovering the two commanderies of Liáodōng and Xuántú,
and returned to encamp at Lóngchéng.
Chuí定都Zhōngshān.
The assembled officials urged him to assume the imperial title,
prepare the ceremonial rites,
and perform the suburban sacrifice by fire.
Chuí followed their advice.
In the eleventh year of Tàiyuán, he presumptuously ascended the throne,
granted amnesty throughout his territory,
and changed the era name to Jiànxīng.
He appointed various officials,
repaired the ancestral temples and altars of the land and grain,
and established Bǎo as the crown prince.
He appointed his Left Chief Clerk Kù Rǔguān Wěi, Right Chief Clerk Duàn Chóng, and Longxiang Zhāng Chóng,
and Zhōngshān Yin Fēng Héng as Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel;
Mùróng Dé as Shìzhōng, Grand Director of Military Affairs within and without, and concurrently Sīlì Xiàowèi;
Fǔjūn Mùróng Lín as Wèi Dàjiāngjūn;
the rest were granted appointments with differing ranks.
He posthumously honored his mother, Lady Lán, as Wénzhāo Huánghòu,
relocated Empress Duàn, the consort of Guǎng,
and had Lady Lán enshrined to receive sacrifices alongside him.
The Erudites Liú Xiáng and Dǒng Mì argued that Yáo's mother was third in妃位 (Imperial Concubine rank),
and did not use her noble status to overshadow Jiāng Yuán,
demonstrating that the way of a sagely king prioritizes impartiality.
Chuí did not agree.

He dispatched his Zhēngxī Mùróng Kǎi, Wèijūn Mùróng Lín, Zhènnán Mùróng Shào, and Zhēnglǔ Mùróng Zhòu, among others, to attack Fú Jiān's Jìzhōu Shepherd Fú Dìng, Zhèndōng Fú Shào, Yōuzhōu Shepherd Fú Mó, and Zhènběi Fú Liàng.
Kǎi wrote a letter to Dìng and the others,
explaining the consequences of their actions (i.e., fortune or misfortune),
and Dìng and the others all surrendered.
Chuí left his crown prince Bǎo to guard Zhōngshān,
and led his generals south to attack Zhái Liáo,
appointing Kǎi as the Vanguard Commander.
Liáo's troops and people were all from Yān and Zhào,
and they all said:
"The son of the King of Tàiyuán
is our parent."
They flocked to him and submitted.
Liáo was frightened
and sent an envoy to request surrender.
When Chuí arrived at Líyáng,
Liáo offered his bare torso as a sign of submission and begged forgiveness;
Chuí treated him with generosity.
He built the Chénghuá Guān for his crown prince Bǎo,
entrusted Bǎo with supervising the affairs of the Ministry of Personnel,
and delegated all matters, great and small, to him,
with Chuí only generally overseeing the main principles.
He established his wife, Lady Duàn, as empress.
He also made Bǎo concurrently Shìzhōng, Dà Chányú, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, and Yōuzhōu Shepherd.
He established a permanent palace (Liú Tái) in Lóngchéng,
and appointed the King of Gāoyáng, Mùróng Lóng, to oversee the affairs of the Liú Tái Shàngshū.
At this time, Mùróng Wěi and other members of the imperial clan who had been harmed by Fú Jiān
were all ritually recalled and buried.
Hé Gēng, the Administrator of Qīnghé, gathered a crowd at Dìnglíng and rebelled,
responding to Zhái Liáo from the south.
[一０]Mùróng Nóng attacked and killed him,
and destroyed the city of Dìnglíng.
He advanced his army into Yè,
and because Yèchéng was vast and difficult to defend,
he built a separate wall east of the main road to Fèngyáng Gate.
His Shàngshū Láng Lóu Huì submitted a memorial, saying:
"The three-year mourning period
is a universal system under heaven.
War and chaos have corrupted the rites,
leading to a system where all officials are appointed without regard to mourning.
People's hearts are driven by ambition and competition,
eagerly seeking honor and advancement,
even to the point of donning mourning attire
to participate in current affairs.
How can this be loyalty to the state?
It is merely a pursuit of profit in the midst of it all.
The sagely kings established their teachings
without diminishing their principles due to adversity,
and without changing their transforming influence due to chaos.
Therefore, they were able to close the door to fierce competition
and block the path of restless ambition.
Your Majesty has risen at the end of many dynasties
and is expanding the enterprise of restoration.
The world is gradually pacifying,
and military implements are being set aside.
It is truly appropriate to cleanse impurities
and follow the old regulations.
If officials encounter a great mourning,
allow them to observe the three-year rite,
then the four directions will recognize your transforming influence,
and people will submit to the rites."
Chuí did not agree.
Zhái Liáo died,
and his son Zhāo succeeded him.
Zhāo attacked and pressured Yèchéng,
but Mùróng Nóng repelled him.
Chuí led his army to attack Zhāo at Huátái,
halting at Líyáng Jīn.
Zhāo held the southern bank to defend.
The generals, fearing Zhāo's well-trained soldiers,
all advised against crossing the river.
Chuí laughed, saying:
"What can those mere lads do?
I shall kill them for you all now."
He then moved his camp to the western ford,
made over a hundred ox-hide boats,
loaded them with feigned troops holding up staffs,
and sailed upstream.
Zhāo had initially deployed his main force to defend Líyáng.
Seeing Chuí heading towards the western ford,
he abandoned his camp and moved west to resist.
Chuí secretly dispatched his Guìlín Wáng Mùróng Zhèn and Piàojì Mùróng Guó to cross Líyáng Jīn by night,
and set up camp south of the river.
Zhāo, hearing this, fled back.
His soldiers were tired and thirsty,
and they ran back to Huátái.
Zhāo took his wife and children and, leading several hundred cavalry, hurried north to Báilù Shān.
Nóng pursued and attacked,
capturing all of Zhāo's followers.
Zhāo fled alone on horseback to Chángzǐ.
The 38,000 households across the seven commanderies Zhāo governed were all restored to their former state.
He relocated over 7,000 households of refugees from Xúzhōu to Líyáng.
At this point, a campaign against Chángzǐ was discussed.
All the generals advised against it,
arguing that Mùróng Yǒng had not yet committed any offense,
and that consecutive years of campaigns
had exhausted the soldiers.
They requested to wait until another year.
Chuí was about to agree,
but when he heard Mùróng Dé's strategy,
he laughed and said:
"My plan is decided!
Moreover, I am old,
and I will empty my bag of wisdom to conquer him.
I will not leave this rebel to burden my descendants."
He then mobilized 70,000 infantry and cavalry,
and dispatched his Dānyáng Wáng Mùróng Zàn and Longxiang Zhāng Chóng to attack Yǒng's brother Zhī at Jìnyáng.
[一一]Yǒng sent his generals Diāo Yún and Mùróng Zhōng to lead 50,000 troops and encamp at Lùchuān.
Chuí dispatched Mùróng Kǎi to exit from Fúsàikǒu,
Mùróng Nóng to enter from Húguān,
while Chuí himself halted southwest of Yè,
not advancing for over a month.
Yǒng thought Chuí was using a deceptive strategy to attack him,
so he ordered all his armies to return and guard Tàiháng Zhǐguān.
Chuí advanced his army, entering through Tiānjǐng Guān,
and arrived at Húbì.
[一二]Yǒng led 50,000 elite soldiers to resist,
blocking the bend of the river to secure his position,
and dispatched envoys to challenge for battle.
Chuí arrayed his forces south of Húbì.
Nóng and Kǎi divided into two wings,
and Mùróng Guó ambushed a thousand soldiers in a deep ravine.
They engaged Yǒng in a great battle.
Chuí led his army in a feigned retreat.
Yǒng pursued for several li.
Guó launched his ambush troops, charging to cut off Yǒng's rear.
Kǎi and Nóng attacked from both sides.
Yǒng's army was utterly defeated,
with over 8,000 heads severed.
Yǒng fled back to Chángzǐ.
Mùróng Zàn attacked and captured Jìnyáng.
Chuí advanced to besiege Chángzǐ.
Yǒng's generals Jiǎ Tāo and others secretly acted as internal sympathizers.
Chuí advanced his army into the city.
Yǒng fled through the North Gate,
but was captured by the vanguard.
He was then condemned and executed,
along with over thirty of the officials he appointed, including Gōngqīng Diāo Yún.
The 76,800 households across the eight old and new commanderies under Yǒng's rule, along with his imperial carriage, robes, musicians, and precious treasures, were all captured.
Thus, all kinds of goods were acquired.
He sent Mùróng Nóng to seize territory in Hénán,
[一三]attacking Lǐnqiu and Yángchéng.
Both were captured.
All the commanderies of Tàishān and Lángyá abandoned their cities and fled.
Nóng advanced his army to the coast,
appointed governors and magistrates, and then returned.
Chuí announced his victory at the ancestral temple in Lóngchéng.
He also said to Cháng Zhōng
: "Who was more virtuous, Yī Yǐn or Zhōu Gōng?"
Zhōng replied
: "Yī Yǐn did not have the familial ties of Zhōu Gōng, yet his achievements benefited an entire era.
When Tài Jiǎ's virtue became corrupt,
he was banished to Tóng Gōng.
He reflected on his transgressions and reformed,
and only then was he restored.
This ensured that the ruler had no grievances,
and the ministers no slander.
The Dao was preserved in the state,
and his excellence overflowed into future generations.
I believe Yī Yǐn's merit was greater than that of Zhōu Dàn."
Shèng said
: "Yī Yǐn, with the prestige of an old minister,
held the important position of À Héng.
When Tài Jiǎ succeeded to the throne,
the way of a ruler was not yet fully established.
Yī Yǐn failed to exert his utmost loyalty in assisting and guiding him,
but instead banished him to Tóng Gōng.
This act was no different from Yí Yì's.
How can he be compared to Zhōu Gōng?"
Láng Fū said
: "Yī Yǐn, in the position of a minister,
could not rectify and control his sovereign.
Fearing that the way of Chéng Tāng would fall into disuse and not be achieved,
he therefore placed him in Tóng Gōng,
to engage with common people,
so that he would learn the hardships of farming.
Only then was he restored to the throne.
This was his loyalty."
Shèng said
: "If Yī Yǐn could depose him and then establish him,
why could he not assist him until he achieved goodness?
If Tài Jiǎ's nature was like that of Jié or Zhòu,
then within three years, he would not have become a virtuous ruler so quickly.
If his nature was originally bright and excellent,
and a righteous heart was easily aroused,
he should have diligently applied the principles of rectification and guidance to assist in perfecting the ruler's virtue.
How could a minister imprison his sovereign and usurp his position?
Moreover, a minister's service to his sovereign
is only limited by his ability.
Why should one harbor wisdom and conceal benevolence to contribute to the ruler's evil?
As for the matter of Tài Jiǎ,
I have already discerned it.
Tài Jiǎ
was a most virtuous ruler.
Seeing that Yī Yǐn had served three dynasties,
and his achievements were without dispute,
he would lose the merit of the illustrious ancestor's entrustment.
Therefore, he concealed his radiant wisdom
and submitted to Yī Yǐn's demotion,
so as to perfect the beauty of Yī Yǐn's loyalty and integrity.
Indeed, only extraordinary people
can accomplish extraordinary deeds.
What is perceived by ordinary people
is also like Tài Bó's three renunciations;
people praise him for his virtue."
Fū said
: "Tài Bó thrice offered the empire,
and it was not until Zhòng Ní that his ultimate virtue was made manifest.
Tài Jiǎ suffered slander throughout the empire,
and only under Your Majesty's reign was his excellence vindicated."
Consequently, they conversed, feasted, and composed poems,
and were granted varying amounts of gold and silk.
Líaoxī Tàishǒu Lǐ Lǎng had been in his commandery for ten years,
maintaining control within its borders.
Shèng suspected him
and repeatedly summoned him, but he refused to go.
Because his mother was in Lóngchéng,
he did not dare to openly rebel.
Instead, he secretly led in Wèi troops,
intending to secure himself.
He then submitted a memorial requesting the dispatch of troops to repel the invaders.
Shèng said
: "This must be a trick."
He summoned Lǐ Lǎng's envoy and questioned him,
and indeed it was confirmed.
He exterminated Lǐ Lǎng's entire clan
and dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Lǐ Hàn to lead cavalry to attack him.
When the army reached Jiàn'ān,
Lǐ Hàn was recalled.
Lǐ Lǎng heard that his family had been executed,
and gathered over three thousand households to fortify himself.
When he heard that Lǐ Hàn had returned midway,
he thought there was an internal disturbance
and no longer prepared defenses.
He left his son Yǎng to guard Lìngzhī
and personally went to Běipíng to welcome the Wèi army.
Lǐ Hàn, having anticipated this,
attacked and captured Lìngzhī.
He sent Guǎngwēi Mèng Guǎngpíng to lead cavalry to pursue Lǐ Lǎng,
catching up with him at Wúzhōng
and beheading him.
Initially,
when Shèng recalled Lǐ Hàn,
none of his officials knew the reason.
After Lǐ Hàn had beheaded Lǐ Lǎng,
Shèng said to his officials
: "The reason I recalled Lǐ Hàn earlier
was precisely for this.
Lǐ Lǎng had just rebelled,
and would certainly fear official authority.
Firstly, he would gather his allies and plunder the good and innocent.
Secondly, he would flee and hide in the mountains and marshes, and could not be pacified quickly.
Therefore, I unexpectedly recalled the army
to make him complacent.
To then suddenly ambush him
was certain to bring victory."
All the officials said
: "This was beyond our comprehension."
When Lǐ Hàn returned from Líaoxī,
he heard that Shèng had killed his general Wèi Shuāng,
and fearing for himself,
abandoned his army and fled.
Afterward, he admitted his guilt,
and his noble rank was restored.
Shèng said to Shìzhōng Sūn Qíng
: "Lǐ Hàn held the command of the three armies
and bore the heavy responsibility of an independent expedition.
He failed to uphold his integrity and die for his country,
but fled without cause.
According to military law,
this is an unforgivable crime.
However, during the late emperor's time of refuge,
people's loyalties wavered,
relatives forgot their kin,
and trusted ministers lost their loyalty.
Lǐ Hàn, despite his physically impaired body,
exerted his strength and gave his life,
with utmost loyalty
that penetrated the bright sun.
Therefore, I have recorded his merit of self-sacrifice
and exempted him from a crime as vast as mountains."
Shèng renounced the title of emperor
and called himself Shùrén Dàwáng.
Wèi attacked Yōuzhōu,
captured Cìshǐ Lú Pǔ, and left.
Mèng Guǎngpíng was dispatched to reinforce,
but it was too late.
Shèng led an army of thirty thousand to attack Gāogōulí,
assaulting Xīnchéng and Nánsū.
He captured them all,
dispersed their accumulated stores,
and moved over five thousand households to Líaoxī.
Shèng received his officials in the Eastern Hall,
examining and evaluating their skills and talents.
Twelve individuals were outstandingly promoted.
He commanded all offices to recommend one civil or military official each who was capable of assisting in governing the world.
He established his son, Líaoxī Gōng Dìng, as the crown prince
and granted a general amnesty for all offenses down to capital crimes.
He hosted a banquet for his officials in Xīnchāng Diàn.
Shèng said
: "Let each of you express your aspirations.
I shall observe them."
Qībīng Shàngshū Dīng Xìn, who was fifteen years old
and Shèng's maternal cousin,
stepped forward and said
: "To be in a high position without arrogance,
to be lofty without peril –
that is my wish."
Shèng laughed and said
: "Young Shàngshū Dīng,
how can you utter such words of a wise elder!"
Shèng governed his subordinates with strict authority,
was arrogant and violent, had few intimates,
and was often suspicious.
Hence, Dīng Xìn's words alluded to this.
Shèng campaigned against the Kùmòxī,
capturing a large number of captives and returning.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Mùróng Guó, along with Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Qín Yú, Duàn Zàn, and others, plotted to lead the imperial guards to attack Shèng.
The plot was discovered,
and they were executed.
Over five hundred people died.
Qián Jiāngjūn, Sīhuǐ Hóu Duàn Jī, Yú's son Xīng, Zàn's son Tài, and others,
taking advantage of the agitated public sentiment,
raised a clamor and shouted loudly in the palace at night.
Shèng heard the disturbance,
led his attendants out to fight,
and the crowd scattered and broke.
Soon after, a bandit from the darkness wounded Shèng.
He was then carried to the front hall,
where he reconfirmed the imperial guard's duties
and summoned his uncle, Héjiān Gōng Xī, to entrust him with his posthumous affairs.
Shèng died before Xī arrived,
at the age of twenty-nine,
having reigned for three years.
He was posthumously given the false title Zhāowǔ Huángdì,
his tomb was named Xīngpíng Líng,
and his temple name was Zhōngzōng.
The imperial historian says: Four stars gathered in the east,
the qi of Jīnlíng was already divided;
five horses floated south,
the heroes of Yùsài were just beginning to be disturbed.
Courts and markets frequently changed,
hardship and worry never ceased.
Mùróng Chuí was endowed by nature with heroic qualities,
his might shook his own dynasty.
Because his heroic strategies aroused suspicion, he sought refuge under Kuānzhèng,
Yǒnggù received him with courtesy,
and Dàomíng served him with all his might.
However, a falcon's nature is hard to restrain,
a wolf's heart is naturally wild.
When Huáinán suffered defeat,
the plot of the three nephews was already hatched;
when Hèshuò's forces were divided,
the auspicious omen of the five wooden pieces began to manifest.
He slew the soaring dragon and soared far away,
crossed Shímén and advanced steadily,
thus causing the Zhái clan to follow him,
and the Yè army to flee in the night.
He gathered the regions of Zhào and Wèi,
and controlled heroes.
With a remnant of his brilliance,
he crushed fifty thousand at Héqu;
with a secret strategy of floating boats,
he recruited seven commanderies at Líyáng.
He restored the old territory of Liáoyīn,
established a new state at Zhōngshān,
imitating the imperial sacrifices to the ancestors,
usurping all the preparations.
When Chóng'ěr returned to Jìn,
he relied on the efforts of five ministers;
when Gōujiàn deceived Wú,
he relied on five thousand soldiers.
How could one whose accomplishments surpassed those of the two hegemons,
whose forces were fewer than a single brigade,
uproot and overturn mountains,
and soar and roar to command the wind and clouds!
Although the people of Wèi forgot their downfall and were again transmitted to the eastern state,
Rènhǎo's remaining generosity shamed the western neighbors,
this truly was Fú Shì's treachery,
not the whale or giant fish of the Jìn imperial house.
Bǎo rose due to empty reputation,
Jùnwén governed the customs,
internal strife brewed,
powerful enemies encroached from without,
though his venom did not affect others, his evil was enough to destroy himself.
Shèng, on the other hand, perfectly embodied filial piety and fraternal love,
and did not let his civil and military virtues decline.
He concealed his brilliance and pacified enemies and bandits,
blamed himself and ceded high danger,
truly a fine captive in a chaotic world.
Xī, however, was not a profound ruler by nature,
his actions were due to his licentious conduct.
His Lírōng-like demeanor
pleased him on the couch;
his Xuánqī-like appearance
was seen as remarkable for his black hair.
He floated light boats on the sea of Qūguāng,
and longed for the morning crossing at the mountain of Jǐngyún.
He adorned his palaces with earth and wood out of arrogance,
and exhausted the complaints of a small territory.
His ancestral sacrifices were annihilated,
and he was driven out by the Féng clan.
The encomium says: Barbarians encroached,
mountains and rivers boiled and surged.
Heaven had not yet regretted the disaster,
and men were not capable.
Swift in movement, agile,
the first to cry out would prosper.
Dàomíng was magnificent,
whipping and driving heroes.
He swept away Yān and pacified Wèi,
Zhāo slaughtered and eternally destroyed.
The great bandit stealthily moved,
and usurped a grand name.
Bǎo's heart gave rise to chaos,
Shèng calmed the family's troubles.
Xī was extremely arrogant and licentious,
people harbored resentment and anger.
His illegitimate deeds brought personal calamity,
a disaster from which there was no escape.
Collated Notes
Record of Events, Volume 25: Qífú Guórén
Qífú Guórén was
a Xiānbēi from Lǒngxī.
In ancient times, there were three tribes: Rúfúsī, Chūlián, and Chìlú.
They came south from Mòběi, emerging from Dàyīn Shān,
and encountered a giant insect on the road,
shaped like a divine turtle,
as large as a mound.
They then killed a horse and sacrificed it,
praying:
"If you are a benevolent god,
then open the road;
if an evil god,
then block it so it is impassable."
Suddenly it disappeared,
and a small child was there.
At that time, an old man of the Qífú tribe had no son,
and asked to adopt him as his son.
Everyone agreed.
The old man was delighted, thinking he had someone to rely on,
and named him Hégān.
Hégān,
in the language of Xià, means 'to rely on'.
At the age of ten,
he was brave and skilled in riding and archery,
able to draw a bow of five hundred catties.
The four tribes admired his heroism and might,
and chose him as their leader,
calling him Qífú Kèhán Tuōduómòhé.
Tuōduó,
means 'neither god nor human'.
Later, there was Yòulín,
who was Guórén's fifth-generation ancestor.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he led five thousand households to move to Xiàyuán,
and his tribe gradually grew strong.
The Xiānbēi Lùjié, with over seventy thousand households,
were encamped at Gāopíng Chuān,
and frequently attacked Yòulín.
Lùjié was defeated
and fled south to Lüèyáng.
Yòulín assimilated all their people,
and consequently settled in Gāopíng Chuān.
After Yòulín died,
his son Jié Quán was established,
and moved to Qiāntún.
After Jié Quán died,
his son Lìnà was established.
He attacked the Xiānbēi Tǔlà at Wūshù Shān,
and campaigned against Wèichí Kěquán at Dàfēi Chuān,
gathering over thirty thousand households.
After Lìnà died,
his younger brother Qígāo was established.
After Qígāo died,
Lìnà's son Shùyán was established.
He attacked the Xiānbēi Mòhóu at Yuàn Chuān,
greatly defeating them,
and receiving the surrender of over twenty thousand households,
consequently settling in Yuàn Chuān.
He appointed his uncle Kēgāo as his tutor,
entrusting him with state affairs.
He appointed Sīyǐn Wūgāo as the Left Auxiliary General,
to guard Càiyuán Chuān;
Chūlián Gāohú as the Right Auxiliary General,
to guard Zhìbiàn Chuān;
and Chìlú Nàhú as the General Who Leads Righteousness,
to guard Qiāntún Shān.
After Shùyán died,
his son Dàhán was established.
At that time, Shí Lè destroyed Liú Yào,
and Dàhán, in fear, moved to Màitián Wúgū Shān.
After Dàhán died,
his son Sīfán was established,
and first moved to Dùjiān Shān.
Soon after, he was attacked by Wáng Tǒng, a general of Fú Jiān,
and his people rebelled and surrendered to Tǒng.
Sīfán sighed and said to his attendants:
"My wisdom is insufficient to resist the enemy,
my virtue is insufficient to appease the people.
Before swords and cavalry even met, my foundation was already ruined.
Seeing the people dispersed,
my position is also hard to maintain.
If I flee to other tribes,
they will certainly not tolerate me.
I will follow the plan of Hūhánxié."
So he went to Tǒng and surrendered to Jiān.
Jiān was greatly pleased,
appointed him Southern Chányú,
and kept him in Cháng'ān.
He appointed Sīfán's uncle Tǔléi as the Protector-General of Valiant Warriors,
to govern his people.
Soon after, the Xiānbēi Bóhán encroached upon Lǒngyòu.
Jiān appointed Sīfán as an Imperial Envoy with Credentials, Director of All Military Affairs for Suppressing the Western Hu, and General Who Guards the West, to campaign against him.
Bóhán, in fear, asked to surrender.
Sīfán then garrisoned Yǒngshì Chuān,
where he exercised great authority and benevolence.
Shēn Yǒng (申永), the Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州) for the Jìn (晉) dynasty, sent an envoy across the sea to establish relations.
Bá (跋) then sent his Middle Secretariat Aide, Lǐ Fú (李扶), to reply.
The Ròurán (蝚蠕) Dàdàn (大但) sent an envoy to present three thousand horses
and ten thousand sheep.
There was a red aura filling the four quarters.
The Grand Astrologer Zhāng Mù (張穆) said to Bá (跋):
"This is the aura of war.
Now, Great Wèi's (大魏) might controls the six directions,
but its envoys are cut off.
Since ancient times, there has never been a situation where neighboring countries, though bordering each other,
do not maintain friendly relations.
To violate righteousness and anger neighbors
is the path to ruin.
It is advisable to send back the former envoy
to mend relations and form an alliance."
Bá (跋) said:
"I shall consider it."
Soon after, a large Wèi (魏) army arrived.
He dispatched Gǔ Ní (古泥), the Right Protector of the Chányú (單于), to lead cavalry to scout them.
Fifteen *lǐ* (里) from the city,
they encountered the army and fled back.
He then sent his generals Yáo Zhāo (姚昭) and Huángfǔ Guǐ (皇甫軌) to resist them in battle.
Huángfǔ Guǐ (皇甫軌) was struck by a stray arrow and died.
As Wèi (魏) had already made preparations,
they withdrew.
Within Bá's (跋) territory, there was an earthquake and mountains collapsed;
the eaves of the Hóngguāng Mén (洪光門) gate broke.
There was another earthquake,
and the right sleeping quarter was damaged.
Bá (跋) asked Mǐn Shàng (閔尚):
"In recent years, there have been repeated seismic changes.
Can you clearly explain the reason?"
Shàng (尚) replied:
"Earth
is *yīn* (陰),
and represents the common people.
Tremors have left and right;
these tremors have all been to the right.
Your servant fears that the common people will move west."
Bá (跋) said:
"I am also very concerned about this."
He dispatched envoys separately to tour the commanderies and states,
to inquire about their hardships and sufferings.
Orphans and the elderly who could not support themselves
were given grain and silk in varying amounts.
Bá (跋) reigned for eleven years.
By this point,
it was the first year of Yuánxī (元熙),
and subsequent events merged with the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
He died in the seventh year of Yuánjiā (元嘉).
His younger brother Hóng (弘) killed Bá's (跋) son Yì (翼) and established himself.
Later, he was attacked by Wèi (魏)
and fled east to Gāogōulì (高句麗).
After two years,
Gāogōulì (高句麗) killed him.
Initially,
Bá (跋) usurped the imperial title in the twentieth year of Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán (孝武太元).
Until Hóng (弘), across two generations,
there were twenty-eight years in total.
[二七]
Féng Sùfú (馮素弗)
was Bá's (跋) eldest younger brother.
He was spirited and had great ambitions,
with a formidable and imposing appearance.
He was heroic and outstanding, unlike others,
chivalrous and unrestrained,
not adhering to minor conventions.
Therefore, people of his time did not consider him extraordinary;
only Wáng Qí (王齊) found him exceptional,
saying:
"He is a talent for bringing order out of chaos."
His sole focus was to associate with the powerful figures of the time,
not concerning himself with property or livelihood.
At twenty,
he personally went to Hán Yè (韓業), the Left Aide to the Minister of the Secretariat under Mùróng Xī (慕容熙), to propose marriage.
Hán Yè (韓業) was angered and refused him.
He again sought the daughter of Gāo Shào (高邵), a Secretariat Aide,
but Gāo Shào (高邵) also refused.
Chéng Zǎo (成藻), the Magistrate of Nángōng (南宮), was a renowned and prominent figure.
Sùfú (素弗) went to him,
but Chéng Zǎo (成藻) ordered his doorkeeper not to admit him.
Sùfú (素弗) entered directly,
and sat opposite Chéng Zǎo (成藻),
as if no one else was present.
They talked and drank for several days.
Chéng Zǎo (成藻) then began to find him extraordinary,
saying:
"I sought a *qíjì* (騏驥) (splendid horse) far away,
not knowing one was nearby in the eastern neighborhood.
How late I am to know you!"
No knight-errant of the age failed to turn to him.
When Xī (熙) usurped the throne,
Sùfú (素弗) served as a Palace Attendant and Minor Commander of the Tent Guards.
Bá's (跋) fraudulent enterprise
was initiated by Sùfú (素弗).
When he became a chief minister,
he was humble and reverent, cautious,
never acting contrary to propriety.
Even the lowliest servants
were treated with equal courtesy.
His carriages, clothing, and residences
were all based on frugality.
He cultivated himself and led his subordinates,
and all officials respected him.
Initially, he served as the Commander of the Capital.
When he garrisoned Yíngqiū (營丘),
the common people sang his praises.
He once said to Hán Yè (韓業):
"You disregarded me before;
now I will take what is mine.
How about that?"
Hán Yè (韓業) bowed and apologized.
Sùfú (素弗) said:
"The past is past;
how could I still settle accounts with you?"
Nevertheless, he treated Hán Yè (韓業) with increasing generosity.
He liked to preserve the existing and restore the extinct,
and to promote old noble families.
He asked the Attendant-in-ordinary Yáng Zhé (陽哲):
"Where are the descendants of the meritorious officials of Qín (秦) and Zhào (趙) now?"
Yáng Zhé (陽哲) replied:
"They are all in the Central Plains;
only Táo Bào's (桃豹) grandson Xiān (鮮) is here."
Sùfú (素弗) summoned him to be Left Constant Attendant.
Commentators attributed to him the demeanor of a prime minister.
He died in the seventh year of Bá's (跋) reign.
Bá (跋) wept for him with profound sorrow.
Until the burial,
he visited seven times.
The court historian commented: Since the Five Hu (五胡) indulged in wickedness,
the Nine Regions (九域) were brought to ruin.
The imperial capital and divine land
were blended with the uncivilized fringes;
great names and precious positions
were all usurped by various barbarian tribes.
It has always been said that the Róngdí (戎狄) are fierce and brutish,
not having peered into morality.
To deceive Heaven and arbitrarily seize destiny
was indeed their norm.
However, Féng Bá (馮跋) came from the Central Plains,
different from the vile hordes.
Taking advantage of the Xīanbéi's (鮮卑) stupidity and tyranny,
he also stole fame on the fringes of the sea.
Yet, among the remnants of the displaced,
few were not heroic and outstanding.
He was fortunately promoted by the masses for his leniency and generosity.
Although he started with self-cultivation,
he rarely achieved perfect virtue in the end.
The old histories state that he believed in and practiced demonic cults,
dismissed and demoted remonstrating officials.
He lacked the talent to govern and lead,
and was not a man of enlightened judgment.
This is true.
He brought calamity and invited invasion,
which indeed was due to this.
Yet he was still able to nurture the common people
and preserve the territory,
issuing commands and decrees
for over twenty years.
Was this the will of Heaven?
It was not due to human effort!
A eulogy states: Guórén (國仁) was brave and martial,
Gānqú (乾歸) was courageous and fierce.
Jiǎojiǎo Chìpán (矯矯熾磐) was outstanding,
decisive when facing critical situations.
Who would have thought that the Xūnlǔ (獯虜)
also harbored deep strategies?
Wén (文) rose from common talent,
rebelling and usurping in turbulent times.
All secretly seized the great treasure,
causing great suffering for us.
Collation notes:
Records of Vassal States, Chapter 26, Tūfà Wūgū (禿髮烏孤).
Tūfà Wūgū
was a Xiānbēi from Héxī.
His ancestors shared a common origin with Later Wèi.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Pǐgū, led his tribe from beyond the northern frontier to relocate to Héxī.
His territory extended east to Màitián and Qiāntún,
west to Shīluó,
south to Jiāohé,
and north to the Great Desert.
When Pǐgū died,
his son Shòutián succeeded him.
Initially,
when Shòutián was in his mother's womb,
his mother, Húyè shì, gave birth to him in her quilt while sleeping.
The Xiānbēi called a quilt
“tūfà,”
and thus he adopted it as his clan name.
When Shòutián died,
his grandson Shùjīnéng succeeded him.
He was brave, resolute, and full of stratagems.
During the Tàishǐ period,
he killed Hú Liè, the Inspector of Qínzhōu, at Wànhúdū,
and defeated Sū Yú, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, at Jīnshān,
thus possessing all the land of Liángzhōu.
Emperor Wǔ ate late on his account.
Later, he was defeated by Mǎ Lóng,
and his subordinates killed him and surrendered.
His cousin Wùwán succeeded him.
When he died,
his grandson Tuījīn succeeded him.
When he died,
his son Sīfùjiān succeeded him,
and his tribal followers gradually grew stronger.
Wūgū was the son of Sīfùjiān.
Upon succeeding to the throne,
he promoted agriculture and sericulture
and cultivated good relations with neighbors.
Lǚ Guāng sent an envoy to appoint him acting Jié, General-in-Chief of Chāmpion, Grand Commander of the Héxī Xiānbēi, and Marquis of Guǎngwǔ County.
Wūgū said to his generals,
“Lǚ shì has sent a distant grant of appointment.
Should I accept it or not?”
The assembly all said,
“Our soldiers and people are not few.
Why should we be subservient to others?”
Wūgū was about to follow their advice,
but his general Shí Zhēnrùoliú said,
“Our foundation is not yet secure.
It is advisable to act according to the times.
Guāng's virtue and governance are clear and bright,
and there are no worries within his territory.
If he were to attack us with deadly force,
we, being small, could not match him,
and even if we regretted it later,
it would be too late.
It is better to accept it and nurture it
to await his weakness.”
Wūgū then accepted it.
Wūgū campaigned against the Yǐfú and Zhéjué tribes,
defeating them greatly.
He sent his general Shí Yìgān to build the Liánchuān fortress to make it his capital.
Wūgū ascended the great mountain of Liánchuān
and wept without speaking.
Shí Yìgān stepped forward and said,
“I have heard that if the ruler is sorrowful, the minister is shamed;
if the ruler is shamed, the minister dies.
Is the cause of Your Majesty's unhappiness
perhaps Lǚ Guāng?
Guāng is already old and frail,
and his armies have suffered repeated defeats.
Now, with the abundance of our soldiers and horses,
and occupying the great rivers,
we can defeat a hundred with one strike.
What is there to fear from Guāng?”
Wūgū said,
“Guāng's decline due to old age
is also known to me.
But my ancestors attracted distant peoples with their virtue,
and diverse tribes feared their might.
Lúlín and Qìhàn, from ten thousand *lǐ* away, submitted to them.
When I took over the enterprise,
various tribes rebelled.
If those nearby are disobedient,
how can those far away be attached?
This is why I weep.”
His general Fú Hún said,
“Why does Your Majesty not mobilize the army and swear to the multitude
to punish their crimes?”
Wūgū followed his advice
and greatly defeated the various tribes.
Lǚ Guāng enfeoffed Wūgū as Duke of Guǎngwǔ Commandery.
He also campaigned against the Yìyún Xiānbēi,
greatly defeating them.
Guāng again sent an envoy to appoint Wūgū General-in-Chief of Pacifying the South, Governor of Yìzhōu, and Left Worthy King.
Wūgū said to the envoy,
“King Lǚ, in the past, with the might of his exclusive campaigns,
then possessed this province,
but he could not pacify distant peoples with virtue
and bestow favor upon the common folk.
His sons are greedy and lecherous,
and his three nephews are wantonly violent.
The commanderies and counties are collapsing,
and the lower classes have no means of livelihood.
How can I defy the will of all under Heaven
and accept an unrighteous title!
The rise of emperors and kings
is not predetermined!
Without the Way, they perish;
with virtue, they prosper.
I will follow the hopes of Heaven and mankind
and become the ruler of all under Heaven.”
He kept their drums, trumpets, and ceremonial feathered standards,
thanked the envoy, and sent him away.
In the first year of Lóng'ān (397 CE),
he proclaimed himself Grand Commander, General-in-Chief, Grand Chányú, and King of Xīpíng,
issued a general amnesty within his territory,
and adopted the era name Tàichū.
He displayed his military might at Guǎngwǔ
and captured Jīnchéng.
Guāng sent General Dòu Gǒu to attack,
and they fought at Jiētíng,
where Dòu Gǒu was greatly defeated.
Lèdū, Huánghé, and Jiāohé, three commanderies under Guāng, surrendered to him,
and tens of thousands of Qiāng and Hú households south of the mountain ranges all submitted to him.
Guāng's generals Yáng Guǐ and Wáng Qǐjī led several thousand households to defect.
Wūgū then changed his title to King of Wǔwēi.
Three years later,
he moved his capital to Lèdū.
He appointed his younger brother Lìlùgū as General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry and Duke of Xīpíng,
stationed at Ānyí;
and Tán as General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry and Duke of Guǎngwǔ,
stationed at Xīpíng.
He appointed Yáng Guǐ as his adviser (*bīnkè*).
Jīn Shíshēng and Shí Liánzhēn,
the heroes and prominent figures of the Four Barbarians;
Yīn Xùn and Guō Xìng,
the virtuous and esteemed of Xīzhōu;
Yáng Tǒng, Yáng Zhēn, Wèi Yīn, Qū Chéngmíng, Guō Huáng, Guō Fèn, Shǐ Gǎo, and Lù Sōng,
the outstanding talents in civil and military affairs;
Liáng Chǎng, Hán Yǐ, Zhāng Chǎng, and Guō Sháo,
the talented and capable men of Zhōngzhōu;
Jīn Shù, Xuē Qiáo,
Zhào Zhèn, Wáng Zhōng, Zhào Cháo, and Sū Bà,
the prominent families of Qín and Yōng—
all held high positions within the court
and governed commanderies and counties externally.
Officials were appointed based on their talents,
and all found their proper place.
Wūgū calmly said to his subordinates,
“The Lǒngyòu region is merely a few small commanderies!
Due to the military chaos,
it has split into more than ten factions.
Gān Guī arbitrarily rules Hénán,
Duàn Yè obstructs troops in Zhāngyè,
the cruel Dī are barely surviving,
stealing and occupying Gūzāng.
Relying on the remaining achievements of my father and elder brothers,
I intend to pacify Xīxià.
Of combining the weak and attacking the ignorant,
which should be first?”
Yáng Tǒng stepped forward and said,
“Gān Guī was originally under my command,
and will eventually submit.
Duàn Yè is a scholar,
his talent is not for governing the world.
Powerful ministers seize command,
and he is not in control of himself.
To attack someone a thousand *lǐ* away,
our grain transport would be cut off.
Moreover, we have good neighborly relations with him,
having promised to share misfortunes and difficulties.
To take advantage of his weakness and decay
would not be a righteous act.
Lǚ Guāng is old and frail,
and his successor is young and ignorant.
His two sons, Zuǎn and Hóng,
though quite accomplished in both civil and military arts,
are suspicious of each other internally.
If heavenly might descends upon them,
they will surely crumble at the first clash.
It is advisable to send the General of Chariots to garrison Hàowèi,
and the General of Pacifying the North to occupy Liánchuān.
Taking advantage of their weaknesses, they should launch attacks alternately,
using various methods to mislead them.
If they rescue their right, strike their left;
if they rescue their left, strike their right.
This will exhaust Zuǎn with constant rushing,
and prevent the people from settling in their agriculture.
Combining the weak and attacking the ignorant,
this is where it lies.
Within two years,
we can conquer Gūzāng while sitting.
Once Gūzāng is taken,
the other two enemies will submit naturally,
without the need for weapons.”
Wūgū agreed with him,
and thus secretly harbored the ambition to annex them all.
At that time, Lìlùgū (利鹿孤), though having usurped the throne,
still acknowledged Yáo Xīng (姚興) as his suzerain.
Yáng Huán's (楊桓) elder brother, Jīng (經), had assisted Yáo Cháng (姚萇) in establishing his reign,
but died young.
Xīng (興), hearing that Huán (桓) had virtue and prestige,
summoned him.
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) held a farewell banquet for Huán (桓) east of the city,
and said to him:
"I had originally planned to accomplish great things with you,
but circumstances have deviated from our original scheme.
The feeling of separation
is indeed deeper than that of the ancients.
However, a Kūn (鯤) cannot move its body
without the vast ocean;
a Fèng (鳳) cannot dry its wings
without a tall Wú (梧) tree.
You possess the talent to assist the age,
a treasure that shines brightly at night.
You should shake your cap strings in the cloud pavilion,
and shine with a value comparable to many cities.
This small region to the west of the river
is not enough to display your abilities.
Exert yourself well to daily renewal,
to achieve great splendor."
Huán (桓) wept and said:
"Your servant previously served the Lǚ (呂) clan,
but his situation was not established.
Your Majesty pardoned your servant from among the captives,
and treated him like an old worthy.
I always hoped to cling to the dragon and attach myself to the phoenix,
and achieve even a small功.
Now that the Dragon Gate has opened,
yet your servant must depart,
how can the longing of Gōnghéng (公衡)
be said to be forgotten!"
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) wept for him.
He then sent Tán (檀) to attack Lǚ Lóng's (呂隆) Chāngsōng (昌松) Grand Administrator Mèng Yī (孟禕) at Xiǎnměi (顯美),
and conquered it.
Tán (檀) captured Yī (禕) and rebuked him, saying:
"To act when the opportunity arises
is rewarded first;
to cling to delusion and not change
is subject to punishment.
I am about to display my might at Yùmén (玉門),
and sweep clean Qín (秦) and Lǒng (隴).
You obstinately defended a poor city,
and delayed the royal ordinances.
The state has its regular punishments,
how can you escape them?"
Yī (禕) replied:
"Your Excellency is clearing the area west of the river,
your fame spreads throughout the realm.
You pacify distant people with civil virtue,
and punish the disobedient with military might.
How much more so for a humble person like Yī (禕),
how dare I defy the Mandate of Heaven!
The punishment of having my drums daubed with blood
is my due.
But one who is loyal to them
is also loyal to this side.
Having received the profound kindness of the Lǚ (呂) clan,
and been entrusted with the duty of a bulwark,
if I had surrendered upon Your Excellency's arrival,
I fear I would incur the wrath of the authorities.
I leave it to your consideration."
Tán (檀) was greatly pleased,
released his bonds,
and treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
He relocated over two thousand households from Xiǎnměi (顯美) and Lìqiān (麗靬) and returned.
Admiring Yī's (禕) loyalty and integrity,
he appointed him Left Sīmǎ (司馬).
Yī (禕) pleaded, saying:
"The Lǚ (呂) clan is about to perish,
and the Holy Court's annexation of the area west of the river
is clearly fated.
But to have failed to protect what I was entrusted with,
and then again to hold a prominent position,
is something I secretly find unsettling.
By Your Excellency's grace,
allow Yī (禕) to be executed at Gūzāng (姑臧);
even in death, I shall not be forgotten."
Tán (檀) magnanimously agreed.
Lǚ Lóng (呂隆) was attacked by Jǔqú Méngxùn (沮渠蒙遜),
and sent envoys to beg for aid.
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) gathered his subordinates to discuss it.
The Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, Póyǎn Lún (婆衍崘), said:
"Gūzāng (姑臧) is now ravaged by famine and exhausted;
grain costs ten thousand coins per shí (石),
and there is no green grass in the fields,
so there is nothing to take for provisions.
Méngxùn (蒙遜) marched a thousand *lǐ* with his army,
and his grain transport is not continuous.
Let the two enemies destroy each other,
so we can exploit their weakness.
If Méngxùn (蒙遜) captures Gūzāng (姑臧),
he will not be able to hold it either.
It is just right for us to take it from him;
we should not save them."
Tán (檀) said:
"Lún (崘) knows one thing,
but not the other.
Although Gūzāng (姑臧) is now depleted and exhausted,
its location is strategically important,
the nexus of Hēxī (河西).
It cannot be allowed for Méngxùn (蒙遜) to occupy it;
we should rescue it quickly."
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) said:
"The words of the Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry [Tán (檀)]
are also my thoughts."
Thereupon, he dispatched Tán (檀) with ten thousand cavalry to rescue them.
When he reached Chāngsōng (昌松), Méngxùn (蒙遜) had already retreated.
Tán (檀) relocated over five hundred households from Liángzé (涼澤) and Duànzhǒng (段冢) and returned.
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) became ill.
He issued an order, saying:
"There are many troubles internal and external,
and the affairs of state are extensive.
Let the Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry [Tán (檀)] succeed me in the enterprise,
to fulfill the will of the former king."
He was on the throne for three years and then died.
He was buried southeast of Xīpíng (西平).
His self-proclaimed posthumous title was King Kāng (康王).
His younger brother Tán (檀) succeeded him.
Tùfǎ Tán (禿髮檀)
Tán (檀) was intelligent and alert in his youth,
possessing talent and strategy.
His father marveled at him,
and said to his sons:
"Tán (檀) has clear insight and competence;
he is not of your caliber."
Therefore, his elder brothers
did not pass the succession to their sons, wishing to transmit it to Tán (檀).
When Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) ascended the throne,
he merely folded his hands,
entrusting all important military and state affairs to him.
In the first year of Yuánxīng (元興), he usurped the title of King of Liáng (涼王),
moved to Lèdū (樂都),
